title: Microstructural development of human newborn cerebral white matter assessed in vivo by diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging.
text: Studying the architecture of white matter in the developing human brain using diffusion tensor MRI can reveal developmental abnormalities that may result in functional disabilities. In this study, we applied a line scan diffusion-weighted MRI sequence to measure the apparent diffusion coefficient and calculate relative anisotropy in cerebral white matter in preterm (n = 17) and full-term infants (n = 7) at early gestational ages. To assess the effects of prematurity on white matter development, we also re-evaluated a subset of early gestation preterm infants (n = 10) at term age. Our findings indicate that the mean apparent diffusion coefficient in the central white matter decreased significantly towards term age, from 1.8 microm2/ms to 1.2 microm2/ms. Conversely, the posterior limb of the internal capsule showed a similar mean apparent diffusion coefficient at both time points, with slightly higher values at 28 weeks compared to term age. Relative anisotropy was significantly higher in areas closer to term birth, with the internal capsule exhibiting higher absolute values compared to the central white matter. Moreover, preterm infants at term age showed lower mean diffusion coefficients and higher relative anisotropy in both regions compared to full-term infants. Non-myelinated fibers in the corpus callosum were visible by diffusion tensor MRI as early as 28 weeks, and full-term and preterm infants at term showed distinct differences in white matter fiber organization. These findings suggest that quantitative assessment of water diffusion by diffusion tensor MRI provides valuable insights into the microstructural development of cerebral white matter in living infants.

title: Induction of myelodysplasia by myeloid-derived suppressor cells.
text:
Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are age-dependent stem cell malignancies characterized by shared features with an activated adaptive immune response and ineffective hematopoiesis. In this study, we discovered that myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC), which are typically linked to immunosuppression, inflammation, and cancer, were significantly expanded in the bone marrow of MDS patients and played a pathogenetic role in the development of ineffective hematopoiesis. These clonally distinct MDSC overproduce suppressive cytokines and function as potent apoptotic effectors targeting autologous hematopoietic progenitors.
We found that the interaction between the proinflammatory molecule S100A9 and CD33 drives MDSC expansion. The S100A9/CD33 ligand-receptor pair recruits components to CD33's immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motif (ITIM), leading to the secretion of the suppressive cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β by immature myeloid cells. In a transgenic mouse model, bone marrow accumulation of MDSC was associated with the development of progressive multilineage cytopenias and cytological dysplasia. Remarkably, early maturation of MDSC by either all-trans-retinoic acid treatment or active immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif-bearing (ITAM-bearing) adapter protein (DAP12) interruption of CD33 signaling rescued the hematologic phenotype. These findings suggest that primary bone marrow expansion of MDSC driven by the S100A9/CD33 pathway perturbs hematopoiesis and contributes to the development of MDS.

title: BC1 RNA, the transcript from a master gene for ID element amplification, is able to prime its own reverse transcription.
text: ID elements are short interspersed elements (SINEs) found in high copy number throughout many rodent genomes. BC1 RNA, a related transcript, is derived from a single copy BC1 RNA gene. The BC1 RNA gene has been shown to be a key regulatory gene for amplification of ID elements in rodent genomes through a process called retroposition. Retroposition involves multiple regulatory steps, including transcription in the appropriate tissue, transcript stability, and priming of the RNA transcript for reverse transcription and integration. This study specifically focuses on the priming step of reverse transcription. BC1 RNA gene transcripts have been found to efficiently self-prime their own reverse transcription through a site-specific and intramolecular process, a consequence of the unique secondary structure of the 3' region. The fact that a gene that has been actively amplified throughout rodent evolution is capable of self-priming reverse transcription suggests that self-priming is a critical feature in establishing the BC1 RNA gene as a master gene for amplification of ID elements.

title: The DNA Methylome of Human Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells
text:
DNA methylation plays an essential role in various biological processes that impact human health and disease. Recent technological advancements enable the comprehensive analysis of the entire genome (methylome) of human cells, including peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), which are a crucial source of cells for clinical blood tests worldwide.
Using whole-genome bisulfite sequencing at a coverage of 24.7-fold (12.3-fold per strand), we characterized the methylome of human PBMCs from a single Asian individual whose genome was previously sequenced in the YH project. Our analysis found that approximately 68% of CpG sites and less than 0.2% of non-CpG sites are methylated in PBMCs, indicating that non-CpG cytosine methylation is rare in these cells.
Our methylome analysis revealed a rich epigenetic landscape, featuring 20 distinct genomic features, including regulatory, protein-coding, non-coding, RNA-coding, and repeat sequences. Integrating our methylome data with the YH genome sequence enabled us to identify 599 haploid differentially methylated regions (hDMRs) covering 287 genes. Of these, over 80% displayed allele-specific expression (ASE), indicating that allele-specific methylation (ASM) is a common phenomenon in PBMCs.
Our findings are consistent with recent studies that demonstrate the power of new sequencing technologies in large-scale epigenomics research. Together, these studies provide a comprehensive resource for future epigenomic research and highlight the importance of considering epigenetic variations in understanding human health and disease.

title: The human myelin basic protein gene is included within a 179-kilobase transcription unit: expression in the immune and central nervous systems.
text: Two human Golli (gene expressed in the oligodendrocyte lineage)-MBP (myelin basic protein) cDNAs have been isolated from a human oligodendroglioma cell line. Analyzing these cDNAs enabled researchers to determine the entire structure of the human Golli-MBP gene. The Golli-MBP gene, consisting of the MBP transcription unit, spans approximately 179 kilobases and comprises 10 exons, with seven of these exons making up the MBP gene. The human Golli-MBP gene contains two transcription start sites, resulting in alternatively spliced transcripts. At least two Golli-MBP transcripts, containing the first three exons of the gene and one or more MBP exons, are produced from the first transcription start site. In contrast, the second family of transcripts contains only MBP exons and produces the well-known MBPs. RNA blot analysis revealed that Golli-MBP transcripts are expressed in fetal tissues, including the thymus, spleen, and human B-cell and macrophage cell lines, as well as in fetal spinal cord. These findings suggest that the expression of exons encoding the autoimmunogen/encephalitogen MBP in the central nervous system is linked to cells and tissues of the immune system through the normal expression of the Golli-MBP gene. Additionally, these findings establish that this genetic locus, which includes the MBP gene, is conserved among species, providing further evidence that the MBP transcription unit is an integral part of the Golli transcription unit. The structural arrangement of these genes may play an important role in their genetic function and/or regulation.

title: Targeting A20 Decreases Glioma Stem Cell Survival and Tumor Growth
text: Glioblastomas, a deadly form of cancer, are characterized by a functional hierarchy maintained by self-renewing glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs). GSCs are regulated by unique molecular pathways compared to the bulk tumor, which could be targeted for therapeutic intervention. Interestingly, we found that A20 (TNFAIP3), a regulator of cell survival and NF-κB signaling, is overexpressed in GSCs at both the mRNA and protein levels. To investigate the functional significance of A20 in GSCs, we used lentiviral-mediated delivery of short hairpin RNA (shRNA) totarget A20 expression. Inhibiting A20 expression resulted in decreased GSC growth and survival, as well as decreased cell-cycle progression and p65/RelA phosphorylation. Moreover, GSCs were less sensitive to TNFalpha-induced apoptosis upon A20 knockdown, but became more sensitive when exposed to TNFalpha. The reduced ability of GSCs to self-renew in response to A20 knockdown was also observed in primary and secondary neurosphere formation assays. Notably, mice bearing human glioma xenografts exhibited increased survival upon A20 targeting. In silico analysis of a glioma patient genomic database revealed that A20 overexpression and amplification are inversely correlated with survival. These findings suggest that A20 contributes to glioma maintenance by promoting GSC survival, which is a novel tumor-enhancing mechanism. Although inactivating mutations in A20 in lymphoma suggest a tumor-suppressive role for A20, our data suggest a tumor-enhancing function in glioma. Therefore, caution should be exercised when developing A20 anticancer therapies, as their effects may vary depending on the tumor type.

title: Efficient targeting of expressed and silent genes in human ESCs and iPSCs using zinc-finger nucleases
text:
Harnessing the full potential of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) requires efficient methods for genetic modification. Nevertheless, existing techniques for generating cell type-specific lineage reporters, as well as reliable tools for disrupting, repairing, or overexpressing genes through gene targeting, are often ineffective and are not commonly used. Here, we report the highly efficient use of zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs) for targeting three genes in human pluripotent cells.
Firstly, we used ZFNs to target the OCT4 (POU5F1) locus, generating OCT4-eGFP reporter cells that allow for monitoring the pluripotent state of hESCs. Secondly, we inserted a transgene into the AAVS1 locus, creating a robust drug-inducible overexpression system in hESCs. Finally, we demonstrated the ability of ZFNs to target non-expressed genes in hESCs and hiPSCs by specifically targeting the PITX3 gene, generating reporter cells in the process.

title: Empirical Bayesian models for analysing molecular serotyping microarrays
text:
Microarrays hold great promise for molecular diagnostics, allowing for the simultaneous testing of numerous biomarkers in a single assay. In the context of infectious diseases, microarrays can be used to identify the presence of specific bacterial serotypes in clinical samples. In this study, we used a microarray designed to molecularly serotype Streptococcus pneumoniae, which incorporated oligonucleotide probes for all known capsular polysaccharide synthesis genes. The data from the microarray was analyzed using an empirical Bayesian model to determine the probabilities of combinations of serotypes present in a given sample.
Our approach takes into account the dependencies between serotypes, both those arising from genes they share and those resulting from homologous genes with similar sequences. To provide additional information for serotypes with high genetic similarity, we included extra probes on the microarray. Once a serotype combination was identified with high probability, a Bayesian random effects model was applied to determine the relative abundance of each serotype within the combination.
To evaluate the accuracy of our analysis, we applied the methods to experimental data from samples containing individual serotypes and combinations of serotypes with known levels of abundance. Our results showed that the Bayesian model was able to uniquely identify 22 of the 24 known serotypes of S. pneumoniae tested as individual samples. Additionally, the model was able to detect combinations of serotypes within samples, and provide an approximate measure of the percentage abundance of each serotype within the combination.
In conclusion, our study demonstrates the potential of microarrays for molecular serotyping of S. pneumoniae and highlights the advantages of using empirical Bayesian models for integrating multiplexed microarray data. The ability to detect and quantify multiple serotypes in a single assay offers a powerful tool for improving our understanding of the epidemiology of infectious diseases and for developing novel diagnostic strategies.

title: Bayesian measures of model complexity and fit
text: In this study, we address the challenge of comparing complex hierarchical models where the number of parameters is not explicitly defined. By leveraging an information-theoretic approach, we derive a measure called pD, which represents the effective number of parameters in a model. pD is calculated as the difference between the posterior mean of the deviance and the deviance at the posterior means of the parameters of interest. In general, pD approximately corresponds to the trace of the product of Fisher's information and the posterior covariance, which, in normal models, is the trace of the 'hat' matrix projecting observations onto fitted values. We explore the properties of pD in exponential families and show that it can be used as a Bayesian measure of fit or adequacy. Furthermore, we demonstrate how pD can be used to construct a deviance information criterion for model comparison, which is related to other information criteria and has an approximate decision-theoretic justification. We illustrate the procedure with several examples and compare it with alternative Bayesian and classical approaches. Throughout, we emphasize that the quantities involved are trivial to compute in a Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis.

title: Simplifying likelihood ratios
text: Likelihood ratios are a powerful tool for evaluating the accuracy of diagnostic tests, yet they are often overlooked due to the complexity of interpreting them. Conversion between "probability" and "odds" of disease requires a calculator, which can make the process challenging for clinicians. This article presents a simplified approach to interpreting likelihood ratios, eliminating the need for calculators, nomograms, or conversions to "odds" of disease. By following this method, clinicians can improve their diagnostic decision-making at the bedside through practical examples.

title: induction of early IFN-inducible genes in the absence of type
text: Recognition of influenza virus (Flu) by TLR7 on plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) leads to the production of type I interferon (IFN) in significant amounts. Synthetic TLR7 ligands, such as CL097, can induce the maturation of pDCs, characterized by the expression of costimulatory molecules and the production of proinflammatory cytokines, but they result in low levels of IFN-alpha production. To investigate the TLR7 signaling in pDCs and how different profiles are induced, we studied the effects of two TLR7 ligands (Flu and CL097) on the activation of blood-isolated pDCs and the human GEN2.2 pDC cell line. Our findings revealed that type I IFN production by pDCs correlates with the translocation of interferon regulatory factor 7 (IRF7) into the nucleus, which is induced by the two TLR7 ligands. Interestingly, we observed the rapid expression of IFN-inducible genes, such as mxa, cxcl10, and trail, within 4 hours of stimulation, despite the lack of type I IFN production. This expression is controlled by STAT1 phosphorylation and is independent of type I IFN. Meanwhile, STAT1 activation was found to be strictly dependent on the PI3K-p38MAPK pathway, revealing a novel signaling pathway leading to the rapid expression of IFN-inducible genes after TLR7 triggering. Overall, our findings demonstrate that pDCs possess the capacity to promptly respond to viral infection during the early phases of the innate immune response.

title: Arteriolar function in visceral adipose tissue is impaired in human obesity.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the relationship between the phenotype of adipose tissue and the function of the microvasculature in fat depots. Specifically, the study aimed to characterize the vasomotor function of small arterioles isolated from visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue in obese individuals undergoing bariatric surgery.
Methods and Results:
In 30 obese patients (age 42±11 years, body mass index 46±11 kg/m(2)), the researchers collected adipose tissue from the visceral and subcutaneous depots during surgery. The vasomotor function of small arterioles from these depots was assessed using videomicroscopy. The results showed that endothelium-dependent vasodilation was severely impaired in visceral arterioles compared to subcutaneous depots (P<0.001 by ANOVA). Nonendothelium-dependent responses to papaverine and nitroprusside were similar. The study also found that visceral fat exhibited higher expression of proinflammatory, oxidative stress-related, hypoxia-induced, and proangiogenic genes, increased activated macrophage populations, and a higher capacity for cytokine production ex vivo.
Conclusion:
The study provides clinical evidence that the visceral microenvironment may be intrinsically toxic to arterial health, suggesting a potential mechanism by which visceral adiposity burden is linked to atherosclerotic vascular disease. The findings also support the concept that both adipose tissue quality and quantity play significant roles in shaping cardiovascular phenotypes in human obesity.

title: Common Carotid Intima Media Thickness and Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index Correlate with Local but Not Global Atheroma Burden: A Cross Sectional Study Using Whole Body Magnetic Resonance Angiography
text:
Background: Common carotid intima media thickness (CIMT) and ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI) are commonly used as surrogate markers of atherosclerosis. However, their correlation with global atherosclerotic burden has not been well-established. This study aimed to compare CIMT and ABPI with atheroma burden as measured by whole body magnetic resonance angiography (WB-MRA).
Methods: We recruited 50 patients with symptomatic peripheral arterial disease and measured CIMT using ultrasound during rest and exercise. We also performed ABPI using a 1.5T MRI scanner with 4 volume acquisitions and divided the WB-MRA data into 31 anatomical arterial segments. Each segment was scored based on the degree of luminal narrowing, and the scores were summed to calculate a standardized atheroma score.
Results: The atherosclerotic burden was high with a standardized atheroma score of 39.5±11. CIMT showed a positive correlation with the whole body atheroma score (β=0.32, p=0.045), but this was primarily due to its correlation with the neck and thoracic segments (β=0.42, p=0.01). In contrast, ABPI correlated with the whole body atheroma score (β=-0.39, p=0.012), which was primarily due to a strong correlation with the ilio-femoral vessels (β=-0.45, p=0.005). On multiple linear regression analysis, no correlation was found between CIMT and global atheroma burden (β=0.13, p=0.45), while the correlation between ABPI and atheroma burden persisted (β=-0.45, p=0.005).
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that ABPI, but not CIMT, correlates with global atheroma burden as measured by WB-MRA in patients with symptomatic peripheral arterial disease. The strong correlation between ABPI and ilio-femoral atheroma burden suggests that this parameter may be a useful indicator of global atherosclerotic burden.

title: Loss of immune escape mutations during persistent HCV infection in pregnancy enhances replication of vertically transmitted viruses
text: Globally, approximately 1% of pregnant women are persistently infected with the hepatitis C virus (HCV). Mother-to-child transmission of HCV occurs in 3-5% of pregnancies and accounts for the majority of new childhood infections. HCV-specific CD8(+) cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) play a crucial role in clearing acute HCV infections, but in the majority of persistent infections, these cells become dysfunctional or recognize mutant viruses that evade T cell recognition. Increased HCV replication during pregnancy may further impair HCV-specific CTLs, limiting their ability to selectively target persistent viruses. To investigate this possibility, we studied the viral quasispecies in the circulation of two women during and after pregnancy. Our findings showed a loss of escape mutations in HLA class I epitopes during pregnancy, which was associated with the emergence of more fit viruses. CTL selective pressure was reestablished after childbirth, at which point escape mutations in these epitopes predominated in the quasispecies, and viral load decreased significantly. Notably, the viruses transmitted perinatally were those that had reverted to their previously optimized replicative fitness. Our results indicate that the immunoregulatory changes of pregnancy reduce CTL selective pressure on HCV class I epitopes, thereby allowing for the vertical transmission of viruses with enhanced replicative fitness.

title: The journey of developing hematopoietic stem cells.
text: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) undergo a complex developmental process during embryogenesis, involving multiple anatomical sites. Once HSC precursors are specified from mesoderm, they mature into functional HSCs through self-renewing divisions, generating a pool of HSCs. During this process, developing HSCs migrate through various embryonic niches, which provide important signals for their establishment and the conservation of their self-renewal ability. Recapitulating these processes in vitro can help generate and expand HSCs for their clinical potential. Understanding the interactions between developing HSCs and their niches is crucial for generating HSCs from embryonic stem cells.

title: The sacroiliac joint in the spondyloarthropathies.
text:
The term spondyloarthropathy (SpA) encompasses a group of related inflammatory joint diseases characterized by distinct clinical features and a unique association with the HLA-B27 molecule. Five subgroups can be differentiated, including ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease, and undifferentiated SpA. The sacroiliac joints are the primary site of involvement in SpA, with ankylosing spondylitis being the most prominent form, where the majority of patients are affected early in the disease.
Using dynamic magnetic resonance imaging, recent studies have visualized both acute and chronic changes in the sacroiliac joints, helping to overcome diagnostic challenges in early stages. An inflammatory infiltrate containing T cells, macrophages, and various cytokines has been identified in biopsy specimens obtained via guided computed tomography. The absence of reactive arthritis-associated bacterial DNA in these biopsy samples suggests that the pathogenesis of SpA and the reason for the sacroiliac joints' predisposition remain unclear.
While the genetic background of SpA may have a role in initiating bacterial infections, the exact nature of this relationship is still unresolved. In chronic disease, autoimmune mechanisms are thought to play a more significant role.

title: A rapid method for extraction of cotton (Gossypium spp.) genomic DNA suitable for RFLP or PCR analysis
text: Isolation of high-quality genomic DNA from Gossypium (cotton) species can be challenging due to the presence of high levels of polysaccharides, oxidizable quinones, and other interfering substances. We have developed a procedure that consistently yields satisfactory-sized and quality genomic DNA for RFLP (restriction fragment length polymorphism) and PCR (polymerase chain reaction) analysis, as well as for most common cloning applications. Throughout the procedure, various antioxidants, phenol-binding reagents, and phenol oxidase inhibitors are used to mitigate the effects of these interfering substances. Additionally, early in the procedure, nuclei are isolated to remove most polysaccharides, resulting in higher-quality DNA.

title: Cross sectional stature and weight reference curves for the UK, 1990.
text: The most recent reference curves for stature and weight in the UK were first published in 1966, but there is growing concern that these curves may not accurately reflect the growth patterns of children today. To address this concern, new reference curves were estimated using data from seven national sources and the Cole's LMS method. These curves provide efficient estimates of the conventional centiles and fit well to the data. Comparatively, the new curves differ significantly from the existing curves at key ages for both stature and weight. As a result, it is proposed that the updated curves presented here should replace the existing UK reference curves.

title: The suture provides a niche for mesenchymal stem cells of craniofacial bones
text:
Bone tissue undergoes continuous regeneration, which is supported by stem cells. Recent studies have shown that perivascular mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) contribute to the turnover of long bones. However, the identity and regulatory environment of craniofacial bone MSCs, which are flat bones that develop from a distinct embryonic origin than long bones, remain unknown.
Our study identifies Gli1+ cells within the suture mesenchyme as the primary MSC population for craniofacial bones. These cells are not associated with blood vessels, give rise to all craniofacial bones in the adult, and are activated during the repair process after injury. Gli1+ cells are typical MSCs in vitro, and ablation of these cells leads to craniosynostosis and the stopping of skull growth, indicating that they are an essential stem cell population.
Using Twist1(+/-) mice with craniosynostosis, our study suggests that craniosynostosis may result from a diminished population of suture stem cells. Our findings indicate that the craniofacial sutures provide a unique niche for MSCs for craniofacial bone homeostasis and repair.

title: Cardiac neural crest cells contribute to the dormant multipotent stem cell in the mammalian heart
text:
In a breakthrough study, researchers found that cardiac neural crest-derived cells in the fetal heart form clonal spheroids in serum-free medium, which express markers of undifferentiated neural precursor cells, such as nestin, Musashi-1, and multiple drug resistance transporter gene 1. Following differentiation, these markers are lost and replaced by the expression of neuron-specific proteins, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and smooth muscle actin (SMA). Cardiosphere-derived cells transplanted into chick embryos migrate to the truncus arteriosus and cardiac outflow tract and contribute to dorsal root ganglia, spinal nerves, and aortic smooth muscle cells.
Using double transgenic mice encoding protein 0–Cre/Floxed-EGFP, the researchers investigated the lineage of the undifferentiated and differentiated neural crest-derived cells in the fetal myocardium. They found that undifferentiated cells expressed GATA-binding protein 4 and nestin but not actinin, while the differentiated cells were identified as cardiomyocytes. These findings suggest that cardiac neural crest-derived cells migrate into the heart, remain there as dormant multipotent stem cells, and under the right conditions, differentiate into cardiomyocytes and typical neural crest-derived cells, including neurons, glia, and smooth muscle cells.
In summary, the study demonstrates that cardiac neural crest-derived cells have the ability to differentiate into various cell types, including cardiomyocytes, and can remain in the heart as dormant stem cells, ready to differentiate under the right conditions. This finding may have important implications for the study and treatment of cardiac disease.

title: The mammalian target of rapamycin signaling pathway mediates epileptogenesis in a model of temporal lobe epilepsy.
text:
Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying epileptogenesis is crucial for the development of more effective treatments for epilepsy. Recently, we discovered that the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway plays a role in epileptogenesis, and mTOR inhibitors can prevent epilepsy in a mouse model of tuberous sclerosis complex. To investigate the potential role of mTOR in temporal lobe epilepsy, we examined the pathway's involvement in a rat model of status epilepticus initiated by kainate.
Our findings reveal that acute kainate-induced seizures activate the mTOR pathway in a biphasic manner, as evidenced by an increase in phospho-S6 (P-S6) expression. The initial P-S6 increase starts approximately one hour after seizure onset, peaks at 3-6 hours, and returns to baseline by 24 hours in both the hippocampus and neocortex, indicating widespread activation of mTOR signaling by acute seizure activity. Following resolution of status epilepticus, a second increase in P-S6 is observed in the hippocampus, starting at 3 days, peaking 5-10 days later, and persisting for several weeks after kainate injection. This second increase in P-S6 correlates with the development of chronic epileptogenesis in the hippocampus.
In line with our previous findings, we found that treatment with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin before kainate injection blocks both the acute and chronic phases of seizure-induced mTOR activation and reduces kainate-induced neuronal cell death, neurogenesis, mossy fiber sprouting, and the development of spontaneous epilepsy. Interestingly, late treatment with rapamycin after termination of status epilepticus only blocks the chronic phase of mTOR activation and reduces mossy fiber sprouting and epilepsy but not neurogenesis or neuronal death.
Our findings demonstrate that the mTOR signaling pathway plays a critical role in epileptogenesis in the kainate rat model and that mTOR inhibitors have potential antiepileptogenic effects in this model.

title: Acute administration of recombinant Angiopoietin-1 ameliorates multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome and improves survival in murine sepsis.
text:
The protein Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) plays a crucial role in protecting the endothelium in the pathophysiology of multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) in sepsis. Recent research suggests that the function of Ang-1 is inhibited by its antagonist Angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2) during sepsis. To investigate whether reversing the suppression of Ang-1 and elevation of Ang-2 could protect against MODS, we examined whether intravenously administering recombinant human (rh) Ang-1 to mice with polymicrobiological abdominal sepsis could improve outcomes.
We induced sepsis in mice by cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) and treated them with either 1 μg of intravenous rhAng-1 or control buffer immediately after CLP induction and every 8 hours thereafter. Sham-operated animals served as time-matched controls. Our results showed that compared to buffer-treated controls, rhAng-1-treated septic mice had significant improvements in various hematologic and biochemical indicators of MODS. Additionally, rhAng-1 stabilized endothelial barrier function, as evidenced by reduced protein leakage from lung capillaries into the alveolar compartment. Histological analysis revealed that rhAng-1 treatment attenuated leukocyte infiltration in the lungs and kidneys of septic mice, probably due to reduced endothelial adhesion molecule expression in rhAng-1-treated mice. Finally, the protective effects of rhAng-1 treatment were reflected by an improved survival time in a lethal CLP model.
In conclusion, our study demonstrates that intravenous rhAng-1 treatment alone is sufficient to significantly improve various organ dysfunctions and survival time in a clinically relevant murine sepsis model, probably by preserving endothelial barrier function. Further research is needed to explore the potential clinical application of this therapy concept.

title: Mechanisms linking obesity to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes
text: Obesity increases the risk of developing insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. In obese individuals, adipose tissue releases excessive amounts of non-esterified fatty acids, glycerol, hormones, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and other factors that contribute to insulin resistance. When insulin resistance combines with dysfunctional pancreatic islet β-cells, which are responsible for releasing insulin, the body's ability to regulate blood glucose levels is compromised. This is a critical factor in the development of type 2 diabetes. This knowledge is driving research into the molecular and genetic basis of the disease and new approaches to its prevention and treatment.

title: Tracking the fate of glomerular epithelial cells in vivo using serial multiphoton imaging in novel mouse models with fluorescent lineage tags
text: Podocytes play a crucial role in maintaining the kidney's filtration system, but studying them in an intact kidney has been challenging due to technical limitations. We overcome these challenges by developing serial multiphoton microscopy (MPM) to visualize the motion of podocytes and parietal epithelial cells (PECs) in vivo over several days. In podocin-GFP mice, podocytes formed random clusters and migrated into the parietal Bowman's capsule after unilateral ureteral ligation. The simultaneous migration of multiple podocytes was observed in podocin-confetti mice using cell-specific expression of CFP, GFP, YFP, or RFP. In PEPCK-GFP mice, serial MPM revealed PEC-to-podocyte migration and nanotube connections. Our findings suggest a highly dynamic glomerular environment and cellular composition, which could advance our understanding of glomerular injury and regeneration.

title: CTCF binding at the H19 imprinting control region mediates maternally inherited higher-order chromatin conformation to restrict enhancer access to Igf2.
text:
The H19 imprinting control region (ICR) is believed to regulate the silencing of the maternally inherited Igf2 allele through a CTCF-dependent chromatin insulator. The ICR has been shown to physically interact with a silencer region in Igf2, as well as with a differentially methylated region (DMR)1. However, the mechanisms by which CTCF influences the chromatin loop and prevents distal enhancers from accessing Igf2 are not fully understood.
To investigate this, we employed systematic chromosome conformation capture (3C) analysis in the Igf2/H19 region spanning over 160 kb. Our findings revealed that enhancers interact with Igf2 promoters on the paternal chromosome, but on the maternal allele, CTCF binding within the H19 ICR prevents this interaction. CTCF binding in the maternal ICR also regulates its interaction with matrix attachment region (MAR)3 and DMR1 at Igf2, thereby forming a tight chromatin loop around the maternal Igf2 locus. This structure may contribute to the silencing of Igf2.
Additionally, we detected mutation of CTCF binding sites in the H19 ICR, leading to loss of CTCF binding and de novo methylation of a CTCF target site within Igf2 DMR1. These results demonstrate that CTCF plays a crucial role in epigenetic regulation of higher-order chromatin structure and gene silencing over long distances in the genome.
In summary, our results provide insights into the mechanisms of imprinting control in the Igf2/H19 locus, highlighting the importance of CTCF in coordinating regional epigenetic marks and regulating gene expression.

title: De novo assembly of a PML nuclear subcompartment occurs through multiple pathways and induces telomere elongation.
text: Tumor cells without telomerase use an alternative way to grow, called ALT (alternative lengthening of telomeres). This pathway involves DNA repair and recombination to keep the cells dividing. One of the key features of this process is the build-up of a protein called PML in the telomere DNA. By studying how the PML protein is formed, we found that certain proteins can help create these protein-filled compartments. These proteins include PML, Sp100, TRF1, TRF2, NBS1, MMS21, SUMO1, Rad9, Rad17, and Rad51. The proteins work together in a specific way to create these compartments, which are called ALT-associated PML bodies (APBs). The APBs can extend the telomeres through a process called DNA repair, which we know because they also colocalize with sites of non-replicative DNA synthesis and histone H2A.X phosphorylation, and result in longer telomere repeat lengths. These findings suggest that APBs are an important step in the ALT pathway.

title: Effects of an opal termination codon preceding the nsP4 gene sequence in the O'Nyong-Nyong virus genome on Anopheles gambiae infectivity.
text: The genome of the alphavirus encodes four non-structural proteins, nsP1, nsP2, nsP3, and nsP4. During translation, the polyprotein P123 is produced when the termination codon between nsP3 and nsP4 is reached. However, in some cases, translation can continue beyond the opal termination codon, leading to the production of the polyprotein P1234. Evolutionary pressures have maintained the presence of both the opal termination codon and an open reading frame (arginine) in the alphavirus genome, indicating that both are important. ONNV (O'nyong-nyong virus) replicates in both vertebrate and invertebrate hosts, and the predominance of a particular codon at this locus in the viral quasispecies may depend on the host. To investigate the functional significance of the opal stop codon in ONNV, we constructed mutants with an opal, ochre, or amber stop codon in place of the arginine between nsP3 and nsP4. We found that the presence of an opal stop codon near the beginning of nsP4 nearly doubled the infectivity of ONNV compared to the arginine codon. Although the frequency of dissemination of the opal virus did not significantly differ from that of the arginine virus on days 8 and 10, the opal virus disseminated earlier. Sequence analysis of RNA isolated from mosquito bodies and heads showed that the codon usage at this position corresponded with the virus administered in the blood meal, suggesting that de novo mutation at this position is rare in mosquitoes. Taken together, these findings suggest that the primary fitness advantage provided by the opal codon is related to mosquito infectivity.

title: Down-regulation of a host microRNA by a Herpesvirus saimiri noncoding RNA.
text: T cells infected with Herpesvirus saimiri produce seven uncharacterized viral non-coding RNAs called HSURs. We discovered that specific sequences in HSURs 1 and 2 may serve as binding sites for three host cell microRNAs (miRNAs). Using coimmunoprecipitation assays, we confirmed that HSURs 1 and 2 interact with the predicted miRNAs in virus-infected T cells. Surprisingly, one of these miRNAs, miR-27, is significantly downregulated in transformed cells, leading to changes in the expression of miR-27 target genes. Our experiments showed that HSUR 1 directs the degradation of mature miR-27 in a sequence-specific and binding-dependent manner, demonstrating a novel viral strategy to manipulate host cell gene expression through the miRNA pathway.

title: HTRF: A Technology Tailored for Drug Discovery –A Review of Theoretical Aspects and Recent Applications
text: Homogeneous Time Resolved Fluorescence (HTRF) is the most frequently employed generic assay technology for measuring analytes in a homogeneous format, making it the ideal platform for drug target studies in high-throughput screening (HTS). This technology combines fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) with time-resolved measurement (TR). In TR-FRET assays, a signal is generated when a donor and acceptor molecule are in close proximity, resulting in fluorescent resonance energy transfer. By using dual-wavelength detection, buffer and media interference are significantly reduced, and the final signal is proportional to the extent of product formation. HTRF is often sensitive and robust, allowing for miniaturization into 384 and 1536-well plate formats. This technology has been applied to various antibody-based assays, including GPCR signaling (cAMP and IP-One), kinases, cytokines, and biomarkers, as well as assays for protein-protein, protein-peptide, and protein-DNA/RNA interactions. Since its introduction to the drug-screening field over a decade ago, HTRF has been used to expedite the study of GPCRs, kinases, new biomarkers, protein-protein interactions, and other targets of interest. Additionally, it has been utilized as an alternative method for bioprocess monitoring. The first-generation HTRF technology, which uses Europium cryptate as a fluorescence donor to monitor reactions between biomolecules, was enhanced in 2008 through the introduction of a second-generation donor, Terbium cryptate (Tb). Tb possesses different photophysical properties compared to Europium, including increased quantum yield and a higher molar extinction coefficient. Furthermore, Tb can serve as a donor fluorophore to green-emitting fluors due to its multiple emission peaks, including one at 490 nm. All Terbium HTRF assays can be read on the same HTRF-compatible instruments as Europium HTRF assays. In conclusion, HTRF is a highly sensitive, robust technology for detecting molecular interactions in vitro and is widely used for both primary and secondary screening phases of drug development. This review covers the general principles of HTRF and its current applications in drug discovery.

title: Chk1 inhibits replication factory activation but allows dormant origin firing in existing factories
text: Origins of replication are activated by loading MCM2-7 hexamers before entering the S phase. However, only about 10% of these licensed origins are typically used in S phase, with the remaining ones remaining dormant. When DNA replication is hindered, dormant origins nearby initiate to ensure that all DNA is eventually replicated. Contrary to this, replicative stress triggers the activation of ataxia telangiectasia and rad-3-related (ATR) and Checkpoint kinases 1 (Chk1), which hinder origin firing. In this study, we show that at low levels of replication stress, ATR/Chk1 predominantly suppresses the initiation of new replication factories by inhibiting the activation of new factories, thereby reducing the number of active factories. At the same time, inhibition of replication fork progression allows dormant origins to initiate within existing replication factories. The inhibition of new factory activation by ATR/Chk1 therefore redirects replication towards active factories where forks are inhibited, and away from regions that have yet to start replication. This minimizes the harmful consequences of fork stalling and prevents similar problems from arising in unreplicated regions of the genome.

title: Fra-1 protooncogene regulates IL-6 expression in macrophages and promotes the generation of M2d macrophages
text:
The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a crucial role in the growth and progression of tumor cells. M2d macrophages, the major inflammatory component of the TME, are influenced by the TME and adopt an immunosuppressive role that promotes tumor metastasis and progression. Fra-1, an activator protein, forms heterodimers with Jun partners and regulates gene transcription. Fra-1 has been implicated in tumorigenesis and progression, yet its functional role in the differentiation of M2d macrophages is poorly understood.
Our study demonstrates that 4T1 mammary carcinoma cells, when co-cultured with RAW264.7 macrophage cells, direct the differentiation of RAW264.7 cells into M2d macrophages. The 4T1 cells induce an overexpression of Fra-1 in RAW264.7 cells, which then binds to the interleukin 6 (IL-6) promoter to increase cytokine production. IL-6 acts in an autocrine manner to skew RAW264.7 macrophage cell differentiation towards M2d macrophages.
These findings provide new insights into strategies to reverse M2d macrophage-induced immune tolerance, which can improve the efficacy of immunotherapeutic approaches.

title: Analysis of SiO2 nanoparticles binding proteins in rat blood and brain homogenate
text: A variety of nanoparticles, including titanium oxide (TiO2), zinc oxide, aluminum oxide, gold oxide, silver oxide, iron oxide, and silica oxide, are commonly used in various products such as chemicals, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and electronics. Recently, SiO2 nanoparticles have been found to have an inert toxicity profile with no association with irreversible toxicological changes in animal models, leading to an increase in their exposure. SiO2 nanoparticles are used in a range of applications, including strengthening fillers for construction materials and non-toxic platforms for biomedical applications such as drug delivery and theragnostics. However, recent in vitro experiments have shown that SiO2 nanoparticles can be cytotoxic. To investigate the potentially toxic pathways of SiO2 nanoparticles, we analyzed the adsorbed protein corona on the surface of SiO2 nanoparticles in the blood and brain of rats. Four types of SiO2 nanoparticles were investigated, and the protein corona was analyzed using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry technology. A total of 115 and 48 plasma proteins from rats were identified as bound to negatively charged 20 nm and 100 nm SiO2 nanoparticles, respectively, and 50 and 36 proteins were found for 20 nm and 100 nm arginine-coated SiO2 nanoparticles, respectively. We found higher numbers of proteins adsorbed onto the 20 nm sized SiO2 nanoparticles than onto the 100 nm sized nanoparticles, regardless of charge. Additionally, more proteins were found bound to arginine-coated positively charged SiO2 nanoparticles than to the negatively charged nanoparticles. The bound proteins were further analyzed using ClueGO, a Cytoscape plugin used to identify protein ontology and biological interaction pathways. The proteins bound on the surface of nanoparticles may affect functional and conformational properties and distributions in various biological processes.

title: Inferring nucleosome positions with their histone mark annotation from ChIP data
text:
The nucleosome is the fundamental unit of chromatin organization, consisting of two copies each of the four core histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, and approximately 147 base pairs of DNA. Post-translational modifications of the histone proteins, such as methylation or acetylation, play a crucial role in chromatin gene regulation. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) is a powerful tool for genome-wide analysis of histone modifications, enabling the detection of specific nucleosomes and their associated modifications. However, the processing and interpretation of ChIP-seq data requirements sophisticated computational methods.
To address this challenge, we developed NucHunter, a novel algorithm that leverages ChIP-seq data to predict positioned nucleosomes and annotate them with histone modification intensities. We demonstrate that these annotations can be used to infer nucleosomal states and their correlations with specific genomic features and chromatin-related processes, such as transcriptional start sites, enhancers, elongation by RNA polymerase II, and chromatin-mediated repression. NucHunter can be applied to a variety of ChIP-seq experiments focused on different histone modifications, allowing researchers to predict positioned nucleosomes and identify distinct histone modification patterns associated with different chromatin states.
The software is freely available at [http://epigen.molgen.mpg.de/nuchunter/](http://epigen.molgen.mpg.de/nuchunter/) and is accompanied by a comprehensive documentation and tutorial to facilitate its use. With NucHunter, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationship between chromatin structures and gene regulation, ultimately leading to novel insights into the mechanisms of chromatin-mediated gene control.

title: Generation of large numbers of dendritic cells from mouse bone marrow cultures supplemented with granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor
text: Dendritic cells, which present antigens to T cells and activate immune responses, are derived from bone marrow, specifically through the MHC class II-rich dendritic cell lineage. However, bone marrow precursors lack mature dendritic cells, and a substantial number of less-mature cells need to be identified. Using a modified method from mouse blood, dendritic cell growth can be induced from MHC class II-negative precursors in marrow. The process involves removing nonadherent, newly formed granulocytes through gentle washes during the first 2-4 days of culture, leaving behind proliferating clusters loosely attached to a more firmly adherent stroma. These clusters can be isolated by 1-g sedimentation and, upon reculture, large numbers of dendritic cells are released. The resulting dendritic cells express high levels of MHC class II products and function as powerful accessory cells for initiating mixed leukocyte reactions. Notably, the use of macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) generates all three lineages of myeloid cells (granulocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells), while granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) generates only dendritic cells. With the ability to generate >5 x 106 dendritic cells in a single week from precursors within the large hind limb bones of a single animal, marrow progenitors can serve as a major source of dendritic cells for future molecular and clinical studies.

title: Insulin action and resistance in obesity and type 2 diabetes
text: Excessive nutrition is a crucial precursor to type 2 diabetes. It boosts insulin production, but hinders its metabolic effects in the liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue. Nonetheless, conflicting evidence highlights the dearth of knowledge regarding the timing of these events during the progression of obesity and diabetes, underscoring a fundamental gap in our comprehension of metabolic disorders. This Perspective examines alternative viewpoints and recent findings on the temporal and mechanistic connections between elevated insulin levels, obesity, and insulin resistance. Although significant attention has been focused on the early stages of the insulin signaling cascade, insulin resistance in obesity is primarily initiated downstream of these stages. New discoveries have also revealed the intricate metabolic dialogue between the liver, adipose tissue, pancreas, and skeletal muscle in the development of insulin resistance. Over the past five years, these and other advances offer both exciting opportunities and daunting challenges for the development of novel therapeutic strategies to combat type 2 diabetes.

title: Effect of lowering blood pressure on cardiovascular events and mortality in patients on dialysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
text:
Patients undergoing dialysis face a significantly higher risk of cardiovascular mortality and morbidity compared to the general population. However, there is limited research on the effectiveness and tolerability of lowering blood pressure in this population. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to assess the impact of blood pressure lowering in dialysis patients.
We searched major medical databases, including Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, for trials published between 1950 and November 2008, without any language restrictions. We extracted a standardized dataset from eligible trials and performed a meta-analysis using a random effects model.
Our analysis included eight relevant trials that provided data on 1679 patients and 495 cardiovascular events. We found that blood pressure lowering treatment was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events (relative risk (RR) 0.71, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.55-0.92, p=0.009), all-cause mortality (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66-0.96, p=0.014), and cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.50-0.99, p=0.044) compared to control regimens. The effects were consistent across various patient groups included in the studies.
Our findings suggest that treatment with blood pressure lowering agents should be considered a standard of care for individuals undergoing dialysis to reduce their high risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.

title: Interaction of an adenovirus E3 14.7-kilodalton protein with a novel tumor necrosis factor alpha-inducible cellular protein containing leucine zipper domains.
text: Early region 3 (E3) of group C human adenoviruses (Ad) encodes several proteins that inhibit the activity of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha), including a 14.7-kDa protein (E3-14.7K) and a heterodimer containing two polypeptides of 10.4 and 14.5 kDa. To investigate the mechanism by which these viral proteins inhibit TNF-alpha functions, the E3-14.7K protein was used to screen a HeLa cell cDNA library in a yeast two-hybrid system to identify interacting proteins. A novel protein containing multiple leucine zipper domains without any significant homology to known proteins was identified and named FIP-2 (for 14.7K-interacting protein). FIP-2 interacted with E3-14.7K both in vitro and in vivo, and colocalized with the viral protein in the cytoplasm, particularly near the nuclear membrane. While FIP-2 does not cause cell death on its own, it can reverse the protective effect of E3-14.7K on cell killing induced by overexpression of the intracellular domain of the 55-kDa TNF receptor or by RIP, a death protein involved in the TNF-alpha and Fas apoptosis pathways. Deletion analysis revealed that the reversal effect of FIP-2 depends on its interaction with E3-14.7K. Three major mRNA forms of FIP-2 have been detected in multiple human tissues, and expression of the transcripts was induced by TNF-alpha treatment in a time-dependent manner in two different cell lines. FIP-2 has consensus sequences for several potential posttranslational modifications. These findings suggest that FIP-2 is one of the cellular targets for Ad E3-14.7K, and that its mechanism of affecting cell death involves the TNF receptor, RIP, or a downstream molecule affected by either of these two molecules.

title: PML induces compaction, TRF2 depletion and DNA damage signaling at telomeres and promotes their alternative lengthening.
text: Telomeres are the protective endcaps of chromosomes, and when theyShorten, the cell may enter senescence or apoptosis. Cancer cells can evade these cellular processes by activating an alternative lengthening mechanism (ALT). One distinct aspect of this pathway is the formation of promyelocytic leukemia (PML) nuclear bodies (APBs) at telomeres. To comprehend the role ofAPBs in ALT cells, we conducted an automated 3D fluorescence microscopy screen and advanced image analysis of a human ALT cell line. Our experiments identified 29 proteins that contribute to APB formation, including proteins that regulate telomere and chromatin structure, protein sumoylation, and DNA repair. By integrating these findings, we discovered that APBs cluster telomere repeats, compact telomeres, and reduce the levels of the shelterin protein TRF2 (also known as TERF2). These changes promote DNA damage response in APBs and are associated with increased ATM kinase phosphorylation. We propose that APBs protect telomeres by inducing DNA damage response in ALT-positive cancer cells through altering the telomere chromatin state to activate ATM phosphorylation.

title: Gr-1+CD11b+ myeloid cells tip the balance of immune protection to tumor promotion in the premetastatic lung.
text: Despite understanding the mechanisms by which a primary tumor influences a distant organ after tumor cell migration, the processes by which a primary tumor affects a chosen distant organ before tumor cell arrival remain unknown. This study found that the number of Gr-1+CD11b+ immature myeloid cells increased significantly in the lungs of mice bearing mammary adenocarcinomas before tumor cell arrival. In premature lungs, these cells reduced the production of interferon-gamma and increased pro-inflammatory cytokines, also produced large amounts of matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9) and promoted vascular remodeling. The MMP9 production and activity were specifically limited to organs and tissues with abundant Gr-1+CD11b+ cells. Our work uncovered a novel tumor-enabling mechanism for Gr-1+CD11b+ cells that transforms the premetastatic lung into an inflammatory and proliferative environment, reduces immune protection, and promotes metastasis through aberrant vasculature formation. As a result, inhibiting Gr-1+CD11b+ cells could correct the premature lung environment, strengthen host immune surveillance, and inhibit tumor metastasis.

title: Activin/Nodal signalling in stem cells.
text: The Activin/Nodal growth factor pathway plays a far-reaching role in various biological processes, including early cell fate decisions, organogenesis, and adult tissue maintenance. In this overview, we delve into the mechanisms by which the Activin/Nodal pathway regulates stem cell function across different stages of development. We highlight recent findings that implicate Activin/Nodal signaling in pathological conditions, such as cancer stem cells and their potential as a therapeutic target. Furthermore, we discuss open questions and future directions regarding the role of Activin/Nodal signaling in stem cell self-renewal, differentiation, and proliferation.

title: Distinct RNA-dependent RNA polymerases are required for RNAi triggered by double-stranded RNA versus truncated transgenes in Paramecium tetraurelia
text: In many eukaryotic organisms, RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRPs) play critical roles in the RNA interference (RNAi) pathway. These enzymes have been found to be involved in the recognition and processing of abnormal transcripts, which triggers the RNAi process, as well as in the amplification of the silencing response. In the ciliate Paramecium tetraurelia, RdRP genes have been tested for their functions in both experimentally induced and endogenous RNAi mechanisms. Our findings indicate that the putatively functional RDR1 and RDR2 genes are required for the accumulation of both primary small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and a distinct class of small RNAs suggesting secondary siRNAs. In contrast, the RDR3 gene is necessary for siRNA accumulation when RNAi is triggered by truncated transgenes. Our data further suggest that RDR3 is involved in the accumulation of endogenous siRNAs and in the regulation of the surface antigen gene family. Interestingly, while only one of these genes is normally expressed in any clonal cell line, the knockdown of RDR3 leads to the co-expression of multiple antigens. These results provide evidence for a functional specialization of Paramecium RdRP genes in distinct RNAi pathways operating during vegetative growth.

title: Mechanisms of Renal Cell Apoptosis Induced by Cyclosporine A: A Systematic Review of in vitro Studies
text: Background: Chronic cyclosporine A (CsA) nephrotoxicity (CCN) is a significant cause of chronic kidney disease with little effective treatment. Objective: To identify the mechanisms of renal cell death in CCN, we examined all in vitro studies on this topic. Methods: We collected in vitro studies on the mechanisms of renal cell death induced by CsA from medical databases (Medline, Embase, and ISI) and evaluated their quality based on in vitro standards. We then extracted the data and synthesized the results using the PICOS framework. Results: Our findings indicate that CsA upregulates Fas and Fas-L expression, increases apoptosis-related enzymes (caspase-2, -3, -4, -7, -8, -9, and -10), and downregulates Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL. Additionally, CsA induces oxidative stress, damages the antioxidant defense system, increases the expression of HERP, GRP78, and CHOP, and induces renal cell death. Finally, we found that CsA increases iNOS and p53 expression in cultured renal cells. Conclusions: Our study suggests that at least four pathways are involved in renal cell death induced by CsA in different cell types. These pathways may provide potential targets for interventions, but confirmation of these findings in vivo is needed.

title: Blood stem cells emerge from aortic endothelium by a novel type of cell transition
text: The ontogeny of haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) during embryonic development remains contentious, particularly their possible lineage relationship to vascular endothelial cells. The first anatomical site from which cells with long-term HSC potential have been isolated is the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM), specifically the vicinity of the dorsal aortic floor. While some authors have suggested that HSCs may originate directly from the aortic floor into the dorsal aortic lumen, others propose that they first arise within the underlying mesenchyme. Here, we employ non-invasive, high-resolution imaging of live zebrafish embryos to demonstrate that HSCs emerge directly from the aortic floor through a unique process that does not involve cell division but rather a concerted bending and egress of single endothelial cells from the aortic ventral wall into the sub-aortic space. These cells then undergo transformation into haematopoietic cells, a process that is directionally polarized in both the dorso-ventral and rostro-caudal dimensions, and depends on the expression of Runx1. In Runx1-deficient embryos, the exit events are initially similar but occur at a reduced frequency and often culminate in the violent death of the exiting cell. Our findings unequivocally establish the haemogenic potential of the aortic floor and reveal a novel mechanism of HSC emergence, which we term endothelial haematopoietic transition.

title: Probable person to person transmission of novel avian influenza A (H7N9) virus in Eastern China, 2013: epidemiological investigation
text:
Objective: To investigate the ability of the novel avian influenza H7N9 virus to transmit from person to person and its efficiency.
Design: Epidemiological investigations conducted after a family cluster of two patients with avian H7N9 infection in March 2013.
Setting: Wuxi, Eastern China.
Participants: Two patients, their close contacts, and relevant environments.
Methods: Samples from the patients and environments were collected and tested using real-time reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR), viral culture, and haemagglutination inhibition assay. Any contacts who became ill had samples tested for avian H7N9 by rRT-PCR. Paired serum samples were obtained from contacts for serological testing by haemagglutination inhibition assays.
Main Outcomes Measures: Clinical data, history of exposure before the onset of illnesses, and results of laboratory testing of pathogens and further analysis of sequences and phylogenetic tree to isolated strains.
Results: The index patient became ill five to six days after his last exposure to poultry. The second patient, his daughter aged 32, who provided unprotected bedside care in the hospital, had no known exposure to poultry. She developed symptoms six days after her last contact with her father. Two strains were isolated successfully from the two patients. Genome sequence and analyses of phylogenetic trees showed that both viruses were almost genetically identical. Forty-three close contacts of both patients were identified. One had mild illness but had negative results for avian H7N9 by rRT-PCR. All 43 close contacts tested negative for haemagglutination inhibition antibodies specific for avian H7N9.
Conclusions: The infection of the daughter probably resulted from contact with her father (the index patient) during unprotected exposure, suggesting that in this cluster the virus was able to transmit from person to person. The transmissibility was limited and non-sustainable.

title: Genetic Variation in the Interleukin-28B Gene Is Associated with Spontaneous Clearance and Progression of Hepatitis C Virus in Moroccan Patients
text:
Background: The IL28B gene has been found to be associated with treatment outcomes, spontaneous clearance, and progression of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Our study aimed to investigate the role of polymorphisms in the IL28B gene in predicting the outcome of HCV infection in a Moroccan population.
Methods: We analyzed a cohort of 438 individuals, including 232 patients with persistent HCV infection, 68 individuals who had naturally cleared the virus, and 138 healthy controls. We genotyped the IL28B SNPs rs12979860 and rs8099917 using a TaqMan 5' allelic discrimination assay.
Results: We found that the protective alleles of the rs12979860 and rs8099917 polymorphisms were more common in individuals who had spontaneously cleared the virus. Individuals with the C/C genotype for the rs12979860 polymorphism were 4.69 times more likely to have cleared the virus, and those with the T/T genotype for the rs8099917 polymorphism were 3.55 times more likely to have cleared the virus. Additionally, patients with advanced liver disease were more likely to carry the T/T genotype for the rs12979860 polymorphism and the G allele for the rs8099917 polymorphism.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that polymorphisms in the IL28B gene play a role in both spontaneous clearance and progression of HCV infection in the Moroccan population. These results have implications for personalized medicine and the development of new treatments for HCV infection.

title: CD127 expression inversely correlates with FoxP3 and suppressive function of human CD4+ T reg cells
text: T regulatory cells (Tregs) are essential regulators of immune tolerance. Traditionally, Tregs have been defined by expressing CD4, CD25, and the transcription factor FoxP3. However, these markers have proven to be insufficient for identifying Tregs in humans with accuracy. We found that the expression of the IL-7 receptor (CD127) is down-regulated on a subset of CD4+ T cells in peripheral blood. Our results show that the majority of these cells are also FoxP3+, including those with low or no CD25 expression. Using a combination of CD4, CD25, and CD127, we were able to isolate a highly purified population of Tregs, accounting for significantly more cells than previously identified using other surface markers. These cells were highly suppressive in functional suppression assays, and cells separated based solely on CD4 and CD127 expression were found to be anergic. Remarkably, cells from this subset were as suppressive as the classic CD4+CD25hi Treg cell subset, despite representing at least three times as many cells. Finally, we demonstrate that CD127 can be used to quantify Treg cell subsets in individuals with type 1 diabetes, supporting the use of CD127 as a biomarker for human Tregs.

title: Environmental factors that influence the cutaneous production of vitamin D
text: All vertebrates, including humans, receive the majority of their daily vitamin D requirement through incidental exposure to sunlight. When the solar ultraviolet B photons (290-315 nm) present in sunlight interact with the skin, they trigger the photolysis of 7-dehydrocholesterol, resulting in the formation of precholecalciferol. Subsequently, precholecalciferol undergoes a thermal rearrangement of its double bonds to produce cholecalciferol. Factors such as skin pigmentation, aging, and the application of sunscreen can reduce the amount of cholecalciferol produced in the skin. The number of solar ultraviolet B photons that reach the earth's surface is influenced by factors such as latitude, season, and time of day, as well as ozone pollution in the atmosphere, which can impact the amount of cholecalciferol produced in the skin. In Boston, for example, exposure to sunlight during the months of November through February will not result in significant production of cholecalciferol in the skin. Additionally, exposure to sunlight through glass windows will not lead to any production of cholecalciferol, as windowpane glass absorbs ultraviolet B radiation. It is estimated that vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency are common among elderly people, particularly those who are immobile or live in areas with limited sunlight exposure during the winter months. Vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency can exacerbate osteoporosis, cause osteomalacia, and increase the risk of skeletal fractures. To prevent vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency, it is recommended to encourage responsible sunlight exposure and/or consuming a multivitamin tablet that contains 10 micrograms (400 IU) vitamin D.

title: Genomic imprinting in development, growth, behavior and stem cells.
text: Certain genes in mammals are subject to genomic imprinting, which means they are preferentially expressed from a single parental allele. This selective expression of a limited number of genes is essential for normal development, as they often regulate fetal growth directly. Recent research has also shown that imprinted genes play intricate roles in the brain, with significant impacts on behavior and neuronal function. Furthermore, new studies have demonstrated the importance of proper expression of specific imprinted genes in induced pluripotent stem cells and adult stem cells. As this review highlights, the complex nature and developmental significance of imprinted genes are becoming increasingly apparent.

title: Quantitative Detection of Hepatitis C Virus RNA by Light Cycler PCR and Comparison with Two Different PCR Assays
text: The novel Light Cycler technology was utilized for the detection of hepatitis C virus (HCV) RNA in clinical samples. Sera from 81 patients were evaluated using Light Cycler PCR, AMPLICOR HCV Monitor assay, and an in-house PCR. Our findings show that Light Cycler is a rapid and reliable method for both detecting and quantifying HCV RNA.

title: Targeting arginine metabolism pathway to treat arginine-dependent cancers.
text: Armed with the vast differences in metabolism between tumor and normal cells, researchers have been driven to develop metabolism-based anti-tumor therapeutics. One such approach involves targeting arginine, a semi-essential amino acid that normal cells can both produce and absorb from the outside world. However, certain tumors have abnormalities in enzymes involved in arginine metabolism, rendering them reliant on extracellular arginine to sustain vital biological functions. This dependency is known as arginine auxotrophy. By exploiting this characteristic, researchers have investigated the use of arginine deprivation therapy, which involves inhibiting the uptake of arginine through the use of arginine deiminase (ADI) and arginase I. This strategy has shown promising efficacy against arginine-auxotrophic tumors. By combining the insights of both clinical oncologists and laboratory scientists, this article provides a comprehensive overview of the potential of arginine deprivation as a novel cancer therapy.

title: Rank Signaling Links the Development of Invariant γδ T Cell Progenitors and Aire+ Medullary Epithelium
text: The medulla of the thymus provides a specialized microenvironment for the negative selection of T cells, with the presence of Aire-expressing medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) during the embryonic-neonatal period being both necessary and sufficient to establish long-lasting tolerance. Here, we showed that the emergence of the first cohorts of Aire(+) mTECs at this critical developmental stage, prior to the selection of the αβ T cell repertoire, was coordinately regulated by Rankl(+) lymphoid tissue inducer cells and invariant Vγ5(+) dendritic epidermal T cell (DETC) progenitors that are the first thymocytes to express the products of gene rearrangement. In turn, the generation of Aire(+) mTECs then fostered Skint-1-dependent, but Aire-independent, DETC progenitor maturation and the emergence of an invariant DETC repertoire. Therefore, our data assign a functional significance to the temporal development of Vγ5(+) γδ T cells during thymus medulla formation for αβ T cell tolerance induction and demonstrate a Rank-mediated reciprocal link between DETC and Aire(+) mTEC maturation.

title: Long-term immune deficiency after allogeneic stem cell transplantation: B-cell deficiency is associated with late infections.
text: In this study, the immune reconstitution of 140 patients who were 2 years disease-free and underwent myeloablative allogeneic transplantation was analyzed. The study found that there were defects in CD4 and CD8 cells, including naive, terminally differentiated, memory, and activated subsets. Natural killer cells normalized at six months, while CD19(+)/CD5(+) B cells expanded after three months and persisted with a defect in memory B cells. Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGvHD) did not significantly affect CD8 subsets, but significantly affected naive and competent CD4 subsets. However, the most significant impact of cGvHD was on B-cell subsets, particularly on the memory B population. The study found that the cumulative incidence of late severe infections was low (14% at four years). Using Cox's models, low B-cell counts at 12 and 24 months were associated with the hazard of developing late infections, particularly if patients did not develop cGvHD.

title: The stimulatory potency of T cell antigens is influenced by the formation of the immunological synapse.
text: T cell activation is contingent upon the interaction between the T cell receptor and peptide-major histocompatibility (pMHC) ligands. Despite understanding the factors that influence the stimulatory potential of a pMHC molecule, the reasons behind this phenomenon remain elusive. Our study reveals that a peptide exhibiting characteristics of a weak agonist stimulates T cells to proliferate more than the wild-type agonist ligand. Using an in silico approach, we suspected that the inability to form the central supramolecular activation cluster (cSMAC) might underlie the enhanced proliferation. This hypothesis was corroborated by experiments demonstrating that enhancing cSMAC formation reduced the stimulatory capacity of the weak peptide. Our findings underscore the complexity of the interplay between various factors in determining the quality of a T cell antigen.

title: Control of glutamate clearance and synaptic efficacy by glial coverage of neurons.
text: A study examining excitatory synaptic transmission in the rat hypothalamic supraoptic nucleus found that the clearance of glutamate from the extracellular space is closely linked to the degree of astrocytic coverage surrounding neurons. Specifically, decreased glutamate clearance, whether induced pharmacologically or due to a decrease in nearby glial coverage, altered the release of transmitters from presynaptic metabotropic glutamate receptors. These findings suggest that astrocytic wrapping of neurons plays a critical role in regulating synaptic efficacy in the central nervous system.

title: Duration of androgen suppression in the treatment of prostate cancer.
text:
BACKGROUND: The use of radiotherapy in combination with long-term medical suppression of androgens (> or = 2 years) has been shown to improve overall survival in patients with locally advanced prostate cancer. In this study, we compared the outcomes of patients with locally advanced prostate cancer who received either short-term or long-term androgen suppression in addition to external-beam radiotherapy.
METHODS: We randomly assigned patients who had received external-beam radiotherapy and 6 months of androgen suppression to either no further treatment (short-term suppression) or 2.5 years of further treatment with a luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone agonist (long-term suppression). The noninferiority of short-term suppression compared to long-term suppression was evaluated, with a hazard ratio of more than 1.35 for overall survival and a one-sided alpha level of 0.05. An interim analysis showed futility, and the results were presented with an adjusted one-sided alpha level of 0.0429.
RESULTS: A total of 1113 patients were registered, of whom 970 were randomly assigned, 483 to short-term suppression and 487 to long-term suppression. After a median follow-up of 6.4 years, 132 patients in the short-term group and 98 in the long-term group had died, with 47 deaths due to prostate cancer in the short-term group and 29 in the long-term group. The 5-year overall mortality for short-term and long-term suppression was 19.0% and 15.2%, respectively, with a hazard ratio of 1.42 (95.71% confidence interval, 1.79; P=0.65 for noninferiority). Common adverse events included fatigue, diminished sexual function, and hot flushes in both groups.
CONCLUSIONS: The combination of radiotherapy plus 6 months of androgen suppression did not demonstrate noninferiority compared to the combination of radiotherapy plus 3 years of androgen suppression in the treatment of locally advanced prostate cancer. (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00003026.)

title: A Functional Neuroimaging Study of Sound Localization: Visual Cortex Activity Predicts Performance in Early-Blind Individuals
text: Blind individuals often demonstrate enhanced nonvisual perceptual abilities, and the neural basis of this improved performance remains largely unexplored. Previous behavioral studies showed that some early-blind individuals localize sounds more accurately than sighted controls using monaural cues. To investigate the neural basis of these differences in humans, we conducted functional imaging studies using positron emission tomography (PET) and a speaker array that allowed for pseudo-free-field presentations within the scanner. Notably, during binaural sound localization, the sighted control group showed decreased cerebral blood flow in the occipital lobe, which was not observed in early-blind individuals. In contrast, during monaural sound localization (one ear plugged), a subgroup of early-blind subjects who were behaviorally superior at sound localization exhibited two activation foci in the occipital cortex. This effect was not seen in blind persons who did not show superior monaural sound localization abilities, nor in sighted individuals. Remarkably, the degree of activation of one of these foci was strongly correlated with sound localization accuracy across the entire group of blind subjects. These findings suggest that blind individuals who perform better than sighted individuals rely on the occipital cortex to carry out auditory localization under monaural conditions. We therefore conclude that computations in the occipital cortex are specifically involved in the enhanced capacity to use monaural cues. Our findings shed light not only on intermodal compensatory mechanisms but also on individual differences in these mechanisms, as well as on inhibitory patterns that differ between sighted individuals and those who lost their vision early in life.

title: High-Infiltration of Tumor-Associated Macrophages Predicts Unfavorable Clinical Outcome for Node-Negative Breast Cancer
text:
