With access to MetaADEDB available for free at <http://www.lmmd.org/online_services/metaadedb>, this database and method offer a valuable tool for searching known side effects or predicting potential side effects of a given drug or compound.

title: Genetic Tests for Ecological and Allopatric Speciation in Anoles on an Island Archipelago
text: Darwin's research on the Galapagos and Wallace's work in Indonesia highlighted the importance of islands in evolutionary studies, particularly in the context of allopatric speciation. Despite the current shift in understanding towards other modes of speciation, island radiations, such as those found in the Lesser Antilles, continue to be seen as exemplars of this process. Geological and molecular phylogenetic evidence suggests that the Martinique anoles provide examples of secondary contact between island species. Four precursor island species, with up to 8 million years of divergence, coalesced to form the current island of Martinique. Moreover, adjacent anole populations exhibit adaptations to distinct habitat zones, allowing for both allopatric and ecological speciation to be investigated in this system. We took advantage of this opportunity for replicated island coalescence and independent ecological adaptation to conduct an extensive population genetic study using neutral nuclear hypervariable markers. Our findings indicate that, despite substantial periods of spatial isolation, the putative allospecies show less reproductive isolation than conspecific populations in adjacent habitats in all three cases of subsequent island coalescence. Interestingly, there is greater genetic isolation across the xeric/rainforest ecotone than is associated with any secondary contact. This supports the potential for ecological speciation, despite the lack of complete allopatric speciation. Additionally, this study helps explain the relatively low number of anole species found in the Lesser Antilles compared to the Greater Antilles.

title: Deficiency and pharmacological stabilization of mast cells reduce diet-induced obesity and diabetes in mice
text: Although mast cells have traditionally been linked to allergic responses, recent research suggests that these cells may also play a role in other prevalent diseases, including multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, aortic aneurysm, and cancer. This study uncovers evidence that mast cells also contribute to diet-induced obesity and diabetes. Specifically, white adipose tissue (WAT) from obese individuals and mice harbors more mast cells than WAT from lean counterparts. Moreover, genetic or pharmacological depletion of mast cells, or their stabilization, in mice consuming a Western diet leads to a reduction in body weight gain, inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and proteases in serum and WAT, alongside improved glucose homeostasis and energy expenditure. Mechanistic studies reveal that mast cells contribute to WAT and muscle angiogenesis, as well as cell apoptosis and cathepsin activity. Adoptive transfer experiments involving cytokine-deficient mast cells demonstrate that these cells, upon producing interleukin-6 (IL-6) and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), promote mouse adipose tissue cysteine protease cathepsin expression, apoptosis, and angiogenesis, thereby exacerbating diet-induced obesity and glucose intolerance. Our findings, mostraving reduced obesity and diabetes in mice treated with clinically available mast cell-stabilizing agents, suggest the potential of developing novel therapies for these ubiquitous human metabolic disorders.

title: Familial aphasic episodes: another variant of partial epilepsy with simple inheritance?
text: We report on a family with partial epilepsy displaying a pattern of simple inheritance. Affected members commonly experience aphasic episodes with secondary generalization, with onset occurring either during adolescence or adulthood. The response to medication has varied significantly among patients. Notably, no neurological defects or decline in intelligence was observed. This case represents another rare example of familial partial epilepsy with neocortical epilepsy features, highlighting the diversity of this condition.

title: Endosome-ER Contacts Control Actin Nucleation and Retromer Function through VAP-Dependent Regulation of PI4P
text: VAP (VAPA and VAPB) is an evolutionarily conserved protein that plays a crucial role in generating tethers between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and other membranes, thereby facilitating lipid exchange across adjacent bilayers. In this study, we investigate the role of VAP in regulating PI4P levels on endosomes and its impact on WASH-dependent actin nucleation on these organelles and the function of the retromer, a protein complex responsible for endosome-to-Golgi trafficking. Our results reveal that VAP recruits recruitment to retromer budding sites on endosomes through an interaction with the retromer SNX2 subunit, which in turn influences the levels of phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P) on these organelles. We find that cells lacking VAP exhibit elevated levels of PI4P, actin comets, and trans-Golgi proteins on endosomes, which can be mimicked by downregulation of OSBP, a protein that interacts with VAP and PI4P transports. These findings shed light on the mechanisms by which the ER can control budding dynamics and cytoskeletal associations with nearby membranes through direct bilayer lipid modifications. In summary, our data provide insights into the VAP-mediated regulation of endosomal tethers and its impact on the cytoskeleton, revealing a complex interplay between ER-endosome interactions and cytoskeletal organization.

title: Anaphase-Promoting Complex/Cyclosome–Dependent Proteolysis of Human Cyclin a Starts at the Beginning of Mitosis and Is Not Subject to the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint
text: Cyclin A is a stable protein in the S and G2 phases, but its stability is compromised when cells enter mitosis and it is almost completely degraded before the metaphase to anaphase transition. Microinjection of antibodies against subunits of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) or against human Cdc20 (fizzy) arrested cells at metaphase and stabilized both cyclins A and B1. In contrast to cyclin B1, cyclin A was efficiently polyubiquitylated by Cdc20 or Cdh1-activated APC/C in vitro, and the degradation of cyclin A was not delayed by the spindle assembly checkpoint. On the other hand, the degradation of cyclin B1 was accelerated by inhibition of the spindle assembly checkpoint. These findings suggest that the APC/C is activated as cells enter mitosis and targets cyclin A for degradation immediately, whereas the spindle assembly checkpoint delays the degradation of cyclin B1 until the metaphase to anaphase transition. Notably, the "destruction box" (D-box) of cyclin A is 10-20 residues longer than that of cyclin B. Overexpression of wild-type cyclin A delayed the metaphase to anaphase transition, whereas expression of cyclin A mutants lacking a D-box arrested cells in anaphase.

title: Human T Cell Leukemia Virus Reactivation with Progression of Adult T-Cell Leukemia-Lymphoma
text:
BACKGROUND: Adult T-cell leukemia-lymphoma (ATLL) has a very poor prognosis, even with various treatment regimens. Virus expression is typically low or absent at diagnosis, suggesting that secondary genetic or epigenetic changes play a role in disease pathogenesis.
METHODS AND FINDINGS: In a phase II clinical trial, we investigated the effectiveness of combination chemotherapy followed by antiretroviral therapy in treating ATLL. Nineteen patients were enrolled between 2002 and 2006 at five medical centers and received infusional chemotherapy with etoposide, doxorubicin, and vincristine, daily prednisone, and bolus cyclophosphamide (EPOCH) for two to six cycles until maximal clinical response. After chemotherapy induction, viral RNA expression increased (median fold change 190), and virus replication occurred, coinciding with disease progression. Eleven patients achieved an objective response, with a median duration of response of 13 months, and two complete remissions. However, seven patients were on study for less than one month due to progressive disease or chemotherapy toxicity.
CONCLUSIONS: While EPOCH chemotherapy followed by antiretroviral therapy is an active therapeutic regimen for ATLL, viral reactivation during induction chemotherapy may contribute to treatment failure. Alternative therapies that simultaneously prevent virus expression and are cytocidal for malignant cells are urgently needed in this disease.

title: Montelukast and fluticasone compared with salmeterol and fluticasone in protecting against asthma exacerbation in adults: one year, double blind, randomised, comparative trial.
text:
Objective:
To assess the effectiveness of adding montelukast or salmeterol to inhaled fluticasone propionate in patients whose asthma symptoms are inadequately controlled with fluticasone alone.
Design and Setting:
A 52-week, double-blind, multicenter clinical trial was conducted to compare the efficacy of montelukast versus salmeterol added to inhaled fluticasone propionate in patients with uncontrolled asthma.
Participants:
A total of 1490 patients aged 15-72 years with a history of chronic asthma for over a year, a baseline FEV1 value of 50-90% predicted, and a beta agonist improvement of > or = 12% in FEV1 were enrolled in the study.
Main Outcome Measures:
The primary endpoint was the percentage of patients experiencing at least one asthma exacerbation during the 52-week trial period.
Results:
Compared to the group receiving salmeterol and fluticasone, 20.1% of patients in the montelukast and fluticasone group experienced an asthma exacerbation (P = 0.011), indicating that the addition of montelukast to fluticasone was non-inferior to the addition of salmeterol to fluticasone in controlling asthma exacerbations. Additionally, salmeterol and fluticasone significantly improved FEV1 before a beta agonist was administered and morning peak expiratory flow, whereas FEV1 after a beta agonist was used and improvements in asthma-specific quality of life and nocturnal awakenings were similar between the groups (P < or = 0.001). Montelukast and fluticasone also significantly reduced peripheral blood eosinophil counts compared to salmeterol and fluticasone (P = 0.011). Both treatments were generally well tolerated.
Conclusion:
The addition of montelukast to inhaled fluticasone propionate may provide equivalent clinical control to salmeterol in patients whose asthma symptoms remain uncontrolled by fluticasone alone.

title: Control of assembly and function of glutamate receptors by the amino-terminal domain.
text: The extracellular domains of the ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits, known as amino-terminal domains (ATDs), play a crucial role in regulating a wide range of receptor functions, including subunit assembly, receptor trafficking, channel gating, agonist potency, and allosteric modulation. Different ionotropic glutamate receptor classes and subunits have distinct features, which may be regulated by the ATDs in unique ways. This knowledge has important implications for the targeting of the ATDs for the modulation of glutamatergic signaling, with emerging evidence suggesting that NMDA receptor antagonists that interact with the GluN2B ATD show promise in animal models of ischemia, neuropathic pain, and Parkinson's disease.

title: Fission yeast and other yeasts as emergent models to unravel cellular aging in eukaryotes.
text: In recent years, simple organisms such as yeasts and worms have played a significant role in aging research. Studies conducted in Saccharomyces cerevisiae have helped elucidate numerous molecular mechanisms underlying cellular aging and uncovered novel longevity genes. These genes have proven to be conserved across multicellular eukaryotes, leading to the extension of these discovery approaches to other yeast models, including Schizosaccharomyces pombe, Candida albicans, Kluyveromyces lactis, and Cryptococcus neoformans. In fission yeast, researchers have identified links between asymmetrical cell division and nutrient signaling pathways with aging. This review aims to summarize the current knowledge on the mechanisms controlling both replicative and chronological aging in S. pombe and other emerging yeast models.

title: Centrifugal elutriation as a method for isolation of large numbers of functionally intact human peripheral blood monocytes.
text: Centrifugal elutriation was employed to isolate human peripheral blood monocytes (HPBM) from mononuclear cells collected as a secondary component after platelet concentration. HPBM were obtained in two populations: total HPBM and small/large monocytes (SM/LM). The elutriation process was carried out at 3,500 rpm in Ca++- and Mg++-free PBS without EDTA. Average recovery of 5.05 x 10^8 HPBM was achieved with a purity of 95% +/- 3%. SM and LM populations were isolated by splitting the total HPBM into two equal populations, with purities of 92% +/- 3% and 93% +/- 3%, respectively, based on nonspecific esterase staining. The elutriation media did not affect viability as determined by trypan blue exclusion. All three HPBM populations were histochemically and functionally purified from the lymphocyte population, as demonstrated by lack of reactivity to leu-1 and leu-7 and depletion of NK cell activity. HPBM populations were enriched in HLA-Dr, OKM-1, OKM-5, MY-8, and leu M-3 monoclonal antibody marker staining. There were no differences in percent positive cells between SM and LM populations for any of the monocyte-specific monoclonal antibodies. All three populations demonstrated antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity against human red blood cells, with LM exhibiting greater lysis (27.0% +/- 5%) than SM (7% +/- 3%).

title: Asthma in United States Olympic athletes who participated in the 1996 Summer Games.
text:
The prevalence of asthma among highly competitive athletes appears to be increasing, according to a study conducted on United States Olympic athletes at the 1996 Summer Olympic Games in Atlanta. The study analyzed responses to a medical history questionnaire completed by 699 athletes and found that:


15.3% of athletes had a previous diagnosis of asthma, and 13.9% recorded use of an asthma medication.
One hundred seventeen (16.7%) reported use of an asthma medication, a diagnosis of asthma, or both, which was used as the basis for the diagnosis of asthma.
Seventy-three (10.4%) of the athletes were currently taking an asthma medication at the time they were processed in Atlanta or noted that they took asthma medications on a permanent or semipermanent basis and were considered to have active asthma.
The study found that athletes who participated in cycling and mountain biking had the highest prevalence of having been told they had asthma or had taken an asthma medication in the past (50%). The frequency of active asthma varied from 45% of cyclists and mountain bikers to none of the divers and weight lifters.
Compared to athletes who participated in the 1984 Summer Olympic Games, more than 11% of the athletes who participated in the 1996 Olympic Games might have been considered to have had asthma based on less restrictive criteria.
The study suggests that asthma may influence the sport that an athlete chooses and concludes that asthma appeared to be more prevalent in athletes who participated in the 1996 Summer Games than in the general population or in those who participated in the 1984 Summer Games.

title: Relapse specific mutations in NT5C2 in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia
text:
Original Text:
The poor prognosis of relapsed childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) stemmed from its intrinsic resistance to treatment, despite intensive retreatment. The underlying mechanisms were unknown. By analyzing the transcriptome profiles of bone marrow specimens from ten individuals with pediatric B-lymphoblastic leukemia using RNA sequencing, we identified 20 newly acquired, novel nonsynonymous mutations not present at initial diagnosis. Two individuals had relapse-specific mutations in the same gene, NT5C2, which encodes a 5'-nucleotidase. Full-exon sequencing of NT5C2 was conducted in 61 additional relapse specimens, revealing additional mutations in five cases. Enzymatic analysis of mutant proteins showed that base substitutions conferred increased enzymatic activity and resistance to treatment with nucleoside analog therapies. Interestingly, all individuals who harbored NT5C2 mutations relapsed early, within 36 months of initial diagnosis (P = 0.03). These findings suggest that mutations in NT5C2 are associated with the outgrowth of drug-resistant clones in ALL.

title: Relationship between Sloan-Kettering virus expression and mouse follicular development
text: Sloan-Kettering virus gene product (Ski) is a unique nuclear oncoprotein that belongs to the ski/sno proto-oncogene family. Ski exhibits multiple functions across various cell types, including the ability to induce both oncogenic transformation and terminal muscle differentiation when expressed at high levels. As important transcription regulators of the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) superfamily, Ski/SnoN typically form heterodimers and are crucial for the regulation of follicle development. Previous studies have established the importance of SnoN in follicle development, prompting this investigation to elucidate the relationship between Ski expression and mouse follicular development in ovaries of neonatal and gonadotropin-induced immature mice. Utilizing immunohistochemical and real-time PCR techniques, the study observed high levels of Ski protein expression in oocyte nuclei at postnatal day 1. As follicular development advances, the localization of Ski shifts from oocyte nuclei to the perinuclear space, and its total levels decrease. During the estrous cycle, Ski expression is evident at proestrus and estrus, with a slight decrease at metestrus and a marked increase at diestrus. Following gonadotropin injection, Ski is detected in the perinuclear space and displays a lower level of expression in oocyte nuclei. Once the follicle undergoes luteinization, Ski is found in the corpus luteum. Real-time PCR results also revealed that Ski mRNA expression is inversely correlated with ovulation-related genes during cumulus expansion, and its expression levels significantly decrease as the follicles mature. Ski is expressed in a specific manner throughout follicle development, ovulation, and luteinization, indicating that it plays crucial roles in these processes, particularly during the early stages of follicular development.

title: Involvement of CB1 cannabinoid receptors in emotional behaviour
text: Rationale: Endogenous and exogenous cannabinoids interacting with the CB1 receptor are linked to the regulation of a variety of behavioral and neuroendocrine functions, including emotional responses and learning and memory processes. Recently, mice lacking the CB1 receptor have been genetically engineered, providing a valuable tool to investigate the endogenous cannabinoid system's neurophysiology. Objectives: To delve into the role of the CB1 receptor in specific emotional behaviors, such as aggression, anxiety, depression, and learning, using CB1 knockout mice. Methods: We analyzed the spontaneous behaviors of CB1 knockout mice and wild-type controls under different behavioral paradigms, including the light/dark box, chronic unpredictable mild stress, resident–intruder test, and active avoidance task. Results: Our findings revealed that CB1 knockout mice exhibited increased aggression in the resident–intruder test and an anxiogenic response in the light/dark box. Additionally, these mice showed increased sensitivity to depressive-like responses in the chronic unpredictable mild stress procedure, indicating an increased vulnerability to develop an anhedonic state. Finally, CB1 knockout mice displayed enhanced conditioned responses in the active avoidance task, suggesting improved learning and memory processes. Conclusions: Together, these findings suggest that endogenous cannabinoids acting through the CB1 receptor are involved in regulating emotional behavior and play a role in the physiological processes underlying learning and memory.

title: Exosomal levels of miRNA-21 from cerebrospinal fluids associated with poor prognosis and tumor recurrence of glioma patients
text: Glioma, the most common type of primary brain tumors, is known to utilize extracellular vesicles, such as exosomes, to facilitate cell-cell communication by transporting cell-derived proteins and nucleic acids, including microRNAs (miRNAs). In this study, we examined the levels of cancer-related miRNAs in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with recurrent glioma and compared them to levels in serum and exosomes. We found that the levels of exosomal miR-21 in the CSF of glioma patients were significantly higher than in non-tumor control groups, such as brain trauma patients. Additionally, we discovered that CSF-derived exosomal miR-21 levels correlated with tumor spinal/ventricle metastasis and recurrence with anatomical site preference. Furthermore, we found that miR-21 levels were associated with tumor grade of diagnosis and negatively correlated with the median values of patient overall survival time. To further investigate the role of miR-21 in glioma, we suppressed its expression in U251 cells using a lentiviral inhibitor and observed up-regulation of its target genes, PTEN, RECK, and PDCD4, at the protein level. Based on our findings, we conclude that exosomal miR-21 levels could serve as a promising indicator for glioma diagnosis and prognosis, particularly in predicting tumor recurrence or metastasis.

title: Age‐associated microRNA expression in human peripheral blood is associated with all‐cause mortality and age‐related traits
text: Recent studies have provided evidence of the relationship between DNA methylation and the expression of protein-coding genes and human aging. However, the connection between microRNA expression and age and age-related clinical outcomes has not been thoroughly investigated. To address this gap, we analyzed the expression of 127 microRNAs in whole blood from 5221 adults and found that the majority of microRNAs were underexpressed in older individuals. Our integration of microRNA and mRNA expression data revealed age-associated changes in mRNA expression possibly driven by age-associated microRNAs in pathways involving RNA processing, translation, and immune function. We developed a linear model predicting microRNA age based on the expression levels of 80 microRNAs and found that microRNA age correlated modestly with predicted age based on DNA methylation and mRNA expression. We used the difference between microRNA age and chronological age as a biomarker of accelerated aging and found that it was associated with all-cause mortality, coronary heart disease, hypertension, blood pressure, and glucose levels. Based on these findings, we constructed a microRNA age prediction model that could potentially detect accelerated aging and predict risks for age-related diseases.

title: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
text:
AIMS: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) is clinically and pathologically diverse. Despite associations with genetic mutations in MAPT, GRN, and C9ORF72, the underlying mechanisms of non-genetic FTLD remain unclear. Epigenetic modulators, such as histone deacetylases (HDACs), may contribute to the dysregulation of transcriptional activity, which is thought to underlie the neurodegenerative process.
METHODS: We examined the distribution and intensity of HDACs 4, 5, and 6 in immunostained sections of temporal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum from 33 pathologically confirmed cases of FTLD and 27 controls.
RESULTS: We found increased cytoplasmic immunostaining for HDAC4 and HDAC6 in granule cells of the dentate gyrus in FTLD cases overall, and specifically in cases with tau-Pick pathology compared to tau-MAPT and controls. No differences were observed between different FTLD subtypes or between genetic and non-genetic forms of FTLD. HDAC5 immunostaining did not change in any FTLD or control cases.
CONCLUSIONS: Dysregulation of HDAC4 and HDAC6 may contribute to the pathogenesis of FTLD-tau associated with Pick bodies, although the lack of HDAC5 immunostaining suggests that these changes do not directly contribute to the formation of Pick bodies.

title: Evolution and Impact of Subclonal Mutations in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
text: Clonal evolution is a crucial aspect of cancer progression and relapse. In a study of 149 chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) cases, we integrated whole-exome sequencing and copy number analysis to identify the fraction of cancer cells harboring specific somatic mutations. We found that driver mutations were primarily clonal (such as MYD88, trisomy 12, and del(13q)) or subclonal (including SF3B1 and TP53), with the latter representing earlier or later events in CLL evolution. Using samples from 18 patients at two time points, we discovered that 10 of 12 CLL cases treated with chemotherapy underwent clonal evolution, primarily involving subclones with driver mutations (such as SF3B1 and TP53) that expanded over time. Additionally, the presence of a subclonal driver mutation was found to be an independent risk factor for rapid disease progression. Our study uncovered patterns of clonal evolution in CLL, shedding light on its stepwise transformation, and linked the presence of subclones to unfavorable clinical outcomes.

title: The transcriptional program of sporulation in budding yeast
text: During the developmental process of sporulation in budding yeast, diploid cells give rise to haploid cells through a complex series of events known as meiosis and spore morphogenesis. To gain insights into the genetic mechanisms underlying this process, DNA microarrays containing most of the yeast genes were employed to examine changes in gene expression during sporulation. The analysis revealed at least seven distinct temporal patterns of gene induction. One transcription factor, Ndt80, appeared to play a crucial role in the induction of a large group of genes near the end of meiotic prophase. By examining the sequences of coordinately expressed genes, consensus sequences believed to be responsible for temporal regulation could be identified. The temporal expression pattern of these genes provided valuable clues about the potential functions of hundreds of previously uncharacterized genes, some of which have their vertebrate homologs that may be involved in gametogenesis.

title: Grass plants bind, retain, uptake, and transport infectious prions.
text: Prions, the protein-based pathogens responsible for prion diseases, can be transmitted through environmental contamination. In this study, we investigated the binding and retention of infectious prion protein (PrP(Sc)) on plants. We discovered that small amounts of PrP(Sc) in diluted brain homogenate or bodily fluids (urine and feces) can attach to the roots and leaves of wheat grass. Ingesting prion-tainted plants efficiently infected hamsters, indicating that the prion-plant interaction occurs with prions from diverse origins, including chronic wasting disease. Our findings also revealed that spraying prion-containing preparations onto leaves retained infectious proteins for several weeks, and plants can absorb prions from contaminated soil and transport them to their aerial parts (stem and leaves). These results demonstrate that plants can effectively bind and transfer infectious prions, suggesting a potential role of environmental prion contamination in horizontal disease transmission.

title: Innate lymphoid cells mediate influenza-induced airway hyper-reactivity independently of adaptive immunity
text: Individuals with asthma, a significant public health concern, are at a heightened risk of developing serious illness from influenza virus infection, but the specific mechanisms by which influenza A contributes to airway disease and asthma are not fully understood. Using a mouse model, we discovered that influenza infection can cause acute airway hyper-reactivity (AHR), a hallmark of asthma, in the absence of T helper type 2 (TH2) cells and adaptive immunity. Instead, influenza infection activates this response through a previously unidentified pathway that relies on the interleukin 13 (IL-13)–IL-33 axis and a unique population of innate lymphoid cells called 'natural helper cells'. Influenza A virus infection, which activates the NLRP3 inflammasome, leads to a marked increase in IL-33 production by alveolar macrophages, which in turn activates natural helper cells to produce large amounts of IL-13.

title: The behaviour change wheel: A new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions
text:
Improving the design and implementation of evidence-based practices depends on successful behavior change interventions. This requires a valid method for characterizing interventions and linking them to an analysis of the targeted behavior. While various frameworks for behavior change interventions exist, it is unclear how well they serve this purpose. To address this gap, this paper evaluates existing frameworks and develops a new framework that overcomes their limitations.
We conducted a systematic search of electronic databases and consulted with behavior change experts to identify existing frameworks of behavior change interventions. These were evaluated based on three criteria: comprehensiveness, coherence, and a clear link to an overarching model of behavior. A new framework was developed to meet these criteria, which we term the "Behavior Change Wheel" (BCW). The BCW consists of three essential conditions for behavior change: capability, opportunity, and motivation (referred to as the "COM-B system"). These conditions serve as the hub of the BCW, surrounded by nine intervention functions aimed at addressing deficits in one or more of these conditions. Seven policy categories that can enable these interventions are positioned around the BCW.
We tested the reliability of the BCW by applying it to two domains of behavior change: tobacco control and obesity. The BCW proved able to characterize interventions within the English Department of Health's 2010 tobacco control strategy and the National Institute of Health and Clinical Excellence's guidance on reducing obesity.
Interventions and policies aimed at changing behavior can be usefully characterized using the BCW, which consists of a "behavior system" at the hub, surrounded by intervention functions and then by policy categories. While more research is needed to determine how well the BCW can lead to more efficient design of effective interventions, it holds promise for improving the design and implementation of evidence-based practices.

title: Intermittent prophylaxis with oral truvada protects macaques from rectal SHIV infection.
text: HIV continues to spread globally, primarily through sexual contact. Despite advances in treatment and care, preventing transmission through vaccines or microbicides has proven challenging. A potential strategy to avoid transmission is prophylactic treatment with antiretroviral drugs before exposure to HIV. Currently, clinical trials are underway evaluating the efficacy of daily treatment with reverse transcriptase inhibitors such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or Truvada (TDF + emtricitabine). Our hypothesis was that intermittent prophylactic treatment with long-acting antiviral drugs would be as effective as daily dosing in blocking early viral replication and preventing mucosal transmission. To test this, we administered prophylactic Truvada to macaque monkeys and exposed them rectally to simian-human immunodeficiency virus (SHIV) once a week for 14 weeks. We found that a simple regimen of oral Truvada given 1, 3, or 7 days before exposure, followed by a second dose 2 hours after exposure, was as protective as daily drug administration. Additionally, a two-dose regimen initiated 2 hours before or after virus exposure was effective, and doubling the Truvada concentration in both doses provided full protection. Delaying the first dose until 24 hours after exposure showed no protection, highlighting the importance of blocking initial replication in the mucosa. Our results suggest that intermittent prophylactic treatment with an antiviral drug can be highly effective in preventing SHIV infection, with a wide window of protection. These findings strengthen the possibility of developing practical, cost-effective strategies to prevent HIV transmission in humans.

title: RNA is favourable for analysing EGFR mutations in malignant pleural effusion of lung cancer.
text: Malignant pleural effusion (MPE) can be a valuable source for evaluating the EGFR status in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, direct sequencing of genomic DNA from MPE samples is not sensitive for EGFR mutation detection. To determine whether RNA-based EGFR analysis is less prone to interference from non-tumor cells with lower EGFR expression, we compared three methods (RNA-based sequencing versus DNA-based sequencing and mass-spectrometric analysis) in a cohort of 150 lung adenocarcinoma patients receiving first-line tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). We found that EGFR mutations were more frequently identified by RNA-based sequencing than by DNA-based sequencing and mass-spectrometric analysis (67.3% versus 44.7% and 46.7%, respectively). Additionally, RNA-based sequencing was better at predicting the clinical efficacy of first-line TKIs. In patients with acquired resistance, EGFR sequencing from RNA provided satisfactory detection of T790M (54.2%). These results demonstrate that using RNA as a template for EGFR sequencing greatly improves sensitivity for EGFR mutation detection from MPE samples in NSCLC, highlighting RNA as the preferred source for analyzing EGFR mutations from heterogeneous MPE specimens.

title: Pharmacological correction of a defect in PPARγ signaling ameliorates disease severity in Cftr-deficient mice
text: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (Cftr) gene, which disrupts its function as an apical chloride channel that supports bicarbonate transport. Individuals with cystic fibrosis exhibit thickened, retained mucus in their airways and organs, as well as other abnormalities, including inflammation, alterations in lipid metabolism, and insulin resistance. Our study reveals that colonic epithelial cells and whole lung tissue from Cftr-deficient mice are affected in their function of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma (PPAR-gamma), encoded by Pparg. This defect contributes to a maladaptive gene expression program. We found that the endogenous PPAR-gamma ligand, 15-keto-prostaglandin E(2) (15-keto-PGE(2)), is reduced in amount in these cells. Treatment of Cftr-deficient mice with the synthetic PPAR-gamma ligand rosiglitazone partially normalizes the altered gene expression pattern and reduces disease severity. Rosiglitazone has no effect on chloride secretion in the colon but increases expression of genes encoding carbonic anhydrases 4 and 2 (Car4 and Car2), increases bicarbonate secretion, and reduces mucus retention. These findings indicate a reversible defect in PPAR-gamma signaling in Cftr-deficient cells that can be pharmacologically corrected to alleviate the severity of the cystic fibrosis phenotype in mice.

title: Visualization of volatile substances in different organelles with an atmospheric-pressure mass microscope.
text: We have developed a cutting-edge mass microscope (mass spectrometry imager with spatial resolution higher than the naked eye) equipped with a chamber for laser desorption/ionization (AP-LDI) and a quadrupole ion trap time-of-flight (QIT-TOF) analyzer. The optical microscope combined with the mass spectrometer allowed us to precisely identify the specific tissue region before performing imaging mass spectrometry (IMS). A highly focused ultraviolet laser was used to achieve high spatial resolution. The atmospheric pressure ion-source chamber enables analysis of fresh samples with minimal loss of their intrinsic water or volatile compounds. Mass-microscopic AP-LDI imaging of freshly cut ginger rhizome sections revealed the presence of 6-gingerol ([M + K](+) at m/z 333.15, positive mode; [M - H](-) at m/z 293.17, negative mode) and monoterpene ([M + K](+) at m/z 191.09), which are compounds closely related to pungency and flavor, respectively. We applied AP-LDI-tandem MS/MS analyses to compare authentic signals from freshly cut ginger directly with a standard reagent, allowing us to evaluate the quality of plants at the organelle level.

title: Coding of Sweet, Bitter, and Umami Tastes Different Receptor Cells Sharing Similar Signaling Pathways
text: Mammals have the ability to detect a wide range of chemical stimuli through their sense of taste. Two distinct families of receptors, known as T1Rs and T2Rs, are responsible for detecting sweet, amino acids, and bitter compounds. We have discovered that eliminating TRPM5, a taste TRP ion channel, or PLCbeta2, a phospholipase C specifically expressed in taste tissue, completely abolishes the ability to detect sweet, amino acid, and bitter flavors, but does not affect sour or salty tastes. This suggests that although the receptors involved in detecting these flavors are different, they all converge on the same signaling molecules. Using taste-blind animals, we next explored how the different taste modalities are represented at the cellular level. We found that mice engineered to restore function to PLCbeta2 in bitter receptor-expressing cells are able to detect bitter flavors normally, but do not perceive sweet or amino acid stimuli. This suggests that the encoding of bitter flavors is independent of sweet and amino acids, and that taste receptor cells are not broadly tuned across these modalities.

title: Green synthesis of silver nanoparticles and characterization of their inhibitory effects on AGEs formation using biophysical techniques
text: Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) resulting from non-enzymatic glycation are a key factor in the secondary complications of diabetes. Researchers are currently exploring new compounds that could potentially inhibit AGEs formation without altering the normal structure and function of biomolecules. Several natural and synthetic compounds have been proposed as AGE inhibitors. In this study, we investigated the inhibitory effects of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) on AGEs formation. AgNPs (average size of 30.5 nm) synthesized from Aloe Vera leaf extract were characterized using UV-Vis spectroscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and dynamic light scattering (DLS) techniques. We evaluated the inhibitory effects of AgNPs on AGEs formation by measuring the degree of reactivity of free amino groups (lysine and arginine residues), protein-bound carbonyl and carboxymethyl lysine (CML) content, and the impact on protein structure using various physicochemical techniques. Our results showed that AgNPs significantly inhibit AGEs formation in a concentration-dependent manner and have a positive effect on protein structure. These findings strongly suggest that AgNPs may have a therapeutic role in diabetes-related complications.

title: Myosin Light Chain–activating Phosphorylation Sites Are Required for Oogenesis in Drosophila
text: The Drosophila sqh gene encodes the regulatory myosin light chain (RMLC) of nonmuscle myosin II. Biochemical analysis of vertebrate nonmuscle and smooth muscle myosin II has revealed that phosphorylation of specific amino acids in the RMLC significantly enhances the actin-dependent myosin ATPase and motor activity in vitro. To investigate the in vivo importance of these sites in Drosophila, we created transgenes that modified these amino acids and examined their phenotypes in an sqh null mutant background during oocyte development in female Drosophila. Germ line cystoblasts completely lacking the sqh gene exhibit severe defects in proliferation and cytokinesis, with abnormal ring canals and accumulation of myosin heavy chain aggregates. In contrast, transgenes sqh -A20 and sqh -A21, in which both serine-21 and threonine-20 are replaced by alanines, behave similarly to the null allele, with no heavy chain aggregates observed. In contrast, expression of sqh -A21, which only alters the primary phosphorylation target serine-21 site, partially restores functionality to germ line myosin II, allowing cystoblast division and oocyte development, although with some cytokinesis failure, defects in rapid cytoplasmic transport from nurse cells to cytoplasm, and some damaged ring canals. Substituting a glutamate for serine-21 (mutant sqh -E21) allows oogenesis to be completed with minimal defects, producing eggs that can develop normally to produce fertile adults. In contrast, flies expressing sqh -A20, in which only the secondary phosphorylation site is absent, appear to be entirely wild type. These genetic findings suggest that phosphorylation at serine-21 is critical for RMLC function in vivo, but the function can be partially provided by phosphorylation at threonine-20.

title: Stages of the pathologic process in Alzheimer disease: age categories from 1 to 100 years.
text:
A comprehensive analysis of 2,332 non-selected brains from individuals aged 1 to 100 years revealed intriguing insights into the progression of tauopathy associated with sporadic Alzheimer's disease (AD). Using immunocytochemistry (AT8) and Gallyas silver staining, 342 cases were found to be negative in the Gallyas stain, but only 10 were immunonegative when re-evaluated with AT8. Notably, 58 cases displayed subcortical tau predominantly in the locus coeruleus, with no detectable cortical tau (subcortical Stages a-c).
Cortical involvement (abnormal tau in neurites) was first identified in the transentorhinal region (Stage 1a, 38 cases), followed by the appearance of pretangle material (Stage 1b, 236 cases). Pretangles gradually transformed into argyrophilic neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) that progressed in parallel with NFT Stages I to VI. Pretangles were predominantly found in subcortical regions in younger individuals (chiefly before age 40). Of the total cases, 1,031 (44.2%) exhibited β-amyloid plaques. Intriguingly, the first plaques appeared in the neocortex after the onset of tauopathy in the brainstem. Plaques generally developed in the 40s in 4% of all cases, culminating in their tenth decade (75%). β-amyloid plaques and NFTs were found to be significantly correlated (p < 0.0001).
These findings suggest that tauopathy associated with sporadic AD may initiate earlier than previously thought, potentially in the lower brainstem instead of the transentorhinal region.

title: Coronary bypass graft patency in patients with diabetes in the Bypass Angioplasty Revascularization Investigation (BARI).
text:
Scarce research has examined the long-term fate of bypass grafts between patients with and without diabetes, leaving uncertainty about whether diabetes inherently predicts poor clinical outcome after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).
METHODS
Among 1526 patients in the Bari study who underwent CABG as their initial revascularization procedure, 99 of 292 (34%) with treated diabetes mellitus (TDM) (those on insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents) and 469 of 1234 (38%) without TDM had follow-up angiography. Angiograms obtained at the longest interval from initial surgery and before any percutaneous graft intervention (average 3.9 years) were evaluated. On average, 3.0 grafts were placed during initial CABG for patients with TDM (n=297; internal mammary artery [IMA], 33%) and 2.9 grafts for patients without TDM (n=1347; IMA, 34%). Patients with TDM were more likely than those without to have small (<1.5 mm) grafted distal vessels (29% vs. 22%) and vessels of poorer quality (9% vs. 6%).
ON FOLLOW-UP ANGIOGRAPHY, 89% of IMA grafts were free of stenoses > or =50% among patients with TDM versus 85% among patients without TDM (P=0.23). Similarly, for vein grafts, the corresponding percentages were 71% versus 75% (P=0.40). After adjusting for confounding variables, TDM was unrelated to having a graft stenosis > or =50% (adjusted odds ratio, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.58 to 1.32).
CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, our findings indicate that diabetes does not adversely affect the patency of internal mammary artery (IMA) or vein grafts over an average 4-year follow-up period. Previous differences in survival between CABG-treated patients with and without diabetes may be primarily due to differential risk of mortality from non-cardiac causes rather than poor graft patency.

title: A novel ATAC-seq approach reveals lineage-specific reinforcement of the open chromatin landscape via cooperation between BAF and p63
text:
Background: Open chromatin regions are closely linked with active regulatory elements during development and are often disrupted in diseases. The BAF (SWI/SNF) complex, which has been shown to play a crucial role in development, can remodel chromatin structure in vitro and control access to a limited number of regions in vivo. However, the underlying mechanisms by which BAF regulates the open chromatin landscape to control developmental processes, such as human epidermal differentiation, remain unclear.
Results: By employing a novel "on-plate" ATAC-sequencing approach that profiles open chromatin landscapes with minimal adherent cells, we discover that the BAF complex is essential for maintaining approximately 11.6% of open chromatin regions in epidermal differentiation. These BAF-dependent regions are highly cell type-specific and are enriched for binding sites for p63, a master transcription factor crucial for epidermal cell differentiation. Intriguingly, the DNA sequences near p63 binding sites are more likely to undergo nucleosome formation and are inaccessible in other cell types without p63, precluding unwanted activation. In epidermal cells, BAF and p63 cooperate to maintain 14,853 open chromatin regions, and BAF and p63 work together to position nucleosomes away from p63 binding sites and recruit transcriptional machinery to regulate cell fate determination.
Conclusions: Our study demonstrates that BAF displays remarkable specificity in regulating the open chromatin landscape during epidermal differentiation by cooperating with the p63 transcription factor to maintain lineage-specific open chromatin regions. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying developmental processes and inform strategies to direct cell fate decisions in disease contexts.

title: Aging, habitual exercise, and dynamic arterial compliance.
text:
Older adults experience a reduction in the flexibility of large arteries in the chest and heart area, which is an independent risk factor for developing heart disease. Researchers wanted to determine the effectiveness of regular exercise in improving this condition.
The study consisted of two parts. In the first part, researchers compared the flexibility of arteries in 151 healthy men aged 18 to 77 years. They found that flexibility decreased with age, regardless of how active the men were. However, men who were more active in their younger years had higher flexibility in their arteries than those who were less active.
In the second part of the study, researchers looked at the effects of exercise on flexibility in 20 middle-aged and older sedentary men. They found that a 3-month exercise program, which primarily consisted of walking, significantly improved flexibility in the arteries. Importantly, these changes were independent of other factors such as weight loss, blood pressure, or oxygen consumption.
Overall, the study suggests that regular aerobic exercise can help restore flexibility in the arteries of middle-aged and older adults, which may help lower the risk of heart disease.

title: A comparison of cancer screening practices in cancer survivors and in the general population: the Korean national health and nutrition examination survey (KNHANES) 2001–2007
text: This study aimed to investigate cancer screening rates among cancer survivors in Korea and to compare these rates to those of two control groups: individuals with other chronic diseases but no history of cancer, and individuals without any chronic diseases or cancer history. The study analyzed data from 15,556 adults aged ≥30 years who participated in the 2001, 2005, and 2007 Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys (KNHANES). The study assessed cancer screening rates according to national guidelines for breast, cervical, gastric, and colorectal cancer and compared them to the two control groups. Cancer survivors had higher screening rates for all four cancer sites compared to the control groups, but the difference was only statistically significant for breast cancer after adjusting for gender, age, marital status, education, income, working status, health insurance, smoking, and drinking status, and self-reported health status. Despite this, screening rates among cancer survivors were still suboptimal, emphasizing the need for more comprehensive strategies to address second primary cancer screening and prevention.

title: Negative effect of the transcriptional activator GAL4
text: The yeast transcriptional activator GAL4 binds specific sites on DNA to activate the transcription of adjacent genes, with its distinct activating regions rich in acidic residues. It has been proposed that these regions interact with other protein components of the transcriptional machinery, such as the TATA-binding protein or RNA polymerase II, while the DNA-binding region positions the activating region near the target gene. Our studies demonstrate that various GAL4 derivatives, when overexpressed in yeast, inhibit the transcription of genes lacking GAL4 binding sites. More efficient activators inhibit more strongly, and inhibition does not depend on the DNA-binding domain. We propose that this inhibition, which we call "squelching," reflects a titration of the transcription factor GAL4 by its own activating region.

title: The Bayh–Dole Act and university research and development
text: The present study investigates the connection between university research and development (R&D) endeavors and the Bayh-Dole Act. This legislation considerably simplified the process of universities securing patents from research funded by the federal government, potentially serving as an incentive for universities to alter their R&D activities. The Act may prompt universities to divert resources away from basic research (which does not generate licensing fees) and redirect them towards applied research (which generates patents and licensing fees). Moreover, industry may be more inclined to fund university R&D projects due to the increased ease of patenting the results. Unlike existing literature which relies on patent data (a measure of research output), this study employs research and development data (a measure of inventive input) to examine the impact of the Act.

title: The relation between past exposure to fine particulate air pollution and prevalent anxiety: observational cohort study
text:
Objective: To determine whether higher past exposure to particulate air pollution is associated with an increased prevalence of high symptoms of anxiety among women.
Design: Observational cohort study.
Setting: Nurses' Health Study.
Participants: 71,271 women residing throughout the contiguous United States who had valid estimates of exposure to particulate matter and data on anxiety symptoms.
Main Outcome Measures: Meaningfully high symptoms of anxiety, defined as a score of 6 points or greater on the phobic anxiety subscale of the Crown-Crisp index, administered in 2004.
Results: Of the 71,271 eligible women, 15% had high anxiety symptoms. Exposure to particulate matter was characterized using estimated average exposure to PM2.5 (<2.5 μm in diameter) and PM2.5-10 (2.5 to 10 μm in diameter) in the one month, three months, six months, one year, and 15 years prior to assessment of anxiety symptoms. Significantly increased odds of high anxiety symptoms were observed with higher exposure to PM2.5 for multiple averaging periods, with the highest odds ratio observed for exposure in the prior one month (odds ratio per 10 µg/m(3) increase: 1.12, 95% confidence interval 1.06 to 1.19). Models including multiple exposure windows suggested that short-term averaging periods were more relevant than long-term averaging periods. No association was found between anxiety and exposure to PM2.5-10, and residential proximity to major roads was not related to anxiety symptoms in a dose-dependent manner.
Conclusions: Exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) was associated with high symptoms of anxiety, with more recent exposures potentially more relevant than more distant exposures. Reducing exposure to ambient PM2.5 may reduce the population-level burden of clinically relevant symptoms of anxiety.

title: A mitochondrially targeted compound delays aging in yeast through a mechanism linking mitochondrial membrane lipid metabolism to mitochondrial redox biology☆
text: A recent study uncovered a natural mechanism for slowing down aging in yeast through the use of a specific compound that targets mitochondrial redox processes. This compound, lithocholic bile acid, enters yeast cells, primarily accumulates in the inner mitochondrial membrane, and triggers an age-related remodeling of phospholipid synthesis and movement within both mitochondrial membranes. As yeast cells age, this remodeling of mitochondrial phospholipid dynamics leads to significant changes in the composition of mitochondrial membrane phospholipids, which in turn alters mitochondrial abundance and morphology. These changes have a profound impact on mitochondrial respiration, the maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential, the balance of mitochondrially produced reactive oxygen species, and the coupling of electron transport to ATP synthesis, all of which are critical components of cellular longevity.

title: Isolation from African Sykes' monkeys (Cercopithecus mitis) of a lentivirus related to human and simian immunodeficiency viruses.
text: An analysis of serum samples from 100 wild-caught or colony-born Sykes' monkeys (Cercopithecus mitis) in Kenya revealed that 59 animals had antibodies cross-reactive to human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) and to simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs). When researchers isolated viruses from five of six seropositive, asymptomatic Sykes' monkeys, they found a lentivirus designated SIVsyk. The virus shared similarities with other SIVs and HIVs in terms of its morphology, reverse transcriptase enzyme, and ability to replicate in and be cytopathic for certain cell lines. However, SIVsyk differed from other SIVs in that it failed to replicate in normal human, mangabey, and macaque peripheral blood mononuclear cells and serum from seropositive Sykes' monkeys, and immunoprecipitated env antigens from HIV-1 as well as from HIV-2, SIVsmm, and SIVagm. These findings indicate a high prevalence of natural infection in Sykes' monkeys in Kenya with a unique lentivirus that may have a limited host range and antigenic cross-reactivity.

title: Role of the Single-Stranded DNA–Binding Protein SsbB in Pneumococcal Transformation: Maintenance of a Reservoir for Genetic Plasticity
text: Bacteria house a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein (SSB) that plays a crucial role in genome maintenance. In Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae, an alternative SSB, SsbB, is specifically expressed during periods of competence for genetic transformation, although its exact function has been enigmatically unclear. To investigate SsbB's role, we compared a null mutant (ssbB(-)) and a C-ter truncation (ssbBΔ7) of SsbB in S. pneumoniae, the latter constructed because SSBs' acidic tail has emerged as a key site for interactions with partner proteins. Our findings indicate that SsbB directly protects internalized ssDNA, with abundant SsbB potentially binding up to 1.15 megabases (half a genome equivalent) of ssDNA. We also show that SsbB contributes to the processing of ssDNA into recombinants and is essential for chromosomal transformation at high DNA concentrations, while inhibiting plasmid transformation. Interestingly, the latter observation explains a long-standing observation that plasmid transformation is very inefficient in S. pneumoniae compared to chromosomal transformation, while the former supports our previous suggestion that SsbB creates a reservoir of ssDNA, allowing successive recombination cycles. Notably, the SsbBΔ7 mutant still maintains the reservoir function, suggesting that the C-terminal region of SsbB is not required for processing protein(s) to access stored ssDNA. Based on our findings, we propose that the evolutionary purpose of SsbB and its abundance is to maintain this reservoir, which enhances the genetic plasticity of S. pneumoniae by increasing the likelihood of multiple transformation events in the same cell.

title: Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly
text: The intricate nature of the human brain has presented a challenge for studying various brain disorders in non-human models, necessitating the development of an in vitro system for human brain development. Our group has established a three-dimensional organoid culture system, termed cerebral organoids, derived from human pluripotent stem cells. These organoids differentiate into distinct brain regions, including a cerebral cortex housing progenitor populations that organize and produce mature cortical neuron subtypes. Moreover, cerebral organoids mimic the features of human cortical development, such as characteristic progenitor zone organization and the presence of outer radial glial stem cells. To further elucidate the potential of these organoids, we employed RNA interference and patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells to model microcephaly, a condition that has proven difficult to recapitulate in mouse models. Our findings demonstrate premature neuronal differentiation in patient organoids, a defect that may contribute to the disease phenotype. Collectively, these results demonstrate the ability of three-dimensional organoids to recapitulate both developmental processes and disease mechanisms in the most complex human tissue.

title: Localization of a gene for partial epilepsy to chromosome 10q
text: There is compelling evidence for a genetic component to epilepsy, yet it is generally assumed that this genetic contribution only applies to 'generalized' epilepsies, with most 'partial' forms being non-genetic. In a familial linkage analysis of a single family consisting of 11 affected individuals, we uncovered strong evidence for the localization of a gene responsible for partial epilepsy. This susceptibility gene maps to chromosome 10q, with a maximum two-point lod score of 3.99 at θ=0.0. All affected individuals share a single haplotype for seven tightly linked contiguous markers, with a maximum lod score of 4.83 at θ=0.0. Further analysis placed the susceptibility locus within a 10 centimorgan interval.

title: Metastatic colonization requires the repression of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition inducer Prrx1.
text: The epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) plays a crucial role in embryonic development, allowing for the formation of tissues from distant cell sources. However, the process of EMT is also exploited by cancer cells for metastasis. Although the relevance of EMT in cancer is still debated, our findings suggest that the homeobox factor Prrx1 plays a pivotal role in cancer metastasis. We demonstrate that Prrx1 is an EMT inducer that confers migratory and invasive properties on cancer cells. The loss of Prrx1 function is necessary for cancer cells to metastasize in vivo, and the acquisition of Prrx1 expression is associated with the reversal of EMT and the gain of stem cell properties. Unlike traditional EMT transcription factors, Prrx1 uncouples EMT and stemness, making it a potential biomarker for patient survival and lack of metastasis.

title: A cohort study of the risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 in relation to papillomavirus infection.
text:
Background: Human papillomavirus (HPV) has been linked to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), but the exact timing of the infection and the development of CIN is not fully understood. Additionally, the relative importance of specific HPV types, other sexually transmitted diseases, and other risk factors is unclear.
Methods: We conducted a prospective study of 241 women who presented for evaluation of sexually transmitted diseases and had negative cervical cytology tests. The women were followed every four months with cytology and colposcopy examinations of the uterine cervix and tests for HPV DNA and other sexually transmitted diseases.
Results: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 was confirmed by biopsy in 28 women. Using survival analysis, the cumulative incidence of CIN at two years was 28% among women with a positive HPV test and 3% among those without detectable HPV DNA. The risk was highest among those with HPV type 16 or 18 infection (adjusted relative risk compared to those without HPV infection: 11; 95% confidence interval: 4.6-26; attributable risk: 52%). All 24 cases of CIN grade 2 or 3 among HPV-positive women were detected within 24 months after the first positive HPV test. After adjusting for HPV infection, the development of CIN was also associated with younger age at first intercourse, the presence of serum antibodies to Chlamydia trachomatis, the presence of serum antibodies to cytomegalovirus, and cervical infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Conclusions: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia is a common and likely early manifestation of cervical infection by HPV, particularly types 16 and 18. The findings highlight the importance of HPV testing in the management of cervical disease.

title: Investigating survival prognosis of glioblastoma using evolutional properties of gene networks
text: In recent years, there has been a surge of interest and numerous publications on applying graph theory techniques to construct and analyze biologically-informed gene networks from cancer cell line data sets. Most of these studies have focused on representing the network topologically and have not investigated the application of graph theoretical methods to evolutionary investigations of cancer. A number of these studies have used graph theory metrics, such as degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality, to identify important hub genes in these networks. However, these studies have not fully explored the importance of genes throughout the different stages of the disease. Previous publications on human glioblastoma have identified four subtypes of glioblastoma in adults based on signature genes. For example, Verhaak et al. found that the subtypes correspond to a narrow median survival range, from 11.3 months for the most aggressive subtype to 13.1 months for the least aggressive one. In this work, we present an evolutionary graph theory study of glioblastoma based on survival data categorization, confirming genes associated with different survival times identified using established graph theory metrics. Our study extends the application of graph theoretical approaches to evolutionary studies of cancer cell line data.

title: Compound heterozygous ZMPSTE24 mutations reduce prelamin A processing and result in a severe progeroid phenotype.
text: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS; OMIM 176670) is a rare and devastating disorder that mimics premature aging in affected children. Typically, these children appear normal at birth but develop failure to thrive within the first two years of life. Additional features may include alopecia, micrognathia, loss of subcutaneous fat with prominent veins, abnormal dentition, sclerodermatous skin changes, and osteolysis of the clavicles and distal phalanges. The mean age of death is typically at age 13 years, often due to atherosclerosis. HGPS is primarily sporadic in occurrence, but a genetic cause has been identified through the detection of de novo heterozygous mutations in the LMNA gene in the majority of HGPS patients. In addition, a family showing autosomal recessive inheritance of homozygous LMNA mutations has been reported. The LMNA gene encodes lamins A and C, which are components of the nuclear lamina, a meshwork underlying the nuclear envelope that provides structural support and is also involved in chromatin organization and gene expression. Recent studies have linked mutations in LMNA to at least eight inherited disorders, known as laminopathies, which affect various tissues including muscle, neurons, skin, bone, and adipose tissue. Notably, these disorders share common genetic defects, leading to reevaluation of their clinical presentation and the recognition of significant phenotypic overlap. HGPS exhibits phenotypic similarities to other laminopathies, such as atypical Werner's syndrome and mandibuloacral dysplasia. These diseases are characterized by lipodystrophy, which is a prominent feature of another laminopathy, familial partial lipodystrophy of the Dunnigan variety. Mandibuloacral dysplasia has been further classified into two subtypes.

title: Reliability of patient responses in pay for performance schemes: analysis of national General Practitioner Patient Survey data in England
text: The objective of this study was to evaluate the robustness of patient responses to a national survey of patient experience as a basis for providing financial incentives to doctors. The design of the study involved analyzing the representativeness of the respondents compared to the general population and comparing practice response rates to questionnaire scores. The results showed that the overall response rate was 38.2% (2.2 million responses), which is comparable to other surveys using similar methodology in the UK. However, men, young adults, and people living in deprived areas were underrepresented among respondents. When examining the reliability of the survey, two questions that triggered payments to general practitioners were found to be reliable measures of practice performance, with average practice-level reliability coefficients of 93.2% and 95.0%. Furthermore, less than 3% and 0.5% of practices had fewer than the required number of responses to achieve conventional reliability levels of 90% and 70%, respectively. Lastly, the study found that a change to the payment formula in 2009 resulted in an increase in the average impact of random variation in patient scores on payments to general practitioners compared to payments made in 2007 and 2008. Overall, the study suggests that there is little evidence to support the concern that low response rates and selective non-response bias have led to systematic unfairness in payments attached to questionnaire scores. However, the study raises important issues regarding the validity and reliability of payments based on patient surveys and provides valuable lessons for the UK and other countries considering the use of patient experience in pay for performance schemes.

title: Impact of low alcohol verbal descriptors on perceived strength: An experimental study
text: The study examines how consumers perceive the strength and appeal of alcohol products when labeled with different verbal descriptors, such as "low," "light," or "reduced." The research employed a within-subjects experimental design, where participants rated the strength and appeal of various terms for either wine or beer, depending on their drinking preferences. The results show that the verbal descriptors form two clusters, with some terms considered lower in strength than others. The study finds that the appeal of alcohol products decreases as the verbal descriptors imply a deviation from the "regular" strength. The findings have policy implications regarding lower strength alcohol labeling and will inform public health outcomes. The study expands on existing knowledge by providing evidence on how consumers perceive verbal descriptors of alcohol product strength and their associated appeal.

title: Transgenic Interleukin 10 Prevents Induction of Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis
text: The effectiveness of interleukin 10 (IL-10) in treating autoimmune-mediated central nervous system inflammation is debated. Research using the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model, utilizing various IL-10 administration methods and routes, has revealed that these variables may impact IL-10's immunoregulatory function. To investigate these factors' influence on IL-10's regulation of EAE pathogenesis, we analyzed transgenic mice expressing a human IL-10 (hIL-10) gene under the control of a class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) promoter. These mice are highly resistant to EAE induced by active immunization, and this resistance is mediated by the suppression of autoreactive T cell function. In contrast, myelin-reactive T helper 1 cells are induced but remain nonpathogenic in the IL-10 transgenic mice. Antibody depletion confirmed that EAE resistance is dependent on the presence of the transgenic IL-10. Transgenic mice expressing the hIL-10 gene but not the endogenous murine IL-10 gene demonstrated that transgenic IL-10 from MHC class II–expressing cells is sufficient to block induction of EAE. This study shows that IL-10 can completely prevent EAE if present at appropriate levels and times during disease induction.

title: Autosomal dominant immune dysregulation syndrome in humans with CTLA4 mutations
text: The protein cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4) plays a critical role in regulating immune responses, and its dysfunction can lead to autoimmune disorders. In this study, we investigated a large family with a complex, autosomal dominant immune dysregulation syndrome characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia, recurrent infections, and multiple autoimmune features. We identified a heterozygous nonsense mutation in exon 1 of CTLA4 in these individuals. Screening of 71 unrelated patients with similar clinical symptoms revealed five additional families with undescribed splice site and missense mutations in CTLA4. While clinical penetrance was incomplete, we found that CTLA-4 protein expression was reduced in regulatory T cells (Treg cells) in both patients and carriers with CTLA4 mutations. Treg cells were present at elevated numbers, but their suppressive function, CTLA-4 ligand binding, and transendocytosis of CD80 were impaired. Moreover, we observed decreased circulating B cell numbers in these individuals. Our findings suggest that mutations in CTLA4, leading to CTLA-4 haploinsufficiency or impaired ligand binding, disrupt T and B cell homeostasis and contribute to a complex immune dysregulation syndrome.

title: Specific inhibition of cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 by PD 0332991 and associated antitumor activity in human tumor xenografts.
text: PD 0332991 is a highly specific inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (Cdk4/6), with an IC50 value of 0.011 micromol/L and 0.016 micromol/L, respectively, against these enzymes compared to a panel of 36 additional protein kinases. It demonstrates potent antiproliferative activity against Rb-positive tumor cells in vitro, leading to a G1 cell cycle arrest and a concomitant reduction in phospho-Ser780/Ser795 on the Rb protein. Following oral administration to mice bearing Colo-205 human colon carcinoma, PD 0332991 exhibits marked tumor regression. Moreover, therapeutic doses of PD 0332991 eliminate phospho-Rb and the proliferative marker Ki-67 in tumor tissue, as well as down-regulate genes under E2F-mediated transcriptional control. These results suggest that inhibition of Cdk4/6 alone is sufficient to cause tumor regression and a net reduction in tumor burden in some tumors.

title: Neutrophils support lung colonization of metastasis-initiating breast cancer cells
text: Despite progress in developing drugs that target cancer cells, treatments for metastatic tumors often fail. The established dependency of cancer cells on their microenvironment suggests targeting the non-cancer cell component of the tumor may lead to novel therapeutic strategies. However, the poorly characterized contribution of host responses during tumor growth and metastasis represents a limitation. We identify neutrophils as the main component and driver of metastatic establishment within the pre-metastatic lung microenvironment in mouse breast cancer models. Neutrophils play a fundamental role in inflammatory responses, and their contribution to tumorigenesis is controversial. By blocking neutrophil recruitment to the pre-metastatic site, we demonstrate that neutrophils specifically support metastatic initiation. Importantly, we find that neutrophil-derived leukotrienes aid colonization of distant tissues by selectively expanding the sub-pool of cancer cells with high tumorigenic potential. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of the leukotriene-generating enzyme arachidonate 5-lipoxygenase (Alox5) abrogates neutrophil pro-metastatic activity and reduces metastasis. Our results highlight the effectiveness of targeted therapy against a specific tumor microenvironment component and suggest that neutrophil Alox5 inhibition may limit metastatic progression.

title: Effect of Previous Miscarriage on Depressive Symptoms During Subsequent Pregnancy and Postpartum in the First Baby Study
text: Our research aimed to test the hypothesis that nulliparous women with a history of miscarriage are at increased risk of depression during late pregnancy and in the postpartum period, compared to women without such a history. We conducted a secondary analysis of a large longitudinal cohort study, the First Baby Study, and analyzed 448 pregnant women with a history of miscarriage and 2,343 pregnant women without a history of miscarriage. We used logistic regression models and generalized estimating equations to estimate the odds of depression (score >12 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) at various time points. Our findings revealed that while women with a history of miscarriage were not more likely to score in the probable depression range during the third trimester or at 6 or 12 months postpartum, they were more likely to score in this range at 1 month postpartum, after adjusting for sociodemographic factors (odds ratio = 1.66, 95% CI = 1.03-2.69). Specifically, our data suggest that women with a history of miscarriage may be more vulnerable to depression during the first month postpartum, although this effect does not seem to persist beyond this time period. Overall, our findings support the importance of raising awareness regarding this issue and encourage further research to identify potential risk factors for depression among women with a history of miscarriage.

title: IL-1β, IL-4 and IL-12 control the fate of group 2 innate lymphoid cells in human airway inflammation in the lungs
text: Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) secrete type 2 cytokines, which play a protective role against parasitic infections but can also contribute to various inflammatory respiratory diseases. Our study reveals that interleukin 1β (IL-1β) directly activates human ILC2s, while IL-12 triggers the conversion of these activated ILC2s into interferon-γ (IFN-γ)-producing ILC1s, which can be reversed by IL-4. This highlights the plasticity of ILCs, which is evident in diseased tissues of patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). These tissues exhibit signatures of IL-12 or IL-4 and the accumulation of ILC1s or ILC2s, respectively. Moreover, we found that eosinophils, which produce IL-4, exhibit cross-talk with IL-5-producing ILC2s, further underscoring the complex interplay between these cell types. Based on our findings, we propose that IL-12 and IL-4 govern the functional identity of ILC2s and their imbalance leads to the perpetuation of type 1 or type 2 inflammation.

title: Summary
text: Steroid receptor RNA activator (SRA), the sole known RNA coactivator, enhances transactivation by nuclear receptors (NRs). We discovered that SLIRP (SRA stem-loop interacting RNA binding protein), a protein expressed in both normal and tumor tissues, binds to a specific substructure of SRA called STR7. SLIRP possesses an RNA recognition motif (RRM) and represses NR transactivation in a SRA- and RRM-dependent manner. Additionally, SLIRP augments the effect of Tamoxifen and modulates the association of SRC-1 with SRA. SHARP, another RRM-containing corepressor, also binds STR7, further reinforcing repression. Interestingly, SLIRP colocalizes with SKIP (Chr14q24.3), a NR coactivator, and reduces SKIP-mediated NR signaling. Moreover, SLIRP is recruited to endogenous promoters (pS2 and metallothionein), with the latter recruitment being dependent on SLIRP. Notably, most of the endogenous SLIRP is found in the mitochondria. Our results demonstrate that SLIRP regulates NR transactivation, suggest the possibility of its role in mitochondrial function regulation, and provide mechanistic insight into the interactions between SRA, SLIRP, SRC-1, and NCoR.

title: Naringenin inhibits allergen-induced airway inflammation and airway responsiveness and inhibits NF-kappaB activity in a murine model of asthma.
text:
Naringenin, a flavonoid compound, has anti-inflammatory and immune-modulating properties, which were investigated for their potential to attenuate allergen-induced airway inflammation in a mouse model of asthma. In this study, mice were sensitized and challenged with ovalbumin, and some were administered naringenin before the challenge. The study evaluated the development of airway inflammation and airway reactivity, as well as the levels of specific cytokines and chemokines in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and serum.
Naringenin treatment significantly reduced ovalbumin-induced airway inflammation and airway reactivity in experimental mice. It also decreased the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-13 (IL-13), in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and serum. Additionally, naringenin inhibited the degradation of IκBα in the lungs and DNA-binding activity of nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), which are key regulators of inflammation. The levels of chemokines CCL5 and CCL11, as well as the enzyme inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), were also significantly reduced.
The results of this study suggest that naringenin may play a protective role in the development of asthma by inhibiting the inflammatory response and reducing the expression of pro-inflammatory genes. The anti-inflammatory effects of naringenin may be mediated by its ability to inhibit NF-κB and reduce the expression of its target genes, leading to a decrease in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.

title: The evolution of Fox genes and their role in development and disease
