text: The forkhead box (Fox) family of transcription factors, originating from unicellular eukaryotes, has undergone expansion through multiple duplication events and gene loss over time, resulting in over 40 members in mammals. Fox genes have evolved to take on specialized functions in various biological processes, with mutations in these genes having a significant impact on human disease, resulting in phenotypes such as cancer, glaucoma, and language disorders. In this summary, we provide an overview of the evolution of the Fox gene family and highlight the diverse roles of different Fox subfamilies in developmental processes, from organogenesis to speech acquisition.

title: Emergent structures and dynamics of cell colonies by contact inhibition of locomotion
text: Cells within tissues can adopt a wide range of organizational patterns based on their functional demands. Drastic changes in organization, such as epithelial-mesenchymal transitions or spheroidal aggregate formation, are commonly associated with tissue development or cancer progression. To investigate the organization of cell colonies, we employ computer simulations of self-propelled particles with generic cell-like interactions. The interplay between cell softness, cell-cell adhesion, and contact inhibition of locomotion (CIL) leads to various cellular structures and collective dynamics observed in different tissue phenotypes. These include regular spatial distributions of cells, dynamic cell clusters, gel-like networks, collectively migrating monolayers, and 3D aggregates. We provide analytical predictions for transitions between non-cohesive, cohesive, and 3D arrangements. Moreover, we demonstrate how CIL yields an effective repulsion that hinders the formation of cohesive tissues, yet promotes collective cell motion and ensures tensile intercellular stresses in continuous monolayers. Our findings highlight the crucial role of CIL in determining the emergent structures and dynamics of cell colonies.

title: Failure of cell cleavage induces senescence in tetraploid primary cells
text: Tetraploidy can arise from various mitotic or cleavage defects in mammalian cells, leading to aneuploidy when tetraploid cells continue to divide. The arrest of the tetraploid cell cycle is a critical cellular control. Here, we explore the senescence of primary rat embryo fibroblasts (REF52) and human foreskin fibroblasts after drug- or small interfering RNA (siRNA)-induced failure of cell cleavage. In contrast to T-antigen-transformed REF52 and p53+/+ HCT116 tumor cells, which rapidly become aneuploid by continuing to cycle after cleavage failure, tetraploid primary cells quickly become quiescent, as determined by the loss of the Ki-67 proliferation marker and the fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator/late cell cycle marker geminin. The arrest is not due to DNA damage, as the γ-H2AX DNA damage marker remains at control levels after tetraploidy induction. Finally, arrested tetraploid cells become senescent, as determined by SA-β-galactosidase activity. Notably, the tetraploid arrest is dependent on p16INK4a expression, as siRNA suppression of p16INK4a bypasses tetraploid arrest, allowing primary cells to become aneuploid. Therefore, we conclude that tetraploid primary cells can become senescent without DNA damage and that the induction of senescence is essential for tetraploidy arrest.

title: Cell death: the significance of apoptosis.
text: Cell death can be classified based on morphological or biochemical criteria, or on the circumstances surrounding its occurrence. Currently, the only unequivocal evidence of cell death is irreversible structural alteration, although biochemical indicators of cell death are being studied to determine their universality. However, measuring cell function or reproductive capacity does not always differentiate between death and dormant states from which recovery may be possible. Additionally, it has been feasible to categorize dying cells into two distinct patterns of morphological change, which are often associated with different circumstances. One pattern, termed "coagulative necrosis," involves swelling and rupture of cell membranes, leading to the dissolution of organized structure and evoking exudative inflammation. The other pattern, characterized by cell condensation with maintenance of organelle integrity and the formation of surface protuberances that separate as membrane-bounded globules, is phagocytosed and digested by resident cells in tissues, with no associated inflammation.

title: The mitochondrial RNA-binding protein GRSF1 localizes to RNA granules and is required for posttranscriptional mitochondrial gene expression.
text: RNA-binding proteins play a crucial role in posttranscriptional gene regulation, controlling the processing, storage, and handling of cellular RNAs. Our findings reveal that GRSF1, previously implicated in the translation of influenza mRNAs, is targeted to mitochondria, where it forms granules that coincide with foci of newly synthesized mtRNA next to mitochondrial nucleoids. GRSF1 prefers to bind RNAs transcribed from three adjacent genes on the light strand of mtDNA, including the ND6 mRNA and the long noncoding RNAs for cytb and ND5, each of which contains multiple binding sites. By silencing GRSF1 through RNA interference, we found that mitochondrial RNA stability, mRNA and lncRNA loading onto the mitochondrial ribosome, and ribosome assembly are all disrupted, resulting in a specific defect in protein synthesis and a failure to produce normal amounts of oxidative phosphorylation complexes. These results imply that GRSF1 is a central regulator of posttranscriptional mitochondrial gene expression.

title: Identification and purification of a 62,000-dalton protein that binds specifically to the polypyrimidine tract of introns.
text: A protein of molecular size 62,000 daltons (p62) was identified in HeLa cell nuclear extracts through UV cross-linking to mRNA precursors. p62 specifically binds to the polypyrimidine tract of the 3' splice site region of introns. Following purification to homogeneity, p62 binds the polypyrimidine tract of pre-mRNAs without requiring the AG dinucleotide at the 3' splice site. Alterations in the polypyrimidine tract that reduce the binding of p62 result in a corresponding decrease in the efficiency of formation of a U2 snRNP/pre-mRNA complex and splicing. p62 remains bound to the pre-mRNA within the spliceosome, suggesting that it plays a critical role in recognizing the 3' splice site during splicing. The protein is referred to as a polypyrimidine tract binding protein (pPTB).

title: Capsule endoscopy in acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage: a prospective cohort study.
text:
Background and Study Objectives:
Capsule endoscopy may play a crucial role in the assessment of patients experienced with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in the emergency department.
Patients and Methods:
We evaluated adult patients with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in the emergency departments of two academic centers. Patients swallowed a wireless video capsule, immediately followed by a nasogastric tube aspiration, and later by esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). We compared capsule endoscopy with nasogastric tube aspiration for determining the presence of blood and with EGD for identifying peptic/inflammatory lesions, safety, and patient satisfaction.
Results:
The study enrolled 49 patients (32 men and 17 women, mean age 58.3 ± 19 years), but three patients did not complete the capsule endoscopy, and five were intolerant of the nasogastric tube. Blood was detected in the upper gastrointestinal tract significantly more often by capsule endoscopy (15/18, 83.3%) than by nasogastric tube aspiration (6/18, 33.3%; P = 0.035). There was no significant difference in identifying peptic/inflammatory lesions between capsule endoscopy (27/40, 67.5%) and EGD (35/40, 87.5%; P = 0.10, OR = 0.39, 95% CI = 0.11-1.15). Capsule endoscopy reached the duodenum in 45/46 patients (98%). One patient (2.2%) had self-limited shortness of breath, and one (2.2%) had coughing during capsule ingestion.

Conclusions: In an emergency department setting, capsule endoscopy appears feasible and safe for patients presenting with acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Capsule endoscopy identifies gross blood in the upper gastrointestinal tract, including the duodenum, significantly more often than nasogastric tube aspiration and identifies inflammatory lesions, as well as EGD. Capsule endoscopy may facilitate patient triage and earlier endoscopy, but should not be considered a substitute for EGD.

title: Electroporation of Cas9 protein/sgRNA into early pronuclear zygotes generates non-mosaic mutants in the mouse.
text: The CRISPR/Cas9 system is a potent tool for uncovering the functions of genes across a wide range of organisms, including mice. To obtain genetically modified embryos or mice using this method, Cas9 mRNA and sgRNA are typically introduced into zygotes through microinjection or electroporation. However, the majority of mutants generated with this approach are genetically mosaic, consisting of multiple cell types carrying distinct mutations, which complicates the analysis of phenotypes in founder embryos or mice. To streamline the analysis and shed light on the roles of genes in developmental processes, we developed a method for producing non-mosaic mouse mutant embryos. By introducing Cas9 protein and sgRNA into in vitro fertilized (IVF) zygotes through electroporation, we were able to initiate the genome editing process before the first replication of the mouse genome. As a result, all cells in the mutant embryo carried the same set of mutations, eliminating the problem of mosaicism/allele complexity in founder mutant embryos or mice generated using the CRISPR/Cas9 system.

title: Molecular Basis for Target RNA Recognition and Cleavage by Human RISC
text: The RNA-Induced Silencing Complex (RISC) is a ribonucleoprotein entity composed of a small single-stranded RNA molecule (siRNA) and an active Argonaute protein. This complex is capable of cleaving messenger RNAs (mRNAs) that complement the siRNA. While the mechanism of RISC cleavage is well understood, the process of target recognition remains enigmatic. Our study demonstrates, both in vitro and in vivo, that the accessibility of the target site directly correlates with the efficiency of cleavage, indicating that RISC is unable to cleave structured RNA. During target recognition, RISC temporarily interacts with single-stranded RNA non-specifically and promotes siRNA-target RNA annealing. Additionally, the 5' part of the siRNA within RISC forms a thermodynamic threshold that stabilizes the association between RISC and the target RNA. Our findings provide crucial insights into the mechanisms of RNA interference by revealing the essential features of RISC and target RNAs.

title: Cancer associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in tumor microenvironment.
text: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a vital component of the tumor microenvironment, promoting the growth and invasion of cancer cells through various mechanisms. CAFs exhibit remarkable heterogeneity due to their diverse origins, but their distinct morphological features and physiological functions have been well- characterized. The interplay between cancer cells and CAFs is central to the progression of cancer, and understanding this relationship is crucial for the development of effective cancer therapies. In this review, we will explore the latest findings on the role of CAFs in tumorigenesis and metastasis, as well as the potential therapeutic implications of targeting CAFs in cancer treatment.

title: Cold Exposure Promotes Atherosclerotic Plaque Growth and Instability via UCP1-Dependent Lipolysis
text: The molecular mechanisms underlying the increased cardiovascular risk associated with cold exposure remain unclear. However, our study reveals that cold-stimulated food-intake-independent lipolysis leads to a significant increase in plasma levels of small low-density lipoprotein (LDL) remnants, accelerating the development of atherosclerotic lesions in mice. In two genetic mouse models (apolipoprotein E (-/-) [ApoE(-/-)] and LDL receptor (-/-) [Ldlr(-/-)] mice), persistent cold exposure stimulated atherosclerotic plaque growth by enhancing lipid deposition. Moreover, we observed a significant increase in inflammatory cells and plaque-associated microvessels in cold-acclimated ApoE (-/-) and Ldlr (-/-) mice, leading to plaque instability. Deletion of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), a key mitochondrial protein involved in thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (BAT), in the ApoE (-/-) strain completely protected mice from the cold-induced atherosclerotic lesions. Cold acclimation also reduced plasma levels of adiponectin, and systemic delivery of adiponectin protected ApoE (-/-) mice from plaque development. These findings provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying low-temperature-associated cardiovascular risks.

title: Mild overexpression of MeCP2 causes a progressive neurological disorder in mice.
text: Mutations in the X-linked methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene, which encodes a transcriptional repressor, are responsible for Rett syndrome and related neurodevelopmental disorders. The majority of mutations associated with disease are loss-of-function mutations, but the specific aspect of MeCP2 function that underlies these phenotypes remains unidentified. To investigate, we overexpressed wild-type human MeCP2 in transgenic mice using a large genomic clone containing the entire human MECP2 locus. Surprisingly, these mice exhibited enhanced motor and contextual learning and enhanced synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus around 10 weeks of age. However, after 20 weeks, the mice developed seizures, became hypoactive, and approximately 30% of them died by 1 year of age. These findings indicate that in vivo MeCP2 levels must be tightly regulated, and that even mild overexpression of this protein can be detrimental. Moreover, these results suggest that duplications or gain-of-function mutations in MECP2 might underlie some cases of X-linked delayed-onset neurobehavioral disorders.

title: Alcohol Sales and Risk of Serious Assault
text:
BACKGROUND: Alcohol is a leading cause of unintentional injuries, including motor vehicle crashes. Prior studies on the association between alcohol consumption and violent injuries were limited to survey data and a single trauma center, without adequate controls. One major limitation was the inability to capture comprehensive data on alcohol sales across different regions. In Ontario, alcohol is primarily sold through government-run retail outlets, and hospitals are funded through a provincial healthcare system. We conducted a population-based case-crossover analysis to assess the risk of hospitalization due to assault in relation to retail alcohol sales across Ontario.
METHODS AND FINDINGS: We analyzed all hospital cases of assault between April 1, 2002, and December 1, 2004, including individuals aged 13 years and older. On the day before each assault case's hospitalization, we compared the volume of alcohol sold at the closest store to the victim's home with the volume sold at the same store 7 days earlier. We used conditional logistic regression to determine the associated relative risk (RR) of assault per 1,000 l higher daily sales of alcohol. Our sample consisted of 3,212 persons admitted to hospital for assault, of whom 25% were aged 13-20 years, and 83% were male. A total of 1,150 assaults (36%) involved the use of a sharp or blunt weapon, and 1,532 (48%) arose during an unarmed brawl or fight. For every 1,000 l more of alcohol sold per store per day, the RR of being hospitalized for assault was 1.13 (95% CI 1.02-1.26). The risk was higher among males (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.05-1.33), youth aged 13-20 years (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.99-1.46), and those living in urban areas (RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.06-1.35).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that there is a strong association between retail alcohol sales and the risk of assault, particularly among young urban men. Given the similarity between this risk and the risk of driving while impaired, we recommend considering novel prevention methods to address alcohol-related violence.

title: miR-375 inhibits autophagy and reduces viability of hepatocellular carcinoma cells under hypoxic conditions.
text:
In this study, we investigated the role of microRNAs (miRNAs) in regulating the autophagy of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells under hypoxic conditions. We used gain- and loss-of-function methods to evaluate the effect of miRNAs on autophagy in human HCC cell lines (Huh7 and Hep3B) and analyzed the growth of HCC xenograft tumors in nude mice.
Our results showed that miR-375 was down-regulated in HCC cells and tissues, and it inhibited autophagy under hypoxic conditions by suppressing the conversion of LC3I to LC3II and thereby autophagic flux. The ability of miR-375 to inhibit autophagy was independent of its ability to regulate 3'-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase-1-AKT-mammalian target of rapamycin signaling, but instead involved suppression of ATG7, an autophagy-associated gene. miR-375 bound directly to a predicted site in the 3' untranslated region of ATG7. Up-regulating miR-375 or down-regulating ATG7 inhibited mitochondrial autophagy of HCC cells, reduced the elimination of damaged mitochondria under hypoxia, increased release of mitochondrial apoptotic proteins, and reduced viability of HCC cells. In mice, xenograft tumors that expressed miR-375 had fewer autophagic cells, larger areas of necrosis, and grew more slowly than tumors from HCC cells that expressed lower levels of miR-375.
Our findings suggest that miRNAs that inhibit autophagy of cancer cells might be developed as therapeutics.

title: Pseudouridine profiling reveals regulated mRNA pseudouridylation in yeast and human cells
text: Modification of RNA nucleosides after transcription occurs in all living organisms. Pseudouridine, the most abundant modified nucleoside found in non-coding RNAs, enhances the function of transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA by stabilizing the RNA structure. Initially, it was believed that messenger RNAs (mRNAs) do not contain pseudouridine, but artificial pseudouridylation was shown to significantly affect mRNA function by facilitating non-canonical base pairing in the ribosome decoding center. However, as there was no evidence of naturally occurring mRNA pseudouridylation, the physiological relevance of this modification was unclear. To address this question, we developed Pseudo-seq, a high-resolution method for identifying pseudouridine modification sites in RNAs. Using this method, we accurately identified known modification sites as well as many novel sites in non-coding RNAs and found hundreds of pseudouridylated sites in mRNAs. Genetic analysis revealed that most of these new modification sites were regulated in response to environmental signals, such as nutrient deprivation in yeast and serum starvation in human cells. These findings suggest a mechanism for rapidly rewiring the genetic code through inducible mRNA modifications, and provide a resource for identifying the targets of pseudouridine synthases implicated in human disease.

title: The descent of memory T-cell subsets
text: The immune system has evolved over time to enhance its capability to protect the host from infectious agents through continuous development of greater complexity. This complexity manifests in the form of immunological memory, which provides long-lasting protection and lengthens the lifespan of the host. The generation of various subsets of memory T cells with distinct homing and functional properties broaden our defensive capabilities. There is ongoing debate regarding the developmental relationship of memory T-cell subsets, but recent discoveries suggest that it is likely that two distinct lineages make up the memory CD8+ T-cell population that develops in response to infection.

title: Differential distribution of IL28B.rs12979860 single-nucleotide polymorphism among Egyptian healthcare workers with and without a hepatitis C virus-specific cellular immune response
text: The present study aimed to investigate the distribution and correlation of a specific genetic variant, IL28B.rs12979860, with HCV-specific cell-mediated immune (CMI) responses among Egyptian healthcare workers (HCWs). The study included 402 HCWs who were divided into four groups based on their HCV status: seronegative aviremic subjects (n=258), seronegative viremic subjects (n=25), subjects with spontaneously resolved HCV infection (n=41), and chronic HCV patients (n=78). The study found that the frequency of the IL28B.rs12979860 C allele homozygosity was significantly higher among the seronegative aviremic HCWs (49%) compared to the other groups, while the frequency of the T allele was highest among the chronic HCV patients (19%). However, the study did not find any significant relationship between the IL28B genotypes and the outcome of HCV-specific CMI responses in any of the four groups. These findings suggest that the IL28B.rs12979860 genotype distribution may differ among Egyptian HCWs with different HCV status, but it does not predict the outcome of HCV-specific CMI responses.

title: TCR ligand density and affinity determine peripheral induction of Foxp3 in vivo
text: T cell receptor (TCR) activation is crucial for the extra-thymic differentiation of forkhead box p3(+) (Foxp3(+)) regulatory T cells. Several lines of evidence suggest that weak TCR stimulation favors the induction of Foxp3 in the periphery; however, it remains unclear how the potency of the TCR ligand impacts this process. To investigate, we assessed the density and affinity of TCR ligands that promote Foxp3 induction in vivo. Our findings revealed that a low dose of a potent agonist led to optimal Foxp3 induction in vivo. Initial Foxp3 induction by weak agonist peptide could be enhanced by inhibiting TCR-peptide major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) interactions or modifying peptide dose. However, time-lapse experiments showed that Foxp3-positive cells induced by weak agonist stimulation were deleted along with their Foxp3-negative counterparts, whereas Foxp3-positive cells induced by low doses of the strong agonist persisted. Our results suggest that the cumulative quantity of TCR stimulation, defined by pMHC ligand potency, density, and duration of interactions, determines initial peripheral Foxp3 induction. However, the persistence of induced Foxp3(+) T cells is influenced by non-interchangeable factors, including TCR ligand potency and density, which dictate the route to peripheral tolerance.

title: Electromagnetic interference from radio frequency identification inducing potentially hazardous incidents in critical care medical equipment.
text:
Healthcare applications of autoidentification technologies, such as radio frequency identification (RFID), have been proposed to enhance patient safety and the tracking and tracing of medical equipment. However, little is known about the potential risks of RFID interference with critical care equipment. To investigate this, we assessed and classified incidents of electromagnetic interference (EMI) caused by RFID on 41 medical devices in a controlled environment at the Academic Medical Centre in Amsterdam.
Using a standardized test protocol, we tested the RFID systems in the presence and absence of medical devices and classified the incidents according to a critical care adverse event scale as hazardous, significant, or light. We found that the passive 868 MHz RFID signal induced more incidents than the active 125 kHz signal, with a median distance of 30 cm between the RFID reader and the medical device. Our findings suggest that implementation of RFID in the critical care environment should include on-site EMI testing and updates to international standards.

title: Potent RNAi by short RNA triggers.
text:
RNA interference (RNAi) is a way for cells to turn off certain genes by using a small piece of RNA to guide the breakdown of a matching gene. This process involves a complex called RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) and a small piece of RNA called a small interfering RNA (siRNA). The siRNA is designed to match a specific gene, and when it finds a matching gene, it tells the RISC complex to break it down.
In this study, researchers made synthetic siRNAs with shorter lengths to see if they could be used to trigger RNAi in human cells. They found that a shorter siRNA of 16 nucleotides (nt) was more effective at knocking down a specific gene than a longer siRNA of 19 nt. They also found that the 16-nt siRNA had a higher capacity to load onto the RISC complex. These results suggest that cells may be able to use shorter siRNAs as triggers for RNAi, which could be useful for treating diseases.
In summary, the study found that a shorter siRNA of 16 nt can be used to trigger RNAi in human cells and that this shorter siRNA is more effective at knocking down a specific gene than a longer siRNA. Additionally, the study found that the 16-nt siRNA has a higher capacity to load onto the RISC complex. These results suggest that shorter siRNAs could be used as triggers for RNAi, which could be useful for treating diseases.

title: IL-23–responsive innate lymphoid cells are increased in inflammatory bowel disease
text: The IL-23/IL-17 axis has been implicated in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), with IL-23-driven inflammation primarily linked to Th17 cells. However, recent findings have identified a novel population of innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) in mice that produce IL-17, IL-22, and IFN-γ in response to IL-23 and mediate innate colitis. The role of these ILC populations in human health and disease is currently poorly understood. In this study, we analyzed the role of IL-23-responsive ILCs in the human intestine in both control and IBD patients. Our results showed increased expression of the Th17-associated cytokine genes IL17A and IL17F among intestinal CD3⁻ cells in IBD, with expression limited to CD56⁻ ILCs. Additionally, we found that IL-23 induces IL22 and IL26 in the CD56⁺ ILC compartment. Interestingly, we observed a significant and selective increase in CD127⁺CD56⁻ ILCs in the inflamed intestine in Crohn's disease (CD) patients but not in ulcerative colitis patients. These findings suggest that IL-23-responsive ILCs are present in the human intestine and that intestinal inflammation in CD is associated with the selective accumulation of a phenotypically distinct ILC population characterized by inflammatory cytokine expression. ILCs may contribute to intestinal inflammation through cytokine production, lymphocyte recruitment, and organization of the inflammatory tissue, making them a novel tissue-specific target for subtypes of IBD.

title: Scaling of Dorsal-Ventral Patterning by Embryo Size-Dependent Degradation of Spemann’s Organizer Signals
text: Spemann's organizer plays a pivotal role in dorsal-ventral (DV) patterning during amphibian embryonic development by secreting regulatory proteins, including Chordin, which antagonizes ventralizing bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs). The resulting DV patterning is remarkably robust, allowing an embryo with its ventral half removed to develop into a smaller but proportionally patterned larva. We investigate the mechanism underlying this robust patterning and find that it relies on facilitated Chordin degradation and the expression of the Chordin-proteinase inhibitor Sizzled on the opposing side. Sizzled, which is stable and widely distributed along the DV axis, stabilizes Chordin and extends its distribution in the ventral direction. This expanded Chordin distribution limits BMP-dependent Sizzled production, creating an axis-wide feedback loop that shapes Chordin's activity. By employing bisection assays, we demonstrate that Chordin degradation is regulated dynamically by embryo-size-coupled Sizzled accumulation. We propose a scaling model that enables the DV pattern to adjust proportionally to embryonic axis size.

title: Augmenting Antitumor Immune Responses with Epigenetic Modifying Agents
text:
Cancer cells often turn off genes that help the immune system recognize and attack them. This happens during the process of tumor growth. When this happens, the cancer cells can avoid being detected by the immune system. This can lead to evasion of immune surveillance.
Also, the cancer cells in the tumor microenvironment can change the immune cells that are there. They can make the immune cells less able to recognize and attack the cancer cells. This is done by altering the expression of immune suppressive cytokines. As a result, the immune cells in the tumor microenvironment become less effective at presenting antigens to T-cells and at killing cancer cells.
However, there is a potential way to reverse this immune suppression. It involves using epigenetic modifications to reactivate the genes that help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. Preclinical studies have shown that this can improve the ability of immune cells to present antigens, activate T-cells, and break down suppressive mechanisms. Clinical trials are now using epigenetic therapies either alone or in combination with immunotherapies to enhance clinical outcomes.
In simpler language, cancer cells can turn off genes that help the immune system recognize and attack them. This makes it harder for the immune system to detect and attack the cancer cells. But, researchers are finding ways to "reset" these genes by using epigenetic modifications. This can help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells more effectively. Clinical trials are already testing this approach in combination with other treatments to see if it can improve cancer treatment outcomes.

title: Activation of proteinase-activated receptor 2 in human osteoarthritic cartilage upregulates catabolic and proinflammatory pathways capable of inducing cartilage degradation: a basic science study
text:
Proteinase-activated receptors (PARs) are a family of G protein-coupled receptors that are activated by serine-dependent cleavage, leading to the generation of a tethered activating ligand. In this study, we investigated the in situ levels and modulation of PAR-2 in human normal and osteoarthritis (OA) cartilage/chondrocytes, as well as the role of PAR-2 in the synthesis of major catabolic factors in OA cartilage.
Using real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction and immunohistochemistry, we found that PAR-2 expression was significantly upregulated in OA compared to normal cartilage. Furthermore, we found that PAR-2 levels were significantly upregulated by interleukin 1 beta (IL-1β) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) as well as by a specific PAR-2-activating peptide (PAR-2-AP). In contrast, the inhibition of p38, a signalling pathway involved in PAR-2 activation, significantly downregulated PAR-2 levels.
We also found that PAR-2 activation induced the synthesis of matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-1 and cyclooxygenase 2 (COX-2) in OA cartilage, as well as the phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 (Erk1/2) and p38 within 5 minutes of incubation. These results suggest that PAR-2 activation may play a role in the pathogenesis of OA, and that targeting PAR-2 could be a potential new therapeutic strategy for the treatment of OA.
In conclusion, this study provides evidence that PAR-2 is upregulated in OA cartilage and that its activation leads to the synthesis of MMP-1 and COX-2. Furthermore, the results suggest that p38 signalling pathway plays a major role in regulating PAR-2 activity in OA chondrocytes. These findings provide a new insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying OA and identify PAR-2 as a potential new therapeutic target for the treatment of OA.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps enriched in oxidized mitochondrial DNA are interferogenic and contribute to lupus-like disease
text: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are implicated in autoimmune disorders, but their mechanisms of formation and function during sterile inflammation remain unclear. Ribonucleoprotein immune complexes (RNP ICs), which stimulate NETosis, depend on mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) for maximum NET induction. After RNP IC stimulation of neutrophils, mitochondria become hypopolarized and migrate to the cell surface. The extracellular release of oxidized mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is pro-inflammatory in vitro and, when injected into mice, stimulates type I interferon (IFN) signaling through a STING-dependent pathway. Mitochondrial ROS are also required for spontaneous NETosis in low-density granulocytes from individuals with systemic lupus erythematosus and chronic granulomatous disease, despite the absence of NADPH oxidase activity. In vivo mitochondrial ROS inhibition reduces disease severity and type I IFN responses in a mouse model of lupus. These findings underscore the role of mitochondria in both NET formation and the production of pro-inflammatory oxidized mtDNA in autoimmune diseases.

title: Microenvironment rigidity modulates responses to the HER2 receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor lapatinib via YAP and TAZ transcription factors.
text:
Stiffness, a crucial biophysical property of the extracellular matrix, plays a significant role in modulating various cellular functions, including proliferation, invasion, and differentiation. Furthermore, stiffness may also impact the effectiveness of therapeutic interventions, particularly in the context of cancer treatments. Despite its importance, the mechanisms underlying the impact of stiffness on therapeutic responses are not well understood.
Tumor progression is marked by changes in the biophysical properties of the underlying tissue, and we aimed to investigate the role of matrix stiffness in modulating the sensitive versus resistant states of HER2-amplified breast cancer cells in response to the HER2-targeted kinase inhibitor lapatinib. Our findings revealed that the antiproliferative effect of lapatinib was inversely proportional to the elastic modulus of the adhesive substrata.
To delve further into the mechanisms underlying this observation, we examined the role of mechanosensitive transcription coactivators YAP and TAZ in modulating lapatinib resistance. We found that down-regulation of YAP and TAZ, either through siRNA or with the small-molecule inhibitor verteporfin, eliminated the modulus-dependent lapatinib resistance. Additionally, reduction of YAP in vivo in mice led to a trend of increasing sensitivity to lapatinib as YAP levels decreased, highlighting the critical role of stiffness in modulating the efficacy of HER2 pathway-targeted therapeutics via the mechanotransduction arm of the Hippo pathway.
In conclusion, our findings provide new insights into the complex interplay between stiffness, cellular signaling pathways, and therapeutic responses in cancer. These findings may have implications for the development of targeted therapies that take into account the stiffness of the underlying tissue, with the potential to improve treatment outcomes in cancer patients.

title: Effective population size and patterns of molecular evolution and variation
text: The population size, Ne, plays a vital role in determining the rate of change in a population's genetic composition due to genetic drift, which is the random sampling of genetic variants in a finite population. Ne is essential in determining the level of variability within a population and the effectiveness of selection relative to drift. This article examines the properties of Ne in various biologically relevant situations and the factors that influence it. Specifically, selection can result in Ne varying across the genome, and advances in genomic technologies have provided novel insights into the role of selection in shaping Ne.

title: Is emotional dysregulation part of the psychopathology of ADHD in adults?
text: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent condition in adulthood. This disorder is characterized by symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. There is ongoing debate whether symptoms of emotional dysregulation should be included as a core aspect of ADHD. Currently, neither the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) nor the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV) and the upcoming DSM-5 include emotional dysregulation as a defining feature of ADHD. Some authors (e.g., Wender, 1995) propose a more nuanced understanding of adult ADHD by incorporating the subjective experiences of adult patients, including symptoms of emotional symptoms. Empirical studies have demonstrated sufficient reliability and validity to this approach. Emotional dysregulation symptoms are distinct and separable from the psychopathology of ADHD. Pharmacological and psychotherapeutic interventions can help alleviate these symptoms. This review highlights the crucial role of emotional symptoms in ADHD symptomatology, emphasizing their importance in future research.

title: A neural basis for melanocortin-4 receptor regulated appetite
text:
The text would read as follows:
Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)- and agouti-related peptide (AgRP)-expressing neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARC) are reciprocally regulated by caloric depletion, with opposing effects on homeostatic satiety. Specifically, these neurons stimulate and inhibit feeding, respectively. The bimodal nature of these effects is largely due to the antagonistic actions of these ligands at downstream melanocortin-4 receptors (MC4R) in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH). Although the neural circuitry underlying this population is still unclear, we have used mice expressing Cre recombinase in MC4R neurons to demonstrate bidirectional control of feeding following real-time activation and inhibition of PVH(MC4R) neurons. Furthermore, we have identified these cells as a functional extension of ARC(AgRP) neuron-driven hunger. Additionally, we have revealed that this function is mediated by a PVH(MC4R) → lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPBN) pathway. Activation of this circuit encodes positive valence, but only in calorically depleted mice. Therefore, the satiating and appetitive nature of PVH(MC4R) → LPBN neurons supports the principles of drive reduction and highlights this circuit as a promising target for antiobesity drug development.

title: Lymph node T cell responses predict the efficacy of live attenuated SIV vaccines
text:
Here is a possible reconstruction of the given text with a more formal and complex sentence structure:
The live attenuated simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) vaccines (LAVs) remain the most effective vaccines in nonhuman primate models of HIV and AIDS, yet the underlying mechanisms of their potent protectionremain largely unexplored. By virtue of our investigation, we have found that the level of protection against intravenous challenge with wild-type SIVmac239 correlates closely with the magnitude, diversity, and functionality of SIV-specific, effector-differentiated T cells in the lymph node, rather than with the responses of such T cells in the blood or with other immune parameters, such as cellular, humoral, and innate immune components.
Our findings indicate that the preservation of protective T cell responses is intrinsically linked to the sustained replication of LAV in the lymph node, predominantly in follicular helper T cells. This observation underscores the significance of lymphoid tissue-based, effector-differentiated, SIV-specific T cell responses, which can interdict and impede early wild-type SIV amplification, and if present in adequate frequencies, might even result in the complete clearance of infection. This insight provides a rationale for the development of secure, persistent vectors that can elicit and maintain such responses.

title: Activation of Serotonin 2C Receptors in Dopamine Neurons Inhibits Binge-like Eating in Mice
text: Neural networks that control binge eating are not fully understood, and effective treatments for this disorder are limited. We used a combination of techniques, including neuroanatomical, pharmacological, electrophysiological, CRISPR-Cas9, and chemogenetic approaches, to investigate the role of 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) receptors in the regulation of binge-like eating behavior in mice. Our results showed that 5-HT activates dopamine (DA) neurons through a 5-HT2CR-mediated mechanism, and activation of this midbrain 5-HT→DA neural circuit inhibits binge-like eating behavior in mice. We also found that drugs that target the 5-HT2CR, such as fluoxetine, d-fenfluramine, and lorcaserin, act on 5-HT2CRs expressed by DA neurons to inhibit binge-like eating in mice. These findings suggest that the 5-HT2CR population in DA neurons may be a potential target for antibinge therapies, and provide preclinical evidence that 5-HT2CR agonists could be used to treat binge eating.

title: Restoration of chaperone-mediated autophagy in aging liver improves cellular maintenance and hepatic function
text: Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), a specialized mechanism for the degradation of cytosolic proteins in lysosomes, plays a crucial role in maintaining cellular quality control. A decline in CMA activity with aging has been observed, which can lead to the accumulation of altered proteins, disrupted cellular homeostasis, and eventually, functional loss characteristic of aged organs. To determine if preserving CMA activity until late in life could prevent these negative aging features, we generated a double transgenic mouse model in which the abundance of the lysosomal receptor for CMA, which decreases with age, could be modulated. We investigated the consequences of maintaining CMA activity until advanced ages in aged rodents at the cellular and organ levels. Our results show that preventing the age-dependent decrease in receptor abundance leads to maintained CMA activity and lower intracellular accumulation of damaged proteins, improved ability to handle protein damage, and enhanced organ function.

title: The Incidence and Repetition of Hospital-Treated Deliberate Self Harm: Findings from the World's First National Registry
text:
BACKGROUND: Suicide is a critical public health concern, with over one million deaths by suicide occurring annually worldwide. Deliberate self-harm (DSH) is the leading risk factor for suicide, yet few countries have reliable data on DSH. We established a national DSH registry in the Republic of Ireland to determine the incidence of hospitalized DSH at the national level, as well as the variety of presentations and patterns associated with DSH and repeat instances.
METHODS AND FINDINGS: Between 2003 and 2009, data on DSH presentations to all 40 hospital emergency departments in Ireland were collected by trained data registration officers using standardized methods of case identification and definition. A total of 75,119 DSH presentations involving 48,206 individuals were recorded, with an incidence rate that decreased from 209 (95% CI: 205-213) per 100,000 in 2003 to 184 (95% CI: 180-189) per 100,000 in 2006, then increased to 209 (95% CI: 204-213) per 100,000 in 2009. Annual changes in the male rate were significant, with successive 10% increases in 2008 and 2009. Significant age variations were observed, with peak rates among women in the 15-19 age group (620 (95% CI: 605-636) per 100,000) and among men in the 20-24 age group (427 (95% CI: 416-439) per 100,000). Repetition rates varied significantly by age, method of self-harm, and number of previous episodes.
CONCLUSION: The population-based data collected through the national DSH registry provide an important indicator of the mental health burden and suicide risk in the community. The increased DSH rate among Irish men in 2008 and 2009 parallels the country's economic recession. These findings emphasize the need for effective interventions to reduce DSH repetition rates as a high priority for health systems.

title: A Common Mechanism of Cellular Death Induced by Bactericidal Antibiotics
text: Antibiotic mode of action is categorized based on the interaction between the drug and the bacterial cell. Two key factors determine this classification: whether the inhibition of cellular function is lethal to bacteria and the type of drug-target interaction. Here, we show that the three primary classes of bactericidal antibiotics, regardless of their drug-target interaction, induce the production of highly harmful hydroxyl radicals in both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. In contrast, bacteriostatic drugs do not produce hydroxyl radicals. Our findings reveal that the mechanism of hydroxyl radical formation induced by bactericidal antibiotics involves an oxidative damage cell death pathway involving the tricarboxylic acid cycle, transient depletion of NADH, destabilization of iron-sulfur clusters, and stimulation of the Fenton reaction. Our results suggest that all three major classes of bactericidal drugs can be enhanced by targeting bacterial systems that repair hydroxyl radical damage, such as proteins involved in triggering the DNA damage response, including RecA.

title: Increased atherosclerosis in mice reconstituted with apolipoprotein E null macrophages.
text: Macrophages derived from macrophage-specific apoE-deficient mice (apoE null) exhibit increased foam cell formation in atherosclerotic lesions. To investigate the in vivo role of apoE secretion by macrophages in atherogenesis, bone marrow transplantation was employed in C57BL/6 mice. After 13 weeks on an atherogenic diet, C57BL/6 mice reconstituted with apoE null marrow developed significantly more atherosclerosis compared to controls, despite similar serum cholesterol and lipoprotein profiles. Conversely, apoE expression was undetectable in macrophage-derived foam cells from apoE null mice. These findings support a protective role of apoE expression by macrophages in early atherogenesis.

title: Endothelium-mediated relaxation of porcine collateral-dependent arterioles is improved by exercise training.
text:
BACKGROUND: Impairment of endothelium-dependent modulation of coronary tone in the collateral-dependent coronary microcirculation has been observed. To investigate the effect of exercise training on this phenomenon, we used a porcine model of chronic coronary occlusion and collateral development.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We studied adult female miniature swine that were subjected to chronic, progressive ameroid occlusion of the proximal left circumflex coronary artery (LCx) for 2 months. After this period, the animals were randomly assigned to either an exercise-training (EX) group or a sedentary (SED) group. The EX group underwent 16 weeks of treadmill running, while the SED group was confined to a cage. Coronary arterioles (approximately 100 microm in diameter) were isolated from the collateral-dependent LCx region (distal to the occlusion) and the nonoccluded left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) region of each heart. The vessels were then studied using in vitro videomicroscopy or frozen for analysis of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (ecNOS) mRNA using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) techniques. We found that relaxation to the endothelium-dependent vasodilator bradykinin was decreased in arterioles isolated from the collateral-dependent LCx region of SED animals compared to the nonoccluded LAD region. However, this difference was not observed in arterioles isolated from EX animals. Nitroprusside-induced relaxation was not affected by either chronic occlusion or exercise. Notably, ecNOS mRNA expression was significantly decreased in arterioles isolated from the LCx region of SED animals. After training, ecNOS mRNA expression was not different between LAD and LCx arterioles.
CONCLUSIONS: These results suggest that exercise training enhances bradykinin-mediated relaxation of collateral-dependent LCx arterioles, which is likely due to increased endothelial nitric oxide synthase (ecNOS) mRNA expression and NO production. Our findings provide evidence that exercise training can improve endothelial function in the collateral-dependent coronary microcirculation.

title: Loss of the RhoGAP SRGP-1 promotes the clearance of dead and injured cells in Caenorhabditis elegans
text: In multicellular organisms, bodies rapidly eliminate dead cells. Many pathways that facilitate this process have been conserved throughout evolution. We discovered srgp-1 as a negative regulator of cell clearance in both Caenorhabditis elegans and mammalian cells. Reduced srgp-1 function enables enhanced engulfment of dying cells, while srgp-1 overexpression hinders the removal of apoptotic cell corpses. We found that SRGP-1 functions in cell engulfment and serves as a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for CED-10 (Rac1). Notably, loss of srgp-1 function promotes the removal of both dead and precariously damaged cells, while impaired engulfment allows these cells to evade clearance, leading to extended survival. We propose that C. elegans employs the engulfment mechanism as part of an ancestral, yet evolutionarily conserved, surveillance system that detects and eliminates unfit cells within a tissue.

title: Abnormalities in the myeloid progenitor compartment in Down syndrome fetal liver precede acquisition of GATA1 mutations.
text: Children with Down syndrome (DS) are at a higher risk of developing acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL) in early childhood. At least two genetic events are required for the development of DS-AMKL, including trisomy 21 (T21) and N-terminal-truncating GATA1 mutations. To investigate the role of T21 in DS-AMKL, researchers compared the second-trimester hemopoiesis in DS fetuses without GATA1 mutations to gestation-matched normal controls. They found that megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor frequency was increased in all DS fetuses' livers, but not marrow, with common myeloid progenitors and GM progenitors commensurately reduced. Additionally, the clonogenicity of DS-FL (fetal liver) CD34(+) cells was markedly increased, affecting megakaryocyte-erythroid and GM progenitors, and replating efficiency of CFU-GEMM (colony-forming unit-granulocyte, erythrocyte macrophage, megakaryocyte) progenitors was also enhanced. These findings suggest that T21 alone significantly disturbs fetal liver hemopoiesis and provide a testable hypothesis to explain the increased susceptibility to GATA1 mutations in DS-AMKL and DS-associated transient myeloproliferative disorder.

title: Regulatory and metabolic rewiring during laboratory evolution of ethanol tolerance in E. coli
text: Understanding the genetic basis of adaptation is a fundamental problem in biology, yet elucidating the underlying molecular mechanisms has proven challenging due to the complexity of fitness changes resulting from perturbations to multiple pathways. To tackle this challenge, we have developed a combined experimental/computational framework to identify the genetic basis of ethanol tolerance in Escherichia coli. We employed fitness profiling to measure the effects of single-locus perturbations on ethanol tolerance, followed by a module-level computational analysis to organize the contributing loci into cellular processes and metabolic pathways, such as osmoregulation and cell wall biogenesis, that significantly impact ethanol tolerance. Surprisingly, our findings revealed that a major component of adaptation involves rewiring metabolic pathways to enhance intracellular ethanol degradation and assimilation. Through phenotypic and metabolomic analysis of laboratory-evolved ethanol-tolerant strains, we investigated accessible routes of ethanol tolerance and observed that these evolved strains largely follow the adaptive paths inferred from our coarse-grained search of the fitness landscape.

title: Familial risk of lymphoproliferative tumors in families of patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia: results from the Swedish Family-Cancer Database.
text: The genetic factors contributing to the etiology of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) are supported by findings from family and population studies. However, the extent to which other malignancies with similar genetic factors impact familial risk is unknown. To investigate, we analyzed data from the Swedish Family-Cancer Database, examining cancer diagnoses in 14,336 first-degree relatives of 5,918 CLL cases and 28,876 first-degree relatives of 11,778 controls between 1958 and 1998. Using marginal survival models, we found that relatives of CLL cases were significantly more likely to develop CLL (relative risk [RR] = 7.52; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 3.63-15.56), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (RR = 1.45; 95% CI = 0.98-2.16), and Hodgkin lymphoma (RR = 2.35; 95% CI = 1.08-5.08). Risk was similar across parent-child, sibling-child, and offspring relationships, as well as between males and females. The age of the case at diagnosis did not impact risk to relatives. Analyzing the data using life table methods revealed no indication of anticipation. Our findings suggest that the genetic factors underlying CLL are also present in other lymphoproliferative malignancies, indicating a shared underlying genetic pathway. However, due to the relatively small absolute excess risk to relatives, clinically diagnosed CLL is uncommon.

title: Collagen/Polypropylene composite mesh biocompatibility in abdominal wall reconstruction.
text:
BACKGROUND: Previous studies have shown that direct peritoneal placement of polypropylene mesh leads to the development of extensive visceral adhesions, making it a contraindicated method. To address this issue, researchers have developed various coatings to enhance the properties of polypropylene mesh. Collagen, a protein with unique biocompatibility and cell ingrowth potential, is one such coating. The aim of this study was to evaluate the long-term effects of an acetic acid-extracted collagen coating on surgical aspects and biomechanical properties of polypropylene mesh implanted in direct contact with viscera in a rat model.
METHODS: Forty adult Wistar rats were randomly divided into two groups: experimental (polypropylene mesh with acetic acid-extracted collagen coating) and control (polypropylene mesh only). The standard mesh implantation procedure was followed for both groups. The rats were euthanized 3 months after surgery, and the adhesion area, adhesion severity, strength of incorporation, and inflammatory response to the mesh were evaluated.
RESULTS: The results showed a significant reduction in adhesion area in the experimental group (14.5% vs 69.9%, p < 0.001). The severity of adhesions was also decreased in the experimental group, with grades 0 and 1 adhesions being more common (p < 0.04 and p < 0.002, respectively), and grade 3 adhesions being less common (p < 0.0001). An association between adhesion area and severity was found (p < 0.0001). Complications, strength of incorporation, and inflammatory response to the mesh were similar in both groups.
CONCLUSIONS: The findings of this study suggest that the acetic acid-extracted collagen coating reduces visceral adhesions to polypropylene mesh in a rat model. The coating does not increase complications or alter the incorporation of the mesh into the surrounding tissue. These results have important implications for the development of novel coatings to prevent adhesions in humans.

title: Microvessel Density and Status of p53 Protein as Potential Prognostic Factors for Adjuvant Anthracycline Chemotherapy in Retrospective Analysis of Early Breast Cancer Patients Group
text:
A considerable subset of patients with early-stage breast cancer may not benefit from anthracycline-based chemotherapy. The goal of this retrospective study was to investigate the impact of microvessel density (MVD) and p53 protein status on 5-year disease-free survival (DFS) in patients with early-stage breast cancer treated with anthracyclines in an adjuvant setting. The study also assessed correlations between MVD, p53 status, and other clinicopathological parameters.
Immunohistochemical analysis of MVD and p53 status was performed on tissue samples from 172 women with early-stage breast cancer (clinical stages T1-2, N1-N2, M0). The study found that 123 tumors (71.5%) had low MVD (≤ 214.8 microvesells/mm2), while 49 tumors (28.5%) had high MVD (>214.8 microvesells/mm2). The proportion of high MVD tumors was significantly higher in tumors with negative estrogen or progesterone receptors (P = 0.029) and in tumors with high grade (P = 0.000).
p53 positivity was detected in 50 tumors (29.1%), and it was significantly associated with high grade (P = 0.000), steroid receptor negativity (P = 0.000), cytokeratin 5/6 positivity (P = 0.026), topoisomerase IIα overexpression (P = 0.005), and higher proliferation rate (P = 0.001). In univariate analysis, higher MVD and p53 negativity were significantly related to longer DFS (median follow-up 36 months). In multivariate Cox regression analysis, MVD was independently associated with DFS.
The study suggests that higher MVD is a favourable prognostic factor for early advanced breast cancer patients who receive adjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy. These findings may help identify patients who are likely to benefit from anthracycline-based chemotherapy and may improve treatment outcomes for early-stage breast cancer patients.

title: Ranking of elimination feasibility between malaria-endemic countries
text: The research conducted through the Global Malaria Eradication Program (1955-1972) revealed a set of common technical and operational factors that contributed to the success of some countries in eliminating malaria. These factors were mapped for all malaria-endemic countries and combined to create an objective, relative ranking of countries based on their elimination feasibility. The analysis was conducted separately for Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, and the limitations of the approach were discussed. The rankings suggested that malaria elimination would be most feasible in countries in the Americas and Asia, and least feasible in countries in central and west Africa. Interestingly, the results varied when measuring feasibility based on technical or operational factors, highlighting the unique challenges faced by each country. It is important to note that these rankings are not intended to be prescriptive, predictive, or to provide absolute assessments of feasibility, but rather to demonstrate that spatial information can be used to quickly and evidence-based assess the relative feasibility of malaria elimination by country.

title: Genetics of obesity in adult adoptees and their biological siblings.
text: An adoption study was conducted to investigate the genetic effects of obesity in adulthood. Adoptees who were separated from their biological parents at a young age were compared to their full and half siblings who were raised by their natural parents. The adoptees fell into four categories based on their weight: thin, medium weight, overweight, and obese. Weight and height were measured for 115 full siblings of 57 adoptees and 850 half siblings of 341 adoptees. The results showed that the body mass index (BMI) of full siblings significantly increased with the weight of the adoptees. In contrast, the BMI of half siblings showed a gradual but weaker increase across the four weight groups of adoptees. There were no significant interactions between sex, sex of the siblings, or sex of the common parent. Interestingly, the study found a striking and significant increase in BMI between full siblings of overweight and obese adoptees, suggesting that genetic factors independent of sex may play a role in adult obesity. These findings support the idea that there are genetic factors that contribute to obesity, which may involve both polygenic and major gene effects.

title: 2010 rheumatoid arthritis classification criteria: an American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism collaborative initiative.
text:
The goal of this study was to develop new classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) that are more sensitive in detecting early disease. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) collaborated on this project, dividing it into three phases. The aim was to identify factors that distinguish patients with high risk of persistent and/or erosive disease from those with other conditions presenting with undifferentiated inflammatory synovitis.
The new criteria set defines definite RA based on the presence of synovitis in at least one joint, absence of a more suitable alternative diagnosis, and achieving a total score of 6 or higher (out of a possible 10) from individual scores in four domains: number and site of involved joints (range 0-5), serological abnormality (range 0-3), elevated acute-phase response (range 0-1), and symptom duration (with two levels, range 0-1).
The new classification system shifts the current paradigm of RA by focusing on features of early disease associated with persistent and/or erosive disease, rather than defining the disease by its late-stage characteristics. This redefinition will encourage earlier diagnosis and treatment to prevent or minimize the undesirable sequelae that are currently the defining features of the disease construct 'RA'.

title: A role for fibroblasts in mediating the effects of tobacco-induced epithelial cell growth and invasion.
text: Cigarette smoke and smokeless tobacco contain harmful compounds that can lead to cancer. However, little is known about how these compounds cause cancer cells to grow and progress. In this study, we investigated the effects of smokeless tobacco extracts on human oral fibroblasts. We found that exposure to these extracts increased the levels of damaging free radicals, DNA damage, and DNA breaks in a dose-dependent manner. Long-term exposure to the extracts also caused fibroblasts to enter a state of senescence, characterized by reduced growth and changes in the secretions they produce. When we exposed fibroblasts to smokeless tobacco extracts and cocultured them with immortalized but noncancerous keratinocytes, we found that factors secreted by the altered fibroblasts increased the proliferation and invasiveness of partially transformed epithelial cells. Additionally, the extracts caused partially transformed keratinocytes to lose the expression of important proteins that help maintain epithelial cell functions, such as E-cadherin and ZO-1, and involucrin. These changes are indicative of compromised epithelial function and a higher risk of cancer progression. Our findings suggest that fibroblasts may contribute to cancer development by promoting the aggressive growth and invasion of mutant epithelial cells. Therefore, tobacco may not only initiate DNA changes in epithelial cells but also support the growth and invasion of these cells by creating a procarcinogenic environment in the surrounding tissue.

title: ImmTAC-redirected tumour cell killing induces and potentiates antigen cross-presentation by dendritic cells
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) are thought to play a crucial role in promoting a diverse and durable T cell response against cancer through the process of antigen cross-presentation. entrance of new immunotherapeutic agents into tumor eradication may depend on their ability to induce antigen cross-presentation. Immunomobilizing monoclonal TCRs (T cell receptors) against cancer, known as ImmTACs, are a novel class of soluble bi-specific anti-cancer agents that combine pico-molar affinity TCR-based antigen recognition with T cell activation via a CD3-specific antibody fragment. ImmTACs specifically recognize human leucocyte antigen (HLA)-restricted tumor-associated antigens presented by cancer cells, leading to T cell redirection and a potent anti-tumor response. Using an ImmTAC specific for a HLA-A*02-restricted peptide derived from the melanoma antigen gp100 (termed IMCgp100), we observed that ImmTAC-mediated melanoma cell death leads to cross-presentation of melanoma antigens by DCs. These cross-presented antigens can activate both melanoma-specific T cells and polyclonal T cells redirected by IMCgp100, with the latter feature enhancing the prospect of breaking tolerance in the tumor microenvironment. The mechanism of DC cross-presentation occurs through the rapid and direct capture of membrane fragments from dying tumor cells by DCs. Cross-presentation of gp100-peptide-HLA complexes by DCs was visualized and quantified using a fluorescently labeled soluble TCR. These data demonstrate how ImmTACs interact with both the innate and adaptive components of the immune system, thereby increasing the likelihood of eliciting an effective and durable anti-tumor response in patients.

title: Basal keratinocyte tetrasomy in low-grade squamous intra-epithelial lesions of the cervix is restricted to high and intermediate risk HPV infection but is not type-specific
text: According to a study published in the journal Cancer Research Campaign in 2000, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection may be an early event in the development of cervical cancer, with additional genetic changes needed for biological transformation. The study analyzed 179 low-grade cervical squamous intra-epithelial lesions (SILs) and 15 normal cervices for the presence of HPV using both in situ hybridization and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The PCR was performed with GP5+/GP6+ primers followed by hybridization using probes for low-risk HPVs (HPV 6, 11, 40, 42, 43, 44), intermediate-risk HPVs (HPV 31, 33, 35, 39, 51, 52, 58, 59, 66, and 68), and high-risk HPVs (HPV 16, 18, 45, and 56). Interphase cytogenetic analysis using pericentromeric probes for chromosomes 1, 3, 4, 6, 10, 11, 17, 18, and X was also performed to identify numerical chromosomal abnormalities. The study found that tetrasomy, or the presence of four copies of a particular chromosome, was detected in 17 of 46 (36%) of epithelia infected with high- or intermediate-risk HPVs, but not in any of the epithelia infected with low-risk HPVs (n = 62). This suggests that the induction of tetrasomy is a property restricted to high and intermediate-risk HPV types, but it is not type-specific. However, the factors that determine which lesions will develop this abnormality are still unclear.

title: “Rapid-Impact Interventions”: How a Policy of Integrated Control for Africa's Neglected Tropical Diseases Could Benefit the Poor
text: Over the past two decades, significant progress has been made in controlling several major human tropical infections. Noteworthy achievements include substantial reductions in the prevalence and incidence of so-called neglected diseases such as lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, guinea worm, leprosy, and trachoma (Box 1). These neglected diseases are often poverty-related and stigmatizing, primarily affecting rural areas of low-income countries and fragile states (Box 2). Despite being around for millennia, these diseases have been a persistent burden on humanity. However, with aggressive regional vertical interventions, there is now a possibility that some neglected tropical infections could be brought under control and potentially eliminated in certain areas of endemicity (Box 2). Even more encouragingly, disease eradication for guinea worm infection may be achievable in the near future (Box 2 and Box 9).

title: FTY720 (fingolimod) is a neuroprotective and disease-modifying agent in cellular and mouse models of Huntington disease.
text: Huntington disease (HD) is a genetic neurodegenerative disorder without a known cure or way to slow its progression. In this study, we explored whether FTY720, the first approved oral therapy for multiple sclerosis, might be effective in HD models and potentially serve as an alternative treatment approach. We employed preclinical target validation paradigms to assess the in vivo efficacy of chronic FTY720 administration in R6/2 HD mouse models. Our findings demonstrate that FTY720 improved motor function, extended survival, and reduced brain atrophy in R6/2 mice. The beneficial effect of FTY720 administration was accompanied by enhanced neuronal activity and connectivity, as well as a significant reduction in mutant huntingtin aggregates. Moreover, increased phosphorylation of mutant huntingtin at serine 13/16 residues, which are predicted to mitigate protein toxicity, was observed in response to FTY720 treatment.

title: Specificity Residues Determine Binding Affinity for Two-Component Signal Transduction Systems
text:
Two-component systems (TCS) are composed of histidine kinases (HKs) and their cognate response regulators, allowing bacteria to detect and respond to a wide range of stimuli. HKs phosphorylate and dephosphorylate their cognate response regulators (RRs) in response to specific stimuli, generally showing high specificity and requiring appropriate association between HK and RR proteins. The Myxococcus xanthus genome encodes one of the largest repertoires of signaling proteins in bacteria (685 open reading frames [ORFs]), including at least 127 HKs and at least 143 RRs, with 27 bona fide NtrC-family response regulators and 21 of which are encoded adjacent to their predicted cognate kinases. Using system-wide profiling methods, we determined that the HK-NtrC RR pairs display a kinetic preference during both phosphotransfer and phosphatase functions, thereby defining cognate signaling systems in M. xanthus. Isothermal titration calorimetry measurements indicated that cognate HK-RR pairs interact with dissociation constants (Kd) of approximately 1 µM, while noncognate pairs had no measurable binding. Furthermore, a chimera generated between the histidine kinase, CrdS, and HK1190 revealed that residues conferring phosphotransfer and phosphatase specificity dictate binding affinity, thereby establishing discrete protein-protein interactions that prevent cross-talk. Our findings indicate that binding affinity is a critical parameter governing system-wide signaling fidelity for bacterial signal transduction proteins.
The significance of this study lies in its systematic approach to investigating specificity for a family of two-component signaling proteins in Myxococcus xanthus. Our results demonstrate that previously identified specificity residues dictate binding affinity, and that phosphatase specificity follows phosphotransfer specificity for cognate HK-RR pairs. The data suggest that preferential binding affinity is the basis for signaling fidelity in bacterial two-component systems. This study provides a framework for understanding the specificity of signal transduction in bacteria and has important implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies against bacterial infections.

title: hnRNP A1 associates with telomere ends and stimulates telomerase activity.
text: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein enzyme complex that replicates short DNA sequences called telomeres by reverse-transcribing an RNA template. However, the presence of G-quadruplex structures in the DNA substrate can hinder telomerase activity. Our findings show that hnRNP A1, a protein previously implicated in telomere length regulation, binds to both single-stranded and structured telomeric repeats in human DNA. In the latter case, it disrupts their higher-order structure. Using an in vitro telomerase assay, we observed that depletion of hnRNP A/B proteins significantly reduced telomerase activity, which was fully restored upon addition of purified recombinant hnRNP A1. This suggests that hnRNP A1 functions as an auxiliary, if not essential, factor in the telomerase holoenzyme. Furthermore, our study shows that hnRNP A1 associates with human telomeres in vivo using chromatin immunoprecipitation. We propose that hnRNP A1 stimulates telomere elongation by unwinding G-quadruplex or G-G hairpin structures that form at each translocation step.

title: Rapamycin passes the torch: a new generation of mTOR inhibitors
text: Mammalian Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) is an unconventional protein kinase that regulates cellular growth and metabolism in response to nutrients, growth factors, and energy levels within the cell. It is frequently disrupted in cancer and metabolic disorders, leading to dysregulated cellular growth and proliferation. Rapamycin, an allosteric inhibitor of mTOR, was approved as an immun suppressant in 1999, with recent interest focusing on its potential as an anti-cancer drug. However, the effectiveness of rapamycin and its analogues (rapalogues) has been inconsistent, despite isolated successes in certain cancer subsets. New generations of ATP-competitive inhibitors that directly target the mTOR catalytic site demonstrate potent and comprehensive inhibition of mTOR and are now in early clinical trials, with the potential to fully exploit the therapeutic potential of targeting this key cellular regulator.

title: Dynamic capsule restructuring by the main pneumococcal autolysin LytA in response to the epithelium
text: Bacterial pathogens produce intricate carbohydrate capsules to evade the host's immune system. Conversely, these capsules render the bacteria more susceptible to antimicrobial peptides found on epithelial surfaces. Our study reveals that when encapsulated pneumococci encounter these peptides, they quickly shed their capsules through a process dependent on the suicidal amidase enzyme LytA. In contrast to classical bacterial autolysis, the capsule removal occurs circumferentially around the cell and is crucial for bacterial survival. Both autolysis and capsule shedding rely on LytA's cell wall hydrolytic activity. Notably, the mechanism by which pneumococci shed their capsules during early acute lung infection of mice allows for increased invasion of epithelial cells. The previously unappreciated role of LytA in removing capsule to counteract antimicrobial peptides may explain why nearly all clinical isolates of pneumococci preserve this enzyme despite the lethal selective pressure of antibiotics.

title: The mammalian Scribble polarity protein regulates epithelial cell adhesion and migration through E-cadherin
text: Scrib (Scrib) is a crucial protein in Drosophila melanogaster that plays a vital role in synaptic function, neuroblast differentiation, and epithelial polarity. Additionally, it acts as a tumor suppressor. In rodents, Scrib has been implicated in receptor recycling and planar polarity, but not in apical/basal polarity. Our study reveals that reducing Scrib levels disrupts the adhesion between Madin–Darby canine kidney epithelial cells, leading to a mesenchymal appearance, increased migration, and loss of directionality. Although the tight junction assembly is delayed, the cells remain polarized when cultured as a monolayer. These effects are unrelated to Rac activation or Scrib binding to βPIX, and instead, Scrib depletion disrupts E-cadherin–mediated cell–cell adhesion. The morphological and migratory changes are similar to those observed in E-cadherin knockdown cells. Adhesion is partly restored by expressing an E-cadherin–α-catenin fusion protein, but not by E-cadherin–green fluorescent protein. These findings suggest that Scrib stabilizes the interaction between E-cadherin and catenins, and this regulation may be a mechanism by which Scrib functions as a tumor suppressor by regulating epithelial cell adhesion and migration.

title: Histone acetylation and DNA demethylation of T cells result in an anaplastic large cell lymphoma-like phenotype.
text: An important feature of anaplastic large cell lymphoma is the significant repression of the T-cell expression program, despite its T-cell origin. The reasons for this down-regulation of the T-cell phenotype are still unknown. To investigate whether epigenetic mechanisms are responsible for the loss of the T-cell phenotype, we treated anaplastic large cell lymphoma and T-cell lymphoma/leukemia cell lines with epigenetic modulators to induce DNA demethylation and histone acetylation. Global gene expression data from treated and untreated cell lines were generated and analyzed, and differentially expressed genes were evaluated using real-time reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction and western blot analysis. Additionally, histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation was analyzed by chromatin immunoprecipitation. Our findings indicate that combined DNA demethylation and histone acetylation of anaplastic large cell lymphoma cells were unable to restore their T-cell phenotype. Instead, the treatment induced the up-regulation of anaplastic large cell lymphoma-specific genes, such as ID2, LGALS1, and c-JUN, and almost completely abolished the T-cell phenotype, including CD3, LCK, and ZAP70. Furthermore, suppressive trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 27 was observed in anaplastic large cell lymphoma cells, which is consistent with its absence in primary tumor samples as revealed by immunohistochemistry. These findings suggest that epigenetically activated suppressors, such as ID2, contribute to the down-regulation of the T-cell expression program in anaplastic large cell lymphoma, which is maintained by trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 27.

title: YEASTRACT: providing a programmatic access to curated transcriptional regulatory associations in Saccharomyces cerevisiae through a web services interface
text: The YEASTRACT information system (http://www.yeastract.com) has been expanded and updated to better support the analysis of transcriptional regulation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Last updated in June 2010, the database now contains over 48,200 regulatory associations between transcription factors (TFs) and target genes, including 298 specific DNA-binding sites for 110 characterized TFs. The system has been enhanced to provide detailed information on the experimental evidences that support these associations, with a new categorization system for direct or indirect evidences. Users can now restrict their queries to only include regulatory associations with experimental evidence for direct action of TFs in the promoter region of their target genes. In addition, the database is now available through a machine-readable web service interface, allowing users to retrieve and exploit the data using their own implementation of additional functionalities. The YEASTRACT information system is further complemented with several computational tools that facilitate the use of the curated data to answer a range of important biological questions. Since its initial release in 2006, YEASTRACT has been widely used by hundreds of researchers around the world, and we expect that the updated system will continue to be a valuable resource for yeast biologists and systems biology researchers.

title: Mechanisms that Specify Promoter Nucleosome Location and Identity
text: The chromatin structure of eukaryotic gene promoters generally features a nucleosome-free region (NFR) flanked by at least one H2A.Z variant nucleosome. Despite computational predictions of nucleosome positions being less accurate, we show that the essential RSC remodeling complex in S. cerevisiae helps resolve the discrepancy between theoretical and experimental findings. In RSC-depleted cells, NFRs shrink, resulting in the average position of flanking nucleosomes moving towards predicted sites. Promoter nucleosome positioning requires the essential Myb family proteins Abf1 and Reb1, whose binding sites are enriched in NFRs.
