Unlike other methods, Lifeact does not interfere with actin dynamics in vitro or in vivo, and its chemically modified form allows for visualizing actin dynamics in non-transfectable cells.

title: Robustness of Random Forest-based gene selection methods
text: Gene selection is a crucial aspect of microarray data analysis, as it provides insight into the underlying mechanisms of a phenomenon being investigated. However, gene selection in noisy microarray data is a challenging task, leading to the use of machine learning methods, including Random Forest-based feature selection. In this study, four state-of-the-art Random Forest-based methods were compared for gene selection, focusing on stability and post-selection accuracy. The analysis revealed that while all methods had equivalent post-selection accuracy in the validation of Random Forest classifiers, they significantly differed in terms of the number of selected genes and stability of selection. The Boruta algorithm stood out by predicting the most genes as important, while the post-selection classifier error rate, a commonly used quality measure, was found to be potentially deceptive. When considering the number of consistently selected genes, the Boruta algorithm was the best performer, although it was also the most computationally intensive. To reduce computational demands, the Boruta algorithm's computational requirements could be reduced by using a similar but simplified classifier, Random Ferns. Finally, the minimal optimal selection methods were found to select a significant proportion of false positives.

title: Improved variant discovery through local re-alignment of short-read next-generation sequencing data using SRMA
text: A crucial step in next-generation sequencing analysis is aligning short reads to a reference genome, with each read aligning independently. However, reads that observe the same non-reference DNA sequence are highly correlated, providing an opportunity to improve our understanding of the target genome's true variation. To address this, we present SRMA, a novel short-read realigner that exploits this correlation to generate a more accurate consensus of the underlying DNA sequence.

title: Functional elements within the dynein microtubule-binding domain
text: Dynein interacts with microtubules through an ATP-sensitive binding site located in a structurally complex region of the heavy chain, near the fourth P-loop motif. Despite extensive research, the mechanisms by which binding affinity is regulated during ATP hydrolysis remain poorly understood. To gain insights, we conducted a thorough analysis of the microtubule binding site using fragment expression, alanine substitution, and peptide competition. Our findings reveal three distinct clusters of amino acids that are crucial for physical interactions with microtubules, with two of these clusters sharing similarity with MAP1B. Amino acid substitutions within any of these regions can weaken or eliminate microtubule binding, indicating that these sites are highly coordinated. Interestingly, a peptide that displaces MAP1B from microtubules also perturbs dynein binding, supporting previous studies suggesting similar interaction sites. Moreover, we identified four amino acids whose substitutions affect the motor protein's release from the microtubule, suggesting that nucleotide-sensitive affinity may be locally regulated at the site of contact. Our work represents the first comprehensive study of dynein-microtubule interactions and provides a framework for understanding the mechanisms underlying affinity modulation.

title: The Transcription Factors Egr2 and Egr3 Are Essential for the Control of Inflammation and Antigen-Induced Proliferation of B and T Cells
text: Lymphocytes effectively respond to pathogens with minimal inflammation, but the underlying mechanisms are not yet understood. In this study, we found that deleting both transcription factors Egr2 and Egr3 in lymphocytes led to a lethal autoimmune disorder characterized by excessive serum proinflammatory cytokines and impaired antigen receptor-induced cell proliferation in B and T cells. Interestingly, Egr2- and Egr3-deficient B and T cells displayed elevated STAT1 and STAT3 activity, whereas antigen receptor-induced AP-1 activation was significantly impaired. Our findings revealed that Egr2 and Egr3 directly regulate the expression of suppressor of cytokine signaling-1 (SOCS1) and SOCS3, which inhibit STAT1 and STAT3, and also counteract the function of BATF, an AP-1 inhibitor, in B and T cells. These results uncover the crucial role of Egr2 and Egr3 in regulating B and T cell function during adaptive immune responses and homeostasis by promoting antigen receptor signaling and controlling inflammation.

title: Effect of hyperosmolality on alkaline phosphatase and stress-response protein 27 of MCF-7 breast cancer cells
text: MCF-7, a cancer cell line derived from a human breast tumor, has very low levels of an enzyme called alkaline phosphatase (ALP). This enzyme is heat-stable and is affected by certain amino acids, such as L-phenylalanine and L-phenylalanylglycylglycine, but not by others, such as L-homoarginine, 1-bromotetramisole, or levamisole. These findings suggest that MCF-7 cells produce a specific form of ALP that is commonly expressed in many human tumors. In contrast to other human cancer cells, MCF-7 cells do not have a significant increase in ALP activity when exposed to glucocorticoids or sodium butyrate. However, exposure to high salt concentrations (hyperosmolality) causes a large increase in ALP activity, which can be blocked by the drug cycloheximide. The results of these experiments were confirmed using cell-free assays and cytochemical and immunocytochemical assays on whole cells. To explore further, the effects of these agents on two stress-response proteins (srp 27 and srp 72) were examined using specific immunocytochemical assays. These tests showed that neither protein is affected by glucocorticoids, while sodium butyrate has no effect on srp 27 but changes the distribution of srp 72 within the cells. Finally, hyperosmolality increased srp 27 levels without affecting srp 72.

title: The Bile Acid Chenodeoxycholic Acid Increases Human Brown Adipose Tissue Activity.
text:
Renewed Interest in Brown Adipose Tissue: A Target for Metabolic Disease
Recent research has reignited enthusiasm for brown adipose tissue (BAT) as a potential solution for metabolic disorders, courtesy of the discovery of functional BAT in humans. In contrast to rodents, where BAT can be activated by bile acids, which activate type 2 iodothyronine deiodinase (D2) in BAT through the G-protein-coupled receptor TGR5, resulting in enhanced oxygen consumption and energy expenditure. To investigate the effects of oral supplementation with the bile acid chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) on human BAT activity, we examined the results of 12 healthy female subjects receiving CDCA for two days, which showed increased BAT activity and whole-body energy expenditure. In contrast, in vitro treatment of primary human brown adipocytes derived from CDCA or specific TGR5 agonists boosted mitochondrial uncoupling and D2 expression, a phenomenon that was absent in primary white adipocytes. These findings signify bile acids as a prime target for stimulating BAT in humans.

title: RNase H and Postreplication Repair Protect Cells from Ribonucleotides Incorporated in DNA
text: The integrity of the genome is put to the test when ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTPs) are incorporated in place of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) during replication. While DNA replicases exhibit selectivity towards dNTPs, the presence of rNTPs can lead to misincorporation. We discover that an accumulation of ribonucleoside monophosphates (rNMPs) in the genome triggers replication stress and has detrimental consequences, particularly when RNase H1 and RNase H2 are deficient. These enzymes remove rNMPs from the chromosomes. We find that postreplication repair (PRR) pathways-dependent on MMS2 and Pol ζ-are essential for countering the effects of rNMPs in the genome. Interestingly, Pol ζ can efficiently replicate over 1-4 rNMPs. Moreover, cells lacking RNase H accumulate mono- and polyubiquitylated PCNA and display a persistently activated PRR. Our findings highlight a crucial function for RNase H1, RNase H2, template switch, and translesion DNA synthesis in overcoming rNTPs incorporated during DNA replication. These insights may provide a mechanistic understanding of the pathogenesis of Aicardi-Goutières syndrome.

title: Selective elimination of high constitutive activity or chemokine binding in the human herpesvirus 8 encoded seven transmembrane oncogene ORF74.
text: Human herpesvirus 8-encoded Open Reading Frame 74 (ORF74) is a seven transmembrane (7TM) receptor that is highly active and responsive to angiogenic chemokines, such as growth-related oncogene-alpha. However, it is also subject to inhibition by angiostatic chemokines, such as interferon-gamma-inducible protein. Transgenic mice expressing ORF74 under the control of the CD2 promoter develop highly vascularized tumors resembling Kaposi's sarcoma. Through targeted mutagenesis, we generated three distinct forms of ORF74: a receptor with normal constitutive signaling but lacking chemokine binding and action, an ORF74 with high constitutive activity but selectively defeated by angiogenic chemokines, and an ORF74 lacking constitutive activity but able to be stimulated by agonist chemokines. These mutant forms can presumably be used in transgenic animals to elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying ORF74's transforming activity.

title: An insulin-like signaling pathway affects both longevity and reproduction in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: Mutations in the daf-2 and age-1 genes in Caenorhabditis elegans lead to a significant increase in lifespan as well as a developmental arrest at the dauer diapause stage. These genes encode components of an insulin-like signaling pathway, which acts at a similar point in the genetic epistasis pathway for dauer arrest and longevity. The daf-2 and age-1 genes regulate the activity of the daf-16 gene, and mutations in daf-16 cause a dauer-defective phenotype. In addition, weak daf-2 alleles and maternally rescued age-1 alleles that extend lifespan but do not arrest at the dauer stage also reduce fertility and viability. Furthermore, age-1(hx546) has reduced maternal and zygotic age-1 activity. DAF-16 mutations suppress all of the daf-2 and age-1 phenotypes, including dauer arrest, life span extension, reduced fertility, and viability defects. These findings demonstrate that insulin signaling, mediated by DAF-2 through the AGE-1 phosphatidylinositol-3-OH kinase, regulates reproduction and embryonic development, as well as dauer diapause and life span. Moreover, DAF-16 transduces these signals, indicating that the regulation of fertility, life span, and metabolism by an insulin-like signaling pathway is similar to the endocrine regulation of metabolism and fertility by mammalian insulin signaling.

title: Estimating prion concentration in fluids and tissues by quantitative PMCA
text: Prions, the protein-based pathogens responsible for prion diseases, can be identified with exceptional sensitivity through protein misfolding cyclic amplification (PMCA) technology. In this study, we outline a quantitative PMCA protocol to measure the minute levels of prions in biological samples. By employing this method, we determined the concentrations of misfolded prion protein (PrPSc) in the brains, spleens, blood, and urine of hamsters infected with scrapie.

title: Positional cloning of the APECED gene
text: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type I (APS 1, also known as APECED) is an autosomal-recessive disorder mapped to human chromosome 21q22.3 between markers D21S49 and D21S171 through linkage studies. We have recently identified a novel gene in this region, AIRE (autoimmune regulator), which encodes a protein consisting of transcription factor-like motifs, including two zinc-finger (PHD-finger) motifs, a proline-rich region, and three LXXLL motifs. Investigations of Swiss and Finnish APECED patients have revealed two mutations in this gene: a C→T substitution that substitutes a stop codon (TGA) for Arg 257 (CGA) and an A→G substitution that replaces the Lys 83 (AAG) with a Glu codon (GAG). The predominant mutation in Finnish APECED patients is the Arg257stop (R257X) mutation, which was detected in 10 of 12 examined alleles. These findings implicate the AIRE gene as the underlying cause of APECED. The discovery of the responsible gene should facilitate genetic testing and potential treatment for the disease, as well as broaden our understanding of the mechanisms behind autoimmune disorders in general.

title: AMP-Activated Protein Kinase: An Ubiquitous Signaling Pathway With Key Roles in the Cardiovascular System
text: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) plays a crucial role in maintaining cellular and systemic energy homeostasis. Over the past two decades, it has become evident that AMPK regulates a myriad of cellular functions and has distinct roles in cardiovascular tissues. AMPK regulates cardiac metabolism and contractile function, as well as promotes anticontractile, anti-inflammatory, and antiatherogenic actions in blood vessels. In this review, we discuss the role of AMPK in the cardiovascular system, including the molecular basis of genetic mutations that alter cardiac physiology and the proposed mechanisms by which AMPK influences vascular function under normal and abnormal conditions.

title: Differentiation of trophoblast stem cells into giant cells is triggered by p57/Kip2 inhibition of CDK1 activity.
text: During mammalian development, the process of genome endoreduplication is rare and its mechanism is unknown. However, recent studies have shed light on this process. When fibroblast growth factor 4 (FGF4) is deprived, trophoblast stem (TS) cells differentiate into non-proliferating trophoblast giant (TG) cells, which are essential for embryo implantation. Our findings show that inhibiting cyclin-dependent protein kinase 1 (CDK1) triggers differentiation of TS cells into TG cells. Interestingly, inhibition of CDK1 causes endoreduplication in embryonic stem cells, indicating that this enzyme plays a specific role in programmed polyploidization. In contrast, FGF4 deprivation in TS cells results in CDK1 inhibition through the overexpression of two CDK-specific inhibitors, p57/KIP2 and p21/CIP1. Mutant TS cells revealed that p57 is essential for endoreduplication by inhibiting CDK1, while p21 prevents the induction of apoptosis. Additionally, CDK2 is required for endoreduplication when CDK1 is inhibited. Notably, p57 expression is restricted to G-phase nuclei, allowing CDK activation of S phase. Therefore, endoreduplication in TS cells is triggered by p57 inhibition of CDK1, which is accompanied by the suppression of the DNA damage response by p21.

title: Atg5-independent autophagy regulates mitochondrial clearance and is essential for iPSC reprogramming
text: The generation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) is accompanied by a significant metabolic shift from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis during the reprogramming process. However, the underlying mechanism of this metabolic reprogramming remains unclear. Our findings indicate that an Atg5-independent autophagic process plays a crucial role in mitochondrial clearance, which is a key event involved in the metabolic switch. We discovered that inhibiting this autophagy process, but not canonical autophagy, impedes mitochondrial clearance, thereby preventing iPSC induction. Furthermore, our results suggest that AMPK is upstream of this autophagic pathway and can be targeted by small molecules to modulate mitochondrial clearance during metabolic reprogramming. Our study not only highlights the importance of Atg5-independent autophagy in establishing pluripotency, but also reveals a common metabolic switch between iPSC generation and tumorigenesis.

title: A mutation in Orai1 causes immune deficiency by abrogating CRAC channel function
text: The stimulation of immune cells with antigens triggers the influx of calcium ions (Ca2+) through release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels, which in turn activates the transcription factor NFAT and amplifies the immune response to pathogens. Previous studies have demonstrated that cells from patients suffering from one type of hereditary severe combined immune deficiency (SCID) syndrome are impaired in store-operated Ca2+ entry and CRAC channel function. To identify the underlying genetic defect in these patients, we employed a combination of two unbiased genome-wide approaches: a modified linkage analysis with single-nucleotide polymorphism arrays and a Drosophila RNA interference screen designed to identify regulators of store-operated Ca2+ entry and NFAT nuclear import. Both approaches converged on a novel protein called Orai1, which comprises four putative transmembrane segments. Further investigations revealed that SCID patients are homozygous for a single missense mutation in ORAI1, and the expression of wild-type Orai1 in SCID T cells restores store-operated Ca2+ influx and the CRAC current (ICRAC). Our findings suggest that Orai1 is a critical component or regulator of the CRAC channel complex, essential for proper immune function.

title: Estimates of global prevalence of childhood underweight in 1990 and 2015.
text:
The United Nations Millennium Development Goal is to reduce the prevalence of underweight among children under 5 years by half between 1990 and 2015. To estimate trends in childhood underweight by geographic regions, we conducted a time series analysis of prevalence data from 1965 to 2002 collected from 139 countries through the World Health Organization Global Database on Child Growth and Malnutrition. Our study found that:
* Globally, the prevalence of underweight is expected to decrease from 26.5% in 1990 to 17.6% in 2015, a change of -34% (95% CI: -43% to -23%).
* In developed countries, the prevalence is expected to decrease from 1.6% to 0.9%, a change of -41% (95% CI: -92% to 343%).
* In developing regions, the prevalence is expected to decline from 30.2% to 19.3%, a change of -36% (95% CI: -45% to -26%).
* In Africa, the prevalence of underweight is projected to increase from 24.0% to 26.8%, a change of 12% (95% CI: 8%-16%).
* In Asia, the prevalence is expected to decrease from 35.1% to 18.5%, a change of -47% (95% CI: -58% to -34%).
* Worldwide, the number of underweight children is expected to decline from 163.8 million in 1990 to 113.4 million in 2015, a change of -31% (95% CI: -40% to -20%).
* However, neither the world as a whole nor the developing regions are expected to achieve the Millennium Development Goals, mainly due to the deteriorating situation in Africa, where all subregions, except Northern Africa, are expected to fail to meet the goal.

In conclusion, there is an overall improvement in the global situation, but it is not expected to lead to achieving the Millennium Development Goals, particularly in Africa.

title: Canonical Wnt signaling regulates organ-specific assembly and differentiation of CNS vasculature.
text: Each organ in the body relies on a network of blood vessels for essential nutrients and oxygen. However, the vasculature associated with individual organs varies significantly in terms of structure and molecular composition. The vascular system of the central nervous system (CNS), for example, features a tightly sealed endothelium that forms a specialized barrier, known as the blood-brain barrier. In contrast, blood vessels of other organs are more porous. During the development of the CNS, two Wnt ligands, Wnt7a and Wnt7b, are produced by the neuroepithelium and directly target the vascular endothelium. Using genetic mouse models, we found that the CNS utilizes the canonical Wnt signaling pathway to promote the formation and differentiation of the organ's vasculature.

title: Bone progenitor dysfunction induces myelodysplasia and secondary leukemia
text: Mesenchymal cells play a crucial role in the 'stroma' of both normal and malignant tissues, with specific mesenchymal cell types involved in the regulatory niches of stem cells. By investigating how mesenchymal osteolineage cells modulate haematopoiesis, our study reveals that deleting Dicer1 specifically in mouse osteoprogenitors, but not in mature osteoblasts, disrupts the integrity of haematopoiesis. Myelodysplasia and acute myelogenous leukaemia resulting from this deletion had intact Dicer1, indicating that perturbation of specific mesenchymal subsets of stromal cells can perturb differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis in heterogeneous cells, leading to disrupted tissue homeostasis. Furthermore, our findings suggest that primary stromal dysfunction can give rise to secondary neoplastic disease, supporting the theory of niche-induced oncogenesis.

title: Generating diploid embryos from Xenopus tropicalis.
text: Xenopus tropicalis offers a remarkable advantage in the ease with which diploid embryos can be produced year-round. By administering human chorionic gonadotropin, an investigator can generate a large number of synchronized embryos through in vitro fertilization or a substantial quantity from a mating pair. This ability to induce ovulations on demand enables a wide range of experiments, including experimental embryology, molecular manipulation of gene products, and genetics.

title: Oct4-Induced Pluripotency in Adult Neural Stem Cells
text: Four transcription factors, Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc, can induce pluripotency in mouse and human fibroblasts. Previously, we identified that direct reprogramming of adult mouse neural stem cells (NSCs) can be achieved by co-expressing Oct4 and either Klf4 or c-Myc. Interestingly, NSCs endogenously express all four factors, along with other intermediate reprogramming markers. We now report that exogenous expression of Oct4 is sufficient to generate pluripotent stem cells from adult mouse NSCs. These one-factor induced pluripotent stem cells (1F iPS) are numerously comparable to embryonic stem cells in vitro and in vivo. Notably, these cells can be efficiently differentiated into NSCs, cardiomyocytes, and germ cells in vitro, as well as form teratomas and transmit germline in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that Oct4 is both required and sufficient to directly reprogram NSCs to pluripotency.

title: Getting started with yeast.
text:
Publisher Summary:
Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a type of yeast, has emerged as a versatile model organism due to its ease of genetic manipulation. Despite being a eukaryote, yeast boasts a relatively simple genetic makeup compared to other eukaryotes, making it an ideal system for molecular biology studies. The following properties contribute to yeast's suitability for research:
1. Rapid growth and cell dispersion for easy replica plating and mutant isolation.
2.well-defined genetic system, enabling the identification and manipulation of specific genes.
3. A highly versatile DNA transformation system, allowing for the introduction of foreign DNA into yeast cells.
4. The ability to transform yeast cells with plasmids carrying structural genes corresponding to any genetic trait.
5. Efficient homologous recombination, allowing researchers to direct cloned sequences to specific locations in the genome.
6. In contrast to other organisms, integrative recombination of transforming DNA in yeast occurs exclusively via homologous recombination.
7. Yeast's non-pathogenic nature makes handling the organism relatively safe.
8. Commercial availability of large quantities of normal baker's yeast, providing an affordable source for biochemical studies.
9. The development of DNA transformation techniques has made yeast particularly accessible to gene cloning and genetic engineering methods.
In summary, yeast's simplicity, ease of manipulation, and versatility make it an ideal model system for exploring genetic mechanisms and developing genetic engineering techniques.

title: PCNA functions as a molecular platform to trigger Cdt1 destruction and prevent re-replication
text: In metazoans, the proteolytic degradation of the replication licensing factor Cdt1 during S phase is a crucial mechanism that limits DNA replication to a single round per cell cycle. In Xenopus egg extracts, Cdt1 is destroyed on chromatin during DNA replication, and this process requires interaction with proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), a homotrimeric processivity factor for DNA polymerases. Cdt1 binds to PCNA through a conserved motif in all metazoans, and removing PCNA from egg extracts inhibits replication-dependent Cdt1 degradation. Mutation of the PCNA-interaction motif leads to a stabilized Cdt1 protein that induces re-replication. DDB1, a component of the Cul4 E3 ubiquitin ligase that mediates human Cdt1 proteolysis in response to DNA damage, is also required for replication-dependent Cdt1 degradation. Cdt1 and DDB1 interact in extracts, and DDB1 chromatin loading is dependent on the binding of Cdt1 to PCNA, suggesting that PCNA functions as a platform for Cdt1 destruction, ensuring efficient and temporally restricted inactivation of a key cell-cycle regulator.

title: Meiosis in Drosophila: seeing is believing.
text: Exciting breakthroughs have recently been made in our comprehension of Drosophila meiosis thanks to a combination of cytological and genetic techniques. New methods have enabled the characterization of chromosome position and spindle formation during female meiosis I. The proteins encoded by the nod and ncd genes, which are crucial for the proper segregation of chromosomes without exchange events, have been identified as kinesin-like motors. The effects of mutations in these genes on the spindle and chromosomes, as well as the localization of these proteins, have led to a mechanistic model of female meiosis I. In male meiosis I, the genomic regions responsible for homologous pairing have been resolved to specific DNA sequences, providing a foundation for elucidating the molecular basis of meiotic pairing. The cytological techniques available in Drosophila have also facilitated progress in understanding the regulation of sister-chromatid segregation. Recently, the genes mei-S332 and ord, which are essential for sister-chromatid cohesion, have been identified. Additional advances in Drosophila meiosis include the definition of a functional centromere through the use of minichromosome derivatives and the identification of several regulatory genes controlling the meiotic cell cycle.

title: Effect of physical activity on cognitive function in older adults at risk for Alzheimer disease: a randomized trial.
text: According to a randomized controlled trial conducted between 2004 and 2007 in metropolitan Perth, Western Australia, physical activity may help reduce the rate of cognitive decline among older adults at risk of dementia. The study randomly assigned 170 participants between the ages of 50 and 89 who reported memory problems but did not meet criteria for dementia to either an education and usual care group or a 24-week home-based physical activity program. The results showed that participants in the intervention group improved by 0.26 points on the Alzheimer Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog) over 18 months, while those in the usual care group deteriorated by 1.04 points. The absolute difference between the groups was -1.3 points. Additionally, participants in the intervention group improved by 0.73 points on the ADAS-Cog at the end of the intervention, while those in the usual care group improved by 0.04 points. Word list delayed recall and Clinical Dementia Rating sum of boxes also improved modestly, while word list total immediate recall, digit symbol coding, verbal fluency, Beck depression score, and Medical Outcomes 36-Item Short-Form physical and mental component summaries did not change significantly. Overall, the study suggests that a 6-month program of physical activity may provide a modest improvement in cognition over an 18-month follow-up period.

title: Variants at 6q21 implicate PRDM1 in the etiology of therapy-induced second malignancies after Hodgkin's lymphoma
text: Individuals who survived pediatric Hodgkin's lymphoma are at risk of developing secondary malignant neoplasms (SMNs) due to radiation therapy. We discovered two variants at chromosome 6q21 that are associated with SMNs in children treated with radiation therapy but not in adults. These variants are located near the PRDM1 gene, which codes for a protein involved in regulating cell growth and differentiation. Our findings indicate that a new gene-exposure interaction may play a role in the development of SMNs after radiation exposure, specifically involving the PRDM1 protein.

title: Long non-coding RNA profiling of human lymphoid progenitor cells reveals transcriptional divergence of B cell and T cell lineages
text: To investigate the transcriptional landscape that regulates human lymphoid cell development during postnatal life, we employed RNA sequencing to identify long non-coding transcripts (lncRNAs) across human bone marrow and thymic progenitor cells at the earliest stages of B lymphoid and T lymphoid cell specification. Our analysis revealed over 3,000 novel lncRNAs, underscoring the importance of these non-coding RNAs in regulating human lymphoid commitment. LncRNA expression patterns were found to be highly stage-specific and more lineage-specific than protein-coding genes, unveiling a complex regulatory network that shapes the developmental trajectory of lymphoid cells. Remarkably, protein-coding genes co-expressed with neighboring lncRNA genes were found to be enriched in ontologies related to lymphoid differentiation, underscoring the functional interplay between these two types of transcripts. Our study reveals an exquisite cell-type specificity in global lncRNA expression patterns, which in turn reveals new developmental relationships among the earliest progenitor cells in the human bone marrow and thymus.

title: The VTI family of SNARE proteins is necessary for plant viability and mediates different protein transport pathways.
text: The Arabidopsis genome houses a clan of V-SNAREs: VTI11, VTI12, and VTI13. Only VTI11 and VTI12 are expressed at appreciable levels. Although these two proteins share 60% similarity, they complement distinct transport pathways when expressed in the yeast vti1 mutant. Recent studies revealed that VTI11 was the mutated gene in the shoot gravitropic mutant zig. Our findings indicate that the vti11 zig mutant exhibits defects in vascular patterning and auxin transport. An Arabidopsis T-DNA insertion mutant, vti12, displayed a normal phenotype under standard growth conditions. However, under nutrient-poor conditions, vti12 exhibited an accelerated senescence phenotype, suggesting that VTI12 may participate in the plant autophagy pathway. VTI11 and VTI12 could substitute for each other in their respective SNARE complexes, and a double-mutant cross between zig and vti12 was lethal in embryos. These results suggest that some VTI1 protein is required for plant viability, and the two proteins display partial functional redundancy.

title: CLASPs link focal adhesion-associated microtubule capture to localized exocytosis and adhesion site turnover
text: The disassembly of integrin-based focal adhesions (FAs) with the extracellular matrix (ECM) is crucial for coordinated cell migration. In migrating human keratinocytes, FAs form near the leading edge, mature through contractile forces, and then disassemble as the cell body advances. We have found that the clustering of microtubule-associated proteins CLASP1 and CLASP2 around FAs occurs temporally with FA turnover. CLASPs, along with the protein LL5β (also known as PHLDB2), facilitate the disassembly of FAs by recruiting proteins that help break the connections between the cell and the ECM. In addition, CLASPs are required for the degradation of ECM components associated with FAs, and inhibition of matrix metalloproteases slows FA disassembly to a similar extent as when CLASPs or LL5β are depleted. Furthermore, our findings suggest that CLASPs establish a local secretion pathway that facilitates FA turnover by severing cell-matrix connections. This pathway involves the coupling of microtubule organization, vesicle transport, and cell interactions with the ECM, allowing for the efficient delivery, docking, and fusion of exocytic vesicles near FAs.

title: CHD4 Is a RanGTP-Dependent MAP that Stabilizes Microtubules and Regulates Bipolar Spindle Formation
text:
Introduction:
The production of GTP-bound Ran GTPase around chromosomes triggers spindle assembly by activating proteins with nuclear localization signals (NLS). Despite identifying several NLS proteins as spindle assembly factors, we sought to investigate additional proteins with distinct roles in spindle assembly.
Results:
We have discovered a chromatin-remodeling ATPase, CHD4, as a RanGTP-dependent microtubule (MT)-associated protein (MAP). MT binding occurs through the NLS-containing region and chromatin-binding domains. In Xenopus egg extracts and cultured cells, CHD4 dissociates from mitotic chromosomes and partially localizes to the spindle. Depletion of CHD4 from egg extracts significantly reduces the amount of MTs around chromatin and prevents spindle assembly. Furthermore, RNAi-mediated depletion of CHD4 in HeLa and Drosophila S2 cells leads to defects in spindle assembly and chromosome alignment, resulting in chromosome missegregation. Our findings reveal that CHD4 is a RanGTP-dependent MT stabilizer, and it promotes the organization of MTs into bipolar spindles in egg extracts. Importantly, this function of CHD4 is independent of chromatin remodeling.
Conclusion:
Our study uncovers a novel role for CHD4 as a MAP vital for MT stabilization and spindle bipolarity. This discovery expands our understanding of the complex process of spindle assembly and provides insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying chromosome segregation during cell division.

title: Myocardial muscarinic receptor upregulation and normal response to isoproterenol in denervated hearts by familial amyloid polyneuropathy.
text:
INTRODUCTION: Familial amyloid polyneuropathy (FAP) is a rare hereditary disorder that affects the autonomic nervous system, resulting in progressive neurological symptoms. While heart failure is not a common complication of FAP, patients are at increased risk of sudden death, conduction disturbances, and adverse events during anesthesia. Despite the well-known cardiac sympathetic denervation in FAP, the post-synaptic status of the cardiac autonomic nervous system remains unclear.
METHODS: In this study, we evaluated the density and affinity of myocardial muscarinic receptors in 21 patients with FAP (age: 39±11 years; normal coronary arteries; left ventricular ejection fraction: 68±9%) using positron emission tomography (PET) with (11)C-MQNB, a specific hydrophilic antagonist. We also assessed cardiac beta-receptor functional efficiency by measuring the heart rate (HR) response to intravenous infusions of isoproterenol.
RESULTS: Our findings revealed higher myocardial muscarinic receptor density in patients with FAP compared to healthy controls (B'(max): 35.5±8.9 versus 26.1±6.7 pmol/mL; P=0.003), without alterations in receptor affinity. However, the HR response to atropine was blunted in patients with FAP, indicating parasympathetic denervation. Notably, incremental infusions of isoproterenol induced a similar increase in HR in both patient and control groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study demonstrates that cardiac autonomic denervation in FAP leads to an upregulation of myocardial muscarinic receptors, which may contribute to the increased risk of adverse events during anesthesia. However, there is no change in cardiac beta-receptor responsiveness to catecholamines, suggestive of preserved cardiac sympathetic innervation. These findings provide new insights into the neural regulation of the cardiovascular system in FAP and may have clinical implications for anesthetic management in these patients.

title: 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase links oxidative PPP, lipogenesis and tumor growth by inhibiting LKB1-AMPK signaling
text:
The oxidative pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) has been linked to tumor growth, but the specific contribution of 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (6PGD), the third enzyme in this pathway, to tumorigenesis remains unclear. Our study found that suppressing 6PGD resulted in decreased lipogenesis and RNA biosynthesis, and increased ROS levels in cancer cells, thereby attenuating cell proliferation and tumor growth.
We discovered that 6PGD-mediated production of ribulose-5-phosphate (Ru-5-P) inhibits AMPK activation by disrupting the active LKB1 complex, leading to increased acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 and lipogenesis. Ru-5-P and NADPH, the precursors of RNA biosynthesis and lipogenesis, respectively, reveal an additional link between the oxidative PPP and lipogenesis. Our findings suggest that 6PGD could be a potential anticancer target.
To explore this opportunity, we identified and developed specific 6PGD inhibitors, physcion and its derivative S3, which effectively inhibited 6PGD, cancer cell proliferation, and tumor growth in nude mice xenografts without significant toxicity. These results support the potential of targeting 6PGD in cancer treatment.

title: Plant Nuclear RNA Polymerase IV Mediates siRNA and DNA Methylation-Dependent Heterochromatin Formation
text: All eukaryotes possess three DNA-dependent RNA polymerases (Pol I, II, and III) that are crucial for transcribing genetic material. Surprisingly, plant species have a fourth nuclear polymerase, Pol IV, which is accompanied by distinct catalytic subunits. While Pol IV is not essential for viability, its dysfunction leads to impaired association of heterochromatin into chromocenters and results in losses of cytosine methylation at specific genetic loci, including pericentromeric 5S gene clusters and AtSN1 retroelements. Remarkably, Pol IV interacts with a methyltransferase involved in RNA-directed de novo methylation, suggesting a partnership between the two enzymes in the methylation process. Consistently, the elimination of 5S gene and AtSN1 siRNAs in Pol IV mutants supports the hypothesis that Pol IV helps generate siRNAs that target de novo cytosine methylation events crucial for the formation of facultative and higher-order heterochromatin structures.

title: Sema3A regulates bone-mass accrual through sensory innervations
text: Semaphorin 3A (Sema3A) is a diffusible axonal chemorepellent that plays a crucial role in axon guidance. Prior studies have shown that Sema3a-deficient mice exhibit various developmental defects due to abnormal neuronal innervations. Our study demonstrates that Sema3A is extensively expressed in bone and affects osteoblast differentiation in a cell-autonomous manner, leading to reduced bone mass in Sema3a-deficient mice. Interestingly, osteoblast-specific Sema3A-deficient mice (Sema3acol1-/− and Sema3aosx-/− mice) retained normal bone mass despite decreased Sema3A expression in bone, suggesting that neuron-derived Sema3A is responsible for the observed bone abnormalities. Indeed, the number of sensory innervations in trabecular bone was significantly decreased in Sema3asynapsin-/− mice, while sympathetic innervations remained unchanged. Moreover, ablating sensory nerves in wild-type mice led to decreased bone mass, while leaving the low bone mass unchanged in Sema3anestin-/− mice, indicating the critical role of the sensory nervous system in maintaining normal bone homeostasis. Furthermore, our study revealed that neuronal abnormalities in Sema3a-deficient mice, such as olfactory development, are also observed in Sema3asynapsin-/− mice, suggesting that neuron-derived Sema3A regulates neural development in an autocrine manner. Our findings demonstrate that Sema3A regulates bone remodeling indirectly by modulating sensory nerve development, but not directly by acting on osteoblasts.

title: Direct lineage reprogramming: strategies, mechanisms, and applications.
text:
The direct conversion of one specialized cell type into another using defined factors has revolutionized traditional concepts of epigenetic stability in differentiated cells. With the exponential increase in cell types generated through direct conversion in recent years, this strategy has emerged as a promising approach for producing functional cells. Here, we provide an update on recent advances in lineage reprogramming, including:
1. Identification of novel reprogramming factors: Researchers have identified new factors that can be used to induce lineage reprogramming, expanding the repertoire of known reprogramming factors.
2. Molecular mechanisms underlying reprogramming: Studies have shed light on the complex molecular mechanisms involved in lineage reprogramming, including epigenetic changes and the resetting of gene expression.
3. Strategies for generating functionally mature cells: Researchers have developed new methods for generating functionally mature cells through lineage reprogramming, including the use of small molecules and other therapeutic agents.
4. Assays for characterizing induced cells: various assays have been developed to assess the success of lineage reprogramming and the functionality of induced cells, including functional assays and gene expression profiling.
5. Progress toward application of lineage reprogramming: Researchers are making rapid progress toward applying lineage reprogramming to a variety of cell types, including stem cells, and there is great potential for this strategy to be used in regenerative medicine.
6. Major future challenges for lineage reprogramming: Despite the significant advances in lineage reprogramming, there are still major challenges to overcome before this strategy can be widely applied, including the potential for unwanted side effects and the difficulty of generating functional cells in large quantities.

title: Converging Intracranial Markers of Conscious Access
text: In a recent study, we investigated the difference in conscious and nonconscious processing of briefly flashed words by employing a visual masking procedure while recording intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) in ten patients. We observed that nonconscious processing of masked words occurred in various cortical areas within an early time frame (less than 300 milliseconds), accompanied by increased gamma-band activity without detectable long-distance neural activity, suggesting a rapidly dissipating feedforward wave. In contrast, conscious processing of unmasked words showed the convergence of four distinct neurophysiological markers, including sustained voltage changes in the prefrontal cortex, significant increases in gamma-band spectral power, increases in long-distance phase synchrony in the beta range, and increases in long-range Granger causality. These findings provide valuable insights into the neural correlates of conscious access and have important implications for current theoretical discussions on the subject.

title: Hyperglycemia is associated with increased bone mineral density and decreased trabecular bone score in elderly Japanese men: The Fujiwara-kyo osteoporosis risk in men (FORMEN) study.
text:
Study Objective:
The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between glycemic and insulin resistance status, bone microarchitecture, and the roles of pentosidine and bone turnover markers in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
Study Design:
This study was a cross-sectional analysis of 1683 community-dwelling men aged 65 years or older. Participants underwent measurements of bone mineral density (aBMD) and bone microarchitecture, as well as assessments of glycemic and insulin resistance status, bone turnover markers, and pentosidine levels.
Results:
Compared to men without T2DM, those with T2DM had higher aBMD but no significant difference in trabecular bone score (TBS). However, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), and homeostasis model assessment-insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) levels were significantly inversely correlated with TBS after adjusting for age, body mass index (BMI), and aBMD. Multivariate linear regression analyses revealed that glycemic indices, including FPG and HbA1c, were associated with increased aBMD and decreased TBS, while HOMA-IR was associated only with TBS. These associations did not change after further adjusting for bone turnover markers and pentosidine levels.
Conclusion:
The study found that hyperglycemia and elevated insulin resistance were negatively associated with TBS in patients with T2DM, independent of bone turnover and pentosidine levels. These findings suggest that hypoxic and inflammatory effects of hyperglycemia on bone may play a role in the increased fracture risk observed in patients with T2DM.

title: Matrix Remodeling Promotes Pulmonary Hypertension through Feedback Mechanoactivation of the YAP/TAZ-miR-130/301 Circuit.
text: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a complex and life-threatening condition with unknown molecular causes. We discovered that changes in the blood vessels in the lungs lead to PH. In different types of lung blood cells, these changes caused the production of certain proteins that promote the buildup of collagen. This buildup makes the blood vessels stiff and narrow, which can lead to high blood pressure in the lungs. We found that a specific group of proteins, called microRNA-130/301, play a key role in this process. These proteins control the production of other proteins that affect the blood vessels, and together they create a feedback loop that worsens the condition. By targeting these proteins with drugs, we can slow down or stop the progression of PH. Overall, our findings suggest that understanding the molecular mechanisms of PH could lead to new and effective treatments for this deadly disease.

title: Exosomal transfer of stroma-derived miR21 confers paclitaxel resistance in ovarian cancer cells through targeting APAF1
text: Advanced ovarian cancer typically spreads to the visceral adipose tissue of the omentum. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the growth of ovarian cancer cells in this tissue have remained largely unexplored. Here, we leverage next-generation sequencing technology to investigate the ovarian cancer-associated adipocytes (CAAs) and fibroblasts (CAFs) that infiltrate the omentum. Our findings reveal significantly higher levels of microRNA-21 (miR21) isomiRNAs in exosomes and tissue lysates isolated from CAAs and CAFs compared to ovarian cancer cells. Functional studies demonstrate that miR21 is transferred from CAAs or CAFs to the cancer cells, where it suppresses ovarian cancer apoptosis and confers chemoresistance by binding to its direct novel target, APAF1. These findings suggest that the malignant phenotype of metastatic ovarian cancer cells can be altered by miR21 delivered by exosomes derived from neighboring stromal cells in the omental tumor microenvironment. Importantly, these data also support the idea that inhibiting the transfer of stromal-derived miR21 may provide an alternative therapeutic strategy for the treatment of metastatic and recurrent ovarian cancer.

title: Age-related changes in kynurenic acid production in rat brain.
text: Two independent in vitro assays were conducted to investigate the biosynthesis of the broad-spectrum excitatory amino acid receptor antagonist kynurenic acid (KYNA) throughout the lifespan of the adult rat. The enzyme kynurenine aminotransferase, which plays a crucial role in KYNA's anabolism, was found to exhibit steady increases between 3-24 months of age in all five examined brain regions. Unexpectedly, no changes were observed in the liver. The most notable increases were observed in the cortex and striatum, where enzyme activity rose threefold over the course of the study. In addition, KYNA production from its bioprecursor L-kynurenine was investigated in tissue slices and found to be significantly enhanced in the cortex and hippocampus of old animals. Interestingly, the effect of depolarizing agents or sodium replacement was virtually identical in tissues from young and old rats. These findings, which are consistent with previous reports of an age-dependent increase in KYNA concentration in brain tissue, suggest an enhanced KYNA tone in the aged brain. This, combined with the documented decline in excitatory amino acid receptor densities with age, suggests that increased KYNA production may contribute to cognitive and memory dysfunction in old animals.

title: The polycomb group protein Suz12 is required for embryonic stem cell differentiation.
text: Polycomb group (PcG) proteins form complexes called Polycomb repressive complexes (PRCs), which contain PcG proteins EZH2, SUZ12, and EED. PRC2 specifically represses transcription by methylating lysine 27 of histone H3 (H3K27me3). SUZ12 is crucial for PRC2's activity, and its inactivation leads to embryonic lethality in mice. Interestingly, we were able to establish and expand Suz12-deficient mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells in culture. These cells display a global loss of H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) and increased expression of differentiation-specific genes. Moreover, Suz12-deficient ES cells exhibit impaired proper differentiation, characterized by reduced repression of ES cell markers and overexpression of differentiation-specific genes. Furthermore, we found that PcGs are actively recruited to specific genes during ES cell differentiation, despite an increase in H3K27me3 levels. This suggests that PcGs have multiple mechanisms to regulate transcription during cellular differentiation. In summary, our results demonstrate that Suz12 is crucial for establishing specific expression programs necessary for ES cell differentiation. Additionally, we provide evidence that PcGs employ different strategies to regulate gene expression during differentiation.

title: The 1.9 A structure of a proteasome-11S activator complex and implications for proteasome-PAN/PA700 interactions.
text: Proteasomes are cylindrical structures that play a crucial role in various cellular processes by degrading a wide range of cytosolic and nuclear proteins. The catalytic chamber of proteasomes is sealed and protected by axial pores, which are opened by activator complexes to allow substrate access and product release. Recent studies have provided high-resolution structures of wild-type and mutant archaeal proteasomes bound to the activator PA26, which support the notion that an ordered open conformation is essential for proteolysis. These findings also reveal the mechanism of binding, which involves an interaction between the PA26 C terminus and a conserved lysine residue. Interestingly, biochemical assays suggest that this interaction is not unique to PA26, but is also observed with other activators, including PAN and PA700, which are unrelated to each other and ATP-dependent.

title: Innate Immune and Chemically Triggered Oxidative Stress Modifies Translational Fidelity
text: Protein and cell function require high fidelity tRNA aminoacylation, which is accurately transferred by purified aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases with a fidelity of 1 error per 10,000-100,000 couplings. However, the accuracy of tRNA aminoacylation in vivo is uncertain and might be significantly lower, with approximately 1% of methionine (Met) residues used in protein synthesis being misacylated to non-methionyl-tRNAs in mammalian cells. This misacylation increases up to 10fold upon exposure to live or non-infectious viruses, toll-like receptor ligands, or chemically induced oxidative stress. Specifically, Met is misacylated to specific non-methionyl-tRNA families, which are then used in translation. The misacylation is blocked by an inhibitor of cellular oxidases, indicating that reactive oxygen species (ROS) are the misacylation trigger. Of the six amino acids tested, misacylation occurs exclusively with Met, highlighting its importance in protecting proteins against ROS-mediated damage. As Met residues protect proteins against oxidative stress, we propose that Met-misacylation functions adaptively to increase Met incorporation into proteins to protect cells against oxidative stress. Our findings demonstrate the importance of considering alternative iterations of the genetic code and provide new insights into the mechanisms of protein synthesis and cellular defense.

title: Yeast sirtuins and the regulation of aging.
text: The sirtuins are a group of evolutionarily conserved enzymes that rely on NAD+ to deacetylate protein lysine side chains. Based on their dependency on NAD+, sirtuins may be susceptible to changes in NAD+ levels or the production of intermediates, thereby connecting them to cellular metabolism. The Sir2 protein from Saccharomyces cerevisiae is an early member of the sirtuin family and has been well characterized as both a histone deacetylase responsible for the silencing of heterochromatin domains and an advocate for longevity. Deleting SIR2 shortens the replicative life span (RLS), whereas increased gene dosage extends it. Sir2 has also been linked to the beneficial effects of caloric restriction (CR) on life span across various organisms, including yeast and higher eukaryotes. While this theory has faced criticism and debate, it has also propelled the aging research field forward. S. cerevisiae has four additional sirtuin homologs, Hst1, Hst2, Hst3, and Hst4. This review explores the functions of Sir2 and Hst proteins in both replicative and chronological aging, as well as their regulation in response to environmental stressors, such as CR.

title: The effect of combination treatment with aliskiren and blockers of the renin-angiotensin system on hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury: systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Objective:
To assess the safety of using aliskiren in combination with agents that block the renin-angiotensin system through a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Design:
A systematic search of Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and two trial registries yielded randomized controlled trials published up to May 7, 2011.
Study Selection:
Randomized controlled trials that compared combined treatment with aliskiren and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers to monotherapy with these agents for at least four weeks, providing numerical data on adverse event outcomes of hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury.
Data Synthesis:
Examining 10 randomized controlled studies (4814 participants), we found that combination therapy with aliskiren and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers significantly increased the risk of hyperkalaemia compared to monotherapy using angiotensin converting enzymes or angiotensin receptor blockers (relative risk 1.58, 95% CI: 1.24-2.02) or aliskiren alone (1.67, 95% CI: 1.01-2.79). The risk of acute kidney injury did not differ significantly between the combined therapy and monotherapy groups (1.14, 95% CI: 0.68-1.89).
Conclusion:
Our findings suggest that the concurrent use of aliskiren and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers is associated with an increased risk for hyperkalaemia. Combination therapy warrants careful monitoring of serum potassium levels.

title: The ins and outs of DNA transfer in bacteria.
text: The processes of transformation and conjugation enable the transfer of genetic information between bacterial cells or between bacterial and eukaryotic cells, and are, therefore, crucial for the spread of beneficial traits, including antibiotic resistance. Both processes involve the recognition of double-stranded DNA followed by the transfer of single strands. Sophisticated molecular machineries are responsible for facilitating the movement of large DNA molecules through the layers of the cell surface. Up to now, most of the components of these machineries have been identified, and here, we present detailed models of their roles in DNA transport.

title: Synaptic islands defined by the territory of a single astrocyte.
text: In the mammalian brain, astrocytes play a crucial role in neuronal function by synchronizing neuronal firing and coordinating synaptic networks. However, the structural basis of these processes is not well understood. To investigate, we studied the three-dimensional relationships between cortical astrocytes and neurons in the brain. Using a transgenic and viral approach to label astrocytes with enhanced green fluorescent protein, we reconstructed astrocyte structures from tissue sections or live animals in vivo. Our findings revealed that cortical astrocytes occupy distinct territories in the cortex, with each astrocyte wrapping around an average of four to eight neuronal somata. Additionally, we found that a single astrocyte connects with approximately 300 to 600 neuronal dendrites. These observations, combined with recent studies showing that glial Ca2+ signaling is restricted to individual astrocytes in vivo and leads to gliotransmission, suggest the concept of functional islands of synapses within the boundaries of individual astrocytes. These islands of synapses are modulated by the gliotransmitter environment controlled by each astrocyte. Our findings provide a new structurally based conceptual framework for understanding the interactions between neurons and astrocytes in the mammalian brain, and offer avenues for investigating these important neuronal functions.

title: Role of DNA Methylation and Epigenetic Silencing of HAND2 in Endometrial Cancer Development
text:
The rising incidence of endometrial cancer, fueled by the aging and obesity epidemics, highlights the need to understand the environmental and lifestyle factors that contribute to its development. Emerging evidence suggests that epigenetic modifications play a crucial role in this process. This study aimed to investigate the functional significance of epigenetic alterations in endometrial cancer.
Using epigenome-wide methylation analysis, we identified HAND2, a gene encoding a transcription factor expressed in the endometrial stroma, as one of the most commonly hypermethylated genes in endometrial cancer. This finding was validated using candidate gene methylation analysis in multiple clinical sample sets. Furthermore, we found that increased HAND2 methylation was associated with decreased RNA and protein expression, and was seen in premalignant endometrial lesions. Moreover, women with high HAND2 methylation in their premalignant lesions were less likely to respond to progesterone treatment.
In a novel integrative epigenome-transcriptome-interactome analysis, HAND2 emerged as the hub of the most highly ranked differential methylation hotspot in endometrial cancer. Moreover, mice lacking Hand2 specifically in their endometrium developed precancerous endometrial lesions with increasing age, and these lesions also showed a lack of PTEN expression.
Our findings suggest that HAND2 methylation may serve as a useful biomarker for early detection of endometrial cancer and as a predictor of treatment response. However, further validation in prospective studies is required to fully establish the clinical utility of HAND2 DNA methylation.
In summary, this study uncovers the critical role of epigenetic alterations in endometrial cancer development and highlights the potential of HAND2 methylation as a biomarker for early detection and treatment monitoring.

title: Socioeconomic factors, material inequalities, and perceived control in self-rated health: cross-sectional data from seven post-communist countries.
text: This study investigated the relationship between perceived control, socioeconomic variables, and self-reported health in seven post-communist countries (Russia, Estonia, Lithuania, Latvia, Hungary, Poland, and Czech Republic). The study collected data through questionnaire interviews on self-reported health, education, marital status, perceived control based on nine questions, and material deprivation based on access to food, clothing, and heating. The study analyzed data from 5330 men and women aged 20-60. The prevalence of poor health (worse than average) ranged from 8% in the Czechs to 19% in the Hungarians. The age-sex-adjusted odds ratio for university versus primary education was 0.36 (0.26-0.49). The odds ratio per 1 standard deviation increase in perceived control and material deprivation was 0.58 (95% CI 0.48-0.69) and 1.51 (1.40-1.63), respectively. The odds ratio for an increase in inequality equivalent to the difference between the most and the least unequal populations was 1.49 (0.88-2.52) using the material inequality score and 1.41 (0.91-2.20) using the Gini coefficient. After adjusting for individuals' deprivation or perceived control, the effects of both ecological measures of inequality were eliminated. The study found that, as in Western populations, education and material deprivation are strongly related to self-reported health. Perceived control appeared to mediate some of the effects of material deprivation.

title: Integrin αvβ3/c-src “Oncogenic Unit” Promotes Anchorage-independence and Tumor Progression
text: Integrins play a crucial role in regulating the growth, survival, and invasion of tumor cells, with the expression of integrin alpha(v)beta(3) being associated with the progression of various human tumors. Our study reveals a novel, adhesion-independent function of alpha(v)beta(3) integrins in pancreatic cancer and other carcinomas. Specifically, we found that alpha(v)beta(3) expression in carcinoma cells enhances tumor growth in vitro and increases lymph node metastasis in vivo through the recruitment of c-Src to the beta(3) integrin cytoplasmic tail, leading to c-Src activation, Crk-associated substrate (CAS) phosphorylation, and tumor cell survival. This activity is unexpectedly independent of cell adhesion or focal adhesion kinase (FAK) activation. Further investigation using pharmacological blockade of c-Src kinase activity or decreased expression of endogenous alpha(v)beta(3) integrin or c-Src reveals that these manipulations not only inhibit anchorage-independent growth but also suppress metastasis in vivo without affecting tumor cell migration or invasion. These findings highlight an unexpected role for integrins as mediators of anchorage independence, suggesting that an alpha(v)beta(3)-c-Src signaling module may underlie the aggressive behavior of integrin alpha(v)beta(3)-expressing tumors in humans.

title: Genomewide Analysis of PRC1 and PRC2 Occupancy Identifies Two Classes of Bivalent Domains
text: In embryonic stem (ES) cells, overlapping regions of bivalent chromatin, marked by histone modifications H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) and H3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3), are found on the promoters of more than 2,000 genes. To gain insights into the structure and function of these regions, we used chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by ultra high-throughput sequencing (ChIP-seq) to map histone modifications and subunits of Polycomb-repressive complexes 1 and 2 (PRC1 and PRC2) genomewide in human and mouse ES cells. Our findings revealed that bivalent domains can be divided into two classes: those occupied by both PRC2 and PRC1 (PRC1-positive) and those specifically bound by PRC2 (PRC2-only). PRC1-positive bivalent domains appear functionally distinct, as they more efficiently retain H3K27me3 upon differentiation, show greater conservation of chromatin state, and are closely associated with a large number of developmental regulator gene promoters. Additionally, we used computational genomics to identify sequence determinants of Polycomb binding. Our analysis revealed that the locations of PRC2 and PRC1 can be predicted based on the locations, sizes, and underlying motif contents of CpG islands. We propose that large CpG islands depleted of activating motifs maintain epigenetic memory by recruiting the full repertoire of Polycomb complexes in pluripotent cells.

title: Spatiotemporal regulation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition is essential for squamous cell carcinoma metastasis.
text: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is implicated in the transformation of stationary epithelial tumor cells into mobile mesenchymal cells during metastasis, but the involvement of EMT in metastasis remains controversial due to the lack of a mesenchymal phenotype in human carcinoma metastases. We used a spontaneous squamous cell carcinoma mouse model to demonstrate that the activation of the EMT-inducing transcription factor Twist1 is sufficient to prompt carcinoma cells to undergo EMT and disseminate into the bloodstream. Notably, in distant sites, reversing Twist1 activity to allow for the reversion of EMT is crucial for disseminated tumor cells to proliferate and form metastases. Our results provide in vivo evidence of the requirement for "reversible EMT" in tumor metastasis and may help clarify the debate on the significance of EMT in carcinoma metastasis.

title: Control of Apoptosis by Asymmetric Cell Division
text: Two crucial biological processes, asymmetric cell division and programmed cell death (apoptosis), are essential for the development and function of multi-celled organisms. We have found that these processes are interconnected, with asymmetric cell division in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans being mediated by a pathway involving three genes: dnj-11 MIDA1, ces-2 HLF, and ces-1 Snail. These genes control the enzymatic machinery responsible for apoptosis. Interestingly, related proteins, including GlsA from the alga Volvox carteri and Snail, Escargot, and Worniu from Drosophila melanogaster, have been implicated in asymmetric cell division. Therefore, we propose that the C. elegans pathway may be a conserved mechanism across the plant and animal kingdoms. Moreover, based on our findings, we suggest that this pathway directly regulates the apoptotic fate in C. elegans, and potentially in other organisms as well.

title: CXCR2 mediates NADPH oxidase–independent neutrophil extracellular trap formation in cystic fibrosis airway inflammation
text: Upon activation, neutrophils release DNA fibers coated with anti-microbial proteins, forming neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). While NETs are beneficial in innate immune defense, excessive NET formation has been linked to the development of autoinflammatory diseases. However, the regulatory mechanisms of NET formation during chronic inflammation are not well understood. This study investigates the role of the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) CXCR2 in NET formation. Our findings show that CXCR2 mediates NET formation independently of NADPH oxidase and involves Src family kinases. We demonstrate the significance of this mechanism in cystic fibrosis lung disease, a condition characterized by chronic neutrophilic inflammation. We observed abundant NETs in the airway fluids of cystic fibrosis patients and mice with cystic fibrosis lung disease, and the amounts of NETs correlated with impaired lung function. Blocking CXCR2 in the lungs using small-molecule antagonists inhibited NET formation and improved lung function in vivo without affecting neutrophil migration, proteolytic activity, or bacterial clearance. These findings establish CXCR2 as a receptor mediating NADPH oxidase-independent NET formation and provide evidence that targeting this pathway is a promising therapeutic strategy for cystic fibrosis lung disease.

title: Modelling the Impact of Artemisinin Combination Therapy and Long-Acting Treatments on Malaria Transmission Intensity
text:
Introduction:
Malaria is a major public health problem in many parts of the world, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) have been introduced as first-line treatments for uncomplicated malaria in many regions, as they have been shown to significantly lower patient infectiousness and have the potential to reduce population-level transmission of the parasite. However, the impact of ACT and other antimalarial drugs on transmission outcomes can vary depending on factors such as the level of transmission intensity in the area, the efficacy of the drugs, and the duration of the prophylactic effect.
To better understand the potential impact of ACT and other antimalarial drugs on transmission outcomes, a mathematical model was developed to predict the potential reduction in transmission that may be achieved by introducing different types of treatment for symptomatic Plasmodium falciparum malaria in endemic areas. The model combined data from a cross-sectional survey of 5,667 individuals conducted prior to policy change from sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine to ACT with independent estimates of the effects of ACT and other drug types on gametocytaemia and infectiousness to mosquitoes from clinical trial data.
Findings:
The results of the study suggest that ACTs have the potential for transmission reductions approaching those achieved by insecticide-treated nets in lower-transmission settings. However, the absolute number of clinical episodes averted through treatment with ACT was highest in the areas with low initial transmission, with a 53% reduction in prevalence of infection seen in the area with the lowest baseline slide-prevalence (3.7%) compared to an 11% reduction in the highest-transmission setting (baseline slide prevalence = 57.1%). In addition, reducing presumptive treatment through improved diagnosis substantially reduced the number of treatment courses required per clinical episode averted in lower-transmission settings, although there was some loss of overall impact on transmission.
Interestingly, an efficacious antimalarial regimen with no specific gametocytocidal properties but a long prophylactic time was estimated to be more effective at reducing transmission than a short-acting ACT in the highest-transmission setting. This suggests that the duration of the prophylactic effect may be an important factor in determining the overall impact of a particular treatment regimen on transmission outcomes.

title: Systems metabolic engineering of Escherichia coli for L-threonine production
text: Amino acid producers have historically been developed through random mutagenesis due to the complexity and strict regulation of the metabolic network. However, we have successfully utilized systems metabolic engineering to create a genetically defined Escherichia coli strain overproducing L-threonine. By removing feedback inhibitions of aspartokinase I and III (thrA and lysC) and transcriptional attenuation regulations (thrL), we enabled enhanced Thr biosynthesis. Additionally, pathways for Thr degradation were eliminated by deleting tdh and mutating ilvA, and the metA and lysA genes were deleted to increase the availability of precursors for Thr synthesis. Our strategy involves transcriptome profiling combined with in silico flux response analysis to identify and manipulate additional target genes for engineering. We constructed an engineered E. coli strain capable of producing Thr at a high yield of 0.393 g/g glucose and 82.4 g/l Thr through fed-batch culture. This systems metabolic engineering approach can be broadly applied to produce various bioproducts with efficient production.

title: Association Between ADHD and Obesity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
text:
Title: Meta-Analysis Reveals Strong Association between Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and Obesity/Overweight
Introduction:
Impulsivity and inattention associated with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) may lead to increased food intake and subsequent weight gain. However, studies examining the relationship between obesity/overweight and ADHD have yielded conflicting results. This meta-analysis aimed to investigate this association using a broad range of databases and unpublished studies.
Methods:
The authors conducted a meta-analysis of 42 studies that included a total of 728,136 individuals (48,161 ADHD subjects; 679,975 comparison subjects). Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and random-effects models were used to estimate the association between obesity/overweight and ADHD.
Results:
Upon analysis, the authors found a significant association between obesity and ADHD for both children and adults. The pooled prevalence of obesity was increased by about 70% in adults with ADHD (28.2%, 95% CI=22.8-34.4) compared with those without ADHD (16.4%, 95% CI=13.4-19.9), and by about 40% in children with ADHD (10.3%, 95% CI=7.9-13.3) compared with those without ADHD (7.4%, 95% CI=5.4-10.1). After controlling for potential confounding factors, the association between ADHD and obesity remained significant. ADHD was also significantly associated with overweight. Medication use for ADHD did not increase the risk of obesity.
Discussion:
This meta-analysis provides evidence for a strong association between ADHD and obesity/overweight. Further research should investigate the underlying mechanisms and the long-term effects of ADHD treatments on weight in individuals with both ADHD and obesity.
Conclusion:
The findings of this meta-analysis suggest that there is a significant association between ADHD and obesity/overweight. Given the prevalence of ADHD and the increasing prevalence of obesity worldwide, this association has important implications for public health. Further research is needed to understand the underlying mechanisms and to develop effective interventions to address this important health issue.

title: Amyloid-DNA Composites of Bacterial Biofilms Stimulate Autoimmunity.
text: Research into the human microbiome has revealed that both beneficial and harmful bacteria can influence various diseases, including obesity, cancer, and autoimmune disorders, through mechanisms that are not fully understood. One such mechanism was discovered when we found that a component of bacterial biofilms, called curli, binds to bacterial DNA during biofilm formation, leading to the formation of fibrous structures that are capable of activating immune cells, including dendritic cells, to produce inflammatory cytokines such as type I interferons. When these composites were given systemically, they triggered immune activation and the production of autoantibodies in mice prone to lupus. Additionally, we found that infection with curli-producing bacteria in lupus-prone mice resulted in higher autoantibody titers compared to infection with curli-deficient bacteria. These findings suggest that the microbiome and biofilm-producing enteric infections may play a role in the progression of autoimmune diseases and could potentially be targeted for treatment.

title: Comprehensive genomic characterization defines human glioblastoma genes and core pathways
text: Human cancer cells often harbor multiple chromosomal abnormalities, nucleotide substitutions, and epigenetic modifications that drive malignant transformation. The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) pilot project aims to assess the value of comprehensive, multi-dimensional analysis of these molecular characteristics in human cancer and to provide the data rapidly to the research community. In this report, we present an interim integrative analysis of DNA copy number, gene expression, and DNA methylation aberrations in 206 glioblastomas, the most common type of primary adult brain cancer, and nucleotide sequence aberrations in 91 of these glioblastomas. This analysis provides new insights into the roles of ERBB2, NF1, and TP53, uncovers frequent mutations in the phosphatidylinositol-3-OH kinase regulatory subunit gene PIK3R1, and offers a network view of the pathways altered in the development of glioblastoma. Moreover, integration of mutation, DNA methylation, and clinical treatment data reveals a link between MGMT promoter methylation and a hypermutator phenotype resulting from mismatch repair deficiency in treated glioblastomas, a finding with potential clinical implications. Overall, these findings demonstrate the feasibility and potential of TCGA, showcasing its ability to rapidly advance knowledge of the molecular basis of cancer.

title: LY2405319, an Engineered FGF21 Variant, Improves the Metabolic Status of Diabetic Monkeys
text: Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) is a novel metabolic regulator with potential as a treatment for various metabolic disorders. Administration of recombinant wild-type FGF21 to diabetic animals leads to a significant improvement in glycemia and amelioration of other systemic measures of metabolic health. We aimed to investigate the pharmacological effects of a recently identified FGF21 analogue, LY2405319 (LY), in non-human primates with diabetes. Diabetic rhesus monkeys were treated subcutaneously with LY once daily for seven weeks, with escalating doses of 3, 9, and 50 mg/kg. LY therapy led to a swift and substantial reduction in multiple metabolic parameters, including glucose, body weight, insulin, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels, at all doses tested. We also observed favorable changes in the circulating profiles of adipokines, with increased adiponectin and reduced leptin, indicative of direct FGF21 action on adipose tissue. Notably, we demonstrate for the first time that FGF21-based therapy has metabolic efficacy in an animal model with advanced diabetes. While the glycemic efficacy of LY was partially attenuated in this context, its lipid-lowering effect was fully preserved, suggesting that FGF21 may be a useful treatment option even in patients with advanced disease progression. These findings support continued exploration of the FGF21 pathway for the treatment of metabolic disorders.

title: Epigenetic Control of Stem Cell Potential during Homeostasis, Aging, and Disease.
text: Decline in stem cells is a crucial factor in the aging process, as it affects multiple tissues. Epigenetic regulation plays a central role in maintaining stem cell function, and recent research suggests that epigenetic dysregulation contributes to the altered potential of stem cells during aging. Unlike terminally differentiated cells, epigenetic changes in stem cells can be transmitted to progeny beyond self and perpetuated through self-renewal divisions within the stem cell pool. This review focuses on recent studies examining epigenetic regulation of tissue-specific stem cells in homeostasis, aging, and aging-related diseases.

title: Host–Parasite Interactions and the Evolution of Gene Expression
text: Interactions between organisms and pathogens offer a persistent opportunity for evolutionary pressure to shape the development of various traits in both parties involved. By employing a mathematically explicit genomic model, we have investigated how gene expression patterns arise at genetic loci linked to host resistance and parasite infection. Our findings lead to a notable but intuitive conclusion that gene expression should follow distinct trajectories in the two interacting species. Specifically, host resistance loci tend to evolve under a co-expression regime, where multiple alleles of the same gene are shared between individuals. On the other hand, parasite infection loci are more likely to undergo a mono-allelic expression profile, where a single allele is consistently expressed across all individuals.
