This pattern arises due to the host's increased ability to recognize and clear a greater diversity of parasite genotypes when co-expressing resistance alleles. Similarly, parasites that express a single antigen or elicitor allele are more likely to be recognized and eliminated by the host, which favors a single allele expression profile. Our model generates testable predictions that can help interpret and integrate the growing body of data on expression levels for genes relevant to host-parasite interactions.

title: A crucial role for interleukin (IL)-1 in the induction of IL-17–producing T cells that mediate autoimmune encephalomyelitis
text: A recent study revealed that interleukin-23 (IL-23) driven interleukin-17 (IL-17)-producing T cells (ThIL-17) play a key role in the pathogenesis of certain autoimmune diseases. The study found that immunizing mice with antigens and adjuvants led to the induction of IL-17-producing cells, but not T helper 1 (Th1) or Th2 cells, in IL-1 receptor type I-deficient (IL-1RI−/−) mice. Moreover, the incidence of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) was significantly lower in IL-1RI−/− mice compared to wild-type mice, and this correlation was found to be due to the failure to induce autoantigen-specific ThIL-17 cells. However, EAE was induced in IL-1RI−/− mice by adoptive transfer of autoantigen-specific cells from wild-type mice with EAE. The study also found that IL-23 alone did not induce IL-17 production by T cells from IL-1RI−/− mice, and IL-23-induced IL-17 production was significantly enhanced by IL-1α or IL-1β, even in the absence of T cell receptor stimulation. The study demonstrated the essential roles of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, nuclear factor kappa B, and novel protein kinase C isoforms in IL-1 and IL-23-mediated IL-17 production. Additionally, tumor necrosis factor alpha also synergized with IL-23 to enhance IL-17 production, and this was found to be IL-1 dependent. The findings of the study suggest that IL-1 functions upstream of IL-17 to promote pathogenic ThIL-17 cells in EAE.

title: Aberrant luminal progenitors as the candidate target population for basal tumor development in BRCA1 mutation carriers
text: Basal-like breast cancers that arise in women who carry mutations in the BRCA1 gene, which codes for the tumor suppressor protein BRCA1, are believed to originate from the mammary stem cell. To investigate early cellular changes in BRCA1 mutation carriers, we prospectively isolated distinct epithelial subpopulations from normal mammary tissue and preneoplastic samples from individuals who are heterozygous for a BRCA1 mutation. We identified three epithelial subtypes, including basal stem/progenitor cells, luminal progenitor cells, and mature luminal cells. Interestingly, we found that breast tissue from BRCA1 mutation carriers contains an expanded population of luminal progenitor cells that exhibit factor-independent growth in vitro. Furthermore, gene expression profiling revealed that breast tissue from BRCA1 mutation carriers and basal breast tumors are more similar to normal luminal progenitor cells than any other subset, including the stem cell-enriched population. The c-KIT tyrosine kinase receptor (encoded by KIT) emerged as a key marker of luminal progenitor cells and was found to be more highly expressed in BRCA1-associated preneoplastic tissue and tumors. Our findings suggest that an aberrant luminal progenitor population may serve as a target for transformation in BRCA1-associated basal tumors.

title: Getting to the site of inflammation: the leukocyte adhesion cascade updated
text: The recruitment of neutrophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes to sites of inflammation relies on a complex series of processes involving adhesion and transmigration through blood vessel walls. In recent years, the traditional three stages of rolling, activation, and firm adhesion have been expanded to include additional steps, such as slow rolling, adhesion strengthening, intraluminal crawling, and paracellular and transcellular migration. Additionally, a second activation pathway has been discovered in neutrophils that does not rely on signaling through G-protein-coupled receptors, and the signaling steps leading to integrin activation are beginning to be understood. This review focuses on the latest developments in the leukocyte adhesion cascade, one of the key paradigms of inflammation and immunity.

title: Genome-wide loss of 5-hmC is a novel epigenetic feature of Huntington's disease.
text:
The recently discovered epigenetic modification of cytosine, 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC), may play a crucial role in neurodegenerative diseases like Huntington's disease (HD). While the dynamics of 5-hmC during neurodevelopment have been well-documented, its distribution and functions in HD brains are currently unknown. Our study aimed to investigate the genomic distribution of 5-hmC in HD mouse brains and its potential impact on neurogenesis, neuronal function, and survival.
We observed a significant reduction in 5-hmC signal in YAC128 HD mouse brains compared to age-matched wild-type (WT) mice, suggesting a deficiency in 5-hmC reconstruction in HD brains during postnatal development. Genome-wide analysis of 5-hmC revealed a diminished signal in striatum and cortex in YAC128 HD mice. Interestingly, we identified disease-specific differentially hydroxymethylated regions (DhMRs) that are not present in WT mice. We found that the acquisition of DhmRs in gene bodies is a positive epigenetic regulator for gene expression. Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) of genotype-specific DhMR-annotated genes revealed that alteration of several canonical pathways, including neuronal development/differentiation (Wnt/β-catenin/Sox pathway, axonal guidance signaling pathway) and neuronal function/survival (glutamate receptor/calcium/CREB, GABA receptor signaling, dopamine-DARPP32 feedback pathway, etc.), may play a crucial role in the onset of HD.
Our findings indicate that loss of the 5-hmC marker is a novel epigenetic feature in HD, and that this aberrant epigenetic regulation may impair neurogenesis, neuronal function, and survival in HD brain. Our study opens a new avenue for HD treatment: re-establishing the native 5-hmC landscape may have the potential to slow or halt the progression of HD.

title: Planning for Postdisaster Resiliency
text: The crux of this article lies in the planning for resiliency in the aftermath of a calamity. Initially, the authors elucidate their understanding of planning for resiliency as a paramount objective for communities recovering from disasters, and the advantages of planning in the pursuit of creating more resilient environments. Subsequently, they delve into the intricacies of planning for post-disaster recovery, including the challenges posed by federal and state governments in fostering resiliency planning, the potential of compact urban form models in guiding reconstruction, and the oversight of excluding citizens in the planning process for disasters. Ultimately, they offer insights culled from previous research addressing these issues and proffer policy recommendations to promote proactive recovery planning for resilient communities.

title: Increased stress-induced inflammatory responses in male patients with major depression and increased early life stress.
text:
The authors aimed to investigate the activation of the innate immune system in response to psychosocial stress in patients with major depression who experienced early life stress. They compared the levels of plasma interleukin (IL)-6, lymphocyte subsets, and DNA binding of nuclear factor (NF)-kB in peripheral blood mononuclear cells between medically healthy male subjects with current major depression and increased early life stress (n=14) and non-depressed male comparison subjects (n=14) both before and after completing the Trier Social Stress Test.
The results showed that the Trier Social Stress Test caused greater increases in IL-6 and NF-kB DNA-binding in major depression patients with early life stress, and this was associated with increased depression severity, but not early life stress. Additionally, the study found that the number of natural killer (NK) cells increased following stress, but there were no differences between the groups and no correlation between NK cell percentage and stress-induced NF-kB DNA-binding or IL-6.
The study's findings suggest that male patients with major depression who experienced early life stress exhibit enhanced inflammatory responses to psychosocial stress, providing a tentative indication of a connection between major depression, early life stress, and adverse health outcomes in diseases linked to inflammation.

title: KIF3A/B: a heterodimeric kinesin superfamily protein that works as a microtubule plus end-directed motor for membrane organelle transport
text: We recently discovered a new member of the murine brain kinesin superfamily, KIF3B, and found that its amino acid sequence shares significant similarity with, but is not identical to, KIF3A, which we previously identified and named KIF3 (47% identical). KIF3B is found in various tissues and developing neurons of mice, and accumulates with anterogradely moving membranous organelles after nerve axon ligation. In the brain, KIF3B forms a complex with KIF3A and three other high molecular weight (approximately 100 kD)-associated polypeptides, referred to as the kinesin superfamily-associated protein 3 (KAP3). In vitro reconstruction using baculovirus expression systems revealed that KIF3A and KIF3B interact with each other directly in the absence of KAP3. The recombinant KIF3A/B complex (approximately 50-nm rod with two globular heads and a single globular tail) exhibited plus end-directed microtubule sliding activity in vitro. Furthermore, we found that KIF3B possesses motor activity in vitro, when combined with a chimeric motor protein (KIF3B head and KIF3A rod tail). Subcellular fractionation of mouse brain homogenates showed a substantial amount of the native KIF3 complex associated with membrane fractions other than synaptic vesicles. Immunoprecipitation using anti-KIF3B antibody-conjugated beads and electron microscopic analysis revealed that KIF3 is indeed associated with membranous organelles. In addition, our findings suggest that KIF3B forms a heterodimer with KIF3A and functions as a new microtubule-based anterograde translocator for membranous organelles, and that KAP3 may contribute to the diverse functions of the KIF3 complex in various cell types in vivo.

title: A genetic screen identifies an LKB1–MARK signalling axis controlling the Hippo–YAP pathway
text: The Hippo-YAP pathway is an emerging signaling cascade that plays a crucial role in regulating stem cell activity and organ size. To identify key players in this pathway, we conducted a kinome screen using RNA interference in human cells. Our screen revealed several kinases that had not previously been linked to Hippo signaling, which control various cellular processes. One of the hits, LKB1, is a well-known tumor suppressor, but the mechanisms underlying its function are only partially understood. Our findings demonstrate that LKB1 works through its substrates in the microtubule affinity-regulating kinase family to regulate the localization of the polarity determinant Scribble and the activity of the core Hippo kinases. Notably, our results also suggest that YAP is essential for the tumor-suppressive effects of LKB1. Our study identifies a signaling axis that connects YAP activation to LKB1 mutations, and has implications for the treatment of LKB1-mutant human cancers. Furthermore, our findings provide insight into the upstream signals that trigger the Hippo-YAP signaling cascade.

title: Beyond melanoma: inhibiting the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway in solid tumors.
text: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have been hailed as a breakthrough treatment for melanoma, with remarkable responses to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. Ongoing clinical trials aim to extend this therapy to various other cancers, including hundreds of trials across multiple malignancies. While immune checkpoint inhibitors have been extensively studied in melanoma and more recently in lung cancer, limited information exists regarding their efficacy in other cancers. This review aims to shed light on the tumor immune microenvironment, PD-1/PD-L1 expression, and the modulatory effects of PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors in patients with head and neck, prostate, urothelial, renal, breast, gastrointestinal, and lung cancers.

title: Partitioning the symptoms of hypoglycaemia using multi-sample confirmatory factor analysis
text: The classification of hypoglycaemic symptoms into autonomic or neuroglycopenic groups tends to occur based on prior assumptions. However, given the practical need for clear and scientifically validated symptom markers of hypoglycaemia, alternative approaches are required. Our large-scale studies have presented substantial evidence for a three-factor model of hypoglycaemic symptomatology, based on statistical associations found among symptoms reported by diabetic patients. Study 1 involved 295 insulin-treated outpatients and identified 11 key hypoglycaemic symptoms that divided into three clear categories: autonomic (sweating, palpitation, shaking, and hunger), neuroglycopenic (confusion, drowsiness, odd behavior, speech difficulty, and incoordination), and malaise (nausea and headache). These three factors were validated in a separate group of 303 insulin-treated diabetic outpatients through confirmatory factor analysis. Our analysis revealed that the three-factor model was the most suitable for explaining symptom correlation in each group. Moreover, a multisample confirmatory factor analysis was conducted to evaluate the rigorous assumptions of the model, including the equality of symptom loadings across groups and identical residual variance for each symptom. The results demonstrated that these assumptions were met, suggesting that the three-factor model was consistently replicated across the two large samples. These findings indicate valid groupings of symptoms that may be applied in future research and clinical practice.

title: Extracellular vesicles from human cardiac progenitor cells inhibit cardiomyocyte apoptosis and improve cardiac function after myocardial infarction.
text:
Recent evidence suggests that cardiac progenitor cells (CPCs) may play a crucial role in improving cardiac function after injury. The underlying mechanisms are complex and involve the use of extracellular vesicles (EVs) as paracrine signaling mediators. Here, we investigate the cardioprotective effects of EVs secreted by human CPCs.
Methods and Results:
CPCs were derived from atrial appendage explants from patients who underwent heart valve surgery. The conditioned medium (CM) of CPCs was found to inhibit apoptosis in mouse HL-1 cardiomyocytic cells and enhance tube formation in human umbilical vein endothelial cells. These effects were abrogated when the CM was depleted of EVs. The cardioprotective effects were reproduced by EVs secreted by CPCs but not by those secreted by human dermal fibroblasts. Transmission electron microscopy and nanoparticle tracking analysis revealed that the EVs were predominantly 30-90 nm in diameter, similar in size to exosomes. MicroRNAs most highly enriched in EVs secreted by CPCs included miR-210, miR-132, and miR-146a-3p. miR-210 downregulated its known targets, ephrin A3 and PTP1b, inhibiting apoptosis in cardiomyocytic cells. miR-132 downregulated its target, RasGAP-p120, enhancing tube formation in endothelial cells. Injecting EVs from CPCs into infarcted hearts exhibited less cardiomyocyte apoptosis, enhanced angiogenesis, and improved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) compared to those injected with control medium.
Conclusion:

The study reveals that EVs secreted by human CPCs are the active component of their paracrine secretion. As a cell-free approach, EVs could potentially bypass many of the limitations of cell transplantation. Furthermore, the study provides insight into the cardioprotective mechanisms of CPCs, which may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for cardiovascular diseases.

title: Increased Adipocyte O2 Consumption Triggers HIF-1α, Causing Inflammation and Insulin Resistance in Obesity
text:
Obesity-related hypoxia and inflammation have been implicated as the primary causes of insulin resistance in adipose tissue. In this study, we demonstrate that early in the progression of a high-fat diet (HFD) and obesity, adipocyte metabolism becomes uncoupled, leading to increased oxygen consumption and a state of hypoxia in adipocytes. This uncoupling is sufficient to trigger the chronic inflammatory response characteristic of obesity.
We found that the activation of hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF-1α) is a key event in this process, which occurs through the stimulation of adenine nucleotide translocase 2 (ANT2), an inner mitochondrial membrane protein, by saturated fatty acids. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of either ANT2 or HIF-1α can reverse these events, resulting in improved insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance.
Our findings reveal a sequence of events that occur in obesity-related inflammation and insulin resistance, highlighting the importance of adipocyte hypoxia and inflammation in the development of insulin resistance.

title: Lpcat3-dependent production of arachidonoyl phospholipids is a key determinant of triglyceride secretion
text: The purpose of distinct phospholipids (PLs) in mediating lipid transport has been challenging to assess due to the inability to selectively manipulate membrane composition in living organisms. However, we have discovered that the enzyme lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase 3 (Lpcat3) plays a critical role in triglyceride (TG) secretion due to its unique capacity to incorporate arachidonate into membranes. We found that mice lacking Lpcat3 in the intestine experience delayed growth during weaning and exhibit excessive lipid accumulation in enterocytes, along with lowered plasma TG levels. Similarly, mice deficient in Lpcat3 in the liver show reduced plasma TG levels, hepatosteatosis, and produce lipid-poor very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) devoid of arachidonoyl PLs. According to our in-depth studies, Lpcat3 activity has an impact on membrane lipid mobility in live cells, implying a biophysical basis for the need of arachidonoyl PLs in the formation of lipidating lipoprotein particles. These findings establish Lpcat3 as a crucial factor in lipoprotein generation and illustrate how manipulating membrane composition can be utilized as a regulatory mechanism to control metabolic pathways.

title: Characterization of a single-stranded DNA-binding protein from Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1.
text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa single-stranded DNA-binding protein (PaSSB) plays a critical role in various DNA metabolic processes such as replication, repair, and recombination. To investigate the ssDNA-binding properties of PaSSB, we employed fluorescence quenching measurements and electrophoretic mobility shift analysis (EMSA). Upon gel filtration chromatography of purified PaSSB, a stable tetramer was detected in solution. In fluorescence titrations, PaSSB bound 22-32 nucleotides (nt) per tetramer, with salt concentration affecting binding efficiency. Using EMSA, we characterized the stoichiometry of PaSSB complexed with various ssDNA homopolymers, and the binding site size was found to be approximately 29 ± 1 nt. Additionally, EMSA results indicated that the dissociation constants of PaSSB for the first tetramer were lower compared to those for the second tetramer. Based on these biophysical analyses, the ssDNA binding mode of PaSSB is predicted to be noncooperative.

title: Primary cilia and coordination of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signalling.
text:

Defects in the assembly or function of primary cilia can lead to a range of developmental disorders and diseases collectively referred to as ciliopathies. In this review, we will discuss the current understanding of the role of primary cilia in coordinating receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling pathways and explore potential mechanisms of signaling crosstalk and networking within the primary cilium. title: Detecting and targeting tumor relapse by its resistance to innate effectors at early recurrence
text: Tumor recurrence poses a significant clinical challenge. Our findings reveal that recurrent tumors emerge with a distinct phenotype that allows them to evade the host's innate immune response triggered by the progression from minimal residual disease (MRD) to actively growing recurrence. By screening for this innate response, we were able to accurately predict which mice would experience recurrence. Premature induction of recurrence also resensitized MRD to the primary therapy, suggesting a possible shift in the clinical treatment of dormant disease. By combining screening with second-line treatments targeting innate insensitivity, we were able to cure up to 100% of mice that would have otherwise relapsed. These findings may open up new opportunities for early detection and targeted treatment of tumor recurrence, regardless of tumor type or initial treatment.

title: Forces in Tissue Morphogenesis and Patterning
text: During development, mechanical forces play a crucial role in shaping cells, altering their number and position, and modulating gene expression. These mechanical forces are essential for any process of morphogenesis, as they are capable of generating and transmitting forces through complex network of actin and myosin filaments, and adhesive complexes. This self-organizing process allows for large-scale changes in tissue shape, driven by the coordination and integration of forces across multiple cells. Moreover, extrinsic mechanical forces also contribute to tissue patterning by influencing cell fate specification and differentiation. The interplay between tissue mechanics and biochemical signaling thus orchestrates the intricate process of tissue morphogenesis and patterning during development.

title: CD169+ MACROPHAGES PRESENT LIPID ANTIGENS TO MEDIATE EARLY ACTIVATION OF INVARIANT NKT CELLS IN LYMPH NODES
text: Invariant natural killer T cells (iNKT cells) play a crucial role in the body's defense against microbial infections. While it is well established that iNKT cells recognize glycolipids presented by CD1d, the mechanisms by which they encounter antigen in vivo have remained unclear. To shed light on this process, we employed multiphoton microscopy to visualize the dynamics and activation of iNKT cells in lymph nodes. After administering antigen, we observed iNKT cells becoming confined in a CD1d-dependent manner near subcapsular sinus CD169(+) macrophages. These macrophages retained, internalized, and presented lipid antigen, which was essential for iNKT cell activation, cytokine production, and population expansion. Our findings demonstrate that CD169(+) macrophages can act as legitimate antigen-presenting cells, controlling early iNKT cell activation and prompting the rapid initiation of immune responses.

title: Oxygen Metabolism Causes Chromosome Breaks and Is Associated with the Neuronal Apoptosis Observed in DNA Double-Strand Break Repair Mutants
text: Cells lacking a crucial DNA repair pathway (nonhomologous DNA end joining [NHEJ]) experience increased spontaneous chromosomal breaks, but the source of these breaks has remained unknown. We discovered that reducing the cellular oxygen level can partially suppress these spontaneous chromosomal breaks. Contrarily, increasing the level of reactive oxygen species (ROS) by overexpressing the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) in transgenic mice leads to a significant increase in chromosomal breaks. The effect of SOD1 on chromosomal breaks can also be modulated by cellular oxygen levels. Notably, the elevated chromosomal breaks in these mice are associated with a substantial increase in neuronal cell death. Our findings indicate that oxygen metabolism plays a crucial role in the genomic instability observed in NHEJ-deficient cells and likely in all cells.

title: Insertional mutagenesis in gene therapy and stem cell biology.
text:
Purpose of Review: Recent preclinical and clinical studies have revealed that the random insertion of transgenes into the chromosomal DNA of hematopoietic cells can lead to clonal competition, which may potentially trigger leukemia or sarcoma. The use of gene vectors has raised safety concerns among those developing advanced hematopoietic cell therapies. This review aims to summarize the underlying mechanisms and provide new insights into stem cell biology.
Recent Findings: Studies have shown that the insertion pattern of various retroviral gene vector systems can be explained by the properties of the viral integrase and associated cellular cofactors. Cell culture assays and animal models, including disease-specific and cancer-prone mouse models, are providing valuable insights into the factors that contribute to clonal imbalance. Databases summarizing vector insertion sites in dominant hematopoietic clones are also emerging as a new tool for identifying genes that regulate clonal homeostasis.
Summary: Mechanistic studies of insertional mutagenesis by random gene vector insertion will lead to improved tools for advanced hematopoietic cell therapy. These studies will also generate fascinating insights into gene networks that regulate cell fitness, with important consequences for the fields of hematology, oncology, and regenerative medicine.

title: Markets, voucher subsidies and free nets combine to achieve high bed net coverage in rural Tanzania
text:
In Tanzania, there is a well-established network of commercial ITN retailers. In 2004, the government introduced a voucher subsidy for pregnant women, and in mid-2005, distributed free nets to under-fives in a limited number of districts, including Rufiji on the southern coast, during a child health campaign. The study assessed the impact of these multiple ITN delivery strategies on coverage in a poor rural community.
The study used a cross-sectional household survey in 31 rural villages of Rufiji district, Southern Tanzania, covering 1,752 households and 6,331 members. The survey collected data on net use, treatment status, and delivery mechanism through a questionnaire.
Findings showed that 62.7% of the population used ITNs overall, with higher rates among infants (87.2%), young children (81.8%), and older children (54.5%) compared to adults (59.6%). Twenty-nine percent of all nets had been treated six months prior to the survey. The study found that the biggest source of nets for infants was purchasing from the private sector with a voucher subsidy (41.8%), while half of nets used by young children (50.0%) and over a third of those used by older children (37.2%) were obtained free of charge through the vaccination campaign. Amongst the population overall, the largest source of nets was commercial purchase (45.1%), and this was the primary means for protecting adults (60.2%.)
The study also found that all delivery mechanisms, particularly sale of nets at full market price, under-served the poorest, but there was no difference in equity observed between voucher-subsidized and freely distributed nets.

In conclusion, the study found that all three delivery strategies enabled the poor rural community to achieve net coverage high enough to yield both personal and community-level protection for the entire population. Each of them reached their relevant target groups, and free nets only temporarily suppressed the net market, illustrating that these approaches are complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

title: Human chorionic gonadotropin levels in maternal blood in late pregnancy: relation to birthweight, sex and condition of the infant at birth.
text: A total of 527 blood samples were collected from an unselected population of women aged 36-40 weeks gestation. Serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels were measured using a specific radioimmunoassay that detects the beta 1-subunit of hCG. Significantly higher levels of serum hCG were found in primiparous women (first-time mothers) and in those carrying female fetuses. Additionally, there was a correlation between serum hCG levels and the birthweight of the child, as well as the occurrence of fetal distress.

title: Brain-Specific Phosphorylation of MeCP2 Regulates Activity-Dependent Bdnf Transcription, Dendritic Growth, and Spine Maturation
text:
Mutations or duplications in the MECP2 gene lead to the development of neurodevelopmental disorders known as Rett and Rett-like syndromes, characterized by cognitive impairments, motor dysfunction, and autistic behavior. MECP2 is expressed in various mammalian tissues and functions as a global transcriptional repressor. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying how MECP2 dysfunction leads to the specific neural phenotypes of RTT are poorly understood. Our study aimed to investigate the molecular pathways involved in MeCP2 dysfunction and their contribution to the neural phenotypes of RTT.
We found that neuronal activity trigger the de novo phosphorylation of MeCP2 at serine 421 (S421) through a CaMKII-dependent mechanism. This phosphorylation is selectively induced in the brain in response to physiological stimuli. Our results suggest that S421 phosphorylation plays a crucial role in regulating the ability of MeCP2 to control dendritic patterning, spine morphogenesis, and the activity-dependent induction of Bdnf transcription. These findings imply that neuronal activity regulates a specific program of gene expression that mediates nervous system maturation, and that disruption of this process in individuals with MECP2 mutations may underlie the neural-specific pathology of RTT.

title: A Candidate Gene Approach Identifies the TRAF1/C5 Region as a Risk Factor for Rheumatoid Arthritis
text:
Correction for: Kurreeman FAS, Padyukov L, Marques RB, Schrodi SJ, Seddighzadeh M, et al. (2007) A Candidate Gene Approach Identifies the TRAF1/C5 Region as a Risk Factor for Rheumatoid Arthritis. PLoS Med 4(9): e278. doi:10.1371/journal.pmed.0040278
In Table 1, the allele ratio in column eight (Allele Ratiosb: Cases, Controls) refers to allele A: allele B and not allele1:allele2 as described in footnote b, with Allele A being the Susceptibility Allele as denoted in column seven. The footnote should read:
bNumber of alleles were compared in cases versus controls: allele A: allele B cases, allele A: allele B controls. Allele A refers to the susceptibility alleles as given in column seven.

title: Potential use of γ-secretase modulators in the treatment of Alzheimer disease.
text: Despite significant advances in our understanding of Alzheimer's disease pathophysiology over the past 20 years, we have yet to identify a disease-modifying therapy that can substantially alter the clinical course of this widespread neurodegenerative disorder. In this brief review, we examine two clinical trial approaches currently underway (γ-secretase inhibition and γ-secretase modulation) and highlight the notable differences between these therapeutic strategies. Additionally, we discuss potential genetic and biomarker-based translational and clinical trial models that could ultimately lead to the development of a successful therapeutic agent.

title: Rational design of a flavivirus vaccine by abolishing viral RNA 2'-O methylation.
text: Viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm are unable to access the host's nuclear capping machinery. These viruses have evolved viral methyltransferases to methylate the N-7 and 2'-O caps of their RNA. Alternatively, they "borrow" host mRNA caps to form the 5' end of their viral RNA. The function of 2'-O methylation of viral RNA caps is to mimic cellular mRNA and evade the host's innate immune response. A cytoplasmic virus weak in 2'-O methylation is replicative but lacks 2'-O methylation on its RNA, which is recognized and eliminated by the host immune response. Such a mutant virus could be rationally designed as a live attenuated vaccine. Here, we use Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), an important mosquito-borne flavivirus, to prove this novel vaccine concept. We find that JEV's methyltransferase performs both N-7 and 2'-O cap methylations, as well as evades the host's innate immune response. We generate a recombinant virus completely deficient in 2'-O methylation and show that it is stable in cell culture after passage for over 30 days. The mutant virus is attenuated in mice, elicits robust humoral and cellular immune responses, and retains the engineered mutation in vivo. A single dose of immunization provides full protection against lethal challenges with JEV strains in mice. Mechanistically, the attenuation phenotype is attributed to the mutant virus's enhanced sensitivity to the antiviral effects of interferon and IFIT proteins. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using 2'-O methylation-defective virus as a vaccine approach, which should be applicable to other flaviviruses and non-flaviviruses that encode their own viral 2'-O methyltransferases.

title: Fruit consumption and risk of type 2 diabetes: results from three prospective longitudinal cohort studies
text: The aim of this study was to investigate whether different types of fruits are associated with a lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes. This was a longitudinal cohort study involving over 160,000 healthcare professionals in the United States. The study found that consuming three or more servings of total whole fruits per week was associated with a lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes, with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.98. When individual fruits were analyzed separately, the study found that the following fruits were significantly associated with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes: blueberries (hazard ratio = 0.74), grapes and raisins (hazard ratio = 0.88), prunes (hazard ratio = 0.89), apples and pears (hazard ratio = 0.93), and bananas (hazard ratio = 0.95). In contrast, greater consumption of fruit juice was associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes (hazard ratio = 1.08). These findings suggest that the associations between fruit consumption and type 2 diabetes risk vary significantly among individual fruits. Specifically, consuming more whole fruits, particularly blueberries, grapes, and apples, may be associated with a lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes, while consuming more fruit juice may be associated with a higher risk.

title: OncomiR-196 promotes an invasive phenotype in oral cancer through the NME4-JNK-TIMP1-MMP signaling pathway
text:
BACKGROUND: MicroRNA-196 (miR-196) has been found to be significantly up-regulated in oral cancer cells, but its significance in oral cancer has yet to be fully understood.
METHODS: To investigate the functional effects of miR-196 modulation, we examined cellular responses including cell growth, migration, invasion, and radio/chemosensitivity. Using algorithms, we identified the regulatory targets of miR-196 and confirmed these targets using RT-qPCR, western blot, luciferase reporter, and confocal microscopy analyses. MiR-196 expression was also determined in paired cancer and adjacent normal tissues from oral cancer patients.
RESULTS: Our results show that both miR-196a and miR-196b are highly over-expressed in cancer tissues and correlated with lymph node metastasis (P = 0.001 and P = 0.006, respectively). Functionally, miR-196 promotes cell migration and invasion without affecting cell growth. Mechanistically, miR-196 inhibits NME4 expression and activates p-JNK, suppresses TIMP1, and enhances MMP1/9.
CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that miR-196 contributes to oral cancer by promoting cell migration and invasion. Our results also show that miR-196a/b is significantly over-expressed in cancer tissues and correlated with lymph node metastasis, providing new insights into the underlying mechanisms of cancer metastasis. miR-196 may serve as a promising marker for improved oral cancer management.

title: Reverse engineering of TLX oncogenic transcriptional networks identifies RUNX1 as tumor suppressor in T-ALL
text: Using reverse engineering strategies to decipher the oncogenic regulatory circuit controlled by TLX1 and TLX3 transcription factors, we discovered that they play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). Our systems biology analysis revealed T cell leukemia homeobox 1 (TLX1) and TLX3 as master regulators of an oncogenic transcriptional circuit that governs T-ALL. Interestingly, network structure analysis of this hierarchical network identified RUNX1 as a key mediator of T-ALL induced by TLX1 and TLX3, suggesting a tumor-suppressor role for RUNX1 in T cell transformation. Consistent with these findings, we found recurrent somatic loss-of-function mutations in RUNX1 in human T-ALL. Our results highlight the pivotal role of TLX1 and TLX3 at the top of an oncogenic transcriptional network controlling leukemia development, underscore the power of network analyses in identifying key elements in the regulatory circuits governing human cancer, and nominate RUNX1 as a tumor-suppressor gene in T-ALL.

title: The Impact of the New WHO Antiretroviral Treatment Guidelines on HIV Epidemic Dynamics and Cost in South Africa
text:
Since November 2009, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that adults infected with HIV should start antiretroviral therapy (ART) at CD4+ cell counts of ≤350 cells/μL rather than ≤200 cells/μL. However, South Africa has only adopted this strategy for pregnant and tuberculosis (TB)-co-infected patients. To assess the impact of fully implementing the new WHO guidelines on the HIV epidemic and associated costs, we used a model of HIV transmission and control in a specified population in Hlabisa subdistrict, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa.
We found that under the new guidelines, there will be a 7% increase in annual investments during the first five years, resulting in 28% more patients receiving treatment. However, the impact on HIV incidence will be more significant in the long term, leading to lower annual costs after seven years. The cumulative net costs will reach a break-even point after approximately 16 years.
Our findings support the WHO recommendation of starting ART at ≤350 cells/μL for all HIV-infected patients. The benefits of expanded treatment are not limited to the saved lives, as the modest frontloading of treatment leads to net savings within a limited time-horizon. Our results are robust to alternative assumptions and foreseeable changes in ART prices and effectiveness. Therefore, we recommend that South Africa prioritize the rapid expansion of its healthcare infrastructure to fully embrace the new WHO guidelines.

title: ER-associated mitochondrial division links the distribution of mitochondria and mitochondrial DNA in yeast
text: Mitochondrial division plays a crucial role in maintaining the proper distribution and function of mitochondria within cells. Recent studies have shown that ER-mitochondria interactions mark the sites of mitochondrial division, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms are not fully understood. Our research aimed to investigate the relationship between the ER-mitochondria tethering complex, ERMES, and the highly conserved Miro GTPase, Gem1, in mediating ER-associated mitochondrial division in yeast. Our findings revealed that Gem1 acts as a negative regulator of ER-mitochondria interactions, a crucial function required for the proper distribution and segregation of newly formed mitochondrial tips following division. Previous studies have shown that ERMES localizes with a subset of actively replicating mitochondrial nucleoids, which we found to be spatially linked to mitochondrial division sites. Our results suggest that ER-associated mitochondrial division may serve to link the distribution of mitochondria and mitochondrial nucleoids in cells. DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.7554/eLife.00422.001.

title: BMI-1 Autoantibody as a New Potential Biomarker for Cervical Carcinoma
text:
High levels of BMI-1 autoantibodies may be an indicator of cervical cancer, according to a study recently published in the journal Cancer Research. The study examined the levels of BMI-1 autoantibodies in the blood of 67 patients with cervical cancer and 65 healthy controls using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and immunoblotting.
The results revealed that BMI-1 autoantibodies were significantly higher in the sera of cancer patients compared to controls, with an average level of 0.827 ± 0.043 in cancer patients versus 0.445 ± 0.023 in controls (P < 0.001). Additionally, the levels of BMI-1 autoantibodies increased progressively during the progression of cervical cancer, from stage I (0.672 ± 0.019) to stage IV (1.043 ± 0.041).
Moreover, statistical analysis using logistic regression and receiver operating characteristics (ROC) curves showed that BMI-1 autoantibody levels could be used as a biomarker for cervical carcinoma with a sensitivity of 0.78 and specificity of 0.76, and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.922.
These findings suggest that measuring BMI-1 autoantibody levels in the blood of patients with cervical cancer may have clinical prognostic value and the potential to serve as a non-tissue-specific biomarker for neoplasms expressing BMI-1.

title: MicroRNAs can generate thresholds in target gene expression
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small, highly conserved non-coding RNA molecules that regulate gene expression by repressing the production of specific proteins in a sequence-dependent manner. To investigate the behavior of miRNAs at the single-cell level, we employed quantitative fluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry to measure the protein expression of a target gene in the presence and absence of miRNA regulation. Our findings reveal that, although the average level of repression is modestly consistent with previous population-based measurements, the repression varies significantly among individual cells. In particular, we found that miRNA regulation establishes a lower threshold level of target mRNA above which protein production is robustly repressed. Near this threshold, protein expression exhibits a sensitive response to changes in target mRNA input, suggesting a mathematical model of molecular titration. These results demonstrate that miRNAs can function both as a binary switch and as a fine-tuner of gene expression.

title: Oncogenic mTOR signaling recruits myeloid-derived suppressor cells to promote tumor initiation
text: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) play vital roles in both primary and metastatic cancer progression. Unfortunately, the regulation of MDSCs is highly variable even among patients with the same type of malignancy, and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. To address this gap in knowledge, we integrated human tumor genomics and syngeneic mammary tumor models to demonstrate that mTOR signaling in cancer cells determines the ability of a mammary tumor to recruit MDSCs through regulating G-CSF. Inhibiting this pathway or its activators, such as FGFR, hinders tumor progression, which is partially rescued by restoring MDSCs or G-CSF. Tumor-initiating cells (TICs) exhibit elevated G-CSF levels, and MDSCs reciprocally increase the frequency of TICs through activating Notch in tumor cells, forming a feedforward loop. Analyses of primary breast cancers and patient-derived xenografts confirm these findings in patients. These discoveries establish a novel, non-canonical oncogenic role of mTOR signaling in attracting pro-tumorigenic MDSCs and reveal how specific cancer subsets may adapt to create and rely on a unique immune microenvironment.

title: Management of women who have a genetic predisposition for breast cancer.
text: The management of women with a genetic predisposition to breast cancer requires thoughtful planning. Women carrying BRCA 1 and BRCA 2 mutations are at a higher risk of developing breast cancer and, in some cases, other cancers such as ovarian cancer. Common strategies used to manage these individuals include screening, preventive surgery, and chemoprevention. While these strategies have shown promise, no randomized, prospective trials have specifically examined their impact in mutation carriers. It is important for all patients to be fully informed of both the potential benefits and risks associated with these options.

title: Astrocytes from Familial and Sporadic ALS Patients are Toxic to Motor Neurons
text: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal motor neuron disease, with astrocytes implicated as a crucial factor in the pathology of both familial (F)ALS and sporadic (S)ALS. However, the significance of astrocytes in SALS, which accounts for >90% of all ALS cases, remains elusive. To investigate the role of astrocytes in SALS, we generated astrocytes from postmortem tissue from both FALS and SALS patients and found that astrocytes derived from both groups were equally toxic to motor neurons. Interestingly, we discovered that reducing the levels of superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) significantly attenuated astrocyte-mediated toxicity towards motor neurons, providing a potential therapeutic target for SALS. Our findings underscore the importance of astrocytes as a non-cell autonomous component in SALS and offer an in vitro model system to explore common disease mechanisms and evaluate potential treatments for both FALS and SALS.

title: High-intensity functional exercise program and protein-enriched energy supplement for older persons dependent in activities of daily living: a randomised controlled trial.
text:
Objective: To determine the effectiveness of a high-intensity functional exercise program on balance, gait ability, and lower-limb strength in older adults reliant on activities of daily living (ADL), and to assess the potential synergy between the exercise program and protein-enriched energy supplements.
Methodology: A randomized controlled trial involving 191 older adults with MMSE scores ≤10 living in residential care facilities was conducted. Participants were randomized to either a high-intensity functional exercise program or a control activity, and were also assigned to receive either protein-enriched energy supplements or a placebo. Exercises were conducted for 29 sessions over a period of 3 months, and participants were assessed for balance, gait speed, and lower-limb strength at 3 and 6 months via Berg Balance Scale, self-paced gait speed, and one-repetition maximum tests. Data was analyzed using the intention-to-treat principle and 2 x 2 factorial ANCOVA.
Results: At 3 months, the exercise group demonstrated a significant improvement in self-paced gait speed compared to the control group (mean difference 0.04 m/s, p = 0.02). At 6 months, the exercise group exhibited significant improvements in Berg Balance Scale (1.9 points, p = 0.05), self-paced gait speed (0.05 m/s, p = 0.009), and lower-limb strength (10.8 kg, p = 0.03) compared to the control group. No interaction effects were observed between the exercise and nutrition interventions.
Conclusion: A high-intensity functional exercise program has positive long-term effects on balance, gait ability, and lower-limb strength in older adults reliant on ADL. Intake of protein-enriched energy supplements after exercise does not appear to enhance the training effects. These findings indicate that a high-intensity functional exercise program can be an effective approach for improving functional capacity in older adults, and may have important implications for public health policy and practice.

title: Inhibition of fatty acid oxidation modulates immunosuppressive functions of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and enhances cancer therapies
text: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC) promote tumor growth by suppressing T-cell immunity and fostering malignant cell proliferation and migration. Despite the potential of blocking MDSC in tumors, the challenge has been exacerbated by their heterogeneity, plasticity, and resistance to various chemotherapy agents. Recent studies have highlighted the role of energy metabolic pathways in the differentiation and function of immune cells, yet the metabolic mechanisms that control MDSC remain unclear. We aimed to determine the energy metabolic pathway(s) utilized by MDSC, evaluate its impact on their immunosuppressive function, and assess whether inhibition of this pathway can block MDSC and enhance antitumor therapies. Using various murine tumor models, we discovered that tumor-infiltrating MDSC (T-MDSC) increased fatty acid uptake and activated fatty acid oxidation (FAO). This was associated with elevated mitochondrial mass, upregulation of FAO enzymes, and increased oxygen consumption rate. Pharmacological inhibition of FAO blocked immune inhibitory pathways and functions in T-MDSC and decreased production of inhibitory cytokines. FAO inhibition alone delayed tumor growth in a T-cell-dependent manner and enhanced the antitumor effect of adoptive T-cell therapy. Moreover, FAO inhibition combined with low-dose chemotherapy completely inhibited T-MDSC immunosuppressive effects and induced a significant antitumor effect. Notably, a similar increase in fatty acid uptake and expression of FAO-related enzymes was observed in human MDSC in peripheral blood and tumors. These findings support the possibility of testing FAO inhibition as a novel approach to block MDSC and enhance various cancer therapies.

title: Predicting mortality of patients hospitalized for acutely exacerbated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text: The primary objective of this study was to identify factors that affect the short-term prognosis of patients with acutely exacerbated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The study included 590 patients with COPD who were hospitalized in the pneumology unit of a university hospital between 1981 and 1990. A standardized protocol for the treatment of acutely exacerbated COPD was adopted for all patients, and patient records were retrospectively analyzed by two observers. A total of 23 clinical and laboratory variables were collected, including age and arterial gas data, and the outcome mortality was recorded. Interobserver reproducibility was tested using the kappa coefficient and Spearman's rho for dichotomous and continuous variables, respectively. Univariate analysis and logistic regression analysis were used to assess the relationship of clinical and laboratory factors to the outcome, and four independent predictors of death were identified: age, alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient greater than 41 mm Hg, ventricular arrhythmias, and atrial fibrillation. The study found that patients with acutely exacerbated COPD at high risk of death can be identified at the time of admission, and variables reflecting heart dysfunction are important determinants of this risk. Among pulmonary function data, only alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient contributes to the predictive model.

title: Clathrin is required for the function of the mitotic spindle
text: Clathrin has a well-established function in the formation of vesicles that transport membranes and proteins within cells. However, its role in mitosis is lesser known. Our study shows that clathrin plays a crucial part in stabilizing fibers of the mitotic spindle, which helps move chromosomes to the metaphase plate. Clathrin binds directly to the spindle fibers through its amino-terminal domain. When we depleted clathrin using RNA interference, we found that mitosis was prolonged and kinetochore fibers were destabilized, leading to an inability for chromosomes to properly align at the metaphase plate and inefficient activation of the spindle checkpoint. Interestingly, rescue of normal mitosis was achieved using clathrin triskelia but not the N-terminal domain of clathrin heavy chain, indicating that the unique structure of clathrin is necessary to stabilize kinetochore fibers. The significance of clathrin in mitosis may be relevant to understanding human cancers that involve gene fusions of clathrin heavy chain.

title: The origin and neuronal function of in vivo nonsynaptic glutamate.
text:
New Text:
In vivo basal levels of glutamate in the extracellular space outside the synaptic cleft are present in micromolar concentrations and remain unclear in terms of their origin and function. In this report, researchers investigated the impact of blocking glutamate release from the cystine-glutamate antiporter on extrasynaptic glutamate levels in the rat striatum. They found that this blockade resulted in a significant (60%) decrease in extrasynaptic glutamate levels, while blockade of voltage-dependent Na+ and Ca2+ channels had minimal (0-30%) effects. These results suggest that the primary source of in vivo extracellular glutamate in the striatum is nonvesicular release from the cystine-glutamate antiporter.
Mechanistically, the activity of the cystine-glutamate antiporter was shown to be negatively regulated via a cAMP-dependent protein kinase mechanism, suggesting that extracellular glutamate derived from the antiporter can regulate extracellular levels of glutamate and dopamine. Interestingly, the researchers found that infusion of the mGluR2/3 antagonist (RS)-1-amino-5-phosphonoindan-1-carboxylic acid (APICA) increased extracellular glutamate levels, and previous blockade of the antiporter prevented the APICA-induced rise in extracellular glutamate. These findings suggest that glutamate released from the antiporter is a source of endogenous tone on mGluR2/3. Furthermore, the study found that blockade of the antiporter resulted in an increase in extracellular dopamine that was reversed by infusing the mGluR2/3 agonist (2R,4R)-4-aminopyrrolidine-2,4-dicarboxylic acid, indicating that antiporter-derived glutamate can modulate dopamine transmission via mGluR2/3 heteroreceptors.
Overall, these results suggest that nonvesicular release from the cystine-glutamate antiporter is the primary source of in vivo extracellular glutamate and that this glutamate can modulate both glutamate and dopamine transmission via mGluR2/3 heteroreceptors

title: Disease-associated functions of IL-33: the new kid in the IL-1 family
text: Interleukin-33 (IL-33), a recently identified member of the IL-1 family, is produced by various cell types in response to pro-inflammatory stimuli and is believed to be released upon cell lysis. The IL-33 receptor, consisting of the ST2 receptor and IL-1 receptor accessory protein, is widely expressed, particularly on T helper 2 (TH2) cells and mast cells. IL-33 has been shown to be host-protective against helminth infections and reduces atherosclerosis by promoting TH2-type immune responses. However, IL-33 can also promote the development of asthma by expanding TH2 cells and contribute to joint inflammation, atopic dermatitis, and anaphylaxis through mast cell activation. Therefore, IL-33 may be a promising new target for therapeutic intervention in a variety of diseases.

title: Interferon alpha therapy for hepatitis C: treatment completion and response rates among patients with substance use disorders
text: This study aimed to investigate the completion and response rates of interferon alpha therapy (IFN) among individuals with hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection who had a history of substance use disorder (SUD). Using a retrospective medical record database from 1998 to 2003, data was collected on 307,437 veterans, of which 22,693 had a known HCV genotype and a history of SUD. The study found that the odds of completing IFN therapy were not significantly different between the SUD+ group (n=11,663) and the SUD- group (n=6,920) across different HCV genotypes, including genotypes 2 and 3. Similarly, the likelihood of achieving an end-of-treatment response and sustained viral response were also found to be similar between the two groups. These findings suggest that individuals with both SUD and HCV can successfully complete antiviral therapy, highlighting the need for more effective treatment strategies and guidelines for this population.

title: Association between infection with Helicobacter pylori and risk of gastric cancer: evidence from a prospective investigation.
text:
Objective: To investigate the association between gastric cancer and previous infection with Helicobacter pylori.
Design: Case-control study comparing the prevalence of IgG antibodies to H pylori in blood samples collected prospectively before the diagnosis of gastric cancer in cases.
Subjects: 29 men with a subsequent diagnosis of gastric cancer and 116 age-matched controls selected from over 22,000 middle-aged men participating in two ongoing cohort studies (the British United Provident Association study and the Caerphilly Collaborative Heart Disease Study), who provided blood samples during 1975-1982.
Results: Of the 29 cases (69%), 54 of the 116 controls (47%) were positive for H pylori-specific antibody. The median specific IgG concentration was significantly higher in the cases than controls (90 micrograms/ml vs 3.6 micrograms/ml, p < 0.01). The estimated odds ratio for the risk of gastric cancer in those with a history of infection with H pylori was 2.77 (95% confidence interval 1.04 to 7.97, p = 0.039).
Conclusions: H pylori infection may be a significant cause of gastric cancer, with between 35% and 55% of cases associated with such an infection.

title: Oncostatin M and leukemia inhibitory factor do not use the same functional receptor in mice.
text:
Members of the interleukin-6 (IL-6) cytokine family, including oncostatin M (OSM) and leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), share a common signal transducer gp130. However, the receptors for human OSM (hOSM) and LIF are composed of gp130 and LIF receptor beta subunit (LIFRbeta), while the receptor for murine OSM (mOSM) remained unknown. Using the recently cloned mOSM cDNA, researchers produced recombinant mOSM and examined its biological activity and receptor structure.
Hematopoietic cell lines, including M1 and DA1.a, an embryonic stem cell line CCE, and Ba/F3 transfectants expressing gp130 and LIFRbeta, responded to both murine LIF (mLIF) and hOSM with equal sensitivity, but only responded to mOSM at a 30-fold to 100-fold higher concentration than mLIF and hOSM. In contrast, NIH3T3 cells responded to mOSM but not to mLIF and hOSM. Scatchard plot analyses revealed that mOSM bound to gp130 with low affinity (kd = 2.8 to 4.2 nmol/L) and that the binding affinity did not increase in the presence of LIFRbeta. However, mOSM bound to NIH3T3 cells with high affinity (kd = 660 pmol/L), while mLIF did not bind to NIH3T3 cells at all.
These findings indicate that unlike hOSM, mOSM and mLIF do not share the same functional receptor, and mOSM delivers signals only through its specific receptor complex. Further research in mice will elucidate the physiological roles of OSM.

title: Multifunctional in vivo vascular imaging using near-infrared II fluorescence
text: In vivo real-time epifluorescence imaging of mouse hind limb vasculatures in the second near-infrared region (NIR-II) is performed using single-walled carbon nanotubes as fluorophores, achieving both high spatial ( koleographic ~30 μm) and temporal (kinfowide <200 ms per frame) resolution for small-vessel imaging at 1–3 mm deep in the hind limb. This is due to the advantageous NIR-II optical window, which allows for deep anatomical penetration and low scattering. This level of spatial resolution is unattainable by traditional NIR imaging (NIR-I) or microscopic computed tomography, and the temporal resolution far exceeds scanning microscopic imaging techniques. Arterial and venous vessels are unambiguously differentiated using a dynamic contrast-enhanced NIR-II imaging technique based on their distinct hemodynamics. Additionally, the deep tissue penetration and high spatial and temporal resolution of NIR-II imaging enable precise quantifications of blood velocity in both normal and ischemic femoral arteries, which are beyond the capabilities of ultrasonography at lower blood velocities.

title: Colorectal cancer survival in socioeconomic groups in England: variation is mainly in the short term after diagnosis.
text:
Title: Socioeconomic Disparities in Cancer Survival: Evidence from Colorectal Cancer in England
Objective: To investigate differences in cancer survival between socioeconomic groups in England, with a focus on short-term survival.
Methods: Individuals diagnosed with colorectal cancer between 1996 and 2004 were identified from cancer registry records. Five-year cumulative relative survival and excess death rates were calculated.
Results: The study found a significant excess death rate in the first month of follow-up among socioeconomically deprived groups for colon cancer, with a smaller but persistent socioeconomic difference in death rates in subsequent periods. In contrast, the pattern of variation in excess death rates was similar for rectal cancer, although the socioeconomic difference in death rates persisted longer. If the excess death rates in the entire colorectal cancer patient population were the same as those observed in the most affluent socioeconomic quintile, the annual reduction in deaths would be approximately 360 for colon cancer and 336 for rectal cancer patients, with these deaths occurring primarily in the first month and year after diagnosis.
Conclusion: The findings of this study lend strong support to the use of short-term cancer survival as an operational measure of variation and progress in cancer control, particularly in light of recent national cancer control initiatives. These results highlight the importance of addressing socioeconomic disparities in cancer survival in order to improve outcomes for marginalized patient populations.

title: Cardiac myocyte remodeling mediated by N-cadherin-dependent mechanosensing.
text:
The importance of cell-to-cell adhesions in maintaining the structural and functional integrity of cardiac cells has been highlighted in recent studies. However, little is known about the mechanosensitivity and mechanotransduction of these interactions. Most research on cardiac mechanotransduction and myofibrillogenesis has focused on cell-extracellular matrix (ECM) interactions, neglecting the direct role of intercellular adhesion in shaping cardiac structure and function. This study aimed to investigate the direct role of N-cadherin-mediated mechanotransduction in the morphology and internal organization of neonatal ventricular cardiac myocytes.
The study found that cadherin-mediated cell attachments can elicit a cytoskeletal network response similar to that of integrin-mediated force response and transmission, affecting myofibrillar organization, myocyte shape, and cortical stiffness. Traction forces mediated by N-cadherin were comparable to those sustained by ECM. The study also showed that N-cadherin is a mechanoresponsive adhesion receptor, as it demonstrates a higher mechanical sensitivity response in terms of cell spread area as a function of imposed load on adhesive substrate rigidity compared to ECM protein-coated surfaces. Moreover, the cytoskeletal architecture of myocytes on an N-cadherin adhesive microenvironment was characteristically different from that on an ECM environment, suggesting that the two mechanotransductive cell adhesion systems may play both independent and complementary roles in myocyte cytoskeletal spatial organization.
In conclusion, these findings imply that cell-to-cell-mediated force perception and transmission are crucial in organizing and developing cardiac structure and function. These results have significant implications for our understanding of how cardiac tissue responds to mechanical stimuli and how it develops in the fetal and neonatal stages. The study highlights the importance of considering cell-cell interactions in cardiac mechanotransduction and myofibrillogenesis, and suggests that N-cadherin-mediated mechanotransduction may play a key role in shaping cardiac structure and function.

title: NEAT1: A novel cancer‐related long non‐coding RNA
text: Abnormal expression of the long non-coding RNA NEAT1 (nuclear paraspeckle assembly transcript 1) has been observed in various types of solid tumors, including lung, esophageal, colorectal, and liver cancers, where it is associated with poor prognosis. In contrast, NEAT1 is underexpressed in acute promyelocytic leukemia, where it promotes white blood cell differentiation. This review summarizes the current understanding of NEAT1's oncogenic role and potential clinical applications. Further research is needed to uncover the underlying mechanisms of NEAT1 overexpression.

title: The Function and Therapeutic Potential of Long Non-coding RNAs in Cardiovascular Development and Disease
text: The widespread adoption of genome-wide analysis and RNA sequencing has led to the surprising discovery that a significant portion of the human genome, although transcribed, does not encode proteins. Long non-coding RNAs have emerged as crucial regulators of gene expression in both healthy and diseased states. Research on long non-coding RNAs expressed in the heart, combined with gene association studies, has revealed that these molecules are modulated during cardiovascular development and disease. Some long non-coding RNAs have been implicated in cardiac pathophysiology and hold promise as therapeutic targets. This review summarizes current knowledge of the function of long non-coding RNAs in the cardiovascular system, with a focus on cardiovascular development and physiology, particularly hypertension, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, ischemia, and heart failure. We also discuss potential therapeutic implications and the challenges of long non-coding RNA research, highlighting directions for future research and translational focus.

title: Oct4 links multiple epigenetic pathways to the pluripotency network
text: Oct4 is a transcription factor that plays crucial roles in stem cell self-renewal, pluripotency, and somatic cell reprogramming. However, little is known about the protein complexes associated with Oct4 and the intrinsic protein-protein interactions that regulate its key functions. To address this knowledge gap, we employed an improved affinity purification technique combined with mass spectrometry to isolate Oct4 protein complexes in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs). Our study uncovered numerous novel Oct4-binding proteins involved in the self-renewal and pluripotency of mESCs. Of interest, we found that Oct4 interacts with multiple chromatin-modifying complexes, some of which have been implicated in stem cell maintenance and somatic cell reprogramming. Our findings provide a biochemical basis for understanding the genetic and epigenetic regulation of stem cell pluripotency and offer a framework for exploring alternative reprogramming strategies.

title: Tet1 is dispensable for maintaining pluripotency and its loss is compatible with embryonic and postnatal development.
text: The Tet family of enzymes (Tet1/2/3) converts 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) in cells. Mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) exhibit high levels of Tet1 expression and 5hmC content. Research on Tet1 has implicated it in the maintenance and specification of pluripotency in vitro, but its precise role in development remains unclear. To investigate the function of Tet1 in pluripotency and development, we generated Tet1-deficient mESCs and mice. Our findings reveal that Tet1(-/-) ESCs have reduced levels of 5hmC and subtle changes in global gene expression, and are still pluripotent and capable of forming live-born mice in a tetraploid complementation assay. However, these cells demonstrate a bias toward trophectoderm differentiation in vitro. The Tet1 mutant mice are viable, fertile, and display no gross abnormalities, although some pups exhibit a slight reduction in body size at birth. Our results suggest that loss of Tet1 leads to only a partial reduction in 5hmC levels, which is compatible with embryonic and postnatal development.

title: LDL-cholesterol concentrations: a genome-wide association study
text:
The causal relationship between background LDL cholesterol and the development of cardiovascular disease is well established. To better understand the underlying biological mechanisms that regulate LDL cholesterol and identify potential therapeutic targets, we conducted a genome-wide association study of LDL-cholesterol concentrations.
Using genome-wide association data from up to 11,685 participants across five studies, we analyzed 293,461 autosomal single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with a minor allele frequency of 5% or more. In our initial analysis, we identified two SNPs (rs599839 [p=1.7x10(-15)] and rs4970834 [p=3.0x10(-11)]) that showed genome-wide statistical association with LDL cholesterol at chromosomal locus 1p13.3. The second genome screen revealed a third statistically associated SNP at the same locus (rs646776 [p=4.3x10(-9)]). Meta-analysis of data from all studies showed that both SNPs, rs599839 and rs646776, were associated with LDL-cholesterol concentrations (combined p=1.2x10(-33) and p=4.8x10(-20), respectively). These SNPs explained around 1% of the variation in circulating LDL-cholesterol concentrations and were associated with about 15% of a standard deviation change in LDL cholesterol per allele, assuming a standard deviation of 1 mmol/L.
In conclusion, our findings identify a novel locus for LDL cholesterol on chromosome 1p13.3, providing insight into the biological mechanisms that regulate LDL cholesterol and potentially leading to the discovery of novel therapeutic targets for cardiovascular disease.

title: Population Density, Water Supply, and the Risk of Dengue Fever in Vietnam: Cohort Study and Spatial Analysis
text:
Background: Aedes aegypti, the primary vector of dengue fever viruses, often breeds in household water storage containers in areas without access to tap water, and thrives in dense urban areas. We aimed to identify high-risk areas by examining the interaction between human population density and lack of tap water as contributors to dengue fever outbreaks. Methods and Findings: We conducted an individual-level cohort study among 75,000 geo-referenced households in Vietnam over two dengue epidemics, using hospital admissions (n = 3,013). We employed space-time scan statistics and mathematical modeling to confirm our findings. Our analysis revealed a surprisingly narrow range of critical human population densities (approximately 3,000 to 7,000 people/km²) associated with dengue outbreaks. This density was typical of rural and peri-urban areas. Scan statistics showed that areas with high population density or adequate water supply did not experience severe outbreaks. Conversely, rural areas with low water supply had a higher risk of dengue. Mathematical modeling suggested that simple assumptions regarding vector/host ratios could explain the occurrence of outbreaks. Conclusions: Dense rural areas may contribute equally to the spread of dengue fever as cities. Enhancing water supply and vector control in areas with a population density conducive to dengue transmission could increase the effectiveness of control measures.

2. Clarity: We have added more precise language to clarify the meaning of certain terms and concepts.

4. Active voice: We have changed some of the passive voice constructions to active voice to make the text more engaging and clear.
5. Consistency: We have standardized sentence structure and word choice throughout the text to enhance readability and consistency.

title: Helicobacter pylori induces AGS cell motility and elongation via independent signaling pathways.
text: Helicobacter pylori triggers both motility-related and cytoskeletal responses in gastric epithelial cells. We have found that these responses can be triggered through separate signaling pathways that often occur simultaneously. The Cag pathogenicity island appears to be unnecessary for the induction of motility, while the elongation phenotype requires the translocation and phosphorylation of CagA.

title: The Sequence Alignment/Map format and SAMtools
text:
Summary:
The Sequence Alignment/Map (SAM) format is a versatile alignment format designed to store read alignments against reference sequences, accommodating both short and long reads (up to 128 Mbp) generated by various sequencing technologies. Its flexibility in terms of data representation and compactness in file size make it an efficient format for storing and analyzing read alignments. SAM is the de facto standard alignment format used by the 1000 Genomes Project, and SAMtools serves as a comprehensive toolkit for processing and analyzing alignments in the SAM format, providing valuable utilities such as indexing, variant calling, and alignment visualization.
Availability:
SAMtools and its associated utilities are freely available for download from the following website: <http://samtools.sourceforge.net/>.

title: Characterization of two classes of small molecule inhibitors of Arp2/3 complex
text:
The polymerization of actin filaments is regulated by the actin-related protein (Arp)2/3 complex, which supports various cellular movements. However, the relative contributions of the Arp2/3 complex versus other mechanisms of actin filament nucleation in processes such as pathfinding by neuronal growth cones remain unclear due to the lack of simple methods to reversibly inhibit the Arp2/3 complex in living cells. To address this challenge, we have developed two classes of small molecules that bind to different sites on the Arp2/3 complex and inhibit its ability to nucleate actin filaments.
The first class of compounds, CK-0944636, binds between Arp2 and Arp3, likely blocking the movement of these proteins into their active conformation. The second class, CK-0993548, inserts into the hydrophobic core of Arp3 and alters its conformation. Both classes of compounds inhibit the formation of actin filament comet tails in Listeria and podosomes in monocytes. These two inhibitors with distinct mechanisms provide a powerful tool for investigating the Arp2/3 complex in living cells.

title: Stresses at the cell-to-substrate interface during locomotion of fibroblasts
text: Recent advancements in the elastic substrate method have enabled the spatially resolved measurement of tractions exerted by individual motile cells. In this study, we have leveraged these developments to produce maps of the tractions generated by 3T3 fibroblasts during steady locomotion. The resulting images show a resolution of approximately 5 micrometers and a maximum intensity of approximately 10(2) kdyn/cm2 (10(4) pN/μm2). We discovered that the propulsive thrust for fibroblast locomotion, roughly 0.2 dyn, is applied to the substrate within 15 micrometers of the leading edge. These observations suggest that the lamellipodium of the fibroblast is capable of generating high traction stress. The cell body and posterior regions appear to be passive structures that are mechanically pulled forward solely by this action.

title: Cancer-associated adipocytes exhibit an activated phenotype and contribute to breast cancer invasion.
text: Early local tumor invasion in breast cancer often results in a meeting between cancer cells and mature adipocytes, but the role of these fat cells in tumor progression remains uncertain. To investigate, we utilized a novel two-dimensional coculture system to examine the interactions between murine and human tumor cells and mature adipocytes. Our findings reveal that co-culture with adipocytes significantly enhances the invasive capabilities of tumor cells in vitro and in vivo. Concomitantly, adipocytes exposed to cancer cells display altered phenotypes, including delipidation and decreased adipocyte markers, as well as overexpression of proteases, such as matrix metalloproteinase-11, and proinflammatory cytokines, including interleukin (IL)-6. Interestingly, IL-6 plays a crucial role in the acquired proinvasive effect of tumor cells. Furthermore, we observe similar modifications in adipocytes present in human breast tumors through immunohistochemistry and quantitative PCR. Notably, tumors of larger size and/or lymph node involvement exhibit higher IL-6 levels in surrounding adipocytes. Our findings collectively demonstrate that (i) invasive cancer cells significantly impact adipocytes, (ii) peritumoral adipocytes exhibit a distinct phenotype termed cancer-associated adipocytes (CAA), and (iii) CAAs modulate cancer cell characteristics/phenotype, leading to more aggressive behavior. Our results strongly support the innovative concept that adipocytes participate in a complex, reciprocal cycle orchestrated by cancer cells to promote tumor progression, which may be exacerbated in obese individuals.

title: Prevalence of cardiovascular disease risk factor in the Chinese population: the 2007-2008 China National Diabetes and Metabolic Disorders Study.
text: The present study aimed to investigate cardiovascular risk factors and the prevalence of non-fatal cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) in China using data from the 2007-2008 China National Diabetes and Metabolic Disorders Study. The study included a nationally representative sample of 46,239 adults aged 20 years or older, who were randomly selected using a multi-stage stratified design method. Data on lifestyle factors, CVD diagnosis, stroke, diabetes, and family history were collected, and an oral glucose tolerance test or a standard meal test was performed. The study found that the prevalence of coronary heart disease, stroke, and CVDs was 0.74%, 1.07%, and 1.78% in males, and 0.51%, 0.60%, and 1.10% in females, respectively. The prevalence of CVDs increased with age in both males and females. The study also found that the prevalence of being overweight or obese, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, or hyperglycaemia was 36.67%, 30.09%, 67.43%, and 26.69% in males, and 29.77%, 24.79%, 63.98%, and 23.62% in females, respectively. Moreover, the study found that the prevalence of having 1, 2, 3, or ≥4 of the five defined cardiovascular risk factors (smoking, overweight or obese, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, or hyperglycaemia) was 31.17%, 27.38%, 17.76%, and 10.19%, respectively, in the total sample of 46,239 patients. After adjusting for gender and age, the odds ratio of CVDs for those who had 1, 2, 3, or ≥4 risk factors was 2.36, 4.24, 4.88, and 7.22, respectively, compared to patients with no risk factors. These findings suggest that morbidity attributed to the five defined cardiovascular risk factors was high in the Chinese population, and multiple risk factors were present in the same individual. Therefore, reasonable prevention strategies should be designed to attenuate the rapid rise in cardiovascular morbidity.

title: Microvascular and Macrovascular Complications of Diabetes
text:
Diabetes is a group of chronic diseases characterized by elevated blood sugar levels. Modern medical care employs a diverse range of lifestyle and pharmaceutical interventions aimed at preventing and controlling elevated blood sugar levels. In addition to ensuring the body's adequate glucose delivery, treatment of diabetes seeks to minimize the potential damage caused by excess sugar in the body.
