The importance of protecting the body from elevated blood sugar levels cannot be overstated, as the direct and indirect consequences on the body's vascular system are the primary source of morbidity and mortality in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Generally, these adverse effects of elevated blood sugar levels are categorized into two types: macrovascular complications (e.g., coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial disease, and stroke) and microvascular complications (e.g., diabetic nephropathy, neuropathy, and retinopathy). It is crucial for physicians to comprehend the connection between diabetes and vascular disease, as the prevalence of diabetes continues to rise in the United States, and the available treatment options for preventing and managing these complications are becoming more diverse.
 Turning to the specifics of diabetic retinopathy, it is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes and accounts for approximately 10,000 new cases of blindness annually in the United States alone.4 The risk of developing diabetic retinopathy or other microvascular complications of diabetes depends on both the duration and severity of elevated blood sugar levels. Studies have shown that both the severity of hyperglycemia and the presence of hypertension are associated with an increased risk of developing diabetic retinopathy in patients with type 2 diabetes.1,3 The onset of retinopathy may occur as early as 7 years before the diagnosis of diabetes in patients with type 2 diabetes, and most patients with type 1 diabetes will develop evidence of retinopathy within 20 years of diagnosis.2,4 Several proposed pathological mechanisms have been proposed to explain how diabetes may lead to retinopathy, including changes in the blood vessels' structure and function, inflammation, and oxidative stress.
In conclusion, comprehensive management of diabetes and its associated complications requires an understanding of the complex interplay between elevated blood sugar levels, vascular health, and other factors. By staying up-to-date on the latest research and treatment options, physicians can help their patients achieve better outcomes and improve their quality of life.

title: Involvement of S-nitrosylation of actin in inhibition of neurotransmitter release by nitric oxide
text:
INTRODUCTION The role of nitric oxide (NO) as a diffusible messenger in the regulation of pain transmission remains a topic of debate, with pro-nociceptive and anti-nociceptive effects proposed. One mechanism by which NO exerts its effects is through reversible post-translational modification of selective cysteine residues in proteins, known as S-nitrosylation. The distribution and targets of S-nitrosylated proteins in the spinal cord have yet to be fully characterized. In this study, we employed the "biotin-switch" method and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry to investigate S-nitrosylated proteins in the spinal cord.
RESULTS Our findings indicate that actin is the most abundantly S-nitrosylated protein in the spinal cord, with higher levels of S-nitrosylation observed in the S2 fraction compared to the P2 fraction of spinal homogenate. Treatment of PC12 cells with the NO donor SNAP resulted in rapid S-nitrosylation of actin and inhibition of dopamine release from the cells. Similarly to cytochalasin B, which depolymerizes actin, SNAP decreased the amount of filamentous actin cytoskeleton near the plasma membrane. Inhibitors of soluble guanylyl cyclase and cGMP-dependent protein kinase did not attenuate the inhibition of dopamine release.
CONCLUSION Our study demonstrates that actin is a major S-nitrosylated protein in the spinal cord, providing evidence that NO directly modulates neurotransmitter release through S-nitrosylation in addition to phosphorylation by cGMP-dependent protein kinase. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between NO and cGMP-dependent protein kinase in the regulation of pain transmission.

title: Independent Association of Lobular Involution and Mammographic Breast Density With Breast Cancer Risk
text: BACKGROUND Research has shown that lobular involution, or the natural aging process of the breast lobules, is inversely associated with breast cancer risk, while mammographic breast density (MBD) is positively associated with breast cancer risk. To investigate whether lobular involution and MBD are independently associated with breast cancer risk in women with benign breast disease, we conducted a nested cohort study among 2666 women with benign breast disease diagnosed at Mayo Clinic between 1985 and 1991, and with a mammogram available within 6 months of the diagnosis. The women were followed up for an average of 13.3 years to identify any breast cancer incidence. Lobular involution was categorized as none, partial, or complete, and parenchymal patterns were classified according to the Wolfe classification as N1 (nondense), P1, P2 (ductal prominence occupying <25% or >25% of the breast, respectively), or DY (extremely dense). Adjusted Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate the hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations of lobular involution and MBD with breast cancer risk. All statistical tests were two-sided. RESULTS After adjustment for MBD, having no or partial lobular involution was associated with a higher risk of breast cancer than having complete involution (none: HR of breast cancer incidence = 2.62, 95% CI = 1.39 to 4.94; partial: HR of breast cancer incidence = 1.61, 95% CI = 1.03 to 2.53; P(trend) = .002). Similarly, after adjustment for involution, having dense breasts was associated with a higher risk of breast cancer than having nondense breasts (for DY: HR of breast cancer incidence = 1.67, 95% CI = 1.03 to 2.73; for P2: HR of breast cancer incidence = 1.96, 95% CI = 1.20 to 3.21; for P1: HR of breast cancer incidence = 1.23, 95% CI = 0.67 to 2.26; P(trend) = .02). Having a combination of no involution and dense breasts was associated with a higher risk of breast cancer than having complete involution and nondense breasts (HR of breast cancer incidence = 4.08, 95% CI = 1.72 to 9.68; P = .006). CONCLUSION Our findings suggest that lobular involution and MBD are independently associated with breast cancer incidence, and that combined, they are associated with an even greater risk for breast cancer. These findings have important implications for breast cancer screening and prevention in women with benign breast disease.

title: Pleiotropy as a mechanism to stabilize cooperation
text: Most genes influence multiple traits, a phenomenon known as pleiotropy, which poses a significant challenge to evolution as adaptive changes in one trait may be hindered by the potential impact on other traits influenced by the same genes. However, we have found that pleiotropy can have an unanticipated benefit in the context of one of the most enigmatic adaptations—cooperation. In the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum, a remarkable act of cooperation occurs when some cells sacrifice themselves to form a stalk that suspends the other cells as reproductive spores. We have identified a gene, dimA, in D. discoideum, which has two contrasting effects. It is necessary for cells to receive the signaling molecule DIF-1, which triggers cell differentiation into prestalk cells. By ignoring DIF-1, cells can cheat by avoiding the stalk. Nonetheless, our findings reveal that in populations containing wild-type cells, the lack of the dimA gene results in exclusion from spores. This pleiotropic connection between stalk and spore formation restricts the potential for cheating in D. discoideum, as defecting on prestalk cell production leads to an even greater reduction in spores. We propose that the evolution of pleiotropic links between cheating and personal costs can stabilize cooperative adaptations.

title: The homeobox gene goosecoid controls cell migration in Xenopus embryos.
text: Goosecoid (gsc), a homeobox gene expressed specifically in the dorsal blastopore lip of the Xenopus gastrula, plays a crucial role in Spemann's organizer phenomenon. Using lineage tracing and time-lapse microscopy, researchers were able to track the fate of embryonic cells that were microinjected with gsc mRNA. These findings revealed that microinjected gsc has non-cell autonomous effects, recruiting neighboring uninjected cells towards a twinned dorsal axis. Additionally, ectopic expression of gsc mRNA in ventral blastomeres and overexpression of gsc in dorsal blastomeres led to cell movement towards the anterior of the embryo. These results suggest that gsc may play a role in controlling gastrulation movements in groups of cells, rather than dissociated cells, and demonstrate that a vertebrate homeobox gene can regulate region-specific cell migration.

title: Epigenetic switch involved in activation of pioneer factor FOXA1-dependent enhancers.
text: Transcription factors (TFs) bind selectively to specific regions of the mammalian genome known as cis-regulatory elements. Among these regions, enhancers play crucial roles in the regulation of gene expression during development and differentiation. Although much is known about the role of chromatin structure in controlling TF functions, there is still much to be learned about the chromatin structure of enhancers and how it is established. Here, we conducted a genomic analysis of enhancers that recruit FOXA1, a pioneer transcription factor that activates the transcriptional potential of these cis-regulatory sites. Interestingly, we found that FOXA1 binds to regions of the genome showing local DNA hypomethylation, and its cell-type-specific recruitment to chromatin is linked to differential DNA methylation levels at its binding sites. Using neural differentiation as a model, we demonstrated that the induction of FOXA1 expression and its subsequent recruitment to enhancers is associated with DNA demethylation. Concurrently, histone H3 lysine 4 methylation is induced at these enhancers. These epigenetic changes may both stabilize FOXA1 binding and facilitate the subsequent recruitment of transcriptional regulatory factors. Notably, FOXA1-dependent enhancers cloned into reporter constructs were able to recapitulate their cell type specificity, but their activities were inhibited by DNA methylation. Thus, these enhancers function as intrinsic cell-type-specific regulatory regions whose activities need to be potentiated by FOXA1 through the induction of an epigenetic switch involving DNA demethylation.

title: Leptin treatment ameliorates anxiety in ob/ob obese mice.
text: We explored the impact of administered leptin on anxiety-like behavior in ob/ob mice. Over a period of 5 days, we repeatedly injected leptin into these mice. Anxiety was assessed using the standard elevated plus maze, and body weight was measured daily. Our findings revealed that repeated leptin administrations significantly increased the percentage of total entries in the open arms and the number of total entries. Moreover, the body weight was significantly reduced by 13.2% after treatment. Our results suggest that leptin treatment not only alleviates obesity but also reduces anxiety in ob/ob mice. These findings suggest that addressing obesity may hold the key to solving related psychological issues.

title: Predicting new molecular targets for known drugs
text: Although drugs are designed to be specific, they often bind to multiple physiological targets, leading to side effects and varying degrees of efficacy. With many possible drug-target interactions, a computational exploration of these interactions is valuable. In this study, we analyzed 3,665 FDA-approved and investigational drugs in relation to hundreds of targets, each defined by its corresponding ligand. Using this approach, we identified thousands of unanticipated drug-target interactions, and experimentally tested 30 of these combinations. Our results confirmed 23 new drug-target associations, five of which were found to be potent (<100 nM). Additionally, the study confirmed the physiological relevance of one drug, N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT), on serotonergic receptors in a knockout mouse. The systematic and comprehensive approach used in this study may lead to the discovery of side effects and new indications for many drugs.

title: Bone loss and vascular calcification: A bi-directional interplay?
text: Vascular calcification (VC) has emerged as a significant predictor of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Initially thought to be a passive and degenerative process, VC is now recognized as an active process that shares histopathological similarities with bone formation. Both VC and osteoporosis (OP) are influenced by oxidative stress and inflammation, and biochemical factors involved in healthy bone metabolism play a crucial role in regulating VC. These factors include vitamin D, osteoprotegerin, osteopontin, matrix Gla protein, cathepsin K, fibroblast growth factor-23, and fetuin-A. Comprehending the intricate regulatory network that governs this process, with its multiple feedback loops and cross-talk between organs, may help to reduce the prevalence of calcific vasculopathy and OP in the aging population, and to develop novel preventive and therapeutic interventions targeting both conditions.

title: Immobilized chemokine fields and soluble chemokine gradients cooperatively shape migration patterns of dendritic cells.
text: Chemokines orchestrate the migration of immune cells by eliciting either directed or random movement, and by activating integrins to induce cell adhesion. By studying dendritic cell (DC) migration, we found that these different responses depend on the mode of chemokine presentation within tissues. When the chemokine CCL21 is presented on the surface of tissues, it triggers integrin-mediated adhesion and random movement of DCs that is confined to the surface of the chemokine. Conversely, direct contact with CCL21 leads to the removal of the anchoring residues, allowing the chemokine to form soluble gradients that trigger chemotactic movement of DCs. Soluble CCL21functionally resembles the second CCR7 ligand, CCL19, which lacks anchoring residues and forms soluble gradients. Both soluble CCR7 ligands trigger chemotactic movement, but not surface adhesion. The combination of adhesive random migration and directional steering allows for dynamic but spatially restricted locomotion patterns that are similar to those observed in secondary lymphoid organs.

title: Local proliferation dominates lesional macrophage accumulation in atherosclerosis
text: During the inflammatory response that leads to atherogenesis, macrophages accumulate progressively in the growing artery wall. Previous studies have suggested that the entry of circulating monocytes into the arterial wall determines the number of macrophages present. However, recent research has challenged this idea, showing that macrophage accumulation does not always depend on monocyte recruitment in certain inflammatory situations. To gain a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying macrophage accumulation in atherosclerosis, we reexamined the process in mouse models of the disease. We found that macrophages in these lesions turn over rapidly, with the majority of cells replenished through local proliferation rather than the entry of new monocytes. The microenvironment plays a key role in this process, with the involvement of a specific receptor (scavenger receptor A or SR-A) orchestrating macrophage proliferation. Our findings highlight macrophage proliferation as a crucial event in atherosclerosis and identify macrophage self-renewal as a potential therapeutic target for cardiovascular disease.

title: Enzymatically active lysosomal proteases are associated with amyloid deposits in Alzheimer brain.
text: The protein precursor to beta-amyloid in the brains of individuals with Alzheimer's disease is cleaved by proteolytic enzymes, which have not yet been identified. However, sections from Alzheimer's brains showed high levels of immunoreactivity for cathepsins D and B, which are normally found in lysosomes. In situ enzyme histochemistry using synthetic peptides and protein substrates revealed that senile plaques contained the highest levels of enzymatically active cathepsin. At the ultrastructural level, cathepsin immunoreactivity was localized to lysosomal dense bodies and lipofuscin granules in senile plaques and degenerating neurons of Alzheimer's neocortex. These findings suggest that lysosomal proteases derived from degenerating neurons may mediate the proteolytic formation of beta-amyloid. Therefore, we propose that the abnormal localization of cathepsins from the regulated intracellular environment provides a basis for the formation of amyloid precursor protein.

title: Gastric juice miR-129 as a potential biomarker for screening gastric cancer
text:
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play a crucial role in the diagnosis of gastric cancer. Conventional tests for screening gastric cancer have limitations in terms of sensitivity and specificity. miRNAs in peripheral blood have been used as biomarkers of gastric cancer, but most of these miRNAs are also present in other types of cancer. However, the tissue-specific nature of gastric juice allows for the examination of miRNAs in gastric juice as potential biomarkers for gastric cancer.
We collected 141 gastric juice samples from patients with gastric cancer, gastric ulcers, atrophic gastritis, and minimal gastritis, as well as healthy individuals. We detected the levels of gastric juice miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p using quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction. A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was constructed to differentiate between patients with gastric cancer and those with benign gastric diseases. Our results showed that patients with gastric cancer had significantly lower levels of gastric juice miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p compared to patients with benign gastric diseases. The areas under the ROC curve (AUC) for miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p were 0.639 and 0.651, respectively. When combined, the AUC increased to 0.656.
Our findings suggest that gastric juice miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p are potential biomarkers for the screening of gastric cancer. The detection of gastric juice miRNAs is a non-invasive method for the diagnosis of gastric cancer.

title: Epidemiological expansion, structural studies, and clinical challenges of new β-lactamases from gram-negative bacteria.
text: The challenge of β-lactamase evolution in treating infections caused by multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacteria is a major concern for the infectious disease community. Given the sheer number of naturally occurring β-lactamases (over 1,000), attempts to correlate structure and function have become daunting. The emergence of new ESBLs (extended-spectrum β-lactamases) such as KPC serine carbapenemases and metallo-β-lactamases (VIM, IMP, and NDM-1) has further compounded this issue. These newer enzymes are becoming increasingly prevalent across different geographical regions, making the development of new β-lactamase inactivators or β-lactamase-stable β-lactams even more challenging. In light of this, combination therapy may be necessary to combat the ongoing evolution of these enzymes in multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: Robust synchronization of coupled circadian and cell cycle oscillators in single mammalian cells
text: Circadian rhythms and cell cycles are two fundamental, periodic processes with a period ranging from 1 day. As a result, there can be interactions between these cycles, leading to synchronization. To investigate this, we used time-lapse imaging to observe single mammalian NIH3T3 fibroblasts over several days. Thousands of circadian cycles in dividing cells revealed that both oscillators operate in a 1:1 mode-locked state, with cell divisions occurring approximately 5 hours before the peak in circadian Rev-Erbα-YFP reporter expression. It is possible that this synchrony is due to either unidirectional or bidirectional coupling. While cell division can be regulated by the circadian cycle, our findings, combined with stochastic modeling, show that the reverse coupling is the dominant interaction in NIH3T3 cells. Additionally, temperature, genetic, and pharmacological perturbations revealed that the two interacting cellular oscillators can adopt a synchronized state that is robust across a wide range of parameters. These findings have implications for circadian function in proliferative tissues, such as the epidermis, immune system, and cancer.

title: Identification of a Brainstem Circuit Controlling Feeding
text: Hunger, triggered by a negative energy balance, prompts the search for and consumption of food. While the hypothalamus plays a role in this response, the specific functions of other brain regions are less clear. Our research reveals that neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), particularly those that express vesicular transporters for GABA (DRNVgat neurons) or glutamate (DRNVGLUT3 neurons), are reciprocally reactivated by changes in energy balance. Increasing the activity of DRNVgat neurons leads to increased food intake, while decreasing the activity of DRNVGLUT3 neurons leads to decreased food intake and body weight. Furthermore, modifying these neurons in obese (ob/ob) mice normalizes their locomotor activity and suppresses food intake. We also identified druggable targets on these neurons using molecular profiling and found that local infusions of agonists for specific receptors on these neurons have potent effects on feeding. Our findings establish the DRN as a critical node in the regulation of energy balance. TRIPTangle.

title: Infection-induced NETosis is a dynamic process involving neutrophil multitasking in vivo
text: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are released in vitro during the course of several hours, creating a temporary window of vulnerability that invading microorganisms can exploit. Despite their ability to migrate and engulf foreign particles, neutrophils capable of NETosis have yet to be documented in situ. In vivo, we directly observed live polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs) rapidly releasing NETs, which prevented systemic bacterial dissemination, during Gram-positive skin infections. The process of NETosis occurred during the crawling phase, resulting in the deposition of large areas of NETs. Further analysis revealed that NET-releasing PMNs exhibited abnormal nuclei, which were devoid of DNA, and displayed unusual crawling behavior, characterized by erratic pseudopods and hyperpolarization. Our findings suggest that both Toll-like receptor 2 and complement-mediated opsonization play a critical role in regulating NET release, and that live human PMNs injected into mouse skin can form NETS in vivo. Surprisingly, we found that intact anuclear neutrophils were abundant in Gram-positive human abscesses, indicating that early in infection, NETosis involves neutrophils that retain the ability to multitask.

title: Swim training suppresses tumor growth in mice.
text: The current study aimed to investigate the impact of physical training on the development of cancer in mice injected with Ehrlich tumor cells. Male Swiss mice were either subjected to a swim training protocol (5 days/week for 6 weeks, 1 hour at 50% of maximum capacity) or remained sedentary in their cages (sedentary group). The mice were inoculated with Ehrlich tumor cells at the end of the fourth week, and were then killed after 6 weeks of training. The study found that the tumor volume and weight were approximately 270% and 280% higher in sedentary mice compared to trained mice. Furthermore, the number of macrophages in the tumor tissue was significantly lower in trained mice (0.65 +/- 0.16 vs. 1.78 +/- 0.43 macrophages x 10(3) in the sedentary group), and neutrophil accumulation in the tumors was slightly reduced after exercise training. Additionally, the amount of tumor cells was reduced in trained mice. The study also found that exercise capacity was significantly improved in trained mice, as determined by a 440% increase in the exercise time at 50% of maximal capacity. In summary, the study suggests that swim training delays the growth of Ehrlich tumors in mice, accompanied by a reduction in macrophage infiltration and neutrophil accumulation. These findings provide theoretical support for clinical observations that regular physical activity may be a therapeutically important approach to preventing cancer progression and improving cancer treatment outcomes.

title: Lung dendritic cells imprint T cell lung homing and promote lung immunity through the chemokine receptor CCR4
text: T cell migration into the lung is essential for effective lung immunity, but the mechanisms that regulate T cell entry into the lung are not well understood. Our study reveals that lung dendritic cells (DCs) play a crucial role in directing T cell migration into the lung. We found that T cells activated by lung DCs have enhanced migration into the lung in response to inhaled antigens and at homeostatic conditions compared to T cells activated by DCs from other tissues. As a result, T cells activated by lung DCs provide better protection against influenza than T cells activated by DCs from other organs. Lung DCs imprint the expression of the chemokine receptor CCR4 on T cells, which contributes to T cell lung migration. Limiting the migration of CCR4-deficient T cells into the lung reduces their ability to protect against influenza. Thus, lung DCs play a critical role in directing T cell migration into the lung and promoting lung immunity, in part through the expression of CCR4.

title: microRNAs: A Safeguard against Turmoil?
text: Recent findings indicate that microRNAs (miRNAs) play a vital role in various stress responses, beyond their previously recognized function in development. Interestingly, miRNAs, which typically suppress the expression of target transcripts, can actually become activators of expression during times of stress. This phenomenon may be partly explained by novel interactions between miRNA/Argonaute complexes and RNA-binding proteins that reorganize their subcellular localization during stress.

title: Vascular smooth muscle cell calcification is mediated by regulated exosome secretion.
text:
The study investigates the regulation and role of matrix vesicle (MV) biogenesis in vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) calcification. MVs, secreted by VSMCs, form the initial deposit for mineralization, and fetuin-A, a potent circulating inhibitor of calcification, is specifically loaded into MVs. However, the mechanisms of fetuin-A intracellular trafficking and MV biogenesis are poorly understood.
The study employed various methods to investigate MV biogenesis in VSMCs, including labeling with Alexa488-fetuin-A, internalization, trafficking via the endosomal system, exocytosis from multivesicular bodies, and comparative proteomics. The study found that VSMC-derived exosomes were enriched with tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81 and were regulated by sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3. Additionally, elevated extracellular calcium induced sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 expression and the secretion of calcifying exosomes from VSMCs in vitro, and chemical inhibition of sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 prevented VSMC calcification.
In vivo, multivesicular bodies containing exosomes were observed in vessels from chronic kidney disease patients on dialysis, and CD63 colocalized with calcification. Furthermore, factors such as tumor necrosis factor-α and platelet-derived growth factor-BB were found to increase exosome production, leading to increased calcification of VSMCs in response to calcifying conditions.
The study identifies MVs as exosomes and shows that factors that increase exosome release can promote vascular calcification in response to environmental calcium stress. Modulation of the exosome release pathway may be a novel therapeutic target for preventing vascular calcification.

title: Vaccines against malaria
text: There is currently no licensed vaccine available to combat any human parasitic disease, including Plasmodium falciparum malaria, a significant cause of infectious mortality. This void has prompted vaccine developers to explore a range of strategies in the design and development of malaria vaccines. The availability of a safe challenge model for small-scale efficacy testing of vaccine candidates has proven beneficial in this process. Malaria vaccine development has been at the forefront of evaluating novel vaccine technologies, including novel adjuvants, vectored prime-boost regimens, and the concept of community vaccination to curb malaria transmission. Most present vaccine candidates target a single stage of the parasite's life cycle, with vaccines concentrating on the early pre-erythrocytic stages showing the most promise. A protein-based adjuvant vaccine, which works through antibodies against sporozoites, and viral vector vaccines targeting the intracellular liver-stage parasite through cellular immunity have shown partial efficacy in humans, with the anti-sporozoite vaccine currently in phase III trials. However, a more effective malaria vaccine suitable for widespread, cost-effective deployment is likely to require a multi-component vaccine targeting multiple life cycle stages. The most promising near-term approach to create such a product is to combine existing partially effective pre-erythrocytic vaccine candidates.

title: MicroRNA-21 is Induced by Rapamycin in a Model of Tuberous Sclerosis (TSC) and Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)
text: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a complex disease affecting women, is characterized by the proliferation of smooth muscle-like cells in the lung, leading to cystic lung destruction. Additionally, women with LAM may develop renal angiomyolipomas. The underlying genetic cause of LAM is mutations in the tuberous sclerosis complex genes (TSC1 or TSC2), which results in hyperactivation of the mammalian Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway. This in turn can lead to the stabilization of lung function in LAM patients and a decrease in the volume of renal angiomyolipomas upon treatment with the mTOR inhibitor, Rapamycin. However, upon discontinuation of treatment, lung function declines, and angiomyolipomas regrow, suggesting that factors induced by mTORC1 inhibition may promote the survival of TSC2-deficient cells. The potential involvement of microRNA (miRNA) signaling in the response of LAM to mTORC1 inhibition remains unexplored. In this study, we investigated the impact of Rapamycin on miRNA expression in angiomyolipoma-derived cells from LAM patients using two separate screens. Our results identified 18 miRNAs that were upregulated by Rapamycin, while eight were downregulated. Dysregulation of miRNAs 29b, 21, 24, 221, 106a, and 199a was common to both platforms and was classified as candidate "RapamiRs." Validation by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) confirmed that these microRNAs were increased upon mTOR inhibition. Of particular interest, the pro-survival miR-21 was the most significantly upregulated by mTOR inhibition (p < 0.01). Further investigation revealed that the regulation of miR-21 by Rapamycin is independent of cell type. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that Rapamycin upregulates multiple miRNAs in TSC2-deficient patient-derived cells, including pro-survival miRNAs. These findings suggest that the induction of miRNAs may contribute to the response of LAM and TSC patients to Rapamycin therapy.

title: Reduced NF1 expression confers resistance to EGFR inhibition in lung cancer.
text:
Activating mutations within the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) are commonly associated with clinical responsiveness to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as erlotinib and gefitinib. However, resistance to these inhibitors often develops over time, typically due to the emergence of a secondary mutation, most commonly T790M. Through a comprehensive genome-wide siRNA screen in a human lung cancer cell line and thorough analyses of murine EGFR-driven lung adenocarcinomas, our findings indicate that erlotinib resistance is associated with decreased expression of neurofibromin, the RAS GTPase-activating protein encoded by the NF1 gene. Specifically, reduced neurofibromin expression compromises the ability of erlotinib to fully inhibit the RAS-ERS signaling pathway. Intriguingly, treatment of neurofibromin-deficient lung cancers with a mitogen-activated protein kinase (MEK) inhibitor can restore sensitivity to erlotinib. Our findings implicate a subset of patients with EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma who might benefit from combination therapy with EGFR and MEK inhibitors.
In essence, our research uncovered a mechanistic link between EGFR mutations and resistance to TKIs, highlighting the potential of targeting downstream signaling pathways to improve treatment outcomes in EGFR-mutant lung cancer patients.

title: Human IRGM induces autophagy to eliminate intracellular mycobacteria.
text: IRG proteins, involved in immunity, are crucial for defending against intracellular pathogens. Specifically, our study found that murine Irgm1 (LRG-47) guanosine triphosphatase triggers autophagy and forms large autolysosomal organelles, which are essential for eliminating intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Additionally, we discovered a role for human IRG proteins in regulating intracellular pathogens, and our findings indicate that the human Irgm1 ortholog, IRGM, plays a part in autophagy and reduces the intracellular load of bacteria.

title: Implementation of a Clinical Pharmacy Education Program in a Teaching Hospital: Resident Oriented Documentation and Intervention
text: The purpose of this study was to establish a clinical pharmacy education program at Masih Daneshvari Hospital, a university-affiliated hospital located in Tehran, Iran. To accomplish this, the researchers identified the most common pharmacist interventions and areas of potential training for pharmacy students and residents. Clinical pharmacy interventions and drug information forms were completed during the study period, from January 2006 to January 2007. Findings showed a total of 772 interventions were conducted during the study year, with drug information accounting for 22.30% of all interventions, followed by dose adjustment and therapeutic reduction or addition. The average number of medications per patient was 8.62 ± 7.54. The study's results suggest that, although Iran is still in the early stages of developing the pharmacy profession compared to developed countries, there is a high demand for clinical pharmacy services among healthcare providers.

title: The surgical anatomy of the conduction tissues.
text: Based on our cumulative expertise, we have evaluated the arrangement of cardiac conduction tissues as observed by surgeons in both normal and abnormal hearts. The sinus node lies subepicardially in the terminal sulcus, and due to its variable blood supply, the entire superior cavoatrial junction is considered a potential danger area. Contrary to morphologically distinct tracts connecting the sinus node and atrioventricular nodes, the atrioventricular node, which represents the atrial portion of the atrioventricular conduction axis, is entirely contained within the triangle of Koch. This axis terminates through the central fibrous body and branches onto the muscular ventricular septum just beneath the interventricular component of the membranous septum. The location of these structures can be ascertained through examination of the right atrium, left atrium, and aorta. Subsequent consideration is given to the surgical anatomy of abnormal muscular atrioventricular connections prominent in ventricular pre-excitation syndromes. Finally, guidelines are formulated to accurately predict the disposition of conduction tissues in congenitally malformed hearts, taking into account both normal and aberrant chamber connections. The most critical factors in this regard are the alignment between atrial and ventricular septal structures and the pattern of ventricular architecture present.

title: Agreement between an online dietary assessment tool (myfood24) and an interviewer-administered 24-h dietary recall in British adolescents aged 11-18 years.
text: In recent years, the development of new technologies has enabled the assessment of nutritional intake among adolescents through online tools. However, little is known about the accuracy of these tools, particularly among this age group. To address this gap in knowledge, a relative validation study was conducted to assess the accuracy of the online tool myfood24 against a face-to-face interviewer-administered 24-hour multiple-pass recall (MPR) in a sample of 75 British adolescents aged 11-18 years. Participants completed both myfood24 and the interviewer-administered MPR on two non-consecutive days at school. The agreement between the two methods was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Bland-Altman plots, and weighted κ statistics. The results indicated strong agreement between the two methods for energy intake (EI) and macronutrients, with ICC ranging from 0.46 for sodium to 0.88 for EI. There was no significant bias between the two methods for EI, macronutrients, and most reported nutrients. The mean difference between myfood24 and the interviewer-administered MPR for EI was -230 kJ (-55 kcal) (95% CI -490, -30 kJ (-117, -7 kcal)); P = 0.4), with limits of agreement ranging between 39% (3336 kJ (-797 kcal)) lower and 34% (2874 kJ (687 kcal)) higher than the interviewer-administered MPR. Additionally, there was good agreement in terms of classifying adolescents into tertiles of EI (κw = 0.64). The results demonstrated the reliability of myfood24 and its potential to collect dietary data of comparable quality to that obtained through an interviewer-administered MPR.

title: Modulation of cancer chemotherapy by green tea.
text: Biochemical modification has played a crucial role in the development of cancer chemotherapy. We turned our attention to the consumption of common beverages and investigated the effects of green tea and its constituents on the antitumor activity of doxorubicin. We conducted a combined treatment study involving toxorubicin and green tea in Ehrlich ascites carcinoma tumor-bearing mice. Oral administration of green tea significantly enhanced the inhibitory effects of doxorubicin on tumor growth by 2.5-fold. Concurrently, the concentration of doxorubicin in the tumor was raised by the combination of green tea and doxorubicin. In contrast, the increase in doxorubicin concentration in normal tissues following the green tea and doxorubicin combination was not observed. Additionally, the enhancement of the antitumor activity of doxorubicin occurring as a result of green tea was found in M5076 ovarian sarcoma, which has low sensitivity to doxorubicin. These findings suggest that consuming green tea may enhance cancer chemotherapy and improve the quality of life for cancer patients undergoing treatment.

title: Histone deacetylase 5 interacts with Krüppel-like factor 2 and inhibits its transcriptional activity in endothelium.
text:
The article explores the role of histone deacetylase 5 (HDAC5) in regulating the anti-inflammatory and anti-atherosclerotic properties of the endothelium. The study shows that HDAC5 associates with and represses the transcriptional activation of Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2), which is a key regulator of endothelial nitric oxide synthesis (eNOS). The authors found that steady laminar flow can attenuate the association of HDAC5 with KLF2, leading to increased KLF2 transcriptional activity and eNOS expression. Conversely, HDAC5 overexpression or silencing can modulate KLF2 transcription and eNOS expression in endothelial cells. The study also shows that HDAC5 knockout mice have higher levels of eNOS protein and lower levels of pro-inflammatory vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 in the thoracic aorta compared to HDAC5 wild-type mice, suggesting that HDAC5 may be a new therapeutic target for preventing vascular endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular diseases.
In summary, the study demonstrates that HDAC5 plays a crucial role in regulating KLF2 transcriptional activation and eNOS expression in endothelial cells. The findings suggest that targeting HDAC5 may be a promising strategy for preventing vascular endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular diseases.

title: N348I in HIV-1 reverse transcriptase can counteract the nevirapine-mediated bias toward RNase H cleavage during plus-strand initiation.
text: Drug-resistant mutations in HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT) can alter the balance between polymerase and ribonuclease H (RNase H) activities within the enzyme. Recently, we discovered that the N348I mutation in the connection domain causes selective dissociation from RNase H-competent complexes, yet the polymerase-competent complex remains largely unscathed. The N348I mutation has been linked to resistance to non-nucleoside RT inhibitors (NNRTIs), such as nevirapine. However, the underlying mechanism connecting changes in RNase H activity to NNRTI susceptibility remains unclear. In light of recent findings that NNRTIs can manipulate the orientation of RT on its nucleic acid substrate and enhance RNase H activity, we investigated the effect of NNRTIs on primer removal mediated by RNase H. Our results demonstrate that RNase H-mediated primer removal is more efficient in the presence of NNRTIs, but the N348I mutant enzyme can counteract this effect. The tight binding inhibitor efavirenz mitigates the influence of the mutation. Together, these findings provide evidence that N348I can undermine the inhibitory effects of nevirapine during initiation of (+)-strand DNA synthesis, revealing a novel mechanism of resistance. Our findings are consistent with clinical observations, which show a more profound effect of N348I on nevirapine susceptibility compared to efavirenz.

title: Cancer survivorship research: the challenge of recruiting adult long term cancer survivors from a cooperative clinical trials group
text:
INTRODUCTION: With the increasing number of adult cancer survivors, there is a growing need for information on the potential late and long-term effects of cancer treatments. Although few adult cancer patients participate in clinical trials, those who have previously enrolled in these trials are an important source of information on treatment-related late effects.
METHODS: We used the database from five phase III randomized clinical trials from the National Surgical Adjuvant Breast & Bowel Project (NSABP) to recruit and enroll long-term survivors for a study on late health outcomes and quality of life. We describe the challenges encountered during the recruitment of patients more than 5-20 years after treatment.
RESULTS: Sixty-five NSABP treatment sites were invited to participate in the study, and 60 sites agreed to enroll patients. Of the 976 patients invited to participate, 744 (76%) expressed interest, and 708 completed interviews (95% of those expressing interest; 29% of the total potential sample). Multiple barriers to recruitment were identified, including difficulty locating patients, lack of institutional commitment, and lack of patient interest.
CONCLUSIONS: Patients treated on clinical trials are an important potential source for examining the late effects of cancer treatments. However, retrospective recruitment has several limitations. In the future, mechanisms should be established for prospective long-term follow-up to identify and understand the frequency and type of late effects associated with cancer treatments.
IMPLICATIONS FOR CANCER SURVIVORS: As cancer patients are living longer, it will be essential to learn from participants in clinical trials whether specific treatment regimens are associated with any serious late effects. This information can help cancer survivors make informed decisions about their health and potentially improve their quality of life.

title: Arylsulfatase B Improves Locomotor Function after Mouse Spinal Cord Injury
text: Bacterial chondroitinase ABC (ChaseABC) has been used to remove inhibitory chondroitin sulfate chains from chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans to enhance regeneration after spinal cord injury in rodents. We hypothesized that the mammalian enzyme arylsulfatase B (ARSB) would also improve recovery after spinal cord injury in mice. Injection of human ARSB into injured mouse spinal cord eliminated immunoreactivity for chondroitin sulfates within five days, and up to 9 weeks after injury. We observed improvements in locomotor recovery assessed by the Basso Mouse Scale (BMS) in ARSB-treated mice compared to control mice at 6 weeks after injection, and similarly improved functional recovery was observed in mice subjected to severe spinal cord injury. Moreover, ARSB-treated mice displayed more extensive serotonin and tyrosine hydroxylase immunoreactive axons in their spinal cords compared to control mice, with greater axonal penetration beyond the injury site. These results suggest that mammalian ARSB improves functional recovery after central nervous system (CNS) injury. However, the underlying structural and molecular mechanisms remain to be elucidated.

title: The World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS): a short screening scale for use in the general population.
text:
The World Health Organization (WHO) Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) was developed in conjunction with the revision of the WHO Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI) to assess adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). This study evaluates the concordance between the ASRS and a short-form ASRS screener with blind clinical diagnoses in a community sample.
The ASRS includes 18 questions about the frequency of recent DSM-IV Criterion A symptoms of adult ADHD. The ASRS screener consists of six out of these 18 questions that were selected based on stepwise logistic regression to optimize concordance with the clinical classification. The ASRS responses were compared to blind clinical ratings of DSM-IV adult ADHD in a sample of 154 respondents who previously participated in the US National Comorbidity Survey Replication (NCS-R), oversampling those who reported childhood ADHD and adult persistence.
Each ASRS symptom measure was significantly related to the comparable clinical symptom rating, but varied substantially in concordance (Cohen's kappa in the range 0.16-0.81). Optimal scoring to predict clinical syndrome classifications was to sum unweighted dichotomous responses across all 18 ASRS questions. However, due to the wide variation in symptom-level concordance, the unweighted six-question ASRS screener outperformed the unweighted 18-question ASRS in sensitivity (68.7% vs. 56.3%), specificity (99.5% vs. 98.3%), total classification accuracy (97.9% vs. 96.2%), and kappa (0.76 vs. 0.58).
The study concludes that until further research shows that a weighted version of the 18-question ASRS outperforms the six-question ASRS screener, the unweighted screener should be preferred in community surveys and clinical outreach and case-finding initiatives.

title: Human milk proresolving mediators stimulate resolution of acute inflammation
text:
Human milk is endowed with nutrients and bioactive substances that are essential for fetal development and immunological protection. In this study, we investigated the resolving properties of milk using human milk lipid mediator isolates (HLMIs) and assessed their impact on resolution programs in vivo and on human macrophages. Our findings revealed that HLMIs significantly reduce the maximum number of neutrophils (14.6±1.2 × 106–11.0±1.0 × 106 cells per exudate) and shorten the resolution interval (Ri; 50% neutrophil reduction) by 54% compared to peritonitis.
Employing rigorous liquid-chromatography tandem-mass spectrometry (LC-MS-MS)-based lipid mediator (LM) metabololipidomics, we demonstrated that human milk possesses a proresolving LM-specialized proresolving mediator (LM-SPM) signature profile, containing SPMs such as resolvins (Rv), protectins (PDs), maresins (MaRs), and lipoxins (LXs) at bioactive concentrations (pico-nanomolar levels). Specifically, SPMs identified in human milk included D-series Rvs (e.g., RvD1, RvD2, RvD3, AT-RvD3, and RvD4), PD1, MaR1, E-series Rvs (e.g. RvE1, RvE2, and RvE3), and LXs (LXA4 and LXB4). Our findings indicate that individual SPMs, such as RvD2 and MaR1 (50 ng per mouse), can shorten Ri by ∼75%. Notably, milk from mastitis showed higher levels of leukotriene B4 and prostanoids and lower SPM levels. Altogether, these findings provide evidence that human milk exhibits resolving actions through comprehensive LM-SPM profiling, suggesting a novel mechanism in maternal-infant biochemical imprinting.

title: Cerebral perfusion and stroke.
text: Stroke is a complex disorder that arises from multiple underlying disease mechanisms, leading to a disruption of blood flow to the brain and subsequent tissue damage. This review focuses on the mechanisms that regulate normal cerebral blood flow and how they are disrupted in disease states. Specifically, we will explore the concept of the ischemic penumbra, which refers to the region of potentially salvageable tissue that can be saved if blood flow is restored promptly after a stroke. We will examine the empirical evidence for the existence of the ischemic penumbra in human patients.

title: Epigenetic regulation of miR-184 by MBD1 governs neural stem cell proliferation and differentiation.
text:
Methyl-CpG binding protein 1 (MBD1) controls gene expression through an epigenetic mechanism that involves DNA methylation. Previously, we demonstrated that MBD1 deficiency impairs the differentiation and neurogenesis of adult neural stem/progenitor cells (aNSCs). However, the underlying mechanism was unknown.
Our study reveals that MBD1 regulates the expression of several microRNAs in aNSCs, with miR-184 being the most notable example. We found that high levels of miR-184 promote aNSC proliferation but inhibit differentiation, while inhibiting miR-184 rescues the defects associated with MBD1 deficiency.
Furthermore, we discovered that miR-184 regulates the expression of Numblike (Numbl), a regulatory protein involved in brain development. MiR-184 binds to the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of Numbl mRNA and affects its translation. Interestingly, we found that exogenous Numbl expression can rescue the aNSC defects that result from either miR-184 overexpression or MBD1 deficiency, highlighting the interconnectedness of this regulatory network.
In summary, our findings demonstrate the complex interplay between MBD1, miR-184, and Numbl in regulating the balance between proliferation and differentiation of aNSCs. This regulatory network provides a crucial framework for controlling brain development and maintenance.

title: Landscape of genetic lesions in 944 patients with myelodysplastic syndromes
text: High-throughput DNA sequencing significantly contributed to the diagnosis and prognosis of patients with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). We aimed to determine the biological and prognostic significance of genetic aberrations in MDS by analyzing the genomes of 944 patients with various MDS subtypes. Using targeted deep sequencing and array-based genomic hybridization, we identified mutations in 845 patients (89.5%), with 47 genes showing significantly mutated in >10% of cases, including TET2, SF3B1, ASXL1, SRSF2, DNMT3A, and RUNX1. Many of these mutations were associated with higher-risk groups and/or blast elevation. We also investigated the impact of these mutations on patient survival in 875 patients. Univariate analysis identified 25 genes (resulting from 47 genes tested significantly plus PRPF8) that affected survival (P < 0.05), and a novel prognostic model (Model-1) was constructed using 14 genes that combined with conventional factors separated patients into four risk groups with 3-year survival rates of 95.2, 69.3, 32.8, and 5.3% (P < 0.001). Subsequently, a 'gene-only model' (Model-2) was constructed based on 14 genes, which yielded four significant risk groups (P < 0.001). Both models were reproducible in a validation cohort (n = 175 patients; P < 0.001 each). Our findings demonstrate the value of large-scale genetic and molecular profiling of multiple target genes for subclassification and prognostication in MDS patients.

title: Integrated molecular genetic profiling of pediatric high-grade gliomas reveals key differences with the adult disease.
text: Objective: To identify copy number alterations and gene expression signatures specific to pediatric high-grade gliomas (HGG). Methods: We performed high-resolution genomic analysis of 78 de novo pediatric HGGs, including 7 diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas, using single nucleotide polymorphism microarray analysis. Gene expression was analyzed for 53 tumors using gene expression microarrays, and results were compared to publicly available data from adult tumors. Results: We identified significant differences in copy number alterations between childhood and adult glioblastomas. PDGFRA was the predominant target of focal amplification in childhood HGG, including diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas, and gene expression analyses suggested an important role for deregulated PDGFRalpha signaling in pediatric HGG. Unlike adult secondary glioblastomas, no IDH1 hotspot mutations were found in pediatric tumors. Pediatric and adult glioblastomas were distinguished by differences in chromosome gains and losses, with 1q gain occurring at a higher frequency in irradiation-induced tumors. PDGFRA amplification and 1q gain occurred more frequently in pediatric tumors. A subset of pediatric HGGs had minimal copy number changes. Conclusion: Our integrated molecular profiling revealed significant differences in the molecular features underlying pediatric and adult HGG, highlighting the need to tailor treatments to each patient group. PDGFRalpha may be a useful target for pediatric HGG, including diffuse pontine gliomas.

title: Gene set enrichment analysis: a knowledge-based approach for interpreting genome-wide expression profiles.
text: Although genome-wide RNA expression analysis has become a common tool in biomedical research, interpreting the resulting data to extract meaningful biological insights remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, we present Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), a powerful analytical method that focuses on gene sets, or groups of genes with shared biological function, chromosomal location, or regulation. By leveraging the power of gene sets, GSEA yields valuable insights into cancer-related data sets, including leukemia and lung cancer. In contrast to single-gene analysis, which often reveals little similarity between independent studies of patient survival in lung cancer, GSEA uncovers numerous biological pathways that are common to these studies. The GSEA method is available as a freely accessible software package, accompanied by an initial database of 1,325 biologically defined gene sets.

title: The evolution of RNAs with multiple functions.
text: Rising numbers of transcripts have been found to convey both protein-coding and regulatory signals. This unexpected observation challenges traditional views of the gene and prompts questions about the extent to which this phenomenon occurs across the genome, as well as the reasons and mechanisms behind it. To explore this, we examine the evolutionary history of genes in early life on Earth, where proteins likely originated from an RNA-based cellular machinery. As protein-coding genes dominated microbial genomes, but RNA retained other capabilities, we hypothesize that mRNAs have been subject to secondary selection to provide regulatory functions in parallel with protein-coding ones. We also propose that some protein-coding loci have lost their protein-coding functions and acquired more sophisticated trans-regulatory capabilities, perhaps as a result of gene duplication. Furthermore, we suggest that many transcripts have undergone secondary processing to release different products and that novel proteins have emerged within loci initially evolved for regulatory RNA functions. Taken together, these observations suggest a dynamic interplay between different types of informational RNAs in both evolutionary and real time, and challenge the notion that discrete loci may express transcripts with only one function. In conclusion, we propose that many eukaryotic loci have evolved the capacity to perform multiple, overlapping and potentially independent functions as both regulatory and protein-coding RNAs.

title: In Vitro–expanded Antigen-specific Regulatory T Cells Suppress Autoimmune Diabetes
text: The scarcity of CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), their dormant state, and broad antigen specificity pose significant obstacles to harnessing these highly effective immune suppressors to treat autoimmune disorders and organ rejection. In this study, we outline an efficient method to expand antigen-specific Tregs from mice prone to autoimmune diseases. We isolated and amplified purified CD4+ CD25+ Tregs up to 200-fold within just over a week in a culture medium containing anti-CD3, anti-CD28, and interleukin 2. The expanded TregsDisplay a typical cell surface phenotype and exhibit both in vitro and in vivo suppression of effector T cell functions. Most notably, a minimal number of antigen-specific Tregs can reverse disease symptoms after onset, suggesting a novel approach to cellular immunotherapy for autoimmune disorders.

title: Stathmin overexpression identifies high-risk patients and lymph node metastasis in endometrial cancer.
text: Our study aimed to validate the prognostic value of Stathmin expression in a large, prospective, multicenter setting. We conducted immunohistochemical staining on 1,076 endometrial cancer samples from 10 centers to investigate the biomarker's relationship with clinicopathologic variables, including lymph node status and survival. We found that 71% of the patients (n = 763) underwent lymph node sampling, and 12% of these had metastatic nodes (n = 94). Stathmin overexpression was detected in 37% (302 of 818) of curettage and 18% (84 of 477) of hysterectomy specimens. Stathmin overexpression in curettage and hysterectomy specimens was highly correlated and significantly associated with nonendometrioid histology, high grade, and aneuploidy. Additionally, Stathmin analysis in preoperative curettage samples significantly correlated with and was an independent predictor of lymph node metastases. High Stathmin expression was also associated with poor disease-specific survival (P ≤ 0.002) in both curettage and hysterectomy specimens. Overall, our study suggests that Stathmin immunohistochemical staining can identify endometrial carcinomas with lymph node metastases and poor survival. However, further research is needed to determine the marker's value as a predictive tool for response to PI3Kinase inhibition and for stratifying patients for lymph node sampling in endometrial carcinomas.

title: Statin prophylaxis and inflammatory mediators following cardiopulmonary bypass: a systematic review
text:
INTRODUCTION Induction of an inflammatory response is believed to play a significant role in the complications that arise after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Recently, statin drugs have gained recognition for their potent anti-inflammatory effects, which could potentially influence a crucial mechanism of injury during CPB. However, there is presently no definitive evidence to confirm this notion. Our systematic review aimed to evaluate if administering prophylactic statin therapy before CPB can reduce the inflammatory response in individuals undergoing heart surgery.
METHODS We conducted a comprehensive and systematic literature search to identify all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of adults or children undergoing open heart surgery with CPB who received prophylactic statin treatment prior to surgery. We extracted data on inflammatory markers, including interleukins 6 and 8 (IL-6, IL-8), peak high sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha). Two authors independently assessed study quality using standardized instruments, and we pooled data using a random effects model with weighted mean difference as the primary summary statistic. Where data could not be pooled, we conducted descriptive analysis.
RESULTS Eight RCTs were included in the review, with limited data available for each inflammatory outcome. Pooled data demonstrated that statin therapy attenuated the post-CPB increase in IL-6, IL-8, hsCRP, and TNF-alpha (WMD [95% CI] -23.5 pg/ml [-36.6 to -10.5]; -23.4 pg/ml [-35.8 to -11.0]; -15.3 mg/L [CI -26.9 to -3.7]; -2.10 pg/ml [-3.83 to -0.37], respectively). Very limited RCT evidence also suggests that statin therapy may decrease adhesion molecules following CPB, including neutrophil CD11b and soluble P(sP)-selectin.
CONCLUSIONS While the RCT evidence suggests a reduction in post-CPB inflammation with statin therapy, the limitations of the studies prevent a definitive conclusion. Several of the trials were not methodologically rigorous, and statin intervention was highly variable in this small number of studies. Our systematic review reveals a significant gap in the current literature regarding the potential anti-inflammatory effect of statin therapy prior to CPB.

title: Array-based Comparative Genomic Hybridization for Genome-Wide Screening of DNA Copy Number in Bladder Tumors
text: In this study, the genomic profiles of 41 primary bladder tumors were analyzed using array-based comparative genomic hybridization (array CGH). In addition to previously identified alterations in large chromosomal regions, the study identified subtle changes in many small genomic regions, some of which involved high-level amplifications or homozygous deletions. The study detected high-level amplifications in 192 genomic clones, with the most common locations being 6p22.3 (E2F3), 8p12 (FGFR1), 8q22.2 (CMYC), 11q13 (CCND1, EMS1, INT2), and 19q13.1 (CCNE). Homozygous deletions were detected in 51 genomic clones, with four showing deletions in more than one case, including deletions at 9p21.3 (CDKN2A/p16 in nine cases), 8p23.1 (three cases), and 11p13 (two cases). Significant correlations were observed between copy number gains in clones containing CCNE1 and gains in ERBB2, and between gains in CCND1 and deletions of TP53. Additionally, there was a significant complementary association between gains in CCND1 and gains in E2F3. While there was no significant relationship between copy number changes and tumor stage or grade, the study suggests that array CGH will be increasingly important in understanding the pathways involved in bladder tumor biology.

title: Tet2 is required to resolve inflammation by recruiting Hdac2 to specifically repress IL-6
text:
Epigenetic modulators play a crucial role in establishing and maintaining unique cellular identities by controlling chromatin and methylation status. Tet proteins, a family of dioxygenases, catalyze the conversion of 5-methylcytosine to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, influencing chromatin architecture and gene expression. Although the role of Tet proteins in modulating DNA methylation has been well-characterized, their involvement in regulating immunity and inflammation remains poorly understood.
Our study uncovers the unexpected function of Tet2 in actively repressing interleukin-6 (IL-6) transcription during inflammation resolution in innate myeloid cells, including dendritic cells and macrophages. Surprisingly, loss of Tet2 led to increased IL-6 production at the late phase of the inflammatory response. Consistent with this observation, Tet2-deficient mice were more susceptible to endotoxin shock and dextran-sulfate-sodium-induced colitis, displaying a more severe inflammatory phenotype and heightened IL-6 secretion compared to wild-type mice.
We discovered that the IL-6-specific transcription factor IκBζ plays a vital role in targeting Tet2 to the Il6 promoter, revealing distinct regulatory roles of IκBζ during the initial and resolution phases of inflammation. Interestingly, Tet2 mediates the repression of IL-6 transcription through histone deacetylation, a mechanism independent of DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation. Our findings provide insight into the gene-specific transcriptional repression activity of Tet2 and the prevention of constitutive transcription activation at the chromatin level for resolving inflammation.

title: Control of immunity by the TNFR-related molecule OX40 (CD134).
text: TNFR/TNF superfamily members play a crucial role in regulating various immune functions. Recent research has highlighted the significance of the OX40/OX40L interaction in this family, which profoundly influences conventional CD4 and CD8 T cells, as well as NKT cells and NK cells. These molecules also facilitate cross-talk between professional antigen-presenting cells and other cell types, such as mast cells, smooth muscle cells, and endothelial cells. Furthermore, OX40-OX40L interactions have the potential to regulate the differentiation and activity of regulatory T cells. Interestingly, blocking OX40L has shown promise as a therapeutic approach in various animal models of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, and agents that stimulate OX40 signaling are emerging as potential adjuvants for vaccination and cancer treatment.

title: The Drosophila DHR96 nuclear receptor binds cholesterol and regulates cholesterol homeostasis.
text: Maintaining proper cholesterol levels is crucial for normal cellular function, and disruptions in this process can lead to harmful consequences such as hypercholesterolemia. Our research reveals that the Drosophila DHR96 nuclear receptor plays a central role in cholesterol regulation. We found that DHR96 binds cholesterol and regulates the transcription of genes involved in cholesterol uptake, transport, and storage. Mutants of DHR96 are susceptible to cholesterol deficiencies and experience an accumulation of excess cholesterol when fed a high-cholesterol diet. This phenotype can be attributed to the misregulation of Npc1b, an ortholog of the mammalian Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 gene NPC1L1, which is crucial for dietary cholesterol absorption. These findings designate DHR96 as a key regulator of cholesterol homeostasis.

title: A neuroimaging investigation of the association between aerobic fitness, hippocampal volume, and memory performance in preadolescent children.
text: As children are becoming increasingly overweight, unhealthy, and unfit, understanding the neurocognitive benefits of an active lifestyle in childhood has significant public health and educational implications. Animal studies have shown that aerobic exercise is linked to increased cell growth and survival in the hippocampus, as well as enhanced learning and memory skills. Recent research in older adults suggests that high levels of aerobic fitness are associated with increased hippocampal volume and better memory performance. To further explore this relationship in children, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was used to investigate whether higher- and lower-fit 9- and 10-year-olds showed differences in hippocampal volume and whether these differences were related to their performance on memory tasks. It was found that higher-fit children had greater bilateral hippocampal volumes and better relational memory task performance compared to lower-fit children. Additionally, bilateral hippocampal volume was found to mediate the relationship between fitness level (max VO(2)) and relational memory. Contrary to predictions, no relationship was found between aerobic fitness, nucleus accumbens volume, and memory. These findings suggest that aerobic fitness may have a specific effect on the preadolescent human brain, relevant to structure and function of the hippocampus.

title: Association between maternal serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level and pregnancy and neonatal outcomes: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
text:
Objective: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the effect of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OHD) levels during pregnancy on various pregnancy outcomes and birth variables.
Design: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
Data sources: Medline (1966-August 2012), PubMed (2008-August 2012), Embase (1980-August 2012), CINAHL (1981-August 2012), the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, and the Cochrane Database of Registered Clinical Trials.
Study selection: Studies reporting the association between serum 25-OHD levels during pregnancy and the outcomes of interest, including pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, bacterial vaginosis, caesarean section, small for gestational age infants, birth weight, birth length, and head circumference.
Data extraction: Two authors independently extracted data from original research articles, including key indicators of study quality. The most adjusted odds ratios and weighted mean differences were pooled and tested in subgroups representing different patient characteristics and study quality.
Results: A total of 3357 studies were identified and reviewed for eligibility, of which 31 eligible studies were included in the final analysis. Sufficient serum levels of 25-OHD were associated with a decreased risk of gestational diabetes (pooled odds ratio 0.73, 95% confidence interval 0.54 to 0.99), pre-eclampsia (0.85, 0.67 to 1.07), and caesarean section (0.81, 0.68 to 0.97), while insufficient serum levels were associated with an increased risk of gestational diabetes (pooled odds ratio 1.49, 95% confidence interval 1.18 to 1.89), pre-eclampsia (1.79, 1.25 to 2.58), and small for gestational age infants (1.85, 1.52 to 2.26). Pregnant women with low serum 25-OHD levels had an increased risk of bacterial vaginosis and low birthweight infants but not delivery by caesarean section.
Conclusion: Vitamin D insufficiency is associated with an increased risk of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, and small for gestational age infants. Pregnant women with low 25-OHD levels had an increased risk of bacterial vaginosis and lower birth weight infants, but not delivery by caesarean section.

title: β-Adrenergic receptor antagonism prevents anxiety-like behavior and microglial reactivity induced by repeated social defeat.
text: Repeated social defeat in mice has been shown to lead to changes in the brain and immune system that contribute to the development of anxiety-like behavior and psychological disorders. In this study, we found that repeated social defeat increased the expression of c-Fos in brain regions involved in fear and threat appraisal, and promoted anxiety-like behavior in a β-adrenergic receptor-dependent manner. Additionally, there was an increase in the number of certain immune cells (CD11b(+)/CD45(high)/Ly6C(high) macrophages) that trafficked to the brain after social defeat. Furthermore, we observed elevated levels of inflammatory markers (CD14, CD86, and TLR4) on the surface of microglia and macrophages, as well as an increase in the number of deramified microglia in the medial amygdala, prefrontal cortex, and hippocampus. The stress-dependent changes in microglia and macrophages were prevented by propranolol, a β-adrenergic receptor antagonist. Interestingly, microglia isolated from socially defeated mice produced higher levels of inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, tumor necrosis factor-α, and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1) after stimulation with lipopolysaccharide compared to microglia from control mice. Our findings suggest that repeated social defeat-induced anxiety-like behavior and enhanced reactivity of microglia are dependent on the activation of β-adrenergic and IL-1 receptors.

title: In vitro differentiation of transplantable neural precursors from human embryonic stem cells
text: The remarkable potential for development and replication of human embryonic stem (ES) cells holds the promise of an almost limitless supply of specific cell types for transplantation therapies. In this study, we describe the in vitro differentiation, enrichment, and transplantation of neural precursor cells derived from human ES cells. Upon aggregation into embryoid bodies, which are large structures resembling neural tubes, ES cells differentiate in the presence of fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF-2) into neural tube-like structures. Neural precursors within these formations are isolated through selective enzymatic digestion and further purified based on their differential adhesion properties. Upon withdrawal of FGF-2, these precursors differentiate into neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes. Following transplantation into the brain of neonatal mice, human ES cell–derived neural precursors are incorporated into various brain regions and differentiate into both neurons and astrocytes without forming teratomas. These results demonstrate human ES cells as a potential source of transplantable neural precursors for possible nervous system repair.

title: Characterization of prostaglandin E2 production by Candida albicans.
text: Candida albicans produces lipid metabolites that resemble those produced by the host's prostaglandin system. Using mass spectrometry, researchers have shown that C. albicans produces authentic prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) from arachidonic acid. The optimal production of PGE2 occurs at 37 degrees Celsius in stationary-phase culture supernatants and cell-free lysates derived from stationary-phase cells. Notably, PGE2 production is inhibited by both non-specific cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase inhibitors but not by inhibitors specific for the cyclooxygenase 2 isoenzyme. Surprisingly, the C. albicans genome does not contain a cyclooxygenase homolog, but several genes that may play a role in prostaglandin synthesis were investigated. It was found that a C. albicans fatty acid desaturase homolog (Ole2) and a multicopper oxidase homolog (Fet3) are involved in prostaglandin production, with ole2/ole2 and fet3/fet3 mutant strains exhibiting reduced PGE2 levels compared to parent strains. This work demonstrates that the synthesis of PGE2 in C. albicans occurs through novel pathways.

title: A global role for KLF1 in erythropoiesis revealed by ChIP-seq in primary erythroid cells.
text: KLF1 plays a crucial role in directing the differentiation of erythroid cells from bipotent progenitors. To explore the local regulatory context and transcription factor networks that KLF1 operates within, we performed KLF1 ChIP-seq in mouse embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) fetal liver erythroid cells. We discovered at least 945 sites in the genome where endogenous KLF1 binds to DNA, including many in the promoters of erythroid genes such as Hbb-b1. However, the majority of these sites are located far away from any known genes. Our findings suggest that KLF1 primarily functions as a transcriptional activator to regulate diverse aspects of terminal erythroid differentiation, including production of alpha- and beta-globin protein chains, heme biosynthesis, coordination of cell proliferation and anti-apoptotic pathways, and construction of the red blood cell membrane and cytoskeleton. Additionally, we propose new mechanisms for KLF1 collaboration with other transcription factors, such as the erythroid transcription factor GATA1, to maintain homeostasis in the erythroid compartment.

title: KOBAS 2.0: a web server for annotation and identification of enriched pathways and diseases
text: High-throughput experimental technologies generally identify numerous genes associated with or affected by a biological or disease process. From these genes, users seek to identify potential biological pathways and diseases involved. To facilitate this process, we have developed a web server called KOBAS 2.0, which annotates an input set of genes with putative pathways and disease relationships based on mapping to genes with known annotations. KOBAS 2.0 allows for both identity mapping and cross-species sequence similarity mapping. It then applies statistical tests to identify significantly enriched pathways and diseases. KOBAS 2.0 leverages knowledge from 1327 species across 5 pathway databases (KEGG PATHWAY, PID, BioCyc, Reactome, and Panther) and 5 human disease databases (OMIM, KEGG DISEASE, FunDO, GAD, and NHGRI GWAS Catalog). KOBAS 2.0 can be accessed at <http://kobas.cbi.pku.edu.chn>.

title: Translocation of sickle cell erythrocyte microRNAs into Plasmodium falciparum inhibits parasite translation and contributes to malaria resistance.
text:
Hemoglobin-S (HbS) bearing red blood cells, which are responsible for sickle cell disease, exhibit resistance to infection by the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Although the molecular basis of this resistance was previously believed to be multifactorial, our study has shed light on an important mechanism that contributes to this resistance. We found that dysregulated microRNA (miRNA) composition in either heterozygous HbAS or homozygous HbSS red blood cells plays a crucial role in resisting P. falciparum infection.
During the intraerythrocytic life cycle of P. falciparum, miRNAs from the red blood cells can translocate into the parasite. We identified two miRNAs, miR-451 and let-7i, that are particularly enriched in HbAS and HbSS red blood cells and negatively regulate parasite growth. Surprisingly, we discovered that these miRNAs integrated into essential parasite messenger RNAs, leading to impaired ribosomal loading and translational inhibition.
Our findings suggest that sickle cell erythrocytes exhibit cell-intrinsic resistance to malaria in part through an atypical miRNA activity, representing a unique host defense strategy against complex eukaryotic pathogens. This study has shed light on an important mechanism contributing to the resistance of sickle cell anemia patients to malaria infection, which could have significant implications for the development of novel antimalarial therapies.

title: CD28 and ITK signals regulate autoreactive T cell trafficking
text: The activation of self-reactive T cells and their migration to target tissues leads to autoimmune organ damage. Mice lacking the inhibitory receptor cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4) develop fatal autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocyte infiltration into non-lymphoid tissues. Our study shows that the CD28 co-stimulatory pathway regulates the migration of self-reactive CTLA-4-deficient T cells to tissues. Ablation of the CD28-activated Tec family kinase ITK does not prevent spontaneous T cell activation, but instead causes self-reactive CTLA-4-deficient T cells to accumulate in secondary lymphoid organs. Despite excessive spontaneous T cell activation and proliferation in lymphoid organs, ITK-deficient mice are otherwise healthy and mount effective antiviral immune responses, with a long lifespan. Our findings suggest that ITK specifically enables autoreactive T cells to enter tissues to mount destructive immune responses. Interestingly, ITK inhibitors mimic the null mutant phenotype and also prevent pancreatic islet infiltration by damaging T cells in mouse models of type 1 diabetes, highlighting their potential utility for treating human autoimmune diseases.

title: Delayed and Accelerated Aging Share Common Longevity Assurance Mechanisms
