text: Mutant dwarf and calorie-restricted mice exhibit exceptional longevity and healthy aging, whereas mouse models with DNA repair-deficient progeroid syndromes prematurely age and die. By comparing the genome-wide expression profiles of these mice, we discovered unexpected similarities between the two extremes of lifespan. Specifically, we found that both groups exhibited suppressed endocrine and energy pathways, along with increased stress responses. To validate these findings, we analyzed the transcriptomes of liver, lung, kidney, and spleen across the entire murine adult lifespan and confirmed the same genes were differentially expressed in both groups. This systemic response to aging was observed in all four organs, indicating a coordinated transcriptional response. However, on a genome-wide scale, the transcriptomes of naturally aged mice showed a strong association to progeroid mice, but not to long-lived mice. This suggests that endocrine and metabolic changes are indicative of "survival" responses to genotoxic stress or starvation, whereas genome-wide associations in gene expression with natural aging are indicative of biological age, which may delineate pro- and anti-aging effects of treatments aimed at health-span extension.

title: Arginine depletion as a mechanism for the immune privilege of corneal allografts
text: The cornea is a unique tissue that enjoys immunological immunity, or "immune privilege." Previous research has found that arginase, an enzyme that depletes the crucial amino acid arginine, can modulate T-cell function. To investigate the expression of arginase in the cornea and its potential role in immune privilege, we employed a murine transplant model. Our results showed that both the endothelium and epithelium of murine corneas exhibit functional arginase I, which can suppress T-cell proliferation in a culture system. When we administered an arginase inhibitor to recipient mice, the rejection of allogeneic C57BL/6 (B6) corneal grafts accelerated. In contrast, inhibiting arginase activity had no effect on the rejection of primary skin grafts that express little to no arginase. Additionally, arginase inhibition did not impact systemic T-cell proliferation. These findings demonstrate that arginase is functional in the cornea and contributes to immune privilege, and modulation of arginase influences graft survival.

title: Once-a-day Concerta methylphenidate versus three-times-daily methylphenidate in laboratory and natural settings.
text:
The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and duration of action of an extended-release methylphenidate (MPH) preparation, Concerta, compared to immediate-release (IR) MPH thrice daily and placebo in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The study was conducted in both natural and laboratory settings, and involved 68 children aged 6-12 years old.
The study found that both Concerta and IR MPH were significantly more effective than placebo in improving behavior as measured by teacher ratings and individualized target behaviors in the children's regular school settings. In the laboratory setting, the effects of Concerta were found to be equivalent to tid MPH and lasted at least 12 hours after dosing. Additionally, more parents preferred Concerta than tid MPH or placebo. Both medications also improved productivity and accuracy on arithmetic seatwork assignments, as well as disruptive and on-task behavior, and classroom rule following in the laboratory setting.
The results of this study suggest that Concerta is a viable alternative to tid MPH for parents who desire to have medication benefits for their child throughout the day and early evening. The use of a measure of individualized daily target goals, such as the daily report card (DRC), as an objective measure of medication response was found to be effective in both the natural and laboratory settings. Overall, this study supports the efficacy and duration of action of Concerta as a long-acting formulation of MPH for the treatment of ADHD.

title: Leaderless genes in bacteria: clue to the evolution of translation initiation mechanisms in prokaryotes
text:
The Shine-Dalgarno (SD) signal has long been considered the primary translation initiation signal in prokaryotes. However, recent studies have revealed that a significant proportion of genes in archaea lack a 5' untranslated region (5'-UTR) on their messenger RNA (mRNA), termed leaderless genes. Despite the growing importance of leaderless genes, large-scale in silico analyses of translation initiation mechanisms in bacteria are primarily based on the SD-led initiation pathway, with limited study on the leaderless mechanism. To address this knowledge gap, we performed a comprehensive analysis of translation initiation regions of over 950 bacterial and 72 archaeal genomes.
Using an algorithm designed to identify multiple signals in the upstream regions of genes across a genome, we categorized genes into SD-led, TA-led, and atypical genes according to the most likely signal in their upstream sequences. Interestingly, the presence of TA-like signals approximately 10 nucleotides upstream of the translation initiation site (TIS) in bacteria suggests the prevalence of leaderless genes.
Our findings indicate that leaderless genes are widespread, accounting for over twenty percent of genes in Actinobacteria and Deinococcus-Thermus. Analyzing the proportion of leaderless genes across closely related bacterial genomes, we observed a linear dependence of translation initiation mechanism change on phylogenetic relationship. Our macroevolutionary analysis further revealed a decreasing trend in the proportion of leaderless genes in bacteria over evolution.
In conclusion, our study provides a comprehensive view of translation initiation mechanisms in prokaryotes, highlighting the significant role of leaderless genes in bacterial genomes. Our findings underscore the need for a more nuanced understanding of translation initiation mechanisms, particularly in the context of leaderless genes, to advance our understanding of prokaryotic evolution.

title: Neuronal Sirt1 deficiency increases insulin sensitivity in both brain and peripheral tissues.
text: Neuronal Sirt1 is a NAD(+)-dependent class III deacetylase that acts as a cellular energy sensor. Recent studies suggest that Sirt1 activity in the brain may play a key role in the regulation of energy balance and glucose metabolism. To investigate this further, we generated genetically modified mice lacking Sirt1 in neurons (SINKO mice). When compared to mice with normal Sirt1 expression (Sirt1(f/f) mice), SINKO mice were found to be more insulin sensitive, with lower fasting insulin levels, improved glucose tolerance, and enhanced insulin sensitivity during hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp studies. Additionally, the hypothalamus of SINKO mice showed increased insulin sensitivity, as evidenced by increased activation of PI3K, phosphorylation of Akt, and FoxO1 following systemic insulin injection. In contrast, intracerebroventricular injection of insulin led to a greater systemic effect to improve glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity in SINKO mice compared to controls. Mechanistic studies revealed that the enhanced central insulin signaling in SINKO mice was accompanied by increased insulin receptor signal transduction in the liver, muscle, and adipose tissue. In summary, our findings suggest that neuronal Sirt1 negatively regulates hypothalamic insulin signaling, leading to systemic insulin resistance. Interventions that reduce neuronal Sirt1 activity have the potential to improve systemic insulin action and limit weight gain on a high-calorie diet.

title: Candidate Causal Regulatory Effects by Integration of Expression QTLs with Complex Trait Genetic Associations
text: The recent success of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) has led to the challenge of identifying how the reported susceptibility variants contribute to complex traits and diseases. Expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) have been implicated in disease associations through overlaps between eQTLs and GWAS signals, but the abundance of eQTLs and the strong correlation structure (LD) in the genome suggests that some of these overlaps may be coincidental rather than driven by the same functional variants. To address this challenge, we propose an empirical method called Regulatory Trait Concordance (RTC) that integrates eQTLs and GWAS results to identify the subset of association signals that are due to cis eQTLs. We simulated genomic regions with various LD patterns and showed that our score outperforms SNP correlation metrics. Applying RTC to published GWAS loci, we prioritized relevant genes for each complex trait and identified potential disease-causing regulatory effects, particularly in immunity-related conditions. We also extended RTC to trans, where interrogating the whole genome for downstream effects of the disease variant can provide insight into its primary biological effect. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating cellular phenotype associations with organismal complex traits to interpret the genetic effects on these traits.

title: Gender-dependent differences in outcome after the treatment of infection in hospitalized patients.
text: While it is well established that gender can impact disease outcomes, the role of gender in infection has received limited attention. To investigate this, we conducted an observational cohort study among hospitalized patients treated for infection at a university-affiliated hospital over a 26-month period. Our study included 892 patients in the surgical units, with 1470 consecutive infectious episodes (782 in men and 688 in women). We found that there was no significant difference in mortality based on gender during hospitalization for infection overall (men, 11.1% vs women, 14.2%; P = 0.07). However, after controlling for other factors using logistic regression analysis, we found that gender was not independently associated with mortality. However, women were found to be at higher risk for death from hospital-acquired pneumonia, even after accounting for other comorbidities (men, 18% vs women, 34%; P = 0.002). Our results suggest that while gender may not be a predictor of mortality for all infections, women are at a higher risk for death from certain types of infections, such as pneumonia.

title: Comparative Safety of Targeted Therapies for Metastatic Colorectal Cancer between Elderly and Younger Patients: a Study Using the International Pharmacovigilance Database
text: The treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is increasingly shifting towards targeted therapies. However, the post-marketing safety of these agents in the elderly is poorly studied. This study aimed to compare the adverse drug reactions (ADRs) of targeted therapies used for mCRC in real-life settings based on age. VigiBase, a database containing individual case safety reports (ICSRs) from the World Health Organization, was analyzed. All ADR reports for aflibercept, bevacizumab, cetuximab, panitumumab, and regorafenib used in CRC were included. The study found that while serious ADRs were similar between patients aged ≥75 and <75 years for cetuximab and panitumumab, there were significant differences in ADRs for other drugs. For example, cardiac disorders were more reported in elderly patients, with heart failure being more common for bevacizumab, cetuximab, and regorafenib. Respiratory, thoracic, and mediastinal disorders were also more common in the elderly. Encephalopathy was significantly associated with bevacizumab in the elderly only. The study suggests that ADRs related to targeted therapies used for mCRC treatment differ across age groups, but are not systematically more reported or worse in the elderly. Therefore, selected elderly patients can be treated with these targeted therapies.

title: CpG island methylation in premalignant stages of gastric carcinoma.
text: Despite the high frequency of CpG island hypermethylation in gastric carcinoma, there are limited reports on methylation analysis of premalignant lesions. To investigate the frequency and timing of hypermethylation during gastric carcinogenesis, we analyzed the methylation status of five genes (p16, human Mut L homologue 1 (hMLH1), death-associated protein (DAP)-kinase, thromobospondin-1 (THBS1), and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase 3 (TIMP-3)) in non-neoplastic gastric mucosa (n = 118), adenomas (n = 61), and carcinomas (n = 64). Our findings reveal three distinct classes of methylation behaviors in these five genes. Specifically, DAP-kinase was methylated at a similar frequency in all four stages, while hMLH1 and p16 were methylated more frequently in cancer samples than in intestinal metaplasia or adenomas. However, hMLH1 and p16 were not methylated in chronic gastritis. THBS1 and TIMP-3 were methylated in all stages, but showed a significant increase in hypermethylation frequency from chronic gastritis to intestinal metaplasia (P < 0.05) and from adenomas to carcinomas (P < 0.05). The average number of methylated genes was higher in premalignant lesions than in non-metaplastic mucosa (P = 0.001), suggesting that CpG island hypermethylation occurs early in multistep gastric carcinogenesis and accumulates along the progression.

title: Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy: current and emerging treatment options for transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis
text:
Transthyretin familial amyloid polyneuropathy (TTR-FAP) is a fatal disorder characterized by the extracellular deposition of abnormal fibrils derived from misfolded, normally soluble transthyretin (TTR) molecules. The disease is predominantly caused by a point mutation in the TTR gene, inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Over 100 such mutations have been identified, leading to the destabilization of the physiological TTR tetramer, causing the generation of monomers with a tendency for spontaneous conformational changes and self-aggregation.
The primary clinical feature of TTR-FAP is progressive sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy, which predominantly involves small unmyelinated nerve fibers. Early symptoms include dissociated sensory loss, particularly affecting pain and temperature sensation, followed by autonomic neuropathy characterized by orthostatic hypotension, constipation alternating with diarrhea, erectile dysfunction, anhydrosis, and urinary retention or incontinence. Later, involvement of motor fibers causes rapidly progressive weakness and gait disturbances. In addition to the peripheral nervous system, the heart and the gut are frequently affected.
The onset of symptoms in TTR-FAP is bimodal, with two distinct peaks: one at age 33 years (early onset) and another in the sixth decade of life (late onset). The disease course is uniformly progressive and fatal, with an average of 10.8 years between onset of symptoms and death in Portuguese patients and 7.3 years in late-onset Japanese patients. Common causes of death include cachexia, cardiac failure, arrhythmia, and secondary infections.
Liver transplantation is the standard therapy for patients who are in a clinical condition good enough to tolerate this intervention, as it stops the progression of neuropathy by removing the main source of mutant TTR. Recently, orally administered tafamidis meglumine has been approved by European authorities for treatment of FAP. This substance has shown to stabilize the TTR tetramer, improving the outcome of patients with TTR-FAP. Other strategies have been studied in vitro to prevent TTR amyloidosis, including gene therapy, immunization, dissolution of TTR aggregates, and free radical scavengers, but none of them are yet ready for clinical use.

title: Invariant natural killer T cells: bridging innate and adaptive immunity
text: Cells of the innate immune system recognize pathogens through conserved pattern-recognition receptors, while cells of the adaptive immune system recognize pathogens through diverse, antigen-specific receptors generated through somatic DNA rearrangement. Invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells act as a bridge between the two systems, expressing T cell receptors generated through somatic DNA rearrangement but displaying semi-invariant receptors that interact with a limited set of lipid and glycolipid antigens, similar to the pattern-recognition receptors of the innate immune system. Functionally, iNKT cells resemble cells of the innate immune system, rapidly eliciting effector functions upon activation and lacking the ability to develop immunological memory. iNKT cells can be activated in response to multiple stimuli and play a role in regulating various immune responses. Activated iNKT cells produce cytokines that can modulate an adaptive immune response, and various glycolipid antigens have been identified to differentially elicit distinct effector functions in iNKT cells. These reagents have been used to test the hypothesis that iNKT cells can be harnessed for therapeutic purposes in human diseases. Here, we review the innate-like properties and functions of iNKT cells and discuss their interactions with other immune cell types.

title: Olmesartan-based therapies: an effective way to improve blood pressure control and cardiovascular protection.
text: The primary objective of treating hypertension is to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease. Among the different first-line antihypertensive drug classes, angiotensin-receptor blockers are notable for their excellent efficacy and tolerability. Additionally, disrupting the renin-angiotensin cascade has been associated with several benefits in terms of target organ protection and cardiovascular prevention. Of particular interest is olmesartan, which has been extensively studied in trials of organ protection, demonstrating improvements in various disease markers such as microinflammation, plaque volume reduction, vascular hypertrophy regression, and microalbuminuria prevention. Olmesartan has also been examined in combination with either hydrochlorothiazide or amlodipine, as well as with both drugs in a single-pill triple combination, showing enhanced antihypertensive efficacy without significantly impacting tolerability. This treatment approach, which utilizes a drug with such characteristics and the availability of various combination regimens with other first-line drug classes, may represent a viable strategy for achieving blood pressure control in a large percentage of hypertensive patients, which could in turn contribute to better cardiovascular disease prevention.

title: Manslaughter by Fake Artesunate in Asia—Will Africa Be Next?
text: Malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum is a deadly disease, disproportionately affecting the rural poor. Artemisinin derivatives, such as artesunate, are a crucial treatment and control option against increasingly drug-resistant malaria globally. However, since 1998, a severe problem has emerged in mainland Southeast Asia of counterfeit "artesunate" tablets containing no actual artemisinin derivatives, leading to a significant proportion of available artemisinin medications being fake [1-5]. Artemisinin-based medications are highly effective in treating malaria due to their rapid antimalarial activity and excellent tolerability. Since they are relatively costly, there is a demand for cheaper alternatives, particularly among the poorest and most vulnerable populations, who are often targeted by counterfeiters with tragic consequences.

title: Workshop: endothelial cell dysfunction leading to diabetic nephropathy : focus on nitric oxide.
text: Clinical manifestations of diabetic nephropathy are an expression of the underlying diabetic microangiopathy. This review updates and refines the previously proposed Steno hypothesis by suggesting that endothelial cell dysfunction represents a unifying pathophysiological pathway for the development of various diabetic complications. In particular, the ability of glucose to scavenge nitric oxide is proposed as the initial event leading to endothelial dysfunction. As glucose levels remain elevated, advanced glycated end products accumulate and induce the production of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, leading to decreased expression of endothelial nitric oxide synthase and reduced nitric oxide generation. This pathophysiological sequence is thought to maintain endothelial dysfunction, setting the stage for further diabetic complications. By shifting the focus to endothelial dysfunction as the root cause of diabetic complications, new preventive strategies may become available.

title: A nuclear Argonaute promotes multi-generational epigenetic inheritance and germline immortality
text: Epigenetic information is often lost at the start of each new generation. However, some pigenetic information can be passed down from parent to offspring (known as multigenerational epigenetic inheritance). A notable example of this type of inheritance is called double-stranded RNA-mediated gene silencing in Caenorhabditis elegans. This process can be inherited for more than five generations. To learn more about this process, we conducted a study to identify genes that help transmit this gene silencing information to future generations. We found a gene called heritable RNAi defective 1 (hrde-1) that plays a crucial role in this process. The hrde-1 gene encodes a protein called Argonaute that helps silence genes in the germ cells of offspring. In these cells, HRDE-1 works with small interfering RNAs to direct the trimethylation of a histone called H3 at a specific site (H3K9me3) at genes that are silenced by double-stranded RNA. This helps to pass on the silencing information to future generations. Without HRDE-1, this silencing process is lost over time, leading to defects in the formation of gametes (sperm or eggs) and ultimately sterility. These findings suggest that the Argonaute protein HRDE-1 helps to transmit epigenetic information from past generations to future generations, which can regulate important biological processes.

title: Autophagic programmed cell death by selective catalase degradation.
text: Autophagy significantly impacts various essential cellular functions like survival during starvation and regulation of infectious pathogens. Recent discoveries have revealed that autophagy can incite cells towards death, but the mechanism behind this process remains unclear. Our research has exposed that blocking caspases, which lead to cell death by means of autophagy, results in the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), oxidation of membrane lipids, and loss of plasma membrane integrity. Inhibiting autophagy by chemical compounds or reducing expression of key autophagy proteins, such as ATG7, ATG8, and receptor interacting protein (RIP), prevents ROS accumulation and cell death. We discovered that the selective autophagic degradation of the major enzymatic ROS scavenger, catalase, is responsible for the abnormal ROS accumulation. In addition, our findings suggest that caspase inhibition directly triggers catalase degradation, leading to ROS buildup, which can be prevented by autophagy inhibitors. These insights provide new knowledge on the underlying mechanisms of autophagy in cell death and offer valuable insights into the complex interactions between ROS and nonapoptotic programmed cell death.

title: Human epidermal stem cell function is regulated by circadian oscillations.
text: Human skin is adapted to withstand harmful environmental factors that fluctuate over a 24-hour period, yet the mechanisms by which circadian rhythms regulate the function of human epidermal stem cells remain largely unexplored. Our investigation reveals that in both human epidermal stem cells and their differentiated counterparts, key clock genes peak in a systematic and synchronized manner, dividing the day into distinct temporal segments. Each of these successive clock waves is associated with a surge in the expression of particular sets of transcripts, which temporally segregate the predisposition of epidermal stem cells to respond to cues that influence their proliferation or differentiation, such as TGFβ and calcium. We find that disruptions to this intricate circadian mechanism have profound effects on stem cell function in both cell culture and in vivo, leading us to propose that it plays a critical role in maintaining homeostasis by providing epidermal stem cells with environmentally relevant temporal cues throughout the day. Dysregulation of this mechanism may contribute to the development of aging and cancer.

title: Engraftment of engineered ES cell–derived cardiomyocytes but not BM cells restores contractile function to the infarcted myocardium
text:
Cellular cardiomyoplasty is a promising therapy for treating severe heart failure. However, there is ongoing debate over which cell source is most effective. To investigate and compare the fate and functional impact of bone marrow (BM) cells and embryonic stem cell (ES cell)–derived cardiomyocytes after transplantation into the infarcted mouse heart, we conducted a study.
One of the challenges we faced when studying ES cells was their enrichment into cardiomyocytes and their long-term engraftment and tumorigenicity, which are poorly understood. To address this, we generated transgenic ES cells that expressed puromycin resistance and an enhanced green fluorescent protein cassette under the control of a cardiac-specific promoter. Puromycin selection resulted in a highly purified (>99%) cardiomyocyte population, and the yield of cardiomyocytes increased 6–10-fold due to induction of proliferation upon purification. Long-term engraftment (4–5 months) was observed when co-transplanting selected ES cell–derived cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts into the injured heart of syngeneic mice, and no teratoma formation was observed (n = 60).
Our findings demonstrate that ES-based cell therapy is a promising approach for treating impaired myocardial function and provides better results than BM-derived cells. Transplantation of ES cell–derived cardiomyocytes improved heart function, while BM cells had no positive effects. Additionally, no contribution of BM cells to cardiac, endothelial, or smooth muscle neogenesis was detected. These results suggest that ES cells may be a more effective and reliable source of cells for cellular cardiomyoplasty.

title: Hyaluronan impairs vascular function and drug delivery in a mouse model of pancreatic cancer
text: Objective: To investigate the role of hyaluronan (HA), a ubiquitous extracellular matrix component, as a potential therapeutic target in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA). Methods: The authors employed a genetically engineered mouse model of PDA and used enzymatic depletion of HA with a clinically formulated PEGylated human recombinant PH20 hyaluronidase (PEGPH20) to examine tumor perfusion, vascular permeability, and drug delivery. The preclinical utility of PEGPH20 in combination with gemcitabine was assessed through short-term and survival studies. Results: PEGPH20 effectively depleted HA, leading to the re-expansion of PDA blood vessels and increased intratumoral delivery of doxorubicin and gemcitabine. Additionally, PEGPH20 triggered fenestrations and interendothelial junctional gaps in PDA tumor endothelia and promoted a tumor-specific increase in macromolecular permeability. Combination therapy with PEGPH20 and gemcitabine resulted in inhibition of PDA tumor growth and prolonged survival compared to gemcitabine monotherapy, suggesting immediate clinical utility. Conclusion: The study demonstrates that HA impedes the intratumoral vasculature in PDA, emphasizing the potential of enzymatic depletion as a means to enhance drug delivery and treatment response in patients with pancreatic cancer.

title: Ribose 2′-O-methylation provides a molecular signature for the distinction of self and non-self mRNA dependent on the RNA sensor Mda5
text: Higher eukaryotic mRNAs bear 5' cap structures that are modified with ribose 2'O-methylation. Similarly, many viruses that replicate within eukaryotic cells have developed 2'O-methyltransferases to modify their mRNAs autonomously. However, despite extensive research, a clear biological function of 2'O-methylation in mRNA remains elusive. Our study reveals that 2'O-methylation of viral mRNA is crucial for evading the host's type I interferon response. We found that human and mouse coronavirus mutants lacking 2'O-methyltransferase activity displayed heightened expression of type I interferon and were significantly more sensitive to type I interferon. Notably, the induction of type I interferon by these virus mutants was dependent on the cytoplasmic RNA sensor Mda5. This discovery suggests that RNA modifications like 2'O-methylation serve as a molecular signature for distinguishing between self and non-self mRNA.

title: Relationship between activity levels, aerobic fitness, and body fat in 8- to 10-yr-old children.
text: The connections between children's physical activity, aerobic fitness, and body fatness are unclear, and indirect measures such as heart rate (HR) may obscure any relationships. The purpose of this study was to investigate these associations by using a triaxial accelerometer (Tritrac-R3D), a pedometer, and HR measurements. Thirty-four children aged 8-10 years participated in the study. The Tritrac and pedometer were worn for up to 6 days, and HR was measured for one day. The results showed that activity measured by Tritrac or pedometer correlated positively with fitness in the whole group (Tritrac: r = 0.66; pedometer: r = 0.59; P < 0.01), and in boys and girls separately (P < 0.05), and negatively with body fatness in the whole group (r = -0.42; P < 0.05). In contrast, HR did not significantly correlate with fitness, and HR > 139 beats/min correlated positively with body fatness in girls (r = 0.64; P < 0.05). These findings suggest that HR is a misleading measure of activity. This study supports a positive relationship between activity and fitness and suggests a negative relationship between body fatness and activity.

title: Junctional actin assembly is mediated by Formin-like 2 downstream of Rac1
text: Epithelial cell-cell adhesion is crucial for maintaining tissue integrity, and disruptions can lead to the development of cancer. The formation of new adherens junctions (AJ) between individual epithelial cells requires coordinated, spatial actin dynamics, but the mechanisms that control the initiation of actin polymerization are not well understood. To investigate the real-time assembly of actin filaments during the formation of AJ in human breast epithelial cells in three-dimensional environments, we used live cell imaging techniques. Our findings revealed that formin-like 2 (FMNL2) is essential for actin assembly and turnover at newly formed cell-cell contacts, as well as for the formation of epithelial lumens. FMNL2 associates with components of the AJ complex and requires Rac1 activity to mediate its function. We were able to control Rac1 activity in living cells using optogenetic techniques, which allowed us to rapidly induce FMNL2 at epithelial cell-cell contact zones. Our data demonstrate that FMNL2 is a key driver of human epithelial AJ formation downstream of Rac1.

title: Inhibition of HDM2 and activation of p53 by ribosomal protein L23.
text: The connection between cell growth and proliferation has been recognized for some time, although the molecular basis for this relationship is poorly understood. Our research reveals that the ribosomal protein L23 interacts with HDM2, a protein that regulates the tumor suppressor p53. The interaction involves the central acidic domain of HDM2 and the N-terminal domain of L23, as well as the simultaneous yet distinct interaction of L23 and another HDM2-interacting protein, L11, to form a ternary complex. We found that overexpression of L23 inhibits HDM2-induced p53 polyubiquitination and degradation, leading to a p53-dependent cell cycle arrest. Conversely, reducing the levels of L23 leads to nucleolar stress and triggers the translocation of B23 from the nucleolus to the nucleoplasm, resulting in the stabilization and activation of p53. Our data suggest that cells maintain a steady state level of L23 during normal growth, and altering the levels of L23 in response to changing growth conditions may disrupt the integrity of the nucleolus and impact the HDM2-p53 pathway.

title: Association of Blood Monocyte and Platelet Markers with Carotid Artery Characteristics: The Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Carotid MRI Study
text: Background: Atherosclerosis is characterized by the infiltration of inflammatory cells from the circulatory system into the affected tissue. Blood cell activation has been postulated to play a crucial role in the formation of plaques in the carotid wall. Methods: In this study, we analyzed the relationship between various blood cellular markers and quantitative measures of carotid wall components in a cohort of 1,546 participants from the ARIC (Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities) Carotid MRI Study. Carotid imaging was performed using a gadolinium contrast-enhanced MRI, while cellular phenotyping was conducted using flow cytometry. Results: Our findings indicate that monocyte Toll-like receptor (TLR)-2 is associated with larger plaques, while CD14, myeloperoxidase, and TLR-4 are associated with smaller plaques. In contrast, platelet CD40L is associated with smaller plaques and thinner caps, while P-selectin is associated with smaller core sizes. Conclusions: Our results suggest that blood cell activation is significantly associated with atherosclerotic changes in the carotid wall, highlighting the potential role of blood cells in the development and progression of atherosclerosis.

title: Vascular endothelial cadherin controls VEGFR-2 internalization and signaling from intracellular compartments
text: Receptor internalization is a critical step in regulating the intensity, duration, and nature of cellular signaling events. Consecutive endothelial cells are restricted in their growth by contact inhibition and respond poorly to the proliferative signals of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Previous studies have shown that the association of vascular endothelial cadherin (VEC) with VEGF receptor (VEGFR) type 2 contributes to density-dependent growth inhibition (Lampugnani et al., 2003). In the present study, the mechanism by which VEC restricts VEGFR-2 signaling is investigated. It is found that VEGF induces the clathrin-dependent internalization of VEGFR-2. When VEC is absent or not engaged at junctions, VEGFR-2 is internalized more quickly and remains in endosomal compartments for a longer period. Internalization does not terminate the signaling of the receptor; instead, the internalized receptor is phosphorylated, codistributes with active phospholipase C–γ, and activates p44/42 mitogen-activated protein kinase phosphorylation and cell proliferation. Inhibition of VEGFR-2 internalization reestablishes the contact inhibition of cell growth, whereas silencing the junction-associated density-enhanced phosphatase-1/CD148 phosphatase restores VEGFR-2 internalization and signaling. Therefore, VEC restricts cell proliferation by retaining VEGFR-2 at the membrane and preventing its internalization into signaling compartments.

title: Diversification in the HIV-1 Envelope Hyper-variable Domains V2, V4, and V5 and Higher Probability of Transmitted/Founder Envelope Glycosylation Favor the Development of Heterologous Neutralization Breadth
text: The study recently investigated the relationship between plasma neutralization breadth and various factors, including viral load, HLA-A*03 genotype, and subtype C infection, in 21 HIV-1 infected individuals at two sites: Kigali, Rwanda (n = 9) and Lusaka, Zambia (n = 12). By analyzing single-genome sequences of full-length transmitted/founder (T/F) envelope (Env) proteins, the researchers found that all individuals were infected with a highly homogeneous population of viral variants, which were categorized as subtype C (n = 12), A1 (n = 7), or recombinant AC (n = 2). An extensive analysis of variable loop lengths and glycosylation patterns in the T/F Envs revealed that a lower ratio of NXS to NXT-encoded glycan motifs correlated with neutralization breadth. Additionally, comparing amino acid sequence changes, insertions/deletions, and glycan motif alterations between the T/F Env and autologous early Env variants revealed that extensive diversification focused in the V2, V4, and V5 regions of gp120, accompanied by contemporaneous viral escape, favored the development of breadth. These findings suggest that more efficient glycosylation of subtype A and C T/F Envs through fewer NXS-encoded glycan sites may lead to the elicitation of antibodies that can transition from autologous to heterologous neutralizing activity following exposure to gp120 diversification. This Env-antibody co-evolution cycle is further augmented over time by additional viral and host factors. These findings suggest that understanding how variation in the efficiency of site-specific glycosylation influences neutralizing antibody elicitation and targeting could lead to the design of immunogens that can induce antibodies that can transition from autologous to heterologous neutralizing activity.

title: Glycolytic oligodendrocytes maintain myelin and long-term axonal integrity
text: Oligodendrocytes, the glial cells responsible for myelinating axons in the central nervous system, play a crucial role in maintaining long-term axonal integrity. However, the mechanisms underlying this process are not fully understood. To investigate, we generated conditional mutant mice lacking the gene Cox10 (protoheme IX farnesyltransferase), which is essential for the assembly of mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (COX), also known as mitochondrial complex IV. Contrary to expectations, mutant mice did not exhibit glial cell death, but instead displayed severe neuropathy, dysmyelination, abnormal Remak bundles, muscle atrophy, and paralysis in the peripheral nervous system. In contrast, no signs of demyelination, axonal degeneration, or secondary inflammation were observed in the adult central nervous system. Interestingly, while cultured oligodendrocytes are sensitive to COX inhibitors, post-myelination oligodendrocytes in vivo show remarkable tolerance to COX deficiency. Moreover, by employing in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy, we discovered that brain lactate concentrations were elevated in mutants, but only in mice exposed to volatile anaesthetics. This finding suggests that oligodendrocytes in the brain are capable of metabolizing lactate products derived from aerobic glycolysis in a rapid and efficient manner. Given these results, we propose a novel model of axon-glia metabolic coupling in which the myelinating glial cells play a crucial role in maintaining the energetic needs of myelinated axons.

title: Siglec-1 Is a Novel Dendritic Cell Receptor That Mediates HIV-1 Trans-Infection Through Recognition of Viral Membrane Gangliosides
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) play a critical role in inducing immunity against pathogens, but HIV-1 exploits and enhances its spread within clusters of DCs and CD4(+) T cells. Uninfected DCs capture HIV-1 and transfer it to bystander CD4(+) T cells through a process called trans-infection. Early studies identified DC-SIGN, a C-type lectin, as the HIV-1 binding factor on DCs, which interacts with the viral envelope glycoproteins. However, during DC maturation, DC-SIGN is downregulated, and HIV-1 capture and trans-infection are enhanced via a glycoprotein-independent capture pathway that recognizes sialyllactose-containing membrane gangliosides. We now show that the sialic acid-binding Ig-like lectin 1 (Siglec-1, CD169), which is highly expressed on mature DCs, specifically binds HIV-1 and vesicles carrying sialyllactose. Additionally, Siglec-1 is essential for trans-infection by mature DCs, identifying it as a crucial factor in HIV-1 dissemination through infectious DC/T-cell synapses. This novel mechanism highlights a previously unknown way in which HIV-1 spreads in activated tissues.

title: The composition of the gut microbiota throughout life, with an emphasis on early life
text: The gut microbiome has emerged as a crucial component of human health. As the immune system develops, the microbiota in the gut plays a vital role in intestinal physiology and regulation. mounting evidence suggests that the human gut microbiome is seeded before birth, with the mother's microbiota serving as the initial inoculum. From infancy onward, the microbiota diversifies and matures, eventually reaching adulthood-like composition by the end of the first 3-5 years of life. Perinatal factors, including mode of delivery, maternal diet, genetics, and mucin glycosylation, influence microbial colonization. Once established, the gut microbiota's composition remains relatively stable throughout adulthood, but can be altered by bacterial infections, antibiotic use, lifestyle changes, surgery, and long-term dietary shifts. These changes can increase the risk of disease. Therefore, establishing and maintaining a healthy gut microbiota throughout life can reduce the risk of disease in both early and late stages. This review discusses recent studies on early colonization and the factors that influence this process, highlighting their impact on health.

title: Intrauterine protein restriction combined with early postnatal overfeeding was not associated with adult-onset obesity but produced glucose intolerance by pancreatic dysfunction
text: In this study, we investigated the effects of intrauterine protein restriction (IPR) combined with overfeeding during lactation on adult-onset obesity and metabolic disorders. After birth, litters from dams fed a control (17% protein) or low protein (6% protein) diet were adjusted to have either four or eight pups, respectively. All offspring were fed a 12% protein diet from weaning until they were 90 days old. Compared to the control (CC) group, the low protein (LO) group had higher relative and absolute food intakes, oxygen consumption, and carbon dioxide production, as well as lower brown adipose tissue weight and lipid content, while the CC group had higher relative food intake, brown adipose tissue weight, and lipid content, and lower oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production, and spontaneous activity. Fasting serum glucose levels were similar among the groups, but the area under the glucose curve was higher in the LO and CO rats than in the LC and CC rats. Additionally, basal insulinemia and homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) were lower in the LO group than in the other groups, and the total area under the insulin curve was similar between the LO and CC groups, but lower than the CO and LC groups. Finally, kitt (a measure of insulin sensitivity) was higher in the LO, LC, and CO groups than in the CC group. Taken together, these findings suggest that IPR followed by overfeeding during lactation does not induce obesity in adulthood, but rather produces glucose intolerance by impairing pancreatic function.

title: Somatic coding mutations in human induced pluripotent stem cells
text: Transcription factors that are specifically defined can cause epigenetic reprogramming of adult mammalian cells into induced pluripotent stem cells. Although DNA factors are incorporated during some reprogramming methods, it is unclear whether the genome remains unchanged at the nucleotide level. We investigated this by analyzing 22 human induced pluripotent stem (hiPS) cell lines that were reprogrammed using five different methods. We found that these cells contained, on average, five protein-coding point mutations in the regions sampled. Most of these mutations were non-synonymous, nonsense, or splice variants, and were enriched in genes associated with cancer. Furthermore, we discovered that at least half of these reprogramming-related mutations existed in fibroblast progenitors at low frequencies beforehand, while the remainder arose during or after the reprogramming process. Therefore, hiPS cells undergo both genetic and epigenetic modifications. Therefore, extensive genetic screening should be performed as a standard procedure to ensure the safety of hiPS cells before their use in clinical applications.

title: Cell cycle, CDKs and cancer: a changing paradigm
text: Cell cycle defects associated with tumors are often caused by alterations in cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) activity. Uncontrolled CDKs lead to unscheduled proliferation, genomic instability, and chromosomal aberrations. Current models argue that mammalian CDKs are crucial for advancing each cell cycle phase, making it unlikely that therapeutic strategies targeting CDK activity will selectively impact tumor cells. However, recent genetic insights reveal that while CDK1 is essential for the cell cycle, interphase CDKs are only required for the proliferation of specialized cells. New evidence suggests that tumor cells might also need specific interphase CDKs to proliferate. Therefore, selective CDK inhibition may have therapeutic potential against specific human cancers.

title: Sudden infant death syndrome.
text: Despite a decline in SIDS cases over the past two decades, it remains the leading cause of death for infants aged 1 month to 1 year in developed countries. Behavioral risk factors identified in epidemiological studies include sleeping in the prone or side position, exposure to smoke, soft bedding and sleep surfaces, and overheating. Evidence suggests that using a pacifier at sleep time and sharing a room without bed sharing can reduce the risk of SIDS. While the exact cause of SIDS is unknown, immature cardiorespiratory autonomic control and a failure of arousal responsiveness from sleep are important factors. Genetic polymorphisms related to serotonin transport and autonomic nervous system development may make affected infants more vulnerable to SIDS. Public health campaigns have been successful in reducing SIDS incidence by 50-90%, but more efforts are needed to further lower the incidence, such as reducing prenatal smoke exposure and improving other recommended infant care practices. Ongoing research is necessary to uncover the underlying pathophysiology of SIDS.

title: Regulation of heterochromatic silencing and histone H3 lysine-9 methylation by RNAi.
text: Eukaryotic heterochromatin is distinguishable by an increased concentration of repetitive sequences and transposable elements, as well as altered histones, which in turn impact both gene expression and chromosome segregation. In the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, we inactivated the genes encoding argonaute, dicer, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which are essential for the RNA interference (RNAi) machinery. This resulted in an abnormal accumulation of complementary transcripts derived from centromeric heterochromatic repeats. Concurrently, we observed transcriptional deregulation of transgenes integrated at the centromere, along with a decrease in histone H3 lysine-9 methylation and impairment of centromere function. We propose that double-stranded RNA generated from centromeric repeats functions in the maintenance and formation of heterochromatin via the RNAi pathway.

title: Conformational Changes during Pore Formation by the Perforin-Related Protein Pleurotolysin
text: The largest superfamily of pore-forming proteins, known as membrane attack complex/perforin-like (MACPF) proteins, play crucial roles in both immunity and pathogenesis. These proteins consist of soluble monomers that assemble into large transmembrane pores through conformational changes that remain poorly understood. Here, we present an 11 Å resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the fungal toxin Pleurotolysin (Ply), along with crystal structures of its components (the lipid-binding PlyA protein and the pore-forming MACPF component PlyB). These data reveal a 13-fold pore 80 Å in diameter and 100 Å in height, with each subunit composed of a PlyB molecule atop a membrane-bound dimer of PlyA. The resolution of the EM map, combined with biochemical and computational experiments, allowed for confident assignment of subdomains in a MACPF pore assembly. The major conformational changes in PlyB involve a ∼70° opening of the bent and distorted central β-sheet of the MACPF domain, accompanied by extrusion and refolding of two α-helical regions into transmembrane β-hairpins (TMH1 and TMH2). We structurally characterized three different disulfide bond-trapped prepore intermediates and used molecular modeling and flexible fitting to generate a potential trajectory of β-sheet unbending. Our findings suggest that MACPF conformational change is triggered by the disruption of a conserved helix-turn-helix motif located at the top of TMH2. Following the release of TMH2, the transmembrane regions assemble into β-hairpins via "top-down zippering" of backbone hydrogen bonds to form the membrane-inserted β-barrel. The intermediate structures of the MACPF domain during refolding into the β-barrel pore provide a structural framework for the transition from soluble monomer to pore, which may be conserved across the entire superfamily. Interestingly, the TMH2 region is crucial for the release of both TMH clusters, which may explain why this region is targeted by endogenous inhibitors of MACPF function.

title: The widespread regulation of microRNA biogenesis, function and decay
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a diverse group of molecules that play a critical role in regulating gene expression in eukaryotic organisms. These small RNA molecules, typically around 21 nucleotides in length, are involved in a wide range of cellular and developmental processes. Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in understanding the mechanisms that govern miRNA biogenesis and function. However, recent research has also revealed that miRNA regulators themselves are subject to complex regulation. A variety of protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions have been identified, which serve to control miRNA metabolism and function in a context-specific manner. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the role of miRNAs in various cellular processes and diseases.

title: The cytidine deaminase CEM15 induces hypermutation in newly synthesized HIV-1 DNA
text: The high frequency of mutations during reverse transcription plays a crucial role in the genetic diversity of primate lentiviral populations. This process is the main driving force behind the development of drug resistance and escape from immune surveillance. One of the characteristic features of primate lentiviruses, including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), is G to A hypermutation during replication in vivo and in cell culture. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying this process are not yet fully understood. Here, we demonstrate that CEM15 (also known as apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like 3G; APOBEC3G), an endogenous inhibitor of HIV replication, is a cytidine deaminase that can induce G to A hypermutation in newly synthesized viral DNA. This effect can be counteracted by the HIV virion infectivity factor (Vif). It appears that this viral DNA mutator is a viral defense mechanism in host cells that may induce either lethal hypermutation or instability of the incoming nascent viral reverse transcripts, which could account for the Vif-defective phenotype. Additionally, the accumulation of CEM15-mediated non-lethal hypermutation in the replicating viral genome could significantly contribute to the genetic variation of primate lentiviral populations.

title: Variants in the Toll-interacting protein gene are associated with susceptibility to sepsis in the Chinese Han population
text:
Introduction:
Deregulated or excessive immune responses triggered by Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling pathways and their negative regulators contribute to the development of sepsis. This study aimed to investigate the association between genetic variants in TLR signaling pathway genes and their negative regulators and susceptibility to sepsis in the Chinese Han population.
Methods:
We enrolled 378 patients with severe sepsis and 390 healthy control subjects. We genotyped 12 tag single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in five genes (TLR2, TLR4, TLR9, MyD88, and TOLLIP) using direct sequencing. The mRNA expression levels of TOLLIP were determined using real-time quantitative PCR assays, and the concentrations of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) were measured by ELISA.
Results:
Our results showed that the minor C-allele of rs5743867 in TOLLIP was significantly associated with decreased risk of sepsis after adjusting for covariates in multiple logistic regression analysis (Padj = 0.00062, ORadj = 0.71, 95% CI = 0.59-0.86). A 3-SNP haplotype block harboring the associated SNP rs5743867 also displayed strong association with omnibus test P value of 0.00049. Haplotype GTC showed a protective role against sepsis (Padj = 0.0012), while haplotype GCT showed an increased risk for sepsis (Padj = 0.00092). After exposure to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), TOLLIP mRNA expression levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from homozygotes for the rs5743867C allele were significantly higher than in heterozygotes and homozygotes for the rs5743867T allele (P = 0.013 and P = 0.01, respectively). Moreover, the concentrations of TNF-α and IL-6 in culture supernatants were significantly lower in the subjects of rs5743867CC genotype than in CT and TT genotype subjects (P = 0.016 and P = 0.003 for TNF-α; P = 0.01 and P = 0.002 for IL-6, respectively).

Conclusion:
Our findings indicated that the variants in TOLLIP were significantly associated with sepsis susceptibility in the Chinese Han population. These results provide new insights into the genetic basis of sepsis susceptibility and may help identify individuals who are at risk of developing sepsis.

title: Children's estimates of food portion size: the development and evaluation of three portion size assessment tools for use with children.
text: A number of methods have been developed to help individuals estimate portion sizes, but their application in improving portion size estimation among children has not been examined systematically. The goal of this study was to create portion size assessment tools specifically designed for children and to evaluate the accuracy of children's estimates of portion size using these tools. The tools included food photographs, food models, and an interactive portion size assessment system (IPSAS). A total of 201 children, aged 4-16 years, were given known quantities of food to eat in a school setting. Food leftovers were then weighed. Children estimated the amount of each food using each tool 24 hours after consuming it. The age-specific portion sizes used in the study were based on the portion sizes typically consumed by children in a national survey. Interestingly, significant differences were found in the accuracy of estimates made using the three tools. Children of all ages performed well when using the IPSAS and food photographs. In contrast, the accuracy and precision of estimates made using the food models were poor. Notably, estimates of the amount of food served were more accurate than estimates of the amount consumed. Additional findings revealed that issues surrounding the reporting of leftover food can have an impact on the accuracy of estimates of actual food consumption. The IPSAS showed potential for assessing dietary intake in children. Nevertheless, before the tool can be applied in a practical setting for assessing dietary intake among children, it will be necessary to expand the tool to cover a wider range of foods and to validate its use in real-life situations.

title: A 3D Map of the Yeast Kinetochore Reveals the Presence of Core and Accessory Centromere-Specific Histone
text:
The developing yeast kinetochore is approximately 68 nanometers in length with a slightly larger diameter than a 25 nanometer microtubule. The kinetochores from the 16 chromosomes are organized in a stereotypic cluster surrounding central spindle microtubules. Quantitative analysis of the inner kinetochore cluster (Cse4, COMA) reveals structural features not apparent in singly attached kinetochores. The cluster of Cse4-containing kinetochores is physically larger perpendicular to the spindle axis compared to the cluster of Ndc80 molecules. If there were a single Cse4 molecule or nucleosome at the kinetochore attached to each microtubule plus end, the cluster of Cse4 would appear geometrically identical to Ndc80. Therefore, the structure of the inner kinetochore at the chromosome surface remains unresolved.
We used point fluorescence microscopy and statistical probability maps to determine the two-dimensional mean position of representative components of the yeast kinetochore relative to the mitotic spindle in metaphase. Comparison of the experimental images to three-dimensional architectures produced by convolution of mathematical models reveals a pool of Cse4 displaced from Cse4 at the kinetochore and kinetochore microtubule plus ends. The pool of displaced Cse4 can be experimentally depleted in mRNA processing pat1Δ or xrn1Δ mutants. The peripheral Cse4 molecules do not template outer kinetochore components. This study suggests the presence of an inner kinetochore plate at the centromere-microtubule interface in budding yeast, and provides insight into the number of Ndc80 molecules at the microtubule attachment site.

title: American Society of Clinical Oncology policy statement: the role of the oncologist in cancer prevention and risk assessment.
text:
Oncologists are well positioned to utilize risk assessment and cancer prevention strategies to prevent or slow the progression of cancer in both cancer survivors and individuals at high risk of developing the disease. As experts in the field of cancer care, oncologists can leverage their knowledge of the natural history and prognosis of various cancers to advise patients on the risk of second malignancies and treatment-related cancers. Furthermore, oncologists are well-positioned to participate in community-based cancer prevention activities, as recognized leaders in the full spectrum of cancer care.
Despite the critical role that oncologists play in cancer prevention, economic barriers such as inadequate or lack of insurance may limit patient access to these services. Additionally, inadequate reimbursement for existing and developing interventions may discourage patients from seeking out these services. To address these challenges, the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) is committed to supporting oncologists in their broad involvement in cancer prevention.
This statement provides examples of risk assessment and prevention activities that oncologists should offer their patients, highlights opportunities for coordination between oncologists and primary care physicians in prevention education and the coordination of care for cancer survivors, provides details on ASCO's efforts to educate and train oncologists on prevention, and proposes improvements to the payment environment to encourage patient access to these services.

title: The BLM helicase contributes to telomere maintenance through processing of late-replicating intermediate structures
text: Werner's syndrome (WS) and Bloom's syndrome (BS) are cancer predisposition disorders caused by a loss of function of the RecQ helicases WRN and BLM, respectively. Both disorders are characterized by defects in DNA replication, an increase in hyperrecombination events, and chromosomal aberrations, which are hallmarks of cancer. Inefficient replication of the G-rich telomeric strand can contribute to chromosomal aberrations in WS cells, suggesting a link between WRN, telomeres, and genomic stability. Our findings indicate that BLM also plays a role in maintaining telomere structure. Telomere defects (TDs) are observed in BLM-deficient cells at an elevated frequency, which is similar to the frequency observed in cells lacking a functional WRN helicase. Loss of both helicases exacerbates TDs and chromosome aberrations, suggesting that BLM and WRN function independently in telomere maintenance. Our results also show that BLM localization, particularly its recruitment to telomeres, changes in response to replication dysfunction, such as in WRN-deficient cells or after aphidicolin treatment. Exposure to replication challenges leads to an increase in decatenated DNA structures and late-replicating intermediates (LRIs), which are visible as BLM-covered ultra-fine bridges (UFBs) in anaphase. A subset of UFBs originates from telomeric DNA, and their frequency correlates with telomere replication defects. We propose that the BLM complex contributes to telomere maintenance through its activity in resolving LRIs.

title: Formation of a thymus from rat ES cells in xenogeneic nude mouse↔rat ES chimeras.
text: Researchers are actively investigating various conditions for differentiating embryonic stem (ES) cells or induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells into specific cell types. However, producing a functional organ with a three-dimensional structure in vitro remains a challenge. In this paper, we describe the creation of a green fluorescent protein-expressing rat ES cell line and the production of mouse-rat ES chimera by injecting rat ES cells into mouse blastocysts. The rat ES cells contributed to various organs in the chimera, including germ cells. Interestingly, when we injected ES cells into blastocysts of nu/nu mice lacking a thymus, the resulting chimeras produced thymus tissue derived from rat ES cells. These chimeric animals may provide a valuable method for deriving various organs from ES or iPS cells.

title: Wnt/beta-catenin signaling is required for CNS, but not non-CNS, angiogenesis.
text:
Despite the essential role of central nervous system (CNS) blood vessels, the molecular mechanisms regulating CNS angiogenesis and the blood-brain barrier (BBB) formation are largely unexplored. Our study aims to elucidate the role of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in regulating the formation of CNS blood vessels.
First, we utilize the analysis of TOP-Gal Wnt reporter mice to identify that canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling is selectively activated in CNS, but not non-CNS, blood vessels during development. This activation correlates with the expression of different Wnt ligands by neural progenitor cells in distinct locations throughout the CNS, including Wnt7a and Wnt7b in ventral regions and Wnt1, Wnt3, Wnt3a, and Wnt4 in dorsal regions.
Furthermore, we demonstrate that blocking Wnt/β-catenin signaling in vivo specifically disrupts CNS, but not non-CNS, angiogenesis. These defects include a reduction in vessel number, loss of capillary beds, and the formation of hemorrhagic vascular malformations that remain adherent to the meninges. Additionally, our experiments reveal that Wnt/β-catenin signaling regulates the expression of the BBB-specific glucose transporter glut-1.
Taken together, these findings provide essential evidence for the crucial role of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in driving CNS-specific angiogenesis and offer molecular insight into the connection between angiogenesis and BBB formation.

title: Cyanidin-3-rutinoside, a natural polyphenol antioxidant, selectively kills leukemic cells by induction of oxidative stress.
text:
Anthocyanins are a group of naturally occurring phenolic compounds found in various fruits and vegetables in the human diet. These compounds have been shown to have a range of biological activities, including anti-mutagenic and anticarcinogenic effects, which are thought to be due to their antioxidant properties. In this study, we focused on the effects and mechanisms of the most common type of anthocyanins, cyanidin-3-rutinoside, in several types of leukemia and lymphoma cell lines.
We found that cyanidin-3-rutinoside, extracted and purified from the black raspberry cultivar Jewel, induced apoptosis in HL-60 cells in a dose- and time-dependent manner. However, this compound paradoxically also induced the accumulation of peroxides, which play a role in the induction of apoptosis in HL-60 cells. Additionally, cyanidin-3-rutinoside treatment resulted in the activation of p38 MAPK and JNK signaling pathways, which contributed to cell death by activating the mitochondrial pathway mediated by Bim. Down-regulation of Bim or overexpression of Bcl-2 or Bcl-x(L) significantly blocked apoptosis. Notably, cyanidin-3-rutinoside treatment did not lead to increased ROS accumulation in normal human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and had no cytotoxic effects on these cells.
Overall, these results suggest that cyanidin-3-rutinoside has potential as a treatment for leukemia, as it is widely available and selective towards tumor cells.

title: Gout-associated uric acid crystals activate the NALP3 inflammasome
text: Development of the acute and chronic inflammatory responses characterized as gout and pseudogout are associated with the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) or calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals, respectively, in joints and surrounding tissues. Although MSU crystals were initially identified as the causative agent of gout in the 18th century and more recently as a 'danger signal' released from dying cells, there is limited understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying MSU- or CPPD-induced inflammation. Our findings reveal that MSU and CPPD activate the caspase-1-activating NALP3 (also known as cryopyrin) inflammasome, leading to the production of active interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18. Macrophages from mice lacking specific components of the inflammasome, such as caspase-1, ASC, and NALP3, are impaired in crystal-induced IL-1β activation. Moreover, there is an impaired neutrophil influx in an in vivo model of crystal-induced peritonitis in inflammasome-deficient mice or mice lacking the IL-1β receptor (IL-1R). These findings provide insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying the inflammatory conditions of gout and pseudogout, and further support a crucial role of the inflammasome in several autoinflammatory diseases.

title: Hematopoietic stem cell quiescence promotes error-prone DNA repair and mutagenesis.
text: Most adult stem cells, including hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), are typically in a dormant or resting state in the body. This state is believed to be an important protective mechanism for stem cells, as it minimizes the harmful effects of cellular respiration and DNA replication. However, our research has shown that HSC quiescence can also have negative consequences. We found that HSCs have unique mechanisms to ensure their survival in response to ionizing radiation (IR), such as increased expression of pro-survival genes and strong activation of the p53-mediated DNA damage response. We discovered that quiescent and proliferating HSCs are equally protected from radiation damage, but they employ different types of DNA repair mechanisms. Specifically, quiescent HSCs rely on non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)-mediated DNA repair, which can lead to the acquisition of genetic rearrangements that persist in vivo and contribute to hematopoietic problems. Our findings suggest that quiescence can be a double-edged sword, making HSCs inherently vulnerable to mutations following DNA damage.

title: Recruitment of Nck by CD3ϵ Reveals a Ligand-Induced Conformational Change Essential for T Cell Receptor Signaling and Synapse Formation
text: Investigations into how membrane receptors initiate signal transduction upon ligand binding are under intense scrutiny, with a particular focus on the T cell receptor complex (TCR-CD3). This complex is composed of TCR alpha/beta ligand binding subunits bonded to CD3 subunits responsible for signal transduction. While it has been theorized that TCR-CD3 may undergo a conformational change upon ligand binding, concrete evidence has yet to be found. Our findings provide strong support for the idea that ligand engagement of TCR-CD3 results in a conformational change that exposes a proline-rich sequence in CD3 epsilon, leading to the recruitment of the adaptor protein Nck. This process occurs independent of and earlier than tyrosine kinase activation. Furthermore, by interfering with Nck-CD3 epsilon association in vivo, we demonstrate that TCR-CD3 recruitment of Nck is crucial for the maturation of the immune synapse and T cell activation.

title: Pseudo-Seq: Genome-Wide Detection of Pseudouridine Modifications in RNA.
text: RNA molecules harbor a diverse array of chemically distinct, post-transcriptionally modified bases. The most commonly observed modified base in cellular RNA, pseudouridine (Ψ), has been mapped to hundreds of sites in mRNAs, many of which are dynamically regulated. Although the pseudouridine landscape has been investigated in only a limited number of cell types and growth conditions, the enzymes responsible for mRNA pseudouridylation are ubiquitously conserved, suggesting that numerous novel pseudouridylated sites remain to be discovered. To address this, we have developed Pseudo-seq, a technique that enables the genome-wide identification of pseudouridylation sites with single-nucleotide resolution. In this chapter, we provide a detailed description of Pseudo-seq, including protocols for RNA isolation from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Pseudo-seq library preparation, and data analysis. We describe the processing and mapping of sequencing reads, the computational identification of sites of pseudouridylation, and the assignment of sites to specific pseudouridine synthases. The approach presented here is easily adaptable to any cell or tissue type for which high-quality mRNA can be isolated, allowing for the identification of novel pseudouridylation sites and a deeper understanding of their regulation and functions.

title: The Mammalian Epigenome
text: Molecular alterations to DNA and histone proteins form a dynamic regulatory system that controls chromatin structure and genome function. The epigenome, which refers to the complete set of these alterations across the genome, is influenced by both genetic and environmental factors. The epigenetic landscape within a given cell is determined by a combination of genetic predisposition, cellular lineage, and external inputs. With the completion of the Human Genome Project, researchers are now focused on deciphering the complex epigenetic codes that govern how genetic information is translated into distinct cellular phenotypes across a wide range of developmental stages, tissue types, and disease states. In this review, we will discuss recent advances in the field, including large-scale studies, cutting-edge technologies, and the challenges that remain.

title: Microtubule-associated histone deacetylase 6 supports the calcium store sensor STIM1 in mediating malignant cell behaviors.
text:
STIM1, a protein found in the endoplasmic reticulum, plays a crucial role in regulating calcium levels within cancer cells. Specifically, STIM1 promotes cell growth, migration, and angiogenesis in breast and cervical cancers. Our study reveals that HDAC6, a microtubule-associated histone deacetylase, regulates the activation of STIM1-mediated store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) between cervical cancer cells and normal cervical epithelial cells.
Using confocal microscopy, we found that microtubule integrity is essential for STIM1 trafficking to the plasma membrane and interaction with Orai1, a key pore subunit of SOCE. Cancer cells exhibited higher levels of STIM1 and Orai1 compared to normal cervical epithelial cells. Furthermore, we discovered that HDAC6 is overexpressed in cancer cells, accompanied by hypoacetylated alpha-tubulin. Inhibition of HDAC6 using the specific inhibitor tubastatin-A resulted in reduced STIM1 translocation to the plasma membrane and blocked SOCE activation in cancer cells. Additionally, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of HDAC6 prevented STIM1 membrane trafficking and downstream calcium influx, as demonstrated by total internal reflection fluorescence images and intracellular calcium measurements. In contrast, HDAC6 inhibition did not affect interactions between STIM1 and the microtubule plus end-binding protein EB1.
Our findings suggest that targeting HDAC6 could be a promising strategy for blocking malignant cell behavior in cancer. Analysis of surgical specimens revealed that most cervical cancer tissues overexpressed STIM1 and Orai1, along with hypoacetylated alpha-tubulin. Together, our results identify HDAC6 as a key regulator of STIM1-mediated SOCE in cancer cells.

title: The tumor necrosis factor family receptors RANK and CD40 cooperatively establish the thymic medullary microenvironment and self-tolerance.
text: Medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) establish T cell self-tolerance through the expression of autoimmune regulator (Aire) and peripheral tissue-specific self-antigens. However, the mechanisms underlying mTEC development remain largely unclear. Our study demonstrates that receptor activator of NF-κB (RANK) and CD40 signals play a crucial role in regulating mTEC development. In embryonic development, RANK signaling was found to be essential for mTEC development, while in postnatal mice, cooperation between CD40 and RANK signals was required for successful mTEC development and establishment of the medullary microenvironment. When fetal thymic stroma cells were stimulated in vitro with RANK or CD40 ligands, mTEC development occurred in a TRAF6-, NIK-, and IκB kinase beta (IKKβ)-dependent manner. These findings demonstrate that there is a developmental-stage-dependent cooperation between RANK and CD40 signals in promoting mTEC development, thereby establishing self-tolerance.

title: Rare and common variants: twenty arguments
text: Genome-wide association studies have significantly advanced our understanding of the genetic roots of disease risk. However, the fact that they typically only identify a small fraction of the total number of causal genetic variants has led to differing opinions regarding whether most of the variability is due to rare variants of large effect or common variants of very small effect. In this review, I will examine 20 arguments for and against each of these models and conclude that both types of effects can be reconciled.

title: DNA methylation status predicts cell type-specific enhancer activity.
text: The selective binding of glucocorticoid receptor (GR) to specific regions of chromatin, known as distal regulatory elements, is associated with cell type-specific areas of freely accessible chromatin. These regions can either preexist in the chromatin (pre-programmed) or be created de novo by the receptor. The mechanisms responsible for these sites' creation and maintenance remain poorly understood. Interestingly, we observe a global trend of increased CpG density in pre-programmed regions, suggesting their demethylated state plays a crucial role in maintaining open chromatin in a tissue-specific manner. On the other hand, sites that are actively opened by GR (de novo) are characterized by lower CpG density and are distinguished by their lack of suppressive methyl-cytosine content. These de novo sites form a unique class of enhancers. Moreover, treatment with glucocorticoids leads to rapid changes in methylation levels at select CpGs within de novo sites. Furthermore, we identify GR-binding regions with CpGs at strategic locations, and our findings demonstrate that DNA methylation can significantly impact GR-DNA interactions in vitro. Our study establishes a direct link between tissue-specific chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and transcription factor binding, and highlights the crucial role of DNA methylation in facilitating the regulation of genes by nuclear receptors.

title: BLM helicase facilitates telomere replication during leading strand synthesis of telomeres
text: New findings suggest that the Bloom syndrome-associated helicase, BLM, plays a crucial role in telomere replication by facilitating the progression of replication forks through G-rich telomeric DNA. To investigate this, researchers employed single molecule analysis of replicated DNA (SMARD) to determine the contribution of BLM helicase to telomere replication. In contrast to cells lacking BLM, replication forks initiating from origins within the telomere moved slower through the G-rich strand when synthesized by the leading strand synthesis pathway. Furthermore, the presence of a G-quadruplex (G4) stabilizer in these cells further slowed down fork progression through the telomere. Interestingly, the study also revealed that deficiency in BLM or another G4-unwinding helicase, Werner syndrome-associated helicase WRN, led to a remarkable increase in G4 structures in cells. Remarkably, the deficiency of either helicase resulted in a more significant increase in G4 DNA detected in the telomere compared to G4 observed genome-wide. Taken together, these findings suggest that BLM helicase facilitates telomere replication by resolving G4 structures formed during the replication of the G-rich strand by leading strand synthesis.

title: Reflecting on 25 years with MYC
text: Approximately 25 years ago, the human homologue of a retroviral oncogene, MYC, was identified. Since then, MYC research has been prolific and the advances remarkable. Looking back, it is incredible how each new insight into MYC regulation and function has also influenced numerous biological fields, including our comprehension of molecular oncogenesis as a whole. Here, we review the key advances in MYC biology and speculate on the future of MYC research.

title: Protective effects of exercise and phosphoinositide 3-kinase(p110alpha) signaling in dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
text: Regular physical activity protects against cardiovascular disease, and the physiological increase in cardiac muscle mass associated with exercise is typically benign, unlike the harmful hypertrophy that occurs with disease. The p110alpha isoform of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) plays a crucial role in the achievement of the beneficial cardiac hypertrophy brought on by exercise. It is unclear, however, if this gene or others that are activated in the heart of an athlete could have an impact on heart function and longeavity in a setting of heart failure. To investigate the possible impact of progressive exercise training and PI3K(p110alpha) activity on survival and/or cardiac function in two models of heart disease, we subjected a transgenic mouse model of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) to swim training, genetically crossed cardiac-specific transgenic mice with increased or decreased PI3K(p110alpha) activity to the DCM model, and subjected PI3K(p110alpha) transgenics to acute pressure overload (ascending aortic constriction). We evaluated life span, cardiac function, and markers of pathological hypertrophy. Exercise training and greater cardiac PI3K(p110alpha) activity prolonged survival by 15 to 20 % in the DCM model. In contrast, decreased PI3K(p110alpha) activity drastically shortened lifespan by approximately 50%. Increased PI3K(p110alpha) activity also had favorable effects on cardiac function and fibrosis in the pressure-overload model and reduced pathological growth.
