Sixty esteemed experts in MDR-TB assemblyd in Washington D.C. and Cape Town, South Africa, to deliberate on crucial MDR-TB trial-related issues, including: standardization of terminology, clinical trial capacity building, and formulation of treatment regimens that promote adherence, stave off resistance, and hold clinical relevance for special populations, such as children and those co-infected with HIV. Building upon this knowledge, the gathering aimed to generate a robust evidence foundation to facilitate regulatory approval and improved treatment guidelines. Discussions focused on investigational treatment combinations currently under evaluation in Phase 2B and Phase 3 trials, as well as promising new regimens and combinations slated for examination in the near future. These include approaches designed to enable more efficient and all-oral treatment regimens to enhance treatment completion rates. The hope is that by illuminating these challenges, a clearer path will emerge towards identifying effective, tolerable treatments that can be effectively implemented worldwide.

title: Para-aortic splanchnopleura from early mouse embryos contains B1a cell progenitors
text: Definitive erythropoiesis in birds arises from stem cells that emerge in the splanchnopleural mesoderm near the embryonic aorta, according to embryological studies (1-4). However, in mammals, the yolk sac is thought to be the exclusive provider of haematopoietic stem cells during ontogeny (5). Although some studies have suggested alternative intraembryonic sources of stem cells in mice (6, 7), the yolk sac remains the primary source of haematopoietic stem cells in mammals. To investigate the possibility of alternative sources of haematopoietic stem cells, we grafted intraembryonic splanchnopleura from 10- to 18-somite mouse embryos into immunodeficient SCID mice. Our results showed significant amounts of donor-derived serum IgM, normal numbers of IgM-secreting plasma cells, and the Bla (IgMa brightB220dullCD5+) cell subset were fully reconstituted by donor progenitors three to six months after engraftment. Interestingly, our experiments revealed a previously unrecognized site of haematogenesis, which occurs 12 hours before the colonization of the fetal liver, the previously known site of haematopoiesis in the embryo.

title: Establishment in culture of pluripotential cells from mouse embryos
text: Pluripotent cells are present in a mouse embryo until at least an early post-implantation stage, as evidenced by their ability to contribute to the formation of chimeric animals and teratocarcinomas. Prior to this study, it was not possible to establish progressively growing cultures of these cells in vitro, and cell lines could only be obtained after teratocarcinoma formation in vivo. We report here the establishment of pluripotent cell lines derived directly from in vitro cultures of mouse blastocysts. These cells are capable of differentiating either in vitro or after inoculation into a mouse as a tumor in vivo, and have a normal karyotype.

title: MHC class II interaction with CD4 mediated by a region analogous to the MHC class I binding site for CD8
text: The interactions between major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules and either CD4 or CDS coreceptors play a pivotal role in the selection of mature T cells in the thymus. Once mature, each of these two glycoproteins exhibits a specific bias in recognizing MHC molecules through their T-cell receptors. CD4+ T cells are responsible for recognizing antigens in association with MHC class II molecules, while CD8+ T cells recognize antigens through MHC class I molecules. Convincing evidence has demonstrated physical interactions between CD4/MHC class II molecules and CD8/MHC class I molecules through cell adhesion assays. Further investigation has identified a specific binding site for CDS on class I molecules, and a structurally analogous region in the MHC class IIβ-chain β2 domain has been discovered to be critical for function with both mouse and human CD4.

title: Instability and decay of the primary structure of DNA
text: Although DNA serves as the repository of genetic information, its chemical stability is somewhat limited. DNA degradation occurs at significant rates in vivo through mechanisms such as hydrolysis, oxidation, and non-enzymatic methylation. These processes are counteracted by specialized DNA repair mechanisms. The spontaneous degradation of DNA is likely to play a key role in processes such as mutagenesis, carcinogenesis, and aging, and can also hinder the recovery of DNA fragments from ancient fossils.

title: Single-cell proteomic analysis of S. cerevisiae reveals the architecture of biological noise
text:
Objective: Quantifying Cellular Behavior with High resolution
Challenges in Measuring Protein Abundance:
A crucial objective in biology is to obtain a precise and quantitative description of cellular behavior. However, this task has been impeded by the difficulty in measuring protein abundance and its variability. Until now, methods for measuring protein levels have been limited, resulting in an incomplete understanding of cellular processes.
 strategy: Flow cytometry and GFP-tagged yeast strains
To overcome these limitations, we have developed a novel approach that combines high-throughput flow cytometry with a library of GFP-tagged yeast strains. This allows for the rapid and precise monitoring of protein levels at the single-cell level. By measuring the protein abundance of over 2,500 proteins in both rich and minimal media, we gained a comprehensive understanding of the cellular response to these conditions.
Single-Cell Data: Noise in Protein Expression
Our single-cell data revealed that the noise in protein expression is predominantly driven by the stochastic production and destruction of messenger RNAs. Beyond this global trend, there are significant differences in protein-specific noise levels that are closely correlated with a protein's mode of transcription and function. For example, proteins that respond to environmental changes exhibit higher levels of noise, while those involved in protein synthesis are relatively quiet.
Structure of Biological Noise:
These findings reveal a remarkable structure to biological noise, suggesting that protein noise levels may have been selected to reflect the costs and potential benefits of variation. Our results provide new insights into the intricate regulatory mechanisms that govern cellular processes and highlight the importance of considering the role of noise in protein abundance.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study demonstrates the power of combining high-throughput flow cytometry and a library of GFP-tagged yeast strains to monitor protein levels at the single-cell level. By revealing the structure of biological noise, we gain a deeper understanding of the regulatory mechanisms that govern cellular processes and the role of noise in protein abundance. These findings have significant implications for fields such as medicine, agriculture, and biotechnology, where an understanding of cellular processes is critical for advancing research and developing new therapies.

title: Direct conversion of fibroblasts to functional neurons by defined factors
text: Cellular differentiation and lineage commitment are considered to be stringent and irreversible processes during development. Recent research has shown that mouse and human fibroblasts can be transformed into a pluripotent state with a combination of four transcription factors. This raised the question of whether transcription factors could directly induce other defined somatic cell fates, beyond an undifferentiated state. We hypothesized that combinatorial expression of neural-lineage-specific transcription factors could directly convert fibroblasts into neurons. Starting from a pool of nineteen candidate genes, we identified a combination of only three factors, Ascl1, Brn2 (also known as Pou3f2), and Myt1l, that efficiently convert mouse embryonic and postnatal fibroblasts into functional neurons in vitro. These induced neuronal (iN) cells express multiple neuron-specific proteins, generate action potentials, and form functional synapses. The ability to generate neurons from non-neural lineages has significant implications for investigations into neural development, modeling of neurological diseases, and regenerative medicine.

title: Inflammasome-mediated dysbiosis regulates progression of NAFLD and obesity
text: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common form of liver disease worldwide, and its progression can lead to chronic hepatic inflammation, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Despite being a leading cause of liver disease, the causes of NAFLD's progression to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) are not well understood. Our study reveals that two inflammasomes, NLRP6 and NLRP3, and the effector protein IL-18 play a crucial role in regulating NAFLD/NASH progression, as well as various aspects of metabolic syndrome by modulating the gut microbiota. We used different mouse models to show that defective inflammasomes lead to increased hepatic steatosis and inflammation, which are exacerbated by the influx of TLR4 and TLR9 agonists into the portal circulation. Additionally, co-housing inflammasome-deficient mice with wild-type mice accelerates hepatic steatosis and obesity. Our findings highlight the central role of the gut microbiota in the pathogenesis of NAFLD and its progression to NASH, and suggest that altered interactions between the gut microbiota and the host play a crucial role in the development of multiple metabolic syndrome-associated abnormalities.

title: Chromatin remodelling at promoters suppresses antisense transcription
text: Chromatin plays a crucial role in organizing the DNA within eukaryotic cells, allowing for efficient packaging and regulation of gene expression. To investigate the mechanisms underlying chromatin structure and transcriptional regulation in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we have focused on the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complex Isw2. Our findings reveal that Isw2 plays a critical role in positioning nucleosomes adjacent to promoter regions, positioning them at the interface between gene and intergenic sequences. Remodeling by Isw2 is directional, resulting in increased nucleosome occupancy in the intergenic region. The loss of Isw2 function leads to inappropriate transcription, generating both coding and noncoding transcripts. Our studies demonstrate that Isw2 repositions nucleosomes to regulate transcription directionality by preventing transcription initiation from cryptic sites, thereby providing insight into chromatin organization on a global scale and shedding light on the mechanisms underlying transcriptional regulation.

title: The Human Mitochondrial DEAD-Box Protein DDX28 Resides in RNA Granules and Functions in Mitoribosome Assembly.
text:
Mitochondrial ribosomes are specialized for the synthesis of 13 key proteins that form the oxidative phosphorylation system. Despite their importance, the mechanisms of mitoribosome biogenesis, compartmentalization, and the factors involved remain largely uncovered. We have recently identified the DEAD-box protein DDX28 as a critical component of RNA granules required for the biogenesis of the large subunit (mt-LSU) of mitochondrial ribosomes. DDX28 interacts with 16S rRNA and the mt-LSU, and our findings indicate that it plays a crucial role during the early stages of mt-LSU biogenesis, specifically in the compartment defined by RNA granules near the mitochondrial nucleoids.
Upon RNAi-mediated silencing of DDX28 in HEK293T cells, mt-LSU protein levels and mitochondrial protein synthesis are severely impaired, leading to a reduced abundance of 16S rRNA and mt-LSU components. These findings demonstrate the essential role of DDX28 in the early stages of mt-LSU biogenesis, highlighting its importance in maintaining proper mitochondrial function.

title: Conversion of Adult Pancreatic α-cells to β-cells After Extreme β-cell Loss
text: Pancreatic insulin-producing beta-cells have a long lifespan, typically replicating little in healthy conditions throughout an individual's lifetime. However, they exhibit increased self-duplication in response to elevated metabolic demand or injury, resulting in beta-cell loss. The ability of adult mammals to differentiate (regenerate) new beta-cells after complete beta-cell loss, such as in diabetes, is uncertain. This process would involve differentiation from precursor cells or an alternative non-beta-cell source. Our study demonstrates beta-cell regeneration in a transgenic model of diphtheria-toxin-induced acute selective near-total beta-cell ablation. When given insulin, the mice survived and showed increased beta-cell mass over time. Lineage-tracing to label glucagon-producing alpha-cells before beta-cell ablation revealed that a large fraction of regenerated beta-cells originated from alpha-cells, highlighting an unappreciated degree of pancreatic cell plasticity. This discovery raises the possibility of harnessing inter-endocrine cell conversion in adult pancreas for diabetes therapies, either through in vitro differentiation settings or by inducing regeneration.

title: Driver mutations in histone H3.3 and chromatin remodelling genes in paediatric glioblastoma
text: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a dangerous brain tumor in both adults and children. However, studies have found differences in the genetic changes that occur in these two groups. To better understand the underlying causes of these differences, researchers sequenced the exomes (the proteins on the surface of genes) of 48 pediatric GBM samples. They found that 44% of the tumors had mutations in a specific pathway involving three proteins: H3.3-ATRX-DAXX. These mutations were observed in 31% of the tumors and led to changes in the structure of the histone proteins, which are crucial for regulating gene expression. The researchers also found that 31% of the samples had mutations in two other proteins, ATRX and DAXX, which are involved in the same pathway. In addition, 54% of all cases had mutations in the TP53 gene, which is a well-known tumor suppressor gene. Finally, the researchers found that H3F3A mutations, which are specific to glioblastoma, were highly prevalent in children and young adults. They also found that the presence of these mutations was strongly associated with specific gene expression profiles and with alternative lengthening of telomeres, a mechanism that helps to explain the differences in GBM pathogenesis between children and adults. In summary, this study provides new insights into the genetic changes that occur in pediatric glioblastoma and highlights the importance of the H3.3-ATRX-DAXX pathway in its development.

title: Translational control of intron splicing in eukaryotes
text: Most eukaryotic genes are interrupted by non-coding introns that must be accurately removed from pre-messenger RNAs to produce translatable mRNAs. Splicing is guided locally by short conserved sequences, but genes typically contain many potential splice sites, and the mechanisms specifying the correct sites remain poorly understood. In most organisms, short introns cannot be efficiently predicted solely on the basis of sequence motifs. In multicellular eukaryotes, long introns are recognized through exon definition, and most genes produce multiple mRNA variants through alternative splicing. The nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway may further shape the observed sets of variants by selectively degrading those containing premature termination codons, which are frequently produced in mammals. Here, we showcase that tiny introns in the ciliate Paramecium tetraurelia are under strong selective pressure to cause premature termination of mRNA translation in the event of intron retention, and this bias is observed among short introns of plants, fungi, and animals. By diminishing the expression of UPF1, a protein crucial in NMD, we demonstrate that the intrinsic efficiency of splicing varies significantly among introns and that NMD activity can considerably reduce the proportion of unspliced mRNAs. Our findings suggest that, independent of alternative splicing, species with abundant introns have come to rely on NMD to compensate for suboptimal splicing efficiency and accuracy.

title: Alternatively activated macrophages produce catecholamines to sustain adaptive thermogenesis
text: All homeotherms rely on thermogenesis to maintain their body temperature, ensuring that cellular functions and physiological processes can continue in chilly environments. According to the prevailing model, when the hypothalamus detects cold temperatures, it triggers sympathetic activity, resulting in the release of noradrenaline in brown and white adipose tissue. Noradrenaline acts on β(3)-adrenergic receptors to induce lipolysis in white adipocytes and stimulate the expression of thermogenic genes, such as Ppargc1a, Ucp1, and Acsl1, in brown adipocytes. However, the identification of all the cell types involved in this efferent loop is not well established. We investigated the role of interleukin-4 (IL-4)-stimulated alternative macrophage activation in adaptive thermogenesis in mice. We discovered that exposure to cold temperatures rapidly activates alternative macrophages in adipose tissue, which secrete catecholamines that induce thermogenic gene expression in brown adipose tissue and lipolysis in white adipose tissue. The absence of alternatively activated macrophages impaired metabolic adaptations to cold, while administration of IL-4 increased thermogenic gene expression, fatty acid mobilization, and energy expenditure, all of which were macrophage-dependent. Our findings reveal a novel function for alternatively activated macrophages in the orchestration of the mammalian stress response to cold.

title: Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres Mediated by Mitotic DNA Synthesis Engages Break-Induced Replication Processes.
text: Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is a telomerase-independent mechanism that allows certain cancer cells to maintain their telomeres. By studying telomerase-positive cells and their ALT-derived human cell lines, we discovered that ALT cells have more fragile telomeres, indicating issues with telomere replication. In response to these problems, ALT cells engage in mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS) at telomeres in a RAD52-dependent, but RAD51-independent, manner. This process is similar to break-induced replication in yeast. Telomeric MiDAS is a conservative DNA synthesis process that may lead to genomic duplications in cancer. We found that the TIMELESS/TIPIN complex suppresses telomere clustering and telomeric MiDAS, while the SMC5/6 complex promotes them. In summary, ALT cells display more telomere replication defects, resulting in persistent DNA damage responses at telomeres, which lead to the engagement of telomeric MiDAS triggered by DNA replication stress, potentially driving genomic duplications in cancer.

title: Light acts directly on organs and cells in culture to set the vertebrate circadian clock.
text: In vertebrates, the expression of clock genes is widespread and not limited to traditional clock structures. For example, the expression of the Clock gene in zebrafish exhibits strong circadian oscillations in various tissues both in vivo and in vitro, demonstrating that endogenous oscillators exist in peripheral organs. A defining characteristic of circadian clocks is their ability to be set or entrained to the local time, typically through exposure to environmental light-dark cycles. An intriguing question is whether peripheral oscillators are entrained by signals from central pacemakers, such as the eyes, or are they directly light-responsive. To investigate this, we have shown that peripheral organ clocks in zebrafish are set by light-dark cycles in culture, and we have also demonstrated that a zebrafish-derived cell line contains a circadian oscillator that is similarly light-entrained.

title: Small molecule inhibition of the KRAS–PDEδ interaction impairs oncogenic KRAS signalling
text: The oncogenic KRAS protein is a primary target in cancer drug discovery, yet direct interference with its signaling pathway has yet to lead to clinically useful drugs. The proper localization and signaling of farnesylated KRAS are regulated by the prenyl-binding protein PDEδ, which maintains the spatial organization of KRAS by facilitating its movement in the cytoplasm. Here, we report that disrupting the binding of mammalian PDEδ to KRAS using small molecules presents a novel opportunity to inhibit oncogenic RAS signaling by altering its localization to endomembranes. Through biochemical screening and structure-based hit optimization, we identified inhibitors of the KRAS-PDEδ interaction that selectively bind to the prenyl-binding pocket of PDEδ with nanomolar affinity, inhibit oncogenic RAS signaling, and suppress the proliferation of human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells that rely on oncogenic KRAS. Our findings may inspire new drug discovery efforts aimed at the development of drugs targeting oncogenic RAS.

title: Evolution of novel cooperative swarming in the bacterium Myxococcus xanthus
text: Cooperation among individuals is essential for evolutionary progress to advanced levels of biological organization. During such transitions, groups of individuals at one level (e.g., single cells) collaborate to form functioning units at a higher level (e.g., multicellular organisms). Although observing the evolution of cooperation in higher eukaryotes can be challenging, microorganisms offer a unique opportunity for direct observation. In this study, we explore the evolution of novel cooperative behavior in experimental lineages of the bacterium Myxococcus xanthus. Natural strains of M. xanthus exhibit socially dependent swarming across soft surfaces through a mechanism called 'S-motility,' which requires the presence of extracellular type IV pili. However, lineages of M. xanthus unable to produce pili underwent a new mechanistic shift towards cooperative swarming. This evolved swarming was found to be mediated, at least in part, by increased production of an extracellular fibril matrix that binds cells together, thereby augmenting group expansion. Notably, while individual cells incur a cost by producing the fibril matrix, the enhanced group cohesion leads to a significant increase in population growth. Our findings illustrate that fundamental transitions to basic cooperation can easily unfold in bacteria, underscoring the adaptation potential of microorganisms.

title: Exon duplication and divergence in the human preproglucagon gene
text: Glucagon is a 29-amino acid hormone produced by the pancreas that counteracts the blood glucose-lowering effects of insulin by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Recently, the structure of the hamster pancreatic glucagon precursor has been determined through the sequence of a cloned cDNA. Proglucagon is a 180-amino acid protein that comprises five functional regions: a signal peptide or pre-peptide, an NH2-terminal peptide (also known as glicentin-related pancreatic peptide, GRPP), glucagon, and two carboxy-terminal glucagon-like peptides (GLP-1 and GLP-2). The sequences of two non-allelic anglerfish pancreatic glucagon precursors have also been determined, and their organization is similar but not identical to the hamster protein, lacking the polypeptide segment corresponding to hamster GLP-2. The presence of three regions possessing internal homology within proglucagon, including glucagon, GLP-1, and GLP-2, suggests that the structure of the preproglucagon gene may provide insight into the evolution of this polyprotein. We have also isolated and sequenced the human preproglucagon gene, and found that the organization of the human precursor is identical to the hamster protein, containing at least three intervening sequences that divide the protein-coding portion of the gene into four regions: the signal peptide and part of the NH2-terminal peptide, the remainder of the NH2-terminal peptide, glucagon, GLP-1, and GLP-2. These findings suggest that triplication and subsequent sequence divergence of an exon encoding glucagon or a glucagon-like peptide produced this polyprotein precursor.

title: BH1 and BH2 domains of Bcl-2 are required for inhibition of apoptosis and heterodimerization with Bax
text: BCL-2 was first identified as a gene located at the t(14;18) chromosomal breakpoint in follicular B-cell lymphoma (1-3). BCL-2 has a unique oncogenic role in promoting cell survival by inhibiting multiple forms of programmed cell death (4-13). A family of related proteins, including BCL-2, share two highly conserved regions known as the Bcl-2 homology 1 (BH1) and Bcl-2 homology 2 (BH2) domains (Fig. 1). One of these proteins, BAX, heterodimerizes with BCL-2 and when overexpressed, counteracts the pro-survival effects of BCL-2 (14). We found that mutating BCL-2 at specific sites in the BHl or BH2 domains completely abolished its ability to inhibit apoptosis in response to interleukin-3 deprivation, γ-irradiation, and glucocorticoid treatment. Interestingly, these mutations also disrupted BCL-2's heterodimerization with BAX, yet still allowed for BCL-2 homodimerization. These results indicate that the BH1 and BH2 domains play a functional role in BCL-2's anti-apoptotic activities and suggest that BCL-2 exerts its effects through heterodimerization with BAX.

title: KAP1 controls endogenous retroviruses in embryonic stem cells
text: Over four decades of the mammalian genome are derived from retroelements, with approximately a quarter being endogenous retroviruses (ERVs). Some of these are still active, such as in mice, where the highly polymorphic early transposon (ETn)/MusD and intracisternal A-type particles (IAP) are found. ERVs are silenced during early embryogenesis by histone and DNA methylation, although the mechanisms behind this are still unknown. KAP1 (KRAB-associated protein 1, also known as tripartite motif-containing protein 28, TRIM28) represses genes by recruiting the histone methyltransferase SETDB1, heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1), and the NuRD histone deacetylase complex, but few of its physiological targets are known. Two lines of evidence suggest that KAP1-mediated repression could contribute to the control of ERVs: first, KAP1 can cause permanent gene silencing during early embryogenesis, and second, a KAP1 complex silences the retrovirus murine leukaemia virus in embryonic cells. Consistent with this hypothesis, we show that KAP1 deletion leads to a significant upregulation of a range of ERVs, particularly IAP elements, in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells and early embryos. We also demonstrate that KAP1 acts synergistically with DNA methylation to silence IAP elements, and that it is enriched at the 5′ untranslated region (5′UTR) of IAP genomes, where KAP1 deletion leads to the loss of histone 3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3), a hallmark of KAP1-mediated repression. Correspondingly, IAP 5′UTR sequences can impose in cis KAP1-dependent repression on a heterologous promoter in ES cells. Our findings establish that KAP1 controls endogenous retroelements during early embryonic development.

title: The TOR signalling pathway controls nuclear localization of nutrient-regulated transcription factors.
text: The rapamycin-sensitive TOR signaling pathway in Saccharomyces cerevisiae activates a cell growth program in response to nutrients such as nitrogen and carbon. The TOR1 and TOR2 kinases (TOR) regulate cytoplasmic protein synthesis and degradation through the conserved TAP42 protein. Although the mechanism by which TOR controls nuclear events such as global repression of starvation-specific transcription is unclear, our study reveals that TOR inhibits transcription of genes expressed upon nitrogen limitation by promoting the association of the GATA transcription factor GLN3 with the cytoplasmic protein URE2. The binding of GLN3 to URE2 requires TOR-dependent phosphorylation of GLN3, which is also dependent on the TOR effector TAP42. Additionally, TOR inhibits expression of carbon-source-regulated genes by stimulating the binding of the transcriptional activators MSN2 and MSN4 to the cytoplasmic 14-3-3 protein BMH2. Overall, the TOR signaling pathway broadly controls nutrient metabolism by sequestering multiple transcription factors in the cytoplasm.

title: Inhibition of pluripotential embryonic stem cell differentiation by purified polypeptides
text: Murine embryonic stem (ES) cells are derived directly from early embryos and possess the ability to differentiate into all adult tissues, including the germline. These cells serve as both a cellular vector for generating transgenic animals and a useful system for identifying factors that control differentiation during early development. In particular, ES cells are shown to respond to a polypeptide factor termed ES cell differentiation inhibitory activity (DIA), which is produced by Buffalo rat liver cells. DIA specifically inhibits the spontaneous differentiation of ES cells in vitro, allowing them to grow as homogeneous stem cell populations without the need for feeder cells. ES cell pluripotency, including the ability to give rise to functional gametes, is preserved during prolonged culture in Buffalo rat liver media, which provides a source of DIA. Further investigation reveals that DIA is related in structure and function to recently identified haemopoietic regulatory factors, including human interleukin for DA cells and leukaemia inhibitory factor. These findings suggest that DIA and human interleukin DA/leukaemia inhibitory factor are multifunctional regulatory factors with distinct biological activities in both early embryonic and haemopoietic stem cell systems.

title: Pancreatic cancer genomes reveal aberrations in axon guidance pathway genes
text: Pancreatic cancer is a deadly malignancy with limited effective treatment options. In an effort to better understand the genomic alterations driving this disease, we performed exome sequencing and copy number analysis on a prospectively accrued cohort of 142 early-stage (I and II) sporadic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma tumors. Our detailed analysis of 99 informative tumors identified a high degree of heterogeneity, including 2,016 non-silent mutations and 1,628 copy-number variations. We identified 16 significantly mutated genes, reinforcing previous findings on KRAS, TP53, CDKN2A, SMAD4, MLL3, TGFBR2, ARID1A, and SF3B1, and uncovering novel mutated genes such as EPC1, ARID2, ATM, ZIM2, MAP2K4, NALCN, SLC16A4, and MAGEA6. Integrative analysis of in vitro functional data and animal models provided supportive evidence for the potential roles of these genetic aberrations in carcinogenesis. Pathway-based analysis of recurrently mutated genes recapitulated clustering in core signaling pathways in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and identified new mutated genes in each pathway. Additionally, we found frequent and diverse somatic mutations in genes traditionally involved in embryonic regulatory axon guidance, such as SLIT/ROBO signaling, which was also observed in murine Sleeping Beauty transposon-mediated somatic mutagenesis models of pancreatic cancer. This finding supports the potential involvement of axon guidance genes in pancreatic carcinogenesis.

title: Rejuvenation of aged progenitor cells by exposure to a young systemic environment
text: The decreased capacity for tissue regeneration is a hallmark of aging, and this decline may be attributed to age-related changes in tissue-specific stem cells. A reduction in skeletal muscle stem cell (satellite cell) activity due to a loss of Notch signaling leads to impaired regeneration of aged muscle. Similarly, a decline in hepatic progenitor cell proliferation resulting from the formation of a complex involving cEBP-α and the chromatin remodeling factor brahma (Brm) hinders the regenerative capacity of aged liver. To investigate the impact of systemic factors on aged progenitor cells from these tissues, we established parabiotic pairings (i.e., a shared circulatory system) between young and old mice (heterochronic parabioses), exposing old mice to factors present in young serum. Notably, heterochronic parabiosis restored Notch signaling activation, proliferation, and regenerative capacity in aged satellite cells. Exposing satellite cells from old mice to young serum augmented the expression of the Notch ligand (Delta), enhanced Notch activation, and increased proliferation in vitro. Moreover, heterochronic parabiosis heightened aged hepatocyte proliferation and restored the cEBP-α complex to levels comparable to those in young animals. These findings suggest that the age-related decline in progenitor cell activity can be influenced by systemic factors that change with age.

title: Continuous single-cell imaging of blood generation from haemogenic endothelium
text:
Despite decades of research, the identity of the cells responsible for generating the first haematopoietic cells in mammalian embryos remains a mystery. The debate rages on as to whether these cells arise from mesodermal cells, mesenchymal progenitors, bipotent endothelial-haematopoietic precursors, or haemogenic endothelial cells. However, the proximity of endothelial and blood cells at sites of embryonic haematopoiesis, as well as their similar gene expression, has led some to propose that the endothelium may be the source of blood cells. Unfortunately, the lack of suitable technology has hindered attempts to observe the emergence of blood cells at the single-cell level, and the existence of haemogenic endothelial cells remains a matter of debate.
In this study, we employed new imaging and cell-tracking methods to investigate the developmental origin of mammalian blood. By continuously monitoring mouse mesodermal cells as they differentiate into endothelial cells and blood colonies over a long period of time, we were able to detect haemogenic endothelial cells that give rise to blood cells. Using simultaneous detection of morphology and multiple molecular and functional markers, we identified both living endothelial and haematopoietic cells. We found that detachment of nascent blood cells from the endothelium is not directly linked to asymmetric cell division, and haemogenic endothelial cells are specified from cells already expressing endothelial markers. These findings significantly improve our understanding of the developmental origin of mammalian blood and the potential generation of haematopoietic stem cells from embryonic stem cells.

title: Formation of germ-line chimaeras from embryo-derived teratocarcinoma cell lines
text: Recent advances in culture techniques have made it possible to obtain embryo-derived pluripotent cells with a normal karyotype and high differentiative potential1-3. To explore the potential of these cells as functional germline cells, we investigated their ability to form chimaeras in mice using three independently isolated XY cell lines (EK.CP1, EK.CC1.1, and EKCC1.2). Our results show that a Whopping 50% of live-born animals are chimaeric, and we have successfully generated seven functional germline chimaeras in male mice derived from these cell lines.

title: Chloroquine resistance not linked to mdr-like genes in a Plasmodium falciparum cross
text: Chloroquine is thought to fight malaria caused by the Plasmodium falciparum parasite by building up in the acidic vesicles of the parasite and impacting its function (1-4). However, resistant parasites quickly expel the drug without any changes, reducing its accumulation in the vesicles (5). The discovery that verapamil can partially reverse chloroquine resistance in vitro led researchers to propose that the pump-mediated efflux mechanism may be similar to that found in mammalian multidrug-resistant tumor cell lines (6). It is known that P. falciparum has at least two mdr-like genes (7,8), one of which has been linked to chloroquine resistance (7,9,10). In order to determine if either of these genes is involved in chloroquine resistance, researchers crossed chloroquine-susceptible and chloroquine-resistant clones of P. falciparum and examined 16 independent recombinant progeny. These findings suggest that the genetic locus governing chloroquine efflux and resistance is unrelated to known mdr-like genes.

title: Identification of a cold receptor reveals a general role for TRP channels in thermosensation
text: The intricate mechanisms by which our bodies perceive cold temperatures are largely unexplored. However, researchers have gained valuable insights into this process through the use of pharmacological agents, such as menthol, which cause a cooling sensation. By studying the menthol receptor, specifically the CMR1 receptor found in trigeminal sensory neurons, scientists have discovered that it is activated not only by menthol but also by cool to cold temperatures. This cold- and menthol-sensitive receptor, CMR1, belongs to the TRP family of excitatory ion channels and is believed to act as a transducer of cold stimuli in the somatosensory system. These findings, combined with the previous identification of heat-sensitive channels VR1 and VRL-1, reveal that TRP channels are responsible for detecting temperatures across a wide range and are the primary temperature sensors in the mammalian peripheral nervous system.

title: Surface mechanics mediate pattern formation in the developing retina
text: The formation of biological structures involves organizing different types of cells into a spatial arrangement. In this study, we investigate the physical basis of the patterning of the Drosophila retina in vivo. We show that E- and N-cadherins are involved in the adhesion of retinal epithelial cells along their apical surfaces. Unexpectedly, we find that the differential expression of N-cadherin within a sub-group of retinal cells (cone cells) leads to their shape being configured in a way that minimizes their surface contact with surrounding cells. The cells within this sub-group pack together in the same manner as soap bubbles do, resulting in a complex spatial pattern of cells that is created through the mechanics of cellular surface interactions. Thus, the simple patterned expression of N-cadherin leads to a complex pattern of cells due to the inherent tendency of surfaces to minimize their area.

title: Role of inscuteable in orienting asymmetric cell divisions in Drosophila
text: Drosophila neuroblasts and epithelial cells in the procephalic neurogenic region undergo division perpendicular to the surface, segregating the proteins Numb and Prospero into the basal daughter cell. Our findings demonstrate that the orientation of the mitotic spindle and correct localization of Numb and Prospero in these cells require the presence of the Inscuteable gene. Intriguingly, ectopic expression of Inscuteable in other epithelial cells leads to spindle reorientation, highlighting the protein's role in establishing polarity for asymmetric cell division. Prior to mitosis, Inscuteable localizes to the apical cell cortex, suggesting that it functions in establishing polarity for cell division.

title: Specific interference by ingested dsRNA.
text: In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, a genetic phenomenon known as interference has been observed, where the expression of a single gene can be specifically reduced through the microinjection of a corresponding fragment of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). One striking aspect of this process is the spreading effect, where interference is observed in a broader region of the animal after the injection of dsRNA into the extracellular body cavity. Our findings demonstrate that C. elegans can respond to dsRNA encountered in the environment in a gene-specific manner. Normally, these nematodes feed on bacteria, ingesting and grinding them in the pharynx and then absorbing bacterial contents in the gut. We have discovered that Escherichia coli bacteria expressing dsRNAs can elicit specific interference effects on nematode larvae that feed on them.

title: Bacterial RNA and small antiviral compounds activate caspase-1 through cryopyrin/Nalp3
text: Mutations in the CIAS1 gene are associated with three autoinflammatory disorders: familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome, and neonatal-onset multiple-system inflammatory disease. The CIAS1 gene codes for cryopyrin, a member of the NOD-LRR protein family that plays a key role in activating intracellular host defense signaling pathways. Cryopyrin forms a multi-protein complex called the inflammasome, which includes the apoptosis-associated speck-like protein (ASC) and caspase-1. The inflammasome is essential for the activation of caspase-1 and the production of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and interleukin-18 (IL-18) in response to bacterial RNA and certain compounds, such as R837 and R848. In contrast, the secretion of tumor-necrosis factor-α and IL-6, as well as the activation of NF-κB and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), are not affected by cryopyrin deficiency. These findings reveal a crucial role for cryopyrin in host defense through bacterial RNA-mediated activation of caspase-1 and provide insights into the pathogenesis of autoinflammatory syndromes.

title: Control of cortical GABA circuitry development by Nrg1 and ErbB4 signalling
text:
Schizophrenia is a complex disorder that affects the proper functioning of several brain systems crucial for cognitive function and social behavior. While the earliest symptoms of the disease typically appear during late adolescence or early adulthood, research suggests that schizophrenia has a strong genetic component and is, in fact, a neurodevelopmental disorder. Several studies have identified neuregulin 1 (NRG1) and its receptor ERBB4 as key risk genes for schizophrenia, although the precise role of these genes in the disease mechanism remains unclear.
Our study reveals that NRG1 and ERBB4 signaling plays a critical role in the development of inhibitory circuitries in the mammalian cerebral cortex. Unlike the prevailing view that these genes are involved in the formation and function of excitatory synapses between pyramidal cells, we found that ERBB4 is primarily expressed in certain classes of interneurons, including parvalbumin-expressing chandelier and basket cells. In these cells, ERB4 localizes to axon terminals and postsynaptic densities, where it promotes the formation of axo-axonic inhibitory synapses. We also discovered that ERB4 expression in GABA-containing interneurons regulates the formation of excitatory synapses onto these cells. In contrast, ERB4 is dispensable for excitatory transmission between pyramidal neurons.
Our findings suggest that NGR1 and ERBB4 signaling are essential for the wiring of GABA-mediated circuits in the postnatal cerebral cortex. This provides a new perspective on the involvement of these genes in the etiology of schizophrenia.

* Changing "expressing" to "expressing" in the fourth sentence to avoid repetition.

title: Obesity as a medical problem.
text: Obesity has become so widespread among the world's population that it is now eclipsing undernutrition and infectious diseases as the most significant source of ill health. In particular, obesity is linked to diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease, certain types of cancer, and sleep-breathing disorders. Obesity is defined as a body-mass index (BMI) of 30 kg m(-2) or higher, but this does not account for the severe health consequences associated with milder degrees of overweight, nor the adverse impact of internal fat deposits. The global obesity epidemic is fueled by a combination of genetic susceptibility, increased access to high-calorie foods, and decreased physical activity in modern society. Obesity should no longer be viewed solely as a cosmetic issue affecting certain individuals; it is a global health crisis that threatens overall well-being.

title: Nonlinear Elasticity in Biological Gels
text: Most synthetic materials, by contrast, become more pliable as they are deformed. This nonlinear elastic response, crucial for the proper functioning of certain tissues, has been observed since at least the 19th century, but the molecular structure and underlying design principles remain a mystery. Current models require intricate, uniquely structured materials to account for this response. In this article, we demonstrate that a much simpler molecular theory can explain strain stiffening in a wide range of biopolymer gels composed of purified cytoskeletal and extracellular proteins. This theory shows that systems of semi-flexible chains, such as filamentous proteins arranged in an open, cross-linked meshwork, inherently stiffen at low strains without the need for complex structures or multiple elements with diverse intrinsic stiffnesses.

title: Live-cell delamination counterbalances epithelial growth to limit tissue overcrowding
text:
The maintenance and development of epithelial tissues depend on a delicate balance between growth and cell death. Despite significant progress in understanding the mechanisms that regulate tissue growth, the processes that control the fine tuning of growth and cell death to ensure proper tissue organization are still poorly understood. To address this gap in knowledge, we have used the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster as a model system to identify a novel mechanism of cell delamination that promotes tissue organization.
In crowded regions of the tissue, a proportion of cells undergo a sequential loss of cell-cell junctions and a progressive loss of apical area, eventually being pushed out by their neighbors. We have recapitulated this process using a simple computational model of epithelial mechanics, showing that stochastic cell loss relieves overcrowding as the system approaches equilibrium. Importantly, this process of delamination occurs before the onset of programmed cell death, providing a mechanism for tissue organization that is distinct from apoptosis-mediated cell extrusion.
Overall, this study reveals a simple mechanism that permits epithelia to adapt to changes in growth, providing important insights into the early stages of cancer development. The observation that live-cell delamination links epithelial hyperplasia to cell invasion highlights the potential role of this mechanism in cancer progression.

title: Broad antiretroviral defence by human APOBEC3G through lethal editing of nascent reverse transcripts
text: To replicate, viruses typically need to overcome the host's natural defenses within cells. One way that viruses achieve this is by producing specialized proteins that counter the antiviral activity of APOBEC3G (apolipoprotein B mRNA-editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like 3G; also known as CEM15), a protein expressed in high levels in human T cells. When produced in the presence of APOBEC3G, viruses that lack the Vif protein are unable to infect cells. APOBEC3G is related to APOBEC1, which is part of an RNA-editing complex that changes a cytosine residue in apoB messenger RNA. Members of the APOBEC family also have the ability to mutate DNA by deaminating cytosine, but it is unclear if this editing potential plays a role in HIV inhibition. Here, we demonstrate that APOBEC3G does, in fact, exert its antiviral effect during reverse transcription by triggering G-to-A hypermutation in the emerging retroviral DNA. Additionally, we find that APOBEC3G can act on a wide range of retroviruses beyond HIV, suggesting that this innate defense mechanism is a broad way for the body to combat these types of viruses.

title: Generation of cell polarity in plants links endocytosis, auxin distribution and cell fate decisions
text:
Dynamically polarized membrane proteins play a crucial role in intercellular communication, a fundamental aspect of multicellular development. Efflux carriers for the signaling molecule auxin from the PIN family are key markers of cell polarity in plants and are essential for auxin distribution-dependent development, including embryo patterning, organogenesis, and tropisms. The polar localization of PINs determines the direction of intercellular auxin flow, but the mechanisms that generate this polarity are poorly understood.
We use real-time PIN tracking to demonstrate that after synthesis, PINs are initially delivered to the plasma membrane in a non-polar manner, and their polarity is established through subsequent endocytic recycling. We find that interfering with PIN endocytosis either through auxin or manipulation of the Arabidopsis Rab5 GTPase pathway prevents PIN polarization. Disruption of PIN polarization leads to temporary changes in asymmetric auxin distribution during embryogenesis and an increased local auxin response in apical embryo regions.
This results in the ectopic expression of auxin pathway-associated root-forming master regulators in embryonic leaves and the transformation of leaves into roots. Our findings reveal a two-step mechanism for the generation of PIN polar localization and highlight the essential role of endocytosis in this process. Furthermore, we demonstrate the connection between endocytosis-dependent polarity of individual cells and auxin distribution-dependent cell fate establishment, which is crucial for multicellular patterning.

title: Congenital leptin deficiency is associated with severe early-onset obesity in humans.
text: The obesity of the ob/ob mouse is caused by genetic mutations in the leptin gene, a protein produced by fat cells that greatly influences appetite and energy expenditure. There is no comparable evidence in humans regarding leptin's role in controlling fat mass. We investigated two severely obese children from the same consanguineous family and found that their serum leptin levels were very low despite their substantially elevated body fat, and in both instances, a homozygous frame-shift mutation was discovered, deleting a single guanine nucleotide at codon 133 of the leptin gene. This finding suggests that leptin deficiency may play a crucial role in the regulation of energy balance in humans, providing the first genetic evidence of leptin's importance in this process.

title: Targeting of cell-surface β-amyloid precursor protein to lysosomes: alternative processing into amyloid-bearing fragments
text:
Progressive deposition of the amyloid beta-peptide is an early and consistent feature of Alzheimer's disease. The beta-peptide is released through proteolytic cleavage of the beta-amyloid precursor protein (betaAPP), a membrane-spanning glycoprotein expressed in most mammalian cells. The normal secretion of betaAPP involves a cleavage in the beta-peptide region, releasing a soluble extramembranous portion and retaining a 10K C-terminal fragment in the membrane. However, this secretory pathway precludes beta-amyloid formation, so we sought an alternative proteolytic processing pathway that could generate beta-peptide-bearing fragments from full-length betaAPP.
Using living human endothelial cells, we discovered that the antibody treatment caused reinternalization of mature betaAPP from the cell surface and its targeting to endosomes/lysosomes. After cell-surface biotinylation, full-length biotinylated betaAPP was recovered inside the cells. Purification of lysosomes directly demonstrated the presence of mature betaAPP and a wide array of beta-peptide-containing proteolytic products. Our findings define a second processing pathway for betaAPP and suggest that it may be responsible for generating amyloid-bearing fragments in Alzheimer's disease.

title: A keratin cytoskeletal protein regulates protein synthesis and epithelial cell growth
text: Cellular growth, or an increase in mass and size, is a highly regulated cellular event. The Akt/mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) signaling pathway plays a central role in controlling protein synthesis and thus cell growth, tissue growth, and organism growth. An example of a physiological context requiring rapid cell growth is tissue repair in response to injury. Here, we demonstrate that keratin 17, an intermediate filament protein rapidly induced in wounded stratified epithelium, regulates cell growth by binding to the adaptor protein 14-3-3σ. Keratinocytes lacking keratin 17 in mice (ref. 4) display decreased protein translation and are smaller in size, which correlates with decreased Akt/mTOR signaling activity. Additionally, other signaling kinases exhibit normal activity, indicating a specific defect in this system. Two amino acid residues located in the amino-terminal head domain of keratin 17 are essential for the serum-dependent relocalization of 14-3-3σ from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and for the subsequent stimulation of mTOR activity and cell growth. These findings uncover a novel and unexpected role for the intermediate filament cytoskeleton in influencing cell growth and size by regulating protein synthesis.

title: Co-crystal structure of the HNF-3/fork head DNA-recognition motif resembles histone H5
text: The three-dimensional structure of an HNF-3/fork head DNA-recognition motif complexed with DNA has been resolved through X-ray crystallography at 2.5 Å resolution. This α/β protein interacts with B-DNA as a monomer, involving both backbone and direct/water-mediated major and minor groove base contacts. This results in a 13° bend in the DNA. The transcription factor adopts a structure similar to that of histone H5, with the amino terminus composed of three compact α-helices that expose the third helix to the major groove. The remaining portion of the protein features a twisted, antiparallel β-structure and random coil that interacts with the minor groove.

title: A Mechanism Linking Extra Centrosomes to Chromosomal Instability
text: Chromosomal instability (CIN) is a prevalent feature of many tumors and is often associated with the presence of extra centrosomes. However, a direct mechanistic link between these two factors has not been established. It has been proposed that extra centrosomes contribute to CIN by promoting multipolar anaphase, a highly abnormal cell division that results in three or more aneuploid daughter cells. To investigate this hypothesis, we used long-term live-cell imaging to examine the division patterns of cells with extra centrosomes. Our results show that cells with multiple centrosomes rarely undergo multipolar cell divisions, and the progeny of these divisions are often inviable. This suggests that multipolar divisions are not the primary cause of chromosomal instability. In contrast, we found that CIN cells with extra centrosomes frequently undergo bipolar cell divisions, but display a higher frequency of lagging chromosomes during anaphase. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we generated cell lines with varying centrosome numbers and observed that extra centrosomes are sufficient to promote chromosome missegregation during bipolar cell division. These segregation errors are the result of cells passing through a transient 'multipolar spindle intermediate', during which time merotelic kinetochore-microtubule attachment errors accumulate before centrosome clustering and anaphase. Our findings provide a direct mechanistic link between extra centrosomes and CIN, two common characteristics of solid tumors. We propose that this mechanism may be a common underlying cause of chromosomal instability in human cancer.

title: Haematopoietic stem cells and early lymphoid progenitors occupy distinct bone marrow niches
text: Although haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are commonly believed to exist within a specialized microenvironment or niche, most experiments manipulating the HSC niche have actually affected other types of progenitor cells. This raises the question of whether HSCs and restricted progenitors reside within separate, specialized niches or if they share a common environment. To investigate this, we examined the sources of the chemokine CXCL12, which is important for HSC and restricted progenitor maintenance. Using Cxcl12(DsRed) knock-in mice that express DsRed in Cxcl12-expressing cells, we found that CXCL12 was primarily produced by perivascular stromal cells, endothelial cells, osteoblasts, and some haematopoietic cells. Deleting CXCL12 from haematopoietic cells or a specific type of supporting cell had limited effects on HSCs or restricted progenitors. However, deleting CXCL12 from endothelial cells, perivascular stromal cells, or osteoblasts had different effects on HSCs and restricted progenitors. Deletion of CXCL12 from endothelial cells depleted HSCs but not myeloerythroid or lymphoid progenitors. Deletion of CXCL12 from perivascular stromal cells depleted HSCs and certain restricted progenitors and mobilized these cells into the circulation. Deletion of CXCL12 from osteoblasts depleted certain early lymphoid progenitors but not HSCs or myeloerythroid progenitors, and did not mobilize these cells into the circulation. Our findings suggest that different types of stem and progenitor cells reside in distinct cellular niches within the bone marrow: HSCs are found in a perivascular niche, while early lymphoid progenitors are found in an endosteal niche.

title: Broad neutralization coverage of HIV by multiple highly potent antibodies
text: Highly versatile antibodies against highly varied viral pathogens are greatly sought after to treat or protect against globally circulating viruses. Here, we examined the neutralizing antibody repertoires of four human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infected donors with impressively broad and potent neutralizing responses and recovered 17 new monoclonal antibodies that neutralize broadly across clades. Many of the new monoclonal antibodies are almost tenfold more potent than the recently characterized PG9, PG16, and VRC01 broadly neutralizing monoclonal antibodies and 100-fold more potent than the initial prototype HIV broadly neutralizing monoclonal antibodies. The monoclonal antibodies largely mirror the neutralization breadth observed in the corresponding donor serum and many recognize novel epitopes on envelope (Env) glycoprotein gp120, providing new targets for vaccine design. Analyzing neutralization with the full set of available broadly neutralizing monoclonal antibodies reveals that certain combinations offer significantly enhanced coverage of the vast diversity of global circulating viruses and these combinations could be incorporated into active or passive immunization regimens. Overall, the isolation of multiple HIV broadly neutralizing monoclonal antibodies from multiple donors, collectively providing broad coverage at low concentrations, is a highly encouraging sign for the development of an effective antibody-based HIV vaccine.

title: Coordination of Rho GTPase activities during cell protrusion
text: GTPases Rac1, RhoA, and Cdc42 collaborate to regulate cytoskeleton dynamics. Recent biosensor studies have shown that all three GTPases are activated at the leading edge of migrating cells, and biochemical evidence suggests that they may reciprocally regulate one another: Cdc42 can activate Rac1 (Reference 8), and Rac1 and RhoA are mutually inhibitory. However, the precise spatiotemporal coordination of these GTPases at the seconds and micrometer scales of individual protrusion events has remained unexplored. To investigate GTPase coordination in mouse embryonic fibroblasts, we simultaneously visualized two GTPase biosensors and employed a 'computational multiplexing' approach that could decode the relationships between multiple protein activities observed in separate experiments. Our findings revealed that RhoA is activated at the cell edge in sync with edge advancement, whereas Cdc42 and Rac1 are activated 2 micrometers behind the edge with a delay of 40 seconds. This suggests that Rac1 and RhoA operate antagonistically through spatial separation and precise timing, with RhoA playing a role in the initial stages of protrusion, while Rac1 and Cdc42 activate pathways involved in reinforcing and stabilizing newly extended protrusions.

title: Understanding mechanisms underlying human gene expression variation with RNA sequencing
text:
Understanding the genetic mechanisms that govern variations in gene expression is a crucial objective of both medical and evolutionary genetics. Studies on expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) have become a vital tool for achieving this aim. Although all eQTL research conducted so far has involved analyzing messenger RNA levels using expression microarrays, recent advances in RNA sequencing have empowered researchers to examine transcript variations at unprecedented resolution.
We conducted RNA sequencing on 69 lymphoblastoid cell lines derived from unrelated Nigerian individuals who have been extensively genotyped by the International HapMap Project. By pooling the data from these individuals, we generated a map of the transcriptional landscape of these cells, which revealed extensive utilization of unannotated untranslated regions and over 100 putative novel protein-coding exons. By using the genotypes from the HapMap project, we identified over 1,000 genes where genetic variation affects overall expression levels or splicing. Our findings demonstrate that eQTLs near genes tend to function by an allele-specific expression mechanism, and that genetic variations that influence the inclusion of an exon are enriched in and around the consensus splice sites. Our results exemplify the power of high-throughput sequencing for the joint analysis of transcriptional variations across individuals.

title: Mesenchymal and haematopoietic stem cells form a unique bone marrow niche
text: The cellular components of the haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niche in the bone marrow are not fully understood, with research pointing to osteoblasts, endothelial cells, and perivascular cells as potential players. However, our study reveals that mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), identified by nestin expression, are a crucial component of the HSC niche. Nestin+ MSCs account for the majority of bone-marrow colony-forming unit fibroblastic activity and can be cultivated as non-adherent 'mesenspheres' that self-renew and expand in serial transplantations. These cells are spatially associated with HSCs and adrenergic nerve fibers and express high levels of genes involved in HSC maintenance. Furthermore, we found that the expression of these genes, as well as genes involved in osteoblast differentiation, is selectively downregulated during enforced HSC mobilization or β3 adrenoreceptor activation. Intriguingly, parathyroid hormone administration leads to an increase in the number of bone marrow nestin+ cells and favors their osteoblastic differentiation, while in vivo depletion of nestin+ cells significantly reduces HSC content in the bone marrow. Importantly, purified HSCs home near nestin+ MSCs in the bone marrow of lethally irradiated mice, and in vivo depletion of nestin+ cells reduces the homing of haematopoietic progenitors to the bone marrow. These findings reveal an unprecedented partnership between two distinct somatic stem cell types and suggest the existence of a unique niche in the bone marrow made up of heterotypic stem cell pairs.

title: Response to self antigen imprints regulatory memory in tissues
text:
The maintenance of immune homeostasis in tissues is achieved through a delicate balance between pathogenic T-cell responses directed at tissue-specific antigens and the tissue's ability to inhibit these responses. The mechanisms by which tissues and the immune system communicate to establish and maintain immune homeostasis are currently unknown. However, clinical evidence suggests that chronic or repeated exposure to self-antigen within tissues can lead to the attenuation of pathological autoimmune responses, possibly as a means to mitigate inflammatory damage and preserve function. Many human organ-specific autoimmune diseases are characterized by the initial presentation of the disease being the most severe, with subsequent flares being of lesser severity and duration. In fact, these diseases often spontaneously resolve, despite persistent tissue autoantigen expression. In the practice of antigen-specific immunotherapy, allergens or self-antigens are repeatedly injected into the skin, leading to a diminution of the inflammatory response after each successive exposure. These findings suggest that tissues acquire the ability to attenuate autoimmune reactions upon repeated exposure to antigens, but the mechanism by which this occurs is unknown.
Our study shows that upon expression of self-antigen in a peripheral tissue, thymus-derived regulatory T cells (Treg cells) become activated, proliferate, and differentiate into more potent suppressors, which mediate resolution of organ-specific autoimmunity in mice. After resolution of the inflammatory response, activated Treg cells are maintained in the target tissue and are primed to attenuate subsequent autoimmune reactions when antigen is re-expressed. Therefore, Treg cells function to confer 'regulatory memory' to the target tissue. These findings provide a framework for understanding how Treg cells respond when exposed to self-antigen in peripheral tissues and offer mechanistic insight into how tissues regulate autoimmunity.

title: Reprogramming of human somatic cells to pluripotency with defined factors
text: Pluripotency refers to the ability of cells in early embryos to differentiate into any of the cell types in the organism. Embryonic stem cells are cells derived from the embryo that retain this pluripotency and are valuable tools for researching how tissues form. Recently, scientists have discovered that by expressing four specific transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and Myc) in murine fibroblasts, they can reprogram these cells directly to pluripotency, yielding induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. Using the same factors, the researchers have also derivated iPS cells from fetal, neonatal, and adult human primary cells, including dermal fibroblasts isolated from a skin biopsy of a healthy human subject. Human iPS cells are similar in morphology and gene expression to embryonic stem cells and can also form teratomas in immune-deficient mice. These findings demonstrate that specific factors can reprogram human cells to pluripotency, providing a method for establishing patient-specific cells in culture.

title: Haematopoietic stem cells do not asymmetrically segregate chromosomes or retain BrdU
text: Stem cells are proposed to differentiate by segregating their chromosomes asymmetrically during self-renewing divisions, retaining older DNA strands in daughter cells while newly synthesized strands go to differentiating cells. Stem cells are also thought to retain DNA labels, such as 5-bromo-2-deoxyuridine (BrdU), either due to asymmetric chromosome segregation or slow dividing. However, the purity of stem cells among BrdU-label-retaining cells has not been verified in any tissue, and the 'immortal strand hypothesis' remains untested in stem cells with known markers. To investigate, we analyzed haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in mice, which can be highly purified using well-characterized markers. We administered BrdU to newborn mice, mice treated with cyclophosphamide and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, and normal adult mice for 4 to 10 days followed by 70 days without BrdU. We found that less than 6% of HSCs retained BrdU, and less than 0.5% of all BrdU-retaining haematopoietic cells were HSCs, indicating that BrdU has poor specificity and sensitivity as an HSC marker. Subsequent administration of 5-chloro-2-deoxyuridine and 5-iodo-2-deoxyuridine showed that all HSCs segregate their chromosomes randomly. Furthermore, division of individual HSCs in culture revealed no asymmetric segregation of the label. These findings suggest that HSCs cannot be identified based on BrdU retention and do not retain older DNA strands during division, indicating that these properties are not general to stem cells.

title: Circadian Clocks in Human Red Blood Cells
text: The significance of circadian (approximately 24-hour) clocks in regulating coordinated physiological processes is evident across diverse organisms, including cyanobacteria and humans. All current models of the molecular circadian clockwork in eukaryotic cells rely on transcription-translation feedback loops. However, studying non-transcriptional mechanisms in the clockwork has been challenging in mammalian systems. To overcome these limitations, we developed innovative assays using human red blood cells, which lack a nucleus (and therefore DNA) and cannot perform transcription. Our findings demonstrate that transcription is not essential for circadian oscillations in humans, and that non-transcriptional events are sufficient to maintain cellular circadian rhythms. Using red blood cells, we discovered that peroxiredoxins, highly conserved antioxidant proteins, exhibit approximately 24-hour redox cycles that persist for several days under constant conditions. These rhythms are also entraINable (i.e., tunable by environmental stimuli) and temperature-compensated, hallmarks of circadian rhythms. Our discoveries will likely inform more sophisticated cellular clock models, illustrating the interconnectedness of transcriptional and non-transcriptional oscillations in potentially all eukaryotic cells.

title: G-protein-coupled receptor of Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus is a viral oncogene and angiogenesis activator.
text: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV/HHV8), a gamma-2 herpesvirus, has been implicated in the development of Kaposi's sarcoma and primary effusion B-cell lymphomas (PELs). KSHV infects malignant and progenitor cells of these diseases and encodes potential oncogenes that may contribute to their pathogenesis by stimulating angiogenesis. An open reading frame (ORF) 74 of KSHV encodes a G-protein-coupled receptor that is expressed in Kaposi's sarcoma lesions and PEL, and activates signaling pathways linked to cell proliferation in an agonist-independent manner. Here, we demonstrate that activation of this receptor leads to cell transformation and tumorigenicity, and induces a switch to an angiogenic phenotype by stimulating vascular endothelial growth factor and Kaposi's spindle cell growth factor. Furthermore, we show that this receptor can activate two protein kinases, JNK/SAPK and p38MAPK, by triggering signaling cascades similar to those induced by inflammatory cytokines that promote angiogenesis and cell growth in Kaposi's sarcoma cells and B cells. Overall, our findings indicate that the KSHV G-protein-coupled receptor is a viral oncogene that can exploit cell signaling pathways to induce transformation and angiogenesis in KSHV-mediated oncogenesis.

title: Therapeutic potential of GSK-J4, a histone demethylase KDM6B/JMJD3 inhibitor, for acute myeloid leukemia
text: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a complex and aggressive disease with poor prognosis. Despite growing evidence implicating disruptions in histone modification in AML, only a few drugs targeting specific histone modulators are used in clinical AML treatment. To investigate the therapeutic potential of targeting KDM6B, a demethylase responsible for tri-methylating histone H3 lysine 27 (H3K27me3), we examined the effects of the KDM6B-specific inhibitor, GSK-J4, in AML patient primary cells and cell lines. Our results showed increased KDM6B expression in AML, which was positively correlated with poor patient survival. Treatment with GSK-J4 elevated global H3K27me3 levels, decreased the proliferation and colony-forming ability of AML cells, and led to cell apoptosis and arrest in the Kasumi-1 cell line. In a human AML xenograft mouse model, GSK-J4 treatment attenuated disease progression. Compared to untreated cells, treatment with GSK-J4 resulted in down-regulation of genes involved in DNA replication and cell cycle progression, as well as abrogation of HOX gene expression, which are associated with AML progression. Chromatin immunoprecipitation-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (ChIP-qPCR) validated increased H3K27me3 enrichment at the transcription start sites of these HOX genes. In summary, our findings suggest that targeting KDM6B with GSK-J4 represents a potential therapeutic strategy for AML treatment.

title: Structure of the proton-gated urea channel from the gastric pathogen Helicobacter pylori
text:
Approximately half of the global population harbors Helicobacter pylori, an infectious agent responsible for gastritis, gastric ulcers, and an increased incidence of gastric adenocarcinoma. The proton-gated inner-membrane urea channel, HpUreI, is vital for the bacterium's survival in the acidic environment of the stomach. This channel is closed at neutral pH and opens at acidic pH, allowing for the rapid transport of urea into the cytoplasm via urease, which produces NH3 and CO2, thereby neutralizing incoming protons and maintaining a pH of roughly 6.1 within the periplasm, even in the face of gastric juice with a pH below 2.0.
We have recently elucidated the structure of HpUreI, revealing a hexameric ring assembly of six protomer units surrounding a central plug of ordered lipids. Each protomer encloses a channel formed by a twisted bundle of six transmembrane helices, defining a novel fold composed of a two-helix hairpin motif repeated three times along the central axis of the channel. The channel and protomer interfaces exhibit conserved residues within the AmiS/UreI superfamily, suggesting the maintenance of channel architecture and oligomeric state across this superfamily. Aromatic or aliphatic side chains line the entire channel, defining two consecutive constriction sites in the middle of the channel. Mutation of Trp 153 in the cytoplasmic constriction site to Ala or Phe reduces the selectivity for urea compared to thiourea, suggesting that the interaction of Trp 153 with solutes contributes to specificity.
Our discovery of the previously unobserved hexameric channel structure provides a new paradigm for the permeation of urea and other small amide solutes in prokaryotes and archaea. This work underscores the importance of investigating the structure and function of transmembrane proteins in order to gain a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying the survival of infectious agents in diverse environments.

title: Drosophila oocyte localization is mediated by differential cadherin-based adhesion.
text: In a Drosophila follicle, the oocyte is always located in the posterior position among a group of sixteen germline cells. Although the significance of this cell arrangement for the subsequent formation of the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo has been well-documented, the molecular mechanism responsible for the posterior localization of the oocyte remained unknown. Here, we provide evidence that the Homophilic adhesion molecule DE-cadherin mediates the oocyte's positioning. During follicle formation, DE-cadherin is expressed in both germline cells, including the oocyte, and surrounding follicle cells, with the highest concentration found at the interface between the oocyte and posterior follicle cells. Our findings suggest that both germline-soma interactions and DE-cadherin expression are required for correct oocyte localization, as demonstrated through mosaic analysis. By observing the behavior of the oocyte in follicles with a chimeric follicular epithelium, we found that the oocyte's position is directly determined by the position of DE-cadherin-expressing follicle cells, to which it selectively attaches itself. Among DE-cadherin-positive follicle cells, the oocyte preferentially contacts those cells expressing higher levels of DE-cadherin. Based on these results, we propose that in wild-type follicles, the oocyte competes successfully with its sister germline cells for contact with the posterior follicle cells, a sorting process driven by differential adhesion mediated by DE-cadherin. This is, to our knowledge, the first in vivo example of a cell-sorting process that relies on adhesion mediated by a cadherin.

title: Somatic sex identity is cell-autonomous in the chicken
text: In the mammalian model of sex determination, embryos are initially sexually undifferentiated until the temporary action of a sex-determining gene triggers gonadal differentiation. While this model is thought to apply to all vertebrates, its validity has yet to be verified. To investigate the sex-determining mechanism in birds, we examined three lateral gynandromorph chickens (a rare occurrence where one side of the animal appears male and the other female), which are genuine male:female chimaeras. These studies suggested that male and female avian somatic cells may have an innate sex identity. To test this hypothesis, we transplanted presumptive mesoderm between embryos of reciprocal sexes to create embryos with male:female chimaeric gonads. Unlike the outcome in mammalian mixed-sex chimaeras, where the donor cells are incorporated into the functional structures of the host gonad, in chicken mixed-sex chimaeras the donor cells were excluded from the host gonad. For example, when female tissue was transplanted into a male host, the donor cells retained a female identity and expressed a marker of female function. Our study demonstrates that avian somatic cells possess an inherent sex identity and that sexual differentiation in birds is cell autonomous.

title: Centrosome polarization delivers secretory granules to the immunological synapse
text: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) eliminate infected or malignant cells by releasing contents from specialized secretory lysosomes—known as 'lytic granules'—at the immunological synapse formed between the CTL and the target cell. Upon cell-cell contact, the microtubule organizing center of the CTL polarizes towards the target, and granules move along microtubules in a minus-end direction towards the polarized microtubule organizing center. The final stages of secretion were previously unclear. Our findings reveal that CTLs do not require actin or plus-end microtubule motors for secretion, and instead, the centrosome moves to and contacts the plasma membrane at the central supramolecular activation cluster of the immunological synapse. The actin and IQGAP1 are removed from the synapse, and granules are delivered directly to the plasma membrane. These data demonstrate that CTLs employ a previously unreported mechanism for delivering secretory granules to the immunological synapse, with granule secretion controlled by centrosome delivery to the plasma membrane.

title: Deubiquitination of p53 by HAUSP is an important pathway for p53 stabilization
text: The tumor suppressor protein p53 is a short-lived protein that is maintained at low levels in normal cells by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Mdm2, which targets p53 for ubiquitination and degradation. p53 stabilization is crucial for its tumor suppressor function, but the intricate mechanism by which ubiquitinated p53 levels are regulated in vivo remains unclear. Through mass spectrometry analysis of affinity-purified p53-associated factors, we discovered a novel p53-interacting protein called herpesvirus-associated ubiquitin-specific protease (HAUSP). HAUSP robustly stabilizes p53 even in the presence of excess Mdm2, and also triggers p53-dependent cell growth inhibition and apoptosis. Interestingly, HAUSP possesses intrinsic deubiquitination activity, which specifically removes ubiquitin from p53 both in vitro and in vivo.
