In contrast, expression of a mutant form of HAUSP that lacks enzymatic activity leads to increased p53 ubiquitination and destabilization. These findings reveal a crucial mechanism by which p53 can be stabilized through direct deubiquitination, and suggest that HAUSP may play a tumor suppressor role in vivo by stabilizing p53.

title: Defective tryptophan catabolism underlies inflammation in mouse chronic granulomatous disease
text: Fifty years ago, chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) was first identified as a fatal condition in children that impaired their ability to fight infections. Since then, significant breakthroughs have been made, including discoveries of insufficient white blood cell function and genetic abnormalities that contribute to the disease. Inherited disorder patients lack NADPH oxidase activity, which prevents them from producing reactive oxygen species, such as superoxide anion, making them particularly susceptible to recurring bacterial and fungal infections. Additionally, patients experience chronic inflammatory conditions and granuloma formation in internal organs. The underlying mechanisms of increased microbial virulence and exacerbated inflammatory responses were previously unknown, but we have found that a superoxide-dependent step in the kynurenine pathway of tryptophan metabolism is blocked in CGD mice, resulting in uncontrolled Vγ1+ γδ T-cell activity, excessive production of interleukin (IL)-17, impaired regulatory T-cell function, and acute inflammatory lung injury. Although neutralizing IL-17 or reducing γδ T-cell numbers offers some benefits, complete recovery and reversal of the hyperinflammatory phenotype are achieved through the administration of a natural kynurenine compound downstream of the blockade in the pathway. Effective treatment also involves co-administering recombinant interferon-γ (IFN-γ), which restores production of downstream immunoactive metabolites and enables the emergence of regulatory Vγ4+ γδ and Foxp3+ αβ T cells. Remarkably, the lack of reactive oxygen species actually contributes to the hyperinflammatory phenotype associated with NADPH oxidase deficiencies through a dysfunctional kynurenine pathway of tryptophan catabolism. However, reactivating this pathway downstream of the superoxide-dependent step can reverse this condition.

title: Experimental and theoretical study of mitotic spindle orientation
text: The microenvironment of a cell and its adhesiveness play a crucial role in the regulation of spindle orientation in living organisms. By combining theoretical and experimental approaches, we have investigated spindle orientation in HeLa (human) cells. Our findings reveal that spindle orientation can be understood as a result of the interactions between cortical force generators and spindle microtubules, which are activated by cortical cues. We develop a simple physical model to describe this spindle mechanics, enabling us to calculate the angular profiles of the torque acting on the spindle and the angular distribution of spindle orientations. Our model account for the preferred spindle orientation and the full angular distribution of spindle orientations observed in various cellular microenvironment geometries. Additionally, it accurately describes asymmetric spindle orientations observed under specific distributions of cortical cues. Our study demonstrates that, under a few simple assumptions, a quantitative description of spindle orientation can be provided for adherent cells.

title: CHROMOTHRIPSIS FROM DNA DAMAGE IN MICRONUCLEI
text:
Recent advances in genome sequencing have unveiled an intriguing genomic phenomenon, termed chromothripsis, in both cancer and congenital disorders. Chromothripsis characteristically exhibits extensive genomic rearrangements and a distinctive oscillating pattern of DNA copy number levels, all confined to a limited number of chromosomes. While the underlying mechanism of chromothripsis remains elusive, we previously proposed that it might arise from the physical segregation of chromosomes within aberrant nuclear structures termed micronuclei.
To investigate this hypothesis, we employed a combination of live cell imaging and single-cell genome sequencing. Our findings demonstrate that micronucleus formation can indeed give rise to a spectrum of genomic rearrangements, some of which recapitulate all the features of chromothripsis. These events are exclusive to the mis-segregated chromosome and occur within a single cell division. Furthermore, our experiments have shown that the mechanism of chromothripsis can involve the fragmentation and subsequent reassembly of a single chromatid from a micronucleus.
Collectively, these studies establish a previously unrecognized mutational process, with chromothripsis representing one of its extreme outcomes.

title: DNA-binding factors shape the mouse methylome at distal regulatory regions
text: Epigenetic methylation of cytosines is crucial in mammalian genomes, but the underlying rules are not yet fully understood. To gain insights, we generated high-resolution methylomes in mouse stem cells and neuronal progenitors. Advanced analytics revealed low-methylated regions (LMRs), accounting for approximately 30% of the methylome, which are predominantly found in CpG-poor distal regulatory areas. These regions are characterized by their location, DNase I hypersensitivity, and the presence of enhancer chromatin marks and enhancer activity in reporter assays. LMRs are occupied by DNA-binding factors, and their presence is necessary and sufficient to establish LMRs. Strikingly, cell-type-specific LMRs are also occupied by cell-type-specific transcription factors, as revealed by comparing methylomes from neurons and stem cells. This study provides a comprehensive reference methylome for mice and demonstrates that DNA-binding factors directly influence DNA methylation, allowing for the identification of active regulatory regions.

title: Molecular basis of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase II activity
text: RNA polymerase II (Pol II) is responsible for DNA-dependent RNA synthesis during transcription. However, recent findings suggest that Pol II also possesses intrinsic RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) activity. This means that Pol II can synthesize RNA molecules without the presence of DNA, using a homopolymeric RNA template or an RNA-DNA hybrid. Our study demonstrates the RdRP activity of Pol II using a pure polymerase, an RNA template-product scaffold, and nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs). Crystallography revealed the template-product duplex in the site occupied by the DNA-RNA hybrid during transcription. RdRP activity resides in the active site used during transcription, but it is slower and less processive than DNA-dependent activity. Remarkably, we were able to obtain RdRP activity using part of the hepatitis delta virus (HDV) antigenome. The presence of transcription factor IIS (TFIIS) with Pol II can cleave one HDV strand, create a reactive stem-loop in the hybrid site, and extend the new RNA 3' end. Short RNA stem-loops with a 5' extension are sufficient for activity, but their growth to a critical length appears to impair processivity. Our findings provide a fascinating insight into the evolution of Pol II, as they suggest that it may have evolved from an ancient RNA replicase that duplicated RNA genomes.

title: Bacteria activate sensory neurons that modulate pain and inflammation
text: Nociceptor sensory neurons are specifically designed to detect potential harmful stimuli, safeguarding the organism by triggering the sensation of pain and eliciting defensive behaviors. Bacterial infections produce pain through mysterious molecular mechanisms, although they are believed to be secondary to immune activation. Here, we provide evidence that bacteria directly activate nociceptors, and that the immune response mediated through TLR2, MyD88, T cells, B cells, and neutrophils and monocytes is not essential for Staphylococcus aureus-induced pain in mice. We found that mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia in mice are correlated with the number of live bacteria present, rather than tissue swelling or immune activation. Bacteria trigger changes in neuron calcium levels and action potentials, in part by using bacterial N-formylated peptides and the pore-forming toxin α-haemolysin through distinct mechanisms. Abolishing Nav1.8-lineage neurons, which include nociceptors, eliminated pain during bacterial infection, but this resulted in increased local immune infiltration and enlargement of the draining lymph node. This study reveals an unexpected role for the nervous system in host-pathogen interactions, demonstrating that bacterial pathogens produce pain by directly activating sensory neurons that modulate inflammation.

title: E2F1-3 Switch from Activators in Progenitor Cells to Repressors in Differentiating Cells
text: In the established model of mammalian cell cycle regulation, the retinoblastoma protein (Rb) functions to prevent cells from entering the S phase by binding and sequestering E2f activators (E2f1, E2f2, and E2f3), which are widely viewed as the ultimate effectors of a transcriptional program that drives cells to enter and progress through S phase. Using a panel of tissue-specific cre-transgenic mice and conditional E2f alleles, we investigated the effects of E2f1, E2f2, and E2f3 triples deficiency in murine embryonic stem cells, embryos, and small intestines. Our findings reveal that in normal progenitor cells, E2f1-3 functions as transcriptional activators, which is opposite to the current understanding. In contrast, E2f1-3 plays a crucial role in maintaining cell survival in proliferating cells rather than being essential for cell division. In differentiating cells, E2f1-3 works in conjunction with Rb to silence E2f-target genes and facilitate exit from the cell cycle. The depletion of Rb in differentiating cells leads to a switch in E2f1-3's function from repressors to activators, resulting in the uncontrolled activation of E2f-responsive genes and ectopic cell divisions. The loss of E2f1-3 completely abrogated these phenotypes caused by Rb deficiency, providing insight into the activator versus repressor functions of E2f1-3 in vivo. This study highlights two distinct roles for E2f1-3 in dividing versus differentiating cells and under normal versus cancer-like cell cycles.

title: K-Ras(G12C) inhibitors allosterically control GTP affinity and effector interactions
text:
K-Ras somatic mutations are the most prevalent oncogenic lesions in human cancer, often resulting in poor responsiveness to standard therapeutic approaches. The challenges in targeting this oncogene directly are attributed to its picomolar binding affinity for both GTP and GDP, as well as the lack of known allosteric regulatory sites. Oncogenic mutations in K-Ras lead to functional activation of Ras family proteins by impairing GTP hydrolysis, resulting in diminished regulation by GTPase activity. Consequently, the proportion of active GTP-bound Ras increases due to a higher affinity for GTP compared to GDP.
In this study, we report the development of small molecules that selectively bind to an oncogenic mutant form of K-Ras (G12C) without affecting the wild-type protein. Crystallographic analysis revealed the formation of a novel pocket beneath the effector binding switch-II region, which is unique to the mutant protein. The designed inhibitors bind to K-Ras(G12C) by exploiting this pocket, thereby disrupting both switch-I and switch-II regions. This results in a shift in the nucleotide preference from GTP to GDP and impairs binding to Raf. Our findings provide structure-based validation of a new allosteric regulatory site on K-Ras that can be specifically targeted in mutant forms of the protein.

title: Cyclin A Regulates Kinetochore-Microtubules to Promote Faithful Chromosome Segregation
text: The most conspicuous stage in cell division is metaphase, where chromosomes align and attach to spindle microtubules through bi-oriented kinetochore-microtubule (k-MT) connections. Attempts to attach correctly are impaired with early mitosis (prometaphase), which has led to the persistence chromosomal irregularities in aneuploid tumor cells that misplace entire chromosomes and display chromosomal instability. The means by which error correction is applied robustly in prometaphase to achieve error-free mitosis remain unknown. Our research shows that k-MT attachments are significantly less stable in prometaphase cells compared to those in metaphase. The switch towards more stable k-MT attachments in metaphase requires the degradation of cyclin A through the proteasome. Overexpression of cyclin A inhibits the stabilization of k-MTs even in aligned chromosomes, whereas their premature stabilization in cyclin-A-deficient cells results in higher rates of chromosome mis-segregation. As a result, the stability of k-MT attachments increases noticeably among all chromosomes as cells transition from prometaphase to metaphase. Cyclin A creates a cellular environment that promotes microtubule detachment from kinetochores in prometaphase to ensure faithful chromosome segregation and efficient error correction.

title: Induced pluripotent stem cells from a spinal muscular atrophy patient
text: Spinal muscular atrophy is one of the most common inherited forms of neurological disorders leading to infant mortality. Patients experience selective loss of lower motor neurons resulting in muscle weakness, paralysis, and eventually death. Although patient fibroblasts have been used extensively to research spinal muscular atrophy, motor neurons have a unique anatomy and physiology that may contribute to their vulnerability to the disease process. In this study, we generated induced pluripotent stem cells from skin fibroblast samples taken from a child with spinal muscular atrophy. These cells proliferated vigorously in culture, retained the disease genotype, and produced motor neurons exhibiting specific deficits compared to those derived from the child's unaffected mother. This is the first investigation to demonstrate the use of human induced pluripotent stem cells to model the specific pathology observed in a genetically inherited disease. As such, it represents a promising resource for exploring disease mechanisms, evaluating new drug candidates, and developing novel therapies.

title: A role for mitochondria in NLRP3 inflammasome activation
text: The NLRP3 inflammasome is triggered by a variety of host 'danger' signals, including infection and metabolic dysregulation. Prior studies suggested that NLRP3 inflammasome activity is negatively regulated by autophagy and positively regulated by reactive oxygen species (ROS) produced by an unknown organelle. Our findings show that blocking mitophagy/autophagy leads to the accumulation of damaged, ROS-generating mitochondria, which in turn activates the NLRP3 inflammasome. Resting NLRP3 localizes to endoplasmic reticulum structures, while on inflammasome activation both NLRP3 and its adaptor ASC redistribute to the perinuclear space where they co-localize with endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria organelle clusters. Interestingly, both ROS generation and inflammasome activation are suppressed when mitochondrial activity is impaired by inhibiting the voltage-dependent anion channel. This suggests that the NLRP3 inflammasome senses mitochondrial dysfunction and may help explain the frequent association of mitochondrial damage with inflammatory diseases.

title: Break-induced telomere synthesis underlies alternative telomere maintenance
text:
Homology-directed DNA repair is crucial for maintaining the genome's integrity through templated DNA synthesis. In certain types of human cancer, alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) relies on homology-directed DNA repair to maintain telomere length. Despite significant progress in understanding how DNA damage triggers DNA replication, the mechanisms that govern the assembly and execution of a DNA replication complex (break-induced replisome) at telomeres or other regions of the mammalian genome remain poorly understood.
In this study, we define break-induced telomere synthesis and demonstrate that it utilizes a specialized replisome, which underlies ALT telomere maintenance. When DNA undergoes double-strand breaks, it triggers unidirectional replication of telomeres through a long-tract process. The initial sensor of telomere damage is replication factor C (RFC), which loads proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA). This in turn triggers the predominance of DNA polymerase δ (Pol δ) through its POLD3 subunit. Breaking the template-dependent synthesis of telomeres requires RFC-mediated PCNA loading, but is independent of other replisome components, such as ATM and ATR, as well as the homologous recombination protein Rad51.
In summary, our findings show that the recognition of telomere damage by the break-induced replisome triggers homology-directed telomere maintenance. This inception of telomere damage recognition marks the beginning of a complex series of events that ultimately result in the proper maintenance of telomere length in the genome.

title: Innate immunity induced by composition-dependent RIG-I recognition of hepatitis C virus RNA
text: Innate immune defenses are crucial for controlling viral infections, and these defenses are triggered by the host recognition of viral molecular patterns known as pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is an RNA virus that affects approximately 200 million people globally. Infection is regulated by hepatic immune defenses activated by the cellular RIG-I helicase, which recognizes PAMP RNA by binding to it and signaling the activation of interferon regulatory factor 3. This leads to the expression of interferon-α/β and antiviral/interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), which restrict the virus's replication. We have identified the polyuridine motif in the 3' non-translated region of the HCV genome as the PAMP substrate of RIG-I and demonstrated that similar homopolyuridine or homopolyriboadenine motifs present in the genomes of RNA viruses are the main determinants of RIG-I recognition and immune activation in human and murine cells. The 5' terminal triphosphate on the PAMP RNA is necessary but not sufficient for RIG-I binding, which is primarily dependent on the homopolymeric ribonucleotide composition, linear structure, and length of the RNA motif. The HCV PAMP RNA stimulates RIG-I-dependent signaling in vivo, leading to a hepatic innate immune response, and triggers interferon and ISG expression in vitro, providing an effective means of suppressing HCV infection. These findings represent a significant advance by identifying specific homopolymeric RNA motifs within the genome of HCV and other RNA viruses as the PAMP substrate of RIG-I, and by demonstrating immunogenic features of the PAMP-RIG-I interaction that could be harnessed as an immune adjuvant for vaccine and immunotherapy approaches.

title: Generation of transgenic non-human primates with germline transmission
text:
The Callithrix jacchus, or common marmoset, is gaining popularity as a non-human primate model in biomedical research due to its relatively high reproductive rate. This makes it a promising candidate for genetic modification through transgenic technology. However, previous attempts to produce transgenic non-human primates have been met with limited success, with transgene expression largely restricted to the germline.
In this study, we successfully used lentiviral vectors in sucrose solution to introduce the transgene into marmoset embryos, resulting in transgenic offspring that expressed the transgene in various organs. What's more, we were able to transmit the transgene germline, ensuring that the transgenic offspring developed normally.
The creation of transgenic marmosets offers a valuable new animal model for studying human disease, thanks to their close genetic relationship with humans. This model will be particularly useful in many areas of biomedical research.

title: Induction of human neuronal cells by defined transcription factors
text: Somatic cell nuclear transfer, cell fusion, or the expression of lineage-specific factors have been shown to induce cell-fate changes in various somatic cell types. Recently, we observed that forcefully expressing a combination of three transcription factors, Brn2 (also known as Pou3f2), Ascl1, and Myt1l, can efficiently convert mouse fibroblasts into functional induced neuronal (iN) cells. In this study, we demonstrate that the same three factors can generate functional neurons from human pluripotent stem cells as early as 6 days after transgene activation. When combined with the basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor NeuroD1, these factors can also convert fetal and postnatal human fibroblasts into iN cells displaying typical neuronal morphologies and expressing multiple neuronal markers, even after downregulating the exogenous transcription factors. Most importantly, the vast majority of human iN cells are capable of generating action potentials and mature to form synaptic contacts when co-cultured with primary mouse cortical neurons. Our findings demonstrate that non-neural human somatic cells, as well as pluripotent stem cells, can be converted directly into neurons by lineage-determining transcription factors. These methods may provide a means for generating patient-specific human neurons for in vitro disease modeling or future applications in regenerative medicine.

title: PAAR-repeat proteins sharpen and diversify the Type VI secretion system spike
text:
The bacterial Type VI secretion system (T6SS) is a complex, dynamic machinery that plays a crucial role in the ecology of many Gram-negative bacteria. T6SS enables these bacteria to translocate a wide range of toxic effector molecules, allowing them to kill both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. The T6SS organelle is structurally similar to the contractile tails of bacteriophages, and it is thought to attack cells by first penetrating them with a trimeric protein complex called the VgrG spike. While the exact composition of the T6SS organelle and the mechanisms of effector selection and delivery are still unknown, our research has shed light on the role of a specific protein family: the PAAR (proline-alanine-alanine-arginine) repeat proteins.
We have discovered that PAAR proteins are essential for T6SS-mediated secretion and target cell killing in Vibrio cholerae and Acinetobacter baylyi. Using crystal structures of PAAR-repeat proteins bound to VgrG-like partners, we have shown that these proteins sharpen the tip of the T6SS spike complex. This sharp conical extension, we propose, plays a key role in attaching effector domains to the spike, allowing for simultaneous delivery of multiple toxins into target cells in a single contraction-driven translocation event.
Our findings offer a new model of the T6SS organelle, in which the VgrG-PAAR spike complex is decorated with multiple effectors that are delivered in a coordinated manner. This novel mechanism of multi-factorial secretion enables T6SS-harboring bacteria to exert a far greater toxic impact on their surroundings than was previously understood. The implications of these discoveries are significant, as they highlight the complexity and sophistication of the interactions between bacteria and their environment, and provide new avenues for exploring the mechanisms of bacterial virulence.

title: Replication stress activates DNA repair synthesis in mitosis
text: Oncogenes have been implicated as a driving force behind tumorigenesis by inducing DNA replication stress. Many chromosomal rearrangements characteristic of human cancers originate from specific regions of the genome called common fragile sites (CFSs). These sites are prone to gaps or breaks in the chromosomes during cell division, particularly when the cells have been exposed to replicative stress. The MUS81–EME1 structure-specific endonuclease plays a crucial role in the formation of chromosome gaps or breaks at CFSs following replicative stress. Our findings demonstrate that entry of cells into mitotic prophase leads to the recruitment of MUS81 to these sites. The nuclease activity of MUS81 then promotes POLD3-dependent DNA synthesis at CFSs, which in turn reduces the likelihood of chromosome mis-segregation and non-disjunction. We propose that the attempted condensation of incompletely duplicated loci in early mitosis serves as the trigger for completion of DNA replication at CFS loci in human cells. Interestingly, this POLD3-dependent mitotic DNA synthesis is more pronounced in aneuploid cancer cells that exhibit elevated levels of chromosomal instability (CIN+) and replicative stress. Targeting this pathway may represent a novel therapeutic strategy.

title: A specific amyloid-β protein assembly in the brain impairs memory
text: Memory function declines with age, and it is believed that this decline initially occurs due to changes in synaptic function rather than a loss of neurons. Some individuals go on to develop Alzheimer's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder, later in life. To investigate the cause of memory decline in the absence of neurodegeneration or amyloid-β protein accumulation, we used Tg2576 mice, which express a human amyloid-β precursor protein (APP) variant linked to Alzheimer's disease. Young Tg2576 mice have normal memory and lack neuropathology, while middle-aged mice (6-14 months old) exhibit memory deficits without any detectable loss of neurons. Older mice (>14 months old) show abundant neuritic plaques containing amyloid-β. We found that the memory deficits in middle-aged Tg2576 mice are caused by the extracellular accumulation of a 56-kDa soluble amyloid-β assembly, which we have termed Aβ*56 (Aβ star 56). Aβ*56 purified from the brains of impaired Tg2576 mice disrupts memory when administered to young rats. Based on our findings, we propose that Aβ*56 impairs memory independently of plaques or neuronal loss, and may play a role in cognitive deficits associated with Alzheimer's disease.

title: Cleavage of GSDMD by inflammatory caspases determines pyroptotic cell death
text:
Inflammatory caspases (caspase-1, -4, -5, and -11) play a crucial role in the innate immune response as they contribute to the activation of pyroptosis, a form of programmed cell death that occurs in response to infection. Despite their importance, the mechanism by which inflammatory caspases induce pyroptosis remained elusive. To investigate this, researchers performed genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 nuclease screens in mouse bone marrow macrophages to identify the factors responsible for pyroptosis induced by caspase-11 and caspase-1. The study identified gasdermin D (Gsdmd) as the key factor responsible for the induction of pyroptosis by inflammatory caspases.
Gsdmd-deficient cells were found to be resistant to the induction of pyroptosis by cytosolic lipopolysaccharide and known canonical inflammasome ligands. Additionally, interleukin-1β release was also diminished in Gsdmd-deficient cells, despite intact processing by caspase-1. The study revealed that caspase-1 and caspase-4/5/11 specifically cleaved the linker between the amino-terminal gasdermin-N and carboxy-terminal gasdermin-C domains in GSDMD, which was required and sufficient for pyroptosis. The cleavage released the intramolecular inhibition on the gasdermin-N domain, which showed intrinsic pyroptosis-inducing activity.
Other gasdermin family members were not cleaved by inflammatory caspases, but they shared the autoinhibition. Gain-of-function mutations in Gsdma3, which causes alopecia and skin defects, disrupted the autoinhibition, allowing the gasdermin-N domain to trigger pyroptosis. This study provides new insights into inflammasome-mediated immunity and disease and changes our understanding of pyroptosis and programmed necrosis.

title: Role of corin in trophoblast invasion and uterine spiral artery remodelling in pregnancy
text: During pregnancy, trophoblast invasion and uterine spiral artery remodeling are crucial for reducing maternal vascular resistance and increasing uteroplacental blood flow. Impaired spiral artery remodeling has long been associated with pre-eclampsia, a common pregnancy complication, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Corin (also known as atrial natriuretic peptide-converting enzyme) is a cardiac protease that activates atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), a hormone essential for regulating blood pressure. Surprisingly, corin is also expressed in the uterus during pregnancy. Here, we uncover a novel function of corin and ANP in promoting trophoblast invasion and spiral artery remodeling. We demonstrate that corin- or ANP-deficient mice exhibit high blood pressure and proteinuria, hallmarks of pre-eclampsia. In these mice, trophoblast invasion and uterine spiral artery remodeling were significantly impaired. Consistent with this, ANP potently stimulated human trophoblasts to invade Matrigel. In contrast, uterine Corin messenger RNA and protein levels were significantly lower in patients with pre-eclampsia compared to normal pregnancies. Moreover, we identified Corin gene mutations in pre-eclamptic patients, which decreased corin activity in processing pro-ANP. These findings suggest that corin and ANP are essential for the physiological changes at the maternal-fetal interface, and defects in their function may contribute to pre-eclampsia.

title: Metabolic rescue in pluripotent cells from patients with mtDNA disease
text:
Mitochondria play a crucial role in energy production through oxidative phosphorylation, which depends on the expression of essential genes encoded by mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). Mutations in mtDNA can lead to severe and debilitating disorders with limited treatment options. The clinical manifestations vary depending on the type of mutation and the degree of mtDNA mutation within each cell. Here, we generated genetically corrected pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) from patients with mtDNA disease using two different approaches: inducing pluripotency in patient fibroblasts and using somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) to replace the mutant mtDNA with wild-type mtDNA.
Isogenic iPS cell lines were generated from patients with common heteroplasmic mutations in mtDNA, including 3243A>G, which causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathy and stroke-like episodes (MELAS), and 8993T>G and 13513G>A, implicated in Leigh syndrome. These cell lines were generated by allowing the spontaneous segregation of heteroplasmic mtDNA in proliferating fibroblasts. By using SCNT, we were able to replace the mutant mtDNA in homoplasmic 8993T>G fibroblasts with wild-type mtDNA from a donor oocyte, resulting in corrected Leigh-NT1 PSCs. Although Leigh-NT1 PSCs had a different mtDNA haplotype than the patient, their transcriptomic profiles were similar to those of embryo-derived PSCs carrying wild-type mtDNA, indicating normal nuclear-to-mitochondrial interactions. In addition, genetically rescued patient PSCs displayed normal metabolic function compared to impaired oxygen consumption and ATP production observed in mutant cells. Overall, both reprogramming approaches offer complementary strategies for generating PSCs containing exclusively wild-type mtDNA, either through spontaneous segregation of heteroplasmic mtDNA in iPS cell lines or through mitochondrial replacement by SCNT in homoplasmic mtDNA-based disease.

title: The yeast Pif1p helicase removes telomerase from telomeric DNA
text: Telomeres are the physical ends of eukaryotic chromosomes, and genetic research has shown that the baker's yeast Pif1p DNA helicase can act as a negative regulator of telomerase, the specialized reverse transcriptase responsible for maintaining telomeric DNA. Despite this inhibition being well established, the underlying biochemical mechanisms remained unknown. Our study reveals that in vitro, Pif1p reduces the processivity of telomerase and releases it from telomeric oligonucleotides, resulting in enzymatically active released telomerase that can lengthen a challenging oligonucleotide. In vivo, overexpressing Pif1p leads to reduced telomerase association with telomeres, while depleting cells of Pif1p leads to increased telomere-bound Est1p, a telomerase subunit present on the telomere when telomerase is active. Based on these findings, we propose that Pif1p helicase activity limits telomerase action both in vitro and in vivo by displacing active telomerase from DNA ends.

title: Small regulatory RNAs inhibit RNA Polymerase II during the elongation phase of transcription
text: Eukaryotic cells harbor a diverse array of endogenous small regulatory RNAs that regulate various cellular processes, including heterochromatin formation, developmental timing, defense against parasitic nucleic acids, and genome rearrangement. Many of these small regulatory RNAs are thought to function within the nucleus. For instance, in plants and fungi, short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) associate with nascent transcripts and trigger chromatin and/or DNA modifications. To further elucidate the biological roles of small regulatory RNAs, we conducted a genetic screen to identify factors required for RNA interference (RNAi) in Caenorhabditis elegans nuclei. Here, we reveal that the gene nuclear RNAi defective-2 (nrde-2) encodes an evolutionarily conserved protein that is essential for siRNA-mediated silencing within nuclei. NRDE-2 interacts with the Argonaute protein NRDE-3 within nuclei and is recruited by NRDE-3/siRNA complexes to targeted nascent transcripts, leading to an NRDE-2-dependent silencing of pre-messenger RNAs (pre-mRNAs) 3' to sites of RNAi. Additionally, we observe an NRDE-2-dependent accumulation of RNA polymerase II (RNAP II) at genomic loci targeted by RNAi, as well as NRDE-2-dependent decreases in RNAP II occupancy and transcriptional activity 3' to sites of RNAi. These findings establish NRDE-2 as a component of the nuclear RNAi machinery and demonstrate that metazoan siRNAs can silence nuclear-localized RNAs co-transcriptionally. Furthermore, these results reveal a novel mechanism of RNAP II regulation, where siRNA-directed recruitment of NRDE factors inhibits RNAP II during the elongation phase of transcription.

title: Cdk1 is sufficient to drive the mammalian cell cycle
text: Unicellular organisms, such as yeast, need a single cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk1) to drive cell division. In contrast, mammalian cells are thought to require the coordinated activation of at least four other Cdks (Cdk2, Cdk3, Cdk4, and Cdk6) to progress through interphase and then mitosis. However, recent genetic evidence has challenged this model, showing that mice can survive without any individual interphase Cdks. Additionally, most mouse cell types can proliferate in the absence of two or even three interphase Cdks. Studies have also shown that ablation of some of the activating subunits of Cdks (D-type and E-type cyclins) leads to similar Results. Here, we demonstrate that mouse embryos lacking all interphase Cdks (Cdk2, Cdk3, Cdk4, and Cdk6) undergo organogenesis and development to midgestation. In these embryos, Cdk1 binds to all cyclins, leading to the phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein (pRb) and the expression of genes regulated by E2F transcription factors. Mouse embryonic fibroblasts derived from these embryos proliferate in vitro, although their cell cycle is extended due to inefficient inactivation of Rb proteins. However, they become immortal upon continuous passage. Moreover, embryos lacking Cdk1 fail to develop to the morula and blastocyst stages. These findings indicate that Cdk1 is the only essential cell cycle Cdk, and that it can execute all the events required to drive cell division in the absence of interphase Cdks.

title: Calorie restriction extends Saccharomyces cerevisiae lifespan by increasing respiration
text: Calorie restriction (CR) has been shown to extend the lifespan of a wide range of organisms, making it the only proven method to increase lifespan in mammals. To explore how CR works in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we established a model of CR in this system. Our findings show that limiting glucose or reducing the activity of the glucose-sensing cyclic-AMP-dependent kinase (PKA) can extend lifespan. However, lifespan extension in a mutant with reduced PKA activity requires the presence of Sir2 and NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide). In this study, we investigate how CR activates Sir2 to extend lifespan. Our results reveal that shifting carbon metabolism towards the mitochondrial tricarboxylic acid cycle and the subsequent increase in respiration play a central role in this process. These findings suggest that this metabolic strategy may be applicable to CR in animals.

title: Mosaic PPM1D mutations are associated with predisposition to breast and ovarian cancer
text: Advances in sequencing technologies have opened up new opportunities to investigate the role of rare genetic variations in the development of common diseases. However, challenges remain in study design, data analysis, and replication. By pooling next-generation sequencing data from 507 genes involved in DNA repair in 1,150 samples, and conducting a large-scale sequencing case–control replication study in 13,642 individuals, we found that rare protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in the gene encoding the p53-inducible protein phosphatase PPM1D are associated with an increased risk of breast and ovarian cancer. Specifically, we identified 25 PPM1D PTVs in 7,781 cancer cases compared to 1 PTV in 5,861 controls (P = 1.12 × 10−5), including 18 mutations in 6,912 individuals with breast cancer (P = 2.42 × 10−4) and 12 mutations in 1,121 individuals with ovarian cancer (P = 3.10 × 10−9). Notably, all of the identified PPM1D PTVs were mosaic in lymphocyte DNA and clustered within a 370-base-pair region in the final exon of the gene, carboxy-terminal to the phosphatase catalytic domain. Functional studies revealed that the mutations result in enhanced suppression of p53 in response to ionizing radiation exposure, suggesting that the mutant alleles encode hyperactive PPM1D isoforms. Our findings have implications for the detection and management of breast and ovarian cancer risk, and provide new insights into the role of rare and mosaic genetic variants in common conditions, as well as the use of sequencing in identifying these variants.

title: Immunogenicity of induced pluripotent stem cells
text: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), generated from somatic cells using specific factors, hold great promise for regenerative medicine as a self-renewing source of autologous cells. However, it was previously assumed that these autologous cells would be immune-tolerated by the recipient, without thorough examination of their immunogenicity. We investigate the immunogenicity of iPSCs in this study. We found that embryonic stem cells (ESCs) derived from inbred C57BL/6 (B6) mice can form teratomas in B6 mice without any evident immune rejection. In contrast, allogenic ESCs from 129/SvJ mice fail to form teratomas in B6 mice due to rapid rejection by recipients. We also experimented with reprogramming B6 mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) into iPSCs using either a retroviral approach (ViPSCs) or a novel episomal approach (EiPSCs) that does not integrate genomic material. Interestingly, teratomas formed by B6 ViPSCs were mostly immune-rejected by B6 recipients, and the majority of teratomas formed by B6 EiPSCs were immunogenic in B6 mice with T cell infiltration and apparent tissue damage and regression observed in a small fraction of teratomas. Global gene expression analysis of teratomas derived from B6 ESCs and EiPSCs revealed a number of genes frequently overexpressed in teratomas derived from EiPSCs, and several of these gene products were shown to contribute directly to the immunogenicity of the B6 EiPSC-derived cells in B6 mice. These findings suggest that the immunogenicity of therapeutically valuable cells derived from patient-specific iPSCs should be evaluated before any clinical application of these autologous cells into humans.

title: Direct conversion of human fibroblasts to multilineage blood progenitors
text: Application of reprogrammed human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) is limited by our understanding of lineage specification, similar to embryo-derived stem cells. However, recent studies have shown the ability to generate progenitors and mature cells of the haematopoietic fate directly from human dermal fibroblasts without establishing pluripotency. By ectopically expressing OCT4 (also called POU5F1)-activated haematopoietic transcription factors and specific cytokine treatment, researchers were able to generate cells expressing the pan-leukocyte marker CD45. These unique fibroblast-derived cells gave rise to granulocytic, monocytic, megakaryocytic, and erythroid lineages, and demonstrated in vivo engraftment capacity. Notably, adult haematopoietic programs were activated, indicating that the fibroblasts were redirected to give rise to blood cells without activating embryonic programs. This is distinct from haematopoiesis involving pluripotent stem cells, where embryonic programs are activated. These findings demonstrate the restoration of multipotency from human fibroblasts and suggest an alternative approach to cellular reprogramming for autologous cell-replacement therapies that avoids complications associated with the use of human pluripotent stem cells.

title: Mical links semaphorins to F-actin disassembly
text:
The mechanisms by which instructive cues on the cell surface regulate the actin cytoskeleton are not well understood. Semaphorins, a large family of such cues, have been studied for their role in cell movement, navigation, angiogenesis, immunology, and cancer. However, the molecular links between semaphorins and the precise control of actin cytoskeletal elements remain unclear. Recently, highly unusual proteins called Mical enzymes have been found to associate with plexin receptors on the cell surface and mediate axon guidance, synaptogenesis, dendritic pruning, and other cell morphological changes. Mical enzymes perform redox reactions and contain domains involved in cell morphology regulation, but their role in mediating morphological changes is unknown.
Here, we demonstrate that Mical directly links semaphorins and plexin receptors to the precise control of actin filament dynamics. We show that Mical is both necessary and sufficient for semaphorin-plexin-mediated F-actin reorganization in vivo and in vitro. Moreover, we find that Mical binds F-actin directly and disassembles both individual and bundled actin filaments. Our results also indicate that Mical utilizes its redox activity to alter F-actin dynamics in vivo and in vitro, revealing a previously unknown role for specific redox signaling events in actin cytoskeletal regulation. Therefore, Mical functions as a novel F-actin-disassembly factor that provides a molecular conduit through which actin reorganization—a hallmark of cell morphological changes—can be precisely achieved spatiotemporally in response to semaphorins.

title: Novel Foxo1-dependent transcriptional programs control Treg cell function
text: Regulatory T cells (Tregs), identified by Foxp3 expression, maintain immune homeostasis by suppressing self-destructive immune responses. Foxp3 acts as a late-stage differentiation factor, regulating Treg cell homeostasis and function, while the early Treg-cell lineage commitment is regulated by the Akt kinase and the Foxo family of transcription factors. However, the extent to which Foxo proteins influence Treg cell homeostasis and function beyond the commitment stage remains largely unexplored. Our study reveals that Foxo1 is a crucial regulator of Treg cell function. Treg cells exhibit high levels of Foxo1 and display reduced T-cell receptor-induced Akt activation, Foxo1 phosphorylation, and Foxo1 nuclear exclusion. Mice lacking Treg-cell-specific Foxo1 develop a fatal inflammatory disorder similar to that observed in Foxp3-deficient mice, but without the loss of Treg cells. Genome-wide analysis of Foxo1 binding sites reveals around 300 Foxo1-bound target genes, including the pro-inflammatory cytokine IFNG, which do not appear to be directly regulated by Foxp3. These findings demonstrate that the evolutionarily ancient Akt-Foxo1 signaling module controls a novel genetic program essential for Treg cell function.

title: Functional screening identifies miRNAs inducing cardiac regeneration
text:
In mammals, the growth of the heart during embryonic development is primarily dependent on an increase in the number of cardiomyocytes. Once born, however, these cardiomyocytes cease to proliferate, leading to limited growth of the myocardium through hypertrophic enlargement of existing myocytes. Our study shows that the administration of selected microRNAs (miRNAs) significantly stimulates cardiomyocyte proliferation and promotes cardiac repair.
Using a whole-genome miRNA library, we conducted a high-content microscopy, high-throughput functional screening to identify human miRNAs that promote neonatal cardiomyocyte proliferation. We found that forty miRNAs strongly increased both DNA synthesis and cytokinesis in neonatal mouse and rat cardiomyocytes. Two of these miRNAs, hsa-miR-590 and hsa-miR-199a, were selected for further testing and were shown to promote cell cycle re-entry of adult cardiomyocytes ex vivo and cardiomyocyte proliferation in both neonatal and adult animals. In mice with myocardial infarction, these miRNAs stimulated marked cardiac regeneration and almost complete recovery of cardiac functional parameters. The miRNAs identified have great potential for treating cardiac pathologies resulting from cardiomyocyte loss.

title: Specificity of sensory–motor connections encoded by Sema3e–Plxnd1 recognition
text:
Spinal reflexes are mediated by neural connections between sensory afferents and motor neurons. These circuits demonstrate multiple levels of specificity, with only certain classes of proprioceptive sensory neurons forming direct, monosynaptic connections with motor neurons. These connections are governed by specific rules within the motor pool, meaning that sensory neurons form strong connections with motor neurons that supply the same muscle while avoiding those that supply opposing muscles. This pattern of connectivity is initially established accurately, and this is maintained even in the absence of activity, suggesting that the specificity of wiring relies on the matching of recognition molecules on the surfaces of sensory and motor neurons. However, the specific determinants of fine synaptic specificity in these reflex circuits remain unresolved.
To investigate the origins of synaptic specificity in these reflex circuits, we employed molecular genetic techniques to manipulate recognition proteins expressed by specific subsets of sensory and motor neurons. Our findings reveal that a recognition system involving the expression of class 3 semaphorin Sema3e by select motor neuron pools and its high-affinity receptor plexin D1 (Plxnd1) by proprioceptive sensory neurons is a critical determinant of synaptic specificity in sensory-motor circuits in mice. Altering the profile of Sema3e-Plxnd1 signaling in sensory or motor neurons results in functional and anatomical rewiring of monosynaptic connections, without affecting motor pool specificity. Our data suggest that the patterns of monosynaptic connectivity in this prototypical central nervous system circuit are constructed through a recognition program based on repellent signaling.

title: A chromatin remodelling complex involved in transcription and DNA processing.
text: The packaging of eukaryotic genomes within chromatin creates barriers that hinder the access of enzymes that process DNA. To overcome these barriers, cells contain multiple protein complexes called chromatin remodelling complexes, each consisting of an ATPase subunit from the SNF2/SWI2 superfamily. These complexes increase nucleosome mobility and are closely linked to transcription. In this study, we analyzed SNF2/SWI2- and ISWI-related proteins to identify remodelling complexes that may assist other DNA transactions. We purified a complex from Saccharomyces cerevisiae containing the Ino80 ATPase. The INO80 complex contains approximately 12 polypeptides, including two proteins related to the bacterial RuvB DNA helicase, which catalyzes branch migration of Holliday junctions. The purified complex remodels chromatin, facilitates transcription in vitro, and exhibits 3' to 5' DNA helicase activity. Mutants of ino80 display hypersensitivity to agents that cause DNA damage, in addition to defects in transcription. These findings suggest that chromatin remodelling driven by the Ino80 ATPase may be linked to both transcription and DNA damage repair.

title: Oncogenic pathway signatures in human cancers as a guide to targeted therapies
text: The complex process of developing an oncogenic state involves the accumulation of multiple mutations that disrupt cell signaling pathways crucial to cell growth and fate control. Research has demonstrated the potential of DNA microarray-based gene expression signatures for identifying cancer subtypes, recurrence, and responses to therapies. Studies have also shown the utility of gene expression profiles in analyzing oncogenic pathways. Here, we investigate gene expression signatures that reflect oncogenic pathway activation. These signatures are validated across multiple human cancer datasets and demonstrate associations with disease outcomes and clinically relevant patterns of pathway deregulation. Combining signatures across multiple pathways reveals coordinated patterns of pathway deregulation that distinguish specific cancers and subtypes. Clustering tumors based on pathway signatures accurately predicts prognosis in respective patient subsets, highlighting the pivotal role of oncogenic pathway deregulation in cancer development and progression. Additionally, predictions of pathway deregulation in cancer cell lines can predict sensitivity to therapeutic agents targeting pathway components. This linkage provides a means to utilize oncogenic pathway signatures in guiding targeted therapy.

title: CTCF mediates methylation-sensitive enhancer-blocking activity at the H19/Igf2 locus.
text:
The Insulin-like growth factor 2 (Igf2) and H19 genes are imprinted, resulting in the silencing of the maternal and paternal alleles, respectively. This process depends on an imprinted-control region located two kilobases upstream of H19 ( references 1, 2). On the paternal chromosome, this element is methylated, leading to the silencing of H19 ( references 2-4). In contrast, on the maternal chromosome, the region remains unmethylated, resulting in the silencing of the Igf2 gene located 90 kilobases upstream ( references 5, 6).
We previously proposed that the unmethylated imprinted-control region serves as a chromatin boundary that blocks the interaction of Igf2 with enhancers located 3' of H19 ( references 5, 6). This enhancer-blocking activity is lost when the region is methylated, allowing paternal expression of Igf2.
In this study, using transgenic mice and tissue culture, we demonstrate that the unmethylated imprinted-control regions from mouse and human H19 possess enhancer-blocking activity. Notably, we find that the zinc finger protein CTCF binds to several sites within the unmethylated imprinted-control region, and its binding is abolished by DNA methylation. This is the first example, to our knowledge, of a regulated chromatin boundary in vertebrates.

title: Broad and potent neutralization of HIV-1 by a gp41-specific human antibody
text: Characterization of human monoclonal antibodies has yielded significant insights into the mechanisms of broad HIV-1 neutralization. In this study, we report an HIV-1 gp41 membrane-proximal external region (MPER)-specific antibody, designated 10E8, which demonstrates neutralizing activity against >98% of tested viruses. An evaluation of serum samples from 78 healthy HIV-1-infected individuals revealed that approximately one-quarter of these samples contained MPER-specific antibodies, while approximately 8% demonstrated 10E8-like specificities. In contrast to other neutralizing MPER antibodies, 10E8 demonstrated a unique binding profile, showing no affinity for phospholipids and lacking autoreactivity. Additionally, 10E8 bound to the cell-surface envelope of HIV-1 without the need for phospholipid spacing. Using X-ray crystallography, we identified a specific site of vulnerability on the MPER, comprising a narrow stretch of highly conserved gp41-hydrophobic residues and a critical arginine or lysine residue in the immediate proximity of the transmembrane region. Analyses of resistant HIV-1 variants confirmed the importance of these residues for neutralization. Our findings highlight the highly conserved MPER as a target for potent, non-self-reactive neutralizing antibodies, underscoring the need for HIV-1 vaccine strategies to focus on eliciting antibodies against this region of the HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein.

title: Disruption of the Hepcidin/Ferroportin Regulatory System Causes Pulmonary Iron Overload and Restrictive Lung Disease
text: Recent research suggests that excess iron accumulation in the lungs may play a role in a range of chronic respiratory diseases. However, the exact mechanisms behind this process and its impact on lung function are still unclear. To investigate, we examined mice with a specific genetic mutation that affects iron metabolism. We found that these mice had higher levels of iron in lung cells, including alveolar macrophages, epithelial cells lining the airways, and vascular smooth muscle cells. Notably, this increased iron levels were associated with oxidative stress, restrictive lung disease, and decreased total lung capacity compared to normal mice. These findings suggest that iron may play a role in lung pathology, which has not been previously considered a classical iron-related disorder.

title: Genome-wide genetic analysis of polyploidy in yeast
text: Polyploidy, or the presence of additional sets of chromosomes, occurs during development, cellular stress, disease, and evolution. Despite its prevalence, little is known about the physiological changes that accompany polyploidy. Previously, we described "ploidy-specific lethality," where a gene deletion that is not lethal in haploid or diploid budding yeast becomes lethal in triploids or tetraploids. In this study, we conducted a genome-wide screen to identify ploidy-specific lethal functions. We found that only 39 of 3,740 mutations screened exhibited ploidy-specific lethality, and almost all of these mutations affected genomic stability by impairing homologous recombination, sister chromatid cohesion, or mitotic spindle function. We discovered defects in wild-type tetraploids predicted by the screen, and uncovered mechanisms by which tetraploidization affects genomic stability. We found that tetraploids have a high incidence of syntelic/monopolar kinetochore attachments to the spindle pole, which can be explained by mismatches in the ability to scale the size of the spindle pole body, spindle, and kinetochores. These findings suggest that geometric constraints may have profound effects on genome stability, and this phenomenon may be relevant in a variety of biological contexts, including disease states such as cancer.

title: Diverse and heritable lineage imprinting of early haematopoietic progenitors
text:
The production of blood cells by haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and their progenitors is a subject of ongoing debate, with various models suggesting different paths of cellular differentiation. However, many of these models rely on in vitro clonal assays and population-based tracking in vivo, which may overlook the complex single-cell dynamics present in vivo. To address this limitation, we employ a novel version of 'cellular barcoding' to trace the in vivo fate of hundreds of LMPPs (lymphoid-primed multipotent progenitors) and HSCs at the single-cell level.
Our findings reveal that LMPPs are heterogeneous in the types of blood cells they produce, with some cells preferentially generating lymphoid, myeloid, or dendritic cells. On the other hand, although there is a known lineage bias among some HSCs, most of the cellular output is derived from a small number of HSCs that generate all cell types. Interestingly, when we analyze the output of sibling cells derived from individual LMPPs, we find that they often have similar fates, suggesting that the fate of these progenitors is imprinted early on. Additionally, this imprinting is also observed in dendritic-cell-biased LMPPs, which suggests that dendritic cells may be considered a distinct lineage with their own unique ancestry.
Our data support the idea of a 'graded commitment' model of haematopoiesis, in which heritable and diverse lineage imprinting occurs earlier than previously thought. In this model, HSCs gradually commit to specific lineages during their development, leading to a more diverse range of cellular outputs. Overall, our findings provide new insights into the complex process of blood cell differentiation and highlight the importance of single-cell analysis in understanding the mechanisms of haematopoiesis.

title: Crowding induces live cell extrusion to maintain homeostatic cell numbers in epithelia
text:
For an epithelium to maintain a protective barrier, it must strike a balance between cell division and cell death. Although compensatory cell division can occur in response to cell death, the mechanism by which cell death relieves overcrowding caused by proliferation is unknown. When we induce apoptosis in epithelial cells, dying cells are shed to preserve the barrier. This process involves dying cells signaling to surrounding cells to contract an actomyosin ring that expels the dying cell. However, it remains unclear what drives cell death during normal homeostasis.
We have found in human, canine, and zebrafish cells that overcrowding caused by proliferation and migration leads to the extrusion of live cells to regulate epithelial cell numbers. This process occurs at sites of highest crowding in vivo and can be induced by overcrowding monolayers in vitro. Unlike apoptotic cell extrusion, which requires sphingosine 1-phosphate signaling and Rho-kinase-dependent myosin contraction, live cell extrusion resulting from overcrowding utilizes stretch-activated channel signaling. Moreover, disrupting a stretch-activated channel, Piezo1, in zebrafish prevents extrusion and leads to the formation of epithelial cell masses.
Our findings indicate that during homeostatic turnover, the growth and division of epithelial cells on a confined substratum can cause overcrowding, leading to their extrusion and subsequent death due to the loss of survival factors. These results suggest that live cell extrusion may function as a tumour-suppressive mechanism to prevent the accumulation of excess epithelial cells.

title: Direct observation of ligand recognition by T cells
text: The activation of T cells through the interaction of their T-cell receptors with antigenic peptides bound to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on the surface of antigen-presenting cells (APCs) is a critical step in the adaptive immune system. In this study, we utilize three-dimensional fluorescence microscopy to visualize individual peptide-MHC complexes labeled with the phycobiliprotein phycoerythrin in an effort to investigate T-cell sensitivity and the requirements for forming an immunological synapse in single cells. We find that T cells expressing the CD4 antigen exhibit transient calcium signaling in response to even a single agonist peptide-MHC ligand, and that the organization of molecules in the contact zone of the T cell and APC assumes the characteristics of an immunological synapse when approximately ten agonists are present. This sensitivity is highly dependent on CD4, as blocking this molecule with antibodies renders T cells unable to detect fewer than approximately 30 ligands.

title: Crypt stem cells as the cells-of-origin of intestinal cancer
text: Intestinal cancer begins with mutations in genes such as adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) in the Wnt signaling pathway. However, the original cell of cancer origin remains unclear in most cases. To investigate this, we established a tamoxifen-inducible Cre recombinase mouse model expressing this gene in long-lived intestinal stem cells. We found that deleting the Apc gene in these stem cells leads to their transformation within days, resulting in the formation of microadenomas at the base of the intestinal crypts. These microadenomas show unimpeded growth and can develop into macroscopic adenomas within 3-5 weeks, while maintaining a stem cell/progenitor cell hierarchy in early neoplastic lesions. Interestingly, when Apc is deleted in short-lived transit-amplifying cells using a different Cre mouse strain, the induced microadenomas fail to grow rapidly and remain small even after 30 weeks. This suggests that stem cell-specific loss of Apc leads to progressive growth of neoplastic lesions.

title: Microbial engineering for the production of advanced biofuels
text: Advanced biofuels produced through microbial engineering have similar characteristics to traditional petroleum-based fuels and can seamlessly integrate into existing transportation infrastructure. However, significantly increasing biofuel production requires meticulous manipulation of the microorganism's metabolic pathways, a task that cannot be achieved through a single feedstock or host organism. To enhance fuel production, data-driven and synthetic biology approaches can be leveraged to optimize both the host organism and metabolic pathways. Although there have been some notable achievements, further challenges must be addressed to transition advanced biofuels towards commercialization and to compete with more conventional energy sources.

title: Sperm chromatin proteomics identifies evolutionarily conserved fertility factors
text:
Male infertility has long been a medical enigma of significant concern. The stability of sperm chromatin is a crucial indicator of male fertility and IVF potential, and abnormalities in chromosome number or DNA structure can lead to reproductive failure. By identifying conserved proteins crucial for sperm chromatin organization, we can uncover universal causes of infertility.
To achieve this, we combined proteomics, cytology, and functional analysis in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Our multi-step approach involved purifying chromatin from comparable meiotic cell types, such as those undergoing spermatogenesis or oogenesis, and performing proteomic analysis using multidimensional protein identification technology (MudPIT). We then prioritized sperm proteins based on abundance and subtracted common proteins to eliminate general chromatin and meiotic factors.
Our approach identified 132 proteins essential for fertility, including conserved spermatogenesis-specific proteins that play vital roles in DNA compaction, chromosome segregation, and fertility. Unexpectedly, factors involved in other processes also showed important roles in spermatogenesis. By Knocking out corresponding mouse genes for nematode proteins, we found that 37% (7/19) caused male sterility, providing significant opportunities for identifying causes of male infertility and potential targets for male contraceptives. Our list offers valuable insights into the mechanisms of male fertility and the potential for identifying novel therapeutic targets for male infertility.

title: Nanog safeguards pluripotency and mediates germline development
text: Nanog is a unique homeodomain protein found in mammalian pluripotent cells and developing germ cells. Deletion of Nanog results in embryonic lethality, while constant expression allows for autonomous self-renewal of embryonic stem cells. Nanog is therefore considered a central component of the pluripotent transcriptional network. However, our findings reveal that Nanog fluctuates in mouse embryonic stem cells. Transient downregulation of Nanog appears to predispose cells towards differentiation, but does not indicate commitment. Through genetic deletion, we demonstrate that, although they are prone to differentiate, embryonic stem cells can self-renew indefinitely in the absence of Nanog. Interestingly, expanded Nanog-null cells colonize embryonic germ layers and exhibit multilineage differentiation in both fetal and adult chimaeras. Moreover, these cells are also recruited to the germ line, but primordial germ cells lacking Nanog fail to mature by reaching the genital ridge. This defect is rescued by repair of the mutant allele. Our findings suggest that Nanog plays a critical role in constructing inner cell mass and germ cell states, rather than in the housekeeping machinery of pluripotency. We propose that Nanog stabilizes embryonic stem cells in culture by countering or reversing alternative gene expression states.

title: Succinate is an inflammatory signal that induces IL-1β through HIF-1α
text: Macrophages activated by Gram-negative bacterial products undergo a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis upon the activation of lipopolysaccharide. Our study shows that inhibiting glycolysis using 2-deoxyglucose reduces lipopolysaccharide-induced interleukin-1β production but not tumor-necrosis factor-α in mouse macrophages. A comprehensive metabolic map of lipopolysaccharide-activated macrophages reveals upregulation of glycolytic genes and downregulation of mitochondrial genes, which corresponds to the expression profiles of altered metabolites. Lipopolysaccharide significantly increases the levels of the tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate succinate, with glutamine-dependent anaplerosis as the primary source. The 'GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid) shunt' pathway also contributes to succinate production. Lipopolysaccharide-induced succinate stable hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, an effect that is inhibited by 2-deoxyglucose, with interleukin-1β as a key target. Additionally, lipopolysaccharide increases succinylation of several proteins, highlighting succinate's role as a signaling metabolite in the innate immune response. Our findings demonstrate succinate's crucial role in enhancing interleukin-1β production during inflammation.

title: Planar cell polarity signalling couples cell division and morphogenesis during neurulation
text: Abnormalities in the environment and genetics can lead to defects in the closure of the neural tube during fetal development, occurring in approximately 1 out of every 1,000 births. Studies in mouse and frog models have suggested that Van Gogh-like 2 (Vangl2), a protein involved in planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling, may play a crucial role in controlling neurulation by promoting the convergence of neural progenitors towards the midline. In this study, we investigate the novel role of PCP signaling in neurulation in zebrafish. We find that non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling polarizes neural progenitors along the anteroposterior axis during neurulation. This polarity is temporarily lost during cell division in the neural keel, but is re-established as daughter cells reintegrate into the neuroepithelium. Mutations in zebrafish Vangl2 (trilobite mutants) result in the loss of neural keel cell polarity, disruption of re-integration of daughter cells, and the accumulation of ectopic neural progenitors, leading to neural tube defects (NTDs). Remarkably, blocking cell division leads to the rescue of trilobite neural tube morphogenesis, despite persistent defects in convergence and extension. These findings reveal a function for PCP signaling in coupling cell division and morphogenesis during neurulation and highlight an unrecognized mechanism that may contribute to NTDs.

title: The challenge of new drug discovery for tuberculosis
text: Tuberculosis (TB), now more prevalent than ever before in human history, is caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis pathogen, which employs diverse strategies to survive and evade immune detection within various host tissues. The urgent need to develop new TB drugs has been exacerbated by the emergence of multi-drug-resistant strains of M. tuberculosis, making it essential to re-examine and reposition established drug families to combat the disease effectively. Moreover, a proper understanding of the intricate interactions between the pathogen and its human host is crucial to determining the success of any drug discovery and development strategies. In this review, we delve into cutting-edge TB drug innovations and evolving strategies to accelerate the delivery of newer agents to patients in need.

title: Subunit Arrangement and Phenylethanolamine Binding in GluN1/GluN2B NMDA Receptors
text: Since the discovery that the anti-hypertensive agent ifenprodil has neuroprotective effects by modulating NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptors, researchers have made concerted efforts to elucidate the underlying mechanism of action and develop improved therapeutic compounds based on this knowledge. Neurotransmission mediated by NMDA receptors is crucial for proper brain development and function, and these receptors are comprised of heteromeric ion channels that are activated by the concurrent binding of glycine and glutamate to the GluN1 and GluN2 subunits, respectively. The allosteric regulation of NMDA receptor ion-channel activity by small molecules binding to the amino-terminal domain (ATD) in a subtype-specific manner has been identified as a key feature of these receptors. Ifenprodil and related phenylethanolamine compounds, which specifically inhibit GluN1 and GluN2B NMDA receptors, have been intensively studied for their potential therapeutic applications in various neurological disorders and diseases, including depression, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease. However, the structural basis for the recognition of these compounds and the allosteric inhibition they exert remains largely unexplored due to a lack of detailed structural information. Here, we provide an explanation for the recognition of phenylethanolamines at the interface between GluN1 and GluN2B subunits, rather than within the GluN2B cleft, and reveal the molecular determinants of phenylethanolamine binding through the crystal structure of the heterodimer formed between the GluN1b ATD from Xenopus laevis and the GluN2B ATD from Rattus norvegicus. Additionally, we demonstrate that restrictions on domain movement in the bi-lobed structure of the GluN2B ATD can significantly diminish sensitivity to ifenprodil, highlighting the importance of conformational freedom in the GluN2B ATD for allosteric inhibition of NMDA receptors. These findings pave the way for the development of improved, subtype-specific compounds with therapeutic potential for neurological disorders and diseases.

title: Association of NOD2 leucine-rich repeat variants with susceptibility to Crohn's disease.
text: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, the two main types of chronic inflammatory bowel disease, are complex conditions with unknown origins. Recently, a genetic susceptibility locus for Crohn's disease has been mapped to chromosome 16. To identify the specific genetic variations responsible for the disease, we employed a positional-cloning strategy that incorporates linkage analysis and linkage disequilibrium mapping. Our study found three independent associations between Crohn's disease and genetic variations in the NOD2 gene. These variations include a frameshift variant and two missense variants, which respectively affect the leucine-rich repeat domain and the adjacent region of the NOD2 protein. The NOD2 protein plays a crucial role in activating nuclear factor NF-kB, and its activity is regulated by the carboxy-terminal leucine-rich repeat domain, which inhibits NF-kB activation. Our findings suggest that genetic variations in NOD2 may contribute to the susceptibility of Crohn's disease by altering the recognition of pathogenic components or over-activating NF-kB in monocytes, providing a molecular framework for the pathogenesis of the disease. Further investigation along this line may reveal new therapeutic targets for Crohn's disease.

title: Human cardiovascular progenitor cells develop from a KDR+ embryonic-stem-cell-derived population
text: The functional heart is composed of distinct mesoderm-derived lineages, including cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells. Studies in the mouse embryo and mouse embryonic stem cell differentiation model have shown that these three lineages originate from a common Flk-1+ (kinase insert domain protein receptor, also known as Kdr) cardiovascular progenitor, which represents one of the earliest stages in mesoderm specification to the cardiovascular lineages. To investigate whether a similar progenitor exists during human cardiogenesis, we analyzed the development of cardiovascular lineages in human embryonic stem cell differentiation cultures. Our findings demonstrate that after induction with a combination of activin A, bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4), basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF, also known as FGF2), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF, also known as VEGFA), and dickkopf homolog 1 (DKK1) in serum-free media, human embryonic stem-cell-derived embryoid bodies generate a KDRlow/C-KIT(CD117)neg population that displays cardiac, endothelial, and vascular smooth muscle potential in vitro and, after transplantation, in vivo. When plated in monolayer cultures, these KDRlow/C-KITneg cells differentiate to generate populations consisting of greater than 50% contracting cardiomyocytes. Populations derived from the KDRlow/C-KITneg fraction give rise to colonies that contain all three lineages when plated in methylcellulose cultures. Results from limiting dilution studies and cell-mixing experiments support the interpretation that these colonies are clones, indicating that they develop from a cardiovascular colony-forming cell. These findings identify a human cardiovascular progenitor that marks one of the earliest stages of human cardiac development.

title: Cancer-related inflammation
text: The mediators and cellular effectors of inflammation play a crucial role in the local environment of tumors. In some cases, inflammatory conditions exist before cancerous changes occur, while in others, an oncogenic event creates an inflamed microenvironment that promotes tumor growth. Regardless of its origin, persistent inflammation within the tumor microenvironment has numerous tumor-promoting effects. It fosters the proliferation and survival of malignant cells, supports angiogenesis and metastasis, undermines adaptive immune responses, and modifies responses to hormones and chemotherapeutic agents. Scientists are currently uncovering the molecular pathways involved in this cancer-related inflammation, leading to the discovery of potential target molecules that could lead to improved cancer diagnosis and treatment.

title: ESCRT-III recognition by VPS4 ATPases
text: The ESCRT (endosomal sorting complex required for transport) pathway plays a crucial role in various cellular processes, including endosomal intraluminal vesicle formation, HIV budding, and cytokinesis. VPS4 ATPases are essential for these processes by recognizing membrane-associated ESCRT-III assemblies and catalyzing their disassembly. Our research reveals that the microtubule interacting and transport (MIT) domains of human VPS4A and VPS4B bind to conserved sequence motifs located at the carboxy terminal of the CHMP1-3 class of ESCRT-III proteins. We have structurally characterized VPS4A MIT-CHMP1A and VPS4B MIT-CHMP2B complexes, which show that the C-terminal CHMP motif forms an amphipathic helix that binds in a groove between the last two helices of the tetratricopeptide-like repeat (TPR) of the VPS4 MIT domain, but in an opposite orientation to a canonical TPR interaction. The MIT domain also contains distinct pockets that bind to three conserved leucine residues of the CHMP motif, which are essential for VPS4 recruitment and endosomal protein sorting. Moreover, mutations that inhibit these interactions block VPS4 recruitment and impair HIV budding, further highlighting the importance of this mechanism. Overall, our findings illuminate the molecular mechanism by which VPS4 ATPases recognize and interact with their CHMP substrates to facilitate the membrane fission events necessary for the release of viruses, endosomal vesicles, and daughter cells.

title: Pif1 family helicases suppress genome instability at G-quadruplex motifs
text: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase serves as a prime example of the Pif1 DNA helicase family, which has been conserved throughout evolution, from bacteria to humans. Our findings indicate that Pif1 helicases possess extraordinary G-quadruplex unwinding capabilities, a trait shared among their counterparts across the spectrum of life. What's more, Pif1 helicases from distantly related organisms have been shown to counteract DNA damage triggered by G-quadruplexes in yeast. In the absence of Pif1, these G-quadruplex-induced damages can give rise to novel genetic and epigenetic changes. Lastly, when introduced into yeast, human PIF1 not only suppressed G-quadruplex-related DNA damage but also telomere elongation.

title: Lysyl oxidase is essential for hypoxia-induced metastasis
text: Metastasis is a complex process responsible for the majority of cancer-related deaths, and it is influenced by both the immediate microenvironment (cell-cell or cell-matrix interactions) and the broader tumour microenvironment (e.g. vascularization). Hypoxia (low oxygen levels) has been linked to metastasis and poor patient outcomes, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. Microarray studies have shown that the expression of lysyl oxidase (LOX) is elevated in hypoxic human tumour cells. Interestingly, LOX expression is associated with both tumour suppression and tumour progression, and its role in tumorigenesis appears to depend on the cellular location, cell type, and transformation status. Our findings demonstrate that LOX expression is regulated by the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) and is linked to hypoxia in human breast and head and neck tumours. Patients with high LOX-expressing tumours have poor distant metastasis-free and overall survival rates. Inhibition of LOX leads to the elimination of metastasis in mice with orthotopically grown breast cancer tumours. Mechanistically, secreted LOX is responsible for the invasive properties of hypoxic human cancer cells through focal adhesion kinase activity and cell-matrix adhesion. Furthermore, LOX may be necessary to create a niche permissive for metastatic growth. Our results suggest that LOX is essential for hypoxia-induced metastasis and could be a valuable therapeutic target for preventing and treating metastases.

title: Identification of human brain tumour initiating cells
text: The cancer stem cell (CSC) hypothesis proposes that cancer clones are sustained by a small subset of cells with stem cell properties. While evidence for CSCs in leukemia is well-established, limited data exists for solid tumors, with the exception of breast cancer. Our recent isolation of a CD133+ cell subpopulation from human brain tumors revealed stem cell properties in vitro.
