However, the true measures of CSCs are their ability to self-renew and perfectly recapitulate the original tumor. Here, we describe the development of a xenograft assay identifying human brain tumor initiating cells (TICs) that initiate tumors in vivo. Only the CD133+ brain tumor fraction harbored cells capable of tumor initiation in NOD-SCID (non-obese diabetic, severe combined immunodeficient) mouse brains. Injecting as few as 100 CD133+ cells resulted in tumor formation that could be serially transplanted and molecularly matched the patient's original tumor, while injection of 105 CD133- cells failed to induce tumor formation. This finding provides essential insights into human brain tumor pathogenesis and reinforces the CSC hypothesis as the driving force behind many solid tumors. Moreover, the identification of TICs establishes a previously untapped cellular target for more effective cancer therapies.

title: Anthropometric reference data for international use: recommendations from a World Health Organization Expert Committee.
text: The World Health Organization (WHO) convened an Expert Committee to reassess the use of anthropometry at different stages of life for evaluating health, nutrition, and social wellbeing. The Committee's task included identifying reference data for anthropometric indexes when appropriate, and providing guidelines on how to use the data. For fetal growth, the Committee recommended an existing sex-specific multiracial reference. However, due to the significant technical limitations of the current National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS)/WHO reference and its inadequacy in assessing the growth of breastfed infants, the Committee recommended the development of a new reference for weight and height/length of infants and children, which would be a complex and costly endeavor. Proper interpretation of midupper arm circumference for preschoolers requires age-specific reference data. For adolescent height-for-age, the Committee recommended using the current NCHS/WHO reference. The use of NCHS body mass index (BMI) data, with their upper percentile elevations and skewness, is not ideal for setting health goals; however, these data were provisionally recommended for defining obesity based on a combination of elevated BMI and high subcutaneous fat. The NCHS values were also provisionally recommended as reference data for subscapular and triceps skinfold thicknesses. Guidelines were provided for adjusting adolescent anthropometric comparisons for maturational status. Currently, there is no need for adult BMI reference data; interpretation should be based on pragmatic BMI cutoffs. Finally, the Committee noted that there is a lack of normative anthropometric data for the elderly, particularly for those over 80 years of age. Proper definitions of health status, function, and biological age remain to be developed for this group.

title: Diverse interventions that extend mouse lifespan suppress shared age-associated epigenetic changes at critical gene regulatory regions
text:
Background: Age-related epigenetic alterations are believed to play a crucial role in the aging process. Specifically, age-associated DNA methylation changes have been described as a "clock" that reflects an individual's biological age. However, the impact of various interventions on the epigenome during aging is not well understood. To address this gap in knowledge, we investigated age-associated DNA methylation changes at the whole-genome, single-nucleotide level in mice and evaluated the effect of three longevity-promoting interventions: the Ames dwarfProp1 df/df mutation, calorie restriction, and rapamycin.
Results: In wild-type mice fed an unsupplemented ad libitum diet, age-associated hypomethylation was enriched at super-enhancers in highly expressed genes involved in liver function. Genes with hypomethylated enhancers were found to be enriched for genes that exhibit age-related changes in expression. Conversely, hypermethylation was enriched at CpG islands marked by bivalent activating and repressing histone modifications and resembled hypermethylation in liver cancer. Notably, age-associated methylation changes were found to be suppressed in Ames dwarf and calorie-restricted mice, and to a lesser extent in rapamycin-treated mice.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that age-associated hypo- and hypermethylation events occur at distinct regulatory features of the genome. The results of this study provide a foundation for understanding the epigenetic contribution to healthy aging and longevity, as well as the molecular basis of the DNA methylation clock. The findings also indicate that various longevity-promoting interventions can modulate the epigenome and may exert their beneficial effects, in part, through epigenetic modifications.

title: Extracellular vesicles for drug delivery.
text: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membranous structures derived from cells, serving as a natural means of intercellular communication. Recent advances in understanding their ability to transfer biological information have sparked interest in utilizing EVs as drug delivery vehicles. Compared to existing delivery systems, EVs offer several advantages, such as the ability to cross biological barriers, innate cell targeting properties, and stability in circulation. However, scalable isolation of EVs and efficient drug loading have hindered their therapeutic application. Tuning EVs' intrinsic cell targeting properties through engineering is crucial to achieve targeted drug delivery. In this review, we will discuss recent progress and persistent challenges in developing EVs as drug delivery vehicles.

title: Effects of soy isoflavones and phytate on homocysteine, C-reactive protein, and iron status in postmenopausal women.
text: BACKGROUND Soy protein or its components may have protective effects against atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors, such as high homocysteine (tHcy), C-reactive protein (CRP), and excess body iron, which tend to increase after menopause. OBJECTIVE The primary goal of this study was to assess the independent effect of soy protein components, specifically isoflavones and phytate, on CVD risk factors in postmenopausal women. A secondary objective was to identify other factors, including blood lipids, oxidative stress markers, serum ferritin, plasma folate and vitamin B-12 levels, and body mass index (BMI), that contribute to tHcy and CRP concentrations. DESIGN A double-blind, 6-week study randomly assigned 55 postmenopausal women aged 47-72 years to one of four soy protein treatments (40 g/day): native phytate and native isoflavones, native phytate and low isoflavones, low phytate and native isoflavones, or low phytate and low isoflavones. Variables measured included iron indexes, tHcy, CRP, and BMI. RESULTS Soy protein with native phytate significantly lowered tHcy, transferrin saturation, and ferritin levels, while soy protein with native isoflavones had no effect on these variables. At baseline, BMI was highly correlated with tHcy and CRP, and HDL cholesterol was correlated with CRP. Multiple regression analysis showed that LDL cholesterol and BMI contributed significantly (R2 = 19.9%, P = 0.003) to the overall variance in tHcy. CONCLUSION Consuming phytate-rich foods and maintaining a healthy weight may reduce atherosclerotic CVD risk factors in postmenopausal women, suggesting that these behaviors may have protective effects against CVD.

title: Replication Fork Stability Confers Chemoresistance in BRCA-deficient Cells
text: Cells lacking the Brca1 and Brca2 genes have difficulty repairing DNA double-strand breaks through homologous recombination, making them more sensitive to DNA-damaging agents like cisplatin and PARP inhibitors. Surprisingly, we found that eliminating the MLL3/4 complex protein, PTIP, protects Brca1/2-deficient cells from DNA damage and restores embryonic stem cell viability in Brca2-deficient cells. However, PTIP's absence does not restore homologous recombination activity at double-strand breaks. Instead, it hinders the recruitment of the MRE11 nuclease to stalled replication forks, which protects the developing DNA strands from extensive degradation. In general, acquiring PARP inhibitors and cisplatin resistance in Brca2-deficient tumor cells is linked to replication fork protection, regardless of whether or not Brca2 reversion mutations occur. The disruption of multiple proteins, including PARP1 and CHD4, leads to the same endpoint of replication fork protection, underscoring the complicated ways in which cancer cells evade chemotherapeutic interventions and gain drug resistance.

title: Plasma Corin as a Predictor of Cardiovascular Events in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure.
text: Objective: To investigate the prognostic value of plasma corin in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF). Background: Recent evidence suggests that corin plays a crucial role in regulating blood pressure and cardiac function. Methods: We enrolled 1,148 CHF patients in a prospective cohort study and examined the association between plasma corin levels and clinical prognosis using multivariate Cox regression analysis. Results: Patients with low corin levels (<458 pg/ml) were more likely to be women and hypertensive. Low corin was associated with an increase in New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels, and a decrease in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Multivariate Cox regression analysis revealed that log corin was an independent predictor of major adverse cardiac event(s) (MACE) (hazard ratio: 0.62; 95% confidence interval: 0.39 to 0.95), along with age, diabetes, NYHA functional class, LVEF, eGFR, and log NT-proBNP. Additionally, log corin was a significant predictor of cardiovascular death (p = 0.041) and heart failure rehospitalization (p = 0.015) after adjusting for clinical variables and established biomarkers of adverse prognosis. The Kaplan-Meier survival curves showed that low corin was a significant predictor of MACE in patients with NT-proBNP levels above and below the median. Conclusion: Our study demonstrates that plasma corin is a valuable prognostic marker of MACE in patients with CHF, independent of conventional risk factors.

title: Cryo-EM structures of Tau filaments from Alzheimer’s disease brain
text:
Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, and there are currently no disease-modifying therapies available. The disease is characterized by the presence of abundant neurofibrillary lesions and neuritic plaques in the cerebral cortex. Neurofibrillary lesions are composed of paired helical and straight tau filaments, which are distinct from other neurodegenerative diseases. High-resolution structures of tau filaments are unavailable, and until now, there have been no atomic-level models of these filaments from patient-derived material.
In this study, we utilize cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps at 3.4-3.5 Å resolution, in combination with corresponding atomic models, to investigate paired helical and straight filaments from the brain of an individual with Alzheimer's disease. Our findings demonstrate that these filaments are composed of two identical protofilaments, featuring residues 306-378 of the tau protein, which adopt a combined cross-β/β-helix structure. This structure serves as the seed for tau aggregation, and the observed differences in inter-protofilament packing suggest that paired helical and straight filaments are ultrastructural polymorphs.
Our study highlights the potential of cryo-EM to investigate amyloid filaments from patient-derived material, and paves the way for exploring other neurodegenerative diseases. These findings underscore the importance of advancing techniques for atomic-level modeling of amyloid fibrils, in order to develop novel therapeutic strategies for these devastating disorders.

title: Modulation of the proteoglycan receptor PTPσ promotes recovery after spinal cord injury
text: Contusive spinal cord injury leads to a range of disabilities due to limited neuronal regeneration and functional plasticity. It is well established that an increase in glial-derived chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans (CSPGs) within the glial scar and perineuronal net creates a barrier to axonal regrowth and sprouting. Recently, protein tyrosine phosphatase σ (PTPσ), along with its sister phosphatase leukocyte common antigen-related (LAR) and the nogo receptors 1 and 3 (NgR), have been identified as receptors for the inhibitory glycosylated side chains of CSPGs. Our research shows that PTPσ plays a critical role in converting growth cones into a dystrophic state by stabilizing them within CSPG-rich substrates. We have developed a membrane-permeable peptide mimetic of the PTPσ wedge domain that binds to PTPσ and relieves CSPG-mediated inhibition. Systemic delivery of this peptide over several weeks restored significant serotonergic innervation to the spinal cord below the level of injury and facilitated recovery of both locomotor and urinary functions. Our findings add further insight into the critical role of PTPσ in mediating the growth-inhibited state of neurons due to CSPGs within the injured adult spinal cord.

title: A gp130–Src–YAP module links inflammation to epithelial regeneration
text: Inflammation promotes the regeneration of injured tissues through mysterious mechanisms, some of which involve interleukin (IL)-6 family members, the expression of which is elevated in many diseases, such as inflammatory bowel diseases and colorectal cancer. We discovered in mice and human cells that gp130, a co-receptor for IL-6 cytokines, triggers the activation of YAP and Notch, transcriptional regulators that control tissue growth and regeneration, independently of the gp130 effector STAT3. Through YAP and Notch, intestinal gp130 signaling stimulates epithelial cell proliferation, causes aberrant differentiation, and confers resistance to mucosal erosion. gp130 interacts with related tyrosine kinases Src and Yes, which are activated upon receptor engagement to phosphorylate YAP and induce its stabilization and nuclear translocation. This signaling module is strongly activated upon mucosal injury to promote healing and maintain barrier function.

title: Hemoglobin concentration in white, black, and Oriental children: is there a need for separate criteria in screening for anemia?
text: A study examining the concentration of hemoglobin in different racial groups found that the hemoglobin levels were lower in black individuals compared to white individuals, even after controlling for potential confounding factors such as iron deficiency and genetic disorders. The study analyzed data from 1718 white, 741 black, and 315 Oriental children aged 5-14 years who underwent multiphasic examinations between 1973 and 1975. The results showed that the median hemoglobin concentration was 0.5 g/dl lower in black children compared to white children of both sexes (P less than 0.001), after excluding children with abnormal hemoglobin by electrophoresis and those with a mean corpuscular volume more than 5% below the normal mean for age. These findings suggest that black individuals have a lower concentration of hemoglobin on average, which could result in about 10% of normal black individuals being misdiagnosed as anemic if the same norms are applied.

title: Divergent reprogramming routes lead to alternative stem-cell states
text:
Pluripotency refers to the ability of a cell to differentiate into all three embryonic germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Pluripotent cells can be obtained through two methods: the classic derivation of embryonic stem cells or the reprogramming of somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). The latter involves the forced expression of key transcription factors in somatic cells, leading to their reprogramming into a pluripotent state. However, it is uncertain whether there are additional classes of pluripotent cells or what the range of reprogrammed phenotypes encompasses.
To investigate these questions, we characterized reprogrammed cells without preconceived notions of iPSC states. We found that mouse embryonic fibroblasts, when maintained at high levels of reprogramming factor expression, undergo unique epigenetic modifications to adopt a stable, Nanog-positive, alternative pluripotent state. This discovery proves that the pluripotent spectrum can encompass multiple, distinct cell states.

title: Autophagy mediates degradation of nuclear lamina
text: Macroautophagy, commonly referred to as autophagy, is a cellular process that breaks down various cellular components, including those found in the cytoplasm. Despite significant research on the role of autophagy in cytoplasmic component degradation, little is known about its role in breaking down nuclear components. Our study reveals that the autophagy machinery plays a critical role in the degradation of nuclear lamina components in mammals. The autophagy protein LC3/Atg8, which is involved in autophagy membrane trafficking and substrate delivery, is present in the nucleus and interacts directly with the nuclear lamina protein lamin B1. This interaction does not decrease lamin B1 levels during starvation but instead mediates its degradation upon oncogenic insults, such as those caused by activated RAS. Once delivered to the lysosome, lamin B1 is degraded. Inhibiting autophagy or the LC3-lamin B1 interaction prevents activated RAS-induced lamin B1 loss and attenuates oncogene-induced senescence in primary human cells. Our findings suggest that this newly identified function of autophagy acts as a protective mechanism, guarding cells against tumorigenesis.

title: Pro-resolving lipid mediators are leads for resolution physiology
text: Recent breakthroughs in our comprehension of the mechanisms underlying the resolution of acute inflammation have led to the discovery of a novel class of lipid mediators known as specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs). This group includes the lipoxin, resolvin, protectin, and maresin families. Collectively, these mediators play a critical role in the resolution of inflammation and have been shown to possess potent biological activities when administered in vivo. In animal studies, SPMs have been found to elicit anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving effects, as well as enhance microbial clearance. These mediators have been identified in the context of inflammation resolution, but their conservation across various physiological processes suggests that they may also play a role in host defense, pain modulation, organ protection, and tissue remodeling. This review aims to delve into the mechanisms of SPMs and omega-3 essential fatty acid pathways, providing insight into their broader physiological functions.

title: ZMYND11 links histone H3.3K36me3 to transcription elongation and tumour suppression
text:
The recognition of modified histones by 'reader' proteins plays a crucial role in the regulation of chromatin in eukaryotic cells. Specifically, the trimethylation of lysine 36 on histone H3 (H3K36me3) is deposited on the nucleosomes in the transcribed regions after RNA polymerase II elongation in yeast, which in turn recruits epigenetic regulators to reposition the chromatin to a relatively repressive state, thereby suppressing cryptic transcription. However, relatively little is known about the role of H3K36me3 in transcription regulation in mammals, which is further complicated by the incorporation of the histone variant H3.3 in gene bodies during transcription.
Our study shows that the candidate tumor suppressor ZMYND11 specifically recognizes H3K36me3 on H3.3 (H3.3K36me3) and regulates RNA polymerase II elongation. Structural analysis reveals that, in addition to trimethyl-lysine binding within the PWWP domain, the recognition of H3.3-specific 'Ser 31' residue by ZMYND11 is mediated by the encapsulation of this residue within a composite pocket formed by the tandem bromo-PWWP domains of ZMYND11. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) analysis shows a genome-wide co-localization of ZMYND11 with H3K36me3 and H3.3 in gene bodies, and its occupancy requires the pre-deposition of H3.3K36me3. Although ZMYND11 is associated with highly expressed genes, it functions as an unconventional transcription co-repressor by modulating RNA polymerase II at the elongation stage. ZMYND11 is critical for the repression of a transcriptional program essential for tumor cell growth, and low expression levels of ZMYND11 in breast cancer patients are associated with worse prognosis. Overexpression of ZMYND11 suppresses cancer cell growth in vitro and tumor formation in mice, indicating that ZMYND11 links histone-variant-mediated transcription elongation control to tumor suppression.

title: Autocrine BDNF–TrkB signalling within a single dendritic spine
text: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and its receptor TrkB play a crucial role in various forms of neuronal plasticity, including structural long-term potentiation (sLTP), which is linked to learning in animals. While it is unknown whether BDNF release and TrkB activation occur during sLTP, we aimed to investigate this using a fluorescence resonance energy transfer-based sensor for TrkB and two-photon fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy. We monitored TrkB activity in single dendritic spines of CA1 pyramidal neurons in cultured murine hippocampal slices in response to sLTP induction. Our findings reveal fast (onset < 1 min) and sustained (>20 min) TrkB activation in the stimulated spine, which depends on N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDAR) and calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) signaling as well as postsynaptically synthesized BDNF. We also confirm the presence of postsynaptic BDNF using electron microscopy to localize endogenous BDNF to dendrites and spines of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons. Additionally, we show rapid, glutamate-uncaging-evoked, time-locked BDNF release from single dendritic spines using BDNF fused to superecliptic pHluorin. Our findings reveal a spine-autonomous, autocrine signaling mechanism involving NMDAR-CaMKII-dependent BDNF release from stimulated dendritic spines and subsequent TrkB activation on these same spines, which is essential for both structural and functional LTP.

title: Whole genomes redefine the mutational landscape of pancreatic cancer
text: Pancreatic cancer remains a significant health burden and one of the most deadly forms of cancer. To better understand the genetic underpinnings of this disease, we conducted whole-genome sequencing and copy number variation (CNV) analysis on 100 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDACs). Our findings revealed that chromosomal rearrangements leading to gene disruption are a prevalent feature of PDACs, affecting well-established cancer genes (TP53, SMAD4, CDKN2A, ARID1A, and ROBO2) as well as new candidate drivers of pancreatic carcinogenesis (KDM6A and PREX2). Using patterns of structural variation (alterations in chromosomal structure), we were able to classify PDACs into four subtypes with potential clinical utility. Specifically, we identified a stable subtype, a locally rearranged subtype, a scattered subtype, and an unstable subtype. Our analysis also revealed a significant proportion of PDACs with focal amplifications, many of which harbored druggable oncogenes (ERBB2, MET, FGFR1, CDK6, PIK3R3, and PIK3CA). However, the prevalence of these amplifications was low in individual patients. In addition, we found that genomic instability frequently co-segregated with inactivation of DNA maintenance genes (BRCA1, BRCA2, or PALB2), and a mutational signature of DNA damage repair deficiency was observed in a significant proportion of cases. Of note, four out of five individuals who received platinum therapy and had measures of defective DNA maintenance showed a response to treatment.

title: Human oocytes reprogram adult somatic nuclei of a type 1 diabetic to diploid pluripotent stem cells
text: The transfer of somatic cell nuclei into oocytes has the potential to generate pluripotent stem cells that are comparable to embryonic stem cells, offering promise for autologous cell replacement therapy. Although methods involving transcription factors are commonly used in research to induce pluripotency from somatic cells, there are notable differences between induced pluripotent stem cells and embryonic stem cells that may impact their clinical application. To investigate the factors influencing the efficiency of blastocyst development and stem cell derivation from somatic cells, we systematically examined the parameters involved. Specifically, we investigated the use of both kinase and translation inhibitors, as well as cell culture with histone deacetylase inhibitors. Our findings revealed that improvements to the oocyte activation protocol, such as using diluted Sendai virus in calcium-free medium, can enhance the development of blastocysts. Notably, the efficiency of development varied between oocyte donors, with a negative correlation between the number of days required for oocyte maturation and the developed blastocyst rate. Moreover, we successfully derived diploid pluripotent stem cell lines from somatic cells of a newborn and an adult female with type 1 diabetes using this modified nuclear transfer protocol.

title: A three-dimensional human neural cell culture model of Alzheimer’s disease
text:
Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, characterized by two distinct pathological hallmarks: amyloid-β plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. The amyloid hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease proposes that the excessive accumulation of amyloid-β peptides leads to the formation of neurofibrillary tangles composed of aggregated hyperphosphorylated tau. However, prior studies have failed to elucidate the relationship between these two pathological events using human neuronal cells.
Previous research using mouse models with familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD) mutations has shown that amyloid-β-induced synaptic and memory deficits occur, but these models do not fully recapitulate the other key pathological events of Alzheimer's disease, including the distinct neurofibrillary tangle pathology. Moreover, human neurons derived from Alzheimer's disease patients have demonstrated elevated levels of toxic amyloid-β species and phosphorylated tau, but not amyloid-β plaques or neurofibrillary tangles.
In this study, we resolved this gap in knowledge by using human neural stem-cell-derived three-dimensional (3D) culture systems to investigate the effect of FAD mutations in β-amyloid precursor protein and presenilin 1 on amyloid-β deposition. Our findings demonstrate that FAD mutations are capable of inducing robust extracellular deposition of amyloid-β, including amyloid-β plaques, in a human neural stem-cell-derived 3D culture system. Moreover, the 3D-differentiated neuronal cells expressing FAD mutations displayed high levels of detergent-resistant, silver-positive aggregates of phosphorylated tau in the soma and neurites, as well as filamentous tau, as detected by immunoelectron microscopy.
In addition, we discovered that the inhibition of amyloid-β generation using β- or γ-secretase inhibitors not only decreased amyloid-β pathology but also attenuated tauopathy. Furthermore, we identified glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) as a crucial regulator of amyloid-β-mediated tau phosphorylation. Our findings represent a significant breakthrough in recapitulating Alzheimer's disease pathology in a single 3D human neural cell culture model. This innovative strategy could prove invaluable in the development of more precise human neural cell models of other neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Mesenchymal-endothelial-transition contributes to cardiac neovascularization
text: Cardiac fibroblasts may transform into endothelial cells through endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, but it is unclear whether cardiac fibroblasts can directly contribute to the formation of new blood vessels after heart injury through a process called mesenchymal-to-endothelial transition. Using genetic fate mapping techniques, we have found that cardiac fibroblasts quickly adopt an endothelial-like phenotype after acute ischemic heart injury. These newly developed endothelial cells exhibit the same anatomical and functional characteristics as native endothelial cells. We discovered that the transcription factor p53 regulates this cellular transition. When p53 is absent in cardiac fibroblasts, the formation of fibroblast-derived endothelial cells is significantly reduced, resulting in decreased post-infarct vascular density and worsened cardiac function. Conversely, enhancing the p53 pathway in cardiac fibroblasts increases the conversion of mesenchymal cells to endothelial cells, leading to enhanced vascularity and improved cardiac function. These findings suggest that mesenchymal-to-endothelial transition may contribute to the formation of new blood vessels in the injured heart, a process that could have therapeutic implications for enhancing cardiac repair.

title: Estimation of optimal serum concentrations of 25-hydroxyvitamin D for multiple health outcomes.
text: Recent evidence suggests that vitamin D intakes above the current recommendations may be associated with better health outcomes. However, the optimal serum concentration of 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] has not been established. This review summarizes the findings from studies that evaluated the thresholds for serum 25(OH)D concentrations in relation to bone mineral density (BMD), lower-extremity function, dental health, and the risk of falls, fractures, and colorectal cancer. For all outcomes, the most advantageous serum concentrations of 25(OH)D begin at 75 nmol/L (30 ng/mL), with the best concentrations found between 90 and 100 nmol/L (36-40 ng/mL). These concentrations cannot be reached with the current recommended intakes of 200 and 600 IU vitamin D/day for younger and older adults, respectively. Comparing vitamin D intakes with achieved serum concentrations of 25(OH)D allows for the estimation of optimal intakes. For bone health in younger adults and all studied outcomes in older adults, an increase in the recommended vitamin D intake is warranted. An intake of at least 1000 IU (25 microg) vitamin D (cholecalciferol)/day is needed to bring vitamin D concentrations in at least 50% of the population up to 75 nmol/L. The implications of higher doses for the entire adult population should be addressed in future studies.

title: Cohesin-dependent globules and heterochromatin shape 3D genome architecture in S. pombe
text: Eukaryotic DNA is folded into three-dimensional structures, such as self-associating topological domains, whose borders are enriched in cohesin and CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF), necessary for long-range interactions. Despite understanding how local chromatin interactions influence higher-order folding of chromatin fibers and the role of cohesin in this process, how local chromatin interactions govern higher-order folding of chromatin fibers and the function of cohesin in this process remain unclear. Here, we use genome-wide chromatin conformation capture (Hi-C) analysis to explore the high-resolution organization of the Schizosaccharomyces pombe genome, despite its small size, which possesses fundamental features found in other eukaryotes. Analyzing wild-type and mutant strains reveals key elements of chromosome architecture and genome organization. On chromosome arms, small regions of chromatin locally interact to form 'globules'; this feature requires a distinct function of cohesin from its role in sister chromatid cohesion. Cohesin is enriched at globule boundaries and its loss causes disruption of local globule structures and global chromosome territories. Contrarily, heterochromatin, which loads cohesin at specific sites, including pericentromeric and subtelomeric domains, is dispensable for globule formation but affects genome organization by mediating chromatin fiber compaction at centromeres and promoting prominent inter-arm interactions within centromere-proximal regions, providing structural constraints crucial for proper genome organization. Loss of heterochromatin relaxes constraints on chromosomes, leading to an increase in intra- and inter-chromosomal interactions. Our analyses uncover fundamental genome folding principles that drive higher-order chromosome organization essential for coordinating nuclear functions.

title: A temporal shift in the circuits mediating retrieval of fear memory
text: Fear memories allow animals to avoid danger, increasing their chances of survival. However, little is known about how these memories are retrieved over time. In this study, we investigated the role of the dorsal midline thalamus in retrieving auditory conditioned fear in rats. We found that the thalamus is required for retrieval at late time points (24 hours, 7 days, 28 days) but not at early time points (0.5 hours, 6 hours) after learning. Specifically, the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT), a subregion of the dorsal midline thalamus, showed increased c-Fos expression only at late time points, indicating that the PVT is gradually recruited for fear retrieval. The prelimbic prefrontal cortex (PL), which is necessary for fear retrieval, sends dense projections to the PVT. Retrieval at late time points activated PL neurons projecting to the PVT, and optogenetic silencing of these projections impaired retrieval at late, but not early, time points. In contrast, silencing of PL inputs to the basolateral amygdala impaired retrieval at early, but not late, time points, indicating a time-dependent shift in retrieval circuits. Additionally, retrieval at late time points activated PVT neurons projecting to the central nucleus of the amygdala, and silencing these projections at late, but not early, time points induced a persistent attenuation of fear. Together, these findings suggest that the PVT may serve as a crucial thalamic node recruited into cortico-amygdalar networks for the retrieval and maintenance of long-term fear memories.

title: Derivation of novel human ground state naive pluripotent stem cells
text:
Human embryonic stem (ES) cells can be isolated from the inner cell mass of blastocysts and maintained in vitro in a naive inner-cell-mass-like configuration by providing exogenous stimulation with leukaemia inhibitory factor (LIF) and inhibiting signaling pathways, such as ERK1/ERK2 and GSK3β. Naive human ES cells display characteristics similar to those of mouse ES cells, including Oct4 transcription driven by its distal enhancer, retention of a pre-inactivation X chromosome state, and reduced DNA methylation and H3K27me3 deposition on developmental regulatory gene promoters. Upon withdrawal of the stimulating factors, naive human ES cells can drift towards a primed pluripotent state, similar to that of the post-implantation epiblast.
In contrast, human ES cells share some epigenetic properties with mouse epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs), including the predominant use of a proximal enhancer element to maintain OCT4 expression, pronounced X chromosome inactivation in most female human ES cells, and increased DNA methylation and H3K27me3 deposition on lineage regulatory gene promoters. However, the feasibility of establishing human ground state naive pluripotency in vitro with equivalent molecular and functional features to those of mouse ES cells remains to be defined.
To address this challenge, we have developed defined conditions that allow the derivation of genetically unmodified human naive pluripotent stem cells from already established primed human ES cells, either through induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell reprogramming or directly from blastocysts. The novel naive pluripotent cells we have validated exhibit highly similar molecular characteristics and functional properties to mouse naive ES cells, and distinct from conventional primed human pluripotent cells. For instance, they demonstrate competence in generating cross-species chimaeric mouse embryos that undergo organogenesis following microinjection of human naive iPS cells into mouse morulas.
Overall, our findings open up new avenues for regenerative medicine, patient-specific iPS cell disease modelling, and the study of early human development in vitro and in vivo.

title: Predicting immunogenic tumour mutations by combining mass spectrometry and exome sequencing
text: Human tumors typically harbor a remarkable number of somatic mutations. If presented on major histocompatibility complex class I molecules (MHCI), peptides containing these mutations could potentially be immunogenic as they should be recognized as 'non-self' neo-antigens by the adaptive immune system. Recent work has confirmed that mutant peptides can serve as T-cell epitopes. However, few mutant epitopes have been described due to the laborious process of screening patient tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes for their ability to recognize antigen libraries constructed following tumor exome sequencing. To simplify the discovery of immunogenic mutant peptides, we developed an approach that combines whole-exome and transcriptome sequencing analysis with mass spectrometry to identify neo-epitopes in two widely used murine tumor models. Of the over 1,300 amino acid changes identified, approximately 13% were predicted to bind MHCI, a small fraction of which were confirmed by mass spectrometry. The peptides were then structurally modeled bound to MHCI. Mutations that were solvent-exposed and therefore accessible to T-cell antigen receptors were predicted to be immunogenic. Vaccination of mice confirmed the approach, with each predicted immunogenic peptide yielding therapeutically active T-cell responses. The predictions also enabled the generation of peptide-MHCI dextramers that could be used to monitor the kinetics and distribution of the anti-tumor T-cell response before and after vaccination. These findings suggest that a suitable prediction algorithm may provide an approach for the pharmacodynamic monitoring of T-cell responses as well as for the development of personalized vaccines in cancer patients.

title: In vivo genome editing using Staphylococcus aureus Cas9
text: The RNA-guided endonuclease Cas9 has become a versatile genome-editing platform, but its size hinders its utility for certain research and therapeutic applications, particularly when using the highly adaptable adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery vehicle. To address this limitation, we investigate six smaller Cas9 orthologues and find that Cas9 from Staphylococcus aureus (SaCas9) can edit the genome with similar efficiency to SpCas9, yet is significantly shorter. We package SaCas9 and its guide RNA expression cassette into a single AAV vector and target the cholesterol regulatory gene Pcsk9 in the mouse liver. Within a week of injection, we observe over 40% gene modification, accompanied by substantial reductions in serum Pcsk9 and total cholesterol levels. To further assess the specificity of SaCas9, we use BLESS and demonstrate that its in vivo genome editing has the potential to be both efficient and specific.

title: Effects of exercise intensity on cardiovascular fitness, total body composition, and visceral adiposity of obese adolescents.
text:
Background: Little is known about how the intensity of exercise affects cardiovascular fitness and body composition in obese adolescents.
Objective: Our goal was to investigate the impact of different intensities of physical training on cardiovascular fitness, percentage of body fat (%BF), and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) in obese adolescents.
Design: We recruited 80 obese adolescents (13-16 years old) and randomly assigned them to one of three groups: biweekly lifestyle education (LSE), LSE plus moderate-intensity physical training, or LSE plus high-intensity physical training. The intervention lasted for 8 months, and physical training was offered 5 days per week. The target energy expenditure for all subjects in the physical training groups was 1047 kJ (250 kcal) per session. Cardiovascular fitness was assessed using a multistage treadmill test, %BF was measured using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, and VAT was measured using magnetic resonance imaging.
Results: We found that the high-intensity physical training group had a significantly greater increase in cardiovascular fitness compared to the moderate-intensity group (P = 0.009), but there were no significant differences between the moderate-intensity and LSE alone groups. Additionally, attending training sessions 2 or more days per week in both physical training groups combined resulted in favorable changes in cardiovascular fitness (P < 0.001), %BF (P = 0.001), and VAT (P = 0.029). We did not find any evidence that high-intensity physical training was more effective than moderate-intensity physical training in improving body composition.
Conclusions: Our findings indicate that both high-intensity and moderate-intensity physical training significantly improved cardiovascular fitness in obese adolescents. However, there was no clear effect of the intensity of physical training on body composition. The physical training also reduced both visceral and total-body adiposity, highlighting the importance of exercise intensity in promoting cardiovascular health in this population.

title: Low methionine ingestion by rats extends life span.
text: Dietary energy restriction has been a widely studied method for increasing mammalian lifespan. Our findings indicate that reducing the concentration of the essential amino acid L-methionine in the diet from 0.86% to 0.17% in male Fischer 344 rats leads to a 30% increase in lifespan. Methionine restriction resulted in a complete inhibition of growth, although the rats consumed more food on a body weight basis. Early-life energy consumption studies revealed that the energy intake of 0.17% methionine-fed animals was near normal for their size, although their consumption per animal was lower than that of the larger 0.86% methionine-fed rats. Increasing the energy intake of 0.17% methionine-fed rats did not enhance growth, while restricting the energy intake of 0.85% methionine-fed rats to that of 0.17% methionine-fed animals did not significantly reduce growth. These findings suggest that food restriction was not the primary mechanism underlying the life span extension observed in these experiments. The well-defined biochemical pathways of methionine metabolism and utilization provide a valuable opportunity to uncover the specific mechanism(s) underlying this dietary restriction-related extension of lifespan.

title: Epicatechin and a cocoa polyphenolic extract modulate gene expression in human Caco-2 cells.
text: We performed a functional genomic analysis to investigate the effects of epicatechin and polyphenolic cocoa extract on human colon adenocarcinoma cells (Caco-2). Using specific Human Hematology/Immunology cDNA arrays containing 406 genes, we identified genes that were differentially expressed after treatment. Epicatechin decreased the expression of 21 genes and increased the expression of 24 genes, while the cocoa polyphenolic extract upregulated 24 genes and downregulated 28 genes. The changes in gene expression for ferritin heavy polypeptide 1 (FTH1), mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase 1 (MAPKK1), signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1), and topoisomerase 1 after incubation with epicatechin, and for myeloid leukemia factor 2 (MLF2), CCAAT/enhancer binding protein gamma (C/EBPG), MAPKK1, ATP-binding cassette, subfamily c member 1 (MRP1), STAT1, topoisomerase 1, and x-ray repair complementing defective repair 1 (XRCC1) after incubation with the cocoa polyphenolic extract were validated through reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Furthermore, changes in the messenger RNA levels for MAPKK1, STAT1, MRP1, and topoisomerase 1 after incubation with either epicatechin or cocoa extract were confirmed at the protein level through Western blotting. The changes in the expression of STAT1, MAPKK1, MRP1, and FTH1 genes, which are involved in the cellular response to oxidative stress, are in agreement with the antioxidant properties of cocoa flavonoids. Additionally, the changes in the expression of C/EBPG, topoisomerase 1, MLF2, and XRCC1 suggest novel mechanisms of action of flavonoids at the molecular level.

title: An atlas of active enhancers across human cell types and tissues
text: Enhancers play a critical role in the precise temporal and cell-type-specific activation of gene expression in multicellular eukaryotes. Understanding the properties, regulatory activity, and target genes of enhancers is essential to uncover the mechanisms of differentiation and homeostasis. To address this, we leveraged the FANTOM5 panel of samples, consisting of a wide range of human tissues and cell types, to generate an atlas of active, in vivo-transcribed enhancers. Our findings reveal that enhancers share characteristics with CpG-poor messenger RNA promoters, yet produce bidirectional, exosome-sensitive, and relatively short unspliced RNAs, which are strongly linked to enhancer activity. The atlas enables unprecedented comparisons of regulatory programs between different cells, allowing the identification of disease-associated regulatory single nucleotide polymorphisms and the classification of cell-type-specific and ubiquitous enhancers. Additionally, we explore the functional significance of enhancer redundancy, which explains gene expression strength rather than expression patterns. The online FANTOM5 enhancer atlas represents a unique resource for studies on cell-type-specific enhancers and gene regulation.

title: Precision microbiome reconstitution restores bile acid mediated resistance to Clostridium difficile
text: The gastrointestinal tracts of mammals harbor hundreds of microbial species, some of which contribute to health by conferring colonization resistance against intestinal pathogens. Antibiotics can disrupt these beneficial microbial communities, making individuals more susceptible to infections like Clostridium difficile (C. difficile), which can lead to severe diarrhea and mortality in hospitalized patients. While some intestinal bacteria provide resistance to C. difficile infection, their in vivo inhibitory mechanisms are not well understood. To address this gap in knowledge, we investigated the correlation between specific bacterial taxa and C. difficile infection resistance in mice treated with different antibiotics. Our findings showed that Clostridium scindens, a bile acid 7α-dehydroxylating intestinal bacterium, is associated with resistance to C. difficile infection and can enhance resistance in a secondary bile acid-dependent manner. We also identified a probiotic candidate that corrects a clinically relevant microbiome deficiency, which has implications for the development of targeted antimicrobials and microbiome-based diagnostics and therapeutics for individuals at risk of C. difficile infection.

title: Transcription initiation complex structures elucidate DNA opening
text: Transcription of eukaryotic protein-coding genes starts with the assembly of the RNA polymerase (Pol) II initiation complex and the opening of the promoter DNA. In this study, we used cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to determine the structures of yeast initiation complexes at resolutions of 8.8 Å and 3.6 Å, showing that DNA is positioned and held in place over the Pol II cleft through interactions between the TATA-box-binding protein TBP and transcription factors TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, and TFIIF. The opening of the DNA occurs near the tip of the Pol II clamp and the TFIIE 'extended winged helix' domain, and can occur without the presence of TFIIH. Additionally, we found that the loading of the DNA template strand into the active center may be facilitated by movements of obstructing protein elements triggered by allosteric binding of the TFIIE 'E-ribbon' domain. Our findings provide a comprehensive model for transcription initiation, with a key event being the entrapment of open promoter DNA by extended protein-protein and protein-DNA interactions.

title: Multiple mechanisms disrupt the let-7 microRNA family in neuroblastoma
text: Neuroblastoma often has a poor prognosis when MYCN is genetically amplified. MYCN is a target of let-7, a family of microRNAs that play a role in many cancers as tumor suppressors. However, in neuroblastoma, the overexpression of LIN28B, which inhibits let-7 production, is not necessary for MYCN amplification. Our study shows that despite de-repression of let-7, LIN28B is not essential in MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cell lines. We found that high levels of MYCN messenger RNA in amplified disease are sufficient to absorb let-7, reconciling the dispensability of LIN28B. Interestingly, genetic loss of let-7 is common in neuroblastoma and is inversely associated with MYCN amplification, and independently associated with poor outcomes. This discovery provides a rationale for the chromosomal loss patterns seen in neuroblastoma. We propose that the disruption of let-7 by LIN28B, MYCN sponging, or genetic loss is a unifying mechanism of neuroblastoma development, with broader implications for cancer pathogenesis.

title: Radiation and Dual Checkpoint Blockade Activates Non-Redundant Immune Mechanisms in Cancer
text: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have shown remarkable clinical efficacy, but achieving optimal results will require combining these therapies with each other and other treatments. This raises fundamental questions about how non-redundant mechanisms contribute to cancer resistance. By treating a subset of patients with metastatic melanoma with an anti-CTLA4 antibody and radiation, we observed impressive tumor regression in both irradiated and unirradiated tumors. However, resistance was still prevalent. Through unbiased analysis of mice, we found that upregulation of PD-L1 on melanoma cells was responsible for resistance, which was also associated with T-cell exhaustion. Therefore, the optimal response in melanoma and other cancer types requires the combination of radiation, anti-CTLA4, and anti-PD-L1/PD-1. Anti-CTLA4 primarily inhibits T regulatory cells (Treg cells), leading to an increase in the CD8 T-cell to Treg (CD8/Treg) ratio. Radiation enhances the diversity of the T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire of intratumoral T cells. By promoting the expansion of T cells and shaping the TCR repertoire of the expanded peripheral clones, anti-CTLA4 and radiation work together. Adding PD-L1 blockade reverses T-cell exhaustion and restores the balance between CD8 and Treg cells, further encouraging oligoclonal T-cell expansion. Similarly, in patients on our clinical trial with melanoma who had high levels of PD-L1 expression, resistance to radiation plus anti-CTLA4 was observed, and persistent T-cell exhaustion resulted in rapid disease progression. Therefore, PD-L1 expression on melanoma cells allows tumors to evade anti-CTLA4-based therapy, and the combination of radiation, anti-CTLA4, and anti-PD-L1 promotes an immune response and immunity through distinct mechanisms.

title: G-protein-independent coupling of MC4R to Kir7.1 in hypothalamic neurons
text: The coordinated release of anorexigenic α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH) and orexigenic Agouti-related protein (AgRP) from distinct hypothalamic neurons in the arcuate nucleus activates common neural targets in the central nervous system, playing a crucial role in regulating energy homeostasis. Both peptides bind strongly to the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R), with α-MSH acting as an agonist that activates the Gαs signaling pathway, while AgRP competitively binds to α-MSH and blocks its activation of the receptor, thus inhibiting its constitutive activity. Our findings show that in mice, the regulation of firing activity in neurons from the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) by α-MSH and AgRP is mediated independently of Gαs signaling by ligand-induced coupling of MC4R to the closure of inwardly rectifying potassium channels, Kir7.1. Additionally, AgRP exhibits biased agonist activity, hyperpolarizing neurons by binding to MC4R and opening Kir7.1, unrelated to its inhibition of α-MSH binding. This suggests that Kir7.1 signaling is essential for melanocortin-mediated regulation of energy homeostasis within the PVN. The coupling of MC4R to Kir7.1 may help explain unusual aspects of melanocortin-mediated control of energy homeostasis, such as the gene dosage effect of MC4R and the prolonged effects of AgRP on food intake.

title: Role of ghrelin in the relationship between hyperphagia and accelerated gastric emptying in diabetic mice.
text:
The article investigates the role of ghrelin in diabetic hyperphagia, a common complication of diabetes characterized by excessive hunger and increased food intake. The study uses mice with streptozotocin-induced diabetes and ghrelin receptor knockout (GHS-R(-/-) mice) to compare the effects of ghrelin deficiency on diabetic hyperphagia.
The study found that:
1. Plasma ghrelin levels were increased in diabetic mice to a similar extent in both genotypes.
2. Diabetic GHS-R(+/+) mice exhibited more pronounced hyperphagia than GHS-R(-/-) mice between days 12 and 21.
3. Increases in neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP) mRNA expression were less pronounced in diabetic GHS-R(-/-) than in GHS-R(+/+) mice from day 15 on, whereas decreases in proopiomelanocortin mRNA levels were similar in both genotypes.
4. Gastric emptying was accelerated to a similar extent in both genotypes, starting on day 16.
5. In fundic smooth muscle strips of diabetic GHS-R(+/+) and GHS-R(-/-) mice, neuronal relaxations were reduced, whereas contractions were increased; this increase was related to an increased affinity of muscarinic and tachykinergic receptors.

The study concluded that diabetic hyperphagia is regulated by central mechanisms, which involves ghrelin-signaling pathway affecting the expression of NPY and AgRP in the hypothalamus. The acceleration of gastric emptying, which is unrelated to ghrelin signaling, is not the cause of diabetic hyperphagia and might involve local contractility changes in the fundus.

title: Human serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol response to extended oral dosing with cholecalciferol.
text: The article discusses the study conducted to determine the quantitative relationship between cholecalciferol input and resulting serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentration, as well as to estimate the proportion of the daily requirement met by cholecalciferol reserves in body tissue stores. The study involved administering cholecalciferol orally to 67 men in Omaha, Nebraska, over a period of 20 weeks during the winter, with labeled doses ranging from 0 to 250 microg cholecalciferol. The serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentration was measured at intervals throughout the study, and the results showed that the concentration changed directly proportional to the dose, with a slope of approximately 0.70 nmol/L for each additional 1 microg cholecalciferol input. The study found that the total amount of cholecalciferol needed to sustain the starting 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentration was approximately 96 microg (approximately 3800 IU)/d, with approximately 78-82 microg/d provided by tissue stores. The study concluded that healthy men seem to use around 3000-5000 IU cholecalciferol/d, with a significant portion met by cutaneous production of vitamin D during the preceding summer months. The study emphasizes that current recommended vitamin D inputs are inadequate to maintain serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentration in the absence of substantial cutaneous production of vitamin D.

title: Intratumor heterogeneity and branched evolution revealed by multiregion sequencing.
text: BACKGROUND: Intratumor heterogeneity may hinder personalized-medicine strategies that rely on results from single tumor-biopsy samples. To investigate intratumor heterogeneity, we performed exome sequencing, chromosome aberration analysis, and ploidy profiling on multiple spatially separated samples from primary renal carcinomas and associated metastatic sites. METHODS: We analyzed the consequences of intratumor heterogeneity using immunohistochemical analysis, mutation functional analysis, and profiling of messenger RNA expression. RESULTS: Phylogenetic reconstruction revealed branched evolutionary tumor growth, with a significant proportion of somatic mutations not detectable across every tumor region. Intratumor heterogeneity was observed for a mutation within an autoinhibitory domain of the mTOR kinase, which correlated with S6 and 4EBP phosphorylation in vivo and constitutive activation of mTOR kinase activity in vitro. Mutational intratumor heterogeneity was detected for multiple tumor-suppressor genes, including SETD2, PTEN, and KDM5C, which underwent multiple distinct and spatially separated inactivating mutations within a single tumor, indicating convergent phenotypic evolution. Gene-expression signatures of good and poor prognosis were detected in different regions of the same tumor. Additionally, allelic composition and ploidy profiling analysis revealed extensive intratumor heterogeneity, with 26 of 30 tumor samples from four tumors harboring divergent allelic-imbalance profiles and with ploidy heterogeneity in two of four tumors. CONCLUSIONS: Intratumor heterogeneity may lead to an underestimation of the tumor genomics landscape portrayed from single tumor-biopsy samples and may present major challenges to personalized-medicine and biomarker development. Intratumor heterogeneity, associated with heterogeneous protein function, may foster tumor adaptation and therapeutic failure through Darwinian selection. (Funded by the Medical Research Council and others.)

title: Succession of microbial consortia in the developing infant gut microbiome.
text: The colonization process of the infant gut microbiome has been characterized as chaotic, but this view may be a result of a lack of understanding of the factors influencing its development. To investigate this, we conducted a 2.5-year case study of the assembly of the human infant gut microbiome, relating life events to microbiome composition and function. Sixty fecal samples were collected from a healthy infant and a detailed diary of diet and health status was kept. Using next-generation sequencing of 16S rRNA genes, we found that the phylogenetic diversity of the microbiome increased gradually over time, with changes in community composition following a smooth temporal gradient. However, major taxonomic groups showed abrupt shifts in abundance in response to changes in diet or health. Our analysis revealed that community assembly was non-random, with discrete steps of bacterial succession punctuated by life events. Additionally, we found that the earliest microbiome was enriched in genes facilitating lactate utilization, and that functional genes involved in plant polysaccharide metabolism were present before the introduction of solid food, priming the infant gut for an adult diet. On the other hand, the introduction of table foods led to a sustained increase in the abundance of Bacteroidetes, elevated fecal short chain fatty acid levels, enrichment of genes associated with carbohydrate utilization, vitamin biosynthesis, and xenobiotic degradation, and a more stable community composition, which are all characteristic of the adult microbiome. This study suggests that the seemingly chaotic shifts in the microbiome are associated with life events, although further experiments should be conducted to assess how different infants respond to similar events.

title: gamma-tocopherol, the major form of vitamin E in the US diet, deserves more attention.
text: Gamma-tocopherol, the primary form of vitamin E found in plant seeds, has historically received less attention than its counterpart, alpha-tocopherol, which is prominent in tissues and dietary supplements. However, recent research has highlighted the unique features of gamma-tocopherol and its potential importance to human health. Studies have shown that gamma-tocopherol is a more effective trap for lipophilic electrophiles than alpha-tocopherol, and it is well-absorbed and accumulates in significant amounts in certain human tissues. Upon metabolism, gamma-tocopherol is primarily converted into 2,7,8-trimethyl-2-(beta-carboxyethyl)-6-hydroxychroman (gamma-CEHC), which is mainly excreted in the urine. In contrast, the corresponding metabolite derived from alpha-tocopherol has natriuretic activity, which may be of physiological importance. Gamma-tocopherol and gamma-CEHC, unlike alpha-tocopherol, also inhibit cyclooxygenase activity, thereby displaying anti-inflammatory properties. Moreover, plasma concentrations of gamma-tocopherol have been shown to be inversely associated with the incidence of cardiovascular disease and prostate cancer in both human and animal studies. These findings suggest that gamma-tocopherol may play a significant role in human health beyond its previously recognized functions. Further investigation into the bioavailability, metabolism, chemistry, and non-antioxidant activities of gamma-tocopherol, as well as epidemiological studies examining its relation to cardiovascular disease and cancer, are warranted.

title: Disclosure of APOE genotype for risk of Alzheimer's disease.
text:
BACKGROUND: The apolipoprotein E (APOE) genotype can provide valuable information about an individual's risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. However, genotyping patients and their family members has been discouraged due to concerns about the potential psychological impact of receiving such information. In this study, we aimed to investigate the effects of disclosing APOE genotyping results on symptoms of anxiety, depression, and test-related distress in adult children of patients with Alzheimer's disease.
METHODS: We randomly assigned 162 asymptomatic adults with a parent diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease to receive either their own APOE genotyping results (disclosure group) or not to receive such results (nondisclosure group). We measured symptoms of anxiety, depression, and test-related distress at six-week intervals for one year after disclosure or nondisclosure.
RESULTS: We found no significant differences between the two groups in terms of changes in time-averaged measures of anxiety (4.5 in the disclosure group vs. 4.4 in the nondisclosure group, p=0.84), depression (8.8 in the disclosure group vs. 8.7 in the nondisclosure group, p=0.98), or test-related distress (6.9 in the disclosure group vs. 7.5 in the nondisclosure group, p=0.61). Secondary comparisons between the nondisclosure group and a sub-group of subjects carrying the APOE epsilon4 allele (which is associated with increased risk) also revealed no significant differences. However, the epsilon4-negative subgroup had a significantly lower level of test-related distress than the epsilon4-positive subgroup (p=0.01). Subjects with clinically meaningful changes in psychological outcomes were distributed evenly among the nondisclosure group and the epsilon4-positive and epsilon4-negative subgroups. Baseline scores for anxiety and depression were strongly associated with post-disclosure scores of these measures (p<0.001 for both comparisons).
CONCLUSIONS: The disclosure of APOE genotyping results to adult children of patients with Alzheimer's disease did not result in significant short-term psychological risks. Test-related distress was reduced among those who learned that they were APOE epsilon4-negative. Persons with high levels of emotional distress before undergoing genetic testing were more likely to have emotional difficulties after disclosure. (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00571025.)

title: Blood pressure and incidence of twelve cardiovascular diseases: lifetime risks, healthy life-years lost, and age-specific associations in 1·25 million people
text: Background: Despite the increasing evidence on the associations between blood pressure and cardiovascular disease, the specific relationships between blood pressure and different cardiovascular disease manifestations in contemporary populations remain uncertain. Objectives: To investigate the associations between blood pressure and 12 different presentations of cardiovascular disease in a large contemporary cohort and to estimate the lifetime risks and cardiovascular disease-free life-years lost adjusted for other risk factors. Methods: We conducted a cohort study using linked electronic health records from 1997 to 2010 in the CALIBER programme, including 1.25 million patients aged 30 years or older who were initially free from cardiovascular disease. We measured clinically blood pressure and recorded 12 different cardiovascular disease outcomes over a median follow-up of 5.2 years. Results: We observed 83,098 initial cardiovascular disease presentations and found that the lowest risk for cardiovascular disease was observed in individuals with systolic blood pressure of 90-114 mm Hg and diastolic blood pressure of 60-74 mm Hg, with no evidence of a J-shaped increased risk at lower blood pressures. The associations of high blood pressure varied by cardiovascular disease endpoint, with strongest associations observed for intracerebral haemorrhage, subarachnoid haemorrhage, and stable angina, and weakest associations observed for abdominal aortic aneurysm. Compared to diastolic blood pressure, raised systolic blood pressure had a greater effect on angina, myocardial infarction, and peripheral arterial disease, whereas raised diastolic blood pressure had a greater effect on abdominal aortic aneurysm than did raised systolic pressure. Pulse pressure associations were inverse for abdominal aortic aneurysm and strongest for peripheral arterial disease. Hypertension (blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg or those receiving blood pressure-lowering drugs) was associated with a lifetime risk of overall cardiovascular disease at 30 years of age of 63.3% (95% CI 62.9-63.8) compared to 46.1% (45.5-46.8) for those with normal blood pressure, and resulted in cardiovascular disease-free life-years lost of 5.0 years (95% CI 4.8-5.2). Conclusion: Our study challenges the widely held assumptions that blood pressure has strong associations with the occurrence of all cardiovascular diseases across a wide age range, and that diastolic and systolic associations are concordant. Despite modern treatments, the lifetime burden of hypertension is substantial. These findings emphasize the need for new blood pressure-lowering strategies to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease. Funding: Medical Research Council, National Institute for Health Research, and Wellcome Trust.

title: Can Online Consumers Contribute to Drug Knowledge? A Mixed-Methods Comparison of Consumer-Generated and Professionally Controlled Psychotropic Medication Information on the Internet
text: In this study, the authors aimed to compare the effects of two popular psychotropic medications, escitalopram and quetiapine, as reported by both professionally controlled health websites and consumer-generated websites. They used a stratified random sample of 960 reviews from six websites and found that both medications are most commonly reported to cause symptom improvement or worsening, changes in sleep, and changes in weight and appetite. However, there were significant differences in the types of effects reported and in the frequency of reporting between professional and consumer-generated websites. Specifically, more consumers posting reviews on consumer-generated websites reported symptom worsening on quetiapine, while more consumers posting on professionally controlled websites reported symptom improvement. Additionally, professional descriptions were more likely to list physical adverse effects and warnings about suicidal ideation, while consumer reviews provided richer descriptions of effects in context. The authors conclude that while professional medication descriptions offer a concise and comprehensive listing of drug effects, consumer reviews provide greater context and situational examples of how effects may manifest. The study highlights the importance of integrating consumer-generated content into online health searches to better identify quality health sources on the internet.

title: Effect of supplemental zinc on the growth and serum zinc concentrations of prepubertal children: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
text: Many studies have investigated the impact of zinc supplementation on children's growth, but the results have been inconsistent. To determine the effectiveness of zinc supplementation on prepubertal children's physical growth and serum zinc concentrations, we conducted a meta-analysis of randomized controlled intervention trials. A total of 33 appropriate studies were identified through MEDLINE searches and other methods, and weighted mean effect sizes were calculated using random-effects models. The results showed that zinc supplementation significantly increased height and weight increments, with effect sizes of 0.350 (95% CI: 0.189, 0.511) and 0.309 (0.178, 0.439), respectively. However, there was no significant effect of zinc on weight-for-height indexes. Zinc supplementation also led to a substantial increase in serum zinc concentrations, with an effect size of 0.820 (0.499, 1.14). The responses were stronger in children with low initial weight-for-age z scores and in those aged >6 mo with low initial height-for-age z scores. Our findings suggest that interventions to improve children's zinc nutriture should be considered in populations at risk of zinc deficiency, particularly in areas with high rates of underweight or stunting. Additionally, the population mean serum zinc concentration may serve as a useful indicator of the successful delivery and absorption of zinc supplements in children.

title: Mechanisms of Age-Related Macular Degeneration
text: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a debilitating condition that affects up to 90% of patients, is a leading cause of blindness in older populations worldwide. AMD is classified into two forms: wet and dry, based on the presence or absence of invading blood vessels in the retina. Recent advancements in understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying wet AMD have led to the development of several FDA-approved therapies. However, there are currently no approved treatments for dry AMD. This review aims to provide insight into the key effector pathways involved in the pathogenesis of both forms of AMD, with a particular focus on the defective immune modulation observed in the eye, a typically immune-privileged area. Notably, recent findings in AMD research have also revealed parallelities with other neurodegenerative disorders, highlighting a shared molecular disease pathway. Finally, the potential therapeutic intervention at specific mechanistic steps in AMD pathogenesis is discussed.

title: The N-end rule pathway regulates pathogen responses in plants.
text: To effectively counteract pathogens, plants have developed a multifaceted immune system that is tightly regulated to timely activate, appropriately duration, and adequately amplify defense programs. This complex system relies on the ubiquitin/proteasome system, which controls protein stability in eukaryotes, to coordinate plant immune responses. Specifically, we have found that the N-end rule pathway, a subset of the ubiquitin/proteasome system, plays a crucial role in regulating defense against a wide range of bacterial and fungal pathogens in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. Our results show that this pathway positively regulates the biosynthesis of plant-defense metabolites, such as glucosinolates, as well as the biosynthesis and response to the phytohormone jasmonic acid, which is a key player in plant immunity. Additionally, our findings suggest that the arginylation branch of the N-end rule pathway regulates the timing and amplitude of the defense program against the model pathogen Pseudomonas syringae AvrRpm1.

title: H3K9 demethylase KDM4E is an epigenetic regulator for bovine embryonic development and a defective factor for nuclear reprogramming.
text: Abnormal epigenetic reprogramming often leads to developmental abnormalities in embryos derived from somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) during embryonic genome activation (EGA). In bovine eight-cell SCNT embryos, there is a global pattern of hypermethylation of histone H3 lysine 9 tri- and dimethylation (H3K9me3/2), but the underlying cause remains elusive. In this study, we investigate the role of two histone H3 lysine 9 demethylase genes, lysine-specific demethylase 4D (KDM4D) and 4E (KDM4E), in active H3K9me3/2 demethylation in in vitro fertilized (IVF) embryos and their deficient expression in cloned embryos at the time of EGA. Our findings show that KDM4E plays a more critical role in IVF and SCNT embryonic development, and overexpression of KDM4E can restore the global transcriptome, improve blastocyst formation, and increase the cloning efficiency of SCNT embryos. These results suggest that KDM4E acts as a crucial epigenetic regulator of EGA and a deficient factor responsible for persisting H3K9me3/2 barriers to SCNT-mediated reprogramming. Additionally, we find that interactions between RNA and KDM4E are essential for H3K9 demethylation during EGA. These discoveries expand our understanding of incomplete nuclear reprogramming and have significant implications for the production of transgenic livestock.

title: Risk of gestational hypertension in relation to folic acid supplementation during pregnancy.
text: The researchers examined the relationship between folic acid supplementation and gestational hypertension. The study population consisted of women in the United States and Canada who were part of the Slone Epidemiology Center Birth Defects Study between 1993 and 2000. Women were interviewed within six months after delivery regarding sociodemographic and medical factors, as well as the occurrence of hypertension with or without preeclampsia, and multivitamin use during pregnancy. The relative risks, adjusted for factors such as weight, parity, twin pregnancy, diabetes, smoking, education, and family income, were estimated using Cox regression models. Of 2,100 women, 204 (9.7%) reported gestational hypertension (onset after week 20 of gestation). The multivariate-adjusted relative risk of developing gestational hypertension during the month when folic acid supplementation was used compared to not using folic acid during that same month was 0.55 (95% confidence interval: 0.39, 0.79). These findings suggest that folic acid-containing multivitamins may reduce the risk of gestational hypertension.

title: Aire regulates negative selection of organ-specific T cells
text: Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1 (APS-1) is a rare genetic disorder that results from mutations in the AIRE gene, leading to deficient tolerance mechanisms. APS-1 is characterized by a range of autoimmune diseases affecting different organs, including the pancreas. Currently, it is unclear what specific mechanisms are impaired in APS-1 due to AIRE mutations. To investigate, we examined the fate of autoreactive CD4+ T cells with high affinity for a pancreatic antigen in transgenic mice with an Aire mutation. Our findings reveal a near-complete failure of the thymus to delete organ-specific cells in the presence of an Aire mutation. This suggests that the central mechanism for deleting forbidden T cell clones is crucial for preventing autoimmune diseases, such as APS-1. In other words, the failure of this mechanism leads to the development of autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome 1.

title: Extracellular Acidic pH Activates the Sterol Regulatory Element-Binding Protein 2 to Promote Tumor Progression.
text: The tumor microenvironment's acidic conditions, such as hypoxia and nutrient scarcity, significantly impact cancer progression. However, the role of acidic extracellular pH in cancer progression has been overlooked compared to hypoxia. Our study reveals that an acidic extracellular pH (pH 6.8) triggers the activation of sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2 (SREBP2) through nuclear translocation and promoter binding to its targets, alongside intracellular acidification. Intriguingly, inhibiting SREBP2, but not SREBP1, hinders the upregulation of low pH-induced cholesterol biosynthesis-related genes. Moreover, acyl-CoA synthetase short-chain family member 2 (ACSS2), a direct SREBP2 target, provided a growth advantage to cancer cells under acidic pH. Furthermore, acidic pH-responsive SREBP2 target genes were associated with poorer overall survival in cancer patients. Our findings demonstrate that SREBP2 is a crucial transcriptional regulator of metabolic genes and cancer cell progression, mainly in response to extracellular acidification.

title: Mutation of the Human Circadian Clock Gene CRY1 in Familial Delayed Sleep Phase Disorder
text: Daily patterns of human activity are regulated by an internal biological clock that naturally oscillates at a rate of approximately 24 hours. This internal clock, known as the circadian system, controls various physiological and behavioral processes. However, in some individuals, this system is disrupted, leading to delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD), a common form of insomnia characterized by misaligned sleep episodes. Researchers have now identified a genetic mutation associated with this disorder, found in a dominant variation of the core circadian clock gene CRY1. This altered gene produces an enhanced transcriptional inhibitor that disrupts the normal functioning of other clock proteins, Clock and Bmal1, leading to reduced expression of key transcriptional targets and longer circadian molecular rhythms. The frequency of this mutation is estimated to be up to 0.6%, and subsequent studies of unrelated families suggest that it contributes to late and/or fragmented sleep patterns in a significant portion of the population. This discovery provides clues into the underlying mechanisms of DSPD and may lead to the development of new treatments for this common sleep disorder.

title: Lateral Hypothalamic Signaling Mechanisms Underlying Feeding Stimulation: Differential Contributions of Src Family Tyrosine Kinases to Feeding Triggered Either by NMDA Injection or by Food Deprivation
text: In rats, researchers can experimentally trigger feeding using several methods. Two of these methods are food deprivation and injecting the neurotransmitter l-glutamate (Glu) or its receptor agonist NMDA into the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA). When NMDA is injected into the LHA, the NMDA receptor (NMDA-R) within the LHA is critical for transmitting signals encoded by Glu and stimulating feeding. However, the specific mechanisms involved in this process are unclear. To investigate, researchers examined the role of protein-tyrosine kinases (PTKs) in LHA feeding mechanisms. They found that injections of PTK inhibitors into the LHA significantly suppressed feeding elicited by LHA NMDA injection (up to 69%) but only mildly suppressed deprivation feeding (24%). This suggests that PTKs may play a less critical role in signals underlying this type of feeding behavior.
