In contrast, food deprivation, but not NMDA injection, led to significant increases in the activity of Src PTKs and the expression of Pyk2, an Src-activating PTK. These results demonstrate that while it is easier to suppress NMDA-elicited feeding by PTK inhibitors, food deprivation more readily activates PTKs in vivo. These findings also suggest that using only one feeding stimulation paradigm may underestimate the contributions of signaling molecules to feeding pathways in vivo.

title: Relationship between advanced glycation end‐product accumulation and low skeletal muscle mass in Japanese men and women
text:
The present study aimed to investigate the relationship between advanced glycation end-product accumulation and skeletal muscle mass among middle-aged and older Japanese men and women.
METHODS: A total of 132 participants enrolled in this cross-sectional study. Skin autofluorescence was assessed as a measure of advanced glycation-end products. Appendicular skeletal muscle mass was measured using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, and skeletal muscle index was calculated by dividing appendicular skeletal muscle mass by height squared. Participants were divided into two groups (low skeletal muscle index and normal skeletal muscle index) using the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia's skeletal muscle index criteria for diagnosing sarcopenia. Multivariate logistic regression analysis and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve were used to determine significant factors associated with low skeletal muscle index.
RESULTS: Participants consisted of 70 men (mean age 57 ± 10 years) and 62 women (mean age 60 ± 11 years). There were 31 and 101 participants in the low and normal skeletal muscle index groups, respectively. Skin autofluorescence was significantly higher in the low skeletal muscle index group compared with the normal skeletal muscle index group (P < 0.01). Skin autofluorescence was a significant independent factor associated with low skeletal muscle index based on multivariate logistic regression analysis (odds ratio 15.7, 95% confidence interval 1.85-133.01; P = 0.012). The cut-off for skin autofluorescence was 2.45 arbitrary units, with a sensitivity of 0.75 and specificity of 0.91.
CONCLUSIONS: Skin autofluorescence was an independent factor associated with low skeletal muscle index among middle-aged and older Japanese men and women. The cut-off for skin autofluorescence as a predictor of low skeletal muscle index was 2.45 arbitrary units.

title: Large-Scale Profiling Reveals the Influence of Genetic Variation on Gene Expression in Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells.
text: In this investigation, we employed whole-genome sequencing and gene expression profiling of 215 human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines from various donors to identify genetic variants associated with RNA expression for 5,746 genes. We were able to predict causal variants for these expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) that disrupt transcription factor binding and experimentally validated a subset of them. Moreover, we identified copy-number variant (CNV) eQTLs, including some that appear to affect gene expression by altering the copy number of intergenic regulatory regions. Additionally, we observed effects of rare genic CNVs and regulatory single-nucleotide variants on gene expression, and found that reactivation of gene expression on the X chromosome depends on the position of the gene on the chromosome. Our findings emphasize the utility of iPSCs for genetic association analyses and provide a valuable resource for investigating the genetic regulation of gene expression in pluripotent cells.

title: Ethanol extract of Allium fistulosum inhibits development of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
text:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a major cause of chronic liver disease and is closely linked to metabolic syndrome. In this study, we investigated the effectiveness of ethanol extract of Allium fistulosum (EAF) in preventing NAFLD and explored the possibility of using EAF as a natural product for developing new treatments for NAFLD.
MATERIALS/METHODS We evaluated the preventive effect of EAF on hepatic lipid accumulation using an oleic acid (OA)-induced NAFLD model in vitro and a Western diet (high-fat high-sucrose; WD)-induced obese mouse model. The study included three groups of mice (n = 7): normal diet group (ND), WD group, and WD plus 1% EAF group.
RESULTS Our results showed that EAF reduced OA-stimulated lipid accumulation in HepG2 cells without causing cellular toxicity and significantly inhibited the transcriptional activation of sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 and fatty acid synthase genes. We then examined these effects in vivo by administering EAF to mice fed either a normal or high-fat diet. Compared to normal diet controls, mice fed a high-fat diet exhibited increased body weight, liver weight, epididymal fat weight, and liver fat accumulation, which were significantly attenuated by EAF supplementation.
CONCLUSIONS Our findings suggest that Allium fistulosum attunes the development of NAFLD and EAF exhibits anti-lipogenic activity in the liver. Therefore, EAF represents a promising candidate for developing novel drugs or drug combinations for the prevention and treatment of NAFLD.

title: Cardiovascular risk factors in childhood and carotid artery intima-media thickness in adulthood: the Cardiovascular Risk in Young Finns Study.
text:
In this study, the researchers investigated the relationship between cardiovascular risk factors measured in childhood and adolescence and the development of atherosclerosis in young adulthood. The study included 2229 white adults aged 24-39 years who were examined in childhood and adolescence between 1980 and 1992, and reexamined 21 years later between 2001 and 2002. The researchers measured common carotid artery intima-media thickness (IMT), a marker of preclinical atherosclerosis, in adulthood.
The study found that childhood levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), systolic blood pressure, body mass index, and smoking were associated with adult carotid IMT in multivariable models adjusted for age and sex. The number of risk factors measured in 12- to 18-year-old adolescents, including high levels of LDL-C, systolic blood pressure, body mass index, and cigarette smoking, were directly related to carotid IMT measured in young adults at ages 33-39 years, and remained significant after adjustment for contemporaneous risk variables. The study found that the number of risk factors measured at ages 3 to 9 years demonstrated a weak direct relationship with carotid IMT at ages 24-30 years in men but not in women.
These findings suggest that exposure to cardiovascular risk factors early in life may induce changes in the arteries that contribute to the development of atherosclerosis. The study highlights the importance of identifying and addressing cardiovascular risk factors early in life to prevent the progression of atherosclerosis and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease later in life.

title: MicroRNA-29 induces cellular senescence in aging muscle through multiple signaling pathways
text: The underlying mechanisms of muscle atrophy that occur with aging are still unclear. Through microRNA array and individual qPCR analyses, we discovered a significant up-regulation of miR-29 in muscles of aged rodents compared to young ones. With aging, the levels of p85α, IGF-1, and B-myb in muscles were lower, while the expression of certain cell cycle proteins (p53, p16, and pRB) increased. When miR-29 was expressed in muscle progenitor cells (MPCs), their proliferation was impaired, and SA-βgal expression increased, indicating the development of senescence. The impaired MPC proliferation was caused by interactions between miR-29 and the 3'-UTR of p85α, IGF-1, and B-myb, suppressing the translation of these mediators of myoblast proliferation. In vivo, electroporation of miR-29 into muscles of young mice suppressed the proliferation and increased the levels of cellular arrest proteins, recapitulating aging-induced responses in muscle. A potential stimulus for miR-29 expression is Wnt-3a, as we found that exogenous Wnt-3a stimulated miR-29 expression by 2.7-fold in primary cultures of MPCs. Therefore, aging-induced muscle senescence results from the activation of miR-29 by Wnt-3a, leading to suppressed expression of several signaling proteins (p85α, IGF-1, and B-myb) that coordinate to impair the proliferation of MPCs, contributing to muscle atrophy. The increase in miR-29 provides a potential mechanism for aging-induced sarcopenia.

title: Rictor, a Novel Binding Partner of mTOR, Defines a Rapamycin-Insensitive and Raptor-Independent Pathway that Regulates the Cytoskeleton
text: The mammalian TOR (mTOR) pathway integrates signals from nutrients and growth factors to regulate cell growth, the process by which cells increase in mass and size. mTOR is a large protein kinase and the target of rapamycin, an immunosuppressant with potential anti-cancer applications. mTOR interacts with the raptor and GbetaL proteins to form a complex that is targeted by rapamycin. We have found that mTOR is also part of a distinct complex defined by the novel protein rictor (rapamycin-insensitive companion of mTOR). Rictor shares similarities with previous proteins discovered in D. discoidieum, S. pombe, and S. cerevisiae, including pianissimo, STE20p, and AVO3p. Interestingly, AVO3p is part of a rapamycin-insensitive TOR complex that does not contain the yeast homolog of raptor and signals to the actin cytoskeleton through PKC1. Consistent with this finding, the rictor-containing mTOR complex contains GbetaL but not raptor and does not regulate the mTOR effector S6K1 or bind to FKBP12-rapamycin. Our results suggest that the rictor-mTOR complex modulates the phosphorylation of Protein Kinase C alpha (PKCalpha) and the actin cytoskeleton, indicating that this aspect of TOR signaling is conserved between yeast and mammals.

title: Activation of the estrogen receptor through phosphorylation by mitogen-activated protein kinase.
text: The phosphorylation of the human estrogen receptor (ER) at serine residue 118 is crucial for the full activation of its activation function 1 (AF-1). This serine is phosphorylated by mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) in both in vitro and in vivo studies, using epidermal growth factor (EGF) and insulin-like growth factor (IGF) as stimuli. Overexpression of MAPK kinase (MAPKK) or the guanine nucleotide binding protein Ras, which activates MAPK, leads to increased estrogen-induced and tamoxifen-induced transcriptional activity in wild-type ER, but not in a mutant ER with an alanine at Ser118. This suggests that the activity of the amino-terminal AF-1 of the ER is modulated by the phosphorylation of Ser118 through the Ras-MAPK cascade of growth factor signaling pathways.

title: Regulation of the antimicrobial response by NLR proteins.
text:
Nucleotide-binding, oligomerization domain (NOD)-like receptor (NLR) proteins are a crucial component of the innate immune system, playing a central role in detecting microbial infections and triggering an appropriate response. Dysregulation of NLR function has been linked to both infectious and autoimmune diseases in animals and humans. Although significant progress has been made in understanding NLR function and interactions, many aspects of their mechanisms of sensing, downstream signaling, and in vivo functions remain unclear. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of key NLR family members, their activation by diverse microorganisms, downstream effector functions, and interactions with other innate sensor protein families. Additionally, the review will discuss the role of microbial sensing by NLR receptors in activating the adaptive immune response, which collaborates in the antimicrobial defense.


In this review, we focus on several key NLR family members, including NOD1, NOD2, and NLRC4, which recognize a wide range of microbial pathogens and play a crucial role in initiating the immune response. We also examine the various downstream effector functions mediated by NLR proteins, including the activation of inflammatory responses, cytokine production, and the activation of the adaptive immune system. Furthermore, we discuss the complex interplay between NLR proteins and other innate sensor protein families, such as the pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) and the Toll-like receptors (TLRs).


The activation of NLR proteins by microbial pathogens leads to the recruitment of adaptive immune cells to the site of infection, facilitating the elimination of the pathogen through a coordinated and efficient immune response. This process is critical for the control of infection and the prevention of disease, and dysregulation of NLR function can lead to impaired immune function and increased susceptibility to infection.


In conclusion, NLR proteins play a pivotal role in the early detection of microbial infections and the initiation of a coordinated immune response. Although significant progress has been made in understanding the mechanisms of NLR function, many aspects of these processes remain unclear, highlighting the need for further research into the complex and multifactorial interactions involved in the immune response. By gaining a deeper understanding of NLR function and its interactions with other immune proteins, we may be able to develop novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of infectious and autoimmune diseases.

title: Acetylcysteine for prevention of acute deterioration of renal function following elective coronary angiography and intervention: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
The antioxidant acetylcysteine has been shown to prevent acute contrast nephrotoxicity in patients with impaired renal function undergoing computed tomography scans. However, its effectiveness in preventing deterioration in renal function during coronary angiography is uncertain.
To investigate the preventive role of oral acetylcysteine in patients with moderate renal insufficiency undergoing elective coronary angiography, a prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was conducted from May 2000 to December 2001 at the Grantham Hospital at the University of Hong Kong.
Recruiting 200 Chinese patients aged 68 years ( Mean ± SD, 68 ± 6.5 years) with stable moderate renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance <60 mL/min [1.00 mL/s]), we randomly assigned participants to receive either oral acetylcysteine (600 mg twice daily; n = 102) or matching placebo tablets (n = 98) on the day before and the day of angiography. All patients received a low-osmolality contrast agent.
The primary outcome measure was the occurrence of a more than 25% increase in serum creatinine level within 48 hours after contrast administration. Secondary outcome measures included changes in creatinine clearance and serum creatinine level.
The results showed that 12 control patients (12%) and 4 acetylcysteine patients (4%) developed a more than 25% increase in serum creatinine level within 48 hours after contrast administration (relatively, 0.32; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.10-0.96; P =.03). In addition, serum creatinine levels were lower in the acetylcysteine group (Mean ± SD, 1.22 mg/dL [107.8 micromol/L]; 95% CI, 1.11-1.33 mg/dL vs 1.38 mg/dL [122.9 micromol/L]; 95% CI, 1.27-1.49 mg/dL; P =.006) during the first 48 hours after angiography. Furthermore, acetylcysteine treatment significantly increased creatinine clearance from 44.8 mL/min (0.75 mL/s) (95% CI, 42.7-47.6 mL/min) to 58.9 mL/min (0.98 mL/s) (95% CI, 55.6-62.3 mL/min) two days after the contrast administration (P <.001). The increase in creatinine clearance was not significant in the control group (from 42.1 to 44.1 mL/min [0.70 to 0.74 mL/s]; P =.15).
Interestingly, the benefit of acetylcysteine was consistent among various patient subgroups and persisted for at least 7 days. More importantly, no major treatment-related adverse events were observed.
In conclusion, our findings suggest that acetylcysteine protects patients with moderate chronic renal insufficiency from contrast-induced deterioration in renal function after coronary angiographic procedures, with minimal adverse effects and at a low cost.

title: DNA Methylation in the Human Cerebral Cortex Is Dynamically Regulated throughout the Life Span and Involves Differentiated Neurons
text: The role of DNA cytosine methylation, an epigenetic regulator of chromatin structure and function, in normal and pathological brain development and aging remains unclear. Here, we investigated the DNA methylation status at 50 loci, including 5' CpG islands of genes related to central nervous system (CNS) growth and development, in temporal neocortex samples from 125 subjects ranging in age from 17 weeks gestation to 104 years old. Two psychiatric disease cohorts—defined by chronic neurodegeneration (Alzheimer's) or lack thereof (schizophrenia)—were included. Our results revealed a robust and progressive increase in DNA methylation levels across the lifespan for 8 of the 50 loci (GABRA2, GAD1, HOXA1, NEUROD1, NEUROD2, PGR, STK11, SYK), typically accompanied by decreasing levels of the corresponding mRNAs. Additionally, 16 loci showed a sharp rise in DNA methylation levels within the first few months or years after birth. Limited changes were observed in the Alzheimer's cohort, which may reflect an acceleration of the age-related change in normal brain. Furthermore, methylation studies on sorted nuclei provided evidence for bidirectional methylation events in cortical neurons during the transition from childhood to advanced age, as reflected by significant increases at 3 and a decrease at 1 of 10 loci. Finally, the de novo DNA methyltransferase DNMT3a was expressed across all ages, including a subset of neurons residing in layers III and V of the mature cortex. Overall, our findings suggest that DNA methylation is dynamically regulated in the human cerebral cortex throughout the lifespan, involves differentiated neurons, and affects a substantial portion of genes by an age-related increase.

title: Mulberry leaves (Morus alba L.) ameliorate obesity-induced hepatic lipogenesis, fibrosis, and oxidative stress in high-fat diet-fed mice
text: The text you provided discusses the association of obesity with various chronic diseases, such as fatty liver, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and severe metabolic syndrome. The study investigates the effect of mulberry leaf extract (MLE) on obesity-induced oxidative stress, lipogenesis, and fibrosis in the liver of mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD). The results show that MLE treatment significantly improves the markers of LXRα-mediated lipogenesis and hepatic fibrosis, such as α-smooth muscle actin, while up-regulating lipolysis-associated markers like lipoprotein lipase. Additionally, MLE normalizes the activities of antioxidant enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 and glutathione peroxidase, and reduces the protein levels of 4-hydroxynonenal in the HFD-fed mice. The study suggests that MLE has beneficial effects on obesity-related fatty liver disease by regulating hepatic lipid metabolism, fibrosis, and antioxidant defense system. The findings imply that MLE supplementation may be a potential therapeutic approach for obesity-related diseases, including non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).

title: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors and the risk of hip fractures in elderly patients.
text:
Recent animal studies have shown that 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) lipid-lowering drugs (statins) significantly increase bone formation in animals. However, it is unknown whether statin use in humans results in clinically meaningful bone formation or a reduction in the risk of osteoporotic fractures. To investigate this, we conducted a case-control study of 6110 New Jersey residents aged 65 years or older, comparing patients who had undergone surgical repair of a hip fracture (cases) with age- and sex-matched controls.
We found that use of statins in the prior 180 days or 3 years was associated with a significant reduction in the risk of hip fracture, even after controlling for various demographic and clinical characteristics, including race, insurance status, psychoactive medications, estrogen and thiazide use, ischemic heart disease, cancer, and diabetes mellitus. Specifically, the adjusted odds ratio (OR) for hip fracture was 0.50 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.33-0.76) for statin use in the prior 180 days, and 0.57 (95% CI, 0.40-0.82) for use in the prior 3 years. There was no significant relationship observed between use of nonstatin lipid-lowering agents and hip fracture risk.
The relationship between statin use and hip fracture risk persisted after controlling for additional variables, such as the number of medications, the Charlson comorbidity index score, and hospitalization or nursing home stay in the last 180 days. Excluding patients who were in a nursing home prior to their index date or who died in the year after their index date did not affect the results. Use of nonstatin lipid-lowering agents was not observed to be associated with a reduction in hip fracture risk in any of these alternative models or analyses. In conclusion, our findings support an association between statin use by elderly patients and a reduction in the risk of hip fracture. Further controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings and to exclude the possibility of unmeasured confounders.

title: The quality of modern cross-sectional ecologic studies: a bibliometric review.
text:
Despite its limitations, the ecological study design is widely used by epidemiologists. However, the challenges associated with this design remain unclear, and its application in epidemiological research remains unassessed. This bibliometric review aimed to critically evaluate the characteristics, statistical methods, and reporting of results of modern cross-sectional ecological studies.
A systematic search of 6 major epidemiology journals identified all cross-sectional ecological studies published since January 1, 2000. A total of 125 articles were assessed according to standardized evaluation criteria, revealing several issues with the studies' methods and reporting. Specifically, a significant proportion of studies used unreliable methods (64%) or contained statistical oversights (20%). Moreover, many authors did not properly adjust their outcomes for age or sex (31%), and statistical validity was a potential issue for 20% of regression models. Simple linear regression was the most common analytic approach (31%). Furthermore, many authors omitted important information when discussing the ecological nature of their study (31%), the choice of study design (58%), and the susceptibility of their research to the ecological fallacy (49%).
These findings suggest that there is a need for internationally standardized guidelines for reporting ecological studies. Additionally, greater attention should be given to the relevant biostatistical literature to improve the quality of these studies.

title: Efficacy of Beta1 Integrin and EGFR Targeting in Sphere-Forming Human Head and Neck Cancer Cells
text:
Background: Resistance to radiotherapy remains a significant obstacle in the treatment of cancer, including head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). It has been shown that simultaneous targeting of β1 integrin and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) can exhibit a higher radiosensitizing potential than monotherapy in most HNSCC cancer models. However, the mechanisms underlying this resistance are not fully understood, and tumor-initiating cells (TICs) are thought to play a crucial role in therapy resistance and recurrence. This study investigated the efficacy of targeting β1 integrin/EGFR in combination with X-ray irradiation on the behavior of sphere-forming cells (SFC), which are enriched in TICs.
Methods: HNSCC cell lines (UTSCC15, UTSCC5, Cal33, SAS) were injected subcutaneously into nude mice for tumor take and then plated for primary and secondary sphere formation under non-adhesive conditions, which is believed to enrich for SFC and their self-renewal capacity, respectively. Treatment involved inhibitory antibodies for β1 integrin (AIIB2) and EGFR (Cetuximab) as well as X-ray irradiation (2-6 Gy single doses). Additionally, flow cytometry for TIC marker expression and cell cycle analysis as well as Western blotting for DNA repair protein expression and phosphorylation were performed.
Results: Our findings indicated that the SAS cell line exhibited higher primary and secondary sphere forming capacity compared to other HNSCC cell lines, which was consistent with the tumor take rates of SAS versus UTSCC15 cells. AIIB2 and Cetuximab treatment had minimal cytotoxic and no radiosensitizing effects on SFC. Interestingly, secondary SAS spheres, representing the fraction of surviving SFC after passaging, showed significantly enhanced radiosensitivity compared to primary spheres. However, neither AIIB2 nor Cetuximab significantly altered basal sphere forming capacity and radiosensitivity. Moreover, an increased accumulation of G0/G1 phase cells was observed in secondary SAS spheres, and DNA double-strand break repair showed no difference in ATM and Chk2 dephosphorylation upon irradiation.
Conclusions: In the HNSCC model, sphere-forming conditions select for cells that are resistant to both anti-β1 integrin and anti-EGFR inhibitory antibodies. Our data suggest that primary and secondary sphere formation involve distinct survival strategies independent of β1 integrin and EGFR, and further research is warranted to elucidate the underlying mechanisms for identifying novel, druggable cancer targets in SFC.

title: Anxiety
text: Objective: To evaluate the impact of routinely administered psychiatric questionnaires on the diagnosis, management, and outcomes of psychiatric disorders in non-psychiatric settings. Data Sources: Embase, Medline, PsycLIT, Cinahl, Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, and hand searches of key journals. Methods: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials examining the administration and feedback of psychiatric questionnaires to clinicians in non-psychiatric settings. The review included a narrative overview of study design and endpoints, as well as a random effects quantitative synthesis of comparable studies. Main Outcome Measures: Recognition of psychiatric disorders after feedback of questionnaire results, interventions for psychiatric disorders, and outcome of psychiatric disorders. Results: Nine randomized studies were identified that examined the use of common psychiatric instruments in primary care and general hospital settings. Meta-analytic pooling was possible for four of these studies (2457 participants), which measured the effect of feedback on the recognition of depressive disorders. The results showed that routine administration and feedback of scores for all patients, regardless of score, did not significantly increase the overall rate of recognition of mental disorders such as anxiety and depression (relative risk of detection of depression by clinician after feedback = 0.95, 95% confidence interval = 0.83 to 1.09). Two studies showed that routine administration followed by selective feedback for only high scorers increased the rate of recognition of depression (relative risk of detection of depression after feedback = 2.64, 1.62 to 4.31). However, this increased recognition did not translate into an increased rate of intervention. Overall, studies of routine administration of psychiatric measures did not show an effect on patient outcome. Conclusions: The routine measurement of outcome is a costly exercise with little evidence of benefit in improving psychosocial outcomes of those with psychiatric disorder managed in non-psychiatric settings.

title: The challenges of overcoming antibiotic resistance: Plant extracts as potential sources of antimicrobial and resistance modifying agents
text: The issue of antibiotic resistance, which has restricted the use of affordable and older antibiotics, has led to the need for continued research into new antimicrobial compounds. Understanding the mechanisms of resistance is crucial in developing strategies to address this problem. Antibiotic-resistant bacteria employ various strategies, including active drug efflux, alteration of target sites, and enzymatic degradation, to evade antibiotics. Multi-drug resistance (MDR) pumps, capable of recognizing and expelling a variety of unrelated compounds from bacterial cells, have been characterized in many Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens, including Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli, and mycobacteria. In vitro observations have shown that some chemical compounds (MDR inhibitors or resistance modifying agents) can modify the resistance phenotype in bacteria by working synergistically with antibiotics. These compounds could be used in combination with antibiotics to overcome resistance in bacterial infections. Crude extracts of medicinal plants have been identified as a rich source of potential resistance modifying agents, particularly from the African biosphere, which boasts a diverse range of plant species.

title: The effect of N-acetylcysteine in the nucleus accumbens on neurotransmission and relapse to cocaine.
text: BACKGROUND Previous studies have shown that low levels of glutamate in the nucleus accumbens core (NAcore) can lead to increased synaptic glutamate transmission from the prefrontal cortex (PFC), resulting in relapse to cocaine seeking. Systemic N-acetylcysteine (NAC) has been found to restore glutamate homeostasis, reduce relapse to cocaine seeking, and decrease the potentiation of PFC-NAcore synapses. In this study, we investigated the effects of direct NAC application to the NAcore on relapse and synaptic transmission in PFC-NAcore synapses, as well as the involvement of metabotropic glutamate receptors 2/3 (mGluR2/3) and 5 (mGluR5). METHODS We trained rats to self-administer cocaine for two weeks and then subjected them to extinction training following NAC application. The effects of NAC were studied using in vitro whole cell recordings and primary glial cultures. RESULTS Our results show that direct NAC injection into the NAcore inhibited the reinstatement of cocaine seeking. In vitro recordings revealed that low concentrations of NAC reduced the amplitude of evoked glutamatergic synaptic currents in the NAcore in an mGluR2/3-dependent manner, while high doses of NAC increased amplitude in an mGluR5-dependent manner. Both effects required NAC uptake through cysteine transporters and activity of the cysteine/glutamate exchanger. Additionally, we found that blocking mGluR5 enhanced the inhibition of cocaine seeking by NAC. CONCLUSIONS Our findings demonstrate that the effect of NAC on relapse to cocaine seeking is dependent on the balance between mGluR2/3 and mGluR5 in the NAcore, and that simultaneous inhibition of mGluR5 can enhance the efficacy of NAC. These results provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying cocaine relapse and suggest potential new therapeutic strategies for treating cocaine addiction.

title: A phospholipid transfer function of ER-mitochondria encounter structure revealed in vitro
text:
As phospholipids are primarily synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondrial inner membranes, it is essential for cells to effectively distribute specific phospholipids to various cellular membranes in order to maintain organelle-specific phospholipid compositions. However, the mechanisms by which phospholipids are transferred between the ER and mitochondria are not well understood. The ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES), which was proposed to facilitate phospholipid transfer between these organelles, remains controversial and requires experimental verification.
To address this gap in knowledge, we developed a novel in vitro assay system using isolated yeast membrane fractions to monitor phospholipid exchange between the ER and mitochondria. Our findings reveal that phospholipid transport between these organelles depends on the structural integrity of the membranes rather than on energy sources such as ATP, GTP, or the membrane potential across the mitochondrial inner membrane. Additionally, we found that the ERMES component plays a critical role in the transport of phosphatidylserine from the ER to mitochondria, but not the transport of phosphatidylethanolamine from mitochondria to the ER.
This in vitro assay system provides a powerful tool for analyzing the non-vesicular phospholipid transport between the ER and mitochondria, illuminating the complex mechanisms by which cells distribute specific phospholipids to maintain organelle-specific compositions. Our findings have important implications for understanding how cells regulate the distribution of phospholipids within the cell, and may lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies for diseases characterized by disruptions in phospholipid metabolism.

title: An integrin β3–KRAS–RalB complex drives tumour stemness and resistance to EGFR inhibition
text:
Cancer cells with stem-like properties are extremely aggressive and often exhibit resistance to drugs. In this study, we uncovered that the integrin αvβ3 serves as a marker for breast, lung, and pancreatic carcinomas that possess stem-like properties and are highly resistant to receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as erlotinib. These findings were confirmed both in vitro and in mice that were implanted with patient-derived tumour xenografts or in clinical specimens from lung cancer patients who had developed resistance to erlotinib.
Mechanistically, when unliganded, αvβ3 recruits KRAS and RalB to the tumour cell plasma membrane, leading to the activation of TBK1 and NF-κB. In fact, the expression of αvβ3 and the subsequent activation of the KRAS–RalB–NF-κB pathway are both necessary and sufficient for tumour initiation, independence from the culture medium, self-renewal, and erlotinib resistance. Interestingly, targeting this pathway pharmacologically with bortezomib can reverse both tumour stemness and erlotinib resistance. Therefore, these findings not only identify αvβ3 as a marker/driver of carcinoma stemness but also suggest a promising therapeutic strategy to sensitize such tumours to receptor tyrosine kinase inhibition.

title: Gain of toxic Apolipoprotein E4 effects in Human iPSC-Derived Neurons Is Ameliorated by a Small-Molecule Structure Corrector
text: Tired of seeing promising drug development for Alzheimer's disease (AD) stall in human clinical trials? Take a cue from animal studies and investigate AD in human model systems. Our study leverages human neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells that express apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4), the major genetic risk factor for AD. We discovered that ApoE4-expressing neurons exhibit excessive tau phosphorylation, irrespective of their elevated production of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides. Interestingly, ApoE4 significantly increased Aβ production in human neurons, but not in mouse neurons. Curiously, converting ApoE4 to ApoE3 through gene editing reversed these detrimental effects, indicating the specific toxicity of ApoE4. Functionally, neurons lacking APOE behaved similarly to those expressing ApoE3, and introducing ApoE4 expression recapitulated pathological phenotypes. Remarkably, treating ApoE4-expressing neurons with a small-molecule structure corrector partially rescued their detrimental state, highlighting the potential of correcting the pathogenic conformation of ApoE4 as a viable therapeutic approach for ApoE4-related AD.

title: LncRNA NEAT1/let-7a-5p axis regulates the cisplatin resistance in nasopharyngeal carcinoma by targeting Rsf-1 and modulating the Ras-MAPK pathway.
text: The long non-coding RNA nuclear paraspeckle assembly transcript 1 (NEAT1) has been found to be upregulated in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) and is involved in the development of drug resistance. However, the specific mechanisms by which NEAT1 contributes to drug resistance in NPC are not yet fully understood. To investigate, the expression levels of NEAT1, let-72-5p, and Rsf-1 were analyzed in NPC cells using reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). The effects of NEAT1 and let-72-5p on cell proliferation and cisplatin resistance were evaluated using 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyl tetrazolium bromide (MTT) and 5-ethynyl-20-deoxyuridine (EdU) assays, and protein levels were examined using western blot analysis. Xenograft tumor assays were also performed to evaluate the role of NEAT1 in NPC tumor growth in vivo. The results showed that NEAT1 was upregulated and let-7a-5p was downregulated in NPC tissues and cell lines, and inhibition of NEAT1 significantly decreased cisplatin resistance in NPC cells. NEAT1 was found to interact with let-7a-5p, and a negative correlation between NEAT1 and let-7a-5p expression was observed in NPC tissues. Rsf-1 was confirmed as a target of let-7a-5p. NEAT1 significantly reversed the inhibitory effect of let-7a-5p on cisplatin resistance in NPC cells, and NEAT1 knockdown inhibited the Ras-MAPK signaling pathway in NPC cells. Furthermore, NEAT1 knockdown suppressed tumor growth in the presence of cisplatin in vivo. These findings suggest that the NEAT1/let-7a-5p axis regulates cisplatin resistance in NPC by targeting Rsf-1 and modulating the Ras-MAPK signaling pathway.

title: Antibacterial peptide microcin J25 inhibits transcription by binding within and obstructing the RNA polymerase secondary channel.
text: The antibacterial peptide microcin J25 (MccJ25) hinders bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) transcription by obstructing the RNAP secondary channel. Biochemical experiments indicate that inhibition of transcription occurs either at the level of nucleotide uptake or nucleotide binding by RNAP. Genetic results indicate that inhibition of transcription requires a long sequence of more than 50 amino acid residues within the RNAP secondary channel (also known as the "NTP-uptake channel" or "pore"). Biophysical studies show that inhibition of transcription involves the binding of MccJ25 within the RNAP secondary channel. Molecular modeling suggests that the binding of MccJ25 within the RNAP secondary channel blocks the RNAP secondary channel. We conclude that MccJ25 inhibits transcription by physically obstructing the RNAP secondary channel, effectively creating a "barrier" that prevents transcription from occurring. Disrupting the RNAP secondary channel represents a promising target for drug discovery.

title: Exploring and exploiting the systemic effects of deregulated replication licensing.
text: Maintaining the accurate propagation of genetic material is essential for proper physiological development and overall wellbeing. The replication licensing machinery plays a crucial role in ensuring that replication occurs once per cell cycle, and its proper regulation is necessary to avoid re-replication, which can lead to genomic instability and increase the risk of cancer. This review discusses the mechanistic basis of replication licensing deregulation and its systemic effects, including its role in carcinogenesis and various genetic syndromes. Additionally, recent findings have revealed that above a certain threshold, the replication licensing factor Cdc6 acts as a global transcriptional regulator, highlighting new areas of research. The role of the putative replication licensing factor ChlR1/DDX11, mutated in the Warsaw Breakage Syndrome, in cancer is also examined. Finally, the potential therapeutic advantages of targeting replication licensing factors, with a focus on Cdc6, are discussed.

title: Regulatory principles of pluripotency: from the ground state up.
text: Pluripotency, the remarkable ability of a single cell to generate all the specialized cell types of an adult organism, can be endlessly replicated through the derivation of self-renewing embryonic stem cells (ESCs). This platform provides an invaluable opportunity to investigate cell fate decisions and diseases. Recent breakthroughs have shown that altering specific signaling cues can cause ESCs to enter a uniform "ground state" of pluripotency that more closely resembles the pluripotent naive epiblast. Here, we discuss the external and internal regulatory mechanisms that govern pluripotency and ponder the emerging spectrum of pluripotent states.

title: Neonatal Mortality Levels for 193 Countries in 2009 with Trends since 1990: A Systematic Analysis of Progress, Projections, and Priorities
text:
Studies on childhood mortality have traditionally focused on infant and under-five mortality rates, with limited attention given to neonatal mortality (deaths within the first 28 days of life). However, neonatal mortality accounts for approximately 41% of all child deaths. To better assess progress, we developed annual estimates for neonatal mortality rates (NMRs) and neonatal deaths for 193 countries from 1990 to 2009, with forecasts into the future.
We compiled a comprehensive database of mortality in neonates and children (<5 years) containing 3,551 country-years of data. While reliable civil registration data was available for 38 countries from 1990 to 2009, a statistical model was used to estimate NMRs for the remaining 155 countries, with country consultation conducted to identify data inputs and review estimates. In 2009, an estimated 3.3 million babies died in the first month of life, compared to 4.6 million neonatal deaths in 1990. More than half of all neonatal deaths occurred in five countries: India (27.8% of global livebirths), Nigeria (7.2%), Pakistan (6.9%), China (6.4%), and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (4.6%). From 1990 to 2009, the global NMR declined by 28%, from 33.2 deaths per 1,000 livebirths to 23.9. However, the proportion of child deaths that occur in the neonatal period increased in all regions of the world, and globally, neonatal mortality now accounts for 41% of all child deaths. While some regions saw significant reductions in NMR (halving in some regions), progress has been slowest in regions with high NMRs, highlighting the need for more effective global health programs to address neonatal deaths if the Millennium Development Goal 4 (two-thirds reduction in child mortality) is to be achieved.

title: Neuroprotective Effects of Four Phenylethanoid Glycosides on H2O2-Induced Apoptosis on PC12 Cells via the Nrf2/ARE Pathway
text: Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) is a crucial transcription factor in protecting against oxidative stress and neurodegenerative diseases. The phenylethanoid glycosides (PhGs), including salidroside, acteoside, isoacteoside, and echinacoside, have been shown to display antioxidant and neuroprotective properties. The current study aimed to investigate the neuroprotective effect and molecular mechanism of PhGs, specifically focusing on their interaction with Nrf2. Our results demonstrate that PhGs pre-treatment significantly suppressed oxidative stress-induced cytotoxicity in PC12 cells by promoting the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and reversing the downregulated expression of heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutamate cysteine ligase-catalytic subunit (GCLC), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit (GCLM). Silencing Nrf2 or inhibiting HO-1 with zinc protoporphyrin (ZnPP) abolished the neuroprotective effect of PhGs. Our findings suggest that PhGs may interact with the Keap1-activated Nrf2/ARE pathway, with the glycosides content influencing the potency of the neuroprotective effect. These findings support the hypothesis that PhGs act as direct activators of Nrf2.

title: Mortality risk attributable to high and low ambient temperature: a multicountry observational study
text:
Background: While previous studies have estimated the number of premature deaths attributable to either hot or cold temperatures in specific countries, no study has assessed the total mortality burden from non-optimum ambient temperatures across different climates. We aimed to calculate the total mortality burden attributable to non-optimum temperature, as well as the relative contributions from heat and cold and from moderate and extreme temperatures.
Methods: We collected data on mortality rates for 384 locations across 11 countries, including Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Taiwan, and the UK. We used a standard time-series Poisson model for each location, controlling for trends and day of the week. We estimated temperature-mortality associations using a distributed lag non-linear model with 21 days of lag and pooled the results in a multivariate metaregression that included country indicators and temperature average and range. We calculated attributable deaths for heat and cold, defined as temperatures above and below the optimum temperature, and for moderate and extreme temperatures, defined using cutoffs at the 2·5th and 97·5th temperature percentiles.
Findings: We analyzed 74,225,200 deaths across various periods between 1985 and 2012. In total, 7·71% (95% empirical CI 7·43-7·91) of mortality was attributable to non-optimum temperature in the selected countries during the study period, with notable variations between countries, ranging from 3·37% (3·06 to 3·63) in Thailand to 11·00% (9·29 to 12·47) in China. The temperature percentile of minimum mortality varied from roughly the 60th percentile in tropical areas to about the 80-90th percentile in temperate regions. More temperature-attributable deaths were caused by cold (7·29%, 7·02-7·49) than by heat (0·42%, 0·39-0·44). Extreme cold and hot temperatures were responsible for 0·86% (0·84-0·87) of total mortality.
Interpretation: Our findings reveal that most of the temperature-related mortality burden was attributable to the contribution of cold temperatures. The effect of extreme temperature was significantly less than that attributable to milder but non-optimum weather. These results have important implications for the development of public-health interventions to minimize the health consequences of adverse temperatures, as well as predictions of future effects in climate-change scenarios. Funding: This study was funded by the UK Medical Research Council.

title: Survivin is not required for the endomitotic cell cycle of megakaryocytes.
text:
The chromosome passenger complex, which includes survivin, plays a crucial role in ensuring proper alignment, separation, and cytokinesis during cell division. Survivin is particularly important for the proliferation and survival of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. However, the extent to which survivin is necessary for endomitosis (the process of polyploidization) of megakaryocytes is still a topic of debate.
To investigate the role of survivin in megakaryocyte polyploidization, we analyzing mice with a megakaryocyte-specific deletion of survivin. PF4-Cre/survivin(fl/fl) mice had normal platelet counts and megakaryocytes that reached comparable ploidy states to those of control mice. The CD41(+) cells within these mice showed minimal excisions but increased annexin V staining, suggesting that survivin is required for the survival of megakaryocyte progenitors in vivo. In contrast, megakaryocytes that were genetically modified to lack survivin exhibited robust excisions and an increased degree of polyploidization when studied ex vivo.
Our findings demonstrate that survivin is essential for the survival of megakaryocyte progenitors, but is not required for polyploidization of committed megakaryocytes.

title: β1 integrin mediates an alternative survival pathway in breast cancer cells resistant to lapatinib
text:
The overexpression of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) in 20% of breast cancer tumors has led to the widespread use of HER2-targeted therapies, such as trastuzumab (T) and lapatinib (L). However, these drugs are only partially effective in treating resistant tumors. In this study, we investigated the role of β1 integrin in mediating resistance to L and LT in HER2-overexpressing breast cancer cells.
We established a panel of HER2-overexpressing cell lines that were resistant to L, T, and the LT combination after long-term exposure. We validated these models in three-dimensional (3D) culture and found that the cells were resistant to HER2 and β1 integrin inhibitors. To identify the downstream kinases involved in β1 integrin-mediated resistance, we treated the cells with siRNA against β1 or pharmacological inhibitors of focal adhesion kinase (FAK) and examined their growth inhibitory effects.
Our results showed that β1 integrin-mediated resistance to L and LT involves the upregulation of FAK and other downstream kinases, which abrogates the inhibition of EGFR/HER1, HER2, and HER3. In contrast, trastuzumab-resistant cells showed only modest growth inhibition in response to β1 inhibition.
Our findings suggest that inhibition of β1 integrin or its downstream signaling pathways may be an effective strategy to overcome acquired resistance to HER2-targeted therapies in breast cancer. These results support the clinical investigation of β1 integrin inhibitors as a potential combination therapy with HER2-targeted drugs.

title: Incidence and Trends of Sepsis in US Hospitals Using Clinical vs Claims Data, 2009-2014
text:
The incidence of sepsis is increasing, according to claims-based estimates, while mortality rates from sepsis are decreasing, according to clinical data from electronic health records (EHRs). However, these estimates may lack clinical fidelity due to changes in diagnosis and coding practices over time. To overcome these limitations, this study aimed to estimate the US national incidence of sepsis and trends using detailed clinical data from EHR systems of diverse hospitals.
Using a retrospective cohort study design, the researchers analyzed clinical data from 409 academic, community, and federal hospitals between 2009 and 2014. They identified 173,690 sepsis cases (mean age = 66.5, 42.4% female) among 2,901,019 adults admitted to these hospitals in 2014 (6.0% incidence). Of these, 26,061 (15.0%) died in the hospital, and 10,731 (6.2%) were discharged to hospice.
The study found that sepsis incidence using clinical criteria was stable (0.6% relative change per year, P = .67), while incidence per claims increased significantly (10.3%/y, P < .001). In-hospital mortality using clinical criteria declined (−3.3%/y, P = .004), but there was no significant change in the combined outcome of death or discharge to hospice (−1.3%/y, P = .19). In contrast, mortality using claims declined significantly (−7.0%/y, P < .001), as did death or discharge to hospice (−4.5%/y, P < .001).
Clinical criteria were more sensitive in identifying sepsis than claims (69.7% vs 32.3%, P < .001), with comparable positive predictive value (70.4% vs 75.2%, P = .23). These findings suggest that EHR-based clinical data provide more objective and accurate estimates than claims-based data for sepsis surveillance.

title: Body-mass index and risk of 22 specific cancers: a population-based cohort study of 5·24 million UK adults
text:
Background: High body-mass index (BMI) has been linked to an increased risk of various cancers, but a comprehensive investigation into these associations across different cancer sites is lacking. We aimed to investigate the relationship between BMI and the most common cancers in a large primary care dataset.
Methods: We analyzed data from 5.2 million individuals in the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, with BMI data available. We used Cox models to examine the association between BMI and 22 common cancers, adjusting for potential confounders. We fitted linear and non-linear (spline) models and examined effect modification by sex, menopausal status, smoking, and age. We also calculated population effects and estimated the attributable fraction of cancer cases to excess weight.
Findings: We found associations between BMI and 17 of the 22 cancers examined, with varying effect sizes across cancer sites. A 5 kg/m2 increase in BMI was associated with a roughly linear increase in cancer incidence for the uterus (HR 1.62, 99% CI 1.56-1.69; p<0.0001), gallbladder (HR 1.31, 95% CI 1.12-1.52; p<0.0001), kidney (HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.17-1.33; p<0.0001), cervix (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.03-1.17; p=0.00035), thyroid (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.00-1.19; p=0.0088), and leukemia (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.05-1.13; p≤0.0001). BMI was positively associated with liver (HR 1.19, 95% CI 1.12-1.27), colon (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.07-1.13), ovarian (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.04-1.14), and postmenopausal breast cancers (HR 1.05, 95% CI 1.03-1.07) overall, but these effects varied by underlying BMI or individual-level characteristics. We observed inverse associations with prostate and premenopausal breast cancer risk, both overall (prostate HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.95-1.00; premenopausal breast cancer HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.86-0.92) and in never-smokers (prostate HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.93-0.99; premenopausal breast cancer HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.85-0.94). By contrast, we observed no association in never smokers for lung and oral cavity cancer (lung HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93-1.05; oral cavity HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.91-1.26). Assuming causality, we estimated that 41% of uterine and 10% or more of gallbladder, kidney, liver, and colon cancers could be attributable to excess weight. We estimated that a 1 kg/m2 population-wide increase in BMI would result in 3790 additional annual UK patients developing one of the ten cancers positively associated with BMI.
Interpretation: BMI is associated with cancer risk, with substantial population-level effects. The heterogeneity in the effects suggests that different mechanisms are associated with different cancer sites and different patient subgroups. The findings suggest that population-level interventions to reduce excess weight could have a significant impact on cancer incidence.

title: Cryo-EM structure of a herpesvirus capsid at 3.1 Å
text: Human herpesviruses are among the largest and most intricate viruses when it comes to their molecular structure and genetic makeup. By employing cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) with an optimized image reconstruction strategy, we have successfully determined the capsid structure of herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) at an angstrom resolution of 3.1. This viral structure is composed of approximately 3000 proteins, organized into three types of hexons (central, peripentonal, and edge), pentons, and triplexes. The major capsid protein, VP5, is found in both hexons and pentons, while VP26 proteins are exclusively present in hexons. Triplexes, on the other hand, are comprised of VP23 and VP19C proteins. These proteins form an extensive network of intermolecular interactions, including multiple disulfide bonds and noncovalent interactions, which contribute to the stabilization and assembly of the capsid. The conformational changes induced by the microenvironment of these proteins lead to the formation of 46 different conformers that come together to form a massive, quasi-symmetric shell, highlighting the complex structural and functional nature of HSV.

title: Asymptotic and resampling strategies for assessing and comparing indirect effects in multiple mediator models.
text: In the behavioral sciences, hypotheses involving mediation are frequent. Mediation occurs when a predictor affects a dependent variable indirectly through at least one intervening variable, or mediator. Despite a need for methods to assess mediation involving multiple simultaneous mediators, little attention has been given to this topic in the literature. To address this gap, we provide an overview of simple and multiple mediation and explore three approaches for investigating indirect processes. We also discuss methods for comparing two or more mediators within a single model. To illustrate these concepts, we present an example of assessing and contrasting potential mediators of the relationship between the helpfulness of socialization agents and job satisfaction. Finally, we offer SAS, SPSS, Mplus, and LISREL macros and syntax to facilitate the use of these methods in practical applications.

title: Distinct Metabolomic Signatures Are Associated with Longevity in Humans
text: Changes in metabolism have an impact on lifespan in experimental models, but there is a lack of data on this topic in humans. To investigate, we used liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry to quantify 217 plasma metabolites and examine their relationship to longevity in a large cohort of men and women followed for up to 20 years. Our findings reveal that higher concentrations of the citric acid cycle intermediate, isocitrate, and the bile acid, taurocholate, are associated with lower odds of reaching 80 years of age. Conversely, higher concentrations of isocitrate, but not taurocholate, are linked to poorer cardiovascular health at the outset, as well as an increased risk of future cardiovascular disease and mortality. None of the metabolites studied were associated with cancer risk. These findings suggest that some, but not all, metabolic pathways involved in human longevity are connected to the risk of common causes of death.

title: The expanding problem of adipose depot remodeling and postnatal adipocyte progenitor recruitment.
text: The increasing prevalence of obesity and related metabolic disorders has heightened the need for an in-depth understanding of adipose tissue biology. This encompasses the functions of adipocytes, the manner in which adipose tissue expands during obesity, and the impact of expanded adipose tissue on physiological processes in adults. A growing recognition of the significance of de novo adipocyte differentiation in adipose tissue expansion has emerged. We highlight recent advances in identifying adipose precursor populations that contribute to the physiological postnatal recruitment of white, brown, and beige adipocytes in mice, as well as the complexity of adipose tissue development in vivo.

title: Clonal competition in BcrAbl-driven leukemia: how transplantations can accelerate clonal conversion
text: INTRODUCTION Clonal competition in cancer refers to the process by which the offspring of a single cell clone outcompete or succumb to other rival clones due to variations in their innate qualities, primarily influenced by subsequent genetic mutations. Although the manner in which these mutations arise is well understood in numerous tumors, the dynamic process of clonal selection remains underappreciated. METHODS To investigate the dynamics of clonal competition in BcrAbl-induced leukemia, we employed a γ-retroviral vector library encoding the oncogene in conjunction with genetic barcodes. We analyzed the growth dynamics of transduced cells at the clonal level both in vitro and in vivo using transplanted mice. RESULTS Our findings indicate moderate changes in clonal abundancies in vitro, but surprisingly, we observed monoclonal leukemias in 6/30 mice after transplantation, with only two distinct BcrAbl clones responsible for these developments. To elucidate the origin of these clones, we employed a mathematical model of hematopoietic tissue maintenance, which suggested that a differential engraftment capacity of these two dominant clones could explain our observations. These findings were validated through supplementary transplantation experiments and elevated BcrAbl transcript levels in both clones. CONCLUSION Our research underscores the notion that clonal competition is not a fixed process based solely on genetic mutations, but rather highly dependent on selection mechanisms within a particular environmental context.

title: Open Babel: An open chemical toolbox
text: Computational modeling in chemistry often faces the challenge of converting chemical structures between different formats. While standard formats like Chemical Markup Language (CML) and de facto standards like SMILES exist, the need for interconversion remains due to diverse application areas, differing data stored by various formats, and competition between software providers. To address this issue, we introduce Open Babel, an open-source chemical toolbox that supports over 110 format conversions. Open Babel version 2.3 incorporates a wide range of cheminformatics algorithms, including partial charge assignment, aromaticity detection, and bond order perception, to efficiently handle a broad spectrum of chemical and molecular data. We describe the implementation and key advancements in Open Babel 2.3, as well as various uses of the tool, such as software development, scientific research, and more. Open Babel provides a unified solution to the proliferation of multiple chemical file formats, offering a comprehensive set of features, including conformer searching, 2D depiction, filtering, batch conversion, and substructure and similarity searching. Additionally, it can be used as a programming library by developers working in areas like organic chemistry, drug design, materials science, and computational chemistry. Open Babel is freely available under an open-source license from <http://openbabel.org>.

title: Young adolescents' nutrition assessment on computer (YANA-C)
text:
Objective:
To evaluate the validity and acceptability of the computerized 24-hour recall tool, Young Adolescent's Nutrition Assessment on Computer (YANA-C), in assessing the dietary habits of young adolescents.
Design:
The study compared the food and nutrient intakes reported by YANA-C with those recorded through food diaries (study 1) and 24-hour dietary recall interviews (study 2).
Main Outcome Measures:
The study assessed the intakes of various food groups (e.g., fruits, vegetables, potatoes) and nutrients (energy, carbohydrates, protein, fat, fiber, calcium, vitamin C, and iron) using YANA-C.
Subjects and Setting:
A total of 237 pupils (aged 11-14 years) from two primary and four secondary schools in Belgium-Flanders participated in the study.
Results:

1. YANA-C showed good agreement with both standard methods in categorizing subjects as consumers or non-consumers (κ=0.48-0.92 for study 1 and κ=0.38-0.90 for study 2).
2. Spearman's correlation coefficients for energy and nutrient intakes ranged between 0.44 and 0.79 for study 1 and between 0.44 and 0.86 for study 2.
3. Nutrient and energy intakes were generally higher in YANA-C compared to the food record, but not compared to the interview (except for calcium).
4. The program was evaluated positively by a small number of participants.

Conclusion:

YANA-C is a valuable method for collecting detailed dietary information from young adolescents with relatively low staff resources, making it useful in various nutrition research applications.

title: Antiretroviral Therapy for Prevention of Tuberculosis in Adults with HIV: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
text:
BACKGROUND:
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection is the leading risk factor for developing tuberculosis, with sub-Saharan Africa being particularly affected. According to estimates from 2010, there were approximately 1.1 million new cases of tuberculosis reported among the 34 million people living with HIV globally. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has been identified as a crucial factor in preventing HIV-associated tuberculosis. To assess the impact of ART on the incidence of tuberculosis in adults with HIV infection, we conducted a systematic review of studies that examined the correlation between ART status and tuberculosis incidence in developing countries.
METHODS AND FINDINGS:
We searched various databases, including PubMed, Embase, African Index Medicus, LILACS, and clinical trial registries, for randomized controlled trials, prospective cohort studies, and retrospective cohort studies that met our inclusion criteria. In total, 11 studies were identified, which compared the incidence of tuberculosis among HIV-infected adults based on their ART status for a minimum of 6 months in developing countries. To facilitate meta-analysis, we categorized the baseline CD4 counts into four groups: less than 200 cells/μl, 200–350 cells/μl, greater than 350 cells/μl, and any CD4 count. Our results showed a significant association between ART and reduced incidence of tuberculosis across all CD4 count categories, with hazard ratios ranging from 0.16 to 0.43. There was no significant modification of the hazard ratio by baseline CD4 count category (p = 0.20).
CONCLUSIONS:
Our findings suggest that ART is strongly associated with a reduction in the incidence of tuberculosis across all CD4 count strata. Early initiation of ART may be a crucial component of global and national strategies to control the HIV-associated tuberculosis syndemic.
REVIEW REGISTRATION:
International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews CRD42011001209

title: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and breast cancer: a review of the current evidence.
text: Incidences of breast cancer, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome have increased significantly over the past few decades due to the obesity epidemic, with industrialized countries being particularly affected. Insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, and alterations in growth hormone and steroid hormone signaling associated with diabetes may increase the risk of breast cancer. We reviewed epidemiological studies examining the association between type 2 diabetes and breast cancer risk, as well as the available evidence on the role of hormonal mediators in this association. The combined evidence suggests a moderate connection between type 2 diabetes and breast cancer risk, which appears to be stronger among postmenopausal than premenopausal women. Despite numerous proposed potential pathways, the mechanisms underlying the association between diabetes and breast cancer risk remain unclear, due to the shared risk factors between the two diseases, including obesity, a sedentary lifestyle, and possibly the consumption of saturated fats and refined carbohydrates, which may confound this association. Although the metabolic syndrome is closely related to diabetes and encompasses additional factors that may influence breast cancer risk, the role of the metabolic syndrome in breast carcinogenesis remains unclear and has yet to be studied.

title: Loss of TDP43 inhibits progression of triple-negative breast cancer in coordination with SRSF3
text: Abnormal alternative splicing has been identified as a distinguishing marker of cancer. In this study, we determine TDP43 (TAR DNA-binding protein 43) as an essential regulator of splicing involved in the distinct splicing profile of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Clinical evidence demonstrates that TDP43 is highly expressed in TNBC with poor prognosis. Suppressing TDP43 inhibits the progression of tumors, including proliferation and metastasis, while overexpressing TDP43 promotes the malignancy of mammary epithelial cells. Deep sequencing analysis and functional experiments reveal that TDP43 alters the most splicing events in collaboration with serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 3 (SRSF3), which controls the progression of TNBC. The TDP43/SRSF3 complex regulates specific splicing events, including downstream genes PAR3 and NUMB. The reduced metastasis and proliferation upon the knockdown of TDP43 or SRSF3 are attributable to the regulation of PAR3 and NUMB exon 12 by TDP43 and SRSF3. The TDP43/SRSF3 complex and downstream PAR3 isoform represent potential therapeutic targets for TNBC.

title: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture--pathologic basis of plaque stability and instability.
text:
Atherosclerosis remains a crucial topic in pathology research due to its intricate mechanisms of pathogenesis and significant clinical implications. A large number of diseases with diverse clinical presentations are essentially related to atherosclerosis, including myocardial infarction, stroke, abdominal aneurysms, and lower limb ischemia, which significantly contribute to morbidity and mortality in Western populations. However, despite these various clinical manifestations, most acute events associated with atherosclerosis share a common pathogenetic feature: the rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque. Plaque disruptions can range from minor surface fissures or erosions to deeper intimal tears that penetrate the soft lipid core of lesions, resulting in thrombus formation in all cases. The abdominal aorta is the most prominent site for plaque formation and complications, where the process of plaque disruption and thrombosis can lead to extensive surface ulcerations covering large areas of the aortic wall, as observed in many autopsy cases in older individuals. While atherosclerosis is undisputedly involved in abdominal aneurysm formation, mural thrombosis in these patients surprisingly has a low rate of clinically significant complications, although cholesterol emboli can be found in their kidneys and skin at autopsy. Nonetheless, the impact of the various biologically active mediators released from eroded aortic surfaces on the human body remains unclear. Conversely, occlusive thrombosis is a common and often fatal complication of plaque in small diameter vessels such as coronary arteries.

title: Pioneer factor Pax7 deploys a stable enhancer repertoire for specification of cell fate
text:
Early transcription factors, known as pioneers, have the transformative ability to confer cellular competence for new fate decisions. However, the intricacies of their actions, such as their kinetics and stability, have remained shrouded in mystery. To delve into this process, we focused on the enigmatic Pax7 protein, which expertly unlocks a unique array of enhancers to determine the fate of one particular pituitary lineage.
Pax7's binding to its targeted enhancers occurs swiftly, but the subsequent chromatin remodeling and gene activation are slower-paced. Fascinatingly, the opened enhancers lose their DNA methylation seals and retain a lasting epigenetic imprint, even after Pax7's withdrawal. This latter observation reveals the remarkable potential of transient Pax7 expression in permanently instating cellular identity.
By closely examining the dynamics of Pax7 during pituitary lineage specification, we discovered that it rapidly binds to distinctive heterochromatin regions early on and triggers chromatin opening that persists after Pax7's departure, accompanied by the loss of DNA hypermethylation at the corresponding enhancers. This groundbreaking research underscores the crucial role of transient Pax7 expression in endowing cells with stable identities.

title: Human cancer cells utilize mitotic DNA synthesis to resist replication stress at telomeres regardless of their telomere maintenance mechanism
text: Telomeres and common fragile sites (CFSs) share similarities in their replicative instability, as they both exhibit fragility during DNA replication stress. Similarly, cells dealing with replication stress at CFSs delay the completion of DNA replication until early mitosis, when they switch to a RAD52-dependent form of break-induced replication. We observe a similar phenomenon in human telomeres, where mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS) occurs without the need for the MUS81-EME1 endonuclease. MiDAS at telomeres is not limited to fragile telomeres, but rather a feature of various cell lines regardless of their telomere maintenance mechanism (either telomerase or alternative lengthening of telomeres). MiDAS in telomeres relies on RAD52 and is mechanistically similar to CFS-associated MiDAS, with the key difference being that telomeric MiDAS does not involve MUS81-EME1. According to our model, replication stress triggers a RAD52-dependent bypass of MUS81-EME1 to complete DNA synthesis in mitosis.

title: Low drug levels and thrombotic complications in high‐risk atrial fibrillation patients treated with direct oral anticoagulants
text: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) do not currently require laboratory monitoring, but this study found that measuring DOAC levels at steady state may be useful in predicting thromboembolic events. The study included 565 patients with atrial fibrillation who were started on DOACs and had DOAC-specific measurements (diluted thrombin time or anti-activated factor II calibrated for dabigatran; anti-activated FX calibrated for rivaroxaban or apixaban) performed at C-trough (the lowest level of drug levels) within 15-25 days of starting treatment. The results showed that thromboembolic events occurred in 10 patients who had baseline C-trough levels in the lowest class of drug levels, and the incidence of thromboembolic events was higher among these patients compared to those with higher C-trough levels. The study also found that patients who experienced thromboembolic events had a higher mean CHA2 DS2 -VASc score than the overall patient population. These findings suggest that measuring DOAC levels at steady state may be a useful way to identify patients who are at high risk of thromboembolic events.

title: Consensus guidelines for the detection of immunogenic cell death.
text: Apoptotic cells were traditionally considered immune-tolerant or incapable of eliciting responses to antigens associated with their death. However, our research has uncovered a peculiar type of apoptosis, termed "immunogenic cell death" (ICD), which does not escape the immune system's notice. ICD is characterized by the emissions of immunostimulatory damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) in a specific spatiotemporal configuration. Many established cancer therapies, including chemotherapy and radiation, can induce ICD. Unfortunately, current methods to detect ICD rely on experimental vaccination approaches using immunocompetent mouse models and syngeneic cancer cells, which are impractical for large-scale screening efforts. To address this limitation, we have developed strategies to identify surrogate markers of ICD in vitro and screen large chemical libraries for potential ICD inducers using a high-content, high-throughput platform we recently developed. This platform enables the detection of multiple DAMPs, such as cell surface-exposed calreticulin, extracellular ATP, and high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), as well as the processes that give rise to their emission, including endoplasmic reticulum stress, autophagy, and necrotic plasma membrane permeabilization. We believe that this technology will facilitate the development of next-generation anticancer therapies that are both lethal to malignant cells and capable of converting them into a cancer-specific therapeutic vaccine.

title: Long-Term ERK Inhibition in KRAS-Mutant Pancreatic Cancer Is Associated with MYC Degradation and Senescence-like Growth Suppression.
text: Introduction of compensatory mechanisms and ERK reactivation have limited the effectiveness of Raf and MEK inhibitors in RAS-mutant cancers. We investigated direct inhibition of ERK and its impact on KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer cell lines. We discovered that ERK suppression impeded cell growth in a subset of cell lines and identified synergistic cell death when combined with PI3K inhibition. Unexpectedly, long-term treatment of sensitive cell lines led to cellular senescence, which was mediated by MYC degradation and p16 reactivation. Furthermore, enhanced basal PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling was associated with de novo resistance to ERK inhibitors, as well as resistance mediated by other protein kinases identified through kinome-wide siRNA screening and a genetic gain-of-function screen. Our findings reveal unique consequences of targeting this kinase cascade through ERK inhibition.

title: TRF2 Recruits RTEL1 to Telomeres in S Phase to Promote T-Loop Unwinding
text: Helicase RTEL1 maintains the stability of vertebrate telomeres by promoting t-loop unwinding and preventing telomere fragility. While RTEL1's interaction with PCNA is essential for this process, the mechanism by which RTEL1 interacts with telomeres to facilitate t-loop unwinding is unclear. In this study, we discovered that the shelterin protein TRF2 recruits RTEL1 to telomeres during S phase, which is crucial for preventing catastrophic t-loop processing by structure-specific nucleases. We found that the TRF2-RTEL1 interaction is mediated by a metal-coordinating motif in RTEL1, which is compromised by the Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome (HHS) mutation, RTEL1(R1264H). Conversely, we identified a TRF2(I124D) substitution mutation within the TRFH domain of TRF2, which disrupts RTEL1 binding and phenocopies the RTEL1(R1264H) mutation, leading to aberrant t-loop excision, telomere length heterogeneity, and loss of the telomere as a circle. These results suggest that TRF2 plays a crucial role in recruiting RTEL1 to facilitate t-loop disassembly at telomeres during S phase.

title: Macrophages Facilitate Electrical Conduction in the Heart
text: The roles of heart-specific macrophages in the steady-state heart are unexplored territory. This study sheds light on the filling function of cardiac macrophages in the distal atrioventricular node, where cardiac cells are densely packed with elongated macrophages expressing connexin 43. When linked to spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes through connexin-43-rich gap junctions, cardiac macrophages exhibit a negative resting membrane potential and promptly mirror cardiomyocyte depolarization. In contrast, macrophages positively regulate the resting membrane potential of cardiomyocytes, as simulations suggest, speeding up repolarization. Flashing channelrhodopsin-2-expressing macrophages enhance atrioventricular conduction, whereas erasing connexin 43 in macrophages or genetically lacking them extends atrioventricular conduction. In the Cd11bDTR mouse, deleting macrophages causes continuous atrioventricular block. These data demonstrate that macrophages are indispensable for normal and aberrant cardiac electrical conduction.

title: A Tunable Diffusion‐Consumption Mechanism of Cytokine Propagation Enables Plasticity in Cell‐to‐Cell Communication in the Immune System
text: Immune cells communicate through cytokine exchange to mount an appropriate response, but the distance over which this communication occurs is not well understood. To address this question, we employed theoretical considerations and experimental models of immune responses in vitro and in vivo to determine the spatial extent of cytokine communication in dense tissues. We found that competition between cytokine diffusion and consumption leads to the formation of spatial niches of high cytokine concentrations with well-defined boundaries. These niches scaled with the density of cytokine-consuming cells, which can be modulated during immune responses. In vivo studies revealed interactions on length scales of 80-120 micrometers, resulting in significant cell-to-cell variance in cytokine exposure. This variability arises from the heterogeneous distribution of cytokines in the tissue, which is often overlooked in single-cell studies. Our findings provide a basis for understanding the patterning of immune responses by diffusible factors and the resulting cell-to-cell variability.

title: Cardiac neural crest contributes to cardiomyogenesis in zebrafish.
text: In birds and mammals, cardiac neural crest is a crucial component of heart development, contributing to the formation of the conotruncal cushion and outflow tract septation.
