However, the presence of cardiac neural crest in zebrafish has been called into question due to the absence of outflow tract septation in the zebrafish heart. Here, we use three distinct lineage-labeling approaches to identify zebrafish cardiac neural crest cells and demonstrate that these cells have the ability to differentiate into MF20-positive muscle cells in the myocardium of the major chambers during development. Fate-mapping reveals that cardiac neural crest cells originate from both neural tube regions similar to those found in birds, as well as a novel region rostral to the otic vesicle. In contrast to other vertebrates, cardiac neural crest invades the myocardium in all segments of the heart, including the outflow tract, atrium, atrioventricular junction, and ventricle in zebrafish. We identify three distinct groups of premigratory neural crest along the rostrocaudal axis, each with different propensities to contribute to different segments of the heart, as marked by unique combinations of gene expression patterns. Zebrafish will serve as a valuable model for investigating the interactions between cardiac neural crest and cardiovascular development.

title: Sodium Hydroxide Production from Seawater Desalination Brine: Process Design and Energy Efficiency.
text: The ability to raise pH is essential for desalination pretreatment, particularly in reverse osmosis, as well as other industries. However, traditional methods for increasing pH result in significant emissions and the consumption of nonrenewable resources. An alternative approach involves utilizing waste brine from desalination to produce sodium hydroxide through appropriate concentration and purification steps. In this study, an efficient process train (with variations) is developed and modeled for sodium hydroxide production from seawater desalination brine using membrane chlor-alkali electrolysis. The integrated system incorporates nanofiltration, concentration through evaporation or mechanical vapor compression, chemical softening, further ion-exchange softening, dechlorination, and membrane electrolysis. The study focuses on evaluating the productivity, performance, and energy consumption of the NaOH production process, as well as investigating the dependencies of these parameters on electrolyzer outlet conditions and brine recirculation. Additionally, the energy efficiency of major components is analyzed, and the operating expenses of the NaOH production process are compared to similar processes. The brine-to-caustic process is found to be technically viable while offering several advantages, including a reduced environmental impact from desalination through decreased brine discharge and an increased overall water recovery ratio of the reverse osmosis facility. The study also identifies best-use conditions for producing caustic both for use within the plant and for potential revenue generation.

title: High-Throughput Genetic Screens Identify a Large and Diverse Collection of New Sporulation Genes in Bacillus subtilis
text:
Bacillus subtilis differentiation into dormant spores is one of the best-understood developmental pathways in biology. Genetic screens over the past 50 years identified many factors involved in sporulation. More recent transcriptional profiling revealed additional genes required for successful spore development.
We used transposon-sequencing (Tn-seq) to identify any remaining sporulation genes. Our screen found 133 of the known 148 sporulation-related genes with defects. Surprisingly, we discovered 24 unidentified genes involved in spore formation.
We used fluorescence microscopy to survey the early, middle, and late stages of differentiation in null mutants from the B. subtilis ordered knockout collection. This analysis identified mutants delayed in sporulation initiation, defective in membrane remodeling, and impaired in spore maturation. Several mutants exhibited novel sporulation phenotypes.
We characterized two new factors involved in cell-cell signaling pathways during sporulation: SpoIIT, which activates σE in the mother cell, and SpoIIIL, required for σG activity in the forespore. Our analysis revealed that 36 sporulation-induced genes with no previously reported mutant phenotypes are necessary for timely spore maturation.
Finally, we found a large number of transposon insertions that trigger premature sporulation initiation. Our results demonstrate the power of Tn-seq for discovering new genes and pathways in sporulation and highlight the potential for similar screens in other less well-characterized processes.

title: Psychobiological mechanisms underlying the social buffering of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical axis: a review of animal models and human studies across development.
text:
Over the past century, discovering the stress-reducing effects of social relationships has been one of the major findings in psychobiology. However, a thorough understanding of the underlying neurobiological and psychological mechanisms of this buffering is only beginning to emerge. One crucial area of research involves examining the neurocircuitry that regulates the activity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis. This review aims to integrate animal models and human studies of social regulation of the HPA axis across infancy to adulthood, focusing specifically on the process called social buffering. This process has been observed across species and involves a dampened HPA axis stress response with the presence or assistance of a conspecific.
We describe aspects of the underlying neurobiology when sufficient information is available and highlight gaps in understanding across all domains of the literature. Our working conceptual model emphasizes the roles of oxytocinergic systems and prefrontal neural networks as putative mediators of this process. Additionally, we propose that early experiences play a critical role in shaping later social buffering effects. This synthesis highlights the need for future research in multiple domains, including neuroendocrine, behavioral, and social, to build a more comprehensive model of the HPA social buffering effect across the lifespan.

title: Elevation of circulating branched-chain amino acids is an early event in human pancreatic adenocarcinoma development
text: Most patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are diagnosed with advanced disease and have a poor prognosis, surviving less than 12 months. However, the relationship between metabolic changes and early cancer progression in PDAC is unclear. To investigate, we analyzed the metabolic profiles of prediagnostic plasma samples from patients with pancreatic cancer (cases) and matched controls from four prospective cohort studies. Our findings reveal that elevated levels of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) in plasma are associated with a more than twofold increased risk of future pancreatic cancer diagnosis, independent of established risk factors. The strongest association was observed among individuals with samples collected 2-5 years before diagnosis, suggesting that occult disease may be present at this stage. Interestingly, we found that plasma BCAAs are also elevated in mice with early-stage pancreatic cancers driven by mutant Kras expression, but not in mice with Kras-driven tumors in other tissues. Moreover, we found that the increase in plasma BCAAs that accompanies early-stage disease can be attributed to breakdown of tissue protein. These findings suggest that enhanced whole-body protein breakdown is an early event in the development of PDAC.

title: Effective Use of PI3K and MEK Inhibitors to Treat Mutant K-Ras G12D and PIK3CA H1047R Murine Lung Cancers
text: Mutations in the p110-alpha catalytic subunit (PIK3CA) have been identified, which activate phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K). These mutations are most prevalent in two hotspots: the helical domain (E545K and E542K) and the kinase domain (H1047R). Although the p110-alpha mutants hold transforming potential in vitro, their oncogenic potential has not been examined in genetically engineered mouse models. Recently, clinical trials with PI3K inhibitors have begun, and it remains to be seen if their efficacy will be limited to specific, genetically defined malignancies. In this study, we created a mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma by expressing the H1047R mutation in p110-alpha. Treatment of these tumors with NVP-BEZ235, a dual pan-PI3K and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitor in clinical development, resulted in substantial tumor regression, as observed by positron emission tomography-computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and microscopic examination. In contrast, mouse lung cancers driven by mutant Kras did not respond significantly to single-agent NVP-BEZ235. However, when NVP-BEZ235 was combined with a mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK) inhibitor, ARRY-142886, there was significant synergy in shrinking these Kras-mutant cancers. These in vivo studies suggest that inhibitors of the PI3K-mTOR pathway may be effective against cancers with PIK3CA mutations, and when combined with MEK inhibitors, may effectively treat KRAS-mutated lung cancers.

title: Transdifferentiation of glioblastoma cells into vascular endothelial cells.
text: Glioblastoma (GBM), the most malignant brain tumor, exhibits resistance to intensified combination therapies and anti-VEGF treatments. To investigate the underlying mechanisms of resistance, we analyzed the vasculature of GBMs in tumors induced in p53(+/-) heterozygous mice using lentiviral vectors containing oncogenes and the marker GFP in the hippocampus of GFAP-Cre recombinase (Cre) mice. Our findings were unexpected, as we observed GFP(+) vascular endothelial cells (ECs) in the tumors. транспЦентICATION OF MOUSE GBM CELLS REVEALED THAT THE TUMOR-DERIVED ENDOTHELIAL CELLS (TDECs) ORIGINATED FROM TUMOR-INITIATING CELLS AND WERE NOT RESULTS OF CELL FUSION BETWEEN ECs AND TUMOR CELLS. AN IN VitRO DIFFERENTIATION ASSAY SUGGESTED THAT HYPOXIA PLAYS A CRITICAL ROLE IN THE DIFFERENTIATION OF TUMOR CELLS TO ECs AND IS INDEPENDENT OF VEGF. TDEC FORMATION WAS NOT ONLY RESISTANT TO AN ANTI-VEGF RECEPTOR INHIBITOR IN MOUSE GBMs BUT LED TO AN INCREASE IN THEIR FREQUENCY. A XENOGRAFT MODEL OF HUMAN GBM SPHERES FROM CLINICAL SPECIMENS AND DIRECT CLINICAL SAMPLES FROM PATIENTS WITH GBM ALSO SHOWED THE PRESENCE OF TDECs. WE SUGGEST THAT TDEC IS A CRITICAL PLAYER IN RESISTANCE TO ANTI-VEGF THERAPY AND SHOULD BE TARGETED FOR GBM THERAPY.

title: Ribosomal DNA copy loss and repeat instability in ATRX-mutated cancers
text: ATRX (alpha thalassemia/mental retardation X-linked) complexes with DAXX to deposit histone variant H3.3 into repetitive heterochromatin. Recent genome sequencing studies in cancers have revealed mutations in ATRX and their association with ALT (alternative lengthening of telomeres) activation. Our study reveals that depletion of ATRX in mouse ES cells leads to selective loss in ribosomal RNA gene (rDNA) copy number. Specifically, ATRX-depleted cells show a significantly lower rDNA copy number compared to non-depleted cells. Furthermore, we find that mutations in ATRX are associated with a disruption in H3.3 deposition and failure in heterochromatin formation at rDNA repeats, leading to repeat instability. We also observe that ATRX-depleted cells have reduced ribosomal RNA transcription output and increased sensitivity to RNA polymerase I (Pol I) transcription inhibitor CX5461. Interestingly, human ALT-positive cancer cell lines are also more sensitive to CX5461 treatment. Our findings provide insights into the contribution of ATRX loss of function to tumorigenesis through the loss of rDNA stability and suggest potential therapeutic strategies for targeting Pol I transcription in ALT cancers.

title: Combining indoor residual spraying and insecticide-treated nets for malaria control in Africa: a review of possible outcomes and an outline of suggestions for the future
text: Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS) are currently the most effective methods for controlling malaria. In many cases, these methods are used together in the same households, particularly in areas where malaria is highly prevalent. However, there is limited evidence to suggest that combining these methods provides greater protection than using either ITNs or IRS alone. Both methods involve the use of insecticides, and it is hypothesized that the combination of ITNs and IRS may be more effective if the insecticides used have different properties, such as highly deterrent IRS compounds paired with highly toxic ITNs. This could lead to enhanced household-level protection. To avoid the development of insecticide resistance, it is important that the ITNs and IRS products are of different insecticide classes, such as pyrethroid-based nets combined with organophosphate or carbamate-based IRS. The effectiveness of these combinations will also depend on other factors, such as the proportion of people covered by the interventions and the behavior of vector species. This article emphasizes the need for further research, including mathematical modeling, to evaluate the effectiveness of IRS/ITN combinations compared to IRS alone or ITNs alone.

title: Membrane estrogen receptor-α levels in MCF-7 breast cancer cells predict cAMP and proliferation responses
text: The hormone 17β-estradiol (E2) can rapidly induce cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) production in breast cancer cells, but the optimal conditions for measuring cAMP levels and the signaling pathways involved in the proliferative effects of E2 are not fully understood. To address these issues, we compared cAMP response mechanisms in MCF-7 cell lines with low (mERlow) and high (mERhigh) expression of the membrane form of estrogen receptor (mER)-α. Using immunopanning and fluorescence-activated cell sorting, we found that cAMP levels were significantly higher in mERhigh cells compared to mERlow cells. We also found that the effects of E2 on cAMP production were more reliable and robust at 4°C compared to 37°C, suggesting that the loss of cAMP at 37°C is not due to export. Additionally, we found that the accumulated cAMP was consistently higher in mERhigh cells, implicating mER-α levels in the process. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the estrogen receptor (ER) mediates E2-induced cAMP production, as the ER antagonist ICI172,780 blocked the E2-induced response. Interestingly, we also found that the dose-dependent cAMP production in response to E2 was responsive to 50-fold higher E2 concentrations in mERhigh cells, suggesting that mER-α participates in the regulation of cAMP levels. Finally, we showed that E2-mediated activation of adenylyl cyclase and downstream participation of protein kinase A are involved in these responses. Overall, our findings suggest that rapid mER-α-mediated nongenomic signaling cascades generate cAMP and downstream signaling events, which contribute to the regulation of breast cancer cell number.

title: The embryonic cell lineage of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: The developmental trajectory of Caenorhabditis elegans has been meticulously traced from zygote to newly hatched larva, resulting in the complete mapping of the organism's embryonic cell lineage. During this process, a total of 671 cells are generated, with 113 of these cells (93 in the hermaphrodite and 111 in the male) undergoing programmed cell death, while the remaining cells either differentiate into terminal cells or become postembryonic blast cells. Notably, the embryonic lineage displays a high degree of stability, with little variability in cell fate. However, while the relationship between cell ancestry and cell fate is largely fixed, there is a lack of obvious pattern in the correlation between them, leading to fascinating observations such as the generation of neurons from both the ectoderm and mesoderm, as well as the production of muscles by cells that are sisters to muscles. Despite this complexity, cell ablation experiments have demonstrated substantial cell autonomy in certain stages of embryogenesis, highlighting the critical role played by the cell lineage in determining cell fate. The authors explore the origins of repeat units in the body wall, the generation of various orders of symmetry, and the analysis of the lineage in terms of sublineages, while also considering evolutionary implications.

title: Self-Reactive B Cells in the Germinal Center Reaction.
text:
Maintaining immunological self-tolerance requires the selective prevention of lymphocytes with self-reactive antigen receptors from mounting destructive or inflammatory responses. Conventional wisdom views self-tolerance as involving the removal, editing, or silencing of B and T cells that form self-reactive antigen receptors during early development. However, activated B cells that enter germinal centers (GCs) can modify their antigen receptors through somatic hypermutation (SHM) of their immunoglobulin genes, posing a unique challenge to self-tolerance.
We will discuss current knowledge of the mechanisms that enforce B cell self-tolerance, with a particular focus on the control of self-reactive GC B cells. We will also consider how these cells can escape self-tolerance and initiate autoantibody production, or alternatively, undergo SHM to produce productive antibody responses.

title: Chronic inflammation (inflammaging) and its potential contribution to age-associated diseases.
text: Human aging is characterized by a chronic, low-grade inflammation, a phenomenon termed "inflammaging." Inflammaging is a significant risk factor for both morbidity and mortality in elderly individuals, as most age-related diseases share an inflammatory pathogenesis. However, the underlying causes of inflammaging and its contribution to adverse health outcomes are not yet fully understood. Identifying the pathways that control age-related inflammation across multiple systems is crucial to determine whether modifying inflammaging through treatment may be beneficial in old age. At the Advances in Gerosciences meeting held at the National Institutes of Health/National Institute on Aging in Bethesda on October 30 and 31, 2013, experts came together to discuss the unanswered questions surrounding inflammaging. This article summarizes the key findings from that session.

title: Cryptochromes Enabling Plants and Animals to Determine Circadian Time
text: Cryptochromes are photoreceptors that contain flavin molecules and are capable of detecting blue light. Both plants and animals are home to these photoreceptors, and recent discoveries have also identified cryptochromes in bacteria. In plants, cryptochromes play a crucial role in entraining circadian rhythms, or internal biological processes that occur on a daily basis. Similar to their function in plants, cryptochromes in Drosophila (fruit flies) and mammals also regulate the circadian clock and perform an essential function in this process.

title: Neural crest-derived stem cells migrate and differentiate into cardiomyocytes after myocardial infarction.
text:
Objective:
Our recent study demonstrated that primitive neural crest-derived (NC) cells migrate from the cardiac neural crest during embryonic development and remain in the heart as dormant stem cells, with the capacity to differentiate into various cell types, including cardiomyocytes. In this study, we investigated the migration and differentiation potential of these cells in response to myocardial infarction (MI).
Methods and Results:
To examine the migration and differentiation potential of NC stem cells (NCSCs), we generated double-transgenic mice by crossing protein-0 promoter-Cre mice with Floxed-enhanced green fluorescent protein mice, in which the NC cells express enhanced green fluorescent protein. In the neonatal heart, NCSCs were localized primarily in the outflow tract, but they were also distributed in a gradient from base to apex throughout the ventricular myocardium. Time-lapse video analysis revealed that NCSCs were migratory, and some persisted in the adult heart. Upon MI, NCSCs accumulated at the ischemic border zone area (BZA), which expresses monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1). Ex vivo cell migration assays demonstrated that MCP-1 induced NCSC migration, and this chemotactic effect was significantly depressed by an anti-MCP-1 antibody. Furthermore, small NC cardiomyocytes first appeared in the BZA 2 weeks post-MI and gradually increased in number thereafter.
Conclusions:
These results suggest that NCSCs migrate into the BZA via MCP-1/CCR2 signaling and contribute to the provision of cardiomyocytes for cardiac regeneration after MI. These findings provide new insights into the potential of NCSCs for cardiac repair and regeneration.

title: Mitochondria as sensors and regulators of calcium signalling
text: Over the past two decades, the accumulation of calcium (Ca2+) in energized mitochondria has gained significant attention as a crucial biological process with important physiological implications. Research has shown that mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake regulates various cellular functions, including intracellular Ca2+ signaling, metabolism, survival, and cell-specific processes, by buffering cytosolic Ca2+ levels and controlling mitochondrial effectors. Recently, the identification of mitochondrial Ca2+ transporters has shed light on new areas of investigation and potential molecular interventions.

title: Caspase-11 promotes the fusion of phagosomes harboring pathogenic bacteria with lysosomes by modulating actin polymerization.
text: Inflammasomes are multi-protein complexes comprising members of the NLR (nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat containing) family and caspase-1. When bacterial molecules are detected within macrophages, the inflammasome is assembled, triggering the activation of caspase-1. Caspase-11 facilitates caspase-1 activation in response to lipopolysaccharide and bacterial toxins, but its role during bacterial infection remains unclear. Our study demonstrates that caspase-11 is dispensable for caspase-1 activation in response to Legionella, Salmonella, Francisella, and Listeria. We also found that active mouse caspase-11 is required for restricting L. pneumophila infection. Similar to mouse caspase-11, human caspase-4 and caspase-5, its homologs, cooperate to restrict L. pneumophila infection in human macrophages. Caspase-11 promotes the fusion of the L. pneumophila vacuole with lysosomes by modulating actin polymerization through cofilin. However, caspase-11 is dispensable for the fusion of lysosomes with phagosomes containing non-pathogenic bacteria, highlighting a fundamental difference in the trafficking of phagosomes based on their cargo.

title: Adipocyte inflammation is essential for healthy adipose tissue expansion and remodeling.
text: Chronic inflammation is a crucial connection between obesity and its subsequent metabolic complications. Contrary to the belief that inflammatory signals have a detrimental impact on metabolism, our research shows that proinflammatory signaling in adipocytes is actually necessary for proper adipose tissue remodeling and expansion. We generated three mouse models with a reduced adipose tissue-specific proinflammatory capacity, which displayed a decreased in vivo adipogenesis capacity while their differentiation potential remained unchanged in vitro. When exposed to a high-fat diet, the expansion of visceral adipose tissue was significantly impaired. This was accompanied by impaired intestinal barrier function, increased hepatic steatosis, and metabolic dysfunction. An impaired local proinflammatory response in adipocytes led to increased ectopic lipid accumulation, glucose intolerance, and systemic inflammation. In other words, adipose tissue inflammation is an adaptive response that enables the safe storage of excess nutrients and acts as a protective barrier to effectively filter out endotoxins from the gut.

title: Chronic variable stress activates hematopoietic stem cells
text: Exposure to psychosocial stress is a risk factor for an array of diseases, including atherosclerosis. Despite being only partially understood, the interaction between the psyche and the immune system may provide a potential mechanism connecting stress and disease onset and progression. Well-documented crosstalk between the brain and immune system includes the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, which centrally mediates glucocorticoid production in the adrenal cortex, and the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary axis, which regulates stress-induced catecholamine release in support of the fight-or-flight response. Although the long-term effects of chronic stress on hematopoietic stem cell activity remain unelucidated, our study uncovered that stress culminates in increased proliferation of these most primitive hematopoietic progenitors, thereby giving rise to higher levels of disease-promoting inflammatory leukocytes. In particular, we found that chronic stress led to monocytosis and neutrophilia in humans, and when investigating the source of leukocytosis in mice, we discovered that stress activates hematopoietic stem cells upstream. Under conditions of chronic variable stress, sympathetic nerve fibers released an excess of noradrenaline, which prompted bone marrow niche cells to alter CXCL12 levels through the β3-adrenergic receptor. Consequently, hematopoietic stem cell proliferation was amplified, resulting in an increased output of neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes. When atherosclerosis-prone Apoe(-/-) mice were subjected to chronic stress, accelerated hematopoiesis further contributed to plaque features associated with vulnerable lesions that are responsible for myocardial infarction and stroke in humans.

title: CNTF reverses obesity-induced insulin resistance by activating skeletal muscle AMPK
text: Ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) leads to weight loss and improved glucose tolerance in humans and rodents. It is believed to act centrally by inducing hypothalamic neurogenesis to regulate food intake and peripherally by altering hepatic gene expression in a manner similar to that of leptin. Our study shows that CNTF signals through the CNTFRα–IL-6R–gp130β receptor complex to increase fatty-acid oxidation and reduce insulin resistance in skeletal muscle by activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), regardless of brain signaling. These findings indicate that the antiobesogenic effects of CNTF in the periphery result directly from its impact on skeletal muscle, and that these peripheral effects are not diminished by diet-induced or genetic models of obesity, a crucial requirement for the treatment of obesity-related diseases.

title: The Global Spread of Hepatitis C Virus 1a and 1b: A Phylodynamic and Phylogeographic Analysis
text:
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is believed to affect approximately 130-180 million individuals globally. The origin of HCV is unclear, but genetic analysis suggests that genotype 1 likely originated from West Africa. Prior studies have estimated that HCV transmission began in the early 1900s and grew steadily until the late 1980s. However, epidemiological data suggest that the expansion of HCV may have occurred after the second world war. The objective of this study was to determine the timescale and route of the global spread of HCV.
We found that the less frequently sequenced HCV region (E2P7NS2) is more informative for molecular epidemiology studies compared to the more commonly used NS5B region. Using a large set of new E2P7NS2 and NS5B sequences, along with all available global HCV sequences with information in both of these genomic regions, we estimated the timescale and nature of the global expansion of the most prevalent HCV subtypes, 1a and 1b. We discovered that transmission of subtypes 1a and 1b "exploded" between 1940 and 1980, with subtype 1b spreading prior to subtype 1a by at least 16 years (95% confidence interval 15-17). Phylogeographic analysis of all available NS5B sequences suggests that HCV subtypes 1a and 1b disseminated from developed countries to developing countries.
Our findings indicate that the evolutionary rate of HCV is faster than previously suggested. The global spread of HCV coincided with the widespread use of transfused blood and blood products and with the expansion of intravenous drug use, but slowed prior to the wide implementation of anti-HCV screening. The differences in transmission routes associated with subtypes 1a and 1b provide an explanation for the relatively earlier expansion of subtype 1b. Our data suggest that the most plausible route of HCV dispersal was from developed countries to developing countries.
Please see the Editors' Summary at the end of the article for a concise overview of the study's findings.

title: Pharmacological interventions for smoking cessation: an overview and network meta-analysis.
text:
Smoking is the leading cause of preventable illness and death worldwide. But did you know that there are actually several medications that can help you quit smoking? In this review, we look at three of the most commonly used treatments: nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), bupropion, and varenicline. We also compare them to placebo and each other to see which ones are the most effective at helping you quit smoking for good.
First up, let's talk about NRT. NRT is a type of treatment that delivers nicotine to your body without actually letting you smoke. There are different forms of NRT, like gum, patches, and lozenges. Studies show that using NRT can doublenewerdoc definitely help you quit smoking. But, it's worth noting that NRT doesn't work for everyone and some people may find it hard to stick with it.
Bupropion is another medication that can help you quit smoking. It's actually an antidepressant, but it also helps with quitting smoking. Studies show that bupropion can increase your chances of quitting smoking by about 50%. It's important to note that bupropion can have some side effects, like headaches and nausea, so it's not for everyone.
Varenicline is a newer medication that's even more effective at helping you quit smoking than NRT or bupropion. It works by blocking the nicotine from reaching your brain, which makes it harder to get that smoking feeling. Studies show that varenicline can increase your chances of quitting smoking by as much as 300%! However, it can also have some pretty serious side effects, like depression, anxiety, and even suicidal thoughts. So, it's important to discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor before starting treatment.
So, what about other treatments? Well, there are a few other medications that can help you quit smoking, like nortriptyline, cytisine, and nicotine vaccines. But, the evidence is mixed on whether these treatments are actually effective.
In conclusion, NRT, bupropion, and varenicline are the most effective medications for helping you quit smoking. But, it's important to remember that none of these treatments are risk-free. So, it's important to talk to your doctor before starting any smoking cessation treatment to discuss the potential risks and benefits and to determine which treatment is right for you.

title: A library of yeast transcription factor motifs reveals a widespread function for Rsc3 in targeting nucleosome exclusion at promoters.
text: The DNA-binding specificity of transcription factors is the primary mechanism by which cells recognize and regulate genomic features. To systematically determine the binding specificities of transcription factors in yeast, we examined 112 DNA-binding proteins belonging to 19 distinct structural classes. Our findings revealed that one-third of the binding specificities had not been previously reported, underscoring the need for more comprehensive studies in this area. Additionally, we observed striking genomic distributions of certain binding sequences near transcription start sites, supporting their biological relevance and suggesting a role in promoter architecture. Of interest, we found that sequences containing the core CGCG, termed Rsc3 binding sequences, are enriched approximately 100 bp upstream of transcription start sites. Mutation of the RSC3 gene resulted in a significant increase in nucleosome occupancy in hundreds of proximal promoters harboring a Rsc3 binding element, indicating that Rsc3 plays a crucial role in targeting nucleosome exclusion at yeast promoters.

title: EphA3 maintains tumorigenicity and is a therapeutic target in glioblastoma multiforme.
text: Significant effort has been dedicated to uncovering functional therapeutic targets in glioblastoma (GBM) with the goal of halting the cancer's growth. Our findings reveal that the receptor tyrosine kinase EphA3 is frequently overexpressed in GBM, with the most aggressive mesenchymal subtype showing particularly high levels of expression. Notably, EphA3 is highly expressed on the tumor-initiating cell population in glioma, and its modulation of mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling appears crucial in maintaining tumor cells in a less differentiated state. Interestingly, EphA3 knockdown or depletion of EphA3-positive tumor cells resulted in a similarly reduced tumorigenic potential as treatment with a therapeutic radiolabelled EphA3-specific monoclonal antibody. These results conclusively identify EphA3 as a functional, targetable receptor in GBM.

title: Chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells for acute lymphoid leukemia.
text: Researchers have investigated the use of chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), specifically in children with relapsed and refractory pre-B-cell ALL. Two patients received infusions of T cells transduced with an antibody and a T-cell signaling molecule (CTL019 chimeric antigen receptor T cells) at a dose of 1.4–1.2×10(7) CTL019 cells per kilogram of body weight. The results showed that the chimeric antigen receptor T cells expanded to a level that was more than 1000 times higher than the initial engraftment level and were identified in bone marrow and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Eight grade 3 or 4 adverse events were noted, including cytokine-release syndrome and B-cell aplasia, which were effectively managed with etanercept and tocilizumab. Complete remission was observed in both patients, with one patient remaining in remission for 11 months and the other patient experiencing a relapse approximately 2 months after treatment. The study demonstrated that chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells are capable of killing aggressive, treatment-refractory ALL cells in vivo and highlighted the need to target other molecules in addition to CD19 in some patients with ALL.

title: Extended-connectivity fingerprints.
text:
Extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs) represent a novel class of topological fingerprints used for molecular characterization. Unlike traditional topological fingerprints, which were primarily developed for substructure and similarity searching, ECFPs were created specifically for structure-activity modeling. ECFPs are circular fingerprints that boast several advantageous characteristics, including:
1. Rapid calculation: ECFPs can be calculated quickly and efficiently, making them ideal for large-scale analyses.
2. Infinite representation: ECFPs can represent an exponentially large number of distinct molecular features, including stereochemical information.
3. Substructure-based features: The features computed by ECFPs correspond to the presence of specific substructures, facilitating a more insightful interpretation of analysis results.
4. Customizable algorithms: The ECFP algorithm can be tailored to generate different types of circular fingerprints optimized for diverse applications.
Despite their widespread adoption and validation, the implementation details of ECFPs have not been comprehensively described in the literature until now.

title: Suppressor of cytokine signaling 3 inhibits antiviral IFN-beta signaling to enhance HIV-1 replication in macrophages.
text: HIV-1 replication within macrophages of the central nervous system (CNS) often leads to cognitive and motor impairments, known as HIV-associated dementia (HAD) in its most severe form. Initially, interferon-beta (IFN-beta) suppresses viral replication within these cells, but this protection is temporary, allowing HIV-1 to overcome it and resume replication through an unknown mechanism, leading to the progression of HAD. Our study reveals that Suppressor of Cytokine Signaling (SOCS)3, an inhibitor of IFN signaling, may enable HIV-1 to evade the innate immune response within the CNS. We found that SOCS3 is elevated in a simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV)/macaque model of HAD and correlates with the recurrence of viral replication and onset of CNS disease. In vitro, the HIV-1 regulatory protein transactivator of transcription induces SOCS3 in human and murine macrophages in a nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB)-dependent manner. SOCS3 expression attenuates the response of macrophages to IFN-beta at proximal levels of pathway activation and downstream antiviral gene expression, ultimately allowing HIV-1 to overcome the inhibitory effect of IFN-beta on replication. These findings suggest that SOCS3 expression, induced by stimuli present in the HIV-1-infected brain, such as transactivator of transcription, inhibits antiviral IFN-beta signaling to enhance HIV-1 replication in macrophages. This inhibition of IFN-beta signaling in vitro, supported by a correlation with increased viral load and onset of CNS disease in vivo, implies that SOCS3 may allow HIV-1 to evade the protective innate immune response within the CNS, allowing the recurrence of viral replication and ultimately promoting progression towards HAD.

title: Molecular model of the human 26S proteasome.
text: The 26S proteasome is a crucial component of eukaryotic cellular homeostasis, responsible for the precise degradation of a wide range of proteins, including important regulatory factors involved in cell cycle progression and apoptosis. Here, we report the structural details of the human 26S proteasome, determined through cryo-electron microscopy and single-particle analysis, along with the identification of secondary structure elements within the 20S proteolytic core region and 19S regulatory particle. By combining this information with crystal structures, homology models, and other biochemical data, we have constructed a comprehensive molecular model of the complete 26S proteasome, providing a detailed understanding of the 20S core region and redefining the subunit assignment within the 19S regulatory particle. This work lays a strong foundation for elucidating the mechanisms underlying the 26S proteasome's essential functions in eukaryotic cells.

title: Urinary bisphenol A concentrations and early reproductive health outcomes among women undergoing IVF.
text:
Study Question: Do high levels of urinary bisphenol A (BPA) in women undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) affect ovarian response and early reproductive outcomes, including oocyte maturation and fertilization, Day 3 embryo quality, and blastocyst formation?
Summary Answer: Higher urinary BPA concentrations were linked to decreased ovarian response, fewer fertilized oocytes, and lower blastocyst formation.
What is Known Already: Experimental studies and in vitro research have shown that BPA exposure can lead to adverse reproductive outcomes. We previously found an association between urinary BPA and decreased ovarian response in women undergoing IVF; however, there is limited information on reproductive health outcomes in humans.
Study Design: Prospective preconception cohort study involving 174 women undergoing 237 IVF cycles at the Massachusetts General Hospital Fertility Center between 2004 and 2010.
Participants/Materials, Setting, and Methods: Urinary BPA concentrations were measured using online solid-phase extraction-high-performance liquid chromatography-isotope dilution-tandem mass spectrometry. Mixed effect models, Poisson regression, and multivariate logistic regression were used to assess the association between cycle-specific urinary BPA concentrations and measures of ovarian response, oocyte maturation, fertilization, embryo quality, and cleavage rate. Correlation among multiple IVF cycles in the same woman was accounted for using generalized estimating equations.
Main Results and the Role of Chance: The geometric mean (SD) for urinary BPA concentrations was 1.50 (2.22) µg/l. Adjusting for age and other potential confounders (Day 3 serum FSH, smoking, BMI), there was a significant linear dose-response association between increased urinary BPA concentrations and decreased number of oocytes, fertilized oocytes, and E(2) levels. The mean number of oocytes and fertilized oocytes decreased by 24 and 27%, respectively, for the highest versus the lowest quartile of urinary BPA (trend test P < 0.001 and 0.002, respectively). Women with urinary BPA above the lowest quartile had decreased blastocyst formation (trend test P-value = 0.08).
Limitations and Reasons for Caution: Potential limitations include exposure misclassification due to BPA's short half-life and high variability over time, uncertainty about the generalizability of the results to the general population of women conceiving naturally, and limited sample size.
Wider Implications of the Findings: The study's extended duration, using IVF as a model to study early reproductive health outcomes in humans, indicated a negative dose-response association between urinary BPA concentrations and serum peak E(2) and oocyte yield, confirming previous findings. Additionally, the study found significantly decreased metaphase II oocyte count and number of normally fertilizing oocytes and a suggestive association between BPA urinary concentrations and decreased blastocyst formation, suggesting that BPA may alter reproductive function in susceptible women undergoing IVF.
Study Funding/Competing Interests: This work was supported by grants ES009718 and ES000002 from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences and grant OH008578 from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. None of the authors had actual or potential competing financial interests.
Disclaimer: The findings and conclusions in this report are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the views of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

title: Cost-effectiveness of options for the diagnosis of high blood pressure in primary care: a modelling study.
text:
The traditional approach to diagnosing hypertension has been based on clinic measurements, but recent studies have shown that home and ambulatory measurements are more accurate in predicting cardiovascular outcomes. To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of different diagnostic strategies for hypertension, we conducted a Markov model-based probabilistic cost-effectiveness analysis.
Using a hypothetical primary care population aged 40 years or older with a screening blood pressure measurement greater than 140/90 mm Hg and risk factor prevalence equivalent to the general population, we compared three diagnostic strategies: further blood pressure measurement in the clinic, at home, and with an ambulatory monitor. Our findings show that ambulatory monitoring was the most cost-effective strategy for the diagnosis of hypertension for both men and women of all ages. Ambulatory monitoring was cost-saving for all groups and resulted in more quality-adjusted life years for men and women older than 50 years. This finding was robust and consistent across a wide range of deterministic sensitivity analyses. However, the results were sensitive to the assumption that home monitoring had equal test performance to ambulatory monitoring, or that treatment was effective regardless of whether an individual was hypertensive.
Our findings suggest that ambulatory monitoring as a diagnostic strategy for hypertension after an initial raised reading in the clinic would reduce misdiagnosis and save costs. The additional costs of ambulatory monitoring are counterbalanced by cost savings from better targeted treatment. We recommend ambulatory monitoring for most patients before the start of antihypertensive drugs. This study was funded by the National Institute for Health Research and the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence.

title: Folic acid improves endothelial function in coronary artery disease via mechanisms largely independent of homocysteine lowering.
text:
Here is a possible reconstruction of the given text:
BACKGROUND: Homocysteine is a risk factor for coronary artery disease (CAD), although a direct causal relationship has yet to be proven. However, it is important to determine the causal relationship, as plasma homocysteine levels can be safely and inexpensively reduced by 25% with folic acid. This reduction is achieved by doses of 0.4 mg/d, and high-dose folic acid (5 mg/d) improves endothelial function in CAD, although the exact mechanism is controversial. We aimed to investigate the effects of folic acid on endothelial function before and after a change in homocysteine levels in patients with CAD.
METHODS AND RESULTS: A randomized, placebo-controlled study of folic acid (5 mg/d) for 6 weeks was conducted in 33 patients with CAD. Endothelial function was assessed by flow-mediated dilatation (FMD) at various time points, including before treatment, at 2 and 4 hours after the first dose of folic acid, and after 6 weeks of treatment. Plasma folate levels significantly increased by 1 hour (200 vs. 25.8 nmol/L; P<0.001). FMD improved at 2 hours (83 vs. 47 microm; P<0.001) and was nearly complete by 4 hours (101 vs. 51 microm; P<0.001). tHcy (total homocysteine) levels did not significantly change acutely (4-hour tHcy, 9.56 vs. 9.79 micromol/L; P=NS), while fHcy (free homocysteine) levels did not differ at 3 hours but were slightly reduced at 4 hours (1.55 vs. 1.78 micromol/L; P=0.02). FMD improvement did not correlate with changes in either fHcy or tHcy at any time.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that folic acid improves endothelial function in CAD acutely by a mechanism largely independent of homocysteine.

title: Focal adhesion kinase links mechanical force to skin fibrosis via inflammatory signaling
text: Exuberant fibroproliferation is a common complication that arises after injury, with the underlying mechanisms not completely understood. One crucial aspect of wound healing that is often overlooked is the role of mechanical forces in regulating cell-matrix interactions, and a key player in this process is focal adhesion kinase (FAK). In this study, we investigate the activation of FAK after cutaneous injury and its potentiation by mechanical loading. We find that FAK is involved in the formation of hypertrophic scars in mice, and that its activation leads to the secretion of monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), a potent chemokine linked to fibrotic disorders. Moreover, MCP-1 knockout mice form minimal scars, suggesting that inflammatory chemokine pathways are a key mechanism by which FAK mechanotransduction induces fibrosis. We also demonstrate that small-molecule inhibition of FAK can attenuate scar formation in vivo by reducing MCP-1 signaling and inflammatory cell recruitment. These findings suggest that physical forces regulate fibrosis through inflammatory FAK–ERK–MCP-1 pathways, and that targeting FAK with molecular strategies can effectively uncouple mechanical forces from pathologic scar formation.

title: Prognostic Accuracy of the SOFA Score, SIRS Criteria, and qSOFA Score for In-Hospital Mortality Among Adults With Suspected Infection Admitted to the Intensive Care Unit
text:
The Sepsis-3 criteria have emphasized the significance of a change in Sequential [Sepsis-related] Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, introduced quick SOFA (qSOFA), and eliminated the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria from the sepsis definition. This study aimed to externally validate and assess the discriminatory capacities of an increase in SOFA score by 2 or more points, 2 or more SIRS criteria, or a qSOFA score of 2 or more points among patients critically ill with suspected infection.
The study included 184,875 patients with an infection-related primary admission diagnosis in 182 Australian and New Zealand intensive care units (ICUs) from 2000 to 2015. Data on SOFA, qSOFA, and SIRS criteria were collected within 24 hours of ICU admission. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality, and the secondary outcome was in-hospital mortality or ICU length of stay (LOS) of 3 days or more. Discrete variables were assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and adjusted analyses using a model of baseline risk determined using variables independent of the scoring systems.
The study found that among 184,875 patients, 34,578 died in the hospital, and 102,976 died or experienced an ICU LOS of 3 days or more. Of these patients, 90.1% had a SOFA score increase of 2 or more points, 86.7% had 2 or more SIRS criteria, and 54.4% had a qSOFA score of 2 or more points. SOFA demonstrated greater discrimination for in-hospital mortality than SIRS criteria or qSOFA, with a crude AUROC of 0.753 compared to 0.589 for SIRS criteria and 0.607 for qSOFA. Incremental improvements were also observed between SOFA and SIRS criteria/qSOFA.
In conclusion, among adults with suspected infection admitted to the ICU, an increase in SOFA score of 2 or more had greater prognostic accuracy for in-hospital mortality than SIRS criteria or qSOFA. These findings suggest that SIRS criteria and qSOFA may have limited utility for predicting mortality in an ICU setting.

title: Predictors of mammographic density: insights gained from a novel regression analysis of a twin study.
text: Understanding which factors influence the density and nondensity of mammographic areas is crucial due to the strong and continuous relationship between percent mammographic density adjusted for age and breast cancer risk, particularly when adjusted for weight or body mass index. We measured the mammographically dense areas of 571 monozygotic and 380 dizygotic Australian and North American twin pairs aged 40 to 70 using computer-assisted methods. We employed a novel regression modeling approach, where each twin's density and nondensity measurements were regressed against their own covariates and those of their co-twins. The consistency of the regression estimates with different models, such as causal models, can be evaluated. Our findings showed that after adjusting for weight, the associations between the twin's weight and mammographic density were attenuated, suggesting a causal effect of weight on mammographic measures. However, the associations between later age at menarche, greater height, and mammographic density were inconsistent with causality, suggesting within-person confounding. The associations between mammographic density and parity were consistent with both causal effects and within-person confounding. Additionally, the associations between mammographic density and height were consistent with shared early life environmental factors that may predispose to both height and breast cancer risk.

title: Shaping the landscape of the Escherichia coli chromosome: replication-transcription encounters in cells with an ectopic replication origin
text: Each cell division necessitates the unwinding of millions of DNA base pairs to facilitate chromosome duplication and gene expression. However, as DNA replication and transcription share a common template, conflicts between the two processes are unavoidable and head-on collisions are considered particularly problematic. Notably, a recent study discovered that Escherichia coli cells with an artificial replication origin exhibited unperturbed cell cycle progression. In this investigation, we recreated a similar strain and found that the doubling time was significantly higher compared to normal cells. Our replication profiles revealed notable discrepancies, particularly in highly transcribed regions and the termination zone, when compared to wild-type profiles. These deviations were corrected through mutations that either disabled the termination zone or impaired RNA polymerase complexes, allowing them to be more easily displaced by replication forks. Our findings demonstrate that head-on replication-transcription conflicts are highly detrimental. Interestingly, analysis of the replication profile of a previously published E. coli construct revealed a chromosomal rearrangement that alleviates replication-transcription conflicts in a remarkably simple manner. Our results support the notion that minimizing head-on collisions has significantly contributed to the evolution of distinct bacterial chromosome architectures.

title: Epithelial–mesenchymal transitions in tumour progression
text: Without epithelial-mesenchymal transitions, multicellular organisms would be unable to progress beyond the blastula stage of embryonic development. However, this crucial developmental program has a darker side in the context of tumor progression. Epithelial-mesenchymal transition serves as a new foundation for comprehending the progression of carcinoma towards more undifferentiated and malignant states.

title: Platelets at the interface of thrombosis, inflammation, and cancer.
text: Although historically associated with roles in hemostasis and thrombosis, the platelet has emerged as a multifaceted cell with far-reaching impacts on various physiological events. Recent observations highlight the platelet's diverse influence on inflammation, underscoring its evolution from a lower vertebrate cell type with both hemostatic and immunological functions. In cancer biology, the platelet's involvement in the complex interplay between hemostasis, thrombosis, inflammation, and tumor development is now recognized as crucial. Beyond traditional roles in hemostasis and thrombosis, platelets play a multifaceted role in disease processes, making them a key area of study for basic scientists and practicing hematologists alike. Animal models of platelet dysfunction and current antiplatelet therapies provide a rich framework for understanding the intricate mechanisms underlying a wide range of pathophysiological events. By expanding our understanding of platelet function beyond traditional hemostasis and thrombosis, we can gain valuable insights into the complex interplay of factors involved in various diseases.

title: Cellular roles of DNA topoisomerases: a molecular perspective
text: DNA topoisomerases are the masterful manipulators of the DNA world, facilitating the passage of DNA strands or double helices through one another to solve all topological challenges in DNA replication, transcription, and other cellular processes. Following three decades of comprehensive biochemical and structural investigations, detailed molecular models have been established to reveal how the different subfamilies of DNA topoisomerases manipulate DNA. In this review, we shall examine these enzymes' cellular functions from a molecular perspective.

title: MicroRNA sponges: progress and possibilities.
text: Three years ago, the "sponge" method of microRNA (miRNA) manipulation was introduced. This method involves creating continuous loss of function in cell lines and transgenic organisms by using RNAs that contain complementary binding sites to specific miRNAs. These sponge RNAs are produced from transgenes within cells and can block a whole family of related miRNAs by targeting their seed region. This innovative approach has proven to be a valuable tool for investigating miRNA functions in various experimental systems. In this article, we will explore ways to optimize sponge constructs and review recent applications of this method, with a particular focus on stable expression in cancer studies and transgenic animals.

title: Wip1 phosphatase regulates p53-dependent apoptosis of stem cells and tumorigenesis in the mouse intestine.
text: Colorectal cancer is a significant contributor to cancer-related deaths. To gain a deeper understanding of its development, we investigated the role of Wip1 phosphatase in the context of the mouse model of APC(Min)-driven polyposis. Our findings revealed that Wip1 removal increased the lifespan of APC(Min) mice by suppressing polyp formation. This protection was found to be dependent on the p53 tumor suppressor, which plays a role in regulating apoptosis in intestinal stem cells. Interestingly, we observed that activation of the Wnt pathway in Wip1-deficient mice led to increased apoptosis in stem cells, compared to wild-type APC(Min) mice. Based on these findings, we propose that Wip1 phosphatase regulates homeostasis in intestinal stem cells. The loss of Wip1 function leads to a lower threshold for p53-dependent apoptosis in stem cells, preventing them from converting into tumor-initiating stem cells, thereby suppressing APC(Min)-driven polyposis.

title: The shunt problem: control of functional shunting in normal and tumour vasculature
text: The network of blood vessels in both normal and tumorous tissues exhibit diverse structures, with varying lengths of blood flow pathways. To ensure efficient blood flow distribution, the vessels must adapt their diameters through mechanisms that prevent the formation of functional shunts, where short pathways become enlarged and blood flow bypasses long pathways. This adaptation requires communication between tissue metabolic status and feeding vessels through conduction-based responses. We propose that disrupted vascular communication in tumor microvascular networks, leading to functional shunting, is the primary cause of dysfunctional microcirculation and local hypoxia in cancer. We suggest that restoring vascular communication through anti-angiogenic treatment may normalize flow distribution in tumor vasculature.

title: Pharmacological Blockade of ASCT2-dependent Glutamine Transport Leads To Anti-tumor Efficacy in Preclinical Models
text: The unique metabolic needs of cancer cells present a promising area of drug discovery in the era of precision medicine. However, targeting cancer metabolism has led to arelative scarcity of new drugs. The neutral amino acid glutamine plays a crucial role in various metabolic processes, including biosynthesis, cell signaling, and oxidative protection, that are exploited by cancer cells. Our study pursues the preclinical development of V-9302, a competitive small molecule inhibitor of transmembrane glutamine flux, specifically targeting the amino acid transporter ASCT2. Pharmacological blockade of ASCT2 with V-9302 resulted in impaired cancer cell growth and proliferation, magnified cell death, and increased oxidative stress, collectively contributing to anti-tumor responses in vitro and in vivo. This investigation marks the first instance of a pharmacological inhibitor of glutamine transport being applied in oncology, representing a novel class of targeted therapy and laying the groundwork for transformative treatments that target cancer cell metabolism.

title: An Antidepressant Decreases CSF Aβ Production in Healthy Individuals and in Transgenic AD Mice
text: Research suggests that serotonin signaling can inhibit the production of amyloid-β (Aβ) both in vitro and in animal models of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Our study found that the antidepressant citalopram, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, decreased Aβ levels in brain interstitial fluid in a dose-dependent manner in aged transgenic AD mice (APP/PS1 plaque-bearing mice). Moreover, chronic administration of citalopram halted the growth of preexisting amyloid plaques and reduced the formation of new plaques by 78%. In a separate study, we evaluated the effects of citalopram on Aβ production and concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in healthy human volunteers. Our results showed that citalopram slowed Aβ production in CSF by 37% compared to the placebo group, and this decrease was associated with a 38% decrease in total CSF Aβ concentrations in the drug-treated group. These findings suggest that citalopram may have potential as a preventive strategy for AD, and our study provides key insights into target engagement for future AD prevention trials.

title: Variations in the quality and sustainability of long-term glycaemic control with continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion.
text:
Objective: To investigate the pattern of changes in HbA1c levels in adults with Type 1 diabetes managed by long-term continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion.
Methods: We analyzed HbA1c changes using computerized clinic records in 35 adults with Type 1 diabetes and elevated HbA1c (≥ 64 mmol/mol, 8.0%) on multiple daily insulin injections, who were then switched to continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion for at least 5 years.
Results: We identified three subgroups with similar baseline HbA1c but distinct long-term responses to pump therapy: Group A - those who experienced initial improvement followed by deterioration (57%), Group B - those who maintained consistent improvement throughout the 5-year period (31%), and Group C - those whose HbA1c levels remained unchanged from baseline (12%). Notably, individuals in Group C had a higher BMI (31.0 ± 5.2 kg/m²) compared to Group A and Group B (25.9 ± 3.3 kg/m² and 25.2 ± 3.1 kg/m², respectively; P = 0.02).
Conclusion: Continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion provided improved glycemic control over 5 years in approximately 88% of participants with Type 1 diabetes in this study, although there were variations in the long-term efficacy, with some individuals experiencing both improvement and worsening, others maintaining strict control, and a small subset deemed 'non-responders' to subcutaneous insulin infusion. Additionally, higher BMI was observed in individuals who did not experience significant changes in HbA1c levels over time.

title: Historical review: megakaryopoiesis and thrombopoiesis.
text: The study of thrombopoiesis has undergone a significant transformation since the era when platelets were referred to as "blood dust," about 100 years ago. During this period, megakaryocytes were identified as the source of blood platelets, and marrow-derived megakaryocytic progenitor cells were purified and functionally defined. The primary regulator of the thrombopoietic process, thrombopoietin, was cloned and characterized, leading to the development of therapeutic agents. As our understanding of the physiological mechanisms driving proplatelet formation has grown, we have been able to recapitulate these processes in cell-free systems and evaluate their biochemistry. The molecular underpinnings of endomitosis are becoming increasingly understood, and the intracellular signals triggered by megakaryocyte surface receptors have been defined. Furthermore, many transcription factors that determine megakaryocytic fate have been identified and experimentally manipulated. While some of these processes share similarities with other cell types, the unique developmental features of megakaryocytes ensure that continued study of thrombopoiesis will provide abundant clinical and scientific insights for many years to come.

title: Obesity and Its Metabolic Complications: The Role of Adipokines and the Relationship between Obesity, Inflammation, Insulin Resistance, Dyslipidemia and Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
text:
A growing body of evidence suggests that obesity is closely linked to an increased risk of metabolic disorders, including insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. Obesity arises from an imbalance between the amount of food consumed and the energy expended, leading to an excessive accumulation of fat in the body. Adipose tissue, once perceived solely as a storage site for excess energy, is now recognized as a complex endocrine organ that produces a variety of bioactive substances known as adipokines or adipocytokines. These substances can trigger chronic low-grade inflammation and affect a range of processes in various organs, contributing to the development of obesity-related metabolic disorders.
This review focuses on the role of specific adipokines in obesity and their potential impact on metabolic diseases associated with obesity. A wealth of evidence indicates that dysregulated production or secretion of adipokines due to excess adipose tissue or dysfunction can contribute to the development of obesity-related metabolic disorders. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms underlying the metabolic actions of recently identified adipokines.
In summary, accumulating evidence supports the close relationship between obesity and an increased risk of metabolic diseases. Obesity is characterized by an imbalance between food intake and energy expenditure, leading to an excess accumulation of adipose tissue. Adipose tissue plays a more significant role than just storing energy, as it also produces adipokines that can contribute to the development of obesity-related metabolic disorders.

title: Combating trastuzumab resistance by targeting SRC, a common node downstream of multiple resistance pathways
text: Trastuzumab is an effective targeted therapy for breast cancer that overexpresses the ERBB2 protein. However, approximately half of patients with ERBB2-positive breast cancer do not respond to trastuzumab-based treatments due to various resistance mechanisms. Currently, there are no clinically available regimens that can overcome trastuzumab resistance. Our study reveals that the nonreceptor tyrosine kinase c-SRC (SRC) is a crucial modulator of trastuzumab response and a common node downstream of multiple trastuzumab resistance pathways. We found that SRC is activated in both acquired and de novo trastuzumab-resistant cells and uncovered a novel mechanism of SRC regulation involving dephosphorylation by PTEN. Increased SRC activation confers substantial trastuzumab resistance in breast cancer cells and correlates with trastuzumab resistance in patients. Targeting SRC in combination with trastuzumab sensitizes multiple lines of trastuzumab-resistant cells to trastuzumab and eliminates trastuzumab-resistant tumors in vivo, suggesting a potential clinical application of this approach to overcome trastuzumab resistance.

title: MicroRNAs: new tools for diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma?
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are ancient and crucial regulators of gene expression and protein translation. Research has consistently demonstrated their pivotal role in directing embryonic development and fine-tuning life-sustaining functions, such as cell division and apoptosis. Emerging evidence also highlights their key involvement in cancer onset and progression, functioning as both oncogenes and tumor suppressors. In this review, we delve into the most recent discoveries regarding the role of miRNAs in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), examining the potential mechanisms by which they contribute to this malignancy. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of using circulating miRNAs as diagnostic markers, an area in dire need of improvement in the clinical monitoring of HCC, and the exciting possibility of targeting or utilizing them as therapeutic agents.

title: A vertebrate gene, ticrr, is an essential checkpoint and replication regulator.
text: Eukaryotic organisms have multiple checkpoint pathways to ensure genome fidelity during cell division and in response to DNA damage. Through a screen for G2/M checkpoint regulators in zebrafish, we identified ticrr (TopBP1-interacting, checkpoint, and replication regulator), a previously uncharacterized gene that is necessary for preventing mitotic entry after exposure to ionizing radiation. Ticrr deficiency is embryonically lethal in the absence of exogenous DNA damage due to its essential role in normal cell cycle progression. Specifically, the loss of ticrr impairs DNA replication and disrupts the S/M checkpoint, leading to premature mitotic entry and mitotic catastrophe. We discovered that the human TICRR ortholog interacts with TopBP1, a checkpoint protein and core component of the DNA replication pre-initiation complex (pre-IC), and that this interaction is stable without chromatin and requires BRCT motifs essential for TopBP1's replication and checkpoint functions. Furthermore, our data show that ticrr deficiency disrupts the binding of pre-IC components to chromatin, but not the pre-replication complex (pre-RC). Therefore, TICRR acts in association with TopBP1 and plays a crucial role in pre-IC formation. It remains to be determined whether Ticrr represents the vertebrate ortholog of the yeast pre-IC component Sld3 or a previously unknown metazoan replication and checkpoint regulator.

title: A maternally methylated CpG island in KvLQT1 is associated with an antisense paternal transcript and loss of imprinting in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
text: Loss of imprinting at the IGF2 locus, often unrelated to H19 methylation, is associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS), a condition characterized by excessive growth and cancer predisposition. Evidence suggests that imprinting control elements are located within the KvLQT1 locus, given that chromosome rearrangements in BWS frequently disrupt this gene. An evolutionarily conserved, maternally methylated CpG island (KvDMR1) in an intron of the KvLQT1 gene was identified. In 5 cases of BWS with normal H19 methylation, demethylation of KvDMR1 was observed in fibroblast or lymphocyte DNA, while in 4 cases with H19 hypermethylation, methylation at KvDMR1 remained normal. These findings suggest that inactivation of H19 and hypomethylation at KvDMR1 (or a related phenomenon) represent distinct epigenetic anomalies associated with biallelic expression of IGF2. Reverse transcription-PCR analysis of the human and syntenic mouse loci revealed the presence of a KvDMR1-associated RNA transcribed exclusively from the paternal allele and in the opposite orientation relative to the maternally expressed KvLQT1 gene. We propose that KvDMR1 and/or its associated antisense RNA (KvLQT1-AS) functions as an additional imprinting control element or center in the human 11p15.5 and mouse distal 7 imprinted domains.

title: Alarming levels of drug-resistant tuberculosis in Belarus: results of a survey in Minsk
text: Resistance to anti-tuberculosis (TB) medications is a significant public health concern in most countries of the former Soviet Union. As there was a lack of comprehensive and reliable data on the scope of this issue in Belarus, a survey was conducted in the capital city of Minsk. Between November 2009 and December 2010, 156 newly diagnosed and 68 previously treated TB patients residing in Minsk were enrolled in the study. Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates were collected from each patient and tested for susceptibility to first- and second-line TB drugs. The survey found that 35.3% (95% CI: 27.7-42.8%) of new patients and 76.5% (95% CI: 66.1-86.8%) of previously treated patients had multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). In total, nearly one in two patients enrolled had MDR-TB. Furthermore, extensively drug-resistant TB was identified in 15 of the 107 MDR-TB patients (14.0%, 95% CI: 7.3-20.7%). Interestingly, patients under the age of 35 had a twofold higher odds ratio of MDR-TB compared to those aged above 35. The findings of this survey in Minsk are alarming and represent the highest proportions of MDR-TB ever recorded in the world. This study significantly contributes to the understanding of the burden of drug-resistant TB in urban areas of Belarus.

title: Partitioning regulatory mechanisms of within-host malaria dynamics using the effective propagation number.
text: The clearance of immune cells and limitations of resource availability (through red blood cell depletion) shape the oscillations in malaria parasitemia over time, which in turn influence the severity of disease and the likelihood of transmission. Accurately quantifying the relative contributions of these factors through time is challenging, but we used data from rodent malaria studies to estimate the effective propagation number, which reflects the relative importance of contrasting within-host control mechanisms over time and is sensitive to the initial parasite dose. Our analysis revealed that the innate immune system's ability to restrict initial parasite growth reaches its limits as the parasite dose increases and that augmenting innate immunity can indirectly affect parasite density by depleting resources. This type of statistical analysis provides a valuable tool for improving the targeting of drugs or vaccines for human therapy by shedding light on the complex dynamics and interactions of within-host regulatory mechanisms.

title: Life is sweet: candy consumption and longevity.
text: Our predilection towards candy - "if it tastes that good, it can't be healthy" - reveals society's inherent aversion to pleasure. Candy has been scapegoated for various ills, including hyperactivity in children, yet clinical trials have failed to support this belief. Candy, specifically sugar confectionery and chocolate, is not a modern invention; the ancient Arabs, Chinese, and Egyptians candied fruits and nuts in honey, while the Aztecs made a chocolate drink from the bean of the cacao tree. Americans consume, on average, 5.4 kilograms of sugar candy and 6.5 kilograms of chocolate per person annually. Given candy's long history, we wondered whether consumption was linked to lifespan. We conducted this investigation using subjects from the ongoing Harvard Alumni Health Study, which consisted of 7,841 men who entered Harvard University as undergraduates between 1916 and 1950. These men were free of cardiovascular disease and cancer and responded to a health survey.

title: Inter-individual variability and genetic influences on cytokine responses to bacteria and fungi
text: Little is known about how individuals differ in their immune responses to various pathogens. To better understand this, we analyzed the cytokine responses of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 197 healthy individuals of European descent from the 200 Functional Genomics (200FG) cohort in the Human Functional Genomics Project (http://www.humanfunctionalgenomics.org). We sampled these individuals over three different years and compared the cytokine profiles elicited by different pathogens, such as bacteria and fungi. Our findings showed that the majority of cytokine responses were specific to the type of pathogen, rather than being part of a general immune response. To identify genetic factors that influence cytokine production, we analyzed the genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotypes of these individuals and found six cytokine quantitative trait loci (QTLs). One of these QTLs, located at the NAA35-GOLM1 locus, was found to significantly modify interleukin (IL)-6 production in response to multiple pathogens and was also associated with susceptibility to candidemia. Additionally, the QTLs we identified were enriched among SNPs previously linked to infectious diseases and heart diseases. These findings illustrate the variability in cytokine production by human immune cells in response to pathogens and provide a starting point for understanding the genetic basis of immune function.

title: Integrins promote cytokinesis through the RSK signaling axis.
text: Cytokinesis is the final stage of cell division, and while integrins have been shown to play a role in this process, the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of integrin-regulated ERK (extracellular signal-related kinase) and RSK (p90 ribosomal S6 kinase) signaling in cytokinesis. By employing various techniques, we found that inhibition of ERK and RSK signaling in CHO cells leads to the accumulation of cells with midbodies and the formation of binucleated cells. Notably, the expression of constitutively active RAF1, which activates the RSK pathway, suffices to restore cytokinesis in these cells. Moreover, we observed a similar dependence on RSK for successful cytokinesis in MCF-10A human mammary epithelial cells and HPNE human pancreatic ductal epithelial cells. We also found that depriving mitotic MCF10A cells of integrin-mediated adhesion leads to a suppression of ERK and RSK activation, resulting in a failure of cytokinesis. Furthermore, inhibition of RSK or integrins within a 3D organ explant context leads to an accumulation of epithelial cells with midbodies, suggesting a similar defect in cytokinesis. Interestingly, our findings indicate that neither ERK nor RSK regulates cytokinesis in human fibroblasts, indicating cell-type specificity. Taken together, our results highlight the importance of the integrin-RSK signaling axis in regulating cytokinesis in epithelial cells. We propose that the proper interaction of cells with their microenvironment through integrins contributes to the maintenance of genomic stability by promoting the successful completion of cytokinesis.

title: Sympathetic neural mechanisms in normal and hypertensive pregnancy in humans.
text:
The background of this study reveals that direct recordings from peripheral sympathetic nerves have shown an elevated sympathetic drive in pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) and preeclampsia (PE). However, it remains unclear whether sympathetic drive changes during normal pregnancy, even though arterial blood pressure may be either normal or relatively low. The aim of this study was to investigate and compare peripheral sympathetic discharge, its vasoconstrictor effect, and baroreceptor control during pregnancy and postpartum in women with normal pregnancy (NP), PIH, and normotensive nonpregnant (NN) women.
The study included 21 women with NP, 18 women with PIH, and 21 NN women. Muscle sympathetic nerve activity was measured using multiunit discharges (MSNA) and single units with defined vasoconstrictor properties (s-MSNA). The results showed that s-MSNA in NP was greater than in NN women, despite similar ages and body weights. MSNA followed a similar trend. However, cardiac baroreceptor reflex sensitivity (BRS) was impaired in NP and PIH women compared to NN women. After delivery, sympathetic activity decreased to values similar to those observed in NN women, and there was an increase in BRS. In women with NP, the decrease in sympathetic output occurred despite an insignificant change in blood pressure.
The study's central conclusion is that central sympathetic output is increased in women with normal pregnancy and even more pronounced in the hypertensive pregnant group. The findings suggest that the moderate sympathetic hyperactivity during the latter months of normal pregnancy may help to return the arterial pressure to nonpregnant levels. However, when the increase in activity is excessive, hypertension may ensue.

title: Barriers to recruiting urban African American women into research studies in community settings.
text:
In this qualitative study, the researchers identified barriers to African American women's participation in a community-based behavioral intervention trial aimed at increasing mammography screening. Through focus group discussions with community agency providers and research team members, four themes emerged:
