1. Building relationships with influential community leaders, or "going to the gatekeepers," was seen as crucial for increasing African American women's participation in the trial. These gatekeepers could help promote the trial and address concerns among potential participants.
2. Understanding and respecting the cultural beliefs and practices of African American women was seen as essential for increasing their participation. The researchers found that cultural sensitivity and tailoring the intervention to the community's needs could help build trust and encourage participation.
3. The location of the trial was identified as a significant barrier to participation, particularly if the trial was held in a location that was not easily accessible to African American women. Conducting the trial in a location that was familiar and convenient for the community could help increase participation.
4. Developing protocols, policies, and procedures that were inclusive and sensitive to the needs of African American women was seen as important for increasing their participation in the trial. The researchers found that addressing potential participants' concerns about the trial's structure and procedures could help build trust and encourage participation.
To address these barriers, the researchers provided a checklist of actions that nurse researchers could consider to increase African American women's participation in community trials, including:
1. Building relationships with influential community leaders and organizations
2. Conducting community-based participatory research that is culturally sensitive and tailored to the needs of the community
3. Ensuring the trial location is accessible and convenient for the community
4. Developing protocols, policies, and procedures that are inclusive and sensitive to the needs of African American women
By taking these actions, nurse researchers can help increase participation in community trials among African American women and improve the overall quality and diversity of research studies.

title: Geographical access to healthcare in Northern England and post-mortem diagnosis of cancer.
text: BACKGROUND Previous studies have suggested that the diagnosis of cancer at death, as recorded on registry death certificates, may be associated with issues related to access to healthcare. METHODS We analyzed data from the Northern and Yorkshire Cancer Registry for patients diagnosed with breast, colorectal, lung, ovarian, or prostate cancer between 1994 and 2002. We supplemented these records with measures of travel time to general practitioner and hospital services, as well as social deprivation. Logistic regression was used to identify factors that were associated with the likelihood of a delayed diagnosis at death. RESULTS Our findings indicate that there was no significant association between access to primary care and the odds of a delayed diagnosis at death. However, for all cancer sites except breast, the highest odds of a delayed diagnosis at death were found among individuals living in the highest quartile of hospital travel time. Specifically, the odds were 2.6 times higher for colorectal and ovary tumors in the most deprived and distant travel time quartile compared to the most affluent and proximal areas. CONCLUSIONS Our study suggests that inadequate access to tertiary care, particularly when combined with social disadvantages, may be related to a higher likelihood of a delayed diagnosis at death.

title: Enhanced monocyte Fc phagocytosis by a homologue of interleukin-10 encoded by human cytomegalovirus.
text: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) expresses multiple homologs of human interleukin 10 (hIL-10), which have immunomodulatory properties that may promote viral infection by altering the function of myeloid cells. To investigate, we analyzed the phenotype and phagocytic capabilities of human monocytes exposed to hIL-10, an HCMV-encoded hIL-10 homologue expressed during the productive phase of infection (cmvIL-10), and a differentially spliced form of cmvIL-10 expressed during latent and productive phases of infection (LAcmvIL-10). Our findings showed that hIL-10 and cmvIL-10 increased the expression of Fcgamma receptors, stimulated phagocytosis of IgG-opsonized erythrocytes, and decreased major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC class II; HLA-DR) expression on purified monocytes within 24 hours. In contrast, LAcmvIL-10 decreased HLA-DR expression at later time points (48 hours and 72 hours) but did not increase Fcgamma receptor expression. Our findings suggest that cmvIL-10 promotes the differentiation of monocytes towards a pro-phagocytic phenotype, while LAcmvIL-10 does not affect monocytes through the same mechanisms as cmvIL-10. We discuss the implications of these properties on HCMV pathogenesis.

title: 3D Chromosome Regulatory Landscape of Human Pluripotent Cells.
text: In this study, we delved into the three-dimensional chromosomal regulatory landscape of human embryonic stem cells in their naive and primed states. To render this map, we identified enhancer and insulator elements present in these cells and positioned them within the context of cohesin-interacting CTCF-CTCF loops as revealed by ChIA-PET data. The resulting CTCF-CTCF loops divulged a chromosomal framework of segregated domains, which in turn composed topologically associating domains (TADs) that remained largely intact during the transition between the naive and primed states. Regulatory changes in enhancer-promoter interactions occurred within the insulated regions during cellular transition. The conserved CTCF anchor regions we identified were found to have a significant impact on gene expression and were often implicated in cancer mutations, thus emphasizing their functional importance in cellular regulation. These three-dimensional regulatory maps of human pluripotent cells serve as a robust foundation for exploring the complex interplay between chromosomal structure and gene regulation in both development and disease.

title: Functional analysis via standardized whole-blood stimulation systems defines the boundaries of a healthy immune response to complex stimuli.
text: Standardization of immunophenotyping protocols has become a pressing concern. Our team has developed a set of innovative whole-blood, syringe-based assay systems that can consistently evaluate induced innate or adaptive immune responses. By eliminating preanalytical errors inherent in immune monitoring, we have identified the specific protein signatures triggered by (1) medically relevant bacteria, fungi, and viruses; (2) specific agonists for defined host sensors; (3) clinically employed cytokines; and (4) activators of T cell immunity. Our findings establish initial reference values for cytokines and chemokines in healthy donors and reveal the common phenomenon of failing to release interleukin-1α as an immunological trait. The observed natural variability in the immune response may help explain why some individuals are more prone to disease or response to medical interventions. The implementation of a comprehensive solution for assessing functional immune responses will help facilitate harmonization of clinical trials and data sharing.

title: SATB1 Expression Governs Epigenetic Repression of PD‐1 in Tumor‐Reactive T Cells
text:
Importance of Programmed Cell Death-1 (PD-1) in T Cell Immunity
Contrary to the critical role of PD-1 in restraining T cell effector activity, the mechanisms that regulate its expression remain obscure. Our research uncovered that the chromatin organizer, AT-rich sequence-binding protein-1 (Satb1), curtails PD-1 expression upon T cell activation by recruiting a nucleosome remodeling deacetylase (NuRD) complex to Pdcd1 regulatory regions. Deficiency in Satb1 T cells exhibited a 40-fold increase in PD-1 expression. Tumor-derived transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) decreased Satb1 expression through binding of Smad proteins to the Satb1 promoter. These proteins also competed with the Satb1-NuRD complex for binding to Pdcd1 enhancers, releasing Pdcd1 expression from Satb1-mediated repression. Importantly, our findings suggest that Satb1 functions to prevent premature T cell exhaustion by regulating Pdcd1 expression upon T cell activation. Dysregulation of this pathway in tumor-infiltrating T cells leads to diminished anti-tumor immunity.
[Graphical Abstract]
[Highlights]
T cell activation enhances Satb1 expression in mature CD8+ and CD4+ T cells.
Satb1 recruits the NuRD repression complex, inhibiting Pdcd1 expression.
In tumors, TGF-β reduces Satb1 expression, leading to increased Pdcd1 expression.
Satb1 deficiency in T cells leads to increased PD-1 expression and decreased anti-tumor activity.
Stephen's work indicates that Satb1 controls PD-1 expression during T cell activation through the recruitment of a deacetylase complex to the Pdcd1 gene's regulatory regions. Tumor-derived TGF-β dysregulates this pathway, leading to unchecked PD-1 expression in tumor-infiltrating T cells and inferior anti-tumor immunity.

title: Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in dendritic cells induces IL-1β–dependent adaptive immunity against tumors
text: The effectiveness of cancer-fighting chemotherapy may depend on the presence of certain immune cells called dendritic cells (DCs), which process and present antigens from dying cancer cells to stimulate the production of tumor-specific immune cells called T lymphocytes that produce interferon-γ (IFN-γ). Our study shows that when cancer cells die, they release a molecule called ATP, which triggers a response in DCs through a specific receptor called P2X7. This leads to the activation of a complex called the inflammasome, which includes a protein called NLRP3. The inflammasome triggers the maturation and release of the immune signaling molecule interleukin-1β (IL-1β), which in turn primes IFN-γ–producing CD8+ T cells to attack the cancer cells. We found that the efficiency of chemotherapy depends on the presence of a functional IL-1 receptor 1 and that individuals lacking this receptor or a related protein called caspase-1 are more susceptible to cancer metastasis. These results suggest that the NLRP3 inflammasome plays a critical role in connecting the innate and adaptive immune responses against dying cancer cells.

title: Mfge8 promotes obesity by mediating the uptake of dietary fats and serum fatty acids
text:
Fatty acids play a crucial role in energy storage, cell signaling, and membrane formation. Although the pathways involved in fatty acid uptake are not fully understood, research has shown that the expression of the integrin ligand Mfge8 is increased in obesity and linked to fatty acid absorption and cellular uptake.
In this study, we found that Mfge8 promotes the absorption of dietary triglycerides and cellular uptake of fatty acids. We also discovered that Mfge8-deficient mice are protected from obesity, steatohepatitis, and insulin resistance.
Our findings suggest that Mfge8 regulates fatty acid uptake through the phosphorylation of Akt by phosphatidylinositide-3 kinase and mTOR complex 2, leading to the translocation of Cd36 and Fatp1 from cytoplasmic vesicles to the cell surface. These findings implicate Mfge8 in the regulation of dietary fat absorption and the development of obesity-related complications.

title: RAD52 Facilitates Mitotic DNA Synthesis Following Replication Stress.
text: Homologous recombination (HR) plays a critical role in counteracting DNA replication stress, particularly at common fragile site (CFS) loci. During replication stress at these locations, mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS) is activated, which requires the MUS81-EME1 endonuclease and a non-catalytic subunit of the Pol-delta complex, POLD3. In this study, we investigate the contribution of HR factors to MiDAS in human cells. Our findings reveal that RAD51 and BRCA2 are dispensable for MiDAS, but are necessary to counteract replication stress at CFS loci during the S-phase of the cell cycle. In contrast, MiDAS is RAD52 dependent, and RAD52 is required for the timely recruitment of MUS81 and POLD3 to CFSs in early mitosis. These findings provide further mechanistic insight into MiDAS and define a specific function for human RAD52. Additionally, selective inhibition of MiDAS may represent a potential therapeutic strategy to sensitize cancer cells experiencing replicative stress.

title: Excitotoxic brain injury in adult zebrafish stimulates neurogenesis and long-distance neuronal integration.
text: Zebrafish possess a greater capacity than mammals to repair their central nervous systems following injury. Understanding the differences in regenerative responses between various vertebrate species may provide valuable insights into strategies to enhance repair in humans. Quinolinic acid is an excitotoxin commonly used to induce brain injury in rodents for modeling conditions such as Huntington's disease and stroke. In rodents, quinolinic acid stimulates neurogenesis and the migration of neuroblasts to the injured area, but the majority of new neurons fail to survive and lesion repair remains minimal. To study reparative processes in the zebrafish brain, we used quinolinic acid to lesion the adult telencephalon. We also employed conditional transgenic lineage mapping of adult radial glia stem cells to investigate the survival and integration of neurons generated after injury. Our findings indicate that quinolinic acid lesioning of the zebrafish brain leads to cell death, microglial infiltration, increased cell proliferation, and enhanced neurogenesis in the injured hemisphere. Lesion repair was more pronounced following quinolinic acid injection than after vehicle injection. Using fate mapping of her4-expressing radial glia, we observed an expansion of radial glia stem cells after injury, which gave rise to neurons that migrated to the injured area, survived for at least 8 weeks, and formed long-distance projections that connected the opposite hemisphere. These findings suggest that quinolinic acid lesioning of the zebrafish brain stimulates adult neural stem cells to produce robust regeneration with long-distance integration of new neurons. This model should be useful in elucidating the reparative mechanisms that can be applied to the development of restorative therapies for mammalian brain injury.

title: Germinal Center T Follicular Helper Cells Are Highly Permissive to HIV-1 and Alter Their Phenotype during Virus Replication.
text: HIV-1 replication is primarily confined to CD4(+) T cells within B cell follicles of secondary lymphoid tissues during asymptomatic disease. Limited evidence suggests that a subpopulation of T follicular helper cells (TFH) in germinal centers (GC) is highly susceptible to HIV-1. However, it remains unclear whether GC TFH are the primary HIV-1-producing cells in vivo. In this study, we investigated TFH susceptibility to HIV-1 ex vivo by culturing tonsil cells with HIV-1 GFP reporter viruses. Using flow cytometry, we observed higher proportions of GC TFH (CXCR5(high)PD-1(high)) and CXCR5(+) PD-1(low) cells that were GFP(+) compared to non-GC TFH (CXCR5(+)PD-1(intermediate)) or extrafollicular (EF) cells. When sorted prior to spinoculation, however, GC TFH were more permissive than CXCR5(+) PD-1(low) or EF cells, suggesting that many GC TFH transition to a CXCR5(+) PD-1(low) phenotype during productive infection. In situ hybridization on inguinal lymph node sections from untreated HIV-1-infected individuals without AIDS revealed higher frequencies of HIV-1 RNA(+) cells in GC than non-GC regions of follicle or EF regions. Superinfection of HIV-1-infected individuals' lymph node cells with GFP reporter virus confirmed the susceptibility of follicular cells ex vivo. Immunostaining of lymph node cells from four HIV-infected individuals revealed that 96% of CXCR5(+) CD4(+) cells were located in follicles. Within sorted lymph node cells, CXCR5(+) subsets harbored 11-66-fold more HIV-1 RNA than CXCR5(-) subsets, as determined by RT PCR. These findings strongly suggest that GC TFH are the major HIV-1-producing cells in chronic asymptomatic HIV-1 infection.

title: Risk of death with atypical antipsychotic drug treatment for dementia: meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials.
text:
Context: Atypical antipsychotic medications are commonly used to treat symptoms such as delusions, aggression, and agitation in patients with Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. However, concerns have been raised about the potential risks associated with their use, including an increased risk of cerebrovascular adverse events, rapid cognitive decline, and mortality.
Objective: To assess the evidence for an increased risk of mortality associated with the use of atypical antipsychotic drugs in patients with dementia.
Data Sources: We searched several databases including MEDLINE (1966 to April 2005), the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register (2005, Issue 1), and conference presentations (1997-2004) for studies on atypical antipsychotic drugs used to treat patients with dementia.
Study Selection: We selected randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trials that compared atypical antipsychotic drugs to placebo in patients with Alzheimer's disease or other forms of dementia. A total of 15 trials (9 unpublished) were identified, with a duration of 10 to 12 weeks.
Data Extraction: We extracted data from the selected trials, including baseline characteristics, outcomes, dropouts, and deaths. Treatment exposure was also obtained or estimated.
Data Synthesis: We calculated odds ratios (ORs) and risk differences based on patients randomized and relative risks based on total exposure to treatment. The results showed that death occurred more frequently among patients randomized to atypical antipsychotic drugs (118 [3.5%] vs 40 [2.3%]. The OR by meta-analysis was 1.54; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.06-2.23; P = .02; and risk difference was 0.01; 95% CI, 0.004-0.02; P = .01).
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that atypical antipsychotic drugs may be associated with a small increased risk of death compared to placebo. This risk should be considered in the context of medical need, efficacy evidence, medical comorbidity, and the efficacy and safety of alternative treatments. Individual patient analyses modeling survival and causes of death are needed.

title: PI3K in cancer: divergent roles of isoforms, modes of activation and therapeutic targeting
text: Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases (PI3Ks) play a central role in mediating intracellular signaling in response to extracellular stimuli. The overactivation of PI3K signaling pathways is a common occurrence in human cancers, making them an attractive target for cancer therapy. In this review, we will delve into recent breakthroughs in our understanding of the functions of specific PI3K isoforms in both normal and cancerous signaling pathways, explore the various mechanisms by which PI3K can be upregulated, and examine the current state and future potential of targeting this pathway in the clinical setting.

title: Amphiregulin enhances regulatory T cell-suppressive function via the epidermal growth factor receptor.
text: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a critical player in both tissue development and homeostasis, as well as the pathogenesis of cancer. Interestingly, we have found that Foxp3(+) regulatory T (Treg) cells express EGFR under inflammatory conditions. Upon stimulation with the EGF-like growth factor Amphiregulin (AREG), Treg cells exhibited enhanced function in vitro. In a colitis and tumor vaccination model, AREG was found to be essential for optimal Treg cell function in vivo. Remarkably, mast cell-derived AREG was able to fully restore optimal Treg cell function. These findings uncover EGFR as a key component in the regulation of local immune responses, highlighting a link between mast cells and Treg cells. Targeting this immune regulatory mechanism may contribute to the therapeutic successes of EGFR-targeting treatments in cancer patients.

title: Gonadotrope-specific deletion of Dicer results in severely suppressed gonadotropins and fertility defects.
text: Pituitary gonadotropins follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) are heterodimeric glycoproteins produced by gonadotropes. They regulate the development and function of gonads, including steroidogenesis and gametogenesis, by acting on the gonads. Although research has focused on the transcriptional regulation of gonadotropin subunits, the post-transcriptional regulation of these subunits is poorly understood. To investigate if microRNAs regulate the hormone-specific gonadotropin β subunits in vivo, we deleted the Dicer gene in gonadotropes using a Cre-lox genetic approach. We found that many of the DICER-dependent microRNAs, predicted to bind gonadotropin β subunit mRNAs, were suppressed in purified gonadotropes of mutant mice. The loss of DICER-dependent microRNAs in gonadotropes led to a significant suppression of gonadotropin-β subunit proteins and, consequently, the heterodimeric hormone secretion. Interestingly, the post-gonadectomy-induced increase in pituitary gonadotropin synthesis and secretion were also abolished in mutants, indicating a defective gonadal negative feedback control. Moreover, mutants lacking Dicer in gonadotropes exhibited severely reduced fertility that was restored by exogenous hormones. Our findings reveal that DICER-dependent microRNAs are crucial for maintaining gonadotropin homeostasis and fertility in mice. Furthermore, these studies highlight the role of microRNAs in the regulation of gonadal feedback control of gonadotropin synthesis and secretion, thereby adding a new layer of transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation in gonadotropes to control the hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal axis physiology.

title: Sequential histone-modifying activities determine the robustness of transdifferentiation
text: Interactions between different somatic cell types have been observed in various species, including jellyfish and mice. The consistency and reproducibility of some cell conversions provide untapped opportunities to learn about the mechanisms that ensure reliable cellular transformation. We have discovered that a conserved H3K27me3/me2 demethylase, JMJD-3.1, and the H3K4 methyltransferase Set1 complex collaborate to guarantee invariant transdifferentiation (Td) of postmitotic Caenorhabditis elegans hindgut cells into motor neurons. At the single-cell level, efficient conversion requires a series of histone-modifying activities, which are organized into distinct phases of Td through the nuclear degradation of JMJD-3.1 and phase-specific interactions with transcription factors that play conserved roles in cellular plasticity and terminal fate selection. Our findings parallel the epigenetic mechanisms underlying reliable Td in nature and efficient cell reprogramming in vitro.

title: Normal and leukemic stem cell niches: insights and therapeutic opportunities.
text: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) rely on cues from the bone marrow (BM) microenvironment to maintain their quiescence and adapt blood production to the organism's needs. However, alterations in the BM niche are commonly observed in blood malignancies and contribute to the aberrant function of disease-initiating leukemic stem cells (LSCs). In this review, we examine recent insights into the cellular and molecular determinants of the normal HSC niche and discuss how genetic changes in stromal cells and leukemia-induced BM niche remodeling contribute to blood malignancies. Additionally, we explore how these findings can be applied to non-cell-autonomous therapies targeting the LSC niche.

title: Role of common hypnotics on the phenotypic causes of obstructive sleep apnoea: paradoxical effects of zolpidem.
text: Hypnotics are contraindicated in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) due to concerns of pharyngeal muscle relaxation and delayed arousal worsening hypoxia. However, there is a lack of human data on the effects of hypnotics on respiratory arousal, genioglossus muscle responsiveness, and upper airway collapsibility during sleep. To address this gap, we conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in which 21 individuals with and without OSA (aged 18-65 years) completed 84 detailed sleep studies after receiving temazepam, zolpidem, zopiclone, or placebo on four occasions. Our findings showed that the arousal threshold increased with zolpidem and zopiclone compared to placebo (mean±SD -18.3±10 and -19.1±9 vs -14.6±7 cmH2O; p=0.02 and p<0.001), but not with temazepam (-16.8±9 cmH2O; p=0.17). Additionally, genioglossus muscle activity during stable non-rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and responsiveness during airway narrowing were not different with temazepam and zopiclone compared to placebo, but paradoxically, zolpidem increased median muscle responsiveness threefold during airway narrowing (median -0.15 (interquartile range -1.01 to -0.04) vs -0.05 (-0.29 to -0.03)% maximum EMG per cmH2O epiglottic pressure; p=0.03). Finally, the upper airway critical closing pressure did not change with any of the hypnotics. In summary, these doses of common hypnotics have differential effects on the respiratory arousal threshold but do not reduce upper airway muscle activity or alter airway collapsibility during sleep. Instead, muscle activity increases during airway narrowing with zolpidem.

title: Clinical human papillomavirus detection forecasts cervical cancer risk in women over 18 years of follow-up.
text:
Purpose: To evaluate the long-term (≥10 years) benefits of clinical human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing for cervical precancer and cancer risk prediction.
Methods: Cervicovaginal lavages from 19,512 women attending a health maintenance program were retrospectively tested for HPV using a clinical test. Women with HPV-positive results were further tested for HPV16 and HPV18 individually using a research test. Papanicolaou (Pap) results classified as atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) or more severe were considered abnormal. Women underwent follow-up prospectively with routine annual Pap testing up to 18 years. Cumulative incidence rates (CIRs) of ≥grade 3 cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN3+) or cancer for enrollment test results were calculated.
Results: A baseline negative HPV test provided greater reassurance against CIN3+ over the 18-year follow-up compared to a normal Pap (CIR, 0.90% vs 1.27%). While both baseline Pap and HPV tests predicted who would develop CIN3+ within the first 2 years of follow-up, only HPV testing predicted who would develop CIN3+ 10 to 18 years later (P = .004). HPV16- and HPV18-positive women with normal Pap were at elevated risk of CIN3+ compared to other HPV-positive women with normal Pap and were at similar risk of CIN3+ compared to women with a low-grade squamous intraepithelial Pap.
Conclusion: HPV testing to rule out cervical disease followed by Pap testing and possibly combined with the detection of HPV16 and HPV18 among HPV positives to identify those at immediate risk of CIN3+ would be an efficient algorithm for cervical cancer screening, especially in women aged 30 years or older.

title: MG53 nucleates assembly of cell membrane repair machinery
text: Membrane repair and remodeling is an essential process that maintains cellular integrity and enables efficient cellular function. Our study reveals that MG53, a muscle-specific protein belonging to the tripartite motif family (TRIM72), plays a crucial role in the sarcolemmal membrane-repair machinery. MG53 interacts with phosphatidylserine to associate with intracellular vesicles that traffic to and fuse with sarcolemmal membranes. In mice lacking MG53, myopathy and reduced exercise capacity result from defective membrane-repair capacity. Upon injury to the sarcolemmal membrane, the extracellular oxidative environment is entered through MG53 oligomerization, leading to the recruitment of MG53-containing vesicles to the injury site. Following vesicle translocation, entry of extracellular calcium ions facilitates vesicle fusion to reseal the membrane. Our findings demonstrate that intracellular vesicle translocation and calcium-dependent membrane fusion are two distinct steps involved in the repair of membrane damage, and suggest that MG53 may initiate the assembly of the membrane repair machinery through an oxidation-dependent mechanism.

title: A large-scale replication study identifies TNIP1, PRDM1, JAZF1, UHRF1BP1 and IL10 as risk loci for systemic lupus erythematosus
text: Recent genome-wide association studies have identified at least 15 genetic loci associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). To further investigate these findings, we selected and genotyped additional SNPs from regions showing nominal evidence of association with SLE (P < 0.05) in a previous study, in an independent sample of 1,963 cases and 4,329 controls. This replication effort confirmed five new SLE susceptibility loci (P < 5 × 10−8): TNIP1 (odds ratio (OR) = 1.27), PRDM1 (OR = 1.20), JAZF1 (OR = 1.20), UHRF1BP1 (OR = 1.17), and IL10 (OR = 1.19). Additionally, we identified 21 candidate loci with P ≤ 1 × 10−5 that may contribute to SLE. Furthermore, a screen of alleles associated with other autoimmune diseases revealed five loci (P < 1 × 10−3) that may also play a role in SLE: IFIH1, CFB, CLEC16A, IL12B, and SH2B3. These findings expand the number of confirmed and candidate SLE susceptibility loci and highlight several key immunologic pathways involved in SLE pathogenesis.

title: ARID1A-mutated ovarian cancers depend on HDAC6 activity
text: The ARID1A gene, which encodes a subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex, is the most frequently mutated epigenetic regulator across all human cancers. ARID1A and TP53 mutations are typically mutually exclusive, and as such, therapeutic strategies that corroborate this genetic characteristic have yet to be explored. In this study, we investigate the role of HDAC6 activity in ARID1A-mutated ovarian cancers. We find that HDAC6 activity is essential in these tumors, and that inhibition of HDAC6 using a clinically relevant small-molecule inhibitor significantly improves the survival of mice bearing ARID1A-mutated tumors. This is accompanied by the suppression of growth and dissemination of ARID1A-mutated tumors, but not those that are wild-type. Our results demonstrate that the dependence of HDAC6 activity in ARID1A-mutated cells is directly correlated with the direct transcriptional repression of HDAC6 by ARID1A. Further, we find that HDAC6 inhibition selectively promotes apoptosis in ARID1A-mutated cells, which is mediated by the direct deacetylation of Lys120 of p53 by HDAC6. Notably, ARID1A mutation inactivates the pro-apoptotic function of p53 by upregulating HDAC6, thereby providing a therapeutic strategy for ARID1A-mutated cancers.

title: Solution NMR structure of the TatA component of the twin-arginine protein transport system from gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis.
text: The Tat transport system translocates folded proteins across the cytoplasmic or chloroplast thylakoid membrane of plant cells. The Tat system in most Gram-positive bacteria is composed of two essential proteins, TatA and TatC. TatA is a bifunctional subunit that forms a protein-conducting channel through self-oligomerization and participates in substrate recognition. However, the mechanism of protein translocation remains unclear. In this study, we report the atomic-level structure of the TatA(d) protein from Bacillus subtilis using NMR spectroscopy. The TatA(d) protein has an L-shaped structure consisting of a transmembrane helix and an amphipathic helix, with the C-terminal tail being mostly unstructured. Our results reveal that the transmembrane helix is inserted into the lipid bilayer, while the amphipathic helix faces the membrane-water interface. Furthermore, the structure of TatA(d) highlights the importance of conserved residues in the hinge region, providing new insights into the protein transport mechanism of the Tat system.

title: Autoimmunity due to molecular mimicry as a cause of neurological disease
text:
A hypothesis linking infection with autoimmune disease is molecular mimicry, where an immune response to an environmental agent resembles a host antigen, leading to disease. This theory has been implicated in the development of diabetes, lupus, and multiple sclerosis (MS). However, there is limited direct evidence connecting the causative agents with pathogenic immune reactions in these diseases. Our study provides conclusive evidence establishing a link between viral infection, autoimmunity, and neurological disease in humans.
As a model for molecular mimicry, we focused on patients with human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1)-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP), a condition that can mimic MS. HAM/TSP patients develop antibodies against neurons, which led us to hypothesize that these antibodies would identify a central nervous system (CNS) autoantigen. Through immunoglobulin G isolated from HAM/TSP patients, we discovered heterogeneous nuclear ribonuclear protein-A1 (hnRNP-A1) as the autoantigen. Interestingly, these antibodies also cross-reacted with HTLV-1-tax, an immune response associated with HAM/TSP. Using immunoglobulin G, we specifically stained human Betz cells, whose axons are more prone to damage. In addition, infusing autoantibodies into brain sections inhibited neuronal firing, further supporting their pathogenic role. These findings demonstrate the significance of molecular mimicry between the infecting agent and hnRNP-A1 in autoimmune diseases of the CNS.

title: Altered recognition of antigen is a mechanism of CD8+ T cell tolerance in cancer
text: Antigen-specific CD8+ T-cell tolerance, mediated by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), is a prominent mechanism of tumor evasion. Through the use of in vivo models, we have demonstrated here that MDSCs directly disrupt the binding of specific peptide–major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) dimers to CD8-expressing T cells by nitrating the tyrosine residues in the T-cell receptor (TCR)-CD8 complex. This process renders CD8-expressing T cells incapable of binding pMHC and responding to the specific peptide, despite their ability to respond to nonspecific stimuli. The nitration of TCR-CD8 is orchestrated by MDSCs through an increase in reactive oxygen species and peroxynitrite production during direct cell-cell contact. Molecular modeling has identified specific sites of nitration that may influence the conformational flexibility of TCR-CD8 and its interaction with pMHC. These findings elucidate a previously unappreciated mechanism of T-cell tolerance in cancer, which is also relevant to many pathological conditions characterized by the accumulation of MDSCs.

title: A new genetic subgroup of chronic granulomatous disease with autosomal recessive mutations in p40 phox and selective defects in neutrophil NADPH oxidase activity.
text: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), a rare immunodeficiency disorder characterized by recurrent pyogenic infections and granulomatous inflammation, is caused by mutations in genes encoding subunits of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase. Four of these genes, gp91(phox), p22(phox), p47(phox), and p67(phox), are involved in the production of intracellular superoxide during phagocytosis. A fifth subunit, p40(phox), plays a unique role in phagocytosis-induced superoxide production through its PX domain, which binds to phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PtdIns(3)P). In this study, we report the first case of autosomal recessive mutations in the NCF4 gene, which encodes p40(phox), in a boy with granulomatous colitis. Our findings show that the patient's neutrophils have a significant defect in intracellular superoxide production during phagocytosis, while extracellular release of superoxide is not affected. Genetic analysis of NCF4 revealed compound heterozygosity for a frameshift mutation with a premature stop codon and a missense mutation predicting a R105Q substitution in the PX domain. The parents and a sibling are healthy heterozygous carriers. Our results demonstrate that p40(phox) binding to PtdIns(3)P is essential for phagocytosis-induced oxidant production in human neutrophils, and that the absence of this binding can lead to disease.

title: Birth weight and mammographic density among postmenopausal women in Sweden.
text: Birth weight is a significant predictor of breast cancer risk in adulthood, and the mammary gland mass may represent an intermediate stage in this long process. In this study, we investigated the relationship between birth size measurements and mammographic density, a marker of mammary gland mass, in a population-based sample of 893 postmenopausal women in Sweden. We retrieved information on birth size from birth records and mammography results. Our analysis used computer-assisted semi-automated thresholding of mammographic density using the Cumulus software. The results were analyzed using generalized linear models, controlling for potential confounders. We found that mean mammographic density increased significantly when comparing extreme birth weight categories (from 15.6% to 18.6%) and head circumference categories (from 15.5% to 20.4%). The corresponding linear trends were statistically significant (p values 0.02 and 0.007, respectively). The associations were particularly strong when the cutoff for high versus low mammographic density was set at a relatively high value of 50%. Compared to women born at 3001-3500 grams, women born at >4000g had almost 3-fold increased risk of developing high mammographic density (odds ratio: 2.9, 95% confidence interval: 1.1 to 7.9). No association was found between mammographic density and birth length, which is known to be less accurately measured. These findings suggest that adult breast density, a powerful predictor of breast cancer risk, has intrauterine roots, as reflected in birth size.

title: Oral ciclopirox olamine displays biological activity in a phase I study in patients with advanced hematologic malignancies.
text: Ciclopirox olamine, an antimycotic agent with anticancer properties, was evaluated in a first-in-human phase I trial for patients with relapsed or refractory hematologic malignancies. Oral formulations of ciclopirox olamine were developed and patients were treated with doses ranging from 5-80 mg/m² once daily for five days in 21-day cycles. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies were conducted in a subset of patients, and results showed rapid absorption and clearance with a short half-life. Plasma concentrations of an inactive metabolite were higher than those of ciclopirox. Expression of the survivin protein was repressed in peripheral blood cells from patients treated with doses above 10 mg/m², indicating biological activity of the drug. Dose-limiting gastrointestinal toxicities were observed at high doses, but no dose-limiting toxicity was observed at a lower dose. Two patients exhibited hematologic improvement. Once-daily oral dosing of ciclopirox olamine was well tolerated in these patients, and further optimization of dosing regimens is warranted.

title: Cancer cell–autonomous contribution of type I interferon signaling to the efficacy of chemotherapy
text: Some of the anti-tumor effects of anthracyclines in mice are due to the induction of immune responses through the activation of innate and T cell-mediated pathways. We demonstrate that anthracyclines trigger the rapid production of type I interferons (IFNs) in cancer cells after activation of the endosomal pattern recognition receptor Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3). These IFNs bind to receptors on cancer cells, leading to the release of chemokines, such as C-X-C motif ligand 10 (CXCL10). In mice lacking TLR3 or IFNARs, tumors failed to respond to chemotherapy unless type I IFN or CXCL10, respectively, were artificially supplied. Furthermore, a type I IFN-related signature predicted clinical responses to anthracycline-based chemotherapy in several independent cohorts of patients with breast cancer. Our findings suggest that the anti-tumor effects of anthracyclines mimic those induced by viral infections, and that this 'viral mimicry' may be a hallmark of successful chemotherapy.

title: alphaE-catenin controls cerebral cortical size by regulating the hedgehog signaling pathway.
text: During the formation of organs, cells regulate their growth rates to produce predetermined structures. Our research reveals that deleting the essential adherens junction gene, alphaE-catenin, in the central nervous system leads to abnormal activation of the Hedgehog signaling pathway, resulting in shortened cell cycles, decreased apoptosis, and excessive thickening of the cerebral cortex. We propose that alphaE-catenin connects cell-density-dependent adherens junctions to the Hedgehog signaling pathway, forming a negative feedback loop that controls the size of developing cerebral cortex.

title: Molecular regulation of effector and memory T cell differentiation
text:
Immunological memory, a cornerstone of adaptive immunity, is a primary focus of vaccination strategies. This article highlights groundbreaking advances in our understanding of the diverse T lymphocyte subsets that provide acute and long-term protection against infection. These insights include:
1. New discoveries regarding transcription factors and upstream "pioneering" factors that regulate access to key sites of gene regulation.
2. Metabolic regulators that contribute to the differentiation of effector and memory subsets.
3. A deeper understanding of the ontogeny and defining characteristics of tissue-resident memory lymphocytes.
4. The origins of the remarkable heterogeneity exhibited by activated T cells.
Together, these findings demonstrate progress in uncovering the underlying pathways that govern T cell diversification, but also reveal gaps in our knowledge and the challenges that arise in applying this knowledge to elicit desired T cell responses through vaccination and immunotherapy.

title: Liver-resident macrophage necroptosis orchestrates type 1 microbicidal inflammation and type-2-mediated tissue repair during bacterial infection.
text: Kupffer cells, the fetal-derived phagocytes lining liver sinusoids, play a pivotal role in host defense against enteroinvasive bacteria. During Listeria monocytogenes infection, Kupffer cells undergo early necroptotic death, leading to monocyte recruitment and a type 1 inflammatory response. This raised alarmins (interleukin-33 and interleukin-4) from hepatocytes and basophils, respectively, resulting in the alternative activation of monocyte-derived macrophages. These cells replace previously ablated Kupffer cells, ensuring liver homeostasis restoration. Kupffer cell death serves as a crucial signal initiating type 1 microbicidal inflammation and type-2-mediated liver repair upon bacterial infection. This demonstrates that the classical dichotomy of type 1 and type 2 responses is not absolute, as these responses can develop sequentially during an infection and collaboratively orchestrate liver immune responses and return to homeostasis.

title: Gene regulation in the immune system by long noncoding RNAs
text: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are emerging as crucial regulators of gene expression in the immune system. Research has shown that lncRNAs are specifically expressed in different immune cell types and play a key role in controlling the differentiation and function of innate and adaptive immune cells. In this review, we delve into the mechanisms lncRNAs use to regulate genes involved in the immune response, including direct interactions with chromatin, RNA, and proteins. We also explore new areas of lncRNA biology, such as the functions of enhancer RNAs, circular RNAs, and chemical modifications to RNA in cellular processes. Despite the growing knowledge of lncRNAs in the immune system, there are still significant gaps in understanding their roles in disease, and future studies are needed to uncover the full potential of lncRNAs in immunology.

title: The Ly49Q receptor plays a crucial role in neutrophil polarization and migration by regulating raft trafficking.
text: Neutrophils quickly adapt and move in a directed manner to reach sites of infection and inflammation. Our findings demonstrate that an inhibitory MHC I receptor called Ly49Q plays a crucial role in the rapid polarization and tissue infiltration of neutrophils. During steady state conditions, Ly49Q hinders neutrophil adhesion by preventing focal-complex formation, likely by inhibiting Src and PI3 kinases. Nonetheless, in the presence of inflammatory stimuli, Ly49Q prompts rapid neutrophil polarization and tissue infiltration in an ITIM-domain-dependent manner. These opposing functions are mediated by different utilization of effector phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2. Ly49Q-dependent polarization and migration are likewise affected by Ly49Q's regulation of membrane raft functions. We propose that Ly49Q is essential in switching neutrophils to their polarized morphology and rapid migration upon inflammation by controlling spatiotemporal regulation of membrane rafts and raft-associated signaling molecules.

title: Prevalence of Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus infection in homosexual men at beginning of and during the HIV epidemic.
text:
In the early years of the HIV epidemic in San Francisco, a significant portion of homosexual men were infected with Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), according to some studies. However, direct measurements of KSHV prevalence at the time of the HIV outbreak are lacking. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of KSHV infection in homosexual men in San Francisco from 1978 to 1996 and to examine changes in KSHV prevalence in relation to changes in sexual behavior.
The study analyzed data from a clinic-based sample of 398 individuals and population-based samples from the San Francisco Men's Health Study (MHS), the San Francisco Young Men's Health Study (YMHS), and the San Francisco City Clinic Cohort. The study found that in 1978 and 1979, the prevalence of KSHV infection was 26.5% among the overall sample (weighted for HIV infection) compared to 6.9% in the San Francisco City Clinic Cohort sample. The prevalence of KSHV infection remained relatively stable between 1984 and 1996, with KSHV infection at 29.6% in an MHS sample from 1984 and 1985 and at 26.4% in a YMHS sample from 1995 and 1996. In contrast, the prevalence of HIV infection decreased from 49.5% of 825 in 1984 and 1985 (MHS) to 17.6% of 428 in 1992 and 1993 (YMHS). The study also found that the proportion of men engaging in unprotected receptive anal intercourse with one or more partners declined from 54% to 11% between the 1984 through 1993 period (MHS) and the YMHS in 1992 and 1993, with similar though slightly higher values in the YMHS.
In conclusion, this study found that KSHV infection was already highly prevalent among homosexual men in San Francisco when the HIV epidemic began, and its prevalence has remained relatively constant since then. While there has been a decline in the incidence of Kaposi sarcoma, this is not likely due to a decline in KSHV transmission.

title: Nortriptyline for smoking cessation: a review.
text: The present review examines the effectiveness of nortriptyline in aiding smoking cessation through a meta-analysis of the Cochrane Library. Six placebo-controlled trials demonstrated that nortriptyline (75-100 mg) significantly doubles the likelihood of quitting smoking (OR = 2.1). However, between 4% and 12% of participants dropped out due to adverse events, although no serious side effects were reported. The article finds that nortriptyline's efficacy is not directly related to its antidepressant properties. The drug is found to be an effective aid to smoking cessation, with a magnitude of effect comparable to that of bupropion and nicotine replacement therapies. Although nortriptyline has been tested in only 500 smokers, the finding that it is effective alongside bupropion but not selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitors suggests that dopaminergic or adrenergic, rather than serotonergic, activity may play a crucial role in cessation success. Therefore, until further studies can confirm a low incidence of significant adverse events, nortriptyline should be considered a second-line treatment for smoking cessation.

title: Emotion dysregulation in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
text: Despite recognition of the interplay between attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and emotional regulation, a consensus on how to approach this clinically complex domain remains elusive. This study synthesizes the existing literature using both quantitative and qualitative methods, uncovering three key findings. First, emotion dysregulation is prevalent in ADHD across the lifespan and significantly contributes to impairment. Second, emotion dysregulation in ADHD may stem from difficulties in attending to, recognizing, and allocating attention to emotional stimuli, pointing to dysfunction within the striato-amygdalo-medial prefrontal cortical network. Third, while current ADHD treatments often address emotion dysregulation as a side effect, reframing the clinical picture with an emphasis on this combination of symptoms may lead to novel therapeutic approaches. The authors then explore three models that could explain the overlap between emotion dysregulation and ADHD: (1) emotion dysregulation and ADHD are separate but correlated dimensions, (2) emotion dysregulation is a core ADHD diagnostic feature, or (3) the combination represents a distinct nosological entity separate from both ADHD and emotion dysregulation alone. The differing predictions from each model can inform research on the often-overlooked population of individuals with ADHD and emotion dysregulation.

title: Use of serum C reactive protein and procalcitonin concentrations in addition to symptoms and signs to predict pneumonia in patients presenting to primary care with acute cough: diagnostic study
text:
Background:
Diagnosing pneumonia in primary care settings can be challenging, and current clinical prediction rules are not always accurate. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of selected inflammatory markers, along with symptoms and signs, in predicting pneumonia in patients presenting to primary care with acute cough.
Methods:
The study was conducted over a five-year period in 12 European countries, with 2820 patients aged 18-85 years participating. All patients had a detailed medical history taken, underwent physical examination, and had their blood levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin measured. Chest radiography was performed within seven days of initial consultation, and pneumonia was diagnosed by blinded radiologists. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) was used to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of each predictor.
Results:
Of the 2820 patients enrolled, 140 (5%) had pneumonia. The re-evaluation of a subset of 1675 chest radiographs showed good agreement between the radiologists' assessments (κ = 0.45, 95% CI = 0.36-0.54). Six published symptoms and signs models varied in their discrimination (ROC area = 0.55-0.71). The optimal combination of clinical prediction items, derived from the study population, included the absence of runny nose, presence of breathlessness, crackles, and diminished breath sounds on auscultation, tachycardia, and fever, with an ROC area of 0.70 (0.65-0.75). Adding CRP at the optimal cut-off of >30 mg/L increased the ROC area to 0.77 (0.73-0.81) and improved diagnostic classification (net reclassification improvement = 28%). In the low-risk group (≤2.5% pneumonia), the prevalence of pneumonia was 2%, while in the high-risk group (>20% pneumonia), the prevalence was 31%. The positive likelihood ratio of low, intermediate, and high risk for pneumonia was 0.4, 1.2, and 8.6, respectively. Measurement of procalcitonin did not add relevant additional diagnostic information. A simplified diagnostic score based on symptoms, signs, and CRP >30 mg/L resulted in proportions of pneumonia of 0.7%, 3.8%, and 18.2% in the low, intermediate, and high-risk groups, respectively.
Conclusion:
The study found that a clinical rule based on symptoms and signs, combined with the optimal cut-off level of CRP, performed best in patients with mild or severe clinical presentation. Adding CRP concentration at the optimal cut-off of >30 mg/L improved diagnostic information, but measurement of procalcitonin concentration did not add clinically relevant information in this population. The simplified diagnostic score based on symptoms, signs, and CRP >30 mg/L resulted in a low proportion of pneumonia in the low-risk group and a higher proportion in the high-risk group. These findings can help improve the accuracy of pneumonia diagnosis in primary care settings.

title: Somatic Mutations of the Immunoglobulin Framework Are Generally Required for Broad and Potent HIV-1 Neutralization
text: Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) to HIV-1 hold great significance for vaccine design due to their ability to prevent infection. These antibodies are characterized by a high degree of somatic mutation and are generated by a small proportion of HIV-1-infected individuals over time. The antibodies accumulate mutations in the complementarity determining region (CDR) loops, which come into contact with the antigen. The CDR loops are supported by canonical framework regions (FWRs), which are less tolerant of mutations yet essential for scaffolding the CDR loops. We have found that, unlike most antibodies, including those with limited HIV-1 neutralizing activity, most bNAbs require somatic mutations in their FWRs. Structural and functional analyses reveal that these somatic mutations in FWR residues enhance the breadth and potency of bNAbs by providing increased flexibility and/or direct antigen contact. In bNAbs, FWRs play an essential role beyond simply scaffolding the CDR loops and their unique contribution to potency and breadth should be taken into account in HIV-1 vaccine design.

title: Etiology of type 1 diabetes.
text: Recent genetic mapping and gene-phenotype studies have shed light on the genetic basis of type 1 diabetes. At least ten genes have been identified as strong causal candidates, with known functions that implicate key pathways in the disease. These include HLA class II and I molecules binding to preproinsulin peptides and T cell receptors, T and B cell activation, innate pathogen-viral responses, chemokine and cytokine signaling, and T regulatory and antigen-presenting cell functions. This review focuses on research in the field of type 1 diabetes, aiming to uncover disease mechanisms through genetic approaches. The expression and functions of these pathways, as well as disease susceptibility, are susceptible to influence by both epigenetic and environmental factors. Inherited immune phenotypes may serve as early precursors of type 1 diabetes, providing valuable insights for future clinical trials.

title: Plasticity of epithelial stem cells in tissue regeneration
text: Tissues rely on stem cells for maintaining homeostasis and repair. Recent research has shown that the fate and multilineage potential of epithelial stem cells can change depending on their location within a tissue's resident niche, their response to normal tissue homeostasis, their mobilization to repair a wound, or their transplantation to a new environment. In this Review, we explore how different populations of naturally lineage-restricted stem cells and committed progenitors can exhibit remarkable plasticity and reversibility, reacquiring long-term self-renewing capacities and multilineage differentiation potential during physiological and regenerative conditions. We also examine the implications of cellular plasticity for regenerative medicine and cancer.

title: Atm-deficient mice exhibit increased sensitivity to dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis characterized by elevated DNA damage and persistent immune activation.
text: The function of the ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia mutated) protein, which recognizes and responds to DNA double-strand breaks, in the context of inflammation and inflammatory diseases is not well understood. Previous research has shown that high levels of systemic DNA damage occur in mouse models of intestinal inflammation. To investigate the role of ATM in inflammation, we induced experimental colitis in ATM-deficient, ATM-heterozygous, and wild-type mice using dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) administration. Our results showed that ATM-deficient mice had higher disease activity indices and mortality rates compared to heterozygous and wild-type mice. We also observed increased sensitivity to DNA strand breaks in peripheral leukocytes and micronucleus formation in erythroblasts in ATM-deficient mice, particularly during remission periods and after the end of treatment. Additionally, we found elevated levels of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species-mediated damage, including 8-oxoguanine and nitrotyrosine, in both the distal colon and peripheral leukocytes, with ATM-deficient mice showing more 8-oxoguanine formation than wild-type mice. Furthermore, ATM-deficient mice displayed higher upregulation of inflammatory cytokines and larger percentages of activated CD69+ and CD44+ T cells in the peripheral blood throughout treatment. Our findings suggest that ATM may play a critical role in dampening the deleterious effects of chronic DSS-induced inflammation, maintaining systemic genomic stability and the integrity of the gut epithelial barrier.

title: Activin–like kinase–3 activity is important for kidney regeneration and reversal of fibrosis
text: The transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) superfamily of molecules, including bone morphogenic proteins (BMPs) and TGF-β, play a crucial role in regulating inflammation, apoptosis, and cellular transitions in the kidney. Our findings show that elevated levels of the BMP receptor activin-like kinase 3 (Alk3) in diseased kidneys after injury suggest a protective role for Alk3-mediated signaling in the kidney. Through structure-function analysis and synthetic organic chemistry, we constructed a library of small peptide agonists of BMP signaling that target the Alk3 receptor. One such peptide agonist, THR-123, suppressed inflammation, apoptosis, and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition program and reversed established fibrosis in five mouse models of acute and chronic renal injury. Importantly, THR-123 acted specifically through Alk3 signaling, as mice lacking Alk3 in their tubular epithelium failed to respond to therapy with THR-123. Combining THR-123 with the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor captopril exhibited an additive therapeutic benefit in controlling renal fibrosis. Our results demonstrate the potential of BMP signaling agonists as a new line of therapeutic agents for inducing regeneration, repair, and reversing established fibrosis in the kidney.

title: COHCAP: an integrative genomic pipeline for single-nucleotide resolution DNA methylation analysis
text: COHCAP (City of Hope CpG Island Analysis Pipeline) is a powerful algorithm designed to analyze single-nucleotide resolution DNA methylation data, which can be generated through either an Illumina methylation array or targeted bisulfite sequencing. The primary objective of COHCAP is to identify CpG islands that exhibit a consistent pattern of methylation across individual CpG sites. Currently, COHCAP is the only DNA methylation package that seamlessly integrates with gene expression data to identify a subset of CpG islands that are most likely to regulate downstream gene expression. Additionally, COHCAP can generate lists of differentially methylated CpG islands with a concordance of approximately 50% with gene expression data from both cell line data and heterogeneous patient samples. An example from this article highlights well-known breast cancer biomarkers, such as estrogen receptor, which exhibit a negative correlation between DNA methylation and gene expression. COHCAP also provides visualizations for quality control metrics, regions of differential methylation, and the correlation between methylation and gene expression. This valuable software is available for free download at <https://sourceforge.net/projects/cohcap>

title: Subgrouping of patients with neuropathic pain according to pain-related sensory abnormalities: a first step to a stratified treatment approach.
text:
Patients with neuropathic pain exhibit a range of sensory abnormalities, which form unique patterns or mosaics, known as sensory profiles, in each individual. One theory is that distinct mechanisms of pain generation produce specific sensory abnormalities, leading to differences in how patients perceive and respond to treatment. Although controlled trials of promising new drugs have yielded negative results, this may be due to the heterogeneity of the patient population. By subgrouping patients based on their individual sensory profiles, we can reduce this heterogeneity and improve trial design.
Recent studies have shown that subgroups of patients with neuropathic pain exhibit distinct sensory profiles across different disorders. For example, some patients may have a predominantly sensory profile characterized by hyperalgesia, while others may have a profile dominated by hypoalgesia. These findings suggest that a new classification of neuropathic pain should take into account these subgroups of patients with different sensory profiles.
Sensory phenotyping has the potential to revolutionize clinical trial design by enriching the study population with potential treatment responders. By stratifying patients based on their sensory profiles, we may be able to identify those most likely to benefit from a particular treatment, leading to more effective and personalized care. In conclusion, the development of a new classification system for neuropathic pain that incorporates sensory profiles may lead to better treatment outcomes for patients with this complex and debilitating condition.

title: The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3).
text: A task force of 19 experts in sepsis pathobiology, clinical trials, and epidemiology was convened by the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine to evaluate and update definitions for sepsis and septic shock. The team analyzed electronic health record databases, conducted Delphi processes, and held meetings to generate new definitions and clinical criteria. The task force concluded that the term "severe sepsis" was redundant and recommended defining sepsis as "life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection." For clinical operationalization, organ dysfunction can be represented by an increase in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of 2 points or more, which is associated with an in-hospital mortality greater than 10%. Septic shock was defined as a subset of sepsis characterized by particularly profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities, which are associated with a greater risk of mortality than with sepsis alone. In out-of-hospital, emergency department, or general hospital ward settings, adult patients with suspected infection can be rapidly identified as being more likely to have poor outcomes typical of sepsis if they have at least 2 of the following clinical criteria, which together constitute a new bedside clinical score termed quickSOFA (qSOFA): respiratory rate of 22/min or greater, altered mentation, or systolic blood pressure of 100 mm Hg or less. The updated definitions and clinical criteria are intended to replace previous definitions, offer greater consistency for epidemiologic studies and clinical trials, and facilitate earlier recognition and more timely management of patients with sepsis or at risk of developing sepsis.

title: Stem cell transplantation in patients with autonomic neuropathy due to primary (AL) amyloidosis.
text:
OBJECTIVE: Patients with AL amyloidosis may benefit from high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT), but fluid shifts, sepsis, and cardiac dysrhythmias can make transplantation challenging. Patients with autonomic neuropathy (AN) may experience more complications during and after transplantation. The purpose of this study was to assess the outcome of patients with AN undergoing ASCT.
METHODS: We conducted a case-control study of patients with AL amyloidosis and AN who underwent ASCT, comparing them to a large cohort of patients without AN.
RESULTS: We identified 13 patients with AN who underwent ASCT and a matched control group of 95 patients without AN. Patients with AN had more organs involved (median 2.5 vs 1, p < 0.001) and often had their melphalan conditioning dose reduced by 30% (p = 0.0015). Median hospitalization duration was similar between both groups, as were engraftment kinetics. Atrial fibrillation occurred in all patients with AN but only in one control patient (p < 0.0001). Median overall survival (OS) for patients with AN was 29 months, while >60 months for controls (p < 0.0001). Univariate analysis revealed that cardiac involvement (p = 0.0132), AN (p = 0.0011), glomerular filtration rate (p = 0.038), number of organs involved (p = 0.0064), and NT-pro-BNP (p = 0.039) impacted OS. Multivariate analysis revealed that AN retained an independent adverse impact on OS.
CONCLUSIONS: Patients with AN secondary to AL amyloidosis can undergo ASCT with relative safety. Autonomic neuropathy is an independent, adverse determinant of survival in these patients.

title: MicroRNA-148a regulates LDL receptor and ABCA1 expression to control circulating lipoprotein levels
text: The hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) pathway is crucial for eliminating circulating LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) from the bloodstream. Although the transcriptional regulation of LDLR is well understood, the post-transcriptional mechanisms that regulate LDLR expression are just being discovered. To identify microRNAs (miRNAs) that control LDLR activity in human hepatic cells, we developed a high-throughput genome-wide screening assay. Through this screen, we identified and characterized miR-148a as a negative regulator of LDLR expression and activity, and defined a sterol regulatory element–binding protein 1 (SREBP1)-mediated pathway through which miR-148a regulates LDL-C uptake. In mice, inhibition of miR-148a increased hepatic LDLR expression and decreased plasma LDL-C levels. Moreover, we found that miR-148a regulates hepatic expression of ATP-binding cassette, subfamily A, member 1 (ABCA1) and circulating high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels in vivo. These findings reveal the importance of miR-148a in regulating hepatic LDL-C clearance and demonstrate the potential of inhibiting miR-148a to reduce an elevated LDL-C/HDL-C ratio, a key risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

title: BRACHYURY and CDX2 Mediate BMP-Induced Differentiation of Human and Mouse Pluripotent Stem Cells into Embryonic and Extraembryonic Lineages
text:
The text is rewritten as follows:
BMP is believed to induce the differentiation of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) towards multiple lineages, including mesoderm and trophoblast. However, the BMP-induced trophoblast phenotype has long been a paradox in stem cell biology. To readdress BMP function in hESCs and mouse epiblast-derived cells, we found that BMP4 cooperates with FGF2 (through the ERK pathway) to induce mesoderm and inhibit endoderm differentiation. These conditions resulted in cells that expressed high levels of BRACHYURY (BRA), which preceded the expression of CDX2. Both genes were essential for the expression of mesodermal genes and trophoblast-associated genes. Maximal expression of the latter was observed in the absence of FGF, and these cells coexpressed mesodermal genes while displaying distinct cell surface and epigenetic properties compared to placental trophoblast. Our findings suggest that BMP primarily induces hESCs and mouse pluripotent stem cells to form mesoderm, rather than trophoblast, through the BRA and CDX2 pathway.

title: Degradation of Cellular miR-27 by a Novel, Highly Abundant Viral Transcript Is Important for Efficient Virus Replication In Vivo
text: Cytomegaloviruses produce large amounts of viral microRNAs (miRNAs) during lytic infection, yet, they only modestly impact the cellular miRNA profile. Notably, the most significant alteration upon lytic infection with murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) is the rapid degradation of the cellular miR-27a and miR-27b. We report that this regulation is mediated by the approximately 1.7 kilobase spliced and highly abundant MCMV m169 transcript. The specificity of this regulation is achieved through a single, optimally positioned miRNA binding site located in the 3'-untranslated region (3'-UTR) of m169. This site can be efficiently retargeted to other cellular and viral miRNAs through target site replacement. Expression of the 3'-UTR of m169 by an adenoviral vector was sufficient to recapitulate its function, indicating that no other viral factors are essential in this process. Degradation of miR-27a/b was found to be accompanied by 3'-tailing and -trimming. Surprisingly, this interaction is mutual, suggesting that m169 may be regulated by miR-27a/b. Interestingly, three mutant viruses that cannot target miR-27a/b, either due to disruption of the miRNA target site or target site replacement, showed significant attenuation in multiple organs as early as 4 days post infection, indicating that degradation of miR-27a/b plays a crucial role in efficient MCMV replication in vivo.

title: Social and geographical factors affecting access to treatment of colorectal cancer: a cancer registry study
text:
Objective: To investigate the impact of deprivation on cancer outcomes, specifically stage at diagnosis and receipt of treatment, among patients in a population-based study in the north of England.
Design: Analysis of a Cancer Registry Database. Data included stage and treatment details from the first 6 months.
Setting: Large area in the north of England.
Participants: 39,619 patients with colorectal cancer diagnosed between 1994 and 2002.
Outcomes measured: Stage of diagnosis and receipt of treatment in relation to deprivation and distance from hospital.
Results: Patients in the most deprived quartile were significantly more likely to be diagnosed at stage 4 for rectal cancer (OR 1.516, p<0.05) but less so for colonic cancer. A trend was observed for both sites for patients in the most deprived quartile to be less likely to receive chemotherapy for stage 4 disease. Patients with colonic cancer were significantly less likely to receive any treatment if they came from any but the most affluent area (ORs 0.639, 0.603, and 0.544 in increasingly deprived quartiles). The effect was less pronounced for rectal cancer, and no effect of distance was observed.
Conclusions: Residing in a deprived area is associated with tendencies towards higher stage at diagnosis and reduced receipt of treatment, particularly for colonic cancer. These findings are consistent with other research and suggest that access to diagnosis requires further investigation.

title: Development of candidate genomic markers to select breast cancer patients for dasatinib therapy.
text: The importance of selecting the right patients for targeted therapies is highlighted in the context of phase I/II trials, which are often underpowered to identify predictors of drug response. This research aimed to identify genomic predictors of dasatinib response that could be tested in early-phase clinical trials. The study focused on comparing gene expression profiles of dasatinib-sensitive and resistant cell lines (n = 23) to develop a dasatinib-sensitivity index (modified DS index). Additionally, a Src pathway activity index (revised Src index) was defined using genes induced by Src transfection of mammary epithelial cells, and a dasatinib target index was created using a weighted sum of 19 kinases that bind to dasatinib with variable affinity. The performance of these prediction models was evaluated in independent cell lines with known dasatinib sensitivity, and their feasibility was evaluated in 133 primary breast cancer biopsies. The results showed that the modified DS index demonstrated 90% accuracy in independent breast cancer cell lines (n = 12), and the target index, but not the revised Src index signature, distinguished dasatinib-sensitive and resistant cells (P = 0.0024). The genomic predictors showed acceptable reproducibility in replicate cell line and human gene expression data. When all three predictors were applied to the same 133 patient samples, the predictors identified different patient subsets as potentially sensitive. Therefore, three conceptually different potential predictors of dasatinib response were identified and are being tested in a clinical trial to determine their utility.

title: BEDTools: a flexible suite of utilities for comparing genomic features
text: In genomics research, analyzing correlations between various genomic features is a crucial task. However, handling massive datasets generated by current sequencing technologies using existing web-based methods can be challenging. To address this issue, this article introduces a novel software suite, BEDTools, for the comparison, manipulation, and annotation of genomic features in Browser Extensible Data (BED) and General Feature Format (GFF) format. BEDTools also supports the comparison of sequence alignments in BAM format to both BED and GFF features. The tools are lightning-fast and enable the user to efficiently compare large datasets, including next-generation sequencing data, with both public and custom genome annotation tracks. BEDTools can be combined with other tools and standard UNIX commands, making it an indispensable resource for genomics research and pipelines that can quickly answer complex questions about large genomic datasets. BEDTools was developed in C++ and is freely available at <http://code.google.com/p/bedtools>. Contact the authors at <aaronquinlan@gmail.com> or <imh4y@virginia.edu>. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Vegetarian diet improves insulin resistance and oxidative stress markers more than conventional diet in subjects with Type 2 diabetes
text:
Study Objectives:
The purpose of this 24-week, randomized, open, parallel-design study was to compare the effects of calorie-restricted vegetarian and conventional diabetic diets, both combined with exercise training, on insulin resistance, visceral fat, and oxidative stress markers in patients with type 2 diabetes.
Methods:
Seventy-four participants with type 2 diabetes were randomly assigned to either a vegetarian diet group (n=37) or a control diabetic diet group (n=37). Both diets were isocaloric, with a 500 kcal/day reduction. All meals were provided throughout the study. After 12 weeks, the second 12 weeks of the diet were combined with aerobic exercise training. Participants were evaluated at baseline, 12 weeks, and 24 weeks. The primary outcome measures were insulin sensitivity measured by hyperinsulinaemic isoglycaemic clamp, volume of visceral and subcutaneous fat measured by magnetic resonance imaging, and oxidative stress markers measured by thiobarbituric acid reactive substances. The analysis was based on intention to treat.
Results:
Forty-three percent of participants in the vegetarian group and 5% in the control group reduced their diabetes medication (P < 0.001). Body weight decreased more in the vegetarian group than in the control group (6.2 kg [95% CI 6.6-5.3] vs. 3.2 kg [95% CI 3.7-2.5]; interaction group × time P = 0.001). A greater increase in insulin sensitivity was observed in the vegetarian group (30% [95% CI 24.5-39] vs. 20% [95% CI 14-25], P = 0.04). Both visceral and subcutaneous fat reductions were greater in the vegetarian group (P = 0.007 and P = 0.02, respectively). Plasma adiponectin increased (P = 0.02) and leptin decreased (P = 0.02) in the vegetarian group, with no change in the control group. Vitamin C, superoxide dismutase, and reduced glutathione increased in the vegetarian group (P = 0.002, P < 0.001, and P = 0.02, respectively). Differences between groups were greater after the addition of exercise training. Changes in insulin sensitivity and enzymatic oxidative stress markers correlated with changes in visceral fat.

title: Antidepressant use and risk of adverse outcomes in older people: population based cohort study
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the association between antidepressant treatment and the risk of various potential adverse outcomes in older people with depression, as well as to examine these risks by class of antidepressant, duration of use, and dose. The study used a cohort design and included 60,746 patients aged 65-100 years who were diagnosed with depression in 570 general practices in the UK. The study found that 54,038 patients (89.0%) received at least one prescription for an antidepressant during follow-up, and a total of 1,398,359 antidepressant prescriptions were issued. The study found significant differences in the associations between the antidepressant classes for seven outcomes, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) associated with the highest adjusted hazard ratios for falls and hyponatraemia, and the group of other antidepressants associated with the highest adjusted hazard ratios for all cause mortality, attempted suicide/self harm, stroke/transient ischaemic attack, fracture, and epilepsy/seizures. Tricyclic antidepressants did not have the highest hazard ratio for any of the outcomes. The study also found significantly different associations between individual drugs for the same seven outcomes, with trazodone, mirtazapine, and venlafaxine associated with the highest rates for some of these outcomes. The study suggests that the risks and benefits of different antidepressants should be carefully evaluated when these drugs are prescribed to older people, and further research is needed to confirm these findings.

title: The benefits of statins in people without established cardiovascular disease but with cardiovascular risk factors: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
text:
Objective: To determine whether statin use reduces all-cause mortality and major coronary and cerebrovascular events in individuals without established cardiovascular disease, but with cardiovascular risk factors, and to evaluate these effects in subgroups of men and women, young and older individuals (>65 years), and those with diabetes mellitus.
Design: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Data Sources: Cochrane controlled trials register, Embase, and Medline.
Data Abstraction: Two independent investigators identified studies that assessed the clinical effects of statins vs. a placebo or control group and had at least one year of follow-up, with at least 80% or more participants without established cardiovascular disease, and outcome data on mortality and major cardiovascular disease events. Heterogeneity was evaluated using the Q and I(2) statistics, and publication bias was assessed using visual examination of funnel plots and the Egger regression test.
