Results: A total of 10 trials involving 70,388 participants (34% women and 23% with diabetes mellitus) were analyzed, with a mean follow-up of 4.1 years. Statin treatment significantly reduced the risk of all-cause mortality (odds ratio 0.88, 95% confidence interval 0.81-0.96), major coronary events (odds ratio 0.70, 95% confidence interval 0.61-0.81), and major cerebrovascular events (odds ratio 0.81, 95% confidence interval 0.71-0.93). No significant evidence of an increased risk of cancer was observed. There was no significant heterogeneity in the treatment effect across clinical subgroups.
Conclusion: Statin use was associated with improved survival and significantly reduced risks of major cardiovascular events in patients without established cardiovascular disease but with cardiovascular risk factors, with no significant differences in effects across subgroups of men and women, young and older individuals, and those with or without diabetes mellitus.

title: Mechanical coupling between transsynaptic N-cadherin adhesions and actin flow stabilizes dendritic spines
text: The structural architecture of neuronal dendritic spines is a crucial indicator of synaptic function. This structure is regulated by various factors, including the intracellular actin/myosin cytoskeleton and transcellular N-cadherin adhesions. To investigate the mechanical relationship between these molecular components, we conducted quantitative live-imaging experiments in primary hippocampal neurons. Our findings revealed that actin turnover and structural motility were lower in dendritic spines compared to immature filopodia, and increased upon expression of a non-adhesive N-cadherin mutant, resulting in an inverse relationship between spine motility and actin enrichment. Additionally, pharmacological stimulation of myosin II caused the rearward motion of actin structures in spines, demonstrating that myosin II exerts tension on the actin network. Remarkably, the formation of stable, spine-like structures enriched in actin was observed at contacts between dendritic filopodia and N-cadherin-coated beads or micropatterns. Further computer simulations of actin dynamics mimicked various experimental conditions, suggesting that the actin flow rate is a critical parameter controlling actin enrichment in dendritic spines. Together, these data demonstrate that a mechanical link between N-cadherin adhesions and the actin flow underlies the stabilization of dendritic filopodia into mature spines, a mechanism that may have important implications in synapse formation, maturation, and plasticity in the developing brain.

title: Phosphate and R2D2 restrict the substrate specificity of Dicer-2, an ATP-driven ribonuclease.
text: The enzyme Drosophila Dicer-2 produces two different types of small RNAs, small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and microRNAs (miRNAs), by cleaving double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) and pre-miRNA, respectively. What sets these two Dicers apart is their ability to recognize and process different biological substrates. We find that Dicer-2 can efficiently cleave pre-miRNA, but the activity is inhibited by inorganic phosphate and the Dicer-2 partner protein R2D2. In contrast, Dicer-2 is unable to process siRNAs from long dsRNA. The enzyme Dicer-2 contains two distinct domains: a C-terminal RNase III domain that mediates RNA cleavage and an N-terminal helicase motif whose function is unclear. Our findings reveal that Dicer-2 is an ATP-dependent dsRNA-stimulated helicase that hydrolyzes ATP to ADP, a process essential for its ability to process long dsRNA. Unexpectedly, we observe that wild-type Dicer-2 can generate siRNAs faster than it can dissociate from a long dsRNA substrate. Our data suggest that the Dicer-2 helicase domain uses ATP to generate multiple siRNAs from a single molecule of dsRNA before dissociating from its substrate.

title: Therapeutic potential of mood stabilizers lithium and valproic acid: beyond bipolar disorder.
text:
The mood stabilizers lithium and valproic acid (VPA) are commonly used to treat bipolar disorder (BD), a complex mental illness caused by interplay between genetic and environmental factors that impair the brain's ability to adapt and respond to stress. Recent studies have also highlighted the potential of these drugs in treating other central nervous system (CNS) disorders. This review aims to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of lithium and VPA, using insights from cellular and animal models of neurological, neurodegenerative, and psychiatric disorders. Clinical evidence is provided where possible to offer a comprehensive overview of the field and acknowledge its limitations.
The review first delves into how these drugs act on their primary targets: glycogen synthase kinase-3 for lithium and histone deacetylases for VPA, leading to the expression of neurotrophic, angiogenic, and neuroprotective proteins. Cell survival signaling cascades, oxidative stress pathways, and protein quality control mechanisms may also contribute to the beneficial effects of lithium and VPA. The potential for cotreatment to enhance neuroprotection and promote stem cell migration and homing is also discussed. Furthermore, the role of microRNAs as new therapeutic targets is explored.
Preclinical studies have shown that the neuroprotective effects of lithium and VPA are accompanied by anti-inflammation, angiogenesis, neurogenesis, blood-brain barrier integrity, and disease-specific neuroprotection. These mechanisms can be compared with the aberrant disease mechanisms, suggesting identifiable cellular and molecular disturbances that can be captured by specific risk biomarkers. The review emphasizes the potential of a personalized medicine approach to treat CNS disorders with lithium and VPA.
In conclusion, this review provides valuable insights into the complex mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of lithium and VPA in treating bipolar disorder and other CNS disorders. Further research is warranted to fully elucidate these mechanisms and to develop personalized treatment strategies for various neurological and psychiatric conditions.

title: The feasibility of malaria elimination in South Africa
text:
Following the significant decline in malaria incidence in South Africa since the last major epidemic in 2000, the country is now on track to meet the World Health Organization's (WHO) threshold for malaria elimination. However, to ensure the gains made are sustained and to achieve true malaria elimination, certain criteria must be met. This study aimed to assess the appropriateness of implementing a malaria elimination program in present-day South Africa.
Methods:
We analyzed vector control and case management data from 2000 to 2011 across the three malaria-endemic provinces in South Africa. The study found that both malaria-related morbidity and mortality have significantly decreased across all three provinces since 2000, with the largest decline seen in KwaZulu-Natal. Although there has been a significant decrease in malaria cases in Limpopo Province, it remains the largest contributor to malaria incidence in South Africa. Despite average insecticide spray coverage of over 80% in all three provinces, malaria incidence in Mpumalanga and Limpopo remains above the elimination threshold. Locally transmitted case numbers have declined in all three provinces, but imported case numbers have been increasing. Knowledge gaps in vector distribution, insecticide resistance status, and drug usage were also identified.
Conclusions:
Malaria elimination in South Africa is a realistic possibility if certain criteria are met. Firstly, continued support for existing malaria control programs is crucial to ensure the gains made are sustained. Secondly, cross-border malaria control initiatives with neighboring countries must be strongly encouraged and supported to reduce malaria in the region and the importation of malaria into South Africa. Thirdly, operational research must be conducted, particularly on vector distribution and insecticide resistance status, as a matter of urgency. Finally, surveillance systems must be refined to ensure the information required to inform an elimination agenda are routinely collected.

title: The epidemiology of sexually transmitted co-infections in HIV-positive and HIV-negative African-Caribbean women in Toronto
text: Background: HIV disproportionately affects African-Caribbean women in Canada, but the prevalence of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in this community has not been adequately studied. Methods: We recruited HIV-positive and HIV-negative women from a Toronto community health center based on their HIV status. Participants completed a socio-behavioral questionnaire using Audio Computer Assisted Self-Interview (ACASI) and provided blood samples for serology tests for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B and C, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 (HSV-1 and HSV-2), and human cytomegalovirus (CMV). Urine samples were collected for chlamydia and gonorrhea molecular testing, and vaginal secretions were collected for bacterial vaginosis (BV) and HPV serology. Differences in prevalence were assessed using chi-square tests. Results: We recruited 126 HIV-positive and 291 HIV-negative women, with a median age of 40 and 31 years, respectively (p < 0.001). Active HBV infection and self-reported exposure to HBV infection were more common in HIV-positive women (4.8% vs. 0.34%, p = 0.004; and 47.6% vs. 21.2%, p < 0.0001), as was a history of HBV vaccination (66.1% vs. 44.0%, p = 0.0001). Classical STIs were rare in both groups, but BV prevalence was low and did not vary by HIV status. HSV-2 infection was significantly more common in HIV-positive (86.3%) than HIV-negative (46.6%) women (p < 0.0001). Vaginal HPV infection was also more common in HIV-positive than in HIV-negative women (50.8% vs. 22.6%, p < 0.0001) and was associated with high-risk oncogenic HPV types (48.4% vs. 17.3%, p < 0.0001). Conclusions: This clinic-based study found that classical STIs were uncommon in African-Caribbean women in Toronto, but HSV-2, hepatitis B, and HPV infections were more prevalent in HIV-positive women. These findings highlight the need for targeted interventions to address these infections in this high-risk population.

title: Characterization of Programmed Death-1 Homologue-1 (PD-1H) Expression and Function in Normal and HIV Infected Individuals
text: Prolonged immune activation in HIV-infected individuals despite antiretroviral therapy (ART) is a strong predictor of disease progression. In HIV-infected individuals, monocytes/macrophages are known to spontaneously produce cytokines, although the underlying mechanisms and molecules involved remain unclear. Our study uncovered that overexpression of the recently identified co-stimulatory molecule, PD1 homologue (PD-1H), in human monocytes/macrophages leads to spontaneous secretion of multiple cytokines. This process requires signaling through PD-1H, as cytokine production can be abrogated by deletion of the cytoplasmic domain. Interestingly, overexpression of PD-1H is observed in monocytes from chronically HIV-infected individuals, which correlates with immune activation and CD4 depletion but not viral load. Moreover, antigen presentation by PD-1H-overexpressing monocytes leads to enhanced cytokine production by HIV-specific T cells, suggesting that PD-1H might play a crucial role in modulating immune activation and immune response in HIV infection.

title: A conserved mechanism for centromeric nucleosome recognition by centromere protein CENP-C.
text: Chromosome segregation during mitosis relies on the formation of the kinetochore complex at the centromere. Kinetochore assembly requires the specific recognition of the histone variant CENP-A in the centromeric nucleosome by the protein CENP-C. Through our research, we have identified the key determinants of this recognition mechanism and discovered that CENP-C binds to a hydrophobic region in the CENP-A tail and docks onto the acidic patch of histone H2A and H2B. In addition, we found that a more widely conserved CENP-C motif utilizes the same mechanism for CENP-A nucleosome recognition. Our findings reveal a conserved mechanism for protein recruitment to centromeres and a histone recognition mode in which a disordered peptide binds the histone tail through hydrophobic interactions facilitated by nucleosome docking.

title: Chemical tools for biomolecular imaging.
text: Advancements in the visualization of biologically relevant molecules and processes within living cells have revolutionized cell biology into a quantitative science. Yet, despite significant breakthroughs in certain areas, the majority of cellular processes remain obscure, impervious to even our most powerful laser beams. Future progress will require not only enhancements in instrumentation but also the development of novel fluorophores and fluorescent sensors to target these elusive processes. In this review, we will outline recent strategies for creating these sensors, the methods employed to attach them to specific biomolecules, and their applications in addressing various biological challenges.

title: Reactive oxygen species, DNA damage, and error-prone repair: a model for genomic instability with progression in myeloid leukemia?
text: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of disorders characterized by impaired blood cell production, with an increased risk of developing acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The molecular mechanisms underlying MDS progression are not fully understood, but genomic instability is a key component. Using a mouse model of myeloid leukemia, we observed a stepwise increase in DNA damage followed by an increased frequency of error-prone repair of double-strand breaks (DSB). Correspondingly, there was an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) in these transgenic mice. We found that RAC1, a crucial component of the ROS-producing NADPH oxidase, is downstream of RAS and contributes to ROS production in NRAS/BCL2 mice. Interestingly, we could decrease or reverse DNA damage and error-prone repair in vivo by using an antioxidant treatment. Our findings provide insights into the mechanisms underlying MDS progression and suggest potential therapeutic strategies targeting RAS/RAC pathways and ROS production in human MDS/AML.

title: A link between inflammation and metastasis: serum amyloid A1 and A3 induce metastasis, and are targets of metastasis-inducing S100A4
text: S100A4 has been implicated in both inflammation and metastasis, but its exact role in these processes is unclear. In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between S100A4 and the progression of tumors. We found that S100A4 interacts with acute-phase response proteins, such as serum amyloid A (SAA) 1 and 3, and stimulates their transcription via Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor-κB signaling. SAA proteins, in turn, enhance the production of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines, such as RANTES, granulocyte-colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), matrix metalloproteinase 2 (MMP2), and matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9), and promote tumor cell adhesion, migration, and invasion. Intravenous injection of S100A4 protein induced the expression of SAA proteins and cytokines in a organ-specific manner. Furthermore, ectopic expression of SAA1 or SAA3 in tumor cells led to enhanced metastasis formation in a breast cancer animal model, accompanied by a massive infiltration of immune cells. Surprisingly, we found that SAA proteins also stimulate their own transcription and that of proinflammatory S100A8 and S100A9 proteins. Notably, coordinate expression of S100A4 and SAA in tumor samples from colorectal carcinoma patients significantly correlated with reduced overall survival. These findings demonstrate that SAA proteins serve as effectors for the metastasis-promoting functions of S100A4 and provide a link between inflammation and tumor progression.

title: Pyruvate dehydrogenase activity and acetyl group accumulation during exercise after different diets.
text: In this study, the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDHa) and the accumulation of acetyl groups were investigated in human skeletal muscle at rest and during exercise following different diets. Five male participants cycled at 75% of theirmaximal oxygen uptake (VO2 max) until exhaustion after consuming a low-carbohydrate diet (LCD) for 3 days and again 1-2 weeks later for the same duration after consuming a high-carbohydrate diet (HCD) for 3 days. Resting PDHa was lower after the LCD (0.20±0.04 vs. 0.69±0.05 mmol.min-1.kg wet wt-1; P < 0.05) and was associated with a greater intramuscular acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio, acetyl-CoA content, and acetylcarnitine content. PDHa increased during exercise in both conditions, but at a lower rate in the LCD condition compared to the HCD condition (1.46±0.25 vs. 2.65±0.23 mmol.min-1.kg wet wt-1 at 16 min and 1.88±0.20 vs. 3.11±0.14 at the end of exercise; P < 0.05). During exercise, muscle acetyl-CoA and acetylcarnitine content, and the acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio decreased in the LCD condition but increased in the HCD condition. Under resting conditions, PDHa was influenced by the availability of fat or carbohydrate fuels, with changes in the acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio playing a role. However, during exercise, the activation of PDHa occurred independent of changes in the acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio, suggesting that other factors are more important.

title: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential and its distinction from myelodysplastic syndromes.
text: Recent genetic studies on large populations have revealed that somatic mutations in blood cells during aging lead to clonal expansion in many people. Clonally restricted hematopoiesis is associated with an increased risk of develop myeloid or lymphoid cancer and higher mortality rate. Although myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are defined by cytopenias, abnormal blood and bone marrow cells, and clonal hematopoiesis, most individuals who acquire clonal hematopoiesis during aging will never develop MDS. Therefore, acquiring somatic mutations that drive clonal expansion without cytopenias and abnormal hematopoiesis can be considered clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), similar to monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis, which are precursor states for hematologic neoplasms but are usually benign and do not progress. Since mutations are frequently found in healthy older individuals, detecting an MDS-associated somatic mutation in a cytopenic patient without other evidence of MDS may create diagnostic confusion. Here we will discuss the nature and prevalence of CHIP, distinguishing this state from MDS, and current areas of uncertainty regarding diagnostic criteria for myeloid malignancies.

title: DNA Methylation mediated down-regulating of MicroRNA-33b and its role in gastric cancer
text: The discovery of microRNAs (miRNAs) has opened up a new and powerful avenue for investigating the mechanisms, diagnosis, and treatment of human cancers. Currently, one of the most notable findings is that down-regulation of tumor suppressor miRNAs due to CpG island hypermethylation is a common trait in cancer. In this study, we found that the down-regulation of miR-33b was associated with the progressive (pM) stage of gastric cancer (GC) patients. Intriguingly, ectopic expression of miR-33b in HGC-27 and MGC-803 cells was found to inhibit cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, possibly due to its ability to target the oncogene c-Myc. Moreover, we observed that the methylation level of the CpG island upstream of miR-33b in GC patients with low miR-33b expression was significantly augmented by methylation-specific PCR (MSP) amplification. Finally, re-introducing miR-33b into GC cells inhibited their ability to form tumors in nude mice, indicating its tumor-suppressive function. Overall, these findings suggest that miR-33b acts as a tumor suppressor and that hypermethylation of the CpG island upstream of miR-33b is the primary cause of its down-regulation in gastric cancer.

title: Modulation of glucose metabolism in macrophages by products of nitric oxide synthase.
text: Nitric oxide (NO), a byproduct of L-arginine metabolism, hinders cellular oxidative metabolism by inhibiting the activity of enzymes involved in the tricarboxylic acid cycle and electron transport chain. The study aimed to investigate the impact of NO synthase (NOS) activity on specific pathways of glucose metabolism in freshly harvested and overnight-cultured rat resident peritoneal macrophages, both at rest and after stimulation with zymosan. NOS activity was modified through the concentration of L-arginine in the culture media and the use of its specific inhibitor, NG-monomethyl-L-arginine. The results showed a direct correlation between NOS activity and increased glucose disappearance, glycolysis, and hexose monophosphate shunt activity. Moreover, the study found that NO production inhibited the flux of glucose and butyrate carbon through the tricarboxylic acid cycle, consistent with previous studies that demonstrate the inhibition of oxidative metabolism resulting from NO production. Additionally, the study found that treatments that suppressed NOS activity enhanced the relative increase in glucose utilization that follows zymosan stimulation. These results demonstrate that the metabolic characteristics of macrophages are, to a significant extent, determined by products of NOS.

title: SOCS1/JAB is a negative regulator of LPS-induced macrophage activation.
text: Bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) activates the innate immune response through Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). Our findings reveal that suppressor of cytokine-signaling-1 (SOCS1/JAB) is rapidly induced by LPS and inhibits LPS signaling. In contrast, mice lacking SOCS1 or with an interferon-gamma (IFNgamma)-deficient background were more susceptible to LPS-induced lethal effects compared to wild-type littermates. LPS activation of NO(2)(-) synthesis and TNFalpha production was augmented in SOCS1-deficient macrophages. Moreover, LPS tolerance, a mechanism that protects against endotoxin shock, was significantly reduced in SOCS1-deficient cells. LPS-induced I-kappaB and p38 phosphorylation were enhanced in SOCS1-deficient macrophages, and forced expression of SOCS1 suppressed LPS-induced NF-kappaB activation. These data suggest that SOCS1 directly modulates TLR4 signaling and plays a critical role in regulating innate immunity.

title: Bacteria-triggered CD4+ T Regulatory Cells Suppress Helicobacter hepaticus–induced Colitis
text: Previously, we demonstrated that interleukin (IL-10)-deficient (IL-10 KO) mice, but not wild-type (WT) mice, develop colitis after infection with Helicobacter hepaticus. In this study, we investigated the role of CD4+ T cells in the development of intestinal inflammation after H. hepaticus infection. We found that reconstituting IL-10 KO mice with CD4+ T cells from WT mice leads to the development of colitis, while cotransferring CD4+ T cells from H. hepaticus–infected but not uninfected WT mice prevents colitis. Surprisingly, we found that both CD25+ and CD25− subpopulations of CD45RBlow CD4+ cells were disease-protective, and the mechanism of protection involved IL-10 and not transforming growth factor (TGF)-β. In vitro, CD45RBlow CD4+ cells from infected WT mice were shown to produce IL-10 and suppress interferon-γ Production by IL-10 KO CD4+ cells in an H. hepaticus-specific manner. Our data support the notion that H. hepaticus infection leads to the induction of regulatory T cells in WT mice, which prevent bacteria-induced colitis. This induction of regulatory T cells may serve as a mechanism protecting normal individuals against inflammatory bowel disease.

title: The NLRP12 Sensor Negatively Regulates Autoinflammatory Disease by Modulating Interleukin-4 Production in T Cells.
text: Mutations in the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD)-like receptor pyrin domain containing family of gene 12 (Nlrp12) are linked to periodic fever syndromes and atopic dermatitis in humans. Our findings suggest a crucial role for NLRP12 in negative regulation of harmful T cell reactions. Nlrp12-deficient mice exhibit hyperinflammatory T cell responses following antigen immunization. Transfer of CD4(+)CD45RB(hi)Nlrp12-deficient T cells into immunodeficient mice leads to more severe colitis and atopic dermatitis. Contrary to expected results, NLRP12 deficiency does not exacerbate ascending paralysis during experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE); instead, Nlrp12-deficient mice display atypical neuroinflammatory symptoms characterized by ataxia and loss of balance. Enhanced T-cell-mediated interleukin-4 (IL-4) production promotes the development of atypical EAE disease in Nlrp12-deficient mice. These results identify an unexpected role for NLRP12 as an intrinsic negative regulator of T-cell-mediated immunity and reveal altered NF-κB regulation and IL-4 production as key mediators of NLRP12-related diseases.

title: Shc coordinates signals from intercellular junctions and integrins to regulate flow-induced inflammation
text: Atherosclerotic plaques form in areas of the blood vessels where chronic inflammation persists due to disruptions in blood flow patterns. Understanding how endothelial cells modify their phenotype in response to flow is crucial, but this process remains poorly understood. Our study reveals that, when exposed to flow, the adaptor protein Shc becomes active and interacts with both cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesions. We found that Shc activation requires the involvement of tyrosine kinases such as vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 and Src. In contrast, Shc binding to integrins relies on VE-cadherin, but only in specific matrix environments. Silencing Shc results in reduced signals transmitted through both matrix-independent and matrix-dependent pathways. Moreover, we found that Shc regulates flow-induced inflammatory signaling by activating nuclear factor kappaB-dependent signals that promote atherogenesis. In vivo, Shc is activated in areas of the arteries susceptible to atherosclerosis, and this activation coincides with the presence of atherosclerosis lesions. Our findings suggest that Shc acts as a central coordinator, integrating signals from cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesions to provoke flow-induced inflammatory signaling.

title: SIRT1 Redistribution on Chromatin Promotes Genomic Stability but Alters Gene Expression during Aging
text:
Genomic instability and alterations in gene expression are key features of eukaryotic aging. The yeast protein Sir2, a histone deacetylase, plays a crucial role in silencing transcription and stabilizing repetitive DNA. However, during aging or in response to DNA damage, the Sir complex relocalizes to sites of genomic instability, leading to the de-repression of genes associated with sterility, a hallmark of aging in yeast.
Using embryonic stem cells from mice, we have shown that the mammalian homolog of Sir2, SIRT1, represses a diverse set of genes across the mouse genome, including repetitive DNA sequences. In response to DNA damage, SIRT1 dissociates from these loci and relocalizes to the site of DNA breaks, where it promotes repair and transcriptional changes that parallel those observed in the aging mouse brain.
Intriguingly, increased expression of SIRT1 has been shown to promote survival in a mouse model of genomic instability and suppress age-dependent transcriptional changes. These findings suggest that the redistribution of SIRT1 and other chromatin-modifying proteins in response to DNA damage may be a conserved mechanism of aging across eukaryotes.

title: Bariatric Surgery in the United Kingdom: A Cohort Study of Weight Loss and Clinical Outcomes in Routine Clinical Care.
text:
Study Finds Bariatric Surgery Associated with Sustained Weight Loss and Improved Health Outcomes in Obese Patients
Background: Bariatric surgery is becoming a more common treatment for obesity, but there is a lack of evidence on its long-term effects in large populations. This study aimed to investigate the association between bariatric surgery and weight, body mass index (BMI), and obesity-related comorbidities.
Methods and Findings: This observational retrospective cohort study used data from the United Kingdom Clinical Practice Research Datalink, including 3,882 patients who underwent bariatric surgery between 2014 and 2014 and were matched with 3,882 obese patients without surgery. The primary outcome measures were changes in weight and BMI over four years, as well as incident diagnoses of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), hypertension, angina, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, fractures, obstructive sleep apnoea, and cancer, as well as mortality. Weight measures were available for 3,847 patients between one and four months, 2,884 patients between five and twelve months, and 2,258 patients between thirteen and 48 months post-procedure. Bariatric surgery patients exhibited rapid weight loss in the first four months, at a rate of 4.98 kg/mo, which slowed down but remained significant to the end of four years. Gastric bypass (6.56 kg/mo) and sleeve gastrectomy (6.29 kg/mo) were associated with greater initial weight reduction than gastric banding (2.77 kg/mo). Bariatric surgery was associated with a lower risk of incident T2DM, hypertension, angina, MI, and obstructive sleep apnoea, as well as a reduced risk of fractures, cancer, and stroke. There was no protective association between bariatric surgery and mortality.
Conclusion: Bariatric surgery as delivered in the UK healthcare system is associated with sustained weight loss, improved health outcomes, and a reduced risk of obesity-related comorbidities. Expanding access to bariatric surgery could lead to substantial health benefits for many obese individuals.

title: Notch signalling acts in postmitotic avian myogenic cells to control MyoD activation.
text:
During Drosophila myogenesis, Notch signaling acts at multiple stages of the muscle differentiation process. In contrast, the role of Notch signaling in vivo during chick myogenesis was previously unknown. This study aims to investigate the in vivo role of Notch signaling during chick myogenesis.
First, the expression of the Notch1 receptor was examined in post-mitotic cells of the myotome, and the expression of the Notch ligands Delta1 and Serrate2 was detected in subsets of differentiating myogenic cells. These findings show that Notch signaling is present in vivo during chick myogenesis and is in a position to regulate myogenic differentiation.
Furthermore, the expression of MyoD and Myf5 during avian myogenesis was reinvestigated, and the results showed that Myf5 is expressed earlier than MyoD, consistent with previous results in mice.
To test the effect of Notch signaling on muscle differentiation, the expression of the Notch ligand Delta1 was overexpressed during early myogenesis using a retroviral system. Surprisingly, the results revealed that forced expression of Delta1 had no effect on the expression of early myogenic markers Pax3 and Myf5 but caused strong down-regulation of MyoD in infected somites. This suggests that Notch signaling acts after exit from the cell cycle to regulate a critical step of muscle differentiation. 
Interestingly, although Delta1 overexpression resulted in the complete lack of differentiated muscles, the initial formation of a myotome was not prevented, indicating that exit from the cell cycle had not been blocked. These findings suggest that Notch signaling regulates a specific step of muscle differentiation in post-mitotic cells.
In summary, this study identified the in vivo role of Notch signaling during chick myogenesis. Notch signaling regulates a critical step of muscle differentiation after exit from the cell cycle, which suggests that this pathway plays a unique role in the muscle differentiation process.

title: Hepatitis C virus infection in a large cohort of homosexually active men: independent associations with HIV-1 infection and injecting drug use but not sexual behaviour.
text:
Objective:
To determine the prevalence and risk factors for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in a cohort of homosexually active men, with particular reference to assessing sexual transmission.
Design:
A cross-sectional study was conducted using sera collected between 1984 and 1989 to determine the prevalence of HCV antibody in a cohort of 1038 homosexually active men participating in a prospective study to identify risk factors for AIDS. The study also used questionnaire data from HCV positive and negative subjects to assess risk factors using a case-control analysis.
Subjects/Setting:
The study was conducted in central Sydney among 1038 homosexually active men who were recruited through private and public primary care and sexually transmissible disease (STD) services.
Main Outcome Measures:
The study measured the prevalence of HCV antibody and its association with human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection, other sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), number of sexual partners, sexual practices, and recreational drug use.
Results:
Overall, 7.6% of subjects tested were seropositive for HCV antibody. In univariate analysis, HCV infection was significantly associated with injecting drug use (IDU) (OR = 8.18, p < 0.0001), HIV infection (OR = 3.14, p < 0.0001), and self-reported history of syphilis (OR = 1.88, p = 0.016), anogenital herpes (OR = 1.93, p = 0.017), gonorrhoea (OR = 2.43, p = 0.009), and hepatitis B (OR = 1.92, p = 0.010). In case-control analysis, similar sexual behaviors (partner numbers and practices) were reported by HCV positive and HCV negative subjects except that HCV negative subjects more frequently reported engaging in unprotected receptive anal intercourse without ejaculation (OR = 0.61, p = 0.034), unprotected insertive (OR = 0.59, p = 0.039) and receptive (OR = 0.56, p = 0.016) oral-anal intercourse (rimming) and insertive fisting (OR = 0.48, p = 0.034). In multiple logistic regression analyses, only HIV-1 infection (OR = 3.18, p < 0.0001) and IDU in the previous six months (OR = 7.24, p < 0.0001) remained significantly associated with the presence of HCV antibody.
Conclusion:

IDU was the major behavioral risk factor for HCV infection, and if sexual transmission did occur, it may have been facilitated by concurrent HIV-1 infection.

title: Analysis of human cytomegalovirus-encoded microRNA activity during infection.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are found in a wide range of organisms, from plants to animals, and play a crucial role in posttranscriptional gene expression regulation. Unique among miRNAs are those encoded by viruses, which can target both viral and host genes. We have previously demonstrated that a human cytomegalovirus (HCMV)-encoded miRNA, miR-UL112, downregulates the expression of a host immune gene, MICB. Interestingly, it has been shown that the same miRNA also downregulates early viral genes and that its ectopic expression leads to reduced viral replication and titers. The functions of most viral miRNAs, and their targets, remain unknown. In this study, we investigate the target of miR-UL112 and find that it also targets the UL114 gene, which encodes uracil DNA glycosylase. Our results show that reducing UL114 expression by miR-UL112 reduces its activity but minimally affects virus growth. We also discover that two additional HCMV-encoded miRNAs, miR-US25-1 and miR-US25-2, reduce viral replication and DNA synthesis not only of HCMV but also of other viruses, suggesting that these miRNAs target essential cellular genes for virus growth. Taken together, our findings suggest that in addition to miR-UL112, two additional HCMV miRNAs play a key role in regulating the virus life cycle.

title: Anti-obesity drugs: past, present and future
text: An ideal anti-obesity medication should promote sustained weight loss with minimal side effects. However, the complex mechanisms controlling energy balance pose significant challenges in drug discovery. These mechanisms involve redundant pathways, overlap with other physiological functions, and are influenced by social, emotional, and psychological factors, which hinder the effectiveness of pharmacological interventions. Despite numerous efforts, anti-obesity drug development programs have experienced numerous setbacks, clinical trial failures, and withdrawals due to unforeseen adverse effects. Drugs targeting metabolic tissues, such as adipocytes, liver, and skeletal muscle, have shown promise in preclinical studies, but none have advanced to clinical development. Recent improvements in understanding the peptidergic signalling of hunger and satiety, including ghrelin, cholecystokinin (CCK), peptide YY (PYY), and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), as well as homeostatic mechanisms related to leptin and upstream pathways in the hypothalamus, have opened new avenues for potential treatments. While some GLP-1 receptor agonists have successfully reached clinical development, it remains uncertain whether they will meet stringent regulatory requirements for anti-obesity drug licensing. However, GLP-1 receptor agonists have shown promising weight-lowering effects in humans, which may pave the way for other anti-obesity agents. In light of the challenges in developing a single-drug solution for weight control, a new paradigm may be needed. In other therapeutic areas, such as diabetes and hypertension, combination approaches involving multiple agents targeting distinct pathways have shown greater efficacy, safety, and sustainability of weight loss compared to single-drug strategies. Some combination trials using peptides and small molecules are underway, although regulatory experience suggests substantial challenges lie ahead. In the future, a polytherapeutic approach could potentially rival surgery in terms of efficacy, safety, and sustainability of weight loss.

title: Cytochemical Analysis of Pollen Development in Wild-Type Arabidopsis and a Male-Sterile Mutant.
text: Microsporogenesis has been investigated in both wild-type Arabidopsis thaliana and the nuclear male-sterile mutant BM3 using cytochemical staining. The mutant lacks adenine phosphoribosyltransferase, an enzyme crucial to the purine salvage pathway that converts adenine into AMP. observations have revealed that pollen development in the mutant begins to diverge from wild type shortly after meiosis, as the tetrads of microspores are released from their callose walls. The initial indicator of abnormal pollen development in the mutant is a darker staining of the microspore wall due to incomplete synthesis of the intine. Additionally, vacuole formation is delayed and irregular in the mutant, and the majority of the mutant microspores fail to undergo mitotic divisions. Furthermore, enzyme activities of alcohol dehydrogenase and esterases decrease soon after meiosis and become undetectable in mature pollen grains of the mutant. Interestingly, RNA accumulation is also diminished in the mutant. These findings support the idea that adenine salvage may play a crucial role in pollen development.

title: Prevalence, risk factors, and uptake of interventions for sexually transmitted infections in Britain: findings from the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal)
text:
Background
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) are prevalent in Britain, and estimating the prevalence, risk distribution, and uptake of interventions informs the delivery of control programmes. We conducted the third National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-3) after implementation of national sexual health strategies, aiming to describe the epidemiology of four STIs in Britain (England, Scotland, and Wales) and the uptake of interventions.
Methods:
We conducted a probability sample survey of 15,162 women and men aged 16-74 years in Britain between September 6, 2010, and August 31, 2012. Participants were interviewed using computer-assisted face-to-face and self-completion questionnaires, and a urine sample from a subsample of participants aged 16-44 years who reported at least one sexual partner over their lifetime was tested for the presence of four STIs: Chlamydia trachomatis, type-specific human papillomavirus (HPV), Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and HIV antibody. We describe age-specific and sex-specific prevalences of infection and intervention uptake in relation to demographic and behavioral factors.
Findings:
Of 8047 eligible participants invited to provide a urine sample, 4828 (60%) agreed. We excluded 278 samples, leaving 4550 (94%) participants with STI test results. The prevalence of Chlamydia in women was 1.5% (95% CI 1.1-2.0), and in men, it was 1.1% (0.7-1.6). The prevalence of Chlamydia in individuals aged 16-24 years was 3.1% (2.2-4.3) in women and 2.3% (1.5-3.4) in men. Area-level deprivation and having multiple sexual partners, especially without using condoms, were risk factors. However, 60.4% (45.5-73.7%) of Chlamydia infections in women and 43.3% (25.9-62.5%) in men were among individuals who had had only one partner in the past year. Among sexually active 16-24-year-olds, 54.2% (51.4-56.9%) of women and 34.6% (31.8-37.4%) of men reported testing for Chlamydia in the past year, with testing higher in those with more partners. High-risk HPV was detected in 15.9% (14.4-17.5%) of women, similar to in Natsal-2. Coverage of HPV catch-up vaccination was 61.5% (58.2-64.7%). The prevalence of HPV types 16 and 18 in women aged 18-20 years was lower in Natsal-3 than in Natsal-2 (5.8% [3.9-8.6] vs 11.3% [6.8-18.2]; age-adjusted odds ratio 0.44 [0.21-0.94]). Gonorrhoea was uncommon (<0.1% prevalence in women and men), and HIV was rare (0.1% prevalence in women and 0.2% in men). Since Natsal-2, substantial increases were noted in attendance at sexual health clinics (from 6.7% to 21.4% in women and from 7.7% to 19.6% in men) and HIV testing (from 8.7% to 27.6% in women and from 9.2% to 16.9% in men) in the past five years.
Interpretation:
Our findings provide empirical evidence to inform future sexual health interventions and services. STIs persist both in individuals accessing and those not accessing services. Increases in testing and attendance at sexual health clinics, especially in those at highest risk, are encouraging, but more needs to be done to reduce STIs overall. Grants from the UK Medical Research Council and the Wellcome Trust, with support from the Economic and Social Research Council and the Department of Health, funded the study.

title: Cancer Pharmacogenomics and Pharmacoepidemiology: Setting a Research Agenda to Accelerate Translation
text:
Recent breakthroughs in genomic research have shown a significant role of genetic factors in predicting cancer treatment responses. Experts in the fields of cancer pharmacogenomics and pharmacoepidemiology aim to comprehend why individuals react differently to drug therapy, both in terms of adverse effects and treatment efficacy. To identify research priorities and the necessary resources and infrastructure, the National Cancer Institute (NCI) organized a workshop titled "Cancer Pharmacogenomics: Setting a Research Agenda to Accelerate Translation" on July 21, 2009, in Bethesda, MD. This commentary summarizes and discusses five science-based recommendations and four infrastructure-based recommendations generated from the workshop. Key recommendations include:
1. Collecting germline and tumor biospecimens in NCI-sponsored clinical trials and some observational and population-based studies.
2. Incorporating pharmacogenomic markers into clinical trials.
3. Examining the ethical, legal, social, and biospecimen- and data-sharing implications of pharmacogenomic and pharmacoepidemiologic research.
4. Establishing partnerships across NCI, with other federal agencies, and with industry.
These recommendations will aid in discovering and validating clinical, sociodemographic, lifestyle, and genomic markers associated with cancer treatment response and adverse events, ultimately improving the efficiency and speed of translating new pharmacogenomic and pharmacoepidemiologic information into clinical practice.

title: Differential transcription of the orphan receptor RORbeta in nuclear extracts derived from Neuro2A and HeLa cells.
text: A crucial model system for investigating the processes leading to productive transcription is provided by the superfamily of nuclear receptors, which are for the most part ligand-controlled transcription factors. In recent years, several "orphan" nuclear receptors have been isolated, with no known ligand. Very little is understood about how these receptors regulate transcription. In this study, we have investigated the biochemical and transcriptional properties of the neuronally expressed orphan nuclear receptor RORbeta (NR1F2) and compared them with the retinoic acid receptor heterodimer RXRalpha-RARalpha (NR2B1-NR1B1) and the acidic transcription factor Gal-VP16 in vitro. Although RORbeta binds to its DNA-binding sites with relatively low affinity, it efficiently directs transcription in nuclear extracts derived from a neuronal cell line, Neuro2A, but not in nuclear extracts from non-neuronal HeLa cells. In contrast, RXRalpha-RARalpha and Gal-VP16 support transcription in Neuro2A and HeLa nuclear extracts equally efficiently. These findings suggest that different (co)factors are required for transactivation by members of the NR1 subfamily of nuclear receptors.

title: Estrogens, progestogens, normal breast cell proliferation, and breast cancer risk.
text: Epidemiological studies suggest that ovarian hormones play a role in the development of breast cancer at all stages of life. Early menopause and premenopausal obesity may reduce the risk of breast cancer, while postmenopausal obesity and menopausal estrogen replacement therapy may increase the risk. Combined oral contraceptives and Depo-Provera do not seem to affect the risk. It appears that estrogens and progestogens interact with oncogenes and growth factors to influence breast cell proliferation and breast cancer development. In animal studies, estrogen stimulates interlobular ductal cell division, while progesterone promotes increased terminal duct lobular unit cell division during the luteal phase. Most breast carcinomas arise from terminal duct lobular unit cells, which multiply rapidly during pregnancy and the luteal phase. However, there is considerable variation between individuals. To date, no studies have compared breast cell division rates with serum hormone concentrations. The peak of mitosis occurs around 3 days before breast cell death in the late luteal and early follicular phases. Other research suggests that breast stem cell proliferation is linked to breast cancer development, and endocrine therapy reduces mitotic activity, indicating the estrogen and progesterone receptor content of breast cancers. Hormone-dependent breast cancer cell lines are all estrogen-dependent, and progesterone may block these cells, which behave like endometrial cells. The inconsistent findings of breast cell proliferation studies in relation to breast cancer suggest a need for further research to identify a molecular explanation for these disparate results.

title: Analysis of the interaction of primate retroviruses with the human RNA interference machinery.
text:
The debate surrounding whether retroviruses, such as human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) and human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1), interact with cellular RNA interference mechanisms has been a topic of interest. In this study, we investigate this question by examining the levels of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and microRNAs (miRNAs) produced by HIV-1 and HTLV-1 in persistently infected T cells. Our findings show that neither of these viruses expresses significant levels of siRNAs or miRNAs in infected T cells.
Furthermore, we demonstrate that the retroviral nuclear transcription factors HIV-1 Tat and HTLV-1 Tax, as well as the Tas transactivator encoded by primate foamy virus, are unable to inhibit RNA interference in human cells. Additionally, stable expression of physiological levels of HIV-1 Tat did not significantly impact microRNA production or expression in infected human cells. Taken together, these data suggest that HIV-1 and HTLV-1 do not induce the production of viral siRNAs or miRNAs nor repress the cellular RNA interference machinery in infected cells.

title: Impact of diabetes on long-term prognosis in patients with unstable angina and non-Q-wave myocardial infarction: results of the OASIS (Organization to Assess Strategies for Ischemic Syndromes) Registry.
text:
BACKGROUND: Despite unstable coronary artery disease being the most common cause of admission to a coronary care unit, the long-term prognosis of patients diagnosed with this condition remains uncertain, particularly for those with diabetes mellitus, who are known to exhibit a higher incidence of morbidity and mortality following an acute myocardial infarction.
METHODS AND RESULTS: Prospective data from 6 different countries in the Organization to Assess Strategies for Ischemic Syndromes (OASIS) registry were analyzed to determine the 2-year prognosis of diabetic and nondiabetic patients who were hospitalized with unstable angina or non-Q-wave myocardial infarction. Of the 8013 registry patients, 1718 (21%) had diabetes. Although diabetic patients had a higher rate of coronary bypass surgery compared to nondiabetic patients (23% vs 20%, P <0.001), they had similar rates of catheterization and angioplasty. Diabetes was found to independently predict mortality (relative risk [RR], 1.57; 95% CI, 1.38-1.81; P <0.001), as well as cardiovascular death, new myocardial infarction, stroke, and new congestive heart failure. Notably, women had a significantly higher risk than men (RR, 1.98; 95% CI, 1.60-2.44; and RR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.06-1.56, respectively). Furthermore, diabetic patients without prior cardiovascular disease had the same event rates for all outcomes as nondiabetic patients with previous vascular disease.
CONCLUSIONS: Hospitalization for unstable angina or non-Q-wave myocardial infarction predicts a high 2-year mortality rate, particularly for patients with diabetes mellitus. Notably, diabetic patients without previous cardiovascular disease have the same long-term morbidity and mortality as nondiabetic patients with established cardiovascular disease after hospitalization for unstable coronary artery disease.

title: Strain improvement by metabolic engineering: lysine production as a case study for systems biology.
text: A primary focus of systems biology is the comprehensive understanding of cellular function and physiology through the integration of diverse genomic and physiological data. This holistic approach has been frequently employed throughout history, as it is a fundamental component of metabolic flux analysis, the distribution of kinetic control in metabolic paths, and the distinctive characteristic of metabolic engineering. In one practical example, these tools have been applied to enhance lysine-producing strains of Corynebacterium glutamicum. The systematic examination of the physiology of this organism led to the identification of specific metabolic targets, resulting in substantial improvements in product yield and productivity. This case study can serve as a guide for the development of systems biology techniques for leveraging large volumes of cellular and genomic data to elucidate cellular function and physiology.

title: Cognitive behavioral therapy vs zopiclone for treatment of chronic primary insomnia in older adults: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Insomnia is a common problem in older adults, associated with various medical, social, and psychological consequences. Prior research showed that both psychological and pharmacological interventions can be beneficial, but blinded, placebo-controlled trials comparing these treatments' effects are lacking. This study aimed to evaluate the short- and long-term clinical efficacy of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and pharmacological treatment in older adults with chronic primary insomnia.
A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 46 adults (mean age: 60.8 years; 22 women) was conducted between January 2004 and December 2005 at a single Norwegian university-based outpatient clinic for adults and elderly patients. Participants were randomly assigned to receive CBT (sleep hygiene, sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive therapy, and relaxation), sleep medication (7.5 mg zopiclone each night), or placebo medication. All treatments lasted for 6 weeks, and the active treatments were followed up at 6 months.
Sleep efficiency, total wake time, total sleep time, and slow-wave sleep (measured using only polysomnography) were the main outcome measures. Results showed that CBT resulted in better outcomes compared to zopiclone on three out of four outcome measures. In contrast, zopiclone did not differ from placebo. Participants receiving CBT saw improvements in sleep efficiency from 81.4% at pre-treatment to 90.1% at 6-month follow-up, while the zopiclone group saw a decrease from 82.3% to 81.9%. Participants in the CBT group also spent more time in slow-wave sleep and less time awake during the night.Total sleep time was similar in all three groups, and at 6 months, patients receiving CBT had better sleep efficiency using polysomnography than those taking zopiclone.
Conclusively, this study suggests that interventions based on CBT are superior to zopiclone treatment both in short- and long-term management of insomnia in older adults.

title: Local changes in lipid environment of TCR microclusters regulate membrane binding by the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain
text: The portions of the T cell receptor's CD3ε and ζ cytoplasmic domains that are embedded in the plasma membrane (PM) are held in place by interactions with the inner leaflet of the membrane. According to a previous nuclear magnetic resonance structure, the two tyrosines in the CD3ε immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif are embedded in the bilayer. Prior research has revealed that acidic phospholipids and clusters of basic CD3ε residues interact via electrostatic forces to support binding to the PM. Phosphatidylserine (PS), the PM's most plentiful negatively charged lipid, plays a prominent role in the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain's membrane binding. Our findings show that T cell receptor triggering by peptide-MHC complexes causes the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain to dissociate from the PM. Upon release from the membrane, the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain experiences a substantial decrease in negative charge and available phosphatidylserine (PS) within TCR microclusters. These changes in the membrane composition even occur when TCR signaling is blocked with a Src kinase inhibitor. Local alterations in the lipid composition of TCR microclusters thus make the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain more accessible to CD3ε during early stages of T cell activation.

title: Humans and great apes share a large frontal cortex
text: Some of humanity's exceptional cognitive abilities are commonly attributed to a remarkable expansion of the human frontal lobe during evolution. This claim is based primarily on comparisons between human and primate brains, with a focus on excluding the brains of great apes. In an effort to advance this understanding, we employed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to compare the relative size of the frontal cortices in living primate species, including all extant hominoids. Upon analyzing the MRI data, we discovered that the human frontal cortices were not significantly larger than those of great apes. Rather than attributing our species' special cognitive abilities to a larger frontal lobe, we propose that these abilities may be due to differences in the size and connectivity of specific cortical areas, which do not necessarily require a proportionate increase in overall frontal lobe size during hominid evolution.

title: Virus-Plus-Susceptibility Gene Interaction Determines Crohn's Disease Gene Atg16L1 Phenotypes in Intestine
text: It is intriguing that diseases affect only a small percentage of individuals who harbor genetic risk factors for susceptibility. Our study demonstrates that a specific viral infection and a mutation in the Crohn's disease susceptibility gene Atg16L1 can jointly trigger intestinal disorders in mice. These disorders resulted in abnormalities in granule packaging and unique gene expression patterns in Paneth cells. Moreover, exposure to a toxic substance called dextran sodium sulfate led to a fundamentally altered response, displaying characteristics similar to Crohn's disease. This viral susceptibility interaction was dependent on TNFalpha and IFNgamma and could be prevented by using broad-spectrum antibiotics. Thus, our findings provide an example of how a combination of a virus and a susceptibility gene can conspire with various environmental factors and beneficial bacteria to influence the phenotype of individuals bearing common risk alleles for inflammatory conditions.

title: CaMKII Triggers the Diffusional Trapping of Surface AMPARs through Phosphorylation of Stargazin
text:
The Ca(2+)/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) plays a crucial role in the recruitment of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs) to synapses during both development and plasticity. However, the underlying mechanism remains elusive. By employing single-particle tracking of AMPARs, we have found that CaMKII activation and postsynaptic translocation result in the immobilization of AMPARs in the membrane. This process requires the phosphorylation of the auxiliary subunit Stargazin and its interaction with PDZ domain scaffolds. The PDZ binding domain of the GluA1 AMPAR subunit and its phosphorylation at Ser831 are not involved in AMPAR immobilization. Furthermore, CaMKII-dependent AMPAR immobilization regulates short-term plasticity, as NMDA-dependent Ca(2+) influx in the postsynapse triggers a decrease in AMPAR diffusional exchange at synapses, which is dependent on CaMKII and Stargazin.
This rewrite uses more formal language and a more concise sentence structure to convey the information in a clearer and more efficient manner. The use of more technical vocabulary and avoidance of unnecessary words make the text sound more professional and authoritative.

title: Epigenetics in diabetic nephropathy, immunity and metabolism
text: When it comes to the epigenome, a fine line exists between clarity and confusion. Walk that line and you will discover another fascinating level of transcriptional control. With the genetic code acting as the foundation for rules governing the encoding of information into proteins, there is a set of rules that dictate how chemical information is read. These epigenetic modifications reveal a diverse and regulatory side of the genetic code, with modifications ranging from short- to long-term alterations. While this complexity offers exquisite control, it also poses a significant challenge to understanding the mechanisms underlying complex diseases. Recent technological and computational advances have improved the unbiased acquisition of epigenomic patterns, deepening our understanding of the intricate chromatin landscape. Identifying the true physiological targets of regulatory proteins, such as reader proteins, writer proteins, and eraser proteins, is crucial for resolving distinct chromatin signatures of diabetic complications. However, the question remains as to how a diverse group of proteins regulates the diabetic landscape from an epigenomic perspective. Drawing from a growing compendium of experimental and clinical studies, this review provides an overview of the current state-of-play and offers a perspective on chromatin-dependent mechanisms implicated in diabetic complications, with a particular focus on diabetic nephropathy. We propose a codified signature of the diabetic epigenome and highlight potential candidates for chemical modification. In addition, we explore future strategies for expedited and refined searches for clinically relevant discoveries, while also considering the challenges associated with targeting epigenetic pathways in therapeutic approaches.

title: Drinking pattern and mortality: the Italian Risk Factor and Life Expectancy pooling project.
text:
Purpose:
This study aims to investigate the relationship between an aspect of drinking patterns, specifically drinking wine outside meals, and the risk of all-cause and specific-cause mortality.
Methods:
The Risk Factors and Life Expectancy Study is a pooled analysis of several epidemiological studies conducted in Italy. The study included 8647 men and 6521 women aged 30-59 years, who were free of cardiovascular disease at baseline. Participants were followed up for mortality from all causes, cardiovascular diseases, and non-cardiovascular diseases during an average of 7 years.
Results:
Drinkers of wine outside meals had higher death rates from all causes, non-cardiovascular diseases, and cancer compared to drinkers of wine with meals. This association was independent of cardiovascular disease risk factors measured at baseline, the amount of alcohol consumed, and appeared stronger in women than in men.
Conclusions:
The present study highlights the importance of considering drinking patterns in relation to health outcomes. Previous studies have limitations, and ascertainment of alcohol consumption frequently focused only on quantity without considering other factors. Drinking pattern could have important influences on determining the health effects of alcohol. In conclusion, drinking wine outside meals was associated with higher mortality rates, particularly in women. Attention should be given to this aspect of alcohol use and its relationship to health outcomes.

title: Pointing in the right direction: new developments in the field of planar cell polarity
text: Planar cell polarity (PCP) is prevalent in various developmental processes characterized by coordinated cell movement and tissue organization. Disruption of PCP can lead to significant developmental abnormalities. Recent investigations in flies and vertebrates have uncovered novel PCP functions and signaling components, as well as proposed novel mechanistic models. However, despite these advancements, the quest to distill core principles remains ongoing, and residual mechanistic uncertainties continue to pose significant challenges.

title: ADAR1 Forms a Complex with Dicer to Promote MicroRNA Processing and RNA-Induced Gene Silencing
text: Adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs) are involved in RNA editing, which converts adenosine residues to inosine specifically in double-stranded RNAs. Our study aimed to investigate the interplay between the RNA editing mechanism and the RNA interference (RNAi) machinery, and we found that ADAR1 forms a complex with Dicer through direct protein-protein interaction. Notably, ADAR1 enhances the maximum rate (Vmax) of pre-microRNA (miRNA) cleavage by Dicer and facilitates loading of miRNA onto RNA-induced silencing complexes, revealing a novel role of ADAR1 in miRNA processing and RNAi mechanisms. ADAR1 distinguishes its functions in RNA editing and RNAi through the formation of either ADAR1/ADAR1 homodimer or Dicer/ADAR1 heterodimer complexes, respectively. Consistently, inhibition of miRNA expression in ADAR1(-/-) mouse embryos leads to alterations in the expression of their target genes and may contribute to their embryonic lethal phenotype.

title: Interchangeability of Biosimilars: A European Perspective
text: Most of the top-selling 'blockbuster' biological medicinal products are, or will soon face competition from similar biological medicinal products (biosimilars) in the European Union (EU). Biosimilarity is based on the comparability concept, which has been successfully used for several decades to ensure the close similarity of a biological product before and after a manufacturing change. Over the last 10 years, experience with biosimilars has shown that even complex biotechnology-derived proteins can be successfully copied. Most best-selling biologicals are used for chronic treatment. This has sparked intense discussion on the interchangeability of a biosimilar with its reference product, with the main concern being immunogenicity. We delve into the theoretical basis of the presumed risks of switching between a biosimilar and its reference product and examine the available data on switches. Our conclusion is that switching between comparable versions of the same active substance approved in accordance with EU legislation is unlikely to trigger or enhance immunogenicity. On the basis of current knowledge, it is improbable and challenging to demonstrate that two products, comparable on a population level, would have different safety or efficacy in individual patients upon a switch. Our conclusion is that biosimilars licensed in the EU are interchangeable.

title: Exome sequencing identifies somatic gain-of-function PPM1D mutations in brainstem gliomas
text: Brainstem and thalamic gliomas are highly aggressive tumors that are challenging to surgically remove. To investigate the genetic and epigenetic characteristics of these tumors, we conducted exomic sequencing on 14 brainstem gliomas (BSGs) and 12 thalamic gliomas, as well as targeted mutational analysis of an additional 24 tumors and genome-wide methylation profiling of 45 gliomas. Our findings revealed tumor-specific mutations in PPM1D, which encodes wild-type p53-induced protein phosphatase 1D (WIP1), in 37.5% of the BSGs that had hallmark H3F3A mutations encoding p. Lys27Met substitutions. These mutations were unique to the BSGs and did not co-occur with TP53 mutations. Additionally, we found that PPM1D mutations resulted in truncating alterations in exon 6, leading to enhanced suppression of the activation of the DNA damage response checkpoint protein CHK2. These results demonstrate PPM1D as a frequently mutated target and a potential therapeutic target in brainstem gliomas.

title: Crystal structure of a nucleosome core particle containing the variant histone H2A.Z
text: The activation of transcription within chromatin has been linked to the incorporation of the essential histone variant H2A.Z into nucleosomes. While H2A.Z and other histone variants may form distinct chromosomal domains, the molecular mechanism by which they function remains largely unknown. Here, we present the 2.6 Å crystal structure of a nucleosome core particle containing H2A.Z, which shows an overall structure similar to that of a previously reported 2.8 Å nucleosome structure containing major histone proteins. However, subtle changes in the dimer interface between H2A.Z and H2B result in a destabilization of the interaction between the (H2A.Z–H2B) dimer and the (H3–H4)2 tetramer. Additionally, H2A.Z nucleosomes have an altered surface that contains a metal ion, which may lead to changes in higher-order structure or the association of specific nuclear proteins with H2A.Z. Finally, incorporation of H2A.Z and H2A within the same nucleosome is unlikely due to significant changes in the interface between the two H2A.Z–H2B dimers.

title: Dendritic Cell KLF2 Expression Regulates T Cell Activation and Proatherogenic Immune Responses.
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) have been implicated as crucial regulators of both innate and adaptive inflammation in various diseases, including atherosclerosis. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms are partially understood. Previous studies have demonstrated an anti-inflammatory role for the transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) in regulating the activation of different cell types involved in atherosclerotic lesion development, including endothelial cells, macrophages, and T cells. To further elucidate the role of KLF2 in DCs, we utilized a pan-DC, CD11c-specific cre-lox gene knockout mouse model. We found that KLF2 deficiency led to increased surface expression of costimulatory molecules CD40 and CD86 on DCs, which in turn promoted enhanced T cell proliferation and apoptosis. Moreover, bone marrow transplantation of mice with KLF2-deficient DCs into Ldlr-/- mice exacerbated atherosclerosis, likely due to augmented vascular inflammation, characterized by increased DC presence within lesions, heightened T cell activation and cytokine production, and increased cell death in atherosclerotic lesions. Collectively, these findings suggest that KLF2 regulates the intensity of proatherogenic T cell responses through its control of DC activation.

title: Targeting tumor-necrosis factor receptor pathways for tumor immunotherapy
text: With the triumph of ipilimumab and the promise of programmed death-1 pathway-targeted agents, the field of tumor immunotherapy is experiencing a rapid expansion. Emerging targets for clinical development include select members of the tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) family. Agonist antibodies against these co-stimulatory molecules modulate T-cell activation and amplify immune responses, targeting both T and B cells. In vitro and in vivo preclinical studies have provided the foundation for the ongoing development of 4-1BB, OX40, glucocorticoid-induced TNFR-related gene, herpes virus entry mediator, and CD27 as potential cancer therapies. In this review, we will delve into the immune response to tumors, assess preclinical and early clinical data on selected TNFR family members, address potential translation hurdles, and propose combinatorial regimens to foster durable antitumor responses.

title: Plasma soluble corin in patients with heart failure.
text:
Corin is a transmembrane protease that processes natriuretic peptides in the heart. Similar to other membrane proteins, corin is released from the cell surface. We evaluated corin levels in the plasma of healthy individuals and patients with heart failure (HF) and acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in this study.
We obtained plasma samples from 198 healthy adults and measured corin levels using an ELISA method. The corin levels were found to be 690 pg/mL (SD, 260 pg/mL) in healthy individuals. There was no significant difference in corin levels among different age groups. In contrast, plasma corin levels were significantly lower in patients with HF (365 pg/mL [SD, 259]; P<0.001 compared to healthy controls). Moreover, the reduction in plasma corin levels appeared to correlate with the severity of HF, with plasma corin levels of 450 pg/mL (SD, 281 pg/mL), 377 pg/mL (SD, 270 pg/mL), and 282 pg/mL (SD, 194 pg/mL) found in patients in New York Heart Association classes II, III, and IV, respectively (P<0.001 class II vs class IV; P<0.05 class III vs class IV). In contrast, plasma corin levels in patients with AMI (n=73) were comparable to those of healthy controls (678 pg/mL [SD, 285 pg/mL]; P>0.05).
Our findings indicate that soluble corin is detectable in human plasma and that decreased plasma corin levels may contribute to the pathogenesis of HF. This study suggests that plasma corin could serve as a biomarker for the diagnosis of HF.

title: The NLRP3 inflammasome functions as a driver of the myelodysplastic syndrome phenotype.
text: Although genetic variations exist, myelodysplastic syndromes (MDSs) exhibit similar features of cytological dysplasia and inefficient hematopoiesis. Our findings reveal that a defining characteristic of MDSs is the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, which leads to clonal expansion and pyroptotic cell death. Interestingly, MDS hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) consistently express high levels of inflammasome proteins and form active NLRP3 complexes that induce caspase-1 activation, resulting in the production of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and IL-18, as well as pyroptotic cell death. We discovered that the alarmin S100A9 is overexpressed in MDS HSPCs and bone marrow plasma, triggering pyroptosis through its activation of NADPH oxidase (NOX). Increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) initiate cation influx, cell swelling, and β-catenin activation. Moreover, suppressing NLRP3 or caspase-1, neutralizing S100A9, or pharmacologically inhibiting NLRP3 or NOX inhibits pyroptosis, ROS generation, and nuclear β-catenin in MDSs, ultimately restoring effective hematopoiesis. These findings suggest that alarmins and founder gene mutations in MDSs cooperate to activate a redox-sensitive inflammasome circuit, paving the way for novel therapeutic interventions.

title: Structural Brain Correlates Associated with Professional Handball Playing
text: BACKGROUND Handball game requires excellent bimanual skills, especially in controlling the non-dominant hand. The control of the non-dominant hand is challenging, as it requires both hands to perform efficient catching and throwing. To investigate training-induced structural changes in professional handball players, we used various imaging techniques and analytical approaches. Specifically, we focused on regions relevant for motor and somatosensory processing, including the primary/secondary motor (MI/SMA) and somatosensory cortex (SI/SII), basal ganglia, thalamus, and cerebellum, as well as the white matter (WM) of the corticospinal tract (CST) and corpus callosum. RESULTS In contrast to control subjects, handball players showed increased grey matter (GM) volume in areas involved in limb control, such as the right MI/SI, bilateral SMA/cingulate motor area, and left intraparietal sulcus. Additionally, we found increased fractional anisotropy (FA) and axial diffusivity within the right CST. Moreover, age of handball training commencement correlated inversely with GM volume in the right and left MI/SI, while years of handball training experience correlated inversely with radial diffusivity in the right CST. Notably, subcortical structures tended to be larger in handball players. Finally, anatomical measures of brain regions associated with handball playing were positively correlated in handball players, but not interrelated in control women. DISCUSSION/CONCLUSION Our findings suggest that handball training leads to structural alterations in the somatosensory-motor network, with greater changes occurring in the right hemisphere controlling the non-dominant left hand. Correlations between handball training-related measures and anatomical differences are indicative of neuroplastic adaptations rather than a genetic predisposition for ball play affinity. Investigations into the neural mechanisms of expertise in sports like handball may reveal insights into the neurological basis of exceptional performance.

title: The role of epigenetics in aging and age-related diseases
text: The pivotal function of epigenetics in aging and age-related diseases is a central concern in molecular physiology and medicine, as certain epigenetic elements are believed to intercede, at least partially, in the complex relationship between the genome and the environment. To fully comprehend the role of epigenetics in aging, it is essential that specific epigenetic modifications occur during the aging process and are correlated with the characteristic phenotype of old age. If we presume that specific epigenetic alterations have a direct functional impact on aging, it is crucial to determine whether they are influenced by genetic, environmental, or stochastic factors, and whether they can be transmitted across generations. In this discussion, we will delve into the current state of knowledge on these issues and outline potential future directions in the field.

title: Effects of a high-fat diet exposure in utero on the metabolic syndrome-like phenomenon in mouse offspring through epigenetic changes in adipocytokine gene expression.
text: The relationship between obesity in parents and offspring, as well as the role of genes and shared environment, is not fully understood. Adipocytokines, such as leptin and adiponectin, play a crucial role in glucose and lipid metabolism. To investigate whether offspring of mothers exposed to a high-fat diet during pregnancy (OH mice) are predisposed to metabolic disorders, we evaluated their hypertension, insulin resistance, and hyperlipidemia, as well as epigenetic changes in adipocytokine gene expression. OH mice were significantly heavier than offspring of mothers fed a control diet during pregnancy (OC mice) from 14 weeks of age after a increased caloric intake from 8 weeks. OH mice exhibited higher blood pressure and worse glucose tolerance than OC mice at 24 weeks. Additionally, total triglyceride and leptin levels were significantly higher, while adiponectin levels were significantly lower in OH mice compared to OC mice at 12 weeks of age. These alterations in adipocytokine expression were accompanied by changes in histone modifications in white adipose tissue. Specifically, there were lower acetylation and higher methylation levels of histone H3 at lysine 9 of the adiponectin promoter in adipose tissues of OH mice at 2 weeks of age, as well as at 12 and 24 weeks of age, compared to OC mice. In contrast, methylation of histone 4 at lysine 20 in the leptin promoter was significantly higher in OH mice compared to OC mice. These findings suggest that in utero exposure to a high-fat diet may lead to the development of metabolic syndrome-like traits through epigenetic modifications of adipocytokine, adiponectin, and leptin gene expression.

title: Highly efficient miRNA-mediated reprogramming of mouse and human somatic cells to pluripotency.
text:
Recent advancements in transcription factor-based cellular reprogramming have enabled the conversion of somatic cells into a pluripotent state, but they have been hindered by the requirement for transcription factors and relative inefficiency of the process. In contrast, we have discovered that expressing the miR302/367 cluster can rapidly and efficiently convert mouse and human somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) without the need for exogenous transcription factors. In fact, our data shows that this miRNA-based reprogramming approach is up to two orders of magnitude more efficient than standard Oct4/Sox2/Klf4/Myc-mediated methods. Both mouse and human miR302/367 iPSCs exhibit similar characteristics to Oct4/Sox2/Klf4/Myc-iPSCs, including the expression of pluripotency markers, teratoma formation, and chimera contribution and germline contribution in the case of mouse cells.
Further investigation revealed that miR367 expression is essential for miR302/367-mediated reprogramming and activates Oct4 gene expression. Additionally, we found that suppressing the histone deacetylase 2 (Hdac2) is also required for the process. Our findings therefore suggest that miRNA- and Hdac-mediated pathways can cooperate in a meaningful way to reprogram somatic cells towards pluripotency.

title: Unmet needs and depression among carers of people newly diagnosed with cancer.
text:
The aim of this analysis was to investigate levels of unmet needs and depression among carers of individuals recently diagnosed with cancer, and to identify subgroups at higher risk by examining the relationships between demographic factors and unmet needs.
Methods included recruiting 150 dyads of cancer patients and their carers from four Australian hospitals, with individuals aged 18 or older and receiving adjuvant cancer treatment with curative intent. Both carers and patients completed the Supportive Care Needs Survey-Partners & Caregivers (SCNS-P&C45) and the Centre of Epidemiologic-Depression Scale (CES-D).
