This review focuses on key cellular mechanisms, including the production of pro- and anti-inflammatory mediators, the expression of adhesion molecules, and the impact of oxidant stress during the inflammatory response. Additionally, the roles of nitric oxide in maintaining microcirculatory function and its involvement in peroxynitrite formation are discussed. Emerging mechanisms of protection through ischemic preconditioning are also explored, and potential interventions that mimic these effects are identified as having the greatest potential to improve clinical outcomes following liver surgery involving ischemic stress and reperfusion.

title: Characterization of a FGF19 Variant with Altered Receptor Specificity Revealed a Central Role for FGFR1c in the Regulation of Glucose Metabolism
text: The global pandemic of diabetes and related metabolic conditions demands new treatments that are both effective and safe. FGF19 and FGF21 are members of the FGF family that function as hormones, with remarkable abilities to regulate glucose, lipid, and energy metabolism. Despite their potential, the mechanism behind their effects remains unknown. Both FGF19 and FGF21 activate FGFRs 1c, 2c, and 3c in the presence of co-receptor βKlotho in vitro, but the receptor responsible for their metabolic effects in vivo remains elusive. To uncover this mystery, we created a variant of FGF19, FGF19-7, with altered receptor specificity, biased towards FGFR1c. Our findings show that FGF19-7 is equally effective as wild-type FGF19 in regulating glucose, lipid, and energy metabolism in both obese mouse models and leptin-deficient mice. These results provide the first conclusive evidence of the central role of the βKlotho/FGFR1c receptor complex in glucose and lipid metabolism, and suggest that activating this receptor alone may be sufficient to replicate the metabolic functions of endocrine FGF molecules.

title: Empirical verification of evolutionary theories of aging
text:
We recently identified three long-lived mutant strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae through prolonged exposure to exogenous lithocholic acid. These strains retain their extended lifespan even after numerous passages in medium without the stimulus. In this study, we employed these long-lived yeast mutants to test evolutionary theories of aging. Our findings reveal that the dominant polygenic trait associated with increased lifespan in each mutant strain does not compromise early-life fitness metrics, such as exponential growth rate, post-exponential growth efficiency, and fecundity. Instead, these mutants exhibit enhanced resistance to chronic exogenous stresses and increased susceptibility to programmed cell death. These results support evolutionary theories of programmed aging.
Furthermore, we discovered that under laboratory conditions mimicking natural selection within an ecosystem, each long-lived mutant strain is outcompeted by the shorter-lived wild-type strain. This finding suggests that yeast cells have evolved mechanisms to limit their lifespan as they age. These mechanisms drive the evolution of yeast longevity towards a finite chronological lifespan within ecosystems.

title: Differential regulation of actin microfilaments by human MICAL proteins.
text: The Drosophila melanogaster MICAL protein is indispensable for the neuronal machinery responsible for axonal signaling, which involves plexin- and semaphorin-mediated signaling. Additionally, the Drosophila MICAL protein plays a role in regulating myofilament organization and synaptic structures, serves as an actin-disassembling factor downstream of plexin-mediated axonal repulsion, and regulates actin structures in mammalian cells. In contrast, little is known about the function of the three known mammalian MICAL isoforms (MICAL1, MICAL2, and MICAL3), as well as the MICAL-like proteins MICAL-L1 and MICAL-L2, in non-neuronal cells. This study reveals that human MICALs are essential for normal actin organization in non-neural cells. Further findings show that all three MICALs regulate actin stress fibers, and that the generation of reactive oxygen species by MICAL proteins is crucial for their actin-regulatory function. Notably, while MICAL1 is auto-inhibited by its C-terminal coiled-coil region, MICAL2 remains constitutively active and affects stress fibers, suggesting differential but complementary roles for MICAL1 and MICAL2 in actin microfilament regulation.

title: Suppression of inflammatory and neuropathic pain by uncoupling CRMP-2 from the presynaptic Ca2+ channel complex
text: The use of N-type voltage-gated calcium channel (CaV2.2) blockers to treat pain is hindered by various physiological side effects. Here, we demonstrate that reducing the binding of collapsin response mediator protein 2 (CRMP-2) to CaV2.2 can alleviate inflammatory and neuropathic hypersensitivity. We found that a peptide composed of CRMP-2 fused to the HIV transactivator of transcription (TAT) protein (TAT-CBD3) decreased neuropeptide release from sensory neurons and excitatory synaptic transmission in dorsal horn neurons, as well as reduced meningeal blood flow, nocifensive behavior induced by formalin injection or corneal capsaicin application, and neuropathic hypersensitivity produced by an antiretroviral drug. Interestingly, TAT-CBD3 displayed mild anxiolytic effects without affecting memory retrieval, sensorimotor function, or depression. At higher doses, TAT-CBD3 caused transient episodes of tail kinking and body contortion. By preventing CRMP-2-mediated enhancement of CaV2.2 function, TAT-CBD3 alleviated inflammatory and neuropathic hypersensitivity, a approach that may prove useful in managing chronic pain.

title: Identification and characterization of a common set of complex I assembly intermediates in mitochondria from patients with complex I deficiency.
text: Deficiencies in the activity of complex I (NADH: ubiquinone oxidoreductase) are a primary cause of mitochondrial diseases in humans. Complex I is composed of approximately 46 structural subunits, with both nuclear and mitochondrial DNA encoding these subunits. Enzyme deficiency can result from either impaired catalytic efficiency or an inability to assemble the holoenzyme complex, although the assembly process remains poorly understood. To investigate complex I assembly in muscle mitochondria from patients with deficiencies caused by nuclear or mitochondrial gene defects, we employed two-dimensional Blue-Native/SDS gel electrophoresis and a panel of 11 antibodies targeting structural subunits of the enzyme. Immunoblot analyses of second dimension denaturing gels identified seven distinct complex I subcomplexes in the patients studied, with five of these subcomplexes also visible in non-denaturing gels in the first dimension. Despite variations in the abundance of these intermediates among different patients, a consistent profile of subcomplexes was observed in all cases. In fact, a similar pattern of subcomplexes was seen in a human/mouse hybrid fibroblast cell line with a severe complex I deficiency due to almost complete holoenzyme assembly. These findings suggest that the observed subcomplexes are intermediate stages in the assembly of the holoenzyme complex, indicating a unique assembly pathway for complex I. Our proposed assembly pathway differs significantly from the current model for Neurospora, highlighting the complexity of this process.

title: Leisure time physical activity and mortality: a detailed pooled analysis of the dose-response relationship.
text:
The 2008 Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans recommended that adults should engage in at least 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity or 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week to achieve substantial health benefits. However, the upper limit of longevity benefit or potential harm from increased physical activity is unclear. To investigate this, we pooled data from six studies in the National Cancer Institute Cohort Consortium, including over 1 million adults (ages 21-98) from the United States and Europe.
We observed a 20% lower risk of mortality among individuals who engaged in less than the recommended minimum of physical activity (less than 7.5 metabolic-equivalent hours per week). The risk decreased by 31% at 1-2 times the minimum, by 37% at 2-3 times the minimum, and by 39% at 4-5 times the minimum. However, there was no evidence of harm at 10 or more times the minimum recommended amount. We also observed a similar dose-response relationship for mortality due to cardiovascular disease and cancer.
Our findings suggest that meeting the 2008 Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans minimum by either moderate- or vigorous-intensity activities is associated with nearly the maximum longevity benefit. Healthcare professionals should encourage inactive adults to engage in leisure time physical activity, and there is no need to discourage individuals who already participate in high levels of physical activity.

title: Green tea polyphenol causes differential oxidative environments in tumor versus normal epithelial cells.
text: Green tea polyphenols (GTPPs) have been deemed advantageous to human health, particularly as chemopreventive agents. However, recent studies have revealed that high concentrations of the most abundant GTPP, (-)-epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), can produce cytotoxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) in both tumor and normal cell cultures. If EGCG also leads to the production of ROS in normal epithelial cells, it may be ineffective for topical use at higher doses. To investigate this, the current study examined the oxidative status of normal epithelial, normal salivary gland, and oral carcinoma cells treated with EGCG using ROS measurement and catalase and superoxide dismutase activity assays. The results showed that high concentrations of EGCG induced oxidative stress only in tumor cells, while reducing ROS levels in normal cells to background levels. Additionally, 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) and 5-bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation assays were also compared between two oral carcinoma cell lines treated with EGCG, suggesting that differences in endogenous catalase activity may play a crucial role in reducing oxidative stress provoked by EGCG in tumor cells. Overall, the findings suggest that GTPPs or EGCG activate different oxidative pathways in normal epithelial and tumor cells, supporting either normal cell survival or tumor cell destruction, which may have implications for enhancing the effectiveness of chemo/radiation therapy in cancer treatment.

title: Protein acetylation affects acetate metabolism, motility and acid stress response in Escherichia coli
text: Although protein acetylation is prevalent, its regulatory functions are poorly understood. To investigate its functions, we analyzed the acetylome in Escherichia coli knockout mutants of cobB, the only known sirtuin-like deacetylase, and patZ, the best-known protein acetyltransferase. For four growth conditions, we identified and differentially quantified over 2,000 unique acetylated peptides belonging to 809 proteins. Notably, nearly 65% of these proteins are involved in metabolism. Our findings reveal that the global activity of CobB has a significant impact on physiology by deacetylating a large number of substrates. We also discovered that CobB-controlled acetylation of isocitrate lyase contributes to the fine-tuning of the glyoxylate shunt. Additionally, acetylation of the transcription factor RcsB inhibits DNA binding, activates flagella biosynthesis and motility, and increases acid stress susceptibility. Surprisingly, patZ deletion led to increased acetylation in acetate cultures, suggesting that it regulates the levels of acetylating agents. The insights gained from this study shed light on the functional roles of protein acetylation in metabolic fitness and global cell regulation.

title: Ribosome biogenesis: Achilles heel of cancer?
text:
The nucleolus is a critical structure in eukaryotic cells that plays a central role in ribosome biogenesis. Cancer cells have altered nucleolar morphology due to the up-regulation of ribosomal gene transcription, which is mediated by RNA polymerase I (pol I). The pre-ribosomal RNA (pre-rRNA) transcripts are modified and processed into mature 18S, 5.8S, and 28S rRNAs, and 5S rRNA is transcribed by RNA polymerase III in the nucleoplasm. Oncogenes like c-Myc can upregulate ribosome biogenesis, while tumour suppressors like p53 and Rb suppress ribosome biogenesis. Mutations in these genes lead to deregulated cell cycle control and upregulated ribosome biogenesis.
The nucleolus is also a key cellular stress sensor, and p53 activation plays a central role in cellular stress responses. The increased translational capacity of cancer cells enables them to maintain higher proliferation rates. Recently, two drugs have been identified that target ribosome biogenesis without causing DNA damage: CX-5461 and BMH-21. CX-5461 specifically inhibits pol I transcription by disrupting pre-initiation complex formation at the rDNA promoter, leading to p53 activation via nucleolar stress and inducing autophagy or senescence in multiple types of cancer cells. BMH-21 is a DNA intercalator that inhibits rDNA transcription and induces nucleolar reorganization, resulting in decreased proliferation and cell death. P53 is activated in BMH-21-treated cells, and cancer cells with high demands for ribosome biogenesis are selectively targeted. Moreover, BMH-21 derivatives that can induce DNA damage display lower efficiency in inducing nucleolar stress and inhibiting proliferation. This study finally uncouples DNA damage and nucleolar stress and reveals an Achilles heel in cancer cells, their addiction to ribosome biogenesis.

title: Cell and molecular mechanisms of insulin-induced angiogenesis
text: Angiogenesis, the process of new blood vessel formation from pre-existing vessels, is a crucial component of wound healing. Our studies have shown that insulin stimulates angiogenesis and elucidated the signaling pathways involved in this process. In vivo studies in mice revealed that insulin injection leads to the development of longer vessels with more branches, accompanied by an increase in alpha-smooth muscle actin-expressing cells, indicative of proper vessel maturation. Additionally, we found that insulin promotes human microvascular endothelial cell migration and tube formation, and these effects are independent of VEGF/VEGFR signaling but depend on the insulin receptor itself. Our results further suggest that downstream signaling pathways including PI3K, Akt, sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP-1), and Rac1 are essential for endothelial cell migration and tube formation, and their inhibition leads to a significant decrease in microvessel development. Based on our findings, insulin appears to be a promising candidate for the treatment of ischaemic wounds and other conditions characterized by impaired blood vessel development.

title: Inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin potentiates thrombin-induced intercellular adhesion molecule-1 expression by accelerating and stabilizing NF-kappa B activation in endothelial cells.
text: We investigated the regulatory function of mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) in the mechanism of thrombin-induced intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) gene expression in endothelial cells. Treating HUVECs with rapamycin, an inhibitor of mTOR, before thrombin exposure augmented thrombin-induced ICAM-1 expression. In contrast, overexpressing mTOR inhibited thrombin-induced transcriptional activity of nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), a crucial regulator of ICAM-1 transcription. Our analysis of the NF-κB signaling pathway revealed that inhibiting mTOR enhanced IκB kinase activity, leading to rapid and sustained phosphorylation of IκBα on Ser32 and Ser36, which is essential for IκBα degradation. Consistent with these findings, we observed increased and more stable nuclear localization of RelA/p65 and, subsequently, DNA binding activity of NF-κB by thrombin following mTOR inhibition. These results define a novel mechanism by which mTOR regulates thrombin-induced ICAM-1 expression in endothelial cells by controlling a delayed and transient activation of NF-κB.

title: Homologous recombination resolution defect in werner syndrome.
text: Werner syndrome (WRN), an uncommon autosomal recessive disorder, presents with features of premature aging, genetic instability, and elevated cancer risk. To investigate the interrelationship between WRN cellular phenotypes, we employed three experimental strategies. We found that WRN cellular phenotypes, including limited cell division potential, DNA damage hypersensitivity, and defective homologous recombination (HR), are linked. WRN cell survival and the generation of viable mitotic recombinant progeny were rescued by expressing wild-type WRN protein or the bacterial resolvase protein RusA. Our results also demonstrated that WRN cellular phenotypes rely on RAD51-dependent HR pathways, as demonstrated by using a dominant-negative RAD51 protein to suppress mitotic recombination in WRN and control cells. The suppression of RAD51-dependent recombination significantly improved the survival of WRN cells following DNA damage, illustrating a physiological role for the WRN RecQ helicase protein in RAD51-dependent HR and highlighting a mechanistic connection between defective recombination resolution and limited cell division potential, DNA damage hypersensitivity, and genetic instability in human somatic cells.

title: Risk factors at medical school for subsequent professional misconduct: multicentre retrospective case-control study
text:
Objective: To investigate whether certain factors during medical school are associated with subsequent professional misconduct by doctors.
Design: Matched case-control study.
Setting: Data collected from medical schools and the General Medical Council (GMC).
Participants: 59 doctors who had demonstrated professional misconduct and were under GMC proceedings in 1999-2004, and 236 controls (four for each case) selected using systematic sampling from the same graduation cohorts.
Main outcome measure: Odds ratios were calculated using multivariable conditional logistic regression to identify potential risk factors, including pre-admission characteristics and progress during the course. Data was retrieved from anonymized copies of the students' progress files held by their original medical schools.
Results: Univariate conditional logistic regression analysis revealed that cases were more likely to be male, from a lower social class, and had academic difficulties during their medical course, particularly in the early years. Multivariable analysis showed that male sex (odds ratio 9.80, 95% confidence interval 2.43 to 39.44, P=0.001), lower social class (4.28, 1.52 to 12.09, P=0.006), and failure of early or preclinical examinations (5.47, 2.17 to 13.79, P<0.001) were independently associated with being a case.
Conclusions: This small study suggests that male sex, lower socioeconomic background, and early academic difficulties during medical school may be risk factors for subsequent professional misconduct. Findings are preliminary and should be interpreted with caution. Most doctors with risk factors will not come before the GMC's disciplinary panels.

title: MiD49 and MiD51, new components of the mitochondrial fission machinery.
text: Mitochondria form complex networks through the process of fission and fusion, and we have identified two key proteins that play a crucial role in this process. These proteins, called mitochondrial dynamics proteins (MiD49 and MiD51), are anchored in the outer membrane of mitochondria. MiD49/51 form structures similar to focal adhesions and ring-like structures around mitochondria, similar to the fission mediator dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1). MiD49/51 directly recruit Drp1 to the mitochondrial surface, whereas their inactivation reduces Drp1 association and leads to uncontrolled fusion. Overexpression of MiD49/51 appears to sequester Drp1 away from its normal function at mitochondria, causing fusion tubules to associate with actin filaments. In essence, MiD49/51 are new regulators of mitochondrial division that modulate Drp1's activity at the mitochondrial surface.

title: Maximal activation of transcription by statl and stat3 requires both tyrosine and serine phosphorylation
text: Two key transcriptional factors, Stat1 and Stat3, are activated initially through phosphorylation on multiple tyrosine residues in response to cytokine and growth factor occupancy of cell surface receptors. We have found that in addition to these tyrosine phosphorylation events, phosphorylation on a single serine residue (residue 727) in each protein is also essential for optimal transcriptional activity. Both cytokines and growth factors are capable of inducing the serine phosphorylation of Stat1 and Stat3, revealing that gene activation by these factors, which are initially inactive due to tyrosine phosphorylation, also depends on one or more serine kinases for full activation.

title: Protein restriction during pregnancy affects maternal liver lipid metabolism and fetal brain lipid composition in the rat.
text: Protein restriction during pregnancy can lead to long-term metabolic problems in offspring. Researchers aimed to investigate the impact of protein restriction in pregnant women on maternal liver lipid metabolism at 19 days of gestation (dG) and its effects on fetal brain development. They compared control (C) and restricted (R) pregnant women who were fed with isocaloric diets containing 20 and 10% casein, respectively. At 19 dG, researchers collected maternal blood, livers, and brains, as well as fetal livers and brains. They measured serum insulin and leptin levels in mothers and quantified maternal and fetal liver and brain lipids using gas chromatography. In addition, they measured the expression of liver desaturase and elongase genes in mothers by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). They found that fat body composition, including liver lipids, was lower in R mothers. R mothers also had higher fasting insulin levels at 19 dG compared to C mothers, and this was inversely related to early growth retardation. Moreover, R mothers had higher serum leptin levels than C mothers. Protein restriction significantly reduced the expression of desaturases and elongases in maternal liver and the concentration of arachidonic (AA) and docosahexanoic (DHA) acids. In fetuses from R mothers, there was a reduction in body weight, liver, and brain lipids, including the content of DHA in the brain. This study suggests that protein restriction during pregnancy may have negative effects on normal fetal brain development by altering maternal lipid metabolism.

title: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans mediate internalization and propagation of specific proteopathic seeds.
text: New research suggests that the transcellular transmission of fibrillar protein aggregates is a key driver of neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, in a prion-like manner. Recent studies have demonstrated this phenomenon in both cell and animal models, where protein aggregates are released into the extracellular space and then enter adjacent cells to induce further fibrillization. The mechanism by which these aggregated proteins, such as tau and α-synuclein, enter cells and trigger intracellular fibril formation is currently unknown. Prior research has shown that prion protein aggregates bind to heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) on the cell surface to facilitate the propagation of disease. This study reveals that tau fibril uptake also occurs through HSPG binding, which is blocked in cultured cells and primary neurons by heparin, chlorate, heparinase, and genetic knockdown of a key HSPG synthetic enzyme, Ext1. Interfering with tau's binding to HSPGs prevented the induction of intracellular aggregation and blocked transcellular aggregate propagation. In vivo, the use of a heparin mimetic, F6, blocked neuronal uptake of stereotactically injected tau fibrils. Additionally, this study found that uptake and seeding by α-synuclein fibrils, but not huntingtin fibrils, also occurs through the same mechanism as tau. These findings provide a unifying mechanism for the cellular uptake and propagation of tauopathy and synucleinopathy.

title: Effects of Bifidobacterium animalis administered during lactation on allergic and autoimmune responses in rodents.
text: Probiotics are widely promoted for their positive effects on immune function, and several mechanisms have been attributed to their beneficial effects, including stimulating T helper 1 (Th1) immunity. To investigate the impact of the probiotic Bifidobacterium animalis on Th1- and Th2-mediated immune responses, we used two animal models representing either Th1- or Th2-mediated immune responses: a rat model for experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and a mouse model for respiratory allergy induced by ovalbumin (OVA). We administered B. animalis to the animals when they were 2 weeks old, and then induced respiratory allergy or EAE when they were 6-7 weeks old. In the allergy model, B. animalis modestly reduced the number of infiltrating eosinophils and lymphocytes in the lungs, but had no effect on allergen-specific serum immunoglobulin E levels. In contrast, B. animalis skewed the Th1/Th2 balance towards Th1 in female mice, as evidenced by cytokine profiles assessed after culturing spleen cells with the mitogen concanvalin A (ConA). However, allergen-induced cytokine production in female mice was not affected by B. animalis. In male mice, B. animalis significantly decreased ConA-induced interleukin-13 and showed a trend towards lower levels of OVA-induced Th2 cytokines. In the EAE model, B. animalis significantly reduced the duration of clinical symptoms by almost 2 days in male mice and improved body weight gain during the experimental period compared to the control group. Our findings suggest that B. animalis reduced several immune parameters in both the allergy and autoimmunity models.

title: Planar Cell Polarity Signaling Pathway in Congenital Heart Diseases
text: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a prevalent cardiac condition in humans, despite significant improvements in understanding its underlying mechanisms and identifying associated genes. The underlying cause of most cases of CHD remains elusive. The planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling pathway, which regulates tissue polarity in Drosophila and gastrulation movements and cardiogenesis in vertebrates, has been found to play multiple roles during cardiac differentiation and development. Disruptions in PCP signaling have been linked to some cases of CHD. In this summary, we will discuss the current knowledge on how PCP factors contribute to the pathogenesis of CHD.

title: Cost-effectiveness of human papillomavirus vaccination and screening in Spain.
text:
In Spain, prophylactic vaccination against human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18 is currently being offered free of charge to one birth cohort of girls aged 11-14. However, the country's screening program is facing challenges due to inequitable coverage and overuse of cytology, leading to inefficiencies in the program.
To address these issues, a multi-HPV-type microsimulation model was developed using likelihood-based methods to assess the health and economic impact of adding HPV vaccination to cervical cancer screening in Spain. The model took into account different strategies, including screening alone in women over the age of 25, with varying frequency and test types (cytology, HPV DNA testing).
The study found that after the introduction of HPV vaccination, screening will continue to be necessary, and strategies that incorporate HPV testing are more effective and cost-effective than those that rely solely on cytology. For vaccinated girls, 5-year organized cytology with HPV testing as triage from ages 30 to 65 costs around 24,350 euros per year of life saved (YLS), assuming life-long vaccine immunity against HPV-16/18 with 90% coverage. In contrast, unvaccinated girls would benefit from organized cytology screening with HPV testing as triage, which costs around 16,060 euros per YLS for a 5-year screening program from ages 30 to 65, or around 38,250 euros per YLS for a 4-year screening program from ages 30 to 85.
The cost-effectiveness of these interventions depends on the cost-effectiveness threshold and the vaccine price. However, the study concludes that if high vaccination coverage among pre-adolescent girls is achieved, organized cytology screening with HPV triage starting at ages 30 to at least 65 every 4-5 years represents the best balance between costs and benefits in Spain's cervical cancer screening program.

title: Dosimetry and risk estimates of radioiodine therapy for large, multinodular goiters.
text: In this study, the absorbed doses of radiation in patients with a large, multinodular goiter (> 100 g) were estimated after the therapeutic administration of 131I. The doses were measured using thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLDs) placed on the skin over the thyroid, submandibular gland, and parotid gland, as well as through radioactivity measurements in 6 euthyroid and 6 hyperthyroid patients. The results showed that the cumulated absorbed doses on the skin were 4.2 +/- 1.4 Gy in the thyroid, 1.2 +/- 0.6 Gy in the submandibular gland, and 0.4 +/- 0.2 Gy in the parotid gland. The absorbed doses in the thyroid were calculated to be 94 +/- 25 Gy for euthyroid and 93 +/- 17 Gy for hyperthyroid patients, using an iodine biokinetic model and the MIRD methodology. The extrathyroidal absorbed doses were also calculated to be 0.88 Gy in the urinary bladder, 0.57 Gy in the small intestine, 0.38 Gy in the stomach, and ranged from 0.05 to 0.30 Gy in other organs. The lifetime risk of development of cancer outside the thyroid gland was calculated to be 1.6%, with older patients (65 years and older) having a estimated risk of approximately 0.5%. These findings may help in choosing the treatment regimen for individual patients with a large, multinodular goiter, taking into account their age and overall health.

title: RBM3 regulates temperature sensitive miR-142–5p and miR-143 (thermomiRs), which target immune genes and control fever
text: Fever is often used to diagnose illness, and in critically ill patients, it's associated with a higher risk of death. However, the molecules in the body that control body temperature are not well understood. We discovered that a protein called RBM3, which responds to cold stress and helps regulate other proteins, was less common in 30 patients with fever. We also found that RBM3 was less common in immune cells called macrophages when they were kept at a fever-like temperature (40°C). Interestingly, RBM3 levels were low even when there was no sign of infection. Lower levels of RBM3 led to higher levels of other proteins called thermomiRs, which in turn regulate the production of certain chemicals in the body that can cause fever. These chemicals include IL-6, TLR2, and PGE2. Using immune cells from healthy donors, we found that lower levels of RBM3 led to higher levels of these thermomiRs, and vice versa. Overall, our findings suggest that there may be a negative feedback loop in the body that helps regulate fever by reducing RBM3 levels and increasing the levels of these thermomiRs.

title: Patient preferences and expectations for care: determinants in patients with lumbar intervertebral disc herniation.
text:
Background: Patients with a diagnosis of intervertebral disc herniation have different treatment preferences. This study aims to identify the relationship between specific expectations and these preferences.
Methods: Data were collected from the observational cohort of the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial (SPORT). Patients who declined randomization and received their preferred treatment were included in the study. Baseline preference and expectation data were gathered at the time of enrollment. Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed to identify associations between patient characteristics, treatment preferences, and expectations.
Results: The majority (67%) of patients preferred operative care, while 28% preferred nonoperative treatment, and 6% were unsure. Of those preferring surgery, 53% had a definite preference, while only 18% of those preferring nonoperative care had a definite preference. Patients preferring surgery were younger, had lower levels of education, and higher levels of unemployment/disability. They also reported higher pain, worse physical and mental functioning, more back pain-related disability, a longer duration of symptoms, and more opiate use. Gender, race, comorbidities, and use of other therapies did not differ significantly across preference groups. Patients' expectations regarding improvement with nonoperative care were the strongest predictor of preference.
Conclusion: Patient expectations regarding the benefit of nonoperative treatment are the primary determinant of surgery preference among patients with lumbar intervertebral disc herniation. Demographic, functional status, and prior treatment experience have significant associations with patients' expectations and preferences.

title: Cord factor and peptidoglycan recapitulate the Th17-promoting adjuvant activity of mycobacteria through mincle/CARD9 signaling and the inflammasome.
text: Although adjuvants are essential components of vaccines, their mechanisms of action are inadequately understood. To investigate the mechanisms by which heat-killed mycobacteria in Complete Freund's Adjuvant (CFA) promote Th17 CD4+ T cell responses, we conducted a study. We found that IL-17 Secretion by CD4+ T cells following CFA immunization requires MyD88 and IL-1β/IL-1R signaling. Through measurement of Ag-specific responses after adoptive transfer of OTII cells, we confirmed that MyD88-dependent signaling regulates Th17 differentiation rather than simply producing IL-17. Additional experiments revealed that CFA-induced Th17 differentiation involves IL-1β processing by the inflammasome, and mice lacking caspase-1, ASC, or NLRP3 exhibited partially defective responses after immunization. Biochemical fractionation studies further showed that peptidoglycan is the primary component of heat-killed mycobacteria responsible for inflammasome activation. By analyzing Il1b transcripts in the injection site skin of CFA-immunized mice, we found that signaling through the adaptor molecule caspase activation and recruitment domain 9 (CARD9) plays a crucial role in triggering pro-IL-1β expression. Additionally, we demonstrated that recognition of the mycobacterial glycolipid trehalose dimycolate (cord factor) by the C-type lectin receptor mincle partially explains this CARD9 requirement. Importantly, administration of purified peptidoglycan and cord factor in mineral oil synergized to recapitulate the Th17-promoting activity of CFA, and this response was diminished in caspase-1- and CARD9-deficient mice. Overall, these findings suggest a general strategy for the rational design of Th17-skewing adjuvants by combining agonists of the CARD9 pathway with inflammasome activators.

title: OPA1 gene therapy prevents retinal ganglion cell loss in a Dominant Optic Atrophy mouse model
text:
Dominant optic atrophy (DOA) is a rare and irreversible blinding disease that is one of the most common forms of hereditary optic neuropathy. DOA is caused by a dominant mutation in the OPA1 gene, which encodes a crucial mitochondrial GTPase involved in cell survival and membrane dynamics. Hereditary optic neuropathies typically result in the degeneration of retinal ganglion cells, leading to optic nerve atrophy and progressive vision loss. Despite advances in understanding the disease's pathological mechanisms, DOA remains incurable.
To investigate the potential of gene therapy for treating DOA, we developed a genetically-modified mouse model with vision loss similar to the disease. We utilized an Adeno-Associated Virus carrying the human OPA1 cDNA under the control of the cytomegalovirus promoter for intravitreal injections. Our findings provide the first evidence that gene therapy can be effective in a DOA mouse model, as restoring wild-type OPA1 expression can alleviate retinal ganglion cell degeneration, the hallmark of the disease. These results offer encouraging evidence for gene therapy as a potential treatment for DOA, and suggest that future investigations may lead to clinical trials in humans.

title: Multiple degradation pathways regulate versatile CIP/KIP CDK inhibitors.
text: The mammalian CIP/KIP family of cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitors (CKIs) consists of three proteins: p21(Cip1/WAF1), p27(Kip1), and p57(Kip2). These proteins interact with and inhibit cyclin-CDK complexes, which are crucial regulators of the cell cycle. Beyond their role in the cell cycle, CIP/KIP CKIs have additional functions in transcription, apoptosis, and actin cytoskeletal dynamics. These diverse functions are carried out in different cellular compartments and may seem contradictory given that CKIs have both tumor-suppressing and tumor-stimulating activities. Multiple ubiquitin ligases (E3s) regulate the degradation of p21, p27, and p57 through the proteasome pathway. This review aims to provide an overview of the current understanding of how distinct E3 pathways control the diverse functions of CKIs.

title: Dislocation of a type I membrane protein requires interactions between membrane-spanning segments within the lipid bilayer.
text: The human cytomegalovirus gene product US11 exerts its function by inducing the rapid degradation of class I major histocompatibility complex (MHCI) heavy chains through a mechanism that resembles the endogenous cellular quality control pathway. Specifically, US11 causes the dislocation of MHCI heavy chains from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and subsequent degradation by the proteasome. The transmembrane domain (TMD) of US11 is essential for MHCI heavy chain dislocation, whereas its binding to MHCI is dispensable. A glutamine residue at position 192 in the US11 TMD is crucial for the ubiquitination and degradation of MHCI heavy chains. Cells that express US11 TMD mutants are unable to form MHCI-beta2m complexes and exhibit impaired ER egress, as revealed by further mutagenesis data. This suggests that an alpha-helical structure in the US11 TMD is essential for MHCI heavy chain dislocation, making the presence of such a structure unique among type I membrane proteins. The failure of US11 TMD mutants to catalyze dislocation is further highlighted by their inability to form interhelical hydrogen bonds within the ER membrane, which is a critical requirement for their function.

title: Prostate cancer-associated gene expression alterations determined from needle biopsies.
text:
The purpose of this study is to identify accurate gene expression alterations that distinguish neoplastic from normal prostate epithelium using a method that avoids contamination by unwanted cellular components and is not compromised by acute gene expression changes associated with tumor devascularization and resulting ischemia.
To achieve this, the researchers used an experimental design involving the isolation of approximately 3,000 neoplastic and benign prostate epithelial cells using laser capture microdissection from snap-frozen prostate biopsy specimens provided by 31 patients. The researchers then synthesized cDNA from amplified total RNA and hybridized it to custom-made microarrays composed of 6,200 clones derived from the Prostate Expression Database. They then verified expression differences for selected genes using quantitative reverse transcription-PCR.
The study found 954 transcript alterations associated with cancer (q < 0.01%), including 149 differentially expressed genes with no known functional roles. The gene expression changes associated with ischemia and surgical removal of the prostate gland were absent. The study also found that genes up-regulated in prostate cancer were enriched in categories related to cellular metabolism, energy use, signal transduction, and molecular transport, while genes down-regulated in prostate cancers were enriched in categories related to immune response, cellular responses to pathogens, and apoptosis. In exploratory analyses, down-regulation of androgen receptor was associated with a lower probability of cancer relapse after neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by radical prostatectomy.
In conclusion, the study suggests that assessments of tumor phenotypes based on gene expression for treatment stratification and drug targeting of oncogenic alterations may best be ascertained using biopsy-based analyses where the effects of ischemia do not complicate interpretation.

title: Circulating trimethylamine N‐oxide and the risk of cardiovascular diseases: a systematic review and meta‐analysis of 11 prospective cohort studies
text: Circulating trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a metabolite produced by the gut microbiome, has been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases. However, the quantitative relationship between TMAO levels and cardiovascular event risk has yet to be comprehensively evaluated. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of all available cohort studies examining the association between baseline TMAO levels and subsequent cardiovascular events. We searched the Embase and PubMed databases for relevant cohort studies and extracted the overall hazard ratios (HRs) for the development of cardiovascular events (CVEs) and mortality from the included studies. We evaluated the heterogeneity among the studies using the Cochran's Q test and I2 statistics, and applied either a random-effect or fixed-effect model depending on the level of heterogeneity. Subgroup analysis and meta-regression were used to investigate potential sources of heterogeneity. Our analysis included eleven eligible studies, with three studies reporting both CVE and mortality outcomes, one study reporting only CVEs, and the remaining seven providing mortality data only. We found that higher levels of circulating TMAO were associated with a 23% increased risk of CVEs (HR = 1.23, 95% CI: 1.07-1.42, I2 = 31.4%) and a 55% increased risk of all-cause mortality (HR = 1.55, 95% CI: 1.19-2.02, I2 = 80.8%). We also observed that the latter association may be susceptible to potential publication bias, although sensitivity analysis did not significantly alter the results. Further subgroup analysis and meta-regression did not reveal any significant influences of study location, follow-up duration, publication year, population characteristics, or TMAO sample sources on the results. Collectively, our findings suggest that higher levels of circulating TMAO may independently predict the risk of subsequent cardiovascular events and mortality.

title: PDGF-BB secreted by preosteoclasts induces angiogenesis during coupling with osteogenesis
text: Osteogenesis during bone modeling and remodeling is intricately linked with angiogenesis, a recent study revealed. Specifically, a vessel subtype identified as CD31hiEmcnhi, which is positive for both CD31 and endomucin, plays a crucial role in coupling angiogenesis and osteogenesis. Our findings indicate that platelet-derived growth factor-BB (PDGF-BB) secreted by preosteoclasts triggers CD31hiEmcnhi vessel formation during bone modeling and remodeling. Mice with PDGF-BB deficiency in the tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase–positive cell lineage exhibit significantly reduced trabecular and cortical bone mass, decreased serum and bone marrow PDGF-BB levels, and fewer CD31hiEmcnhi vessels as compared to wild-type mice. In the ovariectomy (OVX)-induced osteoporotic mouse model, serum and bone marrow PDGF-BB levels and CD31hiEmcnhi vessel numbers are significantly lower than in sham-operated controls. Treatment with exogenous PDGF-BB or inhibition of cathepsin K, which increases the number of preosteoclasts and thus endogenous PDGF-BB levels, leads to an increase in CD31hiEmcnhi vessel number and promotes bone formation in OVX mice. Therefore, targeting pharmacotherapies that increase PDGF-BB secretion from preosteoclasts represents a promising new strategy for treating osteoporosis by stimulating angiogenesis and bone formation.

title: Discovery of endothelial to mesenchymal transition as a source for carcinoma-associated fibroblasts.
text:
Activated fibroblasts are present in various tumors and play a crucial role in cancer progression. Myofibroblasts, activated fibroblasts, and perivascular mesenchymal cells such as pericytes contribute to the growth and spread of cancer. The origin of these activated fibroblasts remains a topic of debate, but it is believed that de novo activation of quiescent fibroblasts into alpha-smooth muscle actin (alpha SMA)-positive myofibroblasts is a primary source. Additionally, epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) and bone marrow recruitment are being studied as potential mechanisms for the emergence of a diverse population of carcinoma-associated fibroblasts.
Our findings show that transforming growth factor-beta1 can induce proliferating endothelial cells to undergo a phenotypic conversion into fibroblast-like cells, a process known as endothelial to mesenchymal transition (EndMT). This transition is characterized by the expression of fibroblast-specific protein-1 (FSP1) and a decrease in the expression of CD31/PECAM. We have also observed EndMT in tumors using the B16F10 melanoma model and the Rip-Tag2 spontaneous pancreatic carcinoma model in Tie2-Cre mice crossed with R26Rosa-lox-Stop-lox-LacZ mice, which allows for irreversible labeling of endothelial cells. Our results demonstrate that EndMT is a unique mechanism for the accumulation of carcinoma-associated fibroblasts and suggest that anti-angiogenic treatment of tumors may directly impact these cells, potentially slowing or stopping cancer progression.

title: ERCC1 and MUS81–EME1 promote sister chromatid separation by processing late replication intermediates at common fragile sites during mitosis
text: Chromosomal instability (CIN) is a defining characteristic of cancer initiation and progression. Certain genomic regions, such as common fragile sites (CFSs), are particularly prone to instability under replication stress, contributing to tumor development. Recent research has shed light on the Fanconi anemia (FANC) pathway's role in preventing defective chromosome segregation and CIN in response to replication stress. Notably, FANCD2 is recruited to regions hosting CFSs on metaphase chromosomes. To investigate the mechanisms that protect these regions, we searched for proteins that co-localize with FANCD2 on mitotic chromosomes and identified XPF–ERCC1 and MUS81–EME1, two structure-specific endonucleases. Our findings demonstrate that depletion of either ERCC1 or MUS81–EME1 compromises the accurate processing of replication intermediates or under-replicated DNA that persist at CFSs until mitosis. Additionally, depletion of these endonucleases leads to an increase in the frequency of chromosome bridges during anaphase, which, in turn, enhances the accumulation of DNA damage in the following G1 phase.

title: Engineered RNA viral synthesis of microRNAs.
text:
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression by silencing target genes post-transcriptionally. While hundreds of conserved cellular miRNAs have been identified, miRNAs of viral origin have also been isolated and found to modulate both the viral life cycle and the host cell transcriptome. However, detection of viral-derived miRNAs has generally been limited to DNA viruses, suggesting that RNA viruses may have difficulty exploiting this aspect of transcriptional regulation. The replicative constraints that would result from RNase III processing of a genomic hairpin are thought to limit the generation of RNA virus-derived miRNAs.
To investigate whether RNA viruses can also produce functional miRNAs, we examined whether an influenza virus could be engineered to deliver functional miRNAs without affecting its replication. We designed a modified influenza A virus that expresses the cellular miRNA-124 (miR-124) by inserting its hairpin into an intron of the nuclear export protein transcript. Endogenous processing of the hairpin resulted in functional miR-124, and we found that the virus could produce a miRNA without having a negative impact on its replication. Our study demonstrates that RNA viruses can indeed produce functional miRNAs, suggesting that this level of transcriptional regulation may be more widespread than previously thought, extending beyond DNA viruses.

title: The developmental potential of iPSCs is greatly influenced by reprogramming factor selection.
text: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are frequently generated by introducing Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and Myc (OSKM) into cells. However, iPSCs often exhibit significant variations in quality, as evidenced by their ability to contribute to chimeric embryos and undergo tetraploid complementation in mice. High-quality iPSCs are crucial for future therapeutic applications. Our study reveals that the combination of reprogramming factors used is a key determinant of iPSC quality. Using tetraploid complementation, we found that ectopic expression of Sall4, Nanog, Esrrb, and Lin28 (SNEL) in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) resulted in the generation of high-quality iPSCs more efficiently than other combinations of factors, including OSKM. Although differentially methylated regions, transcript number of master regulators, establishment of specific superenhancers, and global aneuploidy were comparable between high- and low-quality lines, distinct features such as aberrant gene expression, trisomy of chromosome 8, and abnormal H2A.X deposition distinguished high-quality iPSCs from low-quality ones. These findings may also be applicable to human iPSCs.

title: GiardiaDB and TrichDB: integrated genomic resources for the eukaryotic protist pathogens Giardia lamblia and Trichomonas vaginalis
text: GiardiaDB (<http://GiardiaDB.org>) and TrichDB (<http://TrichDB.org>) serve as the genome databases for Giardia lamblia and Trichomonas vaginalis, respectively, and represent the most recent additions to the EuPathDB (<http://EuPathDB.org>) family of functional genomic databases. Both databases utilize the same framework as other EuPathDB sites (CryptoDB, PlasmoDB, and ToxoDB), providing fully integrated and searchable databases. Users can query genomic-scale data through BLAST searches, annotation keywords, gene ID searches, GO terms, sequence motifs, and other protein characteristics. Additionally, functional queries can be formulated based on transcript and protein expression data from various platforms. Phylogenetic relationships can also be investigated. The ability to combine the results from multiple queries and store queries and query results for future use allows for complex, genome-wide mining of functional genomic data.

title: A coding-independent function of gene and pseudogene mRNAs regulates tumour biology
text: The traditional role of messenger RNA (mRNA) is to transport protein-coding information from DNA to sites of protein synthesis. However, since microRNAs (miRNAs) can bind to RNAs, we questioned whether RNAs might have a regulatory function unrelated to their protein-coding ability. As a model for this non-protein-coding role, we investigated the relationship between the mRNAs produced by the tumor suppressor gene PTEN and its pseudogene PTENP1. We found that PTENP1 is biologically active, regulating cellular levels of PTEN and exerting a growth-suppressive effect. Surprisingly, we also discovered that the PTENP1 locus is selectively lost in human cancer. Building on these findings, we expanded our analysis to other cancer-related genes with pseudogenes, such as oncogenic KRAS. Additionally, we demonstrated that transcripts of protein-coding genes like PTEN are also biologically active. These discoveries introduce a novel non-coding function for mRNAs and uncover a regulatory role for expressed pseudogenes in gene expression.

title: Identification of a Multicomponent Complex Required for Outer Membrane Biogenesis in Escherichia coli
text: The outer membrane (OM) of gram-negative bacteria serves as a protective barrier against harmful substances such as antibiotics and detergents. This membrane is composed of a unique bilayer made up of phospholipids, glycolipids, and proteins, which is carefully organized through a mechanism that is poorly understood. To shed light on these processes, we have identified a multiprotein complex involved in the assembly of proteins in the OM of Escherichia coli. Our study also reveals genetic interactions between genes encoding components of this complex and imp, which encodes a protein involved in LPS assembly in the OM. These interactions suggest that YfgL, one of the lipoprotein components of the complex, plays a crucial role in a homeostatic control mechanism that coordinates the overall OM assembly process.

title: Transtheoretical model-based multiple behavior intervention for weight management: effectiveness on a population basis.
text:
BACKGROUND: The increasing prevalence of overweight and obesity emphasizes the need for evidence-based, easily accessible interventions for weight management that can be tailored to a population. The Transtheoretical Model (TTM) offers a promising framework for multiple behavior weight management interventions.
METHODS: We randomly assigned 1277 overweight or obese adults (BMI 25-39.9) to either a no-treatment control group or a home-based, stage-matched multiple behavior intervention for up to three behaviors related to weight management at 0, 3, 6, and 9 months. All participants were reassessed at 6, 12, and 24 months.
RESULTS: Significant treatment effects were observed for healthy eating (47.5% versus 34.3%), exercise (44.9% versus 38.1%), managing emotional distress (49.7% versus 30.3%), and untreated fruit and vegetable intake (48.5% versus 39.0%) progressing to Action/Maintenance at 24 months. The groups differed in weight lost at 24 months. There was a strong co-variation of behavior change, with individuals in the treatment group being 2.5-5 times more likely to make progress on another behavior if they were already progressing to Action/Maintenance on a single behavior. The multiple behavior intervention had a larger impact than single behavior interventions.
CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the potential of TTM-based tailored feedback for improving healthy eating, exercise, managing emotional distress, and weight on a population basis. The treatment produced a high level of population impact that future multiple behavior interventions can aim to surpass.

title: Autoinduction and signal transduction in the regulation of staphylococcal virulence.
text:
Below is a rewritten version of the given text with improved readability and clarity:
The regulatory network of Staphylococcus aureus, involving accessory genes crucial for pathogenesis, is intricate and includes at least four two-component systems, one of which is a quorum sensor (agr), an alternative sigma factor, and a large collection of transcription factors, such as tst and seb. These regulatory genes are believed to function in a time- and population density-dependent manner, integrating external environmental signals with the internal metabolic machinery of the cell to produce specific subsets of accessory/virulence factors at the appropriate time and quantities for the organism's survival. From a pathogenesis perspective, the regulatory agenda is hypothesized to be tuned to specific locations within the host organism. To test this hypothesis, a comprehensive understanding of the regulatory interactions among the organism's multiple controlling systems is necessary. This review aims to integrate a vast body of data towards developing a preliminary model that can guide research towards a full-scale test.

title: Macrophages in the Pathogenesis of Atherosclerosis
text: In atherosclerosis, the buildup of apolipoprotein B-lipoproteins beneath the endothelial cell layer of blood vessels leads to the recruitment of monocytes, immune cells that give rise to macrophages and dendritic cells. Macrophages derived from these recruited monocytes participate in an unresolving, maladaptive inflammatory response that thickens the subendothelial layer due to cell, lipid, and matrix accumulation. Some lesions subsequently develop a necrotic core, triggered by vascular disease, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and sudden cardiac death. This Review highlights the key roles played by macrophages in each stage of disease progression.

title: Three-dimensional superresolution colocalization of intracellular protein superstructures and the cell surface in live Caulobacter crescentus.
text: Recently, advances in single-molecule imaging and photocontrol have enabled sharp optical microscopy of cellular structures beyond the diffraction limit, allowing for non-invasive imaging of structures within living cells. However, live-cell superresolution imaging poses a challenge when it comes to visualizing three-dimensional (3D) structures in their biological context, such as the cell membrane. To address this challenge, we have developed a technique called superresolution by power-dependent active intermittency and points accumulation for imaging in nanoscale topography (SPRAIPAINT). This technique combines the imaging of intracellular enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (eYFP) fusions (SPRAI) with stochastic localization of the cell surface (PAINT) using a single laser. By utilizing simple light-induced blinking of eYFP and collisional flux onto the cell surface by Nile red, we are able to achieve single-molecule localizations without the need for antibody labeling, cell membrane permeabilization, or thiol-oxygen scavenger systems. As a demonstration of this technique, we have successfully imaged the 3D structure of Crescentin-eYFP, a cytoskeletal fluorescent protein fusion, colocalized with the surface of the bacterium Caulobacter crescentus using a double-helix point spread function microscope. The resulting images show excellent 3D colocalization of intracellular protein structures and the cell surface with superresolution optical microscopy, opening up new possibilities for analyzing protein interactions in living cells with unparalleled precision (20-40 nm in 3D) over a large field of view (12 12 μm).

title: Overweight prevalence among youth in the United States: Why so many different numbers?
text: Recent studies have presented various estimates for the prevalence of overweight among youth in the United States, ranging from 11% to 24%. Despite utilizing the same data from the third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III), these studies have produced different estimates. This paper examines the reasons for these discrepancies, including differences in definition, measurement, criteria selection, and comparison groups. Additionally, the paper compares reference percentiles for body mass index (BMI) from several publications and explores the implications of these variations in prevalence estimates. Notably, the differences in published estimates from NHANES III are discussed and explained.

title: Senescence and aging: the critical roles of p53
text: p53 serves as a transcription factor involved in regulating cellular processes, including cell cycle control, DNA repair, apoptosis, and cellular stress responses. Besides inducing cell growth arrest and apoptosis, p53 activation also plays a role in modulating cellular senescence and organismal aging. Senescence is a permanent cell cycle arrest that plays a crucial role in both aging and as a protective response against cancer. Therefore, p53's regulation of senescence contributes to tumor growth suppression, which is dependent on its expression and cellular context. In this review, we will explore the recent advances in understanding the role of p53 in cellular senescence and its implications for cancer therapy. We will also discuss the impact of p53 on animal lifespan and its regulation of multiple physiological pathways, which may contribute to both senescence and aging.

title: Asymmetric cryo-EM reconstruction of phage MS2 reveals genome structure in situ
text: In single-stranded ribonucleic acid (RNA) viruses, the processes of virion assembly and genome packaging are intricately linked. By utilizing cryo-electron microscopy and single particle analysis, we have investigated the asymmetrical structure of bacteriophage MS2, which consists of 178 copies of the coat protein, a single copy of the A-protein, and the RNA genome. This study reveals that within the virion, the viral RNA genome can adopt a specific conformation in situ. The RNA forms a complex network of stem-loops that predominantly bind to coat protein dimers located on one half of the capsid, indicating that the genomic RNA plays a crucial role in both virion assembly and genome packaging.

title: Harnessing transposons for cancer gene discovery
text: Recently, researchers have made progress in harnessing the Tc1/mariner transposon, Sleeping Beauty (SB), to induce cancer in mouse somatic cells with sufficient frequency. Cancer cells resulting from SB insertional mutagenesis can be used to identify the genes and signaling pathways that drive tumor formation. A conditional SB transposition system has also been developed, allowing scientists to selectively model various types of human cancer by limiting the occurrence of SB mutagenesis. Through SB mutagenesis, a comprehensive collection of well-known cancer genes and a multitude of new potential cancer genes and drug targets have been identified.

title: MicroRNA-Containing T-Regulatory-Cell-Derived Exosomes Suppress Pathogenic T Helper 1 Cells
text: Foxp3(+) T regulatory (Treg) cells prevent inflammatory disease, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. RNA interference through gene silencing can occur in a cell-autonomous or non-cell-autonomous manner, providing a means of intercellular regulation. Here, we demonstrate that non-cell-autonomous gene silencing, mediated by miRNA-containing exosomes, is a mechanism employed by Treg cells to suppress T-cell-mediated disease. Treg cells transfer miRNAs to various immune cells, including T helper 1 (Th1) cells, suppressing Th1 cell proliferation and cytokine secretion. Using Dicer-deficient or Rab27a and Rab27b double-deficient Treg cells to disrupt miRNA biogenesis or the exosomal pathway, respectively, we found that miRNAs and exosomes are essential for Treg-cell-mediated suppression. Transcriptional analysis and miRNA inhibitor studies revealed that exosome-mediated transfer of Let-7d from Treg cells to Th1 cells contributes to suppression and prevention of systemic disease. These findings uncover a mechanism of Treg-cell-mediated suppression mediated by miRNA-containing exosomes.

title: Estimating risk curves for first-degree relatives of patients with Alzheimer’s disease: The REVEAL study
text:
Objective: The REVEAL study is a randomized, controlled investigation into the psychological and behavioral implications of disclosing genetic information related to the APOE gene in a risk assessment protocol for first-degree relatives of Alzheimer's disease patients. This article explains the methodology used to estimate the posterior survival curves, which represent the estimated risk of developing Alzheimer's disease based on gender, age, and genotype.
Methods: We used Bayes' rule to calculate the posterior survival curves, incorporating APOE information and data from the MIRAGE study. The study combined survival data from the MIRAGE study and gender- and age-specific APOE odds ratios to create risk curves for males and females within each of the 6 APOE genotypes.
Results: Our analysis resulted in estimates of gender-, age-, and genotype-specific risk that can be used in a risk assessment research study that includes genotype disclosure. By combining comparative genotype relative risk information and survival data from family studies, we were able to generate risk curves tailored to each individual's genetic profile.
Conclusion: The REVEAL study demonstrates the potential of incorporating genotype disclosure into a risk assessment protocol for first-degree relatives of Alzheimer's disease patients. By using a Bayesian approach and combining survival data and APOE odds ratios, we were able to generate gender-, age-, and genotype-specific risk estimates that can be used to inform decision-making in a research setting.

title: Up-regulation of endothelial nitric-oxide synthase by endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor involves mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase C signaling pathways.
text:
Cytochrome P450 (P450)-dependent metabolites of arachidonic acid, known as the epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), have been proposed to be endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factors (EDHF) that affect vascular tone. However, the impact of EDHF on endothelial-derived nitric oxide biosynthesis remains unclear. To investigate this, we examined the regulation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) by EDHF and identified the relevant signaling pathways involved.
We used cultured bovine aortic endothelial cells to transfect the P450 epoxygenases CYP102 F87V mutant, CYP2C11-CYPOR, and CYP2J2, and assessed the effects of endogenously formed or exogenously applied EETs on eNOS expression and activity. Our results showed that transfection with the P450 epoxygenases led to increased eNOS protein expression, which was attenuated by cotreatment with the P450 inhibitor 17-ODYA. Additionally, Northern analysis revealed that P450 transfection led to increased eNOS mRNA levels, suggesting an effect at the pretranslational level. Furthermore, P450 epoxygenase transfection resulted in increased eNOS activity as measured by the conversion of L-arginine to L-citrulline. Interestingly, the addition of synthetic EETs (50-200 nM) to the culture media also increased eNOS expression and activity.
We then investigated the signaling pathways involved in the regulation of eNOS expression by EDHF. Treatment with mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), MAPK kinase, and protein kinase C inhibitors (apigenin, 2'-amino-3'-methoxyflavone (PD98059), and 1-(5-isoquinolinesulfonyl)-2-methylpiperazine (H-7), respectively) significantly inhibited the effects of P450 transfection on eNOS expression. Additionally, overexpression of P450 epoxygenases or addition of synthetic EETs increased Thr495 phosphorylation of eNOS, an effect that was inhibited by both apigenin and PD98059.
To further investigate the in vivo effects of EDHF on eNOS expression, we overexpressed P450 epoxygenases in rats and measured aortic eNOS expression. Our results showed that overexpression of P450 epoxygenases in rats led to increased aortic eNOS expression, providing direct evidence that EDHF can influence vascular eNOS levels in vivo.
Based on our findings, we conclude that EDHF up-regulates eNOS via activation of MAPK and protein kinase C signaling pathways. These results provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying the regulation of endothelial nitric oxide synthesis and have important implications for our understanding of the physiological roles of EDHF in the regulation of vascular tone.

title: Prostaglandin E2 promotes intestinal tumor growth via DNA methylation
text: Despite DNA methylation being acknowledged as a crucial mechanism for silencing tumor-suppressor and DNA-repair genes during tumor initiation and progression, the underlying mechanisms of DNA methylation alterations in cancer remain elusive. Our findings, however, shed light on a previously unknown function of prostaglandin E(2) (PGE(2)) in promoting tumor growth by DNA methylating certain tumor-suppressor and DNA-repair genes. These discoveries expand our understanding of the complex interplay between PGE(2) and cancer.

title: Nef is physically recruited into the immunological synapse and potentiates T cell activation early after TCR engagement.
text: The HIV-1 protein Nef enhances viral pathogenicity and accelerates disease progression in vivo by inducing T cell activation, likely through an unknown mechanism that involves optimizing the intracellular environment for viral replication. Using a novel T cell reporter system, we found that Nef more than doubles the number of cells expressing the transcription factors NF-κB and NFAT after TCR stimulation, indicating a Nef-induced priming of TCR signaling pathways. This effect occurs independently of calcium signaling and involves a proximal step prior to protein kinase C activation. Upon engagement of the TCR by MHC-bound antigen, the formation of the immunological synapse is triggered, recruiting detergent-resistant membrane microdomains, called lipid rafts. Approximately 5-10% of total Nef is localized within these lipid rafts. Using confocal and real-time microscopy, we found that Nef within lipid rafts is rapidly recruited into the immunological synapse within minutes of Ab engagement of the TCR/CD3 and CD28 receptors, a process dependent on the N-terminal domain of Nef encompassing its myristoylation. Nef does not increase the number of cell surface lipid rafts or immunological synapses. Recent studies have shown a specific interaction between Nef and an active subpopulation of p21-activated kinase-2 found only in lipid rafts, suggesting that the co-recruitment of Nef and key cellular partners (e.g., activated p21-activated kinase-2) into the immunological synapse may underlie the increased frequency of cells expressing transcriptionally active forms of NF-κB and NFAT, leading to altered T cell activation.

title: Microenvironmental regulation of tumor progression and metastasis
text: Cancer cells grow and proliferate within a complex microenvironment, which they rely on for continued growth, invasion, and metastasis. Unlike tumor cells, stromal cell types within the tumor microenvironment (TME) are genetically stable and represent a relatively safe therapeutic target, as they are less likely to develop resistance or recur. However, disrupting the pro-tumorigenic TME is a challenging task, as it has various capacities to promote both beneficial and adverse effects during different stages of cancer progression and metastasis. Many studies have also shown that the microenvironment can normalize tumor cells, suggesting that re-educating stromal cells within the TME to have anti-tumorigenic effects may be a more effective cancer treatment strategy. Here, we discuss the paradoxical roles of the TME during specific stages of cancer progression and metastasis, as well as recent attempts to re-educate stromal cells within the TME to combat cancer.

title: Bezafibrate in men with lower extremity arterial disease: randomised controlled trial.
text:
The objective of this study was to assess the effect of bezafibrate on the risk of coronary heart disease and stroke in men with lower extremity arterial disease. The study was conducted as a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial in 85 general practices and nine hospital vascular clinics. A total of 1568 men aged 35-92 years at the time of recruitment were included in the study, with 783 participants receiving bezafibrate and 785 receiving a placebo. The primary outcome measures were the combination of coronary heart disease and stroke, as well as all coronary events, fatal and non-fatal coronary events separately, and strokes alone (secondary end points).
The results showed that bezafibrate did not reduce the incidence of coronary heart disease and stroke. There were 150 and 160 events in the active and placebo groups, respectively (relative risk 0.96, 95% confidence interval 0.76-1.21). There were 90 and 111 major coronary events in the active and placebo groups, respectively (0.81, 0.60-1.08), of which 64 and 65 were fatal (0.95, 0.66-1.37) and 26 and 46 non-fatal (0.60, 0.36-0.99). The study found that bezafibrate may reduce the incidence of non-fatal coronary events, particularly in men aged <65 years at entry, in whom all coronary events may also be reduced. Additionally, bezafibrate reduced the severity of intermittent claudication for up to three years.
In conclusion, bezafibrate has no effect on the incidence of coronary heart disease and stroke combined, but may reduce the incidence of non-fatal coronary events, particularly among younger men.

title: The modulation of human natural killer cell activity by prostaglandins.
text: Studies have suggested that prostaglandins (PGs) play a role in regulating tumor growth in both mice and humans. Given the potential importance of natural killer (NK) cell cytotoxicity in immune surveillance against cancer, it is of interest to investigate whether the PGs produced by tumors may suppress NK activity. To address this question, the effect of various PGs on NK activity was examined using human peripheral mononuclear cells. At high concentrations (10^-6 M), PGE2, PGD2, PGA2, and PGF2 alpha all caused suppression of NK activity, while only PGE2 and PGD2 displayed significant suppression at lower concentrations (10^-8 M). The range of concentrations tested (10^-5 to 10^-9 M) showed that 45% suppression occurred at 10^-8 M PGE2. Pointing to a particular mechanism for this suppression, pretreatment of K562 cells with PGE2 resulted in suppression, while pretreatment of target cells did not. Lastly, the suppressive effects of supernatants obtained from tumor cell lines (polyoma virus-transformed murine fibroblast cell line, PY3T3) on NK activity were also investigated, and it was found that the supernatants' content of PGE accounted for their marked suppressive effect. Altogether, these findings suggest that the production of PGE by tumor cells may play an important role in modulating human NK activity.

title: Association analysis between anterior-pharynx defective-1 genes polymorphisms and Alzheimer's disease.
text: According to recent biological studies, the protein anterior-pharynx defective-1 (APH-1) plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). To investigate the potential association between APH-1 genetic variations and AD, we analyzed the APH-1 genes for sequence variations in a sample of 113 AD patients and 132 controls from Italy. Our study found six different polymorphisms, including three that predict an amino acid substitution (T27I, V199L, and F217L). However, none of these polymorphisms were significantly associated with the disease. Interestingly, we observed a trend for coexistence of the transversion c+651T>G (F217L) with the apolipoprotein E (APOE) epsilon4 allele. Our findings suggest that genetic variations in the coding regions of APH-1a/b are not linked to an increased risk of sporadic AD in our Italian population sample.

title: Dynamic epigenetic regulation of glioblastoma tumorigenicity through LSD1 modulation of MYC expression.
text: According to the available evidence, the aggressiveness of glioblastoma is linked to small subpopulations of cells that have the ability to self-renew and exhibit tumorigenicity. It is still unclear whether tumorigenicity is an inherent property of a select few cells or something that can be acquired spontaneously. To investigate this, we utilized tumor-sphere and xenograft formation assays to evaluate the tumorigenicity of subclones derived from established and primary glioblastoma lines. Our findings suggest that glioblastoma tumorigenicity is primarily determined, yet it can also be acquired at low frequencies spontaneously. Moreover, these dynamic transitions are regulated by epigenetic reprogramming mediated by the lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1). LSD depletion leads to increased trimethylation of histone 3 lysine 4 at the avian myelocytomatosis viral oncogene homolog (MYC) locus, resulting in elevated MYC expression. MYC, in turn, regulates oligodendrocyte lineage transcription factor 2 (OLIG2), SRY (sex determining region Y)-box 2 (SOX2), and POU class 3 homeobox 2 (POU3F2), a core set of transcription factors required for reprogramming glioblastoma cells into stem-like states. Our findings provide a framework for developing glioblastoma therapeutic strategies focused on epigenetic regulation of these key transcription factors.

title: Auditory Cortex Tracks Both Auditory and Visual Stimulus Dynamics Using Low-Frequency Neuronal Phase Modulation
text: Integrating information across multiple sensory domains to form a unified representation of complex sensory inputs is a primary aspect of perception in real-world situations. A fascinating hypothesis emerging from neurophysiology suggests that there is direct and early cross-modal phase modulation, which we investigate and provide evidence for using magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings of participants viewing audiovisual movies. Our findings reveal that low-frequency neural activity in the 2-7 Hz delta and theta bands carries robust and usable information about the temporal structure of stimuli in both sensory modalities, allowing for the continuous tracking of naturalistic audio-visual streams and reflecting cross-sensory interaction in real time. These experiments are the first to show that a specific cortical mechanism, delta-theta phase modulation across early sensory areas, plays a key "active" role in processing and interpreting multi-sensory information in real time.

title: The diagnosis and management of gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants.
text: Gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR) and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) are common in infants during the early months of life. GOR may be a primary gastrointestinal motility disorder or secondary to conditions such as cow's milk protein allergy. Diagnosis can be challenging due to a lack of correlation between symptoms, pH monitoring results, and histology findings. Severe GORD can cause mild symptoms, while minor GOR can lead to severe symptoms. Treatment options include using thickened formula to reduce regurgitation and alginates or proton pump inhibitors to decrease acid reflux. Despite the availability of these therapeutic interventions, the efficacy of prokinetic drugs is not well established, and their long-term side effects have been insufficiently studied, particularly for acid-reducing molecules. Some research has focused on the potential side effects of cisapride, although other molecules have similar effects. Little is known about the nutritional consequences of long-term therapeutic management using these drugs.

title: Increased sensitivity of antigen-experienced T cells through the enrichment of oligomeric T cell receptor complexes.
text: Although memory T cells exhibit a more robust response to antigen stimulation and are more sensitive to low doses of antigen compared to naive T cells, the molecular basis for this increased sensitivity remains unclear. We have previously shown that the T cell receptor (TCR) exists as differently sized oligomers on the surface of resting T cells, with large oligomers being preferentially activated in response to low antigen doses.
