Tumor cells that originate from normal tissue sometimes acquire mutations that can be targeted by lymphocytes. However, cancer cells have evolved to evade the host immune system by producing physiological PD-1 ligands and stimulating PD-1 on lymphocytes. Recent studies have shown that administering monoclonal antibodies that block the binding of PD-1 to its ligands can reactivate T cells and enhance the anti-tumor immune response. In this review, I will provide an overview of T-cell biology and the mechanisms of PD-1 regulation, as well as the current understanding and unanswered questions surrounding this complex molecule.

title: Dissociation of β1- and β2-adrenergic receptor subtypes in the retrieval of cocaine-associated memory.
text: Retrieval of cocaine-associated memories is dependent on the activation of β-adrenergic receptors (β-ARs), specifically the β1-AR subtype. However, the role of β2-ARs in maintaining drug-seeking behavior is unclear. To investigate, we used a cocaine conditioned place preference (CPP) procedure and examined if retrieval of a cocaine CPP memory is mediated by a specific β-AR subtype or collectively by both β1- and β2-ARs. Our findings show that co-blockade of β1- and β2-ARs resulted in a long-lasting retrieval deficit and prevented subsequent cocaine-induced reinstatement. In contrast, administration of a β1-AR antagonist prior to an initial CPP trial dose-dependently reduced expression of a CPP on subsequent drug-free trials, while administration of a β2-AR antagonist had no effect on initial CPP expression but reduced subsequent CPP expression at the highest dose. These results indicate that the β1-AR subtype mediates retrieval of a cocaine CPP and that acutely blocking either β1- or β2-ARs can prevent subsequent cocaine-induced reinstatement. These findings suggest that β-AR antagonists, particularly β1-AR antagonists, could serve as adjuncts for addiction therapies to prevent retrieval of drug-associated memories and provide protection against relapse.

title: Podoplanin-Rich Stromal Networks Induce Dendritic Cell Motility via Activation of the C-type Lectin Receptor CLEC-2
text: To initiate adaptive immunity, dendritic cells (DCs) migrate from parenchymal tissues to lymphoid organs by traversing stromal scaffolds that display the glycoprotein podoplanin (PDPN). PDPN is expressed by lymphatic endothelial and fibroblastic reticular cells and plays a crucial role in separating blood and lymph during development by activating the C-type lectin receptor, CLEC-2, on platelets. Our findings demonstrate a significant role for CLEC-2 in the morphodynamic behavior and motility of DCs. DCs require CLEC-2 to enter lymphatics and navigate through lymph nodes, thereby impairing T cell priming in CLEC-2-deficient DCs. We discovered that CLEC-2 activation by PDPN triggers cell spreading through downregulation of RhoA activity and myosin light-chain phosphorylation, leading to the formation of F-actin-rich protrusions. These protrusions are crucial for efficient motility along stromal surfaces, highlighting the importance of CLEC-2-PDPN interaction in directing DC migration.

title: The Public Health Responsibility Deal: brokering a deal for public health, but on whose terms?
text:
Coalitions of multinational food and drink companies have pledged to reformulate their products and market them responsibly, largely through self-regulated initiatives. However, the integrity of these voluntary efforts has been questioned. An example of a government-led initiative is the Public Health Responsibility Deal in England, which aims to promote public health. This raises the question of whether public leadership can effectively drive voluntary actions towards meaningful public health outcomes.
To investigate, the study focuses on the calorie reduction initiative of the Responsibility Deal. The research methods involved obtaining source material through Freedom of Information requests and analyzing previously unpublished government documentation from 2011 and 2012.
The study finds that the Responsibility Deal approach to calorie reduction involves the food industry in the development of measures, including reformulation and portion control. However, the public health objectives are compromised by the involvement of private interests, resulting in inadequate monitoring and evaluation.
The findings suggest that relying solely on voluntary actions from the food industry is flawed, as it does not prioritize public health interests. Without effective sanctions, the Responsibility Deal approach allows private companies to influence public health policies and strategies to their advantage. In conclusion, government leadership alone is insufficient to drive meaningful public health outcomes through voluntary initiatives.

title: Role of endothelial shear stress in the natural history of coronary atherosclerosis and vascular remodeling: molecular, cellular, and vascular behavior.
text: Although the entire coronary tree is exposed to the atherogenic effects of systemic risk factors, atherosclerotic lesions form specifically at certain arterial regions where low and oscillatory endothelial shear stress (ESS) occur. Low ESS regulates endothelial gene expression through complex mechanoreception and mechanotransduction processes, leading to an atherogenic endothelial phenotype and the formation of early atherosclerotic plaques. Each early plaque has its unique natural history, which depends not only on forming and progressing atherosclerosis but also on the vascular remodeling response. Although the underlying mechanisms of the remodeling of the atherosclerotic wall are not fully understood, the dynamic interplay between the local hemodynamic environment, low ESS in particular, and the biology of the wall is likely to be crucial. In this review, we explore the molecular, cellular, and vascular processes that support the role of low ESS in the natural history of coronary atherosclerosis and vascular remodeling, and we identify possible mechanisms that underlie the different natural history trajectories of individual coronary lesions. Atherosclerotic plaques that are associated with excessive expansive remodeling evolve into high-risk plaques because low ESS persists, thereby promoting continued lipid accumulation, inflammation, oxidative stress, matrix breakdown, and further plaque progression and excessive expansive remodeling. An enhanced understanding of the pathobiological processes responsible for atherosclerosis and vascular remodeling may help identify a high-risk coronary plaque early on and provide a basis for innovative diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for managing coronary patients and preventing acute coronary syndromes.

title: Schistosoma mansoni worms induce anergy of T cells via selective up-regulation of programmed death ligand 1 on macrophages.
text: The parasitic disease Schistosoma mansoni has evolved two distinct strategies to suppress T cell activation in humans. In the early stages of infection (4-12 weeks), both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells are anergized. However, this is replaced by a different mechanism in the chronic stages of infection, where T cell suppression occurs via a NO-dependent mechanism. This suppression is mediated by splenic F4/80+ macrophages (Mphi), which induce anergy of naive T cells through an IL-4-, IL-13-, IL-10-, TGF-beta-, and NO-independent, but cell contact-dependent, mechanism. In vitro studies using isolated F4/80+ Mphi and naive T cells showed that the up-regulation of programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) on Mphi is responsible for anergy induction. The addition of an inhibitory antibody against PD-L1 completely blocked the ability of Mphi to anergize T cells, highlighting a novel mechanism by which S. mansoni has usurped the natural function of PD-L1 to reduce T cell activation during early acute stages of infection before the subsequent emergence of egg-induced T cell suppression in the chronic stages of infection.

title: Thawing Frozen Robust Multi-array Analysis (fRMA)
text:
A novel microarray preprocessing approach called Frozen Robust Multi-array Analysis (fRMA) was recently developed. This method enables individual array preprocessing while retaining the benefits of multi-array preprocessing techniques. The algorithm requires the generation of frozen parameter estimates using a large database of publicly available arrays. However, curating such a database and creating the frozen parameter estimates is time-consuming, limiting the implementation of fRMA to the most commonly used Affymetrix platforms.
To address this limitation, we have developed an R package called frmaTools, which enables users to quickly create their own frozen parameter vectors. The package fits into a preprocessing workflow and discusses the size of the training dataset required to generate reliable frozen parameter estimates. Moreover, we explore specific scenarios where creating an fRMA implementation is essential, and demonstrate that fRMA performs well even when a large database of arrays is unavailable.
In summary, the frmaTools package greatly expands the applicability of the fRMA algorithm by enabling users to easily create their own fRMA implementation. The package is freely available as part of the Bioconductor project.

title: Transcriptional repressor Blimp-1 is essential for T cell homeostasis and self-tolerance
text: Maintaining T cell homeostasis is essential for a healthy immune system, as irregularities in this process can lead to chronic inflammation and the development of autoimmune diseases. Our research reveals that Blimp-1, a transcriptional repressor that plays a critical role in the differentiation of terminal B cells, is also expressed in a subset of antigen-experienced CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Interestingly, mice that were reconstituted with fetal liver stem cells expressing a mutant Blimp-1 lacking the DNA-binding domain developed a severe multiorgan inflammatory disease due to an excessive accumulation of effector and memory T cells. These findings confirm Blimp-1 as a crucial regulator of T cell homeostasis and suggest that it also regulates the differentiation of both B cells and T cells.

title: Nuclear repositioning of the VSG promoter during developmental silencing in Trypanosoma brucei
text: Interphase nuclear repositioning of chromosomes has been linked to epigenetic regulation of RNA polymerase (pol) II transcription. However, the nuclear position-dependent regulation of RNA pol I–transcribed loci remains poorly understood. As a model system, Trypanosoma brucei is valuable for investigating this question due to its two main surface protein genes (procyclin and variant surface glycoprotein (VSG)) transcribed by pol I, which undergo distinct transcriptional activation or downregulation events during developmental differentiation. Although the monoallelically expressed VSG locus is solely located in an extranucleolar body in the bloodstream form, we find that nonmutually exclusive procyclin genes are positioned at the nucleolar periphery. Interestingly, ribosomal DNA loci and pol I transcription activity are also restricted to similar perinucleolar positions. Upon developmental transcriptional downregulation, the VSG promoter rapidly and dramatically moves to the nuclear envelope, followed by chromatin condensation. We propose a model whereby the VSG expression site pol I promoter is selectively targeted by temporal nuclear repositioning during developmental silencing.

title: An administrative claims measure suitable for profiling hospital performance on the basis of 30-day all-cause readmission rates among patients with heart failure.
text:
Introduction:
Hospital readmission within 30 days of discharge is a costly and often preventable event for heart failure patients. To address this issue, we have developed a model approved by the National Quality Forum for public reporting of hospital-level readmission rates by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. In this study, we used a hierarchical logistic regression model to calculate hospital-level risk-standardized 30-day all-cause readmission rates for patients hospitalized with heart failure.
Methods:
We derived our model using Medicare claims data from a 2004 cohort and validated it using claims and medical record data. Our unadjusted readmission rate was 23.6%. The final model included 37 variables and had a discriminatory power ranging from 15% to 37%. The model's c statistic was 0.60, indicating good predictive accuracy. We calculated the 25th and 75th percentiles of the risk-standardized readmission rates across 4669 hospitals, with the 5th and 95th percentiles ranging from 22.2% to 25.1%. We also observed that hospitals with higher readmission rates had higher odds of all-cause readmission.
Results:
Our claims-based model produced estimates that were similar to those derived from a medical record model, with a correlation of 0.97 and a median difference of 0.06 percentage points. These findings suggest that our model may serve as a valid surrogate for medical record-based readmission rates.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our claims-based model of hospital-level risk-standardized readmission rates for heart failure patients may serve as a useful surrogate for those derived from a medical record model. This model has the advantage of being easily applicable and easily accessible, making it a valuable tool for public reporting and quality improvement initiatives.

title: Queueing up for enzymatic processing: correlated signaling through coupled degradation
text: Advances in high-throughput technologies have given rise to complex network diagrams that illustrate the intricate interactions between different cellular species. While these diagrams offer valuable insights into biological systems on a large scale, a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms that underlie these connections is crucial for the continued development of systems and synthetic biology. To shed light on these mechanisms, we employ queueing theory to investigate how "waiting lines" of protein "customers" can become correlated through enzymatic "servers" that are coupled in a downstream manner. Using the E. coli ClpXP degradation machine as a model system, we observe significant cross-talk between two seemingly unrelated networks that are indirectly connected through a common set of processors. Our findings have implications for synthetic biology applications, where the addition of common ClpXP machinery can lead to synchronized behavior between two independent synthetic networks. Our results demonstrate that post-translational processes can create dynamic connections within cellular networks, revealing a previously unexplained link in biological systems.

title: The histone demethylases Jhdm1a/1b enhance somatic cell reprogramming in a vitamin-C-dependent manner.
text: Reprogramming of somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) erases the epigenetic memory of the cell's past, restoring it to aprimitive-like state. Vitamin C amplifies this process, but the underlying mechanisms are still unknown. Our study shows that histone demethylases Jhdm1a/1b are key regulators of somatic cell reprogramming when treated with vitamin C. We discovered that vitamin C leads to demethylation of histone H3 at residue 36 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts in culture and during reprogramming. Among these demethylases, Jhdm1a/1b, which are dependent on vitamin C, were found to be potent regulators of reprogramming through both gain-of-function and loss-of-function approaches. Specifically, Jhdm1b accelerates cell cycle progression and inhibits cell senescence during reprogramming by suppressing the Ink4/Arf locus. Jhdm1b also collaborates with Oct4 to activate the microRNA cluster 302/367, a crucial component of the pluripotency network. Our findings establish a link between histone demethylases and vitamin-C-induced reprogramming, revealing a role for H3K36me2/3 in determining cell fate.

title: Preexisting helminth infection induces inhibition of innate pulmonary anti-tuberculosis defense by engaging the IL-4 receptor pathway
text: Co-infection with helminths and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is common globally, yet the interplay between helminth-induced Th2 responses and the host's ability to control Mtb infection has not been fully explored. Using mice infected with the intestinal helminth Nippostrongylus brasiliensis (Nb), we discovered that transient impairment of resistance to aerosolized Mtb infection occurs in co-infected mice. Furthermore, a second dose of Nb infection significantly increased Mtb bacterial burden in the lungs of co-infected mice. Interestingly, the Th2 response in co-infected animals did not hinder the onset and development of protective Mtb-specific Th1 cellular immune responses. However, the helminth-induced Th2 environment resulted in the accumulation of alternatively activated macrophages (AAMs) in the lungs. In contrast, mice lacking interleukin (IL) 4Rα exhibited improved ability to control Mtb infection, accompanied by significantly reduced AAM accumulation. Moreover, adoptive transfer of IL-4Rα(-/-) macrophines into IL-4Rα(-/-) mice led to a higher Mtb load in the lungs compared to transfer of wild-type macrophages, suggesting a direct contribution of the IL-4R pathway to the heightened susceptibility of co-infected animals. Our findings indicate that the Th2 response can enhance the intracellular persistence of Mtb, in part by mediating the alternative activation of macrophages via the IL-4Rα signaling pathway.

title: Archaea in biogeochemical cycles.
text: Archaea make up a considerable proportion of the microbial population on Earth. Like bacteria, they have developed diverse energy sources and metabolisms, such as using organic or inorganic electron donors and acceptors. Many archaea are capable of carbon fixation from inorganic sources, playing vital roles in Earth's global geochemical cycles and influencing greenhouse gas emissions. Methanogenesis and anaerobic methane oxidation are crucial steps in the carbon cycle, exclusively performed by anaerobic archaea. Thaumarchaeota are responsible for the oxidation of ammonia to nitrite, the only archaeal group that thrives in large numbers in both terrestrial and marine environments around the world. However, sulfur-dependent archaea are primarily found in hot environments, and their activities have the potential to impact the environment through metal leaching and sulfate reduction by anaerobic, nonthermophilic methane oxidizers. While the metabolisms of many archaea, particularly those in the subsurface, remain unexplored, their diverse range of energy sources and metabolic processes are of great interest to scientists.

title: Novel proteinaceous infectious particles cause scrapie.
text: The scrapie agent, upon infection and a prolonged incubation period, causes a degenerative disease of the central nervous system in sheep and goats. Six lines of evidence, including sensitivity to proteases, reveal that this agent contains a protein that is essential for its infectivity. Although the scrapie agent is irreversibly inactivated by alkali, multiple procedures specifically designed to modify nucleic acids fail to cause inactivation. The agent exhibits heterogeneity in terms of size, likely due to its hydrophobicity, with the smallest form possibly having a molecular weight of 50,000 or less. Due to its unique properties, which distinguish it from viruses, plasmids, and viroids, a new term, "prion," is proposed to describe a small proteinaceous infectious particle that is resistant to inactivation by most nucleic acid modification procedures. Understanding the structure of the scrapie agent may have important implications for the understanding of various degenerative diseases.

title: Viral Carcinogenesis.
text:
Cancer has been recognized for thousands of years, with ancient civilizations such as the Egyptians believed that it was caused by the will of the gods. However, this belief was soon challenged by the Greek physician Hippocrates, who proposed that human diseases, including cancer, resulted from an imbalance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. This theory was later replaced by the lymph theory and the blastema theory.
In the late 19th century, the birth of virology occurred when Dimitri Ivanofsky demonstrated that diseased tobacco plants remained infective after filtering their sap through a filter that trapped bacteria. Martinus Beijerinck would call the tiny infective agent a virus and both Dimitri Ivanofsky and Marinus Beijerinck would become the fathers of virology. Not long after, Payton Rous founded the field of tumor virology in 1911 with his discovery of a transmittable sarcoma of chickens by what would come to be called Rous sarcoma virus or RSV for short.
In the subsequent decades, many viruses have been identified as potential causes of cancer, including the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), which was first visualized in Burkitt's lymphoma cells by electron microscopy in 1965. According to the World Health Organization, approximately 22% of worldwide cancers are attributable to infectious etiologies, with viral etiologies estimated at 15-20%.
Throughout the history of tumor virology, research has not only identified viruses as etiologic agents of human cancers but has also provided valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms of all human cancers, including oncogene activation and tumor suppressor gene inactivation.

title: Monitoring spatiotemporal biogenesis of macromolecular assemblies by pulse-chase epitope labeling.
text: Many cellular proteins perform their functions within larger macromolecular structures known as multiprotein complexes. To better understand the formation of these complexes, researchers seek to study the molecular mechanisms involved. We have developed a cutting-edge pulse-chase system that allows for the isolation of newly forming multiprotein complexes in a controlled and timed manner. This system consists of an unnatural amino acid that induces immediate translation of a specific mRNA encoding the protein of interest, followed by a riboswitch that stops translation of the bait mRNA. By carefully controlling the timing of the pulse and chase, we are able to observe the stepwise assembly of multiprotein complexes over time, enabling us to study their spatiotemporal maturation in a way that was previously un possible. Through our validation of this method, we discovered a distinct assembly step during the biogenesis of nucleoporin complexes (NPCs) and were able to directly monitor the maturation of these complexes using immunofluorescence detection and purification of a pulse-labeled ribosomal protein. Our innovative approach demonstrates a powerful tool for investigating the dynamic protein assembly that occurs within cellular networks.

title: Statins in the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease
text: Statins are widely utilized in evidence-based strategies for lowering cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Their use for secondary prevention of CVD is well established, but there is ongoing debate about their expanding role in primary prevention – that is, in individuals without a history of CVD. Initial findings suggest that statins significantly reduce CVD morbidity in primary prevention, but only moderately decrease CVD mortality. Moreover, long-term statin use may lead to adverse effects, such as incident diabetes mellitus. Additionally, the cost-effectiveness of this strategy is uncertain and must be carefully considered against the risk of overmedicating the general population. Data do support the use of statins for primary prevention in high-risk individuals, where the strategy is cost-effective and benefits outweigh risks. However, the benefit-risk profile for primary prevention in low-risk individuals is less clear. Therefore, the prescription of statins for primary prevention should be individualized based on clinical judgment and, particularly for low-risk individuals, must be carefully considered. Moreover, statins may be beneficial for primary prevention of ischaemic stroke and transient ischaemic attack in appropriately selected individuals.

title: Acetylation of apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease-1 regulates Helicobacter pylori-mediated gastric epithelial cell apoptosis.
text:
Background and Aims: Helicobacter pylori infection can induce gastric epithelial cell (GEC) apoptosis through activation of the tumor suppressor p53. p53-mediated apoptosis involves p53 activation, Bax transcription, and cytochrome c release from mitochondria. However, the mechanism by which H pylori regulates p53-mediated apoptosis in GECs is complex and involves the acetylation of a protein called Apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease-1 (APE-1).
Methods: We used immunoblotting, real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction, immunoprecipitation, immunofluorescence microscopy, chromatin immunoprecipitation, mobility shift, DNA binding, and luciferase assays to investigate the effects of H pylori infection and APE-1 acetylation on GEC apoptosis. We used AGS cells (wild-type or with suppressed APE-1), KATO III cells, and cells isolated from gastric biopsy specimens.
Results: H pylori infection increased intracellular calcium ion concentration [Ca2+]i in GECs, which led to acetylation of APE-1. However, the acetylation status of APE-1 did not affect the transcriptional activity of p53. Instead, expression of a form of APE-1 that could not be acetylated increased total and mitochondrial levels of Bax and induced release of cytochrome c and fragmentation of DNA. Expression of wild-type APE-1, on the other hand, reduced these apoptotic events. We identified a negative calcium response element in the human Bax promoter and found that the acetylated APE-1/histone deacetylase-1 repressor complex recruited to the bax nCaRE.
Conclusions: H pylori-mediated acetylation of APE-1 suppresses Bax expression, which in turn prevents p53-mediated apoptosis in GECs. This provides a new insight into the mechanisms of H pylori-induced gastric mucosa damage and cancer development.

title: A beginning of the end: new insights into the functional organization of telomeres
text: Since the first demonstration of their repetitive sequence and distinct replication pathway, telomeres have captivated scientists with their mechanism of protecting chromosome ends. Over the years, much progress has been made, and we now understand that telomeres are composed of the multi-protein/DNA shelterin complex and that the formation of t-loops provides protection from DNA damage mechanisms. The term "t-loops" was coined by comparison to D-loops, which are generated by the insertion of the 3' overhang into telomeric repeats with the help of TRF2. Recent studies have revealed novel forms of chromosome end-structures that suggest telomere organization may play a role in cellular processes beyond its core function in telomere protection and homeostasis. Specifically, we have found that t-loops form in a TRF2-dependent manner at interstitial telomere repeat sequences, which we term "interstitial telomere loops" (ITLs). These structures are also dependent on the association of lamin A/C, a canonical component of the nucleoskeleton that is mutated in various human diseases, including human segmental progeroid syndromes. Our study suggests a mechanistic link between cellular aging (replicative senescence induced by telomere shortening) and organismal aging (modeled by Hutchinson Gilford Progeria Syndrome). We speculate that ITL formation may have implications for gene expression, genome stability, and chromosome structure.

title: Biochemical analysis of TssK, a core component of the bacterial Type VI secretion system, reveals distinct oligomeric states of TssK and identifies a TssK–TssFG subcomplex
text: The Type VI secretion system (T6SS) of gram-negative bacteria is a complex mechanism for injecting toxic proteins into other bacteria or eukaryotic cells. However, the full understanding of the T6SS remains incomplete. In this study, we investigated a crucial component of the T6SS, TssK, using the antibacterial T6SS of Serratia marcescens as a model system. We found that TssK is essential for effector secretion by the T6SS. The native protein appears to localize to the inner membrane, suggesting that it is a membrane-anchored assembly. We also discovered that TssK exists in multiple stable oligomeric forms, including trimer, hexamer, and higher-order species. Native-level purification of TssK identified interacting proteins TssF and TssG, which are conserved T6SS components of unknown function. Surprisingly, we found that TssF and TssG are required for T6SS activity, but not for the proper localization of TssK. We further purified a complex containing TssK, TssF, and TssG in vitro, providing evidence that these three proteins form a new subcomplex within the T6SS. Our findings reveal new insights into the assembly of the T6SS, suggesting that TssK recruits TssFG into the membrane-associated T6SS complex, and that different oligomeric states of TssK may contribute to the dynamic mechanism of the system.

title: Involvement of ER Stress in Dysmyelination of Pelizaeus-Merzbacher Disease with PLP1 Missense Mutations Shown by iPSC-Derived Oligodendrocytes
text: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease (PMD) is a form of X-linked leukodystrophy caused by mutations in the proteolipid protein 1 (PLP1) gene. Although mutated PLP1 proteins have been shown to accumulate in the rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in disease model animals and cell lines, the exact mechanism of PMD has not been fully understood. In this study, we generated induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from two PMD patients carrying missense mutations and differentiated them into oligodendrocytes in vitro. We observed that the PMD iPSC-derived oligodendrocytes mislocalized the mutated PLP1 proteins to the ER and exhibited increased susceptibility to ER stress, leading to increased numbers of apoptotic oligodendrocytes. Additionally, electron microscopic analysis revealed significantly reduced myelin formation accompanied by abnormal ER morphology. These findings demonstrate the involvement of ER stress in the pathogenic dysmyelination of oligodendrocytes in PMD patients with the PLP1 missense mutation.

title: Using Routine Surveillance Data to Estimate the Epidemic Potential of Emerging Zoonoses: Application to the Emergence of US Swine Origin Influenza A H3N2v Virus
text:
Human populations were previously exposed to zoonotic diseases like SARS, causing occasional infections, before emergence. To assess the risk of widespread epidemics in humans, the reproduction number R (the average number of people infected by a single human case) is often used. However, before now, estimating R required extensive investigations into human clusters, which are often resource-intensive and require specialized expertise. Moreover, existing methods do not address important selection and under-ascertainment biases.
In this study, we present a novel approach that overcomes these limitations. Our method is based on a simple mathematical model of disease transmission and only requires data collected through routine surveillance and standard case investigations. We apply it to assess the transmissibility of swine-origin influenza A H3N2v-M virus in the US, Nipah virus in Malaysia and Bangladesh, as well as a non-zoonotic example (cholera in the Dominican Republic). Estimation is based on two straightforward summary statistics: the proportion infected by the natural reservoir among detected cases (G) and among the subset of the first detected cases in each cluster (F). If detection of a case does not affect detection of other cases from the same cluster, R can be estimated by 1 minus G; otherwise, R can be estimated by 1 minus F when the case detection rate is low. In more complex cases, we can still derive bounds on R.
Our approach allows for robust assessment of the risks posed by emerging zoonoses. By deriving transmissibility estimates for the H3N2v-M virus, we can better evaluate the possible pandemic threat it poses.

title: Independently Evolving Species in Asexual Bdelloid Rotifers
text:
Asexuals serve as a critical test case for understanding why species exist. If asexual lineages displayed the same pattern of diversification as sexual ones, it would challenge the long-held belief that sex is essential for species formation. However, until now, empirical evidence has been lacking. Most studies have relied on visual interpretations of genetic and phenotypic patterns, rather than rigorous tests of alternative evolutionary scenarios.
Here, we provide the first definitive evidence that an asexual clade, the bdelloid rotifers, has evolved into distinct evolutionary species. Our comprehensive sampling of the genus Rotaria revealed the presence of well-separated genetic clusters, indicative of independent evolution. Moreover, combining genetic and morphological analyses revealed divergent selection in feeding morphology, indicating niche divergence. Some of the morphologically distinct groups contained multiple genetic clusters, similar to findings of cryptic species in sexual organisms.
Our results demonstrate that the primary drivers of speciation in sexual organisms - population isolation and divergent selection - have the same qualitative effects in an asexual clade. This study also highlights the power of combined molecular and morphological approaches in shedding new light on the nature of species.

title: The Ribosome Biogenesis Factor Nol11 Is Required for Optimal rDNA Transcription and Craniofacial Development in Xenopus
text: The production of ribosomes is essential for life and affects many disorders. Despite this, defects in ribosome biogenesis are increasingly identified as underlying various symptomatic conditions, termed ribosomopathies. We previously discovered that the nucleolar protein NOL11 is vital for optimal pre-rRNA transcription and processing in human cell cultures. However, its role in the development of multicellular organisms remains unknown. Our study reveals a critical function for NOL11 in vertebrate ribosome biogenesis and craniofacial development. We found that Nol11 is highly expressed in the developing cranial neural crest (CNC) of both amphibians and mammals, and its knockdown in Xenopus leads to impaired pre-rRNA transcription and processing, increased apoptosis, and abnormal development of the craniofacial cartilages. Inhibition of p53 rescues the skeletal phenotype, but not the underlying ribosome biogenesis defect, indicating an evolutionarily conserved control mechanism through which ribosome-impaired craniofacial cells are eliminated. Excessive activation of this mechanism impairs craniofacial development. Our findings uncover a novel requirement for Nol11 in craniofacial development, create the first frog model of a ribosomopathy, and provide additional insights into the clinically significant relationship between specific ribosome biogenesis proteins and craniofacial cell survival.

title: Genomic Nucleosome Organization Reconstituted with Pure Proteins
text:
Chromatin remodelers play a crucial role in regulating gene expression by organizing nucleosomes around promoters. However, the complex in vivo environment of factor redundancy and indirect effects makes it challenging to decipher their individual contributions. To address this issue, we aim to reconstitute genome-wide promoter nucleosome organization using purified proteins, which is a critical goal. We achieve this by using purified components of yeast genomic DNA, histones, sequence-specific Abf1/Reb1, and remodelers RSC, ISW2, INO80, and ISW1a to reconstitute four stages of nucleosome architecture. Our findings reveal direct, specific, and sufficient contributions of these proteins, which are validated by in vivo observations.
Firstly, we find that RSC clears promoters by translating poly(dA:dT) into directional nucleosome removal. This process is highly specific and direct. Secondly, we observe partial redundancy among the remodelers, where INO80 can position +1 nucleosomes independently, or ISW2 can position +1 nucleosomes at Abf1/Reb1 sites. This redundancy is recapitulated in vivo. Thirdly, we observe that INO80 and ISW2 each align downstream nucleosomal arrays, which is a critical aspect of promoter chromatin architecture. Lastly, we find that ISW1a tightens the spacing to canonical repeat lengths, which is a crucial factor in establishing core mechanisms of promoter chromatin architecture.
Our study demonstrates that a minimal set of rules and proteins can establish core mechanisms of promoter chromatin architecture through a combination of redundancy and specialization. This finding has important implications for our understanding of gene regulation and the role of chromatin remodelers in this process.

title: Identification of splenic reservoir monocytes and their deployment to inflammatory sites.
text: According to the current paradigm, monocytes are thought to circulate freely and patrol blood vessels, eventually differentiating into dendritic cells (DCs) or macrophages upon entry into tissue. However, our findings indicate that there is a reservoir of undifferentiated monocytes in the spleen that outnumber those in circulation. These splenic monocytes cluster together in the cord-like structures of the subcapsular red pulp and are distinct from both macrophages and DCs. Upon injury to the myocardial tissue, these monocytes exhibit increased motility and excrete the spleen in large numbers to accumulate at the site of injury, where they play a crucial role in the wound healing process. These observations demonstrate the spleen's function as a storage site for monocytes and its ability to rapidly deploy them to areas of inflammation, highlighting the importance of this organ in regulating the body's inflammatory response.

title: Prox1 Is Required for Granule Cell Maturation and Intermediate Progenitor Maintenance During Brain Neurogenesis
text: The dentate gyrus, a region of remarkable cognitive significance, plays a crucial role in the formation of new memories. Recent research has illuminated the role of adult neurogenesis in the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus in the acquisition of novel information. The homeobox gene Prox1, previously implicated in embryonic development, proves to be a vital factor in the maturation of granule cells during both fetal and adult stages. Our findings demonstrate that Prox1 is essential for the proper maturation of granule cells in the dentate gyrus during development and the maintenance of intermediate progenitors during adult neurogenesis. Moreover, we have discovered a previously unappreciated non-cell autonomous regulatory feedback mechanism that controls adult neurogenesis in the subgranular zone of the mammalian brain, which relies on the expression of Prox1 in intermediate progenitors. Finally, our experiments confirm that the ectopic expression of Prox1 can induce premature differentiation of neural stem cells, further highlighting the indispensable role of Prox1 in the dentate gyrus.

title: The abbreviated pluripotent cell cycle.
text: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) exhibit rapid and symmetric cell division, leading to equivalent progeny cells. In contrast, committed cells undergo a longer, more asymmetric cell cycle. Self-renewal of tissue-specific stem cells is maintained through asymmetric cell division, where one progeny cell remains a progenitor while the other differentiates. The pluripotent cell cycle can be broadly categorized into three contexts: temporal, regulatory, and structural. The short G1 period without reduced time allocated to S phase, G2, and mitosis is a key temporal context. While the rules governing hESC proliferation are not yet fully established, evidence suggests a crucial role for the naïve transcriptome in regulating the ESC cell cycle. This supports the need for pluripotent cells to self-propagate while suppressing the expression of genes that confer lineage commitment and/or tissue specificity. In addition, this study considers unique architectural organization and regulatory machinery in nuclear microenvironments that define pluripotency parameters. From both biological and clinical perspectives, understanding control of the abbreviated ESC cycle can offer novel options to coordinate proliferation and differentiation. Examples of applications that benefit from this knowledge include tissue engineering, cell-based therapy, and the mitigation of developmental aberrations.

title: Senescent growth arrest in mesenchymal stem cells is bypassed by Wip1-mediated downregulation of intrinsic stress signaling pathways.
text: Human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) have been extensively studied as a primary adult stem cell source for cell therapy due to their ability to differentiate into multiple cell types. However, growth arrest (also known as premature senescence) in hMSCs cultured in vitro has been a major hindrance to investigating these cells in-depth. Additionally, the inability to maintain constant cell growth restricts the development of additional genetic modifications aimed at achieving specific differentiation to tissues. Despite some studies identifying p16INK4a as responsible for this senescence-like event, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Our observations show that premature growth arrest in hMSCs correlates with p16INK4a induction, accompanied by increased formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) from mitochondria and heightened p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) activity. Introducing Wip1 (wild-type p53 inducible phosphatase-1), a well-characterized stress modulator, decreased p16INK4a expression and inhibited p38 MAPK activity, while failing to affect ROS levels. Furthermore, suppressing stress responses with Wip1 extended the lifespan of hMSCs in culture, maintaining their multilineage differentiation potential. Based on these findings, we propose that senescence growth arrest in hMSCs may result from activation of stress signaling pathways, leading to the onset of stress responses, which are partly enabled by ROS production during prolonged in vitro culture.

title: Understanding the Odd Science of Aging
text:
Here's a possible revision of the given text:
Evolutionary theory suggests that aging is not caused by specific genetic programming, but rather by the limitations of somatic maintenance that have evolved over time. The accumulation of damage to cells and tissues is thought to be the result of these limitations, rather than active gene regulation. Ecological factors such as hazard rates and food availability can influence the trade-offs between investing in growth, reproduction, and somatic survival, leading to differences in life span across species and within populations. Additionally, dietary restriction and other lifestyle factors can impact aging rate by affecting the complexity of cellular and molecular mechanisms involved in damage accumulation and repair. Ultimately, understanding the cellular and molecular basis of aging involves uncovering the intricate interplay of mechanisms that contribute to the buildup of damage and the various systems that strive to maintain cellular homeostasis.

title: Fate mapping reveals origins and dynamics of monocytes and tissue macrophages under homeostasis.
text: Mononuclear phagocytes, including monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, play an essential role in maintaining tissue integrity and immune defense. Recent research suggests that manipulating these cells may have therapeutic potential. However, the specific developmental paths of individual cell populations and the overall organizational structure of this cellular network are not yet well understood. To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a fate-mapping study of the murine monocyte and macrophage compartment using constitutive and conditional CX(3)CR1 promoter-driven Cre recombinase expression. Our findings demonstrate that major tissue-resident macrophage populations, including liver Kupffer cells and lung alveolar, splenic, and peritoneal macrophages, are established before birth and maintain themselves throughout adulthood without reliance on blood monocyte replenishment. Additionally, we showed that short-lived Ly6C(+) monocytes serve as the necessary precursors for the development of blood-resident Ly6C(-) cells, and that the abundance of Ly6C(+) blood monocytes determines the lifespan of their progeny in circulation.

title: Dealing with substantial heterogeneity in Cochrane reviews. Cross-sectional study
text:
Title: Addressing Heterogeneity in Cochrane Reviews: A Study of Methodological Quality and Choice of Statistical Model
Summary:
Dealing with heterogeneity in Cochrane meta-analyses can be challenging, and there is limited advice provided to authors on how to handle it. This study investigated how authors addressed different degrees of heterogeneity in their studies, specifically whether they used a fixed effect model or a random effects model, which assumes that all included studies are estimating the same true effect. The study found that nearly half of the sampled Cochrane reviews (60 out of 100) had substantial heterogeneity (I2 > 50%), with 55% of these reviews using a fixed effect model. However, there was no correlation between I2 and choice of model (P = 0.79). Moreover, 33% of the reviews had major problems in relation to their handling of heterogeneity, including the use of a fixed effect model without a rationale, lack of comment on even severe heterogeneity, and lack of explanations for its likely causes. The problematic reviews had fewer included trials compared to other reviews (P = 0.024). The study suggests that more attention is needed to address these issues, as the problems identified can impact the conclusions of the reviews.

Introduction:
Heterogeneity is a common challenge in meta-analyses, and dealing with it is crucial to ensure accurate and reliable results. However, there is limited advice provided to authors on how to handle heterogeneity in Cochrane reviews. This study aimed to investigate how authors addressed different degrees of heterogeneity in their studies, specifically whether they used a fixed effect model or a random effects model.

Methods:
The study sampled randomly 60 Cochrane reviews from 2008, which presented a result in their first meta-analysis with substantial heterogeneity (I2 > 50%). The reviews were extracted information on choice of statistical model, how the authors had handled the heterogeneity, and assessed the methodological quality of the reviews in relation to this.


Results:
The results showed that nearly half of the sampled Cochrane reviews (60 out of 100) had substantial heterogeneity (I2 > 50%), with 55% of these reviews using a fixed effect model. However, there was no correlation between I2 and choice of model (P = 0.79). Moreover, 33% of the reviews had major problems in relation to their handling of heterogeneity, including the use of a fixed effect model without a rationale, lack of comment on even severe heterogeneity, and lack of explanations for its likely causes. The problematic reviews had fewer included trials compared to other reviews (P = 0.024).



Discussion:
The study findings highlight the need for more attention to be paid to handling heterogeneity in Cochrane reviews. The lack of correlation between I2 and choice of model suggests that authors are not always using the most appropriate model for their data. Moreover, the major problems identified in the handling of heterogeneity can have a significant impact on the conclusions of the reviews. The study suggests that more emphasis should be placed on providing guidance to authors on how to handle heterogeneity, as well as ensuring that reviews are methodologically sound.




Conclusion:
One-third of Cochrane reviews with substantial heterogeneity had major problems in relation to their handling of heterogeneity. More attention is needed to this issue, as the problems identified can be essential for the conclusions of the reviews.

title: Antagonistic Controls of Autophagy and Glycogen Accumulation by Snf1p, the Yeast Homolog of AMP-Activated Protein Kinase, and the Cyclin-Dependent
text: In the yeast species Saccharomyces cerevisiae, glycogen accumulates as a carbohydrate reserve when nutrient availability is low. Yeast mutated in the SNF1 gene, which encodes a protein kinase required for glucose derepression, exhibits diminished glycogen accumulation and inactivation of glycogen synthase. Upon restoration of synthesis in the mutant strain, only transient glycogen accumulation occurs, suggesting the existence of other SNF1-dependent controls of glycogen storage. A genetic screen revealed that two genes involved in autophagy, APG1 and APG13, may be regulated by SNF1. Increased autophagic activity was observed in wild-type cells entering the stationary phase, but this induction was impaired in the SNF1 mutant. Mutants defective in autophagy were able to synthesize glycogen upon approaching the stationary phase, but were unable to maintain their glycogen stores due to impaired subsequent synthesis and enhanced degradation by phosphorylase, Gph1p. Deletion of GPH1 partially reversed the loss of glycogen accumulation in autophagy mutants. Loss of the vacuolar glucosidase, SGA1, also protected glycogen stores, but only very late in the stationary phase. Gph1p and Sga1p may degrade physically distinct pools of glycogen. Pho85p, a cyclin-dependent protein kinase, antagonizes SNF1 control of glycogen synthesis. Induction of autophagy in pho85 mutants entering the stationary phase was exaggerated compared to wild-type cells, but was blocked in apg1 pho85 mutants. The authors propose that Snf1p and Pho85p are, respectively, positive and negative regulators of autophagy, possibly via Apg1 and/or Apg13. Defective glycogen storage in SNF1 cells can be attributed to both impaired synthesis upon entry into the stationary phase and lack of autophagy-mediated glycogen maintenance.

title: Preferential binding of a kinesin-1 motor to GTP-tubulin–rich microtubules underlies polarized vesicle transport
text: The polarized transport of KIF5 within neurons is essential for the formation of neuronal circuits. A motor protein called KIF5, which is a truncated form of the kinesin-1 protein, recognizes axonal microtubules and selectively accumulates at their tips. However, the specific cue that KIF5 recognizes to target these microtubules remains unknown. We discovered that axonal microtubules are preferentially stained by an antibody called hMB11, which is specific to the GTP-tubulin component of microtubules. Using super-resolution microscopy and EM immunocytochemistry, we found that hMB11 is localized at the attachment sites of KIF5. Additionally, we found that the protein EB1, which binds preferentially to GMPCPP microtubules in vitro, also recognizes hMB11 binding sites on axonal microtubules. Further studies revealed that the expression of hMB11 antibody in neurons disrupts the selective accumulation of truncated KIF5 at the tip of axons. In vitro assays showed that the KIF5 motor head binds approximately threefold stronger to GMPCPP microtubules than to GDP microtubules. Taken together, these data suggest that the abundance of GTP-tubulin in axonal microtubules may underlie the selective localization and polarized axonal vesicular transport of KIF5.

title: Developmental biology of the pancreas.
text:
The pancreas is a multifaceted organ consisting of two distinct populations of cells: exocrine cells that secrete digestive enzymes into the digestive tract, and endocrine cells that produce hormones and send them directly into the bloodstream. The pancreas forms from the endoderm during embryonic development, with the dorsal and ventral buds fusing together to create a single organ. Mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians share similar pancreatic histology and development, while fish exhibit a different organization of pancreatic cells, known as Brockmann bodies. Invertebrates do not possess a pancreas, but similar endocrine cells can be found in the gut or brain.
The early pancreatic bud exhibits uniform expression of the homeobox gene IPF-1, which when mutated, leads to the complete absence of the organ. Heterotopic pancreas, or the presence of pancreatic tissue in an unexpected location, and the regenerative capabilities of the pancreas in adults, suggest that only a few proteins distinguish the pancreatic cell state from surrounding tissues. During pancreatic bud development, endocrine cells differentiate before exocrine cells, and co-expression of different hormones is frequently observed in early stages. However, pancreatic endocrine cells are not of neural crest origin, rather they are of endogenous origin.
Observational studies suggest that both endocrine and exocrine cells arise from the same endodermal rudiment. Development of the pancreas in embryonic life requires trophic stimulation from associated mesenchyme, while in postnatal life, all cell types in the pancreas continue to grow. Destruction of acinar tissue through duct ligation or ethionine treatment leads to rapid regeneration, while surgical removal of parts of the pancreas results in incomplete regeneration of both acini and islets. Treatment with alloxan or streptozotocin can lead to permanent depletion of beta cells.
The cell kinetics of the pancreas are not fully understood, but it is believed that there is a continuous slow turnover of cells, fed by a stem cell population in the ducts, and that local controls govern the production rate of each cell type.

title: Long term pharmacotherapy for obesity and overweight: updated meta-analysis.
text:
Objective: To conduct a comprehensive analysis of the long-term efficacy of anti-obesity drugs in reducing weight and improving health status.
Design: An updated meta-analysis of double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials of approved anti-obesity drugs used in adults (age ≥18) for at least one year.
Data sources: Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, the Current Science Meta-Register of Controlled Trials, and reference lists of identified articles, searched from December 2002 to December 2006.
Studies reviewed: 30 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials of one to four years' duration, including 16 orlistat (n=10,631 participants), 10 sibutramine (n=2,623), and four rimonabant (n=6,365) trials.
Results:
* Attrition rates averaged 30-40%.
* Compared to placebo, orlistat reduced weight by 2.9 kg (95% CI: 2.5 kg to 3.2 kg), sibutramine by 4.2 kg (3.6 kg to 4.7 kg), and rimonabant by 4.7 kg (4.1 kg to 5.3 kg).
* Patients receiving active drug treatment were significantly more likely to achieve 5% and 10% weight loss thresholds.
* Orlistat reduced the incidence of diabetes and improved concentrations of total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, blood pressure, and glycaemic control in patients with diabetes, but increased rates of gastrointestinal side effects and slightly lowered concentrations of high-density lipoprotein.
* Sibutramine improved concentrations of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides (corrected), and rimonabant improved concentrations of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides, blood pressure, and glycaemic control in patients with diabetes, but increased the risk of mood disorders.

Conclusion: Orlistat, sibutramine, and rimonabant modestly reduce weight, have differing effects on cardiovascular risk profiles, and have specific adverse effects.

title: The centrosome cycle: Centriole biogenesis, duplication and inherent asymmetries
text: Centrosomes are microtubule-organizing centers within animal cells, playing a crucial role in shaping the microtubule cytoskeleton, serving as the base for primary cilia, and acting as a hub for important signaling pathways. At the core of a typical centrosome are two cylindrical structures called centrioles, which are surrounded by a matrix of associated pericentriolar material. Cells start each cell cycle with a single centrosome, and the duplication of centrioles is tightly regulated, occurring only once per cell cycle and at a specific site in the cell. This duplication mechanism results in the two centrioles differing in age and maturity, which in turn enables them to perform different functions, such as the older centriole initiating the formation of a ciliary axoneme. We delve into the spatial aspects of the centrosome duplication cycle, the mechanisms of centriole assembly, and the potential implications of the inherent asymmetry of centrioles and centrosomes.

title: Osteoclasts control reactivation of dormant myeloma cells by remodelling the endosteal niche
text:
Despite advances in therapies targeting myeloma cell-intrinsic pathways, multiple myeloma remains largely incurable due to disease relapse attributed to dormant myeloma cells residing in specialized niches. These niches are thought to be responsible for resistance to therapy and the repopulation of the tumor. However, the niche itself is poorly understood, and its role in cell-extrinsic control of myeloma cell dormancy and reactivation has been largely unexplored.
In this study, we employ intravital imaging to track individual myeloma cells as they colonize the endosteal niche and transition from an active state to a dormant state. We demonstrate that dormancy is a reversible state that can be "turned on" by interactions with bone-lining cells or osteoblasts, and "turned off" by osteoclasts remodeling the endosteal niche. Notably, dormant myeloma cells are resistant to chemotherapy targeting dividing cells, highlighting the potential for targeting cell-extrinsic mechanisms to overcome cell-intrinsic drug resistance and prevent disease relapse.
In conclusion, this study sheds light on the pivotal role of the endosteal niche in controlling myeloma cell dormancy and disease relapse, and underscores the need to develop strategies that target cell-extrinsic mechanisms to enhance the efficacy of cancer therapy.

title: Human embryonic stem cells with biological and epigenetic characteristics similar to those of mouse ESCs.
text: Human and mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are derived from blastocyst-stage embryos, but they exhibit distinct biological properties, as revealed by molecular analyses. The pluripotent state of human ESCs isolated so far bears a resemblance to that of mouse-derived epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs). To further rewire the identity of conventional human ESCs and transform them into a more immature state similar to that of pluripotent mouse ESCs, we employed the ectopic induction of Oct4, Klf4, and Klf2 factors in combination with LIF and inhibitors of glycogen synthase kinase 3beta (GSK3β) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (ERK1/2) pathway. Forskolin, a protein kinase A pathway agonist, can also induce Klf4 and Klf2 expression as a transient substitute for ectopic transgene expression. Conversely, the epigenetically converted cells display growth properties, an X-chromosome activation state (XaXa), a gene expression profile, and a signaling pathway dependence that are highly similar to those of mouse ESCs. Moreover, the same growth conditions can be used to derive human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells exhibiting similar characteristics as mouse iPS cells. The generation of validated "naïve" human ESCs offers the opportunity to dissect a previously uncharacterized pluripotent state in humans and open up new possibilities for patient-specific, disease-relevant research.

title: IDEAL in meshes for prolapse, urinary incontinence, and hernia repair.
text: Mesh surgeries are among the most commonly performed surgical procedures globally. However, there is currently no standardized analysis of the incidence and prevention of adverse events following mesh implantation. To address this gap, we developed an in vitro test system for assessing the biocompatibility of surgical meshes based on IDEAL criteria. We also explored different coating strategies for optimizing mesh biocompatibility and evaluated their in vivo performance in a sheep model over a period of 24 months. Our findings revealed comparable ranking characteristics among the meshes at every time point after explantation. The in vivo performance of the meshes was predictable with the in vitro test system, and coating the meshes with autologous plasma prior to implantation appeared to have a positive effect on biocompatibility. These results provide a basis for optimizing future meshes and establishing a ranking system for currently available meshes.

title: Heterotopic of bone marrow. Analysis of precursor cells for osteogenic and hematopoietic tissues.
text: In semisyngeneic heterotopic bone marrow transplants, the donor or recipient origin of cells from osteogenic and hematopoietic tissues is identified through the use of chromosome markers (T6) and reverse transplantation into the initial donor line. In syngeneic and semisyngeneic grafts of bone marrow under the renal capsule, both bone and bone marrow form. In allogeneic grafts, only bone forms, which is later resorbed. In 14-month semisyngeneic transplants, the bone marrow consists of recipient cells, both in the proliferating pool and stem cells of hematopoietic tissue. At the same time, osteogenic precursor cells and bone tissue in these transplants are of donor origin. The relationship between determined osteogenic precursor cells (preosteoblasts) and hematopoietic stem cells (or their descendants) is discussed, with osteogenesis being inducible.

title: TRPM7 is required for breast tumor cell metastasis.
text: The TRPM7 protein functions as a Ca2+-permeable nonselective cation channel with kinase activity. Previous studies have linked TRPM7 to the regulation of cell adhesion and migration, but its role in cancer progression remains uncertain. Our study found that high levels of TRPM7 expression in breast cancer patients are associated with poor outcomes. Moreover, we discovered that TRPM7 plays a functional role in metastasis formation in a mouse xenograft model of human breast cancer. Our investigations revealed that TRPM7 regulates myosin II-based cellular tension, thereby affecting the number of focal adhesions, cell-cell adhesion, and the polarized movement of cells. These findings suggest that TRPM7 is part of a mechanosensory complex adopted by cancer cells to facilitate metastasis formation.

title: Frailty Syndrome: A Transitional State in a Dynamic Process
text:
Frailty has historically been associated with disability and comorbidity, and was once thought to be a natural part of aging. However, recent research suggests that frailty may be a distinct clinical syndrome with a biological basis. The frailty process involves a gradual decline in total physiological reserves, leading to a decrease in the body's ability to maintain and repair itself. This decline is characterized by a range of clinical, functional, and biological changes, including wasting (loss of muscle mass and strength, and weight loss), loss of endurance, decreased balance and mobility, slowed performance, relative inactivity, and potentially, decreased cognitive function.
While the early stages of the frailty process may be clinically silent, once depleted reserves reach a certain threshold, the syndrome can become detectable by evaluating clinical, functional, behavioral, and biological markers. Understanding these changes and their underlying mechanisms, particularly in the pre-frail state, may reveal whether frailty is truly reversible. This knowledge can help inform preventative approaches to address the issue.

title: Progression of preclinical diastolic dysfunction to the development of symptoms.
text:
Background: Preclinical diastolic dysfunction (PDD) has been defined as subjects with normal systolic function but diastolic dysfunction without symptoms of heart failure (HF). The clinical phenotype and natural history of this syndrome are poorly defined. This study aimed to determine the clinical phenotype and progression to HF in a cohort of patients with normal systolic function and moderate/severe diastolic dysfunction as determined by Doppler criteria, without any clinical diagnosis of HF or symptoms of HF (specifically dyspnea, edema, or fatigue) at the time of echocardiography.
Methods: The authors used resources of the Mayo Clinic echocardiography database to consecutively select patients who had an echocardiogram in 2005, with moderate/severe diastolic dysfunction by Doppler criteria and ejection fraction (EF) ≥50%. Patients were excluded if they had a diagnosis of HF or any HF symptoms at the time of echocardiography, or grade 3 or higher valvular dysfunction (except tricuspid valve). A total of 82 patients had their medical chart reviewed. The primary endpoint was the time to the development of either HF according to the Framingham criteria or any symptoms of dyspnea, edema, or fatigue.
Results: The median age of the cohort of PDD subjects was 69 years, with a female preponderance (67%). Hypertension was present in 76% of patients, coronary artery disease in 29%, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in 26%, and estimated creatinine clearance <60 ml/min in 51%. The 2-year cumulative probability of development of HF according to the Framingham criteria was 1.9%, but the 2-year cumulative probability of development of any symptoms was 31.1%. The 2-year cumulative probability of cardiac hospitalization was 21.2%. Peripheral vascular disease and hypertension were independently associated with the development of symptoms.
Conclusion: The study found that hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, and renal dysfunction were prevalent in patients with PDD. More importantly, although the progression to the development of clinical HF over 2 years was low, there was a moderate degree of progression to the development of symptoms and cardiac hospitalizations over 2 years. The authors speculate that ventricular-arterial interaction may play a role in the progression of diastolic dysfunction to the development of symptoms.

title: Aspirin in the chemoprevention of colorectal neoplasia: an overview.
text: Numerous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of aspirin in preventing colorectal cancer (CRC) in addition to its well-established benefits in preventing cardiovascular disease. Epidemiological studies have consistently shown an inverse association between aspirin use and CRC risk. A recent pooled analysis of a long-term post-trial follow-up of around 14,000 patients from four randomized cardiovascular disease prevention trials revealed that daily aspirin treatment for approximately five years was associated with a 34% reduction in 20-year CRC mortality. Similarly, a meta-analysis of nearly 3,000 patients with a history of colorectal adenoma or cancer in four randomized adenoma prevention trials showed that aspirin reduced the occurrence of advanced adenomas by 28% and any adenoma by 17%. Aspirin has also been shown to be beneficial in a clinical trial of patients with Lynch syndrome, a hereditary CRC syndrome; in these patients treated with aspirin for at least two years, there was a 50% or more reduction in the risk of CRC commencing five years after randomization and after aspirin had been discontinued. A few observational studies have also demonstrated an increase in survival among patients with CRC who use aspirin. In conclusion, these findings strengthen the case for considering long-term aspirin use in CRC prevention. However, there is still a lack of consensus on the balance of risks and benefits associated with long-term aspirin use, particularly in low-risk populations. Further research is needed to determine the optimal dose for cancer prevention and to elucidate the underlying mechanism of aspirin's anticancer effect.

title: Chemokine receptor trio: CXCR3, CXCR4 and CXCR7 crosstalk via CXCL11 and CXCL12.
text: Despite the established role of chemokines in immunity and endothelial cell activation, recent evidence suggests that CXC Chemokine receptors CXCR3, CXCR4, and CXCR7 play a critical role in the development and progression of solid tumors. The interaction between these receptors and their shared ligands, including I-TAC (CXCL11) and SDF-1 (CXCL12), mediates their effect on tumorigenesis. Over the past decade, CXCR4 has been found to be overexpressed in most human solid tumors, garnering significant attention towards its role in cancer metastasis. In an effort to bolster the existing arsenal of anti-cancer agents, numerous inhibitors of the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis have emerged as potential neo-adjuvant treatments. However, the discovery of CXCR7 as another receptor for CXCL12 with high binding affinity has raised questions about the notion of "selective blockade" of CXCR4 as cancer chemotherapy. Interestingly, CXCR7 can also bind to CXCL11, which is a ligand for CXCR3. Recent studies have shown that CXCR3 and its ligands are overexpressed in different solid tumors and regulate tumor growth and metastasis. Therefore, it is essential to consider the interplay and crosstalk between these three chemokine receptors and their ligand-mediated signaling cascades in the development of effective anti-cancer therapies. Additionally, emerging evidence suggests that these receptors are differentially expressed in tumor endothelial cells and cancer stem cells, highlighting their direct role in regulating tumor angiogenesis and metastasis. In this review, we will focus on the signals mediated by this receptor trio via their shared ligands and their role in tumor growth and progression.

title: Human Cyclin a Is Required for Mitosis until Mid Prophase
text: Using microinjection and time-lapse video microscopy, we have investigated the role of cyclin A in mitosis. By injecting purified, active cyclin A/cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) into synchronized cells at specific stages of the cell cycle, we observed that it can drive G2 phase cells into mitosis within 30 minutes, even up to 4 hours before control cells enter mitosis. However, this premature mitosis is often abnormal, with non-condensed chromosomes and fusion of daughter cells. In contrast, injecting cyclin A/CDK2 into S phase cells has no effect on their progression through the subsequent G2 phase or mitosis. To further investigate the role of cyclin A/CDK2, we also microinjected the amino terminus of p21Cip1/Waf1/Sdi1 (p21N) into cells to inhibit its activity. Our results show that p21N can prevent S phase or G2 phase cells from entering mitosis, and can cause early prophase cells to re-enter the interphase. These findings suggest that cyclin A/CDK2 is a rate-limiting factor required for entering mitosis and progressing through it until late prophase. Additionally, they suggest that cyclin A/CDK2 may be a target of the newly identified prophase checkpoint.

title: Brief, four-session group CBT reduces binge eating behaviors among bariatric surgery candidates.
text:
INTRODUCTION:
The goal of this study was to assess the effectiveness of a brief, four-session cognitive-behavioral group therapy for binge eating among bariatric surgery candidates at an academic medical center. Binge eating has been linked to poorer outcomes among bariatric surgery patients, and binge eating disorder is considered a contraindication in surgery programs, some of which have mandated preoperative binge eating treatment. Despite this, no prior studies have determined whether a preoperative binge eating intervention can effectively reduce binge eating behaviors among severely obese bariatric surgery candidates.
METHODS: A total of 243 bariatric surgery candidates completed a brief cognitive-behavioral group treatment for binge eating behaviors and were assessed using the Binge Eating Scale and reported the number of weekly binge eating episodes at the initial psychological evaluation and again after the group sessions. The study employed a pre-post intervention design.
RESULTS: The findings suggested significant reductions in both binge eating behaviors and cognitions, as well as binge eating episodes, following the group intervention. The intervention's effectiveness did not differ by gender or ethnicity (black versus white).
CONCLUSION: A brief cognitive-behavioral intervention can reduce binge eating behaviors among bariatric surgery candidates. Given the potential impact of binge eating on outcomes, bariatric surgery programs could benefit by treating binge eating before surgery.

title: Influence of smoking cessation after diagnosis of early stage lung cancer on prognosis: systematic review of observational studies with meta-analysis
text:
Objective: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the impact of smoking cessation after lung cancer diagnosis on prognosis.
Design: Randomized controlled trials or observational longitudinal studies that measured the effect of quitting smoking after lung cancer diagnosis on prognostic outcomes.
Data sources: CINAHL (from 1981), Embase (from 1980), Medline (from 1966), Web of Science (from 1966), and CENTRAL (from 1977) up to December 2008, and reference lists of included studies.
Study selection: Randomized controlled trials or observational longitudinal studies that measured the effect of quitting smoking after lung cancer diagnosis on prognostic outcomes, regardless of stage at presentation or tumor histology.
Data extraction: Two researchers independently identified studies for inclusion and extracted data.
Results: Nine out of ten included studies showed that continued smoking was associated with a significant increase in the risk of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 2.94, 95% confidence interval 1.15 to 7.54), recurrence (1.86, 1.01 to 3.41), and development of a second primary tumor (4.31, 1.09 to 16.98), and recurrence (1.26, 1.06 to 1.50) in limited stage small cell lung cancer. None of the studies contained data on the effect of quitting smoking on cancer-specific mortality or on development of a second primary tumor in non-small cell lung cancer. Life table modeling based on the data from this review estimated a 33% five-year survival rate in 65-year-old patients with early stage non-small cell lung cancer who continued to smoke compared with 70% in those who quit smoking. In limited stage small cell lung cancer, an estimated 29% of continuing smokers would survive for five years compared with 63% of quitters based on the data from this review.
Conclusion: This review provides preliminary evidence that smoking cessation after lung cancer diagnosis improves prognostic outcomes. Life table modeling based on the data from this review estimated a larger number of deaths prevented than would be expected from the reduction of cardiorespiratory deaths after smoking cessation, suggesting that most of the mortality gain is likely due to reduced cancer progression. Offering smoking cessation treatment to patients presenting with early stage lung cancer may be beneficial.

title: Epigenetic reprogramming and induced pluripotency.
text: The reprogramming of adult cells into an embryonic-like state, demonstrated through cloning, has revealed that unidentified factors within the oocyte can alter the developmental state of adult cells. More recently, transcription factors have been discovered that can induce pluripotency in somatic cells without the use of oocytes, generating induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. iPS cells offer a valuable tool for investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying epigenetic reprogramming, as well as providing insights into normal development and disease. Additionally, iPS cells may potentially enable customized cell therapy for the treatment of patients.

title: Sex differences in mortality following acute coronary syndromes.
text:
In this study, the authors investigated the relationship between sex and 30-day mortality in patients with acute coronary syndromes (ACS), and whether this relationship was modified by clinical syndrome or coronary anatomy. The study included a large database of patients from 11 international randomized clinical trials, with a total of 136,247 participants, of whom 38,048 (28%) were women. The main outcome measure was 30-day mortality following ACS.
The results showed that the overall 30-day mortality rate was 9.6% for women and 5.3% for men, with an odds ratio (OR) of 1.91 (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.83-2.00). After multivariable adjustment, mortality was not significantly different between women and men (adjusted OR 1.06; 95% CI 0.99-1.15). The authors found a significant sex by type of ACS interaction, with higher mortality among women in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and lower mortality among women in non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and unstable angina. In a cohort of 35,128 patients with angiographic data, women had less severe coronary disease, but after adjustment for angiographic disease severity, the difference in mortality between women and men was no longer significant.
The authors concluded that sex-based differences in 30-day mortality among patients with ACS exist, but are largely explained by clinical differences at presentation and severity of angiographically documented disease.

title: Membrane topology of the 60-kDa Oxa1p homologue from Escherichia coli.
text: We have mapped the membrane organization of a 60-kDa inner membrane protein from Escherichia coli that shares similarity with the recently identified Oxa1p protein in Saccharomyces cerevisiae mitochondria, which is involved in the assembly of mitochondrial inner membrane proteins. Using hydrophobicity and alkaline phosphatase fusion analyses, we have determined that this protein has a topology with six transmembrane segments, including an N-terminal signal sequence that is not present in the mitochondrial Oxa1p. In contrast to partial N-terminal fusion constructs, the full-length protein folds into a protease-resistant conformation, suggesting that critical folding elements are located in the C-terminal region of the molecule.

title: Identifying and Characterizing Interplay between Hepatitis B Virus X Protein and Smc5/6
text: Hepatitis B X protein (HBx) plays a crucial role in the hepatitis B virus (HBV) replication cycle, yet its function has remained elusive until recently. It was discovered that the structural maintenance of chromosome 5/6 complex (Smc5/6) inhibits transcription from the HBV genome (covalently-closed circular DNA, cccDNA), and that HBx redirects the DNA-damage binding protein 1 (DDB1) E3 ubiquitin ligase to target this complex for degradation. By doing so, HBx alleviates transcriptional repression by Smc5/6 and stimulates HBV gene expression. In this review, we delve into the examination of the interplay between HBx and Smc5/6, discussing the mechanisms by which HBx influences cccDNA transcription and the timing of its expression. Additionally, we explore the potential link between HBx and the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

title: Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Vertical Transmission in 12-Month-Old Infants Born to HCV-Infected Women and Assessment of Maternal Risk Factors
text:
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is an underappreciated cause of pediatric liver disease, primarily acquired through vertical transmission (VT) during pregnancy.
