Current guidelines recommend screening infants for HCV RNA at 1-2 months based on earlier data, but recent studies have shown that VT rates are higher than previously thought, ranging from 4% to 15%. To investigate the association between HCV VT and maternal risk factors in a prospective cohort in Cairo, Egypt, we evaluated HCV RNA in infants with HCV VT and assessed maternal risk factors.
Methods: We screened pregnant women for HCV from December 2012 to March 2014, and for those with HCV viremia, their infants were tested for HCV RNA at 12 months using real-time PCR. Maternal risk factors analyzed for HCV VT association included HCV RNA levels, mode of delivery, and maternal IL28B genotype.
Results: Of 2514 women screened, 54 were viremic (2.1%) and gave birth to 56 infants. Of these, 51 infants aged 12 months were tested, and only 7 infants were viremic, with an HCV VT rate of 14.3% (7/49). The median HCV RNA level in these infants was 2100 IU/mL. None of the maternal risk factors analyzed were associated with transmission.
Conclusion: In Egypt, where HCV is highly endemic, we found an overall 12-month HCV VT rate of 14.3%. Further studies should focus on identifying pregnant women more likely to vertically transmit HCV and testing infants earlier to identify those likely to develop chronic liver disease.

title: Long-term follow-up of cervical disease in women screened by cytology and HPV testing: results from the HART study
text: SEVERAL STUDIES HAVE SHOWN THAT TESTING FOR HIGH-RISK HUMAN PAPILLOVIRUS (HPV) TYPES IMPROVES SENSITIVITY FOR CERVICAL INTRAEPITHELIAL NEOPLASIA GRADE 2+ (CIN2+) COMPARED TO CYTOLOGY, THOUGH WITH A MODest LOWER SPECIFICITY. WE OBTAINED FOLLOW-UP RESULTS FOR WOMEN WHO PARTICIPATED IN THE HART STUDY, WHICH COMPARED HPV TESTING (HC-II) WITH CYTOLOGY AS PRIMARY SCREENING MODEL. WITH A MEDIAN FOLLOW-UP OF 6 YEARS, 42 ADDITIONAL CASES OF CIN2+ WERE IDENTIFIED; WOMEN WHO WERE HPV POSITIVE AT baseline WERE MORE LIKELY TO DEVELOP CIN2+ THAN THOSE WHO WERE HPV NEGATIVE (hazard RATIO (HR) 17.2; 95% CONFIDENCE INTERVAL (CI) (9.3-31.6)) AND THE RISK INCREASED WITH INCREASING VIRAL LOAD. COMPARED WITH HPV-NEGATIVE WOMEN (RELATIVE LIGHT UNIT (RLU) <1), THE HR (95% CI) WAS 5.4 (1.6, 18.2) FOR 1-10 RLU AND 25.5 (13.6, 47.9) FOR RLU > OR = 10. POSITIVE CYTOLOGY (BORDERLINE OR WORSE COMPARED WITH NEGATIVE) WAS ALSO PREDICTIVE OF DEVELOPING CIN2+, THOUGH TO A LESSER EXTENT (HR 8.7; 95% CI (4.5-17.1)). ONLY ONE CASE OF CIN3 AND THREE CASES OF CIN2 WERE FOUND IN WOMEN WHO SHOWED A POSITIVE CYTOLOGY RESULT BUT WERE HPV NEGATIVE AT baseline.

title: The Burden of Trachoma in Ayod County of Southern Sudan
text:
Trachoma, a treatable and preventable disease, is a significant cause of blindness in Southern Sudan, according to recent surveys. A cross-sectional two-stage cluster random survey was conducted in Ayod County of Jonglei State to assess the need for interventions to eliminate blinding trachoma. The study found:

1. Prevalence of signs of active trachoma in children 1-9 years of age was high, with:
* Trachomatous inflammation follicular (TF) = 80.1% (95% CI: 73.9-86.3)
* Trachomatous inflammation intense (TI) = 60.7% (95% CI: 54.6-66.8)
* TF and/or TI (active trachoma) = 88.3% (95% CI: 83.7-92.9)

2. Prevalence of trachomatous trichiasis (TT) was 14.6% (95% CI: 10.9-18.3) in adults over 14 years of age, 2.9% (95% CI: 0.4-5.3) in children 1-14 years of age, and 8.4% (95% CI: 5.5-11.3) overall.

3. The prevalence of corneal opacity in persons over 14 years of age with TT was 6.4% (95% CI: 4.5-8.3).

4. There was no statistically significant difference in the prevalence of trachoma signs between genders.

5. Trachoma affected almost all households surveyed: 384/392 (98.0%) had at least one person with active trachoma, and 130 (33.2%) had at least one person with trichiasis.

Based on these findings, the survey confirmed that trachoma is a significant public health problem in Ayod and that the SAFE strategy is warranted to eliminate blinding trachoma. The high prevalence of active trachoma and trichiasis in the study confirms the severe burden of blinding trachoma in post-conflict areas of Southern Sudan.

title: A Century of Cholesterol and Coronaries: From Plaques to Genes to Statins
text: Approximately one-fourth of deaths in developed countries are caused by coronary heart disease, a century of research has shown. The primary culprit behind this is low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, which is carried by specific receptors (LDLRs) in the liver. These receptors play a crucial role in removing LDL from the bloodstream. Mutations that affect the function of these receptors can either raise or lower LDL levels, leading to heart attacks in childhood or reducing the risk of heart attacks, respectively. To eliminate coronary disease, the primary objective should be to lower LDL levels. Fortunately, effective strategies to achieve this goal are already available. The key questions are: who should be treated, when to start treatment, and how long treatment should continue.

title: Perinatal mortality in rural China: retrospective cohort study.
text:
Objective: To investigate the utilization of local civil registration data to assess perinatal mortality in a typical rural county in a less developed province in China between 1999 and 2000.
Design: A retrospective cohort study was conducted by following pregnancies from registration to the outcome of the infant seven days after birth.
Setting: Routine family planning records in 20 rural townships in eastern China were used for the study.
Subjects: A total of 3697 pregnancies registered by the local family planning system during 1999 were included in the study.
Main Outcome Measures: The outcomes measured in the study included abortions, stillbirths, early neonatal mortality, and perinatal mortality.
Results: Only three cases were lost to follow-up. The average age of the women at pregnancy was 25.9 years. Three hundred and twelve pregnancies were aborted, and 240 ended in miscarriage (total 552, 15%). The perinatal mortality rate was 69 per 1000 births, stillbirth rate was 24 per 1000 births, and early neonatal mortality rate was 46 per 1000 live births. The early neonatal mortality rate was 29 in boys and 69 in girls per 1000 live births. The perinatal mortality rate increased significantly with parity and was higher in townships with lower income per capita.
Conclusions: The study found that the family planning system at the most local level is a useful data source for studying perinatal mortality in rural China. The perinatal mortality rate in the study county was higher than previously reported for both rural and urban areas in China. The results by parity and sex of the infant highlight the concern over the impact of the one child policy.

title: Genetic disruption of aurora B uncovers an essential role for aurora C during early mammalian development.
text: Mitosis is regulated by multiple kinases that control cell cycle progression and prevent chromosome mis-segregation. Aurora kinase B interacts with survivin, borealin, and incenp to form the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC), which plays a role in regulating microtubule-kinetochore attachments and cytokinesis. On the other hand, deleting genes for survivin, borealin, or incenp can lead to early embryonic death at the morula stage. However, we found that aurora B is dispensable for CPC function during early cell divisions, and aurora B-null embryos are typically implanted normally. This is because aurora C scales down its expression during later blastocyst stages, which results in abnormalities in the inner cell mass and post-implantation defects in aurora B-null embryos. Conditional deletion of aurora B in cells that do not express aurora C also leads to misaligned chromosomes and lack of chromosome segregation. Reintroducing wild-type, but not kinase-dead, aurora C can rescue these defects, suggesting functional overlap between these two kinases. Furthermore, aurora B-null cells partially arrest in the presence of nocodazole, suggesting that this kinase is not essential for the spindle assembly checkpoint.

title: NuSAP is essential for chromatin-induced spindle formation during early embryogenesis.
text:
The process of mitotic spindle assembly is regulated by two distinct pathways: a centrosomal and a chromosomal route. RanGTP, an essential molecule, controls the latter pathway by releasing microtubule-associated proteins from inhibitory complexes, allowing for the formation of microtubules near chromosomes. However, the specific function of NuSAP, a microtubule- and DNA-binding protein, in vivo remains unknown.
In this study, we investigate the correlation between NuSAP expression and cell proliferation during embryonic development and adulthood. Our findings reveal that NuSAP is highly correlated with cell proliferation, making it a reliable marker of proliferating cells. Moreover, we demonstrate that NuSAP deficiency in mice leads to early embryonic lethality, as spindle assembly in these cells is inefficient and chromosomes remain dispersed in the mitotic cytoplasm. As a result of sustained spindle checkpoint activity, the cells are unable to progress through mitosis, leading to caspase activation and apoptotic cell death.
Our findings underscore the essential role of NuSAP in the proliferation of embryonic cells and highlight the importance of chromatin-induced spindle assembly. This work sheds light on the complex mechanisms underlying cell division and underscores the importance of further investigating the molecular pathways involved in this process.

title: E2F-6: a novel member of the E2F family is an inhibitor of E2F-dependent transcription
text: The E2F family of transcription factors plays a crucial role in regulating genes necessary for proper cell cycle progression. Five E2F family members have been identified so far: E2F1-5. These members are key regulators of gene expression and can be divided into two groups based on their function. E2Fs 1-3 induce S-phase progression when overexpressed in quiescent cells, while E2Fs 4-5 do not. In this study, we identify a new member of the E2F family, E2F-6, which shares significant homology with the other E2Fs in the DNA binding, heterodimerization, and transcriptional activation domains. Unlike the other E2Fs, E2F-6 lacks a transactivation domain, forming a unique third group within the E2F family. E2F-6 is a nuclear protein that forms heterodimers with the DP proteins (both DP-1 and DP-2) in vitro and in vivo. Our results show that the E2F-6-DP complex has high DNA binding activity and prefers a TTTCCCGC E2F recognition site, which is slightly different from the E2F consensus site derived from the E2 promoter (TTTCGCGC). In contrast to the other E2F family members, ectopic expression of E2F-6 inhibits transcription from promoters containing E2F recognition sites rather than activating transcription. Overexpression of E2F-6 also suppresses the transactivational effects of co-expression of E2F-1 and DP-1. The inhibitory effect of E2F-6 is dependent on its DNA binding activity and its ability to form heterodimers with the DPs. Interestingly, ectopic expression of E2F-6 leads to accumulation of cells in S-phase. Our data suggest that E2F-6 expression delays the exit from S-phase rather than inducing S-phase, highlighting the distinct function of E2F-6 compared to the other E2F family members.

title: Enhancement of hippocampal pyramidal cell excitability by the novel selective slow-afterhyperpolarization channel blocker 3-(triphenylmethylaminomethyl)pyridine (UCL2077).
text:
The slow afterhyperpolarization (sAHP) in hippocampal neurons has been implicated in learning and memory, but its specific function in cell excitability and central nervous system function remains unclear due to two main limitations:
1. Currently, there are no effective inhibitors available to reduce the underlying current of sAHP in vivo or in intact in vitro tissue preparations.
2. Although it is known that a small conductance K(+) channel activates after an increase in [Ca(2+)](i) underlies the sAHP, the exact molecular identity of this channel remains unknown.
To overcome these limitations, we investigated the effects of 3-(triphenylmethylaminomethyl)pyridine (UCL2077), a novel compound, on sAHP in hippocampal neurons in culture and in slices. Our results showed that UCL2077 effectively suppressed the sAHP with an IC(50) value of 0.5 microM in culture and approximately 10 microM in slices. UCL2077 was selective, with minimal effects on Ca(2+) channels, action potentials, input resistance, and the medium afterhyperpolarization. Additionally, UCL2077 had little effect on heterologously expressed small conductance Ca(2+)-activated K(+) (SK) channels. Interestingly, UCL2077 and apamin, a selective SK channel blocker, affected spike firing in hippocampal neurons in different ways. These findings suggest that SK channels are unlikely to underlie the sAHP.
Furthermore, this study demonstrates that UCL2077, the most potent and selective sAHP blocker identified to date, is a valuable pharmacological tool for exploring the role of sAHP channels in the regulation of cell excitability in intact tissue preparations and, potentially, in vivo.

title: Lessons from sudden coronary death: a comprehensive morphological classification scheme for atherosclerotic lesions.
text:
This review aims to challenge the traditional paradigm for understanding the final stages of atherosclerosis, which is largely based on observations of autopsy tissues by Davies and colleagues. According to this paradigm, the primary cause of death in atherosclerotic coronary artery disease is the rupture of a severely advanced atherosclerotic lesion. However, recent autopsy studies have suggested that this assumption is incomplete.
To address this gap in understanding, we revisited the morphological classification scheme for lesions proposed by the American Heart Association (AHA). While the AHA scheme is widely used, it has two main limitations: (1) it utilizes a long and complex list of roman numerals and letter codes that are difficult to remember, and (2) it implies a linear and sequential progression of lesion development, which is often ambiguous in practice.
To address these limitations, we have created a simpler and more flexible classification system that is consistent with the AHA categories but easier to use, capable of handling a wide range of morphological variations, and free from overly mechanistic interpretations. The current paradigm is based on the belief that type IV lesions, or "atheromas," as described by the AHA, are stable due to the presence of a smooth muscle cell-rich fibrous cap that contains the fatty, necrotic core. However, Virchow's analysis in 1858 highlighted that the term "atheroma" originally referred to a dermal cyst (Grutzbalg), a fatty accumulation in the skin. This historical context challenges the traditional view of atheroma as a stable lesion and suggests that its development and progression may be more complex than previously thought.

title: Loss of allergen 1 confers a hypervirulent phenotype that resembles mucoid switch variants of Cryptococcus neoformans.
text: The ability of the fungus Cryptococcus neoformans to survive within a host is directly linked to its capacity to undergo changes that evade host defense mechanisms. In contrast to other virulence-associated genes, the loss of the ALL1 gene enhances the pathogen's virulence by disrupting the host-pathogen interaction, which in turn impairs clearance of the fungus. This is evident in animal models, where the ALL1Δ mutant exhibits a phenotype similar to that of the hypervirulent mucoid switch variant, resulting in decreased host survival and elevated intracranial pressure. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that opportunistic pathogens have adapted to their environments through epigenetic downregulation of gene function, leading to increased virulence.

title: Lessons from more than 80 structures of the GluA2 ligand-binding domain in complex with agonists, antagonists and allosteric modulators.
text:
Ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) are a crucial class of ligand-gated ion channels that facilitate rapid synaptic transmission in the central nervous system. These receptors play a pivotal role in the development and function of the nervous system, including learning and memory. However, they have also been implicated in or have a causal role in various brain disorders, such as epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia. The involvement of iGluRs in these diseases has sparked significant interest in their structure and function.
Since the publication of the structure of a recombinant soluble protein comprising the ligand-binding domain of GluA2 in 1998, extensive research has been conducted on the crystal structures of wildtype and mutant proteins, including different ligands. This structural information, combined with functional data, has led to molecular models for receptor activation and desensitization by agonists, inhibition by antagonists, and block of desensitization by positive allosteric modulators. These models have also enabled the design of new selective compounds.
In summary, iGluRs are essential for fast synaptic transmission in the central nervous system, but their dysfunction has been implicated in various brain disorders. Crystal structures of iGluRs and their complexes with ligands have provided valuable insights into their structure and function, enabling the design of new therapeutic compounds for these diseases.

title: Diaphragm Atrophy and Contractile Dysfunction in a Murine Model of Pulmonary Hypertension
text: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) leads to weight loss and dysfunction of the inspiratory (diaphragm) muscles. To investigate the mechanisms of cachexia and diaphragm abnormalities in PH, a mouse model of PH induced by the drug monocrotaline (MCT) has been widely used. However, it is unclear if this model reproduces the weight loss and diaphragm muscle weakness seen in human patients. To address this, we measured body and soleus muscle weight, food intake, and diaphragm contractile properties in mice after 6-8 weeks of saline (control) or MCT injections. Our findings show that PH mice exhibited progressive weight loss, similar food intake between groups, and decreased diaphragm muscle strength, as evidenced by decreased maximal isometric specific force, maximal shortening velocity, and peak power. Additionally, the abundance of select myofibrillar proteins and protein carbonyls in whole-diaphragm lysates were unchanged by PH. These results suggest that the murine model of PH induced by MCT mimics the loss of body weight and diaphragm muscle weakness observed in human PH patients.

title: Identification of an anti-inflammatory protein from Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a commensal bacterium deficient in Crohn's disease.
text:
Background: Crohn's disease (CD)-associated dysbiosis is characterized by a reduced abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, which is known to produce a culture supernatant with anti-inflammatory effects both in vitro and in vivo. However, the chemical composition of these anti-inflammatory compounds has yet to be determined.
Methods: Peptidomic analysis using mass spectrometry was used to identify anti-inflammatory peptides in the culture supernatant of F. prausnitzii. The effectiveness of these peptides was evaluated in vitro by testing their anti-inflammatory activity directly on intestinal epithelial cell lines and on cell lines transfected with a plasmid construct encoding the candidate protein. In vivo, the cDNA of the candidate protein was delivered to the gut of mice through recombinant lactic acid bacteria to prevent colitis induced by dinitrobenzene sulfonic acid (DNBS).
Results: Seven peptides were identified in the F. prausnitzii culture supernatant, which were shown to derive from a single microbial anti-inflammatory molecule (MAM) with a molecular weight of 15 kDa. Notably, 53% of these peptides were non-polar, making it difficult to directly characterize their putative anti-inflammatory activity. Transfection of MAM cDNA into epithelial cells led to a significant decrease in the activation of the nuclear factor (NF)-κB signaling pathway with a dose-dependent effect. Finally, the use of a food-grade bacterium, Lactococcus lactis, delivering a plasmid encoding MAM was able to alleviate DNBS-induced colitis in mice.
Conclusions: This study provides evidence that F. prausnitzii produces a 15 kDa protein with anti-inflammatory properties that can inhibit the NF-κB signaling pathway in intestinal epithelial cells and prevent colitis in an animal model. These findings suggest that modulating the composition of the gut microbiota with this protein could provide a potential therapeutic approach for the treatment of CD.

title: Calcium store sensor stromal-interaction molecule 1-dependent signaling plays an important role in cervical cancer growth, migration, and angiogenesis.
text: Store-operated Ca(2+) entry (SOCE) is the primary mechanism of Ca(2+) entry in non-excitable cells. Stromal-interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) is an endoplasmic reticulum Ca(2+) sensor that activates SOCE in these cells. However, the role of STIM1 in cancer progression has been controversial, and its clinical significance is unclear. Our study shows that STIM1-mediated signaling plays a crucial role in cervical cancer cell proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis. STIM1 is overexpressed in 71% of early-stage cervical cancer tissues, and its expression is associated with the risk of metastasis and survival. EGF stimulation of cancer cells leads to increased interaction between STIM1 and Orai1 in juxta-membrane areas, resulting in Ca(2+) influx. STIM1 activates Ca(2+)-regulated protease calpain and Ca(2+)-regulated cytoplasmic kinase Pyk2, which regulate the focal-adhesion dynamics of migratory cervical cancer cells. Silencing STIM1 in cervical cancer cells leads to a decrease in cell proliferation, an increase in p21 protein levels, and a decrease in Cdc25C protein levels, resulting in cell cycle arrest at the S and G2/M phases. Additionally, STIM1 regulates the production of VEGF in cervical cancer cells. Interference with STIM1 expression or blockade of SOCE activity inhibits tumor angiogenesis and growth in animal models, confirming the essential role of STIM1-mediated Ca(2+) influx in promoting tumor development in vivo. These findings make STIM1-dependent signaling an attractive target for therapeutic intervention.

title: A feasibility study for a randomised controlled trial of the Positive Reappraisal Coping Intervention, a novel supportive technique for recurrent miscarriage
text:
Study Title: Evaluating the Feasibility and Effectiveness of a Novel Supportive Technique (PRCI) in Improving Quality of Life for Women with Prior Recurrent Miscarriages (RM)
Introduction:
Recurrent miscarriage (RM) is defined as the occurrence of three or more consecutive pregnancy losses. Ladies who have experienced RM are at a high risk of psychological distress and anxiety during the waiting period of any subsequent pregnancy, which poses a significant threat to their overall mental well-being. Given the limited availability of support and therapy for these women, this study aims to assess the feasibility and effectiveness of a novel, self-administered intervention, the Positive Reappraisal Coping Intervention (PRCI), in enhancing their quality of life during the challenging waiting period before an ongoing pregnancy can be confirmed.
Methods and Analysis:
This study is a randomized controlled trial (RCT) feasibility study with a qualitative process evaluation component. Participants (n=50) will be randomly assigned to either the PRCI intervention group or the non-intervention group. The PRCI intervention group will receive a customized PRCI card and weekly questionnaires to evaluate their psychological well-being during the waiting period of their new pregnancy, while the non-intervention group will complete the same weekly questionnaires. The qualitative process analysis will involve semistructured interviews (n=20) to gather data on the initial experience of pregnancy following repeated miscarriages.
Ethics and Dissemination:
Ethics approval has been obtained from the National Research Ethics Service Committee South Central-Hampshire A, and participating centers have given National Health Service Research and Development approval. The study findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals, national and international conferences, and lay user groups. The study registration number is ISRCTN43571276, and it was registered on February 18, 2014, after being adopted onto the United Kingdom Clinical Research Network (UKCRN) portfolio. Recruitment of the first participant began on February 4, 2014.

title: Report of the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Workshop on Lipoprotein(a) and Cardiovascular Disease: recent advances and future directions.
text:
According to estimates, approximately 37% of the US population, as determined by National Cholesterol Education Program guidelines, are at high risk of developing coronary artery disease (CAD). In contrast, only 14% of those deemed to be at low risk have increased plasma lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)]. Therefore, there is a clear need to better understand the contribution of Lp(a) to the risk of CAD and other vascular diseases, as well as the underlying mechanisms. However, the complexity and size heterogeneity of Lp(a) have hindered the development of accurate immunoassays to measure Lp(a) concentrations in plasma. This has resulted in significant intermethod variation in Lp(a) values, making it challenging to compare data from different clinical studies and achieve a uniform interpretation of clinical data.
To address these issues, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) convened a workshop to evaluate current knowledge of Lp(a) as a risk factor for atherosclerotic disorders and to develop strategies for improving the accuracy and standardization of Lp(a) immunoassays. The workshop presented new data from various participants and provided research and practical recommendations. This report includes the latest findings and recommendations from the workshop.

title: Classification, functions, and clinical relevance of extracellular vesicles.
text: Cells of both the eukaryotic and prokaryotic types release small, phospholipid-encased vesicles into their environment. The purpose of cellular vesicle release is not entirely clear, but research has shown that eukaryotic vesicles play a role in eliminating cellular waste. However, these vesicles can also pose a hazard to their surroundings, such as in the case of blood, where they can contribute to clotting. Recent evidence suggests that vesicles may serve as cargo containers for eukaryotic cells, allowing them to exchange biomolecules through transmembrane receptors and genetic information. It appears that this form of intercellular communication via extracellular cargo carriers has been conserved throughout evolution, making vesicles a highly efficient, robust, and economic means of exchanging information between cells. Vesicles also protect cells from the buildup of toxins or drugs, contribute to physiology and pathology, and have a wide range of potential clinical applications, including use as biomarkers or anticancer therapy. Additionally, vesicles have the ability to cross the blood-brain barrier, leading some to consider them naturally occurring liposomes. Unfortunately, vesicles can also be used by tumors and infectious diseases to spread and evade the immune system. In this review, we will discuss the different types, nomenclature, functions, and clinical relevance of vesicles.

title: Estimating the sample mean and standard deviation from the sample size, median, range and/or interquartile range
text: In systematic reviews and meta-analyses, researchers often combine the results of multiple clinical trials by pooling the sample mean and standard deviation. However, some trials may have reported results using alternative methods, such as the median, minimum and maximum values, or first and third quartiles. To accommodate these trials, researchers must estimate the sample mean and standard deviation. This paper aims to enhance the existing literature by addressing several limitations. Firstly, we show that the sample standard deviation estimation method in Hozo et al. (2005) has limitations and is often less practical in reality. As a result, we propose a new estimation method that takes into account the sample size. Secondly, we investigate the sample mean and standard deviation estimation problem under more general settings where the first and third quartiles are also available for the trials. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate that our proposed methods significantly improve upon existing methods and contribute to the literature. Finally, we conclude our work with a comprehensive guidance table for performing meta-analysis in various situations.

title: Fascin protein is critical for transforming growth factor β protein-induced invasion and filopodia formation in spindle-shaped tumor cells.
text: Fascin, an actin-binding protein overexpressed in all carcinomas, has been linked to poor prognosis, shorter survival, and more aggressive metastatic disease. It is believed that fascin facilitates tumor metastasis by promoting the formation of invasive membrane protrusions. However, the underlying mechanisms of fascin overexpression in tumors are not yet fully understood. TGFβ, a cytokine produced by tumor and mesenchymal cells, has been shown to promote metastasis in many late-stage tumors. The mechanisms by which TGFβ induces fascin expression in tumor cells remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that TGFβ induces fascin expression in spindle-shaped tumor cells through the canonical Smad-dependent signaling pathway. Fascin plays a critical role in TGFβ-mediated filopodia formation, migration, and invasion in spindle tumor cells. Moreover, our findings reveal a significant correlation between fascin expression and TGFβ1 and TGFβ receptor I levels in a cohort of primary breast tumor samples. Our data suggest that elevated TGFβ levels in the tumor microenvironment may contribute to fascin overexpression in some metastatic tumors. Furthermore, our findings suggest that fascin may play a central role in TGFβ-induced tumor metastasis.

title: DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types
text:
BACKGROUND:
Currently, there is a lack of knowledge on whether DNA methylation levels can accurately predict age across various human tissues and cell types. Additionally, it is unclear whether the resulting age prediction is a biologically meaningful measure.
RESULTS:
I have developed a multi-tissue predictor of age that enables one to estimate the DNA methylation age of most tissues and cell types. This predictor, which is freely available, was created using 8,000 samples from 82 Illumina DNA methylation array datasets, covering 51 healthy tissues and cell types. This analysis revealed several properties of DNA methylation age, including:
1. It is close to zero for embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells.
2. It coincides with cell passage number.
3. It leads to a highly heritable measure of age acceleration.
4. It is applicable to chimpanzee tissues.

ANALYSIS OF CANCER SAMPLES:

An examination of 6,000 cancer samples from 32 datasets showed that all 20 cancer types exhibited significant age acceleration, with an average of 36 years. Low age-acceleration of cancer tissue is linked to a high number of somatic mutations and TP53 mutations, while mutations in steroid receptors significantly accelerate DNA methylation age in breast cancer.
FINAL CHARACTERIZATION OF AGING CLOCK CPG SITES:

I have identified 353 CpG sites that collectively form an aging clock in terms of chromatin states and tissue variance.
CONCLUSIONS:


I propose that DNA methylation age reflects the cumulative effect of an epigenetic maintenance system. This novel epigenetic clock can be used to address a range of questions in developmental biology, cancer, and aging research.

title: Whole-body MR vascular screening detects unsuspected concomitant vascular disease in coronary heart disease patients
text: Coronary heart disease (CHD) patients often exhibit atherosclerotic vascular disease in other vascular areas, and whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can help detect these concomitant pathologies. In the population-based Heinz Nixdorf Recall Study, 327 CHD patients (age 66.4 years on average) underwent MRI of the brain, heart, and whole body to assess the prevalence of vascular abnormalities. Of these patients, 160 showed signs of stroke on MRI, and 77 had a stenosis of 50% or greater in at least one extracerebral peripheral artery (excluding the coronaries), with 28 cases of relevant renal artery stenoses and 20 cases of relevant extracerebral internal carotid artery stenoses. Additionally, 12 of 81 cases with myocardial infarctions and 11 of 16 cases with cerebrovascular infarctions had false negative histories. This whole-body atherosclerosis MR screening program can detect previously unknown concomitant vascular disease in CHD patients, and its prospective value should be assessed in further studies.

title: Key role of Ubc5 and lysine-63 polyubiquitination in viral activation of IRF3.
text: Mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) plays a crucial role in the immune system's response to RNA viruses. MAVS receives signals from receptors in the cytosol of infected cells, which recognize viral RNA. However, the process by which MAVS triggers the production of type-I interferons is not well understood. To investigate, we created a cell-free system that simulates the interaction between mitochondria from infected cells and the cytosol of uninfected cells. Through this system, we identified a protein called Ubc5 as a vital component of IRF3 activation. Using an inducible RNAi strategy, we showed that Ubc5 is necessary for IRF3 activation by viral infection. Furthermore, we found that two ubiquitin-binding domains of the protein NEMO are also required for IRF3 activation. Our findings suggest that the process of K63 polyubiquitination plays a crucial role in IRF3 activation.

title: Profiling of residual breast cancers after neoadjuvant chemotherapy identifies DUSP4 deficiency as a mechanism of drug resistance
text: Approximately 30% of patients with breast cancer achieve a pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). However, many patients still have residual cancer cells after treatment, which is associated with a higher risk of metastatic recurrence and poorer outcomes. We hypothesized that molecular profiling of tumors after NAC would identify genes involved in drug resistance. Using digital transcript counting, we profiled surgically resected breast cancers after NAC and found that low levels of dual specificity protein phosphatase 4 (DUSP4), an ERK phosphatase, were associated with high post-NAC tumor cell proliferation and basal-like breast cancer (BLBC) status. BLBC had higher DUSP4 promoter methylation and gene expression patterns of Ras-ERK pathway activation compared to other breast cancer subtypes. Overexpression of DUSP4 increased chemotherapy-induced apoptosis, while depletion of DUSP4 dampened the response to chemotherapy. Further, reduced DUSP4 expression in primary tumors after NAC was associated with treatment-refractory high Ki-67 scores and shorter recurrence-free survival. Finally, inhibition of mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK) synergized with docetaxel treatment in BLBC xenografts, suggesting that DUSP4 downregulation activates the Ras-ERK pathway in BLBC, leading to an attenuated response to anti-cancer chemotherapy.

title: Age-related behaviors have distinct transcriptional profiles in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text:
There has been a significant interest in identifying biomarkers of aging, which would allow for the prediction of potential vulnerabilities in individuals before they become chronologically expected. Prior attempts to identify these biomarkers have often relied on comparisons between long-lived animals and control subjects, but the manipulation of model systems that prolong lifespan can have unforeseen consequences, making it difficult to interpret the results. The search for predictive biomarkers of aging is challenging, and the identification of metrics that can accurately predict either physiological or chronological age would be highly valuable.
One methodology that has been used to identify biomarkers for various pathologies is gene expression profiling. Here, we report whole-genome expression profiles of individual wild-type Caenorhabditis elegans across their entire lifespan. Each nematode was scored for age-related behavioral phenotypes or survival and then associated with their respective gene expression profiles. This enabled the identification of transcriptional profiles that were highly associated with either physiological or chronological age.
Our approach provides a paradigm for identifying potential biomarkers of aging in higher organisms that can be repeatedly sampled throughout their lifespan. This could lead to a better understanding of the aging process and the development of interventions to promote healthy aging.

title: Synchronization of Diffusively-Connected Nonlinear Systems: Results Based on Contractions with Respect to General Norms
text: Contraction theory offers a sophisticated means of analyzing the behavior of specific nonlinear dynamical systems. In this work, we explore the application of contraction principles to the synchronization of diffusively interconnected components described by nonlinear differential equations. We present estimates on the convergence of the difference in states between components in situations involving line, complete, and star graphs, as well as Cartesian products of these graph topologies. Our approach relies on contraction theory, which utilizes matrix measures derived from norms that are not induced by inner products. While these norms are frequently employed in practice, the traditional proofs cannot leverage Lyapunov-like linear matrix inequalities, and alternative techniques, such as utilizing the Perron-Frobenius Theorem for L1 or L∞ norms, must be employed.

title: GeneTrack--a genomic data processing and visualization framework.
text: With the advent of high-throughput ChIP-chip and ChIP-seq methodologies, researchers are now faced with managing and analyzing vast datasets, which presents significant informatics challenges, particularly for groups with limited computational resources. To address this challenge, we have developed a software platform to store, analyze, and visualize high-resolution genome-wide binding data. GeneTrack streamlines several stages of the typical data analysis pipeline, including smoothing and peak detection, and provides an easy-to-use web interface for disseminating results. Our software is freely available for download via the Google Project Hosting environment at <https://genetrack.googlecode.com>.

title: Multisite optical recording of excitability in the enteric nervous system.
text: A multisite optical recording technique utilizing an array of 464 photodiodes was employed to measure dynamic changes in transmembrane potentials (Vm) of guinea-pig and mouse enteric neurons stained with the voltage-sensitive dye Di-8-ANEPPS. Optical recordings of Vm fluctuations in enteric neurons triggered by depolarizing current pulses or synaptic activation mirrored the Vm variations measured intracellularly in the same neuron. The fractional change in fluorescence during action potentials was -0.09 +/- 0.06%, with a peak-to-peak noise level of 20 +/- 14% of the action potential amplitude. Optical recordings following electrical stimulation of interganglionic nerve strands revealed slow afterhyperbuildup, nicotinergic supra- and subthreshold fast afterhyperbuildup, and the propagation of action potentials along interganglionic strands. Local application of acetylcholine to a single ganglion led to reproducibly and dose-dependently triggered action potential discharge, demonstrating the feasibility of neuropharmacological studies. The optical mapping allowed for the simultaneous recording of action potentials in a large number of neurons with high spatiotemporal resolution, which is not possible with conventional techniques. This technique provides a valuable tool for examining excitability propagation within enteric circuits and assessing the differential activation of enteric populations in response to various stimuli that affect neuronal activity directly or through synaptic mechanisms.

title: Telomere-bound TRF1 and TRF2 stall the replication fork at telomeric repeats.
text: Vertebrate telomeres are composed of tandem repeats of T2AG3 and associated proteins, including the telomeric DNA-binding proteins TRF1 and TRF2. It has been proposed that telomeres alternate between two states: an open state that permits the entry of various regulatory factors and a closed state that excludes them. TRF1 and TRF2 are thought to promote the closure of telomeres. However, the impact of these two states on DNA replication remains poorly understood. To investigate, we studied the effects of TRF1 and TRF2 on telomeric replication in both in vitro and in vivo experiments. By leveraging the in vitro replication system of linear SV40 DNA, we found that telomeric repeats are a suboptimal replication template. Moreover, the addition of recombinant TRF1 and TRF2 significantly slowed the progression of the replication fork at telomeric repeats. When TRF1 was overexpressed in HeLa cells, cells with 4N DNA content accumulated. Cytological analyses revealed that the replication focus overlapped with telomere signals more frequently in TRF1-overexpressing cells than in control cells, suggesting that TRF1 and TRF2 interfere with replication fork progression.

title: Margination of white blood cells in microcapillary flow.
text: The margination of white blood cells (WBCs) towards vessel walls is a crucial step in their efficient adhesion to the vascular endothelium. To better understand this process, we employed numerical simulations using a two-dimensional blood flow model. Our investigation revealed that the hydrodynamic interactions between blood cells and vessel walls, as well as the collective behavior and deformability of WBCs, significantly influence WBC margination. We found that WBC margination is optimal in intermediate ranges of red blood cell (RBC) volume fractions and flow rates, after which it is significantly reduced. The addition of RBC aggregation enhances WBC margination, while the deformability of WBCs reduces it. These findings have been compiled into state diagrams, which provide a comprehensive understanding of WBC margination across a wide range of flow and cell suspension conditions.

title: Lung cancer treatment waiting times and tumour growth.
text: In this single-center prospective audit, we evaluated 29 lung cancer patients who were awaiting potentially curative radiotherapy. Our analysis included all patients assessable for radical treatment by a single consultant during 1999. At the time of evaluation, these patients had recently been diagnosed and staged using a computed tomographic (CT) scan of the chest. They underwent a subsequent CT scan for treatment planning purposes. We measured tumor size on both diagnostic and planning scans and documented the delay between these examinations and the total time from initial hospital visit to start of treatment. Unfortunately, two patients experienced worsening of symptoms while on the waiting list, rendering them ineligible for radical treatment, while another four had tumor progression on planning CT scans, resulting in an inadequate treatment target volume. Thus, 21% of potentially curable patients became incurable while waiting for treatment. The delay between diagnostic and planning CT scans ranged from 18 to 131 days (median = 54), with corresponding increases in cross-sectional tumor size during this period ranging from zero to 373%. The delay between the initial hospital visit and start of treatment varied from 35 to 187 days (median = 94), while the interval between the radiotherapy request and treatment start ranged from 23 to 61 days (median = 44). The limited availability of specialists is frequently cited as the underlying reason for the UK's poor performance in treating lung cancer. Our findings underscore the adverse impact of waiting times on patient outcomes, even among those fortunate enough to receive specialist referral and be deemed suitable for potentially curative treatment.

title: Functional coupling of RNAP II transcription to spliceosome assembly.
text: The pathway of gene expression in higher eukaryotes involves a highly intricate network of physical and functional interactions among the various machinery involved in each step of the process. In this study, we established a highly efficient in vitro system to investigate how RNA polymerase II (RNAP II) transcription is functionally linked to pre-mRNA splicing. Our findings are quite striking, as we have discovered that nascent pre-mRNA synthesized by RNAP II is immediately and quantitatively directed into the spliceosome assembly pathway, whereas nascent pre-mRNA produced by T7 RNA polymerase is quantitatively assembled into an inhibitory complex called the nonspecific H complex, which is composed of various heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein (hnRNP) proteins. This results in a significant increase in both the kinetics of splicing and the overall yield of spliced mRNA relative to the T7 transcription approach. We conclude that RNAP II mediates the functional coupling of transcription to splicing by directing the nascent pre-mRNA into spliceosome assembly, thereby bypassing the interaction of the pre-mRNA with the inhibitory hnRNP proteins.

title: Calicum microdomains form within neutrophils at the neutrophil–tumor cell synapse: role in antibody-dependent target cell apoptosis
text: Calcium (Ca2+) signals are crucial in cellular signal transduction, with particular importance in immune cell activation. In particular, neutrophil-mediated antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxity (ADCC) plays a significant role in tumor cell killing both in vitro and in clinical settings. By using fluorescence techniques, we discovered that neutrophils exhibit Ca2+ signals during ADCC against breast fibrosarcoma cells. These signals are localized at the interface between neutrophils and tumor cells, displaying dynamic features such as movement, fusion, and fission. The signals were blocked by the intracellular Ca2+ buffer BAPTA, indicating a crucial role for active signaling in the formation of these microdomains. Interestingly, the cytoplasm of neutrophils was found to be enriched in STIM1, a key mediator of Ca2+ signaling, while the Ca2+-binding proteins calbindin and parvalbumin were unaffected. Our findings suggest that Ca2+ microdomains at the neutrophil-tumor cell interface are generated through an active signaling process. Since Ca2+ signals within neutrophils are essential for specific tumor cell apoptosis, it is likely that microdomains play a central role in leukocyte-mediated tumor cell destruction.

title: Platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors reduce mortality in diabetic patients with non-ST-segment-elevation acute coronary syndromes.
text: Diabetes mellitus is a crucial risk factor for unfavorable outcomes following acute coronary syndromes (ACS). This disease could lead to increased platelet aggregation, prompting our investigation into whether diabetes patients with ACS benefit particularly from inhibiting the platelet glycoprotein (GP) IIb/IIIa receptor. We conducted a meta-analysis of the diabetic populations enrolled in 6 large-scale platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor ACS trials: PRISM, PRISM-PLUS, PARAGON A, PARAGON B, PURSUIT, and GUSTO IV, consisting of 6458 diabetic patients. Our analysis showed that platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibition was associated with a statistically significant reduction in mortality at 30 days, from 6.2% to 4.6% (OR 0.74; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.92; P=0.007). In contrast, the lack of benefit was observed in 23 072 nondiabetic patients (3.0% versus 3.0%). A statistically significant interaction between platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibition and diabetic status was observed (P=0.036). Out of 1279 diabetic patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) during the index hospitalization, we found a mortality reduction at 30 days from 4.0% to 1.2% (OR 0.30; 95% CI 0.14 to 0.69; P=0.002). Our findings, which encompass the entire large-scale trial experience of intravenous platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors for the medical management of non-ST-segment-elevation ACS, suggest that these agents may significantly reduce mortality at 30 days in diabetic patients. Although not based on a randomized assessment, the survival benefit appears to be more pronounced in patients undergoing PCI. Accordingly, the use of platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors should be strongly considered in diabetic patients with ACS.

title: Glucose deprivation-induced cytotoxicity and alterations in mitogen-activated protein kinase activation are mediated by oxidative stress in multidrug-resistant human breast carcinoma cells.
text: In a previous study, we discovered that depriving human breast carcinoma cells (MCF-7/ADR) of glucose leads to cell death. As a follow-up, we sought to investigate whether metabolic oxidative stress was the underlying cause or at least a contributing factor in this process. Our findings show that the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway is activated within 3 minutes of being placed in glucose-free medium and remains active for 3 hours. Glucose deprivation for 2-4 hours also leads to oxidative stress, as evidenced by a 3-fold increase in the steady state concentration of oxidized glutathione and a 3-fold increase in pro-oxidant production. Interestingly, glucose and glutamate treatment can suppress MAPK activation and rescue cells from cytotoxicity, while glutamate and the peroxide scavenger, pyruvate, can also rescue cells from cell killing and suppress pro-oxidant production. Additionally, the thiol antioxidant, N-acetyl-L-cysteine, can rescue cells from glucose deprivation-induced cytotoxicity and suppress MAPK activation. These results suggest that glucose deprivation-induced cytotoxicity and alterations in MAPK signal transduction are indeed mediated by oxidative stress in MCF-7/ADR cells. Our findings also support the hypothesis that a common mechanism of glucose deprivation-induced cytotoxicity in mammalian cells may involve metabolic oxidative stress.

title: A structural basis for kinetochore recruitment of the Ndc80 complex via two distinct centromere receptors.
text: The Ndc80 complex is the primary microtubule-binding component of the kinetochore. In contrast to the well-known interaction between Ndc80-Nuf2 subunits and microtubules, little is understood about how the Spc24-25 heterodimer connects to centromeric chromatin. This study sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying this connection, revealing how Spc24-25 interacts with the histone-fold protein Cnn1/CENP-T to link microtubules to chromosomes. The Ndc80 receptor motif of Cnn1 is bound by an α helix in a hydrophobic cleft near the interface between Spc24 and Spc25. Point mutations that disrupt the Ndc80-Cnn1 interaction also hinder the binding of the Mtw1 complex and are lethal in yeast. Interestingly, we identify a Cnn1-related motif in the Dsn1 subunit of the Mtw1 complex, which is essential for Ndc80 binding and indispensable for yeast growth. Replacing this region with the Cnn1 peptide restores viability, demonstrating the functionality of the Ndc80-binding module in different molecular contexts. Furthermore, phosphorylation of the Cnn1 N-terminus coordinates the binding of the two competing Ndc80 interaction partners. Our findings provide insightful structural information into the modular binding mechanism of the Ndc80 complex to its centromeric recruiters.

title: Feedback Circuit among INK4 Tumor Suppressors Constrains Human Glioblastoma Development
text: Using a non-heuristic genome topography scan (GTS) algorithm, we have identified patterns of genomic alterations in human glioblastoma (GBM), including frequent codeletion of p18(INK4C) and p16(INK4A). Functional studies revealed that restoration of p18(INK4C) in GBM cells lacking both p16(INK4A) and p18(INK4C) resulted in impaired cell-cycle progression and tumorigenic potential. Conversely, RNAi-mediated depletion of p18(INK4C) in p16(INK4A)-deficient primary astrocytes or established GBM cells led to enhanced tumorigenicity in vitro and in vivo. Moreover, acute suppression of p16(INK4A) in primary astrocytes was accompanied by an increase in p18(INK4C). These findings delineate a feedback regulatory circuit in the astrocytic lineage and demonstrate the tumor suppressor function of p18(INK4C) in human GBM, where it functions cooperatively with other INK4 family members to restrict inappropriate proliferation.

title: The SMC5/6 complex maintains telomere length in ALT cancer cells through SUMOylation of telomere-binding proteins
text: Most cancer cells activate telomerase to extend telomeres and achieve limitless replicative potential. However, some cancer cells are unable to activate telomerase and instead employ telomere homologous recombination (HR) to lengthen telomeres, a process known as alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT). A characteristic of ALT cells is the recruitment of telomeres to PML bodies (termed APBs). Here, we demonstrate that the SMC5/6 complex localizes to APBs in ALT cells and is necessary for directing telomeres to APBs. The MMS21 SUMO ligase, which is a component of the SMC5/6 complex, SUMOylates multiple telomere-binding proteins, including TRF1 and TRF2. Inhibition of TRF1 or TRF2 SUMOylation impedes APB formation. Depletion of SMC5/6 subunits through RNA interference prevents telomere HR in ALT cells, leading to telomere shortening and senescence. Thus, the SMC5/6 complex facilitates telomere HR and elongation in ALT cells by promoting APB formation through SUMOylation of telomere-binding proteins.

title: Dynein pulls microtubules without rotating its stalk.
text: Dynein is a microtubule motor that propels the movement of cilia and flagella through a conformational change in its motor domain. While the exact mechanism has been debated, our new study provides the clearest visual evidence yet of dynein in action. Using a novel imaging technique called "cryo-positive stain" electron microscopy, we were able to observe the stalks of dynein molecules bound to microtubules in sea urchin outer arm dynein. These observations revealed that the stalks are actually active in motility assays, despite earlier assumptions that they acted as a lever arm. Instead, our findings suggest that dynein uses its stalk as a grappling hook, catching and pulling on tubulin subunits 8 nanometers ahead of the motor domain. This new mechanism challenges prevailing models of dynein function.

title: The INO80 chromatin remodeling complex in transcription, replication and repair.
text: The Ino80 ATPase is a member of the SNF2 family of ATPases and forms an integral part of a multisubunit ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complex. Despite sharing a common core of conserved subunits, INO80 complexes from yeast and higher eukaryotes have diverged significantly during evolution, acquiring new subunits with species-specific functions. Recent research has shown that the INO80 complex plays a crucial role in a wide range of chromatin-dependent nuclear processes, including transcription, DNA repair, and DNA replication.

title: VEX1 controls the allelic exclusion required for antigenic variation in trypanosomes.
text: The mechanism of allelic exclusion in African trypanosomes is supported by the exclusive use of RNA polymerase-I (pol-I) to transcribe a single telomeric variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) gene at a time, resulting in superabundant and switchable VSG coats. We identified the trypanosome protein VSG exclusion-1 (VEX1) through a genetic screen for defects in telomere-exclusive expression. VEX1 was found to be sequestered by the active VSG, and the silencing of other VSGs was discovered to be dependent on VEX1's presence. VEX1's regulation of VSGs was found to be both positively and negatively regulated, with the former affecting VSGs and non-telomeric pol-I-transcribed genes, while the latter primarily affected VSGs. Additionally, VEX1-mediated silencing also affected telomeric pol-I-transcribed reporter constructs, but only when they contained blocks of sequence sharing homology with a pol-I-transcribed locus. Based on these findings, we propose that the restricted positive regulation due to VEX1 sequestration, combined with VEX1-dependent homology-dependent silencing, drives a "winner-takes-all" mechanism of allelic exclusion.

title: Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) regulates monocyte differentiation and functions in mBSA and IL-1β-induced arthritis.
text: Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) plays a crucial role in regulating various immune cell populations, including monocytes. In our previous studies, we demonstrated that KLF2 inhibits the pro-inflammatory activation of monocytes. However, the role of KLF2 in arthritis remains unexplored. In this investigation, we observed that KLF2 hemizygous mice displayed a significant increase in the recruitment of inflammatory monocyte subsets, including CD11b(+)F4/80(+)Ly6C(+) cells, to inflammation sites compared to wild-type littermate controls. Simultaneously, we found that inflammatory mediators, such as MCP-1, Cox-2, and PAI-1, were significantly upregulated in bone marrow-derived monocytes from KLF2 hemizygous mice compared to wild-type controls. Moreover, arthritis was more severe in KLF2 hemizygous mice as compared to littermate wild-type controls, accompanied by an increased number of monocytes matured and differentiated towards osteoclastic lineage. This corresponded with higher expression levels of proteins such as HSP60, HSP90, and MMP13, and reduced levels of pPTEN, p21, p38, and HSP25/27 molecules in bone marrow cells from arthritic KLF2 hemizygous mice compared to littermate wild-type controls. Our findings provide new insights into the KLF2-mediated regulation of arthritis through modulation of monocyte differentiation and function.

title: Relationship of collegiate football experience and concussion with hippocampal volume and cognitive outcomes.
text: In this study, we investigated the long-term effects of concussions and years of football experience on the brain volume of collegiate football players. We found that players with a history of concussion had significantly smaller hippocampal volumes compared to those without a history of concussion, and this difference was more pronounced in players with more years of football experience. Additionally, we found a negative correlation between years of football play and reaction time, indicating that longer years of playing football were associated with slower reaction times. These findings suggest that there may be a temporal relationship between concussions, brain volume, and cognitive performance in football players. Further research is needed to determine the nature of this relationship and to better understand the long-term effects of concussions on the brain.

title: STING and the innate immune response to nucleic acids in the cytosol
text: The detection of pathogen-derived nucleic acids in the cytosol is crucial for the activation of the innate immune system against a wide range of bacterial, viral, and eukaryotic pathogens. However, inappropriate responses to cytosolic nucleic acids can lead to severe autoimmune disorders. The host protein STING has been identified as a central signaling molecule in the innate immune response to cytosolic nucleic acids, with particular relevance for responses to cytosolic DNA and the distinct bacterial nucleic acids known as 'cyclic dinucleotides'. This review aims to summarize the current understanding of STING and highlight the numerous unresolved issues in the field.

title: Global Assessment of Genomic Regions Required for Growth in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
text: Elucidating the genomic elements essential for bacterial viability is pivotal to understanding the fundamental physiology of pathogenic microorganisms. Advances in high-density mutagenesis and deep sequencing have enabled the identification of both necessary and conditionally indispensable genes in various bacteria. While genes form a significant portion of the impressive genome of important pathogens, our study aimed to comprehensively identify all genomic segments, including functional genes, domains, and non-coding regions, crucial for the optimal growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a leading global health menace. Our findings revealed that multiple proteins collaborate by possessing both essential and dispensable domains for growth. Moreover, our analysis uncovered a substantial number of non-coding regions, including regulatory elements and non-coding RNAs, that play a critical role in mycobacterial growth. Our analysis showed that the genetic requirements for growth are more intricate than previously supposed using gene-centric approaches.

title: Cyclooxygenase-Dependent Tumor Growth through Evasion of Immunity
text: The processes by which cancer cells, including melanoma, evade the immune system are not fully understood. We have discovered that tumors formed by mutant Braf(V600E) mouse melanoma cells in an immunocompetent host depend on the production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), which suppresses the immune system and promotes tumor-favoring inflammation. Genetic ablation of cyclooxygenases (COX) or prostaglandin E synthases in these cells makes them susceptible to immune control and shifts the tumor inflammatory profile towards pro-immune pathways. This signature is conserved in human cutaneous melanoma biopsies, suggesting that COX activity plays a key role in immune suppression across species. Our preclinical data also show that inhibiting COX synergizes with anti-PD-1 blockade in eradicating tumors, suggesting that COX inhibitors could be useful adjuvants in cancer immunotherapy.

title: Anti-alphav integrin monoclonal antibody intetumumab enhances the efficacy of radiation therapy and reduces metastasis of human cancer xenografts in nude rats.
text: In a previous study, we discovered that intetumumab (CNTO 95), a fully human anti-αv integrin monoclonal antibody, acts as a radiosensitizer in mice with xenograft tumors. Since intetumumab does not react with mouse integrins but does react with rat integrins, we then investigated the potential of combining radiation therapy and intetumumab in human cancer xenograft models in nude rats. Nude rats bearing human head and neck cancer and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) xenografts were treated with intetumumab and fractionated local tumor radiotherapy. Our findings showed that intetumumab alone had a moderate effect on tumor growth, but when combined with radiation therapy, the treatment significantly inhibited tumor growth and produced a better tumor response rate than with radiation therapy alone. In addition, treatment with intetumumab significantly reduced lung metastasis in the A549 NSCLC xenograft model. We also observed an increase in oxygenation and blood perfusion in xenograft tumors after treatment with intetumumab, as measured by microbubble-enhanced ultrasound imaging. Treatment with intetumumab reduced the microvessel density and increased apoptosis in both tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, we found that treatment with intetumumab did not cause histopathologic changes in the lungs or sensitize the sensitive gastrointestinal epithelium to the effects of radiation therapy. Overall, our results suggest that intetumumab can enhance the efficacy of fractionated radiation therapy in human cancer xenograft tumors in nude rats without an increase in toxicity.

title: Methylomic trajectories across human fetal brain development.
text:
Epigenetic processes play a crucial role in regulating gene expression during fetal brain development. The importance of DNA methylation in this process is highlighted by the dynamic expression of de novo DNA methyltransferases during the perinatal period and the neurodevelopmental deficits associated with mutations in the methyl-CpG binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene. However, the temporal changes to the epigenome during fetal brain development have been relatively unexplored until now.
We recently conducted a study that quantified genome-wide patterns of DNA methylation at over 400,000 sites in 179 human fetal brain samples spanning 23 to 184 days post-conception. We found significant changes in DNA methylation across fetal brain development at over 7% of sites, with a enrichment of loci becoming hypomethylated with fetal age. Further analysis revealed that sites associated with developmental changes in DNA methylation during fetal brain development were underrepresented in promoter regulatory regions but overrepresented in regions flanking CpG islands (shores and shelves) and gene bodies.
Interestingly, we also observed significant differences in DNA methylation between males and females at a number of autosomal sites, with some regions showing sex-specific DNA methylation trajectories across brain development. To further explore these findings, we used weighted gene comethylation network analysis (WGCNA) to identify discrete modules of comethylated loci associated with fetal age. These modules were found to be significantly enriched for genes involved in neurodevelopmental processes, highlighting the importance of epigenetic regulation in the development of the fetal brain.
Overall, this study represents the most comprehensive investigation of DNA methylation across human fetal brain development to date, underscoring the dynamic nature of the epigenome during this critical period of prenatal development.

title: Synaptic Determinants of Rett Syndrome
text: There is growing evidence indicating that the structural and molecular organization of synaptic connections is impacted in both human patients and animal models of neurological and psychiatric diseases. As a result of these findings, the concept of synapsopathies has been introduced, which refers to brain disorders related to synaptic function and plasticity. Particularly relevant to diseases featuring mental retardation in their symptomology, such as Rett syndrome (RS), is the close correlation between neurological diseases and synaptic abnormalities. RS (MIM312750) is an X-linked dominant neurological disorder caused by mutations in methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) in the majority of cases. This review focuses on the current knowledge of the synaptic alterations caused by MeCP2 mutations in mouse models of RS, highlights potential experimental therapies in use, and discusses how understanding the effects of diseases such as RS on the brain can bring us closer to identifying the neurobiological bases of human cognition. Different experimental approaches have shown that RS may result from an impairment in the homeostasis of synaptic transmission in specific brain regions, as several forms of experience-induced neuronal plasticity are compromised in the absence of MeCP2. Based on the results presented in this review, it is reasonable to propose that uncovering the neurobiological mechanisms underlying diseases such as RS will put us closer to understanding the human brain and its intricate functional diversity.

title: Depressive symptoms and physical decline in community-dwelling older persons.
text: Older adults in community settings are commonly affected by symptoms of depression. However, it is unclear whether these symptoms directly contribute to subsequent decline in physical function. To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a 4-year prospective cohort study among 1286 individuals aged 71 years and older. We assessed their baseline depressive symptoms using the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale and performed objective tests of physical performance, including standing balance, a 2.4-m (8-ft) walk, and rising from a chair and sitting down. Our results indicate that higher levels of depressive symptoms are associated with greater decline in physical performance over time, even after adjusting for baseline performance score, health status, and sociodemographic factors. Furthermore, the risk of decline was evident among those at the high end of the functional spectrum who reported no disability, suggesting that reducing depressive symptoms could play a role in reducing functional decline in older adults. In conclusion, our study suggests that older adults who experience depressive symptoms are at higher risk of subsequent physical decline, highlighting the importance of addressing depression in prevention and treatment strategies aimed at preserving functional ability in this population.

title: Foxk proteins repress the initiation of starvation-induced atrophy and autophagy programs
text: Autophagy is the primary catabolic response triggered by starvation, and while the regulation of this process within the cytosolic compartment is well understood, the role of nuclear events in modulating autophagy induction or repression is becoming increasingly clear. However, a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms by which sequence-specific transcription factors regulate the expression of genes required for autophagy remains elusive. In this study, we identify Foxk proteins (Foxk1 and Foxk2) as transcriptional repressors of autophagy in muscle cells and fibroblasts. Notably, Foxk1/2 counterbalance the induction of autophagic and atrophic targets by another forkhead transcription factor, Foxo3. Foxk1/2 recruits Sin3A-HDAC complexes to restrain acetylation of histone H4 and suppress the expression of critical autophagy genes. Surprisingly, mTOR promotes the transcriptional activity of Foxk1 by facilitating nuclear entry to restrict basal levels of autophagy in nutrient-rich conditions. Our findings reveal an ancient and conserved mechanism by which nutritional status is interpreted by mTOR to restrict autophagy by repressing essential autophagy genes through Foxk-Sin3-mediated transcriptional control.

title: PRRSV receptors and their roles in virus infection
text: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) has a limited host range and prefers to infect well-differentiated cells of the monocyte/macrophage lineage, such as pulmonary alveolar macrophages and African green monkey kidney cell line MA-104 and its derivatives, including Marc-145, Vero, and CL-2621. The PRRSV infection process involves receptor-mediated endocytosis and replication, and the expression of cellular receptors determines whether cell lines are permissive or non-permissive to infection. Recently, several PRRSV non-permissive cell lines, such as BHK-21, PK-15, and CHO-K1, have been shown to become susceptible to PRRSV infection after expressing recombinant receptor proteins. Heparin sulfate, sialoadhesin, CD163, CD151, and vimentin have been identified as the key PRRSV receptors, each with distinct distribution and function in virus attachment, internalization, and uncoating. The specific function of these receptors has attracted attention due to their potential as targets for designing new anti-viral reagents or recombinant cell lines for isolating viruses or developing more effective vaccines. In this review, we will discuss the role of PRRSV receptors and the molecular mechanisms of the virus-receptor interaction.

title: Kinetic Analysis Reveals the Fate of a MicroRNA following Target Regulation in Mammalian Cells
text: Significant progress has been made in understanding the process of microRNA (miRNA) biogenesis and regulation, but little is known about the fate of miRNAs after they regulate their target molecules. To gain insights into this process, we conducted kinetic analysis of miRNA turnover following termination of biogenesis and during regulation of a target that is not subject to Ago2-mediated catalytic cleavage. By quantifying the number of miRNA and target molecules in steady state and during decay, we found that each miRNA molecule can regulate at least two target transcripts, providing in vivo evidence that the miRNA is not irreversibly sequestered with its target and that the nonslicing pathway of miRNA regulation is multiple-turnover. Using deep sequencing, we further revealed that miRNA recycling is limited by target regulation, which promotes posttranscriptional modifications to the 3' end of the miRNA and accelerates its rate of decay. These studies provide new insights into the efficiency of miRNA regulation and help explain how a miRNA can regulate a large number of transcripts, while identifying one of the mechanisms that impart specificity to miRNA decay in mammalian cells.

title: Estimation of nuclear DNA content in plants using flow cytometry
text: Flow cytometry (FCM) using DNA-selective fluorochromes is currently the preferred method for measuring nuclear DNA content in plants. Its ease of sample preparation and high sample throughput make it more suitable than other methods, such as Feulgen densitometry, for estimating genome size, level of generative polyploidy, nuclear replication state, and endopolyploidy (polysomaty). We provide detailed protocols for preparing suspensions of intact cell nuclei and explain the analysis of nuclear DNA amounts using FCM. We outline the necessary chemicals and equipment, the measurement process, data analysis, and address common problems encountered with plant material, such as interference from secondary metabolites. The importance of proper term usage and genome size principles are also discussed.

title: Predictive value of bone resorption and formation markers in cancer patients with bone metastases receiving the bisphosphonate zoledronic acid.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the correlation between bone metabolism and clinical outcomes in patients with bone metastases receiving bisphosphonate therapy. The study included 1,824 patients, of whom 1,462 were treated with zoledronic acid and 362 with pamidronate. The researchers measured urinary levels of N-telopeptide (Ntx) and serum bone alkaline phosphatase (BAP) in these patients and grouped them based on their baseline and most recent levels of these markers. The study found that patients with high and moderate levels of Ntx had a significantly higher risk of skeletal complications and disease progression compared to those with low levels. Additionally, high Ntx levels were associated with a 4-6 fold increased risk of death in each solid tumor category, while moderate levels were associated with a 2-4 fold increased risk compared to low levels. Similarly, BAP levels also showed a correlation with the risk of negative clinical outcomes. These findings suggest that Ntx provides valuable prognostic information in patients with bone metastases receiving bisphosphonate therapy.

title: Role of CD28-B7 interactions in generation and maintenance of CD8 T cell memory.
text: Although the role of CD28-B7 interactions in activating naive T cells is well-established, the importance of these interactions in generating and maintaining T cell memory is not fully understood. In this study, we investigated the requirement for CD28-B7 interactions in primary T cell activation and immune memory using CD28-deficient (CD28(-/-)) mice and comparison to wild-type (+/+) mice following an acute infection with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV). Our findings showed that during the primary response, both LCMV-specific CD8 T cells were activated and expanded in both +/+ and CD28(-/-) mice, with a slight reduction in the magnitude of the primary CD8 T cell response in CD28(-/-) mice. However, blocking B7-mediated costimulation by CTLA4-Ig treatment of +/+ mice resulted in a similar reduction in anti-LCMV CD8 T cell responses. Importantly, loss of CD28/B7 interactions did not significantly affect the generation and maintenance of CD8 T cell memory, as the magnitude of CD8 T cell memory was only slightly lower in CD28(-/-) mice compared to +/+ mice. Furthermore, LCMV-specific memory CD8 T cells from CD28(-/-) mice showed normal homeostatic proliferation in vivo and conferred protective immunity, indicating that CD28 signaling is not necessary for the proliferative renewal and maintenance of memory CD8 T cells.

title: Systematic reviews from astronomy to zoology: myths and misconceptions.
text:
Systematic literature reviews are widely utilized as a tool for evidence-based decision making. For instance, reviews of randomized controlled trials are frequently employed to answer questions regarding the effectiveness of healthcare interventions. However, the high profile of systematic reviews as a cornerstone of evidence-based medicine has led to several misconceptions about their purpose and methods. One of these misconceptions is the belief that systematic reviews are limited to randomized controlled trials and are unable to evaluate other forms of evidence, such as non-randomized studies or qualitative research. In reality, systematic literature reviews are a method of locating, assessing, and synthesizing evidence. The value of regularly updated systematic reviews in evaluating the effectiveness of healthcare interventions was pointed out by Antman and colleagues, who demonstrated that review articles frequently failed to acknowledge advances in treatment identified by an updated systematic review.
Since the term "meta-analysis" was first coined by Gene Glass in 1976 to refer to the quantitative synthesis of primary study results, it has been recognized that making explicit efforts to reduce bias in the review of literature is crucial. Despite this, claims that systematic reviews are not required or desirable have arisen, and these arguments often stem from misunderstandings about the origins, purpose, methods, and applications of systematic reviews. Eight common myths about systematic reviews have been identified, and this article will examine each of them.

title: Acellular pertussis vaccines protect against disease but fail to prevent infection and transmission in a nonhuman primate model.
text:
Pertussis, a highly contagious respiratory illness caused by the bacterial pathogen Bordetella pertussis, has seen a significant increase in cases in the United States, with a record high of 42,000 cases in 2012. While the resurgence of pertussis is not fully understood, researchers hypothesize that the current acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines may not be effective in preventing both colonization and transmission of the disease.
To test this hypothesis, infant baboons were vaccinated at 2, 4, and 6 months of age with either aP or whole-cell pertussis (wP) vaccines and then challenged with B. pertussis at 7 months. The study found that baboons vaccinated with aP were protected from severe pertussis-associated symptoms, but not from colonization, and were able to transmit the infection to unvaccinated contacts.
