In contrast, vaccination with wP led to a more rapid clearance of the infection compared to both naïve animals and those vaccinated with aP. Additionally, previously infected animals and those vaccinated with wP had strong B. pertussis-specific T helper 17 (Th17) memory and Th1 memory, whereas aP vaccination induced a Th1/Th2 response.
These findings suggest that the use of aP vaccines, which induce an immune response mismatched to that induced by natural infection, may explain the resurgence of pertussis and highlight the need for the development of improved vaccines to effectively control the disease.

title: Specific and cooperative binding of E. coli single-stranded DNA binding protein to mRNA.
text: A fluorometric titration study on the single-stranded DNA binding protein (SSB) from E. coli revealed that the protein selectively and cooperatively binds to its own mRNA. This binding inhibited the in vitro expression of SSb and bla genes, but not the nusA gene, at a physiological concentration of SSB. These findings suggest that the SSB protein plays a crucial role in gene regulation.

title: ACAM2000™: The new smallpox vaccine for United States Strategic National Stockpile
text: Since the eradication of smallpox more than three decades ago, concerns about bioterrorism have led to a renewed interest in smallpox vaccination. During the early 2000s, the previously licensed smallpox vaccine, Dryvax (Wyeth Laboratories, Inc.), was found to be insufficient for vaccinating the entire US population due to its limited supply. Moreover, Dryvax had a questionable safety profile due to its composition of a pool of vaccinia virus strains with varying degrees of virulence, which was grown on the skin of calves, a technique that posed an unnecessary risk of contamination. In response, the US government supported the development of an improved live vaccinia virus smallpox vaccine. This initiative resulted in the development of ACAM2000 (Acambis, Inc.), a single plaque-purified vaccinia virus derivative of Dryvax, aseptically propagated in cell culture. Preclinical and clinical trials conducted in 2008 demonstrated that ACAM2000 shows comparable immunogenicity to Dryvax and causes a similar frequency of adverse events. Additionally, through careful cardiac screening, ACAM2000 was found to result in an unexpectedly high rate of myocarditis and pericarditis. Following successful clinical trials, ACAM2000 received US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval in August 2007, and subsequently replaced Dryvax for all smallpox vaccinations in February 2008. To date, over 200 million doses of ACAM2000 have been produced and stockpiled within the US Strategic National Stockpile. This review focuses on the production, characterization, clinical trials, and adverse events associated with this newly developed smallpox vaccine, ACAM2000.

title: Risk of malignant neoplasms in patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis.
text:
BACKGROUND: For over two decades, there has been debate regarding the association between sarcoidosis and malignancy, particularly lymphoma and lung cancer. The aim of the present study was to determine the incidence of malignancies in a cohort of patients with sarcoidosis by linking their data to a nationwide population-based cancer register.
METHODS: The cohort consisted of 254 patients followed for a median of 25 years until death, emigration, or December 31, 1992, whichever came first. The expected number of cancer cases was calculated using the annual age- and sex-specific cancer rates from the Danish Cancer Registry.
RESULTS: Thirty-six cancers were registered, with three misclassified as sarcoidosis, leaving 33 cancers compared to 23 expected (standardised incidence ratio (SIR) = 1.4; 95% CI 0.99-2.0). Five lung cancers were observed compared to 2.5 expected, resulting in an SIR of 2.0 (95% CI 0.7-4.7). There was no incidence of lymphoma, and only one case of leukaemia. Additionally, there was a significant excess number of pharyngeal cancers, based on two cases (SIR = 15.4; 95% CI 1.7-56).
CONCLUSIONS: This study does not support the theory of an association between sarcoidosis and malignancy. The main reason other studies have shown such an association is likely due to selection bias and misclassification.

title: Rps14 haploinsufficiency causes a block in erythroid differentiation mediated by S100A8 and S100A9
text: The deletion of chromosome 5q (del(5q)) in the myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) subtype is associated with a genetic alteration that leads to heterozygous deletion of RPS14, which encodes the ribosomal protein small subunit 14. We created mice with conditional mutations in Rps14 and found that the erythroid differentiation process is impaired due to the tumor suppressor protein p53 (Trp53 in mice), which results in an age-dependent progression of anemia, megakaryocyte dysplasia, and loss of hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) quiescence. Using quantitative proteomics, we discovered that mutant erythroblasts exhibit increased expression levels of proteins involved in innate immune signaling, specifically the heterodimeric S100 calcium-binding proteins S100a8 and S100a9. S100a8, which displays elevated expression in mutant erythroblasts, monocytes, and macrophages, plays a functional role in the erythroid defect caused by Rps14 haploinsufficiency. We observed that addition of recombinant S100a8 can induce a differentiation defect in wild-type erythroid cells, and genetic inactivation of S100a8 expression can rescue the erythroid differentiation defect of Rps14-haploinsufficient HSCs. Our findings establish a link between Rps14 haploinsufficiency in del(5q) MDS and the activation of the innate immune system, leading to S100A8-S100A9 expression and a p53-dependent erythroid differentiation defect.

title: A Microtubule Interactome: Complexes with Roles in Cell Cycle and Mitosis
text: The cytoskeleton, specifically the microtubules (MTs), play a crucial role in various cellular processes, including the transportation of intracellular materials, maintenance of cell polarity, and regulation of mitosis. These functions are coordinated by MT-associated proteins (MAPs), which work together to bind MTs and modify their properties. Using a combination of cytosomal sedimentation assays, one-dimensional (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE), and mass spectrometry, we identified over 250 MAPs in early Drosophila embryos. To further analyze the cellular function of these novel MAPs, we adopted two complementary approaches. First, we carried out an RNA interference (RNAi) screen to identify 21 previously uncharacterized genes involved in MT organization. Second, we conducted a bioinformatics analysis based on binary protein interaction data to generate putative interaction networks of MAPs. By integrating both approaches, we identified and validated MAP complexes with potential important roles in cell cycle regulation and mitosis. This study demonstrates that a multidisciplinary approach can yield biologically relevant data, and discovers new MAPs, many of which may play crucial roles in cell division.

title: Structure of the Guanine Nucleotide Exchange Factor Sec7 Domain of Human Arno and Analysis of the Interaction with ARF GTPase
text: Sec7-related guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) initiate vesicle budding from the Golgi membrane surface by converting the GTPase ARF to a GTP-bound, membrane-associated form. In this study, we report the crystal structure of the catalytic Sec7 homology domain of Arno, a human GEF for ARF1, at 2.2 angstroms resolution. The Sec7 domain is a long, completely helical protein with a distinctive hydrophobic groove that is evolutionarily conserved. Using structure-based mutagenesis, we identify the groove and an adjacent conserved loop as the ARF-interacting surface. Subsequent protein footprinting experiments localize the sites of Sec7 domain interaction on ARF1 to the switch 1 and switch 2 GTPase regions, allowing us to propose a model for the interaction between ARF GTPases and Sec7 domain exchange factors.

title: Brief Communication Repeated Cocaine Administration Increases Voltage-Sensitive Calcium Currents in Response to Membrane Depolarization in Medial Prefrontal Cortex Pyramidal Neurons
text: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) plays a crucial role in cocaine addiction, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Recent studies have revealed that repeated cocaine administration leads to changes in pyramidal mPFC neurons, including a reduction in voltage-gated potassium currents (VGKCs) and a possible increase in voltage-sensitive calcium currents (I(Ca)). To investigate the functional implications of these changes, we conducted both current-clamp recordings in brain slices and voltage-clamp recordings in freshly dissociated cells in mPFC neurons after chronic cocaine treatment with either a short-term or long-term withdrawal. We found that repeated cocaine administration significantly prolonged the duration of evoked calcium plateau potentials and increased the whole-cell I(Ca) in mPFC neurons after a 3-day withdrawal. Moreover, selective blockade of L-type calcium channels using nifedipine not only increased the threshold but also reduced the duration and amplitude of calcium plateau potentials in both saline- and cocaine-withdrawn mPFC neurons. However, there was no significant difference in the increased threshold, reduced duration, and decreased amplitude of calcium potentials between saline- and cocaine-withdrawn neurons after blockade of L-type calcium channels. Additionally, we observed an increase in amplitude and a prolonged duration of calcium potentials after 2-3 weeks of withdrawal. These findings suggest that chronic exposure to cocaine enhances the responsiveness of I(Ca), particularly via activated L-type calcium channels, to excitatory stimuli in rat mPFC pyramidal neurons.

title: Rational Extension of the Ribosome Biogenesis Pathway Using Network-Guided Genetics
text: The biogenesis of ribosomes is a critical cellular process that is conserved across all eukaryotes and requires over 170 genes to assemble, modify, and transport ribosome components through various cellular compartments. Despite extensive research, it is likely that many additional genes are involved in this pathway. To identify these genes, we employed network-guided genetics, a strategy that leverages recent advances in functional genomic and proteomic studies to predict candidate genes involved in ribosomal biogenesis. We experimentally evaluated over 100 candidate yeast genes using a range of assays and discovered at least 15 new genes, including previously uncharacterized genes. We found that these genes are involved in specific aspects of ribosomal subunit maturation, association with ribosomal particles, and nuclear export of ribosomal subunits, and that some genes are specifically required for the processing of different types of rRNA molecules, including 5S, 7S, 20S, 27S, and 35S rRNAs. These findings greatly expand our understanding of a universally conserved eukaryotic process and add over 10% new genes, many with human orthologs, to the biogenesis pathway.

title: Quantifying Transmission Investment in Malaria Parasites
text:
A significant portion of microparasites infect new hosts with unique life stages, requiring a subpopulation of parasites to forgo reproduction and develop into transmission forms. Transmission stage production has a profound impact on infectivity, host exploitation, and the effectiveness of medical interventions, such as drug treatment. To predict how parasites will respond to public health efforts on both an epidemiological and evolutionary scale, it is essential to understand transmission strategies, which can be challenging to observe directly and often require inference from infection dynamics.
Using malaria as a case study, we evaluated the accuracy of existing methods for inferring transmission stage investment by comparing them to simulated data generated using a model of within-host infection dynamics. We found that existing methods are insufficient and potentially very misleading due to the difficulty in distinguishing transmission stages produced by different generations of parasites.
To overcome this challenge, we developed a new approach that demonstrates significantly improved performance on simulated data. By applying this approach to real data from mice infected with a single Plasmodium chabaudi strain, we discovered that transmission investment varies from zero to 20%, with evidence of variable investment over time in some hosts but not others. These findings suggest that, even in experimental infections where host genetics and other environmental factors are controlled, parasites may exhibit diverse patterns of transmission investment.

title: Roles of induced expression of MAPK phosphatase-2 in tumor development in RET-MEN2A transgenic mice
text: Germline mutations in the RET tyrosine kinase gene are causally linked to the development of multiple endocrine neoplasia 2A and 2B (MEN2A and MEN2B). Nonetheless, elucidating the underlying principles that govern the aberrant signaling pathways initiated by mutant RET remains an enigmatic challenge. In this study, we undertook to investigate the expression of mitogen-activated protein kinase phosphatase-2 (MKP-2) in carcinomas derived from transgenic mice harboring RET mutations. Surprisingly, we discovered that MKP-2 is overexpressed in carcinomas developing from both RET-MEN2A and RET-MEN2B mutant proteins, as well as in response to endogenous RET activation by its ligand, glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF). Intriguingly, MKP-2 was also expressed in a MEN2A-derived cell line (MKK-f), which was established from a mammary tumor developed in a RET-MEN2A transgenic mouse. To further explore the functional significance of MKP-2 upregulation in this context, we evaluated the effect of MKP-2 inhibition on the in vitro and in vivo proliferation of MKK-f cells. Our findings showed that MKP-2 inhibition significantly attenuated the proliferation of MKK-f cells, which was accompanied by a decrease in cyclin B1 expression. Notably, we also found that MKP-2 is extensively expressed in medullary thyroid carcinomas derived from MEN2A patients, suggesting that the enhanced expression of MKP-2 may play a pivotal role in the altered signaling cascade downstream of mutant RET, ultimately leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation.

title: Effects of repeated social stress on leukocyte distribution in bone marrow, peripheral blood and spleen
text: The movement of leukocytes between different body parts plays a crucial role in the immune system's ability to detect and respond to antigens. Repeated social defeat in group-housed male mice leads to changes in leukocyte trafficking, resulting in a redistribution of immune cells in the bone marrow, peripheral blood, and spleen. Exposure to the stressors over a period of 2, 4, or 6 days causes cell mobilization and increased myelopoiesis in the bone marrow, which is accompanied by an accumulation of neutrophils and monocytes in the circulation and spleen. Additionally, there is significant depletion of B cells in the bone marrow and blood, along with an increase in splenic B cells, indicating a redirection of this cell type to the spleen. In contrast, T cells are significantly reduced in these immune compartments. The recruitment of CD11b+ leukocytes (i.e., monocytes/macrophages and neutrophils) from the bone marrow to the spleen may play a critical role in the development of functional glucocorticoid resistance in the murine spleen, which has been linked to repeated social defeat.

title: Lentivirally transduced dendritic cells as a tool for cancer immunotherapy.
text: Gene transfer into dendritic cells (DCs), the immune system's professional antigen-presenting cells, is crucial for cancer immunotherapy. We investigated the influence of several elements (cPPT, trip, WPRE, SIN) on the transduction efficiency of human and murine DCs using lentiviral vectors encoding tNGFR, huIi80MAGE-A3, or huIi80tOVA. Our results demonstrate that a self-inactivating (SIN) lentiviral vector containing the trip element is most effective in transducing human DCs, resulting in stable gene expression in up to 94.6% (murine) and 88.2% (human) of mature DCs without affecting viability, phenotype, or function. In addition, we found that human DCs transduced with trip/SIN tNGFR-encoding lentiviral vectors at an MOI of 15 were capable of stimulating MAGE-A3-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell clones and priming both MAGE-A3-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in vitro. Similarly, murine DCs transduced with huIi80tOVA-encoding lentiviral vectors were able to present OVA peptides in the context of MHC class I and class II and induced a strong OVA-specific cytotoxic T lymphocyte response in vivo, which was protective against subsequent challenge with OVA-expressing tumor cells. Our findings indicate that efficient gene transfer in human and murine DCs can be achieved using lentiviral vectors, and these DCs can elicit antigen-specific immune responses both in vitro and in vivo. The composition of the transfer vector has a significant impact on the transduction efficiency.

title: Global Reorganization of Replication Domains During Embryonic Stem Cell Differentiation
text:
DNA replication in mammals is regulated through the coordinated firing of clusters of DNA sequences, called "replicons," which duplicate megabase-sized chromosome segments at specific times during the S phase of the cell cycle. These replicon clusters coalesce to form subchromosomal units that persist across multiple cell generations, but the molecular boundaries of these units remained elusive until now. Additionally, the extent to which changes in replication timing occur during cell differentiation and their relationship to transcriptional changes have not been thoroughly investigated.
To address these questions, we generated high-resolution replication timing profiles in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) before and after differentiation to neural precursor cells. Our findings reveal that chromosomes can be divided into multimegabase-sized "replication domains," separated by "transition regions" with unique replication kinetics that are consistent with large originless segments. The molecular boundaries of these replication domains are remarkably conserved across distantly related ESC lines and induced pluripotent stem cells.
Notably, differentiation of ESCs is accompanied by the consolidation of smaller, differentially replicating domains into larger, coordinately replicated units whose replication timing is more aligned to the density of LINE-1 transposable elements and not gene density. These changes in replication timing are accompanied by rearrangements in subnuclear position and are more pronounced for weak promoters than strong promoters.
Our results demonstrate that replication profiles are cell-type specific and reveal that chromosome segments undergo significant changes in organization during differentiation. Furthermore, smaller replication domains and a higher density of timing transition regions that interrupt isochore replication timing define a novel characteristic of the pluripotent state.

title: Molecular characterization of the yeast meiotic regulatory gene RIM1.
text:
In the yeast species Saccharomyces cerevisiae, genetic studies have suggested that the RIM1 gene encodes a positive regulator of meiosis. Mutations in the RIM1 gene lead to a partial defect in meiosis and spore formation, as well as reduced expression of IME1, which is necessary for the expression of many meiotic genes. In this study, we investigate the sequence and functional analysis of the RIM1 gene.
The RIM1 gene product (RIM1) contains three regions similar to C2H2 zinc fingers, which are important for its function. We found that substitution of serine for cysteine in each of these regions abolishes RIM1 function. The carboxyl-terminus of RIM1 is enriched in acidic amino acids and is essential for full RIM1 activity. Additionally, we identified two putative cAMP-dependent protein kinase (cAPK) phosphorylation sites in RIM1, one of which, when substituted with alanine, does not affect RIM1 activity, while the other impairs it. These findings suggest that RIM1 may function as a transcriptional activator.
To further investigate the role of RIM1 in meiosis, we created a complete deletion of the RIM1 gene. This null allele, like previously isolated rim1 mutations, causes a partial meiotic defect. However, we found that RIM1 acts independently of the MCK1 and IME4 gene products, which were previously shown to be involved in IME1 expression. Defects associated with rim1, mck1, and ime4 mutations in expression of a meiotic reporter gene (ime2-lacZ) and in sporulation are additive, suggesting that RIM1 acts independently of these genes to stimulate IME1 expression.
In conclusion, our findings provide insight into the molecular mechanism of meiosis in yeast and suggest that RIM1 plays a crucial role in the regulation of IME1 expression through a novel mechanism that is independent of other known regulators of meiosis.

title: Butyrate greatly enhances derivation of human induced pluripotent stem cells by promoting epigenetic remodeling and the expression of pluripotency-associated genes.
text:
According to our study, the naturally occurring fatty acid butyrate significantly enhances the efficiency of converting induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells from human adult or fetal fibroblasts. Butyrate treatment increases the iPS cell derivation efficiency by 15- to 51-fold using either retroviral or piggyBac transposon vectors expressing 4 to 5 reprogramming genes. Interestingly, butyrate stimulation is more effective (>100- to 200-fold) when the KLF4 or MYC transgene is absent. However, butyrate treatment does not affect the properties of the established iPS cell lines, regardless of whether they are derived from an adult patient with sickle cell disease using either the piggyBac or retroviral vectors.
We conducted genome-wide gene expression and promoter DNA methylation microarrays and other epigenetic analyses on established iPS cells and cells from intermediate stages of the reprogramming process to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms of butyrate stimulation. Our findings reveal that butyrate treatment enhances histone H3 acetylation, promoter DNA demethylation, and the expression of endogenous pluripotency-associated genes, such as DPPA2, whose overexpression partially substitutes for butyrate stimulation. Therefore, butyrate as a cell-permeable small molecule provides a convenient tool to further investigate the molecular mechanisms of cellular reprogramming. Additionally, butyrate stimulation offers an efficient method for reprogramming various human adult somatic cells, including cells from patients that are more refractory to reprogramming.

title: Nanoparticle conjugation of CpG enhances adjuvancy for cellular immunity and memory recall at low dose.
text: In subunit vaccines, strong CD8+ T-cell responses are sought after, yet they are difficult to achieve at reasonable doses of adjuvants. We discovered that targeting adjuvants to the lymph node (LN) through ultrasmall polymeric nanoparticles (NPs), which rapidly drain to the LN after intradermal injection, significantly enhances adjuvant efficacy at low doses. By coupling CpG-B or CpG-C oligonucleotides to NPs, we found better dual-targeting of adjuvants and antigens (co-delivered on separate NPs) in cross-presenting dendritic cells, leading to enhanced dendritic cell maturation and T helper 1 (Th1)-cytokine secretion, in turn driving stronger effector CD8+ T-cell activation with enhanced cytolytic profiles and, most significantly, more robust memory recall. Notably, with only 4 μg CpG, NP-CpG-B could substantially protect mice from syngeneic tumor challenge, even after 4 months of vaccination, compared to free CpG-B. These findings demonstrate that nanocarriers can significantly improve vaccine efficacy at a low adjuvant dose, leading to the induction of potent and long-lasting cellular immunity.

title: Induction of pluripotent stem cells by defined factors is greatly improved by small-molecule compounds
text: Reprogramming of mouse and human somatic cells can be achieved through the ectopic expression of transcription factors, but with relatively low success rates. We have found that the addition of DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors significantly improves reprogramming efficiency. Of particular note is valproic acid (VPA), an HDAC inhibitor, which increases reprogramming efficiency by more than 100-fold when used in conjunction with Oct4-GFP as a reporter. Additionally, VPA enables the efficient induction of pluripotent stem cells without the need for introducing the oncogene c-Myc.

title: Noninvasive ventilation for treatment of acute respiratory failure in patients undergoing solid organ transplantation: a randomized trial.
text:
In the realm of critical care, noninvasive ventilation (NIV) has been associated with a lower incidence of endotracheal intubation in patient populations with acute respiratory failure. With this in mind, a prospective, randomized study was conducted at a 14-bed general intensive care unit of a university hospital to investigate the efficacy of NIV in comparison to standard treatment involving supplemental oxygen administration in the management of respiratory failure in recipients of solid organ transplantation.
Fifty-one patients who underwent solid organ transplantation between December 1995 and October 1997 were selected for the study, of which 40 patients were deemed eligible and 20 were randomly assigned to each treatment group. The intervention group received NIV, while the standard treatment group received supplemental oxygen administration. The primary outcome measures included the need for endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation at any time during the study, as well as secondary outcomes such as complications not present at admission, duration of ventilatory assistance, length of hospital stay, and intensive care unit mortality.
Upon entry into the study, the two groups were found to be similar in terms of their baseline characteristics. Within the first hour of treatment, a significant improvement in the ratio of the PaO2 to the fraction of inspired oxygen (FIO2) was observed in 70% of the patients in the NIV group, compared to 25% of the patients in the standard treatment group. The NIV group also exhibited a sustained improvement in PaO2 to FIO2 over time, with 60% of patients showing improvement by the end of the study. These findings were accompanied by a significant reduction in the rates of endotracheal intubation (20% in the NIV group vs 70% in the standard treatment group; P = .002), fatal complications (20% vs 50%; P = .05), length of stay in the intensive care unit by survivors (mean [SD] days, 5.5 [3] vs 9 [4]; P = .03), and intensive care unit mortality (20% vs 50%; P = .05). Hospital mortality, however, did not differ significantly between the two groups.
The results of this study suggest that transplantation programs should consider NIV as a viable treatment option for selected recipients of transplantation experiencing acute respiratory failure. By reducing the incidence of endotracheal intubation and related complications, NIV may improve patient outcomes and reduce healthcare resource utilization in this high-risk population.

title: BIOINFORMATICS APPLICATIONS NOTE
text:
SUMMARY:
MADE4 (Microarray Analysis and Display Environment, version 4) is a software package designed to facilitate multivariate analysis of microarray gene-expression data. The software can accommodate a wide range of gene-expression data formats, leveraging the powerful statistical and visualization capabilities of the R package ade4. In addition to extending these capabilities for microarray analysis, MADE4 provides novel graphical and visualization tools to enhance interpretation of multivariate results.

title: Dual and opposing roles of primary cilia in medulloblastoma development
text: Current research has revealed that primary cilia are essential for Hedgehog (Hh) signaling during mammalian development. It is known that abnormal Hh signaling can lead to cancer, but the role of primary cilia in oncogenesis is not well understood. Cerebellar granule neuron precursors (GNPs) can give rise to medulloblastomas, the most common malignant brain tumor in children. The primary cilium and Hh signaling are necessary for GNP proliferation. We investigated whether primary cilia in GNPs play a role in medulloblastoma growth in mice. Genetic ablation of primary cilia prevented medulloblastoma formation when this tumor was caused by a constantly active Smoothened protein (Smo), an upstream activator of Hh signaling. On the other hand, removing cilia was required for medulloblastoma growth when caused by a constantly active glioma-associated oncogene family zinc finger-2 (GLI2), a downstream transcription factor. Thus, primary cilia have either a promoting or inhibiting effect on medulloblastoma formation, depending on the type of oncogenic event involved. Notably, the presence or absence of cilia was associated with specific subtypes of human medulloblastomas; primary cilia were found in medulloblastomas with activated HH or WNT signaling but not in most medulloblastomas in other molecular subgroups. Primary cilia could serve as a diagnostic tool and provide new insights into the mechanisms of tumorigenesis.

title: RAS genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae: signal transduction in search of a pathway.
text: In the early studies on budding yeasts, Ras proteins were believed to regulate the initiation of the cell cycle in response to nutrient availability. However, more recent research has shed light on the mechanism of Ras-mediated signal transduction, leading to a reevaluation of our understanding of the signal transmitted by Ras. While it is now clear how Ras mediates signal transduction, the signal itself that Ras responds to remains uncertain. Rather than transmitting a clear signal related to cell cycle initiation, it is now thought that Ras plays a role in coordinating cellular metabolism and mass accumulation.

title: Use of synthetic peptides to locate novel integrin alpha2beta1-binding motifs in human collagen III.
text: A set of 57 synthetic peptides spanning the triple-helical domain of human collagen III was utilized to identify binding sites for the collagen-binding integrin alpha2beta1. The ability of the peptides to support Mg2+-dependent binding of various integrin preparations was evaluated. Wild-type integrins (recombinant alpha2 I-domain, alpha2beta1 purified from platelet membranes, and recombinant soluble alpha2beta1 expressed as an alpha2-Fos/beta1-Jun heterodimer) bound well to only three peptides, containing GXX'GER motifs (GROGER and GMOGER, where O is hydroxyproline), and one containing two adjacent GXX'GEN motifs (GLKGEN). Two mutant alpha2 I-domains were tested: the inactive T221A mutant, which recognized no peptides, and the constitutively active E318W mutant, which bound a larger subset of peptides. Adhesion of activated human platelets to GER-containing peptides was higher than that of resting platelets, and HT1080 cells bound well to more of the peptides compared to platelets. Binding of cells and recombinant proteins was abolished by an anti-alpha2 monoclonal antibody (6F1) and by chelation of Mg2+. Weidentified two novel high-affinity integrin-binding motifs in human collagen III (GROGER and GLOGEN) and a third motif (GLKGEN) with intermediate activity. Each motif was verified using shorter synthetic peptides.

title: Locations of cerebral infarctions in tuberculous meningitis
text: In a study of 14 patients with tuberculous meningitis (TBM) and 173 patients with noninflammatory ischemic stroke (IS), the locations of cerebral infarctions were examined. In patients with TBM, 75% of infarctions occurred in the "TB zone" supplied by the medial striate and thalamoperforating arteries, while only 11% occurred in the "IS zone" supplied by the lateral striate, anterior choroidal, and thalamogeniculate arteries. In contrast, in patients with IS, 29% of infarctions occurred in the IS zone, 29% in the subcortical white matter, and 24% in (or involving) the cerebral cortex. Only 11% of infarctions occurred in the TB zone, and bilaterally symmetrical infarctions of the TB zone were common in TBM (71%) but rare in IS (5%).

title: TRP channels of intracellular membranes.
text:
Ion channels are widely recognized for their role in regulating ion flux across the plasma membrane in response to various environmental and intracellular cues. In addition to their functions in the plasma membrane, ion channels can also be found in intracellular membranes, serving a range of physiological functions. These channels can be temporarily localized to intracellular membranes during their synthesis or secretion, or they may be targeted to intracellular membranes through the endocytic pathway. Some intracellular ion channels are involved in maintaining ion homeostasis within organelles, while others play active roles in membrane trafficking and signal transduction.
Transient receptor potential (TRP) proteins, a family of 28 Ca(2+)-permeable channels in mammals, have been shown to localize to intracellular membranes in addition to the plasma membrane. These channels have diverse tissue distribution, subcellular localization, and physiological functions, and recent studies have revealed their involvement in regulating membrane traffic, signal transduction, and vesicular ion homeostasis. This review aims to provide an overview of these recent findings and discuss the basic membrane and electrical properties of TRP-residing compartments.

title: the Development of Autoimmune Myocarditis in Mice by an
text: IL-12, a potent proinflammatory cytokine, exerts its effect by stimulating T-helper (Th) 1 responses. Our study aimed to investigate the role of IL-12 receptor (IL-12R) signaling in the development of murine experimental autoimmune myocarditis (EAM) induced by cardiac myosin immunization. Both IL-12Rβ1-deficient mice and STAT4-deficient mice were found to be resistant to the induction of myocarditis, indicating that IL-12/IL-12R/STAT4 signaling promotes the development of EAM. Contrary to our expectations, we found that interferon (IFN)-gamma, rather than promoting the disease, plays a protective role in EAM. Depletion of IFN-gamma or genetic deficiency in mice exacerbated myocarditis, suggesting that IFN-gamma suppresses EAM by controlling the expansion of activated T lymphocytes. Our findings suggest that IL-12/IL-12R/STAT4 signaling promotes the development of EAM, while IFN-gamma plays a disease-limiting role.

title: The Viral and Cellular MicroRNA Targetome in Lymphoblastoid Cell Lines
text:
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a widespread human herpesvirus associated with various B cell cancers and lymphoproliferative disorders. During latent infection, EBV expresses 25 viral pre-microRNAs (miRNAs) and induces the expression of specific host miRNAs, such as miR-155 and miR-21, which may contribute to viral oncogenesis. So far, only a limited number of EBV miRNA targets have been identified, thus hindering our understanding of EBV's role in pathogenesis and lymphomagenesis.
To fill this knowledge gap, we employed photoactivatable ribonucleoside-enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (PAR-CLIP) combined with deep sequencing and computational analysis to investigate the viral and cellular miRNA targetome in EBV-infected lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs). We identified 7,827 miRNA-interaction sites in 3,492 cellular 3'untranslated regions (UTRs). Of these, 531 sites contained seed matches to viral miRNAs. We further confirmed 24 PAR-CLIP-identified miRNA:3'UTR interactions using reporter assays.
Our findings reveal that EBV miRNAs predominantly target cellular transcripts during latent infection, thereby manipulating the host environment. Moreover, targets of EBV miRNAs are involved in multiple cellular processes relevant to viral infection, including innate immunity, cell survival, and cell proliferation. Lastly, we discovered that myc-regulated host miRNAs from the miR-17/92 cluster can regulate latent viral gene expression. This comprehensive survey of the miRNA targetome in EBV-infected B cells represents a crucial step towards elucidating the functions of EBV-encoded miRNAs and potentially identifying new therapeutic targets for EBV-related malignancies.

title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction Leads to Nuclear Genome Instability via an Iron-Sulfur Cluster Defect
text: Deviations in the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) and genome instability in the nucleus are associated with various human diseases. Here, we investigate the effects of mtDNA loss on nuclear genome stability in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and find that it leads to cellular crisis, characterized by cell cycle arrest and selective pressure. This crisis is not caused by the absence of respiration but rather correlates with a decrease in the mitochondrial membrane potential. Further analysis revealed a defect in iron-sulfur cluster (ISC) biogenesis, which requires normal mitochondrial function. Remarkably, downregulation of non-mitochondrial ISC protein biogenesis was sufficient to induce genomic instability in cells with intact mitochondrial function, suggesting that mitochondrial dysfunction inhibits the production of ISC-containing proteins, which are crucial for maintaining nuclear genome integrity. A video summary of this article is available in the PaperFlick file accompanying the online Supplemental Data.

title: Replisome stall events have shaped the distribution of replication origins in the genomes of yeasts
text: During the S phase of the cell cycle, the entire genome must be perfectly duplicated, with no sections of DNA left unreplicated. To understand the probability of replication failure due to the irreversible stalling of replication forks, we develop a simple mathematical model. Our results show that maximizing the probability of complete genome replication involves evenly spacing replication origins, minimizing the largest inter-origin distances, and positioning the end-most origins close to chromosome ends. We find that origin positions in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae genome follow these predictions, resulting in a maximized probability of complete replication if replication forks stall. Similarly, origin positions in four other yeasts - Kluyveromyces lactis, Lachancea kluyveri, Lachancea waltii, and Schizosaccharomyces pombe - also conform to these predictions. By equating failure rates at chromosome ends with those in chromosome interiors, we estimate a mean per nucleotide fork stall rate of approximately 5 × 10(-8). Using this value in our theoretical predictions, we obtain replication failure rates consistent with data from replication origin knockout experiments. Our theory also suggests that larger genomes, such as those of mammals, will experience a higher probability of replication failure genome-wide and may require additional compensatory mechanisms to maintain accurate DNA replication.

title: Regulation of chromatin by histone modifications
text: Chromatin, far from being a static structure, is actually an intelligent scaffold that can adjust to external stimuli to control the various functions of DNA. A crucial component of chromatin that plays a central role in this regulation is the modification of histones. There is an constantly expanding list of these modifications, and the complexity of their effects is still being uncovered. However, it is evident that histone modifications have fundamental roles in the majority of biological processes that involve the manipulation and expression of DNA. Here, we outline the known histone modifications, locate them in the genome, and discuss some of their functional implications, focusing primarily on transcription, where the majority of research has taken place.

title: Single-Cell Expression Analyses during Cellular Reprogramming Reveal an Early Stochastic and a Late Hierarchic Phase
text: During cellular reprogramming, a minuscule proportion of cells become induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). Past examinations of gene expression during the reprogramming process were conducted on bulk populations of cells, thereby hindering the identification of single-cell events. To address this limitation, we applied two gene expression technologies to profile 48 genes in individual cells at different stages of the reprogramming process. Our findings revealed substantial variations in gene expression between cells during early stages of reprogramming in contrast to later stages. Notably, the expression of Esrrb, Utf1, Lin28, and Dppa2 serves as a better predictor for cells to transition into iPSCs, as compared to the previously suggested reprogramming markers Fbxo15, Fgf4, and Oct4. Early stochastic gene expression during reprogramming is followed by a subsequent hierarchical phase, with Sox2 serving as an upstream factor in a gene expression hierarchy. Finally, downstream factors derived from the late phase, which do not include Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc, and Nanog, can activate the pluripotency circuitry.

title: Scaffold-based three-dimensional human fibroblast culture provides a structural matrix that supports angiogenesis in infarcted heart tissue.
text:
BACKGROUND We have developed techniques to implant angiogenic patches onto the epicardium over regions of infarcted cardiac tissue to promote the revascularization of damaged tissue. In these experiments, we utilized a 3D human dermal fibroblast culture (3DFC) as an epicardial patch. The 3DFC contains viable cells that secrete angiogenic growth factors and has been shown to stimulate angiogenic activity in the past. We hypothesized that a viable 3DFC cardiac patch would stimulate an angiogenic response within an area of infarcted cardiac tissue.
METHODS AND RESULTS To test this hypothesis, we induced a coronary occlusion in severe combined immunodeficient mice and then implanted 3DFCs with or without viable cells onto the epicardium at the site of tissue injury. We compared the results with animals that received infarct surgery but no implant. Fourteen and 30 days after surgery, we exposed the hearts and took photographs, as well as prepared tissue samples for histology and cytochemistry. Our findings showed that the damaged myocardium that received viable 3DFC exhibited a significantly greater angiogenic response (including arterioles, venules, and capillaries) compared to nonviable and untreated control groups.
CONCLUSIONS Based on the findings from this animal model, we conclude that viable 3DFC can stimulate angiogenesis within a region of cardiac infarction and may have the potential to augment a repair response in damaged tissue. Therefore, a potential use for 3DFC is the repair of myocardial tissue damaged by infarction.

title: Global tuberculosis control: lessons learnt and future prospects
text: Tuberculosis (TB) has a long history, but it's not a disease of the past. Despite its decline from the global public health agenda in the 1960s and 1970s, TB resurfaced in the early 1990s due to various factors, including the emergence of the HIV/AIDS pandemic and the rise of drug-resistant strains. More than a century after Robert Koch discovered the tubercle bacillus, we examine the current state of TB control globally and assess the evolution of TB control policies, including DOTS (directly observed therapy, short course) and the Stop TB Strategy. Our review also explores the challenges and obstacles faced by the public health community worldwide in implementing these strategies and whether they can provide insights for future efforts towards eliminating TB.

title: Global prevalence of glaucoma and projections of glaucoma burden through 2040: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text:
Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness globally, with a disproportionate impact on people living in Africa and Asia. To better understand the scope of this burden, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of population-based studies to estimate the global prevalence of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) and primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG).
Our analysis included data from 50 studies involving over 140,000 participants from 140,496 individuals and 112,398 examined individuals. We used a hierarchical Bayesian approach to estimate the pooled prevalence of glaucoma in the population aged 40-80 years, along with 95% credible intervals (CrIs). We also projected the number of glaucoma cases in 2020 and 2040 using the United Nations World Population Prospects.
Our findings indicate that the global prevalence of glaucoma for the population aged 40-80 years is 3.54% (95% CrI, 2.09-5.82). We found that the prevalence of POAG is highest in Africa (4.20%; 95% CrI, 2.08-7.35), and the prevalence of PACG is highest in Asia (1.09%; 95% CrI, 0.43-2.32). In 2013, the number of people (aged 40-80 years) with glaucoma worldwide was estimated to be 64.3 million, increasing to 76.0 million in 2020 and 111.8 million in 2040.
Our Bayesian meta-regression model revealed that men are more likely to have POAG than women (odds ratio [OR], 1.36; 95% CrI, 1.23-1.52), and after adjusting for age, gender, habitation type, response rate, and year of study, people of African ancestry are more likely to have POAG than people of European ancestry (OR, 2.80; 95% CrI, 1.83-4.06), and people living in urban areas are more likely to have POAG than those in rural areas (OR, 1.58; 95% CrI, 1.19-2.04).
Our findings have important implications for glaucoma screening, treatment, and related public health strategies. As the number of people with glaucoma worldwide increases, it is crucial to prioritize the development of effective interventions that can help mitigate the burden of this disease in the affected populations.

title: Gastrointestinal tract as a major site of CD4+ T cell depletion and viral replication in SIV infection.
text: Both human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) replicate best in activated memory CD4(+) T cells, which are abundant in the intestine. In rhesus monkeys infected with SIV, there was a significant and selective depletion of CD4+ T cells in the intestine within days of infection, before any noticeable changes in lymphoid tissues in the periphery. This loss of CD4+ T cells in the intestine coincided with the productive infection of large numbers of mononuclear cells at this site. The intestine emerges as a prime target for SIV replication and the primary location of CD4+ T cell depletion during early SIV infection.

title: Interaction of streptavidin-based peptide-MHC oligomers (tetramers) with cell-surface TCRs.
text: The binding of oligomeric peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) complexes to cell surface T cell receptors (TCR) can be likened to TCR-pMHC interactions at cell-cell interfaces. In this study, we examined the equilibration of streptavidin-based pMHC oligomers (tetramers) and their dissociation kinetics from CD8(pos) T cells from 2C-TCR transgenic mice and from T cell hybridomas that expressed the 2C TCR or a high-affinity mutant (m33) of this TCR. Our findings indicate that the tetramers bound to only 10-30% of the cell-surface TCRs, which is lower than the assumed saturation value used to calculate affinity values (K(D)). This discrepancy is attributed to the loss of tetramers from stained cells due to dissociation. By employing a kinetic model, we found that the dissociation rate and equilibrium constants of the oligomers were influenced by both monovalent association and dissociation rates (k(off) and k(on)), as well as a multivalent association rate (μ) and TCR cell-surface density. Our results suggest that accounting for dissociation rates could explain the previously observed high frequency of tetramer-negative, functionally competent T cells in certain T cell responses.

title: Human monocyte characteristics are altered in hypercholesterolaemia.
text: Human hyperlipidaemia in age/sex/smoking status-matched pairs of patients and controls has been found to affect peripheral blood monocyte characteristics. Hydercholesterolaemic patients' monocytes were more sensitive to stimulation by the agonist N-formyl-methionyl-leucyl-phenylalanine regarding chemokinesis (stimulation index 1.48 +/- 0.17 vs. 1.10 +/- 0.14), chemotaxis (4.05 +/- 0.55 vs. 2.72 +/- 0.24), and adhesion to porcine aortic endothelial monolayers (1.26 +/- 0.05 vs. 1.17 +/- 0.06). However, the patients' monocyte total surface expression of the adhesion glycoprotein CD11b/CD18 (37.5 +/- 7.1 vs. 36.0 +/- 7.1) was increased; however, not CD11c/CD18 (31.6 +/- 7.2 vs. 31.4 +/- 6.8). As well, the monocytes in hyperlipidaemia were larger (9.15 +/- 0.11 microns vs. 8.98 +/- 0.11 microns) such that the surface density of CD11b/CD18 (0.144 +/- 0.029 vs. 0.142 +/- 0.029) remained unchanged. These findings suggest that circulating monocytes in hypercholesterolaemia are functionally different, which may explain the increased involvement of monocytes in hypercholesterolaemia-related atherogenesis.

title: Adult Mammalian Neural Stem Cells and Neurogenesis: Five Decades Later.
text: Adult somatic stem cells in various organs play a critical role in maintaining tissue homeostasis and enhancing plasticity. In the field of neuroscience, research on adult neurogenesis and neural stem cells has made significant strides over the past five decades, leading to a rapidly expanding and established field that has shed light on the mechanisms underlying tissue regeneration and plasticity. This review aims to summarize recent findings and highlight the most pressing questions relevant to adult mammalian neural stem cells, which also have implications for other somatic stem cells. Furthermore, we will discuss emerging areas of research that are steering the field towards a deeper understanding of adult neural stem cells and their potential applications in improving human health.

title: Relationship of ambulatory blood pressure and the heart rate profile with renal function parameters in hypertensive patients with chronic kidney disease.
text: The study examined the relationship between strict blood pressure (BP) control, heart rate (HR) profile, central hemodynamics, and arterial stiffness in relation to renal function parameters in hospitalized hypertensive patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). The study found significant positive relationships between urine albumin excretion rate (UACR) and 24-hour, daytime, and nighttime ambulatory systolic BP, as well as between UACR and 24-hour and daytime HR variability. Additionally, the study found that circulating B-type natriuretic peptide level and hemoglobin A1c were positively related to UACR. In contrast, the study found that 24-hour and nighttime HR variability were positively associated with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), while the circulating pentosidine and nighttime HR had a negative relationship with eGFR. The study did not identify any significant associations between central hemodynamics and arterial stiffness with renal function parameters. These findings suggest that ambulatory BP and the HR profile are closely related to renal function deterioration in hypertensive patients with CKD, and further studies are needed to investigate the causal relationship between these factors and renal function parameters.

title: The frequency and immunodominance of islet-specific CD8+ T-cell responses change after type 1 diabetes diagnosis and treatment.
text:
Objective: Islet-reactive CD8(+) T cells play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of type 1 diabetes in the NOD mouse model. However, the extent to which similar shifts in T-cell responders occur in clinically diagnosed and insulin-treated type 1 diabetic patients remains unclear.
Research Design and Methods: We exploited a recently validated islet-specific CD8(+) T-cell gamma-interferon enzyme-linked immunospot (ISL8Spot) assay to monitor responses against preproinsulin (PPI), glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), insulinoma-associated protein 2 (IA-2), and islet-specific glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunit-related protein (IGRP) epitopes in 15 HLA-A2(+) adult type 1 diabetic patients at early diagnosis and after a median duration of 11 months.
Results: Findings demonstrated a significant decrease in CD8(+) T-cell reactivity over time, with 28.6% of responses showing positivity at the time of diagnosis versus 13.2% at the follow-up (P = 0.003). While GAD and IA-2 autoantibody (aAb) titers remained unchanged in 75% of cases, the proportion of patients responding to PPI and/or GAD epitopes by ISL8Spot decreased from 60-67% to 20% (P < 0.02). Notably, the previously subdominant IA-2(206-214) and IGRP(265-273) peptides emerged as the immunodominant epitopes.
Conclusions: These findings indicate that shifts in both frequency and immunodominance of CD8(+) T-cell responses occur more rapidly than changes in aAb titers, suggesting complementary clinical applications for T-cell and aAb measurements.

title: A Protein Inventory of Human Ribosome Biogenesis Reveals an Essential Function of Exportin 5 in 60S Subunit Export
text: The assembly of ribosomal subunits in eukaryotes is a complex and multistep process that has been largely studied in yeast. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, over 200 factors, including ribosomal proteins and trans-acting factors, are required for the ordered assembly of 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits. However, relatively few human homologs of these factors have been characterized. To investigate the contribution of human factors to ribosomal subunit biogenesis, we employed a systematic RNA interference (RNAi) approach using inducible, fluorescent ribosomal proteins as reporters. By utilizing computer-based image analysis with supervised machine-learning techniques, we identified 153 human proteins that are involved in ribosome synthesis. Our data indicate that core features of ribosome assembly are conserved from yeast to human, but there are also differences, such as in 60S subunit export. Unexpectedly, our RNAi screen revealed a requirement for the export receptor Exportin 5 (Exp5) in the nuclear export of 60S subunits in human cells. Exp5, like the known 60S export receptor Crm1, binds to pre-60S particles in a RanGTP-dependent manner. Interference with either Exp5 or Crm1 function blocks 60S export in both human cells and frog oocytes, while 40S export is compromised only upon inhibition of Crm1. Thus, 60S subunit export depends on at least two RanGTP-binding exportins in vertebrate cells.

title: Binding of the winged-helix transcription factor HNF3 to a linker histone site on the nucleosome.
text: The transcription factor HNF3 and linker histones H1 and H5 possesswinged-helix DNA-binding domains, yet HNF3 and other fork head-related proteins activate genes during development, whereas linker histones compact DNA in chromatin and repress gene expression. We compared how the two classes of factors interact with chromatin templates and found that HNF3 binds DNA at the sides of nucleosome cores, similar to what has been reported for linker histone. A nucleosome structural binding site for HNF3 is occupied at the albumin transcriptional enhancer in active and potentially active chromatin, but not in inactive chromatin in vivo. While wild-type HNF3 protein does not compact DNA extending from the nucleosome, as does linker histone, site-directed mutants of HNF3 can compact nucleosomal DNA if they contain basic amino acids at positions previously shown to be essential for nucleosomal DNA compaction by linker histones. The results illustrate how transcription factors can possess special nucleosome-binding activities that are not predicted from studies of factor interactions with free DNA.

title: Rapid recent growth and divergence of rice nuclear genomes.
text: By leveraging the nuclear DNA of the African rice species Oryza glaberrima as a reference genome, researchers were able to uncover the timing, nature, mechanisms, and specificities of recent genetic evolution in the indica and japonica subspecies of Oryza sativa. The data revealed that both indica and japonica have experienced substantial increases in genome size, with increases of >2% and >6%, respectively, since their divergence from a common ancestor. This expansion is largely attributed to the amplification of LTR-retrotransposons. However, the loss of various classes of DNA sequence through unequal homologous recombination and illegitimate recombination has resulted in a shrinking of the rice genome. Small deletions have been particularly prevalent throughout the genome. In over 1 million bytes of orthologous regions analyzed, no instances of complete gene gain or loss, nor any precise transposon excision, were observed in either indica or japonica. Instead, the sequences between genes revealed a very high rate of divergence, indicating a molecular clock for transposable elements that is at least 2-fold faster than synonymous base substitutions within genes. Additionally, regions prone to frequent insertions and deletions showed higher levels of point mutations. These findings suggest a highly dynamic rice genome with competing processes influencing the generation and removal of genetic variation.

title: Detection of an autoreactive T-cell population within the polyclonal repertoire that undergoes distinct autoimmune regulator (Aire)-mediated selection.
text: The autoimmune regulator (Aire) plays a crucial role in maintaining central tolerance by promoting the display of tissue-specific antigens in the thymus. To investigate the effect of Aire on thymic selection in a physiological setting, we employed tetramer reagents to detect autoreactive T cells specific for the Aire-dependent tissue-specific antigen interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP). We designed two class II tetramer reagents to identify T cells specific for two different peptide epitopes of IRBP. Surprisingly, our analysis of the polyclonal T-cell repertoire revealed a high frequency of activated T cells specific for both IRBP tetramers in Aire(-/-) mice, but not in Aire(+/+) mice. Interestingly, while one tetramer-binding T-cell population was efficiently deleted in the thymus in an Aire-dependent manner, the second tetramer-binding population was not deleted and could be detected in both the Aire(-/-) and Aire(+/+) T-cell repertoires. Our findings suggest that Aire-dependent thymic deletion of IRBP-specific T cells relies on intercellular transfer of IRBP between thymic stroma and bone marrow-derived antigen-presenting cells. Additionally, our data imply that Aire-mediated deletion relies not only on thymic expression of IRBP, but also on proper antigen processing and presentation of IRBP by thymic antigen-presenting cells.

title: Spatial and temporal heterogeneity of Anopheles mosquitoes and Plasmodium falciparum transmission along the Kenyan coast.
text: For one year, researchers studied the seasonal dynamics and spatial distributions of Anopheles mosquitoes and Plasmodium falciparum parasites in 30 villages along the coast of Kenya. Mosquitoes were collected inside homes every two months, and malaria parasite prevalence was checked in local school children at the end of the survey. A total of 5,476 Anopheles gambiae s.l. and 3,461 An. funestus were collected, and the species within the An. gambiae complex were identified through polymerase chain reaction. Anopheles gambiae s.s. was found to be the primary transmitter of P. falciparum along the coast, while An. funestus contributed more than 50% of transmission in Kwale District. The transmission intensity varied widely across locations, with some sites having as few as one or as many as 120 infective bites per person per year. Thirty-two percent of the sites with high malaria prevalence (ranging from 38% to 70%) had entomologic inoculation rates (EIR) below five infective bites per person per year. Mosquito density in Kwale was not significantly affected by rainfall, but both Anopheles gambiae s.l. and An. funestus were positively correlated with rainfall one and three months prior in Malindi and Kilifi Districts, respectively. The study suggests that the relationship between mosquito populations and rainfall is complex and that entomologic surveys alone may not accurately capture transmission intensity. The findings highlight the importance of considering environmental factors, such as rainfall, in predicting malaria transmission and the need for more accurate methods for measuring transmission intensity in field settings.

title: Myelodysplasia and leukemia of Fanconi anemia are associated with a specific pattern of genomic abnormalities that includes cryptic RUNX1/AML1 lesions.
text: In this study, we investigated Fanconi anemia (FA), a genetic disorder associated with bone marrow (BM) failure, myelodysplasia (MDS), and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). We analyzed 57 FA patients with hypoplastic or aplastic anemia (n = 20), MDS (n = 18), AML (n = 11), or no BM abnormality (n = 8). We examined the BM samples using karyotype, high-density DNA arrays, and selected oncogene sequencing. We found a specific pattern of chromosomal abnormalities in MDS/AML, including 1q+ (44.8%), 3q+ (41.4%), -7/7q (17.2%), and 11q- (13.8%). We also observed cryptic RUNX1/AML1 lesions (translocations, deletions, or mutations) in FA for the first time, occurring in 20.7% of cases. In addition, we identified rare mutations in NRAS, FLT3-ITD, MLL-PTD, ERG amplification, and ZFP36L2-PRDM16 translocation, but not in TP53, TET2, CBL, NPM1, and CEBPα. Interestingly, we found that homozygosity regions were more frequently related to consanguinity rather than somatic copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, suggesting that homologous recombination is not a common progression mechanism in FA. Notably, the RUNX1 and other chromosomal/genomic lesions were found at the MDS/AML stages, except for 1q+, which was found at all stages. These findings have implications for staging and therapeutic management in FA patients and may also shed light on the mechanisms of clonal evolution and oncogenesis in a background of genomic instability and BM failure.

title: Molecular and Cellular Approaches for Diversifying and Extending Optogenetics
text:
Optogenetic technologies harness the power of light to regulate biological processes within targeted cells in real-time. Here, we demonstrate the application of molecular trafficking principles to enhance the optogenetic toolbox in several key ways:

1. The development of subcellular and transcellular trafficking strategies allows for optogenetic regulation at the far-red/infrared border and the expansion of control across the full visible spectrum.

2. Our approach enables enhanced potency of optical inhibition without increasing light power requirements through the use of nanoampere-scale chloride-mediated photocurrents, which maintain the light sensitivity and reversible, step-like kinetic stability of earlier optogenetic tools.

3. Furthermore, we have developed generalizable strategies for targeting cells based not only on genetic identity, but also on morphology and tissue topology, allowing for versatile targeting in organisms where promoters are unavailable or genetically intractable. These findings demonstrate the power of cellular biology to expand and refine fast optogenetic technologies for use in intact-systems biology and behavior.

title: An analysis of the Caenorhabditis elegans lipid raft proteome using geLC-MS/MS.
text: Lipid rafts are specialized regions of the cell membrane that are enriched in certain types of lipids, which form "islands" that facilitate various cellular processes. Our study focused on the lipid raft proteome of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, an organism with a well-understood developmental profile. We used geLC-MS/MS to identify 44 proteins in the lipid raft fraction, of which 40 are likely raft proteins based on their predicted functions. Furthermore, we predicted that 21 of these proteins may be GPI-anchored, and two were experimentally confirmed to be so. This study is the first to investigate the lipid raft proteome of C. elegans, providing insight into the diverse roles of raft proteins within the nematode. Our findings suggest that C. elegans may be a useful model organism for the study of lipid rafts and their functions.

title: Geographic distribution of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus soft tissue infections.
text:
Purpose:
This study aims to investigate the spatial patterns of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections in a local region and determine if specific areas are at increased risk of infection.
Methods:
After obtaining Institutional Review Board approval (132603-3), a retrospective chart review was conducted of 614 patients who underwent incision and drainage of an abscess by a single pediatric surgical practice from January 2004 to December 2008. Additionally, previously published data from 195 patients who underwent incision and drainage of an abscess from January 2000 to December 2003 were reviewed.
Results:
The most common organism cultured in the pediatric population undergoing incision and drainage was S aureus (n = 388), of which 258 (66%) were methicillin-resistant. This represents a 21% increase in the rate of MRSA cultures from 2000 to 2003. Geospatial analysis using a geographic information system (GIS) revealed clusters of MRSA cases within a 1.44-km radius between 2000 and 2003 and five separate clusters of more than 20 MRSA infection cases each in three separate cities over the eight-year time span. (P value = .001)


Conclusion:
Methicillin-resistant S aureus has become the most prevalent organism isolated from cultures of community-acquired abscesses requiring incision and drainage in the pediatric population in our local region. Significant clustering of MRSA infections has emerged in several different cities within our geographic region.

title: The right place at the right time: chaperoning core histone variants.
text: Histone proteins play a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis by regulating chromatin structure and epigenetic signaling through dynamic processes of deposition and eviction controlled by specialized chaperones. As histone variants have evolved, a network of functionally specific histone chaperones has emerged, but the molecular details of their specificity for different histone variants are still being uncovered. A comprehensive understanding of these processes is essential to elucidate the genuine functions of histone variants, their chaperones, and their impact on chromatin dynamics.

title: Phosphorylation site mutations in heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) reduce or eliminate silencing activity.
text: Heterochromatin-associated protein 1 (HP1) plays a crucial role in Drosophila, with dosage-dependent effects on the silencing of euchromatic genes mislocalized to heterochromatin. HP1 is multipathed in vivo, and hyperphosphorylation correlates with heterochromatin assembly during development. To investigate the impact of HP1 phosphorylation on its biological activity and biochemical properties, we expressed Drosophila HP1 in lepidopteran cultured cells using a recombinant baculovirus vector. Phosphopeptides were identified using matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization/time of flight mass spectrometry, which revealed target sites for casein kinase II, protein tyrosine kinase, and PIM-1 kinase. Purified HP1 from bacterial (unphosphorylated) and lepidopteran (phosphorylated) cells displayed similar secondary structure. However, phosphorylation did not affect HP1 self-association but altered its DNA binding properties, suggesting that phosphorylation may differentially regulate HP1-dependent interactions. We further investigated the effect of phosphorylation on HP1 activity by introducing serine-to-alanine and serine-to-glutamate substitutions at consensus protein kinase motifs in the HP1 protein. These mutations resulted in reduced or lost silencing activity of mutant HP1 in transgenic flies, indicating that dynamic phosphorylation/dephosphorylation regulates HP1 activity in heterochromatic silencing.

title: Elimination of paternal mitochondria in mouse embryos occurs through autophagic degradation dependent on PARKIN and MUL1
text: A distinctive attribute of mitochondria is their ontogenetic inheritance, yet little is known about the cellular mechanism through which paternal mitochondria, transported by sperm, are eliminated from early mammalian embryos. While autophagy has been linked to nematodes, its conservation in mammals has been debated. We demonstrate that cultured mouse fibroblasts and pre-implantation embryos employ a shared pathway for the removal of mitochondria. Both situations involve mitophagy, where mitochondria are engulfed by autophagosomes and ultimately degraded by lysosomes. The ubiquitin ligases PARKIN and MUL1 play redundant roles in eliminating paternal mitochondria. The process is accompanied by the depolarization of paternal mitochondria and requires the mitochondrial outer membrane protein FIS1, the autophagy adaptor P62, and the PINK1 kinase. Our findings suggest that the strict maternal transmission of mitochondria relies on mitophagy and uncover a collaboration between MUL1 and PARKIN in this process.

title: Ribosome Profiling Provides Evidence that Large Noncoding RNAs Do Not Encode Proteins
text: Large noncoding RNAs are proving to be a crucial aspect of cellular regulation. Evidence suggests that these transcripts primarily act as functional RNAs rather than producing a protein product. A recent study showed that many large intergenic noncoding RNAs (lincRNAs) are bound by ribosomes, leading some to speculate that they may be translated into proteins. However, our findings here show that classical noncoding RNAs and 5' untranslated regions (UTRs) exhibit the same ribosome occupancy as lincRNAs, indicating that ribosome occupancy alone is not a reliable classifier of transcripts as coding or noncoding. Instead, we propose a metric based on the known property of translation, where translating ribosomes are released upon encountering a bona fide stop codon. We find that this metric accurately distinguishes between protein-coding transcripts and all classes of known noncoding transcripts, including lincRNAs. These results suggest that the majority of lincRNAs do not function through encoded proteins.

title: Isolation of a Fusion Transcript, AMLl IETO, With Similarity to
text: We have characterized the chromosome 21 breakpoint region involved in t(8;21)(q22;q22.3) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and identified rearrangements in nine cases using probes from these regions. Additionally, we have isolated cDNA clones from a t(8;21) AML cDNA library that contain fused sequences from chromosomes 8 and 21. The chromosome 8 component, referred to as ETO (for eight twenty-one), spans a large genomic region, as suggested by the analysis of corresponding yeast artificial chromosomes (YACs). The DNA sequence of the chromosome 21 portion of the fusion transcript is derived from the normal AML1 gene. Remarkably, we have found a high degree of similarity (67% identity over 387 bp, with a corresponding 69% amino acid identity) between AML1 and the Drosophila segmentation gene, runt. The result of the translocation is the juxtaposition of 5' sequences of AML1 to 3' sequences of ETO, oriented telomere to centromere on the der(8) chromosome.

title: Treatment of spondyloarthropathy with 5-aminosalicylic acid (mesalazine): an open trial.
text:
Objective: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) and spondyloarthropathy (SpA) are inflammatory diseases of unknown etiology, with various exogenous and endogenous (inherited) factors contributing to their development. Sulfasalazine (SSZ) is commonly used as a disease-modifying drug in the treatment of AS and SpA, although the specific component responsible for its efficacy is unclear. This study aims to investigate the efficacy of 5-acetylsalicylic acid (5-ASA), a component of SSZ, in the treatment of SpA.
Methods: In an open pilot study, 20 patients with SpA who were already taking SSZ were switched to 5-ASA (Pentasa) for a period of time, while another 19 patients with active SpA were treated with 5-ASA without previous SSZ administration. The physician global clinical assessment and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) were used to evaluate the patients' responses.
Results: Of the patients in the first group, 17 (85%) showed significant improvement in physician global clinical assessment compared to their previous SSZ treatment, while the second group exhibited a statistically significant decrease in ESR.
Conclusion: The results of this study suggest that 5-ASA may be the active moiety of SSZ in the treatment of SpA, supporting the hypothesis that it plays a key role in the drug's efficacy. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to determine the optimal dosage and duration of treatment with 5-ASA for SpA.

title: Relationship of physical activity and television watching with body weight and level of fatness among children: results from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.
text:
In this study, the relationship between physical inactivity and weight gain in children of different ethnic groups is examined. The study used a nationally representative cross-sectional survey that included an in-person interview and medical examination of 4063 children aged 8-16 years between 1988 and 1994. The survey oversampled Mexican Americans and non-Hispanic blacks to produce reliable estimates for these groups.
The study found that:
* Eighty percent of children reported performing 3 or more bouts of vigorous activity each week, but this rate was lower in non-Hispanic black and Mexican American girls (69% and 73%, respectively).
* Twenty percent of children participated in 2 or fewer bouts of vigorous activity per week, and the rate was higher in girls (26%) than in boys (17%).
* Overall, 26% of children watched 4 or more hours of television per day, and the highest rates were found in non-Hispanic black children (42%).
* Boys and girls who watch 4 or more hours of television each day had greater body fat and a greater body mass index than those who watched less than 2 hours per day (P < 0.001).

The study's conclusions were that many US children watch a great deal of television and are inadequately vigorously active, with the lowest levels of vigorous activity observed among girls, non-Hispanic blacks, and Mexican Americans. The study highlights the need for intervention strategies to promote lifelong physical activity among US children to prevent adverse health consequences of inactivity.

title: Vascular Calcification in Chronic Kidney Disease is Induced by Bone Morphogenetic Protein-2 via a Mechanism Involving the Wnt/β-Catenin Pathway
text:
Introduction:
Vascular calcification (VC), which is characterized by the transformation of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) into osteoblast-like cells, is an emerging risk factor for accelerated atherosclerosis in chronic kidney disease (CKD). Phosphate has been shown to play a crucial role in regulating VC. This study aimed to investigate the expression of smooth muscle cell or osteogenesis markers in response to high concentrations of phosphate or exogenous bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP-2) in rat VSMCs, as well as to examine the involvement of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in VSMC calcification and osteoblastic differentiation induced by high phosphate or BMP-2.
Methods:
The study used rat VSMCs and examined the expression of different smooth muscle cell or osteogenesis markers in response to high concentrations of phosphate or BMP-2 using qRT-PCR and western blotting. The levels of osteocalcin were measured by radioimmunoassay, and differentiation and calcification of VSMCs were examined by alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity assay and Alizarin staining. Short hairpin RNA-mediated silencing of β-catenin was performed to examine the involvement of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in VSMC calcification and osteoblastic differentiation. Apoptosis was determined by TUNEL assay and immunofluorescence imaging.
Results:
The study found that BMP-2 serum levels were significantly higher in CKD patients than in controls. High phosphate concentrations and BMP-2 induced VSMC apoptosis and upregulated the expression of β-catenin, Msx2, Runx2, and the phosphate cotransporter Pit1, whereas a BMP-2 neutralization antibody reversed these effects. Knockdown of β-catenin abolished the effect of high phosphate and BMP-2 on VSMC apoptosis and calcification.


Conclusion:

This study shows that BMP-2 plays a crucial role in calcium deposition in VSMCs and VC in CKD patients via a mechanism involving the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. These findings provide new insights into the pathogenesis of VC in CKD and may lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies for the prevention and treatment of VC in this condition.

title: Advances in brain tumor surgery.
text: Advances in molecular and translational research, oncology, and surgery have given the medical community reason to believe that intrinsic brain tumors may be treatable. Intraoperative imaging and brain mapping enable surgeons to operate more effectively near sensitive brain areas and perform more radical tumor resections with increased confidence and safety. However, the invasive edges of a neoplasm and microsatellite lesions located far from the primary tumor will never be completely removable by surgery. It is through ongoing research into the most effective delivery of a targeted chemo-biologic agent that we will ultimately be able to manage the underlying cause of treatment failure.

title: Systematic review of controlled clinical trials of gastric lavage in acute organophosphorus pesticide poisoning.
text: Organophosphorus pesticide (OP) self-poisoning is a significant problem in developing rural areas, with limited clinical trial data to guide timely and effective treatment. Despite recognition of adverse effects, gastric lavage is commonly performed in Asia, but its effectiveness remains unproven. Our systematic search identified 56 studies from China, of which only 23 were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with inadequate methodology for quality assessment. The patient population and study treatment protocol were not well-defined, resulting in large variation in case fatality rates (4.5-93%) between studies and study arms. None of the studies compared an intervention with no gastric lavage or provided data on the removal of significant quantities of poison. This highlights the lack of high-quality evidence supporting the clinical effectiveness of gastric lavage for OP pesticide poisoning. Further studies are needed to determine which patients and duration of lavage are most effective, followed by large clinical trials to evaluate the safety and efficacy of gastric lavage, either singly or repeatedly, in acute OP pesticide poisoning.

title: Integrin activation by Fam38A uses a novel mechanism of R-Ras targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum.
