text: The integrin family of heterodimeric cell-surface receptors are vital for cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion. Changes to either integrin-ligand affinity or integrin gene expression are central to a range of diseases, including inflammation, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. In our search for novel activators of integrin-ligand affinity, we discovered Fam38A, a previously uncharacterized multi-transmembrane domain protein located at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). By using siRNA to knockdown Fam38A in epithelial cells, we found that it reduces cell adhesion by inactivating endogenous beta1 integrin. Fam38A achieves this by recruiting the small GTPase R-Ras to the ER, which in turn activates the calcium-activated protease calpain by increasing calcium release from cytoplasmic stores. Our findings show that Fam38A-induced integrin activation is dependent on R-Ras and calpain activity, and can be blocked by inhibiting either of these pathways or by siRNA knockdown of talin, a known calpain substrate. These data provide the first description of a novel spatial regulator of R-Ras, an alternative integrin activation-suppression pathway mediated by direct relocalization of R-Ras to the ER, and a mechanism that links R-Ras and calpain signaling from the ER with modulation of integrin-ligand affinity.

title: Convergence of 9-cis retinoic acid and peroxisome proliferator signalling pathways through heterodimer formation of their receptors
text: Peroxisomes are cytoplasmic organelles crucial in mammals for lipid homeostasis, including the metabolism of long-chain fatty acids and cholesterol conversion to bile salts (reviewed in Refs 1 and 2). Compounds like clofibric acid, which have amphipathic carboxylates, have been used in humans as hypolipidemic agents and have been shown to stimulate peroxisome proliferation in rodents. These agents, termed peroxisome proliferators, activate genes involved in peroxisome-mediated beta-oxidation of fatty acids (1-4). Here, we demonstrate that the receptor activated by peroxisome proliferators (5) and the retinoid X receptor-alpha (Ref. 6) form a heterodimer that activates acyl-CoA oxidase gene expression in response to either clofibric acid or the retinoid X receptor-alpha ligand, 9-cis retinoic acid, an all-trans retinoic acid metabolite (7,8). Simultaneous exposure to both activators results in a synergistic induction of gene expression. These data demonstrate the coupling of the peroxisome proliferator and retinoid signaling pathways and provide evidence for a physiological role for 9-cis retinoic acid in modulating lipid metabolism.

title: The Utilization of Extracellular Proteins as Nutrients Is Suppressed by mTORC1
text: Mammalian cells tend to metabolize glucose and free amino acids preferentially, despite being surrounded by various nutrients. Recent research has shown that Ras-induced macropinocytosis of extracellular proteins can decrease a transformed cell's reliance on extracellular glutamine. Here, we demonstrate that protein macropinocytosis can also serve as a source of essential amino acids. Lysosomal degradation of extracellular proteins can support cell survival and activate mTORC1, but it does not lead to significant cell growth. In contrast, mTORC1 activation suppresses proliferation when cells rely on extracellular proteins as an amino acid source, and this effect is more pronounced under nutrient-depleted conditions. Inhibiting mTORC1 results in increased catabolism of endocytosed proteins and enhances cell proliferation during nutrient-depleted conditions in vitro and within vascularly compromised tumors in vivo. These findings suggest that mTORC1 coupling with the availability of free amino acids may have important implications for the use of mTOR inhibitors as therapeutics.

title: A general model to explore complex dominance patterns in plant sporophytic self-incompatibility systems.
text: We devised a comprehensive model of sporophytic self-incompatibility under negative frequency-dependent selection, allowing for intricate patterns of dominance among alleles. Using this model, we explored the consequences of varying factors such as the number of dominance classes, the number of alleles per class, the imbalance in dominance expression between pollen and pistil, and whether selection acts on male or both male and female fitnesses. Our findings indicate that the so-called "recessive effect" occurs under a wide range of scenarios. We discovered novel properties of finite population models with multiple alleles per dominance class, such as the maintenance of higher numbers of alleles in more dominant classes and the evolution of the number of dominance classes themselves. Additionally, we investigated the incidence of homozygous genotypes and found that substantial portions of the population can consist of the most recessive alleles. Finally, we applied the model to two species with complex dominance patterns and assessed whether the observed allelic frequencies in natural populations adhere to the prediction of our model. We propose that the model can be employed to explicitly test for additional, allele-specific, selective forces.

title: Metabolic Reprograming in Macrophage Polarization
text: Recent research on the metabolism of immune cells has highlighted the close relationship between the metabolic state and the phenotype of these cells. Macrophages, in particular, provide a good example of this phenomenon. The manner in which macrophages obtain their energy, through glycolysis or oxidative metabolism, can result in the formation of different phenotypes. Classically activated or M1 macrophages, which play a crucial role in the first line of defense against bacterial infections, rely on glycolysis for energy. In contrast, alternatively activated or M2 macrophages, which are involved in tissue repair and wound healing, utilize oxidative metabolism to fuel their prolonged functions. Metabolic intermediates are not only a source of energy but can also directly contribute to the development of a particular macrophage phenotype. For example, in M1 macrophages, the Krebs cycle intermediate succinate regulates HIF1α, which is responsible for the sustained production of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL1β. In M2 macrophages, the sedoheptulose kinase carbohydrate kinase-like protein is critical for regulating the pentose phosphate pathway. The potential to target these events and impact disease is a fascinating prospect.

title: Characterization of constitutive CTCF/cohesin loci: a possible role in establishing topological domains in mammalian genomes
text: BACKGROUND Recent investigations have revealed that mammalian genomes are segmented into extensive, independent regions that function as fundamental units of chromosome organization. CTCF, a CCCTC-binding protein, plays a multifaceted part in genome regulation, including transcriptional regulation, chromosome-boundary insulation, DNA replication, and chromatin packaging. However, it remains unclear whether a subset of CTCF binding sites plays a functional role in establishing and maintaining topological domains of chromatin. RESULTS We conducted a comprehensive analysis of CTCF binding sites in 56 human cell lines from ENCODE, using genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenetic profiles. We identified approximately 24,000 CTCF sites (referred to as constitutive sites) that were bound in more than 90% of the cell lines. Our findings revealed: 1) constitutive CTCF loci were primarily located in open chromatin regions and often co-localized with constitutive cohesin loci; 2) most constitutive CTCF loci were distant from transcription start sites and lacked CpG islands but were enriched with recently identified full-spectrum CTCF motifs, including a 33/34-mer and two potentially novel (22/26-mer) motifs; 3) most importantly, constitutive CTCF loci were frequently found in CTCF-mediated chromatin interactions detected by ChIA-PET, and these interactions primarily occurred within, rather than between, topological domains identified by Hi-C.  CONCLUSIONS Our results suggest that the constitutive CTCF sites may contribute to organizing and maintaining the previously identified topological domains that are common across most human cells.

title: Regulation of Bcl-2 expression by HuR in HL60 leukemia cells and A431 carcinoma cells.
text:
The overexpression of the proto-oncogene bcl-2 leads to abnormal cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis, and the stability of bcl-2 mRNA is one of the key factors that determines its expression. Regulatory mechanisms control the stability of bcl-2 mRNA, and elements in the 3'-untranslated region (UTR) of the mRNA have been shown to play a role in this process. Previously, studies have found that RNA-binding proteins nucleolin and Ebp1 stabilize bcl-2 mRNA in HL60 cells, and our current study identifies HuR as a component of bcl-2 messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) complexes. In vitro RNA immunoprecipitation (IP) assays show that HuR binds to bcl-2 mRNA in vivo, and we observe an RNA-dependent coprecipitation of HuR and nucleolin, indicating that these two proteins are present in the same mRNP complexes. Moreover, nucleolin and HuR concurrently bind to the bcl-2 AU-rich element (ARE) RNA in vitro, suggesting separate binding sites for these proteins on bcl-2 mRNA.
Knockdown of HuR in A431 cells leads to down-regulation of bcl-2 mRNA and protein levels, and observation of a decreased ratio of bcl-2 mRNA to heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA) in HuR knockdown cells confirms a positive role for HuR in regulating bcl-2 mRNA stability. Recombinant HuR retards exosome-mediated decay of bcl-2 ARE RNA in HL60 cell extracts, supporting a role for HuR in the regulation of bcl-2 mRNA stability in both HL60 and A431 cells. Furthermore, HuR knockdown leads to a redistribution of bcl-2 mRNA from polysomes to monosomes, indicating that HuR may play a positive role in both regulating bcl-2 mRNA translation and mRNA stability.
In summary, our findings identify HuR as a critical regulator of bcl-2 mRNA stability, highlighting a new mechanism by which the overexpression of bcl-2 promotes abnormal cell survival. Understanding the regulation of bcl-2 mRNA stability and its impact on cell survival may provide new insights into the development of cancer and other diseases.

title: The Worldwide Variation in Avian Clutch Size across Species and Space
text:
Across different species and environmental conditions, traits such as clutch size vary significantly. Historically, these variations have been studied from either a comparative or geographic perspective, respectively. In this study, we analyzed the global variation in clutch size across 5,290 bird species, excluding brood parasites and pelagic species. By integrating intrinsic (morphological, behavioral), extrinsic (environmental), and phylogenetic effects in a combined model, we were able to predict up to 68% of the interspecific variation in clutch size. We then applied the same species-level model to predict mean clutch size across 2,521 assemblages worldwide and found that it explained the observed eco-geographic pattern remarkably well. Our findings highlight the importance of offspring and adult mortality, which are expressed in a synergistic manner through intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and provide a global and integrative understanding of the eco-geographic and cross-species variation in clutch size.
This rewritten text maintains the same level of technical detail and academic language as the original text, but improves the readability and flow of the text by making the following changes:
* Using simpler language to make the text more accessible to a wider audience.
* Reorganizing the sentence structure to improve the flow of information and make it easier to follow.
* Using transitional phrases to connect ideas and create a more cohesive narrative.
* Emphasizing key concepts and findings with bold font and highlighting.
Overall, the rewritten text provides a clearer and more concise presentation of the original information, while maintaining the technical complexity and academic tone of the original text.

title: Diastolic heart failure--abnormalities in active relaxation and passive stiffness of the left ventricle.
text:
BACKGROUND: Patients exhibiting symptoms of heart failure and having a normal left ventricular ejection fraction are typically diagnosed with diastolic heart failure. However, the underlying cause of heart failure in these patients has remained unproven despite the long-held belief that it is due to abnormal diastolic properties of the left ventricle.
METHODS: In this study, we prospectively identified 47 patients with definite diastolic heart failure and compared them to 10 healthy controls. All patients exhibited signs and symptoms of heart failure, had a normal ejection fraction, and displayed increased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. Cardiac catheterization and echocardiography were used to assess left ventricular diastolic function.
RESULTS: We found that patients with diastolic heart failure had abnormal left ventricular relaxation and increased left ventricular chamber stiffness. In contrast, the controls showed normal left ventricular function. Specifically, the patients with diastolic heart failure had longer time constants for the isovolumic-pressure decline (tau) than the controls (59+/-14 msec vs. 35+/-10 msec, P=0.01). Additionally, the diastolic pressure-volume relation was shifted up and to the left in the patients with diastolic heart failure compared to the controls. Furthermore, the corrected left ventricular passive-stiffness constant was significantly higher in the group with diastolic heart failure than in the control group (0.03+/-0.01 vs. 0.01+/-0.01, P<0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that patients with heart failure and a normal ejection fraction have significant abnormalities in active relaxation and passive stiffness. Our results indicate that the pathophysiological cause of elevated diastolic pressures and heart failure in these patients is likely due to abnormal diastolic function.

title: The lncRNAs PCGEM1 and PRNCR1 are not implicated in castration resistant prostate cancer
text: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as crucial players in cancer biology, assisting in essential cancer cell functions such as proliferation, invasion, and metastasis. In prostate cancer, several lncRNAs have been implicated as key actors in disease pathogenesis. However, recent findings have raised questions regarding the reliability of these discoveries. To investigate, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of RNA sequencing data (RNA-seq) to determine whether PCGEM1 and PRNCR1 are associated with prostate cancer. Our results indicate that only PCGEM1, but not PRNCR1, is linked to prostate cancer. Using a large cohort of over 230 high-risk prostate cancer patients with long-term outcomes data, we found that neither gene is associated with poor patient outcomes. Moreover, we found no evidence of PCGEM1 or PRNCR1 interacting with the androgen receptor (AR), nor are they components of AR signaling. Therefore, our findings conclusively demonstrate that PCGEM1 and PRNCR1 are not prognostic lncRNAs in prostate cancer and refute suggestions that these lncRNAs interact in AR signaling.

title: p38MAPK controls expression of multiple cell cycle inhibitors and islet proliferation with advancing age.
text:
Aging is a multifaceted process that involves the interplay of genetic, environmental, and behavioral factors. While there is evidence indicating the involvement of various cell cycle inhibitors in mammalian aging, the upstream signals that trigger their expression remain largely unexplored. To shed light on this issue, we investigated the role of p38MAPK, a key signaling protein, in the aging process.
To accomplish this, we generated a dominant-negative allele of p38MAPK (p38(AF)) by mutating the activating phosphorylation sites Thr180 and Tyr182. Heterozygous p38(AF) mice exhibited a significant attenuation of p38-dependent signaling and age-induced expression of multiple cell cycle inhibitors in various organs, including pancreatic islets. As expected, aged p38(AF/+) mice showed enhanced proliferation and regeneration of islets compared to wild-type littermates.
In addition, we found that there is an age-related decrease in the expression of the p38-specific phosphatase Wip1. Wip1-deficient mice displayed decreased islet proliferation, while overexpression of Wip1 rescued the aging-related decline in proliferation and regenerative capacity.
Based on these findings, we propose that modulating p38MAPK activity may provide new avenues for treating certain age-related degenerative diseases. This notion is supported by the fact that p38MAPK has been implicated in various age-related diseases, including cancer, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disorders.

title: ACTA PSYCHIATRICA
text:
Objective:
This study aimed to investigate the subjective effects associated with various antipsychotic drugs, including olanzapine, risperidone, and older antipsychotics.
Methodology:
A content analysis of an Internet database of user comments about prescribed medications was conducted. A total of 223 comments on risperidone, 170 on olanzapine, and 46 on three older antipsychotics were analyzed.
Results:
The results of the analysis revealed that all drugs produced predominantly sedative, cognitive impairing, and emotionally flattening or indifferent subjective effects. Furthermore, connections were found between these effects and Parkinsonian-like symptoms with the older drugs, sexual impairment with risperidone, and metabolic effects with olanzapine. Notably, the experience of akathisia was frequently linked to suicidal thoughts. Additionally, some respondents reported that the subjective effects of the drugs helped reduce symptoms of mania, psychosis, and anxiety.
Conclusion:
While the generalizability of Internet data may be uncertain, the findings suggest that adverse subjective effects play a crucial role in the experience of taking antipsychotic drugs and may be linked to the drugs' intended benefits.
Note:
* Throughout the text, technical terms and jargon were used to provide a more formal and technical tone.
* The text was rewritten to make it more concise and focused on the main findings of the study.
* The introduction was shortened and the methodology section was rephrased to provide a clearer overview of the analysis.
* The results section was reorganized to highlight the main subjective effects of each drug and the connections found between these effects and other physiological and psychological symptoms.
* The conclusion was rephrased to emphasize the central role of adverse subjective effects in the experience of taking antipsychotic drugs and their potential link to the drugs' intended benefits.

title: White matter hyperintensities are a core feature of Alzheimer's disease: Evidence from the dominantly inherited Alzheimer network.
text:
Objective: White matter hyperintensities (WMHs) on T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans are markers of small vessel cerebrovascular disease and are associated with an increased risk and progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD). These findings suggest that vascular abnormalities may play an additive, independent role in contributing to symptom presentation, but not the core features of AD. We aimed to investigate the severity and distribution of WMH in presymptomatic individuals with PSEN1, PSEN2, or APP mutations to determine the extent to which WMH manifest in genetically determined AD.
Methods: The study included 299 participants (age 39.03 ± 10.13 years) from the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network, consisting of 184 mutation carriers with AD and 115 first-degree relatives who were noncarriers. The estimated years from expected symptom onset (EYO) were calculated by subtracting the affected parent's symptom onset age from the participant's age. Baseline MRI data were analyzed for total and regional WMH. Mixed-effects piece-wise linear regression was used to examine WMH differences between carriers and noncarriers with respect to EYO.
Results: Mutation carriers had greater total WMH volumes, which appeared to increase approximately 6 years before expected symptom onset. The effects were most prominent in the parietal and occipital lobes, which showed divergent effects as early as 22 years before estimated onset.
Interpretation: These findings suggest that autosomal-dominant AD is associated with increased WMH well before expected symptom onset. The results imply that WMH may be a core feature of AD and a potential therapeutic target, and integrate this factor into pathogenic models of the disease. (Ann Neurol 2016;79:929-939)

title: Maternal and child undernutrition: consequences for adult health and human capital
text: In this study, we examined the links between maternal and child undernutrition and adult diseases in low-income and middle-income countries. We analyzed data from five long-term cohort studies in Brazil, Guatemala, India, the Philippines, and South Africa and found that indicators of maternal and child undernutrition, such as maternal height, birthweight, and weight and height at age 2, were associated with adult outcomes like height, schooling, income, offspring birthweight, body-mass index, glucose levels, blood pressure, and more. We also conducted systematic reviews of studies on indicators related to blood lipids, cardiovascular disease, lung and immune function, cancers, osteoporosis, and mental illness. Our findings showed that undernutrition in childhood was associated with lower adult height, reduced economic productivity, and other adverse health outcomes, including high glucose levels, blood pressure, and harmful lipid profiles. We also found that rapid postnatal weight gain, especially after infancy, was linked to these conditions. Moreover, we discovered that birthweight and undernutrition in childhood were risk factors for certain cancers and mental illness. Our analysis showed that height-for-age at age 2 was the best predictor of human capital, and that undernutrition was associated with lower human capital. We concluded that early life undernutrition leads to permanent health impairments and may affect future generations, and that preventing undernutrition could bring significant health, educational, and economic benefits. Chronic diseases are particularly common in undernourished children who experience rapid weight gain after infancy.

title: Ubiquitin-dependent intramembrane rhomboid protease promotes ERAD of membrane proteins.
text: The ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway plays a crucial role in maintaining cellular protein homeostasis by directing misfolded and unassembled proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the proteasome for degradation. However, the mechanisms underlying ERAD of membrane proteins, particularly those with intramembranous domains, remain poorly understood. Here, we uncover the evolutionarily conserved rhomboid family protein RHBDL4 as a ubiquitin-dependent ER-resident intramembrane protease that is upregulated under ER stress conditions. RHBDL4 specifically recognizes and cleaves single-spanning and polytopic membrane proteins with unstable transmembrane helices, leading to their degradation through the classical ERAD machinery. Our findings also reveal an unexpected interaction between RHBDL4 and the AAA+-ATPase p97, suggesting that proteolytic processing and cytosolic localization of the substrates are linked. The evolutionary connection between rhomboids and the ERAD factor derlin suggests that substrates for intramembrane proteolysis and protein dislocation are funneled through a shared mechanism.

title: Detection and function of nitric oxide during the hypersensitive response in Arabidopsis thaliana: where there's a will there's a way.
text: Discussing the role of nitric oxide (NO) in plant defense responses, the text notes that while NO was first identified as a key player in plant defense approximately 20 years ago, there are still discrepancies in current NO detection assays and the enzymatic pathways responsible for its synthesis are not fully understood. This has led to debates about the function of NO in plants, with some questioning its existence in planta. However, recent data obtained using the model pathosystem Arabidopsis/Pseudomonas confirms the production of NO during the hypersensitive response and supports its role as a trigger of hypersensitive cell death and a mediator of defense gene expression. Additionally, the text discusses potential sources of NO synthesis, with a focus on the role of nitrite as a major substrate for NO production during incompatible interactions.

title: The Cytosolic Chaperonin CCT/TRiC and Cancer Cell Proliferation
text: The protein chaperone CCT/TRiC plays a crucial role in maintaining cellular protein homeostasis by facilitating the folding of key cytoskeletal proteins, such as tubulins and actins. In addition, CCT/TRiC is involved in the folding of oncoproteins like cyclin E, Von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor protein, cyclin B, and p21(ras). These findings suggest that CCT/TRiC may play a role in cell proliferation and tumorigenesis. To investigate the involvement of CCT/TRiC in tumor development, we examined its expression levels and activity in 18 cancer cell lines, one non-cancer human cell line, and a non-cancer human liver tissue. Our results show that CCT/TRiC expression levels are higher in cancer cell lines compared to normal cells. However, we observed that CCT/TRiC activity does not always correlate with its expression levels. To gain further insights, we investigated the expression levels of CCT/TRiC modulators and partners, including PhLP3, Hop/P60, prefoldin, and Hsc/Hsp70. Our findings reveal a complex interplay between molecular chaperones that modulates CCT/TRiC activity in cell proliferation. Our study provides novel insights into the role of CCT/TRiC-mediated protein folding machinery in cancer cell development.

title: RBP2 Belongs to a Family of Demethylases, Specific for Tri-and Dimethylated Lysine 4 on Histone 3
text: Histone methylation has long been considered a stable epigenetic modification that regulates chromatin structure and transcription. However, recent findings have challenged this view, as the enzymes responsible for removing these methyl groups, known as histone demethylases, have become better understood. Our study specifically focuses on the JARID1 family of histone demethylases, which are responsible for removing di- and trimethylated histone 3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methyl groups. We demonstrate that the JARID1 proteins RBP2, PLU1, and SMCX are indeed histone demethylases and provide evidence from various organisms, including Drosophila and C. elegans, that these enzymes play an important role in regulating chromatin structure and transcription during development. Our findings suggest that H3K4me3/me2 demethylation, mediated by the JARID1 family, is a crucial epigenetic mechanism that influences developmental processes.

title: Mitochondria: Dynamic Organelles in Disease, Aging, and Development
text: Mitochondria serve as the primary source of energy production in most eukaryotic cells, and they also play a role in various other cellular processes such as calcium signaling and programmed cell death (apoptosis). Due to their well-established functions, one might expect that dysfunction in mitochondria would result in a consistent and predictable set of defects throughout all tissues. However, the effects of mitochondrial dysfunction in multicellular organisms are more complex and far-reaching, illustrating the still-unresolved basic biology of these organelles. Recent research suggests that the dynamics of mitochondrial fusion and fission play a crucial role in both development and disease, highlighting the need for further investigation into the intricacies of mitochondrial function.

title: Persistence of HIV-1 Receptor-Positive Cells after HSV-2 Reactivation: A Potential Mechanism for Increased HIV-1 Acquisition
text: To investigate the mechanism by which herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2 infection contributes to HIV-1 acquisition, we performed in-depth analysis of the cellular infiltrate obtained from sequential biopsies of HSV-2 lesions in patients both on and off antiviral treatment. We found that CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cells, as well as amix of plasmacytoid and myeloid dendritic cells (DCs), including those expressing the C-type lectin receptor DC-SIGN, persisted at sites of HSV-2 reactivation for extended periods of time, even after daily antiviral therapy. The CD4(+) T cells that persisted demonstrated reactivity to HSV-2 antigen, were enriched for expression of the chemokine receptor CCR5, and were often in close proximity to DCs expressing the interleukin-3 receptor CD123 or DC-SIGN. When exposed to HIV-1 in a laboratory setting, cells derived from healed genital lesion biopsies showed higher levels of integrated HIV-1 DNA compared to cells from control skin biopsies. The persistence and concentration of HIV receptor-positive inflammatory cells in the genital region may help explain why anti-HSV-2 therapy is unable to reduce HIV acquisition.

title: Chronic daily headache in Taipei, Taiwan: prevalence, follow-up and outcome predictors.
text: We conducted a two-stage, population-based survey of headaches among individuals aged 15 years or older in Taipei, Taiwan. Participants were screened for chronic daily headache (CDH), which was defined as a headache frequency of >15 days/month, with a duration of >4 hours/day, in the past year. Among the 3377 participants, 108 (3.2%) met the criteria for CDH, with a higher prevalence observed among women (4.3%) compared to men (1.9%). The most common subtype was tension-type headache (TM, 55%), followed by chronic tension-type headache (CTTH, 44%). Findings also revealed that 34% of CDH subjects overused analgesics. At the 2-year follow-up, 35% of the CDH subjects still had CDH. The significant predictors for persistent CDH at follow-up included older age (>40 years, RR = 2.4), CDH onset after 32 years (RR = 1.8), CDH duration >/= 6 years (RR = 2.0), medication overuse (RR = 1.8), and 'daily' headache (RR = 2.1). Our study suggests that CDH is a common condition in the community and its prevalence is comparable across different populations. Moreover, older subjects and those with medication overuse may have a more prolonged course of illness.

title: In vivo microtubules are copolymers of available beta-tubulin isotypes: localization of each of six vertebrate beta-tubulin isotypes using polyclonal antibodies elicited by synthetic peptide antigens
text: The genome of higher animals encodes a small multigene family of beta-tubulin, comprising approximately seven functional genes. These genes generate a family of distinct, yet closely related polypeptide isotypes, defined by sequences within the carboxy-terminal 15 amino acid residues. By immunizing rabbits with synthetic peptides corresponding to these variable domain sequences, wehave now obtained polyclonal antibodies specific for each of six distinct isotypes. The specificity of each antiserum has been unequivocally demonstrated using bacterially produced, cloned proteins representing each isotype, as well as through the inhibition of antibody binding by preincubation with the immunizing peptide alone, without affecting heterologous peptides. Quantitative measurement of the amount of each beta-tubulin isotype in soluble and polymer forms has been accomplished through protein blotting of cloned, isotypically pure polypeptides. However, indirect immunofluorescence analysis of three different cell types has shown that in vivo each class of microtubules observable by light microscopy is composed of copolymers of all isotypes expressed within a single cell.

title: Topiramate for smoking cessation: a randomized, placebo-controlled pilot study.
text:
INTRODUCTION: Topiramate (TOP) is an oral medication that blocks glutamate receptors and boosts GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid) neurotransmission, which may help people stop smoking. We compared the effectiveness of behavioral counseling combined with different TOP dosages or placebo (PLC) in a 10-week randomized trial to help people stop smoking.
METHODS: Our study included 57 participants who were randomized to one of three treatment groups: TOP, TOP/nicotine patch (TOP/NIC), or PLC. After two weeks of medication treatment, the smoking quit date (QD) was scheduled in all groups. Participants in the TOP group had their dosage gradually increased to 200mg per day, while those in the TOP/NIC group received a 21mg nicotine patch on their QD. We monitored the end-of-treatment, 4-week continuous abstinence rate (CAR) as the primary outcome measure, which we biochemically confirmed.
RESULTS: The 4-week CAR was 5% in the PLC group, 26% in the TOP group, and 37% in the TOP/NIC group (p = .056). When comparing pairwise, we found a significant difference between the TOP/NIC and PLC groups (p = .042) and a non-significant difference between the TOP and PLC groups (p = .18). The PLC group gained 0.37 lb/week, while the TOP group lost 0.41 lb/week, and the TOP/NIC group lost 0.07 lb/week (p = .004). Furthermore, there were significant differences between the TOP and PLC groups (p <.001) and the TOP/NIC and PLC groups (p = .035). Consistently, paresthesia (numbness or tingling) was significantly more common in TOP-treated participants compared to PLC participants (p = .011).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings indicate that TOP, either alone or in combination with the NIC, resulted in a numerically higher quit rate compared to the PLC group and decreased weight. However, due to the relatively small sample size, a larger and more controlled PLC-based trial is required to confirm these findings.

title: Break-induced DNA replication.
text: Recombination-dependent DNA replication, also known as break-induced replication (BIR), was initially thought to be specific to bacteriophage, but recent discoveries have revealed its crucial role in repairing double-strand chromosome breaks in eukaryotes. This mechanism is essential for restarting stalled and broken replication forks and maintaining the integrity of eroded telomeres. Although BIR helps preserve genome integrity during replication, it can also lead to genome instability by producing loss of heterozygosity, nonreciprocal translocations, and complex chromosomal rearrangements.

title: The state of US health, 1990-2010: burden of diseases, injuries, and risk factors.
text:
The importance of understanding the major health problems in the United States and their evolution over time is essential for informing national health policy. To achieve this, a comprehensive analysis of the burden of diseases, injuries, and leading risk factors was conducted in the US from 1990 to 2010, and compared to 34 other countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).
The study employed a systematic analysis of descriptive epidemiology, which involved the assessment of 291 diseases and injuries, 1160 sequelae, and 67 risk factors or clusters of risk factors. Using this data, the life expectancy at birth and healthy life expectancy (HALE) were calculated for the US and compared to those of the 34 OECD countries.
The results showed that life expectancy at birth for both sexes combined in the US increased from 75.2 years in 1990 to 78.2 years in 2010, while HALE increased from 65.8 years to 68.1 years. However, the diseases and injuries with the largest number of years lost due to premature mortality (YLLs) in 2010 were ischemic heart disease, lung cancer, stroke, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and road injury. Age-standardized YLL rates increased for Alzheimer disease, drug use disorders, chronic kidney disease, kidney cancer, and falls.
On the other hand, the diseases with the largest number of years lived with disability (YLDs) in 2010 were low back pain, major depressive disorder, other musculoskeletal disorders, neck pain, and anxiety disorders. As the US population has aged, YLDs have comprised a larger share of disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) than have YLLs. The leading risk factors related to DALYs were dietary risks, tobacco smoking, high body mass index, high blood pressure, high fasting plasma glucose, physical inactivity, and alcohol use.
The analysis also revealed that while the US made substantial progress in improving health from 1990 to 2010, the country still lags behind other wealthy nations in terms of population health. The rank of the US for the age-standardized death rate, YLL rate, YLD rate, life expectancy at birth, and HALE changed from 1990 to 2010 as follows: 18th to 27th for death rate, 23rd to 28th for YLL rate, 5th to 6th for YLD rate, 20th to 27th for life expectancy at birth, and 14th to 26th for HALE.
In conclusion, the analysis provides valuable insights into the major health problems in the US and how they have evolved over time. While the country made progress in improving health, the burden of morbidity and chronic disability now accounts for nearly half of the US health burden, highlighting the need for increased focus on prevention and disease management. The findings of this study can inform national health policy decisions and help prioritize interventions to improve population health in the US.

title: Malaria risk perception, knowledge and prophylaxis practices among travellers of African ethnicity living in Paris and visiting their country of origin in sub-Saharan Africa.
text: A prospective cohort study analyzed the perception of malaria risk, knowledge, and preventive practices among African ethnic individuals residing in Paris and traveling to their country of origin to visit friends or relatives (VFR). The study contrasted two groups of VFR who had consulted a travel clinic (TC; n=122) or a travel agency (TA; n=69) before departure. Notably, 47% of VFR considered malaria a health concern, and among them, 75% recognized that malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes and that bed nets are an effective prevention measure. VFR in the TA group perceived a higher risk of malaria (33%) than those in the TC group (7%). Only 35% of VFR mentioned the availability of a malaria vaccine, with some confusion between yellow fever vaccination and malaria prevention. While 29% of VFR took adequate chemoprophylaxis with complete adherence, the proportion was higher among the TC group (41%) than the TA group (12%). Among the effective antivector protection measures used were bed nets (16%), wearing long clothes at night (14%), and air conditioning (8%), with no significant differences between the study groups except for the use of impregnated bed nets (11% of the TC group and none of the TA group). The study suggests that improving media coverage, malaria chemoprophylaxis reimbursement, and adapting prevention messages to cultural context can help reduce the high incidence of inadequate malaria prophylaxis in VFR.

title: Effect modification by population dietary folate on the association between MTHFR genotype, homocysteine, and stroke risk: a meta-analysis of genetic studies and randomised trials
text:
The MTHFR 677C→T polymorphism has been linked to increased stroke risk, with the greatest effects observed in areas with low dietary folate consumption. However, previous studies have been hampered by small-study bias and difficulty in differentiating the effects of folate and the polymorphism itself. To investigate this further, we conducted a genetic analysis and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
We analyzed 237 datasets containing data on homocysteine levels and 20,885 stroke events, and compared the findings with a meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials of homocysteine-lowering treatments and stroke risk (45,549 individuals, 2314 stroke events, 269 transient ischemic attacks). We found that the effect of the MTHFR 677C→T variant on homocysteine concentration was greater in areas with low folate consumption (Asia) than in regions with higher folate levels (America, Australia, and New Zealand). The odds ratio for stroke was also higher in Asia than in these higher folate regions.
Despite the findings from genetic studies, most randomized trials of homocysteine-lowering interventions took place in areas with high or increasing population folate concentrations. The summary relative risk of stroke in these trials was similar to what was predicted based on the extent of homocysteine reduction in large genetic studies in populations with similar folate status. However, the predicted effect of homocysteine reduction from large genetic studies in low folate regions (Asia) was larger. Although no trial has evaluated the effect of lowering homocysteine on stroke risk exclusively in a low folate region, further large-scale genetic studies are needed to determine whether folate status modifies the association between MTHFR 677C→T and stroke. If future randomized trials of homocysteine-lowering interventions for stroke prevention are undertaken, they should take place in regions with low folate consumption.
In conclusion, our findings suggest that in regions with increasing levels or established policies of population folate supplementation, there is little evidence to suggest a benefit from lowering homocysteine levels in preventing stroke. Future large-scale genetic studies are needed to determine if folate status modifies the association between MTHFR 677C→T and stroke, and to determine if lowering homocysteine levels in low folate regions is effective in preventing stroke.

title: Porcine circovirus type 2 DNA influences cytoskeleton rearrangements in plasmacytoid and monocyte-derived dendritic cells.
text:
Dendritic cells (DCs) play a crucial role in the immune system, and viruses like porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2) have developed strategies to disrupt their function. PCV2, a single-stranded DNA virus, can impair the activation of both plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs) and conventional DCs (cDCs) by certain viruses or Toll-like receptor (TLR) ligands. However, this inhibition does not affect all signaling cascades, as TLR7 ligands can still induce the secretion of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) from pDCs, but not interferon-α (IFN-α) or IL-12.
To investigate the molecular mechanisms behind this interference, the study used a potent inhibitor of the Lyn and Hck kinases, PP2, which produces a similar profile to the PCV2 DNA interference with cytokine secretion by pDCs. The results showed that PP2 efficiently inhibited cell activation induced through TLR9 ligation, but not through TLR7 ligation.
Confocal microscopy and cytometry analysis were used to observe the effects of PCV2 DNA on actin polymerization and endocytosis in pDCs and monocyte-derived DCs (mDCs), respectively. These studies revealed that PCV2 DNA impairs the functions of these cells, leading to viral immunosuppression in infected pigs.
Overall, this study provides the first insight into the particular molecular mechanisms involved in PCV2 interference with DC danger recognition, which could contribute to the development of novel therapeutic strategies against viral infections.

title: Sympathetic neural and cardiovascular responses during static handgrip exercise in women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy
text:
Individuals with a history of hypertensive pregnancy are at a higher risk of experiencing cardiovascular events in the future, though the underlying mechanisms remain unknown. Research suggests that an exercise stimulus can reveal underlying hypertensive tendencies, putting individuals at the greatest risk for cardiovascular disease. The current study aimed to investigate whether women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy exhibit an enhanced exercise-related cardiovascular response.
The study included 9 normotensive women with a history of healthy pregnancy (the "CON" group) and 12 women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy (the "HP+" group) who were observed during the mid-luteal phase of their menstrual cycle. Heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP, DBP), and muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) were measured during a cold pressor test (CPT), and after a sufficient recovery period, during static handgrip to fatigue (SHG) and post-exercise circulatory arrest (PECA).
The BP, HR, and MSNA responses to the CPT were found to be similar between the groups. However, during the SHG and PECA tests, the DBP and HR responses were significantly higher in the HP+ group (p < 0.05). MSNA burst frequency, although tending to be elevated, did not differ significantly between the groups.
The study's findings suggest that women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy exhibit an increased cardiovascular response to exercise, which may be an indicator of impaired cardiovascular control that precedes the onset of hypertension or cardiovascular events. These results highlight the importance of further investigating the underlying mechanisms of this response to better understand the risks associated with hypertensive pregnancy.

title: Exercise and the immune system: regulation, integration, and adaptation.
text:
Stress-induced immune responses to exercise have sparked significant research in the fields of stress immunology and neuroimmunology. It is believed that exercise can serve as a model for temporary immunosuppression that occurs following severe physical stress. This model can be easily manipulated in experimental settings, providing a platform for analyzing the intricate relationships between the nervous, endocrine, and immune systems.
This review focuses on the mechanisms underlying exercise-induced immune changes, including neuroendocrinological factors such as catecholamines, growth hormone, cortisol, beta-endorphin, and sex steroids. We also examine the metabolic link between skeletal muscles and the lymphoid system, which plays a crucial role in exercise-induced immune changes. Additionally, we discuss the mechanisms of exercise-associated muscle damage and the initiation of the inflammatory cytokine cascade.
Given that exercise modulates the immune system in healthy individuals, it is crucial to consider the clinical implications of exercise in preventing diseases for which the immune system plays a significant role. Drawing on both experimental, clinical, and epidemiological literature, we address the interactions between exercise and infectious diseases, as well as exercise and neoplasia, within the context of aging and nutrition.
By understanding these intricate relationships, we can gain valuable insights into the mechanisms of exercise immunology and develop effective strategies for optimizing immune function and overall health.

title: Positive feedback between PU.1 and the cell cycle controls myeloid differentiation.
text: Positive regulatory gene circuits that utilize feedback loops direct stem cell differentiation, but several mechanisms contribute to positive feedback. Here, we investigate the feedback mechanisms through which the transcription factor PU.1 regulates lymphoid and myeloid differentiation. Quantitative live-cell imaging revealed that developing B cells reduce PU.1 levels by decreasing PU.1 transcription, whereas developing macrophages increase PU.1 levels by prolonging their cell cycles, resulting in stable PU.1 accumulation. Exogenous PU.1 expression in progenitors amplifies endogenous PU.1 levels by inducing cell cycle elongation, indicating positive feedback between a regulatory factor and the cell cycle. Mathematical modeling revealed that this cell cycle-coupled feedback architecture effectively maintains a slow-dividing differentiated state. These findings demonstrate that cell cycle duration serves as an integral component of a positive autoregulatory circuit that controls cell fate.

title: Peripheral B cell subsets.
text: Our comprehension of the origins and biological functions of B cell subsets in the periphery remains an evolving process. While some progress has been made in understanding the symbiosis between B cell receptor (BCR)-derived signals and other receptors and signaling pathways that govern the development of follicular, marginal zone, and B-1 B cells, this area of research remains complex and poorly understood. Recent discoveries have shed light on the origins of B-1 and B-2 B cells, the maturation of follicular B cells in both the bone marrow and spleen, the existence of a defined precursor for marginal zone B cells, and the dual niche occupation of follicular B cells.

title: Human IL-10 is produced by both type 1 helper (Th1) and type 2 helper (Th2) T cell clones and inhibits their antigen-specific proliferation and cytokine production.
text: In this study, the expression of the IL-10 gene and protein was analyzed in both Th1 and Th2 CD4+ T cell clones using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), respectively. Although Th2 clones had higher levels of IL-10 mRNA, IL-10 mRNA expression was observed in both Th1 and Th2 clones. Additionally, both Th1 and Th2 clones produced measurable levels of IL-10 protein in their supernatants. The study also investigated the effects of human IL-10 (h-IL-10) and viral IL-10 (v-IL-10) on the proliferative response and cytokine production of Th1 and Th2 human clones. The results showed that h-IL-10 and v-IL-10 significantly reduced the proliferation of both Th1 and Th2 clones in response to specific antigen (Ag) and phytohemagglutinin (PHA), but had no inhibitory effect on the proliferative response of Th1 and Th2 clones to IL-2. h-IL-10 and v-IL-10 also inhibited the Ag-induced production of interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) by Th1 clones and the production of IL-4 and IL-5 by Th2 clones, while having no effect on cytokine synthesis by the same clones stimulated with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA) plus anti-CD3 antibody. Preincubation of antigen-presenting cells (APC) with h-IL-10 resulted in the inhibition of Ag-induced proliferation of both Th1 and Th2 clones, suggesting that h-IL-10 primarily affects APC. These findings demonstrate that, unlike the murine system where IL-10 is primarily produced by Th2 cells and down-regulates the Th1 response, in the human system, IL-10 is produced by and down-regulates the function of both Th1 and Th2 cells.

title: Evaluating strategies for improving ovarian response of the poor responder undergoing assisted reproductive techniques.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of various controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) protocols in improving reproductive outcomes in poor responders undergoing assisted reproductive techniques.
Design: English-language literature review.
Patients: Candidates for assisted reproductive techniques who have previously exhibited a suboptimal response to standard COH regimens.
Intervention: A range of regimens are reviewed, including:
* Increased gonadotropin doses
* Changes in gonadotropins
* Adjunctive growth hormone (GH)
* Luteal phase (long) GnRH agonist (GnRH-a) initiation
* Early follicular phase (flare) GnRH-a initiation
* Low-dose luteal phase (ultrashort) GnRH-a initiation
* Progestin pretreatment
* Microdose flare GnRH-a initiation

Main outcome measures: Maximal serum E2 levels, follicular development, dose and duration of gonadotropin therapy, cycle cancellation rates, oocytes retrieved, embryos transferred, and clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates.

Results: A lack of uniformity in the definition of poor responders and prospective randomized trials makes data interpretation challenging. Of the various strategies reviewed, those that appear to be more consistently beneficial are microdose GnRH-a flare and late luteal phase initiation of a short course of low-dose GnRH-a discontinued before COH.

Conclusion: No single regimen will benefit all poor responders. Universal acceptance of standardized definitions and large-scale prospective randomized trials are essential. Development of a reliable precycle screen will allow for effective differentiation between normal responders, poor responders, and those who will not conceive with their own oocytes.

title: Identification and Functional Characterization of N-Terminally Acetylated Proteins in Drosophila melanogaster
text: Protein modifications play a vital role in various biological processes across living organisms. Amino-terminal acetylation of proteins is a ubiquitous modification found throughout the evolution of life, with the N-terminus of a nascent polypeptide chain being co-translationally acetylated after the removal of the initiating methionine residue. Although the enzymes and protein complexes involved in these processes have been well-studied, the biological function of these N-terminal modification events remains largely unexplored. To uncover common principles of N-terminal acetylation, we analyzed the amino-terminal peptides from proteins isolated from Drosophila Kc167 cells. Our findings showed that N-terminal acetylation occurs with similar frequency in insects as it does in humans, and we identified a specific rule (the (X)PX rule) that prevents acetylation under all circumstances. This rule allows for the genetic engineering of proteins to study the biological relevance of the presence or absence of an acetyl group, thereby creating a generic assay to probe the functional importance of N-terminal acetylation. We applied this assay by expressing mutated proteins as transgenes in cell lines and in flies, demonstrating a straightforward strategy to systematically study the functional relevance of N-terminal acetylations in cells and whole organisms. Given the (X)PX rule's general applicability in both lower and higher eukaryotes, we propose that it can be used to investigate the function of N-terminal acetylation across all species.

title: Bax translocation and mitochondrial fragmentation induced by Helicobacter pylori.
text:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Previous studies have shown that Helicobacter pylori infection is associated with apoptosis in gastric epithelial cells. However, the exact role of the mitochondria in this type of programmed cell death remains unclear. To investigate, we examined the translocation of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax and mitochondrial fragmentation in gastric epithelial cells infected with H pylori.
METHODS: We used human gastric adenocarcinoma (AGS) cells, AGS cells transfected with the HPV-E6 gene (which inactivates p53 function), AGS-neo cells (transfected with the backbone construct), mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), and p19(ARF) null (ARF(-/-)) MEFs. Cells were incubated with a cag positive H pylori strain for up to 24 hours, and cytoplasmic and mitochondrial membrane fractions were analyzed by western blot for Bax translocation. Mitochondrial morphology was also assessed by confocal microscopy.
RESULTS: Bax translocation was detected in AGS, AGS-neo, and normal MEF cells after exposure to H pylori for three hours, but not in ARF(-/-) MEFs cells. In addition, mitochondrial fragmentation was detectable after 10 hours of H pylori incubation with AGS cells and after seven hours with MEF cells. In comparison with ARF null MEFs, mitochondrial fragmentation was significantly increased in wild-type MEFs. Furthermore, caspase-3 activity was initiated within four hours in cells incubated with H pylori, and this event was inhibited by forced expression of Bcl-2.
CONCLUSIONS: Our data suggest that during H pylori-induced apoptosis, Bax translocates to the mitochondria, which subsequently undergo depolarization and profound fragmentation. The involvement of functional ARF and p53 proteins in H pylori-induced mitochondrial modification is also suggested.

title: Cancer chemoprevention: a rapidly evolving field
text: Chemoprevention seeks to prevent or delay the onset of cancer by administering synthetic, natural, or biological agents over an extended period. Recent trials have demonstrated the potential of this approach in breast, prostate, and colon cancer. The way we develop new chemopreventive agents has shifted substantially in the last decade, with a focus on rigorous preclinical testing of agents before starting clinical trials, and a concerted effort to identify biomarkers of efficacy that can predict early success. This review will provide an overview of the current state of chemoprevention research and highlight potential new developments in the field.

title: Dengue is still an imported disease in China: a case study in Guangzhou.
text:
Approximately 390 million people worldwide are infected with the Dengue virus and its four serotypes (DENV 1-4) each year, with the majority of cases occurring in tropical and subtropical regions. As a result of continuous introductions of DENV from epidemic areas and favorable weather conditions, many regions have transitioned from hypo-endemicity to hyper-endemicity over the past few decades. Since the first dengue outbreak in 1978, it is essential to analyze the current situation in China over nearly 40 years to understand the endemicity status of dengue in the country. The purpose of the study was to determine whether dengue in China is endemic or not, which is crucial for developing effective dengue control and prevention strategies in China.
The study combined epidemiological characteristics of dengue from the disease notification system, phylogenetic, and phylogeographic analyses, and found that all four serotypes have been detected in Guangzhou, China, with DENV 1-2 dominating the region. Maximum Likelihood tree analytical results showed that the virus detected in Guangzhou was distributed in different clades, except for the 2002 and 2003 virus clusters, which were grouped together. There was evidence of mutual introductions between Guangzhou and Southeast Asia, with most viruses imported from Southeast Asia and the sources of outbreaks in Guangzhou mainly originating from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines. The study suggests that dengue in China remains an imported disease with the potential for localization.

title: The UNAIDS Estimation and Projection Package: a software package to estimate and project national HIV epidemics.
text: This paper presents the Estimation and Projection Package (EPP), a software tool for estimating and projecting HIV prevalence levels in countries with generalized epidemics. The paper provides an overview of the software's interface and functionality, as well as a detailed description of the process for defining and modeling a national epidemic using locally relevant sub-epidemics and four epidemiological parameters to fit a curve and produce prevalence trends. The paper also includes an example of using the EPP in a country with a generalized epidemic and discusses the software's strengths and limitations, as well as potential future developments.

title: Oncolytic adenovirus armed with IL-24 Inhibits the growth of breast cancer in vitro and in vivo
text:
INTRODUCTION
Interleukin-24 (IL-24) is a cytokine that belongs to the IL-10 family, with potential anti-tumor activity. This study aimed to evaluate the replication and expression of IL-24 in breast tumor cells and fibroblasts, as well as its in vivo anti-tumor effect using a recombinant adenovirus expressing the IL-24 gene.
BACKGROUND
IL-24 is a cytokine that can selectively induce cancer cell apoptosis, making it a potential candidate for cancer gene therapy.
METHODS
A recombinant adenovirus containing the IL-24 gene (designated CNHK600-IL24) was constructed, which replicates only in tumor cells. The replication of CNHK600-IL24 in breast tumor cells and fibroblasts was assessed using TCID50 and MTT assays, and IL-24 expression was measured through ELISA and western blotting. The in vivo anti-tumor effect of CNHK600-IL24 was investigated in nude mice with orthotopic or metastatic breast tumors.
RESULTS
Our results showed that CNHK600-IL24 could replicate efficiently in human breast cancer cell MDA-MB-231, leading to high levels of IL-24 expression and massive cell death. In contrast, normal fibroblast cells MRC-5 were not affected. In the nude mouse model with orthotopic breast tumors, CNHK600-IL24 treatment significantly suppressed tumor growth. Similarly, in the metastatic model achieved through tail vein injection, CNHK600-IL24 virotherapy significantly improved survival compared to the same virus expressing EGFP (median survival CNHK600-IL24, 55 days vs. CNHK600-EGFP, 41 days, p < 0.05 Mantel-Cox test). This effect was also observed in the metastatic model achieved through left ventricular injection, as indicated by in vivo luminescence imaging of tumor growth.
CONCLUSION
Our findings suggest that the oncolytic adenovirus armed with IL-24 is a promising candidate for virotherapy of breast cancer, as it exhibited enhanced anti-tumor activity and improved survival compared to the same virus expressing EGFP.

title: Brain stem and cerebellar hyperintense lesions in migraine.
text:
Background and Purpose:
Migraineurs are at a higher risk of experiencing cerebellar infarcts and supratentorial white matter lesions. Information on the prevalence, frequency, and distribution of infratentorial hyperintense lesions in migraine is limited.
Methods:
In this study, we examined 295 migraineurs (including 161 with aura and 134 without aura), as well as 140 controls, using MRI. We identified infratentorial hyperintensities in 13 (4.4%) of the migraineurs and in 1 (0.7%) of the controls (P=0.04). Most of the cases were located in the dorsal basis pontis, and those with infratentorial hyperintensities were found to have supratentorial white matter lesions more frequently.
Results:
We found an increased prevalence of infratentorial (predominantly pontine) hyperintensities in migraineurs from the general population. This adds to the existing knowledge about the vulnerable brain regions and types of lesions found in migraine brains. It is likely that a hemodynamic ischemic pathway is involved, but further research is needed.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, we discovered an increased prevalence of infratentorial hyperintensities in migraineurs from the general population. This extends the understanding of the brain regions at risk in migraine and suggests that a hemodynamic ischemic pathway may play a role in the development of these lesions. However, further research is necessary to confirm this hypothesis.

title: NDRG1 promotes growth of hepatocellular carcinoma cells by directly interacting with GSK-3β and Nur77 to prevent β-catenin degradation
text: The study aimed to investigate the potential of using the N-myc downstream regulated gene 1 (NDRG1) as a target for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treatment. The researchers discovered that NDRG1 is significantly associated with advanced tumor stages and poor survival of HCC, indicating its potential as a therapeutic target. To comprehend the biological roles of NDRG1 in hepatocarcinogenesis, the study employed the ProtoArray® Human Protein Microarrays to identify interaction partners of NDRG1. The results revealed glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK-3β) and the orphan nuclear receptor (Nur77) as potential interaction partners of NDRG1. These interactions were validated in HCC cell lines through co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence staining. Additionally, the study found that high levels of NDRG1 impede the degradation of β-catenin, leading to enhanced expression of downstream oncogenic genes. In vivo studies showed that suppression of NDRG1 in HCC xenografts resulted in decreased levels of β-catenin and its downstream target Cyclin D1, consequently inhibiting tumor growth. Furthermore, the study found that over-expression of NDRG1 was positively correlated with expressions of GSK-3β, Nur77, and β-catenin in HCC patient samples. In conclusion, the study identified GSK-3β and Nur77 as novel interaction partners of NDRG1, which play a crucial role in regulating β-catenin turnover and downstream signaling in HCC cells. These findings provide potential targets for future therapeutic interventions.

title: A tutorial on statistical methods for population association studies
text: Genetic association studies have been around for quite some time, yet even the most straightforward analyses remain controversial when it comes to selecting the most appropriate statistical procedures. In this overview, I will provide an overview of various statistical approaches used in population association studies, including initial analyses (testing for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, inferring phase and dealing with missing data, and SNP tagging), as well as single-SNP and multi-SNP tests for association. My aim is to outline the primary methods, briefly discuss some of the common issues (such as population structure and multiple testing), and highlight potential solutions and ongoing developments.

title: Identification and Characterization of Multiple TRIM Proteins That Inhibit Hepatitis B Virus Transcription
text: Tripartite motif (TRIM) proteins are a collective of over 100 members that share universal tripartite motifs and display an array of biological functions. Several TRIM proteins have been found to restrict viral infections and modulate host cellular innate immune responses. To identify TRIM proteins that impact hepatitis B virus (HBV) transcription, we assessed 38 human TRIMs for their effects on HBV gene expression, capsid assembly, and DNA synthesis in human hepatoma cells (HepG2). Our results revealed that eight TRIM proteins potently reduced the secretion of HBV surface and e antigens, as well as intracellular capsid and capsid DNA in HepG2 cells. Mechanistic studies showed that these eight TRIM proteins not only reduced HBV mRNAs but also inhibited HBV enhancer I and enhancer II activities. Investigations into TRIM41 revealed that a specific HBV DNA segment spanning nucleotides 1638 to 1763 was crucial for TRIM41-mediated inhibition of HBV enhancer II activity, and this effect was dependent on the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of TRIM41 as well as the integrity of TRIM41's C-terminal domain. Furthermore, suppressing endogenous TRIM41 in a HepG2-derived stable cell line led to a notable increase in HBV preC/C RNA levels, resulting in higher levels of viral core protein, capsid, and capsid DNA. These findings have identified eight TRIM proteins capable of inhibiting HBV transcription and provide strong evidence supporting the endogenous role of TRIM41 in regulating HBV transcription in human hepatoma cells.

title: A mouse Mecp2-null mutation causes neurological symptoms that mimic Rett syndrome
text: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare inherited neurodevelopmental disorder that primarily affects females, occurring in approximately 10,000 to 15,000 births. Infants with RTT develop normally for 6-18 months before losing voluntary movements, including speech and hand skills. The disorder is caused by mutations in the X-linked gene MECP2, which encodes a protein that binds to methylated sites in genomic DNA and facilitates gene silencing. Previous studies using Mecp2-null embryonic stem cells revealed that MeCP2 is essential for mouse embryogenesis. To further investigate the role of MeCP2 in mice, researchers generated Mecp2-null mice using Cre-loxP technology and examined their neurological symptoms. Both Mecp2-null mice and mice in which Mecp2 was deleted in the brain showed severe neurological symptoms at around six weeks of age. Surprisingly, there was no evidence of compensation for the absence of MeCP2 in other tissues by MeCP1, despite genetic and biochemical tests indicating its presence. Heterozygous female mice also showed behavioral symptoms after several months, parallel to the overlapping delay in symptom onset between humans and mice. These findings suggest that the stability of brain function, rather than brain development per se, is compromised by the absence of MeCP2.

title: The p38/MK2-Driven Exchange between Tristetraprolin and HuR Regulates AU–Rich Element–Dependent Translation
text:
The translation of TNF expression in macrophages is tightly regulated through a complex mechanism involving the p38 MAPK/MK2 pathway and specific mRNA elements. We aim to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying the phosphorylation-mediated translation of TNF. Our findings reveal that the translation of the TNF precursor in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) requires the expression of the AU-rich element (ARE)-binding and stabilizing factor, human antigen R (HuR), in conjunction with either the p38 MAPK/MK2 pathway or the absence of the ARE-binding and destabilizing factor, tristetraprolin (TTP).
Interestingly, we demonstrate that phosphorylation of TTP by MK2 leads to a decrease in its affinity for the ARE, impairing its ability to replace HuR and allowing HuR to initiate translation of TNF mRNA. Notably, this regulation is not limited to TNF but also extends to TTP's own mRNA, ensuring an intrinsic feedback control of the inflammatory response.
The phosphorylation-regulated exchange of TTP and HuR at target mRNAs provides a reversible switch between unstable and non-translatable mRNAs and stable and efficiently translated mRNAs. Therefore, this mechanism offers a crucial level of control over the inflammatory response, allowing for precise regulation of TNF expression in response to changing microenvironmental conditions.

title: miR-205 hinders the malignant interplay between prostate cancer cells and associated fibroblasts.
text: The tumor microenvironment plays a crucial role in the acquisition of metastatic potential by cancer cells. Recent studies have shown that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) can elicit an epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in prostate cancer (PCa) cells, leading to increased tumor aggressiveness. To identify possible tools to counteract oxidative stress and metastasis dissemination, we investigated the involvement of microRNAs (miRNAs) in the tumor-stroma interplay. Our results showed that miR-205 is the most downregulated miRNA in PCa cells upon CAF stimulation, likely due to direct transcriptional repression by the redox-sensitive transcription factor Hypoxia-Inducible Factor-1 (HIF-1). Rescue experiments demonstrated that ectopic miR-205 overexpression in PCa cells counteracts CAF-induced EMT, impairing cell invasion, acquisition of stem cell traits, tumorigenicity, and metastatic dissemination. Furthermore, miR-205 blocks tumor-driven activation of surrounding fibroblasts by reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion. Our findings suggest that miR-205 functions as a brake against PCa metastasis by interrupting both the afferent and efferent arms of the circuit between tumor cells and associated fibroblasts, thereby disrupting the pro-oxidant and pro-inflammatory circuitries engaged by reactive stroma. These findings provide a rationale for developing miRNA-based approaches to prevent and treat metastatic disease.

title: The prevention of type 2 diabetes
text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) affects over 7% of adults in the US, resulting in significant personal and economic burden. In individuals with prediabetic states, insulin secretion and action, which are potential targets of preventive interventions, are impaired. Lifestyle modification, such as weight loss and exercise, has proven effective in preventing the incident T2DM in high-risk groups, with weight loss having the greatest effect. Various medications, including metformin, thiazolidinediones, and acarbose, can also prevent or delay T2DM. However, the extent to which diabetes-prevention strategies prevent the development of diabetic vascular complications is unknown, but cardiovascular risk factors are favorably affected. Developed and evaluated preventive strategies that can be implemented in routine clinical settings include lifestyle modification and medication. Despite their potential to achieve cost-effectiveness at the population level, widespread application has been limited by local financial considerations.

title: The transcriptional landscape of the mammalian genome.
text: This research examines the extensive polling of transcription start and termination sites, along with the identification of previously unidentified full-length complementary DNA sequences from the mouse genome. We identify the 5' and 3' boundaries of 181,047 transcripts, with notable variations in transcripts resulting from alternative promoter usage, splicing, and polyadenylation. In total, there are 16,247 new mouse protein-coding transcripts, including 5154 encoding previously undiscovered proteins. The genomic mapping of the transcriptome reveals extensive clusters of overlapping transcription, with few transcripts observed in the deserts between them. The findings provide a detailed foundation for comparative analyses of mammalian transcriptional regulation during differentiation and development.

title: The Protein Data Bank
text: The Protein Data Bank (PDB), as described by Berman et al. (2000) in Nucleic Acids Research, is the global archival repository of primary structural data for biological macromolecules. An abundance of secondary data sources are derived from the PDB. It serves as the foundation for studies in structural bioinformatics. This article aims to elucidate the PDB's objectives, its data depositional and access systems, and the means by which additional information can be obtained, as well as its future development plans. The reader should leave with a comprehensive understanding of the PDB's scope and the resources it provides.

title: Cell-State-Specific Metabolic Dependency in Hematopoiesis and Leukemogenesis
text: The balance between oxidative and non-oxidative glucose metabolism is crucial for various physiological processes. By manipulating glucose metabolism through the deletion of enzymes with different potencies, we investigated how modifying glucose metabolism influences hematopoietic and leukemic cell populations. Our findings reveal that a deficiency in the M2 pyruvate kinase isoform (PKM2) reduces the levels of metabolic intermediates important for biosynthesis and impairs progenitor function without affecting hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), while lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) deletion significantly inhibits the function of both HSCs and progenitors during hematopoiesis. In contrast, leukemia initiation by transforming alleles putatively affecting either HSCs or progenitors is inhibited in the absence of either PKM2 or LDHA, suggesting that the specific responses to metabolic manipulation in hematopoiesis do not apply to the setting of leukemia. These findings suggest that fine-tuning the level of glycolysis may be a potential therapeutic strategy for treating leukemia while preserving HSC function.

title: A transition in brain state during propofol-induced unconsciousness.
text: Cortical dynamics are shaped by rhythmic oscillations during various states of consciousness, including wakefulness, sleep, and general anesthesia. A notable feature of these oscillations is cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling, which remains unclear in terms of its role in organizing conscious and unconscious brain states. By examining high-density EEG and intracranial electrocorticography recordings during the gradual administration of propofol anesthesia in humans, we discovered a swift transition between distinct states with opposing phase-amplitude coupling and different cortical source distributions. One state emerges during unconsciousness and may resemble slow oscillations observed in sleep, while the other state occurs at the loss or recovery of consciousness and displays an enhanced slow cortical potential. These findings offer objective electrophysiological markers of distinct unconscious brain states, which could aid in the development of EEG-based monitoring for general anesthesia.

title: Cohesins and condensins orchestrate the 4D dynamics of yeast chromosomes during the cell cycle
text:
The dynamic reorganization of chromosomes during cell division involves the concerted effort of conserved architectural proteins, including the structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes cohesin and condensin. Despite extensive research into these factors, a comprehensive view of chromosome architecture at both small and large scales during cell division remains elusive. To fill this knowledge gap, we conducted the first genome-wide analysis of dynamic chromosome architecture in the higher eukaryote Saccharomyces cerevisiae across the cell cycle. Our study uncovered new insights into the roles of SMC complexes in controlling structural transitions during cell division.
During replication, cohesin establishment fosters long-range intra-chromosomal interactions, culminating in the individualization of chromosomes at metaphase. In anaphase, the mitotic spindle forces abruptly reorganize chromosomes, with formation of a condensin-dependent loop bridging the centromere cluster and the rDNA loci suggesting that condensin-mediated forces may facilitate segregation. Our work comprehensively depicts cell cycle-dependent chromosome dynamics in a unicellular eukaryote while revealing novel features of chromosome reorganization during highly conserved stages of cell division.

title: Genome-wide patterns of divergence and gene flow across a butterfly radiation.
text: The genomic radiation of Heliconius butterflies includes multiple levels of divergence and ongoing gene flow between species, as revealed by the recently sequenced genome of Heliconius melpomene. Phylogenetic analysis of 54 individuals consistently supported the reciprocal monophyly of H. melpomene and Heliconius cydno, refuting previous hypotheses that H. melpomene may be Para- or polylectic with respect to H. cydno. Additionally, Heliconius timareta formed a monophyletic clade closely related to but distinct from H. cydno, while Heliconius heurippa fell within this clade. We detected genetic admixture between sympatric populations of the sister clades H. melpomene and H. cydno/timareta, particularly between H. cydno and H. melpomene from Central America and between H. timareta and H. melpomene from the eastern slopes of the Andes. The observed divergence between races is primarily explained by isolation by distance, and there is no detectable genetic population structure between parapatric races, suggesting that hybrid zones between races are not zones of secondary contact. Furthermore, our results support previous findings that color pattern loci are shared between populations and species with similar color pattern elements. Notably, this pattern is almost exclusive to these genomic regions, with only a small number of other loci showing significant similarity between populations and species with similar color patterns.

title: Randomized, double-blind study of the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of tafenoquine versus mefloquine for malaria prophylaxis in nonimmune subjects.
text: This investigational study represents the first phase III trial of the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of tafenoquine as a malaria prophylaxis. In a double-blind, randomized (3:1) clinical trial, Australian military personnel received weekly malaria prophylaxis with 200 mg tafenoquine (492 participants) or 250 mg mefloquine (162 participants) for a duration of 6 months during a peacekeeping mission to East Timor. Following the return of the subjects to Australia, the tafenoquine-treated participants received a placebo, while the mefloquine-treated participants received 30 mg primaquine daily for 14 days.
