There were no significant differences between the two groups in terms of hematological and biochemical parameters. Treatment-related adverse events were comparable between the two groups (tafenoquine, 13.4%; mefloquine, 11.7%). A total of 3 subjects on tafenoquine (0.6%) and none on mefloquine discontinued prophylaxis due to possible drug-related adverse events. Conversely, no cases of malaria were diagnosed during the deployment period for either group, but 4 cases (0.9%) and 1 case (0.7%) of Plasmodium vivax infection occurred among the tafenoquine and mefloquine groups, respectively, up to 20 weeks after discontinuation of medication. In a subset of participants, treatment-related mild vortex keratopathy was detected in 93% (69 of 74) of t afenoquine-treated subjects, but none were observed in the 21 mefloquine-treated subjects. The vortex keratopathy did not significantly impact visual acuity and completely resolved in all subjects by 1 year. Tafenoquine appears to be safe and well-tolerated as a malaria prophylaxis, with promising efficacy. Although the participants' specific exposure to malaria could not be confirmed in this study, tafenoquine appears to be a highly effective drug for malaria prophylaxis.

title: Domain-wide regulation of DNA replication timing during mammalian development
text: Investigations into replication timing offer a glimpse into the previously inaccessible higher-order levels of chromosome organization and their plasticity during development. Although the mechanisms behind replication timing are not yet fully understood, recent genome-wide studies have provided a comprehensive overview of how replication timing is regulated during many of the early cell fate transitions in mammals. These studies have revealed coordinated changes in specific, defined segments of the genome, spanning up to half of the genome, which are linked to changes in sub-nuclear organization and domain-wide transcriptional potential. Moreover, the conserved replication timing profiles observed in both mice and humans suggest that these changes have significant developmental implications. Therefore, these studies have laid the groundwork for connecting large-scale chromosome structure to function, and suggest that replication plays a crucial role in domain-level genome organization.

title: PU.1-mediated upregulation of CSF1R is crucial for leukemia stem cell potential induced by MOZ-TIF2
text: Leukemias and other cancers have stem cells that self-renew, which helps them persist. Eradication of these stem cells is essential for successful cancer therapy. To evaluate this idea using an acute myeloid leukemia (AML) model induced by the leukemia-associated fusion protein MOZ-TIF2, we discovered that eliminating AML stem cells can cure the disease. The MOZ-TIF2 fusion protein interacts with the transcription factor PU.1, which stimulates the expression of the macrophage colony-stimulating factor receptor (CSF1R) in AML cells. Our findings revealed that PU.1 is crucial for MOZ-TIF2's ability to maintain AML stem cells, and that high levels of CSF1R expression are necessary for leukemia-initiating activity. By using transgenic mice that express a drug-inducible suicide gene controlled by the CSF1R promoter, we were able to eliminate CSF1R-high cells and cure AML. Additionally, suppressing MOZ-TIF2-induced AML in mice deficient in CSF1R or using CSF1R inhibitors slowed down the progression of the disease. Therefore, in this subtype of AML, stem cells are mainly found within the CSF1R-high cell population, and targeting PU.1-mediated upregulation of CSF1R expression may be a promising therapeutic approach.

title: Pharmacological blockage of fibro/adipogenic progenitor expansion and suppression of regenerative fibrogenesis is associated with impaired skeletal muscle regeneration.
text: Acute muscle injury triggers the proliferation and conversion of fibro/adipogenic progenitors (FAPs) into fibroblasts, leading to the deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) and potentially causing permanent tissue scarring. While the inhibition of this process has been shown to be beneficial, the consequences of suppressing it are not fully understood. To investigate, we used a model of acute muscle damage and found that pharmacological inhibition of FAP expansion using Nilotinib, a potent tyrosine kinase inhibitor with antifibrotic activity, has a detrimental effect on the regeneration process. Specifically, Nilotinib inhibits the expansion of satellite cells in vivo after muscle damage, suggesting a non-cell-autonomous effect. Furthermore, Nilotinib impairs the regenerative fibrogenesis by preventing the injury-induced expansion and differentiation of resident CD45(-):CD31(-):α7integrin(-):Sca1(+) mesenchymal FAPs. Our data support the idea that the expansion and transient fibrogenesis observed during regeneration play a critical trophic role in promoting tissue-specific stem cell proliferation and differentiation.

title: Deregulation of Scribble Promotes Mammary Tumorigenesis and Reveals a Role for Cell Polarity in Carcinoma
text:
The loss of cell polarity proteins, such as Scribble, can have a significant impact on the development of cancer in both flies and mammals. In Drosophila, the depletion of Scribble leads to uncontrolled cell proliferation and the induction of neoplasia. However, the role that these proteins play in tumorigenesis in mammals is not well understood.
Our study demonstrates that depleting Scribble in mammary epithelial cells leads to the disruption of cell polarity, inhibition of three-dimensional morphogenesis, and the inhibition of apoptosis. These changes can lead to the formation of dysplastic and neoplastic growths in vivo, which can eventually progress to tumors over time. Interestingly, we found that the loss of Scribble cooperates with oncogenes, such as c-myc, to transform epithelial cells and induce tumors in vivo.
Moreover, our findings suggest that the mislocalization of Scribble from cell-cell junctions is sufficient to promote cell transformation, further highlighting the critical role that this protein plays in maintaining cell polarity and preventing cancer growth. Indeed, spontaneous mammary tumors in mice and humans have been found to have downregulated and mislocalized Scribble.
Taken together, our study suggests that Scribble plays a critical role in inhibiting breast cancer formation by maintaining cell polarity and preventing dysplastic and neoplastic growth. Disruption of these pathways can lead to the uncontrolled proliferation of cells, ultimately resulting in the development of cancer.

title: The Polymeal: a more natural, safer, and probably tastier (than the Polypill) strategy to reduce cardiovascular disease by more than 75%.
text:
OBJECTIVE:
Despite the promise of the Polypill in managing cardiovascular risk, its high costs and potential adverse effects hinder its widespread adoption. To address this challenge, we aimed to develop a tastier and safer alternative - the Polymeal.
METHODS:
We explored the literature to identify the ingredients of the Polymeal, which include wine, fish, dark chocolate, fruits, vegetables, garlic, and almonds. We used data from the Framingham Heart Study and the Framingham Offspring Study to create life tables modeling the benefits of the Polymeal in the general population from age 50, assuming multiplicative correlations.
RESULTS:
Our analysis revealed that consuming the Polymeal can significantly reduce cardiovascular disease events by 76%. For men, taking the Polymeal daily resulted in an increase in total life expectancy of 6.6 years, an increase in life expectancy free from cardiovascular disease of 9.0 years, and a decrease in life expectancy with cardiovascular disease of 2.4 years. Similarly, for women, the Polymeal resulted in an increase in total life expectancy of 4.8 years, an increase in life expectancy free from cardiovascular disease of 8.1 years, and a decrease in life expectancy with cardiovascular disease of 3.3 years.
CONCLUSION:
Our findings suggest that the Polymeal offers a practical, non-pharmacological, and cost-effective alternative to reduce cardiovascular morbidity and enhance life expectancy in the general population. Its tasty ingredients make it a more appealing option compared to the Polypill, which could lead to increased adoption and implementation in population-based health strategies.

title: Islet-Like Clusters Derived from Mesenchymal Stem Cells in Wharton's Jelly of the Human Umbilical Cord for Transplantation to Control Type 1 Diabetes
text:
Interest in developing renewable sources of islet-replacement tissue for type I diabetes mellitus has grown significantly. Human mesenchymal cells isolated from the Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord (HUMSCs) have shown promise as a valuable source for islet generation. In this study, we demonstrate the successful differentiation of HUMSCs into mature islet-like cell clusters in vitro and their ability to produce insulin in vivo.
Our findings indicate that HUMSCs may be the preferential source of stem cells for converting into insulin-producing cells. The ease of obtaining and processing HUMSCs compared to embryonic and bone marrow stem cells makes them a highly promising candidate for islet-replacement therapy.
To investigate the potential of HUMSCs as a source of islet cells, we induced the cells to transform into islet-like cell clusters in vitro through stepwise culturing in neuron-conditioned medium. These cell clusters were then transplanted into the liver of streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats via laparotomy. Glucose tolerance was measured on week 12 after transplantation accompanied by immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy analysis. Our results showed that the islet-like cell clusters contained human C-peptide and released human insulin in response to physiological glucose levels. Real-time RT-PCR detected the expressions of insulin and other pancreatic beta-cell-related genes (Pdx1, Hlxb9, Nkx2.2, Nkx6.1, and Glut-2) in these islet-like cell clusters. Additionally, we found special fused liver cells that were characterized by human insulin and nuclei-positive staining and possessing secretory granules.
Our findings demonstrate that HUMSCs can be successfully differentiated into mature islet-like cell clusters with insulin-producing ability both in vitro and in vivo. The use of HUMSCs as a source of islet cells has the advantage of a large potential donor pool, rapid availability, no risk of discomfort for the donor, and low risk of rejection.

title: Use of perioperative hydroxyethyl starch 6% and albumin 5% in elective joint arthroplasty and association with adverse outcomes: a retrospective population based analysis
text:
Objective: To determine whether the use of hydroxyethyl starch 6% and albumin 5% in the perioperative setting of elective joint arthroplasties is associated with an increased risk of complications.
Design: Retrospective cohort study using population-based data from 2006 to 2013.
Setting: Data were collected from 510 hospitals across the United States participating in the Premier Perspective database.
Participants: A total of 1,051,441 patients undergoing elective total hip and knee arthroplasties.
Exposures: Perioperative fluid resuscitation with hydroxyethyl starch 6%, albumin 5%, or neither.
Main Outcome Measures: Acute renal failure and thromboembolic, cardiac, and pulmonary complications were assessed as the main outcomes.
Results: Compared to patients who did not receive any colloid, perioperative fluid resuscitation with hydroxyethyl starch 6% or albumin 5% was found to be associated with an increased risk of acute renal failure (odds ratios 1.23, 95% confidence interval 1.13-1.34 and 1.56, 1.36-1.78, respectively). Similarly, use of hydroxyethyl starch 6% was associated with an increased risk of most other complications, while use of albumin 5% showed an increased risk of these complications as well. A recent decrease in hydroxyethyl starch 6% use was noted, while use of albumin 5% increased.
Conclusions: This study, similar to those in critically ill patients, showed that use of hydroxyethyl starch 6% in the elective perioperative orthopedic setting was associated with an increased risk of acute renal failure and other complications. Similar findings were seen with albumin 5%. These results raise concerns regarding the widespread use of these colloids in elective joint arthroplasty procedures.

title: BMAL1 and CLOCK, Two Essential Components of the Circadian Clock, Are Involved in Glucose Homeostasis
text: The generation of circadian timing is facilitated by a distinct set of autoregulatory interactions, known as the molecular clock. Behavioral rhythms are likewise regulated by the molecular clock. We have discovered a role for Bmal1 and Clock in the regulation of glucose homeostasis. Inactivation of these known clock proteins, Bmal1 (Mop3) and Clock, suppresses the diurnal variation in glucose and triglycerides. The metabolic pathway known as gluconeogenesis is abolished in the absence of Bmal1, and its activity is likewise diminished in Clock mutants. However, the counterregulatory response of corticosterone and glucagon to insulin-induced hypoglycaemia remains intact. Moreover, a high-fat diet modifies carbohydrate metabolism by amplifying circadian fluctuations in glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, and mutation of Clock restores the chow-fed phenotype. Bmal1 and Clock, which are central to the molecular clock, exert profound control over the recovery from insulin-induced hypoglycaemia. Furthermore, asynchronous dietary cues may influence glucose homeostasis by interacting with peripheral molecular clocks.

title: Mechanisms of progression and regression of renal lesions of chronic nephropathies and diabetes.
text: The incidence of chronic kidney diseases is rising globally, posing a significant public health concern. While genetic factors contribute to susceptibility and disease progression, proteinuria has been identified as an independent predictor of outcomes. Reducing urinary protein levels through medication and a low-protein diet can slow the decline of renal function in individuals with nondiabetic and diabetic nephropathies, potentially leading to remission and renal lesion regression in both animal models and humans. In animal studies, regression of glomerular structural changes is linked to glomerular remodeling, which can be observed through 3D reconstruction of the glomerular capillary tuft. This allows for quantification of sclerosis volume reduction and capillary regeneration upon treatment. The regeneration of capillary segments may be attributed to the contribution of resident cells, or possibly the involvement of progenitor cells from renal or extrarenal sources. This review highlights recent advances in our understanding of the mechanisms and molecules involved in renal tissue repair, ultimately leading to the regression of renal injury.

title: Contemporary type 1 diabetes pregnancy outcomes: impact of obesity and glycaemic control.
text:
Objective: To compare the outcomes of pregnancies in women with type 1 diabetes and those without, and to investigate the effects of obesity and glycemic control on these outcomes.
Design and Setting: Historical cohort study in a specialist diabetes and maternity network in Victoria, Australia.
Participants: All singleton births (at least 20 weeks gestation) between 2010 and 2013 were analyzed, including 107 pregnancies to women with type 1 diabetes and 27,075 pregnancies to women without diabetes. Women with type 2 diabetes or gestational diabetes were excluded.
Methods: Data were extracted from the Birthing Outcomes System database and associations between type 1 diabetes and pregnancy outcomes were analyzed using multivariable regression.
Main Outcome Measures: Mode of birth, maternal and neonatal outcomes.
Results: Women with type 1 diabetes had higher mean body mass index (BMI) compared to women without diabetes (27.3 kg/m2 vs 25.7 kg/m2, p=0.01) and were more likely to have a shorter median gestation period for their babies (37.3 weeks vs 39.4 weeks, p<0.001) and were more likely to be large for gestational age (LGA) (adjusted odds ratio (aOR), 7.9; 95% CI, 5.3-11.8). Women with type 1 diabetes were also more likely to have induced labor (aOR, 3.0; 95% CI, 2.0-4.5), caesarean delivery (aOR, 4.6; 95% CI, 3.1-7.0), or preterm birth (aOR, 6.7; 95% CI, 4.5-10.0); their babies were more likely to have shoulder dystocia (aOR, 8.2; 95% CI, 3.6-18.7), hypoglycemia (aOR, 10.3; 95% CI, 6.8-15.6), jaundice (aOR, 5.1; 95% CI, 3.3-7.7), respiratory distress (aOR, 2.5; 95% CI, 1.4-4.4), or to suffer perinatal death (aOR, 4.3; 95% CI, 1.9-9.9). In women with type 1 diabetes, greater obesity was associated with increased odds for an LGA baby or congenital malformation, and increased HbA1c levels were associated with preterm birth and perinatal death.
Conclusion: Women with type 1 diabetes, even when managed in a specialist setting, still experience adverse obstetric and neonatal outcomes. Poor glycemic control is not wholly responsible for adverse outcomes, reinforcing the importance of other risk factors, such as obesity and weight gain.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of Vitamin D Action
text: The hormonal metabolite of vitamin D, 1α,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (1,25D), triggers biological responses by binding to the vitamin D receptor (VDR). Upon occupancy by 1,25D, VDR forms a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor (RXR), which then binds to specific regions of genes involved in vitamin D-mediated functions, such as calcium and phosphate absorption, and bone mineral remodeling. The specific genes regulated by 1,25D depend on the cell type and the presence of other coactivators or corepressors. For instance, 1,25D induces the expression of genes involved in bone mineral remodeling, including RANKL, SPP1 (osteopontin), and BGP (osteocalcin), in bone cells. In intestinal cells, 1,25D induces the expression of genes involved in calcium absorption, such as TRPV6, CaBP9k, and claudin 2. In addition, 1,25D regulates genes involved in renal calcium and phosphate reabsorption, such as TRPV5, klotho, and Npt2c. Unliganded VDR can also function in keratinocytes to regulate mammalian hair cycling by controlling genes such as CASP14, S100A8, SOSTDC1, and others involved in Wnt signaling. Furthermore, alternative, non-vitamin D ligands of VDR, such as lithocholic acid, docosahexaenoic acid, and curcumin, have been identified. The combination of these alternative ligands and 1,25D/VDR control of gene expression may play a role in delaying chronic age-related diseases such as osteoporosis, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

title: Quantitative Temporal Viromics: An Approach to Investigate Host-Pathogen Interaction
text:
A comprehensive, quantitative analysis of how viral and host proteins change over time during a productive infection can provide valuable insights into the complex interactions between viruses and their hosts. To achieve this, we developed a cutting-edge technique called "quantitative temporal viromics" (QTV), which utilizes multiplexed tandem-mass-tag-based mass spectrometry.
Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is not only a significant pathogen but also a master of evading the immune system. By employing QTV, we mapped how HCMV manipulates the expression of over 8,000 host proteins, including more than 1,200 cell-surface proteins, to subvert host defense mechanisms. QTV also predicted the expression of natural killer and T cell ligands, as well as 29 viral proteins present on the cell surface, which could serve as potential therapeutic targets. Temporal profiles of over 80% of HCMV's canonical genes and 14 noncanonical open reading frames were detailed.
QTV is a powerful tool that can reveal important principles of viral infection, and its applicability is not limited to any particular virus with a well-established in vitro model. In conclusion, our systematic analysis of temporal changes in host and viral proteins offers a dynamic understanding of the intricate relationships between viruses and their hosts.

title: Interactions between sleep, circadian function, and glucose metabolism: implications for risk and severity of diabetes.
text: Sleep disruptions, including insufficient sleep and fragmented rest, have been linked to abnormal glucose metabolism and an increased risk of developing diabetes. Scientific experiments have provided valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms. Large-scale observational studies suggest that these sleep disturbances are associated with an elevated risk of developing diabetes. Obstructive sleep apnea, which combines sleep fragmentation and low oxygen levels, is a significant risk factor for insulin resistance and potentially diabetes. The question of whether improving glycemic control in type 2 diabetes patients through sleep apnea treatment is still a matter of debate. Recent research has also shone light on the connection between sleep disturbances during pregnancy and the development of gestational diabetes and high blood sugar levels, with potential consequences for both mother and child health. Studies in animal models have also identified disrupted circadian rhythms as a likely contributor to unfavorable metabolic outcomes. This review aims to provide a comprehensive update on the current state of knowledge regarding the relationships between sleep disturbances, circadian dysfunction, and glucose metabolism, drawing on both experimental, prospective, and interventional studies.

title: Antibody-Based HIV-1 Vaccines: Recent Developments and Future Directions
text:
In May 2007, the Global HIV Vaccine Enterprise convened a two-day workshop to discuss humoral immune responses to HIV and approaches to design vaccines that induce viral neutralizing and other potentially protective antibody responses. The workshop aimed to identify key scientific issues, gaps, and opportunities that have emerged since the Enterprise Strategic Plan was first published in 2005, and to make recommendations that Enterprise stakeholders can use to plan new activities.
Most effective viral vaccines work, at least in part, by generating antibodies that inactivate or neutralize the invading virus. Since acquired immune responses to HIV have been shown to protect against infection and disease, the existing data strongly suggest that an optimally effective HIV-1 vaccine should elicit potent antiviral neutralizing antibodies. However, unlike acute viral pathogens, HIV-1 chronically replicates in the host and evades the antibody response, posing major obstacles to vaccine development. Current HIV vaccine candidates do not elicit neutralizing antibodies against most circulating virus strains, highlighting the need to improve vaccine design.
The workshop focused on four key areas that could provide key information to bring the field closer to an effective antibody-based HIV-1 vaccine:
1. Structure-assisted immunogen design: Understanding the three-dimensional structure of the HIV-1 envelope protein (Env) could facilitate the design of immunogens that more effectively stimulate neutralizing antibodies.
2. Role of Fc receptors and complement: Fc receptors and complement are important mediators of antibody-dependent virus neutralization. Understanding their role in HIV-1 neutralization could inform vaccine design.
3. Assay standardization and validation: Consistent and validated assays for measuring HIV-1 neutralization are crucial for evaluating vaccine efficacy. Workshop participants emphasized the need for standardized assays to compare vaccine-elicited neutralizing antibodies across different studies.
4. Immunoregulation of B cell responses: HIV-1 evades the immune response by exploiting B cell regulation. Understanding mechanisms of B cell regulation could inform strategies to improve vaccine-elicited neutralizing antibody responses.
In summary, the workshop highlighted the need to improve vaccine design to elicit neutralizing antibodies against the majority of circulating HIV-1 strains. The four identified areas offer promising avenues for research to address these challenges and bring the field closer to an effective antibody-based HIV-1 vaccine.

title: Targeted therapy for cancer stem cells: the patched pathway and ABC transporters
text: Certain types of leukemia, brain cancer, and breast cancer exhibit a small population of tumor cells with stem cell-like characteristics and the ability for self-renewal. These 'cancer stem cells' account for a mere 1% of the cells in a tumor, making them challenging to detect and study. Like normal stem cells, cancer stem cells possess properties that enable them to evade conventional cancer therapies such as chemotherapy and radiation. These cells display high levels of ABC drug transporters, which confer resistance; are relatively quiescent; have enhanced DNA repair mechanisms; and are less susceptible to undergo apoptosis. Developing combined cancer therapy strategies that target both cancer stem cells and non-stem cells may lead to increased treatment efficacy. Here, efforts to inhibit the Hedgehog/Patched signaling pathway, essential for embryonic growth and differentiation, and the ABCG2 drug efflux transporter will be discussed.

title: Increased in vivo amyloid-β42 production, exchange, and loss in presenilin mutation carriers.
text: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is believed to be caused by an imbalance in the production and clearance of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides. Autosomal dominant AD (ADAD) caused by mutations in the presenilin (PSEN) gene may result from an increase in Aβ42 production in the central nervous system (CNS). While this has been demonstrated in rodent models of ADAD, it has not been observed in human carriers of PSEN mutations. To investigate the effect of PSEN mutations on Aβ production and turnover in humans, we used compartmental modeling of stable isotope labeling kinetic (SILK) studies in mutation carriers and noncarriers. We found that CNS Aβ42 production rates were 24% higher in mutation carriers compared to noncarriers, and this increase was independent of fibrillar amyloid deposits quantified by positron emission tomography (PET) using the amyloid tracer Pittsburgh compound B (PIB). Moreover, the fractional turnover rate of soluble Aβ42 relative to Aβ40 was 65% faster in mutation carriers, which correlated with amyloid deposition. These findings support the hypothesis that Aβ42 is overproduced in the CNS of humans with PSEN mutations, and demonstrate that soluble Aβ42 turnover and exchange processes are altered in the presence of amyloid plaques, leading to reduced Aβ42 concentrations in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Additionally, we observed reversible exchange of Aβ42 peptides with preexisting unlabeled peptide in the presence of plaques.

title: Basic residues in the T-cell receptor ζ cytoplasmic domain mediate membrane association and modulate signaling.
text: The T-cell receptor (TCR) is composed of a TCRαβ heterodimer, a TCRζ homodimer, and CD3γε and CD3δε heterodimers. Despite extensive research, the specific mechanism of T-cell activation following TCR ligand binding remains unclear. Earlier studies proposed that the cytoplasmic tail of CD3ε binds to the plasma membrane through a basic residue-rich stretch (BRS) and suggested that dissociation from the membrane is crucial for phosphorylation. In this study, we demonstrate that BRS motifs within the cytoplasmic tail of TCRζ mediate association with the plasma membrane and that TCR engagement leads to TCRζ dissociation from the membrane. This dissociation requires phosphorylation of the TCRζ immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs by lymphocyte cell-specific protein tyrosine kinase (Lck), but not ζ-chain-associated protein kinase 70 binding. Mutations of the TCRζ BRS motifs that disrupt this membrane association attenuate both proximal and distal responses triggered by TCR engagement. These mutations appear to alter the localization of TCRζ with respect to Lck as well as the mobility of the TCR complex. Our findings reveal that tyrosine phosphorylation of the TCRζ cytoplasmic domain regulates its association with the plasma membrane and underscore the functional significance of TCRζ BRS motifs.

title: Policies for alcohol restriction and their association with interpersonal violence: a time-series analysis of homicides in Cali, Colombia.
text:
Cali, Colombia, has a high incidence of interpersonal violence deaths, including homicides. To address this issue, various alcohol control policies have been implemented, but their impact on homicide rates remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate whether different alcohol control policies were associated with changes in homicide incidence rates in Cali.
Methods:
An ecological study was conducted between 2004 and 2008 using a time-series design. The study period consisted of 446 non-consecutive days when the most restrictive policies were in effect, 1277 non-consecutive days when moderately restrictive policies were in effect, and 104 non-consecutive days when lax policies were in effect. The incidence rate of homicides and unintentional injury deaths (excluding traffic events) was compared between periods when different policies were in effect using conditional autoregressive negative binomial regressions.
Results:
The study found that homicide rates were significantly higher during periods when moderately restrictive policies were in effect compared to periods when the most restrictive policies were in effect (incidence rate ratio (IRR) 1.15, 90% confidence interval (CI) 1.05-1.26, P = 0.012). Moreover, homicides were even more common during periods when lax policies were in effect compared to periods when the most restrictive policies were in effect (IRR 1.42, 90% CI 1.26-1.61, P < 0.001). In contrast, the study found no significant association between less restrictive policies and unintentional injury deaths.
Conclusion:
Extension of alcohol sales and consumption hours was associated with an increased risk of homicides in Cali. Strong restrictions on alcohol availability may reduce the incidence of interpersonal violence events in communities with high homicide rates. These findings suggest that implementing and enforcing stricter alcohol control policies could help reduce homicide rates in Cali, Colombia.

title: Effects of SNF1 on Maltose Metabolism and Leavening Ability of Baker's Yeast in Lean Dough.
text: Baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) maltose metabolism is impaired in lean dough due to glucose repression, which slows down the fermentation process. To enhance maltose metabolism and leavening ability, it is crucial to alleviate this glucose repression. The Snf1 protein kinase is essential for responding to glucose repression and necessary for transcribing glucose-repressed genes, including the maltose-utilization genes (MAL). In this study, we constructed and characterized industrial baker's yeast strains with overexpressed or deleted Snf1 to investigate the effect on maltose utilization, growth, and fermentation characteristics, as well as MAL gene expression and enzyme activity. Our results indicate that overexpressing Snf1 led to significant enhancements in MAL expression levels and enzyme activities, resulting in an 18% increase in maltose metabolism in a low sugar model liquid dough fermentation medium (LSMLD) containing glucose and maltose and a 15% increase in leavening ability in lean dough. These findings provide valuable insights into breeding industrial baker's yeast for rapid fermentation.

title: Review article
text: Ribosomopathies constitute a group of disorders where genetic anomalies impair the biogenesis and function of ribosomes, leading to distinct clinical manifestations. Congenital mutations in genes encoding ribosomal proteins, such as RPS19, can cause Diamond-Blackfan anemia, a disorder characterized by hypoplastic, macrocytic anemia. Various other genes involved in ribosome biogenesis have been implicated in other rare congenital syndromes, including Schwachman-Diamond syndrome, dyskeratosis congenita, cartilage-hair hypoplasia, and Treacher Collins syndrome. Moreover, 5q- syndrome, a subtype of myelodysplastic syndrome, is caused by a somatic deletion of chromosome 5q, resulting in haploinsufficiency of the ribosomal protein RPS14 and an erythroid phenotype analogous to Diamond-Blackfan anemia. Acquired anomalies in ribosome function have been associated with a broader spectrum of human malignancies. The p53 signaling pathway acts as a surveillance system for protein synthesis and genome integrity, and is activated by defects in ribosome biogenesis. This pathway appears to play a crucial role in the clinical features of ribosomopathies. Elucidating the mechanisms underlying how specific aberrations in ribosome biogenesis give rise to distinct clinical syndromes may lead to novel therapeutic strategies for these diseases.

title: PD-L1 expression in human cancers and its association with clinical outcomes
text: PD-L1 is a molecule that inhibits T cell activation, leading to tumor progression. Overexpression of PD-L1 in various cancers, including gastric cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, esophageal cancer, pancreatic cancer, ovarian cancer, and bladder cancer, is associated with poor clinical outcomes. In contrast, PD-L1 expression is associated with better outcomes in breast cancer and Merkel cell carcinoma. The prognostic value of PD-L1 expression in lung cancer, colorectal cancer, and melanoma is controversial. Blocking antibodies targeting PD-1 and PD-L1 have shown remarkable response rates in cancer patients with PD-L1-overexpressing tumors. However, relying solely on PD-L1 as a predictive biomarker for cancer immunotherapy is uncertain due to the variability in PD-L1 immunohistochemistry staining. Factors that influence the accuracy of PD-L1 immunohistochemistry staining include differences in antibodies used, different cut-off values for positivity, and non-uniform expression of PD-L1 in tumors, as well as the impact of sampling time and location. Therefore, a better understanding of the tumor microenvironment and the use of complementary biomarkers, such as gene markers and combined indexes, are necessary to identify patients who will benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade therapy.

title: Primate cytomegaloviruses encode and express an IL-10-like protein.
text: An ORF (open reading frame) in rhesus cytomegalovirus (RhCMV) has been found to share homology with interleukin-10 (IL-10). This IL-10-like protein is derived from a multispliced, polyadenylated early gene transcript spanning part of the UL111A ORF of human CMV (HCMV). Immunological investigations have confirmed the expression of the IL-10-like protein in both tissue culture and RhCMV-infected rhesus macaques. Subsequently, conserved ORFs were identified in human, baboon, and African green monkey CMV, and a fully processed transcript was mapped in fibroblasts infected with the Towne strain of HCMV. The presence of this previously unidentified ORF suggests that the protein may play a crucial role in the persistence and pathogenesis of primate CMV.

title: Genome Sequencing and Analysis of the Tasmanian Devil and Its Transmissible Cancer
text:
The Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii), the largest carnivorous marsupial, is endangered due to a contagious facial cancer that spreads through direct contact with infected individuals. In this study, we sequenced, assembled, and annotated the Tasmanian devil genome and whole-genome sequences of two geographically distant subclones of the cancer. Our analysis suggests that the cancer originated from a female Tasmanian devil and has since evolved and spread across Tasmania through a clonal lineage.
The Tasmanian devil cancer genome contains over 17,000 somatic mutations, indicating a distinct mutational process. Genotyping of somatic mutations in 104 tumorsfrom geographically and temporally diverse Tasmanian devils reveals the pattern of evolution and spread of this parasitic clonal lineage. We observe a selective sweep in one geographical area and the persistence of parallel lineages in other populations.
By analyzing the genome of the Tasmanian devil cancer, we gain insights into the evolutionary history and spread of this aggressive disease. Our findings highlight the importance of genomic analysis in understanding the biology of cancer and its impact on endangered species.

title: A Temporarily Distinct Subpopulation of Slow-Cycling Melanoma Cells Is Required for Continuous Tumor Growth
text: Melanomas are highly diverse tumors, yet their distinct subpopulations' biological significance remains uncertain. By utilizing the H3K4 demethylase JARID1B (KDM5B/PLU-1/RBP2-H1) as a marker, we have characterized a small subset of slowly cycling melanoma cells that cycle with doubled frequencies of over 4 weeks within the rapidly proliferating main population. Isolated JARID1B-positive melanoma cells yield a highly proliferative progeny. JARID1B silencing leads to an initial acceleration of tumor growth subsequent to exhaustion, implying that the JARID1B-positive subpopulation is fundamental to continuous tumor growth. JARID1B expression is dynamic and deviates from a hierarchical cancer stem cell model, as both JARID1B-negative cells can become positive, and single melanoma cells can be tumorigenic regardless of selection. These findings provide a novel understanding of melanoma heterogeneity, positing that tumor maintenance is a dynamic process mediated by a temporarily distinct subpopulation.

title: A map of human circular RNAs in clinically relevant tissues
text:
Cellular circular RNAs (circRNAs), generated through head-to-tail splicing, are present in all multicellular organisms examined to date. Recently, circRNAs have emerged as a substantial class of RNA that functions as post-transcriptional regulators. Additionally, many circRNAs exhibit tissue- and stage-specific expression patterns. Their exceptional stability and specificity make circRNAs promising candidates for clinical biomarker research.
We present a circRNA expression resource of 20 clinically relevant human tissues. In these tissues, we observed highly tissue-specific circRNA expression patterns. We also observed that circular RNA transcripts were often more abundant than their linear host RNAs. Furthermore, we identified potential biomarkers among the 71 validated circRNAs. Our findings emphasize the need to investigate circRNAs in human disease mechanisms.
Key takeaways:
* A comprehensive catalog of circRNAs in 20 clinically relevant human tissues.
* High tissue specificity of circRNA expression.
* Circular RNA transcripts often outnumber their linear host RNAs.
* Differential expression of circRNAs in genes associated with disease phenotypes.


In conclusion, circRNAs exhibit tissue-specific expression patterns and have the potential to serve as clinical biomarkers. The presented resource and findings provide a solid foundation for further investigating the role of circRNAs in human disease mechanisms.

title: Arp2/3 complex inhibition radically alters lamellipodial actin architecture, suspended cell shape, and the cell spreading process
text: Recent research has investigated the dendritic actin cytoskeleton in the cell edge's lamellipodial (LP) region by experimentally decreasing the activity of the actin filament nucleator and branch former, the Arp2/3 complex. Building on these studies, this paper extends the examination of the Arp2/3 complex's role in the actin cytoskeleton by pharmacologically inhibiting it in sea urchin coelomocytes, which have an unusually broad LP region and exhibit exaggerated centripetal flow. Using light and electron microscopy, the study demonstrates that inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex via the drug CK666 significantly alters the LP actin architecture, slows centripetal flow, causes a lamellipodial-to-filopodial shape change in suspended cells, and induces a novel actin structural organization during cell spreading. A common feature of the CK666 phenotype in coelomocytes is the formation of transverse actin arcs, which are arrested by a formin inhibitor. The study also shows that CK666 treatment produces actin arcs in other cells with broad LP regions, such as fish keratocytes and Drosophila S2 cells. The authors hypothesize that the actin arcs visible upon Arp2/3 complex inhibition in coelomocytes may represent an amplified manifestation of elongated mother filaments that could potentially serve as a scaffold for the formation of the dendritic actin network.

title: Synergistic Activation of HIV-1 Expression by Deacetylase Inhibitors and Prostratin: Implications for Treatment of Latent Infection
text: The persistence of HIV-1 reservoirs in individuals treated with Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy (HAART) poses a significant challenge to virus eradication. To address this challenge, we investigated the synergistic activation of HIV-1 production by combining clinically used histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACIs) with prostratin, a non-tumor-promoting nuclear factor (NF)-κB inducer. Using the latently-infected U1 monocytic cell line and latently-infected J-Lat T-cell clones, we demonstrated that the combination of these compounds strongly activated HIV-1 production. We showed that this synergism was due, at least partially, to the synergistic recruitment of unresponsive cells into the expressing cell population. The combined treatment также caused a more pronounced nucleosomal remodeling in the U1 viral promoter region than the treatments with the compounds alone, which correlated with a synergistic reactivation of HIV-1 transcription. The physiological relevance of the prostratin+HDACI synergism was demonstrated in CD8(+)-depleted peripheral blood mononuclear cells from HAART-treated patients with undetectable viral load, and in resting CD4(+) T cells isolated from similar patients, where the combination reactivated viral replication. Our results suggest that combining different types of proviral activators may have important implications for reducing the size of latent HIV-1 reservoirs in HAART-treated patients.

title: Centrosome aberrations: cause or consequence of cancer progression?
text: Most human tumors exhibit anomalies in centrosomes, indicating an underlying disruption in the normal structure, duplication, or division of these organelles. Centrosomes play a crucial role in the organization of microtubule arrays throughout the cell cycle, which in turn affects both the architecture of the tissue and the accuracy of chromosome segregation. However, the causes of centrosomal abnormalities in tumors and their impact on the generation of invasive, genetically unstable cells during cancer progression remain unclear.

title: Autonomic neuropathy, QT interval lengthening, and unexpected deaths in male diabetic patients
text: Measurements of QT intervals were taken over RR intervals ranging from 500 ms to 1000 ms in 13 healthy male subjects, 13 male diabetic subjects without autonomic neuropathy, and 13 with autonomic neuropathy. Consistently, there was a direct linear relationship between QT and RR in all subjects. The gradient of the regression line was significantly greater in the autonomic neuropathy group compared to the normal group. In a separate cohort of 32 male diabetic subjects with varying degrees of autonomic dysfunction, QT and QTC lengths increased significantly at the second visit, unrelated to age or the interval between recordings, corresponding with changes in autonomic function. Of the 71 male diabetic subjects under the age of 60 who were followed for 3 years, 13 had passed away, with 8 of these deaths being unexpected. Interestingly, QT and QTC lengths were significantly longer in those who later died, despite similar ages and duration of diabetes, among those with autonomic neuropathy. Our findings suggest that the relationship between QT and RR intervals is altered in diabetic autonomic neuropathy, and that changes in QT length over time parallel changes in autonomic function. Additionally, there may be an association between QT interval prolongation and the risk of dying unexpectedly in diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

title: Incidence of cancer after immunosuppressive treatment for heart transplantation.
text: Prolonged or intense immunosuppressive therapy following organ transplantation is associated with an elevated risk of cancer. A notable disparity in cancer incidence is observed between heart and heart-lung transplant recipients compared to renal transplant patients. Notably, the incidence of lymphomas is significantly higher in cardiac recipients relative to renal patients. Furthermore, there is a nearly twofold increase in all neoplasms and a sixfold increase in visceral tumors in cardiac recipients compared to renal transplant patients. Several factors may contribute to these differences. In cardiac allograft recipients, intensive immunosuppression is often used to treat acute rejection, and this era of polypharmacy, typically involving triple therapy, has led to a higher number of cardiac transplants.

title: Nucleating actin for invasion
text: The migration of cancer cells into surrounding tissue is an essential step in the processes of metastasis, which remains the most significant cancer-related cause of mortality. This process requires the formation of complex structures, including invadopodia and pseudopodia, which rely on regulated actin assembly. In human cells, there is a diverse array of specialized actin nucleation factors that play critical roles in cancer cell migration, including formins, spire proteins, and Arp2/3-regulating proteins. Research investigating the mechanisms of these actin nucleation factors may ultimately lead to the development of novel treatments for invasive and metastatic cancer.

title: GFI1 and GFI1B control the loss of endothelial identity of hemogenic endothelium during hematopoietic commitment.
text: Recent research has revealed that during embryonic development, hematopoietic progenitors and stem cells originate from hemogenic endothelium precursors through a process termed endothelial to hematopoietic transition (EHT). Transcription factor RUNX1 plays a crucial role in this process, but the specific molecular mechanisms involved are not yet fully understood. In this study, we identified Gfi1 and Gfi1b as direct targets of RUNX1 and key regulators of EHT. These transcription factors are able to induce, in the absence of RUNX1, the downregulation of endothelial markers and the formation of round cells, a characteristic of E HT. Conversely, blood progenitors in Gfi1- and Gfi1b-deficient embryos maintain the expression of endothelial genes, and are unable to disseminate from the yolk sac and colonize embryonic tissues. Our findings demonstrate a critical and specific role for the GFI1 transcription factors in the initial steps of the process leading to the generation of hematopoietic progenitors from hemogenic endothelium.

title: An RNA-directed nuclease mediates post-transcriptional gene silencing in Drosophila cells.
text: In a diverse array of organisms, including Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, planaria, hydra, trypanosomes, fungi, and plants, the introduction of double-stranded RNAs leads to a specific inhibition of gene expression. This phenomenon, known as RNA interference or post-transcriptional gene silencing, may offer protection against viruses, regulate transposition, or modulate gene expression. To shed light on the underlying mechanisms, we have taken a biochemical approach. Here, we show that 'loss-of-function' phenotypes can be created in cultured Drosophila cells by introducing specific double-stranded RNAs. This is accompanied by a significant decrease in the levels of the corresponding cellular messenger RNAs. Secretions from transfected cells contain a nuclease enzyme that specifically degrades exogenous transcripts homologous to the introduced double-stranded RNA. Following partial purification, the sequence-specific nuclease co-sediments with a distinct, approximately 25-nucleotide RNA species that may serve as a specificity factor through homology to the substrate mRNAs.

title: Expression of basal cell keratin 15 and keratin 19 in oral squamous neoplasms represents diverse pathophysiologies.
text: The epithelium of humans contains keratin, which is expressed during cell differentiation. Depending on the target cell type, different types of keratin are expressed, and their changes are believed to reflect alterations in cell properties. Basal cells of the oral epithelium express keratin 5 (K5), K14, K15, and K19, but the alterations in their expressions in tumors are unclear. To address this issue and explore potential diagnostic applications, we analyzed the expression of these keratins in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and squamous intraepithelial neoplasm (SIN). cDNA microarray analysis of 43 OSCC revealed slight upregulation of KRT14, downregulation of KRT15 and KRT19, and unchanged KRT5 expression. There were significant variations in KRT15 and KRT19 expressions across each cancer. Well-differentiated OSCC tend to express more KRT15 and less KRT19 compared to moderately- or poorly-differentiated OSCC. KRT15 was positively correlated with differentiation-related keratin, KRT13. These findings were further investigated through immunohistochemical examination. K5 and K14 were ubiquitously expressed in all 50 OSCC and 50 SIN examined, while K15 and K19 were generally downregulated, but were retain in about half of the cases and showed diverse expression patterns. K15-positive cancers tend to display a well-differentiated phenotype, while K19-positive cancers tend to have more invasive tumor fronts. Most K19-positive cancers appeared to develop with little associated SIN. K19 was consistently downregulated in high-grade SIN, while K15 was downregulated mainly in high-grade SIN. In summary, K15 and K19, unlike K5 or K14, express themselves differently in both SIN and OSCC, which reflects their differences in pathogenesis and biological behaviors, suggesting their potential applications as markers for subclassifying OSCC and SIN.

title: Exosomes in Plasma of Patients with Ovarian Carcinoma: Potential Biomarkers of Tumor Progression and Response to Therapy.
text:
Study Examines Role of Exosomes in Ovarian Cancer Progression and Response to Therapy
Introduction:
In ovarian cancer (OvCa) patients, exosomes released from tumor cells in the bloodstream may play a role in tumor progression and therapy resistance. This study aims to investigate the association between exosome presence/protein content in plasma and disease outcome, response to standard therapy, and tumor resistance to therapies in OvCa patients at diagnosis and during treatment.
Methods:
Exosomes were isolated from the plasma of 22 OvCa patients, 10 patients with benign tumors, and 10 healthy controls (NC) using ultracentrifugation. Exosomes were visualized using scanning electron microscopy, and their protein content was measured. Western blot analysis was used to evaluate the presence of MAGE 3/6 and TGF-β1 in exosomes.
Results:
OvCa patients' plasma contained higher levels of exosomal proteins compared to plasma from patients with benign tumors or NC. Exosomes from OvCa patients carried TGF-β1 and MAGE3/6, which distinguished OvCa patients from those with benign tumors and NC. High protein levels of exosomes were seen in newly diagnosed patients, but the protein content of isolated exosomes was significantly higher in advanced stages of OvCa patients. Exosome levels varied during/after chemotherapy, and correlations between the changes in exosomal protein levels and clinical data suggested that the protein content of exosomes might be useful in predicting responses to therapy and prognosis in OvCa patients.
Conclusion:
Analysis of plasma exosomes offers a novel approach to diagnosis and monitoring response to therapies in OvCa patients. This study suggests that exosomes may be used as a potential biomarker for predicting disease outcome and response to therapy in OvCa patients. However, further research is needed to validate these findings and explore their clinical implications.

title: Insecticide impregnated curtains to control domestic transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis in Venezuela: cluster randomised trial.
text:
Objective: To assess the impact of insecticide-impregnated curtains on the transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis.
Design: Cluster randomized controlled trial with a household interview survey, observational study of people's behavior, and entomological study using light traps to capture sandflies inside homes.
Setting: 14 urban sectors in Trujillo, Venezuela.
Participants: 2913 inhabitants of 569 houses.
Intervention: Sectors were paired based on their 12-month cumulative incidence of cutaneous leishmaniasis, and one sector in each pair was randomly allocated to receive polyester curtains impregnated with lambdacyhalothrin (intervention group), while the other sector received curtains without insecticide or no curtains (control group). A follow-up household survey was conducted after 12 months.
Main Outcome Measures: Reduction in the abundance of sandflies indoors and 12-month incidence of clinical cases of cutaneous leishmaniasis.
Results: Transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis occurred primarily in the domestic setting, with an incidence of 4% over 12 months. The mean number of sandflies per trap per night was 16. After follow-up, the 12-month incidence of cutaneous leishmaniasis was 0% in the intervention group and 8% in the six pairs of control groups that received unimpregnated curtains (mean difference 8, 95% confidence interval 4.22 to 11.78; P=0.001). There were significantly fewer sandflies in the intervention group (2 versus 15, mean difference 13 sandflies per trap; 95% confidence interval 4.22 to 11.78; P<0.001).
Conclusion: Insecticide-impregnated curtains provide a high degree of protection against indoor transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis.

title: Chronic pancreatitis is essential for induction of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by K-Ras oncogenes in adult mice.
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA), one of the most deadly forms of cancer in humans, frequently involves the activation of K-Ras oncogenes through somatic mutations. We have discovered that expressing an endogenous K-Ras(G12V) oncogene in embryonic cells of acinar/centroacinar lineage leads to the formation of pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasias (PanINs) and invasive PDA, suggesting that PDA originates from the differentiation of acinar/centroacinar cells or their precursors into ductal-like cells. Interestingly, adult mice are resistant to the development of K-Ras(G12V)-induced PanINs and PDA, but they can develop the full spectrum of PanINs and invasive PDA if challenged with a mild form of chronic pancreatitis. These findings suggest that the development of PDA involves a combination of genetic (e.g., somatic K-Ras mutations) and nongenetic (e.g., tissue damage) events during adulthood.

title: Relative roles of direct regeneration versus paracrine effects of human cardiosphere-derived cells transplanted into infarcted mice.
text:
Cardiac cell therapy is effective due to multiple biological mechanisms, including direct cell regeneration and paracrine factors. Here, we investigate the relative importance of these mechanisms using human cardiac progenitor cells, cultured as cardiospheres (CSps) or as CSp-derived cells (CDCs), in a Scid mouse model of acute myocardial infarction.
In vitro, we found that CSps and CDCs secrete various growth factors, including vascular endothelial growth factor, hepatocyte growth factor, and insulin-like growth factor 1. These factors promote the survival and function of neonatal rat ventricular myocytes and human umbilical vein endothelial cells.
In vivo, when CDCs were transplanted into the peri-infarct zone of mice, they increased the expression of Akt, decreased apoptosis, and improved capillary density, indicating enhanced tissue resilience. Based on the number of human-specific cells and their impact on capillary density and myocardial viability, direct differentiation accounted for 20-50% of the observed effects.
Our findings suggest that transplanted CDCs serve as "role models," recruiting endogenous regeneration and improving tissue resistance to ischemic stress. The contribution of the role model effect is comparable to or greater than direct regeneration, highlighting the importance of this mechanism in cardiac cell therapy.

title: The IC(50) of anti-Pfs25 antibody in membrane-feeding assay varies among species.
text: Plasmodium falciparum surface protein 25 (Pfs25) is a promising target for transmission-blocking vaccines (TBVs). In vitro studies have shown that anti-Pfs25 antibodies can inhibit the development of oocysts in membrane-feeding assays, and correlational analysis has demonstrated that the activity of these antibodies is directly related to the antibody titer. To further investigate the potential of Pfs25 as a TBV candidate, we purified Pfs25-specific IgGs and measured the amount of antibody required to inhibit 50% of oocyst development (IC50). Our findings revealed that the IC50 values were 15.9, 4.2, 41.2, and 85.6 microg/mL for mouse, rabbit, monkey, and human, respectively. These values were significantly different among species, suggesting that data obtained from animal studies may not directly translate to human immunization. Furthermore, we observed different patterns of competition among species when testing anti-Pfs25 sera against six mouse monoclonal antibodies, and the avidity of antibodies also varied across species. These findings highlight the complexity of the immune response to Pfs25 and the challenges of developing a TBV that can effectively neutralize the parasite in humans.

title: Single-Cell RNA-Seq Reveals Dynamic, Random Monoallelic Gene Expression in Mammalian Cells
text: In most studies of diploid cell populations, expression is observed from both alleles. However, genome-wide analyses of single cells are scarce, hindering our understanding of allelic expression patterns. To address this limitation, we conducted global allelic expression analysis across individual cells of mouse preimplantation embryos of mixed background (CAST/EiJ × C57BL/6J). Our findings revealed that approximately 12-24% of autosomal genes exhibit monoallelic expression. Interestingly, this monoallelic expression was observed to be independent and dynamic, with considerable variation in expression levels among closely related embryonic cells. Similar patterns were observed in mature cells, emphasizing the de novo inactivation of the paternal X chromosome. Our results suggest that in mammalian cells, independent and stochastic allelic transcription leads to abundant random monoallelic expression.

title: Lipopolysaccharide-dependent prostaglandin E(2) production is regulated by the glutathione-dependent prostaglandin E(2) synthase gene induced by the Toll-like receptor 4/MyD88/NF-IL6 pathway.
text: Macrophages produce a substantial amount of PGE(2) during inflammation, which regulates various immune responses. PGE(2) inhibits the production of cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-12 within macrophages. A crucial enzyme involved in the biosynthesis of PGE(2) is membrane-bound glutathione-dependent PGE(2) synthase (mPGES), which is generated by the cyclooxygenase-2-mediated PGE(2) biosynthetic pathway. We discovered that mPGES is activated in macrophages in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation. Conversely, mice lacking Toll-like receptor 4, MyD88, or NF-IL6, an essential transcription factor, failed to exhibit increased mPGES expression or PGE(2) production in response to LPS stimulation. To elucidate the function of mPGES in vivo, we generated mice deficient in mPGES and evaluated their response to LPS. The mice showed no prominent enhancement in PGE(2) production in response to LPS. However, they were unimpaired in their ability to produce inflammatory cytokines and displayed a normal response to LPS-induced shock. Therefore, mPGES is fundamentally involved in LPS-induced PGE(2) production, but is dispensable for modulating inflammatory responses.

title: A microRNA feedback loop regulates global microRNA abundance during aging.
text: During aging, the levels of many microRNAs (miRNAs) change globally across various organisms and tissues. However, the underlying mechanisms and biological relevance of these changes are largely unexplored. To investigate the genetic network controlling miRNA transcription and processing during aging in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, we analyzed the expression of miRNA biogenesis genes and their interactions with transcription factors and aging-associated miRNAs. Our findings revealed that miRNA biogenesis genes are highly interconnected with transcription factors, and we identified a specific miRNA, miR-71, that regulates the expression of ALG-1/Argonaute post-transcriptionally during aging. Interestingly, mutants of miR-71 exhibited globally increased miRNA expression, accompanied by widespread dysregulation of mRNA expression and diminished variability in life span. These observations suggest that the progressive molecular decline often attributed to accumulated damage over an organism's life may be partially mediated by a miRNA-directed mechanism of age-associated decline.

title: Early lymphocyte expansion is severely impaired in interleukin 7 receptor-deficient mice
text: Interleukin 7 (IL-7) stimulates the proliferation of B cell progenitors, thymocytes, and mature T cells through its interaction with the high affinity receptor (IL-7R), which belongs to the hematopoietin receptor superfamily. To further investigate the role of IL-7 and its receptor during B and T cell development, we generated mice that were genetically deficient in IL-7R. These mutant mice exhibited a drastic reduction in thymic and peripheral lymphoid cellularity. By analyzing lymphoid progenitor populations in IL-7R-deficient mice, we identified the developmental stages affected by the mutation and found a critical role for IL-7R during early lymphoid development. Interestingly, these studies suggest that the phase of thymocyte expansion occurring before the onset of T cell receptor gene rearrangement is reliant on, and mediated by, the high affinity receptor for IL-7.

title: Immune Activation with HIV Vaccines
text: The pursuit of a safe and effective HIV vaccine remains a crucial and complex objective in the field of HIV-AIDS research. Recent advancements using a poxvirus vector priming and envelope protein boosting approach have demonstrated a modest but statistically significant level of efficacy, thus establishing the possibility of a vaccine preventing HIV infection (1). Ongoing efforts are focused on enhancing the durability and efficacy of these strategies. However, the results of two vaccine concepts based on recombinant adenovirus serotype-5 (rAd5) (3-5) have raised concerns about potential constraints, as these vaccines might actually increase susceptibility to HIV infection. This raises the question of whether similar issues might affect other recombinant adenovirus vectors currently in development or other vector-based vaccines.

title: Distribution of dystrophin- and utrophin-associated protein complexes during activation of human neutrophils.
text:
Background: Dystrophins and their associated proteins play important structural and signaling roles in non-muscle tissues, but their expression and localization in neutrophils have not been well characterized. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the pattern of expression, cellular distribution, and interaction with actin filaments of dystrophin and utrophin gene products and their associated proteins in resting and fMLP-activated human neutrophils.
Methods: Immunoblot analysis and confocal microscopy were used to investigate the expression of dystrophin and utrophin protein complexes in resting and fMLP-activated human neutrophils. Immunoprecipitation assays were performed to verify the presence of protein complexes.
Results: The study demonstrated the presence of two dystrophin-associated protein complexes in resting and fMLP-activated neutrophils. The first complex consists of Dp71d/Dp71Δ(110)(m) and dystrophin-associated proteins (β-dystroglycan, α-syntrophin, α-dystrobrevin-1, and -2). The second complex contains Up400, instead of Dp71d/Dp71Δ(110)(m), as a central component of the dystrophin-associated protein complexes (DAPC). Confocal analysis also showed the subcellular redistribution of Dp71d/Dp71Δ(110)(m) and Up400 in F-actin-based structures displayed during the activation process with fMLP.
Conclusion: The study found the existence of two protein complexes formed by Dp71d/Dp71Δ(110)(m) or Up400 associated with DAPs in resting and fMLP-treated human polymorphonuclears. The interaction of these complexes with the actin cytoskeleton suggests their dynamic participation in the chemotaxis process. This study provides new insights into the expression and function of dystrophin and utrophin in non-muscle cells and highlights their importance in neutrophil biology.

title: Global and regional burden of hospital admissions for severe acute lower respiratory infections in young children in 2010: a systematic analysis
text: The global incidence of hospital admissions and deaths due to severe acute lower respiratory infections (ALRI) in children under the age of 5 is unknown. To estimate this burden, we conducted a systematic review of studies published between 1990 and 2012, as well as 28 unpublished population-based studies. We found that in 2010, there were approximately 11.9 million episodes of severe ALRI and 3.0 million episodes of very severe ALRI that resulted in hospital admissions in young children worldwide. We also estimated that roughly 265,000 in-hospital deaths occurred in young children, with 99% of these deaths occurring in developing countries. These findings suggest that while 62% of children with severe ALRI are treated in hospitals, 81% of deaths occur outside of hospitals. Improved hospital access and reduced inequities, such as those related to sex and rural status, could significantly decrease mortality related to ALRI. Additionally, community-based management of severe disease could be an important complementary strategy to reduce pneumonia mortality and health inequities. Funding for this study was provided by the World Health Organization (WHO).

title: Identification of a novel p53 functional domain that is necessary for mediating apoptosis.
text: The ability of p53 to induce apoptosis relies on its DNA-binding function, but the transactivation-deficient p53(Gln22-Ser23) can still induce apoptosis. Previous studies have shown that the region between residues 23 and 97 in p53 is essential for this activity. In an effort to more precisely map a domain necessary for apoptosis within the N-terminus, we observed that deleting the N-terminal 23 amino acids somewhat compromises, but does not completely abolish, p53-mediated induction of apoptosis. Surprisingly, p53(Delta1-42), which lacks the N-terminal 42 amino acids and a previously defined activation domain, retains the ability to induce apoptosis at an even higher level than wild-type p53. A more extensive deletion, which eliminates the N-terminal 63 amino acids, completely abrogates p53's ability to mediate apoptosis. In addition, we found that both p53(Delta1-42) and p53(Gln22-Ser23) can activate a subset of cellular p53 targets. Furthermore, we showed that residues 53 and 54 are crucial for the apoptotic and transcriptional activities of both p53(Delta1-42) and p53(Gln22-Ser23). Our data suggest that within residues 43-63 lies an apoptotic domain as well as another transcriptional activation domain. We therefore propose that the apoptotic activity in p53(Gln22-Ser23) and p53(Delta1-42) is still transcription-dependent.

title: Risk of breast cancer in relation to blood lipids: a prospective study of 31,209 Norwegian women
text: In this prospective study, the relationship between blood lipids and breast cancer risk was investigated. Between 1977 and 1983, 31,209 Norwegian women aged 20-54 years underwent a health screening conducted by the Norwegian National Health Screening Services. The screening consisted of a questionnaire, anthropometric measurements, and non-fasting blood draws for the analysis of total serum cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), and high density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol. Low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol was calculated using Friedewald's formula. During the 7-13 years of follow-up, 302 breast cancer cases were identified through linkage with the Norwegian Cancer Registry. After adjusting for some of the known risk factors of breast cancer, the relative risk of women in the highest quartile of TC compared to those in the lowest quartile was 0.87 (95% CI=0.61-1.23). The corresponding relative risks and CIs were 0.82 (CI=0.58-1.16) for TG, 1.02 (CI=0.73-1.42) for HDL, and 0.93 (CI=0.67-1.29) for LDL. No association between breast cancer risk and blood lipids was observed in the total population, nor when the data were divided into those diagnosed before or after the age of 50 as a dividing line between pre- and postmenopausal diagnosis.

title: Involvement of lysosomal dysfunction in autophagosome accumulation and early pathologies in adipose tissue of obese mice
text:
There is ongoing debate about whether obesity accelerates or slows down the process of autophagy in adipose tissue. To shed light on this issue, we focused on the function of lysosomes and the levels of proteases involved in autophagy, both in vivo and in vitro.
Our initial findings revealed that the formation of autophagosomes was enhanced in obese adipose tissue, but the process of autophagic clearance was impaired. At the same time, we discovered that protein and activity levels of Cathepsin L (CTSL) were decreased, while the activity of Cathepsin B (CTSB) was significantly higher in obese adipose tissue. Additionally, cellular senescence and inflammasomes were activated in obese adipose tissue.
In 3T3L1 adipocytes, downregulation of CTSL impaired autophagic clearance, upregulated CTSB expression, promoted cellular senescence, and activated inflammasomes. Upregulation of CTSB further activated inflammasomes. Our findings suggest that dysfunction in lysosomes, as observed in obese adipose tissue, leads to reduced autophagic clearance, resulting in the accumulation of autophagosomes. Concurrently, lysosomal abnormalities, including decreased CTSL function and compensatory CTSB activation, contribute to cellular senescence and inflammasome activation.
Our findings strongly indicate that lysosomal dysfunction is a key player in the early pathologies of obese adipose tissue.

title: ARNO regulates VEGF-dependent tissue responses by stabilizing endothelial VEGFR-2 surface expression.
text:
Background:
Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) promotes angiogenesis by inducing vessel permeability, proliferation, and migration of endothelial cells, which is crucial in ischemic diseases. ADP-ribosylation factor (ARF) nucleotide-binding site opener (ARNO) is a guanine exchange factor involved in cellular signaling through ARF GTPases. However, the role of ARNO in VEGF-dependent endothelial processes has not been investigated. Therefore, we aimed to determine whether ARNO plays a role in VEGF-mediated activation of endothelial cells and thereby vessel permeability.
Methods and Results:
ARNO expression was observed in endothelial cells in vitro through RT-PCR, western blotting, and immunofluorescence, as well as in vivo through immunohistochemical staining of mouse aorta. Treatment with the cytohesin inhibitor SecinH3 or ARNO siRNA obstructed VEGF-dependent Akt activation, as demonstrated by phosphorylated Akt detection, and endothelial cell proliferation, as measured by MTT reduction. Additionally, ARNO suppression reduced VEGF-induced permeability in mouse cremaster muscle vessels in vivo, as detected by fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-dextran extravasation. Furthermore, ARNO knockdown accelerated ligand-induced reduction in vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2 (VEGFR-2) surface expression, internalization, and degradation, as evaluated through flow cytometry and western blotting.
Conclusion:
Our findings reveal a novel and essential role for endothelial ARNO in VEGF-dependent initiation of angiogenesis by regulating VEGFR-2 internalization in endothelial cells, leading to Akt pathway activation, vessel permeability, and endothelial proliferation. Accordingly, ARNO may be a critical player in endothelial signaling and angiogenesis.

title: Effects of Hypoxia and Oxidative Stress on Expression of Neprilysin in Human Neuroblastoma Cells and Rat Cortical Neurones and Astrocytes
text: The pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD), characterized by the accumulation of extracellular deposits of β-amyloid peptide (Aβ) in the brain, has been linked to vascular disorders such as ischemia and stroke. Aβ is produced continuously in the brain through the cleavage of amyloid precursor protein (APP) by β- and γ-secretases, and certain Aβ species are toxic to neurons. The brain has an endogenous mechanism of Aβ removal through proteolytic degradation, with the zinc metalloproteinase neprilysin (NEP) playing a critical role in regulating Aβ concentration. Down-regulation of NEP has been implicated in the development of AD. By comparing the effects of hypoxia and oxidative stress on the expression and activity of the Aβ-degrading enzyme NEP in human neuroblastoma NB7 cells and rat primary cortical neurons, we found that hypoxia reduced NEP expression at the protein and mRNA levels, as well as its activity. Conversely, in astrocytes, hypoxia increased NEP mRNA expression.

title: Genetics and Beyond – The Transcriptome of Human Monocytes and Disease Susceptibility
text:
Background: Gene expression variability in humans may be linked to both genetic and non-genetic factors, which could have a significant impact on physiological and disease processes. To gain a deeper understanding of the overall variability of gene expression, we assessed the transcriptome of circulating monocytes in 1,490 unrelated individuals and investigated its association with over 675,000 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 10 common cardiovascular risk factors.
Methodology/Principal Findings: We identified 2,745 expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) in the monocyte transcriptome, with the majority (90%) being cis-actively modulated. Although associations identified by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of lipids, body mass index, and blood pressure were rarely compatible with mediation by monocyte expression level at the locus, we found 1,662 expression traits significantly associated with at least one risk factor at a study-wide level (P<3.9x10(-7)). Genome-wide interaction analyses revealed that genetic variability and risk factors mostly acted additively on gene expression. By characterizing the correlation among expression traits, the variability of risk factors could be summarized by a limited set of independent gene expressions, which may have biological and clinical relevance. For instance, expression traits associated with cigarette smoking were more strongly associated with carotid atherosclerosis than smoking itself.
Conclusions/Significance: This study demonstrates that the monocyte transcriptome is a powerful integrator of both genetic and non-genetic influences that can have a significant impact on disease pathophysiology and risk assessment.

title: Molecular mechanisms of (-)-epicatechin and chlorogenic acid on the regulation of the apoptotic and survival/proliferation pathways in a human hepatoma cell line.
text: Dietary polyphenols have been linked to a lower risk of developing chronic diseases, but the specific molecular mechanisms underlying this protection are still unclear. To investigate these mechanisms, we focused on the effects of (-)-epicatechin (EC) and chlorogenic acid (CGA) on the regulation of apoptotic and survival/proliferation pathways in human hepatoma cells (HepG2). Our findings showed that EC or CGA treatment for 18 hours had a minimal impact on cell viability and reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation, with EC alone promoting cell proliferation and CGA increasing glutathione levels. Notably, neither EC nor CGA induced the caspase cascade involved in apoptosis, and the expression levels of Bcl-xL and Bax were unchanged. Instead, EC treatment led to a sustained activation of the major survival signals AKT/PI-3-kinase, whereas CGA exposure showed a more pronounced activation of the ERK pathway. These results suggest that EC and CGA do not have any significant effect on apoptosis and instead enhance the intrinsic cellular tolerance against oxidative stress by activating survival/proliferation pathways or increasing antioxidant potential in HepG2 cells.

title: Wnt5a mediates nerve growth factor-dependent axonal branching and growth in developing sympathetic neurons.
text: Nerve growth factor (NGF) impacts the survival and growth of neurons in the peripheral nervous system, but the mechanisms underlying its regulation of axonal growth and target innervation are still being elucidated. Here, we identify Wnt5a, a member of the Wnt family of secreted growth factors, as a key downstream effector of NGF in promoting axonal branching and growth in developing sympathetic neurons. Wnt5a is expressed in sympathetic neurons when their axons are innervating NGF-expressing targets, and NGF:TrkA signaling enhances Wnt5a expression in these neurons. We find that Wnt5a rapidly induces axon branching and has a long-term effect on promoting axon extension. We also discover that loss of Wnt5a function is necessary for NGF-dependent axonal branching and growth, but not survival, in vitro. In addition, Wnt5a(-/-) mice display reduced innervation of NGF-expressing target tissues and a subsequent increase in neuronal apoptosis, suggesting that Wnt5a plays a critical role in NGF-mediated innervation. Our results define a novel regulatory pathway in which Wnt5a, expressed in sympathetic neurons in response to target-derived NGF, regulates innervation of peripheral targets.

title: The Snf1 kinase controls glucose repression in yeast by modulating interactions between the Mig1 repressor and the Cyc8-Tup1 co-repressor.
text: In lower eukaryotes, the mechanism of glucose repression is a conserved and widely distributed pathway that regulates carbon metabolism. Key components of this pathway include the yeast Snf1 kinase, the Mig1 DNA-binding repressor, and the Cyc8(Ssn6)-Tup1 co-repressor complex. Previous studies suggested that the translocation of Mig1 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, upon its phosphorylation by Snf1 in the nucleus, is the critical step in releasing glucose repression. However, in this report, we re-evaluate this model and find that the coordinated action of Mig1 and Cyc8-Tup1 in repressing GAL1 transcription is not dependent on Cyc8-Tup1's physical association with the promoter DNA. Instead, we demonstrate that both negative regulators occupy GAL1 continuously under either repressive or activating conditions, with the majority of Mig1 redistributed to the cytoplasm upon activation.
