Furthermore, we show that Snf1-dependent phosphorylation of Mig1 disrupts its interaction with Cyc8-Tup1, and propose that regulation of this interaction, rather than Mig1's cytoplasmic localization, is the molecular switch that controls transcriptional repression and de-repression.

title: ARID1A mutations in endometriosis-associated ovarian carcinomas.
text: Ovarian clear-cell and endometrioid carcinomas may evolve from endometriosis, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying this transformation remain obscure. To investigate these events, we conducted a comprehensive genomic analysis of 18 ovarian clear-cell carcinomas and one ovarian clear-cell carcinoma cell line, identifying somatic mutations in the ARID1A gene (the AT-rich interactive domain 1A [SWI-like] gene) in six of the samples. ARID1A codes for BAF250a, a fundamental component of the SWI–SNF chromatin remodeling complex. We expanded our sequencing analysis to include an additional 210 ovarian carcinomas and a second ovarian clear-cell carcinoma cell line, as well as immunohistochemical evaluation of BAF250a expression in an additional 455 ovarian carcinomas. Our findings revealed that ARID1A mutations are present in 55% of ovarian clear-cell carcinomas (46%), 30% of endometrioid carcinomas, and none of the 76 high-grade serous ovarian carcinomas. Furthermore, 17 carcinomas exhibited two somatic mutations each. Loss of BAF250a protein expression was observed in strong correlation with the ovarian clear-cell carcinoma and endometrioid carcinoma subtypes, as well as the presence of ARID1A mutations. In two patients, ARID1A mutations and loss of BAF250a expression were present in both the tumor and adjacent atypical endometriosis, but not in distant endometriotic lesions. These findings implicate ARID1A as a tumor-suppressor gene frequently disrupted in ovarian clear-cell and endometrioid carcinomas, suggesting that this event may occur early in the transformation of endometriosis into cancer. (Funded by the British Columbia Cancer Foundation and the Vancouver General Hospital–University of British Columbia Hospital Foundation.)

title: The ALS-associated proteins FUS and TDP-43 function together to affect Drosophila locomotion and life span.
text:
The aggressive neurodegenerative disease amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) shares some clinical and pathological similarities with frontotemporal dementia (FTD), a rare early-onset neurodegenerative disorder. Recent studies have revealed that the RNA/DNA-binding proteins fused in sarcoma (FUS) and TAR DNA binding protein-43 (TDP-43) are genetically and pathologically associated with familial forms of ALS and FTD. It remains unclear whether perturbing these proteins leads to disease through mechanisms unrelated to their normal functions or by disrupting critical molecular processes.
In this study, we investigated the role of FUS and TDP-43 in Drosophila using mutants with disrupted homologs of these proteins. We found that flies with mutated FUS had reduced adult viability, diminished locomotor speed, and shortened lifespan compared to control flies. These phenotypes were fully rescued by wild-type human FUS but not by ALS-associated mutant FUS proteins. A mutation in the Drosophila homolog of TDP-43 displayed similar but more severe deficits. Through cross-rescue analysis, we demonstrated that FUS acts downstream of TDP-43 in a common genetic pathway in neurons. Additionally, we found that these proteins associate with each other in an RNA-dependent complex. Our findings suggest that FUS and TDP-43 collaborate in vivo and imply that molecular pathways requiring the combined activities of these proteins may be disrupted in ALS and FTD.

title: Non-canonical PI3K-Cdc42-Pak-Mek-Erk Signaling Promotes Immune-Complex-Induced Apoptosis in Human Neutrophils
text: Neutrophils are crucial immune cells that defend the body against bacterial and fungal infections. However, they also play a significant role in the inflammatory response. Many of neutrophil surface receptors regulate important cellular processes by activating PI3K, an enzyme involved in cell signaling. We find that stimulating human neutrophils with insoluble immune complexes triggers a previously unknown, PI3K-dependent, non-canonical signaling pathway involving PI3Kβ/δ, Cdc42, Pak, MEK, and Erk. This pathway is rare as it does not involve Ras/Raf-mediated Erk activation or PI3K-mediated activation of Cdc42. Moreover, comparing immune-complex- and fMLF-induced signaling unveils distinct differences in the pathways used by human and murine neutrophils. The novel pathway identified in this study could be essential for resolving inflammation in chronic inflammatory diseases that rely on immune-complex-driven neutrophil activation.

title: Inflammation-induced tumorigenesis in the colon is regulated by caspase-1 and NLRC4.
text: Chronic inflammation is known to increase the risk of developing cancer, but the exact mechanism behind this association remains unclear. The inflammasome, a protein complex consisting of NOD-like receptor (NLR) family members, has been shown to orchestrate various immune responses, but its role in inflammation-induced cancer is poorly understood. Using the azoxymethane and dextran sodium sulfate colitis-associated colorectal cancer model, we found that mice lacking caspase-1 (Casp1(-/-)) had enhanced tumor formation. Contrary to our expectations, the role of caspase-1 in tumorigenesis was not related to its regulation of colonic inflammation, but rather its regulation of colonic epithelial cell proliferation and apoptosis. Specifically, caspase-1-deficient mice showed enhanced colonic epithelial cell proliferation in the early stages of injury-induced tumor formation and reduced apoptosis in advanced tumors. Based on these findings, we propose a model in which the NLRC4 inflammasome plays a central role in inflammation-induced tumor formation by regulating the epithelial cell response to injury.

title: The nuclear receptors SF1 and LRH1 are expressed in endometrial cancer cells and regulate steroidogenic gene transcription by cooperating with AP-1 factors.
text: Excessive exposure to estradiol poses the primary risk factor for endometrial cancer. High estradiol levels in the endometrium of cancerous women are most likely attributable to the overproduction of these hormones by the tumor itself. Endometrial cancer cells express genes that encode enzymes involved in estradiol synthesis. Through RT-PCR and Western blot analysis, we found that nuclear receptors SF1 and LRH1, known regulators of steroidogenic gene expression in gonadal and adrenal cells, are also present in endometrial cancer cell lines. Our results demonstrate that SF1 and LRH1 can activate the promoters of three human steroidogenic genes - STAR, HSD3B2, and CYP19A1 PII - through transient transfections. Forskolin, but not PMA, could also activate these promoters. Additionally, we discovered that both SF1 and LRH1 can cooperate with AP-1 family members c-JUN and c-FOS, known to enhance the proliferation of endometrial carcinoma cells, to further enhance activation of the STAR, HSD3B2, and CYP19A1 PII promoters. In summary, our findings provide new insights into the mechanisms of steroidogenic gene expression in endometrial cancer cells and the regulation of estradiol biosynthesis by tumor cells.

title: Dietary factors in chronic inflammation: food tolerances and intolerances of a New Zealand Caucasian Crohn's disease population.
text:
The relationship between diet and the symptoms of Crohn's disease (CD) has been well-documented, and while no single diet works for everyone, most CD patients are aware of foods that positively or negatively affect their symptoms. This study aimed to categorize foods based on their impact on CD symptoms in a New Zealand Caucasian population.
 Four hundred and forty-six subjects from two centers in New Zealand were recruited for the study, and an extensive dietary questionnaire was used to record participants' self-reported dietary tolerances and intolerances. The questionnaire included 257 food items grouped into 15 categories. Statistically significant differences were found among participants' responses to foods within each category. A two-dimensional graphical summary allowed for the stratification of foods based on their potential beneficial or adverse effects.
A small number of foods were found to be consistently beneficial for CD patients, including white fish, salmon, tuna, gluten-free products, oatmeal, bananas, boiled potatoes, sweet potatoes (kumara), pumpkin, soya milk, goat's milk, and yogurt. On the other hand, foods that are typically considered detrimental to CD patients include grapefruit, chili or chili sauce, corn and corn products, peanuts, cream, salami, curried foods, cola drinks, high-energy drinks, beer, and red wine. Interestingly, some foods that were beneficial for one group of subjects were detrimental to others, such as soya milk, goat's milk, yogurt, oatmeal, kiwifruit, prunes, apple, broccoli, cauliflower, linseed, pumpkin seed, sunflower seed, ginger, and ginger products, beef, lamb, liver, and oily fish.
While it was not possible to identify a specific group of foods that should be avoided by all CD patients, the wide range of detrimental items suggests that maintaining a diet that promotes remission is likely to be challenging, and personalized diets may be particularly important for these individuals.

title: Age as a risk factor for thrombocytopenia and anaemia in children treated for acute uncomplicated falciparum malaria.
text: OF ANTAEMIA & HAEMODYNAMICS IN CHILDREN WITH ACUTE UNDERMINFIELDS Malaria is frequently associated with anaemia in children, but studies examining the relationship between malaria and leucocyte and platelet counts are inconsistent. This study aimed to investigate the effect of age, gender, parasite density, and temperature on haematological parameters in children with acute uncomplicated malaria. METHODS We examined haematological parameters in children with acute uncomplicated malaria and correlated them with age, sex, temperature, and parasite density using statistical analysis software. RESULTS Six hundred and ninety-five children with acute uncomplicated malaria participated in the study, with a mean age of 51.7 months ± 33.8 months. At presentation, anaemia was observed in 43.8% of patients, and children under the age of 5 had a significantly lower haematocrit (28.4% ± 4.8) compared to older children (32.8% ± 4.8) (p < 0.001). There was no significant difference in haematocrit between days 14 and 28. Leucocytosis was more common than leucopenia (9.5% vs 3%). Thrombocytopenia was observed in 59.3% of enrolled patients, with more than half of these patients recovering by day 28. Baseline platelet count was related to days 14 (r = 0.6, p < 0.0001) and 28 (r = 0.2, p = 0.0015) and the haematocrit on day 28 (r = 0.12, p = 0.00197). Platelet count showed no correlation with temperature, parasite density, or leucocyte count. Haematocrit correlated with age (r = 0.4, p < 0.0001), but not with parasite density or temperature. Leucocyte count showed no correlation with age or parasite density. CONCLUSION Thrombocytopenia was the most common haematological finding in this study, and may be of diagnostic importance. Anaemia and leucocytosis were more common in children under the age of 5. Haematocrit and leucocyte count were significantly related to age, while parasite density and temperature showed no correlation with haematological parameters.

title: Discovery of endogenous catecholamines in lymphocytes and evidence for catecholamine regulation of lymphocyte function via an autocrine loop.
text: Recent findings have demonstrated the presence of catecholamines and their metabolites within single lymphocytes and cell extracts using capillary electrophoresis with electrochemical detection. The observation that pharmacological inhibition of tyrosine hydroxylase decreases observed catecholamine levels implies that lymphocytes are capable of producing these compounds. Intracellular dopamine levels were found to be elevated by exogenous dopamine, suggesting a mechanism of cellular uptake. Moreover, incubation with either dopamine or L-DOPA, a precursor of dopamine, resulted in a dose-dependent inhibition of lymphocyte proliferation and differentiation. These results collectively suggest the existence of an autocrine loop, whereby lymphocytes regulate their own activity.

title: Structure-based drug design identifies polythiophenes as antiprion compounds
text: Prions, the cause of transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, lack a cure. Prions are composed of misfolded and aggregated cellular prion protein (PrPC), termed PrPSc. In this study, we investigated the antiprion properties of luminescent conjugated polythiophenes (LCPs), which bind and stabilize ordered protein aggregates. To determine the minimum requirements for antiprion activity, we administered a library of structurally diverse LCPs to the brains of prion-infected mice via osmotic minipumps. Our findings showed that antiprion activity necessitated a minimum of five thiophene rings bearing regularly spaced carboxyl side groups. Furthermore, solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analyses and molecular dynamics simulations revealed that anionic side chains interacted with complementary, regularly spaced cationic amyloid residues of model prions. By applying these findings, we were able to design a new set of LCPs with optimized binding. These new compounds exhibited robust prophylactic and therapeutic potency in prion-infected mice, with the lead compound extending survival by >80% and showing activity against both mouse and hamster prions, as well as efficacy upon intraperitoneal administration into mice. These results demonstrate the feasibility of targeted chemical design in developing compounds that could potentially treat diseases characterized by aberrant protein aggregation, such as prion disease.

title: Comparisons of patient and physician expectations for cancer survivorship care.
text:
Study Examines Disparities in Expectations for Cancer Survivorship Care Among Patients and Physicians
Objective: To compare the expectations of cancer survivors and their physicians regarding physician involvement in primary cancer follow-up, cancer screening, general preventive health, and management of comorbidities.
Methods: A survey was conducted among 992 eligible survivors and 607 physicians to assess their expectations regarding the roles of primary care providers (PCPs) and oncologists in cancer survivorship care.
Results: Of the 992 survivors and 607 physicians surveyed, 535 (54%) and 378 (62%) were included in the analysis, respectively. Among physician respondents, 255 (67%) were primary care physicians, and 123 (33%) were oncologists. There were significant discrepancies between patients and their oncologists regarding expectations for screening for cancers other than the index cancer (agreement rate, 29%), with patients anticipating much more involvement from their oncologists. In contrast, expectations between patients and their primary care physicians were most discrepant for primary cancer follow-up (agreement rate, 35%), with PCPs indicating they should contribute a much greater part to this aspect of care. Expectations between patients and their primary care physicians were generally more concordant than between patients and their oncologists. PCPs and oncologists showed high discordances in their perceptions of their respective roles for primary cancer follow-up, cancer screening, and general preventive health (agreement rates of 3%, 44%, and 51%, respectively). Both PCPs and oncologists indicated that they should carry substantial responsibility for primary cancer follow-up.
Conclusion: This study reveals significant discrepancies in the expectations of cancer survivors and their physicians regarding the roles of primary care providers and oncologists in cancer survivorship care. These findings underscore the need to establish survivorship care planning as a standard component of cancer management to address these uncertainties and improve care outcomes.

title: MHC class I antigen presentation: learning from viral evasion strategies
text: The presentation of peptides by cell surface molecules (MHC class I) to immune cells is a crucial security measure that aids the body in identifying and combating dangerous pathogens. Having said that, viruses have evolved sophisticated strategies to stop certain stages of the MHC class I antigen presentation pathway and make it impossible for viral peptides to be exhibited. This review will demonstrate how an understanding of mechanisms of immune evasion can advance our understanding of interactions between viruses and hosts, as well as our knowledge of the MHC class I presentation pathway and other cellular pathways.

title: T cell receptor-proximal signals are sustained in peripheral microclusters and terminated in the central supramolecular activation cluster.
text: T cell receptor (TCR) signaling is initiated and maintained in microclusters, but its presence in the TCR-rich central supramolecular activation cluster (cSMAC) remains ambiguous. Our research revealed that the cSMAC, formed by the fusion of microclusters, contains higher levels of CD45 and lipid lipobisphosphatidic acid compared to microclusters, making it an area enriched in membrane protein degradation. Calcium signaling through TCR is inhibited within 2 minutes of anti-MHCp treatment and 1 minute of latrunculin-A treatment. TCR-MHCp interactions in the cSMAC persist for 10 minutes without supporting signaling, indicating that these interactions are not sufficient to sustain signaling. In contrast, TCR microclusters are resistant to disruption by anti-MHCp and latrunculin-A treatments. Our findings suggest that TCR signaling is sustained by stabilized microclusters and terminated in the cSMAC, a structure responsible for TCR degradation. Our study also highlights the role of F-actin in TCR signaling beyond microcluster formation.

title: The role of red cell distribution width in the prognosis of patients with gastric cancer.
text: BACKGROUND Although the red cell distribution width (RDW) has been identified as a reliable predictor of prognosis in several cancer types, its prognostic value in gastric carcinoma remains unexplored. OBJECTIVE To investigate the prognostic significance of RDW in gastric cancer patients. METHODS We retrospectively analyzed the data of 172 gastric cancer patients who underwent curative surgery over a five-year period. The study population was divided into two groups based on their RDW levels: high RDW (RDW ≥ 16, n= 62) and low RDW (RDW < 16, n= 110). We evaluated the association between RDW and clinicopathological factors, postoperative mortality, and survival outcomes. RESULTS Overall mortality and postoperative 60-day mortality were 55% and 14%, respectively. A marginally significant association between RDW and mortality was observed (p= 0.063). Preoperative RDW levels were significantly higher in patients with short-term mortality (17.9 ± 4.3 vs. 16 ± 3.2, p= 0.015). In the high RDW group, the incidence of advanced gastric cancer was significantly higher (75 vs. 51%, p= 0.002), while disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) were lower (p= 0.035 and p= 0.04, respectively). CONCLUSION Our findings suggest that high RDW values are associated with a higher frequency of advanced cancer and shorter survival time, although the relationship between RDW and overall survival was only marginally significant.

title: Vascular responsiveness in isolated perfused kidneys of diabetic hypertensive rats.
text: The study aimed to investigate the effects of diabetes and hypertension on the renal vascular system using isolated perfused kidneys from streptozotocin (STZ)-diabetic Wistar-Kyoto (WKY) rats and diabetic spontaneously hypertensive (SHR) rats. The results show that both the diabetic and hypertensive states were associated with an increased wet kidney weight. The contractile responses of the renal arterial system to phenylephrine (PhE), serotonin (5-HT), and angiotensin II (Ang II) were not affected by the diabetic state in both diabetic WKY rats and normoglycemic WKY rats. However, simultaneously occurring diabetes impaired the enhanced vascular reactivity in the hypertensive state. After precontraction with 3 x 10(-6) mol/l PhE, endothelium-dependent and endothelium-independent vasodilator drugs caused the same vasodilator response in the preparations taken from the four groups of animals. In conclusion, the isolated diabetic state did not influence the vasoconstriction caused by various agonists, but the enhanced vascular reactivity in the hypertensive state was blunted by simultaneously occurring diabetes mellitus. Endothelium-dependent and -independent vasorelaxation were not affected by either the hypertensive or diabetic state.

title: DNA replication is required To elicit cellular responses to psoralen-induced DNA interstrand cross-links.
text: Following treatment with DNA interstrand cross-links (ICLs), mammalian cells display chromosome breakage or cell cycle delay with a 4N DNA content. In order to further understand the nature of the delay, a protocol was developed to generate ICLs during specific intervals of the cell cycle. Synchronous populations of G(1), S, and G(2) cells were treated with photoactivated 4'-hydroxymethyl-4,5',8-trimethylpsoralen (HMT) and scored for normal passage into mitosis. Unlike the effects of ionizing radiation, ICLs introduced during G(2) did not result in a G(2)/M arrest, mitotic arrest, or chromosome breakage. Instead, subsequent passage through S phase was required to trigger both chromosome breakage and arrest in the next cell cycle. Similarly, ICLs introduced during G(1) did not cause a G(1)/S arrest. These findings suggest that DNA replication is necessary to elicit the cellular responses of cell cycle arrest and genomic instability after psoralen-induced ICLs. In primary human fibroblasts, the 4N DNA content cell cycle arrest triggered by ICLs was prolonged but reversible. Using kinetic analysis, it was found that these cells could remove up to approximately 2,500 ICLs/genome at a rate of 11 ICLs/genome/h.

title: DNA methylation and healthy human aging
text: The process of aging is characterized by a series of cellular and molecular changes, including senescence, telomere shortening, and shifts in gene expression. Epigenetic modifications are also altered over the lifespan, suggesting that epigenetic changes play a crucial role in the aging process. Among the epigenetic marks studied, DNA methylation has been the most extensively investigated, as it involves the presence of methyl groups at CpG dinucleotides, which are often found near gene promoters and influence gene expression levels. Early studies revealed that global levels of DNA methylation increase during the first few years of life and then decrease starting in late adulthood. However, recent technological advancements have led to the discovery of increases in variability of DNA methylation with age, as well as specific site-specific patterns. Additionally, certain CpG sites have been shown to be highly associated with chronological age, allowing for the prediction of age through a small number of these sites. These observations suggest the existence of two dominant mechanisms contributing to age-related DNA methylation changes: epigenetic drift and the epigenetic clock. This review focuses on the dynamics of DNA methylation throughout healthy human aging, discussing how interactions between the genome, environment, and epigenome influence aging rates. Additionally, the impact of determining 'epigenetic age' on human health is discussed, along with important caveats to existing and future studies.

title: Parathyroid hormone-induced E4BP4/NFIL3 down-regulates transcription in osteoblasts.
text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH), a key regulator of bone metabolism, activates the PTHR1 receptor on the surface of osteoblasts, initiating signaling that leads to the transcription of primary response genes. These primary genes, including the adenovirus E4 promoter-binding protein/nuclear factor regulated by IL-3 (E4bp4), control the expression of downstream PTH targets. We discovered that PTH rapidly induced E4bp4 mRNA in osteoblastic cells without requiring new protein synthesis. PTH also caused the synthesis of E4BP4 protein and its binding to a specific DNA sequence (EBPRE). Overexpression of E4BP4 inhibited the activity of a promoter-reporter construct containing the EBPRE, whereas PTH treatment enhanced the activity of the same construct in primary mouse osteoblasts. Additionally, E4BP4 overexpression inhibited PTH-induced activity of a cyclooxygenase-2 promoter-reporter construct. These findings suggest that E4BP4 may play a role in suppressing PTH-induced gene transcription in osteoblasts.

title: Molecular basis of synaptic vesicle cargo recognition by the endocytic sorting adaptor stonin 2
text:
Synaptic transmission relies on the efficient recycling of synaptic vesicles (SVs) through clathrin-mediated endocytosis. However, the mechanism by which specific SV proteins are targeted for internalization has remained unclear. Stonins are evolutionarily conserved adaptors that play a crucial role in the sorting of SV proteins during endocytosis. Our research has uncovered the molecular determinants for recognizing synaptotagmin, a key SV protein, by stonin 2 or its Caenorhabditis elegans orthologue UNC-41B.
The interaction between synaptotagmin and stonin 2 occurs through the direct attachment of basic residues on the cytoplasmic domain of synaptotagmin to a beta strand within the mu-homology domain of stonin 2. We found that mutating specific amino acids within this beta strand of stonin 2, such as K783, Y784, and E785, to alanine significantly reduces the association between stonin 2 and synaptotagmin, as well as the accumulation of stonin 2 at synapses and the facilitation of synaptotagmin internalization.
Furthermore, we discovered that stonin-binding-defective UNC-41B, the C. elegans orthologue of stonin 2, is unable to rescue paralysis in stonin mutant animals, indicating that the mechanism of stonin-mediated SV cargo recognition is conserved from worms to mammals.
In summary, our findings provide insight into the selective targeting of SV proteins for internalization and highlight the critical role of stonins in this process.

title: Size separation of circulatory DNA in maternal plasma permits ready detection of fetal DNA polymorphisms.
text:
Background: Noninvasive prenatal diagnosis has recently adopted fetal DNA analysis in maternal plasma, particularly for the detection of fetal genetic traits that are absent from the mother's genome, such as RHD or Y-chromosome-specific sequences. However, analyzing other fetal genetic traits has been challenging due to the dominance of maternal DNA in the circulation. We investigated whether distinct biochemical properties distinguish fetal and maternal circulating DNA.
Methods: We analyzed plasma DNA by agarose gel electrophoresis and measured the fractions of fetal and maternal DNA in size-fractionated fragments using real-time PCR. We also used highly polymorphic chromosome-21-specific microsatellite markers to determine paternally and maternally inherited fetal genetic traits.
Results: Size fractionation of circulatory DNA revealed that the majority of cell-free fetal DNA had a molecular size of <0.3 kb, whereas maternal DNA was significantly larger than 1 kb. Analysis of size-fractionated DNA from maternal plasma samples allowed for the easy detection of paternally and maternally inherited microsatellite markers.
Conclusions: Size selection of circulatory DNA fragments smaller than approximately 0.3 kb enables easier analysis of both paternally and maternally inherited DNA polymorphisms.

title: The intravascular volume effect of Ringer's lactate is below 20%: a prospective study in humans
text:
Isotonic crystalloids play a crucial role in managing perioperative fluid needs. Isooncotic preparations like human albumin or hydroxyethyl starch maintain their intravascular volume when infused to compensate for acute blood losses, as demonstrated in recent studies. However, the possible advantages of using colloids over crystalloids when treating hypovolemia remain inconclusive. Based on general physiological knowledge and clinical experience, crystalloids are expected to have a more significant intravascular volume effect than colloids.
To investigate this hypothesis, we conducted a prospective study in ten healthy adult females, using double-tracer blood volume measurements to assess changes in blood volume before and after intended normovolemic hemodilution. The study involved substituting the three-fold amount of withdrawn blood with Ringer's lactate, and the resulting deficits were substituted with half the volume of 20% human albumin. We observed a significant decrease in blood volume after hemodilution (-459 ± 185 ml; P < 0.05) and a significant increase in interstitial water content (+2,157 ± 606 ml; P < 0.05). The volume effect of Ringer's lactate was 17 ± 10%. The infusion of 245 ± 64 ml of 20% human albumin in this situation restored blood volume back to baseline values, with a volume effect of 184 ± 63%.
Our findings suggest that substitution of isolated intravascular deficits in healthy adults with the three-fold amount of Ringer's lactate impedes maintenance of intravascular normovolemia. The main side effect was an impressive interstitial fluid accumulation, which was partly restored by the intravenous infusion of 20% human albumin. We recommend substituting the five-fold amount of crystalloids or using an isooncotic preparation when managing acute bleeding in patients where edema prevention might be advantageous.

title: Fibroblast Growth Factor 21 Prevents Atherosclerosis by Suppression of Hepatic Sterol Regulatory Element-Binding Protein-2 and Induction of Adiponectin in Mice
text:
Background: Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) is a metabolic hormone that has diverse effects on glucose and lipid metabolism, as well as insulin sensitivity. While its role in the cardiovascular system is not well understood, it has been shown to be involved in the regulation of atherosclerosis.
Methods and Results: To investigate the role of FGF21 in atherosclerosis, we evaluated the impact of FGF21 deficiency and replenishment in apolipoprotein E(-/-) mice. We found that FGF21 deficiency exacerbates atherosclerosis in these mice, leading to premature death and accompanied by low levels of adiponectin and severe hypercholesterolemia. Replenishment of FGF21 protected against atherosclerosis in these mice through two independent mechanisms: inducing adipocyte production of adiponectin, which in turn inhibits neointima formation and macrophage inflammation in blood vessels, and suppressing hepatic expression of the transcription factor sterol regulatory element-binding protein-2 (SREBP-2), thereby reducing cholesterol synthesis and attenuating hypercholesterolemia. Chronic treatment with adiponectin partially reversed atherosclerosis in FGF21-deficient apolipoprotein E(-/-) mice, but did not affect hypercholesterolemia. Conversely, hepatic expression of SREBP-2 abrogated the cholesterol-lowering effects of FGF21.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that FGF21 protects against atherosclerosis by fine-tuning the multiorgan crosstalk among the liver, adipose tissue, and blood vessels.

title: VARNA: Interactive drawing and editing of the RNA secondary structure
text:
VARNA is a powerful tool designed to automate the drawing, visualization, and annotation of RNA secondary structures. As a companion software for web servers and databases, Varna offers a range of innovative features to facilitate the analysis and understanding of RNA structures.
Features of Varna include four advanced drawing algorithms, compatibility with popular input/output formats such as dbn, ct, bpseq, and RNAML, and the ability to export drawings in five different picture formats, including pixel-based options like JPEG and PNG, and vector-based formats like SVG, EPS, and XFIG.
In addition to its automated drawing capabilities, Varna also allows manual modification and structural annotation of resulting drawings through an interactive point-and-click interface within a web server or through command-line arguments. This enables users to fine-tune the visualization of their RNA structures and add additional information as needed.
VARNA is a free software release, available under the terms of the GPLv3.0 license, and can be accessed at the project's official website: <http://varna.lri.fr>. Supplementary data are also available at Bioinformatics online.

title: C-reactive protein decreases interleukin-10 secretion in activated human monocyte-derived macrophages via inhibition of cyclic AMP production.
text:
Objective: C-Reactive Protein (CRP), a marker of cardiovascular disease risk, may also play a role in the development of atherosclerosis. Atherosclerotic plaques have been shown to express CRP and Interleukin-10 (IL-10), an anti-inflammatory cytokine. We investigated the effect of CRP on Lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced IL-10 secretion in human Monocyte-Derived Macrophages (HMDMs) and examined the potential mechanism underlying this effect.
Methods: We incubated HMDMs with CRP and measured the effects on LPS-induced IL-10 mRNA and protein expression, as well as the secretion of other cytokines. We also evaluated the role of CRP in regulating the cAMP signaling pathway, which is involved in the regulation of IL-10 expression.
Results: Our results show that CRP significantly decreased LPS-induced IL-10 mRNA and protein expression, as well as secretion of IL-8, IL-6, and Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) from HMDMs. CRP alone increased secretion of IL-8, IL-6, and TNF, and did not inhibit LPS-induced secretion of these cytokines. We also found that Fc gamma receptor I antibodies reversed CRP-mediated IL-10 inhibition. Additionally, CRP significantly decreased intracellular cAMP, phosphorylation of cAMP response element binding protein (pCREB), and adenyl cyclase activity. cAMP agonists reversed CRP-mediated IL-10 inhibition. Overexpression of wild-type and constitutively active CREB in THP-1 cells revealed attenuation of the inhibitory effect of CRP on LPS-induced IL-10 levels. CRP also inhibited hemoglobin:haptoglobin-induced IL-10 and heme oxygenase-1. Furthermore, administration of human CRP to rats significantly decreased IL-10 levels.
Conclusions: Our study provides novel evidence that CRP, by decreasing IL-10, alters the anti-inflammatory/pro-inflammatory balance, accentuating inflammation, which is pivotal in atherothrombosis.

title: The DNA polymerase activity of Pol ε holoenzyme is required for rapid and efficient chromosomal DNA replication in Xenopus egg extracts
text: DNA polymerase ε (Pol ε) plays a crucial role in DNA replication, repair, and cell-cycle checkpoint control in eukaryotic cells. Despite the well-established functions of replicative Pol α and Pol δ, the specific role of Pol ε in chromosomal DNA replication remains unclear. To elucidate the role of Pol ε, this study employed a Xenopus egg extract DNA replication system. Previous studies have shown that depletion of Pol ε in Xenopus egg extracts leads to impaired initiation timing and elongation of chromosomal DNA replication, resulting in reduced accumulation of replicative intermediates and products. Restoration of normal replication is achieved through the addition of Pol ε holoenzyme, but not polymerase-deficient forms of Pol ε or incomplete enzyme complexes. This study also provides evidence that Pol ε holoenzyme interacts directly with GINS, Cdc45p, and Cut5p, which are essential for initiation of chromosomal DNA replication in eukaryotic cells. These findings suggest that the DNA polymerase activity of Pol ε holoenzyme is essential for normal chromosomal DNA replication in Xenopus egg extracts, indicating a distinct role of Pol ε in higher eukaryotes compared to yeasts, where Pol ε has been shown to be non-essential for replication.

title: DAF-16/FOXO employs the chromatin remodeller SWI/SNF to promote stress resistance and longevity
text: Organisms face constant challenges and require adaptive responses to survive, and the forkhead box O (FOXO) transcription factor DAF-16 (also referred to as DAF-16/FOXO) plays a central role in these responses. However, little is known about how DAF-16/FOXO regulates its target genes. To address this gap in knowledge, we used a proteomic approach to identify the bindings partners of DAF-16/FOXO in Caenorhabditis elegans, and evaluated their functions through RNA interference. Our findings revealed several candidate DAF-16/FOXO cofactors, including the chromatin remodeller SWI/SNF. We found that DAF-16/FOXO and SWI/SNF form a complex and co-localize at DAF-16/FOXO target promoters. Crucially, we showed that DAF-16/FOXO relies on SWI/SNF to facilitate its recruitment to target promoters, leading to the activation of transcription by remodeling local chromatin. These findings have significant implications for the regulation of lifespan in animals, as we demonstrate that SWI/SNF is essential for DAF-16/FOXO-mediated processes such as dauer formation, stress resistance, and longevity promotion. Our study provides insights into the mechanisms of DAF-16/FOXO-mediated transcriptional regulation and establishes a critical link between ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling and lifespan regulation.

title: Association of type and location of BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations with risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
text:
Here is a rewritten version of the text with improved readability and clarity:
The study aimed to identify specific mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes that are associated with an increased risk of breast and ovarian cancer. The researchers analyzed data from over 20,000 women who carried disease-associated mutations in these genes and found that the location and type of mutation can significantly impact cancer risk.
The study identified several genetic regions that were associated with an elevated risk of breast cancer, including regions located on chromosomes 1, 4, and 11. These regions were found to be associated with a higher risk of breast cancer, particularly in BRCA1 mutation carriers. In addition, the study identified a region on chromosome 13 that was associated with a lower risk of ovarian cancer, particularly in BRCA2 mutation carriers.
The study also found that mutations that confer nonsense-mediated decay can result in different breast or ovarian cancer risks and an earlier age of breast cancer diagnosis for both BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carriers. The researchers concluded that these findings may have implications for risk assessment and cancer prevention decision-making for individuals carrying BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations.
Overall, the study provides important insights into the complex relationship between genetic mutations and cancer risk and highlights the need for further research in this area to improve cancer prevention and treatment strategies.

title: Endogenous bone marrow MSCs are dynamic, fate-restricted participants in bone maintenance and regeneration.
text: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), despite their widespread clinical application, are still shrouded in mystery regarding their inherent functional capacities within the body. In an effort to elucidate the mysteries of MSCs, we conducted genetic pulse-chase experiments that revealed a fascinating dichotomy between osteoblastic cells, which are brief and non-replicative in nature, and bone-marrow-derived, Mx1(+) stromal cells, which possess "MSC" characteristics. These cells exhibit the remarkable ability to respond to tissue stress and migrate to sites of injury, thereby supplying newly formed osteoblasts during the fracture healing process. Single-cell transplantation experiments further substantiated their remarkable capabilities by yielding progeny that both preserve progenitor function and differentiate into osteoblasts, resulting in the formation of new bone. Additionally, these cells display a remarkable capacity for local and systemic translocation and serial transplantation. While MSCs in vitro meet current definitions, they are osteolineage restricted in vivo in both growing and adult animals, suggesting that the bone-marrow-derived MSC population may consist of a heterogeneous population of fate-restricted stem/progenitor cells, whose dynamic and stress-responsive nature fulfills the high cell replacement demands of the adult skeleton.

title: Dscam and DSCAM: complex genes in simple animals, complex animals yet simple genes.
text: Cadherins and immunoglobulin (Ig) proteins give rise to a diverse array of surface receptors that serve as both cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) and signal-transducing receptors. These receptors rely on a high degree of specificity in both homophilic binding and heterophilic interactions. The Drosophila receptor Dscam is a notable example of homophilic binding specificity, involved in various biological processes such as neural wiring and innate immunity. Through the use of alternatively spliced Ig-domains, an estimated 18,000 isoform-specific homophilic receptor pairs can be generated. Although isoform diversity in Dscam is unique to arthropods, recent genetic analysis of vertebrate DSCAM (Down Syndrome Cell Adhesion Molecule) genes has revealed a conserved set of molecular functions underlying neural wiring. This review covers the multiple functions of Dscam across different species, highlighting its remarkable versatility and conserved basic functions in neural development. The unprecedented expansion of complex alternative splicing in arthropods has yielded a diverse array of surface receptors critical for cell-cell communication, neuronal self-recognition, and innate immune defenses. We propose a hypothesis that reconciles the striking differences in Dscam and DSCAM gene structures with their conserved functions in molecular recognition and neural circuit formation.

title: Differential innate immune response programs in neuronal subtypes determine susceptibility to infection in the brain by positive stranded RNA viruses
text:
Although brain neurons' susceptibility to microbial infections is a crucial factor in determining clinical outcomes, little is known about the specific molecular mechanisms that govern this vulnerability. Our study aimed to investigate the differential susceptibility of two types of neurons, granule cells from the cerebellum and cortical neurons from the cerebral cortex, to replication of various positive-stranded RNA viruses.
We discovered that these neurons have distinct innate immune programs that affect their susceptibility to viral infection ex vivo and in vivo. By introducing genes that were more highly expressed in granule cell neurons into cortical neurons, we identified three interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), including Ifi27, Irg1, and Rsad2 (also known as Viperin), which play a crucial role in the antiviral response against different neurotropic viruses.
Furthermore, we found that the epigenetic state and microRNA (miRNA)-mediated regulation of ISGs are correlated with enhanced antiviral response in granule cell neurons. Our findings suggest that neurons from evolutionarily distinct brain regions have unique innate immune signatures, which likely contribute to their relative permissiveness to infection.
In summary, our study uncovered the molecular factors governing the differential susceptibility of brain neurons to microbial infections, providing new insights into the mechanisms underlying neurological disorders.

title: Small-airway obstruction and emphysema in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text:
Background: In patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the airways with diameters less than 2 mm are majorly affected. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the relationship between small-airway obstruction and emphysematous destruction in COPD.
Methodology: We used multidetector computed tomography (CT) to analyze the number of airways measuring 2.0 to 2.5 mm in diameter in lung samples from 78 patients with different stages of COPD, as determined by Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) scoring. We also measured the extent of emphysema (mean linear intercept), the number of terminal bronchioles per milliliter of lung volume, and the minimum diameters and cross-sectional areas of terminal bronchioles using microCT in samples from patients with COPD and control samples.
Results: On multidetector CT, we found that the number of airways measuring 2.0 to 2.5 mm in diameter was significantly reduced in patients with GOLD stage 1 disease (P=0.001), GOLD stage 2 disease (P=0.02), and GOLD stage 3 or 4 disease (P<0.001) compared to control samples. MicroCT analysis of isolated lungs from patients with GOLD stage 4 disease showed a significant reduction (81-99.7%) in the total cross-sectional area of terminal bronchioles and a reduction (72-89%) in the number of terminal bronchioles (P<0.001). Furthermore, we found that the narrowing and loss of terminal bronchioles preceded emphysematous destruction in COPD (P<0.001).
Conclusion: Our results indicate that narrowing and disappearance of small conducting airways before the onset of emphysematous destruction can explain the increased peripheral airway resistance observed in COPD. (Funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and others.)

title: Stepwise Histone Replacement by SWR1 Requires Dual Activation with Histone H2A.Z and Canonical Nucleosome
text: Histone variant H2A.Z-containing nucleosomes are prevalent at most eukaryotic promoters, facilitated by the conserved SWR1 complex, which replaces histone H2A in conventional nucleosomes with H2A.Z through an ATP-dependent process. Here, we investigate the heterogeneity of promoter-proximal nucleosomes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, revealing a range of H2A.Z content, including nucleosomes containing one, two, or zero H2A.Z molecules. The SWR1-mediated replacement of H2A.Z occurs in a stepwise, unidirectional manner, generating heterotypic nucleosomes as intermediate stages and homotypic H2A.Z nucleosomes as final products. Remarkably, the ATPase activity of SWR1 is specifically stimulated by H2A-containing nucleosomes without leading to histone H2A eviction, and further addition of free H2A.Z-H2B dimer leads to hyperstimulation, eviction of nucleosomal H2A-H2B, and deposition of H2A.Z-H2B. These findings suggest that the collaboration of H2A-containing nucleosome and free H2A.Z-H2B dimer functions as both effector and substrate for SWR1, governing the specificity and outcome of the replacement reaction.

title: Logic of the yeast metabolic cycle: temporal compartmentalization of cellular processes.
text: Yeast grown under continuous, nutrient- restricted conditions demonstrate robust, highly periodic cycles characterized by respiratory bursts. Microarray analysis reveals that over half of the yeast genome is expressed in a periodic manner during these metabolic cycles. Genes encoding proteins with similar functions exhibit synchronized temporal expression patterns, while genes associated with energy and metabolism display exceptionally robust periodicity in their expression. Crucial cellular and metabolic processes occur in synchrony with the metabolic cycle, indicating that key functions in a simple eukaryotic cell are organized in temporal compartments.

title: Molecular pathways: induction of polyploidy as a novel differentiation therapy for leukemia.
text: Differentiation therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for targeting specific types of hematologic malignancies. One notable example is the use of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), which has significantly improved patient outcomes. Based on this success, we hypothesized that compounds inducing terminal megakaryocyte differentiation could be effective treatments for acute megakaryocytic leukemia (AMKL) and primary myelofibrosis (PMF). Using a high-throughput chemical screening approach, we identified small molecules that promote polyploidization, a process by which cells accumulate DNA to 32N or greater, making further cell division impossible. As polyploidization is an irreversible process, it offers a potential way to reduce the tumor burden. Clinical trials with polyploidy inducers, such as aurora kinase A inhibitors, are underway for various malignancies, and trials specifically for AMKL and PMF are in development. This novel form of differentiation therapy may soon become clinically available.

title: Dual mutations in the AML1 and FLT3 genes are associated with leukemogenesis in acute myeloblastic leukemia of the M0 subtype
text: Genetic alterations in the transcription factor AML1 have been linked to leukemogenesis in acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML). Specifically, internal tandem duplications (ITDs) in the juxtamembrane domain and mutations in the second tyrosine kinase domain of the Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3) gene are the most common genetic changes observed in AML. However, these mutations alone do not appear to be sufficient to cause leukemia. To investigate whether both AML1 and FLT3 mutations play a role in leukemic transformation, we analyzed the genes in AML M0 subtype, where AML1 mutations are predominantly found. We discovered that eight of 51 patients had a mutation in the Runt domain of the AML1 gene, including one heterozygous missense mutation with normal function, five heterozygous frameshift mutations, and two biallelic nonsense or frameshift mutations, resulting in haploinsufficiency or complete loss of AML1 activity. In contrast, a total of 10 of 49 patients had a mutation in the FLT3 gene. Interestingly, we found that five of eight patients with AML1 mutations also had the FLT3 mutation, while five of 41 patients without AML1 mutations had the FLT3 mutation (P=0.0055). These results suggest that reduced AML1 activities may predispose cells to acquire the activating FLT3 mutation as a secondary event leading to full transformation in AML M0.

title: Unravelling mechanisms of p53-mediated tumour suppression
text: The tumour suppressor protein p53 is a crucial player in responding to diverse stress signals and coordinating specific cellular responses to safeguard against tumour formation. These responses include transient cell cycle arrest, cellular senescence, and apoptosis, all of which are vital for tumour suppression. However, more recent research has challenged the idea that these canonical cellular responses are the only means by which p53 contributes to tumour suppression. In fact, p53 has been shown to have a broader range of functions, including modulating metabolism, stem cell maintenance, invasion and metastasis, as well as communication within the tumour microenvironment. In this Opinion article, we delve into both the traditional p53 functions and the emerging p53-regulated processes that play a crucial role in tumour suppression.

title: Stem cell-related "self-renewal" signature and high epidermal growth factor receptor expression associated with resistance to concomitant chemoradiotherapy in glioblastoma.
text: The purpose of this study was to identify specific molecular profiles associated with resistance to standard of care therapy, including concomitant chemoradiotherapy with the alkylating agent temozolomide, in glioblastomas. The study analyzed the gene expression profiles of 80 glioblastomas and found an expression signature dominated by HOX genes, including Prominin-1 (CD133), which was a predictor of poor survival in patients treated with concomitant chemoradiotherapy. This association was validated in an independent data set. The study also found that the HOX signature and EGFR expression were independent prognostic factors in multivariate analysis, adjusted for the O-6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) methylation status and age. The study provided the first clinical evidence for the implication of a "glioma stem cell" or "self-renewal" phenotype in treatment resistance in glioblastoma. The biological mechanisms identified in this study are likely to guide future targeted therapies and marker development for individualized treatment and patient selection.

title: Heterogeneity Underlies the Emergence of EGFRT790 Wild-Type Clones Following Treatment of T790M-Positive Cancers with a Third-Generation EGFR Inhibitor.
text:
Title: Rociletinib Resistance in EGFR-Mutant Lung Cancers: The Role of Tumor Heterogeneity
Introduction:
Rociletinib is a third-generation EGFR inhibitor that has shown promising activity in lung cancers with the T790M mutation, a key resistance mechanism to first-generation EGFR inhibitors. However, little is known about the resistance mechanisms that emerge in T790M-positive cancers treated with rociletinib. In this study, we investigated the tumor heterogeneity of T790M-positive cancers at progression and its impact on rociletinib response.
Methods:
We biopsied patients with T790M-positive lung cancers at the time of rociletinib progression and analyzed the T790M status and other resistance mutations. We also performed longitudinal circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) analysis to assess the emergence of resistance mutations.
Results:
Our results showed that half of the T790M-positive cancers analyzed were T790-wild-type at progression, suggesting that T790-wild-type clones can emerge as the dominant source of resistance. We also found that tumor heterogeneity has important clinical implications, as the pretreatment fraction of T790M-positive cells can affect response to rociletinib. Additionally, plasma ctDNA analysis revealed an increase in the plasma EGFR-activating mutation, and T790M heralded rociletinib resistance in some patients, while in others, the activating mutation increased but T790M remained suppressed.
Conclusion:
Our findings highlight the importance of targeting both T790-wild-type and T790M-positive clones in order to improve outcomes in patients with EGFR-mutant lung cancers treated with rociletinib. The use of combination regimens that include targeting T790-wild-type clones may help overcome resistance mechanisms and improve treatment response.

title: Extrathymic Generation of Regulatory T Cells in Placental Mammals Mitigates Maternal-Fetal Conflict
text: T regulatory (Treg) cells, which are controlled by the X-encoded transcription factor Foxp3, are generated in the thymus (tTreg) and outside of it (peripheral, pTreg). A deficiency in these cells leads to fatal autoimmunity. Our study shows that a Foxp3 enhancer, conserved noncoding sequence 1 (CNS1), essential for pTreg but dispensable for tTreg cell production, is present only in placental mammals. CNS1 is made up of mammalian-wide interspersed repeats (MIR) that have undergone retrotransposition during early mammalian evolution. During pregnancy, pTreg cells specific to a particular paternal alloantigen are generated in a CNS1-dependent manner and accumulate in the placenta. Furthermore, when mated with allogenic, but not syngeneic, males, CNS1-deficient females exhibit increased fetal resorption accompanied by increased immune cell infiltration and defective remodeling of spiral arteries. Our findings suggest that, during evolution, a CNS1-dependent mechanism of extrathymic differentiation of Treg cells emerged in placental animals to maintain maternal-fetal tolerance.

title: Acquired EGFR C797S mutation mediates resistance to AZD9291 in non–small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR T790M
text: Here, we investigated cell-free plasma DNA (cfDNA) from individuals with advanced lung cancer who had developed resistance to the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) AZD9291. We first performed next-generation sequencing on cfDNA from seven subjects and identified an acquired EGFR C797S mutation in one; when expressed in a cell line, this mutant EGFR construct rendered it resistant to AZD9291. Subsequent droplet digital PCR analysis of cfDNA samples from 15 AZD9291-treated individuals revealed that all initially carried the T790M mutation, but upon developing resistance, three distinct molecular subtypes emerged: six cases acquired the C797S mutation, five cases maintained the T790M mutation without acquiring the C797S mutation, and four cases lost the T790M mutation despite harboring the underlying EGFR activating mutation. Our findings offer valuable insights into the diverse mechanisms by which tumors develop resistance to AZD9291 and underscore the need for therapies that can overcome resistance mediated by the EGFR C797S mutation.

title: The Translation Initiation Factor 3f (eIF3f) Exhibits a Deubiquitinase Activity Regulating Notch Activation
text:
The activation of the mammalian Notch receptor following ligand binding requires a series of events, including metalloprotease-cleavage, endocytosis, monoubiquitination, and finally processing by the gamma-secretase enzyme, resulting in a soluble, transcriptionally active form of the receptor. Notch1 is proposed to be monoubiquitinated before its gamma-secretase cleavage, with the targeted lysine localized to its submembrane domain. Investigating the regulation of thisstep by a deubiquitinase (DUB) activity could provide new insights into the mechanisms of Notch receptor activation and downstream signaling.
An immunofluorescence-based screening of an shRNA library allowed us to identify eIF3f, a subunit of the translation initiation factor eIF3, as a DUB targeting the activated Notch receptor. We found that eIF3f has an intrinsic DUB activity. Knocking down eIF3f leads to an accumulation of monoubiquitinated forms of activated Notch, which is counteracted by wild-type (WT) eIF3f but not by a catalytically inactive mutant. Additionally, we show that eIF3f is recruited to activated Notch on endocytic vesicles by the putative E3 ubiquitin ligase Deltex1, which acts as a bridging factor. Finally, catalytically inactive forms of eIF3f and shRNAs targeting eIF3f repress Notch activation in a coculture assay, suggesting that eIF3f is a new positive regulator of the Notch pathway.
Our findings support two novel conclusions: (1) The activated form of Notch needs to be deubiquitinated before being processed by the gamma-secretase activity and entering the nucleus, where it carries out its transcriptional function. (2) The enzyme responsible for this deubiquitination activity is eIF3f, which, until now, was primarily known as a translation initiation factor. These data improve our understanding of Notch signaling and open new avenues of research into the Zomes family and translation initiation factors.

title: Focal contacts as mechanosensors: externally applied local mechanical force induces growth of focal contacts by an mDia1-dependent and ROCKindependent mechanism
text: The transition of cell-matrix adhesions from initial punctate focal complexes to mature elongated form, known as focal contacts, requires GTPase Rho activity. Specifically, activation of myosin II-driven contractility by a Rho target, Rho-associated kinase (ROCK), was shown to be essential for focal contact formation. To investigate the mechanism of Rho-dependent induction of focal contacts and to elucidate the role of cell contractility, we applied mechanical force to vinculin-containing dot-like adhesions at the cell edge using a micropipette. Local centripetal pulling led to local assembly and elongation of these structures, and their development into streak-like focal contacts, as revealed by the dynamics of green fluorescent protein-tagged vinculin or paxillin and interference reflection microscopy. Inhibition of Rho activity by C3 transferase suppressed this force-induced focal contact formation. However, constitutively active mutants of another Rho target, the formin homology protein mDia1 (Watanabe, N., T. Kato, A. Fujita, T. Ishizaki, and S. Narumiya. 1999. Nat. Cell Biol. 1:136–143), were sufficient to restore force-induced focal contact formation in C3 transferase-treated cells. Force-induced formation of the focal contacts still occurred in cells subjected to myosin II and ROCK inhibition. Therefore, as long as mDia1 is active, external tension force can bypass the requirement for ROCK-mediated myosin II contractility in the induction of focal contacts. Our experiments show that integrin-containing focal complexes behave as individual mechanosensors that assemble in response to local force.

title: Maternal Protein Restriction Affects Postnatal Growth and the Expression of Key Proteins Involved in Lifespan Regulation in Mice
text: In previous studies, we found that maternal protein restriction in rodents during early life influences growth rates and ultimately affects lifespan. Low birth weight resulting from maternal protein restriction followed by catch-up growth (recuperated animals) was associated with a shorter lifespan, whereas protein restriction and slow growth during lactation (postnatal low protein: PLP animals) led to an increase in lifespan. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we investigated the effects of maternal diet on organ growth, metabolic parameters, and the expression of insulin/IGF1 signaling proteins and Sirt1 in the muscle of male mice at weaning. PLP mice, which experienced protein restriction during lactation, had lower fasting glucose and insulin levels, suggesting enhanced insulin sensitivity. These mice also had higher relative weights of the brain and thymus, and increased expression of insulin receptor substrate 1 and protein kinase C zeta, which are beneficial to longevity. In contrast, recuperated animals had reduced levels of several insulin signaling proteins, including PI3 kinase subunits p85alpha, p110beta, and protein kinase C zeta, which may predispose them to insulin resistance. Sirt1 protein expression was also decreased in the offspring of recuperated mothers. These findings suggest that maternal protein restriction can affect major metabolic pathways involved in the regulation of lifespan at a young age, which may explain the impact of maternal diet on longevity.

title: ‘Short stature in children - a questionnaire for parents’: a new instrument for growth disorder-specific psychosocial adaptation in children
text: According to recent studies, children with and without growth disorders show comparable psychosocial adaptation. However, there is a lack of sensitive and specific methods for analyzing and comparing their quality of life. To address this gap, we developed a new questionnaire for parents of short-statured children. The questionnaire employs both qualitative and quantitative approaches to gather specific information about individual stress factors and sources of support. We administered the questionnaire to 442 parents of children with growth retardation resulting from different causes. Principal component analysis revealed four dimensions of psychosocial adaptation: suffering, future anxieties, behavioral problems, and coping efforts. The questionnaire exhibited sufficient reliability, and a comparison of two growth disorder groups (achondroplasia and growth hormone deficiency) showed growth disorder-specific but not significantly different profiles of psychosocial adaptation. Furthermore, we found a shift in stress factor patterns in children with achondroplasia, indicating more physical restrictions. These findings demonstrate the validity and utility of the new questionnaire in providing growth disorder-specific information on individual stress factors, resources, and psychosocial adaptation.

title: Alphavirus-derived small RNAs modulate pathogenesis in disease vector mosquitoes.
text: Mosquito-borne viruses contribute significantly to human and animal illness. A biological transmission cycle involving virus replication in a vulnerable vertebrate host and mosquito is necessary to sustain these viruses in nature. Although the vertebrate infection is brief and connected to disease, ongoing transmission of these viruses depends on the establishment of a prolonged, non-harmful infection in the mosquito host. Research has demonstrated that the antiviral RNA interference (RNAi) response limits the replication of RNA viruses in flies. However, the significance of this defense pathway in mammals remains uncertain. The differences between the immune responses of mammals and mosquitoes may explain why these viruses do not generally cause disease in the latter. We identified small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) derived from the virus, 21 nucleotides in length, in Aedes aegypti infected with the mosquito-borne virus, Sindbis (SINV). These siRNAs had an uneven distribution that spanned the length of the SINV genome. To determine the role of siRNAs in restricting the virulence of these viruses, mosquitoes were infected with recombinant alphaviruses expressing suppressors of RNA silencing. Decreased survival was observed in mosquitoes in which the accumulation of siRNAs was suppressed. As a result, these findings suggest that an extra siRNA pathway is essential to the survival of mosquitoes infected with alphaviruses and, thus, the preservation of these viruses in nature.

title: Nuclear RNAi maintains heritable gene silencing in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: RNA interference (RNAi) inheritance is a characterized phenomenon in Caenorhabditis elegans, where the progeny of exposed individuals exhibit the capacity to silence genes that were targeted by RNAi in the previous generation. To elucidate the underlying mechanism of RNAi inheritance, we conducted an investigation focused on the specific systems involved in this process. We discovered that exposure to double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) leads to the heritable expression of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and the heritable deposition of histone 3 lysine 9 methylation (H3K9me) markers in the progeny. Notably, siRNAs become detectable before the appearance of H3K9me marks, suggesting that chromatin modifications are not directly inherited but rather reestablished in the inheriting progeny. This observation is reinforced by the notable enhancement of H3K9me marks in inheriting progeny compared to animals directly exposed to dsRNA, implying that germ-line transmission of silencing signals might improve the efficiency of siRNA-mediated H3K9me marking. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the nuclear RNAi (Nrde) pathway plays a crucial role in maintaining heritable RNAi silencing in C. elegans. The Argonaute (Ago) NRDE-3 associates with heritable siRNAs and, in collaboration with the nuclear RNAi factors NRDE-1, NRDE-2, and NRDE-4, promotes siRNA expression in inheriting progeny. These results provide conclusive evidence that siRNA expression is heritable in C. elegans and elucidate an RNAi pathway that maintains the expression of siRNAs and the silencing of target genes in the progeny of animals exposed to dsRNA.

title: Cancer survivors in the United States: prevalence across the survivorship trajectory and implications for care.
text:
BACKGROUND: Cancer survivors represent a growing population, diverse in their needs for medical care, psychosocial support, and practical assistance. This study aims to provide an overview of the prevalent cancer survivor population in the United States, including the number of survivors and their prevalence by cancer site and time since diagnosis.
METHODS: Using incidence and survival data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Program and population projections from the United States Census Bureau, we obtained prevalence data for 2012 and projected figures for 2022. We estimated cancer prevalence using the Prevalence Incidence Approach Model, assuming constant future incidence and survival trends but dynamic projections of the U.S. population.
RESULTS: As of January 1, 2012, there were approximately 13.7 million cancer survivors living in the United States. This number is projected to reach 18 million by 2022, with 64% of survivors having survived 5 years or more after diagnosis, 40% having survived 10 years or more, and 15% having survived 20 years or more. We anticipate an approximately 37% increase in the number of people who have lived 5 years or more after their cancer diagnosis over the next decade, to 11.9 million.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings highlight the growing need for a coordinated agenda for research and practice to address the long-term medical, psychosocial, and practical needs of cancer survivors across the survivorship trajectory. Accurate prevalence estimates will inform the national research agenda and future projections regarding the health service needs of this population.
IMPACT: This study's prevalence estimates will provide valuable insights for policymakers, healthcare providers, and cancer survivors themselves, enabling them to better understand the population's needs and develop appropriate strategies for addressing them.

title: Human aneuploidy: mechanisms and new insights into an age-old problem
text: At least 10% of human pregnancies involve trisomic or monosomic (aneuploid) embryos, with the incidence potentially exceeding 50% for women nearing the end of their reproductive years. Despite extensive research, the molecular basis for aneuploidy remains unknown, as errors occur almost exclusively in the oocyte. However, recent studies in humans and model organisms have illuminated the intricate nature of meiotic defects, suggesting that the age-related increase in errors in the human female is not attributed to a single factor, but rather the result of an interplay between specialized oogenesis and various endogenous and exogenous factors.

title: The Drosophila hindgut lacks constitutively active adult stem cells but proliferates in response to tissue damage.
text: Recent research has challenged the long-held view that the adult Drosophila hindgut is home to active, tissue-replenishing stem cells, similar to those found in the midgut. Instead, our studies have revealed that the hindgut lacks active stem cells and exhibits minimal cell turnover. These findings contradict prior proposals that the hindgut is generated by stem cells located within the anterior region during larval/pupal development. However, when the hindgut is damaged, we observed increased cell proliferation within a ring of quiescent stem cells at the anterior pylorus. This suggests that the hindgut does not function as a model of tissue maintenance through constitutively active stem cells, but may provide insight into mechanisms of stress-induced tissue repair.

title: Vitamin d deficiency in postmenopausal women - biological correlates.
text:
INTRODUCTION: Low levels of vitamin D (VD) have been linked to secondary hyperparathyroidism and the negative consequences that come with it, such as reduced bone mineral density (BMD), an increased risk of fractures and falls. This study aims to investigate the VD status and associated biological factors in a group of postmenopausal women.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: In this study, 123 postmenopausal women evaluated at the C.I.Parhon National Institute of Endocrinology, the Pituitary and Neuroendocrine Diseases department were examined. All patients had been referred for BMD evaluation by their primary care physician. The evaluation included measurements of serum total and ionized calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), 25 hydroxi vitamin D (25OHD), parathyroid hormone (PTH), osteocalcin, and bone mineral density (BMD) using central DXA osteodensitometry. Furthermore, the study included 32 women who were already taking VD supplements at the time of the evaluation.
RESULTS: The results showed that 91.9% of the participants had VD levels below 30 ng/ml, with 74.8% having VD deficiency and 17.1% having VD insufficiency. Only 8.1% of the participants had sufficient VD levels. A history of fragility fractures was present in 45.83% of osteoporotic patients, 27.27% of osteopenic patients, and 15.15% of those with normal BMD. In addition, 32 women (26%) were taking VD supplements at the time of the evaluation, and among these subjects, the 25OHD levels were significantly higher in those with prior fragility fractures (p=0.018) and osteoporosis (p=0.008). Furthermore, a negative correlation was found between VD levels and PTH, ALP, and osteocalcin. Moreover, the bone markers evaluated had a significant inverse correlation with the radius BMD, T and Z scores (p=0.004). Finally, 27.17% of the cases with VD deficiency had secondary hyperparathyroidism, and the 25OHD levels were significantly lower in these cases (p=0.000).
CONCLUSIONS: This study highlights the under-recognition and under-treatment of VD insufficiency, which could lead to secondary hyperparathyroidism. It also emphasizes the need for more active primary prevention measures to address this issue. Furthermore, the results suggest that VD supplementation is not being complied with as much in participants without osteoporosis or fragility fractures.

title: CD44v6 is a marker of constitutive and reprogrammed cancer stem cells driving colon cancer metastasis.
text: The elusive nature of cancer metastasis, where cancer cells spread to distant organs, remains poorly understood. In colorectal cancer, cancer stem cells (CR-CSCs) are believed to play a pivotal role in this process, but the mechanisms behind their acquisition of metastatic traits are obscure. Here, we uncovered a crucial insight: all CR-CSCs express CD44v6, a surface protein that is necessary for their migration and the generation of metastatic tumors. Interestingly, CD44v6 expression is low in primary tumors but is concentrated within specific, clonogenic CR-CSC populations. We found that cytokines produced by tumor-associated cells, such as hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), osteopontin (OPN), and stromal-derived factor 1α (SDF-1), can upregulate CD44v6 expression in CR-CSCs by activating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, which promotes migration and metastasis. Surprisingly, we discovered that CD44v6- cells, the non-stem counterparts of CR-CSCs, do not give rise to metastatic lesions, but upon treatment with cytokines, they can acquire CD44v6 expression and metastatic capacity. Moreover, inhibition of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) selectively killed CD44v6+ CR-CSCs and impaired metastatic growth. Importantly, low levels of CD44v6 were found to associate with improved patient survival in our cohort studies. Overall, our findings suggest that the metastatic process in colorectal cancer is driven by CR-CSCs through the expression of CD44v6, which serves both as a functional marker and potential therapeutic target.

title: Senescent Cells, Tumor Suppression, and Organismal Aging: Good Citizens, Bad Neighbors
text: Cells from organisms with regenerative capacities can temporarily exit the cell cycle in response to various stresses, such as damaged telomeres, DNA damage, strong growth signals, and disrupted chromatin. This temporary pause, termed cellular senescence, is regulated by proteins like p53 and RB and serves as a powerful defense mechanism against cancer. However, as senescent cells accumulate over time, they can develop distinguishing characteristics that may contribute to aging and certain age-related diseases, including late-life cancer. In other words, the senescence response can have seemingly contradictory effects, promoting early-life survival by preventing the development of cancer but potentially limiting lifespan as senescent cells build up.

title: Advances in high-resolution imaging--techniques for three-dimensional imaging of cellular structures.
text: A central objective in biology is to investigate how cellular organization is linked to function. To achieve this aim, a deeper comprehension of organelle composition and structure is essential. Although visualizing cellular organelles through fluorescence or electron microscopy (EM) has become a common tool for cell biologists, recent innovations are providing a more detailed understanding of the cell than ever before. Specifically, cutting-edge light microscopy techniques are achieving resolutions below the diffraction limit, and EM tomography supplies high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) images of cellular structures. The ability to perform both fluorescence and electron microscopy on the same sample (correlative light and electron microscopy, CLEM) enables the identification of where a fluorescently labeled protein is positioned relative to organelle structures visualized by EM. Here, we review the current state-of-the-art in 3D biological imaging techniques, with a focus on recent advances in electron microscopy and fluorescence super-resolution techniques.

title: Quercetin attenuates vascular calcification by inhibiting oxidative stress and mitochondrial fission.
text:
Vascular calcification is a strong predictor of increased cardiovascular problems and death, and it's especially common in people with chronic kidney disease. In this study, we looked at how quercetin affects vascular calcification caused by oxidative stress and abnormal mitochondrial dynamics. We tested this in both lab dishes and live animals.
When we treated vascular smooth muscle cells with a substance called inorganic phosphate (Pi), they started to calcify and show signs of damage to their mitochondria. This included decreased energy production and abnormalities in the structure of their mitochondria. We also saw similar damage in rats that had been given a substance to cause vascular calcification.
When we exposed these cells to quercetin, it blocked the damage caused by Pi and reduced the amount of mitochondrial fragmentation. This led to a decrease in the number of apoptotic (dying) cells and an reduction in the amount of calcium deposits. Quercetin also significantly reduced vascular calcification in rats that had been given the substance to cause it.
In summary, our findings suggest that quercetin reduces vascular calcification by protecting smooth muscle cells from damage caused by oxidative stress and promoting their survival by inhibiting the fragmentation of their mitochondria.

title: The M/GP5 Glycoprotein Complex of Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome Virus Binds the Sialoadhesin Receptor in a Sialic Acid-Dependent Manner
text: The porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) poses a significant threat to swine health globally and is currently the most prevalent viral disease affecting the swine industry. Prior research has identified crucial virus receptors and entry mediators on host cells, yet the viral counterparts for these molecules have remained elusive, hindering the development of new-generation vaccines. This study aimed to identify the viral counterparts for sialoadhesin, a vital PRRSV receptor on macrophages. To achieve this, a soluble form of sialoadhesin was constructed and validated, which demonstrated the ability to bind PRRSV in a sialic acid-dependent manner and neutralize PRRSV infection of macrophages. Our findings confirmed the role of sialoadhesin as an essential PRRSV receptor on macrophages. Interestingly, we found that the M/GP(5) glycoprotein complex of PRRSV, which contains sialic acids, serves as the ligand for sialoadhesin. The interaction between sialoadhesin and PRRSV was found to be dependent on the sialic acid binding capacity of sialoadhesin and the presence of sialic acids on GP(5).
