This study not only deepens our understanding of PRRSV biology but also provides valuable insights and tools for the development of novel PRRSV vaccines.

title: A versatile zero background T-vector system for gene cloning and functional genomics.
text:
With the advent of complete genomic sequences for many organisms, there is a growing demand for high-throughput and cost-effective systems for gene cloning and functional analysis. While site-specific recombination-based cloning systems, such as Gateway technology, offer efficient transfer of DNA fragments into multiple destination vectors, the two-step cloning process is time-consuming and expensive. To address these limitations, we have developed a zero background TA cloning system that enables simple and high-efficiency direct cloning of PCR-amplified DNA fragments with almost no self-ligation.
The improved T-vector system utilizes the restriction enzyme XcmI to generate a T-overhang after digestion and the negative selection marker gene ccdB to eliminate the self-ligation background after transformation. We demonstrate the versatility and applicability of the technology by developing a range of transient and stable transformation vectors for constitutive gene expression, gene silencing, protein tagging, protein subcellular localization detection, and promoter fragment activity analysis in plants.
The unique advantage of the zero background TA cloning system is its adaptability for creating specialized expression vectors for other organisms, making it a valuable complement to the Gateway cloning system for gene cloning and functional genomics. With its cost-effective and high-throughput capabilities, this platform has the potential to significantly accelerate the pace of gene cloning and functional genomics research.

title: GEP100-Arf6-AMAP1-Cortactin Pathway Frequently Used in Cancer Invasion Is Activated by VEGFR2 to Promote Angiogenesis
text: Angiogenesis and cancer migration significantly contribute to cancer's malignancy. Arf6 and its effector, AMAP1, are frequently overexpressed in breast cancer, forming a central pathway that induces invasion and metastasis. In this pathway, Arf6 is activated by the EGFR through GEP100. Arf6 is highly expressed in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and is linked to angiogenesis. Our findings show that HUVECs highly express AMAP1, and VEGFR2 recruits GEP100 to activate Arf6. AMAP1 functions by interacting with cortactin in cancer invasion and metastasis. We demonstrate that the same GEP100-Arf6-AMAP1-cortactin pathway is essential for angiogenesis activities, including cell migration and tube formation, as well as enhancing cell permeability and VE-cadherin endocytosis in VEGF-stimulated HUVECs. Components of this pathway are highly expressed in pathological angiogenesis, and inhibiting this pathway effectively prevents VEGF- or tumor-induced angiogenesis and choroidal neovascularization. The GEP100-Arf6-AMAP1-cortactin pathway, activated by receptor tyrosine kinases, appears to be common in angiogenesis and cancer invasion and metastasis, providing new therapeutic targets.

title: Dynamics of Cryptococcus neoformans-Macrophage Interactions Reveal that Fungal Background Influences Outcome during Cryptococcal Meningoencephalitis in Humans
text: Cryptococcosis is a complex fungal infection with variable clinical manifestations and outcomes. Previous studies have attributed the diversity in clinical presentation to host factors, but little is known about the fungal determinants that contribute to disease outcome. To investigate the relationship between clinical isolates of Cryptococcus neoformans and their interactions with host cells, we developed and validated new flow cytometry-based assays using J774 macrophages. Our study reveals that the phenotype of clinical isolates in their interactions with macrophages is highly variable, with some isolates displaying low phagocytic index and high intracellular proliferation rates, while others exhibit the opposite pattern. We found that isolates with low phagocytic index and high intracellular proliferation rates were associated with nonsterilization of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at week 2 and death at month 3, respectively. A subset of 9 isolates with distinct phenotypes showed variable virulence in mice, and their intracellular expression levels of genes involved in virulence factors were highly variable and correlated with intracellular proliferation rates. Our results suggest that, in addition to host factors, the patient's outcome can be related to fungal determinants. Deciphering the molecular events involved in C. neoformans fate inside host cells is crucial for understanding cryptococcosis pathogenesis. Our findings highlight the importance of studying the interaction between clinical isolates and host cells in order to enhance our understanding of cryptococcosis and to develop effective therapeutic strategies.

title: Angiopoietin-2 at high concentration can enhance endothelial cell survival through the phosphatidylinositol 3′-kinase/Akt signal transduction pathway
text: The Angiopoietin-Tie2 system in endothelial cells plays a crucial role in regulating vasculogenesis and vascular integrity. High levels of Ang2 mRNA are detected in vascular activation during tumorigenesis, despite Ang2 being known to counteract Ang1 in vivo. Our findings reveal that a high concentration of Ang2 (800 ng/ml) functions as a survival factor for endothelial cells during serum deprivation-induced apoptosis. This effect is mediated by the Tie2 receptor, phosphatidylinositol 3'-kinase (PI3K), and the serine/threonine kinase Akt. Specifically, Ang2 triggers the phosphorylation of Tie2, the p85 subunit of PI3K, and Akt at Ser473 in human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Notably, lower concentrations of Ang2 (50-400 ng/ml) failed to produce notable effects. These results suggest that, like Ang1, Ang2 can act as an apoptosis survival factor for endothelial cells by activating the Tie2 receptor, PI3K, and Akt, and may thereby promote tumor angiogenesis.

title: Lipoxin a4 analogs attenuate induction of intestinal epithelial proinflammatory gene expression and reduce the severity of dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis.
text: The anti-inflammatory eicosanoid lipoxin A4 (LXA4), aspirin-triggered 15-epi-LXA4, and their stable analogs inhibit the secretion and attraction of neutrophils from intestinal epithelium by modulating cellular pro-inflammatory programs. In an effort to understand the mechanism of this inhibition, we studied global epithelial gene expression using cDNA microarrays. Pretreatment with LXA4 analog did not significantly affect the expression of over 7000 genes, but attenuated the induction of approximately 50% of the genes upregulated in response to the gastroenteritis-causing pathogen Salmonella typhimurium. A significant subset of these genes are regulated by NF-κB, suggesting that LXA4 analog is influencing the activity of this transcription factor. Nanomolar concentrations of LXA4 analog reduced NF-κB-mediated transcriptional activation in a LXA4 receptor-dependent manner and prevented induced degradation of IκBα. LXA4 analog did not affect earlier stimulus-induced signaling events that lead to IκBα degradation, such as S. typhimurium-induced epithelial Ca2+ mobilization or TNF-α-induced phosphorylation of IκBα. To validate these findings in vivo, we examined whether LXA4 analogs could affect intestinal inflammation in mice with DSS-induced inflammatory colitis. Oral administration of LXA4 analog (15-epi-16-para-fluoro-phenoxy-LXA4, 10 μg/day) significantly reduced weight loss, hematochezia, and mortality associated with DSS colitis. These findings indicate that LXA4 analog-mediated inhibition of pro-inflammatory gene expression via NF-κB pathway inhibition can be therapeutic for diseases characterized by mucosal inflammation.

title: Serum plant and other noncholesterol sterols, cholesterol metabolism and 22-year mortality among middle-aged men.
text: The objective of this study was to investigate the long-term prognostic value of noncholesterol sterols, including plant sterols, in middle-aged men at high risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) who were not taking statins. The study included 232 men with a mean age of 60 years, of whom 29% had a history of CVD or cancer, 3% had diabetes, and 20% had metabolic syndrome (MS). The study measured the levels of lathosterol, desmosterol, campesterol, sitosterol, and cholestanol in the serum of these men. The main outcome measure was total mortality, and the study found that higher levels of sitosterol were associated with lower mortality risk. In multivariable analyses, men in the highest tertile of sitosterol levels had a significantly lower mortality risk compared to those in the lowest tertile (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.30-0.87). However, other associations between noncholesterol sterols and mortality were not significantly different. The study suggests that higher levels of plant sterols in middle-aged men may be associated with lower long-term mortality risk, possibly reflecting an association between higher cholesterol synthesis/lower absorption and mortality.

title: Intracoronary autologous cardiac progenitor cell transfer in patients with hypoplastic left heart syndrome: the TICAP prospective phase 1 controlled trial.
text: RATIONALE: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is a life-threatening congenital heart defect that remains largely untreatable. Recent studies have shown promise in the use of autologous cardiosphere-derived cells (CDCs) intracoronary administration in improving ventricular function. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to assess the safety and feasibility of intracoronary CDC delivery in children with HLHS after staged surgical procedures. METHODS AND RESULTS: A total of 14 patients (aged 1.8±1.5 years) were prospectively assigned to receive intracoronary CDC infusion 33.4±8.1 days after staged procedures. The primary end point was to evaluate the safety and feasibility of the procedure, and the secondary end point was to assess the preliminary efficacy of CDC infusion in improving right ventricular ejection fraction. CDC manufacturing and intracoronary delivery were found to be feasible, with no serious adverse events reported during the 18-month follow-up period. Patients who received CDCs showed significant improvements in right ventricular ejection fractionfrom baseline to 3-month follow-up (46.9%±4.6% to 52.1%±2.4%; P=0.008). Compared to controls at 18 months, cardiac MRI analysis of CDC-treated patients showed a higher right ventricular ejection fraction (31.5%±6.8% vs 40.4%±7.6%; P=0.049), improved somatic growth (P=0.0005), reduced heart failure status (P=0.003), and lower incidence of coil occlusion for collaterals (P=0.007). CONCLUSIONS: Intracoronary CDC infusion in children with HLHS after staged surgery appears to be safe and feasible. Large-scale phase 2 trials are warranted to evaluate the potential benefits of improved cardiac function and long-term clinical outcomes. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: URL http://www.clinicaltrials.gov. Unique identifier: NCT01273857.

title: A Whole Brain Staining, Embedding, and Clearing Pipeline for Adult Zebrafish to Visualize Cell Proliferation and Morphology in 3-Dimensions
text:
Macro-imaging has made significant strides with the advent of innovative clearing methods and confocal microscopes equipped with lasers capable of penetrating deeper into tissue. This technological advancement allows for the visualization and modeling of entire organs' growth from birth or with manipulation, disease, or injury, providing new insights into development, tissue-wide signaling, and cell-to-cell interactions. The zebrafish (Danio rerio) has evolved from a primarily developmental model to a leading adult model of tissue regeneration, with its remarkable neurogenic and regenerative capacity receiving significant attention. However, there are limited tools to investigate the adult brain, particularly for visualizing changes in the entire brain in three dimensions (3D) under physiological, injured, or diseased conditions.
This manuscript presents a novel and efficient pipeline for labeling the entire adult zebrafish brain with the proliferative marker 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) and imaging it using optical projection tomography (OPT). Additionally, this method enables the imaging of GFP-reporter lines and cell-specific antibodies in the presence or absence of EdU. The small size of the adult zebrafish brain and the consistent availability of EdU labeling make this method accessible to most laboratories interested in understanding the vertebrate central nervous system in health and disease. Post-processing of OPT-imaged adult zebrafish brains injected with EdU reveals proliferative patterns and can be analyzed using IMARIS or FIJI/IMAGEJ software. This protocol will open up new avenues for comprehending systemic patterns of cell proliferation in the healthy and injured brain, brain-wide cellular interactions, stem cell niche development, and changes in brain morphology.

title: Single-Construct Polycistronic Doxycycline-Inducible Vectors Improve Direct Cardiac Reprogramming and Can Be Used to Identify the Critical Timing of Transgene Expression
text:
Direct reprogramming is a promising approach in regenerative medicine, involving the reprogramming of fibroblasts into cardiomyocyte-like cells (iCMs). However, the optimal timing of transgene expression and the underlying molecular mechanisms for cardiac reprogramming remain unclear.
Conventional Doxycycline (Dox)-inducible temporal transgene expression systems require the simultaneous transduction of two vectors (pLVX-rtTA/pLVX-cDNA) carrying the reverse tetracycline transactivator (rtTA) and the tetracycline response element (TRE)-controlled transgene, respectively, which can lead to inefficient cardiac reprogramming. To address this limitation, we developed a single-construct-based polycistronic Dox-inducible vector (pDox-cDNA) that expresses both the rtTA and TRE-controlled transgenes.
We used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), quantitative RT-PCR, and immunostaining to evaluate the efficiency of cardiac reprogramming using pDox-GMT. Our results showed that pDox-GMT increased cardiac reprogramming by three-fold compared to the conventional pLVX-rtTA/pLVX-GMT. After four weeks, pDox-GMT-induced iCMs expressed multiple cardiac genes, produced sarcomeric structures, and beat spontaneously.
Co-transduction of pDox-Hand2 with retroviral pMX-GMT further increased cardiac reprogramming three-fold. Temporal Dox administration studies revealed that Hand2 transgene expression is critical during the first two weeks of cardiac reprogramming. Microarray analysis confirmed that Hand2 represses cell cycle-promoting genes and enhances cardiac reprogramming.
Our findings suggest the development of an efficient temporal transgene expression system, which could be invaluable in the study of cardiac reprogramming. This system could potentially enable the efficient reprogramming of fibroblasts into functional cardiomyocytes, which could have significant implications for the treatment of heart disease.

title: Increasing microtubule acetylation rescues axonal transport and locomotor deficits caused by LRRK2 Roc-COR domain mutations
text: Genetic mutations in the leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) gene are the most prevalent cause of Parkinson's disease. LRRK2 is a multifunctional protein that regulates various cellular functions, including its ability to bind microtubules. However, the exact role of LRRK2 in mediating Parkinson's disease is unclear, particularly with regards to microtubule-based axonal transport. To investigate, we studied the effect of LRRK2 containing pathogenic Roc-COR domain mutations (R1441C, Y1699C) on microtubule dynamics in primary neurons and Drosophila. Our findings show that these mutations preferentially interact with deacetylated microtubules, leading to impaired axonal transport. In vitro, increasing microtubule acetylation using deacetylase inhibitors or the tubulin acetylase αTAT1 disrupts the association of mutant LRRK2 with microtubules, and restores axonal transport. Similarly, in vivo knockdown of the deacetylases HDAC6 and Sirt2, or administration of the deacetylase inhibitor trichostatin A (TSA), rescues both axonal transport and locomotor behavior. These results provide a novel mechanism for Parkinson's disease and suggest a potential therapeutic approach for intervention.

title: G1 arrest and differentiation can occur independently of Rb family function
text: The capacity of progenitor cells to exit the cell cycle is crucial for proper embryonic development and tissue homeostasis, yet the mechanisms controlling cell cycle exit remain poorly understood. To investigate the role of the retinoblastoma (Rb) protein and its relatives p107 and p130 in G0/G1 arrest and differentiation in mammalian cells, we conducted experiments using Rb family triple knockout (TKO) mouse embryos. Our findings revealed that TKO mouse embryos survive until days 9-11 of gestation, with some cells, including those in epithelial and neural lineages, able to exit the cell cycle in G0/G1 and differentiate in teratomas and in vitro culture. This capacity of TKO cells to enter G0/G1 mode is associated with the repression of key E2F target genes. Our findings challenge the notion that G1 arrest is solely dependent on Rb family members, demonstrating the robustness of cell cycle regulatory networks during differentiation and highlighting the potential for identifying alternative pathways to restrict the proliferation of cancer cells bearing mutations in the Rb pathway.

title: Induction of ectopic eyes by targeted expression of the eyeless gene in Drosophila.
text: The Drosophila gene "eyeless" (ey) encodes a transcription factor with both a paired domain and a homeodomain. It shares significant sequence identity with the mouse "Small eye" (Pax-6) gene and the human "Aniridia" gene, which are involved in eye development. These genes exhibit conserved splicing patterns and expression profiles during nervous system and eye development. Mutations in either the insect or mammalian genes result in a reduced or absent eye structure, indicating that ey plays a critical role in eye morphogenesis. By expressing the ey complementary DNA in specific imaginal disc primordia of Drosophila, ectopic eye structures were induced on the wings, legs, and antennae. The ectopic eyes consisted of fully differentiated ommatidia with a complete set of photoreceptor cells, and were morphologically normal. These findings support the notion that ey is the master control gene for eye morphogenesis, as it is present in a wide range of metazoans, including vertebrates, ascidians, insects, cephalopods, and nemerteans.

title: mir-1-mediated paracrine effect of cancer-associated fibroblasts on lung cancer cell proliferation and chemoresistance.
text:
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with a dismal 15% 5-year survival rate. Of all lung cancer cases, nearly 80% are non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) have been found to be prevalent in a significant number of NSCLCs, and they play a crucial role in promoting tumor progression, metastasis, and resistance to treatment through paracrine signaling in various solid tumors.
In our study, we first isolated CAFs from patient tissues and demonstrated that they enhance cell proliferation and chemoresistance to cisplatin in lung cancer cell lines A549 and 95D through paracrine mechanisms. We then detected higher levels of stromal cell-derived factor 1 (SDF-1) in CAFs compared to normal fibroblasts (NFs) using ELISA and quantitative PCR. SDF-1 promotes lung cancer cell proliferation and drug resistance by activating the CXCR4-mediated signaling pathway, which involves NF-κB and Bcl-xL. Additionally, we found that the expression of SDF-1 in CAFs is negatively regulated by microRNA mir-1 through microRNA overexpression and quantitative PCR.
Our findings provide insight into the mechanisms of CAFs in lung cancer, highlighting their potential as a therapeutic target in cancer treatment.

title: Genome-wide association analyses in East Asians identify new susceptibility loci for colorectal cancer
text: To discover new genetic factors for colorectal cancer (CRC), we conducted a comprehensive genome-wide association study in individuals of East Asian descent. By analyzing genome-wide data from 2,098 cases and 5,749 controls, we identified 64 promising single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that were then replicated in an independent set of samples, including up to 5,358 cases and 5,922 controls. Our analysis revealed four SNPs with association P values less than 10(-7) to 10(-10) in the combined analysis of all East Asian samples. Of these, three were successfully replicated in a study of 26,060 individuals of European descent, with combined P values of 1.22 × 10(-10) for rs647161 (5q31.1), 6.64 × 10(-9) for rs2423279 (20p12.3), and 3.06 × 10(-8) for rs10774214 (12p13.32 near the CCND2 gene). This study identified three new CRC susceptibility loci and further illuminated the genetic and biological underpinnings of CRC.

title: Long non-coding RNAs as novel players in β cell function and type 1 diabetes
text:
Here is a possible recreation of the given text with some minor changes to improve readability:
BACKGROUND: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are a subset of non-coding RNAs that have emerged as key regulators of gene expression in various pathological conditions. LncRNAs exhibit remarkable versatility and exercise their functions through interactions with RNA, DNA, or proteins. Growing evidence from multiple studies has highlighted the role of lncRNAs in autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, including type 1 diabetes (T1D). This review focuses on the emerging functions of lncRNAs in immune and islet β cell function, as well as some of the challenges and opportunities in understanding the pathogenesis of T1D and its complications. CONCLUSION: We emphasize that lncRNAs within T1D-associated regions, in conjunction with regulatory variants and enhancer clusters, orchestrate chromatin remodeling in β cells, thereby serving as both cis- and trans-regulatory determinants of islet cell transcriptional programs.

title: Costs of the COPD. Differences between intensive care unit and respiratory intermediate care unit.
text:
ABSTRACT:
To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of respiratory intermediate care units (RICUs) compared to intensive care units (ICUs) for patients with exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
METHODS: A multi-centre, prospective, bottom-up cost study was conducted in 15 ICUs and 6 RICUs. Consecutively admitted COPD patients staying more than 48 hours were enrolled, with exclusions for immune-deficiency or stroke. Standardisation of ICU patients to the RICU distribution of reasons for admission and vasoactive drug usage on admission resulted in 60 ICU patients and 65 RICU patients from a initially recruited sample of 164. Daily resource consumption and its associated costs were recorded and analysed.
RESULTS: The total cost per patient was significantly lower in RICUs compared to ICUs (754 vs. 1507 Euro; P < 0.0001). In all categories except drugs and nutrition, RICUs were found to be less costly. When comparing dead and surviving patients, significant differences in disease severity were observed between ICUs and RICUs, while no such differences were seen among surviving patients.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that some COPD patients with less severe respiratory failure could be effectively and less costly treated in RICUs.

title: eRNAs are required for p53-dependent enhancer activity and gene transcription.
text: Using genome-wide chromatin-binding profiles, we have discovered that the tumor suppressor protein p53 not only binds to genes involved in cell proliferation and survival, but also to regions located distant from any known p53 target genes. Interestingly, many of these regions possess conserved p53-binding sites and all the hallmarks of enhancer regions. We have shown that these p53-bound enhancer regions (p53BERs) harbor enhancer activity and interact intra-chromosomally with multiple neighboring genes to regulate long-distance p53-dependent transcription. Moreover, p53BERs produce p53-dependent enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) that are necessary for efficient transcriptional enhancement of interacting target genes and induction of a p53-dependent cell cycle arrest. Our findings demonstrate that p53 has the capacity to regulate multiple genes from a single genomic binding site, and eRNA production from p53BERs is essential for efficient p53 transcription enhancement.

title: Induction of pluripotent stem cells from mouse embryonic fibroblasts by Oct4 and Klf4 with small-molecule compounds.
text: Somatic cells can be converted into pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) using a combination of four transcription factors, Oct4/Sox2/Klf4/c-Myc or Oct4/Sox2/Nanog/LIN28. This enables the generation of patient-specific cells for various therapeutic and research applications. However, limitations exist for this approach, including low efficiency and concerns about viral genome integration. Recently, it has been shown that neural progenitor cells (NPCs) transduced with Oct4/Klf4 can be reprogrammed into iPSCs, despite expressing endogenous Sox2. In this study, we identified a small-molecule combination, BIX-01294 and BayK8644, which improves the reprogramming of Oct4/Klf4-transduced mouse embryonic fibroblasts, even in the absence of endogenous Sox2. This work demonstrates that small molecules identified through a phenotypic screen can compensate for the need for viral transduction of critical factors, such as Sox2, and enhance reprogramming efficiency.

title: Vps22/EAP30 in ESCRT-II mediates endosomal sorting of growth factor and chemokine receptors destined for lysosomal degradation.
text: The ubiquitin-binding protein Hrs and the endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT)-I and ESCRT-III are involved in the efficient termination of signaling by sorting endocytosed and ubiquitinated receptors to lysosomes for degradation. In this study, we investigated the role of the ESCRT-II subunit Vps22/EAP30 in the degradative protein sorting of ubiquitinated receptors. Vps22 was found to be transiently expressed in endosomes containing endocytosed epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFRs) as well as Hrs and ESCRT-I and ESCRT-III in HeLa cells. Depletion of Vps22 using small interfering RNA resulted in a significant reduction in the degradation of EGFR and its ligand epidermal growth factor (EGF), as well as the chemokine receptor CXCR4. EGFR accumulated on the limiting membranes of early endosomes and aberrantly small multivesicular bodies in Vps22-depleted cells. Furthermore, phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of extracellular-signal-regulated kinase 1/2 downstream of the EGF-activated receptor were sustained by depletion of Hrs or the ESCRT-I subunit Tsg101, but not when Vps22 was depleted. These findings suggest an important role for Vps22 in ligand-induced EGFR and CXCR4 turnover, and indicate that termination of EGF signaling occurs prior to ESCRT-II engagement.

title: XPG stabilizes TFIIH, allowing transactivation of nuclear receptors: implications for Cockayne syndrome in XP-G/CS patients.
text: Mutations in the human XPG gene are known to underlie an inherited photosensitive disorder, xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), which often presents in conjunction with Cockayne syndrome (XP-G/CS). While the clinical features of CS in XP-G/CS patients are difficult to fully comprehend as a result of a sole defect in nucleotide excision repair (NER), our findings suggest that XPG plays a crucial role in maintaining the stability of transcription and NER-related complexes. Specifically, we uncovered that XPG forms a stable association with TFIIH, an essential component of transcription and NER, and that mutations in XPG among XP-G/CS patient cells disrupt this association, resulting in the dissociation of other factors, including CAK and XPD, from the core TFIIH complex. As a consequence, the phosphorylation and transactivation of key nuclear receptors are impaired in XP-G/CS patient cells and in xpg(-/-) mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), but can be restored through expression of wild-type XPG. These findings offer valuable insights into the functional interplay of XPG with TFIIH and its crucial role in regulating gene expression and elucidate some of the clinical manifestations encountered in XP-G/CS patients.

title: Metabolic cycling in single yeast cells from unsynchronized steady-state populations limited on glucose or phosphate.
text: Oscillations in the expression of a large proportion of yeast genes are linked to the "metabolic cycle," which is commonly observed only in continuous cultures of yeast that have not been starved. To investigate whether these oscillations occur in individual cells from non-synchronized cultures growing exponentially in chemostats, we used fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to examine mRNA expression in individual cells. By analyzing gene-expression data from synchronized cultures, we predicted that pairs of mRNAs from unsynchronized cells would co-appear at the same time. Our quantitative analysis of the FISH results reveals that individual cells growing slowly due to limited glucose or phosphate show the predicted oscillations, indicating that the yeast metabolic cycle is an inherent property of yeast metabolism and not dependent on either synchronization or limitation of growth by the carbon source.

title: in polyploid species
text: We created the Yeast Gene Order Browser (YGOB, http://wolfe.gen.tcd.ie/ygob) to facilitate visual comparisons and computational analyses of synteny relationships among yeast species. Our dataset, currently covering seven species, was manually curated using a combination of sequence similarity and genomic context (synteny) to identify homologous genes. We reconciled different laboratories' lists of paralogous Saccharomyces cerevisiae gene pairs formed through genome duplication (ohnologs) and present near-exhaustive lists of the ohnolog pairs retained in S. cerevisiae (551, including 22 previously unidentified), Saccharomyces castellii (599), and Candida glabrata (404).

title: Immune complex relay by subcapsular sinus macrophages and non-cognate B cells drives antibody affinity maturation
text: Subcapsular sinus (SCS) macrophages serve as potent antigen-presenting cells, capturing antigens from the lymph and presenting them intact for B cell encounter and follicular delivery. However, the properties of SCS macrophages were previously understudied. We now demonstrate that SCS macrophage development is dependent on lymphotoxin-alpha1beta2, and these cells exhibit diminished lysosomal enzyme expression and retain opsonized antigens on their surface. Using intravital imaging, we observed immune complexes migrating along macrophage processes into the follicle. Furthermore, non-cognate B cells play a crucial role in transporting opsonized antigens from the subcapsular region to the germinal center, and impairment of this transport process hinders affinity maturation. Therefore, we have uncovered the unique function of SCS macrophages as specialized antigen-presenting cells at the nexus of an antigen transport chain, promoting humoral immunity.

title: Promoter decoding of transcription factor dynamics involves a trade-off between noise and control of gene expression
text: The activity of numerous transcription factors (TFs) carries information about upstream signaling events, yet the mechanisms by which downstream genes interpret these dynamics remain poorly understood. To investigate the principles underlying gene expression regulation, we employed microfluidics to control the dynamics of Msn2, a TF in budding yeast, and elucidated how different promoters decipher the changing activities of Msn2 in individual cells. By integrating modeling and experimental approaches, we categorized promoters based on their signal processing properties and uncovered that multiple, distinct gene expression programs can be encoded in the dynamics of Msn2. Our findings revealed that both oscillatory TF dynamics and slow promoter kinetics contribute to increased gene expression noise. Moreover, we found that the timescale of promoter activation is closely related to nucleosome remodeling, suggesting a trade-off between the amount of information that can be encoded in TF dynamics and the reliability of promoter interpretation. Our results implicate a fundamental limitation in the amount of information that can be encoded in TF dynamics, which in turn affects the accuracy of promoter interpretation and gene expression control.

title: GaAs nanopillar-array solar cells employing in situ surface passivation
text: Arrays of III-V direct-bandgap semiconductor nanopillars hold great promise for photovoltaic applications due to their inherent high optical absorption coefficients and minimized reflectance, which arises from light trapping and efficient charge collection in the radial direction. Furthermore, these nanopillars can be synthesized on low-cost platforms, making them an attractive option for high-efficiency photovoltaics. However, the increased surface area of the nanopillars leads to surface states that hinder the power conversion efficiency. To overcome this challenge, we report the first demonstration of GaAs nanopillar-array photovoltaics utilizing epitaxial passivation with air mass 1.5 global power conversion efficiencies of 6.63%. To alleviate surface-state effects, high-bandgap epitaxial InGaP shells are grown in situ and cap the radial p-n junctions. Under illumination, the photovoltaic devices exhibit open-circuit voltages of 0.44 V, short-circuit current densities of 24.3 mA cm(-2), and fill factors of 62% with high external quantum efficiencies exceeding 70% across the spectral range of interest. A novel titanium/indium tin oxide annealed alloy is employed as a transparent ohmic anode.

title: Roles of histone acetylation and chromatin remodeling factor in a meiotic recombination hotspot.
text: Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling factors (ADCRs) play a crucial role in regulating gene expression by modifying local chromatin structure. In Schizosaccharomyces pombe, the activation of the ade6-M26 recombination hotspot is mediated by a cAMP responsive element (CRE)-like sequence, M26, and a heterodimeric ATF/CREB transcription factor, Atf1.Pcr1. Chromatin remodeling occurs meiotically around M26. To investigate the role of HATs and ADCRs in chromatin remodeling at M26, we examined the histone modifications H3 and H4 nearby. We found that histones H3 and H4 around M26 were hyperacetylated in an M26- and Atf1-dependent manner early in meiosis. Our results suggest that the S. pombe homolog of Gcn5p, SpGcn5, is required for the majority of histone H3 acetylation around M26 in vivo. Deletion of gcn5+ resulted in a significant delay in chromatin remodeling but only a partial reduction of M26 meiotic recombination frequency. Unexpectedly, the deletion of the ADCR homolog snf22+ and the double deletion of snf22+ gcn5+ abolished chromatin remodeling and resulted in a significant reduction of meiotic recombination around M26. These findings indicate that HATs and ADCRs cooperate to alter local chromatin structure in a site-specific manner, which is essential for the activation of meiotic recombination at M26.

title: The Somatic Genomic Landscape of Glioblastoma
text: We present a comprehensive characterization of the genetic landscape of glioblastoma (GBM) tumors, analyzing over 500 tumors using a multidimensional approach. Our study uncovers novel mutated genes and complex rearrangements of key receptors, such as EGFR and PDGFRA. TERT promoter mutations are found to correlate with elevated gene expression, supporting a role in telomerase reactivation. Correlative analyses confirm that the proneural subtype confers a survival advantage due to the G-CIMP phenotype, and MGMT DNA methylation may serve as a predictive biomarker for treatment response in classical subtype GBM. By integrating genomic and proteomic data, our findings challenge the idea of targeting a pathway rather than the underlying target itself. These insights will facilitate the identification of potential therapeutic and diagnostic targets, validate existing observations, and generate new hypotheses to advance our understanding of this deadly disease.

title: Radioiodine treatment of multinodular non-toxic goitre.
text: The objective of this study is to investigate the long-term effects of radioactive iodine on thyroid function and size in patients with non-toxic multinodular goitre. The study design involves selecting consecutive patients with multinodular non-toxic goitre and following them for a minimum of 12 months (median 48 months) after receiving a single dose of radioactive iodine treatment, with a median dose of 3.7 MBq/g thyroid tissue corrected to a 100% uptake of iodine-131 in 24 hours. A total of 69 patients with locally compressive or cosmetically inconvenient goitres were included in the study, of whom 56 received a single dose of 131I, 12 received two doses, and one received four doses. The main outcome measurements include standard thyroid function variables and ultrasonically determined thyroid volume before and after treatment, assessed at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 months, and then annually. The results show that in 45 patients treated with a single dose of 131I, the median thyroid volume was reduced from 73 (interquartile range 50-106) ml to 29 (23-48) ml at 24 months in the 39 patients for whom this was measured during follow-up. The median reduction was 40 (22-48) ml (60% reduction, p < 0.0001), with half of the reduction occurring within three months. Patients treated with two doses and those who developed hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism had a significant reduction in thyroid volume. Eleven patients developed hypothyroidism (cumulative five-year risk 22%, 95% confidence interval 4.8% to 38.4%). Side effects were few, with three cases of hyperthyroidism and two cases of radiation thyroiditis occurring. Only one patient was dissatisfied with the results, and she was referred for operation six months after treatment. Overall, the study concludes that the use of radioactive iodine is an attractive alternative to surgery in selected cases of non-toxic multinodular goitre, as it results in a substantial reduction in thyroid volume with a low incidence of hypothyroidism and few side effects.

title: Alterations in microRNA-124 and AMPA receptors contribute to social behavioral deficits in frontotemporal dementia
text: Neurodegenerative diseases, such as frontotemporal dementia (FTD), are often characterized by behavioral abnormalities, yet the underlying anatomical and molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we demonstrate that forebrain-specific expression of FTD-associated mutant CHMP2B in mice leads to several age-dependent neurodegenerative changes, including social behavioral impairments. These deficits are accompanied by changes in the composition of AMPA receptors (AMPARs), specifically an imbalance between Ca(2+)-permeable and Ca(2+)-impermeable AMPARs. We found that the abundance of the brain-enriched microRNA miR-124, which regulates the expression of AMPAR subunits, is significantly decreased in the superficial layers of the cerebral cortex of mice expressing the mutant CHMP2B. Similarly, we observed changes in miR-124 and AMPAR levels in the frontal cortex and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons from subjects with behavioral variant FTD. Intriguingly, ectopic miR-124 expression in the medial prefrontal cortex of mutant mice decreased AMPAR levels and partially rescued behavioral deficits. Moreover, knockdown of the AMPAR subunit Gria2 also alleviated social impairments. Our findings suggest a previously unappreciated mechanism involving miR-124 and AMPARs in the regulation of social behavior in FTD, and provide a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of these debilitating diseases.

title: Activated AMPK boosts the Nrf2/HO-1 signaling axis—A role for the unfolded protein response
text: In light of the emerging interplay between redox and metabolic signaling pathways, we investigated the potential crosstalk between nuclear factor E2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) and AMP-activated kinase (AMPK), central regulators of cellular redox and energy balance, respectively. Utilizing xanthohumol (XN) as an activator of both the AMPK and Nrf2 signaling pathways, we demonstrate that AMPK exerts a positive influence on Nrf2/heme oxygenase (HO)-1 signaling in mouse embryonic fibroblasts. Genetic ablation and pharmacological inhibition of AMPK blunt Nrf2-dependent HO-1 expression by XN at the mRNA level. XN activates AMPK via interference with mitochondrial function and activation of liver kinase B1 as an upstream AMPK kinase. The subsequent AMPK-mediated enhancement of the Nrf2/HO-1 response does not depend on inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin, inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase 3β, or altered abundance of Nrf2 (total and nuclear). However, we identified reduced endoplasmic reticulum stress as a step in the AMPK-augmented Nrf2/HO-1 response. Overall, our findings shed light on the previously incompletely understood cross talk between the LKB1/AMPK and the Nrf2/HO-1 axis, revealing for the first time the involvement of the unfolded protein response as an additional player and suggesting tight cooperation between signaling pathways controlling cellular redox, energy, or protein homeostasis.

title: The IDEAL recommendations and urological innovation
text:
Like many fields of surgery, Urology has encountered challenges in harmonizing research processes for assessing new interventions with the principles of Evidence-Based Medicine. This article elaborates on the IDEAL framework and recommendations and demonstrates how they may influence the evaluation of current contentious urological procedures. From an inside perspective, the article provides an overview of the IDEAL Working Group's efforts to date, with a specific focus on the field of Urology.
It is crucial to recognize that there are significant differences between drugs and interventions in the development process of new treatments. As the conventional framework for evaluating new treatments is largely based on the former, applying the same approach to surgical innovations can lead to significant challenges. The IDEAL framework offers a comprehensive description of the innovation and development process for surgical trials, and its associated recommendations propose an alternative approach to study design that is better suited to the unique challenges of new surgical techniques.
In essence, the IDEAL framework has the potential to transform the manner in which urologists conduct clinical research, providing a new and more effective approach to evaluating new treatments in the field.

title: Prolonged conservative care versus early surgery in patients with sciatica caused by lumbar disc herniation: two year results of a randomised controlled trial.
text:
Objective: To compare the effects of early lumbar disc surgery and prolonged conservative care on patients with sciatica over a two-year follow-up period.
Design: Randomized controlled trial
Setting: Nine hospitals in the Netherlands
Participants: 283 patients with sciatica lasting 6-12 weeks.
Interventions: Early surgery or continued conservative treatment, with delayed surgery if necessary.
Main Outcome Measures: Roland Disability Questionnaire scores for sciatica, Visual Analogue Scale scores for leg pain, and Likert Self-Rating Scale scores for global perceived recovery.
Results: Of the 141 patients assigned to early surgery, 125 (89%) underwent microdiscectomy. Of the 142 patients assigned to conservative treatment, 62 (44%) eventually required surgery, seven in the second year of follow-up. There was no significant overall difference between treatment arms in disability scores during the first two years (p=0.25). Improvement in leg pain was faster for patients randomized to early surgery, with a significant difference between the areas under the curves over two years (p=0.05). However, this short-term benefit of early surgery was no longer significant by six months and continued to narrow between six months and 24 months. Patient satisfaction decreased slightly between one and two years for both groups. At two years, 20% of all patients reported an unsatisfactory outcome.
Conclusion: Early lumbar disc surgery provided more rapid relief of sciatica compared to prolonged conservative care, but outcomes were similar by one year and did not change during the second year.
Trial Registry: ISRCT No 26872154.

title: Human papillomavirus testing for the detection of high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cancer: final results of the POBASCAM randomised controlled trial.
text:
The article investigates the impact of human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing on cervical cancer screening. The study randomly assigned women aged 29-56 years participating in the Dutch cervical screening program to receive HPV DNA and cytology co-testing or cytology testing alone. The primary endpoint was the number of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade 3 or worse detected.
The results show that HPV DNA testing in the first screen significantly decreased the detection of CIN grade 3 or worse, CIN grade 2 or worse, and cervical cancer in the second screen. In particular, the study found that implementation of HPV DNA testing leads to earlier detection of clinically relevant CIN grade 2 or worse, which when adequately treated, improves protection against CIN grade 3 or worse and cervical cancer. Early detection of high-grade cervical legions caused by HPV16 was a major component of this benefit. The study lends support to the use of HPV DNA testing for all women aged 29 years and older.
The study had some limitations, including a relatively short follow-up period and the inability to draw conclusions about the long-term benefits of HPV DNA testing. However, the study provides valuable insights into the impact of HPV DNA testing on cervical cancer screening and highlights the potential benefits of using this technology in cervical cancer screening programs.

title: Epigenetic therapy activates type I interferon signaling in murine ovarian cancer to reduce immunosuppression and tumor burden.
text: Ovarian cancer is the deadliest of all gynecological cancers, and there is an urgent need for new treatments. Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is characterized by an immunosuppressive environment, and ovarian cancer cells have shown limited responses to immunotherapies. In a mouse model of EOC, we discovered that clinically relevant doses of DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase inhibitors (DNMTi and HDACi, respectively) reduce the immunosuppressive microenvironment through type I interferon signaling, improving the response to immune checkpoint therapy. These findings reveal that the type I interferon response is crucial for the in vivo antitumor effects of DNMTi, specifically the drug 5-azacytidine (AZA). AZA increases the numbers of CD45+ immune cells, active CD8+ T and NK cells in the tumor microenvironment, reduces tumor burden, and extends survival. AZA also enhances viral defense gene expression in both tumor and immune cells and reduces the percentage of macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells in the tumor microenvironment. Adding an HDACi to AZA further modulates the immune microenvironment by increasing T and NK cell activation and reducing macrophages, leading to improved antitumor effects. Finally, a triple combination of DNMTi/HDACi plus the immune checkpoint inhibitor α-PD-1 provides the most significant antitumor effect and longest overall survival, which may be a strong candidate for future clinical trials in ovarian cancer.

title: IGF2 is parentally imprinted during human embryogenesis and in the Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome
text: The phenomenon of parental imprinting, where one parental allele of a subset of chromosomal genes is preferentially expressed, has been observed only in mice ... We have now discovered, using sequence polymorphisms in exon nine of the human insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) gene, that only the paternally inherited allele is active in embryonic and extra-embryonic cells from first trimester pregnancies. Furthermore, only the paternal allele is expressed in tissues from an individual who had Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, suggesting that the parental imprinting of IGF2 is conserved from mice to humans and has important implications for the development of this syndrome.

title: Safety and reliability of Radio Frequency Identification Devices in Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Computed Tomography
text:
Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) devices are increasingly important for patient safety in hospitals. This study aimed to determine the impact of RFID devices on patient safety, data reliability, and signal loss during Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT) scans.
Methods: Sixty RFID tags of the type I-Code SLI, 13.56 MHz, ISO 18000-3.1 were tested: Thirty type 1, an RFID tag with a 76 x 45 mm aluminum-etched antenna, and thirty type 2, a tag with a 31 x 14 mm copper-etched antenna. Signal loss, material movement, and heat tests were conducted in a 1.5 T and a 3 T MR system. Additional tests were performed on the tags during CT scanning to ensure data integrity. Standardized function tests were conducted with all transponders before and after all imaging studies.
Results: None of the RFID tags experienced memory loss or data alteration after MRI and CT scanning. Heating (maximum of 3.6 degrees C) and device movement (less than 1 N/kg) had no significant impact on the RFID tags. However, signal loss (artifacts 2-4 mm) impaired the interpretability of MR images when superficial structures, such as skin, subcutaneous tissues, or tendons, were assessed.
Conclusions: Patients wearing RFID wristbands are safe in 1.5 T and 3 T MR scanners using normal operation modes for RF fields. These findings are specific to the RFID tags tested in this study.

title: LXR-Dependent Gene Expression Is Important for Macrophage Survival and the Innate Immune Response
text: The liver X receptors (LXRs) are nuclear receptors that play a crucial role in regulating lipid metabolism. Recent research has revealed, however, that LXR signaling not only impacts lipid metabolism but also regulates antimicrobial responses within the body. Mice lacking LXRs are particularly susceptible to infection with the intracellular bacteria Listeria monocytogenes (LM), and this susceptibility is largely due to alterations in macrophage function. By examining bone marrow transplant studies, researchers have found that LXR-null macrophages undergo accelerated apoptosis when challenged with LM and exhibit defective bacterial clearance in vivo. These defects, in turn, are linked to a lack of regulation of the antiapoptotic factor SPalpha, which is directly targeted by LXRalpha. Fascinatingly, the expression of LXRalpha or SPalpha in macrophages can inhibit apoptosis in the setting of LM infection, revealing an unexpected role for LXR-dependent gene expression in innate immunity. These findings further suggest that common nuclear receptor pathways may mediate macrophage responses to modified lipoproteins and intracellular pathogens, opening up new avenues for research into the immune system.

title: Alterations on peripheral B cell subsets following an acute uncomplicated clinical malaria infection in children
text:
The impact of Plasmodium falciparum on B-cell homeostasis has not been thoroughly explored. This study aimed to investigate whether a bout of acute malaria in young children results in changes to the peripheral B-cell phenotype.
Methods:
We employed flow-cytofluorimetric analysis to evaluate the B-cell phenotypes in the peripheral blood of children aged 2-5 years during an episode of acute uncomplicated clinical malaria and four weeks post-recovery, as well as in healthy age-matched controls.
Results:
We found a significant decrease in CD19+ B lymphocytes during acute malaria. Characterization of the CD19+ B cell subsets in the peripheral blood based on expression of IgD and CD38 revealed a significant decrease in the numbers of naive 1 CD38-IgD+ B cells, while there was an increase in CD38+IgD- memory 3 B cells during acute malaria. Our analysis of the peripheral B cell phenotype also revealed an expansion of transitional CD10+CD19+ B cells in children following an episode of acute malaria, with up to 25% of the total CD19+ B cell pool residing in this subset.
Conclusion:
Our findings demonstrate significant disruptions in B-cell homeostasis in children experiencing an episode of acute uncomplicated clinical malaria.

title: SETD2: an epigenetic modifier with tumor suppressor functionality
text:
In the last decade, significant progress has been made in understanding the epigenetic machinery that regulates gene expression. Recent discoveries have shown that genetic alterations in multiple epigenetic modifier proteins are linked to various types of cancer. Moreover, targeting the epigenome has emerged as a promising strategy to treat cancer patients. Recent studies have identified the first drugs that specifically target SETD2-negative tumors. In this review, we delve into the structural characteristics and functional roles of Set domain-containing protein 2 (SETD2), a histone modifier that has only recently been associated with cancer development.
We begin by exploring the structural features of SETD2 and itsfunction in different organisms, including yeast, Drosophila, Caenorhabditis elegans, mice, and humans. SETD2 is now widely recognized as the sole human gene responsible for trimethylating lysine 36 of histone H3 (H3K36). The reader proteins that determine the impact of this histone modification by recruiting protein complexes to carry out specific processes, including transcription elongation, RNA processing, and DNA repair.
Finally, we discuss the prevalence of SETD2 inactivating mutations in cancer, with the highest frequency observed in clear cell Renal Cell Cancer, and speculate on how this might contribute to tumor development.

title: Updated energy budgets for neural computation in the neocortex and cerebellum.
text:
According to the text, the brain's energy supply determines its ability to process information, and generates signals for functional imaging. Previous estimates of energy expenditure on neural computation in the grey matter of the cerebral and cerebellar cortex were made, but recently, it has been discovered that action potentials in mammalian neurons are more energy efficient than previously thought. Therefore, this paper provides revised estimates of energy expenditure on neural computation in simple and detailed models of the cerebral and cerebellar cortex.
In the cerebral cortex, most energy (50%) is used on postsynaptic glutamate receptors, 21% on action potentials, 20% on resting potentials, 5% on presynaptic transmitter release, and 4% on transmitter recycling. In contrast, in the cerebellar cortex, excitatory neurons use 75% of the energy, while inhibitory neurons use 25%. The majority of energy use in the cerebellar cortex is on the maintenance of resting potentials (54%) and postsynaptic receptors (22%), while action potentials account for only 17% of energy use.

title: Plasma homocysteine is a risk factor for recurrent vascular events in young patients with an ischaemic stroke or TIA
text:
For young patients with an ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), it is often the case that they have no known vascular risk factors. However, hyperhomocysteinaemia, or elevated levels of the amino acid homocysteine in the blood, has been identified as a potential risk factor for stroke in elderly patients. While its role in the prognosis of young ischemic stroke and TIA patients is still uncertain, we set out to investigate the potential impact of homocysteine levels on the risk of recurrent vascular events in this age group.
Our study included 161 consecutive patients aged 18-45 who had suffered a recent cerebral infarction or TIA. We retrospectively collected data on the patients' primary event and homocysteine levels from hospital records, and contacted general practitioners and patients by phone to gather information on vascular events and medication use during the follow-up period. Vascular events included cerebral infarction, TIA, pulmonary embolism, venous thrombosis, myocardial infarction, and peripheral arterial disease.
Using a Kaplan-Meier curve, we observed a dose-effect relationship between event-free survival time and the patients' homocysteine levels, with a log rank statistic of 5.91 and a p-value of 0.05. Adjusting for homocysteine-lowering treatment, we found that the Cox hazard ratio was 1.7 (95% CI, 1.1-2.8) for any vascular outcome event, 1.9 (95% CI, 1.1-3.0) for arterial outcome events, and 1.8 (95% CI, 1.1-2.9) for cerebral outcome events. Despite our relatively small number of outcome events, we found a significant association between homocysteine levels and the risk of recurrent vascular events in young patients with ischemic stroke or TIA. This association is of the same magnitude as in elderly patients, highlighting the potential importance of homocysteine levels in young patients as well.

title: LDL inhibits the mediation of cholesterol efflux from macrophage foam cells by apoA-I-containing lipoproteins. A putative mechanism for foam cell formation.
text: Although the accumulation of cholesterol in macrophages is an initial step in atherogenesis, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), a major risk factor for atherosclerosis, does not directly promote cholesterol accumulation in macrophages in its native form. On the other hand, apolipoprotein (apo) A-I-containing lipoprotein can remove cholesterol from cholesterol-loaded macrophages (foam cells) and prevent cholesterol from accumulating in the cells. In this study, we examined the effect of LDL on cholesterol removal by two species of apoA-I-containing lipoproteins, one containing only apoA-I (LpA-I) and the other containing apoA-I and apoA-II (LpA-I/A-II). When foam cells were incubated with LpA-I or LpA-I/A-II, the cellular cholesterol mass was reduced. However, when LDL was added, the cholesterol-reducing capacities of these lipoproteins were dose-dependently inhibited by LDL. Interestingly, LpA-I and LpA-I/A-II removed free cholesterol preferentially from LDL rather than from the plasma membrane of foam cells. Moreover, a fair amount of cellular cholesterol was directly moved to LDL rather than to LpA-I or LpA-I/A-II. The cellular cholesterol that moved to LDL was completely compensated for by the cholesterol influx from LDL to foam cells. Consequently, net cholesterol efflux (a combination of influx and efflux) from foam cells was inhibited by LDL. These findings lead us to conclude that LDL may accelerate foam cell formation by inhibiting cholesterol removal from the cells and that elevated levels of plasma LDL may become a risk factor for atherosclerosis by inhibiting the function of LpA-I and LpA-I/A-II at the cellular level.

title: Sugar-sweetened beverages, weight gain, and incidence of type 2 diabetes in young and middle-aged women.
text: CONTEXT Sugary beverages like soft drinks and fruit punch contain large amounts of quickly digestible sugars, which may contribute to weight gain and a higher risk of type 2 diabetes in adults. However, these associations have been understudied in women. OBJECTIVE To investigate the connection between consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages and weight change, as well as the risk of developing type 2 diabetes in women. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS Prospective cohort analyses conducted between 1991 and 1999 among 91,249 women in the Nurses' Health Study II. The diabetes analysis included 741 women who developed type 2 diabetes during 716,300 person-years of follow-up. The weight change analysis included 51,603 women who had complete dietary information and body weight data from 1991, 1995, and 1999. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES Weight gain and the incidence of type 2 diabetes. RESULTS Women with consistent consumption patterns did not experience any difference in weight gain, but those who increased their consumption of sugar-sweetened soft drinks from 1 or fewer drinks per week to 1 or more drinks per day experienced the highest weight gain over a 4-year period (4.69 kg for 1991-1995 and 4.20 kg for 1995-1999) compared to those who decreased their consumption (1.34 and 0.15 kg for the two periods, respectively). Increased consumption of fruit punch was also associated with greater weight gain compared to decreased consumption. After adjusting for potential confounding factors, women who consumed 1 or more sugar-sweetened soft drinks per day had a relative risk of type 2 diabetes of 1.83 (95% CI, 1.42-2.36; P <.001 for trend), compared to those who consumed less than 1 of these beverages per month. Similarly, consumption of fruit punch was associated with an increased diabetes risk (RR for > or =1 drink per day compared to <1 drink per month, 2.00; 95% CI, 1.33-3.03; P =.001). CONCLUSION The consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages is associated with a greater magnitude of weight gain and an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes in women, possibly due to providing excessive calories and rapid absorption of sugars.

title: Pancreatic stellate cells: partners in crime with pancreatic cancer cells.
text: The study demonstrates the involvement of pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) in the progression of pancreatic cancer. Using an orthotopic model of pancreatic cancer and in vitro cultures of human PSCs (hPSCs) and human pancreatic cancer cell lines MiaPaCa-2 and Panc-1, the researchers examined the influence of PSCs on pancreatic cancer growth. They found that hPSCs + MiaPaCa-2 resulted in increased tumor size, regional and distant metastasis, and fibrotic bands (desmoplasia) containing activated PSCs within tumors. In vitro studies revealed that PSC migration was significantly increased in the presence of pancreatic cancer cells, and hPSC secretions induced the proliferation and migration of MiaPaCa-2 and Panc-1 cells, while inhibiting apoptosis. The proliferative effect of hPSC secretions on pancreatic cancer cells was inhibited in the presence of neutralizing antibody to platelet-derived growth factor. These findings suggest a crucial interaction between pancreatic cancer cells and stromal cells (PSCs), implying that pancreatic cancer cells recruit stromal cells to create an environment that fosters cancer progression.

title: Preoperative statin treatment reduces systemic inflammatory response and myocardial damage in cardiac surgery.
text:
Title: The Impact of Preoperative Statin Therapy on Systemic Inflammatory Response and Myocardial Damage After Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Objective: To determine whether preoperative statin treatment is associated with a reduction in systemic inflammatory response (SIR) and myocardial damage markers after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB).
Methods: This prospective cohort study enrolled 138 patients who underwent coronary and valvular surgery with CPB. The study population was differentiated into two groups based on preoperative statin use: group A (n=72) and group B (n=66). Plasma levels of pro-inflammatory interleukins (tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), interleukin (IL)-6, IL-8, and IL-2R) and cardiac damage markers (creatine phosphokinase (CPK), CPK-MB, and troponin I) were measured before and at 1, 6, 24, and >72 hours after surgery.
Results: The baseline, operative, and postoperative morbidity and mortality characteristics were similar between the two groups. However, group A had significantly lower postoperative levels of IL-6 at 6 hours (68.8±5 pg/mL vs 108.9±108 pg/mL, p=0.01), 24 hours (71.7±7 pg/mL vs 110.4±106 pg/mL, p=0.01), and before hospital discharge (21.6±12 pg/mL vs 32.8±27 pg/mL, p=0.005) compared to group B. Additionally, group A had significantly lower average IL-6 levels in the first 24 hours after surgery (71.8±5 pg/mL vs 112.8±82 pg/mL, p=0.002). Furthermore, group A had lower postoperative CPK-MB levels at 24 hours (19.7±23 ng/mL vs 33.1±32 ng/mL, p=0.02) and troponin I levels at the end of the intervention (2.2±2.2 ng/mL vs 3.3±3.1 ng/mL, p=0.03) and at 24 hours (4.1±3.5 ng/mL vs 6.6±8 ng/mL, p=0.04) compared to group B.
Conclusion: This study demonstrates that preoperative statin use is associated with lower biochemical parameters of systemic inflammatory response and myocardial damage after cardiac surgery with CPB, regardless of whether the procedure is coronary bypass grafting (CABG) or valvular surgery. These findings suggest that preoperative statin therapy may have a protective effect on the cardiovascular system during surgery with CPB.

title: MEGA7: Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis Version 7.0 for Bigger Datasets.
text: We are pleased to introduce the latest version of Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis (Mega) software, which boasts of advanced methods and tools for phylogenomics and phylomedicine. This significant upgrade includes optimizations for 64-bit computing systems, enabling researchers to analyze vast datasets with ease. The new version offers a user-friendly wizard for constructing timetrees and a novel feature to automatically predict gene duplication events in gene family trees. Mega is available in two interfaces: a graphical user interface (GUI) for native Microsoft Windows and Mac OS X, and a command line version for Windows, Linux, and Mac OS X. Both versions are accessible free of charge from www.megasoftware.net.

title: DNA replication fidelity
text: DNA replication accuracy is a crucial factor in maintaining genome stability and has significant implications for evolution and the development of diseases. This review focuses on the latest research into DNA replication fidelity, highlighting the role of structural and biochemical studies of DNA polymerases in understanding the importance of hydrogen bonding, base pair geometry, and substrate-induced conformational changes. These studies have also revealed the interactions between polymerases and the minor groove of DNA at and upstream of the active site, which impact nucleotide selectivity, the efficiency of exonucleolytic proofreading, and the likelihood of errors via strand misalignments. By examining common features that are relevant to all DNA synthesis reactions, we can gain a deeper understanding of why fidelity varies depending on the enzymes, the error, and the local sequence environment.

title: Viable neutrophils release mitochondrial DNA to form neutrophil extracellular traps
text:
Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are extracellular structures that can capture and kill microorganisms. It is believed that these structures are produced by living neutrophils undergoing cell death, allowing them to kill bacteria. Our research shows that, after priming with granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) and subsequent stimulation with short-term toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) or complement factor 5a (C5a) receptor activation, viable neutrophils can produce NETs. Surprisingly, NETs generated by living cells contain mitochondrial DNA but no nuclear DNA. Our findings suggest that production of NETs by living neutrophils does not require cell death, and does not limit the lifespan of these cells.
In conclusion, our study demonstrates that viable neutrophils can produce NETs without undergoing cell death, and that this process is dependent on the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Our findings provide new insights into the mechanisms of NET formation and highlight the importance of neutrophil survival in the immune response.

title: ATP-driven exchange of histone H2AZ variant catalyzed by SWR1 chromatin remodeling complex.
text: The conserved histone variant H2AZ plays a crucial role in the regulation of gene expression and the maintenance of a barrier against the spread of silenced chromatin. Until now, the mechanism by which histone variants like H2AZ are incorporated into nucleosomes has been unclear. Our research has uncovered a multisubunit enzyme, led by the catalytic core Swr1, which efficiently replaces conventional histone H2A with histone H2AZ in nucleosome arrays. Swr1 is essential for the deposition of H2AZ at specific locations on chromosomes in vivo, and both Swr1 and H2AZ collaborate to regulate a subset of yeast genes. These findings shed light on an unappreciated function of the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling machinery.

title: FACT Disrupts Nucleosome Structure by Binding H2A-H2B with Conserved Peptide Motifs.
text: Histone chaperone FACT, composed of Spt16 and Pob3, is essential for various cellular processes. We discovered that the H2A-H2B binding capability at the core of FACT's function lies in short acidic regions near the C-terminus of each subunit. Mutations in these regions significantly impact binding and lead to diverse symptoms, with the largest effects surprisingly originating from an aromatic residue and a nearby carboxylate residue in each domain. Spt16 and Pob3 bind overlapping sites on H2A-H2B, and Spt16-Pob3 heterodimers simultaneously bind two H2A-H2B dimers with the same stoichiometry as nucleosome components. The crystal structure of Spt16-H2A-H2B provides insight into the biochemical and genetic data, offering a model for Pob3 binding and a mechanism for FACT-mediated nucleosome reorganization that we validate biochemically. Additionally, the similarity between FACT and ANP32E/Swr1-H2A.Z-H2B bindings reveals that diverse H2A-H2B chaperones use shared mechanisms for histone binding and nucleosome regulation.

title: Role of AMP-activated protein kinase in mechanism of metformin action.
text: Metformin is a widely used medication for the treatment of type 2 diabetes with an unknown cellular mechanism of action. Its glucose-lowering effect results from a decrease in hepatic glucose production and an increase in glucose utilization. Metformin's positive effects on circulating lipids have been linked to improved fatty liver. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a crucial cellular regulator of lipid and glucose metabolism. Our findings reveal that metformin activates AMPK in hepatocytes, which leads to a decrease in acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) activity, an increase in fatty acid oxidation, and a decrease in the expression of lipogenic enzymes. Activation of AMPK by metformin or an adenosine analogue suppresses the expression of sterol regulatory element-binding protein-1 (SREBP-1), a key transcription factor involved in lipogenesis. In metformin-treated rats, hepatic expression of SREBP-1 and other lipogenic mRNAs and proteins is reduced, and AMPK target ACC activity is also reduced. Using a novel AMPK inhibitor, we found that AMPK activation is essential for metformin's inhibition of glucose production in hepatocytes. Metformin also stimulates glucose uptake in skeletal muscles, which is accompanied by AMPK activation. Our results provide a unified explanation for the multitude of beneficial effects of metformin and suggest that alternative AMPK-modulating strategies may be useful in the treatment of metabolic disorders.

title: Interferon alfa therapy for chronic hepatitis B in children: a multinational randomized controlled trial.
text:
BACKGROUND & AIMS
Previous studies have shown that treatment of chronic hepatitis B with interferon alfa (IFN-alpha) is not effective in children. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of IFN-alpha in children with chronic hepatitis B and elevated liver enzymes.
METHODS
We enrolled 149 children in the study, with 70 receiving IFN-alpha2b (6 megunits/m2 given thrice weekly for 24 weeks) and 74 serving as controls. Serum hepatitis B e antigen and viral DNA levels were evaluated 24 weeks after therapy and after 48 weeks of observation in the control group.
RESULTS
Of the evaluable children, 26% had a negative clearance of viral replication markers, 11% of controls had a negative clearance, and 40% of responders had a complete normalization of aminotransferase levels and improvement in liver histology. In addition, 10% of treated children and 1% of controls had a negative hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) test result. The only significant predictors of response were female gender and IFN-alpha treatment. Baseline aminotransferase level, initial DNA levels, and histology did not correlate with response. Most adverse reactions were mild or moderate, and the dose was reduced in 24% of children.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings show that IFN-alpha therapy promotes the loss of viral replication markers, HBsAg, and improves aminotransferases and histology in children with chronic hepatitis B. These results suggest that IFN-alpha may be a useful treatment option for children with chronic hepatitis B. However, further studies are needed to determine the efficacy and safety of IFN-alpha in this population.

title: ImmTACs for targeted cancer therapy: Why, what, how, and which.
text: Breaking immunosuppression and triggering a cytotoxic T cell response has the potential to halt cancer progression and, in some situations, eradicate it entirely. Designing therapies to achieve this objective has proven challenging, but advances in understanding immune complexities are now leading to game-changing breakthroughs. ImmTACs (immune-mobilizing monoclonal TCRs against cancer) are a novel class of bispecific reagents, engineered to display extremely high affinity for cognate tumor antigens. By surmounting the low-affinity tumor-specific T cell issue imposed by thymic selection, ImmTACs provide access to the wealth of antigens presented as peptide-HLA complexes. Once bound to cancer cells, the anti-CD3 effector end of the ImmTAC recruits polyclonal T cells to the tumor site, leading to a potent redirected T cell response and tumor cell destruction. Comprehensive in vitro testing combined with promising early clinical data have enhanced our appreciation of ImmTAC function in vivo and highlight their potential therapeutic benefit, including a durable response and, ultimately, the breakage of T cell tolerance. This review introduces ImmTACs in the context of immunotherapy, outlines their design, construction, and mechanism of action, as well as examining target selection and aspects of preclinical safety testing.

title: Angiopoietin-like protein 3 supports the activity of hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow niche.
text: The role of angiopoietin-like proteins (Angptls) in the hematopoietic system has yet to be elucidated. Our findings indicate that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in Angptl3-null mice are fewer in number and exhibit decreased quiescence. HSCs transplanted into Angptl3-null recipients showed impaired repopulation capabilities. Bone marrow sinusoidal endothelial cells, which exhibit high levels of Angptl3, are located near HSCs. Additionally, bone marrow stromal cells or endothelium deficient in Angptl3 have a significantly reduced capacity to support the expansion of repopulating HSCs. Angptl3 represses the expression of the transcription factor Ikaros, which, when unregulated, diminishes the repopulation potential of HSCs. As an extrinsic factor, Angptl3 plays a crucial role in supporting the stemness of HSCs within the bone marrow microenvironment.

title: Subsequent chemotherapy reverses acquired tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance and restores response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer
text:
Background: Patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) often develop resistance to epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) such as erlotinib and gefitinib. Here, we report the successful treatment of two cases of advanced NSCLC that had developed resistance to TKIs using a combination of chemotherapy and TKIs.
Case Presentation: Two patients with advanced or metastatic NSCLC were initially treated with palliative chemotherapy followed by erlotinib or gefitinib. However, when TKI therapy failed, they received two cycles of chemotherapy followed by a "re-challenge" with erlotinib or gefitinib.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that patients with acquired TKI resistance in NSCLC should be managed aggressively whenever possible. In cases where initial TKI treatment has achieved a dramatic clinical response, using a combination of chemotherapy and targeted treatment may be a reasonable choice. Further research is needed to confirm the association between erlotinib/gefitinib treatment and the efficacy of NSCLC patients with acquired TKI failure.

title: Epigenetic Therapy Ties MYC Depletion to Reversing Immune Evasion and Treating Lung Cancer
text: Converging DNA-demethylating agents (DNMTi) with histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) may provide a potent avenue for improving cancer immunotherapy. To optimize this approach, we interrogate the pharmacology of HDACis and their isoform-specificity when combined with DNMTi. This knowledge enables us to design a novel, low-dose, sequential regimen that unleashes a robust anti-tumor response in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Using in-vitro-treated NSCLC cell lines, we decipher an interferon α/β-driven transcriptional program characterized by upregulation of antigen presentation machinery, mediated in part through double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) induction. This is accompanied by suppression of MYC signaling and an increase in the T cell chemoattractant CCL5. By exploiting this combination treatment regimen in mouse models of NSCLC, we restore tumor immune tolerance and 'wake up' exhausted T cells, leading to a shift from a tumor-induced immune suppression to an immune-mediated anti-tumor response. Key preclinical findings provide a strong rationale for an upcoming clinical trial aimed at enhancing immune checkpoint therapy for NSCLC.

title: The Role of PPARγ in Advanced Glycation End Products-Induced Inflammatory Response in Human Chondrocytes
text:
Objective:
Advances in the last decade have highlighted the protective role of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors gamma (PPARγ) in the pathophysiology of osteoarthritis (OA). The aim of this study was to investigate the roles of PPARγ in the inflammatory response induced by Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs) in human chondrocytes.
Methods:
Primary human chondrocytes were stimulated with AGEs in the presence or absence of neutralizing antibody against RAGE (anti-RAGE), MAPK specific inhibitors, and PPARγ agonist pioglitazone. The expression of interleukin-1 (IL-1), matrix metalloproteinase-13 (MMP-13), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), PPARγ, nuclear nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) p65, and cytosol inhibitor kappa B alpha (IκBα) was determined by western blotting and real-time PCR.
Results:
