SRm160 and a related protein SRm300 (the 300-kD nuclear matrix antigen recognized by mAb B4A11) form a complex that is essential for the splicing of specific pre-mRNAs. The SRm160/300 complex associates with splicing complexes and enhances splicing through interactions with SR family proteins. Binding of SRm160/300 to pre-mRNA is typically also dependent on U1 snRNP and is reinforced by U2 snRNP. As a result, SRm160/300 forms various interactions with components attached directly to critical sites within pre-mRNA. The findings suggest that a complex of nuclear matrix proteins SRm160 and SRm300 functions as a coactivator of pre-mRNA splicing.

title: Comparison of pioglitazone vs glimepiride on progression of coronary atherosclerosis in patients with type 2 diabetes: the PERISCOPE randomized controlled trial.
text: A study published in 2006 compared the effects of pioglitazone, an insulin sensitizer, with glimepiride, an insulin secretagogue, on the progression of coronary atherosclerosis in patients with type 2 diabetes. The study was a double-blind, randomized, multicenter trial conducted at 97 academic and community hospitals in North and South America from 2003 to 2006. A total of 543 patients with coronary disease and type 2 diabetes were enrolled in the study and randomized to receive either glimepiride or pioglitazone for 18 months, with titration to maximum dosage if tolerated. Coronary intravascular ultrasonography was performed on 360 patients at study completion to measure the progression of coronary atherosclerosis. The results showed that the least squares mean percent atheroma volume (PAV) increased by 0.73% in the glimepiride group and decreased by 0.16% in the pioglitazone group (P = 0.002). An alternative analysis that imputed values for noncompleters based on baseline characteristics showed an increase in PAV of 0.64% in the glimepiride group and a decrease of 0.06% in the pioglitazone group (between-group P = 0.02). Pioglitazone was also found to have a significant effect on serum lipid levels, with increases in high-density lipoprotein levels and decreases in triglyceride levels compared to glimepiride. However, pioglitazone was associated with a higher rate of hypoglycemia and edema, while glimepiride was associated with a higher rate of fractures and decreased hemoglobin levels. Overall, the study found that pioglitazone had a significantly lower rate of progression of coronary atherosclerosis compared to glimepiride in patients with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease.

title: Staphylococcus aureus RNAIII coordinately represses the synthesis of virulence factors and the transcription regulator Rot by an antisense mechanism.
text: Staphylococcus aureus' intracellular effector, RNAIII, plays a crucial role in the quorum-sensing system, regulating the expression of numerous virulence genes. We demonstrate that the 3' domain of RNAIII functions as an antisense RNA, binding to specific mRNAs and repressing their expression at the post-transcriptional level. This involves the formation of long RNA duplexes, leading to translation initiation repression and subsequent depletion of the mRNA pool. Additionally, we show that RNAIII regulates rot mRNA translation through a limited number of base pairings, indirectly activating the synthesis of several exoproteins. These findings highlight the multifaceted regulatory mechanisms employed by RNAIII and its 3' domain in the establishment of S. aureus' virulence factor network.

title: Human Cytomegalovirus Latency-Associated Proteins Elicit Immune-Suppressive IL-10 Producing CD4+ T Cells
text:
Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous human herpesvirus that persistently infects humans for life after primary infection. In healthy individuals, the virus is well controlled by the HCMV-specific T cell response. A unique feature of this persistence is the establishment of viral latency, which differs from lytic infection characterized by extensive viral gene expression and virus production. In contrast, latency in cells of the myeloid lineage involves highly restricted expression of viral genes such as UL138 and LUNA.
We report that both UL138- and LUNA-specific T cells are detectable in healthy HCMV seropositive individuals and are primarily mediated by CD4+ T cells. These UL138-specific CD4+ T cells can mediate MHC class II restricted cytotoxicity and demonstrate IFNγ effector function in both lytic and latent infection contexts. In contrast to CD4+ T cells specific to antigens expressed solely during lytic infection, the UL138 and LUNA-specific CD4+ T cell responses include cells that secrete the immunosuppressive cytokine IL-10. We also show that IL-10-expressing CD4+ T cells target latently expressed US28 and UL111A. Our findings suggest that latency-associated gene products of HCMV elicit CD4+ T cell responses in vivo, which can mediate effector function against both lytically and latently infected cells. Notably, this response includes a subset of cells that produce the immunosuppressive cytokine IL-10, indicating that HCMV manipulates the T cell responses to latency-associated antigens to maintain latent carriage in vivo.

title: Pamidronate induced anti-proliferative, apoptotic, and anti-migratory effects in hepatocellular carcinoma.
text:
BACKGROUND/AIMS:
Small GTPases of the Ras and Rho families play a crucial role in human tumorigenesis and metastasis. Recent studies have shown that pamidronate inhibits the mevalonate pathway, which is essential for the prenylation of these small GTPases. We aimed to explore the potential therapeutic benefits of pamidronate in the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
METHODS:
We investigated the effect of pamidronate on cell proliferation in five hepatoma cell lines using the MTT assay. Apoptosis was evaluated using DAPI and a histone ELISA assay. Cell migration was assessed using a Modified Boyden Chamber. To evaluate the anti-proliferative effect of pamidronate in vivo, tumor volumes were monitored in nude mice following subcutaneous inoculation of PLC/PRF/5 cells and intraperitoneal injection of pamidronate.
RESULTS:
Pamidronate inhibited cell growth in all hepatoma cell lines examined. The levels of membrane-associated Ras and phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinase 2 (ERK2) were significantly reduced following pamidronate treatment. Pamidronate increased apoptosis and cleavage of Caspase-3 and -9. Moreover, pamidronate suppressed membrane-associated RhoA and cell motility. In vivo, tumor volumes were significantly decreased by pamidronate at three weeks (P < 0.03).
CONCLUSIONS:
Our findings suggest that pamidronate has potential therapeutic applications in inducing anti-proliferative, apoptotic, and anti-migratory effects in HCC. These results provide a rationale for further investigating the use of pamidronate as a treatment for HCC.

title: Defective regulation of adipose tissue autophagy in obesity
text:
The text provided below is a rewrite of the original text with some revisions to improve readability and clarity:
Objectives: Autophagy, a highly regulated process, plays a crucial role in controlling various cellular functions, including organelle recycling, nutrient availability, and tissue differentiation. Recent research has shown increased autophagic activity in the adipose tissue of obese individuals, suggesting a potential link between autophagy and obesity-related insulin resistance. While body mass reduction is the most efficient approach to address insulin resistance in overweight individuals, the impact of weight loss on adipose tissue autophagy remains unclear.
Study Design: Adipose tissue autophagy was examined in mice and humans.
Methods: A mouse model of diet-induced obesity and diabetes was maintained on a 15-day, 40% calorie restriction diet. At baseline, autophagy markers were higher in obese mice compared to lean controls. Upon caloric restriction, autophagy increased in lean mice, while it decreased in obese mice. Reintroduction of ad libitum feeding was enough to rapidly reduce autophagy in lean mice and increase it in obese mice. In the second part of the study, autophagy was evaluated in subcutaneous adipose tissue samples from nine obese-non-diabetic and six obese-diabetic subjects undergoing bariatric surgery for body mass reduction. Samples were collected during surgery and approximately one year later. Markers of systemic inflammation, including tumor necrosis factor-1α, interleukin (IL)-6, and IL-1β, were also evaluated.
Results: Obesity and caloric overfeeding were associated with increased autophagy in the adipose tissue, and body mass reduction led to a decrease in autophagy. These findings suggest that the regulation of autophagy in the adipose tissue is defective in obesity. When obese-diabetic subjects underwent improved metabolic control following calorie restriction, autophagy and inflammation were found to be regulated independently.
Implications: The study findings suggest that weight loss may help regulate autophagy in the adipose tissue, leading to improved metabolic health. However, further research is needed to fully understand the relationship between autophagy, obesity, and insulin resistance.

title: Recovery of visual response of injured adult rat optic nerves treated with transglutaminase.
text: Injury to central nervous system (CNS) axons in adult mammals does not allow for spontaneous regeneration due to inhibitory molecules released by oligodendrocytes. In contrast, the regeneration of CNS axons in fish is associated with the presence of a transglutaminase enzyme. This enzyme dimerizes interleukin-2, producing a cytotoxic molecule that is toxic to oligodendrocytes in vitro. When this nerve-derived transglutaminase was applied to rat optic nerves following injury, leading to the loss of visual evoked potential response to light, the recovery of this response was observed within 6 weeks after injury. Moreover, transmission electron microscopy analysis revealed the simultaneous appearance of axons in the distal stump of the optic nerve.

title: Cell survival during complete nutrient deprivation depends on lipid droplet-fueled β-oxidation of fatty acids.
text: Cells exposed to various forms of stress synthesize triacylglycerols and create lipid droplets (LD), but the significance of this response is unclear. To determine if lipid droplet formation has a protective role in cells that are committed to die, we utilized complete nutrient deprivation in cell culture as a simple model of stress. Complete nutrient deprivation induced lipid droplet biogenesis in human LN18 glioblastoma and HeLa cells, as well as in CHO and rat primary astrocytes. In each cell type, death was linked to depletion of lipid droplets and was accelerated by inhibiting lipid droplet formation after pharmacological inhibition of Group IVA phospholipase A2 (cPLA2α) or downregulating ceramide kinase. Additionally, nutrient deprivation induced β-oxidation of fatty acids, which was sensitive to cPLA2α inhibition, and cell survival in these conditions became solely dependent on fatty acid catabolism. These findings demonstrate that, during nutrient deprivation, cell viability is sustained by β-oxidation of fatty acids, which requires the formation and mobilization of lipid droplets.

title: Molecular and cytogenetic changes involved in the immortalization of nasopharyngeal epithelial cells by telomerase.
text: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a prevalent disease in Hong Kong and southern China, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is believed to play a crucial role in its development. However, most previous studies on the transformation mechanisms of EBV genes were conducted in either NPC or non-nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, which may not accurately represent premalignant nasopharyngeal epithelial cells. To address this limitation, we established a representative cell system using telomerase to immortalize primary non-malignant nasopharyngeal biopsies. Our results showed that the newly immortalized nasopharyngeal epithelial cell line, referred to as NP460hTert, harbors genetic alterations previously identified in premalignant and malignant nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, such as inactivation of p16 by homozygous deletion of the p16(INK4A) locus and downregulation of RASSF1A expression. Interestingly, the deletion of the p16(INK4A) locus appeared to be the most crucial event leading to immortalization of nasopharyngeal epithelial cells by telomerase, and occurred before RASSF1A downregulation. Additionally, our analysis revealed a gain of a 17q21-q25 fragment on chromosome 11p15 in all NP460hTert cells, which is a gain that has been previously reported in NPC. Furthermore, we observed activation of NF-κB in immortalized NP460hTert cells at later population doublings, which may play a role in the survival of immortalized NP epithelial cells. Finally, we found that the upregulation of Id1, a gene commonly expressed in various cancers, including NPC, in immortalized NP460hTert cells. Our findings suggest that the establishment of an immortalized nasopharyngeal epithelial cell line harboring common genetic alterations present in premalignant and cancerous nasopharyngeal epithelial cells may provide a valuable tool to investigate early events involved in NPC carcinogenesis, particularly in the role of EBV infection in NPC development.

title: Cellular nucleic acid binding protein suppresses tumor cell metastasis and induces tumor cell death by downregulating heterogeneous ribonucleoprotein K in fibrosarcoma cells.
text:
The protein Cellular Nucleic Acid Binding Protein (CNBP) has been implicated in the development of vertebrate craniofacial structures and certain human diseases, including Myotonic Dystrophy Type 2 (DM2) and Sporadic Inclusion Body Myositis (sIBM). CNBP regulates cell proliferation and survival by DNA binding, which promotes nucleic acid rearrangements through an ATP-independent process. Various methods were used in this study to investigate the role of CNBP in human fibrosarcoma cells, including cell viability assays, wound-scratch assays, chemotaxis assays, invasion assays, circular dichroic (CD) spectroscopy, NMR spectroscopy, chromatin immunoprecipitation, expression and purification of recombinant human CNBP, electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA), surface plasmon resonance (SPR), fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) analyses, luciferase reporter assay, Western blotting, and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC).
The study found that overexpressing CNBP led to increased cell death and decreased cell motility and invasiveness in human fibrosarcoma cells. CNBP was found to transcriptionally downregulate the expression of Heterogeneous Ribonucleoprotein K (hnRNP K) by forming G-quadruplexes in the hnRNP K promoter. The G-quadruplex stabilizing ligand tetra-(N-methyl-4-pyridyl) porphyrin (TMPyP4) could also interact with and stabilize the G-quadruplex, leading to downregulation of hnRNP K transcription.
The results of this study suggest a new approach for controlling hnRNP K expression and may have implications for the design and development of new anticancer drugs.

title: The DHR96 nuclear receptor regulates xenobiotic responses in Drosophila.
text: Exposure to foreign substances like plant toxins, pollutants, or prescription drugs triggers a defense response in organisms, leading to the activation of genes that encode crucial detoxification enzymes. Although the study of xenobiotic responses has been extensive in vertebrates, relatively little effort has been dedicated to exploring a simplified genetic system for delving into the molecular basis of this coordinated transcriptional response. We aim to address this gap by investigating the effect of phenobarbital treatment on approximately 1000 transcripts in Drosophila. Furthermore, we investigate the role of the Drosophila ortholog of the human SXR and CAR xenobiotic receptors, DHR96, in this response. Our results demonstrate that a DHR96 null mutant exhibits increased sensitivity to the sedative effects of phenobarbital and the pesticide DDT, along with defects in the expression of various phenobarbital-regulated genes. Additionally, we find that metabolic and stress-response genes are controlled by DHR96, indicating its central role in coordinating multiple response pathways. This work establishes a novel model system for uncovering the genetic control of xenobiotic stress responses.

title: A primate virus generates transformed human cells by fusion
text: A model that encompasses both the genesis and unpredictable nature of cancer suggests that cancer cells are an unplanned outcome of events that promote genetic and epigenetic diversity. The widely accepted notion is that these events stem from mutations that affect chromosome separation or stability. However, genetic and epigenetic variability can also be triggered by cell fusion, which is often caused by viruses. Despite the fact that cells fused by viruses are normally considered harmless since they perish, our study reveals that a primate virus utilizes both viral and exosomal proteins involved in cell fusion to produce transformed, proliferating human cells. Individual cells, although they are unable to divide after fusion, can become transformed by expressing an oncogene or a modified tumor suppressor p53 in just one of the fusion partners. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that this virus can generate viable, oncogenically transformed cells by fusing cells that are otherwise destined to die. Therefore, we propose that viruses can contribute to carcinogenesis by fusing cells.

title: TAA1-Mediated Auxin Biosynthesis Is Essential for Hormone Crosstalk and Plant Development
text: Plants have developed remarkable resilience by adapting their growth and development in response to environmental changes. The interplay between hormonal and developmental signals is a crucial mechanism that enables this incredible plasticity. For instance, the hormone ethylene plays a critical role in plant development, and its response varies depending on tissue type, developmental stage, and environmental conditions. By examining the Arabidopsis wei8 mutant, we have discovered that a small group of genes is responsible for tissue-specific responses to ethylene. Biochemical analysis revealed that WEI8 encodes a long-sought tryptophan aminotransferase, TAA1, which is involved in the indole-3-pyruvic acid (IPA) branch of the auxin biosynthetic pathway. Our findings establish a connection between local auxin production, tissue-specific ethylene effects, and organ development. Therefore, the IPA route of auxin production is essential in generating robust auxin gradients in response to environmental and developmental cues.

title: A research agenda for public health workforce development.
text: Over the past few decades, public health research has primarily concentrated on categorical rather than cross-cutting or systems-level issues. Insufficient attention has been given to the infrastructure necessary to support public health programs. This article presents the findings of an interactive process to develop a research agenda for public health workforce development, with the aim of informing all stakeholders in the public health system. This interdisciplinary field of inquiry examines the public health workforce in terms of costs, quality, accessibility, delivery, organization, financing, and outcomes of public health services, with the goal of increasing knowledge and understanding of the relationships among workforce, structure, processes, and effects of public health services. Through meetings of expert panels held between 2000 and 2003, a logic model and five priority research areas were developed. To advance cross-cutting and systems-focused research, innovative public-private partnerships will be necessary.

title: Parallel processing in the mammalian retina
text: Our eyes transmit multiple "images" of the external world to the brain, each with a specific characterization. These images include line drawings (contours), watercolor paintings (colour images), and moving pictures (movies). This process is known as parallel processing and begins as early as the first synapse of the retina, the cone pedicle. At this stage, the molecular composition of the transmitter receptors on the postsynaptic neurons determines which images are transmitted to the inner retina. Within the second synaptic layer, known as the inner plexiform layer, complex inhibitory and excitatory interactions are represented by circuits that act as filters, selectively transmitting only the most relevant "images" to the brain.

title: Oxymetholone Therapy of Fanconi Anemia Suppresses Osteopontin Transcription and Induces Hematopoietic Stem Cell Cycling
text: Androgens are widely used to treat Fanconi anemia (FA) and other bone marrow failure syndromes, but their exact mechanism of action is not fully understood. To investigate the therapeutic efficacy and mechanism of action of oxymetholone (OXM), aged Fancd2(-/-) mice were used. These mice recapitulate key human FA phenotypes, including reduced bone marrow cellularity, red blood cell macrocytosis, and peripheral pancytopenia. Interestingly, chronic OXM treatment significantly improved these hematological parameters and stimulated the proliferation of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. Additionally, RNA-Sequencing analysis indicated that downregulation of osteopontin may play a crucial role in the drug's action. Consistent with increased stem cell proliferation, competitive repopulation assays revealed that chronic OXM therapy eventually resulted in stem cell exhaustion. These findings expand our understanding of the regulation of hematopoietic stem cell proliferation and have direct clinical implications for the treatment of bone marrow failure.

title: A point mutation in KINDLIN3 ablates activation of three integrin subfamilies in humans
text: Heterogeneous deficiency diseases afford unique opportunities to delineate the contributions of individual molecules to human physiology and to identify destructive processes precipitated by their malfunction. We describe a deficiency disorder in two unrelated human siblings, exhibiting profuse bleeding, frequent infections, and osteopetrosis at an early age, symptoms that are more severe than those documented for patients with leukocyte adhesion deficiency III (LAD-III). Mechanistically, these symptoms stem from an inability to catalyze the activation of integrins expressed on hematopoietic cells, including platelets and leukocytes. Isolated lymphocyte cell lines from the two individuals displayed integrin activation defects. Proteins previously linked to integrin activation, such as Ras-associated protein-1 (RAP1) and calcium and diacylglycerol-regulated guanine nucleotide exchange factor-1 (CALDAG-GEF1), were present and operational in these cell lines. The genetic basis for this disease was traced to a point mutation in the coding region of the KINDLIN3 (official gene symbol FERMT3) gene. Following expression of wild-type KINDLIN-3 in immortalized lymphocytes, their integrins became responsive to activation signals. These findings identify a hereditary disease that enrages the well-being of affected individuals and underscores an essential role of KINDLIN-3 in integrin activation in humans. Moreover, allogenic bone marrow transplantation was shown to alleviate the symptoms of the disorder.

title: Fasting Activation of AgRP Neurons Requires NMDA Receptors and Involves Spinogenesis and Increased Excitatory Tone
text: AgRP neuron activity is responsible for promoting feeding and weight gain, while the activity of nearby POMC neurons has the opposite effect. However, the role of excitatory glutamatergic input in modulating these neurons has remained elusive. To address this question, we generated mice lacking NMDA receptors (NMDARs) on either AgRP or POMC neurons. Surprisingly, deletion of NMDARs from AgRP neurons resulted in a significant reduction in weight, body fat, and food intake, whereas deletion from POMC neurons had no effect. Our findings indicate that AgRP neurons are more dependent on NMDARs for their activity than POMC neurons. We also observed that AgRP neurons have a higher density of dendritic spines compared to POMC neurons, and that fasting induced an increase in glutamatergic input onto AgRP neurons, which was parallel to an increase in spines. This suggests that fasting-induced synaptogenesis and spinogenesis are mediated by glutamatergic synaptic transmission and its modulation by NMDARs. In summary, our results demonstrate that glutamatergic synaptic transmission and its modulation by NMDARs play essential roles in controlling AgRP neurons and their response to fasting.

title: Prevalence and Causes of Blindness and Low Vision in Southern Sudan
text:
In southern Sudan, it is believed that background blindness and low vision are prevalent. However, the true extent and regional distribution of these conditions remain largely unquantified. To address this knowledge gap, our study aimed to:
1. Estimate the prevalence of blindness and low vision in Mankien payam (district), southern Sudan.
2. Identify the primary causes of blindness and low vision in the area.
3. Determine targets for blindness prevention programs in Mankien payam.
By achieving these objectives, our study aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the magnitude and causes of blindness and low vision in southern Sudan, which can inform strategies to address these issues and improve the quality of life for individuals in this region.

title: Origin of nitrite and nitrate in nasal and exhaled breath condensate and relation to nitric oxide formation.
text:
Introduction:
Elevated concentrations of nitrate and nitrite have been detected in exhaled breath condensate (EBC) in individuals with airway diseases, leading to speculation about increased nitric oxide (NO) metabolism. However, the underlying sources of nitrate and nitrite in the airways remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the origins of nitrate and nitrite in the airways by comparing the levels of these compounds in EBC, nasal condensate, saliva, and tracheal aspirate.
Methods:
Seventeen tracheostomised and 15 non-tracheostomised subjects were recruited for the study. Nitric oxide, nitrite, and nitrate levels were measured in EBC, nasal condensate, and saliva before and after sodium nitrate ingestion (10 mg/kg) and use of antibacterial mouthwash (chlorhexidine 0.2%). Tracheal aspirate was collected from the tracheostomised subjects.
Results:
Oral nitric oxide levels significantly increased by 90% in tracheostomised subjects after sodium nitrate ingestion, while tracheal nitric oxide levels were unaffected. Oral EBC nitrite levels increased by 23-fold at 60 minutes post-ingestion, while tracheal EBC nitrite levels showed only a minor increase. Nitrate levels were similar in oral and tracheal EBC after nitrate ingestion. Non-tracheostomised subjects showed similar increases in oral nitric oxide and EBC nitrite levels after nitrate ingestion and chlorhexidine mouthwash. Nasal nitrite levels were not affected by nitrate ingestion or mouthwash. Mouthwash with deionised water did not affect nitrite levels in oral EBC or saliva, while significant reductions were observed after antibacterial mouthwash.
Discussion:
The study findings suggest that plasma nitrate is taken up by the lower airways but not the nasal airways, therefore, nitrate levels in EBC are influenced by dietary intake. Nitrate is reduced to nitrite by bacterial activity primarily in the oropharyngeal tract of healthy individuals. Oropharyngeal nitrite seems to contribute to exhaled NO in non-inflamed airways, and there is also a substantial contribution of nitrite from the oropharyngeal tract during standard collection of EBC. These findings have implications for the diagnosis and treatment of airway diseases.
Conclusion:

In conclusion, the study provides new insights into the origins of nitrate and nitrite in the airways. The data suggest that bacterial activity in the oropharyngeal tract plays a key role in reducing nitrate to nitrite, and this is the primary source of nitrite in EBC. These findings have important implications for the diagnosis and treatment of airway diseases, as well as for the development of new therapeutic strategies that target the oropharyngeal tract.

title: AZD9150, a next-generation antisense oligonucleotide inhibitor of STAT3 with early evidence of clinical activity in lymphoma and lung cancer
text: Next-generation sequencing technologies have significantly advanced our understanding of cancer genetics. Antisense technology holds great potential to translate these advancements into improved cancer therapeutics, as antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) inhibitors can be designed based on gene sequence information alone. Recent human clinical data have demonstrated the potent activity of systemically administered ASOs targeting genes expressed in the liver. We report on the preclinical activity and initial clinical evaluation of a class of ASOs modified with constrained ethyl groups for targeting the gene encoding the transcription factor STAT3, a difficult protein to inhibit therapeutically. Systemic delivery of the unformulated ASO, AZD9150, decreased STAT3 expression in a wide range of preclinical cancer models and showed antitumor activity in lymphoma and lung cancer models. The preclinical activity of AZD9150 translated into single-agent antitumor activity in patients with highly treatment-refractory lymphoma and non–small cell lung cancer in a phase 1 dose-escalation study.

title: Evidence of a pluripotent human embryonic stem cell line derived from a cloned blastocyst.
text: Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) technology has recently enabled the generation of animals with a shared genetic makeup. In this study, we detail the derivation of a pluripotent embryonic stem (ES) cell line, known as SCNT-hES-1, from a cloned human blastocyst. The SCNT-hES-1 cells exhibited typical ES cell morphology and surface markers and were capable of differentiating into embryoid bodies in vitro and forming teratomas in vivo containing cell derivatives from all three embryonic germ layers in severely immunocompromised mice. Following over 70 passages, SCNT-hES-1 cells maintained normal karyotypes and were genetically identical to the somatic nuclear donor cells. While we cannot completely rule out the possibility of a parthenogenetic origin, genomic analyses conclusively support a SCNT-derived origin of these human ES cells.

title: Ultrarapid drug metabolism: PCR-based detection of CYP2D6 gene duplication.
text: The enzyme debrisoquine 4-hydroxylase (CYP2D6), which metabolizes a wide range of drugs, exhibits significant genetic variability among individuals. The activity of this enzyme can vary greatly between subjects, ranging from ultrafast to complete inactivity. As a result, the metabolic capacity of individuals differs, leading to intersubject differences in therapeutic efficacy and side effects at standard doses. Approximately 7% of Caucasians possess inherited alleles with multiply functional CYP2D6 genes, resulting in an increased expression of the enzyme. Identifying individuals with ultra-rapid drug metabolism (UM) is clinically significant for adjusting drug dosages and avoiding misdiagnosis of non-compliance. In our study, we employed newly developed PCR assays to detect the UM genotype in a population of 202 psychiatric patients. We found a 3.5% prevalence of UM individuals carrying duplicate active CYP2D6 genes.

title: The Actions of Synaptically Released Zinc at Hippocampal Mossy Fiber Synapses
text: Zn2+ is abundant in synaptic vesicles of hippocampal mossy fibers. We employed Zn2+ chelators and mocha mutant mice to investigate its physiological function in this pathway. Zn2+ does not contribute to the unique presynaptic plasticities observed at mossy fiber synapses, but it is co-released with glutamate from these synapses, both spontaneously and in response to electrical stimulation, where it exerts a notable regulatory influence on NMDA receptors. Zn2+ tends to occupy the high-affinity binding site of NMDA receptors at mossy fiber synapses, while the lower affinity voltage-dependent Zn2+ site is occupied during action potential-driven release. We conclude that Zn2+ acts as a modulatory neurotransmitter released from mossy fiber synapses and plays a significant role in shaping the NMDA receptor response at these synapses.

title: Association between folate intake from different food sources in Norway and homocysteine status in a dietary intervention among young male adults.
text:
The present study aimed to investigate the effect of a dietary intervention that combined nutrition information with increased access to vegetables, fruits, and wholegrain bread. The study investigated changes in the consumption of these food groups and estimated nutrients, as well as the relationship between changes in folate intake and plasma total homocysteine (tHcy) levels.
The 5-month intervention study involved 376 male recruits from the Norwegian National Guard, with 105 participants in the control group from the Norwegian National Guard, Heggelia. The intervention group showed a significant increase in the intake of vegetables, fruits, berries, and juice (P < 0.001), as well as wholegrain bread (P < 0.001). The intervention group also showed a higher increase in dietary fiber and folate intake compared to the control group (P < 0.001 for both). The relative contribution of folate intake from fruits, vegetables, and wholegrain bread was significantly higher in the intervention group compared to the control group (P < 0.001 for all). Furthermore, the study found an inverse association between the increased intake of folate from wholegrain bread and reduced levels of plasma tHcy (P = 0.017).
In summary, the dietary intervention resulted in increased intakes of vegetables, fruits, and wholegrain bread, leading to a higher folate intake from these sources. This increased folate intake was inversely related to reduced tHcy levels. These findings suggest that combining nutrition information with increased availability of healthy food options can lead to improved dietary habits and potentially better cardiovascular health.

title: Beta interferon controls West Nile virus infection and pathogenesis in mice.
text:
Research involving mice lacking the plasma membrane receptor for type I interferon (IFN-αβR(-)(/)(-)) has revealed that IFN signaling plays a crucial role in restricting the tropism, dissemination, and lethality of viral infections, including West Nile virus (WNV) and other pathogenic viruses. However, the specific functions of individual IFN subtypes are not yet fully understood. In this study, we used IFN-β(-)(/)(-) mice to investigate the antiviral and immunomodulatory functions of this IFN subtype in restricting WNV infection.
IFN-β(-)(/)(-) mice were found to be more susceptible to WNV infection than wild-type mice, with greater overall mortality and more rapid progression of the infection. This was accompanied by enhanced viral replication in various tissues, including macrophages, dendritic cells, fibroblasts, and cerebellar granule cell neurons. Interestingly, viral titers were higher in ex vivo cultures of these cell types from IFN-β(-)(/)(-) mice than in wild-type cells. These findings suggest that IFN-β directly controls WNV replication in these cell types.
While no major deficits in WNV-specific antibodies or CD8(+) T cells were observed in IFN-β(-)(/)(-) mice, we did detect an altered CD4(+) CD25(+) FoxP3(+) regulatory T cell response, with greater numbers of these cells after infection. These results suggest that IFN-β controls WNV pathogenesis by restricting infection in key cell types and by modulating T cell regulatory networks.
In conclusion, this study provides further insight into the role of IFN-β in restricting viral infection and modulating the immune response. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the specific functions of individual IFN subtypes in the context of viral infection and immune defense.

title: Frontrunners of T cell activation: Initial, localized Ca2+ signals mediated by NAADP and the type 1 ryanodine receptor
text: T cell activation serves as theinitiating switch for the adaptive immune system. Intracellular calcium (Ca2+) signaling is essentialfor T cell activation, beginning with brief, localized Ca2+ signals that occur initially. The secondary messenger nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP) forms rapidly upon T cell activation and stimulates early Ca2+ signaling. Using a high-resolution imaging technique that incorporates multiple fluorescent Ca2+ indicator dyes, we characterized these early signaling events and investigated the channels involved in NAADP-dependent Ca2+ signals. Within seconds of activating either primary murine T cells or human Jurkat cells with beads coated with an antibody against CD3, we observed Ca2+ signals with diametersthat were close to the limit of detection and located near the activation site at the plasma membrane. In Jurkat cells in which the ryanodine receptor (RyR) was knocked down or in primary T cells from RyR1−/− mice, either these early Ca2+ signals were not detected or their number was significantly reduced. Local Ca2+ signals observed within 20 ms after microinjection of Jurkat cells with NAADP were also sensitive to RyR knockdown. In contrast, the potential NAADP target channel TRPM2 (transient receptor potential channel, subtype melastatin 2) was not requiredfor the formation of initial Ca2+ signals in primary T cells. Through our high-resolution imaging method, we characterized early Ca2+ release events in T cells and obtained evidence for the involvement of RyR and NAADP in such signals.

title: A missense LAMB2 mutation causes congenital nephrotic syndrome by impairing laminin secretion.
text: Laminin β2 is a crucial element of laminin-521, a fundamental component of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). Mutations in LAMB2, specifically the R246Q mutation, have been linked to Pierson syndrome, a severe congenital nephrotic syndrome with ocular and neurological defects. In contrast, individuals with LAMB2 missense mutations, such as R246Q, may exhibit less severe extrarenal defects but still experience congenital nephrotic syndrome. To investigate the mechanism underlying proteinuria in these individuals, we generated three transgenic mouse lines in which the R246Q-mutant rat laminin β2 replaced the wild-type mouse laminin β2 in the GBM. These transgenic mice showed significantly less severe proteinuria compared to their non-transgenic Lamb2-deficient littermates, with the level of proteinuria correlating inversely with R246Q-LAMB2 expression. At the onset of proteinuria, the expression and localization of proteins associated with the slit diaphragm and foot processes were normal, and there were no visible ultrastructural abnormalities. Low transgene expressors developed heavy proteinuria, foot process effacement, GBM thickening, and renal failure by 3 months, while high expressors displayed only mild proteinuria by 9 months. In vitro studies revealed that the R246Q mutation impairs the secretion of laminin. These findings suggest that the R246Q mutation causes nephrotic syndrome by disrupting the secretion of laminin-521 from podocytes into the GBM. However, increased expression of the mutant protein can partially overcome this secretion defect and enhance glomerular permselectivity.

title: Interleukin-33 prevents apoptosis and improves survival after experimental myocardial infarction through ST2 signaling.
text:
BACKGROUND:
ST2 is an interleukin (IL)-1 receptor family member with membrane-bound (ST2L) and soluble (sST2) isoforms, and sST2 serves as a biomarker for poor outcomes in patients with myocardial infarction (MI). IL-33, a recently discovered ligand for ST2, can activate nuclear factor kappaB, potentially regulating apoptotic cell death. We sought to test the hypothesis that IL-33 is cardioprotective after MI through ST2 signaling.
METHODS AND RESULTS:
We protected cultured cardiomyocytes from hypoxia-induced apoptosis using IL-33, and this cardioprotection was partially inhibited by sST2. IL-33 increased expression of antiapoptotic factors, including XIAP, cIAP1, and survivin. To investigate the cardioprotective role of IL-33 in vivo, we conducted a blinded and randomized study of ischemia/reperfusion in rats. IL-33 reduced cardiomyocyte apoptosis, suppressed caspase-3 activity, and increased expression of an IAP family member protein. IL-33 decreased both infarct and fibrosis volumes at 15 days, and both echocardiographic and hemodynamic studies revealed that IL-33 improved ventricular function. To determine whether cardioprotection by IL-33 is mediated through ST2 signaling, we conducted a randomized and blinded study of ST2(-/-) versus wild-type mice in 98 mice subjected to MI. At 4 weeks after MI, IL-33 reduced ventricular dilation and improved contractile function in wild-type mice but not in ST2(-/-) mice. Moreover, IL-33 improved survival after MI in wild-type but not in ST2(-/-) mice.
CONCLUSIONS: IL-33 prevents cardiomyocyte apoptosis and improves cardiac function and survival after MI through ST2 signaling.

title: The impact of open versus closed format ICU admission practices on the outcome of high risk surgical patients: a cohort analysis
text:
In 2000, the organizational structure of the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) at Zaandam Medical Centre (ZMC) transitioned from an open to a closed format. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of this change on patient outcomes in high-risk surgical patients.
Medical records of consecutive high-risk surgical patients admitted to the ICU between 1996 and 1998 (open format) and 2003 and 2005 (closed format) were reviewed. Patients were defined as high-risk based on the Identification of Risk in Surgical patients (IRIS) score. The study assessed mortality, morbidity, ICU length of stay (LOS), and hospital LOS.
The mortality rate in the ICU patients was 25.7% in the open format group and 15.8% in the closed format group (p = 0.01). Morbidity also decreased from 48.6% to 46.1% (p = 0.6), with a slight decrease in hospital LOS from 17 days to 21 days (p = 0.03).
This study suggests that a closed ICU format may be more advantageous in minimizing the adverse effects of high-risk surgery and ensuring optimal care for these patients. High-risk surgical patients require specialized treatment and close monitoring to ensure maximum safety. Our findings support the idea that a closed ICU format can provide a safer environment for these patients.

title: Induction therapy with autologous mesenchymal stem cells in living-related kidney transplants: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
BACKGROUND: Antibody-based induction therapy combined with calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) has shown to reduce acute rejection rates in kidney transplant recipients; however, opportunistic infections and CNI toxicities remain a significant challenge. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have successfully treated graft-versus-host disease, and this study aimed to assess the replacement of antibody induction therapy with autologous MSCs in patients with end-stage renal disease undergoing ABO-compatible, cross-match-negative kidney transplants from living-related donors.
METHODS: This single-center, prospective, open-label, randomized study enrolled 159 patients between February 2008 and May 2009. Patients were inoculated with marrow-derived autologous MSCs (1-2 x 10(6)/kg) at kidney reperfusion, and two weeks later, and were randomly assigned to receive standard-dose (n = 53) or low-dose (n = 52) CNIs. A control group of 51 patients received anti-IL-2 receptor antibody plus standard-dose CNIs. The primary outcome measure was the incidence of acute rejection and renal function (estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR]) at 1 year, with secondary measures including patient and graft survival and adverse events.
RESULTS: Patient and graft survival at 13 to 30 months were similar in all groups. At 6 months, 4 of 53 patients (7.5%) in the autologous MSC plus standard-dose CNI group (95% CI, 0.4%-14.7%; P = 0.04) and 4 of 52 patients (7.7%) in the low-dose group (95% CI, 0.5%-14.9%; P = 0.046) had biopsy-confirmed acute rejection, compared to 11 of 51 controls (21.6%; 95% CI, 10.5%-32.6%). None of the patients in either autologous MSC group had glucorticoid-resistant rejection, while 4 patients (7.8%) in the control group did (95% CI, 0.6%-15.1%; overall P = 0.02). Renal function recovered faster among both MSC groups, showing increased eGFR levels during the first month after surgery compared to the control group. Patients receiving standard-dose CNI had a mean difference of 6.2 mL/min per 1.73 m(2) (95% CI, 0.4-11.9; P = 0.04) and those in the low-dose group had a mean difference of 10.0 mL/min per 1.73 m(2) (95% CI, 3.8-16.2; P = 0.002). Furthermore, combined analysis of MSC-treated groups revealed a significantly decreased risk of opportunistic infections in the MSC-treated groups compared to the control group (hazard ratio, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.20-0.85; P = 0.02).
CONCLUSION: In this study, the use of autologous MSCs compared to anti-IL-2 receptor antibody induction therapy resulted in lower incidence of acute rejection, decreased risk of opportunistic infections, and better estimated renal function at 1 year.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT00658073.

title: Cerebral cortex assembly: generating and reprogramming projection neuron diversity
text: The cortical region of the mammalian brain is crucial for advanced cognitive, motor, and associative functions. Within the central nervous system (CNS), the cortex stands out as a prime example of remarkable neuronal diversity, categorized into two main groups: excitatory projection neurons (PNs) and inhibitory interneurons (INs). This review focuses on recent advances in understanding the strategies and mechanisms that shape PN diversity during embryonic development, and examines how these classes persist throughout an organism's lifetime. Furthermore, we speculate on the intriguing possibility that PNs could be reprogrammed to enhance cortical plasticity in adults through directed changes to their class-specific features.

title: Mechanical modulation of receptor-ligand interactions at cell-cell interfaces.
text:
Cell surface receptors have been extensively studied due to their role in initiating and regulating signal transduction cascades, leading to various functional cellular outcomes. One class of immune receptors, such as T-cell antigen receptors, whose ligands are anchored to the surfaces of other cells, remains poorly understood. The mechanism by which ligand binding initiates receptor phosphorylation, termed "receptor triggering," is controversial. Recent direct measurements of the receptor-ligand complex lifetimes at the cell-cell interface revealed that these lifetimes are shorter than those in solution, but the underlying mechanism is unknown. At the cell-cell interface, the receptor-ligand complex spans a short intermembrane distance of 15 nm compared to long surface molecules (LSMs) whose ectodomains span over 40 nm, and these LSMs include phosphatases such as CD45 that dephosphorylate the receptor. It has been proposed that size-based segregation of LSMs from the receptor-ligand complex is a mechanism of receptor triggering, but it is unclear whether this mechanism can support such small-scale segregation.
To investigate, we developed a nanometer-scale mathematical model that couples membrane elasticity with the compressional stiffness and lateral mobility of LSMs. Our findings show robust supradiffusive segregation of LSMs from a single receptor-ligand complex. The model predicts that LSM redistribution will result in a time-dependent tension on the complex, leading to a decreased two-dimensional lifetime. Interestingly, the model predicts a nonlinear relationship between the three- and two-dimensional lifetimes, which can enhance the ability of receptors to discriminate between similar ligands.
In conclusion, our study demonstrates that theoretical modeling can provide important insights into the mechanisms underlying receptor triggering. The predicted supradiffusive segregation of LSMs from a receptor-ligand complex and the nonlinear relationship between the three- and two-dimensional lifetimes provide new directions for future experimental studies.

title: High-performance neuroprosthetic control by an individual with tetraplegia.
text:
BACKGROUND: Loss of arm function due to paralysis or amputation can result in significant impairment in everyday activities, including the inability to manipulate, grasp, and carry objects. Brain-machine interfaces (BMIs) have the potential to restore some of these lost functions. In this study, we investigated the feasibility of using BMIs to control a high-performance prosthetic limb in an individual with tetraplegia.
METHODS: We implanted two 96-channel intracortical microelectrodes in the motor cortex of a 52-year-old individual with tetraplegia and conducted BMI training for 13 weeks. The goal was to enable the participant to control an anthropomorphic prosthetic limb with seven degrees of freedom (three-dimensional translation, three-dimensional orientation, and one-dimensional grasping) using the BMI interface. The participant's ability to control the prosthetic limb was evaluated using clinical measures of upper limb function.
FINDINGS: The participant was able to move the prosthetic limb in a three-dimensional workspace on the second day of training and demonstrated robust seven-dimensional movements after 13 weeks of training. The participant's success rate in target-based reaching tasks increased from 6.2% (chance level) to 91.6% (mean), with improvements observed in completion time (from 148 seconds to 112 seconds) and path efficiency (from 0.30 to 0.38). The participant was also able to use the prosthetic limb to perform skilful and coordinated reach and grasp movements, resulting in significant gains in tests of upper limb function. No adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The findings of this study suggest that BMIs have the potential to restore natural and intuitive command signals for hand placement, orientation, and reaching in individuals with long-term paralysis. If further developed and refined, BMIs could enable individuals with paralysis or amputation to perform everyday activities with greater ease and independence.
FUNDING: This study was supported by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, National Institutes of Health, Department of Veterans Affairs, and the UPMC Rehabilitation Institute.

title: Phase locking and multiple oscillating attractors for the coupled mammalian clock and cell cycle.
text: Daily synchronous patterns of cell division are observed across various species, suggesting that the circadian clock and cell cycle oscillators are coupled. While the mechanistic interactions between these oscillators are known for mammals, the impact of their coupling on cell and clock progression, as well as its biological relevance, remains unexplored. To address this question, we used multispectral imaging of single live cells, computational methods, and mathematical modeling to investigate the daily rhythm at the tissue level in proliferating mouse fibroblasts. Our findings show that unsynchronized cells robustly phase-lock their cell cycle and circadian clocks in a 1:1 ratio, resulting in synchronized oscillations with a common frequency in an expanding cell population. Dexamethasone-induced synchronization reveals additional clock states, including a low-period phase-locked state and higher-period coexisting states. Cells transition to these states after dexamethasone synchronization. The synchronization of cell division at the single-cell level has significant implications, as disordered circadian function has been linked to the pathogenesis of many diseases, including cancer.

title: Moderate effect of artemisinin-based combination therapy on transmission of Plasmodium falciparum.
text:
Background: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) reduces both microscopically confirmed gametocytemia and mosquito infection. However, recent molecular studies have shown that submicroscopic gametocytemia are common. This study aimed to determine the effects of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) monotherapy, SP plus amodiaquine (AQ), SP plus artesunate (AS), and artemether-lumefantrine (AL; Coartem) on submicroscopic gametocytemia and infectiousness in children.
Methods: In this randomized clinical trial, 528 children aged 6 months to 10 years were enrolled and assigned to one of four treatment groups. Gametocytemia were detected using both microscopy and Pfs25 RNA-based quantitative nucleic acid sequence-based amplification (Pfs25 QT-NASBA). Transmission was evaluated through membrane-feeding assays.
Results: The prevalence of gametocytes, as determined by Pfs25 QT-NASBA, was 89.4% (219/245) at enrollment and decreased after treatment with SP plus AS, SP plus AQ, and AL. Membrane-feeding assays revealed that the proportion of infectious children was significantly higher than expected based on microscopy findings, with a fourfold increase in infectiousness. ACT did not significantly reduce the proportion of infectious children, but it did reduce the proportion of infected mosquitoes.
Conclusions: Submicroscopic gametocytemia are common after treatment and contribute significantly to mosquito infection. While ACT reduces the proportion of infected mosquitoes, its effect on malaria transmission appears to be moderate and limited to the duration of gametocyte carriage and the proportion of mosquitoes that are infected by carriers. These findings should be interpreted in the context of transmission intensity.

title: Lip movements entrain the observers’ low-frequency brain oscillations to facilitate speech intelligibility
text: During fluent speech, lip movements offer visual timing cues that aid in speech perception. By utilizing MEG, we directly investigated the relationship between these visual cues and rhythmic brain activity in participants who are both listening to and observing the speaker. Our initial investigation revealed a close coordination between the neural oscillations in the visual cortex and the speaker's lip movements, indicating significant entrainment. To isolate the visual signal's influence, we employed partial coherence to filter out the coherent auditory speech signal's contribution to the lip-brain coherence. Analyzing the synchronization between different attentional conditions revealed that enhancing visual attention improves the coherence between neural activity in the visual cortex and the speaker's lips. Moreover, we discovered a significant partial coherence between the left motor cortex and lip movements, which directly predicted comprehension accuracy. Our findings underscore the significance of visually entrained and attention-modulated rhythmic brain activity in facilitating enhanced audiovisual speech processing.

title: Loss of DExD/H box RNA helicase LGP2 manifests disparate antiviral responses.
text: Two key intracellular receptors, RIG-I and MDA5, recognize virus infection and produce type I interferons (IFNs) through their ability to recognize viral RNA. A third helicase gene, Lgp2, is similar to Rig-I and Mda5 but lacks the domain responsible for activating caspases and recruiting other proteins. To investigate the role of Lgp2 in IFN production, we generated mice lacking this gene and observed that their cells were more sensitive to the induction of type I IFN by cytosolic polyinosinic/polycytidylic acid. Despite this sensitization, we found that the ability of Lgp2 to inhibit IFN-beta transcription was not compromised, suggesting that Lgp2 is not the primary negative regulator of type I IFN production. Our findings also indicate that Lgp2-deficient mice were resistant to lethal vesicular stomatitis virus infection, which is recognized specifically by RIG-I, but showed a defect in type I IFN production against encephalomyocarditis virus infection, which activates MDA5-dependent innate immune responses. Overall, our data suggest a distinct regulatory role for LGP2 in triggering innate immune signaling pathways following RNA virus infection.

title: Three-dimensional, single-molecule fluorescence imaging beyond the diffraction limit by using a double-helix point spread function.
text:
We have achieved three-dimensional single-molecule fluorescence imaging beyond the optical diffraction limit using a wide-field microscope equipped with a novel double-helix point spread function (DH-PSF). The DH-PSF design features a high and uniform Fisher information density, with two prominent lobes in the image plane that orientate themselves with the axial position of the emitter. By localizing individual fluorescent molecules in a thick polymer sample to within 10-20 nanometers over a depth of field of 2 micrometers in a single 500-millisecond acquisition, we demonstrate the capability of our technique to achieve superresolution imaging of high concentrations of molecules in all three dimensions.
To further enhance the resolution, we utilize a photoactivatable fluorophore, which enables repeated imaging of sparse subsets with the DH-PSF microscope, resulting in superior 3D imaging beyond the Rayleigh diffraction limit. The combination of optimized optical PSF design and digital postprocessing methods opens up new possibilities for improving resolution in imaging techniques.

title: A unique cell division machinery in the Archaea.
text: In contrast to the cell division machineries found in bacteria, euryarchaea, and eukaryotes, no division components have been identified in the second major archaeal phylum, Crenarchaeota. However, our study reveals that a three-gene operon, cdv, in the crenarchaeon Sulfolobus acidocaldarius, forms a distinct cell division machinery. The operon is activated at the onset of genome segregation and division and the Cdv proteins polymerize between segregating nucleoids, persisting through cell division to form a smaller structure during constriction. Interestingly, the cdv operon is down-regulated after UV irradiation, indicating inhibition of division in response to DNA damage, similar to eukaryotic checkpoint systems. Moreover, the cdv genes show a unique phylogenetic range compared to FtsZ-based archaeal division systems, where either one or the other system is present in most archaeal lineages. Two of the Cdv proteins, CdvB and CdvC, share homology with components of the eukaryotic ESCRT-III sorting complex involved in budding of luminal vesicles and HIV-1 virion release, suggesting similar mechanisms and a common evolutionary origin.

title: Modelling and rescuing neurodevelopmental defect of Down syndrome using induced pluripotent stem cells from monozygotic twins discordant for trisomy 21
text: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common genetic condition causing intellectual disability and other developmental abnormalities. To better understand how this condition develops, we created induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from twins who had trisomy 21. By doing this, we could avoid the differences in genetic background that might affect our results. Our analysis of the iPSCs and early development showed that Down syndrome has a unique pattern of gene expression, which we called the "developmental disease transcriptional signature." We also found that the iPSCs had problems forming neurons and glia in mice and in a lab dish. These problems were associated with changes in the structure and number of neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, and with abnormal expression of genes involved in brain development. We also found that a protein called DYRK1A on chromosome 21 might be responsible for these problems. Interestingly, we found that treating the iPSCs with a drug or by blocking the DYRK1A protein with small RNA molecules could fix some of these problems.

title: Programmed death-1–induced interleukin-10 production by monocytes impairs CD4+ T cell activation during HIV infection
text: During HIV infection, the replication of the virus and the migration of microbes from the gut to the bloodstream lead to an overactive immune response, known as hyperimmune activation. This can cause a decline in the number of CD4+ T cells. Two proteins, Programmed death-1 (PD-1) and interleukin-10 (IL-10), are upregulated during HIV infection. Blocking the interactions between PD-1 and programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) and between IL-10 and IL-10 receptor (IL-10R) can lead to the clearance of viruses and improved T cell function in animal models of chronic viral infections. Interestingly, we have found that high levels of microbial products and inflammatory cytokines in the blood of HIV-infected individuals lead to an increase in the expression of PD-1 on monocytes, which correlates with high levels of IL-10 in the plasma. When PD-1 on monocytes is triggered by PD-L1 on other cells, it leads to the production of IL-10, which in turn causes CD4+ T cell dysfunction. Our findings suggest a new function for PD-1, whereby microbial products inhibit T cell expansion and function by increasing PD-1 expression and IL-10 production by monocytes after the binding of PD-1 by PD-L1.

title: A general role for splicing enhancers in exon definition.
text: Exonic splicing enhancers (ESEs) play a crucial role in defining exons by modulating the recruitment of splicing factors to adjacent introns. Our study reveals that ESEs can activate suboptimal 5' and 3' splice sites independently when located on different exons. However, when situated within the same exon, ESEs simultaneously activate the same weak 5' and 3' splice sites. These findings indicate that a single ESE can orchestrate the recognition of both exon/intron junctions within the same splicing event. Our results suggest that ESEs recruit a multi-component complex consisting of splicing machinery components necessary for 5' and 3' splice site selection.

title: SecDFyajC is not required for the maintenance of the proton motive force.
text: The SecDFyajC protein of Escherichia coli plays a crucial role in the export of proteins outside the cell in vivo. However, the specific function of SecDFyajC in protein translocation remains unclear. To investigate this, we evaluated the role of SecDFyajC in maintaining the proton motive force, or the energy gradient across the inner membrane of the cell. Our findings showed that inner membrane vesicles (IMVs) lacking SecDFyajC have a reduced ability to generate a stable proton motive force when energized with succinate. This effect was not observed when NADH was used as an electron donor. Additionally, the proton motive force generated in SecDFyajC-depleted vesicles was found to stimulate protein translocation to the same extent as in IMVs containing SecDFyajC. Further analysis revealed that the reduced proton motive force in SecDFyajC-depleted vesicles was due to lower levels of the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase, which is repressed by growth on glucose media. These results collectively suggest that SecDFyajC is not essential for proton motive force-driven protein translocation.

title: The serine protease inhibitor SerpinA3N attenuates neuropathic pain by inhibiting T cell-derived leukocyte elastase
text: Neuropathic pain is a significant and intractable clinical problem, with an incomplete understanding of its pathophysiology. Recent gene expression profiling studies have identified potential targets for pain therapy, but classical study designs have yielded inconsistent results due to the differential expression of hundreds of genes between sham and nerve-injured groups, which can be challenging to validate. To address this, we used two outbred strains of rats that are genetically similar but differentially bred for differences in neuropathic pain sensitivity. We found that SerpinA3N, a serine protease inhibitor, was upregulated in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) after nerve injury, and its mouse homolog was further validated. Mice lacking SerpinA3N exhibited increased neuropathic mechanical allodynia compared to wild-type (WT) mice, and exogenous delivery of SerpinA3N attenuated mechanical allodynia in WT mice. Additionally, we observed that T cells infiltrate the DRG after nerve injury and release leukocyte elastase (LE), which was inhibited by SerpinA3N derived from DRG neurons. Genetic loss of LE or exogenous application of a LE inhibitor (Sivelastat) in WT mice attenuated neuropathic mechanical allodynia. Overall, our findings reveal a novel and clinically relevant role for SerpinA3N and the crosstalk between neurons and T cells in the modulation of neuropathic pain.

title: Tissue Transglutaminase Is an Integrin-Binding Adhesion Coreceptor for Fibronectin
text: The protein tissue transglutaminase binds tightly to fibronectin in a laboratory setting through its 42-kD gelatin-binding domain. We have found that cell-surface transglutaminase facilitates the adhesion and spreading of cells on the 42-kD fibronectin fragment, which lacks regions that bind to integrins. Overexpressing tissue transglutaminase results in more of it being present on the cell surface, enhances adhesion and spreading on both the 42-kD fibronectin fragment and the full-length protein, amplifies the phosphorylation of focal adhesion kinase in response to adhesion, and increases the size of focal adhesions. These effects are unique to tissue transglutaminase and are not seen with its functional cousin, a catalytic subunit of factor XIII. Tissue transglutaminase's adhesive properties do not require its cross-linking activity but instead depend on its stable noncovalent association with integrins. Transglutaminase interacts directly with multiple integrins from the β1 and β3 subfamilies, but not with those from the β2 integrin subfamily. Complexes of tissue transglutaminase and integrins are formed inside the cell during synthesis and accumulate on the cell surface and in focal adhesions. Our results demonstrate that tissue transglutaminase acts as an integrin-associated coreceptor to promote cell adhesion and spreading by interacting with fibronectin.

title: Imaging the expression of transfected genes in vivo.
text: For the first time, successful gene transduction has been demonstrated in vivo using an appropriate combination of "marker gene" and "marker substrate" in an experimental animal model. The herpes simplex virus 1 thymidine kinase (HSV1-tk) gene was selected as an example of a marker gene, and the recombinant STK retrovirus containing HSV1-tk was used to transduce RG2 glioma cells in vitro and in vivo. RG2TK+ cell lines expressing the HSV1-tk gene and three potential marker substrates for the HSV1-TK enzyme were evaluated. The results showed that radiolabeled 5-iodo-2'-fluoro-2'deoxy-1-beta-D-arabinofuranosyluracil (FIAU) was a significantly better marker substrate for the HSV1-TK enzyme compared to 5-iodo-2'-deoxyuridine or ganciclovir. The magnitude of FIAU accumulation in different RG2TK+ clones corresponded to their sensitivity to ganciclovir and the level of HSV1-tk mRNA expression. Imaging the expression of HSV1-tk in transduced RG2 tumor cells was demonstrated in animals using quantitative autoradiography, and the results showed that 2-[14C]FIAU accumulation was high in RG2TK+ brain tumors growing in one hemisphere and very low in nontransduced RG2 tumors in the contralateral hemisphere. Transduction of RG2 tumor cells with the HSV-tk gene in vivo resulted in tumors that accumulated FIAU to high levels and produced clearly defined images, suggesting that a clinically applicable method for imaging HSV1-tk gene expression can be implemented using existing clinical imaging techniques.

title: Engulfment of apoptotic cells: signals for a good meal
text: The removal of dying cells by immune cells is an essential mechanism that helps maintain the body's homeostasis, and any disruptions to this process can lead to serious immune-related issues. In recent years, groundbreaking research has shed new light on the process of phagocytosis, including how immune cells locate and consume apoptotic cells, how they recognize and engulf these targets, and how they maintain cellular balance after the 'meal'. Several newly discovered factors influencing this process have been identified, while others that were once thought to be key players require revision. This review aims to summarize these recent advancements and highlight the most pressing questions still remaining in this field.

title: Related IgA1 and IgG producing cells in blood and diseased mucosa in ulcerative colitis.
text:
Background: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by an infiltration of the colonic mucosa with plasma cells producing IgG autoantibodies. It is unclear whether this responses represents a local mucosal response that has switched to IgG or a peripheral response that may have been initiated by peripheral antigen that homed to the colonic mucosa. The clonal distribution of IgG secreting cells and isotype switched variants in UC is also unknown.
Aims: To investigate the clonal distribution of mucosal IgG in UC and to search for related IgG and IgA secreting cells in normal and diseased mucosa and blood in UC. To investigate characteristics that may discriminate between the mucosal and peripheral repertoire in the normal mucosa and in UC.
Methods: Blood and normal and diseased mucosa from two patients with UC were studied. Immunoglobulin gene analysis and clone-specific polymerase chain reaction were used to investigate the clonal distribution and characteristics of IgG and related IgA in the mucosa and blood of patients with UC.
Results: The IgG response in the mucosa of UC patients included widespread clones of cells that were present in both the diseased mucosa and blood but were scarce in normal mucosa. Clonally related IgA class switch variants, all IgA1, were detected but only in the diseased mucosa and blood. This suggests that these clones home preferentially to the diseased mucosa. Additionally, J(H)1 usage was characteristic of the peripheral repertoire, and examples of J(H)1 usage were observed in mucosal IgG in UC.
Conclusions: These data suggest that a peripheral response is expressed and expanded in the colonic mucosa in UC.

title: Geovisual analytics to enhance spatial scan statistic interpretation: an analysis of U.S. cervical cancer mortality
text:
Kulldorff's spatial scan statistic and its implementation, SaTScan, are widely used for detecting and evaluating geographic clusters, but two issues hinder their effective interpretation: (1) the lack of cartographic support for understanding the clusters in a geographic context, and (2) the sensitivity of results to parameter choices, which are critical for identifying and interpreting clusters. We address these issues by integrating novel and established geovisual analytics methods to improve the interpretation of SaTScan results. In a case study analyzing cervical cancer mortality in the US, we demonstrate our approach by providing an interactive visual interface to support the interpretation of SaTScan results, and by conducting multiple SaTScan runs with systematically selected parameters to investigate cluster result stability. Our method distinguishes between heterogeneous and homogeneous clusters and evaluates their stability across different analytic scales.
Our approach combines SaTScan with a visual analytic platform, allowing users to interactively explore and compare SaTScan results produced by different parameter choices. We visualize Standardized Mortality Ratio and reliability scores for all counties to identify stable, homogeneous clusters. Our analysis compares favorably to methods such as Empirical Bayes Smoothing and Kafadar spatial smoother. We developed and implemented our geovisual analytics approach in our Java-based Visual Inquiry Toolkit.

title: Neurological development of 5-year-old children receiving a low-saturated fat, low-cholesterol diet since infancy: A randomized controlled trial.
text:
Early childhood nutrition plays a vital role in preventing atherosclerosis, a condition characterized by the buildup of plaque in the arteries. While it is established that early nutritional habits can help prevent atherosclerosis, there is limited research on their effect on neurological development during the first five years of life. This study aimed to investigate the impact of parental counseling on the dietary habits of children during their early years, and its effect on their neurological development.
The study was conducted as a randomized controlled trial in an outpatient clinic in Turku, Finland, between 1990 and 1996. A total of 1062 seven-month-old infants and their parents were recruited at well-baby clinics, and 496 of these children were available for neurodevelopmental testing at the age of five. The participants were randomly assigned to either an intervention group or a control group.
The intervention group received individualized counseling from healthcare professionals to limit their fat intake to 30% to 35% of their daily energy, with a saturated:monounsaturated:polyunsaturated fatty acid ratio of 1:1:1, and a cholesterol intake of less than 200 mg/d. The control group received usual health education. The researchers evaluated the nutrient intake, serum lipid concentrations, and neurological development of the children in both groups at age five.
The results of the study showed that the intervention group had significantly lower intakes of fat, saturated fat, and cholesterol than the control group. At age five, the mean percentage of daily energy intake for total fat, saturated fat, and cholesterol in the intervention group were 30.6%, 11.7%, and 164.2 mg, respectively, compared to 33.4%, 14.5%, and 192.5 mg in the control group. The serum cholesterol concentrations were 3% to 5% lower in the intervention group compared to the control group. Additionally, the neurological development of the children in the intervention group was at least as good as that of the children in the control group. The relative risks for the intervention group to fail tests of speech and language skills, gross motor functioning plus perception, and visual motor skills were 0.95, 0.95, and 0.65, respectively, compared to the control group.
In conclusion, this study suggests that repeated child-targeted dietary counseling of parents during the first five years of a child's life can lessen age-associated increases in children's serum cholesterol levels and is compatible with normal neurological development.

title: Vasodilator responses of coronary resistance arteries of exercise-trained pigs.
text:
background: The purpose of this study was to investigate whether exercise training enhances the vasodilator response of coronary resistance arteries in pigs.
methods and results: The study included Yucatan miniature pigs that were randomly divided into exercise-trained (ET) and sedentary (SED) control groups. The ET group underwent progressive treadmill training for 16-20 weeks, while the SED group remained inactive. Coronary resistance arteries of 64-157 microns in diameter were isolated for in vitro testing of endothelium-independent dilators, including sodium nitroprusside and adenosine, as well as endothelium-dependent dilator bradykinin. The relaxation responses to these dilators were not altered by exercise training. However, endothelium-dependent relaxation to bradykinin was enhanced in coronary resistance arteries from the ET group, indicative of increased endothelium-derived relaxing factor/nitric oxide production. To determine the mechanism underlying this training-induced change, responses to bradykinin were examined in the presence of indomethacin and nitro-monomethyl L-arginine (L-NMMA). Indomethacin and L-NMMA both inhibited the bradykinin-induced relaxation in vessels from both groups, but the training-induced enhancement of bradykinin responses was still present in vessels from the ET group. L-NMMA caused greater inhibition of bradykinin-induced relaxation in coronary resistance arteries from the ET pigs compared to the SED pigs, and eliminated the training-induced enhancement of bradykinin responses.
conclusions: These results suggest that exercise training enhances bradykinin-induced vasodilation through increased endothelium-derived relaxing factor/nitric oxide production by the L-arginine/nitric oxide synthase pathway.

title: Modulation of mitochondrial function and morphology by interaction of Omi/HtrA2 with the mitochondrial fusion factor OPA1.
text: The loss of Omi/HtrA2 function has been linked to nerve cell death in mouse models and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's and Huntington's disease. Omi/HtrA2 is a serine protease that is released from the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol, where it plays a protective role against cellular stress. However, the specific molecular mechanisms are not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigated the effects of Omi/HtrA2 deficiency on mitochondrial structure and function. We found that Omi/HtrA2 loss led to an accumulation of reactive oxygen species and a reduction in mitochondrial membrane potential. Using live cell imaging and electron microscopy, we observed elongated mitochondria in Omi/HtrA2-deficient cells, which was accompanied by abnormal cristae structure. We also found a selective up-regulation of the mitochondrial fusion protein OPA1 in Omi/HtrA2-deficient cells. Complementation of knockout cells with a wild-type Omi/HtrA2 restored the mitochondrial morphology and OPA1 levels. Furthermore, we demonstrated direct interaction between Omi/HtrA2 and endogenous OPA1 through co-immunoprecipitation. These findings suggest that impaired mitochondrial dynamics play a critical role in neurodegenerative disorders, and that Omi/HtrA2 is an important regulator of mitochondrial morphology and OPA1.

title: Four prognostic groups predict long-term survival from prostate cancer following radiotherapy alone on Radiation Therapy Oncology Group clinical trials.
text: In this study, we aimed to identify prognostic subgroups of men with clinically localized prostate cancer (CAP) treated with external beam radiotherapy (XRT) based on the combinations of their Gleason score (GS), T stage, and pathologic lymph node status. We analyzed data from 1557 men enrolled in four Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG) Phase III randomized trials conducted between 1975 and 1992. We found that combining patients based on their pretreatment DSS risk factors into four subgroups identified by their GS, T stage, and lymph node status led to a grouping of patients with similar risk of dying from prostate cancer. We found that the 5-, 10-, and 15-year disease-specific survival (DSS) rates were 96%, 86%, and 72%; 94%, 75%, and 61%; 83%, 62%, and 39%; and 64%, 34%, and 27% for Groups 1 through 4, respectively. These findings provide a basis for estimating the long-term DSS for men treated with XRT alone and should facilitate the design of future prospective randomized trials.

title: The pathogenesis of bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice.
