text: Administration of 0.5 mg bleomycin to mice every 2 weeks for 4 weeks led to the induction of pulmonary fibrosis. Initially, endothelial cells in the intima of pulmonary arteries and veins became edematous and separated from the underlying basement membrane, forming large blebs. This occurred after 2 weeks and was accompanied by the infiltration of perivascular spaces by lymphocytes and plasma cells. After 4 weeks, significant capillary endothelial blebbing and interstitial edema were observed, along with multifocal necrosis of type 1 alveolar epithelial cells and fibrinous exudation into the alveoli. The repair process was characterized by the proliferation and metaplasia of type 2 epithelial cells, fibroblastic organization of alveolar fibrin, and fibrosis of the interstitium within 8 to 12 weeks. The consistent induction of changes similar to those seen in diffuse pulmonary fibrosis or fibrosing alveolitis in humans suggests that bleomycin-induced lung injury may serve as a suitable model for investigating this poorly understood group of diseases.

title: The DNA damage response during mitosis.
text: The cellular system known as the DNA damage response (DDR) is intrinsic to cells and is activated when DNA damage is detected. The DDR's duty is to halt the cell cycle and fix the damaged DNA. DDR can either enable a cell to undergo repair or trigger its elimination through apoptosis or senescence. Depending on the stage of the cell cycle, the intensity of DDR signaling can alter. Specifically, only a slight reaction to DNA double strand breaks was found during mitosis. Research initially revealed that cells that were exposed to radiation during mitosis still reproduced without mending broken chromosomes. Those observations indicated a reduction in DNA repair and a lack of an immediate DNA damage-induced cell cycle arrest. New studies have shed light on how DDR signaling is mechanically rewired during mitosis. Mitotic cells do not simply inactivate the entire DDR, but instead designate their DNA damage for repair after mitotic exit. This information is essential for cancer therapy since it frequently includes drugs that induce DNA damage as well as medications that hinder mitotic progression. The review discussed in this article examines the molecular particulars of DDR signaling during mitosis and the repercussions of experiencing DNA damage during mitosis for a cell's fate.

title: Model-based Geostatistics
text: Geostatistics is focused on resolving estimation and prediction issues for spatially continuous phenomena using a limited number of data points collected across various locations. By employing general statistical principles of modeling and inference, model-based geostatistics offers a systematic approach to tackle complex geostatic problems. This groundbreaking volume is the first comprehensive treatment of model-based geostatistics, providing a thorough understanding of its applications and potential.

title: Placebo-Controlled Trials and Active-Control Trials in the Evaluation of New Treatments. Part 1: Ethical and Scientific Issues
text:
The article discusses the use of placebo-controlled trials in the development of new pharmaceuticals. Placebo-controlled trials are often challenged as unethical when a known effective treatment exists for a condition, but the authors argue that these trials can be ethically conducted even when effective therapy is available. They cite the Declaration of Helsinki, which states that "in any medical study, every patient, including those of a control group, if any, should be assured of the best proven diagnostic and therapeutic method." However, the authors argue that this sentence does not necessarily bar placebo-controlled trials whenever an effective treatment exists. They provide several reasons for this conclusion:
1. The requirement that all patients receive the best proven diagnostic and therapeutic method would bar not only placebo-controlled trials but also active-control and historically controlled trials.
2. It does not seem reasonable to consider as equivalent all failures to use known effective therapy.
3. There is good reason to doubt that the phrase was intended to discourage placebo-controlled trials.
The authors also discuss the issue of informed consent in placebo-controlled trials and the limitations of active-control equivalence trials (ACETs). They argue that ACETs are frequently needed to demonstrate the effectiveness of new treatments and that these trials cannot be replaced by placebo-controlled trials showing that a new drug is equivalent or noninferior to a known effective agent. The authors conclude that placebo-controlled trials may be ethically conducted even when effective therapy exists, as long as patients will not be harmed by participation and are fully informed about their alternatives.

title: Breath-methane in patients with cancer of the large bowel.
text: In a study of 30 patients with cancer of the large bowel, 24 (80%) had measurable levels of methane in their breath, compared to 25 (39%) of 64 patients with non-malignant large-bowel disease and 83 (40%) of 208 subjects without large-bowel disease. These findings suggest that there may be a distinction in anaerobic intestinal flora between patients with cancer of the large bowel and those without the disease. This distinction may have developed before the tumor formed or, alternatively, may result from the tumor.

title: Immune cells contribute to the maintenance of neurogenesis and spatial learning abilities in adulthood
text: Adult neurogenesis, or the birth of new neurons in the adult brain, has been shown to be mediated by T lymphocytes and microglia. This study demonstrates that an enriched environment can induce neurogenesis in the hippocampus, which is associated with the recruitment of T cells and the activation of microglia. In immune-deficient mice, however, hippocampal neurogenesis is impaired and cannot be enhanced by environmental enrichment. Interestingly, the introduction of T cells recognizing a specific CNS antigen can restore and boost hippocampal neurogenesis in these mice. Additionally, these same T cells are required for spatial learning and memory, as well as the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor in the dentate gyrus. This suggests that there may be a common immune-associated mechanism underlying different aspects of hippocampal plasticity and cell renewal in the adult brain.

title: Sperm cross-over activity in regions of the human genome showing extreme breakdown of marker association.
text: Recent studies on population diversity have offered profound, albeit indirect, insights into meiotic recombination across the human genome, revealing a landscape dominated by thousands of cross-over hotspots. However, only a few of these putative hotspots have been directly examined for cross-over activity. In this study, we aim to identify highly active cross-over hotspots by using a novel approach based on the extreme breakdown of marker association for high-resolution sperm cross-over analysis. This strategy led to the isolation of the most active cross-over hotspots to date. These hotspots exhibit morphology, sequence characteristics, and cross-over processes similar to those observed at less active hotspots, but their activity in sperm cannot be predicted from population diversity information. Some of these hotspots also showed evidence of biased gene conversion accompanying cross-over, which was sometimes correlated with variations in cross-over activity between men and presence/absence polymorphism in two hotspots. In contrast to expectations, the most active hotspots showed no evidence of rapid rate evolution or variation in activity between men, suggesting that extreme hotspots may be less vulnerable to attenuation by meiotic drive in favor of mutations that suppress recombination. Notably, these extremely active hotspots provide a valuable resource for elucidating meiotic recombination mechanisms and pathways in humans.

title: An efficient nonviral method to generate integration-free human-induced pluripotent stem cells from cord blood and peripheral blood cells.
text: The development of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) provides a valuable opportunity to use patient-specific somatic cells for disease modeling and drug discovery. To facilitate research using these cells, it is crucial to obtain iPSCs from easily accessible and less invasive tissues, such as blood. We have previously reported the efficient generation of human iPSCs from adult fibroblasts using a combination of plasmids encoding OCT3/4, SOX2, KLF4, L-MYC, LIN28, and shRNA for TP53. In this study, we modified this protocol to enable efficient iPSC induction from CD34+ cord blood cells and peripheral blood isolated from healthy donors using the same plasmid vectors. Initially, the plasmid mixture was able to induce iPSCs, but the efficiency was low. The addition of EBNA1, a critical factor for episomal amplification of the vectors, via an additional plasmid significantly improved the efficiency of iPSC induction, with the highest efficiency observed when inducing iPSCs from αβT cells. Using this approach, we were able to establish iPSC lines from seven healthy donors ranging in age from their 20s to their 60s. This method will be useful for generating patient-specific integration-free iPSCs and could also be applied to the generation of clinical-grade iPSCs in the future.

title: A rapamycin-sensitive signaling pathway contributes to long-term synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus.
text: New forms of long-lasting behavioral and synaptic plasticity require the synthesis of new proteins, such as long-term potentiation (LTP) that persists for over an hour. However, the signaling mechanisms that connect synaptic events to protein translation machinery during long-lasting synaptic plasticity are not well understood. One significant signaling pathway that is triggered by growth factors and results in the translation of specific mRNAs is the rapamycin-sensitive kinase mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), also known as FRAP and RAFT-1. mTOR, eukaryotic initiation factor-4E-binding proteins 1 and 2, and eukaryotic initiation factor-4E are present in the rat hippocampus, as revealed by Western blot analysis, and can be detected in the cell bodies and dendrites of hippocampal slices through immunostaining studies. In cultured hippocampal neurons, these proteins are present in dendrites, often near the presynaptic protein synapsin I. Moreover, their distribution overlaps entirely with the postsynaptic protein PSD-95 at synaptic sites. These observations suggest a postsynaptic localization for these proteins. Disrupting mTOR signaling with rapamycin leads to a reduction in late-phase LTP expression induced by high-frequency stimulation, with the early phase of LTP remaining unaffected. Rapamycin also hinders the synaptic potentiation induced by brain-derived neurotrophic factor in hippocampal slices. These findings demonstrate an essential role for rapamycin-sensitive signaling in the expression of two forms of synaptic plasticity that involve new protein synthesis. The localization of this translational signaling pathway at postsynaptic sites may provide a means of controlling local protein synthesis at potentiated synapses.

title: The FASEB Journal express article 10.1096/fj.00-0815fje. Published online June 27, 2001. Essential role for cholesterol in synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration
text:
Our previous research suggested a connection between lipid metabolism and amyloid beta protein (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease, which we referred to as 'the missing link in Alzheimer's puzzle' (FASEB J., Vol. 12, p. 1097, 1998). In the current study, we investigated the role of cholesterol in synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration using a combination of advanced technologies, including adult rat hippocampal slice culture, a well-established method for limiting cholesterol efflux, lipid metabolic labeling, extracellular recording of CA1 field excitatory postsynaptic potentials (fEPSPs), and immunofluorescence.
KEY FINDINGS

1. Increased cholesterol efflux impairs both short- and long-term synaptic plasticity: Synaptic plasticity is an essential feature of the central nervous system (CNS) that allows synapses to 'remember' past activity and adapt current synaptic function accordingly. In this study, we sought to determine whether increased cholesterol efflux, induced ex vivo using normal human CSF-HDL3 and methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) (a natural and model cholesterol absorption inhibitor), would have any impact on synaptic plasticity. Our findings demonstrated that enhanced cholesterol efflux indeed impairs both short-term and long-term synaptic plasticity, suggesting that cholesterol play a crucial role in maintaining optimal synaptic function.

title: Functional inhibition of osteoblastic cells in an in vivo mouse model of myeloid leukemia.
text: Pancytopenia, a primary complication of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), remains poorly understood. To delve into its underlying mechanisms, we utilized an immunocompetent murine model of AML. Leukemic mice displayed a suppression of osteoblastic cells, resulting in lower serum levels of the bone formation marker osteocalcin. Additionally, we observed a decrease in osteoprogenitor cells and endosteal-lining osteopontin(+) cells, as well as diminished osteocalcin mRNA expression in CD45(-) marrow cells. This led to a severe depletion of mineralized bone. Osteoclasts exhibited only a transient increase without significant bone resorption, and their inhibition only partially restored bone loss. In vitro experiments suggested that a leukemia-derived secreted factor might inhibit osteoblastic cells. Given that the chemokine CCL-3 was recently found to inhibit osteoblastic function in myeloma, we examined its expression in our model and in AML patient samples. Our findings showed that CCL-3 mRNA was significantly increased in malignant marrow cells from leukemic mice and in samples from AML patients. In light of these results, we propose that targeting the uncoupling of osteoblastic and osteoclastic cells may represent a novel approach to promote normal hematopoiesis in patients with myeloid neoplasms.

title: Fibroblast heterogeneity in the cancer wound
text: Fibroblasts play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity and function of healthy tissues, and they temporarily participate in tissue repair after acute inflammation. However, during chronic inflammatory states such as cancer, fibroblasts can assume an aberrant stimulatory role and contribute to the development of the tumor microenvironment. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) can modulate the tumor microenvironment and influence the behavior of neoplastic cells, either promoting or inhibiting tumor growth. The diverse functions of fibroblasts demonstrate their inherent plasticity, providing new opportunities for understanding and treating malignancies. In this article, we discuss the emerging themes of CAF biology in the context of tumorigenesis and therapy.

title: Cohort profile: the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS).
text: The China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) is a nationally representative, longitudinal survey of individuals aged 45 or older in China, as well as their spouses. The study assesses the social, economic, and health circumstances of community-dwelling residents, with a focus on the health and economic adjustments resulting from China's rapidly aging population. The national baseline survey for CHARLS was conducted between June 2011 and March 2012, using a face-to-face computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) and gathering physical measurements and blood samples at every two-year follow-up. A pilot study was conducted in two provinces of China in 2008, involving 2685 individuals, who were later resurveyed in 2012. To ensure the highest standards of research practice and international comparability of findings, CHARLS was harmonized with leading international research studies, such as the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) model. For more information, please contact Dr. Yaohui Zhao at yhzhao@nsd.edu.cn. All data collected by CHARLS are maintained at the National School of Development of Peking University and will be available to researchers worldwide at the study website. The 2008 pilot data for CHARLS are currently available at: http://charls.ccer.edu.cn/charls/. The national baseline data for the study are expected to be released in January 2013.

title: Central role of Th2/Tc2 lymphocytes in pattern II multiple sclerosis lesions
text:
OBJECTIVE: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a complex central nervous system (CNS) disease characterized by diverse pathological processes, including immune cell infiltration, humoral factor deposition, and loss of oligodendrocyte and myelin proteins. Based on histopathological criteria, four distinct lesion patterns have been identified. Pattern II is characterized by the simultaneous deposition of antibodies and complement proteins, in addition to T-cell infiltration. Given the limited access to brain-infiltrating T cells in MS, identifying and characterizing these cells is essential for understanding the pathogenic mechanisms of the disease.
METHODS: To address this objective, we employed next-generation sequencing to identify clonally expanded T cells in demyelinating pattern II brain autopsy lesions. Isolation of these T cells as clones from autologous cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and functional characterization were also conducted.
RESULTS: Our study revealed the presence of clonally expanded CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in demyelinating pattern II brain lesions. For the first time, these T cells were isolated as live T-cell clones. Functional analysis revealed that T cells releasing Th2 cytokines and capable of providing B cell help predominate the T-cell infiltrate in pattern II brain lesions.
INTERPRETATION: These findings provide the first functional evidence for the putative role of Th2/Tc2 cells in pattern II MS, challenging the conventional view of Th2 cells as protective in MS. Our observations have important implications for future treatment strategies in pattern II MS patients.

title: Coordinated oscillations in cortical actin and Ca2+ correlate with cycles of vesicle secretion
text: The actin cortex serves an ambiguous role in the exocytosis of secretory granules, simultaneously facilitating and hindering the process. Until now, it was unclear how cells reconciled these opposing functions. By investigating mast cells, we discovered that antigen activation triggers oscillations in calcium (Ca2+) and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) levels, leading to cyclic recruitment of N-WASP and cortical actin. Our experimental and computational analysis indicates that vesicle fusion coincides with the observed changes in actin and Ca2+ levels. The vesicle secretion cycle begins with actin capture of vesicles when cortical F-actin levels are high, followed by vesicle passage through the cortex when F-actin levels are low, and finally, vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane when Ca2+ levels rise. This orchestrated balance of Ca2+, PI(4,5)P2, and cortical F-actin allows cells to enhance secretion efficiency, revealing how the actin cortex can serve both as a carrier and a barrier for vesicle secretion.

title: WK175, a novel antitumor agent, decreases the intracellular nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide concentration and induces the apoptotic cascade in human leukemia cells.
text: We have recently developed a novel class of antitumor agents that demonstrate potent growth-inhibitory activity against various tumor cells cultured in vitro. As a representative model compound, we chose WK175, which exhibited strong in vitro efficacy. WK175 selectively reduces the intracellular levels of NAD+, leading to apoptotic cell death without causing DNA damage. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we conducted time-course studies in THP-1 (a human monocytic leukemia cell line) cells and found that WK175 activation of the apoptotic death signaling pathway involves the permeability transition pore, caspase 3, and caspase 9. Inhibition of these proteins by specific inhibitors confirmed their involvement in the WK175-induced apoptotic cascade. These results suggest that the decreased NAD+ concentration is the initiating event leading to the antitumor effect of WK175.

title: Husbands' involvement in delivery care utilization in rural Bangladesh: A qualitative study
text:
In Bangladesh, a major contributor to high maternal mortality rates is the lack of access to professional delivery care. To gain a deeper understanding of this issue, a qualitative study was conducted to examine the role of husbands during pregnancy and childbirth. Specifically, the study aimed to investigate the factors that influence husbands' support for their wives in utilizing professional maternal health services.
The study was conducted in a rural sub-district of Netrokona district, Bangladesh, and involved 20 semi-structured interviews with husbands in households that had recently given birth. The husbands were selected based on their household income, ethnicity, and proximity to the nearest hospital. The interviews were conducted in Bangla and later translated and analyzed using NVivo 9.0.
The study found that husbands who supported their wives in utilizing professional delivery care provided emotional, instrumental, and informational support during delivery. In contrast, husbands whose wives used untrained traditional birth attendants at home were uninvolved during delivery and believed that childbirth should take place at home according to local traditions.
The study's findings have significant implications for program planners, who should develop culturally sensitive strategies to involve husbands in maternal health interventions. Specifically, education campaigns targeted at husbands may be effective in promoting the use of professional delivery care among rural Bangladeshi women.

title: Mapping Meiotic Single-Strand DNA Reveals a New Landscape of DNA Double-Strand Breaks in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
text: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), which are produced by the Spo11 protein, catalyze meiotic recombination. Previous DSB mapping studies used rad50S or sae2Δ mutants, which are defective in break processing, to accumulate Spo11-linked DSBs and identify large (≥ 50 kb) "DSB-hot" regions that are separated by "DSB-cold" domains of similar size. Although substantial recombination occurs in some DSB-cold regions, indicating that DSB patterns are not typical in rad50S or sae2Δ mutants, we recently developed a novel method to map genome-wide single-strand DNA (ssDNA)-associated DSBs in repair-defective dmc1Δ and dmc1 rad51Δ mutants. DSBs were identified at known hot spots and in most previously defined "DSB-cold" regions, including near centromeres and telomeres. Although approximately 40% of the genome is DSB-cold in rad50S mutants, analysis of meiotic ssDNA from dmc1Δ showed that most of these regions have substantial DSB activity. Southern blot assays of DSBs in selected regions in dmc1Δ, rad50S, and wild-type cells confirmed these findings, indicating that DSBs are distributed much more uniformly than previously believed. Comparisons of DSB signals in dmc1, dmc1 rad51, and dmc1 spo11 mutant strains identified Dmc1 as a crucial strand-exchange activity genome-wide and confirmed that Spo11-induced lesions initiate all meiotic recombination.

title: Alterations in liver ATP homeostasis in human nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: a pilot study.
text:
The mechanisms driving the progression from fatty liver to steatohepatitis and cirrhosis are not well understood, and animal studies have suggested that altered hepatic energy homeostasis may play a role. To investigate this further, the authors of this study assessed the ability of patients with fatty liver disease to recover from hepatic ATP depletion.
The study included 8 patients with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and 7 healthy age- and sex-matched controls. The authors measured the levels of ATP in the liver before and after inducing transient hepatic ATP depletion through fructose injection. They found that patients had lower ATP levels in the liver than controls both before and after depletion, but controls were able to replenish their hepatic ATP stores during the 1-hour follow-up period. In contrast, patients were not able to fully recover their ATP levels.
The authors also found that body mass index (BMI) was inversely correlated with hepatic ATP recovery, even in controls. While BMI was higher in patients than controls, neither fatty liver nor serum aminotransferase elevations were strong predictors of hepatic ATP recovery. These findings suggest that impaired recovery from hepatic ATP depletion is a key feature of obesity-related nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.

title: Blockade of class IB phosphoinositide-3 kinase ameliorates obesity-induced inflammation and insulin resistance.
text: Obesity and insulin resistance, hallmarks of metabolic syndrome, are intricately linked with a chronic, low-grade inflammatory state defined by aberrant macrophage infiltration into adipose tissues. Although it has been established that chemokines stimulate leukocyte migration by activating class IB phosphoinositide-3 kinase (PI3Kγ) in inflammatory settings, the functional role of PI3Kγ in obesity-induced macrophage infiltration into tissues, systemic inflammation, and the development of insulin resistance remains understudied. In the present investigation, we employed murine models of both diet-induced and genetically induced obesity to investigate the role of PI3Kγ in the accumulation of tissue macrophages and the onset of obesity-induced insulin resistance. Mice lacking p110γ (Pik3cg(-/-)), the catalytic subunit of PI3Kγ, displayed improved systemic insulin sensitivity, accompanied by heightened insulin signaling in the tissues of obese animals. In adipose tissues and livers of obese Pik3cg(-/-) mice, there was a pronounced reduction in the number of infiltrated proinflammatory macrophages, leading to the attenuation of inflammatory reactions in these tissues. Furthermore, bone marrow-specific deletion and pharmacological inhibition of PI3Kγ also alleviated obesity-induced macrophage infiltration and insulin resistance. These findings suggest that PI3Kγ plays a pivotal role in the development of both obesity-induced inflammation and systemic insulin resistance, highlighting PI3Kγ as a potential therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes.

title: Identifying common impairments in frail and dependent older people: validation of the COPE assessment for non-specialised health workers in low resource primary health care settings
text:
Caring for Older People (COPE) is a multidimensional assessment tool designed to help community health workers (CHWs) identify and address clinically significant impairments in older adults in resource-poor settings. To evaluate the tool's effectiveness, CHWs assessed 150 older adults identified as frail or dependent using the COPE assessment tool, which gathered information on impairments in nutrition, mobility, vision, hearing, continence, cognition, mood, and behavior. These assessments were then compared to clinical examinations conducted by local physicians using the EASY-Care assessment tool.
The results showed that the COPE tool was easy to administer and provided CHWs with a better understanding of older adults' needs. However, the agreement between CHW and clinician assessments was only moderate (ranging from 45.8% to 91.3%) for most impairments. Notably, the prevalence of impairments was higher according to clinicians, particularly for visual impairment (98.7% vs 45.8%), cognitive impairment (78.4% vs. 38.2%), and depression (82.0% vs. 59.9%). Additionally, the COPE tool identified the majority of cases (72.2-98.5%) that were confirmed by clinicians as having clinically relevant problems. The levels of disability and needs for care among those identified by COPE were also higher than those identified by clinicians alone.
In conclusion, the COPE tool is a useful tool for identifying specific impairments in frail and dependent older adults in resource-poor settings. The tool is effective at targeting attention towards those with the most significant unmet needs, and can help improve the delivery of healthcare services to this vulnerable population.

title: The carboxyl terminus of human cytomegalovirus-encoded 7 transmembrane receptor US28 camouflages agonism by mediating constitutive endocytosis.
text: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) encodes four 7 transmembrane (7TM) chemokine receptors, including US28, which has been shown to exhibit both ligand-independent, constitutive activity and endocytosis. In this study, we investigate the separability of these two properties by creating chimeric and mutant US28 proteins with altered cytoplasmic tail (CT) or signaling properties. We find that the CT domain of US28 regulates receptor endocytosis independently of the signaling ability of the core domain, and this property is transposable to other 7TM receptors. Deletion of the US28 CT results in reduced constitutive endocytosis and enhanced signaling capacity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the constitutive endocytic property of US28 affects the action of its chemokine ligand fractalkine/CX3CL1, which acts as an agonist on US28 in the absence of the CT domain. This finding illustrates the important role of endocytic properties in modulating the activities of 7TM receptors and their ligands.

title: Geometry, epistasis, and developmental patterning.
text: Developmental signaling networks are composed of numerous components that are challenging to quantify in an embryo. Geometric reasoning enables the classification of a hierarchical structure of phenotypic models, comprising a limited number of composite variables, whose parameters can be defined using in vivo data. The development of the vulva in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans serves as a paradigm for the integration of two signaling pathways: induction by EGF and lateral signaling through Notch. Available data on the relative probabilities of the three potential terminal cell types in diverse genetic backgrounds, as well as timed ablation of the inductive signal, support one geometric model and enable the fitting of most of its parameters. This model is fully dynamic and encompasses both signaling and commitment, predicting correlated cell fate probabilities for crosses between any two genetic backgrounds/conditions. The two signaling pathways are combined additively, without interactions, and epistasis is solely the result of the nonlinear dynamical flow in the landscape defined by the geometric model. This approach quantitatively accounts for genetic experiments purporting to show mutual pathway repression. Additionally, the model quantifies the contributions of both extrinsic and intrinsic sources of noise in the penetrance of mutant phenotypes in signaling hypomorphs, and explains available experiments with no additional parameters. Finally, data from anchor cell ablation allow the parameters required to describe Notch autocrine signaling to be defined.

title: Table of Contents
text: The development of the C. elegans embryo is largely influenced by the formation of its epidermis, or hypodermis, a single layer of epithelial cells that encases the animal. The morphogenesis of the epidermis is a complex process involving cell-cell interactions with internal tissues, such as the developing nervous system and musculature, through multiple stages. Genetic analysis of mutants with abnormal epidermal structure has revealed key steps in epidermal development. In the wild type, epidermal cells are derived from among the four early blastomeres on the dorsal side of the embryo. The specification of epidermal fate is regulated by a hierarchy of transcription factors. Subsequent dorsal intercalation of epidermal cells involves a rearrangement of these cells. Most epidermal cells fuse to form multinucleate syncytia. The dorsal epidermal sheet undergoes epiboly to enclose the rest of the embryo in a process known as ventral enclosure, which requires both a continuous epidermal layer and functional neuroblasts. At least three distinct mechanisms are involved in the enclosure of different areas of the epidermis. Following enclosure, the epidermis extends, a process mediated by coordinated cell shape changes. Epidermal actin microfilaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments are essential for elongation, as are body wall muscles. The mature shape of the epidermis is maintained by the collagenous exoskeleton, secreted by the apical surface of the epidermis.

title: High-throughput sequencing reveals extensive variation in human-specific L1 content in individual human genomes.
text: Using next-generation sequencing, we developed a method to identify the insertion sites of nearly all members of the human-specific L1 retrotransposon family in any human genome. By incorporating diagnostic nucleotides, we were able to locate approximately 800 L1Hs copies, specifically within the pre-Ta, Ta-0, and Ta-1 L1Hs subfamilies, with over 90% of sequenced reads corresponding to human-specific elements. On average, we found that any two individual genomes differ at approximately 285 sites regarding L1 insertion presence or absence. To investigate this further, we analyzed 25 individuals, including 15 unrelated individuals, at 1139 sites, consisting of 772 shared with the reference genome and 367 non-reference L1 insertions. Our findings indicate that L1Hs profiles mirror genetic ancestry, and we were able to determine the chromosomal distribution of these elements. Based on these data, we estimate that the rate of L1 retrotransposition in humans is between 1/95 and 1/270 births, and the number of dimorphic L1 elements in the human population with gene frequencies greater than 0.05 is between 3000 and 10,000.

title: Nationwide trends in incidence, treatment and survival of colorectal cancer patients with synchronous metastases
text: In this study, we aimed to investigate trends in the incidence, treatment, and survival of colorectal cancer (CRC) patients with synchronous metastases (Stage IV) in the Netherlands over a 16-year period (1996-2011). We analyzed a nationwide, population-based dataset of 160,278 CRC patients, dividing the period into four consecutive periods and using Chi-square tests for trend analysis. Our findings revealed a significant increase in the proportion of Stage IV CRC patients from 19% (1996-1999) to 23% (2008-2011, p < 0.001), primarily due to a major increase in the incidence of lung metastases (from 1.7% to 5.0% of all CRC patients). During the study period, the resection of the primary tumor in Stage IV patients decreased (from 65% to 46%), while the use of systemic treatment and metastasectomy increased (from 29% to 60%). Additionally, an increase in metastasectomy was found in patients with only one metastatic site, particularly in patients with liver-only disease (from 5% to 18%, p < 0.001). Median survival for all Stage IV CRC patients improved from 7 to 12 months, with significant improvements in survival for patients with liver- or lung-only metastases (from 9 to 16 months and from 12 to 24 months, respectively, both p < 0.001). Overall, while survival has improved for Stage IV CRC patients over the past two decades, the prognosis of these patients has become increasingly diverse.

title: The curious case of the tumour virus: 50 years of Burkitt's lymphoma
text: Fifty years ago, Burkitt's lymphoma (BL) was first identified, and shortly afterwards, the detection of the first human tumour virus, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), in BL tumours occurred. Over time, the intricate relationship between EBV and BL has become increasingly complex. Initially, it was believed that EBV played a significant role in the development of BL, but subsequent research has revealed a more nuanced understanding of the intricate cellular and molecular interactions between EBV and B cells. Only recently have we begun to grasp the complex interplay between EBV and B cells, which can lead to the formation of BL. In this discussion, we delve into the intertwined histories of EBV and BL, and examine the cofactors involved in BL pathogenesis, including malaria and the MYC translocation.

title: Nanotoxicology: An Emerging Discipline Evolving from Studies of Ultrafine Particles
text:
Although humans have been exposed to airborne nanosized particles (NSPs; < 100 nm) throughout their evolutionary stages, the exposure has exponentially increased over the past century due to human-generated sources. The rapid development of nanotechnology is expected to become a new source of exposure via inhalation, ingestion, skin absorption, and injection of engineered nanomaterials. There is an urgent need for information on the safety and potential hazards of these particles, which can be gained from examining the results of studies on older biokinetic NSPs and newer epidemiologic and toxicologic studies with airborne ultrafine particles. The field of nanotoxicology, which can be defined as the safety evaluation of engineered nanostructures and nanodevices, can be derived from these studies. Some emerging concepts of nanotoxicology can be identified from the results of these studies, including:
1. Inhalation of specific sizes of NSPs results in efficient deposition in all regions of the respiratory tract through diffusional mechanisms. The small size allows for uptake into cells and transcytosis across epithelial and endothelial cells into the blood and lymph circulation, reaching potentially sensitive target sites such as bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen, and heart.
2. NSPs penetrating the skin can distribute via uptake into lymphatic channels. Endocytosis and biokinetics are greatly influenced by the NSP surface chemistry (coating) and in vivo surface modifications. The greater surface area per mass of NSPs renders them more active biologically, with the potential for inflammatory and pro-oxidant, but also antioxidant, activity.
3. Evidence of mitochondrial distribution and oxidative stress response after NSP endocytosis suggests the need for further research on their interactions with subcellular structures.
4. When assessing the safety of engineered NSPs, it is crucial to select appropriate and relevant doses/concentrations, as well as consider the likelihood of increased effects in a compromised organism. Additionally, the potential benefits of possible desirable effects should be taken into account.
5. An interdisciplinary team approach, involving toxicology, materials science, medicine, molecular biology, and bioinformatics, is necessary for nanotoxicology research to arrive at an appropriate risk assessment.

title: ADHD medications and risk of serious cardiovascular events in young and middle-aged adults.
text:
Certainly! Here's a reformulated version of the text:
Background: More than 1.5 million US adults use stimulants and other medications prescribed for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), which can increase heart rate and blood pressure, posing concerns about their cardiovascular safety. This study aimed to investigate whether current use of these medications is associated with a higher risk of serious cardiovascular events in young and middle-aged adults.
Methodology: This was a retrospective, population-based cohort study conducted using electronic health care records from four study sites (OptumInsight Epidemiology, Tennessee Medicaid, Kaiser Permanente California, and the HMO Research Network). Data from 150,359 adults aged 25-64 who dispensed medication for ADHD were analyzed, with each medication user matched to two nonusers based on study site, birth year, sex, and calendar year. Participants were followed for up to 806,182 person-years, during which 1357 cases of myocardial infarction (MI), 296 cases of sudden cardiac death (SCD), and 575 cases of stroke occurred.
Results: During the study period, there were 107,322 person-years of current use (median duration of 0.33 years), with a crude incidence rate of 1.34 (95% CI: 1.14-1.57) for MI, 0.30 (95% CI: 0.20-0.42) for SCD, and 0.56 (95% CI: 0.43-0.72) for stroke. In comparison, remote users had a crude incidence rate of 1.03 (95% CI: 0.86-1.24) for MI, 0.24 (95% CI: 0.16-0.34) for SCD, and 0.46 (95% CI: 0.35-0.60) for stroke. Multivariable-adjusted rate ratios showed that current use of ADHD medications was not associated with an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events (RR = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.72-0.96). Similarly, new users of these medications had an adjusted RR of 0.77 (95% CI: 0.63-0.94).
Conclusion: The study found that among young and middle-aged adults, current or new use of ADHD medications was not associated with an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events. These findings may be due to healthy-user bias, as individuals using these medications may have different health characteristics than nonusers. Further research is needed to confirm these results and to evaluate the cardiovascular safety of these medications.

title: The Rho GEFs LARG and GEF-H1 regulate the mechanical response to force on integrins
text: The response of individual cells to mechanical forces is a crucial area of interest for biologists, as forces can significantly impact cellular behavior. Applying forces to integrins leads to cytoskeletal rearrangements and growth of the associated adhesion complex, resulting in increased cellular stiffness, known as reinforcement. While RhoA has been implicated in reinforcement, the molecular mechanisms that govern its activity are unclear. By combining biochemical and biophysical approaches, we identified two guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), LARG and GEF-H1, as key regulators of the cellular response to force. Our findings show that activation of integrins under tensional forces triggers the activation of these two GEFs and their recruitment to adhesion complexes. Interestingly, we discovered that LARG is activated by the Src family tyrosine kinase Fyn, whereas GEF-H1's catalytic activity is enhanced by an ERK-mediated signaling cascade involving FAK and Ras.

title: Cell death from antibiotics without the involvement of reactive oxygen species.
text: Recent investigations have suggested that traditional antibiotics may kill bacteria by stimulating the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). If this theory holds true, it could pave the way for new strategies to enhance the effectiveness of antibiotics. In this study, we directly tested this notion. Contrary to expectations, antibiotic treatment did not accelerate the formation of hydrogen peroxide in Escherichia coli and did not increase intracellular free iron, a crucial component for the production of lethal damage. Lethality persisted even in the absence of oxygen, and DNA repair mutants were not more sensitive, casting doubt on the idea that toxicity results from oxidative DNA lesions. Our findings indicate that these antibiotic exposures did not generate ROS, and lethality most likely resulted from direct inhibition of cell wall assembly, protein synthesis, and DNA replication.

title: Pioneer Transcription Factors Target Partial DNA Motifs on Nucleosomes to Initiate Reprogramming
text: Pioneer transcription factors (TFs) initially open up silent chromatin, thereby initiating cellular changes, using various types of DNA binding domains (DBDs). FoxA, the prototype pioneer TF, features a winged helix DBD that resembles the structure of linker histones, allowing it to bind target sites on nucleosomes and compacted chromatin. In this study, we compare the ability of Oct4 (POU DBD), Sox2 (HMG box DBD), Klf4 (zinc finger DBD), and c-Myc (bHLH DBD) to target nucleosomes and compacted chromatin in somatic cells during reprogramming. In vitro, purified Oct4, Sox2, and Klf4 proteins can bind nucleosomes. In vivo, these factors preferentially bind to silent sites enriched with nucleosomes. Pioneer activity essentially refers to a DBD's ability to recognize and bind to partial nucleosome motifs on the surface of the nucleosome. This recognition can occur through cooperative binding between factors. Our findings provide insight into how pioneer factors can selectively target unoccupied regions of chromatin.

title: Experimental Evolution of an RNA Virus in Wild Birds: Evidence for Host-Dependent Impacts on Population Structure and Competitive Fitness
text: Within the realm of viruses, RNA viruses exhibit populations that are both genetically and phenotypically complex. Heterogeneity in RNA virus genomes arises due to the error-prone replication process and is partially understood. Understanding how natural selection molds RNA virus populations is crucial, as it can inform treatment strategies and enhance control measures. To explore this, we allowed West Nile virus (WNV) to replicate in wild-caught American crows, house sparrows, and American robins. By comparing the phenotype and population diversity of WNV after five sequential passages in each bird species, we discovered that fitness gains occur in a species-specific manner, with the greatest replicative fitness gains in robin-passaged WNV and the least in WNV passaged in crows. Moreover, sequencing data revealed that intrahost WNV populations were strongly influenced by purifying selection, while the overall complexity of the viral populations was similar among passaged hosts. However, the selective pressures that control WNV populations varied among bird species, with crow-passaged WNV populations containing the most unique mutations and defective genomes, but the lowest average mutation frequency. These findings suggest that virus replication in the most disease-susceptible bird species is positively associated with virus mutational tolerance, likely via complementation, and negatively associated with the strength of selection. These differences in genetic composition likely have distinct phenotypic consequences for the virus populations. In conclusion, these results provide important insights into how different hosts may contribute to the emergence of RNA viruses.

title: sasCIF: an extension of core Crystallographic Information File for SAS
text: Different data acquisition packages used at various small angle scattering facilities employ distinct formats for storing both raw and processed data. To promote seamless data exchange between laboratories, there has been a consensus among the small angle scattering community to adopt an ASCII format for one-dimensional data, which incorporates a self-explanatory header containing essential details about the sample and instrumentation conditions followed by raw or processed data in a tabular format. This format, known as sasCIF, has been designed as an extension of the core CIF (Crystallographic Information File) dictionary.

title: Migratory dendritic cells transfer antigen to a lymph node-resident dendritic cell population for efficient CTL priming.
text: Skin dendritic cells (DCs) are believed to play a crucial role in initiating local T cell immunity. Our study found that after skin infection with herpes simplex virus (HSV), cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activation required MHC class I-restricted presentation by non-migratory CD8(+) DCs rather than skin-derived DCs. Although migratory DCs did not directly present antigen, blocking their exit from infected skin significantly inhibited class I-restricted presentation and HSV-specific CTL responses. These findings support the idea that migrating DCs transport antigen to lymphoid-resident DCs for presentation and CTL priming, with the latter then amplifying the process through a larger network of DCs to efficiently activate T cells. Notably, robust CTL responses were observed with a relatively small number of skin-emigrant DCs, suggesting that inter-DC antigen transfer functions to amplify presentation across a larger network of DCs.

title: Thrombopoietin-induced Polyploidization of Bone Marrow Megakaryocytes Is Due to a Unique Regulatory Mechanism in Late Mitosis
text:
Megakaryocytes undergo a distinct differentiation process, becoming polyploid through repeated cycles of DNA synthesis without dividing. However, the mechanism behind this polyploidization remains unknown. Some scientists have suggested that polyploidization occurs when megakaryocytes skip a round of mitosis after DNA replication. To investigate this, we conducted immunohistochemical studies on mouse bone marrow megakaryocytes during thrombopoietin-induced polyploidization.
Our findings revealed that megakaryocytes enter mitosis and progress through normal prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, and up to anaphase A, but not to anaphase B, telophase, or cytokinesis. During anaphase A, we observed that multiple spindle poles form, and the nuclear membrane breaks down. The sister chromatids are aligned on a multi-faceted plate, and the centrosomes are symmetrically located on either side of each face of the plate. Following anaphase A, a set of sister chromatids moves into the multiple centrosomes. Notably, the pair of spindle poles in anaphase are located close to each other, likely due to the lack of movement of spindle poles during anaphase B.
These observations suggest that polyploidization of megakaryocytes is not simply a result of skipping mitosis, and that the megakaryocytes must have a unique regulatory mechanism in anaphase. Factors that regulate anaphase, such as microtubule motor proteins, may be involved in this polyploidization process.
In summary, our study provides evidence that megakaryocyte polyploidization is a complex process that involves the unique regulation of mitosis and may involve factors such as microtubule motor proteins.

title: Unifying Viral Genetics and Human Transportation Data to Predict the Global Transmission Dynamics of Human Influenza H3N2
text:
Sophisticated epidemiological modeling of global human movement patterns is crucial for predicting the spread of infectious diseases such as influenza. While standard epidemiological data offer valuable insights, they often fail to capture the complex dynamics of dispersal at various geographical scales. Recent advances in evolutionary analyses of viral genomes have provided valuable information on the spatial dynamics of influenza viruses, yet these analyses have largely overlooked the wealth of data on human mobility. To address this limitation, we have developed a phylogeographic approach that integrates human movement data and viral gene sequences to elucidate the global spread of human influenza subtype H3N2 and predict the spatial spread of human influenza A viruses worldwide.
By employing a framework that estimates the migration history of human influenza while simultaneously testing and quantifying a range of potential predictive variables of spatial spread, we found that the global dynamics of influenza H3N2 are driven by air passenger flows, whereas at more local scales, spread is also determined by processes that correlate with geographic distance. Our findings highlight the central role of mainland China and Southeast Asia in maintaining a source population for global influenza diversity. By comparing the model output with the known pandemic expansion of H1N1 during 2009, we demonstrated that predictions of influenza spatial spread are most accurate when data on human mobility and viral evolution are integrated.
In conclusion, the integrated approach introduced here offers great potential for epidemiological surveillance through phylogeographic reconstructions and for improving predictive models of disease control. By combining data on human mobility with the spatial information inherent in sampled viral genomes, we can provide a more nuanced understanding of the global dynamics of influenza viruses and enhance our ability to predict and control future outbreaks.

title: Microtubule sliding activity of a kinesin-8 promotes spindle assembly and spindle length control
text:
Molecular motors play crucial roles in mitotic spindle formation, either by regulating individual microtubules or by crosslinking and sliding microtubule arrays. Kinesin-8 motors, in particular, are well-known for their regulatory functions in controlling microtubule dynamics. These motors possess microtubule-destabilizing activities and restrict spindle length in a wide range of cell types and organisms.
In this study, we investigate the antiparallel sliding activity of Kip3, a kinesin-8 motor in budding yeast. We identify complementary mutants of Kip3 that separate its sliding and microtubule-destabilizing activities, allowing us to determine the in vivo importance of this sliding activity. In conjunction with Cin8, a kinesin-5 family member, the sliding activity of Kip3 promotes bipolar spindle assembly and maintains genome stability.
We propose a "slide-disassemble" model, where the sliding and destabilizing activities of Kip3 are balanced during pre-anaphase, enabling normal spindle assembly. However, in late anaphase, the destabilizing activity of Kip3 takes over, inhibiting spindle elongation and ultimately leading to spindle disassembly.

title: A Pharmacological Map of the PI3-K Family Defines a Role for p110α in Insulin Signaling
text: Phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3-Ks) are an emerging class of promising drug targets, but the distinct functions of PI3-K isoforms remain poorly understood. To address this, we designed a unique approach to probe the PI3-K family using a diverse panel of inhibitors. Biochemical assays revealed hidden similarities across target proteins and chemical scaffolds, while crystal structures of inhibitors bound to p110γ revealed a flexible region exploited by selective compounds. We then utilized this chemical array to determine the PI3-K isoforms required for insulin signaling. Our findings indicate that p110α is the primary insulin-responsive PI3-K in cultured cells, while p110β is dispensable but sets a threshold for p110α activity. In vivo studies using these compounds revealed that targeting p110α blocked the acute effects of insulin treatment, while inhibition of p110β had no effect. These results demonstrate the power of a systematic matrix of inhibitors to validate targets within a protein family.

title: Identification of Epstein-Barr virus nuclear antigen 1 protein domains that direct interactions at a distance between DNA-bound proteins.
text: The EBNA1 protein of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) interacts directly with and activates DNA replication from the EBV latent origin of replication, oriP, through two noncontiguous subelements. This interaction is facilitated by the looping mechanism of EBNA1 molecules bound to oriP, which efficiently interact with each other. We have previously mapped a region of EBNA1, referred to as the looping region, that plays a critical role in mediating these interactions. Our findings now demonstrate that two fragments of this region, consisting mainly of an eight-amino-acid repeat, can mediate homotypic interactions when transferred to another DNA-binding protein. These protein interactions are reliant on DNA binding, as they are only detected when the proteins are bound to DNA.

title: Primary prevention of hypertension: clinical and public health advisory from The National High Blood Pressure Education Program.
text:
In 1993, the National High Blood Pressure Education Program Coordinating Committee published its initial statement on primary hypertension prevention. This updated report from 2019 incorporates new and additional scientific evidence from the literature. The current recommendations for primary prevention of hypertension involve a population-based approach and a targeted strategy focused on individuals at high risk of developing hypertension. These two strategies are complementary and emphasize six effective approaches for preventing hypertension:
1. Engage in moderate physical activity
2. Maintain a healthy body weight
3. Limit alcohol consumption
4. Reduce sodium intake
5. Eat a potassium-rich diet
6. Consume a diet low in saturated and total fat and high in fruits, vegetables.
By implementing these strategies in public health and clinical practice, we can prevent blood pressure from rising and decrease elevated blood pressure levels for individuals with high normal blood pressure or hypertension.

title: Formins: intermediates in signal-transduction cascades that affect cytoskeletal reorganization.
text: The regulation of cell growth and orientation relies on a dynamic actin cytoskeleton that can adapt in response to developmental and environmental stimuli. In animals and fungi, formins are among the four primary classes of poly-L-proline-containing (PLP) proteins involved in signal transduction pathways that lead to reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton. Investigation of the Arabidopsis genome reveals that formins are the sole conserved profilin-binding PLP proteins in plants, and they exhibit distinct structural differences compared to their animal and fungal counterparts, suggesting the possibility of novel mechanisms of control or unique functions in plant formins.

title: Genetic variability in GLP-1 receptor is associated with inter-individual differences in weight lowering potential of liraglutide in obese women with PCOS: a pilot study
text:
The study investigated the inter-individual differences in the weight-lowering potential of GLP-1 receptor agonists (RAs) in obese women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Despite being clinically unpredictable, the role of genetic variability of GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) was evaluated using common GLP-1R single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in 57 obese women with PCOS who were assigned to liraglutide 1.2 mg daily subcutaneously for 12 weeks. The study found that:
* Twenty out of 57 subjects were strong responders and lost 7.38 ± 1.74 kg, compared to 2.11 ± 2.17 kg lost in poor responders.
* Carriers of at least one polymorphic rs10305420 allele had a poor treatment response compared to carriers of two wild type alleles (odds ratio (OR) = 0.27, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.09-0.85, P = 0.025).
* Carriers of at least one polymorphic rs6923761 allele had a tendency towards stronger treatment response compared to carriers of two wild type alleles (OR = 3.06, 95% CI = 0.96-9.74, P = 0.058).
* Fasting glucose and glucose after oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) decreased comparably in both groups when compared to baseline, but no within-treatment differences were found in androgen profile.
* Gastrointestinal adverse events were transit and balanced between strong and poor responders.
* The GLP-1R rs10305420 polymorphism explained some of the inter-individual differences in response to liraglutide regarding weight loss in obese PCOS women.
Despite the clinical unpredictability of weight loss response to GLP-1R agonists, the genetic variability of GLP-1R was shown to play a role in the response to liraglutide in obese women with PCOS. The study found that carriers of at least one polymorphic rs10305420 allele had a lower weight loss response, while carriers of at least one polymorphic rs6923761 allele had a tendency towards a stronger treatment response. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to explore the potential of genetic testing to predict treatment response in obese individuals with PCOS.

title: Cost-effectiveness of aromatase inhibitor co-treatment for controlled ovarian stimulation.
text: Background: The clinical efficacy and cost-effectiveness of utilizing the aromatase inhibitor letrozole in combination with follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) during intrauterine insemination (IUI) for various indications were contrasted in this study. Methods: Four hundred and thirty-two consecutive patients who underwent 872 IUI cycles were included in the study, with the majority of them being divided into two groups: Group I, comprising 308 patients who underwent 589 IUI cycles with letrozole and FSH for diverse indications, including anovulation (143 cycles), male factor infertility (147 cycles), unexplained infertility (250 cycles), endometriosis (18 cycles), and combined indications (31 cycles), and Group II, consisting of 124 patients who underwent 283 IUI cycles and received FSH alone for ovarian factor infertility (82 cycles), male factor infertility (66 cycles), unexplained infertility (114 cycles), endometriosis (13 cycles), and other indications (8 cycles). The primary outcome measures included the number of mature follicles >16 mm in diameter, FSH dose used per cycle, clinical pregnancy rate, and cost-effectiveness ratio per pregnancy. Results: The requirement for FSH dose during ovarian stimulation was found to be significantly lower when letrozole was used (P < 0.0001). Although a significantly higher number of follicles >16 mm and endometrial thickness at the day of hCG administration were observed in Group II (P < 0.0001), the pregnancy rate per started and per completed cycles were similar in Group I and Group II (14.4% and 15.9%, respectively). Additionally, the IUI cancellation rate was significantly lower when letrozole was used (P = 0.05%). The cost per cycle was significantly lower in Group I compared to Group II (468.93 Canadian dollars +/- 418.18 vs. 1067.28 +/- 921.43; P < 0.0001). The cost-effectiveness ratio was 3249.42 dollars in the letrozole group and 6712.00 dollars in the FSH-only group. Conclusion: The findings of this study suggest that the use of letrozole in combination with FSH during IUI may be a more cost-effective ovarian stimulation protocol than FSH alone. A randomized controlled trial is needed to further substantiate these findings and determine the optimal circumstances for its use.

title: The cost effectiveness of stereotactic radiosurgery versus surgical resection in the treatment of solitary metastatic brain tumors.
text: Solitary metastatic brain tumors are the most common type of intracranial neoplasms encountered by neurosurgeons. Surgical resection of brain metastasis combined with whole brain radiotherapy (WBR) significantly improves survival in comparison to WBR alone. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SR) also provides similar results to surgical resection. To evaluate the economic efficiency of these treatment options, we analyzed the results of surgical resection and SR studies published between 1974 and 1994. We included studies that met the following criteria: at least 75% of patients received WBR, study dates were in the computed tomography era, operative morbidity, mortality, and median survival were reported, and cobalt-60 gamma unit was used for SR. Three surgical resection studies and one SR study met these requirements. We developed a model to estimate typical resource usage for uncomplicated procedures, reported complications, and subsequent craniotomies for both treatment options. Costs were estimated from the societal perspective using the 1992 Medicare Provider Analysis and Review database with average cost:charge ratios for surgery and WBR. A survey of capital and operating costs from five sites was used for radiosurgery. Our analysis revealed that radiosurgery had lower costs for uncomplicated procedures ($20,209 vs $27,587), average complication costs per case ($2,534 vs $2,874), and total costs per procedure ($22,743 vs $30,461). Radiosurgery was more cost-effective ($24,811 vs $32,149 per life year) and had better incremental cost effectiveness ($40,648 vs $52,384 per life year) than surgical resection. A sensitivity analysis revealed that significant changes in key assumptions would be required to alter the analysis outcome. Equalizing the incremental cost effectiveness of the two treatments would require one of the following: 1) a 38.7% reduction in SR annual case volume, 2) a 34.7% increase in SR procedure cost, 3) a 18.8% reduction in surgical resection procedure cost, 4) a 240.5% increase in SR morbidity cost, 5) a 12.7% reduction in SR median survival, 6) a 16.8% increase in surgical resection median survival. Eliminating all surgical resection morbidity costs would still result in superior incremental cost effectiveness for SR.

title: Trans-ancestry mutational landscape of hepatocellular carcinoma genomes
text: Various epidemiological factors are linked to the prevalence of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) across different populations. However, the global scope of genetic alterations in HCC genomes specific to distinct ancestral backgrounds remains largely unexplored. Through analysis of genomic data from 503 liver cancer cases sourced from diverse populations, we uncovered 30 candidate driver genes and 11 core pathway modules. Our collaborative effort with two large-scale cancer genome projects also translated into the identification of unique mutational signatures in 608 liver cancer cases, predominantly found in Asian cases. This work provides new insights into the ancestry-correlated mutational processes involved in HCC development. Specifically, we found that a combination of hotspot TERT promoter mutation, TERT focal amplification, and viral genome integration occurs in over 68% of cases, underscoring TERT as a central and ancestry-independent node in hepatocarcinogenesis. The identification of novel alterations in genes encoding metabolic enzymes, chromatin remodelers, and a high frequency of mTOR pathway activations offers promising avenues for therapeutic and diagnostic strategies.

title: Organization of the mitotic chromosome.
text: For over a century, the internal organization of mitotic chromosomes has remained a mystery. Despite their recognizability, the three-dimensional structure of chromosomes during cell division has yet to be fully understood. To address this, we employed chromosome conformation capture techniques, including 5C and Hi-C, across different cell cycle phases. Our findings reveal two distinct three-dimensional folding states of the human genome during these stages. In interphase, highly compartmentalized and cell type-specific organization was observed in nonsynchronous cells. However, in metaphase, we discovered a locus-independent, homogenous folding state that is common to all chromosomes and consistent among different cell types. Using polymer simulations, we found that metaphase Hi-C data do not fit traditional hierarchical models and are best described by a linearly organized, longitudinally compressed array of consecutive chromatin loops. This discovery provides new insights into the general principle of metaphase chromosome organization.

title: Compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome.
text: The concept of Compensatory Anti-Inflammatory Response Syndrome (CARS) was introduced in 1997 by Roger Bone (1941-1997) to describe the consequences of counter-regulatory mechanisms activated to limit excessive inflammation in patients with sepsis or systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). One of the key consequences of CARS is the immune system's modification, which can heighten intensive care patients' susceptibility to hospital-acquired infections. This finding is supported by animal studies, but the results are sensitive to experimental conditions. Circulating leukocytes undergo alterations in sepsis and SIRS patients, as well as in animal models of these conditions. However, this is not a global defect in immune cell function, but rather a reprogramming of circulating leukocytes. Within tissues, leukocytes are activated or primed rather than immunosuppressed. Therefore, CARS can be viewed as an adaptive, compartmentalized response aimed at silencing certain acute pro-inflammatory genes while maintaining the potential expression of genes involved in anti-infectious processes.

title: Quantum dots spectrally distinguish multiple species within the tumor milieu in vivo
text: A solid tumor is composed of cancer and host cells embedded in an extracellular matrix, nourished by blood vessels. To fully understand tumor pathophysiology, it is crucial to identify and monitor the different components of the tumor in real-time. However, standard fluorophores often hinder the simultaneous imaging of these components. To overcome this limitation, we employed multiphoton microscopy techniques and transgenic mice expressing green fluorescent protein, in combination with customized quantum dot preparations. These fluorescent semiconductor nanocrystals enabled us to simultaneously image and differentiate tumor vessels from perivascular cells and the matrix. Moreover, we used them to assess the accessibility of particles of different sizes to the tumor. Additionally, we successfully monitored the recruitment of quantum dot–labeled bone marrow–derived precursor cells to the tumor vasculature. These findings demonstrate the versatility of quantum dots in studying tumor pathophysiology and opening up new avenues for treatment.

title: Arginase I: a limiting factor for nitric oxide and polyamine synthesis by activated macrophages?
text:
The text can be rewritten as follows:
Arginase hydrolyzes arginine into ornithine and urea, which can regulate nitric oxide (NO) and polyamine synthesis. To investigate whether cytosolic arginase isoform expression (arginase I) limits NO or polyamine production in activated RAW 264.7 macrophage cells, we measured NO synthesis in cells overexpressing arginase I or beta-galactosidase and treated them with interferon-gamma, lipopolysaccharide, or 8-bromo-cAMP (8-BrcAMP). Overexpression of arginase I had no effect on NO synthesis, while cells overexpressing arginase I produced twice as much putrescine and spermidine after activation as cells expressing beta-galactosidase. These results indicate that endogenous levels of arginase I are limiting for polyamine synthesis but not for NO synthesis in activated macrophage cells. Additionally, this study demonstrates that it is possible to modulate arginase I levels enough to affect polyamine synthesis without affecting induced NO synthesis.

title: Opposing Effects of PKCθ and WASp on Symmetry Breaking and Relocation of the Immunological Synapse
text: The immunological synapse (IS) is the junction between a T cell and an antigen-presenting cell, and is composed of supramolecular activation clusters (SMACs). To date, no studies have been conducted on the dynamics of naive T cell IS formation. Our findings indicate that IS formation during antigen recognition is a cyclical process involving two distinct phases: stable IS formation and autonomous naive T cell migration. The migration phase is driven by protein kinase theta (PKCtheta), which is localized to the F-actin-dependent peripheral (p)SMAC. Interestingly, PKCtheta-deficient T cells exhibited hyperstable IS in vitro and in vivo, with fast oscillations in the distal SMAC, but reduced slow oscillations in pSMAC integrity. IS reformation is mediated by the Wiscott Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASp). WASp-deficient T cells showed normal IS formation, but were unable to reform IS after migration unless PKCtheta was inhibited. Our findings suggest that PKCtheta and WASp have opposing effects on IS stability, with PKCtheta promoting pSMAC symmetry breaking and WASp facilitating IS reformation.

title: Integrins regulate microtubule nucleating activity of centrosome through mitogen-activated protein kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase (MEK/ERK) signaling.
text:
Microtubule nucleation is an essential step in the formation of the microtubule cytoskeleton, and we have shown that androgen and Src promote this process by accumulating γ-tubulin at the centrosome. Here, we investigate the mechanisms by which androgen and Src regulate microtubule nucleation and explore the potential role of integrins in these processes. We employ a tyrosine-to-alanine substitution in the membrane-proximal NPIY motif of the integrin β1 tail to perturbe integrin function and examine the impact on microtubule nucleation and γ-tubulin accumulation at the centrosome.
Our results indicate that the formation of the androgen receptor-Src complex and the activation of downstream signaling pathways are significantly suppressed when cells are adhered by the mutant integrin. Inhibitor studies reveal that microtubule nucleation requires MEK/ERK signaling but not PI3K/AKT signaling. Interestingly, the expression of activated RAF-1 is sufficient to rescue microtubule nucleation inhibited by the mutant integrin by promoting the centrosomal accumulation of γ-tubulin. Our findings establish a novel integrin signaling paradigm, where integrins regulate microtubule nucleation by promoting the formation of androgen receptor-Src signaling complexes that activate the MEK/ERK signaling pathway.

title: Consumption of added sugars from liquid but not solid sources predicts impaired glucose homeostasis and insulin resistance among youth at risk of obesity.
text: Little is known about the long-term associations between sugar consumption (both solid and liquid sources) and glucose-insulin homeostasis in youth. This study aimed to investigate these associations among Caucasian children aged 8-10 years with at least one obese biological parent, using data from the QUébec Adipose and Lifestyle InvesTigation in Youth (QUALITY) cohort (n = 630) followed up 2 years later (n = 564). Sugar intake was assessed through three 24-hour dietary recalls at baseline. The study found that added sugar intake from either liquid or solid sources was not significantly associated with changes in adiposity measures (fat mass, body mass index, or waist circumference) over two years. However, a higher consumption (10g/day) of added sugars from liquid sources was associated with higher fasting glucose levels, higher fasting insulin levels, higher homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), and lower Matsuda-insulin sensitivity index (Matsuda-ISI) in all participants (P < 0.01). No associations were observed between solid source added sugar consumption and these outcomes. Overweight/obese children at baseline had greater increases in adiposity indicators, fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR, and decreases in Matsuda-ISI, compared to normal-weight children, during the two-year follow-up. Consumption of added sugars from liquid sources was found to be a risk factor for the development of impaired glucose homeostasis and insulin resistance over two years among youth at risk of obesity.

title: Towards an improved investment approach for an effective response to HIV/AIDS.
text:
Significant changes are necessary to adopt a more targeted and strategic approach to investment in response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic, leading to long-term benefits. Under the current system, advocacy for resources has relied on a commodity-based approach that has resulted in the scaling up of numerous strategies without considering their relative effectiveness. In contrast, our proposed strategic investment framework aims to improve the management of national and international responses to HIV/AIDS by incorporating efficiency gains through community mobilization, synergies between program elements, and the extension of antiretroviral therapy for HIV transmission prevention.
The framework consists of three categories of investment: six basic programmatic activities, interventions to create an enabling environment, and programmatic efforts in other health and development sectors related to HIV/AIDS. According to our estimates, achieving universal access to HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support by 2015 will require an annual investment of at least US$22 billion. Comparing the proposed framework with continuation of current approaches, we estimate that it will avert 12·2 million new HIV infections and 7·4 million deaths from AIDS between 2011 and 2020, resulting in 29·4 million life-years gained. Additionally, the framework is cost-effective, with an estimated cost of $1060 per life-year gained, and the additional investment proposed would be largely offset by savings in treatment costs alone.

title: Pivotal Roles of T-Helper 17-Related Cytokines, IL-17, IL-22, and IL-23, in Inflammatory Diseases
text: T-helper 17 (Th17) cells are defined by their production of interleukin-17 (IL-17, also referred to as IL-17A), IL-17F, IL-21, and IL-22, as well as potentially tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and IL-6 upon certain stimulation. The cytokines produced by Th17 cells, including IL-23, which promotes their development, as well as IL-17 and IL-22 produced by these cells, play crucial roles in various inflammatory diseases, such as experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis, colitis, and Concanavalin A-induced hepatitis. In this review, we highlight the functional characteristics of Th17 cells and their associated cytokines, with a particular focus on their involvement in mouse models and human inflammatory diseases.

title: LXRS and FXR: the yin and yang of cholesterol and fat metabolism.
text: Liver X receptors (LXRs) and farnesoid X receptors (FXR) are nuclear receptors that function as intracellular sensors for sterols and bile acids, respectively. In response to their ligands, these receptors trigger transcriptional responses that maintain a delicate balance of cholesterol and bile acid metabolism. LXRs not only facilitate the effective storage of energy from carbohydrates and fatty acids, but also contribute to a decrease in triglyceride levels and modulation of glucose metabolism. The intricate, dual interplay between these two receptor systems suggests that they co-evolved to form a highly sensitive and efficient system for maintaining total body fat and cholesterol homeostasis. Recent evidence suggests that the specific action of these receptors in various tissues also plays a crucial role in maintaining the proper function of the cardiovascular, immune, reproductive, endocrine pancreas, renal, and central nervous systems. As such, LXRs and FXR represent promising therapeutic targets for the prevention and treatment of a wide range of metabolic and lipid-related diseases.

title: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus/human herpesvirus type 8-positive solid lymphomas: a tissue-based variant of primary effusion lymphoma.
text: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as human herpesvirus type 8, is consistently identified in Kaposi's sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma (PEL), and multicentric Castleman's disease. Here we report four cases of KSHV-bearing solid lymphomas that occurred in AIDS patients (cases 1-3) and in a HIV-negative person (case 4). The patients presented with extranodal masses in the abdomen (cases 1, 3, and 4) or skin (case 2), and nodal involvement, along with Kaposi's sarcoma (case 3). The gastrointestinal tract was involved in two patients (cases 1 and 3). Unlike KSHV-negative AIDS-associated diffuse large cell lymphomas, KSHV-positive solid lymphomas exhibited PEL-like cell morphology and expression of a set of genes previously shown to define PEL tumor cells. Our results suggest that KSHV-positive solid lymphomas should be considered as a tissue-based variant of classical PEL, regardless of HIV status.

title: STAR: ultrafast universal RNA-seq aligner.
text:
MOTIVATION: The accurate alignment of high-throughput RNA-seq data remains a formidable challenge due to the complex, non-contiguous nature of transcript structures, relatively short read lengths, and the steadily increasing throughput of sequencing technologies.
