Current RNA-seq aligners struggle with high mapping error rates, slow mapping speed, limitations in read length, and biases in their alignment strategies.
RESULTS: To tackle the large (over 80 billion reads) ENCODE Transcriptome RNA-seq dataset, we developed the Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference (STAR) software program, which capitalizes on an innovative RNA-seq alignment algorithm that utilizes a previously unexplored sequential search strategy in uncompressed suffix arrays. This approach enables STAR to outperform other aligners by more than 50-fold in terms of mapping speed, achieving the alignment of 550 million 2 × 76 bp paired-end reads per hour on a modest 12-core server, while concurrently improving alignment accuracy and sensitivity. In addition to unbiased de novo detection of canonical junctions, STAR can also identify non-canonical splices and chimeric (fusion) transcripts, and can map full-length RNA sequences. We experimentally validated 1960 novel intergenic splice junctions with an 80-90% success rate using Roche 454 sequencing of reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction amplicons, further corroborating the exceptional mapping strategy employed by STAR.
AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: STAR is implemented as a standalone C++ code and is freely distributed under the GPLv3 license. The software can be downloaded from the following URL: <http://code.google.com/p/rna-star/>.

title: Effect of alendronate on risk of fracture in women with low bone density but without vertebral fractures: results from the Fracture Intervention Trial.
text:
The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of alendronate sodium in reducing the risk of fractures in postmenopausal women who have low bone mineral density (BMD) but no vertebral fractures. The study was a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled trial conducted at 11 community-based clinical research centers. A total of 4432 women aged 54 to 81 years with a femoral neck BMD of 0.68 g/cm2 or less were randomly assigned to receive either alendronate or placebo for 4 years. All participants received a supplement containing calcium and vitamin D. The main outcome measures were clinical fractures confirmed by x-ray reports, new vertebral deformities detected by morphometric measurements on radiographs, and BMD measured by dual x-ray absorptiometry.
The results showed that alendronate increased BMD at all sites studied and reduced clinical fractures from 312 in the placebo group to 272 in the intervention group, but the reduction was not statistically significant. Alendronate did significantly reduce the risk of clinical fractures among women with baseline osteoporosis at the femoral neck (>2.5 SDs below the normal young adult mean), with a 36% reduction in the risk of fractures (P < 0.001). However, there was no significant reduction among women with higher BMD. Alendronate also decreased the risk of radiographic vertebral fractures by 44% overall, with a treatment-control difference of 1.7% and an NNT of 60. The study found no significant increase in the risk of gastrointestinal or other adverse effects associated with alendronate use.
In conclusion, the study found that 4 years of alendronate therapy safely increased BMD and decreased the risk of first vertebral deformity in postmenopausal women with low BMD but without vertebral fractures. Alendronate significantly reduced the risk of clinical fractures among women with osteoporosis but not among women with higher BMD. These findings suggest that alendronate may be a useful treatment option for postmenopausal women with low BMD and a low risk of fractures.

title: AP-1/sigma1B-adaptin mediates endosomal synaptic vesicle recycling, learning and memory.
text: Synaptic vesicle recycling involves the AP-2/clathrin-mediated endocytosis pathway, but it is unknown whether the endosomal pathway is also essential. Mice lacking the tissue-specific AP-1-sigma1B complex display impaired synaptic vesicle recycling in hippocampal synapses. The ubiquitously expressed AP-1-sigma1A complex mediates protein sorting between the trans-Golgi network and early endosomes in vertebrates. Vertebrates express three sigma1 subunit isoforms: A, B, and C, with the highest expressions found in the brain. Reduced synaptic vesicle reformation in cultured neurons from sigma1B-deficient mice is observed upon stimulation, and large endosomal intermediates accumulate. These mice exhibit impaired motor coordination and severely compromised long-term spatial memory, indicating a molecular mechanism underlying a severe human X-chromosome-linked mental retardation.

title: Update of the FANTOM web resource: high resolution transcriptome of diverse cell types in mammals
text: With the initial release of the fifth iteration of the Functional Annotation of Mammalian Genomes (FANTOM5) collaborative project, we aggregated a wealth of primary data and database systems into the FANTOM web resource (<http://fantom.gsc.riken.jp>). This comprehensive platform was designed to facilitate researchers' exploration of transcriptional regulation and cellular states. Throughout the collaboration, we have continuously expanded and enhanced the database systems, and we believe that our data and web resources are indispensable tools for the scientific community to gain a deeper understanding of mammalian cellular organization. In this article, we outline the contents of FANTOM5, report recent updates to the web resource, and provide insights into future developments.

title: Adverse Events Associated With the Treatment of Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
text:
The management of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) poses significant clinical challenges, particularly due to the long duration of treatment and the use of multiple second-line drugs. Adverse drug events (ADEs) are a major clinical consideration in patients receiving anti-MDR-TB treatment, with a high incidence of side effects observed in patients undergoing therapy.
To investigate the frequency and type of ADEs associated with MDR-TB therapy, a systematic review of the literature was conducted using the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Studies were included if they reported available ADE data for patients treated with a regimen including second-line drugs for MDR-TB.
The review identified 5346 patients, of which 2602 (57.3%) experienced at least one type of ADE. The three most common side effects observed were gastrointestinal disorders (32.1%), ototoxicity (14.6%), and psychiatric disorders (13.2%). Subgroup analyses based on various characteristics (such as study population, previous tuberculosis treatment, human immunodeficiency virus prevalence, and length of treatment) did not reveal any significant differences between groups.
Among the 1519 patients who developed ADEs with available data on impact on MDR-TB therapy, 70.4% required a change in MDR-TB treatment. These findings suggest that ADEs are common among MDR-TB patients and can significantly impact treatment outcomes. Therefore, close monitoring and aggressive management of side effects are essential during MDR-TB therapy, particularly for ototoxicity and psychiatric disorders.

title: Presynaptically Localized Cyclic GMP-Dependent Protein Kinase 1 Is a Key Determinant of Spinal Synaptic Potentiation and Pain Hypersensitivity
text:
The potentiation of synaptic transmission, or long-term potentiation (LTP), in spinal neurons that receive inputs directly from the periphery has been proposed to contribute to pain hypersensitivity in various diseases. Previous studies have implicated the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor-nitric oxide (NO) pathway and the downstream second messenger, cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), in these processes. However, the specific targets of cGMP in the spinal cord that mediate LTP and contribute to pain sensitivity are still unclear.
Our study found that Protein Kinase G1 (PKG-I), which is localized presynaptically in nociceptor terminals, plays a crucial role in the expression of spinal LTP. We used the Cre-loxP system to generate nociceptor-specific knockout mice lacking PKG-I specifically in presynaptic terminals of nociceptors in the spinal cord, while sparing post-synaptic neurons and other tissues. Using patch clamp recordings, we found that activity-induced LTP at synapses between nociceptors and spinal neurons projecting to the periaqueductal grey (PAG) was completely abolished in these knockout mice, although basal synaptic transmission was unaffected. Our results suggest that presynaptic mechanisms involving an increase in release probability from nociceptors are operational in the expression of synaptic LTP on spinal-PAG projection neurons.
Furthermore, we identified inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor 1 and myosin light chain kinase as key phosphorylation targets of presynaptic PKG-I in nociceptive neurons. Behavioural analyses in vivo showed marked defects in these mice in several models of activity-induced nociceptive hypersensitivity, and pharmacological studies identified a clear contribution of PKG-I expressed in spinal terminals of nociceptors to pain sensitivity. Overall, our findings suggest that presynaptic PKG-I plays a critical role in regulating pain sensitivity in the spinal cord.

title: A Sleeping Beauty mutagenesis screen reveals a tumor suppressor role for Ncoa2/Src-2 in liver cancer.
text: The Sleeping Beauty (SB) transposon mutagenesis system is a powerful tool that enables the discovery of mutations that speed up the development of tumors. In this study, we sought to identify mutations that collaborate with MYC, one of the most frequently dysregulated genes in human cancer. We performed a forward genetic screen using a mouse model of MYC-induced liver cancer that was generated through SB-mediated mutagenesis. We sequenced insertions in 63 liver tumor nodules and found at least 16 genes/loci that contribute to accelerated tumor growth. To further validate these findings, we used RNAi-mediated knockdown in a liver progenitor cell line, which demonstrated that three of these genes, Ncoa2/Src-2, Zfx, and Dtnb, act as tumor suppressors in liver cancer. Furthermore, deleting Ncoa2/Src-2 in mice increases their susceptibility to diethylnitrosamine-induced liver tumorigenesis. These results uncover genes and pathways that prevent MYC-mediated liver tumorigenesis, providing potential targets for cancer therapy.

title: Protein-Protein Interaction Inhibition (2P2I)-Oriented Chemical Library Accelerates Hit Discovery.
text: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) represent a promising area of opportunity for therapeutic intervention. Recently, we and other researchers have identified key factors that can help identify the next generation of innovative drugs for targeting PPIs. Using these rules, we designed an oriented chemical library containing 1664 structurally diverse compounds, which we evaluated on a series of representative protein-protein interfaces using homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF) technology. Our analysis showed significant enrichment factors for certain PPI classes, indicating higher "druggability" potential. As a proof-of-concept, we focused on selectivity profiles, 3D molecular modes of action resolved by X-ray crystallography, and biological activities of hits targeting well-defined "druggable" bromodomains of the bromo and extraterminal (BET) family. Our study demonstrates the power of machine learning-based oriented chemical libraries in accelerating the identification of hits targeting PPIs. A wider application of this method to a larger set of compounds can lead to the discovery of original and potent probes for this challenging class of targets.

title: Molecular characterization of endometrial cancer: a correlative study assessing microsatellite instability, MLH1 hypermethylation, DNA mismatch repair protein expression, and PTEN, PIK3CA, KRAS, and BRAF mutation analysis.
text:
This study aimed to comprehensively analyze the molecular genetic alterations in a large cohort of endometrial cancers using multiple techniques. Ninety-six cases were evaluated for genomic alterations, including microsatellite instability (MSI), MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, p53 and mismatch repair protein expression (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), and mutations in PTEN, PIK3CA, KRAS, and BRAF. The results showed that:
• At least one alteration was identified in 55% of the specimens tested for PTEN, making it the most common abnormality in this study.
• A PIK3CA alteration was observed in 17% of the specimens.
• Twenty-nine of 94 (31%) MSI-positive tumors exhibited an MSI-H phenotype.
• Of the 29 MSI-H cases, 83% were positive for methylation of the MLH1 promoter region.
• Twenty-three of 28 MSI-H cases with immunohistochemistry results showed loss of expression of MLH1/PMS2 (n=19), MSH2/MSH6 (n=2), or MSH6 only (n=2).
• Of the 19 MSI-H cases with loss of MLH1/PMS2 on immunohistochemistry, 18 were positive, and 1 was equivocal for MLH1 promoter hypermethylation.
• Twelve of 94 cases (13%) analyzed for KRAS mutations were found to have a mutation.
• No BRAF V600E mutations were identified.

This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the molecular genetic alterations in endometrial cancers, highlighting the frequency and characteristics of these alterations in a large cohort of cases. The results suggest that MSI, MLH1 promoter methylation, and loss of MLH1/PMS2 expression are common alterations in endometrial cancers, and that PIK3CA and KRAS mutations are also present in a significant proportion of cases. This study contributes to our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying endometrial cancer development and progression.

title: Identification of indole-3-carboxylic acid as mediator of priming against Plectosphaerella cucumerina.
text: The Arabidopsis plant's resistance to the necrotrophic pathogen Plectosphaerella cucumerina is mediated by a combination of multiple hormonally-controlled signaling pathways. The priming agent β-aminobutyric acid (BABA) is able to effectively induce resistance against this pathogen by stimulating the deposition of callose-rich cell walls. In the current research, it is demonstrated that BABA-Induced Resistance (BABA-IR) against P. cucumerina in Arabidopsis has additional components, including the induction of defenses mediated by indolic derivatives. A chromatographic approach for detecting and characterizing metabolites that are enhanced by BABA compared to water-treated plants when the challenge is present has been developed. Using this analytical system, a signal at m/z 160 was primed by BABA in infected plants, which was subsequently identified as the indole-derivative metabolite indole-3-carboxylic acid (I3CA). Quantification of I3CA in primed plants showed that this indolic metabolite is specifically primed by BABA upon P. cucumerina infection, while other indolic compounds such as IAA and camalexin are not. These observations suggest that priming is not a single mechanism but rather a multicomponent defense.

title: Evaluation of networks of randomized trials.
text: Randomized trials can either be viewed as individual experiments or as part of a larger body of evidence. The scope and complexity of available randomized data vary across topics. Systematic reviews can help identify gaps in the existing evidence, highlight discrepancies between trials, and inform future trials. A recent development in systematic reviews, mixed treatment comparison (MTC) meta-analysis, has gained popularity. MTC meta-analysis can provide valuable insights into the available randomized evidence from collections of trials and compare multiple treatments. However, evaluating networks of trials poses unique challenges. In this article, we explore the statistical methodology for MTC meta-analysis. We discuss methods for evaluating inconsistency, gaps in the existing literature, and the implications of these findings for future trial planning. Specifically, we examine the concepts of network geometry and asymmetry, and propose metrics for assessing these factors.

title: Metabolic regulation by the mitochondrial phosphatase PTPMT1 is required for hematopoietic stem cell differentiation.
text:
The regulation and coordination of mitochondrial metabolism in relation to hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) self-renewal and differentiation is not fully understood. In this study, we investigate the role of PTPMT1, a PTEN-like mitochondrial phosphatase, in mitochondrial metabolism and its impact on HSC function.
Using inducible or hematopoietic-cell-specific knockout mice, we found that depletion of PTPMT1 led to hematopoietic failure due to changes in the cell cycle and a block in the differentiation of HSCs. Surprisingly, the HSC pool was increased by approximately 40-fold in PTPMT1 knockout mice. Reintroduction of wild-type PTPMT1, but not catalytically deficient or truncated PTPMT1 lacking mitochondrial localization, restored differentiation capabilities of PTPMT1 knockout HSCs.
Further analysis revealed that PTPMT1 deficiency altered mitochondrial metabolism, and phosphatidylinositol phosphate substrates of PTPMT1 directly enhanced fatty-acid-induced activation of mitochondrial uncoupling protein 2. Notably, depletion of PTPMT1 from myeloid, T lymphoid, or B lymphoid progenitors did not cause any defects in lineage-specific knockout mice, suggesting a unique role of PTPMT1 in regulating HSC metabolism.
Overall, this study establishes a crucial role of PTPMT1 in the metabolic regulation of HSC function, providing new insights into the complex interplay between mitochondrial metabolism and HSC biology.

title: GSK-3-mediated phosphorylation enhances Maf-transforming activity.
text:
Here is a possible reconstruction of the given text with improved readability:
The Maf oncoproteins are a type of transcription factor belonging to the AP-1 superfamily. They are involved in various cellular processes, including development, metabolism, and tumorigenesis. Studies have shown that Maf proteins are overexpressed in approximately 50% of human multiple myelomas. Our research has discovered that Maf proteins' transforming activity is regulated by GSK-3-dependent phosphorylation, and that phosphorylation by GSK-3 can increase the oncogenic potential of a protein. Through microarray analysis, we have identified a gene-expression subprogram under the control of GSK-3-mediated Maf phosphorylation that plays a role in extracellular matrix remodeling and is relevant to cancer progression. Additionally, we found that GSK-3 phosphorylates MafA on multiple residues, including S61, T57, T53, and S49, leading to its ubiquitination and degradation. However, this phosphorylation paradoxically increases MafA's transcriptional activity by recruiting the coactivator P/CAF. We further demonstrate that P/CAF shields MafA from ubiquitination and degradation, suggesting that, after the release of the coactivator complex, MafA becomes polyubiquitinated and degraded to bring the response to an end.

title: NETs are a source of citrullinated autoantigens and stimulate inflammatory responses in rheumatoid arthritis.
text: Early events leading to the development of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are not well understood, but the formation of autoantibodies to citrullinated protein antigens (ACPAs) is considered a key pathogenic event. In this study, we investigated whether abnormal neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation occurs in RA, identified its triggers, and examined its harmful inflammatory consequences. Circulating and synovial fluid neutrophils from RA patients showed enhanced NETosis compared to neutrophils from healthy controls and those with osteoarthritis (OA). Furthermore, NETs infiltrated RA synovial tissue, rheumatoid nodules, and skin, and correlated with ACPA presence and levels as well as systemic inflammatory markers. RA sera and immunoglobulin fractions from RA patients with high levels of ACPA and/or rheumatoid factor significantly enhanced NETosis, and the NETs induced by these autoantibodies displayed distinct protein content. During NETosis, neutrophils externalized the citrullinated autoantigens implicated in RA pathogenesis, and anti-citrullinated vimentin antibodies potently induced NET formation. Additionally, inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-17A (IL-17A) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) induced NETosis in RA neutrophils. Furthermore, NETs significantly augmented inflammatory responses in RA and OA synovial fibroblasts, including induction of IL-6, IL-8, chemokines, and adhesion molecules. These findings suggest that accelerated NETosis may play a key role in RA pathogenesis by externalizing citrullinated autoantigens and immunostimulatory molecules, leading to aberrant adaptive and innate immune responses in the joint and periphery, and perpetuating disease mechanisms.

title: Is autoimmunity the Achilles' heel of cancer immunotherapy?
text: The introduction of immuno-oncology as a game-changing strategy for metastatic cancer requires clinicians to integrate this innovative approach with traditional treatments like chemotherapy, radiation, and targeted small-molecule compounds. It is equally essential to comprehend the limitations and adverse effects of immunotherapy, which may seem less toxic compared to other cancer treatments at first glance. However, as immunotherapy gains wider adoption, particularly as first- and second-line treatments, immunotoxicity and autoimmune side effects are emerging as potential limitations. In this Perspective, we explore evidence indicating that the occurrence of immunotoxicity can be a positive sign for patients, and discuss possible mechanisms related to the induction of autoimmunity. We also investigate ways to mitigate immunotoxicity and envision the future direction of research and reporting to minimize it.

title: Trophoblast differentiation defect in human embryonic stem cells lacking PIG-A and GPI-anchored cell-surface proteins.
text: Human embryonic stem (hES) cells possess the ability to differentiate into various cell types derived from the three embryonic germ layers and extraembryonic tissues, such as trophoblasts. However, the underlying mechanisms governing the lineage choices of hES cells are still poorly understood. To investigate this, we established two independent hES cell clones that lack a specific group of cell surface molecules known as glycosyl-phosphatidyl-inositol-anchored proteins (GPI-APs). We found that the GPI-AP deficiency in these two hES clones is due to a deficiency in the expression of the PIG-A gene, which is essential for the first step of GPI synthesis. Surprisingly, GPI-AP-deficient hES cells were able to form embryoid bodies and initiate cell differentiation into the three embryonic germ layers. However, they failed to form trophoblasts upon differentiation induction through embryoid body formation or by adding exogenous BMP4. The inability of GPI-AP-deficient hES cells to form trophoblasts was attributed to the lack of GPI-anchored BMP coreceptors, which resulted in an impaired full BMP4 signaling activation in these cells. This study reveals that GPI-AP-enhanced full activation of BMP signaling is requirement for trophoblast formation in human hES cells.

title: CRISPR Interference Limits Horizontal Gene Transfer in Staphylococci by Targeting DNA
text: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in bacteria and archaea is facilitated through phage transduction, transformation, or conjugation, with the latter being particularly crucial for the dissemination of antibiotic resistance. The acquisition of Clustered, Regularly Interspaced, Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR) loci grants bacteria sequence-directed immunity against phages. A clinical isolate of Staphylococcus epidermidis possesses a CRISPR spacer that matches the nickase gene present in the majority of staphylococcal conjugative plasmids, and we investigate the implications of this observation. Our findings demonstrate that CRISPR interference hinders conjugation and plasmid transformation in S. epidermidis. Despite the restoration of the target sequence in the spliced mRNA following intron insertion, we reveal that the interference machinery directly targets DNA. This work suggests that CRISPR loci can counter multiple mechanisms of HGT and potentially restrict the spread of antibiotic resistance in pathogenic bacteria.

title: Development of leukemia in donor cells after allogeneic stem cell transplantation--a survey of the European Group for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (EBMT).
text: Leukemia in donor cells (donor cell leukemia; DCL) is a rare but severe complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation (SCT) that has been poorly understood, including its incidence, potential pathogenetic factors, therapeutic options, and outcome. To address these knowledge gaps, a questionnaire survey was conducted among European Blood and Marrow Transplantation Group (EBMT) centers, which collected data on 10489 allogeneic SCTs performed between 1982 and 2003. The survey identified 14 cases of DCL, most of which had a myeloid phenotype (7 cases of acute myeloid leukemia, 3 each of acute lymphocytic leukemia and 1 case of chronic myeloid leukemia). Molecular analysis of chimerism was used to demonstrate the donor cell origin in most cases. The DCL type and cytogenetic alterations were found to be independent of the original disease. The median time between transplantation and diagnosis of DCL was 17 months (4-164). The survey did not identify any specific conditioning, donor, graft manipulation, graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis, or subsequent complications as risk factors for DCL. Chemotherapy induced remissions in DCL, and 2 of 5 patients remain alive in remission after a second transplant. Furthermore, the study found that donors are not at an increased risk of developing hematologic malignancies, with a median follow-up period of 9 years (range 6-30 years). These findings suggest that DCL is an extremely rare complication of allogeneic SCT, and treatment attempts with chemotherapy and a second SCT are justified. Moreover, the study provides reassurance that donors are not at risk of developing hematologic malignancies.

title: Lack of evidence of transfusion transmission of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in a US surveillance study.
text:
Since 2004, there have been several reported cases of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) transmitted through blood transfusions in the United Kingdom, raising concerns about the potential risk of similar transmissions of non-variant or classic forms of CJD.
In this study, researchers identified 36 blood donors who later developed CJD and 436 recipients of their blood components. They determined the vital status of each recipient and, if deceased, the cause of death by matching their personal identifiers with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Death Index database. The study included 91 alive recipients, 329 deceased recipients, and 16 lost to follow-up. The total person-years survived by these groups was 2096.0. The study found that 144 recipients survived for 5 years or longer after transfusion, and 68 of them had received blood donated 60 or fewer months before the onset of CJD in the donor. However, no recipient was found to have developed CJD.
The results of this large, ongoing study suggest that there is no evidence of transfusion transmission of CJD. These findings reinforce the conclusion that the risk of transfusion transmission of prion disease by CJD donors is significantly lower than the comparable risk of transmission by vCJD donors.

title: Large-scale hypomethylated blocks associated with Epstein-Barr virus-induced B-cell immortalization.
text: DNA methylation alterations are ubiquitous in human cancer from its earliest detectable stages. A logical approach to comprehending the mechanism and timing of altered DNA methylation involves examining it in the context of cancer development caused by a specific agent. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a human oncogenic herpesvirus linked to lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, can also be utilized commonly in the laboratory to immortalize human B-cells cultured. We performed whole-genome bisulfite sequencing of normal B-cells, activated B-cells, and EBV-immortalized B-cells from the same three people to discover the effect of alteration on the methylome. Surprisingly, large-scale hypomethylated regions, which along comprise two-thirds of the genome, were induced by EBV immortalization rather than by B-cell activation per se. These areas largely corresponded to hypomethylated areas detected in human cancer and were linked with gene-expression hypervariability, similar to human cancer, and consistent with a model of epigenomic change promoting tumor cell heterogeneity. In addition, we describe small-scale alterations in DNA methylation near CpG islands. These results suggest that methylation disruption is an early and vital step in the malignant transformation process.

title: Stem cell self-renewal specified by JAK-STAT activation in response to a support cell cue.
text: Adult stem cells, such as those found in blood, skin, and sperm, are generated throughout life from a pool of stem cells that have the capacity to divide and differentiate. These stem cells are sustained by their microenvironment, or "niche," which regulates their fate decisions. Although the niche influences stem cell self-renewal, few signals that direct this process have been identified. Here, we investigate the role of apical hub cells in the Drosophila testis as a niche that supports stem cell self-renewal. Hub cells produce the ligand Unpaired (Upd), which activates the JAK-STAT pathway in nearby germ cells, instructing them to self-renew and maintain their stem cell population.

title: Effects of interventions in pregnancy on maternal weight and obstetric outcomes: meta-analysis of randomised evidence
text: Objective: To assess the effects of dietary and lifestyle interventions during pregnancy on maternal and fetal outcomes. Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Data Sources: Major databases from inception to January 2012 without language restrictions. Study Selection: Randomized controlled trials evaluating any dietary or lifestyle interventions during pregnancy and their effects on obstetric outcomes. Data Synthesis: Summary of results as relative risks for dichotomous data and mean differences for continuous data. Results: Forty-four relevant randomized controlled trials (7278 women) were identified, evaluating three categories of interventions: diet, physical activity, and a mixed approach. Overall, there was a 1.42 kg reduction in gestational weight gain with any intervention compared to control. The combined interventions did not result in significant differences in birth weight or the incidence of large or small for gestational age babies, but physical activity was associated with reduced birth weight. Interventions were also associated with a reduced risk of pre-eclampsia and shoulder dystocia, with no significant effects on other critical outcomes. Dietary interventions led to the largest reduction in maternal gestational weight gain and improved pregnancy outcomes compared to other interventions. Conclusion: Dietary and lifestyle interventions during pregnancy can reduce maternal gestational weight gain and improve outcomes for both mother and baby. Among the interventions, those based on diet are the most effective and are associated with reductions in maternal gestational weight gain and improved obstetric outcomes. However, the overall evidence rating for important outcomes such as pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension, and preterm delivery was low to very low.

title: Tetraspanin 3 Is Required for the Development and Propagation of Acute Myelogenous Leukemia.
text: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a fierce cancer affecting both adults and children and often relapses following treatment. Therefore, uncovering the signals that promote AML growth is crucial to develop novel therapies. In this study, we discovered that Tetraspanin 3 is a target of the RNA-binding protein Musashi 2, which plays a pivotal role in AML. To investigate the function of Tspan3 in AML, we generated mice lacking Tspan3 and found that they displayed no overt defects. However, deletion of Tspan3 impaired the self-renewal and disease progression of leukemia stem cells and significantly improved survival in mouse models of AML. Moreover, inhibition of Tspan3 in AML patient samples led to a blockade of growth, indicating that Tspan3 is also crucial in human disease. Our findings further reveal that Tspan3 deficiency hinders responses to the chemokine CXCL12/SDF-1 and results in abnormalities in AML localization within the niche, thereby identifying Tspan3 as a significant regulator of aggressive leukemias and uncovering a role for Tspan3 in oncogenesis.

title: Reorganization of enhancer patterns in transition from naive to primed pluripotency.
text: Naive and primed pluripotency demonstrate distinct signaling requirements, transcriptomes, and developmental properties, yet share key transcriptional regulators such as Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog. We find that transition between these two pluripotent states is linked to widespread relocalization of Oct4, accompanied by global rearrangement of enhancer chromatin landscapes. Our genomic and biochemical investigations identify mediators of primed state-specific Oct4 binding, including Otx2 and Zic2/3. Strikingly, premature Otx2 overexpression can orchestrate an exit from the naive state, leading to the transcription of a sizable subset of primed pluripotency-related genes and redirection of Oct4 to previously inaccessible enhancer sites. However, the capacity of Otx2 to colonize new enhancer regions depends on its levels, cis-encoded properties of the sites, and the signaling environment. Our findings elucidate the regulatory mechanisms underlying pluripotency and underscore the importance of transcription factors such as Otx2 and Oct4 in pioneering new enhancer sites, with their capacity being highly context-dependent.

title: Topoisomerase II plays an essential role as a swivelase in the late stage of SV40 chromosome replication in vitro.
text: The study examined the effects of topoisomerases I and II on the replication of SV40 DNA using an in vitro replication system containing purified proteins that mimic the monopolymerase reaction. In the presence of both topoisomerases, two distinct nascent DNA strands were formed. One product resulted from the replication of the leading template strand and was approximately half the size of the template DNA, while the other product originated from the lagging template strand and consisted of shorter DNAs. The study found that for the replication of naked SV40 DNA, either topoisomerase I or II maintained replication fork movement and supported complete leading strand synthesis. However, when SV40 chromosomes were replicated with the same proteins, reactions containing only topoisomerase I produced shorter leading strands. In contrast, reactions supplemented with topoisomerase II or containing only topoisomerase II produced mature size DNA products. The study also found that the presence of crude extracts of HeLa cells and the topoisomerase II inhibitor VP-16 blocked elongation of the nascent DNA during SV40 chromosome replication. These results suggest that topoisomerase II plays a crucial role as a swivelase in the late stage of SV40 chromosome replication in vitro.

title: Bromodomain Proteins Contribute to Maintenance of Bloodstream Form Stage Identity in the African Trypanosome
text:
Trypanosoma brucei, the agent of African trypanosomiasis, is transmitted to mammalian hosts by the tsetse fly. In the fly, the parasite's surface is covered with invariant procyclin, while in the mammalian host, it resides extracellularly in the bloodstream form (BF) and is heavily covered with highly immunogenic Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG). In the BF, the parasite varies the highly immunogenic surface VSG using a repertoire of approximately 2500 distinct VSG genes. Recent findings in mammalian systems suggest a role for histone acetyl-lysine recognizing bromodomain proteins in maintaining stem cell fate, leading us to hypothesize that bromodomain proteins may play a similar role in maintaining the BF cell fate in trypanosomes.
We employed small-molecule inhibitors and genetic mutants for individual bromodomain proteins to investigate the function of these proteins in trypanosomes. RNA-seq experiments revealed changes in the transcriptome similar to those observed during differentiation from the BF to the insect stage, and these changes were recapitulated at the protein level by the appearance of insect-stage proteins on the cell surface. Furthermore, inhibition of bromodomain proteins disrupted two major BF-specific immune evasion mechanisms employed by trypanosomes to evade mammalian host antibody responses. Specifically, monoallelic expression of the highly variable VSG is disrupted, and rapid internalization of antibodies bound to VSG on the surface of the trypanosome is blocked.
Our findings suggest that bromodomain proteins play a crucial role in maintaining the bloodstream stage identity and immune evasion of trypanosomes. Notably, bromodomain inhibition resulted in a decrease in virulence in a mouse model of infection, implying that these proteins could be potential therapeutic targets for trypanosomiasis.
Using a 1.25 Å resolution crystal structure of a trypanosome bromodomain in complex with I-BET151, we identified a novel binding mode of the inhibitor, providing a valuable starting point for the development of rational drug designs.

title: Timing requirements for insulin/IGF-1 signaling in C. elegans.
text: The insulin/IGF-1 signaling pathway plays a crucial role in determining the lifespan, reproductive success, and ability to enter a state of dormancy (diapause) in various organisms. Due to its fundamental importance in animal physiology, we investigated when during an organism's life this pathway is necessary to regulate these different processes. Our findings reveal that in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, the pathway acts during adulthood, up until relatively advanced ages, to influence aging. In contrast, it controls diapause during development. Moreover, we found that the pathway regulates longevity and reproduction independently of each other, indicating that life-span regulation can be dissociated from other physiological processes that might seem to compromise an organism's quality of life.

title: Predominance of Type 1 Innate Lymphoid Cells in the Rectal Mucosa of Patients With Non-Celiac Wheat Sensitivity: Reversal After a Wheat-Free Diet
text:
Objective:
Non-celiac wheat sensitivity (NCWS) is defined as a response to ingested wheat following the exclusion of celiac disease and wheat allergy. However, the underlying mechanisms of NCWS are not fully understood, and this study aimed to investigate the inflammatory response in the rectal mucosa of patients with well-defined NCWS.
Methods:
This prospective study included 22 patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)-like clinical presentation, diagnosed with NCWS through a double-blind placebo-controlled challenge. Eight IBS patients who did not improve on a wheat-free diet were used as controls. Two weeks after oral challenge with 80 grams of wheat per day, cells were isolated from rectal biopsies and characterized using fluorescence-activated cell sorting analysis for intracellular cytokines and surface markers.
Results:
Rectal biopsies from wheat-challenged NCWS patients revealed a significant mucosal CD45(+) infiltrate composed of CD3(+) and CD3(-) lymphocytes, with the latter producing more interferon (IFN)-γ than IBS controls. Approximately 30% of IFN-γ-producing CD45(+) cells were T-bet(+), CD56(-), NKP44(-), and CD117(-), indicating the presence of type-1 innate lymphoid cells (ILC1). The number of IFN-γ-producing ILC1 cells significantly decreased in 10 patients after they resumed a wheat-free diet for two weeks.
Conclusions:
These findings suggest that, in patients with active NCWS, IFN-γ-producing ILC1 cells infiltrate the rectal mucosa, providing evidence for the role of this innate lymphoid cell population in the pathogenesis of NCWS.

title: Folding and Self-Assembly of the TatA Translocation Pore Based on a Charge Zipper Mechanism
text:
We present a novel concept for the folding and self-assembly of complexes consisting of pore-forming TatA subunits from the Twin-arginine translocase and other membrane proteins, enabled by electrostatic "charge zippers." Each TatA subunit is composed of a transmembrane segment, an amphiphilic helix (APH), and a densely charged C-terminal region (DCR). The complementary charge sequence between the DCR and APH suggests that the protein can be "zipped up" by forming a ladder of seven salt bridges. This results in a transmembrane pore that can self-assemble through both intra- and intermolecular salt bridges, with the length of the pore matching the lipid bilayer thickness.
To validate this concept, we employed molecular dynamics simulations and experimental assays to investigate the monomer-oligomer equilibrium of specific charge mutants. Our findings support the idea that similar "charge zippers" can be employed for other membrane-associated proteins, such as the biofilm-inducing peptide TisB, the human antimicrobial peptide dermcidin, and the pestiviral E(RNS) protein.
In summary, our concept proposes that the pore-forming TatA complex and other membrane proteins can self-assemble through electrostatic "charge zippers," allowing for the formation of transmembrane pores that can be exploited for a variety of biotechnological applications.

title: Molecular mechanisms of ribosomal protein gene coregulation.
text:
The 137 ribosomal protein genes (RPGs) in Saccharomyces provide a model for understanding how gene regulation is coordinated. To investigate the regulatory mechanisms involved, we analyzed the position and function of the transcription factors that control RPG expression, as well as the chromatin structure near the RPGs. Our findings reveal that the transcription factors Rap1, Fhl1, Ifh1, Sfp1, and Hmo1 are involved in the regulation of RPGs, and that Hmo1 plays a particularly important role in this process.
We found that Hmo1 cross-links to promoter DNA in an RPG-specific manner, and that it extended 20-50 base pairs downstream of Fhl1. When RPGs are repressed, Fhl1 remains in place, while Hmo1 dissociates, leading to an upstream shift of the +1 nucleosome. This shift is reflected in the Hmo1 extension and the core promoter region. Our results suggest that Fhl1 and Hmo1 may create two regulatory barriers that position the +1 nucleosome into either an activating or a repressive state.
In addition, we found that specific TFIID subunits cross-linked to Rap1 sites, providing further evidence for the role of sequence-specific DNA binding in regulating nucleosome positioning and transcription complex assembly. Overall, our findings shed light on how gene coregulation has evolved in concert with coding sequences, and provide a detailed picture of the regulatory mechanisms that control RPG expression.

title: Lipoatrophy and severe metabolic disturbance in mice with fat-specific deletion of PPARγ.
text: Adipose tissue plays a crucial metabolic role, and its dysfunction is linked to the onset of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. As the master regulator of adipocyte differentiation and function, the nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) has been extensively studied in vitro. Despite previous attempts at generating fat-specific knockouts of the murine PPARγ gene, the in vivo effects of such deletions were minimal. To address this, we generated Adipoq-Cre mice, which allow for adipose-specific recombination, and observed a unique fat-specific PPARγ knockout (PPARγ FKO) mouse model. At 3 months of age, these mice displayed almost no visible brown or white adipose tissue, and instead had enlarged pancreatic islets, massive fatty livers, and elevated blood glucose and serum insulin levels, indicative of extreme insulin resistance. Additionally, PPARγ FKO mice exhibited delayed hair coat formation, lack of dermal fat, disrupted mammary gland development, and high bone mass, highlighting the important role of adipose PPARγ in various tissues. Therefore, our findings underscore the necessity of fat PPARγ in adipose formation, whole-body metabolic homeostasis, and the normal development of fat-containing tissues.

title: Fluconazole prophylaxis: can we eliminate invasive Candida infections in the neonatal ICU?
text:
Purpose of Review:
In light of the high mortality rate and risk of neurodevelopmental impairment associated with fungal infections in preterm infants, preventing invasive Candida infections in these vulnerable patients should be a primary concern in every neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).
Recent Findings:
Even with prompt or empiric treatment, the mortality rate and incidence of neurodevelopmental impairment remain unacceptably high in infants weighing less than 1000 grams. Several studies have investigated the effectiveness and safety of fluconazole prophylaxis in high-risk infants, with compelling results. These studies have shown that fluconazole prophylaxis significantly reduces the incidence of invasive Candida infections in both high-risk and low-risk infants, with a mortality rate from all causes that is 25% lower. Moreover, these studies have demonstrated that targeting fluconazole prophylaxis to infants who are either <1000 g or < or =27 weeks can eliminate these infections as a cause of neurodevelopmental impairment and mortality.
Summary:
Targeting fluconazole prophylaxis to infants who are either <1000 g or < or =27 weeks is highly effective, safe, and inexpensive, and can eliminate invasive Candida infections as a cause of mortality and neurodevelopmental impairment in preterm infants.

title: Fumarase deficiency in dichorionic diamniotic twins.
text: Fumarase deficiency is an uncommon autosomal recessive inherited mistake in the Krebs Tricarboxylic Acid cycle. Heavy neurological symptoms are inherently associated with fumarase deficiency, typically presenting as microcephaly, dystonia, global developmental delays, seizures, and early mortality in infancy. Additionally, heterozygous carriers of the condition face an increased risk of developing hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma. We detail a non-consanguineous family in which a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy resulted in twin boys diagnosed with fumarase deficiency through biochemical, enzymatic, and molecular testing. The affected twins displayed hepatic involvement. An exclusive mutation in the fumarate hydratase gene was identified within this family.

title: Angiopoietin-2 is increased in sepsis and inversely associated with nitric oxide-dependent microvascular reactivity
text:
INTRODUCTION: Angiopoietin-2 (ang-2), a protein released by endothelial cell Weibel-Palade bodies (WPBs) and involved in angiogenesis, is elevated in severe sepsis, but the underlying mechanisms are still unclear. Nitric oxide (NO) has been shown to inhibit WPB exocytosis and decrease endothelial NO bioavailability in sepsis, potentially contributing to increased endothelial activation and capillary leak. We hypothesized that endothelial NO bioavailability would be inversely correlated with ang-2 concentrations in sepsis.
METHODS: In this study, we measured plasma ang-2, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and endothelial-active cytokines in 83 patients with early sepsis and 41 hospital controls, as well as related these markers to reactive hyperemia-peripheral arterial tonometry (RH-PAT), a measure of endothelial NO bioavailability.
RESULTS: Our results showed that plasma ang-2 levels were significantly elevated in sepsis (median [interquartile range (IQR)]: severe sepsis 12.4 [8.5-33.4], sepsis without organ failure 6.1 [5.0-10.4], controls 2.7 [2.2-3.6], P < 0.0001). There was a negative correlation between ang-2 and RH-PAT (r = -0.38, P < 0.0001) and a positive correlation between ang-2 and IL-6 (r = 0.57, P < 0.0001) and degree of organ failure (sequential organ function assessment score) (r = 0.58, P < 0.0001). The correlation between ang-2 and RH-PAT persisted after controlling for sepsis severity. In a longitudinal mixed-effects model, recovery of RH-PAT over time was associated with decline in ang-2.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that ang-2 is elevated in proportion to sepsis severity, and inversely correlated with NO-dependent microvascular reactivity. Impaired endothelial NO bioavailability may contribute to increased endothelial cell release of ang-2, endothelial activation, and capillary leak. Agents that increase endothelial NO bioavailability or inhibit WPB exocytosis and/or ang-2 activity may have therapeutic potential in sepsis.

title: Ecologic versus individual-level sources of bias in ecologic estimates of contextual health effects.
text:
A significant number of researchers have attempted to advocate for ecological (aggregate) studies by arguing that the primary objective of these studies is the estimation of contextual or group-level effects, rather than individual-level effects. However, critics argue that these attempts are often undermined by the fact that ecological effect estimates are inevitably used as estimates of individual effects, despite disclaimers. Moreover, there is a subtle problem where ecological variation in the distribution of individual effects can bias ecological estimates of contextual effects, a phenomenon that is common in studies of ecosocial factors and health outcomes due to the fact that social context is not randomly allocated across typical analysis units (administrative regions).
Ecological data, by definition, contain only marginal observations on the joint distribution of individually defined confounders and outcomes, thereby failing to identify either contextual or individual-level effects. While ecological studies can still be useful with appropriate caveats, their limitations are best addressed through multilevel study designs that obtain and use both individual- and group-level data. However, these studies often share certain unique problems with ecological studies, such as problems arising from inappropriate aggregation and issues related to temporal changes in covariate distributions.

title: Left–right asymmetry in the vertebrate embryo: from early information to higher-level integration
text: Although vertebrates appear symmetrical on the outside, there are numerous internal asymmetries in the placement and arrangement of organs during embryonic development. These asymmetries are established through complex epigenetic and genetic mechanisms during embryogenesis. Recent studies in various model organisms have shed light on how this laterality information is generated and transmitted to different regions of the embryo. While commonalities are emerging in the processes used by different vertebrates to specify the left-right axis, there are also divergences in these mechanisms. Interestingly, recent findings have also revealed connections between the establishment of left-right asymmetries and the symmetrical growth of the anterior-posterior axis.

title: Obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cancer: the insulin and IGF connection.
text: According to epidemiological research, there is a strong correlation between obesity and the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D), which in turn may increase the risk of cancer and cancer-related mortality. The connection between these diseases appears to be influenced by factors such as insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, elevated levels of IGF, and inflammatory markers. Treatment with medications such as metformin and exogenous insulin for T2D may also play a role in cancer risk and mortality. Innovative therapies targeting the insulin and IGF1 systems are currently being explored for their potential use in cancer treatment.

title: Non-coding RNAs: Functions and applications in endocrine-related cancer.
text:
A substantial portion of the human genome is transcribed into non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), which have challenged the traditional central dogma of molecular biology. Research has shown that ncRNAs play a crucial role in transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression. Interestingly, many ncRNAs are dysregulated in cancer, and recent studies aim to harness this knowledge for the development of cancer biomarkers and anti-cancer drugs. In particular, endocrine-related cancers, which have relatively low survival rates, are in need of such advancements.
This review summarizes the roles and clinical implications of newly discovered ncRNAs, including long ncRNAs, PIWI-interacting RNAs, tRNA- and Y RNA-derived ncRNAs, and small nucleolar RNAs, in endocrine-related cancers affecting both sexes. The review focuses on recent studies highlighting discoveries in ncRNA biology and expression in cancer, and concludes with a discussion on the challenges and future directions, including clinical application. ncRNAs hold great promise as diagnostic tools and therapeutic targets, but further research is necessary to realize their potential.

title: NMR structural and kinetic characterization of a homeodomain diffusing and hopping on nonspecific DNA.
text: Protein-DNA interactions that are not specific are inherently dynamic and involve both the diffusing of the protein along the DNA and hopping from one DNA molecule or segment to another. Understanding how gene regulatory proteins interact nonspecifically with DNA in terms of both structure and dynamics is difficult due to the experimental observables being an average of rapidly exchanging states. Through the use of various NMR spectroscopic techniques, such as relaxation analysis, paramagnetic relaxation enhancement, and residual dipolar couplings, we have characterized the structural and kinetic aspects of the interaction of the HoxD9 homeodomain with a nonspecific, 24-bp DNA duplex in a system in which the protein is not constrained to any particular site. The data reveal that HoxD9 binds to nonspecific DNA in the same manner and orientation as it does in the specific complex. However, the mobility of arginine side-chains contacting the DNA is increased in the nonspecific complex compared to the specific one. Additionally, the kinetics of intermolecular translocation between two different nonspecific DNA molecules have been analyzed, revealing that direct transfer from one nonspecific complex to another nonspecific DNA molecule occurs without passing through the intermediate of free protein. This finding provides a simple mechanism for accelerating the target search in vivo for the specific site in a sea of nonspecific sites by allowing for more effective sampling of available DNA sites as the protein jumps from one segment to another.

title: MHC Haplotype Matching for Unrelated Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation
text: The current standards for selecting unrelated donors for hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) involve matching the alleles of each human leukocyte antigen (HLA) locus within the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). However, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) continues to be a significant and potentially life-threatening complication even after HLA-identical unrelated HCT. The MHC contains over 400 genes, but the total number of transplantation antigens remains unclear. Identifying genes that influence transplantation outcome could be possible through linkage disequilibrium (LD)-mapping approaches if the expanded MHC haplotypes of the unrelated donor and recipient could be clarified.

title: The SIR2/3/4 complex and SIR2 alone promote longevity in Saccharomyces cerevisiae by two different mechanisms. Genes Dev 13
text: The SIR genes in yeast are critical determinants of lifespan. Our findings indicate that the Sir proteins' role in life span regulation is unrelated to their involvement in non-homologous end joining. The short lifespan of sir3 or sir4 mutants is primarily caused by the concurrent expression of a and alpha mating-type information, which leads to an increase in recombination in rDNA, likely resulting in the production of extrachromosomal rDNA circles. Similarly, the short lifespan of sir2 mutants is a direct result of their inability to repress recombination generated by the Fob1p-mediated replication block in the rDNA. Sir2p is a limiting factor in promoting yeast longevity, and increasing the gene dosage extends the life span in wild-type cells. The conservation of SIR2 in mammalian aging indicates a possible role for this protein in this process.

title: Meta-analysis identifies common variants associated with body mass index in East Asians
text: Through genome-wide association studies (GWAS) conducted in populations of East Asian descent, we have identified multiple genetic loci associated with obesity or body mass index (BMI). To further investigate these findings and validate the associations, we performed a meta-analysis of approximately 2.4 million single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in 27,715 East Asians, followed by in silico and de novo replication studies in 37,691 and 17,642 additional East Asians, respectively. Our analysis identified ten BMI-associated loci with genome-wide significance (P < 5.0 × 10(-8)), including seven previously identified loci (FTO, SEC16B, MC4R, GIPR-QPCTL, ADCY3-DNAJC27, BDNF and MAP2K5) and three novel loci in or near the CDKAL1, PCSK1 and GP2 genes. Furthermore, three additional loci nearly reached the genome-wide significance threshold, including two previously identified loci in the GNPDA2 and TFAP2B genes and a newly identified signal near PAX6, all of which were associated with BMI with P < 5.0 × 10(-7). These findings may shed light on novel pathways involved in obesity and highlight the importance of conducting genetic studies in non-European populations.

title: Phosphorylation of histone H3(T118) alters nucleosome dynamics and remodeling
text:
Nucleosomes, the building blocks of chromatin, function as both regulators and barriers to gene expression, replication, and repair. Post-translational modifications (PTMs) of histone proteins within nucleosomes control these processes. One such modification is phosphorylation of histone H3 at threonine 118 (H3(T118ph)). Our study focused on the effects of H3(T118ph) on nucleosome dynamics.
We expressed H3(T118ph) using protein ligation techniques and observed its impact on nucleosome behavior. Our findings reveal that H3(T118ph) reduces the binding strength between DNA and histone proteins by 2 kilocalories per mole, increases nucleosome mobility by 28 times, and enhances DNA accessibility near the dyad region by 6 times. Moreover, H3(T118ph) accelerates the disassembly of nucleosomes by the MSH2-MSH6 complex and enables disassembly by the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeler, suggesting that H3(T118ph) can directly modulate and potentially reprogram chromatin remodeling reactions.
In summary, our study uncovers the effects of H3(T118ph) on nucleosome dynamics and highlights its potential as a regulator of chromatin remodeling. Our findings demonstrate the importance of considering the modifications of histone proteins in the context of chromatin structure and function.

title: Mechanosignaling through YAP and TAZ drives fibroblast activation and fibrosis.
text:
Feedback loop drives fibrosis: YAP/TAZ coordinate matrix stiffness-regulated fibroblast activation.
Disease-driven fibrosis is fueled by a self-sustaining loop in which the stiff extracellular matrix (ECM) activates fibroblasts, which in turn produce more ECM components, making the surrounding environment even more stiff. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. We identify yes-associated protein (YAP) and transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ), key regulators of the Hippo signaling pathway, as central elements of this vicious cycle. YAP and TAZ are highly expressed in fibrotic lung tissue, especially in elongated fibroblastic cells, where TAZ shows prominent nucleus accretion. When cultured on stiff matrices, YAP and TAZ accumulate in fibroblast nuclei, leading to enhanced matrix production, contraction, and proliferation. Inhibiting YAP and TAZ together in vitro significantly reduces these fibroblast functions exclusively on stiff matrices. Their targets, including plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, are regulated by matrix stiffness independently of transforming growth factor-β signaling. Immortalized fibroblasts expressing active YAP or TAZ mutants can grow uninhibited on soft matrices, then promote fibrosis when transferred to the lung, demonstrating the capacity of fibroblast YAP/TAZ activation to drive a profibrotic response in vivo. Altogether, these findings establish YAP and TAZ as mechanoactivated coordinators of the matrix-amplifying feedback loop that perpetuates fibrosis.

title: Control of cellular cholesterol efflux by the nuclear oxysterol receptor LXR alpha.
text:
Nuclear receptor LXR alpha plays a crucial role in regulating the metabolism of cholesterol in cells. Previous studies have shown that LXR alpha regulates the conversion of cholesterol to bile acids. Our current research aims to uncover the role of LXR alpha in controlling cellular cholesterol efflux. 
We found that expression of LXR alpha in NIH 3T3 fibroblasts or RAW264.7 macrophages, or treatment of these cells with oxysterol ligands of LXR, resulted in a 7- to 30-fold increase in the mRNA encoding the putative cholesterol/phospholipid transporter ATP-binding cassette (ABC)A1. In contrast, the induction of ABCA1 mRNA in response to oxysterols was significantly attenuated in cells that constitutively express dominant-negative forms of LXR alpha or LXR beta that lack the AF2 transcriptional activation domain. 
Our findings suggest that cellular cholesterol efflux is primarily controlled at the transcriptional level by a nuclear receptor-signaling pathway. Oxysterol ligands of LXR are able to stimulate efflux in response to cellular sterol loading, leading to the induction of the ABCA1 transporter and the lipid efflux to extracellular acceptors. These results have important implications for our understanding of mammalian cholesterol homeostasis and suggest new opportunities for pharmacological regulation of cellular lipid metabolism.

title: Circadian regulation of intracellular G-protein signalling mediates intercellular synchrony and rhythmicity in the suprachiasmatic nucleus
text: Thousands of cellular clocks in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the body's central clock, exhibit synchronous oscillations, which are orchestrated by poorly understood cell-cell communication mechanisms. Here, we discover that the amount of RGS16 (regulator of G protein signalling 16), a protein liable to turn off Gαi, rises at a selective circadian time to grant time-dependent activation of intracellular cyclic AMP signalling in the SCN. gene ablation of Rgs16 leads to a loss of circadian cAMP generation, resulting in longer circadian periods in behavioral rhythm. The precisely timed regulation of the cAMP signal by clock-controlled RGS16 is essential for the dorsomedial SCN to maintain a normal phase relationship with the ventrolateral SCN. Therefore, RGS16-dependent temporal regulation of intracellular G protein signaling coordinates the intercellular synchrony of SCN pacemaker neurons, thereby establishing a 24-hour rhythm in behavior.

title: MDC1 collaborates with TopBP1 in DNA replication checkpoint control
text: Human TopBP1 plays a crucial role in regulating the DNA replication checkpoint. In this study, we identified MDC1, a key checkpoint protein involved in the cellular response to DNA double-strand breaks, as a TopBP1-interacting protein. The specific interaction between TopBP1 and MDC1 is mediated by the fifth BRCT domain of TopBP1 and the Ser-Asp-Thr (SDT) repeats of MDC1. We also demonstrated that TopBP1 accumulation at stalled replication forks is enhanced by the H2AX/MDC1 signaling pathway. Furthermore, MDC1 is essential for ATR-dependent Chk1 activation in response to replication stress. Taken together, our findings suggest that MDC1 plays a critical role in multiple aspects of the DNA damage response and DNA replication checkpoint.

title: Deregulated DNA polymerase β strengthens ionizing radiation-induced nucleotidic and chromosomal instabilities
text: DNA polymerase β (Pol β) is an error-prone enzyme that has been found to be overexpressed in several human tumors. By using a few modified CHO cells that differed only in their exogenous expression of Pol β, we showed here that cells overexpressing Pol β are significantly more sensitive to IR treatments, leading to increased apoptosis. Moreover, the surviving cells displayed a hypermutator phenotype, which we found to be mediated by multiple pathways involving Pol β, including (i) an increased capacity to incorporate mutagenic dGTP analogs, such as 8-oxo-dGTP, one of the most abundant purine-derived nucleotides exposed to γ-irradiation, (ii) the induction of IR-induced DNA breaks, and (iii) accumulation of chromosome aberrations induced by radiation. Our findings suggest that alterations in Pol β expression in irradiated cells strengthen both cell death and genetic changes associated with a malignant phenotype, providing new insights into the cellular response to radiation and its carcinogenic consequences.

title: Chromosome 7 gain and DNA hypermethylation at the HOXA10 locus are associated with expression of a stem cell related HOX-signature in glioblastoma
text:
Background HOX genes are a group of developmental genes that are not expressed in either the developing forebrain or normal brain. In glioblastoma, aberrant expression of a HOX-gene-dominated stem-cell signature has been linked to increased resistance to chemo-radiotherapy and sustained proliferation of glioma initiating cells. Our study aims to investigate the epigenetic and genetic alterations that interact with the expression of this signature in glioblastoma.
Results We observe extensive DNA methylation of the HOXA locus at 7p15.2 in glioblastoma compared to non-tumor brain tissue. This hypermethylation is associated with a gain of chromosome 7, a hallmark of glioblastoma, and may function as a rescue mechanism by preventing unwanted gene expression due to tumor-driven gene dosage increases. We identify a specific CpG island within the alternative promoter of the HOXA10 gene that escapes hypermethylation in HOX-high glioblastoma. An additive effect of gene copy gain at 7p15.2 and DNA methylation at key regulatory CpGs in HOXA10 is found to be significantly associated with HOX-signature expression. Furthermore, we observe concordance between methylation status and the presence of active or inactive chromatin marks in glioblastoma-derived spheres, with HOX-high spheres exhibiting higher levels of active chromatin marks and HOX-low spheres displaying higher levels of inactive chromatin marks.
Conclusions Based on our findings, we propose that co-evolution and interaction between gene copy gain, which is associated with a gain of chromosome 7, and additional epigenetic alterations are key mechanisms that coordinate and activate a misguided HOX transcriptional program in glioblastoma.

title: Probing the phenomenon of trained immunity in invertebrates during a transgenerational study, using brine shrimp Artemia as a model system
text: The study on the invertebrate's innate immune system revealed the intriguing concept of trained immunity, where the immune system exhibits adaptive features. However, the long-term memory characteristics of the innate immune system and the underlying mechanisms remain obscure. To investigate this phenomenon, we utilized the invertebrate model Artemia and conducted a transgenerational study to determine if trained immunity exists and to identify the mechanisms involved. Our findings indicated the presence of memory and partial discrimination in Artemia's immune system, as evidenced by increased resistance towards a homologous bacterial strain for three consecutive generations. This enhanced resistance was linked to elevated levels of hsp70 and hmgb1 signaling molecules and modifications in the expression of essential innate immunity-related genes. Furthermore, we discovered stochastic patterns in the acetylation and methylation levels of H4 and H3K4me3 histones, respectively, in the progenies of ancestors challenged with bacteria. Our findings suggest that the innate immune responses in invertebrates have the potential to be trained, and epigenetic reprogramming of select innate immune effectors may play a central role in the mechanisms leading to trained immunity.

title: Using Structural Information to Change the Phosphotransfer Specificity of a Two-Component Chemotaxis Signalling Complex
text:
Two-component signal transduction pathways, comprising histidine protein kinases (HPKs) and their response regulators (RRs), are widely used by bacteria to respond to environmental cues. In fact, some bacteria have over 150 different two-component systems, each with a high degree of specificity to prevent unwanted interactions. One of the best-understood pathways is the chemotaxis pathway, which plays a crucial role in bacterial migration towards attractants and away from repellents.
In this study, we present the 1.40 Å crystal structure of the histidine-containing phosphotransfer domain of the chemotaxis HPK, CheA(3), in complex with its cognate RR, CheY(6). Our findings reveal that a methionine finger on CheY(6) specifically interacts with a hydrophobic pocket in CheA(3), allowing for high-specificity protein-protein interactions. By using site-directed mutagenesis and surface plasmon resonance studies, we found that this methionine is essential for the interaction between CheA(3) and CheY(6). Additionally, we demonstrated that introducing this methionine and an adjacent alanine residue into non-cognate CheYs significantly altered their specificity, allowing them to interact with and transfer phosphate from CheA(3)-P.
The structure presented here has provided valuable insights into the determinants of specificity in the CheA-CheY interaction, enabling the successful reengineering of phosphotransfer signaling. In summary, our findings highlight the complex regulation of two-component signal transduction pathways and the mechanisms used by bacteria to ensure proper coordination of cellular responses.

title: Combination varenicline and bupropion SR for tobacco-dependence treatment in cigarette smokers: a randomized trial.
text: Combining varenicline and bupropion sustained-release (SR) therapy may lead to higher smoking abstinence rates compared to varenicline monotherapy, according to the results of a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled clinical trial conducted between October 2009 and April 2013 at three midwestern clinical research sites. The study included 506 adult cigarette smokers who were randomly assigned to receive either varenicline and bupropion SR or varenicline and placebo for 12 weeks. At week 12, 53.0% of the combination therapy group achieved prolonged smoking abstinence and 56.2% achieved 7-day point-prevalence smoking abstinence, compared to 43.2% and 48.6%, respectively, in the varenicline monotherapy group. The results were confirmed at weeks 26 and 52, with 36.6% and 38.2% of the combination therapy group achieving prolonged abstinence and 36.6% and 39.2% achieving 7-day point-prevalence abstinence, respectively. However, neither outcome was significantly different at 52 weeks. The study also found that participants in the combination therapy group reported more anxiety and depressive symptoms compared to those in the varenicline monotherapy group. The authors conclude that while combined use of varenicline and bupropion, compared to varenicline alone, may increase smoking abstinence at 12 and 26 weeks, further research is needed to determine the role of combination therapy in smoking cessation.

title: Effect of a C/EBP gene replacement on mitochondrial biogenesis in fat cells.
text: CCAAT/enhancer-binding proteins, C/EBPα and C/EBPβ, are essential for the differentiation and maturation of fat cells. Previous investigations revealed that replacing C/EBPα with C/EBPβ in the mouse genome, resulting in beta/beta alleles, inhibits lipid accumulation in white adipose tissue (WAT). In this study, beta/beta mice had a longer lifespan and higher energy expenditure compared to their control littermates due to enhanced WAT energy oxidation. The WAT of beta/beta mice was rich in metabolically active, thermogenic mitochondria, which are known for their ability to burn energy. The beta/beta allele exerted its effect by elevating the expression of the G protein alpha stimulatory subunit (Galphas) in WAT. Overexpression of Galphas in fat-laden 3T3-L1 cells was found to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis, similar to the WAT of beta/beta mice, and significantly reduce the stored lipid pool.

title: Variable breakpoints target PAX5 in patients with dicentric chromosomes: a model for the basis of unbalanced translocations in cancer.
text: Despite the variability in breakpoint locations in acquired chromosomal abnormalities, such as dicentric chromosomes in B cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia, single genes can be targeted through various mechanisms. Using FISH and molecular copy number counting, we identified 5 fusion gene partners with PAX5: LOC392027 (7p12.1), SLCO1B3 (12p12), ASXL1 (20q11.1), KIF3B (20q11.21), and C20orf112 (20q11.1). In each predicted fusion protein, the DNA-binding paired domain of PAX5 was present. Quantitative PCR demonstrated that both deletion and fusion events resulted in underexpression of PAX5, which led to altered expression of its target genes, EBF1, ALDH1A1, ATP9A, and FLT3. Deletion and mutation of the homologous PAX5 allele further supported the critical role of PAX5. Our findings indicate that specific gene loci can be targeted by heterogeneous translocation breakpoints in human cancer, acting through various mechanisms. This approach may provide insight into the identification of cancer genes in solid tumors, where unbalanced chromosomal rearrangements are prevalent and few genes have been identified. It is likely that this strategy will reveal similar mechanisms of cancer pathogenesis in other types of cancer.

title: Copyright � 1996, American Society for Microbiology Endotoxin-Induced Enhancement of Glucose Influx into
text:
Hypoglycemia is one of the most harmful metabolic disorders caused by endotoxemia. In animal models of endotoxemia, there is a significant increase in glucose consumption in organs rich in macrophages. However, the exact mechanism by which endotoxin (LPS) affects the uptake of glucose by macrophages has not been fully understood. To address this, we conducted a study to investigate the direct effect of LPS on glucose uptake by macrophages.
Our results showed that the consumption and uptake of glucose, as measured using 2-deoxy-D-[3H]glucose, were significantly increased by two to threefold in murine peritoneal exudate macrophages in culture after stimulation with 3 ng of LPS per ml. The rate of glucose uptake reached a plateau after 20 minutes of stimulation and remained at the maximum as long as LPS was present. Additionally, northern (RNA) blot analysis using cDNA probes for five known isoforms of glucose transporter (GLUT) revealed that the expression of GLUT by macrophages was restricted to the GLUT1 isoform during LPS stimulation, and the amount of GLUT1 mRNA was increased by the stimulation.
These findings suggest that the rapid and sustained glucose influx into macrophages via GLUT1 plays a crucial role in the development of systemic hypoglycemia during prolonged endotoxemia.

title: Factors associated with American Board of Medical Specialties member board certification among US medical school graduates.
text:
ABMS member board certification is emerging as a key measure of physician quality. To identify factors associated with this certification among US medical school graduates, we conducted a retrospective study of a national cohort of 1997-2000 graduates, monitoring their progress through March 2, 2009. Our findings reveal that graduates in certain specialty categories were more likely to be board certified, while others were less likely.
We analyzed data from 42,440 graduates, and found that 37,054 (87.3%) were board certified. Across all specialty categories, graduates who scored in the top tertile on the US Medical Licensing Examination Step 2 Clinical Knowledge were more likely to be certified. The lowest odds were observed for emergency medicine (87.4% vs 73.6%; odds ratio [OR], 1.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.03-3.20), while the highest odds were noted for radiology (98.1% vs 74.9%; OR, 13.19; 95% CI, 5.55-31.32).
In contrast, graduates who identified as underrepresented racial/ethnic minorities were less likely to be board certified, with a range of 83.5% to 95.6% across specialty categories. Specifically, the odds of certification were lower for pediatrics (AOR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.33-0.58) and other nongeneralist specialties (AOR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.96), compared to white graduates.
Our findings also revealed that graduates with higher levels of debt were less likely to be board certified. Specifically, obstetrics/gynecology graduates were less likely to be certified for every $50,000 unit increase in debt (AOR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.83-0.96). In contrast, family medicine graduates were more likely to be certified for each $50,000 unit increase in debt (AOR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.01-1.26).
Overall, our study shows that demographic and educational factors significantly impact ABMS member board certification among US medical school graduates. By identifying these factors, our findings can help inform decision-making and strategies to improve physician quality and address disparities in medical education.

title: Body-mass index and mortality in Korean men and women.
text: BACKGROUND: Obesity is linked to various health risks, but its role as a predictor of mortality remains disputed. METHODS: We examined the relationship between body weight and death risk in a 12-year prospective study of 1,213,829 Korean individuals between the ages of 30 and 95. We analyzed 82,372 deaths from all causes and 48,731 deaths from specific diseases (including 29,123 from cancer, 16,426 from atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and 3362 from respiratory disease) in relation to body mass index (BMI), calculated as weight in kilograms divided by squared height in meters. RESULTS: Across both sexes, the average baseline BMI was 23.2, and death rate showed a J-shaped association with BMI, regardless of smoking history. The lowest risk of death from any cause occurred among individuals with a BMI of 23.0-24.9. In all groups, respiratory death risk was higher among individuals with lower BMI, while cancer and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease death risk were higher among those with higher BMI. The relative risk of death associated with BMI decreased with increasing age.
