CONCLUSIONS: Underscoring the significance of body weight as a predictor of death, both underweight, overweight, and obese men and women had higher death rates than their normal-weight counterparts. The association between BMI and death varied according to cause of death and was influenced by age, sex, and smoking history.

title: Human iPSC-based modeling of late-onset disease via progerin-induced aging.
text: Reprogramming somatic cells to induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) effectively remodels their identity to an embryonic state, posing a significant challenge for modeling age-related disorders. In this investigation, we outline a methodology to introduce aging-related traits into human iPSC-derived cell lines and demonstrate its application in the modeling of Parkinson's disease (PD). Our approach involves the expression of progerin, a truncated form of lamin A associated with premature aging. We discovered that expressing progerin in iPSC-derived fibroblasts and neurons induces multiple aging-related markers and features, including dopamine-specific phenotypes such as neuromelanin accumulation. Inducing aging in PD iPSC-derived dopamine neurons revealed disease characteristics that require both aging and genetic susceptibility, including pronounced dendrite degeneration, progressive loss of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression, and enlarged mitochondria or Lewy-body-precursor inclusions. Our findings suggest that progerin-induced aging can be utilized to unveil late-onset age-related disease features in iPSC-based disease models.

title: SNAREs — engines for membrane fusion
text: Since the late 1980s, the discovery of SNARE proteins has illuminated their importance as integral components of protein complexes that regulate membrane fusion. Although SNARE proteins exhibit significant sequence diversity, their mechanism of action appears to be highly conserved, allowing them to adapt to a wide range of fusion reactions, including those involved in cell proliferation, membrane repair, cytokinesis, and synaptic transmission. As research continues to uncover the intricate details of these nanoscale machines, a fascinating picture is emerging.

title: Maintaining the norm: T-cell homeostasis
text: Immunologists have long been fascinated by the longevity of naive and memory T cells, but the factors that govern their survival and maintenance have remained elusive. In recent years, however, it has become increasingly clear that the homeostasis of these subsets is remarkably dynamic and tightly regulated by intrinsic signals, such as cytokines and self-peptide-MHC ligands for the T-cell receptor. These homeostatic mechanisms may have a profound impact on the ability of the T-cell pool to respond to both foreign and self-antigens.

title: Cell type of origin influences the molecular and functional properties of mouse induced pluripotent stem cells
text: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have been generated from various somatic cell populations through the forced expression of specific factors. However, it remains unclear whether iPSCs derived from different cell types share similar molecular and functional properties. In this study, we investigated the transcriptional and epigenetic profiles of iPSCs derived from mouse fibroblasts, hematopoietic cells, and myogenic cells. Our results show that these iPSCs exhibit distinct patterns of gene expression and epigenetic marks, indicating that cellular origin plays a significant role in determining their differentiation potentials in vitro. Moreover, we found that continuous passaging of iPSCs largely abolishes these differences, suggesting that early-passage iPSCs retain a transient epigenetic memory of their somatic cells of origin. These findings have important implications for the use of iPSCs in disease modeling and potential therapeutic applications, as they suggest that early-passage iPSCs may be more reflective of their original cellular source.

title: Spatiotemporal control of mitosis by the conserved spindle matrix protein Megator
text: A putative spindle matrix, whose existence and functionality have been the subject of controversy, is thought to play a key role in the movement of chromosomes during cell division. Our study has shown that Megator (Mtor), the Drosophila counterpart of the human nuclear pore complex protein Translocated Promoter Region (Tpr), and the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC) protein Mad2 form a conserved complex that localizes to a nuclear-derived spindle matrix in living cells. Using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching techniques, we have found that Mtor is retained around spindle microtubules, exhibiting distinct dynamic properties. Mtor/Tpr promotes the recruitment of Mad2 and Mps1, but not Mad1, to unattached kinetochores (KTs), leading to normal mitotic duration and SAC response. At anaphase, Mtor plays a role in spindle elongation, which affects normal chromosome movement. Based on our findings, we propose that Mtor/Tpr functions as a spatial regulator of the SAC, ensuring efficient recruitment of Mad2 to unattached KTs at the onset of mitosis and proper spindle maturation. Additionally, the enrichment of Mad2 in a spindle matrix helps confine the action of a diffusible "wait anaphase" signal to the vicinity of the spindle, thereby ensuring proper chromosome movement.

title: Randomized trial of folic acid supplementation and serum homocysteine levels.
text:
Background: Lowering serum homocysteine levels through folic acid supplementation has been shown to reduce mortality from ischemic heart disease. While it is known that higher doses of folic acid (1 mg/d) result in maximal homocysteine reduction, the effect of lower doses (relevant to food fortification) is unclear.
Methods: We randomized 151 patients with ischemic heart disease to one of five dosages of folic acid (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0 mg/d) or placebo. Fasting blood samples for serum homocysteine and serum folate analysis were taken at baseline, after 3 months of supplementation, and 3 months after folic acid supplementation was discontinued.
Results: As the dosage of folic acid increased, the median serum homocysteine level decreased, with the maximum reduction observed at 0.8 mg of folic acid per day (2.7 micromol/L, 23%). The response to folic acid was greater in individuals with higher initial serum homocysteine levels, but there were statistically significant reductions across all initial levels. In addition, serum folate level increased approximately linearly (5.5 nmol/L for every 0.1 mg of folic acid). Placebo group results showed large within-person fluctuations in serum homocysteine levels over time, indicating that monitoring individual reductions is impractical.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that a dosage of 0.8 mg/d of folic acid is necessary to achieve the maximum reduction in serum homocysteine levels across the full range of homocysteine levels in the population. Current US food fortification levels will achieve only a minor portion of the achievable homocysteine reduction.

title: Adherens junctions in Drosophila retinal morphogenesis.
text: Adherens junctions, comprising classic cadherins, play a crucial role in animal morphogenesis. Despite the well-established importance of cadherins in development, the mechanisms regulating adherens junction function during morphogenesis remain an area of active research. Adherens junctions are involved in the formation of simple cell patterns, as well as more complex cell shape changes and movements, which rely on the dynamic regulation of adherens junctions.

title: Multiple roles of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in skeletal development, growth, and repair.
text: Publisher's Summary: This chapter delves into the critical roles of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in skeletal morphogenesis, discusses potential future research directions, and highlights some of the challenges faced in the field. VEGF regulates osteoclastic differentiation, migration, and activity, making it a central coordinator of the entire process. VEGF is essential for osteoclastic activity at both the initial stage of bone formation and during bone growth. Several factors, including prostaglandins E1 and E2, BMP-4, BMP-6, BMP-7, FGF-2, TGF-β, endothelin-1, IGF-1, and vitamin D3, induce VEGF expression in osteoblasts by activating various signaling pathways. The repair of bone fractures, like bone development during embryonic development, highlights the involvement of VEGF in bone healing. Bone fractures can heal in two distinct ways: stabilized fractures undergo intramembranous ossification, while unstable fractures undergo endochondral ossification. The similarity between bone development and fracture healing, along with VEGF's expression at fracture sites, suggests its involvement in bone repair as it is in bone formation.

title: Effectiveness of thigh-length graduated compression stockings to reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis after stroke (CLOTS trial 1): a multicentre, randomised controlled trial
text: In this randomized controlled trial, we investigated the effectiveness of thigh-length graduated compression stockings (GCS) in preventing deep vein thrombosis (DVT) after stroke. 2518 patients admitted to hospital within 1 week of an acute stroke and who were immobile were enrolled from 64 centers in the UK, Italy, and Australia. Patients were randomly assigned to either routine care plus thigh-length GCS (n=1256) or routine care plus avoidance of GCS (n=1262). Compression Doppler ultrasound of both legs was performed at days 7-10 and, when practical, again at 25-30 days after enrolment. The primary outcome was the occurrence of symptomatic or asymptomatic DVT in the popliteal or femoral veins. Analysis was by intention to treat. The results showed that the primary outcome occurred in 126 (10.0%) patients in the GCS group and 133 (10.5%) patients in the avoid GCS group, with a non-significant absolute reduction in risk of 0.5% (95% CI -1.9% to 2.9%). However, skin breaks, ulcers, blisters, and skin necrosis were significantly more common in patients allocated to GCS than in those allocated to avoid their use (64 [5%] vs 16 [1%]; odds ratio 4.18, 95% CI 2.40-7.27). These findings do not support the use of thigh-length GCS in patients admitted to hospital with acute stroke. National guidelines for stroke may need to be revised based on these results. The study was funded by the Medical Research Council (UK), Chief Scientist Office of Scottish Government, Chest Heart and Stroke Scotland, Tyco Healthcare (Covidien) USA, and UK Stroke Research Network.

title: Streptococcus pneumoniae early response genes to human lung epithelial cells
text: The article investigates the gene expression changes in Streptococcus pneumoniae, a pathogenic bacterium that infects the respiratory tract, upon exposure to human lung epithelial cells. The study used TIGR (JCVI) microarray technology to analyze the transcriptional responses of an encapsulated pathogenic pneumococcal strain, TIGR4, upon exposure to human lung epithelial cells A549 for 0.5 and 1 hours. The results showed that different gene expression profiles were observed at the two incubation time points, with most genes being down-regulated at 0.5 hours and up-regulated at 1 hour. Specifically, genes involved in ribonucleotide biosynthesis were down-regulated at both time points, while genes associated with cell envelope, energy metabolism, transport, and protein synthesis were mostly up-regulated at 1 hour. The study also compared the transcriptomes of TIGR4 in response to human macrophages for the same time periods, revealing a set of genes that exhibited similar expression changes upon exposure to both types of host cells. These genes included cell envelope-associated bgaA and nanA, and uncharacterized gene clusters such as SP1677-SP1680 and SP1688-SP1690. Overall, the study suggests that at the early stage of interaction with host epithelial cells, complex gene regulation and expression changes occur in bacteria, some of which may play an essential role in the establishment of infection.

title: Proteomic identification of a novel isoform of collapsin response mediator protein-2 in spinal nerves peripheral to dorsal root ganglia.
text: Primary afferent fibers arise from pseudounipolar sensory cells in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and transmit external stimuli received in the skin to the spinal cord. In this study, we employed a proteomic approach to investigate the polarity of primary afferent fibers. We dissected lumbar spinal nerve segments, both central and peripheral to the DRG, from 5-week-old Wistar rats and subjected the lysates to large-scale 2-dimensional electrophoresis (2-DE) at pH 5-6. Among the approximately 800 protein spots detected in the central and peripheral fractions, we identified a unique spot in the peripheral fraction with a molecular weight (MW) of 60 kDa and pI of 5.6 as an isoform of collapsin response mediator protein-2 (CRMP-2). Using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) and Western blots with anti-CRMP-2 antibodies that recognize residues 1-17 and 486-528, we confirmed that this novel spot was periCRMP-2. Interestingly, this spot was detected only in the peripheral fraction, but not in the central fraction, DRG, or other regions of the brain. Additionally, we found that the expression of periCRMP-2 decreased following sciatic nerve injury. These findings suggest that periCRMP-2 is a C-terminal truncated isoform that is specifically polarized in the peripheral side of spinal nerves and may play a role in nerve degeneration and regeneration.

title: Empirical statistical estimates for sequence similarity searches
text:
The FASTA package of sequence comparison programs has been updated to provide more accurate statistical estimates for local sequence similarity scores with gaps. The new approach uses the extreme value distribution to estimate the mean and variance of the local similarity scores of unrelated sequences, and then corrects the scores for the expected effect of library sequence length. This enables accurate estimates to be calculated for both FASTA and Smith-Waterman similarity scores for protein/protein, DNA/DNA, and protein/translated-DNA comparisons.
The accuracy of the statistical estimates was evaluated for 54 protein families using FASTA and Smith-Waterman scores, and the results showed that the probability estimates calculated from the distribution of similarity scores are generally conservative, as are probabilities calculated using the Altschul-Gish lambda, kappa, and eta parameters. Furthermore, the performance of several alternative methods for correcting similarity scores for library-sequence length was evaluated using 54 protein superfamilies from the PIR39 database and 110 protein families from the Prosite/SwissProt rel. 34 database. The results showed that both regression-scaled and Altschul-Gish scaled scores perform significantly better than unscaled Smith-Waterman or FASTA similarity scores. When the Prosite/SwissProt test set is used, regression-scaled scores perform slightly better; when the PIR database is used, Altschul-Gish scaled scores perform best.
Overall, the length-corrected similarity scores improved the sensitivity of database searches, and the statistical parameters derived from the distribution of similarity scores provided accurate estimates of statistical significance that can be used to infer sequence homology.

title: Steroid hormone signalling links reproduction to lifespan in dietary-restricted Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: Dietary restriction (DR) has been shown to increase healthspan and longevity in various species, including primates, but it often comes at the cost of impaired reproductive function. It is unclear whether signals linked to the reproductive system contribute to or are necessary for DR's effects on lifespan. To investigate, we examined the expression of the cytochrome P450 DAF-9/CYP450 and the production of the steroid hormone Δ(7)-dafachronic acid (DA) in Caenorhabditis elegans under DR conditions. We found that DA signaling through the non-canonical nuclear hormone receptor NHR-8/NHR and the nutrient-responsive kinase let-363/mTOR is essential for DR-mediated longevity in C. elegans. Moreover, steroid signaling also affects germline plasticity in response to nutrient deprivation, and this is required to achieve lifespan extension. These findings demonstrate that steroid signaling plays a central role in integrating nutrient and steroid hormone signals to regulate lifespan in response to nutrient availability.

title: Regulation and effects of hypothalamic galanin: relation to dietary fat, alcohol ingestion, circulating lipids and energy homeostasis.
text: Galanin (GAL) is known to stimulate feeding behavior, displaying distinct properties and functions compared to other feeding stimulants, such as neuropeptide Y and agouti-related protein. In contrast to other feeding peptides, hypothalamic GAL is relatively unresponsive to food deprivation and changes in corticosterone, glucose utilization, dietary carbohydrate, and leptin. This suggests that GAL is not essential under conditions of food scarcity or low-energy, high-carbohydrate diets. On the other hand, recent findings indicate that GAL in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) plays a key role in adapting to conditions of positive energy balance characterized by excess consumption of fat and alcohol. GAL in the PVN is activated by a high-fat diet and alcohol consumption, with peak activation occurring during the middle of the active feeding cycle, when fat and triglyceride levels naturally increase. Central injection of GAL in the PVN leads to enhanced food and alcohol consumption, and a stronger feeding response is observed in rats maintained on a fat-rich diet. These findings support the existence of non-homeostatic, positive feedback circuits between GAL and both dietary fat and alcohol, which contribute to the large meal size, overconsumption of alcohol, and obesity associated with fatty foods.

title: Evidence-based interventions for improvement of maternal and child nutrition: what can be done and at what cost?
text: According to the text, maternal undernutrition contributes to approximately 800,000 neonatal deaths annually, while stunting, wasting, and micronutrient deficiencies underlie nearly 3.1 million child deaths every year. While progress has been made through various interventions implemented at scale, there is still a need to improve access to these interventions, particularly in poor populations, to accelerate gains in reducing child mortality. The article conducted a comprehensive update of interventions to address undernutrition and micronutrient deficiencies in women and children, using standard methods to assess emerging new evidence for delivery platforms. The analysis suggests that access to ten evidence-based nutrition interventions can reduce child mortality by 15%, with a total additional annual cost of approximately Int$9.6 billion per year. However, the article also stresses that continued investments in nutrition-specific interventions, when linked to nutrition-sensitive approaches such as women's empowerment, agriculture, food systems, education, employment, social protection, and safety nets, can greatly accelerate progress in countries with the highest burden of maternal and child undernutrition and mortality.

title: FGF regulates TGF-β signaling and endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition via control of let-7 miRNA expression.
text: Maintaining normal endothelial function is crucial for various aspects of blood vessel health, but the regulatory mechanisms behind this process are not well understood. In this study, we found that disrupting the baseline fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling to the endothelium leads to a significant reduction in let-7 microRNA levels, which, in turn, leads to increased expression of transforming growth factor (TGF)-β ligands and receptors, and activation of TGF-β signaling, ultimately resulting in endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Endo-MT). We also found that Endo-MT plays a key role in neointima formation in a mouse transplant arteriopathy model and in rejection of human transplant lesions. The decline in endothelial FGF signaling is caused by the development of an FGF resistance state, characterized by inflammation-induced reduction in FGF signaling components. These findings demonstrate FGF signaling's critical role in maintaining endothelial homeostasis and reveal an unexpected connection between Endo-MT and vascular pathology.

title: Nuclear Receptors, RXR, and the Big Bang
text: Isolation and analysis of genes encoding receptors for steroids, retinoids, vitamin D, and thyroid hormone revealed a conserved template for nuclear hormone receptors. This discovery led to the identification of numerous related proteins, termed orphan receptors. Further characterization of these orphan receptors, particularly the retinoid X receptor (RXR), positioned nuclear receptors at the center of the "Big Bang" of molecular endocrinology. This Review provides a personal perspective on nuclear receptors and explores their integrated and coordinated signaling networks, which are essential for multicellular life. The RXR heterodimer and its associated ligands play a key role in this process, and their transcriptional mechanism is a crucial component of nuclear receptor function.

title: A genome-wide short hairpin RNA screening of jurkat T-cells for human proteins contributing to productive HIV-1 replication.
text: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) have been deployed to hinder HIV-1 replication. However, a problem arises due to the rapid mutation of viral sequences when targeted by siRNAs and cytotoxicity when cellular genes are knocked down. In search of cellular proteins that contribute to HIV-1 replication without causing significant cytotoxicity, we utilized a shRNA library that targets 54,509 human transcripts. We then constructed a comprehensive population of Jurkat T-cell clones, each expressing a unique shRNA, and infected them with HIV-1. Surviving clones represented moieties silenced for human mRNAs essential for viral replication, but whose chronic knockdown did not lead to cytotoxicity. Through this process, 252 individual Jurkat mRNAs were identified, of which 22 were further verified for their contributions to HIV-1 replication. Five mRNAs, including NRF1, STXBP2, NCOA3, PRDM2, and EXOSC5, were investigated for their role in distinct steps of the HIV-1 life cycle. Our findings were compared to previous studies that used siRNA-based screens in HeLa or 293T cells, highlighting similarities and differences.

title: UNR facilitates the interaction of MLE with the lncRNA roX2 during Drosophila dosage compensation.
text: Dosage compensation is a regulatory mechanism that helps balance the expression of genes on the X chromosome between male and female organisms. In the fruit fly Drosophila, this process involves non-coding RNAs and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) whose functions are not fully understood. Our study reveals that an RBP called UNR plays a crucial role in the targeting of a male-specific complex to the X chromosome. UNR facilitates the interaction between two key subunits of this complex: the RNA helicase MLE and the long non-coding RNA roX2.

title: BMP/SMAD1 signaling sets a threshold for the left/right pathway in lateral plate mesoderm and limits availability of SMAD4.
text: Bistability in developmental pathways refers to the generation of binary outputs from graded or noisy inputs. Thresholds are crucial for bistability. The specification of the left/right (LR) axis in vertebrate embryos involves bifurcation from a graded TGF-beta member NODAL in the left lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) which is regulated by feedforward and feedback loops. Our study revealed that BMP/SMAD1 signaling sets a repressive threshold for NODAL-dependent nodal activation in LPM, thereby limiting the available SMAD4. This repressive threshold is essential for the bifurcational output of the LR system.

title: Human Macrophages Infected with a High Burden of ESAT-6-Expressing M. tuberculosis Undergo Caspase-1- and Cathepsin B-Independent Necrosis
text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infects lung macrophages, which, instead of eliminating the pathogen, are manipulated by the bacteria to create an environment conducive to intracellular replication and spread to adjacent cells. The role of host cell death during Mtb infection is debated, as the bacilli have been shown to be both anti-apoptotic, keeping the host cell alive to avoid the antimicrobial effects of apoptosis, and pro-necrotic, killing the host macrophage to allow infection of neighboring cells. Since mycobacteria activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages, we investigated whether Mtb could induce one of the recently described inflammasome-linked cell death modes, pyroptosis and pyronecrosis, which are mediated by caspase-1 and cathepsin-B, respectively. We infected human monocyte-derived macrophages with virulent (H37Rv) Mtb at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1 or 10. The higher MOI led to increased release of IL-1β, while a low MOI showed no IL-1β response. Infected macrophages were collected, and cell viability was determined by assessing DNA integrity, mitochondrial membrane potential, plasma membrane integrity, and HMGB1 release. We found that infection with H37Rv at an MOI of 10, but not MOI 1, over two days resulted in extensive DNA fragmentation, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, loss of plasma membrane integrity, and HMGB1 release. Although we observed plasma membrane permeabilization and IL-1β release from infected cells, the cell death induced by Mtb was not dependent on caspase-1 or cathepsin B. Instead, it was found to be dependent on mycobacterial expression of ESAT-6. We conclude that as the number of virulent Mtb inside the human macrophage increases, ESAT-6-dependent necrosis occurs, activating caspase-1 in the process.

title: Differentiation of Human Induced-Pluripotent Stem Cells into Smooth-Muscle Cells: Two Novel Protocols
text:
Conventional methods for converting human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) into smooth muscle cells (SMCs) are often inefficient and may result in SMCs with an incomplete or mixed phenotype. To address this limitation, we present two novel protocols for differentiating hiPSCs into SMCs with predominantly contractile or synthetic phenotypes.
Flow cytometry analysis of smooth muscle actin (SMA) expression revealed that approximately 45% of the cells generated with each protocol exhibited an SMC phenotype, and the populations could be purified to ~95% through metabolic selection. Moreover, assessments of cellular mRNA and/or protein levels showed that SMCs obtained via the Contractile SMC protocol and those differentiated via a traditional protocol exhibited similar expression profiles for SMA, myosin heavy chain II, collagen 1, calponin, transgelin, connexin 43, and vimentin. In contrast, SMCs generated using the Sythetic SMC protocol displayed reduced calponin expression, increased collagen 1 expression, and increased connexin 43 expression compared to traditional SMCs. These differences were further reflected in functional assays, where Contractile SMCs exhibited more extensive decline in two-dimensional surface area in response to carbachol treatment, while Synthetic SMCs displayed greater cell migration and proliferation.
Collectively, these findings demonstrate that our novel differentiation protocols can effectively generate SMCs from hiPSCs with predominantly contractile or synthetic phenotypes.

title: Conserved Histone Variant H2A.Z Protects Euchromatin from the Ectopic Spread of Silent Heterochromatin
text: The presence of boundary elements hinders the spread of heterochromatin, although these sites do not fully account for the maintenance of adjacent euchromatin. Specifically, histone variant H2A.Z (Htz1 in yeast) substitutes for conventional H2A in many nucleosomes, leading to the activation of nearby genes. Microarray analysis revealed that these genes cluster near telomeres, and their reduced expression in htz1Delta cells was completely reversed upon deletion of SIR2 (sir2Delta), suggesting that H2A.Z antagonizes telomeric silencing. Additionally, Htz1-activated genes located near the silent HMR mating-type locus can be bypassed by either sir2Delta or a deletion encompassing the silencing nucleation sites in HMR. In htz1Delta cells, Sir2 and Sir3 spread into adjacent euchromatic regions, leading to changes in histone H4 acetylation and H3 4-methylation indicative of ectopic heterochromatin formation. Htz1 is enriched in these euchromatic regions, and it acts in conjunction with a boundary element to prevent the spread of heterochromatin. This highlights the presence of elements within both euchromatin and heterochromatin that antagonize the conversion to the opposite chromatin state.

title: COMMD proteins, a novel family of structural and functional homologs of MURR1.
text: MURR1 is a multifunctional protein that inhibits nuclear factor kappaB (NF-κB), a transcription factor with multiple roles in immunity, apoptosis, cell cycle regulation and oncogenesis. We have identified a new family of proteins with homology to MURR1. These proteins form multimeric complexes and are responsible for the identification in a screen for MURR1 associated factors. The family is defined by the presence of a unique motif known as the COMM (copper metabolism gene MURR1) domain, which acts as a protein-protein interaction interface. Similarly, several of these factors associate with and inhibit NF-κB, similar to MURR1. The proteins, designated as COMMD or COMM domain containing 1-10, are highly conserved across multicellular eukaryotic organisms and make up a novel family of structural and functional homologs of MURR1. Interestingly, the prototypical member of this family, MURR1/COMMD1, regulates NF-κB activity in the nucleus by disrupting its association with chromatin, rather than preventing its translocation or binding to cognate motifs.

title: Occurrence of chromosome 9 and p53 alterations in multifocal dysplasia and carcinoma in situ of human urinary bladder
text: To investigate the genetic changes that occur in flat urothelial lesions, including carcinoma in situ (CIS) and moderate dysplasias (DII), we examined 33 CIS and 16 DII samples from 21 patients using dual color fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and DNA sequencing. We looked at the chromosomal regions most often affected in bladder cancer, including 9q22 (FACC), 9p21 (CDK), 17p13 (p53), and related centromeric probes. The data showed that nearly identical deletion frequencies were observed on chromosomes 9 and 17 for CIS and p53, with a lower deletion rate in DII compared to CIS. A strong correlation was found between the results of FISH and LOH analyses. p53 mutations were detected in 72% of CIS and 67% of DII samples. In three of 16 patients with multifocal tumors, oligoclonal lesions were identified by LOH analyses, and sequencing of p53 revealed two different p53 deletions in two cases. Our findings suggest that chromosome 9 deletions cannot be used as a marker of papillary growth, as they are found in both flat lesions associated with papillary tumors and those that are not. The similar distribution and lower amount of genetic changes in DII suggest that DII may be a possible precursor lesion of CIS.

title: Fresh meat and further processing characteristics of ham muscles from finishing pigs fed ractopamine hydrochloride.
text:
The feed additive Ractopamine hydrochloride (RAC) has consistently shown improved carcass cutting yields in finishing pigs, but its effects on further processing characteristics are less clear. Some studies have reported that RAC can lead to higher ultimate pH values in pig muscles, which could potentially result in better protein interaction and improved textural properties in cured and smoked hams. To investigate this further, an experiment was conducted to determine whether RAC-fed pigs produce hams with higher ultimate pH values, and if so, whether this leads to improved texture and water retention in the processed hams.
Two hundred hams from barrows and gilts were selected based on their HCW and were fed either a RAC or control diet. After fabrication into different cuts, the hams were processed into cured and smoked hams. The results showed that RAC significantly increased cutting yields of the whole ham (%, inside, outside, and knuckle) compared to the control group (P < 0.0001). Moreover, the ultimate pH values of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, semimembranosus, and adductor muscles were found to be 0.06 pH units higher in pigs fed RAC (P < 0.05), with the biceps femoris showing a slightly higher increase of 0.04 pH units (P = 0.02). Additionally, cured hams from RAC-fed pigs were heavier at all stages of production. No significant differences were observed in binding strengths or protein fat-free values between RAC- and control-fed hams.
In summary, the study found that RAC can increase cutting yields, total weight of cured hams, and ultimate muscle pH, suggesting that it can be fed to pigs without affecting further processed ham characteristics.

title: Translocated LPS Might Cause Endotoxin Tolerance in Circulating Monocytes of Cystic Fibrosis Patients
text: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is an inherited multifactorial disease caused by genetic abnormalities in the gene that encodes a chloride channel. The lungs of CF patients are consistently infected with various pathogens, but bacteremia has rarely been observed in this condition. Moreover, circulating monocytes in CF patients exhibit a heightened Endotoxin Tolerance (ET) state, characterized by a significant reduction in their inflammatory response to bacterial stimuli. Although this phenomenon has been previously described, the underlying mechanism responsible for ET induction in CF patients remains unknown. In this study, we investigated the possibility of microbial/endotoxin translocation from a localized infection in the lungs to the bloodstream as a potential cause of ET induction in CF patients. Plasma analysis of fourteen CF patients revealed elevated levels of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) compared to healthy volunteers and patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). In vitro experiments showed that endotoxin concentrations found in plasma of CF patients were capable of inducing an ET phenotype in monocytes from healthy controls. These findings are consistent with the absence of bacterial DNA in CF plasma, suggesting that soluble endotoxin in the bloodstream of CF patients is responsible for the ET observed in their circulating monocytes.

title: Effect of mammographic screening from age 40 years on breast cancer mortality in the UK Age trial at 17 years' follow-up: a randomised controlled trial.
text: In this study, we evaluated the long-term effects of age-specific mammographic screening on breast cancer mortality in women aged 39-41. The UK Age trial randomized these women to either annual screening up to age 48 or usual medical care with screening starting at age 50. We found that annual screening led to a significant reduction in breast cancer mortality in the first 10 years after diagnosis, but not thereafter. The overall breast cancer incidence during the 17-year follow-up was similar between the intervention and control groups. Our results suggest that early mammography screening may reduce breast cancer mortality in this age group, although further research is needed to fully understand the long-term effects. The study was funded by the National Institute for Health Research Health Technology Assessment program and the American Cancer Society, among others.

title: Concordance, disease progression, and heritability of coeliac disease in Italian twins.
text:
Objective: To understand the genetic and environmental factors that contribute to developing coeliac disease (CD) by studying twins.
Method: We analyzed 23 monozygotic (MZ) and 50 dizygotic (DZ) twin pairs, where at least one member had CD. We used DNA fingerprinting to determine zygosity and genotyped for HLA-DQ and DR alleles. We also analyzed the disease status of the twin pair using antibody tests and biopsies.
Results: We found that MZ twins were more likely to have CD than DZ twins. The occurrence of CD was higher in MZ twins, and the concordance rate was higher in MZ twins than in DZ twins. Most of the twin pairs with CD received a diagnosis within two years. We also found that a large proportion of the variation in CD was due to genetic factors.
Conclusion: MZ twins are more likely to have CD than DZ twins, and a large proportion of the variation in CD is due to genetic factors. Our findings suggest that genetics play a significant role in the development of CD.

title: A literature review of the safety of medical body area network devices in magnetic resonance imaging
text:
Electromagnetic fields and wireless technology are an integral part of modern life. The use of Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) machines to clarify internal human structures and function in healthcare is becoming more prevalent. With the rapid development of wireless devices, their miniaturization, and application as clinical tools, there is an expanding intersection zone. However, there is a lack of safety standards for newer wireless technologies, including those used in Medical Body Area Networks (MBAN) when used in MRI machines.
To address this issue, we conducted a review of the clinical scientific literature and the United States Food and Drug Administration adverse events database. Unfortunately, we found no published studies specifically addressing the safety of wireless devices potentially used in MBAN in MRI machines. We propose the addition of a research track to evaluate the safety of MBAN devices in MRI machines. This will enable the informed design of current and future MBAN components, devices, and systems to avoid potential patient adverse events resulting from the unintended consequences of concurrently using these technologies in MRI machines.

title: Synaptic glutamate release by ventromedial hypothalamic neurons is part of the neurocircuitry that prevents hypoglycemia.
text: Experimental evidence has confirmed the significance of neuropeptides in the hypothalamus. However, due to challenges in studying their functions in living organisms, the roles of fast-acting neurotransmitters such as glutamate and GABA remain largely unknown. Synaptic vesicles known as VGLUTs for glutamate and VGAT for GABA are responsible for the uptake and release of neurotransmitters from synapses. Ventromedial hypothalamic (VMH) neurons are primarily glutamatergic and express VGLUT2. To assess the role of glutamate release from VMH neurons, mice were genetically engineered to lack VGLUT2 selectively in a specific subset of VMH neurons called SF1 neurons. These mice exhibited hypoglycemia during fasting due to impaired increases in the glucose-raising pancreatic hormone glucagon and impaired induction of liver mRNAs encoding PGC-1alpha and the gluconeogenic enzymes PEPCK and G6Pase. Additionally, these mice had defective counterregulatory responses to insulin-induced hypoglycemia and 2-deoxyglucose (an antimetabolite). Therefore, glutamate release from VMH neurons is an essential component of the brain circuitry that helps prevent hypoglycemia.

title: c-Src and cooperating partners in human cancer.
text: The proto-oncogene c-src is infrequently mutated in human cancers, and when overexpressed in normal cells, it exhibits little to no oncogenic potential. This has led to questions about its role in the development of human tumors. However, recent research has revealed that c-Src, a non-receptor tyrosine kinase, exhibits elevated protein levels and activity in a wide range of human cancers. In addition, it has been found to play a crucial role in multiple signaling pathways that regulate cell proliferation, survival, metastasis, and angiogenesis, making it an attractive target for cancer therapy.

title: Type 1 diabetes-associated IL2RA variation lowers IL-2 signaling and contributes to diminished CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cell function.
text:
Numerous studies have shown that regulatory T cells (Tregs) from individuals with various human autoimmune diseases, including type 1 diabetes, are deficient in their ability to control excessive immune responses compared to healthy, non-diseased individuals. It is unclear whether this dysfunction is cause by perturbations in the immune system during disease development or is a primary event. Genetic variations in genes involved in Treg function, such as IL2RA, have been linked to an increased risk of autoimmune diseases. However, the relationship between these genetic variations and Treg function has not been fully explored.
We aimed to address this gap in knowledge by investigating the impact of an IL2RA haplotype associated with type 1 diabetes on Treg fitness and suppressive function. We conducted our studies using healthy human subjects to minimize any confounding effects of disease. Our results showed that the presence of the autoimmune disease-associated IL2RA haplotype leads to decreased IL-2 responsiveness in activated CD4+ T cells, as measured by phosphorylation of STAT5a, and lower levels of FOXP3 expression by Tregs. Additionally, we found that these Tregs had reduced ability to suppress the proliferation of autologous effector T cells.
Our findings provide a molecular and cellular mechanisms explanation for how genetic variations in the IL-2RA gene contribute to the susceptibility to autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.

title: Hematopoietic stem cells and other hematopoietic cells show broad resistance to chemotherapeutic agents in vivo when overexpressing bcl-2.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the effect of overexpressing the bcl-2 protein on the resistance of various cell types, including hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), to chemotherapeutic agents.
Methods:
Transgenic mice that overexpress the bcl-2 protein (H2K-bcl-2) were treated with several chemotherapeutics, including 5-fluoruracil, cyclophosphamide, and busulfan, to evaluate the contribution of increased bcl-2 levels to the response to these drugs in vivo. Cell populations were enumerated using flow cytometry, and HSC were studied using FACS purification and long-term reconstitution assays in vivo. In vitro resistance to chemotherapeutics was confirmed by short-term proliferation assays with different amounts of chemotherapeutics.
Results:
Overexpression of bcl-2 alone protected many cell types, although protection levels varied between populations and agents. However, even sensitive populations returned to pre-treatment levels faster in transgenic mice. bcl-2 overexpression also prevented the dramatic changes in HSC following 5-fluoruracil treatment (downregulation of c-kit, upregulation of Lin, less efficient long-term reconstitution). In vitro studies demonstrated increased resistance of bcl-2 overexpressing HSC to chemotherapeutic agents.

Conclusions:
Increased expression of bcl-2 in HSC and their progeny confers broad resistance to chemotherapeutic agents. The ability to differentially regulate sensitivity to apoptosis of bystander and tumor cells is clinically important.

title: Direct sensing of systemic and nutritional signals by hematopoietic progenitors in Drosophila
text:
The Drosophila lymph gland is a hematopoietic organ that displays similarities to the mammalian myeloid system. Progenitor cells, which are most similar to common myeloid progenitors in mammals, proliferate and differentiate into three types of mature cells: plasmatocytes, crystal cells, and lamellocytes. These immature cells then mature into cells reminiscent of mammalian myeloid cells.
During the early stages of larval development, the lymph gland contains only progenitor cells, while in the third instar, a specific region called the medullary zone contains immature blood cells that are undergoing maturation. Another group of cells called the posterior signaling center acts as a haematopoietic niche.
Similar to mammalian myeloid cells, Drosophila blood cells are capable of responding to various stresses, such as hypoxia, infection, and oxidative stress. However, the mechanisms by which myeloid progenitors in Drosophila detect and respond to systemic signals to regulate cell fate determination have not been well characterized.
Our study found that the haematopoietic progenitors in Drosophila are direct targets of both systemic (insulin) and nutritional (essential amino acid) signals. These signals promote Wingless (WNT in mammals) signaling, which plays a crucial role in maintaining the progenitors.
We expect that this research will shed light on possible direct signal sensing mechanisms employed by myeloid progenitors in mammals.

title: Regulation of autophagy by cytoplasmic p53
text: Various cellular stressors, including p53 activation, can induce autophagy. Our research shows that inhibiting, depleting, or deleting p53 in human, mouse, and nematode cells undergoing knockout, knockdown, or pharmacological p53 inhibition can stimulate autophagy. Enhanced autophagy helped p53-deficient cancer cells survive under conditions of hypoxia and nutrient scarcity, allowing them to maintain high ATP levels. Inhibiting p53 resulted in autophagy in enucleated cells, and cytoplasmic, not nuclear, p53 could repress the enhanced autophagy of p53-deficient cells. Many different inducers of autophagy, such as starvation, rapamycin, and toxins affecting the endoplasmic reticulum, triggered proteasome-mediated degradation of p53 through a pathway dependent on the E3 ubiquitin ligase HDM2. Inhibiting p53 degradation prevented the activation of autophagy in several cell lines in response to various stimuli, providing evidence of a crucial signaling pathway linking autophagy to the dysregulation of p53 in cancer.

title: The Neurobiology of Sleep: Genetics, cellular physiology and subcortical networks
text: To gain a deeper understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying sleep, it is crucial to examine this ubiquitous mammalian behavior at multiple levels of biological organization. At the molecular level, the circadian rhythm of sleep involves interconnected positive and negative feedback loops involving circadian genes and their protein products in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which are synchronized to ambient conditions through light exposure. This circadian information is then integrated with homeostatic sleep need in anterior hypothalamic nuclei. These nuclei interact with arousal systems in the posterior hypothalamus, basal forebrain, and brainstem to control sleep onset. During sleep, an ultradian oscillator in the mesopontine junction regulates the recurring alternation of rapid eye movement (REM) and non-REM sleep. The sleep cycle is accompanied by neural modulatory influences on forebrain structures that impact behavior, consciousness, and cognition.

title: Suppression of intestinal neoplasia by deletion of Dnmt3b
text: Abnormal gene silencing accompanied by DNA methylation is linked to the progression of many tumors, including those that exhibit global DNA methylation loss. To investigate the role of de novo methyltransferase Dnmt3b in this process, we employed conditional inactivation of Dnmt3b in Apc(Min/+) mice. We found that the loss of Dnmt3b had no effect on microadenoma formation, which is considered the initial stage of intestinal tumor development. However, we observed a substantial decrease in the formation of macroscopic colonic adenomas. Intriguingly, many large adenomas exhibited areas of Dnmt3b inactivation, indicating that Dnmt3b is required for the initial growth of macroscopic adenomas but is not essential for their maintenance. These findings support a role for Dnmt3b in the transitional stage between microadenoma formation and large colonic tumor growth and suggest that Dnmt3b, and by extension de novo methylation, are not necessary for continued tumor growth after this transition has occurred.

title: Epithelium-intrinsic NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome drives infected enterocyte expulsion to restrict Salmonella replication in the intestinal mucosa.
text: The intestinal mucosa separates the host from the microbiota, but certain pathogens, such as Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm), can invade and compromise this barrier. Despite being well-studied, the mechanisms by which the body defends itself against acute insults remain incompletely understood. To investigate this further, we utilized a murine model of Salmonella enterocolitis and analyzed the mechanisms that limit the growth of pathogens within the epithelium during early infection. Although the epithelium-invading S.Tm initially replicate, this intraepithelial replicative niche is restricted by the expulsion of infected enterocytes into the lumen. This mechanism is compromised in the absence of certain inflammasome components (NAIP1-6, NLRC4, caspase-1/-11) or when they are specifically ablated in the epithelium, resulting in a 100-fold increase in intraepithelial loads and accelerated colonization of the lymph nodes. Interestingly, the cytokines downstream of inflammasome activation, interleukin (IL)-1α/β and IL-18, are not essential for epithelial restriction of early infection. These data demonstrate the importance of an epithelium-intrinsic inflammasome in driving the expulsion of infected cells to restrict the pathogen's intraepithelial proliferation, which potentially represents a general defense mechanism against mucosal infections.

title: GEMC1 is a TopBP1 interacting protein required for chromosomal DNA replication
text: Recent research has shed light on the factors required for chromosomal DNA replication in single-celled eukaryotes, but the mechanisms involved in multicellular organisms remain poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, we identified a novel vertebrate protein named GEMC1 (geminin coiled-coil containing protein 1), which plays a crucial role in chromosomal DNA replication. GEMC1 is highly conserved across vertebrates and is more highly expressed in proliferating cells. By using Xenopus laevis egg extracts, we found that Xenopus GEMC1 (xGEMC1) interacts with the checkpoint and replication factor TopBP1, which facilitates the binding of xGEMC1 to chromatin during the formation of pre-replication complexes (pre-RCs). We discovered that xGEMC1 interacts directly with other replication factors, including Cdc45 and the kinase Cdk2-CyclinE, and becomes heavily phosphorylated through these interactions. Phosphorylated xGEMC1 stimulates the initiation of DNA replication, while depletion of xGEMC1 hinders the onset of DNA replication due to impaired Cdc45 loading onto chromatin. Inhibition of GEMC1 expression with morpholino and siRNA oligos also prevents DNA replication in embryonic and somatic vertebrate cells. These findings suggest that GEMC1 facilitates the initiation of chromosomal DNA replication in multicellular organisms by mediating TopBP1- and Cdk2-dependent recruitment of Cdc45 to replication origins.

title: Does an arthroscopic suture bridge technique maintain repair integrity?: a serial evaluation by ultrasonography.
text:
Unannealed biomechanical studies suggest that the suture bridge technique can enhance rotator cuff tendon footprint contact area, holding strength, and mean contact pressure. Building upon these findings, this study aimed to investigate the following questions:
1. Would the suture bridge technique result in a high rate of cuff integrity after surgery?
2. Would the fixation status of the repaired cuff change over time?
3. Could preoperative factors predict postoperative cuff integrity?
4. Would patients who experienced retears have less favorable pain, functional scores, range of motion, and muscle strength compared to those with intact repairs?

To answer these questions, a prospective study was conducted on 78 patients who underwent arthroscopic repairs using the suture bridge technique. The integrity of the rotator cuff repair was evaluated using ultrasonographic evaluation at 4.5 and 12 months after surgery. The results showed that intact cuffs were present in 91% of patients at 4.5 months postoperatively, which were maintained at the 12-month follow-up. The failure rates were 17.6% for massive tears, 11.1% for large tears, 6.3% for medium tears, and none for small tears. Preoperative fatty degeneration of the supraspinatus muscle was found to be a strong predictor of cuff integrity. No correlation was found between the integrity and clinical outcomes except for a temporary decrease in abduction strength at 6 months. The arthroscopic repair using the suture bridge technique was able to achieve a low retear rate in shoulders treated for rotator cuff tears, with no influence of retear on the outcome.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE Level IV, therapeutic study.

title: Widespread and tissue specific age-related DNA methylation changes in mice.
text: Abnormal methylation of promoter CpG islands in cancer is associated with silencing of tumor-suppressor genes, and age-related hypermethylation in normal appearing mucosa may serve as a risk factor for human colon cancer. The question remains as to whether this age-related DNA methylation phenomenon is exclusive to human tissues. To investigate, we conducted comprehensive DNA methylation profiling of promoter regions in aging mouse intestine using a combination of methylated CpG island amplification and microarray analysis. By comparing 3-month-old and 35-month-old C57BL/6 mice, we identified 774 genes (21% of 3627 detectable autosomal genes) that displayed increased methylation, and 466 genes (13% of 3627) that showed decreased methylation using pyrosequencing to quantitatively validate the microarray data. We found linear age-related methylation changes at 12 genomic regions examined, including three, seven, and six loci showing similar changes in lung, liver, and spleen tissues, respectively. There was partial conservation between age-related hypermethylation in human and mouse intestines, and Polycomb targets in embryonic stem cells were enriched among the hypermethylated genes. Our findings demonstrate a high prevalence of hyper- and hypomethylation as a function of age in normal mouse small intestine tissues and strong tissue-specificity to the process. We conclude that epigenetic deregulation is a ubiquitous feature of aging in mammals.

title: Environmental and economic costs of soil erosion and conservation benefits.
text: Soil erosion poses a significant environmental challenge to the long-term sustainability and productivity of agriculture. Over the past 40 years, roughly one-third of the world's arable land has been lost due to erosion, with this amount continuing to increase at a rate of more than 10 million hectares per year. Furthermore, with an additional 250,000 people joining the global population every day, the increasing demand for food to feed this growing population, combined with the decline in per capita food productivity, threatens the ability of agriculture to meet the world's growing food needs.

title: Association between influenza vaccination and cardiovascular outcomes in high-risk patients: a meta-analysis.
text: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors other than traditional ones are associated with fatal and non-fatal atherothrombotic events. This study aimed to determine if influenza vaccination reduces the risk of CVD events. Data from 1946 to 2013 from MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library Central Register of Controlled Trials were analyzed in a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials comparing influenza vaccine to placebo or control in patients at high risk of CVD. The goal was to identify whether the use of influenza vaccine reduces the risk of cardiovascular events. Two researchers independently extracted data from published and unpublished studies on trial design, baseline characteristics, outcomes, and safety events. High-quality studies were defined as those with appropriate methods of randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and complete follow-up. Cardiovascular events, cardiovascular mortality, all-cause mortality, and specific cardiovascular events were analyzed using random-effects Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals. The analysis was stratified by subgroups of patients with and without a history of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) within 1 year of randomization. The findings showed that in published and unpublished randomized clinical trials of 6735 patients aged 67 years (51.3% women and 36.2% with a cardiac history), influenza vaccine was associated with a lower risk of composite cardiovascular events (2.9% vs 4.7%; RR, 0.64 [95% CI, 0.48-0.86], P=0.003) in the published trials. The treatment effect interacted with the presence or absence of recent ACS (P < 0.02). The results were unaffected by adding unpublished data. The conclusion was that in a meta-analysis of RCTs, the use of influenza vaccine was associated with a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, with the greatest treatment effect seen in patients with the most active coronary disease.

title: Baby hands that move to the rhythm of language: hearing babies acquiring sign languages babble silently on the hands
text:
The universal "ba, ba, ba" sound that babies produce around 7 months of age has captivated scientists due to its potential insights into language acquisition mechanisms and evolutionary origins. However, the underlying biological basis of babbling remains a mystery, with some theories proposing it as a non-linguistic motor activity driven by the baby's growing control over the mouth and jaw, while others argue it is a linguistic activity reflecting the babies' early sensitivity to specific phonetic-syllabic patterns.
To investigate, researchers conducted a study over a period of 12 months with two groups of hearing babies: three acquiring spoken language (Group 1: "speech-exposed") and three using sign language only (Group 2: "sign-exposed"). Despite Group 2's exposure to sign language, which does not involve the mouth, the motoric hypothesis would predict similar hand activity to that seen in Group 1. However, the researchers discovered that the sign-exposed hearing babies' hand activity differed depending on whether they were producing linguistic or non-linguistic activity, with linguistic activity produced at a low frequency of approximately 1 Hz and non-linguistic activity produced at a higher frequency of approximately 2.5 Hz. Interestingly, these babies were able to babble systematically on their hands without the use of the mouth, indicating that babbling is fundamentally a linguistic activity.
The researchers concluded that all babies are born with an innate sensitivity to specific rhythmic patterns at the heart of human language, which enables them to use these patterns in their early babbling stages. This finding challenges the assumption that babbling is solely a motoric activity and highlights the critical role of language acquisition in shaping the baby's cognitive and motor Development.

title: The Ten-Eleven Translocation-2 (TET2) gene in hematopoiesis and hematopoietic diseases
text: Inactivation of the Ten-Eleven Translocation-2 (TET2) gene through mutations, deletions, and IDH1/2 (Isocitrate Dehydrogenase 1 and 2) gene mutations is a common occurrence in both myeloid and lymphoid malignancies, as well as in healthy individuals with clonal hematopoiesis. TET2 gene mutations, similar to those found in myeloid and lymphoid malignancies, also accumulate with age in otherwise healthy individuals. TET2 is one of three evolutionarily conserved dioxygenases, known as the TET family, that catalyze the conversion of 5-methylcytosine (5-mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC) and promote DNA demethylation. TET dioxygenases require 2-oxoglutarate, oxygen, and Fe(II) for their activity, and this activity is enhanced in the presence of ascorbic acid. TET2 is the most expressed TET gene in hematopoietic tissue, particularly in hematopoietic stem cells. In addition to its hydroxylase activity, TET proteins also recruit the O-linked β-D-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) transferase (OGT) enzyme to chromatin, which promotes post-transcriptional modifications of histones and facilitates gene expression. The TET2 level is regulated by interactions with IDAX, which originated from the TET2 gene during evolution, as well as by microRNA miR-22. TET2 has diverse functions during hematopoiesis, including stem-cell self-renewal, lineage commitment, and terminal differentiation of monocytes. Analysis of Tet2 knockout mice, which are viable and fertile, demonstrated that Tet2 functions as a tumor suppressor whose haploinsufficiency leads to myeloid and lymphoid transformations. This review summarizes the recently identified TET2 physiological and pathological functions and discusses how this knowledge may impact our therapeutic approaches in hematological malignancies and potentially other tumor types.

title: Impaired Awareness of Hypoglycemia in a Population-Based Sample of Children and Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes
text:
The objective of this study was to determine the prevalence and clinical associations of impaired awareness of hypoglycemia in a population-based sample of children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes.
To achieve this, the researchers used a validated questionnaire to assess hypoglycemia awareness in 656 patients with type 1 diabetes over a six-month period. The results showed that impaired awareness of hypoglycemia was present in 29% of patients.
Patients with impaired awareness of hypoglycemia had earlier onset of diabetes, were younger, and had lower mean levels of A1C since diabetes onset and at their last visit compared to those without impaired awareness. Moreover, the overall rate of severe hypoglycemia was 24.5 episodes per 100 patient-years in the preceding year, and the rate was significantly higher in those with impaired awareness (37.1 vs. 19.3 episodes per 100 patient-years, P < 0.001).
The study found that among patients aged <6 years, 59% of care providers reported impaired awareness of hypoglycemia, and the rate of severe hypoglycemia was significantly higher in those reporting impaired awareness (33.3 vs. 52 episodes per 100 patient-years, P = 0.02). Additionally, more patients with recurrent hypoglycemia reported impaired awareness of hypoglycemia (47 vs. 28%, P = 0.03).
These findings suggest that impaired awareness of hypoglycemia is a significant problem in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes and highlight the importance of screening for this condition as part of routine diabetes care.

title: Enhancing circadian clock function in cancer cells inhibits tumor growth
text: Investigating the relationship between circadian rhythms and cancer, we examined the effects of disrupting the circadian clock on cell cycle progression and proliferation in B16 melanoma cells and tumors. Our results showed that clock genes were decreased in B16 cells and tumors, but treating the cells with drugs that induce circadian rhythmicity, such as dexamethasone, forskolin, and heat shock, caused a reversal in this pattern, leading to a decrease in the number of cells in S phase and an increase in the number of cells in G1 phase. This resulted in a slowing down of B16 cell proliferation in vitro and tumor growth in vivo. Similar effects were observed in human colon carcinoma HCT-116 cells. Additionally, we found that dexamethasone's effects on tumor growth and cell cycle events were not due to an increase in apoptosis or an enhancement of immune cell recruitment to the tumor. Moreover, knocking down the essential clock gene Bmal1 in B16 tumors abolished the effects of dexamethasone on tumor growth and cell cycle events. Our findings demonstrate that the effects of dexamethasone on cell cycle and tumor growth are mediated by the tumor-intrinsic circadian clock, highlighting the potential of enhancing circadian clock function as a novel strategy to control cancer progression.

title: Distinct functions of nucleotide-binding/hydrolysis sites in the four AAA modules of cytoplasmic dynein.
text:
Cytoplasmic dynein is a microtubule-based motor protein that plays a crucial role in intracellular retrograde transport along microtubule filaments. The motor domain of dynein consists of six tandemly linked AAA (ATPases associated with diverse cellular activities) modules, with the first four containing predicted nucleotide-binding/hydrolysis sites (P1-P4). To elucidate the functions of these multiple nucleotide-binding/hydrolysis sites, we expressed and purified Dictyostelium dynein motor domains containing mutations that block nucleotide binding at each of the four AAA modules and examined their biochemical properties in detail.
Notably, the P1 mutant was trapped in a strong-binding state even in the presence of ATP, and consequently lost its motile activity. In contrast, mutation in the P2 or P4 site did not affect the apparent binding affinity of the mutant for microtubules in the presence of ATP, but reduced ATPase and microtubule sliding activities. These findings suggest that ATP binding and hydrolysis at the P1 site are essential for the motor activities of cytoplasmic dynein. Moreover, the results indicate that the other nucleotide-binding/hydrolysis sites regulate the motor activities, with nucleotide binding at the P3 site being critical for microtubule-activated ATPase and motile activities of cytoplasmic dynein.
In conclusion, the present study reveals that the motor activities of cytoplasmic dynein are dependent on ATP binding and hydrolysis at a specific site (P1), while other sites (P2 and P4) play a regulatory role in modulating these activities. The findings provide new insights into the mechanism of intracellular transport and highlight the importance of evaluating the functional roles of multiple nucleotide-binding/hydrolysis sites in motor proteins.

title: Over-expression of RCAN1 causes Down syndrome-like hippocampal deficits that alter learning and memory.
text: Individuals with Down syndrome (DS) exhibit alterations in brain structure, including abnormalities in neurotransmission and signaling pathways that govern brain function. A large number of genes are simultaneously expressed at altered levels in DS, making it challenging to identify the specific gene(s) responsible for particular abnormalities and the underlying molecular pathways. To shed light on this complex issue, we generated RCAN1-TG mice to investigate the consequences of over-expressing RCAN1 and explore its contribution to the brain phenotype of DS. RCAN1-TG mice display structural brain abnormalities in regions affected in DS, including a reduced volume and number of neurons in the hippocampus. Additionally, the density of dendritic spines on RCAN1-TG hippocampal pyramidal neurons is decreased. Furthermore, we observed deficits in hippocampal-dependent learning and short- and long-term memory, as well as a failure to maintain long-term potentiation (LTP) in hippocampal slices. Following LTP induction, we observed diminished calcium transients and decreased phosphorylation of CaMKII and ERK1/2-proteins, which are critical for LTP maintenance and memory formation. Our findings strongly suggest that RCAN1 plays a crucial role in normal brain development and function, and its up-regulation likely contributes to the neural deficits associated with DS.

title: Vitamins E and C in the prevention of prostate and total cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial.
text:
Context: Many individuals take vitamins in the hope of preventing chronic diseases such as cancer. Vitamins E and C are among the most common individual supplements, and a large-scale randomized trial suggested that vitamin E may reduce the risk of prostate cancer, although few trials have been powered to address this relationship. No previous trial has examined vitamin C alone in the prevention of cancer in men at usual risk.
Objective: To evaluate whether long-term supplementation with vitamins E and C decreases the risk of prostate and total cancer events among men.
Design, Setting, and Participants: The Physicians' Health Study II is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled factorial trial conducted among 14,641 male physicians in the United States aged 50 years or older, including 1307 men with a history of prior cancer at randomization. The trial began in 1997 and continued until its scheduled completion on August 31, 2007.
Intervention: Individual supplements of 400 IU of vitamin E every other day and 500 mg of vitamin C daily.
Main Outcome Measures: Prostate and total cancer.
Results: During a mean follow-up of 8.0 years, there were 1008 confirmed incident cases of prostate cancer and 1943 total cancers. Compared with placebo, vitamin E had no effect on the incidence of prostate cancer (active and placebo vitamin E groups, 9.1 and 9.5 events per 1000 person-years; hazard ratio [HR], 0.97; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.85-1.09; P = .58) or total cancer (active and placebo vitamin E groups, 17.8 and 17.3 cases per 1000 person-years; HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.95-1.13; P = .41). There was also no significant effect of vitamin C on total cancer (active and placebo vitamin C groups, 17.6 and 17.5 events per 1000 person-years; HR, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.92-1.10; P = .86) or prostate cancer (active and placebo vitamin C groups, 9.4 and 9.2 cases per 1000 person-years; HR, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.90-1.15; P = .80). Neither vitamin E nor vitamin C had a significant effect on colorectal, lung, or other site-specific cancers. Adjustment for adherence and exclusion of the first 4 or 6 years of follow-up did not alter the results. Stratification by various cancer risk factors did not demonstrate any significant modification of the effect of vitamin E on prostate cancer risk or either agent on total cancer risk.
Conclusion: In this large, long-term trial of male physicians, neither vitamin E nor C supplementation reduced the risk of prostate or total cancer. These data provide no support for the use of these supplements for the prevention of cancer in middle-aged and older men.
Trial Registration: clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT00270647.

title: Micromanagers of gene expression: the potentially widespread influence of metazoan microRNAs
text: Our proposal suggests that the unique microRNA landscape within each cell type acts as a critical regulator, suppressing the expression of thousands of mRNAs and providing a crucial context for understanding the evolution of all metazoan mRNA sequences. By dampening the expression of genes that should not be expressed in a particular cell type, microRNAs significantly reduce protein output to insignificant levels. Conversely, for genes that require customized expression in different cell types, microRNAs adjust dosage to achieve a more uniform level within each cell type while allowing for additional layers of gene control that integrate with transcriptional and other regulatory processes to significantly expand the complexity of metazoan gene expression.

title: The Kinase Regulator Mob1 Acts as a Patterning Protein for Stentor Morphogenesis
text: Morphogenesis and pattern formation are crucial processes in any living being, whether single-celled or multi-celled. However, unlike the developmental biology of plants and animals, the underlying mechanisms of morphogenesis and pattern formation in individual cells are still largely unexplored. Although all cells exhibit patterns, they are most pronounced in ciliates, which is why we have turned to a classic unicellular model organism, the giant ciliate Stentor coeruleus. In this study, we discovered that the RNA interference (RNAi) machinery is conserved in Stentor. By using RNAi, we identified the kinase coactivator Mob1, which has conserved functions in cell division and morphogenesis across plants and animals, as an asymmetrically localized patterning protein essential for global patterning during development and regeneration in Stentor. Our findings reopen the door for Stentor as a model system for regeneration.

title: Measurement and clinical monitoring of human lymphocyte clonality by massively parallel VDJ pyrosequencing.
text: The extensive variety of immune receptors generated by B and T cells enables the recognition of diverse threats to the host organism. In this study, we demonstrate that massively parallel DNA sequencing of rearranged immune receptor loci can provide direct detection and tracking of immune diversity and expanded clonal lymphocyte populations in both physiological and pathological contexts. DNA was isolated from blood and tissue samples, a range of redundant primers were used to amplify diverse DNA rearrangements, and the resulting mixtures of barcoded amplicons were sequenced using long-read ultra deep sequencing. Singles DNA molecules were then characterized based on the DNA sequences that had been joined to form functional (or nonfunctional) immune effectors. Current experimental designs can accommodate up to 150 samples in a single sequencing run, with the depth of sequencing sufficient to identify both stable and dynamic aspects of the immune repertoire in both healthy individuals and patients with hematological malignancies. These data provide a high-resolution picture of immune spectra in normal individuals and in patients with hematological malignancies, shedding light on both the initial emergence of clonal tumor populations and the later suppression or re-emergence of such populations after treatment.

title: Can we apply the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel definition of the metabolic syndrome to Asians?
text:
The text you provided is well-written and clear, but I can provide a more concise and straightforward rewording of it for you:
The limited availability of information on the metabolic syndrome in Asians prompted this study to determine the optimal waist circumference for diagnosing central obesity in this population and to estimate the prevalence of the metabolic syndrome in an Asian population.
The study used data from the 1998 Singapore National Health Survey, a cross-sectional survey involving 4,723 men and women of Chinese, Malay, and Asian-Indian ethnicity aged 18-69 years. The study found that a waist circumference of >80 cm in women and >90 cm in men was a more appropriate definition of central obesity in this population.
The study then determined the prevalence of the metabolic syndrome using the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP ATP III) criteria with and without the modified waist circumference criteria. The results showed that decreasing waist circumference increased the crude prevalence of the metabolic syndrome from 12.2% to 17.9% in Asians. The study also found that the prevalence of the metabolic syndrome was higher in men than in women, and that the prevalence was significantly higher in Asian Indians than in other ethnic groups.
In conclusion, the study found that the NCEP ATP III criteria, applied to an Asian population, underestimate the population at risk. Using a lower waist circumference cutoff, the prevalence of the metabolic syndrome in Asians is comparable to that in Western populations. The study highlights the need to consider ethnic differences when applying diagnostic criteria for the metabolic syndrome in different populations across Asia.

title: Serotonin and fluoxetine levels in plasma and platelets after fluoxetine treatment in depressive patients.
text:
Major depressive disorder, a mood disorder, is characterized by complex alterations in neurotransmitters such as serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. Specifically, there is significant evidence of abnormalities in serotonin neurotransmission. Biochemical parameters of serotonin transmission, including the amount of 5-hydroxytryptamine in plasma and platelets, have been utilized to identify changes related to depression. Recently, these parameters have also been used to investigate the mechanism of action of antidepressant drugs, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
This study aimed to explore the interaction between plasma and platelet levels of fluoxetine and serotonin after administering fluoxetine to depressed patients. In total, 12 patients with major depression (meeting DSM-IV criteria) received a single oral dose of fluoxetine in the morning, starting with 5 mg for the first 5 days, followed by 10 mg from day 6 to day 10, and culminating in 20 mg from day 11 to day 40. Blood samples were collected at 0, 7, 10, and 24 hours after drug administration on the first day of fluoxetine 5 mg and on days 11 and 40 of fluoxetine 20 mg (the 30th day of treatment, respectively). Plasma fluoxetine and serotonin levels significantly increased after drug administration, reaching their highest levels on the 30th day of fluoxetine 20 mg. Fluoxetine was also detectable in platelets, with a time variant similar to plasma levels. Conversely, platelet serotonin levels decreased after drug administration, with the lowest values observed on the 30th day of fluoxetine 20 mg.

title: The histone acetyltransferase MOF is a key regulator of the embryonic stem cell core transcriptional network.
text: Pluripotent embryonic stem cells (ESCs) possess the ability to self-renew and rapidly respond to differentiation cues, both of which are regulated by epigenetic mechanisms. Our study reveals that the histone acetyltransferase Mof plays a critical role in maintaining ESC self-renewal and pluripotency. Mof-deficient ESCs lose their characteristic morphology, alkaline phosphatase (AP) staining, and differentiation potential, and exhibit aberrant expression of the core transcription factors Nanog, Oct4, and Sox2. Importantly, the phenotypes of Mof-null ESCs can be partially rescued by Nanog overexpression, suggesting that Mof functions upstream of Nanog in ESCs. Genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) and transcriptome analyses further demonstrate that Mof is an integral component of the ESC core transcriptional network and that Mof primes genes for diverse developmental programs. Additionally, we find that Mof is required for the recruitment of Wdr5 and histone H3K4 methylation at key regulatory loci, highlighting the interconnectedness of various chromatin regulators in ESCs.

title: Role of the CXCR4/SDF-1 chemokine axis in circulating neutrophil homeostasis.
text: The bone marrow is the main site for neutrophil production and release into the circulation. As the CXC chemokine receptor-4/stromal derived factor-1 (CXCR4/SDF-1) axis plays a central role in the interactions between hematopoietic stem cells, lymphocytes, and developing neutrophils in the marrow, we investigated whether reciprocal CXCR4-dependent mechanisms are involved in neutrophil release and return to the marrow after circulating. Neutralizing antibody to CXCR4 significantly reduced marrow retention of infused neutrophils (from 45.7% ± 0.5% to 6.9% ± 0.5%) and mobilized neutrophils from the marrow (from 34.4% ± 4.4%). As neutrophils mature and become activated, CXCR4 expression and SDF-1-induced calcium flux decrease, which is associated with decreased marrow homing in vivo.
