The binding of transcription factors such as Sp1, Sp3, and NF1-C to the first 227 base pairs of the 5' flanking DNA (-227/LUC) is crucial for basal transcription in human NCI-H295A adrenal cells. However, human placental JEG-3 cells do not express -227/LUC, even when transfected with a vector expressing steroidogenic factor 1 (SF-1). Therefore, other factors are necessary for basal expression of P450c17.
Deoxyribonuclease I footprinting and EMSAs identified a GATA consensus site at -64/-58 and an SF-1 site at -58/-50 in the P450c17 promoter. RT-PCR analysis identified GATA-4, GATA-6, and SF-1 in NCI-H295A cells and GATA-2 and GATA-3, but not GATA-4, GATA-6, or SF-1 in JEG-3 cells. Cotransfection of either GATA-4 or GATA-6 without SF-1 activated -227/LUC in JEG-3 cells, while cotransfection of GATA-2 or GATA-3 with or without SF-1 did not. Surprisingly, mutation of the GATA binding site in -227/LUC increased GATA-4 or GATA-6-induced activity, while mutation of the Sp1/Sp3 site decreased it. Additionally, promoter constructs including the GATA site, but excluding the Sp1/Sp3 site at -196/-188, were not activated by GATA-4 or GATA-6.
Glutathione-S-transferase pull-down experiments and coimmunoprecipitation demonstrated interaction between GATA-4 or GATA-6 and Sp1, but not Sp3. Chromatin immunoprecipitation assays confirmed that this GATA-4/6 interaction with Sp1 occurred at the Sp site in the P450c17 promoter in NCI-H295A cells. Demethylation with 5-aza-2-deoxycytidine permitted JEG-3 cells to express endogenous P450c17, SF-1, GATA-4, GATA-6, and transfected -227/LUC. These findings suggest that GATA-4 or GATA-6 and Sp1 regulate the expression of P450c17 in adrenal NCI-H295A cells, and that methylation of P450c17, GATA-4, and GATA-6 silences the expression of P450c17 in placental JEG-3 cells.

title: Performance of an abbreviated version of the Lubben Social Network Scale among three European community-dwelling older adult populations.
text:
Purpose:
There is a necessity for accurate and reliable short scales to evaluate social networks and social support systems and identify social isolation in elderly individuals.

Design and Methods:
The present study is a cross-national and cross-cultural evaluation of the effectiveness of an abbreviated version of the Lubben Social Network Scale (LSNS-6) in identifying social isolation among community-dwelling older adult populations in three European countries. Based on the concept of a lack of redundancy in social ties, clinical cut-points of the LSNS-6 were defined to determine individuals at risk of social isolation.
Results:
The LSNS-6 and two subscales (Family and Friends) exhibited high levels of internal consistency, stable factor structures, and strong associations with criterion variables. The proposed clinical cut-points showed good convergent validity, identifying 20% of respondents in Hamburg, 11% of those in Solothurn (Switzerland), and 15% of those in London as at risk of social isolation.
Implications:
We conclude that abbreviated scales such as the LSNS-6 should be included in clinical practice protocols of gerontological professionals. Screening older individuals based on the LSNS-6 provides quantitative data about their family and friendship ties, and identifies those at increased risk of social isolation who may benefit from in-depth assessments and targeted interventions.

title: The PneuCarriage Project: A Multi-Centre Comparative Study to Identify the Best Serotyping Methods for Examining Pneumococcal Carriage in Vaccine Evaluation Studies
text:
Title: Comparison of Pneumococcal Serotyping Methods for Carriage Studies: A Multi-centre Study
Background:
The pneumococcus is a pathogenic bacterium that primarily resides in the nasopharynx, with over 90 serotypes identified. Understanding pneumococcal carriage is crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of pneumococcal vaccines. Traditional serotyping methods are time-consuming and insufficient for detecting multiple serotype carriage, while new methods have been developed over the past decade. We conducted the PneuCarriage project, a large, international multi-centre study to identify the most effective pneumococcal serotyping methods for carriage studies.
Methods and Findings:
We distributed reference sample sets to 15 research groups for blinded testing, and 20 serotyping methods were used to test 81 laboratory-prepared (spiked) samples. The top-performing methods were then applied to 260 nasopharyngeal samples collected from children in six high-burden countries. Sensitivity and positive predictive value (PPV) were determined for each method, as well as for the traditional serotyping method (which identified over 98% of the dominant serotype). Alternate methods showed varying levels of sensitivity, with 7-99% sensitivity for the dominant serotype and 8-100% PPV. Only 15 methods were able to detect the dominant serotype with ≥70% sensitivity, and only 8 methods were able to detect minor serotypes with similar accuracy. For the field samples, the overall sensitivity ranged from 74.2% to 95.8% (with the microarray method showing the highest sensitivity at 95.8%), and PPV ranged from 82.2% to 96.4% (with the microarray method showing the highest PPV at 93.7%).
Limitations:



Conclusion:

title: Ribosome-Mediated Specificity in Hox mRNA Translation and Vertebrate Tissue Patterning
text: Throughout history, the ribosome has been considered a complex ribozyme with constitutive rather than regulatory capabilities in the translation of mRNA. However, our recent discoveries have challenged this view, as we have identified mutations in the Ribosomal Protein L38 (Rpl38) gene in mice that lead to surprising tissue-specific patterning defects, including extreme transformations of the axial skeleton. Interestingly, global protein synthesis remains unchanged in Rpl38 mutant embryos, yet the translation of a specific subset of Homeobox mRNAs is disrupted. Our data suggest that RPL38 acts as a regulatory component of the ribosome, facilitating 80S complex formation on these mRNAs and conferring transcript-specific translational control. Moreover, our findings indicate that Rpl38 is particularly enriched in regions of the embryo where loss-of-function phenotypes occur. This raises the possibility that the activity of ribosomal proteins (RPs) may be tightly regulated to introduce a new level of specificity in the control of gene expression and mammalian development. By screening for dynamic regulation of individual RPs within the vertebrate embryo, we have uncovered a surprising degree of control over RP activity, which may play a crucial role in the development of specific tissues and organs. These findings challenge our previous understanding of the ribosome's role in mRNA translation and highlight the complexity and specificity of the regulation of gene expression in mammalian development.

title: Growth and invasion of human melanomas in human skin grafted to immunodeficient mice.
text: In this study, an orthotopic model of human melanoma was developed by injecting malignant cells into human skin grafted onto nude and SCID mice. The melanoma cells proliferated and invaded the human skin grafts with characteristic patterns, with three of six tumors growing as multiple nodules and infiltrating the grafts without major architectural changes in the dermis, while the others invaded the dermis along collagen fibers with prominent endothelial vessels. In contrast, melanoma cells inoculated into mouse skin grew as diffusely expanding nodules that did not invade the murine dermis. In the human skin grafts, human melanoma cells were found to be angiogenic for human blood vessels, while murine vessels were only present at the periphery of the grafts. The tumor cells also invaded the human vessels, and four out of seven cell lines metastasized to the lungs, indicating that this model is useful for studying the interactions between normal and malignant human cells in vivo.

title: Myeloperoxidase: friend and foe.
text: Neutrophilic polymorphonuclear leukocytes (neutrophils) are specially designed to engulf and destroy microorganisms. When coated with opsonins (usually complement and/or antibody), microorganisms bind to specific receptors on the surface of the phagocyte, leading to membrane invagination and the incorporation of the microorganism into an intracellular phagosome. This triggers a rapid increase in oxygen consumption, with most of the excess oxygen being converted into highly reactive oxygen species (ROS). Additionally, cytoplasmic granules release their contents into the phagosome, leading to the death of the ingested microorganism. One of the antimicrobial systems formed in the phagosome consists of myeloperoxidase (MPO), released during degranulation, hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), formed through the respiratory burst, and a halide, particularly chloride. The initial product of the MPO-H2O2-chloride system is hypochlorous acid, which can then undergo further reactions to produce chlorine, chloramines, hydroxyl radicals, singlet oxygen, and ozone. These toxic agents can be released to the outside of the cell and contribute to the pathogenesis of disease. This review will consider the potential sources of H2O2 for the MPO-H2O2-halide system, the toxic products of the MPO system, the evidence for MPO involvement in microbicidal activity, the involvement of MPO-independent antimicrobial systems, and the role of the MPO system in tissue injury. It is concluded that the MPO system plays an important role in the microbicidal activity of phagocytes.

title: Role of microsomal prostaglandin E synthase-1 in the facilitation of angiogenesis and the healing of gastric ulcers.
text: The significance of prostaglandin E (PGE) in various biological events highlights the need to investigate the role of PGE synthases (PGESs) in vivo. Specifically, there has been no report on the functional relevance of microsomal PGES-1 (mPGES-1) in the physiological healing processes of gastric ulcers and angiogenesis, which is crucial for healing. To address this knowledge gap, we examined the involvement of mPGES-1 in the healing of gastric ulcers and angiogenesis using mPGES-1 knockout (KO) mice and their wild-type (WT) counterparts. We induced gastric ulcers in both groups by applying 100% acetic acid to the serosal surface and measured the ulcer areas subsequently. Notably, mPGES-1 and cyclooxygenase-2 were expressed in granulation tissues compared to normal stomach tissues. We observed that the healing of acetic acid-induced ulcers was significantly delayed in mPGES-1 KO mice compared to WT, accompanied by reduced angiogenesis in ulcer granulation tissues, as evidenced by decreased CD31 mRNA levels determined by real-time PCR and microvessel density in granulation tissues. Moreover, we found that the mRNA levels of proangiogenic growth factors, such as transforming growth factor-β, basic fibroblast growth factor, and connective tissue growth factor, were reduced in mPGES-1 KO mice compared to WT in ulcer granulation tissues. These findings suggest that mPGES-1 plays a crucial role in enhancing the ulcer-healing processes and angiogenesis indispensable to ulcer healing. Therefore, the use of a selective mPGES-1 inhibitor should be approached with caution in patients with gastric ulcers.

title: Echocardiographic Evidence of Innate Aortopathy in the Human Intracranial Aneurysm
text:
Introduction:
Intracranial aneurysm (IA) is found to be more prevalent in patients with coarctation of the aorta or bicuspid aortic valve compared to the general population, indicating a shared underlying pathophysiology. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between IA and aortopathy by analyzing the echocardiographic aortic root dimension (ARD) in patients with IA.
Methods:
We retrospectively analyzed 260 consecutive patients with IA who underwent echocardiography at our institution between 2008 and 2010. The patients were divided into two groups based on their ARD: an eccentric group (patients aged <55 years with at least one ruptured aneurysm, an aneurysm ≥7 mm in size, or multiple aneurysms) and a non-eccentric group (remainder of the patients). The clinical, angiographic, and echocardiographic findings of the two groups were compared.
Results:
Our results showed that ARD was significantly larger in the eccentric group than in the non-eccentric group (P = 0.049). Multivariable analysis confirmed this finding (P = 0.02). Subgroup analysis of patients aged <55 years revealed similar results for ARD (P = 0.03), whereas hypertension was more associated with the non-eccentric group (P = 0.01). Additionally, height was found to be inversely related to aneurysm size after adjusting for age, sex, weight, ARD, smoking status, and number of aneurysms (P = 0.004).
Discussion:
Our findings suggest that a certain group of IA patients share a common intrinsic wall defect with aortopathy. The shared neural crest cell origin may contribute to this phenomenon. These findings have important implications for the diagnosis and treatment of IA and aortopathy.
Conclusion:
Our study demonstrates a strong association between IA and aortopathy, suggesting that these conditions may share a common pathophysiology. Further research is needed to fully understand the underlying mechanisms and to develop effective prevention and treatment strategies for these conditions.

title: Aortic and large artery compliance in end-stage renal failure.
text: The pulse wave velocity (PWV) was measured in the aorta, right leg, and arm of 90 healthy controls (CS) and 92 hemodialysis (HD) patients of similar age and mean arterial pressure (MAP). Blood chemistry and echographic dimensions of the aorta were also assessed in all subjects. Unlike femoral and brachial PWV, which were only mildly elevated in HD patients (P < 0.05), aortic PWV was significantly increased (1113 ± 319 cm/s) in HD compared to CS (965 ± 216 cm/s; P = 0.0016). Additionally, aortic diameters were larger in HD, both at the aortic root (32.7 ± 4 mm vs. 28.2 ± 2.8 mm; P < 0.0001) and aortic bifurcation (16.9 ± 3.1 mm vs. 14.6 ± 2.2 mm; P < 0.0001). Although MAP was similar in HD and CS (109.9 ± 19.3 mmHg vs. 110.2 ± 17.2 mmHg), pulse pressure was significantly higher in HD patients (76.6 ± 23.7 mmHg vs. 63.9 ± 22 mmHg; P = 0.007). Furthermore, aortic PWV increased with age (P < 0.0001) and MAP (P < 0.0001) in both populations. The presence of aortic calcification showed a borderline relationship with the increase in aortic PWV (P = 0.050 in CS and P = 0.069 in HD). These findings suggest that the aortic wall compliance is decreased in HD patients, resulting in an increase in the pulsatile component of arterial pressure.

title: The DNA polymerase λ is required for the repair of non-compatible DNA double strand breaks by NHEJ in mammalian cells
text: Recently identified DNA polymerase lambda (polλ) has eluded its cellular function despite its involvement in chromosomal DNA repair. Our study revealed that polλ plays a crucial role in repairing DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) via non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) in mammalian cells.expression of an inactive form of polλ (polλDN) reduces the frequency of NHEJ events following I-Sce-I-induced DSBs, while inactive forms of its homologues polβ and polμ do not. This effect is specific to events that require DNA end processing before ligation, and is associated with the occurrence of large deletions near the induced DSB. Furthermore, polλDN-expressing cells exhibit enhanced sensitivity and genomic instability in response to ionizing radiation, similar to that of NHEJ-defective cells. Our findings support the notion that polλ plays a key role in repairing a subset of DSBs in genomic DNA, thereby contributing to the maintenance of genetic stability mediated by the NHEJ pathway.

title: Angina with "normal" coronary arteries: sex differences in outcomes.
text:
Background:
Several studies have shown that women with nonobstructive coronary disease have a higher rate of subsequent investigations, rehospitalizations for recurrent chest pain, and repeat coronary angiography compared to men. However, the sex specificity of this finding is not clear. To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted an evaluation of sex differences in rehospitalization for acute coronary syndrome (ACS) or chest pain in patients with "angiographically normal" coronaries.
Methods:
We conducted a retrospective cohort study using prospectively collected angiographic and clinical data on all patients in British Columbia, Canada, who presented for their first cardiac catheterization with suspected ischemic heart disease but angiographically normal coronaries.
Results:
Our analysis included 32,856 patients, of which 7.1% were men and 23.3% were women. Among angiographically normal patients, women were significantly older and more likely to have hypertension, prior stroke, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and peripheral vascular disease than men. Despite these differences in comorbidities, there was no significant variation in the Canadian Cardiovascular Society class of angina between men and women. Within one year of their initial catheterization, 1.0% of patients died (19 women, 18 men), and 0.6% had a stroke (13 women, 9 men). However, we found a significant difference in rehospitalization rates between men and women, with women being readmitted to hospital for ACS or chest pain requiring catheterization at a rate that was more than 4 times higher than men (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 4.06, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.15-14.31).
Conclusions:
Our findings have important social and economic implications and suggest that traditional diagnostic methods may not be optimal for women. In a contemporary, population-based cohort presenting for cardiac catheterization for suspected ischemia, we found that women with angiographically normal coronaries were significantly more likely to be readmitted to hospital for ACS/chest pain within 180 days compared to men. These observations suggest that there may be a need to reevaluate the diagnostic approach for women with chest pain, particularly those with angiographically normal coronaries.

title: Keratin-dependent regulation of Aire and gene expression in skin tumor keratinocytes
text: Intermediate filament protein keratin 17 (K17) is significantly increased in skin diseases caused by inflammation and many tumors originating from epithelial cells. We found that a transcription factor called autoimmune regulator (Aire) is expressed in tumor keratinocytes in a K17-dependent manner. Aire is necessary for the rapid onset of skin tumor generation in mice. We discovered that the expression of Aire in keratinocytes relies on the interaction between K17 and a protein called heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein hnRNP K. Additionally, K17 and Aire colocalize in the nucleus of tumor-prone keratinocytes, and both proteins bind to specific DNA sequences in genes involved in inflammatory responses. These findings provide new insights into the roles of K17 and Aire in inflammatory and immune responses in diseased epithelia.

title: Flow-Dependent Regulation of Kruppel-Like Factor 2 Is Mediated by MicroRNA-92a.
text:
The transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) is critical for preserving endothelial function, which is downregulated when atheroprotective flow is present. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play a significant role in regulating gene expression at the post-transcriptional level. In this study, we investigated the role of miR-92a in the flow-regulated KLF2.
Using Dicer knockdown, we identified KLF2 as a miRNA target in human umbilical vein endothelial cells. In silico analysis predicted that miR-92a could bind to the 3' untranslated region of KLF2. Overexpression of miR-92a decreased the expression of KLF2 and several endothelial genes, including nitric oxide synthase and thrombomodulin, at the mRNA and protein levels. Conversely, inhibition of miR-92a led to increased expression of these genes. Subsequent experiments demonstrated that atheroprotective laminar flow downregulated the level of miR-92a precursor and induced KLF2 expression, which was subsequently reduced by miR-92a precursor. In addition, we found that the level of miR-92a was lower in human umbilical vein endothelial cells exposed to atheroprotective pulsatile shear flow compared to atheroprone oscillatory shear flow. Immunoprecipitation experiments showed that pulsatile shear flow decreased the functional targeting of miR-92a precursor/KLF2 mRNA in human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Consistently, mice receiving miR-92a precursor in the carotid arteries exhibited impaired vasodilatory response to flow.
In conclusion, atheroprotective flow patterns reduce the level of miR-92a, leading to increased expression of KLF2, which maintains endothelial homeostasis.

title: Effectiveness of a diabetes education and self management programme (DESMOND) for people with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus: three year follow-up of a cluster randomised controlled trial in primary care
text: To determine whether the benefits of a six-hour structured education and self-management program for individuals with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus persist over time, a three-year follow-up was conducted among 731 participants from 207 general practices in 13 primary care sites in the United Kingdom. The program was delivered by two trained healthcare professionals in the community compared to usual care. The primary outcome was glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels, and secondary outcomes included blood pressure, weight, blood lipid levels, smoking status, physical activity, quality of life, beliefs about illness, depression, emotional impact of diabetes, and drug use. Findings showed that HbA1c levels at three years had decreased in both groups, with no significant difference between the intervention and usual care groups after adjusting for baseline and cluster (difference -0.02, 95% confidence interval -0.22 to 0.17). While the intervention group showed sustained benefits in four out of five health beliefs compared to the baseline at three years (P<0.01), depression scores and quality of life did not differ at three years. The study concluded that a single education and self-management program for individuals with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus did not demonstrate significant differences in biomedical or lifestyle outcomes at three years, although there were sustained improvements in some illness beliefs. The trial was registered with Current Controlled Trials ISRCTN17844016.

title: Acetylation of Histone H3 Lysine 56 Regulates Replication-Coupled Nucleosome Assembly
text: Chromatin assembly factor 1 (CAF-1) and Rtt106 play a crucial role in the process of depositing newly synthesized histones onto replicating DNA, forming nucleosomes that are essential for maintaining genome stability and inherited chromatin structures in proliferating cells. However, the underlying mechanisms of histone acetylation in this replication-coupled nucleosome assembly pathway remain unclear. Our study demonstrates that histone H3 acetylated at lysine 56 (H3K56Ac) is incorporated onto replicating DNA and, by enhancing the binding affinity of CAF-1 and Rtt106 for histone H3, H3K56Ac enhances the ability of these histone chaperones to assemble DNA into nucleosomes. Genetic analysis reveals that H3K56Ac acts in a nonredundant manner with the acetylation of the N-terminal residues of H3 and H4 in nucleosome assembly, providing a mechanism by which H3K56Ac regulates this process. These findings shed light on the role of H3K56Ac in replication-coupled nucleosome assembly mediated by CAF-1 and Rtt106.

title: Selective inhibition of Ras-dependent cell growth by farnesylthiosalisylic acid.
text: S-trans,trans-Farnesylthiosalicylic acid (FTS) is a novel farnesylated carboxylic acid derivative with potential as a therapeutic agent. In vitro studies have shown that FTS acts as a potent and selective inhibitor of the enzyme prenylated protein methyltransferase (PPMTase), which methylates the carboxyl-terminal S-prenylcysteine in a variety of prenylated proteins, including Ras. While FTS does not affect protein prenylation, it is able to inhibit methylation of these proteins in cell-free systems and intact cells, with a higher concentration requirement in intact cells. The results suggest that FTS may specifically interfere with the interaction of Ras with a farnesylcysteine recognition domain in the cell membrane. Importantly, FTS has been shown to reduce levels of Ras in cell membranes and inhibit Ras-dependent cell growth in vitro, independent of methylation. These effects are observed in Ras-transformed cell lines, such as EJ cells, and are reversed by FTS treatment. Additionally, FTS has been found to inhibit the mitogenic effects of epidermal and basic fibroblast growth factors, suggesting its selectivity towards Ras growth signaling. These findings raise the possibility that FTS may be a potential therapeutic agent for the treatment of cancers driven by Ras mutations.

title: NADPH oxidase controls phagosomal pH and antigen cross-presentation in human dendritic cells.
text: The phagocyte NADPH oxidase, NOX2, plays a crucial role in the bactericidal activity of phagocytic cells and innate immunity. Recently, we discovered that NOX2 activity in mouse dendritic cells (DCs) helps prevent acidification of phagosomes, allowing for better antigen presentation. To investigate the function of NOX2 in regulating phagosomal pH in human DCs, we analyzed the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and phagosomal/endosomal pH in monocyte-derived DCs and macrophages (M(diameter)s) from healthy donors and patients with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). Interestingly, we found that human M(diameter)s are better at acidifying their phagosomes than human DCs, which is reflected in higher expression of the vacuolar proton ATPase (V-H(+)-ATPase). However, phagosomal ROS production was actually higher in M(diameter)s due to increased gp91phox expression and recruitment to phagosomes. In contrast, in the absence of active NOX2, phagosomal and endosomal pH decreased. Moreover, impairment of antigen cross-presentation was observed in both the presence of a NOX2 inhibitor and in DCs derived from patients with CGD. Therefore, we conclude that NOX2 activity regulates phagosomal and endosomal pH in human DCs and is essential for efficient antigen cross-presentation.

title: Activation of fast skeletal muscle troponin as a potential therapeutic approach for treating neuromuscular diseases
text: Reduced neural input in neuromuscular diseases leads to muscle weakness due to decreased density of muscle innervation, lower rates of neuromuscular junction activation, or inefficient synaptic transmission. To address this issue, we created CK-2017357, a small-molecule fast-skeletal-troponin activator that enhances muscle strength by amplifying the muscle's response when neural input is diminished. Selectively binding to the fast-skeletal-troponin complex, CK-2017357 slows the rate of calcium release from troponin C and increases muscle sensitivity to calcium. As a result, the force-calcium relationship of muscle fibers shifts towards higher forces at lower calcium levels, and the force-frequency relationship of nerve-muscle pairs also shows an increase in muscle force production. We demonstrate that administration of single doses of CK-2017357 to a model of neuromuscular disease myasthenia gravis leads to immediate improvements in muscle force and grip strength. This suggests that targeting the fast-skeletal-troponin complex with CK-2017357 may provide a new therapeutic approach for improving physical activity in diseases where neuromuscular function is compromised.

title: Cortactin regulates cofilin and N-WASp activities to control the stages of invadopodium assembly and maturation
text: Invadopodia are protrusions on the surface of invasive cancer cells that degrade the surrounding matrix. The mechanisms controlling their formation and maturation remain unclear. By dissecting the stages of invadopodium assembly and maturation, we found that cortactin phosphorylation acts as a Master switch during these processes. Specifically, cortactin phosphorylation regulates cofilin and Arp2/3 complex-dependent actin polymerization. Cortactin directly binds cofilin and inhibits its severing activity, but cortactin phosphorylation releases this inhibition, allowing cofilin to sever actin filaments and create barbed ends at invadopodia, thus supporting Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization. After barbed end formation, cortactin is dephosphorylated, blocking cofilin severing activity and stabilizing invadopodia. These findings reveal novel mechanisms of actin polymerization in invadopodia of metastatic carcinoma cells and define four distinct stages of invadopodium assembly and maturation, including invadopodium precursor formation, actin polymerization, stabilization, and matrix degradation.

title: Calreticulin exposure dictates the immunogenicity of cancer cell death
text: Anthracyclin-treated cancer cells are particularly effective in triggering an immune response against the tumor, whereas other DNA-damaging agents like etoposide and mitomycin C do not induce the same immune response. We found that anthracyclins cause the rapid transfer of a protein called calreticulin (CRT) to the cell surface. Blocking or reducing CRT reduces the ability of dendritic cells to engulf and present anthracyclin-treated tumor cells to the immune system, effectively neutralizing their immunogenicity in mice. We discovered that the anthracyclin-induced CRT translocation can be mimicked by inhibiting a complex called protein phosphatase 1/GADD34. Re-administering CRT or inhibiting the protein phosphatase 1/GADD34 complex restored the immunogenicity of cells killed by etoposide and mitomycin C and improved their antitumor effects in vivo. These findings identify CRT as a critical factor in determining immune responses against cancer and offer a possible strategy for immunogenic chemotherapy.

title: In vivo disruption of Xenopus U3 snRNA affects ribosomal RNA processing.
text: Researchers injected DNA oligonucleotides complementary to sequences located in the 5' third of U3 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNA) into Xenopus oocyte nuclei to Disrupt endogenous U3 snRNA. The effects of this treatment on ribosomal RNA (rRNA) processing were then examined. The team found that some species of toads exhibit a single rRNA processing pathway, whereas in other toads, two distinct rRNA processing pathways can coexist within a single oocyte. Disruption of U3 snRNA in toads with the single rRNA processing pathway led to a decrease in 20S and '32S' pre-rRNA. In contrast, in toads with two rRNA processing pathways, an increase in '36S' pre-rRNA was observed in the second pathway. This study represents the first in-vivo demonstration of U3 snRNA's role in rRNA processing. The cleavage site #3 is situated at the interface between the internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS 1) and the 5.8S rRNA and connects all of the affected rRNA intermediates: 20S and '32S' are the products of site #3 cleavage in the first pathway, while '36S' serves as the substrate for cleavage at site #3 in the second pathway. The researchers propose that U3 snRNP folds pre-rRNA into a conformation that determines the correct cleavage at processing site #3.

title: A genome-wide siRNA screen reveals diverse cellular processes and pathways that mediate genome stability.
text:
The importance of signaling pathways that respond to DNA damage in maintaining genome stability cannot be overstated. In cancer and other diseases, disruptions in these pathways can lead to genetic instability and uncontrolled proliferation. To identify additional genes involved in genome stabilization, we employed a genome-wide siRNA screen using phosphorylation of the histone variant H2AX as a marker of DNA damage. Interestingly, we found hundreds of genes whose downregulation led to increased levels of H2AX phosphorylation (gammaH2AX), including many links to cellular complexes and genes with unclassified functions.
Our findings highlight the critical role of mRNA-processing factors in preventing DNA damage, with aberrant RNA-DNA structures sometimes causing damage. Furthermore, we observed a connection between elevated gammaH2AX levels and Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) syndrome, a neurological disorder. Surprisingly, we found that several CMT proteins are involved in the DNA-damage response, underscoring the broader connections between genome stability and other biological processes. These data underscore the importance of considering the interconnectedness of biological pathways in maintaining genome stability.

title: Alphavbeta6-Fyn signaling promotes oral cancer progression.
text:
In our previous studies, we demonstrated that integrin beta6 is overexpressed in invasive oral squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and correlates with the progression of oral tumors. However, the mechanism by which integrin beta6 promotes oral cancer progression is not well understood. The aim of the present study was to investigate whether integrin beta6 signaling activates Fyn and thereby promotes oral SCC progression.
We analyzed the integrin beta6 signaling complex and examined the function of these signaling molecules in oral SCC cells. Our findings showed that upon ligation of integrin beta6 with fibronectin, beta6 complexed with Fyn and activated it. The activation of Fyn recruited and activated focal adhesion kinase (FAK) to this complex. This complex was necessary to activate Shc and couple beta6 signaling to the Raf-ERK/MAPK pathway. This pathway transcriptionally activated the matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3) gene and promoted oral SCC cell proliferation and experimental metastasis in vivo. Our findings suggest that integrin beta6 signaling activates Fyn and thereby promotes oral cancer progression.

title: miRNA-dependent gene silencing involving Ago2-mediated cleavage of a circular antisense RNA.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are approximately 22 nucleotides in length non-coding RNAs that typically bind to the 3' untranslated region (UTR) of target messenger RNAs (mRNAs) in the cytoplasm, leading to mRNA degradation and translational repression. Here, we investigate the possibility that miRNAs can also regulate gene expression by targeting non-coding antisense transcripts in human cells. Specifically, we demonstrate that miR-671 directs cleavage of a circular antisense transcript of the Cerebellar Degeneration-Related protein 1 (CDR1) locus in an Ago2-slicer-dependent manner. The resulting downregulation of circular antisense has a concomitant decrease in CDR1 mRNA levels, independent of heterochromatin formation. Our study provides the first evidence for non-coding antisense transcripts as functional miRNA targets and uncovers a novel regulatory mechanism involving a positive correlation between mRNA and antisense circular RNA levels.

title: Regulation of Serum Amyloid A3 (SAA3) in Mouse Colonic Epithelium and Adipose Tissue by the Intestinal Microbiota
text: The gut microbiome has been implicated as an environmental factor that influences the development of metabolic and inflammatory diseases in mammals. Recent studies have shown that gut bacteria-derived lipopolysaccharide (LPS) can trigger obesity and insulin resistance in mice, but the molecular mechanisms underlying microbial regulation of host metabolism and inflammation have not been fully explored. We investigated the role of the gut microbiome in the regulation of hepatic serum amyloid A (SAA) proteins, which are known markers and mediators of inflammation in insulin resistance. Our findings revealed that SAA3 expression was significantly augmented in adipose and colonic tissue of mice exposed to gut microbes. Furthermore, we found that the Toll-like receptor (TLR)/MyD88/NF-κB signaling axis played a role in the regulation of SAA3 expression in the colon. Our data suggest that LPS, and potentially other products of the indigenous gut microbiota, may contribute to the elevation of cytokine expression in tissues and exacerbate chronic low-grade inflammation observed in obesity. Overall, this study provides new insights into the mechanisms by which the gut microbiome influences host metabolism and inflammation, and highlights the potential of the gut microbiome as a therapeutic target for the prevention and treatment of metabolic disorders.

title: Reversing the tide — diagnosis and prevention of T2DM in populations of African descent
text: Populations of African descent are leading the global epidemic of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Delayed diagnosis exacerbates the burden of the disease, leading to preventable complications. Earlier detection would result in reduced undiagnosed T2DM, more accurate statistics, better resource allocation, and improved health outcomes. An underappreciated factor contributing to undiagnosed T2DM in these populations is that traditional screening tests for hyperglycemia (fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c) perform suboptimally. To address this challenge, combining tests or adding glycated albumin (a nonfasting marker of glycemia) may be beneficial. However, it is important to recognize that individuals of African, Caribbean, or African-American descent may have varying responses to diagnostic tests and interventions due to differences in diet, exercise, body mass index (BMI), environment, gene-environment interactions, and the prevalence of sickle cell trait. Intensive lifestyle interventions have been shown to be effective in the primary prevention of T2DM in the African-American population, but they have not been as effective in the secondary prevention. Lack of health literacy and poor glycemic control in Africa and the Caribbean make customized lifestyle interventions a promising approach for both primary and secondary prevention. In conclusion, diagnosing and preventing T2DM requires tailored strategies that are sensitive to the diversity within populations of African descent.

title: Biofeedback and relaxation in the treatment of migraine headaches: comparative effectiveness and physiological correlates.
text: A total of 27 migraine patients were divided into three equal groups and received different types of biofeedback training: thermal biofeedback, frontalis EMG biofeedback, or relaxation training. Each group underwent training under "massed" practice conditions (nine sessions per week) for a total of 18 training sessions and six test-generalization sessions. Noteworthy improvements in headaches were observed across all groups, with the thermal biofeedback group displaying the most significant improvements, exhibiting near complete elimination of migraine attacks by the end of training and maintaining this performance for at least six months following training. Additionally, an examination of skin temperature and EMG changes within the three groups throughout the training period pointed towards a distinct correlation between skin temperature control and reduction in migraine headache symptoms, suggesting that further investigation into this relationship is warranted.

title: Fine-scale chromatin interaction maps reveal the cis-regulatory landscape of human lincRNA genes
text: Recent advances in chromosome conformation capture techniques have significantly expanded our knowledge of the three-dimensional (3D) organization of genomes. However, these methods are limited by their reliance on restriction enzymes, which can only provide a coarse-grained resolution. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel approach called DNase Hi-C, which utilizes DNase I for chromatin fragmentation and achieves greatly improved efficiency and resolution compared to traditional Hi-C methods. By integrating DNase Hi-C with DNA-capture technology, we have established a high-throughput approach for targeted mapping of fine-scale chromatin architecture. We applied this targeted DNase Hi-C method to investigate the 3D organization of 998 large intergenic noncoding RNA (lincRNA) promoters in two human cell lines. Our findings unveil the intricate mechanisms of lincRNA expression, which involve both super-enhancers and the Polycomb repressive complex. Furthermore, our results provide the first comprehensive view of the cell type-specific 3D organization of lincRNA genes.

title: BASOPHILS AND THE T HELPER 2 ENVIRONMENT CAN PROMOTE THE DEVELOPMENT OF LUPUS NEPHRITIS
text: In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), autoantibodies can target the kidney, leading to functional failure and potential mortality. Our findings reveal that activation of basophils through autoreactive IgE leads to their migration to lymph nodes, promoting the differentiation of T helper type 2 (T(H)2) cells and enhancing the production of self-reactive antibodies that cause lupus-like nephritis in mice lacking the Src family protein tyrosine kinase Lyn (Lyn(-/-) mice). Individuals with SLE also exhibit elevated serum IgE, self-reactive IgEs, and activated basophils that express CD62 ligand (CD62L) and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II molecule human leukocyte antigen-DR (HLA-DR), which are associated with increased disease activity and active lupus nephritis. Additionally, basophils were found in the lymph nodes and spleen of individuals with SLE. Our study shows that in Lyn(-/-) mice, basophils and IgE autoantibodies cooperate to amplify autoantibody production that leads to lupus nephritis, and in individuals with SLE, IgE autoantibodies and activated basophils are factors associated with disease activity and nephritis.

title: Behavioral treatment of obesity in patients encountered in primary care settings: a systematic review.
text: In 2011, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) approved a program that allows primary care practitioners to provide intensive behavioral weight loss counseling to obese patients. This program involves 14 face-to-face sessions lasting 10-15 minutes each, spread over a period of 6 months. However, a systematic review of studies on behavioral counseling for overweight and obese patients recruited from primary care found that there is limited research on primary care practitioners providing this type of care. The review included 12 randomized controlled trials involving 3893 participants and found that interventions that included both reduced energy intake and increased physical activity, as well as having more treatment sessions, were associated with greater weight loss. The findings suggest that trained interventionists, who provide counseling in person or by telephone, could be considered for treating overweight or obesity in patients encountered in primary care settings.

title: Guanylate binding protein 1 is a novel effector of EGFR-driven invasion in glioblastoma
text:
Although GBP1 (guanylate binding protein 1) was one of the first interferon-inducible proteins identified, its function remains largely unknown. However, recent studies have shown that EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) activation, often through mutation or amplification, is a common genetic alteration in various human tumors, including glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). GBM is characterized by independent yet interconnected features of extensive invasion into normal brain parenchyma, rapid growth, necrosis, and angiogenesis.
In this study, we discovered that EGFR activation stimulates GBP1 expression in GBM cell lines through a signaling pathway involving Src and p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase. Moreover, we identified YY1 (Yin Yang 1) as the downstream transcriptional regulator that regulates EGFR-driven GBP1 expression. GBP1 was found to be necessary for EGFR-mediated MMP1 (matrix metalloproteinase 1) expression and glioma cell invasion in vitro. Interestingly, deregulation of GBP1 expression did not affect glioma cell proliferation, but overexpression of GBP1 enhanced glioma cell invasion through MMP1 induction, which was independent of its GTPase activity. In addition, reducing GBP1 levels by RNA interference in invasive GBM cells significantly inhibited their ability to infiltrate the brain parenchyma of mice.
Our findings reveal that GBP1 is a novel link between EGFR activity and MMP1 expression and suggest that it may be a promising therapeutic target for inhibiting GBM invasion. Notably, GBP1 expression was highly correlated with EGFR expression in both human GBM tumors and cell lines, particularly those of the neural subtype. Together, these results provide new insights into the complex mechanisms underlying GBM invasion and open up potential avenues for the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

title: ATP binding to PAN or the 26S ATPases causes association with the 20S proteasome, gate opening, and translocation of unfolded proteins.
text:
The archaeal ATPase protein PAN, similar to its eukaryotic counterpart the 26S proteasome-regulatory ATPase, binds to the 20S proteasome when exposed to ATP or ATPγS, but not ADP. Using electron microscopy (EM), PAN appears as a two-ring structure that caps the 20S proteasome, resembling two densities in the 19S complex.
The N terminus of the archaeal 20S alpha subunits functions as a gate that keeps seven-residue peptides from entering the proteasome, while allowing tetrapeptides to pass through. Upon association with the 20S particle, PAN stimulates gate opening. Interestingly, although degradation of globular proteins requires ATP hydrolysis, the PAN-20S complex with ATPγS can translocate and degrade unfolded and denatured proteins. In fact, both rabbit 26S proteasomes and the PAN-20S complex can degrade these unfolded proteins upon binding to ATP, without hydrolysis.
In summary, while unfolding of proteins requires energy from ATP hydrolysis, simply binding to ATP allows the PAN-20S complex to associate, open the gate, and translocate unfolded substrates into the proteasome, which can occur through a facilitated diffusion mechanism mediated by the ATPase.

title: Cytokines and anti-cytokine biologicals in autoimmunity: present and future.
text: The mounting appreciation of cytokines' significance in autoimmune disorders, particularly the central role of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFalpha) in the inflammatory and destructive processes common to various human autoimmune diseases, has led to the development of a new generation of therapeutics: TNFalpha blocking agents. This article reviews the current understanding of cytokines' function in autoimmunity, based on both laboratory and clinical studies. We also discuss potential future directions for anti-TNFalpha therapy, including combination therapy with other anti-cytokine or anti-T cell agents, as well as the use of small molecules targeting molecules involved in TNFalpha production, such as NF-kappaB and p38 MAPK. The future development of anti-TNFalpha and anti-cytokine therapies holds promise.

title: Vegetarian dietary patterns and mortality in Adventist Health Study 2.
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the connection between vegetarian dietary patterns and mortality. We conducted a prospective cohort study among 96,469 Seventh-day Adventist men and women in North America, and collected data on their dietary patterns through a food frequency questionnaire. We categorized their dietary patterns into five categories: non-vegetarian, semi-vegetarian, pesco-vegetarian, lacto-ovo-vegetarian, and vegan. We then analyzed the relationship between these dietary patterns and mortality rates over a five-year follow-up period, using the National Death Index to identify deaths.
Our findings showed that vegetarian dietary patterns were associated with lower all-cause mortality and certain cause-specific mortality rates. Specifically, we found that the adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality among all vegetarians combined was 0.88, compared to non-vegetarians. Within the vegetarian groups, we found that vegans had an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.85, while lacto-ovo-vegetarians had a hazard ratio of 0.91, pesco-vegetarians had a hazard ratio of 0.81, and semi-vegetarians had a hazard ratio of 0.92. These associations were more pronounced in men than in women.
These findings suggest that a vegetarian diet may be beneficial for reducing mortality rates, particularly in men. The mechanisms underlying these associations are not fully understood, but may be related to the vegetarian diet's emphasis on plant-based foods, which are rich in nutrients and phytochemicals that have been shown to have protective effects against various diseases. Our study provides further evidence to support the recommendation to adopt a vegetarian diet for overall health and well-being.

title: TEAD mediates YAP-dependent gene induction and growth control.
text: The transcriptional coactivator YAP has been linked to oncogenesis and is frequently amplified in human cancers. Recent research has shown that YAP is phosphorylated and inhibited by the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway. This study demonstrates that the TEAD family of transcription factors plays a crucial role in mediating YAP-dependent gene expression. TEAD is also essential for YAP-induced cell proliferation, transformation, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The gene encoding the cysteine-rich protein CTGF has been identified as a direct YAP target involved in cell growth. Furthermore, our findings reveal a functional connection between YAP and TEAD in both humans and Drosophila, with TEAD serving as a critical component of the Hippo pathway that regulates YAP's biological functions.

title: Direct isolation of human central nervous system stem cells.
text: Stem cells, which are special cells with the ability to renew themselves and differentiate into different cell types, have the potential to repair or replace damaged tissue. We have successfully isolated and studied clonogenic human central nervous system stem cells (hCNS-SC) directly from fresh human fetal brain tissue using antibodies and fluorescence-activated cell sorting. These hCNS-SC are identified as 5F3 (CD133)(+) cells, 5E12(+), CD34(-), CD45(-), and CD24(-/lo). By analyzing these cells, we found that single CD133(+) CD34(-) CD45(-) cells can initiate neurosphere cultures, which are clusters of cells that can differentiate into both neurons and glial cells. Furthermore, when single cells from these cultures are replated and cultured again, they can maintain their ability to self-renew and differentiate into different cell types. When we transplanted these sorted and expanded hCNS-SC into immunodeficient neonatal mice, the cells showed potent engraftment, proliferation, migration, and neural differentiation, demonstrating their potential for use in the treatment of neurological disorders.

title: p53 mutation in breast cancer. Correlation with cell kinetics and cell of origin.
text:
Several studies have investigated the expression of cytokeratins (CKs), vimentin, the epithelial growth factor receptor (EGFR), the oestrogen receptor (ER), and the progesterone receptor (PgR) in breast cancer, but none have directly compared p53 mutations with these phenotypic and differentiation markers in the same case. To fill this knowledge gap, the present study evaluated the expression of p53 and bcl-2 proteins in relation to phenotypic characteristics and cellular kinetic parameters (mitotic index and apoptotic index) in 37 cases of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and 27 cases of infiltrating ductal carcinoma (IDC) of the breast. The study also examined p53 gene mutation by polymerase chain reaction single strand conformation polymorphism (SSCP) analysis.
Results showed that 13 cases (8 DCIS and 5 IDC) exhibited expression of CK8, CK14, CK18, vimentin, and EGFR, consistent with a stem cell phenotype, while 44 cases (27 DCIS and 17 IDC) showed expression of CK8 and CK1, weak or negative expression of CK18, and were negative for vimentin and EGFR, consistent with a luminal cell phenotype. Notably, DCIS and IDC cases with a stem cell phenotype were ER/PgR negative and intermediately or poorly differentiated, while those with a luminal cell phenotype were ER/PgR positive and well or intermediately differentiated. Further analysis revealed that intermediately or poorly differentiated cases with a stem cell phenotype had higher proliferative activity (percentage of MIB-1 positive cells) compared to intermediately or well-differentiated cases with a luminal cell phenotype. Both DCIS and IDC cases with a stem cell phenotype were p53 positive and bcl-2 negative by immunohistochemistry, while IDC cases with a stem cell phenotype had a reduction in both mitotic index and apoptotic index compared to DCIS. Most of the tumors showing a more differentiated phenotype (luminal) were p53 negative and bcl-2 positive, and cell kinetic parameters increased from DCIS to IDC. These findings suggest that the existence of subsets of DCIS and IDC that may be derived from subpopulations of normal breast cells with different control mechanisms of cell proliferation and neoplastic progression.

title: Cardiorespiratory fitness and body mass index as predictors of cardiovascular disease mortality among men with diabetes.
text:
Background: There is ongoing debate about whether higher levels of cardiorespiratory fitness—a marker of regular physical activity—are associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality in overweight and obese individuals with diabetes. Our study aimed to quantify the independent and joint relationships between cardiorespiratory fitness and body mass index (BMI) with CVD mortality in men with diabetes.
Methods: We conducted a prospective observational study using data from the Aerobics Center Longitudinal Study. The study included 2316 men with no prior history of stroke or myocardial infarction, who were diagnosed with diabetes (mean age: 50 years), and had a medical examination that included a maximum exercise test, with mortality surveillance through December 31, 1998. BMI was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters. The main outcome measure was CVD mortality, which was analyzed across different levels of fitness, with stratification by BMI.
Results: During a mean follow-up of 15.9 years, we observed 179 CVD deaths and 36,710 man-years of exposure. In a model adjusted for age, examination year, fasting glucose level, systolic blood pressure, parental history of premature CVD, total cholesterol level, cigarette smoking, abnormal resting and exercise electrocardiograms, we found that men with a low fitness level had a significantly higher adjusted risk of mortality compared to normal weight men with a high fitness level. Specifically, the hazard ratio for CVD mortality was 2.7 (95% confidence interval: 1.3-5.7) in normal weight men, 2.7 (95% confidence interval: 1.4-5.1) in overweight men, and 2.8 (95% confidence interval: 1.4-5.1) in class 1 obese men, compared to normal weight men with a high fitness level.
Conclusion: In this cohort of men with diabetes, low fitness level was found to be associated with an increased risk of CVD mortality within normal weight, overweight, and class 1 obese weight categories.

title: Effect of screening on cervical cancer mortality in England and Wales: analysis of trends with an age period cohort model.
text:
In 1997, the percentage of women dying from cervical cancer was 7% lower than in the previous year and had decreased by over 25% since 1992. This significant reduction is likely due to the implementation of cervical screening programs, although other factors such as strong cohort effects have contributed to fluctuations in mortality rates in the past.
To estimate the impact of cervical screening on mortality rates, we analyzed mortality data from death registrations in England and Wales, using mid-year population estimates to calculate rates in 5-year age bands. We adjusted mortality rates since 1993 upward by 4% to account for changes in the classification of cause of death.
Our model took into account the effects of age, year of birth, and a smoothly varying age effect, birth cohort effect, and age-dependent explore factors on mortality rates. By accounting for these factors, we were able to isolate the beneficial effects of cervical screening and estimate its impact on mortality rates over time.

title: The regulation of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors by Src kinase.
text: Src family kinases (SFKs) play a crucial role in regulating various cellular processes by interacting with growth factors, G-protein-coupled receptors, and ligand-gated ion channels. Recent studies have highlighted SFKs as a central hub for multiple signaling pathways that control N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptors in the central nervous system. SFKs associate with NMDA receptors through both indirect and direct binding mechanisms, forming an SFK signaling complex with protein tyrosine phosphatase α and C-terminal Src kinase. Early research revealed that intramolecular interactions within the SH2 or SH3 domain of SFKs maintain their inhibited state. Disruption of these interactions can lead to the activation of SFKs, involving multiple signaling pathways in the regulation of this process. The enzyme activity of SFKs exhibits a graded response, with varying levels corresponding to different activation states. It has been proposed that the SH2 and SH3 domains may also enhance the catalytic activity of protein tyrosine kinases, such as Abl. Recent findings suggest that the stability of neuronal Src protein is linked to its enzyme activity, and that the SH2 and SH3 domain interactions can regulate both the activation and enzyme activity of active neuronal Src. Together, these discoveries unveil new mechanisms governing SFK regulation.

title: The art and design of genetic screens: RNA interference
text: The groundbreaking gene knockdown technique of RNAi has unlocked innovative possibilities for genetic screens in model organisms and human cells. This article delves into the current state-of-the-art for RNAi screening and stresses the significance of well-designed assays and sophisticated analytical approaches for large-scale screening experiments. From high-throughput screens using simplified homogeneous assays to microscopy and whole-animal experiments, the success of vast RNAi surveys hinges on the thoughtful creation of phenotypic assays and their interpretation within a meaningful biological context, much like traditional genetic screens in the past.

title: Computer assisted learning in undergraduate medical education.
text:
It is widely acknowledged that the education of undergraduate medical students can be significantly enhanced through the use of computer-assisted learning. The wide range of online options available, as seen in the accompanying figure, are likely to make learning more engaging, effective, and retained. However, it is important to note that this assumption is not necessarily correct, and there are potential pitfalls to consider.
Why invest in computer-assisted learning? While individual lecturers and departments are already introducing computer-based applications, a planned and coordinated approach is preferable to haphazard expansion. Additionally, computer-assisted learning is convenient and flexible, allowing for fewer face-to-face lectures and seminars, and placing fewer geographical and temporal constraints on staff and students. Students at peripheral hospitals or primary care centers may particularly benefit from this approach.
Unique presentation benefits: Computer-based presentations are particularly well-suited to subjects that are visually intensive, detail-oriented, and difficult to conceptualize, such as complex biochemical processes or microscopic images. Moreover, "virtual" cases may reduce the need to use animal or human tissue in learning.
Personalized learning: Computer-assisted learning allows each learner to progress at their preferred pace, repeating, interrupting, and resuming learning as desired. This can be particularly beneficial for weaker students.
Economies of scale: Once an application is set up, the incremental cost of offering it to additional students is relatively small.
Competitive advantage: A "leading edge" virtual campus is likely to attract top students, and the quality of information technology can be used to discriminate between medical schools.
Achieving the ultimate goal of higher education: The goal of higher education is to link people into learning communities. Computer applications, especially the internet and world wide web, are an efficient way of doing this.
Expanding pedagogical horizons: The most controversial argument for computer-assisted learning is that it can expand pedagogical horizons, offering new and innovative ways of teaching and learning. While there are potential pitfalls to consider, the benefits of computer-assisted learning make it an important area of investment for medical education.

title: Combined Impact of Health Behaviours and Mortality in Men and Women: The EPIC-Norfolk Prospective Population Study
text:
BACKGROUNDThere is a large body of evidence suggesting that lifestyle factors have a significant impact on health outcomes, but the cumulative effect of multiple behaviors on mortality in the general population is not as well understood. To address this knowledge gap, we aimed to quantify the joint effect of four health behaviors on mortality in a large, longitudinal study of men and women aged 45-79 living in the general community in the United Kingdom.
METHODS AND FINDINGSWe analyzed the prospective relationship between lifestyle and mortality in a population of 20,244 men and women who were free of cardiovascular disease and cancer at baseline surveys conducted between 1993 and 1997. Participants were awarded one point for each health behavior they engaged in, including current non-smoking, physical activity, moderate alcohol consumption (1-14 units per week), and fruit and vegetable intake of at least five servings per day. The resulting score ranged from 0 to 4. After an average follow-up period of 11 years, we observed 1,987 deaths. We found that the age-sex-body mass index- and social class-adjusted relative risks (95% confidence intervals) for all-cause mortality were 1.39 (1.21-1.60), 1.95 (1.70-2.25), 2.52 (2.13-3.00), and 4.04 (2.95-5.54) for participants who had three, two, one, and zero health behaviors compared to four, respectively. The strongest trends were observed for cardiovascular deaths. In conclusion, our findings suggest that combining four health behaviors is associated with a 4-fold difference in total mortality, equivalent to being 14 years younger in chronological age.

title: Increased Cell Bond Tension Governs Cell Sorting at the Drosophila Anteroposterior Compartment Boundary
text: Animal development has evolved a conserved strategy of dividing proliferating tissues into compartments to control growth and patterning of tissues [1-6]. Signals across compartment boundaries can lead to localized expression of secreted proteins, organizing tissue growth and patterning. The formation and maintenance of these compartments requires sharp and straight interfaces, which stabilize the position of growth-promoting molecules and ensure proper body plan development. However, mechanisms to maintain compartment boundaries in proliferating tissues during cell division are not fully understood. To address this question, we quantitatively analyzed cell morphology and laser ablation of cell bonds near the anteroposterior compartment boundary in developing Drosophila wings. Our findings revealed that cell bond tension is significantly increased along this compartment boundary compared to the rest of the tissue, and that this increase is reduced in the presence of Y-27632, an inhibitor of Rho-kinase. Using simulations with a vertex model, we demonstrated that a 2.5-fold increase in local cell bond tension is sufficient to guide cell rearrangement after cell division and maintain compartment boundaries. These results provide a physical mechanism by which localized increases in Myosin II-dependent cell bond tension can direct cell sorting at compartment boundaries.

title: Plant products as antimicrobial agents.
text: The pursuit of drugs and dietary supplements derived from plants has gained traction in recent years. Ethnopharmacologists, botanists, microbiologists, and natural-products chemists are scouring the planet in search of phytochemicals and "leads" with potential applications in infectious disease treatment. While approximately 25-50% of current pharmaceuticals originate from plants, none are currently used as antimicrobials. Traditional healers have long relied on plant-based remedies to prevent and cure infectious conditions, and Western medicine is now attempting to replicate these successes. Plants are abundant in a diverse array of secondary metabolites, such as tannins, terpenoids, alkaloids, and flavonoids, which have demonstrated antimicrobial properties in vitro. This review aims to provide an overview of current botanical screening efforts, as well as in vivo studies examining their effectiveness and toxicity. The structure and antimicrobial properties of phytochemicals will also be explored. Given the increasing popularity of unregulated botanical preparations and their widespread use by the public, clinicians must consider the potential consequences of patients self-medicating with these products.

title: Nature, Nurture, or Chance: Stochastic Gene Expression and Its Consequences
text: Gene expression is inherently probabilistic, with random fluctuations in transcription and translation resulting in cell-to-cell variations in mRNA and protein levels. This variability persists across a wide range of organisms, from microorganisms to multicellular animals, and is influenced by both the physical parameters that govern gene expression and the structure of the gene network. Stochastic gene expression has far-reaching consequences for cellular function, with benefits in certain situations, such as the stress response, metabolism, development, the cell cycle, circadian rhythms, and aging, and detrimental effects in others.

title: Nuclear Hormone Receptor NHR-49 Controls Fat Consumption and Fatty Acid Composition in C. elegans
text:
Here is a possible revision of the text:
The nuclear hormone receptors (NHRs) of mammals, including the liver X receptor, farnesoid X receptor, and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), play a crucial role in regulating energy metabolism. As a result, targeting these receptors is a promising approach for treating metabolic disorders such as diabetes and obesity. However, a comprehensive understanding of NHRs' regulatory networks has been hampered by a lack of easily manipulated experimental systems. Our study demonstrates that deleting the NHR gene nhr-49 in Caenorhabditis elegans leads to worms with increased fat content and shorter lifespan. Through a quantitative RT-PCR screen, we identified 13 genes involved in energy metabolism that are influenced by nhr-49. We found that nhr-49 acts as a key regulator of fat metabolism by modulating pathways that control fat consumption and fatty acid saturation. Notably, we discovered that the two phenotypes of the nhr-49 knockout are distinct and separable, with the high-fat phenotype resulting from reduced expression of enzymes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, and the shortened adult life span due to impaired expression of a stearoyl-CoA desaturase. Although nhr-49 shares sequence similarity with the mammalian hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 receptor, its biological activities are most similar to those of the mammalian PPARs, indicating an evolutionarily conserved role for NHRs in regulating fat metabolism. Our findings in C. elegans provide novel insights into how NHR regulatory networks are coordinated to govern fat metabolism.

title: Folate and vitamin B6 from diet and supplements in relation to risk of coronary heart disease among women.
text: High levels of homocysteine in the blood, known as hyperhomocysteinemia, have been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. However, there is limited information available on the exact relationship between folate and vitamin B6 intake and the incidence of nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI) and fatal coronary heart disease (CHD). To investigate this association, a large-scale prospective cohort study was conducted among a group of 80,822 female participants free of cardiovascular disease, cancer, hypercholesterolemia, or diabetes. Participants completed a detailed food frequency questionnaire to determine their usual intake of folate and vitamin B6, and the incidence of nonfatal MI and fatal CHD was monitored over a period of 14 years. The study found that those with higher intakes of folate and vitamin B6 had a significantly lower risk of CHD compared to those with lower intakes, even after controlling for various cardiovascular risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, alcohol consumption, fiber intake, vitamin E intake, and saturated, polyunsaturated, and trans fat intake. Specifically, the relative risks of CHD were found to be 0.69 and 0.67, respectively, for folate and vitamin B6 intake. Additionally, the study revealed that women who regularly consumed multiple vitamins had a lower risk of CHD compared to those who did not, and that the inverse association between a high-folate diet and CHD was strongest among women who consumed up to 1 alcoholic beverage per day or more than 1 drink per day. These findings suggest that intake of folate and vitamin B6 above the current recommended dietary allowance may play a crucial role in the primary prevention of CHD among women.

title: Control of oocyte meiotic maturation and fertilization.
text: Sexual reproduction relies on meiosis to produce haploid gamete nuclei, which then fuse after fertilization to form a diploid zygote. In most animal species, oocytes enter a state of dormancy during meiotic prophase, and undergo meiotic maturation in response to intercellular signaling. This process involves a critical transition between diakinesis and metaphase of meiosis I, accompanied by changes in the nuclear envelope, cytoskeleton rearrangement, and meiotic spindle assembly. In essence, meiotic maturation is essential for meiosis and prepares the oocyte for fertilization. In the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, the processes of meiotic maturation, ovulation, and fertilization are synchronized: sperm use the major sperm protein as a hormone to trigger oocyte meiotic maturation, and the maturing oocyte in turn signals its own ovulation, facilitating fertilization. This chapter highlights recent advances in understanding the signaling pathways and gametic interactions required for fertilization.

title: From Cell Differentiation to Cell Collectives: Bacillus subtilis Uses Division of Labor to Migrate
text:
The structure of cells, arising from their interactions, can lead to collective properties that are adaptive and allow cells to tackle environmental challenges more effectively than they could alone. One challenge that is particularly important for microorganisms is migration. In this study, we demonstrate how the division of labor between two distinct cell types, which emerge during Bacillus subtilis sliding motility, drives flagellum-independent migration.
Cell clusters organize themselves into neatly aligned cell chains that form filamentous loops at the edge of the colony. Using time-lapse microscopy, we showed that these loops move by pushing themselves away from the colony. The formation of these bundles relies critically on the harmonious interaction between surfactin-producing and matrix-producing cells. We propose that surfactin-producing cells reduce friction between cells and their substrate, allowing matrix-producing cells to form bundles more efficiently. The folding properties of these bundles determine the rate of colony expansion.
Our study highlights how the simple arrangement of cells within a community can lead to a remarkable ecological advantage. This underlying mechanism is crucial to understanding the diverse origins of multicellularity.

title: Tissue-resident macrophages self-maintain locally throughout adult life with minimal contribution from circulating monocytes.
text: Contrary to previous belief, evidence gathered over time indicates that resident tissue macrophages in the steady state are maintained locally, rather than derived from monocytes. Using parabiosis and fate-mapping techniques, we found that monocytes do not significantly contribute to tissue macrophages in the steady state. Instead, we found that after depletion of lung macrophages, the majority of repopulation occurred through stochastic cellular proliferation in situ, which was dependent on macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-Csf) and granulocyte macrophage (GM)-CSF. Additionally, we discovered that after bone marrow transplantation, host macrophages retained the capacity to expand when the development of donor macrophages was compromised. This expansion of host macrophages was functional and prevented the development of alveolar proteinosis in mice transplanted with GM-Csf-receptor-deficient progenitors. These results lead us to conclude that tissue-resident macrophages and circulating monocytes should be classified as distinct mononuclear phagocyte lineages that are maintained independently in the steady state.

title: Registration and real-time visualization of transcranial magnetic stimulation with 3-D MR images
text:
The following is a rewritten version of the given text with improved readability and clarity:
This paper presents a method for real-time registration and visualization of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) results on the corresponding anatomical locations in magnetic resonance images (MRIs) of the brain. The method involves three main steps:
1. Digitization of the patient's scalp in physical space using a magnetic-field digitizer, following a specific pattern.
2. A registration process that minimizes the distance between the digitized points and a segmented scalp surface extracted from the MRI. This allows the physician to track the movement of the coil in real-time and adjust its position to the desired anatomical location.
3. Amplitude of motor evoked potentials is projected onto the segmented brain to create functional brain maps. The registration process achieves subpixel accuracy in a simulation study, with a point-to-surface root-mean-square error of 1.17 ± 0.38 mm in a 24-subject study.

title: Enzymatic targeting of the stroma ablates physical barriers to treatment of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDAs) are characterized by a robust inflammatory response. We found that this response generates extremely high interstitial fluid pressures (IFPs) that exceed previously measured or theorized levels for solid tumors. These high pressures can lead to vascular collapse, significantly impeding the perfusion, diffusion, and convection of small molecule therapeutics. We discovered that hyaluronan, also known as hyaluronic acid (HA), is the primary component responsible for these barriers. By using an enzymatic agent to remove stromal HA in autochthonous murine PDA, we were able to normalize IFP and re-expand the microvasculature. When combined with the standard chemotherapeutic, gemcitabine, this treatment permanently alters the tumor microenvironment and consistently achieves objective tumor responses, resulting in a significant increase in overall survival.

title: Circulating adiponectin, leptin and adiponectin-leptin ratio and endometrial cancer risk: Evidence from a meta-analysis of epidemiologic studies.
text: In this meta-analysis, we investigated the associations between circulating adiponectin, leptin, and adiponectin-leptin (A/L) ratio and endometrial cancer risk by pooling data from 13 studies including 1,963 endometrial cancer cases and 3,503 noncases. We used random-effects models to estimate summary odds ratios (SOR) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We found that compared to individuals with low concentrations of adiponectin, leptin, and A/L ratio, those with high concentrations had a significantly reduced risk of endometrial cancer (SOR = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.34-0.65, I(2) = 63.7%; SOR = 2.19, 95% CI: 1.44-3.31, I(2) = 64.2%; and SOR = 0.45, 95% CI: 0.24-0.86, I(2) = 90.1%, respectively). Additionally, we found that a 18% reduction in risk occurred for each 5 μg/mL increment in circulating adiponectin concentrations (SOR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.74-0.90, I(2) = 49%, n = 8). Stratifying by study characteristics and whether these studies considered or adjusted for potential confounders, the findings were robust. We did not observe any evidence of publication bias. In conclusion, our findings suggest that elevated circulating adiponectin and A/L ratio, or decreased leptin levels, are associated with a reduced risk of endometrial cancer. Further prospective studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

title: CDE-1 Affects Chromosome Segregation through Uridylation of CSR-1-Bound siRNAs
text: We have investigated the function of a germline-specific nucleotidyltransferase protein, CDE-1, in the context of RNA interference (RNAi) and chromosome segregation in Caenorhabditis elegans. Our findings indicate that CDE-1 localizes specifically to mitotic chromosomes in embryos, a phenomenon that requires the interaction with the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase EGO-1 and the Argonaute protein CSR-1. We demonstrate that CDE-1 is crucial for the uridylation of CSR-1-bound small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), and that in the absence of CDE-1, these siRNAs accumulate to inappropriate levels, leading to defects in both meiotic and mitotic chromosome segregation. Increased levels of siRNAs are associated with aberrant gene silencing, which is likely attributable to the inappropriate loading of CSR-1 siRNAs into other Argonaute proteins. Based on our data, we propose a model in which CDE-1 regulates specific EGO-1-generated siRNAs within the CSR-1-mediated, chromosome-associated RNAi pathway, thereby differentiating it from other endogenous RNAi pathways. The conservation of CDE-1 across species suggests that similar sorting mechanisms may operate in other organisms, including mammals.

title: Localized diacylglycerol drives the polarization of the microtubule-organizing center in T cells
text: The repositioning of the T cell microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) toward the presenting antigen cell enables the directed secretion of cytokines and lytic factors. By using single-cell photoactivation of the T cell antigen receptor, we demonstrate that MTOC polarization is driven by the local buildup of diacylglycerol (DAG). MTOC reorientation is closely followed by the production of DAG and then by the recruitment of the microtubule motor protein dynein. Halting the production of DAG or disrupting its localization hinders MTOC recruitment. Localized DAG accumulation is also essential for cytotoxic T cell-mediated killing. Moreover, photoactivation of DAG itself can induce a temporary MTOC polarization. Our data identify a DAG-dependent pathway that signals via dynein to control microtubule polarity in T cells.

title: Dual roles of plcA in Listeria monocytogenes pathogenesis.
text: The plcA gene of Listeria monocytogenes encodes a secreted phosphatidylinositol-specific phospholipase C (Pl-PLC).
