Recent research has shown that mutations within the plcA gene can lead to reduced virulence in mice and various effects when examined in tissue culture models of infection. Genetic analysis has revealed that many of these effects are due to the loss of readthrough transcription from plcA into the downstream gene prfA, which encodes a crucial transcription factor involved in the regulation of numerous L. monocytogenes virulence genes. Constructing an in-frame deletion within plcA did not affect the expression of prfA, allowing for a direct assignment of the role of Pl-PLC in pathogenesis. Pl-PLC was found to play a significant role in enabling L. monocytogenes to evade phagocytosis by primary murine macrophages. Intriguingly, this defect primarily manifested in the liver of infected mice, but not in the spleen.

title: Fine-tuning in regulation of Clp protein content in Bacillus subtilis.
text: Clp-mediated proteolysis in Bacillus subtilis appears to play a significant role, particularly under stressful conditions. Calibrated Western blot analyses were used to estimate the approximate number of heat-inducible Clp proteins within a single cell. These numbers suggest that different Clp ATPases do not compete for the proteolytic subunit ClpP. Coimmunoprecipitation experiments revealed specific interactions between ClpX, ClpP, ClpC, and ClpE. Notably, ClpE and ClpX are rapidly degraded in wild-type cells during prolonged heat stress, while remaining stable in a clpP mutant, indicating ClpP-dependent degradation. Furthermore, ClpCP seemed to be involved in the degradation of the short-lived ClpE ATPase, suggesting a negative "autoregulatory" circuit for this particular Clp ATPase at the posttranslational level. The half-life of stress-inducible clp mRNAs during exponential growth and heat shock was analyzed to reveal precise regulation of Clp protein synthesis at the posttranscriptional level to meet the needs of B. subtilis.

title: A C-Type Lectin Collaborates with a CD45 Phosphatase Homolog to Facilitate West Nile Virus Infection of Mosquitoes
text: West Nile virus (WNV) is the most prevalent arthropod-borne flavivirus in the United States, yet the molecular mechanisms behind its transmission from mosquitoes to humans remain unclear. Our findings reveal that an Aedes aegypti C-type lectin, called mosGCTL-1, plays a crucial role in WNV infection. We show that mosGCTL-1 is induced by WNV, interacts with the virus in a calcium-dependent manner, and facilitates infection in both in vivo and in vitro experiments. Moreover, we identify a mosquito homolog of human CD45, called mosPTP-1, which recruits mosGCTL-1 to enable viral attachment to cells and enhance viral entry. In vivo experiments demonstrate that mosGCTL-1 and mosPTP-1 work together to facilitate WNV infection in mosquitoes. Similar to Aedes aegypti, we observed these genes' participation in WNV infection in another natural vector of the virus, Culex quinquefasciatus. In vivo experiments also revealed that blocking WNV infection in mosquitoes using mosGCTL-1 antibodies during the blood-feeding process was effective. Our findings provide a molecular understanding of the interactions between flaviviruses and their arthropod vectors, which may lead to strategies to control viral dissemination in nature.

title: Use of human embryonic stem cells to model pediatric gliomas with H3.3K27M histone mutation
text: Over 70% of diffuse intrinsic pediatric gliomas, a highly aggressive brainstem tumor, harbor heterozygous mutations that result in a K27M amino acid substitution (where methionine replaces lysine 27) in the tail of histone H3.3. The role of this mutation in tumorigenesis is still not fully understood. To investigate, we employed a human embryonic stem cell model. Our findings reveal that H3.3K27M expression collaborates with p53 loss and PDGFRA activation in neural progenitor cells derived from human embryonic stem cells, leading to neoplastic transformation. Through genome-wide analysis, we discovered that the modified precursors are reset to a more primitive stem cell state, marked by extensive modifications to histone marks at key regulatory genes. Subsequently, we identified a compound that targets the protein menin as an inhibitor of tumor cell growth both in vitro and in vivo.

title: Basis for avid homologous DNA strand exchange by human Rad51 and RPA.
text: Human Rad51 (hRad51), a protein that belongs to a conserved family of general recombinases, has been shown to exhibit a remarkable ability to facilitate the alignment and exchange of homologous DNA molecules. By promoting the efficient strand exchange of paired molecules over long distances (up to 5.4 kilobases), hRad51 plays a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of genomic DNA. Interestingly, the efficiency of homologous DNA pairing and strand exchange is found to be strongly dependent on the presence of a heterotrimeric single-stranded DNA binding factor, hRPA, and optimal conditions that reduce the interactions between the homologous duplex and the hRad51-single-stranded DNA nucleoprotein filament. These findings suggest that the homologous DNA pairing and strand exchange system described may be valuable for elucidating the mechanism of hRad51 function and identifying its functional interactions with other recombination factors.

title: A multiple indicators multiple causes model of late-life depression in Latin American countries
text:
The Euro-D depression scale consists of symptom clusters that may vary in their impact on older adults due to differences in demographic and cognitive characteristics. This theory requires further investigation, and the role of measurement bias on the findings needs to be established.
Methodology:
A sample of 10,405 community-dwelling older adults from six Latin American countries were examined using a Multiple Indicators Multiple Causes (MIMIC) model to investigate measurement bias and the relationship between Euro-D symptom clusters and background variables.
Results:
The Euro-D factor structure was consistently supported across all countries, with a two-dimensional structure of affective suffering and motivation disturbance. Although measurement invariance could not be assumed across countries, the measurement bias was minor. Both Euro-D factors were found to be age-independent but gender-related, with larger differences observed for affective suffering than for motivation disturbance. Additionally, the impact of verbal fluency impairment was more pronounced on motivation disturbance.
Limitation:
The study's analytical methods could only examine indicator threshold invariance. The generalization of the findings to clinical populations needs to be examined. A wider range of cognitive tests is required. The study did not investigate the additional factors that could have contributed to the variation in Euro-D scores across countries, which was beyond the scope of the study.
Conclusion:
The current study provides evidence for the construct validity of Euro-D and the possible differential association of depression symptom clusters with gender and verbal fluency in older adults. An understanding of the heterogeneity of late-life depression may have clinical implications for the diagnosis and treatment of depression in old age.

title: Microvesicles derived from human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells stimulated by hypoxia promote angiogenesis both in vitro and in vivo.
text: Although mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been increasingly investigated as a potential treatment for various diseases, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, human umbilical cord (UC)-derived MSCs were exposed to hypoxic conditions, and the microvesicles (MVs) in the supernatant were collected, observed under an electron microscope, and identified using flow cytometry. The results indicated that upon hypoxic stimulation, MSCs released a significant amount of MVs, which were approximately 100 nm in diameter. The MVs were found to be similar in phenotype to the parent MSCs, with the exception of a negative reaction to the platelet-derived growth factor receptor. Using a DiI-labeling assay, it was observed that MSC-MVs could be internalized into human UC endothelial cells (UC-ECs) within 8 hours of addition to the culture medium. Additionally, using carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester labeling and MTT assays, it was found that MSC-MVs promoted the proliferation of UC-ECs in a dose-dependent manner. Moreover, MVs were able to enhance in vitro capillary network formation of UC-ECs in a Matrigel matrix. In a rat hindlimb ischemia model, both MSCs and MSC-MVs were shown to significantly improve blood flow recovery compared to the control medium (P<0.0001), as assessed by laser Doppler imaging analysis. These findings suggest that MV release is one of the primary mechanisms underlying the success of MSC therapy by promoting angiogenesis.

title: Evaluation of oxidative status and depression-like responses in Brown Norway rats with acute myeloid leukemia
text: A recent study has shown that leukemia in rats is associated with increased oxidative stress, which may play a role in the development of depression in cancer patients. To investigate this further, researchers induced acute myeloid leukemia in Brown Norway rats and evaluated their behavior in a forced swim test. They also measured various antioxidant parameters, such as glutathione content and ferritin mRNA expression, in the rats' spleen, brain cortex, and hippocampus. The study found that leukemic rats showed signs of oxidative stress and reduced antioxidant activity in their brain tissues, which was associated with alterations in the expression of N-methyl-D-aspartic (NMDA) receptors. Specifically, there was an increase in the potency of the neurotransmitter glycine to bind to NMDA receptors in the leukemic rats, which is a hallmark of depression. Additionally, the study found that the 5-HT2A receptors were upregulated in the cortex of leukemic rats, which is also a feature of depression. These findings suggest that oxidative stress may play a role in the development of depression in cancer patients, and that disturbances in the antioxidant system and NMDA receptors may be involved in this process.

title: Distinct roles for DNA-PK, ATM and ATR in RPA phosphorylation and checkpoint activation in response to replication stress
text: DNA damage encountered by DNA replication forks poses the risk of genome instability, a precursor to cancer development. Damage checkpoint systems halt cell cycle progression, prompt repair, and induce programmed cell death in cases of severe damage. These checkpoints are crucial components of the DNA damage response network, actively suppressing tumor growth. DNA damage and disruptions to replication machinery lead to the accumulation of single-stranded DNA, which then triggers the activation of Ataxia Telangiectasia and Rad3 Related (ATR) kinase and the phosphorylation of the RPA32 subunit of Replication Protein A. This leads to the activation of Chk1 and an arrest in the cell cycle. DNA-dependent Protein Kinase Catalytic Subunit (DNA-PKcs), a kinase related to ATM and ATR, has well-documented functions in DNA double-strand break repair but poorly understood roles in replication stress-induced RPA phosphorylation. Our findings demonstrate that DNA-PKcs mutant cells fail to arrest replication following stress, and mutations in RPA32 phosphorylation sites targeted by DNA-PKcs increase the proportion of cells in mitosis, impair ATR signaling to Chk1 and result in a G2/M arrest defect. Inhibition of ATR and DNA-PK (but not ATM) mimics the defects observed in cells expressing mutant RPA32. Cells expressing mutant RPA32 or DNA-PKcs exhibit sustained H2AX phosphorylation in response to replication stress that persists in cells entering mitosis, indicating improper mitotic entry with unrepaired damage.

title: The essential Schizosaccharomyces pombe Pfh1 DNA helicase promotes fork movement past G-quadruplex motifs to prevent DNA damage
text:
Background: G-quadruplexes (G4s) are stable, non-canonical DNA secondary structures composed of stacked arrays of four guanines, held together by Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds. G4 motifs, found throughout bacterial and eukaryotic genomes, can be isolated in vitro. The budding yeast Pif1 DNA helicase, as well as Pif1 family helicases from bacteria, robustly unwind G4 structures in vitro and suppress G4-induced DNA damage in vivo.
Results: We investigated the genomic distribution and evolutionary conservation of G4 motifs in four fission yeast species and examined the relationship between G4 motifs and Pfh1, the sole S. pombe Pif1 family helicase. By employing chromatin immunoprecipitation combined with deep sequencing, we discovered that many G4 motifs in the S. pombe genome were associated with Pfh1. Additionally, cells depleted of Pfh1 displayed increased fork pausing and DNA damage near G4 motifs, as indicated by high DNA polymerase occupancy and phosphorylated histone H2A levels, respectively. Notably, G4 motifs were found underrepresented in genes, but Pfh1-associated G4 motifs were more frequently located on the transcribed strand of highly transcribed genes, suggesting a role for Pfh1 in replication or transcription at these sites.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that in the absence of functional Pfh1, unresolved G4 structures can cause fork pausing and DNA damage, which are reminiscent of those associated with human tumors. These findings highlight the importance of Pfh1 in maintaining genomic stability and suggest that dysregulation of Pfh1 may contribute to the development of cancer.

title: Wnt7a signaling promotes dendritic spine growth and synaptic strength through Ca²⁺/Calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II.
text: Maintaining a delicate balance between excitatory and inhibitory synapses is essential for proper brain function. Wnt proteins promote synapse formation by enhancing synaptic assembly. However, it remains unclear whether Wnt signaling differentially regulates the formation of excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Our study reveals that Wnt7a preferentially stimulates the formation of excitatory synapses. In hippocampal neurons, Wnt7a increases the number of excitatory synapses while leaving inhibitory synapses unaltered. We find that Wnt7a or the post-synaptic expression of Dishevelled-1 (Dvl1), a key component of the Wnt signaling pathway, enhances the frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) but not miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs). Wnt7a also increases the density and maturity of dendritic spines, and this effect is lost when Wnt7a-Dvl1 is deficient. Using a postsynaptic reporter for Ca(2+)/Calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) activity, we show that Wnt7a rapidly activates CaMKII in spines. Importantly, inhibition of CaMKII abolishes the effects of Wnt7a on spine growth and excitatory synaptic strength. These findings indicate that Wnt7a signaling is essential for regulating spine growth and synaptic strength through the local activation of CaMKII at dendritic spines. Therefore, disruptions in Wnt7a signaling may contribute to neurological disorders characterized by impaired excitatory signaling.

title: Bitter taste receptors and α-gustducin regulate the secretion of ghrelin with functional effects on food intake and gastric emptying.
text:
The study aimed to investigate the relationship between bitter taste receptors (T2Rs) and ghrelin secretion in the stomach. Ghrelin is a hunger hormone with gastroprokinetic properties, but the factors controlling its secretion are unknown. T2Rs and gustatory G proteins, including α-gustducin and α-transducin, are expressed in the gut and are involved in the chemosensation of nutrients. The study used mouse models to investigate whether T2R-agonists affect ghrelin release and food intake.
The stomach contains two ghrelin cell populations: cells containing octanoyl and desoctanoyl ghrelin, which colocalized with α-gustducin and α-transducin, and cells staining for desoctanoyl ghrelin. The study found that gavage of T2R-agonists increased plasma octanoyl ghrelin levels in wild-type (WT) mice, but the effect was partially blunted in gustaton knockout (gust(-/())) mice. Intragastric administration of T2R-agonists increased food intake during the first 30 min in WT mice but not in gust(-/-) and ghrelin receptor knockout (GRKO) mice. This increase was accompanied by an increase in the mRNA expression of agouti-related peptide in the hypothalamus of WT mice but not in gust(-/-) mice. The temporary increase in food intake was followed by a prolonged decrease (next 4 h), which correlated with an inhibition of gastric emptying. The delay in emptying, which was partially counteracted by ghrelin, was not mediated by cholecystokinin and GLP-1 but involved a direct inhibitory effect of T2R-agonists on gastric contractility.
The study provides functional evidence that activation of bitter taste receptors stimulates ghrelin secretion. This discovery may lead to novel therapeutic applications for the treatment of weight and gastrointestinal motility disorders by modulating endogenous ghrelin levels through the activation of T2Rs by tastants. In summary, the study demonstrates that T2Rs play a critical role in regulating ghrelin secretion and food intake, providing a new perspective on the complex interplay between taste and gut hormones in the regulation of appetite and gastrointestinal function.

title: Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors regulate growth of human glioblastoma via Akt activation.
text: New evidence suggests that glioblastoma cells release and exploit glutamate to promote their own growth and migration through autocrine or paracrine loops involving calcium-permeable AMPA-type glutamate receptors. Our findings reveal that calcium signaling through AMPA receptors controls the proliferation and motility of glioblastoma cells by activating Akt. Specifically, calcium influx through phosphorylated Akt at Ser-473 enhances cell growth and mobility. In contrast, introduction of a dominant-negative form of Akt inhibits cell proliferation and migration, while the delivery of a constitutively active form of Akt protects tumor cells from apoptosis induced by the conversion of calcium-permeable AMPA receptors to impermeable receptors. These results indicate that Akt functions as an downstream effector of calcium signaling mediated by AMPA receptors in glioblastoma cells, and that the activation of the glutamate-AMPA receptor-Akt pathway may contribute to the aggressive and invasive nature of these tumors. This novel pathway presents a potential new therapeutic target for the treatment of glioblastoma.

title: The Extracellular Surface of the GLP-1 Receptor Is a Molecular Trigger for Biased Agonism
text: Ligand-directed signal bias offers tremendous potential for manipulating molecular events, with the promise of creating safer and more effective therapeutics. Key to unlocking this potential is a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying ligand binding and intracellular signaling. Activation of class B G protein-coupled receptors, for instance, is facilitated by the interaction between the peptide N terminus and the receptor core. By employing advanced analytical techniques that allow us to isolate and study the distinct effects of ligand binding on pathway-specific signaling, we have gained valuable insights into the initiation of receptor activation and the mechanistic basis for biased agonism. Our findings reveal that peptide agonists can interact with different regions of the receptor extracellular surface to modulate effector coupling and achieve biased signaling, providing a solid foundation for the rational design of biased agonists.

title: A local macrophage chemokine network sustains protective tissue-resident memory CD4 T cells
text: CD8 tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells play a crucial role in local control of viral infections, but the role of CD4 TRM is less clear. To investigate this, we used parabiotic mice to show that a preexisting pool of CD4 TRM cells in the genital mucosa are essential for full protection from a lethal herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2) infection. Using a local network of macrophages, chemokines maintained vaginal CD4 TRM in memory lymphocyte clusters (MLCs), independent of circulating memory T cells. Within these MLCs, CD4 TRM cells were enriched in clones that expanded in response to HSV-2, highlighting the importance of establishing a pool of CD4 TRM for protection against sexually transmitted viruses such as HSV-2. Our findings provide valuable insights into how such a pool of CD4 TRM may be established.

title: Influence of smoking and plasma factors on patency of femoropopliteal vein grafts.
text:
Objective: To determine the effects of smoking, plasma lipids, lipoproteins, apolipoproteins, and fibrinogen on the patency of saphenous vein femoropopliteal bypass grafts at one year.
Design: Prospective study of patients with saphenous vein femoropopliteal bypass grafts enrolled in a multicenter trial.
Setting: Surgical wards, outpatient clinics, and home visits coordinated by two tertiary referral centers in London and Birmingham.
Participants: 157 patients (mean age 66.6 years, SD 8.2) with saphenous vein femoropopliteal bypass grafts, 113 with patent grafts and 44 with occluded grafts one year after bypass.
Main Outcome Measure: Cumulative percentage patency at one year.
Results: The following markers were significantly higher in patients with occluded grafts compared to those with patent grafts: blood carboxyhemoglobin concentration (p < 0.05), plasma thiocyanate concentration (p < 0.01), and plasma concentrations of fibrinogen (p < 0.001) and apolipoproteins AI (p < 0.04) and (a) (p < 0.05). Serum cholesterol concentrations were significantly higher in patients with grafts that remained patent one year after bypass (p < 0.005). Analysis of smoking markers revealed that a quarter of patients (40) were untruthful about quitting smoking. Patency of grafts in smokers was significantly lower at one year by life table analysis compared to non-smokers (63% vs 84%, p < 0.02). Patency was significantly higher by life table analysis in patients with a plasma fibrinogen concentration below the median compared to those with a concentration above (90% vs 57%, p < 0.0002). Unexpectedly, increased plasma low-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentration was significantly associated with improved patency at one year (85% at values above the median compared to 68% at values in the lower half of the range, p < 0.02).
Conclusion: Plasma fibrinogen concentration was the most important variable predicting graft occlusion, followed by smoking markers. A more forceful approach is needed to stop patients from smoking, and therapeutic measures to improve patency of vein grafts should focus on decreasing plasma fibrinogen concentration rather than serum cholesterol concentration.

title: No effect of dietary fat on short-term weight gain in mice treated with atypical antipsychotic drugs
text:
Here is a rewritten version of the text:
Background: Atypical antipsychotic drugs (AAD) are known to induce significant weight gain in female C57BL/6J mice. However, the impact of dietary fat on this effect is unknown. Objectives: To investigate whether a high-fat diet exacerbates the obesigenic effects of AAD in this mouse model. Methods: Female C57BL/6J mice were treated with AAD for 3 weeks and fed either a low-fat or high-fat diet (4.6 vs 15.6% fat by wt). Food intake, body weight, body composition, and serum lipids were measured during treatment with optimized doses of olanzapine, quetiapine, and risperidone. Energy intake and feed efficiency were calculated. Group differences in change were analyzed via repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA). Serum lipid concentrations, energy intake, and feed efficiency were compared using two-way ANOVA. Results: AAD-treated mice gained significantly more weight than controls after 3 weeks (P<0.001). Treatment and diet had significant effects on food intake and energy intake over time (P<0.001). AAD-treated mice had significantly higher feed efficiency than controls (P<0.05), although there was no significant interaction between treatment and diet (P=0.65). Risperidone low-fat mice gained significantly more absolute fat mass than placebo low-fat mice (P<0.05). All treatment groups, except quetiapine low-fat and olanzapine high-fat, gained significantly more absolute lean mass than placebo controls (P<0.05). Cholesterol levels were significantly lower in quetiapine and risperidone than placebo (P<0.05). Risperidone low-fat mice had significantly higher triglyceride levels than placebo and risperidone high-fat mice (P<0.05). Conclusions: The results of this study suggest that a high-fat diet does not increase AAD-induced body weight gain in female mice during a 3-week treatment period.

title: The role of free radicals in cold injuries.
text: Cold injury is tissue trauma caused by exposure to cold temperatures, even for a brief period in a severely cold and windy environment. When frozen tissue is rewarmed, it is associated with the generation of free oxygen radicals, which can lead to cellular damage. The current understanding of the mechanism of action of free oxygen radicals during rewarming is discussed in this review. Decreased energy stores during ischaemia result in the accumulation of adenine nucleotides and the liberation of free fatty acids, which can lead to the breakdown of lipid membranes. Upon rewarming, these fatty acids are metabolized through cyclo-oxygenase and adenine nucleotides are metabolized through the xanthine oxidase pathway, potentially contributing to the formation of free oxygen radicals. Leukocytes may also play a significant role in the pathogenesis of cold injury. Oxygen radical scavengers, such as superoxide dismutase and catalase, can help reduce cold-induced injury, but their effectiveness is limited due to their inability to easily cross the plasma membrane. Liquid soluble antioxidants are likely to be more effective due to their presence in membranes where peroxidative reactions can be arrested.

title: SIRT1 deacetylase in SF1 neurons protects against metabolic imbalance.
text: Chronic consumption of high-calorie diets leads to obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), which affect a substantial portion of the global population. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms that protect against diet-induced metabolic disruption is of the utmost medical significance. In this study, we found that mice lacking the protein SIRT1 in certain neurons are more susceptible to weight gain and T2DM due to their inability to efficiently burn energy. Conversely, mice with an increased amount of SIRT1 in these neurons are less likely to develop obesity and insulin resistance, likely due to their enhanced energy expenditure and increased insulin sensitivity in muscle tissue. Our findings demonstrate the protective role of SIRT1 in these neurons against the metabolic imbalances caused by a high-calorie diet.

title: mTOR supports long-term self-renewal and suppresses mesoderm and endoderm activities of human embryonic stem cells.
text: Although the recent discovery of the transcriptional regulatory circuit involving SOX2, NANOG, and OCT4 has shed light on the mechanisms governing human embryonic stem cell (hESC) pluripotency, the intricate signaling networks that control this property remain largely unexplored. We investigate the role of mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), a serine/threonine protein kinase, in regulating hESC long-term undifferentiated growth. Our findings indicate that mTOR plays an essential role in maintaining hESC pluripotency, as inhibition of mTOR function impairs pluripotency, ceases cell proliferation, and enhances mesoderm and endoderm activities in hESCs. At the molecular level, mTOR integrates signals from external pluripotency-promoting factors and represses the transcriptional activities of certain genes, as revealed through genome-wide microarray analysis. Specifically, mTOR suppresses the expression of developmental genes, which is crucial for the maintenance of hESC pluripotency. These findings unveil a novel signaling pathway by which mTOR regulates stem cell fate choices. Our discoveries could contribute to the development of successful strategies for tissue repair and regeneration.

title: Intrinsic genetic characteristics determine tumor-modifying capacity of fibroblasts: matrix metalloproteinase-3 5A/5A genotype enhances breast cancer cell invasion
text: The study investigated the role of stromal fibroblasts in promoting tumor invasion in breast cancer, specifically examining the impact of genetic variations in matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) genes on fibroblast-mediated tumor cell invasion. Primary fibroblasts were isolated from breast cancer patients (n = 13) and non-cancer patients (n = 19), and their ability to promote invasion was measured in in vitro assays. The study found that tumor-derived fibroblasts had higher levels of invasion compared to normal fibroblasts (p = 0.041). The MMP-3 5A/5A genotype was found to contribute to the higher levels of invasion in tumor fibroblasts, with higher levels of MMP-3 release observed in these cells. In contrast, normal fibroblasts did not exhibit higher levels of invasion or enhanced MMP release, suggesting that more complex changes occur in tumor-derived fibroblasts. The study suggests that a high-expressing MMP-3 genotype may promote tumor progression more effectively in women with breast cancer.

title: Hallmarks of Cancer: The Next Generation
text: The hallmarks of cancer constitute six biological capabilities that tumors acquire during their development. These hallmarks provide an organizing principle for understanding the complexities of neoplastic disease. They include sustaining proliferation, evading growth suppressors, resistance to cell death, replicative immortality, angiogenesis, and invasiveness leading to metastasis. Underlying these hallmarks are genome instability, which generates the genetic diversity enabling their acquisition, and inflammation, which supports multiple hallmark functions. In the last decade, conceptual progress has added two emerging hallmarks of potential generality: reprogramming of energy metabolism and evading immune destruction. Tumors also exhibit complexity in terms of the repertoire of recruited, seemingly normal cells that contribute to the acquisition of hallmark traits by creating the "tumor microenvironment." Recognition of the widespread applicability of these concepts will likely impact the development of new cancer treatments.

title: BCR/ABL oncogenic kinase promotes unfaithful repair of the reactive oxygen species-dependent DNA double-strand breaks.
text:
Here is a possible revision of the given text:
The oncogenic BCR/ABL tyrosine kinase in Ph-positive leukemia cells leads to persistent DNA damage through the induction of reactive oxygen species (ROSs). This results in the formation of double-strand breaks (DSBs) in S and G(2)/M cell cycle phases, which are then repaired through homologous recombination repair (HRR) and nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) mechanisms. Interestingly, a higher mutation rate is observed in HRR products derived from BCR/ABL-positive cells compared to normal counterparts. Moreover, exclusive to BCR/ABL cells, large deletions are observed in NHEJ products. Together, these findings suggest a sequential series of events that contribute to genomic instability in Ph-positive leukemias, namely: BCR/ABLactivity --> ROSs --> DNA damage --> DSBs in proliferating cells --> inefficient HRR and NHEJ repair.

title: Cancer risks attributable to low doses of ionizing radiation: assessing what we really know.
text:
High doses of ionizing radiation have severe consequences for human health, including cancer induction. However, the impact of low doses of radiation is less clear-cut and has significant societal implications in areas such as cancer screening, nuclear power, occupational exposure, frequent flying, space exploration, and radiological terrorism. We address two key questions:
Firstly, what is the lowest dose of X- or gamma radiation at which there is sufficient evidence of increased cancer risk in humans? Epidemiological data suggests that this threshold is around 10-50 millisieverts (mSv) for an acute exposure and 50-100 mSv for a prolonged exposure.
Secondly, how can we extrapolate cancer risk estimates to even lower doses? While a linear extrapolation of cancer risks from intermediate to very low doses may currently appear to be the most appropriate approach, supported by experimentally grounded, quantifiable biophysical arguments, it is likely to result in an underestimate of some radiation-induced cancer risks and an overestimate of others.
In summary, while high doses of ionizing radiation have clear deleterious consequences, the risks of low-dose radiation are more complex and have significant societal implications. Addressing these questions can help us better understand and manage the risks associated with low-dose radiation exposure.

title: Laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation for alleviating chronic pelvic pain: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Chronic pelvic pain is a prevalent condition that significantly impacts an individual's quality of life, productivity, and healthcare usage. One potential treatment option for patients with chronic pelvic pain is laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA). In this study, we aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of LUNA in reducing pain and improving quality of life in patients with chronic pelvic pain.
The study was a randomized, controlled trial conducted at 18 hospitals in the UK, involving 487 women with chronic pelvic pain lasting longer than 6 months. Participants were randomly assigned to either LUNA or laparoscopy without pelvic denervation (no LUNA). The primary outcome measures were pain levels, assessed using a visual analogue scale, and health-related quality of life, measured through a generic instrument called EuroQoL EQ-5D and EQ-VAS.
Our findings indicate that after a median follow-up of 69 months, there were no significant differences in pain levels between the LUNA and no LUNA groups. Specifically, there were no differences in the worst pain level, noncyclical pain, dysmenorrhea, or dyspareunia between the two groups. Additionally, no differences were observed between the groups in terms of quality of life.
Overall, our study suggests that LUNA does not result in significant improvements in pain or quality of life compared to laparoscopy without pelvic denervation in patients with chronic pelvic pain. While LUNA may be a viable treatment option for some patients, further research is needed to determine its effectiveness and potential benefits.

title: Identification of bone and liver metastases from breast cancer by measurement of plasma alkaline phosphatase isoenzyme activity.
text: Plasma alkaline phosphatase isoenzyme activities were investigated in patients with breast cancer to diagnose and monitor bone and liver metastases. Our findings revealed that bone alkaline phosphatase activity was elevated in 42% of the 50 patients with radiologically confirmed bone metastases, whereas total alkaline phosphatase activity was increased in only 20% of these patients. Moreover, liver alkaline phosphatase activity was markedly elevated in 48% of the 25 patients with liver metastases, with all patients having concurrent bone metastases. Notably, bone alkaline phosphatase activity was significantly higher in patients with symptomatic bone disease. Isoenzyme determination provided valuable information that would have altered patient management in five of the 20 patients who were monitored serially. While measurement of alkaline phosphatase isoenzyme activity is less sensitive than imaging procedures, it can effectively screen for and detect a sizable proportion of bone and liver metastases, and provide useful objective evidence of their response to treatment.

title: Recommendations on how to ensure the safety and effectiveness of biosimilars in Latin America: a point of view
text: In recent decades, the use of biotechnology-derived medicines has significantly increased. Despite undergoing rigorous characterization and clinical studies to prove their safety and effectiveness, biosimilars are complex molecules that can be affected by small changes in their purification and production process. Regulatory authorities in Latin America have begun to establish standardized pathways for the commercial licensure of biosimilars. To ensure that a biosimilar lives up to its potential in real-world clinical use, a comprehensive post-licensing monitoring system must be put in place. This system is the only way to accurately determine the similarity between the original biologic and its biosimilar. Pharmacovigilance allows regulatory authorities to assess a drug's performance in the marketplace and make informed decisions about its safety and effectiveness. Developing an effective pharmacovigilance system for biological medicines involves several steps and processes. To help policy makers in Latin America address the challenges surrounding the establishment of an effective pharmacovigilance system, the Americas Health Foundation convened a group of experts to discuss the topic and provide recommendations for implementation. The group discussed current challenges and gaps in pharmacovigilance in Latin America, focusing on the major issues associated with the traceability and pharmacovigilance of biosimilars after their approval. The recommendations developed should enable countries to accurately document the safety and performance of a biosimilar as experienced by patients in real-life settings and have a significant impact on the successful implementation of pharmacovigilance of biosimilars throughout the region.

title: Coordinated regulation of sulfur and phospholipid metabolism reflects the importance of methylation in the growth of yeast
text: A yeast strain deficient in Met4p, the primary transcriptional regulator of the sulfur assimilation pathway, cannot produce methionine. This seemingly simple auxotroph fails to grow well in rich media containing excess methionine, resulting in small colonies on yeast extract/peptone/dextrose plates. In contrast, overnight cultures reveal the presence of abundant fast-growing large colonies, suggesting that spontaneous suppressor mutations arise at a high frequency. To identify these suppressor mutations, we employed genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism and standard genetic analyses. The most common suppressors were found to be loss-of-function mutations in OPI1, which encodes a transcriptional repressor involved in phospholipid metabolism. By using a novel system that enables rapid and specific degradation of Met4p, we were able to investigate the dynamic expression of all genes following loss of Met4p. These experiments revealed that Met4p activates genes involved in maintaining S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) levels, while Opi1p represses these genes. SAM serves as a methyl donor in three Opi1p-regulated reactions, leading to the production of the abundant membrane phospholipid, phosphatidylcholine. Our findings indicate that rapidly growing cells require a significant amount of methylation, likely for the biosynthesis of phospholipids.

title: Glossary of reference terms for alternative test methods and their validation.
text: This glossary was created to serve as a comprehensive reference source for professionals working in the field of alternatives to animal testing. It has been compiled from various existing reference documents sourced from different organizations and is intended to provide a central point of reference on alternative testing methods. With the rapid growth of new alternative test methods and approaches over the past few decades, it was recognized that a consolidated, revised, and harmonized collection of terms used in the validation of these methods was necessary. Our glossary aims to provide valuable insights into the validation of novel or updated testing methods consistent with current approaches. Additionally, given the continuous emergence of new developments and technologies, this glossary is designed to be a dynamic and continuously updated resource. An internet-based version of this compilation can be found at <http://altweb.jhsph.edu>, allowing for seamless additions of new material.

title: Combinatorial transcriptional control in blood stem/progenitor cells: genome-wide analysis of ten major transcriptional regulators.
text:
Combinatorial transcription factor (TF) interactions play a crucial role in shaping cellular phenotypes, particularly in stem cell formation, maintenance, and differentiation. In this study, we present the most comprehensive genome-wide binding data set for ten key regulators of blood stem/progenitor cells, including SCL/TAL1, LYL1, LMO2, GATA2, RUNX1, MEIS1, PU.1, ERG, FLI-1, and GFI1B. By performing genome-wide computational analysis of complex binding patterns followed by functional validation, we have uncovered several exciting findings:
First, we identify a novel combinatorial interaction between seven TFs (SCL, LYL1, LMO2, GATA2, RUNX1, ERG, and FLI-1) that had not been previously recognized.
Second, we demonstrate that direct protein-protein interactions between four key regulators (RUNX1, GATA2, SCL, and ERG) play a crucial role in stabilizing complex binding to DNA.
Third, we show that compound heterozygosity for Runx1 and Gata2 results in severe hematopoietic defects in mice at midgestation, highlighting the importance of these interactions in hematopoiesis.
Overall, this study illustrates the power of genome-wide analysis in revealing novel functional insights into the transcriptional control of stem and progenitor cells.

title: Influence of CYP2D6 Polymorphisms on Serum Levels of Tamoxifen Metabolites in Spanish Women with Breast Cancer
text:
BACKGROUND Estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer tumors rely on estrogen signals for growth and proliferation, and can be managed through anti-estrogen therapy with tamoxifen. However, some women with these tumors may have reduced response to tamoxifen due to specific genetic variations. Specifically, common gene variants in the CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 enzymes can impact how the body metabolizes tamoxifen, leading to lower levels of the drug's active metabolites.
METHODS In this study, we examined 90 Spanish women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer who were candidates for tamoxifen therapy. We used the AmpliChip CYP450 test to determine the variability in the CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genes. We then measured the levels of tamoxifen and its metabolites in their plasma using high-performance liquid chromatography.
RESULTS Our results showed that 80% of the patients were extensive metabolizers of the CYP2D6 enzyme, 12.2% were intermediate metabolizers, 2.2% were ultra-rapid metabolizers, and 5.6% were poor metabolizers. The prevalence of the CYP2D6*4 allele, which is associated with reduced metabolism of tamoxifen, was 35%. In addition, we found that the CYP2C19*2 allele, which has been linked to breast cancer outcomes, was present in 15.6% of the studied alleles.
CONCLUSION Our findings suggest that genotyping for the CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genes may be useful in predicting which patients are likely to respond well to tamoxifen therapy. Specifically, women with the CYP2D6*4/*4 genotype had lower levels of the active metabolites of tamoxifen, 4-hydroxy tamoxifen and endoxifen. Therefore, genetic testing may help guide personalized treatment strategies for breast cancer patients.

title: Role of tumor associated macrophages in tumor angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis
text:
Angiogenesis, or the formation of new blood vessels, is crucial for the growth and survival of malignant tumors. Macrophages, which are recruited and reprogrammed by tumor cells, play a significant role in this process by producing and secreting angiogenic factors. These factors, including angiogenin-2, TIE2 ligand, and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A), stimulate the recruitment of TIE2 receptor-expressing monocytes (TEM) into the tumor site, leading to the formation of new blood vessels.
In addition to TEM, tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) also contribute to angiogenesis by producing and secreting various angiogenic factors, including VEGFA, matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), thymidine phosphorylase (TP), urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA), and adrenomedullin (ADM). These factors not only support angiogenesis but also lymphangiogenesis, the formation of new lymphatic vessels. TAM can express LYVE-1, a marker of lymphatic endothelium, and can trans-differentiate into lymphatic endothelial cells, contributing to tumor lymphangiogenesis.
Recently, a new pro-angiogenic factor, YKL-40, was discovered. YKL-40 belongs to a family of mammalian chitinase-like proteins (CLP) that act as cytokines or growth factors. Production of YKL-40 in macrophages is antagonistically regulated by cytokines, and it has been shown to induce angiogenesis in vitro and in animal tumor models. YKL-40-neutralizing monoclonal antibody can block tumor angiogenesis and progression, suggesting that YKL-40 may be a promising target for anti-angiogenic therapy. The roles of YKL-39 and SI-CLP in tumor angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis remain to be investigated.

title: The HIV Treatment Gap: Estimates of the Financial Resources Needed versus Available for Scale-Up of Antiretroviral Therapy in 97 Countries from 2015 to 2020
text:
Background: In 2015, the World Health Organization (WHO) revised its guidelines recommending that all people living with HIV, regardless of CD4 count, initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) upon diagnosis. However, few studies have projected the global resources needed for rapid scale-up of ART. The Health Policy Project conducted modeling analyses for 97 countries to estimate eligibility for and numbers on ART from 2015 to 2020, along with the facility-level financial resources required.
Methods and Findings: Current coverage levels and future need for treatment were based on country-specific epidemiological and demographic data. Simulated annual numbers of individuals on treatment were derived from three scenarios: (1) continuation of countries' current policies of eligibility for ART, (2) universal adoption of aspects of the WHO 2013 eligibility guidelines, and (3) expanded eligibility as per the WHO 2015 guidelines and meeting the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS "90-90-90" ART targets. We modeled uncertainty in the annual resource requirements for antiretroviral drugs, laboratory tests, and facility-level personnel and overhead. We estimate that 25.7 million adults and 1.57 million children could receive ART by 2020 if countries maintain current eligibility plans and increase coverage based on historical rates, which may be ambitious. If countries uniformly adopt aspects of the WHO 2013 guidelines, 26.5 million adults and 1.53 million children could be on ART by 2020. Under the 90-90-90 scenario, 30.4 million adults and 1.68 million children could receive treatment by 2020. The facility-level financial resources needed for scaling up ART in these countries from 2015 to 2020 are estimated to be US$45.8 billion under the current scenario, US$48.7 billion under the WHO 2013 scenario, and US$52.5 billion under the 90-90-90 scenario. After projecting recent external and domestic funding trends, the estimated 6-year financing gap ranges from US$19.8 billion to US$25.0 billion, depending on the costing scenario and the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief contribution level, with the gap for ART commodities alone ranging from US$14.0 to US$16.8 billion.
Limitations: The study is limited by excluding above-facility and other costs essential to ART service delivery and by the availability and quality of country- and region-specific data.
Conclusions: The projected number of people receiving ART across three scenarios suggests that countries are unlikely to meet the 90-90-90 treatment target (81% of people living with HIV on ART by 2020) unless they adopt a test-and-offer approach and increase ART coverage. Our results suggest that future resource needs for ART scale-up are smaller than stated elsewhere but still significantly threaten the sustainability of the global HIV response without additional resource mobilization from domestic or innovative financing sources or efficiency gains. As the world moves towards adopting the WHO 2015 guidelines, advances in technology, including the introduction of lower-cost, highly effective antiretroviral regimens, whose value are assessed here, may prove to be "game changers" that allow more people to be on ART with the resources available.

title: Distinction and relationship between elongation rate and processivity of RNA polymerase II in vivo.
text: A number of proteins and drugs have been linked to the transcriptional elongation process mediated by RNA polymerase II (Pol II), but the factors that govern the elongation rate (nucleotide additions per minute) and processivity (nucleotide additions per initiation event) in live organisms are poorly understood. Our study reveals that a mutation in the Rpb2 subunit of Pol II results in reduced elongation rate and processivity in vivo. Contrary to putative elongation factors tested, none of them affected the elongation rate, but mutations in the THO complex and Spt4 significantly reduced processivity. The drugs 6-azauryracil and mycophenolic acid also reduce both elongation rate and processivity, and this processivity defect is exacerbated by mutations in Spt4, TFIIS, and CTDK-1. Our findings suggest that in vivo, a lower Pol II elongation rate leads to premature dissociation along the chromatin template, and that Pol II processivity can be decoupled from elongation rate.

title: Neurite sprouting and synapse deterioration in the aging Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system.
text: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans serves as a powerful model organism for the investigation of age-related neural degeneration. In contrast to other organisms, where neuronal death and loss of processes are evident, the aging nervous system of C. elegans exhibits subtle morphological changes that are not immediately apparent. However, recent studies have employed cutting-edge imaging techniques, including fluorescence microscopy and electron microscopy (EM), to capture the intricate details of aging neural processes at the molecular level. These investigations have uncovered two primary morphological alterations in the aging C. elegans nervous system: the formation of novel outgrowths from specific neurons, and the deterioration of synaptic integrity. branches arise from the primary dendrite or emerge from somata in a subset of aging neurons, often accompanied by mitochondria. lower levels of insulin signaling occur, preserving the structural integrity of certain ALM and PLM neurons into old age. transcription factors, such as DAF-16/FOXO and heat shock factor transcription factor HSF-1, play a neuroprotective role, with HSF-1 exhibiting cellular autonomy in this capacity. electron microscopic evaluation of synapse-rich regions reveals a striking decline in synaptic vesicle numbers and a reduction of presynaptic density size. Interestingly, animals that remain mobile into old age exhibit fewer synaptic declines than their Debilitated counterparts, suggesting a correlation between synaptic health and locomotor function. These findings underscore the similarity between the aging C. elegans nervous system and the mammalian brain, implying a shared response to aging. Elucidating the intricate mechanisms of neuronal aging in C. elegans may ultimately inform the development of interventions aimed at preserving cognitive function in mammals.

title: Determinants of adolescent physical activity and inactivity patterns.
text:
Although there is recognition of the significance of environmental factors in shaping physical activity patterns, little empirical research has been conducted to investigate their impact on adolescents' physical activity and inactivity levels. This study aimed to investigate the environmental and sociodemographic determinants of physical activity and inactivity among US subpopulations of adolescents.
We define environmental factors as modifiable aspects of the physical environment that directly influence the opportunity to engage in physical activity. Our study examined the correlations between sociodemographic and environmental factors and physical activity and inactivity levels, with the implication that findings could inform societal-level intervention strategies to promote physical activity and reduce inactivity among adolescents.
The study population consisted of nationally representative data from the 1996 National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health, including 17,766 US adolescents enrolled in middle and high schools (3,933 Non-Hispanic Blacks, 3,148 Hispanics, and 1,337 Asians). Physical activity and inactivity levels were assessed through questionnaires that recorded hours of inactivity (TV/video viewing and video/computer games) and times of moderate to vigorous physical activity per week. Outcome variables were categorized into three levels of physical activity (0-2 times/week, 3-4 times/week, and >/=5 times/week) and three levels of inactivity (0-10 hours/week, 11-24 hours/week, and >/=25 hours/week).
Environmental and sociodemographic correlates of physical activity and inactivity served as exposure and control variables, including sex, age, urban residence, participation in school physical education programs, use of community recreation centers, total reported incidents of serious crime in the neighborhood, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, generation of residence in the United States, presence of mother/father in the household, pregnancy status, work status, in-school status, region, and month of interview. Logistic regression models were used to investigate sex and ethnic interactions in relation to environmental and sociodemographic factors to examine the potential impact of physical education and recreation programs and sociodemographic factors on physical activity and inactivity patterns.
Our results showed that moderate to vigorous physical activity was lower and inactivity was higher among Non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic adolescents. Participation in school physical education programs was significantly low among these adolescents and decreased with age. Participation in daily school physical education (PE) program classes and use of a community recreation center were associated with an increased likelihood of engaging in high levels of moderate to vigorous physical activity. Maternal education was inversely associated with high inactivity patterns, while high family income was associated with increased moderate to vigorous physical activity and decreased inactivity. High neighborhood serious crime level was associated with a decreased likelihood of falling in the highest category of moderate to vigorous physical activity.
In conclusion, our findings reveal significant associations between modifiable environmental factors, such as participation in school PE and community recreation programs, and physical activity patterns of adolescents. Despite the substantial impact of participation in school PE programs on physical activity patterns among US adolescents, few adolescents participated in such programs; only 21.3% of all adolescents. These findings can inform intervention strategies aimed at promoting physical activity and reducing inactivity among adolescents, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds.

title: Suicide prevention strategies: a systematic review.
text:
In 2002, it was estimated that approximately 877,000 lives were lost worldwide due to suicide. While some developed nations have implemented national suicide prevention plans, the effectiveness of these plans is often not evaluated. This study aimed to examine the evidence for the effectiveness of specific suicide-prevention interventions and make recommendations for future prevention programs and research.
The study included relevant publications published between 1966 and 2005, which were identified through electronic searches of MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and PsychINFO databases. The studies evaluated interventions in various domains, including education and awareness for the general public and professionals, screening tools for at-risk individuals, treatment of psychiatric disorders, restricting access to lethal means, and responsible media reporting of suicide.
The study found that education of physicians and restricting access to lethal means were effective in preventing suicide. However, other methods, including public education, screening programs, and media education, require more testing. The study also concluded that ascertaining which components of suicide prevention programs are effective in reducing suicide rates is essential to optimize the use of limited resources.
In conclusion, the study emphasizes the need for more evidence-based interventions to prevent suicide. While education of physicians and restricting access to lethal means have shown promise, other approaches require further evaluation to determine their effectiveness. By identifying the most effective interventions, resources can be allocated more efficiently to maximize the impact of suicide prevention efforts.

title: Oxidative damage of DNA confers resistance to cytosolic nuclease TREX1 degradation and potentiates STING-dependent immune sensing.
text: Immune sensing of DNA is crucial for antiviral immunity, but it can also trigger autoimmune diseases such as lupus erythematosus (LE). We have provided evidence for the involvement of a specific DNA modification in the detection of cytosolic DNA. This modification, 8-hydroxyguanosine (8-OHG), is a marker of oxidative damage in DNA and effectively enhances the immune system's recognition of cytosolic DNA. 8-OHG reduces the vulnerability of cytosolic DNA to degradation by the 3' repair exonuclease 1 (TREX1). This process occurs physiologically in pathogen DNA during exposure to lysosomal reactive oxygen species (ROS), as well as in neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) DNA during the oxidative burst. Notably, 8-OHG is also abundant in UV-exposed skin lesions of LE patients, and it colocalizes with type I interferon (IFN). Injecting oxidized DNA into the skin of lupus-prone mice resulted in lesions that closely resemble the lesions found in patients. Therefore, oxidized DNA serves as a prototypic damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) with significant implications for infection, sterile inflammation, and autoimmunity.

title: IL-18 induction of osteopontin mediates cardiac fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction in mice.
text: Osteopontin (OPN), a crucial component of the extracellular matrix, is associated with the fibrotic process during tissue remodeling. OPN and the cytokine interleukin (IL)-18 have been shown to be elevated in a range of human cardiac pathologies. In this study, we investigated the role of IL-18 in regulating cardiac OPN expression and the subsequent interstitial fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction. We found that IL-18 and OPN expression increased parallel to each other in murine models of left ventricular pressure and volume overload. Administering exogenous recombinant (r)IL-18 for two weeks increased cardiac OPN expression, interstitial fibrosis, and diastolic dysfunction. Activating the T helper (Th)1 lymphocyte phenotype with a selective toll-like receptor (TLR)9 agonist led to increased cardiac IL-18 and OPN expression, which was associated with elevated cardiac fibrillar collagen concentrations and interstitial fibrosis resulting in diastolic dysfunction. rIL-18 also induced OPN expression and protein levels in primary cardiac fibroblast cultures. Conditioned media from TLR9-stimulated T lymphocyte cultures induced IL-18 and OPN expression in cardiac fibroblasts, while blocking the IL-18 receptor with a neutralizing antibody abolished the increase in OPN expression. Furthermore, mutating the transcriptional factor interferon regulatory factor (IRF)1 or using IRF1 small interfering RNA (siRNA) resulted in decreased expression of IL-18 and OPN in cardiac fibroblasts. Notably, in mice with pressure overload, IRF1-mutant mice showed a downregulation of IL-18 and OPN expression in cardiac tissue, reduced cardiac fibrotic development, and improved left ventricular function compared to wild-type mice. These findings provide direct evidence that the induction of IL-18 regulates OPN-mediated cardiac fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction.

title: Hematopoietic stem cell: self-renewal versus differentiation.
text: The mammalian blood system, composed of more than 10 distinct mature cell types, is predicated on a single cell type: hematopoietic stem cell (HSC). Within this system, only HSCs possess the dual capabilities of multipotency and self-renewal. Multipotency allows for differentiation into all blood cell types. Self-renewal allows HSCs to regenerate themselves without differentiating. Since mature blood cells (MBCs) have limited lifespans, HSCs must constantly produce more differentiated progenitors while maintaining the HSC pool size throughout an organism's life by exacting a balance between self-renewal and differentiation. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms of HSC self-renewal and differentiation has been a central concern. In this review, we focus on the hierarchical structure of the hematopoietic system, current knowledge of the microenvironment and molecular signals regulating HSC self-renewal and differentiation in adults, and the growing utilization of systemic approaches to comprehend HSC biology.

title: RSEM: accurate transcript quantification from RNA-Seq data with or without a reference genome
text:
Here is a possible reconstruction of the text in a more formal and structured style:
Background:
RNA-Seq is revolutionizing the field of transcriptomics by providing a high-throughput approach for measuring transcript abundance. However, one of the main challenges in transcript quantification from RNA-Seq data is the handling of reads that map to multiple genes or isoforms. This issue is particularly important when there is no available genome sequence for the organism being studied, as it can be difficult to determine which transcripts are isoforms of the same gene.
Results:
We present RSEM, a user-friendly software package for quantifying gene and isoform abundances from single-end or paired-end RNA-Seq data. RSEM outputs abundance estimates, 95% credibility intervals, and visualization files, and can also simulate RNA-Seq data. Unlike other existing tools, RSEM does not require a reference genome, making it particularly useful for quantification with de novo transcriptome assemblies. Our results show that RSEM has superior or comparable performance to quantification methods that rely on a reference genome on both simulated and real data sets.
Conclusions:
RSEM is an accurate and user-friendly software tool for quantifying transcript abundances from RNA-Seq data. Its ability to effectively use ambiguously-mapping reads allows for accurate gene-level abundance estimates with large numbers of short single-end reads. On the other hand, estimates of the relative frequencies of isoforms within single genes may be improved through the use of paired-end reads, depending on the number of possible splice forms for each gene. Our findings provide valuable guidance for the cost-efficient design of quantification experiments with RNA-Seq, which is currently relatively expensive.

title: A synthetic Escherichia coli predator–prey ecosystem
text: We have created a novel synthetic ecosystem featuring two populations of Escherichia coli, which communicate and cooperate through quorum sensing and circuitously regulate each other's survival and gene expression via genetically engineered gene circuits. This system mimics the intricate dynamics of canonical predator-prey relationships, with predatory cells inducing the expression of a lethal protein in the prey, and the prey countering this with the production of an antidote protein in the predator. The resulting populational dynamics can lead to extinction, coexistence, or oscillations between the predator and prey populations, as experimentally demonstrated through long-term cultivation in microchemostats. By integrating experimental observations with a simple mathematical model, we can predictably investigate the complex interactions between interacting populations.

title: Funnel trap for the capture of phlebotomine sand flies (Diptera: Psychodidae) from tree holes.
text: A funnel trap that fits over holes leading into hollow trees was used to capture adult phlebotomine sand flies, Lutzomyia shannoni Dyar, on Ossabaw Island in Chatham County, Georgia. These insects rest in hollow trees during the day and were collected by funnel traps as they emerged from the tree holes at night. The trap is lightweight, durable, inexpensive, waterproof, and selective. In fact, a single investigator was able to capture over 100 healthy L. shannoni flies per night during July and August 1988, when adult flies were abundant on the island.

title: Cystine/glutamate exchange regulates metabotropic glutamate receptor presynaptic inhibition of excitatory transmission and vulnerability to cocaine seeking.
text:
Withdrawal from chronic cocaine reduces extracellular glutamate levels in the nucleus accumbens by decreasing the cystine/glutamate exchange (xc-) mechanism. Activating xc- with N-acetylcysteine restores extracellular glutamate levels and prevents cocaine-induced drug seeking. It was hypothesized that activating xc- increases glutamatergic tone on presynaptic group II metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR2/3) and thereby inhibits excitatory transmission.
In the first experiment, the capacity of glutamate generated from xc- to regulate excitatory transmission via mGluR2/3 was determined. Physiological levels of cystine (100-300 nm) were restored to acute tissue slices from the nucleus accumbens or prefrontal cortex. Cystine increased glutamate efflux and decreased miniature EPSC (mEPSC) and spontaneous EPSC (sEPSC) frequency, as well as evoked EPSC amplitude. These effects of cystine were presynaptic, as there was no change in mEPSC or sEPSC amplitude, and an increase in the evoked EPSC paired-pulse facilitation ratio. The cystine-induced reduction in EPSCs was reversed by blocking either xc- or mGluR2/3.
In the second experiment, blocking mGluR2/3 prevented the ability of N-acetylcystine to inhibit the reinstatement of drug seeking in rats trained to self-administer cocaine. These data demonstrate that non-synaptic glutamate derived from xc- modulates synaptic glutamate release and regulates cocaine-induced drug seeking.

title: Survival analysis: time-dependent effects and time-varying risk factors.
text: In traditional Kaplan-Meier or Cox regression analysis, a baseline risk factor is generally linked to mortality throughout the follow-up period. Nonetheless, changes may occur during follow-up, such as a fluctuating or strengthening of associations over time or a change in the risk factor itself. This paper focuses on the short-term versus long-term effects (time-dependent effects) of a fixed baseline risk factor. An example is provided showing that underweight is a significant risk factor for mortality in dialysis patients, particularly in the short term. In contrast, overweight exhibits a stronger association with mortality in the long term than in the short term. The analysis of how time-varying risk factors (time-dependent risk factors) relate to mortality is also demonstrated by addressing the pitfall of adjusting for sequelae. A clear research question guides the proper analysis of effects over time. Both types of questions, those pertaining to time-dependent effects and those pertaining to time-dependent risk factors, can be addressed with time-dependent Cox regression analysis. It will be shown that using time-dependent risk factors typically means focusing on short-term effects only.

title: Control of interneuron dendritic growth through NRG1/erbB4-mediated kalirin-7 disinhibition
text: Neuregulin 1 (NRG1) is a secreted trophic factor that activates the postsynaptic erbB4 receptor tyrosine kinase. Both NRG1 and erbB4 have been implicated in schizophrenia, but the downstream targets of their interaction are not well characterized. ErbB4 is abundant in interneurons, and NRG1-mediated erbB4 activation has been shown to modulate interneuron function, although the role of NRG1-erbB4 signaling in regulating interneuron dendritic growth is not well understood. Our study reveals that NRG1/erbB4 promote the growth of dendrites in mature interneurons through kalirin, a key regulator of dendritic morphogenesis. Recent research has linked the KALRN gene to schizophrenia, highlighting the potential role of kalirin in disease pathology. Our findings suggest that phosphorylation of kalirin's C terminus is essential for the effects of NRG1-erbB4 signaling on interneuron dendritic growth, and that understanding how these signals modulate dendritic morphogenesis may provide insight into the alterations in cortical circuits that occur in schizophrenia.

title: Use of gene-expression profiling to identify prognostic subclasses in adult acute myeloid leukemia.
text:
Background: In patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the presence or absence of recurrent cytogenetic aberrations serves as a vital tool for determining the most appropriate treatment. However, current classification methods fail to adequately reflect the molecular heterogeneity of the disease, resulting in challenges in treatment stratification, particularly for patients with intermediate-risk AML exhibiting a normal karyotype.
Methods: We employed complementary-DNA microarrays to ascertain the levels of gene expression in peripheral blood samples or bone marrow samples from a total of 116 adult AML patients, including 45 with a normal karyotype. We utilized unsupervised hierarchical clustering analysis to identify distinct molecular subgroups based on their gene expression signatures. Subsequently, we applied a refined supervised learning algorithm to develop a gene-expression-based clinical outcome predictor using a training set comprising samples from 59 patients. The predictive power of the algorithm was validated using an independent validation group comprising the remaining 57 patients.
Results: Unsupervised analysis uncovered novel molecular subtypes of AML, including two prognostically relevant subgroups in AML with a normal karyotype. Using the supervised learning algorithm, we constructed an optimal 133-gene clinical outcome predictor that accurately predicted overall survival among patients in the validation group (P=0.006), including the subgroup of patients with AML with a normal karyotype (P=0.046). In a multivariate analysis, the gene-expression predictor emerged as a strong independent prognostic factor (odds ratio, 8.8; 95% confidence interval, 2.6 to 29.3; P<0.001).
Conclusions: The application of gene-expression profiling enables the molecular classification of adult AML with increased accuracy.

title: Perspectives on public health workforce research.
text: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Office of Workforce and Career Development is dedicated to cultivating a skilled, sustainable, and diverse public health workforce through evidence-based training, career development, and strategic workforce planning with the goal of enhacing population health outcomes. This article examines previous research on public health workforce priorities, identifying eight major themes, and proposes a strategic framework for public health workforce research comprising six functional areas: definition and standards, data, methodology, evaluation, policy, and dissemination and translation. To prioritize the development of an actionable research agenda, we constructed a matrix of key challenges in workforce analysis based on public health workforce categories, conducted extensive reviews of relevant methods and approaches, and explored new tools and approaches for addressing priority areas. Finally, we consider how methods from multiple disciplines of social sciences can inform the development of a research framework for advancing public health workforce research and policy.

title: Gene targeting using zinc finger nucleases
text: The capability to precisely manipulate the genome of mammalian cells has far-reaching implications for both basic and applied research. Gene targeting involves introducing a DNA molecule into a cell, which replaces the corresponding chromosomal segment through homologous recombination, providing a precise method for manipulating the genome. Historically, the application of gene targeting to mammalian cells has been limited by its relatively low efficiency. However, zinc finger nucleases (ZFNs) have shown promise in enhancing the efficiency of gene targeting by introducing DNA double-strand breaks in target genes, which then trigger the cell's endogenous homologous recombination machinery. Recent studies have demonstrated that ZFNs can achieve targeting frequencies of up to 20% in a disease-causing gene in human cells. Future work will be necessary to translate these in vitro findings to in vivo applications and to determine whether ZFNs may unintentionally create genomic instability.

title: relative expression results in real-time
text: Real-time reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) followed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is the most appropriate method for detecting and quantifying messenger RNA (mRNA). It offers exceptionally high sensitivity, consistent reproducibility, and a vast range of quantification. Recently, relative expression analysis has gained popularity, wherein the expression of a target gene is standardized using a non-regulated reference gene. A variety of mathematical equations and models have been developed to calculate an expression ratio based on RT-PCR efficiency and the crossing point deviation of an unknown sample compared to a control. However, these existing equations and models only allow for the determination of a single transcription difference between one control and one sample. To address this limitation, a novel software tool named REST (relative expression software tool) was established. REST compares two groups, with up to 16 data points in a sample and 16 in a control group, for reference, and up to four target genes. The mathematical model used is based on PCR efficiencies and the mean crossing point deviation between the sample and control group. Subsequently, the expression ratio results of the four investigated transcripts are tested for significance using a randomization test. In this article, we explain the development and application of REST and discuss the advantages of relative expression in real-time PCR using REST. The latest version of REST software and instructions for proper use can be downloaded from <http://www.wzw.tum.de/gene-quantification/>.

title: Pain attacks in non-complicated and complicated gallstone disease have a characteristic pattern and are accompanied by dyspepsia in most patients: the results of a prospective study.
text:
Objective: To characterize the pain pattern and associated digestive symptoms in patients with symptomatic gallstone disease.
Methods: A total of 220 patients with symptomatic gallstone disease, including those with complicated disease (acute cholecystitis and common bile duct stones), were interviewed using detailed questionnaires to assess pain patterns and symptoms of indigestion.
Results: The majority of patients (66%) experienced pain in the right upper quadrant (RUQ), including the upper midline epigastrium. Pain was localized in a defined area (90%) with a point of maximum intensity. The pain was referred to the back in 63% of patients, and the mean visual analogue scale (VAS) score was very high (90 mm on a 0-100 scale). A pattern of incipient or low-grade warning pain with a subsequent relatively steady state until subsiding in the same fashion was present in 90% of patients. An urge to walk around was experienced by 71%. Pain attacks occurred mainly at night (77%), lasting for more than one hour and almost never less than half an hour. Sixty-six percent of patients were intolerant to at least one kind of food, but only 48% to fatty foods. Symptoms of functional indigestion, such as gastroesophageal reflux, dyspepsia, or irritable bowel symptoms, were seen in the vast majority of patients in association with attacks.
Conclusion: The pain pattern in gallstone-associated pain follows a characteristic distribution in the majority of patients, with a defined area of maximum intensity and referral to the back. The majority of patients experience functional indigestion, particularly of the reflux type or dyspepsia, in association with attacks.

title: Prevalence and cardiovascular disease correlates of low cardiorespiratory fitness in adolescents and adults.
text: In a recent study, researchers investigated the prevalence of low fitness in the US population aged 12-49 years. They found that approximately 7.5 million adolescents and 8.5 million adults had low fitness, with a higher prevalence among non-Hispanic blacks and Mexican Americans compared to non-Hispanic whites. The study used data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 1999-2002 and found that low fitness was associated with an increased prevalence of CVD risk factors, including overweight or obesity, high total cholesterol levels, and low levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. The study suggests that promoting physical activity and exercise in the US population could help reduce the burden of CVD risk factors.

title: In situ regulation of DC subsets and T cells mediates tumor regression in mice.
text:
Vaccines don't work well for people with cancer that has spread, as the cancer cells need very powerful and sustained attacks from specialized immune cells called cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) to kill the cancer cells and remove them. Recent studies have shown that some types of immune cells called dendritic cells (DCs) can change the way they work to help fight cancer. These DCs can make proteins called cytokines that help CTLs and another type of immune cell called T regulatory (Treg) cells work better.
We tried to find a way to improve the immune response against cancer by controlling the activity of these DCs in mice using special materials that contain proteins and other substances that can be used to activate the DCs. We found that the number of pDCs and CD8(+) DCs, as well as the amount of a protein called interleukin-12, were important factors in determining how well the immune system could fight cancer. When we used these materials to vaccinate the mice, we found that the immune system was able to recognize and kill cancer cells more effectively, and the cancer cells were unable to grow back. This suggests that the local activity of pDCs and CD8(+) DCs at the vaccine site may be important for the success of cancer treatment.
