These results provide a way to design new vaccines that could be more effective at treating cancer.

title: VEGF inhibits tumor cell invasion and mesenchymal transition through a MET/VEGFR2 complex.
text: Inhibition of VEGF signaling in mouse models of glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) and some patients treated with bevacizumab leads to a more invasive phenotype. Here, we show that VEGF directly regulates tumor cell invasion by enhancing the recruitment of protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B) to a MET/VEGFR2 heterocomplex, thus suppressing HGF-dependent MET phosphorylation and tumor cell migration. VEGF blockade, on the other hand, restores and increases MET activity in GBM cells in a hypoxia-independent manner. This results in a program that resembles epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, marked by a switch from T-cadherin to N-cadherin and enhanced mesenchymal features. Inhibition of MET in GBM mouse models blocks the mesenchymal transition and invasion induced by VEGF ablation, resulting in improved survival.

title: Interaction between Oct3/4 and Cdx2 Determines Trophectoderm Differentiation
text: The first cell lineage to differentiate in mammalian embryonic development is called the Trophectoderm (TE), which gives rise to the placenta. Despite being a crucial event in early mammalian development, the molecular mechanisms underlying the differentiation of TE are still poorly understood. Embryonic stem (ES) cells can be induced to differentiate into the TE lineage by repressing the POU-family transcription factor, Oct3/4. We have shown that overexpressing Caudal-related homeobox 2 (Cdx2) can also induce the differentiation of ES cells into TE cells. Interestingly, while Cdx2 is not essential for TE differentiation induced by Oct3/4 repression, it plays a crucial role in the self-renewal of Trophoblast stem (TS) cells. In preimplantation embryos, Cdx2 coexpresses with Oct3/4 and the two proteins form a complex that reciprocally regulates their target genes in ES cells, suggesting that a reciprocal inhibition between lineage-specific transcription factors may be involved in the first differentiation event of mammalian development.

title: SSEA-1 is an enrichment marker for tumor-initiating cells in human glioblastoma.
text: The expression of CD133+ in human glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) cells is believed to enrich for tumor stem cells (TSCs) or tumor-initiating cells (TICs), however, approximately 40% of freshly isolated GBM specimens lack CD133+ tumor cells, casting doubt on the universal applicability of this marker. We demonstrate that stage-specific embryonic antigen 1 (SSEA-1/LeX)+ GBM cells possess the functional characteristics of TSCs/TICs, including: (1) SSEA-1+ cells are highly tumorigenic in vivo compared to SSEA-1- cells; (2) SSEA-1+ cells can give rise to both SSEA-1+ and SSEA-1- cells, forming a cellular hierarchy; and (3) SSEA-1+ cells exhibit self-renewal and multilineage differentiation potential. A distinct subpopulation of SSEA-1+ cells was found in 24 of 24 primary GBMs examined, and most CD133+ tumor cells were also SSEA-1+, suggesting that SSEA-1 may serve as a general TSC/TIC enrichment marker in human GBMs.

title: Temporal regulation of topoisomerase IV activity in E. coli.
text: We isolated a mutant allele of DNAX, which codes for the tau and gamma subunits of the DNA polymerase III holoenzyme, that leads to extreme filamentous cell morphology without affecting cell growth or DNA replication. This phenotype results from a defect in the proper decatenation of daughter chromosomes during rapid cell growth. In contrast to wild-type cells, in which ParC, a subunit of topoisomerase IV, is associated with the replication factory, the mutant cells exhibit a uniform distribution of ParC throughout the nucleoid. The distribution of ParE, the other subunit of topoisomerase IV, remains unaltered. Furthermore, the majority of topoisomerase IV activity in synchronized cell populations is observed later in the cell cycle, when DNA replication is almost complete. These observations suggest that in vivo, the activity of topoisomerase IV may be dependent on the release of ParC from the replication factory.

title: Molecularly targeted therapy based on tumour molecular profiling versus conventional therapy for advanced cancer (SHIVA): a multicentre, open-label, proof-of-concept, randomised, controlled phase 2 trial.
text: The SHIVA trial was a phase 2, open-label, randomized, controlled study that evaluated the efficacy of molecularly targeted agents in patients with advanced cancer who had failed standard-of-care therapy. The study was conducted at eight academic centers in France and included adult patients with any type of metastatic solid tumor, provided they had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1, had accessible disease for biopsy or resection, and had at least one measurable lesion. Molecular profiling was conducted on each patient's tumor to identify potential molecular alterations that could be targeted with one of ten molecularly targeted agents available. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either the matched molecularly targeted agent or treatment at physician's choice. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival in the intention-to-treat population, which was not assessed by independent central review. Safety was evaluated in any patients who received at least one dose of their assigned treatment. The study found that the use of molecularly targeted agents outside their indicated indications did not improve progression-free survival compared to treatment at physician's choice in heavily pretreated patients with cancer. The study suggests that off-label use of molecularly targeted agents should be discouraged, but enrollment in clinical trials should be encouraged to identify predictive biomarkers of efficacy.

title: CRTC2 (TORC2) contributes to the transcriptional response to fasting in the liver but is not required for the maintenance of glucose homeostasis.
text: The liver plays a crucial role in maintaining glucose homeostasis by either promoting glucose storage or production, depending on the body's physiological state. The cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) is a primary regulator of genes involved in coordinating the liver's response to fasting, but the mechanism by which it activates these genes remains unclear. To investigate the role of CREB's cofactor, CRTC2 (CREB-regulated transcription coactivator 2, previously TORC2), we generated mice lacking CRTC2 and examined their hepatic glucose metabolism in vivo. Our findings showed that CRTC2-deficient hepatocytes produced less glucose in response to glucagon, which correlated with decreased CREB binding to key genes involved in gluconeogenesis. However, despite reduced expression of CREB target genes, including PEPCK, G6Pase, and PGC-1alpha, no hypoglycemia was observed in mutant mice. These results provide genetic evidence supporting a role for CRTC2 in the transcriptional response to fasting, but suggest that it plays only a limited role in maintaining glucose homeostasis.

title: Ancient Hybridization and an Irish Origin for the Modern Polar Bear Matriline
text:
Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) are among the species most vulnerable to the rapidly changing Arctic climate, and their survival is a global concern. However, there is a lack of understanding about the evolutionary history of polar bears, which could significantly impact future conservation strategies. In this study, we used a spatially explicit phylogeographic model to estimate the evolutionary dynamics of 242 brown bear and polar bear matrilines sampled across their past and present geographic ranges.
Our results show that the current distribution of these matrilines was shaped by a combination of regional stability and rapid, long-distance dispersal from ice-age refugia. Additionally, we found evidence of multiple instances of hybridization between polar bears and brown bears throughout the Late Pleistocene.
The reconstructed matrilineal history of brown and polar bears has two striking features. First, it is punctuated by dramatic and discrete climate-driven dispersal events. Second, opportunistic mating between these two species as their ranges overlapped has left a strong genetic imprint. In particular, we found evidence of a likely genetic exchange with extinct Irish brown bears, which may have contributed to the origin of the modern polar bear matriline. This suggests that interspecific hybridization may be more common and could be a mechanism by which species deal with marginal habitats during periods of environmental deterioration.

title: FBW7 ubiquitin ligase: a tumour suppressor at the crossroads of cell division, growth and differentiation
text: FBW7 (F-box and WD repeat domain-containing 7) is a crucial component of an evolutionarily conserved SCF-type ubiquitin ligase complex, which plays a vital role in regulating cellular growth and division. FBW7 recognizes and degrades key proto-oncogenes, including MYC, cyclin E, Notch, and JUN, making it a tumor suppressor. The regulatory network of FBW7 is disrupted in many human malignancies, leading to cancer-associated mutations in both FBW7 and its substrates. Loss of FBW7 function causes chromosomal instability and tumorigenesis, further emphasizing its critical role in cancer development. This review focuses on the structural and functional aspects of FBW7 and its significance in cancer biology.

title: Hypoglycemic episodes and risk of dementia in older patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
text:
Although acute hypoglycemia may be linked to cognitive impairment in children with type 1 diabetes, no studies have examined whether hypoglycemia is a risk factor for dementia in older patients with type 2 diabetes. To determine if severe hypoglycemic episodes are associated with an increased risk of dementia in older patients with type 2 diabetes, we conducted a longitudinal cohort study of 16,667 patients with a mean age of 65 years and type 2 diabetes who were members of an integrated healthcare delivery system in Northern California.
We found that at least one episode of hypoglycemia was diagnosed in 8.8% of patients, and dementia was diagnosed in 11% of patients during follow-up. Patients who had at least three episodes of hypoglycemia had a graded increase in risk of dementia, with fully adjusted hazard ratios of 1.94 (95% CI, 1.42-2.64). The attributable risk of dementia between individuals with and without a history of hypoglycemia was 2.39% per year (95% CI, 1.72%-3.01%). When examining emergency department admissions for hypoglycemia (535 episodes), results were similar, with fully adjusted HRs of 1.42 (95% CI, 1.12-1.78) and 2.36 (95% CI, 1.57-3.55) for 1 and 2 or more episodes, respectively. Our findings suggest that a history of severe hypoglycemic episodes is associated with an increased risk of dementia in older patients with type 2 diabetes. Whether minor hypoglycemic episodes also increase the risk of dementia remains unknown.

title: Defective mast cell effector functions in mice lacking the CRACM1 pore subunit of store-operated calcium release–activated calcium channels
text: CRACM1 (also known as Orai1) forms the pore subunit of store-operated calcium release-activated calcium channels. A mutation in the gene encoding CRACM1 has been linked to severe combined immunodeficiency disease in humans. To investigate CRACM1's role further, we generated CRACM1-deficient mice and measured their expression levels using β-galactosidase activity. CRACM1-deficient mice were found to be smaller in size. Mast cells derived from these mice showed impaired degranulation and cytokine secretion, and their allergic responses in vivo were inhibited. We detected robust CRACM1 expression in muscles and certain regions of the brain, heart, and kidney, but not in lymphoid tissues such as the thymus and spleen. In contrast, CRACM2 was found to be more abundant in mouse T cells. Consistent with these findings, store-operated calcium influx and T cell development and proliferation were not affected in CRACM1-deficient T cells. Our results demonstrates CRACM1's critical role in mouse mast cell effector function, while calcium release-activated calcium channels in mouse T cells are functional even in the absence of CRACM1.

title: MicroRNA-7: A miRNA with expanding roles in development and disease.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a group of small, non-coding RNA molecules (average length: 22 nucleotides) that play a crucial role in post-transcriptional gene regulation. They achieve this by bonding with mRNA transcripts harboring specific target sequences, leading to either accelerated mRNA decay or translation inhibition. Given their involvement in the expression of genes involved in various aspects of normal cell development and function, it is not surprising that misregulated miRNA expression is linked to numerous human diseases. Their significant role in controlling cellular physiology and pathological processes has established miRNAs as potential therapeutic targets, as well as diagnostic and prognostic tools in human health. MicroRNA-7 (miR-7) is a highly conserved miRNA with restricted spatiotemporal expression during development and adulthood. In humans and mice, miR-7 is generated from three distinct genes, indicating both redundancy and the importance of this miRNA in regulating essential cellular functions. This review examines the expanding role of miR-7 in relation to health, with a focus on organ differentiation and development, as well as various diseases affecting the brain, heart, endocrine pancreas, and skin, and cancer. As our understanding of miR-7 grows, so too does the complexity of its regulation and potential functional applications from both a biomarker and therapeutic standpoint.

title: Integration-free induced pluripotent stem cells model genetic and neural developmental features of down syndrome etiology.
text: Down syndrome (DS), the most common congenital cause of mental retardation in humans, is characterized by cognitive deficits resulting from abnormal cellular processes during development and in adult tissues. However, the underlying mechanisms of DS etiology remain inadequately understood. To investigate the potential of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) in modeling DS phenotypes, we generated bona fide DS and wild-type (WT) nonviral iPSCs through episomal reprogramming. Our findings revealed that DS iPSCs selectively overexpressed chromosome 21 genes, a result consistent with gene dosage alterations. Notably, DS and WT iPSCs displayed similar lineage potency, differentiation kinetics, proliferation, and axon extension at early time points. However, at later time points, DS cultures showed a twofold bias toward glial lineages. Furthermore, DS neural cultures demonstrated increased sensitivity to oxidative stress-induced apoptosis, which could be mitigated by the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine. Our results highlight the complexity of genetic alterations resulting from trisomy 21, which are likely to contribute to the developmental phenotypes in DS brains. Additionally, the increased sensitivity to oxidative stress in DS neural cultures suggests that this may play a role in the accelerated neurodegeneration observed in DS. Our findings provide a proof of concept for screening corrective therapeutics using DS iPSCs and their derivatives, and highlight the potential of nonviral DS iPSCs as a discovery platform for modeling complex human diseases in vitro.

title: In Vivo CRISPR/Cas9 Gene Editing Corrects Retinal Dystrophy in the S334ter-3 Rat Model of Autosomal Dominant Retinitis Pigmentosa
text: Genome editing via Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeat (CRISPR)/Cas9 has the potential to treat inherited diseases in patients. As a proof of concept, we demonstrated that CRISPR/Cas9 can be used in vivo to specifically ablate the rhodopsin gene harboring the dominant S334ter mutation (Rho(S334)) in rats that model severe autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa. Following a single subretinal injection of guide RNA/Cas9 plasmid combined with electroporation, we observed allele-specific disruption of Rho(S334), preventing retinal degeneration and improving visual function.

title: Vitamin D insufficiency and the blunted PTH response in established osteoporosis: the role of magnesium deficiency
text:
This study aimed to investigate the relationship between vitamin D insufficiency, magnesium (Mg) deficiency, and the calcium-parathyroid hormone (PTH) endocrine axis in patients with established osteoporosis. The study included 30 patients (10 women) who were divided into three groups based on their vitamin D and PTH levels. The results showed that:
* All subjects within the low vitamin D and low PTH group had evidence of Mg depletion, as measured by the Mg loading test.
* Following the magnesium loading test, there was an increase in calcium levels and a rise in PTH levels compared to baseline.
* Following oral supplementation, bone turnover increased, as measured by C-terminal telopeptide (CTX) and procollagen type I carboxyterminal peptide (P1CP) levels.
The study found that in patients with established osteoporosis, there is a distinct group with a low vitamin D and a blunted PTH level, and that Mg deficiency is an important contributing factor. The study also showed that the magnesium loading test is a useful tool for assessing Mg deficiency in patients with established osteoporosis.

title: Novel syndromes associated with JC virus infection of neurons and meningeal cells: no longer a gray area.
text:
The recent surge in the availability of immunomodulatory medications has been linked to the emergence of novel JC virus (JCV)-associated brain syndromes in patients with autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis, Crohn's disease, and psoriasis. In the last decade, three previously unrecognized syndromes have been discovered, caused by JCV infection of neurons and meningeal cells.
Previous assumptions held that JCV only infected oligodendrocytes and astrocytes in the white matter of the brain of immunosuppressed individuals. However, recent findings have revealed that JCV-infected glial cells are frequently found at the gray-white matter junction or exclusively within the gray matter, leading to demyelination in the cortex. Mutations in JCV can also alter its tropism, resulting in the involvement of other cell types, such as neurons and meningeal cells, and producing clinically distinct entities.
These new developments in JCV infection pose challenges for clinicians and researchers alike, as they highlight the complexity of JCV pathogenesis and tropism. Further research is needed to fully understand the biology of this polyomavirus and to develop effective therapies for affected patients. While increased awareness of these syndromes may lead to early diagnosis, it is crucial to remain vigilant and open to the possibility of additional JC variants or yet unknown polyomaviruses associated with neurological diseases.

title: Phosphoinositide 3-kinase signalling pathways in tumor progression, invasion and angiogenesis.
text:
INTRODUCTION:
The PI3K signaling pathway has emerged as a crucial player in tumor progression, rivaling the Ras-MAPK pathway in its importance. This review aims to examine the current evidence for PI3K's involvement in human cancers, discuss the mechanisms by which its activation promotes tumor progression, and explore its potential as a novel anticancer target.
METHODS:
A comprehensive analysis of recent literature on the role of PI3K in tumor progression was conducted using Medline. The review focused on the mechanisms of action of PI3K and its clinical implications.
Results:
Evital evidence suggests that misregulation of the PI3K pathway is a common feature of many types of cancer, either due to loss of the suppressor protein PTEN or constitutive activation of PI3K isoforms or downstream elements such as AKT and mTOR. This activation enhances cell survival, proliferation, cytoskeletal deformability, and motility - key factors in tumor invasion. Additionally, the PI3K pathway is involved in various aspects of angiogenesis, including upregulation of angiogenic cytokines in response to tumor hypoxia or oncogene activation, and endothelial cell responses to these cytokines. These cytokines signal through receptors such as VEGF-R, FGF-R, and Tie-2, potentiating processes essential for neoangiogenesis, including cell proliferation, migration, differentiation into tubules, and "invasion" of these capillary sprouts into the extracellular matrix (ECM).
CONCLUSIONS:
A deeper understanding of the role of the PI3K pathway in cancer will lead to the development of more potent and selective inhibitors, which could be a useful adjunct to conventional therapies, potentially disrupting tumor progression at several key points, including cell survival, invasion, and angiogenesis.

title: Complementary foods for infant feeding in developing countries: their nutrient adequacy and improvement
text:
Objective:
To assess the energy and nutrient adequacy of various plant-based complementary foods used in developing countries, including Africa, India, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, and Thailand.
Methodology:
The study calculated the energy, nutrient, and anti-nutrient (dietary fiber and phytic acid) content (per 100 g as consumed, per 100 kcal, and per day) of 23 plant-based complementary foods consumed in developing countries. This was done by using food composition values based on chemical analysis for trace minerals, non-starch polysaccharide, and phytic acid, as well as literature reviews. The results were then compared with the estimated nutrient needs (per day; per 100 kcal) from complementary foods for infants aged 9-11 months, assuming average breast milk volume and composition and three complementary feedings per day, each of 250 g.
Key Findings:
Complementary foods should provide around 25-50% of the daily requirements for protein, riboflavin, and copper, 50-75% for thiamin, calcium, and manganese, and 75-100% for phosphorus, zinc, and iron. Most or all of these foods appear to meet the estimated daily nutrient needs (per day; per 100 kcal) for protein, thiamin, and copper, but not for calcium, iron, and, in some cases, zinc, even if moderate bioavailability for iron and zinc is assumed. Some of those made from rice are also inadequate in riboflavin (per day; per 100 kcal).
Conclusion:
Even if strategies to improve the bioavailability of iron and zinc are employed, they are unlikely to overcome deficits in calcium, iron, and zinc. Therefore, research into the feasibility of fortifying plant-based complementary foods in developing countries with calcium, iron, and zinc is urgently needed.
Sponsorship:
This study was supported by the Micronutrient Initiative through the Canadian International Development Agency.

title: Early aging and age-related pathologies in mice deficient in BMAL1, the core componentof the circadian clock.
text: Mice lacking the circadian transcription factor BMAL1 (brain and muscle ARNT-like protein) exhibit impaired circadian behavior and a loss of rhythmicity in the expression of target genes. In this study, we found that Bmal1-deficient mice have shorter lifespans and display various symptoms of premature aging, including sarcopenia, cataracts, reduced subcutaneous fat, organ shrinkage, and others. Interestingly, the early aging phenotype in Bmal1-deficient mice is associated with increased levels of reactive oxygen species in certain tissues. These findings, when combined with previous research on the role of CLOCK/BMAL1 in controlling stress responses, may provide a mechanistic explanation for the early onset of age-related pathologies in the absence of BMAL1.

title: A self-inactivating lentiviral vector for SCID-X1 gene therapy that does not activate LMO2 expression in human T cells.
text: To develop safer and more effective vectors for gene therapy of X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID-X1), we evaluated new self-inactivating lentiviral vectors based on the HIV virus. We tested the CL20i4-hgamma(c)-Revgen vector, which contains the entire human common gamma chain (γ(c)) genomic sequence driven by the γ(c) promoter, and the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector, which uses a promoter fragment from the eukaryotic elongation factor alpha (EF1alpha) gene to express a codon-optimized human γ(c) cDNA. Both vectors contain a 400-bp insulator fragment from the chicken beta-globin locus within the self-inactivating long-terminal repeat. In mouse SCID-X1 transplantation models, transduction of bone marrow cells with either vector restored T, B, and natural killer lymphocyte development and function. In addition, transduction of human CD34(+) bone marrow cells from SCID-X1 patients with either vector restored T-cell development in an in vitro assay. In safety studies using a Jurkat LMO2 activation assay, only the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector lacked the ability to transactivate LMO2 protein expression, while the CL20i4-hgamma(c)-Revgen vector significantly activated LMO2 protein expression. Moreover, the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector did not cause tumors in transplanted mice. These findings suggest that the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector may be suitable for testing in a clinical trial based on its preclinical demonstrations of efficacy and safety.

title: Genetic Variants at Newly Identified Lipid Loci Are Associated with Coronary Heart Disease in a Chinese Han Population
text:
Recently, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have discovered new genetic locations linked to blood lipid levels in whites. We investigated whether these variants are related to the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) in the Chinese Han population.
METHODOLOGY / RESULTS We conducted a two-stage case-control study in the Chinese Han population. The first stage, with 1,376 CHD cases and 1,376 sex- and age-matched controls, examined the association between five newly identified lipid-related single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) found in GWAS of whites and CHD risk in Chinese. We validated these SNPs in the second stage, involving 1,269 cases and 2,745 controls. Additionally, we examined the link between these SNPs and blood lipid levels in 4,121 controls. We identified two novel SNPs: rs599839 in CELSR2-PSRC1-SORT1 and rs16996148 in NCAN-CILP2, which were significantly linked to decreased CHD risk in the Chinese population (odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) in the dominant model: 0.76 (0.61-0.90; P = 0.001), 0.67 (0.57-0.77; P = 3.4 × 10(-8)), respectively). Multiple linear regression analyses using the dominant model indicated that rs599839 was significantly associated with reduced LDL cholesterol levels (P = 0.022), while rs16996148 was significantly linked to increased LDL and HDL cholesterol levels (P = 2.9 × 10(-4) and 0.001, respectively).
CONCLUSION / SIGNIFICANCE We have identified two novel SNPs in newly identified lipid-related loci that are significantly related to CHD susceptibility in the Chinese Han population.

title: Spare respiratory capacity rather than oxidative stress regulates glutamate excitotoxicity after partial respiratory inhibition of mitochondrial complex I with rotenone.
text: The use of rotenone to inhibit mitochondrial complex I in rodents reproduces certain aspects of Parkinson's disease, leading researchers to investigate the mechanism by which rotenone enhances neuronal cell death. In an acute glutamate excitotoxicity model of primary rat cerebellar granule neurons, rotenone was found to increase mitochondrial superoxide levels and potentiate glutamate-induced calcium deregulation, the first irreversible stage of necrotic cell death. However, the addition of a cell-permeant O2*- trap did not prevent the adverse effects of rotenone. To quantify the bioenergetic consequences of rotenone addition, cell respiration was monitored. Glutamate activation of NMDA receptors utilized the full respiratory capacity of the in situ mitochondria, with over 80% of the glutamate-stimulated respiration attributed to increased cellular ATP demand. At 20 nM, rotenone inhibited both basal and glutamate-stimulated cell respiration and caused respiratory failure in the presence of glutamate. Additionally, inhibition of ATP synthase by oligomycin was also toxic in the presence of glutamate. These findings suggest that, in the rotenone model of partial complex I deficiency under these specific conditions, cell vulnerability is primarily determined by spare respiratory capacity rather than oxidative stress.

title: Isolated liver perfusion for non-resectable liver tumours: a review.
text: Many treatments have been proposed for non-resectable primary or secondary hepatic cancer, but the outcomes have generally been underwhelming. Isolated Hepatic Perfusion (IHP) was first attempted four decades ago, but it gained acceptance only recently following impressive tumor responses obtained through isolated limb perfusion with melphalan and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) for melanomas and sarcomas. The surgical isolation of the liver is a technically complex operation that enables the safe administration of high doses of chemotherapeutics and TNF. Percutaneous techniques using balloon occlusion catheters are less invasive but result in higher leakage rates from the perfusion circuit into the systemic circulation. Several phase I-II trials have shown that IHP can achieve high tumor response rates, even when there is resistance to systemic chemotherapy. However, no significant advantage in overall survival has been demonstrated so far. IHP offers distinct pharmacokinetic advantages for locoregional chemotherapy and biotherapy, and may also allow gene therapy with minimal systemic exposure and toxicity. At present, IHP remains an experimental treatment modality and should therefore be employed only in controlled trials.

title: Combinatorial control of exon recognition.
text: Pre-mRNA splicing is a crucial process that allows for the expression of most metazoan genes. This process is carried out by the spliceosome, which removes non-coding intronic sequences and assembles exons into mature mRNAs prior to export and translation. The complexity of higher eukaryotic genes and the lack of splice site conservation require a high degree of precision from the splicing machinery in recognizing and pairing splice sites. The spliceosome efficiently removes introns ranging in size from 100 to 100,000 bases, while also accommodating a large number of alternative splicing events between different cell types, during development, or during other biological processes. This flexibility allows the spliceosome to efficiently identify and process exons within a given pre-mRNA, depending on multiple parameters such as splice site strength, the presence or absence of splicing regulators, RNA secondary structures, the exon/intron architecture, and the pre-mRNA synthesis process itself. The relative contributions of these parameters influence how efficiently splice sites are recognized and flanking introns are removed.

title: High CTLA-4 expression on Th17 cells results in increased sensitivity to CTLA-4 coinhibition and resistance to belatacept.
text: The CD28/cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4) blocker belatacept selectively inhibits alloreactive T cell responses, but its use is often associated with a high incidence of acute rejection following renal transplantation. To investigate the reason behind this, we examined the etiology of belatacept-resistant graft rejection. T cells differentiate into distinct subsets of memory T cells, each with its unique function in protecting against diverse pathogens. Of particular interest are T helper 1 (Th1) and T helper 17 (Th17) cells, which are pro-inflammatory CD4+ lineages that provide immunity to pathogens and can cause harm in autoimmune diseases. We observed that both Th1 and Th17 memory subsets contain a similar number of divided cells after allogeneic stimulation. However, Th17 memory cells express much higher levels of the coinhibitory molecule CTLA-4 than Th1 cells. Belatacept inhibits Th1 responses while augmenting Th17 cells due to their greater sensitivity to coinhibition by CTLA-4. Interestingly, Th17 cells from renal transplant recipients are resistant to ex vivo CD28/CTLA-4 blockade with belatacept, and an increased frequency of Th17 memory cells is associated with acute rejection during belatacept therapy. These findings highlight important differences in costimulatory and coinhibitory requirements between CD4+ memory subsets, and demonstrate that the diversity of pathogen-derived memory T cells has implications for immunomodulation strategies.

title: A small molecule modulates Jumonji histone demethylase activity and selectively inhibits cancer growth
text: The potential for pharmacological inhibition of general transcriptional regulators is significant in blocking cancer growth through simultaneous targeting of multiple tumorigenic signaling pathways. Innovative cell-based screens have led to the identification of a unique small molecule (JIB-04) that specifically inhibits the activity of the Jumonji family of histone demethylases in vitro, in cancer cells, and in tumors in vivo. Unlike existing inhibitors, JIB-04 is not a competitive inhibitor of α-ketoglutarate. In cancer cells, but not in normal cells, JIB-04 alters a subset of transcriptional pathways and inhibits viability. In mice, JIB-04 reduces tumor burden and prolongs survival. Notably, patients with breast tumors that overexpress Jumonji demethylases have significantly lower survival rates. Therefore, JIB-04, a novel inhibitor of Jumonji demethylases in vitro and in vivo, presents a promising therapeutic and research tool for cancer treatment and validates the use of unbiased cellular screens for discovering chemical modulators with disease relevance.

title: Gq protein alpha subunits Galphaq and Galpha11 are localized at postsynaptic extra-junctional membrane of cerebellar Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal cells.
text: Following the activation of cell surface receptors, the alpha subunit of the Gq subclass of GTP-binding proteins activates the phosphoinositide signaling pathway. In this study, we investigated the expression and localization of Gq protein alpha subunits in the adult mouse brain using in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry. Of the four members of the Gq protein alpha subunits, Galphaq and Galpha11 were predominantly expressed in the brain. The highest level of Galphaq transcription was observed in cerebellar Purkinje cells (PCs) and hippocampal pyramidal cells, while Galpha11 was primarily expressed in hippocampal pyramidal cells. An antibody against the C-terminal peptide common to Galphaq and Galpha11 strongly labeled the cerebellar molecular layer and hippocampal neuropil layers. Immunogold particles were mainly located on the cytoplasmic face of postsynaptic cell membranes of PCs and pyramidal cells and were almost excluded from the junctional membrane. Using double immunofluorescence, Galphaq/Galpha11 was extensively colocalized with metabotropic glutamate receptor mGluR1alpha in dendritic spines of PCs and with mGluR5 in hippocampal pyramidal cells. These findings suggest that peri-junctional stimulation of group I metabotropic glutamate receptors is mediated by Galphaq and/or Galpha11, leading to the activation of the intracellular effector, phospholipase Cbeta.

title: The Bloom's syndrome gene product is homologous to RecQ helicases
text: The Bloom's syndrome (BS) gene, BLM, plays a critical role in maintaining genomic stability in somatic cells. A candidate for BLM was identified through a novel mapping method that involved selecting a cDNA derived from a 250 kb segment of the genome and mapping it using somatic crossover points. The cDNA was from individuals with BS who had undergone intragenic recombination within the BLM region. Analysis of the candidate gene revealed a 4437 bp cDNA that encodes a 1417 amino acid peptide with homology to the RecQ helicases, a subfamily of DExH box-containing DNA and RNA helicases. The presence of chain-terminating mutations in the candidate gene in individuals with BS confirmed that it was indeed BLM.

title: Preventing obesity in children and adolescents.
text:
In this review, we explore the natural progression of obesity in children, introducing family-based and school-based interventions that can prevent or slow its onset. While childhood is a critical period for weight management, the adolescent years also present challenges. While it's unclear whether early adiposity rebound is solely caused by changes in body fat, caution is warranted during this period. Family and school environments offer prime opportunities for preventive measures.
An effective approach involves examining factors that impact energy balance and identifying more immediate influences on these factors. For instance, television viewing has a significant impact on both energy intake and expenditure, making it a viable target for interventions. By providing anticipatory guidance to pediatricians, parents can be educated on modifying their child's television use to promote healthier habits. Similarly, school-based interventions focusing on dietary choices and sedentary behavior can likewise promote lasting changes.

title: Culture of Preimplantation Mouse Embryos Affects Fetal Development and the Expression of Imprinted Genes1
text: Culture of preimplantation mammalian embryos and cells can impact their subsequent growth and differentiation. In a previous study, we found that culturing mouse embryonic stem cells led to alterations in genomic imprinting and reduced their potential to develop into normal fetuses. To investigate if the same holds true for preimplantation mouse embryos, we cultured them in a chemically defined medium (M16) with or without fetal calf serum (FCS). Only a third of the blastocysts derived from two-cell embryos cultured in M16 medium supplemented with FCS developed into viable Day 14 fetuses after transfer to recipients. These M16 + FCS fetuses were lighter than controls and M16 fetuses, and displayed decreased expression of the imprinted H19 and insulin-like growth factor 2 genes, as well as increased expression of the imprinted gene Grb10. In contrast, the growth factor receptor binding gene Grb7 was drastically reduced in expression in most of these fetuses. Interestingly, no changes were observed for the imprinted gene Mest. Overall, our findings suggest that preimplantation culture in the presence of serum can have far-reaching effects on the regulation of multiple growth-related imprinted genes, leading to abnormal fetal growth and development.

title: Results of screening for intracranial aneurysms in patients with coarctation of the aorta.
text:
The following is a rewritten version of the given text:
Background and Purpose:
Intracranial aneurysms (IAs) are found in approximately 2.3% of adults, with a mean age of detection at 52 years. However, their prevalence is significantly lower in young adults, <0.5%. Early studies suggest that 10%-50% of patients with aortic coarctation may have IAs. The recommendations for screening are varied, and this study aimed to investigate the prevalence of IAs through screening with magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) in patients with coarctation.
Methods:
This study included consecutive patients older than 16 years of age with coarctation who underwent brain MRA between May 1999 and October 2007. The MRA was performed using a 1.5T scanner with a 3D time-of-flight protocol, simultaneously imaging the heart and aorta. The cerebral MRAs were double-reported by a neuroradiologist. The results were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and continuous variables were compared using Student t tests and Mann-Whitney U tests (categorical variables, by using the Fisher exact test).
Results:
A total of 117 MRAs were double-reported, with a median age of 29 ± 11 years (range, 16-59 years). IAs were found in 12 patients (10.3%), with a mean diameter of 3.9 mm (range, 2.0-8.0 mm). Patients with aneurysms were older (median, 37 years; range, 16-50 years) than those without (median, 23 years; range, 16-59 years; Z = -2.01, P = .04). Hypertension was more common in those with IAs (83% vs. no IA 43%, P = .01). No significant association was found between ascending aortopathy, bicuspid aortic valves, and IAs.
Conclusions:
The study found that patients with coarctation have a higher prevalence of IAs, occurring at an earlier age than in population studies. Whether routine screening is appropriate for this group of patients is unclear. Hypertension is likely to be an important pathophysiologic factor.

title: A new look at the heart in diabetes mellitus: from ailing to failing
text: This review discusses some of the mechanisms that contribute to the increased risk of cardiovascular disease in patients with diabetes. Advanced imaging techniques such as single photon emission computed tomography or photon emission tomography with radioactive labeled analogues of norepinephrine have shown that patients with Type I and Type II diabetes have cardiac sympathetic dysfunction and incompetence, both early and late, in the disease process. Myocardial blood flow assessment with photon emission tomography has also revealed that endothelial-dependent vasodilation is significantly reduced in relation to cardiac sympathetic dysfunction. Additionally, signs of endothelial activation have been found early in patients with Type I and Type II diabetes, even in the absence of clinical evidence of vascular disease. This activation, alongside meticulous glucose control and rapid recompensation of hyperglycaemia in patients with acute coronary syndrome, plays a crucial role in determining macrovascular mortality. Cardiac sympathetic dysfunction can partially normalize with near-normalization of glycaemia. These findings highlight the importance of early detection and intervention to prevent the progression of cardiovascular disease in patients with diabetes.

title: Genetic and epigenetic mutations affect the DNA binding capability of human ZFP57 in transient neonatal diabetes type 1
text: In the mouse, ZFP57 harbors three Cys2His2 zinc finger domains (ZF) that recognize a methylated target sequence (TGC(met)CGC) using its first and second ZFs. In this study, we demonstrate that the human ZFP57 (hZFP57), containing six Cys2His2 ZFs, binds the same methylated sequence through its third and fourth ZFs and identify key amino acids crucial for DNA interaction. Furthermore, we provide evidence linking hZFP57 mutations and hypomethylation of the TNDM1 ICR to Transient Neonatal Diabetes Mellitus type 1, which likely results in loss of hZFP57 binding to the TNDM1 locus and PLAGL1 activation.

title: Physiological astrocytic calcium levels stimulate glutamate release to modulate adjacent neurons.
text: Astrocytes can release glutamate in response to changes in intracellular calcium levels, which can signal to adjacent neurons. However, it is unclear whether this mechanism is used during normal brain function or is activated only in pathological conditions. To shed light on this question, we employed flash photolysis to elevate intracellular calcium in astrocytes and measured the resulting glutamate release and its effects on neighboring neurons. Our findings demonstrate that modest increases in astrocytic calcium levels (ranging from 84 to 140 nM) can elicit substantial glutamatergic currents in nearby neurons, with a Hill coefficient of 2.1 to 2.7. Since agonists like glutamate, norepinephrine, and dopamine can all raise astrocytic calcium levels to over 1.8 microM, these studies demonstrate that the astrocytic glutamate release pathway is activated at physiological intracellular calcium levels. Therefore, this calcium-dependent mechanism of glutamate release from astrocytes is functional within the normal range of astrocytic calcium levels and can be used as a signaling pathway in the nervous system.

title: Albumin and furosemide therapy in hypoproteinemic patients with acute lung injury.
text:
Objective: To investigate the effectiveness of diuresis and colloid replacement therapy in improving pulmonary physiology in critically ill patients with acute lung injury and hypoproteinemia.
Design: A prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
Setting: All adult intensive care units in two university hospitals.
Patients: Thirty-seven mechanically-ventilated patients with acute lung injury and serum total protein level </=5.0 g/dL.
Interventions: A 5-day protocolized regimen of 25 g of human serum albumin every 8 hours, along with continuous infusion of furosemide, or dual placebo, targeted to diuresis, weight loss, and serum total protein.
Outcome Measures: Change in weight, serum total protein, fluid balance, hemodynamics, respiratory system compliance, and oxygenation.
Results: Baseline characteristics were similar between the treatment and control groups (n = 19 and n = 18, respectively), with trauma being the major cause of acute lung injury. The treatment group experienced significant improvements in Pao2/Fio2 ratio within 24 hours (from 171 to 236, p =.02), accompanied by weight loss and fluid balance changes. Respiratory mechanics were unchanged, while mean arterial pressure increased from 80 to 88 mm Hg (p =.10) and heart rate decreased from 110 to 95 beats/min (p =.008) over time in the treatment group. There was no significant difference in mortality observed between the groups, although favorable trends were seen in measures of intensive care.
Conclusion: Albumin and furosemide therapy improves fluid balance, oxygenation, and hemodynamics in hypoproteinemic patients with acute lung injury. Further study is needed to determine the effect of this simple therapy on cost, outcomes, and other patient populations.

title: Advances in functional and structural mr image analysis and implementation as fsl
text: Advanced techniques for interrogating and analyzing neuroimaging data have significantly impacted the versatility, sensitivity, and breadth of neuroimaging experiments. The development of these methodologies has enabled researchers to tackle scientific questions that were previously unaddressable, and as such, has become a prominent area of research in its own right. In this paper, we provide a review of the research conducted by the Analysis Group at the Oxford Centre for Functional MRI of the Brain (FMRIB). This research has primarily focused on the creation of novel methodologies for analyzing both structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. Most of the work outlined in this paper has been developed into freely available software tools within FMRIB's Software Library (FSL).

title: Metformin—mode of action and clinical implications for diabetes and cancer
text: For decades, metformin has been the go-to treatment for diabetes mellitus, but its underlying mechanisms remained poorly understood. Recent breakthroughs have revealed that this drug not only lowers glucose levels but also holds promise for targeting metabolic differences in abnormal metabolic signaling. By uncovering the key mechanisms of metformin's action, we can develop novel treatments. The central component of metformin's mechanism is modulating cellular energy metabolism. Metformin inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis and opposes the action of glucagon, leading to defective cAMP and protein kinase A signaling. Additionally, metformin's inhibition of mitochondrial complex I results in impaired lipid metabolism. While the glucose-lowering effect of metformin is dispensable for 5'-AMP-activated protein kinase, it plays a crucial role in enhancing insulin sensitivity. Furthermore, metformin may also influence tumorigenesis, both indirectly through reduced insulin levels and directly through the induction of energetic stress. While these off-target effects require further investigation, our updated understanding of metformin's antigluconeogenic action in the liver has significant implications for the treatment of diabetes mellitus and cancer.

title: Characteristics of the Earliest Cross-Neutralizing Antibody Response to HIV-1
text: New analyses of HIV-1-infected individuals have revealed that the development of broadly cross-reactive neutralizing antibody responses occurs in approximately 10-30% of cases. The timing of the emergence of these responses is currently unknown, as is whether they emerge in response to a single or multiple regions of the viral envelope glycoprotein (Env). To investigate this further, we analyzed cross-neutralizing antibody responses in longitudinal plasma samples collected shortly after and up to seven years after infection. Our findings indicate that anti-HIV-1 cross-neutralizing antibody responses first emerge on average at 2.5 years post-infection, with rare cases showing development as early as 1 year. If these responses do not develop within the first 2-3 years of infection, it is unlikely that they will occur later on. Our study suggests a link between the development of cross-neutralizing antibody responses and specific activation markers on T cells, as well as plasma viremia levels. The earliest cross-neutralizing antibody responses target a limited number of Env regions, primarily the CD4-binding site and epitopes that are not present on monomeric Env, but are present on the virion-associated trimeric Env form. In contrast, the neutralizing activities of plasmas from individuals who did not develop cross-neutralizing antibody responses target epitopes on monomeric gp120 other than the CD4-BS. Our study provides valuable insights into the interaction between the human immune system and HIV, and may inform the development of effective immunization protocols. Specifically, emphasis should be placed on eliciting antibodies against complex epitopes present on the virion-associated envelope spike, as these are key components of the earliest cross-neutralizing activities of HIV-1-infected plasmas.

title: Gender, age, and heart failure with preserved left ventricular systolic function.
text:
Study Objectives:
This research aimed to determine if women are more likely than men to experience heart failure (HF) with preserved systolic function after adjusting for potential confounding variables, including age.
Background: Previous studies have shown an association between female gender and preserved left ventricular systolic function (LVSF) in patients with HF, but these studies have limitations due to referral biases, small sample sizes, or the inability to adjust for a wide range of potential confounding variables.
Methods: This cross-sectional study used retrospective medical chart abstraction of a national sample of Medicare beneficiaries hospitalized with the principal discharge diagnosis of HF in acute-care nongovernmental hospitals in the U.S. between April 1998 and March 1999. To be included in the analysis, patients had to be aged 65 years or older, have documentation of LVSF, and corroboration of the diagnosis of HF. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify the correlates of preserved LVSF, which was defined as qualitatively normal function or quantitatively reported ejection fraction ≥0.50. Stratified regressions by gender were performed to identify significant interactions.
Results: Of the 19,710 patients in the analysis, preserved LVSF was present in 6,700 (35%), and 79% of these patients were women. In contrast, among the 12,956 patients with impaired LVSF, only 49% were women. Patients with preserved LVSF were 1.5 years older than those with impaired LVSF after adjustment for age and other patient factors. After adjusting for age and other patient factors, female gender remained strongly associated with preserved LVSF (calculated risk ratio = 1.71; 95% confidence interval 1.63 to 1.78). The association was consistent across all age groups, and was similar in patients with or without coronary artery disease, hypertension, pulmonary disease, renal insufficiency, or atrial fibrillation.
Conclusions: In elderly patients hospitalized with HF, preserved systolic function is primarily a condition of women, independent of important demographic and clinical characteristics.

title: YAP/TAZ-Dependent Reprogramming of Colonic Epithelium Links ECM Remodeling to Tissue Regeneration
text: The process of tissue regeneration involves dynamic cellular adaptations to the injured environment, which are currently poorly understood at the cellular level. To shed light on this phenomenon, we examined colonic regeneration in a mouse dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) colitis model and discovered that the epithelium undergoes a transient reprogramming into a primitive state. This is characterized by the re-expression of fetal markers and the suppression of adult stem and differentiated cell markers. The cell fate change is orchestrated by remodeling the extracellular matrix (ECM), increased FAK/Src signaling, and ultimately YAP/TAZ activation. In a controlled cell culture system mimicking the ECM remodeling observed in vivo, we found that a collagen 3D matrix supplemented with Wnt ligands is sufficient to sustain endogenous YAP/TAZ activity and induce cell fate conversion. This simple model provides evidence that cellular reprogramming is a crucial element in tissue regeneration.

title: Summary
text:
Here is a potentially more clear and concise version of the text:
Glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and podocalyxin are essential for maintaining the morphology of podocytes, the specialized epithelial cells that line the glomerular tubule. We demonstrated that GBM and laminin, but not collagen IV, up-regulate the expression of podocalyxin in human glomerular epithelial cells. Scanning electron microscopy revealed that laminin induces a modified morphology of podocytes with process formation, which is more extensive in the presence of GBM. Under high magnification, podocytes appear ruffled. Using transmission electron microscopy, we observed raised areas on the basal cell surface in the presence of anti-podocalyxin antibody. Additionally, we found that anti-podocalyxin antibody increased the adhesion and spreading of podocytes to both collagen IV and laminin, suggesting that podocalyxin inhibits cell-matrix interactions. In podocytes expressing podocalyxin, the presence of anti-podocalyxin antibody partially reversed the inhibition of adhesion to collagen IV provoked by anti-beta1 integrin antibody, indicating that podocalyxin may compete with beta1-related cell adhesion. Our findings suggest that the observed podocalyxin-mediated inhibition of binding to the matrix may contribute to the specialized conformation of the basal surface of podocytes.

title: Mfold web server for nucleic acid folding and hybridization prediction
text: The abbreviated name "mfold web server" refers to a suite of software applications available on the World Wide Web (WWW) for predicting the secondary structure of single-stranded nucleic acids. The primary goal of this web server is to provide easy access to RNA and DNA folding and hybridization tools for the scientific community at large. By leveraging universally available web graphical user interfaces (GUIs), the server overcomes the challenge of portability associated with these software applications. The server provides detailed output, including structure plots with or without reliability information, single strand frequency plots, and "energy dot plots," for the folding of individual sequences. Additionally, bulk servers offer less detailed information but in a faster time frame and for large numbers of sequences simultaneously. The portal for the mfold web server is accessible at <http://www.bioinfo.rpi.edu/applications/mfold>, which will be referred to as "MFOLDROOT" throughout this text.

title: Grip strength in healthy caucasian adults: reference values.
text:
Study Objective:
The primary goal of this investigation was to update existing reference data on handgrip strength for healthy adults of both genders spanning a wide age range and to identify potential influencing factors.
Methodology:
Intra- and inter-individual variations of grip strength, as well as their relationship to various anthropometric factors, were analyzed in a standardized manner for 769 healthy adults (403 women and 366 men) between the ages of 20 and 95 years. Handgrip strength measurements were taken in neutral positions of the arm, forearm, and wrist using a Baseline digital hydraulic dynamometer (NexGen Ergonomics Inc., Quebec, Canada) in both hands.
Results:
The study found that, on average, women had significantly weaker handgrip strength than men, with an approximate ratio of left to right hand of .95 in both genders. Handgrip strength peaks in both genders around the age of 35 and decreases with age thereafter. Anthropometric variables such as forearm circumference and length, hand size, and body mass index showed positive correlations with grip strength. However, body mass index, type of work, and hand dominance only had a partial or no correlation with grip strength. Gender and age, followed by parameters representing body length and obesity, were found to have the highest predictive value for handgrip strength and were therefore entered into the generation of prediction equations.
Conclusion:

Based on the study findings, the researchers recommend adjusting measured values for intraindividual comparison and including anthropometric characteristics. Hand dominance can be ignored. The regression equations generated may prove useful for clinicians or those who utilize normative values within software to provide more accurate predictions of strength scores for specific applications.

title: Association Between Biomarkers of Ovarian Reserve and Infertility Among Older Women of Reproductive Age
text: The text discusses the findings of a study examining the association between biomarkers of ovarian reserve and reproductive potential among women aged 30-44 years who had been trying to conceive for 3 months or less. The study found that levels of antimüllerian hormone (AMH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and inhibin B were not associated with reduced fertility in this population. Specifically, women with low AMH levels did not have a significantly lower probability of conceiving by 6 or 12 cycles of attempt compared to women with normal levels. Similarly, women with high serum FSH values did not have a significantly lower probability of conceiving by 6 or 12 cycles of attempt compared to women with normal values. However, women with high urinary FSH values had a slightly lower probability of conceiving by 6 cycles of attempt. The study did not find an association between inhibin B levels and the probability of conceiving in a given cycle. These findings suggest that biomarkers indicating diminished ovarian reserve are not useful for assessing natural fertility in this population of women.

title: Matrix-embedded osteocytes regulate mobilization of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells.
text: The bone marrow (BM) niche is home to multiple cell types that regulate the migration of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs) out of the niche and into the circulation. Here, we demonstrate that osteocytes, the primary cellular component of mature bone, play a crucial role in regulating HSPC egress. After administering granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), which is clinically used to mobilize HSPCs, we observe changes in the morphology and gene expression of the osteocytic network that occur before changes in osteoblasts. These rapid responses are likely mediated by the sympathetic nervous system, as osteocytes express the β2-adrenergic receptor. In mice with targeted ablation of osteocytes or a disrupted osteocyte network, we find that the number of HSPCs in the BM remains unchanged but the ability to mobilize HSPCs in response to G-CSF is impaired. These findings suggest that the BM/bone niche interface is tightly regulated from within the bone matrix and establish a critical physiological role for skeletal tissues in hematopoietic function.

title: Generation of Genetically Modified Mice by Oocyte Injection of Androgenetic Haploid Embryonic Stem Cells
text: Haploid cells are suitable for genetic analysis. Recent advances in the derivation of mouse haploid embryonic stem cells (haESCs) through parthenogenesis have enabled genetic screening in mammalian cells. However, the successful generation of live animals from these haESCs, which is essential to extend genetic analysis to the organism level, has Yet to be achieved. Here, we report the derivation of haESCs from androgenetic blastocysts. These cells, referred to as AG-haESCs, retain some paternal imprints, express typical ESC pluripotency markers, and contribute to various tissues, including the germline, upon injection into diploid blastocysts. Amazingly, live mice can be obtained by injecting AG-haESCs into MII oocytes, and these mice exhibit haESC-carried genetic traits and develop into fertile adults. Furthermore, gene targeting via homologous recombination is feasible in the AG-haESCs. Our findings demonstrate that AG-haESCs can be used as a genetically tractable fertilization agent for the production of live animals through injection into oocytes.

title: The impact of hydroxyethyl starches in cardiac surgery: a meta-analysis
text:
Recent studies have raised concerns about the safety of hydroxyethyl starches (HESs) in septic patients, but it is unclear if this applies to less vulnerable patient populations. To evaluate the impact of different HES generations on safety and efficacy endpoints in cardiac surgery patients, we conducted a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs).
We searched multiple databases, including PubMed, EMBase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, for RCTs comparing HES to other colloid or crystalloid solutions during open heart surgery. Our results showed that older starches with higher molecular weights led to higher blood loss and transfusion requirements compared to other volume substitutes. However, the latest-generation tetrastarch (130/0.4) performed better than albumin, gelatin, and crystalloids in terms of blood loss, transfusion needs, and length of stay in the intensive care unit and hospital.
Specifically, the tetrastarch showed a statistically significant reduction in blood loss and transfusion requirements compared to gelatin and crystalloids. Additionally, the tetrastarch led to shorter lengths of stay in the intensive care unit and hospital compared to gelatin and crystalloids. These findings suggest that tetrastarch may be a safer alternative to older starches and other colloid or crystalloid solutions in cardiac surgery patients.
However, our safety analysis raised some concerns regarding coagulation issues with older starches, which may require further investigation in future trials. In conclusion, our meta-analysis suggests that tetrastarch may be a viable option for cardiac surgery patients, but further trials are needed to fully assess its safety profile.

title: Place of care in advanced cancer: a qualitative systematic literature review of patient preferences.
text:
BACKGROUND: It is generally accepted that a significant number of patients prefer to die at home rather than in a hospital or other institutional setting. However, there is limited research on the preferences of advanced cancer patients specifically regarding the place of terminal care and death.
AIM: To conduct a systematic literature review of the preferences for place of care and death among advanced cancer patients.
METHOD: We conducted database searches of MEDLINE (1966-1999), PsychLit (1974-1999), and Bath Information Data Service (BIDS) (1981-1999) to identify studies that investigated the preferences of patients, the general public, and healthcare professionals regarding the place of terminal care and death. Studies were assessed and data extracted and synthesized according to the guidelines of the NHS Centre for Reviews and Dissemination, and were graded according to their design and methodological rigor.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies that investigated the preferences of patients, the general public, and healthcare professionals were identified. These studies obtained views prospectively and retrospectively from patients, family members, and professionals. The majority of studies found that patients preferred to receive end-of-life care at home, ranging from 49% to 100% of respondents. In contrast, inpatient hospice care was the most preferred option among healthcare professionals. The general public also showed a preference for inpatient hospice care, especially among those with recent experience of a close friend or relative's death or dying. When the views of patients, families, and professionals were compared, all respondents generally agreed on the preferred place of care, with patients expressing the strongest preference for home care. However, only two studies provided longitudinal data, and nine of the eighteen studies had major design or reporting flaws, such as poor response rates, unclear or unsystematic methods of eliciting preferences, or other sample or measurement bias.
CONCLUSIONS: Home care is the most common preference among advanced cancer patients, with inpatient hospice care as the second preference. Providing care in a patient's preferred location could be an important outcome for services and indicates that meeting patient preferences regarding the place of terminal care and death could have significant clinical and ethical implications. Future studies should prioritize the development of more robust and reliable methods for assessing patient preferences in this area.

title: Linkage Disequilibrium Mapping of       CHEK2: Common Variation and Breast Cancer Risk
text: Background Checkpoint kinase 2 (CHEK2) plays a crucial role in preventing the development of cancer by inducing cell cycle arrest and promoting DNA repair in genetically damaged cells. Previous research has revealed a significant association between the CHEK2 gene and breast cancer etiology, focusing primarily on the rare 1100delC mutation. However, the impact of common polymorphisms within this gene on breast cancer risk remains unexplored. To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a study aimed at investigating the influence of common CHEK2 variants on population-level breast cancer risk by employing a comprehensive set of tagging single nucleotide polymorphisms (tagSNPs) that capture the majority of genetic diversity within the gene. Methods and Findings We analyzed 14 commonly occurring SNPs spanning 52 kilobases (kb) of the CHEK2 gene in a sample of 92 Swedish women. Our results indicate that these typed SNPs are sufficient to capture association signals from untyped SNPs in the same region. Six of the 14 SNPs were found to be well-correlated with both haplotypic and single SNP variations within CHEK2. We genotyped these six tagSNPs in a sample of 1,577 postmenopausal breast cancer cases and 1,513 population controls. However, we failed to identify any compelling associations between common CHEK2 haplotypes and breast cancer risk. The 1100delC mutation, which is rare in our Swedish population (0.7% in cases and 0.4% in controls), was associated with an odds ratio of 2.26 (95% confidence interval, 0.99–5.15) when compared to non-carriers. Our sample is representative of a Northern European population, as evidenced by estimates of the population frequency and the odds ratio of the 1100delC mutation.

title: Decoding Mammalian Ribosome-mRNA States by Translational GTPase Complexes
text:
In eukaryotic cells, the accurate synthesis of proteins relies on a group of translational GTPases that collaborate with specific decoding factors to decipher the mRNA code on ribosomes. Through the determination of ribosome-bound decoding factor⋅GTPase structures representing different stages of translation elongation (aminoacyl-tRNA⋅eEF1A), termination (eRF1⋅eRF3), and ribosome rescue (Pelota⋅Hbs1l), our study uncovered how each decoding factor capitalizes on the flexibility of the ribosomal decoding center to modify ribosomal proteins and rRNA to varying degrees, resulting in distinct levels of large-scale ribosome movements. Comprehensive comparisons of the structures revealed that each decoding factor employs distinct strategies to communicate information from the decoding center to the associated GTPase. Additionally, our results provide a structural blueprint for how the ribosome recognizes and selectively engages with different decoding factor⋅GTPase complexes to ensure fidelity in protein synthesis.
Structural snapshots of the translation termination pathway further elucidated the conformational changes that coordinate the incorporation of decoding factors into the peptidyl transferase center. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of how the mammalian ribosome recognizes and binds to different decoding factor⋅GTPase complexes, and how these interactions enable accurate protein synthesis. In summary, this study reveals the intricate mechanism of translational GTPases and their collaboration with decoding factors to ensure faithful translation of mRNA into protein in eukaryotic cells.

title: Intestinal Cgi-58 Deficiency Reduces Postprandial Lipid Absorption
text: CGI-58, a protein linked with lipid droplets (LDs), promotes triglyceride (TG) hydrolysis in vitro. Mutations in human CGI-58 lead to TG accumulation in various tissues, including the intestine. Enterocytes are thought to lack TG-rich LDs, but a fatty meal triggers temporary cytosolic LD accumulation. These LDs are eventually cleared, suggesting the presence of TG hydrolytic machinery in enterocytes. However, the identities of these proteins remain unknown. We investigated the role of intestine-specific CGI-58 inactivation in mice and found that it significantly reduces postprandial plasma TG concentrations and intestinal TG hydrolase activity, resulting in a 4-fold increase in intestinal TG content and large cytosolic LD accumulation in absorptive enterocytes during the fasting state. Intestine-specific CGI-58 knockout mice showed mild but significant decreases in intestinal fatty acid absorption and oxidation. Surprisingly, inactivation of CGI-58 in the intestine led to increased plasma and intestinal cholesterol levels, while reducing hepatic cholesterol levels, without affecting intestinal cholesterol absorption or fecal neutral sterol excretion. Our findings suggest that intestinal CGI-58 is essential for efficient postprandial lipoprotein-TG secretion and maintaining hepatic and plasma lipid homeostasis. Our animal model will be useful in identifying how intestinal fat metabolism contributes to the pathogenesis of metabolic disorders, such as obesity and type 2 diabetes.

title: Transglutaminase 2 Undergoes a Large Conformational Change upon Activation
text: Human transglutaminase 2 (TG2), a member of a large family of enzymes that facilitate protein cross-linking, plays a crucial role in extracellular matrix biology across various tissues. However, its structural characterization has been limited due to the inaccessibility of its active site in crystallized forms of vertebrate transglutaminases. We have now successfully trapped human TG2 in complex with an inhibitor mimicking inflammatory gluten peptide substrates, and have solved its crystal structure at 2-angstrom resolution. The inhibitor maintains TG2 in a unique extended conformation, significantly different from previously crystallized transglutaminase structures. The active site is exposed, revealing the catalytic process takes place in a tunnel bridged by two tryptophan residues, which separate acyl-donor and acyl-acceptor and stabilize tetrahedral reaction intermediates. Site-directed mutagenesis experiments were conducted to study the acyl-acceptor side of the tunnel, leading to mutants with an increased preference for hydrolysis over transamidation. These findings provide a foundation for comprehending the catalytic and non-catalytic roles of TG2 in biology, as well as shedding light on how the autoantibody response to TG2 is induced in celiac sprue patients.

title: Lactic acidosis in patients with diabetes treated with metformin.
text:
Dear Editor,
From May 1995, when metformin was introduced in the United States, to June 30, 1996, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) received reports of lactic acidosis in 66 patients treated with metformin. Of these patients, 47 had their diagnosis confirmed through circulating lactate values (>5 mmol per liter) using established criteria for the diagnosis of lactic acidosis (Table 1).1,2 Among the 47 patients with confirmed diagnoses, 43 had one or more risk factors for lactic acidosis, including 30 (64%) with preexisting cardiac disease, of whom 18 had histories of congestive heart failure. . . .

title: The Apaf-1 apoptosome induces formation of caspase-9 homo- and heterodimers with distinct activities
text: According to conventional beliefs, initiator caspases are activated through proximity-induced homodimerization, but some research suggests that during apoptosis, caspase-9 may instead form a holoenzyme with the Apaf-1 apoptosome. Using a novel site-specific crosslinking technique, we provide the first direct evidence that procaspase-9 homodimerizes within the apoptosome, significantly increasing its binding affinity for the complex and inducing selective intramolecular cleavage at Asp-315. Interestingly, procaspase-9 can also bind to the NOD domain in Apaf-1, leading to the formation of a heterodimer that more effectively activates procaspase-3. Following cleavage, the intersubunit linker and associated conformational changes in caspase-9-p35/p12 inhibit its ability to form homodimers and heterodimers, but feedback cleavage by caspase-3 at Asp-330 removes the linker and partially restores activity to caspase-9-p35/p10. Thus, the apoptosome plays a crucial role in the formation of caspase-9 homo- and heterodimers, both of which are influenced by cleavage and contribute to its overall function.

title: Repositioning of aurora B promoted by chiasmata ensures sister chromatid mono-orientation in meiosis I.
text: During meiosis I, sister chromatids are juxtaposed or fused and oriented in a mono-way, while homologous chromosomes paired by chiasmata (bivalents) become bioriented. In the absence of chiasmata, biorientation of sister chromatids (univalents) has been observed in some species, including humans, although it carries a risk of aneuploidy. Our findings in fission yeast reveal that biorientation of fused sister kinetochores predominates during early prometaphase I prior to chiasmata, leading to abnormal anaphase upon loss of the spindle assembly checkpoint. When univalents are connected by chiasmata or an artificial tether, they are converted to monopolar attachments, which are then stabilized. This appears to be achieved by positioning kinetochores at the outer edge of the bivalent, while bringing the Aurora B protein, which destabilizes kinetochore-microtubule attachments, inward. Our research clarifies how chiasmata promote biorientation of bivalents over univalents at meiosis I.

title: Biophysical Constraints Arising from Compositional Context in Synthetic Gene Networks.
text:
Synthetic gene expression is susceptible to the intricate compositional context within genes (promoter structure, intergenic spacers, and ribosome binding sites). Conversely, the impact of the spatial arrangement and orientation of genes on expression levels in synthetic gene networks remains largely unexplored. To investigate the effects of intergenic context on gene expression, we evaluated the expression of genes arranged in convergent, divergent, or tandem orientations. Our findings indicate that inducing convergent genes resulted in up to 400% higher expression levels, greater ultrasensitivity, and a wider dynamic range compared to divergent- or tandem-oriented genes. Moreover, we discovered that the orientation of genes affects expression levels even when both genes are induced.
We propose that transcriptional interference in divergent and tandem genes, mediated by supercoiling, underlies the observed differences in expression levels. To test this hypothesis, we employed modeling and in vitro supercoiling relaxation experiments. Our results confirmed the mediating role of supercoiling and suggested that treatment with gyrase, an enzyme involved in DNA replication and repair, abrogated the intergenic context effects on expression levels.
Building on these findings, we redirected our efforts towards engineering a toggle switch with convergent genes, taking advantage of supercoiling effects to enhance threshold detection and switch stability. This approach yielded improved performance in detecting and switching between different expression states.
In summary, our study demonstrates the importance of intergenic compositional context in shaping gene expression in synthetic gene networks. By leveraging the principles of supercoiling and manipulating gene orientation, we were able to design and optimize a toggle switch with enhanced performance. These findings open up new avenues for the engineering of synthetic gene networks with optimized expression control.

title: Glucose repression in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
text:
Glucose serves as the primary source of energy for the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Although yeast cells can utilize a variety of carbon sources, the presence of glucose has a profound impact on the cell's metabolic activities. Specifically, glucose represses various molecular processes involved in the use of alternate carbon sources, as well as respiration and gluconeogenesis. This dominant influence of glucose on yeast carbon metabolism is mediated by several interconnected signaling and metabolic pathways that primarily regulate transcriptional activity, but can also reach post-transcriptional and post-translational levels.
This review focuses on the effects of glucose repression on yeast carbon metabolism, with a particular emphasis on the roles of the Snf3/Rgt2 glucose-sensing pathway and Snf1 signal transduction in establishing and relieving glucose repression.

title: The p21 Cdk-interacting protein Cip1 is a potent inhibitor of G1 cyclin-dependent kinases.
text: The protein kinase Cdk2, which is dependent on cyclins, associates with cyclins A, D, and E and has been linked to the regulation of the G1 to S phase transition in mammals. To identify potential regulators of Cdk2, we employed an advanced two-hybrid system to isolate human genes encoding proteins that interact with Cdk2. One of these genes encodes a novel 21-kDa protein called CIP1, which is present in immunoprecipitates containing cyclin A, cyclin D1, cyclin E, and Cdk2. p21CIP1 is a potent, tight-bindings inhibitor of Cdks and can inhibit the phosphorylation of Rb by cyclin A-Cdk2, cyclin E-Cdk2, cyclin D1-Cdk4, and cyclin D2-Cdk4 complexes. Further experiments showed that CIP1 and SV40 T antigen act in a mutually exclusive manner to regulate cell cycle progression.

title: Exploring the temporal structure of heterochronous sequences using TempEst (formerly Path-O-Gen)
