title: ERS/ESTS clinical guidelines on fitness for radical therapy in lung cancer patients (surgery and chemo-radiotherapy).
text: A multidisciplinary collaboration involving experts from the European Respiratory Society (ERS) and the European Society of Thoracic Surgery (ESTS) was conducted to develop recommendations and provide clinicians with up-to-date guidelines for assessing the fitness of lung cancer patients for surgery and chemo-radiotherapy. The project was divided into distinct topics, each assigned to at least two experts, who conducted their own literature searches according to their individual strategies. The draft reports produced by the experts were reviewed, discussed, and voted upon by the entire panel of experts. The evidence supporting each recommendation was summarized and graded using the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network Grading Review Group criteria. The resulting clinical practice guidelines included a functional algorithm for risk stratification of lung resection candidates, focusing on cardiological evaluation, forced expiratory volume in 1 second, systematic carbon monoxide lung diffusion capacity, and exercise testing. In contrast to lung resection, for which the scientific evidence is more robust, the panel was unable to recommend any specific test, cut-off value, or algorithm for assessment before chemo-radiotherapy due to the lack of available data. The experts recommend that lung cancer patients should be managed in specialized settings by multidisciplinary teams.

title: The Ran GTPase regulates mitotic spindle assembly
text: Ran is a ubiquitous nuclear GTPase with a well-established function in nuclear transport during interphase, although its roles in mitotic regulation are less clear. The GTPase state of Ran is controlled by two regulatory proteins: RanGAP1, a GTPase-activating protein, and RCC1, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor. Ran also interacts with RanBP1, a guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitor. RanBP1 has a high affinity for GTP-bound Ran, and it acts as a cofactor for RanGAP1, increasing the rate of GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis on Ran by approximately tenfold. RanBP1 levels fluctuate throughout the cell cycle. Our unpublished findings have shown that increased levels of RanBP1 prolong mitosis in mammalian cells and Xenopus egg extracts. To investigate the effect of elevated RanBP1 levels on mitosis, we studied the impact of exogenous RanBP1 on spindle assembly in Xenopus egg extracts during M phase. Our results indicate that Ran's role in spindle assembly is unrelated to nuclear transport and is likely mediated by alterations in microtubule dynamics.

title: A summary of the effects of antihypertensive medications on measured blood pressure.
text: Epidemiological studies examining family data on blood pressure (BP) are commonly hampered by the effects of blood pressure-lowering medications. We conducted a systematic review of 137 clinical trials involving monotherapy and 28 trials involving combination therapy, which collectively included 11,739 participants. We categorized the six major classes/groups of antihypertensive medications by ethnicity: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, alpha1-blockers, cardioselective beta-blockers (beta1-blockers), calcium channel blockers, thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics, and loop diuretics. Our findings indicate that for ethnic groups combined, monotherapy with ACE inhibitors, alpha1-blockers, and beta1-blockers resulted in an average reduction of systolic and diastolic BP by 12.5/9.5 mm Hg, while calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, and loop diuretics resulted in an average reduction of 15.3/9.8 mm Hg. However, ACE inhibitors, alpha1-blockers, and beta1-blockers were less effective in African Americans compared to non-African Americans, while calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, and loop diuretics were more effective in African Americans. For two-drug combination therapy, the BP-lowering effect of the second medication was 84% and 65% for systolic and diastolic BP, respectively. Our findings may be used to impute the pretreatment BP levels, thereby improving the power of epidemiologic analysis in studies where use of antihypertensive medications is a confounding factor in BP measurements.

title: Stem Cells and Early Lineage Development
text: The recent generation of pluripotent stem cell lines from various sources, including reprogrammed adult somatic cells, has raised questions about the equivalency of these different pluripotent states. Researchers have identified at least two distinct states representing epiblast progenitors in the blastocyst and pluripotent progenitors in the gastrulating embryo. Determining the initial developmental state of these pluripotent lines is crucial for establishing the starting point for differentiation towards therapeutically relevant cell types.

title: Divergent clonal evolution of castration resistant neuroendocrine prostate cancer
text: An increasingly recognized mechanism of resistance to androgen receptor (AR)-directed therapy in prostate cancer involves epithelial plasticity, where tumor cells exhibit low to absent AR expression and often display neuroendocrine features. Despite progress in understanding the etiology and molecular basis of this "alternative" treatment-resistant cell state, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. The present study sheds light on this resistance mechanism by analyzing whole-exome sequencing data of metastatic biopsies from patients. The findings point to a complex model of divergent clonal evolution, where CRPC-Adeno and CRPC-NE tumors show substantial genomic overlap. In contrast, genome-wide DNA methylation analysis revealed marked epigenetic differences between CRPC-NE tumors and CRPC-Adeno. The study suggests that epigenetic modifiers may play a role in the emergence of an "AR-indifferent" cell state, which is resistant to AR-directed therapy. These findings support the notion that divergent clonal evolution is a mechanism of treatment resistance in advanced prostate cancer.

title: S-phase-promoting cyclin-dependent kinases prevent re-replication by inhibiting the transition of replication origins to a pre-replicative state
text:
In the process of DNA replication and cell division, the activation of kinase complexes involving cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks) triggers these processes. However, previous assumptions suggested that the association of Cdks with different types of cyclins determines whether DNA replication (S phase) or cell division (M phase) will occur. New findings in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae challenge this idea, as it has been discovered that individual B-type cyclins (encoded by genes CLB1-CLB6) can have functions in both processes.
Results from S. cerevisiae strains lacking a certain type of Cdk (C1b1-C1b4) have shown that these cells can undergo DNA replication once but fail to enter mitosis. Researchers have discovered genes that allow such cells to undergo an extra round of DNA replication without mitosis. Specifically, the Clb5 kinase, which promotes S phase, remains active during the G2-phase arrest of cells in the parental strain, but its activity declines rapidly in sim mutants. Furthermore, increased expression of the CLB5 gene prevents re-replication. This suggests that a cyclin B-kinase that promotes DNA replication in G1-phase cells can prevent re-replication in G2-phase cells.
Inactivation of C1b kinases by expression of the specific C1b-Cdk1 inhibitor p40SIC1 is sufficient to induce a prereplicative state at origins of replication in cells blocked in G2/M phase by nocodazole. Re-activation of C1b-Cdk1 kinases induces a second round of DNA replication.
Based on these findings, the authors propose that S-phase-promoting cyclin B--Cdk complexes prevent re-replication during S, G2, and M phases by inhibiting the transition of replication origins to a pre-replicative state. This model can explain why origins "fire" only once per S phase and why S phase is dependent on the completion of the preceding M phase.

title: E-cadherin engagement stimulates proliferation via Rac1
text: Studies have shown that E-cadherin plays a role in suppressing tumor growth and inhibiting cell proliferation in culture. Our experiments revealed that reducing the number of cells seeded in a monolayer culture of normal rat kidney-52E (NRK-52E) or MCF-10A epithelial cells led to the release of cells from growth arrest. However, unexpectedly, further reducing the number of cells seeded to the point where they were isolated from neighboring cells actually decreased proliferation. Microengineered substrates were used to investigate the role of E-cadherin in proliferation, and our findings showed that engagement of E-cadherin stimulated proliferation at intermediate seeding densities. The proliferation arrest at high densities was not caused by E-cadherin, but instead resulted from a decrease in cell spreading due to crowding. Induction of Rac1 activity, which was specifically triggered by E-cadherin engagement at intermediate seeding densities, was found to be essential for the cadherin-stimulated proliferation. The regulation of Rac1 activation by E-cadherin was mediated by p120-catenin. Together, these findings demonstrate that E-cadherin plays a stimulatory role in proliferative regulation and uncover a simple mechanism by which cell-cell contact can modulate epithelial cell proliferation in different settings.

title: Structure of Actin-related protein 8 and its contribution to nucleosome binding
text: Nuclear actin-related proteins (Arps) are constituents of various chromatin remodeling complexes, yet their molecular functions within these complexes remain elusive. Through the crystal structure of the INO80 complex subunit Arp8 in its ATP-bound form, we have shed light on the mysterious functions of Arp8. Intriguingly, human Arp8 contains several insertions within the conserved actin fold, which are responsible for its inability to polymerize. Notably, one of these insertions wraps over the active site cleft and appears to stiffen the domain architecture, while shared nucleotide-binding features with actin suggest an allosterically controlled ATPase activity. Quantitative binding studies with nucleosomes and histone complexes have revealed that Arp8 and the Arp8-Arp4-actin-HSA subcomplex of INO80 strongly prefer nucleosomes and H3-H4 tetramers over H2A-H2B dimers, indicating that Arp8 functions as a nucleosome recognition module. In contrast, Arp4 exhibits a preference for free (H3-H4)(2) over nucleosomes and may potentially serve as a pivotal player in (dis)assembly processes during chromatin remodeling.

title: Regulation of β-Adrenergic Receptor Signaling by S-Nitrosylation of G-Protein-Coupled Receptor Kinase 2
text: beta-adrenergic receptors (beta-ARs), which are representative prototypical G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), play a crucial role in controlling various physiological processes. The GPCR kinases (GRKs) inhibit G-protein signaling by targeting receptors for endocytosis. Although nitric oxide (NO) and/or S-nitrosothiols (SNOs) can preserve beta-AR signaling in vivo, the underlying molecular mechanisms are still unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that SNOs enhance beta-AR expression and prevent agonist-induced receptor downregulation in mice, and in cells, SNOs reduce GRK2-mediated beta-AR phosphorylation and subsequent recruitment of beta-arrestin to the receptor, thus attenuating receptor desensitization and internalization. In both cell and tissue samples, GRK2 is S-nitrosylated by SNOs and NO synthases, and GRK2 S-nitrosylation increases upon stimulation of multiple GPCRs with agonists. We identify Cys340 of GRK2 as the primary site of inhibition by S-nitrosylation. Our research thus uncovers a central mechanism by which GPCR signaling is regulated.

title: Electroporation enables the efficient mRNA delivery into the mouse zygotes and facilitates CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing
text: Recent advances in the CRISPR/Cas9 system have significantly reduced the time required to generate mutant mice, yet the inclusion of a time-consuming microinjection step continues to limit its widespread application in high-throughput genetic analysis. To address this challenge, we have developed a simple, efficient, and large-scale genome editing method that replaces microinjection with electroporation of RNAs encoding the CRISPR/Cas9 system. We demonstrate the versatility of this method by performing single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN)-mediated knock-in experiments in mouse embryos, paving the way for large-scale genetic analysis in this model organism.

title: Summary
text: The genetic disorders Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) and restrictive dermopathy (RD) result from the accumulation of farnesylated prelamin A due to flaws in the lamin A maturation pathway. Both conditions present with aging symptoms that are accelerated. Despite knowing how prelamin A accumulation gives rise to these accelerated aging traits, the underlying mechanism remains a mystery. Our study unveils that in HGPS and RD fibroblasts, DNA damage checkpoints are persistent due to compromised genomic integrity. Disabling the checkpoint kinases ataxia-telangiectasia-mutated (ATM) and ATM- and Rad3-related (ATR) in these patient cells can partially overcome early replication arrest. Treating patient cells with a protein farnesyltransferase inhibitor (FTI) did not reduce DNA double-strand breaks and damage checkpoint signaling, although treatment significantly restored the abnormal nucleus shape. This suggests that DNA damage accumulation and aberrant nuclear morphology are distinctive phenotypes resulting from prelamin A buildup in these progeroid syndromes. Since DNA damage accumulation is a significant contributor to the symptoms of HGPS, our findings challenge the possibility of treating HGPS with FTIs alone.

title: The Buccaneer software for automated model building. 1. Tracing protein chains.
text: A novel approach for automatically tracing protein chains in experimental electron density maps is presented. This technique leverages the repeated application of an oriented electron density likelihood target function to identify likely Cα positions. The target function is applied in two stages: (1) to identify seed positions in the map and (2) to grow these initial Cα positions into extended chain fragments. Techniques for combining these fragments into an initial chain trace are also discussed.

title: Expression profile of genes modulated by Aloe emodin in human U87 glioblastoma cells.
text: Glioblastoma, the most aggressive and malignant form of glioma, appears to be resistant to various conventional chemotherapeutic agents. Therefore, researchers have been investigating potential targets to modulate specific molecular pathways involved in glioblastoma development and progression. Aloe emodin is believed to influence the expression of various genes in cancer cells. To understand the molecular mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effect of Aloe emodin on gene expression profiles in the human U87 glioblastoma cell line, researchers used microarray technology. The study revealed a total of 8,226 gene alterations out of 28,869 genes after treatment with 58.6 μg/ml for 24 hours. Of these, 34 genes showed statistically significant changes (p < 0.05), with 22 genes up-regulated and 12 genes down-regulated in response to Aloe emodin treatment. The genes were grouped into clusters based on their biological functions, revealing induction of expression of genes involved in apoptosis (programmed cell death) and tissue remodeling in U87 cells (p < 0.01). The study also confirmed these findings through quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). These results provide valuable insights into potential molecular targets for cancer therapy based on Aloe emodin treatment.

title: The miniature genome of a carnivorous plant Genlisea aurea contains a low number of genes and short non-coding sequences
text:
Background: Genlisea aurea (Lentibulariaceae) is a carnivorous plant with a uniquely small genome size of 63.6 megabases (Mb), one of the smallest known among higher plants. Analysis of genome size and phylogenetic data suggests that this condition is evolutionarily derived within the genus. Therefore, G. aurea serves as an ideal model organism for investigating the evolutionary mechanisms underlying genome reduction.
Results: We have sequenced and assembled the G. aurea genome through de novo drafting. The assembly consists of 10,687 contigs totaling 43.4 Mb and includes 17,755 complete and partial coding protein genes. Comparative analysis with the genome of Mimulus guttatus, another representative of the higher core Lamiales clade, reveals significant differences in gene content and non-coding region length.
Conclusions: Genome reduction was a complex process involving gene loss, reduction of intron and intergenic region lengths, but not intron loss. Gene loss is more prevalent among multigenic family members, indicating that genetic redundancy is essential for genome size reduction.

title: Abnormal Spine Morphology and Enhanced LTP in LIMK-1 Knockout Mice
text: In vitro experiments have suggested a role for the LIM kinase family in regulating cofilin phosphorylation and actin dynamics. Moreover, abnormal expression of LIMK-1 has been linked to Williams syndrome, a mental disorder marked by severe visuospatial cognitive impairments. However, the in vivo function of these kinases remains unclear. By studying LIMK-1 knockout mice, we have found significant in vivo involvement of LIMK-1 in regulating cofilin and the actin cytoskeleton. Our results demonstrate that the knockout mice display notable abnormalities in dendritic spine morphology and synaptic function, including enhanced hippocampal long-term potentiation. The knockout mice also exhibit altered fear responses and spatial learning. These findings indicate that LIMK-1 plays a critical role in dendritic spine morphogenesis and brain function.

title: Wdr5 Mediates Self-Renewal and Reprogramming via the Embryonic Stem Cell Core Transcriptional Network
text: The transcriptional and epigenetic networks of embryonic stem (ES) cells are crucial for self-renewal maintenance, but their functional interplay remains unclear. Our study reveals that WD repeat domain 5 (Wdr5), a core member of the mammalian Trithorax (trxG) complex, is positively correlated with the undifferentiated state and regulates ES cell self-renewal. We find that Wdr5, an "effector" of histone H3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3), interacts with the pluripotency transcription factor Oct4. Genome-wide protein localization and transcriptome analyses show overlapping gene regulatory functions between Oct4 and Wdr5. The Oct4-Sox2-Nanog circuitry and trxG complex collaborate in activating transcription of key self-renewal regulators, and Wdr5 is necessary for efficient formation of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. We propose an integrated model of transcriptional and epigenetic control, orchestrated by select trxG members, to maintain ES cell self-renewal and facilitate somatic cell reprogramming.

title: Neurons derived from reprogrammed fibroblasts functionally integrate into the fetal brain and improve symptoms of rats with Parkinson's disease.
text:
The long-term goal of nuclear transfer or alternative reprogramming techniques is to create personalized donor cells for transplantation therapy, avoiding immunorejection, a significant challenge in current transplantation medicine. It was recently demonstrated that the transcription factors Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc can reprogram mouse fibroblasts into induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. However, the therapeutic potential of iPS cells for neural cell replacement strategies had yet to be explored. Our study aimed to investigate the ability of iPS cells to differentiate into neural precursor cells and produce mature neurons and glia in culture and in vivo.
Using mouse iPS cells, we were able to efficiently generate neural precursor cells that were capable of differentiating into both neurons and glia in vitro. When transplanted into the fetal mouse brain, the cells migrated to various brain regions and differentiated into different types of neurons and glia, including glutamatergic, GABAergic, and catecholaminergic subtypes. Electrophysiological recordings and morphological analysis revealed that the grafted neurons had mature neuronal activity and were functionally integrated into the host brain. In addition, we were able to induce iPS cells to differentiate into dopamine neurons of midbrain origin and transplant them into the adult brain, where they were able to improve behavior in a rat model of Parkinson's disease.
To minimize the risk of tumor formation, we used fluorescence-activated cell sorting to separate contaminating pluripotent cells and committed neural cells from the grafted cells. Our findings demonstrate the potential of directly reprogrammed fibroblasts for neuronal cell replacement therapy in the animal model, suggesting a promising avenue for treating various neurological disorders.

title: Responses of primate frontal cortex neurons during natural vocal communication.
text:
The controversial history of the role of primate frontal cortex in vocal communication and its implications for language evolution has been a subject of debate. While evidence suggests that vocalization processing occurs in ventrolateral prefrontal cortex neurons, the primary location of vocal-motor activity has been conjectured to be subcortical. Direct observation of neural activity during natural vocal communication in freely moving animals has been limited due to the use of restraint chair studies in previous research.
In this study, we recorded the activity of single neurons across multiple regions of prefrontal and premotor cortex in freely moving marmosets engaged in a natural vocal behavior called antiphonal calling. Our aim was to investigate whether neurons in the marmoset frontal cortex exhibited responses during vocal signal processing and/or vocal motor production during active, natural communication. We observed motor-related changes in single neuron activity during vocal production, but relatively weak sensory responses for vocalization processing during this natural behavior. Vocal motor responses occurred both before and during call production and were typically synchronized with the timing of each vocalization pulse. Despite the relatively weak sensory responses, a population classifier was able to distinguish between neural activity that occurred during presentations of vocalization stimuli that elicited an antiphonal response and those that did not. These findings provide insight into the role that nonhuman primate frontal cortex neurons play in natural communication and establish a foundation for further testing the functional contributions of these neocortical areas during vocal behaviors.

title: Salt-inducible kinase 2 links transcriptional coactivator p300 phosphorylation to the prevention of ChREBP-dependent hepatic steatosis in mice.
text:
The association between obesity and type 2 diabetes has been linked to increased lipogenesis in the liver, which leads to fat accumulation in hepatocytes, a condition known as hepatic steatosis. This condition is a common cause of liver dysfunction in the United States. Carbohydrate-responsive element-binding protein (ChREBP), a transcriptional activator of glycolytic and lipogenic genes, has emerged as a key player in the development of hepatic steatosis in mice. However, the molecular mechanisms responsible for enhancing its transcriptional activity remain unclear.
In this study, we identified histone acetyltransferase (HAT) coactivator p300 and serine/threonine kinase salt-inducible kinase 2 (SIK2) as key upstream regulators of ChREBP activity. In cultured mouse hepatocytes, we showed that glucose-activated p300 acetylated ChREBP on Lys672, leading to increased transcriptional activity and lipogenesis. SIK2 inhibited p300 HAT activity by direct phosphorylation on Ser89, leading to decreased ChREBP-mediated lipogenesis in hepatocytes and mice overexpressing SIK2. Both liver-specific SIK2 knockdown and p300 overexpression led to hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance, and inflammation, phenotypes that were reversed by SIK2/p300 co-overexpression. Additionally, in mouse models of type 2 diabetes and obesity, low SIK2 activity was associated with increased p300 HAT activity, ChREBP hyperacetylation, and hepatic steatosis.
Our findings suggest that inhibition of hepatic p300 activity may be a beneficial treatment for hepatic steatosis in obesity and type 2 diabetes. Additionally, identifying SIK2 activators and specific p300 inhibitors as potential targets for pharmaceutical intervention may lead to new therapeutic strategies for managing liver dysfunction associated with these conditions.

title: A Role for NuSAP in Linking Microtubules to Mitotic Chromosomes
text: The spindle apparatus is a microtubule (MT)-based mechanism that attaches to and segregates chromosomes during cell division, including mitosis and meiosis. Self-organization of the spindle around chromatin involves the assembly of MTs, their attachment to chromosomes, and organization into a bipolar array. A regulator of spindle self-organization is RanGTP, which is generated at chromatin and activates a set of soluble, Ran-regulated spindle factors such as TPX2, NuMA, and NuSAP. The exact mechanisms by which these spindle factors direct and attach MTs to chromosomes are still open questions. Recently, the nucleolar and spindle-associated protein (NuSAP) was identified as an essential MT-stabilizing and bundling protein that is enriched at the central part of the spindle. In this study, we use biochemical reconstitution to show that NuSAP can efficiently adsorb to isolated chromatin and DNA and produce and retain high concentrations of MTs in the immediate vicinity of chromatin or DNA. Additionally, we find that NuSAP-chromatin interaction is subject to Ran regulation and can be suppressed by Importin alpha (Impalpha) and Imp7. We propose that the presence of MT binding agents such as NuSAP, which can be directly immobilized on chromatin, are critical for targeting MT production to vertebrate chromosomes during spindle self-organization.

title: Molecular features of cellular reprogramming and development
text: Over time, somatic cells become more specialized in their functions during ontogeny, but they can be manipulated in the laboratory to become other types of cells, including those with the ability to develop into any type of cell. Early attempts at nuclear reprogramming facing significant technological challenges, including somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) and cell fusion, which made it difficult to understand the exact regulatory programs that control cell identity. However, the discovery of reprogramming through the ectopic expression of a specific set of transcription factors, known as direct reprogramming, provided a more manageable platform to explore the molecular characteristics of cellular specification and differentiation, cell type stability, and pluripotency. We will discuss how cellular identity is maintained and controlled during developmental transitions, focusing on the transcriptional and epigenetic regulation of these processes, as they have been studied using direct reprogramming.

title: Small molecule modifiers of circadian clocks
text: Circadian clocks regulate the 24-hour cycle of vital physiological and behavioral processes in response to environmental changes daily. These clocks are remarkably accurate under constant conditions, yet highly responsive to resetting signals. With the core oscillator's molecular composition largely established, recent research has shifted towards exploring mechanisms/molecules that alter the clock. Specifically, small molecule modifiers, both intrinsic and extrinsic, are emerging as valuable tools for grasping basic clock biology and developing potential therapeutics for clock-related diseases. This review will concentrate on synthetic compounds capable of modifying circadian clocks' period, phase, or amplitude, with an emphasis on the mammalian clock. We will discuss the potential of utilizing these small molecule modifiers in both basic and applied research.

title: NVP-BEZ235, a dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor, prevents PI3K signaling and inhibits the growth of cancer cells with activating PI3K mutations.
text: Deregulation of the Phosphatidylinositol-3-Kinase (PI3K) pathway is a common occurrence in human cancer, often caused by inactivation of the tumor suppressor phosphatase and tensin homologue deleted from chromosome 10 or activating mutations of p110-alpha. These mutations lead to oncogenic activity of the enzyme and contribute to resistance to the anti-HER2 antibody trastuzumab. The PI3K pathway is therefore a promising target for cancer therapy. We have investigated NVP-BEZ235, a dual inhibitor of PI3K and the downstream mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR). NVP-BEZ235 inhibited the activation of downstream effectors, including Akt, S6 ribosomal protein, and 4EBP1, in breast cancer cells. The antiproliferative activity of NVP-BEZ235 was superior to that of the allosteric selective mTOR complex inhibitor everolimus in a panel of 21 cancer cell lines with different origins and mutation status. The described activation of Akt due to mTOR inhibition was prevented by higher doses of NVP-BEZ235. NVP-BEZ235 reversed the hyperactivation of the PI3K/mTOR pathway caused by oncogenic mutations of p110-alpha, E545K, and H1047R, and inhibited the proliferation of HER2-amplified BT474 cells that are resistant to trastuzumab. In trastuzumab-resistant BT474 H1047R breast cancer xenografts, NVP-BEZ235 inhibited PI3K signaling and showed potent antitumor activity. In treated animals, complete inhibition of PI3K signaling was observed in the skin at pharmacologically active doses, suggesting that the skin may serve as a surrogate tissue for pharmacodynamic studies. In summary, NVP-BEZ235 inhibits the PI3K/mTOR axis and exhibits antiproliferative and antitumoral activity against cancer cells with both wild-type and mutated p110-alpha, making it a promising target for cancer therapy.

title: Pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and pharmacogenetic determinants of osteonecrosis in children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
text: In this study, we investigated the association between glucocorticoid-induced osteonecrosis and various factors in children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) treated with steroids. We prospectively screened 364 children with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the hips and knees, regardless of symptoms, and found that the cumulative incidence of any (grade 1-4) osteonecrosis was 71.8%, and the incidence of symptomatic (grade 2-4) osteonecrosis was 17.6%. We identified two risk factors for symptomatic osteonecrosis: age >10 years (odds ratio [OR] 4.85, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.5-9.2, P = .00001) and more intensive treatment (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.2-4.9, P = .011). We also found that lower albumin (P = .05) and elevated cholesterol (P = .02) levels were associated with symptomatic osteonecrosis. Moreover, severe osteonecrosis (grade 3 or 4) was linked to poor dexamethasone clearance (P = .0005). When we adjusted for clinical features and polymorphisms of ACP1 (a gene that regulates lipid levels and osteoblast differentiation), we found that the association between osteonecrosis and rs12714403 polymorphism (OR 5.6, 95% CI 2.7-11.3, P = 1.9 × 10(-6)) remained significant. Our findings suggest that older age, lower albumin, higher lipid levels, and dexamethasone exposure are associated with osteonecrosis, and that inherited genomic variation may play a role in the development of this complication.

title: Prevention of Rectal SHIV Transmission in Macaques by Daily or Intermittent Prophylaxis with Emtricitabine and Tenofovir
text:
Background: Despite the lack of an effective vaccine, HIV continues to spread globally, underscoring the need for alternative strategies to limit its transmission. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with antiretroviral drugs may be a promising intervention if highly effective and cost-effective PrEP modalities are identified. To evaluate the efficacy of different PrEP regimens, we conducted a study in macaques using daily and intermittent PrEP regimens with increasing antiviral activity.
Methods and Findings: We employed a repeat-exposure macaque model with 14 weekly rectal virus challenges. Each of six rhesus macaques in groups 1-3 received a different PrEP regimen, consisting of subcutaneous emtricitabine (FTC), oral FTC and tenofovir-disoproxil fumarate (TDF), or subcutaneous FTC and a higher dose of TDF, respectively. A fourth group of six macaques received an intermittent PrEP regimen similar to group 3, but only 2 hours before and 24 hours after each weekly challenge. The results were compared to 18 untreated control macaques. The risk of infection was 3.8-7.8 times lower in macaques treated with daily PrEP (groups 1 and 2), and all six animals in group 3 were protected. In contrast, breakthrough infections with blunted viremias occurred in two of six animals in group 3, and all six animals in group 4 (receiving intermittent PrEP) were protected.
Conclusions: This study suggests that single antiretroviral drugs may provide some protection against HIV infection, but a combination of drugs may be needed to increase protection. Intermittent PrEP, delivered 2 hours before and 24 hours after each challenge, provides comparable protection to daily PrEP in this SHIV/macaque model. These findings support PrEP trials in humans and identify promising PrEP modalities.

title: Direct-coupling analysis of residue co-evolution captures native contacts across many protein families
text: The uniformity in the three-dimensional structures of homologous proteins imposes strict constraints on their sequence variability, suggesting that the correlation among amino acid compositions at different sequence positions can be exploited to infer the spatial organization within the tertiary protein structure. To distinguish between direct and indirect correlations, a recently developed method called Direct Coupling Analysis (DCA) has been employed (Weigt et al., 2009, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences). In this study, we have created a computationally efficient implementation of DCA, enabling us to evaluate the accuracy of contact prediction by analyzing a large number of protein domains based solely on their sequence information. Our findings demonstrate that DCA successfully predicts a considerable number of contacts, which aligns with the global structure of the contact map for most of the protein domains examined. Moreover, our analysis uncovers additional signals beyond intra-domain contact predictions, such as those arising from alternative protein conformations, ligand-mediated residue couplings, and inter-domain interactions in protein oligomers. These findings suggest that contacts predicted by DCA can serve as a reliable guide for facilitating computational predictions of alternative protein conformations, protein complex formation, and even the de novo prediction of protein domain structures, provided a large number of homologous sequences are available due to advances in genome sequencing.

title: Variation in antibiotic prescribing and its impact on recovery in patients with acute cough in primary care: prospective study in 13 countries.
text:
Objective: To investigate the variation in antibiotic prescribing patterns for acute cough in different European countries and assess the impact on recovery.
Design: Cross-sectional observational study involving primary care clinicians from 14 research networks in 13 European countries.
Participants: Adults presenting with new or worsening cough or clinical symptoms suggesting lower respiratory tract infection.
Main Outcome Measures: Antibiotic prescribing rates by clinicians and total symptom severity scores over time.
Results: A total of 3402 participants were enrolled (clinicians completed case report forms for 99% [3368] of participants, and 80% [2714] returned symptom diaries). The mean symptom severity scores at presentation ranged from 19 (scale range 0-100) in networks based in Spain and Italy to 38 in the network based in Sweden. Antibiotic prescribing varied widely between networks, ranging from 20% to nearly 90% (53% overall), with different classes of antibiotics prescribed. The most commonly prescribed antibiotic was amoxicillin, but this varied from 3% of antibiotics prescribed in the Norwegian network to 83% in the English network. Fluoroquinolones were not prescribed at all in three networks, but were prescribed for 18% in the Milan network. After adjusting for clinical presentation and demographics, significant differences remained in antibiotic prescribing, ranging from Norway (odds ratio 0.18, 95% confidence interval 0.11-0.30) to Slovakia (11.2, 6.20-20.27) compared with the overall mean (proportion prescribed: 0.53). Recovery rates were similar for patients who were and were not prescribed antibiotics once clinical presentation was taken into account (coefficient -0.01, P<0.01).
Conclusions: The considerable variation in antibiotic prescribing for acute cough in Europe cannot be explained by differences in clinical presentation. There is no association between antibiotic prescribing patterns and clinically important differences in recovery.
Trial Registration: Clinicaltrials.gov NCT00353951.

title: Dorsomorphin, a Selective Small Molecule Inhibitor of BMP Signaling, Promotes Cardiomyogenesis in Embryonic Stem Cells
text:
Pluripotent embryonic stem (ES) cells hold great promise as a source of cells for regenerative therapy due to their ability to differentiate into any cell type in the body. However, the mechanisms underlying lineage specification of these cells are not well understood, and generating sufficient quantities of desired cell types remains a significant challenge. Small molecules, particularly those that modulate key developmental pathways, have the potential to serve as tools for studying in vitro lineage specification and directing the differentiation of stem cells towards specific cell types.
Our study demonstrates the use of dorsomorphin, a selective small molecule inhibitor of BMP signaling, to induce myocardial differentiation in mouse ES cells. We found that dorsomorphin treatment during the initial 24 hours of ES cell differentiation robustly increases the yield of spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes with a 20-fold increase compared to untreated controls. In contrast, the endogenous BMP antagonist Noggin only weakly induces cardiomyogenesis. Quantitative PCR analyses of differentiating ES cells revealed that pharmacological inhibition of BMP signaling during the early critical stage promotes the development of the cardiomyocyte lineage, but reduces the differentiation of endothelial, smooth muscle, and hematopoietic cells.
Our findings suggest that administration of a selective small molecule BMP inhibitor during the initial stages of ES cell differentiation significantly promotes the differentiation of primitive pluripotent cells towards the cardiomyocytic lineage, apparently at the expense of other mesodermal lineages. These results demonstrate the potential of small molecule modulators of developmental pathways, such as dorsomorphin, as versatile pharmacological tools for stem cell research and regenerative medicine.

title: Cineradiography of Monkey Lip-Smacking Reveals Putative Precursors of Speech Dynamics
text: A distinctive attribute of speech is its characteristic 5 Hz rhythm. One theory proposes that this rhythm emerged through modifications to facial movements in ancestral primates. If this hypothesis has any validity, a comparative analysis may provide insight. To test this idea, we employed cineradiography (X-ray movies) to quantify and characterize the internal dynamics of the macaque monkey vocal tract during lip-smacking (a rhythmic facial expression) and chewing. Previous studies in humans revealed that speech movements are faster than chewing movements, and the coordination between vocal tract structures is different between the two behaviors. If speech evolved from a rhythmic ancestral facial movement, it is hypothesized that monkey lip-smacking versus chewing should also exhibit these distinctions. Our findings indicate that the lips, tongue, and hyoid move with a 5 Hz speech-like rhythm during lip-smacking, yet this rhythm is not observed during chewing. Moreover, the functional coordination between these structures differed for each behavior. These data offer empirical support for the notion that the human speech rhythm evolved from the rhythmic facial expressions of ancient primates.

title: Interneuronal DISC1 regulates NRG1-ErbB4 signalling and excitatory-inhibitory synapse formation in the mature cortex.
text: The neuroprotective protein Neuregulin-1 (NRG1) and its receptor ErbB4 play crucial roles in neurodevelopment, but the mechanisms underlying their signaling in the mature brain are poorly understood. Discoidin (DISC1), a multifunctional scaffold protein, has been shown to mediate various cellular processes. Here, we present a functional link between DISC1 and NRG1-ErbB4 signaling in mature cortical interneurons. Using cell type-specific gene modification in vitro and in vivo, including in a mutant DISC1 mouse model, we demonstrate that DISC1 inhibits NRG1-induced ErbB4 activation and signaling. This effect is likely mediated by competitive inhibition of ErbB4 binding to PSD95. Additionally, we show that interneuronal DISC1 influences NRG1-ErbB4-mediated phenotypes in the fast spiking interneuron-pyramidal neuron circuit. Post-mortem brain analysis and some genetic studies have reported deficits in interneurons and genes involved in DISC1, NRG1, and ErbB4 in schizophrenia. Our findings suggest a potential mechanism by which cross-talk between DISC1 and NRG1-ErbB4 signaling may contribute to these deficits.

title: The Proto-Oncogene c-maf Is Responsible for Tissue-Specific Expression of Interleukin-4
text: The molecular underpinnings of the distinct cytokine expression profiles of CD4+ T helper 1 (Th1) and Th2 subsets remain enigmatic. Our study uncovers that the proto-oncogene c-maf, a basic region/leucine zipper transcription factor, controls tissue-specific expression of interleukin-4 (IL-4). c-Maf is specifically expressed in Th2 cell clones and is induced during normal precursor cell differentiation along a Th2, but not Th1, lineage. c-Maf binds to a c-Maf response element (MARE) located in the proximal IL-4 promoter adjacent to a site footprinted by extracts from Th2 cell clones. By introducing c-Maf into Th1 cells, B cells, and nonlymphoid cells, we found that it transactivates the IL-4 promoter, a function that maps to the MARE and Th2-specific footprint. Additionally, we discovered that c-Maf works in conjunction with the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NF-ATp) to initiate endogenous IL-4 production by B cells. Manipulation of c-Maf may have implications for modifying Th subset ratios in human disease.

title: hClock gene expression in human colorectal carcinoma.
text: In this study, we aimed to investigate changes in the expression of the human Circadian Clock (hClock) gene in colorectal carcinomas (CRCs) and to explore the possible implications. Previous research has shown that disruptions to the circadian rhythm are one of the underlying factors that contribute to the development of CRCs. However, the molecular modifications to the circadian genes involved in CRCs have yet to be studied. Using immunofluorescence and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis, we examined the expression of hCLOCK protein and gene in 30 cases of CRC. Our results showed that the hCLOCK protein was expressed in all specimens obtained from CRC patients, with higher levels of expression observed in the tumor tissues compared to non-cancerous tissues. The hClock gene was expressed in all specimens, with significantly higher expression observed in CRC cases compared to non-cancerous tissues. We also found a strong positive linear correlation between hClock gene expression and protein expression in human CRCs, as well as correlation with other clock-controlled genes such as ARNT, HIF-1α, and VEGF. These findings suggest that hCLOCK may interact with HIF-1α/ARNT and stimulate VEGF expression, leading to tumor angiogenesis and metastasis. Additionally, our results indicate that hClock is stably expressed in human colorectal mucosa and play an important role in regulating the expression of downstream clock-controlled genes.

title: The Antiretroviral Therapy in Lower Income Countries (ART-LINC) Collaboration and ART Cohort Collaboration (ART-CC) groups Summary
text: In this study, we compared the baseline characteristics and outcomes of HIV-1-infected patients starting highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) in low-income and high-income settings. We analyzed data from 4810 treatment-naïve adult patients from 18 HAART programs in Africa, Asia, and South America (low-income settings) and 22,217 patients from 12 HIV cohort studies in Europe and North America (high-income settings). We found that patients in low-income settings had lower CD4 cell counts, were more likely to be female, and more likely to start treatment with a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) compared to patients in high-income settings. Although the median number of CD4 cells gained and the percentage of patients reaching HIV-1 RNA levels lower than 500 copies/mL were similar at 6 months, mortality was higher in low-income settings (124 deaths during 2236 person-years of follow-up) compared to high-income settings (414 deaths during 20,532 person-years). The adjusted hazard ratio (HR) of mortality comparing low-income with high-income settings decreased from 4.3 (95% CI 1.6-11.8) during the first month to 1.5 (0.7-3.0) during months 7-12. Providing treatment free of charge in low-income settings was associated with lower mortality (adjusted HR 0.23; 95% CI 0.08-0.61). Our findings suggest that patients starting HAART in resource-poor settings have increased mortality rates in the first months on therapy, which may be reduced by timely diagnosis and assessment of treatment eligibility, as well as the provision of free HAART.

title: A family of phosphoinositide 3-kinases in Drosophila identifies a new mediator of signal transduction
text:
Mammalian phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI 3-kinases) play essential roles in receptor-mediated signal transmission and have been implicated in processes such as transformation and cell growth. In yeast, PI 3-kinase activity is required for protein transport. Using PCR, we identified three distinct PI 3-kinases in Drosophila: PI3K_92D, which is similar to p110 alpha; PI3K_59F, which is homologous to Vps34p; and PI3K_68D, a novel PI 3-kinase that is ubiquitously expressed throughout the Drosophila life cycle. PI3K_68D encodes a protein of 210 kDa lacking sequences implicated in linking p110 PI 3-kinases to p85 adaptor proteins, but with an amino-terminal proline-rich sequence that could bind to SH3 domains and a carboxy-terminal C2 domain. In vitro biochemical assays revealed that PI3K_68D has a unique substrate specificity, preferring phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate, and is unable to phosphorylate phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate, the putative in vivo substrate for p110.
Our findings establish a family of PI 3-kinases in Drosophila, including a novel class represented by PI3K_68D. PI3K_68D has the potential to interact with signaling proteins containing SH3 domains, lacks p85-adaptor-binding sequences, has a calmodulin-independent phospholipid-binding domain, and shows a limited in vitro substrate specificity, suggesting that it could activate a distinct signal transduction pathway.

title: Mammalian RAD52 Functions in Break-Induced Replication Repair of Collapsed DNA Replication Forks
text: Human cancers are characterized by the presence of oncogene-induced DNA replication stress (DRS), which renders them reliant on repair pathways such as break-induced replication (BIR) for damaged DNA replication forks. To gain insight into BIR, we conducted a targeted siRNA screen for genes that are essential for G1 to S phase progression when oncogenic cyclin E is overexpressed. Among the top hits was RAD52, a gene that is dispensable for normal mouse development. In cells where DNA replication forks collapsed due to oncogenes or chemicals, the Rad52 protein localized to DRS foci. By depleting Rad52 with siRNA or knocking out the gene using CRISPR/Cas9, we discovered that restarting collapsed DNA forks and repairing DNA damage in cells experiencing DRS became compromised. In fact, homozygous deletion of the Rad52 gene in cancer-prone, heterozygous APC mutant mice significantly suppressed tumor growth and lengthened lifespan. These findings suggest that mammalian RAD52 helps repair collapsed DNA replication forks in cancer cells.

title: Neural crest cell lineage segregation in the mouse neural tube.
text: Neural crest (NC) cells originate in the dorsal neural tube (NT) and migrate into the embryo to give rise to various cell types. A significant question that remains unresolved is when and how the fate of NC cells is determined. There is evidence for multipotent NC cells that make their fates known during or after migration. Some studies suggest that the NC may be divided into subpopulations of distinct precursors within the NT. We investigated this question in the mouse embryo and found that a particular subpopulation of cells on the most dorsomedial aspect of the NT express the receptor tyrosine kinase Kit (previously known as c-kit), emigrate exclusively into the developing dermis, and then express markers characteristic of the melanocyte lineage. These cells are thus melanocyte progenitor cells, and they are generated primarily at the midbrain-hindbrain junction and cervical trunk, with significant numbers also present in the lower trunk. Other cells within the dorsal NT are Kit-, migrate ventrally, and, starting from embryonic day 9.5, express the neurotrophin receptor p75. These cells are likely to give rise to ventral NC derivatives such as neurons and glia. The p75+ cells are located ventrolateral to the Kit+ cells in areas of the NT where these two cell types are found. These data provide direct in vivo evidence for NC lineage segregation within the mouse neural tube.

title: How absolute is zero? An evaluation of historical and current definitions of malaria elimination
text:
A comprehensive understanding of the terminology used in malaria control and elimination initiatives is crucial to ensure accurate forecasting of resource and operational requirements. However, a lack of clarity surrounds key terms such as "control," "elimination," and "eradication," resulting in ongoing debates and confusion. To address this issue, this paper provides a historical review of commonly used terms and their underlying mathematical concepts, using simple branching process models to illustrate their application in program planning.
The paper argues that current conceptions of elimination are insufficient for providing practical strategic milestones for malaria control and elimination programs. Instead, new conceptual definitions are suggested to more precisely describe the old goals of "control"—now referred to as "controlled low-endemic malaria"—and "elimination." Additionally, the paper proposes a third state, "controlled non-endemic malaria," to describe the epidemiological condition in which endemic transmission has been interrupted, but malaria resulting from onward transmission from imported infections continues to occur at a sufficiently high level that elimination has not been achieved.
To make these concepts relevant, measurable, and achievable for a particular environment, the paper discusses guidelines for deriving operational definitions and metrics. The paper concludes that a more nuanced understanding of these terms is necessary to effectively eliminate malaria and provides a framework for operationalizing these concepts in program planning and implementation.

title: Fission Yeast Scm3: A CENP-A Receptor Required for Integrity of Subkinetochore Chromatin
text: The mechanisms governing the specific insertion of CENP-A at centromeres are inadequately understood. Mis16 and Mis18 are essential for the localization of CENP-A at centromeres and share a conserved structure across fission yeast and humans. Fission yeast sim1 mutants that abrogate kinetochore domain silencing are defective in Scm3(Sp), the ortholog of budding yeast Scm3(Sc). Scm3(Sp) depends on Mis16/18 for its centromere localization, similar to how they are recruited to centromeres in late anaphase. Of note, Scm3(Sp) coimmunopurifies with CENP-A(Cnp1) and associates with CENP-A(Cnp1) in vitro, yet localizes independently of intact CENP-A(Cnp1) chromatin and is differentially released from chromatin. While Scm3(Sc) has been proposed to form a distinct hexameric nucleosome with CENP-A(Cse4) and histone H4 at budding yeast point centromeres, we favor a model in which Scm3(Sp) acts as a CENP-A(Cnp1) receptor/assembly factor, collaborating with Mis16 and Mis18 to receive CENP-A(Cnp1) from the Sim3 escort and orchestrate the assembly of CENP-A(Cnp1) into subkinetochore chromatin.

title: The Molecular Basis for Oat Intolerance in Patients with Celiac Disease
text:
Background: Celiac disease is a small intestinal inflammatory disorder characterized by malabsorption, nutrient deficiency, and a range of clinical manifestations. It is caused by an inappropriate immune response to dietary gluten and is treated with a gluten-free diet. Recent feeding studies have found that oats are safe for celiac disease patients and are now often included in their diet. This study aimed to investigate whether oat intolerance exists in celiac disease and to characterize the cells and processes underlying this intolerance.
Methods and Findings: We selected nine adults with celiac disease who had a history of oats exposure for the study. Four of the patients had clinical symptoms on an oats-containing diet, and three of these patients had intestinal inflammation typical of celiac disease at the time of oats exposure. We established oats-avenin-specific and -reactive intestinal T-cell lines from these three patients, as well as from two other patients who appeared to tolerate oats. The avenin-reactive T-cell lines recognized avenin peptides in the context of HLA-DQ2, which have sequences rich in proline and glutamine residues similar to wheat gluten epitopes. Deamidation (glutamine->glutamic acid conversion) by tissue transglutaminase was involved in the avenin epitope formation.
Conclusions: We conclude that some celiac disease patients have avenin-reactive mucosal T-cells that can cause mucosal inflammation. Oat intolerance may be a reason for villous atrophy and inflammation in patients with celiac disease who are eating oats but otherwise adhering to a strict gluten-free diet. Clinical follow-up of celiac disease patients eating oats is advised.

title: A comparison of continuous and bi-level positive airway pressure non-invasive ventilation in patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: a meta-analysis
text:
Study: Comparison of Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) and Bi-Level Positive Airway Pressure (BiPAP) Noninvasive Ventilation in Patients with Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema
Introduction:
We conducted a study to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) compared to bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP) noninvasive ventilation in patients with cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
Methods: We systematically searched the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, EMBASE, and MEDLINE databases for randomized controlled studies that compared CPAP and BiPAP treatment in patients with cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Two reviewers assessed the quality of the studies and independently extracted the data.
Results: Our analysis included seven randomized controlled studies involving a total of 290 patients with cardiogenic pulmonic edema. We found that hospital mortality and the risk of requiring invasive ventilation were not significantly different between patients treated with CPAP and those treated with BiPAP. Stratifying studies based on whether they used fixed or titrated pressure during BiPAP treatment and studies involving patients with or without hypercapnia did not change the results. Additionally, the duration of noninvasive ventilation required to resolve pulmonary edema and the length of hospital stay were not significantly different between the two groups. However, there was an insignificant trend towards an increase in new onset acute myocardial infarction in patients treated with BiPAP.

Conclusion: Our findings suggest that BiPAP does not offer any significant clinical benefits over CPAP in patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Given the limited data available, the choice of modality will depend on the equipment available until a large randomized controlled trial shows significant clinical benefits and cost-effectiveness of BiPAP versus CPAP in patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

title: CaMKII induces permeability transition through Drp1 phosphorylation during chronic β-AR stimulation
text:
The mechanism by which chronic activation of β-adrenergic receptors (β-ARs) leads to the opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) is unclear. However, our study has shed light on this phenomenon, demonstrating that chronic administration of isoproterenol (ISO) can cause persistently increased mPTP openings, which ultimately lead to mitochondrial damage and cardiac dysfunction.
We have found that this effect is mediated by the phosphorylation of the mitochondrial fission protein, dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent kinase II (CaMKII) at a specific serine site (S616). Inhibiting Drp1 activity or mutating this phosphorylation site abolishes the ability of CaMKII or ISO to induce mPTP opening and myocyte death in vitro, and rescues heart hypertrophy in vivo.
Notably, our study has also revealed that in human failing hearts, the phosphorylation of Drp1 at S616 is significantly increased. These findings uncover a downstream pathway linked to chronic β-AR stimulation, where CaMKII, Drp1, and mPTP work together to connect cytosolic stress signals with mitochondrial dysfunction in the heart. This mechanistic insight provides new avenues for the development of therapeutic strategies to prevent or treat cardiac dysfunction associated with chronic β-AR stimulation.

title: MicroRNA Response of Primary Human Macrophages to Arcobacter Butzleri Infection
text: The burgeoning role of microRNAs (miRNAs) in infectious diseases is becoming increasingly evident, and their potential use as diagnostic tools and therapeutic targets has become the primary focus of research. To investigate the immune signaling of macrophages in response to Arcobacter (A.) butzleri infection, an emerging foodborne pathogen that causes gastroenteritis, we evaluated the expression of miRNAs in primary human macrophages infected with A. butzleri. Our research revealed the expression of several miRNAs previously linked to bacterial infections, such as miR-155, miR-125, and miR-212, which play a crucial role in fine-tuning the immune response through Toll-like receptor signaling. Additionally, we identified novel miRNAs, such as miR-3613, miR-2116, miR-671, miR-30d, and miR-629, that were differentially regulated in A. butzleri-infected cells. These miRNAs target pathways involved in apoptosis and endocytosis, which may be essential for A. butzleri pathogenesis. Our findings contribute significantly to the understanding of the interaction between A. butzleri and human innate immune cells, illuminating the underlying regulatory mechanisms in macrophages during infection.

title: The circadian factor Period 2 modulates p53 stability and transcriptional activity in unstressed cells
text:
Human Period 2 (hPer2) is a transcriptional regulator at the core of the circadian clock mechanism, responsible for maintaining the negative feedback loop that sustains the clock. Its dysfunction has been implicated in various human diseases, including cancer and increased genetic stress susceptibility. To identify an uncharacterized checkpoint node in which circadian components integrate environmental stress signals with the DNA damage response, we investigated hPer2's role in modulating the activity of the tumor suppressor protein p53.
We found that hPer2 binds to the C-terminal half of human p53 (hp53) and forms a stable trimeric complex with hp53's negative regulator, Mdm2, preventing Mdm2 from ubiquitinating and degrading hp53 by the proteasome. Lower expression of hPer2 resulted in reduced hp53 protein levels, while its overexpression affected both hp53 stability and transcriptional activity of targeted genes. In essence, our findings show that hPer2 plays a crucial role in maintaining basal levels of hp53, enabling the cell to rapidly respond with a transcriptional program when needed, thereby improving the cell's ability to withstand genotoxic stress.

title: Properties of Commelina yellow mottle virus's complete DNA sequence, genomic discontinuities and transcript suggest that it is a pararetrovirus.
text:
The second group of plant viruses known to possess a circular double-stranded DNA genome are the non-enveloped bacilliform viruses. In this study, we have characterized the viral transcript and determined the complete sequence of the genome of Commelina mellow mottle virus (CoYMV), a member of this group.
Using viral transcript analysis, we observed that CoYMV encodes a single terminally-redundant genome-length plus 120 nucleotide transcript, with a fraction of the transcripts being polyadenylated. Our analysis of the genome sequence revealed that the genome is 7489 base pairs in size and contains three open reading frames that could encode proteins of 23, 15, and 216 kDa. The functionality of the 25 and 15 kDa proteins is currently unknown. The 216 kDa polypeptide displays similarities to the coat protein and protease/reverse transcriptase polyprotein of cauliflower mosaic virus, suggesting that it is a polyprotein that is proteolytically processed to yield the virion coat protein, a protease, and replicase (reverse transcriptase and ribonuclease H).
The genome of CoYMV is composed of two complementary strands, each interruptede by site-specific discontinuities. The locations of these discontinuities, as well as the presence of a region on the CoYMV transcript capable of annealing with the 3'-end of cytosolic initiator methionine tRNA, suggest replication through reverse transcription. To test this hypothesis, we constructed a construct containing 1.3 CoYMV genomes and used Agrobacterium-mediated infection to infect Commelina diffusa, the natural host of CoYMV.
We hope that this study will provide valuable insights into the structure and function of non-enveloped bacilliform viruses, and will contribute to our understanding of the complex interactions between plant viruses and their hosts.

title: The Glucocorticoid Receptor Inhibits
text: Glucocorticoids suppress NFκB-mediated activation of pro-inflammatory genes such as interleukin-8 (IL-8) and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1). Our experiments indicate that the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) mediates this effect by interacting with NFκB through protein-protein interactions. Specifically, we found that the GR's zinc binding region (ZBR), which includes its DNA binding and dimerization functions, directly binds to the dimerization domain of the RelA subunit of NFκB in vitro. Moreover, we demonstrate in vivo and in vitro that GR does not disrupt NFκB's ability to bind to its response elements. In transient transfections, we discovered that the GR ligand binding domain is essential for repressing NFκB, but not for associating with it. GR can also repress an NFκB derivative bearing a heterologous activation domain. To investigate the mechanism by which GR regulates NFκB-activated transcription, we used chromatin immunoprecipitation assays in untransfected A549 cells. As expected, we found that the inflammatory signal TNFα stimulates pre-initiation complex (PIC) assembly at the IL-8 and ICAM-1 promoters, leading to phosphorylation of the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II (pol II) at serines 2 and 5 in its carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) heptapeptide repeats (YSPTSPS). Remarkably, GR does not inhibit PIC assembly under repressing conditions, but rather interferes with the phosphorylation of serine 2 of the pol II CTD.

title: Regulation of myeloid cell function through the CD200 receptor.
text: Myeloid cells play a crucial role in chronic inflammatory diseases due to their ability to exhibit pro-inflammatory, destructive, and remodeling actions. The protein CD200 is expressed on a range of cell types, while the recently discovered CD200R is found on myeloid cells and T cells. Deleting CD200 in vivo leads to myeloid cell dysregulation and heightened susceptibility to autoimmune inflammation, suggesting that the CD200-CD200R interaction plays a role in immune suppression. Our study demonstrates that CD200R agonists suppress myeloid cell function in vitro and define a dose-response relationship between receptor expression and cellular inhibition. We also demonstrate that CD200R agonists inhibit cytokine secretion from mouse peritoneal macrophages stimulated with IFN-gamma and IL-17, but not with LPS. Inhibition of cytokine production was only observed in low CD200R-expressing cells when the CD200R agonists were further cross-linked. Additionally, we show that CD200R agonists inhibit IL-5 and IL-13 secretion from human PBMCs, with inhibition seen only when the CD200R on monocytes was cross-linked, but not on CD4+ T cells. Overall, our findings provide direct evidence that the CD200-CD200R interaction controls myeloid cell function in both murine and human systems, suggesting potential clinical applications for CD200R agonists in the treatment of chronic inflammatory diseases.

title: Management of hepatitis C disease among VA patients with schizophrenia and substance use disorders.
text:
Objective: To compare rates of hepatitis C (HCV) infection, testing, and treatment among patients with schizophrenia, a substance use disorder, or co-occurring schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and a substance use disorder, and a control group.
Methods: Data was obtained from 293,445 patients of the Northwest Veterans Healthcare Administration.
Results: The substance use disorder group composed 13.6% of the sample, while the schizophrenia group consisted of 1.6% and the co-occurring disorders group was 1.4%. These groups were found to be approximately four, two, and six times more likely as the control group to receive HCV testing and incur HCV infection, respectively. However, the rate of interferon (IFN) therapy was significantly lower for the substance use group and the group with co-occurring disorders, although the magnitude of the differences was not substantial, suggesting that these high-risk groups were not excluded from IFN therapy.

title: Equity in adherence to antiretroviral therapy among economically vulnerable adolescents living with HIV in Uganda
text: Research from sub-Saharan Africa indicates that children marginalized by poverty have been disproportionately affected by HIV, with many contracting the virus through mother-to-child transmission. For adolescents living with HIV, adherence to life-saving treatment regimens is often influenced by a complex mix of economic and social factors that affect their families and exacerbate health problems. Using data from the National Institute of Child and Human Development (NICHD)-funded Suubi+Adherence study, we examined how individual and composite measures of equity relate to self-reported adherence among Ugandan adolescents aged 10-16 (n = 702) living with HIV. Our findings showed that greater ownership of assets, specifically having seven or more tangible assets, was associated with higher odds of self-reported adherence (OR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.00-2.85). Additionally, we found that proximity to the nearest health clinic had an impact on adherence, with youth living closest to a clinic being more likely to report optimal adherence (OR = 1.49, 95% CI: 0.92-2.40). Moreover, by examining the impact of composite equity scores on adherence, we discovered that adolescents with greater economic advantage in household assets, financial savings, and caregiver employment had higher odds of adherence by a factor of 1.70 (95% CI: 1.07-2.70). These findings suggest that addressing economic and social inequities may be beneficial for increasing adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) among economically vulnerable youth, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. This study is one of the first to investigate the question of equity in adherence to ART among economically vulnerable youth with HIV.

title: High-Resolution Phenotypic Profiling Defines Genes Essential for Mycobacterial Growth and Cholesterol Catabolism
text: The intricate networks of cellular metabolism are highly interconnected, and perturbations in individual enzymes can have far-reaching consequences. As a result, global gene expression profiling methods are limited in their ability to predict how the loss of a single functional gene will affect the cell. In this study, we employed a novel approach to global phenotypic profiling to directly identify the genes required for the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. By combining high-density mutagenesis and deep-sequencing, we were able to characterize the composition of complex mutant libraries exposed to various conditions and unambiguously identify the genes essential for Mtb growth in vitro. This approach proved to be a significant improvement over previous methods. To explore the functions that are required for persistence in the host, we focused on the pathways involved in the utilization of cholesterol, a critical carbon source during infection. Our findings reveal that few of the genes we identified had previously been linked to this adaptation through transcriptional profiling, and only a small fraction were encoded in the chromosomal region known to encode sterol catabolic functions. Surprisingly, these genes comprise a large percentage of those previously shown to be required for bacterial growth in mouse tissue. This work represents the most comprehensive genetic characterization of a sterol catabolic pathway to date and suggests potential roles for uncharacterized virulence genes, while also precisely mapping genes encoding potential drug targets.

title: Tyrosine phosphorylation regulates the endocytosis and surface expression of GluN3A-containing NMDA receptors.
text: Regulation of receptor trafficking governs synaptic transmission, plasticity, and development by modifying the composition of excitatory synapses. GluN3A (previously known as NR3A), a distinct member of the NMDA receptor (NMDAR) subunit family, confers low calcium permeability and reduced magnesium sensitivity upon NMDAR channels. Due to these unique properties, GluN3A subunits restrict the maturation and plasticity of excitatory synapses, indicating the need for GluN3A removal as a crucial step in neuronal circuit development. However, the molecular signals directing GluN3A endocytosis remain unresolved. By identifying a novel endocytic motif (YWL) located within the cytoplasmic C-terminal tail of GluN3A, we elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying GluN3A internalization. Alanine mutations within the YWL motif hindered clathrin-mediated endocytosis, resulting in accumulation of GluN3A-containing NMDARs at the cell surface. In contrast, mimicking phosphorylation of the tyrosine residue within the YWL motif fostered internalization and reduced the cell-surface expression of GluN3A-containing NMDARs, as confirmed by immunocytochemical and electrophysiological investigations in recombinant systems and rat neurons in primary culture. Our findings uncover a novel signaling mechanism that links the functional surface expression of GluN3A-containing receptors to the phosphorylation state of GluN3A subunits, providing a molecular framework for the control of NMDAR subunit composition with broader implications for synaptic plasticity and neural development.

title: Myeloid-specific Krüppel-like factor 2 inactivation increases macrophage and neutrophil adhesion and promotes atherosclerosis.
text:
In a previous study, it was shown that hemizygous deficiency of the transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) in mice with elevated cholesterol levels leads to increased atherosclerosis. However, the specific cell type responsible for this effect was not identified. To investigate this further, researchers generated mice with cell-specific KLF2 inactivation in myeloid cells, which includes macrophages and neutrophils.
The results showed that macrophages and neutrophils isolated from these mice had similar responses to activation and lipid accumulation as compared to normal myeloid cell-specific KLF2(+/+) mice. However, the myeloid-specific KLF2(-/-) cells adhered more strongly to endothelial cells. In addition, fewer myeloid-specific KLF2(-/-) neutrophils survived in culture compared to normal myeloid cell-specific KLF2(+/+) neutrophils.
When the myeloid-specific KLF2(-/-) mice were mated to mice lacking the low-density lipoprotein (LDLR) gene and then fed a high-fat and high-cholesterol diet, significant increases in atherosclerosis were observed in the myeloid-specific KLF2(-/-)LDLR(-/-) mice compared to the myeloid-specific KLF2(+/+)LDLR(-/-) mice. The increased atherosclerosis in the myeloid-specific KLF2(-/-)LDLR(-/-) mice was accompanied by elevated neutrophil and macrophage accumulation and oxidative stress in the artery walls, as evidenced by increased levels of myeloperoxidase, chlorinated, and nitrosylated tyrosine epitopes. 
In conclusion, this study suggests that KLF2 expression in myeloid cells plays a role in regulating atherosclerosis, and the increased neutrophil accumulation and atherosclerosis progression in myeloid-specific KLF2 defective mice highlight the importance of neutrophils in promoting vascular oxidative stress and atherosclerosis. Overall, the results suggest that increasing KLF2 expression may be a novel strategy for prevention and treatment of atherosclerosis.

title: Epidemiology of Staphylococcus aureus blood and skin and soft tissue infections in the US military health system, 2005-2010.
text:
The rate of hospital-onset methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections is decreasing, but the incidence of community-onset S. aureus infections is less well-known. To address this knowledge gap, this observational study aimed to characterize the overall and annual incidence rates of community-onset and hospital-onset S. aureus bacteremia and skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) in a national healthcare system, as well as to evaluate trends in the incidence rates of S. aureus bacteremia and SSTIs and the proportion due to MRSA.
Methods:
The study included all Department of Defense TRICARE beneficiaries from January 2005 to December 2010, with medical records reviewed to identify and classify all annual first-positive S. aureus blood and wound or abscess cultures as methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) or MRSA, and as community-onset or hospital-onset infections (isolates collected >3 days after hospital admission). The primary outcome measures were unadjusted incidence rates per 100,000 person-years of observation, the proportion of infections due to MRSA, and annual trends for 2005-2010 (examined using the Spearman rank correlation test or the Mantel-Haenszel χ2 test for linear trend).
Results:
During 56 million person-years of observation (non-active duty: 47 million person-years; active duty: 9 million person-years), there were 2643 blood and 80,281 wound or abscess annual first-positive S. aureus cultures. The annual incidence rates for S. aureus bacteremia ranged from 3.6 to 6.0 per 100,000 person-years, while the incidence rates for SSTIs ranged from 122.7 to 168.9 per 100,000 person-years. The incidence rates for community-onset MRSA bacteremia decreased from 1.7 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI, 1.5-2.0 per 100,000 person-years) in 2005 to 1.2 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI, 0.9-1.4 per 100,000 person-years) in 2010 (P = .005 for trend). The incidence rates for hospital-onset MRSA bacteremia also decreased from 0.7 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI, 0.6-0.9 per 100,000 person-years) in 2005 to 0.4 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI, 0.3-0.5 per 100,000 person-years) in 2010 (P = .005 for trend). Concurrently, the proportion of community-onset SSTIs due to MRSA peaked at 62% in 2006 before decreasing annually to 52% in 2010 (P < .001 for trend).
Discussion:
In conclusion, this study found that the incidence rates of both community-onset and hospital-onset MRSA bacteremia decreased in parallel, while the proportion of community-onset SSTIs due to MRSA has more recently declined. These findings suggest a decline in the overall incidence of MRSA infections in the Department of Defense population. However, continued surveillance and infection control measures are necessary to further reduce the incidence of these infections.

title: Potentiation of NMDA currents by pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide in neonatal rat sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
text: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were made from sympathetic preganglionic neurons (SPNs) in the intermediate-lateral cell column of thoracolumbar spinal cord slices of 12- to 16-day-old rat pups, and the effects of pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP)-38 on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)- and kainate (KA)-induced inward currents were investigated. PACAP, at concentrations (10-30 nM) that had no significant impact on holding currents, reversibly augmented NMDA-induced currents but not KA-induced currents. At higher concentrations (>30 nM), PACAP produced a sustained inward current. The potentiating effect of PACAP was abolished by prior incubation of the slices with the adenylate cyclase inhibitor MDL-12,330A (25 μM). Furthermore, superfusing the slices with the membrane-permeable cyclic AMP analogue N6,2'-O-dibutyryladenosine 3':5'-cyclic monophosphate (100-300 μM) in the presence of the phosphodiesterase inhibitor 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (700 μM) increased the NMDA currents. These findings suggest that PACAP selectively enhances NMDA receptor-mediated responses in rat SPNs, probably through a cyclic AMP-dependent mechanism, implicating PACAP in synaptic plasticity.

title: Aberrant Expression of RCAN1 in Alzheimer’s Pathogenesis: A New Molecular Mechanism and a Novel Drug Target
text:
Alzheimer's disease (AD), a devastating neurodegenerative disorder, is the leading cause of dementia in the elderly.
