Characterized by three hallmarks of neuropathology, including neuritic plaque deposition, neurofibrillary tangle formation, and neuronal loss, AD is a complex andmultifactorial disorder. Recent evidence suggests that dysregulation of the regulator of calcineurin 1 (RCAN1) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of AD. Aberrant RCAN1 expression can lead to neuronal apoptosis and Tau hyperphosphorylation, resulting in neuronal loss and neurofibrillary tangle formation.
This review aims to provide an overview of the recent advances in our understanding of the regulation of RCAN1 expression and its physiological functions. We will also summarize the AD risk factors that lead to RCAN1 dysregulation, which can cause neuronal loss, synaptic impairments, and neurofibrillary tangle formation. Additionally, we will discuss the potential underlying mechanisms of RCAN1 dysregulation and its impact on APP processing, Aβ generation, and neuritic plaque formation.
Finally, we will outline the potential of targeting RCAN1 as a new therapeutic approach for AD. By understanding the role of RCAN1 in AD pathogenesis, we may be able to develop novel therapeutic strategies to slow or halt disease progression, ultimately improving the lives of millions of people affected by this devastating disorder.

title: Congruent Visual Speech Enhances Cortical Entrainment to Continuous Auditory Speech in Noise-Free Conditions.
text:
Unlabeled:
The synchrony of auditory and visual speech cues enhances our comprehension of a speaker, even in quiet conditions. When incongruent auditory and visual information is presented simultaneously, it can interfere with a listener's perception and even lead them to perceive incorrect information. Research into the neural basis of these effects has mostly focused on the specific case of discrete audiovisual syllables, with less attention given to the case of natural, continuous speech. Recent studies using multivariate analysis methods have demonstrated that cortical response measures to continuous auditory speech can be obtained easily. In this work, we apply these methods to the case of audiovisual speech and present a novel framework for indexing multisensory integration in the context of continuous speech. Specifically, we investigate how the temporal and contextual congruency of ongoing audiovisual speech affects the cortical encoding of the speech envelope in humans through electroencephalography (EEG). We find that the cortical representation of the speech envelope is enhanced by the presentation of congruent audiovisual speech in quiet conditions. This enhancement is likely due to the contribution of neural generators that are not active during unimodal stimulation and is most prominent at the temporal scale corresponding to syllabic rate (2-6 Hz). Moreover, our data suggest that neural entrainment to the speech envelope is disrupted when the auditory and visual streams are incongruent both temporally and contextually.
Significance Statement: Seeing a speaker's face while they talk significantly improves comprehension of what they are saying. This is because the speaker's facial movements provide additional information about the speaker's message, but also indicate when the speaker is producing the message. Studying how the brain combines information from continuous auditory and visual speech has been challenging due to the difficulty of measuring the brain's response to these stimuli simultaneously. Here, we introduce a new approach using relatively inexpensive and non-invasive scalp recordings. Specifically, we show that the brain's representation of auditory speech is enhanced when the accompanying visual speech signal shares the same timing. This enhancement is most pronounced at a time scale corresponding to the mean syllable length.

title: Telomere tethering at the nuclear periphery is essential for efficient DNA double strand break repair in subtelomeric region
text: In the yeast species Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which lacks lamins, the nuclear pore complex (NPC) has been proposed to play a role in organizing chromatin. Using fluorescence microscopy in living cells, we have shown that nucleoporin proteins from the Nup84 core complex, specifically Nup84p, Nup145Cp, Nup120p, and Nup133p, anchor telomere XI-L at the nuclear periphery. Our findings indicate that the integrity of this complex is necessary for the repression of a URA3 gene located in the subtelomeric region of this chromosome end. Moreover, altering the integrity of this complex reduces the efficiency of repairing a DNA double-strand break (DSB) only when it occurs in the subtelomeric region, even though the repair machinery is functional. These observations confirm and expand the role of the NPC, specifically the Nup84 complex, in organizing chromatin function. Our results also demonstrate that anchoring of telomeres is crucial for effective repair of DSBs in this region and is essential for maintaining genome integrity.

title: p63 Regulates adult neural precursor and newly born neuron survival to control hippocampal-dependent Behavior.
text: The intricate mechanisms governing the survival of adult neural precursor cells (NPCs) and their role in maintaining adult neurogenesis are currently imperfectly understood. To investigate the function of p63, a p53 family member, in adult NPC function, we conducted experiments in mice. Our findings demonstrate that conditional ablation of p63 in adult NPCs or p63 haploinsufficiency resulted in a decrease in the number of NPCs and newborn neurons in the neurogenic regions of the hippocampus, lateral ventricles, and olfactory bulb. These reductions were attributed to increased apoptosis of NPCs and newborn neurons, which were rescued by inhibition of caspase activity, p53, or the p53 apoptotic effector PUMA (p53-upregulated modulator of apoptosis). Moreover, these cellular deficits had functional consequences, leading to impairments in hippocampal-dependent memory formation. Our results indicate that p63 plays a critical role in regulating the number of adult NPCs and adult-born neurons, as well as neural stem cell-dependent cognitive functions. Notably, these findings suggest that p63 inhibits p53-dependent cell death, thereby maintaining the pool of NPCs and promoting adult neurogenesis.

title: Tyrosine-Phosphorylated Caveolin-1 Blocks Bacterial Uptake by Inducing Vav2-RhoA-Mediated Cytoskeletal Rearrangements
text: Some bacterial adhesins may promote a pathogen's extracellular lifestyle rather than entering host cells. However, little is known about the signals that occur during these interactions. In this study, we found that Neisseria gonorrhoeae (P(+)GC), which produces type IV pili (Tfp), induces an immediate recruitment of caveolin-1 (Cav1) in host cells. This recruitment prevents bacterial internalization by triggering cytoskeletal rearrangements through downstream phosphotyrosine signaling. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of potential interaction partners for tyrosine-phosphorylated Cav1 and found that it directly interacts with the Rho-family guanine nucleotide exchange factor Vav2. Both Vav2 and its substrate, the small GTPase RhoA, were shown to play a direct role in the Cav1-mediated prevention of bacterial uptake. Our findings demonstrate how Tfp-producing bacteria evade host cell uptake. Additionally, our data provide a mechanistic link between Cav1 phosphorylation and pathogen-induced cytoskeleton reorganization, advancing our understanding of caveolin function.

title: Effects of GC Bias in Next-Generation-Sequencing Data on De Novo Genome Assembly
text:
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) has revolutionized genome assembly due to its exponential increase in data throughput and drastic decrease in cost when compared to traditional Sanger sequencing. However, NGS presents new computational challenges for de novo genome assembly, including the impact of GC bias. While it is known that GC bias can affect genome assembly, the extent of its influence is not fully understood. In this study, we systematically investigated the effects of GC bias on genome assembly.
Our findings reveal that the impact of GC bias on assembly completeness depends on its degree. When the level of GC bias is mild, it only slightly lowers assembly completeness. However, as the degree of GC bias increases, the fragmentation of assembly due to GC bias can be explained by the uneven distribution of read coverage across the genome. Specifically, regions with low GC content experience lower read coverage, leading to fragmented assemblies. This phenomenon is observed across all assemblers evaluated.
Increasing the total amount of NGS data can rescue the assembly fragmentation caused by GC bias, but the required amount of data varies depending on the genome's GC content distribution. Notably, both low and high coverage depths due to GC bias result in lower assembly accuracy. These insights provide valuable guidelines for improving de novo genome assembly in the presence of GC bias.

title: Cancer inhibition through circadian reprogramming of tumor transcriptome with meal timing.
text: Disrupting the body's internal clock can accelerate the growth of cancer, while reinforcing the circadian rhythm can actually halt it. To explore this phenomenon, we studied mice with pancreatic adenocarcinoma (n = 77) and synchronized them to a specific schedule for food intake based on their natural circadian rhythm. We found that when the mice ate according to their natural circadian rhythm, their cancer growth was significantly slower compared to when they ate at random times. We also found that the circadian rhythm of critical genes involved in cellular stress, cell cycle, and metabolism was not affected by the feeding schedule, but the expression of these genes in the tumors did change in a 24-hour rhythmic pattern. In particular, we found that the expression of genes involved in heat shock proteins, such as Hspa8 and Cirbp, and the cyclin A2 gene Ccna2, was significantly upregulated in tumors when the mice ate according to their natural circadian rhythm. In contrast, the feeding schedule did not affect the expression of these genes in the rest of the body. Our findings suggest that targeting the body's internal clock may be a promising new approach to cancer therapy.

title: Role of chicken melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 in induction and activation of innate and adaptive immune responses to infectious bursal disease virus in cultured macrophages
text: The present study aimed to investigate the role of chicken melanoma-differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) in recognizing and responding to infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV) infection in chicken macrophages. Our findings show that IBDV infection in HD11 cells led to a significant increase in IBDV titers and RNA loads, up to 3.4 × 107 plaque-forming units (PFU)/mL and 1114 ng/µL, respectively, at 24 hours post-infection (hpi). Moreover, IBDV infection induced the upregulation of various genes involved in the innate immune response, including MDA5 (59-fold), interferon-β (IFN-β) (693-fold), dsRNA-dependent protein kinase (PKR) (4-fold), 2’, 5’-oligoadenylate synthetase (OAS) (286-fold), myxovirus resistance gene (Mx) (22-fold), interleukin-1β (IL-1β) (5-fold), IL-6 (146-fold), IL-8 (4-fold), IL-10 (4-fold), inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) (15-fold), and major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC class I) (4-fold). The study also showed that nitric oxide production in the culture supernatants increased significantly (p < 0.05) up to 6.5 μM at 24 hpi. Notably, chMDA5-knockdown HD11 cells had significantly higher IBDV RNA loads at 24 hpi and significantly lower nitric oxide production and expression levels of chicken MDA5, IFN-β, PKR, OAS, Mx, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12(p40), IL-18, IL-10, iNOS, MHC class I and CD86 at 24 hpi. Furthermore, overexpression of chMDA5 in HD11 cells resulted in significantly reduced IBDV titers and RNA loads and significantly increased nitric oxide production at 16 and 24 hpi. Additionally, chMDA5 overexpression led to significantly higher expression levels of chicken MDA5, IFN-β, PKR, OAS, Mx, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12(p40), IL-10 and iNOS at 2 hpi. Taken together, these findings suggest that chMDA5 senses IBDV infection in chicken macrophages, and this is associated with IBDV-induced expression of IFN-β and initiation of an innate immune response that in turn activates the adaptive immune response and limits IBDV replication.

title: Age-Associated Sperm DNA Methylation Alterations: Possible Implications in Offspring Disease Susceptibility
text: Recent evidence suggests that paternal aging may play a role in the susceptibility of offspring to certain diseases. It is well-established that various neuropsychiatric disorders (such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder), trinucleotide expansion associated diseases (like myotonic dystrophy and Huntington's disease), and even some forms of cancer have increased incidence in the offspring of older fathers. Despite substantial epidemiological evidence supporting these findings, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. However, it is believed that epigenetic modifications, particularly DNA methylation alterations, may play a role. In this study, we investigated the impact of aging on DNA methylation in mature human sperm. Using a methylation array approach, we evaluated changes in sperm DNA methylation patterns in 17 fertile donors by comparing two samples collected from each individual 9-19 years apart. Our findings identified 139 regions of significantly hypomethylated DNA with age and 8 regions of significantly hypermethylated DNA with age. We confirmed a subset of these alterations in an independent cohort, and found that 117 genes were associated with these regions of methylation changes (promoter or gene body). Interestingly, some of the age-related changes in sperm DNA methylation were found in genes previously linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. While our data does not establish a causal relationship, it raises the possibility that the age-associated methylation of these candidate genes in sperm may contribute to the increased incidence of neuropsychiatric and other disorders in the offspring of older males. Further studies are needed to determine whether and to what extent a causal relationship exists.

title: Mutations in the nuclear bile acid receptor FXR cause progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis
text: Neonatal cholestasis is a life-threatening condition that requires prompt diagnosis, and it can be caused by mutations in several genes. However, some cases of familial cholestasis cannot be explained by known genetic mutations. Here, we report on four individuals from two unrelated families with neonatal cholestasis and mutations in NR1H4, a gene that encodes the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), a nuclear hormone receptor that regulates bile acid metabolism. Clinical features of severe, persistent NR1H4-related cholestasis in newborns include rapid progression to end-stage liver disease, vitamin K-independent coagulopathy, low to normal serum gamma-glutamyl transferase activity, elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein levels, and undetectable liver bile salt export pump (ABCB11) expression. Our findings underscore the critical role of FXR in regulating bile acid metabolism and liver protection.

title: Phase II study of panobinostat in combination with bevacizumab for recurrent glioblastoma and anaplastic glioma.
text:
BACKGROUND: Panobinostat, a histone deacetylase inhibitor, has shown antineoplastic and antiangiogenic effects in glioma, which may be enhanced when combined with bevacizumab. We conducted a multicenter phase II trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of panobinostat plus bevacizumab in patients with recurrent high-grade glioma (HGG).
METHODS: Patients with recurrent HGG were treated with oral panobinostat at a dose of 30 mg three times per week, every other week, in combination with bevacizumab at a dose of 10 mg/kg every other week. The primary endpoint was the 6-month progression-free survival (PFS6) rate for participants with recurrent glioblastoma (GBM). An exploratory arm of the study evaluated patients with recurrent anaplastic glioma (AG).
RESULTS: At the interim analysis, the GBM arm of the study did not meet criteria for continued accrual, and the arm was closed. A total of 24 patients with GBM were enrolled before closure. The PFS6 rate was 30.4% (95% CI: 12.4%-50.7%), with a median PFS of 5 months (range: 3-9 months) and a median overall survival (OS) of 9 months (range: 6-19 months). The AG arm of the study continued to accrue patients, and a total of 15 patients were enrolled. The PFS6 rate was 46.7% (range: 21%-73%), with a median PFS of 7 months (range: 2-10 months) and a median OS of 17 months (range: 5 months-27 months).
CONCLUSIONS: The phase II study of panobinostat plus bevacizumab did not meet criteria for continued accrual, and the GBM cohort of the study was closed. Although the addition of panobinostat to bevacizumab was relatively well tolerated, it did not significantly improve PFS6 compared to historical controls of bevacizumab monotherapy in either cohort.

title: Blood monocytes consist of two principal subsets with distinct migratory properties
text: Peripheral blood monocytes are a diverse group of white blood cells in the bloodstream. Researchers used a mouse model to study how these cells function in the body and how they can be used in therapy for inflammatory diseases. They found that monocytes in mice can be divided into two main groups based on how they behave in the body. One group is called CX(3)CR1(lo)CCR2(+)Gr1(+), and the other is called CX(3)CR1(hi)CCR2(-)Gr1(-). These groups have different functions and can differentiate into dendritic cells in the body, which are important for fighting infection. The researchers also found that the levels of CX(3)CR1 expression on these cells can be used to identify two main types of monocytes in humans, called CD14(+)CD16(-) and CD14(lo)CD16(+) monocytes. These cells share similarities with the mouse subsets and may be targeted for therapy in inflammatory diseases.

title: The Spemann Organizer Signal noggin Binds and Inactivates Bone Morphogenetic Protein 4
text: The signals emitted by the Spemann organizer of the embryonic gastrula have the ability to directly induce neural tissue from the ectoderm and dorsalize ventral mesoderm to form muscle. These activities are mirrored by the secreted polypeptide noggin, which is expressed at the appropriate time and place to participate in the organizer signal. Conversely, the organizer signal is antagonized by bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), which induce epidermis and ventral mesoderm instead. Interestingly, our findings reveal that noggin protein exhibits high binding affinity for BMP4 and can abolish its activity by blocking its interaction with cognate cell-surface receptors. These data suggest that the noggin secreted by the organizer plays a crucial role in patterning the embryo by disrupting BMP signaling.

title: A Conserved MST-FOXO Signaling Pathway Mediates Oxidative-Stress Responses and Extends Life Span
text: Oxidative stress impacts cell survival and homeostasis, but the underlying biological mechanisms remain mysterious. In this study, we uncover that the protein kinase MST1 mediates oxidative stress-induced cell death in primary mammalian neurons by directly activating the FOXO transcription factors. MST1 phosphorylates FOXO proteins at a conserved site within the forkhead domain, disrupting their interaction with 14-3-3 proteins, promoting FOXO nuclear translocation, and thereby inducing cell death in neurons. Furthermore, we extend the MST-FOXO signaling link to nematodes, demonstrating that the C. elegans MST1 ortholog CST-1 influences life span and aging processes. Knockdown of CST-1 shortens life span and accelerates tissue aging, while overexpression of cst-1 promotes life span and delays aging, with the latter occurring in a daf-16-dependent manner. The identification of FOXO transcription factors as major and evolutionarily conserved targets of MST1 suggests that MST kinases play important roles in various biological processes, including cellular responses to oxidative stress and longevity.

title: Physician Emigration from Sub-Saharan Africa to the United States: Analysis of the 2011 AMA Physician Masterfile
text:
The large-scale emigration of physicians from sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) to high-income nations is a pressing development concern. Our study aimed to investigate current trends of SSA physicians in the US physician workforce.
We analyzed data from the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Health Workforce Statistics and the 2011 American Medical Association Physician Masterfile (AMA-PM) on physicians trained or born in SSA countries practicing in the US. We estimated emigration proportions, year of entry to the US, years of practice before emigration, and length of time in the US.
According to the 2011 AMA-PM, 10,819 physicians were born or trained in 28 SSA countries. Of these, 68% were trained in SSA, 20% were trained in the US, and 12% were trained outside both SSA and the US. We estimated that active physicians (aged ≤ 70 years) represented 96% of the total. Migration trends among SSA-trained physicians increased from 2002 to 2011 for all but one source country, with the exception of South Africa. The increase in last-decade migration was over 50% in Nigeria and Ghana, over 100% in Ethiopia, and over 200% in Sudan. Liberia was the most affected country, with 77% of its estimated physicians emigrating to the US. On average, SSA-trained physicians have been in the US for 18 years, with nearly half emigrating during the implementation years (1984-1999) of structural adjustment programs.
Our findings suggest that the emigration of SSA physicians to the US will persist unless far-reaching policies are implemented by both the US and SSA countries.

title: Kynurenic Acid Is a Nutritional Cue that Enables Behavioral Plasticity
text: The kynurenine pathway of tryptophan metabolism plays a role in the development of various brain diseases, although its functional significance remains unclear. Our study has revealed that kynurenic acid, a product of this pathway, acts as a regulator of food-dependent behavioral flexibility in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Fasting in C. elegans alters a range of behaviors, including feeding rate upon encountering food again, and this effect is mediated by changes in the levels of neurally produced kynurenic acid. When animals fast, levels of kynurenic acid are depleted, leading to increased activity of NMDA-receptor-expressing interneurons and the activation of a neuropeptide-Y-like signaling pathway that enhances serotonin release upon food re-encounter. Following refeeding, kynurenic acid levels are replenished, ending the enhanced feeding period. These findings suggest that a physiological function of kynurenic acid is to directly connect metabolism with activity in NMDA and serotonergic circuits, which regulate a wide range of behaviors and physiological processes.

title: Comprehensive Identification and Annotation of Cell Type-Specific and Ubiquitous CTCF-Binding Sites in the Human Genome
text:
Chromatin insulators are DNA elements that regulate gene expression by either preventing silencing of gene expression through maintained boundaries of heterochromatin or blocking interactions between enhancers and promoters, thereby preventing gene activation. The protein CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) is the only known protein involved in establishing insulators in vertebrates. While CTCF has been implicated in various regulatory functions, its study has been limited to a small number of cell types across the human genome. As a result, it is unknown whether cell type-specific differences in CTCF-binding sites are functionally significant.
In this study, we aim to identify and characterize cell type-specific and ubiquitous CTCF-binding sites in the human genome across 38 cell types designated by the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) consortium. These cell type-specific and ubiquitous CTCF-binding sites exhibit unique and versatile transcriptional functions, as well as characteristic chromatin features. Additionally, we investigate the insulator barrier function of CTCF and explore its novel role in DNA replication. These findings represent a crucial step towards a comprehensive and systematic understanding of CTCF-dependent insulators and their diverse roles in the human genome.

title: Experimental and Theoretical Approaches to Conscious Processing
text: Recent research and theoretical models have made progress in uncovering the mystery of connecting subjective conscious experience with measurable neuronal activity. This review focuses on the specific challenge of determining how external or internal information transitions from nonconscious processing to conscious processing, marked by the existence of a reportable subjective experience. By combining neuroimaging and neurophysiological data gathered during minimal contrasts between conscious and nonconscious processing, researchers have identified objective neural measures of conscious access, including late amplification of relevant sensory activity, long-distance synchronization at beta and gamma frequencies, and "ignition" of a large-scale prefrontal-parietal network. These findings are compared to current theoretical models of conscious processing, such as the Global Neuronal Workspace (GNW) model, which proposes that conscious access occurs when incoming information is made globally available to multiple brain systems through a network of neurons with long-range axons densely distributed in prefrontal, parieto-temporal, and cingulate cortices. The clinical implications of these results for conditions such as general anesthesia, coma, vegetative state, and schizophrenia are also discussed.

title: Reconstruction of the yeast Snf1 kinase regulatory network reveals its role as a global energy regulator
text: Highly conserved across eukaryotic cells, the AMP-activated kinase (AMPK) plays a central role in regulating carbon metabolism. To map the complete network of interactions surrounding AMPK in yeast (Snf1) and to evaluate the function of its regulatory subunit Snf4, we measured global mRNA, protein, and metabolite levels in wild-type, Deltasnf1, Deltasnf4, and Deltasnf1Deltasnf4 knockout strains. By utilizing four newly developed computational tools, including a novel DOGMA sub-network analysis, we demonstrated the benefits of integrating multi-level omics data to uncover the global Snf1 kinase function in yeast. We showed for the first time the comprehensive regulation of Snf1 on gene and protein expression levels, and revealed that yeast Snf1 has a significantly more extensive role in controlling energy metabolism than previously reported. Additionally, we identified complementary roles of Snf1 and Snf4, similar to the function of AMPK in humans. Our findings indicate that Snf1 acts as a low-energy checkpoint, and that yeast can be used more extensively as a model system for investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying the global regulation of AMPK in mammals, which failure can lead to metabolic diseases.

title: Influence of Steroid Hormone Signaling on Life Span Control by Caenorhabditis elegans Insulin-Like Signaling
text: Sterol-sensing nuclear receptors and insulin-like growth factor signaling have evolved to play vital roles in aging control. In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, bile acid-like steroid hormones called dafachronic acids (DAs) impact longevity by binding to and regulating the activity of the conserved nuclear receptor DAF-12, and the insulin receptor (InsR) ortholog DAF-2 regulates life span by inhibiting the FoxO transcription factor DAF-16. The mechanisms by which the DA/DAF-12 pathway interacts with DAF-2/InsR signaling to control life span are not well understood. To investigate this, we specifically examined the roles of liganded and unliganded DAF-12 in life span control in the context of reduced DAF-2/InsR signaling. Our findings reveal that in animals with reduced daf-2/InsR activity, both liganded and unliganded DAF-12 promote longevity. However, in daf-2/InsR mutants, liganded and unliganded DAF-12 act in opposing ways to control life span. These results establish new roles for a conserved steroid signaling pathway in life span control and elucidate the complex interactions among DA biosynthetic pathways, DAF-12, and DAF-2/InsR signaling in aging.

title: Asymmetric Cell Divisions Sustain Long-Term  Hematopoiesis from Single-sorted Human Fetal Liver Cells
text: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in adult bone marrow are thought to have originated from fetal liver precursors. To investigate the cellular mechanisms involved in long-term hematopoiesis, we analyzed single-sorted candidate HSCs from fetal liver cultured in a mix of stimulatory cytokines over 8-10 days. The number of cells in primary cultures varied from 10,000 cells. We then recloned individual cells in slow-growing colonies and found that the number of cells in subclones differed significantly. These findings suggest that primitive hematopoietic cells undergo asymmetric cell division, with differing proliferative potential and cell cycle properties among daughter cells. This continuous generation of functional heterogeneity among clonal progeny supports the idea that intrinsic mechanisms control stem cell fate and sustain hematopoiesis both in vitro and in vivo.

title: Reprogramming factor expression initiates widespread targeted chromatin remodeling.
text: Despite significant progress in characterizing the transcription factor-driven reprogramming of somatic cells to an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) state, numerous mechanistic questions remain unresolved. To elucidate the early events in the reprogramming process, we conducted a systematic analysis of the transcriptional and epigenetic changes that occur during early factor induction after specific divisions. Our observations revealed rapid, genome-wide modifications in euchromatic histone H3K4me2 at over a thousand loci, including large subsets of pluripotency-related or developmentally regulated gene promoters and enhancers. Conversely, patterns of repressive H3K27me3 modification remained relatively unchanged, with focused depletion observed specifically at regions where H3K4 methylation is gained. These chromatin regulatory events preceded transcriptional changes within the corresponding loci, providing evidence for an early, organized, and population-wide epigenetic response to ectopic reprogramming factors. Our findings clarify the temporal order through which somatic identity is reset during the reprogramming process.

title: Stroke and migraine--the spectrum of cause and effect.
text: The connection between migraines and strokes is intricate. While a stroke may occur simultaneously with a migraine, migraines can also increase the risk of stroke in women under 45 years of age and possibly in men who experience migraine with aura. In contrast, a stroke may resemble a migraine, but migraine symptoms can also be indicative of underlying cerebrovascular disorders. True migraine-related stroke is rare. The precise mechanisms of stroke occurring during a migraine episode are not yet understood, but they likely involve a complex interaction between the dynamic changes in brain blood flow and pre-existing stroke risk factors.

title: MicroRNA Regulation of Cbx7 Mediates a Switch of Polycomb Orthologs during ESC Differentiation
text: The Polycomb Group (PcG) of chromatin modulators controls pluripotency and differentiation. Mammalian genomes contain multiple homologs of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (PRC1) components, including five orthologs of the Drosophila Polycomb protein (Cbx2, Cbx4, Cbx6, Cbx7, and Cbx8). Our study has identified Cbx7 as the primary Polycomb ortholog of PRC1 complexes in embryonic stem cells (ESCs). During ESC differentiation, the expression of Cbx7 is downregulated, followed by the upregulation of Cbx2, Cbx4, and Cbx8, which are directly repressed by Cbx7. Increasing Cbx7 expression inhibits differentiation and X chromosome inactivation, while decreasing Cbx7 levels induces differentiation and releases lineage-specific markers. In a functional screen, we identified the miR-125 and miR-181 families as regulators of Cbx7 that are induced during ESC differentiation. Ectopic expression of these miRNAs accelerates ESC differentiation by regulating Cbx7. These findings establish a crucial role for Cbx7 and its regulatory miRNAs in maintaining pluripotency.

title: Differences in the Clinical Effects of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers: A Critical Review of the Evidence
text: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is a crucial player in the pathophysiology of hypertension and related cardiovascular events. While both angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor antagonists (ARBs) are essential in treating hypertension, recent years have shown that they may have distinct cardiovascular protective effects. As our understanding of their non-overlapping mechanisms of action grows, the number of studies investigating their differences will likely increase. ACE inhibitors are a safe therapeutic option for hypertensive patients with cardiological comorbidities.

title: A talin-dependent LFA-1 focal zone is formed by rapidly migrating T lymphocytes
text: Cells such as fibroblasts and endothelial cells migrate through the coordinated responses of distinct integrin-containing focal adhesions and complexes. However, the organization of integrins on highly motile T lymphocytes remains poorly understood. We investigated the distribution, activity, and cytoskeletal linkage of integrin lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 (LFA-1) on human T lymphocytes migrating on endothelial cells and ligand intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1). Unlike other cell types, the pattern of total LFA-1 on T lymphocytes varies from low expression in lamellipodia to high expression in the uropod. However, high-affinity, clustered LFA-1 is restricted to a mid-cell zone that remains stable over time and across ICAM-1 densities. Talin is essential for the stability and formation of the LFA-1 zone, and disruption of the talin-integrin link leads to loss of zone integrity and a significant decrease in migration speed on ICAM-1. We termed this unique adhesive structure the "focal zone," which differs from previously described integrin-containing attachments displayed by other cell types.

title: Tricyclic antidepressants and headaches: systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and relative adverse effects of tricyclic antidepressants in the treatment of migraine, tension-type, and mixed headaches.
Design: Meta-analysis.
Sources: Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Trials Registry, and PsycLIT.
Studies Reviewed: Randomized trials of adults receiving tricyclics as the only treatment for a minimum of four weeks.
Data Extraction: Frequency of headaches (number of headache attacks for migraine and number of days with headache for tension-type headaches), intensity of headache, and headache index.
Results: A total of 37 studies met the inclusion criteria. Tricyclics significantly reduced the number of days with tension-type headache and the number of headache attacks from migraine compared to placebo (mean standardized mean difference: -1.29, 95% confidence interval: -2.18 to -0.39 and -0.70, -0.93 to -0.48). However, tricyclics were less effective than selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in reducing headaches (mean standardized mean difference: -0.80, 95% confidence interval: -2.63 to 0.02 and -0.20, -0.60 to 0.19). The effect of tricyclics increased with longer duration of treatment (β=-0.11, 95% confidence interval: -0.63 to -0.15; P<0.0005). Tricyclics were also more likely to reduce the intensity of headaches by at least 50% than either placebo (tension-type: relative risk 1.41, 95% confidence interval: 1.02 to 1.89; migraine: 1.80, 1.24 to 2.62) or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (1.73, 1.34 to 2.22 and 1.72, 1.15 to 2.55). Tricyclics were more likely to cause adverse effects than placebo (1.53, 95% confidence interval: 1.11 to 2.12) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (2.22, 1.52 to 3.32), including dry mouth (P<0.0005 for both), drowsiness (P<0.0005 for both), and weight gain (P<0.001 for both), but did not increase dropout rates (placebo: 1.22, 0.83 to 1.80, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: 1.16, 0.81 to 2.97).
Conclusion: Tricyclic antidepressants are effective in preventing migraine and tension-type headaches and are more effective than selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, although with greater adverse effects. The effectiveness of tricyclics seems to increase over time.

title: Functional Consequences of Splicing of the Antisense Transcript COOLAIR on FLC Transcription
text: Antisense transcription is prevalent across many genomes, but the extent to which it plays a functional role is a matter of debate. We are investigating the functional properties of a set of long noncoding antisense transcripts, collectively referred to as COOLAIR, produced at the Arabidopsis FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC). COOLAIR begins just downstream of the primary sense transcript poly(A) site and either terminates prematurely or extends into the FLC promoter region. Our findings demonstrate that the splicing of COOLAIR is crucial for its function. This was revealed through an analysis of a hypomorphic mutation in the core spliceosome component PRP8, which perturbs a cotranscriptional feedback mechanism linking COOLAIR processing to histone demethylation and reduced FLC transcription within the FLC gene body. The significance of COOLAIR splicing in this repression mechanism was further confirmed by disrupting COOLAIR production and mutating the proximal splice acceptor site. Our findings suggest that changes in the splicing of a long noncoding transcript can quantitatively influence gene expression through cotranscriptional coupling mechanisms.

title: Nuclear Factor-�B Affects Tumor Progression in a Mouse Model of Malignant Pleural Effusion
text: We generated a novel mouse model of malignant pleural effusion (MPE) by directly injecting Lewis lung cancer (LLC) cells into the pleural space of syngeneic C57B/6 mice. The resulting pleural effusions shared similar cellular and biochemical features with human MPEs. When we implanted and grew pleural tumors, it triggered a host inflammatory response characterized by the influx of various inflammatory cells into the pleural fluid. In vitro and in vivo, LLC cells showed high basal nuclear factor (NF)-κB activity, which we utilized to drive expression of a NF-κB-dependent green fluorescent protein-firefly luciferase fusion reporter construct. This allowed us to trace pleural tumors intravitally. Inhibiting NF-κB in LLC cells did not affect their viability in culture, but injecting LLC cells expressing a dominant NF-κB inhibitor led to decreased tumor burden, decreased pleural effusion volume, and decreased pleural effusion tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) levels. These findings suggest that tumor NF-κB activity plays a crucial role in mediating the development and progression of MPE.

title: A phase I study of PF-04449913, an oral hedgehog inhibitor, in patients with advanced solid tumors.
text:
The purpose of this study was to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of PF-04449913, an investigational drug, and evaluate its safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and preliminary antitumor activity in patients with advanced tumors.
The study used an open-label, multicenter, phase I design with a 3+3 design and dose escalation/de-escalation to identify the MTD. PF-04449913 was administered orally once daily in 28-day treatment cycles, starting at 80 mg/day. A total of 23 patients were enrolled, and 19 were evaluable for dose-limiting toxicity (DLT). The MTD was estimated to be 320 mg/day, and the recommended phase II dose was not determined.
PF-04449913 was generally well tolerated at doses of 80-320 mg/day, with the most common adverse events (AEs) being grade 1-2 dysgeusia, fatigue, decreased appetite, nausea, dizziness, dehydration, and diarrhea. Grade 3 AEs occurred only in patients receiving the 640 mg/day dose, and no grade 4-5 AEs were reported. Pharmacokinetic analysis revealed dose-proportional kinetics with biphasic elimination, supporting once-daily dosing. PF-04449913 modulated hedgehog signaling at the dose levels tested, as demonstrated by >80% downregulation of GLI1 expression in the skin of treated patients. Eight patients (34.8%) achieved stable disease, and three patients with disease progression at enrollment had prolonged disease stabilization (≥6 months).
In conclusion, the results of this study suggest that PF-04449913 is tolerable and worthy of further investigation in patients with advanced solid tumors.

title: Histone levels are regulated by phosphorylation and ubiquitylation dependent proteolysis
text: Histone levels are tightly regulated to prevent harmful effects such as genomic instability and increased sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents resulting from the accumulation of highly basic proteins when DNA replication slows or stops. Although chromosomal histones are stable, excess (non-chromatin-bound) histones are rapidly degraded through a Rad53 (radiation-sensitive 53) kinase-dependent process in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Here, we demonstrate that excess histones associate with Rad53 in vivo and undergo modifications such as tyrosine phosphorylation and polyubiquitylation before their proteolysis by the proteasome. We identified the Tyr 99 residue of histone H3 as critical for efficient ubiquitylation and degradation of this histone. We also identified the ubiquitin conjugating enzymes (E2) Ubc4 and Ubc5, as well as the ubiquitin ligase (E3) Tom1 (temperature-dependent organization in the mitotic nucleus 1), as enzymes involved in the ubiquitylation of excess histones. Regulated histone proteolysis has significant implications for maintaining epigenetic marks on chromatin, genomic stability, and the packaging of sperm DNA.

title: TLR-activated B cells suppress T cell-mediated autoimmunity.
text: TLRs detect microbial infections and activate immune responses. Dendritic cells, macrophages, and B lymphocytes express TLRs, and MyD88 is a signaling adaptor protein involved in this process. The impact of TLR-activated B cells on T cell-mediated inflammation is not well understood. In this study, we investigate the role of TLR-activated B cells in a T cell-mediated autoimmune disease called experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) by using mice with genetic deficiencies in MyD88 or specific TLRs. Our results show that TLR signaling in B cells suppresses inflammatory T cell responses (both Th1 and Th17) and promotes recovery from EAE. Specifically, only certain TLRs are required on B cells for resolving EAE, and these TLRs are not essential for disease initiation. We found that Mycobacterium tuberculosis components in the adjuvant provide TLR agonists that control the regulatory function of B cells, which in turn limits autoimmune disease. Our data suggest that B cells act as a bridge between recognition of microbial products through TLRs and suppression of a T cell-mediated autoimmune disease. In summary, TLR signaling in B cells plays a crucial role in regulating immune responses and preventing autoimmune diseases.

title: Successful expansion of functional and stable regulatory T cells for immunotherapy in liver transplantation
text:
Strategies to prevent organ transplant rejection are under intense investigation, with a focus on regulatory T cells (Tregs) due to their potential to induce tolerance in transplant recipients. A recent clinical trial, ThRIL, launched at King's College London, aims to use Treg cell therapy to achieve this goal. The trial's success could revolutionize the management of transplant patients, making it possible for them to receive drug-free transplants in the future.
This study is the first to report the manufacture of clinical-grade Tregs from prospective liver transplant recipients using a proprietary GMP isolation technique and expansion methods involving anti-CD3/CD28 beads, IL-2, and rapamycin. The resulting cells were found to be a highly pure and stable population of Tregs (>95% CD4+CD25+FOXP3+), with sufficient numbers for clinical use.
Our study demonstrated that the expansion of Tregs using this protocol resulted in superior functional cells compared to freshly isolated cells, while also preventing their conversion to Th17 cells under pro-inflammatory conditions. The final Treg product was manufactured in the clinical research facility (CRF), paving the way for its clinical application.
The results presented in this manuscript, combined with the anticipated clinical outcomes from ThRIL, will undoubtedly inform improved strategies for managing liver transplant recipients.

title: A framework for improving microRNA prediction in non-human genomes
text: Has there been significant attention recently on predicting novel pre-microRNAs (miRNAs) from genomic sequences? Not really. While previous studies have shown promising results when using human-trained methods on non-human genome sequences, there has been a concerning trend of poor specificity (the ability to accurately reject non-miRNA sequences) in these studies. Given that the ratio of true miRNA sequences to pseudo-miRNA sequences is about 1:1000, the large number of false positives arising from low specificity renders most existing tools inapplicable to non-human genomes. To address this issue, we have developed a framework called SMIRP, which leverages sequence conservation and phylogenetic distance information to create species-specific miRNA prediction systems. Our study shows substantial improvements in specificity and precision for four non-human test species when our framework is applied to three different prediction systems using both human-specific and taxon-wide training data. Notably, the SMIRP framework is applicable to all miRNA prediction systems, and we expect substantial improvements in precision and specificity, regardless of the machine learning technique chosen.

title: CD8 Cells of Patients with Diffuse Cutaneous Leishmaniasis Display Functional Exhaustion: The Latter Is Reversed, In Vitro, by TLR2 Agonists
text: Localized (LCL) and diffuse (DCL) cutaneous leishmaniasis are caused by Leishmania mexicana (Lm). DCL patients exhibit a poor cellular immune response, leading to chronicity of the infection. It has been proposed that CD8 T lymphocytes (CD8) play a crucial role in infection clearance, although the role of CD8 cytotoxicity in disease control has not been clearly elucidated. Lesions of DCL patients have shown to have lower numbers of CD8 compared to patients with LCL, and leishmanicidal treatment restores CD8 levels. The enhanced response of CD8 towards Leishmania parasites led researchers to investigate possible functional differences between CD8 from patients with LCL and DCL. CD8 cells from DCL patients displayed decreased cytotoxicity, antigen-specific proliferation, and IFNγ production when stimulated with Leishmania-infected macrophages (MOi). In contrast, LCL patients showed higher levels of these functions. Furthermore, DCL patients had fewer TUNEL+ cells in their lesions, indicating a state of cellular exhaustion. To restore the functional capacity of CD8 cells from DCL patients, researchers preincubated them with TLR2 agonists, including Lm lipophosphoglycan (LPG) or Pam3Cys. This led to the restoration of cytotoxicity, antigen-specific proliferation, and IFNγ production, while also reducing the expression of the exhaustion marker PD-1. These findings suggest that the CD8 response is essential for controlling Lm infection in LCL patients and that chronic infection in DCL patients leads to functional exhaustion of CD8 T lymphocytes, which may contribute to disease progression. This study is the first to demonstrate the presence of functionally exhausted CD8 T lymphocytes in DCL patients and the potential benefits of pre-stimulation with TLR2 ligands in restoring their effector mechanisms.

title: Enhancer Evolution across 20 Mammalian Species
text: The mammalian radiation has concurrently witnessed significant alterations in the non-coding regions of the genome, yet an in-depth comprehension of the evolution of regulatory mechanisms in mammals remains unfulfilled. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of the evolution of promoters and enhancers that are active in the liver of 20 mammalian species from six distinct orders by profiling the genomic enrichment of histone H3 acetylation at lysine 27 (H3K27ac) and histone H3 trimethylation at lysine 4 (H3K4me3). Our findings establish that the rapid evolution of enhancers is a ubiquitous characteristic of mammalian genomes, with most recently evolved enhancers originating from ancestral DNA exaptation rather than lineage-specific expansions of repeat elements. In contrast, the majority of liver promoters exhibit partial or complete conservation across these species. The data presented in this study additionally reveal that recent evolutionary changes in enhancers are often linked to genes under positive selection, providing insight into the regulatory adaptations that underlie mammalian genomic evolution. These findings offer a valuable perspective on the functional genetics that govern the evolution of mammalian regulatory elements.

title: IDH1 mutations alter citric acid cycle metabolism and increase dependence on oxidative mitochondrial metabolism.
text: Gene mutations in the isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IDH1/2) occur in various types of cancer, yet the metabolic implications of these genetic alterations remain poorly understood. In this study, we employed (13)C metabolic flux analysis on a panel of isogenic cell lines harboring heterozygous IDH1/2 mutations. We discovered that under hypoxic conditions, IDH1-mutated cells exhibited enhanced oxidative tricarboxylic acid metabolism and decreased reductive glutamine metabolism compared to IDH2-mutated cells. However, selectively inhibiting the mutated IDH1 enzyme function failed to restore the impaired reductive carboxylation capacity. Moreover, this metabolic reprogramming made IDH1-mutated cells more sensitive to hypoxia or inhibition of the electron transport chain in vitro. Finally, IDH1-mutated cells showed poor growth as subcutaneous xenografts in a hypoxic in vivo environment. Together, our findings suggest potential therapeutic strategies to exploit the unique metabolic vulnerabilities associated with IDH1 mutations.

title: The assessment of the prognostic value of tumor markers and cytokines as SCCAg, CYFRA 21.1, IL-6, VEGF and sTNF receptors in patients with squamous cell cervical cancer, particularly with early stage of the disease
text: The purpose of this study is to assess the predictive value of tumor markers, including squamous cell carcinoma antigen (SCCAg), cytokeratin-19 fragment (CYFRA 21.1), interleukin 6 (IL-6), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor I (sTNF RI), and sTNF RII, in patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. We analyzed 138 patients with stages I-IVA according to the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) classification, who were followed up for 10 years. During this time, 56 relapses and 53 deaths occurred, and recurrent disease was confirmed in 45% of patients. We measured the pretreatment serum levels of these tumor markers in all patients and evaluated their prognostic value in terms of disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) using the log-rank test and Cox regression model. Additionally, we conducted receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis to determine the markers' predictive power for disease recurrence and death. Our findings revealed that the largest area under the curve was observed for SCCAg and IL-6 for patients with recurrence, and for SCCAg and VEGF for patients who died. Cox analysis showed that independent prognostic factors for DFS were SCCAg and IL-6, while for OS, the factors were IL-6, SCCAg, and VEGF. However, in patients with early-stage disease, VEGF, CYFRA 21.1, and IL-6 were significant predictors of OS. Our study suggests that serum levels of VEGF, CYFRA 21.1, and IL-6 before treatment in patients with early-stage cervical cancer are important prognostic factors.

title: Combination of platelet count and mean platelet volume (COP-MPV) predicts postoperative prognosis in both resectable early and advanced stage esophageal squamous cell cancer patients
text: The purpose of this study is to identify the most powerful predictor of survival among routine blood tests for patients with esophageal squamous cell cancer (ESCC). We evaluated various laboratory parameters, including red blood cell indices (hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, and red blood cell distribution width), platelet morphology (mean platelet volume and platelet count), coagulation status (D-dimer), and tumor biomarker (CA19-9), as well as inflammatory markers (neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio and platelet-lymphocyte ratio). A total of 468 patients diagnosed with ESCC between 2005 and 2008 were retrospectively analyzed. Using univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards analyses, we found that platelet count (PLT) and mean platelet volume (MPV) were significantly associated with overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS). Specifically, patients with both elevated PLT and MPV had a worse prognosis. We also found that the combination of PLT and MPV (COP-MPV) was an independent prognostic factor for OS and DFS in multivariate analyses. In subgroup analyses of early (stages I and II) and locally advanced (stage III) patients, COP-MPV remained significantly associated with OS and DFS in each group. Our findings suggest that COP-MPV may be a promising predictor of postoperative survival in ESCC patients.

title: Dementia incidence and mortality in middle-income countries, and associations with indicators of cognitive reserve: a 10/66 Dementia Research Group population-based cohort study
text:
Background: Limited studies have investigated dementia incidence in countries with low or middle incomes, suggesting a lower prevalence compared to high-income countries. We aimed to determine incidence of dementia according to 10/66 Dementia Research Group and Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) IV criteria, as well as the effect of dementia at baseline on mortality and the independent effects of age, sex, socioeconomic position, and cognitive reserve.
Methods: We conducted a population-based cohort study of individuals aged 65 and older living in urban and rural sites in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Peru, Mexico, and China. We assessed cognitive function using questionnaires and obtained information on age, sex, education, literacy, occupational attainment, and household assets. Mortality data was obtained from all sites, and for participants who had passed away, we interviewed a friend or relative to determine the likelihood of dementia before death.
Results: 12,887 participants were interviewed at baseline, of whom 11,718 were dementia-free. Over 34,718 person-years of follow-up, the incidence of 10/66 dementia varied between 18·2 and 30·4 per 1000 person-years, and were 1·4-2·7 times higher than the incidence of DSM-IV dementia (9·9-15·7 per 1000 person-years). Mortality hazards were 1·56-5·69 times higher in individuals with dementia at baseline compared to those who were dementia-free. Informant reports suggested a high incidence of dementia before death, which if included, could result in a 4-19% higher overall incidence. 10/66 dementia incidence was independently associated with age, female sex, and low education, but not with occupational attainment.
Interpretation: Our findings support the cognitive reserve hypothesis, showing that in middle-income countries as in high-income countries, education, literacy, verbal fluency, and motor sequencing confer substantial protection against the onset of dementia.
Funding: This study was funded by the Wellcome Trust Health Consequences of Population Change Programme, WHO, US Alzheimer's Association, and FONACIT/CDCH/UCV.

title: Regulation of immune responses by extracellular vesicles
text: Extracellular vesicles, including exosomes, are small membrane-bound compartments derived from multivesicular bodies or the plasma membrane. Most cells release these vesicles, which then enter the body's fluids. The contents of extracellular vesicles include a subset of proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids derived from the parent cell. It is believed that these vesicles play a crucial role in intercellular communication, both locally and systemically, by transferring their contents between cells. Extracellular vesicles are involved in various physiological processes and have important roles in immune regulation, with vesicles from both non-immune and immune cells playing a significant role in this process. Additionally, extracellular vesicle-based therapeutics are being developed and clinically tested for the treatment of inflammatory diseases, autoimmune disorders, and cancer. Given the significant therapeutic potential of extracellular vesicles, this Review focuses on their role in modulating immune responses and their potential therapeutic applications.

title: Risk of cancer after low doses of ionising radiation: retrospective cohort study in 15 countries.
text:
Objective: To provide accurate estimates of the risk of cancer after prolonged exposure to low levels of ionizing radiation and to strengthen the scientific basis of radiation protection standards for environmental, occupational, and medical diagnostic exposures.
Design: Multinational retrospective cohort study of cancer mortality among nuclear industry workers in 15 countries.
Participants: 407,391 workers individually monitored for external radiation exposure over a total of 5.2 million person-years.
Main Outcome Measurements: Estimates of excess relative risks per sievert (Sv) of radiation dose for mortality from cancers other than leukemia and from leukemia excluding chronic lymphocytic leukemia, which are the primary causes of death of concern for radiation protection authorities.
Results: The excess relative risk for cancers other than leukemia was found to be 0.97 per Sv (95% confidence interval: 0.14-1.97). Analyses of causes of death related or unrelated to smoking suggest that while confounding by smoking may be present, it is unlikely to fully explain this increased risk. The excess relative risk for leukemia excluding chronic lymphocytic leukemia was found to be 1.93 per Sv (<0-8.47). Based on these estimates, it is estimated that 1-2% of cancer deaths among nuclear workers in this cohort may be attributable to radiation exposure.
Conclusions: These estimates, derived from the largest study of nuclear workers ever conducted, are higher than but statistically compatible with the risk estimates used in current radiation protection standards. The findings suggest that there is a small excess risk of cancer, even at the low doses and dose rates typically received by nuclear workers in this study.

title: Gamma-Secretase Represents a Therapeutic Target for the Treatment of Invasive Glioma Mediated by the p75 Neurotrophin Receptor
text: The protein p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75(NTR)) plays a central role in the highly invasive nature of malignant gliomas. Our research reveals that neurotrophin-dependent regulated intramembrane proteolysis (RIP) of p75(NTR) is essential for its ability to promote glioma invasion. We have identified a novel approach to targeted glioma therapy by exploiting this process. We found that expressing chimeras of p75(NTR) that are resistant to cleavage or treating animals with clinically applicable gamma-secretase inhibitors led to a significant reduction in glioma invasion and increased survival. Notably, we observed proteolytic processing of p75(NTR) in patient tumor samples and brain tumor initiating cells, indicating the potential of targeting this protein for clinical application in the treatment of malignant glioma.

title: Preliminary assessment of inhaled nitric oxide for acute vaso-occlusive crisis in pediatric patients with sickle cell disease.
text: The text discusses the potential benefits of inhaled nitric oxide (INO) therapy for the treatment of vaso-occlusive crises in pediatric patients with sickle cell disease. The study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial conducted at an urban, tertiary care children's hospital in the United States. Twenty patients aged 10 to 21 years with severe acute vaso-occlusive crisis were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive either INO (80 ppm with 21% final concentration of inspired oxygen) or placebo (21% inspired oxygen) for 4 hours. The primary outcome measures were the change in pain levels at 4 hours compared to preinhalation pain, measured on a 10-cm visual analog scale (VAS), and secondary outcome measures included pain over 6 hours, parenteral narcotic use over 24 hours, duration of hospitalization, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and methemoglobin concentration. The results showed that the INO group had a greater reduction in pain levels compared to the placebo group, with a 1-cm/h greater reduction in pain over 4 hours. Additionally, morphine use over 6 hours was significantly less in the INO group, but the difference was only observed over 4 hours and 24 hours. The duration of hospitalization was similar between the two groups. No INO toxicity was observed. The study suggests that INO may be beneficial for acute vaso-occlusive crisis in pediatric patients with sickle cell disease, and these preliminary results warrant further investigation.

title: Corresponding author:
text: Over the years, techniques for cytogenetic analysis have advanced and become an integral part of laboratory testing, providing valuable diagnostic and predictive information in blood disorders. Chromosomal aberrations, including karyotypic abnormalities, contribute to understanding the molecular basis of disease, enabling the rational application of therapeutic interventions. While metaphase cytogenetics (MC) has been a major driving force in this field, recent innovations in molecular technologies have complemented MC and overcome many of its limitations, including the need for cell culture. Whole genome scanning approaches, such as comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) and single nucleotide polymorphism arrays (SNP-A), enable the analysis of unbalanced chromosomal abnormalities. SNP-A combines copy number detection and genotyping, allowing the diagnosis of copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, a lesion that cannot be detected by MC but may have significant pathogenetic implications. These whole genome scanning arrays have the advantage of detecting chromosomal defects in a higher proportion of patients with hematologic malignancies compared to traditional cytogenetics. The detection of new chromosomal aberrations, including somatic uniparental disomy, may lead to the development of more accurate prognostic schemes in many diseases.

title: Rare Variants Create Synthetic Genome-Wide Associations
text:
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified at least 2,000 common variants associated with common diseases or traits (<http://www.genome.gov/gwastudies>). Many of these variants have been successfully replicated, leading to extensive resequencing efforts to identify the causal site. However, we propose an alternative explanation: uncommon or rare variants may create "synthetic associations" by occurring more frequently in association with one of the alleles at the common site. Although synthetic associations are a theoretical possibility, they have never been systematically explored.
Using simple computer simulations, we show that under reasonable genetic models, synthetic associations are not only possible but inevitable. We demonstrate that rare causal mutations responsible for both hearing loss and sickle cell anemia create genome-wide significant synthetic associations, extending over a 2.5-Mb interval encompassing scores of associated variants.
Our findings highlight the importance of considering the possibility of synthetic associations in the interpretation and follow-up of GWAS signals. Common variants may not always be the causal site, and uncommon or rare variants may create false positives that can lead to misinterpretation of the results.

title: Decoding of Cytoplasmic Ca2+ Oscillations through the Spatial Signature Drives Gene Expression
text: Cytoplasmic Ca2+ oscillations are a fundamental signaling mechanism that triggers various cellular responses across different cell types [1, 2]. Oscillations are more efficient at low stimulus intensities, suggesting they are the primary signaling mechanism in physiological conditions [3]. These oscillations regulate downstream signals by changing Ca2+ concentration levels, leading to the activation of specific targets [4-6]. Our study found that the spatial Ca2+ gradient within the oscillation plays a crucial role in this process. When plasmalemmal Ca2+ efflux was inhibited, Ca2+ oscillations in mast cells induced over a range of agonist concentrations in the presence of external Ca2+ were indistinguishable from those in the absence of Ca2+. However, only oscillations with accompanying Ca2+ entry through store-operated CRAC channels triggered gene expression. In contrast, increased cytoplasmic Ca2+ buffering prevented oscillations but failed to activate gene expression. We propose that local Ca2+ influx, rather than global Ca2+ oscillations, is the primary driver of gene expression at physiological levels of stimulation. Our findings suggest that the primary role of Ca2+ oscillations may be to activate CRAC channels, thereby generating localized Ca2+ signals that drive gene expression. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spatial profile of a Ca2+ oscillation provides a unique mechanism by which a pleiotropic messenger specifically activates gene expression.

title: Effect of glucosamine on pain-related disability in patients with chronic low back pain and degenerative lumbar osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Background:
Chric low back pain (LBP) with degenerative lumbar osteoarthritis (OA) is a common condition affecting a large portion of the adult population. Despite the increasing use of glucosamine by patients with chronic LBP, little is known about its effectiveness in this context.
Objective:
To investigate the effect of glucosamine on pain-related disability in patients with chronic LBP and degenerative lumbar OA.
Methods:
A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial was conducted at the Oslo University Hospital Outpatient Clinic in Oslo, Norway, involving 250 patients aged 25 years or older with chronic LBP (>6 months duration) and degenerative lumbar OA. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either 1500 mg of oral glucosamine or placebo daily for 6 months, with assessments of effect performed after the intervention period and at 1-year follow-up.
Primary Outcome Measures:
The primary outcome measure was pain-related disability assessed using the Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ). Secondary outcome measures included numerical scores from pain-rating scales obtained at rest and during activity, as well as quality-of-life measures evaluated using the EuroQol-5 Dimensions (EQ-5D) instrument. Data were collected at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 and 6 months, and again at 1 year following the intervention. Group differences were analyzed using linear mixed models analysis.
Results:
At baseline, the mean RMDQ score was 9.2 (95% confidence interval [CI], 8.4-10.0) for the glucosamine group and 9.7 (95% CI, 8.9-10.5) for the placebo group (P = .37). After 6 months, the mean RMDQ score was the same for both groups (5.0; 95% CI, 4.2-5.8). At 1 year, the mean RMDQ scores were 4.8 (95% CI, 3.9-5.6) for the glucosamine group and 5.5 (95% CI, 4.7-6.4) for the placebo group (P = .72). No significant difference in change between groups was found when assessed after the 6-month intervention period and at 1 year: RMDQ (P = .91), LBP at rest (P = .97), LBP during activity (P = .97), and quality-of-life EQ-5D (P = .20). Mild adverse events were reported in 40 patients in the glucosamine group and 46 in the placebo group (P = .48).
Conclusion:
Among patients with chronic LBP and degenerative lumbar OA, 6-month treatment with oral glucosamine did not result in reduced pain-related disability after the 6-month intervention and after 1-year follow-up. These findings suggest that glucosamine may not be an effective treatment for managing chronic LBP and degenerative lumbar OA.

title: Adult cervicocerebral artery dissection: a single-center study of 301 Finnish patients.
text:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE:
There have been limited studies investigating potential risk factors, comorbidities, and prognostic markers in adults with spontaneous cervicocerebral artery dissections (CAD). To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a retrospective, hospital-based analysis of factors associated with CAD and its prognosis in 301 Finnish patients diagnosed between 1994 and 2007.
METHODS:
We analyzed the clinical and demographic data of patients with CAD and identified potential risk factors, comorbidities, and prognostic markers. Two thirds of the patients were male (68%), and women were found to be younger than men. Migraine, particularly with visual aura, was more common in patients with CAD compared to the general Finnish population (36% of all patients). Smoking was also more prevalent among patients with CAD.
RESULTS:
At 3 months, 83% of patients reached a favorable outcome. Occlusion of the dissected artery, internal carotid artery dissection (ICAD), and recent infection in infarction patients were associated with a poorer outcome. Notably, ICAD patients had fewer brain infarctions but more severe strokes compared to non-ICAD patients. A total of 2.3% of patients died during the follow-up period (mean 4.0 years, 1186 patient years), and six patients experienced verified CAD recurrences.
CONCLUSIONS:
Our study provides evidence for the association of CAD with male sex and potential links to smoking and migraine. Occlusion of the dissected artery, ICAD, and infection were found to be associated with poorer outcomes in patients with CAD. These findings underline the importance of early diagnosis and appropriate management of CAD to improve patient outcomes.

title: Genetic variation and gastric cancer risk: a field synopsis and meta-analysis.
text:
Here is a possible reconstruction of the original text using a more formal and objective tone:
Background: A growing body of literature has investigated the genetic susceptibility to sporadic gastric carcinoma, but a comprehensive overview and quantitative summary of these findings has been lacking.
Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of the evidence on the association between DNA variation and risk of developing stomach cancer. To assess the credibility of the results, we applied the Venice criteria and calculated false positive report probability (FPRP) to validate the significance of the findings. Subgroup analyses were performed based on ethnicity (Asian vs Caucasian), tumour histology (intestinal vs diffuse), tumour site (cardia vs non-cardia), and Helicobacter pylori infection status (positive vs negative).
Results: Our literature search identified 824 eligible studies comprising 2,530,706 subjects (cases: 261,386 (10.3%)). We performed primary and subgroup meta-analyses on 156 variants involving 101 genes, and identified 11 variants that were significantly associated with disease risk and had a high level of summary evidence: MUC1 rs2070803 at 1q22 (diffuse carcinoma subgroup), MTX1 rs2075570 at 1q22 (diffuse), PSCA rs2294008 at 8q24.2 (non-cardia), PRKAA1 rs13361707 at 5p13 (non-cardia), PLCE1 rs2274223 at 10q23 (cardia), TGFBR2 rs3087465 at 3p22 (Asian), PKLR rs3762272 at 1q22 (diffuse), PSCA rs2976392 at (intestinal), GSTP1 rs1695 at 11q13 (Asian), CASP8 rs3834129 at 2q33 (mixed), and TNF rs1799724 at 6p21.3 (mixed). We also identified polymorphisms with lower quality significant associations (n=110).
Conclusions: Our findings identify several high-quality biomarkers of gastric cancer susceptibility, which will form the basis of an annually updated online resource that will inform future screening programs.

title: Structure and function of the blood–brain barrier
text:
The central nervous system (CNS) relies on a tightly regulated microenvironment for proper neural signaling. At three key interfaces, cells act as barriers between the bloodstream and the CNS, known as the blood-brain barrier (BBB), blood-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) barrier, and arachnoid barrier. The BBB, specifically, is the primary site of blood-CNS exchange and is composed of a physical barrier formed by endothelial tight junctions and a transport barrier resulting from membrane transporters and vesicular mechanisms. Associated cells, such as astrocytic glial cells, pericytes, and microglia, play crucial roles in maintaining the structure and function of the BBB.
The development of the BBB in embryos and changes that occur in pathology are also important factors to consider. The BBB is subject to both short-term and long-term regulation, which can be disrupted in disease states. Any drug discovery and delivery program aiming to target or avoid the CNS must take into account the unique characteristics of the BBB. By understanding the structure, function, and regulation of the BBB, researchers can develop more effective and safer treatments for various neurological disorders.

title: Golli protein negatively regulates store depletion-induced calcium influx in T cells.
text: Calcium influx is pivotal for T cell activation and differentiation, but the intricate mechanisms governing this process are not fully understood. Our findings reveal that the golli protein, a splice variant of the myelin basic protein gene, plays a crucial role in regulating calcium influx in T cells. Golli-deficient T cells exhibited hyperproliferation and enhanced calcium entry upon T cell receptor stimulation. Our studies demonstrated that golli regulates calcium influx in T cells by inhibiting the store depletion-induced calcium influx. The myristoylation site of golli is essential for its inhibitory action, as membrane association of golli is necessary for its function. These findings suggest that golli operates in a unique manner to modulate T cell activation through the regulation of calcium homeostasis.

title: Extracellular vesicles derived from renal cancer stem cells induce a pro-tumorigenic phenotype in mesenchymal stromal cells
text: Renal carcinomas have been shown to harbor a population of cancer stem cells (CSCs) with self-renewing capacity and tumor-promoting potential. These CSCs secrete large amounts of extracellular vesicles (EVs) that can transfer various molecules, including proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids, and induce epigenetic changes in target cells. Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (MSCs) are susceptible to tumor signals and can be recruited to the tumor microenvironment. The exact role of MSCs in tumor development is still under debate, with both pro- and anti-tumorigenic effects reported. In this study, we investigated the involvement of renal CSC-derived EVs in the interaction between tumor and MSCs. We found that CSC-derived EVs promoted persistent changes in MSCs, characterized by increased expression of genes associated with cell migration (CXCR4, CXCR7), matrix remodeling (COL4A3), angiogenesis (IL-8, Osteopontin, Myeloperoxidase), and tumor growth. EV-stimulated MSCs exhibited enhanced migration toward the tumor conditioned medium in vitro and supported tumor growth and vascularization in vivo when co-injected with renal tumor cells. In conclusion, CSC-derived EVs induce phenotypical changes in MSCs that are associated with tumor growth.

title: In vivo effect of chronic hypoxia on the neurochemical profile of the developing rat hippocampus.
text: The study investigated the impact of chronic postnatal hypoxia on the developing hippocampus in a rat model. Using in vivo 1H NMR spectroscopy at 9.4 T, the researchers evaluated a neurochemical profile consisting of 15 metabolites and 2 metabolite ratios in the hippocampus of exposed rats (n = 23) from postnatal day (P) 3 to P28, compared to normoxic controls (n = 14). The results showed that chronic hypoxia altered the concentrations of several neurochemicals, including aspartate, creatine, phosphocreatine, GABA, glutamate, glutamine, glutathione, myoinositol, N-acetylaspartate (NAA), phosphorylethanolamine, and glutamate/glutamine (Glu/Gln) ratios. Specifically, the increased phosphocreatine/creatine (PCr/Cr) ratio indicated decreased brain energy consumption. The elevated glutamate, Glu/Gln ratio, and GABA levels suggested suppressed excitatory neurotransmission in an energy-limited environment. Decreased NAA and phosphorylethanolamine indicated reduced neuronal integrity and phospholipid metabolism. These alterations in hippocampal neurochemistry during development may underlie some of the cognitive deficits observed in human infants at risk of chronic hypoxia.

title: Noncoding Transcription by RNA Polymerase Pol IVb/Pol V Mediates Transcriptional Silencing of Overlapping and Adjacent Genes
text: Widespread transcription of eukaryotic genomes extends beyond genes and encompasses intergenic and noncoding regions. Despite its prevalence, the functional significance of this pervasive noncoding transcription remains largely unexplored. Our findings reveal that Arabidopsis RNA polymerase IVb/Pol V, a multisubunit nuclear enzyme essential for siRNA-mediated gene silencing of transposons and repetitive sequences, also transcribes intergenic and noncoding regions. This enables the formation of heterochromatin and silencing of adjacent and overlapping genes. Pol IVb/Pol V transcription relies on the chromatin-remodeling protein DRD1 but is unrelated to siRNA biogenesis. However, both Pol IVb/Pol V transcription and siRNA production are necessary to silence transposons, suggesting that Pol IVb/Pol V produces RNAs or chromatin structures that act as scaffolds for siRNA-mediated heterochromatin-forming complexes. Our findings offer a solution to a paradox in epigenetic regulation: the need for transcription to silence the same region.

title: Intestinal microbiota metabolism of L-carnitine, a nutrient in red meat, promotes atherosclerosis
text: The gut microbiota metabolizes choline and phosphatidylcholine, producing trimethylamine (TMA), which is further metabolized to a proatherogenic compound, trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO). We demonstrate that the gut microbiota's metabolism of dietary L-carnitine, found in red meat, also generates TMAO and accelerates atherosclerosis in mice.
