Interestingly, omnivorous humans produced more TMAO than vegans or vegetarians after consuming L-carnitine through a microbiota-dependent mechanism. The presence of specific bacterial taxa in human feces was associated with both plasma TMAO concentrations and dietary status. Plasma L-carnitine levels in subjects undergoing cardiac evaluation were found to predict increased risks for both prevalent cardiovascular disease (CVD) and incident major adverse cardiac events (myocardial infarction, stroke or death), but only among subjects with concurrently high TMAO levels. Chronic dietary L-carnitine supplementation in mice significantly altered the composition of cecal microorganisms, enhanced the synthesis of TMA and TMAO, and exacerbated atherosclerosis, but this effect was not observed if the intestinal microbiota was concurrently suppressed. In contrast, dietary supplementation with TMAO or either carnitine or choline reduced in vivo reverse cholesterol transport in mice with an intact intestinal microbiota. These findings suggest that the gut microbiota may play a significant role in the established link between high levels of red meat consumption and CVD risk.

title: Hepatotoxicity associated with antiretroviral therapy in adults infected with human immunodeficiency virus and the role of hepatitis C or B virus infection.
text:
The use of antiretroviral drugs, including protease inhibitors, to treat human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection has been associated with hepatotoxicity, particularly in individuals coinfected with hepatitis C or B virus. To investigate if the incidence of severe hepatotoxicity is similar across all antiretroviral drug combinations and to determine the role of chronic viral hepatitis in its development, a prospective cohort study was conducted at an urban HIV clinic.
A total of 298 patients receiving new antiretroviral therapies between January 1996 and January 1998 were included in the study, of whom 211 (71%) received protease inhibitors as part of combination therapy (median follow-up, 182 days) and 87 (29%) received dual nucleoside analog regimens (median follow-up, 167 days). Of the participants, 154 (52%) had chronic hepatitis C and 8 (2.7%) had chronic hepatitis B virus infection.
Severe hepatotoxicity was observed in 31 (10.4%) of the 298 patients, and ritonavir use was associated with a higher incidence of toxicity (30%; 95% CI, 17.9%-44.6%). However, no significant difference in hepatotoxicity incidence was detected in other treatment groups, including nucleoside analogs (5.7%; 95% CI, 1.2%-12.9%), nelfinavir (5.9%; 95% CI, 1.2%-16.2%), saquinavir (5.9%; 95% CI, 0.15%-28.7%), and indinavir(6.8%; 95% CI, 3.0%-13.1%). Additionally, chronic viral hepatitis was associated with an increased risk of severe hepatotoxicity among patients prescribed non-ritonavir regimens (relative risk, 3.7; 95% CI, 1.0-11.8), but most patients with chronic hepatitis C or B virus infection (88%) did not experience significant toxic effects.
In multivariate logistic regression analysis, only ritonavir (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 8.6; 95% CI, 3.0-24.6) and a CD4 cell count increase of more than 0.05 x 10(9)/L (AOR, 3.6; 95% CI, 1.0-12.9) were associated with severe hepatotoxicity. No irreversible outcomes were seen in patients with severe hepatotoxicity.
The study suggests that ritonavir may increase the risk of severe hepatotoxicity, but hepatotoxicity is not necessarily more common in individuals with chronic viral hepatitis. Therefore, withholding protease inhibitor therapy from individuals coinfected with hepatitis B or C virus is not justified.

title: Mutations in the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase pathway predict for antitumor activity of the inhibitor PX-866 whereas oncogenic Ras is a dominant predictor for resistance.
text: The novel phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor PX-866 was assessed against 13 experimental human tumor xenografts derived from various cell lines. Mutations in PI3K (PIK3CA) and loss of PTEN activity were not necessarily predictive of sensitivity to the antitumor effects of PX-866, unless Wild-type Ras was present. In contrast, the presence of oncogenic Ras was the dominant factor contributing to resistance, even in tumors with coexisting PIK3CA mutations. The level of PI3K signaling activity, as measured by phosphorylated Ser(473)-Akt, failed to predict the in vivo antitumor response to PX-866. Furthermore, reverse-phase protein array analysis revealed that the Ras-dependent downstream targets c-Myc and cyclin B were elevated in cell lines resistant to PX-866 in vivo. Investigations using an H-Ras construct showed that mutant Ras can mediate resistance through its ability to utilize multiple signaling pathways for tumorigenesis. The identification of Ras and downstream signaling pathways driving resistance to PI3K inhibition may serve as a valuable guide for patient selection as inhibitors enter clinical trials and for the development of rational combinations with other molecularly targeted agents.

title: Changing mortality patterns in East and West Germany and Poland. II: short-term trends during transition and in the 1990s.
text:
The aim of this study is to examine the trends in life expectancy and cause-specific mortality patterns in the former German Democratic Republic (GDR) and Poland during the political transition period and in the 1990s, both in East Germany and Poland.
The study uses decomposition methods to examine changes in life expectancy by age and cause of death, using data from 1988/89 and 1990/91 for the GDR and Poland, and from 1992-97 for Germany and 1991-96 for Poland. The results show that:
In both the GDR and Poland, male life expectancy at birth declined by nearly one year during transition, primarily due to increases in death rates from external causes and circulatory diseases. Female life expectancy in Poland deteriorated by 0.3 years, mainly due to rising circulatory mortality among the elderly, while in East Germany, rising death rates among children and young adults were almost offset by declining circulatory mortality among those over 70. Between 1991/92 and 1996/97, male life expectancy at birth increased by 2.4 years in the former GDR, 1.2 years in the old Federal Republic, and 2.0 years in Poland (women: 2.3, 0.9, and 1.2 years). In East Germany and Poland, the overall improvement was largely due to falling mortality among men aged 40-64, while those over 65 contributed the largest proportion to life expectancy gains in women. The decrease in deaths among men aged 15-39 accounted for 0.4 years of life expectancy at birth in East Germany and Poland, primarily due to greater decreases from external causes. Among those over 40, absolute contributions to changing life expectancy were greater in the former GDR than in the other two entities in both sexes, primarily due to circulatory diseases. A persisting East-west life expectancy gap in Germany of 2.1 years in men in 1997 was largely due to external causes, diseases of the digestive system, and circulatory diseases. Higher death rates from circulatory diseases among the elderly largely explain the female life expectancy gap of approximately one year.

In conclusion, this study provides further insights into the health effects of political transition. The post-transition improvements in life expectancy and mortality have been much steeper in East Germany compared to Poland. Changes in dietary patterns and medical care may have played a significant role in shaping post-transition mortality trends.

title: 0021-972X/06/$15.00/0 The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism 91(3):760–771 Printed in U.S.A. Copyright © 2006 by The Endocrine Society doi: 10.1210/jc.2005-1923 REVIEW: Aromatase Inhibitors for Ovulation Induction
text:
For the past 40 years, clomiphene citrate (CC) has been the primary treatment for anovulation in infertile women. However, CC has known side effects, including antiestrogenic effects on the endometrium and cervix, which can impair fertility, and a higher risk of multiple pregnancies compared to natural cycles. In light of these issues, we propose the use of aromatase inhibitors (AIs) as a new method of ovulation induction. This review aims to compare the physiological mechanisms of action and efficacy of CC and AIs in inducing ovulation, either alone or in combination with gonadotropins.
We conducted a systematic review of published studies using the Entrez-PubMed search engine, identifying both controlled and noncontrolled studies that compared CC and AI treatment for ovulation induction or augmentation. Due to the recent acceptance of AIs for ovulation induction, few controlled studies were found, and the majority of studies were pilot or preliminary comparisons.
Our findings suggest that AIs are as effective as CC in inducing ovulation, without the antiestrogenic side effects. AIs also result in lower serum estrogen concentrations and are associated with good pregnancy rates with a lower incidence of multiple pregnancy compared to CC. When used in combination with gonadotropins for assisted reproductive technologies, AIs reduce the dose of FSH required for optimal follicle recruitment and improve the response to FSH in poor responders.
Based on the preliminary evidence, it appears that AIs may replace CC in the future due to their similar efficacy with a reduced side effect profile. However, definitive studies in the form of randomized controlled trials comparing CC with AIs are currently lacking, and worldwide experience with AIs for ovulation induction is increasing.

title: Patent ductus arteriosus: lack of evidence for common treatments.
text: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is a common diagnosis among extremely premature infants, particularly those with lung disease. Despite decades of research, the question of whether the benefits of treatments to prevent ductal patency or promote closure outweigh the risks of these treatments remains unanswered. The authors generally avoid using treatments designed to close the PDA. This review discusses three reasons for this cautious approach: the rates of spontaneous closure of the ductus arteriosus; the adverse effects of persistent ductal patency; and the benefits and risks of treatments for closure.

title: Gene therapy of arthritis with TCR isolated from the inflamed paw.
text:
In recent years, the treatment of autoimmune diseases has witnessed significant advancements through the use of biological agents. However, these therapies can sometimes be accompanied by severe side effects, such as tuberculosis and other types of infection. To address this issue, there is an urgent need for non-systemic and lesion-specific methods of delivering therapeutic agents. In our attempt to treat a mouse model of arthritis, we focused on using T cells that expressed a regulatory molecule and were specifically guided to the inflamed paw.
We began by identifying the TCR alpha beta genes present in the inflamed paw of mice with collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) through a combination of single-strand chain polymorphism analysis of TCR and single-cell sorting. We discovered an expanded clone designated B47, which is autoreactive but not specifically directed towards type II collagen. In vivo, TCR genes from B47-transduced T cells accumulated in the inflamed paw. Following the injection of cells cotransduced with the B47 and soluble TNFRIg genes, significant suppression of CIA was observed, which was correlated with the amount of TNFRIg transcripts in the hind paw rather than the serum concentrations of TNFRIg. Additionally, T cells cotransduced with the B47 and intracellular Foxp3 genes exhibited significant suppression of CIA, characterized by reduced expression of TNF-alpha, IL-17A, and IL-1beta, and bone destruction. Notably, these T cells also suppressed the progression of established CIA. Therefore, immunosuppressive therapy using autoreactive TCR is a promising therapeutic strategy for arthritis, and these T cells can deliver either soluble or intracellular suppressive molecules.

title: Melatonin: A Mitochondrial Targeting Molecule Involving Mitochondrial Protection and Dynamics
text: Melatonin is thought to be primarily synthesized within mitochondria. This idea is backed by the recent discovery that aralkylamine N-acetyltransferase/serotonin N-acetyltransferase (AANAT/SNAT) is located in mitochondria of oocytes, and that isolated mitochondria can generate melatonin. It is also suggested that melatonin acts as a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant. It accumulates in mitochondria with a high concentration gradient, likely due to active transport via mitochondrial melatonin transporters. Melatonin protects mitochondria by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS), inhibiting the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP), and activating uncoupling proteins (UCPs). This maintains the optimal mitochondrial membrane potential and preserves mitochondrial functions. Additionally, melatonin regulates mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics, typically reducing mitochondrial fission and elevating fusion. Mitochondrial dynamics exhibit an oscillatory pattern that correlates with the melatonin circadian secretory rhythm in pinealeocytes and likely in other cells. Furthermore, recent research has uncovered melatonin's role in promoting mitophagy and maintaining homeostasis of mitochondria.

title: Self-reported health status and access to health services in a sample of prisoners in Italy
text:
The present study aimed to investigate the self-reported health status, quality of life, and access to health services among male prisoners in Italy. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 908 prisoners, and 650 of them responded to the questionnaire. The results showed that approximately 31% and 43% of prisoners reported poor perceived health status and poor quality of life, respectively. Additionally, 60% of prisoners stated that their health had worsened or greatly worsened during their time in prison.
The study found that older age, lower education, psychiatric disorders, self-reported health problems on prison entry, and suicide attempts within prison were significantly associated with a worse perceived health status. It was also found that 30% of prisoners reported having a health problem present on prison entry, and the most frequently reported health problems included dental health problems, arthritis or joint pain, eye problems, gastrointestinal diseases, emotional problems, and high blood pressure.
The study also examined the frequency of medical encounters among prisoners, and it was found that prisoners encountered general practitioners an average of six times in the previous year. The frequency of medical encounters was significantly associated with older age, sentenced prisoners, psychiatric disorders, and self-reported health problems on prison entry.
The findings of the study suggest that prisoners have a perceived poor health status, and there is a need for specific care needs and health promotion programs. Programs for the correction of risk behaviors and the prevention of long-term effects of incarceration on prisoners' health are strongly needed.

title: BH3-only Protein Noxa Is a Mediator of Hypoxic Cell Death Induced by Hypoxia-inducible Factor 1α
text: Hypoxia, a common cause of cell death and underlying numerous diseases such as stroke and chronic degenerative disorders, triggers a variety of cellular responses to adapt to altered metabolic demands and decreased oxygen availability. In our study, we used polymerase chain reaction–based suppression subtractive hybridization to identify genes differentially expressed in response to hypoxia. Among these genes, we found the BH3-only Bcl-2 family protein Noxa, which plays a crucial role in p53-induced apoptosis. Our results show that the Noxa promoter directly responds to hypoxia through the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-1α. By suppressing Noxa expression with antisense oligonucleotides, we could rescue cells from hypoxia-induced death and reduce infarction volumes in an animal model of ischemia. Furthermore, our findings indicate that reactive oxygen species (ROS) and cytochrome c release contribute to Noxa-mediated hypoxic cell death. Overall, our study uncovers the mechanism by which Noxa is induced by HIF-1α and mediates hypoxic cell death.

title: Neutrophil extracellular chromatin traps connect innate immune response to autoimmunity
text:
Autoantibodies to DNA and histones (chromatin) are the distinct antigen specificity in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and related musculoskeletal disorders. However, the underlying mechanisms that induce these autoantibodies remain unknown. This situation has recently shifted with the discovery of Neutrophil Extracellular Chromatin Traps (NETs) and their role in immune responses to various microbial pathogens.
At the heart of an infectious process, neutrophils exude various antimicrobial defenses, including the release of nuclear chromatin into the extracellular space. The released NETs, a complex network of nuclear chromatin and antimicrobial proteins, trap and degrade microbial pathogens. Here, we assess the evidence supporting NETs versus apoptotic bodies as a source of nuclear antigens in autoimmunity. Additionally, we discuss the possibility that NET chromatin serves as a vital component of immune deposits in the pathogenesis of glomerulonephritis in SLE and other autoimmune-related immune complex diseases.

title: Bcl2 Regulation by the Melanocyte Master Regulator Mitf Modulates Lineage Survival and Melanoma Cell Viability
text: Kit/SCF signaling and Mitf-dependent transcription play critical roles in melanocyte development and pigmentation. To identify Mitf-dependent Kit transcriptional targets in primary melanocytes, microarray analyses were performed. Among the identified targets was BCL2, which was found to be crucial for melanocyte survival and function. Germline deletion of BCL2 resulted in melanocyte loss, and co-deletion of Mitf and Bcl2 led to marked phenotypic synergy in mice. Chromatin immunoprecipitation assays confirmed Mitf's regulation of BCL2 in both melanocytes and melanoma cells. Moreover, Mitf also controls BCL2 expression in osteoclasts, and Mitf-deficient mice and Bcl2-deficient mice exhibited severe osteopetrosis. Disruption of Mitf in melanocytes or melanoma resulted in increased apoptosis, which could be rescued by BCL2 overexpression. Interestingly, primary human melanoma expression microarray analyses revealed strong nearest neighbor linkage between MITF and BCL2, highlighting the pivotal roles of both factors in the melanocyte lineage and the well-documented resistance of melanoma to treatment.

title: YOKO HONDA AND SHUJI HONDA 1
text: The daf-2 gene network in Caenorhabditis elegans regulates longevity, with mutations in the daf-2 gene conferring a life extension (Age) phenotype and the formation of a growth-arrested larval form specialized for dispersal (constitutive dauer). The Age phenotype is potentiated by mutations in the clk-1 gene, which encodes a homologue of yeast CAT5/COQ7 involved in ubiquinone biosynthesis. This study also revealed that the daf-2 mutation confers an oxidative stress resistance (Oxr) phenotype, which is regulated by the insulin-like signaling pathway from daf-2 to the daf-16 gene, a homologue of the HNF-3/forkhead transcription factor. Investigation of the insulin-like signaling pathway's regulation of antioxidant defense gene expression revealed that the mRNA level of the sod-3 gene, which encodes Mn-superoxide dismutase (SOD), is significantly higher in daf-2 mutants than in the wild type. The increased sod-3 gene expression phenotype is regulated by the insulin-like signaling pathway, with the clk-1 mutation enhancing it in the daf-2 mutant. These findings suggest that the daf-2 gene network controls longevity by regulating the Mn-SOD-associated antioxidant defense system, which plays a role in efficient life maintenance at the dauer stage.

title: Brown Fat and Browning for the Treatment of Obesity and Related Metabolic Disorders
text: Brown fat is a specific type of fat deposit that can increase metabolic rate and produce heat. With the recent discovery of active brown fat in adult humans and new transcription factors controlling brown adipocyte differentiation, the field of brown fat research has experienced a surge in interest and growth. Brown fat expansion or activation leads to increased energy expenditure and a negative energy balance in mice, hindering weight gain. Brown fat can utilize glucose and lipids and improve glucose metabolism and blood lipids without weight loss. Cold exposure or beta adrenergic agonists can induce the browning of white adipose tissue. The inducible brown adipocyte, which develops through thermogenic activation of white adipose tissue, has a distinct origins and molecular signature compared to classical brown adipocytes but shares characteristics such as high mitochondria content, UCP1 expression, and thermogenic capacity upon activation. Increasing browning may also enhance whole brown fat activity. Recent human studies have shown that findings in mice can be replicated in humans, making brown fat a promising target for treating obesity and related disorders.

title: Hypoxia-induced energy stress regulates mRNA translation and cell growth.
text: Oxygen deprivation (hypoxia) has significant effects on cell metabolism and growth. Cells can adapt to low oxygen levels in part by activating hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF). Our research reveals that hypoxia inhibits protein synthesis by suppressing key regulatory factors, including eIF2alpha, eEF2, and the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) effectors 4EBP1, p70S6K, and rpS6, regardless of HIF. Hypoxia leads to energy starvation and the activation of the AMPK/TSC2/Rheb/mTOR pathway. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation in hypoxia also leads to the inhibition of eEF2. Moreover, the long-term effects of hypoxia on cellular bioenergetics and mTOR inhibition are significant. Additionally, mutations in the TSC2 tumor suppressor gene can provide a growth advantage to cells by blocking hypoxic mTOR inhibition and G1 cell cycle arrest. Finer insight into the mechanisms of eIF2alpha, eEF2, and mTOR inhibition can demonstrate how cells conserve energy during low oxygen conditions, thereby promoting survival.

title: The dystonia-associated protein torsinA modulates synaptic vesicle recycling.
text: The loss of a glutamic acid residue in the AAA-ATPase (ATPases associated with diverse cellular activities) torsinA is responsible for most cases of early onset autosomal dominant primary dystonia. In this study, we discovered that snapin, which binds SNAP-25 (synaptosome-associated protein of 25,000 Da) and enhances the association of the SNARE complex with synaptotagmin, interacts with both wild type and mutant torsinA. Snapin co-localized with endogenous torsinA in dense core granules in PC12 cells and was recruited to perinuclear inclusions containing mutant DeltaE-torsinA in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. Subsequent investigation into synaptic vesicle recycling revealed that overexpression of wild type torsinA negatively impacts the process, while overexpression of DeltaE-torsinA leads to increased uptake of the lipophilic dye FM1-43. Conversely, knockdown of either snapin or torsinA using small interfering RNAs resulted in an inhibitory effect on the exo-endocytic process. Additionally, down-regulation of torsinA caused the persistence of synaptotagmin I on the plasma membrane, which closely resembles the effect observed upon overexpression of the DeltaE-torsinA mutant. These findings suggest that torsinA functions together with snapin in regulated exocytosis, and that DeltaE-torsinA exerts its pathological effects through a loss of function mechanism, which may impair neuronal uptake of neurotransmitters, such as dopamine, leading to the development of dystonic movements.

title: In vivo electroporation in the embryonic mouse central nervous system
text: This protocol describes a basic method for in vivo electroporation in the nervous system of embryonic mice. The delivery of electrical pulses following microinjection of DNA into the brain ventricle or spinal cord central canal enables efficient transfection of genes into the nervous system. This is achieved using forceps-type electrodes that stabilize the uterus and/or yolk sac containing the embryo. More than ten embryos can be operated on within 30 minutes, with >90% of operated embryos surviving and >90% of survivors exhibiting appropriate gene expression. Notably, gene expression in neurons persists for an extended period, even at postnatal stages, allowing this method to be used to elucidate the roles of genes in both embryonic development and higher-order functions of the nervous system, such as learning.

title: Hierarchical phylogenetic models for analyzing multipartite sequence data.
text:
There is ongoing debate about how to incorporate information from multi-partite sequence data in phylogenetic analyses. One approach is the "strict combined-data" method, which involves concatenating all partitions and estimating a single evolutionary history to maximize the explanatory power of the data. However, this approach can be limited by the potential for conflicts between partitions. Another approach is the "consensus/independence" method, which involves analyzing each partition separately and then combining the results to determine a consensus evolutionary history. This approach can also lead to conflicts, especially when the partitions have different evolutionary histories.
To address these limitations, some researchers have used a combination of methods, such as "mixtures across the model space" of a strict combined-data approach and a priori independent parameters. However, this approach can be complex and difficult to interpret.
We propose an alternative middle ground: a Bayesian hierarchical phylogenetic model. Our hierarchical framework enables researchers to pool information across data partitions to improve estimate precision in individual partitions while permitting estimation and testing of tendencies in across-partition quantities. For example, we can estimate the distribution from which individual topologies relating the sequences within a partition are drawn. We use standard hierarchical priors on continuous evolutionary parameters across partitions, while the structure on topologies varies depending on the research problem.
We illustrate our model with three examples. In the first example, we explore the evolutionary history of the guinea pig (Cavia porcellus) using alignments of 13 mitochondrial genes. The hierarchical model provides significantly more precise continuous parameter estimates than an independent parameter approach without losing the salient features of the data. In the second example, we analyze the frequency of horizontal gene transfer using 50 prokaryotic genes. We assume an unknown species-level topology and allow individual gene topologies to differ from this with a small estimable probability. Inferring the species and individual gene topologies simultaneously returns a transfer frequency of 17%. In the third example, we examine HIV sequences longitudinally sampled from HIV+ patients. We ask whether post-treatment development of CCR5 coreceptor virus represents concerted evolution from mid-disease CXCR4 virus or reemergence of initial infecting CCR5 virus. The hierarchical model pools partitions from multiple unrelated patients by assuming that the topology for each patient is drawn from a multinomial distribution with unknown probabilities. Preliminary results suggest evolution and not reemergence.

title: Up-to-date catalogues of yeast protein complexes
text: Gold standard datasets on protein complexes are crucial for inferring and validating protein-protein interactions. Despite significant progress in characterizing protein complexes in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, many researchers continue to rely on the manually curated complexes catalogued by the Munich Information Center of Protein Sequences database. Although this catalogue has been an invaluable resource, it no longer accurately reflects the current state of knowledge. Here, we present two curated protein complex catalogues as a result of systematic curation efforts. The first catalogue, denoted as CYC2008, is a comprehensive list of 408 manually curated heteromeric protein complexes supported by small-scale experiments reported in the current literature. This catalogue represents the most up-to-date reference set for biologists interested in discovering protein interactions and complexes. The second catalogue, denoted as YHTP2008, includes 400 high-throughput complexes annotated with current literature evidence. Of these, 262 have some overlap with CYC2008 complexes. Additional evidence for interacting subunits is provided for 68 complexes that have only partial or no overlap with CYC2008 complexes, and literature evidence was not found for 100 complexes. Some of these partially supported and unsupported complexes may be worthwhile candidates for experimental validation. Both catalogues are freely available at: <http://wodaklab.org/cyc2008/>.

title: Synergistic Mechanisms of DNA Demethylation during Transition to Ground-State Pluripotency
text: Pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) exist in a dynamic state of reversible molecular configurations, spanning from a naive, ground-state in 2i to metastable embryonic stem cells (ESCs) in serum to lineage-primed epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs). To investigate the role of DNA methylation (5mC) across different pluripotent states, we mapped genome-wide 5mC and 5-hydroxymethycytosine (5hmC) in multiple PSCs. Ground-state ESCs display an altered distribution of 5mC and 5hmC at regulatory elements, with significantly lower absolute levels compared to ESCs in serum. Conversely, EpiSCs exhibit increased promoter 5mC and reduced 5hmC, which contributes to their limited developmental potential. Upon switching to 2i, there is a rapid onset of both the ground-state gene expression program and global DNA demethylation. Mechanistically, the repression of de novo methylases by PRDM14 leads to slow hypomethylation, while TET1/TET2-mediated 5hmC conversion enhances both the rate and extent of hypomethylation, resulting in a synergistic effect during the transition to ground-state pluripotency, leading to a highly hypomethylated state.

title: Febrile seizures in the developing brain result in persistent modification of neuronal excitability in limbic circuits
text: Febrile (fever-induced) seizures affect approximately 3-5% of infants and young children. Despite the relatively high incidence of these seizures, there has been debate about their potential contribution to the development of epilepsy later in life. To better understand the long-term effects of febrile seizures on the brain, we developed a new rat model of complex febrile seizures and employed patch clamp techniques to examine the effects on hippocampal synaptic transmission. Our findings indicate that seizures induced by hyperthermia in immature rats result in a selective increase in inhibitory synaptic transmission in the hippocampus that persists into adulthood. This observation challenges the widely held view that early-life febrile convulsions are harmless.

title: Identification of an allele of VAM3/SYP22 that confers a semi-dwarf phenotype in Arabidopsis thaliana.
text: The short stem and midrib (ssm) mutants of Arabidopsis thaliana display both semi-dwarf and wavy leaf phenotypes due to defects in the elongation of stem internodes and leaves. Importantly, these abnormalities cannot be rescued by exogenous phytohormones. ssm was initially identified as a single recessive mutant in the ecotype Columbia (Col-0), but genetic crossings have revealed that this mutant phenotype can be restored in Col-0 by another gene that is functional in the ecotype Landsberg erecta (Ler) but not in Col-0. Following the mapping of the gene responsible for the ssm mutants, a small deletion within the sixth intron of a gene encoding a syntaxin, VAM3/SYP22, was discovered. This mutation seems to cause a peptide insertion in the deduced VAM3/SYP22 polypeptide sequence due to defective splicing of the shortened sixth intron. Notably, when compared to the wild-type Ler genome, the wild-type Col-0 genome contains a single base pair deletion causing a frameshift mutation in SYP23, a gene with the highest known homology to VAM3/SYP22. These findings suggest that VAM3/SYP22 and SYP23 have overlapping functions and that the vesicle transport mediated by these syntaxins is crucial for shoot morphogenesis.

title: Class Ia MHC-deficient BALB/c mice generate CD8+ T cell-mediated protective immunity against Listeria monocytogenes infection.
text: CD8(+) T cells are essential for establishing immunity against intracellular pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes. In this study, we employed class Ia MHC-deficient mice, which have a reduced number of circulating CD8(+) T cells, to investigate the protective capacity of class Ib MHC-restricted T cells during L. monocytogenes infection. To leverage the K(b-/-)D(b-/-) mutation, which was backcrossed onto a C.B10 (BALB/c congenic at the H-2 locus with C57BL/10) genetic background, as BALB/c mice are more prone to Listeria infection than other commonly analyzed mouse strains, such as C57BL/6. C.B10 K(b-/-)D(b-/-) mice immunized with a sublethal dose of L. monocytogenes displayed full protection against a subsequent lethal infection. Adoptive transfer of Listeria-immune splenocyte subsets into unprimed K(b-/-)D(b-/-) mice revealed that CD8(+) T cells were the dominant component of this protective immune response. We isolated a CD8(+) T cell line from the spleen of a Listeria-infected class Ia MHC-deficient mouse, which specifically recognized Listeria-infected cells in vitro, as demonstrated by IFN-gamma secretion and cytotoxicity assays. Adoptive transfer of this T cell line alone conferred significant protection against L. monocytogenes challenge. These findings suggest that even a limited number of class Ib MHC-restricted T cells are sufficient to generate the rapid recall response needed for protection against secondary infection with L. monocytogenes.

title: Upregulated PD-1 Expression Is Associated with the Development of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, but Not the PD-1.1 Allele of the PDCD1 Gene
text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease with genetic inheritance that involves multiple organ systems. Programmed death 1 (PD-1), a protein that regulates T cell activity, has been identified as a potential candidate gene in the development of SLE. To investigate the role of PD-1 in SLE, 30 patients with the disease and 30 healthy controls were recruited, and their PD-1 expression levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were measured using flow cytometry and quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). The study found that the PD-1 expression levels of SLE patients were significantly higher than those of healthy controls. Moreover, the upregulated PD-1 expression levels in SLE patients were closely associated with the SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI) scores. No significant association was found between PD-1 expression levels and a specific single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP), rs36084323. The results suggest that elevated PD-1 expression may contribute to the pathogenesis of SLE, and could potentially serve as a biomarker for SLE diagnosis. Additionally, the use of PD-1 inhibitors may be a promising therapeutic approach for managing SLE.

title: Endothelial cell membranes contain podocalyxin--the major sialoprotein of visceral glomerular epithelial cells
text: Podocalyxin, the primary sialoprotein in the glycocalyx of glomerular podocytes, has been found to have a wider distribution beyond the glomeruli. In this study, we employed a monospecific antibody produced through affinity purification on nitrocellulose transfers of glomerular podocalyxin to investigate its extraglomerular localization. By indirect immunofluorescence, we observed the presence of podocalyxin in various organ tissues, including the lung, heart, kidney, small intestine, brain, pancreas, aorta, and peripheral blood vessels of the liver. Further examination through immunoelectron microscopy revealed that podocalyxin was localized on the luminal membrane domain of endothelial cells, with a patchy distribution, both in pre-embedding and post-embedding procedures. To confirm these findings, we conducted immunoblotting analysis on SDS extracts of lung tissue, which reinforced the presence of podocalyxin in endothelial plasma membranes. Our results indicate that (a) podocalyxin is a ubiquitous component of endothelial plasma membranes, (b) it is confined exclusively to the luminal membrane domain, and (c) its distribution on the endothelial cell surface is irregular.

title: Teratogen-Induced Oxidative Stress Targets Glyceraldehyde-3-Phosphate Dehydrogenase in the Organogenesis Stage Mouse Embryo
text: Exposure of mouse embryos to the teratogen hydroxyurea (HU) during the organogenesis stage can cause curly tails and limb malformations, and oxidative stress has been implicated as a contributing factor. Hydroxyurea (HU) generate reactive aldehydes when it interacts with polyunsaturated bilipid membranes, with 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) being one of the most cytotoxic of these compounds. The goal of the current study was to investigate whether gestational day 9 exposure to hydroxyurea (HU) in CD1 mice results in region-specific 4-HNE-protein adducts in the embryo and to identify the proteins targeted. Unexpectedly, three proteins involved in energy metabolism, including glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase 2, and aldolase 1, A isoform, showed increased 4-HNE-protein adduct formation in the caudal region of exposed embryos. Furthermore, HU exposure led to increased nuclear translocation of GAPDH in this region, which may play a role in the reactivation of oxidized proteins involved in DNA repair and the stimulation of E1A-associated P300 protein/creb-binding protein (p300/CBP) activity, leading to cell death in a p53-dependent pathway. These findings suggest that GAPDH is a redox-sensitive target in the embryo and may play a role in the stress response during development.

title: Recurrent venous thromboembolism and bleeding complications during anticoagulant treatment in patients with cancer and venous thrombosis.
text: A small proportion of patients with deep vein thrombosis may experience recurrent venous thromboembolic complications or bleeding during anticoagulant treatment, and this risk is higher in patients with concomitant cancer. A prospective follow-up study aimed to determine whether cancer patients have a higher risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism or bleeding compared to those without cancer. Of the 842 included patients, 181 had known cancer at entry. The 12-month cumulative incidence of recurrent thromboembolism in cancer patients was 20.7% (95% CI, 15.6%-25.8%) compared to 6.8% (95% CI, 3.9%-9.7%) in patients without cancer, resulting in a hazard ratio of 3.2 (95% CI, 1.9-5.4). Similarly, the 12-month cumulative incidence of major bleeding was higher in cancer patients (12.4% (95% CI, 6.5%-18.2%)) compared to patients without cancer (4.9% (95% CI, 2.5%-7.4%), with a hazard ratio of 2.2 (95% CI, 1.2-4.1). These findings show that cancer patients with venous thrombosis are at a higher risk of recurrent thromboembolic complications and major bleeding during anticoagulant treatment, which is correlated with the severity of the cancer. Existing anticoagulation strategies may be insufficient to manage these risks, and new treatment approaches are needed.

title: Fitting multilevel models in complex survey data with design weights: Recommendations
text:
BACKGROUND: Multilevel models (MLM) offer researchers a powerful approach to understanding the complex relationships between individual-level determinants and contextual factors, such as geographic areas, in the analysis of public health data. However, there is a lack of consensus on how to handle design weights in complex survey data when using MLM. Simulation studies suggest that scaling design weights using two methods can improve the accuracy of MLM fitting, but there is limited guidance on how to apply these methods in practice.
METHODS: This study compares the performance of unweighted and scaled-weighted MLM analyses using data from the 2005-2006 National Survey of Children with Special Health Care Needs (NS-CSHCN), which collected data from children clustered within states. The study examines the impact of different outcome types (categorical vs. continuous), model types (level-1, level-2, or combined), and software programs (Mplus, MLwiN, and GLLAMM) on the performance of scaled-weighted and unweighted analyses.
RESULTS: The results show that scaled-weighted estimates and standard errors differ slightly from unweighted analyses, but the differences are minimal and do not lead to different inferential conclusions. Additionally, the study found minimal differences across software programs, which increasing confidence in the results and inferential conclusions independent of software choice.
CONCLUSION: Given the importance of design weights in MLM, analysts should consider scaling the weights and using software that properly accounts for the scaled weights in the estimation process. By doing so, researchers can ensure that their analyses accurately reflect the complex relationships between individual-level determinants and contextual factors in public health data.

title: Functional outcomes of multi-condition collaborative care and successful ageing: results of randomised trial
text:
The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of integrated care for chronic physical diseases and depression in reducing disability and improving quality of life among middle-aged and elderly patients. The study design was a randomized controlled trial, conducted at 14 primary care clinics in Seattle, Washington, comparing the outcomes of patients receiving integrated care to those receiving usual care.
Participants were recruited from clinics based on their diagnosis of diabetes or coronary heart disease, or both, along with raised blood pressure, elevated lipid levels, or signs of depression (measured by PHQ-9 score ≥ 10). The intervention involved a "treat to target" program for controlling diabetes and risk factors for coronary heart disease, alongside collaborative care for managing depression through self-management support, monitoring of disease control, and pharmacotherapy.
The primary outcome measures were the Sheehan Disability Scale, Global Quality of Life Rating, and World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS-2), which measure disability in activities of daily living (mobility, self-care, and household maintenance). The study found that patients receiving integrated care showed greater improvements in disability and quality of life compared to usual care at six and 12 months, with a significant difference in Sheehan Disability Scale scores (-0.9, 95% confidence interval -1.5 to -0.2; P = 0.006) and global quality of life ratings (0.7, 0.2 to 1.2; P = 0.005). Although there was a trend towards greater improvement in disabilities in activities of daily living (-1.5, -3.3 to 0.4; P = 0.10), the difference did not reach statistical significance.

In conclusion, the study found that integrated care that addresses chronic physical diseases and comorbid depression can significantly reduce social role disability and enhance global quality of life among middle-aged and elderly patients.

title: A Comparison of Cost Effectiveness Using Data from Randomized Trials or Actual Clinical Practice: Selective Cox-2 Inhibitors as an Example
text:
Background: Data on absolute risks of outcomes and patterns of drug use in cost-effectiveness analyses are often derived from randomized clinical trials (RCTs). This study aimed to assess the external validity of previously published cost-effectiveness studies by comparing the data used in these studies (typically based on RCTs) to observational data from real-world clinical practice. As an example, the selective Cox-2 inhibitors (coxibs) were examined.
Methods and Findings: The UK General Practice Research Database (GPRD) was utilized to estimate the exposure characteristics and individual probabilities of upper gastrointestinal (GI) events during current exposure to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or coxibs. A basic cost-effectiveness model was developed to evaluate two alternative strategies: prescription of a conventional NSAID or coxib. The outcomes included upper GI events recorded in GPRD and hospitalizations for upper GI events recorded in the national registry of hospitalizations (Hospital Episode Statistics) linked to GPRD. Prescription costs were based on the number of tablets prescribed as recorded in GPRD and the 2006 cost data from the British National Formulary. The study population included over 1 million patients prescribed conventional NSAIDs or coxibs. Only a minority of patients used the drugs long-term and daily (34.5% of conventional NSAIDs and 44.2% of coxibs), whereas coxib RCTs required long-term daily use for at least 6-9 months. The mean cost of preventing one upper GI event as recorded in GPRD was $104k (ranging from $64k with long-term daily use to $182k with intermittent use), and $298k for hospitalizations. The mean costs over calendar time were $58k during 1990-1993 and $174k during 2002-2005. Comparatively, using RCT data rather than GPRD data for event probabilities, the mean cost was $16k with the VIGOR RCT and $20k with the CLASS RCT.
Conclusions: The published cost-effectiveness analyses of coxibs lacked external validity, did not represent patients in actual clinical practice, and should not have been used to inform prescribing policies. External validity should be an explicit requirement for cost-effectiveness analyses.

title: 7α, 25-dihydroxycholesterol-mediated activation of EBI2 in immune regulation and diseases
text: In 1993, researchers identified EBI2 (also known as GPR183) as one of the main genes induced in Burkitt's lymphoma cells by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection. Later, in 2009, it was discovered that EBI2 plays a crucial role in regulating B cell migration and responses. Consequently, an effort was made to find the endogenous ligand of EBI2. In 2011, two groups simultaneously reported the identification of 7α, 25-dihydroxyxcholesterol (7α, 25-OHC), an oxysterol, as the most likely physiological ligand of EBI2. Subsequent studies further elucidated how 7α, 25-OHC binds to EBI2 and how a local gradient of 7α, 25-OHC can regulate the migration, activation, and functions of various immune cells, including B cells, T cells, dendritic cells (DCs), monocytes/macrophages, and astrocytes. The discovery of 7α, 25-OHC as a G protein-coupled receptor ligand revealed a previously unknown signaling system of oxysterols, a class of molecules with profound biological functions. Dysregulation of oxysterol synthesis or function is believed to contribute to a wide range of diseases, including inflammation, autoimmune diseases, cardiovascular diseases, neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, and metabolic diseases such as diabetes, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Therefore, EBI2 may represent a promising target for therapeutic interventions for human diseases.

title: PrimPol Bypasses UV Photoproducts during Eukaryotic Chromosomal DNA Replication
text: DNA damage can hinder the DNA replication machinery, leading to genetic instability. Consequently, various mechanisms have evolved to complete genome duplication without a pristine DNA template, but identifying the enzymes involved remains a challenge. Here, we investigate the role of Primase-Polymerase (PrimPol; CCDC111), a conserved primase-polymerase found in both archaea and eukaryotes, in chromosomal DNA replication. Our findings reveal that PrimPol is crucial for replication fork progression on damaged DNA templates caused by ultraviolet (UV) light exposure. Specifically, PrimPol mediates translesion synthesis (TLS) of UV lesions, which enables replication fork progression without relying on the Pol η-dependent pathway. Moreover, we show that PrimPol is also essential for efficient replication fork progression during an unperturbed S phase. These findings demonstrate that PrimPol is a vital component of replication fork progression in eukaryotic cells.

title: The novel immunosuppressive enzyme IL4I1 is expressed by neoplastic cells of several B-cell lymphomas and by tumor-associated macrophages
text: Our previous research revealed strong IL4I1 gene expression in primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) and identified the protein as a secreted L-phenylalanine oxidase. We recently discovered that this protein inhibits T-cell proliferation in vitro. To further investigate the role of IL4I1 in malignancies, we analyzed its protein expression in 315 human lymphoid and non-lymphoid malignancies. We found that IL4I1 expression was very frequent in tumors beyond PMBL, and it was detected in tumor-associated macrophages from most of the tumors and in neoplastic cells from follicular lymphoma, classic and nodular lymphocytic predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, and small lymphocytic lymphoma, three of which are germinal center derived. In addition, IL4I1-positive tumor cells were detected in rare cases of solid cancers, such as mesothelioma. The enzymatic activity corresponded to the protein expression, suggesting that IL4I1 is functional in vivo. Different tumor types appeared to impact various infiltrating lymphocyte populations, which in turn could influence tumor evolution. In the case of follicular lymphoma cells, which are sensitive to antitumor cytotoxic T cells and depend on interactions with local T helper cells for survival, high IL4I1 expression seemed linked to the absence of bone marrow involvement and a more favorable prognosis. These findings suggest evaluating IL4I1 as a prognostic factor.

title: Poor prognosis in carcinoma is associated with a gene expression signature of aberrant PTEN tumor suppressor pathway activity.
text: The future of cancer management lies in pathway-specific therapy, with a particular focus on the oncogenic phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway. Despite its prevalence in solid tumors, there is currently no reliable method for detecting PI3K pathway activation in human tumors. By taking advantage of the relationship between the loss of the negative regulator PTEN and the activation of the PI3K pathway, we developed and validated a microarray gene expression signature for detecting PTEN loss in breast cancer (BC) using immunohistochemistry (IHC). Our findings show that the most significant gene in the signature is PTEN itself, indicating that PTEN mRNA levels are the primary determinant of PTEN protein levels in BC. Interestingly, some PTEN IHC-positive BCs exhibited the signature of PTEN loss, which was associated with moderately reduced PTEN mRNA levels and specific types of PIK3CA mutations and/or amplification of HER2. This suggests that the signature is more sensitive than PTEN IHC for identifying tumors with pathway activation. In independent data sets of breast, prostate, and bladder carcinoma, the prediction of pathway activity by the signature correlated significantly with poor patient outcome. Furthermore, stathmin, encoded by the signature gene STMN1, was identified as an accurate IHC marker of the signature and had prognostic significance in BC. Stathmin also demonstrated pathway-pharmacodynamic activity in vitro and in vivo, suggesting that the signature or its components may be clinically useful tests for stratifying patients for anti-PI3K pathway therapy and monitoring therapeutic efficacy. These findings highlight the enormous potential impact of pathway inhibition on patient survival, particularly in light of the observed association between aberrant PI3K pathway signaling and metastasis across carcinoma types.

title: Suppression of subtelomeric VSG switching by Trypanosoma brucei TRF requires its TTAGGG repeat-binding activity
text:
Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite responsible for human African trypanosomiasis, frequently changes its major surface antigen (VSG) in the bloodstream of its mammalian host to evade the host immune response. VSGs are expressed exclusively from subtelomeric loci, and previous studies have shown that telomere proteins TbTIF2 and TbRAP1 play crucial roles in VSG switching and VSG silencing regulation, respectively. Our new findings reveal that the telomere-bound protein TbTRF also plays a critical role in VSG switching regulation, as a transient depletion of TbTRF leads to a significant increase in VSG switching events.
We have solved the nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) structure of the DNA-binding Myb domain of TbTRF, which folds into a canonical helix-loop-helix structure that is conserved among Myb domains of mammalian TRF proteins. Interestingly, the TbTRF Myb domain tolerates the presence of a bulky "J" base in T. brucei telomere DNA, and the DNA-binding affinity of TbTRF is not affected by the presence of J either in vitro or in vivo.
Furthermore, we discovered that point mutations in the Myb domain of TbTRF that significantly reduce its in vivo telomere DNA-binding affinity also lead to significantly higher VSG switching frequencies, indicating that the telomere DNA-binding activity of TbTRF is crucial for its role in VSG switching regulation. In conclusion, our findings underscore the vital role of TbTRF in regulating VSG switching in T. brucei and provide new insights into the mechanisms of telomere-mediated gene regulation in this parasite.

title: CD4+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity eliminates primary tumor cells in metastatic melanoma through high MHC class II expression and can be enhanced by inhibitory receptor blockade
text: Metastatic melanoma is a rapidly progressing disease with a high mortality rate and limited treatment options. Immunotherapy based on tumor-targeting cytotoxic T cell responses has shown promise in treating this disease. To investigate the potential of using CD4+ cytotoxic T cells in the development of this approach, we examined the frequency and efficacy of these cells in metastatic melanoma patients and explored the regulatory mechanisms controlling their cytotoxicity. Our findings indicate that naturally occurring CD4+ cytotoxic T cells can be recovered from metastatic melanoma patients at significantly higher frequencies than in healthy controls. These cells were capable of killing autologous tumor cells without the need for CD8+ T cells or other cell types. However, several restrictive factors were identified, including the requirement for high MHC class II expression on melanoma cells, which was not satisfied in a subset of melanomas. In addition, the granzyme B and perforin release by activated CD4+ cytotoxic T cells was reduced after coculturing with autologous melanoma cells, which exhibited low LAMP-1 expression and low granzyme B and perforin secretion in the supernatant. These findings suggest that inhibitory mechanisms are present to suppress CD4+ cytotoxic T cells. Blockade of PD-1 and CTLA-4 enhanced the cytolytic activity of CD4+ T cells, but this effect was only observed in MHC class II high melanomas. Our study shows that CD4+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity can eliminate primary melanoma cells, but the efficacy of this approach depends on MHC class II expression.

title: The epidemiology and iatrogenic transmission of hepatitis C virus in Egypt: a Bayesian coalescent approach.
text: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a major culprit in the development of liver cancer and cirrhosis, and Egypt has been recording the highest HCV prevalence worldwide. In this study, we employ a sophisticated Bayesian inference framework to reconstruct the transmission dynamics of HCV in Egypt by analyzing genomic sequences of the virus isolated from the sampled population. Our findings indicate that the actual number of HCV infections in Egypt experienced rapid exponential growth between 1930 and 1955. This rapid spread of the virus provides convincing genetic evidence that the Egyptian HCV outbreak was initiated and propagated by extensive anti-schistosomiasis injection campaigns during this period. Although our analysis shows that HCV transmission has gradually decreased over time, we predict that the virus will continue to persist in Egypt for several decades to come. The combination of population genetic and epidemiological approaches employed in this study provides detailed insights into the historical trends of HCV prevalence in Egypt. Moreover, since our results are consistent with a demographic scenario postulated beforehand, they also serve as a reliable test of inference methods based on the coalescent process.

title: Improving population representation through geographic health information systems: mapping the MURDOCK study.
text: This paper explores methods for evaluating and optimizing recruitment strategies to ensure representative sampling in population-based studies. The authors apply these methods to the Measurement to Understand Reclassification of Disease of Cabarrus/Kannapolis (MURDOCK) study, a longitudinal health study covering Kannapolis and Cabarrus County, North Carolina. While efforts have been made to recruit a representative registry of participants, unintentional bias remains a possibility. The study uses geospatial referencing to track participants' locations and compare them to demographic data from the 2010 Census. The study found that areas with low recruitment rates had higher proportions of minority and younger populations, indicating a need for targeted recruitment strategies in these areas. Additionally, the study found that participants from farther away from the enrollment site were underrepresented, suggesting that distance to the site may be a significant barrier to participation. These findings have broader implications for improving representative sampling in population-based studies.

title: Haplotype-based variant detection from short-read sequencing
text: Direct haplotype detection from short-read DNA sequencing data requires modifying existing small-variant detection methods. To address this challenge, we have developed a Bayesian statistical framework that can effectively model multiallelic loci across sets of individuals with varying copy number. As part of this development, we have also created an implementation of this framework in a haplotype-based variant detector called FreeBayes.

title: Longitudinal Genome-Wide Association of Cardiovascular Disease Risk Factors in the Bogalusa Heart Study
text: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, and recent genome-wide association studies (GWA) have implicated many genetic locations associated with CVD risk factors in adults. However, it is unclear if these locations predict trait levels at all ages, how trait development over time, or if they could be used to screen individuals who are pre-symptomatic to provide the opportunity for preventive measures before disease onset. To address these questions, we conducted a GWA study on participants in the longitudinal Bogalusa Heart Study (BHS) and characterized the association between genetic factors and the development of CVD risk factors from childhood to adulthood. We discovered 7 genome-wide significant associations involving CVD risk factors, two of which have been previously reported. We tested top regions for replication in the Young Finns Study (YF) and found two strong associations: rs247616 in CETP with HDL levels (combined P = 9.7 x 10(-24)), and rs445925 at APOE with LDL levels (combined P = 8.7 x 10(-19)). We found that SNPs identified in adult cross-sectional studies tend to have age-independent effects in the BHS with effect sizes consistent with previous reports. Previously identified variants were associated with adult trait levels above and beyond those seen in childhood; however, variants with time-dependent effects were also promising predictors. This is the first GWA study to evaluate the role of common genetic variants in the development of CVD risk factors in children as they advance through adulthood, highlighting the utility of using longitudinal studies to identify genetic predictors of adult traits in children.

title: Actin and serum response factor transduce physical cues from the microenvironment to regulate epidermal stem cell fate decisions
text:
The maintenance of epidermal tissue homeostasis is critical for overall skin health, and this process is regulated by a delicate balance between stem cell renewal and differentiation. External cues play a crucial role in this regulation, as the extracellular matrix (ECM) provides important signals that direct the fate of epidermal cells. To gain a deeper understanding of the molecular pathways involved in epidermal differentiation, we employed a highly precise approach: engineering single-cell microenvironments in which specific variables were quantitatively controlled.
Using micropatterned surfaces, we were able to isolate the signaling pathways that govern epidermal stem cell differentiation when exposed to restricted ECM contact. Notably, human epidermal stem cells on small (20 μm diameter) circular islands remained rounded and differentiated at a higher frequency than those on large (50 μm diameter) islands. Differentiation was found to be ECM composition and density-independent, rather, the actin cytoskeleton plays a crucial role in mediating shape-induced differentiation by regulating serum response factor (SRF) transcriptional activity.
Our findings demonstrate that biophysical cues are ultimately translated into transcriptional responses that determine epidermal cell fate. Specifically, knockdown of SRF or its co-factor MAL inhibited differentiation, while overexpression of MAL stimulated SRF activity and involucrin expression. SRF target genes FOS and JUNB were also found to be essential for differentiation, with c-Fos mediating serum responsiveness, and JunB being regulated by actin and MAL.
In summary, our study demonstrates the pivotal role of external cues in directing epidermal stem cell differentiation through the activation of specific signaling pathways. By engineering microenvironments that allow for precise control of these signals, we uncovered new insights into the molecular mechanisms that govern epidermal homeostasis. These findings have important implications for our understanding of epidermal development, homeostasis, and disease, and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for skin-related disorders.

title: Reproducibility and automatic measurement of QT dispersion.
text: The aim of this study was to evaluate the reproducibility of QT dispersion measurements obtained from abnormal electrocardiograms (ECGs) in patients with previous myocardial infarction, using both observer-based and automated methods. The study included 70 patients and employed standard 12-lead ECGs recorded at 25 mm/s. The images were scanned into a personal computer and analyzed using specialized software. The study compared the reproducibility of QT dispersion measurements obtained using a user-interactive and an automatic measurement system. The results showed that the reproducibility of the RR interval was excellent across all methods (mean absolute errors of 3-4 ms, relative errors of 0.3-0.5%). The reproducibility of the mean QT interval was good, with intrasubject errors of 6 ms (1.4%), interobserver errors of 7 ms (1.8%), and observer-vs-automatic measurement errors of 10 and 11 ms (2.5 and 2.8%). However, the reproducibility of QTc dispersion measurements was poor across all methods, with intrasubject errors of 12 ms (17.3%), interobserver errors of 15 ms (22.1%), and observer-vs-automatic measurement errors of 30 and 28 ms (35.4 and 31.9%). These findings suggest that the poor reproducibility of QT dispersion measurements limits its usefulness as a clinical tool, particularly for predicting adverse events. The study highlights the need for any automated system to be able to accurately measure difficult-to-relabel T waves in addition to common ones to be useful for measuring QT dispersion.

title: Inhibition of LSD1 sensitizes glioblastoma cells to histone deacetylase inhibitors.
text:
Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a particularly aggressive brain tumor that remains largely unresponsive to treatment despite advances in cancer therapy. One promising avenue for cancer therapy is targeting enzymes involved in epigenetic alterations, as these enzymes play critical roles in cellular processes that lead to tumor formation. Several histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors have been developed and tested in GBM with moderate success. Our study aimed to investigate the effects of combining HDAC inhibitors with a specific enzyme called lysine specific demethylase 1 (LSD1).
We found that treating GBM cells with HDAC inhibitors led to an accumulation of histone methylation, which is removed by LSD1. To evaluate the potential of combining LSD1 inhibition with HDAC inhibitors, we knocked down LSD1 in GBM cells using short hairpin RNA or pharmacological means and treated them with HDAC inhibitors. We observed a significant increase in caspase-dependent apoptosis (>2-fold) in LSD1-knockdown GBM cells treated with HDAC inhibitors. Interestingly, we also found that pharmacologically inhibiting LSD1 with the monoamine oxidase inhibitor tranylcypromine, in combination with HDAC inhibitors, led to synergistic apoptotic cell death in GBM cells. This effect was not observed in normal human astrocytes.
Our results suggest that LSD1 and HDACs cooperate to regulate key pathways of cell death in GBM cell lines, but not in normal counterparts. This finding validates the use of combined LSD1 and HDAC inhibitors as a potential therapeutic approach for GBM.

title: Challenges for malaria elimination in Zanzibar: pyrethroid resistance in malaria vectors and poor performance of long-lasting insecticide nets
text:
BACKGROUND: The use of long-lasting insecticide treated nets (LLINs) and indoor residual house spraying (IRS) is the primary strategy for controlling malaria vectors in Zanzibar. The present study aimed to assess the insecticide susceptibility status of malaria vectors and evaluate the durability and efficacy of LLINs on the island.
METHODS: Mosquitoes were collected from Pemba and Unguja islands in 2010-2011 for WHO susceptibility tests. One hundred and fifty LLINs were collected from households on Unguja, and their physical condition was recorded. The efficacy and total insecticide content of the nets were then tested.
RESULTS: Species identification revealed that over 90% of the Anopheles gambiae complex consisted of An. arabiensis, with a small number of An. gambiae s.s. and An. merus present. Susceptibility tests showed that An. arabiensis from Pemba was resistant to the pyrethroids used for LLINs and IRS, while mosquitoes from Unguja Island were fully susceptible to all pyrethroids tested. A physical inspection of 150 LLINs revealed that two-thirds were damaged after only three years in use. The used nets had a significantly lower (p < 0.001) mean permethrin concentration of 791.6 mg/m2 compared to 944.2 mg/m2 for new ones. The efficacy of the LLINs decreased significantly against both susceptible An. gambiae s.s. colony mosquitoes and wild-type mosquitoes from Pemba after just six washes (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The sustainability of the gains achieved in malaria control in Zanzibar is seriously threatened by the resistance of malaria vectors to pyrethroids and the short-lived efficacy of LLINs. This study highlights the challenges of achieving malaria elimination in even relatively well-resourced and logistically manageable areas like Zanzibar with the current control measures. The use of LLINs and IRS may require adaptation and improvement to address these issues and achieve malaria elimination goals.

title: Proliferating cell nuclear antigen acts as a cytoplasmic platform controlling human neutrophil survival
text: Neutrophil apoptosis, a crucial process for resolving inflammation, is only partially understood at the molecular level. In this study, we uncover a survival pathway mediated by proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), a nuclear factor involved in DNA replication and repair, which plays a key role in regulating neutrophil lifespan. Our findings show that mature neutrophils, despite their inability to proliferate, express high levels of PCNA in their cytosol, particularly in association with procaspases, implying that PCNA functions to prevent their activation. Notably, cytosolic PCNA levels decrease during apoptosis, while in vitro and in vivo exposure to the survival factor granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) leads to increased PCNA abundance. Peptides derived from the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21, which compete with procaspases to bind PCNA, triggered neutrophil apoptosis, demonstrating that specific modifications of PCNA protein interactions can impact neutrophil survival. Furthermore, overexpression of PCNA in neutrophil-derived PLB985 myeloid cells significantly renders them more resistant to apoptosis induced by TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand or gliotoxin. Conversely, decreasing PCNA expression after transfecting cells with PCNA small interfering RNA sensitizes them to apoptosis. Finally, a mutation in the PCNA interdomain-connecting loop, the binding site for many partners, significantly reduces the PCNA-mediated antiapoptotic effect. These findings identify PCNA as a crucial regulator of neutrophil lifespan and provide a novel target to modulate pathological inflammation.

title: Development of the Human Infant Intestinal Microbiota
text: Soon after birth, a new microbial ecosystem is established in the gastrointestinal tract of a human being. While this process is an integral part of human biology, the timing and sources of the microorganisms involved, as well as how they impact human development, physiology, and disease, are still poorly understood. To shed light on these questions, we designed a microarray to detect and quantify the small subunit ribosomal RNA (SSU rRNA) gene sequences of diverse bacterial species and taxonomic groups. Using this tool in conjunction with sequencing of cloned libraries of PCR-amplified SSU rDNA, we analyzed the microbial communities present in stool samples from 14 healthy, full-term infants, including a set of dizygotic twins, at various stages throughout the first year of life. To investigate the origins of the infant microbiota, we also profiled vaginal and milk samples from the mothers, as well as stool samples from the mothers, fathers, and two siblings. Our findings revealed significant variation in the composition and temporal patterns of the microbial communities between infants, despite some temporal consistencies in the twins. By the end of the first year of life, the microbial ecosystems in each baby had become more similar to the adult gastrointestinal tract profile.

title: Combinatorial modulation of galP and glk gene expression for improved alternative glucose utilization
text:
Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) serves as a critical precursor for the anaerobic production of succinate and malate. Despite increasing PEP availability via inactivation of carbohydrate phosphotransferase systems (PTS), the resulting strain displayed a suboptimal glucose utilization rate. To enhance anaerobic glucose utilization and efficient production of succinate and malate, a combinatorial approach involving modulation of galactose permease (galP) and glucokinase (glk) gene expression was pursued in the chromosome of an Escherichia coli strain with inactivated PTS.
To construct artificial regulatory parts, including promoter and messenger RNA stabilizing regions (mRS), λ-Red recombination was employed in the E. coli chromosome. The mRS libraries were selected based on their constitutive expression under various cultivation conditions. A straightforward one-step recombination method was then used to modulate galP and glk gene expression with different regulatory parts. The glucose utilization rates of the resulting strains were evaluated, and a positive correlation was observed between expression strength and glucose utilization rates for both genes. Combinatorial modulation exhibited a synergistic effect on glucose utilization rate, resulting in the highest rate (1.64 g/L h) recorded, which was approximately tenfold higher than the PTS-deficient strain and 39% higher than the wild-type E. coli.
These modulated strains hold promise for efficient anaerobic production of succinate and malate.

title: Matrix eQTL: Ultra fast eQTL analysis via large matrix operations
text:
The goal of expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) mapping is to identify specific regions of the genome that influence the expression of genes. This technique is used to investigate the regulatory mechanisms of normal tissues and to search for genetic factors contributing to complex diseases like cancer, diabetes, and cystic fibrosis. Modern eQTL datasets contain millions of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and thousands of transcripts measured across hundreds of samples. Due to the large number of SNP-transcript pairs to be analyzed, eQTL analysis is computationally demanding, making it challenging to study the entire dataset. As a result, researchers often prioritize a subset of transcripts and SNPs for analysis, limiting the scope of the study. With the increasing availability of larger genotype and gene expression datasets, there is a growing need for efficient eQTL analysis tools.
To address this challenge, we developed Matrix eQTL, a fast and versatile method for performing eQTL analysis using linear models. Matrix eQTL can model and test associations using both linear regression and ANOVA models, and include covariates to account for factors like population structure, gender, and clinical variables. Additionally, it supports testing of heteroscedastic models and models with correlated errors. In our evaluation on large datasets, Matrix eQTL was found to be thousands of times faster than existing popular software for QTL/eQTL analysis. Matrix eQTL is available as both Matlab and R packages, making it easy to use on Windows, Mac OS, and Linux systems. You can download the software from the following address: <http://www.bios.unc.edu/research/genomic_software/Matrix_eQTL>

title: The structure of DdrB from Deinococcus: a new fold for single-stranded DNA binding proteins
text: Deinococcus spp. are renowned for their exceptional ability to rapidly recover from severe genomic fragmentation in response to exposure to extreme levels of ionizing radiation or desiccation. Despite being initially characterized over 50 years ago, the molecular mechanism underlying this remarkable repair process remains inadequately comprehended. Here, we present the 2.8 Å crystal structure of DdrB, a unique single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein exclusive to Deinococcus spp. that plays a pivotal role in DNA recovery following damage. DdrB forms a pentameric ring capable of binding single-stranded DNA but not double-stranded DNA. Interestingly, the crystal structure reveals a novel fold that is distinct from any other single-stranded binding (SSB) protein that has been characterized to date. The need for a distinct ssDNA binding function in response to severe damage suggests that DdrB may serve more than just standard SSB protein functions, such as protecting ssDNA, but also in protein recruitment or DNA architecture maintenance. mechanisms of DdrB action in damage recovery are discussed.

title: N348I in the Connection Domain of HIV-1 Reverse Transcriptase Confers Zidovudine and Nevirapine Resistance
text: The study investigated the in vivo relevance of the N348I mutation in the connection domain of the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) reverse transcriptase (RT) and its role in drug resistance. The mutation was found to increase in prevalence from 1% in treatment-naive individuals to 12.1% in treatment-experienced patients, and was highly associated with mutations in the RT and protease genes. The study also showed that N348I decreased the susceptibility of HIV-1 to zidovudine, nevirapine, and efavirenz, and potentiated resistance to these drugs when combined with other mutations. Biochemical analyses provided further evidence for the role of N348I in drug resistance and suggested a molecular mechanism for how it contributes to resistance. Overall, the study highlights the importance of monitoring the emergence of resistance mutations in HIV-1 RT and the need for continued research on the mechanisms of drug resistance in order to improve HIV therapy.

title: Dual Targeting of PDGFRα and FGFR1 Displays Synergistic Efficacy in Malignant Rhabdoid Tumors
text: Subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex are frequently mutated in a considerable portion of human cancers. Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs), which are aggressive and lethal pediatric cancers, exhibit a deficiency in the SMARCB1 subunit of the SWI/SNF complex. As part of an integrated molecular profiling and chemical biology approach, we have discovered that the receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) PDGFRα and FGFR1 are coactivated in MRT cells, and that dual inhibition of these receptors has synergistic efficacy. Inhibitor combinations targeting both receptors and the dual inhibitor ponatinib lead to suppression of the AKT and ERK1/2 signaling pathways, resulting in apoptosis. MRT cells that have developed resistance to the PDGFRα inhibitor pazopanib are susceptible to FGFR inhibitors. Additionally, we found that PDGFRα levels are regulated by SMARCB1 expression, and our findings were validated by analyzing clinical specimens, which revealed the expression of both PDGFRα and FGFR1 in rhabdoid tumor patients. These results support a promising therapeutic strategy for cancers with SWI/SNF deficiencies, which involves exploiting the dependencies of RTK coactivation for tumor cells.

title: A nano-positioning system for macromolecular structural analysis
text: Flexible domains within macromolecules and macromolecular complexes are often difficult to locate with standard structural biology techniques. To address this challenge, we have developed a method that combines single-molecule measurements with X-ray crystallography data using probabilistic data analysis. This method not only determines the most likely position of a fluorescently labeled domain but also provides a complete three-dimensional probability distribution of the experimental uncertainty. With this approach, single-pair fluorescence resonance energy transfer measurements can now be used as a quantitative tool for investigating the position and dynamics of flexible domains within macromolecular complexes. We applied this method to investigate the position of the 5' end of nascent RNA exiting transcription elongation complexes of yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) RNA polymerase II, and studied the effect of transcription factor IIB on the position of the RNA.
