title: Tumor-associated macrophages correlate with the clinicopathological features and poor outcomes via inducing epithelial to mesenchymal transition in oral squamous cell carcinoma
text: BACKGROUND Both tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and the epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) of cancer cells play critical roles in facilitating the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). However, the extent to which TAMs can drive EMT in OSCC remains unexplored. RESULTS In this study, we investigated the expression of macrophage markers CD68 and CD163, epithelial marker E-cadherin, and mesenchymal marker vimentin in 127 OSCC patients through semi-quantitative immunohistochemistry. Our findings revealed that CD68 and CD163 were expressed not only in infiltrating TAMs but also in cancer cells themselves. High levels of CD68-positive macrophages were associated with poor overall survival. Interestingly, both CD163 expression in macrophages and cancer cells were linked to poor overall survival, with a significant prognostic impact in OSCC. Moreover, incubation of TAMs-conditioned medium led to the acquisition of a fibroblast-like appearance in cancer cells (HN4, HN6, and SCC9), accompanied by altered expressions of E-cadherin and vimentin. These changes were correlated with enhanced migration and invasion abilities. CONCLUSIONS Our results indicatethat TAMs play a crucial role in promoting EMT in OSCC, thereby contributing to tumor progression.

title: Geometric cues for directing the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells.
text: Substantial efforts have been devoted to deciphering the variables that influence the lineage commitment of stem cells. This study unveils that cell shape, irrespective of soluble factors, exerts a profound impact on the differentiation of human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) from bone marrow. When subjected to competing soluble differentiation signals, cells cultured in rectangles with increasing aspect ratios and in shapes with pentagonal symmetry but varying subcellular curvature, exhibit distinct adipogenesis and osteogenesis profiles. The results demonstrate that geometric features that enhance actomyosin contractility promote osteogenesis and are in line with the in vivo microenvironment of differentiated cells. Pharmacological agents disrupting the cytoskeleton validate the pivotal role of focal adhesion and myosin-generated contractility during differentiation. Microarray analysis and pathway inhibition studies imply that contractile cells drive osteogenesis by augmenting c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK1/2) activation, while also elevating wingless-type (Wnt) signaling. In conclusion, this work uncovers the significance of geometric shape cues in coordinating the mechanochemical signals and paracrine/autocrine factors that direct MSCs towards appropriate fates.

title: Amyloid accumulation is a late event in sporadic Alzheimer's disease-like pathology in nontransgenic rats
text: The amyloid cascade hypothesis proposes that the deposition of the amyloid beta (Aβ) peptide in the brain is a key event in the onset of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, recent research suggests that amyloid toxicity may no longer be considered the primary cause of sporadic AD, which leads to cognitive decline. Using accelerated senescence non-transgenic OXYS rats, we have found that accumulation of Aβ is a later event in AD-like pathology. Our results show that age-related increases in Aβ1–42 levels and extracellular Aβ deposits in the brain of OXYS rats occur later than synaptic losses, neuronal cell death, mitochondrial structural abnormalities, and hyperphosphorylation of the tau protein. We identified genetic variants associated with the risk of either late-onset or early-onset AD, including App, Apoe4, Bace1, Psen1, Psen2, and Picalm. We found that nonsynonymous SNPs were located only in the genes Casp3 and Sorl1 in OXYS rats, indicating that these rats may serve as a model for sporadic AD. It is possible that multiple age-associated pathological processes may occur before toxic amyloid accumulation, which in turn triggers the final stage of sporadic AD.

title: Estimating low-density lipoprotein cholesterol by the Friedewald equation is adequate for classifying patients on the basis of nationally recommended cutpoints.
text: In a study of 4736 participants, we compared LDL cholesterol values obtained using the Friedewald formula (total cholesterol minus HDL cholesterol minus VLDL cholesterol estimated as triglycerides divided by 5) with those obtained through lipoprotein fractionation. We found that when triglycerides were less than 2.0 g/L, approximately 90% of estimated LDL cholesterol values were within +/- 10% of measured values. However, this proportion decreased to 72% and 39% at triglyceride concentrations of 2.0-4.0 g/L and 4.0-6.0 g/L, respectively. Alternative formulas for estimating VLDL cholesterol were not more accurate. Despite this, the use of estimated LDL for risk classification based on National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel cutpoints of 1.30 and 1.60 g/L was considered acceptable, particularly when triglyceride concentrations were less than or equal to 5.0 g/L. Only 11% of classifications were shifted across one cutpoint, and fewer than 1% were misclassified two cutpoints high. Refinements to the estimation model did not significantly improve LDL estimation or risk classification concordance.

title: Conditional Kif3a ablation causes abnormal hedgehog signaling topography, growth plate dysfunction, and excessive bone and cartilage formation during mouse skeletogenesis.
text:
Here is a possibly improved version of the text:
Motor protein Kif3a and primary cilia play crucial roles in regulating key developmental processes, but their involvement in skeletogenesis is poorly understood. To investigate, we generated mice lacking Kif3a in cartilage and examined the cranial base and synchondroses. Kif3a deficiency resulted in delayed growth rate and abnormal cranial base development, which was evident through both anatomical and micro-computed tomography (microCT) analysis in newborn animals. Additionally, Kif3a deficiency significantly altered synchondrosis growth plate structure and function, with the severity of these changes increasing over time. By postnatal day (P)7, mutant growth plates displayed atypical zones of chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy, characterized by elevated Col2a1 gene expression but minimal expression of Indian hedgehog (Ihh), Col10a1, Vegf, Mmp13, and Sp7. Concurrently, unexpected events occurred in surrounding perichondrial tissues, including excessive intramembranous ossification along the perichondrial border and ectopic cartilage formation. To identify possible causes for these latter occurrences, we examined hedgehog signaling patterns and intensity by evaluating Patched 1, Gli1, and syndecan 3 expression, and found that hedgehog signaling was minimal within mutant growth plates as early as P0, yet surprisingly was higher and widespread in mutant perichondrial tissues. Lastly, we studied the effects of Ihh deficiency in cartilage, finding that cranial base abnormalities only minimally resembled those seen in Kif3a-deficient mice. In summary, Kif3a and primary cilia contribute uniquely to cranial base development and synchondrosis growth plate function. Their deficiency leads to irregular hedgehog signaling topography, growth plate dysfunction, and unacceptable responses and processes in surrounding perichondrial tissues, including ectopic cartilage formation and excessive intramembranous ossification.

title: Morin Attenuates Ovalbumin-Induced Airway Inflammation by Modulating Oxidative Stress-Responsive MAPK Signaling.
text:
Morin, a plant-derived active ingredient, has shown promising anti-inflammatory effects in various diseases. However, its impact on pulmonary diseases, particularly asthma, remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the potential of morin in reducing airway inflammation in chronic asthma, with a focus on oxidative stress modulation.
We used ovalbumin-sensitized mice and human bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) to examine the effects of morin on airway inflammation. In vivo, morin significantly attenuated the infiltration of inflammatory cells into the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) and around the respiratory tracts and vessels. Additionally, morin suppressed goblet cell hyperplasia and collagen deposition/fibrosis, and dose-dependently inhibited the increases in IgE, TNF-α, IL-4, IL-13, matrix metalloproteinase-9, and malondialdehyde. In BECs challenged with tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), morin significantly decreased the levels of eotaxin-1, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, IL-8, and intercellular adhesion molecule-1. Moreover, morin abolished the increases in intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation, indicating that ROS/MAPK signaling contributes to the relief of airway inflammation.
Our findings demonstrate for the first time that morin alleviates airway inflammation in chronic asthma, likely through the oxidative stress-responsive MAPK pathway. These results highlight morin as a potential agent for asthma management, suggesting a novel profile of morin as an anti-inflammatory drug.

title: Spontaneous autoimmunity prevented by thymic expression of a single self-antigen
text: The expression of self-antigens in the thymus plays a crucial role in the elimination of autoreactive T cells, helping to maintain the body's unresponsiveness to its own tissues. The Autoimmune regulator (Aire) gene, which is defective in autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1, has been shown to enhance the thymic expression of self-antigens. However, a direct correlation between specific thymic self-antigens and a single autoimmune phenotype in this model has remained obscure. Our findings indicate that autoimmune eye disease in aire-deficient mice develops as a result of the loss of thymic expression of a singular eye antigen, interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP). Moreover, the absence of IRBP expression solely in the thymus, even in the presence of aire expression, is enough to trigger spontaneous eye-specific autoimmunity. These results suggest that the failure of thymic expression of a single self-antigen can be enough to cause organ-specific autoimmune disease in otherwise self-tolerant individuals.

title: Preventing bacterial DNA release and absent in melanoma 2 inflammasome activation by a Legionella effector functioning in membrane trafficking.
text: Legionella pneumophila, the pathogen responsible for Legionnaires' pneumonia, homes within a specialized vacuole structure called the Legionella-containing vacuole (LCV). The LCV resists fusion with lysosomes and allows for efficient bacterial replication within host macrophages, which relies on a Dot/Icm type IVB secretion system. An essential effector translocated by this system is SdhA, which promotes intracellular growth of L. pneumophila and prevents host cell death. Interestingly, our study found that the absence of SdhA led to increased caspase-1 activation and IL-1β secretion, as well as macrophage pyroptosis during Legionella infection. These inflammasome activation phenotypes were unrelated to the established flagellin-NAIP5-NLRC4 axis and instead relied on the DNA-sensing AIM2 inflammasome. We discovered that Legionella DNA is released into macrophage cytosol, and this effect is significantly enhanced in the absence of SdhA. Surprisingly, SdhA possesses a functional Golgi-targeting GRIP domain, which is required for preventing AIM2 inflammasome activation. Ectopically expressed SdhA forms a unique ring-shaped membrane structure, suggesting a role in membrane trafficking and maintaining LCV membrane integrity. Our findings suggest a possible connection between LCV trafficking/maturation and suppression of host innate immune detection, mediated by the function of SdhA.

title: Cytosolic viral sensor RIG-I is a 5'-triphosphate-dependent translocase on double-stranded RNA.
text:
Retinoic acid inducible-gene I (RIG-I) is a cytosolic protein with multiple domains that detects viral RNA and triggers an antiviral response. Two N-terminal domains, called caspase activation and recruitment domains (CARDs), transmit the signal, while a regulatory domain prevents signaling when no viral RNA is present. RIG-I can recognize two different molecular patterns, 5'-triphosphate and double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), which allow it to distinguish between pathogenic and self-RNA. However, the function of the DExH box helicase domain, which is also essential for activity, is less clear.
Using single-molecule protein-induced fluorescence enhancement, we discovered that RIG-I has a significant adenosine 5'-triphosphate-powered dsRNA translocation activity. The CARDs greatly suppress translocation in the absence of 5'-triphosphate, and the activation of 5'-triphosphate causes RIG-I to preferentially translocate on dsRNA in cis. This integration of two RNA molecular patterns may provide a means to specifically detect and combat replicating viruses.

title: Human Cytomegalovirus-Encoded Interleukin-10 Homolog Inhibits Maturation of Dendritic Cells and Alters Their Functionality
text: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) may use its viral interleukin-10 homolog (cmvIL-10) to impair the function of dendritic cells (DCs), crucial regulators of adaptive immunity. We hypothesized that cmvIL-10 inhibits DC maturation and cytokine production, preventing the activation and polarization of naive T cells towards protective gamma interferon-producing effectors. Our analysis showed that cmvIL-10 is expressed with late gene kinetics, and its effects are mediated through the IL-10 receptor. Treatment of immature DCs (iDCs) with supernatant from HCMV-infected cultures inhibited DC maturation and proinflammatory cytokine production, and incubation of iDCs with recombinant cmvIL-10 recapitulated these inhibitory effects. Additionally, cmvIL-10 had long-term effects on DCs, enhancing their migration towards a lymph node homing chemokine while reducing their cytokine production. However, cmvIL-10 did not affect the ability of mature DCs (mDCs) to secrete IL-12, even when restimulated by the activated T-cell signal CD40 ligand. Interestingly, cmvIL-10 also induced endogenous cellular IL-10 expression in DCs, partially contributing to its anti-inflammatory effects. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that cmvIL-10 has a profound impact on DC function at all stages of activation, leading to long-term functional alterations in these important immune regulators.

title: Model for unidirectional movement of axonemal and cytoplasmic dynein molecules
text: A novel model for the unidirectional movement of dynein is proposed based on structural data and biochemical experimentation. In this model, the binding affinity of dynein for microtubules is independent of their nucleotide state, and the change from strong to weak microtubule binding is natural, occurring due to the variation in relative orientation between the stalk and microtubule as the stalk rotates during nucleotide state transitions. Therefore, the enigmatic communication from the ATP binding site in the globular domain to the far MT-binding site in the tip of the stalk, which is a requirement in conventional models, is not needed. With this model, the previously observed experimental results, such as the effect of ATP and ADP bindings on dissociation of dynein from microtubules, the processive movement of single-headed axonemal dyneins at saturating ATP concentrations, the load dependence of step size for the processive movement of two-headed cytoplasmic dyneins, and the dependence of stall force on ATP concentration, can be accurately explained.

title: The inflammasome component NLRP3 impairs antitumor vaccine by enhancing the accumulation of tumor-associated myeloid-derived suppressor cells.
text:
Title: NLRP3 Inflammasome Regulates Antitumor Immunity through MDSC Accumulation
Abstract:
The NLRP3 inflammasome is a proteolysis complex that activates proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18. However, its role in antitumor immunity remains unknown. We investigated the function of NLRP3 in the immune response to melanoma cells using dendritic cell vaccination. The absence of NLRP3 led to a 4-fold improvement in survival, with enhanced immunity may due to increased CD8+ T cells. The reduction of tumor-associated myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in Nlrp3-deficient mice contributed to the improved immune response. Our findings suggest that NLRP3 may play a critical role in impeding antitumor immune responses, providing novel strategies to enhance vaccine efficacy by limiting NLRP3 signaling.
Introduction:
The NLRP3 inflammasome plays a crucial role in innate immunity by processing and releasing proinflammatory cytokines. However, its involvement in antitumor immunity has yet to be investigated. Dendritic cell vaccination is a promising approach to elicit antitumor immunity, but its efficacy may be hampered by the presence of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), which can inhibit T cell activation.
Methods:
We employed dendritic cell vaccination against the poorly immunogenic melanoma cell line B16-F10 in wild-type (WT) and NLRP3-deficient (Nlrp3(-/-) mice. The survival of vaccinated mice was evaluated using a mouse model of melanoma, and the immune response was analyzed by flow cytometry and adoptive transfer experiments.
Results:
Vaccination of Nlrp3-deficient mice showed a relative 4-fold improvement in survival compared to WT mice. Enhanced immunity was found to depend on CD8+ T cells and exhibited immune specificity and memory. We observed a significant decrease in the number of tumor-associated MDSCs in Nlrp3-deficient mice. Moreover, adoptive transfer experiments demonstrated that Nlrp3(-/-) MDSCs were less efficient in reaching the tumor site. Depleting MDSCs with an anti-Gr-1 antibody increased the survival of tumor-bearing wild-type mice but not Nlrp3(-/-) mice.
Discussion:

Our findings formally demonstrate a novel role for NLRP3 in regulating antitumor immunity through MDSC accumulation. The absence of NLRP3 resulted in reduced MDSCs in tumors, leading to enhanced antitumor immunity. Our results suggest that NLRP3 plays a critical role in hampering antitumor immune responses, providing a potential therapeutic target to improve the response to antitumor vaccines by limiting NLRP3 signaling.
Conclusion:


NLRP3 may pose an unanticipated obstacle to antitumor immunity, and targeting NLRP3 may improve vaccine efficacy. Inhibition of NLRP3 may be a potential strategy to enhance antitumor immunity and boost vaccine efficacy by limiting NLRP3 signaling in tumors. Further investigations are needed to confirm our findings and explore the clinical implications of targeting NLRP3 in cancer treatment.
In summary, our study reveals a critical function of NLRP3 in regulating antitumor immunity through MDSC accumulation. The findings suggest that targeting NLRP3 may be a novel strategy to improve the response to antitumor vaccines and enhance cancer therapy.
Keywords: NLRP3, inflammasome, dendritic cell vaccination, melanoma, MDSCs.

title: Natural Killer Cells for Immunotherapy – Advantages of the NK-92 Cell Line over Blood NK Cells
text: Natural killer (NK) cells are potent cytotoxic effector cells for cancer therapy and potentially for severe viral infections. However, isolating enough functionally active NK cells from a patient's blood can be technically challenging due to their low representation (only making up 10% of lymphocytes) and potential dysfunction. Alternative methods involve obtaining cells from a healthy donor, but this requires depleting the allogenic T cells to prevent graft-versus-host reactions. Established cytotoxic cell lines have been derived from patients with clonal NK-cell lymphoma, which can be expanded in culture with IL-2. Except for the NK-92 cell line, none of the other six known NK cell lines have consistently shown high antitumor cytotoxicity. NK-92 cells are also the only cell line product that has been safely infused into patients with advanced cancer, with measurable clinical benefit and minimal side effects.

title: Differential activation of DNA-PK based on DNA strand orientation and sequence bias
text:
DNA-PKcs and Ku are crucial components of the enzymatic complex responsible for repairing DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) through non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Ku, a heterodimeric protein, binds to DNA ends and facilitates the recruitment of the catalytic subunit, DNA-PKcs. Our studies focused on the impact of DNA strand orientation and sequence bias on the activity of DNA-PK. Moreover, we investigated the effect of the position and strand orientation of cisplatin adducts on the kinase's activity.
To achieve this, we prepared a series of duplex DNA substrates with site-specific cisplatin–DNA adducts placed in three different orientations on the duplex DNA. Terminal biotin modification and streptavidin (SA) blocking were employed to direct DNA-PK binding to the unblocked termini with a specific DNA strand orientation and cisplatin–DNA adduct position. Kinase activity was measured, and the results reveal that DNA strand orientation and sequence bias significantly influence kinase activation, only a portion of which can be attributed to Ku-DNA binding activity. Furthermore, the position of cisplatin–DNA adducts resulted in varying degrees of inhibition depending on distance from the terminus as well as strand orientation. These findings highlight the importance of local variations in DNA structure, chemistry, and sequence on DNA-PK activation and potentially NHEJ.

title: Regulators of Trypanosoma brucei Cell Cycle Progression and Differentiation Identified Using a Kinome-Wide RNAi Screen
text: The African trypanosome, Trypanosoma brucei, maintains a complex link between cell cycle regulation and differentiation throughout its life cycle. While there have been significant changes in phosphorylation noted between the mammalian bloodstream form and insect procyclic form, relatively little is known about the parasite's protein kinases (PKs) involved in cellular proliferation and differentiation. To address this knowledge gap, a T. brucei kinome-wide RNAi cell line library was generated, allowing for independent, inducible knockdown of each of the parasite's 190 predicted PKs. Screening this library using a cell viability assay identified at least 42 PKs necessary for normal bloodstream form proliferation in culture. A secondary screen identified 24 PKs whose RNAi-mediated depletion resulted in various cell cycle defects, including those in G1/S, kinetoplast replication/segregation, mitosis, and cytokinesis, with 15 of these being novel cell cycle regulators. Additionally, two novel PKs, repressor of differentiation kinase 1 (RDK1) and RDK2, were identified, which upon depletion promote bloodstream to procyclic form differentiation. RDK1 is a membrane-associated STE11-like PK, whereas RDK2 is a NEK PK essential for parasite proliferation. RDK1 collaborates with the PTP1/PIP39 phosphatase cascade to prevent uncontrolled bloodstream to procyclic form differentiation, while RDK2 acts as a PK whose depletion efficiently induces differentiation in the absence of known triggers. This RNAi kinome library provides a valuable tool for functional analysis of cell signaling pathways in African trypanosomes, as well as drug target identification and validation.

title: Chemotherapy options in elderly and frail patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (MRC FOCUS2): an open-label, randomised factorial trial
text:
Elderly and frail cancer patients often receive reduced doses of chemotherapy due to their poor health. We designed the FOCUS2 trial to investigate whether chemotherapy doses can be reduced further while still providing effective treatment. In this open, 2 × 2 factorial trial, we randomly assigned 61 UK cancer centers to treat 459 patients with advanced colorectal cancer who were considered unfit for full-dose chemotherapy. We looked at the effects of four different chemotherapy regimens: 48-hour intravenous fluorouracil with levofolinate (group A), oxaliplatin and fluorouracil (group B), capecitabine (group C), or oxaliplatin and capecitabine (group D). We found that the addition of oxaliplatin to chemotherapy did not significantly improve progression-free survival, but the substitution of fluorouracil with capecitabine did not improve global quality of life. The risk of toxic effects was not significantly higher with oxaliplatin than with fluorouracil, but capecitabine was associated with a higher risk of toxic effects. Baseline symptoms, extent of disease, and use of oxaliplatin were predictive of better overall treatment utility. Our results suggest that frail and elderly cancer patients can participate in randomized controlled trials with appropriate chemotherapy doses, and that a combination of chemotherapy regimens may be preferable to single-agent chemotherapy. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings and to identify the most effective chemotherapy regimen for this patient population.
The FOCUS2 trial was funded by Cancer Research UK and the Medical Research Council.

title: Whole-genome sequencing of Oryza brachyantha reveals mechanisms underlying Oryza genome evolution
text: The untapped genetic potential of wild species within the genus Oryza holds valuable agronomic gene variants for rice improvement. We present a de novo assembled genome sequence of Oryza brachyantha, spanning 261 megabases. The compact genome of Oryza brachyantha is characterized by low activity of long-terminal repeat retrotransposons and massive internal deletions of ancient long-terminal repeat elements, resulting in a compact genome. We identified 32,038 protein-coding genes in the Oryza brachyantha genome, of which only 70% are located in collinear positions compared to the rice genome. Investigating the breakpoints of non-collinear genes suggests that double-strand break repair through non-homologous end joining plays a crucial role in gene movement and erosion of collinearity in the Oryza genomes. The transition of euchromatin to heterochromatin in the rice genome is accompanied by segmental and tandem duplications, further expanded by transposable element insertions. The high-quality reference genome sequence of Oryza brachyantha serves as a valuable resource for functional and evolutionary studies within the Oryza genus.

title: Ultrasound imaging for lumbar punctures and epidural catheterisations: systematic review and meta-analysis.
text:
Objective:
To determine whether ultrasound imaging can improve the success rate of lumbar punctures or epidural catheterizations, compared to traditional palpation methods, and if so, whether it can reduce the number of traumatic procedures, insertion attempts, and needle redirections.
Design:
Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
Data Sources:
Ovid Medline, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials up to May 2012, without restriction by language or publication status.
Review Methods:
Randomized trials that compared ultrasound imaging with no imaging (standard method) in the performance of lumbar punctures or epidural catheterizations were identified.
Results:
14 studies with 1334 patients were included (674 patients assigned to the ultrasound group, 660 to the control group). Five studies evaluated lumbar punctures, and nine evaluated epidural catheterizations. Ultrasound imaging reduced the risk of failed procedures (risk ratio 0.21 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.43), P < 0.001). Risk reduction was similar when subgroup analysis was performed for lumbar punctures (risk ratio 0.19 (0.07 to 0.56), P = 0.002) or epidural catheterizations (risk ratio 0.23 (0.09 to 0.60), P = 0.003). Ultrasound imaging also significantly reduced the number of traumatic procedures (risk ratio 0.27 (0.11 to 0.67), P = 0.005), insertion attempts (mean difference -0.44 (-0.64 to -0.24), P < 0.001), and needle redirections (mean difference -1.00 (-1.24 to -0.75), P < 0.001).
Conclusions:
Ultrasound imaging can reduce the risk of failed or traumatic lumbar punctures and epidural catheterizations, as well as the number of needle insertions and redirections. Ultrasound may be a useful adjunct for these procedures.

title: Guidance of B cells by the orphan G protein-coupled receptor EBI2 shapes humoral immune responses.
text: Humoral immunity relies on both quick and long-term antibody production in response to invading pathogens. This is achieved by the generation of distinct populations of B cells, including extrafollicular plasmablasts and follicular germinal center (GC) B cells. However, the signals that guide B cells to these different compartments have not been fully understood. Our study reveals that the expression of the orphan G protein-coupled receptor Epstein-Barr virus-induced gene 2 (EBI2, also known as GPR183) by activated B cells is essential for their movement to extrafollicular sites and the induction of early plasmablast responses. Conversely, downregulation of EBI2 enables B cells to access the center of follicles and promotes efficient GC formation. EBI2 therefore provides a previously uncharacterized dimension to B cell migration that is crucial for coordinating rapid versus long-term antibody responses.

title: SIRT1 is required for long-term growth of human mesenchymal stem cells
text: Human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) hold great therapeutic potential due to their ability to self-renew and differentiate into various cell types. However, MSCs often undergo senescence when cultured in vitro, and the underlying molecular mechanisms are not well understood. In this study, we found that the levels of NAD-dependent protein deacetylase SIRT1 vary in human bone marrow-derived MSCs (B-MSCs) and adipose tissue-derived MSCs after multiple passages in cell culture. Using lentiviral shRNA, we demonstrated that reducing SIRT1 in human MSCs at an early passage slows down cell growth and accelerates cellular senescence. Conversely, increasing SIRT1 delays senescence in B-MSCs that have been cultured for an extended period, and the cells maintain their adipogenic and osteogenic potential. Moreover, we found that the delayed accumulation of the protein p16 is involved in the SIRT1-mediated effect. Interestingly, resveratrol, a compound known to activate SIRT1 deacetylase activity, only transiently promotes proliferation of B-MSCs. These findings shed light on the role of SIRT1 in the aging of normal diploid cells and may contribute to the prevention of MSCs senescence, which is crucial for MSCs-based tissue engineering and therapies.

title: Rapid and persistent modulation of actin dynamics regulates postsynaptic reorganization underlying bidirectional plasticity
text: The synapse, a highly organized cellular structure, undergoes reorganization in response to changes in input signals. The mechanisms underlying this reorganization are not yet fully understood. One potential locus for these changes is actin, as it plays a crucial role in both the cytoskeleton and scaffolding of synapses. Actin exists in a dynamic equilibrium between two forms, F-actin and G-actin, which are modulated by cellular signaling. Using a novel FRET-based imaging technique to monitor this equilibrium, we found that tetanic stimulation resulted in a rapid and persistent shift towards F-actin in the dendritic spines of rat hippocampal neurons. This enlarges the spines and increases postsynaptic binding capacity. In contrast, prolonged low-frequency stimulation resulted in a shift towards G-actin, leading to a loss of postsynaptic actin and structure. This bidirectional regulation of actin is critical for protein assembly and disassembly, and provides a substrate for bidirectional synaptic plasticity.

title: Sublime Microglia: Expanding Roles for the Guardians of the CNS
text:
Recent research has challenged the long-held belief that microglia in the central nervous system (CNS) solely operate in disease states. Instead, emerging evidence suggests that these immune cells play a more active role in shaping the CNS, refining neuronal connections, and contributing to plasticity. These physiological functions of microglia in the normal CNS begin during development and persist into adulthood.
In this article, we aim to develop a comprehensive framework for understanding the roles of microglia beyond their traditional function in neuroinflammation. We will explore the rich array of signaling and communication mechanisms employed by microglia, which are equally important in both healthy and diseased states.
By reconsidering the functions of microglia in the CNS, we may gain new insights into the mechanisms underlying neural development and function, and potentially identify new therapeutic targets for a range of neurological disorders.

title: Cancer after pre-eclampsia: follow up of the Jerusalem perinatal study cohort.
text:
Objective:
To compare the incidence of cancer in women with and without a history of pre-eclampsia.
Design: Cohort study.
Setting: Jerusalem perinatal study of women who delivered in three large hospitals in West Jerusalem during 1964-76.
Participants: 37,033 women.
Main Outcome Measures: Age-adjusted and multivariate-adjusted hazard ratios for cancer incidence for the entire cohort and for women who were primiparous at study entry.
Results: Cancer developed in 91 women who had pre-eclampsia and 2,204 who did not (hazard ratio 1.27, 95% confidence interval 1.03-1.57). The risk of site-specific cancers was increased, particularly of the stomach, ovary epithelium, breast, and lung or larynx. The incidence of cancer of the stomach, breast, ovary, kidney, and lung or larynx was increased in primiparous women at study entry who had a history of pre-eclampsia.
Conclusions: A history of pre-eclampsia is associated with increased risk of overall cancer incidence and several specific sites. This may be explained by shared environmental and genetic factors between the development of pre-eclampsia and cancer in this population.

title: Keeping your senescent cells under control
text:
Cellular senescence is a state of permanent cell cycle arrest that can occur in response to various forms of cellular damage or stress, such as telomere shortening, DNA damage, or oncogene activation. This phenomenon has been shown to be a potent failsafe mechanism against tumorigenesis, as senescent cells are unable to divide and potentially prone to undergo programmed cell death, thereby preventing the proliferation of premalignant cells. However, senescence can also have negative effects on organ maintenance by limiting the regenerative potential of tissues and organs.
Recent in vivo studies have demonstrated that senescence can occur in various cell types and can contribute to the cytotoxicity of certain anticancer agents. Interestingly, senescent cells have been observed in aged or damaged tissues, and it is thought that senescence checkpoints may affect the regenerative reserve of tissues and organismal aging.
One of the key mechanisms by which senescence regulates cellular behavior is through the secretion of a myriad of cytokines and growth factors, known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). While the SASP can have pro-tumorigenic effects, such as enhancing the tumorigenicity of surrounding breast cancer cells, it can also have anti-tumor effects, such as inducing apoptosis of tumor cells.
Recent studies have identified microRNAs (miRNAs) as central players in controlling the SASP. Specifically, miR-146a/b have been shown to negatively regulate the secretion of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and IL-8, two of the SASP. Inhibition of these miRNAs could potentially increase IL-6 levels in senescent cells, stabilizing the senescence program and reducing the risk of malignant transformation. However, it should be noted that the SASP can also act as a mitogen for surrounding cells, potentially increasing the risk of malignant transformation.
Overall, the study of senescence and its regulatory mechanisms holds great promise for our understanding of aging and cancer. By delving into the complex interplay between cellular stress responses, senescence, and tumorigenesis, we may uncover new opportunities for therapeutic intervention and disease prevention.

title: Role for insulin signaling in catecholaminergic neurons in control of energy homeostasis.
text:
Dopaminergic midbrain neurons play a crucial role in regulating food palatability and the reward associated with eating. By integrating signals on these factors into the complex control of energy homeostasis, these neurons help us maintain a healthy weight and body composition. To better understand the mechanisms underlying this process, we investigated the role of insulin receptor (IR) signaling in dopaminergic neurons of mice.
To do this, we inactivated IR signaling in tyrosine hydroxylase (Th)-expressing cells of mice (IR(ΔTh)). As expected, this resulted in increased body weight, fat mass, and hyperphagia (excessive food intake). Interestingly, insulin acutely stimulated the firing frequency of dopaminergic ventral tegmental area/substantia nigra (VTA/SN) neurons in only 50% of these neurons. Moreover, mice with inactivated IR signaling in these neurons exhibited altered responses to cocaine under food-restricted conditions.
Taken together, these findings provide in vivo evidence for the critical role of insulin signaling in catecholaminergic neurons in controlling food intake and energy homeostasis. By dysregulating these neurons, insulin signaling may contribute to the development of metabolic disorders such as obesity.

title: [New guidelines to evaluate the response to treatment in solid tumors].
text: Anticancer drugs undergo a process of evaluation to assess their effectiveness in shrinking tumors. In the 1970s, the International Union Against Cancer and the World Health Organization (WHO) developed specific criteria for evaluating tumor response. In 1994, several organizations involved in cancer research collaborated to review and update these criteria based on their collective experience and knowledge. After several years of intensive discussions, new guidelines were developed and are now replacing the previous WHO criteria. Simultaneously, one of the participating groups developed a novel approach to measuring tumor response by analyzing unidimensional measurements of tumor lesions instead of the traditional bidimensional method. This innovative model has been extensively validated by the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) Group and has been incorporated into the current guidelines. This special article provides an overview of the philosophical principles underlying response evaluation and proposes a novel model that combines the assessment of all existing lesions, characterized by target lesions (to be measured) and nontarget lesions, to derive an overall response to treatment. The article also provides a detailed codification of methods for assessing tumor lesions and covers all other aspects of response evaluation, which have been reviewed and updated where necessary.

title: Structural Rearrangements of NR1/NR2A NMDA Receptors during Allosteric Inhibition
text: The N-terminal domain (NTD) of ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) subunits plays a crucial role in subunit oligomerization. In N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors (NMDARs), the NTDs of NR2A and NR2B subunits also bind to the endogenous inhibitor Zn(2+). However, the molecular mechanisms by which the NTDs communicate with the rest of the receptor to promote its inhibition are still unknown. In this study, we identify the dimer interface between the agonist-binding domain (ABD) as a crucial structural determinant that regulates the inhibition of NMDARs. The strength of this interface also influences proton inhibition, another form of allosteric modulation of NMDARs. Our findings suggest that conformational rearrangements at the ABD dimer interface are a conserved mechanism across all iGluR subfamilies, serving different functions depending on the receptor type. In AMPA and kainate receptors, this mechanism mediates fast desensitization, while in NMDARs, it regulates allosteric inhibition.

title: The role of iron in Mycobacterium smegmatis biofilm formation: the exochelin siderophore is essential in limiting iron conditions for biofilm formation but not for planktonic growth
text: Mycobacteria species form intricate biofilm communities at liquid-air interfaces and solid surfaces. The development of Mycobacterium smegmatis biofilms requires supplemental iron at concentrations above 1 μM ferrous sulphate, although planktonic growth can occur without iron addition. Genetic analysis of M. smegmatis using microarray technology reveals that genes involved in iron uptake and siderophore synthesis are significantly induced during biofilm formation, indicating a response to iron scarcity, even when 2 μM iron is present. The acquisition of iron under these conditions is mainly mediated by the exochelin synthesis and uptake pathways, and a mutant lacking these genes exhibits a striking defect in iron uptake, suggesting a regulatory role of iron in the transition to biofilm growth. In contrast, while the expression of genes encoding mycobactin and iron ABC transport operons is greatly increased during biofilm formation, mutants in these systems can still form biofilms in low-iron conditions (2 μM). A correlation between iron availability and the levels of matrix-attached fatty acids suggests a possible metabolic function in the later stages of biofilm maturation, in addition to the early regulatory role. M. smegmatis surface motility also requires iron availability, with both supplemental iron and the exochelin pathway playing a role in its acquisition.

title: Plasma lipids and prolactin in patients with breast cancer.
text: In a study comparing pre- and postmenopausal women with benign or malignant breast disease, several differences were observed in circulating plasma prolactin and lipid levels. Plasma lipids, phospholipids, triglycerides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids were significantly higher in blood samples collected from breast cancer patients before surgery. HDL-Cholesterol levels were also lower in these patients. These differences persisted when the patient groups were divided according to menopausal status. Plasma prolactin concentrations were found to be higher in cancer patients compared to non-cancer patients, with a more pronounced increase in premenopausal than postmenopausal patients. Premenopausal patients with invasive or poorly differentiated breast cancer had significantly higher prolactin levels than those with non-invasive disease. No correlations were found between plasma prolactin and any of the lipid fractions.

title: expression by oxidized linoleic
text:
Hypercholesterolemia is associated with impaired vascular relaxations due to endothelial dysfunction. However, early stages of hypercholesterolemia are characterized by an increase in endothelial production of nitric oxides (NO). Prior studies have shown that oxidized low-density lipoprotein (LDL) has both stimulatory and inhibitory effects on endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) expression, with lysophosphatidyl choline (LPC) being a mediator of these effects. Another biologically active component of oxidized LDL is 13-hydroperoxyoctadecadienoic acid (13-HPODE), an oxidized form of linoleic acid.
The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of 13-HPODE on eNOS expression in bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs). The study found that a 24-hour treatment with 13-HPODE led to a dose-dependent increase in eNOS mRNA levels, as demonstrated by Northern analysis. Time-response studies showed that 13-HPODE treatment significantly increased eNOS mRNA levels at 12 and 24 hours. Additionally, the study found that 13-HPODE treatment significantly increased eNOS protein content and enzyme activity. Nuclear run-on studies revealed that the rate of transcription of the eNOS gene was significantly elevated 4 hours after 13-HPODE treatment, and actinomycin D studies demonstrated that the half-life of eNOS mRNA was increased from 6 hours to 12 hours after 13-HPODE treatment.
These findings suggest that endothelial cells may attempt to compensate for oxidative injury by increasing eNOS expression in early stages of hypercholesterolemia. Overall, the study highlights the complex mechanisms involved in endothelial dysfunction and the potential role of 13-HPODE in modulating these processes.

title: Specific killing of multiple myeloma cells by (-)-epigallocatechin-3-gallate extracted from green tea: biologic activity and therapeutic implications.
text: Green tea extract, specifically epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), is an antioxidant with both chemopreventive and chemotherapeutic properties. Our evaluation of its efficacy in multiple myeloma (MM) revealed that EGCG induces dose- and time-dependent growth arrest and subsequent apoptotic cell death in MM cell lines, including those dependent on interleukin-6 (IL-6), and primary patient cells, without significantly affecting the growth of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and normal fibroblasts. Treatment with EGCG also resulted in significant apoptosis in human myeloma cells grown as tumors in immunodeficient mice. We found that EGCG interacts with the 67-kDa laminin receptor 1 (LR1), which is elevated in myeloma cell lines and patient samples compared to normal PBMCs. Silencing LR1 using RNA interference abolished EGCG-induced apoptosis in myeloma cells, suggesting that LR1 plays a crucial role in mediating the antimyeloma effects of EGCG while sparing PBMCs. Analysis of gene expression changes revealed that EGCG treatment activates distinct pathways of growth arrest and apoptosis in MM cells, including the upregulation of death-associated protein kinase 2, Fas ligand, Fas, caspase 4, p53-like proteins (p73, p63), positive regulators of apoptosis (CARD10, CARD14), and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (p16 and p18). These findings demonstrate the potent and specific antimyeloma activity of EGCG and support its potential as a clinical therapeutic agent.

title: Pharmacologic inhibition of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 arrests the growth of glioblastoma multiforme intracranial xenografts.
text: The activation of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (cdk4/6) is a prevalent feature in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) tumors, making it a promising target for the development of small molecule inhibitors. In this study, we investigated the molecular determinants and in vivo response of diverse GBM cell lines and xenografts to PD-0332991, a cdk4/6-specific inhibitor. Using a panel of 16 GBM cell lines with different genetic backgrounds, we found that PD-0332991 induced a potent G(1) cell cycle arrest and induction of senescence in all Rb-proficient cell lines, regardless of other genetic mutations. In contrast, 5 cell lines with homozygous inactivation of Rb were completely resistant to treatment. Moreover, short hairpin RNA depletion of Rb expression resulted in resistance of GBM cells to PD-0332991, further emphasizing the requirement of Rb for sensitivity to cdk4/6 inhibition. The in vitro data were further validated in vivo, where PD-0332991 efficiently crossed the blood-brain barrier and suppressed the growth of intracranial GBM xenograft tumors, including those that had recurred after initial therapy with temozolomide. Notably, no mice receiving PD-0332991 died as a result of disease progression during treatment. Furthermore, the combination of PD-0332991 and radiation therapy resulted in significantly increased survival benefits compared to either therapy alone. Our findings support the evaluation of PD-0332991 in clinical trials against both newly diagnosed and recurrent GBM, with Rb status emerging as the primary determinant of potential benefit from this therapy.

title: Choosing Haplotype-Tagging SNPS Based on Unphased Genotype Data Using a Preliminary Sample of Unrelated Subjects with an Example from the Multiethnic Cohort Study
text: To identify haplotype-tagging single nucleotide polymorphisms (htSNPs) for our study on the genetic variation of prostate and breast cancer risk in a multiethnic cohort (MEC), we adopt an approach that combines genotyping a high density of SNPs in and around candidate genes with a statistical algorithm to estimate haplotype frequencies. We first apply this method on a preliminary sample of 70 control subjects from the five ethnic groups in the MEC, and then use the haplotype frequencies to evaluate the performance of a set of candidate htSNPs that will be genotyped in a much larger case-control sample. To optimize the selection of htSNPs, we calculate the coefficient of determination, R2h, which measures the uncertainty of the number of copies of common haplotypes carried by an individual. We choose the candidate set of htSNPs that maximizes the minimum value of R2h across the common haplotypes, h.

title: A model for the role of gut bacteria in the development of autoimmunity for type 1 diabetes
text: mounting evidence supports the role of the gut microbiome in the development of type 1 diabetes. Experimental studies have shown that treating diabetes-prone rodents with probiotics or antibiotics can prevent the onset of the disease. These findings are echoed in recent studies of children at high genetic risk of developing the disease, which have found significant differences in gut microbiome composition between those who go on to develop autoimmunity and those who remain healthy. However, these differences are not consistent across all studies due to the powerful influence of environmental factors, such as diet and geography, on the composition of the microbiome. By controlling for these confounding factors, researchers have discovered bacterial associations with disease, such as the strong link between the dominant bacterial species, Bacteroides dorei, and type 1 diabetes in a human cohort from a single Finnish city. Additionally, recent DNA methylation analyses suggest that a comprehensive epigenetic analysis of the gut microbiome may be warranted. This model proposes that a diet high in fat and low in resistant starch may be the primary driver of gut dysbiosis, leading to a lack of butyrate production by gut bacteria and a permeable gut followed by autoimmunity. Bacteroides, a genus of bacteria, is thought to play a key role in these changes in butyrate production.

title: METHODS AND RESULTS
text: Cytoscape is an open-source software platform designed to integrate complex networks of biological interactions with high-throughput expression data and other molecular states. While it can be applied to any system of molecular components and interactions, Cytoscape's full potential is realized when used in conjunction with vast databases of protein-protein, protein-DNA, and genetic interactions, which are increasingly available for both humans and model organisms. The Cytoscape platform offers basic functionalities through its software Core to visualize and query the network, integrate it with expression profiles, phenotypes, and other molecular states, and link the network to databases of functional annotations. The Core is highly extensible through a plugin architecture, allowing for rapid development of additional computational analyses and features. Examples of Cytoscape plugins include a search for interaction pathways correlating with changes in gene expression, a study of protein complexes involved in cellular recovery from DNA damage, the construction of a physical/functional interaction network for Halobacterium, and integration with detailed stochastic gene regulatory models.

title: Dual Regulation of miRNA Biogenesis Generates Target Specificity in Neurotrophin-Induced Protein Synthesis
text: Control of translation is a key mechanism for regulating gene expression. The induction of protein synthesis by brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays a crucial role in long-term changes to synaptic function, but the mechanism by which BDNF targets specific mRNAs for translation is not well understood. We have found that BDNF rapidly increases the levels of Dicer, which leads to higher levels of mature microRNAs (miRNAs) and the formation of RNA processing bodies in neurons. BDNF also rapidly induces the protein Lin28, causing the loss of Lin28-regulated miRNAs and a corresponding increase in the translation of their target mRNAs. The binding sites for Lin28-regulated miRNAs are necessary and sufficient to make a transcript responsive to BDNF. Lin28 deficiency or the expression of a Lin28-resistant Let-7 precursor miRNA inhibits BDNF translation specificity and BDNF-dependent dendrite arborization. Our results demonstrate that the specificity of BDNF-regulated translation depends on a two-part posttranscriptional control of miRNA biogenesis that enhances mRNA repression in association with GW182 while selectively derepressing and increasing translation of specific mRNAs.

title: A Viral microRNA Cluster Strongly Potentiates the Transforming Properties of a Human Herpesvirus
text: The oncogenic Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a human herpesvirus, induces proliferation of resting B lymphocytes upon infection, its primary reservoir in vivo. While viral latent proteins are essential for perpetuating B cell growth, it remains uncharacterized whether they constitute a sufficient factor. Recent discoveries have revealed that EBV encodes miRNAs (microRNAs), which are expressed in infected B cells and some EBV-linked lymphomas. These EBV miRNAs are grouped into two clusters located either near the BHRF1 gene or within the viral BART transcripts. To investigate the function of the BHRF1 miRNA cluster, we generated a virus mutant lacking its three members (Δ123) and a revertant virus. Our findings indicate that the transformative potential of the Δ123 EBV mutant is significantly diminished (>20-fold) compared to wild-type or revertant viruses. B cells exposed to the knockout virus displayed a slower growth rate, and a two-fold decrease in the proportion of cells entering the S phase of the cell cycle. Moreover, these cells exhibited higher levels of latent gene expression and viral protein production compared to their wild-type counterparts. These results suggest that the BHRF1 miRNAs augment B cell expansion at lower levels of latent gene expression. This miRNA cluster's dual function of expanding the virus reservoir while reducing viral antigenic load may enable EBV to persist within the host. Therefore, targeting the BHRF1 miRNAs with novel therapies may provide a potential approach for treating certain EBV-related lymphomas.

title: EMSY overexpression disrupts the BRCA2/RAD51 pathway in the DNA-damage response: implications for chromosomal instability/recombination syndromes as checkpoint diseases
text:
EMSY connects the BRCA2 pathway to sporadic breast/ovarian cancer. This protein functions as a nucleus-based binding partner of the BRCA2 N-terminal region, which is critical in controlling chromatin/transcription regulation. However, when EMSY is amplified or overexpressed, it suppresses BRCA2's potential to activate transcription, and this leads to unstable chromosomes, a hallmark of hereditary breast/ovarian cancer. Additionally, EMSY may play a role in the DNA damage response by localizing to sites of DNA damage and repair, suggesting that its overexpression may also suppress BRCA2 in these processes. Using a well-established recombination/repair assay system, we demonstrate that a slight increase in EMSY levels can indeed repress these processes independently of transcriptional interference/repression. Since EMSY, RPA, and PALB2 all bind to the same BRCA2 region, these findings further support a scenario where: (a) EMSY amplification may mimic BRCA2 deficiency by overriding RPA and PALB2, thereby crippling the BRCA2/RAD51 complex at DNA damage and replication/transcription sites; and (b) BRCA2/RAD51 may coordinate these processes by utilizing at least EMSY, PALB2, and RPA. We extensively discuss the molecular details of how this can occur to understand its implications for a novel recombination mechanism that appears to be a checkpoint rather than a DNA repair system, with important implications for cancer predisposition, targeted therapy, and prevention.
In summary, EMSY regulates the BRCA2 pathway in sporadic breast/ovarian cancer by suppressing BRCA2 transcriptional activity, leading to chromosomal instability. Overexpression of EMSY may also affect BRCA2's role in DNA damage response and recombination/repair by suppressing these processes. A better understanding of the molecular mechanisms involved can provide valuable insights into the development of novel cancer therapies and prevention strategies.

title: Original Article
text:
The study investigated the effects of supplementing with dehydrated fruit and vegetable juice concentrates (Juice Plus+R) on various biomarkers of health in Japanese adults. The study was double-blind, placebo-controlled and involved 60 participants (39 males and 21 females) aged 27.8 years with a body mass index (BMI) of 22.1. Participants were randomized into two groups and received either the supplement or a matching placebo for 28 days. Blood and urine samples were collected at baseline, day 14, and day 28 for analysis.
The results showed that supplementation with the fruit and vegetable juice concentrate significantly increased the levels of serum beta-carotene, lycopene, and alpha-tocopherol by 528%, 80.2%, and 39.5%, respectively, compared to the placebo group. Additionally, supplementation led to a 174.3% increase in serum folate levels and a corresponding decrease in plasma homocysteine levels of -19.9%. Measures of oxidative stress, such as serum lipid peroxides and urine 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), also decreased significantly after supplementation. Notably, the benefits of supplementation were similar in smokers and non-smokers.
In conclusion, the study demonstrates that supplementation with dehydrated fruit and vegetable juice concentrates is a highly bioavailable source of phytonutrients that can improve antioxidant status, folate levels, and reduce markers of oxidative stress and homocysteine levels. These benefits were observed in both smokers and non-smokers, highlighting the potential of this supplement to improve overall health and reduce disease risk.

title: NCBI GEO: archive for functional genomics data sets—update
text: The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO, <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/>) is a publicly accessible repository for high-throughput microarray and next-generation sequence functional genomic data sets contributed by the research community. GEO supports the archival of raw data, processed data, and metadata, which are meticulously indexed, cross-linked, and searchable. All data are freely available for download in various formats. In addition, GEO offers a range of user-friendly web-based tools and strategies to aid in querying, analyzing, and visualizing data. This article provides an overview of the current status and recent database developments, including the introduction of GEO2R, a user-friendly R-based web application that facilitates the analysis of GEO data.

title: Viral Paratransgenesis in the Malaria Vector Anopheles gambiae
text:
Paratransgenesis, the genetic manipulation of insect symbiotic microorganisms, is being considered as a potential method to control vector-borne diseases such as malaria. However, the feasibility of paratransgenic malaria control has been hindered by the lack of suitable symbiotic microorganisms for the major vectorAnopheles gambiae. In contrast, densonucleosis viruses (DNVs) are attractive agents for viral paratransgenesis due to their ability to infect important vector insects, be genetically manipulated, and be transmitted to subsequent generations. However, An. gambiae has been shown to be refractory to DNV dissemination.
We recently discovered, cloned and characterized the first known DNV (AgDNV) capable of infection and dissemination in An. gambiae. We also developed a flexible AgDNV-based expression vector to express any gene of interest in An. gambiae using a two-plasmid helper-transducer system. To demonstrate the proof of concept of the paratransgenesis strategy, we used this system to transduce the expression of an exogenous gene (enhanced green fluorescent protein; EGFP) in An. gambiae mosquitoes. Wild-type and EGFP-transducing AgDNV virions were highly infectious to An. gambiae larvae, disseminated to and expressed EGFP in epidemiologically relevant adult tissues such as midgut, fat body, and ovaries, and were transmitted to subsequent generations. These proof-of-principle data suggest that AgDNV could be used as part of a paratransgenic malaria control strategy by transduction of anti-Plasmodium peptides or insect-specific toxins in Anopheles mosquitoes. AgDNV will also be an extremely valuable tool as an effective and easy-to-use laboratory tool for transient gene expression or RNAi in An. gambiae.

title: The polycomb group protein L3mbtl2 assembles an atypical PRC1-family complex that is essential in pluripotent stem cells and early development.
text: Research has shown that L3mbtl2 is involved in transcriptional repression and chromatin compaction, but its biological function remains unknown. Our study reveals that disrupting L3mbtl2 leads to embryonic lethality during gastrulation. Compromised proliferation and abnormal differentiation of L3mbtl2-deficient embryonic stem (ES) cells were also observed. We found that L3mbtl2 regulates genes by recruiting a complex similar to Polycomb Repressive Complex1 (PRC1) and including G9A, Hdac1, and Ring1b. The presence of L3mbtl2 at target genes is associated with H3K9 dimethylation, low histone acetylation, and H2AK119 ubiquitination. Genome-wide analysis revealed that the L3mbtl2-dependent complex predominantly regulates genes not bound by canonical PRC1 and PRC2. However, some developmental regulators are repressed by the combined activity of all three complexes. Overall, our study has uncovered a highly selective, essential role for an atypical PRC1-family complex in ES cells and early development.

title: Long-term effect of aspirin on cancer risk in carriers of hereditary colorectal cancer: an analysis from the CAPP2 randomised controlled trial
text:
BACKGROUND: Observational studies have shown that regular aspirin use is associated with a reduced risk of colorectal cancer. However, previous randomized controlled trials have not specifically focused on preventing colorectal cancer as a primary endpoint. The CAPP2 trial aimed to investigate the antineoplastic effects of aspirin and a resistant starch in individuals with Lynch syndrome, the most common inherited colorectal cancer syndrome. Our study reports the long-term follow-up results of participants randomly assigned to aspirin or placebo.
METHODS: In the CAPP2 randomized trial, individuals with Lynch syndrome were randomly assigned to aspirin or placebo in a 2x3 factorial design for up to 4 years. Participants were masked to treatment allocation, and the primary endpoint was the development of colorectal cancer. Analysis was conducted using intention-to-treat and per-protocol methods. This trial is registered with ISRCTN59521990.
RESULTS: A total of 861 participants were randomly assigned to aspirin or placebo, and the mean follow-up time was 55.7 months. Among the 48 participants who developed 53 primary colorectal cancers, the aspirin group had 18 cases, and the placebo group had 30 cases. The intention-to-treat analysis showed a hazard ratio of 0.63 (95% CI 0.35-1.13, p=0.12), and the incidence rate ratio was 0.56 (95% CI 0.32-0.99, p=0.05). The results were similarly significant when analyzing participants who completed 2 years of intervention (258 aspirin and 250 aspirin placebo). The hazard ratio was 0.41 (95% CI 0.19-0.86, p=0.02), and the incidence rate ratio was 0.37 (95% CI 0.18-0.78, p=0.008). No adverse event data were available post-intervention, but during the intervention, adverse events did not differ between the aspirin and placebo groups.
INTERPRETATION: Our findings suggest that 600 mg of aspirin per day for a mean of 25 months substantially reduced colorectal cancer incidence after 55.7 months in individuals with hereditary colorectal cancer. Further studies are needed to determine the optimal dose and duration of aspirin treatment. The study was funded by the European Union, Cancer Research UK, Bayer Corporation, National Starch and Chemical Co, UK Medical Research Council, Newcastle Hospitals trustees, Cancer Council of Victoria Australia, THRIPP South Africa, The Finnish Cancer Foundation, SIAK Switzerland, and Bayer Pharma.

title: Drosophila CPEB Orb2A Mediates Memory Independent of Its RNA-Binding Domain
text:
The synthesis of new proteins at activated synapses is believed to play a crucial role in long-term memory formation. The CPEB family of RNA binding proteins, including Drosophila Orb2, has been implicated in this process. However, the specific mechanisms by which these molecules regulate memory formation are still poorly understood.
To investigate the role of the Orb2 protein in long-term memory formation, we used gene targeting and site-specific transgenesis to specifically modify the endogenous Orb2 gene in Drosophila. Our findings indicate that the Orb2A and Orb2B isoforms, although both essential, have distinct functions in memory formation. These two isoforms share some common domains, such as glutamine-rich and RNA-binding regions, but have different requirements for their functions.
We discovered that Orb2A induces Orb2 complexes in a manner dependent on both its glutamine-rich region and neuronal activity. This suggests that Orb2A acts in an unconventional manner to form stable Orb2 complexes that are essential for memory to persist. In contrast, Orb2B is thought to act as a conventional CPEB, regulating the transport and/or translation of specific mRNAs.
Overall, our study sheds light on the complex mechanisms involved in long-term memory formation and highlights the importance of Orb2A and Orb2B in this process. Further research is needed to fully understand the role of these proteins and their implications for memory formation in other organisms.

title: Functional hemichannels in astrocytes: a novel mechanism of glutamate release.
text: The expression and potential functions of unopposed gap junction hemichannels in the brain are poorly understood. However, recent findings suggest that these hemichannels can function independently in astrocytes. Using immunocytochemistry, dye uptake, and HPLC analysis, we demonstrate that astrocytes in vitro express functional hemichannels that can mediate robust efflux of glutamate and aspartate. We confirm the functional hemichannels by showing that extracellular lucifer yellow (LY) can enter astrocytes in a nominal divalent cation-free solution (DCFS) and that the passage can be blocked by gap junction blocking agents. Glutamate/aspartate release (or LY loading) in DCFS is blocked by multivalent cations (Ca2+, Ba2+, Sr2+, Mg2+, and La3+) and gap junction blocking agents (carbenoxolone, octanol, heptanol, flufenamic acid, and 18alpha-glycyrrhetinic acid) with affinities similar to those reported for blocking gap junction intercellular communication. Furthermore, glutamate efflux via hemichannels is accompanied by reduced glutamate uptake and is not significantly mediated by reversal of the glutamate transporter. In contrast, glutamate release in DCFS is not blocked by glutamate transporter blockers. Additionally, blocking intracellular Ca2+ mobilization by BAPTA-AM or thapsigargin does not inhibit glutamate release in DCFS. Interestingly, divalent cation removal also induces glutamate release from intact CNS white matter (acutely isolated optic nerve), which is blocked by carbenoxolone, suggesting the existence of functional hemichannels in situ. Our results suggest that astrocyte hemichannels may play a significant role in regulating extracellular glutamate levels in the brain, with implications for both normal and pathological brain function.

title: Human Rad52 binds and wraps single-stranded DNA and mediates annealing via two hRad52–ssDNA complexes
text: Rad52 facilitates the repair of damaged DNA by promoting the annealing of complementary strands bound by replication protein A (RPA). To investigate the mechanism by which human Rad52 (hRad52) interacts with and mediates annealing of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA)-RPA complexes, we employed a fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) assay that incorporated two fluorescent dyes into DNA substrates. Our results indicate that hRad52 bound to ssDNA or ssDNA-RPA complexes in two different modes depending on concentration, with either ssDNA wrapped around the protein ring or stretched between multiple hRad52 rings at low and high concentrations, respectively. Annealing by hRad52 occurred most efficiently when each complementary DNA strand or complex was bound by hRad52 in a wrapped configuration, suggesting that hRad52 facilitates homology search and annealing via two hRad52-ssDNA complexes. In contrast, mutants of hRad52 (RQK/AAA) and hRad52(1-212) that impaired its ability to bind hRPA protein competed with hRPA for ssDNA binding and failed to counteract hRPA-mediated duplex destabilization, highlighting the significance of hRad52-hRPA interactions in promoting efficient DNA annealing.

title: Mendelian Randomization Study of B-Type Natriuretic Peptide and Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence of Causal Association from Population Studies
text:
Original text:
 background Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested that there is an inverse association between levels of the N-terminal fragment of pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) in blood and the risk of developing T2D, but the prospective relationship between these factors is unclear because it may be confounded by other variables.
Rewritten text:
Background: Genetic and epidemiological evidence suggests that there may be an inverse association between levels of NT-pro-BNP in blood and the risk of developing T2D, but the prospective nature of this relationship is uncertain due to potential confounding factors.

Original text:
Methods and findings: We conducted a prospective case-cohort study and genotyped three T2D case-control studies for the variant rs198389 within the BNP locus. We combined our results with existing data from a meta-analysis of 11 case-control studies. Using Mendelian randomization, we compared the observed association between rs198389 and T2D to that expected based on the NT-pro-BNP level to T2D association and the NT-pro-BNP difference per C allele of rs198389. In participants of our case-cohort study who were free of T2D and cardiovascular disease at baseline, we observed a 21% (95% CI 3%-36%) reduced risk of incident T2D per one standard deviation (SD) higher log-transformed NT-pro-BNP level in analysis adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, systolic blood pressure, smoking, family history of T2D, history of hypertension, and levels of triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol. The association between rs198389 and T2D observed in case-control studies (odds ratio = 0.94 per C allele, 95% CI 0.91-0.97) was similar to that expected (0.96, 0.93-0.98) based on the pooled estimate for the NT-pro-BNP level to T2D association and the difference in NT-pro-BNP levels (0.22 SD, 0.15-0.29) per C allele of rs198389. No significant associations were observed between the rs198389 genotype and potential confounders.
Rewritten text:
Methods and findings: We conducted a prospective case-cohort study and genotyped three T2D case-control studies for the variant rs198389 within the BNP locus. We combined our results with existing data from a meta-analysis of 11 case-control studies. No significant associations were observed between the rs198389 genotype and potential confounders.

title: brain organization
text: A temporary activation of estrogen receptors (ER) in the developing brain during a limited perinatal "window of time" is recognized as a crucial mechanism for the diminishment of neural control over reproductive function and sexual behavior in females.Two main ER isoforms, alpha and beta, are present in neural circuits governing ovarian cycle and sexual behavior. Using highly selective ER agonists, this study provides the first evidence for distinct contributions of individual ER isoforms to the defeminization process. Neonatal activation of ERalpha in female rat pups leads to abrogation of cyclic ovarian activity and female sexual behavior in adulthood, with concurrent male-like alterations in the anteroventral periventricular (AVPV) and sexually dimorphic nucleus of the preoptic area (SDN-POA). In contrast, exposure to an ERbeta-selective agonist induces persistent estrus and a strong defeminizing effect on the hypothalamic gonadotropin "surge generator" AVPV, but fails to influence female sexual behavior or morphometric features of the SDN-POA. Notably, despite co-localization in several brain regions involved in reproductive function control, ER isoforms seem to convey distinct, non-additive chemical signals during neonatal brain organization.

title: Thresholds for the cost–effectiveness of interventions: alternative approaches
text: Many countries use the cost-effectiveness thresholds recommended by the World Health Organization's Choosing Interventions that are Cost-Effective project (WHO-CHOICE) when evaluating health interventions. This project sets the threshold for cost-effectiveness as the cost of the intervention per disability-adjusted life-year (DALY) averted less than three times the country's annual gross domestic product (GDP) per capita. Highly cost-effective interventions are defined as meeting a threshold per DALY averted of once the annual GDP per capita. However, we argue that relying on these thresholds compromises the value of cost-effectiveness analyses and renders them too simplistic for practical decision-making in public health. There is little theoretical justification for using these thresholds, as they ignore the relative values of locally-applicable interventions and oversimplify the consideration of affordability. Furthermore, the WHO-CHOICE thresholds are set so low that few interventions with evidence of efficacy can be excluded. These thresholds are also of little use in assessing the trade-offs that decision-makers must confront. Instead, we propose alternative approaches to evaluating the cost-effectiveness of health interventions, which take into account the local applicability and affordability of interventions, and provide a more nuanced assessment of their value.

title: Effect of low doses of ionising radiation in infancy on cognitive function in adulthood: Swedish population based cohort study.
text:
Aim: To investigate the impact of low-dose ionizing radiation exposure in infancy on cognitive function in adulthood.
Design: Population-based cohort study.
Setting: Sweden.
Participants: 3094 male subjects who received radiation therapy for cutaneous hemangiomas before the age of 18 months between 1930 and 1959.
Main Outcome Measures: Radiation doses to the frontal and posterior regions of the brain were measured, and the association between radiation dose and intellectual capacity at the ages of 18 or 19 was assessed using cognitive tests (learning ability, logical reasoning, and spatial recognition) and high school attendance.
Results: The proportion of boys who attended high school decreased as radiation dose to both the frontal and posterior regions of the brain increased. The multivariate odds ratio for the frontal dose was 0.47 (95% CI: 0.26-0.85, P < 0.0003), and for the posterior dose it was 0.59 (0.23-1.47, P < 0.0005). A negative dose-response relationship was also observed for the three cognitive tests measuring learning ability and logical reasoning, but not for the test of spatial recognition.
Conclusions: This study found that low levels of ionizing radiation exposure in infancy have a lasting impact on cognitive abilities in adulthood.

title: Differential effects of charybdotoxin on the activity of retinal ganglion cells in the dark- and light-adapted mouse retina
text:
Here is a possible reconstruction of the given text in a more formal and technical style:
Patch-clamp experiments were performed on retinal ganglion cells in the mouse retina to investigate the effects of BK(Ca) channel blockade on neural activity. Under dark adaptation, blockade of BK(Ca) channels resulted in increased spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) and light-evoked On-EPSCs, as well as decreased light-evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs). Conversely, under light adaptation, blockade of BK(Ca) channels led to decreased light-evoked On-EPSCs, as well as decreased spontaneous IPSCs and light-evoked On- and Off-IPSCs. Moreover, blockade of BK(Ca) channels significantly altered the outputs of RGCs by transforming light-evoked responses into a bursting pattern and increasing the light-evoked depolarization of the membrane potentials, while having no significant effect on peak firing rates of light-evoked responses.

title: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome: review of the phenotype
text: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is a rare and well-known condition characterized by distinct physical features resembling premature aging in children. Key symptoms include short stature, low body weight, early hair loss, lipodystrophy, scleroderma, restricted joint mobility, osteolysis, and aged-like facial features. Cardiovascular problems often lead to early death. Cognitive development is typically normal. Data from 10 cases in our study and 132 cases from the literature reveal an incidence of approximately 1:4,000,000 in the Netherlands over the past century, with a slight sex ratio bias towards males (1.2:1). The primary symptoms usually appear before the age of 3, with failure to thrive (55%), hair loss (40%), skin problems (28%), and lipodystrophy (20%) being the most common initial signs. Children with HGPS typically have a height of less than 13 years and a weight of 14.5 kilograms. Osteolysis is widespread but primarily affects the viscerocranium, while lipodystrophy is generalized, with the exception of abdominal fat deposits. Cardiovascular issues are diverse, with both early onset and later onset being common. Stroke and coronary dysfunction are the most frequent problems. Pathological findings in coronary arteries and aorta resemble those of elderly individuals, but can also be more limited. Loss of smooth muscle cells is the most notable finding. The average age of death is 12.6 years. HGPS can be classified into two subtypes: classical HGPS, which follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance and is characterized by spontaneous mutations, and non-classical progeria, which has a slower progression of growth retardation, longer persistence of scalp hair, less severe lipodystrophy, less severe osteolysis in the face, and longer survival into adulthood.
