The inheritance pattern of non-classical progeria is likely autosomal recessive. The underlying cause of HGPS is an abnormal Lamin A, either due to a mutated LMNA gene or abnormal post-translational processing (ZMPSTE24 gene mutations). Therapeutic strategies are being developed to target the various pathways involved in the disease, such as RNA interference techniques and inhibition of the dominant-negative influence of abnormally formed Lamin A on normally formed Lamin A.

title: Identification of an autoantigen demonstrates a link between interstitial lung disease and a defect in central tolerance.
text:
Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a common manifestation of systemic autoimmunity, characterized by progressive inflammation or scarring of the lungs. This can lead to significant impairment in gas exchange, resulting in hypoxemia, pulmonary hypertension, and even death. Despite being prevalent, the underlying mechanisms of ILD are not well understood, including the role of specific defects in immune tolerance. Additionally, it is unclear whether autoimmune responses targeting the lung parenchyma are central to ILD pathogenesis, particularly in cases of isolated idiopathic forms.
Our research has shed light on the origins of ILD by identifying a specific defect in central tolerance brought about by mutations in the autoimmune regulator gene (Aire). We found that this defect leads to the development of an autoreactive T cell response to a lung antigen named vomeromodulin, resulting in similar lung pathology in both human patients and mice with Aire deficiencies. This novel model system allows us to delve into the fundamental mechanisms underlying ILD pathogenesis, providing vital insights into disease progression.

title: In vivo role of ER-associated peptidase activity in tailoring peptides for presentation by MHC class Ia and class Ib molecules
text: The protein ERAP1 helps finalize the processing of proteins that will be presented to the immune system on the surface of cells. To understand the role of ERAP1 in the body, we created mice without the ERAP1 protein. We found that the surface expression of certain proteins called H-2Kb and H-2Db, which are important for presenting antigens to immune cells, was much lower in these mice. Although cells from these mice couldn't present some antigens as well as they should, they also had some unexpected changes in their ability to present antigens to immune cells. For example, some antigens were presented more effectively than usual. These findings tell us that ERAP1 plays an important role in preparing proteins for presentation to the immune system by MHC class Ia and class Ib molecules.

title: PD 0332991, a selective cyclin D kinase 4/6 inhibitor, preferentially inhibits proliferation of luminal estrogen receptor-positive human breast cancer cell lines in vitro
text:
Introduction: Abnormalities in cell cycle regulators have been linked to the development of human malignancies, including breast cancer. PD 0332991 is an orally active, highly selective inhibitor of the cyclin D kinases (CDK)4 and CDK6, which has shown the ability to block the phosphorylation of retinoblastoma (Rb) in a low nanomolar range. To determine predictors of response to this inhibitor, we evaluated the sensitivity of a panel of molecularly characterized human breast cancer cell lines to PD 0332991 and analyzed the associated gene expression data.
Methods: Forty-seven human breast cancer and immortalized cell lines representing the known molecular subgroups of breast cancer were treated with PD 0332991 to determine their IC50 values. These data were then correlated with baseline gene expression data to identify genes associated with response to the inhibitor.
Results: Our results showed that cell lines representing the luminal estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) subtype (including those that are HER2 amplified) were the most sensitive to growth inhibition by PD 0332991, while nonluminal/basal subtypes were the most resistant. Through statistical analysis, we identified 450 differentially expressed genes between sensitive and resistant cells. Analysis of these genes revealed elevated levels of pRb and cyclin D1, and decreased levels of CDKN2A (p16) in the most sensitive lines. Cell cycle analysis demonstrated G0/G1 arrest in sensitive cell lines, and Western blot analysis showed that Rb phosphorylation was blocked in sensitive lines but not in resistant lines. Additionally, we found that PD 0332991 had synergistic effects with tamoxifen and trastuzumab in ER+ and HER2-amplified cell lines, respectively, and enhanced sensitivity to tamoxifen in cell lines with conditioned resistance to ER blockade.
Conclusions: These findings suggest that CDK4/6 inhibition may play a role in some breast cancers, and our results identify potential criteria for patient selection in clinical studies of PD 0332991.

title: Identification of secreted proteins that mediate cell-cell interactions in an in vitro model of the lung cancer microenvironment.
text: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells with somatic mutations in K-ras can attract a variety of cell types (collectively referred to as "stromal cells") that may promote or hinder tumor growth through poorly understood mechanisms. To investigate this, we hypothesized that stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment modify the tumor cell secretome, including proteins necessary for tumor growth and proliferation, and developed an in vitro model to test this idea. Culturing a mutant K-ras lung adenocarcinoma cell line (LKR-13) with lung stromal cells, such as macrophages, endothelial cells, or fibroblasts, enhanced stromal cell migration, formed new blood vessels, increased LKR-13 cell proliferation, and regulated the release of proteins involved in angiogenesis, inflammation, cell growth, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. These proteins include CXCL1, which has been linked to NSCLC development, and IL-18, whose function in this context is unknown. Using genetic and pharmacological methods to inhibit CXCL1 and IL-18, we found that stromal cell migration, LKR-13 cell proliferation, and LKR-13 cell tumorigenicity require these proteins. Therefore, we conclude that stromal cells enhance LKR-13 cell tumorigenicity by altering the secretome of LKR-13 cells. Strategies targeting tumor-stromal cell interactions may serve as promising therapeutic approaches in NSCLC patients.

title: Tightrope act: autophagy in stem cell renewal, differentiation, proliferation, and aging
text: Autophagy is a cellular process that breaks down damaged organelles and protein aggregates. Stem cells, which have the ability to self-renew and differentiate, require autophagy more than other cell types due to their limited capacity to dilute cellular waste and spent organelles due to quiescence. We review the current literature on the role of autophagy in embryonic and adult stem cells, including hematopoietic, mesenchymal, and neuronal stem cells, highlighting the diverse and contrasting roles autophagy plays in their biology. Additionally, we discuss the few studies on stem cells, lysosomal activity, and autophagy, and highlight the need for novel techniques to detect autophagy in primary cells in order to study its importance in stem cells during transplantation, a promising therapeutic approach for many diseases.

title: Variant Histone H2A.Z Is Globally Localized to the Promoters of Inactive Yeast Genes and Regulates Nucleosome Positioning
text: H2A.Z is an evolutionarily conserved histone variant that plays a crucial role in transcriptional regulation, antisilencing, silencing, and genome stability. However, the mechanisms by which H2A.Z regulates these functions are not yet fully understood, mainly due to the scarcity of information on its spatial distribution along chromosomes and its role in shaping chromatin structure. To address this gap in knowledge, we used chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled with tiling arrays of microarrays to map H2A.Z across the yeast genome at an approximately 300-base pair resolution. Our findings indicate that H2A.Z is associated with 4,862 small regions (typically one or two nucleosomes wide) in the promoter regions of inactive genes scattered throughout the genome. Additionally, we demonstrate that H2A.Z can regulate nucleosome positioning at the GAL1 promoter. We observed that within H2A.Z-associated domains, called HZAD (H2A.Z-associated domains), the regions where H2A.Z shows an antisilencing function are localized in a more extensive pattern, suggesting that H2A.Z regulates both silencing and transcriptional activation through different mechanisms. Our results suggest that the incorporation of H2A.Z into specific promoter-bound nucleosomes reconfigures chromatin structure to poise genes for transcriptional activation. Our findings have implications for the understanding of higher eukaryotes.

title: Collective trauma in northern Sri Lanka: a qualitative psychosocial-ecological study
text:
BACKGROUND: Complex post-conflict and natural disaster situations have a profound impact on individual psychology, family dynamics, community structures, and societal norms. Just as the mental health effects on an individual's psyche can result in both non-pathological distress and psychiatric disorders, massive trauma and loss can fundamentally alter family and social processes at various levels.
METHOD: This qualitative, ecological study utilizes naturalistic, psychosocial ethnography in Northern Sri Lanka, where the researcher actively participates in psychosocial and community mental health programs among the Tamil community. Data is gathered through participant observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions with community-level relief and rehabilitation workers, government officials, and non-governmental personnel. The study compares the community effects of chronic, man-made disaster (war) with the contexts before and after the tsunami.
RESULTS: The study reveals profound social transformations at the family and community levels. In contrast to the tsunami's less pronounced effects, the chronic war situation led to more fundamental changes in community functioning. Family dynamics show single-parent families, mistrust among members, and altered child-rearing practices. Communities demonstrate increased dependence, passivity, and suspicion, complemented by a breakdown in traditional structures, institutions, and ways of life, as well as deterioration in social norms and ethics. A variety of community-level interventions are attempted in response to these findings.
CONCLUSION: Trauma resulting from conflict, war, and disasters has far-reaching impacts on family and community dynamics, leading to fundamental changes at the collective level. Successful relief, rehabilitation, and development programs will require integrated, multi-level approaches to address the issue of collective trauma.

title: Guidelines for the selection of highly effective siRNA sequences for mammalian and chick RNA interference.
text:
In this study, we examined the relationship between short interfering RNA (siRNA) sequences and their ability to induce RNA interference (RNAi) in four exogenous and two endogenous genes in mammalian and Drosophila cells. Our findings show that highly effective siRNAs for systematic mammalian functional genomics can be designed using a set of rules that govern siRNA sequence preferences. These rules indicate that siRNAs that satisfy certain conditions are capable of effectively silencing genes in mammalian cells. Specifically, siRNAs that meet the following conditions are highly effective:
* A/U at the 5' end of the antisense strand
* G/C at the 5' end of the sense strand
* At least five A/U residues in the 5' terminal one-third of the antisense strand
* The absence of any GC stretch of more than 9 nt in length.
SiRNAs that do not meet these conditions are less effective or fail to silence genes entirely in mammalian cells. Similarly, these rules were found to be applicable to DNA-based RNAi in mammalian cells and in ovo RNAi using chick embryos. However, siRNA sequence preferences were much less pronounced in RNAi experiments conducted in Drosophila.

title: Overview of the CCP4 suite and current developments
text: The CCP4 (Collaborative Computational Project, Number 4) software suite is a comprehensive collection of programs, data, and software libraries designed to facilitate macromolecular structure determination through X-ray crystallography. The suite boasts flexibility, allowing users to employ a variety of methods to achieve their goals. The programs are sourced from multiple locations but are united through a standardized infrastructure consisting of common file formats, data objects, and graphical interfaces. Automation pipelines are incorporated into the suite, streamlining the structure solution process. Following a brief overview of the CCP4 software's evolution over the last 30 years, an in-depth look at the current suite is provided. While detailed explanations are furnished in the accompanying articles, here, we illustrate how the individual programs contribute to a robust software package.

title: Histone Demethylase Expression Enhances Human Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer Efficiency and Promotes Derivation of Pluripotent Stem Cells.
text: The low efficiency of human embryonic stem cell (hESC) derivation through somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) hinders its potential application. Forming blastocysts from human SCNT embryos is a challenging task with limited success, and only a select few oocyte donors exhibit success. Previous studies in mice revealed that reducing histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) through ectopic expression of the H3K9me3 demethylase Kdm4d improves SCNT embryo development. Building upon these findings, we investigated the effect of overexpressing another H3K9me3 demethylase, KDM4A, on human SCNT. Our results show that overexpressing KDM4A significantly enhances the blastocyst formation rate in human SCNT embryos, facilitating efficient derivation of SCNT-derived ESCs using adult Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) patient somatic nuclei donors. This conserved mechanism has the potential to improve SCNT in various contexts, including regenerative medicine.

title: Interface Contractility between Differently Fated Cells Drives Cell Elimination and Cyst Formation
text: Although cellular mechanisms for suppressing tumors are well-studied, little is known about the mechanisms that prevent abnormal cells from forming in epithelial tissues. Recent research in Drosophila imaginal discs has shown that ectopic expression of transcription factors that determine cell fate causes abnormal epithelial cysts to form. Cysts do not develop solely within affected cells but rather through the juxtaposition of two cell populations with diverse fates. The juxtaposition of wild-type and aberrantly specified cells at their shared interface leads to increased contractility at adherens junctions and along basal interfaces. Experimental simulations of 3D vertex models have validated the findings, demonstrating that enhanced interface contractility is sufficient to explain many morphogenetic behaviors, including cyst formation by medium-sized clusters, segregation of large cells by smooth boundaries or apical constriction in small groups, and elimination of single, aberrant cells by apoptosis. When lateral interface contractility is high, aberrant single cells are eliminated from tissues, and cysts form when the elimination of such cells fails and they proliferate to intermediate-sized cell clusters. The results provide a new perspective on morphogenetic mechanisms that arise from cell-fate heterogeneities within tissues, maintaining or disrupting epithelial homeostasis.

title: Resonating circadian clocks enhance fitness in cyanobacteria.
text: Certain organisms exhibit enhanced longevity, growth rates, and developmental pace when exposed to a light/dark cycle that resonates optimally with their internal circadian clock. However, there is a lack of evidence demonstrating that the synchronization between the endogenous clock and the environmental cycle directly improves reproductive fitness. To investigate the adaptive significance of circadian programming, we evaluated the relative fitness of cyanobacterial strains with different circadian periods under competitive conditions. Our results indicate that strains with a circadian period similar to that of the light/dark cycle were favored under competition, suggesting the action of soft selection.

title: Stromal Fibroblasts Present in Invasive Human Breast Carcinomas Promote Tumor Growth and Angiogenesis through Elevated SDF-1/CXCL12 Secretion
text: Breast carcinomas often consist of a majority of stromal cells, including fibroblasts, yet the mechanisms by which these cells contribute to tumor growth are poorly understood.To investigate this, we used a co-implantation tumor xenograft model, showing that fibroblasts from human breast carcinomas (CAFs) promoted the growth of admixed breast carcinoma cells significantly more than normal mammary fibroblasts derived from the same patients. CAFs, which exhibit characteristics of myofibroblasts, play a central role in promoting tumor cell growth by secreting stromal cell-derived factor 1 (SDF-1). These fibroblasts also promote angiogenesis by recruiting endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) into carcinomas, an effect mediated in part by SDF-1. Furthermore, CAF-secreted SDF-1 directly stimulates tumor growth through the cognate receptor CXCR4, which is expressed by carcinoma cells. Our findings suggest that fibroblasts within invasive breast carcinomas contribute to tumor promotion primarily through the secretion of SDF-1.

title: Embryonic Origin of Postnatal Neural Stem Cells
text: Adult neural stem/progenitor cells located in the walls of the lateral ventricles within the brain generate various types of neurons for the olfactory bulb (OB). The position of these cells determines which types of OB neurons they produce. Our study shows that the majority of mouse B1 cell precursors are produced between embryonic days (E) 13.5 and 15.5, and remain largely inactive until they become reactivated after birth. Using a retroviral library containing over 100,000 genetic tags, we found that B1 cells share a common progenitor with embryonic cells of the cortex, striatum, and septum, but this lineage relationship is lost before E15.5. The regional specification of B1 cells becomes evident as early as E11.5 and is spatially associated with the production of neurons that populate different areas of the forebrain. This study reveals the early embryonic regionalization of postnatal neural stem cells and the lineage relationship between them and embryonic progenitor cells.

title: The Opa1-Dependent Mitochondrial Cristae Remodeling Pathway Controls Atrophic, Apoptotic, and Ischemic Tissue Damage
text: Mitochondrial structural changes occur during apoptosis and autophagy in vivo, but it is unclear if these changes are actually relevant to tissue damage. To investigate this, we looked at the role of the optic atrophy 1 (OPA1)-dependent cristae remodeling pathway in vivo and found that it regulates the response of multiple tissues to different types of damage, including apoptotic, necrotic, and atrophic stimuli. Genetic inhibition of the cristae remodeling pathway in vivo does not affect development, but it does protect mice from various types of damage, including muscular atrophy, heart and brain damage, and hepatocellular apoptosis. Our results suggest that the OPA1-dependent cristae remodeling pathway is a fundamental, targetable determinant of tissue damage in vivo.

title: First Proposal of Minimum Information About a Cellular Assay for Regenerative Medicine
text:
Advancements in stem cell research have given rise to an influx of studies in regenerative medicine across various institutions and companies globally. However, the lack of a standardized format for experimentation hinders reproducibility and data sharing among laboratories or cell banks. To improve information flow in stem cell and derivative cell research, we propose a minimum information standard to comprehensively describe cellular assay data, thereby facilitating practical regenerative medicine. Drawing from the existing Minimum Information About a Cellular Assay framework, we have developed Minimum Information About a Cellular Assay for Regenerative Medicine (MIACARM), which enables the description of complex cellular experiments using detailed taxonomy of human cell types. By employing controlled vocabularies, such as ontologies, MIACARM provides a central platform for cellular assay data exchange among cell banks and registries operating at over 20 sites worldwide.
Currently, there are over 20 human cell information storage facilities globally. However, the lack of a standardized format for experiments hampers reproducibility and data exchange among different laboratories or cell providers. This collaborative effort by scientists from stem cell banks and cellular information registries across the US, UK, Europe, and Japan aims to address this issue by introducing new minimum information guidelines, MIACARM, to promote data exchange and streamline practical regenerative medicine.

title: The PAR proteins: fundamental players in animal cell polarization.
text: The PAR gene family was identified through genetic screens for regulators of cytoplasmic partitioning in the early embryo of the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, and encodes six distinct proteins essential for asymmetric cell division in the worm zygote. Some PAR proteins are localized asymmetrically and form physical complexes with one another. Notably, PAR proteins have been found to regulate cell polarity in various contexts across different animal species, suggesting they are part of an ancient and fundamental mechanism for cell polarity determination. Although the full mechanisms of PAR protein function are still unclear, advances in cell biology and biochemistry are beginning to elucidate how PAR proteins polarize cells.

title: Prions Adhere to Soil Minerals and Remain Infectious
text: An unidentified environmental reservoir of infectivity contributes to the natural transmission of prion diseases (transmissible spongiform encephalopathies [TSEs]) in sheep, deer, and elk. Prion infectivity may enter soil environments through shedding from diseased animals and the decomposition of infected carcasses. The disposal of TSE-infected cattle, sheep, and deer in burial has led to the unintentional introduction of prions into subsurface environments. In this study, we investigated the potential of soil as a reservoir for prion diseases by examining the interaction between the disease-associated prion protein (PrPSc) and common soil minerals. We found that PrPSc adsorbed to two clay minerals, quartz, and four whole soil samples, with the mineral montmorillonite showing strong binding capabilities. We quantified the PrPSc-binding capacities of each mineral and observed that desorption of PrPSc from montmorillonite resulted in cleavage at an N-terminal site, making it difficult to remove the protein. Despite cleavage and strong binding, PrPSc bound to montmorillonite remained infectious. Our findings suggest that PrPSc released into soil environments may be preserved in a bioavailable form, perpetuating prion disease epizootics and exposing other species to the infectious agent.

title: Regulated Accumulation of Desmosterol Integrates Macrophage Lipid Metabolism and Inflammatory Responses
text: The relationship between cholesterol accumulation, inflammation, and LXR-dependent response pathways in atherosclerotic lesions is not well understood. To investigate this, we used lipidomic and transcriptomic approaches to evaluate the effect of diet and LDL receptor genotype on macrophage foam cell formation in the peritoneal cavities of mice. Our findings showed that foam cell formation was associated with significant changes in hundreds of lipid species, unexpected suppression of inflammatory gene expression rather than activation, and the regulated accumulation of desmosterol, which underlies many homeostatic responses, including activation of LXR target genes, inhibition of SREBP target genes, selective reprogramming of fatty acid metabolism, and suppression of inflammatory response genes in macrophage foam cells. These observations suggest that macrophage activation in atherosclerotic lesions results from extrinsic, proinflammatory signals generated within the artery wall that suppress the homeostatic and anti-inflammatory functions of desmosterol.

title: A JOURNAL OF NEUROLOGY
text:
Brain glial cells, outnumbering neurons by a factor of five, have recently garnered attention for their potential involvement in epileptic seizures. Specifically, microglia and astrocytes, which are responsible for surveillance of brain damage that often leads to seizures, are thought to play a key role in these processes. While it has been suggested that seizures may be triggered by immune responses in the brain, the evidence is mixed, with some studies indicating that innate immune responses may lower the seizure threshold in experimental models of epilepsy, yet others have found no proof of an independent role in initiating seizures in vivo.
Our study aimed to further investigate the potential of innate immune responses in the development of epilepsy. We found that cortical innate immune responses alone are capable of producing profound increases in brain excitability, leading to focal seizures. When we applied lipopolysaccharide to the cortex, which binds to toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), the resulting increase in evoked field potential amplitudes and focal epileptiform discharges were significantly reduced by the pre-application of interleukin-1 receptor antagonist.
Our findings suggest an important role of innate immunity in acute seizures. Specifically, the release of interleukin-1 in response to TLR4 detection of danger signals associated with central nervous system infections and brain injury may increase neuronal excitability, leading to seizures. These results highlight the potential of glial inhibition, through pharmacological blockade of TLR4 and the pro-inflammatory mediators released by activated glia, as a means of treating seizure disorders in humans.

title: Sequential domain assembly of ribosomal protein S3 drives 40S subunit maturation.
text:
Eukaryotic ribosomes mature through the association of ribosomal RNA with ribosomal proteins, forming nuclear precursor particles that undergo a complex assembly process coordinated by non-ribosomal factors. In this study, we provide insights into how structural rearrangements in ribosomal protein S3 contribute to the maturation of the 40S subunit. We found that S3 dimerizes and is imported into the nucleus in a rotated conformation, associated with the chaperone Yar1. Initial assembly of S3 with 40S precursors occurs through its C-domain, while the N-domain projects from the 40S surface. Later, the assembly factor Ltv1 replaces Yar1, securing the S3 N-domain in its rotated position and preventing its integration into the 40S subunit. Finally, Ltv1 release, triggered by phosphorylation, and a conformational change in the S3 N-domain result in the stable incorporation of S3, representing a novel assembly mechanism for ribosomal proteins.
In this rewrite, I've attempted to make the language more concise and clear, while still conveying the same information as the original text. I've also tried to make the sentence structure more varied and less repetitive. Let me know if you would like me to make any further changes!

title: Assaying proliferation and differentiation capacity of stem cells using disaggregated adult mouse epidermis
text: In this protocol, we detail the process of isolating and characterizing keratinocytes from adult mouse epidermis, and examining their function in an in vivo skin reconstitution assay using neonatal dermal cells. Additionally, we describe how to subject isolated keratinocytes to clonal analysis in vitro and in vivo, and how to enrich for hair follicle-inducing dermal papilla cells in the dermal preparation. By using these methods, we can compare the capacity of different populations of adult epidermal stem cells to proliferate and differentiate into different lineages. The isolation and grafting of cells for the skin reconstitution assay typically takes place over two days, while clonal growth in culture is assessed after 14 days, and evaluation of the grafts is performed after 4-5 weeks.

title: Telomerase-negative immortalized human cells contain a novel type of promyelocytic leukemia (PML) body.
text: Human cells that are unable to produce telomerase maintain their telomeres through an alternative mechanism called alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT). We have discovered that these ALT cells contain a unique structure called an ALT-associated PML body (APB). APBs are donut-shaped nuclear structures composed of PML protein, telomeric DNA, and the proteins that bind to telomeres, human telomere repeat binding factors 1 and 2. Further analysis revealed that APBs also contain other proteins involved in DNA synthesis and recombination, such as replication factor A, RAD51, and RAD52. Interestingly, APBs first appear during immortalization, which is the process by which these cells become immortal. APBs were found in both ALT tumors and cell lines, but not in mortal cells or in telomerase-positive cell lines or tumors.

title: Prediction of coronary artery disease by a systemic atherosclerosis score index derived from whole-body MR angiography
text: The present study aimed to investigate the relationship between non-invasive whole-body magnetic resonance angiography (WB-MRA) findings, including a systemic atherosclerosis score index (ASI), and the presence of significant coronary artery disease (CAD). WB-MRA was performed on 50 patients scheduled to undergo elective cardiac catheterization for suspected CAD, and the extent of luminal narrowing in 40 extra-cardiac vessel segments was evaluated and assigned scores. The ASI was generated by dividing the sum of scores by analyzable segments. The results showed that patients with significant CAD (n = 27) had higher ASI values compared to those without CAD (n = 22), with a significant correlation between ASI and established cardiovascular risk scores, such as PROCAM and Framingham risk scores. A ROC curve-derived ASI cut-off of > 1.54 was found to be a strong independent predictor of significant CAD, with a sensitivity of 59%, specificity of 86%, and a positive predictive value of 84%. Additionally, the study found that the presence of CAD was associated with a higher likelihood of extra-cardiac stenosis in specific vascular territories, such as the carotid arteries and lower extremities. Overall, the study suggests that WB-MRA may have prognostic implications for identifying patients at risk of significant CAD, particularly those with extra-cardiac manifestations of atherosclerosis.

title: Analysis of re-replication from deregulated origin licensing by DNA fiber spreading
text:
Each human cell division cycle poses a significant challenge: preventing DNA replication origins from initiating more than once, a phenomenon known as re-replication. Acute deregulation of replication control leads to extensive DNA damage, cell-cycle checkpoint activation, and cell death, while moderate deregulation promotes genome instability and tumorigenesis. However, it has been difficult to directly demonstrate re-replication or assess the cell cycle phase-specificity of this process due to the lack of detectable increases in cellular DNA content.
To overcome this limitation, we developed an adaptation of DNA fiber spreading, enabling the direct detection of re-replication on single DNA molecules from human chromosomes. Using this method, we found substantial re-replication within 1 hour of S phase entry in cells overproducing the replication factor, Cdt1. Moreover, a comparison of the HeLa cancer cell line to untransformed fibroblasts revealed that HeLa cells display low-level re-replication in otherwise unperturbed cell cycles. Interestingly, depletion of the Cdt1 inhibitor, geminin, in an untransformed fibroblast cell line led to undetectable re-replication by standard assays, but was readily quantifiable using DNA fiber spreading analysis.
Our findings demonstrate the power of this novel approach for evaluating re-replication and its role in genome stability. By directly evaluating re-replicated DNA molecules, we can gain a deeper understanding of the cellular processes that promote or perturb genome stability, paving the way for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for diseases linked to genome instability.

title: Liver receptor homolog-1 is essential for pregnancy
text: Coordinated effort of several cellular signals and factors is crucial for a successful pregnancy. One key player, liver receptor homolog-1 (Lrh-1), is an orphan nuclear receptor that controls metabolism and hormone production. Its high expression in granulosa cells of ovarian follicles and corpus luteum in rodents and humans is essential for fertility. Genetic ablation of Lrh-1 (Nr5a2) in mice during embryonic development results in lethal defects. Reduction of Lrh-1 in ovarian follicles shows that it regulates genes necessary for both steroid synthesis and ovulation. To study the impact of Lrh-1 on mouse gestation, we disrupted its expression in the corpus luteum, causing luteal insufficiency. Hormone replacement allowed for embryo implantation but was followed by gestational failure, including impaired endometrial decidualization, compromised placental formation, fetal growth restriction, and fetal death. Lrh-1 is also expressed in the human endometrium and a primary culture of human endometrial stromal cells. Reducing NR5A2 transcript abundance through RNA interference blocked decidualization. These findings highlight the vital roles of Lrh-1: maintaining the corpus luteum, promoting decidualization, and establishing the placenta. It has multiple indispensable functions in maintaining a successful pregnancy.

title: Transcriptional Signature and Memory Retention of Human-Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
text: Using mouse and human cells, genetic reprogramming of somatic cells to a pluripotent state (induced pluripotent stem cells or iPSCs) by over-expression of specific genes has been accomplished. However, the similarity between human iPSCs and human Embryonic Stem Cells (hESCs) remains unclear. In this study, we investigated the transcriptional profile of human iPSCs generated without viral vectors or genomic insertions, revealing that these cells are generally similar to hESCs but have significant differences. To generate human iPSCs without viral vectors or genomic insertions, we cloned pluripotent factors Oct4 and Nanog in episomal vectors and transfected them into human fetal neural progenitor cells. Transient expression of these factors, or Oct4 alone, resulted in efficient generation of human iPSCs. This reprogramming strategy revealed a potential transcriptional signature for human iPSCs while retaining the gene expression of the donor cells in human reprogrammed cells without viral and transgene interference. Additionally, the episomal reprogramming strategy provides a safe approach for generating human iPSCs for clinical purposes and basic research.

title: A CXCL1 Paracrine Network Links Cancer Chemoresistance and Metastasis
text:
The relationship between metastasis and chemoresistance in cancer is complex, and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unknown. Our research uncovered a network of communication signals between cancer, immune, and blood vessel cells that drives both processes in breast cancer. Specifically, we found that cancer cells that overexpress CXCL1 and 2 through transcriptional activation or genetic amplification of the CXCL1 4q21 locus are better equipped to survive in metastatic sites.
CXCL1/2 attracts CD11b(+)Gr1(+) myeloid cells into the tumor, which produce chemokines, such as S100A8/9, that enhance cancer cell survival. Notably, chemotherapeutic agents used to treat cancer typically kill cancer cells, but this treatment can also trigger a parallel stromal reaction, leading to TNF-α production by endothelial and other stromal cells. TNF-α then enhances the expression of CXCL1/2 in cancer cells, thereby amplifying the CXCL1/2-S100A8/9 loop and contributing to chemoresistance.
Interestingly, blocking the CXCR2 receptor breaks this cycle and enhances the efficacy of chemotherapy against breast tumors and metastases. Our findings reveal a previously unknown network of interactions between endothelial cells, carcinoma cells, and myeloid cells that link chemoresistance and metastasis, providing potential avenues for therapeutic intervention.

title: Prophylaxis of postoperative vomiting in children undergoing tonsillectomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of prophylactic anti-emetic interventions in children undergoing tonsillectomy. A total of 22 articles were identified, and the outcome of interest was postoperative vomiting (POV) in the first 24 hours. The review found good evidence for the prophylactic anti-emetic effect of dexamethasone (odds ratio (OR) 0.23, 95% CI 0.16-0.33) and the serotinergic antagonists ondansetron (OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.29-0.46), granisetron (OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.06-0.19), tropisetron (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.06-0.35), and dolasetron (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.1-0.59). Metoclopramide was also found to be efficacious (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.34-0.77). The review found insufficient evidence to recommend dimenhydrinate, perphenazine, or droperidol in the doses studied, and gastric aspiration or acupuncture were not found to be effective. The authors concluded that dexamethasone and the anti-serotinergic agents are the most effective agents for the prophylaxis of POV in children undergoing tonsillectomy.

title: A method of comparing the areas under receiver operating characteristic curves derived from the same cases.
text:
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves are a widely used tool for evaluating and comparing the performance of diagnostic technologies and diagnostic algorithms. In this paper, the authors present a novel approach for refining the statistical comparison of the areas under two ROC curves derived from the same set of patients, taking into account the correlation between the areas that is induced by the paired nature of the data.
The authors propose a method that leverages the correspondence between the area under an ROC curve and the Wilcoxon statistic to derive a table that converts the observed correlations in paired ratings of images into a correlation between the two ROC areas. This between-area correlation can be used to reduce the standard error (uncertainty) about the observed difference in areas, resulting in a significant increase in the statistical sensitivity (power) of the comparison.
For studies involving multiple readers, this method provides a measure of a component of the sampling variation that is otherwise difficult to obtain. By accounting for the paired nature of the data, the authors' approach offers a more accurate and robust way to compare the performance of different diagnostic technologies and algorithms. This has important implications for healthcare and research, as it enables more reliable and valid evaluations of new diagnostic tools and techniques.

title: Transient inactivation of Rb and ARF yields regenerative cells from postmitotic mammalian muscle.
text: A significant biological enigma is the limited capacity for tissue regeneration in mammals, While some vertebrates, such as urodele amphibians and teleost fish, can regenerate major structures through cell cycle reentry, mammals lack this mechanism. We wondered if a tumor suppressor protein present in mammals but absent in regenerative vertebrates, known as Ink4a product ARF (alternative reading frame), might be responsible for suppressing regeneration. We found that dual inactivation of ARF and another protein, Rb, led to the reentry of mammalian muscle cells into the cell cycle, loss of differentiation properties, and increased cytokinetic machinery. Single postmitotic myocytes were isolated using laser micro-dissection and transient suppression of ARF and Rb resulted in the formation of myoblast colonies that could differentiate and fuse into myofibers upon transplantation in vivo. These findings suggest that the differentiation of mammalian cells can be reversed by inactivating ARF and Rb, supporting the hypothesis that ARF evolved to suppress regeneration.

title: CENP-B Controls Centromere Formation Depending on the Chromatin Context
text: The centromere is a crucial region of chromatin that directs the accurate transmission of eukaryotic chromosomes during cell divisions. However, the mechanism by which the centromere forms and stabilizes at a specific genomic location is not fully understood. In this study, we investigate the de novo formation of a human/mammalian artificial chromosome (HAC/MAC) with a functional centromere. We demonstrate that the assembly of the centromere on HAC/MAC requires the presence of alpha-satellite DNA containing binding sites for the centromeric CENP-B protein. Interestingly, we find that CENP-B plays a dual role in centromere formation. When alpha-satellite DNA is integrated into a chromosomal site, centromere formation is suppressed in cells expressing CENP-B. However, on these integration sites, CENP-B enhances histone H3-K9 trimethylation and DNA methylation, thereby stimulating the formation of heterochromatin. Therefore, our findings suggest that CENP-B plays a crucial role in ensuring the proper formation of de novo centromeres, while also preventing the formation of excess centromeres on chromosomes.

title: Improved tools for biological sequence comparison.
text:
We have designed and developed three computer programs for comparing protein and DNA sequences: FASTA, FASTP, and RDF2. These programs offer a range of features and functionalities to help users search sequence databases, evaluate similarity scores, and identify periodic structures based on local sequence similarity.
FASTA is a more advanced version of FASTP, which can search both protein and DNA sequence databases. It can compare a protein sequence to a DNA sequence database by translating the DNA data base as it is searched. In addition, FASTA includes an innovative step in the calculation of the initial pairwise similarity score that allows multiple regions of similarity to be combined to increase the scores of related sequences.
RDF2 is a program that evaluates the significance of similarity scores using a shuffling method that preserves local sequence composition. This program can help users determine the likelihood that a given similarity is due to chance rather than a real similarity between the sequences.
LFASTA is a program that visualizes the local similarities between two sequences by displaying all regions of similarity with scores greater than a predetermined threshold. It can display these similarities as a "graphic matrix" plot or as individual alignments, allowing users to quickly identify areas of high similarity between the sequences.
Furthermore, these programs have been modified to accommodate alternative scoring matrices for comparing DNA or protein sequences. This enables users to apply different scoring functions to their sequences and obtain more informative similarity scores.

title: The adverse consequences of unmet need among older persons living in the community: dual-eligible versus Medicare-only beneficiaries.
text:
OBJECTIVE: The goal of this study was to investigate and compare the prevalence of specific adverse consequences associated with unmet needs for assistance among a particularly vulnerable subgroup of older adults who are eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid, compared to those eligible for Medicare only.
METHOD: We used data from the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS), a representative survey of the older Medicare population, to calculate the prevalence of disability-related need for assistance with self-care, household tasks, and mobility activities, as well as the prevalence of adverse consequences resulting from unmet need, among dually eligible and Medicare only individuals.
RESULTS: Approximately 2 million community-dwelling older adults experienced an adverse consequence due to unmet need for assistance with self-care, such as soiling their clothes, while over 2 million experienced adverse consequences due to unmet need for assistance with household tasks, such as going without groceries. Furthermore, over 3 million individuals experienced at least one adverse consequence of unmet need for assistance with mobility-related activities, such as being unable to get out of bed, in the month preceding the NHATS interview. Notably, dually eligible individuals experienced higher rates of 6 of the 11 adverse consequences studied and were more likely to have at least one adverse consequence in all 3 domains compared to others.
DISCUSSION: The findings of this study highlight the importance of addressing the needs of this vulnerable population, particularly in the context of emerging care models aimed at integrating medical care, behavioral health, and long-term services. Indicators of adverse consequences of unmet need could serve as useful tools for monitoring the quality and adequacy of such care systems.

title: Supplementary information: ‘MesoRD User’s Guide ’ and other
text: MesoRD is a tool for stochastic simulation of chemical reactions and diffusion, based on the next subvolume method. This is an exact method for simulating the Markov process associated with the reaction-diffusion master equation. MesoRD is free and open-source software, written in C++ and licensed under the GNU General Public License (GPL). It can run on a variety of operating systems, including Linux, Mac OS X, NetBSD, Solaris, and Windows XP. To download MesoRD, please visit <http://mesord.sourceforge.net>. For additional information, including a user guide and other documents, please visit the MesoRD website. If you have any questions or need further assistance, please contact either Johan Elf at icm.uu.se or Johan Hattne at embl-hamburg.de.

title: Functional anatomy of T cell activation and synapse formation.
text: T cell activation and function depend on a purposeful interaction with antigen-presenting cells. In vivo, these cell-to-cell interactions occur through two distinct dynamics: transient connections formed through brief meets known as immunological kinapses or sustained connections known as immunological synapses. Kinapses typically occur during the steady state and allow for referencing to self-peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) and searching for pathogen-derived pMHC. Synapses, on the other hand, are induced by T cell receptor (TCR) interactions with agonist pMHC under specific conditions and are associated with robust immune responses that generate effector and memory T cells. Recent high-resolution imaging studies have revealed that the synapse is highly coordinated, integrating multiple cell adhesion molecules, TCR recognition of pMHC complexes, and an array of activating and inhibitory ligands to promote or prevent T cell signaling. In this review, we examine the molecular components, geometry, and timing underlying kinapses and synapses, integrate recent molecular and physiological data, and suggest potential future directions.

title: Modulation of Replicative Lifespan in Cryptococcus neoformans: Implications for Virulence
text:
The fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans is known to undergo replicative aging, resulting in increased resistance to host and antifungal-based killing with older cells. Based on this observation, the authors hypothesized that manipulating the generational age of the pathogenic yeast population would affect its virulence. SIR2, a well-conserved histone deacetylase, was investigated as a potential target for anti-aging drugs, as it has been shown to play a role in aging and lifespan in various organisms.
The study found that treatment of C. neoformans with Sir2p-agonists resulted in a significantly prolonged replicative lifespan (RLS), while treatment with a Sir2p-antagonist shortened RLS. These results were dependent on SIR2 and not observed in sir2Δ cells, which have a slightly impaired fitness. As a result, the authors investigated the effect of RLS modulation on C. neoformans in a Galleria mellonella infection model. They found that prolonged RLS resulted in decreased virulence, while shortened RLS enhanced virulence. Additionally, combination treatment with Sir2p agonists and antifungal therapy enhanced the antifungal's effect. Importantly, no difference in virulence was observed when sir2Δ cells were used for infection, confirming target specificity and ruling out non-specific effects of the drugs on the Galleria host.
The study suggests that RLS modulating drugs, such as Sir2p agonists, can shift the lifespan and vulnerability of the fungal population, making them a potential class of novel antifungal drug targets that can enhance antifungal efficacy.

title: Pf4-Cre transgenic mice allow the generation of lineage-restricted gene knockouts for studying megakaryocyte and platelet function in vivo.
text: To generate transgenic mice that specifically express the Cre-recombinase enzyme in megakaryocytes, we modified a mouse Bacterial Artificial Chromosome (BAC) clone through homologous recombination. We replaced the first exon of the platelet factor 4 (Pf4), also known as CXCL4, with a codon-improved Cre cDNA. Consequently, several transgenic strains were obtained, and one strain, Q3, was further studied. By crossing the Q3 mice with the ROSA26-lacZ reporter strain, we discovered that Cre-recombinase activity was confined to megakaryocytes. These findings were corroborated by crossing the Q3 mice with a strain containing loxP-flanked integrin beta1. Following conditional allele excision in megakaryocytes, DNA analysis revealed complete excision, and platelets were almost devoid of the integrin beta1 protein. As a result, the Pf4-Cre transgenic strain will be a valuable tool for investigating megakaryopoiesis, platelet development, and platelet function.

title: LIN-44/Wnt Directs Dendrite Outgrowth through LIN-17/Frizzled in C. elegans Neurons
text:
The proper development of the nervous system relies on the proper formation and morphology of two key functional domains in neurons: axons and dendrites. Although both domains are vital for signal transmission, our understanding of dendrite development is still limited. To address this, we investigated the regulation of dendrite development in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans.
Our findings reveal that the Wnt ligand LIN-44 and its Frizzled receptor LIN-17 play a crucial role in the development of the PQR oxygen sensory neuron. Mutations in either LIN-44 or LIN-17 result in impaired dendrite formation, stunted growth, or misrouting. By manipulating the temporal and spatial expression of LIN-44 and conducting cell-ablation experiments, we discovered that this molecule is patterned during embryogenesis and acts as a proximal cue to determine the site from which the dendrite emerges. In addition, genetic interaction between LIN-44 and LIN-17 indicates that the LIN-44 signal is transmitted through the LIN-17 receptor, which acts cell autonomously in PQR. Furthermore, we found that LIN-17 interacts with another Wnt molecule, EGL-20, and functions independently of the MIG-1/Frizzled pathway in this process.
Our results demonstrate a critical role for Wnt and Frizzled molecules in regulating dendrite development in vivo. This discovery provides new insights into the mechanisms underlying neural development and function, and highlights the importance of further investigating the complex interplay between these molecules in nervous system development and function.

title: Why do general practitioners prescribe antibiotics for upper respiratory tract infections to meet patient expectations: a mixed methods study
text:
Objective:
To investigate the role of patient expectations in general practitioners' (GPs) antibiotic prescribing for upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs).
Methods:
Concurrent explanatory mixed methods approach using a cross-sectional survey and semistructured interviews. Settings: Primary care GPs in Australia. Participants: 584 GPs (response rate of 23.6%) completed the cross-sectional survey. 32 GPs were interviewed individually. Outcome measure: Prescribing of antibiotics for URTI.
Results:
More than half of the GP respondents in Australia reported that they would prescribe antibiotics for an URTI to meet patient expectations. Qualitative findings revealed that 'patient expectations' may be the primary reason for inappropriate prescribing, but it encompasses other factors, including limited time, poor doctor-patient communication, and diagnostic uncertainty. We identified three role archetypes to explain the behavior of GPs in relation to antibiotic prescribing for URTIs. The main themes emerging from the qualitative component showed that many GPs did not think that antibiotic prescribing in primary care was responsible for the development of antibiotic resistance nor that their individual prescribing would make a significant difference in light of larger issues like hospital prescribing or veterinary use. For them, there were minimal negative consequences from their inappropriate prescribing.


Conclusions:
There is a pressing need to raise awareness of the scope and magnitude of antibiotic resistance and the primary care role in contributing to it, as well as the individual prescribing decisions' contribution to the problem.

title: Migraine and cardiovascular disease: systematic review and meta-analysis.
text:
The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the association between migraine and cardiovascular disease, including stroke, myocardial infarction, and death due to cardiovascular disease. The study design was used to investigate the association between migraine and cardiovascular disease by analyzing data from case-control and cohort studies.
The study's data sources were electronic databases such as PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, as well as reference lists of included studies and reviews published until January 2009. The selection criteria were case-control and cohort studies that investigated the association between any migraine or specific migraine subtypes and cardiovascular disease.
Two investigators independently assessed the eligibility of identified studies in a two-step approach, with disagreements resolved by consensus. The studies were grouped according to predetermined categories based on migraine and cardiovascular disease. Data extraction was done by two investigators, and pooled relative risks and 95% confidence intervals were calculated.
The results showed that the studies were heterogeneous in terms of participant characteristics and definition of cardiovascular disease. Nine studies investigated the association between any migraine and ischaemic stroke, with a pooled relative risk of 1.73 (95% CI 1.31 to 2.29). Additional analyses revealed a significantly higher risk among people who had migraine with aura (2.16, 1.53 to 3.03) compared to people who had migraine without aura (1.23, 0.90 to 1.69). Furthermore, the results suggested a greater risk among women (2.08, 1.13 to 3.84) compared to men (1.37, 0.89 to 2.11). Age less than 45 years, smoking, and oral contraceptive use further increased the risk. Eight studies investigated the association between migraine and myocardial infarction (1.12, 0.95 to 1.32), and five between migraine and death due to cardiovascular disease (1.03, 0.79 to 1.34). Only one study investigated the association between women who had migraine with aura and myocardial infarction and death due to cardiovascular disease, showing a twofold increased risk.
In conclusion, migraine is associated with a twofold increased risk of ischaemic stroke, which is only apparent among people who have migraine with aura. The study's findings also suggest a higher risk among women and risk was further magnified for people with migraine who were aged less than 45, smokers, and women who used oral contraceptives. No overall association was found between any migraine and myocardial infarction or death due to cardiovascular disease. Too few studies are available to reliably evaluate the impact of modifying factors, such as migraine aura, on these associations.

title: Effect of Duration and Intermittency of Rifampin on Tuberculosis Treatment Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
text:
Background: Treatment regimens for active tuberculosis (TB) that are intermittent, or use rifampin only during the initial phase, have practical advantages, but their efficacy has been questioned. To assess the impact of duration and intermittency of rifampin use on TB treatment outcomes, we conducted a systematic review of available literature.
Methods and Findings: We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane CENTRAL database for randomized controlled trials published in English, French, or Spanish between 1965 and June 2008. We included studies that used standardized treatment with rifampin-containing regimens and reported bacteriologically confirmed failure and/or relapse in previously untreated patients with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB. We pooled cumulative incidences of treatment outcomes and analyzed them with stratified random effects meta-analyses. Regimens that used rifampin only for the first 1-2 months had significantly higher rates of failure, relapse, and acquired drug resistance compared to regimens that used rifampin for 6 months. This was particularly evident when there was initial drug resistance to isoniazid, streptomycin, or both. However, there was little evidence of a difference in failure or relapse rates with daily or intermittent schedules of treatment administration, although there was insufficient published evidence to support administration of treatment twice weekly throughout therapy.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that TB treatment outcomes are significantly worse with shorter duration of rifampin and/or initial drug resistance to isoniazid and/or streptomycin. Treatment outcomes were similar with all intermittent schedules evaluated, but there is insufficient evidence to support administration of treatment twice weekly throughout therapy.

title: A novel set of DNA methylation markers in urine sediments for sensitive/specific detection of bladder cancer.
text:
This study aims to identify a set of DNA methylation markers in urine sediments for the sensitive and specific detection of bladder cancer.
The experimental design involves profiling 59 tumor-associated genes in bladder cancer cell lines, a small cohort of cancer biopsies, and urine sediments using methylation-specific PCR. From this analysis, 21 candidate genes are selected for further study in a larger cohort of 132 bladder cancer patients, including 8 cases for stage 0a, 68 cases for stage I, 50 cases for stage II, 4 cases for stages III, and 2 cases for stage IV, as well as 23 age-matched patients with noncancerous urinary lesions, 6 neurologic diseases, and 7 healthy volunteers.
The results show that cancer-specific hypermethylation is detected in 15 genes in urine sediments (P < 0.05), confirming the existing diagnosis of 121 out of 132 bladder cancer cases (sensitivity, 91.7%) with 87% accuracy. Notably, a higher detection rate is observed in stage 0a and I disease (75% and 88%, respectively), suggesting the potential of this approach for early diagnosis. Interestingly, the set of methylation markers identified in this study is distinct from that found in previous studies conducted in the United States, indicating a possible epigenetic disparity between American and Chinese cases.
Conclusion: Methylation profiling of an 11-gene set in urine sediments provides a sensitive and specific detection of bladder cancer.

title: Posttranslational Acetylation of α-Tubulin Constrains Protofilament Number in Native Microtubules
text:
Microtubules are composed of linear polymers of α-β tubulin dimers that form a tubular quinary structure. While microtubules assembled from purified tubulin in vitro typically contain between 10 and 16 protofilaments, these structural variations are not observed in cells. This discrepancy suggests that extraneous factors restrict the number of protofilaments in microtubules, but the underlying mechanisms are unknown.
To investigate this phenomenon, we examined the role of acetylation of α-tubulin in constraining protofilament number in C. elegans touch receptor neurons (TRNs). We discovered that mutants lacking α-tubulin acetyltransferase activity have short microtubules with rampant lattice defects and variable protofilament number within and between microtubules. All-atom molecular dynamics simulations suggest that acetylation of lysine 40 promotes the formation of interprotofilament salt bridges, thereby stabilizing lateral interactions between protofilaments and enforcing quinary structure to produce sturdy, structurally uniform microtubules in vivo.
Our findings demonstrate that acetylation of α-tubulin is a crucial constraint on protofilament number in vivo. We propose a structural model whereby this posttranslational modification facilitates the formation of lateral salt bridges, thereby regulating the association between adjacent protofilaments and enabling the formation of homogeneous microtubule populations in vivo.

title: A KEY ROLE FOR OREXIN IN PANIC ANXIETY
text:
Panic disorder is a severe anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent, debilitating panic attacks. Individuals with panic disorder have been found to have decreased activity in the central gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) system, along with exaggerated responses in the autonomic and respiratory systems after intravenous infusions of hypertonic sodium lactate. In a rat model of panic disorder, chronic inhibition of GABA synthesis in the dorsomedial-perifornical hypothalamus leads to anxiety-like states and increased sensitivity to cardioexcitatory responses induced by sodium lactate. This region is rich in neurons that contain orexin (ORX), a neurotransmitter involved in arousal, vigilance, and central autonomic mobilization, all of which are essential components of panic.
Our studies demonstrate that activation of ORX-producing neurons is crucial for developing a panic-prone state in the rat panic model. Silencing the hypothalamic gene encoding ORX (Hcrt) with RNAi or using systemic ORX-1 receptor antagonists blocks panic responses. Furthermore, we discovered that individuals with panic anxiety have higher levels of ORX in their cerebrospinal fluid compared to those without panic anxiety.
Taking these findings together, it is likely that the ORX system plays a role in the pathophysiology of panic anxiety, and targeting the ORX system with antagonists may represent a new therapeutic strategy for treating panic disorder.

title: Local Increases in Mechanical Tension Shape Compartment Boundaries by Biasing Cell Intercalations
text:
Mechanical forces play a crucial role in shaping tissue organization during animal development. Many tissues are organized into distinct, non-overlapping groups of cells called compartments. The boundaries between these compartments exhibit a linear architecture and are associated with signaling centers that influence tissue growth and patterning. Recent studies have shown that local increases in mechanical tension at cell junctions along compartment boundaries can prevent cell mixing and maintain compartmentalization. However, the cellular mechanisms that govern this process are not well understood.
To investigate these mechanisms, we used live imaging and quantitative image analysis to study the dynamics of cell junctions along the anteroposterior compartment boundaries of the Drosophila pupal abdominal epidermis. Our findings show that cell mixing within compartments involves multiple cell intercalations, which occur without altering the frequency or orientation of cell intercalations along the compartment boundaries. Instead, an asymmetry in the shrinkage of junctions during intercalation creates a bias, resulting in cell rearrangements that inhibit cell mixing.
Using simulations, we found that local increases in mechanical tension can account for this bias in junctional shrinkage, thereby maintaining cell populations separate. Our results demonstrate that mechanical forces play a crucial role in maintaining compartmentalization by influencing junctional rearrangements during cell intercalation.

title: MDA5 and PTPN2, two candidate genes for type 1 diabetes, modify pancreatic β-cell responses to the viral by-product double-stranded RNA
text:
The relationship between beta-cells and the immune system in type 1 diabetes (T1D) is complex and involves a "conversation" between these two entities. This dialogue may be influenced by an individual's genetic background. To investigate this conversation, we examined the effect of modulating two candidate genes, MDA5 and PTPN2, on beta-cell responses to double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), a byproduct of viral replication. These genes were selected based on a comparison of known candidate genes for T1D and genes expressed in pancreatic beta-cells, as identified in previous array analysis.
We used INS-1E cells and primary rat beta-cells to transfect small interference RNAs (siRNAs) targeting MDA5 or PTPN2 and then exposed them to intracellular synthetic dsRNA (polyinosinic-polycitidilic acid-PIC). We used real-time RT-PCR, western blot, and viability assays to study gene and protein expression and cell viability.
Our results show that PIC increased MDA5 and PTPN2 mRNA expression, which was inhibited by the specific siRNAs. PIC triggered apoptosis in INS-1E and primary beta-cells, and this was augmented by PTPN2 knockdown (KD), although inhibition of MDA5 did not modify PIC-induced apoptosis. In contrast, MDA5 silencing decreased PIC-induced cytokine and chemokine expression, although inhibition of PTPN2 induced minor or no changes in these inflammatory mediators.
Our findings suggest that changes in MDA5 and PTPN2 expression modify beta-cell responses to dsRNA. MDA5 regulates inflammatory signals, while PTPN2 may function as a defense mechanism against pro-apoptotic signals generated by dsRNA. These two candidate genes for T1D may thus modulate beta-cell apoptosis and/or local release of inflammatory mediators in the course of a viral infection by acting, at least in part, at the pancreatic beta-cell level.

title: Tumor necrosis factor signaling mediates resistance to mycobacteria by inhibiting bacterial growth and macrophage death.
text: Tumor necrosis factor (TNF), a major player in controlling tuberculosis, is believed to protect against the disease by promoting the formation of granulomas, which are clusters of immune cells, including macrophages, that work together to combat infection. Lack of TNF signaling can lead to the progression of tuberculosis in humans, and mortality rates are higher among Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infected mice when TNF signaling is absent. To better understand the role of TNF in mycobacterial infections, we monitored Mycobacterium marinum-infected zebrafish in real-time and conducted a step-by-step analysis of how TNF signaling works in mycobacterial disease. We found that even when only the innate immune system is involved, loss of TNF signaling leads to increased mortality. In the absence of TNF, mycobacterial growth within macrophages accelerates, leading to necrotic death of overloaded macrophages and breakdown of granulomas. TNF does not directly contribute to granuloma formation, but it does so indirectly by restricting mycobacterial growth within macrophages and preventing their necrosis, which helps maintain granuloma integrity.

title: Loss of negative regulation by Numb over Notch is relevant to human breast carcinogenesis
text: The biological interaction between Notch and Numb plays a crucial role in regulating the balance between cell proliferation and differentiation during development and homeostasis. While alterations in Notch signaling have been linked to various human diseases, including cancer, the involvement of Notch in human tumors has remained elusive. Our study reveals that the loss of Numb-mediated control on Notch signaling occurs in approximately 50% of human mammary carcinomas, leading to increased Notch signaling. Mechanistically, Numb functions as an oncosuppressor, as its ectopic expression in Numb-negative tumor cells inhibits proliferation. In contrast, Numb silencing increases Notch signaling in normal breast cells and in Numb-positive breast tumors. Moreover, pharmacological inhibition of Notch can suppress the growth of Numb-negative breast tumors but not Numb-positive ones. Taken together, our findings highlight the importance of the Numb/Notch biological antagonism in maintaining the homeostasis of the normal mammary parenchyma and its disruption in human mammary carcinogenesis.

title: Cortical Dynein Controls Microtubule Dynamics to Generate Pulling Forces that Position Microtubule Asters
text: Dynein at the cortex plays a crucial role in positioning processes, particularly during embryonic cell division and fibroblast migration. To better understand how cortical dynein interacts with microtubule ends to generate force and impact positioning, we have reconstituted the 'cortical' interaction between dynein and dynamic microtubule ends in an in vitro system using microfabricated barriers. Our results show that barrier-attached dynein captures microtubule ends, inhibits growth, and triggers microtubule catastrophes, thereby controlling microtubule length. The subsequent interaction with shrinking microtubule ends generates pulling forces up to several pN. By combining experiments in microchambers with a theoretical description of aster mechanics, we demonstrate that dynein-mediated pulling forces lead to the reliable centering of microtubule asters in simple confining geometries. Our findings demonstrate the intrinsic ability of cortical microtubule-dynein interactions to regulate microtubule dynamics and drive positioning processes in living cells.

title: Breast cancer risk factors in relation to breast density (United States)
text:
In this study, we investigated the relationship between known breast cancer risk factors and breast density in a large cohort of New Hampshire women (n=144,018). We analyzed data from mammography records and patient questionnaires to evaluate the impact of factors such as age, body mass index (BMI), menstrual and reproductive history, and hormone therapy (HT) use on breast density.
Our initial analyses revealed a negative association between age and breast density, as well as a negative association between BMI and breast density. We also found that women who had their first birth at a later age, were premenopausal, or were currently using HT tend to have higher breast density, while those with more parity tend to have lower breast density.
When we stratified the analysis by age and BMI, we found significant interactions between these factors and the risk factors of interest. For example, the positive effect of age at first birth on breast density was only observed in postmenopausal women, and the inverse influence of parity was only significant in women with low BMI. We also found that the positive effect of age at menarsche on breast density was less evident in women with high BMI.
The multivariable model suggested a slight positive influence of family history of breast cancer on breast density. However, the relationship between reproductive factors and breast density was less evident in women with high BMI. Interestingly, we found that density is reduced in young women using HT, but increased in HT users aged 50 or older.
In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the complex relationship between breast cancer risk factors and breast density. While some risk factors, such as age and BMI, have a consistent impact on density across all age groups, others, such as reproductive history and HT use, show more variable effects depending on factors such as age and BMI. These findings have important implications for breast cancer screening and prevention, and highlight the need for further research to better understand the interplay between these factors.

title: Perspective: repression of competition and the evolution of cooperation.
text: Repression of competition within groups emerges as the second major force in the history of life, shaping the evolution of cooperation. When opportunities for competition against neighbors are limited within groups, individuals can increase their success only by enhancing the efficiency and productivity of their group. As a result, characters that repress competition within groups promote cooperation and enhance group success. This idea was first proposed in the context of fair meiosis, where each chromosome has an equal chance of transmission via gametes. Randomized success means that each part of the genome can increase its success only by enhancing the total number of progeny, ultimately benefiting the group. Alexander used this insight to develop theories on the evolution of human sociality, arguing that social structures spread when they repress competition within groups and promote successful group-against-group competition. Buss introduced another example, proposing that metazoan success depended on repressing competition between cellular lineages. Maynard Smith subsequently synthesized these lines of thought and drew connections to other evolutionary concepts. In this paper, I will develop simple mathematical models to illustrate the key processes by which repression of competition evolves. First, I will clarify the main concepts and then provide a historical overview of the idea. Finally, I will summarize recent developments and identify promising areas for future research.

title: Article
text: This study aimed to investigate the effects of RA, a ligand of RARalpha, on immune responses in human and murine colitis. The study found that RA up-regulated FOXP3 expression and down-regulated IL-17 expression in colon biopsies of patients and in colon tissues and MLN of mice with colitis, compared to control groups. Additionally, RA treatment decreased the production of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-17) by LPMCs from mice, while increasing the production of regulatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-beta). In contrast, the antagonist of RARalpha (LE135) had the opposite effect. Furthermore, RA ameliorated TNBS-induced colitis in a dose-dependent manner, as seen by improved body weight and colon inflammation. These findings suggest that RA may have a therapeutic potential in the treatment of inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) by down-regulating colon inflammatory responses.

title: Multiple RNA surveillance pathways limit aberrant expression of iron uptake mRNAs and prevent iron toxicity in S. cerevisiae.
text: Regulation of mRNA expression for iron-uptake proteins is crucial to maintain iron homeostasis and prevent intracellular iron toxicity. Our findings indicate that many mRNAs encoding iron-uptake or mobilization proteins are active in iron-replete conditions independent of the S. cerevisiae RNase III ortholog Rnt1p or the nuclear exosome component Rrp6p. Extended forms of these mRNAs accumulate even in the absence of Rnt1p or the 5'-->3' exonucleases Xrn1p and Rat1p, suggesting that multiple degradative pathways work together to surveil aberrant mRNAs. RNase III-deficient cells are more sensitive to high iron concentrations, implying that Rnt1p-mediated RNA surveillance is essential to prevent iron toxicity. These conclusions suggest that RNA surveillance via multiple ribonucleolytic pathways plays an important role in maintaining iron homeostasis in yeast by avoiding the potentially toxic effects of the iron starvation response in iron-replete conditions.

title: Differential regulation of adherens junction dynamics during apical-basal polarization.
text: Adherens junctions (AJs) in epithelial cells undergo constant turnover to modulate adhesion properties in various physiological and developmental contexts, but the regulation of AJ dynamics during apical-basal polarization of primary epithelia remains unclear. To address this question, we employed novel and genetically validated GFP markers of Drosophila E-cadherin (DE-Cad) and β-catenin (Armadillo, Arm) to quantitatively assess in vivo dynamics of biosynthetic turnover and membrane redistribution through fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) assays. Our data showed that the membrane distribution of DE-Cad and Arm in AJs of polarizing epithelial cells exhibited significantly faster biosynthetic turnover than in polarized cells. Unexpectedly, fast biosynthetic turnover of membrane DE-Cad was found to be microtubule-dependent, whereas the redistribution of Arm in AJs was diffusion-based and qualitatively distinct from the slower exchange-based DE-Cad distribution. Furthermore, biochemical assays revealed that the binding of Arm to DE-Cad was weaker in polarizing cells compared to polarized cells. Our findings indicate that the interaction between DE-Cad and Arm is modulated during apical-basal polarization, suggesting a new mechanism that may play a crucial role in establishing apical-basal polarity by regulating AJ dynamics.

title: Phylogenetic analysis of mRNA polyadenylation sites reveals a role of transposable elements in evolution of the 3′-end of genes
text:
mRNA polyadenylation is a crucial step in the maturation of most eukaryotic messenger RNAs (mRNAs), and it is tightly linked to the termination of transcription in determining the 3' end of genes. It has been observed that many human and mouse genes contain alternative polyadenylation ( Poly(A) ) sites, leading to the generation of mRNA variants containing unique 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) or distinct protein sequences.
In this study, we investigated the conservation and divergence of various types of alternative Poly (A) sites across human, mouse, rat, and chicken. Our findings revealed that the 3' most Poly(A) sites tend to be more highly conserved than upstream sites, whereas Poly(A) sites located upstream of the 3' most exon, also known as intronic Poly(A) sites, tend to be much less conserved. We also observed that genes with a longer evolutionary history are more likely to exhibit alternative polyadenylation, suggesting that new Poly(A) sites may have emerged through evolution. Furthermore, our results showed that non-conserved Poly(A) sites are more frequently associated with transposable elements (TEs) compared to conserved ones, although the frequency of utilization is lower. Different classes of TEs have distinct characteristics in their association with Poly(A) sites through the exaptation of TE sequences into polyadenylation elements.
