Our findings establish a conservation pattern for alternative Poly(A) sites in several vertebrate species, highlighting the dynamic modification of the 3' end of genes through evolution, mediated by TEs.

title: Inter- and Intra-Host Viral Diversity in a Large Seasonal DENV2 Outbreak
text:
BACKGROUND: High levels of genetic diversity are characteristic of RNA viruses due to their error-prone replication process. While several groups have investigated viral variability using different deep sequencing methods, most of these studies have focused on chronic infections in humans. However, there is limited research on the genetic diversity of arthropod-borne, acute viral infections.
METHODS AND PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: To examine the genetic diversity of Dengue Virus 2 (DENV2) isolates from classical and severe cases in a large outbreak in Brazil, we employed two different deep sequencing approaches. Our analysis of the consensus genomes revealed a larger extent of the 2010 epidemic compared to a previous epidemic in another city two years prior (genetic distance = 0.002 and 0.0008, respectively). However, we found a high level of conservation within host populations. Excluding homopolymer regions from 454/Roche-generated sequences revealed 10-44 variable sites per genome population at a frequency of >1%, indicating low intra-host genetic diversity. Surprisingly, only 10% of inter-host variability resulted from non-synonymous mutations, suggesting purifying selection at the population level.
CONCLUSIONS AND SIGNIFICANCE: Our findings challenge the common perception of RNA viruses as highly diverse. Despite their error-prone nature, DENV2 viruses maintain low levels of intra-host variability, which may be due to purifying selection at the population level. This study highlights the need for further investigations into the genetic diversity of arthropod-borne, acute viral infections, which are often overlooked in the context of viral evolution and host-virus interactions.

title: Serum Soluble Corin Deficiency Predicts Major Disability within 3 Months after Acute Stroke
text:
Objective:
To investigate the association between serum soluble corin levels and the risk of poor outcomes within 3 months after stroke. Specifically, we aimed to determine whether high levels of serum soluble corin are associated with a lower risk of major disability or death after stroke.
Methods:
We conducted a prospective study including 522 patients with acute stroke. Serum soluble corin levels were measured at baseline for all participants. The primary outcome measures were major disability or death within 3 months after stroke. Logistic regression analysis was used to examine the association between baseline serum soluble corin levels and the risk of poor outcomes, adjusting for age, sex, baseline National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score, time from onset to hospitalization, smoking status, alcohol consumption, hypertension, diabetes, coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation, family history of stroke, and stroke subtype.
Results:
Our results showed that patients with high levels of serum soluble corin had a significantly lower risk of the composite outcome of major disability or death compared to those with low levels of corin (the lowest tertile). In adjusted analyses, patients with high corin levels still had a lower risk for the composite outcome, and this association remained significant after additional adjustment for other conventional factors. No significant association was found between serum soluble corin levels and other composite outcomes.
Conclusion:
Our findings suggest that serum soluble corin deficiency may be associated with an increased risk of major disability within 3 months after stroke. These results may imply a potential role of corin in stroke prognosis.

title: Altered PTEN expression; a diagnostic marker for differentiating normal, hyperplastic and neoplastic endometrium
text:
HISTORY AND OBJECTIVES Different molecular alterations have been described in endometrioid endometrial carcinoma (EECA). Among them, the most frequently altered is loss of the PTEN protein, a tumor suppressor gene. This study aimed to evaluate the expression pattern of the PTEN gene in normal, hyperplastic, and neoplastic endometrium.
METHODS In a hospital-based study in Tehran, Iran, we evaluated the expression of PTEN using immunohistochemistry (IHC) on 87 consecutive samples, categorized into three groups:
 Group A: Normal proliferative endometrium (n = 29)
Group B: Hyperplastic endometrium (including simple hyperplasia without atypia, n = 21, and complex hyperplasia with atypia, n = 8)
Group C: EECA (n = 29)
We analyzed the immunostaining of cells using arbitrary quantitative methods based on the staining area and intensity of the color reaction.
RESULTS PTEN immunoreactivity was present in all normal proliferative endometrium, all simple hyperplasia, 75% of atypical complex hyperplasia, and in 48% of EECA (P < 0.001). The intensity of PTEN reaction was significantly higher in the proliferative endometrium group compared to the hyperplastic endometrium and EECA groups (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION Our findings indicate that PTEN expression is significantly higher in cyclical endometrium compared to atypical hyperplasia and endometrioid carcinoma.

title: Care Seeking for Neonatal Illness in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review
text:
Despite recent progress in reducing child mortality, neonatal deaths continue to account for 41% of all deaths in children under five years of age globally, with over 90% of these deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Infections are a leading cause of neonatal death, and limited care seeking contributes to high mortality rates. While estimates of care-seeking behaviors in LMICs have been studied, there is a lack of data on this issue, particularly in non-South Asian regions.
To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review of studies that reported the proportion of caregivers who sought care for ill or suspected ill neonates in LMICs. We searched 784 studies and identified 22 studies that provided relevant data from community household surveys, facility-based surveys, and intervention trials. The majority of these studies were conducted in South Asia, in rural areas, and published within the last four years.
Of the 9,098 neonates who were ill or suspected to be ill, 4,320 caregivers sought some type of care, including care from a health facility or provider. However, care seeking ranged between 10% and 100% among caregivers, with a median of 59%. Care seeking from a health care provider yielded a similar range and median, while care seeking at a health care facility ranged between 1% and 100%, with a median of 20%. The estimates were limited by the few studies conducted in urban settings and regions other than South Asia, and there was a lack of consistency in defining illness, care-seeking, and care provider.
Our findings suggest that there is a need for representative data to describe care-seeking patterns in different geographic regions and to better understand the mechanisms to enhance care seeking during this vulnerable time period. Specifically, there is a need to improve the availability and accessibility of healthcare services, particularly in low-resource settings, to reduce neonatal mortality.

title: Synaptic Incorporation of AMPA Receptors during LTP Is Controlled by a PKC Phosphorylation Site on GluR1
text: The incorporation of GluR1-containing AMPA receptors into synapses is essential for various forms of neural plasticity, including long-term potentiation (LTP). Despite the identification of several signaling pathways involved in this process, the direct modifications of GluR1 that control its incorporation into synapses remain unclear. Our study reveals that phosphorylation of GluR1 by PKC at a highly conserved serine 818 residue is increased during LTP and is critical for the expression of LTP. GluR1 is phosphorylated by PKC at this site in both in vitro and in vivo experiments. Furthermore, we found that acute phosphorylation of GluR1 at position 818 by PKC, as well as the introduction of a phosphomimetic mutation, promotes GluR1 incorporation into synapses. Conversely, inhibiting GluR1 phosphorylation at position 818 reduces LTP and hinders the synaptic incorporation of GluR1 driven by PKC. Our findings suggest that the phosphorylation of GluR1 at serine 818 by PKC is a crucial event in the plasticity-driven incorporation of AMPA receptors into synapses.

title: The Bloom's syndrome helicase promotes the annealing of complementary single-stranded DNA
text: The mutated gene in Bloom's syndrome, BLM, encodes a 3'-5' DNA helicase belonging to the highly conserved RecQ family. In addition to its conventional DNA strand separation activity, BLM catalyzes the disruption of non-B-form DNA structures, such as G-quadruplexes, and the branch migration of Holliday junctions. We have recently characterized a novel activity for BLM: the promotion of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) annealing. This activity does not require Mg2+, is inhibited by ssDNA binding proteins and ATP, and is dependent on DNA length. Through an analysis of various truncation mutants of BLM, we found that the C-terminal domain is crucial for ssDNA annealing and identified a 60 amino acid stretch within this domain as being essential for both ssDNA binding and strand annealing. Our findings suggest that the ssDNA annealing activity of BLM plays a crucial role in the processing of DNA intermediates that arise during the repair of damaged replication forks.

title: Bayesian selection of continuous-time Markov chain evolutionary models.
text: In this study, we propose a reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo (RJMCMC) approach for estimating the posterior distribution of phylogenies based on aligned DNA/RNA sequences using several hierarchical evolutionary models. By utilizing an informed yet uninformative prior, we evaluate the advantages of the Bayesian approach to hypothesis testing and estimation in phylogenetics through comparative analysis of different models for infinitesimal rate variation among nucleotides, number of rate classes, and branch length relationships. We use Bayes factors to assess the relative probabilities of these models and the suitability of a molecular clock. Our most general model, initially proposed by Tamura and Nei, involves six parameters that describe the infinitesimal probability of change among nucleotides (A, G, C, T/U), including three parameters for the stationary distribution and two for nucleotide transitions. Nested models include the Hasegawa-Kishino-Yano model with equal transition rates and the Kimura model with a uniform stationary distribution and equal transition rates. Applying these methods to simulated and real data sets, including 16S rRNA sequences from 15 contemporary bacteria, halobacteria, eocytes, and eukaryotes, as well as 9 primates and the entire HIV genome of 11 isolates, we find that the Kimura model is too restrictive, that the Hasegawa-Kishino-Yano model can be rejected for some data sets, and that there is evidence for more than one rate class and a molecular clock among similar taxa. Moreover, we find that the molecular clock can be rejected for more distantly related taxa.

title: The intersection between aging and cardiovascular disease.
text: The human lifespan is increasing, leading to a sharp rise in the proportion of older individuals (65+ years), which will continue to grow over the next two decades. Within this age group, cardiovascular disease will remain the leading cause of death, accompanied by an exponential increase in treatment costs. As aging is an inevitable part of life, it remains a primary risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Although extensive research has focused on both younger and older populations in the cardiovascular field, a significant portion of the underlying genetic mechanisms remain unexplored. Similarly, the molecular biology of aging field has made limited progress in identifying the impact of aging pathways on cardiovascular health. However, this knowledge gap is gradually narrowing, and the two fields are converging. We provide an overview of the key genes involved in controlling lifespan and health span, including sirtuins, AMP-activated protein kinase, mammalian target of rapamycin, and insulin-like growth factor 1, and their roles in regulating cardiovascular health. We will also discuss a series of upcoming review articles that will offer a more comprehensive analysis of studies linking genetic aging and cardiovascular health, as well as future directions in these intrinsically linked fields.

title: Single-RNA counting reveals alternative modes of gene expression in yeast
text: Proper execution of gene expression programs is crucial for cellular function, and accurate control of timing and intensity is essential. However, the mechanisms by which transcriptional machinery fulfills this need are not fully understood. To investigate, we employed an in situ hybridization approach that detects individual mRNA molecules within single yeast cells. Our findings reveal that expression levels for specific genes are higher than previously reported, and cell-to-cell variation is more pronounced than anticipated. Notably, the majority of constitutively expressed genes exhibit minimal expression variation, suggesting that they are transcribed via single transcription initiation events occurring at distinct times. In contrast, the gene PDR5, which is regulated by the transcriptional coactivator complex SAGA, exhibits expression bursts, resulting in more pronounced variation in mRNA abundance. These results provide direct evidence for the existence of multiple expression modes in the transcriptome, offering new insights into how cells modulate their transcriptome.

title: A complete landscape of post-transcriptional modifications in mammalian mitochondrial tRNAs
text: In the mitochondria of mammalian cells, 22 types of transfer RNAs (tRNAs) encoded in mitochondrial DNA play essential roles in the translation of 13 vital subunits of the respiratory chain complexes involved in oxidative phosphorylation. Following transcription, mitochondrial tRNAs are modified by nuclear-encoded tRNA-modifying enzymes. These modifications are necessary for the proper functioning of mitochondrial tRNAs (mt tRNAs), and their absence can lead to harmful consequences. However, the information available on these modifications has been incomplete. To address this issue, we isolated all 22 species of mt tRNAs from bovine liver and comprehensively determined the post-transcriptional modifications in each tRNA using mass spectrometry. Here, we describe the primary structures with post-transcriptional modifications of seven previously uncharacterized mt tRNAs and provide revised information on base modifications in five other mt tRNAs. In the complete set of bovine mt tRNAs, we found 15 species of modified nucleosides at 118 positions (7.48% of total bases). This result provides insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying the decoding system in mammalian mitochondria and enables the prediction of candidate tRNA-modifying enzymes responsible for each modification of mt tRNAs.

title: Preventing coronary heart disease: B vitamins and homocysteine.
text: The list of preventable and reversible risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease continues to expand. Well-established risk factors include cigarette smoking, high blood pressure, physical inactivity, elevated cholesterol, underlying lipoprotein abnormalities, lipoprotein(a), diabetes, overweight, male gender, and age. In the 1990s, there have been numerous studies linking elevated plasma homocysteine levels to arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and evidence suggests that dietary and supplemental folic acid can reduce homocysteine levels. A recent article by Robinson and colleagues in Circulation provides further evidence of the importance of homocysteine and suggests that plasma folate and plasma pyrixodal-l-phosphate (vitamin B6) are protective factors. Their study, which involved 750 patients younger than age 60 with diagnoses within the previous 12 months of coronary, cerebrovascular, or peripheral vascular disease and 800 healthy control subjects, found that men in the highest quintile for fasting total homocysteine (tHcy) had an estimated relative risk of 2.2 compared to the rest of the population, with a striking dose-response relationship and a more-than-multiplicative interaction with cigarette smoking and high blood pressure on vascular disease risk. The corresponding estimated relative risk for coronary heart disease was similar. Robinson and colleagues examined three B vitamins in detail to determine their effects on fasting and post–methionine-loading tHcy levels and any independent effects on cardiovascular disease.

title: Relationship between serum parathyroid hormone levels, vitamin D sufficiency, and calcium intake.
text:
In recent years, there has been increased recognition of the importance of adequate vitamin D status for optimal bone health, but there is no universally accepted ideal intake level. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is commonly used as an indicator of vitamin D status, but no universally agrees upon reference level exists. This study aimed to investigate the relative importance of high calcium intake and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D for maintaining calcium homeostasis, as indicated by serum intact parathyroid hormone (PTH).
A cross-sectional study of 2310 healthy Icelandic adults aged 30-85 years was conducted between February 2001 and January 2003. Participants completed a semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire to assess their vitamin D and calcium intake. They were then divided into groups based on their calcium intake (less than 800 mg/d, 800-1200 mg/d, or more than 1200 mg/d) and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level (less than 10 ng/mL, 10-18 ng/mL, or more than 18 ng/mL). Serum PTH levels were measured as the main outcome.
A total of 944 participants completed the study, with the lowest serum PTH levels found in those with a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of more than 18 ng/mL, and the highest levels found in those with a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of less than 10 ng/mL. At low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels (less than 10 ng/mL), higher calcium intake was associated with higher serum PTH levels (P = 0.04). At a calcium intake of more than 1200 mg/d, there was a significant difference in serum PTH levels between the lowest and highest vitamin D groups (P = 0.04).
The study's findings suggest that ensuring adequate vitamin D status is key to maintaining calcium metabolism, as long as calcium intake levels are above 800 mg/d. Vitamin D supplements are necessary for adequate vitamin D status in northern climates.

title: Sex-specific effects of the DAF-12 steroid receptor on aging in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: Sexually dimorphic differences in longevity and aging are prevalent throughout the animal kingdom. These variations may, in part, be attributable to sex-specific differences in endocrinology. The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans provides a useful model system for investigating these differences. In this study, we aimed to investigate the contribution of sex differences in insulin/insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and steroid endocrinology to aging in C. elegans populations cultivated in liquid media. Our findings suggest that sex differences in steroid endocrinology may play a role in the observed sex differences in aging. In hermaphrodites, mutational loss of the DAF-12 steroid receptor has a similar effect on lifespan as previously observed in plate-cultured populations, with mutant longevity being suppressed in a weak daf-2 insulin/IGF-1 receptor mutant and enhanced in a stronger daf-2 mutant. In contrast, mutation of daf-12 had little effect on aging in male populations, regardless of the strength of the daf-2 mutation. Moreover, while mutation of daf-12 marginally reduced lifespan in daf-2(+) hermaphrodites, as observed in plate-cultured populations, it did not have the same effect in daf-2(+) males. These results suggest that sex differences in steroid endocrinology may play a crucial role in explaining the observed sex differences in aging in C. elegans, similarly to the findings in mammals.

title: Nonclassical binding of formylated peptide in crystal structure of the MHC class lb molecule H2-M3
text: H2-M3 is a class Ib MHC molecule found in mice that exhibits an unusual preference for binding N-formylated peptides, with a 10(4)-fold bias. To delve into the underlying mechanisms of this specificity, we produced and crystallized a soluble form of M3 in complex with a formylated nonamer peptide, fMYFINILTL. Employing X-ray crystallography, we determined the crystal structure of M3 at 2.1 Å resolution. comparison with class I MHC molecules reveals that M3 shares a similar overall structure, yet differs in peptide binding. The A pocket, usually accommodating the unoccupied N-terminus of a bound peptide, is now closed, while the peptide is shifted by one residue, resulting in the P1 side chain being positioned in the B pocket. The formyl group is coordinated by His-9 and a bound water in the groove.

title: Sequential signals toward podosome formation in NIH-src cells
text: Podosomes (also referred to as invadopodia in cancer cells) are actin-rich adhesion structures with matrix degradation capabilities that form in various cell types. Despite their crucial physiological importance, the molecular mechanism of podosome formation remains largely unexplored. To investigate this phenomenon, we examined the molecular mechanisms of podosome formation in this study. Our findings revealed that the expression of different phosphoinositide-binding domains led to the enrichment of PtdIns(3,4)P2 in podosomes found in Src-transformed NIH3T3 (NIH-src) cells. This suggests a vital role of this phosphoinositide in podosome formation. Live-cell imaging analysis revealed that Src expression stimulated podosome formation at adhesion sites in NIH3T3 cells after PtdIns(3,4)P2 accumulation. The adaptor protein Tks5/FISH, which plays a crucial role in podosome formation, was discovered to form a complex with Grb2 at adhesion sites in an Src-dependent manner. Additionally, it was found that N-WASP bound all SH3 domains of Tks5/FISH, which facilitated the formation of circular podosomes. These results indicate that augmenting the N-WASP-Arp2/3 signal was accomplished on the basis of the Tks5/FISH-Grb2 complex at adhesion sites, which is stabilized by PtdIns(3,4)P2.

title: Forebrain engraftment by human glial progenitor cells enhances synaptic plasticity and learning in adult mice.
text: Human astrocytes are significantly larger and more complex than those of lower mammals, suggesting that their role in neural processing has evolved over time. To investigate the cell-autonomous and species-specific properties of human glia, we transplanted human glial progenitor cells (GPCs) into neonatal immunodeficient mice. Following maturation, the host brains exhibited a high number and proportion of both human glial progenitors and astrocytes. The engrafted human glia were electrically connected to host astroglia, but retained the size and complexity of human astroglia and propagated calcium signals 3 times faster than their host. Long-term potentiation (LTP) was significantly enhanced in the human glial chimeric mice, and they also displayed improved learning abilities in various tests such as the Barnes maze, object-location memory, and both contextual and tone fear conditioning. In contrast, mice allografted with murine GPCs showed no enhancement of LTP or learning. These findings suggest that human glia have a unique ability to differentially enhance activity-dependent plasticity and learning in mice.

title: Reprogramming of human fibroblasts to pluripotency with lineage specifiers.
text: Following the initial discovery that OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC overexpression could induce pluripotency in somatic cells, subsequent research has focused on improving our understanding of the reprogramming process by replacing these factors with alternative proteins. However, despite significant efforts, OCT4 has remained a crucial component of the reprogramming process in human cells, seemingly unable to be replaced. Here, we report a novel strategy for achieving this replacement by identifying and leveraging factors previously characterized as lineage specifiers. Through a combination of transcriptome and bioinformatic analysis, we have identified factors that can successfully replace OCT4 and SOX2 in the reprogramming of human fibroblasts. Our findings support a model in which counteracting lineage specification networks underlies the induction of pluripotency, offering new insights into the complex networks involved in cellular reprogramming.

title: Mechanisms of endocytosis.
text:
Endocytic mechanisms play a crucial role in regulating the composition of the plasma membrane and mediating cellular interactions with their environment. In this review, we delve into the intricate details of mammalian endocytic mechanisms, focusing on the cellular proteins that govern these processes. We begin by examining the well-established clathrin-mediated endocytic pathways and then discussed alternative, clathrin-independent mechanisms, including the CLIC/GEEC endocytic pathway, Arf6-dependent endocytosis, flotillin-dependent endocytosis, macropinocytosis, circular doral ruffles, phagocytosis, and trans-endocytosis. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the role of caveolae and caveolin1 in endocytosis.
We recognize the significance of various cellular components, such as lipids, membrane curvature-modulating proteins, small G proteins, actin, and dynamin, in endocytic pathways. Furthermore, we highlight the functional diversity of endocytic pathways and emphasize the importance of understanding these mechanisms to uncover the underlying causes of human diseases.
Overall, our review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of mammalian endocytic mechanisms and their significance in cellular communication and disease processes. Through this study, we hope to inspire further research and shed light on the complex relationships between cellular endocytosis and human health.

title: Birth Size and Breast Cancer Risk: Re-analysis of Individual Participant Data from 32 Studies
text: In this study, we reanalyzed individual participant data from published and unpublished epidemiological studies to investigate the association between birth size and breast cancer risk. We found that birth weight, as well as birth length and head circumference, were positively associated with breast cancer risk. Specifically, for every one-standard-deviation increase in birth weight, the risk of breast cancer increased by 10.6% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 10.2-11.1%). Similarly, for every one-standard-deviation increase in birth length, the risk of breast cancer increased by 10.3% (95% CI: 9.9-10.8%). We also found that head circumference was positively associated with breast cancer risk, with a 10.9% increase in risk for every one-standard-deviation increase (95% CI: 10.3-11.5%). Our results suggest that birth size, particularly birth length, is an independent correlate of breast cancer risk in adulthood.

title: LncRNA-GAS5 induces PTEN expression through inhibiting miR-103 in endometrial cancer cells
text:
Background: Growth arrest-specific 5 (GAS5) has been implicated in multiple cancers, including endometrial carcinoma. However, the mechanisms underlying its expression and function in endometrial cancer are poorly understood.
Results: In this study, we found that GAS5 is down-regulated in endometrial cancer cells using real-time reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and flow cytometry analysis. We also observed that GAS5 stimulates apoptosis in endometrial cancer cells. To investigate the expression of GAS5, PTEN, and miR-103, RT-PCR was performed, and we found that the expression of PTEN was up-regulated when endometrial cancer cells overexpressed GAS5. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that GAS5 may bind to miR-103, which was confirmed through luciferase reporter assay and western blotting. Furthermore, we found that miR-103 mimic decreased the mRNA and protein levels of PTEN, and GAS5 plasmid may reverse this regulation effect in endometrial cancer cells.
Conclusion: Our results demonstrate that GAS5 acts as a tumor suppressor long non-coding RNA in endometrial cancer. By inhibiting the expression of miR-103, GAS5 significantly enhanced the expression of PTEN, leading to increased cancer cell apoptosis. These findings suggest that GAS5 may play an important role in the pathogenesis of endometrial cancer.

title: Modification of kidney barrier function by the urokinase receptor
text: Podocyte dysfunction, characterized by foot process effacement and proteinuria, often marks the beginning of progressive kidney disease. Currently, treatments targeting the cellular origins of the disease are unavailable. This study reveals that inducing urokinase receptor (uPAR) signaling in podocytes leads to foot process effacement and urinary protein loss through a mechanism involving lipid-dependent activation of αvβ3 integrin. Mice lacking uPAR (Plaur−/−) are protected from lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-mediated proteinuria but develop disease after expression of a constitutively active β3 integrin. Gene transfer studies demonstrate that uPAR expression in podocytes, but not in endothelial cells, is necessary for the development of LPS-mediated proteinuria. Mechanistically, uPAR activates αvβ3 integrin in podocytes, promoting cell motility and the activation of small GTPases Cdc42 and Rac1. Inhibition of αvβ3 integrin reduces podocyte motility in vitro and lowers proteinuria in mice, highlighting the importance of uPAR signaling in regulating kidney permeability.

title: Jagged1-induced Notch signaling drives proliferation of multiple myeloma cells.
text: Hematopoietic stem cells express Notch receptors, which interact with their ligands on bone marrow stromal cells toregulate cell fate decisions and survival. We recently demonstrated that Notch signaling is involved in the proliferation and survival of B cell-derived tumor cells in classic Hodgkin disease, and described a novel mechanism for the oncogenic capacity of Notch. In this study, we investigated whether Notch signaling plays a role in the close interactions between malignant plasma cells and their bone marrow microenvironment, which are essential for tumor cell growth in multiple myeloma (MM). Our findings show that Notch receptors and their ligand Jagged1 are highly expressed in cultured and primary MM cells, while non-malignant counterparts have low to undetectable levels of Notch. Functional data suggest that ligand-induced Notch signaling serves as a growth factor for MM cells, and these interactions may contribute to myelomagenesis in vivo.

title: An Extensive MicroRNA-Mediated Network of RNA-RNA Interactions Regulates Established Oncogenic Pathways in Glioblastoma
text: Through an integration of gene expression data and matched microRNA profiles in glioblastoma, we have uncovered a previously unknown layer of posttranscriptional regulation, which involves over 248,000 microRNA (miR)-mediated interactions. These interactions include approximately 7,000 genes that act as "sponges" for miRs and 148 genes that engage in alternative, non-sponge interactions. Biochemical analyses in cell lines have confirmed that this network regulates key drivers of tumor initiation and subtype development, such as PTEN, PDGFRA, RB1, VEGFA, STAT3, and RUNX1. Our findings suggest that these interactions mediate crosstalk between canonical oncogenic pathways. By silencing 13 miR-regulated PTEN genes, we were able to downregulate PTEN in a 3'UTR-dependent manner and increase tumor cell growth rates, providing a mechanistic explanation for the loss of PTEN expression in a significant number of glioma samples with an intact PTEN locus.

title: Direct reprogramming of mouse fibroblasts to neural progenitors.
text:
Induced pluripotency may prove to be a versatile tool for generating a wide range of differentiated cells for cell therapy and drug development. However, the process of reprogramming somatic cells to become induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) can be challenging and time-consuming. We sought to determine if it might be possible to skip the intermediate pluripotent stage and directly convert somatic cells into lineage-specific stem/progenitor cells of another germ layer in a single step.
Our findings demonstrate that a simple and efficient method exists to transdifferentiate fibroblasts into functional neural stem/progenitor cells (NPCs) using transient induction of four reprogramming factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc). Compared to directly converted neurons (or iN cells), the transdifferentiated NPCs have a significant advantage in that they can be expanded in vitro and give rise to multiple neuronal subtypes and glial cells.
Our results provide a valuable new approach to iPSC-factor-based reprogramming, which can be readily modified to serve as a general platform for transdifferentiation. This innovative technique holds great promise for healthcare applications such as regenerative medicine and drug development.

title: Tissue-Specific Knockout of the Insulin Receptor in Pancreatic β Cells Creates an Insulin Secretory Defect Similar to that in Type 2 Diabetes
text: Dysfunction within pancreatic beta cells is a key defect in the development of type 2 diabetes, but the exact relationship to insulin resistance remains unclear. To investigate the role of insulin signaling in beta cells, we employed the Cre-loxP system to specifically inhibit the insulin receptor gene in these cells. The resulting mice exhibited a selective loss of insulin secretion in response to glucose and a gradual decline in glucose tolerance. These findings strongly suggest that the insulin receptor plays a vital functional role in glucose sensing by pancreatic beta cells and implicate defects in insulin signaling within these cells as a contributing factor to the altered insulin secretion observed in type 2 diabetes.

title: Social variations in access to hospital care for patients with colorectal, breast, and lung cancer between 1999 and 2006: retrospective analysis of hospital episode statistics
text:
The study aimed to investigate the relationship between socioeconomic factors, age, sex, and year of admission on the type of hospital admission (emergency vs elective) and surgical procedure for patients with colorectal, breast, and lung cancer.
The study used a repeated cross-sectional design, analyzing individual patient data from April 1999 to March 2006 from the Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) dataset. The study included 564,821 patients aged 50 or older with a diagnosis of colorectal, breast, or lung cancer. The main outcome measures were the proportion of patients admitted as emergencies and the proportion receiving the recommended surgical treatment.
The study found that patients from deprived areas, older people, and women were more likely to be admitted as emergencies. For example, patients in the least deprived fifth of deprivation had a lower odds ratio of 0.63 for breast cancer compared to those in the most deprived fifth. Similarly, patients aged 80-89 had a lower odds ratio of 3.13 for lung cancer compared to those aged 50-59. However, there were no improvements in disparities between age groups over time. Patients from deprived areas were also less likely to receive preferred procedures for rectal, breast, and lung cancer, with a lower proportion of patients in the most deprived fifth undergoing anterior resection for rectal cancer (67.4%) compared to the least deprived fifth (75.5%).
The study also found that men were less likely than women to undergo anterior resection and lung cancer resection, and older people were less likely to receive breast conserving surgery and lung cancer resection. For example, patients aged 80-89 had a lower odds ratio of 0.52 for lung cancer resection compared to those aged 50-59.
In conclusion, despite the implementation of the NHS Cancer Plan, social factors still have a strong influence on access to and the provision of care, particularly for patients from deprived areas. The study highlights the need for targeted interventions to address these disparities and ensure equal access to high-quality cancer care for all patients.

title: Identification of Gene Positioning Factors Using High-Throughput Imaging Mapping
text: The arrangement of genomes within the 3D space of the cell nucleus is not random. To better understand the spatial organization of genomes at a large scale, we have developed HIPMap, a high-precision, high-throughput, and automated pipeline for fluorescent in situ hybridization imaging. Using HIPMap, we conducted an unbiased siRNA screen to identify factors involved in genome organization in human cells. We identified 50 cellular factors essential for proper positioning offunctionally diverse genomic loci. These factors include chromatin remodelers, histone modifiers, and proteins involved in the nuclear envelope and pore. Components of the replication and post-replication chromatin re-assembly machinery are significantly represented among the positioning factors, and timely progression of cells through replication, but not mitosis, is necessary for correct gene positioning. Our results have established a method for large-scale mapping of genome locations and led to the identification of a comprehensive list of cellular factors involved in spatial genome organization.

title: Astrocyte-Mediated Distributed Plasticity at Hypothalamic Glutamate Synapses
text: Afferent stimulation can lead to rapid, feed-forward changes in synaptic strength that are specific to individual synapses. By combining electrophysiology, caged molecule photolysis, and Ca(2+) imaging, we have observed a form of plasticity in which the recruitment of astrocytes in response to afferent activity results in a fast and feed-forward increase in the amplitude of synaptic currents at multiple glutamate synapses on magnocellular neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus. This plasticity is largely multiplicative, suggesting a proportional increase or "scaling" in the strength of all synapses on the neuron. The effect requires a metabotropic glutamate receptor-mediated rise in Ca(2+) in the astrocyte processes surrounding the neuron, followed by the release of the gliotransmitter ATP, which acts on postsynaptic purinergic receptors. These findings provide evidence for a distributed synaptic plasticity mechanism that is rapid, feed-forward, and mediated by the synaptic activation of neighboring astrocytes.

title: Effect of smoking reduction on lung cancer risk.
text:
Many smokers struggle to quit smoking entirely, but reducing the number of cigarettes smoked per day may be a viable harm reduction strategy. However, it remains unclear whether this approach actually reduces the risk of tobacco-related diseases such as lung cancer. In an observational population-based cohort study with up to 31 years of follow-up, researchers from the Copenhagen Centre for Prospective Population Studies investigated the effects of smoking reduction on lung cancer incidence.
The study included 19,714 participants aged 20 to 93 years from four longitudinal studies in Copenhagen and its suburbs. Participants attended two consecutive examinations with a 5- to 10-year interval between 1964 and 1988, during which they provided information on their lifestyle habits, including smoking. The study population was categorized into six groups based on their smoking habits: continued heavy smokers, reducers (who had reduced their smoking by at least 50% without quitting), continued light smokers, quitters, stable ex-smokers, and never smokers.
During the follow-up period until December 31, 2003, there were 864 incident lung cancer cases identified through record linkage with the National Cancer Registry. Using Cox regression analysis, the researchers found that individuals who had reduced their smoking by 50% had a significantly lower risk of developing lung cancer compared to persistent heavy smokers (hazard ratio (HR) = 0.73, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.54-0.98). Similarly, the HR for light smokers was 0.44 (95% CI, 0.35-0.56), compared to persistent heavy smokers, while quitters had a HR of 0.50 (95% CI, 0.36-0.69), stable ex-smokers had a HR of 0.17 (95% CI, 0.13-0.23), and never smokers had a HR of 0.09 (95% CI, 0.06-0.13).
In conclusion, the study suggests that among individuals who smoke 15 or more cigarettes per day, reducing smoking by 50% may significantly reduce the risk of lung cancer.

title: Facilities for macromolecular crystallography at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin
text: Three state-of-the-art macromolecular crystallography (MX) beamlines are available at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin (HZB) for the regional, national, and international structural biology user community. Located within the low-β section of the BESSY II electron storage ring, the cutting-edge beamlines BL14.1, BL14.2, and BL14.3 are fed by a superconducting 7 T wavelength-shifter insertion device. BL14.1 and BL14.2 are energy-tunable in the range of 5-16 keV, while BL14.3 is a fixed-energy side station operating at 13.8 keV. All three beamlines are equipped with high-quality CCD detectors. BL14.1 and BL14.2 are in regular user operation, providing approximately 200 beam days per year and 600 user shifts to about 50 research groups across Europe. BL14.3 has initially served as a test facility and was later brought into regular user mode operation in 2010. BL14.1 has recently been upgraded with a microdiffractometer, including a mini-κ goniometer and an automated sample changer. In addition to the beamlines, the HZB provides user facilities such as office space adjacent to the beamlines, a sample preparation laboratory, a biology laboratory (safety level 1), and high-end computing resources. This article summarizes the instrumentation of the beamlines and the various experimental possibilities available to the user community.

title: PHENIX: a comprehensive Python-based system for macromolecular structure solution
text: Macromolecular X-ray crystallography is widely used to provide a molecular-level understanding of biological processes. However, the process can be time-consuming due to the need for manual interpretation of complex numerical data using various software packages, and the repeated use of interactive three-dimensional graphics. To address these challenges, PHENIX has been developed as a comprehensive system for macromolecular crystallographic structure solution, with a focus on automating all procedures. This has involved the creation of algorithms that minimize or eliminate subjective input, the development of algorithms that automate manual tasks, and the integration of these algorithms into a single framework.

title: Telomeric 3′ Overhangs Derive from Resection by Exo1 and Apollo and Fill-In by POT1b-Associated CST
text: Mammalian telomeres require a 3' overhang for proper protection and maintenance, but excessive resection of the 5' end can lead to telomere shortening. The mechanisms underlying the synthesis of this balance have not been fully understood. To investigate, we analyzed telomeric overhangs throughout the cell cycle and at both leading and lagging telomeres in mouse cells. Our findings reveal that Apollo, a nuclease bound to the shelterin subunit TRF2, initiates the formation of the 3' overhang at leading telomeres but not lagging ones. However, the activity of Apollo is blocked at both ends by the shelterin protein POT1b. Exo1, a nuclease, extensively resects both telomere ends, producing transient long 3' overhangs in S/G2 phase. CST/AAF, a DNA polα.primase accessory factor, binds POT1b and shortens the extended overhangs produced by Exo1, likely through fill-in synthesis. Overall, the synthesis of the 3' overhang in mammalian telomeres is a complex, shelterin-controlled process that ensures the proper functioning of chromosome ends.

title: Targeting BRCA1 and BRCA2 Deficiencies with G-Quadruplex-Interacting Compounds
text: G-quadruplex (G4)-forming genomic sequences, such as telomeres, act as natural barriers to replication forks. When replication forks become stalled, homologous recombination (HR) can be used to stabilize and restart the process, which also helps repair DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) that form at the collapsed forks. We have previously demonstrated that HR facilitates telomere replication. Here, we show that the replication efficiency of guanine-rich (G-rich) telomeric repeats is significantly reduced in cells lacking HR. Treatment with the G4-stabilizing compound pyridostatin (PDS) increases telomere fragility in BRCA2-deficient cells, suggesting that G4 formation contributes to telomere instability. Remarkably, PDS exposure reduces proliferation of HR-defective cells by inducing DSB accumulation, checkpoint activation, and deregulated G2/M progression, as well as exacerbating the replication defect intrinsic to HR deficiency. Interestingly, PDS toxicity extends to HR-defective cells that have acquired olaparib resistance through loss of 53BP1 or REV7. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of G4-stabilizing drugs to selectively target and eliminate HR-compromised cells and tumors, including those resistant to PARP inhibition.

title: Downloaded from
text: Regular physical activity triggers a subclinical inflammatory response, partially mediated by white blood cells, and reflected by increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the blood, including interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α). However, the origin of these cytokines remains unknown. In this study, we investigated changes in plasma cytokine concentrations and their corresponding mRNA expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells following exercise. We recruited ten healthy, untrained males (peak oxygen uptake: 48.8 ± 6.5 ml/kg/min) who underwent 3 hours of cycling and inclined walking at 60-65% of their peak oxygen uptake. Leukocyte subsets in the blood were elevated during and for 2 hours after exercise, after which they returned to normal within 24 hours. Plasma levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α peaked at the end of exercise and remained elevated at 2 hours (IL-6) and up to 24 hours (IL-1β and TNF-α) post-exercise. Our findings also revealed changes in the expression of cytokine genes in circulating mononuclear cells following exercise.

title: Receptor tyrosine kinases endocytosis in endothelium: biology and signaling.
text: Receptor tyrosine kinases play a crucial role in regulating various physiological processes in endothelial cells, including proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis. It is widely accepted that receptor tyrosine kinase signaling takes place both intracellularly and on the plasma membrane, although more research is needed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms. The endocytosis of receptor tyrosine kinases and their subsequent intracellular trafficking affect the spatial and temporal regulation of signaling events. Additionally, signaling endosomes serve as platforms for the compartmentalization of signaling processes. This review aims to summarize the recent advances in our understanding of endothelial receptor tyrosine kinase endocytosis and signaling, using vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2 as a paradigm.

title: Ethnographic study of incidence and severity of intravenous drug errors.
text:
Objective: To determine the prevalence and clinical significance of errors in the preparation and administration of intravenous (IV) drugs, and to identify the specific stages of the process where errors occur.
Methods: This was a prospective ethnographic study using disguised observation, conducted in 10 wards of a teaching and non-teaching hospital in the United Kingdom. Nurses who prepared and administered IV drugs were included in the study. The primary outcome measures were the number, type, and clinical importance of errors identified.
Results: A total of 249 errors were identified, with at least one error occurring in 212 out of 430 IV drug doses (49%, 95% confidence interval 45% to 54%). Of these errors, 1% had potentially severe clinical consequences, 29% were potentially moderate, and 19% were potentially minor. The majority of errors occurred during the preparation of bolus doses or when preparing drugs that required multiple step preparation.
Conclusion: The rate of IV drug errors was found to be high, with most errors resulting in short-term adverse effects, but some potentially serious. A combination of reducing the workload on the ward, providing training, and implementing technology to administer slow bolus doses may be the most effective approach to reducing error rates.

title: Feature Selection with the Boruta Package
text: This article introduces the R package Boruta, which implements a groundbreaking feature selection algorithm for identifying all relevant variables. The algorithm is built upon a Random Forest classification framework and iteratively removes features that are statistically proven to be less important than random probes. Boruta offers a user-friendly interface for utilizing this innovative algorithm. The text provides a concise description of the algorithm and showcases its application through practical examples.

title: Integrin-linked kinase expression is elevated in human cardiac hypertrophy and induces hypertrophy in transgenic mice.
text:
BACKGROUND:
Although numerous signaling pathways have been implicated in experimental cardiac hypertrophy, the molecular mechanisms underlying the hypertrophic response in human heart diseases remain poorly understood. Integrin-linked kinase (ILK) is a multifunctional protein kinase that links beta-integrins to the actin cytoskeleton, suggesting a potential role in mechanotransduction.
METHODS AND RESULTS:
In this study, we found a significant increase in ILK protein levels in hypertrophic ventricles from patients with congenital and acquired outflow tract obstruction. This increase in ILK was associated with activation of Rho family guanine triphosphatases (GTPases), including Rac1 and Cdc42, as well as known hypertrophic signaling kinases, such as extracellular signal-related kinases (ERK1/2) and p70 S6 kinase. To further investigate the role of ILK in cardiac hypertrophy, we used transgenic mice with cardiac-specific expression of a constitutively active ILK (ILK(S343D)) or wild-type ILK (ILK(WT)), and compared their responses to those of mice with cardiomyocyte-restricted expression of a kinase-inactive ILK (ILK(R211A)). Our results show that the constitutively active ILK mouse displayed a compensated ventricular hypertrophic phenotype, with an activation profile of GTPases and downstream protein kinases similar to that observed in human hypertrophy. In contrast, the kinase-inactive ILK mouse was unable to mount a compensatory hypertrophic response to angiotensin II in vivo.
CONCLUSIONS:
Taken together, these findings identify ILK-regulated signaling as a broadly adaptive hypertrophic response mechanism that is relevant to a wide range of clinical heart diseases.

title: Functional and molecular defects of pancreatic islets in human type 2 diabetes.
text: To provide further insight into the primary changes in insulin secretion in type 2 diabetes and the possible mechanisms involved, we conducted a thorough analysis of functional and molecular properties of islets isolated from the pancreas of 13 type 2 diabetic and 13 matched nondiabetic cadaveric organ donors. We found that glucose-stimulated insulin secretion from type 2 diabetic islets was significantly lower than from control islets, while arginine- and glibenclamide-stimulated insulin release was less affected. Additionally, we observed reduced mRNA expression of GLUT1 and -2, glucokinase, and diminished glucose oxidation. Furthermore, AMP-activated protein kinase activation was reduced, and the expression of insulin, pancreatic duodenal homeobox-1 (PDX-1), and forkhead box O1 (Foxo-1) was decreased. Markers of oxidative stress, nitrotyrosine and 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine, were significantly higher in type 2 diabetic than control islets, and their levels were correlated with the degree of glucose-stimulated insulin release impairment. Notably, exposure to glutathione for 24 hours significantly improved glucose-stimulated insulin release and decreased nitrotyrosine concentration, with partial recovery of insulin mRNA expression. These findings provide conclusive evidence that the defects in insulin secretion in type 2 diabetic islets are associated with multiple cellular alterations. Most importantly, our study shows that the functional impairment of type 2 diabetic islets can be, at least in part, reversible. In light of these findings, reducing islet cell oxidative stress may be a potential target for type 2 diabetes therapy.

title: Induction of stem-like cells with malignant properties by chronic exposure of human lung epithelial cells to single-walled carbon nanotubes
text:
The study aimed to investigate the potential carcinogenic effects of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) on human lung cells, with a particular focus on the acquisition of cancer stem cells (CSCs). CNTs have shown great promise in various commercial and biomedical applications, but their long-term health impacts remain a concern. The researchers hypothesized that the exposure to CNTs may lead to the acquisition of CSCs, which are a subpopulation of cells that drive tumor initiation and progression.
The study exposed non-tumorigenic human lung epithelial cells to well-dispersed CNTs for a period of 6 months at a physiologically relevant concentration of 0.02 μg/cm2 surface area dose. The chronically exposed cells were then evaluated for the presence of CSC-like cells using various methods, including tumor spheres and side population (SP) assays. The researchers found that CSC-like cells were present in all clones of chronically exposed lung epithelial cells, and these cells displayed all the biological features of lung CSCs, including self-renewal, aggressive cancer behaviors, and in vivo tumorigenesis. The CSC-like cells also displayed aberrant stem cell markers, such as Nanog, SOX-2, SOX-17, and E-cadherin. Restored expression of the tumor suppressor protein p53 abrogated the CSC properties of the CSC-like cells. The study also identified specific stem cell surface markers, including CD24low and CD133high, which were associated with SWCNT-induced CSC formation and tumorigenesis.
The findings of the study provide new and compelling evidence for the acquisition of CSC-like cells induced by chronic CNT exposure, which are likely to be a major driving force for CNT tumorigenesis. The study supports the adoption of prevention strategies and exposure control for CNTs and suggests that the detection of CSCs and associated surface markers may provide an effective screening tool for predicting the carcinogenic potential of CNTs and related nanoparticles.

title: Reprogramming factor stoichiometry influences the epigenetic state and biological properties of induced pluripotent stem cells.
text:
Sure! Here is a potential revision of the given text:
We investigated the impact of varying the levels and ratios of reprogramming factors on the acquisition of pluripotency in somatic cells. Our findings show that the optimal combination of Oct4, Klf4, c-Myc, and Sox2 leads to the generation of iPS cells that can efficiently produce "all-iPSC mice" with a normal imprinted genotype. Notably, the expression levels of these factors during reprogramming have a significant impact on the epigenetic and biological properties of iPS cells, including the maintenance of imprinting at the Dlk1-Dio3 locus and the lack of tumor formation. Conversely, loss of imprinting at this locus does not necessarily correlate with reduced pluripotency, but rather affects the efficiency of generating "all-iPSC mice." These findings highlight the complexity of defining a universal epigenetic state for iPSCs and ESCs, and suggest that the optimal combination of reprogramming factors may vary depending on the specific cell type and context.

title: Activator protein-1 (AP-1) DNA binding activity is induced by hydroxyurea in organogenesis stage mouse embryos
text: Hydroxyurea is a powerful teratogen, and exposure to it reduces its teratogenicity when combined with free radical scavengers or antioxidants. Activator Protein-1 (AP-1) and NF-κB are transcription factors that play critical roles in embryonic development and the stress response. This study aimed to determine whether teratogenic doses of hydroxyurea cause oxidative stress and alter gene expression by activating these transcription factors. Pregnant mice were given saline or hydroxyurea (400, 500, or 600 mg/kg) on day 9 of gestation, and their offspring were either killed 0.5, 3, or 6 hours after treatment to assess oxidative stress and transcription factor activities, or on day 18 to assess fetal development. Lower doses of hydroxyurea (400 mg/kg) did not affect the offspring, but higher doses (500 or 600 mg/kg) caused dose-dependent increases in fetal resorptions and malformations, such as curly tails, abnormal limbs (oligodactyly, hemimelia, and amelia), and short ribs. Hydroxyurea did not induce oxidative stress, as measured by the glutathione ratio, and it did not alter NF-κB DNA binding activity in the early embryo. However, exposure to hydroxyurea at any dose increased AP-1 DNA binding activity in embryos and yolk sacs 0.5 or 3 hours after treatment. The hydroxyurea-treated embryos showed a dramatic and region-specific increase in c-Fos immunoreactivity. The induction of AP-1 DNA binding activity by hydroxyurea represents an early, sensitive marker of the embryonic response to insult.

title: BCL-6 represses genes that function in lymphocyte differentiation, inflammation, and cell cycle control.
text: BC6, a transcriptional regulator frequently altered in lymphoid malignancies, controls B cell differentiation and inflammation. Through DNA microarray analysis, we identified genes repressed by BC6, including numerous genes involved in B cell activation. Our findings suggest that BC6 modulates B cell receptor signals. BC6 suppression of chemokine genes, such as MIP-1α and IP-10, may also mitigate inflammatory responses. BLIM-1, another BC6 target, is essential for plasmacytic differentiation. Interestingly, BC6 downregulation in plasma cells leads to BLIM-1 repression, thereby controlling plasmacytic differentiation. In fact, inhibition of BC6 function leads to changes characteristic of plasmacytic differentiation, including decreased c-Myc expression and increased p27kip1 expression. These findings imply that malignant transformation by BC6 involves inhibition of differentiation and enhanced proliferation.

title: Local, Efflux-Dependent Auxin Gradients as a Common Module for Plant Organ Formation
text: Plants demonstrate remarkable adaptability and flexibility during their development, surpassing that of animals. This is attributable to their capacity to create new organs, such as lateral roots, leaves, and flowers, after the embryonic stage. During postembryonic development, organ primordia develop from founder cell populations by coordinated cell division and differentiation. We have found that organ formation in Arabidopsis depends on dynamic gradients of the signaling molecule auxin, with maximum concentrations at the primordia tips. These gradients are mediated by asymmetrically localized PIN proteins, which represent a redundant network for auxin distribution in both aerial and underground organs. The polar localization of PIN1 undergoes a dynamic rearrangement that correlates with the establishment of auxin gradients and primordium development. Our findings suggest that PIN-dependent, local auxin gradients represent a unifying mechanism for the formation of all plant organs, regardless of their mature shape or developmental origin.

title: Drosophila MICAL regulates myofilament organization and synaptic structure
text: The comprehensive size and organizational structure of synaptic terminals hold great significance in determining their functional proprieties. In an extensive mutagenesis screen focused on identifying Drosophila mutants with abnormally structured neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), we discovered mutant alleles of the gene encoding the multi-domain protein Drosophila mical, which is characterized by an N-terminal monooxygenase domain. The mical mutations disrupt the normal formation of synaptic boutons, causing them to malposition and cluster along synaptic branches and at nerve entry sites. Interestingly, high expression of MICAL in somatic muscles results in the anomalous subcellular localization and structural organization of contractile muscle filaments, as demonstrated by immunohistochemical staining. Rather than being incorporated into a well-organized sarcomeric pattern, actin and myosin filaments are distorted and accumulate beneath the plasma membrane. Although the contractile elements are severely disrupted, the proposed organizer of sarcomeric structure, D-Titin, is significantly less affected by the mical mutations. Transgenic expression of interfering RNA molecules confirm that MICAL is indispensable in muscles for the proper arrangement of myofilaments. Ultimately, ultrastructural analysis reveals that myosin-rich thick filaments enter submembranous regions and interfere with synaptic development, leading to the observed synaptic growth phenotype. Notably, the filamentous network surrounding synaptic boutons may play a crucial role in restricting the extension of synaptic branches.

title: Viral Infection of Engrafted Human Islets Leads to Diabetes
text: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is characterized by the destruction of the insulin-producing β-cells in the pancreatic islets. Both genetic and environmental factors contribute to the development of T1D. While a viral infection with enteroviruses is suspected to trigger T1D, the causal relationship remains unproven and controversial. In order to resolve this debate, we created a viral infection model using immunodeficient mice that had been transplanted with human islet grafts. We induced hyperglycemia in the mice by selectively ablating their native β-cells. The human islet grafts were then transplanted to restore normoglycemia. The mice were subsequently infected with CVB4, and their glucose levels were monitored. Forty-seven percent of the mice infected with CVB4 developed hyperglycemia. The human islet grafts from the infected mice contained viral RNA, expressed viral proteins, and had reduced insulin levels compared to grafts from uninfected mice. Additionally, we observed the induction of multiple interferon-stimulated genes in the human islet grafts from infected mice, indicating that human islets can become severely dysfunctional after CVB infection, leading to diabetes.

title: MicroRNA-22 (miR-22) Overexpression Is Neuroprotective via General Anti-Apoptotic Effects and May also Target Specific Huntington’s Disease-Related Mechanisms
text:
ABSTRACT:
While numerous factors contributing to neurodegenerative diseases have been identified, relatively few therapeutic approaches have been developed. One possible explanation is that successful treatments may require the simultaneous targeting of multiple molecular pathways. Recently, a new therapeutic strategy has emerged: engaging microRNAs (miRNAs), which allows for the targeting of multiple pathways with a single sequence.
BACKGROUND:
MiRNAs have been identified as a potential therapeutic approach for neurodegenerative diseases due to their ability to regulate multiple cellular pathways. In this study, we focused on miR-22, which has been shown to target multiple genes implicated in Huntington's disease (HD) and is decreased in HD brains. We investigated the neuroprotective effects of increasing miR-22 expression in in vitro models of neurodegeneration.
METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS:
We tested the hypothesis that overexpressing miR-22 would protect against neurodegeneration in in vitro models of HD and other neurodegenerative diseases. We used primary striatal and cortical cultures exposed to a mutated human huntingtin fragment (Htt171-82Q) and primary neuronal cultures exposed to 3-nitropropionic acid (3-NP), a mitochondrial complex II/III inhibitor. Overexpression of miR-22 inhibited neurodegeneration in all three models. Additionally, miR-22 improved neuronal viability in an in vitro model of brain aging. The mechanisms underlying these effects involved the reduction of caspase activation, which was mediated by targeting the pro-apoptotic activities of mitogen-activated protein kinase 14/p38 (MAPK14/p38) and tumor protein p53-inducible nuclear protein 1 (Tp53inp1). Furthermore, miR-22 targeted multiple genes implicated in HD, including HDAC4, REST corepresor 1 (Rcor1), and regulator of G-protein signaling 2 (Rgs2), and also decreased focal accumulation of mutant Htt-positive foci in a HD-specific manner.
CONCLUSIONS:
Our findings demonstrate that miR-22 has multipartite anti-neurodegenerative activities, including the inhibition of apoptosis and the targeting of multiple genes implicated in HD. These results suggest that manipulating miR-22 may be a viable therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases. Further studies are needed to evaluate the feasibility and efficacy of this approach in vivo.

title: Research in cardiovascular care: a position statement of the Council on Cardiovascular Nursing and Allied Professionals of the European Society of Cardiology.
text: To optimize patient care, evidence-based practices are advocated, and research is crucial to inform healthcare professionals of all disciplines in making informed decisions for their daily practice. Recognizing the growing complexity of cardiac care across the lifespan of patients, combined with the expanding opportunities and challenges in multidisciplinary research, the Science Committee of the Council on Cardiovascular Nursing and Allied Professionals (CCNAP) acknowledged the need for a position statement to guide researchers, policymakers, and funding bodies to advance the body of knowledge required to improve cardiovascular care. In this statement, we identify knowledge gaps in current research related to cardiovascular patient care, explore upcoming challenges, and provide recommendations for future research.

title: Genome-Wide Dynamics of Htz1, a Histone H2A Variant that Poises Repressed/Basal Promoters for Activation through Histone Loss
text: Histone variants play a crucial role in specializing chromatin regions, but their impact on transcriptional regulation remains largely unclear. In this study, we aimed to elucidate the genome-wide distribution and dynamics of Htz1, a histone H2A variant found in yeast. Through our experiments, we discovered that Htz1 localizes to hundreds of repressed/basal Pol II promoters and prefers TATA-less promoters. The deposition of Htz1 requires the SWR1 complex, which largely colocalizes with Htz1. We found that Htz1 occupancy correlates with specific histone modifications, and its deposition is partially dependent on the histone acetyltransferase Gcn5 and Bdf1, a member of the SWR1 complex. Interestingly, changes in growth conditions lead to a dramatic redistribution of Htz1 from activated to repressed/basal promoters. Notably, Htz1 promotes full gene activation without negatively impacting repression. Moreover, we discovered that Htz1-bearing nucleosomes can be deposited at repressed/basal promoters and facilitate activation by becoming susceptible to loss, thus exposing the promoter DNA.

title: Metagenomic analysis of microbial consortium from natural crude oil that seeps into the marine ecosystem offshore Southern California
text: Microorganisms play a crucial role in degrading crude oils in marine ecosystems, and understanding this process is essential for improving our knowledge of the marine environment. To gain insights into the microbial hydrocarbon degradation process in marine ecosystems, we collected crude oil from an active seep area in the Santa Barbara Channel (SBC) and generated approximately 52 gigabytes of raw metagenomic sequence data. The assembled data consisted of around 500 megabytes, representing approximately 1.1 million genes derived primarily from chemolithoautotrophic bacteria. While members of the Oceanospirillales bacterial order, which belongs to the Deltaproteobacteria, constituted less than 2% of the assembled genes within the SBC metagenome, they dominated the microbial community associated with the oil plume that developed in the aftermath of the Deepwater Horizon (DWH) blowout in 2010, comprising over 60% of the metagenomic data generated from the DWH oil plume. This suggests that Oceanospirillales may play a less significant role in microbially mediated hydrocarbon conversion within the SBC seep oil as compared to the DWH plume oil. We hypothesize that this difference results from the SBC oil seep being mostly anaerobic, while the DWH oil plume is aerobic. Within the Archaea, the phylum Euryarchaeota recruited more than 95% of the assembled archaeal sequences from the SBC oil seep metagenome, with over 50% of the sequences assigned to members of the orders Methanomicrobiales and Methanosarcinales. These orders contain organisms capable of anaerobic methanogenesis and methane oxidation (AOM) and we hypothesize that these orders, together with their metabolic capabilities, may be fundamental to the ecology of the SBC oil seep.

title: Hmga2 Promotes Neural Stem Cell Self-Renewal in Young but Not Old Mice by Reducing p16Ink4a and p19Arf Expression
text: Stem cells maintain their population throughout life by undergoing self-renewing divisions. However, the self-renewal capacity of these cells declines with age, partly due to increased expression of the tumor suppressor p16(Ink4a). Our research revealed that Hmga2, a transcriptional regulator, is highly expressed in fetal neural stem cells but declines with age. This decrease is partially attributed to the upregulation of let-7b microRNA, which targets HMGA2. Contrary to expectations, Hmga2-deficient mice exhibit reduced stem cell numbers and self-renewal in both the central and peripheral nervous systems, particularly in fetal and young-adult mice, but not old-adult mice. Subsequently, p16(Ink4a) and p19(Arf) expression was increased in Hmga2-deficient fetal and young-adult stem cells, and deleting p16(Ink4a) and/or p19(Arf) partially restored self-renewal capacity. In contrast, let-7b overexpression reduced Hmga2 and raised p16(Ink4a)/p19(Arf) expression. Our findings suggest that Hmga2 promote self-renewal of fetal and young-adult stem cells by reducing p16(Ink4a)/p19(Arf) expression. Aging-related changes in let-7 and Hmga2 expression contribute to the decline in neural stem cell function.

title: Genotoxic Stress Abrogates Renewal of Melanocyte Stem Cells by Triggering Their Differentiation
text: The depletion of somatic stem cells due to the accumulation of DNA damage has been implicated in the emergence of aging-related phenotypes. Hair graying, a common indicator of aging in mammals, is attributable to the inadequate maintenance of melanocyte stem cells (MSCs) over time. In a recent study, we discovered that exposure to ionizing radiation resulted in the irreversible depletion of MSCs in mice. Surprisingly, this DNA-damage response led not to the apoptosis or senescence of MSCs, but rather their differentiation into mature melanocytes within the niche. This debilitating phenomenon ultimately contributes to irreversible hair graying. Notably, the deficiency of Ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM), a pivotal kinase in the DNA-damage response, sensitizes MSCs to ectopic differentiation, indicating that ATM plays a crucial role in maintaining the stem cell quality and quantity by functioning as a "stemness checkpoint."

title: Gemcitabine chemoresistance and molecular markers associated with gemcitabine transport and metabolism in human pancreatic cancer cells
text: To identify predictive molecular markers for gemcitabine resistance, we investigated changes in the expression of four genes associated with gemcitabine transport and metabolism during the development of acquired gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer cell lines. The expression levels of human equilibrative nucleoside transporter-1 (hENT1), deoxycytidine kinase (dCK), RRM1, and RRM2 mRNA were analyzed by real-time light cycler-PCR in various subclones during the development of acquired resistance to gemcitabine. Real-time light cycler-PCR results showed that the expression levels of either RRM1 or RRM2 progressively increased during the development of gemcitabine resistance. Expression of dCK was slightly increased in cells resistant to lower concentrations of gemcitabine, but was decreased below the undetectable level in higher concentration-resistant subclones. Expression of hENT1 was increased in the development of gemcitabine resistance. We found that the ratio of hENT1 × dCK/RRM1 × RRM2 gene expression in gemcitabine-resistant subclones decreased progressively with the development of acquired resistance. Moreover, the expression ratio significantly correlated with gemcitabine sensitivity in eight pancreatic cancer cell lines, whereas no single gene expression level correlated with sensitivity. These findings suggest that the sensitivity of pancreatic cancer cells to gemcitabine is determined by the balance of these four factors involved in gemcitabine transport and metabolism. The ratio of the four gene expression levels correlates with acquired gemcitabine-resistance in pancreatic cancer cells and may be a useful predictive marker for the efficacy of gemcitabine therapy in pancreatic cancer patients.

title: The DNA Damage Machinery and Homologous Recombination Pathway Act Consecutively to Protect Human Telomeres
text: Telomeres act as a protective barrier against the misinterpretation of chromosome ends as DNA damage, thereby preventing the activation of DNA damage checkpoint proteins. However, a paradoxical relationship exists between telomere function and these checkpoint proteins, as the very proteins that are crucial for telomere maintenance, such as ATM and ATR, are also involved in detecting and responding to DNA damage. Until now, a comprehensive molecular model explaining this seemingly contradictory relationship has been lacking. Our investigation reveals that the DNA damage machinery interacts with telomeres in two distinct steps. Initially, the ATR-dependent machinery is attracted to telomeres before replication is complete, likely in response to the formation of single-stranded DNA arising from replication fork stalling. Subsequently, after replication, telomeres draw in ATM and the homologous recombination (HR) machinery. In vivo and in vitro experiments suggest that the HR machinery is essential for the formation of a specialized structure at telomere ends after replication, which is crucial for their proper functioning. Our findings indicate that the recognition of telomere ends as DNA damage is critical for the completion of end replication and for the acquisition of a structure that enables them to function optimally.

title: Sprouty1 Regulates Reversible Quiescence of a Self-Renewing Adult Muscle Stem Cell Pool during Regeneration
text:
Satellite cells are the stem cells responsible for maintaining and repairing skeletal muscle tissue. While they have the ability to self-renew and differentiate following transplantation, their role in endogenous muscle fiber repair remained unclear. The transcription factor Pax7 specifically identifies satellite cells and is crucial for establishing the adult satellite cell population. Using a lineage tracing approach, we discovered that after injury, quiescent adult Pax7(+) cells enter the cell cycle, with a subset returning to quiescence to replenish the satellite cell compartment, while the others contribute to muscle fiber formation.
We found that the expression of Sprouty1 (Spry1), a receptor tyrosine kinase signaling inhibitor, is present in quiescent Pax7(+) satellite cells in uninjured muscle. After injury, Spry1 expression is downregulated in proliferating myogenic cells, and it is reinduced as Pax7(+) cells re-enter quiescence. Our study reveals a role for Spry1 in the return to quiescence and maintenance of the satellite cell pool during muscle repair. This clarifies its important role in adult muscle stem cell biology and tissue repair.

title: Mechanosensitivity in the enteric nervous system
text: The enteric nervous system (ENS) automatically controls the muscles in the gut. Special nerve cells called mechanosensitive enteric neurons (MEN) start movement in the gut by responding to changes in the shape of the gut wall. MEN in the gut mostly respond to squeezing or stretching, rather than to pressure. Some MEN can respond to both squeezing and stretching. Up to 60% of the total number of nerve cells in the ENS can be activated by mechanical stress. When MEN are stimulated, they send electrical signals to other nerve cells. There are two groups of MEN based on how they respond to different types of pressure. One group responds to squeezing, and the other group responds to stretching. The nerve cells in these groups have different ways of adapting to pressure. For example, some nerve cells can quickly adapt to squeezing, while others adapt more slowly to stretching. All MEN have some common features. They receive signals from other nerve cells, are not very sensitive to pressure, and can perform different functions such as controlling other nerve cells or causing muscles to move. This raises the idea that MEN may be able to both sense and control muscle activity at the same time. The specific nerve channels or receptors that the different MEN groups use are not yet understood. Future research will need to incorporate these nerve cells into the neural circuits that control muscle activity. They may work together to control different types of muscle movements or control them separately.

title: Phosphorylation of centromeric histone H3 variant regulates chromosome segregation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
text: The histone H3 variant Centromeric histone H3 (CenH3) is crucial for chromosome segregation in eukaryotes. We investigate post-translational modifications of Saccharomyces cerevisiae CenH3, specifically the phosphorylation of Cse4. Our research demonstrates that mutations in the phosphorylation sites of Cse4 result in growth and chromosome segregation defects when combined with kinetochore mutants like okp1 and ame1. Through the use of a phosphoserine-specific antibody, we observe that the association of phosphorylated Cse4 with centromeres increases in response to defective microtubule attachment or reduced cohesion. We find that evolutionarily conserved Ipl1/Aurora B contributes to the phosphorylation of Cse4, as levels of phosphorylated Cse4 are reduced at centromeres in ipl1 strains in vivo, and in vitro assays show phosphorylation of Cse4 by Ipl1.
