Consistently, we observe that a phosphomimetic cse4-4SD mutant suppresses the temperature-sensitive growth of ipl1-2 and Ipl1 substrate mutants dam1 spc34 and ndc80, which are defective in chromosome biorientation. Moreover, cell biology approaches using a green fluorescent protein-labeled chromosome show that cse4-4SD suppresses chromosome segregation defects in dam1 spc34 strains. Taken together, our findings provide a comprehensive analysis of Cse4 phosphorylation in vivo and in vitro, shedding light on its role in ensuring faithful chromosome segregation.

title: Genome-wide analysis of estrogen receptor binding sites
text: The estrogen receptor (ER) is the primary transcriptional regulator of breast cancer phenotype and a key therapeutic target. By mapping all ER and RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) binding sites on a genome-wide scale, we identified authentic cis-regulatory sites and their corresponding target genes in breast cancer cells. Combining this database with gene expression data revealed distinct temporal mechanisms of estrogen-mediated gene regulation, particularly in the case of estrogen-suppressed genes. Moreover, this resource enabled the identification of cis-regulatory sites in previously unexplored regions of the genome and the cooperating transcription factors involved in estrogen signaling in breast cancer.

title: Replicative aging in yeast: the means to the end.
text: Advancements in aging research are accelerating, and an unexpected driver of this progress is the study of a single-celled eukaryote – yeast. The identification of genetic modulators of replicative life span in yeast is underway, alongside the discovery of the molecular events that accompany aging. Moreover, the conservation of longevity pathways between yeast and complex multicellular eukaryotes is being examined. This review first offers a brief retrospective on the evolution of yeast as a model for aging and then dives into recent breakthroughs that have propelled aging research forward, bridging gaps between yeast and mammalian aging research. Although the elusive answer to what drives aging remains a challenge, progress is being made rapidly towards a definitive solution.

title: Serum high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, metabolic profile, and breast cancer risk.
text:
The prevalence of metabolic syndrome, characterized by obesity, glucose intolerance, low serum high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), high serum triglycerides, and hypertension, is high and rising globally, including in parallel with an increasing incidence of breast cancer. Despite HDL-C's importance in the metabolic syndrome, its role in breast cancer remains unclear.
In two population-based screening surveys conducted between 1977 and 1987 among 38,823 Norwegian women aged 17-54 years, serum HDL-C levels were analyzed using enzymatic assays. Other variables such as height, weight, blood pressure, serum lipids, fat and energy intake, physical activity, parity, oral contraceptive use, hormone therapy use, alcohol intake, and smoking habit were also assessed. Cox proportional hazards modeling was used to compute the relative risk (RR) of breast cancer associated with serum HDL-C levels and to adjust for potential confounding variables. Stratified analyses were performed to evaluate effect modification by body mass index (BMI) and menopausal status. All statistical tests were two-sided.
During a median follow-up of 17.2 years, 708 cases of invasive breast cancer were identified. In multivariable analysis, the risk of postmenopausal breast cancer was inversely associated with quartile of HDL-C (P(trend) = 0.02). Among women with HDL-C above 1.64 mmol/L (highest quartile) versus below 1.20 mmol/L (lowest quartile), the relative risk was 0.75 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.58 to 0.97). The HDL-C association was confined to women with a BMI greater than or equal to 25 kg/m2, for whom the relative risk of postmenopausal breast cancer in those with HDL-C above 1.64 mmol/L versus below 1.20 mmol/L was 0.43 (95% CI = 0.28 to 0.67; P(trend) < 0.001; P(interaction) = 0.001).
In conclusion, low HDL-C, as part of the metabolic syndrome, is associated with an increased risk of postmenopausal breast cancer.

title: Prediction of Chemical-Protein Interactions Network with Weighted Network-Based Inference Method
text: Chemical-protein interaction (CPI) is the central focus of target identification and drug discovery. However, large-scale determination of CPI through in vitro or in vivo experiments poses significant challenges. In contrast, in silico prediction offers several advantages, including cost-effectiveness and high accuracy. Leveraging our previous success in drug-target interaction prediction through network-based inference (NBI) methodology, we have developed node- and edge-weighted NBI methods for CPI prediction. Two comprehensive CPI bipartite networks, extracted from the ChEMBL database, were utilized to evaluate the methods. The first network contains 4,741 compounds and 97 G protein-coupled receptors, while the second network consists of 2,827 compounds and 206 kinases. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) ranged from 0.73 to 0.83 for the external validation sets, indicating the reliability of the predictions. The edge-weighted NBI method revealed the weak-interaction hypothesis in the CPI network. Additionally, we validated our methods by predicting candidate targets for five approved drugs, including imatinib, dasatinib, sertindole, olanzapine, and ziprasidone. The molecular hypotheses and experimental evidence supporting these predictions were further provided, demonstrating the potential value of our methods in understanding the molecular basis of drug polypharmacology and drug repositioning.

title: Exploiting the yeast stress-activated signaling network to inform on stress biology and disease signaling
text: Healthy cells have complex systems in place to monitor their environment and respond accordingly when cellular stress arises. Whether stress is caused by external factors or internal defects, cells must be able to mount precise defenses. This often involves halting cell growth and progression, which helps to limit the transmission of damaged materials and reallocate cellular resources towards defense. The balance between defense and growth is a critical one in cells, with eukaryotic cells poorly understood in this regard. Our recent work on the stress-activated signaling network in budding yeast has shed light on the regulatory networks that control this decision, highlighting similarities between yeast and mammalian stress responses. By exploring these similarities, we can gain valuable insights into signaling defects in human cancers.

title: Cell Stem Cell Review FoxO Transcription Factors and Stem Cell Homeostasis: Insights from the Hematopoietic System
text: The FoxO (forkhead O) family of transcription factors plays a crucial role in various physiological processes, including cell cycle arrest, stress resistance, differentiation, apoptosis, and metabolism. Recent studies have demonstrated that FoxO-dependent signaling is essential for the long-term regenerative potential of the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) compartment. By regulating HSC response to physiological oxidative stress, quiescence, and survival, FoxO function is critical for maintaining the integrity of the HSC compartment. These findings provide evidence for the evolutionarily conserved role of FoxO in promoting stress resistance and longevity across a range of phylogenetic systems. Moreover, these observations have implications for aging in higher organisms and malignant stem cell biology, suggesting that FoxOs may play a significant role in maintaining and protecting stem cell compartments in multiple tissues.

title: A Teratocarcinoma-Like Human Embryonic Stem Cell (hESC) Line and Four hESC Lines Reveal Potentially Oncogenic Genomic Changes
text: The first Swiss human embryonic stem cell (hESC) line, CH-ES1, displays features of a malignant cell line. It originated from the only surviving blastomere of an embryo following cryopreservation, and its karyotype and tumorigenicity resemble those of teratocarcinoma cells more than other hESC lines. To investigate the molecular basis of its oncogenicity, we compared CH-ES1's chromosomal abnormalities and single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to those of the 2102Ep teratocarcinoma line and four hESC lines (H1, HS293, HS401, and SIVF-02) with normal G-banding results. Our findings revealed genomic gains and losses in CH-ES1, including increases in regions containing oncogenes, similar to those observed in teratocarcinomas. Notably, CH-ES1 is trisomic for chromosomes 1, 9, 12, 17, 19, and X. In contrast, even the karyotypically normal hESC lines showed significant genomic changes involving genes linked to cancer. The largest alterations were detected in the H1 line at passage number 56, with 5 Mb duplications in chromosomes 1q32.2 and 22q12.2 observed, although gains and losses were identified already at passage 22. These findings emphasize the importance of monitoring the acquisition of genetic changes by hESCs before their use in regenerative medicine applications and suggest that assessing these changes may help understand the mechanisms of oncogenesis.

title: The Association between Single-Nucleotide Polymorphisms of ORAI1 Gene and Breast Cancer in a Taiwanese Population
text:
Introduction:
Breast cancer is the most common type of cancer affecting women worldwide. Recent research has implicated the ORAI1 gene, which encodes components of store-operated calcium channels, in the progression and metastasis of breast cancer.
Methods:
In this study, we genotyped 384 female patients with breast cancer for five ORAI1 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with a minimum allele frequency (MAF) of >10% using a TaqMan allelic discrimination assay. We used chi-square analyses to compare the genotype and allelic frequencies between control and patient groups.
Results:
Our results showed that two ORAI1 SNPs (rs12320939 and rs12313273) were associated with estrogen receptors (ERs) positivity in breast cancer patients under a recessive model. After correcting for multiple testing using the Bonferroni correction, the significance remained. Additionally, rs12320939 was associated with lymph node involvement in breast cancer patients.
Conclusion:
Our study found that genetic polymorphisms in the ORAI1 gene were strongly associated with lymph node involvement and ERs positivity in breast cancer patients in a Taiwanese population. These findings suggest that ORAI1 may play a pivotal role in the progression and metastasis of breast cancer.

title: Noninvasive Imaging beyond the Diffraction Limit of 3D Dynamics in Thickly Fluorescent Specimens
text: Obtaining optical images of living organisms' dynamics involves balancing the spatial, temporal, and photosensitivity trade-offs. However, capturing rapid 3D dynamics in thick or densely fluorescent specimens proved problematic. Here, we present an innovative approach that combines ultrathin planar illumination created by scanned Bessel beams with super-resolution structured illumination microscopy to explore the dynamics of living specimens over many time points in three dimensions beyond the diffraction limit. We apply this method to study in vivo karyotyping of chromosomes during mitosis and discover unique cytoskeleton dynamics at the dorsal and ventral surfaces of fibroblasts. In contrast to spinning disk confocal microscopy, our method displays significantly reduced photodamage when imaging quick morphological changes in D. discoideum cells, and improved contrast and resolution at depth within developing C. elegans embryos. Bessel beam structured plane illumination thus offers valuable insights into complex biological phenomena requiring subcellular spatiotemporal details in a single or multiple cell context.

title: The Ndc80 Kinetochore Complex Forms Load-Bearing Attachments to Dynamic Microtubule Tips via Biased Diffusion
text:
In this study, we aim to elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying the kinetochore-microtubule interaction during mitosis, a crucial process that occurs in all eukaryotes. The kinetochore, located at the centromere region of a chromosome, plays a pivotal role in this process by coupling to the dynamically changing tips of microtubules. Although genetic, biochemical, and structural studies have implicated the Ndc80 complex as a direct point of contact between kinetochores and microtubules, the dynamic nature of this interaction is poorly understood.
To investigate this phenomenon, we employed in vitro techniques that allow for the manipulation and tracking of individual molecules. Our results demonstrate that the Ndc80 complex is capable of forming the dynamic and load-bearing attachments necessary for coupling kinetochores to the dynamic microtubule tips in vivo. Furthermore, we show that this coupling likely occurs through a biased diffusion mechanism, which is conserved across different species, from yeast to humans.
Our findings reveal how an ensemble of Ndc80 complexes may provide the necessary combination of plasticity and strength to maintain load-bearing tip attachments during both microtubule assembly and disassembly. This ensures the proper progression of mitosis and highlights the importance of the Ndc80 complex in this process. In summary, our study provides new insights into the dynamic nature of the kinetochore-microtubule interaction and its crucial role in mitosis, shedding light on the molecular mechanisms underlying this essential process.

title: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies are associated with a non-MS course in children
text:
Objective: To determine whether detecting myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies (MOG-Abs) in children presenting with acquired demyelinating syndrome (ADS) could predict a demyelination phenotype.
Method: Sixty-five children with a first episode of ADS (12 acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, 24 optic neuritis, 18 transverse myelitis, 11 other clinically isolated syndrome) were retrospectively identified from two national demyelination programs in the United Kingdom and France. Serum samples from these patients were tested for MOG-Abs using a cell-based assay at the time of their presentation. The presence of MOG-Abs was analyzed to predict the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) at a one-year follow-up.
Results: Of the 65 children evaluated, 23 (35%) had detectable MOG-Abs. Notably, the presence of MOG-Abs at the time of presentation significantly predicted a non-MS disease course at the one-year follow-up, with only two (9%) of the 23 MOG-Ab-positive patients being diagnosed with MS compared to 16 (38%) of the 42 MOG-Ab-negative patients (p = 0.019, Fisher exact test). The accuracy of MOG-Abs in predicting a non-MS disease course was found to be high, with a positive predictive value of 91% (95% confidence interval [CI] 72-99), negative predictive value of 38% (95% CI 24-54), positive likelihood ratio of 4.02 (CI 1.0-15.4), and odds ratio of 6.5 (CI 1.3-31.3).
Conclusions: This study found that MOG-Abs are present in 35% of children with ADS, across a range of demyelinating disorders, at the time of presentation. The presence of MOG-Abs can be useful in predicting a non-MS disease course at onset, with a high degree of accuracy. These findings suggest that MOG-Abs may be a valuable tool in the early identification of pediatric patients with a non-MS disease course.

title: Kidney paired donation and optimizing the use of live donor organs.
text: A recent study aimed to assess the potential impact of a national kidney paired donation (KPD) program, accompanied by an optimized matching algorithm, on the number and quality of transplants achievable. The study simulated pools of incompatible donor/recipient pairs and compared the results with currently used schemes in some centers and regions. The findings suggest that a national optimized matching algorithm would lead to more transplants (47.7% vs 42.0%, P<.001), better HLA concordance (3.0 vs 4.5 mismatched antigens; P<.001), more grafts surviving at 5 years (34.9% vs 28.7%; P<.001), and a reduction in the number of pairs required to travel (2.9% vs 18.4%; P<.0.001) compared to extending the currently used first-accept scheme to a national level. Additionally, highly sensitized patients would benefit significantly (2.3% vs 14.1% successfully matched; P<.001) from a national optimized scheme. Even if only 7% of patients awaiting kidney transplantation participated in an optimized national KPD program, the healthcare system could potentially save up to $750 million. The study concludes that a combination of a national KPD program and a mathematically optimized matching algorithm leads to more matches with lower HLA disparity, providing patients with greater opportunities to find high-quality matches and increasing the overall success of transplants.

title: Genetic Interaction between Mutations in c-Myb and the KIX Domains of CBP and p300 Affects Multiple Blood Cell Lineages and Influences Both Gene Activation and Repression
text: Adult blood cell production, or definitive hematopoiesis, depends on the transcription factor c-Myb. The closely related histone acetyltransferases CBP (CREBBP) and p300 (EP300) bind c-Myb through their KIX domains, and mice lacking a p300 KIX domain mutation exhibit blood defects. However, mice lacking the same KIX domain mutation in CBP have normal blood. To investigate, we tested the hypothesis that the CBP KIX domain plays a subordinate role in hematopoiesis through a genetic interaction with c-Myb. We assessed hematopoiesis in mice with mutations in c-Myb and/or the KIX domains of CBP and p300, and measured the impact of KIX domain mutations on c-Myb-dependent gene expression. Our findings show that in the context of a p300 KIX mutation, a CBP KIX domain mutation affects platelets, B cells, T cells, and red blood cells. Gene interaction analysis provides mechanistic evidence that blood defects in KIX mutant mice are due to reduced c-Myb and KIX interaction. Additionally, we demonstrate that the CBP and p300 KIX domains contribute to both c-Myb-dependent gene activation and repression. These results suggest that the KIX domains of CBP, and especially p300, are the primary mediators of c-Myb-dependent gene activation and repression required for definitive hematopoiesis.

title: Comparative determinants of 4-year cardiovascular event rates in stable outpatients at risk of or with atherothrombosis.
text:
Clinicians and trialists have struggled to identify which patients are at highest risk for cardiovascular events. Prior ischemic events, polyvascular disease, and diabetes mellitus have been recognized as predictors of ischemic events, but the relative contributions of these factors to future risk remain unclear.
To categorize the risk of cardiovascular events in stable outpatients with various initial manifestations of atherothrombosis using simple clinical descriptors.
Outpatients with coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, or peripheral arterial disease, or with multiple risk factors for atherothrombosis, were enrolled in the global Reduction of Atherothrombosis for Continued Health (REACH) Registry and followed up for up to 4 years. Patients from 3647 centers in 29 countries were enrolled between 2003 and 2004 and followed up until 2008. The final database lock was in April 2009.
The primary outcome measures were rates of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke.
A total of 45,227 patients with baseline data were included in this 4-year analysis. During the follow-up period, a total of 5481 patients experienced at least 1 event, including 2315 with cardiovascular death, 1228 with myocardial infarction, 1898 with stroke, and 40 with both a myocardial infarction and stroke on the same day. Among patients with atherothrombosis, those with a prior history of ischemic events at baseline (n = 21,890) had the highest rate of subsequent ischemic events (18.3%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 17.4%-19.1%); patients with stable coronary, cerebrovascular, or peripheral artery disease (n = 15,264) had a lower risk (12.2%; 95% CI, 11.4%-12.9%); and patients without established atherothrombosis but with risk factors only (n = 8073) had the lowest risk (9.1%; 95% CI, 8.3%-9.9%) (P < .001 for all comparisons). In addition, in multivariable modeling, the presence of diabetes (hazard ratio [HR], 1.44; 95% CI, 1.36-1.53; P < .001), an ischemic event in the previous year (HR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.57-1.85; P < .001), and polyvascular disease (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.78-2.24; P < .001) each were associated with a significantly higher risk of the primary end point.
Clinical descriptors can assist clinicians in identifying high-risk patients within the broad range of risk for outpatients with atherothrombosis.

title: The association between sterilizing activity and drug distribution into tuberculosis lesions
text: Discovering new antibiotics that can shorten treatment times and combat the growing menace of drug resistance is the primary goal of tuberculosis (TB) drug development. By utilizing a MALDI (matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization) mass spectrometry imaging suite in a biosafety containment facility, we have demonstrated that the essential antibiotics rifampicin and pyrazinamide effectively penetrate sites of TB infection in lung lesions. Rifampicin even accumulates in necrotic caseum, a crucial lesion site where persistent tubercle bacilli reside, in contrast to moxifloxacin, which exhibits limited diffusion in caseum despite its in vitro activity against a subpopulation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. These findings suggest that the uneven spatial distribution and kinetics of drug accumulation within lesions may create temporary and spatial windows of monotherapy in specific niches, allowing the gradual development of multidrug-resistant TB. We propose an alternative model for prioritizing new antibiotic combinations based on the quantitative and spatial distribution of TB drugs within the various lesion types found in human lungs. Our discovery that lesion penetration influences treatment outcomes has significant implications for TB management.

title: Notch signaling: cell fate control and signal integration in development.
text: Notch signaling is an evolutionarily ancient cell interaction mechanism that plays a crucial role in the development of metazoans. Through the exchange of signals between nearby cells, the Notch receptor can enhance and consolidate cell-to-cell differences, ultimately determining the fate of individual cells. Notch signals regulate how cells respond to both intrinsic and extrinsic developmental cues, allowing them to execute specific developmental programs. Notch activity governs the execution of differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis programs, acting as a general developmental tool that influences organ formation and morphogenesis. In essence, Notch signaling is a fundamental mechanism that orchestrates the complex process of cellular communication and cooperation during embryonic development.

title: A long non-coding RNA signature to improve prognosis prediction of colorectal cancer
text: An accumulation of evidence suggests that long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are frequently anomalously expressed in cancer, yet only a few related lncRNA signatures have been established for predicting cancer prognosis. Our goal was to develop a lncRNA signature for improving the prediction of colorectal cancer (CRC) prognosis. Utilizing a lncRNA-mining approach, we performed lncRNA expression profiling in large CRC cohorts from Gene Expression Omulus (GEO), including the GSE39582 test series (N=436), an internal validation series (N=117); and two independent validation series, GSE14333 (N=197) and GSE17536 (N=145). We identified a set of six lncRNAs that were significantly correlated with disease-free survival (DFS) in the test series. Based on this six-lncRNA signature, patients in the test series could be grouped into high-risk and low-risk subgroups with significantly different DFS (HR=2.670; P<0.0001). The prognostic value of this six-lncRNA signature was confirmed in the internal validation series and two additional independent CRC sets. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) showed that the risk score positively correlated with various cancer metastasis-related pathways. Functional experiments revealed that three dysregulated lncRNAs, AK123657, BX648207, and BX649059, were required for efficient invasion and proliferation suppression in CRC cell lines. Our findings may provide an efficient tool for evaluating the clinical prognosis of CRC.

title: Clinical use of bone densitometry: scientific review.
text:
Osteoporosis causes significant morbidity and annually costs $13.8 billion in the United States. Measuring bone mass through densitometry is a crucial step in diagnosing osteoporosis and determining an appropriate treatment plan. Bone mineral densitometry has become more widely available and commonly used in practice.
The objective of this review is to assess the value of various clinical applications of bone densitometry. A MEDLINE search was conducted to update previous meta-analyses of the relationship between different measures of bone density and the risk of vertebral and hip fractures. Data from the prospective Study of Osteoporotic Fractures were used to estimate the risk of fracture based on bone density and age in postmenopausal white women.
The review emphasizes meta-analyses and systematic reviews when available. Bone mineral density (BMD) predicts fracture and can be combined with age to estimate absolute fracture risk in postmenopausal white women. Hip BMD predicts hip fracture more strongly than other BMD measurements. However, there is insufficient data to translate BMD results into fracture risk for men and non-white women. The benefit of fracture prevention treatments depends on BMD, with women with osteoporosis having a greater risk of fractures and greater benefit from treatments than those without osteoporosis.
Guidelines based on systematic reviews and a cost-effectiveness analysis suggest that measuring BMD in white women over 65 years old and potentially using risk factors to select younger postmenopausal women for densitometry is worthwhile. Other potential clinical applications of BMD that have not been adequately studied include screening men and non-white women, monitoring BMD in patients receiving treatment, and using BMD to identify patients who should be evaluated for secondary causes of osteoporosis.

title: Vascular Calcifying Progenitor Cells Possess Bidirectional Differentiation Potentials
text: Vascular calcification is a complex phenomenon that lacks an effective treatment option. In this study, we aimed to investigate the modulation or reversal of calcification by identifying and investigating the calcifying/decalcifying potential of progenitor cells. We used cells from the aortas of mice and sorted them into four groups based on the expression of Sca-1 and PDGFRα markers. Our results showed that Sca-1(+) progenitor cells have greater osteoblastic differentiation potential than Sca-1(-) progenitor cells. Among Sca-1(+) progenitor populations, Sca-1(+)/PDGFRα(-) cells exhibited bidirectional differentiation potential towards both osteoblastic and osteoclastic lineages, while Sca-1(+)/PDGFRα(+) cells differentiated into an osteoblastic lineage unidirectionally. When treated with a PPARγ agonist, Sca-1(+)/PDGFRα(-) cells preferentially differentiated into osteoclast-like cells. Our findings suggest that a subtype of bone marrow-derived and vessel-resident progenitor cells could be a therapeutic target for preventing vascular calcification. Furthermore, activation of PPARγ may be an option to reverse calcification.

title: Physiological relevance of cell cycle kinases.
text: The foundational study on the cell division cycle and its regulation by protein kinases was initially conducted in yeast and other model organisms. This pioneering work identified key regulatory mechanisms that are conserved in mammals. However, recent research in various cell types and genetic models has provided a new perspective on the function of these major cell cycle regulators in different tissues. Here, we review the physiological significance of mammalian cell cycle kinases, including cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks), Aurora and Polo-like kinases, and mitotic checkpoint regulators (Bub1, BubR1, and Mps1), as well as less-studied enzymes such as Cdc7, Nek proteins, or Mastl. We discuss their roles in development, tissue homeostasis, and human disease, with a particular emphasis on the control of self-renewal or asymmetric cell division in stem/progenitor cells and the ability to regenerate injured tissues. Additionally, we highlight their previously unexpected functions in metabolism, cardiovascular function, or neuron biology, and the potential therapeutic benefits of modulating their enzymatic activity in human disease. Overall, this review provides a comprehensive overview of the importance of mammalian cell cycle kinases in maintaining cellular homeostasis and their potential as therapeutic targets for various diseases.

title: Matrix Metalloproteinase 1 Is Necessary for the Migration of Human Bone Marrow-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells Toward Human Glioma
text: Human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have increasingly been utilized as cellular vectors for delivering therapeutic genes to tumors. However, the underlying mechanism of cellular mobilization remains inadequately understood. In this investigation, MSCs displaying similar cell surface markers and multilineage differentiation potential were isolated from various donors. Notably, distinct MSC isolates displayed varied migration ability towards human glioma cells. We hypothesized that unique molecular signals might be responsible for the varying tumor tropisms exhibited by different MSC isolates. To test this hypothesis, we compared the gene expression profiles of tumor-trophic MSCs with those of non-tumor-trophic MSCs. Our findings revealed that matrix metalloproteinase 1 (MMP1) gene expression and protein activity were elevated by 27-fold and 21-fold, respectively, in highly migratory MSCs compared to poorly migratory MSCs. Functional inactivation of MMP1 abrogated the migratory potential of MSCs towards glioma-conditioned medium. Conversely, rescuing the non-migratory phenotype of poorly migratory MSCs with either recombinant MMP1 or conditioned medium from highly migratory MSCs rendered the cells responsive to the signaling cues from glioma cells in vivo. Moreover, blocking the interaction of MMP1 and its cognate receptor, PAR1, diminished the migratory ability of MSCs. Taken together, this study provides the first evidence that MMP1 is crucially involved in the migration capacity of MSCs, acting through the MMP1/PAR1 axis.

title: Bullying in school: are short pupils at risk? Questionnaire study in a cohort.
text:
Bullying remains a prevalent issue in schools and can have detrimental effects on its victims. Research has shown that bullying can lead to antisocial behavior in adulthood and that victims are generally weaker than their bullies. This suggests that shorter students are more likely to be victims and less likely to be the aggressors.
To investigate this further, the Wessex growth study surveyed 92 shortnormal adolescents who were below the third centile for height at school entry, as well as 117 controls matched for age and sex. These participants completed a bullying questionnaire based on work by Whitney and Smith. There were no significant differences in sex or social class between the groups, and the mean age (range) was 14.7 (13.4-15.7) years. The mean height SD scores were: short pupils −1.90 (−3.53 to −0.01), controls 0.31 (−1.41 to 0.30).
Note: The term "short normal" is used in the original text to describe the participants who were below the third centile for height at school entry. In this rewritten version, the term "shorter students" is used to make the language more clear and concise.

title: Inflammasome-induced IL-1β secretion in microglia is characterized by delayed kinetics and is only partially dependent on inflammatory caspases.
text: Inflammasomes are multicomponent complexes that connect host defense and stress signaling to the processing of the pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-1β (IL-1β). Although inflammasome activation has been well-studied in hematopoietic macrophages and dendritic cells, less is known about microglia, the resident tissue macrophages of the brain that originate from a distinct progenitor. To compare inflammasome-mediated activation in different types of macrophages, we isolated primary microglia and hematopoietic macrophages from adult, healthy rhesus macaques. We examined the expression profiles of NOD (nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain)-like receptors, adaptor proteins, and caspases and elucidated inflammasome activation and regulation in great detail. Here, we demonstrate that primary microglia respond to the same innate stimuli as hematopoietic macrophages. However, microglial responses are more persistent due to the lack of negative regulation on pro-IL-1β expression. In contrast, while caspase 1, 4, and 5 activation is crucial for inflammasome-induced IL-1β secretion by hematopoietic macrophages, microglial secretion of IL-1β is only partially reliant on these inflammatory caspases. These findings highlight key cell type-specific differences that may inform the development of strategies to modulate innate immune responses in the brain.

title: microRNA-29a suppresses cell proliferation by targeting SPARC in hepatocellular carcinoma.
text: In the current study, we created a lentivirus vector encoding the miR-29a precursor and established two stable cell lines, PLC-29a and 97L-29a, which overexpress miR-29a. TaqMan RT-PCR confirmed the overexpression of miR-29a, and its inhibition of the growth of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cell lines MHCC-97L and PLC was observed. Dual-luciferase reporter assays showed that miR-29a directly targets the 3' untranslated region (UTR) of SPARC mRNA. Silencing SPARC expression by RNAi knockdown resulted in a similar effect as miR-29a overexpression on HCC cell growth regulation. Moreover, we found that miR-29a levels were significantly lower in HCC tissues compared to nearby non-cancerous liver tissues from 110 patients with HCC, suggesting that the expression of miR-29a is important in the regulation of the SPARC-AKT pathway and HCC growth.

title: Another Barrier to Regeneration in the CNS: Activated Macrophages Induce Extensive Retraction of Dystrophic Axons through Direct Physical Interactions
text: Injured axons in the adult central nervous system (CNS) suffer lengthy retraction from the initial site of injury after spinal cord injury, a process accompanied by macrophage infiltration. While the inflammatory cells' direct involvement in this process has been unclear, our study sheds light on the matter. Using in vivo and in vitro experiments, we investigated the role of macrophages in axonal retraction within the dorsal columns after spinal cord injury and found that retraction occurs between days 2 and 28 post-lesion, with ED-1+ cells associated with the ends of injured axons. We also determined that depleting infiltrating macrophages using clodronate liposomes resulted in a significant reduction in axonal retraction. Our findings shed light on the mechanism of axonal retraction, revealing that macrophage-axon interactions are essential for this process. Time-lapse imaging of adult dorsal root ganglion neurons in an in vitro model of the glial scar showed that adhesive contacts and physical interplay between macrophages and dystrophic axons lead to extensive axonal retraction. Our results indicate that only dystrophic adult axons are susceptible to macrophage "attack," and both primary macrophages and microglia require activation to induce axonal retraction. Surprisingly, contact with astrocytes had no deleterious effect on adult dystrophic axons, suggesting that the induction of extensive retraction is specific to phagocytic cells. Our findings demonstrate a direct role of activated macrophages in axonal retraction through physical cell-cell interactions with injured axons.

title: Large-Scale Movements of IF3 and tRNA during Bacterial Translation Initiation
text: In the process of bacterial translation initiation, three factors (IFs 1-3) play a crucial role in selecting the initiator tRNA and identifying the start codon on the 30S ribosomal subunit. To shed light on this process, we have obtained 11 single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) reconstructions of the complex formed between the 30S subunit, initiator tRNA, mRNA, and IFs 1-3, revealing different stages of the initiation pathway. IF1 provides essential anchoring points for IF2 and IF3, which in turn enhance their functions. IF2 adopts an extended conformation that enables it to capture the formylmethionyl group on tRNA, while IF3 undergoes significant conformational changes to accommodate the formylmethionyl-tRNA (fMet-tRNA(fMet)) in the P site for start codon recognition.

title: Corresponding Author:
text: In higher eukaryotes, introns are excised from protein-coding mRNAs via the spliceosome, a massive complex composed of five non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) and approximately 200 proteins. By analyzing the divergence of spliceosomal proteins across various basal eukaryotic lineages, it is possible to infer properties of the splicing system in the last common ancestor of extant eukaryotes, as well as the eukaryotic ancestor itself. We propose that, just as intron length has increased in multicellular eukaryotes, the spliceosome has also become more complex throughout eukaryotic evolution. However, the examination of spliceosomal component distribution suggests that all key components found in modern eukaryotes were already present in the eukaryotic ancestor, including small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) protein components and many splicing-related proteins. Both major and trans-splicing are likely to have been present, and the spliceosome had likely formed connections with other cellular processes such as transcription and capping. However, there is currently no evidence indicating that U12-dependent minor splicing was present in the eukaryotic ancestor. While the last common ancestor of extant eukaryotes appears to possess significant molecular complexity, inference about earlier stages in eukaryotic evolution is not possible from this study.

title: 2D and 3D Stem Cell Models of Primate Cortical Development Identify Species-Specific Differences in Progenitor Behavior Contributing to Brain Size.
text:
Researchers have long believed that variations in the size and complexity of the cerebral cortex are responsible for cognitive differences between humans and other animals. To investigate this further, scientists compared cortical progenitor cell output in humans and three nonhuman primates using directed differentiation of pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) in both adherent two-dimensional (2D) and organoid three-dimensional (3D) culture systems.
Clonal lineage analysis revealed that cortical progenitors in primates proliferate for a longer time period, producing early-born neurons, compared to rodents, where this expansion phase ceases before neurogenesis begins. The extent of this additional cortical progenitor expansion differs among primates, resulting in variations in the number of neurons generated by each progenitor cell. Interestingly, the regulation of cortical size through this mechanism occurs cell autonomously in culture, suggesting that individual cortical progenitor cell clonal output plays a role in regulating primate cerebral cortex size.

title: Multicolor “DiOlistic” Labeling of the Nervous System Using Lipophilic Dye Combinations
text: We present a novel technique for rapid labeling of a large number of cells in the nervous system using multiple colors. By utilizing lipophilic dye-coated particles delivered via a "gene gun" to neuronal preparations, individual neurons and glia that come into contact with the particles are rapidly labeled. By using particles coated with different combinations of various lipophilic dyes, many cells within a complex neuronal network can be simultaneously labeled with a wide range of colors. This approach is most effective in living tissue but also labels previously fixed tissue. In living tissue, labeled neurons continue to exhibit normal synaptic activity and undergo dendritic remodeling. This technique provides a valuable means of studying the structural plasticity of neuronal circuits in living tissue. Furthermore, the Golgi-like labeling of neurons with multiple colors offers a novel approach to investigating neuronal connectivity.

title: A DNA test to sex most birds.
text: Birds are challenging to sex due to the lack of sex-linked physical characteristics in nestlings, making it difficult to determine the sex of adult birds in over 50% of bird species worldwide. This limitation hinders both evolutionary studies and human-assisted breeding of birds. However, DNA-based sex identification provides a solution. We have developed a test that uses two conserved CHD (chromo-helicase-DNA-binding) genes located on the avian sex chromosomes of all birds, with the exception of ratites (ostriches and related birds). The CHD-W gene is located on the W chromosome and is exclusive to females, while the other gene, CHD-Z, is found on the Z chromosome and occurs in both sexes, with the female version being ZW and the male version being ZZ. The test utilizes PCR with a single set of primers to amplify homologous sections of both genes and detect intron differences. In males, a single CHD-Z band is visible on a gel, while females exhibit a second, distinct CHD-W band.

title: Evidence that Embryonic Neurons Regulate the Onset of Cortical Gliogenesis via Cardiotrophin-1
text: Precursor cells in the developing embryonic cortex undergo a sequential process of generating neurons followed by glial cells, however, the mechanisms that control this transition are not well understood. Using cortical precursor cultures that mimic the in vivo differentiation pattern, we have shown that cortical neurons produce and secrete the neurotrophic cytokine cardiotrophin-1. This cytokine triggers the gp130-JAK-STAT pathway and is essential for the timely generation of astrocytes in vitro. Our findings suggest that a similar process occurs in vivo. In utero electroporation of neurotrophic cytokines in the environment of embryonic cortical precursors leads to premature gliogenesis, while disrupting the gp130 signaling pathway delays the normal timely appearance of astrocytes. Furthermore, the neonatal cardiotrophin-1-deficient cortex contains fewer astrocytes. These results highlight a neural feedback mechanism in which newly born neurons produce cardiotrophin-1, which instructs multipotent cortical precursors to generate astrocytes, thereby ensuring that gliogenesis occurs after neurogenesis is mostly complete.

title: The Inhibition of TDP-43 Mitochondrial Localization Blocks Its Neuronal Toxicity
text:
Genetic mutations in the gene encoding TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TARDBP, also known as TDP-43) lead to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a debilitating neurodegenerative disease. An accumulation of TDP-43 in the cytoplasm is a hallmark of various neurodegenerative diseases. However, the underlying mechanisms by which TDP-43 contributes to ALS pathophysiology remain unclear. Our recent findings reveal that TDP-43 accumulates in the mitochondria of neurons in individuals with ALS or frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Disease-associated mutations further increase TDP-43's mitochondrial localization. Within the mitochondria, TDP-43 interacts specifically with messenger RNAs (mRNAs) encoding subunits of respiratory complex I, including ND3 and ND6. These interactions lead to a decline in the expression of these subunits and the breakdown of complex I, a crucial bioenergetic process.
We found that suppressing TDP-43's mitochondrial localization abolishes the mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal loss caused by TDP-43 mutations in transgenic mouse models. These findings suggest that targeting TDP-43's mitochondrial localization may offer a promising therapeutic strategy for treating neurodegenerative diseases.
In summary, this study uncovers a novel mechanism by which TDP-43 contributes to ALS pathophysiology through its mitochondrial localization. By targeting TDP-43's mitochondrial localization, we may be able to develop new therapeutic approaches for treating neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Effect on the quality of peer review of blinding reviewers and asking them to sign their reports: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Anxiety about bias, lack of accountability, and poor quality of peer review has led to questions about the imbalance in anonymity between reviewers and authors. To investigate whether blinding reviewers to the authors' identities and requiring them to sign their reports could improve the quality of peer review, we conducted a randomized controlled trial.
Setting: A general medical journal.
Participants: A total of 420 reviewers from the journal's database.
Intervention: We modified a paper accepted for publication to introduce 8 areas of weakness. Reviewers were randomly allocated to 5 groups. Groups 1 and 2 received manuscripts from which the authors' names and affiliations had been removed, while groups 3 and 4 were aware of the authors' identities. Groups 1 and 3 were asked to sign their reports, while groups 2 and 4 were asked to return their reports unsigned. The fifth group was sent the paper in the usual manner of the journal, with authors' identities revealed and a request to comment anonymously. Group 5 differed from group 4 only in that its members were unaware that they were taking part in a study.
Main outcome measure: The number of weaknesses in the paper that were commented on by the reviewers.
Results: Reports were received from 221 reviewers (53%). The mean number of weaknesses commented on was 2 (1.7, 2.1, 1.8, and 1.9 for groups 1, 2, 3, and 4 and 5 combined, respectively). There were no statistically significant differences between groups in their performance. Reviewers who were blinded to authors' dentities were less likely to recommend rejection than those who were aware of the authors' identities (odds ratio, 0.5; 95% confidence interval, 0.3-1.0).
Conclusions: Neither blinding reviewers to the authors and origin of the paper nor requiring them to sign their reports had any effect on the rate of detection of errors. Such measures are unlikely to improve the quality of peer review reports.

title: 2001. Comparison of three management strategies for patients with atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance. Baseline results from a randomized trial
text:
More than 2 million US women receive an uncertain cervical cytology diagnosis (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance [ASCUS]) annually. Effective colposcopy triage strategies are needed to distinguish between those with underlying disease and those without, without excessive follow-up testing.
The ASCUS/LSIL (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) Triage Study (ALTS) is a multicenter randomized trial comparing the sensitivity and specificity of three management strategies for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 (CIN3): immediate colposcopy (considered the reference standard), HPV testing with cytology results, or cytology results alone. This article reports on the enrollment results for 3488 women with a referral diagnosis of ASCUS.
The underlying prevalence of histologically confirmed CIN3 among participants with ASCUS was 5.1%. HPV testing had a sensitivity of 96.3% (95% CI: 91.6-98.8%) for detecting CIN3 or above, with 56.1% referred to colposcopy. Sensitivity of a single repeat cytology specimen with a triage threshold of HSIL or above was 44.1% (95% CI: 35.6-52.9%), with 6.9% referred. Sensitivity of a lower cytology triage threshold of ASCUS or above was 85.3% (95% CI: 78.2-90.8%), with 58.6% referred.
HC2 testing for cancer-associated HPV DNA is a viable alternative for managing women with ASCUS. It has greater sensitivity for detecting CIN3 or above, and its specificity is comparable to a single additional cytologic test indicating ASCUS or above.

title: Cell Stem Cell Article In Vivo Fate Analysis Reveals the Multipotent and Self-Renewal Capacities of Sox2 + Neural Stem Cells in the Adult Hippocampus
text: To delve into the characteristics of adult neural stem cells (NSCs), we utilized Sox2-GFP transgenic mice for generation and analysis. Within the subgranular zone (SGZ), Sox2-GFP cells exhibit markers indicative of progenitors, yet they comprise two distinct populations with differently elevated proliferation rates. Lentivirus- and retrovirus-based fate-tracing studies revealed that Sox2-positive cells in the SGZ have the potential to give rise to both neurons and astrocytes, underscoring their multifaceted nature at both the population and single-cell levels. A subset of Sox2-positive cells produces progeny that retain Sox2, highlighting Sox2-positive cells as the primary source of adult NSCs. In response to mitotic signals, increased proliferation of Sox2-positive cells is coupled with the generation of Sox2-positive NSCs and neuronal precursors. It is possible that an asymmetric distribution of Sox2-positive NSCs may play a crucial role in maintaining a constant size of the NSC pool while also producing newly generated neurons during adult neurogenesis.

title: Past exposure to sun, skin phenotype, and risk of multiple sclerosis: case-control study.
text:
Objective: To investigate whether past high levels of sun exposure are linked to a reduced risk of multiple sclerosis.
Design: Population-based case-control study.
Setting: Tasmania, latitudes 41-3 degrees South.
Participants: 136 cases with multiple sclerosis and 272 controls randomly selected from the community and matched on sex and year of birth.
Main Outcome Measure: Multiple sclerosis defined by both clinical and magnetic resonance imaging criteria.
Results: Higher sun exposure during the ages of 6-15 (averaging 2-3 hours or more per day during summer weekends and holidays) was associated with a lower risk of multiple sclerosis (adjusted odds ratio 0.31, 95% confidence interval 0.16 to 0.59). Greater exposure in winter appeared more important than in summer. Additionally, greater actinic damage was independently associated with a decreased risk of multiple sclerosis (0.32, 0.11 to 0.88 for grades 4-6 disease). A dose-response relation was found between multiple sclerosis and decreasing sun exposure during the ages of 6-15 and with actinic damage.
Conclusion: Higher levels of sun exposure during childhood and early adolescence are associated with a reduced risk of multiple sclerosis. It is possible that inadequate ultraviolet radiation exposure may contribute to the development of multiple sclerosis.

title: Endocytic Trafficking of Rac Is Required for the Spatial Restriction of Signaling in Cell Migration
text: The small GTPases Rab5 and Rac are crucial for the proper execution of endocytosis and actin remodeling, respectively. Coordinating these processes is essential to achieve spatial restriction of intracellular signaling, which is necessary for a variety of cellular functions, including polarized cell behaviors. Our findings reveal that endocytosis mediated by clathrin and Rab5 is required for the activation of Rac triggered by signaling molecules. Rac activation occurs on early endosomes, where the Rac Guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) Tiam1 is also recruited. Subsequent recycling of Rac to the plasma membrane allows for localized signaling, leading to the formation of actin-based migratory protrusions. Therefore, the trafficking of Rac through the endocytic pathway is crucial for the precise spatial resolution of Rac-dependent signaling. Our studies also demonstrate that a Rab5-Rac circuitry regulates the morphology of motile mammalian tumor cells and primordial germinal cells during zebrafish development, suggesting that this circuitry is crucial for controlling migratory programs in various cell types, both in vitro and in vivo.

title: Significance of stem cell marker Nanog gene in the diagnosis and prognosis of lung cancer
text: The current study aimed to investigate the potential of the Nanog gene as a diagnostic and prognostic marker for lung cancer. A total of 100 patients diagnosed with lung cancer between April 2013 and May 2015 were enrolled in the study, of which 50 were categorized as lung cancer (group A) and 50 as squamous cell lung carcinoma (group B). Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) was used to detect cancer and adjacent tissues, and Nanog gene expression was evaluated in both patient groups. Our findings showed that there was no significant difference in age, gender, disease stage, or lymph node metastasis between the two groups. However, Nanog gene expression in patients with carcinoma was significantly higher than in adjacent tissues (p < 0.05). Moreover, differentiated and well-differentiated carcinoma tissue showed higher Nanog gene expression than poorly differentiated and undifferentiated carcinoma (p < 0.05). In addition, the expression of Nanog in normal cells was significantly higher than in normal lung tissues and benign lesions in lung cancer stem cells. Additionally, we observed that Nanog was highly expressed in CD44+ cells, and Nanog expression in lung cancer stem cells was significantly higher (p < 0.05). Our results suggest that the expression of the Nanog gene is significantly higher in patients with stage III and IV lung cancer compared to stage I and II disease. Furthermore, higher Nanog expression was associated with a lower degree of cell differentiation in lung cancer. These findings suggest that the Nanog gene may serve as a useful biomarker for the diagnosis and prognosis of lung cancer.

title: Current knowledge and future directions of TLR and NOD signaling in sepsis
text: Over time, the incidence of sepsis has been on the rise, accompanied by an elevated risk of mortality from the condition. The US witnesses a substantial financial burden of sepsis care annually. Death from sepsis is understood to be a complex process that arises from the failure of the body's immune system to maintain homeostasis in the presence of microbial pathogens. Initially discovered in Drosophila, the Toll-like receptor (TLR) family plays a critical role in recognizing microbial pathogens through their ability to sense invading microorganisms and trigger intracellular signal transduction pathways. The NOD signaling pathway, which is also involved in bacteria recognition, synergizes with the TLR family in coordinating an effective immune response for eradicating invading microbial pathogens. TLRs and NOD1/NOD2 detect different pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Research into modulating TLR and NOD signaling has generated significant interest as a potential therapeutic approach for managing sepsis, but to date, none of the targeted molecules have demonstrated efficacy in clinical trials.

title: Concentration Sensing by the Moving Nucleus in Cell Fate Determination: A Computational Analysis
text:
During the development of the vertebrate neuroepithelium, the nucleus in neural progenitor cells (NPCs) undergoes interkinetic nuclear migration, moving from the apex towards the base and then back to the apex, before dividing. The fate of the resulting daughter cells is thought to depend on the sampling by the moving nucleus of a spatial concentration profile of the cytoplasmic Notch Intracellular Domain (NICD). However, the complex stochastic motions of the nucleus, including random waiting and back-and-forth movements, can expose the nucleus to varying levels of cytoplasmic NICD throughout its journey. Despite the stochastic nature of nuclear migration, we aimed to investigate how the position of the nucleus can determine the fate of daughter cells.
To address this question, we developed a mathematical model that accounts for reaction, diffusion, and nuclear accumulation of NICD in NPCs during interkinetic nuclear migration (INM). Utilizing experimentally measured trajectory-dependent probabilities of nuclear turning, waiting times, and average nuclear speeds in NPCs of the developing zebrafish retina, we performed stochastic simulations to compute the nuclear trajectory-dependent probabilities of NPC differentiation. Comparison with experimentally measured nuclear NICD concentrations and trajectory-dependent probabilities of differentiation enabled the estimation of the NICD cytoplasmic gradient.
Our findings reveal that spatially polarized production of NICD, rapid NICD cytoplasmic consumption, and the time-averaging effect of nuclear import/export kinetics are sufficient to explain the experimentally observed differentiation probabilities. Our computational studies provide quantitative support for the nuclear concentration-sensing mechanism for NPC fate determination in the zebrafish retina.

title: Odorant-specific adaptation pathways generate olfactory plasticity in C. elegans
text: After prolonged exposure to an odorant, the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans experiences a reduced response to the odorant for several hours. This specific olfactory adaptation is odorant-specific, meaning that animals can adapt independently to different odorants detected by a single pair of olfactory neurons called the AWC neurons. The genetic basis of olfactory adaptation is complex, involving multiple genes that are required for adaptation to different odorants. Animals lacking the gene adp-1 fail to adapt to a subset of AWC-sensed odorants, and this adp-1-related process is dependent on calcium. Conversely, mutations in the gene osm-9 affect adaptation to a different but overlapping subset of AWC-sensed odorants. Notably, mutations in adp-1 and osm-9 do not impair the ability of unadapted animals to respond to odorants, emphasizing that odorant sensation and odorant adaptation are distinct processes.

title: Genome-wide dFOXO targets and topology of the transcriptomic response to stress and insulin signalling
text: FoxO transcription factors, whose activity is suppressed by insulin/insulin-like growth factor signaling (IIS), play a central role in numerous physiological processes across different organisms. By employing genomic tools, we uncovered over 700 direct target genes of dFOXO in adult female Drosophila. dFOXO is crucial for the transcription of several IIS components and interacting signaling pathways, such as the TOR pathway, in wild-type flies. The genomic locations occupied by dFOXO in adults differ from those observed in larvae or cultured cells. These locations remain unchanged upon exposure to stress or reduced IIS, but dFOXO binding is increased, and additional targets are activated, upon genetic reduction in IIS. We identify the subset of the IIS transcriptional response directly controlled by dFOXO and demonstrate that some of the indirect effects do not require dFOXO. Promoter analysis uncovered GATA and other forkhead factors as potential mediators of the indirect effects. Moreover, we exhibit genome-wide conservation of dFOXO targets between Drosophila and the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, with a prominent enrichment of regulators, including the dHR96/daf-12 nuclear hormone receptor, in a second tier of regulators.

title: Stable partnership and progression to AIDS or death in HIV infected patients receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy: Swiss HIV cohort study.
text:
Objective: To investigate the association between a stable partnership and clinical outcomes in HIV-infected patients receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).
Design: Prospective cohort study of adults with HIV (Swiss HIV cohort study) conducted at seven outpatient clinics across Switzerland.
Participants: A total of 3736 patients who started HAART before 2002 (median age 36 years, 29% female, median follow-up time of 3.6 years).
Main outcome measures: Time to AIDS or death (primary endpoint), death alone, increases in CD4 cell counts of at least 50 and 100 above baseline, optimal viral suppression (viral load below 400 copies/ml), and viral rebound.
Results: Of the 3736 participants, 2985 (80%) reported a stable partnership on at least one occasion. At the time of starting HAART, 52% (545/1042) of participants reported a stable partnership, and after five years of follow-up, 46% (190/412) of participants reported a stable partnership. In an analysis stratified by previous antiretroviral therapy and clinical stage when starting HAART, the adjusted hazard ratio for progression to AIDS or death was 0.79 (95% confidence interval 0.63-0.98) for participants with a stable partnership compared to those without. Adjusted hazards ratios for other endpoints were 0.59 (0.44-0.79) for progression to death, 1.15 (1.06-1.24) for an increase in CD4 cells of 100 counts/microl or more, and 1.06 (0.98-1.14) for optimal viral suppression.
Conclusion: This study found that a stable partnership is associated with a slower rate of progression to AIDS or death in HIV-infected patients receiving HAART.

title: Specific deficit of the ON response in visual transmission by targeted disruption of the mGIuR6 gene
text: Taking advantage of the specialized expression of metabotropic glutamate receptor subtype 6 (mGluR6) in retinal ON bipolar cells, we developed knockout mice lacking mGluR6 expression. Homozygous mutant mice displayed a loss of ON responses to light but preserved OFF responses, suggesting that mGluR6 plays a crucial role in synaptic transmission to ON bipolar cells. Remarkably, the mutant mice showed no detectable changes in retinal cell organization or the projection of optic fibers to the brain. We further evaluated the visual behaviors of the mGluR6-deficient mice using shuttle box avoidance behavior experiments with light exposure as a conditioned stimulus. The findings highlight the essential role of mGluR6 in transmitting visual information through the ON bipolar cell pathway.

title: Common BRCA1 variants and susceptibility to breast and ovarian cancer in the general population.
text: Most cases of young onset breast cancer and ovarian cancer are believed to be caused by inherited mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. However, these mutations are rare in the general population and are thought to account for only a small percentage of breast cancer cases. A larger proportion of breast cancer may be due to common variants that have a less significant individual risk. We have examined the frequency of four common polymorphisms in the BRCA1 gene - Gln356Arg, Pro871Leu, Glu1038Gly and Ser1613Gly - in large groups of breast and ovarian cancer cases and matched controls. Due to strong linkage disequilibrium, these polymorphisms combine into only three haplotypes with a frequency greater than 1.3%. The most common haplotypes, characterized by the alleles Gln356Pro871Glu1038Ser1613 and Gln356Leu871Gly1038Gly1613, have frequencies of 0.57 and 0.32, respectively, and there is no significant difference in their frequencies between cancer patients and controls. However, our data suggest that the Arg356 allele may have a different genotype distribution in breast cancer patients compared to controls (Arg356 homozygotes are more frequent in the control groups, P = 0.01), which may indicate that it may provide protection against breast cancer. If this finding is confirmed, it may provide insight into the structural features of the BRCA1 protein that are important for its function.

title: Exercise causes a tissue-specific change of NO production in the kidney and lung.
text: Exercise induces changes in local vascular tone, leading to an increase in systemic blood flow and a redistribution of blood flow to working muscles. This raises the question of whether exercise affects nitric oxide (NO) production in internal organs such as the kidney and lung. To investigate this, we studied the effect of exercise on NO synthase (NOS) mRNA and protein expression, NOS activity, and tissue levels of nitrite/nitrate (stable end products of NO) in the kidneys and lungs of rat. We found that exercise significantly decreased expression of endothelial NOS (eNOS) mRNA in the kidneys compared to control rats, while exercise increased expression of eNOS protein in the lungs. Western blot analysis confirmed these findings. Meanwhile, neither neuronal NOS (nNOS) mRNA and protein nor inducible NOS (iNOS) mRNA and protein in the kidneys and lungs differed between exercise and control rats. NOS activity in the kidneys was lower in exercise rats, while it was higher in the lungs. Interestingly, iNOS activity in both organs did not differ between exercise and control rats. Finally, we observed that tissue levels of nitrite/nitrate were lower in the kidneys and significantly higher in the lungs of exercise rats. In conclusion, our results demonstrate that exercise has a tissue-specific effect on NO production in the kidney and lung.

title: Ballistic labeling and dynamic imaging of astrocytes in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures
text:
The morphology of protoplasmic astrocytes in mammalian central nervous system (CNS) tissues in vivo is highly complex and intricate, with multiple fine protrusions and processes. However, when these cells are dissociated and cultured in vitro, they often adopt a flattened, fibroblast-like morphology with only a few simple processes. Using fluorescent labeling and confocal reconstruction techniques, we have demonstrated that a significant proportion of astrocytes in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures exhibit a more native, complex cytoarchitecture, with many fine spine- or veil-like protrusions.
In this study, we used ballistic delivery of gold or tungsten particles carrying cDNAs (Biolistics), lipophilic dyes (DiOlistics), or fluorescent intracellular calcium indicators (Calistics) to label dozens of astrocytes in single slice cultures. We found that expression of a membrane-targeted form of enhanced green fluorescent protein (Lck-GFP) is more effective than soluble GFP for visualizing fine astrocytic processes. Time-lapse confocal imaging of Lck-GFP transfected astrocytes or "calistically" labeled astrocytes showed structural remodeling and calcium transients, respectively. This approach provides a valuable in vitro system for investigating the functional architecture, development, and dynamic remodeling of astrocytes and their interactions with neurons and other glia in live mammalian brain tissues.

title: A bipotential precursor population for pancreas and liver within the embryonic endoderm.
text: The pancreas emerges independently from the dorsal and ventral domains of embryonic gut endoderm during embryonic development. Gene inactivation experiments in mice have revealed factors crucial for the development of the dorsal pancreas, but the factors responsible for the emergence of the ventral pancreas have remained obscure. In this study, we investigated the hypothesis that the emergence of the ventral pancreas is linked to the emergence of the liver. We found that both the liver and ventral pancreas are specified in the same general domain of cells at the same time during embryonic development. Using embryo tissue explantation experiments, we discovered that the default fate of the ventral foregut endoderm is to activate the pancreas gene program. However, FGF signaling from the cardiac mesoderm diverts this endoderm to instead express genes for liver. Our findings suggest that the cell type choice for pancreas or liver is not determined by a contest for growth or viability. The expression of cardiac mesoderm-derived FGF leads to the local production of sonic hedgehog, which inhibits the formation of the pancreas but not the liver. This study highlights the bipotential nature of the precursor cell population for pancreas and liver during embryonic development, as well as the role of FGF in directing their fate. The recapitulation of these processes in the adult pancreas and their evolution in different organisms provide insight into the developmental mechanisms that give rise to these complex organs.

title: ErbB4-neuregulin signaling modulates synapse development and dendritic arborization through distinct mechanisms.
text: Alterations in the function of neuregulin-1 (NRG1)/ErbB4 have been linked to schizophrenia, with affected individuals displaying abnormalities in glutamatergic synaptic transmission and neuronal circuits. However, the role of NRG1/ErbB4 in shaping synapse development and neuronal connectivity remains insufficiently explored. Our study demonstrates that ErbB4 is expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory interneurons at postsynaptic sites, and its overexpression enhances the size of presynaptic inputs without affecting their number. Conversely, knockdown of ErbB4 using shRNA diminishes the size of presynaptic inputs. We found that ErbB4-mediated synapse maturation requires its extracellular domain, whereas its tyrosine kinase activity is dispensable for this process. Furthermore, depletion of ErbB4 leads to a decrease in the number of primary neurites, and stimulation of ErbB4 using a soluble form of NRG1 triggers exuberant dendritic arborization through the activation of the tyrosine kinase domain of ErbB4 and the phosphoinositide 3-kinase pathway. These findings suggest that NRG1/ErbB4 signaling differentially regulates synapse maturation and dendritic morphology through two distinct mechanisms: trans-synaptic signaling and tyrosine kinase activity, respectively.

title: Dynamic Helix Interactions in Transmembrane Signaling
text: The challenge of studying how protein transmembrane domains transmit signals across membranes is a formidable one. Here, we examine the factors that have contributed to the success of these efforts and reflect on the insights gained from them. Unfortunately, it appears that some of the most fascinating aspects of transmembrane helix interactions may be the most difficult to investigate using current methods.

title: Association between smoking and risk of bladder cancer among men and women.
text:
Previous research has shown that the population attributable risk (PAR) of bladder cancer due to tobacco smoking is 50% to 65% in men and 20% to 30% in women. Additionally, current smoking triples the risk of bladder cancer compared to never smoking. However, as smoking prevalence and cigarette composition have changed over the past 30 years, it is important to revisit these risk estimates.
In this study, we aimed to evaluate the association between tobacco smoking and bladder cancer in the National Institutes of Health-AARP (NIH-AARP) Diet and Health Study cohort. We included 281,394 men and 186,134 women who completed a lifestyle questionnaire and were followed up between 1995 and 2006. We found that former smokers and current smokers had higher risks of bladder cancer than never smokers, with a summary risk estimate of 2.22 and 4.06, respectively. The PAR for ever smoking in our study was 0.50 in men and 0.52 in women.
Compared to the pooled estimate of US data from cohorts initiated between 1963 and 1987, the relative risks for smoking in the more recent NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study cohort were higher, with PARs for women comparable to those for men. These findings suggest that the association between smoking and bladder cancer remains strong and that smoking cessation may help to reduce the burden of this disease.

title: Leptin regulates glutamate and glucose transporters in hypothalamic astrocytes.
text: Glial cells play a vital role in modulating the activity of neurons, and their involvement in appetite and energy balance is gaining attention. Leptin, a key regulator of appetite and metabolism, has been shown to affect the structure and morphology of glial cells. Our study demonstrates that the metabolic state and leptin levels also impact the expression of astrocyte-specific glutamate and glucose transporters, indicating that metabolic signals have an effect on synaptic efficiency and glucose uptake, ultimately affecting neuronal function. We discovered that basal and glucose-stimulated electrical activity of hypothalamic proopiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons in mice were altered in the offspring of mothers fed a high-fat diet. In adulthood, changes in body weight and fasting also affected the expression of glucose and glutamate transporters. These findings suggest that the metabolic state of the entire organism has a profound impact on hypothalamic glial cell activity, highlighting the importance of these cells in the development of obesity.

title: Metabolic phenotyping of human blood plasma: a powerful tool to discriminate between cancer types?
text:
BACKGROUND:
Mounting evidence suggests that cancer cell metabolism differs from that of normal cells. However, the specificity of cancer metabolite profiles across different tumor types remains unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate whether the plasma metabolic phenotype can distinguish between lung and breast cancer.
PATIENTS AND METHODS:
The proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectra of plasma were analyzed into 110 integration regions, each reflecting the metabolic phenotype. These regions were used to train a classification model that discriminated between 80 female breast cancer patients and 54 female lung cancer patients with adenocarcinoma. Model performance was validated using permutation testing and an independent validation cohort of 60 female breast cancer patients and 81 male lung cancer patients with adenocarcinoma.
RESULTS:
The model correctly classified 99% of breast cancer patients and 93% of lung cancer patients with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.96. Consistent performance was observed in the validation cohort, with a sensitivity of 89%, specificity of 82%, and AUC of 0.94. Decreased levels of sphingomyelin and phosphatidylcholine (phospholipids with choline head group) and increased levels of phospholipids with long, saturated fatty acid chains were associated with more rigid cell membranes in lung tumors, which were less sensitive to lipid peroxidation. In contrast, the other discriminating metabolites pointed to a more pronounced response of the body to the Warburg effect in lung cancer.
CONCLUSION:
Metabolic phenotyping of plasma can effectively differentiate between lung and breast cancer, suggesting that the metabolite profile reflects more than a generic cancer marker.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT02362776.

title: Direct in vivo assessment of microcirculatory dysfunction in severe falciparum malaria.
text:
Study Reveals Microcirculatory Changes in Severe Malaria
This research aimed to investigate and quantify changes in the microcirculation on the mucosal surface of patients with severe malaria through direct in-vivo observation using orthogonal polarization spectral (OPS) imaging.
Methods:
The microcirculation in the rectal mucosa of adult patients with severe malaria was assessed using OPS imaging at admission and then daily. Comparison groups consisted of patients with uncomplicated falciparum malaria, patients with bacterial sepsis, and healthy individuals.
Results:
Erythrocyte velocities were directly measured in 43 adult patients with severe falciparum malaria, of whom 20 died. The microcirculation exhibited disturbed blood flow with heterogeneous obstruction that corresponded to the severity of the disease. Blocked capillaries were found in 29 patients (67%) and were associated with hyperdynamic blood flow (erythrocyte velocity >750 mm/s) in adjacent vessels in 27 patients (93%). The proportion of blocked capillaries correlated with the base deficit in plasma and lactate concentration. Abnormalities resolved when the patients recovered. In contrast, healthy individuals and patients with uncomplicated malaria or sepsis did not show stagnant erythrocytes, and hyperdynamic blood flow was prominent in patients with sepsis.

Conclusion:
Patients with severe falciparum malaria display extensive microvascular obstruction that corresponds to the severity of the disease. This finding highlights the critical role that microvascular obstruction plays in the pathophysiology of severe malaria and underscores the distinct difference between the microvascular pathophysiology of malaria and bacterial sepsis.

title: Multiple archaeal groups mediate methane oxidation in anoxic cold seep sediments.
text: No microorganism capable of anaerobic growth on methane as the sole carbon source has been cultivated yet, thus information about these microorganisms has been inferred from geochemical and microbiological observations of field samples. Stable isotope analysis of lipid biomarkers and rRNA gene surveys have implicated specific microbes in the anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM). In this study, we used combined fluorescent in situ hybridization and secondary ion mass spectrometry analyses to identify anaerobic methanotrophs in marine methane-seep sediments. Our results provide direct evidence for the involvement of at least two distinct archaeal groups (ANME-1 and ANME-2) in AOM at methane seeps. While both archaeal groups often occurred in direct physical association with bacteria, they were also observed as monospecific aggregations and as single cells. The ANME-1 archaeal group was more frequently found in monospecific aggregations or as single filaments, suggesting it may not always have a bacterial partner. Bacteria associated with both archaeal groups included close relatives of Desulfosarcina species. Isotopic analyses revealed that monospecific archaeal cells and cell aggregates were active in anaerobic methanotrophy, as were multispecies consortia. Overall, the data indicate that the microbial species and biotic interactions mediating anaerobic methanotrophy are diverse and complex. The results also show that highly structured ANME-2/Desulfosarcina consortia are not the sole entities responsible for AOM at marine methane seeps, as other microbial groups, including ANME-1 archaea, are capable of anaerobic methane consumption, either as single cells, in monospecific aggregates, or in multispecies consortia.

title: N-cadherin in the spotlight of cell-cell adhesion, differentiation, embryogenesis, invasion and signalling.
text: Cell migration is a crucial process that plays a significant role in various stages of development, from embryogenesis to adulthood, and also in certain pathological conditions. Cadherins, particularly the neural cell adhesion molecule N-cadherin, play a vital role in cell migration. In embryonic development, N-cadherin is the key molecule during gastrulation and neural crest development. N-cadherin-mediated contacts trigger various signaling pathways, including those involving Rho GTPases and tyrosine kinase signaling (e.g., through the fibroblast growth factor receptor). In cancer, cadherins regulate the balance between suppression and promotion of invasion. E-cadherin functions as an invasion suppressor and is downregulated in most carcinomas, while N-cadherin, an invasion promoter, is frequently upregulated.
