text: Understanding the global chromatin structure and gene expression programs of human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) can provide a powerful tool for determining whether these cells have similar pluripotent states. Recent studies have suggested that ESCs and iPSCs represent distinct pluripotent states with significantly different gene expression profiles. In this study, we compare global chromatin structure and gene expression data for a panel of human ESCs and iPSCs. Using genome-wide maps of nucleosomes marked with histone H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, we find little difference between ESCs and iPSCs in terms of these modifications. Similarly, gene expression profiles reveal that the transcriptional programs of ESCs and iPSCs show only a few consistent differences. Although some variation in chromatin structure and gene expression was observed in these cell lines, these variations were unable to distinguish ESCs from iPSCs.

title: Myeloid Cells Expressing VEGF and Arginase-1 Following Uptake of Damaged Retinal Pigment Epithelium Suggests Potential Mechanism That Drives the Onset of Choroidal Angiogenesis in Mice
text: While data suggests that both myeloid cell accumulation and complement activation occur during choroidal neovascularization (CNV), a clear explanation for the angiogenic drive that promotes pathological angiogenesis has not been presented. One possible explanation is the early and specific activation and conditioning of the myeloid cell infiltrate. Using a laser-induced CNV murine model, we have identified that the early recruitment of macrophages derived from monocytes and microglia, prior to angiogenesis and contemporaneous with lesional complement activation, is a crucial event. These early-recruited macrophages expressed a specific gene signature, including high levels of Arg-1 expression. Additionally, accumulating macrophages from the retina and peripheral blood were activated at the site of injury, displaying enhanced VEGF expression, and notably prior to exaggerated VEGF expression from the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). These initial events, including distinct VEGF (+) Arg-1(+) myeloid cells, subsided when CNV was established and RPE-VEGF expression was maximal. Depletion of inflammatory CCR2-positive monocytes confirmed the origin of infiltrating monocyte Arg-1 expression, and CNV suppression followed depletion. Our in vitro data also supported a myeloid cell uptake of damaged RPE or its derivatives as a mechanism generating VEGF (+) Arg-1(+) phenotype in vivo. These results provide a potential early driver of angiogenesis via myeloid-derived VEGF drive following uptake of damaged RPE, and offer an explanation for why CNV develops during any stage of macular degeneration, which can be explored further for therapeutic gain.

title: Monitoring Tumorigenesis and Senescence In Vivo with a p16INK4a-Luciferase Model
text: Experimental monitoring of cancer and aging within living organisms remains challenging. Here, we describe a luciferase knockin mouse (p16(LUC)) that reliably detects the expression of p16(INK4a), a tumor suppressor and aging biomarker. Lifelong assessment of luciferase activity in p16(+/LUC) mice revealed an exponential increase in luminescence with age, which varied significantly among a group of contemporarily housed, syngeneic mice. Contrary to expectations, expression of p16(INK4a) with aging did not predict cancer development, suggesting that the accumulation of senescent cells is not the primary determinant of cancer-related death. In all 14 tumor models tested, expression of p16(LUC) was focally activated by early neoplastic events, offering visualization of tumors with enhanced sensitivity compared to other imaging modalities. Activation of p16(INK4a) was observed in both the emerging neoplasm and surrounding stromal cells. This work suggests that p16(INK4a) activation is a common feature of all emerging cancers, making the p16(LUC) allele a sensitive, unbiased reporter of neoplastic transformation.

title: The Bacteroides sp. 3_1_23 Pif1 protein is a multifunctional helicase
text: Bacteroides sp. 3_1_23 (BsPif1) DNA helicase is a member of the 5'-to-3' helicase superfamily that is widespread across bacteria and eukaryotes, playing essential roles in maintaining genomic stability. Despite extensive research on eukaryotic Pif1 helicases, including yeast and human Pif1 proteins, the functions and biochemical properties of prokaryotic Pif1 helicases have remained largely unexplored. In this study, we investigated the expression, purification, and biochemical properties of BsPif1. Our findings demonstrate that BsPif1 binds to a wide range of DNA substrates, including partial duplex DNA with 5'-overhangs, fork-like substrates, D-loop structures, and flap-like substrates, indicating its potential role in resolving stalled DNA replication forks and enhancing Okazaki fragment maturation. Remarkably, BsPif1 also resolves R-loop structures and unwinds DNA-RNA hybrids, similar to its eukaryotic counterparts. Furthermore, BsPif1 exhibits efficient activity against G-quadruplexes and disrupts nucleoprotein complexes. These results suggest that prokaryotic Pif1 helicases may play a crucial role in resolving common problems that arise during DNA transactions. Interestingly, our findings reveal that BsPif1 shares similarities with both yeast and human Pif1 in terms of substrate specificity, helicase activity, and mode of action, suggesting that prokaryotic Pif1 helicases may play similar functional roles in vivo.

title: Netting neutrophils in autoimmune small-vessel vasculitis
text: Small-vessel vasculitis (SVV) is a chronic autoinflammatory condition closely associated with antineutrophil cytoplasm autoantibodies (ANCAs). Our findings indicate that ANCA-activated neutrophils release chromatin structures known as neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), which contain the targeted autoantigens, proteinase-3 (PR3) and myeloperoxidase (MPO). The accumulation of NETs in inflamed kidneys and the presence of circulating MPO-DNA complexes suggest that NET formation plays a key role in triggering vasculitis and fostering an autoimmune response against neutrophil components in individuals with SVV.

title: Control of Nutrient Stress-Induced Metabolic Reprogramming by PKCζ in Tumorigenesis
text: Cancer cells exhibit heightened metabolic activity to sustain their rapid growth and survival under conditions of nutrient stress. Our findings reveal that PKCζ deficiency fosters the adaptability of cancer cells to redirect their metabolism towards utilizing glutamine through the serine biosynthetic pathway when glucose is scarce. PKCζ suppresses the expression of key enzymes PHGDH and PSAT1 and phosphorylates PHGDH to hamper its enzymatic function. Notably, mice lacking PKCζ exhibit enhanced tumorigenesis in the intestine and increased levels of these metabolic enzymes, while patients with low PKCζ levels have a poor prognosis. Additionally, PKCζ and caspase-3 activities are correlated with PHGDH levels in human intestinal tumors, conclusively demonstrating that PKCζ acts as a critical metabolic tumor suppressor in both mice and humans with cancer.

title: XRCC4's interaction with XLF is required for coding (but not signal) end joining
text: XRCC4 and XLF are closely related proteins that play critical roles in DNA Ligase IV function. XRCC4 forms a tight complex with DNA Ligase IV, while XLF interacts directly with XRCC4. Both XRCC4 and XLF can form homodimers that can polymerize into heterotypic filaments independently of DNA Ligase IV. Recent structural and biochemical data suggest that XRCC4 and XLF cooperate to generate a filamentous structure that facilitates the linking of DNA molecules. Our findings indicate that reducing XRCC4's interaction with XLF leads to DNA repair deficits, including an unexpected shortcoming in VDJ coding, but not signal end joining. These data support a model in which XRCC4/XLF complexes keep DNA ends together, a requirement for successful coding end joining, but not for signal end joining. Furthermore, our data suggest that DNA-PK-mediated phosphorylation of XRCC4/XLF complexes disrupt DNA bridging in vitro, indicating a regulatory function for this phosphorylation event.

title: Loss of imprinting in colorectal cancer linked to hypomethylation of H19 and IGF2.
text: Epigenetic alterations in human cancers include global DNA demethylation, gene demethylation, and hypermethylation of promoters, as well as loss of imprinting (LOI) of the insulin-like growth factor-II gene (IGF2). Previously described mechanisms for LOI involve hypermethylation of a differentially methylated region (DMR) upstream of the H19 gene, leading to the activation of the usually silent maternal allele of IGF2. However, our findings suggest that this mechanism does not apply to colorectal cancers, which exhibit hypomethylation of the H19 DMR and a DMR upstream of exon 3 of IGF2 in both cancerous tissue and normal mucosa from the same patients, as well as in cell lines with somatic cell knockout of DNA methyltransferases DNMT1 and DNMT3B. These data indicate that hypomethylation may play a role in LOI, challenging the prevailing IGF2-H19 enhancer competition model for IGF2 imprinting in the human colon. Instead, an alternative model involving a transcriptional repressor acting on the usually silent maternal allele of IGF2 may be at play.

title: Management of patients with sore throats in relation to guidelines: An interview study in Sweden
text:
Objective: To investigate how Swedish general practitioners (GPs) manage patients with a sore throat in relation to current guidelines, as revealed through semi-structured interviews.
Design: A qualitative content analysis was conducted to analyze the interviews.
Setting: Swedish primary care.
Subjects: A strategic sample of 25 GPs was interviewed.
Main Outcome Measures: The GPs' perceived management of sore throat patients was evaluated.
Results: The study found that nine of the interviewed GPs adhered to current guidelines for sore throat management, while 16 were non-adherent. The two groups differed in terms of their knowledge of guidelines, with adherent GPs sharing knowledge within their primary care team while non-adherent GPs relied on idiosyncratic knowledge. Adherent GPs had a lower concern for bacterial infections and differential diagnosis, and they targeted patient history and examination more than non-adherent GPs. Non-adherent GPs reported difficulties in getting patients to avoid antibiotics, while adherent GPs did not.
Conclusion: The study revealed that while two-thirds of the GPs were non-adherent and had a liberal approach to antibiotics, one-third were guideline adherent with a restrictive view on antibiotics. Non-adherent GPs had significant knowledge gaps, and adherent GPs had discussed guidelines within their primary care team. Guideline implementation was found to be promoted by knowledge shared in team discussions.

title: Catch and release: how do kinetochores hook the right microtubules during mitosis?
text: Sport fishermen rely on tension to prevent hooked fish from escaping. In a similar manner, at the molecular level, a technique known as "angler's trick" is employed at kinetochores to ensure accuracy during cell division. Specifically, the mitotic spindle attaches randomly to chromosomes, but then stabilized attachments are secured through the tension exerted by opposing microtubules. Unstable attachments, without tension, release quickly, allowing the spindle to reorient and biorient correctly. This phenomenon, known as tension-induced stability, is not limited to mitosis, but also plays a role in other physiological processes such as cell adhesion, motility, hemostasis, and tissue morphogenesis. Here, we review the mechanisms that stabilize kinetochore attachments and explore the potential applicability of these principles to other force-activated systems. While there has been significant focus on one kinase-based mechanism in the mitosis field, it is likely that multiple mechanisms work together to secure properly bioriented kinetochores, and insights from other tension-sensitive systems may also be relevant.

title: Label-free in vivo imaging of myelinated axons in health and disease with spectral confocal reflectance microscopy
text:
We have developed a novel technique for high-resolution in vivo imaging of myelinated axons in the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerve without the need for fluorescent labeling. Our method, based on spectral confocal reflectance microscopy (SCoRe), utilizes a conventional laser-scanning confocal system to generate images by combining the simultaneously reflected signals from multiple lasers of different wavelengths. Unique and striking color patterns are generated that enable the tracing of myelinated fibers in dense axonal areas, highlighting nodes of Ranvier and Schmidt-Lanterman incisures. These patterns can also be used to detect various myelin pathologies.
By employing SCoRe, we were able to perform chronic brain imaging up to 400 μm deep, capturing the de novo myelination of mouse cortical axons in vivo. Additionally, we demonstrated the feasibility of imaging myelinated axons in the human cerebral cortex. The integration of SCoRe constitutes a significant addition to the evolving toolbox for imaging myelination in living animals and may potentially have implications for imaging myelinated axons in humans.

title: Applicability of current staging/categorization of α-synuclein pathology and their clinical relevance
text: In Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), alpha-synuclein (alphaS) pathology tends to follow a predictable topographic distribution. Currently, there are two staging/categorization systems, Braak's and McKeith's, used to assess alphaS pathology and its relationship to clinical symptoms such as dementia and extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). In this study, we analyzed the applicability of these systems in a cohort of 226 alphaS-positive individuals. The cohort was selected from a larger autopsy sample of 1,720 based on the detection of alphaS-immunoreactivity (IR) in one of the most vulnerable nuclei, including the dorsal motor nucleus of vagus, substantia nigra, and basal forebrain. The frequency of alphaS-IR lesions in the cohort was 14%. Each subject with available material was assigned a neuropathological stage/category of PD/DLB based on the current staging/categorization systems. The neuropathological data was then analyzed in relation to dementia and EPS. The results showed that 83% of subjects showed a distribution pattern of alphaS-IR that was compatible with the current staging/categorization systems. Interestingly, around 55% of subjects with widespread alphaS pathology (Braak's PD stages 5-6) did not exhibit clinical signs of dementia or EPS. Similar findings were observed in subjects who fulfilled the McKeith criteria for diffuse neocortical category and displayed only mild concomitant Alzheimer's disease-related pathology, with 48% being demented and 54% displaying EPS. However, around 17% of subjects deviated from the suggested caudo-rostral propagation, suggesting alternative routes of progression, possibly due to concomitant diseases and genetic predisposition. In conclusion, our findings confirm that the current staging/categorization systems can be applied to most subjects with alphaS pathology. However, the observation that around half of subjects with abundant alphaS pathology remain neurologically intact raises questions about whether these systems fully capture the actual disease process.

title: Batf is important for IL-4 expression in T follicular helper cells
text: Besides T helper (Th)-2 cells, T follicular helper (Tfh) cells are a prominent population of IL-4-producing T cells, responsible for regulating type 2 humoral immunity; however, the transcriptional control of IL-4 production in Tfh cells remains largely unexplored. Our study, on the other hand, reveals that the basic leucine zipper transcription factor ATF-like, Batf, plays a crucial role in IL-4 expression in Tfh cells rather than in classical Th2 cells. In detail, Batf, in collaboration with interferon regulatory factor (IRF) 4, Stat3, and Stat6, triggers IL-4 production in Tfh cells by directly binding to and activating the CNS2 region within the IL-4 locus. Additionally, Batf-to-c-Maf signaling is a significant determinant of IL-4 expression in Tfh cells. consequences of Batf deficiency in Tfh cells, leading to impaired generation of IL-4-producing T cells, which in turn leads to reduced protection against allergic asthma. Overall, our findings suggest a positive role of Batf in fostering the generation of pro-allergic IL-4-producing Tfh cells.

title: Autocrine VEGF Signaling Synergizes with EGFR in Tumor Cells to Promote Epithelial Cancer Development
text: It has been established that tumor cells produce VEGF, which acts on endothelial cells to promote angiogenesis and tumor growth. In mouse skin tumors, we have found that VEGF produced by tumor cells acts on those cells in a cell-autonomous and angiogenesis-independent manner to promote proliferation. VEGF is upregulated in tumors that express a protein called SOS, and its deletion in epidermal cells leads to delayed tumorigenesis by suppressing angiogenesis and tumor cell proliferation. Deletion of a receptor called Flt1 in the epidermis also impairs tumorigenesis and proliferation. However, surprisingly, complete tumor inhibition occurs in the absence of VEGF in mice with a specific genetic mutation, suggesting that VEGFR and EGFR work together in neoplastic cells to promote tumor growth. Our findings reveal that K5-SOS upregulates VEGF, Flt1, and Neuropilin-1 in an Erk-dependent manner, creating an autocrine proliferation loop. Conversely, EGFR prevents tumor cells from undergoing apoptosis. Additionally, we found that Flt1 is upregulated in human squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and its inhibition in SCC cells impairs proliferation. Therefore, our findings indicate that VEGF is not only involved in angiogenesis but also acts as a potent growth factor for epidermal tumors.

title: Discovery and development of the Polo-like kinase inhibitor volasertib in cancer therapy
text: Due to their critical role in regulating cell cycles, the Polo-like kinase (Plk) family, particularly Plk1, has emerged as a promising therapeutic target in oncology. Recently, several Plk1 inhibitors have been developed, with some agents showing encouraging results in early-stage clinical trials. This review focuses on volasertib (BI 6727), a potent and selective Plk inhibitor, which has shown promising activity in various cancer cell lines and xenograft models of human cancer. Trials conducted so far suggest that volasertib has clinical efficacy across a range of malignancies, with the most promising results seen in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Notably, recent phase II data have demonstrated that volasertib combined with low-dose cytarabine (LDAC) was associated with higher response rates and improved event-free survival compared to LDAC alone in patients with previously untreated AML. Considering its potentially manageable safety profile and the significant unmet need in this patient population, volasertib is currently in phase III development as a potential treatment for AML patients who are ineligible for intensive remission induction therapy. In this review, we delve into the underlying biology of Plk1 inhibitors in cancer, the clinical development of volasertib in solid tumors and AML, and the potential identification of biomarkers that could predict response to volasertib and inform its clinical use.

title: Babies driving robots: self-generated mobility in very young infants
text: Infants' ability to generate mobility through their own movement is essential for their cognitive, social, and motor development. For some children with special needs, this mobility can only be achieved through the use of assistive technology such as power wheelchairs. Previously, infants under 24 months were not considered candidates for power mobility training. However, recent research has shown that younger infants can learn to use their reaching and grasping abilities to navigate power mobility. This interdisciplinary study combines previous work on motor development and learning in infants with special needs, as well as the application of robot technology for rehabilitation, to investigate whether young infants can drive a mobile robot without formal training. The pilot study focused on two infants who were observed over multiple sessions, and the results indicate that these infants increased their overall session time, the percentage of time spent driving, and the total distance traveled. These findings suggest that young infants can independently move themselves using a mobile robot without training, and provide a foundation for further research on training methods to enhance self-generated mobility in infants with special needs. Future studies will explore various training and technology combinations to reduce barriers to exploration and advance the cognitive, social, and motor development of infants with special needs.

title: Effects of Abciximab on the architecture of platelet-rich clots in patients with acute myocardial infarction undergoing primary coronary intervention.
text:
Here is a possible revision of the text:
BACKGROUND: Abciximab plus aspirin has been shown to improve the TIMI 3 flow rate of the infarct-related artery in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention or thrombolysis. The present study aimed to investigate whether the reperfusion efficacy of abciximab is related to changes in clot architecture in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI).
METHODS AND RESULTS: In a double-blind fashion, 23 AMI patients in the ADMIRAL trial received either abciximab or placebo before primary stenting. Ex vivo platelet-rich clots (PRC) were assessed for viscoelastic (G' in dyne/cm(2)) and morphological (mean platelet aggregate surface area [SAG] in micrometer(2)) indexes before and after bolus administration of abciximab or placebo. Abciximab significantly reduced G' by 63% (P=0.0001) and SAG by 65% (P=0.0007), whereas no effect was observed in the placebo group. These abciximab-related changes increased fibrin exposure by reducing platelet-aggregate surface area, potentially improving endogenous fibrinolysis. These effects were observed in all patients, regardless of previous heparin administration.
CONCLUSIONS: Abciximab significantly reduces platelet aggregate size and increases fibrin accessibility of ex vivo PRC in AMI patients, which may contribute to better coronary artery patency observed with abciximab. These findings highlight the potential mechanisms underlying the reperfusion efficacy of abciximab in improving cardiac function in AMI patients.

title: Natural Mutagenesis of Human Genomes by Endogenous Retrotransposons
text: Two abundant classes of mobile genetic elements, Alu and L1 elements, continue to introduce new retrotransposon insertions into human genomes. According to estimates, these elements have generated millions of new germline insertions across individual human genomes globally. Despite the prevalence of these insertions, current technologies are limited in their ability to detect most of the young insertions, making it challenging to assess the true extent of germline mutagenesis caused by endogenous human retrotransposons. In this study, we describe innovative techniques for detecting these young retrotransposon insertions and demonstrate that they are indeed abundant in human populations. Furthermore, we found that high frequencies of new somatic L1 insertions occur in human lung cancer genomes. Genome-wide analysis suggests that altered DNA methylation may play a role in the high levels of L1 mobilization observed in these tumors. Our findings indicate that transposon-mediated mutagenesis is vast in human genomes and is likely to have a significant impact on human biology and disease.

title: Knowledge of young African American adults about heart disease: a cross-sectional survey
text:
Background: African Americans experience higher rates of cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality compared to other ethnic groups, making young adults an important target for intervention strategies to reduce disease risk. The study aimed to assess the level of knowledge of lifestyle risk factors for CVD among young African American adults in Phoenix, Arizona, and use the findings to inform the development of CVD outreach programs tailored to this population.
Methods: A convenience sample of 172 African American men and women between 18 and 26 years old completed a questionnaire adapted from the American Heart Association's national surveys. Descriptive statistics were analyzed by age, gender, education level, and health status variables including body mass index (BMI), smoking status, and physical activity.
Results: While some aspects of heart disease were well-known among young adult African Americans, knowledge of certain other important risk factors (menopause) and preventive behaviors (eating fewer animal products) was inconsistent and variable. Differences in knowledge of individual variables were greater among those with higher education levels than by gender overall. The predictors of a summary CVD knowledge score included higher education, female gender, and high self-efficacy (R2 = 0.158, p < 0.001). Additionally, predictors of self-efficacy in changing CVD risk were higher education and perceived low risk of CVD (R2 = 0.064, p < 0.001), explained 6% of the variance.
Conclusion: Assessing the baseline knowledge of CVD is crucial in designing and implementing successful health promotion programs. Identifying areas of strengths and weaknesses in knowledge can guide the tailoring of programs for greater effectiveness. Further research can help to identify the range of other characteristics that determine knowledge and risk perception.

title: Recent insights into the role of Notch signaling in tumorigenesis
text: Members of the Notch family of transmembrane receptors play a crucial role in determining cell fate. Over the past decade, it has become evident that Notch signaling is involved in the development of hematologic and solid malignancies. Various cellular processes and microenvironmental cues associated with tumorigenesis, such as proliferation, apoptosis, adhesion, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and angiogenesis, are modulated by Notch signaling. It is becoming increasingly apparent that Notch signaling can act as both an oncogene and a tumor suppressor. This review delves into recent findings on the molecular and functional aspects of Notch-mediated neoplastic transformation, as well as cellular mechanisms that may help explain the complex role of Notch in tumorigenesis.

title: BRIEFINGS IN FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS AND PROTEOMICS. VOL 5. NO 3. 209^221 doi:10.1093/bfgp/ell028 Histone acetylation in gene regulation
text: Chromatin, the complex nucleoprotein structure that houses genetic information, is dynamic and plays a crucial role in regulating various biological processes. Post-translational modifications of key proteins are a vital aspect of gene regulation in eukaryotic cells, and one of the most extensively studied modifications is acetylation of lysine residues on the N-terminal histone tails. This review delves into the enzymes that control both histone and non-histone protein acetylation levels in the cell, with a particular focus on their impact on cancer.

title: Efficacy of monthly tafenoquine for prophylaxis of Plasmodium vivax and multidrug-resistant P. falciparum malaria.
text: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, the efficacy of tafenoquine in preventing malaria was assessed. A total of 205 Thai soldiers received either a loading dose of tafenoquine 400 mg daily for 3 days, followed by single monthly 400-mg doses (n = 104) or placebo (n = 101) for up to 5 consecutive months. The study found that among volunteers who completed follow-up (96 tafenoquine and 91 placebo recipients), there were 22 P. vivax, 8 P. falciparum, and 1 mixed infection. All infections except one P. vivax occurred in placebo recipients, indicating that tafenoquine provided 97% protective efficacy against all malaria (95% confidence interval [CI], 82%-99%), 96% protective efficacy against P. vivax malaria (95% CI, 76%-99%), and 100% protective efficacy against P. falciparum malaria (95% CI, 60%-100%). The study also showed that monthly tafenoquine was safe and well tolerated, highlighting its potential as a prophylactic treatment against malaria in tropical regions.

title: Headache, migraine, and structural brain lesions and function: population based Epidemiology of Vascular Ageing-MRI study
text:
Objective: To investigate the relationship between overall and specific headaches and the volume of white matter hyperintensities, brain infarcts, and cognitive function in a population-based study.
Design: Cross-sectional study.
Setting: Epidemiology of Vascular Ageing study in Nantes, France.
Participants: 780 community-dwelling participants (mean age 69, 58.5% women) with detailed headache assessment.
Main Outcome Measures: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was conducted to assess volume of white matter hyperintensities and classification of infarcts using a standardized assessment grid. Cognitive function was evaluated through a battery of tests, including the mini-mental state examination.
Results: Among the participants, 163 (20.9%) reported a history of severe headache, and 116 had migraine, of whom 17 (14.7%) reported aura symptoms. An association was found between any history of severe headache and increasing volume of white matter hyperintensities. The adjusted odds ratio for the highest volume of white matter hyperintensities was 2.0 (95% confidence interval 1.3 to 3.1, P for trend 0.002) for participants with any history of severe headache compared to those without severe headache in the lowest volume category. The association pattern was similar for all headache types. Migraine with aura was the only headache type strongly associated with volume of deep white matter hyperintensities (odds ratio 12.4, 1.6 to 99.4, P for trend 0.005) and brain infarcts (odds ratio 3.4, 1.2 to 9.3). Brain infarcts were primarily located outside the cerebellum and brain stem. No evidence was found for cognitive impairment associated with any headache type or brain lesions.
Conclusions: In this population-based study, any history of severe headache was associated with increased volume of white matter hyperintensities. Migraine with aura was the only headache type associated with brain infarcts. There was no evidence that headache of any type or in combination with brain lesions was associated with cognitive impairment.

title: Characterization of adipocytes derived from fibro/adipogenic progenitors resident in human skeletal muscle
text: A new population of fibro/adipogenic progenitors has been discovered located between skeletal muscle fibers. The aim of this study was to determine the extent these progenitors differentiate into fully functional adipocytes. The characterization of muscle progenitor-derived adipocytes is crucial for understanding muscle homeostasis, as they are believed to be the cellular origin of intermuscular adipose tissue that develops in various pathophysiological situations. CD15+/PDGFRα+CD56- progenitors were isolated from 15 human muscle biopsies and their differentiation into adipocytes was investigated. Adipogenic differentiation was found to be regulated by the same factors as differentiation of progenitors derived from white subcutaneous adipose tissue. Moreover, basic adipocyte functions, such as triglyceride synthesis and lipolysis, occurred at levels similar to those observed with subcutaneous adipose tissue progenitor-derived adipocytes. However, muscle progenitor-derived adipocytes were found to be insensitive to insulin-induced glucose uptake, which was associated with impaired phosphorylation of key insulin-signaling effectors. These findings suggest that muscle adipogenic progenitors give rise to bona fide white adipocytes that exhibit an unexpected insulin resistance.

title: Membrane lipids in invadopodia and podosomes: Key structures for cancer invasion and metastasis
text: Invadopodia are protrusions on the surface of invasive cancer cells that degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM). Similar structures called podosomes are found in oncogene-transformed fibroblasts and cells from the monocyte lineage, including macrophages and osteoclasts. These structures are believed to play important roles in remodeling the ECM around cancer cells during invasion and metastasis. Much research has focused on identifying the molecular components and regulators of invadopodia/podosomes, which could serve as potential therapeutic targets for malignant cancers. However, the mechanisms by which these components are assembled into invadopodia/podosomes and how assembly is spatially and temporally regulated remain poorly understood. This review will summarize recent advances in the molecular mechanisms of invadopodia/podosome formation, with a particular emphasis on the roles of lipid rafts and phosphoinositides.

title: CCR2 and CXCR4 regulate peripheral blood monocyte pharmacodynamics and link to efficacy in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis
text: BACKGROUND CCR2 plays a pivotal role in regulating the movement of monocytes to areas of inflammation, making it a prime target for the treatment of inflammatory diseases. To investigate the pharmacodynamic effects of CCR2 blockade, we examined the effects of a potent small molecule antagonist on the peripheral blood monocyte compartment in both acute and chronic inflammatory conditions. RESULTS Our findings demonstrate that CCR2 antagonism in vivo leads to a rapid decrease in the number of circulating Ly6Chi monocytes, with the majority of these cells being sequestered in the bone marrow due to their CXCR4 expression. This suggests that CCR2 plays a key role in regulating monocyte dynamics in vivo. Additionally, we found that CCR2 antagonism leads to increased levels of circulating CCL2 and CCL7 levels, indicating that CCR2 is involved in regulating the levels of its ligands under homeostatic conditions. Finally, we observed that the pharmacodynamic changes caused by CCR2 antagonism are apparent even after chronic dosing in a mouse model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, where CCR2 blockade resulted in a significant reduction in disease severity, as evidenced by a decreased accumulation of monocytes and other cells in the central nervous system. CONCLUSION These findings demonstrate that targeting CCR2 in vivo has predictable pharmacodynamic effects that can be leveraged to align drug engagement with biological effects on disease activity.

title: Displacement of a DNA binding protein by Dda helicase
text: Recent studies have demonstrated that Bacteriophage T4 Dda helicase exhibits activity as a monomer in unwinding short duplex oligonucleotides and displacing streptavidin from 3'-biotinylated oligonucleotides. However, the helicase's activity for streptavidin displacement and DNA unwinding increases with the number of Dda molecules bound to the substrate molecule. To investigate the helicase's ability to displace DNA binding proteins, a substrate was designed with a DNA binding site for the Escherichia coli trp repressor incorporated into an oligonucleotide substrate for Dda helicase containing single-stranded overhangs. Our results show that a single Dda monomer is insufficient to displace the E. coli trp repressor from double-stranded DNA under single turnover conditions, although the substrate is unwound and the repressor is displaced when the single-stranded overhang is long enough to accommodate two Dda molecules. The quantity of product formed increases when the substrate can accommodate more than two Dda molecules. These findings suggest that multiple Dda molecules cooperate to displace DNA binding proteins in a manner that correlates with the helicase's DNA unwinding and streptavidin displacement activities. To explain these observations, we propose a cooperative inchworm model for the activities of Dda helicase.

title: Control of Developmental Regulators by Polycomb in Human Embryonic Stem Cells
text: Polycomb group proteins are crucial for early development in multicellular organisms, but their functions in human development are not well understood. To investigate, we mapped the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) subunit SUZ12 across the entire non-repeat portion of the human genome in embryonic stem (ES) cells. Surprisingly, we found that SUZ12 is distributed across a significant number of genes encoding key developmental regulators. These genes are characterized by trimethylation of histone H3K27, transcriptional repression, and high conservation across the genome. Interestingly, we discovered that PRC2 target genes are preferentially activated during ES cell differentiation, and ES cell regulators OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG cooccupy a notable subset of these genes. These findings suggest that PRC2 occupies a unique collection of developmental genes in ES cells that must be repressed to maintain pluripotency and are poised for activation upon differentiation.

title: PAD4 is essential for antibacterial innate immunity mediated by neutrophil extracellular traps
text: Neutrophils capture and eliminate bacteria through the formation of highly condensed chromatin structures, known as neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). We previously found that peak citrullination of histone proteins, catalyzed by peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (PAD4), is correlated with chromatin decondensation during NET formation. However, the functional significance of PAD4 in NET-mediated bacterial capture and killing remained unclear. To investigate this, we generated PAD4-deficient mice and found that they are unable to form NETs upon stimulation with chemokines or exposure to bacteria, and are therefore impaired in bacterial elimination. In a mouse model of necrotizing fasciitis, PAD4-deficient mice were found to be more susceptible to bacterial infection than wild-type mice. Additionally, our findings showed that citrullination of histones and nucleosomes inhibited, rather than enhanced, bacterial killing by neutrophils, indicating that PAD4 primarily functions in chromatin decondensation to form NETs rather than increasing histone-mediated bacterial killing. Overall, our study defines a novel role for histone hypercitrullination in the innate immune response during bacterial infection.

title: Human ‘brite / beige’ adipocytes develop from capillary networks and their implantation improves metabolic homeostasis in mice
text:
Uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) is abundantly expressed in brown adipose tissue, where it modulates energy metabolism by decoupling the electron transport process from ATP production. UCP1 is also found in peripheral white adipose tissue, specifically in adipocytes termed "brite" (brown-in-white) or "beige," which exhibit a hybrid phenotype combining features of both brown and white adipocytes. The presence of brite or beige adipocytes in humans is positively correlated with a lean, metabolically healthy phenotype, although whether a causal relationship exists is currently unclear.
In this study, we investigate the proliferative potential of human brite/beige adipocyte progenitors in response to pro-angiogenic factors. We discover that these progenitors proliferate in association with expanding capillary networks, leading to the formation of adipocytes that express UCP1 and exhibit uncoupled respiration. When implanted into normal chow-fed or high-fat diet (HFD)-fed glucose-intolerant NOD-scid IL2rg(null) (NSG) mice, activated beige/brite adipocytes significantly enhance systemic glucose tolerance. These adipocytes also express a range of neuroendocrine and secreted factors, including the pro-protein convertase PCSK1, which has been implicated in human obesity.
Our findings suggest that pro-angiogenic conditions drive the proliferation of human beige/brite adipocyte progenitors, and activated beige/brite adipocytes may contribute to systemic glucose homeostasis through a neuroendocrine mechanism. These findings have important implications for the development of therapeutic strategies aimed at improving metabolic health.

title: Mindfulness meditation and improvement in sleep quality and daytime impairment among older adults with sleep disturbances: a randomized clinical trial.
text:
This randomized clinical trial aimed to assess the effectiveness of a mindfulness meditation intervention, known as Mindful Awareness Practices (MAPS), in improving sleep quality among older adults with moderate sleep disturbances. The study was conducted at a medical research center from January to December 2012, and included 47 participants (mean age 66.3 years, SD=7.4). The participants were randomly assigned to either the MAPS intervention (n=24) or a sleep hygiene education (SHE) intervention (n=25).
The MAPS intervention consisted of a 6-week program (2 hours per week) with assigned homework, while the SHE intervention involved a similar structure but focused on sleep hygiene habits. The primary outcome measure was the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), which was administered at baseline and post-intervention. Secondary outcomes included measures of insomnia symptoms, depression, anxiety, stress, and fatigue, as well as inflammatory signaling via nuclear factor (NF)-κB.
The results of the study showed that the MAPS intervention led to significant improvement in sleep quality compared to the SHE intervention, as measured by the PSQI. Specifically, the mean PSQI scores were 10.2 (1.7) at baseline and 7.4 (1.9) at post-intervention in the MAPS group, while the scores were 10.2 (1.8) at baseline and 9.1 (2.0) at post-intervention in the SHE group. The between-group difference in mean PSQI scores was 1.8 (95% CI, 0.6-2.9), with an effect size of 0.89. The MAPS group also showed significant improvement relative to the SHE group on secondary health outcomes of insomnia symptoms, depression symptoms, fatigue interference, and fatigue severity (P<.05 for all). In contrast, no significant between-group differences were observed for anxiety, stress, or NF-κB. Interestingly, both groups showed a significant decline in NF-κB concentrations over time (P<.05).
The study's findings suggest that a community-accessible MAPs intervention may improve sleep quality among older adults with moderate sleep disturbances, and this effect may carry over into reducing sleep-related daytime impairment, which has implications for quality of life. The study highlights the clinical importance of mindfulness-based interventions in possibly serving to remediate sleep problems among older adults in the short term. The study was registered at clinicaltrials.gov (Identifier: NCT01534338).

title: THE ORIGIN AND DIFFERENTIATION OF MICROGLIAL CELLS DURING DEVELOPMENT
text: Certain scholars suggest that microglia originate from the neuroepithelium, yet the prevailing belief is that microglial cells are of mesodermal origin and belong to the monocyte/macrophage cell lineage. These cells enter the developing central nervous system (CNS) from the bloodstream, ventricular space, or meninges. Afterward, microglial cells are distributed relatively evenly throughout the entire nervous parenchyma. Stereotyped patterns of migration have been observed during development, where long-distance tangential migration precedes radial migration of individual cells. Microglial cells migrating through the nervous parenchyma are ameboid microglia, which appear to differentiate into ramified microglia upon reaching their final location. This is supported by the presence of cells exhibiting intermediate features between those of ameboid and ramified microglia. The factors that control the invasion of the nervous parenchyma, migration within the developing CNS, and differentiation of microglial cells are not well understood and are thought to depend on environmental factors such as soluble or cell-surface bound molecules and components of the extracellular matrix. Microglial cells within the developing CNS are involved in clearing cell debris and withdrawing misdirected or transitory axons, and presumably support cell survival and neurite growth.

title: Integrin αvβ8-Mediated TGF-β Activation by Effector Regulatory T Cells Is Essential for Suppression of T-Cell-Mediated Inflammation
text: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are essential for maintaining immune homeostasis by suppressing self-destructive T cell responses. However, the mechanisms by which Tregs regulate immune responses during inflammation are not fully understood. In this study, we investigated the role of the integrin αvβ8 in Treg-mediated suppression. We found that effector Tregs express high levels of αvβ8, which enables them to activate latent transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β). While Treg-cell-specific deletion of αvβ8 did not result in spontaneous inflammation, Treg cells lacking αvβ8 were unable to suppress pathogenic T cell responses during active inflammation. These findings highlight the importance of effector Treg-cell-mediated activation of latent TGF-β in suppressing self-destructive T cell responses during active inflammation, identifying a key mechanism for maintaining immune homeostasis.

title: Effects of treatment for intestinal helminth infection on growth and cognitive performance in children: systematic review of randomised trials.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the effects of anthelmintic drug treatment on growth and cognitive performance in children.
Data Sources: Electronic databases including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group controlled trial register, Cochrane controlled trials register, Embase, and Medline. Additionally, citations of all identified trials were consulted, and contact was made with the World Health Organization and field researchers.
Review Methods: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials in children aged 1-16 that compared anthelmintic treatment with placebo or no treatment was conducted. The validity and data abstraction were assessed independently by two reviewers.
Main Outcome Measures: The primary outcomes were growth and cognitive performance.
Results: Thirty randomized controlled trials involving over 15,000 children were identified. The effects on mean weight were unremarkable, and there was heterogeneity in the results. However, there were some positive effects on mean weight change after a single dose of any anthelmintic, with pooled estimates of 0.24 kg (95% CI 0.15 kg to 0.32 kg; fixed effects model) and 0.38 kg (0.01 kg to 0.77 kg; random effects model). Results from trials of multiple doses showed mean weight change in up to one year of follow-up of 0.10 kg (0.04 kg to 0.17 kg; fixed effects) or 0.15 kg (0.00 to 0.30; random effects). At more than one year of follow-up, mean weight change was 0.12 kg (-0.02 kg to 0.26 kg; fixed effects) and 0.43 (-0.61 to 1.47; random effects). The results on cognitive performance were inconclusive.
Conclusions: There is some limited evidence that routine treatment of children in areas where helminths are common has effects on weight gain, but this is not consistent between trials. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether this intervention improves cognitive performance.

title: Choosing appropriate substitution models for the phylogenetic analysis of protein-coding sequences.
text: Despite the prevalence of phylogenetic inference of protein-coding sequences in the literature, few studies have incorporated evolutionary models that account for the genetic code. This oversight is compounded by the exclusion of codon-based models from commonly used model selection techniques, which is possibly due to the perceived computational burden associated with these models. To address this issue, we investigated a computationally efficient alternative to traditional nucleotide substitution models, which incorporates codon position (CP). We examined the suitability of different models for alignments of 177 RNA virus genes and 106 yeast genes, using a total of 11 substitution models, including one codon model and four CP models. Our results reveal that the majority of gene alignments are best described by CP substitution models, rather than by standard nucleotide models, and this is particularly true without the added computational cost of full codon models. These findings have significant implications for phylogenetic inference of coding sequences, as they demonstrate that incorporating CPs into substitution models not only represents a computationally viable alternative to traditional approaches but may also frequently lead to more statistically robust conclusions.

title: Polycomb Proteins Remain Bound to Chromatin and DNA during DNA Replication In Vitro
text:
During development, the transcriptional status of a gene can be maintained through multiple rounds of cell division due to epigenetic effects. These effects are believed to reflect changes in chromatin folding and histone modifications or variants at target genes, but little is known about how these chromatin features are inherited through cell division. Maintaining transcription states can be challenging due to DNA replication, which disrupts or dilutes chromatin-associated proteins and histone modifications.
Polycomb group protein complexes, such as those belonging to the PRC1 class, are essential for development and are believed to heritably silence transcription by altering chromatin folding and histone modifications. It is unclear whether these complexes and their effects are maintained during DNA replication or subsequently re-established. However, our research suggests that when PRC1-class Polycomb complex-bound chromatin or DNA is replicated in vitro, Polycomb complexes remain bound to replicated templates. The retention of Polycomb proteins through DNA replication may contribute to the maintenance of transcriptional silencing through cell division.

title: Control of CNS Cell-Fate Decisions by SHP-2 and Its Dysregulation in Noonan Syndrome
text:
In the developing mammalian central nervous system (CNS), growth factors guide multipotent precursors to differentiate into neurons or glia, a process crucial for proper neural function. Disruptions in this process can lead to neural dysfunction and cognitive impairments. We have found that genetic mutations in the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2, as seen in Noonan Syndrome (NS), can perturb the balance between neuron and glial cell fate, leading to learning disabilities and mental retardation.
In our study, we investigated the role of SHP-2 in neural cell fate decisions in cultured cortical precursors and in the embryonic cortex. We found that genetic knockdown of SHP-2 inhibited basal neurogenesis and promoted earlier and more extensive astrocyte formation. Conversely, expression of an NS-associated SHP-2 mutant enhanced neurogenesis and inhibited astrogenesis. Similarly, mice with a genetic mutation that mimics NS exhibited perturbed neural cell fate decisions.
Our findings suggest that SHP-2 regulates the balance between neuron and glial cell fate during the neurogenic phase, and perturbations in this balance may contribute to the cognitive impairments seen in NS patients. This discovery sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying neural development and offers potential therapeutic targets for the treatment of NS and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Global Regulation of H2A.Z Localization by the INO80 Chromatin-Remodeling Enzyme Is Essential for Genome Integrity
text:
Sure! Here's a potential revision of the given text:
INO80 is a conserved enzyme across evolution that relies on ATP to remodel chromatin and participate in various cellular processes, including transcription, DNA repair, and replication. Specifically, we have found that the yeast INO80 protein plays a crucial role in regulating genome-wide distribution of the histone H2A.Z. When INO80 is absent, H2A.Z nucleosomes become mislocalized, leading to reduced responsiveness of H2A.Z levels at promoters to transcriptional changes. Our data also suggest that INO80 has the ability to exchange histones, specifically replacing nucleosomal H2A.Z/H2B with free H2A/H2B dimers. Interestingly, genetic interactions between INO80 and Htz1 support a model in which INO80 removes unacetylated H2A.Z from chromatin to promote genome stability.

title: Rho GTPase signalling in cell migration
text: Cells migrate in various ways due to their environment, including the composition of the extracellular matrix, interactions with other cells, and chemical stimuli. Rho GTPases play a crucial role in all types of cell migration, although the specific contribution of each Rho GTPase varies depending on the environment and cell type. In this review, I will discuss recent advances in our understanding of how Rho GTPases contribute to different types of migration, comparing lamellipodium-driven versus bleb-driven migration modes. I will also explore how cells migrate across the endothelium and the roles of other less-well characterized members of the Rho family in addition to Rho, Rac, and Cdc42, which are already known to regulate migration.

title: A Novel Adaptor Protein Orchestrates Receptor Patterning and Cytoskeletal Polarity in T-Cell Contacts
text: The recognition of antigens by T cells is mediated by the formation of a specialized junction between the T cell and the antigen-presenting cell, which is regulated by the recruitment and exclusion of specific proteins at the contact area. The mechanisms underlying these events remain unknown. Here, we demonstrate that the engagement of the adhesion molecule CD2 initiates a process of protein segregation, CD2 clustering, and cytoskeletal polarization. While protein segregation is independent of the cytoplasmic domain of CD2, CD2 clustering and cytoskeletal polarization require an interaction between the CD2 cytoplasmic domain and a novel SH3-containing protein called CD2AP. CD2AP likely facilitates receptor patterning in the contact area by linking specific adhesion receptors to the cytoskeleton.

title: Operable non-small cell lung cancer diagnosed by transpleural techniques : do they affect relapse and prognosis?
text:
Aim: To determine whether transpleural methods for diagnosing peripheral lung cancer, such as needle aspiration or tumor excision, have an impact on relapse and prognosis due to their potential to spread malignant cells from the tumor.
Design: A retrospective study.
Setting: A National referral hospital.
Participants: A review of 239 patients who underwent surgery between 1990 and 1998 and for whom non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) of less than 3 cm in maximum diameter was completely resected. The duration of postoperative follow-up ranged from 12 to 105 months, with a median period of 45 months.
Interventions: The transbronchial method involved using a bronchoscope, while the transpleural method included needle aspiration cytology or tumor excision. Dichotomous variables included gender, histologic type of squamous cell carcinoma or other type of carcinoma, pathologic stage, and whether the diagnostic method was the transbronchial type only (first-line method) or the transpleural type (second-line method).
Results: NSCLC was diagnosed in 45 patients through the transpleural technique and in 194 patients through the transbronchial technique. There were no significant statistical differences in age, gender, histologic type, pathologic stage, and tumor size between the two groups. There were 42 relapses, with 7 occurring in the transpleural technique group and 35 in the transbronchial technique group (p = 0.90). Of the 7 patients in the transpleural group, there were 4 distant metastases and 3 local relapses, while of the 35 patients in the transbronchial group, there were 20 distant metastases and 15 local relapses (p = 0.99). Pleural carcinomatosis occurred in none of the 45 patients in the transpleural group and in 1 case (0.5%) in the 194 patients in the transbronchial group (p = 0.99). Patients in the transpleural group had a statistically better 5-year survival rate than patients in the transbronchial group (79.4% vs 60.3%, p = 0.04). This finding was confirmed as an independent prognostic factor in a multivariate analysis.
Conclusion: Transpleural methods appear to be a viable approach for diagnosing operable lung cancer that is challenging to diagnose using bronchoscopy, as these methods did not have a significant impact on relapse and prognosis in the patients in this study.

title: Characterization of the adipocyte cellular lineage in vivo
text: Mature adipocytes arise from the proliferation and differentiation of precursor cells. Our previous research revealed that adipocyte progenitors in white adipose tissue (WAT) are identified as Lin(-):CD29(+):CD34(+):Sca-1(+):CD24(+) (CD24(+)) cells, which are capable of generating functional WAT (reference). To uncover the adipocyte cellular lineage in vivo, we utilized several Cre recombinase mouse models. Although it was proposed that white adipocytes originate from endothelial and haematopoietic lineages, our findings show that neither of these lineages label white adipocytes. However, platelet-derived growth factor receptor α (PdgfRα)-Cre tracing labels all white adipocytes. Analyzing WAT from PdgfRα-Cre reporter mice identifies CD24(+) and Lin(-):CD29(+):CD34(+):Sca-1(+):CD24(-) (CD24(-)) cells as adipocyte precursors. Our data demonstrate that CD24(+) cells give rise to the CD24(-) population in vivo, and the CD24(-) cells express late markers of adipogenesis. Based on these findings, we propose a model where CD24(+) adipocyte progenitors differentiate into CD24(-) preadipocytes, which eventually become mature adipocytes. This characterization of the adipocyte cellular lineage will facilitate the study of the mechanisms that regulate WAT formation in vivo and WAT mass expansion in obesity.

title: Reducing Plasmodium falciparum Malaria Transmission in Africa: A Model-Based Evaluation of Intervention Strategies
text: Over the past decade, there has been a scaling-up of malaria interventions across Africa. However, it remains unclear what the overall reduction in transmission is achievable with the currently available tools. To address this question, we developed an individual-based simulation model for Plasmodium falciparum transmission in an African context, incorporating the three major vector species (Anopheles gambiae s.s., An. arabiensis, and An. funestus) and parameters obtained by fitting the model to parasite prevalence data from 34 transmission settings across Africa. We explored the impact of continued roll-out of long-lasting insecticide treated nets (LLINs), additional rounds of indoor residual spraying (IRS), mass screening and treatment (MSAT), and a future RTS,S/AS01 vaccine in six representative settings with varying transmission intensity (as summarized by the annual entomological inoculation rate, EIR), vector-species combinations, and patterns of seasonality. We considered a realistic target of 80% coverage of interventions and found that in low-transmission settings (EIR approximately 3 ibppy), LLINs have the potential to reduce malaria transmission to low levels (<1% parasite prevalence in all age-groups) provided usage levels are high and sustained. In two of the moderate-transmission settings (EIR approximately 43 and 81 ibppy), additional rounds of IRS with DDT coupled with MSAT could drive parasite prevalence below a 1% threshold. However, in the third (EIR = 46) with An. arabiensis prevailing, these interventions are insufficient to reach this threshold. In both high-transmission settings (EIR approximately 586 and 675 ibppy), either unrealistically high coverage levels (>90%) or novel tools and/or substantial social improvements will be required, although considerable reductions in prevalence can be achieved with existing tools and realistic coverage levels. Our findings suggest that interventions using current tools can result in major reductions in P. falciparum malaria transmission and the associated disease burden in Africa. In low- to moderate-transmission settings where vectors are primarily endophilic, a comprehensive and sustained intervention program can achieve reductions to the 1% parasite prevalence threshold. However, in high-transmission settings and those in which vectors are mainly exophilic, additional new tools that target exophagic, exophilic, and partly zoophagic mosquitoes will be required to achieve further reductions in transmission.

title: Golgi Export of the Kir2.1 Channel Is Driven by a Trafficking Signal Located within Its Tertiary Structure
text: Despite the significance of the Golgi apparatus in protein trafficking, the mechanisms that sort newly synthesized proteins for transport to the cell surface are poorly understood. In this study, we uncover a unique aspect of protein transport by demonstrating that the potassium channel Kir2.1, which is associated with Andersen-Tawil syndrome, is selectively incorporated into Golgi export carriers through an unusual signal-dependent mechanism. Contrary to conventional trafficking signals, which are typically composed of short linear peptide sequences, the exit of Kir2.1 from the Golgi is determined by specific residues embedded within the convergence of two distinct protein domains. This signal patch serves as a recognition site for interaction with the AP1 adaptor complex, thereby marking Kir2.1 for inclusion in clathrin-coated vesicles at the trans-Golgi. The identification of a trafficking signal in the tertiary structure of Kir2.1 provides valuable insight into how protein conformation is linked to Golgi export, highlighting a quality control process that plays a crucial role in ensuring the proper functionality of proteins.

title: Characteristics of Body Fat, Body Fat Percentage and Other Body Composition for Koreans from KNHANES IV
text: Optimal measurement of body fat mass has become increasingly crucial with the rising prevalence of obesity. In this study, we analyzed fat and muscle mass of Koreans using the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey IV (KNHANES IV). Our sample consisted of 10,456 participants (ages 20-85 years old; 4,476 men and 5,980 women). Body composition was measured using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, and reference values were established using the LMS method. We found that the fat mass index (FMI, body fat mass/height(2); kg/m(2)) of Korean men did not exhibit a significant correlation with age (P = 0.452), whereas the ratio of percentage of fat in the trunk and legs showed a positive correlation with age in both genders (P < 0.001). Furthermore, the appendicular lean mass/height(2) (kg/m(2)) of Korean men showed a negative correlation with age (P < 0.001). In contrast, the ratio of appendicular lean mass/height(2) in women increased with age (P < 0.001). Using the FMI classification, we determined the rates of obesity to be 6.1% (FMI > 9 kg/m(2)) in men and 2.7% (FMI > 13 kg/m(2)) in women. Our findings indicate that muscle mass decreases and obesity increases with aging in Korean men, while both fat mass and obesity increase with aging in Korean women.

title: The Evolution of Dominance in Sporophytic Self-Incompatibility Systems. II. Mate Availability and Recombination
text: Self-incompatibility through sporophytic recognition (SSI) is a self-pollen recognition system that promotes outcrossing in plants. In SSI systems, recognition is typically controlled by a complex locus (5-locus) composed of genes that determine pollen and stigma specificity. Experimental studies have shown that S-alleles can be dominant, recessive, or codominant, with the dominance level of a given S-allele depending on whether pollen or stigma specificity is examined. In this and the companion paper by Llaurens and colleagues, the evolution of dominance in single-locus SSI is explored using numerical models and simulation. Particular attention is directed towards factors that can cause S-allele dominance to differ in pollen versus stigma. The effect of recombination between the S-locus and modifier locus is also examined. The models predict that a limited number of compatible mates are required for the evolution of S-allele dominance in the stigma, but not in the pollen. Tight linkage between the S-locus and modifier locus promotes the evolution of S-allele dominance hierarchies. Model results are interpreted in light of published information on the molecular basis of dominance in SSI systems and reported S-allele dominance relationships in various species. These studies show that dominant S-alleles are more common in the pollen than in the stigma, a pattern that is consistent with the prediction that mate limitation is relatively infrequent in natural populations with SSI.

title: Neurological outcomes of animal models of uterine artery ligation and relevance to human intrauterine growth restriction: a systematic review
text:
The present review investigates the molecular, neurological, and behavioral consequences of uterine artery ligation in animal models. We examine the similarity of these findings to the pathological and functional phenotypes characteristic of cerebral palsy and its associated developmental comorbidities in humans.
METHODS:
We conducted a PubMed database search for studies using the uterine artery ligation model published between 1990 and 2013. From the included studies, we summarized and analyzed the relevant neuroanatomical and behavioral deficits.
RESULTS:
Our analysis of 25 studies revealed a gradient of reduced body weight with sparing of brain mass in fetuses with growth restriction. The somatosensory cortex, hippocampus, and corpus callosum showed significant reductions in size. However, the motor cortex appeared to be relatively spared. Upregulation of apoptotic proteins and downregulation of proteins essential for neuronal survival, growth, and differentiation were observed. Diffuse neuronal apoptosis and astrogliosis occurred in various brain regions, and white matter injury involved oligodendrocyte precursor maturation arrest, hypomyelination, and aberrant myelin organization. Animals with growth restriction presented with deficits in gait, memory, object recognition, and spatial processing.
INTERPRETATION:
Our findings suggest that neuronal death, white matter injury, motor abnormalities, and cognitive deficits are crucial outcomes of uterine artery ligation in animal models. As these phenomena resemble the deficits observed in human cerebral palsy, this model is clinically relevant.

title: The fidelity of the ligation step determines how ends are resolved during Nonhomologous end joining
text: Nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) can effectively repair chromosome breaks despite diverse end structures, but the mechanisms underlying this process are not yet fully understood. In order to shed light on how NHEJ works, we analyzed the cellular NHEJ of ends with systematically mispaired and damaged termini. Our findings revealed that NHEJ is highly proficient at bypassing subtle terminal mispairs and radiation-induced damage through direct ligation. However, the efficiency of bypass decreases as the severity of the mispair increases, with only 6% of bypass products remaining at the highest level of mispair severity. Interestingly, our data suggest that the cell has evolved a strategy to compensate for this decrease in bypass efficiency by increasing the levels of end processing by nucleases and polymerases. Specifically, the cell favors pathways with the fewest number of steps required to generate a substrate suitable for ligation. This suggests that both the frequency and nature of end processing are tailored to meet the needs of the ligation step. Based on these observations, we propose a model where the ligase plays a central role in organizing all steps of NHEJ within a stable paired-end complex, Thus limiting end processing and associated errors.

title: Laminin-based cell adhesion anchors microtubule plus ends to the epithelial cell basal cortex through LL5α/β
text: LL5beta has been identified as a microtubule-anchoring factor that attaches EB1/CLIP-associating protein (CLASP)-bound microtubule plus ends to the cell membrane. In this study, we demonstrate that LL5beta and its homologue LL5alpha (LL5s) localize to the basal side of fully polarized epithelial sheets alongside autocrine laminin-5 and its receptors, integrins alpha3beta1 and alpha6beta4. Our results show that depletion of either laminin receptor integrin results in the loss of cortical localization of LL5s, while LL5 depletion reduces the amount of integrin alpha3 at the basal cell membrane. Intriguingly, activation of integrin alpha3 is sufficient to initiate LL5 accumulation at the cell membrane. LL5s form a complex with the cytoplasmic tails of these integrins, though the nature of their interaction may be indirect. By analyzing the three-dimensional distribution of microtubule growth in epithelial sheets using EB1-GFP and RNA interference, we discovered that LL5s are essential for maintaining the density of growing microtubules selectively at the basal cortex. Together, these findings reveal that signaling from laminin-integrin associations anchors microtubule plus ends to the epithelial basal cell membrane.

title: DNA topoisomerases: structure, function, and mechanism.
text: Topoisomerases solve the topological problems encountered during DNA replication, transcription, recombination, and chromatin remodeling by introducing temporary single- or double-strand breaks in the DNA. Additionally, these enzymes fine-tune the steady-state level of DNA supercoiling to facilitate interactions with proteins and prevent excessive supercoiling, which is detrimental. Recent crystal structure solutions of topoisomerase fragments representing various classes of enzymes have provided insightful mechanistic information. Notably, despite a lack of sequence homology, prokaryotic type IA and eukaryotic type IIA topoisomerases, as well as the type IIA enzymes from eukaryotes, share structural folds that are thought to reflect functional motifs in critical regions of the enzymes. Type IB enzymes, on the other hand, have a unique structure that is distinct from other known topoisomerases, but are similar to a class of enzymes referred to as tyrosine recombinases. Common structural themes among all topoisomerases include hinged clamps that open and close to bind DNA, DNA binding cavities for temporary DNA storage, and the coupling of protein conformational changes to DNA rotation or DNA movement. For type II topoisomerases, the binding and hydrolysis of ATP further modulate conformational changes in the enzymes to effect changes in DNA topology.

title: Pilot testing of dipsticks as point-of-care assays for rapid diagnosis of poor-quality artemisinin drugs in endemic settings
text: High-quality artemisinin drugs are critical for malaria treatment, but the growing presence of low-quality drugs in many endemic areas hinders effective disease management. To develop a rapid point-of-care assay for detecting counterfeit and substandard artemisinin drugs in resource-limited settings, we used specific monoclonal antibodies against artesunate and artemether and created prototypes of lateral flow dipstick assays. In this pilot study, we evaluated the feasibility of these dipsticks in different endemic areas and their performance when used by untrained personnel. Our results showed that the dipstick tests can be performed successfully by various investigators with the included instruction sheet, and none of the artemether and artesunate drugs collected from local pharmacies failed the test. We conclude that simple dipstick assays, with potential future optimizations to test conditions and sensitivity, could serve as a qualitative and semi-quantitative screening tool for rapid detection of counterfeit artemisinin drugs in endemic areas.

title: Increased Microerythrocyte Count in Homozygous α+-Thalassaemia Contributes to Protection against Severe Malarial Anaemia
text:
Here is a reformulated version of the text:
BACKGROUND The inherited hemoglobin disorder alpha(+)-thalassemia results from decreased alpha-globin chain synthesis, leading to microcytosis and an increased red blood cell count. Individuals homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassemia are immune to severe malaria, including severely anemic malaria (SMA, Hb concentration < 50 g/l). However, we wondered if this genotype provides additional protection during acute malaria, beyond its protective effect against severe malaria. METHODS AND FINDINGS We analyzed data from children in Papua New Guinea who participated in a case-control study to assess the genotype-specific reduction in red blood cell count and hemoglobin levels in response to acute malaria. We observed a median reduction of approximately 1.5 x 10^12 red blood cells/L in all malaria-infected children compared to healthy community children (P < 0.001). We developed a mathematical model that predicts that children homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassemia lose less hemoglobin than children of normal genotype for a reduction in red blood cell count of over 1.1 x 10^12 cells/L due to the lower mean cell hemoglobin value in homozygous alpha(+)-thalassemia. In addition, homozygous alpha(+)-thalassemia children require a 10% greater reduction in red blood cell count than children of normal genotype (P = 0.02) for hemoglobin levels to fall to 50 g/L, the threshold for SMA. We estimated that the hematological profile of children homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassemia reduces the risk of SMA during acute malaria compared to children of normal genotype (relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.24-1.12; P = 0.09). CONCLUSIONS The increased red blood cell count and microcytosis in children homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassemia may contribute significantly to their protection against SMA. A lower hemoglobin concentration per red blood cell and a larger population of red blood cells may be a biologically advantageous strategy against the significant reduction in red blood cell count that occurs during acute Plasmodium falciparum infection. This hematological profile may reduce the risk of anemia from other Plasmodium species and other causes. Other host genetic variations that result in increased red blood cell count and microcytosis may also provide a similar advantage.

title: Construction of Escherichia coli K-12 in-frame, single-gene knockout mutants: the Keio collection
text: We have thoroughly and precisely eliminated all non-essential genes in Escherichia coli K-12 using single-gene deletions. We employed a one-step approach that inserted a kanamycin cassette flanked by FLP recognition target sites into open-reading frame coding regions, effectively inactivating chromosomal genes. Of the total of 4288 genes targeted, we were able to successfully delete 3985 genes through this method. To preclude problems that may arise in high-throughput studies, two independent mutants were created for every deleted gene. These mutants, referred to as the 'Keio collection,' offer a novel resource for investigating unknown gene functions, gene regulatory networks, and the effects of mutations in a standard E. coli K-12 background. Unfortunately, we were unable to disrupt 303 genes, including 37 genes with unknown functions, which are potential essential genes. The distribution of these mutants is being managed through GenoBase (http://ecoli.aist-nara.ac.jp/).

title: Validated RealTime reverse transcriptase PCR methods for the diagnosis and pathotyping of Eurasian H7 avian influenza viruses
text: Avian influenza (AI), caused by H7 AI viruses (AIVs) of both low pathogenicity (LP) and high pathogenicity (HP), are notifiable poultry diseases. The objects of this study were to design and validate two RealTime reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reactions (RRT PCRs) for detecting Eurasian H7 AIVs and pathotyping them. The H7 RRT PCRs targeted the (i) hemagglutinin HA2 region and (ii) cleavage site CS region of the haemagglutinin gene. These RRT PCRs were validated against 65 H7 AIVs, 57 non-H7 AIVs, and 259 poultry swabs, comparing their performance to that of the M gene (AI generic) RRT PCR and virus isolation (VI). An additional 38 swabs and 20 tissue specimens were used for extended validation. The results showed that both H7 RRT PCRs amplified all 61 Eurasian lineage H7 AIVs tested, while none of the 57 non-H7 AIVs were detected. The diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of the H7 HA2 RRT PCR were 95.4% and 64.6%, respectively, while those of the H7 CS RRT PCR were 97.9% and 99.6%, respectively. In comparison, the H7 HA2 RRT PCR was more sensitive than virus isolation, while the H7 CS RRT PCR provided an opportunity for rapid pathotyping of H7 AIVs.

title: Interleukin-6 receptor pathways in coronary heart disease: a collaborative meta-analysis of 82 studies
text:
Background: Persistent inflammation has been implicated in the development of cardiovascular disease. Interleukin-6 receptor (IL6R) signaling plays a crucial role in this process, leading to downstream inflammatory cascades. To investigate the potential link between IL6R signaling and coronary heart disease, we studied a functional genetic variant known to affect IL6R signaling.
Methods: In a collaborative meta-analysis, we examined the frequency of a functional genetic variant, Asp358Ala (rs2228145), in IL6R in a large cohort of participants. We also compared the frequency of this variant in a group of patients with coronary heart disease and in a control group. To gain insights into possible mechanisms, we evaluated the variant's effect on localized gene expression and post-lipopolysaccharide stimulation of interleukin 6.
Findings: Our analysis revealed that the minor allele frequency of Asp358Ala was 39%. However, we found no significant associations between this variant and traditional cardiovascular risk factors, such as lipid levels, blood pressure, body mass index, and smoking. By contrast, we observed significant increases in IL6R and interleukin 6 concentrations in individuals carrying the Asp358Ala allele. Additionally, there was a reduced concentration of C-reactive protein and fibrinogen in this group. Furthermore, we found that the frequency of Asp358Ala was associated with a reduced risk of developing coronary heart disease. We did not observe any significant relationships between this variant and IL6R mRNA levels or interleukin-6 production in monocytes.
Interpretation: Our large-scale human genetic and biomarker analysis provides evidence for a causal association between IL6R-related pathways and coronary heart disease. Funding: British Heart Foundation; UK Medical Research Council; UK National Institute of Health Research, Cambridge Biomedical Research Centre; BUPA Foundation.

title: Plasma exosomes can deliver exogenous short interfering RNA to monocytes and lymphocytes
text:
Despite the promise of RNA interference (RNAi) and its potential for use in cancer therapy, several technical hurdles must be overcome. The major obstacle in RNAi-based therapeutics is delivering nucleic acids across the cell's plasma membrane.
