This study demonstrates that exosome vesicles derived from human cells can effectively deliver short interfering RNA (siRNA) to human mononuclear blood cells. Exosomes are nanoscale vesicles of endocytic origin involved in cell-to-cell communication, including antigen presentation, tolerance development, and RNA transport.
Using optimized methods, we introduced siRNA into human exosomes of various origins. Plasma exosomes (exosomes from peripheral blood) were then used as a gene delivery vector (GDV) to transport exogenous siRNA to human blood cells. Our findings show that the vesicles effectively delivered the administered siRNA into monocytes and lymphocytes, resulting in selective gene silencing of mitogen-activated protein kinase 1. These results suggest that human exosomes can be used as a GDV to deliver heterologous nucleic acids, such as therapeutic siRNAs.

title: Quantitative analysis of tumor-derived methylated p16INK4a sequences in plasma, serum, and blood cells of hepatocellular carcinoma patients.
text:
Purpose and Experimental Design:
Using real-time quantitative methylation-specific PCR (RTQ-MSP), we quantified the amount of methylated p16INK4a sequences in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) collected from 49 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) at three different time points: preoperatively, intraoperatively, and postoperatively.
Results:
RTQ-MSP was able to detect as little as 10 genome-equivalents of methylated p16INK4a sequences. We expressed the amount of methylated p16INK4a sequences in terms of the methylation index, which is the percentage of bisulfite-converted unmethylated and methylated p16INK4a sequences that are methylated. We observed methylated p16INK4a sequences in the peripheral circulation of 80% (23 of 29) of HCC patients. There was no significant difference in the detectability and concentrations of methylated p16INK4a sequences between preoperative plasma and serum samples from HCC patients. Before surgical resection, the p16INK4a methylation indices ranged from 0.2 to 100% and from 0.012 to 0.075% in the patients' plasma and buffy coat samples, respectively. After surgical resection, the median p16INK4a methylation indices in plasma and buffy coat samples decreased 12- and 15-fold, respectively.
Conclusions:
Our results demonstrate the clinical usefulness and effectiveness of peripheral blood RTQ-MSP for detecting and monitoring HCC. The amount of methylated p16INK4a sequences in the peripheral circulation may be used as a useful biomarker for HCC diagnosis, treatment response, and monitoring. Additionally, our findings suggest that intraoperative sampling may not be necessary for ctDNA analysis in HCC patients.

title: Dynamic control of excitatory synapse development by a Rac1 GEF/GAP regulatory complex.
text: The small GTPase Rac1 plays a crucial role in orchestrating actin-dependent remodeling for various cellular processes, including synapse development. However, the mechanisms behind the regulation of Rac1 signaling by its activators (GEFs) and inhibitors (GAPs) are largely unclear. In this study, we identify a regulatory complex comprising a Rac-GEF (Tiam1) and a Rac-GAP (Bcr) that cooperate to control excitatory synapse development. Disruption of Bcr function within this complex leads to increased Rac1 activity and excessive synaptic growth, which is rescued by Tiam1 inhibition. Furthermore, we reveal that EphB receptors utilize the Tiam1-Bcr complex to regulate synaptogenesis, with Tiam1 inducing Rac1-dependent spine formation, while Bcr prevents Rac1-mediated receptor internalization, promoting spine growth over retraction. Our findings demonstrate the importance of a Rac-specific GEF/GAP complex in maintaining optimal levels of Rac1 signaling, providing a crucial insight into the regulation of small GTPases.

title: 4-1BB Costimulation Ameliorates T Cell Exhaustion Induced by Tonic Signaling of Chimeric Antigen Receptors
text: Chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) targeting CD19 have demonstrated potent antitumor responses in hematologic malignancies, with significant tumor regression observed in some cases. However, the efficacy of CARs targeting other antigens has been less impressive, and it remains unclear whether this is due to the greater susceptibility of hematologic malignancies to CAR therapies or to superior functionality of the CD19 CAR itself. To investigate this phenomenon, we studied the phosphorylation of the CD3-ζ chain of CARs and found that tonic phosphorylation of this chain, triggered by antigen-independent clustering of CAR single-chain variable fragments, can lead to early exhaustion of CAR T cells, which limits their antitumor efficacy. This activation was observed in all CARs studied, except for the highly effective CD19 CAR, which showed a distinct pattern of CD3-ζ phosphorylation. Further analysis revealed that CD28 costimulation augments, while 4-1BB costimulation reduces, exhaustion induced by persistent CAR signaling. These findings provide important insights into the mechanisms underlying the antitumor effects of CD19 CARs and the observations that CD19 CAR T cells incorporating the 4-1BB costimulatory domain are more persistent than those incorporating CD28 in clinical trials. This study sheds light on the potential factors contributing to the impressive efficacy of CD19 CARs and highlights the importance of carefully selecting costimulatory domains in CAR design.

title: Ultrafast Evolution and Loss of CRISPRs Following a Host Shift in a Novel Wildlife Pathogen, Mycoplasma gallisepticum
text: Rates of genome evolution in human pathogens are well-documented, but less is known about bacterial pathogens in the wild, particularly during and after host switches. Mycoplasma gallisepticum (MG), a pathogenic bacterium, has evolved predominantly in poultry before recently infecting wild house finches (Carpodacus mexicanus), a common North American songbird. This study investigates the genome and rates of genome evolution in House Finch isolates of MG, as well as in poultry outgroups. Using whole-genome sequences of 12 House Finch isolates across a 13-year serial sample and four additional newly sequenced poultry strains, we estimate a nucleotide diversity of only 2% in House Finch isolates as compared to ancestral poultry strains, and a nucleotide substitution rate of 0.8-1.2 × 10^(-5) per site per year in both poultry and House Finches, which is unusually high for bacteria. Furthermore, we find high diversity and complete turnover of CRISPR arrays in poultry MG strains before the switch to the House Finch host, but there is progressive loss of CRISPR repeat diversity and cessation of novel CRISPR repeat recruitment after the invasion of House Finches. Notably, recent (2007) House Finch MG strains retain only about 50% of the CRISPR repertoire found in (1994-1995) strains and have lost the CRISPR-associated genes required for CRISPR function. Our results suggest that genome evolution in bacterial pathogens of wild birds can be extremely rapid, and in this case, it is accompanied by apparent functional loss of CRISPRs.

title: Inducing Tumor Immunity through the Selective Engagement of Activating Fcγ Receptors on Dendritic Cells
text:
The capture and presentation of tumor antigens by dendritic cells (DCs) is crucial for the induction of tumor-specific immunity. However, the process of transitioning from antigen capture to T cell stimulation requires a maturation signal, which can be negatively influenced by the presence of immune complexes (ICs). While ICs can enhance antigen capture, they are ineffective at inducing DC maturation, naive T cell activation, and protective immunity.
We have discovered that interfering with the inhibitory signal delivered by FcγRIIB on DCs converts ICs into potent maturation agents, leading to T cell activation. By applying this approach to immunization with DCs pulsed ex-vivo with ICs, we have generated antigen-specific CD8+ T cells in vivo and achieved efficient protective immunity in a murine melanoma model. These findings suggest that ICs may normally function to maintain tolerance through their binding to inhibitory FcγRs on DCs, but they can be converted to potent immunogenic stimuli by selective engagement of activating FcγRs. This mechanism provides a novel approach to the development of tumor vaccines.

title: Homocysteine and the risk of ischemic stroke in a triethnic cohort: the NOrthern MAnhattan Study.
text:
Background and Purpose: The exact level of total homocysteine (tHcy) that increases the risk of ischemic stroke is still unknown, and no prospective cohort studies have enrolled enough elderly minority subjects. To investigate this association, we conducted a multiethnic prospective study of the relationship between mild to moderate fasting tHcy levels and the incidence of ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, and vascular death.
Methods: We analyzed data from 2939 participants (mean age, 69 ± 10 years; 61% women, 53% Hispanics, 24% blacks, and 20% whites) in a population-based cohort study. We measured baseline values of tHcy and methylmalonic acid at the time of enrollment. Using Cox proportional models, we calculated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) after adjusting for age, race, education, renal insufficiency, B12 deficiency, and other potential risk factors.
Results: Our adjusted HR for a tHcy level ≥15 micromol/L compared to <10 micromol/L was highest for vascular death (HR = 6.04; 95% CI, 3.44 to 10.60), followed by combined vascular events (HR = 2.27; 95% CI, 1.51 to 3.43), ischemic stroke (HR = 2.01; 95% CI, 1.00 to 4.05), and nonvascular death (HR = 2.02; 95% CI, 1.31 to 3.14). Elevations of tHcy of 10 to 15 micromol/L were not significantly predictive of ischemic stroke, but increased the risk of vascular death (HR = 2.27; 95% CI, 1.44 to 3.60) and combined vascular events (HR = 1.42; 95% CI, 1.06 to 1.88). The effect of tHcy was stronger among whites and Hispanics compared to blacks.
Conclusions: Our study found that total Hcy elevations above 15 micromol/L are an independent risk factor for ischemic stroke, while mild elevations of tHcy of 10 to 15 micromol/L are less predictive. The vascular effects of tHcy were found to be greater among whites and Hispanics compared to blacks. Our findings suggest that measuring tHcy levels may be a valuable tool in assessing cardiovascular risk, particularly among whites and Hispanics.

title: Expression and purification of recombinant methylated HBHA in Mycobacterium smegmatis.
text:
The Heparin-Binding Haemagglutinin (HBHA) is a key adhesin involved in Mycobacterium tuberculosis dissemination from the primary infection site, making it a promising candidate for developing a new vaccine against tuberculosis. Recently, methylation of HBHA was identified as a novel post-translational modification, imparting important immunological properties to the protein. Since recombinant HBHA expressed in E. coli lacks methylation, we explored the possibility of producing methylated HBHA in fast-growing mycobacteria for use in immunological and biochemical studies.
We generated constructs containing the complete HBHA coding sequence cloned in the plasmid pMV206, under the control of either a strong promoter (hsp60) or its own promoter. The constructs were electroporated into Mycobacterium smegmatis, and the resulting recombinant strains were analyzed for HBHA protein expression using monoclonal antibodies D2 and E4. Our findings showed that high levels of intact protein can be toxic to the mycobacteria, while methylated HBHA can only be obtained in M. smegmatis using a weaker promoter sequence. Additionally, the expression of the complete HBHA gene is necessary to produce methylated HBHA.
To overcome these limitations, we constructed a recombinant M. smegmatis strain (pMV3-38) that expresses a histidine-tagged methylated HBHA that can be easily purified. This approach should enable the rapid evaluation of a new HBHA-based vaccine candidate for tuberculosis using fast-growing strains of M. smegmatis.

title: Detection of alternative lengthening of telomeres by telomere quantitative PCR
text: Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is one of two crucial telomere length maintenance mechanisms in cancer cells, allowing for their unlimited proliferative potential. Current methods for detecting ALT in tumors are time-consuming and require substantial quantities of tumor tissue, making it challenging to investigate the prevalence and prognostic significance of ALT in large tumor populations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel diagnostic strategy using telomere quantitative PCR to identify ALT. This protocol is significantly faster than conventional methods and simultaneously assesses two distinct characteristics of ALT cells: long telomeres and the presence of C-circles (partially double-stranded circles of telomeric C-strand DNA). By requiring only 30 ng of genomic DNA, this protocol will facilitate large-scale studies of ALT in tumors and can be easily adopted by clinical laboratories.

title: Noise and interlocking signaling pathways promote distinct transcription factor dynamics in response to different stresses
text: All cells possess sophisticated stress-sensing networks that detect and adapt to changing environmental conditions. Yeast cells, in particular, detect stress through a variety of signaling pathways that converge on the transcription factors Msn2 and Msn4. These proteins respond to stress by initiating rapid, unpredictable movements into and out of the nucleus. To gain insights into the role of Msn2/4 nuclear localization dynamics, we combined advanced live-cell imaging techniques with computational modeling of stress-sensing signaling networks. Our findings reveal that different signaling pathways, including Ras/protein kinase A, AMP-activated kinase, the high-osmolarity response mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway, and protein phosphatase 1, regulate Msn2 activation in distinct ways in response to varying stresses. Additionally, we discovered that brief periods of nuclear localization elicit a more robust transcriptional response than sustained nuclear residence. By employing stochastic modeling, we were able to simulate Msn2's responses to different stresses in silico and demonstrate that bursts of localization arise from noise in the signaling pathways, which are amplified by the limited number of Msn2 molecules present in the cell. This noise allows genetically identical cells to exhibit diverse behaviors in response to an uncertain environment, allowing them to balance growth and survival in an unpredictable world.

title: Long-term financing needs for HIV control in sub-Saharan Africa in 2015-2050: a modelling study.
text:
Objective:
To estimate the present value of current and future funding required for HIV treatment and prevention in 9 sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries, which account for 70% of the HIV burden in Africa, under different scenarios of intervention scale-up. To analyze the gaps between current expenditures and funding obligations and discuss the policy implications of future financing needs.
Design:
We used the Goals module in Spectrum to provide a range of estimates for future financing obligations, using the most up-to-date cost and coverage data. Four different scale-up scenarios were applied, varying by treatment initiation threshold and service coverage level. We compared the model projections to current domestic and international financial sources available in selected SSA countries.
Results:
In the 9 SSA countries, the estimated resources required for HIV prevention and treatment in 2015-2050 range from US$98 billion to maintain current coverage levels for treatment and prevention with eligibility for treatment initiation at CD4 count of <500/mm(3) to US$261 billion if treatment were to be extended to all HIV-positive individuals and prevention scaled up. With the addition of new funding obligations for HIV, which arise implicitly through commitment to achieve higher than current treatment coverage levels, overall financial obligations (sum of debt levels and the present value of the stock of future HIV funding obligations) would rise substantially.
Conclusions:
Investing upfront in scale-up of HIV services to achieve high coverage levels will reduce HIV incidence, prevention, and future treatment expenditures by realizing long-term preventive effects of ART to reduce HIV transmission. Future obligations are too substantial for most SSA countries to be met from domestic sources alone. New sources of funding, in addition to domestic sources, include innovative financing. Debt sustainability for sustained HIV response is an urgent imperative for affected countries and donors.

title: Cell-mediated immunity and antibody responses elicited by attenuated Salmonella enterica Serovar Typhi strains used as live oral vaccines in humans.
text:
The urgent need for improved typhoid vaccines is hindered by a lack of understanding of the specific factors that contribute to immunity against Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi) infections in humans. Although antibodies to S. Typhi O, H, and Vi are believed to play a role in protecting against infection, it is unclear whether these antibodies act as the primary mechanism of protection or work in conjunction with other immune responses, such as cell-mediated immunity (CMI).
CMI responses triggered by immunization with attenuated S. Typhi oral vaccines include the production of type 1 cytokines (e.g., interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor-alpha), and the activation of classical major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class Ia-restricted and novel, nonclassical MHC class Ib (HLA-E)-restricted CD8(+) cytotoxic T cell responses. The immune response to S. Typhi vaccination is more complex and comprehensive than previously thought, with various immune mechanisms contributing to protection. However, the specific immune correlates of protection remain largely unexplored.

title: Extensive Promoter-Centered Chromatin Interactions Provide a Topological Basis for Transcription Regulation
text: The understanding of higher-order chromosomal organization for transcription regulation in eukaryotes is limited, and the current study aimed to fill this gap using a novel approach called Genome-Wide Chromatin Interaction Analysis with Paired-End-Tag sequencing (ChIA-PET). By analyzing long-range chromatin interactions associated with RNA polymerase II in human cells, the study uncovered extensive interactions between promoters, both within and outside of genes, forming higher-order clusters. These clusters revealed cooperative gene expression, with promoters interacting with each other to control transcription. Notably, cell-specific chromatin interactions were found to provide structural frameworks for cell-specific transcription, and genetically-identified disease-associated noncoding elements were shown to be spatially associated with corresponding genes through long-range interactions. Overall, the study provided insights into transcription regulation through three-dimensional chromatin interactions in human cells, both for housekeeping and cell-specific genes.

title: Resazurin microtiter assay plate: simple and inexpensive method for detection of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
text: A novel method for detecting multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis is described, which involves measuring the reduction of resazurin. Eighty clinical isolates were tested against isoniazid and rifampin, and results were compared with those of the proportion method at 7 days. The method showed excellent specificity and sensitivity. Moreover, it is simple, cost-effective, and rapid, and can potentially be used with other antituberculosis drugs.

title: The pervasiveness and plasticity of circadian oscillations: the coupled circadian-oscillators framework.
text:
MOTIVATION: Circadian rhythms have been observed across various organisms, including animals, plants, fungi, and cyanobacteria, and play a fundamental role in regulating the internal homeostasis and behavior of these systems. Genetically encoded molecular clocks, which consist of negative transcription/translation feedback loops and rely on only a dozen genes, are central to maintaining these rhythms. However, high-throughput gene expression studies reveal that a significantly larger fraction of transcripts in a typical tissue oscillate with the day-night cycle, and the oscillating species vary depending on the tissue type. This suggests that a much larger fraction of all transcripts and potentially other molecular species may exhibit circadian rhythms.
RESULTS: To quantify the pervasiveness and plasticity of circadian rhythms, we conducted a large-scale analysis aggregating the results of 18 circadian transcriptomic studies and 10 circadian metabolomic studies in mice using different tissues and conditions. We found that over half of protein-coding genes in the cell can produce transcripts that exhibit circadian rhythms in at least one condition, and similar results were observed for measured metabolites. Genetic or environmental perturbations can disrupt existing rhythms by altering their amplitudes and phases, suppressing them, or giving rise to novel circadian rhythms. The oscillating species and their oscillations provide a characteristic signature of the physiological state of the corresponding cell/tissue. Molecular networks containing many oscillator loops that have been sculpted by evolution over two trillion day-night cycles have an intrinsic circadian frequency. These loops are coupled by shared nodes in a large network of coupled circadian oscillators, with clock genes forming a major hub. Cells can program and reprogram their circadian repertoire through epigenetic and other mechanisms.
AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: High-resolution and tissue/condition-specific circadian data and networks are available at http://circadiomics.igb.uci.edu. For more information, contact pfbaldi@ics.uci.edu.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Additional supplementary data can be found at Bioinformatics online.

title: Gene–environment interactions in 7610 women with breast cancer: prospective evidence from the Million Women Study
text: The text provides information about a study investigating the combined effects of low-penetrance genetic susceptibility polymorphisms and environmental factors on breast cancer incidence. The study was conducted in a large UK prospective cohort, and the authors analyzed the genotypes of 12 polymorphisms in relation to ten established environmental risk factors for breast cancer. The results showed that none of the 120 comparisons yielded significant evidence of a gene-environment interaction, and there was little evidence that the genotypic relative risks were affected by use of hormone replacement therapy. One of the polymorphisms (MAP3K1-rs889312) was found to be correlated with height, with carriers of the high-risk C allele being significantly shorter than non-carriers. The study suggests that the risks of breast cancer associated with low-penetrance susceptibility polymorphisms do not vary significantly with these ten established environmental risk factors. The study was funded by Cancer Research UK and the UK Medical Research Council.

title: Thrombocytopenia as an Indicator of Malaria in Adult Population
text:
Objective: To evaluate the predictive value of thrombocytopenia in malaria diagnosis.
Methods: This was a prospective observational study conducted at the Medical Unit of Hayat Abad Medical Complex during November 2008 to November 2010. We included all adult patients with fever and thrombocytopenia presenting to the medical unit. Platelet counts were recorded for all patients, and malaria diagnosis was made using microscopy and/or rapid diagnostic tests.
Results: A total of 228 patients with fever and thrombocytopenia were enrolled in the study, of whom 121 (53%) were diagnosed with malaria. Of these, 82 (68%) had falciparum malaria, while 39 (32%) had vivax infection. The mean platelet count for the malaria patients was 101,000/dL (SD ± 47,500), with a median of 75,000/dL. In contrast, the platelet count for the 107 patients who did not have malaria ranged between 10,000 and 150,000/dL, with a mean value of 58,000/dL (SD ± 54,000), and a median of 50,000/dL.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that the presence of thrombocytopenia may be a predictor of malaria in adults. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings and to determine the clinical utility of thrombocytopenia as a diagnostic tool for malaria.

title: AMPA receptor ligand binding domain mobility revealed by functional cross linking.
text: Glutamate receptors in the central nervous system (CNS) are primarily mediated by glutamate receptor (GluR) subtypes, with the AMPA subtype exhibiting rapid kinetics involving activation, deactivation, and desensitization on a millisecond timescale or faster. Recent research has focused on understanding the structure and function of GluR2, a key subtype involved in excitatory synaptic transmission. Using multi-channel rapid perfusion techniques, the study examined the state-dependence of intermolecular disulfide cross-links between the lower D2 lobes of the ligand binding cores in GluR2 Cys mutants. The study found that under reducing conditions, both wild-type GluR2 and mutants with cysteine substitutions (G725C and S729C) exhibit normal activation and desensitization kinetics. However, the mutants can be efficiently trapped in non-conducting states when oxidized. In contrast, the I664C mutant is only partially inactivated under oxidizing conditions. The study also found that spontaneous trapping of the receptors in the absence of glutamate is due to two motions: spontaneous breaking of the D1 dimer interface and hyperextension of the lower lobes of the ligand binding core. These findings suggest that the glutamate binding domains are surprisingly mobile in the absence of ligand, which could influence receptor activity in the brain. The study employed various conditions, including the presence of the competitive antagonist CNQX, the weak partial agonist kainate, and the L483Y mutation that stabilizes the D1 dimer interface, to assess spontaneous trapping in different situations. These results suggest that the data obtained provide valuable insights into the structure and function of glutamate receptors in the CNS, which could have implications for understanding receptor activity in the brain.

title: Ncf1 (p47phox) Is Essential for Direct Regulatory T Cell Mediated Suppression of CD4+ Effector T Cells
text:
Background: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain how regulatory T cells (Tregs) suppress effector T cells (Teffs), but none have been proven conclusively. Our previous data suggest that Tregs may modulate the microenvironment's redox state, which could play a role in suppression. We tested the hypothesis that oxidants produced by Tregs directly suppress Teffs.
Methods/Principal Findings: Tregs and Teffs were isolated from wild type (WT) or Ncf1(p47phox)-deficient mice, which lack NADPH oxidase function. Teffs were labeled with CFSE and co-cultured with unlabeled Tregs at varying ratios in the presence of anti-CD3/CD28-coated beads for 3 days. Treg-mediated suppression was quantified by flow cytometric analysis of CFSE dilution in Teffs. The presence of antioxidants (NAC or 2-mercaptoethanol) or inhibitors of NADPH oxidase (diphenyleneiodonium or VAS-2870) reduced WT Treg-mediated suppression. The suppression was partially dependent on TGFβ, which could be blocked with neutralizing antibodies. Exogenous TGFβ treatment resulted in suppression of Teff proliferation, which could be overcome with NAC. Ncf1-deficient Teff were less sensitive to suppression by exogenous TGFβ, and Ncf1-deficient Tregs suppressed Ncf1-deficient Teff poorly compared to wild type controls. Partial reconstitution of suppression occurred in assays with WT Tregs and Ncf1-deficient Teff.
Conclusions/Significance: Our findings demonstrate that NADPH oxidase-derived ROS play a role in direct Treg-mediated suppression of CD4+ Teffs. This process is blocked by thiol-containing antioxidants, NADPH oxidase inhibitors, or a lack of Ncf1 expression in Tregs and Teffs. Oxidants may represent a potential new target for modulating Treg function.

title: Oxidative damage targets complexes containing DNA methyltransferases, SIRT1, and polycomb members to promoter CpG Islands.
text: Cancer cells display concurrent losses and gains in global DNA methylation. We have found that treating cells with hydrogen peroxide can recruit DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) to damaged chromatin. DNMT1 becomes part of a complex containing DNMT3B and members of the polycomb repressive complex 4 upon hydrogen peroxide treatment. These proteins relocalize from non-CG-rich to CG-rich regions. Key components are similarly enriched at gene promoters in an in vivo colitis model. Although high-expression genes enriched for complex components exhibit histone mark and nascent transcription changes, CpG island-containing low-expression genes undergo promoter DNA methylation, suggesting that oxidative damage leads to the formation and relocalization of a silencing complex that may help explain cancer-specific aberrant DNA methylation and transcriptional silencing.

title: Expression profiles during dedifferentiation in newt lens regeneration revealed by expressed sequence tags
text:
Adult newts have the remarkable ability to regenerate their lenses from pigmented epithelial cells (PECs) of the dorsal iris through a process called dedifferentiation. The goal of this research was to obtain sequence resources for a study on newt lens regeneration and to gain insights into the molecular mechanisms of dedifferentiation at the genetic level.
To achieve this, mRNA was isolated from iris tissue during dedifferentiation and converted into a cDNA library. From this library, 10,449 clones were sequenced and analyzed, resulting in the identification of 780 contigs and 1,666 singlets. These sequences were then annotated, revealing the presence of cancer- and apoptosis-related genes during newt dedifferentiation. Additionally, several candidate genes that may play a role in the reprogramming process during dedifferentiation were also identified.
The study's findings indicate that the expression of cancer- and apoptosis-related genes may be a hallmark of dedifferentiation in newts. The obtained EST (expression sequence tag) resource provides a valuable tool for future research on newt dedifferentiation, and the sequenced data are now available in the GenBank database (accession numbers FS290155-FS300559).

title: In vivo proliferation and cell cycle kinetics of long-term self-renewing hematopoietic stem cells.
text: Rare hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) must undergo an extensive expansion to produce mature blood cells. Phenotypic isolation of HSC from mice allows for direct measurement of their proliferation kinetics. We investigated the proliferation and cell cycle dynamics of long-term self-renewing HSC (LT-HSC) in normal adult mice. Approximately 5% of LT-HSC were found to be in the S/G2/M phases of the cell cycle, while another 20% were in the G1 phase at any given time. Using BrdUrd incorporation, we determined the rate at which different cohorts of HSC entered the cell cycle over time. About 50% of LT-HSC incorporated BrdUrd by 6 days, with over 90% incorporation by 30 days. By 6 months, nearly all (99%) of LT-HSC had incorporated BrdUrd. We estimated that approximately 8% of LT-HSC entered the cell cycle asynchronously per day. Nested reverse transcription-PCR analysis revealed high levels of cyclin D2 expression in LT-HSC. Although approximately 75% of LT-HSC are quiescent in G0 at any given time, all HSC are recruited into the cell cycle on a regular basis, with 99% of LT-HSC dividing on average every 57 days.

title: The role of the tissue omega-6/omega-3 fatty acid ratio in regulating tumor angiogenesis
text: Angiogenesis plays a critical role in tumor growth and metastasis. It is well established that the metabolites of omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids, which are obtained through the diet and cannot be synthesized de novo in mammals, have different effects on cellular processes. Omega-6 fatty acid (n-6 FA)-derived metabolites promote angiogenesis by increasing growth factor expression, whereas omega-3 fatty acids (n-3 FA) have anti-angiogenic and antitumor properties. However, most studies have failed to consider the role of the n-6 FA/n-3 FA ratio in angiogenesis, instead examining the absolute levels of n-6 and n-3 FA. This review highlights the biochemical interactions between n-6 and n-3 FA and focuses on how the n-6/n-3 FA ratio in tissues regulates tumor angiogenesis. We suggest that future studies should consider the n-6/n-3 FA ratio as a key element in experimental design and analysis. Additionally, we recommend that clinical interventions aim to both reduce n-6 metabolites and simultaneously increase n-3 FA intake.

title: The Natural Statistics of Audiovisual Speech
text:
Humans, like other living beings, are exposed to a continuous stream of stimuli that are intricate, multimodal, extensive, and time-varying in nature. This complex input space must be translated and sampled by our sensory systems and transmitted to the brain for further processing. To streamline this process, it is assumed that the brain relies on statistical patterns in the stimulus space. So far, these ideas have been tested mostly on unimodal signals and natural environments. However, there is a significant gap in our understanding of how the brain processes multisensory signals, such as human speech. Specifically, we lack a clear understanding of how the brain pieces together audiovisual speech signals to form a perceived representation versus what is inherently embedded within the signal structure of the stream itself.
In this study, we aimed to fill this knowledge gap by identifying the major statistical features of audiovisual speech. Our findings include:
1. Robust associations and close temporal synchrony between the area of the mouth opening and the acoustic envelope.
2. Strongest correlation between the area of the mouth opening and vocal tract resonances.
3. Temporal modulation of both area of the mouth opening and voice envelope in the 2-7 Hz frequency range.
4. Consistent timing of mouth movements relative to the onset of the voice, between 100 and 300 ms.

We interpret these findings in the context of recent neural models of speech communication, which suggest that speech communication is a mutually coupled, multisensory event, where the output of the signaler is matched to the neural processes of the recipient.

title: Establishment of human iPSC-based models for the study and targeting of glioma initiating cells
text: Glioma tumour-initiating cells (GTICs) can arise from the transformation of neural progenitor cells (NPCs). Research on GTICs has primarily focused on isolating and studying primary tumors, as well as using human embryonic materials. Recently, the genetic landscape of human gliomas has been comprehensively mapped. Specifically, dysregulation of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) and tumor suppressor p53 signaling was found in approximately 90% and 86% of primary tumors, respectively. In this study, we investigate the use of human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) to model gliomagenesis. We find that dysregulation of RTK and p53 signaling in hiPSC-derived NPCs (iNPCs) recapitulates GTIC properties in vitro. When these cells are transplanted into mice, they form highly aggressive tumors composed of undifferentiated stem cells and their differentiated progeny. Notably, metabolic modulation compromises the viability of GTICs. Finally, we screen a library of 101 anti-cancer compounds and identify three molecules that specifically target transformed iNPCs and primary GTICs. Overall, our results highlight the potential of hiPSCs for studying human tumorigenesis.

title: Thyroid Hormone Receptor Repression Linked to Type I Pneumocyte Associated Respiratory Distress Syndrome
text: The lung is a defining feature of air-breathing animals, but the pathway regulating the formation of type I pneumocytes, which are responsible for gas exchange, remains poorly understood. In contrast, the glucocorticoid receptor and its cognate ligand have been known to promote the maturation of type II pneumocytes. However, prenatal administration of glucocorticoids is commonly used to alleviate the severity of infant respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). Interestingly, we have discovered that mutations in the nuclear co-repressor SMRT (silencing mediator of retinoid and thyroid hormone receptors) in C57BL/6 mice (SMRTmRID) lead to a previously unidentified respiratory distress syndrome caused by prematurity of the type I pneumocytes. Unlike glucocorticoid-responsive RDS, SMRT-induced RDS is unresponsive to glucocorticoid treatment. Surprisingly, treatment with anti-thyroid hormone drugs (propylthiouracil or methimazole) completely rescues SMRT-induced RDS, suggesting an unexpected and crucial role for the thyroid hormone receptor (TR) in lung development. We found that TR and SMRT control type I pneumocyte differentiation through the transcription factor Klf2, which in turn appears to directly activate the type I pneumocyte gene program. Intriguingly, mice lacking lung Klf2 fail to produce mature type I pneumocytes and die shortly after birth, closely recapitulating the SMRTmRID phenotype. These findings identify TR as a second nuclear receptor involved in lung development, specifically type I pneumocyte differentiation, and suggest a potential new therapeutic approach for RDS that is unresponsive to glucocorticoids.

title: Assessing the ceRNA hypothesis with quantitative measurements of miRNA and target abundance.
text: Recent research has suggested that competitive endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs) can act as sponges for microRNAs (miRNAs) by binding to their target sites. It is important to consider the quantitative relationship between an miRNA and its endogenous target sites in order to fully understand this phenomenon. To investigate this, we altered the abundance of intracellular target sites in hepatocytes and livers by expressing an miR-122 target and measured the effects on miR-122 target genes. We found that target repression was released in a threshold-like manner at high target site abundance (≥1.5 × 10(5) added target sites per cell), and this threshold was insensitive to the effective levels of the miRNA. Additionally, we found that global target site abundance in hepatocytes did not change significantly in response to extreme metabolic liver disease models, suggesting that modulation of miRNA target abundance is unlikely to have a significant impact on gene expression and metabolism through a ceRNA effect.

title: Immunological mechanisms for desensitization and tolerance in food allergy
text:
Food allergy is a significant public health concern in westernized countries, affecting approximately 5% of children and 3-4% of adults. However, the existing therapies for food allergy are limited, and allergen-specific immunotherapy is currently being extensively evaluated, although it is still in the experimental stage. The optimal treatment protocol, including the route of administration, target maintenance dose, and duration of maintenance therapy, as well as the ideal patient candidate, is still being studied and determined.
The mechanisms underlying successful food desensitization are not yet fully understood, mainly due to the lack of a standard immunotherapy protocol. However, research suggests that these mechanisms may involve the suppression of mast cells and basophils, the development of food-specific IgG4 antibodies, a decrease in the food-specific IgE/IgG4 ratio, the expansion and up-regulation of regulatory T cells, a shift from a Th2 to a Th1 immune profile, and the development of anergy or deletion in antigen-specific cells. Further studies are required to fully elucidate these mechanisms and identify valuable biomarkers for monitoring and evaluating food-allergic patients undergoing immunotherapy.

title: Prodromal non-motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease
text: The motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD), including bradykinesia, muscular rigidity, and tremor, are caused by the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Recent neuropathological studies have shown that Lewy bodies, the characteristic pathological hallmark of PD, are found in multiple neuronal cell types throughout the brain, with an ascending gradient of involvement from the medulla oblongata to the neocortex. This updated understanding of PD as a severe multisystemic neurodegenerative disorder highlights the importance of identifying prodromal non-motor symptoms, such as autonomic disturbances, olfactory dysfunctions, depression, and sleep disorders (including REM-sleep behavior disorder). Studies have shown that these symptoms may appear before the onset of motor symptoms and could potentially contribute to an early diagnosis of PD. Several tests are available to detect these prodromal symptoms, which could also be used in the future to evaluate the effectiveness of neuroprotective agents.

title: Erythroid Krüppel-Like Factor Directly Activates the Basic Krüppel-Like Factor Gene in Erythroid Cells �
text: The Sp/Krüppel-like factor (Sp/Klf) family comprises roughly 25 zinc finger transcription factors that recognize CACCC boxes and GC-rich elements. In this study, we investigate basic Krüppel-like factor (Bklf/Klf3) and find that its expression in erythroid tissues is highly dependent on another family member, erythroid Krüppel-like factor (Eklf/Klf1). Our results show that Bklf mRNA is significantly reduced in erythroid tissues from Eklf-null murine embryos. We discover that Bklf is driven by two promoters; a ubiquitously active GC-rich upstream promoter, 1a, and an erythroid downstream promoter, 1b. Transcripts from the two promoters encode identical proteins. Interestingly, both the ubiquitous and erythroid promoters are dependent on Eklf in erythroid cells, and Eklf also activates both promoters in transient assays. Using an inducible form of Eklf, we demonstrate activation of the endogenous Bklf gene in the presence of an inhibitor of protein synthesis. Chromatin immunoprecipitation assays confirm that Eklf associates with both Bklf promoters. Eklf is typically an activator of transcription, whereas Bklf is known to be a repressor. Our findings support the hypothesis that feedback cross-regulation occurs within the Sp/Klf family in vivo.

title: Noncanonical Wnt Signaling Promotes Obesity-Induced Adipose Tissue Inflammation and Metabolic Dysfunction Independent of Adipose Tissue Expansion
text:
Dysfunction in adipose tissue has been recognized as a crucial factor in the development of insulin resistance in obese individuals. Cell culture and mouse studies have suggested that canonical Wnt proteins play a role in regulating adipose tissue growth. However, recent evidence suggests that endogenous Wnt proteins do not appear to play a significant role in adipose tissue dysfunction, while the function of noncanonical Wnt signaling remains poorly understood.
In this study, we investigate the role of Wnt5a-mediated noncanonical Wnt signaling in adipose tissue dysfunction. We find that Wnt5a expression is significantly increased in visceral fat relative to subcutaneous fat in obese individuals. Ablation of Wnt5a in obese mice leads to improved insulin sensitivity, accompanied by reduced adipose tissue inflammation. Conversely, overexpression of Wnt5a in myeloid cells exacerbates adipose tissue inflammation and leads to more pronounced impairments in glucose homeostasis. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Wnt5a promotes the expression of proinflammatory cytokines in macrophages, leading to defective insulin signaling in adipocytes. Exogenous interleukin-6 administration can restore insulin resistance in Wnt5a-deficient mice, suggesting a central role for this cytokine in Wnt5a-mediated metabolic dysfunction.
Together, these findings support the idea that noncanonical Wnt signaling contributes to insulin resistance in obesity independent of adipose tissue expansion. This suggests that targeting noncanonical Wnt signaling may be a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of obesity-related metabolic disorders.

title: A cluster of ribosome synthesis factors regulate pre-rRNA folding and 5.8S rRNA maturation by the Rat1 exonuclease
text: The enzyme Rat1 degrades pre-rRNA fragments and processes the 5' ends of the 5.8S and 25S rRNAs. UV crosslinking revealed Rat1 binds to multiple sites on the pre-rRNA, consistent with its known functions. The major 5.8S 5' end is generated by Rat1 digestion of the ITS1 spacer from site A(3). Processing from A(3) requires a cluster of proteins, including Cic1, Erb1, Nop7, Nop12, and Nop15, which exhibit interdependent pre-rRNA binding. Surprisingly, these proteins were not crosslinked near site A(3), but instead bound regions around the 3' end of the 5.8S rRNA and the 5' end of the 25S rRNA, which are base paired in mature ribosomes, as well as the ITS2 spacer that separates these rRNAs. In contrast, the protein Nop4, which is required for endonucleolytic cleavage in ITS1, binds the pre-rRNA near the 5' end of the 5.8S rRNA. ITS2 undergoes structural remodeling in vivo, and chemical probing suggests that the A(3) cluster is necessary for this reorganization, potentially regulating the timing of processing. We propose that Nop4 and the A(3) cluster establish long-range interactions between the 5.8S and 25S rRNAs, which are subsequently maintained by ribosomal protein binding.

title: Synergistic activity of the histone deacetylase inhibitor suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid and the bisphosphonate zoledronic acid against prostate cancer cells in vitro.
text: Bisphosphonates are widely used to treat malignant bone diseases by inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and having direct effects on cancer cells. In this study, we investigated whether the anticancer activity of the third-generation bisphosphonate zoledronic acid (ZOL) could be enhanced by combining it with the histone deacetylase inhibitor suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA). We found that ZOL and SAHA worked together to induce cell death in prostate cancer cell lines LNCaP and PC-3, resulting in a synergistic effect as shown by combination index isobologram analysis. The combination of ZOL and SAHA caused dissipation of the mitochondrial transmembrane potential, activation of caspase-3, and DNA fragmentation, indicating that the combination of the two agents led to the initiation of apoptosis. Since ZOL inhibits the mevalonate pathway, which prevents protein prenylation, we examined whether the mevalonate pathway was also the target of the cooperative action of ZOL and SAHA. Our findings showed that geranylgeraniol, but not farnesol, significantly reduced ZOL/SAHA-induced cell death, indicating that the synergistic action of the agents was due to the inhibition of geranylgeranylation. Consistently, a direct inhibitor of geranylgeranylation, GGTI-298, synergized with SAHA to induce cell death, while an inhibitor of farnesylation, FTI-277, had no effect. Additionally, SAHA synergized with mevastatin, an inhibitor of the proximal enzyme in the mevalonate pathway. These in vitro findings provide a basis for exploring the potential of combining SAHA and ZOL, or other inhibitors of the mevalonate pathway, as a promising strategy for anticancer therapy in vivo.

title: The Immune Response to Melanoma Is Limited by Thymic Selection of Self-Antigens
text: The limited expression of melanoma-associated antigens (MAAs) to normal melanocytes and melanomas makes them an ideal target for immunotherapy and melanoma vaccines. However, the self-derived nature of MAAs can limit immune responses to these antigens due to thymic tolerance. The extent of this limitation is not fully understood. The autoimmune regulator (AIRE) controls the expression of tissue-specific self-antigens in thymic epithelial cells (TECs), which determines the fate of auto-reactive thymocytes. A deficiency in AIRE leads to an expanded autoreactive immune repertoire in both humans, including APECED patients, and mice. Interestingly, we found increased IgG levels to melanoma cells in APECED patients, correlating with autoimmune skin features. Additionally, enhanced CD4(+) and MAA-specific CD8(+) T cell responses were observed in AIRE(-/-) mice after melanoma challenge, highlighting the role of thymic expression of gp100 in shaping the T cell repertoire. TRP-2 (tyrosinase-related protein), on the other hand, is absent from TECs, resulting in the presence of TRP-2-specific CD8(+) T cells in both AIRE(-/-) and AIRE(+/+) mice. This study underscores the importance of investigating thymic expression of self-antigens before incorporating them into vaccination and immunotherapy strategies.

title: Murine embryonic stem cell differentiation is promoted by SOCS-3 and inhibited by the zinc finger transcription factor Klf4.
text: Homozygous embryonic stem (ES) cells with a mutation in the Shp-2 gene (Shp-2(Delta46-110)) exhibit hypersensitivity to leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) and increased phosphorylation of signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT3) upon LIF stimulation. Given this phenomenon, we hypothesized that LIF-responsive genes in Shp-2(Delta46-110) cells may be potential targets for genes vital for ES cell self-renewal. Using microarray analysis, we identified 41 genes whose expression was modified by LIF in Shp-2(Delta46-110) ES cells. Of these, we validated the induction of two significantly up-regulated genes, suppressor of cytokine signaling-3 (SOCS-3) and Kruppel-like factor 4 (Klf4), using Northern blotting. Additionally, we found that ES cells overexpressing SOCS-3 had a decreased capacity to differentiate into hematopoietic progenitors, whereas ES cells overexpressing Klf4 had a greater capacity to self-renew as evidenced by increased secondary embryoid body (EB) formation. Furthermore, Klf4-transduced d6 EBs showed higher levels of Oct-4 expression, indicating that Klf4 promotes ES cell self-renewal. These findings confirm the negative role of SOCS-3 in LIF signaling and reveal a novel function for Klf4 in ES cell biology.

title: MicroScope—an integrated microbial resource for the curation and comparative analysis of genomic and metabolic data
text:
MicroScope is an integrated platform dedicated to both the systematic updating of microbial genome annotation and to comparative analysis. The platform provides comprehensive data from completed and ongoing genome projects, including automatic and expert annotations, as well as data from post-genomic experiments such as transcriptomics and mutant collections. This enables users to refine and expand their understanding of gene functions. MicroScope features a range of tools and graphical interfaces for analyzing genomes and manually curating gene annotations in a comparative context. Since its initial release in January 2006, the platform has undergone continuous updates, including the addition of new data content and analysis tools. The most recent update was published in 2009 in the Database journal.
Today, MicroScope houses data for over 1600 microbial genomes, with approximately 300 of these genomes being manually curated and maintained by biologists. The platform receives around 50,000 expert annotations each year, which contribute to the improvement of microbial genome annotations. The platform's user-friendly interface has been significantly redesigned, and new tools have been developed and integrated to facilitate expert annotation. Additionally, in the context of the European Microme project (Framework Program 7 Collaborative Project), MicroScope is becoming a resource for the curation and analysis of both genomic and metabolic data. As more projects focus on the study of environmental bacterial (meta)genomes capable of metabolizing a diverse range of chemical compounds with industrial relevance, the importance of MicroScope as a resource for precision genome annotation and analysis will continue to grow.

title: Comparison of Maximal Oxygen Consumption Between Black and White Prepubertal and Pubertal Children
text: The aim of this study was to determine if there were any differences in maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) between two groups of black and white children, and if so, to determine whether these differences were related to hematologic profiles, body composition, or physical activity/inactivity levels. Forty-five prepubertal and 42 pubertal, clinically normal black and white children participated in the study. Body composition was measured using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, and visceral adipose tissue and s.c. adipose tissue were assessed using computed tomography scans of the abdomen. Physical activity/inactivity was evaluated using a questionnaire. The results showed that black prepubertal and pubertal children had lower VO2max values compared to white children (prepubertal: 28.8 ± 7.8 vs. 35.0 ± 6.5 mL/kg/min, p < 0.01; pubertal: 33.7 ± 6.4 vs. 40.4 ± 10.2 mL/kg/min, p < 0.05). Black children also had lower hemoglobin (Hb) concentrations and hematocrits than white children (prepubertal: 12.1 ± 0.5 vs. 12.8 ± 0.9 g/dL, p < 0.001; 35.6 ± 1.4 vs. 37.4 ± 2.3%, p < 0.01, respectively; pubertal: 13.0 ± 0.9 vs. 13.6 ± 0.7 g/dL, p < 0.05; 37.7 ± 2.5 vs. 39.5 ± 2.1%, p < 0.05, respectively). These findings suggest that black prepubertal and pubertal children had lower VO2max compared to their white peers matched for age, pubertal stage, and body mass index, which could be attributed at least in part to their lower Hb concentrations and more sedentary lifestyle. Further investigations could explore the relationship between Hb flow rate (a function of Hb × maximal cardiac output) and VO2max in black and white children.

title: Retinoic acid inhibits Th17 polarization and enhances FoxP3 expression through a Stat-3/Stat-5 independent signaling pathway.
text: CD4(+) helper T (Th) cells play a critical role in maintaining a delicate balance between host defense and autoimmune disease. Two important populations of helper T cells are the proinflammatory, interleukin-17 (IL-17)-producing (Th17) cells and the anti-inflammatory forkhead box P3-positive (FoxP3(+)) T regulatory (Treg) cells. Our study shows that all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and other agonists of the retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARalpha) inhibit the formation of Th17 cells and promote FoxP3 expression. Conversely, inhibition of retinoic acid signaling hinders transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta1) induction of FoxP3. The effect of ATRA is independent of IL-2, signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 (Stat5), and Stat3, revealing a novel mechanism for the induction of FoxP3 in CD4 T cells. Previous studies have demonstrated that vitamin A derivatives are protective in animal models of autoimmune disease, and the present data suggest a previously unappreciated role for RARalpha in the regulation of CD4(+) T-cell differentiation, providing a mechanistic explanation for the anti-inflammatory effects of retinoic acid.

title: British Journal of Nutrition (2003), 89, 295–301 q The Authors 2003 DOI: 10.1079/BJN2002776 Plasma homocysteine concentration is decreased by dietary intervention*
text: In this study, we investigated the impact of a high intake of natural folate from food on plasma total homocysteine (tHcy) concentrations in healthy females. Thirty-seven participants completed a crossover dietary intervention, with a baseline period and two 5-week diet periods (low- and high-folate diets) separated by a 3-week washout. The low-folate diet contained one serving of vegetables and fruit per day, while the high-folate diet included at least seven servings of vegetables, berries, and citrus fruit per day. We measured serum and red blood cell (RBC) folate, serum vitamin B12, and plasma tHcy concentrations at the beginning and end of each diet period. Our results show that a high intake of fresh berries, citrus fruit, and vegetables significantly increased serum and RBC folate concentrations and decreased plasma tHcy concentrations. Specifically, the mean concentration of serum and RBC folate increased by 78% and 14%, respectively, in response to the high-folate diet (P<0.001). In contrast, the serum concentration of vitamin B12 remained unchanged during the intervention. Overall, these findings suggests that a diet rich in fresh folate-containing foods can effectively increase serum and RBC folate and decrease plasma tHcy concentrations.

title: Achieving increased resolution and more pixels with Superresolution Optical Fluctuation Imaging (SOFI)
text: Superresolution Optical Fluctuation Imaging (SOFI) initially demonstrated the potential to enhance imaging resolution by a factor of square root of 2. This technique has been further improved by re-weighting the Optical Transfer Function (OTF) and exploiting cross-cumulants to achieve a fair approximation of the underlying Point-Spread Function (PSF). As demonstrated, SOFI images can be resolved with twice the diffraction limit, resulting in a significant improvement in the imaging resolution of near-infrared quantum dot labeled tubulin-network of 3T3 fibroblasts.

title: Evaluation of reagent strips in detecting asymptomatic bacteriuria in early pregnancy: prospective case series.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the performance of reagent test strips in screening pregnant women for asymptomatic bacteriuria at their first antenatal clinic visit.
Design: Prospective case series.
Setting: Antenatal clinic of a large inner-city maternity hospital.
Subjects: All women attending for their first antenatal clinic visit. Patients taking antibiotics for any reason and those with urinary tract symptoms were excluded.
Intervention: A midstream urine specimen was divided into two parts; the first half was sent for microscopy and formal bacteriological culture, while the second half was tested using a commercial reagent strip test for the presence of blood, protein, nitrite, and leucocyte esterase.
Main Outcome Measures: Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value of the reagent strips in diagnosing asymptomatic bacteriuria (defined as 10(5) colony-forming units/ml urine).
Results: Sensitivity was low, ranging from 33% when all four tests were used in combination. Specificity was high, with typical values of 99% or more. Positive predictive value reached a maximum of 69%, while negative predictive value was typically 95% or more.
Conclusion: Urine reagent strips are not sufficiently sensitive to be of use in screening pregnant women for asymptomatic bacteriuria, and therefore many patients would be missed. In light of the potentially serious sequelae of this condition in pregnant women, we recommend that formal bacteriological investigation remain the investigation of choice in this group of patients.

title: Wnt5a functions in planar cell polarity regulation in mice.
text: Planar cell polarity (PCP) refers to the polarization of cells within a two-dimensional planar sheet. In vertebrates, a distinctive epithelial PCP is observed in the uniform orientation of stereociliary bundles of sensory hair cells in the mammalian cochlea. Concurrently, planar polarization is also required for the process of convergent extension (CE), which involves a polarized cellular movement that occurs during the closure of the neural tube and the extension of the cochlea. Studies in Drosophila and vertebrates have shown that there is a conserved PCP pathway, which involves Frizzled (Fz) receptors. Using the cochlea as a model system, this study aims to investigate the involvement of known ligands of Fz, Wnt morphogens, in the regulation of PCP. Specifically, we investigate the reciprocal expression pattern of Wnt5a and the secreted frizzled-related protein 3 (Sfrp3 or Frzb) along the axis of planar polarization in the cochlear epithelium. We also assess the effect of Wnt5a on the regulation of cochlear extension and stereociliary bundle orientation in vitro, and examine the role of Wnt5a in the proper subcellular distribution of a PCP protein, Ltap/Vangl2. Furthermore, we investigate the genetic interaction between Wnt5a and Ltap/Vangl2 for the uniform orientation of stereocilia, cochlear extension, and neural tube closure. Our findings demonstrate that Wnt5a functions in the regulation of PCP in mice.

title: The RNA Polymerase “Switch Region” Is a Target for Inhibitors
text: The antibiotic myxopyronin (Myx) inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) by targeting the RNAP "switch region" - the hinge that regulates the opening and closing of the RNAP active center cleft. Through a combination of genetic, biochemical, and structural approaches, we demonstrate that Myx interacts with the RNAP switch region to prevent the RNAP from interacting with promoter DNA. We define the specific contacts between Myx and RNAP and the changes in RNAP conformation that result from Myx binding. Our findings suggest that Myx functions by interfering with the opening of the RNAP active-center cleft during transcription initiation. Additionally, we show that structurally related antibiotics, such as corallopyronin (Cor) and ripostatin (Rip), also target the RNAP switch region and function in a similar manner to Myx. Unlike previously characterized RNAP inhibitors, which target distant regions of the enzyme, the RNAP switch region is distant from the targets of Myx, Cor, and Rip, indicating that these antibiotics represent a new class of broad-spectrum antibacterial agents.

title: How reliable are light traps in estimating biting rates of adult Anopheles gambiae s.l. (Diptera: Culicidae) in the presence of treated bed nets?
text:
The study investigated the effectiveness of light traps in comparing to human bait catches in estimating the biting rates of Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes in two types of communities in southern Sierra Leone. The communities were:
1. Areas where most of the inhabitants slept under treated bed nets.
2. Areas where most of the inhabitants slept without bed nets. The study found that the number of female A. gambiae mosquitoes caught in these communities by light traps was strongly correlated (r > or = 0.72) with those from corresponding human biting catches performed either on the same or adjacent nights.
However, the study found that the relative sampling efficiency of light traps varied slightly but significantly with mosquito abundance in villages with treated bed nets, but not in those without them. Despite this, the relationship between relative sampling efficiency and mosquito abundance did not differ significantly between the two types of village.
Ultimately, the study concluded that light traps can be used as a proxy for human bait catches in estimating the biting rates of A. gambiae mosquitoes in the two communities. The study found that there was insufficient evidence to suggest that the presence of treated nets altered the relative efficiency of light traps, and any bias was minor and unlikely to have practical importance.

title: Development of a novel mouse glioma model using lentiviral vectors
text: We have developed a novel method for inducing glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) in adult, immunocompetent mice through the injection of Cre-loxP–controlled lentiviral vectors expressing oncogenes. By targeting fewer than 60 glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)-positive cells in the hippocampus, subventricular zone, or cortex of Tp53-heterozygous mice, we were able to generate GBM in these areas. In contrast, tumors were rarely observed when the mice were transduced in the cortex. Furthermore, we demonstrated that brain tumor cells isolated from mice with GBM can form GBM-like tumors in naive recipient mice, and these tumors contain CD133+ cells, form tumorspheres, and can differentiate into neurons and astrocytes. Our findings suggest that the use of Cre-loxP–controlled lentiviral vectors is a novel and region-specific method for generating a GBM model in adult mice.

title: Research Letters
text: We describe a case of preclinical variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) in an individual who died from an unrelated disorder 5 years after receiving a blood transfusion from a donor who later developed vCJD. Prion protein levels were detected using western blot, paraffin-embedded tissue blot, and immunohistochemistry in the spleen, but not in the brain. Immunohistochemistry for prion protein was also positive in a cervical lymph node. The patient was a heterozygote at codon 129 of the PRNP gene, indicating that vulnerability to vCJD infection is not restricted to individuals with the methionine homozygous PRNP genotype. These findings have significant implications for future estimates and surveillance of vCJD in the UK.

title: Swi1Timeless Prevents Repeat Instability at Fission Yeast Telomeres
text: Genomic instability stemming from DNA replication stress has been implicated in the development of cancer and genetic disorders in humans. When left unchecked, replication stress, such as fork stalling and collapse, can occur frequently throughout the genome, particularly at natural barriers like replication impediments. The fork protection complex (FPC) has been shown to play a crucial role in maintaining stalled replication forks at specific locations, including eukaryotic ribosomal DNA genes and the mating type locus in fission yeast. However, little is understood about the FPC's role in other natural replication barriers, such as telomeres. Telomeres are notoriously difficult to replicate due to the presence of repetitive GT-rich sequences and telomere-binding proteins. Despite this, the mechanisms that govern telomere replication remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the role of the fission yeast Swi1(Timeless) protein in telomere replication. Our findings reveal that loss of Swi1 leads to telomere shortening in a telomerase-independent manner, accompanied by an increased recruitment of Rad52 recombinase and more frequent amplification of telomere/subtelomeres. These changes are reminiscent of tumor cells that utilize the alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) pathway to maintain telomere length. Our results suggest that Swi1 plays a critical role in ensuring telomere replication by suppressing recombination and repeat instability at telomeres. Our findings may also shed light on the potential role of Swi1 in regulating telomere stability in cancer cells.

title: Prediction of guide strand of microRNAs from its sequence and secondary structure
text:
This study aimed to develop machine learning models for predicting the guide strands of microRNAs (miRNAs), which are produced by the sequential processing of a long hairpin RNA transcript by Drosha and Dicer, RNase III enzymes. The models were trained and tested on a dataset of 329 miRNA and 329 miRNA* pairs using cross-validation technique. The results showed that the best performance was achieved using binary pattern, with an accuracy of 0.708. Furthermore, integrating secondary structure features with binary pattern improved the accuracy to 0.719. A web server was developed based on the SVM models described in this study (http://crdd.osdd.net:8081/RISCbinder/).
The study's findings suggest that the guide and passenger strands of miRNA precursors can be distinguished based on their nucleotide sequence and secondary structure. These models have the potential to improve the field of RNA silencing technology and the understanding of microRNA processing.

The following is a summary of the main points in the text:
* Researchers have developed machine learning models to predict guide strands of miRNAs.
* Models were trained and tested on a dataset of 329 miRNA and 329 miRNA* pairs using cross-validation technique.
* The results achieved using binary pattern were the highest accuracy of 0.708.
* Integrating secondary structure features with binary pattern improved the accuracy to 0.719.
* A web server was developed based on the SVM models described in this study (http://crdd.osdd.net:8081/RISCbinder/).
* The study's findings suggest that the guide and passenger strands of miRNA precursors can be distinguished based on their nucleotide sequence and secondary structure.
* These models have the potential to improve the field of RNA silencing technology and the understanding of microRNA processing.

title: NIPBL, encoding a homolog of fungal Scc2-type sister chromatid cohesion proteins and fly Nipped-B, is mutated in Cornelia de Lange syndrome
text: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is a multifactorial disorder marked by distinctive facial features, intellectual disability, growth retardation, and limb abnormalities. Recently, we identified and studied a novel gene, NIPBL, which is mutated in individuals with CdLS. We determined the gene's structure and the corresponding genes in mice, rats, and zebrafish, and named the encoded protein Delangin. Vertebrate Delangins exhibit significant similarity to their invertebrate and plant homologs, including Scc2-type sister chromatid cohesion proteins, and Drosophila Nipped-B. We propose that disrupted Delangin function may inappropriately activate DLX genes, thereby contributing to the proximodistal limb patterning defects in CdLS. usual genome analyses often find individual Delangin or Nipped-B-like orthologs in diploid animal and plant genomes. The evolution of an ancient sister chromatid cohesion protein into a gene involved in developmental gene regulation suggests similarities between CdLS and Roberts syndrome.

title: Impaired FANCD2 monoubiquitination and hypersensitivity to camptothecin uniquely characterize Fanconi anemia complementation group M.
text:
The text can be rewritten as follows:
FANCM is a key component of the Fanconi anemia (FA) core complex, and one FA patient (EUFA867) with biallelic mutations in FANCM has been reported. Interestingly, EUFA867 also carries biallelic mutations in FANCA. Upon correction of the FANCA defect in EUFA867 lymphoblasts, a "clean" FA-M cell line was generated, which was hypersensitive to mitomycin C. Unlike cells defective in other core complex members, FANCM(-/-) cells were proficient in monoubiquitinating FANCD2 and were sensitive to the topoisomerase inhibitor camptothecin, a feature shared only with the FA subtype D1 and N. Furthermore, FANCM(-/-) cells were sensitive to UV light. Notably, both FANCM and a C-terminal deletion mutant were able to rescue the cross-linker sensitivity of FANCM(-/-) cells, while a FANCM ATPase mutant was unable to do so. These findings suggest that FANCM functions in both FA core complex-dependent and -independent manner.

title: Vesicular Glycolysis Provides On-Board Energy for Fast Axonal Transport
text: Rapid axonal transport (RAT) relies on a steady supply of energy over long distances to fuel the molecular motors that move vesicles. Our findings demonstrate that glycolysis provides ATP for the RAT of vesicles. Although inhibiting ATP production in mitochondria did not affect vesicle mobility, pharmacological or genetic inhibition of the glycolytic enzyme GAPDH significantly reduced transport in cultured neurons and Drosophila larvae. GAPDH localizes to vesicles through a huntingtin-dependent mechanism and is transported on rapidly moving vesicles within axons. Purified motile vesicles exhibited GAPDH enzymatic activity and produced ATP. Finally, we show that vesicular GAPDH is essential and sufficient to provide on-board energy for rapid vesicular transport. Although detaching GAPDH from vesicles slowed transport, targeting GAPDH to vesicles was sufficient to enhance FAT in GAPDH-deficient neurons. This specifically localized glycolytic machinery can provide constant energy independently of mitochondria, supporting the processive movement of vesicles over long distances in axons.

title: RB loss in resistant EGFR mutant lung adenocarcinomas that transform to small-cell lung cancer
text: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are successful in treating non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLCs) with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations. However, most patients will experience a relapse within an average of 1 year after continuous treatment. Interestingly, a subset of these resistant cancers undergo a fundamental transformation from NSCLC to small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). While the underlying molecular changes remain unidentified, analysis of tumor samples and cell lines from resistant EGFR mutant patients revealed that Retinoblastoma (RB) is lost in all SCLC transformed cases, but rarely in those that remain NSCLC. Furthermore, these resistant SCLC transformed cancers exhibit increased levels of neuroendocrine markers and decreased EGFR expression, as well as greater sensitivity to BCL2 family inhibition compared to resistant NSCLCs. These findings suggest that this subset of resistant cancers eventually adopt many of the molecular and phenotypic characteristics of classical SCLC.

title: Periostin Deficiency Increases Bone Damage and Impairs Injury Response to Fatigue Loading in Adult Mice
text: 골파괴와 Callus formation이 흥ione befprevention fractures are essential. Periostin (Postn), a matricellular protein, mediates the adaptive response of cortical bone to loading. However, the effect of periostin on damage and injury response to fatigue is unknown. To investigate this, we subjected Postn(-/-) and Postn(+/+) mice to axial compression fatigue on their tibia, and observed changes in bone structure and properties. In Postn(+/+) mice, cracks and surface damage (CsNb, CsS) increased 1 hour after fatigue, with decreased strength compared to non-fatigued tibia. At 15 days, woven bone formation (CtTV and CtBV) was observed in 75% of the fatigued bones, indicating a bone repair response. Cortical porosity and remodeling also significantly increased in the fatigued tibia of Postn(+/+) mice. In contrast, Postn(-/-) mice showed detectable cracks even in the absence of fatigue, with decreased collagen crosslinks and tissue hardness compared to Postn(+/+). Fatigue significantly increased CsNb and CsS in Postn(-/-), but was not associated with changes in CtTV and CtBV. Additionally, cortical porosity and remodeling did not increase in Postn(-/-), and damage remained high even after 30 days. As a result, strength remained compromised in Postn(-/-). Furthermore, the degree of anisotropy (DA) in osteocytic lacunae changed after fatigue in Postn(+/+), but not in Postn(-/-). These observations suggest that periostin influences bone materials properties, damage accumulation, and repair, including local modeling/remodeling processes in response to fatigue. Therefore, the level of periostin expression may influence the propensity to fatigue fractures.

title: Preferential occupancy of histone variant H2AZ at inactive promoters influences local histone modifications and chromatin remodeling.
text: The histone variant H2AZ (Htz1) plays a crucial role in transcriptional regulation, the prevention of unwanted chromatin spread, and genome stability. Our comprehensive analysis of the genome-wide distribution of Htz1, performed using an SWR1-dependent approach, revealed that it is widely dispersed throughout the genome, with a preference for intergenic regions. Contrary to expectations, the level of Htz1 occupancy is inversely correlated with transcription rates and the presence of RNA polymerase II under different growth conditions. Although Htz1 does not directly regulate transcriptional repression on a genome-wide scale, its presence under inactive conditions is essential for optimal activation of a subset of genes. In addition, Htz1 is not primarily responsible for nucleosome positioning, even at promoters where it is highly enriched. Furthermore, our biochemical experiments demonstrated that the incorporation of Htz1 into nucleosomes inhibits the activities of histone modifying enzymes involved in transcription, including Dot1, Set2, and NuA4, and also impedes the mobilization of nucleosomes by chromatin remodeling complexes. Taken together, these findings suggest that Htz1 may serve to identify and mark quiescent promoters, thereby ensuring proper activation.

title: Genomic organisation and transcription characterisation of the gene encoding Leishmania (Leishmania) amazonensis arginase and its protein structure prediction.
text: The genomic organization of the gene encoding Leishmania (Leishmania) amazonensis arginase, as well as its flanking regions, was characterized. The size of the transcribed RNA was determined, allowing us to map the genomic sites signaling for RNA trans-splicing and putative polyadenylation regions. The general organization was compared with genes encoding other proteins already described in organisms of the Trypanosomatid family. The complete nucleotide sequence of the arginase open reading frame was obtained, and the three-dimensional structure of the enzyme was inferred through a computational analysis of the deduced amino acid sequence, based on the established crystal structure described for Rattus norvergicus arginase. The human liver arginase sequence was analyzed in the same way, and the comparison of the presumed structure of both the Leishmania and human enzymes identified some differences that may be exploited in chemotherapeutic studies.

title: Endometrial carcinoma risk among women diagnosed with endometrial hyperplasia: the 34-year experience in a large health plan
text:
Endometrial hyperplasia (EH) can be classified into two severity levels: simple hyperplasia (SH) and complex hyperplasia (CH), as well as two subtypes of atypical hyperplasia (AH): simple atypical hyperplasia (SAH) and complex atypical hyperplasia (CAH). Predicting the risk of endometrial carcinoma (EC) progression based on these classifications is essential, but there is a lack of data on the progression of EH.
To address this gap, we conducted a nested case-control study of EH progression, including 138 cases diagnosed with EH and ultimately developing EC at least one year after their initial diagnosis (median time: 6.5 years). We also included 241 controls who were individually matched on age, date, and follow-up duration and counter-matched on EH classification. Using a centralized pathology panel and medical record review, we calculated rate ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) adjusted for treatment and repeat biopsies.
Our findings showed that AH significantly increased the risk of EC, with an RR of 14 (95% CI: 5–38) compared to disordered proliferative endometrium (DPEM) as the referent. The highest risk of EC progression was observed within one to five years after AH (RR=48, 95% CI: 8–294), but the risk remained elevated for more than five years after AH (RR=3.5, 95% CI: 1.0–9.6). In contrast, the progression risks for SH (RR=2.0, 95% CI: 0.9–4.5) and CH (RR=2.8, 95% CI: 1.0–7.9) were substantially lower than the progression risk for DPEM.
Our findings suggest that the higher progression risks for AH may justify management guidelines that differentiate between atypical and non-atypical EH. These guidelines could focus on more aggressive management of AH, considering its higher risk of progression to EC.
