title: Redefining the Genetic Hierarchies Controlling Skeletal Myogenesis: Pax-3 and Myf-5 Act Upstream of MyoD
text: We investigated the roles of Pax-3, Myf-5, and their mutant combinations in programming skeletal myogenesis by analyzing mice with genetic modifications to these genes. We found that homozygous mutations in splotch and Myf-5 resulted in distinct perturbations and early muscle defects in embryos. Interestingly, double homozygotes for splotch and Myf-5 had a striking phenotype absent in individual mutants: a complete absence of body muscles. Importantly, MyoD activation failed to rescue this double mutant phenotype, indicating that Pax-3 and Myf-5 define two distinct myogenic pathways, with MyoD acting downstream of these genes for myogenesis in the body muscles. Surprisingly, this genetic hierarchy does not appear to operate for head muscle formation.

title: Assessment of Volume Depletion in Children with Malaria
text:
Background: The extent of volume depletion in severe malaria is currently unknown, although knowledge of fluid compartment volumes can aid in treatment. To assist in the management of severely ill children and test the hypothesis that changes in fluid compartment volumes reflect disease severity, we measured body fluid compartment volumes in Gabonese children with malaria.
Methods and Findings: We used tracer dilution with heavy water and bromide to estimate total body water volume (TBW) and extracellular water volume (ECW) in children with severe or moderate malaria, and derived intracellular water volume (ICW) from these parameters. Bioelectrical impedance analysis measurements were taken daily until discharge and calibrated against dilution methods. Sixteen children had severe and 19 moderate malaria. Severe childhood malaria was associated with a significant depletion of TBW (mean [SD] of 37 [33] ml/kg, or 6.7% [6.0%]) relative to measurements at discharge, which is defined as mild dehydration in other conditions. ECW measurements were normal on admission in children with severe malaria and did not rise in the first few days of admission. Volumes in different compartments (TBW, ECW, and ICW) were not related to hyperlactataemia or other clinical and laboratory markers of disease severity. Moderate malaria was not associated with a depletion of TBW.

title: NSOM/QD-Based Direct Visualization of CD3-Induced and CD28-Enhanced Nanospatial Coclustering of TCR and Coreceptor in Nanodomains in T Cell Activation
text: We have recently advanced the use of near-field scanning optical microscopy (NSOM) and immune-labeling quantum dots (QD) to image the specific TCR response during in vivo clonal expansion. Through the application of dipole-polarization and dual-color imaging, we were able to scan cell-membrane molecules at the best-optical lateral resolution and demonstrate the distinct distribution of CD3, CD4, or CD8 molecules as single QD-bound molecules or nano-clusters on the cell membrane of unstimulated primary T cells. Approximately 6-10% of CD3 molecules were found to co-cluster with CD4 or CD8 as 70-110 nm nano-clusters without forming larger nano-domains. Following ligation of the TCR/CD3 complex, CD3 nanoscale co-clustering or interaction with CD4 or CD8 co-receptors formed 200-500 nm nano-domains or larger micro-domains. This nano-spatial co-clustering of CD3 and CD4 or CD3 and CD8 was found to be an intrinsic event of TCR/CD3 ligation, rather than solely dependent on MHC engagement, and was driven by Lck phosphorylation. Furthermore, CD28 co-stimulation significantly enhanced TCR/CD3 nanoscale co-clustering or interaction with CD4 co-receptor within nano- or micro-domains on the membrane, while CD28 co-stimulation did not enhance CD8 clustering or CD3-CD8 co-clustering in nano-domains, although it did increase the molecular number and density of CD3 clustering in larger nano-domains. These findings provide novel insights into the interaction between the TCR/CD3 complex and CD4 or CD8 co-receptors during T-cell activation.

title: Hoxa9 transforms primary bone marrow cells through specific collaboration with Meis1a but not Pbx1b.
text: Studies have shown that Hoxa9, Meis1, and Pbx1 proteins are involved in leukemic transformation in both mice and humans. These proteins interact with each other, with Hoxa9 cooperatively binding to consensus DNA sequences with Meis1 and Pbx1. In this investigation, we sought to determine whether Hoxa9 could collaborate with either Pbx1 or Meis1 to transform hemopoietic cells. We used primary bone marrow cells that had been retrovirally engineered to overexpress Hoxa9 and Meis1 simultaneously, and found that these cells induced growth factor-dependent oligoclonal acute myeloid leukemia in syngenic mice within 3 months of transplantation. In contrast, overexpression of Hoxa9, Meis1, or Pbx1 alone, or a combination of Hoxa9 and Pbx1, failed to transform these cells acutely within 6 months post-transplantation. Similar results were obtained when FDC-P1 cells, which had been engineered to overexpress these genes, were transplanted to syngenic recipients. These findings demonstrate a specific collaboration between a member of the Hox family and one of its DNA-binding partners in the transformation of hemopoietic cells.

title: Tyr26 phosphorylation of PGAM1 provides a metabolic advantage to tumours by stabilizing the active conformation
text: The mechanisms by which oncogenic signaling coordinates glycolysis and anabolic biosynthesis in cancer cells remain unclear. Recently, we reported that the glycolytic enzyme phosphoglycerate mutase 1 (PGAM1) regulates anabolic biosynthesis by controlling intracellular levels of its substrate 3-phosphoglycerate and product 2-phosphoglycerate. We have now discovered a novel mechanism in which Y26 phosphorylation enhances PGAM1 activation by releasing an inhibitory subunit, E19, that blocks the active site, stabilizing cofactor 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate binding and H11 phosphorylation. Additionally, we have determined the crystal structure of H11-phosphorylated PGAM1, which reveals that phospho-H11 activates PGAM1 by promoting substrate 3-phosphoglycerate binding. Further, we have found that Y26 phosphorylation of PGAM1 is common in human cancer cells and contributes to the regulation of 3-phosphoglycerate and 2-phosphoglycerate levels, promoting cancer cell proliferation and tumor growth. Since PGAM1 is a negative transcriptional target of TP53, and is therefore frequently upregulated in human cancers, these findings suggest that Y26 phosphorylation represents an additional mechanism underlying PGAM1 upregulation.

title: Spatial and Temporal Clustering of Dengue Virus Transmission in Thai Villages
text:
Transmission of dengue viruses (DENV), the leading cause of arboviral disease worldwide, varies over time and space due to a complex interplay of factors involving the human host, virus, mosquito vector, and environment. Understanding these factors is crucial for effective surveillance and disease prevention measures. To investigate the hypothesis that DENV transmission is spatially and temporally focused, we conducted cluster investigations in Thai villages with active and non-active transmission of the virus.
Our findings reveal that DENV transmission is remarkably focal within hyperendemic rural areas of Thailand. Among 556 village children enrolled as neighbors of 12 dengue-positive and 22 dengue-negative index cases, all 27 DENV infections (4.9% of enrollees) occurred in positive clusters (p < 0.01; attributable risk [AR] = 10.4 per 100; 95% confidence interval 1-19.8 per 100]. In positive clusters, 12.4% of enrollees became infected within a 15-day period, and DENV infections were concentrated centrally near homes of index cases. However, as only one of 217 pairs of serologic specimens tested in positive clusters revealed a recent DENV infection that occurred before cluster initiation, we attribute the observed DENV transmission after cluster investigation to recent virus transmission activity. Notably, all eight (0.8%) DENV-infected mosquitoes collected were from houses in positive clusters, with none found in control clusters or schools. Distinguishing features between positive and negative clusters included greater availability of piped water in negative clusters (p < 0.01) and a greater number of Ae. aegypti pupae per person in positive clusters (p = 0.04). Conducting cluster investigations revealed that during primarily DENV-4 transmission seasons, the ratio of inapparent to symptomatic infections was nearly 1:1 among child enrollees. 
Despite the limitations of our study, such as the inability to sample all children and mosquitoes within each cluster and reliance on serologic evidence of interval infections in enrollees due to restrictions on blood collection frequency in children, our findings suggest that active school-based dengue case detection prompting local spraying could contain recent virus introductions and reduce the longitudinal risk of virus spread within rural areas. These findings emphasize the importance of exploring the complex interplay of host immune and behavioral factors that impact DENV transmission and informing the development of effective prevention strategies. Cluster methodology has the potential to serve as a valuable research tool in investigating other temporally and spatially clustered infectious diseases.

title: Secondary T cell–T cell synaptic interactions drive the differentiation of protective CD8+ T cells
text: Immunization leads to the differentiation of CD8+ T cells, which acquires effector capabilities and transitions into a memory pool. T cell priming occurs through an immunological synapse formed with an antigen-presenting cell (APC). By disrupting synaptic stability at varying times, we found that CD8+ T cell differentiation requires additional interactions beyond those with APCs. We identified a critical differentiation phase that required interactions between primed T cells. We discovered that T cell-T cell synapses play a pivotal role in generating protective CD8+ T cell memory. T cell-T cell synapses enable T cells to polarize the critical secretion of interferon-γ (IFN-γ) towards each other. Collective activation and homotypic clustering facilitate cytokine sharing and act as regulatory stimuli for T cell differentiation.

title: The Histone H3 Lysine-27 Demethylase Jmjd3 Links Inflammation to Inhibition of Polycomb-Mediated Gene Silencing
text: Epigenetic chromatin markers hinder the ability of specialized cells to adjust gene expression programs in response to environmental signals and to change their identity. Proteins of the Polycomb group (PcG) mediate gene silencing and repress transdifferentiation by relying on the tri-methylation of histone H3 lysine 27 (H3K27me3). However, white blood cells called macrophages can change their identity when they migrate to inflamed areas, but it is unclear whether inflammation influences the PcG-mediated silencing. Our investigation shows that the JmjC-domain protein Jmjd3 is a histone H3K27me demethylase that is activated in macrophages in response to bacteria-derived compounds and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Jmjd3 binds to genes regulated by the Polycomb group and controls their H3K27me3 levels and transcriptional activity. The discovery of an inducible enzyme that removes a histone mark that regulates cell differentiation and identity provides a connection between inflammation and changes in the epigenome, which could explain the adaptability of macrophages and the aberrant differentiation in chronic inflammation.

title: Apolipoprotein E and atherosclerosis: beyond lipid effect.
text:
Apolipoprotein E (apoE) is a human protein that plays a multifaceted role in various physiological processes, including plasma lipoprotein metabolism, coagulation, oxidative processes, macrophage, glial cell, and neuronal cell homeostasis, adrenal function, central nervous system physiology, inflammation, and cell proliferation. The apoE gene is located on chromosome 19 and exists in three allelic forms (e2, e3, and e4) that determine six possible apoE genotypes and plasma phenotypes. The e4 allele is associated with higher levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and is considered proatherogenic, while the e2 allele is associated with lower LDL-C levels and is thought to have the opposite effect, although it may also be associated with increased plasma triglycerides and lipoprotein remnants.
However, the relationship between apoE and atherosclerosis is complex and not fully understood, and various mechanisms have been proposed to explain the link between the two. Despite this, apoE mimetic peptides that promote LDL clearance are currently being tested in animals for potential clinical applications.
In contrast to humans, the situation is relatively simpler in animals, particularly in mice, which have been useful for testing mechanisms related to apoE and atherosclerosis.

title: Exploitative and Hierarchical Antagonism in a Cooperative Bacterium
text: In the highly social prokaryote Myxococcus xanthus, cooperation between close relatives may lead to noncooperation with other genotypes of the same species. This noncooperation can manifest as outright aggression or social exploitation. In this study, we characterized the social interactions among nine developmentally proficient strains of M. xanthus isolated from different locations. We found that in most pairings, at least one competitor exhibited strong antagonism towards its partner, and a majority of mixes showed bidirectional antagonism that decreased total spore production, even to the point of driving entire populations to extinction. The primary determinant of competitive superiority was not the sporulation efficiency of unmixed populations, but rather differential response to mixing. In some competitive pairings, the dominant partner sporulated more efficiently in mixed populations than in clonal isolation. This finding represents a novel form of exploitation in bacteria, where socially competent genotypes exploit other genotypes. This is the first documentation of social exploitation among natural bacterial isolates, and patterns of antagonistic superiority form a highly linear dominance hierarchy. In addition, at least some competition pairs construct chimeric, rather than segregated, fruiting bodies. These findings suggest that cooperation between clone-mates in M. xanthus is accompanied by intense antagonism towards distinct social types of the same species, and that this antagonism may have large effects on local population sizes and dynamics. Furthermore, the finding of several cases of facultative social exploitation among these natural isolates suggests that such exploitation may occur frequently in nature in many prokaryotes with cooperative traits.

title: Mental Health Conditions Among Patients Seeking and Undergoing Bariatric Surgery: A Meta-analysis.
text:
The importance of bariatric surgery in achieving sustained weight loss and improved physical health outcomes for severely obese individuals is well-established. However, mental health conditions such as depression and binge eating disorder are common among patients seeking bariatric surgery, and their impact on postoperative outcomes is not fully understood.
To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a systematic review of studies published between 1988 and 2015 on the prevalence of mental health conditions among bariatric surgery candidates and recipients, as well as the association between preoperative mental health conditions and postoperative outcomes. Our findings revealed that the most common mental health conditions among bariatric surgery patients were depression (19%) and binge eating disorder (17%). However, the evidence regarding the association between preoperative mental health conditions and weight loss outcomes was inconsistent.
While bariatric surgery was associated with decreased prevalence of depression (7%-74%) and decreased severity of depressive symptoms (40%-70%) compared to preoperative levels, there was no consistent association between mental health conditions and postoperative weight loss. These findings suggest that bariatric surgery may have a positive impact on mental health outcomes, but the relationship between mental health and weight outcomes is more complex than previously thought.
In conclusion, our study highlights the importance of considering mental health in the treatment of severely obese individuals seeking bariatric surgery. While bariatric surgery may improve mental health outcomes, it is not a guarantee of weight loss success. Further research is needed to better understand the interplay between mental health and weight outcomes, and to develop personalized treatment plans that address both aspects of health.

title: The Nuclear Effector of Wnt-Signaling, Tcf1, Functions as a T-Cell–Specific Tumor Suppressor for Development of Lymphomas
text: The HMG-box transcription factor Tcf1 is crucial for T-cell development in the thymus and mediates the cellular response to Wnt signals. previous studies have shown that mice lacking Tcf1 (Tcf1-/- mice) have developmental blocks during T-cell development, resulting in a small thymus. Surprisingly, many Tcf1-deficient mice spontaneously develop thymic lymphomas, with 50% of mice developing a thymic lymphoma/leukemia by 16 weeks of age. These lymphomas are clonal, highly metastatic, and exhibit high levels of Wnt signaling when crossed with Wnt reporter mice, as well as high expression of Wnt target genes Lef1 and Axin2. In contrast to wild-type thymocytes, where Tcf1 is more highly expressed than Lef1, Tcf1-deficient thymocytes display a predominance of Wnt inhibitory isoforms. The loss of Tcf1 function as a repressor of Lef1 leads to high Wnt activity, which in turn drives lymphoma development. Notably, the development of thymic lymphomas in Tcf1-deficient mice is exacerbated by activating Notch1 mutations. Therefore, Notch1 and loss of Tcf1 function synergize as oncogenic events. Tcf1 deficiency predisposes to the development of thymic lymphomas by leading to ectopic upregulation of Lef1 due to the lack of Tcf1 repressive isoforms. Furthermore, cooperating activating mutations in Notch1 often occur in these tumors. Thus, Tcf1 functions as a T-cell-specific tumor suppressor gene, in addition to its well-established role as a Wnt responsive transcription factor. In summary, Tcf1 acts as a molecular switch between proliferative and repressive signals during T-lymphocyte development in the thymus.

title: Activator Control of Nucleosome Occupancy in Activation and Repression of Transcription
text: The relationship between chromatin structure and gene expression is a topic of intense research. The universal transcription factor Gal4 was found to remove promoter nucleosomes as it triggers transcription, but the mechanisms behind this process were unclear. In contrast, the presence of nucleosomes was thought to be required for repression of transcription. However, our new quantitative assay has shown that nucleosomes are not necessary for repression. We were able to follow the time courses of nucleosome removal and reformation in wild-type and mutant yeast cells upon activation and repression of the GAL genes. When galactose inhibitor Gal80 is removed, Gal4 quickly recruits SWI/SNF to the genes, leading to nucleosome removal. Without SWI/SNF, Gal4's action still results in nucleosome removal, but this process is significantly delayed. When glucose is added to cells growing in galactose, transcription is repressed. However, if galactose remains present, Gal4 continues to work, recruiting SWI/SNF and maintaining a nucleosome-free promoter, even though it is repressed. This requirement for galactose is removed in a mutant where Gal4 works constitutively. These findings show that an activator can control chromatin structure both during activation and repression by recruiting an enzymatic machine that removes promoter nucleosomes. Our results reveal that promoter nucleosome removal occurs invariably during activation, while nucleosome reformation is not required for repression. The discovery of two routes to nucleosome removal and transcription activation, one that requires the action of SWI/SNF recruited by the activator, and a slower route that does not, sheds new light on the early events of gene activation. Additionally, our findings contradict the widely held idea that nucleosomes are required for repression, as repression sets in efficiently regardless of promoter nucleosome reformations. This nucleosome occupancy assay will be useful in exploring other outstanding questions in the field.

title: Contractile forces sustain and polarize hematopoiesis from stem and progenitor cells.
text: The ability of stem cells to self-renew and differentiate relies on specific cellular processes, including asymmetric division and polarized motility. These processes are regulated by non-muscle myosin-II (MII) forces and the mechanical properties of the extracellular matrix. By using mass spectrometry-calibrated intracellular flow cytometry to study human hematopoiesis, we have discovered that MIIB is a major isoform that is highly polarized in hematopoietic stem cells and progenitors (HSC/Ps) and decreases in differentiated cells through an asymmetric division mechanism. In contrast, MIIA is constitutively expressed and can be activated by dephosphorylation during cytokine-induced differentiation of cells grown on stiff, endosteum-like matrices. In vivo, MIIB is essential for the generation of blood, while MIIA is required for sustained HSC/P engraftment. Interestingly, inhibition of both MII isoforms in culture using blebbistatin enriches for long-term hematopoietic multilineage reconstituting cells by 5-fold or more, as assessed in vivo. Additionally, megakaryocytes become more polyploid, producing 4-fold more platelets. Overall, MII plays a multifaceted role in polarized division and niche sensing.

title: Critical Role of the Virus-Encoded MicroRNA-155 Ortholog in the Induction of Marek's Disease Lymphomas
text:
Despite the well-established roles of some oncogenes in cancer development, microRNAs (miRNAs) have increasingly been implicated in various human cancers. The discovery of miRNAs in oncogenic herpesviruses, such as KSHV, has highlighted their potential to contribute to the oncogenic capabilities of these viruses. However, demonstrating the direct in vivo role of virus-encoded miRNAs in neoplastic diseases is challenging in the absence of suitable animal models. To address this limitation, we used rapid-onset Marek's disease (MD) lymphomas in chickens, which provide an excellent natural disease model, to examine the oncogenic potential of virus-encoded miRNAs.
Our results showed that deleting the six-miRNA cluster 1 from the viral genome abolished the oncogenicity of the virus, and this effect was primarily due to the single miRNA within the cluster, miR-M4, which is the ortholog of cellular miR-155. We confirmed the definitive role of this miR-155 ortholog in oncogenicity by rescuing the oncogenic phenotype with either the miR-M4 or the cellular homolog, gga-miR-155. This is the first demonstration of the direct in vivo role of a virus-encoded miRNA in inducing tumors in a natural infection model. Furthermore, the use of viruses deleted in miRNAs as effective vaccines against virulent MDV challenge offers the prospect of generating genetically defined attenuated vaccines.

title: Functional insights into the role of nuclear-retained long noncoding RNAs in gene expression control in mammalian cells
text: The mammalian genome hosts a vast array of long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) genes, which have been shown to play crucial roles in regulating gene expression. Recent studies have revealed the involvement of several lncRNAs in epigenetic gene regulation, transcriptional control, and post-transcriptional regulation. These non-coding RNAs are located in various subcellular compartments and the majority of them are retained in the nucleus, which are broadly classified as nuclear-retained lncRNAs (nrRNAs). The identified functions of nrRNAs include providing structural support to the hierarchical organization of the nucleus, influencing the recruitment of chromatin modifier factors to specific chromatin sites, and involvement in various diseases. This review will summarize the recent findings on the roles of mammalian nrRNAs in controlling gene expression by affecting chromatin organization, transcription, pre-mRNA processing, nuclear organization, and their involvement in disease.

title: Downregulation of TAP1 in B lymphocytes by cellular and Epstein-Barr virus-encoded interleukin-10.
text: Virally infected cells degrade intracellular viral proteins through proteolytic degradation and present the resulting peptides in association with major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules to CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). These cells are normally susceptible to CTL-mediated elimination. However, some viruses have developed strategies to evade the immune system by interfering with the pathway of antigen presentation. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) expresses a late protein, the BCRF1 gene product vIL-10, which bears sequence similarity to human interleukin-10 (hIL-10). Our findings demonstrate that vIL-10 downregulates the expression of one of the two transporter proteins (TAPs) involved in antigen presentation. Similarly, hIL-10 exhibits the same effect. The downregulation of TAP1 gene expression leads to a reduction in the transport of peptide antigens into the endoplasmic reticulum, as shown in the TAP-specific peptide transporter assay, their loading onto empty MHC I molecules, and the subsequent translocation to the cell surface. Consequently, IL-10 causes a general decrease in surface MHC I molecules on B lymphocytes, which may impact the recognition of EBV-infected cells by cytotoxic T cells.

title: TGF-β and Insulin Signaling Regulate Reproductive Aging via Oocyte and Germline Quality Maintenance
text: Reproductive aging is one of the earliest physiological changes that humans and Caenorhabditis elegans experience. While somatic aging has been extensively studied in both species, the mechanisms that regulate reproductive aging are still not well understood. However, our study has uncovered a critical role for TGF-β signaling and insulin/IGF-1 pathway in regulating reproductive aging in C. elegans. We found that TGF-β regulates multiple aspects of the reproductive process, including embryo quality, oocyte fertilizability, chromosome segregation fidelity, DNA damage resistance, and oocyte and germline morphology. Specifically, TGF-β activity regulates reproductive span and germline/oocyte quality non-cell-autonomously and is temporally and transcriptionally distinct from its regulation of growth. Additionally, upregulation of chromosome segregation, cell cycle, and DNA damage response genes in TGF-β mutant oocytes may contribute to the decline in oocyte quality in aged mammalian oocytes. Our findings suggest striking similarities between the reproductive aging processes in C. elegans and humans, including the correlation between reproductive aging and declining oocyte quality, as well as the shared genetic mechanisms involved in oocyte quality maintenance.

title: The Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition Generates Cells with Properties of Stem Cells
text: The epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a crucial developmental program that often plays a role in cancer metastasis and invasion. In this study, we investigated the induction of EMT in immortalized human mammary epithelial cells (HMLEs) and found that it leads to the acquisition of mesenchymal traits and the expression of stem cell markers. Moreover, we observed that cells undergoing EMT exhibit increased mammosphere formation, which is a hallmark of mammary epithelial stem cells. Interestingly, stem cells isolated from HMLE cultures and mammary glands/carcinomas also express EMT markers, highlighting a direct link between EMT and the gain of epithelial stem cell properties. Furthermore, transformed HMLE cells that have undergone EMT exhibit enhanced mammosphere, soft agar colony, and tumor formation capabilities. These findings provide conclusive evidence of the direct relationship between EMT and the acquisition of epithelial stem cell properties.

title: NEMO Prevents RIP Kinase 1-Mediated Epithelial Cell Death and Chronic Intestinal Inflammation by NF-κB-Dependent and -Independent Functions
text: Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) play a crucial role in maintaining gut immune homeostasis, and dysregulation of IEC functions can contribute to the development of inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). In particular, the nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) essential modulator (NEMO) has been shown to be essential for IEC function and survival. Depletion of NEMO in IECs can lead to Paneth cell apoptosis and impaired antimicrobial factor expression in the ileum, as well as colonocyte apoptosis and microbiota-driven chronic inflammation in the colon. Interestingly, while combined deficiency of RelA, c-Rel, and RelB in IECs leads to Paneth cell apoptosis, it does not cause colitis, suggesting that NEMO may prevent colon inflammation through NF-κB-independent functions. Moreover, inhibition of receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) kinase activity or combined deficiency of Fas-associated via death domain protein (FADD) and RIPK3 can prevent epithelial cell death, Paneth cell loss, and colitis development in mice with epithelial NEMO deficiency. These findings suggest that NEMO may be a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of colitis in patients with NEMO mutations and possibly in IBD, as inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity could help prevent IEC death and inflammation in the gut.

title: Suppression of Myc oncogenic activity by ribosomal protein haploinsufficiency
text: The Myc oncogene regulates the expression of several components involved in protein synthesis, including ribosomal proteins, translation initiation factors, RNA polymerase III, and ribosomal DNA. While it remains unclear how increased protein synthesis capacity affects the complexity of cancer development, we used ribosomal protein heterozygous mice as a genetic tool to restore normal protein synthesis levels in Emu-Myc/+ transgenic mice. Our findings show that the oncogenic potential of Myc is diminished when protein synthesis is restored. We discovered that Myc's ability to increase protein synthesis directly enhances cell size and speeds up cell cycle progression independently of known cell cycle targets regulated by Myc. Additionally, when we restored normal protein synthesis levels in Myc-overexpressing precancerous cells, they were more efficiently eliminated through programmed cell death. Our findings uncover a new mechanism connecting elevated protein synthesis rates to a specific translation initiation defect in the regulation of selective messenger RNAs. We discovered that an aberrant increase in cap-dependent translation downstream of Myc hyperactivation specifically impairs the translational switch to internal ribosomal entry site (IRES)-dependent translation required for accurate mitotic progression. This defect results in reduced mitotic-specific expression of the endogenous IRES-dependent form of Cdk11 (also known as Cdc2l and PITSLRE), which leads to cytokinesis defects and is associated with increased centrosome numbers and genome instability in Emu-Myc/+ mice. When translational control is re-established in Emu-Myc/+ mice, genome instability is repressed. Our discoveries highlight the highly specific consequences of translational control disturbances in gene expression, genome stability, and cancer initiation, which have far-reaching implications for understanding cancer formation at the post-genomic level.

title: Susceptibility to exacerbation in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text:
Although the significance of exacerbations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is well established, our comprehension of their recurrence, determining factors, and consequences remains limited. In a large observational cohort study, we aimed to assess the hypothesis that a specific subtype of COPD, characterized by a high frequency of exacerbations, exists independently of disease severity.
We analyzed the occurrence and correlations of exacerbations in 2138 patients enrolled in the Evaluation of COPD Longitudinally to Identify Predictive Surrogate Endpoints (ECLIPSE) study over a three-year period. Exacerbations were defined as events that required antibiotic or corticosteroid prescription (or both) or hospitalization (severe exacerbations). Our findings revealed that exacerbation frequency increased progressively with the severity of COPD, with rates of 0.85, 1.34, and 2.00 per patient in stage 2, 3, and 4 disease, respectively. Notably, 22% of stage 2 patients, 33% of stage 3 patients, and 47% of stage 4 patients experiencing two or more exacerbations during the first year of follow-up. The most significant predictor of exacerbations across all stages was a history of prior events, highlighting the importance of personalized prevention strategies. Moreover, we discovered that the frequent-exacerbation phenotype remained relatively stable over three years and could be predicted based on the patient's recall of previous treated events. Additional correlations were observed between this phenotype and history of gastroesophageal reflux or heartburn, poorer quality of life, and elevated white-cell count.
Our study suggests that while exacerbations become more frequent and severe with advancing COPD severity, there exists an independent susceptibility phenotype that may influence the targeting of prevention strategies across the disease spectrum. (Funded by GlaxoSmithKline; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00292552.)

title: Sympathetic baroreflex gain in normotensive pregnant women.
text: During normotensive pregnancy, there is an increase in muscle sympathetic nerve activity while mean arterial pressure is maintained or reduced, suggesting a resetting of the baroreflex set point. We hypothesized that spontaneous sympathetic baroreflex gain would be reduced in normotensive pregnant women compared to nonpregnant matched controls. To investigate this, we measured integrated muscle sympathetic burst incidence, total sympathetic activity, and R-R interval at rest in 11 pregnant women (age 33 ± 1 weeks gestation, height 23.5 ± 0.9 kg/m2) and 11 nonpregnant controls (age 29 ± 1 year, height 25.2 ± 1.7 kg/m2). Our results showed that pregnant women had elevated baseline sympathetic burst incidence and total sympathetic activity compared to controls. Despite similar mean and diastolic blood pressure levels between the two groups, the baroreflex gain calculated as the linear relationship between sympathetic burst incidence and diastolic blood pressure was reduced in pregnant women. Furthermore, sympathetic and cardiovagal gains were negatively correlated in pregnant women. These findings suggest that the influence of the sympathetic nervous system over arterial blood pressure is reduced in normotensive pregnancy, likely through a baroreceptor-dependent mechanism.

title: Facilitators and Impediments of the Pluripotency Reprogramming Factors' Initial Engagement with the Genome
text:
The aberrant expression of transcription factors can reset cellular identity, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. To shed light on this process, we mapped the distribution of Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc (O, S, K, and M) on the human genome during the initial 48 hours of converting fibroblasts to pluripotency. Three key observations emerged from our study:
Firstly, c-Myc plays an unexpected role in facilitating the engagement of OSK chromatin domains, which are crucial for reprogramming. Secondly, O, S, and K act as pioneer factors at enhancers of genes that promote reprogramming, suggesting their early involvement in the process. Finally, we identified megabase-scale chromatin domains marked by H3K9me3, including many genes essential for pluripotency, that initially reject OSKM binding and hinder the efficiency of reprogramming.
In summary, our findings highlight the complex and diverse nature of the initial factor binding events that occur during cellular reprogramming, suggesting that a minority of cells must overcome these barriers to achieve pluripotency.

title: Fibrillar Collagen Inhibits Arterial Smooth Muscle Proliferation through Regulation of Cdk2 Inhibitors
text: Arterial smooth muscle cells (SMCs) are temporarily halted in the G1 phase of the cell cycle when they come into contact with polymerized type I collagen fibrils, while monomeric collagen actually promotes SMC proliferation. The enzymes cyclin E-associated kinase and cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (cdk2) are prevented from functioning properly on polymerized collagen, and the levels of the cdk2 inhibitors p27Kip1 and p21Cip1/Waf1 increase significantly compared to SMCs grown on monomeric collagen. In fact, p27Kip1 binds to the cyclin E-cdk2-p21Cip1/Waf1 complex in these SMCs. Interestingly, monovalent blocking antibodies to alpha2 integrins, which are responsible for adhesion to both types of collagen, mimic these effects when SMCs are grown on monomeric collagen. Furthermore, polymerized collagen rapidly suppresses the activity of p70 S6 kinase, a potential regulator of p27Kip1. It follows that fibrillar collagen specifically regulates early integrin signaling, which may ultimately lead to increased levels of cdk2 inhibitors and decreased SMC proliferation.

title: Memory CD4+ T cells induce innate responses independently of pathogen
text: Studies have shown that recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) can trigger intense innate inflammatory responses. We questioned whether the adaptive immune system could also influence the character and magnitude of these initial inflammatory responses. We discovered that the reaction of memory, but not naive, CD4+ T cells can significantly enhance the production of multiple innate inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (IICs) in the lung, and this leads to early control of the virus during influenza infection. Memory CD4+ T cell-induced IICs and viral control depend on cognate antigen recognition and are most effective when memory cells are either Th1 or Th17 polarized. However, this process does not require the production of interferon-γ (IFN-γ) or tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and is independent of activated pathogen recognition pathways. This findings represent a previously unidentified mechanism by which memory CD4+ T cells can trigger an early innate response to enhance immune protection against pathogens.

title: Direct Upregulation of STAT3 by MicroRNA-551b-3p Deregulates Growth and Metastasis of Ovarian Cancer.
text:
Introduction:
Ovarian cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths in women, and high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) is the most aggressive and common subtype. Cancer cells display uncontrolled proliferation and resistance to apoptosis, leading to poor clinical outcomes. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that play a critical role in the regulation of gene expression and have been implicated in cancer development and progression. In this study, we investigated the role of miRNA 3q26.2 in HGSOC and explored its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target.
Methods:
We used a combination of bioinformatic and experimental approaches to investigate the expression of miRNA 3q26.2 in HGSOC cells. We used cell viability assays, Western blotting, and luciferase reporter assays to study the functional effects of miRNA 3q26.2 on cell proliferation, apoptosis, and transcriptional activation.
Results:
Our results showed that miRNA 3q26.2 is overexpressed in HGSOC cells compared to normal ovarian cells. Overexpression of miRNA 3q26.2 led to increased expression of the mature microRNA miR551b-3p, which is known to be associated with poor clinical outcome in HGSOC. In addition, we found that miR551b-3p contributes to resistance to apoptosis and increased survival and proliferation of cancer cells in vitro and in vivo. We also demonstrated that miR551b-3p upregulates STAT3 protein levels by binding to the STAT3 promoter and recruiting RNA polymerase II and the TWIST1 transcription factor. Furthermore, inhibition of miR551b reduced STAT3 expression in ovarian cancer cells in vitro and in vivo and reduced ovarian cancer growth in vivo.
Discussion:
Our findings suggest that miRNA 3q26.2 plays a critical role in the development and progression of HGSOC by upregulating the expression of miR551b-3p, which in turn regulates STAT3 expression. miR551b-3p is a promising candidate biomarker and therapeutic target in ovarian cancer, and our data provide a rationale for the use of anti-miR551b therapy in the treatment of HGSOC. Future studies will focus on further elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying the actions of miR551b-3p and developing new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of ovarian cancer.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study highlights the potential of miRNA 3q26.2 as a biomarker and therapeutic target in HGSOC. By identifying the molecular mechanisms underlying the actions of miR551b-3p, we have provided a rationale for the use of anti-miR551b therapy in the treatment of HGSOC, and our findings underscore the importance of targeting miRNAs in ovarian cancer. Further research is needed to validate our findings and to determine the clinical utility of miRNA-targeted therapies in ovarian cancer.

title: Human albumin administration in critically ill patients: systematic review of randomised controlled trials.
text: Objective: To assess the effect of administering human albumin or plasma protein fraction on mortality rates in critically ill patients. Design: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials comparing administration of albumin or plasma protein fraction with no administration or crystalloid solution in patients with hypovolaemia, burns, or hypoalbuminaemia. Subjects: A total of 30 randomized controlled trials involving 1419 patients were included in the review. Main Outcome Measure: Mortality rates at the end of follow-up for each trial were the primary outcome measure. Results: The results showed that the risk of death in the albumin-treated group was higher than in the comparison group for each patient category. Specifically, the relative risk of death after albumin administration was 1.46 (95% CI: 0.97-2.22) for hypovolaemia, 2.40 (95% CI: 1.11-5.19) for burns, and 1.69 (95% CI: 1.07-2.67) for hypoalbuminaemia. The pooled relative risk of death with albumin administration was 1.68 (95% CI: 1.26-2.23), with a fixed effects model indicating a 6% (95% CI: 3%-9%) increase in the risk of death with albumin. Conclusion: The data suggest that there is no evidence that albumin administration reduces mortality rates in critically ill patients with hypovolaemia, burns, or hypoalbuminaemia, and a strong suggestion that it may increase mortality. These findings imply that use of human albumin in critically ill patients should be urgently reviewed and rigorously conducted, randomized controlled trials should be the basis for any future recommendations.

title: A fine-scale map of recombination rates and hotspots across the human genome.
text: High-resolution genetic maps, which detail the varying recombination rates across a genome, are a vital tool for various genetic analyses. We have generated a detailed genetic map of the human genome based on statistical evaluations of genetic variation data and identified over 25,000 recombination hotspots, along with their associated motifs and sequence contexts. The study reveals notable differences in the behavior of recombination rates at both large (megabase) and small (kilobase) scales, leading us to propose a two-stage model of recombination. According to this model, hotspots are random features within a larger framework in which long-range recombination rates are constrained.

title: Mental Health Support Provided Throughout the Bariatric Surgery Clinical Pathway in French Specialized Care Centers for Obesity
text: According to international guidelines, pre-operative psychological assessment is recommended for bariatric surgery candidates. Therefore, healthcare teams caring for bariatric patients should include a mental health provider, such as a psychologist or psychiatrist. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the psychology and psychiatry resources and practices in France's 37 specialized obesity centers (CSOs), established by the French Ministry of Health. The CSO coordinators were contacted via email to gather basic information on the centers, such as the number of bariatric procedures. Then, psychologists and psychiatrists from each center completed an anonymous questionnaire assessing their professional practices and organization of care pathways. A total of 81% (26/32) of CSO coordinators responded to the survey. The results revealed significant differences and shortages in terms of psychology and psychiatry resources. Most psychologists (26/31) and psychiatrists (10/10) stated that they typically meet new patients only before or after surgery (56% and 30%, respectively), but some psychologists and psychiatrists (14%) do not meet all patients (before and/or after surgery). Notwithstanding, all professionals provide psychology assessments, and around 75% of them offer a psychological follow-up, indicating similar practices among psychologists and psychiatrists. Our findings highlight the importance of psychological/psychiatric evaluations in French CSOs and stress the scarcity of mental health providers in some of these services. Post-operative psychological follow-up is typically not provided. It is recommended to create clear guidelines for long-term post-operative psychological or psychiatric follow-up.

title: Calcium: Regulation of cell death: the calcium–apoptosis link
text: The choice is yours: to live or to die? This pertinent question poignantly illustrates the dual nature of calcium (Ca2+) in living organisms - a survival factor or a merciless killer. It has long been acknowledged that Ca2+ signals regulate a wide range of essential cellular functions and are crucial for cell survival. However, more recent research has revealed that excessive or disrupted intracellular Ca2+ compartmentalization can lead to cytotoxicity and trigger either apoptotic or necrotic cell death.

title: Breaking the code of DNA binding specificity of TAL-type III effectors.
text: Many bacteria rely on the injection of effector proteins through type III secretion to manipulate cellular processes in eukaryotic cells. TAL (transcription activator-like) effectors from plant pathogenic Xanthomonas are key virulence factors that function as transcriptional activators in the plant cell nucleus by directly binding to DNA with a central domain composed of tandem repeats. In this study, we investigate how the specificity of TAL effectors is encoded. Each repeat contains two hypervariable amino acid residues that recognize one base pair in the target DNA. We used computational methods to predict recognition sequences of TAL effectors and experimentally validated these predictions. Our findings demonstrate the modular protein architecture of TAL effectors, enabling the creation of artificial effectors with new specificities. This study sheds light on the functionality of a unique DNA binding domain and paves the way for the design of DNA binding domains for biotechnology applications.

title: Interferon-Gamma at the Crossroads of Tumor Immune Surveillance or Evasion
text: Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) is a multifunctional cytokine with both anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic properties, making it an important player in the immune response to cancer. Despite its potential as a therapeutic agent, IFN-γ-based treatments have had limited success in clinical trials. Recent studies suggest that IFN-γ may also promote tumor growth and progression through mechanisms such as insensitivity to IFN-γ signaling, downregulation of major histocompatibility complexes, and upregulation of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase and programmed cell-death ligand 1. However, the overall impact of IFN-γ on patient survival remains positive in certain cancers. Therefore, further research is needed to uncover the intricate and highly regulated mechanisms of IFN-γ in the tumor microenvironment. This review aims to summarize current knowledge on the pro- and antitumorigenic effects of IFN-γ and its potential as a therapeutic target for cancer treatment, with a focus on identifying IFN-γ-responsive patients who may benefit from these treatments.

title: Role of antioxidants in paraquat toxicity.
text:
Paraquat, a highly toxic quarternary nitrogen herbicide, has been associated with numerous cases of acute poisoning and death over the past few decades. The mechanisms of paraquat toxicity involve the generation of superoxide anions, which can lead to the formation of more toxic reactive oxygen species such as hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radicals. Additionally, the oxidation of cellular NADPH, the primary source of reducing equivalents for intracellular reduction of paraquat, disrupts important NADPH-requiring biochemical processes. Respiratory failure due to an oxidative insult to the alveolar epithelium with subsequent obliterating fibrosis is the major cause of death in paraquat poisoning.
Currently, management of paraquat poisoning is largely supportive and involves modifying the toxicokinetics of the poison. Unfortunately, there are no true pharmacological antagonists for paraquat, and chelating agents capable of binding the poison in the blood or other tissues are also unavailable. Given that paraquat induces its toxic effects through oxidative stress-mediated mechanisms, innovations in the management of paraquat poisoning are being directed towards the use of antioxidants. This review provides an overview of the current status of antioxidants in ameliorating or treating the toxic effects produced by paraquat.

title: Nucleation of nuclear bodies by RNA
text: The genesis of the distinct functional compartments within the mammalian cell nucleus remains largely obscure. In particular, the initial stage of nucleation necessary for nuclear body formation is poorly understood. Here, we uncover a vital role for RNA in the formation of these nuclear structures. Our findings demonstrate that both coding and non-coding RNAs can act as structural elements and initiators of nuclear body formation. We find that specific RNAs recruit and accumulate proteins residing within these bodies, leading to their formation. These results highlight the significance of transcription in nuclear body formation, and suggest that RNA serves as a scaffold in the creation of key nuclear structures, including histone loci bodies, nuclear speckles, paraspeckles, and nuclear stress bodies. These findings establish that RNA-mediated biogenesis of nuclear bodies is a universal principle of nuclear organization.

title: Evaluation of human papillomavirus testing in primary screening for cervical abnormalities: comparison of sensitivity, specificity, and frequency of referral.
text: The study aimed to evaluate the accuracy of human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade 3 or cancer. The study included 4075 women who attended Planned Parenthood clinics in Washington State and were simultaneously screened using thin-layer Pap and HPV DNA testing by two different methods. The results showed that HPV DNA testing had higher sensitivity but lower specificity than thin-layer Pap screening for detecting CIN 3 or higher. The study found that the strategy requiring repeat positive PCR tests on two visits had the highest sensitivity (84.2%) and specificity (86.2%) among the seven colposcopy triage strategies evaluated. Additionally, the study found that HPV testing was more accurate in older women (> or = 30 years) compared to younger women. The study concluded that in some settings, HPV DNA testing may be a reasonable alternative to cytology-based screening for reproductive-age women, particularly in settings where screening intervals are long or haphazard.

title: Breaking the chains: structure and function of the deubiquitinases
text: Ubiquitination is a reversible protein modification that plays a crucial role in various cellular processes. Recent advancements have led to a deeper understanding of a superfamily of enzymes known as deubiquitinases (DUBs), which remove ubiquitin from proteins. Contrary to their uniform naming, DUBs exhibit a vast array of distinct mechanistic features. Despite the small number (less than 100) of DUBs, these enzymes are subject to multiple layers of regulation that control their activity and specificity, suggesting a high degree of selectivity. Due to their widespread involvement in crucial regulatory pathways, DUBs may emerge as promising new therapeutic targets.

title: Replication protein A: a heterotrimeric, single-stranded DNA-binding protein required for eukaryotic DNA metabolism.
text: Replication protein A, also known as replication factor A (RFA) or human single-stranded DNA-binding protein (hSSDP), is a crucial single-stranded DNA-binding protein that plays a vital role in multiple processes in eukaryotic DNA metabolism, including DNA replication, DNA repair, and recombination. RPA homologues have been identified in all eukaryotic organisms examined and are constituted of abundant heterotrimeric proteins, each consisting of subunits of approximately 70, 30, and 14 kDa. These proteins bind nonspecifically to single-stranded DNA and interact with/or modify the activities of various proteins. In cells, RPA is phosphorylated by DNA-dependent protein kinase when bound to single-stranded DNA (during S phase and after DNA damage), potentially playing a coordinating role in DNA metabolism. Additionally, RPA may also modulate gene expression.

title: Internal fixation versus nonoperative treatment of displaced 3-part proximal humeral fractures in elderly patients: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Background: The aim of this study was to evaluate the 2-year outcomes of elderly patients with a displaced 3-part fracture of the proximal humerus who were randomly assigned to treatment with a locking plate or nonoperative treatment.
Patients and Methods: We included 60 patients with a mean age of 74 years (ranging from 56 to 92 years), with 81% being women. The primary outcome measures included Constant and Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) scores, as well as health-related quality of life (HRQoL) assessed using the EQ-5D.
Results: At the final 2-year follow-up, the results for range of motion (ROM), function, and HRQoL showed significant improvements in favor of the locking plate group. Specifically, the mean flexion in the locking plate group was 120° compared to 111° in the nonoperative group (P = .36), and the mean abduction was 114° compared to 106° (P = .28). Correspondingly, the mean Constant score improved from 58 to 61 (P = .64), the DASH score decreased from 35 to 26 (P = .19), and the mean EQ-5D (index) score improved from 0.59 to 0.70 (P = .26). However, despite good initial reduction in 86% of fractures in the locking plate group, 13% of patients experienced a fracture complication requiring a major reoperation and 17% required a minor reoperation.
Conclusion: Our findings indicate that treatment with a locking plate provides better functional outcomes and HRQoL compared to nonoperative treatment in elderly patients with a displaced 3-part fracture of the proximal humerus, but at the cost of additional surgical interventions in approximately 30% of patients.

title: Good and bad consequences of altered fatty acid metabolism in heart failure: evidence from mouse models.
text: The historical interpretation of heart failure's shift towards glucose metabolism as an oxygen-sparing mechanism has been challenged by recent data. Contrary to the long-held belief that inhibiting fatty acid oxidation (FAO) is an effective treatment for heart failure, recent studies suggest that relying on glucose metabolism might actually worsen cardiac function. This review aims to provide an overview of the current understanding of metabolic adaptations in heart failure, with a focus on studies using mouse models to investigate the effects of modulating cardiac FA metabolism on cardiac function. By examining the impact of FA metabolism modulation under both ischaemic and non-ischaemic heart failure conditions, we hope to shed light on whether and when these modulations can be protective against heart failure.

title: Pericytes of human skeletal muscle are myogenic precursors distinct from satellite cells
text: Cells derived from blood vessels in human skeletal muscle can regenerate skeletal muscle tissue, similar to embryonic "mesoangioblasts." However, adult cells do not express endothelial markers, but instead express markers of pericytes, such as NG2 proteoglycan and alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and can be isolated from freshly dissociated ALP-positive cells. Unlike conventional myogenic precursors (satellite cells), pericyte-derived cells express myogenic markers only in differentiated myotubes, which they form spontaneously with high efficiency. When transplanted into severe combined immune deficient–X-linked, mouse muscular dystrophy (scid–mdx) mice, pericyte-derived cells colonize host muscle and generate numerous fibers expressing human dystrophin. Similar cells isolated from Duchenne patients, and engineered to express human mini-dystrophin, also give rise to many dystrophin-positive fibers in vivo. These findings suggest that myogenic precursors distinct from satellite cells are associated with the microvascular walls of human skeletal muscle, may represent a correlate of embryonic "mesoangioblasts" present after birth, and may be a promising candidate for future cell-therapy protocols in patients.

title: Ten years' experience with alendronate for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women.
text:
BACKGROUND: Antiresorptive agents are widely used to treat osteoporosis. We report the outcomes of a multinational, double-blind randomized study in which postmenopausal women with osteoporosis were treated with alendronate for up to 10 years.
METHODS: During the initial three-year phase, participants were randomly assigned to receive either alendronate or placebo, with 3 doses per day. Participants in the placebo group who completed the initial phase were given alendronate in years 4 and 5, and then discharged. Those in the active-treatment groups continued to receive alendronate during the initial extension (years 4 and 5) and two further extensions (years 6-7 and years 8-10). Participants in the discontinuation group received alendronate at a dose of 20 mg daily for two years, followed by 5 mg daily in years 3-5, and then five years of placebo. Randomized group assignments and blinding were maintained throughout the 10 years. We analyzed the outcomes of the 247 women who completed all four phases of the study.
RESULTS: Ten years of treatment with 10 mg of alendronate daily resulted in significant increases in bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine (mean increase of 13.7%, 95% CI: 12.0-15.5%), trochanter (mean increase of 10.3%, 95% CI: 8.1-12.4%), femoral neck (mean increase of 5.4%, 95% CI: 3.5-7.4%), and total proximal femur (mean increase of 6.7%, 95% CI: 4.4-9.1%). In contrast, treatment with 5 mg of alendronate daily resulted in smaller gains in BMD. Discontinuation of alendronate resulted in a gradual loss of its effects on BMD and biochemical markers of bone remodeling.
CONCLUSIONS: The therapeutic effects of alendronate were sustained over a 10-year period, and the drug was well tolerated. Discontinuation of alendronate resulted in a gradual loss of its effects on BMD.

title: UCP1-independent signaling involving SERCA2b-mediated calcium cycling regulates beige fat thermogenesis and systemic glucose homeostasis
text: Uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) plays a central role in thermogenesis in brown fat, but its involvement in beige fat is uncertain. We have discovered a UCP1-independent thermogenic mechanism in beige fat that relies on enhanced ATP-dependent calcium cycling by the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase 2b (SERCA2b) and ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2). Inhibition of SERCA2b hinders UCP1-free beige fat thermogenesis in both humans and mice as well as in pigs, which lack a functional UCP1 protein. Conversely, boosting calcium cycling via activation of alpha-1 and/or beta-3 adrenergic receptors or the SERCA2b-RyR2 pathway promotes UCP1-independent thermogenesis in beige adipocytes. Without UCP1, beige fat efficently burns glucose through enhanced glycolysis, tricarboxylic acid metabolism, and pyruvate dehydrogenase activity to generate ATP for thermogenesis through the SERCA2b pathway, making beige fat a 'glucose sink' that improves glucose tolerance independently of body weight loss. Our findings reveal a noncanonical thermogenic mechanism by which beige fat regulates whole-body energy homeostasis through calcium cycling.

title: Poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN) mediates 3′-end maturation of the telomerase RNA component
text: Mutations in the PARN gene, which encodes poly(A)-specific ribonuclease, are responsible for rare genetic disorders such as familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and dyskeratosis congenita. However, the mechanism by which PARN deficiency impairs telomere maintenance remains unclear. To investigate, we used somatic cells and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from patients with dyskeratosis congenita and PARN mutations. Our findings reveal that PARN plays a critical role in the maturation of the telomerase RNA component (TERC). Patient-derived cells and immortalized cell lines with disrupted PARN display decreased levels of TERC. We also found that deep sequencing of TERC RNA 3' termini revealed that PARN is required for the removal of post-transcriptionally acquired oligo(A) tails that target nuclear RNAs for degradation. Remarkably, restoring PARN in these cells normalized the diminished TERC levels and the increased proportion of oligo(A) forms of TERC. Our results provide a new function for PARN in the biogenesis of TERC and offer insights into the molecular links between PARN mutations and telomere diseases.

title: Folic acid supplementation and dietary folate intake, and risk of preeclampsia
text:
Background/Objectives: Folic acid supplementation has been proposed as a potential means of reducing the risk of preeclampsia. However, previous epidemiological studies have yielded inconclusive results. This study aimed to investigate the hypothesis that folic acid supplementation and dietary folate intake before conception and during pregnancy decrease the likelihood of preeclampsia.
Subjects/Methods: A birth cohort study was conducted from 2010 to 2012 at the Gansu Provincial Maternity & Child Care Hospital in Lanzhou, China. A total of 10,041 pregnant women without chronic hypertension or gestational hypertension were enrolled.
Results: Compared to non-users, folic acid supplement users had a lower incidence of preeclampsia (odds ratio (OR) = 0.61, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.43-0.87). A significant dose-response relationship was observed among women who used folic acid supplements during pregnancy only, with a greater reduction in risk observed with longer duration of use (P-trend = 0.007). The reduced risk associated with folic acid supplementation was consistent for mild or severe preeclampsia and for early- or late-onset preeclampsia, although the statistical significance was only reached for mild (OR = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.30-0.81) and late-onset (OR = 0.60, 95% CI: 0.42-0.86) preeclampsia. Similarly, the reduced risk associated with higher dietary folate intake during pregnancy was only observed for severe preeclampsia (OR = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.31-0.87, for the highest quartile of dietary folate intake compared to the lowest).
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that folic acid supplementation and higher dietary folate intake during pregnancy may decrease the risk of preeclampsia. Further studies are needed to confirm these associations.

title: Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq (MACS)
text: We introduce Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq data, MACS, a powerful tool for analyzing ChIP-Seq data generated by next-generation sequencing technologies, such as Solexa's Genome Analyzer. MACS employs a sophisticated empirical modeling approach to estimate the shift size of ChIP-Seq tags, and leverages this information to refine the spatial resolution of predicted binding sites. Additionally, MACS utilizes a dynamic Poisson distribution to account for local genomic biases, leading to more accurate and robust predictions. In contrast to other ChIP-Seq peak-finding algorithms, MACS demonstrates favorable performance and is made freely available to the research community.

title: Familial obesity and leanness.
text: Using the Princeton School District Family Study cohort, our investigation aimed to estimate the prevalence of suspected familial ponderosity and leanness, provide empirical risk estimates for the proportion of probands' first-degree relatives who were similarly affected, and evaluate the contributions of diseases, drugs, and caloric intake to relative obesity and leanness. We analyzed data from 379 probands, including 125 whites and 52 blacks from a random recall group and 147 whites and 55 blacks from a hyperlipidemic recall group. We identified suspected familial obesity and leanness in kindreds with at least two first-degree relatives in the same Quetelet index decile as the proband, with top or bottom decile respectively. Our findings revealed that suspected familial obesity was observed in 2.4% and 6% of random and hyperlipidemic recall group whites, respectively, and suspected familial leanness was identified in 2.4% and 1.4% of random and hyperlipidemic recall whites and in 3.8% of randomly recalled blacks. Notably, approximately twice as many first-degree relatives of top Quetelet index decile probands themselves had top decile Quetelet indices, while approximately three times as many first-degree relatives of bottom decile Quetelet index probands themselves had bottom decile Quetelet indices. Additionally, 19% and 31% of top decile Quetelet index white probands from random and hyperlipidemic recall groups came from families where at least two other first-degree relatives were similarly obese, and 18% and 20% of white random and hyperlipidemic recall group probands with bottom decile Quetelet indices had suspected familial leanness. Most subjects with familial obesity or leanness had no overt metabolic or pharmacological explanations for their body habitus, and within-family clustering of hypertension was common in kindreds with suspected familial obesity but absent in kindreds with suspected familial leanness. Our findings suggest that marked within-family clustering of both obesity and leanness is a useful diagnostic marker and that therapeutic intervention to reduce obesity is most effective when targeted at the family level in many kindreds with familial obesity.

title: In-hospital switching of oral P2Y12 inhibitor treatment in patients with acute coronary syndrome undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention: prevalence, predictors and short-term outcome.
text:
In clinical practice, the switching of P2Y12 inhibitors, particularly from clopidogrel to novel agents such as prasugrel and ticagrelor, has become more common due to the availability of these new drugs for patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Using data from the Greek AntiPlatelet REgistry (GRAPE), this study aimed to investigate the prevalence, predictive factors, and short-term outcomes of in-hospital P2Y12 inhibitor switching in 1794 ACS patients undergoing PCI.
The study found that switching occurred in 636 (35.5%) patients, with the majority of these switches occurring between prasugrel and ticagrelor (90.4%), followed by switching from clopidogrel to a novel agent (5.3%), and between novel agents (4.3%). Predictive factors for switching included presentation to a non-PCI-capable hospital, bivalirudin use, age ≥75 years (inverse predictor), and regional trends.
Using propensity-matched pairs analysis, the study found that switching from clopidogrel to a novel agent was associated with higher rates of bleeding, particularly types 1, 2, and any bleeding events, but not with higher rates of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Switching from clopidogrel to a novel agent was associated with lower rates of MACE (8.9%, 1.2%, 12.0%, 3.8% vs 23.7%, 3.8%, 30.6%, 1.2%).
In conclusion, this study suggests that in-hospital switching of P2Y12 inhibitors is common in clinical practice, and is influenced by clinical factors and regional practice differences. While switching to a novel agent may be associated with higher bleeding risk, it may also be associated with lower MACE rates. Further research is needed to determine the optimal approach to antiplatelet therapy in ACS patients undergoing PCI.

title: Structural basis of allosteric and synergistic activation of AMPK by furan-2-phosphonic derivative C2 binding.
text: The metabolic stress-sensing enzyme AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) plays a crucial role in regulating metabolism in response to energy supply and demand. Activating AMPK through drugs may offer a potential treatment for metabolic disorders such as type 2 diabetes. Our crystal structure analysis of AMPK in complex with its activator 5-(5-hydroxyl-isoxazol-3-yl)-furan-2-phosphonic acid (C2) revealed two C2-binding sites in the γ-subunit, distinct from nucleotide-binding sites. The activation of AMPK by C2 works in synergy with the drug A769662, activating AMPK α1-containing complexes independent of upstream kinases. These findings suggest that dual drug therapies could be an effective AMPK-targeting approach to treat metabolic disorders.

title: Validity of age at menarche self-reported in adulthood.
text:
Objective: To assess the accuracy of self-reported age at menarche in adulthood and evaluate the impact of socioeconomic position, education, gynecological experiences, and psychological factors on recall validity.
Design: Prospective birth cohort study set in England, Scotland, and Wales.
Participants: 1050 women from the Medical Research Council National Survey of Health and Development, with two measurements of age at menarche (one recorded in adolescence and the other self-reported at age 48) were analyzed.
Results: The study found that the accuracy of self-reported age at menarche in middle age compared to that recorded in adolescence was moderate (kappa = 0.35, r = 0.66, n = 1050). Validity improved by categorizing age at menarche into three groups: early, normal, and late (kappa = 0.43). Educational level and experiencing stillbirth or miscarriage influenced agreement.
Conclusion: The study's findings cast doubt on the reliability of self-reported age at menarche in middle age, making it necessary for researchers to exercise caution when utilizing this measure. Accuracy was influenced by socioeconomic position, education, gynaecological experiences, and psychological factors.

title: Seroepidemiologic survey of captive Old-World primates for antibodies to human and simian retroviruses, and isolation of a lentivirus from sooty mangabeys (Cercocebus atys).
text: A total of 526 monkeys and apes from 20 genera and 50 species living in US zoos and vivaria were tested for antibodies to three retroviruses, HTLV-I, HTLV-III/LAV, and simian-AIDS retrovirus, type I (SRV-I). The sera were initially screened using ELISA, and ELISA-positive sera, along with ELISA-negative sera from cage contacts, were further tested using Western blotting. A significant number of false-positive and false-negative results were identified. Most true positive reactions in the study were directed towards a single retrovirus, but a few individuals from four species were found to be positive for multiple retroviruses. Specifically, 39 out of 526 (7%) animals were found to be seroreactive to HTLV-I, 21 out of 516 (4%) animals were positive for SRV-I, and 23 out of 526 (4%) animals were found to be seropositive for HTLV-III/LAV. Many of the HTLV-III/LAV seropositive animals were from a mixed-species zoo exhibit containing sooty mangabeys, mandrills, Kolb's guenons, and talapoins. A type D virus was isolated from the blood of three out of ten SRV-I antibody-positive Tonkeana macaques, but not from any of the seropositive talapoins. Additionally, a lentivirus was isolated from the blood of four out of seven HTLV-III/LAV seropositive sooty mangabeys, but not from seropositive talapoins in the same exhibit or from two seropositive colobus from another zoo. The sooty mangabey lentivirus caused generalized lymphadenopathy, leukopenia, and decreased levels of T4 lymphocytes in two experimentally infected rhesus macaques.

title: Coronary plaque disruption.
text: Coronary atherosclerosis is by far the most common cause of ischemic heart disease, and plaque disruption with superimposed thrombosis is the main cause of acute coronary syndromes, including unstable angina, myocardial infarction, and sudden death.1-5 Therefore, understanding why atherosclerosis suddenly becomes life-threatening is crucial for event-free survival. While the volume and severity of stenosis are important factors, the most significant determinants of thrombus formation are the composition and vulnerability of the plaque.6 Lipid-rich and soft plaques are more unstable and prone to rupture than collagen-rich and hard plaques, making them highly thrombogenic.7 This review will explore the potential mechanisms responsible for the sudden conversion of a stable atherosclerotic plaque to a life-threatening atherothrombotic lesion, known as plaque fissuring, rupture, or disruption.8-11 Atherosclerosis is a complex interaction between blood elements, disturbed flow, and vessel wall abnormalities, involving inflammation, growth, degeneration, lipid accumulation, necrosis, calcification/ossification, and thrombosis.12-23 Thrombotic factors may play a role early in atherogenesis, but a flow-limiting thrombus does not develop until mature plaques are present, which is why thrombosis is often classified as a complication rather than a genuine component of atherosclerosis.14,18-21 Mature plaques are characterized by atherosis and sclerosis, and understanding their composition and mechanisms of formation is essential for the development of effective treatments.22-23

title: p16INK4A is a robust in vivo biomarker of cellular aging in human skin.
text: In this study, the relationship between cell-cycle regulating gene p16INK4A and human skin aging was investigated. p16INK4A encodes an inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6, and its expression has been linked to cellular aging and premature senescence. While there is an age-dependent increase in p16INK4A expression in human fibroblast senescence in vitro, little was known about its expression in vivo. To investigate the correlation between p16INK4A expression and donor age in human skin, the study analyzed p16INK4A expression by immunohistochemistry, along with the expression of the p16INK4A repressor BMI1. Skin samples from donors aged 0-20, 21-70, and 71-95 years were selected from a bank of healthy human skin. The results showed that the number of p16INK4A-positive cells was significantly higher in elderly individuals compared to younger age groups in both the epidermis and dermis, which have different proliferative activities. Interestingly, the expression of the BMI1 gene, which represses p16INK4A, was significantly downregulated with increasing donor age. Conversely, no significant age differences were observed for the proliferation marker Ki67. Further immunofluorescence co-expression studies revealed that Ki67-positive cells were negative for p16INK4A and BMI1. Taken together, these findings provide the first in vivo evidence that p16INK4A expression directly correlates with chronological aging of human skin, making it a biomarker for human aging in vivo. These results suggest a model for changes in regulatory gene expression that drive aging in human skin, and highlight the potential of p16INK4A as a marker of aging in vivo.

title: hPrimpol1/CCDC111 is a human DNA primase-polymerase required for the maintenance of genome integrity.
text: Prim-pol is a recently discovered DNA primase-polymerase that belongs to the archaeal-eukaryotic primase (AEP) superfamily. In this study, we characterize a previously unidentified prim-pol in human cells, which we designate hPrimpol1 (human primase-polymerase 1). hPrimpol1 exhibits both primase and DNA polymerase activities in vitro and interacts directly with RPA1 through an RPA1-dependent mechanism. Depletion of hPrimpol1 leads to increased levels of spontaneous DNA damage and defects in the resumption of stalled replication forks. Our findings indicate that hPrimpol1 plays a novel role in responding to DNA replication stress, with both RPA1 binding and primase activity being essential for its cellular function during DNA replication.

title: Functional proteomics identifies miRNAs to target a p27/Myc/phospho-Rb signature in breast and ovarian cancer
text: The myc oncogene is overexpressed in approximately half of all breast and ovarian cancers, however, attempts to target it therapeutically have proven challenging. Myc regulates multiple cellular processes, including the cell cycle, which is linked to cancer cell proliferation and growth. We discovered a protein signature of high myc, low p27, and high phospho-Rb that is significantly correlated with poor patient survival in breast and ovarian cancers. Using a functional proteomics screen of a miRNA library in multiple cell lines and integration of patient tumor data, we identified a panel of five miRNAs (miR-124, miR-365, miR-34b*, miR-18a, and miR-506) as potential tumor suppressors that can reverse the myc-mediated protein signature. Mechanistic studies revealed an RNA-activation function of miR-124, which leads to direct induction of p27 protein levels by binding to and inducing transcription on the p27 promoter region, resulting in a G1 cell cycle arrest. In vivo studies using a xenograft model demonstrated that nanoparticle-mediated delivery of miR-124 can reduce tumor growth and sensitize cells to etoposide, suggesting a potential clinical application of miRNAs as therapeutics to target myc-driven tumor growth.

title: The potential role of miRNAs 21 and 199-a in early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma.
text:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most common types of cancer and a leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Early diagnosis of HCC is crucial, but current methods are limited. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that can regulate gene expression and have been identified as potential biomarkers for HCC. This study aimed to investigate the serum and tissue expression of miR-21 and miR-199-a in HCC patients and determine their potential as early detectors.
