A total of 40 serum and tissue samples (17 from chronic hepatitis and 23 from HCC patients) were collected and analyzed for miR-21 and miR-199-a expression using real-time quantitative reverse-transcriptase PCR (RT-qPCR). The results showed that serum miR-21 expression was significantly increased in HCC patients compared to chronic hepatitis patients (P<0.001), while miR-199-a expression was significantly decreased in HCC patients (P<0.001). Similarly, the median of miR-21 was higher in malignant tissues compared to adjacent non-malignant tissues, although the difference was not statistically significant (P=0.191), while miR-199-a expression was significantly lower in malignant tissues (P<0.001). The area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) for miR-21 and miR-199-a was 0.84 and 0.87, respectively, indicating their potential as circulating biomarkers for HCC.
In conclusion, this study found that miR-21 and miR-199-a expression is significantly altered in HCC patients compared to chronic hepatitis patients and may serve as potential early detection biomarkers for HCC.

title: Tex10 Coordinates Epigenetic Control of Super-Enhancer Activity in Pluripotency and Reprogramming.
text: Super-enhancers (SEs) are large clusters of transcriptional enhancers that are simultaneously occupied by multiple lineage-specific transcription factors, driving the expression of genes that define cell identity. In embryonic stem cells (ESCs), SEs are particularly enriched with the core pluripotency factors Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog. In this study, we aimed to elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying SE activity in pluripotency and reprogramming. Starting from a protein interaction network surrounding Sox2, we identified Tex10 as a key pluripotency factor that plays a functionally significant role in ESC self-renewal, early embryo development, and reprogramming. Texas is enriched at SEs in a Sox2-dependent manner and regulates histone acetylation and DNA demethylation at SEs. Additionally, Tex10 activity is crucial for pluripotency and reprogramming in human cells. Our findings highlight Tex10 as a central component of the pluripotency network and provide insights into its role in epigenetic control of SE activity for cell fate determination.

title: Value of whole brain re-irradiation for brain metastases--single centre experience.
text:
Controversy exists in previous studies regarding the role of repeat whole brain radiation (WBRT) for previously irradiated brain metastases. Our retrospective study aimed to document the practice at Princess Margaret Hospital regarding the re-irradiation of patients with progressive or recurrent brain metastatic disease after initial WBRT.
Methods:
We conducted a comprehensive computerized database analysis to identify patients treated for brain metastases with more than one course of WBRT between 1997 and 2003. Seventy-two patients were treated with WBRT for brain metastases and retreated with WBRT at a later date. The records of these patients were reviewed.
Results:
Our study population had a median age of 56.5 years, with the most common primary sites being lung (51 patients) and breast (17 patients). The most common dose used for initial radiotherapy was 20 Gy/5 fractions (62 patients). The doses used for re-irradiation were 25 Gy/10 fractions (22 patients), 20 Gy/10 fractions (12 patients), 15 Gy/5 fractions (11 patients), and 20 Gy/8 fractions (10 patients). Thirty-one percent of patients experienced a partial clinical response after re-irradiation, 27% remained stable, and 32% deteriorated after re-irradiation. Patients with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status 0-1 at the time of retreatment lived longer. In responders, the mean duration of response was 5.1 months. The median survival after re-irradiation was 4.1 months. One patient experienced memory impairment and pituitary insufficiency after 5 months of progression-free survival.



Conclusion:
Our findings suggest that repeat radiotherapy may be a useful treatment for carefully selected patients. With improved survival and systemic treatment options for patients with metastatic disease, more patients may be candidates for consideration of repeat WBRT for recurrent brain metastases, but prospective studies are needed to further clarify their outcomes.

title: Bisphosphonates in oncology: rising stars or fallen heroes.
text: The incorporation of bisphosphonates in oncology has significantly revolutionized the management of patients with metastatic bone disease. In this manuscript, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the extensive clinical trials supporting the use of bisphosphonates in this context, while also reviewing current and ongoing research. Moreover, we analyze the data highlighting the advantages of bisphosphonate use in preventing treatment-induced bone loss, as well as the intriguing emerging evidence on their potential antitumor effects when used in the adjuvant setting. Finally, we emphasize the need for a careful balance between the benefits and risks of bisphosphonate therapy, including the recently recognized potential risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw.

title: IL-33, a recently identified interleukin-1 gene family member, is expressed in human adipocytes.
text: Obesity is characterized by inflammation in adipose tissue. To investigate whether IL-33, a recently identified member of the IL-1 gene family, and its associated receptors are expressed in human adipocytes, we examined their expression in visceral white fat, preadipocytes, and adipocytes (SGBS cells). Our results showed that IL-33, IL-1RL1, and IL-1RAP were expressed in these cells. Treatment with TNFalpha for 24 hours resulted in a 6-fold increase in IL-33 mRNA levels in preadipocytes and adipocytes. Time-course studies revealed that the increase in IL-33 mRNA with TNFalpha was maximized (>55-fold) at 12 hours, unlike IL-1 beta, which peaked at 2 hours (5.4-fold), and IL-18, which peaked at 6 hours (>1500-fold). Hypoxia (1% O(2), 24 hours) did not alter IL-33 mRNA levels in adipocytes, but preadipocytes showed a 3-fold increase. Our findings suggest that human adipocytes and preadipocytes express IL-33, but the different IL-1 family members exhibit distinct responses to TNFalpha.

title: Imaging techniques for assaying lymphocyte activation in action
text: Advances in imaging techniques have significantly enhanced our comprehension of lymphocyte activation. Technological developments in spatial and temporal resolution, as well as innovative labeling strategies, have enabled researchers to directly observe the activation process in real-time. As a result, the use of imaging methods to study lymphocyte activation has expanded, providing an unparalleled level of cellular and molecular detail in the field. This has led to the verification of some models, the revision of others, and the replacement of outdated concepts with new ones. In this review article, we will survey the current imaging techniques used to assess lymphocyte activation in various contexts, ranging from whole animals to individual molecules, and discuss the strengths and limitations of these methods.

title: Extending healthy life span--from yeast to humans.
text: When organisms such as yeast and rodents experience a reduction in food intake (dietary restriction), they tend to live longer compared to those on a standard diet. Similar observations can be made when the activity of pathways involved in nutrient sensing is diminished through genetic mutations or chemical inhibitors. In rodents, both dietary restriction and reduced nutrient-sensing pathway activity have been shown to reduce the likelihood of age-related functional decline and disease, including tumors and neurodegeneration. Dietary restriction has also been found to increase lifespan and protect against diseases such as diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease in rhesus monkeys, and in humans, it leads to changes that shield against these age-related pathologies. Tumors and diabetes are uncommon in humans with mutations in the growth hormone receptor, and natural genetic variations in nutrient-sensing pathways have been linked to increased human life span. Dietary restriction and reduced nutrient-sensing pathway activity may slow aging through similar mechanisms, which have been conserved throughout evolution. These findings have important implications for the prevention of age-related diseases and the promotion of healthy aging in humans, while also raising questions about potential side effects.

title: Hospital and 1-year survival of patients admitted to intensive care units with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text: In this study, we aimed to describe the outcomes and identify variables associated with hospital and one-year survival for patients with acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) admitted to intensive care units (ICUs). Using a prospective, multicenter, inception cohort design, we collected data from 362 ICU admissions across 40 US hospitals. We found that hospital mortality was 24%, with higher mortality rates among older patients (30% at hospital discharge, 47% at 90 days, 59% at 1 year). Using multiple regression analysis, we identified age, severity of respiratory and nonrespiratory organ system dysfunction, and hospital length of stay before ICU admission as variables associated with hospital mortality. The development of nonrespiratory organ system dysfunction was the major predictor of hospital mortality and 180-day outcomes, whereas respiratory physiological variables were more strongly associated with 180-day mortality rates than hospital death rates. Our findings suggest that the need for mechanical ventilation at ICU admission did not influence either short-term or long-term outcomes. These findings have implications for the management of COPD exacerbations in critically ill patients.

title: Kindlin-3 is essential for integrin activation and platelet aggregation
text: Integrin-mediated platelet adhesion and aggregation are crucial for sealing injuries and preventing excessive blood loss, yet excessive platelet aggregation can lead to arterial thrombosis and cause devastating events such as heart attacks and stroke. To ensure platelets aggregate only at injury sites, integrins on circulating platelets remain in a low-affinity state until activated through binding to a wounded vessel. This activation is mediated by the cytoskeletal protein Talin, which binds to the β subunit cytoplasmic tail of the integrin. Our findings reveal that platelets lacking the adhesion plaque protein Kindlin-3 are unable to activate integrins despite normal Talin expression, leading to severe bleeding and resistance to arterial thrombosis. Furthermore, we have identified Kindlin-3 as a novel and critical element in platelet integrin activation in hemostasis and thrombosis, as it can bind to specific regions of β-integrin tails distinct from those bound by Talin, triggering integrin activation directly.

title: Opening of compacted chromatin by early developmental transcription factors HNF3 (FoxA) and GATA-4.
text: Early transcription factors, HNF3 (FoxA) and GATA-4, are the first known to bind the albumin gene enhancer in liver precursor cells in embryos. To investigate how they access inactive chromatin, we assembled nucleosome arrays containing albumin enhancer sequences and compacted them with linker histone. Surprisingly, HNF3 and GATA-4 still bound their sites in compacted chromatin, even without the presence of ATP-dependent enzymes. The ability of HNF3 to open chromatin is due to a high-affinity DNA binding site and the C-terminal domain of the protein, which interacts with histones H3 and H4. These findings suggest that transcription factors that promote transcription during development are also capable of initiating chromatin opening events.

title: N- and E-cadherins in Xenopus are specifically required in the neural and non-neural ectoderm, respectively, for F-actin assembly and morphogenetic movements.
text: Transmembrane cadherins are calcium-dependent intercellular adhesion molecules that have been found to be sites of actin assembly during adhesive contact formation. While the roles of actin assembly on transmembrane cadherins during development are not fully understood, we have investigated their functions in the developing ectoderm of the Xenopus embryo. Our findings show that F-actin assembly is a primary function of both N-cadherin in the neural ectoderm and E-cadherin in the non-neural (epidermal) ectoderm. Both cadherins are essential for the characteristic morphogenetic movements of these two tissues, but their depletion did not cause dissociation at the neurula stage, likely due to the expression of C-cadherin in each tissue. Interestingly, depletion of each of these cadherins is not rescued by the other or by the expression of C-cadherin, suggesting that each cadherin is expressed in a different domain of the cell membrane. These data highlight the combinatorial nature of cadherin function, the importance of N- and E-cadherin in F-actin assembly, and the specificity of this function to individual cadherins. Our findings also demonstrate how cell adhesion and motility can be combined in morphogenetic tissue movements, generating the form and shape of embryonic organs.

title: Mutation of the fumarase gene in two siblings with progressive encephalopathy and fumarase deficiency.
text: We have identified an inborn error of the tricarboxylic acid cycle, fumarase deficiency, in two siblings born to first cousin parents. The children presented with progressive encephalopathy, dystonia, leucopenia, and neutropenia. Elevated lactate in the cerebrospinal fluid and high fumarate excretion in the urine prompted us to investigate the activities of the respiratory chain and the Krebs cycle, which led to the diagnosis of fumarase deficiency in these two children. The deficiency was severe and present in all tissues examined, affecting both the cytosolic and mitochondrial fumarase isoenzymes equally. Analyzing fumarase cDNA revealed that both patients were homozygous for a missense mutation, a G-955-->C transition, which predicts a Glu-319-->Gln substitution in a highly conserved region of the fumarase cDNA. The parents, who were found to be heterozygous for this mutation, had half the expected fumarase activity in their lymphocytes. This study represents the first molecular characterization of tricarboxylic acid deficiency, a rare inherited inborn error of metabolism in childhood.

title: Adult Neurogenesis Is Sustained by Symmetric Self-Renewal and Differentiation.
text: Somatic stem cells have been identified in various adult tissues, and understanding whether self-renewal occurs symmetrically or asymmetrically is crucial for elucidating the mechanisms underlying long-term stem cell maintenance and the generation of progeny for cellular replacement. In the adult mouse brain, neural stem cells (NSCs) located in the walls of the lateral ventricles (ventricular-subventricular zone [V-SVZ]) persist into adulthood, and their retention is a puzzle that remains unsolved. Utilizing multiple clonal labeling techniques, we have revealed that the vast majority of B1 cells undergo symmetrical cell division, with approximately 20%-30% of these cells exhibiting the capacity for self-renewal, allowing them to remain in the niche for several months before generating neurons, while the remaining 70%-80% of B1 cells engage in consuming divisions, resulting in the depletion of these cells over time. This unique cellular mechanism appears to decouple self-renewal from the generation of progeny, as limited rounds of symmetric self-renewal and consuming symmetric differentiation divisions may be responsible for the observed levels of neurogenesis throughout an organism's lifespan.

title: A common missense variant in NUDT15 confers susceptibility to thiopurine-induced leukopenia
text: Thiopurine therapy, commonly used in autoimmune conditions, can be complicated by life-threatening leukopenia. This leukopenia is related to genetic variations in TPMT (encoding thiopurine S-methyltransferase) in certain populations. Although TPMT mutations are less common in Asians, the incidence of thiopurine-induced leukopenia is higher in Asians than in individuals of European descent. Our study, which used Immunochip-based 2-stage association analysis in 978 Korean patients with Crohn's disease treated with thiopurines, identified a nonsynonymous SNP in NUDT15 (encoding p. Arg139Cys) that was strongly associated with thiopurine-induced early leukopenia (odds ratio (OR) = 35.6; Pcombined = 4.88 × 10−94). In Koreans, this variant demonstrated sensitivity and specificity of 89.4% and 93.2%, respectively, for thiopurine-induced early leukopenia (comparable to 12.1% and 97.6% for TPMT variants). Surprisingly, this SNP was also strongly associated with thiopurine-induced leukopenia in subjects with inflammatory bowel disease of European descent (OR = 9.50; P = 4.64 × 10−4). These findings indicate that NUDT15 is a pharmacogenetic determinant for thiopurine-induced leukopenia in diverse populations.

title: Induction of cell cycle entry eliminates human leukemia stem cells in a mouse model of AML
text: Cancer stem cells have been suggested to play a key role in the initiation, progression, and recurrence of various types of cancer, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Our previous research has shown that CD34+CD38- human primary AML stem cells found in the endosteal region of the bone marrow are relatively resistant to chemotherapy. Using a NOD/SCID/IL2rγnull mouse model of human AML, we have now discovered that these stem cells are in a state of cell cycle quiescence and can be induced to enter the cell cycle with the help of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). When combined with chemotherapy that targets cells in the cell cycle, the addition of G-CSF significantly enhances the induction of apoptosis and elimination of human primary AML stem cells in vivo. This combination therapy leads to improved survival of secondary recipients after transplantation of leukemia cells compared to chemotherapy alone.

title: Reconstitution of the immune system after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in humans
text: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is linked to a severe immune deficiency, putting the patient at a heightened risk of infections. Fortunately, the innate immune system, including epithelial barriers, monocytes, granulocytes, and natural killer cells, begins to recover within weeks after the transplant. In contrast, the adaptive immune system, comprising B and T cells, takes much longer to recover, with T-cell counts normalizing during the first few months post-transplantation, but T-cell immunity may remain impaired for an extended period of time, potentially spanning several years. Over the past decade, significant advancements have been made in understanding the underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon, which may ultimately lead to the development of novel interventions to accelerate recovery.

title: Vision tests in the mouse: Functional phenotyping with electroretinography.
text: Electroretinography (ERG) is a widely used diagnostic technique in clinical ophthalmology, providing objective information about retinal function. In addition, ERG is a valuable tool in basic research, where animal models of inherited retinal diseases have significantly advanced our understanding of the composition of ERG responses and how retinal degenerative pathologies impact retinal function. For example, electrophysiological assessment of genetically engineered mice that mimic human mutations leading to retinal diseases can be directly compared to clinical data. Furthermore, the limitations associated with ERG examinations, such as the length of measurement and range of light intensity, are significantly reduced when working with mice compared to human patients. To obtain accurate and reliable retinal response measurements, several crucial factors must be considered. This paper focuses on these factors and presents exemplary ERG data from normal wild-type mice and transgenic mice with specific functional properties, such as Rho-/- (rod opsin knockout, cone function only) and Cnga3-/- (cone CNG channel deficient, rod function only), to illustrate the contributions of rod and cone systems to ERG responses.

title: Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 is essential for meiosis but not for mitotic cell division in mice
text: We employed homologous recombination in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells to target the locus encoding cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2). Notably, embryonic fibroblasts lacking CDK2 proliferate normally and become immortal after prolonged culture. However, eliminating a conditional CDK2 allele in immortal cells did not significantly affect proliferation. Surprisingly, CDK2-deficient mice are viable and can survive up to two years, suggesting that CDK2 is dispensable for proliferation and survival of most cell types. In contrast, CDK2 plays a crucial role in the completion of prophase I during meiotic cell division in both male and female germ cells, a previously unappreciated function for this cell cycle kinase.

title: Capsaicin-sensitive sensory nerve fibers contribute to the generation and maintenance of skeletal fracture pain.
text: Although skeletal pain can have a profound impact on a patient's quality of life and functional status, there is limited knowledge on the specific populations of nerve fibers responsible for non-malignant bone pain. To address this gap, we conducted a study using neonatal male Sprague-Dawley rats that were treated with capsaicin or vehicle and subjected to femoral fracture at young adulthood (15-16 weeks old). Our findings revealed that capsaicin treatment led to a significant (>70%) depletion in the density of calcitonin-gene related peptide (CGRP+) sensory nerve fibers in the periosteum, but not in 200 kDa neurofilament H (NF200+) sensory nerve fibers. The periosteum, a thin, cellular, and fibrous tissue, plays a crucial role in driving fracture pain. Our results also showed that capsaicin treatment resulted in a 50% reduction in the severity of fracture-induced skeletal pain-related behaviors, such as spontaneous flinching, guarding, and weight bearing, but the time course of these behaviors was unchanged. These findings suggest that both capsaicin-sensitive (primarily CGRP+) C-fibers and capsaicin-insensitive (primarily NF200+) A-delta fibers participate in generating skeletal fracture pain. Skeletal pain can significantly hinder functional recovery after trauma-induced fracture, osteoporosis-induced fracture, and orthopedic surgery procedures such as knee and hip replacements. Understanding the specific populations of sensory nerve fibers involved in skeletal pain may lead to the development of more targeted and effective therapies to alleviate acute and chronic skeletal pain.

title: Surgical therapy for dystonia.
text: Surgical treatments for dystonia have progressed significantly since the early 20th century, with technological advancements and improved understanding of the basal ganglia's role in the disorder leading to enhanced efficacy. Dystonia refers to a type of involuntary movement that can result from various conditions, affecting different parts of the body or in some cases, the entire body. It is crucial to determine whether the underlying cause of dystonia is primary (genetic or idiopathic) or secondary (related to structural, metabolic, or neurodegenerative disorders). Secondary dystonias are more common than primary dystonias and tend to respond less well to treatments such as pallidotomy or deep brain stimulation of the internal segment of the globus pallidum. However, emerging data suggests that the thalamus may be a promising target for treating secondary dystonias. While combinations of bilateral targets are possible with current DBS technology, they are not commonly used due to surgical complications and costs. This review focuses on the evolution of surgical treatments for dystonia, with a comparison of outcomes for primary versus secondary and generalized versus cervical dystonia.

title: MEG3 imprinted gene contribution in tumorigenesis.
text: Maternally expressed gene 3 (MEG3) is a noncoding RNA located on chromosome 14q32 that plays a crucial role in cell proliferation regulation. It is an imprinted gene, meaning its expression is dependent on the parental origin of the gene. MEG3 is capable of interacting with various proteins such as cyclic AMP, p53, MDM2, and GDF15, thus influencing cellular processes. The expression of MEG3 is controlled by epigenetic mechanisms, with aberrant CpG methylation being observed in various cancers. Additionally, gene copy number loss has been linked to tumorigenesis. Studies have shown that MEG3 deletion leads to the upregulation of paternally expressed genes and the downregulation of maternally expressed genes and tumor suppressor miRNAs. However, conflicting evidence exists regarding the exact effects of MEG3 deletion on gene expression. MEG3 has been implicated in tumor suppressor functions and is located on chromosome 14q32, making it a potential tumor suppressor gene. As research continues to uncover the mechanisms of MEG3, its association with tumorigenesis is growing.

title: Uptake of rosuvastatin by isolated rat hepatocytes: comparison with pravastatin.
text: 1. Rosuvastatin, a new 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase inhibitor, selectively targets the liver, and its liver-specific uptake is desirable. The uptake kinetics of rosuvastatin were studied in comparison to those of pravastatin using isolated rat hepatocytes. 2. Both drugs exhibited active transport and passive diffusion processes in their uptake. The Michaelis constant (K(m)) for rosuvastatin (9.17 micro M) was approximately half that of pravastatin (16.5 micro M), while the maximum uptake rate (V(max)) and carrier-mediated uptake clearance (V(max)/K(m)) of rosuvastatin were significantly higher than those of pravastatin (p < 0.01). A greater contribution of carrier-mediated uptake clearance was observed for rosuvastatin (0.903) compared to pravastatin (0.654). 3. Sodium and chloride ions did not significantly influence the uptake of rosuvastatin and pravastatin, but both drugs were inhibited by depletion of cellular ATP and organic anions such as bromosulfophthalein. 4. Rosuvastatin also inhibited the uptake of pravastatin, with an inhibition constant (K(i)) of 2.75 micro M, similar to its K(m). 5. These results indicate that an organic anion transport protein is the primary mediator of hepatic uptake for both rosuvastatin and pravastatin, which occurs in an ATP-dependent manner. While both drugs are taken up via the same transport systems, rosuvastatin demonstrates greater affinity and efficiency than pravastatin.

title: Junctophilin-4, a component of the endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane junctions, regulates Ca2+ dynamics in T cells.
text: Orai1 and STIM1 collaborate to facilitate store-operated Ca(2+) entry (SOCE) in immune cells. STIM1, an ER Ca(2+) sensor, detects Ca(2+) depletion and connects with PM-localized Orai1 channels at ER-PM interfaces. However, the molecular composition of these interfaces in T cells remained unknown. We found that JP4, a junctional protein in excitable cells, is expressed in T cells and localized at ER-PM interfaces to regulate Ca(2+) signaling. Silencing or genetically manipulating JP4 decreased ER Ca(2+) concentration and SOCE in T cells and impaired the activation of NFAT and ERK signaling pathways, resulting in diminished expression of activation markers and cytokines. Mechanistically, JP4 interacts with STIM1 through its cytoplasmic domain and promotes STIM1 recruitment into the interfaces. Moreover, JP4 also forms a complex with junctate, a Ca(2+)-sensing ER-resident protein previously shown to mediate STIM1 recruitment. Our findings suggest that the junctate-JP4 complex at the interfaces cooperates with STIM1 to maintain ER Ca(2+) homeostasis and regulate SOCE in T cells.

title: The PI3K inhibitor arsenal: choose your weapon!
text: Due to its widespread involvement in inflammation and cancer, there has been a growing recognition of the therapeutic potential of inhibitors of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway, leading to increased interest in compounds with suitable pharmacological profiles. These are primarily focused on inhibiting PI3K itself. However, as class I PI3Ks are also essential for a range of normal physiological processes, broad-spectrum PI3K inhibition may be poorly tolerated. In recent years, patents have emerged for a new generation of PI3K inhibitors, with a particular focus on the development of compounds with enhanced isoform selectivity for use as anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory therapies. However, challenges persist in targeting this enzyme family successfully through pharmacological means.

title: Infralimbic BDNF/TrkB enhancement of GluN2B currents facilitates extinction of a cocaine-conditioned place preference.
text: Activation of the tropomyosin-related kinase B (TrkB) receptor enhances the strength of N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor currents in male rat infralimbic prefrontal pyramidal neurons. This increase in NMDA receptor activity is bidirectionally regulated by the signaling cascade involving the TrkB receptor and the GluN2B subunit of NMDA receptors. Specifically, blockade of GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors disrupts the consolidation of extinction of a cocaine-induced conditioned place preference (CPP), while potentiation of TrkB receptor activity with infralimbic infusions of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) or systemic injections of 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (7,8DHF), a newly synthesized TrkB receptor agonist, enhances extinction of the CPP. The 7,8DHF-induced enhancement of extinction is prevented by infralimbic infusions of a GluN2B-specific receptor antagonist, indicating that TrkB receptor activation enhances extinction learning via GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors. These findings suggest that infralimbic TrkB receptor activation may be a useful adjunct for extinction-based therapies for psychiatric disorders associated with reduced BDNF activity.

title: Compaction of chromatin by diverse Polycomb group proteins requires localized regions of high charge.
text:
Polycomb group (PcG) proteins are essential for maintaining the epigenetic silencing of developmental genes across species, from flies to humans. PcG proteins in the Polycomb-repressive complex 1 (PRC1) class inhibit transcription by compacting chromatin, a process conserved from Drosophila to mice. An experimental study revealed that a basic amino acid-rich region is crucial for PRC1's chromatin compaction function, which is unexpectedly found in a different PRC1 subunit, M33, in mice, rather than the previously identified Posterior Sex Combs (PSC) subunit in Drosophila. The study also showed that other PcG proteins from non-Drosophila, non-mouse species can also compact chromatin when containing domains of high positive charge, supporting the hypothesis that compaction is a critical aspect of PcG function.

title: Angiopoietin-like proteins stimulate ex vivo expansion of hematopoietic stem cells
text: The successful ex vivo expansion of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) would greatly enhance the treatment of diseases and contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental mechanisms of stem cell biology. Our study reveals, using microarray analysis, that the HSC-supportive mouse fetal liver CD3+ cells specifically express the proteins angiopoietin-like 2 (Angptl2) and angiopoietin-like 3 (Angptl3). We discovered that culturing highly enriched HSCs for 10 days in the presence of Angptl2 or Angptl3, along with saturating levels of other growth factors, led to a 24- or 30-fold net expansion of long-term HSCs through reconstitution analysis. Remarkably, the coiled-coil domain of Angptl2 was found to be capable of stimulating the expansion of HSCs. Moreover, angiopoietin-like 5, angiopoietin-like 7, and microfibril-associated glycoprotein 4 also supported the expansion of HSCs in culture.

title: Balancing co-stimulation and inhibition with BTLA and HVEM
text: The interaction between B- and T-lymphocyte attenuator (BTLA), a receptor from the immunoglobulin superfamily, and herpesvirus-entry mediator (HVEM), a co-stimulatory tumour-necrosis factor receptor, is a unique case where two different receptor families intersect. This interaction has sparked interest in how receptors from distinct families can interact, and what downstream signaling events might occur upon receptor ligation. Recent investigations have uncovered that engagement of HVEM with its endogenous ligand (LIGHT) from the tumour-necrosis factor family elicits a robust immune response, whereas HVEM interactions with BTLA dampen T-cell responses.

title: Lin28b is sufficient to drive liver cancer and necessary for its maintenance in murine models.
text: Lin28a/b are protein molecules that play a crucial role in regulating stem cell maintenance, metabolism, and tumorigenesis. Poorly differentiated, aggressive cancers often display excessive levels of Lin28 protein, but its specific function in cancer initiation and progression has yet to be fully elucidated. Our research reveals that overexpressing LIN28B leads to the development of hepatoblastoma and hepatocellular carcinoma in mouse models. Moreover, we found that Lin28b overexpression is also present in MYC-driven hepatoblastomas, and deleting Lin28a/b in the liver leads to a reduction in tumor burden, extended latency, and prolonged survival. Notably, both intravenous silencing of Lin28b and conditional Lin28b deletion also exhibit a tumor-inhibiting effect. Igf2bp proteins are upregulated in the context of Lin28B overexpression, with Igf2bp3 specifically playing a crucial role in promoting cell growth. Our results demonstrate that Lin28b is both necessary and sufficient to initiate and maintain liver cancer in multiple mouse models.

title: Nanoenzymology of the 20S proteasome: proteasomal actions are controlled by the allosteric transition.
text: The proteasome is a critical cytosolic proteolytic complex in eukaryotic cells, with both its architecture and enzymatic functions relatively well characterized. Despite long-standing interest, elucidating the underlying mechanisms of the proteasome's enzymatic actions has proven challenging. Recently, we employed tapping mode atomic force microscopy (AFM) in liquid to observe the alpha-rings of the proteasome switching between open and closed conformations, seemingly to control access to the central channel. In this study, we utilize AFM to examine the side-view configuration of 20S proteasome particles and find that they can adopt two stable conformations. The overall shapes of the 20S particles can be classified as either barrel-like or cylinder-like. The relative abundance of these conformers depends on the nature of their interactions with ligands, with barrels dominating in control or inhibited molecules, and cylinders and open molecules prevailing when observed in the presence of peptide substrates. Drawing on these findings, we have developed a two-state model of allosteric transitions to describe the dynamics of proteasomal structure. This model provides a better understanding of the observed properties of the 20S molecule and sets the stage for further investigations into the structural dynamics of the proteasome.

title: Changes in plasma copeptin, the c-terminal portion of arginine vasopressin during water deprivation and excess in healthy subjects.
text:
The stability of arginine vasopressin (AVP) is a challenge in its measurement due to its short half-life. To address this limitation, researchers have turned to its precursor peptide, copeptin, which is more stable and has been shown to be a useful tool in evaluating AVP levels in critically ill patients. The present study aimed to investigate the clinical usefulness of copeptin as a marker of disordered states of blood volume and plasma osmolality.
A prospective observational study was conducted in a university hospital, involving 24 healthy adults. Three techniques were employed to induce changes in plasma osmolality and volume, including a 28-hour water deprivation, a 17-hour hypertonic saline infusion combined with thirsting, and a hypotonic saline infusion with iv desmopressin administration during free water intake.
The results showed that water deprivation led to a significant decrease in body weight, accompanied by a rise in plasma osmolality and an increase in copeptin levels from 4.6 +/- 1.7 pmol/liter to 9.2 +/- 5.2 pmol/liter (P < 0.0001). During hypertonic saline infusion and thirsting, copeptin levels increased from 4.9 +/- 3.0 pmol/liter to 19.9 +/- 4.8 pmol/liter (P < 0.0001). In contrast, during hypotonic saline infusion, plasma osmolality decreased, and copeptin levels decreased from 6.2 +/- 2.4 pmol/liter to 2.4 +/- 2.1 pmol/liter (P < 0.01).
The study demonstrated that copeptin shows identical changes during water disorders as previously observed for AVP. These findings suggest that copeptin may serve as a reliable marker of AVP secretion and potentially replace the measurement of circulating AVP levels in clinical practice.

title: Propagation and recovery of intact, infectious Epstein-Barr virus from prokaryotic to human cells.
text: Currently, manipulating the genetic material of herpesviruses is challenging due to their large genomes. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a system that enables the cloning of any gamma-herpesvirus in Escherichia coli onto an F factor-derived plasmid. Our approach has shown that immortalized B cell lines can be established with recombinant Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), indicating that the F factor-cloned EBV genome possess all the characteristics of wild-type EBV. Given the ability to modify genes in E. coli, this experimental approach provides a means to investigate the functions of EBV in a controlled manner. Furthermore, it is now possible to generate attenuated EBV strains in vitro, allowing for the creation of vaccine strains. By incorporating genes for hygromycin resistance and green fluorescent protein onto the E. coli cloned EBV genome, we can also investigate the target cells of EBV other than B lymphocytes.

title: Chemosensitivity profile assay of circulating cancer cells: prognostic and predictive value in epithelial tumors.
text: The prognostic value of detecting circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in metastatic breast cancer using the CellSearch technology raises additional questions regarding the biological significance of this information. We hypothesized that a drug-resistance profile of CTCs may predict treatment response in cancer patients and could be used for patient selection. In a prospective trial involving 105 patients with carcinoma, CTCs were isolated from peripheral blood, and the expression of genes involved in drug resistance was evaluated in positive samples. The drug-resistance profile was correlated with disease-free survival (DFS) and time to progression (TTP) over a 24-month follow-up. The secondary endpoint was the objective response correlation. Fifty-one percent of patients were found to be positive for CTCs, while all blood samples from healthy donors were negative. The drug-resistance profile correlated significantly with DFS and TTP (p < 0.001 in both). The test had a sensitivity of 98% in predicting treatment response and a specificity of 100% in identifying negative samples. The positive and negative predictive values were 96.5% and 100%, respectively. We identified a drug-resistance profile of CTCs that is predictive of treatment response, independent of tumor type and stage of disease. This approach may represent an initial step towards individualizing chemotherapy in cancer patients.

title: Trends in heart failure incidence and survival in a community-based population.
text: The incidence of heart failure has remained unchanged over the past two decades in the general population, according to a study conducted in Olmsted County, Minnesota. Specifically, among men, the incidence of heart failure was found to be significantly higher (378/100,000 persons) compared to women (289/100,000 persons), and this trend was observed throughout the study period. Despite this, survival rates after a heart failure diagnosis improved over time, with a 5-year age-adjusted survival rate of 43% in the early 1980s compared to 52% in the late 1990s. However, the improvement in survival was not seen in all groups, with women and older individuals experiencing less or no improvement in survival rates. These findings suggest that there may be sex-specific disparities in the treatment and outcomes of heart failure.

title: Doxycycline induces apoptosis in PANC-1 pancreatic cancer cells.
text:
Tetracyclines, such as doxycycline, have been reported to exhibit cytotoxic activity against malignant tumor cells, yet the underlying mechanisms of their effects on cellular proliferation remain insufficiently understood. To investigate the antitumor potential of doxycycline, we examined its effects on human pancreatic cancer cell line, PANC-1, and explored its influence on the expression of a potent proangiogenic factor, interleukin (IL)-8.
Our findings demonstrate that doses of doxycycline in excess of 20 micrograms per milliliter induced cytotoxic effects, leading to G(1)-S cell cycle arrest and DNA fragmentation in PANC-1 cells. Notably, doxycycline consistently activated the transcription of p53, p21, and Fas/FasL-cascade-related genes, while reducing the expression of Bcl-xL and Mcl-1. Moreover, doxycycline at a concentration of 5 micrograms per milliliter below the cytotoxic threshold suppressed both endogenous and paclitaxel-induced IL-8 expression. In a mouse xenograft model, doxycycline treatment resulted in a significant suppression of tumor growth, with an average reduction of 80%.
These findings suggest that doxycycline exerts its antitumor effect by manipulating a complex network of genes involved in apoptotic pathways, rather than solely relying on direct cytotoxicity. Specifically, doxycycline appears to activate proapoptotic genes, inhibit the expression of IL-8, and suppress genes involved in the inhibition of apoptosis. These insights into the mechanisms underlying doxycycline's antitumor activity provide a promising avenue for the development of novel strategies for cancer therapy.

title: Orientationally invariant indices of axon diameter and density from diffusion MRI.
text:
The present study proposes and validates a novel diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique for measuring orientationally invariant indices of axon diameter and density in white matter. These indices offer a more specific measure of white matter microstructure compared to standard indices from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). The proposed technique takes advantage of the orientational invariance property, allowing for fusion with tractography and providing new opportunities for mapping brain connectivity and quantifying disease processes.
To test the method, we adopted a four-compartment tissue model combined with an optimized multishell high-angular-resolution pulsed-gradient-spin-echo acquisition in both simulation and real-world scenarios. Fixed monkey brains were scanned using a preclinical scanner, while live human brains were imaged on a clinical 3T scanner. The human data acquisition took approximately one hour.
Simulation experiments demonstrated that both monkey and human protocols could accurately detect distributions of axon diameters that occur naturally in white matter. We compared the axon diameter index with the mean axon diameter weighted by axon volume. While there was a protocol-dependent difference between the two measures, a strong correlation was observed for the monkey protocol, while a weaker but still discernible correlation was found for the human protocol, where greater diffusivity and lower gradient strength limited sensitivity to larger axons.
Maps of axon diameter and density indices obtained from the monkey and human data in the corpus callosum and corticospinal tract showed patterns consistent with known histological findings. The results represent the first demonstration of orientationally invariant sensitivity to natural axon diameter distributions using both specialized and clinical MRI hardware. This finding motivates further refinement, validation, and evaluation of the technique to better understand the influences of potential confounds.

title: IFI16 and cGAS cooperate in the activation of STING during DNA sensing in human keratinocytes
text: Human cells can detect foreign DNA (exogenous DNA) during infection by using the cytosolic DNA receptor cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS), which produces a second messenger called cyclic GMP-AMP (cGAMP). Other potential DNA receptors have been described, but their roles in the cGAS-cGAMP pathway are currently unclear. Our study shows that interferon-γ inducible protein 16 (IFI16) works with cGAS to detect DNA in human keratinocytes, and both are essential for full activation of an innate immune response to exogenous DNA and DNA viruses. IFI16 also helps activate the STING protein in response to cGAMP, and interacts with STING to promote its phosphorylation and translocation. Our findings suggest that the two DNA sensors IFI16 and cGAS work together to prevent the unnecessary activation of the type I interferon response.

title: Oncostatic effects of the indole melatonin and expression of its cytosolic and nuclear receptors in cultured human melanoma cell lines.
text: Melatonin has been shown to have anti-tumor effects on malignant melanoma in both in vitro and in vivo studies. We examined the growth-inhibiting effects of melatonin over a range of concentrations in four melanoma cell lines (representative of different growth phases and phenotypes) using multiple assays. Melanoma cells were exposed to melatonin at concentrations between 10^-12 and 10^-3 M, and proliferation and clonogenicity were evaluated at 12 hours and 14 days, respectively. Additionally, the expression of cytosolic quinone oxidoreductases NQO1, NQO2 (also known as the MT3 receptor), and nuclear receptor RORalpha was examined using RT-PCR. Melatonin at pharmacologically relevant concentrations (10^-3-10^-7 M) significantly suppressed proliferation in all melanoma cell lines. In SKMEL-188 cells cultured in serum-free media, melatonin at low concentrations (10^-12-10^-10 M) also slightly reduced proliferation. The effects of pharmacological doses of melatonin were confirmed in the clonogenic assay. We detected NQO1 expression in all cell lines, while NQO2 and nuclear receptor RORalpha (including its isoform RORalpha4) were present only in SBCE2, WM-164, and WM-98. These findings suggest that melatonin differentially suppresses proliferation in melanoma cell lines of varying behavior, and the intensity of the anti-tumor response may be related to the cell line-specific pattern of melatonin receptors and cytosolic binding protein expression.

title: Lysosomal localization of TRPML3 depends on TRPML2 and the mucolipidosis-associated protein TRPML1.
text: Mucolipidosis type IV is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder that affects the central nervous system, digestive system, and vision. The disorder is caused by mutations in the TRPML1 gene, which codes for a transmembrane protein involved in lysosomal function. Additionally, mammals have two additional TRPML genes, TRPML2 and TRPML3, which have limited information regarding their propensity to multimerize, distribution in the cell, and mechanisms of trafficking regulation. Our study found that TRPMLs interact with each other to form homomultimers and heteromultimers, with TRPML1 and TRPML2 homomultimers localizing to lysosomes, while TRPML3 homomultimers are mainly found in the endoplasmic reticulum. However, when TRPML1 or TRPML2 is coexpressed with TRPML3, TRPML3 localizes to lysosomes, indicating a hierarchy of subcellular distribution for the TRPMLs. Specifically, TRPML1 and TRPML2 dictate the localization of TRPML3, rather than the other way around.

title: Evolution of metastasis revealed by mutational landscapes of chemically induced skin cancers
text: Humans exhibit a high level of genetic diversity in tumors, but the processes influencing the timing and route of metastatic dissemination among subclones remain unknown. Using whole-exome sequencing of 103 paired benign, malignant, and metastatic skin tumors from genetically diverse mice, we found that most metastases disseminate synchronously from the primary tumor, supporting a parallel model of metastasis over a linear one. Shared mutations between primary carcinomas and their matched metastases have a signature associated with initiating carcinogens, while non-shared mutations are primarily associated with oxidative stress. Our findings imply that intratumoral factors play a role in metastatic seeding, and we also demonstrate the importance of germline polymorphisms in determining allele-specific mutations. Additionally, we identify somatic genetic alterations that are specific to carcinogenesis initiated by Hras or Kras mutations in mice. These findings highlight the potential of using mouse tumors that mimic human genetic diversity to better understand the clonal evolution of metastasis and to test novel therapies.

title: A specific inhibitor of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, 2-(4-morpholinyl)-8-phenyl-4H-1-benzopyran-4-one (LY294002).
text: Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PtdIns 3-kinase) is an enzyme that plays a crucial role in growth factor signal transduction by interacting with both receptor and non-receptor tyrosine kinases, including the platelet-derived growth factor receptor. Investigating the inhibition of PtdIns 3-kinase could provide valuable insights into its function and regulatory mechanisms. Quercetin, a naturally occurring bioflavinoid, has been shown to inhibit PtdIns 3-kinase with an IC50 of 1.3 μg/ml (3.8 μM), while inhibition appeared to be directed towards the ATP-binding site of the kinase. Analogs of quercetin were then evaluated as PtdIns 3-kinase inhibitors, with the most potent ones exhibiting IC50 values in the range of 1.7-8.4 μg/ml. In contrast, genistein, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor of the isoflavone class, did not significantly inhibit PtdIns 3-kinase (IC50 > 30 μg/ml). To further investigate PtdIns 3-kinase inhibitors, other chromones were evaluated. One compound, 2-(4-morpholinyl)-8-phenyl-4H-1-benzopyran-4-one (also known as 2-(4-morpholinyl)-8-phenylchromone, LY294002), selectively and completely abolished PtdIns 3-kinase activity (IC50 = 0.43 μg/ml; 1.40 μM), without affecting PtdIns 4-kinase or tested protein and lipid kinases. Analogs of LY294002 demonstrated a highly selective structure-activity relationship, with small structural changes resulting in significant decreases in inhibition. LY294002 was shown to completely abolish PtdIns 3-kinase activity in fMet-Leu-Phe-stimulated human neutrophils, as well as inhibit proliferation of smooth muscle cells in cultured rabbit aortic segments. Given the central role of PtdIns 3-kinase in growth factor signal transduction, the development of specific inhibitors against the kinase may be beneficial in the treatment of proliferative diseases, as well as in elucidating its biological role in cellular proliferation and growth factor response.

title: A simple two-step protocol for the purification of human pancreatic beta cells
text: Isolating pure human beta cells could be beneficial for various research purposes. However, the lack of specific surface antigens has been a significant challenge. To develop a straightforward method for human beta cell isolation, we aimed to eliminate ductal cells by their expression of carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9), followed by positive selection of beta cells based on their expression of polysialic acid–neural cell adhesion molecule (PSA-NCAM). We investigated the cell type-specific expression of CA19-9, NCAM, and PSA-NCAM in sections of adult human pancreas and cultured primary endocrine and exocrine cells. Dispersed human islet cells were purified in two steps, after 4 days of suspension culture, by binding to magnetic microbeads coupled to antibodies against CA19-9 and PSA-NCAM. We detected NCAM expression in ducts and islets in the human pancreas, while PSA-NCAM immunoreactivity was only observed in islets. PSA-NCAM staining in dispersed cells revealed that the marker is expressed in all endocrine cell types, but not in duct cells. Although purification of dispersed islet cells using PSA-NCAM microbeads alone did not completely eliminate contaminating duct cells, elimination of the duct cells by CA19-9 microbeads followed by positive sorting of the PSA-NCAM-positive cells in five consecutive Islet preparations resulted in 90 to 98% pure endocrine cells, of which 89 to 97% were beta cells. We describe a straightforward and reproducible method for the purification of viable human pancreatic beta cells devoid of exocrine acini and ducts.

title: Prev | Table of Contents Reports Embryonic Stem Cell Lines Derived from Human
text: Human blastocyst-derived, pluripotent cell lines have been developed that possess normal karyotypes, exhibit high levels of telomerase activity, and express surface markers characteristic of primate embryonic stem cells but not other early lineages. Following 4-5 months of undifferentiated proliferation in vitro, these cells retain the potential to form all three embryonic germ layers, including gut epithelium (endoderm), cartilage, bone, smooth muscle, and striated muscle (mesoderm), and neural epithelium, embryonic ganglia, and stratified squamous epithelium (ectoderm). These cell lines hold promise for advancing human developmental biology, drug discovery, and transplantation medicine.

title: Ascorbic-acid transporter Slc23a1 is essential for vitamin C transport into the brain and for perinatal survival
text: The only proven requirement for ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is in preventing scurvy, likely due to its role as a cofactor for enzymes involved in post-translational modifications that stabilize collagen. To investigate this further, we created mice lacking the mouse ortholog of a rat ascorbic acid transporter, Slc23a1 (solute carrier family 23 member 1). In cultured embryonic fibroblasts from these mice, ascorbic acid uptake was significantly reduced, and undetectable or reduced levels of ascorbic acid were observed in the blood and tissues of the mice. Prenatal supplementation of pregnant females did not elevate ascorbic acid levels in Slc23a1-deficient fetuses, suggesting that Slc23a1 is crucial for ascorbic acid transport across the placenta. Slc23a1-deficient mice died shortly after birth due to respiratory failure and intraparenchymal brain hemorrhage. Notably, the lungs of these mice showed no postnatal expansion, but had normal levels of surfactant protein B. The brain hemorrhage was not simply a result of scurvy, as Slc23a1-deficient mice did not exhibit hemorrhage in other tissues, and their skin had normal levels of 4-hydroxyproline despite low ascorbic acid content. Our findings reveal that Slc23a1 is essential for transporting ascorbic acid into many tissues and across the placenta, and deficiency in this transporter is lethal in newborn mice, highlighting a previously unappreciated requirement for ascorbic acid during the perinatal period.

title: MVP-mediated exosomal sorting of miR-193a promotes colon cancer progression
text: Exosomes are rapidly emerging as key players in intercellular communication. So far, the influence of exosome release on both the donor cells and recipient cells has not been extensively studied. To address this gap, we analyzed the exosomal microRNA (miRNA) expression profiles in primary mouse colon tumors, liver metastases of colon cancer, and normal colon tissues. Our findings indicate that advanced disease is characterized by higher levels of tumor suppressor miRNAs encapsulated within exosomes. In particular, miR-193a shows a striking correlation with the major vault protein (MVP). When MVP is knocked out, miR-193a accumulates in the donor cells instead of the exosomes, leading to a halt in tumor progression. Moreover, miR-193a inhibits cell proliferation by targeting Caprin1, which upregulates Ccnd2 and c-Myc. In contrast, human colon cancer patients with more advanced disease feature higher levels of exosomal miR-193a in their circulation. In summary, our results suggest that the action of MVP in directing tumor suppressor miRNA into exosomes promotes tumor progression.

title: Casual blood pressure and neurocognitive function in children with chronic kidney disease: a report of the children with chronic kidney disease cohort study.
text:
Background and Objectives: Children with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at risk of cognitive impairment, with nearly 60% of them having hypertension. However, there is limited information on the impact of hypertension on CKD-related neurocognitive deficits in children. Our study aimed to determine whether children with CKD and elevated blood pressure (EBP) perform poorly on neurocognitive tests compared to those with CKD and normal blood pressure.
Design, Setting, Participants, and Measurements: This was a cross-sectional analysis of the association between auscultatory blood pressure and neurocognitive test performance in children aged 6-17 years enrolled in the Chronic Kidney Disease in Children (CKiD) project.
Results: Of the 383 subjects, 132 (34%) had EBP (systolic blood pressure and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥90th percentile). Subjects with EBP had lower mean (SD) scores on Wechsler Abbreviated Scales of Intelligence (WASI) Performance IQ than those with normal BP (P = 0.03) and WASI Full Scale IQ (P = 0.04). There was an inverse correlation between BP index (subject's blood pressure/95th percentile BP) and Performance IQ score. On multivariate analysis, the association between lower Performance IQ score and increased BP remained significant after controlling for demographic and disease-related variables.
Conclusion: Higher blood pressure was independently associated with decreased WASI Performance IQ scores in children with mild-to-moderate CKD.

title: Bone marrow failure and developmental delay caused by mutations in poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN).
text:
BACKGROUND: Deadenylation, a process regulated by enzymes called deadenylases, plays a critical role in the function and fate of RNA molecules. Among these enzymes, poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN) is particularly interesting due to its role in degrading mRNAs and non-coding RNAs. Despite its importance, there is limited understanding of the biological impact of germline mutations in PARN.
METHODS: To investigate the role of PARN in human disease, we identified mutations in PARN in patients with haematological and neurological manifestations. We performed a range of experiments, including genomic analysis, biochemical assays, and knockdown studies, in human marrow cells and zebrafish.
RESULTS: Our analyses revealed large monoallelic deletions in PARN in four patients with developmental delay or mental illness. One of these patients presented with a severe neurological phenotype, central hypomyelination, and bone marrow failure, and had an additional missense mutation on the non-deleted allele, leading to significantly reduced PARN protein and deadenylation activity. Cellular studies showed that these patient cells had impaired oligoadenylation of specific H/ACA box small nucleolar RNAs, and displayed short telomeres and an abnormal ribosome profile, reminiscent of those observed in some instances of dyskeratosis congenita. Interestingly, knocking down PARN in human marrow cells and zebrafish resulted in impaired haematopoiesis, further supporting the causal link between PARN dysfunction and the observed human disease.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that large monoallelic mutations in PARN can underlie developmental/mental illness, while biallelic mutations can lead to severe bone marrow failure and central hypomyelination. These results highlight the importance of PARN in human health and disease, and underscore the need for further investigations into its role in specific disorders.

title: The changing epidemiology of malaria in Ifakara Town, southern Tanzania.
text: Between 1995 and 2000, there were significant changes in the epidemiology of malaria in Ifakara, southern Tanzania. We documented these changes through parasitological and clinical data from various community and hospital-based studies involving children up to the age of 5. There was a rightward shift and lowering of the age-specific parasite prevalence in community-based cohort studies. The incidence of clinical malaria in placebo-receiving infants in additional study cohorts decreased from 0.8 episodes per infant per year in 1995 to 0.43 episodes per year in 2000, a rate ratio of 0.53 (95% CI: 0.404–0.70, P<0.0001). Concurrently, there was an increase in the total number of malaria admissions and a marked rightward shift in the age distribution of these admissions (median age in 1995: 1.55 years vs. 2.33 in 2000, P<0.0001). However, the burden of malaria deaths remained in infants. We explore how these drastic changes in the epidemiology of malaria may have resulted from the use of currently available malaria control tools. Caution is warranted when interpreting hospital-based data as it is likely to underestimate the impact of anemia on mortality in the community, where most pediatric deaths occur. Even in low to moderate transmission settings, where older children experience most malaria episodes, targeting effective malaria control at infants may lead to significant reductions in infant mortality caused by malaria.

title: MicroRNA-192 in diabetic kidney glomeruli and its function in TGF-beta-induced collagen expression via inhibition of E-box repressors.
text: The key features of diabetic nephropathy (DN) involve the accumulation of extracellular matrix proteins, such as collagen 1-alpha 1 and -2 (Col1a1 and Col1a2). Transforming growth factor beta1 (TGF-beta), a crucial regulator of these extracellular matrix genes, is elevated in mesangial cells (MC) in DN. Through microarray profiling, we discovered that TGF-beta enhanced Col1a2 mRNA in mouse MC (MMC) while simultaneously reducing the mRNA levels of an E-box repressor, deltaEF1. TGF-beta treatment or short hairpin RNAs targeting deltaEF1 increased the activity of upstream E-box elements in the Col1a2 gene. TGF-beta also decreased the expression of Smad-interacting protein 1 (SIP1), another E-box repressor similar to deltaEF1. Our findings were further supported by the observation that SIP1 is a target of microRNA-192 (miR-192), a miR that is highly expressed in the kidney and whose levels are significantly increased in glomeruli isolated from streptozotocin-injected diabetic mice and diabetic db/db mice compared to nondiabetic controls. MiR-192 treatment or transfection with miR-192 decreased endogenous SIP1 expression and reporter activity of a SIP1 3' UTR-containing luciferase construct in MC. Furthermore, miR-192 synergized with deltaEF1 short hairpin RNAs to increase Col1a2 E-box-luc activity. Our results imply a novel mechanism by which miRs play a role in the kidney and DN, by controlling TGF-beta-induced Col1a2 expression by down-regulating E-box repressors.

title: Activation of PAR(2) receptors sensitizes primary afferents and causes leukocyte rolling and adherence in the rat knee joint.
text:
The present study aimed to investigate the role of PAR(2) receptors in the chronic inflammation of arthritis by examining their activation in the rat knee joint. The study used a combination of immunohistochemical analysis and electrophysiological recordings to assess the effects of PAR(2) activation on neuronal activity and leukocyte trafficking in the joint.
Results showed that PAR(2) receptors are expressed in 59% of dorsal root ganglia cells in the knee joint, and that stimulation of PAR(2) with its activating peptide increased joint fibre firing rate during both normal and noxious rotation. Additionally, PAR(2) activation significantly increased leukocyte rolling and adhesion in the synovial vasculature over a 60-min period. The study also demonstrated that the effects of PAR(2) activation are mediated by TRPV1 and NK(1) receptors, as pre-treatment with selective antagonists blocked the responses.
The findings of this study suggest that PAR(2) receptors play an acute inflammatory role in the knee joint, contributing to the chronic inflammation of arthritis via both neuronal sensitization and leukocyte trafficking. These findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying arthritis and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of this debilitating disease.

title: Polyphosphate kinase 1, a central node in the stress response network of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, connects the two-component systems MprAB and SenX3-RegX3 and the extracytoplasmic function sigma factor, sigma E.
text: The regulation of polyphosphate (poly P) metabolism in Mycobacterium tuberculosis affects the stress response. Here, we describe the regulatory framework of a signal transduction pathway involving the two-component system (TCS) SenX3-RegX3, the extracytoplasmic function sigma factor SigE, and the poly P-producing enzyme polyphosphate kinase 1 (PPK1). Our findings reveal that the ppk1 promoter in Mycobacterium tuberculosis is activated under phosphate starvation, which is inhibited by an imperfect palindrome likely representing a binding site for the response regulator RegX3, a component of the two-component system SenX3-RegX3. Moreover, we found that the activity of the ppk1 promoter is abrogated upon deletion of a putative SigE binding site. Furthermore, we demonstrated that SigE binds to the ppk1 promoter in vitro and corroborated its involvement in ppk1 transcription. Additionally, overexpressing RseA (anti-SigE) attenuated ppk1 expression under phosphate starvation, suggesting SigE's role in ppk1 transcription. Combining these findings with our earlier observation that PPK1 can regulate sigE expression via the MprAB TCS, we propose the existence of multiple positive feedback loops in this signaling circuit. This architecture, in combination with the sequestering effect of RseA, may contribute to the persistence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

title: Natural history of asymptomatic unruptured cerebral aneurysms evaluated at CT angiography: growth and rupture incidence and correlation with epidemiologic risk factors.
text: Objective: To investigate the relationship between aneurysm size and epidemiological risk factors using CT angiography. Methods: In this HIPAA-compliant, institutional review board-approved study, patients with known asymptomatic unruptured intracerebral aneurysms were followed up longitudinally with CT angiographic examinations. Aneurysm growth was defined as an increase in one or more dimensions by 5% or more, and the ABC/2 method was used to calculate volume. Logistic regression analysis was used to analyze the associations of epidemiological factors with aneurysm growth and rupture. Inter- and intra-observer agreement coefficients were calculated for dimension, volume, and growth using the Pearson correlation coefficient and difference of means with 95% confidence intervals, the agreement statistic, and the McNemar χ(2) test. Results: A total of 165 patients with 258 aneurysms were included in the study, with a mean follow-up time of 2.24 years from diagnosis. Forty-six of 258 aneurysms grew larger, and spontaneous rupture occurred in four of 228 intradural aneurysms (average size: 6.2 mm). The risk of aneurysm rupture per patient-year was 2.4% (95% CI: 0.5%, 7.12%) with growth and 0.2% (95% CI: 0.006%, 1.22%) without growth (P = 0.034). A 12-fold higher risk of rupture was observed for growing aneurysms (P < 0.002), with high intra- and interobserver correlation coefficients for size, volume, and growth. Tobacco smoking (P < 0.015) and initial size (P < 0.051) were independent covariates that predicted 78.4% of growing aneurysms. Conclusion: These findings support imaging follow-up of all patients with aneurysms, including those with smaller aneurysms than the current 7-mm treatment threshold. Aneurysm growth, size, and smoking were associated with increased rupture risk.

title: A search for the presence of the enteroviral capsid protein VP1 in pancreases of patients with Type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes and pancreases and hearts of infants who died of coxsackieviral myocarditis
text: Using an antiserum raised against a recombinant Coxsackie virus B3 capsid protein (VP1), an immunocytochemical technique was developed that could detect the presence of all Coxsackie B viruses in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded infected tissue culture cells. This technique was applied to autopsy heart and pancreas tissues from 21 patients who were thought to have died of acute Coxsackievirus B myocarditis, and cardiac myocytes were found positive for VP1 in 12 of 20 cases where the heart was available for analysis. Insulitis was present in the pancreas in seven of these cases, and all seven islet endocrine cells containing VP1 were found. In contrast, VP1 was rarely found in exocrine pancreas tissues. Additionally, cells showing positive staining for VP1 typically displayed signs of necrosis. The study also investigated tissues from 88 patients who had died at clinical presentation of Type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus, and no evidence of VP1 was found in the autopsy pancreases. While this study suggests that direct viral cytopathicity is unlikely to be the cause of the destruction of insulin-secreting B cells in the diabetic pancreas, it does not rule out the possibility that a persistent viral infection could lead to their destruction through an autoimmune mechanism.

title: Direct reprogramming of mouse fibroblasts to cardiomyocyte-like cells using Yamanaka factors on engineered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) hydrogels.
text: Reprogramming strategies allow for the rapid conversion of somatic cells into cardiomyocytes or cardiomyocyte-like cells without passing through the pluripotent state. A recently described protocol combines Yamanaka factor induction with pluripotency inhibition followed by BMP4 treatment to efficiently reprogram mouse fibroblasts into beating cardiomyocyte-like cells. The original study was conducted using Matrigel-coated tissue culture polystyrene (TCPS), a stiff material that also non-specifically adsorbs serum proteins. To address this issue, protein adsorption-resistant poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) materials can be covalently modified to present precise concentrations of adhesion proteins or peptides, without the unintended effects of non-specifically adsorbed proteins. In this study, we describe an improved protocol that incorporates custom-engineered materials. We first replicated the Efe et al. protocol on Matrigel-coated TCPS, reprogramming adult mouse tail-tip fibroblasts (TTF) and mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) into cardiomyocyte-like cells that exhibited striated sarcomeric α-actinin staining, spontaneous calcium transients, and visible beating. We then designed PEG culture substrates to promote MEF adhesion via laminin and RGD-binding integrins, resulting in improved proliferation and reprogramming efficiency, as evidenced by increased beating patch number and area, gene expression, and flow cytometry. These findings suggest that cellular reprogramming can be enhanced using custom-engineered materials.

title: Effects of risedronate treatment on vertebral and nonvertebral fractures in women with postmenopausal osteoporosis: a randomized controlled trial. Vertebral Efficacy With Risedronate Therapy (VERT) Study Group.
text:
In this study, the investigators aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of daily oral risedronate treatment for 3 years in postmenopausal women with established osteoporosis to reduce the risk of vertebral and nonvertebral fractures.
110 centers in North America enrolled 2458 ambulatory postmenopausal women aged <85 years with at least one vertebral fracture at baseline. Subjects were randomly assigned to receive either risedronate (2.5 or 5 mg/d) or placebo for 3 years. All subjects received calcium supplementation (1000 mg/d), and vitamin D (up to 500 IU/d) was provided if baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels were low. The primary outcomes were the incidence of new vertebral fractures detected through quantitative and semiquantitative assessments of radiographs, radiographically confirmed nonvertebral fractures, and changes in bone mineral density (BMD) measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA).
Compared with placebo, 5 mg/d of risedronate reduced the cumulative incidence of new vertebral fractures by 41% (41% - 58%) over 3 years (11.3% vs 16.3%; P= .003). A fracture reduction of 65% (38% - 81%) was observed after the first year (2.4% vs 6.4%; P<.001). The cumulative incidence of nonvertebral fractures over 3 years was reduced by 39% (6% - 61%) (5.2% vs 8.4%; P= .02). BMD increased significantly compared with placebo at the lumbar spine (5.4% vs 1.1%), femoral neck (1.6% vs -1.2%), femoral trochanter (3.3% vs -0.7%), and midshaft of the radius (0.2% vs -1.4%). Bone formed during risedronate treatment was histologically normal. The overall safety profile of risedronate, including gastrointestinal safety, was similar to that of placebo.
In conclusion, these data suggest that risedronate therapy is effective and well tolerated in the treatment of women with established postmenopausal osteoporosis.

title: Hypoxia — a key regulatory factor in tumour growth
text: Cells exhibit a range of biological responses when exposed to hypoxic conditions, such as activating signaling pathways that control proliferation, angiogenesis, and death. Cancer cells have adapted these pathways to enable tumors to survive and even grow under hypoxic conditions, and tumor hypoxia is linked to poor prognosis and resistance to radiation therapy. As such, many elements of the hypoxia-response pathway are potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

title: Loss of fibronectin from the aged stem cell niche affects the regenerative capacity of skeletal muscle in mice
text: Age-related changes in the muscle tissue have been shown to impair the function of somatic stem cells, known as muscle stem cells (MuSCs). Our study demonstrates that the aged stem cell niche in skeletal muscle has a significantly reduced amount of a protein called fibronectin (FN). This reduction has detrimental effects on the function and maintenance of MuSCs. In addition, we found that deleting the gene encoding FN from young regenerating muscles recreates the aging phenotype, resulting in a decline in MuSC numbers. Using an extracellular matrix (ECM) library screen and pathway profiling, we identified FN as the preferred adhesion substrate for MuSCs, and found that integrin-mediated signaling through focal adhesion kinase and the p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway is weakened in MuSCs from aged mice due to limited attachments to the niche. Interestingly, we found that restoring FN levels in the aged niche can remobilize stem cells and restore youth-like muscle regeneration. Together, our results suggest that the loss of MuSC adhesion to FN in the niche ECM is an unrecognized aging mechanism.

title: Monitoring starvation-induced reactive oxygen species formation.
text: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) possess the potential to harm cells due to their capacity to oxidize cellular components such as DNA, proteins, and lipids. However, at low concentrations and under strict regulation, these molecules can also function as versatile mediators in various signal transduction pathways, including autophagy. Historically, autophagy has been associated with oxidative stress, playing a role in the degradation of oxidized proteins and organelles. Recently, evidence has emerged suggesting that ROS may also play a signaling role in the regulation of autophagy, leading to either survival or death, depending on the circumstances. To investigate the effects of ROS on this pathway, it is crucial to determine the localization, intensity, kinetics, and essentiality of the oxidative signal in autophagy. Furthermore, once the mechanisms of ROS involvement in autophagy are elucidated, detection and manipulation of ROS formation can be used to monitor and control autophagic activity. This chapter provides an overview of the methods used to examine ROS in the context of autophagy.

title: Why do patients with multimorbidity in England report worse experiences in primary care? Evidence from the General Practice Patient Survey
text:
Study Objective:
To investigate the primary care experiences of individuals with multiple long-term conditions in England using data from the 2012 General Practice Patient Survey.
Design and Methods:
The study analyzed questionnaire data from 906,578 respondents, of which 583,143 reported one or more long-term conditions. Mixed effect logistic regressions were employed to examine patient experience on six items covering three care domains (access, continuity, and communication) and a single item on overall primary care experience. Control variables included sociodemographic characteristics and general practice, while health-related quality of life was assessed using the EuroQoL (EQ-5D) scale.
Results:
Most patients with long-term conditions reported positive experiences of care at their general practice, with adjusted percentages ranging from 74.0% to 93.1% across seven questions. However, the number of comorbid conditions was associated with a decrease in the percentage of patients reporting a positive experience, with the OR reducing from 0.83 to 0.31 as the number of conditions increased from zero to four or more. After adjusting for health-related quality of life, the relationship between comorbid conditions and patient experience was no longer significant. The most significant factor affecting patient experience was pain, among the five quality of life variables included in the analysis.
Conclusion:
Patients with multiple long-term conditions frequently report poorer primary care experiences. However, patient-centred measures of health-related quality of life, particularly pain, are more important than the number of conditions in explaining why patients with multiple long-term conditions report poorer experiences of care.

title: The rice FISH BONE gene encodes a tryptophan aminotransferase, which affects pleiotropic auxin-related processes.
text: Auxin is an essential plant hormone, and its distribution within organs plays a crucial role in plant growth and development. Examining Arabidopsis mutants that were defective in auxin synthesis revealed that the indole-3-pyruvic acid (IPA) pathway, catalyzed by the TRYPTOPHAN AMINOTRANSFERASE OF ARABIDOPSIS (TAA) and YUCCA (YUC) families, is the primary route of indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) synthesis. However, little is known about the molecular mechanisms of auxin synthesis in rice. In this study, we discovered a rice mutant called fish bone (fib), which encodes an ortholog of TAA genes.
