S-nitrosylated GAPDH (SNO-GAPDH) binds to the protein Siah1, which has a nuclear localization signal, and is transported to the nucleus. Our findings reveal a novel mechanism for targeted nitrosylation of nuclear proteins and suggest that protein-protein transfer of nitric oxide groups may be a general mechanism in cellular signal transduction. Specifically, we show that SNO-GAPDH physiologically transnitrosylates nuclear proteins, including the deacetylating enzyme sirtuin-1 (SIRT1), histone deacetylase-2 (HDAC2), and DNA-activated protein kinase (DNA-PK). These findings shed light on the complexities of nitric oxide signaling and highlight the importance of protein targeting in cellular regulation.

title: The transcription factor c-Maf controls the production of interleukin-4 but not other Th2 cytokines.
text: IL-4 promotes the differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into IL-4-producing T helper 2 (Th2) cells. Previous research had suggested, but not definitively proven, that the transcription factor c-Maf directed the tissue-specific expression of IL-4. It was unclear whether c-Maf controlled the transcription of other Th2 cytokine genes. To investigate the role of c-Maf in vivo, we examined cytokine production in mice lacking c-Maf (c-maf(-/-)). We found that CD4+ T cells and NK T cells from c-maf(-/-) mice were significantly deficient in IL-4 production. However, the mice produced normal levels of IL-13 and IgE, and, when differentiated in the presence of exogenous IL-4, c-maf(-/-) T cells produced approximately normal levels of other Th2 cytokines. Our findings suggest that c-Maf has a critical and selective function in IL-4 gene transcription in vivo.

title: Genome-wide association of IL28B with response to pegylated interferon-α and ribavirin therapy for chronic hepatitis C
text: The treatment of patients with chronic hepatitis C using pegylated interferon-alpha (PEG-IFN-α) plus ribavirin (RBV) does not always lead to a sustained virological response (SVR) in all patients. In an effort to identify genetic factors associated with non-response, we conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) on a Japanese population with hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1. We found two genetic variants near the IL28B gene on chromosome 19 that were strongly associated with non-response. These associations were replicated in an independent cohort, and the SNPs were also found to be associated with SVR. In further analysis of the region, seven additional SNPs located near the IL28B gene were found to have the most significant associations. Real-time quantitative PCR assays in peripheral blood mononuclear cells showed lower IL28B expression levels in individuals carrying the minor alleles. These findings suggest that genetic variations in the IL28B gene may play a role in determining response to treatment in patients with chronic hepatitis C.

title: The WUSCHEL-related homeobox gene WOX11 is required to activate shoot-borne crown root development in rice.
text: In rice (Oryza sativa), shoot-borne crown roots are the dominant root type, emerging from lower stem nodes during normal plant development. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing crown root growth are poorly understood. This study identified WOX11, a WUSCHEL-related Homeobox gene, as a crucial regulator of crown root development. WOX11 was found to be expressed in emerging crown roots and later in the root meristem's cell division regions. Its expression can be triggered by exogenous auxin or cytokinin. Reduced or lost function of the WOX11 gene led to a decrease in the number and growth rate of crown roots, while overexpression led to premature crown root growth and an increase in root biomass by producing crown roots at upper stem nodes and the base of florets. The expression of auxin- and cytokinin-responsive genes was altered in WOX11 overexpression and RNA interference transgenic plants. Investigation revealed that WOX11 directly repressed RR2, a cytokinin-responsive type-A regulator gene that is expressed in crown root primordia. The results suggest that WOX11 may serve as a conduit for auxin and cytokinin signaling, influencing cell proliferation during crown root development.

title: Inducible depletion of satellite cells in adult, sedentary mice impairs muscle regenerative capacity without affecting sarcopenia
text: Geriatric frailty is significantly influenced by sarcopenia, the age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength. While the underlying factors behind sarcopenia are still unclear, research suggests that the decline in activity of satellite cells, which are the body's natural muscle stem cells, may play a crucial role. To investigate this hypothesis further, we experimentally depleted satellite cells in young adult mice to assess the impact on muscle regeneration throughout their lives. Our analysis of multiple muscle samples from different cohorts revealed that the muscles maintain their normal size despite reduced regenerative capacity, but exhibit increased fibrosis. These findings suggest that lifelong reduction of satellite cells do not accelerate or exacerbate sarcopenia, and may contribute to age-related muscle fibrosis instead. In other words, satellite cells may not be essential for maintaining muscle size or fiber type composition during aging, but their loss might contribute to the accumulation of scar tissue in muscles with age.

title: Reproductive clonality in protozoan pathogens--truth or artefact?
text:
The long-standing debate surrounding the frequency and significance of genetic exchange in parasitic protozoa has been revived in recent years. Recent claims have been made that dominant clonal evolution can explain the population structures of several key protozoan pathogens. However, we present an alternative perspective, suggesting that much of the apparent clonality may be due to inadequate sampling and study design.
We review current research to understand why sex is difficult to detect in protozoan parasite populations. We compare laboratory models of genetic exchange in parasitic protozoa with natural patterns of genetic diversity and evaluate the fitness advantage of sex at different evolutionary scales. We also discuss approaches to improve the accuracy of efforts to characterize genetic exchange in the field.
Furthermore, we examine the implications of the first population genomic studies for the debate around sex and clonality in parasitic protozoa and consider the limitations of these studies. Finally, we highlight the importance of ongoing research in this area to better understand the role of genetic exchange in the evolution and transmission of parasitic protozoa.

title: The ACF1 complex is required for DNA double-strand break repair in human cells.
text: Double-strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA are repaired through nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR) processes, but the mechanisms by which cells repair DNA damage remain poorly understood. Our research reveals that ATP-dependent chromatin-remodeling factors, such as ACF1 and SNF2H, accumulate rapidly at sites of DSBs and are necessary for DSB repair in human cells. When the expression of ACF1 or SNF2H is reduced, cells become highly sensitive to X-rays and chemical treatments that produce DSBs, and these breaks are left unrepaired. We found that ACF1 interacts directly with KU70 and is required for the accumulation of KU proteins at DSBs. Following treatments that produce DSBs, the KU70/80 complex becomes more closely associated with the chromatin-remodeling factors of the CHRAC complex, which includes ACF1, SNF2H, CHRAC15, and CHRAC17. Additionally, we found that the frequency of NHEJ and HR induced by DSBs in chromosomal DNA is significantly decreased in cells lacking ACF1 or its complexes. Our findings suggest that ACF1 and its complexes play important roles in DSB repair.

title: Findings to date from the ASCUS-LSIL Triage Study (ALTS).
text: There is ongoing debate in the United States regarding the appropriate evaluation and management of low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL) and equivocal (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance [ASCUS]) cervical cytology interpretations. To address this issue, the National Cancer Institute launched the ASCUS-LSIL Triage Study (ALTS): a multicenter, randomized clinical trial comparing three management approaches - immediate colposcopy, cytologic follow-up, and triage by human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing. This article summarizes the key findings of ALTS, as published to date. Participants with ASCUS (n = 3488) or LSIL (n = 1572) were randomly assigned to research arms between 1996 and 1998 and were monitored for two years. The disease outcome was histologic cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 3/cancer. While the prevalence of oncogenic HPV was too high to effectively triage LSIL using HPV DNA testing with Hybrid Capture 2, HPV testing proved useful for women referred with a cytologic interpretation of ASCUS, with sensitivity comparable to immediate colposcopy and a reduced need for colposcopic referrals among older women. Experienced pathologists varied significantly in their interpretations of cervical abnormalities, especially for histologic CIN 1 and cytologic ASCUS. However, a distinct type of ASCUS could be identified with a high positive predictive value for detecting women with underlying high-grade CIN. Additional analyses are ongoing.

title: Marine organisms as a source of new anticancer agents.
text: Throughout the past four decades, various plant and terrestrial microorganism-derived active anticancer agents have been discovered. The initial marine-derived anticancer drug, cytarabine, was isolated from the Caribbean sponge Cryptotheca crypta in the 1980s and has since been used in clinical treatment for leukemia and lymphoma. Additionally, gemcitabine, a fluorinated derivative of cytarabine, has been approved for use in treating patients with pancreatic, breast, bladder, and non-small-cell lung cancer. In recent years, several new marine-derived experimental anticancer agents have entered preclinical and clinical trials, thanks to advancements in deep-sea collection, extraction, and large-scale production through aquaculture and synthesis. This paper will discuss examples of these marine-derived agents currently undergoing preclinical and early clinical evaluation, as well as present a summary of available information on the results of Phase I and II trials of agents such as aplidine, ET-734, dolastatin 10, and bryostatin 1.

title: A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of diindolylmethane for breast cancer biomarker modulation in patients taking tamoxifen
text: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was conducted to investigate the activity and safety of BioResponse DIM® (BR-DIM) in combination with tamoxifen in women taking the drug for breast cancer. One hundred thirty women were enrolled (51 in the placebo group and 47 in the BR-DIM group), and the study found that BR-DIM significantly increased the ratio of 2/16α-hydroxyestrone (2/16α-OHE1) in urine compared to placebo (-0.7 [−1.7, 0.8], P < 0.001). Additionally, BR-DIM led to an increase in serum sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) compared to placebo (+25 ± 22 and +1.1 ± 19 nmol/L, respectively). The study also found that BR-DIM did not result in any changes in breast density measured by mammography or MRI. Interestingly, plasma tamoxifen metabolites (endoxifen, 4-OH tamoxifen, and N-desmethyl-tamoxifen) were reduced in women receiving BR-DIM versus placebo (P < 0.001). The study found minimal adverse events, and there were no differences in adverse events between the two treatment groups. Overall, the study suggests that BR-DIM may promote favorable changes in estrogen metabolism and circulating levels of SHBG in patients taking tamoxifen for breast cancer, and further research is warranted to determine whether BR-DIM may attenuate the clinical benefit of tamoxifen. The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with the identifier NCT01391689.

title: Intracellular coenzymes as natural biomarkers for metabolic activities and mitochondrial anomalies.
text: Mitochondria are crucial for energy metabolism, programmed cell death, and oxidative stress response. Mutations in mitochondrial DNA can impair the structure and function of key enzyme complexes, leading to a variety of illnesses, including cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, and aging. Early detection of mitochondrial and metabolic irregularities is essential for effective diagnosis and therapeutic intervention. Low levels of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) are indicative of impaired cellular oxidation-reduction reactions. Notably, NADH and FAD are naturally fluorescent, allowing for non-invasive imaging of metabolic activities in living cells and tissues. This intriguing property makes them ideal biomarkers for metabolic and mitochondrial functions. Innovative techniques utilizing NADH and FAD autofluorescence can be excited by distinct wavelengths, providing complementary imaging methods that are sensitive to protein binding and local environment, offering new avenues for research into cellular metabolism. This article will delve into the most recent developments concerning intracellular NADH and FAD as potential biomarkers for metabolic and mitochondrial processes.

title: Biochemical differences in the alphabeta T cell receptor.CD3 surface complex between CD8+ and CD4+ human mature T lymphocytes.
text: In this study, we investigated the differences in the T cell receptor (TCR) complex between CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from individuals who are deficient in the CD3gamma molecule. We found that the surface TCR components from CD4+ gamma-deficient T cells were similar in size to those of CD4+ gamma-positive controls, except for a different stoichiometry of alpha-beta-delta-epsilon chains. In contrast, the surface TCR alpha, beta, and CD3delta chains of CD8+ gamma-deficient T cells were not present in their normal sizes. Using confocal immunofluorescence and blue native gel electrophoresis, we found that there was a heterogeneous population of TCR.CD3 in these cells. Furthermore, we performed an epitopic scan using primary peripheral blood T lymphocytes from normal gamma-positive donors and found that the monoclonal antibody RW2-8C8 stained CD8+ T cells better than CD4+ T cells, and this effect was independent of T cell activation or differentiation. Moreover, RW2-8C8 staining of CD8+ T cells was found to be more dependent on lipid raft integrity than that of CD4+ T cells. Finally, immunoprecipitation studies on purified primary CD4+ and CD8+ T cells revealed that there were glycosylation differences between the two. Taken together, these results suggest that there are conformational or topological lineage-specific differences in the TCR.CD3 complex between CD4+ and CD8+ wild-type T cells, which may be relevant for cis interactions during antigen recognition and signal transduction.

title: Circulating mitochondrial DNA in serum of patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
text: Neutrophils play a crucial role in the pathophysiology of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and recent studies have shed light on the role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in this disease. Specifically, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) has been found to be released during NET formation. To investigate the role of mtDNA in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, we measured circulating cell-free mtDNA and genomic DNA in the blood of patients with the disease and healthy controls. Our results showed that both fragments of mtDNA (79 base pairs and 230 base pairs) and genomic DNA were elevated significantly in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis compared to controls. However, only the shorter 79 base pair mtDNA fragment correlated with the active stage of the disease and clinical symptoms. These findings suggest that the mechanism of extracellular release of mtDNA accompanies the active stage of the disease, and circulating mtDNA may serve as a useful biomarker for monitoring treatment. Interestingly, untreated patients had extremely high levels of circulating mtDNA, which suggests that this biomarker has potential for use in clinical settings.

title: Estrogen receptor-alpha promotes alternative macrophage activation during cutaneous repair.
text: Efficient local recruitment of monocytes/macrophages is crucial for tissue repair. Once recruited, macrophages are polarized towards classical (pro-inflammatory) or alternative (pro-healing) activation in response to cytokines, with tight temporal regulation being vital for efficient wound healing. However, the contribution of estrogen and its receptors to macrophage polarization and local effects on wound healing has been largely unexplored. Our study identifies a previously unreported role of estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) in polarizing macrophages from various sources towards an alternative phenotype. Cell-specific ER alpha ablation studies demonstrate an in vivo role for inflammatory cell ERα, but not ERβ, in poor healing associated with altered cytokine profiles and reduced numbers of alternatively activated macrophages. Our findings also reveal intrinsic changes in ERα-deficient macrophages, which are unable to respond to alternative activation signals in vitro. In conclusion, our data demonstrate that inflammatory cell-expressed ERα promotes alternative macrophage polarization, which is beneficial for timely healing. These findings are likely to be relevant to many pathologies involving excessive inflammation.

title: Disturbance in cerebral spinal fluid sphingolipid content is associated with memory impairment in subjects infected with the human immunodeficiency virus
text: Despite the widespread use of antiretroviral therapies to control the replication of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), cognitive dysfunctions known as HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) continue to affect approximately 50% of infected individuals. Currently, there is no biomarker that can identify those at risk of developing HAND. Past studies have identified specific sphingolipid species that are dysregulated in HAND, but the relationship between these biochemical changes and cognitive dysfunction remains unclear. To address this gap in knowledge, we compared levels of sphingomyelin, ceramide, and sterol species in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with performance on standard neurological tests designed to assess cognitive and motor functions in HIV-infected individuals. Our findings revealed that the ratio of sphingomyelin to ceramide for certain acyl chain lengths (C16:0, C18:0, C22:0, and C24:0) was associated with poorer performance on multiple indices of memory. The most significant association was found for the acyl chain of C18:0, which consistently correlated with poor performance on multiple memory tests. These findings suggest that the sphingomyelin:ceramide ratio for C18:0 may serve as a reasonable surrogate marker for memory dysfunction in HIV-infected individuals.

title: An observational study fluid balance and patient outcomes in the Randomized Evaluation of Normal vs. Augmented Level of Replacement Therapy trial.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the relationship between daily fluid balance during intensive care unit (ICU) stay and clinical outcomes in patients enrolled in the Randomized Evaluation of Normal vs. Augmented Level (RENAL) replacement therapy study.
Design: Statistical analysis of data from multicenter, randomized, controlled trials.
Setting: Thirty-five ICUs in Australia and New Zealand.
Patients: Cohort of 1453 patients enrolled in the RENAL study.
Interventions: We examined the association between daily fluid balance and clinical outcomes using multivariable logistic regression, Cox proportional hazards, time-dependent analysis, and repeated measure analysis models.
Measurements and Main Results: During ICU stay, mean daily fluid balance among survivors was -234 mL/day compared to +560 mL/day among nonsurvivors (p < .0001). Mean cumulative fluid balance over the same period was -1941 vs. +1755 mL (p = .0003). A negative mean daily fluid balance during study treatment was independently associated with decreased risk of death at 90 days (odds ratio 0.318; 95% confidence interval 0.24-0.43; p < .000.1) and with increased survival time (p < .0001). In addition, a negative mean daily fluid balance was associated with significantly increased renal replacement-free days (p = .0017), ICU-free days (p < .0001), and hospital-free days (p = .01). These findings were unchanged after applying different statistical models.
Conclusions: In the RENAL study, a negative mean daily fluid balance was consistently associated with improved clinical outcomes. Fluid balance may be a target for specific manipulation in future interventional trials of critically ill patients receiving renal replacement therapy.

title: Prison health care: a review of the literature.
text: The growing prison population has led to a surge in health issues among inmates, creating a complex challenge for corrections officials. Prisons were designed with rehabilitation in mind, but this goal can sometimes clash with the primary aim of providing adequate healthcare. A comprehensive review of the literature reveals that mental health, substance abuse, and infectious diseases are the most pressing health concerns in prison settings. The needs of female prisoners and older inmates differ significantly from those of the general prisoner population, underscoring the importance of tailored approaches. In addition to addressing the immediate health needs of prisoners, prison healthcare services should strive to promote community health and wellbeing through broad-based initiatives. Collaboration between healthcare professionals and corrections officials is crucial for delivering effective healthcare to prisoners, and innovative technologies such as telemedicine offer a promising means of achieving this goal.

title: A Brief History of Long-Term Potentiation
text: Since the groundbreaking discovery of long-term potentiation (LTP) in 1973, a vast number of scientific papers have been published on this captivating phenomenon, which serves as a fascinating cellular model for learning and memory. Although LTP has undergone significant growing pains over the years, it has finally reached adulthood. In this review, the rich history of LTP is explored. It is an exciting time, and the pace of discovery is nothing short of remarkable.

title: Tumor-Induced IL-6 Reprograms Host Metabolism to Suppress Anti-tumor Immunity
text: In patients with cancer, the wasting syndrome known as cachexia is characterized by caloric deficiency. Our study reveals that tumors induce alterations in the host's metabolic response to caloric deficiency, leading to intratumoral immune suppression. We used pre-cachectic mice with transplanted colorectal cancer or autochthonous pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) to explore how tumor-induced IL-6 affects the hepatic ketogenic potential. We found that IL-6 reduces the hepatic ketogenic potential by suppressing PPARalpha, the transcriptional master regulator of ketogenesis. When these mice were subjected to caloric deficiency, the resulting relative hypoketonemia triggered a significant increase in glucocorticoid levels. This hormonal stress response suppressed multiple intratumoral immune pathways. Moreover, we discovered that elevating plasma corticosterone to a level lower than that observed in cachectic mice abolished the response of mouse PDA to an immunotherapy currently in clinical trials. Our findings indicate that tumor-induced IL-6 impairs the ketogenic response to caloric deficiency, leading to a systemic metabolic stress response that hinders anti-cancer immunotherapy.

title: Chaperoning stem cells: a role for heat shock proteins in the modulation of stem cell self-renewal and differentiation?
text: Stem cell self-renewal and differentiation are highly regulated processes, with intrinsic and extrinsic signals playing a crucial role in their control. Molecular chaperones, including heat shock proteins (Hsp), are ubiquitous molecules that modulate protein conformational and complexation states. While the function of Hsp is well understood in differentiated cells, their role in stem cells is less clear. Interestingly, embryonic stem cells have been found to exhibit enhanced stress tolerance and elevated chaperone expression. This review provides a critical evaluation of stem cell research from a molecular chaperone perspective, and proposes a model of chaperone-mediated self-renewal in mouse embryonic stem cells.

title: How much alcohol and how often? Population based case-control study of alcohol consumption and risk of a major coronary event.
text: Objective: To investigate the relationship between the quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and the risk of acute myocardial infarction and coronary death. Design: Case-control study. Setting: Lower Hunter region of New South Wales, Australia, between 1983 and 1994. Subjects: Men and women aged 35-69 years. Main Outcome Measure: Acute myocardial infarction or coronary death. Results: A comparison of alcohol consumption patterns between 11,511 cases of acute myocardial infarction or coronary death and 6077 controls randomly selected from the same study population revealed that men and women who consumed one or two drinks of alcohol on five or six days a week had a lower risk of a major coronary event compared to non-drinkers, after adjusting for the effects of age, smoking, and medical history. This reduction in risk was also seen after excluding non-drinkers who were formerly moderate to heavy drinkers. Additionally, a protective effect of alcohol consumption was found for regular drinkers who consumed one or two drinks in the 24 hours preceding the onset of symptoms. Conclusions: The frequency and quantity of alcohol consumption are significant predictors of the risk of a major coronary event, with the lowest risk found among men and women who consume one to four drinks daily on five or six days a week and among women who consume one or two drinks daily on five or six days a week.

title: Tracking adipogenesis during white adipose tissue development, expansion and regeneration
text: White adipose tissue exhibits remarkable plasticity, and we have developed a novel system to inducibly and permanently label mature adipocytes, which we refer to as the AdipoChaser mouse. Through this system, we have monitored adipogenesis during development, high-fat diet (HFD) feeding, and cold exposure. Interestingly, during cold-induced "browning" of subcutaneous fat, the majority of "beige" adipocytes arise from de novo-differentiated adipocytes. In contrast, epididymal fat exhibits adipogenesis after 4 weeks of HFD feeding, while subcutaneous fat undergoes hypertrophy for a period of up to 12 weeks. Furthermore, gonadal fat develops postnatally, whereas subcutaneous fat develops between embryonic days 14 and 18. Our findings highlight the significant differences in adipogenic potential among various fat depots.

title: Blockade of adrenoreceptors inhibits the splenic response to stroke.
text:
Recent research has highlighted the role of the peripheral immune system in the delayed cellular degeneration that occurs after a stroke. In the permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model of stroke, the spleen experiences a reduction in size. This decrease is caused by the release of immune cells from the spleen. When systemically treating mice with human umbilical cord blood cells (HUCBC) 24 hours after a stroke, the reduction in spleen size is blocked, while the infarct volume is significantly reduced. Splenectomy (removal of the spleen) two weeks before MCAO also reduces infarct volume, suggesting that the spleen plays a detrimental role in stroke-induced neurodegeneration.
After MCAO, the sympathetic nervous system is activated, leading to increased levels of catecholamines in both the spleen and the circulation. These catecholamines bind to alpha and beta adrenoreceptors in the spleen. The current study investigated whether catecholamines regulate the spleen's response to stroke. Male Sprague-Dawley rats were either denervated (had their splenic nerves removed) two weeks before MCAO or received injections of carvedilol (a pan adrenergic receptor blocker), prazosin (an alpha1 receptor blocker), or propranolol (a beta receptor blocker). Denervation did not affect infarct volume or spleen size. Propranolol treatment had no effect on these outcomes, but treatment with either prazosin or carvedilol prevented the reduction in spleen size. However, only carvedilol significantly reduced infarct volume (p < 0.05). These results suggest that circulating catecholamines regulate the spleen's response to stroke through the activation of both alpha and beta adrenergic receptors.

title: Effects of Thiazolidinediones on Stroke Recovery: A Case-Matched Controlled Study
text: Anti-inflammatory therapy reduces the size of an infarction and enhances stroke recovery. Thiazolidinedione peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)gamma agonists have potent anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitizing effects against diabetes. In a study of 30 stroke patients with type 2 diabetes receiving inpatient rehabilitation, those treated with pioglitazone or rosiglitazone showed significantly greater improvement in functional independence measure (FIMTM) scores compared to a control group (25.6 ± 10.2 SD vs. 19.8 ± 10.5, respectively, P = 0.015). There were no significant differences in rehabilitation hospital stay (24.2 ± 7.6 vs. 25.1 ± 7.4 days, P = 0.657) or final discharge destination (home/institution, 19/11 vs. 17/13, P = 0.792) between the two groups. The use of thiazolidinediones was associated with improved functional recovery in stroke patients with type 2 diabetes.

title: Crosstalk between tumor and endothelial cells promotes tumor angiogenesis by MAPK activation of Notch signaling.
text: Progress has been made in understanding the induction of tumor vasculature by secreted angiogenic factors, but little is known about contact-dependent signals that promote tumor angiogenesis. In this study, we investigate the role of Notch ligand Jagged1 in promoting angiogenesis in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) cells. We found that Jagged1 expression in HNSCC cells triggered Notch activation in nearby endothelial cells (ECs) and promoted capillary-like sprout formation. Our results show that Jagged1-expressing HNSCC cells significantly enhance neovascularization and tumor growth in vivo. Furthermore, we found a strong correlation between Jagged1 expression and tumor blood vessel content, and a significant association with HNSCC development. Our findings reveal a novel mechanism by which the direct interaction between tumor cells and ECs promotes angiogenesis through the MAPK and Notch signaling pathways.

title: A Sequential splicing mechanism promotes selection of an optimal exon by repositioning a downstream 5' splice site in preprotachykinin pre-mRNA.
text:
To investigate the molecular basis of alternative splicing, we analyzed the splicing patterns of pre-mRNAs containing an optional exon, E4, from the preprotachykinin gene. This gene encodes multiple tachykinin peptides through alternative splicing of a single pre-mRNA. Our findings revealed that the skipping of E4 is the primary mechanism of alternative splicing in this gene, with a secondary mechanism involving the incorporation of E4 into the final spliced RNA.
To determine the structural changes that promote IVS3 splicing, we investigated the effects of various mutations on splicing activity. We found that a 2-nucleotide substitution at the 5' splice site of E4, changing it to an exact consensus match, GUAAGU, was the most significant mutation in restoring splicing activity. Interestingly, we also found that a 15-nucleotide segment of IVS5 containing GUAAGU, when inserted into a splicing-defective mutant, could recover splicing activity. However, additional sequences in IVS5 were not effective in promoting splicing. Additionally, we observed that the 72-nucleotide L2 exon of adenovirus, without its associated 5' splice site, could activate splicing when juxtaposed to E4.
Our findings suggest that RNA structural changes play a critical role in regulating alternative splicing. The RNA structures of these exons and introns interact in a specific manner, leading to the activation or inhibition of splicing. By understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying alternative splicing, we can gain insights into the regulation of gene expression and its role in various diseases and developmental processes.

title: Melatonin and the circadian regulation of sleep initiation, consolidation, structure, and the sleep EEG.
text: The endogenous melatonin rhythm, controlled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, displays a close association with the endogenous circadian components of sleep propensity and EEG oscillations, such as slow waves and sleep spindles, even when the sleep-wake cycle is desynchronized from the melatonin rhythm. Administering melatonin during the day enhances daytime sleep propensity, as evidenced by shorter sleep onset latency and consolidation. The EEG during daytime sleep following melatonin administration shows features similar to those of nocturnal sleep EEG, including increased sleep spindle activity and reduced slow-wave sleep. Higher doses of melatonin (5 mg or more) prior to nocturnal sleep lead to increased REM sleep. These findings demonstrate that melatonin impacts the primary characteristics of human sleep, including latency to sleep onset, sleep consolidation, slow waves, sleep spindles, and REM sleep. Further studies using physiological doses and delivery systems that generate physiological plasma melatonin profiles are needed to conclusively establish the role of the endogenous melatonin rhythm in the circadian regulation of sleep.

title: Long-term survival, quality of life, and quality-adjusted life-years among critically ill elderly patients.
text:
Objective: To evaluate mortality, quality of life (QOL), and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) in critically ill elderly patients.
Design: Cross-sectional survey.
Setting: Ten-bed medical-surgical intensive care unit (ICU) in a tertiary care university hospital.
Patients: A total of 882 elderly patients (ages 65 and above) and 1,827 controls (ages below 65) were studied during the period of 1995 to 2000.
Intervention: None.
Measurements and Main Results: Mortality was assessed during ICU and hospital stays, as well as 12, 24, and 36 months after ICU discharge. The 3-year cumulative mortality rate among the elderly (57%) was significantly higher than that among controls (40%). Most elderly nonsurvivors died within one month after discharge from the ICU. Day-1 Sequential Organ Failure (SOFA) scores of 15 or higher among elderly patients were associated with a high risk of mortality during the ICU stay. QOL was evaluated using EQ-5D and RAND-36 measures from 10 months to 7 years after discharge. The majority of elderly survivors (88%) reported good or satisfactory health state, and 66% found it to be similar or better than 12 months earlier. Elderly respondents had lower QALYs (21-35%) compared to the mean QALY minus 2 standard deviation units of the age- and gender-adjusted general population.
Conclusion: While high age alone does not justify refusing intensive care, the benefits perceived by intensive care seem to decrease with aging, if reflected as QALYs. However, 97% of elderly survivors lived at home, and 88% of them considered their QOL satisfactory or good after hospital discharge, highlighting the need for more reliable information on the outcome for the elderly.

title: Recent developments and complexities in neutrophil transmigration.
text:
REVIEW OBJECTIVE: Neutrophil migration from the blood to inflamed tissues is a crucial component of innate immunity and a key factor in the development of inflammatory diseases. As this area of leukocyte biology continues to evolve, this review aims to summarize recent findings and highlight the mechanisms underlying neutrophil transmigration.
RECENT FINDINGS: This review will focus on the prerequisites for neutrophil migration, including leukocyte crawling and changes in leukocytes and endothelial cells. Advances in both paracellular and transcellular neutrophil migration through endothelial cells will be discussed, along with the roles and regulation of endothelial cell adhesion molecules. Additionally, the migration of neutrophils through the vascular pericyte coverage and basement membrane will be reviewed.
SUMMARY: The significance of neutrophils in inflammatory diseases highlights the importance of understanding the mechanisms that mediate their migration. A better understanding of these mechanisms may lead to the development of more targeted anti-inflammatory interventions.

title: Exploring the epidemiological characteristics of cancers of unknown primary site in an Australian population: implications for research and clinical care.
text:
Investigating Incidence, Mortality, and Survival Trends of Cancer of Unknown Primary Site (CUP): Clinical Implications
Objective: To explore the incidence, mortality, and survival patterns of cancer of unknown primary site (CUP) in South Australia and examine clinical implications.
Methodology: The study used data from the South Australian Cancer Registry to calculate age-standardized incidence and mortality rates from 1977 to 2004. Disease-specific survival, socio-demographic, histological, and secular predictors of CUP compared to cancers of known primary site and histological types were investigated using multivariable logistic regression.
Results: The study found that incidence and mortality rates for CUP increased by approximately 60% between 1977-80 and 1981-84, with rates peaking in 1993-96. Male to female incidence and mortality rate ratios approximated 1.3:1. Incidence and mortality rates increased with age, and the odds of unspecified histological type were higher for males than females, non-metropolitan residents, low socio-economic areas, and for the period 1977-88 compared to subsequent diagnostic periods. CUP represented a higher proportion of cancers in Indigenous patients. Case survival was 7% at 10 years from diagnosis, with older age, male sex, Indigenous status, lower socio-economic status, and unspecified histology type being predictive of lower case survival.
Conclusion: The study highlights the poor prognosis for CUP, with a modest improvement in survival. The findings identify elevated risk groups for CUP and poorer treatment outcomes, emphasizing the need for increased research and clinical attention in these populations.

title: Alkylating agent melphalan augments the efficacy of adoptive immunotherapy using tumor-specific CD4+ T cells.
text:
In recent years, the immune-enhancing properties of certain chemotherapeutic drugs have gained increasing recognition. This has led to the exploration of combining conventional chemotherapy with immunotherapeutic strategies to achieve long-lasting therapeutic benefits. Previous studies have suggested that melphalan, an alkylating agent commonly used to treat multiple myeloma, has immunomodulatory effects. However, the specific mechanisms underlying these effects are not well understood. In this study, we investigated the impact of melphalan on endogenous immune cells and adoptively transferred tumor-specific CD4+ T cells in tumor-bearing mice.
Our results showed that melphalan treatment resulted in a quick burst of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines during the cellular recovery phase after melphalan-induced myelodepletion and leukodepletion. Following melphalan treatment, tumor cells exhibited characteristics of immunogenic cell death, including the translocation of the endoplasmic reticulum-resident calreticulin to the cell surface and the extracellular release of high-mobility group box 1. Additionally, there was enhanced tumor antigen uptake by dendritic cells in the tumor-draining lymph node. Consistent with these immunomodulatory effects, melphalan treatment of tumor-bearing mice led to the activation of endogenous CD8+ T cells and, more importantly, effectively drove the clonal expansion and effector differentiation of adoptively transferred tumor-specific CD4+ T cells. Interestingly, the combination of melphalan and CD4+ T cell adoptive cell therapy was more effective in prolonging the survival of mice with advanced B cell lymphomas or colorectal tumors compared to either treatment alone. These findings provide insight into melphalan's immunostimulatory effects and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of combining melphalan with adoptive cell therapy using antitumor CD4+ T cells.

title: Influence of cigarette smoking on inhaled corticosteroid treatment in mild asthma.
text:
BACKGROUND: Although inhaled corticosteroids are commonly used to treat asthma, there is limited research on how cigarette smoking affects their effectiveness. Our study aimed to investigate the impact of smoking on the response to inhaled corticosteroid treatment in patients with mild asthma.
METHODS: We conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 38 adult asthma patients, including 21 non-smokers. The patients were randomly assigned to receive either inhaled fluticasone propionate (1000 microg/day) or a placebo for 3 weeks. We measured the patients' responses to treatment using peak expiratory flow (PEF) readings, spirometric parameters, bronchial hyperreactivity, and sputum eosinophil counts. We compared the responses between non-smokers and smokers.
RESULTS: Our results showed that non-smokers had a significantly greater increase in mean morning PEF following inhaled fluticasone (27 l/min compared to -5 l/min in smokers). Non-smokers also had statistically significant improvements in mean morning PEF (27 l/min), forced expiratory volume in 1 second (0.17 l), and geometric mean PC20 (2.6 doubling doses), as well as a significant decrease in the proportion of sputum eosinophils (-1.75%) compared to the placebo group. In contrast, smoking asthmatic patients did not show significant changes in any of these parameters.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that active cigarette smoking impairs the efficacy of short-term inhaled corticosteroid treatment in mild asthma. This has important implications for the management of patients with mild asthma who smoke.

title: Hitting the target: emerging technologies in the search for kinase substrates.
text: Protein kinases can modify their targets' activity, localization, protein association, and stability through phosphorylation. Despite the significance in understanding cellular biology, identifying bona fide substrates of specific protein kinases has been a slow process. Traditional methods, including genetics, yeast two-hybrid screens, and biochemical purification, have been time-consuming and unreliable. However, recent advancements have emerged, such as screening for phosphorylation of proteins from phage expression libraries, peptide library screens to determine optimal motifs preferred by specific kinases, the use of phospho-motif antibodies, and an approach that uses structurally altered kinases and allele-specific adenosine triphosphate analogs and kinase inhibitors. These methods have shown promise in identifying genuine in vivo substrates of certain protein kinases. We discuss the advantages and limitations of these approaches.

title: Histone phosphorylation: a chromatin modification involved in diverse nuclear events.
text: Histone posttranslational modifications are central to various chromatin-related processes, acting as signals for the recruitment, assembly, or retention of chromatin-associated factors. The most well-known function of histone phosphorylation is its role in cellular responses to DNA damage, where phosphorylated histone H2A(X) demarcates large chromatin domains near DNA breaks. However, multiple studies have also shown that histone phosphorylation plays a crucial role in various other chromatin-associated processes, including chromatin remodeling linked to other nuclear events. This review aims to summarize the current understanding of histone phosphorylation and describe the various kinases and phosphatases that regulate it, as well as its key roles in DNA repair, transcription, chromatin compaction during cell division and apoptosis, and the intricate crosstalk between phosphorylation and other histone modifications that enables sophisticated control over chromatin remodeling processes.

title: Neurodevelopmental Outcome After a Single Course of Antenatal Steroids in Children Born Preterm: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
text:
Objective: To systematically review and integrate data on the neurodevelopmental outcome of children after administration of a single course of antenatal corticosteroids for threatened preterm labor.
Data Sources: Medline, Scopus, CENTRAL, and www.clinicaltrials.gov (inception to August 2014) using combinations of the terms "prenatal," "antenatal," "cortico*," "*steroid*," "betamethasone," "dexamethasone," "neurodevelopment*," "*development*," and "follow-up."
Methods of Study Selection: We included randomized and nonrandomized trials reporting on the neurodevelopmental outcomes of children whose mothers were administered a single course of betamethasone or dexamethasone antenatally for threatened preterm birth as opposed to placebo or no treatment.
Results: Summary risk ratio (RR) was calculated for dichotomous data; standardized mean difference was calculated for trials that measured the same outcome but used different methods. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I statistic. Sensitivity and subgroup analyses were planned according to study design, specific steroid, and mean gestational age at birth. A single course of antenatal corticosteroids was associated with reduced risk for cerebral palsy (seven studies; treated: 390 of 5,199, untreated: 146 of 1,379; RR 0.678, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.564-0.815), psychomotor development index less than 70 (two studies; treated: 783 of 3,049, untreated: 258 of 969; RR 0.829, 95% CI 0.737-0.933), and severe disability (five studies; treated: 1,567 of 4,840, untreated: 475 of 1,211; RR 0.787, 95% CI 0.729-0.850). Steroid treatment increased the rates of intact survival (six studies; treated: 1,082 of 2,013, untreated: 273 of 561; RR 1.186, 95% CI 1.056-1.332). Betamethasone was found to significantly decrease the risk for severe disability and increase the rate of intact survival. Dexamethasone increased the rate of intact survival; however, data for dexametasone and the other planned subgroup analyses were limited (fewer than 1,000 children at most). The major limitations involved inclusion of nonrandomized studies and scarcity of data on finer neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Conclusion: A single course of antenatal corticosteroids in women at high risk for preterm birth appears to improve most neurodevelopmental outcomes in offspring born before 34 weeks of gestation.

title: Prognostic impact of minimal pleural effusion in non-small-cell lung cancer.
text: Purpose: Minimal pleural effusion (PE) in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) may signify an early stage of malignant PE, but its clinical significance has rarely been investigated. This study aimed to assess the proportion of minimal PE in NSCLC patients and its impact on survival. Methods: Based on chest computed tomography scans at diagnosis, 2,061 patients were classified into three groups: no PE, minimal PE, and malignant PE. Variables associated with four factors - patient, stage migration, tumor, and treatment - were investigated for correlation with survival. Results: Minimal PE was present in 272 patients (13.2%), with a median survival time of 7.7 months compared to 17.7 months for patients without PE. Minimal PE was significantly associated with worse survival after adjusting for all variables (hazard ratio, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.21-1.62). The prognostic impact of minimal PE was higher in early-stage disease (Pinteraction = .001). In patients with minimal PE, pleural invasion or attachment was observed in 87.8% of cases, and it was an independent factor predicting worse survival (P = .03). Conclusion: Minimal PE is a commonly encountered prognostic factor in NSCLC, especially in early-stage disease. Its presence is associated with worse survival, emphasizing the need for further investigation into its accumulation mechanisms.

title: Fusion proteins for versatile antigen targeting to cell surface receptors reveal differential capacity to prime immune responses.
text: Targeting proteins to antigen-presenting cells (APCs) is a strategic approach to eliciting adaptive immune responses. However, the connection between the chosen target receptor and the quality and quantity of the resulting responses remains poorly understood. We present a strategy for expressing antigens, including hydrophobic proteins, as soluble fusion proteins that are optimized for proteasome-dependent major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I-restricted cross-presentation and form stable complexes with a wide range of targeting antibodies. Upon subcutaneous immunization, these complexes were initially taken up by CD169+ lymph node subcapsular sinus macrophages. In the ovalbumin (OVA) model system, receptor-targeted antigenic complexes primed specific T and B cell responses in vitro and in vivo at least 100-fold more efficiently than antigen alone. A comparison of 10 targeting receptors allowed us to establish a ranking regarding the priming of CD8+ T cell responses and demonstrated striking differences in the relative efficacy of CD8+ and CD4+ T cell subset and B cell priming. The described fusion proteins should facilitate the development of optimized strategies for targeted delivery of protein antigens in the context of tolerization or vaccination.

title: A sequential model for peptide binding and transport by the transporters associated with antigen processing.
text: TAP proteins facilitate the translocation of antigenic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Investigations into the specificity of this process have been hindered by non-TAP-dependent factors that influence the amount of peptide accumulation in the ER during transport assays. To overcome this obstacle, we have developed an overexpression system that allows us to separately quantify binding of peptides to the TAP substrate-binding site and peptide transport by TAP. Our results show that the efficiency of peptide accumulation in the ER parallels the affinity of the peptide for the TAP substrate-binding site, but can be influenced by interactions with the glycosylation system within the ER and, likely, peptide efflux. Interestingly, random peptide mixtures of 9-16 amino acids exhibit significantly higher affinity for the binding site compared to shorter or longer peptides. Additionally, we observed that peptides bind to TAP heteromers in the absence of ATP and are released upon binding of ATP, suggesting a model for TAP function.

title: Outcome of repeated radiosurgery for recurrent metastatic brain tumors.
text:
Objective: We investigated the outcomes of repeat Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKS) for local or distant recurrence after initial radiosurgery.
Methods: A retrospective analysis of 204 patients who underwent GKS was conducted. Of these, 43 patients (21%) received GKS more than once, with 16 patients experiencing recurrence at the previously treated site, 13 with new lesions at remote sites, and 14 with both local recurrence and new lesions.
Results: The median survival from the initial GKS was 36 weeks in all patients and 68 weeks in patients who underwent repeated GKS. The median time from the first GKS to the second was 37 weeks. The median survival from the second radiosurgical intervention was 32 weeks. At 6 months after salvage GKS, the local control rate was 90.7%. The prognostic factor of Radiation Propagation Analysis (RPA) class was the most dominant factor in both initial and salvage GKS.
Conclusion: Recurrence is common after initial radiosurgery for metastatic brain tumors. The survival time and local control rate after salvage GKS are comparable to those after initial radiosurgery. GKS as a salvage treatment may provide additional survival benefit in select patients.

title: Human CYP3A4 and murine Cyp3A11 are regulated by equol and genistein via the pregnane X receptor in a species-specific manner.
text: The pregnane X receptor (PXR) plays a crucial role in the body's adaptive defense system, tasked with eliminating various noxious xenobiotics. PXR activation by both endogenous and exogenous chemicals, including steroids, antibiotics, bile acids, and herbal compounds, leads to the induction of drug metabolism. In this study, we investigated the ability of isoflavones, specifically genistein, daidzein, and the metabolite equol, to activate human and mouse PXR in vitro and in vivo. Using cell-based transient transfection assays and primary hepatocytes, we found that isoflavones, particularly genistein, effectively activated full-length, wild-type mouse PXR, while equol displayed greater potency in activating human PXR. Additionally, we observed that isoflavones induced recruitment of the coactivator steroid receptor coactivator 1 to PXR through a mammalian 2-hybrid assay. Treatment of human hepatocytes with equol resulted in increased expression of Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) mRNA and immunoreactive protein, while treatment of wild-type, but not PXR(-/-) mouse hepatocytes, led to the induction of Cytochrome P450 3A11 (Cyp3A11) mRNA. In contrast, equol had no effect on Cyp3A11 mRNA in vivo. These findings demonstrate a species-specific difference in the activation of PXR by isoflavones, with equol displaying greater potency in human PXR.

title: Metabolism of glucose, glutamine, long-chain fatty acids and ketone bodies by murine macrophages.
text:
In this study, the enzymatic activities of key metabolic enzymes were examined in both elicited macrophages of mice and rat lymph node lymphocytes. The results revealed some interesting differences in metabolic pathways between these two cell types.
Firstly, the activity of hexokinase in macrophages was found to be much higher than in any other major tissue in the body, indicating that glucose is a major source of energy for these cells. Additionally, the activity of hexokinase was higher than that of phosphorylase or 6-phosphofructokinase, suggesting that glucose utilization is more important than glycogen synthesis in macrophages.
Furthermore, the study showed that the rate of glucose utilization by resting macrophages incubated in vitro was significantly lower than the activity of 6-phosphofructokinase, suggesting that glucose metabolism is highly activated during phagocytosis or increased secretory activity.
In contrast, lymphocytes had lower activities of citrate synthase and oxoglutarate dehydrogenase compared to macrophages, indicating that the tricarboxylic acid cycle may play a less important role in energy generation in these cells. Additionally, the activity of 3-oxoacid CoA-transferase was higher in macrophages, but that of 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase was significantly lower in macrophages compared to lymphocytes.
Interestingly, the activity of carnitine palmitoyltransferase was higher in macrophages, suggesting that both acetoacetate and fatty acids can contribute to the tricarboxylic acid cycle as acetyl-CoA substrates. However, no detectable rate of acetoacetate or 3-hydroxybutyrate utilization was observed during incubation of resting macrophages, but the rate of oleate utilization was found to be 1.0 nmol/h per mg of protein or about 2.2% of the activity of palmitoyltransferase.
Finally, the activity of glutaminase was found to be about 4-fold higher in macrophages compared to lymphocytes, suggesting that the rate of glutamine utilization may be very high in these cells. The rate of glutamine utilization by resting incubated macrophages was found to be similar to that reported for rat lymphocytes, but was significantly lower than the activity of glutaminase. Overall, these findings highlight the unique metabolic characteristics of macrophages compared to other immune cells.

title: TGF-beta inhibition of endothelial cell proliferation: alteration of EGF binding and EGF-induced growth-regulatory (competence) gene expression.
text:
Here's a possible revision of the text:
Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) impedes the proliferation of endothelial cells derived from various sources, including human umbilical vein, bovine aorta, and rat heart. Prolonged exposure to TGF-beta also leads to notable changes in the morphology of rat heart endothelial cells, indicating senescence. These changes are accompanied by a reduction in the number of high-affinity receptors for epidermal growth factor (EGF), with minimal impact on total receptor counts. Moreover, TGF-beta treatment decreases the expression of specific competence genes (c-myc, JE, KC) induced by EGF, while the induction of c-fos gene expression by EGF remains unchanged. These findings suggest that growth inhibitors like TGF-beta may modulate the cell's response to growth-stimulatory factors.

title: Human NK cells in acute myeloid leukaemia patients: analysis of NK cell-activating receptors and their ligands
text: NK cell activation is tightly regulated to maintain healthy cells while eliminating malignant ones. NK cells have multiple receptors on their surface that determine whether they are activated to kill target cells. In this study, we found decreased expression of NKp46, NKp30, DNAM-1, CD244, and CD94/NKG2C activating receptors on NK cells from acute myeloid leukaemia patients. This reduction might be caused by chronic exposure to ligands on leukaemic blasts. The study also showed that leukaemic blasts from most patients express ligands for NK cell-activating receptors, with DNAM-1 ligands being frequently expressed and NKG2D ligand MICA/B expressed in half of the patients, while CD48, a ligand for CD244, was expressed in only a quarter of the patients. The diminished expression of NK cell-activating receptors and/or the heterogeneous expression of ligands on leukaemic blasts may impair NK cell-mediated immunosurveillance, leading to inadequate tumour recognition and elimination. A deeper understanding of the activating receptor repertoire on NK cells and their ligands on blasts, along with the possibility to modulate their expression, could open new avenues for NK cell-based immunotherapy against leukaemia.

title: Production of interleukin-6 in contracting human skeletal muscles can account for the exercise-induced increase in plasma interleukin-6.
text:
1. Exercise increases plasma levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6), and previous studies have shown that contracting muscles can produce IL-6. The aim of the current study was to determine whether the IL-6 produced by contracting skeletal muscle accounts for the accumulation of IL-6 in the blood during exercise.
2. Six healthy male participants performed a 5-hour one-legged dynamic knee extensor exercise at 25 watts, which represents 40% of peak power output (Wmax). Arterial-femoral venous (a-fv) differences in IL-6 concentrations between the exercising and resting legs were measured before and every hour during the exercise. Leg blood flow was also measured using ultrasound Doppler technique. IL-6 levels were analyzed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).
3. Arterial plasma concentrations of IL-6 increased 19-fold compared to rest. The a-fv difference in IL-6 over the exercising leg followed the same pattern as the net IL-6 release. In contrast, there was no significant a-fv difference or net IL-6 release in the resting leg. The muscle generated 2.5 kg of active muscle during the last 2 hours of exercise, leading to a median IL-6 production of 6.8 ng min-1 (kg active muscle)-1 (range, 3.96-9.69 ng min-1 kg-1) over this period.
4. During the last 2 hours of exercise, the net IL-6 release from the muscle was 17-fold higher than the elevation in arterial IL-6 concentration, and at 5 hours of exercise, the net release during 1 min was half of the IL-6 content in the plasma. This suggests that there is a high turnover of IL-6 during muscular exercise, which may play a crucial role in maintaining glucose homeostasis during prolonged exercise. These findings suggest that IL-6 produced by skeletal contracting muscle contributes to the maintenance of glucose homeostasis during prolonged exercise.

title: Symptoms of hypoglycemia in children with IDDM.
text:
Objective: To investigate the symptoms of hypoglycemia in children with insulin-dependent diabetes from both the child's and parents' perspectives, and to compare the symptom reporting of diabetic children with that of adult diabetic patients.
Research Design and Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 100 parents and 43 of their children to gather information on the frequency and intensity of hypoglycemia symptoms. The data was analyzed using Principal Components Analysis (PCA) to identify distinct subgroups of hypoglycemia-related symptoms.
Results: The study found that diabetic children and their parents had similar agreement on the relative frequency and intensity of hypoglycemia symptoms reported. PCA analysis revealed that both children and parents identified the same two distinct subgroups of hypoglycemia-related symptoms: behavioral disturbance and autonomic-neuroglycopenic subgroups.
Conclusions: These findings suggest that hypoglycemic symptoms in children with diabetes are distinct from those experienced by adults, with behavioral changes being the primary features of low blood glucose levels. These observations have important implications for parental education on hypoglycemia.

title: Comparative Protein Structure Modeling Using MODELLER.
text: Comparative protein structure modeling is a technique used to predict the three-dimensional structure of a target protein based on its alignment to one or more known protein structures (templates). The prediction process involves fold assignment, target-template alignment, model building, and model evaluation. This unit provides an overview of how to use the MODELLER software to generate comparative models and how to utilize the ModBase database of models. The process is demonstrated through the example of modeling lactate dehydrogenase from Trichomonas vaginalis (TvLDH). Additionally, the text covers common errors in comparative modeling and some of the potential applications of this technique. © 2016 John Wiley & Sons, Inc.

title: IL-6 as a keystone cytokine in health and disease
text: Interleukin 6 (IL-6) has far-reaching effects on the immune system and other cell types, exhibiting hormone-like characteristics that influence homeostasis. IL-6 displays both pro- and anti-inflammatory properties depending on the context, making it a prime target for clinical intervention. However, the complex signaling pathway regulating IL-6 activity presents challenges for effective intervention. Clinical experience with IL-6 antagonists has raised questions about when and how to block this cytokine to improve disease outcomes and patient wellbeing. This review examines the impact of IL-6 on both innate and adaptive immunity and the potential advantages of various IL-6 antagonists. Moreover, insights into the immunobiology of IL-6 will inform clinical decisions regarding the use of these antagonists.

title: Chaperoning 5S RNA assembly.
text:
In eukaryotic cells, three of the four ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs)—5.8S, 18S, and 25S/28S—are derived from a single pre-rRNA transcript and are assembled into ribosomes. The fourth rRNA, 5S, is transcribed by RNA polymerase III and forms a separate 5S ribonucleoprotein particle (RNP) containing ribosomal proteins Rpl5/uL18 and Rpl11/uL5. In mammals, the 5S RNP plays a key role in regulating the homeostasis of the tumor suppressor p53. In yeast or humans, a specialized complex composed of Rpf2 and Rrs1 is responsible for the nucleolar localization of the 5S RNP and its incorporation into pre-ribosomes.
Our study focuses on the structural and functional characterization of the Rpf2-Rrs1 complex, as well as its interactions with the 5S RNA and other ribosomal components. We discovered a unique 5S RNA E-loop-binding module in the Rpf2-Rrs1 complex that interacts with the Rpl5 protein and also contacts the ribosome assembly factor Rsa4 and the 25S RNA. We propose that the Rpf2-Rrs1 complex establishes a network of interactions that guide the incorporation of the 5S RNP into pre-ribosomes in their initial conformation before they rotate to form the central protuberance in the mature large ribosomal subunit.

title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and neutrophil infiltration: role of cigarette smoke and cyclooxygenase products.
text: Cigarette smoke is the primary cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), leading to airway inflammation. Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) is produced within human airways and exhibits both pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory activities. We measured PGE2 concentrations in induced sputum supernatants from different groups of subjects and correlated the values with neutrophil infiltration and the expression of cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2). Cigarette smoke extract (CSE) was used to evaluate the effect of smoking on COX-2 and PGE2 receptor expression as well as on PGE2 release in neutrophils and alveolar macrophages (AM) obtained from normal donors. The effects of PGE2 and PGE receptor agonists and antagonists were investigated on neutrophil adhesion to a human bronchial epithelial cell line (16HBE). We found significantly higher levels of PGE2, COX-2 expression, and neutrophil infiltration in normal smokers and COPD smokers compared to controls and former COPD smokers (P < 0.0001). Induced sputum supernatant caused neutrophil adhesion to 16HBE, which was significantly reduced by PGE2 immunoprecipitation in COPD smokers. In vitro experiments revealed that CSE increased PGE2 release and COX-2 and PGE2 receptor expression in neutrophils and AM, and PGE2 enhanced neutrophil adhesion to 16HBE. A specific E-prostanoid 4 (EP4) receptor antagonist blunted the effect of PGE2. These findings suggest that CSE promotes the induction of COX-2 and contributes to the pro-inflammatory effects of PGE2 in the airways of COPD patients.

title: Non-receptor tyrosine kinase Etk is involved in the apoptosis of small cell lung cancer cells.
text: The study aimed to investigate the role of epithelial and endothelial tyrosine kinase (Etk), also known as Bmx, in the apoptosis of small cell lung cancer (SCLC) cells. The study analyzed the expression levels of Etk in 171 lung cancer specimens, including 71 SCLCs and 100 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cases, using immunostaining. The study also used a parental SCLC cell line (H446) and its Etk-overexpressing subline (H446-Etk) to study the role of Etk in apoptosis induced by doxorubicin. The results showed that high expression of Etk occurred in 74.6% of SCLC cases, but only in 40% of NSCLC cases. The expression levels of Bcl-2, Bcl-X(L), and p53 were analyzed in relation to Etk expression, and it was found that the levels of Bcl-2 and Bcl-X(L) increased significantly in H446-Etk cells compared to H446 cells after doxorubicin treatment, and were positively associated with Etk expression. However, p53 did not correspond with Etk expression, despite a significant decrease in p53 expression with apoptosis in both H446-Etk and H446 cells. After doxorubicin treatment, the cell viability was significantly higher in H446-Etk cells than in parental H446 cells. Lastly, downregulation of Etk using siRNA sensitized H446 cells to doxorubicin-induced apoptosis. The study suggests that upregulation of Etk may be a new mechanism involved in protecting SCLC cells from apoptosis, with Bcl-2 and Bcl-X(L) but not p53 contributing to doxorubicin-induced apoptosis through the Etk pathway.

title: No Pasaran! Role of the axon initial segment in the regulation of protein transport and the maintenance of axonal identity.
text: The transmission of information in the brain relies heavily on the intricate organization of neurons, which is supported by various cellular transport processes. One key component of this architecture is the axon initial segment (AIS), which acts as a central hub for the transmission of signals. The AIS plays a crucial role in both the initiation of action potentials and the regulation of axonal arborization. Through years of research, the main components of the AIS and their interactions have been progressively uncovered, as well as their role in assembly and maintenance. Two mechanisms have been identified that contribute to the regulation of protein transport at the AIS: a surface diffusion barrier and an intracellular traffic filter. However, a more detailed understanding of these processes is still required. Given the recent discoveries regarding the structure of the AIS cytoskeleton, this lecture will explore how a better understanding of the AIS architecture can shed light on its role in regulating protein transport and maintaining axonal identity.

title: The effectiveness of right heart catheterization in the initial care of critically ill patients. SUPPORT Investigators.
text:
Objective: To investigate the association between the use of right heart catheterization (RHC) in the first 24 hours of intensive care unit (ICU) admission and subsequent survival, resource utilization, and clinical outcomes.
Methods: A prospective cohort study was conducted at five US teaching hospitals between 1989 and 1994, including 5735 critically ill adult patients. The main outcomes were survival time, cost of care, intensity of care, and length of stay in the ICU and hospital, obtained from clinical records and the National Death Index. A propensity score was constructed using multivariable logistic regression to adjust for treatment selection bias. Case-matching and multivariable regression modeling techniques were used to estimate the association of RHC with specific outcomes after adjusting for the propensity score. Sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the potential impact of unidentified or missing covariates on the results.
Results: After adjusting for treatment selection bias, RHC was associated with increased 30-day mortality (odds ratio, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.03-1.49). The mean cost per hospital stay was higher ($49 300 vs $35 700) and length of stay in the ICU was longer (14.8 vs 13.0 days) with RHC. Subgroup analysis did not reveal any patient group or site for which RHC was associated with improved outcomes. Patients with higher baseline probability of surviving 2 months had the highest relative risk of death following RHC. Sensitivity analysis suggested that a missing covariate would need to increase the risk of death 6-fold and the risk of RHC 6-fold for a true beneficial effect of RHC to be misrepresented as harmful.
Conclusion: In this observational study, after adjusting for treatment selection bias, RHC was associated with increased mortality and resource utilization. The results of this analysis suggest that the apparent lack of benefit of RHC may be due to treatment selection bias. Confirmation of these findings in other observational studies is necessary, and a randomized controlled trial of RHC may guide patient selection for such a study.

title: Natural history of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and approaches to therapy
text: After cell-to-cell transmission, HTLV-I increases its viral genome through de novo infection and the proliferation of infected cells. In vivo, infected cells are selected by the host's immune system, the genetic and epigenetic environment of proviral integration sites, and other factors during the carrier state. In leukemic cells, Tax gene expression is frequently impaired by genetic and epigenetic mechanisms, allowing ATL cells to evade the host immune system. On the other hand, ATL cells acquire the ability to proliferate without Tax through intracellular genetic and epigenetic changes. Despite advances in supportive care and the development of novel treatment agents, the prognosis for ATLL remains poor. Various therapies, including interferon-α plus zidovudine, intensive chemotherapy, and allogenic stem cell transplantation, have shown improvement in prognosis compared to cyclophosphamide, vestibulotoxin, and prednisolone (CHOP). However, the comparison of different therapeutic approaches is complex due to the varying natural history of ATLL, enrollment of naïve-to-therapy, refractory or relapsed patients, and inconsistent reporting of outcome. Moreover, results from small proof-of-principle studies have not been extended to randomized, controlled trials. Therefore, large, multicenter, international randomized controlled trials are necessary to establish the value of each treatment approach and to avoid further patient suffering.

title: Hierarchical organization of the plasma membrane: investigations by single-molecule tracking vs. fluorescence correlation spectroscopy.
text: Through the use of single-molecule tracking and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) in living cells, groundbreaking observations have been made, providing a novel understanding of molecular diffusion, interaction, and signal transduction in the plasma membrane. It is evident that the plasma membrane is a complex entity, consisting of diverse structures on nanoscale to mesoscale dimensions (2-200 nm) with varying lifetimes, where some membrane molecules temporarily bind together. The dynamic interactions between molecules occur in the time-dependent, inhomogeneous two-dimensional liquid environment of the plasma membrane, which may be a crucial factor in plasma membrane function.

title: Stability of the antimalarial drug dihydroartemisinin under physiologically relevant conditions: implications for clinical treatment and pharmacokinetic and in vitro assays.
text: Artemisinins are highly unstable antimalarial drugs that degrade quickly in the presence of iron, heme, or biological reducing agents. Despite being well-documented, the impact of this instability on their chemical stability and antimalarial activity under diverse in vitro and clinical conditions has received less attention. To fill this knowledge gap, we focused on dihydroartemisinin (DHA), the primary metabolite of other artemisinins, and investigated its behavior in different buffer solutions, plasma, and erythrocyte lysate at various temperatures and pH levels. We evaluated the residual antimalarial activity of DHA using a chemosensitivity assay against Plasmodium falciparum and measured its degradation using high-performance liquid chromatography with electrochemical detection. To examine the role of Fe(II)-heme, we blocked its reactivity with carbon monoxide (CO). Our results showed a significant reduction in DHA's antimalarial activity after incubation in plasma and to a lesser extent in erythrocyte lysate, with activity Halving after 3 hours and almost complete abolition after 24 hours. Similar trends were observed in serum-enriched media, with temperature and pH having a pronounced impact on DHA stability and decomposition. These findings underscore the importance of carefully controlling experimental conditions in in vitro studies, as subtle differences in storage and handling can significantly affect artemisinin stability and efficacy. Disorders such as fever, hemolysis, or acidosis common in malaria patients may contribute to the instability of these drugs and reduce their clinical efficacy.

title: Modulation of anxiety through blockade of anandamide hydrolysis
text: Cannabis contains a psychoactive compound called Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol, which interacts with CB1 cannabinoid receptors in the human brain, producing subjective responses. This suggests that endogenous cannabinoids, such as anandamide, may play a role in regulating emotions. However, the erratic effects of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol complicate the interpretation of these findings and limit the therapeutic potential of direct cannabinoid agonists. A potential solution is to create drugs that enhance the effects of endogenous cannabinoids by preventing their breakdown. Here, we describe a class of potent, selective, and systemically active inhibitors of fatty acid amide hydrolase, the enzyme responsible for degrading anandamide. Similarly to commonly used anti-anxiety drugs, these inhibitors display benzodiazepine-like properties in the elevated zero-maze test and reduce isolation-induced vocalizations in rats. These effects are accompanied by increased brain levels of anandamide and are blocked by CB1 receptor inhibition. Our findings suggest that anandamide is involved in modulating emotional states and that inhibition of fatty acid amide hydrolase may provide a novel approach to anti-anxiety therapy.

title: Familial clustering of reflux symptoms
text: Our study aimed to investigate the prevalence of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) symptoms and medication use among first-degree relatives of patients with known GERD. We conducted a postal questionnaire survey of 418 subjects, including relatives of six groups of patients with different GERD-related conditions. Our findings showed that while infrequent GERD symptoms were equally common among all groups of relatives, frequent symptoms were more common among relatives of patients with abnormal pH studies and/or low lower esophageal sphincter (LOS) pressure. Specifically, 26% of relatives of patients with an abnormal pH study and normal LOS pressure, and 27% of relatives of patients with an abnormal pH study and low LOS pressure, reported frequent GERD symptoms, compared to 9% of relatives of nondyspeptic patients. Similarly, 30% of relatives of patients with Barrett's esophagus reported frequent GERD symptoms, compared to 16% of relatives of patients with a normal pH study and 18% of relatives of patients with a peptic stricture. Our results suggest that there is a familial clustering of GERD symptoms in individuals with GERD and increased esophageal acid exposure, as well as in individuals with Barrett's esophagus.

title: Histone chaperones: 30 years from isolation to elucidation of the mechanisms of nucleosome assembly and disassembly
text: Over three decades have passed since the discovery of nucleosomes in 1974 and the first isolation of a histone chaperone in 1978. Despite the isolation and functional analysis of various types of histone chaperones, the fundamental processes of nucleosome assembly and disassembly have been relatively understudied.Recently, the tertiary structure of a hetero-trimeric complex composed of the histone chaperone CIA/ASF1 and the histone H3-H4 dimer was determined and it was proposed that this complex serves as an intermediate in nucleosome assembly and disassembly reactions. Additionally, CIA was shown biochemically to dissociate the histone (H3-H4)2 tetramer into two histone H3-H4 dimers, implying that CIA regulates the semi-conservative replication of nucleosomes. Our aim is to provide a comprehensive overview of prominent histone chaperones and elucidate the mechanisms that preserve and modify epigenetic information.
