Most prescriptions were written by non-specialists, and the majority of patients were prescribed conventional antipsychotics. Patients who received second-generation antipsychotics were more likely to receive continuous antipsychotic therapy. In addition, many patients received polypharmacy treatments, including comedication for somatic illnesses. Specifically, drugs for the treatment of cardiovascular and metabolic disorders were frequently co-prescribed. Given the majority of antipsychotics are used for disorders other than schizophrenia, it is essential to increase awareness among non-specialists about the drug's indications, efficacy, and side effects. These physicians account for the majority of antipsychotic prescriptions, emphasizing the significance of their knowledge and actions.

title: Structural basis for the activation of microtubule assembly by the EB1 and p150Glued complex.
text: Plus-end tracking proteins, such as EB1 and the dynein/dynactin complex, regulate microtubule dynamics. These proteins are thought to stabilize microtubules by forming a plus-end complex at the growing ends of microtubules with poorly understood mechanisms. In this study, we present the crystal structure of two components of the plus-end complex, the carboxy-terminal dimerization domain of EB1 and the microtubule binding (CAP-Gly) domain of the dynactin subunit p150Glued. Each molecule of the EB1 dimer contains two helices that form a conserved four-helix bundle, while also providing binding sites for p150Glued in its flexible tail region. By combining crystallography, NMR, and mutational analysis, our findings reveal the key interactions between EB1 and p150Glued, which are essential for their function in regulating microtubule polymerization. Additionally, our results show that removing the flexible tail from EB1 enhances its ability to promote microtubule assembly, suggesting that this region negatively regulates EB1 activity. Based on these findings, we propose that EB1 adopts an auto-inhibited conformation, which is relieved by p150Glued as an allosteric activator.

title: Epigenetic regulation of NANOG by miR-302 cluster-MBD2 completes induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming.
text: The majority of somatic cells undergoing induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell reprogramming with Yamanaka factors remain in a stable, partially reprogrammed state, with the underlying molecular mechanisms still unknown. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play a crucial role in mRNA translation and are implicated in the reprogramming process, although the identified miRNA functional targets critical for complete iPS cell reprogramming remain elusive. We beschreyder methyl-DNA binding domain protein 2 (MBD2) as an epigenetic suppressor that inhibits the full reprogramming of somatic cells to iPS cells through direct binding to the NANOG promoter elements, thereby preventing transcriptional activation. By overexpressing the miR-302 cluster, we observed a significant increase in the conversion of partial to fully reprogrammed iPS cells, leading to increased NANOG expression. Our studies provide a direct molecular mechanism involved in achieving a fully reprogrammed iPS cell state in partially reprogrammed cells, which can be used to study disease pathogenesis, drug screening, and potential cell-based therapies.

title: Complex physiology and compound stress responses during fermentation of alkali-pretreated corn stover hydrolysate by an Escherichia coli ethanologen.
text: The physiology of ethanologenic Escherichia coli grown anaerobically in alkali-pretreated plant hydrolysates is not well understood, despite its potential as a sustainable source of ethanol. To investigate how E. coli responds to such hydrolysates, we studied the growth and metabolism of E. coli K-12 ethanologen fermenting a corn stover hydrolysate pretreated with ammonia fiber expansion. Although the hydrolysate contained a high sugar content (approximately 6% glucose and 3% xylose) and relatively low toxicity, E. coli growth ceased before glucose was depleted. However, the cells remained metabolically active and continued converting glucose to ethanol until all glucose was consumed. Gene expression profiling revealed complex and changing patterns of metabolic physiology and cellular stress responses during different phases of growth, including an exponential growth phase, a transition phase, and a stationary phase. During these phases, high cell maintenance and stress response costs were partially mitigated by available free amino acids in the hydrolysate. However, after most amino acids were depleted, the cells entered stationary phase, and ATP derived from glucose fermentation was entirely consumed by cell maintenance in the hydrolysate. Comparative gene expression profiling and metabolic modeling of the ethanologen suggested that the high energetic cost of mitigating osmotic, lignotoxin, and ethanol stress collectively limits growth, sugar utilization rates, and ethanol yields in alkali-pretreated lignocellulosic hydrolysates.

title: Systemic arterial hypertension in children following renal transplantation: prevalence and risk factors.
text:
Background: Proper management of blood pressure (BP) after renal transplantation can improve allograft and patient survival. This study aimed to investigate the distribution of BP and the prevalence of hypertension in children after kidney transplantation, as well as identify clinical and center-specific factors associated with hypertension.
Methods: A retrospective case note review was conducted on all pediatric kidney transplant recipients in the UK, with data collected at 6 months, 1, 2, and 5 years post-transplantation. Hypertensive subjects were defined as those with systolic and/or diastolic BP > 95th percentile. Risk factors and center-specific factors were evaluated using a multivariate model.
Results: Of the 428 patients included in the study, 27.3%, 27.6%, 26.0%, and 25.6% were hypertensive at 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, and 5 years post-transplantation, respectively. At 6 months and 1 year, 58.4% and 52.8% of patients were receiving anti-hypertensive therapy, respectively, with 31.6-36.6% remaining hypertensive. Multivariate analysis revealed that odds ratios for systolic hypertension were 4.16, 2.65, and 2.07 for deceased donor, lowest height z-score quartile, and being on anti-hypertensive medication, respectively. There was significant variation in prevalent rates of hypertension between centers (P < 0.0001), which remained significant after adjusting for other factors in the model (P = 0.003).
Conclusions: Control of BP after kidney transplantation in paediatric centers in the UK remains suboptimal, with over 25% of patients remaining hypertensive 5 years post-transplantation. Significant variations in prevalent rates of hypertension between centers may reflect differences in assessment and management of hypertension. Addressing these variations is crucial for improving BP control and promoting better allograft and patient outcomes.

title: Coupling cAMP signaling to transcription in the liver: pivotal role of CREB and CREM.
text: Transcription factors that bind to cAMP-responsive elements (CREs) in the promoters of various genes belong to the basic domain-leucine zipper superfamily and are composed of three genes in mammals: CREB, CREM, and ATF-1. These proteins are generated through post-transcriptional events such as alternative splicing and regulate gene expression as activators or repressors. Activation is triggered by signaling-dependent phosphorylation of a key acceptor site (Ser133 in CREB) by various kinases, including PKA, CamKIV, and Rsk-2, leading to the interaction with CBP (CREB-binding protein), a co-activator with histone acetyltransferase activity. Repression involves dynamic dephosphorylation of the activators, leading to decreased association with CBP. Another pathway of transcriptional repression on CRE sites involves the inducible repressor ICER (inducible cAMP early repressor), a product of the CREM gene. ICER is an inducible repressor involved in autoregulatory feedback loops of transcription that govern the down-regulation of early response genes, such as c-fos. The liver presents a remarkable setting where cAMP-responsive signaling plays a major role, with a finely tuned program of gene expression triggered by partial hepatectomy, leading to specific checkpoints coordinating a coordinated regeneration of the tissue. Temporal kinetics of transcriptional activation after hepatectomy reveal an early induction pattern for several genes, some of them controlled by the CREB/CREM transcription factors. The robust induction of ICER after partial hepatectomy suggests an important role of CREM in liver physiology, which is further confirmed by the delay in tissue regeneration in CREM-deficient mice. The study of the specific modification codes that histones display during liver regeneration and physiology will provide exciting new insights into the dynamics of chromatin architecture.

title: Comparison of dietary assessment methods in a Southern French population: use of weighed records, estimated-diet records and a food-frequency questionnaire
text:
Study Objective: Develop and validate dietary assessment instruments for the French Mediterranean region.
Methods: Recruited 150 male and female volunteers and administered three assessment methods - a 4-day weighed dietary record (PETRA), a 7-day estimated-diet record (S7) based on a checklist and set of photographs, and a semi-quantitative food-frequency questionnaire (FFQ) - to measure dietary intake. Correlated the results of these assessments to validate their accuracy.
Results: Validation was based on nutrients and foods. Energy-adjusted Pearson correlation coefficients between S4 (the portion of the S7 that coincided with the PETRA record) and PETRA ranged from 0.32 for vitamin E to 0.81 for vitamin C (mean: 0.65 for 21 nutrients). Spearman correlation coefficients ranged from 0.63 for fish and seafood to 0.90 for wine (mean: 0.76 for 16 food groups). There was minimal misclassification in the opposite extreme quartiles. De-attenuated energy-adjusted Pearson correlation coefficients between FFQ and S7 ranged from 0.22 for proteins and monounsaturated fatty acids to 0.80 for iron (mean: 0.45). Less than 10% of subjects were misclassified in the opposite extreme quartiles (except for vitamin C, 12%). Spearman correlation coefficients ranged from 0.25 for green-yellow-red raw vegetables to 0.76 for wine (mean: 0.42). Less than 10% of subjects were misclassified in the opposite extreme quartiles (except for citrus fruit, 11%).
Conclusion: The portion estimation using the set of photographs was validated by the correlation between S4 and PETRA for both nutrients and foods. The FFQ provides a reasonable measure of macronutrient intake and a good measure of micronutrient intake when compared to the literature, but performs less well for food intake. Improving the FFQ by using the set of photographs and adding more questions on under-represented foods can lead to better results.
Sponsorship: This work was financially supported by INSERM contract 91-1006 and the Ardèche and Hérault Committees of the ‘Ligue contre le cancer’.

title: Substrate fate in activated macrophages: a comparison between innate, classic, and alternative activation.
text:
Macrophages play a crucial role in both innate and adaptive immunity, with their activation depending on the balance of signaling pathways. From a functional standpoint, macrophage stimulation can be divided into three main modes: innate, classic, and alternative pathways. These different activations lead to the expression of specific sets of genes involved in the release of pro- or anti-inflammatory stimuli. In this study, we investigated whether specific metabolic patterns depend on the signaling pathway activated.
To achieve this, we employed a [1,2-(13)C(2)]glucose tracer-based metabolomics approach to characterize the metabolic flux distributions in macrophages stimulated through the classic, innate, and alternative pathways. By combining this methodology with mass isotopomer distribution analysis of the newly formed metabolites, our data showed that activated macrophages are primarily glycolytic cells, with a clear distinction between the classic/innate activation and the alternative pathway. Notably, macrophage activation through LPS/IFN-gamma or TLR-2, -3, -4, and -9 results in similar metabolic flux patterns regardless of the pathway activated. However, stimulation through the alternative pathway has limited metabolic effects.
The underlying reason for these differences lies in the switch in the expression of 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase (PFK2) from the liver-type PFK2 to the more active ubiquitous PFK2 isoenzyme, which is triggered by Hif-1alpha activation and leads to increased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate concentration and glycolytic flux. Interestingly, this switch occurs in LPS/IFN-gamma-activated macrophages as well, suggesting that this pathway regulates ubiquitous PFK2 expression through Hif-1alpha-independent mechanisms.
In summary, our findings reveal that macrophage activation through different signaling pathways leads to distinct metabolic responses, highlighting the importance of understanding these differences in immune cell function and dysfunction.

title: The effect of folic acid supplementation on plasma homocysteine in an elderly population.
text:
BACKGROUND Elevated levels of plasma homocysteine are associated with an increased risk of coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, and venous thrombosis. Folic acid has been shown to be the most effective treatment for reducing homocysteine levels. However, the lowest effective dose of folic acid is not well understood, particularly in elderly individuals who are at the highest risk of these conditions.
AIM To investigate the effects of different daily doses of folic acid supplementation (0, 50, 100, 200, 400, and 600 microg) on plasma homocysteine levels in an elderly population.
DESIGN A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
METHODS Participants aged 65-75 years (n=368) were randomly assigned to receive one of the treatments for 6 weeks. Plasma homocysteine levels were measured after 3 and 6 weeks of supplementation.
RESULTS Only the 400 microg and 600 microg groups had significantly lower homocysteine levels compared to the placebo group (p=0.038 and p<0.001, respectively). Using multiple linear regression and each individual's total folic acid intake (diet plus supplement), it was estimated that a total daily folic acid intake of 926 microg per day would be required to ensure that 95% of the elderly population is free of cardiovascular risk due to folate deficiency.
DISCUSSION Achieving a total daily folic acid intake of 926 microg through diet alone is unlikely, and supplementation or fortification of food with folic acid may be necessary to reach this target.

title: Central obesity and hyperinsulinaemia in women are associated with polymorphism in the 5' flanking region of the human insulin gene.
text:
Obesity is a complex disease with a significant genetic component. The distribution of body fat is not uniform, with distinct patterns in the upper and lower body. While the total amount of body fat has a stronger genetic influence, the distribution of fat within the body displays a stronger heritable tendency. Central obesity, characterized by hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance, is associated with non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and atherosclerosis.
To investigate the molecular genetics of central obesity, we analyzed 56 severely obese (mean body mass index of 40), unrelated British Caucasian young women for associations between genetic variants and anthropometric measurements, insulin secretion, and insulin resistance. We examined the insulin receptor, insulin-sensitive glucose transporter, and insulin genes. We found an association between a specific variant of the insulin gene (class 3 allele in the 5' flanking region) and upper body obesity (P = 0.005). This variant was also associated with increased fasting hyperinsulinemia (P = 0.01), enhanced insulin secretion during stimulation (P = 0.01), and impaired insulin sensitivity as measured by the homeostatic model assessment (HOMA; P = 0.008). No such associations were observed with the other genes studied.
These findings suggest that genetic variations in the 5' flanking region of the insulin gene may affect the expression of the gene and influence insulin production in severely obese female subjects.

title: Population density profiles of nasopharyngeal carriage of 5 bacterial species in pre-school children measured using quantitative PCR offer potential insights into the dynamics of transmission.
text: Bacterial vaccines have the potential to reduce the rates of bacterial carriage in the nasopharynx. Typically, the colonization of bacteria in this region is a binary outcome. Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) can accurately measure the quantity of bacterial DNA present in mucosal samples over a wide range. By using culture and single-gene, species-specific qPCR assays for Streptococcus pneumoniae (lytA), Streptococcus pyogenes (ntpC), Moraxella catarrhalis (ompJ), Haemophilus influenzae (hdp), and Staphylococcus aureus (nuc), and standard curves generated against log-phase reference strain broth cultures, we investigated the frequency and peak density distributions of carriage in nasopharyngeal swabs from 161 healthy 2-4-year-old children. The results showed consistent detection between qPCR and culture methods, with most discordance occurring at lower detection thresholds of both methods. The abundance of bacterial DNA in carriage samples varied across five to seven orders of magnitude, with the most abundant species skewed towards high values (modes: S. pneumoniae log3-4, M. catarrhalis and H. influenzae log4-5 CFU/ml broth). The wide range of bacterial DNA concentrations in healthy children carrying these bacteria may indicate that different individuals at different times vary greatly in infectiousness. Understanding the factors that determine colonization density, including the host, microbial, and environmental factors, will allow for more accurate predictions of the effectiveness of vaccines.

title: Circadian mechanisms in murine and human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells following dexamethasone exposure.
text: A group of key regulatory factors control the circadian rhythms in mammalian cells. While the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the brain acts as the central circadian oscillator, circadian clocks are also found in peripheral tissues and cells. Recent research has shown that over 20% of expressed genes in bone and adipose tissues exhibit a circadian pattern of expression. This study investigates the core circadian transcriptional machinery in primary cultures of murine and human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs). Exposure to dexamethasone synchronized the oscillatory expression of genes encoding the albumin D binding protein (dbp), brain-muscle arnt-like 1 (bmal1), period 3 (per3), rev-erb alpha (Rev A), and Rev B. The genes exhibited a mean oscillatory period of 22.2 to 24.3 hours. The peak expression of genes encoding "positive" (bmal1) and "negative" (per3) components of the circadian regulatory apparatus was out of phase with each other by approximately 8-12 hours, consistent with in vivo observations. In vivo, phosphorylation by glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK3β) regulates the turnover of per3 and components of the core circadian regulatory apparatus. In vitro addition of lithium chloride, a GSK3β inhibitor, significantly shifted the acrophase of all genes by 4.2-4.7 hours in BMSCs, although only male murine BMSCs displayed a significant increase in the length of the period of oscillation. We conclude that BMSCs provide a valid in vitro model for studying circadian mechanisms in bone metabolism and stem cell biology.

title: Herpesvirus-encoded GPCRs: neglected players in inflammatory and proliferative diseases?
text: Herpesviruses have incorporated membrane-bound G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) into their viral genomes, which are similar in structure to chemokine receptors. These GPCRs manipulate the host cell's natural signaling networks to support the virus's survival, replication, and disease progression. Specifically, the herpesvirus-encoded chemokine receptors ORF74, BILF1, and US28, found at sites of inflammation and in tumor cells, serve as uniquely vulnerable targets for targeted therapies. Given their high druggability, these viral GPCRs hold promise as antiviral drug targets.

title: Midbody accumulation through evasion of autophagy contributes to cellular reprogramming and tumorigenicity
text: The midbody is a singular organelle formed between daughter cells during cytokinesis, which is essential for their final separation. After division, midbodies persist in cells as midbody derivatives (MBds), but their fate remains unclear. Our study reveals that MBds are passed down asymmetrically to the daughter cell with the older centrosome. MBds are specifically accumulated in stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells, and potential cancer 'stem cells' both in vivo and in vitro. Interestingly, loss of MBds accompanies stem cell differentiation, which is mediated by the binding of the autophagic receptor NBR1 to the midbody protein CEP55. In contrast, differentiation and normal dividing cells do not accumulate MBds and possess high autophagic activity. Stem cells and cancer cells uniquely accumulate MBds by evading autophagosome encapsulation, showing low autophagic activity. MBd enrichment significantly enhances reprogramming to induced pluripotent stem cells and increases the in vitro tumorigenicity of cancer cells. These findings uncover previously unappreciated roles for MBds in stem cells and cancer 'stem cells'.

title: Integrated genomic analysis identifies clinically relevant subtypes of glioblastoma characterized by abnormalities in PDGFRA, IDH1, EGFR, and NF1.
text: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network has recently identified recurring genetic anomalies in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). We have developed a robust gene expression-based molecular classification system for GBM that distinguishes between Proneural, Neural, Classical, and Mesenchymal subtypes. By integrating multiple types of genomic data, we have identified patterns of somatic mutations and DNA copy number variations that are unique to each subtype. Specifically, mutations in EGFR, NF1, and PDGFRA/IDH1 define the Classical, Mesenchymal, and Proneural subtypes, respectively. Our findings reveal a close relationship between subtype and different neural lineages, and we have found that the response to aggressive therapy varies widely between subtypes, with the greatest benefit observed in the Classical subtype and none in the Proneural subtype. This framework provides a unified approach to molecular stratification of GBM, with important implications for future research.

title: Chronic Hepatitis B Infection: A Review
text: Approximately 240 million individuals globally are infected with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV), and 15-40% of untreated individuals with chronic HBV infection may develop cirrhosis, which can lead to liver failure and cancer. Fortunately, evidence suggests that treatment with pegylated interferon or nucleos(t)ide analogues (such as lamivudine, adefovir, entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil, and tenofovir alafenamide) can effectively suppress HBV DNA replication and improve liver inflammation and fibrosis. Long-term viral suppression has been shown to be associated with regression of liver fibrosis and a reduced risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in cohort studies. However, the cure rates after treatment remain low (ranging from 3-7% with pegylated interferon and 1-12% with nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy). Pegylated interferon therapy can be completed in 48 weeks without the development of resistance, but its use is limited by poor tolerability and adverse effects such as bone marrow suppression and exacerbation of existing neuropsychiatric symptoms like depression. Newer agents like entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil, and tenofovir alafenamide may offer a significantly lower risk of drug resistance compared to older agents like lamivudine and adefovir, and should thus be considered as first-line treatment. In conclusion, antiviral therapy with either pegylated interferon or a nucleos(t)ide analogue should be offered to patients with chronic HBV infection and liver inflammation in an effort to slow the progression of liver disease. Nucleos(t)ide analogues are therefore recommended as first-line therapy, as most patients will require indefinite treatment due to low cure rates.

title: CD64 expression distinguishes monocyte-derived and conventional dendritic cells and reveals their distinct role during intramuscular immunization.
text:
In this article, we delve into the world of dendritic cells (DCs) residing within skeletal muscles, shedding light on their mysterious nature. Although most vaccines are administered intramuscularly (i.m.), little is known about the DCs that inhabit these tissues. By employing a distinguishing marker, we distinguish between conventional DCs and monocyte-derived DCs (Mo-DCs) within muscles. We discover the distinct DC subsets present in skeletal muscles and their counterparts in draining lymph nodes (LNs). Our findings reveal the functional specialization of muscle DCs and the role of adjuvants in enhancing their migratory and functional behavior.
Using alum as an adjuvant, we demonstrate that i.m. administration of antigen (Ag) leads to the presence of large numbers of conventional DCs that belong to the CD8α+ and CD11b+ types. Both types of DCs can capture Ag and migrate to draining LNs, where they efficiently activate naive T cells. In contrast, Mo-DCs are as numerous as conventional DCs in alum-injected muscles, but only a small fraction migrates to draining LNs, indicating that alum itself has a limited capacity to induce Mo-DC migration. We identify that the addition of small amounts of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to alum enhances Mo-DC migration, which in turn amplifies the overall immunogenicity of Ag presented by muscle-derived DCs. This study highlights the importance of acknowledging the diverse migratory and functional behaviors of muscle DCs and Mo-DCs during i.m. vaccination, underscoring the need to understand the role of adjuvants in light of this heterogeneity.

title: T-cell-antigen recognition and the immunological synapse
text: Over the past five years, there has been considerable excitement in the field of T-cell recognition due to the discovery of the immunological synapse, a complex cellular structure that forms at the interface of a T cell and a cell expressing the appropriate peptide-MHC complexes. Advances in imaging technologies have enabled us to shed light on the role of cell surface molecules and the signaling modules they engage in during cell-to-cell communication. The pace of progress has been so rapid that T-cell recognition may become the first system in which the molecular basis of cell-cell recognition is fully understood.

title: Key interactions by conserved polar amino acids located at the transmembrane helical boundaries in Class B GPCRs modulate activation, effector specificity and biased signalling in the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor.
text:
Class B G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) have the potential to exhibit biased agonism in response to ligand stimulation, activating multiple signaling effectors. Our previous study identified key tale-surface (TM) domain polar amino acids crucial for the function of the GLP-1 receptor, a key therapeutic target for diabetes and obesity. This study combines mutagenesis, pharmacological characterization, molecular modeling, and computational analysis to identify additional highly conserved polar residues in Class B GPCRs that are important for GLP-1 receptor stability and signalling specificity.
We predict that:
(i) Positively charged residues (R3.30227, K4.64288, R5.40310) located at the extracellular boundaries of TMs 3, 4, and 5 stabilize extracellular loop 2, crucial for ligand affinity and receptor activation.
(ii) A predicted hydrogen bond network between residues in TMs 2 (R2.46176), 6 (R6.37348), and 7 (N7.61406 and E7.63408) at the cytoplasmic face of the receptor is important for stabilizing the inactive receptor and directing signalling specificity.
(iii) Residues at the bottom of TM 5 (R5.56326) and TM6 (K6.35346 and K6.40351) are crucial for receptor activation and downstream signalling.
(iv) Residues predicted to be involved in stabilization of TM4 (N2.52182 and Y3.52250) also influence cell signaling.
Overall, this work expands our understanding of peptide-mediated signalling by the GLP-1 receptor.

title: Influence of lifestyle modification on arterial stiffness and wave reflections.
text: Arterial stiffness and wave reflections have a significant impact on cardiovascular function and disease risk, and are associated with a higher mortality rate in patients with end-stage renal failure and essential hypertension. As a result, preventing and treating arterial stiffness is crucial. Given the recognition of arterial stiffening as a key precursor of cardiovascular disease (CVD), it is essential to understand the role of lifestyle modifications in preventing and reversing arterial stiffening. While available evidence suggests that lifestyle modifications, such as aerobic exercise and sodium restriction, are clinically effective interventions for preventing and treating arterial stiffening, more research is needed to fully understand their utility in managing this condition. Therefore, lifestyle modifications should be considered as a first-line therapeutic approach for arterial stiffening, but further investigation is needed to optimize their use.

title: Effect of exercise-induced ischemia on QT interval dispersion.
text: Increased dispersion of the duration of ventricular repolarization (QT dispersion) is associated with increased vulnerability to arrhythmias. This study aimed to investigate the effect of exercise on QT dispersion in patients with ischemic heart disease (IHD). QT dispersion, corrected QT dispersion, and percentage change in uncorrected and corrected QT dispersion between rest and peak exercise were measured in 14 members of a control group, 17 patients with IHD, and 14 patients with IHD taking beta-blockers (IHD-B). All subjects underwent a standard Bruce protocol exercise test, and QT intervals were measured at rest and peak exercise using a digitizing tablet interfaced to a personal computer. QT dispersion at rest was significantly increased in the IHD group compared to the control and IHD-B groups, respectively (corrected QT dispersion in milliseconds: 74 +/- 7, 40 +/- 4, 49 +/- 5, p < 0.03). The corrected QT dispersion at peak exercise was higher in the IHD group compared to the control group (57 +/- 5 vs 26 +/- 3 msec, p < 0.03). Additionally, the percentage change in QT dispersion with exercise was significantly higher in the IHD group (52% +/- 5%) compared to the control group (28% +/- 4%, p < 0.002) and the IHD-B group (30% +/- 3%, p < 0.01). These findings suggest that a larger mean QT dispersion at peak exercise and an increased percentage change in QT dispersion with exercise may contribute to the increased susceptibility of the IHD group for arrhythmias. The cardioprotective effects of beta-blockers may be explained by their ability to blunt exercise-related changes in QT dispersion.

title: Effects of powered mobility on self-initiated behaviors of very young children with locomotor disability.
text: This research study examines the impact of powered mobility on the spontaneous behavior of six children with diverse disabilities, aged 23-38 months, who learned to use motorized wheelchairs in under three weeks. Using a multiple baseline design, two-hour observation periods were video-recorded at 10-day intervals before and after they achieved independent mobility. The study analyzed the frequency of self-initiated interactions with objects, spatial exploration, and communication with caregivers.Results showed that three children exhibited increased behavior in all three areas, while one child increased in two categories but decreased in interactions with objects. Moreover, two children displayed increased spatial exploration only.

title: BCR/ABL modifies the kinetics and fidelity of DNA double-strand breaks repair in hematopoietic cells.
text: The oncogenic BCR/ABL tyrosine kinase promotes the repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). Upon gamma-irradiation, BCR/ABL-positive leukemia cells exhibit an increased number of DSBs compared to normal cells. These lesions are repaired in a time-dependent manner through the BCR/ABL-activated non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) followed by homologous recombination repair (HRR) mechanisms. However, mutations and large deletions were detected in HRR and NHEJ products, respectively, in BCR/ABL-positive leukemia cells. We suggest that unreliable repair of DSBs may contribute to genomic instability in Philadelphia chromosome-positive leukemias.

title: Bone morphogenetic protein signaling in nephron progenitor cells
text: Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling is crucial in multiple stages of kidney development and significantly impacts the outcome of kidney injury. Additionally, BMP treatment is a vital component of protocols for differentiating nephron progenitors from pluripotent stem cells. This review examines the role of BMP signaling in influencing nephron progenitor cells in each of these contexts.

title: Computational analysis of 3'-ends of ESTs shows four classes of alternative polyadenylation in human, mouse, and rat.
text: Alternative initiation, splicing, and polyadenylation are crucial mechanisms employed by many organisms to generate diversity among mature mRNA transcripts derived from the same transcription unit. While previous computational analyses of alternative polyadenylation have primarily focused on polyadenylation activities within or downstream of the standard 3'-terminal exons, our study presents a genome-wide analysis of patterns of alternative polyadenylation in the human, mouse, and rat genomes across the entire transcribed regions of mRNAs using 3'-ESTs with aligned poly(A) tails to genomic sequences. Our analysis reveals four distinct classes of patterns of alternative polyadenylation: tandem poly(A) sites, composite exons, hidden exons, and truncated exons. Based on our findings, we estimate that at least 49% (human), 31% (mouse), and 28% (rat) of polyadenylated transcription units exhibit alternative polyadenylation. Moreover, a portion of these alternative polyadenylation events result in the generation of new protein isoforms.

title: Epigenetic instability in ES cells and cloned mice.
text: Cloning through nuclear transfer (NT) is a less efficient process, resulting in the death of most clones before birth and surviving individuals often exhibiting growth abnormalities. In an effort to investigate the relationship between gene expression and survival, as well as fetal overgrowth, we examined imprinted gene expression in both cloned mice and their embryonic stem (ES) cell donor populations. Our findings revealed that the epigenetic state of the ES cell genome is highly unstable, and variation in imprinted gene expression was observed in most cloned mice, even those derived from the same subclone of ES cells. Notably, many of these animals survived to adulthood despite widespread epigenetic abnormalities in their genomes, suggesting that mammalian development may be surprisingly resilient to genome-wide epigenetic alterations. These data suggest that even seemingly normal cloned animals may harbor subtle abnormalities in gene expression.

title: Successful three-way kidney paired donation with cross-country live donor allograft transport.
text: Offering transplantation opportunities to patients with incompatible live donors through kidney paired donation (KPD) is seen as a crucial strategy in addressing the organ availability crisis. According to estimates, implementing a national KPD program in the United States could result in an additional 1000-2000 transplants per year. Most of these transplants could be performed within the participants' local or regional area, but patients with rare blood types or broad HLA sensitization may benefit from larger geographic matching. In this scenario, either patients or organs would need to travel to optimize the benefits of a national program. In this study, we report on how a triple KPD enabled a highly sensitized patient (PRA 96%) to receive a well-matched kidney from a live donor located on the opposite coast. The kidney was removed in San Francisco and transported to Baltimore for reperfusion 8 hours later. The patient experienced prompt function and, one year later, had a serum creatinine level of 1.1 mg/dl. This case serves as a model for addressing the challenges involved in implementing a comprehensive KPD program on a large scale in the United States.

title: Role of PACAP and VIP in astroglial functions.
text: Astrocytes account for a significant portion of the human brain's volume, comprising at least half. In addition to their supporting functions, astrocytes play key roles in regulating stem cell proliferation, synaptic plasticity, and neuroprotection. These cells are also involved in neuronal physiology, responding to neurotransmitters and neuropeptides, and releasing regulatory factors known as gliotransmitters. During development and adulthood, astrocytes express specific receptors for pancreatic and insulin-like peptides (PACAP and VIP), which modulate various astrocyte activities such as proliferation, plasticity, glycogen production, and biosynthesis of neurotrophic factors and gliotransmitters.

title: A subset of 26S proteasomes is activated at critically low ATP concentrations and contributes to myocardial injury during cold ischemia.
text: The mechanisms by which molecules contribute to myocardial injury during warm or cold ischemia are not well understood. Although proteasomes are thought to play a role in ischemia-reperfusion injury, their functions during the ischemic period are not well characterized. Since donor hearts are often exposed to prolonged global cold ischemia before transplantation, we investigated the role and regulation of the proteasome during cold ischemic storage of rat hearts in relation to myocardial ATP content. Our findings show that cardiac proteasome peptidase activity increases by 225% as myocardial ATP levels decrease during cold ischemic storage in University of Wisconsin solution for up to 48 hours. Adding a specific proteasome inhibitor to the solution inhibited proteasome activity in cardiac extracts, reduced edema formation, and preserved the ultrastructural integrity of cardiomyocytes. Using purified 20S/26S proteasome enzyme preparations, we found that this activation is attributed to a subset of 26S proteasomes that are stable at low ATP concentrations, and that ATP inhibits their activity. Maximal activation occurs at low ATP levels. These data suggest that proteasome activation is a pathophysiologically relevant mechanism of cold ischemic myocardial injury, and that a subset of 26S proteasomes may be a cell-destructive protease that is activated as ATP levels decline. Proteasome inhibition during cold ischemia preserves the ultrastructural integrity of cardiomyocytes.

title: Coping and satisfaction with growth hormone treatment among short-stature children.
text:
Children's ability to cope with a chronic medical condition requiring prolonged treatment serves as an indicator of the quality of treatment and its impact on their quality of life, as well as that of their parents. This study specifically looked at how well children with short stature (2 Standard Deviations or more below average for their age and gender) coped with growth hormone (GH) treatment for at least a year, and the factors that affected their ability to do so.
The study included 96 patients, with 53 being male, who were treated with daily injections at home for 12 to 66 months. The questionnaire used to assess their ability to cope and degree of satisfaction and compliance with treatment showed no significant differences between genders, the presence of an underlying disease, age at which treatment started, or duration of treatment. Despite the fact that the full impact of GH treatment on final height is still unknown, the study found high levels of satisfaction and compliance with treatment among the children.

title: Risk for breast cancer development determined by mammographic parenchymal pattern.
text:
A classification system for identifying women at risk of developing breast cancer based solely on the mammographic appearance of the breast parenchyma has been developed. This system categorized patients into four groups based on their mammography results, with each group having a distinct incidence of breast cancer development.
The study, conducted over a five-year period at Hutzel Hospital in Detroit, reviewed the mammograms of all women aged 30 or older. The average follow-up time was approximately 2.5 years. The four groups had incidence rates of breast cancer of 0.1, 0.4, 1.7, and 2.2, respectively.
The parenchymal patterns identified in the study are described in detail, along with criteria for their identification. This classification system can help healthcare providers to better assess and manage breast cancer risk for their patients.

title: Accurate coarse-grained modeling of red blood cells.
text: We establish a systematic coarse-graining technique for modeling red blood cells (RBCs) using insights from mean-field theory. Our three-dimensional RBC membrane model takes into account the bending energy, in-plane shear energy, and constraints of fixed surface area and fixed enclosed volume. The coarse-graining method is versatile and can be applied at various levels of coarse-graining without requiring any adjustable parameters. We investigate the sensitivity of the coarse-grained model and validate its behavior against both experimental data and dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) simulations of RBCs in different flow conditions, such as capillary and shear flows.

title: Mice deficient in CD4 T cells have only transiently diminished levels of IFN-gamma, yet succumb to tuberculosis.
text: CD4 T cells play a crucial role in protecting against Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. To investigate the mechanism of this protection, two mouse models lacking CD4 T cells were used. Transgenic mice lacking either MHC class II or CD4 molecules were found to be more susceptible to M. tuberculosis infection than wild-type mice, with MHC class II-deficient mice being more susceptible than CD4-deficient mice. However, the relative resistance of CD4-deficient mice was not attributed to an increased number of double-negative (CD4-8) T cells. Analysis of in vivo IFN-gamma production in the lungs of infected mice revealed that both mutant mouse strains were temporarily impaired in their ability to produce IFN-gamma following infection. By 2 weeks post-infection, IFN-gamma production in the mutant mice was reduced by over 50% compared to wild-type mice. However, by 4 weeks post-infection, both mutant and wild-type mice had similar levels of IFN-gamma mRNA and protein production. In CD4 T cell-deficient mice, IFN-gamma production was actually due to CD8 T cells, suggesting that early events in M. tuberculosis infection are critical determinants of the course of the infection. This study supports the hypothesis that CD4 T cells play an important role in protecting against M. tuberculosis infection early in the infection process.

title: Treatment and management of graft-versus-host disease: improving response and survival.
text: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) remains a significant clinical challenge following allogenic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, with ongoing research focusing on developing a standardized therapeutic strategy. Despite significant progress in understanding the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and risk factors for both acute and chronic forms of the disease, a uniform treatment approach is still lacking. Initial treatment with corticosteroids has shown good evidence, but the most effective management of steroid-refractory GVHD remains controversial, with current practices reliant on smaller studies and varying between institutions. Early diagnosis, multidisciplinary collaboration, and adequate supportive care, including infection prophylaxis, are crucial in improving outcomes for these patients. It is hoped that future systematic research efforts and the identification of new therapeutic targets will lead to improved treatment outcomes. This review aims to provide an overview of existing options for the management and treatment of acute and chronic GVHD.

title: The value of self-report assessment of adherence, rhinitis and smoking in relation to asthma control.
text: Objective: To investigate the utility of self-report measures of inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) adherence, degree of rhinitis, and smoking status in predicting asthma control. Methods: Patients prescribed ICS for asthma at 85 UK practices were asked to complete a validated questionnaire assessing asthma control (Asthma Control Questionnaire; ACQ) and adherence (Medication Adherence Report Scale). Additionally, patients were asked to report on their smoking status and the severity of their rhinitis using a two-item measure and a single-item measure, respectively. Complete anonymized questionnaires were analyzed, and associations between the variables were assessed using odds ratios and regression analysis. Results: Of 3916 participants, complete questionnaires were available for 3916. Poor asthma control (ACQ >1.5) was associated with reported rhinitis (OR = 4.62, 95% CI: 3.71-5.77), smoking (OR = 4.33, 95% CI: 3.58-5.23), and low adherence to ICS (OR = 1.35, 95% CI: 1.18-1.55). The degree of rhinitis was also found to be important, with those reporting severe rhinitis experiencing the worst asthma control, followed by those reporting mild rhinitis and then those reporting no rhinitis symptoms (F(2, 3913) = 128.7, p <.001). There was a relationship between the number of cigarettes smoked each day and asthma control (F(5, 655) = 6.08, p <.001). Conclusions: The study demonstrates that poor asthma control is associated with self-reported rhinitis, smoking, and low medication adherence. These potentially modifiable predictors of poor asthma control can be identified through a brief self-report questionnaire used routinely as part of an asthma review.

title: Development of a syngeneic mouse model for events related to ovarian cancer.
text: Mouse ovarian surface epithelial cells (MOSEC) were obtained from virgin, mature mice through mild trypsinization and were repeatedly passaged in vitro. Early passage cells (<20 passages) exhibited a cobblestone morphology and contact inhibition of growth. Following approximately 20 passages in vitro, cobblestone morphology and contact inhibition of growth were lost. Tumor forming potential was assessed by subcutaneously and intraperitoneally injecting early and late passage cells into athymic and syngeneic C57BL6 mice. Early passage MOSEC did not form tumors in vivo, while late passage MOSEC formed tumors in the subcutaneous and peritoneal cavities of mice, with a highly malignant neoplasm comprising both carcinomatous and sarcomatous components. Late passage MOSEC expressed cytokeratin and failed to respond to gonadotropin stimulation with ovarian steroid production in vitro. Ten clonal lines were established from late passage MOSEC, each of which formed multiple peritoneal tumors and ascitic fluid after intraperitoneal injection into C57BL6 mice. Cytogenetic analysis of three cell lines revealed that they were polyploid with near-tetraploid modal chromosome numbers, and common clonal chromosome gains and losses included +5, +15, +19, and -X, -3, -4. One cell line had a clonal translocation between chromosomes 15 and 18, while another had a small marker chromosome; however, common structural abnormalities were not observed. These data demonstrate the development of a mouse model for studying events relevant to ovarian cancer in humans. The ability of MOSEC to form extensive tumors within the peritoneal cavity, similar to those seen in patients with Stage III and IV cancer, and the ability to produce tumors in mice with intact immune systems, makes this model unique for investigating molecular and immune interactions in ovarian cancer development.

title: Hypoxia in cancer: significance and impact on clinical outcome
text:
Hypoxia, a defining feature of advanced solid tumors, holds a pivotal position in the tumor (patho-)physiome due to its potential to promote tumor progression and resistance to treatment. Hypoxia presents a "Janus face" in tumor biology, as it can lead to both restricted proliferation and differentiation, as well as aggressive tumor growth. Unlike standard prognostic factors such as tumor stage and lymph node involvement, hypoxia has been identified as an unfavorable prognostic indicator for patient outcome. Studies investigating tumor hypoxia using direct oxygenation assessment have shown poorer disease-free survival in patients with hypoxic cervical cancers or soft tissue sarcomas. In head and neck cancers, hypoxia has been shown to be prognostic for survival and local control.
However, technical limitations of direct oxygen sensing techniques have prompted the use of surrogate markers for tumor hypoxia, such as hypoxia-related endogenous proteins (e.g., HIF-1α, GLUT-1, CA IX) or exogenous bioreductive drugs. In many, but not all, studies, these markers have demonstrated prognostic significance for patient outcome. The prognostic value of exogenous markers, on the other hand, appears to be limited. Non-invasive assessment of hypoxia using imaging techniques such as PET or SPECT detection of radiolabeled tracers or MRI techniques (e.g., BOLD) may provide further insights into patient prognosis, although clinical experience with these methods is currently limited. Additionally, variations in treatment protocols, endpoint characterization, and methodological differences (e.g., different immunohistochemical staining procedures) may impact the power of the prognostic marker used.

title: Knowledge and Practice of Standard Precautions and Awareness Regarding Post-Exposure Prophylaxis for HIV among Interns of a Medical College in West Bengal, India.
text:
Study Objectives:
To evaluate the knowledge of interns regarding standard precautions and post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV, and identify any gaps between knowledge and practice in these areas. Additionally, the study aimed to determine the perceived barriers that hinder adherence to standard precautions among the interns.
Study Design:
A cross-sectional study was conducted among 130 interns of the 2010-2011 batch from a government-run medical college in Kolkata, India. A self-administered questionnaire was used to assess the interns' knowledge on basic components of standard precautions and post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV. The questionnaire also included open-ended questions to gather information on the reasons for non-adherence to standard precautions and any specific comments.
Results:
The study found that while the interns had good knowledge of personal protective equipment, hand washing, safe handling, and disposal of needles and sharp objects, they did not always practice these precautions effectively. The main reasons for non-adherence were difficulties in handling needles, wearing gloves, discomfort when wearing aprons, the inconvenience of frequent hand-washing, and the unavailability of equipment. Although the majority of respondents were aware of washing wounds with soap and water, around 32.3% were unaware that antiseptics could cause more damage. Only 63.8% of the respondents were aware of reporting any incidents of occupational exposure, and the knowledge on post-exposure prophylaxis regimens was found to be poor.
Conclusion:
The study revealed a significant gap between the interns' knowledge and practice of standard precautions, emphasizing the need for continuous on-site training, supportive supervision, and monitoring of their activities. The findings suggest that more efforts are required to address the barriers to adherence to standard precautions, particularly in the areas of hand washing and needle handling. The study highlights the importance of improving the knowledge and practice of standard precautions among healthcare professionals to prevent occupational exposure to HIV and other bloodborne pathogens.

title: Viruses and microRNAs
text: The discovery of RNA interference (RNAi) and cellular microRNAs (miRNAs) has revolutionized the field of biological research and revealed a previously unexplored level of post-transcriptional gene regulation. Recently,virally encoded miRNAs have been identified in several pathogenic human viruses, raising questions about their potential functions. I propose that these miRNAs may have played a significant role in shaping the evolution of viruses and continue to influence their in vivo tissue tropism. As our understanding of viral miRNA function grows, it may also provide new insights into how latent viral infections, such as herpesviruses, evade the host's immune system. Furthermore, research into viral miRNA function may lead to novel approaches for treating diseases caused by these viruses.

title: Economic impact of primary open-angle glaucoma in Australia.
text:
GLAUCOMA AS A LEADING CAUSE OF IRREVERSIBLE BLINDNESS: AN ECONOMIC PERSPECTIVE
Glaucoma, the world's leading cause of irreversible blindness, poses dire public health and economic consequences. To assess the economic impact of this condition, we conducted a comprehensive review of published randomized trials and population-based studies since 1985. Our study aimed to estimate the cost-effectiveness of interventions aimed at preventing vision loss from primary open-angle glaucoma, taking into account both financial costs (in Australian dollars) and disability-adjusted life years.
The prevalence of glaucoma in Australia is expected to increase significantly, from 208,000 cases in 2005 to 379,000 cases in 2025, as the population ages. This growth will result in increased health system costs, which are projected to rise from $AU355 million to $AU784 million over the same time period. The total costs of glaucoma, including indirect costs and losses in well-being, are estimated to increase from $AU1.9 billion to $AU4.3 billion in Australia by 2025.
Our findings highlight the substantial economic burden posed by primary open-angle glaucoma. This dynamic model provides a valuable tool for policymakers to better understand the ongoing economic impact of interventions aimed at preventing visual impairment and blindness from glaucoma. By continuously monitoring and analyzing the economic consequences of this condition, we can work towards improving the prevention and management of glaucoma, ultimately reducing its devastating impact on public health and the economy.

title: The LIM domain-containing homeo box gene Xlim-1 is expressed specifically in the organizer region of Xenopus gastrula embryos.
text: A newly discovered cysteine-rich motif, named LIM, has been found in the homeobox genes lin-11, Isl-1, and mec-3 in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans. We analyzed the relevant genes in Xenopus laevis and identified a closely related gene, Xlim-1. Xlim-1 mRNA is present in low amounts in the unfertilized egg, with a significant peak of expression during the gastrula stage, followed by a decrease, and then an increase during the tadpole stage. The brain shows the highest levels of Xlim-1 mRNA in adult tissues. The maternal and late expression phases of the Xlim-1 gene suggest that it plays multiple roles at distinct stages of the Xenopus life cycle. In the gastrula embryo, Xlim-1 mRNA is localized in the dorsal lip and the dorsal mesoderm, which is part of Spemann's organizer. Explant experiments showed that Xlim-1 mRNA is induced by the mesoderm-inducing factors activin A and retinoic acid, with the combination of both inducers leading to enhanced induction. The structure, inducibility, and localized expression in the organizer of the Xlim-1 gene suggest that it has a role in establishing body pattern during gastrulation.

title: Signal transduction proteins that associate with the platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) receptor mediate the PDGF-induced release of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase from permeabilized cells.
text:
In a study by Stanton et al. (1991), rat kidney cells were found to rapidly release glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) in response to peptide growth factors (Stanton, R.C., Seifter, J.L., Boxer, D.C., Zimmerman, E., and Cantley, L. C. (1991) J. Biol. Chem. 266, 12442-12448). To investigate the signal transduction pathways involved in G6PD release, two cell lines transfected with wild type or mutant platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) receptors (PDGFR) were studied using two permeabilization protocols. PDGF was found to significantly increase G6PD release in cells transfected with wild type PDGFR within 1 minute, while it failed to stimulate G6PD release in cells transfected with tyrosine kinase-deficient PDGFR. Similarly, PDGF did not stimulate G6PD release in cells transfected with partially autophosphorylation-deficient PDGFR, in which four known signaling proteins do not associate with the PDGFR. However, the PDGF-stimulated release of G6PD was partially restored in PDGFR mutants in which either phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase or phospholipase C gamma 1 could associate with the PDGFR. Moreover, the study found no basal or PDGF-stimulated phosphorylation of G6PD. The results indicate that:

1. release of G6PD requires intrinsic PDGFR tyrosine kinase activity.
2. release of G6PD requires PDGFR autophosphorylation.
3. release of G6PD is mediated by signaling proteins that associate with the PDGFR.
4. release of G6PD is not mediated by direct phosphorylation of G6PD.

In summary, the study demonstrates that the release of G6PD from rat kidney cells is mediated by signaling pathways involving the PDGF receptor, and that the activity of the tyrosine kinase of the PDGF receptor is essential for this process.

title: Microarrays for the study of viral gene expression during human cytomegalovirus latent infection.
text: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is one of the largest known DNA viruses, ubiquitously present in the human host. Following resolution of the primary, productive infection, HCMV persists in the host by establishing a lifelong latent infection in myeloid lineage cells, such as monocytes and their progenitors. The majority of adults with HCMV infection are asymptomatic, but the virus can cause neurological deficits in infants and remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in immunosuppressed individuals. Microarray-based studies have provided valuable insights into the genes that are transcriptionally active during both the productive and latent phases of HCMV infection. This chapter outlines the methodology for investigating genes in HCMV using microarrays, utilizing two cell types: productively infected human foreskin fibroblasts and latently infected primary human myeloid progenitor cells.

title: Physiological implications of hydrogen sulfide: a whiff exploration that blossomed.
text:
Over the centuries, the life-sustaining role of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) has evolved from microorganisms to plants, invertebrates, vertebrates, and finally to mammals. However, for centuries, H2S was only known for its toxicity and environmental hazards. Only over the past decade has its physiological significance been recognized. The discovery of endogenous H2S production in mammalian cells marked the beginning of this shift, and the identification of H2S as a gasotransmitter has led to a flurry of research on its various physiological functions.
H2S-producing enzymes are expressed in various systems, including the cardiovascular, nervous, immune, renal, respiratory, gastrointestinal, reproductive, liver, and endocrine systems. These enzymes play a crucial role in regular system function, which affects the release of H2S. Through its many molecular targets, such as ion channels and signaling proteins, H2S mediates various physiological functions.
Disruptions in H2S metabolism can lead to a wide range of diseases, including hypertension, atherosclerosis, heart failure, diabetes, cirrhosis, inflammation, sepsis, neurodegenerative diseases, erectile dysfunction, and asthma, among others. To address these problems, novel technologies for detecting endogenous H2S production have been developed, while novel H2S-based therapeutic compounds have been invented to treat diseases associated with abnormal H2S metabolism. While challenges still exist, research into the physiology and medicine of H2S is now entering an era of rapid exponential exploration.

title: TatC is a specificity determinant for protein secretion via the twin-arginine translocation pathway.
text: The recent discovery of a widespread translocation route, especially required for proteins bearing a twin-arginine motif in their signal peptide, has centered attention on its membrane-bound components, with TatC as a primary focus. Unlike most organisms whose genomes have been fully sequenced, the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis contains two tatC-like genes (tatCd and tatCy). The resulting TatCd and TatCy proteins may play a role in the transport of approximately 27 proteins boasting putative twin-arginine signal peptides, with around 6-14 of these proteins expected to be secreted into the growth medium. Using a proteomics-based approach, we found that PhoD of B. subtilis, a phosphodiesterase belonging to a novel protein family, gets secreted via the twin-arginine translocation pathway. Surprisingly, TatCd plays a pivotal role in the secretion of PhoD, whereas TatCy is not indispensable for this process. Therefore, TatC appears to function as a specificity determinant for protein secretion through the Tat pathway. In light of our observations, we postulate that the TatC-determined pathway specificity stems from specific interactions between TatC-like proteins and other pathway components, such as TatA, of which three paralogues are present in B. subtilis.

title: Function and regulation of SUMO proteases
text: The covalent bonding of small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) to proteins is highly dynamic, and both SUMO conjugation and cleavage can be regulated. Protein desumoylation is carried out by SUMO proteases, which play a crucial role in controlling various cellular mechanisms, including transcription, cell division, and ribosome biogenesis. Recent breakthroughs have led to the discovery of two novel classes of SUMO proteases, greater understanding of SUMO protease specificity, and the revelation of previously unrecognized SUMO protease functions in key cellular pathways. These advances, along with new connections between SUMO proteases and the recently discovered SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligases (STUbLs), make this an exciting time to study these enzymes.

title: Review article: prebiotics in the gastrointestinal tract.
text:
BACKGROUND Prebiotics are short-chain carbohydrates that modulate the composition and metabolism of the gut microbiota in a beneficial manner, thereby promoting health benefits similar to those of probiotics, albeit at a lower cost and with less potential risks. This review aims to evaluate the available scientific evidence on the prebiotic effects on gut function and human health.
METHODS A comprehensive search of the Science Citation Index was conducted using the keywords "prebiotic," "microbiota," "gut bacteria," "large intestine," "mucosa," "bowel habit," "constipation," "diarrhea," "inflammatory bowel disease," "Crohn's disease," "ulcerative colitis," "pouchitis," "calcium," and "cancer," focusing primarily on studies conducted in humans and reports published in the English language. Despite efforts to identify relevant clinical trials or meta-analyses in the Cochrane Library, no relevant studies were found.
RESULTS The review identified three prebiotics—oligofructose, galacto-oligosaccharides, and lactulose—that demonstrably alter the gut microbiota by increasing the populations of Bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus. These carbohydrates are fermented and lead to the production of short-chain fatty acids and intestinal gas; however, their effects on bowel habit are relatively minor. Few randomized-controlled trials have been conducted in a clinical context, although animal studies have shown anti-inflammatory effects in inflammatory bowel disease and increased calcium absorption.
CONCLUSIONS Although prebiotics are still in the early stages of research and development, their potential to modify the gut microbiota in a manner that promotes direct health benefits at a lower cost and with less potential risks makes them an attractive area of investigation. Further research is warranted to fully elucidate the prebiotic effects on gut function and human health.

title: Pain catastrophizing and general health status in a large Dutch community sample.
text: The current study aimed to investigate the relationship between pain catastrophizing and general health status in a Dutch adult population, including various subgroups with musculoskeletal pain. As part of exploratory rather than statistical reasons, the study also replicated previous studies on the factor structure, reliability, and validity of the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS). Our findings showed that among different pain subgroups, catastrophizing explained unique variance in predicting various aspects of general health status beyond pain intensity, age, gender, and chronicity. Strongest associations were found between catastrophizing and mental health, general health perception, social functioning, and vitality. Moreover, the association between catastrophizing and general health status was not moderated by pain chronicity. The results of the confirmatory factor analysis confirmed a three-factor model of the PCS, which was invariant across different subgroups of people with musculoskeletal pain. The inter-factor correlations were high, and the incremental explanatory power of the three-factor model over a one-factor model was only slightly better. This implies that a one-factor model could also be justified, at least in the general community. Across various pain subgroups, the reliability of the PCS total and subscales was adequate. Additionally, the study provided further evidence for the concurrent validity of the PCS.

title: Variability in risk of gastrointestinal complications with individual non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: results of a collaborative meta-analysis.
text:
The objective of this systematic review was to compare the relative risks of serious gastrointestinal complications associated with different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The review included 12 controlled epidemiological studies that investigated the relation between drug use and admission to hospital for haemorrhage or perforation. The main outcome measures were estimated relative risks of gastrointestinal complications with each drug, with exposure to ibuprofen used as the reference.
The results of the review showed that ibuprofen had the lowest or equal lowest relative risk of gastrointestinal complications in 10 of the 11 studies included in the review. Pooled relative risks calculated with exposure to ibuprofen as the reference were significantly greater than 1.0, with an interval of point estimates ranging from 1.6 to 9.2. Overall, ibuprofen was associated with the lowest relative risk, followed by diclofenac. Azapropazone, tolmetin, ketoprofen, and piroxicam ranked highest for risk, while indomethacin, naproxen, sulindac, and aspirin occupied intermediate positions. Higher doses of ibuprofen were associated with relative risks similar to those observed with naproxen and indomethacin.
The review's conclusions suggested that the low risk of serious gastrointestinal complications associated with ibuprofen is likely due to the low doses of the drug used in clinical practice. In higher doses, ibuprofen is associated with a similar risk to other NSAIDs. Using low-risk drugs in low doses as first-line treatment would significantly reduce morbidity and mortality due to serious gastrointestinal toxicity from these drugs.

title: Accuracy of weighed dietary records in studies of diet and health.
text:
Objective:
To perform an independent evaluation of the accuracy of seven-day weighed dietary records in measuring habitual dietary intake, as the most commonly used technique in studies examining the relationship between diet and health.
Design:
Subjects selected from the Northern Ireland diet and health study by stratified random sampling were re-evaluated to represent the range of energy intakes in the study. The subjects were 31 free-living adults (16 men and 15 women).
Setting:
Northern Ireland

Main Outcome Measures:

* Energy intake measured through seven-day weighed dietary records
* Total energy expenditure estimated concurrently using the doubly labeled water technique

Results:

The average recorded energy intake was significantly lower than the measured expenditure in the entire group (9.66 MJ/day compared to 12.15 MJ/day, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.45 to 3.53 MJ/day). Among those in the upper third of energy intakes, the mean ratio of intake to expenditure was nearly 1.0, indicating accurate records (men 1.01 (0.11), women 0.96 (0.08]). In the middle and lower thirds, the ratios for men were 0.74 (0.05) and 0.70 (0.07), respectively, and for women 0.89 (0.07) and 0.61 (0.07).

Conclusions:

These results suggest a serious bias in the reporting of habitual energy intake. If confirmed, they may have significant implications for the interpretation of many nutritional studies.

title: A novel family of sequence-specific endoribonucleases associated with the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats.
text: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPRs) work in conjunction with the associated CAS proteins to protect microbial cells from foreign genetic elements using unknown molecular mechanisms. All CRISPR systems contain proteins of the CAS2 family, indicating that these uncharacterized proteins play a central role in this process. Here, we show that the CAS2 proteins are a novel family of endoribonucleases. Our findings reveal that six purified CAS2 proteins from different organisms can cleave single-stranded RNAs preferentially within U-rich regions. A specific CAS2 enzyme, SSO1404 from Sulfolobus solfataricus, cleaves the phosphodiester bond on the 3'-side of the RNA and produces 5'-phosphate- and 3 '-hydroxyl-terminated oligonucleotides. Crystal structure analysis of SSO1404 at 1.6 Å resolution has revealed the first ribonuclease with a ferredoxin-like fold. Our mutational studies have identified six crucial residues (Tyr-9, Asp-10, Arg-17, Arg-19, Arg-31, and Phe-37) that are essential for enzymatic activity, and we propose that Asp-10 may be the main catalytic residue. Therefore, CAS2 proteins are sequence-specific endoribonucleases, and their role in the CRISPR-mediated anti-phage defense mechanism may involve the degradation of phage or cellular mRNAs.

title: Menstrual and reproductive factors in relation to mammographic density: the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation (SWAN)
text: Research has suggested that factors related to menstruation and reproduction may increase the risk of breast cancer through a pathway that includes increased mammographic density. In order to investigate this association, we measured the area of radiographic density and the total breast area on mammograms from 801 participants in the Study of Women's Health Across the Nation (SWAN), a multi-ethnic cohort of pre- and early perimenopausal women. Using multivariable linear regression, we found that the following menstrual and reproductive factors were independently associated with percent mammographic density: older age at menarche (related to the age at which a girl first begins menstruating), premenstrual cravings and bloating, younger age at first full-term birth (related to the age at which a woman gives birth for the first time), greater number of births, and premenopausal status (related to the stage of a woman's reproductive cycle). After adjusting for other factors such as age, race/ethnicity, study site, body mass index (BMI), and smoking, the only factor that remained associated with percent density was the number of births. Additionally, we found that the association between number of births and percent density was stronger among women who were in the lowest BMI tertile (a category of body size). These findings support a mechanism by which parity (the number of births a woman has) may influence breast cancer risk through mammographic density among pre- and early perimenopausal women, and suggest that body size may play a role in this association.

title: Genetic and environmental determinants of 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels in Hispanic and African Americans.
text: Background: Vitamin D deficiency is linked to various adverse health outcomes, yet little is known about the genetic epidemiology of vitamin D or its metabolites in different racial/ethnic groups. Objective: To investigate the relationship between genetic variations in vitamin D-related genes and plasma levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D [1,25(OH)2D] in Hispanic Americans (HAs) and African Americans (AAs). Design and Settings: Cross-sectional study of 1,534 subjects recruited from three locations in the US: Los Angeles, California (AAs; 513 individuals from 42 families), San Luis Valley, Colorado (HAs; 513 individuals from 30 families), and San Antonio, Texas (HAs; 504 individuals from 58 families). Main Outcome Measures: Plasma levels of 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D were measured. Results: Plasma levels of 25(OH)D were highest in SLV-HAs (18.3 ± 7.7 ng/ml), lower in SA-HAs (14.6 ± 6.4 ng/ml), and lowest in AAs (11.0 ± 5.4 ng/ml). Similarly, levels of 1,25(OH)2D were similar in AAs (43.5 ± 13.9 pg/ml) and SLV-HAs (43.2 ± 13.3 pg/ml), but higher in SA-HAs (48.6 ± 17.0 pg/ml). Adjusting for gender and age within each site revealed that two single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the vitamin D binding protein gene (DBP), rs4588 and rs7041, were associated with 25(OH)D, and one SNP in the DBP, rs4588, was associated with 1,25(OH)2D at all three study centers. Conclusion: SNPs in the DBP are associated with levels of 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D in HA and AA participants in the Insulin Resistance Atherosclerosis Family Study, highlighting the need for further investigation into the genetic epidemiology of vitamin D in different racial/ethnic groups.

title: Changes in the levels of inositol phosphates after agonist-dependent hydrolysis of membrane phosphoinositides.
text:
In this study, the formation of inositol phosphates in response to agonists was investigated in several tissues, including brain slices, parotid gland fragments, and the insect salivary gland. The tissues were first incubated with [3H]inositol, which was incorporated into the phosphoinositides. The researchers then used various techniques, such as anion-exchange and high-resolution anion-exchange chromatography, high-voltage paper ionophoresis, and paper chromatography, to identify and separate the different inositol phosphates present in the tissues.

One of the most notable findings of this study was the enormous increase in inositol 1,4-bisphosphate observed in the insect salivary gland and parotid gland after stimulation with 5-hydroxytryptamine and carbachol, respectively. Carbachol also led to a significant increase in the level of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate in the parotid gland. In contrast, stimulation of brain slices with carbachol resulted in only a modest increase in the levels of these bis- and trisphosphates.


Finally, the study showed that the earliest event in the stimulus-response pathway is the hydrolysis of polyphosphoinositides by a phosphodiesterase to yield inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and inositol 1,4-bisphosphate, which are subsequently hydrolyzed to inositol 1-phosphate and inositol. The absence of inositol 1:2-cyclic phosphate could indicate that phosphatidylinositol is not catabolized by its specific phosphodiesterase or that any cyclic derivative liberated is rapidly hydrolyzed by inositol 1:2-cyclic phosphate 2-phosphohydrolase. Overall, this study provides important insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the signaling pathways involved in the response to agonists in various tissues.

title: RNA editing in brain controls a determinant of ion flow in glutamate-gated channels.
text: L-glutamate, the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, regulates ion channels that facilitate rapid neural communication. Using cDNA cloning, the subunit components of two related classes of glutamate receptor channels have been identified, each containing an arginine or glutamine residue in a specific position. We found that the arginine residue significantly influences the ion flow properties, and in one channel class, it dominates them. We discovered that the DNA sequences encoding the specific channel segment of all subunits contain a glutamine codon (CAG), even though an arginine codon (CGG) is present in the mRNAs of three subunits. Considering that multiple genes and alternative exons were excluded as sources for the arginine codon, we propose that RNA editing alters the subunit transcripts of the two glutamate receptor classes with varying efficiency and selectivity.

title: Post-translational modifications of the beta-1 subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase affect enzyme activity and cellular localization.
text: The AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a ubiquitous mammalian enzyme crucial in the adaptation of cells to metabolic stress. The enzyme is composed of a catalytic alpha subunit and regulatory beta and gamma subunits, each belonging to a larger isoform family. AMPK is allosterically regulated by AMP and phosphorylation of the alpha subunit. The beta subunit is post-translationally modified by myristoylation and multi-site phosphorylation. In our current study, we investigated the impact of modifying the beta-1 subunit on enzyme activity, heterotrimer assembly, and subcellular localization. We used site-directed mutagenesis and expression of subunits in mammalian cells. Removing the myristoylation site (G2A mutant) resulted in a 4-fold increase in enzyme activity and a relocalization of the beta subunit from a particulate extranuclear distribution to a more homogeneous cell distribution. Mutating the serine-108 phosphorylation site to alanine showed no change in cell localization but was associated with enzyme inhibition. In contrast, mutations in the phosphorylation sites, SS24, 25AA, and S182A, had no effect on enzyme activity but resulted in nuclear redistribution of the subunit.
