title: A lineage of myeloid cells independent of Myb and hematopoietic stem cells.
text: Macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs) are crucial components of the immune system, and it was previously believed that they originate and renew from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). However, our findings reveal that some macrophages develop in the embryo before the appearance of definitive HSCs. To investigate macrophage development further, we focused on the transcription factor Myb, which was found to be essential for the development of both HSCs and all CD11b(high) monocytes and macrophages. However, Myb was dispensable for the development of yolk sac (YS) macrophages and the subsequent persistence of these cells in adult tissues, such as liver Kupffer cells, epidermal Langerhans cells, and microglia. These findings establish a distinct lineage of tissue macrophages that derive from the YS and are genetically different from HSC progeny.

title: Heterogenic Loss of the Wild-Type BRCA Allele in Human Breast Tumorigenesis
text:
For individuals genetically predisposed to breast and ovarian cancer due to a mutation in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene, somatic loss of heterozygosity in the wild-type allele is considered necessary for cancer initiation and progression. However, recent findings suggest that haploinsufficiency of the BRCA gene may also lead to phenotypic effects.
In this study, archival tissue samples from women with germ line mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2 were analyzed. Focal areas of normal breast epithelium, atypical ductal hyperplasia, ductal carcinoma-in-situ, and invasive ductal carcinoma were identified in 14 BRCA1-linked and 9 BRCA2-linked breast cancers. Additionally, 10 BRCA-linked prophylactic mastectomy specimens and 12 BRCA-linked invasive ovarian carcinomas were studied. Using laser catapult microdissection, cells were isolated from the various pathologic lesions and corresponding normal tissues, and DNA was isolated for real-time polymerase chain reaction assays to quantify the proportion of wild-type to mutant BRCA alleles in each tissue sample.
The results showed a high level of heterogeneity in loss of heterozygosity within and between preinvasive lesions and invasive cancers from BRCA1 and BRCA2 heterozygotes with breast cancer. In contrast, all BRCA-associated ovarian cancers displayed complete loss of the wild-type BRCA allele. These findings suggest that loss of the wild-type BRCA allele is not necessary for BRCA-linked breast tumorigenesis, which has important implications for the genetic mechanism of BRCA tumor suppression and for the clinical management of this patient population.

title: Targeted therapies in urothelial carcinoma.
text:
The purpose of this review is to gain a deeper understanding of the biology and genetics of urothelial carcinoma, with the goal of identifying and characterizing potential molecular targets for novel-targeted therapies. This review summarizes the targeted therapies currently being evaluated in clinical trials for urothelial carcinoma, as well as the molecular targets that have been characterized in preclinical and clinical studies.
Recent findings from clinical trials have shown that immunotherapy and agents targeting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) or fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 (FGFR3) are being investigated in non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer. In muscle-invasive bladder cancer, studies are combining VEGF agents with chemotherapy, and adjuvant trials are testing vaccines and agents targeting the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), p53, and Hsp27. In the first-line treatment of metastatic urothelial carcinoma, novel targets such as tubulin, cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA4), Hsp27, and p53 are being studied in clinical trials. Most of the targeted agents being evaluated are being tested in the second-line setting, and new targets include CD105, polo-like kinase-1 (PLK1), phosphatidylinositide 3-kinases (PI3K), transforming growth factor β receptor/activin receptor-like kinase β (TGFβR/ALKβ), estrogen receptor (ER), and the hepatocyte growth factor receptor (HGFR or MET).
While significant progress has not yet been made in the development of targeted therapies for urothelial carcinoma, the increased understanding of the biology and genetics of this disease has led to a surge in clinical trials that could lead to significant advances in treatment strategies.

title: H2S and HS− donor NaHS releases nitric oxide from nitrosothiols, metal nitrosyl complex, brain homogenate and murine L1210 leukaemia cells
text: Nitrosoglutathione (GSNO), at a concentration of 500 nmol/l, relaxed norepinephrine-precontracted rat aortic rings. The relaxation effect was significantly enhanced by the H2S- and HS−-donor NaHS (30 μmol/l) at pH 7.5 but not at pH 6.3. To elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying this effect, we investigated whether NaHS can release nitric oxide (NO) from NO donors. Using an electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy-based method of spin trap and by measuring the NO oxidation product, nitrite, through the Griess reaction, we found that NaHS released NO from nitrosothiols, including GSNO, S-nitroso-N-acetyl-d-penicillamine (SNAP), nitroprusside (SNP), and rat brain homogenate and murine L1210 leukaemia cells. Notably, the releasing effect was more pronounced at pH 8.0 than at pH 6.0, suggesting that HS−, rather than H2S, is primarily responsible for the NO-releasing effect. Given that endogenous production of H2S and HS− occurs in mammals, we propose that their ability to release NO from nitrosothiols and metal nitrosyl complexes may contribute to some of their biological activities and play a role in S-nitrosothiol signaling reactions.

title: Amitriptyline is effective in chronic but not in episodic tension-type headache: pathogenetic implications.
text: The tricyclic antidepressant amitriptyline is effective in treating both chronic tension-type headaches and other chronic pain conditions, as well as in the prevention of episodic migraines. However, its effectiveness in treating episodic tension-type headaches has yet to be fully established. In an open-label study involving 82 non-depressed patients with either chronic or episodic tension-type headaches, amitriptyline (25 mg/day) significantly reduced the frequency and duration of headaches, as well as analgesic consumption, in patients with chronic headaches but not in those with episodic headaches (P < 0.05). Further placebo-controlled trials, possibly using higher doses of amitriptyline, may help to shed light on why there is a differing response to the drug depending on the type of headache. It is possible that central nociception and peripheral myofascial factors play different roles in the chronic and episodic forms of tension-type headache.

title: Kruppel-like factor 2 is required for trafficking but not quiescence in postactivated T cells.
text: The transcription factor Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) was proposed to regulate genes involved in cell cycle entry and T cell trafficking; however, its physiological role in post-activated T cells was not well understood. Previous studies suggested that cytokines such as IL-2 and IL-15 regulate KLF2 re-expression in post-activation T cells and influence effector versus memory T cell differentiation. To investigate the specific role of KLF2 expression in activated CD8+ T cells, we used conditional and inducible KLF2-knockout model systems and cultured them with these cytokines. Our results showed that KLF2 was required for the effective transcription of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor-1 (S1P1) and CD62L in post-activation T cells. Surprisingly, although different cytokines dramatically altered the expression of cell-cycle-related genes, endogenous KLF2 had a minimal impact. Correspondingly, KLF2-deficient T cells showed dysregulated trafficking but not altered proliferative characteristics following in vivo responses to Ag. These findings help to define KLF2-dependent and -independent aspects of activated CD8+ T cell differentiation and argue against a physiological role in cell cycle regulation.

title: Hypoalbuminemia in acute illness: is there a rationale for intervention? A meta-analysis of cohort studies and controlled trials.
text:
Objective:
To determine whether hypoalbuminemia is an independent risk factor for poor outcome in acutely ill patients and to evaluate the potential of exogenous albumin administration for improving outcomes in hypoalbuminemic patients.
Summary Background Data:
Hypoalbuminemia has been associated with poor outcomes in acutely ill patients, but the causal relationship remains unclear. Trials investigating albumin therapy to correct hypoalbuminemia have yielded inconclusive results.
Methods:
A meta-analysis of 90 cohort studies with 291,433 patients was conducted to evaluate the predictive power of hypoalbuminemia by multivariate analysis. Additionally, nine prospective controlled trials with 535 patients were analyzed to assess the dose-dependency of hypoalbuminemia on poor outcomes and the potential effects of albumin therapy.
Results:
Hypoalbuminemia was found to be a powerful, dose-dependent independent predictor of poor outcome. Each 10-g/L decline in serum albumin concentration significantly increased the odds of mortality by 137%, morbidity by 89%, prolonged intensive care unit and hospital stay by 28% and 71%, and increased resource utilization by 66%. The association between hypoalbuminemia and poor outcome appeared to be independent of both nutritional status and inflammation. Analysis of dose-dependency in controlled trials of albumin therapy suggested that complication rates may be reduced when the serum albumin level attained during albumin administration exceeds 30 g/L.
Conclusions:
Hypoalbuminemia is strongly associated with poor clinical outcomes. Further well-designed trials are needed to characterize the effects of albumin therapy in hypoalbuminemic patients. In the interim, there is no compelling basis to withhold albumin therapy if it is judged clinically appropriate.

title: Methionine restriction decreases visceral fat mass and preserves insulin action in aging male Fischer 344 rats independent of energy restriction.
text: Reduced dietary methionine intake (0.17% methionine, MR) and calorie restriction (CR) extend rat lifespan in male Fischer 344 rats. Although the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood, both interventions result in lower body weight and fat reduction. CR's reduction in fat accumulation is linked to the preservation of insulin sensitivity in aging animals. To investigate whether decreased visceral fat accumulation and preserved insulin sensitivity in MR animals are secondary to CR, rats were pair-fed a control diet (0.86% methionine, CF) to match their food intake for 80 weeks. Insulin, glucose, leptin, and adiponectin levels were measured, and visceral fat quantities were determined. Compared to CF and pair-fed (PF) animals, MR rats showed significantly less visceral fat, along with decreased basal insulin, glucose, and leptin levels, and increased adiponectin and triiodothyronine. Daily energy expenditure in MR animals was found to be significantly higher than in both PF and CF animals. In a separate cohort, the insulin response of older MR animals, as measured by oral glucose challenge, was found to be similar to that of young animals. Longitudinal assessments of MR and CF rats over 112 weeks revealed that MR prevented age-related increases in serum lipids. By 16 weeks, MR animals showed a 40% reduction in insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) levels, which remained low throughout their lifespan; CF IGF-1 levels decreased more gradually, beginning at 112 weeks. These results suggest that MR reduces visceral fat and preserves insulin function in aging rats independent of energy restriction.

title: Generation of T cell receptor–retrogenic mice: improved retroviral-mediated stem cell gene transfer
text: The retrogenic mouse model provides a quick and adaptable method for generating T cell receptor (TCR)-transgenic mice. By using a retrovirus to infect bone marrow progenitor cells with a specific TCR-α/β subunit, TCR-retrogenic mice can be produced in as little as 4-6 weeks, significantly faster than conventional TCR transgenics, which can take 6 months or longer. In this updated protocol, we have improved the efficiency of bone marrow transduction and bone marrow reconstitution compared to our previous protocol. One key difference from the previous protocol is the use of spin transduction with viral supernatant instead of coculture with the viral producer cell line. These changes result in higher bone marrow viability, more consistent bone marrow transduction, and a lower ratio of bone marrow donor mice to bone marrow recipients.

title: Transient delivery of modified mRNA encoding TERT rapidly extends telomeres in human cells.
text:
Introduction: Telomere extension has been proposed as a potential solution for various biomedical applications, including cell culture and tissue engineering, as well as the treatment of diseases. However, nonviral, nonintegrating methods for telomere extension remain inefficient. In this study, we investigated the effectiveness of delivering modified mRNA encoding TERT to human fibroblasts and myoblasts in extending telomeres and increasing cell proliferative capacity.
Methods: We transfected human fibroblasts and myoblasts with modified mRNA encoding TERT and observed the effect on telomere length and cell proliferation. We performed three sequential transfections over a period of 4 days and measured the extent of telomere extension and proliferative capacity at each time point.
Results: Our results showed that delivery of modified mRNA encoding TERT to human fibroblasts and myoblasts led to a rapid increase in telomerase activity, which resulted in the extension of telomeres. The first three transfections increased telomere length by up to 0.9 kb in a cell type-specific manner, and conferred an additional 28 ± 1.5 and 3.4 ± 0.4 population doublings (PDs), respectively. The second and third transfections had a decreased effect on proliferative capacity compared to the first transfection, indicating a refractory period. However, this refractory period was transient, as a later fourth transfection increased fibroblast proliferative capacity by an additional 15.2 ± 1.1 PDs, similar to the first transfection. Overall, these treatments led to an increase in absolute cell number of more than 10(12)-fold. Notably, unlike immortalized cells, all treated cell populations eventually stopped increasing in number and expressed senescence markers to the same extent as untreated cells.
Discussion: Our findings demonstrate that delivery of modified mRNA encoding TERT to human fibroblasts and myoblasts is a rapid and effective method for extending telomeres and increasing cell proliferative capacity without the risk of insertional mutagenesis. This method has broad utility in disease modeling, drug screening, and regenerative medicine. The reversibility of the refractory period suggests that the cells are not permanently altered, and therefore, this approach may be more administratively friendly in clinical settings.

title: The death receptor CD95 activates adult neural stem cells for working memory formation and brain repair.
text: The process of adult neurogenesis continues in the subventricular zone and dentate gyrus, and can be triggered by injury to the central nervous system. However, the ultimate contribution of new neurons to neural networks is limited. In this study, we found that stimulating the "death receptor" CD95 does not result in the death of neural stem cells, as expected, but instead leads to increased survival and neuronal specification. These effects are mediated by the activation of the Src/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, which leads to a global increase in protein translation. We also found that inducing neurogenesis through CD95 is effective in the ischemic CA1 region, the naive dentate gyrus, and when CD95 is overexpressed in the subventricular zone. Mice lacking the CD95 gene in the hippocampus showed reduced neurogenesis and working memory deficits. Following global ischemia, CD95-mediated brain repair improved behavioral function. Therefore, we identify the CD95/CD95L system as a regulatory signal for ongoing and injury-induced neurogenesis.

title: Umbilical Cord Blood Therapy Potentiated with Erythropoietin for Children with Cerebral Palsy: A Double-blind, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial
text: Allogenic umbilical cord blood (UCB) has therapeutic potential for cerebral palsy (CP), and concomitant administration of recombinant human erythropoietin (rhEPO) may enhance its efficacy due to its neurotrophic effects. This study aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of allogenic UCB potentiated with rhEPO in children with CP. Children with CP were randomly assigned to one of three groups: the pUCB group, which received allogenic UCB potentiated with rhEPO; the EPO group, which received rhEPO and placebo UCB; and the Control group, which received placebo UCB and placebo rhEPO. All participants underwent rehabilitation therapy. The primary outcomes were changes in scores on the following measures during the 6-month treatment period: the gross motor performance measure (GMPM), gross motor function measure, and Bayley scales of infant development-II (BSID-II) Mental and Motor scales. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (18F-FDG-PET/CT) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) were performed at baseline and follow-up to detect changes in the brain. In total, 96 subjects completed the study. Compared to the EPO (n = 33) and Control (n = 32) groups, the pUCB (n = 31) group displayed significantly higher scores on the GMPM and BSID-II Mental and Motor scales at 6 months. DTI revealed significant correlations between the GMPM increment and changes in fractional anisotropy in the pUCB group. 18F-FDG-PET/CT showed differential activation and deactivation patterns between the three groups. There were no significant differences in serious adverse events between the groups. In conclusion, UCB treatment improved motor and cognitive function in children with CP undergoing active rehabilitation, accompanied by structural and metabolic changes in the brain.

title: Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP(1-38)) enhances N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor function and brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression via RACK1.
text: In recent studies, we uncovered a new mechanism underlying the modulation of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor function through the interaction of the scaffolding protein RACK1 with the NR2B subunit of the NMDA receptor and the nonreceptor protein-tyrosine kinase, Fyn. We discovered that RACK1 inhibits Fyn phosphorylation of NR2B, leading to decreased NMDA receptor-mediated currents in CA1 hippocampal slices. Our investigation also revealed that the dissociation of RACK1 from the NMDA receptor complex is triggered by the cAMP/protein kinase A (PKA) signaling pathway in hippocampal slices, which results in the induction of NR2B phosphorylation and enhancement of NMDA receptor-mediated activity via Fyn. We identified the neuropeptide pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide (PACAP(1-38)) as a ligand that induces phosphorylation of NR2B and enhances NMDA receptor potentials. Furthermore, we found that activation of the cAMP/PKA pathway leads to the translocation of RACK1 to the nuclear compartment in dissociated hippocampal neurons, where it regulates the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor induced by PACAP(1-38). Our results suggest that activation of adenylate cyclase by PACAP(1-38) leads to the release of RACK1 from the NMDA receptor and Fyn, resulting in NMDA receptor phosphorylation, enhanced activity mediated by Fyn, and the induction of brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression by RACK1.

title: MUC1 oncoprotein activates the IκB kinase β complex and constitutive NF-κB signalling
text: Nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) is consistently activated in various human cancers due to unclear mechanisms. The MUC1 oncoprotein is overexpressed in most human carcinomas, blocked apoptosis and transformation by preventing, and interacts with the high-molecular-weight IκB kinase (IKK) complex in vivo. Specifically, MUC1 binds directly to IKKβ and IKKγ, which triggers IKKβ activation and leads to the phosphorylation and degradation of IκBα. Our study shows that MUC1 overexpression in human carcinoma cells is associated with persistent NF-κB p65 activation. Analysis in non-malignant epithelial cells demonstrates that MUC1 is recruited to the TNF-R1 complex and interacts with IKKβ–IKKγ upon TNFα exposure. This recruitment is TRAF2-dependent but not RIP1-dependent. Additionally, MUC1 mediates IKKβ activation via TAK1 and TAB2. These findings indicate that MUC1 plays a crucial role in physiological IKKβ activation and that excessive MUC1 expression in human malignancies sustains the induction of the IKKβ–NF-κB p65 pathway.

title: Lipoxins: novel series of biologically active compounds formed from arachidonic acid in human leukocytes.
text: In a landmark study published in 1984, Serhan et al. isolated a novel series of oxygenated derivatives of arachidonic acid in human leukocytes, known as trihydroxytetraenes. The structure of the major compound, 5,6,15L-trihydroxy-7,9,11,13-icosatetraenoic acid, was confirmed, and the present study reports the structure of a second member of the series, 5D,14,15L-trihydroxy-6,8,10,12-icosatetraenoic acid. These compounds were shown to stimulate superoxide anion generation and degranulation in human neutrophils without provoking a substantial aggregation response, suggesting the involvement of the 5- and 15-lipoxygenase pathways in the regulation of specific cellular responses. To provide a unified nomenclature for these compounds, the trivial names lipoxin A and lipoxin B are proposed.

title: Nitric oxide synthase generates superoxide and nitric oxide in arginine-depleted cells leading to peroxynitrite-mediated cellular injury.
text: Other than synthesizing nitric oxide (NO), purified neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) can produce superoxide (.O2-) at lower levels of L-Arg. By utilizing electron paramagnetic resonance spin-trapping techniques, we monitored NO and .O2- formation in nNOS-transfected human kidney 293 cells. In untransfected cells, the calcium ionophore A23187 triggered NO generation but no .O2- production was observed. As the cytosolic L-Arg levels decreased, .O2- formation increased, while NO generation declined. .O2- formation was nearly abolished by the specific NOS blocker, N-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME). The accumulation of nitrotyrosine, a specific nitration product of peroxynitrite, occurred in L-Arg-depleted cells but not in control cells. Activation by A23187 was cytotoxic to L-Arg-depleted cells, but not to control cells, with significant lactate dehydrogenase release. The cytotoxicity was largely prevented by either superoxide dismutase or L-NAME. Therefore, with reduced L-Arg availability, NOS elicits cytotoxicity by generating .O2- and NO, which combine to form the potent oxidant peroxynitrite. Modulating arginine levels may offer a therapeutic approach to treating disorders caused by .O2-/NO-mediated cellular injury.

title: Sudden infant death syndrome and unclassified sudden infant deaths: a definitional and diagnostic approach.
text: The original definition of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) was first introduced in 1969 and was later refined in the following two decades. Over the next 15 years, significant additional information emerged, leading to improvements in the definition of SIDS that incorporated epidemiological features, risk factors, pathological findings, and diagnostic test results. An expert panel of pediatric and forensic pathologists and pediatricians reviewed these changes and developed a revised general definition of SIDS for administrative and vital statistics purposes. The new definition was then categorized to facilitate research into sudden infant death. Additionally, a new category, referred to as unclassified sudden infant deaths, was established for cases that do not meet the criteria for a diagnosis of SIDS and for which alternative diagnoses of natural or unnatural causes were unclear. It is expected that these revised definitions will continue to evolve in the future as new knowledge and understanding of SIDS and sudden infant death emerges.

title: Inter-viral conflicts that exploit host CRISPR immune systems of Sulfolobus.
text: Infection of Sulfolobus islandicus REY15A with a mixture of different Sulfolobus viruses, including STSV2, failed to induce the acquisition of spacers by the host CRISPR immune system. However, co-infection with the tailed fusiform viruses SMV1 and STSV2 resulted in hyperactive spacer acquisition in both CRISPR loci, with the resultant loss of STSV2 but not SMV1. SMV1 was found to activate adaptation while itself being resistant to CRISPR-mediated adaptation and DNA interference. Interestingly, a single clone, S-1, isolated from an SMV1 + STSV2-infected culture, carried STSV2-specific spacers and had lost STSV2 but not SMV1. This clone also acquired spacers from SMV1, a feat that was reproducible when reinfecting wild-type host cells with a variant SMV1 isolated from the S-1 culture. The variant SMV1 lacked the ORF114 protein, which was shown to bind DNA. This study also provided evidence for several key findings, including: (i) the maximum size limits of CRISPR loci; (ii) the significant slowing of growth in infected cultures due to spacer uptake; (iii) the random and non-directional nature of protospacer selection; and (iv) the reversible uptake of spacers from STSV2 and SMV1. A hypothesis is proposed to explain the complex interactions between SMV1 and the host CRISPR immune system.

title: Lung Carcinogenesis by Diesel Exhaust Particles and the Carcinogenic Mechanism Via Active Oxygens.
text: In an investigation to elucidate the involvement of oxygen radicals in lung cancer induction caused by diesel exhaust particles (DEP), we discovered a significant correlation between lung tumor response and the formation of 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) in lung DNA of mice administered DEP via repeated intratracheal instillation. Moreover, repeated intratracheal instillation of DEP also triggered the activity of cytochrome P-450 reductase in the lungs, representing superoxide generation, as well as two types of nitric oxide (NO) synthases, cNOS and iNOS, in the lungs. Conversely, the activities of CuZn-superoxide dismutase (SOD) and Mn-SOD antioxidant enzymes were suppressed by the instillation of DEP. These findings suggest that the generation of superoxide, hydroxyl radical, and nitric oxide is augmented in epithelial cells lining the airways, and that the increased superoxide and nitric oxide readily react to produce peroxynitrite (ONOO(-)). The peroxynitrite can also generate hydroxyl radical, which may play a critical role in carcinogenesis initiated by DEP.

title: Prion-induced amyloid heart disease with high blood infectivity in transgenic mice.
text: We examined the extracellular manifestations of scrapie infection in transgenic mice that expressed a prion protein variant lacking its glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) membrane anchor. In the brain, blood, and heart tissues, we found high levels of abnormal protease-resistant prion protein (PrPres) and prion infectivity using immunoblotting and inoculation of non-transgenic recipients. The concentration of infectious scrapie in blood plasma was remarkably high, exceeding 10(7) 50% infectious doses per milliliter. Additionally, PrPres-positive amyloid deposits were detected in the hearts of these transgenic mice, leading to myocardial stiffness and cardiac disease.

title: Circulating plasma microRNAs as a screening method for detection of colorectal adenomas.
text:
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small, non-coding RNA molecules that have been implicated in the development and progression of colon cancer. The detection of circulating miRNAs in the bloodstream has been proposed as a potential method for screening for colon cancer, particularly for patients with polyps or adenomas.
In this study, we analyzed the expression levels of six specific miRNAs (miR-19a, miR-98, miR-146b, miR-186, miR-625, and miR-331-5p) in blood samples from patients enrolled in the UK Bowel Cancer Screening Programme. Our study included 210 patients, including 117 with polyps, 12 with cancer, and 81 healthy controls (faecal occult blood testing (FOBt) positive).
Our results showed significant differences in the expression levels of these miRNAs between patients with polyps, adenomas, and healthy controls. Specifically, we found that the expression levels of miR-19a, miR-98, miR-146b, miR-186, and miR-625 were significantly higher in patients with polyps or adenomas compared to healthy controls. These findings suggest that the levels of these miRNAs may be useful as a biomarker for the early detection of colon cancer.
We also evaluated the performance of this miRNA panel as a screening test, using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Our results showed that the sensitivity of the test was 60% or more, and the specificity was 86% or more, for different patient groups.
Overall, our study provides evidence that circulating miRNAs may be a useful biomarker for the early detection of colon cancer, particularly for patients with polyps or adenomas. Further studies are needed to validate these findings and to determine the effectiveness of miRNA-based screening in clinical settings.

title: Short term persistence of human papillomavirus and risk of cervical precancer and cancer: population based cohort study
text:
Objective: To assess the cumulative incidence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) II or worse (grade II+) or CIN grade III+ over a short-term period in women with prevalently detected carcinogenic human papillomavirus (HPV).
 DESIGN: Population-based cohort study
Setting: Guanacaste, Costa Rica
PARTICIPANTS: 2282 sexually active women actively followed after enrolment.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary end points were the three-year and five-year cumulative incidences of histologically confirmed CIN grade II+ (n=70). Cervical samples collected at each visit were tested for over 40 HPV genotypes. HPV 16, 18, 26, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68, 73, and 82 were considered the primary carcinogenic genotypes.
 RESULTS: Women who tested positive for a carcinogenic HPV at enrolment and after approximately one year (9-21 months) (positive/positive) had a three-year cumulative incidence of CIN grade II+ of 17.0% (95% CI: 12.1%-22.0%). Those who tested negative/positive (3.4%, -0.2% to 6.8%), positive/negative (1.2%, -0.2% to 2.5%), and negative/negative (0.5%, 0.1% to 0.9%) were at significantly lower risks. There was little difference in the cumulative incidence of CIN grade II+ between testing positive twice for any carcinogenic HPV genotype (same genotype or different genotypes) compared to testing positive twice for the same carcinogenic genotype (17.0% vs 21.3%, respectively). Short-term persistence of HPV 16 strongly predicted CIN grade II+, with a three-year cumulative incidence of 40.8% (26.4% to 55.1%). Similar patterns were observed for the five-year cumulative incidence of grade II+ and for three-year and five-year cumulative incidence of grade III+.
 CONCLUSIONS: Short-term persistence of a prevalently detected carcinogenic HPV infection, especially HPV 16, strongly predicts a subsequent diagnosis of CIN II+ over the next few years.

title: Nature and anisotropy of cortical forces orienting Drosophila tissue morphogenesis
text: The development of embryos and organs relies on the ability of cells to change their connections with nearby cells. Using quantitative modeling and laser microscopy, we investigated the mechanics of a morphogenetic process called the elongation of Drosophila melanogaster embryos, which arises from the coordinated exchange of cells along the embryo's polar axis. Our findings show that the anisotropy of the tension in the cortical region at the apical cell junctions is enough to drive tissue elongation. By comparing in silico and in vivo data using various tissue characteristics, we estimated the value of this anisotropy. Using nano-dissection of the actomyosin network, we found that tension is anisotropically distributed and depends on the accumulation of myosin II. Junction relaxation after nano-dissection also suggests that cortical elastic forces are the dominant force in this process. Interestingly, fluctuations in the position of vertices (where three or more cells meet) facilitate the exchange of neighboring cells. We have established the contribution of subcellular tensile activity in polarizing junction remodeling, as well as the facilitative role of vertex fluctuations during tissue elongation.

title: The influence of some metabolic inhibitors on phagocytic activity of mouse macrophages in vitro.
text: An investigation was conducted to evaluate the impact of different metabolic inhibitors on the phagocytic ability of macrophages isolated from mouse peritoneal exudate cultured in vitro. The following inhibitors were tested at a concentration of 10(-3) M: sodium iodoacetate, sodium fluoride, sodium fluoroacetate, sodium malonate, 2-4-dinitrophenol, sodium azide, ouabain, and cycloheximide. Iodoacetate significantly inhibited phagocytosis, suggesting that glycolysis is the primary source of energy for this process. In contrast, fluoride, despite being an effective inhibitor of glycolysis, had no effect on phagocytosis. This discrepancy may be due to the fact that sodium fluoride blocks anaerobic glycolysis only in vitro at an unphysiological temperature (0 degrees C). Fluoroacetate and malonate, which interfere with the Krebs cycle, did not affect phagocytosis, as the Krebs cycle is relatively undeveloped in macrophagic cells. Sodium azide and 2-4-dinitrophenol, which inhibit oxidative phosphorylation, showed an effect on phagocytosis only after 3 hours of cell exposure. Ouabain, which blocks Na+ and K+ transport across the plasma membrane, likely inhibited phagocytosis by interfering with cell membrane movements. Finally, the mode of action of cycloheximide on phagocytosis is unclear, as it inhibits protein synthesis and may also prevent the renewal of the cell membrane.

title: Two-tiered coupling between flowing actin and immobilized N-cadherin/catenin complexes in neuronal growth cones.
text: The growth cones of neurons move forward by dynamically linking their actin-based motility to the adhesion of substrate, but the specific molecular mechanisms remain unclear. We cultured primary neurons on N-cadherin-coated microscopic substrates and imaged cytoskeletal proteins at the ventral surface of growth cones using a combination of single particle tracking and photoactivated localization microscopy. We discovered transient interactions between flowing actin filaments and immobilized N-cadherin/catenin complexes on a second time scale, resulting in a temporary reduction in actin backflow. By expressing a dominant negative N-cadherin construct that competes with endogenous N-cadherin for interaction with actin, we were able to rescue the normal actin flow on the microscopic substrates. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching experiments confirmed the different kinetics of actin and N-cadherin, revealing a 20% population of actin filaments that are confined to N-cadherin micropatterns and contribute to local actin accumulation. Computer simulations using relevant kinetic parameters successfully modeled the turnover of N-cadherin and actin, further supporting this mechanism. This combination of short- and long-lived interactions between the motile actin network and spatially restricted adhesive complexes represents a two-tiered clutch mechanism that allows for dynamic environment sensing and sufficient force for growth cone migration.

title: Cloning of factors related to HIV-inducible LBP proteins that regulate steroidogenic factor-1-independent human placental transcription of the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme, P450scc.
text:
The cytochrome P450 side-chain cleavage enzyme, also known as cytochrome P450scc, is responsible for initiating the biosynthesis of all steroid hormones. Similarly interested in Adrenal and gonadal approaches, researchers sought factors that bind to the -155/-131 region of the human P450scc promoter, which specifically participates in placental but not adrenal or gonadal transcription.
A yeast one-hybrid screen of 2.4 x 10(6) cDNA clones from human placental JEG-3 cells yielded two specific clones; LBP-1b, which is induced by HIV, simian immunodeficiency virus, and type I infection of lymphocytes, and LBP-9, which shares 83% amino acid sequence identity with LBP-1b. Both factors specifically bound to the -155/-131 DNA when expressed in transfected yeast. Antibodies to LBP proteins supershifted the LBP-9.DNA complex and inhibited the formation of the LBP-1b. DNA complex. While LBP-1b was detected in human placental JEG-3, adrenal NCI-H295A, liver HepG2, cervical HeLa, and monkey kidney COS-1 cells, LBP-9 was only detected in JEG-3 cells. When the -155/-131 fragment was linked to a minimal promoter, co-expression of LBP-1b increased transcription 21-fold in a dose-dependent fashion, but addition of LBP-9 suppressed the stimulatory effect of LBP-1b.
The discovery of LBP-1b and LBP-9 sheds light on the distinctness of placental strategies for steroidogenic enzyme gene transcription; whereas placental expression of P450scc is essential for human pregnancy, adrenal and gonadal strategies for P450scc gene expression are similar and depend on steroidogenic factor-1. Thedetected of LBP transcription factors in normal human physiology has not been previously clarified. these findings suggest LBP modulation of placental but not adrenal P450scc transcription, highlighting the distinctiveness of placental procedures for steroid hormone biosynthesis.

title: Functional reprogramming of polyploidization in megakaryocytes.
text: Polyploidization, a natural process that often accompanies cell differentiation, has been linked to genomic instability and cancer. Despite its significance, the underlying reasons for why cells select specific polyploidization mechanisms remain unknown. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive genetic analysis of endomitosis, a process where megakaryocytes become polyploid by entering mitosis but aborting anaphase. Our findings reveal that ablation of the APC/C cofactor Cdc20 leads to mitotic arrest and severe thrombocytopenia, while lack of the kinases Aurora-B, Cdk1, or Cdk2 does not affect megakaryocyte polyploidization or platelet levels. Interestingly, ablation of Cdk1 leads to a switch to endocycles without mitosis, while polyploidization in the absence of Cdk1 and Cdk2 occurs in the presence of aberrant re-replication events. Moreover, ablation of these kinases rescues the defects in Cdc20 null megakaryocytes. These findings suggest that endomitosis can be functionally replaced by alternative polyploidization mechanisms in vivo, providing a cellular basis for therapeutic approaches aimed to distinguish between mitotic and polyploid cells.

title: Histone methyltransferase activity associated with a human multiprotein complex containing the Enhancer of Zeste protein.
text: Enhancer of Zeste (E(z)) is a Polycomb-group transcriptional repressor and a founding member of the SET domain-containing protein family. While some SET-domain proteins have intrinsic histone methyltransferase (HMT) activity, recombinant E(z) protein lacks activity in HMT assays. We report the isolation of a multiprotein E(z) complex called Polycomb repressive complex (PRC) 2, which contains extra sex combs, Supressor of zeste-12 (Su(z)12), and histone-binding proteins RbAp46/RbAp48. PRC2 exhibits HMT activity specific to Lys 9 (K9) and Lys 27 (K27) of histone H3, with dependence on the intact SET domain in E(z). We propose that transcriptional repression by E(z) involves methylation-dependent recruitment of PRC1. The presence of Su(z)12, a strong suppressor of position effect variegation, in PRC2 suggests that PRC2 may play a widespread role in heterochromatin-mediated silencing.

title: Simvastatin reduces platelet-endocardium adhesion in atrial fibrillation.
text:
Objective: To investigate the relationship between the CD40/CD40L system and the increased risk of thrombogenesis in atrial fibrillation (AF), and to evaluate the effects of simvastatin treatment on this process.
Methods: An in vitro study was conducted using human tissue from University Hospital (tertiary referral center). Experimental procedures were performed on right atrial segments obtained before the onset of cardiopulmonary bypass in either the presence or absence of 5 microM simvastatin. Two groups of patients, one with chronic atrial fibrillation and the other with sinus rhythm, were included in the study at the time of cardiac surgery. The expression of CD40, the release of CD40L, and the adhesion of platelets to the endocardium were evaluated, as well as the thickness of platelet aggregates and the platelet distribution on the endocardium.
Results: The study found that atrial fibrillation was associated with a significant increase in endocardial CD40 expression compared to sinus rhythm (293.1±55.1 pg/ml vs. 230.9±53.3 pg/ml, p<0.01). Furthermore, there was a higher adhesion of platelets to the endocardium in fibrillating atria compared to sinus rhythm atria (10.8±2.2 vs. 5.2±1.3 platelet CD41 AU, p<0.01). Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that about 62% of fibrillating endocardium was covered by platelets, compared to 12% of non-sinus rhythm atria. The addition of simvastatin significantly reduced CD40 expression, as well as platelet adhesion to fibrillating atria, with the effects not being reversed by the addition of mevalonic acid.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that chronic atrial fibrillation acutely upregulates CD40 expression and platelet adhesion to the endocardium, and that simvastatin is effective in modulating this expression, which may contribute to reducing the risk of intra-atrial thrombus formation.

title: Transmission of sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease by blood transfusion: risk factor or possible biases.
text: BACKGROUND The occurrence of transfusion-related transmissions of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) has highlighted the potential risk of other forms of CJD. To investigate, we conducted a case-control study of CJD patients with a definite or probable diagnosis (sporadic CJD, n = 741; genetic CJD, n = 175) and non-CJD patients with a definitive alternative diagnosis (n = 482) with available blood transfusion history. We evaluated the risk of exposure to blood transfusion occurring more than 10 years before disease onset and explored potential confounding factors using univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses. RESULTS In the univariate model, transfusion occurring more than 10 years before clinical onset was found to be significantly more common in sporadic CJD than in other neurological disorders (OR = 4.1). Adjusting for potential confounding factors in multivariate analysis revealed a significant increase in the risk of sporadic CJD after transfusion (OR = 5.05). No significant risk factors were identified in the analysis of genetic CJD patients. CONCLUSION This case-control study is the first to demonstrate a significant risk of transfusion occurring more than 10 years before clinical onset in sporadic CJD patients. While the biological plausibility of these findings is unclear, they suggest that previous epidemiological reports may have underestimated the risk of blood transmission in sporadic CJD.

title: Advantages and pitfalls of fructosamine and glycated albumin in the diagnosis and treatment of diabetes.
text: The accurate diagnosis and monitoring of diabetic patients are crucial in reducing the risk of complications. Currently, diagnostic and prognostic strategies in diabetes rely on two main tests: plasma (or capillary) glucose and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). However, these measures have limitations and can be affected by various clinical and analytical factors. Alternative indices of glucose homeostasis, such as fructosamine and glycated albumin (GA), may provide valuable additional information, especially in patients where HbA1c measurements may be biased or unreliable. These patients include those with rapid changes in glucose homeostasis and larger glycemic excursions, as well as those with red blood cell disorders and renal disease. The available evidence suggests that GA has a superior diagnostic efficiency compared to fructosamine in a wide range of clinical settings. Additionally, the method for measuring GA is more standardized and less susceptible to preanalytical variables than those used for fructosamine. Another advantage of GA over HbA1c is its lower reagent cost and the ability to automate GA analysis on many conventional laboratory instruments. While further studies are needed to fully establish GA as a complement or replacement for HbA1c, the use of GA may improve clinical management in patients where HbA1c values are unreliable.

title: Catalytic-Independent Functions of PARP-1 Determine Sox2 Pioneer Activity at Intractable Genomic Loci.
text: Pioneer transcription factors (TFs) act as genomic first responders by binding to inaccessible regions of chromatin, promoting enhancer formation. The mechanism by which pioneer TFs access chromatin remains an open question. Our study reveals that PARP-1, a nucleosome-binding protein, collaborates with the intrinsic properties of the pioneer TF Sox2 to facilitate its binding to difficult-to-reach genomic locations in embryonic stem cells. These actions of PARP-1 occur independently of its poly(ADP-ribosyl) transferase activity. PARP-1-dependent Sox2-binding sites are located in regions of the genome with relatively high nucleosome occupancy and low co-binding by other transcription factors. PARP-1 stabilizes Sox2 binding to nucleosomes at these suboptimal sites through cooperative interactions on DNA. Our findings illuminate the distinct and extrinsic factors that influence Sox2 pioneer activity. The conditional pioneer activity observed with Sox2 at a subset of binding sites may be a common feature of other pioneer TFs operating at difficult-to-reach genomic locations.

title: Steroid regulation of C. elegans diapause, developmental timing, and longevity.
text: Hormones play a pivotal role in the regulation of major life stage transitions and developmental timing events in various species. In the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, the steroid hormone receptor DAF-12 acts as a central conductor of developmental timing, stage specification, and longevity. DAF-12 integrates environmental and physiological cues to control life history progression, and it is intricately linked to a complex network of pathways that govern diverse biological processes. Recent research has provided valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms governing life stage transitions in the worm and the role of steroid hormone regulation in shaping biological time.

title: A core subunit of Polycomb repressive complex 1 is broadly conserved in function but not primary sequence.
text: Polycomb Group (PcG) proteins regulate heritable gene silencing by altering chromatin structure. A crucial PcG complex, PRC1, compacts chromatin and inhibits chromatin remodeling. In Drosophila melanogaster, the disordered C-terminal region of PSC (PSC-CTR) mediates these non-covalent effects on chromatin, and is essential for survival. Due to the low conservation of PSC-CTR sequence among organisms, the extent of its effects on chromatin outside of Drosophila was unclear. The absence of folded domains made it challenging to comprehend how the PSC-CTR sequence encodes its function. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms and extend of conservation of PSC-CTR activity, we identified and examined 17 PSC-CTR proteins from metazoans spanning chordates to arthropods. Our findings revealed that PSC-CTR sequences are minimally conserved but highly charged and disordered. Active PSC-CTRs, which bind DNA tightly and inhibit chromatin remodeling efficiently, are distinguished from less active ones by the absence of extensive negative charges. We found that increasing the distribution of negative charges can enhance PSC-CTR activity. Using the defined sequence properties, we predicted the presence of active PSC-CTRs in additional diverse genomes. Our analysis indicates extensive conservation of PSC-CTR activity across metazoans. This conclusion could not have been deduced from sequence alignments. Furthermore, we discovered that plant genomes lacking active PSC-CTRs instead contain a functional analogue of PcG protein, EMF1. Our study suggests that a disordered domain with dispersed negative charges underlies PRC1 activity and is conserved across metazoans and plants.

title: Dietary status of trained female cyclists.
text: In this study, the diets of eight highly trained female cyclists were evaluated to assess their nutritional quality. Each cyclist kept a 3-day food record, which was analyzed using a computerized software package to determine the nutrient content of their diets. Additionally, blood samples were collected to evaluate hemoglobin, hematocrit, and albumin levels. The results showed that the cyclists' diets were significantly below the Recommended Daily Allowance (RDA) for several nutrients, including energy (85% RDA), carbohydrates (4.4 gm/kg body weight per day), folic acid (76% RDA), magnesium (81%), iron (59%), and zinc (48%). Moreover, more than one-third of the cyclists failed to meet the RDA for several micronutrients, including pyridoxine, folic acid, cobalamin, vitamin E, magnesium, iron, and zinc. Hemoglobin, hematocrit, and albumin levels were all within the normal range, but the hemoglobin values were mostly in the lower 50% of normal range. The study found that the cyclists' diets were low in foods such as meats, poultry, fish, beans, peas, and nuts, which are important for nutritional quality. The study suggests that these athletes could benefit from nutrition education and diet counseling to improve their dietary quality.

title: Regulation of Pax-3 expression in the dermomyotome and its role in muscle development.
text: Segmented mesoderm in vertebrates gives rise to a diverse array of cell types during embryonic development, including the axial skeleton and muscle. Multiple transcription factors, containing a paired domain (Pax proteins), are expressed in segmented mesoderm during embryogenesis. These include Pax-3 and a related gene, Pax-7, which are expressed in the segmental plate and dermomyotome. In this study, we investigate the role of notochordal signals in patterning the expression of Pax-3, Pax-7, and Pax-9 in somites, and the subsequent differentiation of cell types derived from the somitic mesoderm. We specifically assess the function of the Pax-3 gene in the differentiation of cell types originating from the dermomyotome by analyzing the development of muscle in splotch mouse embryos, which lack a functional Pax-3 gene. Our findings reveal that a population of Pax-3-expressing cells derived from the dermomyotome, which normally migrate into the limb, are absent in homozygous splotch embryos, resulting in lost limb muscles. Notably, no abnormalities were observed in trunk musculature of splotch embryos, indicating that Pax-3 is essential for the development of limb muscles but not trunk muscle.

title: Angiopoietin 2 is a partial agonist/antagonist of Tie2 signaling in the endothelium.
text:
Original Text:
Angiopoietin 2 (Ang2) was initially shown to be a competitive antagonist of Ang1, a receptor tyrosine kinase found in endothelial cells (ECs). However, subsequent studies have reported conflicting results on whether Ang2 acts as an agonist or antagonist of Tie2. Our findings reveal that Ang2 acts as an agonist when Ang1 is absent and as a dose-dependent antagonist when Ang1 is present. Exogenous Ang2 activates Tie2 and the pro-migratory, pro-survival PI3K/Akt pathway in ECs, although with less potency and lower affinity than exogenous Ang1. Interestingly, ECs produce Ang2 but not Ang1, and this endogenous Ang2 maintains Tie2, PI3K, and Akt activities, and promotes EC survival, migration, and tube formation. However, when ECs are stimulated with Ang1 and Ang2, Ang2 dose-dependently inhibits Ang1-induced Tie2 phosphorylation, Akt activation, and EC survival. Our findings demonstrate that Ang2 is both an agonist and an antagonist of Tie2, and that endogenous Ang2 maintains a level of Tie2 activation necessary for various EC functions. These findings may help reconcile conflicting reports of Ang2's effect on Tie2, enhance our understanding of receptor tyrosine kinase signal transduction mechanisms, and inform the targeting of Ang2 and Tie2 in conditions such as sepsis and cancer.

title: Bacteremia caused by a strain of Desulfovibrio related to the provisionally named Desulfovibrio fairfieldensis.
text: Over the course of 5 years, eight isolates of Desulfovibrio spp. were obtained from abdominal or brain abscesses, or blood. Seven of these isolates were part of a mixed flora, while one strain was isolated in pure culture from the blood of a patient with peritonitis of appendicular origin. Analysis of the 16S rRNA gene sequences revealed that this strain was closely related to Desulfovibrio fairfieldensis. This report describes the fourth isolate of D. fairfieldensis to be isolated in pure culture or as a predominant part of the flora, and to be associated with infectious processes. These findings suggest that D. fairfieldensis may have a higher pathogenic potential than other Desulfovibrio species.

title: Vitamin D: The "sunshine" vitamin.
text: Around 50% of the global population suffers from vitamin D insufficiency, affecting an estimated 1 billion people worldwide, regardless of age or ethnicity. This widespread deficiency can be attributed to lifestyle factors such as reduced outdoor activities and environmental factors like air pollution, which limit exposure to sunlight and hinder the skin's ability to produce vitamin D through UVB induction. Considering that hypovitaminosis D is an independent risk factor for total mortality in the general population, it has become a significant public health concern. Recent studies suggest that people may require more vitamin D than previously recommended to prevent chronic diseases. As the number of vitamin D deficient individuals continues to increase, the importance of this hormone in overall health and the prevention of chronic diseases is receiving increased attention in scientific research. Vitamin D insufficiency affects people of all ages, and as few foods contain vitamin D, guidelines recommend supplementation at suggested daily intake and tolerable upper limit levels. Measuring the serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level is often the initial diagnostic test for patients at risk of deficiency. Treatment with either vitamin D2 or vitamin D3 is recommended for deficient individuals. A 2007 meta-analysis found that vitamin D supplementation was associated with a significantly lower mortality rate. This review aims to summarize the mechanisms that are believed to underlie the relationship between vitamin D and health, as well as its biology and clinical implications.

title: Cyclin D1 activation in B-cell malignancy: association with changes in histone acetylation, DNA methylation, and RNA polymerase II binding to both promoter and distal sequences.
text: The expression of the Cyclin D1 gene is deregulated by chromosomal translocations in certain types of cancer, including mantle cell lymphoma and a subset of multiple myeloma. The molecular mechanisms behind this deregulation are not fully understood, but changes in the acetylation and methylation of histones and DNA may play a role. To investigate this further, we examined the patterns of DNA methylation and histone acetylation at the Cyclin D1 locus on chromosome 11q13 in B-cell malignancies. We found that the Cyclin D1 promoter was hypomethylated and hyperacetylated in cells with deregulated Cyclin D1 expression, while the upstream region of the gene was methylated and hypoacetylated in non-expressing cells. Interestingly, we also found that hypomethylated DNA and hyperacetylated histones were present at the Cyclin D1 promoter, but not in the nearby major translocation cluster region, in non-tumorigenic B and T cells. Our results suggest a model where RNA polymerase II binds to IgH regulatory sequences and then activates the Cyclin D1 promoter through either long-range polymerase transfer or tracking.

title: The physiological regulation of toll-like receptor expression and function in humans.
text:
Eleven mammalian toll-like receptors (TLRs) have been identified to date, and they play a crucial role in regulating immune responses. However, the factors that regulate TLR expression and function in vivo are poorly understood. To investigate this, we studied the physiological regulation of TLR expression and function in humans.
We collected peripheral venous blood samples from healthy volunteers at different times of day, specifically during the peak and nadir of the endogenous cortisol concentration, to examine the influence of diurnal rhythmicity on TLR expression and function. We found that TLRs 1, 2, 4, and 9 did not show any diurnal rhythmicity in their expression. However, we observed that the upregulation of costimulatory molecules (CD80 and CD86) and antigen-presenting molecules (MHC class II) on CD14(+) monocytes following activation with specific TLR ligands was greater in samples collected in the evening compared to those collected in the morning.
To examine the influence of physical stress on TLR expression and function, we collected peripheral venous blood samples from healthy volunteers at rest and following 1.5 hours of strenuous exercise in a hot environment (34°C). We found that strenuous exercise resulted in a decrease in the expression of TLRs 1, 2, and 4 on CD14(+) monocytes. Additionally, the upregulation of CD80, CD86, MHC class II, and interleukin-6 by CD14(+) monocytes following activation with specific TLR ligands was decreased in samples obtained following exercise compared to those obtained at rest.
These results demonstrate that TLR function is subject to modulation under physiological conditions in vivo and provide evidence for the role of immunomodulatory hormones in the regulation of TLR function.

title: A review of psychosocial needs of breast-cancer patients and their relatives.
text:
Objective: To identify the psychosocial needs of breast-cancer patients and their relatives, as well as the factors affecting these needs, and to develop a tentative model to guide further research and need assessments in clinical practice.
Background: Women diagnosed with breast cancer face the challenge of dealing with a potentially life-threatening illness, which can be emotionally and physically demanding. The treatment and recovery process can be just as challenging for their relatives. Conducting a need assessment can help clinicians identify the appropriate support and care required by patients and their families.
Design: Literature review
Methodology: A thorough literature search was conducted using electronic databases and specific research terms to identify relevant articles. In total, 20 articles were analyzed.
Results: The needs of patients were found to include:
1. Treatment-related physical and social impairments, such as fatigue, menopausal symptoms, and changes in body image.
2. Emotional distress, including fear of recurrence, anxiety, and depression.
Partners also have specific needs, including:
1. Help to protect themselves and the patient from various threats.
2. Want information about the patient's condition and themselves about the prognosis and perspectives.
There is a lack of knowledge regarding the needs of relatives, and the interaction between patients and their partners can be influenced by factors such as mutual familial support, women's and partners' health, and emotional distress.
Conclusion: A tentative family-based model is proposed to guide further research and clinical support. Further research is needed to determine which psychosocial factors may influence the fulfillment of patients' and relatives' needs.
Implications for Clinical Practice: The proposed model can serve as a framework for healthcare professionals to assess patients' and relatives' met and unmet needs and the real demand for support, counseling, and education.

title: Poly(ADP-ribose) Polymerase 1 Represses Liver X Receptor-mediated ABCA1 Expression and Cholesterol Efflux in Macrophages.
text: Liver X receptors (LXR) are nuclear receptors that play a central role in the reverse cholesterol transport process by activating ATP-binding cassette transporters (ABCA1 and ABCG1) that facilitate cholesterol efflux from cells. mouse models of atherosclerosis have shown that LXR activation reduces atherosclerosis and promotes regression of established plaques. However, the regulatory factors that impact LXR-mediated gene activation in macrophages remain unclear. To identify new regulators of LXR, we used affinity purification and mass spectrometry to analyze LXRα protein complexes and identified poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase-1 (PARP-1) as a LXR-associated protein. PARP-1 interacts with both LXRα and LXRβ. Both PARP-1 depletion and inhibition enhance LXR ligand-induced ABCA1 expression in RAW 264.7 macrophages and primary bone marrow-derived macrophages, but do not affect LXR-mediated expression of other target genes, ABCG1 and SREBP-1c. Chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments confirmed PARP-1 recruitment to the LXR response element in the ABCA1 promoter. Furthermore, we found that LXR is poly(ADP-ribosyl)ated by PARP-1, which may explain how PARP-1 influences LXR function. Importantly, the PARP inhibitor 3-aminobenzamide enhances macrophage ABCA1-mediated cholesterol efflux to lipid-poor apolipoprotein AI. These findings highlight the crucial role of PARP-1 in LXR-regulated lipid homeostasis. Understanding the interplay between PARP-1 and LXR may provide insights into developing novel therapeutics for treating atherosclerosis.

title: Emergency contraception: advance provision in a young, high-risk clinic population.
text:
Objective: To assess the impact of providing emergency contraception in advance on its use and potential secondary effects on regular contraceptive use.
Methods: We conducted a controlled trial among female clients aged 16-24 years at a publicly funded family planning clinic. Participants were randomly assigned to receive advance provision of emergency contraception and education (treatment) or education only (control). Follow-up was conducted among 263 participants (133 treatment, 130 control) and the main outcome measures included emergency contraception knowledge and use, frequency of unprotected sex, and patterns of contraceptive use in the past 4 months.
Results: Participants were aware of emergency contraception at follow-up, but the treatment group was three times more likely to use it (P =.006). Although the treatment group did not report higher frequencies of unprotected sex than the control group, women in the treatment group (28%) were more likely than those in the control group (17%) to report using less effective contraception at follow-up compared with enrollment (P =.05). The proportion of women in both groups who reported consistent pill use increased from enrollment to follow-up (34% versus 45%), but the control group (58%) was more likely than the treatment group (32%) to report consistent pill use at follow-up (P =.03).
Conclusion: Providing emergency contraception in advance increased its use, but education alone did not have a significant impact. Changes in less effective contraceptive methods and patterns of pill use were potential negative effects that need to be explored in relation to observed benefits.

title: Immunophenotypic analysis of AIDS-related diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and clinical implications in patients from AIDS malignancies consortium clinical trials 010 and 034
text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) in patients with HIV infection exhibits clinical heterogeneity, and immunohistochemical markers can predict clinical outcome. In this study, we evaluated the prognostic significance of subtyping DLBCL into germinal center (GC) versus non-GC subtypes, as well as the expression of Ki-67, BCL-2, FOXP1, and Blimp-1/PRDM1 in 81 DLBCLs from patients with AIDS. We found that the GC and non-GC subtypes did not differ significantly in terms of overall survival or CD4 count at cancer presentation. The presence of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was observed in both subtypes, but the frequency was lower in the GC subtype. The expression of FOXP1, Blimp-1/PRDM1, and BCL-2 was not correlated with outcome in HIV-infected patients with DLBCL. Our results suggest that in HIV-infected patients with DLBCL, currently used immunohistochemical markers may not be clinically relevant. The only predictive marker found was Ki-67, where a higher proliferation index was associated with better survival, indicating a better response to therapy in patients with higher proliferation rates.

title: Prion-like activity of Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase: implications for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
text: Neurodegenerative diseases are part of a larger group of disorders known as proteinopathies, which are characterized by the misfolding and aggregation of specific proteins. Recent experimental evidence suggests that prion-like mechanisms may play a role in many common neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, tauopathies, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). These diseases are marked by the aberrant misfolding and aggregation of proteins, which can lead to neurotoxicity and contribute to the progression of the disease. ALS, a lethal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive degeneration of motor neurons, is a classical proteinopathy and is typified by the formation of protein inclusions within and around motor neurons. Misfolded/oxidized SOD1 protein has been shown to be highly toxic to motor neurons and plays a prominent role in the pathology of ALS. Recent research has also identified prion-like properties in both mutant and wild-type SOD1, which may provide the molecular basis for the contiguous spread of the disease through the nervous system. This review will examine the current state of knowledge regarding the prion-like properties of SOD1 and discuss the proposed mechanisms of intercellular transmission.

title: Analysis of Epstein-Barr virus-regulated host gene expression changes through primary B-cell outgrowth reveals delayed kinetics of latent membrane protein 1-mediated NF-κB activation.
text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is an oncogenic human herpesvirus that alters the gene expression of host cells to immortalize primary B cells. In this study, we examined the changes in EBV-regulated host gene expression during primary B-cell infection, from the initial proliferation phase to the formation of lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs). While the majority of EBV-regulated mRNAs were altered during the transition from resting, uninfected B cells to initial B-cell proliferation, a significant number of mRNAs underwent unique changes from early proliferation to LCL outgrowth. We identified perpetually and dynamically EBV-regulated biological processes, protein classes, and transcription factor targets. Early after infection, genes associated with proliferation, stress responses, and the p53 pathway were highly enriched, but the transition from early to long-term outgrowth was characterized by genes involved in the inhibition of apoptosis, actin cytoskeleton, and NF-κB activity. It was previously believed that the primary viral protein responsible for NF-κB activation, latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1), is expressed within 2 days after infection. Our findings indicate that while this is true, LCL-level LMP1 expression and NF-κB activity are not evident until 3 weeks after primary B-cell infection. Additionally, heterologous NF-κB activation during the first week after infection increased the transformation efficiency, while early NF-κB inhibition had no effect on transformation. However, inhibition of NF-κB was not toxic to EBV-infected cells until LMP1 levels and NF-κB activity were high. These findings collectively highlight the dynamic nature of EBV-regulated host gene expression and support the notion that early EBV-infected proliferating B cells have a fundamentally distinct growth and survival phenotype from that of LCLs.

title: Clinical and laboratory features of adult T-cell leukaemia lymphoma in Barbados.
text: In this study, we investigate the clinical and pathological features of 23 Afro-Caribbean patients with adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATLL) who were admitted to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Barbados over a 5-year period. Our sample consisted of 9 males and 14 females, with a median age of 38 years (range: 14-84). Of the 23 patients, 12 had acute leukaemia, 10 had lymphoma (including 4 with solitary extra-nodal lesions), and 1 had the smouldering subtype. Notably, 2 patients had a history of tropical spastic paraparesis/HTLV-I associated myelopathy (TSP/HAM). Unfortunately, the prognosis for these patients was poor, with only 3 complete responses to chemotherapy (CHOP) observed, lasting from 9 to 36 months. Our findings suggest that ATLL in Barbados is similar to the disease in other Caribbean islands and Japan, with one notable exception: the age of onset in Barbados is significantly lower than in Japan.

title: Acoustic landmarks drive delta-theta oscillations to enable speech comprehension by facilitating perceptual parsing.
text: A growing body of research suggests that low-frequency (<10 Hz) oscillations in the auditory cortex are synchronized with incoming speech and other complex auditory signals. Specifically, recent studies have identified critical-band temporal envelopes as the acoustic feature being reflected by the phase of these oscillations. However, the exact mechanism by which this alignment mediates intelligibility remains unclear. Here, we investigate the hypothesis that the ' sharpness' of temporal fluctuations in the critical band envelope acts as a temporal cue to speech syllabic rate, guiding delta-theta rhythms to synchronize with the stimulus and enhance decoding. Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings, we demonstrate that reducing temporal fluctuations at the syllabic rate leads to decreased envelope-tracking activity, while reinstating these fluctuations restores this activity and enhances intelligibility. These findings support the notion that the sharpness of cochlear output fluctuations drives cortical oscillatory activity to track and entrain to the stimulus at its syllabic rate, facilitating parsing of the stimulus into meaningful chunks for further decoding. This process likely improves perception and intelligibility.

title: Crystal structures of complexes of the small ribosomal subunit with tetracycline, edeine and IF3.
text:
The small subunit of the ribosome plays a crucial role in decoding genetic information and initiating protein synthesis. By using X-ray crystallography, we investigated the structures of three complexes of the small subunit of Thermus thermophilus in association with the A-site inhibitor tetracycline, the universal initiation inhibitor edeine, and the C-terminal domain of the translation initiation factor IF3. Our analysis revealed the specific site on the small subunit where tetracycline blocks the A-site, as well as the binding sites of edeine and IF3. Our findings shed light on the mechanisms of initiation and provide new insights into the role of these factors in protein synthesis.
(Note: I have reworded some of the sentences to improve clarity and readability, while trying to preserve the accuracy and scientific content of the original text.)

title: Plasmid-encoded proinsulin preserves C-peptide while specifically reducing proinsulin-specific CD8⁺ T cells in type 1 diabetes.
text: Researchers have long sought a therapy for type 1 diabetes (T1D) that targets the specific autoimmune response in the disease while sparing the rest of the immune system. Proinsulin is a major target of the adaptive immune response in T1D, and scientists hypothesized that an engineered DNA plasmid encoding proinsulin (BHT-3021) might help preserve β cell function in T1D patients by reducing the frequency of insulin-specific CD8⁺ T cells. In a recent study, 80 subjects with recent-onset T1D were randomly assigned to receive intramuscular injections of BHT-3021 or a placebo, twice weekly for 12 weeks. C-peptide levels, an exploratory efficacy measure, and islet-specific CD8⁺ T cell frequencies were monitored in a blinded fashion. Four dose levels of BHT-3021 were evaluated: 0.3, 1.0, 3.0, and 6.0 mg. No serious adverse events related to BHT-3021 were observed, and C-peptide levels improved at all doses, particularly at 1 mg at the 15-week time point (+19.5% BHT-3021 versus -8.8% BHT-placebo, P < 0.026). Proinsulin-reactive CD8⁺ T cells, but not T cells against unrelated islet or foreign molecules, declined in the BHT-3021 arm (P < 0.006). No significant changes were noted in interferon-γ, interleukin-4 (IL-4), or IL-10 production in CD4 T cells. These findings suggest that BHT-3021 reduces the frequency of CD8⁺ T cells reactive to proinsulin while preserving C-peptide over the course of dosing.

title: Dexamethasone and risk of nausea and vomiting and postoperative bleeding after tonsillectomy in children: a randomized trial.
text: A recent study investigated the effectiveness of dexamethasone in preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in pediatric tonsillectomy patients. The experiment was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted at a major teaching hospital in Switzerland between February 2005 and December 2007. A total of 215 children underwent elective tonsillectomy and were randomly assigned to receive either dexamethasone or a placebo intravenously after anesthesia induction. Acetaminophen-codeine and ibuprofen were administered as postoperative analgesics. Follow-up continued until the 10th postoperative day. The primary outcome measure was the prevention of PONV at 24 hours, while secondary endpoints included the reduction in the need for ibuprofen at 24 hours and evaluation of adverse effects. The results showed that 44% of children who received a placebo experienced PONV at 24 hours, compared to 38% of those who received dexamethasone at 0.05, 0.15, or 0.5 mg/kg. In addition, children who received dexamethasone required significantly less ibuprofen. However, there were 26 postoperative bleeding episodes in 22 children, with four percent of children who received a placebo experiencing bleeding, compared to 11%, 4%, and 24% of those who received dexamethasone at 0.05, 0.15, and 0.5 mg/kg, respectively. The trial was stopped early due to safety concerns and the results suggest that dexamethasone decreased the risk of PONV dose-dependently but was associated with an increased risk of postoperative bleeding.

title: Detection of sweet and umami taste in the absence of taste receptor T1r3.
text: The flavor receptors of sugars (sweetness) and glutamate (umami) are believed to be detected by T1r receptors expressed in taste cells. Molecular genetics and heterologous expression suggest that T1r2 and T1r3 serve as sweet-responsive receptors, while T1r1 and T1r3, as well as a truncated form of the type 4 metabotropic glutamate receptor (taste-mGluR4), are umami-responsive receptors. Our findings reveal that mice lacking T1r3 fail to exhibit a preference for artificial sweeteners and display diminished but not completely abolished behavioral and nerve responses to sugars and umami compounds. These results indicate that T1r3-independent sweet- and umami-responsive receptors and/or pathways exist in taste cells.

title: Cyclin A1 is required for meiosis in the male mouse
text: The mammalian A-type cyclin family consists of two members, cyclin A1 (encoded by Ccna1) and cyclin A2 (encoded by Ccna2). Cyclin A2 promotes both the G1/S and G2/M transitions, and deletion of Ccna2 in mice is lethal in embryonic stages. Cyclin A1 is specific to the germ cell lineage in mice and humans, with the highest levels found in the testis and certain myeloid leukemia cells. To investigate the role of cyclin A1 and potential redundancy among the cyclins in vivo, we generated mice with a null mutation of Ccna1. Ccna1-/- males were sterile due to a block in spermatogenesis before the first meiotic division, while females were normal. Meiosis arrest in Ccna1–/– males was associated with increased germ cell apoptosis, desynapsis abnormalities, and reduced activation of Cdc2 kinase at the end of meiotic prophase. Cyclin A1 is essential for spermatocyte passage into the first meiotic division in male mice, a function that cannot be complemented by the co-expressed B-type cyclins.

title: Metabolic effects of isoenergetic nutrient exchange over 24 hours in relation to obesity in women.
text: Utilizing 24-hour whole body indirect calorimetry, the effects of feeding, during a sedentary test day, isoenergetic diets varying in fat (3% or 40% of total energy) and carbohydrate (82% or 45% of total energy) content were examined in three groups of women: lean, obese, and "post-obese" after slimming. Energy expenditure was higher in absolute terms in the obese women. When compared to energy balance, 24-hour energy expenditure was lower by 3-7% when fasting, but there were no significant differences in energy expenditure between the two diets or between the groups. However, the thermogenic effect of the high carbohydrate diet was significantly greater than that of the high fat diet (5.8% vs 3.5% of energy expenditure, P < 0.01). The post-obese group had lower energy expenditure per kilogram of fat-free mass (FFM) than controls when fasting and when high-fat fed, but this trend was not observed in the obese group. Notably, sleeping energy expenditure was particularly low in the post-obese group when high-fat fed. Diurnal variations in respiratory quotient (RQ) were analyzed and found to exhibit a more pronounced rise in morning RQ from the nocturnal minimum in the obese and post-obese groups, which may suggest an energy-saving mechanism through greater availability of stored dietary carbohydrate.

title: Acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease: an integrated clinical syndrome.
text: The previously held belief that individuals who experience acute kidney injury (AKI) tend to fully recover and retain their renal function is no longer accurate. AKI can result in end-stage renal disease (ESRD) directly, and increase the risk of developing chronic kidney disease (CKD) and worsening of underlying CKD. The severity, duration, and frequency of AKI are important predictors of poor patient outcomes. Additionally, CKD is a significant risk factor for the development and progression of AKI.
