Experimental data support the clinical findings and the bidirectional nature of the relationships between AKI and CKD. Reductions in renal mass and nephron number, vascular insufficiency, cell cycle disruption, and maladaptive repair mechanisms are key modulators of progression in patients with and without coexistent CKD. Moreover, the distinction between AKI and CKD may be artificial, and a more integrated approach to understanding this clinical syndrome is warranted. The clinical spectrum of disease state and outcome is determined by host factors, including the balance of adaptive and maladaptive repair mechanisms over time. Therefore, long-term follow-up is crucial for patients with first episodes of AKI, even if they initially presented with normal renal function.

title: Fatty acids as modulators of the immune response.
text: Abundant research has demonstrated that fatty acids can regulate inflammation and immune responses. Many of these studies have focused on omega-3 fatty acids, which have shown potent anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties in various diseases, including autoimmunity, arthritis, and infection. However, the evidence from human trials is less conclusive. This review provides a historical context for understanding how fatty acids affect the immune system and critically evaluates the evidence from two recent landmark reports from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality regarding the effectiveness of omega-3 fatty acids in treating rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, and other immune-mediated diseases. Additionally, the review examines the results of human clinical trials investigating the impact of various bioactive fatty acids on ex vivo and in vivo immune responses, highlighting limitations in experimental design and immune assays commonly used. The disparity between expected and observed results in this field has been a source of disappointment, and recommendations for improving both animal-based and human studies are provided.

title: Common and rare variants in multifactorial susceptibility to common diseases
text: Here, we provide a historical perspective on the search for genetic variants that influence an individual's susceptibility to chronic diseases, from the groundbreaking work of RA Fisher to the current excitement of whole-genome association studies (WGAS). We then delve into the underlying concepts of identifying common variants as disease causal factors and contrast them with the basic ideas behind the rare variant hypothesis. The identification of rare variants involves carefully selectering candidate genes, utilizing highly efficient resequencing techniques, and assessing the functional consequences of the implicated variant. We believe that this approach can be successfully employed currently to uncover the contribution of rare variants to the complex inheritance of common diseases, which could pave the way for the implementation of much-needed preventative screening programs.

title: Cell-cell adhesion and signalling.
text: Recent discoveries have shed light on the signaling pathways activated by Rho small GTPases, which play a crucial role in coordinating cell-cell adhesion, stability, and functionality. Of particular interest is the intricate interplay between adherens junctions, Rho protein activation, and the dynamic interplay between microtubules, actin filaments, and intermediate filaments. This interplay has profound implications for the functional regulation of cell-cell adhesion and suggests a more integrated understanding of signaling processes.

title: Fibroblast growth factor 21 as an emerging metabolic regulator: clinical perspectives.
text: Fibroblast Growth Factor 21 (FGF21) is a metabolic hormone produced by the liver and expressed in adipocytes and the pancreas. It regulates glucose and lipid metabolism through various actions in these tissues and the brain. In mice, fasting leads to increased expression of FGF21 in the liver, which stimulates gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and ketogenesis as an adaptive response to fasting and starvation. In the fed state, FGF21 acts as an autocrine factor in adipocytes, regulating the activity of PPAR-γ through a feed-forward loop mechanism. Recombinant FGF21 administration has been shown to confer multiple metabolic benefits in obese mice and diabetic monkeys, including improved insulin sensitivity, blood glucose, lipid profile, and body weight, without exhibiting mitogenic or other side effects. However, in human studies, high circulating FGF21 levels are found in obesity and related cardiometabolic disorders, including the metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and coronary artery disease. These findings suggest the presence of FGF21 resistance or compensatory responses to the underlying metabolic stress, and the need for supraphysiological doses of FGF21 to achieve therapeutic efficacy. On the other hand, serum FGF21 has been identified as a potential biomarker for the early detection of these cardiometabolic disorders. This review summarizes recent advances in understanding the physiological and clinical aspects of FGF21.

title: Assessment of the cerebral circulation in adults with coarctation of the aorta.
text:
Objective: To investigate the prevalence of intracranial aneurysms (IA) in adults with coarctation of the aorta (CoA) and identify potential risk factors.
Background: There is a fivefold increase in the frequency of IA in adults with CoA; however, current guidelines for management of adults with CoA do not universally recommend computed tomography angiography (CTA) or magnetic resonance imaging of the intracranial vessels.
Methods: Prospectively enrolled adults aged ≥18 years with CoA underwent CTA of the intracranial vessels from January 2008 to February 2011. Data on prognostic variables were analyzed using Fisher's exact and two sample t-test.
Results: A total of 43 patients (58% female, 33.55 ± 10.21 years) completed CTA of the intracranial vessels, and five patients (11%) were found to have IA. The age of patients with IA was significantly higher than those without (45.6 ± 8.17 vs. 30.89 ± 7.89, P = 0.0003). No statistically significant differences were detected between measurements of fasting lipid profiles, C-reactive protein, brain natriuretic peptide, and homocysteine levels among CoA patients with and without IA (P = not significant).
Conclusion: Prospective screening of adults with CoA confirmed the increased prevalence of IA but also identified increased age as the sole risk factor, suggesting that screening is justified particularly in the fourth and fifth decades of life. Further studies are required to investigate the development, natural history, and treatment of IA.

title: Bioenergetic aspects of apoptosis, necrosis and mitoptosis
text:
In this review, I discuss the interplay between bioenergetic processes and programmed cell death phenomena, including apoptosis and necrosis, as well as mitochondrial suicide (mitoptosis). Based on my analysis, I have reached the following conclusions:
(I) ATP and elevated mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ) are necessary for certain stages of apoptosis and necrosis.
(II) Apoptosis, even when it occurs with increased ΔΨ and ATP levels, ultimately results in a collapse of ΔΨ and decreased ATP levels.
(III) A moderate decrease in ATP levels for short or long periods of time leads to apoptosis or necrosis, respectively. In some cases, cell death is mediated by a ΔΨ-dependent overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) by the initial (Complex I) and middle (Complex III) spans of the respiratory chain. ROS trigger mitoptosis, which is thought to eliminate intracellular mitochondria with ROS overproduction. Massive mitoptosis can result in cell death due to the release of cell death proteins from the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol.
In summary, my review highlights the vital role of bioenergetics in programmed cell death, particularly in the regulation of ΔΨ and ATP levels, which are essential for various stages of apoptosis and necrosis. Understanding these interrelations can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms of cell death and may have implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for cancer and other diseases.

title: Embryonic stem cells require Wnt proteins to prevent differentiation to epiblast stem cells
text:
Pluripotent stem cells exist in two states: naive and primed, as exemplified by mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and more developed epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs; reference). In the naive state of ESCs, the genome displays an unusual open conformation and exhibits minimal repressive epigenetic marks. Conversely, EpiSCs have activated their epigenetic machinery, allowing differentiation towards embryonic cell types. The transition from naive to primed pluripotency represents a crucial stage in cellular differentiation. However, the signaling pathways governing this fundamental process remain unclear.
Our research reveals that paracrine and autocrine Wnt signals are essential self-renewal factors for ESCs, and are required to inhibit their differentiation into EpiSCs. Additionally, we find that Wnt proteins, in combination with the cytokine LIF, are sufficient to support ESC self-renewal in the absence of any undefined factors, and can be used to derive new ESC lines, including those from non-permissive mouse strains. Our findings not only demonstrate that Wnt signals regulate the naive-to-primed pluripotency transition, but also identify Wnt as a crucial and limiting factor in ESC self-renewal.

title: CLIP identifies Nova-regulated RNA networks in the brain.
text: Nova proteins are specific to neurons and are the target of paraneoplastic opsoclonus myoclonus ataxia (POMA), an autoimmune neurological disorder characterized by abnormal motor inhibition. Nova proteins regulate pre-messenger RNA splicing in neurons by directly binding to RNA. To identify Nova RNA targets, we developed a method called CLIP (cross-linking and immunoprecipitation) to purify protein-RNA complexes from mouse brains. Using this method, we identified 34 transcripts that were identified multiple times. Thirty-four percent of these transcripts encode proteins involved in the neuronal synapse, while 29% are involved in neuronal inhibition. These splicing targets were confirmed in Nova-deficient mice, including c-Jun N-terminal kinase 2, neogenin, and gephyrin, which encodes a protein that clusters inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric acid and glycine receptors. CLIP reveals that Nova regulates a coherent set of RNAs encoding multiple components of the inhibitory synapse, which may explain why abnormal motor inhibition occurs in POMA.

title: Anti-Angiogenic Activity of Selected Receptor Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors, PD166285 and PD173074: Implications for Combination Treatment with Photodynamic Therapy
text:
Angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels from existing vasculature, is essential for tumor growth. This process involves coordinated signaling between endothelial and tumor cells through angiogenic growth factor signaling. Disrupting these events can have significant implications for slowing down tumor growth. To investigate the anti-angiogenic and anti-tumor activities of two compounds, PD166285 and PD173074, in combination with photodynamic therapy (PDT), we evaluated their effects on RTK signaling in vitro and in vivo.
PD166285, a broad-spectrum RTK inhibitor, inhibited the activation of PDGFR-β, EGFR, and FGFR1TKs, as well as c-src TK, with an IC50 concentration range of 7-85 nM. In contrast, PD173074, a selective FGFR1TK inhibitor, demonstrated >100-fold selective growth inhibitory action towards human umbilical vein endothelial cells compared to a panel of tumor cell lines, with an IC50 concentration of 26 nM. Both compounds inhibited the formation of microcapillaries on Matrigel-coated plastic, indicating anti-angiogenic activity.
In vivo anti-angiogenesis studies in mice revealed that oral administration of either PD166285 (1-25 mg/kg) or PD173074 (25-100 mg/kg) generated dose-dependent inhibition of angiogenesis. Treatment with these compounds in combination with PDT resulted in significantly prolonged tumor regression compared to PDT alone (p<0.001). Many long-term survivors were also observed in the combination treatment groups. PD166285 and PD173074 displayed potent anti-angiogenic and anti-tumor activity, prolonging the duration of anti-tumor response to PDT.
Our findings suggest that interfering with membrane signal transduction by inhibitors of specific RTKs, such as FGFR1TK, may lead to the development of new chemotherapeutic agents that can limit tumor angiogenesis and regrowth following cytoreductive treatments such as PDT.

title: The VirB type IV secretion system of Bartonella henselae mediates invasion, proinflammatory activation and antiapoptotic protection of endothelial cells.
text:
Bartonella henselae, an arthropod-borne zoonotic pathogen, infects both feline reservoir hosts and incidentally infected humans, causing a range of clinical manifestations. Unique to this pathogen, B. henselae can colonize the human vascular endothelium, leading to inflammation and the formation of vasoproliferative lesions known as bacillary angiomatosis and bacillary peliosis. In vitro studies using cultured human endothelial cells revealed that the Type IV secretion system (T4SS) VirB is essential for establishing intraerythrocytic infection in mammalian reservoirs. Furthermore, we discovered that the VirB T4SS mediates most of the virulence attributes associated with the interaction between B. henselae and human endothelial cells, including:
1. Rearrangement of the actin cytoskeleton, leading to bacterial aggregate formation and internalization by the invasome structure.
2. Proinflammatory activation via NF-κB, resulting in cell adhesion molecule expression and chemokine secretion.
3. Inhibition of apoptotic cell death, leading to enhanced endothelial cell survival.
4. Cytostatic and cytotoxic effects at high bacterial titers, interfering with a potent VirB-independent mitogenic activity.
Our findings indicate that the VirB T4SS is a major virulence determinant of B. henselae, allowing the pathogen to target multiple endothelial cell functions.

title: Serum Cystatin C Is Related to Pulse Wave Velocity Even in Subjects with Normal Serum Creatinine
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between serum cystatin C and arterial stiffness in individuals with normal serum creatinine levels. A total of 2,018 participants (1,120 males and 898 females) were enrolled. We found a positive correlation between serum cystatin C levels and brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity (baPWV) in males, and in females, a positive correlation was observed between baPWV and serum cystatin C levels.
Using stepwise multivariate regression analysis, we identified age, waist circumference, heart rate, cystatin C level, triglyceride level, and fasting glucose as independent contributors to baPWV in males, while in females, age, heart rate, cystatin C level, fasting glucose, and insulin level were significant variables. Notably, these findings suggest that serum cystatin C may be a more predictable marker of arterial stiffness than serum creatinine and creatinine-based glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
In conclusion, this study's findings confirm that serum cystatin C is related to pulse wave velocity even in subjects with normal serum creatinine levels. Our results imply that cystatin C could be a more reliable marker of arterial stiffness than serum creatinine and creatinine-based GFR.

title: Screening for inhibition of Vibrio cholerae VipA-VipB interaction identifies small-molecule compounds active against type VI secretion.
text:
The type VI secretion system (T6SS) is the most prevalent bacterial secretion system and a crucial virulence mechanism employed by Gram-negative bacteria to either target eukaryotic cells or combat other microbes. The components of T6SS are highly variable, but some are deemed essential for its function. In Vibrio cholerae, two homologous proteins, VipA and VipB, have been identified in all T6SSs studied so far. The binding of an α-helical region of VipA to VipB is necessary for secretion to occur. In this study, we aimed to investigate whether this interaction could be blocked and hypothesized that such inhibition would result in the abrogation of T6S.
To achieve this, we utilized a library of 9,600 small-molecule compounds in a bacterial two-hybrid system (B2H) to identify compounds that could potentially block the binding of VipA-VipB. After excluding compounds that showed cytotoxicity towards eukaryotic cells, inhibited growth of Vibrio, or inhibited an unrelated B2H interaction, 34 compounds were further investigated for their ability to influence the T6SS-mediated secretion of hemolysin-coregulated protein (Hcp) or phospholipase A1 (PLA1) activity. Two compounds, KS100 and KS200, showed intermediate or strong effects in both assays. Analogues of these compounds were generated, and potent inhibitory compounds with desirable physicochemical properties were identified through in silico analysis. Since these compounds target a virulence mechanism without affecting bacterial replication, they have the potential to mitigate virulence with minimal risk for development of resistance.

title: Early life compartmentalization of human T cell differentiation and regulatory function in mucosal and lymphoid tissues
text:
The mechanisms of immune response during early life remain poorly understood, particularly in regards to the stimulation of the immune system and the proper activation of T cells. T cells play a crucial role in adaptive immunity, and studies in mice suggest that the localization of T cell subsets in tissues is crucial for both immune protection and regulation. However, the early development and function of T cells in human tissues remain unexplored.
To address this knowledge gap, we analyzed T cells in lymphoid and mucosal tissues from pediatric organ donors aged 0-2 years and compared them to T cells from adult organ donors. Our findings revealed significant differences in the composition and function of T cells in pediatric and adult tissues. In contrast to adult tissues, which are predominantly composed of memory T cells, pediatric blood and tissues contain a much higher proportion of naive T cells that recently emigrated from the thymus. Additionally, effector memory T cells (T(EM)) were primarily found in the lungs and small intestine. Furthermore, regulatory T cells (T(reg)) comprised a substantial portion (30-40%) of CD4(+) T cells in pediatric tissues, but were present at much lower frequencies (1-10%) in adult tissues.
Surprisingly, we found that early T cell functionality in pediatric tissues was confined to mucosal sites, such as the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts, which have the lowest T(reg):T(EM) cell ratios. This suggests that the immune system has mechanisms in place to control immune responses in early life, primarily in situ.
In conclusion, our findings provide new insights into the development and function of T cells in early life and shed light on the mechanisms that regulate the immune response during this critical period of growth and development.

title: Circulating microRNAs as biomarkers for hepatocellular carcinoma.
text: In this study, we aimed to investigate the potential of measuring serum levels of microRNAs (miRNAs) miR-16, miR-195, and miR-199a in differentiating hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) from chronic liver diseases (CLDs). We analyzed sera from 105 HCC patients, 107 CLD patients, and 71 normal control subjects using real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction. Our results showed that serum levels of miR-16 and miR-199a were significantly lower in HCC patients than in CLD patients or control subjects (P<0.01). As a single marker, miR-16 had the highest sensitivity for HCC, followed by miR-199a, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), des-gamma-carboxyprothrombin (DCP), AFP-L3%, and miR-195. The combination of miR-16, AFP, AFP-L3%, and DCP yielded the optimal combination of sensitivity (92.4%) and specificity (78.5%) for HCC overall and when analysis was restricted to patients with tumors size smaller than 3 cm. As a second-line HCC marker, miR-16 yielded positive HCC predictions in 18 of 26 (69.2%) HCC patients with negative results on all three conventional markers, most of whom had tumors size smaller than 3 cm; miR-16 was falsely positive in only 12 of 96 (12.5%) CLD patients. Our findings suggest that the addition of miR-16 to conventional serum markers improves sensitivity and specificity for HCC, and further prospective studies are warranted to explore the use of miR-16 as a second-line marker.

title: Mitochondrial haplogroups and hypervariable region polymorphisms in schizophrenia: a case-control study.
text: Earlier studies have detected associations between mitochondrial haplogroups and schizophrenia (SZ) in various populations. However, no study has investigated the relationship between major mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) haplogroups and SZ in the Chinese Han population. Our study aimed to evaluate the association between mtDNA haplogroups and SZ onset in the Chinese Han population using a case-control design. We conducted mtDNA sequencing of the hypervariable regions (HVR1, HVR2, and HVR3) in a sample of 298 SZ patients and 298 controls. Haplotypes were classified into 10 major haplogroups: A, B, CZ, D, F, G, M, N, N9a, and R. Our findings revealed that only haplogroup N9a showed a nominally significant association with protection from SZ (1.68% vs. 6.38%, p=0.004, OR=0.251 (0.092-0.680); adjusted for age and sex: p=0.006, OR=0.246 (0.090-0.669)). Additionally, three HVR polymorphisms showed nominally significant differences between SZ patients and controls, all of which are linked to haplogroup N9a. Our results suggest that mtDNA haplogroup N9a may be a protective factor against SZ.

title: Resolution of acute inflammation in the lung.
text: Acute inflammation in the lungs is important for our health. Both the acute inflammatory response and its resolution are crucial for protecting our bodies. When microbes, irritants, or injured tissue enter the lungs, the body mounts an immediate response to defend itself. To avoid harming nearby healthy tissue, the lungs produce specialized proteins called resolving mediators, including lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, and maresins. These proteins help stop inflammation by interacting with specific receptors on immune cells and other lung tissue to slow down or stop the inflammatory response. However, problems with this process are common in many lung diseases, such as chronic inflammation. In this review, we will explore the molecular and cellular mechanisms that help resolve acute inflammation in the lungs.

title: The calcium sensor STIM1 is regulated by androgens in prostate stromal cells.
text:
Background: Prostate development and maintenance in adults depend on the interaction of stromal and glandular components. Androgens regulate this process by directly affecting the stroma. In this study, we investigated whether there is a direct relationship between androgens and another critical regulator of stromal cells, intracellular calcium (Ca2+).
Methods: We examined gene expression changes in prostate stromal cells that were treated with dihydrotestosterone (DHT) with respect to untreated cells using Affymetrix gene expression arrays. We also identified Ca2+-regulated features with Gene Ontology (GO). The changes in intracellular calcium levels were measured in Fluo-4-loaded cells using fluorescence microscopy. Androgen regulation was confirmed by chromatin immunoprecipitation.
Results: We found that prostate stromal cell cultures can be sorted based on their expression of integrin α1 β1, which concentrates cells expressing the androgen receptor (AR). We identified a key functional category within the androgen-regulated gene expression signature that focused on calcium signaling-related genes. STIM1 was identified as a significantly differentially expressed gene with four relevant associated GO terms. DNA sequence analysis revealed that the promoter region of STIM1 contained putative androgen response element sequences, and the AR binding ability of STIM1 was confirmed. Androgens directly regulate STIM1 expression, and the effects of STIM1 on store-operated calcium entries are inhibited upon STIM1 knock-down. Lowering STIM1 expression in prostate stromal cells decreased basal Ca2+ levels, the amount of Ca2+ released by thapsigargin, and the amount of Ca2+ in the store following TG-induced depletion.
Conclusion: Our findings indicate a direct relationship between androgens and the regulation of intracellular calcium levels through the STIM1 gene. The AR regulates the promoter region of STIM1, leading to changes in calcium signaling.

title: Role of soluble guanylate cyclase in dilator responses of the cerebral microcirculation.
text: The responses of cerebral blood vessels to nitric oxide (NO) are mediated by two mechanisms: one dependent on soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) and the other independent of it. In an experiment conducted on anesthetized rabbits, we tested the hypothesis that the vasodilation of cerebral microvessels in response to NO is dependent on sGC activation. The diameters of cerebral arterioles (initial diameter = 94 ± 5 micrometers) were measured using a closed cranial window. We found that the vasodilation produced by YC-1 (3-(5'-hydroxymethyl-2'-furyl)-1-benzyl indazole), an NO-independent activator of sGC, was blocked by ODQ (1H-[1,2,4]oxadiazolo[4,3,-a]quinoxalin-1-one)(10 microM), an inhibitor of sGC. These results indicate that sGC is functionally important in cerebral arterioles. Moreover, acetylcholine (which stimulates endogenous production of NO by the endothelium) produced vasodilation of cerebral arterioles that was inhibited by ODQ. For instance, 1 microM acetylcholine dilated cerebral arterioles by 34 ± 7 and 5 ± 1% in the absence and presence of ODQ (10 microM), respectively. In contrast, increases in arteriolar diameter in response to sodium nitroprusside (1 microM, an NO donor) were inhibited by approximately 80% by ODQ, but were not affected by 17-ODYA (10 microM) or clotrimazole (10 microM), inhibitors of the cytochrome P450 pathway. These findings suggest that the dilatation of the cerebral microcirculation in response to exogenously applied and endogenously produced NO is dependent, in large part, on sGC activation.

title: Noxa controls Mule-dependent Mcl-1 ubiquitination through the regulation of the Mcl-1/USP9X interaction.
text: The regulation of Mcl-1, a critical pro-survival protein, is tightly controlled, and its down-regulation favors apoptosis. Mcl-1 interacts with various BH3-only proteins, including Noxa, which plays a key role in modulating Mcl-1 expression. In this study, we demonstrated that Noxa triggers the degradation of Mcl-1 at the mitochondria, a process that requires the E3 ligase Mule. Interestingly, our findings also revealed that Noxa over-expression leads to a decrease in the interaction between USP9X, a deubiquitinase, and Mcl-1, resulting in an increase in the number of polyubiquitinated Mcl-1 forms. Furthermore, Noxa over-expression increases the interaction between Mule and Mcl-1, accompanied by a decrease in the interaction between Mule and USP9X. These changes ultimately lead to the degradation of Mcl-1 by the proteasome machinery, adding complexity to the process. Overall, the involvement of Noxa in Mcl-1 proteasomal degradation adds a new layer of regulatory interactions to this important pathway.

title: Paediatric HIV infection.
text: By the year 2000, there will be approximately six million pregnant women and five to ten million children infected with HIV-1. In response, intervention strategies have been formulated and some have already been implemented. A crucial aspect of these strategies is taking into account that the majority of HIV-1 infected individuals reside in developing countries. Moreover, further research is needed to fully understand the immunological and virological factors involved in HIV-1 transmission from mother to child, as well as the differential disease progression in infected children and the transient nature of infection.

title: Potential role of NF-kappaB in adult neural stem cells: the underrated steersman?
text:
Neural stem cells serve as precursors for neurons and glial cells during brain development, proliferating, migrating, and differentiating into specific lineages. Recent discoveries have unveiled adult neural stem cells within the central nervous system, with emerging knowledge on the regulation of stem cell proliferation, migration, and differentiation by soluble factors such as chemokines and cytokines. However, the downstream signal transduction mechanisms of these factors remain unclear. This review aims to illustrate potential evidence for a central role of transcription factor nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) in critical signal transduction processes.

NF-κB is an inducible transcription factor discovered in lymphocytes by David Baltimore's laboratory and has since been found in neurons, glia, and neural stem cells. It is involved in diverse biological processes, including inflammation, innate immunity, development, apoptosis, and anti-apoptosis. Recent studies reveal that NF-κB family members are ubiquitously expressed in the nervous system, where they play a crucial role in neuronal plasticity, learning, memory consolidation, neuroprotection, and neurodegeneration.



NF-κB is composed of three subunits: two DNA-binding and one inhibitory subunit. Activation of NF-κB occurs in the cytoplasm, leading to the degradation of the inhibitory subunit and permitting the nuclear import of the DNA-binding subunits. Once within the nucleus, several target genes can be activated. This review proposes a model delineating the multifaceted function of NF-κB on neural stem cells. Additionally, the potential role of NF-κB in brain cancer stem cells is discussed.



In conclusion, this review provides insight into the complex regulation of neural stem cell proliferation, migration, and differentiation, focusing on the potential central role of NF-κB in these processes. Understanding these mechanisms may shed light on the development of novel therapeutic strategies for neurological disorders.

title: Intrauterine factors and risk of breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of current evidence.
text:
BACKGROUND: Recent research suggests that prenatal experiences may influence a woman's risk of developing breast cancer later in life. Researchers have explored various potential mechanisms, including exposure to maternal sex hormones and growth hormones, germ-cell mutations, the formation of cancer stem cells, and genetic or epigenetic events. In this study, we systematically reviewed and quantified the available data on perinatal factors and breast cancer risk.
METHODS: We conducted a comprehensive literature search for studies examining the association between perinatal factors and breast cancer risk. We analyzed each of the perinatal factors separately, including birthweight, birth length, parental age at delivery, gestational age, exposure to diethylstilbestrol during pregnancy, being a twin, having maternal pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, and other factors.
FINDINGS: Our analysis of 57 studies published between 1980 and 2007 revealed several significant associations. Higher birthweight and birth length were associated with an increased risk of breast cancer, while higher maternal age and paternal age were linked to a decreased risk. Additionally, maternal pre-eclampsia or eclampsia and twin membership were associated with a lower risk of breast cancer. However, we found no association between breast cancer risk and gestational age at birth or maternal diethylstilbestrol exposure during pregnancy.
INTERPRETATION: Our findings suggest that the prenatal environment plays a significant role in determining a woman's risk of developing breast cancer later in life. Further research is needed to uncover the underlying mechanisms responsible for this association.

title: Helicobacter hepaticus does not induce or potentiate colitis in interleukin-10-deficient mice.
text: The study aimed to investigate whether Helicobacter hepaticus can cause colitis in mice lacking the interleukin-10 gene (IL-10(-/-) mice) and if it can enhance colitis in specific-pathogen-free (SPF) IL-10(-/-) mice. To do this, germfree IL-10(-/-) mice on either a mixed (C57BL/6 x 129/Ola) or inbred (129/SvEv) genetic background were orally infected with H. hepaticus ATCC 51448 and rectally administered with the bacteria. In a second experiment, germfree IL-10(-/-) mice were colonized with stool from SPF mice that either did or did not have endogenous H. hepaticus. After 7-9 weeks, weight loss and mortality were monitored, the colon was isolated for histology, and mesenteric lymph node cells were tested for T-cell activation markers. The findings showed that IL-10(-/-) mice monoassociated with H. hepaticus for up to 16 weeks exhibited minimal histologic colitis or increased IL-12 production. SPF IL-10-knockout mice showed no significant difference in weight loss, mortality rate, histologic scores, colonic IL-12 secretion, or T-cell activation between being exposed to or not exposed to H. hepaticus. Therefore, the study concluded that H. hepaticus does not induce or exacerbate disease in IL-10(-/-) mice and therefore is not necessary to cause colitis in genetically susceptible hosts.

title: Metabolic interplay between glycolysis and mitochondrial oxidation: The reverse Warburg effect and its therapeutic implication.
text:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a type of liver cancer, often has a aggressive growth pattern. The Warburg effect, which is the increased use of glycolysis (a process for converting glucose to energy) in cancer cells, may contribute to this aggressive behavior. However, studies have shown that the Warburg effect has limitations, such as high levels of mitochondrial respiration (the process of using energy in the cell) and low levels of glycolysis in cancer cells.
To explain these contradictory findings, a "reverse Warburg effect" has been proposed. This means that some cancer cells might be using a different process to get energy, called oxidative phosphorylation (the process of using energy in the cell using oxygen). Additionally, there may be a group of cells surrounding the tumor called the stromal compartment, which could be providing lactate (a byproduct of glycolysis) to the cancer cells. This interaction would prevent the tumor microenvironment from becoming too acidic, making it harder for the cancer cells to be targeted by treatments that rely on this acidity.
Understanding how cancer cells can change their metabolism to adapt to different conditions offers new possibilities for developing treatments that target the hypoxic (low-oxygen) tumor microenvironment and overcome the limitations of glycolytic inhibitors.

title: Enhanced waterlogging tolerance in barley by manipulation of expression of the N‐end rule pathway E3 ligase PROTEOLYSIS6
text: Enhanced tolerance of crops to low oxygen levels (hypoxia) during flooding is a crucial goal for food security. In Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) Heynh., the N-end rule pathway of targeted proteolysis regulates plant responses to hypoxia by controlling the stability of group VII ethylene response factor (ERFVII) transcription factors, which are regulated by the oxidation status of the amino terminal (Nt)-cysteine (Cys). Here, we demonstrate that the barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) ERFVII BERF1 is a substrate of the N-end rule pathway in vitro. Furthermore, we show that Nt-Cys acts as a sensor for hypoxia in vivo, as the stability of the oxygen-sensor reporter protein MCGGAIL-GUS increased in waterlogged transgenic plants. Transgenic RNAi barley plants with reduced expression of the N-end rule pathway N-recognin E3 ligase PROTEOLYSIS6 (HvPRT6) showed increased expression of hypoxia-associated genes and altered seed germination phenotypes. In addition, in response to waterlogging, transgenic plants showed sustained biomass, enhanced yield, retention of chlorophyll, and enhanced induction of hypoxia-related genes. HvPRT6 RNAi plants also displayed reduced chlorophyll degradation in response to continued darkness, often associated with waterlogged conditions. Barley Targeting Induced Local Lesions IN Genomes (TILLING) lines, containing mutant alleles of HvPRT6, showed increased expression of hypoxia-related genes and phenotypes similar to RNAi lines. Our findings indicate that the N-end rule pathway represents a promising target for plant breeding to enhance tolerance to waterlogging in barley and other cereals.

title: A SUMO-Dependent Protein Network Regulates Chromosome Congression during Oocyte Meiosis
text: During the meiotic division of Caenorhabditis elegans eggs, a multi-protein complex called the Rothplein complex (RC) forms between homologous chromosomes. The RC promotes chromosome congression through the actions of the chromokinesin KLP-19, but the mechanism of RC formation has remained unclear. We found that the SUMO E3 ligase GEI-17/PIAS plays a crucial role in KLP-19 recruitment to the RC. Using proteomic analysis, we discovered that KLP-19 is a SUMO substrate in vivo. In vitro experiments revealed that KLP-19 is efficiently sumoylated in a GEI-17-dependent manner, while GEI-17 undergoes extensive auto-sumoylation. GEI-17 and another RC component, the kinase BUB-1, contain functional SUMO interaction motifs (SIMs), which allow them to recruit SUMO-modified proteins, including KLP-19, into the RC. Our findings highlight the importance of SUMO-SIM networks in regulating the assembly of dynamic protein complexes.

title: Prediagnostic levels of C-peptide, IGF-I, IGFBP -1, -2 and -3 and risk of endometrial cancer.
text:
Investigating the Link Between Chronic Hyperinsulinemia and Endometrial Cancer
Chronic hyperinsulinemia, a condition characterized by excess insulin production, is associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer, according to a new study. This finding is consistent with previous research, which has shown that conditions related to chronic hyperinsulinemia, such as obesity, noninsulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, and polycystic ovary syndrome, are also associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer.
In the study, the researchers investigated the association between pre-diagnostic blood concentrations of C-peptide (a marker of pancreatic insulin production), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-I), insulin-like growth factor-binding proteins (IGFBP-1, -2, and -3), and endometrial cancer risk. The study included 166 women with primary invasive endometrial cancer and 315 matched controls, of whom 44 case and 78 control subjects were premenopausal at recruitment.
The results showed that endometrial cancer risk increased with increasing levels of C-peptide, up to an odds ratio (OR) of 4.76 [95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.91-11.8] for the highest quintile. This association remained after adjustment for body mass index (BMI) and other confounders. In contrast, IGFBP-1 levels were inversely related to endometrial cancer, but the association was weakened and lost statistical significance after adjustment for confounders. Risk was unrelated to levels of IGF-I, IGFBP-2, and IGFBP-3.
The study suggests that chronic hyperinsulinemia, as reflected by increased circulating C-peptide, is associated with increased endometrial cancer risk. The findings provide evidence for the potential role of chronic hyperinsulinemia in the development of endometrial cancer and suggest that reducing insulin resistance through lifestyle changes or medication may help prevent the disease.

title: Interactions between SRY and SOX genes in mammalian sex determination.
text: The SRY gene located on the Y chromosome of mammals is believed to play a crucial role in determining testis development. However, the exact mechanism of its action remains unclear. Early studies proposed that SRY directly activates other genes in the testis-determining pathway. This paper presents an alternative hypothesis, which suggests that SRY functions indirectly by interacting with related genes SOX3 (from which SRY evolved) and SOX9 (involved in vertebrate gonad differentiation). According to this hypothesis, in females, SOX3 inhibits SOX9 function, while in males, SRY inhibits SOX3 and allows SOX9 to perform its testis-determining role. This hypothesis makes specific predictions about the phenotypes of individuals with deficiencies or overproduction of any of the three genes, and can explain the observed cases of XX(SRY-) males and transdifferentiation in the absence of SRY. Furthermore, this hypothesis suggests a possible evolutionary scenario in which the dominant SRY sex-determining system of present-day mammals may have emerged from an ancient system dependent on SOX3 dosage.

title: Chromatin immunoprecipitation and microarray-based analysis of protein location
text:
Genome-wide location analysis, also known as ChIP-Chip, is a powerful technique for identifying protein-DNA interactions in living cells. This method combines chromatin immunoprecipitation and DNA microarray analysis to detect the locations of proteins on the genome. Here's how it works:
1. Crosslinking cells: To capture protein-DNA interactions in vivo, cells are treated with a chemical crosslinking agent to form covalent bonds between proteins and DNA.
2. Cell lysis and DNA fragmentation: After crosslinking, cells are lysed to release the chromatin and fragment the DNA.
3. Immunoprecipitation: The desired protein is immunoaffinity purified, along with any associated DNA fragments.
4. Enrichment and labeling: The enriched DNA population is then labeled, typically with a fluorescent dye, and combined with a differentially labeled reference sample.
5. Microarray analysis: The labeled DNA samples are then applied to DNA microarrays, which are designed to detect enriched signals on specific genome regions.
6. Data analysis: Various computational and bioinformatic approaches are used to normalize the enriched and reference channels, connect signals to specific genome locations, provide confidence metrics, and generate maps of protein-genome occupancy.
This process takes approximately 1 week to complete once sufficient numbers of cells have been obtained and has been used to produce high-quality ChIP-chip results in many different cell and tissue types. The experimental protocols involve:
7. Cell harvesting: Cells are harvested and processed for crosslinking.
8. Crosslinking reactions: Cells are treated with a chemical crosslinking agent to capture protein-DNA interactions in vivo.
9. DNA fragmentation and purification: After crosslinking, cells are lysed to release the chromatin and fragment the DNA, and the desired protein is immunoaffinity purified.
10. Enrichment and labeling: The enriched DNA population is then labeled, typically with a fluorescent dye, and combined with a differentially labeled reference sample.
111. Microarray analysis: The labeled DNA samples are then applied to DNA microarrays, which are designed to detect enriched signals on specific genome regions.
12. Data analysis: Various computational and bioinformatic approaches are used to normalize the enriched and reference channels, connect signals to specific genome locations, provide confidence metrics, and generate maps of protein-genome occupancy.

title: Spatial and temporal clusters of Barmah Forest virus disease in Queensland, Australia.
text:
Objective:
To detect spatial and temporal clusters of Barmah Forest virus (BFV) disease in Queensland, Australia, using geographical information systems and spatial scan statistics (SaTScan).
Methods:
We collected BFV disease cases, population data, and statistical local area (SLA) boundaries from Queensland Health and the Australian Bureau of Statistics during 1992-2008. A retrospective Poisson-based analysis using SaTScan software and method was performed to identify purely spatial and space-time BFV disease clusters. The spatial cluster size was set to a proportion of the population, and a 200 km radius, with varying time windows from 1 to 12 months for the space-time analysis.
Results:
The spatial scan statistic revealed a most likely significant purely spatial cluster (including 23 SLAs) and a most likely significant space-time cluster (including 24 SLAs) in a similar location. Additional secondary clusters were identified from both analyses in various locations.
Conclusions:

This study confirms the presence of statistically significant BFV disease clusters in Queensland, Australia. The study also demonstrates the utility and applicability of SaTScan in analyzing ongoing surveillance data to identify clusters to inform the development of effective BFV disease prevention and control strategies in Queensland, Australia.

title: Surfactant Protein B Suppresses Lung Cancer Progression by Inhibiting Secretory Phospholipase A2 Activity and Arachidonic Acid Production
text:
Background and Objectives: Radiotherapy is commonly used to treat patients with inoperable cancer, including advanced stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, radioresistance is a major obstacle in radiotherapy, and its mechanism is not fully understood. In this study, we investigated the role of surfactant protein B (SP-B) in radioresistance using NSCLC cells.
Methods: To investigate the mechanism of radioresistance regulated by SP-B, we established the ΔSFTPB A549 cell line and analyzed SP-B expression. We also analyzed the change in SP-B expression in response to ionizing radiation (IR) in A549 and NCI-H441 cell lines. In addition, we used conditioned media (CM) from NSCLC cells to evaluate the downstream signaling pathway. Finally, we assessed the in vivo effects of SP-B through a mouse xenograft model using intratumoral injection of CM.
Results: Our results showed that in response to IR, NSCLC cell lines exhibited decreased SP-B expression, which was regulated by the TGF-β signaling pathway. Moreover, we found that decreased SP-B expression stimulated cell survival and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in NSCLC cells. In addition, treatment with CM from irradiated cells activated sPLA2, enhanced protein kinase Cδ-MAPKs signaling pathway, and increased arachidonic acid production. We confirmed the in vivo roles of SP-B through the mouse xenograft model.
Conclusion: Our findings revealed that down-regulation of SP-B was involved in the radiation-induced metastatic conversion of NSCLC and provided evidence that SP-B acted as a suppressor of NSCLC progression. Overall, our study shed light on the mechanism of radioresistance and suggested a potential therapeutic strategy for improving the effectiveness of radiotherapy in NSCLC treatment.

title: Liraglutide improves hippocampal synaptic plasticity associated with increased expression of Mash1 in ob/ob mice
text:
Objective: Consuming a high-fat diet has adverse effects on cognitive function, particularly in the hippocampus. Activating GLP-1 signaling can alleviate these detrimental effects, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. This study examined the effects of daily subcutaneous treatment with GLP-1 mimetic, Liraglutide, on synaptic plasticity, hippocampal gene expression, and metabolic control in obese diabetic mice.
Results: Long-term potentiation (LTP) in the CA1 area was completely abolished in obese mice compared to lean controls. However, Liraglutide treatment restored LTP to a level similar to that in lean controls. Treatment with Liraglutide also increased the expression of Mash1 and synaptophysin in the hippocampus, while decreasing the expression of neurotrophic tyrosine kinase receptor-type 2 and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Additionally, Liraglutide significantly reduced plasma glucose levels and improved insulin concentrations, and reduced the glycaemic excursion following an intraperitonal glucose load. It also enhanced the insulin response to glucose, but did not affect O2 consumption, CO2 production, respiratory exchange ratio, or energy expenditure. On day 21, accumulated food intake and number of feeding bouts were significantly reduced, although simple energy restriction was not responsible for these beneficial effects.
Conclusion: Liraglutide elicits beneficial effects on metabolic control and synaptic plasticity in mice with severe obesity and insulin resistance, mediated in part through increased expression of Mash1, believed to improve hippocampal neurogenesis and cell survival.

title: Post-transcriptional regulation of IME1 determines initiation of meiosis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
text: The IME1 gene of Saccharomyces cerevisiae is essential for the initiation of meiosis. The transcription of IME1 is detectable under conditions that stimulate meiosis, such as nitrogen and glucose starvation and the presence of specific gene products. This study reveals that IME1 is also subject to translational regulation. Translation of IME1 mRNA can occur under nitrogen starvation or G1 arrest conditions. Elevated transcription of IME1 in the absence of nutrients is also capable of triggering translation. Four distinct conditions were identified that result in the expression of Ime1 protein in vegetative cultures: the presence of IME1 on a multi-copy plasmid, elevated transcription provided by a Gal-IME1 construct, G1 arrest induced by alpha-factor treatment, and G1 arrest following mild heat shock treatment of cdc28 diploids. Our findings indicate that starvation is not only necessary for transcription and efficient translation of IME1, but also for either activating Ime1 protein or inducing/activating another factor that, either alone or in combination with Ime1, triggers meiosis.

title: Targeted proteomics reveals compositional dynamics of 60S pre-ribosomes after nuclear export
text: The construction and intracellular targeting of eukaryotic pre-ribosomal particles involves a diverse array of transiently associating trans-acting assembly factors, energy-consuming enzymes, and transport factors. However, the ability to rapidly and reliably measure the co-enrichment of multiple factors with maturing pre-ribosomal particles presents a major biochemical bottleneck in understanding their function and the precise contribution of over 50 energy-consuming steps that drive ribosome assembly. To address this challenge, we developed a workflow that combines genetic trapping, affinity-capture, and selected reaction monitoring mass spectrometry (SRM-MS). By exploiting this approach, we were able to interrogate the dynamic proteome of pre-60S particles after nuclear export and uncover assembly factors that travel with pre-60S particles to the cytoplasm, where they are released before initiating translation. Furthermore, we identified a novel shuttling factor that facilitates nuclear export of pre-60S particles. Our workflow also allowed us to capture and quantitate protein interaction networks of trapped intermediates of macromolecular complexes, providing a reliable discovery tool to unveil dynamic processes that contribute to their in vivo assembly and transport.

title: Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea and incident stroke: the sleep heart health study.
text:
RATIONALE: Although obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with physiological disturbances that increase the risk of hypertension and cardiovascular disease, it is unclear whether OSA is linked to an increased risk of ischemic stroke in the general population.
OBJECTIVES: To determine the incidence of ischemic stroke in a community-based sample of men and women with varying levels of OSA.
METHODS: Baseline polysomnography (PSG) was conducted between 1995 and 1998 in a longitudinal cohort study. The primary exposure was the obstructive apnea-hypopnea index (OAHI), and the outcome was incident ischemic stroke.
RESULTS: A total of 5,422 participants without a history of stroke at the baseline examination and untreated for sleep apnea were followed for a median of 8.7 years. One hundred ninety-three ischemic strokes occurred. After adjusting for covariates, a significant positive association between ischemic stroke and OAHI was observed in men (P value for linear trend: P = 0.016). Men in the highest OAHI quartile (>19) had an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.86 (95% confidence interval, 1.1-7.4). In the mild to moderate range (OAHI, 5-25), each one-unit increase in OAHI was estimated to increase stroke risk by 6% (95% confidence interval, 2-10%). In contrast, stroke was not significantly associated with OAHI quartiles in women, but an increased risk was observed at an OAHI greater than 25.
CONCLUSIONS: The significant adjusted association between ischemic stroke and OAHI in community-dwelling men with mild to moderate sleep apnea suggests that targeting this population for stroke prevention trials may be warranted.

title: Reproducibility of 31P cardiac magnetic resonance spectroscopy at 3 T.
text: The present study aimed to leverage the enhanced clinical field strength of 3 Tesla (3T) to develop and optimize a chemical shift imaging (CSI) acquisition protocol, resulting in high-quality spectra with exceptional specificity to the myocardium. The proposed protocol was designed to be clinically feasible, ensuring prompt analysis without compromising the quality of the data. To achieve this, the study investigated the variability in CSI data obtained from healthy male subjects scanned twice at 3T, utilizing an novel analysis method that solely relied on anatomical location for spectral analysis. The results demonstrated that the optimized CSI protocol at 3T delivered consistent and reliable data with minimal inter- and intra-subject variability. Specifically, the mean phosphocreatine (PCr)/adenosine triphosphate (ATP) value remained consistent across both scans (2.07 +/- 0.38 and 2.14 +/- 0.46), indicating no significant difference between the two scans. The intra-subject variability and inter-observer variability were assessed at 0.43 +/- 0.35 (20%) and 0.14 +/- 0.24, respectively, without any notable differences between analyses. Furthermore, the inter-observer variability demonstrated an intra-class correlation coefficient of 0.763, underscoring the robustness of the analysis procedure. The improvement in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at 3T resulted in increased spatial resolution and myocardial specificity without compromising reproducibility when compared to previous studies at 1.5 T. Overall, the present study successfully implemented a CSI acquisition protocol that consistently produces high-quality spectra with minimal variability, ensuring reliable myocardial mapping.

title: Nuclear HuR accumulation through phosphorylation by Cdk1.
text: A protein predominantly binding RNA, HuR, moves to the cytoplasm in response to stress and proliferation signals, where it stabilizes or modifies the translation of target mRNAs. Here, we present evidence that HuR's phosphorylation at S202 by the G2-phase kinase Cdk1 affects its distribution. HuR was specifically phosphorylated in synchronized G2-phase cultures; its cytoplasmic levels increased by inhibiting Cdk1 and declined in response to activating Cdk1. In contrast, the constitutively cytoplasmic HuR(S202A) mutant was not phosphorylated. Using a novel anti-phospho-HuR(S202) antibody, phospho-HuR(S202) was shown to be predominantly nuclear. The increased cytoplasmic presence of unphosphorylated HuR was linked to its decreased association with 14-3-3 and heightened binding to target mRNAs. Our findings suggest that Cdk1 phosphorylates HuR during G2, thus retaining it in the nucleus in association with 14-3-3 and hindering its post-transcriptional function and anti-apoptotic influence.

title: Surgical Resection for Patients with Solid Brain Metastases: Current Status
text: Up to 40% of cancer patients develop brain metastases, and their management has seen significant advancements in recent years. Three key developments have contributed to this progress: improved imaging and detection techniques, better management of the underlying systemic disease, and enhanced surgical techniques, including image-guided surgery. Class I data suggests that surgical intervention is often a more effective treatment for brain metastases compared to whole brain radiation. Additionally, there is evidence to suggest that even in areas of the brain with high levels of brain activity, metastases can be safely removed. The overall complication rate is low, and the recurrence rate is less than 10%. Surgery is typically recommended for patients with the following characteristics: a mass with an unknown primary, a symptomatic mass in eloquent areas, a mass with significant edema requiring high-dose steroids, a mass larger than 3 cm, or when radiosurgery may also be an option. The debate surrounding radiosurgery or whole brain radiation as an adjunct to surgical removal is ongoing and requires further evaluation.

title: Clinical features and treatment of peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum.
text: In this study, the authors aimed to better understand the clinical features, diagnosis, and management of peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum (PPG), an uncommon skin condition that primarily affects patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The study included 7 patients with PPG who were observed at a university-affiliated community setting over a 10-year period (1988-1999). The patients had a variety of IBD types, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, and some had associated disorders, such as abdominal cancer. The study found that while PPG is most commonly associated with IBD, it can occur in the absence of IBD. The authors also noted that biopsy of the skin lesion is not diagnostic, but can rule out other potential causes. Relocation of the stoma may lead to new ulceration and should be avoided. Trauma to the skin of a predisposed patient can trigger the pustules or ulcerations associated with pathergy. Effective treatments for PPG included topical and systemic corticosteroids, immunosuppressive drugs, and biologic agents. The study concluded that PPG can occur in both IBD patients and those without IBD, and that careful evaluation and management are necessary to prevent complications and improve outcomes.

title: The Tof1p-Csm3p protein complex counteracts the Rrm3p helicase to control replication termination of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
text: The termination of replication forks in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is regulated in a specific and polar manner by the interaction between the Fob1p replication terminator protein and the Tandem Ter sites located in the non-transcribed spacers. Here, we demonstrate, through both 2D gel analyses and chromatin immunoprecipitations (ChIP), that there is a second level of global control mediated by the intra-S-phase checkpoint protein complex of Tof1p and Csm3p, which protects stalled forks at Ter sites against the activity of the Rrm3p helicase ("sweepase"). The sweepase tends to release arrested forks by transiently displacing the Ter-bound Fob1p. Consistently, very few replication forks were arrested at the natural replication termini in the absence of the two checkpoint proteins. In the absence of the Rrm3p helicase, there was a slight enhancement of fork arrest at the Ter sites. Simultaneous deletions of the TOF1 (or CSM3), and the RRM3 genes restored fork arrest by removing both the fork-releasing and fork-protection activities. Other genes such as MRC1, WSS1, and PSY2 involved in the MRC1 checkpoint pathway were not involved in this global control. This observation suggests that Tof1p-Csm3p function differently from MRC1 and the other above-mentioned genes. This mechanism is not restricted to the natural Ter sites but was also observed at fork arrest caused by the meeting of a replication fork with transcription approaching from the opposite direction.

title: Association of hypomethylation of LINE-1 repetitive element in blood leukocyte DNA with an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma
text:
The following is a rewritten version of the given text:
This study aimed to investigate the association between global DNA hypomethylation in blood leukocyte DNA and the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The study included 315 HCC cases and 356 age, sex, and HBsAg status-matched controls. The degree of methylation in blood leukocyte DNA was evaluated using a combination of bisulfite-polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and pyrosequencing on long interspersed element-1 (LINE-1) repeats. The study found that the median methylation level in HCC cases (77.7% 5-methylcytosine (5mC)) was significantly lower than that in controls (79.5% 5mC) (P=0.004, Wilcoxon rank-sum test). The odds ratios (ORs) of HCC for individuals in the third, second, and first (lowest) quartiles of LINE-1 methylation were 1.1 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.7–1.8), 1.4 (95% CI 0.8–2.2), and 2.6 (95% CI 1.7–4.1) (P for trend <0.001), respectively, compared to individuals in the fourth (highest) quartile. The study also found a 1.9-fold (95% CI 1.4–2.6) increased risk of HCC among individuals with LINE-1 methylation below the median compared to individuals with higher (>median) LINE-1 methylation. The results suggest that individuals with global hypomethylation in blood leukocyte DNA may be at an increased risk of HCC. The study's findings provide the first evidence that global hypomethylation detected in the easily obtainable DNA source of blood leukocytes may help identify individuals at risk of HCC.

title: The ketogenic diet for the treatment of childhood epilepsy: a randomised controlled trial.
text:
BACKGROUND:
The ketogenic diet has been used extensively to treat children with drug-resistant epilepsy since the 1920s. Our study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of the ketogenic diet in a randomized controlled trial.
METHODS:
We recruited 145 children aged 2-16 years who experienced at least one seizure per day (or more than seven seizures per week) and had failed to respond to two or more antiepileptic medications. The participants were randomly assigned to receive the ketogenic diet either immediately or after a 3-month delay (control group). The study was conducted at two hospital centers or a residential center for children with epilepsy, and the families were not blinded to the group assignment. We recorded early withdrawals and assessed seizure frequency on the diet after 3 months. The primary outcome was a reduction in seizures, and we analyzed the data intention-to-treat. We also assessed the tolerability of the diet using a questionnaire at 3 months. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT00564915).
FINDINGS:
Of the 145 children enrolled, 73 were assigned to the ketogenic diet, and 72 were assigned to the control group. We had data available for 103 children, including 54 on the diet and 49 controls. Of the children who did not complete the trial, 16 did not receive their intervention, 16 did not provide adequate data, and 10 withdrew from the treatment before the 3-month review. After 3 months, the mean percentage of baseline seizures was significantly lower in the diet group compared to the controls (62.0% vs 136.9%, 75% decrease, 95% CI 42.4-107.4%; p<0.0001). Twenty-eight children (38%) in the diet group had greater than 50% seizure reduction, and five children (7%) had greater than 90% seizure reduction, compared to four (6%) controls (p<0.0001). There was no significant difference in the efficacy of the treatment between symptomatic generalised or symptomatic focal syndromes. The most common side effects reported at the 3-month review were constipation, vomiting, lack of energy, and hunger.
INTERPRETATION:
Our results support the use of the ketogenic diet in children with treatment-resistant epilepsy. The study was funded by the HSA Charitable Trust, Smiths Charity, Scientific Hospital Supplies, and the Milk Development Council.

title: Building-in biosafety for synthetic biology.
text: As synthetic biology advances, practical applications are transitioning from theoretical foundations and lab-based research to real-world implementation. However, a pressing concern with microbial systems is that self-replicating, reengineered cells could lead to unintended consequences if they escape or overwhelm their intended environment. To tackle this biosafety issue, various mechanisms for limiting microbial replication and horizontal gene transfer have been proposed. These include using toxin-antitoxin pairs, conditional plasmid replication, or requiring a specific metabolite for cellular function. While refining the existing genetic code or tailoring orthogonal systems, such as xeno nucleic acids, promises future advancements in 'firewalls' separating natural and synthetic cells, this work focuses on what can be achieved with current technology. We summarize the state-of-the-art in biosafety design and provide general recommendations (e.g., short environmental retention times) for current synthetic biology projects to better isolate themselves against potential negative impacts.

title: Sustained active site rigidity during synthesis by human DNA polymerase μ
text: Human DNA polymerase μ (Pol μ) is the only template-dependent enzyme capable of repairing double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) with unpaired 3' ends through nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ). To investigate this function, we structurally characterized the catalytic cycle of Pol μ for single-nucleotide incorporation. Our findings reveal that, unlike other template-dependent DNA polymerases, Pol μ undergoes limited conformational changes upon dNTP binding or catalysis, primarily involving the flexible loop 1 region. Specifically, the loop 1 region moves upon DNA binding, indicating a significant structural rearrangement. Interestingly, Pol μ variants with mutations in loop 1 exhibit altered catalytic properties and are partially defective in NHEJ. These results suggest that specific loop 1 residues contribute to Pol μ's exceptional ability to catalyze template-dependent NHEJ of DSBs with unpaired 3' ends.

title: Angiopoietin-1 requires p190 RhoGAP to protect against vascular leakage in vivo.
text:
Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1), a ligand of the endothelium-specific receptor Tie-2, inhibits permeability in the mature vasculature, but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Our study shows that Ang-1 signals Rho family GTPases to organize the cytoskeleton in a manner that enhances the permeability barrier function of the endothelium. Specifically, Ang-1 phosphorylates Tie-2 and its downstream effector, phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, leading to the activation of one GTPase, Rac1, and the inhibition of another, RhoA. The loss of either part of this dual effect abolishes the cytoskeletal and anti-permeability actions of Ang-1, suggesting that coordinated GTPase regulation is essential for the vessel-sealing effects of Ang-1.
p190 RhoGAP, a GTPase regulatory protein, plays a crucial role in this coordinating function. Phosphorylation of p190 RhoGAP by Ang-1 requires Rac1 activation and is necessary for RhoA inhibition. Remarkably, Ang-1 prevents the cytoskeletal and pro-permeability effects of endotoxin only when p190 RhoGAP is present. Treatment with p190 RhoGAP small interfering RNA completely abrogates the ability of Ang-1 to rescue endotoxemia-induced pulmonary vascular leak and inflammation in mice.
Our findings provide mechanistic insights into the protective effects of Ang-1 against endotoxin. By modulating the endothelial cytoskeleton through coordinated and opposing effects on Rho GTPases, Ang-1 offers a specific therapeutic strategy for treating life-threatening endotoxemic conditions such as sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome.

title: Vesicular trafficking of semaphorin 3A is activity-dependent and differs between axons and dendrites.
text: In the developing nervous system, secreted semaphorins act as guidance cues. Although the mechanisms of their transport and secretion are poorly understood, our findings indicate that endogenous semaphorin 3A (Sema3A) is distributed punctately in axons and dendrites of cultured cortical neurons. Co-localization of GFP-Sema3A with secretory vesicle cargo proteins suggests that it is transported via secretory vesicles. Using live-cell imaging, we observed highly dynamic trafficking of GFP-Sema3A vesicles in axons and dendrites, with distinct properties in each region regarding directionality, velocity, mobility, and pausing time. In contrast to dendrites, where GFP-Sema3A vesicles are stationary and move equally frequently in both directions, axonal transport is faster without interruption and predominantly in the anterograde direction. Disruption of microtubules, but not actin filaments, impairs GFP-Sema3A transport. We found that depolarization arrests axonal transport of GFP-Sema3A vesicles, while action potential blockade using tetrodotoxin (TTX) accelerates axonal transport, but not dendritic transport. These findings suggest that axons and dendrites regulate the trafficking of Sema3A and other secretory vesicles in distinct ways, with axons specializing in fast, uninterrupted anterograde transport. Moreover, neuronal activity regulates secretory vesicle trafficking in axons by a depolarization-evoked trafficking arrest.

title: Frequency of Intracranial Aneurysms Determined by Magnetic Resonance Angiography in Children (Mean Age 16) Having Operative or Endovascular Treatment of Coarctation of the Aorta (Mean Age 3).
text: Coarctation of the aorta (CofA) has been linked to an elevated risk of intracranial aneurysm (IA). This magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) study assesses the prevalence of IAs in 80 children treated in early childhood for CofA. MRA was performed at a median age of 15.7 ± 7.1 years, and surgical or endovascular treatment for CofA occurred at a median age of 2.6 ± 4.4 years. None of the patients had IAs. Contrary to findings in adult patients with late treatment for CofA, this first systematic study of early-treated children did not confirm the association between CofA and IAs. Our results call into question the previously observed developmental relationship between CofA and IAs and suggest that modifiable risk factors, such as hypertension, may play a role in IA development in patients with CofA who are diagnosed and treated in adulthood. In conclusion, our data suggest that early treatment of CofA can potentially reduce the formation of IAs in children, making MRA screening less necessary in this young population.

title: Transcriptional profiling of the heart reveals chamber-specific gene expression patterns.
text: Investigating the genetic basis of cardiac chamber-specific gene expression is crucial for understanding the normal development and function of the heart. To achieve this, we conducted a comprehensive, nearly genome-wide transcriptional profiling of the four heart chambers and the interventricular septum. Our rigorous statistical analysis enabled the identification of both known and novel members of gene families believed toplay important roles in cardiac development and function, including LIM proteins, homeobox proteins, Wnt and T-box pathway proteins, as well as structural proteins like actins and myosins. Furthermore, we identified thousands of additional differentially expressed genes, for which little structural or functional information is currently available. By clustering these genes based on their known and unknown functions, we uncovered signaling pathways that are essential for the development and maintenance of chamber-specific features. To facilitate future research in this area, we have created a searchable internet database that allows for the study of the chamber-specific expression of any gene represented on our comprehensive microarray. We anticipate that further investigating the genes identified through this effort will provide insights into the specialization of heart chamber tissues and their distinct functions in cardiac development, aging, and disease.

title: CD34+ hematopoietic stem-progenitor cell microRNA expression and function: a circuit diagram of differentiation control.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs), a relatively new class of epigenetic elements, are small non-coding RNAs that bind to the 3' untranslated region of messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and inhibit their translation into proteins. miRNAs play vital roles in various cellular processes, including metabolism, apoptosis, differentiation, and development. In our study, we investigated the expression of 33 miRNAs in CD34+ hematopoietic stem-progenitor cells (HSPCs) derived from normal human bone marrow and mobilized human peripheral blood stem cell harvests. We then combined these data with mRNA expression data from human HSPCs and miRNA-mRNA target predictions to create an innovative database called the Transcriptome Interaction Database. Computational predictions from the Transcriptome Interaction Database indicated that miRNAs regulate hematopoietic differentiation by controlling mRNA translation. Based on these predictions, we proposed a model in which miRNAs control different stages of hematopoiesis by regulating the expression of genes essential for hematopoiesis. To validate these predictions, we investigated the effect of miRNAs on several target mRNAs and found that their translation is indeed decreased by miRNAs. Finally, we focused on miRNA-155 for further characterization in hematopoiesis, as we predicted that it would regulate both myeloid and erythroid differentiation. As expected, transduction of miRNA-155 significantly reduced both myeloid and erythroid colony formation in normal human HSPCs.

title: Acute exercise activates nuclear factor (NF)-kappaB signaling pathway in rat skeletal muscle.
text: Two studies were conducted to investigate the effects of an acute bout of physical exercise on the nuclear protein kappaB (NF-κB) signaling pathway in rat skeletal muscle. In Study 1, rats were placed on a treadmill for 1 hour at a speed of 25 m/min and a grade of 5%, or until exhaustion (Ex), and compared with acontrol group (C) that received an injection of pyrrolidine dithiocarbamate (PDTC, 100 mg/kg, i.p.) 24 and 1 hour prior to the exercise bout. Additionally, three other groups of rats were injected with either lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 8 mg/kg, i.p.), t-butylhydroperoxide (tBHP, 1 mmol/kg, i.p.), or saline (C) and were killed at resting condition. The results showed that rats that exercised (Ex) had higher levels of NF-κB binding and protein content in muscle nuclear extracts compared to the C rats. In contrast, cytosolic IκBα and IκB kinase (IKK) contents were decreased, while phospho-IκBα and phospho-IKK contents were increased in Ex rats compared to C rats. The exercise-induced activation of the NF-κB signaling cascade was partially abolished by PDTC treatment. In Study 2, the time course of exercise-induced NF-κB activation was examined, revealing that the highest levels of NF-κB binding were observed at 2 hours post-exercise. Decreased cytosolic IκBα and increased phospho-IκBα content were found 0-1 hour post-exercise, while P65 reached peak levels at 2-4 hours. These data suggest that the NF-κB signaling pathway can be activated in a redox-sensitive manner during muscular contraction, likely due to increased oxidant production. The cascade of intracellular events may be the precursor to the previously reported elevated gene expression of manganese superoxide dismutase.

title: Staphylococcus aureus RNAIII and the endoribonuclease III coordinately regulate spa gene expression.
text: Staphylococcus aureus RNAIII is one of the largest regulatory RNAs, which controls the expression of several virulence genes encoding exoproteins and cell-wall-associated proteins. RNAIII repreesses the expression of the spa gene (coding for the surface protein A) at multiple levels, including transcriptional repression and post-transcriptional regulation. We demonstrate that RNAIII-mediated repression of spa gene expression occurs through both transcriptional and translational mechanisms, involving the double-strand-specific endoribonuclease III (RNase III). The 3' end domain of RNAIII interacts with the 5' region of the spa mRNA through an initial loop-loop interaction, effectively inhibiting the formation of the translation initiation complex in vitro. However, the coordinated action of RNase III is essential in vivo to degrade the mRNA and irreversibly arrest translation, demonstrating that RNase III plays a crucial role in the degradation of targeted paired RNAs. These findings add to the complexity of the Staphylococcus aureus virulon's expression.

title: Fast calcium and voltage-sensitive dye imaging in enteric neurones reveal calcium peaks associated with single action potential discharge.
text: Slow changes in intracellular calcium ([Ca(2+)](i)) levels reflect increased neuronal activity, according to our study. Using single-trial fast [Ca(2+)](i) imaging with a sampling rate of at least 200 Hz, we found that each peak corresponds to a single spike discharge recorded by consecutive voltage-sensitive dye (VSD) imaging in enteric neurons and nerve fibers. Fast [Ca(2+)](i) imaging also revealed subthreshold fast excitatory postsynaptic potentials. Nicotine-evoked [Ca(2+)](i) peaks were reduced by -conotoxin and blocked by ruthenium red or tetrodotoxin. Importantly, fast [Ca(2+)](i) imaging can be used to directly record single action potentials in enteric neurons. [Ca(2+)](i) peaks require the opening of voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels as well as calcium release from intracellular stores.

title: New colorimetric cytotoxicity assay for anticancer-drug screening.
text: We have developed a speedy, sensitive, and economical approach for measuring the cellular protein content of both adherent and suspension cultures in 96-well microtiter plates. This method is suitable for both standard laboratory applications and massive-scale operations, such as the National Cancer Institute's disease-oriented in vitro anticancer-drug discovery screen, which demands the utilization of millions of culture wells annually. We fixed the cells with trichloroacetic acid and stained them for 30 minutes with 0.4% (wt/vol) sulforhodamine B (SRB) dissolved in 1% acetic acid. Unbound dye was removed by four washes with 1% acetic acid, and protein-bound dye was extracted with 10 mM unbuffered Tris base [tris (hydroxymethyl)aminomethane] for determination of optical density in a computer-interfaced, 96-well microtiter plate reader. The SRB assay results were linear with the number of cells and the values for cellular protein measured by both the Lowry and Bradford assays over a range of cell densities from sparse subconfluence to multilayered supraconfluence. The signal-to-noise ratio at 564 nm was approximately 1.5 with 1,000 cells per well. Our novel SRB assay exhibited a superior sensitivity compared to several fluorescence assays and was more sensitive than both the Lowry and Bradford assays and 20 other visible dyes. The SRB assay provides a colorimetric end point that is nondestructive, indefinitely stable, and visible to the naked eye. It offers a sensitive measure of drug-induced cytotoxicity, is valuable in quantifying clonogenicity, and is well-suited for large-scale, automated drug screening.
