To investigate this mutation, the researchers recorded the light-evoked response of the retina, known as the electroretinogram (ERG), in affected mice. They also measured cortical potentials with a scalp electrode to evaluate visual transmission. The inheritance pattern of the nob mutation was determined by breeding nob animals with normal mice.
The results showed that the photoreceptor-mediated ERG component (a-wave) was normal in nob mice, but the major response component reflecting postreceptoral neuronal activity (b-wave) was missing. Visually-driven cortical activity was also abnormal in nob animals.
Using light microscopy, the researchers found that the nob retina appeared to have a normal cytoarchitecture.
Based on these findings, the researchers conclude that the nob defect disrupts the transmission of visual information through the retina, making these mice a valuable model for studying outer retinal synaptic function. They also suggest that the mutant mouse may provide a model for the complete form of congenital stationary night blindness, a human disorder characterized by a profound loss of rod-mediated visual sensitivity.

title: Differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells and embryonic stem cells into steroidogenic cells using steroidogenic factor-1 and liver receptor homolog-1.
text:
In our previous work, we demonstrated that mesenchymal stem cells could be differentiated into steroidogenic cells by treatment with steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1) and 8-bromo-cAMP. We also showed that the use of liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1), another member of the nuclear receptor 5A family, in combination with 8-bromo-cAMP, could also induce the differentiation of human mesenchymal stem cells into steroid hormone-producing cells. However, we found that these approaches were not effective in differentiating other types of undifferentiated cells, such as embryonic stem cells or embryonal carcinoma cells, likely due to the cytotoxic effects of overexpressing the nuclear receptor 5A family.
To overcome this limitation, we generated embryonic stem cells carrying the tetracycline-regulated SF-1 gene at the ROSA26 locus. The embryonic stem cells were first differentiated into a mesenchymal cell lineage by culturing on collagen IV-coated dishes and treating with retinoic acid pulses before expression of SF-1. Notably, the untreated embryonic stem cells were unable to be converted into steroidogenic cells by expression of SF-1 in the absence of leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), likely due to their inability to survive. However, when the differentiated cells were induced to express SF-1, they exhibited characteristics of adrenocortical-like cells and produced a large amount of corticosterone. These findings indicated that pluripotent stem cells could be differentiated into steroidogenic cells by the nuclear receptor 5A family of proteins via the mesenchymal cell lineage. This approach may provide a source of cells for future gene therapy for diseases caused by steroidogenesis deficiencies.

title: Chronic daily headache. A clinical and psychological profile before and after treatment.
text:
To evaluate the clinical and personality characteristics of patients with chronic daily headaches before and after treatment, 20 patients were assessed using the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) and the Strait and Trait Anxiety Index 1,2 (STAI). The study found two distinct groups based on their personality profiles:
Group 1 (n=6) had a "conversion V" configuration, with elevated scores on scales measuring hypochondria and hysteria, while the depression scale was slightly lower. Group 2 (n=13) showed elevated scores on scales measuring depression and other MMPI scales. One patient had no scale elevation. Both groups had high STAI 1,2 scores. Almost all patients experienced psychosomatic symptoms and migraine features. Headache occurrence, severity, and duration were recorded regularly, and the MMPI and STAI were administered again after treatment. Improvement in headaches and decreased scores on several MMPI and STAI scales were observed. However, 12 of 20 patients retained a "conversion V" configuration after treatment. The study conclusion highlights that chronic daily headaches were likely transformed migraines in most cases and were accompanied by anxiety levels in all patients and hysteric traits in some. With time, these patients may develop a depressive disorder. After treatment, hysterical traits persist at a lower level in those who exhibited these traits before treatment, and may be unmasked in those who had depression.

title: Potassium channel structure and function as reported by a single glycosylation sequon.
text:
Inwardly rectifying potassium channels (IRKs) are highly potassium-selective, integral membrane proteins that help maintain the resting membrane potential and cell volume. Integral membrane proteins as a class are frequently N-glycosylated, with the attached carbohydrate being extracellular and potentially modulating function. However, the dynamic effects of glycosylation on IRKs have yet to be demonstrated at the molecular level.
To investigate this, the study focused on ROMK1, a member of the IRK family. ROMK1 has a single N-glycosylation consensus sequence, making it an ideal candidate for studying glycosylation. The research showed that ROMK1 is expressed in a functional state in the plasma membrane of an insect cell line (Spodoptera frugiperda, Sf9) and exists in two forms: glycosylated and unglycosylated. To test functionality, glycosylation was abolished either by an N117Q mutation or by treatment with tunicamycin.
The results showed that whole cell currents were greatly reduced in both unglycosylated forms compared to the wild type. Single channel currents revealed a dramatic decrease in opening probability, po, as the main cause. These findings confirmed that the N-glycosylation sequon is extracellular, in line with current topological models of IRKs, and indicated that sequon occupancy by carbohydrate stabilizes the open state of ROMK1.

title: Role of the novel Th17 cytokine IL-17F in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD): upregulated colonic IL-17F expression in active Crohn's disease and analysis of the IL17F p.His161Arg polymorphism in IBD.
text:
Interleukin-17F (IL-17F), produced by IL-23R-expressing Th17 cells, is a novel member of the IL-17 cytokine family. In light of the association of IL23R with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), we investigated the role of IL-17F in IBD, including its intestinal gene expression and the effect of the IL17F p. His161Arg polymorphism on disease susceptibility and phenotype in Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). Additionally, we analyzed the IL17F p. His161Arg polymorphism for potential epistasis with IL23R and NOD2/CARD15 variants.
We found that intestinal IL-17F mRNA expression was 4.4-fold higher in inflamed colonic lesions of CD compared to uninflamed biopsies (P = 0.016), but not in UC. However, the mean intestinal IL-17F mRNA expression was higher in UC than in CD (P < 0.0001). The IL17F p. His161Arg substitution was observed at similar frequencies in IBD patients and controls and was not associated with any specific disease phenotype. We did not find evidence for epistasis between the IL17F p. His161Arg polymorphism and IBD-associated single nucleotide polymorphisms within the IL23R gene.
In conclusion, intestinal IL-17F gene expression is increased in active CD, but the IL17F p. His161Arg polymorphism does not contribute to IBD susceptibility and does not show any epistatic interaction with CD-associated IL23R variants.

title: Targeting brain cancer: advances in the molecular pathology of malignant glioma and medulloblastoma
text: Brain tumors are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality across various age groups, and among the most common types are malignant gliomas in adults and medulloblastoma in children. Over the past two decades, there has been a significant upsurge in research on these malignancies, which has greatly enhanced our understanding of their basic biology and disease mechanisms. This Review provides an overview of these advances in the light of the evolving concept of molecular pathology, and explores the implications of this knowledge for the development of novel treatment strategies.

title: Rapid helper T-cell recovery above 200 × 106/l at 3 months correlates to successful transplant outcomes after allogeneic stem cell transplantation
text: The current study aims to assess the significance of quantifying peripheral lymphocyte subsets, particularly CD4+ helper T-cell recovery, in predicting post-allogenic stem cell transplantation outcomes, including overall survival (OS) and non-relapse mortality (NRM). A total of 69 allogenic recipients with various diagnoses, including acute myeloid leukemia (42), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (5), chronic myeloid leukemia (15), non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (5), and high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome (2), were included in the study. Peripheral lymphocyte subset counts (CD3+ T cells, CD3+4+ helper T cells, CD3+8+ cytotoxic T cells, CD19+ B cells, and CD56+ natural killer cells) were measured at 3, 6, and 12 months following transplantation. The CD4+ helper T-cell reconstitution at 3 months was found to be strongly correlated with OS (P<0.0001), NRM (P=0.0007), and opportunistic infections (P=0.0108) at a cutoff value of 200 × 106/l CD4+ helper T cells. Additionally, rapid CD4+ helper T-cell recovery was associated with higher CD4+ helper T-cell transplant dose (P=0.006) and donor type (P<0.001). Furthermore, early CD4+ helper T-cell recovery at 3 months correlated with a subsequent faster helper T-cell recovery until 12 months, but not with B-cell recovery. In a multivariate analysis, rapid recovery of CD4+ helper T cells at 3 months was identified as a favorable prognostic factor, along with higher CD34+ cell transplant dose, in terms of OS (P=0.001) and NRM (P=0.005).

title: Generating an iPSC bank for HLA-matched tissue transplantation based on known donor and recipient HLA types.
text: The likelihood of immunological rejection of Human Leukocyte Antigens (HLA)-mismatched induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) hinders their therapeutic potential. In contrast, we demonstrate a practical method for utilizing an existing tissue bank of 150 homogamously HLA-typed volunteers to generate an iPSC stem cell bank that can match 93% of the UK population with minimal immunosuppression. Our model offers a pragmatic approach for leveraging existing HLA-typed samples to create a more comprehensive and diverse iPSC stem cell bank, thereby circumventing the need for extensive typing of a large number of individuals.

title: Promiscuous gene expression and the developmental dynamics of medullary thymic epithelial cells.
text: Thymic epithelial cells (TEC) create the structural and functional environment necessary for the formation and quality control of the T cell repertoire. Additionally, they provide an extraordinary source of various tissue-restricted antigens (TRA), a feature known as promiscuous gene expression (pGE). The regulation of pGE is linked to the cell biology of TEC subtypes, including their turnover and developmental interrelationships, which are not well understood. The observation that pGE is primarily a characteristic of mature medullary TEC (mTEC) suggests that the full implementation of pGE depends on mTEC differentiation. Here, we demonstrate that the emergence of TEC subsets and pGE is closely correlated during ontogeny, and we provide evidence that mature CD80pos mTEC develop from an immature CD80neg subset. This differentiation process occurs continuously in the postnatal thymus. While mature mTEC have a short lifespan (2-3 weeks), immature mTEC consist of two distinct pools: a smaller cycling pool and a larger non-cycling pool. The latter may serve as a reservoir of committed precursors, maintaining the renewal process. Our data indicate that mTEC are a highly dynamic cell population, suggesting that the availability and display of TRA in the thymus undergo a continuous tempo-spatial reorganization.

title: Evaluation of HER-2/neu amplification and other biological markers as predictors of response to neoadjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy in primary breast cancer: the role of anthracycline dose intensity.
text:
Objective: The debated role of HER-2/neu status as a predictor of response to anthracycline-based chemotherapy remains unresolved. This study aimed to assess the contribution of HER-2/neu gene amplification and other biomarkers in determining response to different doses of neoadjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy.
Methods: We retrospectively analyzed the clinical and pathological records of 115 primary breast cancer patients who received neoadjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy. The patients were divided into two groups based on the dose intensity of anthracyclines: high-dose (doxorubicin ≥20 mg/m2/week and/or epirubicin ≥30 mg/m2/week) and moderate-low dose (less than high-dose). HER-2/neu status was determined by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) on tumor samples before chemotherapy.
Results: HER-2/neu amplification was observed in 29 (25%) of the 115 tumors, with 18 (15%) from the moderate-low dose and 11 (9%) from the high-dose group. In the univariate analysis, a high Ki67 index (>20%) and positive clinical axillary nodes were significantly predictive of an objective tumor response (P = 0.033 and 0.001, respectively). multivariate analysis revealed that Ki67 was the only factor predictive of response (OR = 3.08, 95% CI = 1.1-8.5, P = 0.03). HER-2/neu status and hormonal receptor status (HR) were not significantly associated with response to different anthracycline dose intensities.
Conclusion: In this study, no significant dose-response relationship was observed according to HER-2/neu status. These findings suggest that HER-2/neu status may not be a reliable predictor of response to anthracycline-based chemotherapy in breast cancer patients.

title: Radioactive labeling of mitochondrial translation products in cultured cells.
text: The mammalian mitochondrial genome harbors 37 genes, of which 13 encode polypeptide subunits vital to the enzyme complexes of the oxidative phosphorylation system. These genes also encode rRNAs and tRNAs that are essential for their translation. The mitochondrial translation apparatus is located in the mitochondrial matrix and serves exclusively to synthesize these 13 enzyme subunits. Mitochondrial diseases in humans are often linked to defects in mitochondrial translation, manifesting as a decrease in the overall rate of mitochondrial protein synthesis, a decrease in the synthesis of specific polypeptides, the production of abnormal polypeptides, or alterations in the stability of specific translation products. These changes in mitochondrial translation can be detected using a simple technique that benefits from the insensitivity of the mitochondrial translation machinery to antibiotics that completely inhibit cytoplasmic translation. By specifically labeling mitochondrial translation products with radioactivity, their distribution on gradient gels can be visualized in cultured cells. This analysis of mitochondrial translation in patient cell biopsies is a valuable tool for investigating disease-causing mutations in both the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.

title: Caenorhabditis elegans cyclin A- and B-type genes: a cyclin A multigene family, an ancestral cyclin B3 and differential germline expression.
text: We have isolated cDNA clones for Cyclin A1, B, and B3 in Caenorhabditis elegans. Cyclin A1 and B are most closely related to their counterparts in other species, while Cyclin B3 shares a closer relationship with the recently discovered chicken Cyclin B3. Our findings confirm the conservation of Cyclin B3 throughout evolution. Cyclin A1 belongs to an A-type multigene family, but the cDNA only detects a single band on northern blots. In contrast, three transcripts are observed for the Cyclin B cDNA, with one specific to the paternal germline. The remaining two transcripts, along with the Cyclin A1 and Cyclin B3 transcripts, are most abundant in the maternal germline and present at low levels in other tissues. Notably, the 3' untranslated regions of each Caenorhabditis cyclin cDNA contain multiple potential translational control elements, similar to those found in Xenopus and Drosophila maternal cyclin mRNAs, which play a critical role in oogenesis and early embryogenesis.

title: A comparison of pharmacological (amitriptyline HCL) and nonpharmacological (cognitive-behavioral) therapies for chronic tension headaches.
text: Forty-one individuals with recurrent tension headache were randomly assigned to either cognitive-behavioral therapy (delivered through a predominantly home-based treatment protocol) or amitriptyline therapy (with dosage tailored to 25, 50, or 75 mg/day). Cognitive-behavioral therapy and amitriptyline both showed significant improvements in headache frequency, with 56% and 27% reductions in headache index, respectively, when evaluated using patient-reported outcomes. Similarly, 94% and 69% of patients perceived at least some improvement with cognitive-behavioral therapy and amitriptyline, respectively, as rated by neurologists. In cases where differences in treatment effectiveness were observed (headache index, somatic complaints, perceived control of headache activity), cognitive-behavioral therapy tended to produce more positive outcomes than amitriptyline. However, neither treatment completely resolved headache problems.

title: Homeostasis model assessment: insulin resistance and β-cell function from fasting plasma glucose and insulin concentrations in man
text: The steady-state basal plasma glucose and insulin concentrations are governed by a feedback loop, and a computer-based model has been used to predict the homeostatic concentrations that result from varying degrees of β-cell deficiency and insulin resistance. By comparing a patient's fasting values with the model's predictions, a quantitative assessment can be made of the contributions of insulin resistance and deficient β-cell function to fasting hyperglycemia (homeostasis model assessment, HOMA). The accuracy and precision of the estimate have been evaluated by comparing it with independent measures of insulin resistance and β-cell function obtained through hyperglycemic and euglycemic clamps and an intravenous glucose tolerance test. The estimate of insulin resistance obtained through HOMA correlated well with estimates obtained through the euglycemic clamp (Rs = 0.88, p < 0.0001), fasting insulin concentration (Rs = 0.81, p < 0.0001), and hyperglycemic clamp (Rs = 0.69, p < 0.01). Conversely, there was no correlation with any aspect of insulin-receptor binding. The estimate of deficient β-cell function obtained through HOMA correlated with that derived through the hyperglycemic clamp (Rs = 0.61, p < 0.01) and with the estimate from the intravenous glucose tolerance test (Rs = 0.64, p < 0.05). However, the low precision of the estimates from the model (coefficients of variation: 31% for insulin resistance and 32% for β-cell deficit) limits its use. Nonetheless, the correlation of the model's estimates with patient data supports the hypothesis that basal glucose and insulin interactions are predominantly determined by a simple feedback loop.

title: Clinical benefits and considerations of bisphosphonate treatment in metastatic bone disease.
text: Patients with metastatic bone disease are at risk of developing skeletal-related events that can negatively impact their quality of life, leading to loss of autonomy and functional capabilities. Fortunately, bisphosphonates have become a crucial component in the treatment of patients with bone metastases, as they delay the onset and reduce the risk of skeletal-related events while also alleviating bone pain in various cancer types. Among bisphosphonates, zoledronic acid has proven to be particularly effective and safe in treating bone lesions from different cancer types, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, lung cancer, and multiple myeloma. Recent studies have shown that administering zoledronic acid before the onset of bone pain can provide additional clinical benefits and positively impact survival in certain patient subsets. Specifically, normalization of elevated levels of N-telopeptide of type I collagen (NTX), a biomarker of bone resorption, has been observed in the majority of patients treated with zoledronic acid, and this normalization has been linked to improved survival outcomes. These findings are particularly significant in patients with breast cancer, prostate cancer, lung cancer, or other solid tumors, as normalization of NTX levels has been shown to correlate with extended survival.

title: Distinct memory CD4+ T cells with commitment to T follicular helper- and T helper 1-cell lineages are generated after acute viral infection.
text: CD4(+) T follicular helper (Tfh) cells are crucial for triggering germinal center reactions, which are necessary for producing long-lasting antibody responses. However, it is unclear if CD4(+) memory T cells retain their Tfh cell lineage after eliminating the antigen. Through the use of adoptive transfer of antigen-specific memory CD4(+) T cell subpopulations in the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection model, we discovered distinct memory CD4(+) T cell populations with a commitment to either Tfh- or Th1-cell lineages. Our conclusions are based on gene expression profiling, epigenetic studies, and phenotypic and functional analyses. Our findings indicate that CD4(+) memory T cells "remember" their previous effector lineage after antigen clearance, with the ability to quickly reacquire their lineage-specific effector functions upon antigen reencounter. These findings have significant implications for vaccine design, as improving the generation and activation of Tfh cells may be used to boost vaccine-induced protective immunity.

title: Control of synapse development and plasticity by Rho GTPase regulatory proteins
text:
Synapses are specialized cell-cell contacts that facilitate communication between neurons. Most excitatory synapses in the brain are located on dendritic spines, which are small actin-rich protrusions extending from dendrites. During development and in response to environmental stimuli, spines undergo significant changes in shape and number, thought to play a role in processes such as learning and memory. Abnormalities in spine development are associated with various brain disorders, underscoring the importance of understanding the mechanisms that regulate their formation and plasticity.
Rho-family GTPases, critical actors of the actin cytoskeleton, play essential roles in the development and remodeling of spines and synapses. Precise regulation of Rho GTPase activity is required for their function, as aberrant signaling can lead to spine and synapse defects and cognitive impairments. Rho GTPases are activated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and inhibited by GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs).
We propose that Rho-family GEFs and GAPs provide the spatiotemporal regulation and signaling specificity necessary for proper Rho GTPase function. These proteins possess several distinct features, including multiple GEFs and GAPs per Rho GTPase, developmentally regulated expression, discrete localization, ability to bind to and organize specific signaling networks, and tightly regulated activity. Recent studies have identified several Rho-family GEFs and GAPs that contribute to spinogenesis and synaptogenesis, occupying distinct biochemical niches critical for synaptic development.
In conclusion, Rho-family GTPases, GEFs, and GAPs play a crucial role in regulating the formation and plasticity of spines and synapses, with dysregulation of these mechanisms contributing to various brain disorders. Elucidating the mechanisms of Rho GTPase regulation is essential for understanding cognition and disease.

title: Rate and molecular spectrum of spontaneous mutations in the bacterium Escherichia coli as determined by whole-genome sequencing.
text:
Knowing the rate and type of mutations that happen spontaneously is important for understanding how living things change over time. In this report, we looked at how many mutations happened in wild-type Escherichia coli bacteria and a bacterial strain that doesn't have a system to fix mistakes during replication. We found:
1. The rate of mutations in wild-type E. coli is about 1 mutation per 1000 genetic instructions per generation.
2. Mutations in wild-type E. coli tend to have more A:T base pairs than G:C base pairs. However, when the bacteria don't have a working system to fix mistakes, the bias switches to more G:C base pairs.
3. When the bacteria replicate, A:T base pairs are more likely to switch places with G:C base pairs on the template strand. The opposite is true for base pairs on the leading strand.
4. Mutations tend to happen more often at certain positions in the genetic code. These positions are especially likely to have an A base pair replaced by a T base pair, or a G base pair replaced by a C base pair.
5. These findings suggest that the rate of small mutations (where one or a few base pairs change) is higher at repeat sequences. However, these events occur at a much slower rate than base-pair substitutions (where a larger section of the genetic code changes).
Mismatch repair is a genetic system that helps fix mistakes during replication. We found that many bacteria in nature don't have this system, which could be an adaptation. By comparing wild-type E. coli and MMR-defective strains, we may gain a deeper understanding of how mutation rates and spectra vary among organisms and how they are affected by the environment.

title: Apolipoprotein E4 as a predictor of outcomes in pediatric mild traumatic brain injury.
text: The epsilon4 allele of the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene has been associated with unfavorable outcomes in adults with traumatic brain injury (TBI), with similar patterns observed in children. This study investigated the relationship between the APOE epsilon4 allele and outcomes in children with mild TBI. The study included 99 children aged 8-15 who were admitted to the Emergency Department with mild TBI, of whom 28 had at least one epsilon4 allele. Demographic characteristics were similar between the two groups. Children with an epsilon4 allele were more likely to have a Glasgow Coma Scale score of less than 15, but did not differ from those without an epsilon4 allele on other measures of injury severity. However, children with an epsilon4 allele performed better than those without on a test of constructional skill, despite not differing on any other neuropsychological tests. Additionally, children with and without an epsilon4 allele did not differ on measures of post-concussive symptoms. Overall, the findings suggest that the APOE epsilon4 allele does not consistently relate to the outcomes of mild TBI in children.

title: Do physicians follow systemic treatment and funding policy guidelines?
text: Background: The use of bisphosphonates for the prevention of skeletal-related events in women with bone metastases from breast cancer is well established. To evaluate the use of bisphosphonates in clinical practice, we retrospectively reviewed the medical charts and electronic files of patients who received clodronate or pamidronate at three Canadian cancer centers between January 2000 and December 2001. Methods: We assessed the time between the diagnosis of bone metastases and the initiation of bisphosphonates, as well as whether physicians followed local treatment guidelines and funding policies. Results: Our findings show a significant improvement in the time between diagnosis and initiation of bisphosphonates, going from a median of 155 days in 1998 to 24 days in 2001. However, only 67% of patients received oral clodronate as their first bisphosphonate, despite a local funding policy recommending this. Furthermore, despite one center's guidelines recommending that bisphosphonates be discontinued when the patient is progressing, 90% of patients remained on bisphosphonates until they died. Conclusions: While considerable effort is devoted to creating evidence-based treatment guidelines, the implementation of these guidelines in clinical practice often falls short. Despite the creation of guidelines and policies, physicians still manage a significant proportion of patients outside of these guidelines, but within evidence-based recommendations. Therefore, there is a need for either the development of guidelines and policies that are more likely to be followed or the implementation of methods to ensure that restrictive policies are actually enforced.

title: Increased resting energy expenditure and weight loss are related to a systemic inflammatory response in lung cancer patients.
text:
The following is a rewritten version of the given text:
Objective: To investigate the relationship between increased resting energy expenditure (REE) and weight loss in lung cancer patients with a systemic inflammatory response.
Methods: REE was measured via indirect calorimetry using a ventilated hood system. The levels of soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor 55 (sTNF-R55), sTNF-R75, soluble intercellular adhesion molecule (sICAM)-1, soluble E (sE)-selectin, lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-binding protein (LBP), interleukin (IL)-6, and TNF-alpha were measured using sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). C-reactive protein (CRP) was measured through turbidimetry. A cross-sectional study was conducted to compare inflammatory mediators among hypermetabolic (REE/Harris Benedict (HB) equation ≥ 110%) vs. normometabolic (REE/HB < 110%) patients and among patients who lost weight (≥ 10% loss of preillness weight) vs. those whose weight remained stable.
Results: Eighty-seven patients with primary non-small-cell lung cancer were examined in the study. The mean REE expressed as a percentage of the HB reference values was 118% ± 12%; 67 patients were considered hypermetabolic. Twenty-six patients experienced a significant weight loss of more than 10% of their preillness weight. Hypermetabolic patients exhibited significantly elevated levels of sTNF-R55, sE-selectin, LBP, and CRP compared to normometabolic patients. Weight loss was associated with increased levels of the sTNF-Rs, sICAM-1, IL-6, LBP, and CRP.
Conclusion: Hypermetabolism and weight loss are closely related to the presence of a systemic inflammatory response, as evidenced by enhanced levels of inflammatory mediators and acute phase proteins in patients with primary non-small-cell lung cancer.

title: Exercise capacity and body mass as predictors of mortality among male veterans with type 2 diabetes.
text:
Objective:
To assess the relationship between exercise capacity and mortality in a cohort of male veterans with type 2 diabetes.
Research Design and Methods:
The study included 831 male patients with type 2 diabetes (mean age: 61 years) who underwent exercise testing for clinical reasons between 1995 and 2006. BMI was calculated, and patients were classified into three categories (18.5-24.9 kg/m2, 25.0-29.9 kg/m2, and > or =30 kg/m2). Exercise capacity was measured in metabolic equivalents (METs) and classified as <5.0 or > or =5.0 METs. The relationship between exercise capacity, BMI, and other clinical variables with all-cause mortality was assessed using Cox proportional hazards model. Study participants were followed up for mortality until June 30, 2006.
Results:
During a mean follow-up of 4.8 years, 112 patients died, resulting in an average annual mortality rate of 2.2%. With every 1-MET increase in exercise capacity, there was a 10% survival benefit (hazard ratio: 0.90 [95% CI: 0.82-0.98]; p < 0.01). However, BMI was not significantly associated with mortality after adjusting for age, ethnicity, examination year, BMI, presence of cardiovascular disease (CVD), and CVD risk factors. Diabetic patients who achieved <5 maximal METs were found to be 70% more likely to die than those who achieved > or =5 maximal METs after adjusting for confounding variables.
Conclusion:

There was a strong inverse association between exercise capacity and mortality in this cohort of men with documented diabetes. This relationship was found to be independent of BMI after adjusting for other clinical variables.

title: Impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia: a review.
text: Impaired awareness of hypoglycemia (IAH) is an acquired complication of insulin therapy that affects individuals with type 1 and insulin-treated type 2 diabetes mellitus. This condition is characterized by a diminished or absent ability to recognize the onset of hypoglycemia. Typically, deficiencies in the counter-regulatory hormonal responses to hypoglycemia co-exist in these individuals. The combination of IAH and counter-regulatory failure significantly increases the risk of severe hypoglycemia. To identify individuals at risk in a clinical setting, scoring systems have been developed. The primary treatment for IAH is strict avoidance of hypoglycemia.

title: A chikungunya fever vaccine utilizing an insect-specific virus platform
text:
Traditionally, vaccine development has been challenged by a trade-off between immunogenicity and safety. Live-attenuated vaccines generally provide rapid and durable immunity but often come with reduced safety compared to inactivated vaccines. In contrast, inactivated vaccines have increased safety but may require multiple doses and boosters to elicit an immune response. To overcome these limitations, we developed the insect-specific alphavirus, Eilat virus (EILV), as a vaccine platform.
To address the chikungunya fever (CHIKF) pandemic, we created a chimeric virus containing the chikungunya virus (CHIKV) structural proteins by using an EILV cDNA clone. The recombinant EILV/CHIKV was structurally identical to wild-type CHIKV at the nanoscale, as determined by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, and mimicked the early stages of CHIKV replication in vertebrate cells, from attachment and entry to viral RNA delivery. However, the recombinant virus remained completely incapable of productive replication, ensuring a high degree of safety. A single dose of EILV/CHIKV produced in mosquito cells elicited rapid (within 4 days) and long-lasting (>290 days) neutralizing antibodies that provided complete protection in two different mouse models. In nonhuman primates, EILV/CHIKV elicited rapid and robust immunity that protected against viremia and telemetrically monitored fever. Our EILV platform represents the first structurally native application of an insect-specific virus in preclinical vaccine development, highlighting the potential application of such viruses in vaccinology.

title: Molecular elements of low-oxygen signaling in plants.
text: Oxygen and its limitations are becoming increasingly important factors in plant fitness, growth, and development. Recent research has shed light on the mechanisms by which plants perceive and respond to oxygen. Our findings suggest that oxygen is perceived by plant cells through an oxygen-mediated branch of the N-end rule pathway for protein degradation, which targets a specific clade of ethylene responsive transcription factors (ERF-VII). An additional regulatory step involves the aerobic sequestration of an ERF-VII protein at the plasma membrane, followed by its timely release when hypoxia occurs. In the absence of oxygen, the transient accumulation of reactive hydrogen peroxide leads to the induction of an additional set of genes involved in both signaling and the attenuation of oxidative stress. Moreover, we have found that temporary hypoxic environments created as a result of dense cell packing can trigger cell-fate determination in maize anthers, while limited oxygen delivery in bulky fruit or tuber tissues growing in aerobic conditions can stimulate anaerobic-like responses. These advances highlight the critical role of hypoxia in plant development and underscore the importance of considering it in agricultural practices and breeding programs.

title: Purification, characterization, and sequence analysis of a potential virulence factor from Porphyromonas gingivalis, peptidylarginine deiminase.
text: The onset and progression of adult-onset periodontitis have been associated with the infection of the gingival sulcus by Porphyromonas gingivalis, an opportunistic pathogen that employs a brevity of virulence factors to evade the host's immune system. A common characteristic shared by many other oral pathogens is the production of ammonia, which serves as a protective mechanism during acidic oral environments. Additionally, the production of ammonia by P. gingivalis has been proposed as a virulence factor due to its detrimental effects on neutrophil function. In this study, we have successfully purified and characterized a peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD) from a prokaryote, which exhibits biochemical properties that suggest its potential as a virulence factor. PAD deiminates the guanidino group of carboxyl-terminal arginine residues on various peptides, including the vasoactive peptide-hormone bradykinin, resulting in the formation of ammonia and a citrulline residue. The purified protein has an estimated molecular mass of 46 kDa, whereas the DNA sequence predicts a full-length protein of 61.7 kDa. PAD is optimal activity at 55 degrees Celsius, stable at low pH, and exhibits the highest activity above pH 9.0. Interestingly, in the presence of stabilizing factors, PAD is resistant to limited proteolysis and retains significant activity after brief exposure to boiling. We propose that PAD, in collaboration with arginine-specific proteinases from P. gingivalis, fosters the growth of the pathogen in the periodontal pocket, initially by bolstering its survivability and then by facilitating its evasion of host humoral defenses.

title: Traumatic encephalopathy: review and provisional research diagnostic criteria.
text:
Objective: To determine the frequency of neurobehavioral signs and symptoms reported in published cases of traumatic encephalopathy (TE) in order to develop clinical diagnostic criteria with predictive validity.
Introduction: Since 1928, there have been reports of persistent or progressive neurological or neurobehavioral changes following one or more head injuries. However, no diagnostic criteria have been established or accepted for the clinical diagnosis of TE. Provisional research diagnostic criteria are needed not only for meaningful diagnosis but also to facilitate research on the epidemiology, etiology, course, prognosis, imaging, and biomarkers of TE, as well as its neuropathological features and potential treatments.
Methods: All 436 published cases of TE in various languages were reviewed, and all symptoms and signs reported were classified and enumerated. Ninety-seven cases met inclusion criteria based on sufficient documentation of the history and neurobehavioral examination. Provisional research diagnostic criteria for clinically probable and clinically possible TE were developed based on the most frequently reported clinical features.
Results: The provisional diagnostic criteria for TE presented here are the first published criteria based on a systematic analysis of its clinical characteristics.
Conclusion: The provisional diagnostic criteria for TE presented here are a step toward scientifically derived consensus criteria, which are essential to accelerate progress in the investigation of this important condition.

title: Hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus infection.
text: In the United States, an estimated 200,000 individuals are simultaneously infected with both the hepatitis C virus (HCV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). As HIV-infected individuals have experienced prolonged life expectancy due to highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), liver disease has emerged as a prominent cause of morbidity and mortality among this population. HIV infection appears to exacerbate all stages of HCV infection, leading to increased viral persistence and accelerated progression of HCV-related liver disease. In turn, hepatitis C can complicate the management of HIV infection by increasing the incidence of liver toxicity associated with antiretroviral medications. The medical management of hepatitis C in HIV-infected individuals remains contentious due to the interplay of both infections and potential drug interactions, as well as the scarcity of published information. Nevertheless, the burden of liver disease is significant enough to warrant immediate management of HIV/HCV-coinfected individuals before more data becomes available. Therefore, the management of hepatitis C must be based on data obtained from individuals without HIV, and an understanding of the interactions between both infections. Ongoing studies of therapy in HIV/HCV-coinfected individuals are necessary to guide the management of these patients in the future.

title: Role of the vascular endothelial growth factor pathway in tumor growth and angiogenesis.
text: New blood vessel formation, or angiogenesis, is a crucial process in the growth and spread of tumors. As such, understanding the molecular mechanisms behind tumor angiogenesis has been a key area of focus in cancer research. The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) pathway has been identified as a major regulator of this process. The VEGF/VEGF-receptor axis involves multiple ligands and receptors with distinct binding specificities, expression patterns, and functions. Activation of this pathway triggers a network of signaling processes that promote endothelial cell growth, migration, and survival, as well as vessel permeability. Additionally, VEGF has been implicated in the mobilization of endothelial progenitor cells from the bone marrow to areas of neovascularization. Given the established role of VEGF in tumor angiogenesis and cancer pathogenesis, researchers have designed and developed agents that selectively target this pathway. Studies with anti-VEGF/VEGF-receptor therapies have shown that these agents can significantly inhibit angiogenesis and tumor growth in preclinical models. Most recently, an anti-VEGF antibody (bevacizumab) has been shown to improve survival and response rates when used in combination with chemotherapy in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer, further validating the importance of VEGF pathway inhibitors as a new treatment modality in cancer therapy.

title: Frozen robust multiarray analysis (fRMA).
text: Robust multiarray analysis (RMA) is the most commonly used preprocessing algorithm for Affymetrix and Nimblegen gene expression microarrays. RMA modularly performs background correction, normalization, and summarization. The last two steps require analyzing multiple arrays simultaneously. RMA's ability to share information across samples comes with several benefits. For example, the summarization step uses a parametric model that considers probe-specific effects, assumed to be constant across arrays, and enhances outlier detection. Residuals obtained from the fitted model can create useful quality metrics. However, RMA's reliance on multiple arrays has two drawbacks: (1) it cannot be used in clinical settings where samples must be processed individually or in small batches and (2) data sets preprocessed separately cannot be compared. To address these limitations, we propose a preprocessing algorithm called frozen RMA (fRMA). fRMA allows for individual or small batch processing of microarrays and combines the data for analysis using information from the large publicly available microarray databases. Specifically, probe-specific effects and variances are precomputed and frozen, and these are then used in conjunction with data from new arrays to normalize and summarize the data. We find that fRMA performs equally well as RMA when analyzing the data as a single batch and outperforms RMA when analyzing multiple batches. The fRMA methods are available in the R package fRMA and can be downloaded from the software section of <http://rafalab.jhsph.edu>.

title: Hypoxia in relation to vasculature and proliferation in liver metastases in patients with colorectal cancer.
text:
Research Objective: To investigate hypoxia in liver metastases of colorectal cancer by analyzing pimonidazole binding, glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) and carbonic anhydrase IX (CA-IX) expression, proliferation, and vascularity, and to compare GLUT1 and CA-IX expression in corresponding primary tumors.
Methods and Materials: Twenty-five patients with liver metastases of colorectal cancer scheduled for metastasectomy were included in the study. The hypoxia marker pimonidazole and proliferation marker iododeoxyuridine were administered before surgery. The frozen metastases were then stained with immunofluorescence, and pimonidazole binding, vascularity, and proliferation were analyzed quantitatively. Thirteen paraffin-embedded primary tumors were stained immunohistochemically for GLUT1 and CA-IX expression, which were analyzed semiquantitatively in primary tumors and corresponding liver metastases.
Results: In liver metastases, pimonidazole binding showed a pattern consistent with diffusion-limited hypoxia, with a mean pimonidazole-positive fraction of 0.146 and a mean distance from vessels to pimonidazole-positive areas of 80 microm. Pimonidazole binding often co-localized with GLUT1 or CA-IX expression, but microregional areas of mismatch were also observed. No correlation was found between the level of pimonidazole binding and GLUT1 or CA-IX expression. In some patients, a significant fraction (up to 30%) of proliferating cells was present in pimonidazole-stained areas. Expression of CA-IX in primary tumors and metastases showed a significant correlation, which was absent for GLUT1 expression.
Conclusions: Compared to other tumor types, liver metastases of colorectal cancer contain large amounts of hypoxic cells. The lack of correlation between pimonidazole binding and GLUT1 and CA-IX expression raises questions about the usefulness of these markers for measuring hypoxia in liver metastases.

title: Unmet needs mediate the relationship between symptoms and quality of life in breast cancer survivors
text: This study aimed to investigate the symptoms, unmet needs, and quality of life (QoL) reported by women at 6 months to <2 years and 2 to 5 years after surgery and adjuvant treatment for breast cancer. The study also evaluated the relationship among these variables using structural equation modeling. The study included 113 and 137 survivors at <2 years and 2 to 5 years, respectively, who completed the Memorial Symptom Assessment Scale, the Supportive Care Needs Survey-34, and the Medical Outcomes Study 12-item Short Form Health Survey version 2.0 during their medical follow-up. The results showed that the mean number of symptoms and unmet needs were 5.43 and 3.0, respectively, for survivors at <2 years, and 5.24 and 2.42, respectively, for survivors at 2 to 5 years following treatment. The most common reported symptoms were related to physical domains. No significant differences were found between the two survivor groups on the Memorial Symptom Assessment Scale scores. Survivors at <2 years reported significantly higher scores in Psychological and Health Care System/Information needs (p < 0.01), and lower composite scores in physical and mental QoL (p < 0.05) than those at 2 to 5 years post-treatment. Significant direct and indirect effects were found of symptom burden through unmet needs on survivors’ physical and mental QoL after adjustment for survival time, and the models showed a good fit. The study suggests that breast cancer survivors continue to experience many symptoms regardless of their survivorship period, and unmet needs mediate the relationship between symptom burden and survivors’ QoL.

title: Phagocytosis and deposition of vascular beta-amyloid in rat brains injected with Alzheimer beta-amyloid.
text: The presence of extracellular deposits of beta-amyloid protein in the brain is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD). To investigate the effect of amyloid in an animal model, researchers injected isolated amyloid cores from AD brains into the cortex and hippocampus of rats. As a control, they also injected lipofuscin, a major contaminant of the plaque core preparation, into the opposite side of the brain to stimulate a similar phagocytic cell response. Rats were sacrificed at different intervals (2 days, 7 days, and 1 month) after injection, and amyloid was detected using four different histochemical techniques. The researchers found that both amyloid and lipofuscin moved from the injection site into undamaged neuropil, persisted for at least 1 month, and were associated with increases in glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and microglia (OX-42) staining. By 1 week, many of the amyloid cores were engulfed by phagocytes. Some of the beta-amyloid-containing phagocytes migrated to vessels and ventricles, and by 1 month, a significant amount of the amyloid was directly associated with vessels. These findings suggest that phagocytic cells can internalize exogenous amyloid and attempt to clear it from the central nervous system (CNS). Therefore, the observed distribution of amyloid is not necessarily the initial site of deposition.

title: Specific sites in the C terminus of CTCF interact with the SA2 subunit of the cohesin complex and are required for cohesin-dependent insulation activity.
text: Recent studies have revealed that the protein CTCF, which plays a crucial role in organizing chromatin structure within the eukaryotic nucleus, relies on recruiting the cohesin complex for both its insulation and organization functions. Our findings show that direct interactions between the cohesin subunit SA2 and specific regions of the C-terminal tail of CTCF are essential for CTCF's activity. All other cohesin components are recruited through their interaction with SA2. Expression of CTCF mutants lacking the C-terminal domain or with mutations within it disrupts the normal expression profile of imprinted genes IGF2-H19 and also impairs CTCF's insulation activity. These results demonstrate that specific regions on the C terminus of CTCF are critical for cohesin binding and insulator function. Notably, the only direct interaction between CTCF and cohesin involves contact between CTCF and SA2, which is located external to the cohesin ring. This suggests that SA2 may bind to CTCF first, and the cohesin ring may assemble subsequently.

title: Interleukin 6 plays a key role in the development of antigen-induced arthritis.
text: In order to investigate the direct role of interleukin (IL-6) in the development of rheumatoid arthritis, IL-6-deficient mice (IL-6 -/-) were backcrossed for eight generations into C57BL/6 mice, a strain prone to antigen-induced arthritis (AIA). Compared to wild-type (IL-6 +/+) littermates, IL-6 -/- mice displayed mild arthritis, and Safranin O staining revealed well-preserved articular cartilage in these mice. Furthermore, the mRNA expression of IL-1 beta and tumor necrosis factor alpha, but not IL-6, was found to be comparable in the inflamed joints of IL-6 -/- mice, suggesting that IL-6 may play a more crucial role in cartilage destruction than either IL-1 beta or tumor necrosis factor alpha. In addition, IL-6 -/- mice exhibited reduced in vitro proliferative responses in lymph node cells and decreased in vivo antibody production upon antigen stimulation, and their lymph node cells produced more Th2 cytokines than IL-6 +/+ mice. These results suggest that IL-6 may contribute to the development of AIA both at the inductive and effector phases, and blocking IL-6 may be beneficial in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis.

title: Relation between renal function within the normal range and central and peripheral arterial stiffness in hypertension.
text:
In this study, we investigated the relationship between renal function and arterial stiffness in patients with essential hypertension. We included 305 patients, aged 48±11 years, with normal renal function (serum creatinine values <1.4 mg/dL in men and <1.2 mg/dL in women), who were free from overt cardiovascular disease. We measured arterial stiffness using noninvasive pulse wave velocity (PWV) determinations in the aorta and upper limbs.
Our results showed that glomerular filtration rate (GFR), estimated using the Mayo clinic equation, was inversely correlated with large-artery stiffness, as assessed by aortic PWV (r=-0.34, P<0.001), and with peripheral artery stiffness, as assessed by upper-limb PWV (r=-0.25, P<0.001). In a multivariate linear regression analysis, aortic PWV was independently predicted by age (β=0.48, P<0.001), mean arterial pressure (β=0.14, P=0.013), and GFR (β=-0.13, P=0.029). Upper-limb PWV was predicted by GFR (β=-0.24, P<0.001) and mean arterial pressure (β=0.20, P<0.001).
Our findings indicate that in hypertensive patients with normal renal function, there is an inverse relationship between GFR and stiffness of both central elastic and peripheral muscular arteries. These relations are in part independent from the effects of age, sex, and blood pressure values. Our results highlight the importance of considering renal function when assessing arterial stiffness in hypertensive patients, as it may help identify individuals at higher risk of cardiovascular disease.

title: Comparative gene expression profiling of in vitro differentiated megakaryocytes and erythroblasts identifies novel activatory and inhibitory platelet membrane proteins.
text: To identify novel platelet receptors, we compared the transcriptomes of in vitro differentiated megakaryocytes (MKs) and erythroblasts (EBs). We obtained RNA from purified, biochemically paired MK and EB cultures and analyzed it using cDNA microarrays. Bioinformatic analysis of MK-up-regulated genes revealed 151 transcripts encoding transmembrane domain-containing proteins. Many of these were known platelet genes, but a number of previously unidentified or poorly characterized transcripts were also discovered. These included G6b, G6f, LRRC32, LAT2, and the G protein-coupled receptor SUCNR1, which encode proteins with structural features or functions suggesting a role in platelet function modulation. Immunoblotting on platelets confirmed the presence of these proteins, and flow cytometric analysis confirmed their surface expression on platelets. Through comparative analysis of expression in platelets and other blood cells, we showed that G6b, G6f, and LRRC32 are specifically expressed in the platelet lineage, while LAT2 and SUCNR1 were also detected in other blood cells. The identification of the succinate receptor SUCNR1 on platelets is particularly interesting, as physiologically relevant concentrations of succinate were shown to enhance the effects of low doses of various platelet agonists.

title: Topographic mapping of VMH → arcuate nucleus microcircuits and their reorganization by fasting
text: In the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC), neurons that produce the protein pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) inhibit feeding, while neurons that produce neuropeptide-Y (NPY) stimulate feeding. To investigate how neurons in the ventromedial hypothalamic nucleus (VMH), a known satiety center, regulate these feeding-related neurons, we observed the synaptic inputs projecting to POMC and NPY neurons in brain slices from genetically engineered mice. Our findings indicate that POMC neurons receive strong excitatory inputs from the medial VMH (mVMH), while NPY neurons receive weak inhibitory inputs only from within the ARC. Interestingly, the strength of the excitatory input from the mVMH to POMC neurons is reduced by fasting. These data reveal a novel, anatomically distinct circuit that is dynamically regulated by nutritional state in a manner consistent with the VMH's known role as a satiety center.

title: The human immunodeficiency virus type 1 nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor resistance mutation I132M confers hypersensitivity to nucleoside analogs.
text: In a earlier study, we discovered a rare mutation in the reverse transcriptase (RT) gene of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1), specifically the I132M mutation, which grants resistance to non-nucleoside RT inhibitors (NNRTIs) such as nevirapine and delavirdine. Our latest research investigated the impact of this mutation on viral replication capacity and resistance to other RT inhibitors. To our surprise, the data revealed that I132M actually confers heightened sensitivity to nucleoside analogs like lamivudine (3TC) and tenofovir at both the virus and enzyme levels. Further studies using subunit-selective mutagenesis and transient kinetic analysis showed that the mutation in the p51 subunit of RT is responsible for the increased sensitivity to these drugs, which is due to a decrease in the enzyme's affinity for the natural dCTP substrate and an increase in its affinity for 3TC-triphosphate. Additionally, the replication capacity of HIV-1 containing I132M is significantly impaired, which can be partially or completely compensated for by the A62V or L214I mutation, respectively. Overall, these findings help shed light on the rare occurrence of I132M selection in patients whose NNRTI regimens are failing, and demonstrate that a single mutation outside of the polymerase active site and within the p51 subunit of RT can significantly impact nucleotide selectivity.

title: AFF1 and AFF4 differentially regulate the osteogenic differentiation of human MSCs
text: Members of the AFF (AF4/FMR2) protein family, including AFF1 and AFF4, act as scaffolding proteins that integrate the activity of two transcription elongation factors, positive elongation factor b (P-TEFb) and ELL1/2, in the formation of super elongation complexes (SECs). Although their role in osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) is unclear, this study reveals that depleting AFF1 with small interfering RNA (siRNA) leads to increased alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, enhanced mineralization, and upregulated expression of osteogenic-related genes. Conversely, depletion of AFF4 significantly hinders the osteogenic potential of MSCs. The study also shows that overexpression of AFF1 and AFF4 has different effects on osteogenic differentiation in vitro and MSC-mediated bone formation in vivo. Mechanistically, AFF1 regulates the expression of DKK1 through its binding to the DKK1 promoter region. Depleting DKK1 in HA-AFF1-overexpressing MSCs rescues the impaired osteogenic differentiation. Furthermore, the study reveals that AFF4 is enriched in the promoter region of ID1. AFF4 knockdown blunts the BRE luciferase activity, SP7 expression, and ALP activity induced by BMP2 treatment. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that AFF1 and AFF4 differentially regulate osteogenic differentiation in human MSCs.

title: Markers of myocardial damage and inflammation in relation to long-term mortality in unstable coronary artery disease. FRISC Study Group. Fragmin during Instability in Coronary Artery Disease.
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the predictive value of troponin T, C-reactive protein, and fibrinogen levels in patients with unstable coronary artery disease (CAD) for long-term mortality from cardiac causes. We analyzed data from 917 patients enrolled in the Fragmin during Instability in Coronary Artery Disease trial, and followed them for a mean of 37.0 months.
We found that patients with low levels of troponin T (less than 0.06 microg/liter) had a low risk of death from cardiac causes (1.2%), compared to those with higher levels (0.06-0.59 microg/liter: 8.7%, and at least 0.60 microg/liter: 15.4%). Similarly, patients with low levels of C-reactive protein (less than 2 mg/liter) had a low risk of death (5.7%), while those with higher levels had a progressively higher risk (7.8% for 2-10 mg/liter, and 16.5% for more than 10 mg/liter). Additionally, we found that patients with low levels of fibrinogen (less than 3.4 g/liter) had a low risk of death (5.4%), while those with higher levels had a higher risk (12.0% for 3.4-3.9 g/liter, and 12.9% for at least 4.0 g/liter).
We also conducted a multivariate analysis and found that levels of troponin T and C-reactive protein were independent predictors of the risk of death from cardiac causes. These findings suggest that elevated levels of troponin T and C-reactive protein are strongly related to the long-term risk of death from cardiac causes in patients with unstable CAD. These markers are additive with respect to each other and other clinical indicators of risk, and can be useful in identifying patients at high risk of death from cardiac causes.

title: Loss of lamin B1 results in prolongation of S phase and decondensation of chromosome territories.
text: Nuclear lamin B1 (LMNB1) makes up a significant portion of the structural proteins in the lamina mesh within cells. To investigate its role, we silenced LMNB1 expression in the colon cancer cell line DLD-1 and observed a dramatic redistribution of the histone H3K27me3 mark from the cell periphery to a more homogeneous distribution throughout the nucleus. Additionally, we observed telomere shortening, increased frequency of micronuclei and nuclear blebs, and changes in alternative splicing of multiple genes in LMNB1-depleted cells. Using 3D-FISH analysis, we found that the volume and surface area of chromosome territories were significantly larger in LMNB1-deficient cells, pointing to a role for LMNB1 in maintaining chromatin condensation during interphase. These changes led to a prolonged S phase due to the activation of the Chk1 checkpoint. Furthermore, silencing of LMNB1 resulted in increased enlargement of nuclear speckles and extensive changes in alternative splicing of various genes. Overall, our findings suggest that the nuclear lamina plays a mechanistic role in organizational chromosome architecture, maintaining genome integrity, and proper alternative splicing.

title: Human artificial chromosomes with alpha satellite-based de novo centromeres show increased frequency of nondisjunction and anaphase lag.
text: Human artificial chromosomes have been employed to mimic the requirements for human chromosome segregation and to investigate the characteristics of sequences capable of performing centromere functions. Natural human centromeres require specialized chromatin comprising alpha satellite DNA bound to epigenetically modified histones and centromere-specific proteins. Although various types of alpha satellite DNA have been utilized to create de novo centromeres in artificial chromosome assays, the extent to which they recapitulate normal centromere function remains unexplored. We have employed two types of alpha satellite DNA, DXZ1 (from the X chromosome) and D17Z1 (from chromosome 17), to construct human artificial chromosomes. Notably, artificial chromosomes have displayed higher levels of segregation errors during individual cell divisions using an anaphase assay compared to natural human chromosomes (P < 0.001). Abnormally small chromosomes derived from chromosomes 17 and the X chromosome have also demonstrated increased missegregation, indicating that overall chromosome size and/or structure may influence chromosome segregation fidelity. Moreover, we have observed variable centromeric DNA content and/or epigenetic assembly among different artificial chromosomes, which suggests that these factors may impact the mitotic behavior of artificial chromosomes.

title: Identification of a human HLA-E-restricted CD8+ T cell subset in volunteers immunized with Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi strain Ty21a typhoid vaccine.
text: Our previous research on volunteers immunized with Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi) has suggested a significant role for CD8+ T cells in host defense. In this study, we identify a novel subset of HLA-E-restricted S. Typhi-specific CD8+ T cells derived from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) of Ty21a typhoid vaccinees. These cells can effectively kill S. Typhi-infected targets without sharing classical HLA class I molecules with them, using a FAS-independent, granule-dependent mechanism that involves the release of granzyme B and the inhibition of concanamycin and strontium ions. Our findings also demonstrate that the expression of HLA-E molecules on the surface of S. Typhi-infected targets makes them susceptible to lysis, and that anti-HLA-E antibodies can partially block these responses. Additionally, we show that presentation of S. Typhi antigens via HLA-E can stimulate the production of interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma). Increases in the net frequency of IFN-gamma-producing cells were observed when targets were coated with peptides containing S. Typhi groEL HLA-E binding motifs. These results suggest that HLA-E binds nonamer peptides derived from bacterial proteins and triggers CD8+-mediated lysis and IFN-gamma production when exposed to infected targets, which may contribute to host defense against intracellular bacterial infections.

title: Costs and cost-effectiveness of alternative tuberculosis management strategies in South Africa--implications for policy.
text:
Objective:
Conduct an economic analysis of the Hlabisa community-based directly observed therapy management strategy for tuberculosis and project the costs of three alternative strategies.
Setting:
Hlabisa health district, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa.

Methods: An economic analysis comparing the current tuberculosis management strategy in Hlabisa with three alternative strategies (the Hlabisa strategy prior to 1991 based on hospitalization, the national strategy, and sanatorium care) in terms of costs to both health service and patient, and of cost-effectiveness.

Results:
The current Hlabisa strategy was found to be the most cost-effective, with a cost of R3799 per patient cured, whereas the strategy used prior to 1991 had a cost of R98307, the national strategy had a cost of R9940, and sanatorium care had a cost of R11145. Between 71% and 88% of treatment costs were found to lie with the health service, with hospitalization (R119 per day) being the most expensive item. Prolonged hospitalization was found to be extremely expensive, but community care was cheaper (R28 for a community clinic visit and R7 for a community health worker visit). The total cost of supervising a patient in the community under the current Hlabisa strategy was R503, equivalent to 4.2 days in hospital, while drug costs (R157) were equivalent to just 1.3 days in hospital.

title: Interleukin-18 null mutation increases weight and food intake and reduces energy expenditure and lipid substrate utilization in high-fat diet fed mice
text:
The objective of this study is to investigate the impact of interleukin-18 (IL-18) on weight gain, energy intake, whole-body energy expenditure, and lipid metabolism in high-fat diet-fed mice. The researchers aim to determine whether IL-18 modulates basal metabolic rate and metabolic processes in addition to its known role in modulating food intake and energy metabolism during sickness.
To achieve this, the researchers compared the food intake, metabolism, and motor activity of IL-18 knockout mice with their wildtype littermates. They also evaluated the anorectic effects of intracerebroventricular IL-18 administration in IL-18 receptor knockout, IL-18/IL-18R knockout, and wildtype mice.
The results showed that IL-18 knockout mice were overweight at 6 months of age and gained excess weight on both low-fat and high-fat diets, consumed more high-fat food, and showed reduced whole-body energy expenditure and increased respiratory exchange ratios. Additionally, the energy expenditure of IL-18 knockout mice was found to be reduced across different fasting and feeding conditions, diets, levels of physical activity, and times of day, indicating actions on basal metabolic rate. The circadian amplitude of energy expenditure was also blunted in IL-18 knockout mice, but not in food intake, motor activity, or respiratory exchange ratio. Furthermore, central IL-18 administration reduced high-fat diet intake in wildtype mice, but not in mice lacking the IL-18 receptor.
The findings of this study suggest that endogenous IL-18 has a suppressive effect on appetite and promotes energy expenditure and lipid fuel substrate utilization not only during sickness but also in healthy adults consuming high-fat diets.

title: Notch activation promotes cell proliferation and the formation of neural stem cell-like colonies in human glioma cells
text: Our study aimed to investigate the potential roles of Notch signaling in the formation of cancer stem cells and cancer cells with a stem cell phenotype in human glioma. Using RT-PCR, we found that most human astrogliomas of different grades expressed moderate to high levels of Notch receptors and ligands, including Hes5 but not Hes1, which are downstream molecules of the Notch pathway. We detected mRNA encoding different types of Notch receptors in human glioma cell lines BT325, U251, SHG-44, and U87, but only active form of Notch1 (NIC) was detected in SHG-44 and U87 cells by Western blot. Interestingly, proliferation of these two glioma cell lines appeared faster than that of the other two lines in which NIC was not detected. To evaluate the effects of Notch signaling on glioma cells, weconstitutive transfected NIC of Notch1 into SHG-44 cells. Our results showed that over-expression of NIC in SHG-44 cells promoted the growth and colony-forming activity of these cells. Furthermore, over-expression of NIC increased the formation of neurosphere-like colonies in the presence of growth factors, which expressed nestin and could be induced to express neuron-, astrocyte-, or oligodendrocyte-specific markers, consistent with the phenotypes of neural stem cells. These findings suggest that Notch signaling promotes the formation of cancer stem cell-like cells in human glioma.

title: Rodent models in bone-related research: the relevance of calvarial defects in the assessment of bone regeneration strategies.
text: In vivuous research involving animal models has been a widely utilized experimental system in bone-related biomedical research since it allows for the collection of relevant data regarding physiological and pathological conditions, which can be used to develop more effective clinical interventions. Animal models, specifically rodent models, have been extensively used and have contributed significantly to the development and establishment of various translational approaches aimed at regenerating bone tissue. The calvarial defect model has been particularly useful in basic and applied research, but its controversial use is due to the inability of critical and subcritical size defects to spontaneously heal. This work aims to discuss the advantages and limitations of using rodent models in bone-related biomedical research, with a particular focus on the problematic issues surrounding the use of calvarial critical and subcritical size defects. Additionally, the work provides surgical protocols for establishing both defects in rat calvarial bone, as well as examples of the most commonly used techniques for accessing bone tissue repair.

title: The transcriptional responses of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to inhibitors of metabolism: novel insights into drug mechanisms of action.
text: A study on the Mycobacterium tuberculosis microarray profiles revealed a comprehensive understanding of the bacteria's transcriptional responses to drugs and growth-inhibitory conditions. The analysis uncovered 150 underlying clusters of coordinately regulated genes, providing a glimpse into the full metabolic potential of the organism. These findings were validated through biochemical analysis for two previously uncategorized agents, pyridoacridones and phenothiazines. The study showed that transcriptional profiling of both crude and purified natural products can offer valuable insights into the mechanism of action and detoxification of these compounds before purification, guiding the drug discovery process. Notably, the transcriptional profile of a crude marine natural product aligned with the predicted mechanism from the pure active component, underscoring the potential of this approach. The discovered gene clusters also shed light on the metabolic response of bacteria to drug-induced stress and offered a rational basis for selecting critical metabolic targets for screening new agents with improved activity against this important human pathogen.

title: Electron microscopic studies of macrophages in early human yolk sacs.
text: The distribution and fine structure of macrophages were investigated in 10 human embryos ranging in age from 6 to 7 weeks gestation (5.5 to 12 mm crown-rump length). Macrophages were discovered in the mesenchymal tissues and blood vessels outside of the yolk sac, and they were found to be present in the intravascular space before the appearance of bone marrow and lymphatic tissues. In addition to macrophages, fibroblastic cells and cells of the erythropoietic series were also observed in the extravascular tissue. The macrophages displayed various cellular structures indicating a transition from immature to mature forms, and they showed robust phagocytic activity, engulfing and digesting both primitive erythroblasts and occasional platelets. The macrophages were positively stained for lysosomal enzymes and exhibited numerous pleomorphic heterophagolysosomes displaying different stages of digestion. It is uncertain whether intravascular macrophages derive from migrated extravascular macrophages or phagocytic endothelial cells. The phagocytosis and degradation of erythroblasts appear to be a primary function of yolk sac macrophages. Moreover, the presence of macrophages in mitosis suggests their proliferation in situ.

title: Urban malaria and anaemia in children: a cross-sectional survey in two cities of Ghana.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the epidemiology of urban malaria, a growing concern in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in Ghana.
Methods:
Cross-sectional surveys were conducted in Accra and Kumasi, Ghana, to determine risk factors for malaria infection and anemia in children aged 6-60 months. Malaria prevalence rates varied between urban communities, ranging from 2% to 33%. Approximately 47% of children were anemic (Hb<11.0 g/dl). The study identified factors associated with malaria prevalence, including low socio-economic status, age, and anemia. The attributable risks of anemia and severe anemia (Hb<8.0 g/dl) caused by malaria were 5% and 23%, respectively.
Conclusions:
Urban malaria exhibited heterogeneity and complexity, which differed from rural areas. The study highlighted the importance of targeting specific areas or districts to effectively control malaria. Moreover, the most vulnerable group, the urban poor, should be prioritized when designing control measures. A thorough assessment of malaria risk patterns is necessary to guide an integrated control program.

title: Nitrite infusions to prevent delayed cerebral vasospasm in a primate model of subarachnoid hemorrhage.
text: The study aimed to investigate whether infusions of nitrite can prevent delayed cerebral vasospasm in anesthetized cynomolgus monkeys after subarachnoid hemorrhage. The study included 14 monkeys, with 3 receiving a 90-mg sodium nitrite intravenous solution infused over 24 hours, 3 receiving a 180-mg sodium nitrite intravenous solution infused over 24 hours, and 8 receiving a control saline solution infusion. The infusions were administered continuously for 14 days, and the monkeys were evaluated using arteriography on days 7 and 14. The results showed that sodium nitrite infusions increased blood and cerebrospinal fluid nitrite levels, prevented the development of vasospasm, and correlated with the formation of S-nitrosothiol in cerebrospinal fluid. There was no evidence of nitrite toxicity in the study. The study concluded that subacute sodium nitrite infusions prevented delayed cerebral vasospasm in the primate model of subarachnoid hemorrhage.

title: Developmental gene networks: a triathlon on the course to T cell identity
text: Cells acquires their definitive identities by triggering combinations of transcription factors that initiate and sustain expression of the appropriate cell type-specific genes. T cell development compartmentalizes into three critical phases, each governed by distinct transcription factor clusters that regulate progenitor cell migration to the thymus, proliferation, lineage commitment, and sensitivity to T cell receptor signals, all prior to the designation of cells to particular effector programs. Each phase is indispensable for proper T cell development, and the mechanisms that define each phase's boundaries are equally crucial. Unless cells halt one set of regulators before starting the following gene network phase, they are predisposed to transforming into leukemia.

title: A tumor necrosis factor-α–mediated pathway promoting autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
text: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is caused by mutations in either the PKD1 or PKD2 genes, which encode polycystin-1 and polycystin-2, respectively. We found that tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), an inflammatory cytokine present in the cystic fluid of ADPKD patients, disrupts the localization of polycystin-2 to the plasma membrane and primary cilia through a scaffold protein called FIP2, which is induced by TNF-α. Treatment of mouse embryonic kidney organ cultures with TNF-α led to the formation of cysts, and this effect was stronger in Pkd2+/− kidneys. TNF-α also stimulated cyst formation in vivo in Pkd2+/− mice. Conversely, treatment of Pkd2+/− mice with the TNF-α inhibitor etanercept prevented cyst formation. These findings suggest a pathway between TNF-α signaling, polycystins, and cystogenesis, where the activation of this pathway may reduce the amount of functional polycystin-2 below a critical threshold, leading to the ADPKD cellular phenotype.

title: Inappropriate inhaler use: assessment of use and patient preference of seven inhalation devices. EDICI.
text:
Inefficient inhaler technique is a common problem that can lead to poor drug delivery, reduced disease control, and increased inhaler use. The aim of our study was to assess patients' preferences for different inhaler devices and determine if patient preference is related to ease of use. We also wanted to determine the best method for selecting an inhaler based on patient technique and device cost.
One hundred patients were trained in the use of seven different inhaler devices in a random order. After training, patients were assessed on their inhaler technique using predetermined criteria. Patients were then asked to select their top three preferred inhalers and which, if any, they currently used. Our results showed that the breath-actuated inhalers (Easi-Breathe and Autohaler) had the best technique, with 91% of patients showing good technique. In contrast, the pressurized metered dose inhaler (pMDI) had the lowest technique scores, despite being the most commonly prescribed. The Easi-Breathe was the most popular device among patients, followed by the Autohaler, Clickhaler, and Accuhaler.
Interestingly, despite being the most commonly prescribed device, only 55% of patients currently used the pMDI, and only 79% of patients tested could use it effectively even after expert instruction.
