Additionally, the relaxant effect of vagal stimulation was ablated by hexamethonium, an inhibitor of ganglionic nicotinic receptors, indicating that ganglionic transmission does not rely on NO release from preganglionic neurons. However, hexamethonium did not inhibit the gastric relaxation induced by increasing the intragastric pressure, which is also mediated by NO, consistent with our previous findings. The selective inhibition by hexamethonium of only the vagally mediated relaxation but not of the pressure-induced relaxation of the stomach suggests the existence of at least two distinct neuronal pathways capable of generating NO and contributing to gastric accommodation of food or fluid.

title: Efficient T cell activation requires an optimal dwell-time of interaction between the TCR and the pMHC complex
text: Cytotoxic T cell (CTL) activation by antigen is dependent on the specific detection of peptide-major histo-compatibility class I (pMHC) molecules on the target cell surface by the T cell receptor (TCR). To investigate the effect of mutations in the antigen-binding site of a Kb-restricted TCR on T cell activation, antigen binding, and dissociation from antigen, we examined these parameters for variants derived from a Kd-restricted peptide that was recognized by a CTL clone. Using these two independent systems, our data demonstrate that T cell activation can be impaired by mutations that either decrease or increase the binding half-life of the TCR-pMHC interaction. Our findings indicate that efficient T cell activation occurs within a finite dwell-time range of the TCR-pMHC interaction, which is consistent with the exclusion of either extremely low or high affinity T cells from the expanded population during immune responses.

title: Crystal structure of human insulin-regulated aminopeptidase with specificity for cyclic peptides.
text: Insulin-regulated aminopeptidase (IRAP or oxytocinase) is a membrane-bound zinc-metallopeptidase that is involved in the cleavage of neuroactive peptides in the brain, resulting in memory-enhancing effects when inhibited. We have recently determined the crystal structure of human IRAP, which reveals a unique, four-domain arrangement with a large, mostly buried cavity adjacent to the active site. This structure provides insight into the GAMEN exopeptidase loop's unusual conformation compared to other aminopeptidases, thereby explaining IRAP's specificity for cyclic peptides such as oxytocin and vasopressin. Furthermore, computational docking of IRAP-specific cognitive enhancers into the crystal structure suggests a molecular basis for their structure-activity relationships, and demonstrates that the structure will be a valuable tool in the development of new classes of cognitive enhancers for treating various memory disorders, including Alzheimer's disease.

title: Glutathione and glutathione-dependent enzymes represent a co-ordinately regulated defence against oxidative stress.
text: Glutathione, a tripeptide molecule, plays a crucial role in protecting cells against oxidative stress, which occurs when the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the cell exceed its antioxidant capacity. Chronic oxidative stress can lead to cellular dysfunction, DNA damage, and protein inactivation, and is associated with various diseases, including cancer, arthritis, and neurodegenerative disorders. Glutathione is central to a complex detoxification system that involves multiple mechanisms for scavenging free radicals, reducing peroxides, and conjugating electrophilic compounds. This article discusses how glutathione biosynthesis, glutathione peroxidases, glutathione S-transferases, and glutathione S-conjugate efflux pumps work together in an integrated fashion to allow cellular adaptation to oxidative stress. The antioxidant responsive element (ARE) is a cis-actor that is found in the promoters of many genes that are inducible by oxidative and chemical stress, and is involved in transcriptional activation through basic leucine zipper transcription factors such as Nrf and small Maf proteins. The intracellular sensor(s) for ROS and thiol-active chemicals that induce genes through the ARE are described, and the mechanisms involved in regulation of ARE-driven gene expression are discussed. This knowledge has significant medical implications, as it may help to explain how normal cells adapt to oxidative stress, and how acquired resistance to cancer chemotherapeutic drugs can occur.

title: Does socioeconomic status matter? A meta-analysis on parent training effectiveness for disruptive child behavior.
text: Disadvantaged socioeconomic status (SES) is often believed to hinder the effectiveness of parent training programs. However, the influence of SES on program effectiveness has been largely overlooked, with an emphasis instead on initial problem severity. In our meta-analysis, we examined whether SES affects parent training program effectiveness at both immediate post-treatment and 1-year follow-up, while controlling for levels of initial problem severity. We analyzed 75 studies on parent training programs to reduce disruptive child behavior and found that, at immediate post-treatment, disadvantaged samples benefited less from parent training when they had low levels of initial problem severity. However, at follow-up, disadvantaged samples benefited less from parent training regardless of initial problem severity. Initial problem severity was a strong predictor of effect sizes both immediately post-treatment and at follow-up. Our findings suggest that parent training programs are equally effective for disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged families immediately post-treatment, at least when initial problems are severe. However, maintaining treatment gain may be more challenging for disadvantaged families, indicating a need for sustained family support.

title: Infectiousness of malaria-endemic human populations to vectors.
text: Although human populations' infectiousness to mosquitoes plays a critical role in determining the prevalence and severity of malaria transmission, this parameter has been rarely estimated in the field. Traditional approaches to measuring malaria transmission have relied on the presence of asexual parasites or gametocytes in humans as proxies for infectiousness. Here, we present empirical data from Africa and Papua New Guinea that establish a remarkable lack of correlation between the infectiousness of human populations and mosquito-to-human transmission intensity across a wide range of transmission intensities. We compare these findings with the predictions of a stochastic simulation model of Plasmodium falciparum epidemiology, which predicted little variation in human infectiousness for entomologic inoculation rates (EIRs) above approximately 10 infectious bites per year. The model's predictions are consistent with the findings in the field data, suggesting that interventions aimed at reducing mosquito-to-human transmission will have little to no impact on human infectiousness in most rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa, without achieving very large reductions in transmission. Therefore, interventions should be complemented with measures aimed at reducing the density or infectiousness of blood stage parasites.

title: Molecular analysis of circulating tumour cells—biology and biomarkers
text: Growing evidence suggests that single-site biopsies may not fully capture the genomic landscape of a tumor, as intratumoral heterogeneity is increasingly recognized. As more targeted therapies enter the clinic, it is crucial to screen tumors for genetic abnormalities and identify resistance mechanisms upon disease progression. However, obtaining multiple biopsies from different locations within the tumor and over time is impractical, uncomfortable for patients, and carries risks. To address this challenge, we investigate the potential of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) captured from a non-invasive blood test. These cells can be easily sampled serially, making them a promising tool for understanding intratumoral heterogeneity and tumor evolution. Various technologies, including the validated CellSearch® system, are available for detecting and isolating CTCs. Recent discoveries of CTCs relate to mechanisms of hematological spread previously described in preclinical models, such as epithelial-mesenchymal transition and collective cell migration, as well as the presence of tumor-initiating cells within the circulation. Advances in single-cell molecular analysis are expanding our understanding of metastasis, and the combination of CTC and cell-free DNA assays is expected to provide valuable blood-borne biomarkers for real-time patient monitoring and treatment stratification.

title: Endoplasmic reticulum stress contributes to beta cell apoptosis in type 2 diabetes
text:
The following is a rewritten version of the given text in a more formal and academic tone:
Increased lipid supply can lead to the demise of beta cells, which may play a role in the reduction of beta cell mass in type 2 diabetes. We aimed to investigate whether endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress is instrumental in lipid-induced apoptosis in beta cells and whether ER stress is present in the islets of an animal model of diabetes and in humans with type 2 diabetes. We examined the expression of genes involved in ER stress in insulin-secreting MIN6 cells exposed to elevated lipids, in islets isolated from db/db mice, and in pancreas sections of individuals with type 2 diabetes. We also conducted experiments to assess whether overproduction of the ER chaperone heat shock 70 kDa protein 5 (HSPA5, previously known as immunoglobulin heavy chain binding protein [BIP]) could mitigate lipid-induced apoptosis. Our findings suggest that the pro-apoptotic fatty acid palmitate triggers a robust ER stress response in MIN6 cells, which was almost absent in cells treated with the non-apoptotic fatty acid oleate. Time-dependent increases in the mRNA levels of activating transcription factor 4 (Atf4), DNA-damage inducible transcript 3 (Ddit3, previously known as C/EBP homologous protein [Chop]), and DnaJ homologue (HSP40) C3 (Dnajc3, previously known as p58) correlated with increased apoptosis in palmitate-treated MIN6 cells, but not in oleate-treated cells. Notably, overproduction of HSPA5 in MIN6 cells significantly protected against lipid-induced apoptosis. In the islets of db/db mice, various genes associated with ER stress were also upregulated, and we observed an increase in the processing (activation) of X-box binding protein 1 (Xbp1) mRNA, confirming the existence of ER stress. Lastly, our study revealed increased islet protein production of HSPA5, DDIT3, DNAJC3, and BCL2-associated X protein in pancreas sections from type 2 diabetes individuals. Our findings suggest that ER stress is present in type 2 diabetes and plays a crucial role in the underlying beta cell failure.

title: Coactivator SRC-2-dependent metabolic reprogramming mediates prostate cancer survival and metastasis.
text: The text provided highlights the significance of metabolic pathway reprogramming in cancer cell growth and survival, specifically focusing on the role of the transcriptional coregulator steroid receptor coactivator 2 (SRC-2), also known as NCOA2, in driving glutamine-dependent de novo lipogenesis in tumor cells. The study found that SRC-2 is highly overexpressed in a variety of tumors, including prostate cancer, and plays a crucial role in promoting lipogenesis and reprogramming glutamine metabolism through retrograde TCA cycling. The activation of SRC-2 was shown to be mTORC1-dependent and leads to the activation of key transcription factors involved in lipogenic pathways, such as SREBP-1. Metabolic profiling of human prostate tumors revealed a significant increase in the SRC-2-driven metabolic signature in metastatic tumors compared to localized tumors, supporting the idea that SRC-2 plays a crucial role in cancer metastasis. Additionally, inhibition of SRC-2 in murine models significantly impaired the survival, growth, and metastasis of prostate cancer cells, suggesting that targeting this pathway may be a promising therapeutic strategy for prostate cancer treatment. Overall, the study highlights the importance of understanding the underlying regulators of the tumor metabolic program and identifying potential therapeutic targets, such as SRC-2, to combat cancer.

title: In vitro substrate specificity of protein tyrosine kinases
text:
Protein tyrosine kinases display a wide range of substrate specificity, as evidenced by the indiscriminate phosphorylation of synthetic peptides such as P60stc autophosphorylation site peptides and angiotensin by these enzymes. This observation has led to the belief that protein tyrosine kinases are highly promiscuous, with little in vitro site specificity. However, recent studies have challenged this view, suggesting that protein tyrosine kinases exhibit more specificity than previously thought.
Researchers have obtained synthetic peptides with high substrate activity for specific groups of protein tyrosine kinases, and modifications to these peptides have identified kinase substrate determinants residing near the target tyrosine amino acid residue. Moreover, several protein kinases have been shown to be regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation at specific sites, with highly specific protein tyrosine kinases mediating this process. These and other studies contributing to the evolving view of in vitro substrate specificity of protein tyrosine kinases are reviewed in this work.

title: Relative effectiveness of clinic and home blood pressure monitoring compared with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring in diagnosis of hypertension: systematic review
text:
Objective: To compare the accuracy of clinic and home blood pressure measurements with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring as the reference standard for diagnosing hypertension.
 DESIGN: Systematic review with meta-analysis using hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (ROC) models.
DATA SOURCES: Medline (from 1966), Embase (from 1980), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, DARE, Medion, ARIF, and TRIP up to May 2010.
Eligibility Criteria: Studies that examined the diagnosis of hypertension in adults of all ages using home and/or clinic blood pressure measurements compared to those made using ambulatory monitoring with clearly defined thresholds to diagnose hypertension.
RESULTS: Of the 20 eligible studies, only seven (clinic) and three (home) could be directly compared to ambulatory monitoring thresholds of 135/85 mm Hg. Compared to these thresholds, clinic measurements had a mean sensitivity and specificity of 74.6% (95% CI: 60.7%-84.8%) and 74.6% (47.9%-90.4%), respectively, while home measurements had a mean sensitivity and specificity of 85.7% (78.0%-91.0%) and 62.4% (48.0%-75.0%).
CONCLUSIONS: Neither clinic nor home measurements had sufficient sensitivity or specificity to be recommended as a single diagnostic test. If ambulatory monitoring is used as the reference standard, treatment decisions based solely on clinic or home blood pressure readings may result in substantial overdiagnosis. Ambulatory monitoring before starting lifelong drug treatment may lead to more appropriate targeting of treatment, particularly around the diagnostic threshold.

title: Purification and characterization of mouse hematopoietic stem cells.
text: In this study, researchers isolated bone marrow hematopoietic stem cells from mice using various phenotypic markers. These cells have the ability to proliferate and differentiate with high efficiency into myelomonocytic cells, B cells, or T cells. In fact, only 30 of these cells are needed to save 50% of lethally irradiated mice and reconstitute all blood cell types in the survivors.

title: Regulation of arabinose and xylose metabolism in Escherichia coli.
text: Bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, often consume one sugar at a time when fed multiple sugars through a process known as carbon catabolite repression. For example, they will initially consume glucose before moving on to lactose. Additionally, glucose also represses the consumption of other sugars, such as arabinose and xylose. In this study, we explored a second hierarchy in E. coli, focusing on the consumption of arabinose and xylose when grown in a mixture of the two pentoses. We found that E. coli will consume arabinose before xylose, and this repression is dependent on the AraC protein. Specifically, arabinose-bound AraC binds to the xylose promoters and suppresses gene expression. These findings demonstrate that sugar utilization in E. coli involves multiple layers of regulation, with cells consuming glucose first, then arabinose, and finally xylose. These results may have implications for the metabolic engineering of E. coli strains capable of producing chemicals and biofuels from mixtures of hexose and pentose sugars derived from plant biomass.

title: MicroRNA expression profiling of human metastatic cancers identifies cancer gene targets.
text: Microscopic non-coding RNA molecules (microRNAs) play a crucial role in the development and progression of cancer, and their expression patterns differ between normal tissues and cancers. However, the specific role of microRNAs in the metastatic process remains unclear. To identify a distinct microRNA expression signature characteristic of metastatic tumors, we performed a microarray analysis on 43 pairs of primary tumors (10 colon, 10 bladder, 13 breast, and 10 lung cancers) and one of their corresponding metastatic lymph nodes. Our analysis revealed a metastatic cancer microRNA signature consisting of 15 overexpressed and 17 underexpressed microRNAs. These results were confirmed through qRT-PCR analysis. Some of the microRNAs identified in our study have been previously linked to cancer progression, including miR-10b, miR-21, miR-30a, miR-30e, miR-125b, miR-141, miR-200b, miR-200c, and miR-205. To further validate our findings, we performed immunohistochemical analysis on a small series of paired colon, breast, and bladder cancers and their corresponding metastatic lymph nodes for three well-established miRNA target genes (PDCD4, DHFR, and HOXD10). Our results showed that the immunohistochemical expression of these targets corresponded closely with the deregulation of the corresponding microRNAs. Our findings suggest that specific microRNAs may directly contribute to cancer metastasis and may serve as a novel tool for identifying metastatic cancer gene targets.

title: Circos: an information aesthetic for comparative genomics.
text: We developed a visualization tool called Circos to aid in the identification and analysis of similarities and differences that arise from comparisons of genomes. Our tool is effective in displaying variation in genome structure and, more broadly, any other type of positional relationship between genomic intervals. Data for these analyses are commonly produced through sequence alignments, hybridization arrays, genome mapping, and genotyping studies. Circos uses a circular ideogram layout to facilitate the display of relationships between pairs of positions using ribbons, which encode the position, size, and orientation of related genomic elements. Circos is capable of displaying data as scatter plots, line plots, histograms, heat maps, tiles, connectors, and text. Additionally, Bitmap or vector images can be created from GFF-style data inputs and hierarchical configuration files, which can be easily generated by automated tools, making Circos ideal for fast deployment in data analysis and reporting pipelines.

title: Pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic and clinical profile of novel antiplatelet drugs targeting vascular diseases.
text: The current gold standard antiplatelet agent, clopidogrel, has several limitations that have sparked the search for more effective platelet antagonists. Researchers are exploring various drugs that target the purinergic P2Y12 receptor, including prasugrel, an oral irreversible thienopyridine; ticagrelor, an oral reversible P2Y12 receptor inhibitor; cangrelor, an intravenous P2Y12 receptor antagonist; elinogrel, a direct-acting reversible P2Y12 receptor inhibitor; BX 667, an orally active and reversible small-molecule P2Y12 receptor antagonist; SCH 530348, SCH 205831, SCH 602539, and E5555, highly selective and orally active antagonists on the protease-activated receptor 1. In addition, new drugs targeting other platelet targets, such as terutroban, an oral thromboxane receptor inhibitor; ARC1779, a nuclease-resistant aptamer that inhibits von Willebrand factor-dependent platelet aggregation; ALX-0081, a bivalent humanized nanobody targeting the GPIb binding site of von Willebrand factor; and AJW200, an IgG4 monoclonal antibody of von Willebrand factor, are being developed. The pharmacology and clinical profiles of these new agents suggest they may provide more consistent, rapid, and potent platelet inhibition than existing treatments, but further comparisons in well-designed, randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings.

title: BLM is required for faithful chromosome segregation and its localization defines a class of ultrafine anaphase bridges.
text: Mutations in the BLM gene are associated with Bloom's syndrome, a disorder characterized by an increased risk of cancer and chromosomal instability. To investigate the role of BLM in ensuring faithful chromosome segregation in human cells, we examined the behavior of BLM-defective cells during mitosis. Our findings indicate that BLM-defective cells display a higher frequency of anaphase bridges and lagging chromatin compared to isogenic corrected derivatives that ectopically express the BLM protein. In normal mitotic cells, BLM localizes to anaphase bridges, where it co-localizes with its cellular partners, topoisomerase IIIα and hRMI1 (BLAP75). By using BLM staining as a marker, we identified a novel class of ultrafine DNA bridges in anaphase, which we termed BLM-DNA bridges, that are surprisingly prevalent in the anaphase population of normal human cells. These bridges frequently link centromeric loci and are present at an elevated frequency in BLM-deficient cells. Based on these results, we propose that sister-chromatid disjunction is often incomplete in human cells even after the onset of anaphase. Our findings suggest a model for the action of BLM in ensuring complete sister chromatid decatenation in anaphase.

title: Association Between High Serum Soluble Corin and Hypertension: A Cross-Sectional Study in a General Population of China.
text:
Here's the rewritten text with corrections and improvements:
BACKGROUND: Corin has been suggested to be associated with hypertension based on cellular and animal studies. However, there is a lack of population-based evidence to support this association, which hinders the translation of basic research findings to clinical and preventive practice. Our study aimed to investigate the association between serum corin levels and hypertension in a general population of China.
METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study from January to May 2010 on 2,498 participants aged 30 years or older living in Gusu district of Suzhou. We measured serum soluble corin and blood pressure.
RESULTS: Participants with hypertension had higher levels of serum corin compared to those without hypertension (median [interquartile range]: 1,836.83 pg/mL vs. 1,579.14 pg/mL, P < 0.001). A positive association was observed between higher serum corin levels and the prevalence of hypertension (odds ratio [OR] = 2.01, P < 0.001). In multivariate analysis, participants in the third (OR = 1.43, P = 0.007) and fourth (OR = 1.96, P < 0.001) quartiles had significantly increased odds of hypertension compared to those in the lowest quartile of serum corin. ORs of hypertension positively and significantly increased with serum corin levels (P for trend <0.001). Moreover, the association remained significant in subgroups defined by age, body mass index, total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and fasting plasma glucose (all P < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that hypertensive participants had higher levels of serum corin compared to non-hypertensive participants, implying that corin may play a role in the pathophysiology of hypertension.

title: Shared and distinct genetic variants in type 1 diabetes and celiac disease.
text:
The text can be rewritten with a more formal and objective tone as follows:
BACKGROUND:
Two inflammatory disorders, type 1 diabetes and celiac disease, have been found to co-segregate in populations, suggesting a shared genetic origin. Since both diseases are associated with the HLA class II genes on chromosome 6p21, we investigated whether non-HLA loci are also shared between the two diseases.
METHODS:
We genotyped and analyzed the DNA samples of 8064 patients with type 1 diabetes, 9339 control subjects, and 2828 families providing 3064 parent-child trios (consisting of an affected child and both biological parents) to identify any associated loci. In addition, we analyzed 18 loci associated with type 1 diabetes in 2560 patients with celiac disease and 9339 control subjects.
RESULTS:
Three loci associated with celiac disease (RGS1 on chromosome 1q31, IL18RAP on chromosome 2q12, and TAGAP on chromosome 6q25) were also associated with type 1 diabetes (P < 1.00 x 10(-4)). A novel 32-bp insertion-deletion variant on chromosome 3p21 was identified as a type 1 diabetes locus (P = 1.81 x 10(-8)) and was also associated with celiac disease. In addition, PTPN2 on chromosome 18p11 and CTLA4 on chromosome 2q33 were found to be associated with both type 1 diabetes and celiac disease. The IL18RAP and TAGAP alleles were found to confer protection in type 1 diabetes and susceptibility in celiac disease. Loci with distinct effects in the two diseases included INS on chromosome 11p15, IL2RA on chromosome 10p15, and PTPN22 on chromosome 1p13 in type 1 diabetes and IL12A on 3q25 and LPP on 3q28 in celiac disease.
CONCLUSIONS:
Our results suggest that both type 1 diabetes and celiac disease share common genetic susceptibility, indicating the presence of common biological mechanisms, such as autoimmunity-related tissue damage and intolerance to dietary antigens, as etiological features of both diseases.

title: Promotion of tumorigenesis by heterozygous disruption of the beclin 1 autophagy gene.
text: Malignant cells often exhibit defects in the process of autophagy, a genetically conserved pathway for degrading lengthy proteins and cytoplasmic organelles, but thus far, there is no direct genetic evidence for a role of autophagy genes in tumor suppression. Interestingly, around 40-75% of cases of sporadic breast, ovarian, and prostate cancer in humans exhibit monoallelic deletion of the beclin 1 autophagy gene. To investigate this phenomenon further, we generated a targeted mouse mutant model to test the hypothesis that monoallelic deletion of beclin 1 might promote tumorigenesis. Our findings reveal that heterozygous disruption of beclin 1 leads to an increase in the frequency of spontaneous malignancies and accelerates the development of hepatitis B virus-induced premalignant lesions. In contrast, molecular analyses of tumors in beclin 1 heterozygous mice show that the remaining wild-type allele is neither mutated nor silenced. Furthermore, disruption of beclin 1 in heterozygous mice results in enhanced cellular proliferation and reduced autophagy in vivo. These findings establish beclin 1 as a haplo-insufficient tumor-suppressor gene and provide persuasive genetic evidence that autophagy is a novel mechanism of cell-growth regulation and tumor suppression. Notably, mutation of beclin 1 or other autophagy genes may contribute to the development of human cancers.

title: Treatment-related mortality with bevacizumab in cancer patients: a meta-analysis.
text:
Fatal adverse events (FAEs) have been reported in cancer patients treated with the widely used angiogenesis inhibitor bevacizumab in combination with chemotherapy, with an unclear role in treatment-related mortality. To investigate this further, a systematic review and meta-analysis of published randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted to determine the overall risk of FAEs associated with bevacizumab.
The review included 16 RCTs with a total of 10,217 patients with various advanced solid tumors. The overall incidence of FAEs with bevacizumab was found to be 2.5% (95% CI, 1.7%-3.9%). Compared to chemotherapy alone, the addition of bevacizumab was associated with an increased risk of FAEs, with a relative risk (RR) of 1.46 (95% CI, 1.09-1.94; P = .01; incidence, 2.5% vs 1.7%). This association varied significantly with the type of chemotherapeutic agents used (P = .045) but not with tumor types (P = .13) or bevacizumab doses (P = .16). Bevacizumab was also associated with an increased risk of FAEs when used in conjunction with taxanes or platinum agents (RR, 3.49; 95% CI, 1.82-6.66; incidence, 3.3% vs 1.0%), but not when used with other agents (RR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.25-2.88; incidence, 0.8% vs 0.9%). The most common causes of FAEs were hemorrhage (23.5%), neutropenia (12.2%), and gastrointestinal tract perforation (7.1%).
In conclusion, this meta-analysis found that bevacizumab in combination with chemotherapy or biological therapy, compared to chemotherapy alone, was associated with increased treatment-related mortality. The increased risk of FAEs with bevacizumab was largely driven by the use of taxanes or platinum agents. These findings highlight the importance of careful monitoring and management of potential adverse events in cancer patients treated with bevacizumab-based therapies.

title: Quiescent and active hippocampal neural stem cells with distinct morphologies respond selectively to physiological and pathological stimuli and aging.
text: New neurons are generated in the adult hippocampus throughout life by neural stem/progenitor cells (NSCs), and neurogenesis is a plastic process that can be influenced by external stimuli. We found that Canonical Notch signaling through RBP-J is essential for hippocampal neurogenesis. Notch signaling helps to distinguish different populations of Sox2(+) NSCs, and within these populations, cells can switch between being actively dividing or quiescent. Radial and horizontal NSCs respond differently to neurogenic stimuli, with physical exercise activating the quiescent radial population, and epileptic seizures resulting in an increase in the horizontal NSC pool. Interestingly, a decrease in neurogenesis in aged mice is associated with a loss of actively dividing horizontal NSCs, rather than a complete loss of stem cells. Additionally, we found that the transition to a quiescent state can be reversed, leading to a rejuvenation of neurogenesis in the brain. This discovery of multiple NSC populations with Notch dependence and distinct responses to stimuli, as well as their reversible quiescence, has important implications for our understanding of the mechanisms of adaptive learning and regenerative therapy.

title: Low serum vitamin D is associated with high risk of diabetes in Korean adults.
text: New research suggests that vitamin D may play a significant role in glucose metabolism, particularly in Asian populations. While a low vitamin D level has been linked to an increased risk of diabetes mellitus in other populations, this correlation has not been consistently demonstrated in Asians. To explore this relationship further, researchers analyzed data from a large, population-based survey of Korean adults aged 20 or older, conducting cross-sectional analyses on 5787 participants (2453 men and 3334 women). Diabetes mellitus was defined as fasting plasma glucose ≥7 mmol/L or current use of oral hypoglycemic agents or insulin. Insulin resistance was assessed using homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) and quantitative insulin sensitivity check index (QUICKI). Compared to individuals with sufficient serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) concentrations ≥75 nmol/L, the odds ratio (95% CI) for diabetes mellitus were 1.73 (1.09-2.74), 1.30 (0.91-1.84), and 1.40 (0.99-1.98) for serum 25(OH)D concentrations <25, <50, and 50-<75 nmol/L, respectively, after multiple adjustments (P-trend < 0.0001). Additionally, the serum 25(OH)D level was inversely associated with HOMA-IR (β = -0.061; P = 0.001) and positively associated with QUICKI (β = 0.059; P = 0.001) in overweight or obese participants. These findings suggest that a low serum vitamin D concentration is a risk factor for diabetes mellitus in Korean adults, and that the concentration is inversely associated with insulin resistance in those who are overweight or obese.

title: When NK cells overcome their lack of education.
text: The immune system's cells have developed diverse molecular mechanisms to perceive their surroundings and react to alterations in self. NK cells, a type of lymphocyte with both effector and regulatory functions, are particularly adept at adapting to changes in self. In a study published in the current issue of the JCI, Tarek and colleagues reveal the therapeutic potential of manipulating NK cell adaptation to self through an innovative mAb-based therapy against neuroblastoma (NB). This groundbreaking approach is likely to spur further research into NK cell therapies.

title: Toll-like receptor-3 mediates HIV-1 transactivation via NFκB and JNK pathways and histone acetylation, but prolonged activation suppresses Tat and HIV-1 replication.
text: Research has implicated TLR3 in the pathogenesis of various viral infections, including those caused by SIV and HIV-1. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects are not well understood, and it is unclear whether HIV interacts with TLR3 to influence disease progression. To investigate this, we explored the impact of TLR3 ligands on HIV-1 transcription using primary human macrophages and cell lines with integrated HIV-1 promoters. Our findings demonstrate that TLR3 activation leads to the upregulation of transcription factors, such as c-Jun, CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein alpha (CEBPA), signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT)-1, STAT-2, RELB, and nuclear factor kappa-B1 (NFκB1), which are known to regulate HIV promoter activity. Additionally, we found that TLR3 activation enhances HIV-1 transcription through the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and NFκB pathways. These effects were accompanied by epigenetic modifications, including decreased histone deacetylase activity, increased histone acetyl transferase (HAT) activity, and increased acetylation of histones H3 and H4 at specific positions in the HIV-1 promoter. However, prolonged TLR3 activation decreased HIV-1 transcription, HAT activity, and Tat transcription, and inhibited viral replication. These findings suggest that TLR3 acts as a viral sensor to mediate viral transcription, cellular signaling, innate immune responses, and inflammation in HIV-infected individuals. Our study provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying these TLR3-mediated effects.

title: Patent ductus arteriosus: are current neonatal treatment options better or worse than no treatment at all?
text: There is a lack of consensus among neonatologists regarding the timeline for closing a moderate-sized patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in infants, with some believing it should be closed by 1-2 years old, while others may wait until the child does not require mechanical ventilation. While 95% of neonatologists agree that a PDA should be closed in infants born before 28 weeks who require mechanical ventilation, the proportion of neonatologists treating a PDA in infants who do not require mechanical ventilation varies widely. The uncertainty surrounding PDA closure is compounded by the lack of randomized controlled trials specifically addressing the risks and benefits of closing a PDA in these infants. New findings suggest that early pharmacologic treatment may have several short-term benefits for preterm newborns, while ductus ligation may introduce its own set of potential complications that could counteract the benefits of closure.

title: A conserved phosphatase cascade that regulates nuclear membrane biogenesis.
text: A newly identified family of phosphatases, belonging to the haloacid dehalogenase superfamily, shares a conserved catalytic motif, DXDX(T/V). One member of this family, Dullard, was recently shown to play a role in regulating neural tube development in Xenopus (Satow et al., 2002). Our study reveals that Dullard and Nem1p, a protein from yeast, share similar functions in mammalian and yeast cells, respectively. Both proteins have similar domains and substrate preferences and localize to the nuclear envelope. Moreover, we demonstrate that human Dullard can rescue the abnormal nuclear envelope morphology of nem1Delta yeast cells, effectively replacing Nem1p. Interestingly, Nem1p has been shown to dephosphorylate the yeast phosphatidic acid phosphatase, Smp2p (Santos-Rosa et al., 2005), and we find that Dullard dephosphorylates the mammalian phosphatidic acid phosphatase, lipin. Taken together, these findings suggest that Dullard participates in a conserved phosphatase cascade that regulates nuclear membrane biogenesis, from yeast to mammals.

title: Increased expression of CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 in ovarian/peritoneal endometriotic lesions.
text: Endometriosis is a disease that affects up to 10% of premenopausal women and is dependent on estrogen. We aimed to investigate whether different endometriosis sites have unique local estrogen concentrations due to distinct enzymes responsible for estrogen metabolism. Cytochrome P450 (CYP) 1A1 and CYP1B1 mRNA and protein expressions in deep-infiltrating (rectal, retroperitoneal, and uterine) lesions, superficial (ovarian and peritoneal) lesions, and eutopic and healthy (control) endometrium were evaluated using real-time PCR and western blot. A cross-sectional study with 58 premenopausal women revealed increased CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 mRNA expression in superficial lesions compared to healthy endometrium. CYP1A1 mRNA expression was also higher in superficial lesions than in eutopic endometrium. Interestingly, CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 expression was similar in stromal cells isolated from ovarian lesions, rectal lesions, and eutopic endometrium. However, there was a longer half-life of estradiol (measured by HPLC-MS-MS) in ovarian endometriotic stromal cells compared to paired eutopic stromal endometrial cells. Our findings suggest that there is a site-dependent regulation of CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 in ovarian/peritoneal lesions and ovarian endometriotic stromal cells, while these cells have a slower metabolism.

title: Eset partners with Oct4 to restrict extraembryonic trophoblast lineage potential in embryonic stem cells.
text: The histone H3 Lysine 9 (H3K9) methyltransferase Eset is a crucial epigenetic regulator in the development of the inner cell mass (ICM). Although ICM-derived embryonic stem (ES) cells are normally unable to contribute to the trophectoderm (TE) in blastocysts, depletion of Eset using short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) leads to differentiation into trophoblast-like cells and the upregulation of trophoblast-associated gene expression. Through chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) analysis, we identified Eset target genes with Eset-mediated H3K9 trimethylation. We found that genes highly expressed in the TE, such as Tcfap2a and Cdx2, are bound and repressed by Eset. Additionally, single-cell PCR analysis revealed that the expression of Cdx2 and Tcfap2a is also induced in Eset-depleted morula cells. Interestingly, Eset-depleted cells can incorporate into the TE of a blastocyst and eventually contribute to placental tissues. Furthermore, coimmunoprecipitation and ChIP assays showed that Eset interacts with Oct4, which in turn recruits Eset to repress the expression of trophoblast-associated genes. Our results suggest that Eset restricts the extraembryonic trophoblast lineage potential of pluripotent cells and connects an epigenetic regulator to a key cell fate decision through a pluripotency factor.

title: Suicides after pregnancy in Finland, 1987-94: register linkage study.
text:
Objective: To determine the rates of suicide associated with different stages of pregnancy in Finland.
Design: Register linkage study.
Information on suicides in women of reproductive age was linked with the Finnish birth, abortion, and hospital discharge registers to identify how many women who committed suicide had experienced a completed pregnancy within the year prior to their death.
Setting: Nationwide data from Finland.
Subjects: Women who committed suicide between 1987 and 1994.

Results: A total of 73 suicides were associated with pregnancy, representing 5.4% of all suicides in women in this age group. The mean annual suicide rate was 11.3 per 100,000. The suicide rate associated with birth was significantly lower (5.9), while the rates associated with miscarriage (18.1) and induced abortion (34.7) were significantly higher than in the general population. The risk associated with birth was higher among teenagers, while the risk associated with abortion was elevated in all age groups. Women who had committed suicide tended to come from lower socioeconomic backgrounds and were more likely to be unmarried compared to other women who had experienced a completed pregnancy.

Conclusions: The increased risk of suicide after an induced abortion suggests that either common risk factors contribute to both suicide and abortion or that abortion may have harmful effects on mental health.

title: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis: a rare or very rare clinical entity?
text:
Lactic acidosis associated with biguanide therapy, particularly metformin, is a recognized complication with potential clinical significance. While the incidence of metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA) is lower than that of phenformin-induced lactic acidosis, it continues to be reported sporadically, raising concerns for clinicians. In this review, we examine the current global data on the prevalence of MALA, its risk factors, and practical guidelines for metformin use to minimize the risk of this potential hazard.
METHODS:
We conducted an extensive literature search using Medline and Ovid databases (1965-1998) with the following keywords: 'type 2 diabetes mellitus,' 'oral hypoglycemic drugs,' 'biguanides,' 'metformin-associated lactic acidosis,' and 'renal impairment.'
RESULTS:
MALA is a rare clinical entity, approximately 20 times less common than phenformin-induced lactic acidosis. Renal impairment is the major precipitating factor for MALA in metformin-treated patients. In some cases, no identifiable precipitating factors were found, and the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Based on previous reports, practical recommendations for metformin use to minimize the risk of MALA are listed.
CONCLUSIONS:
The low prevalence of MALA is comparable to the prevalence of sulphonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia. Metformin has numerous beneficial metabolic effects in the management of Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Provided that the recommended guidelines for metformin use are strictly adhered to, its widespread use would be safe, and the incidence of MALA will further reduction.

title: Inborn errors of human JAKs and STATs.
text: Mutations in the genes encoding two of the four human JAKs (JAK3 and TYK2) and three of the six human STATs (STAT1, STAT3, and STAT5B) have been identified. We review the disorders associated with these mutations, highlighting the insights into the molecular and cellular pathogenesis provided by the discovery of inborn errors of cytokines, hormones, and their receptors, including those interacting with JAKs and STATs. While the functions of JAKs and STATs are largely conserved between mammals, including mice, significant phenotypic differences have emerged between mice and humans carrying biallelic null alleles of JAK3, TYK2, STAT1, or STAT3. Moreover, the high degree of allelic heterogeneity at these loci has revealed a diverse range of immunological and clinical phenotypes, which had not been anticipated.

title: Mental health problems of homeless children and families: longitudinal study.
text:
Objective:
To assess the mental health needs of homeless children and families before and after rehousing, and to identify the local strategies that can be implemented to address these needs.
Design:
Cross-sectional and longitudinal study.
Setting:
City of Birmingham.

Subjects:
58 rehoused families with 103 children aged 2-16 years and 21 comparison families of low socioeconomic status in stable housing, with 54 children.
Main Outcome Measures:
Mental health problems in children and mothers, including symptoms of anxiety and depression, and level of communication between parents and children.
Results:
Mental health problems were significantly higher in rehoused mothers and their children compared to the comparison group. Specifically, 26% of rehoused mothers and 5% of comparison mothers had mental health problems, and 39% of rehoused children and 11% of comparison children had mental health problems. Homeless mothers had significantly less social support at follow-up compared to the comparison group. Additionally, mothers with a history of abuse and poor social integration were more likely to have children with persistent mental health problems.
Conclusions:
Homeless families have a high level of complex needs that cannot be met by conventional health services and arrangements. Local strategies for rapid rehousing into permanent accommodation, effective social support and health care for parents and children, and protection from violence and intimidation should be developed and implemented to address these needs.

title: The flip side of perception-action coupling: locomotor experience and the ontogeny of visual-postural coupling.
text: The potential impact of motor development on psychological function is once again a topic of significant theoretical and practical interest. This renewed focus has stemmed from a shift in approach, deviating from earlier studies that aimed to predict long-term psychological functions based on early motor assessments, to a current attempt to understand how the acquisition of motor skills influences psychological changes. This paper explores the link between the acquisition of one specific motor skill, prone locomotion, and the resulting developmental changes in an infant's ability to regulate posture based on visual information. The argument is presented that the onset of prone locomotion triggers the need for infants to differentiate and process visual information more effectively, with the goal of efficiently controlling subtasks within the larger task of locomotion, such as steering, maintaining postural control, and attending to the surface of support. The paper then outlines a research program aimed at determining whether locomotor experience directly influences improvements in postural control or merely signifies maturational progression. Additionally, a hypothesis is proposed that connects the emergence of height awareness to an infant's ability to regulate posture based on peripheral visual input. The theoretical framework underlying this paper is the principle of probabilistic epigenesis, which suggests that the development of one ability can lead to a multitude of changes in both similar and unrelated domains.

title: Crystal structure of the first plant urease from jack bean: 83 years of journey from its first crystal to molecular structure.
text: Urease, a nickel-dependent metalloenzyme, is synthesized by plants, bacteria, and fungi. It catalyzes the hydrolysis of urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. Although the amino acid sequences of plant and bacterial ureases are similar, they have distinct biological activities. Plant ureases, but not bacterial ureases, possess insecticidal properties independent of their ureolytic activity. Currently, the structural information available is limited to bacterial ureases, although the jack bean urease (Canavalia ensiformis; JBU) from plants is the most well-studied enzyme and was crystallized in 1926. To better understand the biological properties of plant ureases, including the mechanism of insecticidal activity, we initiated structural studies on some of these enzymes. Here, we report the crystal structure of JBU, the first plant urease structure, at 2.05 Å resolution. The active-site architecture of JBU is similar to that of bacterial ureases, containing a bi-nickel center. JBU has a bound phosphate and a covalently modified residue (Cys592) by β-mercaptoethanol at its active site, and the concomitant binding of multiple inhibitors (phosphate and β-mercaptoethanol) is not observed in bacterial ureases. By correlating the structural information of JBU with available biophysical and biochemical data on the insecticidal properties of plant ureases, we propose that the amphipathic β-hairpin located in the entomotoxic peptide region of plant ureases may form a membrane insertion β-barrel, similar to that found in β-pore-forming toxins.

title: Studies of nuclear and cytoplasmic behaviour during the five mitotic cycles that precede gastrulation in Drosophila embryogenesis.
text:
Using differential interference contrast optics and cinematography, we have investigated the morphological changes that occur in the living, syncytial embryo of Drosophila from stage 10 to 14 of embryogenesis, just prior to and during the formation of the cellular blastoderm. Additionally, we have supplemented these studies with data collected from fixed, stained, whole embryos. Our findings include:
* The average duration of nuclear cycles 10-13 is approximately 9, 10, 12, and 21 minutes, respectively, at 25°C.
* The duration of the mitotic period without a discrete nuclear envelope in cycles 10-13 is approximately 3, 3, 3, and 5 minutes, respectively.
* The length of nuclear cycle 14 varies positionally throughout the embryo, with the shortest cycles lasting approximately 65 minutes.
* In living embryos, syncytial blastoderm nuclei enter and leave mitosis in two waves originating from the opposite anterior and posterior poles of the embryo and terminating in the midregion, taking approximately half a minute to travel over the embryonic surface.
* Yolk nuclei divide in synchrony with the migrating nuclei at nuclear cycles 8 and 9, and after cycle 10, they cease dividing and become polyploid.
* The syncytial embryo has at least three distinct levels of cytoskeletal organization, including structured domains of cytoplasm organized around each blastoderm nucleus, radially directed tracks orienting colchicine-sensitive saltatory transport throughout the peripheral cytoplasm, and a long-range organization of the core of the embryo making possible coherent movements of the large inner yolk mass in concert with each nuclear cycle.
* This highly organized cytoplasm may be involved in providing positional information for the important process of nuclear determination that occurs during these stages.

title: Activation of liver X receptors and retinoid X receptors prevents bacterial-induced macrophage apoptosis.
text:
Microbe-macrophage interactions play a pivotal role in the development of various infections. Some bacterial pathogens have been shown to induce macrophage apoptosis, which allows them to evade the host's innate immune response and establish a foothold in the body. Recent research has uncovered a previously unsuspected function for liver X receptors (LXRs) and retinoid X receptors (RXRs) in regulating macrophage survival. Specifically, activation of LXRs and RXRs inhibits macrophage apoptosis in response to withdrawal of macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) and various inducers of apoptosis. These findings suggest that LXR/RXR agonists may be leveraged as a strategy to enhance innate immunity to bacterial pathogens that induce apoptotic programs, thereby preventing them from evading the host's immune response.
 Expression profiling studies revealed that LXR/RXR agonists induce the expression of antiapoptotic regulators, including AIM/CT2, Bcl-X(L), and Birc1a. In contrast, they inhibit the expression of proapoptotic regulators and effectors, including caspases 1, 4/11, 7, and 12; Fas ligand; and Dnase1l3. The combination of LXR/RXR agonists was more effective than either agonist alone at inhibiting apoptosis in response to various inducers of apoptosis. Moreover, this combination acted synergistically to induce expression of AIM/CT2. Inhibition of AIM/CT2 expression in response to LXR/RXR agonists partially reversed their antiapoptotic effects, suggesting a potential mechanism for their mediating their protective effects.
 These findings underscore the importance of LXRs and RXRs in regulating macrophage survival and suggest that LXR/RXR agonists may provide a new avenue for enhancing the host's defense against bacterial pathogens that induce apoptotic programs.

title: p53 binding to nucleosomal DNA depends on the rotational positioning of DNA response element.
text: The binding of the p53 tumor suppressor protein to specific DNA sequences is a crucial aspect of its function. To better understand how p53 recognizes DNA in the presence of nucleosomal structures, we investigated the binding of the p53 DNA binding domain (p53DBD) and full-length wild-type p53 protein to a single p53 response element (p53RE) placed near the nucleosomal dyad in six different orientations. Our findings indicate that the strongest p53 binding occurs when the p53RE in the nucleosome is bent in the same direction as observed in solution and co-crystal structures. However, if the orientation of the binding site in the core particle is shifted by approximately 180 degrees, the p53RE becomes inaccessible to p53. Our results suggest that the orientation of the binding sites on a nucleosome may play a significant role in the initial p53-DNA recognition and subsequent cofactor recruitment.

title: Diminished sympathetic nervous system activity in genetically obese (ob/ob) mouse.
text: To investigate the dysregulation of the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) in genetically obese mice (ob/ob), norepinephrine (NE) turnover was measured in the heart and interscapular brown adipose tissue (IBAT) of ob/ob and lean mice. The results show that SNS activity is reduced by 33-56% in the heart and by 45-73% in IBAT of ob/ob mice compared to lean controls at ambient temperature (22°C). However, during cold exposure (4°C), NE turnover increased equally in both ob/ob and lean mice, but the rates remained lower in the obese mice than in the lean despite the gradual development of hypothermia in the ob/ob mice. Administration of naltrexone, a long-acting opiate antagonist, failed to reverse the suppression of SNS activity observed in the ob/ob mice. These findings suggest that the reduced SNS activity in ob/ob mice may contribute to their defective thermogenesis.

title: Quality of life of young adults with idiopathic short stature: effect of growth hormone treatment. Dutch Growth Hormone Working Group.
text: The study aimed to evaluate the impact of recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) treatment on the quality of life of adults diagnosed with idiopathic short stature (ISS) during childhood. The study included 89 subjects, with 24 treated with rhGH from childhood and 65 never treated. At the time of the interview, the treated subjects had reached their final height, which was significantly lower than the control subjects (p < 0.001). Although the subjects reported experiencing negative events related to their height, the majority were not willing to trade-off their height for increased benefits. The personality of the subjects was not found to be significantly different from a norm group. The treated subjects were highly satisfied with the rhGH treatment, overestimating the actual height gain of 12-13 cm. Overall, the study found that rhGH therapy does not appear to affect the quality of life of adults with ISS.

title: Neighborhood Racial/Ethnic Concentration, Social Disadvantage, and Homicide Risk: An Ecological Analysis of 10 U.S. Cities
text: Homicide is a leading cause of death among African American and Hispanic men in the US. We investigated how neighborhood characteristics associated with social disadvantage contribute to racial/ethnic homicide gaps in 10 cities. Our hypothesis was that (1) higher concentrations of African Americans and Hispanics would be linked to higher homicide rates, and (2) adjusting for neighborhood characteristics such as unemployment, median household income, low educational attainment, and female headship would reduce the relationship between racial/ethnic concentration and homicide. Using Poisson regression models that accounted for spatial autocorrelation, we found that homicide rates were higher in neighborhoods with greater concentrations of African Americans and Hispanics, but the association was reduced after adjusting for social disadvantage variables, particularly the percentage of female heads of household and individuals with less than a high school education. Additionally, we found that the relationship between neighborhood racial/ethnic concentration and homicide was better explained by social disadvantage variables in some cities than in others. Based on our findings, policymakers may consider implementing policies that expand early childhood education programs, increase access to higher education, and encourage economic and community development in disadvantaged neighborhoods.

title: Preterm patent ductus arteriosus: A continuing conundrum for the neonatologist?
text: Managing preterm patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) remains a complex challenge. On one hand, the physiological and statistical associations with adverse outcomes suggest that it is a pathological condition. On the other hand, clinical trials of treatment strategies have failed to demonstrate any long-term benefits. Ultrasound studies have suggested that the haemodynamic impact of PDA may occur earlier after birth than previously thought, within the first few hours after delivery. However, the optimal time to treat PDA remains unclear. Historically, studies have primarily focused on symptomatic or pre-symptomatic treatment, with limited trials testing the effectiveness of no treatment at all. Prophylactic treatment, while the best-studied regimen, has shown improvements in some short-term outcomes but has not translated to any tangible benefits in longer-term outcomes. Neonatologists have been reluctant to participate in trials that test treatment against a never-treat approach. Recent observations of the early postnatal haemodynamic significance suggest that targeting treatment based on the constrictive response of the duct in the early postnatal period may be the most effective strategy. A pilot trial of this approach showed a reduction in pulmonary haemorrhage incidence, but more trials are needed to confirm its efficacy.

title: Political and economic aspects of the transition to universal health coverage.
text: Countries have achieved universal health coverage through diverse pathways and health systems, yet they share common features on their journey towards this goal. A significant political push, often driven by various social forces, results in the creation of public programs or regulations that expand access to care, promote equity, and distribute financial risks. This is frequently accompanied by an increase in national income and health spending, which enables the purchase of more health services for a growing population. Moreover, there is a noticeable trend towards pooling a greater share of health spending, either through taxes or mandatory insurance schemes, which is a crucial factor in achieving universal health coverage. This paper examines common patterns in countries that have successfully achieved universal health care access and explores how economic growth, demographics, technology, politics, and health spending have contributed to this major public health development.

title: Wedelolactone protects human bronchial epithelial cell injury against cigarette smoke extract-induced oxidant stress and inflammation responses through Nrf2 pathway.
text: Cigarette smoke constitutes the primary root cause of the development of various pulmonary afflictions, including lung cancer, through the activation of oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, leading to the formation of lesions in normal human bronchial epithelial (NHBE) cells. Notably, Wedelolactone (WEL), a natural compound derived from Eclipta prostrata L., has shown promise in inhibiting the proliferation and growth of cancer cells. In this study, we investigated the effects of WEL on NHBE cell injury induced by cigarette smoke extract (CSE) in vitro. Our findings demonstrate that pre-treatment with WEL at concentrations ranging from 2.5 to 20 microM offered a significant protective effect against 10% CSE-induced cell death in NHBE cells. Furthermore, WEL exhibited a dose-dependent ability to reverse the activities of SOD, CAT, GSH, and MDA to normal levels. Additionally, we observed a significant reduction in the protein expressions of COX-2 and ICAM-1, which are associated with inflammatory responses, upon WEL pre-treatment compared to 10% CSE treatment. The expressions of antioxidases such as NAD(P)H dehydrogenase:Quinone 1 (NQO1) and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) were also significantly reduced by WEL pre-treatment. Of note, Nrf2 inhibitor all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) declined the expressions of these antioxidases remarkably. These results suggest that WEL protects NHBE cells against CSE-induced injury by modulating the Nrf2 signaling pathway. Our findings indicate that WEL may serve as a promising agent in protecting against CSE-induced lung injury.

title: IL-17 promotes tumor development through the induction of tumor promoting microenvironments at tumor sites and myeloid-derived suppressor cells.
text:
Research into the role of immune responses in tumor development has been a central focus of tumor biology and immunology. Specifically, the cytokine IL-17 has been found to play a contentious role in tumor development. While IL-17-producing cells are present in cancer patients and tumor-bearing mice, the exact mechanisms by which IL-17 contributes to tumor growth are not yet fully understood.
In the current study, we found that the development of tumors was inhibited in mice lacking the IL-17 receptor (IL-17R). Conversely, mice deficient in both IL-17R and interferon gamma receptor (IFN-gammaR) exhibited increased tumor growth compared to wild-type mice. Additionally, neutralizing IL-17 with antibodies inhibited tumor growth in wild-type mice, while systemic administration of IL-17 promoted tumor growth.
Our findings revealed that the IL-17R deficiency led to increased CD8 T cell infiltration into tumors, while simultaneously reducing the infiltration of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) within tumors. In contrast, administration of IL-17 resulted in decreased CD8 T cell infiltration and increased MDSC infiltration. Further analysis showed that IL-17 was essential for the development and tumor-promoting activity of MDSCs in tumor-bearing mice.
Our study provides new insights into the role of IL-17 in tumor development and highlights the importance of targeting IL-17 in cancer treatment. The mechanisms by which IL-17 mediates its tumor-promoting effects through regulation of MDSCs are a primary focus of future research.

title: Circulating tumor cells and [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography for outcome prediction in metastatic breast cancer.
text: In this study, we investigated the prognostic value of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) and positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) monitoring during systemic therapy for metastatic breast cancer (MBC). We analyzed 115 MBC patients who underwent CTC counts and FDG-PET/CT scans at baseline and during therapy, and evaluated the correlation between CTC levels and PET/CT response. Our results showed that midtherapy CTC counts predicted overall survival in univariate and multivariate analyses, with a median overall survival time of 14 months. Among patients with fewer than five CTCs at midtherapy, FDG-PET/CT predicted overall survival in 31 (91%) of 34 discordant patients. These findings suggest that detection of five or more CTCs during therapeutic monitoring can accurately predict prognosis in MBC, and that FDG-PET/CT deserves a role in patients with fewer than five CTCs at midtherapy. Prospective trials are needed to determine the most sensitive and cost-effective modality for therapeutic monitoring in MBC.

title: Phylogenetic analysis of Portuguese Feline Immunodeficiency Virus sequences reveals high genetic diversity.
text: Feline Immunodeficiency Virus (FIV) is a Lentivirus responsible for an immunodeficiency-like disease in domestic cats. Through analysis of the genetic diversity of the V3-V5 region of the env gene, FIV is categorized into five phylogenetic subtypes (A, B, C, D, and E) with a global distribution. To investigate the subtype diversity of FIV in Portugal, a serological survey was conducted over the course of one year at the Veterinary Faculty Hospital in Lisbon, Portugal, to identify seropositive animals. Two viral genomic regions were amplified using nested PCR, sequenced, and the phylogenetic relationships between 24 newly obtained Portuguese FIV sequences and other previously published FIV isolates were analyzed. The introduction of these sequences resulted in the identification of a new subclustering within subtype B, containing most of the new Portuguese sequences. Additionally, a new cluster emerged, consisting of two highly divergent new sequences that may represent a new subtype. The study of these new FIV isolates revealed the presence in Portugal of a unique viral population with subclustering within subtype B and distinct sequences compared to the five known subtypes, providing valuable insights into FIV's genetic diversity.

title: Aire deficiency promotes TRP-1-specific immune rejection of melanoma.
text:
The thymic transcription factor autoimmune regulator (Aire) plays a crucial role in preventing autoimmunity by promoting the expression of tissue-specific self-antigens, including many cancer antigens. For instance, Aire-deficient patients are prone to develop vitiligo, an autoimmune disease that affects melanocytes, often triggered by effective immunotherapies against melanoma. To investigate the potential link between Aire deficiency and enhanced immune responses to cancer, we hypothesized that eliminating Aire in mice might increase immune responses to cancer and provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms.
In this study, we discovered that Aire deficiency leads to a reduction in thymic expression of TRP-1 (TYRP1), a self-antigen specific to melanocytes and a cancer antigen in melanomas. Interestingly, Aire deficiency did not affect the number of regulatory T cells in the thymus, yet it resulted in defective negative selection of TRP-1-specific T cells, without the observed reduction in regulatory T cells. This led to elevated immune responses against melanoma, characterized by suppressed melanoma growth. Intriguingly, we found that transplantation of Aire-deficient thymic stroma into an otherwise Aire-wild-type host was enough to enhance immune rejection of melanoma, offering a potential strategy to boost immune responses against cancer.
In summary, our discoveries indicate that Aire deficiency can bolster immune responses against melanoma by enhancing the negative selection of TRP-1-specific T cells, which leads to suppressed melanoma growth. Remarkably, manipulating TRP-1-specific T-cell negative selection may represent a logical strategy to enhance immune rejection of melanoma.

title: Mass screening programmes and trends in cervical cancer in Finland and the Netherlands.
text: With respect to cervical cancer management, Finland and the Netherlands exhibit comparable characteristics, including fertility rate, age at first birth, and a national screening program for several years. This study aims to compare the trends in incidence and mortality from cervical cancer in Finland and the Netherlands in relation to the introduction and intensity of their screening programs. Therefore, incidence and mortality rates were calculated using Cancer Registries in both countries. Data on screening intensity was obtained from the Finnish Cancer Registry and the Dutch evaluation center at ErasmusMC-Rotterdam. Women aged 30-60 have been screened every 5 years in Finland since 1992 and in the Netherlands since 1996. Similarly, screening protocols for smear taking and referral to a gynecologist are comparable. Notably, incidence and mortality rates have declined more in Finland. In 2003, age-adjusted incidence and mortality in Finland were 4.0 and 0.9 per 100,000 woman-years, respectively, while in the Netherlands they were 4.9 and 1.4 per 100,000 woman-years. Additionally, excess smear use in the Netherlands was estimated at 24 per 1,000 women during a 5-year interval, compared to 121 in Finland. The decline in mortality in Finland seems to be largely attributed to the screening program, whereas in the Netherlands, it was initially believed to be a natural decline. Also, differences in risk factors, such as population density and percentages of immigrants and female smokers, may play a role. Furthermore, the greater excess smear use in Finland may have influenced incidence.

title: Biochemical characterization of the Ran-RanBP1-RanGAP system: are RanBP proteins and the acidic tail of RanGAP required for the Ran-RanGAP GTPase reaction?
text: RanBP proteins have been shown to enhance the efficiency of the RanGAP-mediated GTPase reaction on Ran. Previous studies had suggested that RanBP1 was located away from the active site of the reaction, yet we reexamined the process using fluorescence spectroscopy under pre-steady-state conditions and found that RanBP1 does not affect the rate-limiting steps of the reaction, such as GTP cleavage or product release. However, RanBP1 does influence the dynamics of the Ran-RanGAP interaction, remarkably stimulating the association reaction by 20-fold, causing it to be under diffusion control (4.5 x 10(8) M(-1) s(-1)). By establishing a valuable kinetic system for analyzing the interaction, we also discovered, to our surprise, that the highly conserved acidic C-terminal end of RanGAP is not essential for the switch-off reaction. Contrary to previous findings, our genetic experiments in Saccharomyces cerevisiae revealed that the acidic tail of RanGAP plays a crucial role in microtubule organization during mitosis, suggesting that it is involved in a process during mitosis.

title: Concomitant induction of CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses in volunteers immunized with Salmonella enterica serovar typhi strain CVD 908-htrA.
text: Type 1 cell-mediated immunity may play a crucial role in the protection against typhoid fever. In order to investigate the vaccine candidate, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi) strain CVD 908-htrA, which is a leading live attenuated oral vaccine against typhoid fever, we assessed the specific immune responses against S. Typhi elicited by immunization with CVD 908-htrA in both high (4.5 x 108 CFU) and low (5 x 107 CFU) doses. Our results demonstrated potent cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) responses and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) secretion by CD8+ T cells following immunization with CVD 908-htrA in six out of eight vaccinees (four in the high dose group and two in the low dose group). An increase in the frequency of IFN-γ-secreting cells (SFC) in the presence of S. Typhi-infected targets was observed, with means of 221 +/- 41 SFC/106 PBMC and 233 +/- 87 SFC/106 PBMC in the high and low dose groups, respectively. Strong CD4+ T cell responses were also observed. Furthermore, a significant correlation was found between the volunteers who responded with IFN-γ SFC to stimulation with S. Typhi-infected cells and those who released IFN-γ in response to stimulation with soluble S. Typhi flagella (STF) Ag (r = 0.822, p < 0.001), as well as between CTL and IFN-γ production to STF (r = 0.818, p = 0.013). These findings are consistent with a crucial role of type 1 immunity in controlling typhoid infection and support the ongoing evaluation of CVD 908-htrA as a potential typhoid vaccine candidate.

title: The diverse functions of GAPDH: views from different subcellular compartments.
text: Recent studies have revealed multiple roles for glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) beyond its cytoplasmic location under basal conditions. GAPDH is also found in nucleus, mitochondria, and small vesicular fractions. When cells encounter stress, GAPDH undergoes dynamic re-distribution within the cell. This review focuses on the multifunctional properties of GAPDH, including its oligomerization, posttranslational modification, and subcellular localization. We describe the mechanisms by which S-nitrosylation of GAPDH under oxidative stress can lead to cell death/dysfunction by nuclear translocation of GAPDH, which is counteracted by a cytosolic protein called GOSPEL. GAPDH is also implicated in various diseases such as neurodegenerative disorders and cancers. Therapeutic strategies based on molecular understanding of GAPDH are discussed.

title: Exercise-induced asthma: a practical guide to definitions, diagnosis, prevalence, and treatment.
text: Exercise-induced asthma is characterized as an intermittent narrowing of the airways, demonstrated by a decrease in lung function, which can cause wheezing, chest tightness, coughing, and difficulty breathing. This occurs in people who have chronic asthma, as well as those who do not typically experience asthma symptoms. A definitive diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating a significant drop in lung function (typically 13-15% for forced expiratory volume in one second, FEV1, and 15-20% for peak expiratory flow rate, PEFR) after exercise, accompanied by associated symptoms. Studies show that this condition is prevalent among individuals who participate in recreational sports and highly competitive athletes, with approximately 12-15% of unselected athletes exhibiting positive exercise challenges. Treatment approaches include non-pharmacological measures, such as exploiting the refractory period after exercise and prewarming the air, as well as medications, including beta-agonists, cromolyn, and nedocromil. With proper management, individuals with exercise-induced asthma can potentially participate and excel at the highest levels of athletic competition.

title: Effect of sample quality on the sensitivity of endoscopic biopsy for detecting gastric and duodenal lesions in dogs and cats.
text:
BACKGROUND: The quality of histopathology slides from endoscopic biopsies of dogs and cats varies, but the impact of biopsy quality on diagnostic accuracy is unknown.
HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesize that the quality of endoscopic biopsy samples affects the ability to diagnose histologic lesions in the stomach or duodenum of dogs and cats. We predicted that more samples would be needed to diagnose lesions in poor-quality tissue specimens.
ANIMALS: We examined histopathology slides from 99 dogs and 51 cats as clinical cases at 8 veterinary institutions or practices in 5 countries.
METHODS: We graded the quality of the histologic section of tissue (inadequate, marginal, adequate), the type of lesion (lymphangiectasia, crypt lesion, villus blunting, cellular infiltrate), and the severity of the lesion (normal, mild, moderate, severe). We determined the sensitivity of different quality tissue samples for finding different lesions.
RESULTS: Our findings showed that fewer tissue samples were required from dogs for diagnosis, with improvements in quality from inadequate to marginal to adequate. Similarly, duodenal lesions in cats showed a trend towards fewer samples being needed, except for moderate duodenal infiltrates where quality of tissue sample made no difference. Gastric lesions in dogs and mild gastric lesions in cats also showed a similar trend, while the number of samples needed to diagnose moderately severe gastric lesions in cats was not affected by tissue sample quality.
CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Our results demonstrate a significant impact of endoscopic biopsy quality on diagnostic accuracy, with differences in sensitivity between biopsies of canine and feline tissues. This highlights the importance of careful sample processing and evaluation to improve diagnosis and clinical decision-making.

title: G-quadruplexes significantly stimulate Pif1 helicase-catalyzed duplex DNA unwinding.
text: The evolutionarily preserved G-quadruplexes (G4s) are inherited faithfully and perform various cellular functions, including telomere maintenance, gene regulation, DNA replication initiation, and epigenetic regulation. In contrast to the Watson-Crick base-pairing found in duplex DNA, G4s are formed through Hoogsteen base pairing and are highly stable and compact DNA structures. Failure to resolve G4s in the cell hinders DNA-based transactions and leads to genome instability. Cells have evolved specialized helicases to unwind G4s. We used a recombinant form of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase to investigate Pif1-mediated DNA unwinding on a substrate mimicking an ongoing lagging strand synthesis impaired by G4s, which resembles a replication origin and a G4-structured flap in Okazaki fragment maturation. Our findings show that the presence of G4s significantly enhances Pif1's ability to unwind duplex DNA. Further studies reveal that this stimulation is caused by G4-enhanced Pif1 dimerization, which is essential for duplex DNA unwinding. This work sheds new light on the properties and functions of G4s. We explore the observed activation phenomenon in relation to the possible regulatory role of G4s in rapidly reactivating the stalled lagging strand synthesis by aiding the replicator in recognizing and activating the replication origin, as well as quickly removing the G4-structured flap during Okazaki fragment maturation.

title: Diffusion tensor imaging detects and differentiates axon and myelin degeneration in mouse optic nerve after retinal ischemia.
text: Both axon and myelin degeneration significantly impact the long-term disability of patients with white matter disorders. However, the clinical manifestations of the neurological dysfunction caused by white matter disorders cannot determine the origin of neurological deficits. A non-invasive biological marker capable of detecting and differentiating axon and myelin degeneration would be a significant addition to currently available tools. Directional diffusivities derived from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) have been previously proposed by this group as potential biological markers to detect and differentiate axon and myelin degeneration. To further test the hypothesis that axial (lambdaparallel) and radial (lambdaperpendicular) diffusivities reflect axon and myelin pathologies, respectively, the optic nerve was examined serially using DTI in a mouse model of retinal ischemia. A significant decrease of lambdaparallel, the putative DTI axonal marker, was observed 3 days after ischemia without concurrently detectable changes in lambdaperpendicular, the putative myelin marker.
