Our findings suggest that BAF250a is a vital component of the gene regulatory machinery in ES cells, controlling self-renewal, differentiation, and cell lineage decisions.

title: Metabolic shutdown in Escherichia coli cells lacking the outer membrane channel TolC.
text: The transmembrane protein TolC is a crucial component of multidrug efflux and type I secretion systems in Escherichia coli. Disabling TolC leads to increased susceptibility to antibiotics and impairment of secretion of toxic proteins. Contrary to expectations, we discovered that the loss of TolC has a profound impact on cell growth, particularly in minimal glucose medium. This effect was further exacerbated by the simultaneous loss of ygiB and ygiC genes, which are located near tolC on the chromosome, as well as their homologues yjfM and yjfC found elsewhere on the genome. Our findings indicate that the growth inhibition is caused by a depletion of the crucial metabolite NAD+ and a resulting high NADH/NAD+ ratio. The increased levels of PspA and decreased NADH oxidation rates in TolC-deficient membranes suggest that the membrane is under stress and that a proton motive force is dissipating. We conclude that inactivation of TolC leads to metabolic shutdown in E. coli cells grown in minimal glucose medium. The TolC-related phenotype can be partially restored by expressing the ygiBC and yjfMC genes, which have independent functions that complement those of TolC.

title: Acyl and total ghrelin are suppressed strongly by ingested proteins, weakly by lipids, and biphasically by carbohydrates.
text:
Context: Ghrelin, an orexigenic hormone, can increase body weight by stimulating appetite and fat storage. Its circulating levels increase before meals and decrease after food ingestion. Understanding how specific types of ingested macronutrients influence ghrelin regulation can inform the development of weight-reducing diets.
Objective: The aim of this study was to investigate how ingestion of carbohydrates, proteins, or lipids affects acyl (bioactive) and total ghrelin levels in human subjects, with a hypothesis that lipids would suppress ghrelin levels to a lesser extent than carbohydrates or proteins.
Design: This randomized, within-subjects cross-over study was conducted at a university clinical research center.
Participants: Sixteen healthy human subjects participated in the study.
Interventions: Isocaloric, isovolemic beverages composed primarily of carbohydrates, proteins, or lipids were provided.
Main Outcome Measures: The study measured the magnitude of postprandial suppression of total and acyl ghrelin levels using a novel acyl-selective, two-site ELISA.
Results: All beverages suppressed plasma acyl and total ghrelin levels. A significant effect of macronutrient class on the decay rate of both acyl and total ghrelin was observed, with a ranking of protein > carbohydrate > lipid. Total ghrelin nadir levels were significantly lower after both carbohydrate and protein beverages compared to lipid beverages. In the first 3 postprandial hours, the ranking for acyl and total ghrelin suppression was carbohydrate > protein > lipid, while in the subsequent 3 hours, there was a notable rebound above preprandial values of acyl and total ghrelin after carbohydrate ingestion alone.
Conclusion: These findings suggest possible mechanisms underlying the effects of high-protein/low-carbohydrate diets to promote weight loss and high-fat diets to promote weight gain.

title: Hydrogen sulfide increases nitric oxide production with calcium-dependent activation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase in endothelial cells.
text: Recent research has revealed that hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is synthesized in mammalian tissues through multiple enzymatic pathways. Numerous studies have demonstrated that H2S exhibits vasodilatory and antihypertensive effects in the cardiovascular system, despite the lack of understanding regarding the intracellular mechanisms of its vasodilation and interactions with other endothelium-derived relaxing factors, such as nitric oxide (NO). To investigate the direct regulation of endothelial NO synthase (eNOS) activity and NO production by H2S, we evaluated the effect of a H2S donor, naHS, on NO production in cultured endothelial cells. Our findings showed that naHS dose-dependently increased NO production in endothelial cells, which was abolished by a calcium chelator (BAPTA-AM) but not by the absence of extracellular calcium. Furthermore, the NaHS-induced NO production was partially blocked by inhibitors of ryanodine receptor (dantrolene) or inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor (xestospongin C). NaHS significantly elevated intracellular calcium concentrations, which was attenuated by dantrolene or xestospongin C. Additionally, NaHS triggered phosphorylation of eNOS at the activating phosphoserine residue 1179. Interestingly, the NaHS-induced eNOS phosphorylation and NO production were resistant to inhibition by a PI3K/Akt inhibitor (wortmannin). Overall, these data suggest that H2S directly acts on endothelial cells to induce eNOS activation and NO production by releasing calcium from the intracellular store in the endoplasmic reticulum, which may provide insight into the mechanisms underlying its vasodilatory function.

title: Fear of falling and visual field loss from glaucoma.
text:
Objective: To investigate whether visual field (VF) loss caused by glaucoma is associated with a greater fear of falling.
Design: A prospective, observational study.
Participants: 83 glaucoma patients with bilateral VF loss and 60 control subjects without significant VF loss, recruited from patients with a suspicion of glaucoma.
Methods: Participants completed the University of Illinois at Chicago Fear of Falling Questionnaire, and VF loss severity was assessed using Rasch analysis.
Main Outcome Measures: Ability to perform tasks without fear of falling was expressed in logits, with lower scores indicating less ability and greater fear of falling.
Results: Glaucoma patients had greater VF loss than control subjects (median better-eye mean deviation [MD] of -8.0 decibels [dB] vs. +0.2 dB; P<0.001), but did not differ in age, race, gender, employment status, body mass index (BMI), grip strength, cognitive ability, mood, or the presence of other illnesses (P ≥ 0.1 for all). In multivariate models, glaucoma subjects reported greater fear of falling compared to controls (β = -1.20 logits; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.87 to -0.53; P = 0.001), and fear of falling increased with greater VF loss severity (β = -0.52 logits per 5-dB decrement in the better eye VF MD; 95% CI, -0.72 to -0.33; P<0.001). Other variables predicting greater fear of falling included female gender (β = -0.55 logits; 95% CI, -1.03 to -0.06; P = 0.03), higher BMI (β = -0.07 logits per 1-unit increase in BMI; 95% CI, -0.13 to -0.01; P = 0.02), living with another adult (β = -1.16 logits; 95% CI, -0.34 to -1.99 logits; P = 0.006), and greater comorbid illness (β = -0.53 logits/1 additional illness; 95% CI, -0.74 to -0.32; P<0.001).
Conclusions: Bilateral VF loss resulting from glaucoma is associated with a greater fear of falling, with an impact greater than several other risk factors. Given the physical and psychological consequences associated with fear of falling, significant improvements in quality of life may be achieved in patients with VF loss by screening for, and developing interventions to minimize, fear of falling.

title: Repeat instability: mechanisms of dynamic mutations
text: Repeat-causing genetic instability is a significant and distinct form of mutation associated with over 40 neurological, neurodegenerative, and neuromuscular disorders. DNA repeat expansion mutations are dynamic and ongoing within tissues and across generations. The patterns of inherited and tissue-specific instability are determined by both gene-specific cis-elements and trans-acting DNA metabolic proteins. Repeat instability is likely the result of unusual DNA structures forming during DNA replication, repair, and recombination. Advances in experimental understanding of the mechanisms of repeat instability have expanded our knowledge of this mutational process, revealing unexpected ways in which metabolic pathways can either drive or protect against repeat instability.

title: Demographic Risk Factors for Alcohol-Related Aggression In and Around Licensed Venues.
text:
FEW studies have examined the interplay between gender and both area-level and individual socio-economic status (SES) as predictors of alcohol-related aggression (ARA) in and around licensed premises. The current study aimed to investigate these factors and their relationship with ARA in a sample of 697 men and 649 women aged 16-47.
METHODS Participants completed a patron intercept survey as part of a larger study assessing trends in harm and stakeholders' views surrounding local community-level interventions in dealing with alcohol-related problems in the night-time economy. Binary logistic regression analyses revealed that age, gender, occupational category, area-level SES, and level of intoxication at the time of interview were all significant predictors of ARA involvement. Being male doubled the odds of involvement in ARA, while age served as a protective factor. Blue collar workers had more than double the odds of ARA involvement compared to professionals, while individuals living in the most socio-economically disadvantaged areas were over twice as likely to report experiencing ARA compared to those living in the most advantaged areas. However, the predictive model showed that the effects of age, occupational category, and area-level SES were only significant for male participants, with greater intoxication no longer a predictor.
CONCLUSIONS The results suggest that ARA is more likely to occur among men, those in blue collar occupations, and individuals living in low SES areas. This suggests that both individual and area-level disadvantage may play a role in ARA.

title: Schizophrenia susceptibility pathway neuregulin 1–ErbB4 suppresses Src upregulation of NMDA receptors
text: According to recent research, altered function of the N-methyl D-aspartate (NMDA) subtype of glutamate receptor (GluNMDAR) is believed to be a key mechanism underlying cognitive impairments in individuals with schizophrenia. Specifically, it is hypothesized that excessive signaling between the genes NRG1 and ERBB4 leads to hypofunction of GluNMDARs in the brain, contributing to cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. However, the current study contradicts this hypothesis, as it shows that neuregulin 1β-ErbB4 (NRG1β-ErbB4) signaling does not result in general impairment of GluNMDAR function. Instead, the study reveals that NRG1β-ErbB4 signaling specifically suppresses the enhancement of synaptic NMDAR currents mediated by the nonreceptor tyrosine kinase Src in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Furthermore, NRG1β-ErbB4 signaling prevents the induction of long-term potentiation at hippocampal Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses and suppresses Src-dependent enhancement of NMDAR responses during theta-burst stimulation. Additionally, NRG1β-ErbB4 signaling inhibits the phosphorylation of GluN2B by Src kinase activity. Based on these findings, the study proposes that NRG1-ErbB4 signaling contributes to cognitive dysfunction in schizophrenia by aberrantly suppressing Src-mediated enhancement of synaptic NMDAR function.

title: Intestinal bacteria and the regulation of immune cell homeostasis.
text: The human intestine is inhabited by an estimated 100 trillion bacteria, with some playing a crucial role in maintaining normal physiology while others have been linked to the development and progression of inflammatory diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and asthma. This review delves into the impact of bacterial signals on the immune system in both health and disease, exploring the composition of the intestinal microbiome, known immunoregulatory molecules produced by bacteria, and the mammalian innate immune receptors that recognize them. We examine how bacterial signals modulate immune cell function and discuss the potential of using bacterial communities or their products in the prevention or treatment of human diseases. Finally, we reflect on the challenges that lie ahead in this field and the potential for future breakthroughs.

title: Sympathetic activation during early pregnancy in humans.
text: In this study, the researchers investigated whether sympathetic activity increases during early pregnancy in humans. They enrolled 11 healthy women who were without prior hypertensive pregnancies and measured sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) and various physiological parameters, including blood pressure, heart rate, total peripheral resistance, renin, and aldosterone, both in the mid-luteal phase (PRE) and early pregnancy (EARLY, at 6.2 ± 1.2 weeks of gestation). The results showed that MSNA was significantly higher during EARLY than during PRE, both at rest and during upright tilt. Furthermore, resting diastolic pressure trended lower, heart rate was similar, total peripheral resistance decreased, sympathetic vascular transduction was blunted, and renin and aldosterone levels were higher during EARLY than during PRE. These findings challenge conventional thinking about blood pressure regulation during pregnancy and suggest that sympathetic activation may provide the substrate for pregnancy-induced cardiovascular complications.

title: Psychological adaptation in children with idiopathic short stature treated with growth hormone or placebo.
text: The study investigated the effects of growth hormone (GH) on the psychological adjustment of children and adolescents with idiopathic short stature (ISS). Sixty-eight participants, aged 9-16 years, with significant ISS were randomly assigned to receive either GH or a placebo three times a week until their height velocity slowed down. At baseline and annually thereafter, parents and children completed behavioral and self-concept questionnaires. The results showed that the two groups had similar behavioral and self-concept profiles during the first two years of the study. However, in years three and four, behavioral problems, as reported by parents on the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL), appeared to decrease more in the GH-treated group compared to the placebo-treated group. Additionally, the GH-treated group did not show any significant differences in competency domains or self-concept, as measured by the Self-Perception Profile (SPP), at any point during the study. The study found no association between short stature and psychological adaptation or self-concept in children with ISS. The trend toward improved problem behaviors observed in the GH-treated group suggests that GH treatment may have a positive impact on adaptation, psychosocial function, or quality of life in children with ISS, although further research is needed to confirm this finding.

title: Distinct and essential roles of transcription factors IRF-3 and IRF-7 in response to viruses for IFN-alpha/beta gene induction.
text: The activation of the interferon (IFN)-alpha/beta gene transcription in virus-infected cells is a critical event in the innate immune system. Mice lacking the transcription factor IRF-3 are more susceptible to viral infections. In embryonic fibroblasts, virus-induced IFN-alpha/beta gene expression levels are reduced, and the spectrum of IFN-alpha mRNA subtypes is altered. Furthermore, cells that are also deficient in IRF-7 expression are unable to induce these genes in response to any of the viruses tested. However, by co-expressing both IRF-3 and IRF-7, a normal profile of IFN-alpha/beta gene induction can be achieved in these cells, demonstrating the essential and distinct roles of the two factors in ensuring the efficient and diverse expression of IFN-alpha/beta genes for the antiviral response.

title: Interleukin-2- and interferon-gamma-secreting T cells in normal and diseased human intestinal mucosa.
text: A sensitive reverse hemolytic plaque assay was used to detect lymphokine-secreting T cells, while Northern blot analysis was employed to detect the expression of lymphokine messenger RNA (mRNA) in the mucosa of children with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis (UC), as well as in histologically normal mucosa from patients without inflammatory bowel disease. In contrast to the mucosa of most patients with UC and control subjects, where IL-2- and IFN-gamma-secreting cells were scarce or present at low levels, the mucosa of patients with Crohn's disease displayed readily detectable lymphokine-secreting cells (ranging from 3-18%). Consistent with this finding, IFN-gamma mRNA was detected in 5 out of 6 Crohn's tissues by Northern blot analysis, but only in 1 out of 5 UC samples and none of the nine samples of control mucosa. These studies suggest that there is an ongoing cell-mediated immune response in the mucosa of Crohn's disease.

title: Metabolic reprogramming of stromal fibroblasts through p62-mTORC1 signaling promotes inflammation and tumorigenesis.
text:
The tumor microenvironment, or the surrounding tissue of a tumor, plays a crucial role in cancer progression. However, the specific mechanisms by which stromal cells, or cells in the tumor microenvironment, influence the epithelium are not well understood. Our research found that levels of a protein called p62 were reduced in the stroma of several tumors, and that its loss in the tumor microenvironment or stromal fibroblasts led to increased tumorigenesis of epithelial prostate cancer cells.
We discovered that the mechanism underlying this process involves the regulation of cellular redox through an mTORC1/c-Myc pathway of stromal glucose and amino acid metabolism. This results in increased stromal IL-6 production, which is necessary for tumor promotion in the epithelial compartment. In other words, p62 acts as an anti-inflammatory tumor suppressor by modulating metabolism in the tumor stroma.

title: Drosophila RNAi screen reveals CD36 family member required for mycobacterial infection.
text: Certain pathogens, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, have the ability to survive within the hostile intracellular environment of a macrophage. To identify the host factors required for mycobacterial entry and survival within macrophages, we conducted a genome-wide RNA interference screen in Drosophila macrophage-like cells using Mycobacterium fortuitum. This screen revealed factors that are essential for general phagocytosis, as well as those that are specifically required for mycobacterial infection. One of these factors, Peste (Pes), is a member of the CD36 family and is essential for mycobacterial uptake, but not for the uptake of Escherichia coli or Staphylococcus aureus. Additionally, our findings suggest that mammalian class B scavenger receptors (SRs) play a crucial role in pattern recognition and innate immunity by mediating the uptake of bacteria into non-phagocytic cells. Specifically, SR-BI and SR-BII were found to uniquely mediate the uptake of M. fortuitum, highlighting a conserved role for class B SRs in the immune response.

title: Knowledge, attitudes, and practice on second primary cancer screening among cancer survivors: a qualitative study.
text:
Objective: This study aimed to investigate the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of cancer survivors regarding second cancer screening.
Methods: We conducted three focus group interviews with 13 disease-free stomach, colorectal, breast, and thyroid cancer survivors. We identified and categorized recurrent issues through thematic analysis.
Results: None of the participants were familiar with the term "SPC," and they were unable to distinguish it from "recurrence" or "metastasis." The survivors believed they had been cured and were not aware of their increased risk of SPC. Although they had high awareness of cancer screening, they struggled to differentiate between "cancer screening" and "routine surveillance tests" after cancer treatment. The survivors stated that they would have undergone SPC screening if they had been informed about it. They trusted physicians as the most credible source of screening information.
Conclusion: Cancer survivors had limited knowledge about SPC, and a lack of information was the primary obstacle to SPC screening.
Practice Implications: An educational intervention could help cancer survivors comprehend their risk of SPC and the necessity of screening after the first cancer.

title: LncRNA HANR Promotes Tumorigenesis and Increase of Chemoresistance in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
text:
Background/Aims: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the 5th most common cancer worldwide and the 3rd leading cause of cancer-related death. Recent studies have demonstrated critical roles for long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in various cancers, including HCC. However, the mechanisms of lncRNAs in HCC tumorigenesis and chemoresistance remain unclear.
Methods: In this study, we identified a HCC-expressed lncRNA termed HANR (HCC associated long non-coding RNA) through microarray analysis and validated its up-regulated expression through quantitative PCR. RNA pull-down and pathway analyses were conducted to investigate physical and functional interactions with HANR. In vivo experiments were performed to assess tumorigenesis and chemoresistance in HCC. Additionally, HANR expression was detected in HCC patient specimens using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Xenograft and orthotopic mice models were constructed to evaluate the effect of HANR on tumorigenesis and chemoresistance in vivo.
Results: Our findings showed that HANR was up-regulated in HCC patient samples and cell lines. Elevated HANR expression in HCC was associated with poor patient survival. Knock-down of HANR led to suppressed HCC xenograft/orthotopic tumor growth, increased apoptosis, and enhanced chemosensitivity to doxorubicin, whereas over-expression of HANR exhibited the opposite effects. Mechanistically, HANR was found to bind to GSKIP and regulate the phosphorylation of GSK3β in HCC.
Conclusion: Our results suggest that HANR plays a crucial role in HCC tumorigenesis and chemoresistance, and may serve as a promising therapeutic target for chemosensitization of HCC cells to doxorubicin. This finding may have important implications for the future development of HCC therapies.

title: Dissection of signaling cascades through gp130 in vivo: reciprocal roles for STAT3- and SHP2-mediated signals in immune responses.
text: We created a series of genetically modified mouse lines, where the cytokine receptor gp130-dependent STAT3 and/or SHP2 signals were disrupted. We replaced the mouse gp130 gene with human gp130 mutant cDNAs. The SHP2-deficient mice (gp130F759/F759) were born normally but exhibited enlarged spleens and lymph nodes and an exaggerated acute phase response. In contrast, STAT3-deficient mice (gp130FXQ/FXXQ) died shortly after birth, similar to gp130-deficient mice (gp130D/D). The gp130F759/F759 mice showed prolonged gp130-induced STAT3 activation, indicating a negative regulatory role for SHP2. We observed increased production of Th1-type cytokines, IgG2a, and IgG2b in the gp130F759/F759 mice, while these immune responses were reduced in the gp130FXXQ/FXXQ mice. These findings suggest that the balance of positive and negative signals generated through gp130 regulates immune responses.

title: Viral interleukin-10 expressed by human cytomegalovirus during the latent phase of infection modulates latently infected myeloid cell differentiation.
text: The human cytomegalovirus UL111A gene is active during both latent and productive infections and encodes proteins similar to interleukin-10 (IL-10). We investigated whether viral IL-10 produced during latency affects the differentiation of latently infected myeloid progenitor cells. Comparing infections with the parental virus or mock infection, latent infection with a virus lacking the gene encoding viral IL-10 led to increased production of cytokines associated with dendritic cell (DC) formation and a higher proportion of myeloid DCs. These findings indicate that viral IL-10 restricts the ability of latently infected myeloid progenitors to differentiate into DCs, suggesting an immunomodulatory role for viral IL-10 that could hinder the host's ability to clear latent virus.

title: Bortezomib enhances dendritic cell (DC)-mediated induction of immunity to human myeloma via exposure of cell surface heat shock protein 90 on dying tumor cells: therapeutic implications.
text: Most conventional cancer chemotherapies are immunosuppressive and inhibit the immunogenic death of tumor cells. However, Bortezomib, a specific inhibitor of the 26S proteasome, has shown promise in clinical trials against various human tumors, including myeloma. Our research reveals that the uptake of human myeloma cells by dendritic cells (DCs) after tumor cell death induced by Bortezomib, but not by gamma irradiation or steroids, leads to the induction of antitumor immunity, including against primary tumor cells, without the need for additional adjuvants. The delivery of activating signals from Bortezomib-killed tumor cells to DCs depends on cell-cell contact between DCs and dying tumor cells and is mediated by the exposure of heat shock protein 90 (hsp90) on the surface of dying cells, which is induced by Bortezomib. The combination of Bortezomib and geldanamycin (an hsp90 inhibitor) leads to increased apoptosis of tumor cells, but abrogates their immunogenicity. These findings suggest that exposure of endogenous heat shock proteins on the surface of dying cells, which is induced by drugs like Bortezomib, may serve as a mechanism of immunogenic death of human tumors. Targeting Bortezomib specifically to tumors may enhance their immunogenicity and induced immune response against them.

title: Survivin depletion preferentially reduces the survival of activated K-Ras-transformed cells.
text: To identify potential cancer-specific targets, we conducted a synthetic lethal screen using a library of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) targeting approximately 4,000 genes in the DLD-1 colon carcinoma cell line, which expresses an activated form of the K-Ras oncogene. We found that siRNAs targeting baculoviral inhibitor of apoptosis repeat-containing 5 (survivin) significantly reduced the survival of activated K-Ras-transformed cells compared to their normal isogenic counterparts, in which the mutant K-Ras gene had been disrupted (DKS-8). Concurrently, survivin siRNA induced a transient G(2)-M arrest and marked polyploidy, accompanied by increased activation of caspase-3 in activated K-Ras cells. These findings suggest that tumors harboring the activated K-Ras oncogene may be particularly susceptible to inhibitors of the survivin protein.

title: Small molecules enable cardiac reprogramming of mouse fibroblasts with a single factor, Oct4.
text: Recent research has demonstrated that mouse fibroblasts can be transformed into cardiac cells through the forced expression of multiple transcription factors and microRNAs. However, for potential use of this reprogramming strategy in cell-based therapy or in vivo cardiac regeneration, it is highly desirable to reduce or eliminate genetic manipulations through the use of small molecules. In this study, we report the identification of a defined small-molecule cocktail that enables the efficient conversion of mouse fibroblasts into cardiac cells with only one transcription factor, Oct4, without any evidence of a pluripotent state. Small-molecule-induced cardiomyocytes spontaneously contract and exhibit a ventricular phenotype, and these induced cardiomyocytes also pass through a cardiac progenitor stage. This study provides a foundation for future pharmacological reprogramming approaches and offers a small-molecule condition for investigating the mechanisms underlying the cardiac reprogramming process.

title: A switch from white to brown fat increases energy expenditure in cancer-associated cachexia.
text: Cancer-related cachexia (CAC) is a wasting syndrome characterized by systemic inflammation, body weight loss, and atrophy of white adipose tissue (WAT) and skeletal muscle. Despite limited therapeutic options, recent research has shown that a phenotypic shift from WAT to brown fat, known as WAT browning, occurs in the early stages of CAC. Brown fat is characterized by increased expression of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), which uncouples mitochondrial respiration to generate heat instead of ATP. Our findings suggest that WAT browning contributes to increased lipid mobilization and energy expenditure in cachectic mice. Chronic inflammation and the cytokine interleukin-6 (IL-6) have been shown to increase UCP1 expression in WAT, while treatments that reduce inflammation or block β-adrenergic receptors can reverse WAT browning and alleviate the severity of cachexia. Furthermore, UCP1 staining has been observed in WAT samples from CAC patients, highlighting the potential of targeting WAT browning as a therapeutic approach to improve the condition of cancer patients.

title: Potential Mechanisms of Action of Lithium in Bipolar Disorder
text:
Over half a century has passed since lithium was first introduced as a treatment for bipolar disorder, and since then, a wealth of empirical evidence has accumulated to support its efficacy in this role. However, despite its widespread use, the specific mechanisms by which lithium exerts its mood-stabilizing effects are not yet fully understood. To shed light on these mechanisms, this paper reviews the literature on the effects of lithium on mood, cognition, brain structure, neurotransmission, and intracellular and molecular pathways.
A comprehensive search of databases including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and PsycINFO revealed a large body of studies that have investigated the effects of lithium on acute mania, long-term mood stability, and prophylaxis. While lithium has been shown to be effective in these areas, its efficacy in treating depression is less clear-cut. However, lithium possesses a unique anti-suicidal property that sets it apart from other agents.
In terms of cognition, studies suggest that lithium may reduce cognitive decline in patients, although further investigation is needed to confirm this. Interestingly, lithium appears to preserve or increase the volume of brain structures involved in emotional regulation, such as the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala, which may reflect its neuroprotective effects.
At a neuronal level, lithium reduces excitatory neurotransmission (dopamine and glutamate) but increases inhibitory neurotransmission (GABA). These broad effects are underpinned by complex neurotransmitter systems that strive to achieve homeostasis through compensatory changes. For example, lithium targets second-messenger systems that further modulate neurotransmission. Specifically, the effects of lithium on the adenyl cyclase and phospho-inositide pathways, as well as protein kinase C, may serve to dampen excessive excitatory neurotransmission.
In addition to these mechanisms, it has been proposed that the neuroprotective effects of lithium are key to its therapeutic actions. Lithium has been shown to reduce oxidative stress, increase protective proteins such as brain-derived neurotrophic factor and B-cell lymphoma 2, and inhibit apoptotic processes through inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase 3 and autophagy.
Overall, it is clear that the processes which underpin the therapeutic actions of lithium are complex and interrelated. While the specific mechanisms by which lithium exerts its mood-stabilizing effects are not yet fully understood, the available evidence suggests that its neuroprotective effects are a key component of its therapeutic actions. Further research is needed to fully elucidate these mechanisms and to identify new targets for the development of more effective and safer mood stabilizers.

title: The role of autophagy in cancer development and response to therapy
text: Autophagy is a cellular process marked by dynamic changes to subcellular membranes, resulting in the degradation of cytoplasmic proteins and organelles. This process is crucial for cellular adaptation to stress or starvation. While much research has explored the significance of autophagy in cancer, the question of whether it hinders tumorigenesis or functions as a rescue mechanism for cancer cells under unfavorable conditions remains unresolved. Currently, our understanding of the role of autophagy in cancer development and response to therapy is vast, but more work is needed to fully elucidate its mechanisms and potential as a therapeutic target. Additionally, investigating methods to manipulate the autophagic process could provide insights into improving cancer treatments.

title: The quest to overcome resistance to EGFR-targeted therapies in cancer
text: Patients with metastatic lung, colorectal, pancreatic, or head and neck cancers who initially benefit from treatments targeting the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) ultimately develop resistance. As our understanding of the various mechanisms of resistance grows, the challenge of eradicating tumors that are resistant to EGFR inhibitors becomes more daunting. However, this increased knowledge also provides an opportunity to develop novel mechanism-based inhibitors and combination therapies that can prevent or overcome resistance. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the resistance pathways to EGFR-targeted therapies in lung, colorectal, and head and neck cancers, and discuss therapeutic strategies designed to circumvent these resistance mechanisms.

title: An organ culture model for the study of metanephric development.
text: A murine whole organ metanephric culture system was designed to investigate the developmental aspects of mammalian nephrogenesis. Metanephros and ureteric bud tissue were removed from CFI albino mouse embryos at 13.5 +/- 0.4 days gestation and cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's Minimal Essential Medium supplemented with 20% donor bovine serum at 37°C in a mixed air-5% CO2 environment. Under the experimental conditions employed, the metanephric explants displayed organotypic tubular and glomerular epithelial development. By 72 hours of culture, a well-developed proximal tubule with microvilli, characteristic intracellular organelles, and intercellular junctions had formed. By 120 hours of culture, unique devascularized glomeruli composed of parietal and visceral epithelial layers had formed, with visceral epithelial cells forming foot processes and slit pore diaphragms, and producing islands of basement membrane. Notably, endothelial or mesangial elements were not present at any stage in organ culture development, indicating that advanced nephrogenesis can occur following initial epithelial-mesenchymal induction even in the absence of vascularization. The whole organ culture model system allows for the isolation of renal structural development from the influences of perfusion and urine formation, providing a highly controlled environment for studying normal and abnormal mammalian renal development.

title: Molecular layers underlying cytoskeletal remodelling during cortical development
text: During the development of neural cells, the cytoskeleton undergoes significant changes and reorganization to enable the sequential steps of neurogenesis, cell migration, and terminal differentiation. It is apparent from examining the mechanisms involved in these processes that different configurations of the cytoskeleton predetermine the proper execution of each step and distinguish cohorts of proteins whose functions are essential for controlling neuronal migration yet not terminal differentiation. These combinatorial protein functions are also predetermined by regulated gene expression and the precise subcellular localization of their protein products. In the context of recent data on the regulation of the cytoskeleton during the maturation of cortical neurons in the developing brain, we expand upon this view.

title: Strong bias in the bacterial CRISPR elements that confer immunity to phage.
text: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)–Cas systems provide adaptive immunity against phage through spacer-encoded CRISPR RNAs that are complementary to invasive nucleic acids. Here, we challenge Streptococcus thermophilus with a bacteriophage and use PCR-based metagenomics to monitor phage-derived spacers daily for 15 days in two experiments. While spacers that target the host chromosome are rare and strongly selected against, suggesting autoimmunity is lethal, we observe early dominance by a few spacer sub-populations and rapid oscillations in sub-population abundances. In both CRISPR systems and replicate experiments, a few spacers account for the majority of spacer sequences. Furthermore, we detect a strong and reproducible bias in the phage genome locations from which spacers derive, which may reflect selection for specific spacers based on location and effectiveness.

title: Chronic hypoxia induces modification of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor in rat brain.
text: This study investigated the binding of the radioligand [3H]MK-801 to the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor in membranes isolated from the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and corpus striatum of 3-week-old rats exposed to 10 weeks of intermittent hypobaric hypoxia (at an altitude of 4300 m and a pressure of 450 Torr) and compared the results to those of normoxic controls. The research showed that the hypoxic animals had significant reductions in the binding sites for [3H]MK-801 (Bmax) and a decrease in the dissociation constant (Kd) compared to the controls. In the cerebral cortex, both glutamate (100 microM) and glycine (10 microM) enhanced [3H]MK-801 binding by two to threefold, but the EC50 value for glutamate was higher in the hypoxic cortical membranes than in the controls (0.44 microM vs. 0.28 microM). No significant differences were found in the EC50 value of glycine. These findings indicate that the NMDA receptor is altered in various brain regions of rats exposed to a hypoxic environment during development.

title: Cannabinoids in Clinical Practice
text: Cannabis has the potential for clinical use, but much of the available information is unreliable and based solely on anecdotal reports. The most significant natural cannabinoid is tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC), but others, such as cannabidiol (CBD) and cannabigerol (CBG), also have therapeutic effects. These constituents may interact with each other, and their effects may not be entirely accounted for by THC alone. For example, CBD reduces anxiety caused by THC. A standardized extract of the herb may be more beneficial in practice and clinical trials have been conducted to assess its effectiveness. While the mechanism of action is not fully understood, cannabinoid receptors have been identified, and natural ligands have been found. Cannabis is frequently used by patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) to manage muscle spasms and pain, and in an experimental model of MS, low doses of cannabinoids alleviated tremors. Most controlled studies have focused on THC, but this does not mirror the typical clinical scenario. Small clinical trials have shown that THC is effective as an analgesic, and CBD and CBG also have analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties, suggesting that drugs without psychoactive properties can be developed. Patients given the synthetic derivative nabilone for neurogenic pain preferred cannabis herb and reported that it relieved not only pain but the associated depression and anxiety. Cannabinoids are also effective in chemotherapy-induced emesis, and nabilone has been licensed for this use for several years. Currently, the synthetic cannabinoid HU211 is undergoing trials as a protective agent after brain trauma. Anecdotal reports of cannabis use include case studies in migraine and Tourette's syndrome, and as a treatment for asthma and glaucoma. While the smoking aspect of cannabis may pose safety concerns, the overall safety profile is relatively good. However, adverse reactions include panic or anxiety attacks, which are more common in the elderly and in women, and less likely in children. While psychosis has been cited as a cannabis side effect, a review of psychiatric hospital admissions found no evidence of this. However, it may exacerbate existing symptoms. The slow elimination of cannabinoids from the body has implications for cognitive tasks, especially driving and operating machinery, although driving impairment with cannabis is only moderate, and there is a significant interaction with alcohol. Standardized natural and synthetic compounds have the advantage of being more reliable and consistent, but may not have the overall therapeutic effect of the herb.

title: Large deformation of red blood cell ghosts in a simple shear flow.
text: Red blood cells alter their shape in response to local blood flow conditions. This deformability impacts their functional performance and the fluid dynamics of blood. To simulate three-dimensional membrane-fluid interactions, we use the immersed boundary method, validated for both neo-Hookean and Evans-Skalak models. We investigate the behavior of initially oblate spheroidal red blood cells, and show that the cell membrane exhibits asymptotic behavior as the dilation modulus to extensional modulus ratio increases, providing good area conservation. We also observe tank treading behavior and calculate its period.

title: Preoperative C-reactive protein predicts long-term mortality and hospital length of stay after primary, nonemergent coronary artery bypass grafting.
text:
BACKGROUND: Elevated preoperative C-reactive protein (CRP) levels have been linked to increased morbidity and mortality after cardiac surgery. This study aims to investigate the significance of lower CRP levels (less than 10 mg/l) in predicting long-term, all-cause mortality and hospital length of stay in patients undergoing primary, nonemergent coronary artery bypass graft-only surgery.
METHODS: We evaluated the association between preoperative CRP levels categorized into four groups (< 1, 1-3, 3-10, and > 10 mg/l) and 7-yr all-cause mortality and hospital length of stay in 914 prospectively enrolled primary, nonemergent coronary artery bypass graft-only surgical patients using a proportional hazards regression model.
RESULTS: A total of 87 patients (9.5%) died during a mean follow-up period of 4.8 +/- 1.5 years. After adjusting for potential confounders using a proportional hazards model, the 3-10 and > 10 mg/l preoperative CRP groups were significantly associated with long-term, all-cause mortality (hazard ratios [95% CI]: 2.50 [1.22-5.16], P = 0.01; and 2.66 [1.21-5.80], P = 0.02, respectively) and extended hospital length of stay (1.32 [1.07-1.63], P < 0.001; and 1.27 [1.02-1.62], P = 0.001, respectively).
CONCLUSION: Our findings indicate that preoperative CRP levels as low as 3 mg/l are associated with increased long-term mortality and extended hospital length of stay in relatively lower-acuity patients undergoing primary, nonemergent coronary artery bypass graft-only surgery. These important findings may enable more objective risk stratification of patients who present for uncomplicated surgical coronary revascularization.

title: Transcript assembly and quantification by RNA-Seq reveals unannotated transcripts and isoform switching during cell differentiation.
text: High-throughput mRNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) holds the potential for simultaneous discovery and abundance estimation of transcripts. However, this requires algorithms that bypass prior gene annotations and account for alternative transcription and splicing events. To address this challenge, we have developed an open-source software program called Cufflinks. We evaluated Cufflinks by analyzing >430 million paired 75-bp RNA-Seq reads from a mouse myoblast cell line over a time series of differentiation. The results showed the detection of 13,692 known transcripts and 3,724 previously unannotated ones, with 62% of the latter being supported by independent expression data or homologous genes in other species. Across the time series, 330 genes exhibited complete changes in the dominant transcription start site (TSS) or splice isoform, while 1,304 other genes showed subtle shifts. These findings demonstrate that Cufflinks can uncover the remarkable regulatory flexibility and complexity present in even well-studied biological models, such as muscle development, and enhance genome annotation through transcriptome-based analysis.

title: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in the United Kingdom: analysis of epidemiological surveillance data for 1970-96.
text:
The goal of this study is to investigate any potential changes in the occurrence of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) in the United Kingdom following the outbreak of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), also known as mad cow disease. The study design involves two sources of data: (a) referral of suspected cases by neurologists, neuropathologists, and neurophysiologists, and (b) death certificates. The study population consists of all 662 patients identified as sporadic cases of CJD in England and Wales during 1970-84, and the entire UK during 1985-96. The main outcome measures include the age distribution of patients, age-specific time trends of disease, occupational exposure to cattle, and potential exposure to the causative agent of BSE.
The results show an increase in the number of sporadic CJD cases recorded annually in England and Wales during the study period, with the greatest increase among people aged over 70. Additionally, there was a statistically significant excess of cases among dairy farm workers and their spouses, as well as among individuals at increased risk of contact with live cattle infected with BSE. Furthermore, during 1994-6, there were six deaths from sporadic CJD in the UK in patients aged under 30.
The study's conclusions suggest that the increase in the incidence of sporadic CJD and the high incidence among dairy farmers in the UK may not be related to BSE. The most notable change in the pattern of CJD in the UK after the BSE epidemic is the incidence among a group of exceptionally young patients with a distinct and unusual neuropathological profile. The outcome of mouse transmission studies and the future incidence of the disease in the UK and other countries will be important in determining whether the agent causing BSE has infected humans.

title: Documented head injury in early adulthood and risk of Alzheimer's disease and other dementias.
text:
Background: The relationship between antecedent head injury and the development of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is inconclusive.
Objective: To investigate the association between early adult head injury, as documented by military hospital records, and dementia in late life, and to evaluate the interaction between head injury and apolipoprotein E (APOE) epsilon4 as risk factors for dementia.
Methods: This study employed a population-based prospective historical cohort design. The sample consisted of male World War II Navy and Marine veterans who were hospitalized during their military service with either a nonpenetrating head injury or another unrelated condition. In 1996-1997, military medical records were abstracted to document the occurrence and details of closed head injury. The entire sample was then evaluated for dementia and AD using a multi-stage procedure. Of the 548 veterans with head injury and 1228 without head injury who completed all assigned stages of the study, the authors estimated the risk of dementia, specifically AD, using proportional hazards models.
Results: Both moderate (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.32; 95% CI = 1.04-5.17) and severe (HR = 4.51; 95% CI = 1.77-11.47) head injuries were found to be associated with an increased risk of AD. These results were also observed for dementia in general. The authors found an inconclusive association between mild head injury and dementia. Stratifying the results by the number of APOE epsilon4 alleles, the authors observed a nonsignificant trend toward a stronger association between AD and head injury in individuals with more epsilon4 alleles.
Conclusions: Moderate and severe head injuries in young men may be associated with an increased risk of AD and other dementias in late life, although the authors cannot rule out the possibility that other unmeasured factors may be influencing this association.

title: Transient receptor potential channels as drug targets: from the science of basic research to the art of medicine.
text: The Trp gene family is composed of a diverse group of ion channels known as transient receptor potential (TRP) proteins, which play a crucial role in cellular sensing and signaling pathways. In mammals, there are 28 TRP channel genes that encode cation-selective ion channels with unique permeation and gating properties. These proteins are involved in a wide range of physiological processes, including the regulation of musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, genitourinary, and nervous system function. Mutations in the genes encoding TRP channels, known as "TRP channelopathies," have been linked to a number of hereditary diseases that affect these systems. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the functional properties of mammalian TRP channels, their involvement in acquired and hereditary diseases, and their potential as drug targets for therapeutic intervention.

title: Identification of genes associated with the astrocyte-specific gene Gfap during astrocyte differentiation.
text: The arrangement of chromosomes and genes within the mammalian cell nucleus is not random, and gene clustering plays a crucial role in transcriptional regulation. However, the significance of gene clustering and their expression during the differentiation of neural precursor cells (NPCs) into astrocytes remains poorly understood. To investigate this, we used a genome-wide enhanced circular chromosomal conformation capture (e4C) technique to identify genes associated with the astrocyte-specific gene glial fibrillary acidic protein (Gfap) during astrocyte differentiation. We identified 18 genes that were specifically associated with Gfap and expressed in NPC-derived astrocytes. Our findings provide further evidence for the functional importance of gene clustering in transcriptional regulation during NPC differentiation.

title: Ketamine reduces LPS-induced HMGB1 via activation of the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway and NF-κB suppression.
text:
Original Text:
Background: Ketamine, as an anesthetic agent, possesses anti-inflammatory properties. In this study, we investigate whether ketamine inhibits the release of high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), a late-phase cytokine of sepsis, in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated macrophages through the induction of heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1).
Methods: Macrophages were pre-incubated with various concentrations of ketamine before being treated with LPS (1 μg/mL). The cell culture supernatants were collected to measure inflammatory mediators (HMGB1, nitric oxide, tumor necrosis factor-α, and interleukin 1β) using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Moreover, HO-1 protein expression, the phosphorylation and degradation of IκB-α, and the nuclear translocation of nuclear factor E2-related factor 2 and nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) p65 were assessed by Western blot analysis. To further elucidate the role of HO-1 in this process, tin protoporphyrin (SnPP), an HO-1 inhibitor, was employed.
Results: Ketamine treatment exhibited a dose-dependent attenuation of the increased levels of proinflammatory mediators (HMGB1, nitric oxide, tumor necrosis factor α, and interleukin 1β) and a concomitant augmentation of HO-1 protein expression in LPS-activated macrophages. Moreover, ketamine suppressed the phosphorylation and degradation of IκB-α, as well as the LPS-stimulated nuclear translocation of NF-κB p65 in macrophages. The present study also demonstrated that ketamine induced HO-1 expression through the nuclear translocation of nuclear factor E2-related factor 2 in macrophages. The effects of ketamine on LPS-induced proinflammatory cytokines production were partially reversed by the HO inhibitor SnPP.
Conclusion: Ketamine inhibits the release of HMGB1 in LPS-stimulated macrophages, and this effect is, at least in part, mediated by the activation of the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway and NF-κB suppression.

Here's the rewritten text with a more complex vocabulary and sentence structures:

The cell culture supernatants were collected to measure inflammatory mediators (HMGB1, nitric oxide, tumor necrosis factor-α, and interleukin 1β) using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. In addition, HO-1 protein expression, the phosphorylation and degradation of IκB-α, and the nuclear translocation of nuclear factor E2-related factor 2 and nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) p65 were evaluated by Western blot analysis. title: Association Between Early Screening for Patent Ductus Arteriosus and In-Hospital Mortality Among Extremely Preterm Infants.
text:
There is currently no consensus on the screening and treatment of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in extremely preterm infants. Our study aimed to evaluate the association between early screening echocardiography for PDA and in-hospital mortality in this population.
We conducted a comparison of preterm infants who were screened for PDA early in their hospital stay (n=605) and those who were not (n=605) in a national prospective population-based cohort study. We used propensity score matching and instrumental variable analysis to adjust for potential selection bias.
Our results showed that early screening echocardiography was associated with a lower hospital death rate and a lower rate of pulmonary hemorrhage. Among the 1513 preterm infants included in the study, 847 were screened for PDA and 666 were not. The exposed infants were treated for PDA more frequently during their hospitalization than the nonexposed infants. The adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality was 0.62 (95% CI, 0.37 to 1.04) in the overall cohort, suggesting a reduced risk of death among the exposed infants.
However, our results also showed that the instrumental variable analysis, which was used to adjust for potential selection bias, yielded an adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality that was less conclusive. This suggests that there may be some ambiguity in the interpretation of our findings and that longer-term evaluation is needed to provide clarity.
Overall, our study suggests that early screening echocardiography for PDA may be associated with improved outcomes in extremely preterm infants, including lower in-hospital mortality and pulmonary hemorrhage rates. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings and to determine the optimal screening and treatment strategy for PDA in this population.

title: Role of birthweight in the etiology of breast cancer.
text: Breast cancer may originate before birth. We examined the existing literature on the association between birthweight and the risk of breast cancer. To date, 26 research papers have been published on this topic. The majority of studies indicate a positive correlation between birthweight and premenopausal breast cancer, but not postmenopausal breast cancer. The relative risk estimate for breast cancer among women with high birthweight compared to those with low birthweight, combined from all studies including both pre- and postmenopausal breast cancer, was found to be 1.23 (95% confidence interval 1.13-1.34). The mechanisms underlying this association are likely linked to elevated levels of growth factors, which may increase the number of susceptible stem cells in the mammary gland or initiate tumors through genetic mutations. Abnormalities in the expression of growth hormone genes, such as insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2), due to loss of imprinting (LOI), may also play a role. These abnormalities have been found in both mammary tumor tissue and high birthweight individuals, suggesting a possible epigenetic mechanism. Further research is needed to fully understand the role of environmental factors in epigenetic regulation of gene expression and its relationship to breast cancer risk.

title: An activator of the cAMP/PKA/CREB pathway promotes osteogenesis from human mesenchymal stem cells.
text:
Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are a type of adult stem cell found in various tissues throughout the body. These stem cells have the ability to differentiate into different cell types, including osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes. As stem cells are highly versatile and can give rise to multiple cell types, their differentiation is tightly regulated to ensure proper tissue function. This regulation presents a potential opportunity for developing new therapeutic approaches using MSCs.
The discovery of small molecules that can stimulate the osteogenic differentiation of MSCs could lead to the development of a new anabolic drug for treating osteoporosis, a condition characterized by a loss of bone density. Our research identified CW008, a derivative of pyrazole-pyridine, as a potential therapeutic agent. CW008 promotes osteoblast differentiation of human MSCs in culture and increases bone formation in ovariectomized mice.
Our findings indicate that CW008 acts by activating the cAMP/PKA/CREB signaling pathway and inhibiting leptin secretion, both of which are critical regulators of osteogenic differentiation. These results suggest that CW008 may be a useful tool for the treatment of bone-related diseases and for studying bone biology.
In summary, our research on MSCs has identified a potential therapeutic agent that can stimulate osteogenic differentiation and increase bone formation. The finding of this small molecule provides new insights into the regulation of MSCs differentiation and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic approaches for bone-related disorders.

title: Magnesium sulphate for women at risk of preterm birth for neuroprotection of the fetus.
text:
BACKGROUND
Clinical and experimental evidence suggests that magnesium sulfate given before birth may protect the fetus's nervous system. This review aims to determine if magnesium sulfate given during pregnancy reduces the risk of cerebral palsy and other neurological defects in preterm births.
OBJECTIVES
We searched medical databases to find studies that tested the effectiveness of magnesium sulfate in reducing the risk of cerebral palsy and other neurological defects in preterm births. We categorized the studies based on their primary purpose (neuroprotection vs. other reasons) and extracted data from the trials.
MAIN RESULTS
Five trials involving 6145 babies found that antenatal magnesium sulfate therapy significantly reduced the risk of cerebral palsy and substantial gross motor dysfunction in preterm births. However, there was no significant effect on pediatric mortality or other neurological impairments. The number of women needed to be treated to benefit one baby by avoiding cerebral palsy is 63 (95% confidence interval: 43 to 87).
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS
The results of this review support the use of magnesium sulfate as a neuroprotective agent in preterm births. The beneficial effects of magnesium sulfate on cerebral palsy and gross motor function in early childhood indicate that further evaluation is needed to assess the long-term effects of magnesium sulfate on the nervous system.

title: The growing landscape of lysine acetylation links metabolism and cell signalling
text: Lysine acetylation is a widespread post-translational modification that connects metabolism and cell signaling. Advances in mass spectrometry have allowed for a deeper understanding of lysine acetylation, revealing its involvement in various biological processes through the regulation of protein interactions, activity, and localization. Additionally, proteins can undergo other types of acylations, such as formylation, butyrylation, propionylation, succinylation, malonylation, myristoylation, glutarylation, and crotonylation. The interplay between lysine acetylation and cellular metabolism is further highlighted by the presence of metabolite-sensitive acylations, which can be selectively removed by sirtuin deacylases. These recent findings suggest new functions for different lysine acylations and deacylating enzymes and uncover the mechanisms by which acetylation regulates various cellular processes.

title: COMPASS, a histone H3 (Lysine 4) methyltransferase required for telomeric silencing of gene expression.
text: The Trx family of proteins plays a vital role in regulating gene expression in certain organisms. Recently, we discovered and characterized COMPASS, a multiprotein complex that includes Trx-related protein Set1 from yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Surprisingly, our findings show that COMPASS functions as a methyltransferase in vitro, catalyzing the methylation of the fourth lysine of histone H3. Moreover, Set1 and other COMPASS components are essential for histone H3 methylation in vivo and the transcriptional silencing of a gene located near a chromosome telomere.

title: Free water elimination diffusion tractography: A comparison with conventional and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, diffusion tensor imaging acquisitions.
text:
PURPOSE: This study evaluates the ability of free water elimination (FWE) diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) methods to reduce cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) partial volume effects (PVEs) in deterministic tractography reconstructions.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Ten healthy individuals were scanned with "traditional," FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery), and FWE DTI scans. Deterministic tractography reconstructions of the fornix, corpus callosum, and cingulum bundles were performed using each modality. The FWE DTI scan was performed twice to match either total acquisition time (long FWE) or number of measurements (encoding directions, short FWE) to the FLAIR and "traditional" DTI scans. PVE resolution was determined based on reconstructed tract volume. All reconstructions underwent blinded review for anatomical correctness, symmetry, and completeness.
RESULTS: Reconstructions of the fornix demonstrated that the FWE and FLAIR scans produce more complete and anatomically plausible tract reconstructions than "traditional" DTI. Additionally, tract reconstructions using FWE-DTI were significantly larger than when FLAIR was used with DTI (p < 0.0005). FLAIR and FWE methods led to signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) reductions of 33% and 11%, respectively, compared with conventional DTI. The long and short FWE acquisitions did not significantly differ (p ≥ 0.31) from each other for any of the reconstructed tracts.
CONCLUSION: The FWE diffusion model overcomes CSF PVE without incurring the time, SNR, and volumetric coverage penalties associated with FLAIR DTI.

title: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials of acupuncture in the treatment of depression.
text: Acupuncture has gained popularity as a complementary and alternative treatment for depression. This review analyzed randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the effects of acupuncture on depression. METHODS: We searched MEDLINE, Allied and Complementary Medicine, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials for RCTs that compared acupuncture with control conditions in the treatment of depression. We assessed the methodology of the RCTs using the Jadad criteria and evaluated elements of research design, including randomization, blinding, and assessment of attrition rates. RESULTS: Of the 9 RCTs examined, 5 were deemed to have low quality based on the Jadad criteria. The odds ratios derived from the RCTs suggested some evidence for the effectiveness of acupuncture in treating depression. However, placebo acupuncture treatment was often no different from intended verum acupuncture. LIMITATIONS: The RCTs reviewed had limitations such as small sample sizes, imprecise enrollment criteria, problems with randomization and blinding, and brief duration of study. CONCLUSIONS: While the evidence suggests a potential role for acupuncture in treating depression, it is inconclusive due to the limitations of the existing RCTs. However, there is a growing effort to standardize complementary approaches to depression, and further systematic research is warranted to fully understand the effectiveness of acupuncture in treating depression.

title: Genome-Wide Gene-Sodium Interaction Analyses on Blood Pressure: The Genetic Epidemiology Network of Salt-Sensitivity Study.
text: In this study, we conducted genome-wide analyses to identify genomic regions that interact with sodium levels and impact blood pressure (BP) in a dataset of 1876 Chinese individuals from the Genetic Epidemiology Network of Salt-Sensitivity (GenSalt) study. We used single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) and gene-based tests to identify these associations. Our findings showed that several novel BP loci were identified, including UST rs13211840 (P=3.13×10(-9)) for diastolic BP, CLGN rs2567241 (P=3.90×10(-12)) and LOC105369882 rs11104632 (P=4.51×10(-8)) for systolic BP, and CLGN variant rs2567241 for diastolic BP (P=3.11×10(-22)) and mean arterial pressure (P=2.86×10(-15)). In addition, we identified eight novel BP loci through gene-based analysis, including MKNK1 (P=6.70×10(-7)), C2orf80 (P<1.00×10(-12)), EPHA6 (P=2.88×10(-7)), SCOC-AS1 (P=4.35×10(-14)), SCOC (P=6.46×10(-11)), CLGN (P=3.68×10(-13)), MGAT4D (P=4.73×10(-11)), ARHGAP42 (P≤1.00×10(-12)), CASP4 (P=1.31×10(-8)), and LINC01478 (P=6.75×10(-10)). These findings suggest that multiple genomic regions interact with sodium levels to influence BP, and highlight the importance of further investigating these loci in larger populations.

title: Percentile curves for hemoglobin and red cell volume in infancy and childhood.
text: Percentile curves were created for hemoglobin and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) in children ranging from 0.5 to 16 years of age using data from several populations of non-indigent white children living near sea level. To ensure accuracy, subjects with laboratory evidence of iron deficiency, thalassemia minor, or hemoglobinopathy were excluded from the reference population. A total of 9,946 children were included in the hemoglobin reference population and 2,314 in the MCV reference population. These percentile curves are particularly useful in the diagnosis and screening of iron deficiency and thalassemia minor.

title: Preservation of pancreatic beta-cell function and prevention of type 2 diabetes by pharmacological treatment of insulin resistance in high-risk hispanic women.
text: Type 2 diabetes often results from the gradual deterioration of pancreatic beta-cell function in response to chronic insulin resistance. We investigated whether improving insulin sensitivity could maintain pancreatic beta-cell function and delay or prevent the onset of type 2 diabetes in high-risk Hispanic women with a history of gestational diabetes. Participants were randomized to receive either a placebo or the insulin-sensitizing drug troglitazone (400 mg/day) in a double-blind manner. Fasting glucose levels were measured every 3 months, and oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTTs) were conducted annually to detect diabetes. Intravenous glucose tolerance tests (IVGTTs) were performed at baseline and 3 months later to identify early metabolic changes associated with any protection from diabetes. Women who did not develop diabetes during the trial underwent OGTTs and IVGTTs 8 months after stopping study medications. During a median follow-up of 30 months, the average annual diabetes incidence rate in the 236 women who returned for at least one follow-up visit was 12.1% in the placebo group and 5.4% in the troglitazone group (P < 0.01). Treatment with troglitazone delayed or prevented the onset of type 2 diabetes in high-risk Hispanic women, and this protection was associated with the preservation of pancreatic beta-cell function. Specifically, the degree of reduction in endogenous insulin requirements 3 months after randomization predicted the extent of protection from diabetes, and this effect persisted 8 months after stopping study medications. Furthermore, the protective effect of troglitazone was associated with a reduction in the secretory demands placed on beta-cells by chronic insulin resistance.

title: Androgen regulation of micro-RNAs in prostate cancer.
text:
The background of androgens' role in the growth of both androgen-dependent and castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) has been well-established. However, only a limited number of microRNAs (miRNAs) have been investigated as potential androgen regulators. In this study, we aimed to identify androgen-regulated miRNAs in both cell lines and xenograft models.
We used the LNCaP cell line, which we have previously established and overexpresses the androgen receptor (AR), along with the VCaP cell line, and 13 intact-castrated prostate cancer (PC) xenograft pairs, as well as clinical specimens of untreated PC and CRPC. Our results showed that 17 miRNAs were significantly upregulated or downregulated upon dihydrotestosterone (DHT) treatment in the cell lines, and 42 after castration in the AR-positive xenografts. Only four miRNAs (miR-10a, miR-141, miR-150*, and miR-1225-5p) displayed consistent androgen regulation in both cell lines and xenografts. Of these, miR-141 had higher expression in PC and CRPC compared to benign prostate hyperplasia. Moreover, ectopic overexpression of miR-141 enhanced growth of parental LNCaP cells, while inhibition of miR-141 by anti-miR-141 suppressed the growth of the LNCaP subline overexpressing AR.
In conclusion, our findings suggest that only a limited number of miRNAs are androgen-regulated in both cell lines and xenograft models, and among them, miR-141 exhibited upregulated expression in cancer tissues. The overexpression of miR-141 increased growth of LNCaP cells, which may suggest a potential role in the progression of PC.

title: Relationship between drug treatment services, retention, and outcomes.
text: INTRODUCTION This long-term study employed path analyses to investigate the relationships between treatment processes and outcomes among patients enrolled in community-based drug treatment programs. METHODS A total of 1,939 patients from 36 outpatient and residential treatment facilities in 13 California counties were assessed at intake, discharge, 3-months post-admission, and 9-months post-admission. Path analyses were conducted to examine how the quantity and quality of services received in the initial 3-months of treatment are linked to treatment retention and outcomes at the 9-month follow-up. Patients were considered to have a favorable outcome if they did not use drugs, were not involved in criminal activity, and lived in the community for at least 30 days prior to the follow-up assessment. The path analyses controlled for patients' baseline characteristics. RESULTS Findings showed that greater service intensity and satisfaction were positively related to either treatment completion or longer treatment retention, which in turn were associated with favorable treatment outcomes. Patients with greater problem severity received more services and were more likely to be satisfied with treatment. These patterns held true for patients regardless of whether they were treated in outpatient or residential programs. CONCLUSIONS The strong correlation between process measures, such as higher levels of service intensity, satisfaction, and either treatment completion or retention, and treatment outcomes suggests that improving these fundamental elements of the treatment process will lead to better treatment outcomes.

title: Breast cancer mortality trends in the United States according to estrogen receptor status and age at diagnosis.
text:
Since 1990, there has been a significant decline in overall breast cancer mortality rates in the United States, with a 24% decrease observed during this period. This decrease has been attributed to the use of mammography screening and adjuvant systemic therapy. However, the effectiveness of these modalities may depend on the expression of estrogen receptors (ER) and age. To examine breast cancer mortality trends in the United States based on ER status and age, we analyzed data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) program from 1990 to 2003.
We calculated trends in incidence-based mortality (IBM), annual hazard rates for breast cancer deaths after diagnosis, and relative hazard rates for women with ER-positive and ER-negative tumors. These hazard rates were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for stage and grade, and stratified by age at diagnosis.
Our results show that IBM and annual hazard rates for breast cancer deaths decreased among women with both ER-positive and ER-negative tumors during the study period. However, the declines were greater for women with ER-positive tumors, with a 38% decrease observed among women younger than 70 years and a 14% decrease among women 70 years or older.
Our findings suggest that additional emphasis should be placed on improving outcomes for breast cancer patients older than 70 years and those of all ages with ER-negative tumors, as mortality rates in these groups remain unacceptably high. Overall, these results highlight the importance of continued investment in breast cancer research and the need for more effective treatment strategies for this devastating disease.

title: An adenovirus mutant that replicates selectively in p53-deficient human tumor cells.
text: The human adenovirus E1B gene produces a 55-kilodalton protein that inhibits the activity of the cellular tumor suppressor protein p53. Research has shown that a mutant adenovirus lacking this viral protein can infect and lyse p53-deficient human tumor cells, but not cells that retain functional p53. Conversely, introducing the 55-kilodalton protein into p53-deficient cells makes them susceptible to infection with the mutant virus. Injections of the mutant virus into p53-deficient human cervical carcinomas growing in nude mice led to a significant reduction in tumor size, with 60% of the tumors regressing completely. These findings suggest that mutant adenoviruses could potentially be used to treat certain human cancers.

title: Immune reconstitution after cord blood transplantation: peculiarities, clinical implications and management strategies.
text: Umbilical cord blood (UCB) has emerged as a promising alternative source of hematopoietic stem cells for patients lacking suitable donors. Historical challenges with UCB transplantation include delayed engraftment, poor immune reconstitution, and increased risk of infection. However, more recent studies have suggested that adjusting conditioning regimens, particularly by omitting in vivo T-cell depletion, can significantly enhance post-transplant T-cell expansion and facilitate an expedient immune recovery. The unique characteristics of UCB cells, the significance of thymic function, and the impact of conditioning regimens and graft-versus-host disease on immune reconstitution are detailed. The review also highlights available data on UCB and third-party peripheral blood derived anti-viral cell therapy, which presents a novel approach to manage UCB recipients experiencing viral complications in the post-transplant period.

title: OVEREXPRESSION OF BOTH CLOCK AND BMAL1 INHIBITS ENTRY TO S PHASE IN HUMAN COLON CANCER CELLS.
text:
Many physiological, biochemical, and behavioral processes operate under the circular rhythm, or circadian rhythm, which is generated by an internal timing mechanism called the biological clock in almost all living organisms, from bacteria to mammals. The biological clock's core circadian oscillator consists of a positive regulatory feedback loop involving CLOCK and BMAL1 proteins. In addition to its role in regulating the circadian rhythm, the biological clock also controls cellular processes through two distinct mechanisms: the cell cycle and the cell rhythm. However, the relationship between these two mechanisms remains controversial, and therefore, the aim of this study was to investigate the effect of Clock and Bmal1 on cell cycle progression, with a particular focus on the G1 phase.
To achieve this goal, the researchers used a vector-based approach with the tetracycline operator-repressor system to simultaneously induce Bmal1 and Clock expression in SW480/T-REx/Clock/Bmal1 cells. The results showed that the induction of both Clock and Bmal1 had a profound effect on cell cycle progression, as it inhibited cell growth and caused a significant increase in the proportion of cells in the G1 phase. Moreover, overexpression of Clock and Bmal1 prevented the cells from entering the G2/M phase in response to Paclitaxel treatment, making the cells more resistant to the drug.
In conclusion, the study found that overexpression of both Clock and Bmal1 suppressed cell growth and hinted that these proteins may play a role in preventing cells from entering the G1 to S phase of the cell cycle by suppressing CyclinD1 expression, which could contribute to acquiring resistance to Paclitaxel.

title: Composition of gall bladder stones associated with octreotide: response to oral ursodeoxycholic acid.
text: Octreotide, an effective treatment for acromegaly, can lead to the formation of gallstones in approximately 13% to 60% of patients. Knowledge of the composition of these stones is crucial for understanding their pathogenesis, treatment, and prevention. In this study, chemical analysis of gallstones retrieved during cholecystectomy from two patients revealed that they were primarily composed of cholesterol (71% and 87% by weight). In the remaining 12 patients, localized computed tomography of the gallbladder indicated that eight had stones with attenuation scores of less than 100 Hounsfield units, indicating that they were likely made of cholesterol-rich, dissolvable stones. Gallbladder bile was obtained through ultrasound-guided fine needle puncture in six patients, and all showed supersaturated bile with high cholesterol saturation indices (mean of 1.19, range of 0.08 to 1.53). Additionally, all six patients had abnormally rapid cholesterol microcrystal nucleation times, and in four cases, cholesterol microcrystals were observed in the bile immediately after sampling. Of the 12 patients deemed eligible for oral ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) treatment, two had a blocked cystic duct and were not started on UDCA, while one was lost to follow-up. After one year of treatment, five of the remaining nine patients showed partial (n=3) or complete (n=2) gallstone dissolution, indicating that their stones were cholesterol-rich. According to actuarial analysis, the combined gallstone dissolution rate was 58.3% (95% CI: 15.9%). In conclusion, octreotide-induced gallstones are generally small, multiple, and cholesterol-rich, although some patients may present with blocked cystic ducts and/or gallstones containing calcium, similar to spontaneous gallstone disease.

title: Imiquimod 5% cream for the treatment of superficial basal cell carcinoma: results from a randomized vehicle-controlled phase III study in Europe.
text:
Background: Imiquimod is an immune response modifier that activates toll-like receptor 7, inducing cytokine production and a subsequent innate and adaptive immune response.
