Clinical studies have demonstrated that imiquimod 5% cream can induce clinical and histological clearance of superficial basal cell carcinoma (sBCC).
Objectives: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of imiquimod 5% cream in a randomized, double-blind, parallel, vehicle-controlled phase III clinical study conducted in Europe for the treatment of sBCC.
Methods: Eligible subjects with at least one histologically confirmed sBCC tumor were randomly assigned to apply either imiquimod or vehicle cream to the affected area once daily for seven times per week for six weeks. The treated area was clinically evaluated for treatment response at 12 weeks after completion of treatment and histologically evaluated for response using a standardized scoring system. Safety assessments, including adverse events and local skin reactions, were conducted throughout the study.
Results: A total of 166 subjects were enrolled in the study. For the intent-to-treat analysis, there was a statistically significant difference between the imiquimod and vehicle groups in terms of composite clearance rates (both clinical and histological assessments) and histological clearance rates. Specifically, 77% and 6% of subjects in the imiquimod group and vehicle group, respectively, achieved composite clearance, while 80% and 6% achieved histological clearance. The most common safety findings were investigator-assessed local skin reactions and spontaneous reports by subjects of application site reactions, which occurred more frequently in the imiquimod group than in the vehicle group.
Conclusions: Imiquimod 5% cream administered once daily for seven times per week for six weeks is a safe and effective treatment for sBCC compared to vehicle cream, as demonstrated by the significant differences in composite and histological clearance rates.

title: Changing the course of pancreatic cancer--Focus on recent translational advances.
text:
Over the past decade, groundbreaking preclinical research has shed light on the complex nature of pancreatic cancer. While the majority of pancreatic cancers are KRAS-mutated, not all tumors are equally dependent on the KRAS pathway. Despite encouraging early results from KRAS-targeting therapies, clinical trials have faced disappointing outcomes. However, 'synthetic lethal' approaches hold promise in this context. Contrary to previous beliefs, the pancreatic cancer stromal microenvironment appears to have both protective and hindering effects on tumor progression. While stromal barriers can impede drug delivery, the stroma can also protect the tumor in certain situations. Clinical trials aimed at manipulating stromal components are underway.
Specifically, BRCA mutation-related pancreatic tumors account for a unique subtype with increased sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents and PARP inhibition. DNA repair defects in cancer stretch beyond germ line BRCA mutations, suggesting expanded therapeutic potential for DNA repair-targeting agents.
In addition, immune-based strategies are currently being investigated in pancreatic cancer, including combinatorial approaches using immune-modifying agents and vaccines. Although early single-agent checkpoint inhibitor trials have been unsuccessful, the pursuit of an 'immune-therapy responsive' profile in pancreatic cancer remains an area of active research.

title: Swc2 is a widely conserved H2AZ-binding module essential for ATP-dependent histone exchange
text: Histone H2AZ is selectively incorporated into specific regions of chromatin to modulate chromosome functions. In yeast, the SWR1 complex, comprised of multiple proteins, is responsible for ATP-dependent exchange of histone H2A with H2AZ. Through our research, we uncovered interactions between SWR1 components and H2AZ, revealing a connection between the ATPase domain of Swr1 and three subunits essential for H2AZ binding. We discovered that Swc2 directly binds to H2AZ and is crucial for its transfer, while Swc6 and Arp6 are required for the association of Swc2 and nucleosome binding. Additionally, Swc5 and Yaf9 are necessary for H2AZ transfer but do not affect nucleosome binding. Finally, we found that the C-terminal α-helix of H2AZ is critical for its recognition by SWR1. This work sheds light on the initial stages of histone exchange.

title: Detection, characterization, and spontaneous differentiation in vitro of very small embryonic-like putative stem cells in adult mammalian ovary.
text: The present study aimed to uncover the stem cell potential of ovarian surface epithelium (OSE) in adult rabbit, sheep, monkey, and menopausal human ovaries. Two distinct populations of putative stem cells (PSCs) were identified in OSE scraped samples: smaller than 1 μm PSCs with pluripotent markers (Oct-4 and SSEA-4) and larger than 4 μm PSCs with a tissue-committed progenitor stem cell phenotype (Oct-4 and minimal SSEA-4 expression). Pluripotent gene transcripts were detected in both human and sheep OSE by reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction. PSCs spontaneously differentiated into oocyte-like structures, parthenote-like structures, embryoid body-like structures, cells with neuronal-like phenotype, and embryonic stem cell-like colonies, while epithelial cells underwent mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition in 3 weeks of OSE culture. Germ cell markers were immunolocalized in oocyte-like structures. In conclusion, contrary to the existing view of OSE as a bipotent source of oocytes and granulosa cells, mammalian ovaries contain distinct very small embryonic-like PSCs and tissue-committed progenitor stem cell populations that have the potential to differentiate into oocyte-like structures in vitro, while mesenchymal fibroblasts form supporting granulosa-like somatic cells. Further research at the single-cell level, including complete gene expression profiling, is needed to determine whether postnatal oogenesis is a conserved phenomenon in adult mammals.

title: Rearrangement of CRLF2 is associated with mutation of JAK kinases, alteration of IKZF1, Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, and a poor outcome in pediatric B-progenitor acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
text: Gene expression profiling of 207 pediatric patients with high-risk B-precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) revealed that 29 out of 207 cases (14%) had significantly elevated expression of CRLF2 (cytokine receptor-like factor 2). Further analysis revealed that each of these 29 cases harbored a unique genomic rearrangement of CRLF2. Specifically, 18 out of 29 cases (62%) had a translocation of the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene IGH@ on 14q32 to CRLF2 in the pseudoautosomal region 1 of Xp22.3/Yp11.3, while 10 cases (34%) had a 320-kb interstitial deletion centromeric of CRLF2, resulting in a P2RY8-CRLF2 fusion. One case had both IGH@-CRLF2 and P2RY8-CRLF2 rearrangements, and another case had a novel CRLF2 rearrangement. Only two out of 29 cases were diagnosed with Down syndrome. The presence of CRLF2 rearrangements was associated with specific genetic mutations, including activating mutations in JAK1 or JAK2, deletion or mutation of IKZF1, and Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (P < .001 for each). Notably, patients with CRLF2 rearrangements had significantly poorer treatment outcomes compared to those without these rearrangements (35.3% vs 71.3% relapse-free survival at 4 years; P < .001). These findings suggest that the cooperative action of CRLF2 expression, JAK kinase mutations, and IKZF1 alterations may promote B-cell leukemogenesis, highlighting the importance of targeting these pathways in the treatment of this disease.

title: Substrate requirements for ErmC' methyltransferase activity.
text: ErmC' is an enzyme that confers resistance to the macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B group of antibiotics by methylating 23S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) at a specific adenine residue (A-2085 in Bacillus subtilis and A-2058 in Escherichia coli). Through cloning and expressing the gene for ErmC' in E. coli, the protein was purified to near homogeneity. Investigations into the substrate requirements of ErmC' revealed that a 262-nucleotide RNA fragment within domain V of B. subtilis 23S rRNA can be used efficiently as a substrate for methylation at A-2085. kinetic studies of the monomethylation reaction showed that the apparent Km of this 262-nucleotide RNA oligonucleotide was significantly higher than the value determined for full-size and domain V 23S rRNA, and the Vmax for this fragment also rose notably. Based on the kinetic data presented, a model of RNA-ErmC' interaction involving multiple binding sites is proposed.

title: Validity of the World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) Screener in a representative sample of health plan members.
text: The validity of the World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) Screener was examined in a sample of individuals enrolled in a large health plan in the US. A subset of 668 subscribers was administered the ASRS Screener twice to assess test-retest reliability and then a third time with a clinical interviewer for DSM-IV adult ADHD diagnoses. The data were weighted to account for differences between the sample and the population in terms of socio-demographics and past medical claims. The internal consistency reliability of the continuous ASRS Screener ranged from 0.63 to 0.72, while test-retest reliability (Pearson correlations) ranged from 0.58 to 0.77. A four-category version of the ASRS Screener showed strong agreement with clinician diagnoses, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.90. The brief nature and ability to differentiate between DSM-IV cases and non-cases make the six-question ASRS Screener an attractive tool for use in both community-based epidemiological surveys and clinical outreach and case-finding initiatives.

title: The body-mass index of twins who have been reared apart.
text: To assess the relative importance of genetic and environmental factors on body mass index (BMI), we studied identical and fraternal twins who were either raised together or apart. Our sample consisted of 93 pairs of identical twins raised apart, 154 pairs of identical twins raised together, 218 pairs of fraternal twins raised apart, and 208 pairs of fraternal twins raised together. We found that the intra-pair correlation coefficients for BMI among identical twins raised apart were 0.70 for men and 0.66 for women, which provided the most direct estimates of the relative importance of genetic influences (heritability) on BMI. These estimates were slightly lower than those obtained from twins raised together in previous studies. Using maximum-likelihood model-fitting analyses, we estimated heritability to be 0.74 for men and 0.69 for women. Non-additive genetic variance had a significant impact on the estimates of heritability, particularly among men. In contrast, unique environmental factors, such as those that are specific to each individual, contributed approximately 30% of the variance in BMI. Sharing the same childhood environment did not play a significant role in the similarity of BMI among twins later in life. Our findings suggest that genetic influences on BMI are substantial, while the childhood environment has little to no impact. These results corroborate and extend previous studies on twins and adoptees.

title: A study of high cell density cultivation process of recombinant Helicobacter pylori multi-epitope vaccine engineering bacteria.
text:
Objective:
To develop a high cell density cultivation process for recombinant Helicobacter pylori multi-epitope vaccine engineering bacteria BIB.
Methods:
Based on the results of shake flask fermentation, the process was scaled up to a 50 L fermenter to optimize and validate the factors influencing the yield of the target protein, including the fermentation medium, initial seed inoculum size, inducer concentration, induction start time, induction duration, inducer addition strategy, and feeding strategy.
Results:
After 8 hours of incubation in modified TB medium at 37°C, the BIB working seed was inoculated at 5% (v/v) and induced for an additional 11 hours with a final lactose concentration of 5 mmol/L. During the growth phase, glucose was added at a rate of 80 ml/h as the carbon source, and in the induction phase, glycerol was added at a rate of 40 ml/h as the carbon source. Ammonia water was added dropwise to maintain a pH of approximately 7.0, and the revolution speed was adjusted to maintain a dissolved oxygen concentration above 30%. The final output of bacterial biomass was approximately 70 g/L, and the expression amount of the target protein rBIB was around 32%.
Conclusion:
After high cell density cultivation of the recombinant engineering bacteria, the expression and yield of the target protein rBIB significantly increased.

title: Phorbol esters and cytokines regulate the expression of the NEMO-related protein, a molecule involved in a NF-kappa B-independent pathway.
text: The NF-κB signaling pathway plays a pivotal role in immune, inflammatory, and apoptotic responses. Recently, we identified NEMO (NF-κB Essential Modulator) as a crucial component of this pathway. NEMO is a structural and regulatory subunit of the high molecular kinase complex (IKK) responsible for phosphorylating NF-κB inhibitors. Database searches led to the isolation of a cDNA encoding a protein called NRP (NEMO-related protein), which shares significant homology with NEMO. Our findings demonstrate that NRP is present in a distinct high molecular weight complex, devoid of known IKK members. Despite this, we were unable to observe any effect of NRP on NF-κB signaling. However, treatment with phorbol esters led to NRP phosphorylation and a decrease in its half-life, an effect that could be inhibited by K-252a and stauroporin. Additionally, we found that de novo expression of NRP can be induced by interferon and tumor necrosis factor alpha, with a synergistic effect on NRP expression. Moreover, our results indicate that endogenous NRP associates with the Golgi apparatus. Similar to NEMO, we discovered that NRP interacts with two kinases, suggesting that NRP may play a similar role in another signaling pathway.

title: Tailoring Nutritional Advice for Mexicans Based on Prevalence Profiles of Diet-Related Adaptive Gene Polymorphisms
text:
In Mexico, certain genetic adaptations, known as Diet-related Adaptive Gene (DRAG) polymorphisms, have been found to be associated with an increased risk of chronic diseases in specific populations. The country's population is composed of Amerindians (AM), Mestizos, and individuals with varying degrees of AM, European (EUR), and African ancestry. In order to develop effective prevention and treatment strategies, it is essential to consider the genetic makeup of the Mexican population and its cultural food traditions.
To achieve this goal, we aimed to provide a prevalence profile of several DRAG polymorphisms across different regions of Mexico, including the Central West (CW) region. Using geographic heat maps generated through ArcGIS software, we analyzed the distribution of polymorphisms such as MTHFR C677T (rs1801133), ABCA1 Arg230Cys (rs9282541), APOE T388C (rs429358)/C526T (rs7412), and LCT C-13910T (rs4988235) as well as AMY1 copy number variation (CNV). In addition, we obtained new data through allelic discrimination-real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) assays for these polymorphisms and the AMY1 CNV in CW Mexico subpopulations with varying proportions of AM and EUR ancestry.
Our findings showed that the AM groups in the CW region exhibited the highest frequencies of the MTHFR 677T, ABCA1 230C, and APOE ε4 adaptive alleles, followed by Mestizos with intermediate AM ancestry. Meanwhile, the LCT-13910T allele frequency was highest in Mestizos-EUR, while the AMY1 diploid copy number was found to be approximately 6.82 ± 3.3 copies. The heat maps revealed a heterogeneous distribution of the DRAG polymorphisms, where AM groups exhibited the highest frequencies of the adaptive alleles, followed by Mestizos.
In light of these genetic differences, it is crucial to provide genome-based nutritional advice on a regionalized and individualized basis, tailoring it to the traditional food culture and available food sources in each region. This approach may help promote healthier dietary patterns and reduce the risk of chronic diseases in the Mexican population.

title: Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Through Inhibition of the Renin-Angiotensin System
text: The growing prevalence of type 2 diabetes mellitus poses a significant health challenge, associated with elevated morbidity and mortality rates. In light of this alarming trend, preventing the onset of this disease should be accorded paramount importance in the near future. Various pharmacological interventions have demonstrated efficacy in clinical trials, including antidiabetic drugs such as metformin, acarbose, and troglitazone, as well as antiobesity agents like orlistat. It is worth noting that arterial hypertension, a condition characterized by insulin resistance, often precedes the development of type 2 diabetes by several years. While certain antihypertensive medications may exacerbate insulin resistance and impair glucose tolerance, newer agents exhibit neutral or even slightly beneficial metabolic effects. A number of clinical trials have examined the impact of ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor antagonists (ARAs) on insulin sensitivity in hypertensive individuals, with inconsistent results. Specifically, half of the studies conducted with ACE inhibitors in non-diabetic individuals demonstrated a slight but statistically significant increase in insulin sensitivity, while the other half failed to reveal any significant changes. The effects of ARAs on insulin sensitivity are generally neutral. The mechanisms underlying the improvement of glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity through the inhibition of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) are complex and involve several factors, such as enhanced blood flow and microcirculation in skeletal muscles, which facilitates insulin and glucose delivery to insulin-sensitive tissues, as well as improved insulin signalling at the cellular level and increased insulin secretion by β cells. Recent large-scale clinical studies have demonstrated a consistent reduction in the incidence of type 2 diabetes in hypertensive patients treated with either ACE inhibitors or ARAs for 3–6 years, when compared to other antihypertensive medications. These findings are particularly noteworthy, as they suggest that targeting the RAS through the use of these drugs may represent a novel strategy for preventing the development of type 2 diabetes. From a theoretical perspective, these observations highlight the complexity of the pathogenesis, prevention, and treatment of type 2 diabetes, and underscore the need for continued research in this area. From a practical standpoint, the potential to reduce the burden of type 2 diabetes through the use of these therapies is substantial, and warrants further investigation.

title: Randomized dose-finding clinical trial of oncolytic immunotherapeutic vaccinia JX-594 in liver cancer
text: Oncolytic viruses and immunotherapeutics have complementary mechanisms of action that are both self-amplifying in tumors, yet the impact of dose on patient outcome is unclear. JX-594 (Pexa-Vec) is a oncolytic and immunotherapeutic vaccinia virus. To determine the optimal JX-594 dose in patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), we conducted a randomized phase 2 dose-finding trial (n = 30). Radiologists infused low- or high-dose JX-594 into liver tumors on days 1, 15, and 29; infusions resulted in detectable intravascular JX-594 genomes. Equivalent objective intrahepatic modified response evaluation criteria in solid tumors (mRECIST) (15%), Choi (62%) response rates, and intrahepatic disease control (50%) were observed in injected and distant non-injected tumors at both doses. JX-594 replication and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) expression preceded the induction of anticancer immunity. Contrary to tumor response rate and immune endpoints, patient survival duration was significantly related to dose (median survival of 14.1 months compared to 6.7 months on the high and low dose, respectively; hazard ratio 0.39; P = 0.020). JX-594 demonstrated both oncolytic and immunotherapy mechanisms of action, tumor responses, and dose-dependent survival in individuals with HCC.

title: Misread protein creates membrane channels: an essential step in the bactericidal action of aminoglycosides.
text:
Aminoglycosides have pleiotropic effects, including the irreversible uptake and blockade of initiating ribosomes, which were previously unexplained. However, our findings suggest that incorporation of misread proteins into the membrane can account for the membrane damage and bactericidal action. The sequence of events involves the following steps:
1. Initial entry of the antibiotic into the cell
2. Interaction with chain-elongating ribosomes, leading to misreading and incorporation of misread protein into the membrane
3. Creation of abnormal channels in the membrane, allowing for increased (and irreversible) entry of the antibiotic
4. Blockade of initiating ribosomes, which are essential for protein synthesis
Our findings can explain several previously unexplained observations, including:
1. The requirement for protein synthesis during, but not after, the lag phase before membrane damage
2. The ability of streptomycin-resistant cells to take up streptomycin after treatment with another aminoglycoside
3. The acceleration of streptomycin uptake by puromycin at moderate concentrations and the inhibition of streptomycin uptake by high concentrations of puromycin
These findings suggest that normal membrane proteins must be selected not only for a hydrophobic anchoring surface but also for a tight fit in the membrane.

title: Rate of cervical cancer, severe intraepithelial neoplasia, and adenocarcinoma in situ in primary HPV DNA screening with cytology triage: randomised study within organised screening programme.
text:
The objective of this randomized controlled trial was to compare the performance and impact of primary human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA screening with cytology triage versus conventional cytology on cervical cancer and severe pre-cancerous lesions in a population-based screening program in southern Finland.
58,076 women, aged 30-60, were invited to participate in the routine population-based screening program for cervical cancer between 2003 and 2005. The women were randomly assigned to either primary HPV DNA screening with cytology triage (intervention) or conventional cytological screening (reference). The primary outcomes measured were the rates of cervical cancer, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade III, and adenocarcinoma in situ (referred to as CIN III+) during 2003-2007, detected through record linkage between files from the screening registry and the national cancer registry.
The results showed that among the 95,600 woman-years of follow-up in the HPV arm, there were 76 cases of CIN III+ (including six cervical cancers), while in the conventional arm, there were 53 cases of CIN III+ (including eight cervical cancers). The relative rate of CIN III+ in the HPV arm versus the conventional arm was 1.44 (95% confidence interval 1.01 to 2.05) among all women invited for screening and 1.77 (1.16 to 2.74) among those who attended. The relative rate of CIN III+ among women with a normal or negative test result was 0.28 (0.04 to 1.17). The rate of cervical cancer between arms was 0.75 (0.25 to 2.16) among women invited for screening and 1.98 (0.52 to 9.38) among those who attended.
Overall, the study suggests that primary HPV screening with cytology triage is more sensitive than conventional cytology in detecting CIN III+ lesions, and that the findings have importance regarding cancer prevention, despite the small number of cases of cervical cancer observed. The trial was registered with Current Controlled Trials ISRCTN23885553.

title: Metabolic syndrome as a risk factor for diabetes.
text:
The metabolic syndrome was first characterized as a condition of insulin resistance, marked by the clustering of metabolic traits such as high triglycerides, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high blood pressure, abdominal obesity, and varying degrees of impaired glucose regulation. Different definitions have been proposed by various expert groups, but epidemiological studies demonstrate that they all associate the metabolic syndrome with a similar elevated cardiometabolic risk, which is significantly higher for developing diabetes (ranging from 3-20 fold), depending on the number of components present and the inclusion of impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance or both. The latter is thought to indicate a failure of the beta cell to produce enough insulin to compensate for insulin resistance, leading to an altered disposition index and an increased risk of developing Type 2 diabetes.
There has been no clinical trial conducted on individuals diagnosed with the metabolic syndrome, but structured lifestyle changes have been tested in people with impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance, with successful results in reducing the incidence of Type 2 diabetes by almost 50%, provided a weight loss of at least 5% is achieved. Oral antidiabetic and anti-obesity drugs have also shown some success, but to a lesser extent. Fibrates have been found to reduce or delay the onset of diabetes in some cases, while statins have been controversial. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are the antihypertensive medications least associated with an increased risk of developing diabetes.

title: The fallacy of the ecological fallacy: the potential misuse of a concept and the consequences.
text: Ecological studies have been subject to criticism in epidemiological contexts due to the "ecological fallacy." While the empirical evidence suggests that correlations derived from ecological- and individual-level analyses are not comparable, the underlying conceptual issues remain a challenge. This paper proposes a new approach to addressing these issues by conceptualizing them as validity problems, rather than problems unique to ecological-level analyses. This perspective acknowledges the potential inference problems in individual-level studies while also highlighting the unique contributions of ecological variables to our understanding of disease causation and the design of effective interventions. By expanding the terrain for cause identification and intervention, this approach can lead to a more nuanced and effective approach to public health.

title: Blocking caspase-activated apoptosis improves contractility in failing myocardium.
text: The study investigated the role of caspase activation in cardiac contractility and sarcomere organization in the development of congestive heart failure (CHF). In a rabbit model of heart failure, the researchers used in vivo transcoronary adenovirus-mediated gene delivery to deliver a potent caspase inhibitor, p35, to failing myocytes. They found that caspase activation was associated with a reduction in contractile force of failing myocytes, leading to destroyed sarcomeric structure. Conversely, genetic manipulation of hearts to express p35 prevented the rise in caspase 3 activity and DNA-histone formation, leading to a significant improvement in left ventricular pressure rise and decreased end-diastolic chamber pressure. In vitro studies also demonstrated that microinjection of activated caspase 3 into the cytoplasm of intact myocytes induced sarcomeric disorganization and reduced contractility of the cells. These results suggest that caspases have a direct impact on cardiac function and may lead to novel therapeutic strategies via antiapoptotic regimens.

title: Development and validation of QRISK3 risk prediction algorithms to estimate future risk of cardiovascular disease: prospective cohort study
text:
Objective:
Develop and validate updated QRISK3 prediction models to estimate the 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease in both men and women, taking into account potential new risk factors.
Design:
Prospective open cohort study.
Setting:
General practices in England providing data for the QResearch database.

Participants:
1309 QResearch general practices in England: 981 practices were used to develop the scores, and a separate set of 328 practices were used to validate the scores.

7.89 million patients aged 25-84 years were in the derivation cohort, and 2.67 million patients in the validation cohort.


Methods:
Cox proportional hazards models in the derivation cohort to derive separate risk equations for men and women for evaluation at 10 years.
Risk factors considered included those already in QRISK2 (age, ethnicity, deprivation, systolic blood pressure, body mass index, total cholesterol: high density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio, smoking, family history of coronary heart disease in a first-degree relative aged less than 60 years, type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, treated hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease (stage 4 or 5)) and new risk factors (chronic kidney disease (stage 3, 4, or 5), a measure of systolic blood pressure variability (standard deviation of repeated measures), migraine, corticosteroids, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), atypical antipsychotics, severe mental illness, and erectile dysfunction diagnosis or treatment in men).


Measures of calibration and discrimination were determined in the validation cohort for men and women separately and for individual subgroups by age group, ethnicity, and baseline disease status.

Main outcome measures:
Incident cardiovascular disease recorded on any of the following three linked data sources: general practice, mortality, or hospital admission records.

Results:
363,565 incident cases of cardiovascular disease were identified in the derivation cohort during follow-up, arising from 50.8 million person years of observation.


All new risk factors considered met the model inclusion criteria except for HIV/AIDS, which was not statistically significant.
The models had good calibration and high levels of explained variation and discrimination. In women, the algorithm explained 59.6% of the variation in time to diagnosis of cardiovascular disease (R2, with higher values indicating more variation), and the D statistic was 2.48 and Harrell's C statistic was 0.88 (both measures of discrimination, with higher values indicating better discrimination). The corresponding values for men were 54.8%, 2.26, and 0.86.


Overall performance of the updated QRISK3 algorithms was similar to the QRISK2 algorithms.


Conclusion:

Updated QRISK3 risk prediction models were developed and validated, taking into account potential new risk factors. The inclusion of additional clinical variables in QRISK3 (chronic kidney disease, a measure of systolic blood pressure variability (standard deviation of repeated measures), migraine, corticosteroids, SLE, atypical antipsychotics, severe mental illness, and erectile dysfunction) can help enable doctors to identify those at most risk of heart disease and stroke.

title: The importance of engaging policy-makers at the outset to guide research on and introduction of vaccines: the use of policy-maker surveys.
text:
Conducting face-to-face surveys of policy-makers and other influential leaders is a valuable tool for identifying key issues in the introduction of new vaccines at an early stage. These surveys can help:
1. Identify major issues related to the introduction of new vaccines, including potential challenges and obstacles.
2. Identify key decision-makers and influencers in a country's introduction of vaccines, including policy-makers, healthcare professionals, and other stakeholders.
3. Understand the data needs of policy-makers to overcome obstacles to vaccine introduction, including data on disease burden, vaccine effectiveness, and distribution and financing strategies.
4. Inform vaccine-introduction strategies by identifying feasible and financially sustainable means of distributing, targeting, and financing vaccines.
5. Provide insights into the opinions and beliefs of decision-makers on new-generation vaccines against cholera, typhoid fever, and shigellosis, as well as future vaccines against dengue fever/dengue haemorrhagic fever.
The methodology used in conducting these surveys involves face-to-face interviews with policy-makers and other influential leaders, which can help to ensure that research activities respond to the needs of policy-makers in countries endemic for the target diseases.
The surveys also provide valuable lessons on methodological issues, including the importance of using local language and culture-specific materials to increase response rates and the need for careful sampling and data analysis techniques to ensure the accuracy of survey findings.
Overall, conducting face-to-face surveys of policy-makers and other influential leaders can help to identify key issues and inform vaccine-introduction strategies, ultimately leading to improved vaccine uptake and disease control.

title: Histone acetyltransferase PCAF regulates inflammatory molecules in the development of renal injury.
text: Kidney diseases, including chronic kidney disease (CKD) and acute kidney injury (AKI), are associated with systemic inflammation. The mechanisms that modulate inflammation in these renal injuries remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the role of p300/CBP-associated factor (PCAF), a histone acetyltransferase, in the regulation of inflammatory genes in kidney disease. Our results demonstrate that PCAF is overexpressed in the kidneys of db/db mice and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-injected mice. Concomitantly, there is an increase in global histone acetylation, including H3K18ac, and the upregulation of pro-inflammatory genes, such as intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), in these renal injuries. Furthermore, we observed that increased H3K18ac is recruited to the promoters of ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and MCP-1 in the kidneys of LPS-injected mice. In vitro studies showed that PCAF knockdown in human renal proximal tubule epithelial cells (HK-2) leads to decreased expression of inflammatory molecules, including VCAM-1, ICAM-1, p50 subunit of nuclear factor kappa B (p50), and MCP-1 at the mRNA and protein levels, alongside a reduction in H3K18ac levels. Consistently, overexpression of PCAF elevates the expression of these inflammatory molecules. Notably, PCAF deficiency also inhibits palmitate-induced recruitment of H3K18ac to the promoters of ICAM-1 and MCP-1, as well as decreases the upregulation of these inflammatory molecules by palmitate. Overall, our findings demonstrate that PCAF plays a critical role in regulating inflammatory genes through H3K18ac, providing a potential therapeutic target for inflammation-related renal diseases.

title: T1 mapping for myocardial extracellular volume measurement by CMR: bolus only versus primed infusion technique.
text:
The aim of this study was to evaluate the accuracy of the "bolus only" T1 mapping cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) technique for measuring myocardial extracellular volume fraction (ECV). Previous studies have shown that ECV can be measured with T1 mapping before and after contrast agent infusion, but it was unknown if the bolus only approach could provide accurate measurements.
Background: Myocardial ECV can be measured with T1 mapping, but the contrast agent distribution between blood and myocardium must be in equilibrium. One way to achieve equilibrium is through a primed contrast infusion (EQ-CMR), but this approach may not always be feasible. The bolus only approach, which measures ECV immediately after contrast administration, has potential as an alternative. However, there is limited data to support its use.
Methods: One hundred forty-seven subjects (50 healthy volunteers, 25 hypertrophic cardiomyopathy patients, 22 severe aortic stenosis patients, 20 amyloid patients, and 30 chronic myocardial infarction patients) underwent both bolus only and infusion ECV measurements. In 18 subjects with severe AS, the results were compared with histological CVF.
Results: The ECV measurements by both techniques showed a strong correlation with histological CVF (r² = 0.69, p < 0.01 and r² = 0.71, p < 0.01). Across healthy and diseased states, there was a strong correlation between the techniques (r² = 0.97). However, when ECV was above 0.4, the bolus only technique consistently measured higher ECV values (mean difference ± limit of agreement for ECV <0.4 = -0.004 ± 0.037 and ECV >0.4 = 0.040 ± 0.075, p < 0.001).
Conclusion: The bolus only, T1 mapping-derived ECV measurement is sufficient for ECV measurement across a range of cardiac diseases, and this approach is histologically validated in aortic stenosis. However, when ECV is above 0.4, the bolus only technique consistently measures higher ECV values compared to the infusion technique. This study demonstrates the potential of the bolus only approach as an alternative method for ECV measurement in cardiac magnetic resonance imaging.

title: Cytomegalovirus US2 destroys two components of the MHC class II pathway, preventing recognition by CD4+ T cells
text: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous herpesvirus that can cause severe disease in immunocompromised individuals undergoing bone marrow or tissue transplantation, or those with Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS). HCMV establishes lifelong, latent infections and, upon periodic reactivation, exploits a diverse panel of immune evasion proteins to evade the host's immune system. Key host cells for HCMV include monocytes/macrophages, which serve as both a latent reservoir and a means of dissemination throughout the body. In addition to endothelial and glial cells, these cells can also express Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class II proteins and present antigens to CD4+ T lymphocytes. Surprisingly, we found that the HCMV protein US2 targets two critical proteins in the MHC class II antigen presentation pathway: HLA-DR-α and DM-α. Our results contrast with prior findings showing US2's ability to degrade Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class I proteins, which share only limited homology with class II proteins. By reducing or abolishing antigen presentation, US2 may enable HCMV-infected macrophages to remain relatively undetected by CD4+ T cells, a property that would be advantageous following virus reactivation.

title: CD169-positive macrophages dominate antitumor immunity by crosspresenting dead cell-associated antigens.
text: The activation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) targeting tumors is vital for eliciting an immune response against cancer. To activate these CTLs, antigen-presenting cells (APCs) must first acquire tumor-associated antigens from dead tumor cells. However, little is known about how APCs in draining lymph nodes acquire and present these antigens. Our study shows that macrophages, specifically CD169(+) macrophages, phagocytose dead tumor cells via lymphatic flow and crosspresent tumor antigens to CD8(+) T cells. Subcutaneous immunization with irradiated tumor cells protects mice from syngenic tumors. However, the activation and subsequent immunity of tumor-antigen-specific CD8(+) T cells are severely impaired in mice depleted of CD169(+) macrophages. Unlike migratory dendritic cells (DCs) and lymph node-resident conventional DCs, CD169(+) macrophages are not essential for crosspresenting tumor antigens to CD8(+) T cells. Therefore, we have identified CD169(+) macrophages as the dominant lymph node-resident APCs involved in activating early tumor antigen-specific CD8(+) T cells.

title: Emerging mechanisms in morphogen-mediated axon guidance.
text: In the early stages of animal development, specialized molecules called morphogens, such as Sonic hedgehog (Shh), Wnt, and TGFbeta/Bmp, create gradients that control cell growth and dictate the ultimate fate and characteristics of target cells. These morphogens activate established signaling pathways that regulate gene expression, playing a crucial and evolutionarily conserved role in the assembly of neural circuits. Shh, Wnt, and TGFbeta/Bmp signaling are essential for neural polarization, axon and dendrite development, and synaptogenesis, a series of processes that require rapid and local changes in cytoskeletal organization and plasma membrane components. The question remains as to whether mechanisms used by morphogens to influence growth cones are similar to those employed in their role in cell specification. This review aims to provide insight into this question by highlighting recent advances that demonstrate how Shh, Wnt, and TGFbeta/Bmp have adapted their "classical" signaling pathways or adopted new molecular mechanisms to regulate different aspects of neuronal circuit formation.

title: Lessons learnt from malaria epidemics in the Islamic Republic of Iran.
text: The Islamic Republic of Iran is in the early stages of malaria control, but malaria outbreaks still pose a significant threat in the southern regions of the country. This study examines the epidemiological characteristics and underlying factors of 60 malaria outbreaks that occurred in Sistan va Baluchestan province between 2005 and 2009. Using a zero-truncated negative binomial model, the researchers investigated the relationship between various predictor variables and the total number of malaria cases. The outbreaks were primarily concentrated in the southern part of the province, with the majority occurring between July and October, peaking in August. The majority of the outbreaks were small in scale (68.3% had fewer than 100 cases) and short-lived (51.7% lasted less than a month). Plasmodium falciparum was found in 46.7% of the outbreaks. The study identified increased rainfall rates and population movements as the most significant predictive factors. These findings may aid in the development of an epidemic investigation and reporting system as Iran transitions into the malaria elimination phase.

title: Autoradiography of chromosomal DNA fibers from Chinese hamster cells.
text: Historical challenges in determining the length of DNA molecules in chromosomes of higher organisms have hindered our comprehension of chromosome structure. Despite efforts to estimate DNA lengths through electron microscopy, the true extent of DNA in higher organisms has remained elusive. Solari (1) has recorded the longest DNA measured to date - a 93 μm-long DNA fiber from a sea urchin sperm.

title: Epigenetic memory and preferential lineage-specific differentiation in induced pluripotent stem cells derived from human pancreatic islet beta cells.
text: Human-induced pluripotent stem cells (HiPSCs) appear to be very similar to human embryonic stem cells (HESCs). By using two genetic lineage-tracing systems, we demonstrated the ability to generate iPSC lines from human pancreatic islet beta cells. These reprogrammed cells acquired markers of pluripotency and differentiated into the three embryonic germ layers. Notably, beta cell-derived iPSCs (BiPSCs) maintained open chromatin structure at specific beta-cell genes, along with a unique DNA methylation signature that distinguishes them from other PSCs. BiPSCs also showed an increased capacity to differentiate into insulin-producing cells in both in vitro and in vivo settings, compared to ESCs and non-beta iPSCs. Our findings suggest that the epigenetic memory of the beta cell of origin may predetermine BiPSCs to differentiate more readily into insulin-producing cells. These results indicate that the phenotype of HiPSCs may be influenced by their cells of origin and that their skewed differentiation potential may be an advantageous trait for cell replacement therapy.

title: CCL2/monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 mediates enhanced transmigration of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infected leukocytes across the blood-brain barrier: a potential mechanism of HIV-CNS invasion and NeuroAIDS.
text:
HIV infection of leukocytes leads to altered transmigration and BBB permeability
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is associated with encephalitis and dementia, which are characterized by leukocyte infiltration into the central nervous system (CNS), microglia activation, abnormal chemokine expression, breakdown of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and eventual neuronal loss. While it is known that HIV infection can affect the ability of leukocytes to migrate into the CNS, little is understood about the impact of HIV infection on leukocyte transmigration in response to chemokines and BBB integrity. Our study aims to address this knowledge gap by investigating the effect of HIV infection on leukocyte transmigration across a tissue culture model of the human BBB in response to the chemokine CCL2.
Our findings demonstrate that HIV infection of human leukocytes leads to increased transmigration across the BBB in response to CCL2, as well as disruption of the BBB, with evidence of enhanced permeability, reduced tight junction proteins, and expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMP)-2 and MMP-9. In contrast, HIV-infected cells did not migrate in the absence of CCL2, and this condition did not affect BBB integrity. The chemokines CXCL10/interferon-gamma-inducible protein of 10 kDa, CCL3/macrophage inflammatory protein-1alpha, or CCL5/RANTES did not enhance HIV-infected leukocyte transmigration or BBB permeability. Instead, the increased capacity of HIV-infected leukocytes to transmigrate in response to CCL2 was found to be associated with their increased expression of CCR2, the chemokine receptor for CCL2. These results suggest that CCL2 plays a key role in the infiltration of HIV-infected leukocytes into the CNS and the subsequent pathology characteristic of NeuroAIDS.

title: Prostaglandin E2 as an inhibitory modulator of fibrogenesis in human lung allografts.
text:
The article investigates the role of prostaglandin (PG)E2 in modulating the fibrotic differentiation of human lung allograft-derived mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs) in bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS). The study aims to uncover the regulators of fibrotic differentiation of resident mesenchymal cells in the lung and understand the mechanisms underlying the development of BOS.
The study examines the effects of PGE2 on the proliferation, collagen secretion, and α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) expression of lung-resident MSCs (LR-MSCs) derived from patients with and without BOS. The researchers employ pharmacologic and small-interfering RNA approaches to identify the downstream signaling pathway involved in the suppressive effects of PGE2 on LR-MSCs.
The results indicate that PGE2 treatment of LR-MSCs inhibits their proliferation, collagen secretion, and α-SMA expression. The study shows that the PGE2/E prostanoid (EP)2/adenylate cyclase pathway is involved in these suppressive effects. The researchers find that endogenous PGE2 secretion is upregulated by interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), which ameliorates myofibroblast differentiation of LR-MSCs in vitro. Conversely, inhibition of PGE2 by indomethacin augments α-SMA expression. The study reveals that BOS LR-MSCs secrete significantly less PGE2 than non-BOS LR-MSCs and are defective in their ability to induce cyclooxygenase-2, which impairs their capacity to up-regulate PGE2 synthesis in response to IL-1β. Moreover, BOS LR-MSCs demonstrate resistance to the inhibitory actions of PGE2, accompanied by a reduction in the EP2/EP1 ratio.
The study concludes that the PGE2 axis plays an important role in braking fibrotic differentiation of LR-MSCs, and this failure is associated with BOS. The findings suggest that targeting the PGE2/EP2 axis may provide a therapeutic strategy for preventing or treating BOS in lung transplant patients.

title: Association of DNA polymerase mu (pol mu) with Ku and ligase IV: role for pol mu in end-joining double-strand break repair.
text: Mammalian DNA polymerase mu (Pol mu) shares similarities with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase, but its functional significance in cells remains unclear. Our findings reveal that upon exposure to ionizing radiation (IR), Pol mu protein levels increase. Concomitantly, Pol mu forms discrete nuclear foci, which largely converge with IR-induced foci of gammaH2AX, a previously characterized marker of sites of DNA double-strand breaks. This suggests that Pol mu plays a part in the cellular response to DNA double-strand breaks. Moreover, Pol mu interacts with the nonhomologous end-joining repair factor Ku in cell extracts and requires both Ku and another end-joining factor, XRCC4-ligase IV, to form a stable complex on DNA in vitro. Pol mu then facilitates the stable recruitment of XRCC4-ligase IV to Ku-bound DNA and ligase IV-dependent end joining, differing from the related mammalian DNA polymerase beta, which showsreduced ability to form a complex with Ku and XRCC4-ligase IV and is less efficient in facilitating joining mediated by these factors. Our data support a crucial role for Pol mu in the end-joining pathway for repair of double-strand breaks.

title: Stromal-epithelial metabolic coupling in cancer: integrating autophagy and metabolism in the tumor microenvironment.
text: Cancer cells do not exist as uniform populations in vivo, but are embedded in "cancer cell nests" surrounded by stromal cells, including cancer-associated fibroblasts. It is plausible that stromal fibroblasts influence the metabolism of nearby cancer cells, and vice versa. We propose that the Warburg effect in cancer cells may result from their isolation from their normal stromal context or tumor microenvironment. In fact, when cancer cells are co-cultured with fibroblasts, cancer cells increase their mitochondrial mass, while fibroblasts lose their mitochondria. A deeper analysis reveals that aggressive cancer cells are "parasites" that employ oxidative stress as a "weapon" to extract nutrients from surrounding stromal cells. Oxidative stress in fibroblasts triggers autophagic mitophagy, leading to the breakdown of mitochondria and the production of energy-rich nutrients such as lactate and ketones. These nutrients are then available to feed cancer cells. This mechanism would allow cancer cells to survive and proliferate during metastasis without relying on blood vessels for nutrient supply. We term this new paradigm "The Autophagic Tumor Stroma Model of Cancer Metabolism", or the "Reverse Warburg Effect". Additionally, glutaminolysis in cancer cells, which promotes mitochondrial metabolism, aligns with this model.

title: Oxidative stress in renal dysfunction: mechanisms, clinical sequelae and therapeutic options
text: Oxidative stress has been linked to the escalating incidence of cardiovascular events in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly as traditional cardiovascular risk factors are unable to account for the significant cardiovascular morbidity and mortality observed in this population group. Oxidative stress is characterized by elevated oxidant activity and reduced antioxidant capacity in patients with renal impairment, and this increases proportionately with the severity of renal dysfunction. Inflammation, which is also prevalent in CKD, further exacerbates the oxidant generation process. The two primary consequences of oxidative stress are endothelial dysfunction and left ventricular hypertrophy, which have detrimental cardiovascular implications. With our enhanced understanding of oxidative stress, it is now crucial to identify effective interventions that mitigate it in order to reverse endothelial dysfunction and left ventricular hypertrophy, thereby abating the clinical sequelae of these abnormalities.

title: Effect of age, sex, and sites on the cellularity of the adipose tissue in mice and rats rendered obese by a high-fat diet.
text:
In a study conducted on Swiss mice, the size and number of parietal fat pads were determined during gestation, lactation, and post-weaning stages. The mice were fed a high-fat diet (40% lard w/w) ad libitum, and their offspring received the same diet throughout their life. Two groups of mothers were studied: one group was fed a high-fat diet during gestation and lactation, while the other group was fed a control diet.
When the mice were 2 weeks old, those suckled by obese mothers had fatter parametrial pads compared to the control group. This difference was attributed solely to an increase in fat cell size. After weaning, the obese mice displayed a continuous increase in fat cell number until the 18th week of age, while the control group did not show any change in cell number. Similarly, when a high-fat diet was introduced to adult rats, they also exhibited an increase in fat cell number.
The study compared three sites of fat pads (perirenal, epididymal, and subcutaneous) in both sexes at 32 weeks of age. The high-fat-fed group showed an increase in weight in all three sites, which was attributed to hyperplasia in the perirenal site, hypertrophy in the epididymal and subcutaneous sites, and hyperplasia plus hypertrophy in the parametrial site. It was observed that in each sex, the adipose tissue sites in the obese mice responded differently to the diet, suggesting that the level of fat in the diet plays a crucial role in both the formation and maturation of new fat cells and in the regulation of fat cell lipid content. The study concluded that these processes may act together or separately according to the adipose tissue site.

title: Transcriptional integration of mitochondrial biogenesis.
text: Gene regulatory factors encoded in the nucleus are crucial for mitochondrial function and biogenesis. Some of these factors work exclusively within the mitochondria to regulate transcription, translation, and other functions. Others govern the expression of genes in the nucleus necessary for mitochondrial metabolism and organelle biogenesis. The PGC-1 family of transcriptional coactivators plays a pivotal role in transmitting and integrating physiological signals that regulate metabolism, differentiation, and cell growth to the transcriptional machinery responsible for controlling mitochondrial function. As a result, the PGC-1 coactivators act as a central component of the transcriptional regulatory circuitry that coordinates the energy-producing functions of mitochondria in response to metabolic demands, aging, and disease.

title: RFID system evaluation against radiated transient noise
text: In this study, the impact of transient noise on a radiofrequency identification (RFID) system according to the ISO/IEC 14443 type-B standard is investigated in real-time communication systems operating at 13.56 MHz. The study examines the effects of transient bursts on the digital communication system in a controlled environment by varying the level, frequency, and duration of the interference. Two methods are used to evaluate the impact of transient noise: direct observation of RFID equipment in the presence of transient signals, and capturing and analyzing the interference in the time domain using simulation. The RFID system is found to be susceptible to various types of errors due to transient noise. It is essential to measure and evaluate the transient phenomena in the time domain to ensure that the RFID system does not have potential susceptibility problems.

title: Musculoskeletal pain in Europe: its impact and a comparison of population and medical perceptions of treatment in eight European countries.
text:
Objectives:
* To assess the impact of musculoskeletal pain (MP) on the population.
* To compare the management of MP between primary care physicians and the general population.
* To identify misconceptions about treatment options for MP.

Methods:

* A total of 5803 people with MP and 1483 primary care physicians in eight European countries were interviewed by telephone using a structured questionnaire.
* The questionnaire assessed usual management of MP, perceived benefits and risks of treatment, and current health status (SF-12).

Results:

* Primary care physicians perceive MP to be well managed, with the majority offering some form of treatment to presenting patients.
* However, from a population perspective, up to 27% of people with pain do not seek medical help, and of those who do, several wait months/years before seeing a doctor.
* Only 55% or fewer patients who have seen a doctor are currently receiving prescription treatment for their pain.
* Communication between doctors and patients is poor, with few patients receiving information about their condition, and many having misconceptions about treatment options.

Conclusions:

* Management of MP is similar across eight European countries, but there is discordance between physician and patient perspectives of care.
* Some people with pain have never sought medical help despite being in constant/daily pain.
* Those who do seek help receive little written information or explanation, and many have misperceptions about the benefits and risks of treatment that limit their ability to actively participate in decisions about their care.

title: [Palliative care in Germany].
text: In Germany, the delivery of palliative care remains inadequate for both inpatients and outpatients. However, over the past 15 years, progress has been made in the country, drawing increased attention to the plight of the terminally ill and their families. As a result, specialized palliative care structures have been established. While the situation for inpatients in hospitals and hospices is pleasing, albeit not yet satisfactory, there is a more pressing need for outpatient care. Currently, financial resources for palliative care are inadequate, and more need to be made available to meet the growing demand. It is crucial to recognize the needs of the terminally ill, their families, and friends, and prioritize this issue on the healthcare agenda. While recent developments in the federal government and states are promising, there is still hope for improvement in the coming years.

title: A view to a kill: the bacterial type VI secretion system.
text: The bacterial type VI secretion system (T6SS) is structurously and mechanistically analogous to an intracellular membrane-attached contractile phage tail. Recent investigations reveal that a rapid conformational transformation in the structure of a sheath protein complex propels T6SS spike and tube components, as well as antibacterial and antieukaryotic effectors, out of predatory T6SS-bearing cells and into prey cells. The contracted organelle is then recycled through an ATP-dependent process. T6SS is regulated at both transcriptional and posttranslational levels, with the latter involving the detection of membrane perturbation in some species. Additionally, T6SS can target not only eukaryotic cells but also other bacteria coinfecting a mammalian host, underscoring its importance in both environmental ecosystems and the context of infection and disease. This review highlights recent advances in our understanding of the structure, mechanical function, assembly, and regulation of the T6SS.

title: Open Access Increases Citation Rate
text:
PLoS Biology publishes a research article by Gunther Eysenbach that provides robust evidence that open-access (OA) articles are more immediately recognized and cited than non-OA articles. The study compared citations of OA and non-OA articles published in the same journal, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), and found that OA articles gained a significant citation advantage during the 4-16 months following publication. Specifically, OA articles were twice as likely to be cited 4-10 months after publication and almost three times as likely between 10-16 months compared to non-OA articles. The study also looked at the impact of self-archiving non-OA articles and found that self-archived articles were also cited less often than OA articles from the same journal.
The study has several implications. First, it provides objective support to the belief that open-access publication speeds up scientific dialogue between researchers. Second, it highlights the challenges to the long-term future of open access, such as varying attitudes of authors at different stages of their career, access to appropriate funds, and the potential for hybrid journals to dilute the open-access advantage. Despite these challenges, the study's findings should embolden open-access advocates, as they provide tangible evidence for what has seemed obvious all along.

title: Serum immunoglobulin A from patients with celiac disease inhibits human T84 intestinal crypt epithelial cell differentiation.
text:
INTRODUCTION & OBJECTIVES Celiac disease is characterized by dysfunction in the crypt-villus axis of the small intestine, involving immunoglobulin (Ig) A deposits underneath the epithelium. The goal of this study was to investigate whether celiac disease-specific serum IgA (reactive for reticulin/endomysial autoantigens) disrupts the communication between mesenchymal cells and epithelial cells.
METHODS We induced differentiation of T84 epithelial cells in three-dimensional collagen gel cultures with either IMR-90 fibroblasts or transforming growth factor beta. We then assessed the effects of purified celiac IgA and monoclonal tissue transglutaminase antibodies (CUB7402) on these cocultures.
RESULTS Our findings showed that active celiac disease IgA, which reacts with tissue transglutaminase, significantly inhibited T84 epithelial cell differentiation (P < 0.001) and increased epithelial cell proliferation (P = 0.024). Similar effects were observed with antibodies against tissue transglutaminase.
CONCLUSIONS Our primary finding indicates that celiac disease-specific autoantibodies disrupt transforming growth factor beta-mediated fibroblast-epithelial cell communication in this in vitro crypt-villus axis model. These results suggest that celiac disease-specific autoantibodies may also contribute to the formation of the gluten-dependent jejunal mucosal lesion in celiac disease.

title: Pathogenesis of diseases associated with antineutrophil cytoplasm autoantibodies.
text:
Steering towards an understanding of the underlying mechanisms of diseases associated with circulating antineutrophil cytoplasm autoantibodies (ANCA), such as primary vasculitides and inflammatory bowel diseases, remains an area of interest. In the present review, we delve into the mechanisms that give rise to the development of ANCA, including the potential role of microbial superantigens and the potential flaws in the process of apoptosis or the removal of apoptotic cells.
Subsequently, we focus our attention on the contribution of ANCA to the manifestation of clinical symptoms and the pathogenic function of ANCA itself, including the accessibility of ANCA antigens as targets for circulating antibodies and the mode of action of ANCA. We also explore mechanisms of neutrophil activation by ANCA, such as the engagement of Fcgamma receptors, the possible mechanisms of neutrophil-mediated tissue damage, and the neutrophil-endothelial interaction.

title: The common marmoset as a novel animal model system for biomedical and neuroscience research applications.
text: The common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), a miniature primate of the New World, has gained significant attention in the fields of biomedical science and neuroscience due to its (i) ability to cross-react with human cytokines or hormones, (ii) ease of handling due to its diminutive size, (iii) exceptional reproductive prowess, (iv) establishment of basic research tools, and (v) unique behavioral and cognitive characteristics. Researchers have developed various neurological disease models, such as Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, stroke, multiple sclerosis, and spinal cord injury, using the common marmoset. We recently created transgenic common marmosets with germline transmission, which will serve as a novel animal model for studying human diseases. In this review, we recapitulate the recent progress of biomedical research and neuroscience using the common marmoset as an exceptional model system.

title: Liver receptor homolog-1 regulates the transcription of steroidogenic enzymes and induces the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into steroidogenic cells.
text: Studies have shown that Steroidogenic Factor-1 (SF-1, also known as Ad4BP) plays a primary role in regulating genes related to steroid production. However, research has revealed that the mRNA for Liver Receptor Homolog-1 (LRH-1), a member of the NR5A nuclear receptor family, is expressed at significantly higher levels in human gonads compared to SF-1 mRNA. Our previous work demonstrated that SF-1 can induce the differentiation of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) into steroidogenic cells, such as Leydig or adrenocortical cells. Introducing LRH-1 into human MSCs (hMSCs) using cAMP also led to the expression of steroidogenic enzymes, including CYP17, and the differentiation of these cells into steroid hormone-producing cells. Promoter analysis, EMSA, and chromatin immunoprecipitation assay using LRH-1-transduced hMSCs revealed that three LRH-1 binding sites are responsible for the transactivation of the CYP17 promoter. Immunohistochemical studies also showed that LRH-1 protein is expressed in human Leydig cells. Moreover, the CYP17 promoter region was found to be highly methylated in hMSCs, but demethylation was observed after the introduction of LRH-1 and cAMP treatment. These findings suggest that LRH-1 may play a crucial role in regulating the steroidogenic lineage in MSCs and contribute significantly to steroid hormone production in human Leydig cells.

title: Checkpoint responses to replication fork barriers.
text: Maintaining the fidelity of DNA replication is crucial for preserving genome integrity. When an active replication fork is disrupted, various cellular pathways are activated to stabilize the replication apparatus and resolve the issue. However, if the problem is not resolved, the fork may collapse, exposing free DNA ends to potential misprocessing. In prokaryotes, replication fork collapse can trigger the activity of recombination proteins to restore the fork. Recent research has shown that recombination is closely linked to replication in eukaryotic cells, and that recombination proteins are recruited to stalled, but not collapsed, replication forks. This review focuses on the different types of potential replication fork barriers (RFBs) that can arise during DNA replication, and how these unique RFBs can result in distinct DNA structures at stalled replication forks. The DNA structure checkpoints that operate during S phase respond to different RFBs in distinct ways, and we therefore discuss the processes controlled by the DNA replication checkpoints, with a particular emphasis on the function of the intra-S phase checkpoint, which stabilizes stalled forks.

title: Ecology, economics and political will: the vicissitudes of malaria strategies in Asia.
text: The documented history of malaria in parts of Asia stretches back over 2,000 years, during which the disease has played a significant role in the socioeconomic landscape of many nation-states, waxing and waning in power and prosperity. On a smaller time scale, the last half century has witnessed a microcosm of history, with large fluctuations in endemicity and impact of malaria across the diverse ecosystems of rice fields, rainforests, mountains, and plains. This period has been marked by dramatic changes in social and economic structure, population size, density, and mobility, and political structures, all of which have influenced the evolving face of malaria in this vast region of the world. Although the majority of global malaria cases currently reside in Africa, Asia was once home to a larger number of cases before successful malaria control programs were implemented, and now harbors a global threat in the form of the epicenter of multidrug-resistant Plasmodium falciparum, which is gradually spreading across the tropical world. The latter reflects the economic changes of recent decades, particularly the mobility of populations in search of commerce, trade, and personal fortunes, or caught in the turmoil of physical conflicts. The period from the 1950s to the 1990s saw near "eradication" of malaria followed by resurgence in Sri Lanka, control and resurgence in India, the impact of war and post-war instability on drug resistance in Cambodia, an increase in severe and cerebral malaria in Myanmar during prolonged political turmoil, and the essential disappearance of the disease from most of Thailand, except for forested border areas where it remains momentarily intractable. Both positive and negative experiences offer lessons in the debate between eradication and control as alternative strategies. China has long aimed for "basic elimination," or eradication by another name, despite WHO dictates, and has shown that, with community organization, extensive attention to case detection, management, and focus elimination, plus the political will at all levels of society, it is possible to eliminate malaria from large areas of a vast nation and maintain near-eradication status in those areas. However, China has not succeeded in the international border regions of the tropical south where unfettered population movement complicates the program. Thailand, Malaysia, and to some extent Vietnam have also reached essential elimination in their rice field plains through vigorous vertical programs, but fall short at their forested borders. Economics is central to the history of the rise and fall of nations, and to the history of disease in the people who constitute nations. The current fascination with free-market economics as the primary driver of national wealth places limitations on the involvement of communities in malaria management, and the task of malaria control or elimination needs to be clearly linked to the basic macroeconomic process that preoccupies governments. Historically, malaria has had a severe and measurable negative impact on the productivity of nations. Economic models need to be revised with political eloquence and integrated with technical and demographic strategies. Recent decades in Chinese malaria history offer some relevant lessons for this context.

title: Global and regional risk of disabling sequelae from bacterial meningitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: In this study, we aimed to estimate the global and regional risks of severe and minor sequelae resulting from bacterial meningitis. We conducted a systematic review of published papers from 1980 to 2008 and identified 132 studies that met our inclusion criteria. Our findings revealed that the median risk of experiencing at least one major or minor sequela after hospital discharge was 19.9% (range: 12.3-35.3%). The risk of experiencing at least one major sequela was 12.8% (range: 7.2-21.1%), while the risk of experiencing at least one minor sequela was 8.6% (range: 4.4-15.3%). The median risk of experiencing at least one major sequela varied by region and income, with the highest risks observed in the African and southeast Asian regions. Specifically, the all-cause risk of a major sequela was twice as high in the African region (pooled risk estimate: 25.1% [95% CI: 18.9-32.0%]) and the southeast Asian region (21.6% [95% CI: 13.1-31.5%]) compared to the European region (9.4% [95% CI: 7.0-12.3%]; overall I(2)=89.5%, p<0.0001). We also found that the risks of long-term disabling sequelae were highest in low-income countries, where the burden of bacterial meningitis is greatest. Notably, most reported sequelae could have been averted by vaccination with Hib, pneumococcal, and meningococcal vaccines.

title: Efficacy of human papillomavirus testing for the detection of invasive cervical cancers and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia: a randomised controlled trial.
text:
Background: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) testing is more sensitive but less specific than cervical cytology for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of cervical cancer screening policies based on HPV testing.
Methods: Between March 2004 and December 2004, women aged 25-60 years were randomly assigned to either conventional cytology or HPV testing in combination with liquid-based cytology (first phase) or alone (second phase). Women aged 35-60 years who were HPV-positive in the first phase were referred for colposcopy, while those aged 25-34 years were referred only if cytology was also abnormal or HPV testing was persistently positive. In the second phase, women in the HPV group were referred for colposcopy if the HPV test was positive. Two rounds of screening occurred in each phase, and all women had cytology testing only at the second round. The primary endpoint was the detection of grade 2 and 3 CIN, and invasive cervical cancers during the first and second screening rounds.
Findings: In total, 47,001 women were randomly assigned to the cytology group and 47,369 to HPV testing. Among the 33,851 women from the cytology group and 32,998 from the HPV-testing group who had a second round of screening, no invasive cancers were detected in the HPV group during round two, compared with nine in the cytology group (p=0.004). Overall, 18 invasive cancers were detected in the cytology group versus seven in the HPV group (p=0.028) in the two rounds of screening. Among women aged 35-60 years, the relative detection (HPV vs cytology) was 2.00 (95% CI 1.44-2.77) for CIN2, 2.08 (1.47-2.95) for CIN3, and 2.03 (1.60-2.57) for CIN2 and 3 together at round one. At round two, the relative detection was 0.54 (0.23-1.28) for CIN2, 0.48 (0.21-1.11) for CIN3, and 0.51 (0.28-0.93) for CIN2 and 3 together. Among women aged 25-34 years, there was significant heterogeneity between phases in the relative detection of CIN3. Pooling both phases, the detection ratio of CIN2 for women aged 25-34 years was 4.09 (2.24-7.48) at round one and 0.64 (0.23-1.27) at round two.
Interpretation: HPV-based screening is more effective than cytology in preventing invasive cervical cancer, by detecting persistent high-grade lesions earlier and providing a longer low-risk period. However, in younger women, HPV screening leads to over-diagnosis of regressive CIN2. Funding: European Union, Italian Ministry of Health, Regional Health Administrations of Piemonte, Tuscany, Veneto and Emilia-Romagna, and Public Health Agency of Lazio.

title: Microcytosis, iron deficiency and thalassaemia in a multi-ethnic community: a pilot study.
text: The high frequency of microcytosis (defined as mean cell hemoglobin <27 pg) among individuals with no other abnormalities often creates confusion in the screening process for hemoglobin disorders. To address this issue, we conducted a small pilot study to evaluate whether routinely proceeding to plasma ferritin and HPLC assays using the original sequestrene blood sample can help resolve confusion. The study included 1,302 individuals referred to a North London district general hospital by their General Practitioner (GP) for a full blood count. Ethnicity was determined through a questionnaire. In North European individuals, microcytosis occurred in 3% of males (half of whom were iron-deficient) and 11% of females (most of whom were iron-deficient). In contrast, among ethnic minorities, microcytosis was present in 35% of males (one-tenth of whom were iron-deficient) and 45% of females (less than half of whom were iron-deficient). As a result, an exclusion diagnosis of "probable alpha thalassaemia" could be made in the remaining individuals. We conclude that when microcytosis is present, using the original sequestrene sample for routine plasma ferritin assay and hemoglobinopathy screening can lead to a more efficient and cost-effective laboratory service for primary care and maternity services.

title: Crystal structure of the human AAA+ protein RuvBL1.
text: RuvBL1 is a highly conserved eukaryotic protein from the AAA(+)-family of ATPases, involved in various cellular processes such as signaling pathways, chromatin remodeling, transcriptional regulation, and DNA repair. In this study, we present the three-dimensional structure of the selenomethionine variant of human RuvBL1, refined to 2.2 angstrom resolution using diffraction data. The crystal structure reveals a hexamer formed by ADP-bound RuvBL1 monomers. Each monomer contains three domains: the first and third domains are involved in ATP binding and hydrolysis, while the second domain, which is unique among AAA(+) proteins and not present in the bacterial homolog RuvB, is a novel DNA/RNA-binding domain. Surprisingly, although ATPase activity is essential for RuvBL1's functions in vivo, we could only detect a marginal activity with the purified protein. Structural homology and DNA binding studies suggest that the second domain is responsible for RuvBL1's interaction with single-stranded DNA/RNA and double-stranded DNA. The structure of the RuvBL1.ADP complex, combined with our biochemical results, reveals that RuvBL1 requires one or more as yet undetermined cofactors for its enzymatic activity, although it has all the structural characteristics of a molecular motor, including the ability to act as an ATP-driven helicase.

title: Characteristics of a monoclonal antibody (RM124) against acute myelocytic leukemia cells.
text: A monoclonal antibody was produced against cells from an experimental rat model of myelocytic leukemia (BNML). The characteristics of this rat model are similar to those of human acute myelocytic leukemia. The monoclonal antibody (MCA) RM124 was examined for its labeling pattern on BNML leukemia cells, normal rat bone marrow cells, and hemopoietic stem cells (HSC) using flow cytometry and complement-dependent cytotoxicity assays. Flow cytometry revealed that MCA-RM124 labeled BNML leukemia cells at a much higher rate compared to normal bone marrow cells, including CFU-S and CFU-C. However, only a subpopulation of normal granulocytes showed cross-reactivity, with a lower labeling density. Complement-dependent cytotoxicity assays showed that MCA-RM124 selectively killed leukemic cells, while retaining minimal activity towards normal HSCs (CFU-S).

title: Quantitative assessment of T-cell repertoire recovery after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
text: The impaired recovery of T cells and restricted diversity of T cell receptor (TCR) following allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) pose significant risks of infection and cancer relapse. However, the accurate quantification of TCR diversity in these individuals has been challenging due to technical limitations. To address this challenge, we employed a novel approach that integrates 5' rapid amplification of complementary DNA ends PCR with deep sequencing to assess TCR diversity in 28 recipients of allo-HSCT. Utilizing a single oligonucleotide pair, we were able to accurately determine the frequency of individual TCRs in duplicate blood samples.
