In a Phase I trial, rH-TNF was administered via a five-day continuous intravenous (IV) infusion, repeated every 28 days. Thirty-eight treatment courses were given to 19 patients, starting with a dose of 5 x 10^4 U/m2/d, which was escalated to 1.0 x 10^5, 2.0 x 10^5, 2.4 x 10^5, and 3.0 x 10^5 U/m2/d. Mild and self-limiting systemic side effects, including fever, chills, hypotension, fatigue, anorexia, and headaches, were observed. At the maximum tolerated dose of 3.0 x 10^5 U/m2/d, dose-limiting hematologic toxicity, characterized by transient thrombocytopenia and leukopenia, was seen. Additionally, elevated bilirubin levels were noted at higher dose levels. Lipoprotein analysis revealed that the five-day rH-TNF treatment resulted in decreased high-density lipoproteins and increased triglycerides and very-low-density lipoproteins. Pharmacokinetic studies using an ELISA test showed that plasma rH-TNF levels remained below 0.2 U/mL. Based on these findings, the recommended Phase II dose of rH-TNF administered as a five-day continuous infusion is 2.4 x 10^5 U/m2/d.

title: Tissue-specific expression and regulation of sexually dimorphic genes in mice.
text: We present a comprehensive analysis of sex differences in gene expression across multiple somatic tissues from 334 mice derived from an intercross between inbred mouse strains C57BL/6J and C3H/HeJ. Utilizing a large number of individuals enabled the detection of relatively small differences in expression between sexes, while the intercross provided insight into the genetic control of sexually dimorphic gene expression. Through microarray analysis of 23,574 transcripts, we found that the extent of sexual dimorphism in gene expression was more pronounced than previously recognized, with thousands of genes showing sexual dimorphism in liver, adipose, and muscle, and hundreds of genes sexually dimorphic in brain. These genes exhibited highly tissue-specific patterns of expression and were enriched for distinct pathways represented in the Gene Ontology database. Chromosomal enrichment was observed not only on the sex chromosomes but also on several autosomes, and genetic analyses revealed global regulation of subsets of sexually dimorphic genes through expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) hotspots that exhibited tissue-specific control. Additionally, many tissue-specific transcription factor binding sites were found to be enriched in the sexually dimorphic genes.

title: The role of prevention in oncology practice: results from a 2004 survey of American Society of Clinical Oncology members.
text:
In 2004, the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Cancer Prevention Committee conducted a survey among its members to assess their involvement in cancer prevention activities. The survey consisted of updated items related to genetics, chemoprevention, and survivorship. The sample included 2,000 domestic members and a convenience sample of 3,144 international members. Of the 49.7% of domestic members who responded, the majority were younger than 51.7 years old (P < .01). Similarly, 465 international members responded, with the majority (43.2%) being 51-65 years old.
Overall, 35% of respondents had received formal instruction in cancer prevention and control. The majority of respondents expected an increase in prevention, screening, early detection, and risk reduction/genetic counseling in their practices in the next five years. Most respondents reported caring for cancer survivors, including providing general medical care, and either directly providing or referring patients for cancer prevention and control services, such as cancer screening, tobacco and nutrition counseling, risk reduction, and chemoprevention.
Multivariable modeling revealed that fewer perceived barriers to the inclusion of cancer prevention activities in clinical practice existed among those practicing in an academic setting, seeing a higher proportion of patients without a cancer diagnosis, having formal training in prevention and control, expecting an increase in prevention activities in the next five years, and providing community advice on prevention.
The study found that despite a desire for more specific educational programs in cancer prevention and control, barriers to the inclusion of these activities in oncology clinical practice exist. However, a substantial proportion of ASCO members reported an interest in cancer prevention and control activities, with a desire for more training in this emerging area of oncology practice.

title: Stress-dependent regulation of FOXO transcription factors by the SIRT1 deacetylase.
text: The Sir2 deacetylase plays a crucial role in extending the lifespan of various species. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms are not yet fully understood. Our study reveals that in mammalian cells, the Sir2 homolog SIRT1 regulates the cellular response to stress by influencing the activity of the FOXO family of transcription factors, which act as sensor proteins for the insulin signaling pathway and regulators of organismal longevity. SIRT1 and the FOXO transcription factor FOXO3 form a complex in cells under stress conditions, and SIRT1 deacetylates FOXO3 in vitro and within cells. This dual effect of SIRT1 on FOXO3 function has two distinct outcomes: (1) SIRT1 enhances FOXO3's ability to induce cell cycle arrest and resistance to oxidative stress, and (2) SIRT1 inhibits FOXO3's ability to induce cell death. Therefore, one possible mechanism by which members of the Sir2 family may contribute to organismal longevity is by modulating FOXO-dependent responses away from apoptosis and towards stress resistance.

title: TLR-Mediated Innate Production of IFN-γ by CD8+ T Cells Is Independent of Glycolysis.
text: CD8(+) T cells can respond to unrelated infections without specific antigen (Ag) recognition through an immune response that is independent of Ag. This rapid and innate-like immune response enables Ag-experienced T cells to alert other immune cell types to pathogenic intruders. In this study, we found that murine CD8(+) T cells can detect TLR2 and TLR7 ligands, leading to the rapid production of interferon gamma (IFN-γ) but not tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) or interleukin-2 (IL-2). Importantly, Ag-experienced T cells activated by TLR ligands produce sufficient IFN-γ to augment the activation of macrophages. Unlike Ag-specific reactivation, TLR-dependent production of IFN-γ by CD8(+) T cells relies solely on newly synthesized transcripts without inducing mRNA stability. Furthermore, the production of IFN-γ upon TLR triggering requires the activation of the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and serine-threonine kinase Akt, and protein synthesis relies on the activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin. We investigated the energy source responsible for the TLR-induced production of IFN-γ and found that, unlike Ag-specific cytokine production, which requires a glycolytic switch for optimal cytokine release, mitochondrial respiration provides sufficient energy for TLR-induced IFN-γ production. To our knowledge, this is the first report describing TLR-mediated bystander activation, which leads to a short boost of IFN-γ production that activates Ag-experienced CD8(+) T cells, prime macrophages, and limits T cell responses to unrelated infections.

title: Recommendations for the presurgical psychosocial evaluation of bariatric surgery patients.
text: Psychosocial factors have a considerable impact on the long-term success of bariatric surgery, including emotional adjustment, adherence to postoperative lifestyle guidelines, weight loss outcomes, and improvement or resolution of co-morbidities. As such, it is crucial that bariatric behavioral health professionals with specialized knowledge and experience play a key role in evaluating and caring for patients both before and after surgery. The assessing clinician assumes several important roles in the multidisciplinary management of bariatric patients, such as identifying potential obstacles to optimal surgical outcomes and providing recommendations to the patient and bariatric team on how to address these issues. This document outlines recommendations for the psychosocial evaluation of bariatric surgery patients, including the qualifications of those conducting these assessments, the communication of evaluation results and suggested treatment plan, and the extension of behavioral healthcare to the entire duration of the surgical and postoperative process.

title: Simian immunodeficiency virus–induced mucosal interleukin-17 deficiency promotes Salmonella dissemination from the gut
text: Salmonella Typhimurium causes a localized intestinal infection in immunocompetent individuals, whereas HIV-infected individuals develop a life-threatening blood infection. In this study, we demonstrate that Simian Immunodeficiency Virus (SIV) infection leads to a depletion of T Helper Type 17 (TH17) cells in the ileal mucosa of rhesus macaques, impairing the mucosal barrier's ability to stop Salmonella Typhimurium from spreading. In contrast, SIV-negative macaques exhibit a dominant TH17 gene expression profile in response to Salmonella Typhimurium infection in ligated ileal loops, including the expression of Interleukin-17 (IL-17) and IL-22. However, TH17 cell depletion is observed in SIV-infected rhesus macaques, resulting in diminished TH17 responses to Salmonella Typhimurium and increased bacterial dissemination. IL-17 receptor-deficient mice exhibit higher systemic dissemination of Salmonella Typhimurium from the gut, suggesting that IL-17 deficiency leads to impaired mucosal barrier function. Our findings indicate that SIV infection impairs the IL-17 axis, an essential component of the mucosal immune response that prevents systemic microbial dissemination from the gastrointestinal tract.

title: An adoption study of human obesity.
text: We investigated the impact of genetic and family environmental factors on human adiposity in a sample of 540 adult Danish adoptees, selected from a population of 3580 and divided into four weight classes: thin, median weight, overweight, and obese. Our findings revealed a strong correlation between the weight class of the adoptees and the body mass index (BMI) of their biological parents, with a significance level of less than 0.0001 for mothers and less than 0.02 for fathers. Contrary to our expectations, there was no significant association between the weight class of the adoptees and the BMI of their adoptive parents. Moreover, the relation between biological parents and adoptee weight class was apparent across the full range of body fatness, from very thin to very obese. Our results suggest that genetic factors play a crucial role in determining human adiposity in adults, while the family environment has no apparent effect on weight classification.

title: Redox-dependent downregulation of Rho by Rac
text: Rac and Rho GTPases serve as crucial regulators of actin cytoskeleton remodeling during cell spreading and migration. Here, we demonstrate that Rac-mediated production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) leads to a decrease in Rho activity. The redox-dependent reduction in Rho activity is essential for Rac-induced formation of membrane ruffles and integrin-mediated cell spreading. The pathway linking ROS generation to the downregulation of Rho involves the inhibition of low-molecular-weight protein tyrosine phosphatase (LMW-PTP) and an increase in tyrosine phosphorylation and activation of its target, p190Rho-GAP. Our findings illuminate a novel mechanism for the connection between changes in cellular redox state and the control of actin cytoskeleton rearrangements by Rho GTPases.

title: The epidemiology of trachoma in Eastern Equatoria and Upper Nile States, southern Sudan.
text:
The objective of this study was to assess the prevalence and geographical distribution of trachoma in southern Sudan, specifically in the states of Eastern Equatoria and Upper Nile. Despite limited surveys and anecdotal data suggesting that trachoma is endemic in these regions, the magnitude and distribution of the disease were largely unknown.
To address this gap, the researchers conducted population-based cross-sectional surveys in nine sites in southern Sudan between September 2001 and June 2004. The surveys used a two-stage random cluster sampling method with probability proportional to size to select the sample. Trachoma grading was done using the World Health Organization (WHO) simplified grading system.
The findings of the study revealed that a total of 17,016 persons were examined, with a response rate of 86.1% of the enumerated population. The prevalence of signs of active trachoma in children aged 1-9 years was found to be:
TF=53.7% (95% confidence interval (CI)=52.1-55.3); TI=42.7% (95% CI=41.2-44.2); TF and/or TI=64.1% (95% CI=62.5-65.5). The prevalence of trichiasis (TT) in children aged less than 15 years was 1.2% (95% CI=0.9-1.4), while TT prevalence in persons aged 15 years and above was 9.2% (95% CI=8.6-9.9). Interestingly, women were found to be more likely to have trichiasis compared to men (odds ratio (OR)=1.57; 95% CI=1.34-1.84).
Based on these findings, the researchers estimated that there is a backlog of 178,250 (lower and upper bounds=156,027-205,995) persons requiring surgery, and that the entire population of over 3.9 million people in the study regions is in need of the SAFE strategy to control blinding trachoma.

In conclusion, the study findings indicate that trachoma is a significant public health problem in the surveyed regions of southern Sudan, particularly in children. The high prevalence of active trachoma and trichiasis in children underscores the urgent need to implement trachoma control interventions in these regions.

title: A single residue determines the cooperative binding property of a primosomal DNA replication protein, PriB, to single-stranded DNA.
text: PriB is a protein that plays a crucial role in reinitiating DNA replication in bacteria. We compared the DNA-binding properties of PriB from Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium LT2 (StPriB) and Escherichia coli (EcPriB). Our findings reveal that the only residue that differs between the two proteins is a single amino acid (V6) in EcPriB, which is replaced by A6 in StPriB. Previous structural studies had shown that this residue is located on the interface of PriB dimers and does not affect its ability to bind to single-stranded DNA (ssDNA). However, our results demonstrate that the binding mechanism of StPriB to DNA is significantly different from that of EcPriB. Unlike EcPriB, which forms a single complex with ssDNAs of various lengths, StPriB forms multiple distinct complexes. Based on these findings, we propose binding modes for stable complexes of PriB with ssDNA of 25 nucleotides (nt), such as (EcPriB)25 and (StPriB)25.

title: Genomic organization and chromosomal location of the human dsRNA adenosine deaminase gene: the enzyme for glutamate-activated ion channel RNA editing.
text: The characterization of the human gene encoding double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) adenosine deaminase (DRADA) has been conducted. This nuclear-localized enzyme plays a crucial role in RNA editing, which is essential for the expression of specific subtypes of glutamate-gated ion channel subunits. The DRADA gene spans approximately 30 kilobase pairs and consists of 15 exons. The transcription of the DRADA gene, initiated at multiple sites located 164 to 216 nucleotides upstream of the translation initiation codon, is driven by a putative promoter region devoid of typical TATA or CCAAT box-like sequences. The gene encodes three dsRNA binding motifs (DRBM), each consisting of 70 amino acid residues and encoded by two exons flanked by an intervening sequence. This discovery supports the notion that the dsRNA binding domains may comprise two distinct functional subdomains. Using fluorescent in situ hybridization, the DRADA gene has been localized to the long arm of chromosome 1, region q21. The presented gene structure and sequence information will facilitate investigations into the potential involvement of DRADA in inherited diseases that may result from malfunction of glutamate-gated ion channels.

title: "We charge them; otherwise we cannot run the hospital" front line workers, clients and health financing policy implementation gaps in Ghana.
text: This study investigates the discrepancies in policy implementation regarding user fees and health insurance in providing financial access to primary healthcare for children under five in Ghana. METHODS We employed a mix of data analysis, focus groups, in-depth interviews, and a structured questionnaire to gather information. RESULTS Providers adjusted their interpretations of exemption policies, sometimes offering partial or no exemptions, despite clients who were aware or suspected their entitlements failed to request them due to concerns about negative reactions from providers. Providers attributed their modifications to the uncertainty and delays in reimbursement, threatening their institutions' financial viability. Although low at the time of the study, insurance coverage was not significantly influencing implementation arrangements. However, unchanged underlying goal conflicts, resource constraints, working conditions, and relationships between frontline workers and clients remained, persisting implementation gaps for the health insurance policy. CONCLUSIONS Policies that disregard frontline workers' incentives and fail to align them with policy objectives can face implementation gaps, as demonstrated by the exemptions policy.

title: EML4-ALK translocation predicts better outcome in lung adenocarcinoma patients with wild-type EGFR.
text:
INTRODUCTION: The Echinoderm microtubule-associated protein like 4 (EML4) fusion with anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) represents a novel target in a subset of non-small cell lung cancer, particularly adenocarcinoma. The EML4-ALK fusion is exclusive to epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations. To gain insight into the impact of EML4-ALK on the prognosis of non-small cell lung cancer, we investigated EML4-ALK expression in lung adenocarcinoma from patients with wild-type EGFR and analyzed their clinical treatment outcomes.
METHODS: We enrolled lung adenocarcinoma patients with malignant pleural effusions and wild-type EGFR for EML4-ALK analysis using reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and direct sequencing. Demographic data, EML4-ALK status, and survival data were analyzed. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was performed on available tumor samples to validate the PCR results. Additionally, K-ras mutation analysis was conducted in patients without the EML4-ALK fusion gene.
RESULTS: A total of 116 patients with wild-type EGFR RT-PCR results were included in the analysis. None of the patients received ALK inhibitor therapy. We identified 39 patients (34%) with the EML4-ALK fusion gene, and the concordance rate between RT-PCR and FISH was 85%. The K-ras mutation rate in patients without the EML4-ALK fusion gene was 6.5%. Multivariate analysis revealed that patients with better performance status (p < 0.001) and EML4-ALK translocation (p = 0.017) had longer overall survival. No significant differences were found between patients with variant 1 and non-variant 1 EML4-ALK fusion genes in terms of clinical factors and survival outcomes.
CONCLUSION: For lung adenocarcinoma patients with wild-type EGFR, EML4-ALK translocation is associated with longer overall survival.

title: Transcriptional Repression of Gata3 Is Essential for Early B Cell Commitment
text: The underlying mechanisms for silencing alternative fates in early B cell precursors remain unclear. To investigate, we utilized both gain-of-function and loss-of-function approaches, as well as a synthetic Zinc-finger polypeptide (6ZFP) engineered to block transcription factor binding to a specific cis-element. Using this approach, we found that the transcription factor EBF1 promotes B cell lineage commitment by directly repressing the expression of the T cell-lineage-specific Gata3 gene. Strikingly, Ebf1-deficient lymphoid progenitors displayed increased T cell lineage potential and high levels of Gata3 transcript expression, while enforced EBF1 expression blocked T cell differentiation and rapidly reduced Gata3 mRNA levels. Remarkably, 6ZFP-mediated disruption of EBF1 binding to the Gata3 regulatory region restored Gata3 expression, aborted EBF1-driven suppression of T cell differentiation, and prevented B cell differentiation through a GATA3-dependent mechanism. Furthermore, we found that EBF1 binding to the Gata3 regulatory site induced repressive histone modifications across this region, thus identifying a crucial transcriptional circuit for B cell lineage commitment.

title: Isolation and partial characterization of an unusual human immunodeficiency retrovirus from two persons of west-central African origin.
text: An uncommon human retrovirus was isolated from two patients in Belgium with persistent generalized lymphadenopathy, who originated from West-Central Africa. Although the virus shared similarities with human immunodeficiency retrovirus type 1 (HIV-1) and HIV-2 in terms of biological and morphological properties, notable antigenic differences were observed. The viral proteins also varied in molecular weight compared to the corresponding HIV-1 and HIV-2 proteins. Partial chemical cleavage of the most highly conserved viral proteins revealed patterns that differed from those of HIV-1 and HIV-2. Additionally, nucleic acid hybridization experiments could differentiate between the virus types. Sequence analysis of the viral U3 region showed a unique enhancer organization not found in other immunodeficiency viruses, indicating that the new isolate is more closely related to HIV-1 than to HIV-2, but it distinctly differs in several key aspects.

title: Role of circulating nitrite and S-nitrosohemoglobin in the regulation of regional blood flow in humans.
text: In order to investigate the relative contributions of endothelial-derived nitric oxide (NO) and intravascular nitrogen oxide species in the regulation of human blood flow, we simultaneously measured forearm blood flow and arterial and venous levels of plasma nitrite, low-molecular-weight S-nitrosothiols, and red cell S-nitrosohemoglobin (SNO-Hb) at rest and during regional inhibition of NO synthesis, followed by forearm exercise. Surprisingly, we found significant circulating arterial-venous plasma nitrite gradients, indicating a novel delivery source for intravascular NO. Additionally, we found that consumption of nitrite increased significantly with exercise during the inhibition of regional endothelial synthesis of NO. The role of circulating S-nitrosothiols and SNO-Hb in the regulation of basal vascular tone was less clear, as low-molecular-weight S-nitrosothiols were undetectable and S-nitroso-albumin levels were two logs lower than previously reported, with most of it formed in the venous circulation. In contrast, SNO-Hb was measurable in the human circulation (brachial artery levels of 170 nM in whole blood), but arterial-venous gradients were not significant, and delivery of NO from SNO-Hb was minimal. In conclusion, our data suggest that (i) circulating nitrite is bioactive and provides a delivery gradient of intravascular NO, (ii) S-nitroso-albumin does not deliver NO from the lungs to the tissue but forms in the peripheral circulation, and (iii) SNO-Hb and S-nitrosothiols play a minimal role in the regulation of basal vascular tone, even during exercise stress.

title: Extra centrosomes and/or chromosomes prolong mitosis in human cells
text: By employing laser microsurgery and cell fusion, we have investigated the impact of additional centrosomes and/or chromosomes on the duration of mitosis in human cells. Our findings reveal that increasing the number of chromosomes leads to an approximate 10-minute prolongation of a 20-minute division, while doubling the number of centrosomes adds approximately 30 minutes to the duration. These results indicate that extra centrosomes and/or chromosomes prolong mitosis by delaying the satisfaction of the spindle assembly checkpoint. This finding suggests that mitosis can be prolonged through non-genetic means, and extra chromosomes and centrosomes likely contribute to the elevated mitotic index observed in many tumors.

title: Familial recurrence-pattern analysis of nonsyndromic isolated cleft palate--a Danish Registry study.
text: The discovery of an association between genetic variation at the transforming growth-factor alpha (TGFA) locus and nonsyndromic isolated cleft palate (CP) represents a significant breakthrough in our understanding of this condition. The present study was conducted to assess the feasibility of identifying genetic links to potential CP-susceptibility loci, such as TGFA, using information on the familial recurrence pattern of CP. Taking advantage of the high ascertainment and uniform registration of CP in Denmark, the study estimated the recurrence risks for first-, second-, and third-degree relatives of 1,364 nonsyndromic CP probands to be 2.74% (72/2,628), 0.28% (3/1,068), and 0.00% (0/360), respectively. These estimates are comparable to previously published estimates based on questionnaire and interview data. However, the population prevalence of nonsyndromic CP was found to be significantly higher than previously reported (0.058% [1,456/2,523,023]). Analyses of these and other published data, using a method presented by Risch, suggested that major-locus or additive multilocus inheritance of CP is unlikely. The familial recurrence pattern was consistent with CP being caused by multiple interacting loci, with a single locus accounting for more than a sixfold increase in the risk to first-degree relatives of CP probands being unlikely, but a single locus accounting for a threefold increase providing a good fit to the data. Such a locus could potentially be detected in a realistic sample of affected sib pairs.

title: Gene methylation in gastric cancer.
text: Gastric cancer is one of the most prevalent forms of cancer and ranks second in cancer-related deaths worldwide, with over 70% of cases occurring in developing countries. Early on in the molecular biology revolution, cancer research primarily focused on genetic alterations, including gastric cancer. Epigenetic mechanisms play a crucial role in the development and maintenance of tissue-specific gene expression patterns in mammals. Disruptions to these processes can result in altered gene function and malignant cell transformation. Recent advancements in the rapidly evolving field of cancer epigenetics have revealed extensive reprogramming of every aspect of the epigenetic machinery in cancer, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, nucleosome positioning, non-coding RNAs, and microRNAs. Aberrant DNA methylation within the promoter regions of genes, leading to the inactivation of tumor suppressor and other cancer-related genes in cancer cells, is the most well-defined epigenetic hallmark in gastric cancer. The use of gene methylation as a target for cancer detection and diagnosis in biopsy specimens and non-invasive body fluids, such as serum and gastric washes, has led to numerous studies exploring its application in gastric cancer. This review will focus on the most common and significant phenomenon of epigenetics, DNA methylation, in gastric cancer and highlight the impact that epigenetics has had on this field.

title: Klebsiella aerogenes urease gene cluster: sequence of ureD and demonstration that four accessory genes (ureD, ureE, ureF, and ureG) are involved in nickel metallocenter biosynthesis.
text: The region located upstream of the Klebsiella aerogenes urease structural genes was sequenced and found to contain an open reading frame that could encode a 29.8-kDa peptide. Deletions were generated in this gene, denoted ureD, and in each of the genes (ureE, ureF, and ureG) located downstream of the three structural genes. Transformation of the mutated plasmids into Escherichia coli led to high levels of urease expression, but the enzyme was inactive (deletions in ureD, ureF, or ureG) or only partially active (deletions in ureE). Ureases were purified from the recombinant cells and found to be identical to control enzyme when analyzed by gel filtration chromatography and sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, but their activity levels were found to correlate with nickel contents as analyzed by atomic absorption analysis. Tentative identification of UreD, UreE, UreF, and UreG peptides was carried out through gel electrophoretic comparison of mutant and control cell extracts, in vivo expression of separately cloned genes, or in vitro transcription-translation analyses. These assignments were confirmed for UreE and UreG through amino-terminal sequencing. The amounts of UreF (apparent M(r), 27,000) and UreD (apparent M(r), 29,300) were found to be significantly reduced, possibly due to the lack of good ribosome binding sites in the regions upstream of these open reading frames. These results demonstrate that all four accessory genes are essential for the functional incorporation of the urease metallocenter.

title: Hepatic polyploidy and liver growth control.
text: Cellular polyploidy is detected in all differentiated mammalian tissues, including the liver, both in normal instances and during disease states. As our understanding of polyploidy's significance grows, studies have shown that cells with higher ploidy classes tend to progress toward terminal differentiation and cellular senescence at a higher rate, increasing their likelihood of undergoing apoptosis. Genetic abnormalities, such as impaired DNA repair mechanisms, may contribute to hepatocellular polyploidy. Emerging models suggest that extensive polyploidy could lead to organ failure and, in some cases, oncogenesis by activating precancerous cell clones.

title: Disturbances in the positioning, proliferation and apoptosis of neural progenitors contribute to subcortical band heterotopia formation.
text: Cortical malformations, particularly intractable epilepsy, frequently coincide with other developmental disorders. By leveraging the spontaneous genetic rat model of subcortical band heterotopia (SBH), associated with epilepsy, we investigate the evolutionary events underlying SBH formation in the neocortex. Our findings demonstrate that Pax6(+) and Tbr2(+) progenitors are mispositioned in the neocortex of tish(+/-) and tish(-/-) rats throughout neurogenesis. Furthermore, these mispositioned tish(-/-) progenitors exhibit an extended cell cycle due to an elongated period in G(2)+M+G(1). This mislocalization is unrelated to disintegration of adherens junctions or loss of radial glial polarity in the ventricular zone (VZ), as determined by immunohistochemical staining with phalloidin (to identify F-actin), aPKC-λ, and Par3. However, vimentin immunohistochemistry reveals that the radial glial scaffold is disrupted in the region of the tish(-/-) heterotopia. Additionally, lineage tracing experiments using in utero electroporation in tish(-/-) neocortex demonstrate that mispositioned progenitors fail to maintain contact with the ventricular surface, and ventricular/subventricular zone (SVZ) progenitors produce neurons that migrate into both the heterotopia and cortical plate (CP). Combining these observations, we elucidate a series of developmental errors that underlie SBH formation, distinct from the initial mistake in neuronal migration.

title: Sex-related differences in the presentation, treatment and outcomes among patients with acute coronary syndromes: the Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events.
text:
Objective: To assess whether there are any differences in the severity, management, and outcomes of acute coronary syndromes (ACS) between men and women undergoing coronary angiography.
Methods: The study included 7638 women and 19,117 men who underwent coronary angiography as part of the Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) from 1999 to 2006. The severity of coronary artery disease was classified as mild ( < 50% stenosis in all epicardial vessels) or advanced (> = 50% stenosis in one or more epicardial vessels).
Results: Women were older and had more cardiovascular risk factors than men. Men and women presented with chest pain equally, but women were more likely to experience jaw pain and nausea. Women were more likely to have mild/normal disease (12% vs 6%, p < 0.001) and less likely to have left-main and three-vessel disease (27% vs 32%, p < 0.001) or undergo percutaneous coronary intervention (65% vs 68%, p < 0.001). Women with advanced disease had a higher risk of death (4% vs 3%, p < 0.01). After adjusting for age and disease severity, women were more likely to have adverse outcomes (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and rehospitalization) at six months compared to men (odds ratio 1.24, 95% confidence interval 1.14-1.34), but the sex difference in mortality was no longer significant after adjustment.
Conclusions: Women with ACS were more likely to have cardiovascular disease risk factors and atypical symptoms such as nausea compared with men, but were more likely to have mild/normal angiographic coronary artery disease. Further research is needed to understand the relationship between disease severity and sex differences in ACS outcomes.

title: GITR, a member of the TNF receptor superfamily, is costimulatory to mouse T lymphocyte subpopulations.
text: GITR (glucocorticoid-induced TNFR family related gene) is a member of the TNFR superfamily (TNFRSF) that is expressed in a range of cell types, including T lymphocytes. Due to its high similarity in the cytoplasmic region with other established costimulatory members of the TNFRSF, we investigated whether GITR plays a costimulatory role in different T lymphocyte subpopulations. Our findings indicate that the proliferation response of both CD8+ and CD4+ peripheral T cell subpopulations was enhanced when a GITR costimulus was added to an anti-CD3 stimulus. Additionally, expression of the primary activation-induced receptor (IL-2Ralpha) and production of IL-2 and IFN-gamma were increased more with a GITR costimulus compared to anti-CD3 alone. Furthermore, GITR stimulation also activated the MAPK signaling pathway. Interestingly, CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cell (Treg cell) proliferation was triggered by the GITR costimulus, which was followed by the loss of the anergic phenotype and suppressor activity. However, unstimulated GITR(-/-) CD4+CD25+ cells and GITR(+/+) CD4+CD25+ cells had equal suppressor activity on CD4+CD25- responder cells. These findings demonstrate a novel role for GITR as a costimulatory molecule on T cell subsets.

title: PI3K and cancer: lessons, challenges and opportunities
text: The pivotal function of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) activation in tumor cell biology has prompted an extensive effort to target PI3K and its downstream kinases, such as Akt and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), in cancer treatment. However, recent clinical data have revealed limited single-agent activity of inhibitors targeting PI3K, Akt, or mTOR even at tolerable doses. One exception is the response to PI3Kδ inhibitors in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, where both cell-intrinsic and -extrinsic activities contribute to efficacy. We will examine the challenges and opportunities for the clinical development of PI3K–AKT–mTOR pathway inhibitors. By focusing on patient selection, enhancing our understanding of immune modulation, and strategically combining inhibitors, we should be able to realize the potential of these promising targeted anticancer agents.

title: Sequence-based species delimitation for the DNA taxonomy of undescribed insects.
text: Accelerating the cataloging of undescribed insect species using automated DNA-based approaches is promising, yet large-scale species discovery from sequence data still lacks adequate procedures. To address this issue, we applied mitochondrial DNA variation to delimit species within the poorly known beetle radiation of the genus Rivacindela in arid Australia. We sampled 468 individuals from 65 sites and multiple morphologically distinguishable types, and analyzed three mtDNA genes (cytochrome oxidase subunit 1, cytochrome b, and 16S ribosomal RNA). Our quantitative evaluation identified 46 or 47 putative species based on distinctive fixed characters. The distinct boundaries between groups were also evident from a Notable increase in branching rate in clock-constrained calibrated trees. We combined Yule models with coalescence theory to develop a new likelihood method, which identified the point of transition from species-level to population-level evolutionary processes. Fitting the location of the switches from speciation to coalescent nodes on the ultrametric tree of Rivacindela resulted in a transition at 0.43 Mya, leading to an estimate of 48 putative species (confidence interval of 47–51 clusters within 2 logL units). The entities delineated in this manner exhibited biological properties consistent with traditionally defined species, including geographic range coherence, morphological congruence, and typical sequence divergence among closely related insect species. The discovery of discontinuous evolutionary groupings that are easily recognizable in patterns of sequence variation enables largely automated species delineation from DNA surveys of local communities, providing a promising framework for taxonomy in this poorly known insect group.

title: CCR6 regulates the migration of inflammatory and regulatory T cells.
text: In autoimmune diseases, Th17 cells and regulatory T (Treg) cells play opposite roles, but the mechanisms behind their proper migration to inflamed tissues are not fully understood. In this study, we discovered that both Th17 and Treg cells express the chemokine receptor CCR6. However, the expression of CCR6 on Th17 cells is regulated by TGF-beta and requires two nuclear receptors, RORalpha and RORgamma. Th17 cells also produce the CCR6 ligand CCL20, which is induced by TGF-beta and IL-6, and requires STAT3, RORgamma, and IL-21. CCL20 production by Th17 cells promotes the migration of Th17 and Treg cells in vitro in a CCR6-dependent manner. Conversely, the absence of CCR6 on Th17 cells leads to a reduction in the severity of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis and Treg and Th17 cell recruitment into inflamed tissues. Our findings suggest that CCR6 plays a crucial role in the migration of Treg and Th17 cells.

title: Inhibition of receptor-mediated calcium influx in T cells by unsaturated non-esterified fatty acids.
text: Investigating the impact of omega-3, omega-6, and omega-9 unsaturated fatty acids (UFAs) on receptor-mediated calcium influx, researchers utilized an T-cell line (JURKAT) and anti-CD3 antibodies (OKT3) to increase intracellular calcium levels. The study discovered that all UFAs, as well as nickel ions and 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate, significantly reduced the OKT3-induced sustained increase in intracellular calcium to basal levels. Despite the activation of protein kinase C (PKC) by non-esterified fatty acids, as previously demonstrated in studies using H-7 and analysis of PKC-dependent phosphorylation of 19 and 80 kDa marker substrates, the study found that UFA-induced inhibition of calcium entry was not mediated by PKC. Using flow cytometry analysis, the researchers also determined that UFAs did not interfere with antibody-receptor binding. Notably, the effect of UFAs was reversed when the fatty acids were added after their inhibition of OKT3-induced calcium increase had returned to basal levels. The findings of this study and possible mechanisms by which UFAs inhibit receptor-mediated calcium influx were discussed.

title: Deleted in liver cancer-1 (DLC-1): a tumor suppressor not just for liver.
text: Originally isolated as a potential tumor suppressor gene, Deleted in Liver Cancer 1 (DLC-1) was named due to its frequent deletion in hepatocellular carcinoma. Subsequent studies revealed that DLC-1 down-regulation, through both genomic deletion and DNA methylation, is associated with multiple cancer types, including lung, breast, prostate, kidney, colon, uterus, ovary, and stomach. Re-expressing DLC-1 in cancer cells leads to reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and focal adhesions, which significantly inhibits cell growth, reinforcing its role as a tumor suppressor. This tumor suppressive function is attributed to DLC-1's RhoGTPase activating protein (RhoGAP) activity, steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR)-related lipid transfer (START) domain, and localization within focal adhesions, which is mediated by the Src Homology 2 (SH2) domains of tensins in a phosphotyrosine-independent manner. Therefore, analyzing the expression and subcellular localization of DLC-1 could serve as a valuable marker for cancer prognosis, while targeting DLC-1 and its downstream signaling molecules may offer a therapeutic strategy for cancer treatment.

title: Interaction of Helicobacter pylori with gastric epithelial cells is mediated by the p53 protein family.
text: Although the p53 tumor suppressor has been extensively studied, many questions remain about the roles of p73 and p63, its homologs, in regulating cellular processes such as apoptosis, cell differentiation, and drug sensitivity. Recent evidence suggests that both p73 and p63 play important roles in these processes. To investigate their roles in H pylori infection, we cocultured gastric epithelial cells with H pylori and assessed their functions using luciferase reporter, real-time polymerase chain reaction, immunoblotting, and cell survival assays. We also used short hairpin RNA and dominant-negative mutants to inhibit the activity of p73 and p63 isoforms. Our results showed that H pylori infection leads to a robust up-regulation of p73 protein in vitro and in vivo, which in turn up-regulates pro-apoptotic genes such as NOXA, PUMA, and FAS receptor in gastric epithelial cells. Down-regulation of p73 activity suppressed cell death and Fas receptor induction by H pylori. Our findings also revealed that bacterial virulence factors within the cag pathogenicity island, c-Abl tyrosine kinase, and interaction with p63 isoforms control the activity of p73. Overall, our study implicates p73 in H pylori-induced apoptosis and suggests that the p53 family may play a role in the epithelial cell response to H pylori infection.

title: Brown and white adipose tissues: intrinsic differences in gene expression and response to cold exposure in mice
text: Brown adipocytes burn energy, while white adipocytes serve as an energy storage site. We investigated the ability of different white adipose tissue depots to adopt a brown-like phenotype through cold exposure. By comparing gene expression in white fat at thermoneutrality to that in brown fat, we identified a "brite" transcriptional signature. This study uncovered novel targets for understanding the process of "browning," including genes, pathways, and regulatory motifs. For instance, neuregulin 4 was found to be more highly expressed in brown adipose tissue and upregulated in white fat upon cold exposure. Cell studies suggest that it plays a role in increasing adipose tissue innervation in response to cold by promoting neurite outgrowth. To further understand the discrete properties of different adipose depots, we developed a cell culture system that allows for in vitro study of depot-specific differences. The key transcriptional events that underlie the transition of white adipose tissue to a brown-like state are crucial, as they offer a promising approach to combat metabolic disorders such as obesity and type 2 diabetes.

title: Continuous glucose monitoring in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes (CONCEPTT): a multicentre international randomised controlled trial
text:
Type 1 diabetes during pregnancy is a high-risk condition for both the mother and the baby. Generally, the mother experiences fluctuating blood sugar levels, which can lead to neonatal complications. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) helps to improve glucose control, essential for positive outcomes. A recent study investigated the effectiveness of CGM on maternal glucose control and obstetric/neonatal health outcomes.
The study was a multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial that included participants aged 18 to 40 with type 1 diabetes, who were receiving intensive insulin therapy. The participants were recruited from 31 hospitals across Canada, England, Scotland, Spain, Italy, Ireland, and the USA. The study included two parallel trials for pregnant and non-pregnant participants. The participants were randomly assigned to either CGM in addition to capillary glucose monitoring or capillary glucose monitoring alone.
The study outcomes were measured in all randomized participants with baseline assessments. The primary outcome was the change in HbA1c from randomization to 34 weeks' gestation in pregnant participants and to 24 weeks or conception in non-pregnant participants. Secondary outcomes included obstetric and neonatal health outcomes, assessed with all available data without imputation.
The study found small differences in the HbA1c of pregnant participants using CGM (mean difference -0.19%; 95% CI -0.34 to -0.03; p=0.0207). Pregnant CGM users spent more time in the target range (68% vs 61%; p=0.0034) and less time in hyperglycemic status (27% vs 32%; p=0.0279) than did pregnant control participants, with a similar number of severe hypoglycemic events (18 CGM and 21 control) and time spent hypoglycemic (3% vs 4%; p=0.10). Significant improvements in neonatal health outcomes were observed, such as a lower incidence of large for gestational age (odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.90; p=0.0210), fewer neonatal intensive care admissions lasting more than 24 h (0.48; 0.26 to0.86; p=0.0157), fewer episodes of neonatal hypoglycemia (0.45; 0.22 to0.89; p=0.0250), and one-day shorter length of hospital stay (p=0.0091). The study found no apparent benefit of CGM in non-pregnant participants.
Adverse events occurred in 51 (48%) of CGM participants and 43 (40%) of control participants in the pregnancy trial, and in 12 (27%) of CGM participants and 21 (37%) of control participants in the planning pregnancy trial. Serious adverse events occurred in 13 (6%) participants in the pregnancy trial (8 [7%] CGM, 5 [5%] control) and in three (3%) participants in the planning pregnancy trial (2 [4%] CGM and 1 [2%] control). The most common adverse events were skin reactions occurring in 49 (48%) of 103 CGM participants and 8 (8%) of 104 control participants during pregnancy and in 23 (44%) of 52 CGM participants and 5 (9%) of 57 control participants in the planning pregnancy trial. The most common serious adverse events were gastrointestinal (nausea and vomiting in 4 participants during pregnancy and 3 participants planning pregnancy).
In conclusion, the study found that the use of CGM during pregnancy in patients with type 1 diabetes is associated with improved neonatal outcomes, which are likely to be attributed to reduced exposure to maternal hyperglycemia. CGM should be offered to all pregnant women with type 1 diabetes using intensive insulin therapy. This study is the first to indicate potential for improvements in non-glycemic health outcomes from CGM use. The study was funded by the Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation, Canadian Clinical Trials Network, and National Institute for Health Research.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps: Is immunity the second function of chromatin?
text: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are composed of structured chromatin components, which are adjacently bound to select cytoplasmic proteins. These NETs are secreted by white blood cells called neutrophils, potentially as an last-resort measure, to combat microbial infections. The release of chromatin from neutrophils occurs through a novel form of cell death termed "NETosis." This review aims to explore our current understanding of NET structure composition, their functionality during infections and as danger signals, as well as their growing significance in autoimmunity and coagulation.

title: Phosphorylation of p35 and p39 by Cdk5 determines the subcellular location of the holokinase in a phosphorylation-site-specific manner.
text: Cdk5, a member of the cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk) family, is activated by neuronal activators p35 or p39. Cdk5 regulates various neuronal functions, including migration, synaptic activity, and neuronal death. While it is known that p35 and p39 impart cytoplasmic membrane association of p35-Cdk5 and p39-Cdk5 through myristoylation, the relationship between cellular localization and different functions is not fully understood. To investigate the role of Cdk5 activity in the subcellular localization of p35-Cdk5 and p39-Cdk5, we examined the effect of Cdk5 activity on the localization of these proteins. Our findings showed that Cdk5 activity phosphorylates p35 and p39 at specific sites, regulating their cytoplasmic localization and perinuclear accumulation. Interestingly, Cdk5 activity was necessary to retain Cdk5-activator complexes in the cytoplasm, but small amounts of p35 and p39 were detected in the nucleus. Notably, p39 had a higher propensity to accumulate in the nucleus than p35, and phosphorylation at Thr84, specific to p39, regulated the potential nuclear localization activity of the Lys cluster in p39. These results suggest that the subcellular localization of the Cdk5-activator complexes is determined by their kinase activity and implicate a role for p39-Cdk5 in the nucleus.

title: Interleukin-12 and -23 Control Plasticity of CD127(+) Group 1 and Group 3 Innate Lymphoid Cells in the Intestinal Lamina Propria.
text: Human group 1 ILCs comprise at least three distinct subsets, including NK cells, CD127(+) ILC1, and intraepithelial CD103(+) ILC1. In inflamed intestinal tissues from Crohn's disease patients, the number of CD127(+) ILC1 increases at the expense of ILC3. Our findings reveal that the differentiation of ILC3 into CD127(+) ILC1 is reversible in both in vitro and in vivo environments. CD127(+) ILC1 can differentiate into ILC3 in response to interleukin-2 (IL-2), IL-23, and IL-1β, with the transcription factor RORγt playing a crucial role in this process. Moreover, we observed a higher proportion of CD14(+) dendritic cells (DCs) in resection specimens from Crohn's disease patients, which in vitro promote the polarization of ILC3 towards CD127(+) ILC1. In contrast, CD14(-) DCs favor the differentiation of CD127(+) ILC1 towards ILC3. These observations suggest that environmental cues determine the composition, function, and phenotype of CD127(+) ILC1 and ILC3 in the gut.

title: Transcriptional regulation of neuronal genes and its effect on neural functions: expression and function of forkhead transcription factors in neurons.
text: The forkhead box transcription factor, class O (FOXO), is a mammalian homologue of DAF-16, which regulates the lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans. FOXO includes subfamilies of forkhead transcription factors such as AFX, FKHRL1, and FKHR. FKHR is phosphorylated on three sites (Thr-24, Ser-256, and Ser-319) in a phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt-dependent manner, thereby inhibiting death signals. In this study, we investigate the dephosphorylation of FKHR in response to transient forebrain ischemia in neurons of gerbil and mouse brains. We found that the activation of FKHR preceded delayed neuronal death in vulnerable hippocampal regions following ischemic brain injury. The activation of FKHR was accompanied by an increase in DNA binding activity for FKHR-responsive elements on the Fas ligand promoter. We also identified FKHR-induced downstream targets such as Fas ligand and Bim in brain ischemia. As a result, we propose a new strategy to rescue neurons from delayed neuronal death by promoting the survival signaling. We found that inhibiting protein tyrosine phosphatases with Sodium orthovanadate up-regulated Akt activity in the brain and rescued neurons from delayed neuronal death by inhibiting FKHR-dependent or -independent death signals in neurons.

title: ERAAP synergizes with MHC class I molecules to make the final cut in the antigenic peptide precursors in the endoplasmic reticulum.
text: The major histocompatibility complex class I molecules display peptides (pMHC I) on the cell surface for immune detection by CD8(+) T cells. These peptides are generated through the breakdown of intracellular polypeptides by the proteasome in the cytoplasm and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by the ER aminopeptidase associated with antigen processing (ERAAP). To investigate the obscure mechanism of ERAAP function in vivo, we analyzed naturally processed peptides in cells with or without the necessary MHC I and ERAAP. In the lack of MHC I, ERAAP degraded the antigenic precursors in the ER. Nonetheless, MHC I molecules could bind to proteolytic intermediates and were fundamental for the formation of the final peptide by ERAAP. Therefore, ERAAP collaborates with MHC I to create the final pMHC I repertoire.

title: Estimates of animal and plant protein intake in US adults: results from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 1988-1991.
text:
The objective of this study was to investigate the sources of protein intake among different subgroups of the US adult population, including those defined by race-ethnicity, age, and gender, using data from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) conducted from 1988 to 1991.
The study population consisted of 7,924 adult participants in NHANES. Data on protein sources and intake were obtained through a 24-hour dietary recall.
The main source of protein in the American diet is animal protein, which accounts for 69% of total protein intake. Within animal protein, meat, fish, and poultry contribute the most, with 42% of total animal protein intake. Dairy protein is the second most common source of protein, accounting for 20% of total protein intake.
By contrast, plant protein sources are less common, with grains contributing the most, at 18% of total protein intake. Women consume a lower percentage of beef (14%) and pork (7%) protein compared to men (18% and 9%, respectively), while also consuming a higher percentage of poultry (13%), dairy (22%), and fruit and vegetable (11%) protein compared to men (11%, 19%, 4%, and 9%, respectively).
Blacks report consuming a higher percentage of poultry (18%) and pork (11%) protein and a lower percentage of dairy protein (14%) compared to whites (12%, 7%, and 22%, respectively) and Mexican-Americans (11%, 8%, and 17%, respectively). Mexican-Americans consume a higher percentage of legume (7%) and egg (7%) protein compared to whites (4% and 4%, respectively) and blacks (4% and 5%, respectively). Whites consume a higher percentage of grain protein (19%) compared to blacks (16%) and Mexican-Americans (15%).
In conclusion, these findings demonstrate that while the percentage of total energy from protein may be similar across different subgroups, the sources of protein differ significantly. These differences should be taken into account when providing nutrition education to specific populations.

title: CYP18A1, a key enzyme of Drosophila steroid hormone inactivation, is essential for metamorphosis.
text:
Ecdysteroids are a type of steroid hormone that play a crucial role in regulating significant developmental transitions in insects. Both increases and decreases in the levels of active hormones are important for the coordination of molting and metamorphosis, making both ecdysteroid biosynthesis and inactivation essential for proper development. We have found that the Drosophila melanogaster Cyp18a1 gene encodes a cytochrome P450 enzyme (CYP) with 26-hydroxylase activity, a key step in ecdysteroid metabolism. This gene has a clear ortholog in most insects and crustaceans. When Cyp18a1 is overexpressed in Drosophila S2 cells, a significant conversion of 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) into 20-hydroxyecdysonoic acid is observed, a multi-step process involving the formation of 20,26-dihydroxyecdysone as an intermediate. In Drosophila larvae, Cyp18a1 is expressed in many tissues that respond to 20E.
We have investigated the consequences of inactivating Cyp18a1 on Drosophila development, using null alleles generated by removing a P element and RNAi knockdown of the gene. Both methods result in pupal lethality, which may be due to impaired ecdysteroid breakdown. Our data suggest that inactivating 20E leads to developmental problems, and that CYP18A1 is a crucial enzyme in this process.

title: The sialyltransferase ST3GAL6 influences homing and survival in multiple myeloma.
text:
Glycosylation is a complex process by which oligosaccharide chains are covalently attached to proteins or lipids, and changes in this process, particularly increased sialylation, have been linked to cancer progression. Specifically, altered sialylation has been associated with the transformation and metastasis of multiple myeloma (MM) cells. While the role of sialylation in MM cell trafficking has been explored, the specific gene involved in this process, β-galactoside α-2,3-sialyltransferase, ST3GAL6, has remained unexamined.
Our study aims to investigate the role of ST3GAL6 in MM cell adhesion and migration. We found high expression of this gene in both MM cell lines and patients. ST3GAL6 is responsible for generating functional sialyl Lewis X, a critical component of selectin ligands in humans. In MM patients with high expression of ST3GAL6, we found a poor prognosis, as evidenced by inferior overall survival.
To validate our findings, we conducted in vitro experiments where we knocked down ST3GAL6 in MM cells. Our results showed a significant decrease in sialic acid levels on the cell surface, which led to a reduction in adhesion to bone marrow stromal cells and fibronectin, as well as transendothelial migration. These effects were replicated in vivo, where we found decreased homing and engraftment of ST3GAL6-knockdown MM cells to the bone marrow niche, accompanied by reduced tumor burden and improved survival.
Our study demonstrates that altered glycosylation, particularly sialylation, plays a crucial role in MM cell adhesion and migration. The identification of ST3GAL6 as a key player in this process provides new insights into MM biology and opens up potential therapeutic strategies for the treatment of this disease.

title: New developments in the epidemiology of cancer prognosis: traditional and molecular predictors of treatment response and survival.
text: Throughout history, numerous epidemiological studies have been conducted to identify factors that may influence cancer risk. In addition, there has been a longstanding tradition of examining potential genetic changes within cancer cells to predict recurrence and/or mortality after diagnosis. While these methods have proven useful, there has been relatively little focus on evaluating the molecular changes that occur within cancer cells during the early stages of disease progression.

title: Behavioral effects of estrogen receptor gene disruption in male mice.
text: Gonadal steroid hormones regulate sexually dimorphic brain development and behaviors by interacting with nuclear receptors. By manipulating these receptors, we can investigate molecular events in neurons related to instinctual mammalian behaviors. Our study employed transgenic mice lacking the estrogen receptor (ERKO) to investigate the role of ER activation by endogenous estrogen in the development of male- typical behaviors. Contrary to expectations, ERKO mice, despite being infertile, displayed normal motivation to mate but had reduced intromissions and virtually no ejaculations. Aggressive behaviors were significantly decreased, and male-typical offensive attacks were rarely observed in ERKO males. Furthermore, disrupting the ER gene resulted in demasculinized open-field behaviors. Interestingly, despite the apparent lack of functional ER protein in the brain, the androgen-dependent system appeared normal in ERKO mice. These findings suggest that ER gene expression during development plays a crucial role in organizing male-typical aggressive and emotional behaviors in addition to simple sexual behaviors.

title: High-Density Lipoproteins Exert Pro-inflammatory Effects on Macrophages via Passive Cholesterol Depletion and PKC-NF-κB/STAT1-IRF1 Signaling.
text: Membrane cholesterol is involved in various cellular signaling pathways and functions, but the impact of cholesterol depletion by high-density lipoproteins (HDLs) on inflammatory responses in macrophages has been largely unexplored. However, our study reveals an unexpected pro-inflammatory effect of HDL-mediated cholesterol depletion and lipid raft disruption in murine and human primary macrophages in vitro. These pro-inflammatory effects were also observed in vivo in peritoneal macrophages from apolipoprotein A-I transgenic mice, which have elevated HDL levels. Our findings suggest that low HDL levels compromise the innate immune response required for clearing bacterial infections in the lungs. We used various techniques, including expression analysis, chromatin immunoprecipitation-polymerase chain reaction (ChIP-PCR), and combinatorial pharmacological and genetic intervention studies, to reveal that both native and reconstituted HDL enhance Toll-like receptor-induced signaling by activating a protein kinase C (PKC)-nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1)/inositol-requiring protein 1 (IRF1) axis, leading to increased inflammatory cytokine expression. Our results demonstrate that HDL's pro-inflammatory activity supports the proper functioning of macrophage immune responses.

title: Hypoxia of the renal medulla--its implications for disease.
text: In land mammals, the kidney plays a crucial role in conserving water in arid environments through the Renal Medullary Concentrating Mechanism (RMCM). This mechanism, located in the medulla of the kidney, functions to reabsorb water and concentrate urine up to four times the osmolality of plasma. To achieve this, the RMCM employs a countercurrent system of vessels and tubules that actively reabsorbs sodium in a low-oxygen environment. This unique gradient of osmolality is essential for the kidney's water conservation activities. However, hypoxia of the medulla may increase susceptibility to acute and chronic renal injury, a phenomenon that will be discussed in this review. The RMCM is critical for maintaining proper kidney function, and dysfunction of this mechanism can lead to significant consequences for the animal's overall health.

title: Troponin concentrations for stratification of patients with acute coronary syndromes in relation to therapeutic efficacy of tirofiban. PRISM Study Investigators. Platelet Receptor Inhibition in Ischemic Syndrome Management.
text: A significant challenge for physicians is to identify patients with acute coronary syndromes who may benefit from treatment with glycoprotein-IIb/IIIa-receptor antagonists. In order to determine whether troponin concentrations can be used to stratify patients for benefit from treatment with tirofiban, we conducted a study involving 2222 patients with coronary artery disease who had experienced chest pain in the previous 24 hours. Baseline measurements of troponin I and troponin T were taken, and patients were randomly assigned to receive either tirofiban or heparin. The results showed that 629 (28.3%) patients had troponin I concentrations higher than the diagnostic threshold of 1.0 microg/L, and 644 (29.0%) had troponin T concentrations higher than 0.1 microg/L. The 30-day event rates (death, myocardial infarction) were significantly higher in patients with troponin-I-positive status (13.0%) compared to those with a negative status (4.9%, p<0.0001). Similarly, the 30-day event rates were higher in troponin-T-positive patients (13.7%) compared to those with a negative status (3.5%, p<0.001). In troponin-I-positive patients, tirofiban was found to lower the risk of death (adjusted hazard ratio 0.25 [95% CI 0.09-0.68], p=0.004) and myocardial infarction (0.37 [0.16-0.84], p=0.01) after 48 hours of infusion treatment. This benefit was observed in both medically managed patients (0.30 [0.10-0.84], p=0.004) and those undergoing revascularization (0.37 [0.15-0.93], p=0.02). Conversely, no treatment effect was observed in troponin-I-negative patients. Similar findings were observed in troponin-T-positive patients. Our results indicate that troponin I and troponin T can reliably identify high-risk patients with acute coronary syndromes who will benefit from tirofiban treatment, regardless of whether they are managed medically or undergo revascularization.

title: Evolution and function of ubiquitin-like protein-conjugation systems
text: Ubiquitin modifies other proteins through a covalent process. In recent years, numerous proteins have been found that share only subtle similarities with ubiquitin yet can also attach to other proteins. This has led to new insights into the evolutionary origins of the ubiquitin system, as parallels have been discovered between the activation of ubiquitin and the biosynthesis of certain enzyme cofactors.

title: Inflammatory biomarkers and exacerbations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text:
Background: Exacerbations of respiratory symptoms in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have significant and long-lasting consequences for patients. This study aimed to investigate the hypothesis that elevated levels of inflammatory biomarkers in individuals with stable COPD are associated with an increased risk of exacerbations.
Methods: This prospective cohort study included 61,650 participants from the Copenhagen City Heart Study (2001-2003) and the Copenhagen General Population Study (2003-2008). Of these, 6574 had COPD, defined as a ratio between forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity below 0.7. Baseline levels of C-reactive protein (CRP), fibrinogen, and leukocyte count were measured in participants at a time when they were not experiencing symptoms of exacerbations. Exacerbations were recorded and defined as short-course treatment with oral corticosteroids alone or in combination with an antibiotic or as a hospital admission due to COPD. Levels of CRP, fibrinogen, and leukocyte count were categorized as high or low according to cut points of 3 mg/L, 14 μmol/L, and 9 ×10(9)/L, respectively.
Results: During the follow-up period, 3083 exacerbations were recorded (mean, 0.5/participant). In the first year of follow-up, multivariable-adjusted odds ratios for having frequent exacerbations were 1.2 (95% CI, 0.7-2.2; 17 events/1000 person-years) for individuals with 1 high biomarker, 1.7 (95% CI, 0.9-3.2; 32 events/1000 person-years) for individuals with 2 high biomarkers, and 3.7 (95% CI, 1.9-7.4; 81 events/1000 person-years) for individuals with 3 high biomarkers compared with individuals who had no elevated biomarkers (9 events/1000 person-years; trend: P = 2 × 10(-5)). Corresponding hazard ratios using maximum follow-up time were 1.4 (95% CI, 1.1-1.8), 1.6 (95% CI, 1.3-2.2), and 2.5 (95% CI, 1.8-3.4), respectively (trend: P = 1 × 10(-8)). The addition of inflammatory biomarkers to a basic model including age, sex, FEV1 percent predicted, smoking, use of any inhaled medication, body mass index, history of previous exacerbations, and time since most recent prior exacerbation improved the C statistics from 0.71 to 0.73 (comparison: P = 9 × 10(-5)). Relative risks were consistent in those with milder COPD, in those with no history of frequent exacerbations, and in the 2 studies separately. The highest 5-year absolute risks of having frequent exacerbations in those with 3 high biomarkers (vs no high biomarkers) were 62% (vs 24%) for those with Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) grades C-D (n = 558), 98% (vs 64%) in those with a history of frequent exacerbations (n = 127), and 52% (vs 15%) for those with GOLD grades 3-4 (n = 465).
Conclusion: Simultaneously elevated levels of CRP and fibrinogen and leukocyte count in individuals with COPD were associated with increased risk of having exacerbations, even in those with milder COPD and in those without previous exacerbations. Further investigation is needed to determine the clinical value of these biomarkers for risk stratification.

title: Gene supplementation therapy for recessive forms of inherited retinal dystrophies
text: Over the past decade, gene supplementation therapy for inherited retinal degeneration has made significant progress. Early studies in animal models of disease showed modest improvements in retinal function and survival, which were further enhanced by advancements in the vectors used for gene transfer to the retina. In 2008, clinical trials for Leber congenital amaurosis caused by retinal pigment epithelium 65 deficiency began, and the results demonstrated the safety and efficacy of gene therapy for inherited retinal dystrophy. In this review, we will assess the development of gene supplementation therapy in the retina and explore the potential to treat various forms of inherited retinal degeneration with gene therapy.

title: Complex Tissue and Disease Modeling using hiPSCs.
text: Advancements in genetic models derived from human pluripotent stem cells have unlocked new opportunities for deciphering disease mechanisms and drug testing. However, it is possible that the true nature of a disease or a drug's interaction with the body can only be fully grasped when all the cells and surrounding components of a tissue are present and functionally mature. To fully leverage these models, it is likely that complex, multi-cellular structures that mimic the intricate architecture of tissue niches will be needed. Recent research has made significant strides in creating human tissue mimics, and we provide suggestions on how to further advance this field.

title: Reprogramming somatic cells towards pluripotency by cellular fusion.
text: Pluripotent cells emerge within the inner cell mass (ICM) of mammals, possessing the potential to generate all cell types of the adult organism through a process of commitment and directed differentiation. Although extensively studied over several decades, the mechanisms that govern cell fate selection and stabilization, as well as those that can be engineered to reverse it, remain partially understood. Reprogramming of somatic cells towards a pluripotent-like state can be achieved through various experimental approaches, including nuclear transfer, the provision of a defined cocktail of transcription factors, or fusion with a pluripotent stem cell partner. These techniques have been used to demonstrate the remarkable epigenetic plasticity of terminally differentiated cell types, as well as to identify the factors essential for pluripotent conversion. In this review, we summarize recent advances in cell fusion-based studies to better comprehend the basis of pluripotency and the epigenetic mechanisms underlying cell type interconversion.

title: Anorectic drugs and pulmonary hypertension from the bedside to the bench.
text: For more than three decades, drugs used for weight reduction, such as aminorex, a corticosteroid, and fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine, which decrease serotonin levels, have been utilized as an aid in weight loss for obese individuals. However, these drugs have been linked to a significant health issue, primary pulmonary hypertension (PPH), which caused an epidemic in Europe during the late 1960s and early 1970s after the use of aminorex, and later with fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine. Due to their connection to PPH, these drugs have been withdrawn from the market voluntarily. The underlying cause of PPH in patients treated with these drugs is uncertain; however, recent evidence suggests that abnormalities in potassium channels and 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), or serotonin, may play a role. Experimental evidence also suggests that these drugs inhibit 4-aminopyridine-sensitive currents in potassium channels, leading to vasoconstriction in pulmonary resistance vessels and perhaps smooth muscle cell proliferation. Additionally, 5-HT causes pulmonary artery vasoconstriction and smooth muscle cell proliferation, and its levels are known to be high in those with fenfluramine-induced PPH. However, a direct cause-and-effect relationship has not yet been confirmed. Despite the negative health consequences of these drugs, the epidemics of anorectic-related PPH have provided valuable insights into the causes of PPH unrelated to anorectic agents.

title: B-catenin deficiency, but not Myc deletion, suppresses the immediate phenotypes of APC loss in the liver.
text: Approximately 30% of hepatocellular carcinomas (HCCs) exhibit dysregulated Wnt signaling, making it essential to identify the downstream pathways activated by Wnt signaling. Using cre-lox technology, we deleted the Apc gene in adult mouse livers and observed a rapid increase in nuclear beta-catenin and c-Myc within 4 days of gene deletion, leading to induced proliferation and hepatomegaly. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we investigated the impact of APC inactivation in the presence or absence of beta-catenin and c-Myc. Our findings revealed that beta-catenin loss rescues both the proliferation and hepatomegaly phenotypes after APC loss, while c-Myc deletion had no effect on these phenotypes in the liver, indicating distinct Wnt signaling pathways within the liver compared to the intestine. Specifically, the majority of Wnt targets in the liver are beta-catenin-dependent but c-Myc-independent, which has important implications for our understanding of HCC development.

title: Uncoupling Mitochondrial Respiration for Diabesity.
text: Until recently, the mechanism of adaptive thermogenesis was believed to be attributed to the expression of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) in brown and beige adipocytes. UCP1 is known to catalyze a proton leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane, resulting in uncoupled oxidative metabolism and a subsequent increase in energy expenditure without the production of ATP. As such, increasing brown and beige adipose tissue with augmented UCP1 expression was considered a viable target for obesity-related disorders. However, recent findings have uncovered an UCP1-independent pathway to uncouple mitochondrial respiration. A secreted enzyme, PM20D1, which is enriched in UCP1+ adipocytes, exhibits both catalytic and hydrolytic activity, reversibly forming N-acyl amino acids. These N-acyl amino acids act as endogenous uncouplers of mitochondrial respiration at physiological concentrations. Intriguingly, administration of PM20D1 or its products to diet-induced obese mice leads to improved glucose tolerance, resulting from increased energy expenditure. In short-term studies, treated animals demonstrate no toxicity and exhibit a 10% weight loss primarily consisting of adipose tissue. Further exploration of this metabolic pathway may uncover novel therapeutic strategies for diabesity, the combined disease state of diabetes and obesity.

title: A functional polymorphism in the prodynorphin gene promotor is associated with temporal lobe epilepsy.
text: The PDYN gene, which encodes the anticonvulsant peptide dynorphin, is a promising candidate for a seizure suppressor gene and potential modulator of susceptibility to temporal lobe epilepsy. We investigated this possibility through a case-control association study involving 155 patients with non-lesional temporal lobe epilepsy and 202 controls. Our findings revealed that low expression of the PDYN promoter L-alleles was associated with an increased risk of temporal lobe epilepsy in individuals with a family history of seizures. Additionally, regardless of familial background, individuals who were homozygous for the L-allele were found to have a higher risk of experiencing secondarily generalized seizures and status epilepticus.

title: Cardiovascular and renal benefits of dry bean and soybean intake.
text: Beans and soybeans are nutrient-dense and fiber-rich, providing high-quality protein sources. Studies have shown that consuming both dry beans and soybeans have protective and therapeutic effects on overall health. Dry beans have been found to lower serum cholesterol levels, improve diabetic state, and provide metabolic benefits for weight control. Soybeans are unique in their isoflavone content, including genistein and diadzein, which have various biological functions. Soybeans and soy-based foods have been shown to have multifaceted health-promoting effects, including cholesterol reduction, improved vascular health, maintained bone density, and reduced menopausal symptoms. While soy appears to have salutary effects on renal function, the mechanisms are not well understood. While populations consuming high levels of soy have lower cancer prevalence, experimental data are insufficient to establish a protective role for soy. As the availability of legume products and resources increases, incorporating dry beans and soyfoods into the diet can be practical and enjoyable. With the shift towards a more plant-based diet, dry beans and soy can be potent tools in the prevention and treatment of chronic diseases.

title: Nonuniform probability of glutamate release at a hippocampal synapse.
text: A modification in the likelihood of neurotransmitter release (Pr) is a fundamental mechanism underlying synaptic plasticity. Although Pr is often assumed to be consistent across all terminals within a single synapse, this assumption cannot be justified given the heterogeneous size and structure of synaptic terminals in the central nervous system. Pr was measured at excitatory synapses on cultured hippocampal neurons by analyzing the gradual block of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor-mediated synaptic currents through the irreversible opening of the channel by MK-801. Pr varied non-uniformly (ranging from 0.09 to 0.54) among terminals arising from a single axon, with most exhibiting a low Pr. Interestingly, terminals with higher Pr are more susceptible to activity-dependent modulation that occurs during long-term potentiation.

title: An autoimmune disease, APECED, caused by mutations in a novel gene featuring two PHD-type zinc-finger domains
text: Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy (APECED) is the sole identified systemic autoimmune disorder with a well-established monogenic etiology, and the first autoimmune condition located outside the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region. The underlying biochemical deficiency in APECED remains unidentified. Our team has isolated a novel gene, AIRE, encoding a hypothetical nuclear protein sporting two PHD-type zinc-finger motifs, suggesting its role in transcriptional regulation. Five mutations in AIRE have been found in individuals with this condition. This discovery represents the first instance of a single-gene defect underlying a systemic human autoimmune disorder, offering an opportunity to investigate the molecular foundations of autoimmunity.

title: NuA4 lysine acetyltransferase Esa1 is targeted to coding regions and stimulates transcription elongation with Gcn5.
