HUVECs were cultured continuously in the presence of increasing concentrations of oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) for 4, 6, 12, and 24 hours to identify early- and late-induced genes, respectively, with non-stimulated controls taken at 0 hours. We evaluated the expression of pro-inflammatory adhesion molecules, such as vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), intracellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), E-selectin, KLF-2, and its target genes endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) by real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) or Western blot analysis.
To determine the effect of Tregs on KLF-2 expression in HUVECs, we cultured HUVECs alone or with anti-CD3 mAbs activated Tregs, followed by addition of ox-LDL (50 mg/L) for 6 hours. We compared the expression levels of pro-inflammatory adhesion molecules, KLF-2, eNOS, and PAI-1 in these cultures to the expression levels in control cultures. Our results showed that ox-LDL treatment increased the expression of pro-inflammatory adhesion molecules and decreased the expression of eNOS, accompanied by a significant decrease in KLF-2 expression, with a dose- and time-dependent manner.

Furthermore, we found that the inhibitory effect of ox-LDL on KLF-2 expression was reversed by the addition of Tregs. To investigate the possible mechanism underlying this observation, we used small interfering RNA (siRNA) to reduce endogenous KLF-2 expression and found that this led to a partial reversal of the suppressive effect of Tregs on HUVECs activation. These findings strongly suggest that KLF-2 plays a critical role in the Tregs-mediated protection of endothelial function by regulating pro-inflammatory adhesion molecules expression.
Our results also indicate that Tregs-mediated KLF2 expression in HUVECs impaired by ox-LDL requires both cell-to-cell contact and soluble factors, which further highlights the complex interplay of cellular and molecular mechanisms involved in this process.
In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that Tregs can protect endothelial function by regulating KLF-2 and its downstream transcriptional targets, which is largely dependent on cell-to-cell contact and soluble factors. These observations have important implications for our understanding of the mechanisms underlying endothelial dysfunction and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the prevention and treatment of endothelial-related diseases.

title: Metformin Normalizes Type 2 Diabetes-Induced Decrease in Cell Proliferation and Neuroblast Differentiation in the Rat Dentate Gyrus
text: In this study, we investigated the effects of metformin, one of the most commonly prescribed drugs for treating type 2 diabetes, on cell proliferation and neuroblast differentiation in the subgranular zone of the hippocampal dentate gyrus (SZDG) in Zucker diabetic fatty (ZDF) rats, which are a model for type 2 diabetes. To do this, we orally administered metformin to 14-week-old ZDF rats for two weeks, and then sacrificed the animals at 16 weeks of age. During this period, we observed that blood glucose levels were higher in vehicle-treated ZDF rats compared to Zucker lean control (ZLC) rats. Notably, metformin treatment significantly decreased blood glucose levels from 15.5 weeks of age. In the SZDG, we found that the number of Ki67-positive cells (a marker for cell proliferation) and doublecortin-positive cells (a marker for differentiated neuroblasts) were significantly lower in vehicle-treated ZDF rats compared to ZLC rats. Interestingly, metformin treatment led to a significant increase in the number of Ki67- and doublecortin-positive cells in the SZDG compared to the vehicle-treated ZDF group. These results suggest that diabetes significantly reduces cell proliferation and neuroblast differentiation in the SZDG, but metformin treatment can normalize this reduction in the diabetic rats.

title: Molecular mechanisms underlying tumor dormancy.
text: Evidence suggests that a significant portion of otherwise healthy individuals harbor dormant, microscopic tumors. These undetectable tumors are common and highly prevalent, with the ability to remain asymptomatic due to their small size and non-invasive nature. Advancements in diagnostic imaging and molecular biology have made it clear that these neoplasms can remain dormant for extended periods of time without expanding in size. One crucial mechanism behind tumor dormancy is the tumor population's capacity to induce angiogenesis, which hinders the tumor's expansion. Most tumors are believed to arise as microscopic, non-angiogenic neoplasms that cannot grow in size until a blood supply is established. It is becoming increasingly clear that cancer does not progress in a continuous, exponential manner, but rather in stages. Clinical cancer is usually diagnosed at late, symptomatic stages, when tumors have grown to a detectable size. Dormancy in primary tumors refers to the time between the carcinogenic transformation event and the onset of inexorable growth, while it can also occur in minimally residual or occult disease from treated tumors or micro-metastases. The existence of dormant tumors has significant implications for early cancer detection and treatment. Understanding the regulatory mechanisms involved in these processes could lead to the identification of novel early cancer biomarkers and the development of dormancy-promoting tumor therapies. Despite their high prevalence and clinical importance, this area of cancer research has been understudied. In this mini-review, we summarize observations, models, and experimental approaches to study tumor dormancy. We also discuss analogies and distinctions between tumor dormancy and cellular dormancy, as well as the "exit from tumor dormancy" and "onset of the angiogenic switch".

title: The myeloid transcription factor GATA-2 regulates the viral UL144 gene during human cytomegalovirus latency in an isolate-specific manner.
text: It is commonly accepted that after initial infection, human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) establishes a lifelong latent infection in specific progenitor cells and other myeloid lineage cells. In this study, we found that the viral UL144 gene is expressed during latent infection in two cell types within the myeloid lineage, CD34(+) and CD14(+) monocytes, and that the UL144 protein is functional in these cells. Interestingly, this latency-associated expression of UL144 varies among HCMV isolates and is dependent on the presence of functional GATA-2 transcription factor binding sites in the UL144 promoter, as opposed to the latency-associated gene LUNA, which is also regulated by GATA-2 but expresses uniformly during latent infection regardless of virus isolate. Upon further examination of the HCMV latency-associated transcriptome, our findings suggest that the transcriptome may be highly variable among virus isolates and is influenced by the specific combination of transcription factor binding sites present in the promoters of latency-associated genes.

title: How to control residual cardiovascular risk despite statin treatment: focusing on HDL-cholesterol.
text: Managing dyslipidemia in high-risk patients with cardiovascular disease involves reducing low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C) levels as the primary target. However, even after achieving low LDL-C targets, some patients may still experience cardiovascular events. This is possibly due to elevated triglyceride (TG) levels and low high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C) levels, which are recognized as independent risk factors for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Atherogenic dyslipidemia, characterized by low HDL-C, high TG, and small, dense LDL particles, is a common phenotype in subjects with insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome. To further reduce the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD), raising HDL-C and lowering TG levels may serve as secondary therapeutic targets for patients who achieve LDL-C levels below current recommendations but are still at risk of CHD. While increasing HDL-C levels alone has not been confirmed to reduce CHD in large randomized clinical trials, the importance of functional HDL in reducing CHD remains controversial. Large CHD endpoint trials that include many patients with diabetes are currently underway to evaluate combination treatments with statin and niacin, fibrates, or cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitors compared to statin alone treatments. This review discusses the rationale and importance of increasing HDL-C levels with and without lowering TG levels in the treatment and prevention of cardiovascular events.

title: The prevalence of congenital malformations is still higher in pregnant women with pregestational diabetes despite near-normal HbA1c: a literature review.
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the association between maternal hyperglycemia during pregnancy and the risk of congenital malformations in women with pregestational diabetes (both type 1 and type 2). We also focused on the impact of maternal glycemic control, specifically HbA1c levels in early pregnancy, on the risk of congenital malformations.
Our literature review included original studies published in English after 1997 that reported data on congenital malformations and HbA1c levels in pregnant women with pregestational diabetes. We included nine studies with a total of 6225 women with type 1 diabetes and 2334 women with type 2 diabetes.
Our findings revealed that the prevalence of congenital malformations was significantly higher in women with pregestational diabetes compared to the background population (6.4% vs 4.3%). Within the group of women with pregestational diabetes, those with HbA1c levels below 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) in early pregnancy had a twofold increased risk of congenital malformations compared to those with HbA1c levels of 53-64 mmol/mol (7.0-8.0%).
In conclusion, our study showed that pregnant women with pregestational diabetes are at a threefold higher risk of congenital malformations compared to the background population. However, maintaining HbA1c levels below 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) in early pregnancy may also increase the risk of congenital malformations.

title: Local and systemic insulin resistance resulting from hepatic activation of IKK-beta and NF-kappaB.
text: We have demonstrated that obesity and a high-fat diet (HFD) lead to the activation of NF-κB and its downstream targets in the liver. To mimic this state of chronic, subacute inflammation in mice, we selectively expressed a constitutively active form of IKK-b in hepatocytes using transgenic mice, referred to as LIKK mice. These mice exhibited a type 2 diabetes phenotype characterized by hyperglycemia, profound hepatic insulin resistance, and moderate systemic insulin resistance, including effects in muscle. We found that the hepatic production of proinflammatory cytokines, including IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-alpha, was increased in LIKK mice to a similar extent as in mice fed an HFD. Parallel increases in cytokine signaling were observed in the liver and muscle of LIKK mice. We also found that insulin resistance could be improved by systemic neutralization of IL-6 or salicylate inhibition of IKK-β. Interestingly, hepatic expression of the IκBα superrepressor (LISR) reversed the phenotype of both LIKK mice and mice fed an HFD. These findings suggest that lipid accumulation in the liver leads to subacute hepatic inflammation through NF-κB activation and downstream cytokine production, which in turn causes insulin resistance both locally in the liver and systemically.

title: Homelessness and health.
text: Homelessness has a profound impact on the health of tens of thousands of Canadians, leading to a higher risk of early mortality and an array of health issues, such as seizures, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, musculoskeletal disorders, tuberculosis, and skin and foot problems. The unique challenges faced by homeless individuals hinder their access to quality healthcare, highlighting the need for further research to develop more effective strategies for delivering care to this vulnerable population.

title: Serum metabolomics in animal models and human disease.
text:
Objective of Review:
This study aims to explore recent applications of serum metabolomics in both human and animal studies. The primary focus is on comprehending the intrinsic variability in human metabolism and the use of serum metabolomics in disease classification.
Recent Findings:
Several studies have utilized serum metabolomics to develop non-invasive biomarkers of disease and/or monitor the effects of nutritional and genetic interventions. While significant progress has been made in identifying common changes in aging, menopause, and cancer, challenges in interpreting these findings persist. These include the small sample sizes in most human studies and the disparities between human and rodent metabolomes. However, a comprehensive metabolic screen of over 1,000 healthy individuals (the HUMSERM project) has illuminated numerous variables that can be used to refine the interpretation and design of future human studies, as well as data mining.
Summary:
While some common serum metabolome alterations have been identified, inconsistencies persist. A comprehensive human serum metabolome database would be valuable in guiding future research in both humans and animals.

title: Differential Requirement of the Extracellular Domain in Activation of Class B G Protein-coupled Receptors.
text: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) from the secretin-like (class B) family play a crucial role in hormonal homeostasis and are vital drug targets for the treatment of metabolic disorders and neuronal diseases. These receptors consist of a large N-terminal extracellular domain (ECD) and a transmembrane domain (TMD) with the characteristic GPCR arrangement of seven transmembrane helices. Class B GPCRs are activated by peptide hormones with their C termini attached to the ECD and their N termini attached to the TMD. It is believed that the ECD functions as an affinity trap to bind and localize the hormone to the receptor, allowing the N termini of the hormone to insert into the TMD and induce conformational changes that activate downstream signaling. However, our research reveals that class B GPCRs exhibit diverse requirements for the ECD in hormone activation. In certain receptors, such as corticotrophin-releasing factor receptor 1 (CRF1R), parathyroid hormone receptor (PTH1R), and pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide type 1 receptor (PAC1R), the ECD is essential for high-affinity hormone binding, but this requirement can be bypassed by proximity and mass action effects. In contrast, the ECD is necessary for signaling even when the hormone is covalently linked to the TMD in receptors like glucagon receptor (GCGR) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R). Additionally, our findings indicate that small molecules that interact with the intracellular side of GLP-1R can activate the receptor only when the ECD is present, suggesting a direct role of the ECD in GLP-1R activation.

title: Genome-wide maps of histone modifications unwind in vivo chromatin states of the hair follicle lineage.
text:
Using mouse skin as a model, we investigate the intricate mechanisms that govern the regenerative capabilities of hair follicle stem cells (HF-SCs). By analyzing the changes in chromatin structure and gene expression in quiescent and activated HF-SCs, as well as their progeny, we uncover a complex network of regulatory elements involved in the maintenance of stem cell identity.
We find that polycomb-group (PcG)-mediated trimethylation of histone H3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me3) plays a crucial role in the progression of HF-lineage commitment. In HF-SCs, PcG represses the expression of genes involved in non-skin lineages and hair follicle differentiation, while in the committed, transit-amplifying (TA) progeny, these regulators remain PcG-repressed, and HF-SC regulators acquire H3K27me3 marks. Interestingly, genes that are poised in embryonic stem cells and active in HF-SCs, but repressed in TA progeny, encode key transcription factors and signaling regulators that are essential for balancing HF-SC quiescence.
Our findings reveal the importance of chromatin mapping in understanding the complex behavior of HF-SCs and define the roles of PcG-mediated repression in governing a fate switch between quiescence and activation. By elucidating the molecular mechanisms that govern the regenerative capabilities of HF-SCs, we provide new insights into the mechanisms that control tissue homeostasis and repair.

title: Two classes of endogenous small RNAs in Tetrahymena thermophila.
text: In Tetrahymena thermophila, small RNAs play a crucial role in RNA interference (RNAi) pathways, regulating RNA cleavage, translational repression, or DNA/chromatin modification. Specifically, approximately 27-30-nucleotide (nt) RNAs govern developmentally regulated DNA elimination through an RNAi mechanism. This study characterizes the sequence features of these RNAs and a second, approximately 23-24-nt RNA class representing a different RNAi pathway. Notably, these findings unveil the existence of multiple endogenous RNAi pathways in the unicellular T. thermophila, a complexity previously thought to be exclusive to multicellular organisms.

title: The binding of maize DHN1 to lipid vesicles. Gain of structure and lipid specificity.
text:
Dehydrins (DHNs; late embryogenesis abundant D-11) are a family of plant proteins that are induced in response to abiotic stresses such as drought, low temperature, and salinity, or during the late stages of embryogenesis. The proteins have been found to be intrinsically unstructured, but they contain a specific sequence known as the "K segment" that resembles a class A2 amphipathic alpha-helical domain found in other proteins. The presence of the K segment raises the question of whether DHNs bind lipids, bilayers, or phospholipid vesicles.
To investigate, we studied the binding of maize (Zea mays) DHN DHN1 to lipid vesicles containing acidic phospholipids. We found that DHN1 bound more favorably to smaller vesicles than to larger ones, and that the association of DHN1 with vesicles resulted in an apparent increase in the protein's alpha-helicity. These findings suggest that DHNs, and possibly similar plant stress proteins in the late embryogenesis abundant and cold-regulated classes, may undergo function-related conformational changes at the water/membrane interface, potentially related to the stabilization of vesicles or other endomembrane structures under stress conditions.

title: Requirement of heterochromatin for cohesion at centromeres.
text: Centromeres are often characterized by heterochromatin, but the role of this silent chromatin during cell division remains a mystery. As cells divide, newly replicated sister chromatids must stick together until anaphase, when the cohesin protein Scc1/Rad21 is broken. In metazoans, chromosome arm cohesins dissolve during prophase, leaving centromeres as the only remaining connection between sister chromatids. It is unclear what distinguishes centromere cohesion from arm cohesion. In fission yeast, the Heterochromatin protein 1 counterpart Swi6 is crucial for maintaining sister centromere cohesion. Swi6 is necessary for the Rad21-cohesin's association with centromeres but not along chromosome arms, indicating that it plays a key role in separating centromere cohesion from arm cohesion. Therefore, one of the functions of centromeric heterochromatin is to attract cohesin protein, thereby ensuring sister centromere cohesion and proper chromosome segregation during cell division.

title: Gene expression in human skeletal muscle: alternative normalization method and effect of repeated biopsies
text: The reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) method has recently gained popularity in determining transcription and mRNA content in rodent and human muscle samples. However, relying on endogenous controls for adjusting cDNA variance between samples is not always optimal. To address this limitation, we investigated several new normalization methods, including the use of cDNA content determined by PicoGreen and OliGreen fluorophores. We also examined the effects of repeated muscle biopsies on mRNA gene expression and the spatial heterogeneity of mRNA expression across the muscle. Our results show that standard curves constructed from oligo standards revealed high sensitivity and linearity (R2>0.99) with both OliGreen and PicoGreen reagents, when analyzing serial dilutions of RT samples. Additionally, we found that PicoGreen reagent detected RNA:DNA hybrid content in RT samples with high sensitivity. Standard curves constructed from double-stranded lambda DNA (1-10 ng) and serial dilutions of RT samples resulted in linearity with R2>0.99. Our findings suggest that PicoGreen and OliGreen may serve as potential alternatives for normalization in human gene expression studies. Furthermore, our study found that multiple muscle biopsies obtained from the same muscle did not influence the mRNA response induced by an acute exercise bout for any of the genes examined.

title: The Impact of Location of Progressive Visual Field Loss on Longitudinal Changes in Quality of Life of Patients with Glaucoma.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between changes in quality of life (QoL) scores and rates of progressive visual field loss in different regions of the visual field in patients with glaucoma.
The study included 236 patients with glaucomatous visual field loss who were followed for an average of 4.3±1.5 years. Each year, the patients completed the 25-item National Eye Institute Visual Functioning Questionnaire (NEI VFQ-25) and had standard automated perimetry (SAP) tests conducted every 6 months. The visual field loss was categorized into four different regions: central inferior, central superior, peripheral inferior, and peripheral superior. The study found a significant association between changes in QoL scores and changes in different regions of the visual field. Specifically, a 1 decibel (dB)/year decline in binocular mean sensitivity in the central inferior area was associated with a decline of 2.6 units/year in NEI VFQ-25 scores (R(2) = 35%; P < 0.001). The association was weaker for the central superior, peripheral superior, and peripheral inferior areas (R(2) values of 30%, 24%, and 19%, respectively). Moreover, patients who had worse visual field sensitivity at baseline experienced greater declines in QoL scores over time.
In conclusion, the study found that progressive decline in sensitivity in the central inferior area of the visual field had the strongest association with longitudinal decline in QoL in patients with glaucoma.

title: Use of thiazolidinediones and the risk of bladder cancer among people with type 2 diabetes: a meta-analysis.
text:
Background: Patients with type 2 diabetes have a 40% higher risk of developing bladder cancer compared to the general population. Thiazolidinediones, particularly pioglitazone, have been linked to this increased risk. To investigate this association, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies examining the risk of bladder cancer among adults with type 2 diabetes taking thiazolidinediones.
Methods: We searched major biomedical databases and grey literature sources from inception to March 2012 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort studies, and case-control studies that reported on incident bladder cancer among individuals with type 2 diabetes who either (v. never) were exposed to pioglitazone, rosiglitazone, or any thiazolidinedione. We selected 4 RCTs, 5 cohort studies, and 1 case-control study for analysis, with a total of 2,657,365 patients, of whom 3643 had bladder cancer, for an overall incidence rate of 53.1 per 100,000 person-years.
Results: The one RCT that investigated pioglitazone use found no significant association with bladder cancer (risk ratio [RR] 2.36, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.91-6.13). However, the cohort studies of thiazolidinediones (pooled RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.04-1.26; I(2) = 0%) and of pioglitazone specifically (pooled RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.07-1.39; I(2) = 0%) showed significant associations with bladder cancer. In contrast, no significant association was observed in the two RCTs that evaluated rosiglitazone use (pooled RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.34-2.23; I(2) = 0%).
Interpretation: Our findings support the hypothesis that thiazolidinediones, particularly pioglitazone, are associated with an increased risk of bladder cancer among adults with type 2 diabetes. These results suggest that healthcare providers should exercise caution when prescribing thiazolidinediones, particularly pioglitazone, to patients with type 2 diabetes.

title: Immune signaling by RIG-I-like receptors.
text:
Here is a possible revision of the text:
The RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs) RIG-I, MDA5, and LGP2 play a crucial role in sensing virus infection and initiating antiviral immunity. These receptors detect viral RNA ligands or processed self-RNA in the cytoplasm and trigger innate immunity and inflammation, leading to the regulation of gene expression that controls infection. RLRs also cooperate with other factors in signaling crosstalk networks, such as Toll-like receptors, to modulate the adaptive immune response. The regulation of RLR signaling occurs at various levels, including autoregulation, ligand and cofactor interactions, and posttranslational modifications. Dysregulation of RLR expression or abnormal RLR signaling has been implicated in the development of autoimmune diseases, highlighting the importance of understanding RLR signaling mechanisms to develop RLR-targeted therapeutics for antiviral and immune-modifying applications.

title: Ionizing radiation-induced long-term expression of senescence markers in mice is independent of p53 and immune status.
text: Irradiation has been shown to induce the formation of senescence markers, a phenotype that coincides with lifelong impaired repair and regeneration of irradiated tissues. We hypothesized that IR-induced senescence markers could persist long-term in vivo, potentially contributing to the permanent loss of tissue function. Our study shows that mouse tissues exposed to a sublethal dose of IR display persistent (up to 45 weeks, the maximum time analyzed) DNA damage foci and increased p16(INK4a) expression, two hallmarks of cellular senescence and aging. BrdU-labeling experiments revealed that IR-induced damaged cells are partially eliminated, virtually independent of the DNA damage response modulator p53 and the presence of an intact immune system. Surprisingly, the accumulation of damaged cells occurred without relying on p53, as their levels were similar in wild-type and Rag2(-/-) gammaC(-/-) mice, which are deficient in T, B, and NK cells. Our findings thus provide strong evidence that exposure to IR causes long-term expression of senescence markers in vivo, an effect that may contribute to the reduced tissue functionality commonly observed in cancer survivors.

title: Cranial neural crest and the building of the vertebrate head
text: The formation of the skull in vertebrates is a multi-step process involving complex molecular and morphogenetic events that result in unique craniofacial structures for each species. A specific type of neural cell called the neural crest plays a crucial role in this process, serving as the main source of craniofacial mesenchyme. There has been debate about the extent to which the neural crest contains intrinsic patterning information, but recent advances have shown that environmental signals also play a crucial role in coordinating craniofacial morphogenesis in both space and time.

title: Tamoxifen resistance in MCF7 cells promotes EMT-like behaviour and involves modulation of beta-catenin phosphorylation.
text: In our previous studies, we demonstrated that breast cancer cells exhibit altered growth rates and aggressive behavior after acquiring endocrine resistance. To investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying this phenomenon, we examined the integrity of the protein complex responsible for cell-cell adhesion in our tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer model. In vitro culture experiments revealed that tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells (TamR) had loosely packed colonies with disrupted cell-cell junctions, indicating a shift towards an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Neutralizing E-cadherin function promoted the invasion and inhibited the aggregation of endocrine-sensitive MCF7 cells, while having little impact on TamR cells. Additionally, TamR cells displayed increased levels of tyrosine-phosphorylated beta-catenin and decreased levels of serine/threonine-phosphorylated beta-catenin, accompanied by loss of association between beta-catenin and E-cadherin, and elevated cytoplasmic and nuclear beta-catenin levels. Inhibition of EGFR kinase activity in TamR cells reduced beta-catenin tyrosine phosphorylation, increased beta-catenin-E-cadherin association, and promoted cell-cell adhesion. These findings suggest that homotypic adhesion in tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer cells is dysfunctional due to EGFR-driven modification of beta-catenin phosphorylation and may contribute to the enhanced aggressive phenotype and transition towards a mesenchymal phenotype in vitro.

title: Expression profiles of Toll-like receptors in non-small cell lung cancer and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
text: In this study, the expression of Toll-like receptors (TLRs) was investigated in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) from patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), and healthy controls. TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, TLR7, TLR8, and TLR9 mRNA expression was quantified using real-time reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), while TLR3, TLR7, and TLR9 protein expression was assessed on BALF T-lymphocytes using flow cytometry. The results showed that TLR3 mRNA expression was significantly higher in NSCLC patients compared to IPF patients and controls, while TLR7 mRNA expression was significantly higher in both NSCLC and IPF groups compared to controls. TLR9 expression at the mRNA level was significantly higher in both NSCLC and IPF groups compared to controls. Additionally, TLR2 mRNA expression was significantly higher in IPF patients compared to controls. Flow cytometry revealed decreased TLR3 and TLR9 expression in IPF patients compared to the NSCLC group and decreased TLR9 expression in IPF compared to the controls. TLR2 protein expression was significantly higher in IPF patients compared to NSCLC patients. These findings suggest that increased expression of endosomal TLRs in NSCLC patients and elevated expression of TLR2 in pulmonary fibrosis are the main results of this study, which do not provide support for a common TLR pathway hypothesis between NSCLC and IPF.

title: A protein farnesyltransferase inhibitor ameliorates disease in a mouse model of progeria.
text: Progerias are uncommon genetic conditions that manifest through accelerated aging. Certain progeroid disorders are caused by mutations that result in the accumulation of a modified form of prelamin A, a protein crucial to the structural framework of the cell nucleus. In progeria, the abnormal accumulation of modified prelamin A disrupts this framework, leading to distorted nuclei. Previous studies have shown that inhibiting the enzyme farnesyltransferase (FTI) can reverse this cellular abnormality. We investigated the efficacy of an FTI, ABT-100, in Zmpste24-deficient mice, a mouse model of progeria. The mice treated with FTI exhibited improved body weight, grip strength, bone density, and percentage of survival at 20 weeks of age. These findings suggest that FTIs may have potential benefits for humans with progeria.

title: A rare mutation in UNC5C predisposes to late-onset Alzheimer's disease and increases neuronal cell death
text: We have identified a rare genetic mutation, T835M (rs137875858), in the UNC5C netrin receptor gene that is associated with an increased risk of late-onset Alzheimer's disease. This mutation was found to segregate with disease in two families in an autosomal dominant pattern and was also associated with disease across four large case-control cohorts (odds ratio = 2.15, Pmeta = 0.0095). The mutation alters a conserved residue in the hinge region of UNC5C and, in vitro studies have shown that it leads to increased cell death in human HEK293T cells and in rodent neurons. Additionally, neurons expressing T835M UNC5C were found to be more susceptible to cell death from various neurotoxic stimuli, including β-amyloid (Aβ), glutamate, and staurosporine. Considering the high expression of UNC5C in the adult nervous system, particularly in the hippocampus, we propose that one possible mechanism by which T835M UNC5C contributes to the risk of Alzheimer's disease is by increasing susceptibility to neuronal cell death, particularly in vulnerable regions of the disease brain.

title: Treatment of active tuberculosis in HIV-coinfected patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text:
Background: Patients with HIV infection and tuberculosis (TB) are at a higher risk of death, treatment failure, and relapse. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and cohort studies were conducted to evaluate the impact of duration and dosing schedule of rifamycin and use of antiretroviral therapy in the treatment of active TB in HIV-positive patients.
Methods: Included studies had to have confirmed microbiological diagnosis of TB, failure, and/or relapse, and patients received standardized rifampin- or rifabutin-containing regimens. Pooled cumulative incidence of treatment failure, death during treatment, and relapse were calculated using random-effects models. Multivariable meta-regression was performed using negative binomial regression.
Results: After screening 5158 citations, 6 randomized trials and 21 cohort studies were included. Relapse was more common with regimens using 2 months of rifamycin (adjusted risk ratio, 3.6; 95% confidence interval, 1.1-11.7) than with regimens using rifamycin for at least 8 months. Compared with daily therapy in the initial phase (n=3352 patients from 35 study arms), thrice-weekly therapy (n=211 patients from 5 study arms) was associated with higher rates of failure (adjusted risk ratio, 4.0; 95% confidence interval, 1.5-10.4) and relapse [adjusted risk ratio, 4.8; 95% confidence interval, 1.8-12.8). There were trends toward higher relapse rates if rifamycins were used for only 6 months, compared with > or =8 months or if antiretroviral therapy was not used.
Conclusions: This review raises serious concerns regarding current recommendations for the treatment of HIV-TB coinfection. The data suggest that at least 8 months of rifamycin therapy, initial daily dosing, and concurrent antiretroviral therapy might be associated with better outcomes, but adequately powered randomized trials are urgently needed to confirm this.

title: Crystal structure and association behaviour of the GluR2 amino-terminal domain.
text: Neurotransmission is rapid and mediated largely by ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs), which are tetrameric, ligand-gated ion channel proteins composed of three subfamilies: AMPA, kainate, and NMDA receptors. These receptors share a common modular-domain architecture, but each subfamily forms active channels exclusively through the assembly of subunits within the same subfamily. While the molecular basis for this subfamily-specific assembly is not fully understood, we propose mechanisms by which the amino-terminal domain (ATD) of AMPA receptors guides receptor assembly based on crystal structures of the GluR2-ATD. Specifically, we found that the ATDs of GluR1 and GluR2 form tightly associated dimers, providing a molecular explanation for how the ATD directs subfamily-specific receptor assembly.

title: Deficiency in l-serine deaminase results in abnormal growth and cell division of Escherichia coli K-12.
text: The loss of the ability to deaminate L-serine drastically impairs growth and cell division in Escherichia coli K-12. A strain from which the genes (sdaA, sdaB, tdcG) coding for this organism's three L-serine deaminases have been deleted grows well in glucose minimal medium but, upon subculture into minimal medium with glucose and casamino acids, exhibits abnormal cell growth, resulting in the formation of large, aberrant cells that often lyse. When inoculated into Luria-Bertani (LB) broth with or without glucose, the bacteria form elongated filaments. The provision of S-adenosylmethionine restores cell division in LB broth with glucose, and significantly improves growth in medium with casamino acids. Based on these findings, we propose that E. coli cell replication is regulated by methylation, and that an elevated intracellular L-serine concentration, in the presence of other amino acids, depletes the cell of S-adenosylmethionine, thereby preventing normal cell division.

title: Stem cell characteristics in prostate cancer cell lines.
text:
The recent studies suggest the existence of a small, stem-like cell population in various human cancers, including prostate cancer (PCa). This study aimed to investigate the stem cell properties of six established PCa cell lines (DU145, DuCaP, LAPC-4, 22Rv1, LNCaP, and PC-3) in vitro.
The study design included low-density plating and serial passaging to test the colony-forming efficiency and self-renewal ability of morphologically distinguishable holoclones and paraclones. The expression of the putative stem cell marker CD133 and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) was analyzed using flow cytometry and immunohistochemical staining.
The results demonstrated that five out of six cell lines formed clear holo-, mero-, and paraclones. However, unlike paraclones, the DU145 holoclones were able to be maintained in culture for several passages, indicating self-renewal ability. Using FACS analysis, only a small fraction (0.01%) of CD133(+) cells were detected in DU145 cells, and they did not show more holoclone formation than marker-negative cells or unselected cells. Immunohistochemistry revealed alpha2-integrin and BCRP as potential stem cell markers and CK5 with the combination of CK18 to distinguish transient amplifying cells.
Overall, these findings suggest that stem-like cells may be present in some established PCa cell lines, but CD133 selection does not enrich for these cells.

title: Resistance to antimicrobials in humans and animals.
text: The emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) began to raise concerns in the mid-20th century, with reports of its dangers in clinical medicine and the use of antibiotics in animal feed as growth promoters by the 1990s.1-3 Initially, overuse of antimicrobials was seen as the primary culprit and reducing their use was believed to be the solution. However, the issue is not that simple. The concept of overuse has proven too simplistic, as evidence of overprescribing as the sole cause of AMR is lacking. In fact, multiple factors contribute to the development of AMR, including the spread of resistant bacteria through the food chain, hospital acquired infections, and the use of antibiotics in agriculture. Therefore, simply reducing antibiotic use may not be enough to address the problem. A more comprehensive approach is needed, including public information campaigns, surveillance of resistance, targets for hospital acquired infections, and the establishment of an overarching advisory body on all aspects of antibiotic use.

title: Unmet needs and depressive symptoms among low--income older adults.
text:
In previous studies, researchers have identified several factors that contribute to the development of late-life depression, including declining health, social isolation, and financial difficulties. On the other hand, social support from family and friends, as well as religiousness, have been found to be protective factors against depression. In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between unmet needs for home- and community-based services and depressive symptoms in low-income older adults, while controlling for these known risk and protective factors.
To assess the depressive symptoms of 213 community-residing older adults, we conducted in-depth interviews using the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS). We also explored the older adults' perceived unmet needs in the areas of personal assistance, instrumental support, emotional support, and other facilitative/enabling services. Our findings revealed a positive association between the number of unmet needs and depressive symptoms, although the explained variance of GDS scores was relatively small.
Our results suggest that low-income older adults' perceived unmet needs for home- and community-based services may contribute significantly to their depressive symptoms. This finding has important implications for future research and practice, highlighting the need for targeted interventions that address the social determinants of health and aim to improve access to home- and community-based services for low-income older adults. By doing so, we can help mitigate the negative impact of unmet needs on depressive symptoms and promote the overall well-being of this vulnerable population.

title: A key role for Ctf4 in coupling the MCM2-7 helicase to DNA polymerase alpha within the eukaryotic replisome.
text: The eukaryotic replisome plays a critical role in maintaining genome stability, yet its structure remains poorly understood. In our previous work, we discovered that regulatory proteins assemble around the MCM2-7 helicase at replication forks in yeast to form the replisome progression complex (RPC), which may connect MCM2-7 to other replisome components. Recently, we found that the RPC interacts with DNA polymerase alpha, which primed each Okazaki fragment during lagging strand synthesis. Our data suggest that a complex comprising the GINS and Ctf4 components of the RPC serves as the critical link between MCM2-7 and DNA polymerase alpha. Interestingly, other studies have shown that the Mrc1 subunit of RPCs binds DNA polymerase epsilon, which synthesizes the leading strand at replication forks. Our findings demonstrate that coupling MCM2-7 to replicative polymerases is a crucial aspect of the regulation of chromosome replication in eukaryotes, highlighting the essential role of Ctf4 in this process. Crucially, we also observed that cells lacking both Ctf4 and Mrc1 experience chronic activation of the DNA damage checkpoint during chromosome replication, hindering their progression through the cell cycle.

title: Data analysis methods for detection of differential protein expression in two-dimensional gel electrophoresis.
text: Advancements in microarray technology have prompted statisticians and bioinformaticians to create novel statistical approaches for evaluating disparate biological samples. The ultimate objective is to identify a limited number of differentially expressed genes from a vast pool of thousands. Similarly, quantitative proteomics, which involves the analysis of protein expression through two-dimensional gel electrophoresis, shares some similarities with transcriptomic studies. Therefore, this investigation aimed to assess a range of data analysis methodologies commonly used in array analysis by employing numerous proteomic data sets comprising hundreds of proteins. Interestingly, the significance analysis of microarrays technique demonstrated superiority in identifying differentially expressed proteins compared to the Student's t test, even with a limited number of replicates. This approach will help avoid wasting time and resources on false positives and ensure that meaningful information is not lost due to false negatives.

title: A clinical approach to circadian rhythm sleep disorders.
text:
Circadian rhythm sleep disorders are characterized by complaints of insomnia and excessive sleepiness due to alterations in the body's internal clock or misalignment between the body's internal rhythm and the 24-hour social and physical environment. In addition to physiological and environmental factors, maladaptive behaviors often play a significant role in the development of these disorders. This review will focus on the clinical approach to identifying and managing the various circadian rhythm sleep disorders, including delayed sleep phase disorder, advanced sleep phase disorder, non-entrained type, irregular sleep-wake rhythm, shift work sleep disorder, and jet lag disorder.
Diagnostic tools such as sleep diaries and wrist activity monitoring can be useful in confirming the diagnosis. As behavioral and environmental factors are often involved, a multimodal approach is usually necessary. Treatment options include sleep hygiene education, timed exposure to bright light, avoidance of bright light at the wrong time of day, and pharmacological approaches, such as melatonin. However, it is important to note that the use of melatonin is not an FDA-approved indication for treating circadian rhythm sleep disorders.

title: SIVrcm infection of macaques.
text: In a previous study, we identified and characterized SIVrcm, a unique primate lentivirus detected in a Red-Capped Mangabey (RCM) kept as a household pet in Gabon. SIVrcm differs from HIV-1 and HIV-2/SIV groups of primate lentiviruses. This report presents additional in vitro replication studies and results of SIVrcm infection in macaques. SIVrcm exhibited limited cytopathic effects in Molt 4 Clone 8 cells and rhesus and human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). In vivo, SIVrcm was found to be non-pathogenic in rhesus macaques after 200 days and in cynomolgous macaques after one year, although it did result in a chronic infection in both species.

title: Integrating nutrition security with treatment of people living with HIV: lessons from Kenya.
text:
The increased caloric requirements of individuals living with HIV, the undesirable side effects of treatment exacerbated by malnutrition, and the declines in adherence and potential increased drug resistance highlight the need for more effective interventions to improve the nutrition security of individuals receiving antiretroviral treatment. To address these challenges, this study aimed to identify the key benefits and challenges of interventions aimed at strengthening the nutrition security of people living with HIV who are receiving antiretroviral treatment.
Qualitative research was conducted in western Kenya in 2005 and 2006 on a short-term nutrition intervention that provided free antiretroviral treatment to people living with HIV. Results showed that patients who received the nutrition intervention reported improved adherence to their medication, reduced side effects, and increased appetite. Many clients also reported weight gain, recovery of physical strength, and resumption of work activities. These improvements were seen to have a positive impact on the support they received from family and community.
These findings provide additional empirical evidence to support calls for a more comprehensive and holistic approach to addressing the coexistence of HIV and chronic nutrition insecurity. While short-term nutritional support to individuals is important, longer-term livelihood security programming for communities affected by HIV is also crucial. To address these challenges, interdisciplinary research and intersectoral action from the agriculture and health sectors are necessary.

title: Acylated and desacyl ghrelin stimulate lipid accumulation in human visceral adipocytes
text:
Objective: To investigate the impact of obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D) on the circulating forms of the orexigenic hormone ghrelin, and their potential role in the control of adipogenesis in humans.
Methods: Plasma concentrations of acylated and desacyl ghrelin were measured in 80 subjects, and the expression of the ghrelin receptor (growth hormone secretagogue receptor, GHS-R) was analyzed in omental adipose tissue using western blot and immunohistochemistry. The effect of acylated and desacyl ghrelin on adipogenesis was determined in vitro in omental adipocytes.
Results: Circulating acylated ghrelin levels were increased, while desacyl ghrelin levels were decreased, in obesity and T2D. Body mass index, waist circumference, insulin, and Homeostasis Model Assessment (HOMA) index were positively correlated with acylated ghrelin levels. Obese individuals showed lower protein expression of GHS-R in omental adipose tissue. Incubation with both acylated and desacyl ghrelin significantly increased PPARγ and SREBP1 mRNA levels, as well as several fat storage-related proteins, in differentiating omental adipocytes. Both ghrelin forms also stimulated intracytoplasmic lipid accumulation.
Conclusions: Both acylated and desacyl ghrelin stimulate lipid accumulation in human visceral adipocytes. The elevated circulating concentrations of acylated ghrelin in obese individuals may contribute to excessive fat accumulation in obesity.

title: Significant correlation between LKB1 and LGR5 gene expression and the association with poor recurrence-free survival in rectal cancer after preoperative chemoradiotherapy
text: The objective of the current study was to investigate whether the levels of gene expression for LKB1 and LGR5 are associated with clinical outcomes in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer treated with preoperative chemoradiotherapy (CRT). cells were obtained from 52 patients with locally advanced rectal cancer who underwent preoperative CRT. Total RNA was isolated from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues using microdissection, and the expression levels of LKB1 and LGR5 genes were measured using real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction and immunohistochemistry. Additionally, in vitro studies were conducted using colon cancer cell lines to examine the serial changes in LKB1, LGR5, and PRKAA1 (AMPK) gene expression following irradiation. Our findings indicate that specimens obtained from patients with poor pathological response and tumor recurrence had significantly higher levels of LKB1 and LGR5 gene expression compared to those without these characteristics (P < 0.05). Furthermore, there was a significant positive correlation between LKB1 and LGR5 gene expression after CRT (Spearman's ρ: 0.429, P = 0.0023). Patients with high expression levels of both LKB1 and LGR5 had a significantly lower recurrence-free survival compared to those in the other group (P = 0.0055, 95% confidence interval: 1.39–11.08). Finally, in vitro studies revealed a similar pattern of serial gene expression among LKB1, LGR5, and PRKAA1 following irradiation. These results suggest that LKB1 and LGR5 expression may contribute to resistance to CRT, thereby influencing tumor relapse in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer treated with preoperative CRT.

title: Evaluating the impact of pharmacists in mental health: a systematic review.
text:
For over three decades, healthcare professionals have sought to enhance the treatment outcomes of individuals with mental health conditions by integrating various practitioners into collaborative care models. Clinical pharmacists have been instrumental in these efforts, contributing their skills in capacities such as educator, consultant, and provider. To evaluate the impact of pharmacists in mental healthcare, we conducted a systematic review of the literature from 1972 to 2003, identifying approximately 35 publications. However, only 16 studies were deemed scientifically rigorous enough to be evaluated and compared.
The 16 studies were conducted across various healthcare organizations, including Veterans Administration hospitals, health maintenance organizations, community mental health clinics, and nursing homes. Half of the studies focused on inpatient settings, while the remaining were conducted in outpatient settings. The studies investigated the roles of pharmacists in providing treatment recommendations and patient education (nine studies), serving as providers (with prescriptive authority) (five studies), and delivering education to psychiatric staff (two studies). Most of the studies were prospective in design, but only three incorporated a randomization procedure for patients or facilities.
The results of the 16 studies were positive, displaying improvements in outcomes, prescribing practices, patient satisfaction, and resource utilization. However, most of the studies were small, and limitations in study design hindered further comparison. Notwithstanding these limitations, the long-standing success of pharmacists in mental healthcare settings and the promising results of these studies suggest that additional, multicenter, cost-effectiveness trials are necessary to further support the role of the psychiatric pharmacist.

title: Multicenter phase II study of lapatinib in patients with brain metastases from HER2-positive breast cancer.
text:
BRAIN METASTASES IN HER2+ BREAST CANCER PATIENTS
Approximately one-third of patients with advanced HER2+ breast cancer will develop brain metastases. Effective treatment options for these patients are limited, posing a significant clinical challenge. In a small phase 2 trial, lapatinib, an EGFR/HER2 inhibitor, showed promise in reducing CNS lesions. The current study aimed to further evaluate the CNS activity of lapatinib.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
Eligible patients had HER2+ breast cancer, progressive brain metastases, prior trastuzumab therapy, and cranial radiotherapy. The primary endpoint was CNS objective response, defined as a 50% or greater reduction in CNS lesion volume without increasing steroid use, worsening neurological symptoms, or extra-CNS disease progression.
RESULTS
Of the 242 enrolled patients, 6% showed CNS objective responses to lapatinib. In an exploratory analysis, 21% of patients experienced a 20% or greater reduction in their CNS lesion volume. A statistically significant association was observed between volumetric reduction and improvements in progression-free survival and neurological symptoms. Of the 50 evaluable patients who entered the lapatinib plus capecitabine extension, 20% experienced a CNS objective response, and 40% experienced a 20% or greater reduction in their CNS lesion volume.
CONCLUSIONS
This study demonstrates the modest CNS antitumor activity of lapatinib. The addition of capecitabine to lapatinib regimens may enhance CNS response rates. Further research is warranted to investigate lapatinib-based regimens for CNS metastases in HER2+ breast cancer patients.

title: Control of signaling-mediated clearance of apoptotic cells by the tumor suppressor p53
text: The inadequate clearance of dying cells can lead to irregular immune responses, such as unresolved inflammation and autoimmune conditions. Our findings demonstrate that the tumor suppressor p53 regulates the phagocytic removal of apoptotic cells through its target, Death Domain1α (DD1α), implying that p53 promotes both the proapoptotic pathway and postapoptotic events. DD1α functions as an engulfment ligand or receptor that interacts with homophilic intermolecular interactions at intercellular junctions of apoptotic cells and macrophages, distinct from other typical scavenger receptors that recognize phosphatidylserine on the surface of dead cells. Deficiency in DD1α leads to in vivo defects in clearing dying cells, resulting in multiple organ damage indicative of immune dysfunction. p53-induced expression of DD1α prevents the persistence of cell corpses, ensuring efficient generation of appropriate immune responses.

title: Circulating tumor DNA as a non-invasive substitute to metastasis biopsy for tumor genotyping and personalized medicine in a prospective trial across all tumor types.
text: Cell-free tumor DNA (ctDNA) has the potential to enable non-invasive diagnostic tests for personalized medicine, offering similar molecular information as invasive tumor biopsies. In the histology-independent phase II SHIVA trial, patients are matched with targeted therapeutics based on previous screening of multiple somatic mutations using metastatic biopsies. As an ancillary study, we compared de novo detection of somatic mutations in plasma DNA to metastasis biopsies in 34 patients with 18 different tumor types, scanning 46 genes and over 6800 COSMIC mutations using a multiplexed next-generation sequencing panel. In 27 patients, 28 of 29 mutations identified in metastasis biopsies (97%) were detected in matching ctDNA. Of these 27 patients, one additional mutation was found only in ctDNA. In the seven other patients, mutation detection from metastasis biopsy failed due to insufficient biopsy material, but was successful in all plasma DNA samples, revealing three more potential actionable mutations. These results suggest that ctDNA analysis could serve as an alternative or supplement to tissue biopsies for mutation detection in selecting personalized therapies based on a patient's tumor genetic makeup, regardless of cancer type or metastatic site.

title: TGF-beta suppresses tumor progression in colon cancer by inhibition of IL-6 trans-signaling.
text: Changes in TGF-beta signaling have been observed in colorectal cancer, but the molecular consequences are still unclear. To investigate this further, we used transgenic mice that overexpress TGF-beta or a dominant-negative TGF-betaRII. Our results demonstrate that TGF-beta signaling in tumor-infiltrating T cells controls the growth of abnormal epithelial cells in experimental colorectal cancer, as evident from histological analysis and a novel high-resolution chromoendoscopy system. At the molecular level, TGF-beta signaling in T cells regulates STAT-3 activation in tumor cells through IL-6. Specifically, IL-6 signaling requires soluble IL-6R from tumor cells rather than membrane-bound IL-6R, and inhibition of TGF-beta-dependent IL-6 trans-signaling prevented tumor progression in vivo. In conclusion, our data provide new insights into TGF-beta signaling in colorectal cancer and suggest innovative therapeutic strategies for colorectal cancer treatment by targeting TGF-beta-dependent IL-6 trans-signaling.

title: New opportunities: the use of nanotechnologies to manipulate and track stem cells.
text: Nanotechnologies are revolutionary tools that could significantly enhance the measurement, comprehension, and manipulation of stem cells. Examples of such technologies include the use of magnetic nanoparticles and quantum dots for labeling and tracking stem cells in vivo, as well as the delivery of genes, oligonucleotides, and proteins/peptides into cells using nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes, and polyplexes. Additionally, engineered nanometer-scale scaffolds can be employed for stem cell differentiation and transplantation. This review analyzes the application of nanotechnologies in stem cell tracking, differentiation, and transplantation, while also addressing any potential safety concerns regarding their cytotoxicity.

title: The emergence of order in the Drosophila pupal retina.
text:
During the process of pupation, a highly organized and complex system of cellular interactions is established in the developing Drosophila eye. This system involves the emergence of eight distinct cell types, including the primary, secondary, and tertiary pigment cells, as well as the four cells that form the bristle. These cells form a intricate lattice-like structure that interweaves between the autonomously developing ommatidia, with the lattice being refined through the removal of excess cells.
Studies have shown that during both larval and pupal development, local cell-cell contacts play a crucial role in determining the fate of individual cells. For example, cells that come into contact with the anterior or posterior cone cells in an ommatidium are fated to become primary pigment cells, while cells that contact primary pigment cells from different ommatidia become secondary and tertiary pigment cells.
In contrast to ommatidial development, bristle development is a distinct process that involves the formation of four cells within each bristle group, which are thought to arise from a single founder cell. These cells do not make stereotyped contacts with surrounding ommatidial cells during their early differentiation, but instead form particular contacts within the bristle group. Additionally, differentiation of the bristles radiates from the center of the eye to the edges, rather than the more uniformly distributed pattern observed in ommatidial development.
During the final stages of retinal development, programmed cell death leads to the removal of cells from the lattice, and subsequent structure production is specific to each cell type. This process allows for the establishment of a highly specialized and functional retina, with the intricate interplay of cellular interactions and local cell-cell contacts playing a crucial role in determining the final structure and function of the eye.

title: Gene expression analysis by cDNA microarray in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
text:
Background: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is a common type of cancer in humans, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its malignancy are not well understood. Comprehensive gene expression profiling is crucial for gaining insights into the disease.
Methods: We used cDNA microarray analysis to examine the expression patterns of 16,617 genes in nine OSCC patients.
Results: We identified 47 genes with altered expression among all cases and categorized their ontology into 10 categories. To validate the microarray data, the expression of genes such as TGFBI, FADD, and DUSP1 was analyzed using reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Hierarchical clustering analysis revealed that the nine cases could be divided into two clusters.
Conclusions: We suggest that the 47 identified genes play a functional role in oral squamous cell carcinogenesis. Additionally, the gene expression patterns observed through hierarchical clustering analysis may reflect degrees of differentiation. The postoperative recovery was uneventful, and all patients are currently free of tumor. As the number of cases accumulates and more cases are observed over a longer period, the 5-year survival rate data will be added. This will enable the representation of OSCC malignancy based on these gene expression patterns.

title: Risk factors associated with symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux.
text: LACK OF DATA ON RISK FACTORS FOR GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX IN THE UNITED STATES Patients with gastroesophageal reflux are often advised to modify their lifestyle, but there are no population-based data on the risk factors for reflux in the US. STUDY DESIGN We conducted a cross-sectional study in an age- and gender-stratified random sample of the population of Olmsted County, Minnesota. We mailed a self-report questionnaire to residents aged 25-74 years, which assessed reflux symptoms and potential risk factors. Logistic regression was used to determine the odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for reflux symptoms (heartburn or acid regurgitation) associated with potential risk factors. RESULTS OF THE STUDY Overall, 1,524 (72%) of 2,118 eligible respondents participated. The following factors were found to be independently associated with frequent (at least weekly) reflux symptoms: a body mass index (BMI) of over 30 kg/m2 (OR = 2.8; CI, 1.7-4.5), a family history of heartburn or esophageal/gastric disease (OR = 2.6; CI, 1.8-3.7), a history of smoking (OR = 1.6; CI, 1.1-2.3), consuming more than seven drinks per week (OR = 1.9; CI, 1.1-3.3), and a higher psychosomatic symptom checklist score (OR per 5 units = 1.4; CI, 1.3-1.6). CONCLUSION Obesity is a significant risk factor for gastroesophageal reflux, although the effectiveness of weight reduction in preventing reflux remains to be proven. The finding that a family history is also a risk factor suggests that there may be a genetic component to the disorder.

title: A mathematical investigation of the effects of inhibitor therapy on three putative phosphorylation cascades governing the two-component system of the agr operon.
text: Two-component systems (TCSs) are extensively employed by bacteria to detect specific external stimuli and initiate an appropriate response through a phosphorylation cascade within the cell. The TCS of the agr operon in the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus functions as part of a regulatory process called quorum sensing, a cell-to-cell communication mechanism used to assess population density. By manipulating this "knowledge," S. aureus coordinates the production of its arsenal of virulence factors required for infection. To gain a deeper understanding of this process, we have developed three models of the agr operon, each featuring a distinct phosphorylation cascade for the TCS, as the precise nature of the cascade is not fully understood. Utilizing numerical and asymptotic techniques, we investigate the impact of inhibitor therapy, a novel approach to controlling bacterial infections by attenuating virulence, on each of these three cascades. Our findings, if validated through experimental data, provide insights into the potential effectiveness of such therapy. Furthermore, the TCS models presented here are relevant to many other bacteria, as TCSs are widely conserved throughout the bacterial kingdom.

title: Coregulators in nuclear estrogen receptor action: from concept to therapeutic targeting.
text: Estrogens play a crucial role in regulating various physiological processes across different tissues, including the male and female reproductive systems, breast, skeletal, nervous, cardiovascular, digestive, and immune systems. The majority of these activities are mediated through two distinct estrogen receptors, ERalpha and ERbeta, which function as hormone-inducible transcription factors. Recent research has shown that the recruitment of coregulatory proteins to these receptors is essential for their ability to respond appropriately to hormones, interpret extracellular signals, condensate chromatin, and communicate with the general transcription apparatus at target gene promoters. Additionally, the presence of corepressors, which function as negative regulators of ER activity, adds an extra layer of complexity to ER function. This review also discusses ongoing efforts to develop pharmaceutical agents that target ER-cofactor interactions as therapies for estrogen-related disorders.

title: Autophagy and mTORC1 regulate the stochastic phase of somatic cell reprogramming
text: We demonstrate the robust induction of autophagy during the conversion of mouse fibroblasts into induced pluripotent stem cells using four reprogramming factors (Sox2, Oct4, Klf4, and c-Myc, collectively referred to as 4F). This process occurs independently of p53 activation and is mediated by the synergistic suppression of mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and the upregulation of autophagy-related genes. The 4F factors collaboratively repress mTORC1, with Klf4 and c-Myc inducing autophagy-related genes while Sox2 and Oct4 inhibit them. Interestingly, inhibition of mTORC1 promotes cell reshaping (mitotic remodeling and cell size reduction), while mTORC1 activation appears to hinder reprogramming by triggering autophagy. Surprisingly, autophagy does not contribute to cell reshaping during reprogramming, instead concentrating on degrading p62, which accumulates in autophagy-deficient cells and facilitates reprogramming. Our findings expose a complex signaling network involving mTORC1 inhibition and autophagy induction in the initial stages of reprogramming, where a delicate balance determines the efficiency of the process.

title: Lithium Therapy Improves Neurological Function and Hippocampal Dendritic Arborization in a Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 1 Mouse Model
text:
Background: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) is a dominantly inherited neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor and cognitive dysfunction. Caused by an expanded polyglutamine tract in ataxin 1 (ATXN1), SCA1 pathogenesis involves a complex process that begins with misfolding of ATXN1, leading to impaired interactions and transcriptional dysregulation. Lithium, which has shown neuroprotective effects in various conditions, may exert its effects by modulating gene expression.
Methods and Findings: To investigate the efficacy of lithium treatment in a knock-in mouse model of SCA1 (Sca1154Q/2Q mice), we fed these mice either regular chow or chow supplemented with 0.2% lithium carbonate. Our results showed that dietary lithium carbonate supplementation improved motor coordination, learning, and memory in Sca1154Q/2Q mice, both before and after symptom onset. Neuropathologically, lithium treatment attenuated the reduction of dendritic branching in mutant hippocampal pyramidal neurons. Additionally, lithium treatment restored the levels of isoprenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase (Icmt; alternatively, Pccmt), a protein that is down-regulated early in the course of SCA1 pathogenesis.
Conclusions: The positive effects of lithium on multiple behavioral measures and hippocampal neuropathology in an authentic disease model make it a promising candidate treatment for human SCA1 patients. The finding that lithium can restore a protein that is altered early in the disease process suggests that it may be able to slow or halt the progression of SCA1. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms underlying lithium's neuroprotective effects and to determine its potential as a therapeutic option for SCA1 patients.

title: The progression from hypertension to congestive heart failure.
text:
The study aimed to investigate the relative and population-attributable risks of hypertension in the development of congestive heart failure (CHF), to determine the time course of progression from hypertension to CHF, and to identify risk factors that contribute to the development of overt heart failure in hypertensive subjects.
Design: Inception cohort study
Setting: General community
Participants: Original Framingham Heart Study and Framingham Offspring Study participants aged 40 to 89 years and free of CHF, with a starting point of January 1, 1970.
Exposure measures: Hypertension (defined as blood pressure of at least 140 mm Hg systolic or 90 mm Hg diastolic, or current use of medications for hypertension treatment) and other potential CHF risk factors were assessed at periodic clinic examinations.
Outcome measure: Development of CHF.
Results: A total of 5143 eligible subjects contributed 72422 person-years of observation. Over a mean follow-up period of 14.1 years, there were 392 new cases of heart failure; in 91% (357/392) of these cases, hypertension occurred before the development of heart failure. After adjusting for age and heart failure risk factors in proportional hazards regression models, hypertension had a 2-fold increased risk of developing heart failure in men and a 3-fold increased risk in women. Hypertension accounted for 39% of CHF cases in men and 59% in women. Myocardial infarction, diabetes, left ventricular hypertrophy, and valvular heart disease were identified as predictive risk factors for CHF in both sexes. Survival following the onset of hypertensive CHF was poor, with only 24% of men and 31% of women surviving 5 years.
Conclusion: Hypertension was the most common risk factor for CHF in this population-based sample, accounting for a large proportion of heart failure cases. Early and aggressive blood pressure control strategies are likely to offer the greatest promise for reducing the incidence of CHF and its associated mortality.

title: Association of plasma resistin with glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria in hypertensive adults.
text: In a recent study, we investigated the relationship between plasma resistin levels and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in a cohort of 1575 hypertensive adults without known coronary heart disease or stroke. The study included 857 blacks and 718 non-Hispanic whites. Resistin was measured using a solid phase sandwich immunoassay, eGFR was estimated from serum creatinine, and albuminuria was expressed as urine albumin:creatinine ratio. After adjusting for coronary heart disease risk factors, use of renin-angiotensin blockers, and statins, we found that higher plasma resistin levels were associated with lower eGFR in both ethnic groups (P<0.0001). This association remained significant after additional adjustment for a marker of insulin resistance (homeostasis model assessment for insulin resistance) and a marker of inflammation (plasma C-reactive protein). Furthermore, we observed that higher plasma resistin levels were associated with a higher urine albumin:creatinine ratio in black subjects with diabetes (P<0.0001) and non-Hispanic white subjects with diabetes (P=0.032), independent of coronary heart disease risk factors, hypertension medication use, and statin use. These findings suggest that in adults with hypertension, higher circulating resistin levels are associated with a lower estimated glomerular filtration rate and with increased urine albumin:creatinine ratio in the presence of concomitant diabetes, independently of coronary heart disease risk factors and markers of insulin resistance and inflammation.

title: Large-scale candidate gene scan reveals the role of chemoreceptor genes in host plant specialization and speciation in the pea aphid.
text: Comprehending the underlying factors of speciation is crucial to understanding patterns of biodiversity. Identifying the genetic adjustments that give rise to adaptation and reproductive isolation is essential to connect barriers to gene flow to the underlying causes of divergence. In this study, we present a novel approach to the genetics of speciation, which should complement the commonly used methods of quantitative trait locus mapping and genome-wide scans for selection. We implemented a large-scale candidate gene approach through sequence capture, with a focus on identifying the genetic changes underlying reproductive isolation in the pea aphid, a model system for the study of ecological speciation. By means of targeted resequencing, we were able to scale up the candidate gene approach and specifically investigate the role of chemosensory gene families in host plant specialization. Screening for the signature of divergence under selection at 172 candidate and noncandidate loci revealed a small number of loci that show high levels of differentiation among host races, which almost all correspond to odorant and gustatory receptor genes. This study provides the first indication that some chemoreceptor genes, which are often clustered together in the genome, may play a key role in local adaptation and reproductive isolation in the pea aphid and potentially other phytophagous insects. Our approach offers a new avenue for the functional genomics of ecological speciation.

title: The cancer stem cell hypothesis: a guide to potential molecular targets.
text: Conventional cancer theories posits that tumors arise from uncontrolled cell growth due to the gradual accumulation of random mutations in genes that regulate cell division. However, several discrepancies with this theory have been reported earlier. These contradictions may be resolved by the existence of residual tumor cells, known as Cancer Stem Cells (CSCs), which are responsible for initiating and maintaining tumors, spreading them to other parts of the body, and causing tumors to recur. In this review, we will summarize the current understanding of CSCs, with a focus on identifying specific markers of these cells and discussing the potential clinical applications of targeting them for cancer treatment.

title: Serum amyloid A: An acute-phase protein involved in tumour pathogenesis
text: The synthesis of acute-phase protein serum amyloid A (SAA) is primarily regulated by inflammation-associated cytokines, and high levels of SAA in the blood may serve as a marker for acute and chronic inflammatory diseases. However, SAA is also produced in non-hepatic tissues, such as human cancer metastases and cancer cell lines. A growing body of in vitro research suggests that SAA may play a role in carcinogenesis and malignant diseases. Recent findings indicate that SAA could be included in a group of biomarkers to detect a pattern of physiological events that reflect the growth of malignancy and the host response. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the various ways in which SAA may contribute to tumor development, accelerate tumor progression and metastasis, and shed light on its possible role as a linking factor between chronic inflammation and neoplasia.

title: Body size and outcomes on peritoneal dialysis in the United States.
text:
Background: Being overweight has been cited as a relative contraindication for peritoneal dialysis. However, there is limited evidence to support this opinion.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 418,021 Medicare patients initiating dialysis between 1995 and 2000, of which 7% were underweight, 27% were overweight, and 23% were obese at the time of dialysis initiation. We evaluated the association between BMI category and peritoneal dialysis initiation, as well as survival outcomes among patients initiating peritoneal dialysis.
Results: Our results showed that compared to patients with normal BMI, underweight, overweight, and obese patients had adjusted odds of initiating peritoneal dialysis of 0.70, 1.12, and 0.87, respectively. Among peritoneal dialysis patients, adjusted mortality hazard ratios in the first, second, and third year were 1.45, 1.28, and 1.17 for the underweight group, respectively; 0.84, 0.89, and 0.98 for the overweight group, respectively; and 0.89, 0.99, and 1.00 for the obese group, respectively. Except for higher third-year mortality in the obese group, the associations were similar after censoring at a switch to hemodialysis. For transplantation, the corresponding results were 0.76, 0.90, and 0.88 for the underweight group, respectively; 0.95, 1.06, and 0.93 for the overweight group, respectively; and 0.62, 0.68, and 0.71 for the obese group, respectively. For switching to hemodialysis, hazards ratios were 0.92, 0.97, and 0.80 for the underweight group, respectively; 1.07, 1.11 (P < 0.05), and 1.03 for the overweight group, respectively; and 1.28 (P < 0.05), 1.29 (P < 0.05), and 1.36 (P < 0.05) for the obese group, respectively.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that overweight and obese patients on peritoneal dialysis have longer survival than those with lower BMI, despite lower transplantation and technique survival rates. This suggests that BMI category may not be a relative contraindication for peritoneal dialysis.

title: The anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome: a machine designed to destroy
text: The anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) is a multifunctional enzyme that plays a crucial role in both cellular processes within and outside of the eukaryotic cell cycle. As the most sophisticated molecular machine known to date, it catalyzes ubiquitin ligation reactions with incredible precision, comprising over a dozen subunits that coalesce into a massive 1.5-megadalton complex.
