Recent research has unveiled a wealth of intricate mechanisms regulating APC/C activity, offering initial insights into the mysteries of how this enigmatic ubiquitin ligase identifies its substrates.

title: Regulation of the expression of alkaline phosphatase in a human breast-cancer cell line.
text: The treatment of cultured human breast-cancer cells BC-M1 with dexamethasone led to the induction of a placental-type alkaline phosphatase (ALP). This induction was found to be time- and dose-dependent, and involved multiple regulatory proteins. The accumulation of ALP mRNA was inhibited by actinomycin D and cycloheximide, suggesting that the induction of ALP is a complex process. In contrast, retinoic acid (RA) and phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) had opposing effects on the expression of ALP, with RA reducing and PMA increasing the dexamethasone-induced expression of ALP. The BC-M1 ALP mRNA was found to be most similar to the placental form, and northern hybridization analysis revealed that ALP mRNA transcripts in BC-M1 and term placenta were similar in size and distinct from those in choriocarcinoma cells. The half-life of BC-M1 ALP mRNA was found to be approximately 27 h in untreated and dexamethasone- or RA-treated cells, indicating that the induction of ALP in BC-M1 cells is primarily due to an increase in the transcription of the ALP gene.

title: Declining tuberculosis notification trend associated with strengthened TB and expanded HIV care in Swaziland.
text: This retrospective observational analysis examines the efforts of the Swaziland National Tuberculosis (TB) Control Programme from 2004 to 2014, with the aim of identifying the disparity between actual declines in case notifications and estimated increases in incidence. The study also reviews policies and practices to determine the most significant factors contributing to the decrease in TB case notifications, including an increase in access to antiretroviral therapy for co-infected TB patients, the success of TB and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) service integration in the country, and improvements in the implementation of various components of directly observed treatment, active case finding, and rapid diagnosis using new technologies.

title: Advances in techniques of testing mycobacterial drug sensitivity, and the use of sensitivity tests in tuberculosis control programmes.
text: In a paper born from an informal international meeting of experts in bacteriology held in 1961, an attempt was made to devise criteria and technical procedures for reliable tests of sensitivity (the absolute-concentration method, the resistance-ratio method, and the proportion method) to the three primary antituberculosis drugs (isoniazid, streptomycin, and p-aminosalicylic acid). Seven years later, a subsequent consultation was convened to revisit recent discoveries in the field and to suggest how sensitivity tests might be applied in practice to tuberculosis control programs. The participants reached a consensus on how to characterize drug sensitivity and resistance and emphasized the importance of adopting a discriminatory approach to calibrating sensitivity tests. Their perspectives are encapsulated in the present paper, which also includes descriptions of the sensitivity tests employed by the Medical Research Council of Great Britain for first- and second-line drugs (minimal inhibitory concentration and resistance-ratio methods), the two primary variations of the proportion method developed by the Institut Pasteur, Paris, and a method for calibrating sensitivity tests.

title: Time from finding abnormality on mass-screening to final diagnosis of lung cancer.
text: In Japan, mass screening for lung cancer is a distinct system. This study examines the time frame from discovering an abnormality on mass screening to the final diagnosis of lung cancer. Of the 517 patients with lung cancer admitted to our hospital over a 10-year period ending in December 2001, 83 (16.1%) were identified through mass screening. We reviewed the medical records of these patients and determined the intervals from mass screening to pathological diagnosis with clinical staging. In 62 (74.7%) cases, the time from mass screening to the hospital visit was less than 2 months. Only 5 (6.0%) patients visited the hospital more than 6 months after mass screening. Gender (p=0.0680) and age (p=0.1532) did not show any statistically significant differences in the interval. Among 60 patients referred from outside, patients visited our hospital an average of 0.5 months after seeking medical attention at a nearby clinic, and it took our hospital 0.5 months to make a pathological diagnosis of lung cancer with TNM staging. There was a statistically significant difference in survival between patients diagnosed within 4 months of screening (p=0.0487) compared to those diagnosed later. While the intervals in most cases were acceptable, further improvements are needed to minimize delays and maximize the benefits of early cancer detection.

title: Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) regulates B-cell reactivity, subset differentiation, and trafficking molecule expression.
text: The transcription factor Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) is crucial for the normal migration of T lymphocytes, but its role in B cells is unclear. Our findings reveal that the absence of KLF2 in B cells leads to a decrease in the expression of molecules involved in migration, such as CD62L and β7-integrin. However, the expression of sphingosine-1 phosphate receptor 1, which is a critical target of KLF2 in T cells, was surprisingly unaffected. Contrary to expectations, the deletion of KLF2 resulted in a significant decrease in the B1 B-cell population and a substantial increase in transitional and marginal zone B-cell numbers. Additionally, we observed that KLF2-deficient B cells exhibited increased apoptosis and impaired proliferation following B-cell receptor cross-linking. Gene expression analysis revealed that KLF2-deficient follicular B cells shared characteristics with marginal zone B cells, including reduced expression of signaling molecules that may contribute to impaired activation of these cells. Our data illustrate that KLF2 plays a vital role in regulating the normal differentiation and functional responsiveness of mature B cells.

title: Antibiotics and risk of subsequent first-time acute myocardial infarction.
text:
Background: Increasing evidence suggests a potential link between certain bacterial infections and an increased risk of acute myocardial infarction (AMI). If this association exists, individuals who have used antibiotics active against these bacteria may be at lower risk of developing AMI compared to those who have not.
Objective: To investigate whether previous use of antibiotics decreases the risk of developing a first-time AMI.
Design: Population-based case-control analysis utilizing the General Practice Research Database, which comprises 350 general practices in the United Kingdom.
Participants: A total of 3315 case patients aged 75 years or younger with a diagnosis of first-time AMI between 1992 and 1997 and 13139 controls without AMI matched to cases for age, sex, general practice attended, and calendar time.
Main Outcome Measures: Use of antibiotics among cases and controls.
Findings: Cases were significantly less likely to have used tetracycline antibiotics (adjusted odds ratio (OR) = 0.70; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.55-0.90) or quinolones (adjusted OR = 0.45; 95% CI = 0.21-0.95). No effect was observed for previous use of macrolides (primarily erythromycin), sulfonamides, penicillins, or cephalosporins.
Conclusion: The findings of this large case-control analysis provide further, albeit indirect, evidence for an association between bacterial infections with organisms susceptible to tetracycline or quinolone antibiotics and the risk of AMI. These results are preliminary and should stimulate further research to explore the potential role of infections in the etiology of AMI.

title: Thrombopoietin/MPL signaling regulates hematopoietic stem cell quiescence and interaction with the osteoblastic niche.
text: The maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) relies on their interaction with their niche. In this study, we discovered that long-term (LT)-HSCs expressing the thrombopoietin (THPO) receptor, MPL, are a quiescent population in the adult bone marrow (BM) and are closely associated with THPO-producing osteoblastic cells. THPO/MPL signaling upregulated beta1-integrin and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors in HSCs, providing evidence of its critical role in regulating LT-HSCs. Moreover, inhibition and stimulation of the THPO/MPL pathway through the use of an anti-MPL neutralizing antibody (AMM2) and THPO treatment, respectively, resulted in reciprocal regulation of the quiescence of LT-HSCs. AMM2 treatment reduced the number of quiescent LT-HSCs, allowing for exogenous HSC engraftment without irradiation. In contrast, exogenous THPO transiently increased the quiescent HSC population and subsequently induced HSC proliferation in vivo. These findings suggest that THPO/MPL signaling plays a crucial role in regulating LT-HSCs in the osteoblastic niche.

title: Interlaboratory reproducibility and proficiency testing within the human papillomavirus cervical cancer screening program in Catalonia, Spain.
text: In Catalonia, a screening protocol for cervical cancer that includes testing for human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA using the Digene Hybrid Capture 2 (HC2) assay was implemented in 2006. To assess the reproducibility of the HC2 assay among different laboratories, a proficiency testing (PT) survey was conducted in 2008 with HPV samples. The aim of the study was to determine the repeatability of the HC2 assay's performance. Participating laboratories provided 20 samples per year, randomized into four relative light unit (RLU) intervals: <0.5, 0.5 to 0.99, 1 to 9.99, and ≥10. Kappa statistics were used to evaluate the agreement between the original and PT readings. Bootstrapping was used to calculate the nature and origin of discrepant results. A total of 946 specimens were retested. The kappa values for positive/negative categorical classification and the four RLU intervals were 0.91 and 0.79, respectively. Sample retesting yielded consistently lower RLU values than the original test, regardless of the time elapsed (median, 53 days). The probability of clinically discrepant results upon retesting varied according to the RLU value, with samples in the 0.5 to 5 interval showing a 10.80% probability (95% CI, 7.86 to 14.33) compared to 0.85% for samples outside this interval (95% CI, 0.17 to 1.69). Overall, the HC2 assay showed high interlaboratory concordance. The study identified differential confidence thresholds and provided guidelines for future interlaboratory PT to ensure the high analytical quality of HPV DNA detection for cervical cancer prevention.

title: The role of regulatory variation in complex traits and disease
text: In recent years, there has been rapid progress in identifying genetic locations that influence a wide range of traits, from growth and fitness in simple organisms to disease in humans. However, a significant gap remains in understanding the underlying mechanisms that connect these genetic variants to their resulting traits. Emerging studies on the genetics of gene expression have shed light on this issue, providing a crucial tool for bridging the gap between DNA sequence variations and their phenotypic consequences. In this review, we will delve into the molecular nature of regulatory variants, exploring their impact on the transcriptome and proteome. We will also discuss conceptual advances from model organism studies and highlight examples of direct genetic pathways leading from specific polymorphisms to changes in gene expression, eventually culminating in changes in physiology and disease risk.

title: Adhesion disengagement uncouples intrinsic and extrinsic forces to drive cytokinesis in epithelial tissues.
text: Cytokinesis is characterized by the invagination of a cell by a contractile actomyosin ring. In epithelial tissues, E-cadherin-mediated adhesion connecting the cell cortex facilitates the formation of new junctions between adjacent cells during cytokinesis. However, the mechanisms underlying invagination, new junction formation, and tissue integrity maintenance remain unclear. Previous studies on Drosophila embryos have revealed that apical-basal cleavage is polarized, with invagination occurring faster on the basal side than on the apical side. The contraction of the actomyosin ring is controlled by septin filaments and Anillin, but the mechanism by which polarized cleavage occurs remains unclear. Our findings indicate that mechanical anchorage of the actomyosin ring to E-cadherin complexes is responsible for polarized cleavage. The formation of the new junction requires the disengagement of adhesion between the cells in the cleavage furrow, followed by the formation of new E-cadherin complexes at the newly formed interface. The disengagement of adhesion is influenced by the tension exerted by the cytokinetic ring and neighboring cells. By uncovering the intrinsic and extrinsic forces essential for cytokinesis, we have developed a framework for understanding how tissue cohesion is maintained during epithelial cell division.

title: The epithelial inward rectifier channel Kir7.1 displays unusual K+ permeation properties.
text: Researchers have isolated cDNA sequences of rat and human proteins that encode a 360 amino acid polypeptide with a structure typical of inwardly rectifying potassium channels (Kir). The newly discovered proteins, known as Kir7.1, share only 37% of their sequence with other Kir subunits and have unique amino acids at conserved sites, particularly in the pore region. Study of rat brain tissue revealed that Kir7.1 was prominently expressed in secretory epithelial cells of the choroid plexus, as confirmed through in situ patch-clamp measurements. When Kir7.1 was expressed in Xenopus oocytes, it generated macroscopic Kir currents with a minimal dependence on external potassium concentration. The study also found that a methionine at position 125 in the pore region of Kir7.1, which is different from the usual arginine found in other Kir channels, affects the channel's ability to regulate potassium permeability. Replacing this residue with the conserved arginine in mutant Kir7.1 channels restored the dependence of K+ permeability on extracellular potassium concentration and increased the sensitivity of the channel to the ion Ba2+. These findings suggest that the site in the pore region is essential for regulating potassium permeability in Kir channels.

title: Oral fingolimod (FTY720) for relapsing multiple sclerosis.
text: Fingolimod (FTY720) is a new oral immunomodulatory drug being investigated for the treatment of relapsing multiple sclerosis. In a phase II proof-of-concept study, we randomly assigned 281 patients to receive either oral fingolimod at doses of 1.25 mg or 5.0 mg, or placebo, once daily for 6 months, with monthly magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and clinical evaluations. The primary endpoint was the total number of gadolinium-enhanced lesions recorded on T1-weighted MRI at monthly intervals. In an extension study, patients who received placebo were randomly assigned to one of the fingolimod doses, and the number of lesions and clinical disease activity were evaluated over an additional 6 months. Results showed that fingolimod significantly reduced the number of lesions detected on MRI and clinical disease activity compared to placebo, with the lowest median number of lesions observed in the 1.25 mg dose group. The annualized relapse rate was also significantly lower in the fingolimod groups compared to the placebo group. Common adverse events included nasopharyngitis, dyspnea, headache, diarrhea, and nausea, and there was an increased incidence of clinically asymptomatic elevations of alanine aminotransferase levels with fingolimod. One case of the posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome occurred in the 5.0 mg group. Fingolimod was also associated with a reduction in heart rate and a modest decrease in forced expiratory volume in 1 second. These results suggest that fingolimod may be effective in reducing disease activity in multiple sclerosis, and larger, longer-term studies are warranted to confirm these findings. (ClinicalTrials.gov numbers: NCT00333138 [core study] and NCT00235430 [extension].)

title: Nonoverlapping functions of DNA polymerases mu, lambda, and terminal deoxynucleotidyltransferase during immunoglobulin V(D)J recombination in vivo.
text: DNA polymerases pol mu, pol lambda, and TdT are members of the pol X family that share similar protein structures and functional domains. While pol mu fails to participate in heavy chain gene rearrangement, pol lambda is recruited during heavy chain rearrangement at an initial step preceding TdT action, as evidenced by shorter heavy chain junctions in pol lambda-deficient animals. In contrast to previous in vitro studies, analysis of animals lacking these enzymes reveals no overlapping or compensatory activities for V(D)J recombination between pol mu, pol lambda, and TdT. This diverse usage of polymerases with distinct catalytic specificities may reflect the specific function of the third hypervariable region for each immunoglobulin chain, with pol lambda maintaining large heavy chain junctional heterogeneity and pol mu ensuring restricted light chain junctional variability.

title: Moderate regular exercise increases basal production of nitric oxide in elderly women.
text: Vascular endothelial cells produce nitric oxide (NO), a powerful vasodilator and potential anti-atherosclerotic agent. As such, it has been proposed that NO may play a role in regulating vascular tone and preventing the progression of atherosclerosis. However, NO activity declines with aging. In a previous study, we found that intense aerobic exercise training in young adults resulted in significantly higher plasma nitrite/nitrate (NOx) concentrations. Based on these findings, we hypothesized that even mild regular exercise training could increase NO production in inactive older adults. We measured plasma NOx concentrations before and after a 3-month aerobic exercise training program (cycling on a leg ergometer at 80% ventilatory threshold for 30 minutes, 5 days/week) in elderly women. Additionally, we assessed the plasma concentration of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), a secondary messenger of NO, in the same samples. The individual ventilatory threshold increased significantly after the 3-month exercise training program. Blood pressure at rest also significantly decreased following exercise training. These findings suggest that a 3-month exercise training program in older women produced favorable physiological effects. Plasma NOx concentrations significantly increased as a result of exercise training, and plasma cGMP concentrations also increased. The present study suggests that even a mild, regular aerobic endurance exercise program can increase NO production in sedentary older adults, which may have beneficial effects (i.e., antihypertensive and anti-atherosclerotic effects through endogenous NO) on the cardiovascular system.

title: Competition between target sites of regulators shapes post-transcriptional gene regulation
text: Post-transcriptional gene regulation (PTGR) of mRNA turnover, localization, and translation is mediated by microRNAs (miRNAs) and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). These regulators exert their effects by binding to specific sequences within their target mRNAs. Mounting evidence indicates that competition for binding is a fundamental principle of PTGR. miRNAs can be neutralized and sequestered by their target mRNAs through a process termed 'sponging,' and competition between binding sites on different RNAs may lead to regulatory crosstalk between transcripts. Here, we employ quantitative modeling to explore competition effects under physiological conditions and examine the role of endogenous sponges in light of the key features that have emerged.

title: Primary prevention of ischemic stroke: A statement for healthcare professionals from the Stroke Council of the American Heart Association.
text:
Stroke is the third leading cause of death in the United States, with an estimated 700,000 incident strokes occurring annually and 4.4 million stroke survivors. (1-3) The economic burden of stroke was estimated to be $51 billion in 1999, including both direct and indirect costs. (3) Despite advances in treatment for acute ischemic stroke, including tissue plasminogen activator, the best approach to reducing the burden of stroke remains prevention. (4-5) Identifying and targeting high-risk or stroke-prone individuals can help reduce the burden of stroke. (6) However, epidemiological data suggest a leveling off of prior declines in stroke-related mortality and a possible increase in stroke incidence. (7-8)
The American Heart Association's Stroke Council formed an ad hoc writing group to review and summarize the existing evidence on various stroke risk factors. (9) The writing group used a literature review, reference to previously published guidelines, and expert opinion to formulate recommendations. (9) The level of evidence and strength of recommendations for each risk factor are listed in Tables 2-4. (9) The tables show the estimated prevalence, population attributable risk, relative risk, and risk reduction with treatment for each factor when known. (9) Population attributable risk reflects the proportion of ischemic strokes in the population that can be attributed to a particular risk factor and is calculated as 100 times the proportion of strokes that can be attributed to the risk factor divided by the total number of strokes plus the proportion of strokes that can be attributed to the risk factor. (9) ...
References: (1-9)
Note: The numbers in parentheses refer to the sources used in the text.

title: Chimeric live, attenuated vaccine against Japanese encephalitis (ChimeriVax-JE): phase 2 clinical trials for safety and immunogenicity, effect of vaccine dose and schedule, and memory response to challenge with inactivated Japanese encephalitis antigen.
text: ChimeriVax-JE is a live, attenuated vaccine against Japanese encephalitis, generated through the use of the yellow fever (YF) 17D vaccine as a vector. In a double-blind, phase 2 trial, 99 adult participants were administered either the vaccine, placebo, or YF 17D vaccine (YF-VAX). The safety profile of ChimeriVax-JE was assessed, and it was found to be well-tolerated, with no significant differences in adverse events observed between the treatment groups. Viremias resulting from the administration of ChimeriVax-JE and YF-VAX were of short duration and low titer, and 82 (94%) of 87 subjects administered graded doses (1.8-5.8 log(10)) of ChimeriVax-JE developed neutralizing antibodies. Additionally, a second dose administered 30 days later failed to exhibit a booster effect. Previous inoculation with YF did not interfere with ChimeriVax-JE, but there was a non-statistically significant suggestion that ChimeriVax-JE interfered with YF-VAX administered 30 days later. A separate study investigated immunological memory in individuals who had received ChimeriVax-JE 9 months prior to challenge with inactivated mouse-brain vaccine (JE-VAX). Anamnestic responses were observed in preimmune individuals. These findings indicate that ChimeriVax-JE is a safe and effective vaccine, eliciting protective levels of neutralizing antibodies following a single dose.

title: Global prevalence of anxiety disorders: a systematic review and meta-regression.
text:
The following is a rewritten version of the given text with improved readability and clarity:
INTRODUCTION
The literature on the global prevalence of anxiety disorders is diverse and inconsistent. To address this issue, a systematic review and meta-regression analysis were conducted to estimate the prevalence of anxiety disorders worldwide and identify the factors that contribute to variability in these estimates. The findings will inform the forthcoming Global Burden of Disease study.
METHODS
A comprehensive search of electronic databases, reference lists, review articles, and expert networks identified prevalence studies of anxiety disorders published between 1980 and 2009. A total of 87 studies from 44 countries were included in the analysis. Substantive and methodological factors associated with inter-study variability were identified through meta-regression analyses, and the global prevalence of anxiety disorders was calculated adjusting for study methodology.
RESULTS
The prevalence of anxiety disorders varied widely across studies, with estimates ranging from 0.9% to 28.3% for current prevalence and 2.4% to 29.8% for past-year prevalence. Substantive factors, such as gender, age, culture, conflict, and economic status, and urbanicity, explained the greatest proportion of variability between studies. Methodological factors, including prevalence period, number of disorders, and diagnostic instrument, accounted for an additional 13% of variance between studies.
GLOBAL PREVALENCE
The global current prevalence of anxiety disorders adjusted for methodological differences was estimated to be 7.3% (4.8-10.9%), ranging from 5.3% (3.5-8.1%) in African cultures to 10.4% (7.0-15.5%) in Euro/Anglo cultures.

CONCLUSIONS
Anxiety disorders are common, and the factors identified in this study explain much of the variability in prevalence estimates. Attention should be paid to cultural differences in responses to survey instruments for anxiety disorders. The findings of this study inform the forthcoming Global Burden of Disease study, which will provide a comprehensive overview of the global burden of mental disorders.

title: Expression of optineurin, a glaucoma-linked gene, is influenced by elevated intraocular pressure.
text: Recently, a protein called Optineurin (OPTN) was found to be associated with 16.7% of families with primary open-angle glaucoma. The function of OPTN in the eye is currently unknown, but it is present in the trabecular meshwork, which plays a crucial role in maintaining intraocular pressure (IOP). To gain insights into the role of OPTN in the development of glaucoma, we investigated its expression in response to factors known to be associated with the disease, including elevated IOP, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFalpha), and dexamethasone (DEX). We performed these treatments in human organ cultures under conditions mimicking physiological pressure. Our findings reveal that OPTN is significantly upregulated after 2, 4, and 7 days of sustained elevated IOP. Moreover, OPTN expression is induced 2.3-fold by TNFalpha and 2.6-fold by prolonged DEX treatment. These results suggest that OPTN is part of the transcriptome responding to glaucomatous insults and provide evidence for the protective role of this protein in the trabecular meshwork.

title: Prevention of malaria in long-term travelers.
text:
Long-term travelers face unique challenges when it comes to preventing malaria. Unlike short-term travelers, who are primarily protected by guidelines aimed at preventing Plasmodium falciparum infections, long-term travelers require more comprehensive strategies to address the higher risk of malaria associated with extended stays in endemic regions. The aim of this study was to examine the risk of malaria in long-term travelers, explore recent developments in personal protective measures, and evaluate the safety and tolerability of malaria chemoprophylaxis during long-term use. The study also considered alternative prevention strategies, including continuous chemoprophylaxis, stand-by emergency self-treatment, seasonal prophylaxis, and methods to prevent primary infection and relapses from Plasmodium vivax malaria.
A comprehensive search of scientific literature was conducted to identify relevant studies and articles, with a cutoff date of July 2006. The search terms used included "long-term travel" and "malaria prevention," "long-term malaria chemoprophylaxis," and "insect repellent and malaria." Additional references were obtained from the bibliographies of selected articles, dissertations, and conference proceedings on travel medicine. No language restrictions were applied.
The findings of the study indicate that long-term travelers are at a higher risk of malaria than short-term travelers. Unfortunately, long-term travelers often underuse personal protective measures and adhere poorly to continuous chemoprophylaxis regimens. To address these challenges, various strategies are used during long-term stays, including discontinuation of chemoprophylaxis after the initial period, sequential regimens with different medications, stand-by emergency self-treatment, and seasonal chemoprophylaxis targeting high-incidence periods or locations. Each of these strategies has its advantages and drawbacks.
Counterfeit drugs sold in countries endemic for malaria pose a significant concern for long-term travelers who purchase medications overseas. Additionally, vivax malaria can cause significant illness in travelers, but relapses of vivax malaria are not prevented by the current first-line chemoprophylaxis regimens. The study concludes that prevention of malaria in long-term travelers is a complex issue that requires expert advice from travel medicine specialists. Personalized recommendations for malaria prevention in long-term travelers are essential.

title: Activation of AMPKα2 in adipocytes is essential for nicotine-induced insulin resistance in vivo
text:
Cigarette smoking may seem to have a paradoxical effect on human bodies, promoting both weight loss and insulin resistance (IR) simultaneously. Despite being aware of this phenomenon, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we seek to uncover the truth by evaluating the role of nicotine, a primary component of cigarette smoke.
We found that nicotine, when introduced into adipocytes, selectively activates AMP-activated protein kinase α2 (AMPKα2). This triggers the degradation of MAP kinase phosphatase-1 (MKP1) through a proteasome-dependent process. As a consequence, the irregular activation of p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase and c-Jun N-terminal kinase follows, which leads to a heightened phosphorylation of insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS1) at serine 307. This phosphorylation ultimately results in IRS1 degradation, inhibition of protein kinase B, and the loss of insulin-mediated inhibition of lipolysis.
Nicotine's ability to stimulate lipolysis leads to weight loss, but this benefit is accompanied by an adverse effect: elevated levels of circulating free fatty acids, which can trigger IR in insulin-sensitive tissues. Ironically, despite decreasing total body adiposity, those who smoke tend to develop IR.
We now confirm that AMPKα2 is a crucial factor in nicotine-induced whole-body insulin resistance, even if fat storages are reduced.

title: Availability of evidence of benefits on overall survival and quality of life of cancer drugs approved by European Medicines Agency: retrospective cohort study of drug approvals 2009-13
text:
Study Examines Availability of Data on Cancer Drug Benefits in Europe
Objective: To assess the availability of data on the overall survival and quality of life benefits of cancer drugs approved in Europe.
Design: Retrospective cohort study setting: Publicly accessible regulatory and scientific reports on cancer approvals by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) from 2009 to 2013.
Main outcome measures: Pivotal and postmarketing trials of cancer drugs according to their design features (randomization, crossover, blinding), comparators, and endpoints. Availability and magnitude of benefit on overall survival or quality of life determined at time of approval and after market entry. Validated European Society for Medical Oncology Magnitude of Clinical Benefit Scale (ESMO-MCBS) used to assess the clinical value of the reported gains in published studies of cancer drugs.
Results: From 2009 to 2013, the EMA approved the use of 48 cancer drugs for 68 indications. Of these, eight indications (12%) were approved on the basis of a single-arm study. At the time of market approval, there was significant prolongation of survival in 24 of the 68 (35%). The magnitude of the benefit on overall survival ranged from 1.0 to 5.8 months (median 2.7 months). At the time of market approval, there was an improvement in quality of life in seven of 68 indications (10%). Out of 44 indications for which there was no evidence of a survival gain at the time of market authorization, in the subsequent postmarketing period, there was evidence for extension of life in three (7%) and reported benefit on quality of life in five (11%). Of the 68 cancer indications with EMA approval, and with a median of 5.4 years' follow-up (minimum 3.3 years, maximum 8.1 years), only 35 (51%) had shown a significant improvement in survival or quality of life, while 33 (49%) remained uncertain. Of 23 indications associated with a survival benefit that could be scored with the ESMO-MCBS tool, the benefit was judged to be clinically meaningful in less than half (11/23, 48%).
Conclusions: This systematic evaluation of oncology approvals by the EMA in 2009-13 shows that most drugs entered the market without evidence of benefit on survival or quality of life. At a minimum of 3.3 years after market entry, there was still no conclusive evidence that these drugs either extended or improved the lives of most cancer patients. When there were survival gains over existing treatment options or placebo, they were often marginal.

title: A cluster randomized, controlled trial of breast and cervix cancer screening in Mumbai, India: methodology and interim results after three rounds of screening.
text:
Cervical and Breast Cancers: A Major Global Health Burden and a New Screening Trial
Cervical and breast cancers are the most common types of cancer affecting women worldwide, and they pose a significant health burden, particularly in developing countries. To address this issue, a cluster-randomized, controlled screening trial was conducted at the Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai, India, with funding from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) of the United States. The trial began in May 1998 and will continue for eight years, with four rounds of screening at two-year intervals.
The screening trial involves trained primary health workers providing health education and visual inspection of the cervix using 4% acetic acid-based visual inspection of the cervix (VIA) to the participants. In addition, clinical breast examination (CBE) will also be conducted. The control arm receives only health education.
After three rounds of screening, the methodology and interim results were presented. The screening arm showed high participation rates, low attrition rates, good compliance to diagnostic confirmation, significant downstaging, and excellent treatment completion rate, along with improving case fatality ratios. The study also found significant differences between the ever-screened and never-screened participants in the screening arm regarding variables such as religion, language, age, education, occupation, income, and health-seeking behavior for gynecological and breast-related complaints.
In contrast, the control arm showed excellent participation rate for health education, low attrition rates, and a good number of symptomatic referrals for both cervical and breast cancers.
Overall, this screening trial has the potential to significantly improve cancer outcomes in developing countries like India and could serve as a model for other countries to follow.

title: Evidence for energy-dependent accumulation of paraquat into rat lung
text:
In the early stages after ingestion, there are no obvious changes in the lungs, which may explain why death occurs weeks later following accidental ingestion. Animal studies have demonstrated that the lung is the primary target organ, but the reason for the lung's ability to retain paraquat is not yet understood.
Here is the rewritten text with some changes to make it more concise and easier to read:
Paraquat, a common herbicide, can cause severe lung damage and fibrosis in humans after accidental ingestion. Animal studies have shown the lung to be the primary target organ, with a high concentration of paraquat there following administration. However, the reasons for the lung's ability to retain paraquat are currently unclear. Initial changes in the lungs after ingestion may not be apparent for several days, which may explain why death occurs weeks later in some cases.

title: Role of gut commensal microflora in the development of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
text: Gut mucosal tolerance has been recognized as a potentially promising pathway for treating autoimmune diseases like human multiple sclerosis and experimental conditions such as experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). There is limited information on the capacity of commensal gut bacteria to promote peripheral immune tolerance. To investigate this further, inbred SJL and C57BL/6 mice were given antibiotics orally to reduce the diversity of gut microorganisms. The results showed that reducing the gut microbiota hindered the development of EAE. Intriguingly, intraperitoneal antibiotic-treated mice did not experience significant changes in gut microflora and still developed EAE at similar rates to untreated mice, suggesting that the reduction in disease activity was due to changes in the gut bacterial population. This protection was associated with lower levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and higher levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and IL-13. Transferring low numbers of IL-10-producing CD25(+)CD4(+) T cells (>75% FoxP3(+)) isolated from the cervical lymph nodes of commensal bacteria into mice protected them from EAE, and in vivo neutralization of CD25(+) cells confirmed the role of regulatory T cells in maintaining peripheral immune homeostasis. Our data demonstrate that modifying the gut commensal bacteria through antibiotics can modulate peripheral immune tolerance, which can protect against EAE. This approach may offer a new therapeutic strategy in treating multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune diseases.

title: Epidemiology of surgically managed pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence.
text:
Objective:
To determine the incidence of surgically managed pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence in a population-based cohort and to describe their clinical characteristics.
Methods:
A retrospective cohort study was conducted using all patients who underwent surgical treatment for prolapse and incontinence at Kaiser Permanente Northwest between 1995 and 2015. In total, 395 women were included in the study, all of whom were aged 20 or older and were members of Kaiser Permanente Northwest. A standardized data-collection form was used to review all inpatient and outpatient charts, and variables examined included age, ethnicity, height, weight, vaginal parity, smoking history, medical history, and surgical history, including the preoperative evaluation, procedure performed, and details of all prior procedures. Age-specific and cumulative incidences were calculated, and the number of primary operations was compared to repeat operations performed for prolapse or incontinence.
Results:
The age-specific incidence of surgical intervention for pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence increased with advancing age. By age 80, the lifetime risk of undergoing a single operation for these conditions was 11.1%. The majority of patients were older, postmenopausal, parous, and overweight, and nearly half were current or former smokers, with one-fifth having chronic lung disease. Reoperation was common (29.2% of cases), and the time intervals between repeat procedures decreased with each successive repair.
Conclusion:
Pelvic floor dysfunction is a significant health concern for older women, as evidenced by the 11.1% lifetime risk of undergoing a single operation for pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence. The large proportion of reoperations highlights the need for further epidemiologic research to determine the etiology, natural history, and long-term treatment outcomes of these conditions.

title: Antihypertensive classes, cognitive decline and incidence of dementia: a network meta-analysis.
text:
OBJECTIVE:
The impact of blood pressure-lowering treatments on preventing cognitive decline and dementia has been inconsistent. To compare the effects of different antihypertensive drug classes on cognitive function and dementia incidence, we conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis of 19 randomized trials (18,515 individuals) and 11 studies (831,674 individuals).
METHODS:
We analyzed the effects of antihypertensive treatment on cognition and dementia incidence in hypertensive patients without prior cerebrovascular disorders using network meta-analysis. The analysis included 15 studies that combined both randomized trials and observational studies.
RESULTS:
Antihypertensive treatment, regardless of drug class, showed beneficial effects on overall cognition (effect size = 0.05, 95% CI = 0.02-0.07) and all cognitive functions except language. Treatment reduced the risk of all-cause dementia by 9% (hazard ratio = 0.91, 95% CI = 0.89-0.94) compared to the control group, with the largest benefits observed with angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs). ARBs were more effective than β-blockers, diuretics, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors in rank. While the mean change in blood pressure did not significantly differ between drug classes, ARBs showed the largest effect.
CONCLUSION:
Our findings suggest that antihypertensive treatment has a beneficial impact on cognitive decline and dementia prevention, with ARBs possibly being the most effective. The results of this study support earlier findings that highlight the significance of blood pressure management in preventing cognitive decline.

title: Abnormal hemoglobins in a quarter million people.
text: Hemolysates from over 250,000 people in Alabama were electrophoresed on cellulose acetate at pH 8.4, and those showing abnormalities were also electrophoresed in citrate agar at pH 6.0. The globin chains of non-Hb S and non-Hb C mutants were electrophoresed in urea-mercaptoethanol buffers at both pH 8.9 and pH 6.0, and 60 of these were structurally analyzed. Among 6,000 samples from whites, only three contained abnormal hemoglobins, including Hb D Los Angeles, Hb J Baltimore, and one unidentified. In contrast, about 29,000 samples from blacks showed electrophoretically detectable abnormalities, most of which were linked to Hb S or C, present at frequencies of around 9% and 3%, respectively. Approximately 1,000 samples were found to have patterns with potential clinical significance. Twenty other mutant hemoglobins were detected in various genetic combinations in 164 families; four of these, Hb Alabama, Montgomery, Titusville, and Mobile, were previously unknown. The methods used are rapid, cost-effective, and well-suited for large-scale surveys. They provide highly specific characterizations of many mutant hemoglobins, and no discrepancies were found between the presumptive identifications based on these characterizations and the definitive identifications obtained through structural analyses.

title: Cellular adaptation to mechanical stress: role of integrins, Rho, cytoskeletal tension and mechanosensitive ion channels.
text: To gain insights into how cells sense and adapt to mechanical stresses, we applied tension forces to magnetic microbeads attached to cell-surface integrin receptors and tracked changes in bead displacement with sub-micrometer resolution using optical microscopy. We identified four types of mechanical responses in cells: (1) an immediate viscoelastic response, (2) early adaptive behavior characterized by attenuation of oscillatory forces with each pulse, (3) later adaptive cell stiffening with sustained (>15 seconds) static stresses, and (4) a large-scale repositioning response with prolonged (>1 minute) stress. Interestingly, these adaptation responses varied biochemically. The immediate and early responses were influenced by dissipating cytoskeletal prestress (isometric tension), while the later adaptive response was not. Repositioning response was blocked when tension was inhibited through interference with Rho signaling, similar to the case of the immediate and early responses, but it was also prevented by blocking mechanosensitive ion channels or by inhibiting Src tyrosine kinases. Furthermore, all adaptive responses were suppressed when cells were cooled to 4°C to slow down biochemical remodeling. Thus, cells employ multiple mechanisms to detect and respond to changes in the level of mechanical stress applied to integrins.

title: Cutting edge: Candida albicans hyphae formation triggers activation of the Nlrp3 inflammasome.
text: The pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β plays a crucial role in antifungal immunity; however, the mechanisms by which fungal pathogens trigger IL-1β secretion are not fully understood. In this study, we investigate the mechanisms of IL-1β release during Candida albicans infection. We found that infection with C. albicans activates the Nlrp3 inflammasome, leading to the release of IL-1β. Interestingly, the ability of C. albicans to transition from a unicellular yeast form to a filamentous form is essential for the activation of the Nlrp3 inflammasome, as C. albicans mutants incapable of forming hyphae exhibited defects in inducing IL-1β secretion from macrophages. Our findings also indicate that Nlrp3-deficient mice are more susceptible to C. albicans infection, consistent with a key role for Nlrp3 in innate immune responses to this pathogen.

title: Type 2 diabetes and subsequent incidence of breast cancer in the Nurses' Health Study.
text:
Objective: Hyperinsulinemia may facilitate mammary carcinogenesis. Insulin resistance, on the other hand, has been linked to an elevated risk of breast cancer and is also characteristic of type 2 diabetes. To investigate this relationship further, we conducted a prospective study evaluating the association between type 2 diabetes and the incidence of invasive breast cancer in the Nurses' Health Study.
Design and Methods: In this large cohort study, we followed 116,488 female nurses aged 30-55 years, who were free of cancer in 1976, for a total of 2.3 million person-years. We identified 6,220 women with type 2 diabetes and 5,189 incident cases of invasive breast cancer during the follow-up period. We gathered data on age, obesity, family history of breast cancer, history of benign breast disease, reproductive factors, physical activity, and alcohol consumption.
Results: During the follow-up period, we observed a modestly elevated incidence of breast cancer among women with type 2 diabetes (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.17; 95% CI 1.01-1.35). This association was apparent among postmenopausal women (1.16; 0.98-1.62) but not premenopausal women (0.83; 0.48-1.42). Additionally, the association was predominant among women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer (1.22; 1.01-1.47).
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that women with type 2 diabetes may have a slightly increased risk of breast cancer. These results highlight the importance of considering the potential effects of insulin resistance on breast cancer risk in the development of prevention and treatment strategies.

title: Virus-encoded microRNAs.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a topic of immense interest due to their regulatory functions in various cellular processes, including immune response, apoptosis, and tumorigenesis. Additionally, several virus families have been found to encode miRNAs, and researchers continue to uncover their roles in the viral life cycle. Despite the identification of over 225 viral miRNAs, a comprehensive understanding of their functions remains limited. This review focuses on a few well-studied viral miRNAs and extrapolates general themes of their activities. These include the regulation of viral gene expression, evasion of host defenses, and a likely key role in maintaining latent and persistent infections. It is hypothesized that while the molecular mechanisms and machinery may be similar, viral miRNAs may utilize distinct target strategies compared to host miRNAs. Specifically, many viral miRNAs may regulate unique viral-encoded transcripts or host genes that are exclusive to the viral miRNA landscape. In order to advance the field, additional functional studies that utilize engineered viral miRNA mutants and relevant infection models are necessary.

title: Wolfram syndrome 1 and adenylyl cyclase 8 interact at the plasma membrane to regulate insulin production and secretion
text: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is responsible for producing and storing insulin in pancreatic beta cells, but when ER stress occurs, it can lead to pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction and contribute to the development of type 2 diabetes. Wolfram syndrome 1 (WFS1) is believed to play a key role in the ER stress signaling pathway, but its direct impact on beta-cell function remains unknown. Our research found that WFS1 is crucial for glucose- and glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1)-stimulated cyclic AMP (cAMP) production and the regulation of insulin biosynthesis and secretion. When glucose is present, WFS1 translocates from the ER to the plasma membrane, where it combines with adenylyl cyclase 8 (AC8), an enzyme essential for cAMP synthesis in beta cells. The inhibition of this complex formation by ER stress and mutant WFS1 reduces cAMP synthesis and insulin secretion, indicating that WFS1 has a distinct function outside the ER in regulating both insulin biosynthesis and secretion. These findings suggest that the reduction of WFS1 protein on the plasma membrane contributes to beta-cell dysfunction and the progression of type 2 diabetes.

title: Two Rice GRAS Family Genes Responsive to N-Acetylchitooligosaccharide Elicitor are Induced by Phytoactive Gibberellins: Evidence for Cross-Talk Between Elicitor and Gibberellin Signaling in Rice Cells
text: In this study, we investigate the induction of two GRAS family genes, CIGR1 and CIGR2, in rice in response to the potent elicitor N-acetylchitooligosaccharide (GN). Our data shows that these genes are rapidly induced by exogenous gibberellins, and the induction pattern is dependent on the dose and biological activity of the gibberellins. These results suggest that the induction of CIGR1 and CIGR2 by gibberellin is mediated by a specific receptor and signal transduction pathway. Further pharmacological analysis reveals that the induction of CIGR1 and CIGR2 by gibberellin is dependent on protein phosphorylation/dephosphorylation events. Interestingly, we found that the induction of CIGR1 and CIGR2 by GN is not observed in rice calli derived from slender rice 1, a constitutive gibberellin-responsive mutant, or d1, a mutant deficient in the α-subunit of the heterotrimeric G-protein. These results suggest that the signal transduction cascade from gibberellin is independent of that from GN, and further imply that CIGR1 and CIGR2 have dual, distinct roles in defense and development.

title: Ghrelin's second life: from appetite stimulator to glucose regulator.
text: Ghrelin, a 28-amino acid peptide hormone produced by the stomach, was the first orexigenic hormone discovered outside of the brain. Its octanoyl modification, mediated by ghrelin O-acyltransferase (GOAT), is crucial for its biological activity. Ghrelin stimulates food intake by binding to its receptor (GRLN-R) on hypothalamic neurons. Its widespread expression throughout the body implies a role in multiple physiological functions, including growth hormone release, gastric emptying, and body weight regulation, as well as a potential local function in the pancreas. Recent studies suggest that ghrelin and its receptor play a key role in blood glucose homeostasis, with some studies proposing that ghrelin inhibits insulin secretion, resulting in increased circulating glucose levels. This suggests that ghrelin may be a diabetogenic factor, making it a promising target for developing new therapies for obesity-related type 2 diabetes, a growing health problem worldwide.

title: Histone acetylation and deacetylation in yeast
text: In the yeast species Saccharomyces cerevisiae, histone acetylation and deacetylation occur by directing enzymes called acetyltransferases and deacetylases to specific gene promoters. However, these processes also have a global impact on the majority of nucleosomes in the genome, even in an untargeted manner. Recent research has revealed additional functions for histone acetylation, including its involvement in DNA replication, repair, and the formation of heterochromatin, beyond its conventional role in transcription. Interestingly, certain acetylatable lysine residues can serve as binding sites for regulatory factors. Moreover, histone deacetylation is not only repressive but can actually be necessary for the activation of certain genes.

title: Neuroinflammation in spinal cord injury: therapeutic targets for neuroprotection and regeneration.
text: Traumatic spinal cord injury unleashes a complex local inflammatory response with the potential to both enhance repair and exacerbate pathology. The composition and capabilities of the post-injury immune cascade change over time and distance from the lesion, leading to the production of various cytokines, proteases, and growth factors. These dynamic environments can determine the fate of affected neurons and glia, with microenvironmental cues from the cells themselves playing a crucial role in these outcomes. By manipulating the assembly and phenotype of cells in the neuroinflammatory response, we may harness the potential of this response to promote repair, prevent pain, and facilitate functional recovery. This review focuses on the potential of the neuroinflammatory response to drive outcomes such as regeneration and recovery.

title: Evaluation of systemic amyloidosis by scintigraphy with 123I-labeled serum amyloid P component.
text:
Background:
The progression and distribution of systemic amyloidosis have been challenging to monitor due to the difficulty in detecting amyloid deposits through biopsy alone. Serum amyloid P component (SAP) is a normal circulating protein that can be specially bound to amyloid fibrils, making it a potential marker for amyloid deposits. We aimed to determine whether labeled SAP could be used to identify amyloid deposits in patients with systemic amyloidosis.
Methods:
We administered purified human SAP labeled with iodine-123 to 50 patients with biopsy-confirmed systemic amyloidosis (25 with the primary AL type and 25 with the secondary AA type) and 26 healthy controls. Whole-body images and regional views were obtained after 24 hours and read in a blinded manner.
Results:
In patients with amyloidosis, the 123I-SAP was rapidly and specifically localized to amyloid deposits. The scintigraphic images obtained were characteristic and appeared to accurately assess the extent of amyloid deposition in all 50 patients. In contrast, no uptake of the 123I-SAP was observed in the control group or healthy subjects. Amyloid deposition was confined to the spleen in patients with AA amyloidosis, while the heart, skin, carpal region, and bone marrow showed uptake in patients with the AL type. Positive images were seen in six patients in whom biopsies had been negative or unsuccessful, and amyloid was later found on biopsy or at autopsy. Additionally, progressive amyloid deposition was observed in 9 of 11 patients studied serially.


Conclusion:
Scintigraphy with 123I-SAP can be used for the diagnosis, location, and monitoring of systemic amyloidosis. This non-invasive technique has the potential to accurately assess the extent of amyloid deposition in patients with this condition, providing valuable insights for clinical decision-making and disease management.

title: The Neurovascular Unit Coming of Age: A Journey through Neurovascular Coupling in Health and Disease
text: The concept of the neurovascular unit (NVU), formalized at the 2001 Stroke Progress Review Group meeting of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, highlights the intricate relationship between the brain and its blood vessels. Since then, the NVU has garnered significant attention from the neuroscience community, leading to substantial advances in the field. Here, we will assess the current state of knowledge on the NVU, focusing on one of its most critical roles: the coordination between neural activity and blood flow. The available evidence favors a transformative shift in the mechanisms of neurovascular coupling, transitioning from a unidimensional process involving neuronal-astrocytic signaling to local blood vessels to a complex, multidimensional process involving multiple cell types and signaling pathways that impact the entire cerebrovascular network in a highly orchestrated manner. The growing understanding of NVU dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases also underscores the importance of maintaining neurovascular health to promote brain well-being.

title: Effects of MAL61 and MAL62 overexpression on maltose fermentation of baker's yeast in lean dough.
text: The primary fermentable sugar in lean dough is maltose, and improving the leavening capabilities of baker's yeast in these conditions requires enhancing maltose metabolism. Maltase (alpha-glucosidase, encoded by MAL62) and maltose permease (encoded by MAL61) are the key factors involved in maltose metabolism. Although the major rate-limiting factor in maltose metabolism and leavening ability of baker's yeast in lean dough remains unclear, this study aimed to investigate the decisive factor by constructing MAL61 and/or MAL62 overexpression strains. Our findings revealed that elevated maltose permease activity through MAL61 overexpression had less of an impact on maltose fermentation compared to elevated maltase activity through MAL62 overexpression. Increased maltase activity through MAL62 overexpression led to a substantial 44% improvement in the leavening ability of industrial baker's yeast in lean dough and a 39% increase in maltose metabolism in a medium containing glucose and maltose. Therefore, maltase proved to be the rate-limiting factor in maltose fermentation of industrial baker's yeast in lean dough. This study provides a foundation for breeding industrial baker's yeast for quick dough leavening.

title: Human papillomavirus genotype 31 does not express detectable microRNA levels during latent or productive virus replication.
text: Recent findings have revealed that several pathogenic DNA viruses produce virally encoded microRNAs in infected cells. Specifically, a range of human and animal herpesviruses, as well as members of the polyoma- and adenovirus families, have been found to express microRNAs. While their functions are still unclear, it is likely that these viral microRNAs play a crucial role in viral replication in vivo. In this study, we investigated the microRNAs expressed in human cells during the latent and productive phases of the human papillomavirus genotype 31 (HPV31) replication cycle. Surprisingly, we were unable to identify any HPV31-specific microRNAs after cloning and identifying over 500 cellular microRNAs. We therefore conclude that HPV31, and possibly human papillomaviruses in general, do not express viral microRNAs.

title: Integrated genomic profiling of endometrial carcinoma associates aggressive tumors with indicators of PI3 kinase activation.
text:
Although 75% of endometrial cancers are diagnosed in the early stages, 15% to 20% of these will recur. To identify features that predict recurrent disease, we performed an integrated analysis of genome-wide expression and copy-number data for primary endometrial carcinomas along with extensive clinical and histopathological data. Unsupervised analysis of the expression data revealed two distinct clusters with distinct phenotypes, and these were associated with significant differences in disease-free survival.
To understand the mechanisms behind these differences, we conducted a global genomic survey of amplifications, deletions, and loss of heterozygosity, which identified 11 significantly amplified and 13 significantly deleted regions. We found that amplification of the oncogene PIK3CA was associated with poor prognosis and clustered with an aggressive transcriptional profile. Moreover, samples with PIK3CA amplification showed signs of in vitro activation of PI3 kinase (PI3K), a signature shared by aggressive tumors without PIK3CA amplification. Tumors with loss of PTEN expression or PIK3CA overexpression that did not have PIK3CA amplification also showed high levels of PI3K activation, along with high protein expression of the PI3K pathway member STMN1 and an aggressive phenotype in test and validation datasets. However, mutations of PTEN or PIK3CA were not associated with the same expression profile or aggressive phenotype. STMN1 expression had independent prognostic value. The findings emphasize the utility of comprehensive analysis of the cancer genome in clinically annotated specimens and highlight the importance of the PI3K pathway in patients with aggressive endometrial cancer.

title: Alteration of the Antitumor Immune Response by Cancer-Associated Fibroblasts
text: Within the tumor microenvironment, a specific subtype of cells known as cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) play a pivotal role in the intricate process of tumor-stroma interaction. CAFs, which are among the most prevalent stromal cell populations in most types of human carcinomas, have been implicated in various aspects of tumor progression, including tumor growth, angiogenesis, cancer stemness, extracellular matrix remodeling, tissue invasion, metastasis, and even chemoresistance. In recent years, these activated tumor-associated fibroblasts have also been shown to modulate the anti-tumor immune response on multiple levels. This review aims to provide an overview of our current understanding of how CAFs execute these functions and to explore their potential therapeutic implications.

title: Confusion and memory loss from capsular genu infarction: a thalamocortical disconnection syndrome?
text: We investigated six patients who experienced sudden changes in behavior after an infarction in the inferior genu of the internal capsule. The acute symptoms included fluctuating levels of alertness, inattention, memory loss, apathy, abulia, and psychomotor retardation, which suggested frontal lobe dysfunction. Contralateral hemiparesis and dysarthria were generally mild, except when the infarct extended to the posterior limb. Neuropsychological testing in five patients with left-sided infarcts revealed significant verbal memory loss. Additional cognitive deficits consistent with dementia were identified in four patients. A right-sided infarct caused a temporary impairment in visuospatial memory. Functional brain imaging in three patients showed a focal reduction in hemispheric perfusion that was most prominent in the ipsilateral inferior and medial frontal cortex. We inferred that the capsular genu infarct interrupted the inferior and anterior thalamic peduncles, resulting in functional deactivation of the ipsilateral frontal cortex. These findings suggest that one mechanism for cognitive decline resulting from a lacunar infarct is thalamocortical disconnection of white matter tracts, in some cases leading to "strategic-infarct dementia."

title: Neoadjuvant androgen ablation before radical prostatectomy in cT2bNxMo prostate cancer: 5-year results.
text:
In the initial report of the Lupron Depot Neoadjuvant Prostate Cancer Study Group, patients who received 3 months of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) showed a significant decrease in the positive margin rate compared to those who underwent radical prostatectomy alone. This study, conducted over a period of 5 years, presents the longest follow-up of any neoadjuvant trial to date.
Methods:
A multi-institutional prospective randomized trial was conducted between February 1992 and April 1994 involving patients with stage cT2b prostate cancer. A total of 138 patients received 3 months of leuprolide plus flutamide before radical prostatectomy, while 144 patients underwent radical prostatectomy alone. Patients were followed up every 6 months with serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing for 5 years. Biochemical recurrence was defined as PSA levels greater than 0.4 ng./ml.
Results:
At the 5-year mark, there was no significant difference in the biochemical recurrence rate between the neoadjuvant androgen ablation plus prostatectomy group (64.8%) and the prostatectomy-only group (67.6%). PSA levels were less than 0.4 ng./ml. in 64.8% of the neoadjuvant group and 67.6% of the prostatectomy-only group (p = 0.663).
Conclusion:
While 3 months of ADT before radical prostatectomy appeared to significantly decrease positive surgical margins, the 5-year follow-up shows no improvement in the recurrence rate compared to prostatectomy alone. Until further studies demonstrate improved outcome with longer periods of ADT, induction ADT before radical prostatectomy is not justified.

title: Full-length transcriptome assembly from RNA-Seq data without a reference genome.
text: Advances in massively parallel sequencing allow for extensive exploration of transcriptomes with unprecedented depth and efficiency. However, conventional methods for transcript reconstruction from these data often rely on aligning reads to a reference genome, which can be a limiting factor when dealing with samples lacking a complete or well-annotated genome. To address this challenge, we present the Trinity method for de novo assembly of full-length transcripts, which is evaluated on samples from fission yeast, mouse, and whitefly, where a reference genome is not available. By efficiently constructing and analyzing sets of de Bruijn graphs, Trinity successfully reconstructs a considerable fraction of transcripts, including alternatively spliced isoforms and transcripts from recently duplicated genes. In comparison to other de novo transcriptome assemblers, Trinity consistently recovers more full-length transcripts across a wide range of expression levels, with a sensitivity similar to methods that rely on genome alignments. Our approach provides a comprehensive solution for transcriptome reconstruction in any sample, particularly when a reference genome is unavailable.

title: Growth restricted in vitro culture conditions alter the imprinted gene expression patterns of mouse embryonic stem cells.
text: Embryonic stem (ES) cell-derived clones and chimeras often experience growth abnormalities during fetal development, leading to offspring with increased neonatal mortality and morbidity. studied the role of epigenetic factors in this phenomenon. found that during culture, growth-restricted ES cells exhibit abnormal methylation profiles and altered expression of two important imprinted genes: insulin-like growth factor II (IGF2) and H19. using a mouse model, we showed that culture conditions that simulate fetal development, such as starvation and high cell density, lead to changes in methylation patterns and gene expression that could contribute to growth abnormalities in offspring. this work provides evidence that epigenetic factors play a crucial role in the loss of developmental potential in ES cell-derived clones and chimeras.

title: When is antipsychotic polypharmacy supported by research evidence? Implications for QI.
text:
Concurrent use of multiple standing antipsychotics (antipsychotic polypharmacy) is increasingly common among both inpatients and outpatients. Despite this trend, reviews of research evidence on antipsychotic polypharmacy have not distinguished between appropriate versus inappropriate use.
To investigate the effectiveness of antipsychotic polypharmacy, a systematic review of studies comparing changes in symptoms, functioning, and side effects between patients treated with multiple antipsychotics and patients treated with a single antipsychotic was conducted. The studies were grouped based on whether prescribing was concordant with clinical practice guidelines for multiple antipsychotic use.
The literature review, including three randomized controlled trials, found no evidence to support the use of antipsychotic polypharmacy in patients without a history of treatment resistance to multiple trials of monotherapy. However, limited data suggest that antipsychotic polypharmacy may be beneficial in patients with a history of treatment resistance to multiple monotherapy trials, particularly when clozapine is augmented with a second-generation antipsychotic.
The study's findings emphasize the importance of avoiding antipsychotic polypharmacy in patients without guideline-recommended indications for its use. The Joint Commission has implemented a core measure set for Hospital-Based Inpatient Psychiatric Services, including two measures related to antipsychotic polypharmacy. The first measure assesses the overall rate of antipsychotic polypharmacy, while the second measure evaluates whether clinically appropriate justification has been documented to support the use of more than one antipsychotic medication.

title: The Liverpool uveal melanoma liver metastases pathway: outcome following liver resection.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the outcomes of patients undergoing liver resection for metastases from uveal melanoma.
Methods: Over a 9-year period, patients with uveal melanoma metastases were included. High-risk patients were offered 6-monthly non-contrast liver magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) surveillance after treatment of the primary uveal melanoma. Following the detection of liver metastases, patients underwent contrast-enhanced (Primovist®) liver MRI, computer tomography (CT) of the thorax, and staging laparoscopy.
Results: A total of 155 patients with uveal melanoma liver metastases were referred, of which 17 patients underwent liver resection (11.0%). One patient was treated with percutaneous radio-frequency ablation. Majority of patients who underwent liver resection had multiple metastectomies (n = 8) and three patients had major liver resections. The median overall survival for patients treated with surgery/ablation was 27 months (14-90 months), which was significantly better than patients treated palliatively (median = 8 months, P < 0.001). Among patients who underwent surgery, 11 had recurrent disease (median = 13 months). Patients who had undergone a major liver resection had a significantly poorer disease-free survival (P = 0.037).
Conclusion: Patients who can undergo surgical resection for metastatic uveal melanoma have a more favorable survival compared to those who do not.

title: Smooth muscle lineage diversity in the chick embryo. Two types of aortic smooth muscle cell differ in growth and receptor-mediated transcriptional responses to transforming growth factor-beta.
text: In avian embryo lineage studies, we have identified two types of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in the tunica media of large elastic arteries: one that originates from the cardiac neural crest and is ectodermal in nature (Ect), and another that arises from local mesenchyme of mesodermal origin (Mes). To investigate whether the differing embryonic lineages give rise to SMCs with distinct growth and differentiation properties, we isolated Ect and Mes SMCs from the Day 14 chick embryo aorta. Surprisingly, despite their different embryonic origins, we found that Ect and Mes SMCs exhibit similar levels of seven smooth muscle differentiation markers in vitro. Conversely, Ect SMCs displayed a greater capacity for growth in serum-free medium compared to Mes SMCs, but only under conditions that allow for short-range cell-cell interactions. Interestingly, we discovered significant lineage-dependent differences in SMC responses to transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta). Exposure to TGF-beta 1 (0.4-400 pmole/liter) consistently increased DNA synthesis in Ect SMCs, whereas in paired cultures of Mes SMCs, TGF-beta 1 was growth inhibitory. Moreover, SMCs transfected with a luciferase reporter gene under the control of TGF-beta 1-response elements showed a 12-fold increase in luciferase activity in Ect SMCs and only a 3-fold increase in Mes SMCs upon TGF-beta 1 treatment (120 pM). In addition, we found that Ect and Mes SMCs expressed similar levels of types I, II, and III TGF-beta receptors, but Mes SMCs produced a fully glycosylated form of the type II TGF-beta receptor subunit, while Ect SMCs elaborated only an unglycosylated form. These findings suggest that different SMC populations within a common vessel wall may respond differently to signals that regulate SMC formation during embryonic development and to factors involved in the progression of vascular disease later in life.

title: THE USE OF LEAD CITRATE AT HIGH pH AS AN ELECTRON-OPAQUE STAIN IN ELECTRON MICROSCOPY
text:
Aqueous solutions of lead salts (1, 2) and saturated solutions of lead hydroxide (1) have been used as stains to enhance the electron-scattering properties of biological materials examined in the electron microscope. While saturated solutions of lead hydroxide (1) stain more intensely than either lead acetate or monobasic lead acetate (1, 2), they form insoluble lead carbonate upon exposure to air, which can contaminate the surface of sections during staining. This has driven the development of elaborate procedures to exclude air or carbon dioxide (3, 4). Several modified lead stains have recently appeared (5-7), which utilize a high pH (approximately 12) and contain small amounts of tartrate (6), a relatively weak complexing agent (8), in addition to lead. These modified stains are less likely to contaminate the surface of the section with precipitated stain products.
The stain reported here differs from previous alkaline lead stains in that the chelating agent, citrate, is present in sufficient excess to sequester all lead present. Lead citrate, which is soluble in high concentrations in basic solutions, is a chelate compound with an apparent association constant (log Ka) between ligand and lead ion of 6.5 (9). Tissue binding sites, likely including organophosphates and other anionic species present in biological components following fixation, dehydration, and plastic embedding, have a greater affinity for this cation than lead citrate, as cellular and extracellular structures in the section sequester lead from the staining solution. Alkaline lead citrate solutions are less likely to contaminate sections, as no precipitates form when droplets of fresh staining solution are exposed to air for periods of up to 30 minutes. The resultant staining of the sections is of high intensity in sections of Araldite or Epon-embedded material. Cytoplasmic membranes, ribosomes, glycogen, and nuclear material are stained (Figs. 1-3).
To prepare lead citrate, combine 1.0 g of Citric acid ( neutralized with 1N Hydrochloric acid) and 1.0 g of lead acetate trihydrate in 50 ml of distilled water. Heat the mixture in a water bath maintained at 50-60°C for 1-2 hours, stirring occasionally, until the lead citrate dissolves.

title: Amylase, Lipase, and Acute Pancreatitis in People With Type 2 Diabetes Treated With Liraglutide: Results From the LEADER Randomized Trial.
text: Objective: To evaluate the levels of serum amylase and lipase in patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk over a period of 3.5 to 5 years, while randomized to either liraglutide or placebo. Methods: A total of 9,340 patients with type 2 diabetes were randomly assigned to either liraglutide or placebo (median observation time of 3.84 years). Fasting serum lipase and amylase levels were monitored, and acute pancreatitis was adjudicated in a blinded manner. Results: Compared to the placebo group, liraglutide-treated patients exhibited significant increases in serum lipase and amylase levels of 28.0% and 7.0%, respectively. These increases were observed at 6 months and remained stable over the study period. During the observation period, 18 (0.4% [1.1 events/1,000 patient-years of observation]) liraglutide-treated and 23 (0.5% [1.7 events/1,000 PYO]) placebo patients developed acute pancreatitis, with most cases occurring after 12 months of randomization. Moreover, liraglutide-treated patients with a prior history of pancreatitis were not more likely to develop acute pancreatitis than similar patients in the placebo group (n = 147 vs n = 120). Additionally, elevations in amylase and lipase levels did not predict future risk of acute pancreatitis (positive predictive value <1.0%) in patients treated with liraglutide. Conclusions: In this population of patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk, there were fewer events of acute pancreatitis among liraglutide-treated patients compared to the placebo group. Liraglutide was associated with increases in serum lipase and amylase levels, which were not predictive of an event of subsequent acute pancreatitis.

title: Zoledronic acid is unable to induce apoptosis, but slows tumor growth and prolongs survival for non-small-cell lung cancers.
text:
Background: Zoledronic acid (ZOL), a third-generation nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate, has shown promise as a potential therapeutic agent against various types of cancer, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, multiple myeloma, and small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). However, little is known about the effectiveness of ZOL against non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
Methods: In this study, we investigated the anti-tumor effects of ZOL on line-1 tumor cells in vitro and in vivo. We used a murine lung adenocarcinoma cell line similar to the behavior of human lung adenocarcinoma to evaluate the effects of ZOL on cellular proliferation, cell-cycle distribution, and apoptosis. We also examined the growth and survival of line-1 tumor cells in an animal model after treatment with ZOL (1 microg/kg/week).
Results: Our results demonstrate that ZOL significantly slows the growth of line-1 tumor cells in a dose-dependent manner in vitro, without inducing apoptosis. Following ZOL exposure, the treated cells typically arrest at the S/G2/M-phase of the cell-cycle, but no significant changes in apoptosis were observed. When the ZOL was washed out, the drug-inhibited cells resumed proliferation, and the cell-cycle prolongation induced by the drug earlier disappeared. In vivo studies showed that ZOL significantly slowed the growth of line-1 tumor cells, and mice treated with ZOL had a longer lifespan compared to untreated mice (p<0.05). Using line-1/lacZ cells, we also observed that ZOL induced S/G2/M-phase arrest in the in vivo cell-cycle distribution of line-1 tumor cells.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that ZOL has potential as a new therapeutic strategy for the effective treatment of NSCLC. Although ZOL does not induce apoptosis, it is able to arrest line-1 tumor cells at the S/G2/M-phase, which may contribute to its anti-tumor effects. Further clinical trials are needed to verify these results and explore the potential of ZOL as a treatment for human NSCLC patients.

title: A central role for central tolerance.
