text: The recent clarification of the role of central tolerance in preventing organ-specific autoimmunity has significantly altered our understanding of self/nonself discrimination. This major shift in paradigm can be attributed to the discovery of the promiscuous expression of tissue-restricted self-antigens (TRAs) by medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs). TRA expression in mTECs closely resembles the entirety of the body's tissues, regardless of their developmental or spatio-temporal expression patterns. This review aims to provide an overview of the current knowledge on the cellular and molecular mechanisms regulating TRA expression in mTECs, outline the relevant processes of antigen presentation and tolerance induction, and delve into the implications of these findings for the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases as well as other biological processes such as fertility, pregnancy, puberty, and tumor defense.

title: Contribution of traditional healers to a rural tuberculosis control programme in Hlabisa, South Africa.
text:
The present study was conducted in the rural health district of Hlabisa, located in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, with the objective of assessing the acceptability and effectiveness of traditional healers as supervisors of tuberculosis (TB) treatment in an existing directly observed treatment, short-course (DOTS) program. The study design was an observational comparison of treatment outcomes among new TB patients in three intervention sub-districts that offered the additional option of traditional healers for DOT supervision, with those in the remainder of the district that were provided with the standard range of options for DOT supervision (health facility, community health worker, and lay persons). Treatment outcomes were compared between these groups, as well as between patients supervised by traditional healers and those supervised by other categories of DOT supervisors.
The study found that there was no significant difference in treatment outcomes between the intervention and control areas (77% vs. 75%, P < 0.5). Among the 275 patients with known outcomes in the intervention area, 48 patients were supervised by traditional healers, and 227 patients were supervised by other categories of DOT supervisors. The treatment completion rate was not significantly higher among patients supervised by traditional healers than among patients supervised by other DOT supervisors (88% vs. 75%, P = 0.3841). Furthermore, interviews with 41 of the 51 traditional healer patients who had completed treatment revealed high levels of satisfaction with the care received.
The findings of this pilot scheme suggest that traditional healers can make an effective contribution to TB program performance in Hlabisa district. However, further evaluation will be necessary as this approach is scaled up.

title: Alzheimer's disease: the two-hit hypothesis.
text: There is a wealth of evidence pointing towards oxidative stress and disrupted mitogenic changes as playing significant roles in the development of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, though these events occur early on, before any noticeable cytopathology, the relationship between them and their role in the disease pathophysiology was previously unclear. Through the study of signaling pathways involved in mitogenic and oxidative stress processes in AD, we propose a "two-hit hypothesis" which suggests that either oxidative stress or abnormalities in mitotic signaling can serve as initiators, but that both mechanisms are necessary to propel disease progression. In this paper, we review the evidence for oxidative stress and aberrant mitotic alterations in AD and elucidate the two-hit hypothesis by elaborating on how both mechanisms are essential and characteristic features of the disease.

title: Toll-like receptor 7 mediates pruritus
text: Toll-like receptors are typically found on immune cells to help regulate the body's initial response to infection. However, our findings suggest that Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) is also expressed in a different type of cell: sensory neurons in the skin. We discovered that TLR7 plays a crucial role in inducing itching (pruritus) in mice, but is not essential for eliciting other types of pain, such as mechanical, thermal, inflammatory, or neuropathic pain. These results suggest that TLR7 may be a promising target for developing anti-itch treatments for skin conditions.

title: Antigen presentation by major histocompatibility complex class I-B molecules.
text: Majority of MHC class I loci, known as Class I-b genes, have been found to be monomorphic or oligomorphic in various organisms, with the mouse being a prominent example. Two distinct features differentiate Class I-b molecules from Class I-a: limited polymorphism and lower surface expression on cells. These traits suggest potential evolutionary and functional implications for this class. Furthermore, Class I-b proteins typically have shorter cytoplasmic domains or instead carry a lipid anchor in lieu of the transmembrane domain. Some are also restricted to a limited distribution of cells or tissues. At least six mouse MHC class I-b molecules have been demonstrated to present antigens to alpha beta or gamma delta T cells. Recent discoveries have provided insight into the functional role of H-2M3a and identified the natural peptide-binding motif of Qa-2. Additionally, significant progress has been made in comprehending other class I-b molecules, including Qa-1, TL, HLA-E, HLA-G, and the MHC-unlinked class I molecule CD1. However, we argue that the historical classification of MHC genes as class I-a and I-b is conceptually misleading, despite its practical utility. With this caveat in mind, we explore the presentation of antigens by MHC class I-b molecules, with a focus on their structure, polymorphism, peptide binding requirements, and cellular expression.

title: Pdgfrβ+ Mural Preadipocytes Contribute to Adipocyte Hyperplasia Induced by High-Fat-Diet Feeding and Prolonged Cold Exposure in Adult Mice.
text: The expansion of white adipose tissue (WAT) in obesity is characterized by the de novo differentiation of new adipocytes; however, the cellular origin of these cells remains unclear. Using Zfp423(GFP) reporter mice, we aimed to investigate the adipose mural (Pdgfrβ(+)) cells and their role in adipocyte development. Our findings revealed distinct mural populations in adipose tissue, with varying levels of the preadipocyte commitment factor Zfp423. The "MuralChaser" lineage tracking system was used to uncover adipose perivascular cells as developmental precursors of adipocytes formed in obesity. Interestingly, Pdgfrβ(+) cells were found to play a limited role in the initial cold-induced recruitment of beige adipocytes in WAT, with increased differentiation observed only after prolonged cold exposure. Our results provide genetic evidence for a mural cell origin of white adipocytes in obesity and suggest that beige adipogenesis may originate from multiple sources.

title: Effect of clinical guidelines on medical practice: a systematic review of rigorous evaluations.
text: Despite increased interest in clinical guidelines, doubts persist regarding their effectiveness. A crucial lack of a comprehensive review has hindered the debate. We have analyzed 59 published evaluations of clinical guidelines that met strict scientific standards; 24 assessed guidelines for specific medical conditions, 27 evaluated preventive care, and 8 examined guidelines for prescribing or support services. Our findings indicate that the introduction of guidelines leads to significant improvements in clinical practice, as demonstrated by 43 out of 59 studies detecting improvements in the process of care and 9 out of 11 studies reporting enhanced outcomes. However, the magnitude of these improvements varies substantially.

title: Threonine as a carbon source for Escherichia coli.
text: Threonine can serve as the sole source of carbon and energy for certain mutants of Escherichia coli K-12 through an aerobic pathway. This pathway involves the conversion of threonine through the action of threonine dehydrogenase, resulting in the formation of aminoketobutyric acid. This compound is then metabolized by aminoketobutyric acid ligase, which produces acetyl coenzyme A and glycine as byproducts. A strain lacking the serine transhydroxymethylase enzyme utilizes this pathway, resulting in glycine excretion as a waste product. The activity of aminoketobutyric acid ligase was confirmed through the use of crude extracts passed through Sephadex G100.

title: Protein S-nitrosylation: a physiological signal for neuronal nitric oxide
text:
Nitric oxide (NO) has been implicated in a wide range of physiological and pathophysiological processes, which are not fully explained by its well-established effects on soluble guanylyl cyclase. While exogenous NO can S-nitrosylate cysteine residues in proteins, the significance of endogenous NO in this process is still uncertain. Using a novel proteomic approach, we identify and characterize a population of proteins that are endogenously S-nitrosylated, and demonstrate the loss of this modification in mice lacking neuronal NO synthase (nNOS). These findings suggest that protein S-nitrosylation serves as a physiological signaling mechanism for nNOS.
In addition, we have identified a diverse range of metabolic, structural, and signaling proteins that may be targeted by neuronally generated NO. These findings provide evidence for the role of NO in modulating various cellular processes, and highlight the importance of protein S-nitrosylation as a regulatory mechanism.
Overall, our results establish protein S-nitrosylation as a key physiological signaling mechanism for nNOS, and provide new insights into the complex interplay between NO and protein signaling in various cellular processes.

title: Hypoxia‐Sensitive COMMD1 Integrates Signaling and Cellular Metabolism in Human Macrophages and Suppresses Osteoclastogenesis
text:
In this study, we investigate the role of COMMD1, a cell-intrinsic negative regulator of osteoclastogenesis, in the augmentation of inflammatory responses and bone destruction under pathological conditions. We found that hypoxia suppresses COMMD1 expression, leading to increased osteoclastogenesis and bone loss in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and inflammatory arthritis models. COMMD1 negatively regulates E2F1-dependent metabolic pathways in macrophages, and downregulation of COMMD1 protein expression by hypoxia enhances RANKL-induced expression of inflammatory and E2F1 target genes, contributing to osteoclastogenesis. Our results identify COMMD1 and the E2F-metabolic pathway as key regulators of osteoclastogenic responses under pathological inflammatory conditions. These findings provide a mechanism by which hypoxia exacerbates inflammation and bone destruction, and suggest that COMMD1 may be a therapeutic target for treating bone-related diseases.
Graphical Abstract:

Highlights:
1. COMMD1 is a negative regulator of osteoclast differentiation.
2. COMMD1 suppresses bone loss in RA and inflammatory arthritis models.
3. COMMD1 negatively regulates E2F1-dependent metabolic pathways in macrophages.
4. Hypoxia suppresses COMMD1 expression to augment osteoclastogenesis.
5. Pathways that promote osteoclastogenesis are well characterized, but less is known about negative regulators that suppress pathological bone loss.
6. Murata et al. identify COMMD1 as an inhibitor of osteoclastogenesis that restrains NF-κB- and E2F1-CKB-mediated metabolic pathways in macrophages.

title: Production of tyrosol by Candida albicans biofilms and its role in quorum sensing and biofilm development.
text:
Candida albicans, a common fungal pathogen, produces two quorum-sensing molecules: tyrosol and farnesol. Tyrosol accelerates the morphological transition from yeasts to hyphae, while farnesol blocks this transition. In this study, we investigated the secretion of tyrosol by C. albicans and its potential role in biofilm development.
We found that both planktonic cells and biofilms of four C. albicans strains, including three mutants with defects in the Efg 1 and Cph 1 morphogenetic signaling pathways, produced extracellular tyrosol during growth at 37°C. There was a positive correlation between tyrosol production and biomass for both cell types. However, biofilm cells produced at least 50% more tyrosol than planktonic cells when tyrosol production was related to cell dry weight.
The addition of exogenous farnesol to a wild-type strain inhibited biofilm formation by up to 33% after 48 hours. Exogenous tyrosol had no effect, but scanning electron microscopy revealed that tyrosol stimulated hypha production during the early stages (1-6 hours) of biofilm development.
Simultaneous addition of tyrosol and farnesol at different concentrations indicated that the action of farnesol was dominant, and 48-hour biofilms formed in the presence of both compounds consisted almost entirely of yeast cells. When biofilm supernatants were tested for their abilities to inhibit or enhance germ tube formation by planktonic cells, the results showed that tyrosol activity exceeded that of farnesol after 14 hours, but not after 24 hours, and that farnesol activity increased significantly during the later stages (48-72 hours) of biofilm development.
Our findings support the conclusion that tyrosol acts as a quorum-sensing molecule for both biofilms and planktonic cells, with its action being most significant during the early and intermediate stages of biofilm formation.

title: Regulated nucleo/cytoplasmic exchange of HOG1 MAPK requires the importin beta homologs NMD5 and XPO1.
text: MAP kinase signaling pathways play a crucial role in transmitting extracellular signals from the cell surface to the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. However, the mechanisms by which signals cross the nuclear envelope remain poorly understood. We investigated the distribution and translocation of MAP kinases in yeast cells exposed to changes in osmolarity, and found that the HOG1 MAP kinase cascade is activated in response to increased osmolarity. Using GFP fusions, we found that HOG1, PBS2, and STE11 reside in the cytoplasm of unstressed cells, while only HOG1 translocates to the nucleus in response to osmotic stress. This translocation occurs rapidly, is transient, and correlates with the phosphorylation and activation of the MAP kinase by its upstream kinase. Interestingly, phosphorylation of HOG1 is necessary and sufficient for its nuclear translocation, as a catalytically inactive kinase that is phosphorylated is translocated to the nucleus with the same efficiency as the wild-type. In contrast, the import of the MAPK into the nucleus under stress conditions requires the activity of a novel importin beta homolog, NMD5, rather than the classical importin alpha/ beta heterodimer. Similarly, the export of dephosphorylated HOG1 from the nucleus requires the activity of the NES receptor XPO1/CRM1. Our findings elucidate the requirements for the regulated nuclear transport of a stress-activated MAP kinase.

title: FBW7 regulates endothelial functions by targeting KLF2 for ubiquitination and degradation
text: The protein FBW7, which functions as a substrate-binding subunit of the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex SCFFBW7, plays a crucial role in various physiological and pathological processes, including endothelial function. Despite FBW7's importance in vessel development, its role in endothelial cells has yet to be explored. In this study, we discovered that FBW7 is a key regulator of endothelial function, including angiogenesis, leukocyte adhesion, and barrier integrity. Using RNA interference, we found that depleting FBW7 significantly impairs angiogenesis in both in vitro and in vivo settings. We identified the zinc finger transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) as a physiological target of FBW7 in endothelial cells. FBW7-mediated KLF2 destruction depends on the phosphorylation of KLF2 by glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3) at two conserved phosphodegrons. Mutating these phosphodegron motifs abolishes FBW7-mediated degradation and ubiquitination of KLF2. Our findings suggest that FBW7 is essential for the regulation of endothelial cell migration, angiogenesis, inflammation, and barrier integrity. Moreover, FBW7-mediated KLF2 degradation is critical for angiogenesis in teratomas and zebrafish development. Overall, our results provide valuable insights into the mechanisms of FBW7 and its role in endothelial function.

title: Role of RhoA-specific guanine exchange factors in regulation of endomitosis in megakaryocytes.
text: Polyploidy can precede aneuploidy in cancer, but it has a different mechanism in megakaryocytes (Mks). Unlike aneuploidy, polyploidization in Mks is a highly controlled process that requires specific gene downregulation. Using primary cells, we discovered that two key guanine exchange factors, GEF-H1 and ECT2, must be downregulated for Mk polyploidization. The first (2N-4N) endomitotic cycle requires downregulation of GEF-H1, while subsequent cycles (>4N) require downregulation of ECT2. Exogenous expression of both GEF-H1 and ECT2 prevents endomitosis and leads to proliferation of 2N Mks. Additionally, we found that the mechanism by which polyploidization is prevented in Mks lacking Mkl1, which is mutated in megakaryocytic leukemia, is through elevated GEF-H1 expression. Interestingly, shRNA-mediated GEF-H1 knockdown alone can rescue this ploidy defect, offering new insights into the mechanisms of normal and malignant megakaryocytopoiesis, as well as aberrant mitosis in aneuploid cancers.

title: Optimal therapy for reduction of lipoprotein(a).
text: There is a growing body of evidence suggesting that Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] has atherogenic and pro-thrombotic potential, as well as a causative role in coronary heart disease and stroke. Currently, most approaches for reducing Lp(a) levels focus on therapies for hyperlipoproteinemia(a), including apheresis techniques, nicotinic acid, and statins. However, none of these strategies have been shown to be effective or convenient for patients, and new approaches are being explored. Promising results are emerging from the use of therapeutic interventions that target inflammatory pathways, such as inhibition of Interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling with natural compounds (e.g., Ginko biloba) or the IL-6 receptor antibody Tocilizumab. These approaches may not only lower Lp(a) levels but also reduce cardiovascular risk for patients. Additionally, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin may help decrease the plasma concentration of Lp(a) and modulate its influence on platelets. Overall, we highlight the need for novel approaches to effectively lower Lp(a) levels and reduce cardiovascular risk.

title: Early gastric cancer and dysplasia.
text: Since the inception of early gastric cancer in Japan in 1962, its treatment has undergone a significant transformation from curative surgical resection to minimally invasive endoscopic resection, with the latter encompassing a range of techniques, from polypectomy to the more recent endoscopic submucosal dissection. As the global experience with these endoscopic methods has grown and gained acceptance, research has shown that they are comparable in effectiveness to historical surgical outcomes in appropriately selected patients. In turn, the criteria for endoscopic resection have expanded to provide a greater number of patients with improved quality of life, avoiding the morbidity and mortality associated with surgery. This article traces the evolutionary role of endoscopic and surgical therapy in early gastric cancer.

title: The impact of homelessness on children.
text: This article examines and evaluates the impact of homelessness on children, highlighting the significant obstacles they face in terms of their ability to thrive and reach their full potential. Homeless children are at risk of encountering a range of challenges, including health issues, hunger and malnutrition, delays in development, emotional distress, behavioral problems, and underperforming in school. Several factors may contribute to these outcomes, such as inadequate living conditions, instability in housing and shelters, lack of access to essential services, and barriers to obtaining necessary support. To address these issues, the article argues that public policy interventions are necessary to address the unique needs of homeless children.

title: Strategies of microbial cheater control.
text: The potential advantages of cooperation among microorganisms can be subverted by genetic conflict within social groups, manifesting as "cheating." To ensure the success of cooperation as an evolutionary strategy, it is essential to mitigate or prevent the negative effects of this conflict. To provide a conceptual framework for future research in microbial behavioural ecology, we propose a range of hypothetical mechanisms that could limit the emergence and spread of cheating behaviors.

title: Golden Hours in Severe Paraquat Poisoning-The Role of Early Haemoperfusion Therapy.
text:
Paraquat is a widely ingested poison in Southern India, with no antidote and a high fatality rate. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of early hemoperfusion as a treatment for paraquat poisoning.
Methods:
This retrospective analysis included 101 patients admitted to a Tertiary Medical College Hospital between 2012 and 2015 with a history of paraquat consumption. Patients were divided into two groups based on the timing of hemoperfusion: early (≤6 hours) and late (>6 hours). The outcome of paraquat poisoning, including survival rate, was compared between the two groups.
Results:
A total of 62 patients died, with a significantly higher mortality rate in those who received only gastric lavage and symptomatic treatment compared to those who received hemoperfusion (92.1% vs 42.9%). Early hemoperfusion was found to be more effective in improving survival rates.
Conclusion:
Early hemoperfusion is a valuable treatment for severe paraquat poisoning, significantly improving survival rates. This study highlights the importance of prompt treatment and the potential benefits of early hemoperfusion in the management of paraquat poisoning.

title: Changes in the prevalence of cerebral palsy for children born very prematurely within a population-based program over 30 years.
text:
Although cerebral palsy (CP) among extremely premature infants has been reported as a significant morbidity outcome, comparing published CP rates from various sites over different birth years can be challenging. To assess changes in population-based, gestational age-specific prevalence rates of CP among extremely premature infants over 30 years, we conducted a prospective population-based longitudinal outcome study in Northern Alberta.
We included 2318 infants born between 1974 and 2003, with gestational ages of 20 to 27 weeks and birth weights of 500 to 1249 grams, of whom 62% died, 1% were lost to follow-up, and 37% received multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental assessment by age 2 years. We determined the population-based prevalence rates of CP among these survivors and used logistic regression with linear spline to assess changes in CP prevalence over time.
Our findings revealed that at age 2 years, 14.2% of 858 survivors had CP. The diagnosis was confirmed for each child by age 3 years or older. We observed a significant increase in population-based survival among those whose gestational age was 20 to 25 weeks, from 4% to 31% (P < 0.001), while CP prevalence per 1000 live births increased monotonically from 0 to 110 until the years 1992-1994 (P < 0.001) and decreased thereafter to 22 in the years 2001-2003 (P < 0.001). Among those whose gestational age was 26 to 27 weeks, population-based survival increased from 23% to between 75% and 80% (P < 0.001), while CP prevalence per 1000 live births increased monotonically from 15 to 155 until the years 1992-1994 (P < 0.001) and then decreased to 16 in the years 2001-2003 (P < 0.001). For all survivors born in the years 2001-2003, CP prevalence was 19 per 1000 live births.
Our findings indicate that population-based CP prevalence rates for children whose gestational age was 20 to 27 weeks and whose birth weight ranged from 500 to 1249 grams have shown steady reductions in the last decade, with stable or reducing mortality, reversing trends prior to 1992-1994.

title: Desferrioxamine treatment of porphyria cutanea tarda in a patient with HIV and chronic renal failure.
text: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) can arise in HIV patients. Current research suggests that HIV infection might hinder the hepatic cytochrome oxidase system, resulting in porphyrin metabolism issues. Furthermore, chronic hemodialysis in renal failure may serve as a risk factor for PCT. In addition to the contributory factors associated with HIV infection, it is possible that porphyrin buildup resulting from renal failure may play a role in the development of this disease. We present a case of PCT in an HIV-1 infected patient undergoing blood dialysis, who was unresponsive to antimalarials but effectively treated with desferrioxamine.

title: Mutations in G protein beta subunits promote transformation and kinase inhibitor resistance
text: Activating mutations in genes encoding G protein α (Gα) subunits occur in approximately 4-5% of all human cancers, while oncogenic alterations in Gβ subunits, such as GNB1 and GNB2, have remained uncharacterized. Our study uncovers recurrent mutations in GNB1 and GNB2 that confer cytokine-independent growth and activate canonical G protein signaling. Our findings indicate that different mutations in GNB1 cluster by lineage, with examples including all 11 GNB1 K57 mutations in myeloid neoplasms and seven of eight GNB1 I80 mutations in B cell neoplasms. We also demonstrate that expression of patient-derived GNB1 variants in Cdkn2a-deficient mouse bone marrow followed by transplantation leads to either myeloid or B cell malignancies. Treatment with the dual PI3K-mTOR inhibitor BEZ235 suppresses GNB1-induced signaling and markedly increases survival in vivo. Interestingly, mutations in the gene encoding GNB1 frequently cooccur with oncogenic kinase alterations, including the BCR-ABL fusion protein, the V617F substitution in JAK2, and the V600K substitution in BRAF. Coexpression of patient-derived GNB1 variants with these mutant kinases results in inhibitor resistance in each context. Our findings suggest that GNB1 and GNB2 alterations confer transformed and resistance phenotypes across a range of human tumors and may be targetable with inhibitors of G protein signaling.

title: Isolation of major pancreatic cell types and long-term culture-initiating cells using novel human surface markers.
text: We have developed a novel set of cell surface markers for isolating and studying the various cell types present in the human pancreas. To identify these markers, we utilized hybridoma technology and immunized Balb/C mice with either intact or dissociated human islets. We then analyzed the antibodies generated by these mice for their specificity and reactivity on the surface of pancreatic cells using immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry. The identified antibodies were used to separate populations of alpha, beta, exocrine, and duct cells from primary human pancreas using FACS, and to characterize the detailed cell composition of human islet preparations. Additionally, these antibodies were employed to show that human islet expansion cultures originate from non-endocrine cells and that insulin expression levels can be increased to up to 1% of normal islet cells by subpopulation sorting and overexpression of transcription factors Pdx-1 and ngn3, representing an improvement over previous results with this culture system. These methods enable the analysis and isolation of functionally distinct pancreatic cell populations, which may have implications for cell therapy.

title: Re-engineered CD40 receptor enables potent pharmacological activation of dendritic-cell cancer vaccines in vivo
text: Despite promising clinical outcomes from dendritic cell (DC) vaccine trials, there is a need to improve DC vaccine design. Although many potential antigens have been identified, methods to enhance antigen presentation by DCs have not advanced radically. We have created an effective, drug-inducible CD40 (iCD40) receptor that allows for control activation of DCs in vivo. iCD40 is composed of a membrane-bound cytoplasmic domain of CD40 fused with drug-binding domains. This innovation enables the receptor to respond to a lipid-permeable, high-affinity dimerizer drug while avoiding negative feedback mechanisms. As a result, iCD40-expressing DCs remain activated in vivo for a more extended period, leading to a magnitude greater CD8+ T-cell response, including the elimination of previously established solid tumors, compared to activating DCs ex vivo (P < 0.01). Moreover, iCD40-mediated DC activation exceeded the activation of full-length, endogenous CD40 receptors both in vitro and in vivo. Because iCD40 is secluded from the external environment and can only be activated within an immunological synapse, iCD40-expressing DCs have an extended lifespan and are likely to result in more potent vaccines, possibly even in immune-compromised patients.

title: Effect of homocysteine lowering on mortality and vascular disease in advanced chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
High levels of homocysteine in patients with chronic kidney disease have been linked to an increased risk of mortality and vascular disease. While folic acid and B vitamins have been shown to lower homocysteine levels in this population, it is unclear whether these supplements also reduce mortality.
To investigate this, a double-blind randomized controlled trial was conducted among 2056 participants with advanced chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal disease and high homocysteine levels. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a daily capsule containing 40 mg of folic acid, 100 mg of pyridoxine hydrochloride (vitamin B6), and 2 mg of cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12) or a placebo. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality, and secondary outcomes included myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, amputation of all or part of a lower extremity, and the composite of these three plus all-cause mortality, as well as time to initiation of dialysis and time to thrombosis of arteriovenous access in hemodialysis patients.
The results of the study showed that treatment with high doses of folic acid and B vitamins had no significant effect on mortality or the incidence of vascular disease. Specifically, there were 448 deaths in the vitamin group and 436 deaths in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR], 1.04; 95% CI, 0.91-1.18), and no significant differences were observed for secondary outcomes such as MI, stroke, and amputations, or for the composite of these outcomes plus mortality, time to dialysis, or time to thrombosis in hemodialysis patients.
In conclusion, this study suggests that treatment with high doses of folic acid and B vitamins does not improve survival or reduce the incidence of vascular disease in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal disease. These findings do not support the use of these supplements in this population as a means of reducing mortality or morbidity.

title: Treated individuals who progress to action or maintenance for one behavior are more likely to make similar progress on another behavior: coaction results of a pooled data analysis of three trials.
text: This study aimed to investigate the phenomenon of coaction, which refers to the probability of taking effective action on one behavior being related to taking effective action on a second behavior. The study compared treatment and control groups in three behavior pairs: diet and sun protection, diet and smoking, and sun protection and smoking. The study analyzed pooled data from three randomized trials of Transtheoretical Model (TTM) tailored interventions, with a total of 9461 participants in the U.S. in 1999. The study found that the treatment group had a greater likelihood of taking action on a second behavior compared to the control group, with two of the behavior pairs being significant at 12 and 24 months. The combined odds ratios (ORs) for the treatment and control groups at 12 and 24 months were 1.63 and 1.85 for the treatment group, and 1.20 and 1.10 for the control group. These findings were consistent with results found in previous studies applying TTM tailoring to energy balance behaviors, and suggest that there is more coaction within the treatment group. The study concluded that future research should identify predictors of coaction in more multiple behavior change interventions.

title: Trabecular bone score as an indicator for skeletal deterioration in diabetes.
text:
Introduction:
Trabecular bone score (TBS) is a novel texture index that measures the variation in gray levels of lumbar spine dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry images. This index has been shown to be related to bone microarchitecture independent of bone mineral density (BMD). Our study aimed to investigate the relationship between TBS and insulin resistance in diabetic patients.
Methods:
We conducted a cross-sectional study using data collected from participants in an ongoing prospective cohort study between 2009 and 2010. A total of 1229 men and 1529 postmenopausal women aged 50 or older were included in the study. Measurements of biochemical parameters, TBS, and BMD were performed.
Results:
Our results showed that TBS was significantly lower in men with diabetes compared to nondiabetic men (1.287 ± 0.005 vs 1.316 ± 0.003, P < .001). In contrast, BMD was significantly higher in men with diabetes (1.135 ± 0.010 vs 1.088 ± 0.006 g/cm(2)). In women, TBS was significantly lower in those with diabetes only in an unadjusted model (1.333 ± 0.004 vs 1.353 ± 0.003). However, in women younger than 65 years, TBS was significantly lower in those with diabetes even after adjusting for covariates (P < .001). There was no association between diabetes and BMD at femur sites in both genders. TBS was negatively correlated with glycated hemoglobin, fasting plasma glucose, fasting insulin, and homeostasis model assessment for insulin resistance in both genders.
Discussion:
Our findings suggest that TBS may be an indicator of skeletal deterioration in diabetic patients with high BMD. The inverse association between TBS and insulin resistance may be useful in identifying patients at risk of skeletal deterioration. However, further studies are needed to confirm these findings and explore the potential clinical applications of TBS in diabetes management.

title: Full activation of the T cell receptor requires both clustering and conformational changes at CD3.
text: The triggering of T cell receptors (TCRs) involves both clustering of receptors and conformational changes at the cytoplasmic tails of CD3 subunits. The mechanism by which ligand binding to TCRalphabeta confers these conformational changes is unclear. Using well-defined ligands, we found that inducing the conformational change requires both multivalent engagement and the constraints imposed by the plasma membrane on TCR-CD3 clusters. This conformational change is elicited by cooperative rearrangements of two TCR-CD3 complexes and does not require changes in the structure of the TCRalphabeta ectodomains. When ligands bind to TCRalphabeta, a conformational change occurs at the CD3 subunits, which reverts upon ligand dissociation. This change is essential for T cell activation. Our permissive geometry model provides a molecular mechanism for how the information from ligand binding to TCRalphabeta is transmitted to the CD3 subunits and intracellular signaling machinery.

title: Class III PI3K Vps34 plays an essential role in autophagy and in heart and liver function.
text: A critical regulator of autophagy is the Class III PI3K Vps34 (also known as PIK3C3). Although Vps34 has been shown to play a crucial role in autophagy in yeast, its function in mammals was previously unknown. To better understand the physiological function of Vps34 and its role in autophagy, we generated Vps34-deficient mice, in which the expression of Cre recombinase results in the deletion of exon 4 of Vps34, leading to a frameshift mutation deleting 755 of the 887 amino acids in Vps34. Acute ablation of Vps34 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) infected with adenoviral Cre results in diminished localized production of phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate and a blockade of both endocytic and autophagic degradation. Starvation-induced autophagosome formation is also blocked in Vps34-deficient MEFs and liver. Liver-specific Albumin-Cre;Vps34-deficient mice exhibited hepatomegaly and hepatic steatosis, as well as impaired protein turnover. Ablation of Vps34 in the heart of muscle creatine kinase-Cre;Vps34-deficient mice resulted in cardiomegaly and decreased contractility. Interestingly, while amino acid stimulation-induced mTOR activation was suppressed in the absence of Vps34, the steady-state level of mTOR signaling was unchanged in Vps34-null MEFs, liver, or cardiomyocytes. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that Vps34 plays a critical role in regulating functional autophagy and is essential for normal liver and heart function.

title: Sex-based differences in the effect of digoxin for the treatment of heart failure.
text: BACKGROUND The Digitalis Investigation Group trial found that treatment with digoxin did not decrease overall mortality among patients with heart failure and depressed left ventricular systolic function, despite a slight reduction in hospitalizations. However, the study did not evaluate sex-based differences in the effect of digoxin therapy, despite the fact that epidemiologic features, causes, and prognosis of heart failure vary between men and women. METHODS In this post-hoc analysis, we investigated whether sex-based differences existed in the effect of digoxin therapy among the 6800 patients in the Digitalis Investigation Group study. We used Mantel-Haenszel tests of heterogeneity and a multivariable Cox proportional-hazards model adjusted for demographic and clinical variables to evaluate the interaction between sex and digoxin therapy on the primary end point of death from any cause. RESULTS We found an absolute difference of 5.8% (95% confidence interval, 0.5-11.1) between men and women in the effect of digoxin on the rate of death from any cause (P=0.034 for the interaction). Specifically, women who were randomly assigned to digoxin had a higher rate of death than women who were randomly assigned to placebo (33.1% vs. 28.9%; absolute difference, 4.2%, 95% confidence interval, -0.5-8.8). In contrast, the rate of death was similar among men randomly assigned to digoxin and men randomly assigned to placebo (35.2% vs. 36.9%; absolute difference, -1.6%, 95% confidence interval, -4.2-1.0). The multivariable analysis revealed that digoxin was associated with a significantly higher risk of death among women (adjusted hazard ratio for the comparison with placebo, 1.23; 95% confidence interval, 1.02-1.47), but it had no significant effect among men (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.93; 95% confidence interval, 0.85-1.02; P=0.014 for the interaction). CONCLUSIONS Our findings indicate that the effect of digoxin therapy differs between men and women, with digoxin therapy being associated with an increased risk of death from any cause among women, but not men, with heart failure and depressed left ventricular systolic function.

title: Recipient-type specific CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells favor immune reconstitution and control graft-versus-host disease while maintaining graft-versus-leukemia.
text: CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) play a crucial role in preventing autoimmune diseases specific to organs and in inducing tolerance to allogeneic organ transplants. Recent studies have shown that high numbers of Tregs can modulate graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) when administered alongside allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in mice. In a clinical setting, it would be challenging to obtain a sufficient number of freshly purified Tregs from a single donor to produce a therapeutic effect. Therefore, we expanded regulatory T cells ex vivo by stimulating them with allogeneic APCs, which resulted in the production of alloantigen-specific regulatory T cells. Here, we demonstrate that Tregs specific to the recipient's alloantigens control GVHD while promoting immune reconstitution. In contrast, irrelevant Tregs only provide partial protection against GVHD. Additionally, specific Tregs showed enhanced survival in grafted animals, while irrelevant Tregs did not. Furthermore, the use of specific Tregs did not interfere with any potential graft-versus-tumor activity. These findings suggest that using recipient-type specific Tregs may be a promising approach for controlling GVHD in future clinical trials.

title: Expression of the gene encoding the chemorepellent semaphorin III is induced in the fibroblast component of neural scar tissue formed following injuries of adult but not neonatal CNS.
text: This study investigates the expression of the chemorepellent molecule semaphorin III (D)/collapsin-1 (sema III) after central nervous system (CNS) lesions in rats. Scar tissue composed of spindle-shaped cells with high levels of sema III mRNA was found in lesioned areas of the lateral olfactory tract (LOT), cortex, perforant pathway, and spinal cord. These cells were found to express proteins characteristic of fibroblast-like cells. Additionally, the receptor neuropilin-1, which binds sema III, was expressed in injured neurons, as well as in scar-associated cells and blood vessels around the lesion site. In contrast to lesions in mature CNS tissue, LOT transection in neonates did not induce sema III mRNA expression within cells in the lesion, and instead, vigorous axonal regeneration occurred. The co-expression of sema III and neuropilin-1 in the scar suggests that these molecules play a role in CNS scar formation. The discovery that sema III is secreted by injured CNS cells and can inhibit the outgrowth of axons provides evidence that chemorepulsive semaphorins may contribute to the inhibition of axonal regeneration in the adult CNS. The lack of sema III expression in the absence of lesions in neonates suggests that inactivating sema III in scar tissue may be a promising means to promote long-distance regeneration in the adult CNS.

title: The relationship of the level of cyclic amp to differentiation in primary cultures of chick muscle cells.
text: The influence of elevated levels of cAMP on the differentiation of primary chick myoblast cultures has been investigated. At 24 hours after plating, 0.1 mM but 2 cAMP or 1 mM 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine was added to the cultures and maintained throughout the 70-hour incubation period. Both treatments significantly prolonged the time required for myoblast fusion, but had no noticeable impact on the increase in creatine phosphokinase activity. Morphological examination of the cells revealed no differences in the relative numbers of myoblasts and fibroblasts between the control, but 2 cAMP, and 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine cultures, but the latter treatment appeared to inhibit cell proliferation to some extent.

title: Intact endothelial autophagy is required to maintain vascular lipid homeostasis.
text: The role of autophagic flux within the vascular endothelial layer is inadequately understood. However, our study has shown that oxidized and native low-density lipoprotein (LDL) stimulate autophagosome formation in primary endothelial cells. Using confocal and electron microscopy, we observed that excess native or modified LDL is engulfed within autophagic structures. Moreover, we found that transiently knocking down the essential autophagy gene ATG7 leads to increased levels of intracellular (125)I-LDL and oxidized LDL (OxLDL) accumulation, suggesting that autophagy may play a crucial role in regulating excess lipids in endothelial cells. To further investigate the physiological significance of these findings, we used mice with a conditional deletion of ATG7 within the endothelium. Our results demonstrate that endothelial autophagy is critical in limiting lipid accumulation within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choroidal endothelium of the eye, both in an acute model of lipid excess and in a chronic model of lipid overload. Our findings suggest that strategies that stimulate autophagy or preserve its age-dependent decline may be beneficial in treating atherosclerotic vascular disease.

title: Induction of circadian gene expression in human subcutaneous adipose-derived stem cells.
text:
OBJECTIVE:
This study aims to investigate the circadian expression of genes encoding the transcriptional apparatus in murine adipose tissues. Specifically, the study tests the hypothesis that human subcutaneous adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs) can serve as an in vitro model to evaluate the activity of the core circadian transcriptional apparatus.
METHODS AND PROCEDURES:
To test this hypothesis, the study employed primary cultures of undifferentiated and adipocyte-differentiated ASCs. The cells were treated with dexamethasone, rosiglitazone, or 30% fetal bovine serum. The response of undifferentiated ASCs to dexamethasone was further evaluated in the presence of lithium chloride, an inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase 3, a key component of the circadian apparatus. Total RNA was harvested at 4-hour intervals over 48 hours and analyzed using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR).
RESULTS:
The study found that adipocyte-differentiated cells responded faster to treatments than their undifferentiated counterparts, but the period of circadian gene oscillation was longer in the adipocyte-differentiated cells. The study also showed that dexamethasone induced circadian gene expression patterns with mean periods of 25.4 and 26.7 hours in undifferentiated and adipocyte-differentiated ASCs, respectively. Both rosiglitazone and serum shock significantly lengthened the period of circadian gene expression in adipocyte-differentiated ASCs compared to undifferentiated ASCs. Additionally, the study found that lithium chloride inhibited adipogenesis and significantly lengthened the period of Per3 and Rev-erbalpha gene expression profiles by over 5 hours in dexamethasone-activated undifferentiated ASCs.
DISCUSSION:
These findings support the initial hypothesis and demonstrate the validity of ASCs as an in vitro model for studying circadian biology in human adipose tissue. The study's results provide new insights into the regulation of circadian genes in adipose tissue and highlight the potential of ASCs as a tool for investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying circadian rhythms in humans.

title: BCL9 promotes tumor progression by conferring enhanced proliferative, metastatic, and angiogenic properties to cancer cells.
text: Various components of the Wnt signaling cascade have been shown to exhibit both tumor suppressor and oncogenic properties across multiple human cancers, emphasizing the significance of this pathway in oncogenesis and the need for further exploration of Wnt signaling components as potential cancer therapeutic targets. In this study, we employ expression profiling analysis, in vitro, and in vivo functional studies to demonstrate that the Wnt pathway component BCL9 functions as a novel oncogene in human multiple myeloma and colon carcinoma. Our findings show that BCL9 enhances beta-catenin-mediated transcriptional activity regardless of Wnt signaling component mutational status and promotes increased cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and metastatic potential by fostering the loss of epithelial and gain of mesenchymal-like phenotypes. Most importantly, BCL9 knockdown exhibits significant anti-tumor effects in xenograft mouse models of cancer by reducing tumor load, metastasis, and host angiogenesis through down-regulation of c-Myc, cyclin D1, CD44, and vascular endothelial growth factor expression in tumor cells. Together, these findings suggest that deregulation of BCL9 contributes significantly to tumor progression. The diverse roles of BCL9 highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for treating various cancers exhibiting aberrant Wnt signaling.

title: Programmed cell death pathways in cancer: a review of apoptosis, autophagy and programmed necrosis.
text: Programmed cell death (PCD), encompassing apoptosis, autophagy, and programmed necrosis, is believed to be a cellular response to any pathological stimulus, mediated by an intrinsic program. These three forms of PCD may work together to determine the fate of malignant cells; apoptosis and programmed necrosis consistently contribute to cell death, while autophagy can exhibit either pro-survival or pro-death behavior. Recent evidence has significantly expanded our knowledge of cancer onset and progression, shedding light on the complex interplay between these three modes of PCD. Unlocking the PCD signaling pathways may lead to the development of novel, targeted anti-cancer therapies. With this in mind, this review aims to provide an overview of the apoptosis, autophagy, and programmed necrosis pathways, as well as the regulation of apoptosis-related microRNAs in cancer. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of PCD and the intricate interplay between these three forms of cell death may enable researchers and clinicians to harness them for the discovery of new drug targets, paving the way for more effective cancer treatments in the future.

title: Loss of gametophytic self-incompatibility with evolution of inbreeding depression.
text: Gametophytic self-incompatibility (SI) in plants is a widespread mechanism that prevents self-fertilization and the detrimental effects of inbreeding depression. However, this mechanism often evolves into self-compatibility over time. We investigate the genetic mechanisms behind the breakdown of gametophytic SI, taking into account a dynamic model of inbreeding depression that allows for partial purging of nearly recessive lethal mutations through selfing, as well as the impact of pollen limitation and sheltered load linked to the S-locus. We consider two mechanisms for the breakdown of gametophytic SI: a nonfunctional S-allele and an unlinked modifier locus that inactivates the S-locus. Our findings show that under a range of conditions, self-compatible alleles can invade a self-incompatible population. The invasion of self-compatible genotypes is more likely to occur when the S-allele is nonfunctional, and the spread of these genotypes is favored by high or low selfing rates, a small number of S-alleles, and pollen limitation. The maintenance of gametophytic SI is attributed to a combination of high inbreeding depression in self-incompatible populations, coupled with intermediate selfing rates and sheltered load linked to the S-locus. Observed parameter values suggest that these factors contribute to the maintenance of gametophytic SI.

title: The oncogenic microRNA miR-22 targets the TET2 tumor suppressor to promote hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal and transformation.
text: MicroRNAs are frequently dysregulated in cancer, and in particular, miR-22 is upregulated in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and leukemia, with poorer prognosis correlating with its aberrant expression. To elucidate its function in hematopoietic stem cells and malignancy, we generated transgenic mice conditionally expressing miR-22 in the hematopoietic compartment. These mice displayed diminished global 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC) levels and augmented hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal, accompanied by impaired differentiation. In contrast, miR-22 inhibition retarded proliferation in both mouse and human leukemic cells. Over time, miR-22 transgenic mice evolved MDS and hematological malignancies. We also identified TET2 as a key target of miR-22 in this context, with ectopic TET2 expression countering the miR-22-induced phenotypes. Decreased TET2 protein levels correlated with poorer clinical outcomes and miR-22 overexpression in MDS patients. These findings designate miR-22 as a potent oncogenic factor and highlight the importance of dysregulation in the miR-22/TET2 regulatory network in hematopoietic malignancies.

title: Transmission of atherosclerosis susceptibility with gut microbial transplantation.
text: According to recent research, there may be a link between intestinal microbe metabolism of certain dietary nutrients and the development of atherosclerotic heart disease. In this study, we investigate whether gut microbe transplantation can transmit the production of trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), which is associated with atherosclerosis susceptibility. Our findings indicate that a strong association exists between TMAO levels and atherosclerosis in a mouse diversity panel. We selected two inbred mouse strains, one prone to atherosclerosis and high in TMAO production, and another resistant to atherosclerosis and low in TMAO production, to receive cecal microbial transplantation into apolipoprotein e null mice. The recipients of the C57BL/6J microbes showed choline diet-dependent enhancement in atherosclerotic plaque burden compared to the recipients of the NZW/LacJ microbes. We found that microbial DNA analyses in feces and cecum revealed the transplantation of donor microbial community features into the recipients, with differences in taxa proportions between donor strains that were transmissible to the recipients and tended to coincide with TMAO levels. Additionally, we identified specific taxa that correlated with TMAO levels in donors and recipients and with atherosclerotic lesion area in recipients. Our findings suggest that atherosclerosis susceptibility may be transmitted via gut microbiota transplantation, highlighting the potential of the gut microbiome as a novel therapeutic target for modulating atherosclerosis susceptibility.

title: The complete primary structure of the spermadhesin AWN, a zona pellucida-binding protein isolated from boar spermatozoa.
text: AWN is a protein found in the secretions of male boars that becomes associated with the surface of sperm cells during ejaculation. It is believed to play a role in the initial stages of fertilization by mediating sperm adhesion to the egg's zona pellucida through a carbohydrate-recognition mechanism. To determine the complete primary structure of AWN, we used a combination of protein-chemical and mass spectrometric methods. Our findings revealed that AWN exists in two isoforms, AWN-1 and AWN-2, which differ in their N-terminal acetylation. The amino acid sequence of AWN consists of 133 residues and contains two disulfide bridges between nearest-neighbor cysteine residues. Phylogenetic analysis of AWN proteins showed significant similarity only to AQN-1 and AQN-3, two other boar spermadhesins.

title: What influences government adoption of vaccines in developing countries? A policy process analysis.
text: This study seeks to develop a framework for analyzing the process by which governments adopt new vaccines, particularly in developing country settings. To illustrate the relevance of key explanatory factors identified in the literature and the need to go beyond a variable-centric approach, the paper examines the early adoption of Hepatitis B vaccines in Taiwan and Thailand. These cases demonstrate the importance of considering the policy context and decision-making process in determining the pace and extent of vaccine adoption. Furthermore, the study highlights the feasibility of modeling "causal diversity" – the complex set of conditions leading to decisional outcomes – across a range of country contexts. A deeper understanding of how government decision-makers process information and the parameters of decision-making processes may enable both analysts (in predicting the institutionalization of new vaccines) and advocates (in crafting targeted strategies to accelerate their diffusion).

title: Benzodiazepines and injurious falls in community dwelling elders.
text:
Benzodiazepines are commonly prescribed drugs for the elderly, but they are associated with a heightened risk of falling, which can lead to severe consequences. In this study, we aimed to estimate the impact of benzodiazepine-induced injurious falls in a population of elderly individuals.
A nested case-control study was conducted using data collected over 10 years in the French PAQUID community-based cohort. The main outcome measure was the occurrence of an injurious fall, defined as a fall resulting in hospitalization, fracture, head trauma, or death. Controls (matched 3:1 with cases) were selected based on age and other factors. Benzodiazepine exposure was determined by analyzing the use of benzodiazepines in the 2 weeks preceding the fall.
Our results showed a significant association between benzodiazepine use and the occurrence of injurious falls, with a higher risk observed in subjects aged 80 years or older. The adjusted odds ratio for injurious falls in subjects exposed to benzodiazepines was 2.2 (95% CI: 1.4-3.4) in subjects aged 80 years or older and 1.3 (95% CI: 0.9-1.9) in subjects aged <80 years. The population attributable risk for injurious falls in subjects exposed to benzodiazepines was 28.1% (95% CI: 16.7-43.2) in subjects aged 80 years or older. The incidence of injurious falls in subjects aged 80 years or older exposed to benzodiazepines was 2.8/100 person-years, with over 9% of these falls being fatal. Taking into account population estimates, benzodiazepine use could be responsible for nearly 20,000 injurious falls and over 1800 deaths in subjects aged 80 years or older in France every year.
Our findings highlight the need for new strategies to limit the use of benzodiazepines in the elderly, given the significant morbidity and mortality associated with their use. While existing guidelines on benzodiazepine use have not been effective in preventing their misuse, it is crucial to develop new approaches to minimize their misuse and prevent the serious consequences of injurious falls in the elderly.

title: Effect of women's nutrition before and during early pregnancy on maternal and infant outcomes: a systematic review.
text: According to current understanding of biological processes, the nutritional status of women before and during early pregnancy may significantly impact early developmental processes and pregnancy outcomes. We conducted a systematic review of research articles to investigate the effect of maternal nutrition before and during early pregnancy (less than 12 weeks gestation) on maternal, neonatal, and child health outcomes. Our review included 45 articles, consisting of nine intervention trials and 32 observational studies, which were identified through database searches and review articles. Our findings suggest that periconceptional folic acid supplementation reduces the risk of neural tube defects, while preconceptional and periconceptional intake of vitamin and mineral supplements is associated with a lower risk of delivering low birthweight and/or small-for-gestational age (SGA) and preterm deliveries (PTD). Additionally, some studies suggest that maternal prepregnancy size, low stature, underweight, and overweight are linked to increased risks of PTD and SGA. While the available data highlight the importance of women's nutrition prior to and during the first trimester of pregnancy, there is a need for further research, particularly in developing country settings, to examine relationships with low birthweight, SGA, PTD, stillbirth, and maternal and neonatal mortality. Specifically, we need to evaluate the effectiveness of periconceptional interventions such as food supplements, multivitamin-mineral supplements, and specific micronutrients (iron, zinc, iodine, vitamin B-6, and B-12) and investigate the relationship between prepregnancy body size and composition and maternal, neonatal, and child health outcomes.

title: Kinesin-2 controls development and patterning of the vertebrate skeleton by Hedgehog- and Gli3-dependent mechanisms.
text: Hedgehog signaling plays a crucial role in the patterning of the vertebrate skeleton. Our study reveals that conditional inhibition of the Kif3a subunit of the kinesin-2 intraflagellar transport motor in mesenchymal skeletal progenitor cells leads to severe patterning defects in the craniofacial region, including split sternum and polydactyly. These deformities resemble those observed in mice with deregulated hedgehog signaling. We demonstrate that in Kif3a-deficient mesenchymal tissues, both the repressor function of Gli3 transcription factor and the activation of Shh transcriptional targets, Ptch and Gli1, are impaired. Quantitative analysis of gene expression shows that the Gli1 transcript level is significantly reduced, while Gli3 expression remains unchanged upon kinesin-2 depletion. Interestingly, our findings suggest that the motor is necessary for the efficient cleavage of the full-length Gli3 transcription factor into a repressor form.

title: Ablation of NF1 function in neurons induces abnormal development of cerebral cortex and reactive gliosis in the brain.
text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a common genetic disorder that affects the growth properties of neural-crest-derived cell populations. In fact, approximately half of NF1 patients experience learning disabilities. To investigate the role of NF1 in development and function, we generated a conditional mutation in the NF1 gene using Cre/loxP technology, circumventing the embryonic lethality of NF1 null mouse embryos. We then introduced a Synapsin I promoter-driven Cre transgenic mouse strain into the conditional NF1 background, which resulted in ablation of NF1 function in most differentiated neuronal populations. Interestingly, these mice exhibited abnormal development of the cerebral cortex, suggesting that NF1 plays an essential role in this aspect of central nervous system (CNS) development. Furthermore, though they were tumor-free, the mice displayed extensive astrogliosis in the absence of obvious neurodegeneration or microgliosis. These findings imply that NF1-deficient neurons are capable of inducing reactive astrogliosis through a non-cell autonomous mechanism.

title: Pathology of postprimary tuberculosis in humans and mice: contradiction of long-held beliefs.
text:
Tuberculosis remains one of the world's leading infectious causes of death, with approximately 80% of all cases caused by postprimary (secondary) tuberculosis in the lung. However, obtaining tissue samples from developing lesions is challenging, and there are no established models of postprimary tuberculosis. In the pre-antibiotic era, when tissue samples were more readily available, researchers described early postprimary tuberculosis as a lipid pneumonia distinct from the caseating granulomas commonly seen today.
To investigate this further, we performed histopathological, immunohistochemical, and acid fast staining on tissue samples from individuals with both primary and postprimary tuberculosis, as well as on mice with reactivation tuberculosis. Our findings confirmed that postprimary tuberculosis begins as a lipid pneumonia in the lung, accompanied by bronchial obstruction and infection restricted to foamy alveolar macrophages. As the disease progresses, cavities form due to a combination of caseation of tuberculous pneumonia and microvascular occlusion, which is characteristic of delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH). Reactivation tuberculosis in mice also begins as a similar tuberculous lipid pneumonia with bronchial obstruction and evidence of DTH participation. Interestingly, both in humans and mice, developing necrosis is associated with the localization of organisms within lipid droplets.
These findings suggest that reactivation tuberculosis in mice can be a valuable model for understanding the development of human postprimary tuberculosis.

title: Secondary aerosolization of viable Bacillus anthracis spores in a contaminated US Senate Office.
text:
In the aftermath of bioterrorist attacks involving letters and mail handling systems in Washington, DC, which resulted in Bacillus anthracis (anthrax) spore contamination in the Hart Senate Office Building and other nearby facilities in the US Capitol, there is an urgent need to understand the nature and extent of indoor secondary aerosolization of B anthracis spores. To address this issue, the study collected air samples, surface dust, and swab samples under semiquiescent (minimal activities) and simulated active office conditions to evaluate the secondary aerosolization of B anthracis spores.
The investigation revealed that viable B anthracis spores reaerosolized under semiquiescent conditions, showing a significant increase in reaerosolization during simulated active office conditions. Specifically, there was a remarkable increase in the number of B anthracis particles collected on open sheep blood agar plates and personal air monitors during active office conditions. Most notably, more than 80% of the B anthracis particles collected on stationary monitors were within the alveolar respirable size range of 0.95 to 3.5 micro meters.
The findings of this study have significant implications for respiratory protection, remediation, and reoccupancy of contaminated office environments. It is clear that proper precautions must be taken to minimize the risk of secondary aerosolization of B anthracis spores, particularly in areas where aerosol exposure could occur, such as air handling systems, ducts, and vents.

title: Fingolimod provides long-term protection in rodent models of cerebral ischemia.
text:
The sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor agonist fingolimod (FTY720), which has demonstrated efficacy in advanced multiple sclerosis clinical trials, attenuates injury caused by reperfusion in various organs, including the heart, liver, and kidney. Therefore, we investigated the therapeutic potential of fingolimod in rodent models of focal cerebral ischemia. To assess the translational significance of these findings, we examined whether fingolimod improves long-term behavioral outcomes, whether delayed treatment is effective, and whether neuroprotection can be achieved in a second species.
We used rodent models of middle cerebral artery occlusion and cell culture models of neurotoxicity and inflammation to explore the therapeutic potential and underlying mechanisms of fingolimod-mediated neuroprotection. In a transient mouse model, fingolimod significantly reduced infarct size, neurological deficit, edema, and the number of dying cells in the core and periinfarct area. Neuroprotection was accompanied by decreased inflammation, as fingolimod-treated mice had fewer activated neutrophils, microglia/macrophages, and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1)-positive blood vessels. Fingolimod-treated mice displayed better behavioral performances up to 15 days after ischemia. Reduced infarct was also observed in a permanent model, even when mice were treated 4 hours after ischemic onset. Similarly, fingolimod attenuated infarct size in a rat model of focal ischemia. While fingolimod did not protect primary neurons against glutamate excitotoxicity or hydrogen peroxide, it decreased ICAM-1 expression in brain endothelial cells stimulated by tumor necrosis factor alpha.
Our findings suggest that anti-inflammatory mechanisms, rather than direct effects on neurons, underlie the beneficial effects of fingolimod after stroke. Activating S1P receptors, a highly promising target in stroke treatment, may offer a novel therapeutic strategy to counteract the detrimental effects of reperfusion injury in various organs, including the brain.

title: Induced regeneration—the progress and promise of direct reprogramming for heart repair
text: The prospect of regenerating cardiac tissue holds great promise for revolutionizing cardiovascular medicine. Recent breakthroughs in stem cell biology and direct reprogramming, or transdifferentiation, have empowered researchers with innovative tools to achieve this goal. In this Review, we delve into the most recent advancements in generating new cardiomyocytes in vitro, as well as the exhilarating progress made towards in vivo reprogramming of cardiac tissue. We also discuss the challenges and controversies that the field faces.

title: "Sandwich"-type immunoassay of carcinoembryonic antigen in patients receiving murine monoclonal antibodies for diagnosis and therapy.
text: In some patients receiving injections of monoclonal antibody, measurements of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) in their blood surged significantly. To detect CEA levels, a monoclonal antibody-based double-determinant enzyme immunoassay was used, in which untreated plasma samples were diluted with an equal volume of buffer containing mouse serum. As the CEA titers increased, so did the levels of human antibody against mouse Ig (HAMA). Interestingly, adsorption of these sera with solid-phase anti-human IgG or Protein A restored CEA titers to their original values, suggesting that the serum factor responsible for false-positive CEA titers was most likely HAMA. Neither adding undiluted mouse serum to the assay mixture nor pretreating plasma specimens with heat to 70 degrees C was able to abolish HAMA interference. In contrast, protein precipitation with polyethylene glycol (130 g/L) or heating plasma samples to 90 degrees C effectively eliminated false-positive CEA titers caused by HAMA, while not reducing authentic CEA levels.

title: Mutant dynactin in motor neuron disease
text: Proposed impairment in axonal transport in motor neurons has been linked to a region of 4 megabases (Mb) at chromosome 2p13 in motor neuron disease. Our study reveals a genetic mutation in this interval that codes for the largest subunit of the axonal transport protein dynactin, resulting in a single base-pair change causing an amino-acid substitution that disrupts the folding of dynactin's microtubule-binding domain. Using binding assays, we found decreased binding of the mutant protein to microtubules, providing evidence that dysfunction of dynactin-mediated transport can cause human motor neuron disease.

title: Thioredoxin mediates oxidation-dependent phosphorylation of CRMP2 and growth cone collapse.
text: Semaphorin3A (Sema3A) serves as a repulsive guidance molecule for axons, effectively inducing collapse of growth cones through the phosphorylation of collapsin response mediator protein 2 (CRMP2). In this study, we investigate the regulatory role of CRMP2 oxidation and thioredoxin (TRX) in the phosphorylation of CRMP2 and subsequent growth cone collapse triggered by Sema3A. Our findings reveal that Sema3A-mediated stimulation produces hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) through the action of molecule interacting with casl (MICAL), which oxidizes CRMP2, leading to the formation of a disulfide-linked homodimer through cysteine-504. The oxidized CRMP2 forms a transient disulfide-linked complex with TRX, subsequently activating phosphorylation of CRMP2 by glycogen synthase kinase-3, resulting in growth cone collapse. Moreover, we successfully reconstituted oxidation-dependent phosphorylation of CRMP2 in vitro using a limited set of purified proteins, thereby elucidating the crucial role of H2O2 and CRMP2 oxidation in Sema3A-induced growth cone collapse, as well as an unappreciated association between TRX and CRMP2 oxidation.

title: Pathologic indicators of degradation and inflammation in human osteoarthritic cartilage are abrogated by exposure to n-3 fatty acids.
text:
The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation on the metabolism of osteoarthritic (OA) cartilage. The study exposed human OA cartilage to n-3 PUFAs or other types of fatty acids and measured the metabolic profile of the cartilage before and after exposure, as well as the expression of certain genes involved in cartilage metabolism.
Results showed that n-3 PUFA supplementation reduced the release of proteoglycan metabolites from OA cartilage explants in a dose-dependent manner, and specifically abolished endogenous aggrecanase and collagenase proteolytic activity. Additionally, expression of mRNA for ADAMTS-4, MMP-13, and MMP-3 was also specifically abolished with n-3 PUFA supplementation. Furthermore, n-3 PUFA supplementation abolished the expression of mRNA for mediators of inflammation (cyclooxygenase 2, 5-lipoxygenase, 5-lipoxygenase-activating protein, tumor necrosis factor alpha, IL-1alpha, and IL-1beta) without affecting the expression of message for several other proteins involved in normal tissue homeostasis.
Overall, these findings suggest that n-3 PUFA supplementation significantly altered the pathologic indicators of human OA cartilage, point toward a potential therapeutic role for n-3 PUFAs in the treatment of OA cartilage metabolism.

title: Interactive effects of oligofructose and obesity predisposition on gut hormones and microbiota in diet-induced obese rats.
text:
Objective:
Oligofructose (OFS) is a prebiotic that modifies gut satiety hormones and microbiota, reducing energy intake and fat mass. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of OFS in diet-induced obese (DIO) and diet-resistant (DR) rats.
Methods: Adult, male DIO, and DR rats were randomly assigned to a high-fat/high-sucrose (HFS) diet or HFS diet supplemented with 10% OFS for six weeks. Body composition, food intake, gut microbiota, plasma gut hormones, and cannabinoid CB(1) receptor expression in the nodose ganglia were measured.
Results: OFS reduced body weight, energy intake, and fat mass in both phenotypes (P < 0.05). OFS altered gut microbiota profiles in DIO and DR rats, with the differences being eliminated by OFS. OFS did not modify plasma ghrelin or CB(1) expression in nodose ganglia, but plasma levels of GIP were reduced, and PYY was elevated (P < 0.05) by OFS.
Conclusion: OFS was able to reduce body weight and adiposity in both prone and resistant obese phenotypes. The OFS-induced changes in gut microbiota profiles, along with changes in gut hormone levels, likely contribute to the sustained lower body weights.

title: RKIKK motif in the intracellular domain is critical for spatial and dynamic organization of ICAM-1: functional implication for the leukocyte adhesion and transmigration.
text: The spatial organization of ICAM-1 on the cell surface may not have been previously linked to its physiological function in leukocyte adhesion and transendothelial migration (TEM). However, our study found that ICAM-1 regulates de novo microvilli elongation and is subsequently clustered on these microvilli. In contrast, truncation of the intracellular domain resulted in uniform distribution of ICAM-1 on the cell surface. Further analysis revealed that the C-terminal 21 amino acids are non-essential, while a segment of 5 amino acids (RKIKK(511)) in the NH-terminal third of the intracellular domain is required for proper localization and dynamic distribution of ICAM-1, as well as its association with F-actin, ezrin, and moesin. Notably, deletion of the (RKIKK(511)) motif significantly delayed LFA-1-dependent membrane projection and decreased leukocyte adhesion and TEM. Treating endothelial cells with cell-permeant penetratin-ICAM-1 peptides comprising ICAM-1 RKIKK sequences inhibited leukocyte TEM. Together, these findings demonstrate that the microvillus ICAM-1 presentation is crucial for leukocyte TEM and suggest a novel regulatory role for ICAM-1 topography in this process.

title: Immunology of the tick-host interaction and the control of ticks and tick-borne diseases.
text: Sixty years have passed since the first experimental vaccine against ticks was administered. Despite this progress has been slow, with the recent commercial release of a recombinant vaccine against Boophilus microplus being a significant development. The specifics of naturally acquired immunity against ticks, particularly in crucial, domesticated ruminant hosts, remain poorly understood. While the characterization of antigens of naturally acquired immunity is still limited, more has been discovered about "concealed" antigens. Critical questions persist regarding the true impact of tick-induced immunosuppression and the effect of immunity on the transmission of tick-borne diseases, despite some exciting and essential recent findings as discussed by Peter Willadsen and Frans Jongejan.

title: Rapid method for the isolation of lipoproteins from human serum by precipitation with polyanions.
text: A method for isolating lipoproteins from human serum is described, involving precipitation with polyanions and divalent cations. This procedure allows for the preparation of low and very low density lipoproteins without the need for ultracentrifugation by precipitating them with heparin and either MnCl2 alone or MgCl2 plus sucrose. The precipitation is reversible, selective, and complete, resulting in highly concentrated isolated lipoproteins that are free of other plasma proteins as determined by immunological and electrophoretic methods. The low density and very low density lipoproteins can then be separated from each other through ultracentrifugation. The advantage of this method is that large quantities of lipoproteins can be prepared with a single preparative ultracentrifugation. Other polyanions, such as dextran sulfate and MnCl2, or sodium phosphotungstate and MgCl2, can also be used to precipitate the low and very low density lipoproteins, resulting in the high density lipoproteins being precipitated by increasing the concentrations of the reagents. These lipoproteins, containing small amounts of protein contaminants, can be further purified through ultracentrifugation at a density of 1.22. With a single preparative ultracentrifugation, immunologically pure high density lipoproteins can be isolated from large volumes of serum.

title: The role of oral antidiabetic agents: why and when to use an early-phase insulin secretion agent in Type II diabetes mellitus
text: New evidence from the 1990s emphasizes the importance of glycemic control in both Type I (insulin-dependent) and Type II (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus. Although measurement of HbA1c is the standard for assessing the impact of glucose control on the development and prevention of diabetic complications, more recent studies suggest that other glucose parameters, such as post-challenge and postprandial hyperglycemic peaks, may also be important indicators of vascular damage in early-stage Type II diabetes. Currently, there is no widely accepted standard approach to pharmacological management of Type II diabetes, although the United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study has shown that reaching near-normal glycemic targets is crucial. Loss of endogenous insulin secretion has been confirmed as a key factor in the progression of Type II diabetes in this study, although early insulinization was not found to be more effective than other forms of therapy. The advent of polypharmacy in recent years has significantly improved the treatment of this disease, and the development of early-phase insulin secretion agents such as nateglinide and repaglinide has further enhanced treatment options.
