These agents can reduce mealtime glucose excursions and HbA1c levels when used alone or in combination with metformin, and their antidiabetic potential is similar to that of the combination treatment with glibenclamide and metformin. Further studies are needed to confirm the long-term effect of these agents on improving life expectancy and reducing diabetic complications in Type II diabetic patients.

title: Layered hydrogels accelerate iPSC-derived neuronal maturation and reveal migration defects caused by MeCP2 dysfunction.
text: Utilizing patient-derived neural progenitor cells (NPCs) in a 3D assay can offer a comprehensive understanding of cellular phenotypes in neurodevelopmental disorders. Unlike 2D systems, which cannot fully replicate the brain's cellular arrangement, the use of layered hydrogels allows for a more accurate representation of the in vivo environment. Here, we designed a novel 3D migration and differentiation assay to investigate how neurodevelopmental disorders, such as Rett syndrome, affect neural development. By utilizing this platform, we discovered a genotype-specific effect of MeCP2 dysfunction on iPSC-derived neuronal migration and maturation, resulting in reduced neurite outgrowth and decreased synapses in 3D layered hydrogels. This innovative 3D system expands the range of neural phenotypes that can be studied in vitro, enabling the assessment of how physical and mechanical stimuli influence neural development and the identification of specific cell arrangements that are crucial for proper neural function.

title: Inducible gene expression: diverse regulatory mechanisms
text: The swift onset of gene expression in response to stimuli chiefly occurs through the control of RNA polymerase II-dependent transcription. In this Review, we delve into the events that unfold during the transcription cycle in eukaryotes that are essential for the expedited and precise activation of gene expression in response to external stimuli. Besides regulated recruitment of the transcription machinery to the promoter, recent discoveries have revealed that additional control steps may include chromatin remodeling and the release of paused polymerase. Furthermore, recent research suggests that certain components of signal transduction pathways also play a key role in activating transcription at target genes.

title: On the origins of ultra-fine anaphase bridges.
text: Chan et al. (2009) investigated the phenomenon of sister-chromatid bridging at fragile site loci during mitosis in response to replication stress. Using techniques such as fluorescence microscopy and chromosome length measurements, they found that the bridge formation was more pronounced at sites of high replication stress, suggesting a link between replication stress and the stability of sister chromatids. Their findings have important implications for our understanding of the mechanisms that govern chromosome segregation and the maintenance of genome stability.

title: Resistance to gefitinib in PTEN-null HER-overexpressing tumor cells can be overcome through restoration of PTEN function or pharmacologic modulation of constitutive phosphatidylinositol 3'-kinase/Akt pathway signaling.
text:
PURPOSE: Tyrosine kinase (TK) inhibitors are emerging as an encouraging new approach for treating tumors that overexpress HER, but their optimal use awaits a clearer understanding of the downstream signaling pathways that contribute to their effectiveness. We reported earlier that both EGFR- and Her2-overexpressing tumors are sensitive to the EGFR-selective TK inhibitor gefitinib (ZD1839, "Iressa"), and the ability of this agent to down-regulate Akt correlated with its sensitivity. However, EGFR-overexpressing MDA-468 cells that lack PTEN function are resistant to ZD1839, and ZD1839 is unable to down-regulate Akt activity in these cells.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: To investigate the role of PTEN function, we generated MDA468 cells with tet-inducible PTEN expression.
RESULTS: We found that the resistance of MDA-468 cells to ZD1839 is caused by EGFR-independent constitutive Akt activation due to the loss of PTEN function in these cells. Reintroducing PTEN function through tet-inducible expression restores ZD1839 sensitivity to these cells and reestablishes EGFR-stimulated Akt signaling. Although implementing full restoration of PTEN function in tumors is challenging clinically, the effects of PTEN loss are primarily attributable to overactive PI3K/Akt signaling, which can be modulated using pharmacological approaches. We found that pharmacologic down-regulation of constitutive PI3K/Akt pathway signaling using the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 similarly restores EGFR-stimulated Akt signaling and sensitizes MDA-468 cells to ZD1839.
CONCLUSIONS: Sensitivity to ZD1839 requires an intact growth factor receptor-stimulated Akt signaling pathway. PTEN loss leads to an uncoupling of this signaling pathway, resulting in ZD1839 resistance, which can be reversed by reintroducing PTEN or using pharmacological approaches to down-regulate constitutive PI3K/Akt pathway activity. These findings have significant predictive and therapeutic implications for cancer treatment.

title: Transcriptome analysis reveals human cytomegalovirus reprograms monocyte differentiation toward an M1 macrophage.
text: Monocytes are the primary targets of Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) infection, and they play a crucial role in the hematogenous dissemination of the virus. After infection, monocytes acquire different functional traits during polarization to either the classical proinflammatory M1 macrophage or the alternative antiinflammatory M2 macrophage. Our hypothesis is that HCMV induces a proinflammatory M1 macrophage following infection to promote viral dissemination, as a proinflammatory state provides the necessary tools to drive infected monocytes from the blood into the tissue. To test this hypothesis, we used Affymetrix Microarray to analyze the transcriptional profile of infected monocytes at a key temporal point following infection. Our results showed that HCMV significantly up-regulated 583 (5.2%) of the total genes and down-regulated 621 (5.5%) of the total genes with a fold change of 1.5 or greater. Ontology analysis revealed that genes involved in classical M1 macrophage activation were specifically stimulated by HCMV infection. Interestingly, we found that 65% of genes associated with M1 polarization were up-regulated, while only 4% of genes associated with M2 polarization were up-regulated. Furthermore, analysis of the monocyte chemokinome at the transcriptional level showed that 44% of M1 and 33% of M2 macrophage chemokines were up-regulated. Using chemokine Ab arrays, we also confirmed the secretion of these chemotactic proteins from HCMV-infected monocytes. Overall, our results indicate that the HCMV-infected monocyte transcriptome exhibited a unique M1/M2 polarization signature that was skewed towards the classical M1 activation phenotype.

title: Antithymocyte globulin treatment for patients with recent-onset type 1 diabetes: 12-month results of a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial.
text:
Background: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the destruction of insulin-producing β cells, leading to uncontrolled hyperglycemia. Preclinical studies and pilot clinical trials have indicated that antithymocyte globulin (ATG), a therapy that targets T cells, may be effective in reducing the autoimmune response and preserving β-cell function. In this phase 2, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial, we investigated the safety and efficacy of rabbit ATG in preserving islet function in participants with recent-onset type 1 diabetes.
Methods: We enrolled participants aged 12-35 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes from 11 sites in the USA. Using a computer-generated randomization sequence, we randomly assigned patients to receive either 6.5 mg/kg ATG or placebo over a four-day period. All participants were masked and managed by an unmasked drug management team until month 3, after which they were managed by an independent, masked study physician and nurse educator. The primary endpoint was the change in 2-hour area under the curve C-peptide response to a mixed meal tolerance test from baseline to 12 months. Analyses were performed by intention to treat. This is an interim analysis of an ongoing trial that will run for 24 months of follow-up and has been registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT00515099).
Findings: Between September 10, 2007, and June 1, 2011, we screened 154 individuals and randomly allocated 38 to ATG and 20 to placebo. We found no significant between-group difference in the primary endpoint: participants in the ATG group had a mean change in C-peptide area under the curve of -0.195 pmol/mL (95% CI -0.292 to -0.098), while those in the placebo group had a mean change of -0.239 pmol/mL (-0.361 to -0.118). All but one participant in the ATG group experienced cytokine release syndrome and serum sickness, which was associated with a transient increase in interleukin-6 and acute-phase proteins. ATG-treated patients had 159 grade 3-4 adverse events, many associated with T-cell depletion, compared with 13 in the placebo group, but we did not observe any between-group difference in the incidence of infectious diseases.
Interpretation: Our findings suggest that a brief course of ATG does not result in the preservation of β-cell function 12 months later in patients with new-onset type 1 diabetes. Generalized T-cell depletion in the absence of specific depletion of effector memory T cells and preservation of regulatory T cells appears to be an ineffective treatment for type 1 diabetes.

title: The nucleosome family: dynamic and growing.
text: Since the discovery of the nucleosome in 1974, scientists have discovered various protein-DNA complexes in which DNA is wrapped around histone complexes of different compositions: octasomes, hexasomes, tetrasomes, "split" half-nucleosomes, and, more recently, bona fide hemisomes. Do these particles exist in living organisms? Under what conditions? What are their physiological implications in the intricate DNA transactions within eukaryotic nuclei? What are their dynamics? This review synthesizes research that spans over three decades and offers a new perspective on the term "nucleosome." Rather than viewing the nucleosome as a singular, static entity, it is now recognized as a family of particles with differing structural and dynamic properties, leading to distinct functionalities.

title: Association between serum corin levels and risk of acute myocardial infarction.
text:
BACKGROUND: Mounting evidence suggests that corin plays crucial roles in regulating salt and water balance, blood pressure, and cardiac function by inducing natriuretic peptides. In light of this, we conducted a case-control study to investigate the association between serum soluble corin levels and acute myocardial infarction (AMI) risk.
METHODS: We enrolled 856 AMI patients and 856 healthy controls, and examined the possible relationship between serum corin levels and AMI susceptibility using a logistic regression model.
RESULTS: AMI patients had higher BMI, were less physically active, and were more likely to have histories of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and smoking in comparison to controls. Notably, serum levels of corin were significantly lower in AMI patients (825±263pg/ml) than in healthy controls (1246±425pg/ml). Moreover, the odds ratio of ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) decreased with increasing levels of serum corin in both men and women (P for trend <0.001) after adjusting for BMI, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, and physical activity.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that reduced serum levels of corin are associated with an increased risk of AMI in both men and women.

title: Crosstalk between the estrogen receptor and the HER tyrosine kinase receptor family: molecular mechanism and clinical implications for endocrine therapy resistance.
text: The evolution and progression of breast cancer are influenced by intricate interactions between steroid receptors, such as the estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor, and growth factor receptor signaling. In recent years, cancer therapy has seen the emergence of various strategies targeting these specific cancer pathways and key molecules, including ER and growth factor receptors, to slow or stop tumor growth. However, success has varied, and both de novo (initial) and acquired resistance have presented challenges. Recent studies of ER biology have provided new insights into ER function in breast cancer, highlighting the critical interplay between the ER and HER (human epidermal growth factor receptor) signaling pathways in the development of resistance to endocrine therapies targeting the ER pathway. The aim of this review article is to summarize current knowledge on the mechanisms of resistance of breast cancer cells to endocrine therapies due to the interplay between the ER and HER signaling pathways and to explore potential new therapeutic strategies that could increase the duration of response and circumvent endocrine-resistant tumor growth.

title: Nuclear PTEN functions as an essential regulator of SRF-dependent transcription to control smooth muscle differentiation
text: The progression of vascular diseases is associated with significant changes in the phenotype and function of vascular smooth muscle cells (SMCs). The expression of contractile genes and SMC differentiation are tightly regulated by the transcription factor serum response factor (SRF), but the mechanisms that control SMC phenotype are not fully understood. Our study reveals a novel function for the lipid and protein phosphatase PTEN in the nucleus, where it acts as an essential regulator of SMC differentiation alongside SRF. PTEN interacts with the N-terminal domain of SRF and promotes SRF binding to critical promoter elements in SMC-specific genes. Factors that induce phenotypic switching lead to the loss of nuclear PTEN, resulting in reduced myogenically active SRF and increased SRF activity on genes involved in proliferation. Interestingly, decreased PTEN expression was observed in intimal SMCs of human atherosclerotic lesions, highlighting the potential clinical implications of these findings.

title: SEROSURVEY FOR FELINE LEUKEMIA VIRUS AND LENTIVIRUSES IN CAPTIVE SMALL NEOTROPIC FELIDS IN SÃO PAULO STATE, BRAZIL
text: Members of the family Retroviridae, including feline leukemia virus (FeLV), Gammaretrovirus, and feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), a Lentivirus, can infect domestic cats (Felis catus) and cause cytoproliferative and cytosuppressive disorders. Unfortunately, these viruses are also prevalent in domestic cats worldwide, and infection can lead to high morbidity and mortality rates. Infection of endangered neotropic small felids, such as those belonging to the species Leopardus pardalis, Leopardus tigrinus, Leopardus wiedii, Herpailurus yaguarondi, and Oncifelis geoffroyi, with these viruses could be devastating. To investigate the prevalence of FeLV and feline lentiviruses in captive neotropic small felids in São Paulo state, Brazil, we tested serum samples from 104 animals using commercially available immunoassays. Fortunately, all results were negative, suggesting that retrovirus infection is not a significant clinical problem in these populations. As domestic cats in São Paulo city are naturally infected with these pathogens, and feral cats are commonly found in zoological facilities in Brazil, it is crucial to take preventive measures to prevent transmission of retroviruses to naive populations of wild and captive neotropic felids in Brazil.

title: Comparing the metabolism of quercetin in rats, mice and gerbils
text: Several species of rodents are being used to investigate the metabolism of quercetin in vivo, but it remains unclear whether they are suitable animal models. To address this, we compared the metabolism of quercetin in Wistar rats (rats), Balb/c mice (mice) and Mongolian gerbils (gerbils). We measured the levels of quercetin metabolites, such as quercetin-3-glucuronide (Q3G), quercetin-3′-sulfate (Q3′S), and methyl-quercetin isorhamnetin (IH), in the plasma, lungs, and livers of these animals using high-performance liquid chromatography after acute and/or chronic quercetin administration. We also investigated the metabolic enzyme activities in the intestinal mucosal membrane and liver. Initially, we found that after acute quercetin administration, the Q3′S level was highest in gerbils. However, after long-term supplementation (20 weeks), Q3G became the dominant metabolite in the plasma, lungs, and livers, followed by IH and Q3′S in all animals, although gerbils still had a higher Q3′S conversion ratio. The average concentration of total quercetin in the plasma of gerbils was highest in both short- and long-term studies. The activities of uridine 5′-diphosphate-glucuronosyltransferase, phenolsulfotransferase, and catechol-O-methyltransferase were induced by quercetin in a dose- and tissue-dependent manner in all animals. Taken together, after long-term quercetin supplementation, the metabolism of quercetin is similar among all animals and resembles that of humans. However, the accumulation of quercetin and Q3′S conversion ratio in gerbils are higher than those in the other animals.

title: Cytokinesis failure generating tetraploids promotes tumorigenesis in p53-null cells
text: A long-standing theory in cancer research is that cell division failure, resulting in genetically unstable tetraploid cells, facilitates the development of aneuploid malignancies. To test this idea, we temporarily blocked cytokinesis in p53-null (p53-/-) mouse mammary epithelial cells (MMECs), allowing for the isolation of diploid and tetraploid cultures. The tetraploid cells displayed an increased frequency of whole-chromosome mis-segregation and chromosomal rearrangements. Only the tetraploid cells were transformed in vitro following exposure to a carcinogen, and in the absence of a carcinogen, only the tetraploid cells gave rise to malignant mammary epithelial cancers when transplanted subcutaneously into nude mice. These tumors all contained numerous non-reciprocal translocations and a 8–30-fold amplification of a chromosomal region containing a cluster of matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) genes. Overexpression of MMP is linked to mammary tumors in humans and animal models, indicating that tetraploidy increases the frequency of chromosomal alterations and promotes tumor development in p53-deficient MMECs.

title: Claspin, a Chk1-regulatory protein, monitors DNA replication on chromatin independently of RPA, ATR, and Rad17.
text: Claspin plays a crucial role in the ATR-dependent activation of Chk1 in Xenopus egg extracts containing unfinished DNA replication. Our findings show that Claspin associates with chromatin in a regulated manner during S phase, with binding depending on the pre-replication complex (pre-RC) and Cdc45, but not on replication protein A (RPA). These dependencies suggest that Claspin binds to chromatin prior to the initiation of DNA unwinding at replication origins. In contrast, both ATR and Rad17 require RPA for binding to DNA. Notably, Claspin, ATR, and Rad17 all bind to chromatin independently, indicating that Claspin monitors DNA replication during S phase. Furthermore, these findings suggest that Claspin, ATR, and Rad17 may coordinate checkpoint regulation by detecting different aspects of the DNA replication fork.

title: Cold-related respiratory symptoms in the general population.
text:
The prevalence and threshold temperatures of self-reported respiratory symptoms associated with cold exposure were investigated in a large population-based study. The study included 6,591 men and women aged 25-74 years from the FINRISK study. Participants were queried about cold-related respiratory symptoms, and the results were expressed as age-adjusted prevalence figures and coefficients from multivariate regressions.
Compared to healthy individuals, people with asthma and chronic bronchitis reported significantly more cold-related respiratory symptoms. The reported threshold temperature for symptom onset was -14°C for males and -15°C for females, and this threshold decreased with age, asthma, and chronic bronchitis. Interestingly, the threshold temperature for mucus production was lower, decreasing by age and asthma. The effects of smoking and education were minimal.
Overall, the study found that cold-related respiratory symptoms are common in individuals with chronic respiratory diseases, and they start to emerge at relatively low temperatures. In a cold climate, these symptoms may have a significant impact on the health-related quality of life.

title: Carvedilol for children and adolescents with heart failure: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Although beta-blockers improve symptoms and survival in adults with heart failure, little is known about these medications in children and adolescents. To investigate the effects of carvedilol in this age group, a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study was conducted among 161 children and adolescents with symptomatic systemic ventricular systolic dysfunction. The study was conducted at 26 US centers and lasted from June 2000 to May 2005.
Participants were randomly assigned to receive placebo or carvedilol in a 1:1:1 ratio, with patients stratified according to whether their systemic ventricle was a left ventricle or not. The primary outcome measure was a composite measure of heart failure outcomes in patients receiving carvedilol, which included individual components of this composite, echocardiographic measures, and plasma b-type natriuretic peptide levels.
Despite the fact that 54 patients were assigned to placebo, 30 improved (56%), 16 worsened (30%), and 8 were unchanged (15%), compared to 58 improved (56%), 25 worsened (24%), and 20 were unchanged (19%) among 103 patients assigned to carvedilol, there was no statistically significant difference between the groups in terms of the composite end point. The study also found a significant interaction between treatment and ventricular morphology, indicating a possible differential effect of treatment between patients with a systemic left ventricle (beneficial trend) and those whose systemic ventricle was not a left ventricle (nonbeneficial trend).
The study's findings suggest that carvedilol does not significantly improve clinical heart failure outcomes in children and adolescents with symptomatic systolic heart failure, although the lower than expected event rates may indicate that the trial was underpowered. However, there may be a differential effect of carvedilol in children and adolescents based on ventricular morphology.

title: The circadian clock gene BMAL1 is a novel therapeutic target for malignant pleural mesothelioma.
text:
Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is a highly aggressive cancer arising from the mesothelial cells lining the parietal pleura, with a poor prognosis. Despite progress in MPM treatment, more efficient therapeutic approaches are still needed. Recently, BMAL1, a component of the circadian clock machinery, has been found to be overexpressed in MPM. Our study aimed to investigate whether BMAL1 could serve as a potential therapeutic target for MPM.
We evaluated BMAL1 expression in MPM cell lines and clinical specimens, and found that it was higher in MPM cells compared to non-tumorigenic mesothelial cells and normal pleural tissue. Interestingly, we observed a rhythmic change in BMAL1 expression in MPM cells following exposure to serum shock, suggesting that the circadian rhythm pathway is disrupted in these cells.
To investigate the role of BMAL1 in MPM, we knocked it down in two MPM cell lines (ACC-MESO-1 and H290) and a non-tumorigenic mesothelial cell line (MeT-5A). Our results showed that BMAL1 knockdown suppressed the proliferation of MPM cells, both in anchorage-dependent and independent clonal growth. The knockdown also led to cell cycle disruption, with an increase in apoptotic and polyploidy cell populations, downregulation of cell cycle regulators Wee1, cyclin B, and p21(WAF1/CIP1), and upregulation of cyclin E.
Notably, BMAL1 knockdown induced mitotic catastrophe in ACC-MESO-1 cells, which expressed the highest level of BMAL1. Additionally, we observed disruption of cell cycle regulators and induction of drastic morphological changes, including micronucleation and multiple nuclei, in these cells.
In conclusion, our findings suggest that BMAL1 plays a critical role in MPM and could serve as a promising therapeutic target for this aggressive cancer.

title: Mechanism and Regulation of DNA-Protein Crosslink Repair by the DNA-Dependent Metalloprotease SPRTN
text:
In this study, we identify the metalloprotease SPRTN as the DPC protease acting in metazoans. Mice lacking SPRTN fail to repair DPCs and are more sensitive to DPC-inducing agents. SPRTN processes DPCs through a unique DNA-induced protease activity, which is regulated by multiple sophisticated mechanisms. Our findings also provide a molecular explanation for why patients with Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome, a premature aging and cancer predisposition disorder, have SPRTN deficiency.
Here is a more concise and clear rewording of the text:
Covalent DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs) are harmful to cells, as they disrupt essential chromatin functions like replication and transcription. Until recently, the mechanisms for repairing DPCs were largely unknown. However, the discovery of a DPC-processing protease in yeast has shed light on these mechanisms. While a DPC protease is believed to exist in higher eukaryotes, its identity remains unknown.
Our study identifies the metalloprotease SPRTN as the DPC protease in metazoans. Mice lacking SPRTN are unable to repair DPCs and are more sensitive to DPC-inducing agents. SPRTN processes DPCs using a unique DNA-induced protease activity, which is regulated by multiple complex mechanisms. Our findings also provide a molecular explanation for why patients with Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome, a premature aging and cancer predisposition disorder, have SPRTN deficiency.

title: 'Zero is not good for me': implications of infertility in Ghana.
text:
BACKGROUND In sub-Saharan Africa, the value placed on children is paramount, and as such, infertility is associated with significant psychological, marital, and social implications. While previous research has explored the impact of infertility on individuals in this region, this study specifically examines the experiences of women in Ghana, West Africa.
METHODS This study employed semi-structured interviews with 107 women aged 21-48 years (mean age 33 years) seeking treatment in gynecological and obstetric clinics in Accra, Ghana. The interviews were analyzed using iterative open coding to identify themes related to mental health, marital strain, social interaction, and gendered experiences.
RESULTS Infertile women in Ghana reported experiencing severe social stigma, marital tension, and a range of mental health difficulties. Many women felt that they were disproportionately blamed for infertility, leading to greater social consequences than their male partners. Non-infertile women in the study also corroborated these findings, emphasizing the significant social consequences of infertility for women in particular.
CONCLUSIONS This study demonstrates that infertility has significant implications for social interactions, marital stability, and mental health in Ghana. These consequences are not perceived to be shared equally between men and women in Ghanaian society.

title: Ethical dilemmas in a randomized trial of asthma treatment: can Bayesian statistical analysis explain the results?
text:
The original objective of the study was to investigate whether the use of bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) ventilation could reduce the need for endotracheal intubation, hospital stay, and hospital charges in patients with status asthmaticus. However, the development of physician treatment bias made it challenging to enroll patients, leading to a premature termination of the study. To address this issue, the authors employed Bayesian statistics to explain the study results.
METHODS: This was a prospective, randomized controlled clinical trial conducted over 34.5 months at an urban university hospital with an emergency department census of 94,000 annual visits. Patients aged 18-75 years with status asthmaticus after initial standard treatment were randomized to receive BiPAP ventilation plus standard treatment or standard treatment alone (non-BiPAP). Exclusions included patients with concurrent cardiac or other pulmonary diseases. The primary outcome measures were endotracheal intubation rate and length of hospital stay. Secondary outcome measures included vital signs (respiratory rate, pulse rate, blood pressure), changes in expiratory peak flow, changes in pulse oximetry values, and hospital charges. Data analysis was performed using Fisher's exact test, Mann-Whitney tests, and Bayesian statistics, with the first enrollment only included in the analysis.
RESULTS: Nineteen patients were enrolled in the BiPAP group, and 16 patients in the non-BiPAP group. The groups were similar in age, sex, initial peak flow rate, and arterial blood gas measurements. There was a 7.3% increase (95% CI = -22 to +45) in the intubation rate in the non-BiPAP group (n = 2) compared with the BiPAP group (n = 1). No significant difference was seen in length of hospital stay or hospital charges, although there was a favorable trend towards the BiPAP group. One patient in the BiPAP group experienced discomfort associated with the nasal BiPAP mask. Bayesian analysis revealed that, at a 95% confidence level, the prior conviction among treating physicians that BiPAP was a successful treatment modality would have had to be 98.9% to explain the observed data.
CONCLUSIONS: Despite the study's premature termination, BiPAP appeared to have no deleterious effects in patients with status asthmaticus, with a trend towards decreased endotracheal intubation rate, decreased length of hospital stay, and decreased hospital charges. However, further study with more patients is needed to determine the clinical and statistical significance of this intervention. The use of Bayesian statistics highlights the importance of considering prior probabilities and treatment effects in the analysis of clinical trial data.

title: Mental health in prison populations. A review--with special emphasis on a study of Danish prisoners on remand.
text:
Objective:
The objective of this review is to examine the existing literature on mental health and psychiatric morbidity in prison populations and compare the findings with a Danish study on remand prisoners.
Method:
The review of the literature is organized into three sections: validity of psychometrics in prison populations, prevalence of psychiatric disorders prior to imprisonment, and incidence of psychiatric disorders during imprisonment. The results are compared with a longitudinal Danish study on remand prisoners in either solitary confinement (SC) or non-SC.
Results:
The study found that many factors need to be considered when addressing mental health issues in prisoners, including international differences, prison setting, demographics, and methodological issues. The prison population worldwide is increasing, and psychometrics may perform differently in prison populations compared to general populations. Psychiatric morbidity, including schizophrenia, is higher in prison populations compared to general populations, with dependence syndromes being the most frequent disorders. The early phase of imprisonment is a vulnerable period with a moderately high incidence of adjustment disorders, and subjects in solitary confinement have twice the incidence of these disorders compared to those in non-SC. Prevalence of psychopathy is lower in European than North American prisons, and medium to high scores of psychopathy are related to higher psychiatric comorbidity. Opioid dependence is the most frequent drug disorder, and subjects using injection represent a more dysfunctional group than subjects using smoke administration. Finally, many mentally ill prisoners remain undetected and undertreated.
Conclusion:
The review highlights the growing population of mentally ill prisoners who are insufficiently detected and treated. Insufficient attention to mental health issues in prisons can result in poor outcomes for both prisoners and society as a whole.

title: Why females live longer than males: control of longevity by sex hormones.
text: Male species have a shorter lifespan compared to females in many species, including humans. We have identified a possible explanation for this phenomenon, which involves the beneficial effects of estrogens on longevity. Estrogens bind to receptors and activate the expression of genes related to longevity, including those encoding antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase. This results in mitochondria from females producing fewer reactive oxygen species compared to males. Unfortunately, administering estrogens can have harmful side effects, including feminization and an increased risk of diseases such as uterine cancer in postmenopausal women. However, compounds found in soy or wine, known as phytoestrogens, may provide some of the beneficial effects of estrogens without these negative side effects. The study of gender differences in longevity can help us better understand the aging process and develop practical strategies to increase lifespan in both females and males.

title: The pre-B-cell receptor: selector of fitting immunoglobulin heavy chains for the B-cell repertoire
text: In this Opinion piece, I delve into the role of the pre-B-cell receptor (pre-BCR) in the development of antigen-specific B cells, exploring its influence on immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) variable-region repertoire selection, precursor B-cell differentiation and proliferation, and IgH allelic exclusion. Drawing parallels with the role of the pre-T-cell receptor (pre-TCR) in T-cell development, I pose questions such as why both lineages utilize a surrogate chain - the surrogate light chain and the pre-TCR α-chain, respectively - as a step towards developing their repertoires of antigen-recognizing cells. This article, combined with the accompanying piece by Harald von Boehmer, aims to shed light on these issues and uncover the functions of the pre-BCR and pre-TCR in lymphocyte differentiation and antigen-receptor allelic exclusion.

title: Helicobacter species methods and protocols. Introduction.
text: Helicobacter infection is a persistent and chronic condition that accounts for the majority of cases of gastric and duodenal ulcers, as well as gastric cancer. The study of this bacteria has greatly benefited from standardization of culture techniques and the use of animal models. The following chapters will delve into the clinical aspects of the infection and provide guidance on optimal investigation techniques.

title: Effectiveness of statin-eluting stent on early inflammatory response and neointimal thickness in a porcine coronary model.
text:
Background: Drug-eluting stents (DES) are commonly used during coronary revascularization due to their ability to significantly reduce rates of restenosis and target lesion revascularization compared to bare metal stents (BMS). However, DES have limitations, such as delayed healing and persistent local inflammation, which can lead to late thrombosis. Statins have been shown to inhibit cell proliferation, inflammation, and restore endothelial function. The present study aimed to evaluate the ability of stent-based cerivastatin delivery to reduce stent-induced inflammatory responses and adverse effects on endothelial function, as well as to inhibit neointimal hyperplasia in a porcine coronary model.
Methods and Results: In this study, 9 pigs had either a cerivastatin-eluting stent (CES) or a BMS implanted in one of their coronary arteries. All animals survived without any adverse effects. Scanning electron microscopy revealed a significant decrease in inflammatory cell infiltration on day 3 after stenting in the treated vessels, with an inflammation score of 1.15±0.12 compared to 2.43±0.34 in the BMS group (p<0.0001). At day 28, endothelial function was preserved in both the CES and BMS groups using intracoronary infusion of bradykinin. Volumetric intravascular ultrasound imaging revealed decreased intimal volume in the CES group (28.3±5.4 vs 75.9±4.2 mm3, p<0.0001). Histomorphometric analysis showed reduced neointimal area (1.74±0.45 vs 3.83±0.51 mm2, p<0.0001) in the CES group, despite similar injury scores (1.77±0.30 vs 1.77±0.22, p=0.97).
Conclusion: In porcine coronary arteries, CES significantly decreased neointimal hyperplasia with a decreased early inflammatory response and without endothelial dysfunction.

title: Genetic variation in West Nile virus from naturally infected mosquitoes and birds suggests quasispecies structure and strong purifying selection.
text: An analysis of genetic diversity within and between naturally infected mosquitoes and birds revealed that West Nile virus (WNV) exists in nature as a quasispecies, with a genetically diverse population of genomes. A 1938 nucleotide fragment comprising the 3' 1159 nt of the WNV envelope (E) coding region and the 5' 779 nt of the non-structural protein 1 (NS1) coding region was amplified and cloned from ten infected birds and ten infected mosquito pools collected on Long Island, NY, during the peak of the 2003 WNV transmission season. The clones were then sequenced, resulting in 20 sequences per specimen. The study found that WNV infections are derived from a genetically diverse population of genomes in nature, with a mean nucleotide diversity of 0.016% within individual specimens and a mean percentage of clones that differed from the consensus sequence of 19.5%. The study also found that WNV sequences in mosquitoes were significantly more genetically diverse than in birds, and that there was no host-dependent bias for particular types of mutations. Non-consensus clones obtained from two avian specimens had highly similar genetic signatures, providing evidence that WNV genetic diversity may be maintained throughout the enzootic transmission cycle. The study further found evidence of purifying selection in both intra- and interhost WNV populations, supporting the observation that WNV populations may be structured as a quasispecies and documenting strong purifying natural selection in WNV populations.

title: Overlapping patterns of IGF2 and H19 expression during human development: biallelic IGF2 expression correlates with a lack of H19 expression.
text: The spatial expression patterns of IGF2 and H19 genes during certain stages of human embryonic/fetal and early postnatal development display notable similarities. However, exceptions were found in specific tissues, such as the ciliary anlage of the embryonic retina and the choroid plexus/leptomeninges, where IGF2 transcripts were detected but not H19. While the choroid plexus/leptomeninges revealed the presence of both parental IGF2 alleles, RNase protection analysis revealed weak P1 promoter activity in these tissues, with P2, P3, and P4 promoters showing activity across all IGF2-expressing tissues. These observations suggest a coordinated control of the reciprocally imprinted and closely linked IGF2 and H19 loci.

title: Intimal smooth muscle cell proliferation after balloon catheter injury. The role of basic fibroblast growth factor.
text: The study investigated the localization and synthesis of basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF) in the rat carotid artery during chronic smooth muscle cell proliferation. Immunostaining revealed the presence of bFGF in the uninjured arterial wall, with a decrease in staining after balloon injury. Western and northern blot analyses showed a decrease in bFGF protein and mRNA levels after injury. A neutralizing antibody to bFGF was administered 4 and 5 days after injury, and it had no effect on intimal smooth muscle cell proliferation. These findings suggest that an increase in bFGF expression is not necessary for chronic smooth muscle cell proliferation observed after balloon catheter injury and that bFGF is not the major mitogen responsible for intimal smooth muscle cell proliferation.

title: Prevention of central venous catheter-associated thrombosis: a meta-analysis.
text:
The use of anticoagulant prophylaxis in patients with central venous catheters is a topic of controversy. To investigate this further, we conducted a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of anticoagulant prophylaxis in patients with central venous catheters.
We searched Medline and EMBASE up to May 2006, supplemented by manual searches of conference proceedings and bibliographies, and included 15 trials in our analysis. Unfractionated heparin infusion, oral fixed low-dose vitamin K antagonist, and subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin were among the regimens evaluated.
Our findings showed that anticoagulant prophylaxis is effective in preventing all catheter-associated deep vein thrombosis in patients with central venous catheters. However, the effectiveness in preventing symptomatic venous thromboembolism, including pulmonary embolism, remains uncertain. The summary relative risks ranged from 0.31 to 0.73 for all catheter-associated deep vein thrombosis, but did not achieve statistical significance for any individual regimen in preventing symptomatic deep vein thrombosis.
In conclusion, our meta-analysis suggests that anticoagulant prophylaxis is effective in preventing catheter-associated deep vein thrombosis in patients with central venous catheters. However, further research is needed to determine the effectiveness of these regimens in preventing symptomatic venous thromboembolism.

title: Long-term efficacy of nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation in adolescents: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
In a double-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) among Dutch adolescents, the short-term efficacy of nicotine patches compared to placebo patches was investigated. The study revealed that nicotine patches were effective in aiding smoking cessation among highly compliant participants at the end of treatment. However, the study aimed to evaluate whether the effects of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) held in 6- (T7) and 12-month (T8) follow-up assessments.
The study involved 257 adolescents aged 12-18 years who were motivated to quit smoking. Participants were randomly assigned to either a nicotine patch (n=182) or a placebo patch (n=180) condition according to a computer-generated list. The participants attended an information meeting followed by a 6- or 9-week treatment. Smoking cessation, compliance, and potential covariates were measured through online questionnaires, and smoking cessation at T8 was biochemically validated by saliva cotinine.
The results showed that at T7, 8.1% and 5.7% of participants in the nicotine and placebo patch groups, respectively, were abstinent. At T8, abstinence was 4.4% and 6.6%, respectively. Intention-to-treat analyses showed no significant effects of NRT on abstinence rates at T7 (OR=1.54, 95% CI=0.57, 4.16) and validated abstinence rates at T8 (OR=0.64, 95% CI=0.21, 1.93) neither after considering compliance nor after adjusting for covariates.
The study's findings indicate that NRT fails in helping adolescents quit smoking at 6- and 12-month follow-ups. This suggests that a more intensive approach is needed to assist youngsters in their quit attempts.

title: Interferon gamma in autoimmunity: A complicated player on a complex stage.
text: Early conceptions of autoimmune disease characterized interferon gamma (IFNγ) as a definitive pro-inflammatory factor. However, recent findings have demonstrated that IFNγ can exhibit both pro- and anti-inflammatory actions, with the final outcome depending on the specific physiological or pathological context being examined. In this review, we will discuss the principal immunomodulatory functions of IFNγ and summarize current evidence on the impact of IFNγ on disease pathology and regulation in various autoimmune diseases and model systems.

title: The first gene of the Bacillus subtilis clpC operon, ctsR, encodes a negative regulator of its own operon and other class III heat shock genes.
text: The Bacillus subtilis clpC operon is regulated by two stress induction pathways, using either σB or a class III stress induction mechanism at a σA-like promoter. When the clpC operon was placed under the control of the IPTG-inducible Pspac promoter, significant repression of the natural clpC promoters fused to a lacZ reporter gene was observed following IPTG induction. This finding strongly suggested negative regulation of the clpC operon by one of its gene products. In fact, the negative regulator could be identified, which is encoded by the first gene of the clpC operon, ctsR, and contains a predicted helix-turn-helix DNA-binding motif. Deletion of ctsR abolished the negative regulation and resulted in high expression of both the clpC operon and the clpP gene under non-stressed conditions. However, a further increase in clpC and clpP mRNA levels was observed after heat shock, even in the absence of σB, suggesting a second induction mechanism at the vegetative promoter. Two-dimensional gel analysis and mRNA studies revealed that the expression of other class III stress genes was at least partially influenced by the ctsR deletion. Further experiments using different clpC promoter fragments either fused to the reporter gene bgaB or used in gel mobility shift experiments with the purified CtsR protein revealed a possible target region where the repressor bound in vivo and in vitro. Our findings demonstrate that the CtsR protein acts as a global repressor of the clpC operon, as well as other class III heat shock genes, by preventing unstressed transcription from either the σB- or σA-dependent promoter, and may be inactivated or dissociate under inducing stress conditions.

title: Role for c-myc in activation-induced apoptotic cell death in T cell hybridomas.
text: Mature T cells and some T cell hybridomas undergo programmed cell death, also known as apoptosis, when activated through the T cell receptor complex. This phenomenon is likely related to antigen-induced negative selection of developing T cells. The activation-induced apoptosis depends on the cell's ability to produce active proteins and RNA, although the genes responsible for this process have not been previously identified. Using antisense oligonucleotides, we found that blocking the constitutive expression of the c-Myc protein in T cell hybridomas disrupts all aspects of activation-induced apoptosis without affecting the production of lymphokines in these cells. These findings suggest that c-Myc expression is a necessary component of activation-induced apoptosis.

title: Examining BCL-2 family function with large unilamellar vesicles.
text:
The BCL-2 family of proteins, which consists of approximately 20 members, plays a crucial role in regulating cell survival and apoptosis. These proteins work together to maintain cell survival or initiate apoptosis, a process of programmed cell death, in response to cellular stress, such as DNA damage. The pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family effectors, BAK and BAX, are activated following cellular stress and compromise the integrity of the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM), leading to the release of pro-apoptotic proteins, such as cytochrome c, into the cytoplasm. These proteins then activate caspases, which ultimately lead to apoptosis.
The BCL-2 family is divided into two subsets: pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic members. Anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, such as BCL-2 related gene, long isoform, BCL-xL; myeloid cell leukemia 1, MCL-1, regulate cellular survival by tightly controlling the interactions between BAK/BAX and the BH3-only proteins capable of directly inducing BAK/BAX activation. In addition, availability of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins is also dictated by sensitizer/de-repressor BH3-only proteins, such as BAD or PUMA, which bind and inhibit anti-apoptotic members.
To study the interactions between BCL-2 family members, researchers use large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs), a biochemical model system. LUVs are composed of defined lipids that are assembled in ratios identified in lipid composition studies from solvent extracted Xenopus mitochondria. This model system allows for direct exploration of BCL-2 family function, as the protein and lipid components are completely defined and tractable. Kinetic analyses of protein interactions and real-time measurements of membrane permeabilization, which are based on LUVs containing a polyanionic dye (ANTS: 8-aminonaphthalene-1,3,6-trisulfonic acid) and cationic quencher (DPX: p-xylene-bis-pyridinium bromide), can also be performed using this model system.
In summary, the BCL-2 family of proteins plays a critical role in regulating cell survival and apoptosis, and their interactions with each other and with lipids in the outer mitochondrial membrane are essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis. The use of LUVs provides a convenient model system to study these interactions in a controlled and defined manner.

title: The Hippo pathway effector YAP controls mouse hepatic stellate cell activation.
text:
Hepatic stellate cell activation is a natural response to liver injury, but when it persists, it can lead to excessive matrix production and the formation of pathological scar tissue, ultimately resulting in fibrosis and cirrhosis. While several signaling pathways have been identified that promote stellate cell activation, the mechanisms that trigger and drive the early stages of activation are not well understood.
We discovered the Hippo signaling pathway and its effector, YAP, as a crucial factor in controlling stellate cell activation. YAP is a transcriptional co-activator that plays a key role in the earliest stages of gene expression during stellate cell activation. When stellate cells are activated in vivo or in vitro, YAP becomes rapidly activated, as evidenced by its nuclear translocation and the induction of YAP target genes. Consistently, YAP was also found to be activated in stellate cells of human fibrotic livers, and its nuclear localization was confirmed.
 Furthermore, we found that inhibition of YAP expression or pharmacological inhibition of YAP prevented hepatic stellate cell activation in vitro and impeded fibrogenesis in mice. These findings suggest that targeting YAP may present a novel approach for the treatment of liver fibrosis.
In summary, our study identifies YAP as a critical driver of hepatic stellate cell activation and highlights the potential of targeting YAP as a therapeutic strategy for the treatment of liver fibrosis.

title: Human Monocytes Engage an Alternative Inflammasome Pathway.
text: Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) is regulated by inflammasome activation, but lipopolysaccharide stimulation of human monocytes produces IL-1β without simultaneously activating the classical inflammasome. This distinct response is specific to humans and involves an "alternative inflammasome" that is independent of pyroptosome formation, pyroptosis induction, and K+ efflux dependence. By analyzing signaling pathways in a monocyte transdifferentiation system, we found that TLR4-mediated signaling upstream of NLRP3 leads to alternative inflammasome activation. This cascade is unique to the alternative inflammasome and does not affect classical NLRP3 activation. Given its involvement in IL-1β production and immune responses, we propose a pivotal role for this signaling cascade in TLR4-driven immunopathology in humans.

title: The use of biosimilars in immune-mediated disease: A joint Italian Society of Rheumatology (SIR), Italian Society of Dermatology (SIDeMaST), and Italian Group of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IG-IBD) position paper.
text: Biological agents have gained extensive use in rheumatology, dermatology, and inflammatory bowel disease over the years. There has been a significant strengthening of evidence regarding their efficacy and safety across these therapeutic indications in the last decade. Biosimilar agents are monoclonal antibodies that are similar to previously approved biologics. In the European Union, they have been approved for all indications in the management of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs), although data are currently only available for rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. Mandatory direct evidence on the efficacy, safety, and immunogenicity of biosimilars is necessary in psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease, as well as in pediatric patients. Drawing on the current evidence in the medical literature, we present the joint official position of the Italian Societies of Rheumatology, Dermatology, and Inflammatory Bowel Disease on the use of biosimilars in IMIDs.

title: The coordination of cyclic microtubule association/dissociation and tail swing of cytoplasmic dynein.
text: The dynein motor domain is composed of a tail, head, and stalk, and is believed to generate force by swinging the tail against the head during its ATPase cycle. To do this, dynein must coordinate the tail swing with microtubule association/dissociation at the tip of the stalk. While the former process is becoming clearer, the latter process remains unclear. Using a single-headed recombinant motor domain of Dictyostelium cytoplasmic dynein, we investigate how the motor domain interacts with microtubules, how the two mechanical cycles (microtubule association/dissociation and tail swing) are coordinated, and which ATPase site in the motor domain regulates this coordination. Based on steady-state and pre-steady-state measurements, we find that the two mechanical cycles proceed synchronously at most intermediate states in the ATPase cycle. The motor domain in the poststroke state binds strongly to the microtubule with a K(d) of approximately 0.2 microM, while most of the motor domains in the prestroke state bind weakly to the microtubule with a K(d) of >10 microM. However, our results suggest that the timings of microtubule affinity change and tail swing are staggered at the recovery stroke step in which the tail swings from the poststroke to the prestroke position. The ATPase site in the AAA1 module of the motor domain is found to be responsible for coordinating these two mechanical processes.

title: A conserved modified wobble nucleoside (mcm5s2U) in lysyl-tRNA is required for viability in yeast.
text:
Transfer RNAs from all organisms (except Mycoplasma) and organelles contain a 2-thiouridine derivative (xm(5)s(2)U) as a wobble nucleoside. These tRNAs read the A- and G-ending codons in the split codon boxes His/Gln, Asn/Lys, and Asp/Glu. In eukaryotic cytoplasmic tRNAs, the conserved constituent (xm(5)-) in position 5 of uridine is 5-methoxycarbonylmethyl (mcm(5)). A protein (Tuc1p) from yeast similar to the bacterial protein TtcA, which is required for the synthesis of 2-thiocytidine in position 32 of the tRNA, was found to be required for the synthesis of 2-thiouridine in the wobble position (position 34). It appears that an ancient member of the TtcA family has evolved to thiolate U34 in tRNAs from organisms in the domains Eukarya and Archaea. Deletion of the TUC1 gene along with a deletion of the ELP3 gene, which results in the lack of the mcm(5) side chain, removes all modifications from the wobble uridine derivatives of the cytoplasmic tRNAs specific for Gln, Lys, and Glu. Surprisingly, overexpression of the mcm(5)s(2)U-lacking tRNA(Lys) alone was sufficient to restore viability in the double mutant elp3 tuc1.
It seems that the primary function of mcm(5)s(2)U34 is to improve the efficiency of reading the cognate codons rather than to prevent mis-sense errors.

title: The molecular requirements for cytokinesis.
text: Following anaphase, animal cells form an actomyosin contractile ring that constricts the plasma membrane to produce two daughter cells connected by a cytoplasmic bridge. This bridge is eventually severed to complete cytokinesis. Researchers have employed various methods to identify proteins involved in cytokinesis in vertebrates, insects, and nematodes. A core group of approximately 20 proteins are consistently involved in cytokinesis in most animal cells, and can be found in the contractile ring, central spindle, RhoA pathway, and on vesicles that expand the membrane and sever the bridge. While cytokinesis necessitates additional proteins, their specificity or requirement for cytokinesis is not universally conserved among animal cells.

title: Ibuprofen for the treatment of patent ductus arteriosus in preterm or low birth weight (or both) infants.
text:
The article compares the effectiveness and safety of ibuprofen versus indomethacin in closing a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in newborn infants. The authors analyzed 33 randomized controlled trials involving 2190 infants and found that:
1. Ibuprofen is as effective as indomethacin in closing a PDA, with a significant reduction in the risk of failure to close the duct (typical RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.20).
2. Ibuprofen reduces the risk of necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) compared to indomethacin (typical RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.93).
3. The duration of ventilatory support was reduced with ibuprofen compared to indomethacin (MD -2.4 days, 95% CI -3.7 to -1.0).
4. Oral ibuprofen is as effective as indomethacin in closing a PDA (typical RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.27).
5. Oral ibuprofen reduces the risk of NEC compared to indomethacin (typical RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.73).
6. The risk of failure to close a PDA was reduced with oral ibuprofen compared to iv ibuprofen (typical RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.64).
The authors conclude that ibuprofen is as effective as indomethacin in closing a PDA and has a lower risk of NEC and transient renal insufficiency. Oro-gastric administration of ibuprofen appears as effective as iv administration. However, further studies are needed to assess the effectiveness of high-dose versus standard-dose ibuprofen, early versus expectant administration of ibuprofen, echocardiographically guided versus standard iv ibuprofen, and continuous infusion versus intermittent boluses of ibuprofen. Additionally, long-term follow-up is needed to evaluate the long-term outcomes of ibuprofen use in infants with PDA.

title: A gradient of template dependence defines distinct biological roles for family X polymerases in nonhomologous end joining.
text: Researchers have discovered that three members of the Pol X family are involved in nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) in mammals. Template-independent TdT promotes diversity during NHEJ-dependent repair of V(D)J recombination intermediates, but the functions of the template-dependent polymerases mu and lambda in NHEJ remain unclear. Our study shows that both pol mu and pol lambda are recruited by NHEJ factors to fill gaps when ends have partially complementary overhangs, indicating equivalent roles in promoting accuracy during NHEJ. However, only pol mu demonstrates a distinctive in vivo role during immunoglobulin kappa recombination, which correlates with its ability to act as a TdT-like enzyme when primer termini lack complementary bases in the template strand. Unlike TdT, synthesis by pol mu in this context is primarily directed by a template from another DNA molecule. This unique template dependence is primarily attributable to a small structural element present in all three polymerases.

title: Involvement of sympathetic nervous system and brown fat in endotoxin-induced fever in rats.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate the role of brown adipose tissue (BAT) and the sympathetic nervous system in the increased heat production associated with endotoxin-induced fever. The study found that oxygen consumption (VO2) increased by 28% over a 4-hour period after two doses of endotoxin (Escherichia coli lipopolysaccharide, 0.3 mg/100 g body weight) administered 24 hours apart. Injection of a mixed beta-adrenoceptor antagonist (propranolol) reduced VO2 by 14% in endotoxin-treated rats, while selective beta 1- (atenolol) or beta 2- (ICI 118551) antagonists suppressed VO2 by 10%. These drugs had no effect on VO2 in control animals. The study also found that BAT thermogenic activity, assessed by measures of in vitro mitochondrial guanosine 5'-diphosphate (GDP) binding, was elevated by 54% in interscapular BAT and by 171% in other BAT depots. Surgical denervation of one lobe of the interscapular depot prevented these responses. Endotoxin failed to stimulate GDP binding in rats fed protein-deficient diets, which may have been due to either a lack of BAT thermogenic activity in control rats fed these diets or a suppression of food intake in the protein-deficient animals by the endotoxin. The results suggest that sympathetic activation of BAT is involved in the thermogenic responses to endotoxin and that these can be modified by dietary manipulation.

title: Metabolic, Epigenetic, and Transgenerational Effects of Gut Bacterial Choline Consumption.
text: Choline is a crucial nutrient and methyl donor that plays a vital role in epigenetic regulation. We examined the impact of gut microbial choline metabolism on bacterial fitness and host biology by creating a community of microorganisms lacking a single choline-utilizing enzyme. Our findings indicate that choline-utilizing bacteria compete with the host for this essential nutrient, significantly affecting plasma and hepatic levels of methyl-donor metabolites and reproducing biochemical signatures of choline deficiency. Mice with high levels of choline-consuming bacteria were found to be more susceptible to metabolic disorders when fed a high-fat diet. Moreover, bacterially induced reduction of methyl-donor availability influenced global DNA methylation patterns in both adult mice and their offspring, leading to behavioral alterations. Our results demonstrate an unappreciated effect of bacterial choline metabolism on host metabolism, epigenetics, and behavior. This work suggests that considering interpersonal differences in microbial metabolism is crucial when determining optimal nutrient intake requirements.

title: Genome-wide analysis reveals SR protein cooperation and competition in regulated splicing.
text: SR proteins, well-characterized RNA binding proteins, play a crucial role in promoting exon inclusion by interacting with exonic splicing enhancers (ESEs). However, it remained unclear whether the regulatory mechanisms identified in model genes apply to other genes in the cell. To address this question, we conducted global analyses of two prototypical SR proteins, SRSF1 (SF2/ASF) and SRSF2 (SC35), using splicing-sensitive arrays and CLIP-seq on mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs). Surprisingly, we found that these SR proteins can promote both inclusion and skipping of exons in vivo, despite their binding patterns not fully explaining such opposite responses. Further investigations revealed that the loss of one SR protein is often accompanied by changes in the interactions between other SR proteins at affected exons. In other words, the specific effects of one SR protein on regulated splicing are dependent on a complex network of interactions with multiple other SR proteins in mammalian genomes.

title: Human tuberculous granulomas induce peripheral lymphoid follicle-like structures to orchestrate local host defence in the lung.
text: The human tuberculous granuloma acts as a crucial foundation for local immune processes that determine the outcome of tuberculosis. Due to the scarcity of relevant information in human patients, the current study aimed to provide insights into the functional and structural characteristics of infected tissue. To achieve this goal, the study investigated the mycobacterial load in lesions and the distribution of infection to various tissue locations, as well as the distribution, functions, and interactions of host immune cells. Early granuloma formation in formerly healthy lung tissue was analyzed to identify the spatiotemporal sequence of cellular infiltration in response to mycobacterial infection. The development of the granuloma was found to consist of an inner cell layer with limited CD8+ cells surrounding the necrotic center and an outer area of lymphocyte infiltration housing mycobacteria-containing antigen-presenting cells, as well as CD4+, CD8+, and B cells in active follicle-like centers resembling secondary lymphoid organs. It is concluded that the follicular structures in the peripheral rim of granulomas serve as a morphological basis for the sustained host response in pulmonary tuberculosis.

title: Eosinophil pathogenicity mechanisms and therapeutics in neuromyelitis optica.
text: Inflammatory demyelinating lesions in neuromyelitis optica (NMO) are characterized by an abundance of eosinophils. To investigate the role of these cells in the pathogenesis of NMO and explore potential therapeutic strategies, we employed cell culture, ex vivo spinal cord slices, and in vivo mouse models of NMO. Our findings indicate that eosinophils Cultured from mouse bone marrow exhibited antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) towards cells expressing the aquaporin-4 protein in the presence of NMO autoantibody (NMO-IgG). Furthermore, eosinophils could stimulate cell killing through a complement-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (CDCC) mechanism when activated by complement. In NMO-IgG-treated spinal cord slice cultures, the inclusion of eosinophils or their granule toxins led to NMO pathology. Interestingly, treatment with second-generation antihistamines, such as cetirizine and ketotifen, which have eosinophil-stabilizing actions, significantly reduced NMO-IgG/eosinophil-dependent cytotoxicity and NMO pathology in both cell culture and mouse models. Our results suggest that eosinophils play a key role in NMO pathogenesis through ADCC and CDCC mechanisms. Moreover, these findings support the potential therapeutic utility of approved eosinophil-stabilizing drugs in the treatment of NMO.

title: Association of cystic fibrosis with abnormalities in fatty acid metabolism.
text:
BACKGROUND:
Individuals with cystic fibrosis have abnormal levels of plasma fatty acids. Previous research has shown that arachidonic acid levels are elevated and docosahexaenoic acid levels are reduced in tissues from mice with cystic fibrosis. In this study, we examined whether humans with mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene exhibit similar alterations in fatty acid metabolism in tissues expressing CFTR.
METHODS:
We analyzed fatty acids from nasal and rectal biopsy specimens, nasal epithelial scrapings, and plasma from 38 subjects with cystic fibrosis, compared to 13 obligate heterozygotes, 24 healthy controls, 11 subjects with inflammatory bowel disease, 9 subjects with upper respiratory tract infection, and 16 subjects with asthma.
RESULTS:

The ratio of arachidonic to docosahexaenoic acid was significantly increased in mucosal and submucosal nasal biopsy specimens (P < 0.001) and rectal biopsy specimens (P = 0.009) from subjects with cystic fibrosis and pancreatic sufficiency and subjects with cystic fibrosis and pancreatic insufficiency, compared to values in healthy control subjects. In nasal tissue, this alteration reflected increased levels of arachidonic acid and decreased levels of docosahexaenoic acid. In nasal cells, the ratio of arachidonic to docosahexaenoic acid was significantly higher in subjects with cystic fibrosis (P < 0.001) compared to healthy controls, with values in obligate heterozygotes intermediate between these two groups (P < 0.001). The ratio was not increased in subjects with inflammatory bowel disease. Subjects with asthma and those with upper respiratory tract infection had intermediate values between those in subjects with cystic fibrosis and healthy controls.
CONCLUSIONS:


Our findings indicate that alterations in fatty acid metabolism similar to those observed in cystic fibrosis-knockout mice are present in CFTR-expressing tissue from individuals with cystic fibrosis. These alterations may play a role in the pathogenesis of cystic fibrosis.

title: Actin dynamics and cell-cell adhesion in epithelia.
text: Latest breakthroughs in intercellular adhesion have underscored the crucial role of adherens junctions in interactions with the underlying actin cytoskeleton. In skin epithelial cells, a dynamic aspect of adherens junction formation involves the formation of filopodia, which extend into adjacent cell membranes, facilitating the clustering of adherens junction protein complexes at their tips. This in turn stimulates actin polymerization at the cytoplasmic interface of these complexes, although the exact mechanism is still unclear. The VASP/Mena family of proteins may be involved in organizing actin polymerization at these sites. In vivo, adherens junction formation relies on filopodia in processes where epithelial sheets need to move closer to form robust intercellular connections, such as during ventral closure in embryonic development or wound healing in postnatal animals.

title: Lamin A-dependent nuclear defects in human aging.
text: Mutations in the nuclear protein lamin A are responsible for the premature aging syndrome Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS). It is unclear whether lamin A plays a role in normal aging. Our study reveals that the same molecular mechanismlinked to HGPS is active in healthy cells. We found that cell nuclei from older individuals exhibit defects similar to those in HGPS patient cells, including changes in histone modifications and increased DNA damage. Notably, these aging-related nuclear defects are caused by occasional, spontaneous use of a cryptic splice site in lamin A that is normally not active. Inhibiting this splice site reverses the nuclear defects associated with aging. These findings suggest that lamin A plays a role in the physiological aging process.

title: Zmpste24 deficiency in mice causes spontaneous bone fractures, muscle weakness, and a prelamin A processing defect.
text: Zmpste24 is a membrane metalloproteinase found in the endoplasmic reticulum of cells. Research on tissues from Zmpste24-deficient mice (Zmpste24(-//-)) has shown that Zmpste24 plays a role in processing proteins that are prenylated with a CAAX motif. In this study, we investigate the effects of Zmpste24 deficiency on mouse health. Zmpste24(-/-) mice grow at a slower rate, appear malnourished, and display progressive hair loss. One of the most striking pathological manifestations is the occurrence of multiple spontaneous bone fractures, similar to thoseseen in mice with osteogenesis imperfecta. The volume of both cortical and trabecular bone is significantly reduced in Zmpste24(-/-) mice. Additionally, Zmpste24(-/-) mice exhibit muscle weakness in both the upper and lower extremities, similar to mice lacking farnesylated CAAX proteins. Processing of prelamin A was found to be defective in fibroblasts lacking Zmpste24, as well as in fibroblasts lacking the CAAX carboxyl methyltransferase Icmt, but was normal in fibroblasts lacking the CAAX endoprotease Rce1. Muscle weakness in Zmpste24(-/-) mice can be attributed to defective prelamin A processing, but the brittle bone phenotype suggests a broader role for Zmpste24 in mammalian biology.

title: Human and other faeces as breeding media of the trachoma vector Musca sorbens.
text:
A study was conducted to investigate the breeding habits of the fly Musca sorbens, which is believed to transmit Chlamydia trachomatis and cause trachoma in humans. The study was conducted in a rural Gambian village where trachoma is endemic. The researchers sought to identify the breeding media of M. sorbens in the village.
To do this, they set up test breeding media on soil-filled buckets and monitored the emergence of adult flies. They found that M. sorbens emerged from human faeces (6/9 trials), calf faeces (3/9), cow faeces (3/9), dog faeces (2/9), and goat faeces (1/9), but not from horse faeces, composting kitchen scraps, or a soil control (0/9 of each).
The results showed that the greatest number of flies emerged from human faeces (1426 flies/kg), with a median time for emergence of 9 days post-oviposition. Of all flies emerging from faeces, 81% were M. sorbens. Interestingly, male and female flies emerging from human faeces were significantly larger than those from other media, suggesting that they would be more fecund and live longer than smaller flies from other sources. Female flies caught from children's eyes were similar in size to those from human faeces, but significantly larger than those from other media.
The study suggests that human faeces are the best larval medium for M. sorbens, although some breeding also occurs in animal faeces. The researchers conclude that removing human faeces from the environment through the provision of basic sanitation is likely to greatly reduce fly density, eye contact, and hence trachoma transmission. However, if faeces of other animals are present, M. sorbens will persist.

title: Current Health and Environmental Status of the Maasai People in Sub-Saharan Africa
text: As time passes, the AIDS pandemic continues to escalate, impacting an estimated 38.6 million people globally. In response, two Cal Poly students are designing a satellite health clinic to serve the Maasai people residing in the Kajiado district of Southern Kenya. The Maasai have traditionally lived as pastoralists, subsisting on their cattle, which they share water with, amplifying the risk of contamination. However, as Kenya's population grows, the land the Maasai have traditionally used for grazing is dwindling. In an effort to adapt, some Maasai have turned to farming to sustain their livelihood. These changes have contributed to the degradation and deforestation of their region. As the Maasai's lifestyle evolves, they are relying more on maize for sustenance, resulting in a shift away from meat and dairy products. These transformations have had a profound impact on the Maasai culture. Our goal is to comprehensively understand these changes and identify potential areas for further support to ensure the Maasai community's survival.

title: Identification and characterization of a widely expressed form of adenylyl cyclase.
text: Scientists discovered a new type of mammalian enzyme called adenylyl cyclase using a technique called reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). They compared the new enzyme to eight already known mammalian enzymes and found that it was the most different, defining a new subclass of adenylyl cyclases. The researchers then studied the gene encoding the new enzyme, called AC9, and found that it was located on human chromosome 16. They detected high levels of the AC9 mRNA in all tissues they tested, including the brain, where it was particularly abundant in certain areas such as the hippocampus, cerebellum, and neocortex. They also created an antibody that could detect the protein produced by the AC9 gene in tissues and cell membranes. They found that the AC9 protein was present at highest levels in brain membranes and that it was stimulated by certain chemicals called Gs alpha. Unlike some other adenylyl cyclases, AC9 was not affected by calcium or by a different type of protein called G protein betagamma subunits. In summary, AC9 is a new type of enzyme that is found in many tissues throughout the body, including the brain, and it is regulated by a different type of protein called G proteins.

title: Expression of Golli mRNA during development in primary immune lymphoid organs of the rat
text: The gene encoding the oligodendrocyte lineage protein Golli (Golli)-MBP contains three exons specific to Golli, alongside eight exons from the classic myelin basic protein (MBP) gene. This results in the production of alternatively spliced proteins that share amino acid sequencing with MBP. Unlike MBP, which is expressed only in the nervous system later in development, Golli gene products are expressed both pre- and post-natally at multiple sites. In this study, we used RT-PCR and 5' RACE to determine the sequence of Golli in rat and found that Golli sequences are expressed in primary lymphoid organs as early as embryonic day 16.5, which may explain the anergic rat T cell response observed in Golli-induced meningitis.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of single baseline measurement of Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay for diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction in emergency department: systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Objective:
To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies to estimate the accuracy of a single baseline measurement of the Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay (Roche Diagnostics) for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction in patients presenting to the emergency department.
Design:

We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies that evaluated the accuracy of a single baseline measurement of the Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay for the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction in patients presenting to the emergency department with suspected acute coronary syndrome. We searched electronic databases including Medline, Embase, and other relevant databases for articles published between January 2006 and December 2013.
Study selection:


We included studies that evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a single baseline measurement of the Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay for the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction in patients presenting to the emergency department with suspected acute coronary syndrome. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts and selected potentially relevant papers.
Data synthesis:


We extracted the data on the methodological quality of the studies using the adapted QUADAS-2 tool, and pooled the summary sensitivity and specificity estimates using hierarchical bivariate models. We also conducted a sensitivity analysis to assess the impact of different cut-off values on the accuracy of the assay.
Results:



Twenty-three studies were included in the review, with a total of 1,178 patients. The results showed that at a cut-off value of 14 ng/L, the summary sensitivity was 89.5% (95% CI 86.3-92.1%) and the summary specificity was 77.1% (95% CI 68.7-83.7%). At a cut-off value of 3-5 ng/L, the summary sensitivity was 97.4% (95% CI 94.9-98.7%) and the summary specificity was 42.4% (95% CI 31.2-54.5%). These results indicate that a single baseline measurement of the Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay could be used to rule out acute myocardial infarction if lower cut-off values are used. However, this method should be part of a comprehensive triage strategy and may not be appropriate for patients who present less than three hours after symptom onset.
Discussion:


The results of this systematic review and meta-analysis indicate that a single baseline measurement of the Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay could be used to rule out acute myocardial infarction if lower cut-off values are used.
