However, this method should be part of a comprehensive triage strategy and may not be appropriate for patients who present less than three hours after symptom onset. Care must also be exercised because of the higher imprecision of the evaluated assay and the greater effect of lot-to-lot reagent variation at low troponin concentrations.
Conclusion:


The results of this systematic review and meta-analysis indicate that a single baseline measurement of the Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay could be used to rule out acute myocardial infarction if lower cut-off values are used. However, this method should be part of a comprehensive triage strategy and may not be appropriate for patients who present less than three hours after symptom onset. Care must also be exercised because of the higher imprecision of the evaluated assay and the greater effect of lot-to-lot reagent variation at low troponin concentrations.

title: Pericyte differentiation.
text: Pericytes are identified in the body based on their location, embedded within the basement membrane of microvessels. They form an essential part of the microvascular wall and are believed to play a role in angiogenesis, although their specific function is not entirely clear. Pericytes derived from the retinal microvasculature have been cultured and distinguished from other stromal cells, such as smooth muscle cells, based on a series of characteristics. In vitro, pericytes form multicellular nodules rich in extracellular matrix, which becomes mineralized when grown in medium containing serum. These findings suggest that pericytes are primitive mesenchymal cells capable of differentiating into an osteogenic phenotype. The differentiation of pericytes is characterized by changes in their response to transforming growth factor beta 1 and the synthesis and/or deposition of various extracellular matrix proteins, including laminin, Type IV collagen, tenascin, Type X collagen, osteonectin, and thrombospondin-1. Angiogenesis is frequently associated with mineralization, and these data suggest that pericytes may contribute to mineralization in vivo.

title: Membrane association of the CD3ε signaling domain is required for optimal T cell development and function.
text: The TCR:CD3 complex transmits crucial signals for optimal T cell development and adaptive immunity. In resting T cells, the CD3ε cytoplasmic tail interacts with the plasma membrane via a basic stretch (BRS). Our study reveals that mice lacking a functional CD3ε-BRS displayed significant reductions in thymic cellularity and limited CD4-CD8-double-negative (DN) 3 to DN4 thymocyte transition, resulting from enhanced DN4 TCR signaling that led to increased cell death and TCR downregulation in subsequent populations. Furthermore, both positive and negative T cell selection were affected in mice lacking a functional CD3ε-BRS, resulting in limited peripheral T cell function and greatly reduced responsiveness to influenza infection. In conclusion, the membrane association of the CD3ε signaling domain is essential for optimal thymocyte development and peripheral T cell function.

title: A new era in ovulation induction.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of aromatase inhibitors in ovulation induction, superovulation, and IVF.
Design: A literature search was conducted using MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Database of systematic reviews, employing keywords such as "aromatase inhibitor," "letrozole," "anastrazole," "ovulation induction," "ovulation," and "superovulation."
Results: Ovulation induction with letrozole is associated with an ovulation rate of 70%-84% and a pregnancy rate of 20%-27% per cycle. In comparison, ovulation and pregnancy rates with letrozole seem higher than those of anastrazole. In superovulation, letrozole is associated with a fewer number of developing follicles and a thicker endometrium. The use of letrozole for superovulation results in a higher pregnancy rate compared to the use of clomiphene citrate (CC) (16.7% vs. 5.6%). The addition of letrozole to FSH treatment leads to a decreased FSH requirement. The pregnancy rate for treatment with letrozole and FSH is similar to that of FSH alone.
Conclusion: Aromatase inhibitors are as effective or more effective than CC in ovulation induction and superovulation. Unlike CC, they do not have an antiestrogenic effect on the endometrium. Given their advantages, they can replace CC as ovulation-inducing drugs. Their role in IVF remains to be determined.

title: Of lineage and legacy: the development of mammalian hematopoietic stem cells
text: The hematopoietic system emerges as one of the first complex tissues in the early stages of mammalian development. The origin of adult bone marrow hematopoietic stem cells is a topic of intense research in the field of developmental hematopoiesis. As blood is a mobile tissue and hematopoietic cells arise from multiple embryonic sites, tracing the origin of the adult mammalian blood system is complicated. The question of how these cells arise and mature is a topic of ongoing debate and research. In addition, there is a focus on understanding the developmental signals that induce the adult hematopoietic stem cell program, as these may provide insights into generating and expanding these clinically important cell populations outside of the body (ex vivo). This review provides a historical overview of and the most recent data on the developmental origins of hematopoiesis.

title: Long crocidolite asbestos fibers cause polyploidy by sterically blocking cytokinesis.
text:
The physical nature of asbestos has been characterized as a carcinogen, with its harmful effects believed to be primarily influenced by fiber dimensions. It is hypothesized that long asbestos fibers may disrupt chromosome distribution during cell division, causing genetic mutations that lead to cancer progression.
Using high-resolution time-lapse light microscopy and serial-section electron microscopy, we have carefully observed individual crocidolite asbestos fibers as they pass through the later stages of cell division in LLC-MK2 epithelial cells. Our findings reveal that long fibers (15-55 micrograms) caught in the cleavage furrow of dividing cells can block cytokinesis, resulting in the formation of binucleated cells.
We discovered that the ends of these blocking fibers are often located within invaginations of the newly formed nuclei. Attachment of the fiber to the nuclear envelope can be observed when a chromatin strand runs along the fiber and into the intercellular bridge. These observations suggest that individual crocidolite fibers can cause genetic changes by directly interfering with cytokinesis, and that fiber length and affinity for the nuclear envelope are critical factors.
Our data provide the first visual evidence that individual asbestos fibers can cause genomic changes at the cellular level, which may serve as an initial step in the development of asbestos-induced cancers.

title: Neural induction and early patterning in vertebrates.
text: In the early stages of vertebrate development, the formation of the nervous system is triggered by signals from a prominent 'organizing' region of the embryo during gastrulation. This phenomenon, known as neural induction, was first discovered and characterized by experimental embryologists studying amphibian embryos. Subsequent research in these model organisms revealed that eliminating transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) signaling in the ectoderm is a key step in the acquisition of neural fate. This observation forms the basis of the 'default' model of neural induction. Endogenous proteins produced by the ectoderm act to inhibit TGFβ ligands, leading to the induction of a non-neural fate in the dorsal ectoderm. In contrast, in the ventral ectoderm, the TGFβ ligands are not inhibited, leading to the induction of a neural fate. This suggests that the molecular mechanisms underlying neural induction are conserved across a wide range of organisms in the evolutionary tree. Further research using embryonic stem cells from mice, primates, and humans should shed light on the role of signaling pathways and their downstream mediators in neural induction in vertebrate embryos.

title: What's in the 'treatment gap'? Ethnographic perspectives on addiction and global mental health from China, Russia, and the United States.
text: Over the past few years, a 'global mental health' movement has gained momentum, prioritizing evidence-based interventions for mental illnesses in low- and middle-income countries. Anthropologists and cultural psychiatrists have engaged in vigorous discussions regarding the appropriateness of this agenda. This article builds on ethnographic fieldwork conducted on substance use disorder management in China, Russia, and the United States, to reflect on these debates. We contend that the 'treatment gaps' framework, which guides much research and intervention under the global mental health rubric, partially obscures the intricate web of institutions, therapeutics, knowledges, and actors involved in managing addiction (and other mental health concerns) in any given context.

title: Generation of mice deficient in both KLF3/BKLF and KLF8 reveals a genetic interaction and a role for these factors in embryonic globin gene silencing.
text: Krüppel-like factors 3 and 8 (KLF3 and KLF8) are closely related transcriptional regulators that bind to similar DNA sequences. Previous studies have shown that in erythroid cells, there is a KLF family regulatory hierarchy, where KLF1 drives the expression of both the Klf3 and Klf8 genes, and KLF3 in turn represses Klf8 expression. However, the contribution of KLF8 to this regulatory network has remained unknown. To investigate, we generated a mouse model with disrupted KLF8 expression. Although these mice are viable but have a reduced lifespan, mice lacking both KLF3 and KLF8 die at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5), indicating a genetic interaction between these two factors. In fetal liver tissue, double mutant embryos for Klf3 and Klf8 show greater dysregulation of gene expression compared to each of the single mutants. Specifically, we observe derepression of embryonic, but not adult, globin expression. Together, these findings suggest that KLF3 and KLF8 have overlapping roles in vivo and play a role in silencing embryonic globin expression during development.

title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis phagosome maturation arrest: selective targeting of PI3P-dependent membrane trafficking.
text: The capacity of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to infiltrate host macrophages and reside within a phagosome that fails to mature into a phagolysosome is crucial for the spread of tuberculosis and the global pandemic affecting billions of people worldwide. Tuberculosis can be considered a disease with a notable element of intracellular traffic and organelle biogenesis. The current understanding of the block in M. tuberculosis phagosome maturation has provided insight into the mechanisms of phagolysosome biogenesis. The maturation block involves disrupting the recruitment and function of Rab proteins, Rab effectors (phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases and tethering molecules such as EEA1), SNAREs (Syntaxin 6 and cellubrevin), and Ca2+/calmodulin signaling. M. tuberculosis analogs of mammalian phosphatidylinositols disrupt these systems and associated processes.

title: SvpA, a novel surface virulence-associated protein required for intracellular survival of Listeria monocytogenes.
text:
A newly discovered protein, designated SvpA, has been identified as a key player in the virulence of the intracellular pathogen Listeria monocytogenes. This 64 kDa protein, encoded by the svpA gene, is both secreted and surface-exposed, as shown by immunogold labeling of whole bacteria with an anti-SvpA antibody. Analysis of the protein sequence suggests that SvpA has a leader peptide, a transmembrane region, and a positively charged tail similar to that of the surface protein ActA, indicating that it may reassociate with the bacterial surface via its C-terminal membrane anchor.
To investigate the role of SvpA in L. monocytogenes virulence, an allelic mutant was constructed by disrupting the svpA gene in the wild-type strain LO28. The mutant showed a striking reduction in virulence in mice, with a 2 log decrease in the LD50 and restricted bacterial growth in organs compared to the wild-type strain. This reduction in virulence was not due to a loss of adherence or reduced expression of known virulence factors, which remained unchanged in the svpA mutant. Instead, it was caused by a limitation in the intracellular growth of mutant bacteria.
Confocal and electron microscopy studies revealed that most SvpA mutant bacteria remained confined within phagosomes, in contrast to wild-type bacteria which rapidly escaped to the cytoplasm. The regulation of SvpA was found to be independent of PrfA, the transcriptional activator of virulence genes in L. monocytogenes, and instead, was controlled by a MecA-dependent regulatory network.
The findings of this study indicate that:
1. SvpA is a novel factor involved in the virulence of L. monocytogenes, promoting bacterial escape from phagosomes of macrophages.
2. SvpA is, at least partially, associated with the surface of bacteria.
3. SvpA is PrfA-independent and controlled by a MecA-dependent regulatory network.

In summary, this study identifies SvpA as a previously unknown protein that plays a crucial role in the virulence of L. monocytogenes by promoting bacterial escape from phagosomes of macrophages. The findings provide new insights into the complex regulatory network that controls the virulence of this intracellular pathogen.

title: Measuring adherence to highly active antiretroviral therapy: implications for research and practice.
text: The revolutionary treatment known as Highly Active Antiretroivelont therapy (HAART) has greatly improved the progression of HIV disease, drastically reducing both HIV-related morbidity and mortality. However, the intricate nature of the typical daily HAART regimen presents a significant challenge, requiring tall levels of adherence for complete and long-term viral suppression and the prevention of drug resistance. As a result, evaluating medication adherence has become crucial. Although various methods for assessing adherence exist, they only measure a subset of behaviors and lack strong predictive validity. Given the significance of adherence to HAART from both an individual and public health perspective, there is a need for ongoing development and validation of measures for assessing adherence.

title: Survival rates of tropical and temperate passerines: a Trinidadian perspective.
text: Data collected through mist nets over a 10-year period in Trinidad were used to estimate the adult survival rates of 17 species of forest passerines. The Trinidadian survival rates (mean of 65%, ranging from 45% to 85%) were significantly higher than the published estimates for European (mean survival of 52%, ranging from 32% to 71%) and North American (mean survival of 53%, ranging from 29% to 63%) passerines of similar body size, indicating a 45% higher mean life expectancy in Trinidad. These findings were further confirmed after controlling for phylogeny using a method of independent contrasts. The study also revealed that transient and/or young birds were a crucial component of the Trinidad data, and analyses that fail to account for their presence may underestimate adult survival rates. This research supports the hypothesis that avian survival rates are higher in humid tropical regions, although the magnitude of the difference may be less than previously suggested.

title: P0 glycoprotein peptides 56–71 and 180–199 dose-dependently induce acute and chronic experimental autoimmune neuritis in Lewis rats associated with epitope spreading
text: Two synthetic peptides, P0 180-199 and P0 56-71, were used to induce experimental autoimmune neuritis (EAN) in Lewis rats. The peptides were administered at either low (50-100 microg/rat) or high (250 microg/rat) doses. The results showed that the onset of clinical signs and the peak of the disease occurred at different times depending on the peptide used. In addition, there were differences in the level of spreading of the epitopes within the peptides, as well as differences in the production of interferon-gamma. The histopathological evaluation of the sciatic nerves revealed similar levels of mononuclear cell infiltration in both types of EAN, but more severe demyelination in the high dose group. These findings support the hypothesis that high dose autoantigen immunization leads to extensive determinant spreading and a chronic course of autoimmune diseases.

title: Interaction between broad-spectrum antibiotics and the combined oral contraceptive pill. A literature review.
text: Opinions on the significance of drug interactions between combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) and broad-spectrum antibiotics vary widely between healthcare professionals in Europe and the US. While rifampicin and griseofulvin have been shown to induce hepatic enzymes and reduce the efficacy of COCPs, the impact of other broad-spectrum antibiotics on contraceptive effectiveness is less clear. There are limited prospective studies on the pharmacokinetics of concurrent COCP and antibiotic use, and few demonstrate any convincing basis for reduced contraceptive efficacy. However, variable contraceptive steroid handling may make some women more susceptible to COCP failure. Given the serious consequences of unwanted pregnancy, a cautious approach involving additional or alternative contraception during short courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics and the initial weeks of long-term antibiotic administration may be warranted to safeguard those women who may be at risk. Conflicting opinions and advice can be confusing for both healthcare professionals and patients, and instructions for additional precautions during and after concurrent COCP and antibiotic use can be complicated. Educating women about the mode of action of COCPs and the times when failure is more likely is crucial for healthcare professionals who prescribe these pills. Professionals who feel that concurrent antibiotic use poses a real threat to COCP efficacy should present advice for additional contraceptive precautions in a simple and consistent manner, backed by written information and reinforced at regular intervals.

title: CLIP-170 interacts with dynactin complex and the APC-binding protein EB1 by different mechanisms.
text: CLIP-170 is a proteins that plays a crucial role in the interactions between endosomes and microtubules, particularly in controlling microtubule dynamics. CLIP-170 is known to localize dynamically to growing microtubule plus ends, where it colocalizes with the dynein activator dynactin and the APC-binding protein EB1. Based on this observation, it is possible that CLIP-170 interacts with dynactin and/or EB1. To investigate this, we used site-specific mutagenesis of CLIP-170 and a transfection/colocalization assay in mammalian tissue culture cells. Our results confirm that CLIP-170 interacts directly or indirectly with both dynactin and EB1. We found that the CLIP-170/dynactin interaction is mediated by the second metal binding motif of the CLIP-170 tail, while the CLIP-170/EB1 interaction does not require metal binding. Additionally, our experiments suggest that the CLIP-170/dynactin interaction occurs via the shoulder/sidearm subcomplex of dynactin and can occur in the cytosol, without requiring microtubule binding. These findings have implications for the targeting of both dynactin and EB1 to microtubule plus ends. Our data suggest that the CLIP-170/dynactin interaction can target dynactin complex to microtubule plus ends, although dynactin likely also targets MT plus ends directly via the microtubule binding motif of the p150(Glued) subunit. We found that CLIP-170 mutants alter p150(Glued) localization without affecting EB1, indicating that EB1 can target microtubule plus ends independently of dynactin.

title: Subcapsular encounter and complement-dependent transport of immune complexes by lymph node B cells
text: The mechanism by which B cells encounter antigens in lymphoid tissues is not fully understood, and it is also unclear how immune complexes are transported to follicular dendritic cells. Using real-time two-photon microscopy, we observed rapid delivery of immune complexes from the lymph to macrophages in the lymph node subcapsular sinus. B cells captured these immune complexes through a complement receptor-dependent mechanism, and this process involved macrophage processes that penetrated the follicle and transported the complexes to follicular dendritic cells. Additionally, cognate B cells captured antigen-containing immune complexes from macrophage processes and migrated to the T zone. Our findings reveal that macrophages lining the subcapsular sinus are an important site of B cell encounter with immune complexes, and that intrafollicular B cell migration facilitates the transport of immune complexes and encounters with cognate antigens.

title: Exercise training-induced adaptations in the coronary circulation.
text:
Exercise training leads to an increase in coronary blood flow capacity, which is caused by modifications to the control of coronary vascular resistance and, consequently, coronary blood flow. The importance of various control systems, such as metabolic, myogenic, endothelium-mediated, and neurohumoral, differs throughout the coronary arterial tree. These systems contribute to regulating coronary vascular resistance in a non-uniform manner, with each level of the coronary arterial tree having a unique distribution of adaptations.
Furthermore, the effects of exercise training are not uniform throughout the coronary tree, with adaptations varying spatially. For instance, endothelium-mediated control plays a significant role in training-induced changes in coronary vascular resistance, and the mode, frequency, and intensity of exercise training bouts, as well as the duration of training, can influence these adaptations.
Exercise training also induces changes in the responses of coronary vascular smooth muscle to vasoactive agents and alters cellular-molecular control of intracellular calcium in coronary vascular smooth muscle in conduit coronary arteries and enhances myogenic reactivity of coronary resistance arteries. Conversely, adenosine sensitivity is increased in conduit coronary arteries and large resistance arteries after training but remains unchanged in small coronary resistance arteries of trained animals.
While much is still unknown, the evidence shows that chronic exercise alters the phenotype of coronary endothelial and vascular smooth muscle cells, with plasticity of these cells playing a crucial role in adaptation of the cardiovascular system in exercise training.

title: Hepatic intra-arterial versus intravenous fotemustine in patients with liver metastases from uveal melanoma (EORTC 18021): a multicentric randomized trial.
text:
BACKGROUND: Uveal melanoma (UM) with metastatic disease limited to the liver is a challenging condition, and the effect of an intrahepatic treatment on survival is uncertain. To investigate this, we conducted a prospective study of the efficacy and safety of hepatic intra-arterial (HIA) versus systemic (IV) fotemustine in patients with liver metastases from UM.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: We randomly assigned 171 patients to receive either HIA or IV fotemustine at 100 mg/m(2) on days 1, 8, 15 (and 22 in the HIA arm only) as induction, followed by a 5-week rest period and subsequent treatments every 3 weeks. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS), and secondary endpoints included response rate (RR), progression-free survival (PFS), and safety.
RESULTS: Our study was stopped early due to results from a futility analysis of overall survival. A total of 155 patients had died, and 16 were still alive (median follow-up 1.6 years, range 0.25-6 years). HIA did not significantly improve OS (median 14.6 months) compared to the IV arm (median 13.8 months), with a hazard ratio of 1.09 (95% confidence interval 0.79-1.50, log-rank P = 0.59). However, there was a significant benefit on PFS for HIA compared to IV, with a median of 4.5 versus 3.5 months, respectively (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.45-0.84, log-rank P = 0.002). The 1-year PFS rate was 24% in the HIA arm versus 8% in the IV arm. An improved RR was seen in the HIA (10.5%) compared to IV treatment (2.4%). In the IV arm, the most common grade ≥3 toxicities were thrombocytopenia (42.1%) and neutropenia (62.6%), whereas 21.2% and 28.7% of patients experienced these toxicities in the HIA arm. The most common grade ≥3 toxicity related to HIA was catheter complications (12%), and liver toxicity (4.5%) apart from two toxic deaths.
CONCLUSION: Our study suggests that HIA treatment with fotemustine did not result in improved OS compared to IV treatment, despite better RR and PFS. Intrahepatic treatment should still be considered experimental. EUDRACT NUMBER AND CLINICALTRIALSGOV IDENTIFIER: 2004-002245-12 and NCT00110123.

title: Comparison of survival between cerebellar and supratentorial glioblastoma patients: surveillance, epidemiology, and end results (SEER) analysis.
text:
Cerebellar glioblastoma multiforme (cGBM) is a rare brain tumor, and there is a common belief that its prognosis is worse than for supratentorial glioblastoma multiforme (sGBM). However, most studies on this topic have been limited in scope and design. This study aimed to investigate the effect of cerebellar location on survival by comparing the overall survival time of cGBM and sGBM patients using a case-control design.
We retrospectively analyzed data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) registry, covering 1973 to 2008. We identified 132 cGBM patients and matched them with 20,848 sGBM patients based on age, extent of resection, decade of diagnosis, and radiation therapy using propensity score matching.
Our findings showed that 37% of cGBM patients were older than 65 years, 62% were men, and 87% were white. Most patients underwent surgery and radiation (74%), while only 26% underwent surgical resection only. The median survival time for the cGBM and sGBM matched cohort was 8 months, but the survival distributions differed (log-rank P = .04). Survival time for cGBM vs sGBM at 2 years was 21.5% vs 8.0%, and 12.7% vs 5.3% at 3 years.
Multivariate analysis of survival among cGBM patients revealed that younger age (P < .0001) and having radiation therapy (P < .0001) were significantly associated with reduced hazard of mortality. Among all patients, multivariate analysis showed that tumor location (P = .03), age (P < .0001), tumor size (P = .009), radiation (P < .0001), and resection (P < .0001) were associated with survival time in the unmatched cohort.
Our findings suggest that cGBM patients have a survival time advantage compared to sGBM patients as the study progresses. These findings indicate that cGBM patients should be treated as aggressively as sGBM patients with surgical resection and radiation therapy.

title: Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans infection (animal experiments).
text:
During a specific phase of infection in white mice injected intraperitoneally with a pure Culture of a proteolytic strain of Candida albicans, both Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans were simultaneously isolated from the peritoneal abscesses, particularly those attached to the stomach, duodenum, pancreas, and upper part of the small intestine. This simultaneous occurrence of the two pathogens was further supported by histopathological examination, which revealed a large number of Staphylococcus aureus present near the center of granulomata caused by Candida albicans.
In light of the fact that the proteolytic byproducts of Candida albicans can serve as a good medium for the growth of Staphylococcus aureus and the latter may be isolated from the intestinal tract of healthy mice, possibly as a transient flora component, the coexistence of these two important etiological agents of endogenous infections as encountered during this study holds significant clinical implications. Moreover, these observations highlight the significance of controlling the bacterial flora of mice in pure mycological studies.

title: Three common functional polymorphisms in microRNA encoding genes in the susceptibility to hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Recent findings have suggested that common genetic variations in microRNAs (miRNAs) may increase the risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, earlier studies and meta-analyses have yielded inconclusive results. This review and meta-analysis aimed to assess whether specific single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the genes encoding miRNAs are associated with susceptibility to HCC and its clinicopathological characteristics in hepatitis B virus (HBV)-related HCC. A computerized search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and China BioMedicine (CBM) databases revealed ten case-control studies with a combined total of 3437 cases and 3437 healthy controls. We identified three common functional SNPs in miRNA-encoding genes: miR-146a G>C (rs2910164), miR-196a-2 C>T (rs11614913), and miR-499 T>C (rs3746444). Our meta-analysis found that the miR-146a C variant was associated with a decreased risk of HCC, particularly among Asian and male populations. In contrast, the miR-196a-2 T variant was associated with an increased susceptibility to HCC in Caucasian populations. However, we failed to find any significant correlations between the miR-499 C polymorphism and HCC risk. When we further stratified the analysis by HBV status, similar trends were observed, but the results were not statistically significant due to small sample sizes. Our findings suggest that SNPs in the genes encoding miR-146a and miR-196a-2 may play a significant role in genetic susceptibility to HCC.

title: Isonicotinamide enhances Sir2 protein-mediated silencing and longevity in yeast by raising intracellular NAD+ concentration.
text: Sirtuins are a family of evolved proteins that rely on NAD+ to function. These proteins regulate gene transcription, cellular metabolism, and aging. Sirtuins require a stable intracellular NAD+ level to function properly. Nicotinamide (NAM), a NAD+ precursor, is produced by the enzyme Pnc1 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. However, NAM can also inhibit sirtuin activity. To overcome this inhibition, the yeast cell produces nicotinic acid (NA) through the NAD+ salvage pathway enzyme Npt1. Isonicotinamide (INAM), an isostere of NAM, stimulates sir2 deacetylase activity in vitro by alleviating NAM inhibition. Our study found that INAM also has an additional mechanism in vivo that increases the intracellular NAD+ concentration. INAM enhances silencing at the rDNA locus but partially suppresses silencing defects in an npt1Δ mutant. Yeast cells grown without NA had a short replicative life span, which was extended by INAM in a SIR2-dependent manner and correlated with increased NAD+. The INAM-induced increase in NAD+ was strongly dependent on Pnc1 and Npt1, suggesting that INAM increases flux through the NAD+ salvage pathway. A part of this effect was mediated by the NR salvage pathways, which generate NAM as a product and require Pnc1 to produce NAD+. Our study also showed that INAM influences the expression of multiple NAD+ biosynthesis and salvage pathways to promote homeostasis during stationary phase.

title: Similar activation of signal transduction pathways by the herpesvirus-encoded chemokine receptors US28 and ORF74.
text: The virus-encoded chemokine receptors US28 from human cytomegalovirus and ORF74 from human herpesvirus 8 are both constantly active. We discovered that both receptors constantly activate the transcription factors nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) and cAMP response element binding protein (CREB), and both pathways can be influenced by their respective endogenous receptor ligands. By adding specific pathway modulators that target the G protein subunit Galphai, phospholipase C, protein kinase C, calcineurin, p38 MAP kinase, and MEK1, we found that both the consistently active receptors and the receptors'ligand-dependent inductions are mediated by several yet similar mechanisms. The NFAT and CREB transcription factors, along with their upstream activators, are known to induce the expression of both host and virus-encoded genes. According to our findings, the activity of these virus-encoded chemokine receptors appears to coordinate host and potentially viral gene expression in a similar manner. ORF74 has been linked to tumorigenesis, so these findings may have important implications for understanding cytomegalovirus-associated pathogenesis.

title: The therapeutic promise of the cancer stem cell concept.
text: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are a unique subpopulation of tumor cells that possess the remarkable ability to initiate and maintain tumors. They have the capacity to differentiate into various cell lineages, giving rise to a large population of non-tumorigenic cancer cells. Recent studies have revealed that CSCs are prevalent in several human malignancies and are associated with disease progression. Indeed, it is now believed that the failure of conventional anticancer therapies to eradicate malignant tumors may be attributed, in part, to the presence of CSCs. Therefore, targeting CSCs with tailored therapeutic approaches may offer a promising strategy to improve clinical cancer therapy, particularly for malignancies that are refractory to conventional treatments.

title: 3'-End processing of pre-mRNA in eukaryotes.
text: Almost all eukaryotic messenger RNAs (mRNAs) undergo endonucleolytic cleavage at their 3' ends, followed by the addition of a poly(A) tail. This process is highly dependent on the presence of specific sequence elements in the mRNA, including the sequence AAUAAA upstream of the cleavage site, a degenerate GU-rich sequence element downstream of the cleavage site, and stimulatory sequences upstream of AAUAAA. Currently, six factors have been identified that carry out these two reactions, and while some of these factors have been purified to homogeneity and their cDNAs cloned, the identity of the endonuclease involved in the process remains unknown. Additionally, the cooperative RNA-protein and protein-protein interactions within the processing complex are still being analyzed, and many details of the mechanism are not yet clear. However, studies on regulated polyadenylation in yeast and other organisms have shown that the sequences directing cleavage and polyadenylation are more degenerate in yeast compared to metazoans, and there is no identified downstream element involved in this process. The list of processing factors may be complete now with approximately a dozen polypeptides, but their functions in the reaction are largely unknown. Furthermore, it is thought that 3' processing is coupled to transcription, with interactions between processing factors and the mRNA cap as well as with RNA polymerase II influencing the process.

title: Structure and developmental regulation of Golli-mbp, a 105-kilobase gene that encompasses the myelin basic protein gene and is expressed in cells in the oligodendrocyte lineage in the brain.
text: We have discovered a novel genetic element, termed the Golli-mbp gene, which encompasses the mouse myelin basic protein (MBP) gene. This gene contains three distinct exons that are alternatively spliced with MBP exons and introns, resulting in a family of MBP-related mRNAs that are subject to individual developmental regulation. These mRNAs are expressed at specific stages of oligodendrocyte differentiation in a temporally controlled manner, suggesting that the MBP gene is part of a more complex gene structure that may play a role in oligodendrocyte differentiation before myelination. Notably, one Golli-mbp mRNA that encodes a protein with antigenic similarity to MBP is also expressed in the spleen and other non-neural tissues.

title: Cardiovascular effects of intensive lifestyle intervention in type 2 diabetes.
text: The impact of intense lifestyle interventions on weight loss for overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes remains uncertain, particularly in terms of their long-term effects on cardiovascular disease outcomes. To investigate this, we conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) among 5145 overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes in 16 study centers across the United States. The study participants were randomly assigned to receive either an intensive lifestyle intervention aimed at promoting weight loss through reduced caloric intake and increased physical activity (intervention group) or standard diabetes support and education (control group). The primary outcome of the study was a composite of fatal or non-fatal cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction, stroke, or hospitalization for angina, measured over a maximum follow-up period of 13.5 years. The trial was stopped early due to a futility analysis when the median follow-up was 9.6 years. We found that the intervention group experienced greater weight loss throughout the study period (8.6% vs. 0.7% at 1 year; 6.0% vs. 3.5% at study end) and notable improvements in glycated hemoglobin levels and initial fitness and cardiovascular risk factors, except for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels. However, the primary outcome occurred in 403 patients in the intervention group and 418 in the control group (1.83 and 1.92 events per 100 person-years, respectively; hazard ratio in the intervention group, 0.95; 95% confidence interval, 0.83 to 1.09; P=0.51). In conclusion, our findings indicate that an intensive lifestyle intervention targeting weight loss does not significantly reduce the rate of cardiovascular events in overweight or obese adults with type 2 diabetes. (Funded by the National Institutes of Health and others; Look AHEAD ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00017953.)

title: Early loss of interneurons and delayed subunit-specific changes in GABA(A)-receptor expression in a mouse model of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
text: Unilateral injection of kainic acid (KA) into the dorsal hippocampus of adult mice triggers spontaneous recurrent partial seizures that mirror histopathological changes observed in human mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we examined alterations in pre- and postsynaptic components of GABAergic neurotransmission in this mouse model at different time points following KA injection, ranging from 1 to 120 days. We employed immunohistochemical techniques to detect markers of GABAergic interneurons (parvalbumin, calbindin-D28k, and calretinin), the type-1 GABA transporter (GAT1), and major GABA(A)-receptor subunits expressed in the hippocampal formation. Our findings revealed a profound loss of hilar cells and limited damage to CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells in the acute phase following KA injection. Moreover, parvalbumin and calbindin-D28k staining of interneurons disappeared irreversibly in CA1 and dentate gyrus (DG), while calretinin staining was spared. The prominent GABA(A)-receptor alpha1 subunit staining of interneurons also disappeared after KA treatment, suggesting acute degeneration of these cells. Interestingly, GAT1 immunoreactivity revealed degenerating terminals at 24 h post-KA in CA1 and DC, which subsided almost completely thereafter. A loss of CA1 and, to a lesser extent, CA3 neurons became evident at 7-15 days post-KA, with a more pronounced reduction after 1 month. In contrast, dentate gyrus granule cells were markedly enlarged and dispersed in the molecular layer, accompanied by a prominent increase in GABA(A)-receptor subunit staining. After 4 months, the dorsal CA1 area was lost almost entirely, CA3 was reduced, and the DG represented most of the remaining dorsal hippocampal formation. No significant morphological alterations were detected in the contralateral hippocampus. These findings suggest that loss of hilar cells and GABAergic neurons contribute to epileptogenesis in this mouse model of MTLE. In contrast, long-term degeneration of pyramidal cells and granule cell dispersion may represent distinct responses to recurrent seizures. Finally, GABA(A)-receptor upregulation in the DG may represent a compensatory response persisting for several months in epileptic mice.

title: Cardiorespiratory adaptation during sleep in infants and children.
text: After birth, the cardiorespiratory control system undergoes maturation, leading to instability in the system during early infancy, particularly during sleep. Over the past decade, there has been increased scrutiny of the effects of different states of alertness on respiratory and cardiac control, with a particular focus on the influence of rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep during the postnatal period. It is notable that newborns spend a significant portion of their time in REM sleep, and this proportion increases in preterm newborns. As infants age from term to six months, the proportion of REM sleep decreases, which may reduce the risk of abnormal sleep-related events. Clinicians must be aware of these developmental changes in sleep patterns to effectively manage issues such as apparent life-threatening events (ALTE), sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), and cardiorespiratory responses to respiratory disorders. While there is a wealth of knowledge on the effects of sleep on respiratory and cardiac control in the first months of life, there is a dearth of data on late infancy and early childhood. This review aims to synthesize available data on the impact of sleep on ventilatory mechanics, including the upper airways and chest wall, ventilation and apnea, gas exchange, chemoreceptor function, and arousal responses, as well as changes in heart rate and heart rate variability, and the occurrence and mechanisms of bradycardia.

title: A Common Signal Patch Drives AP-1 Protein-dependent Golgi Export of Inwardly Rectifying Potassium Channels.
text: Nearly all members of the inwardly rectifying potassium (Kir) channel family share a unique cytoplasmic domain structure that serves as an AP-1 clathrin adaptor-dependent Golgi export signal in one channel, Kir2.1 (KCNJ2). This raises the question of whether Kir channels have a common mechanism for Golgi export. To investigate, we compared two structurally and functionally diverse Kir family members, Kir2.3 (KCNJ4) and Kir4.1/5.1 (KCNJ10/16), which have 50% amino acid identity. Our findings reveal that Golgi export of both channels is blocked upon siRNA-mediated knockdown of the AP-1 γ subunit, consistent with a common AP-1-dependent trafficking mechanism. Using a comprehensive mutagenic analysis guided by homology mapping in atomic resolution models of Kir2.1, Kir2.3, and Kir4.1/5.1, we identified a common structure that serves as a recognition site for AP-1 binding and governs Golgi export. This signal, larger than previously thought, involves a patch of hydrophobic residues from the C-terminal region that form a hydrophobic cleft, an adjacent cluster of basic residues within the N terminus, and a potential network of salt bridges that join the N- and C-terminal poles together. Our findings demonstrate a new proteostatic mechanism that couples protein folding of channels to forward trafficking in the secretory pathway.

title: Statins in the treatment of polycythaemia vera and allied disorders: an antithrombotic and cytoreductive potential?
text: Thrombohaemorrhagic complications pose significant clinical challenges in patients afflicted by the classical chronic Ph-negative myeloproliferative disorders (CMPDs), specifically polycytaemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythaemia (ET), and idiopathic myelofibrosis (IMF). These disorders are characterized by clonal myeloproliferation, myeloaccumulation, and an increased risk of developing myelofibrosis and neoangiogenesis in both the bone marrow and spleen.atabase studies have revealed the anti-thrombotic, anti-proliferative, pro-apoptotic, and anti-angiogenic effects of statins, which are translated into potential clinical benefits in patients with CMPDs through statin therapy.

title: Metabolic analysis of senescent human fibroblasts reveals a role for AMP in cellular senescence.
text: Cellular senescence is widely recognized as a crucial tumor-suppressive mechanism in mammals, and various oncogenic insults, such as ras proto-oncogene activation, can initiate this program. Although it is known that the senescence program is characterized by the upregulation of cell-cycle regulators like p16INK4A and p21CIP-1, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In the context of stress-induced premature senescence, reactive oxygen species (ROS) have been suggested to play a key role in the phenotype. Additionally, alterations in cellular carbohydrate metabolism have been implicated in oncogenic transformation, with the most well-documented example being aerobic glycolysis. However, little is known about the specific metabolic pathways involved in these processes. To investigate this, we analyzed age-dependent changes in cellular carbohydrate metabolism in human fibroblasts undergoing in vitro senescence. Our findings reveal that senescent fibroblasts exhibit a metabolic imbalance, characterized by a severe reduction in ribonucleotide triphosphates (RTPs), including ATP, which are essential for nucleotide biosynthesis and proliferation. ATP depletion in senescent fibroblasts is attributed to dysregulation of glycolytic enzymes, resulting in a significant increase in cellular AMP. Notably, this AMP accumulation leads to premature senescence, suggesting that metabolic regulation plays a critical role in cellular senescence and tumor suppression.

title: Identification of an H2-M3-restricted Listeria epitope: implications for antigen presentation by M3.
text: Through expression cloning, we have identified an H2-M3-restricted epitope on the intracellular bacterial pathogen Listeria monocytogenes. A picomolar concentration of an amino-terminal N-formylated hexapeptide, fMIGWII, effectively targeted cells for lysis by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, while the non-formylated peptide was approximately 100-fold less active. The 185-amino acid protein sequence of this epitope predicts a transmembrane protein with its N-terminal region retaining its structure and adopting an N(out)-C(in) topology. This membrane orientation provides an explanation for the protection of the epitope from deformylases present in the bacterial cell and suggest an explanation for the ability of phagocytes to present H2-M3-restricted bacterial epitopes via a vacuolar TAP-independent mechanism.

title: High-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomographic imaging of cortical and trabecular bone microarchitecture in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
text:
In this study, high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT) was used to evaluate the microarchitecture and biomechanics of the peripheral skeleton in female patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). The study aimed to investigate the potential reasons behind the higher incidence of fragility fractures in T2DM patients, despite normal or elevated bone mineral density (BMD).
The study was a cross-sectional design conducted in patients with T2DM recruited from a diabetic outpatient clinic. A total of 19 elderly female patients with T2DM and 19 age- and height-matched controls were included in the study. HR-pQCT was used to measure bone density, cross-sectional geometry, trabecular and cortical microarchitecture, and compressive mechanical properties at the distal radius and tibia.
Compared to the controls, the T2DM cohort had higher trabecular volumetric BMD adjacent to the cortex and higher trabecular thickness in the tibia. However, the cortical porosity differences were significant in the radius, indicating impaired bone strength. Moreover, pore volume approached significance in the tibia. These findings suggest that T2DM may be associated with impaired resistance to bending loads due to inefficient redistribution of bone mass, characterized by loss of intracortical bone offset by an elevation in trabecular bone density.
In conclusion, the results of this pilot investigation provide a potential explanation for the elevated fracture incidence in patients with T2DM. The findings suggest that T2DM may impair the ability of bone to withstand bending loads, leading to an increased risk of fractures. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings and to explore the underlying mechanisms.

title: Critical role of CD28 in protective immunity against Salmonella typhimurium.
text: Efficient T cell activation needs both T cell receptor (TCR) signals and costimulatory signals. CD28 is one of the molecules that provide costimulatory signals for T cells. We used mice lacking CD28 expression (CD28-/- mice) to investigate its role in the immune response to the intracellular bacterium Salmonella typhimurium, which causes murine typhoid fever. CD28-/- mice were highly susceptible to infection with wild-type S. typhimurium and even failed to control infection with attenuated aroA- S. typhimurium. Further analysis revealed that CD28-/- animals did not produce a T-dependent antibody response and were severely impaired in the production of interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma). Therefore, CD28-mediated cosignaling is essential for immunity against S. typhimurium. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate a crucial role for CD28 in protective immunity against an intracellular microbial pathogen.

title: D3 phosphoinositides and outside-in integrin signaling by glycoprotein IIb-IIIa mediate platelet actin assembly and filopodial extension induced by phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate.
text: Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) triggers the disclosure of a limited number of the rapidly growing (barbed) ends of actin filaments in human blood platelets, leading to the slow and gradual assembly and extension of filopodia. This response is triggered by immunological disturbances in the glycoprotein (GP) IIb-IIIa integrin, and is sensitive to the inhibitor wortmannin. Platelets lacking the GPIIb-IIIa integrin or with this integrin's function impaired by calcium chelation or the peptide RGDS have reduced responsiveness to PMA. The effects of PMA differ from those of >/=5 microM thrombin receptor-activating peptide (TRAP), which triggers rapid and massive actin assembly and lamellar and filopodial extension. However, we found that wortmannin can inhibit filopod formation when the thrombin receptor is activated using suboptimal doses (<1 microM) of TRAP. In addition, phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate inhibits actin filament severing and capping by human gelsolin in vitro. Our findings suggest that D3 polyphosphoinositides and integrin signaling are involved in PMA-stimulated platelet activation, and that D3-containing phosphoinositides generated in response to protein kinase C activation and GPIIb-IIIa signaling serve as late-acting intermediates in filopodial actin assembly.

title: `Gain of function' phenotype of tumor-derived mutant p53 requires the oligomerization/nonsequence-specific nucleic acid-binding domain
text: Mutant p53 proteins can activate the transcription of genes involved in cell proliferation, without using the wild-type p53 DNA-binding site. To investigate the domain requirements for this transactivation, we analyzed the ability of mutant p53 to activate the promoters of human epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), multiple drug resistance 1 (MDR-1), and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) genes. We also identified the structural domain responsible for the "gain of function" property of mutant p53-281G. "Gain of function" was measured by assessing the tumorigenicity of 10,000 murine cells expressing mutant p53 constitutively. We generated internal deletion mutants of p53-281G deleting conserved domains I, II, III, IV, and V, as well as one mutant that eliminates amino acids 100-300, which removes four of the five conserved domains (II-V). Another mutant, p53-281G del 393-327, deletes the oligomerization and non-sequence-specific nucleic acid-binding domains of p53. Our results show that all of these mutants have significantly reduced transactivation ability on the EGFR and MDR-1 promoters, but they significantly activate the PCNA promoter, suggesting that the mechanism of transactivation on the PCNA promoter is different from that of the EGFR and MDR-1 promoters. Notably, the deletion mutant p53-281G del 393-327 was found to be defective in inducing tumor formation in nude mice, despite being constitutively expressed in 10,000 cells, indicating that structural domains near the C-terminus are necessary for "gain of function".

title: Banana contains a diverse array of endogenous badnaviruses.
text: Banana streak disease is caused by multiple badnavirus species, with Banana streak Obino l'Ewai virus being one of the most harmful. This virus has hindered international banana (Musa spp.) breeding programs, as newly developed hybrids are often infected, limiting their potential for further exploitation. It is believed that the virus integrates into the nuclear genome of Musa balbisiana (B genome), one of the wild banana species that contributes to many cultivars grown today. To investigate whether the DNA of other badnavirus species is integrated into the Musa genome, researchers PCR-amplified DNA fragments from Musa acuminata, M. balbisiana, and Musa schizocarpa, as well as the 'Obino l'Ewai' and 'Klue Tiparot' cultivars, and sequenced 103 clones. The results showed remarkable variation, with 36 distinct sequences identified that had less than 85% nucleotide identity to each other. There was no commonality in the sequences amplified from M. acuminata and M. balbisiana, suggesting that integration occurred after these species diverged. Analysis of the rates of non-synonymous and synonymous substitution revealed that the integrated sequences evolved under a high degree of selective constraint, consistent with a living badnavirus. Each distinct sequence is thought to have resulted from an independent integration event.

title: Pregnancy in women with type 1 diabetes: have the goals of St. Vincent declaration been met concerning foetal and neonatal complications?
text:
Objective:
In 1989, the St. Vincent Declaration set a five-year target to match outcomes of pregnancies in women with diabetes to those of the general population. Our study aimed to evaluate if this goal has been met by assessing the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes (T1DM).
Methodology:
We analyzed 12 population-based studies that were published in the last 10 years, incorporating 14,099 women with T1DM and 4,035,373 women from the general population. The prevalence of four foetal and neonatal complications was compared between the two groups.
Results:
Compared to the general population, women with T1DM had a higher risk of congenital malformations (5.0% vs. 2.1%, relative risk [RR] = 2.4), perinatal mortality (2.7% vs. 0.72%, RR = 3.7), preterm delivery (25.2% vs. 6.0%, RR = 4.2), and delivery of large for gestational age infants (54.2% vs. 10.0%, RR = 4.5). Early pregnancy HbA1c was positively associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes.
Conclusion:
Our findings indicate that the goal of the St. Vincent Declaration has not been achieved, as women with T1DM are still at a higher risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes compared to the general population. Efforts to improve pregnancy outcomes in women with T1DM are needed to meet the goals of the St. Vincent Declaration.

title: BP control and left ventricular hypertrophy regression in children with CKD.
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between blood pressure (BP) and left ventricular hypertrophy in children with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Using data from the Chronic Kidney Disease in Children cohort, we prospectively analyzed 478 subjects and found that hypertension in adult patients is linked to the development of left ventricular hypertrophy. However, the association between BP and left ventricular hypertrophy in children with CKD has not been conclusively determined.
To assess the relationship between BP and left ventricular hypertrophy, we measured BP annually and obtained echocardiograms every 2 years. Using linear mixed models, we found that predictors of left ventricular mass index included systolic BP, anemia, and use of antihypertensive medications other than angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers. Additionally, predictors of left ventricular hypertrophy included systolic BP, female sex, anemia, and use of other antihypertensive medications.
Over a period of 4 years, the adjusted prevalence of left ventricular hypertrophy decreased from 15.3% to 12.6% in a systolic BP model and from 15.1% to 12.6% in a diastolic BP model. These findings suggest that a decline in BP may predict a decline in left ventricular hypertrophy in children with CKD, and indicate additional factors that warrant further investigation as predictors of left ventricular hypertrophy in these patients.
In conclusion, our study suggests that hypertension in adult patients with CKD is associated with left ventricular hypertrophy, but the association between BP and left ventricular hypertrophy in children with CKD is not yet conclusively established. Further investigation is needed to identify the factors that predict left ventricular hypertrophy in these patients.

title: Nicotinic Acid Adenine Dinucleotide 2'-Phosphate (NAADP) Binding Proteins in T-Lymphocytes.
text: NAADP (nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate) acts as a messenger to regulate calcium release from intracellular acidic stores. Despite the identification of several channels involved in NAADP-mediated calcium signaling, the NAADP receptor itself remains unidentified. To study NAADP binding proteins, we employed the photoaffinity probe [32P]-5-azido-NAADP ([32P]-5-N3-NAADP) in Jurkat T-lymphocyte extracts. [32P]-5-N3-NAADP photolabeling of Jurkat S100 cytosolic fractions led to the labeling of at least ten distinct proteins, with some showing selectivity for NAADP. Interestingly, certain S100 proteins demonstrated a biphasic response to NAADP, peaking at 100 nM with a five-fold increase, while others were stimulated by low concentrations of unlabeled NAADP. No such response was observed with structurally similar NADP. The photolabeled S100 proteins were successfully resolved using two-dimensional gel electrophoresis. Similarly, when the P100 membrane fraction from Jurkat cells was examined, a 22/23 kDa doublet and a 15 kDa protein were selectively labeled, while NAADP did not increase the labeling of any P100 proteins. Overall, [32P]-5-N3-NAADP photolabeling and two-dimensional electrophoresis represent a promising approach for identifying and characterizing NAADP binding proteins.

title: Loss of subcellular lipid transport due to ARV1 deficiency disrupts organelle homeostasis and activates the unfolded protein response.
text: The ARV1-encoded protein facilitates the transport of sterols from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the plasma membrane. In yeast ARV1 mutants, multiple lipids accumulate in the ER, resulting in sensitivity to drugs that modulate sterol and sphingolipid metabolism. Using fluorescent and electron microscopy, we observed an increase in sterol accumulation, ER membrane expansion, lipid droplet formation, and vacuolar fragmentation in ARV1 mutants. Motif-based regression analysis of ARV1 deletion transcript profiles revealed activation of Hac1p, an integral component of the unfolded protein response (UPR). Consistently, we found constitutive splicing of HAC1 transcripts, induction of a UPR reporter, and elevated expression of UPR targets in ARV1 mutants. The UPR sensor IRE1, present in the ER lumen, exhibited a lethal genetic interaction with ARV1, indicating a requirement for the UPR in cells lacking ARV1. Surprisingly, ARV1 mutants containing a defective variant of Ire1p that cannot sense unfolded proteins were viable. These cells also displayed constitutive HAC1 splicing that interacted with DTT-induced disruption of protein folding. Our findings suggest that a portion of UPR induction in arv1Δ strains is distinct from protein misfolding. Decreased ARV1 expression in murine macrophages resulted in UPR induction, particularly up-regulation of activating transcription factor-4 (CHOP), CHOP (C/EBP homologous protein), and apoptosis. Cholesterol loading or inhibition of cholesterol esterification further elevated CHOP expression in ARV1 knockdown cells. Therefore, loss or down-regulation of ARV1 disrupts membrane and lipid homeostasis, leading to a breach in ER integrity, which in turn triggers the UPR.

title: IL-28, IL-29 and their class II cytokine receptor IL-28R
text: Cytokines play a crucial role in regulating the innate and adaptive immune systems. In our investigation of the human genome, we discovered a group of three cytokines, designated interleukin 28A (IL-28A), IL-28B, and IL-29, that are distantly related to type I interferons (IFNs) and the IL-10 family. Our research revealed that these cytokines, like type I IFNs, are produced in response to viral infection and exhibit antiviral activity. However, they interact with a heterodimeric class II cytokine receptor composed of IL-10 receptor β (IL-10Rβ) and an orphan class II receptor chain, designated IL-28Rα. This newly identified cytokine family may serve as an alternative to type I IFNs in defending against viral infections.

title: High-dose recombinant tumor necrosis factor alpha in combination with interferon gamma and melphalan in isolation perfusion of the limbs for melanoma and sarcoma.
text:
In this study, the researchers aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of combining three agents - recombinant tumor necrosis factor alpha (rTNF alpha), recombinant interferon gamma (rIFN-gamma), and melphalan - in isolation limb perfusion (ILP) for in-transit melanoma and recurrent sarcoma metastases. The triple combination was chosen based on previous studies showing a synergistic antitumor effect of these agents.
Twenty-three patients received a total of 25 ILPs with the triple combination, with 19 females and four males involved in the study. The patients had either multiple progressive in-transit melanoma metastases (stage IIIa or IIIab) or recurrent soft tissue sarcoma. The rTNF alpha was injected as a bolus into the arterial line during ILP, and the total dose ranged between 2 and 4 mg, administered under hyperthermic conditions (40°C to 40.5°C) for 90 minutes. rIFN-gamma was given subcutaneously (SC) on days -2 and -1 and in the perfusate, along with rTNF alpha at a dose of 0.2 mg. Melphalan (Alkeran) was administered in the perfusate at 40 micrograms/mL.
During three ILPs in a pilot study, two severe toxicities were observed, including severe hypotension and transient oliguria, and moderate hypotension lasting for 4 hours followed by severe kidney failure with complete recovery. However, in all 18 ILPs performed in the triple combination protocol, patients received continuous infusion dopamine at 3 micrograms/kg/min from the start of ILP and for 72 hours, and only mild hypotension and transient chills and temperature were observed. Regional toxicity attributable to rTNF alpha was minimal. Hematologic toxicity consisted of neutropenia (one grade 4 and one grade 3) and neutropenia with thrombocytopenia (one grade 4 and three grade 2). Eleven patients had been previously treated with melphalan in ILP or cisplatin.
Of the 23 patients, 21 had complete responses (CRs), with response rates ranging from 4 to 29 months (89%), and two had partial responses (PRs) with response times ranging from 2 to 3 months. Overall disease-free survival and survival rates were 70% and 76%, respectively, at 12 months. The softening of nodules was obvious within 3 days after ILP, and time to definite response ranged between days 5 and 30.
In conclusion, this phase II study suggests that high-dose rTNF alpha can be administered safely by ILP with dopamine and hyperhydration for in-transit melanoma and sarcoma metastases. The combination of rTNF alpha, rIFN-gamma, and melphalan demonstrates high efficacy with minimal toxicity, even after failure of prior therapy with melphalan alone.

title: Methanosphaera stadtmaniae gen. nov., sp. nov.: a species that forms methane by reducing methanol with hydrogen
text:
Methanosphaera stadtmaniae is a microorganism that lacks mobility and has a spherical shape. It obtains energy for growth by reducing methanol to methane using hydrogen. Unlike other methanogenic organisms, it cannot produce methane from hydrogen and carbon dioxide, formate, acetate, or methylamines. Additionally, it cannot grow in the presence of hydrogen and carbon monoxide, nitrate, fumarate, sulfate, or choline. Its optimal pH range is 6.5 to 6.9, and its optimal temperature range is between 36°C and 40°C.
Methanosphaera stadtmaniae is not affected by bile salts, inhibitors of folic acid coenzyme synthesis, cephalothin, or clindamycin. However, it is inhibited by metronidazole, bacitracin, monensin, lasalocid, or bromoethanesulfonate. It requires acetate, carbon dioxide, isoleucine, ammonium, and thiamin for growth, and biotin has a stimulatory effect. This organism does not contain cytochromes, and the mol % G+C of its DNA is 25.8. The composition of its cell wall and 16S rRNA, as well as its immunological fingerprint, indicate that it belongs to a new genus within the Methanobacteriaceae family. The type strain of Methanosphaera stadtmaniae is found in the human large intestine.

title: Generation of induced pluripotent stem cells from Asian patients with chronic neurodegenerative diseases.
text: Induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells derived from disease patients offer a valuable resource for biomedical research and may provide a source for replacement therapies. In this study, we generated iPS cells from Asian patients with chronic degenerative diseases of the nervous system, including spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), Parkinson disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) by introducing four factors (KLF4, SOX2, OCT4, and c-MYC). All of the iPS cells displayed pluripotency similar to that of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and were able to differentiate into various somatic cell types in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, the iPS cells can be committed to differentiate into neural cells, the cell type affected in chronic degenerative diseases. This patient-specific iPS cell line provides a valuable tool for investigating disease mechanisms, discovering and testing new drugs, and developing innovative therapies for chronic neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Embryonic-like stem cell derived from adult bone marrow: immature morphology, cell surface markers, ultramicrostructure and differentiation into multinucleated fibers in vitro.
text: Embryonic-like stem cell (ELSC) isolated from bone marrow may be a better candidate for cell therapy of degenerative muscular disease compared to mesenchymal stem cell (MSC), due to their distinct characteristics. We compared the differences in ELSC and MSC derived from bone marrow by isolating and analyzing their cellular properties. Our results showed that ELSC could be successfully isolated from three adult bone marrow samples using a serum-free medium supplemented with basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF). In contrast, MSC could also be isolated from the same samples using DMEM/F12 medium containing 10% new cattle serum. The ELSC were found to be smaller in size and had a more immature morphology than MSC. Additionally, ELSC exhibited lower expression of Oct-4, Nanog-3, and Sox-2 compared to MSC. Interestingly, both ELSC and MSC could be induced into long, multinucleated fibers expressing myogenin and myosin heavy chain (MHC) in myogenic differentiation medium, but by day 10, the proportion of multinucleated fibers positive for MHC was significantly higher in ELSC (25.0%+/-6.9%) compared to MSC (13.8%+/-7.6%). These findings suggest that ELSC represent an ideal candidate for cell therapy of degenerative muscular disease due to their enhanced myogenic potential.

title: Kinetic evidence for rapid oxidation of (-)-epicatechin by human myeloperoxidase.
text: Researchers have discovered that apocynin needs to be converted into another compound, called "metabolites," in order to stop NADPH oxidase in white blood cells. (-)-Epicatechin, a type of flavan-3-ol found in certain foods, is thought to be a "pretend drug" that helps create these apocynin-like metabolites. (-)-Epicatechin can also increase the amount of nitric oxide in cells, which can help reduce inflammation. Scientists tested how well (-)-epicatechin works as a substrate for an enzyme called myeloperoxidase (MPO). They used a special technique called multi-mixing stopped-flow to see how quickly (-)-epicatechin was converted into other compounds by MPO. They found that (-)-epicatechin was one of the most efficient substances for triggering the action of heme peroxidases, a type of enzyme. The scientists estimated that the rate of (-)-epicatechin being converted into other compounds by MPO was about 1.9 x 10(7) molecules per second and 4.5 x 10(6) molecules per second at a temperature of 25 degrees Celsius and a pH of 7. These findings suggest that (-)-epicatechin can quickly be converted into apocynin-like metabolites by MPO.

title: Using the yeast gene deletion collection to customize gene expression.
text: Despite the relative ease of genome manipulation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, researchers are constantly seeking new and improved methods for substituting yeast promoters. Replacing a gene's native promoter with a heterologous promoter of choice allows for regulated expression and simplifies the task of determining functional relevance. Although various clever chromosomal insertion strategies have been described over the years, the launch of the S. cerevisiae Genome Deletion Project offers an impressive resource for a streamlined workflow. The strategy, as described by Liko et al. on page 728, is surprisingly straightforward. The genome deletion project resulted in a collection of strains in which a single open reading frame (ORF) is replaced with a Kanamycin resistance module. Although the main objective of the collection is to provide a comprehensive resource of all possible knockouts, the authors note that for any given yeast promoter of interest, there may be a strain in which the ORF of interest is still present.

title: Tyrosine phosphorylation and regulation of the AMPA receptor by SRC family tyrosine kinases.
text: The phosphorylation of AMPA receptors is a crucial mechanism for regulating receptor function and underlies various forms of synaptic plasticity in the central nervous system (CNS). While serine and threonine phosphorylation of AMPA receptors has been well-studied, the role of tyrosine phosphorylation on these receptors remains unexplored. Our study reveals that the GluR2 subunit of AMPA receptors is tyrosine-phosphorylated in both vitro and in vivo settings by Src family tyrosine kinases on tyrosine 876 located near the C terminus. Furthermore, treating cultured cortical neurons with GluR agonists leads to increased phosphorylation of tyrosine 876. Interestingly, the association with GluR2-interacting proteins GRIP1/2 is decreased by tyrosine phosphorylation of GluR2, whereas PICK1 interaction remains unchanged. Additionally, mutating tyrosine 876 completely eliminates AMPA- and NMDA-induced internalization of the GluR2 subunit. These findings suggest that tyrosine phosphorylation of tyrosine 876 on the GluR2 C terminus by Src family tyrosine kinases plays a critical role in regulating AMPA receptor function and may be crucial for synaptic plasticity.

title: tBid induces alterations of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation flux by malonyl-CoA-independent inhibition of carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1
text: Recent studies suggest a close relationship between cellular metabolism and the process of programmed cell death (apoptosis). We have investigated changes in lipid metabolism in permeabilized hepatocytes treated with a truncated form of the protein Bid (tBid) in the presence of caspase inhibitors and exogenous cytochrome c. Using labelled palmitate to measure β-oxidation flux, we found that tBid inhibits the breakdown of palmitate, resulting in the accumulation of palmitoyl-CoA and depletion of acetyl-carnitine and acylcarnitines, which are characteristic of inhibition of the enzyme carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1). Our results also showed that tBid decreases CPT-1 activity through a mechanism that is independent of malonyl-CoA, the primary inhibitor of CPT-1, but dependent on a decrease in cardiolipin. Overexpression of the protein Bcl-2, which can interact with CPT-1, counteracted the effects of tBid on β-oxidation. These findings suggest a model in which tBid-induced metabolic dysfunction leads to the accumulation of toxic lipid metabolites, such as palmitoyl-CoA, which may participate in the apoptotic pathway.

title: CD8+ T cells are activated in an antigen-independent manner in HIV-infected individuals.
text: Chronic HIV-1 infection is characterized by the hyperactivation of T cells, particularly CD8(+) T cells. While the mechanisms behind this activation are poorly understood, we have found that CD8(+) T cells are activated in vivo during HIV-1 replication regardless of their antigen specificity. Cytokines present in untreated HIV-1 infection, such as IL-15, can trigger the proliferation and expression of activation markers on CD8(+) T cells in the absence of TCR stimulation. Additionally, DCs activated by HIV-1 or LPS can stimulate CD8(+) T cells in an IL-15-dependent but antigen-independent manner, and IL-15 expression is highly increased in DCs isolated from viremic HIV-1 patients. These findings suggest that CD8(+) T cells are activated by inflammatory cytokines in untreated HIV-1 patients, regardless of their antigen specificity. This contrasts with CD4(+) T cells, whose in vivo activation seems to be biased towards specificities for persistent Ags. Our observations explain the higher abundance of activated CD8(+) T cells compared to CD4(+) T cells in untreated HIV-1 infection.

title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts promote hepatocellular carcinoma metastasis through chemokine-activated hedgehog and TGF-β pathways.
text: Fibroblasts are abundant in the vicinity of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) tumors, as most HCCs arise in fibrotic or cirrhotic livers. However, the role of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in promoting HCC metastasis remains unclear. Our study revealed that CAFs stimulate the migration and invasion of HCC cells in vitro and facilitate the metastasis of HCC to the bone, brain, and lung in NOD/SCID mice. Using the RayBio human chemokine antibody array, we found that CAFs secrete higher levels of CCL2, CCL5, CCL7, and CXCL16 than peri-tumor fibroblasts. These chemokines differentially regulate the migration and invasion of HCC cells. CCL2 and CCL5 promote migration but not invasion, while CCL7 and CXCL16 enhance both migration and invasion. Furthermore, CCL2 and CCL5 activate the hedgehog (Hh) pathway, while CCL7 and CXCL16 enhance the activity of the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) pathway in HCC cells. Neutralizing antibodies against these chemokines attenuate the effects of CAFs on HCC metastasis and inhibit the activation of Hh and TGF-β pathways in HCC cells. In summary, CAFs promote HCC metastasis by secreting chemokines that coordinate the activation of Hh and TGF-β pathways in HCC cells.

title: Mortality risk in patients with dementia treated with antipsychotics versus other psychiatric medications.
text:
Objective: To compare mortality rates in patients with dementia who started new antipsychotic medication versus other psychiatric medications.
Method: A retrospective, cohort study utilized national Department of Veterans Affairs data from fiscal years 2001-2005 on patients aged 65+ who initiated outpatient psychiatric treatment after a dementia diagnosis (N=10,615). Twelve-month mortality rates were compared between patients taking antipsychotics and those taking other psychiatric medications. The authors employed multivariate models and propensity-scoring methods to control for confounding. Additional analyses included a no-medication group and examination of mortality causes.
Results: Results showed that all groups taking antipsychotics had significantly higher mortality rates (22.6%-29.1%) compared to patients taking nonantipsychotic medications (14.6%). After adjusting for potential confounding factors, the mortality risk for atypical and combined atypical/conventional antipsychotics was similar to that for conventional antipsychotics. In contrast, the mortality risk was significantly lower for nonantipsychotic medications compared to conventional antipsychotics. Within the nonantipsychotic medication group, the adjusted mortality risks for individual classes of medications were significantly lower than the risk for antipsychotics. Despite this, mortality risks did not change over the 12-month study period. Additionally, the proportion of patients taking antipsychotics who died from cerebrovascular, cardiovascular, or infectious causes was not significantly higher than the rate for those taking nonantipsychotic psychiatric medications.
Conclusions: The study found that antipsychotic medications used in patients with dementia were associated with higher mortality rates compared to most other medications used for neuropsychiatric symptoms. The exact cause of this association is unclear and may be due to a direct medication effect or the underlying pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric symptoms that prompt antipsychotic use.

title: Glutathione: overview of its protective roles, measurement, and biosynthesis.
text: This introduction marks the beginning of a special issue dedicated to the mighty glutathione (GSH), the most abundant low molecular weight thiol compound produced within cells. GSH plays a crucial role in protecting cells from harmful oxidation and toxicity, maintaining redox balance, and regulating various cellular processes. The review aims to provide a concise overview of GSH's functions, the sources of oxidants and electrophiles, the mechanisms of oxidant elimination through reduction and electrophile detoxification through conjugation with GSH, as well as methods for assessing GSH levels within cells. Additionally, the review covers GSH synthesis, regulation, and therapeutic approaches that manipulate GSH content. The purpose of this introduction is to offer a brief but comprehensive look at some of the key aspects of GSH metabolism as part of this special issue, which will provide a more in-depth analysis of this essential molecule.

title: A wellness class for inpatients with psychotic disorders.
text: The purpose of this project was to educate inpatients with psychotic disorders, many of whom were taking second-generation antipsychotics, on lifestyle changes they could make to combat weight gain.
