To achieve this, a 30-minute, didactic presentation was given by a medical student and a psychology student under the supervision of the primary investigator to all inpatients on a Veterans Affairs acute inpatient schizophrenia treatment unit. The presentation covered topics such as the health benefits of maintaining an ideal body weight through selecting foods according to the USDA Food Pyramid, determining adequate food portions, choosing healthy meals outside the home, and beginning and adhering to an exercise program. Following the presentation, subjects completed a 13-item quiz to assess their knowledge of food and nutrition before and after the presentation. The results showed that fifty patients completed both the pre- and post-presentation tests, with a mean percentage of correct answers on the pre-test of 85.6%, which increased to 89.3% on the post-test, resulting in a statistically significant difference of 3.7% (t = 2.43, df = 49, p < 0.02). The mean percent of improvement was 6.1%. The study demonstrates that psychotic individuals can benefit from educational presentations about nutrition and a healthy lifestyle, and gain an understanding of basic concepts related to food choices and fitness.

title: Heterochromatin integrity affects chromosome reorganization after centromere dysfunction.
text:
The centromere is crucial for passing on genetic information from one generation to the next on eukaryotic chromosomes. Centromere identity can be regulated through epigenetic changes, which can affect genome stability, the evolution of karyotypes, and speciation. However, researchers don't know much about how problems with the centromere can affect the structure of chromosomes.
To investigate this, researchers studied Schizosaccharomyces pombe, a type of fungus. They found that when the centromere is removed in these fungi, some of the surviving cells develop new centromeres at the subtelomeric region of their chromosomes or form acentric chromosomes that are joined with other chromosomes through the fusion of telomeres. The number of new centromeres formed compared to the number of telomere fusions is lower when genes involved in RNA interference-dependent formation of heterochromatin are inactive.
These findings suggest that the way chromosomes are reorganized can affect the course of karyotype evolution. Heterochromatin, a type of chromatin that is rich in RNA, may play a role in this process.

title: Expansion and deletion of CTG repeats from human disease genes are determined by the direction of replication in E. coli
text: Several inherited neurological and neurodegenerative disease genes are linked to the lengthening of CTG repeats. We demonstrate that the frequency of genetic expansions or contractions in Escherichia coli varies depending on the direction of replication. Large expansions predominate when the CTGs are situated in the leading strand template, whereas deletions are more pronounced when they are oriented oppositely. Most deletions produce predictable-sized product classes. The mechanisms of strand slippage and non-classical DMA structures may explain these observations and relate to expansion-deletion mechanisms in eukaryotic chromosomes for disease genes.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps capture and kill Candida albicans yeast and hyphal forms.
text: Neutrophils engulf and destroy microorganisms through phagolysosomal fusion. Recently, we discovered that activated neutrophils form extracellular fibers composed of granule proteins and chromatin. These neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) degrade virulence factors and kill both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Our findings reveal that Candida albicans, a eukaryotic pathogen, induces NET formation and is susceptible to NET-mediated killing. C. albicans is the leading cause of fungal infections in humans, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. One of C. albicans' major virulence traits is its ability to transition between singular budding cells and filamentous hyphae. Our study shows that NETs kill both yeast-form and hyphal cells, and that granule components are responsible for fungal killing. Overall, our findings indicate that neutrophils trap and kill Ascomyces yeasts by forming NETs.

title: Katanin p60-like1 promotes microtubule growth and terminal dendrite stability in the larval class IV sensory neurons of Drosophila.
text:
The shape of dendrites is a crucial factor in determining neuronal function. However, the mechanisms that control the diverse morphologies of dendrites and the extent to which their function relies on these morphologies are still unclear. We have found that a protein called Kat-60L1 plays a key role in regulating the elaborate dendrite morphology and sensory functions of Drosophila larval class IV dendritic arborization neurons.
Kat-60L1 mutants have reduced sensitivity to noxious mechanical and thermal stimuli, and the class IV dendrite branch number and length are also decreased. These findings suggest a direct connection between the full extent of the dendritic arbor and neuronal function. We observed that Kat-60L1 is required for the formation of dynamic, filopodium-like nascent branches in late larval development, and that mutant dendrites have fewer EB1-GFP-labeled microtubules. Our data suggest that Kat-60L1 increases the number of stabilized microtubules within dendrites to establish terminal branch stability and full arbor complexity.
Interestingly, loss of the related microtubule-severing protein Spastin also reduces the class IV dendrite arbor, but microtubule polymerization within dendrites is unaffected. Conversely, overexpression of Spastin destroys stable microtubules within these neurons, while Kat-60L1 has no effect. Our findings suggest that Kat-60L1 regulates the class IV dendritic arbor through microtubule-related mechanisms distinct from Spastin.
Our studies indicate that multiple pathways are involved in regulating dendritic arbor development, working at different developmental stages. This discovery sheds new light on the complex interplay between neuronal morphology and function, with important implications for our understanding of neurobiology and disease.

title: Update on technical issues concerning complementary feeding of young children in developing countries and implications for intervention programs.
text: This paper offers a revision of the 1998 World Health Organization (WHO)/Unicef report on supplementary feeding. Recent research findings corroborate the guidelines outlined in the original report, but updates in energy and micronutrient requirements for infants and young children result in lower recommendations regarding the frequency and energy density of additional foods. Consequently, the list of "problem nutrients" is revised. Without fortification, the levels of iron, zinc, and vitamin B6 in supplementary foods are often insufficient, and the intake of other nutrients may be deficient in some populations. This highlights the need for strategies to ensure adequate consumption of these essential nutrients, as well as optimizing breast milk intake when additional foods are introduced. The impact of supplementary feeding interventions on child growth has been inconsistent, underscoring the importance of more comprehensive programs. A six-step approach to planning, implementing, and evaluating these programs is recommended.

title: Decrease of learning capacity in offspring with increasing paternal age in the rat.
text: At various ages (2.5, 6, 10, 14, 18, and 22 months), 15 male Wistar rats were randomly mated with 2.5-month-old females. In a separate experiment, 15 male Wistar rats at the age of 2.5 months and 15 at the age of 23 months were simultaneously mated with 2.5-month-old females. The offspring's characteristics, such as litter size, sex ratio, gross external malformations, growth pattern, and mortality in the first 13 weeks of life, as well as reproductive capacity at 13 weeks of age, were evaluated. Additionally, the offspring's spontaneous activity and emotionality were measured using an open field test, and their learning capacity was assessed using an avoidance conditioning test, conducted between 10 and 13 weeks of age. Notably, the offspring's learning capacity, expressed as the percentage of success for male or female, showed a consistent and significant decrease as the father's age increased. However, the impact on females was not the same as that on males. The genetic implications of these findings are discussed briefly.

title: Processing of the beta-amyloid precursor. Multiple proteases generate and degrade potentially amyloidogenic fragments.
text: Proteolytic processing of beta-amyloid precursor proteins (APP) is necessary for the release of the beta/A4 protein and its deposition into the amyloid plaques associated with aging and Alzheimer's disease. In cultured human cells, we investigated the role of acidic intracellular compartments in APP processing. Using acidotropic agents and inhibitors of a specific class of lysosomal proteases, along with metabolic labeling and immunoprecipitation, we found that APP is degraded within an acidic compartment to produce at least 12 COOH-terminal fragments. Nine of these fragments likely contain the entire beta/A4 domain and are potentially amyloidogenic. Treatment with E64 or Z-Phe-Ala-CHN2 inhibited the activities of lysosomal cysteine proteases cathepsins B and L, but did not affect the activities of the lysosomal aspartic protease cathepsin D. Instead, the inhibitors prevented further degradation of the fragments. These findings suggest that large numbers of potentially amyloidogenic APP fragments are generated in an acidic compartment by non-cysteine proteases and are then eliminated within lysosomes by cysteine proteases. Immunoblot and immunohistochemical analyses confirmed that chronic cysteine protease inhibition leads to accumulation of potentially amyloidogenic APP fragments in lysosomes. These results provide further support for the hypothesis that an acidic compartment may play a role in amyloid formation and begin to identify the proteolytic events that may be important for amyloidogenesis.

title: Pharmaceutical Public-Private Partnerships in the United States and Europe: Moving from the Bench to the Bedside
text: To address unmet medical needs and enhance industry competitiveness, regulators in both the US and EU have taken steps to bridge the gap between academic research and patient care. A pharmaceutical public-private partnership (PPPP), a legally binding contract between a private pharmaceutical enterprise and a public or private research university, can be a valuable tool for achieving a more efficient outcome in the highly regulated pharmaceutical industry. By creating a binding contract that respects positive social norms, PPPPs can shift the parties away from an inefficient Prisoners' Dilemma Nash Equilibrium towards the Pareto Optimal Frontier. When combined with careful coordination of interdependent actors, PPPPs can increase the likelihood of successful commercialization by altering the incentives compared to more traditional contracts. As PPPPs are less established in Europe than in the US, this article aims to provide a comprehensive roadmap for universities, private firms, and EU policy makers to create efficient PPPPs that promote for-profit innovation in the pharmaceutical industry in Europe. Additionally, the article suggests amendments to US laws governing the patenting of government-funded technology to prevent unnecessary barriers to the sharing of medical discoveries and research tools. Our analysis combines game theory and law and management approaches to create a comprehensive framework for for-profit PPPPs.

title: Chronic stress and psychological well-being: evidence from Thailand on household crowding.
text: This study investigates the impact of household crowding, a form of chronic stress, on psychological well-being. Using data from a large (n = 2017) random sample of households in Bangkok, Thailand, we find that objective household crowding negatively affects psychological well-being, even after controlling for various background characteristics. This detrimental effect is mediated by subjective crowding, which consistently and directly harms well-being. Moreover, we find no evidence of a gender effect. Interestingly, the effects of objective and subjective crowding are similar across different types of households, including two- and three-generation households and one- and multiple-couple households. We also examine the argument that subjective crowding is merely an effect of psychological well-being, and find that this perspective is not supported by the data. Our findings suggest that chronic household crowding poses a significant threat to psychological well-being, highlighting the importance of addressing this issue in various cultural contexts.

title: Age- and sex-specific genomic profiles in non-small cell lung cancer.
text:
Gene expression profiling may provide valuable insights into the underlying differences in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) outcomes between different age and sex groups. To investigate the clinical relevance of these differences, we conducted a retrospective analysis of 787 NSCLC patients at Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, from July 2008 to June 2009. We used lung tumor samples with corresponding microarray and clinical data to describe patterns of oncogenic pathway activation and tumor biology/microenvironment status in these patients.
Our findings revealed distinct patterns of pathway activation in NSCLC subgroups defined by patient age and sex. In patients younger than 70 years, high-risk patients had the shortest 5-year recurrence-free survival and demonstrated increased activation of the Src (25% vs 6%; P < 0.001) and tumor necrosis factor (76% vs 42%; P < 0.001) pathways compared to low-risk patients. In contrast, high-risk patients aged 70 years or older demonstrated increased activation of the wound healing (40% vs 24%; P = 0.02) and invasiveness (64% vs 20%; P < 0.001) pathways compared to low-risk patients. Similarly, in women, high-risk patients exhibited increased activation of the invasiveness (99% vs 2%; P < 0.001) and STAT3 (72% vs 35%; P < 0.001) pathways, while high-risk men showed increased activation of the STAT3 (87% vs 18%; P < 0.001), tumor necrosis factor (90% vs 46%; P < 0.001), EGFR (13% vs 2%; P = 0.003), and wound healing (50% vs 22%; P < 0.001) pathways. Multivariate analyses confirmed the independent clinical relevance of these pathway-based subphenotypes in women (hazard ratio [HR], 2.02; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.34-3.03; P < 0.001) and patients younger than 70 years (HR, 1.83; 95% CI, 1.24-2.71; P = 0.003). These findings were consistently observed in split sample analyses, suggesting their reproducibility.
In conclusion, our study demonstrates that oncogenic pathway activation status is a valuable predictor of outcomes in NSCLC subgroups defined by patient age and sex. These findings warrant validation in independent patient data sets, which could have significant implications for personalized lung cancer treatment strategies.

title: Amelioration of colitis by genetically engineered murine regulatory T cells redirected by antigen-specific chimeric receptor.
text:
Here is a revised version of the text with some improvements in clarity, readability, and consistency:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Therapeutic application of regulatory T cells (Tregs) for inflammatory diseases is limited by the scarcity of antigen-specific Tregs. To overcome this limitation, we employed chimeric immune receptors that redirect effector T cells (Teff) toward specific antigens, potentially providing a useful therapeutic approach for treating a wide range of diseases. METHODS: To enable the approach in a clinical setting, which requires genetic modification of patient Tregs, we describe a novel protocol for efficient retroviral transduction and 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (TNP)-specific expansion of murine naturally occurring regulatory T cells (nTregs) with a 2,4,6-TNP-specific tripartite chimeric receptor. RESULTS: Transduced Tregs maintained their Foxp3 level, could undergo repeated expansion upon ex vivo encounter with their cognate antigen in a major histocompatibility complex-independent, costimulation-independent, and contact-dependent manner, and specifically suppressed Teff cells. Adoptive transfer of small numbers of the transduced nTregs was associated with antigen-specific, dose-dependent amelioration of trinitrobenzenesulphonic acid colitis in vivo. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that nTregs can be efficiently transduced to express functional, antigen-specific chimeric receptors, which enable specific suppression of Teff cells both in vitro and in vivo. This approach may enable future cell-based therapeutic applications in inflammatory bowel disease and other inflammatory disorders.
Key improvements:
1. Clarified the Background and Aims: The original text jumped directly into the methods without providing sufficient context. I added a brief introduction to the therapy involved, the limitations of current approaches, and the potential benefits of using chimeric receptors.
2. Improved readability: The original text used some technical terms that may be unfamiliar to some readers. I tried to simplify the language and provide definitions for technical terms when necessary.
3. Consistency: Some of the sentences in the original text were quite long and convoluted. I broke them up into shorter, simpler sentences, and used more consistent sentence structures throughout the text.
4. Grammar and punctuation: I corrected some grammatical errors and improved punctuation to make the text more readable.

title: Purification and activation properties of UreD-UreF-urease apoprotein complexes.
text: In vitro assembly of the Klebsiella aerogenes urease nickel metallocenter requires the presence of UreD, UreF, and UreG accessory proteins, and is further facilitated by UreE. Previous studies have shown that the urease apoenzyme exists in both uncomplexed form and as UreD-urease and UreD-UreF-urease apoprotein complexes. This study reveals the existence of a distinct series of complexes composed of UreD, UreF, and urease apoenzyme. These novel complexes exhibit unique activation properties compared to urease and UreD-urease complexes, and are resistant to inactivation by nickel chloride. Additionally, the bicarbonate concentration dependence for UreD-UreF-urease apoenzyme activation is significantly lower than that of urease and UreD-urease complexes. Western blot analyses using polyclonal antibodies against urease and UreD revealed that UreD is masked in the UreD-UreF-urease complexes, likely due to the presence of UreF. Our findings suggest that the binding of UreF modulates the UreD-urease apoenzyme activation properties by excluding nickel ions from binding to the active site until after formation of the carbamylated lysine metallocenter ligand.

title: Coordinate regulation of the IL-4, IL-13, and IL-5 cytokine cluster in Th2 clones revealed by allelic expression patterns.
text: The cytokines IL-4, IL-13, and IL-5 are characteristic of the Th2 subset of effector T cells and are frequently co-expressed. These cytokine genes are located within 140 kb of identical DNA in both mouse and human genomes. By using IL-4-expressing CD4+ T cell clones derived from F1 mice, we identified genetic variations for each of these cytokines and evaluated the parental origin of the cytokine mRNAs. Both monoallelic and biallelic expression was observed for each gene, as well as for an additional gene, IL-3, located over 450 kb telomeric on the same chromosome. In most cases (81%), IL-4 was expressed from the same allele as IL-13 or IL-5. In contrast, there was only 52% concordance of these three cytokines at the allelic level among clones that expressed IL-3. Interestingly, independent expression of the cytokine alleles occurs frequently in T cells, but the clustered locus containing IL-4, IL-13, and IL-5 is subject to coordinated regulation.

title: T-cell activation.
Effect of hydroxyethyl starch on bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass: a meta-analysis of randomized trials.
text:
The goal of this study was to investigate the effects of hydroxyethyl starch on bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass surgery. A meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials was conducted to evaluate how hydroxyethyl starch compares to albumin in terms of postoperative blood loss, reoperation for bleeding, and blood product transfusion. The study included 18 trials with a total of 970 patients.
The results showed that hydroxyethyl starch significantly increased postoperative blood loss by 33.3% compared to albumin, with a 95% confidence interval of 18.2% to 48.3% (P < .001). The risk of reoperation for bleeding was also found to be more than doubled by hydroxyethyl starch, with a relative risk of 2.24 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.14-4.40 (P = .020). Furthermore, hydroxyethyl starch increased transfusion of red blood cells, fresh-frozen plasma, and platelets by 28.4%, 30.6%, and 29.8%, respectively, compared to albumin.
In head-to-head comparisons, no significant differences were detected between hydroxyethyl starch 450/0.7 and 200/0.5. However, insufficient data were available for hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.4 versus albumin. Albumin, on the other hand, showed improvements in hemodynamics. The study found no significant differences in fluid balance, ventilator time, intensive care unit stay, or mortality between hydroxyethyl starch and albumin.
Overall, the study suggests that hydroxyethyl starch increases blood loss, reoperation for bleeding, and blood product transfusion after cardiopulmonary bypass surgery. The study also found that the risks associated with hydroxyethyl starch cannot be mitigated by using lower molecular weight and substitution.

title: Downstream of Mutant KRAS, the Transcription Regulator YAP Is Essential for Neoplastic Progression to Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a aggressive and malignant cancer with poor survival rates, often resulting in KRAS mutations. However, KRAS has remained an untargetable therapeutic site. We discovered that the abundance of YAP mRNA, which encodes Yes-associated protein (YAP), a protein regulated by the Hippo pathway during tissue development and homeostasis, is increased in human PDAC tissues compared to normal pancreatic epithelia. In genetically engineered KrasG12D and KrasG12D:Trp53R172H mouse models, pancreas-specific deletion of Yap halted the progression of early neoplastic lesions to PDAC without affecting normal pancreatic development and endocrine function. Although Yap was dispensable for acinar to ductal metaplasia (ADM), an initial step in PDAC progression, Yap was critically required for the proliferation of mutant Kras or Kras:Trp53 neoplastic pancreatic ductal cells in culture and for their growth and progression to invasive PDAC in mice. Yap functioned as a critical transcriptional switch downstream of the oncogenic KRAS–mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, promoting the expression of genes encoding secretory factors that cumulatively sustained neoplastic proliferation, a tumorigenic stromal response in the tumor microenvironment, and PDAC progression in Kras and Kras:Trp53 mutant pancreas tissue. Our findings identify Yap as a critical oncogenic KRAS effector and a potential therapeutic target for PDAC and potentially other KRAS-mutant cancers.

title: Rho, Rac and Cdc42 regulate actin organization and cell adhesion in macrophages.
text:
The role of Rho family proteins in regulating actin organization in cells of haematopoietic origin, specifically in Bac1.2F5 cells, a CSF-1-dependent murine macrophage cell line, has not been well-studied. However, recent findings suggest that these proteins play a crucial role in the regulation of actin filament-based structures in these cells.
CSF-1 stimulates the proliferation and motility of Bac1 cells, and acts as a chemoattractant. This stimulation leads to the rapid reorganization of actin filaments, resulting in the formation of filopodia, lamellipodia, and membrane ruffles at the plasma membrane, as well as the appearance of fine actin cables within the cell interior. Microinjection of constitutively activated (V12)Rac1 stimulates lamellipodium formation and membrane ruffling, while the dominant inhibitory Rac mutant, N17Rac1, inhibits CSF-1-induced lamellipodium formation and leads to cell rounding. V12Cdc42 induces the formation of long filopodia, while the dominant inhibitory mutant N17Cdc42 prevents CSF-1-induced filopodium formation but not lamellipodia. V14RhoA stimulates actin cable assembly and cell contraction, while the Rho inhibitor, C3 transferase, induces the loss of actin cables.
Bac1 cells have cell-to-substratum adhesion sites containing beta1 integrin, pp125FAK, paxillin, vinculin, and tyrosine-phosphorylated proteins. These "focal complexes" are present in both growing and CSF-1-starved cells, but are disassembled upon injection with N17Cdc42 or N17Rac1. Interestingly, beta1 integrin does not disperse until long after focal phosphotyrosine and vinculin staining have disappeared.
Overall, these findings suggest that Cdc42, Rac, and Rho proteins regulate the formation of distinct actin filament-based structures in Bac1 macrophages, and that Cdc42 and Rac are also involved in the assembly of adhesion sites to the extracellular matrix.

title: Visualizing the function and fate of neutrophils in sterile injury and repair
text: Neutrophils have been linked to harmful effects in various inflammatory conditions, where they can cause tissue damage and ultimately lead to their own demise. However, in the context of a fully healed sterile thermal injury to the liver, neutrophils play a crucial role in facilitating the repair process. These cells not only penetrate the injury site but also perform the essential task of breaking down damaged vessels and creating channels for new blood vessel growth. Once these tasks are completed, they do not die at the injury site or get engulfed by other immune cells. Instead, many of these neutrophils embark on a preprogrammed journey that involves a stopover in the lungs to upregulate the expression of a protein called CXCR4 (C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4) before entering the bone marrow, where they ultimately undergo programmed cell death.

title: The effect of mass screening on incidence and mortality of squamous and adenocarcinoma of cervix uteri.
text:
Objective:
To evaluate the effectiveness of the Finnish national cervical cancer screening program in reducing incidence and mortality rates.
Methods:
Cervical cancer incidence and mortality data were obtained from the Finnish Cancer Registry, covering a period from 1953 when the registry was established to 1991. The screening program, administered by a centralized organization, notifies women aged 30-60 every 5 years for screening.
Results:
The mean incidence of cervical carcinoma in the early 1960s was 15.4 per 10(5) woman-years, which decreased to 2.7 per 10(5) woman-years in 1991. Correspondingly, mortality rates also decreased, from 6.6 to 1.4 per 10(5) woman-years during the same period. However, the reduction in incidence was predominantly observed in squamous cell carcinomas, while the mortality rate due to adenocarcinoma decreased in screened birth cohorts, but the incidence rate remained unchanged.
Conclusions:
The Finnish national cervical cancer screening program has been effective in reducing incidence and mortality rates. Continued implementation of the program is crucial. In the future, more attention should be given to glandular cell atypias in cervical smears, which could potentially lead to a decrease in cervical adenocarcinoma incidence.

title: Role of 5-HT in the regulation of the brain-pituitary-adrenal axis: effects of 5-HT on adrenocortical cells.
text:
Serotonin (5-HT) plays a crucial role in regulating the brain-pituitary-adrenal axis. Specifically, 5-HT controls the activity of hypothalamic CRF neurons and pituitary corticotrope cells through activation of 5-HT1A and (or) 5-HT2A/2C receptor subtypes. 5-HT can also trigger the renin-angiotensin system by stimulating renin secretion and enhancing aldosterone production, primarily through activation of 5-HT2 receptors. Locally, 5-HT produced in the adrenal gland stimulates the secretory activity of adrenocortical cells through a paracrine mode of communication. This presence of 5-HT has been demonstrated immunohistochemically and biochemically in various species, including frogs, rats, pigs, and humans.
In vivo and in vitro studies have shown that 5-HT stimulates corticosteroid secretion in various species, including humans. The type of receptor involved in the mechanism of action of 5-HT differs between species, with 5-HT4 receptor subtype playing a key role in the stimulatory effect of 5-HT on adrenocortical cells in frogs and humans. In rats, the effect of 5-HT on aldosterone secretion is mediated through activation of 5-HT7 receptors. Clinical studies have also revealed that 5-HT4 receptor agonists stimulate aldosterone secretion in healthy volunteers and in patients with corticotropic insufficiency and primary hyperaldosteronism.
Local serotonergic control of corticosteroid production is believed to play a crucial role in the physiological control of the adrenal cortex as well as in the pathophysiology of cortisol and aldosterone disorders.

title: Effect of interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor/cachectin on glucose turnover in the rat.
text: In this study, we investigated the impact of recombinant human interleukin-1 beta (IL-1) and recombinant human tumor necrosis factor alpha/cachectin (TNF) on glucose metabolism in healthy rats. We used a primed constant infusion of D-(6-3H)glucose and D-[U-14C]glucose to measure glucose kinetics. During the 6-hour isotope and 4-hour monokine infusion, we measured plasma levels of glucagon and insulin and correlated them with changes in glucose metabolism. Our results showed that IL-1 but not TNF modified glucose kinetics, leading to elevated rates of glucose appearance (Ra) and decreased rates of glucose disappearance (Rd). This was associated with increased levels of glucagon and a decrease in the ratio of insulin to glucagon. Moreover, plasma glucose levels were increased early after IL-1 administration, coinciding with the peak in Ra. Our findings suggest that IL-1 induces the utilization of glucose as a substrate, as evidenced by the augmentation of the metabolic clearance rate (MCR) and the percent of flux oxidized by IL-1. In contrast, TNF failed to modify glucose kinetics. Interestingly, TNF-treated rats increased the percent of glucose recycling, but not the total rate of glucose production. These results suggest that endogenous macrophage products, such as IL-1, play a role in the diverse alterations of carbohydrate metabolism seen during injury and/or infection.

title: Human and murine very small embryonic-like cells represent multipotent tissue progenitors, in vitro and in vivo.
text: This study aimed to investigate the developmental lineage progression of human and mouse very small embryonic-like (HuVSEL or MuVSEL) cells in vitro and in vivo. In the laboratory, these cells differentiated into cells from all three embryonic germ layers. In contrast to control cells, HuVSEL cells produced significant amounts of mineralized tissue in calvarial defects. Immunohistochemistry revealed that HuVSEL cells gave rise to neurons, adipocytes, chondrocytes, and osteoblasts within the calvarial defects. MuVSEL cells also demonstrated the ability to differentiate into similar lineages. The first round of serial transplants of MuVSEL cells into irradiated osseous sites showed that approximately 60% of the cells retained their VSEL cell phenotype, while other cells differentiated into multiple cell types at 3 months. However, secondary transplants did not identify the original VSEL cells, indicating limited self-renewal. However, the study did demonstrate VSEL cell derivatives in situ up to 1 year after transplantation without detecting teratomas. These findings suggest that VSEL cells can produce multiple cell structures both in vitro and in vivo, and provide a foundation for future cell-based regenerative therapies for osseous, neural, and connective tissue disorders.

title: High frequency of p16 (CDKN2/MTS-1/INK4A) inactivation in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
text:
The tumor suppressor gene p16 (CDKN2/MTS-1/INK4A) is inactivated through various genetic mechanisms in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC). We examined 29 invasive primary HNSCCs using immunohistochemistry with a newly developed monoclonal antibody (mAb), DCS-50, to evaluate p16 inactivation. Our findings showed that 24 of 29 (83%) tumors lacked p16 nuclear staining by immunohistochemistry. Further analysis revealed that 16 (67%) of these tumors had homozygous deletions, 5 (21%) were methylated, 1 showed a rearrangement at the p16 locus, and 1 had a frameshift mutation in exon 1. Our results indicate that:
1. Inactivation of the p16 tumor suppressor gene is a common feature of squamous cell carcinomas of the head and neck.
2. P16 is inactivated through multiple and distinct mechanisms, including homozygous deletion, point mutation, and promoter methylation.
3. Immunohistochemical analysis for p16 gene product expression is an accurate and relatively simple method for evaluating p16 gene inactivation.
In summary, our study shows that p16 inactivation is a frequent event in HNSCC and can occur through various mechanisms, including homozygous deletion, point mutation, and promoter methylation. Immunohistochemical analysis for p16 expression is a valuable tool for evaluating p16 gene inactivation in HNSCC.

title: Genome-wide RNAi screen of Ca(2+) influx identifies genes that regulate Ca(2+) release-activated Ca(2+) channel activity.
text: Recent research by our team and other groups has demonstrated a crucial and conserved role of Stim in store-operated Ca(2+) influx and Ca(2+) release-activated Ca(2+) (CRAC) channel activity. Using an unbiased genome-wide RNA interference screen in Drosophila S2 cells, we have identified 75 hits that significantly inhibit Ca(2+) influx upon store depletion by thapsigargin. Among these hits, 11 predicted transmembrane proteins, including Stim, are present. One of these proteins, olf186-F, was found to have a profound effect on Ca(2+) entry and CRAC current upon RNA interference-mediated knockdown. When olf186-F was overexpressed, the CRAC current was increased threefold. Interestingly, cotransfection of olf186-F with Stim led to an 8-fold increase in CRAC current and faster development of the current. olf186-F is a member of a highly conserved family of four-transmembrane spanning proteins with homologs from Caenorhabditis elegans to human. The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca(2+) pump sarco-/ER calcium ATPase (SERCA) and the single transmembrane-soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive (NSF) attachment receptor (SNARE) protein Syntaxin5 are also required for CRAC channel activity, consistent with a signaling pathway in which Stim senses Ca(2+) depletion within the ER, translocates to the plasma membrane, and interacts with olf186-F to trigger CRAC channel activity.

title: Wedelolactone induces growth of breast cancer cells by stimulation of estrogen receptor signalling.
text: Wedelolactone, a plant-derived compound, was shown to exhibit anti-cancer activity against breast and prostate cancer cells in vitro and in vivo by targeting multiple cellular proteins, including androgen receptors, 5-lipoxygenase, and topoisomerase IIα. In this study, a novel biological activity of wedelolactone at low concentrations (nM) was discovered. Wedelolactone acts as an agonist of estrogen receptors (ERα and ERβ), as demonstrated by transactivating estrogen response elements (ERE) in cells expressing either ERα or ERβ, and through molecular docking in the ligand binding pocket of both receptors. In breast cancer cells, wedelolactone stimulates the growth of estrogen receptor-positive cells, expresses estrogen-responsive genes, and activates rapid non-genomic estrogen signaling pathways. These effects can be inhibited by pre-treatment with a pure ER antagonist, ICI 182,780, and are not observed in ER-negative breast cancer cells. Therefore, we conclude that wedelolactone acts as a phytoestrogen in breast cancer cells by stimulating both genomic and non-genomic signaling pathways of the ER.

title: Subpopulations of mouse blood monocytes differ in maturation stage and inflammatory response.
text: Blood monocytes serve as well-characterized precursors for macrophages and dendritic cells in humans, and their subsets have been extensively studied in various disease states. In contrast, mouse monocyte subsets have been minimally characterized. Using flow cytometry, we identified three distinct subsets of mouse monocytes based on their expression of Ly-6C, CD43, CD11c, MBR, and CD62L. These subsets share characteristics of extensive phagocytosis, similar expression of the M-CSF receptor (CD115), and transition into macrophages upon M-CSF stimulation. By depleting blood monocytes with dichloromethylene-bisphosphonate-loaded liposomes and monitoring their repopulation, we demonstrated a developmental relationship between the subsets. Monocytes were Maximally depleted 18 hours after liposome application and subsequently reappeared in the circulation, exclusively consisting of the Ly-6C(high) subset, which resembles bone marrow monocytes. serial flow cytometric analyses of newly released Ly-6C(high) monocytes showed that Ly-6C expression down-regulated while in circulation. Under inflammatory conditions induced by acute infection with Listeria monocytogenes or chronic infection with Leishmania major, there was a significant increase in immature Ly-6C(high) monocytes, similar to the inflammatory left shift of granulocytes. Additionally, acute peritoneal inflammation recruited preferentially Ly-6C(med-high) monocytes. In conclusion, these data identify distinct subpopulations of mouse blood monocytes that differ in maturation stage and capacity to migrate to inflammatory sites.

title: Proteogenomics to discover the full coding content of genomes: a computational perspective.
text:
Proteogenomics, a field that intersects genomics and proteomics, has emerged as a powerful tool for identifying and characterizing protein-coding genes. This technology utilizes tandem mass spectra searches against genomic databases to provide valuable information for gene annotation, which can be challenging or impossible to determine using traditional methods. Examples of the insights gained through proteogenomics include confirmation of translation, identification of gene and exon boundaries, evidence for post-translational processing, and prediction of novel genes. To fulfill its potential, proteogenomics must overcome several technological hurdles, such as improving the speed and accuracy of peptide identification, constructing and searching specialized databases, and correcting for sampling biases.
This article reviews the current state of the field, highlighting its achievements and the role of computation in addressing these challenges. We discuss how advances in technology and algorithms have enabled large-scale proteogenomic studies in various model organisms, including Arabidopsis, yeast, fruit flies, and humans. We also preview the field's future directions, including ongoing efforts to tackle complex gene structures, search against genomes of related species, and reconstruct immunoglobulin genes.

title: The in vitro phosphorylation of p53 by calcium-dependent protein kinase C--characterization of a protein-kinase-C-binding site on p53.
text: We demonstrate in vitro that Ca2+-dependent protein kinase C (PKC) phosphorylates recombinant murine p53 protein on several residues located within a conserved basic region of 25 amino acids in the C-terminal part of the protein. Synthetic p53 peptide (357-381) is also phosphorylated by PKC at multiple Ser and Thr residues, including Ser360, Thr365, Ser370, and Thr377. Our findings further reveal that p53 peptide at micromolar concentrations has the ability to stimulate sequence-specific DNA binding by p53. However, this stimulation is lost upon phosphorylation by PKC. To elucidate the mechanisms that regulate PKC-dependent phosphorylation of p53 peptide, we compared the phosphorylation of recombinant p53 and p53 peptide by PKC. Our results suggest that the phosphorylation of full-length p53 on the C-terminal PKC sites is highly dependent on the accessibility of the phosphorylation sites, and that a domain on p53 distinct from p53 peptide (357-381) is involved in binding PKC. Consequently, we have identified a conserved 27-amino-acid peptide, p53 peptide (320-346), within the C-terminal region of p53 and adjacent to residues 357-381, that interacts with PKC in vitro. This interaction inhibits PKC autophosphorylation and the phosphorylation of substrates, including p53 peptide (357-381), neurogranin, and histone H1. Conventional Ca2+-dependent PKC alpha, beta, and gamma, as well as the catalytic fragment of PKC (PKM), were similarly susceptible to inhibition by p53 peptide (320-346). However, Ca2+-independent PKC delta was much less sensitive to inhibition. These findings shed light on the in vivo phosphorylation of p53 by PKC.

title: Role of ocular pigment epithelial cells in immune privilege
text: The eye's microenvironment is both immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory, with pigment epithelial (PE) cells playing a crucial role. PE cells isolated from the eye have the ability to suppress T cell receptor-mediated activation of T cells and the induction of regulatory T cells in vitro, due to their capacity to produce inhibitory cell-surface and soluble molecules such as CD86 (B7-2), transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, thrombospondin-1, programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1/B7-H1), and cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen 2α. The immunosuppressive properties of cultured ocular PE cells from the iris, ciliary body, and retina can overlap to some extent. Additionally, PE-derived regulatory T cells acquire functions that contribute to immune regulation in the eye. The eye employs multiple strategies to control immune-mediated inflammation, which is known as immune privilege, to prevent extensive damage to bystander cells and potential blindness. This review focuses on the immunosuppressive property and role of ocular PE cells in immune privileged sites.

title: Drug-resistant Salmonella in the United States: an epidemiologic perspective.
text: Salmonellosis poses a considerable health burden in the United States, with over 40,000 reported cases and 500 deaths annually, as well as financial costs exceeding $50 million. Moreover, there is a growing concern about antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella strains, which has significant public health implications. Although the pathway of transmission of the bacteria can be complex, combined epidemiologic and laboratory studies utilizing cutting-edge methods in molecular biology have enabled researchers to trace antimicrobial-resistant Salmonellae back to their source: foods of animal origin. These findings suggest that the antimicrobial drugs to which food animals are exposed create selective pressure that fosters the evolution and persistence of resistant strains.

title: Glutamine-specific N-terminal amidase, a component of the N-end rule pathway.
text: The deamidation of the N-terminal glutamine (Gln) by Nt(Q)-amidase, an N-terminal amidohydrolase, is a key step in the N-end rule pathway of protein degradation. We have detected and purified Ntaq1, the active form of Nt(Q)-amidase, from mouse tissues and analyzed its properties. This enzyme is highly conserved across animals, plants, and some fungi, but has a unique sequence compared to other amidases. Our earlier work in Drosophila revealed that a mutant gene, Cg8253, encoding Nt(Q)-amidase can lead to defects in long-term memory. Other studies have identified protein ligands of the uncharacterized human C8orf32 protein, which we have shown to be the Ntaq1 Nt(Q)-amidase. Surprisingly, recent high-throughput studies have successfully solved the crystal structure of C8orf32 (Ntaq1). Our site-directed mutagenesis and crystal structure analysis indicate that the active site and catalytic mechanism of Nt(Q)-amidase are similar to those of transglutaminases.

title: Brahma-related gene 1-dependent STAT3 recruitment at IL-6-inducible genes.
text: Interleukin 6 (IL-6) is an immune regulation cytokine involved in various cellular processes, including hemopoiesis, proliferation, and tumorigenesis. IL-6 triggers the phosphorylation, dimerization, and nuclear translocation of STAT3, which in turn binds to specific promoters and activates transcription. The yeast-mating type-switching and sucrose-nonfermenting chromatin-remodeling complex, Brg1, is crucial for the recruitment of STAT1 or STAT1/STAT2 complexes to interferon (IFN) targets. We hypothesized that Brg1 might also be necessary for the recruitment of STAT3. In this study, we found that the inducible subset of human IL-6-responsive genes requires Brg1 for their expression. Brg1 is constitutively present at these targets and is necessary for STAT3 recruitment, as well as downstream histone modifications and IL-6-induced chromatin remodeling. Furthermore, IL-6-induced recruitment of STAT3 to the IFN regulatory factor 1 (IRF1) promoter and accompanying mRNA synthesis are Brg1-dependent, despite the fact that STAT1 recruitment to this locus is Brg1-independent. Additionally, Brg1 increased basal expression of interferon-induced transmembrane protein 3 (IFIT3) and interferon-gamma-induced protein 16 (IP-16), as well as basal chromatin accessibility at the IRF1 promoter. Surprisingly, the effect on basal expression was STAT3-independent, as shown through small interfering RNA (siRNA) knockdown. Taken together with previous findings, these data reveal that Brg1 plays a broader role in mediating STAT accessibility at multiple cytokine-responsive promoters, and highlights promoter-specific differences in both the effect of Brg1 on basal chromatin accessibility and on the recruitment of different STAT proteins to the same target.

title: High and low fat consumers, their macronutrient intake and body mass index: further analysis of the National Diet and Nutrition Survey of British Adults.
text:
Objective: To investigate the characteristics of individuals who consume high or low amounts of fat in their diets, specifically in terms of their macronutrient intake and body mass index (BMI).
Design: Reanalysis of data from the Dietary and Nutritional Survey of British Adults. Comparisons were made between groups defined as high and low fat consumers based on 7-day weighed food records, which were considered to be valid for energy intake.
Setting: Data was collected from private households in Great Britain between 1986 and 1987.
Subjects: From a total population of 2197, individuals who were either overweight or underweight, or had an estimated energy intake below 1.2 were excluded. The remaining 1240 subjects were divided into two groups: low fat consumers (6.1% of the total population) and high fat consumers (8.7% of the total population).
Main Outcomes: Macronutrient consumption and BMI.
Results: When the criteria for defining high and low fat groups were changed from fat percentage to fat grams (FATg), 30% of the subjects changed groups. Nutrient intakes differed according to the definition of the groups. High fat FATg group consumed significantly more of all nutrients than the low fat FATg group. However, this was not seen when fat percentage was used, with the high fat group consuming more fat and less carbohydrate. The average BMI tended to be higher in the high fat than the low fat groups, with a particularly large difference observed in the FATg analysis. However, the high fat group contained a wide range of BMIs. Further exploration of BMI in the high fat groups showed that age was the only variable distinguishing individuals in the top and bottom quartiles of BMI.
Conclusions: High and low fat consumers exhibit different characteristics, and these differences are affected by how the groups are defined. High fat consumers tend to have a higher BMI than low fat consumers, but not all high fat consumers are overweight or obese.

title: Quantitative, genome-wide analysis of eukaryotic replication initiation and termination.
text: Many essential aspects of DNA replication, such as the precise locations where synthesis is initiated and terminated, how frequently origins are used, and how fork progression is influenced by transcription, remain poorly understood. By using deep sequencing of Okazaki fragments, we comprehensively document replication fork directionality throughout the genome of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, enabling a systematic analysis of initiation, origin efficiency, fork progression, and termination. Our findings reveal that leading-strand initiation preferentially occurs within a region free of nucleosomes at replication origins. Through the use of a strain that allows early firing of late origins, we demonstrate that replication termination is largely a passive process that does not rely on cis-acting sequences or replication fork pausing. Our analysis of the replication profile reveals that timing is primarily determined by the kinetics of origin firing, allowing us to reconstruct chromosome-wide timing profiles from an asynchronous culture.

title: The murine H19 gene is activated during embryonic stem cell differentiation in vitro and at the time of implantation in the developing embryo.
text: In vitro differentiation of murine embryonic stem cells into embryoid bodies mimics the events that occur in vivo during early embryogenesis. Utilizing this system in conjunction with differential cDNA cloning, we have identified genes whose expression is regulated during early embryonic development. As part of this study, we isolated several cDNA clones, including one that corresponds to the gene H19. This gene is specifically activated in extraembryonic cell types around the time of implantation, suggesting it may play a role at this stage of development. Subsequently, H19 is expressed in all cells of the mid-gestation embryo, with the exception of most cells in the developing central and peripheral nervous systems. Following birth, expression of this gene either ceases or is significantly reduced in all tissues.

title: Localization of Sir2p: the nucleolus as a compartment for silent information regulators.
text: In wild-type budding yeast strains, the proteins encoded by SIR3, SIR4, and RAP1 co-localize with telomeric DNA in a limited number of foci within interphase nuclei. Immunostaining of Sir2p reveals that, in addition to a punctate staining that coincides with Rap1 foci, Sir2p also localizes to a specific subdomain of the nucleolus. This finding is further confirmed through formaldehyde cross-linking and immunoprecipitation with anti-Sir2p antibodies, which demonstrate the presence of Sir2p at both the spacer of the rDNA repeat and at telomeres. In contrast, strains lacking Sir4p exhibit a unique localization pattern of Sir2p and Sir3p, which involves concentration in the nucleolus through a pathway that requires SIR2 and UTH4, a gene involved in yeast longevity. This unexpected localization of Sir2p and Sir3p is surprising, given the known role of silent information regulatory factors (SIRFs) in maintaining rDNA stability and longevity. This discovery defines a new site of action for SIRFs and highlights the complex interplay between different cellular compartments in regulating gene expression and cellular aging.

title: Optogenetics reveal delayed afferent synaptogenesis on grafted human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neural progenitors.
text:
Reprogramming of somatic cells into a pluripotent stem cell state has opened new avenues for cell replacement therapy and disease modeling in various neurological disorders. However, it remains to be seen how well grafted human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) differentiate into functional neurons and integrate into the host circuitry. To address this question, we investigated the functional properties and synaptic integration of hiPSC-derived neurons grafted in an in vitro model of hyperexcitable epileptic tissue (organotypic hippocampal slice cultures, OHSCs) and in vivo in adult rats.
We first differentiated the hiPSCs into long-term self-renewing neuroepithelial stem (lt-NES) cells, which are known to form primarily GABAergic neurons. When differentiated in OHSCs for 6 weeks, lt-NES cell-derived neurons displayed neuronal properties such as tetrodotoxin-sensitive sodium currents and action potentials (APs), as well as both spontaneous and evoked postsynaptic currents, indicating functional afferent synaptic inputs. The grafted cells had a distinct electrophysiological profile compared to host cells in the OHSCs, with higher input resistance, lower resting membrane potential, and APs with lower amplitude and longer duration.
To investigate the origin of synaptic afferents to the grafted lt-NES cell-derived neurons, the host neurons were transduced with Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) and optogenetically activated by blue light. Simultaneous recordings of synaptic currents in grafted lt-NES cell-derived neurons using whole-cell patch-clamp technique at 6 weeks after grafting revealed limited synaptic connections from host neurons. Longer differentiation times, up to 24 weeks after grafting in vivo, revealed more mature intrinsic properties and extensive synaptic afferents from host neurons to the lt-NES cell-derived neurons, suggesting that these cells require extended time for differentiation/maturation and synaptogenesis. However, even at this later time point, the grafted cells maintained a higher input resistance. These data indicate that grafted lt-NES cell-derived neurons receive adequate afferent input from the host brain. Since the lt-NES cells used in this study show a strong propensity for GABAergic differentiation, the host-to-graft synaptic afferents may facilitate inhibitory neurotransmitter release and normalize hyperexcitable neuronal networks in brain diseases, such as epilepsy.

title: Anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody in new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus.
text:
Type 1 diabetes mellitus is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by the destructive action of T lymphocytes on beta cells responsible for insulin production. Prior clinical investigations have demonstrated that continuous immunosuppression can momentarily slow the loss of insulin production. Preclinical studies have suggested that a monoclonal antibody targeting CD3 could both reverse hyperglycemia at onset and induce resistance to recurrent disease.
In this study, we evaluated the efficacy of a non-activating humanized monoclonal antibody against CD3--hOKT3gamma1(Ala-Ala)--on the progressive loss of insulin production in patients with recently diagnosed type 1 diabetes mellitus. Within six weeks after diagnosis, 24 patients were randomly assigned to receive either a single 14-day course of treatment with the antibody or no treatment and were monitored over the subsequent year.
Our findings indicate that treatment with hOKT3gamma1(Ala-Ala) significantly maintained or improved insulin production over a one-year period in nine of the twelve patients in the treatment group, compared to only two of the twelve controls (P=0.01). The treatment effect on insulin responses persisted for at least 12 months after diagnosis. Concomitantly, glycosylated hemoglobin levels and insulin doses were also reduced in the antibody treatment group. More importantly, no severe adverse effects were observed, and the most common side effects consisted of fever, rash, and anemia. Furthermore, the clinical responses were found to be associated with changes in the ratio of CD4+ T cells to CD8+ T cells at 30 and 90 days after treatment.
Our results suggest that treatment with hOKT3gamma1(Ala-Ala) can significantly mitigate the deterioration in insulin production and improve metabolic control during the first year of type 1 diabetes mellitus in most patients. The precise mechanism of action of the anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody may involve direct effects on pathogenic T cells, the induction of regulatory cell populations, or both.

title: Establishment and in vitro differentiation of a new embryonic stem cell line from human blastocyst.
text:
Human embryonic stem cells have the unique ability to proliferate indefinitely in a laboratory dish while maintaining the potential to differentiate into cells from all three embryonic germ layers. These cells offer great promise for studies on gene function, in vitro differentiation, and more. The goal of this study was to establish a new human embryonic stem cell line.
To achieve this, an inner cell mass was removed from a human blastocyst and cultured on mouse embryonic fibroblasts in a specially formulated medium. The established line was evaluated through various methods, including morphological examination, passage number, freezing and thawing, alkaline phosphatase expression, Oct-4 expression, surface marker analysis (using Tra-1-60 and Tra-1-81), and karyotype analysis. Additionally, differentiated cardiomyocytes and neurons were evaluated through transmission electron microscopy and immunocytochemistry.
Our findings reveal the successful derivation of a new human embryonic stem cell line, designated Royan H1. These cells exhibit normal karyotype (XX) and remain undifferentiated in morphology after continuous passaging for over 30 passages. They are also viable after freezing and thawing, and express alkaline phosphatase, Oct-4, Tra-1-60, and Tra-1-81. Importantly, Royan H1 cells can maintain their undifferentiated state when grown on mouse embryonic fibroblast feeder layers, both in the presence and absence of recombinant human leukemia inhibitory factor. Furthermore, these cells can differentiate in vitro into beating cardiomyocytes and neurons in the absence of feeder cells.
In conclusion, our results demonstrate that Royan H1 cells are a newly established human embryonic stem cell line with unique properties and potential applications in various fields of research.

title: Lactate Metabolism in Human Lung Tumors
text: In cultures, cancer cells consume glucose and produce lactate, yet it remains unclear if lactate plays a role in tumor metabolism in living organisms. Previous studies have shown that human non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLCs) utilize glucose in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. We now report that lactate is also a TCA cycle carbon source for NSCLC. In human NSCLC, the presence of high levels of 18fluorodeoxyglucose uptake and aggressive tumor behavior was associated with the greatest lactate utilization. When human NSCLC patients were infused with 13C-lactate, extensive labeling of TCA cycle metabolites was observed. In mice, depleting monocarboxylate transporter-1 (MCT1) from tumor cells eliminated lactate-dependent metabolite labeling, indicating that lactate uptake is mediated by tumor cells. Most strikingly, comparing lactate and glucose metabolism in vivo revealed that lactate's contribution to the TCA cycle far outweighs its contribution from glucose. These findings suggest that tumors, including bona fide human NSCLC, can utilize lactate as a source of energy in vivo.

title: Increased lipid peroxidation as a mechanism of methionine-induced atherosclerosis in rabbits.
text: Methionine is metabolized through the transmethylation/transsulfuration pathway to form homocysteine, which may exert atherogenic effects by various mechanisms, including lipid peroxidation. Accordingly, consuming excessive dietary methionine may lead to the development of atherosclerosis. To investigate this hypothesis, plasma and aortic levels of thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS), as well as activities of aortic and red blood cell superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase (GPX) were measured in rabbits fed a diet rich in 0.3% methionine for 6 or 9 months. Histological examination of aortas was also performed. Feeding rabbits a methionine-enriched diet for 6 or 9 months resulted in significant increases in plasma and aortic TBARS levels and aortic antioxidant enzyme activities, but a decrease in plasma antioxidant activity (AOA) was observed. In red blood cells, SOD activity increased, catalase remained normal, and GPX decreased in the treated animals. Histological examination of aortas revealed typical atherosclerotic changes, such as intimal thickening, cholesterol deposition, and calcification in methionine-fed rabbits. These findings support the idea that a high-methionine diet may induce atherosclerosis in rabbits and suggest disturbances in lipid peroxidation and antioxidant processes as possible mechanisms of its atherogenic influence.

title: Sex differences in sex chromosome gene expression in mouse brain.
text: A pressing question is whether genes located on the sex chromosomes directly influence non-gonadal tissues to produce sex differences in development and function, or whether all sex differences in somatic tissues are induced by gonadal secretions. To investigate this query, we examined whether mouse X-Y homologous gene pairs are expressed in brain in a sex-specific manner. Using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and northern blot analysis, we evaluated mRNA expression in the brains of eight Y-linked genes and their X-linked homologues at three ages: 13.5 days post coitum, the day of birth (P1), and adulthood. Our findings revealed that transcripts of six Y genes were expressed in brain at one or more ages, including Usp9y, Ube1y, Smcy, Eif2s3y, Uty, and Dby. Notably, these genes were also expressed in XY female brain, indicating that they do not require testicular secretions for their expression. In contrast, six X-linked homologues (Usp9x, Ube1x, Smcx, Eif2s3x, Utx, and Dbx) were found to be exclusively expressed in brain, with significantly higher levels of expression observed in female brains compared to male brains, regardless of their X-inactivation status. Interestingly, for five of these gene pairs, the expression of the Y-linked homologue in males was insufficient to compensate for the female bias in X gene expression. Furthermore, we discovered that three X-Y gene pairs (Usp9x/y, Ube1x/y, and Eif2s3x/y) exhibited different patterns of expression in brain, suggesting that they may not be functionally equivalent. These sex differences in X-Y gene expression suggest a range of mechanisms by which these genes may contribute to sex differences in brain development and function.

title: Genome architecture, rearrangements and genomic disorders.
text: An increasing number of human diseases have been found to result from recurrent DNA rearrangements involving unstable genomic regions. These are termed genomic disorders, where the clinical phenotype is a consequence of abnormal gene expression due to the altered dosage of genes located within the rearranged genomic fragments. Both intrachromosomal and interchromosomal rearrangements are facilitated by the presence of region-specific low-copy repeats (LCRs) and occur through nonallelic homologous recombination (NAHR) between paralogous genomic segments. LCRs typically span around 10-400 kb of genomic DNA, share at least 97% sequence identity, and provide the substrates for homologous recombination, making the region prone to rearrangements. Furthermore, it has been suggested that higher-order genomic architecture involving LCRs plays a significant role in the evolution of primate karyotypes, particularly during speciation.

title: painDETECT: a new screening questionnaire to identify neuropathic components in patients with back pain.
text: The goal of this study was to develop and validate a simple, validated screening tool to detect neuropathic pain (NeP) components in chronic low back pain (LBP) patients, and to determine the prevalence of NeP components in a large-scale survey of LBP patients. The research network developed a questionnaire called painDETECT (PD-Q) and validated it in a prospective, multicentre study involving approximately 8000 LBP patients. The results showed that the PD-Q is a reliable screening tool with high sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive accuracy. In an unselected cohort of chronic LBP patients, 37% were found to have predominantly neuropathic pain. Patients with NeP had higher ratings of pain intensity, more severe co-morbidities such as depression, panic/anxiety, and sleep disorders, and poorer quality of life. Based on the prevalence of LBP in the general population, the study estimates that 14.5% of female and 11.4% of male Germans suffer from LBP with a predominant neuropathic pain component. The study demonstrates that simple, patient-based, easy-to-use screening questionnaires can determine the prevalence of NeP components in individual LBP patients and in heterogeneous cohorts of such patients, and that accurate diagnosis is a milestone in choosing appropriate therapy.

title: Scoring of dual fluorescein and ICG inflammatory angiographic signs for the grading of posterior segment inflammation (dual fluorescein and ICG angiographic scoring system for uveitis)
text:
Proposal of a Semiquantitative Dual Fluorescein and Indocyanine Green Angiography Scoring System for Uveitis
Purpose: To develop a scoring system that combines fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography (FA and ICGA, respectively) to assess the progression of uveitis and response to treatment.
Methods: The proposed scoring system was created based on existing FA scoring systems, a standardized ICGA protocol, and schematic interpretation of ICGA findings in posterior uveitis. The scores were assigned based on the impact of each angiographic sign on the appreciation of active intraocular inflammation. To allow for direct comparison between FA and ICGA, the ICGA scores were multiplied by a factor of 2.
 Results: A total maximum score of 40 was assigned to the FA signs, including optic disc hyperfluorescence, macular edema, retinal vascular staining and/or leakage, capillary leakage, retinal capillary nonperfusion, neovascularization of the optic disc, neovascularization elsewhere, pinpoint leaks, and retinal staining and/or subretinal pooling. A total maximum score of 20 was assigned to the ICGA signs, including early stromal vessel hyperfluorescence, choroidal vasculitis, dark dots or areas (excluding atrophy), and optic disc hyperfluorescence.
Conclusion: The proposed combined FA and ICG angiographic scoring system may help assess the magnitude of retinal versus choroidal inflammation, monitor disease progression, and evaluate response to treatment. Further testing in clinical settings and determination of intra- and interobserver variations are needed to validate the system.

title: Improving outcomes of acute kidney injury: report of an initiative
text: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a intricate disorder involving various causative factors and occurring in diverse settings. The disorder presents with a range of clinical manifestations, from minimal elevation in serum creatinine levels to anuric renal failure. To address the complexity of AKI and improve patient outcomes, a multidisciplinary collaborative network, termed the Acute Kidney Injury Network (AKIN), has been established. The AKIN has proposed standardized criteria for diagnosing and categorizing AKI, which will require validation through future studies. The AKIN offers a platform that fosters knowledge acquisition and collaboration, ultimately leading to better patient outcomes.

title: A Screen for Endocytic Motifs
text: Cargo selection into coated vesicles for endocytosis is typically achieved through short linear motifs. Researchers have identified three common motifs for clathrin-mediated endocytosis: YXXPhi, [D/E]XXXL[L/I], and FXNPXY. To discover novel endocytic motifs, scientists generated a library of CD8 chimeras with random sequences in their cytoplasmic tails and used a novel fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-based assay to select for endocytosed constructs. Among the five tails that were most efficiently internalized, only one contained a conventional motif. Two of the tails contained dileucine-like sequences, which appear to be variations of the [D/E]XXXL[L/I] motif. Interestingly, one of the tails contained a novel internalization signal, YXXXPhiN, which was able to function in cells expressing a mutant mu2 that cannot bind YXXPhi, suggesting that it is not a variation of the YXXPhi motif. Similarly, endogenous proteins, including functional YXXXPhiN (in addition to a classical YXXPhi) in cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4), contain similar sequences. Therefore, the repertoire of endocytic motifs is more diverse than previously thought, extending beyond the three well-characterized sorting signals.

title: Microtubule stabilization reduces scarring and causes axon regeneration after spinal cord injury.
text: Hypertrophic scarring and limited intrinsic axon growth potential pose significant challenges for spinal cord repair. These processes are tightly regulated by microtubule dynamics. Notably, moderate microtubule stabilization decreased scar formations after spinal cord injuries in rodents through various cellular mechanisms, including dampening of transforming growth factor-β signaling. It prevented the accumulation of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and made the lesion site conducive to axon regeneration of growth-competent sensory neurons. Microtubule stabilization also promoted the growth of central nervous system axons of the Raphe-spinal tract and led to functional improvements. In essence, microtubule stabilization reduces fibrotic scarring and enhances the capacity of axons to grow.

title: Histone tails: Directing the chromatin response to DNA damage.
text: Substantial investment of energy is devoted to altering large areas of chromatin near DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). Following the formation of DSBs, a diverse array of histone modifications are triggered to create a platform for the inducible and modular assembly of DNA repair protein complexes in the vicinity of the DNA lesion. This complex signaling network is crucial for repairing DNA damage and communicating with cellular processes that occur both nearby and far from the genomic lesion. Failure to properly execute DNA damage-inducible chromatin changes is linked to developmental abnormalities, immunodeficiency, and cancer in both humans and genetically engineered mouse models. This review will discuss the current understanding of DNA damage-responsive histone modifications that occur in mammalian cells, highlighting their role in maintaining genome integrity.

title: Sestrin2 inhibits uncoupling protein 1 expression through suppressing reactive oxygen species.
text: Uncoupling protein 1 (Ucp1), located in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mammalian brown adipose tissue (BAT), generates heat by uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation. When exposed to cold temperatures or excess nutrients, sympathetic neurons stimulate BAT to express Ucp1, leading to increased energy dissipation and thermogenesis. Notably, raised Ucp1 expression leads to reduced obesity in mice and is associated with leanness in humans. Despite the significance of Ucp1 regulation, there is currently limited understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying its expression. This study aims to elucidate the role of Sestrin2 and reactive oxygen species (ROS) in controlling Ucp1 expression. We found that transgenic overexpression of Sestrin2 in adipose tissues inhibited both basal and cold-induced Ucp1 expression in interscapular BAT, leading to decreased thermogenesis and increased fat accumulation. Consistently, BAT from Sestrin2-deficient mice displayed an elevated Ucp1 expression level. Our results indicate that Sestrin2 reduces Ucp1 expression primarily by scavenging ROS. Indeed, treatment with ROS-suppressing chemicals, such as butylated hydroxyanisole and N-acetylcysteine, also inhibited cold- or cAMP-induced Ucp1 expression. Moreover, inhibition of p38 MAPK, a key signaling mediator involved in cAMP-induced Ucp1 expression, was observed in Sestrin2 overexpression or antioxidant treatments. Altogether, these findings suggest that Sestrin2 and antioxidants inhibit Ucp1 expression by suppressing ROS-mediated p38 MAPK activation, highlighting a crucial role of ROS in proper BAT metabolism.

title: The non-catalytic function of XPG protein during dual incision in human nucleotide excision repair.
text: XPG is a member of the FEN-1 structure-specific endonuclease family and has 3'-junction cutting activity on bubble substrates, with the ability to make the 3'-incision in the human dual incision (excision nuclease) repair system. To further investigate the role of XPG in nucleotide excision repair, two specific amino acid residues thought to be involved in DNA binding and catalysis were mutated and the resulting mutant proteins were overproduced using a baculovirus/insect cell system, purified, and characterized. The mutation of amino acid residue D77 had a modest effect on junction cutting and excision activity, resulting in uncoupled 5'-incision by mammalian cell-free extracts. Conversely, the mutation of amino acid residue D812 completely abolished the junction cutting and 3'-incision activities of XPG, but the excision nuclease reconstituted with XPG (D812A) was still able to carry out normal 5'-incision at the 23rd-24th phosphodiester bonds 5' to a (6-4) photoproduct without producing any 3'-incision. These findings suggest that residue D812 is an active site residue of XPG, and that in addition to making the 3'-incision, the physical presence of XPG in the protein-DNA complex is required non-catalytically for subsequent 5'-incision by XPF-ERCC1.

title: A 40-Hz auditory potential recorded from the human scalp.
text: State-of-the-art computer algorithms can decipher the brain's electrical activity in response to sound stimuli, revealing a consistent sequence of brain waves locked in time with the sound. These waves, visible 8-80 milliseconds after the stimulus, demonstrate a distinct pattern resembling 3-4 cycles of a 40-Hz sine wave. This phenomenon, known as the 40-Hz event-related potential (ERP), exhibits intriguing properties. Firstly, it disappears when anesthetized, indicating that adequate processing of sensory information might rely on cyclical brain activity in the 30-50-Hz range, similar to what is observed in the visual and olfactory systems. Secondly, measuring the latency and amplitude of the 40-Hz ERP can provide valuable information on the number and location of auditory nerve fibers that a given tone excites. Thirdly, the response is visible at near-threshold sound intensities, a discovery that could have practical applications in clinical hearing testing.

title: Bile acids: natural ligands for an orphan nuclear receptor.
text: Bile acids influence gene expression related to cholesterol metabolism through mysterious biochemical processes. In the body, small amounts of free and bonded chenodeoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid, and deoxycholic acid activate the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), a nuclear receptor thought to be without a parent molecule (NR1H4). As ligands, these acids and their attachments disrupt FXR's association with a fragment of steroid receptor coactivator 1, leading to evidence of a nuclear signaling pathway involving bile acids and cholesterol metabolism regulation.

title: The yeast ribosomal protein L32 and its gene.
text: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae ribosomal protein gene RPL32 is of particular interest for two reasons: 1) it is located near another ribosomal protein gene, RP29, whose transcription may be regulated by the same control sequences, and 2) RPL32's splicing is believed to be modulated by its own product, ribosomal protein L32. RPL32 has been extensively studied. It is crucial for cell growth, and its sequence suggests that L32 is a protein of 105 amino acids with a basic N-terminus and acidic C-terminus, and is homologous to ribosomal protein L30 in mammals. The reading frame has been confirmed through partial NH2-terminal analysis of L32. The nucleotide sequence predicted an intron of 230 nucleotides, which starts with the unusual sequence GTCAGT and ends 40 nucleotides downstream of the consensus sequence TAC-TAAC. The intron was confirmed through determination of the cDNA clone sequence. Transcription initiates 58 nucleotides upstream of the AUG initiation codon, and the polyadenylation site occurs 100 nucleotides downstream of the termination codon. Regulation of ribosomal protein gene transcription has been linked to two related consensus sequences, and analysis of the intergenic region between RP29 and RPL32 revealed three copies of these sequences. A deletion removing all three sequences reduced synthesis of a L32-LacZ fusion protein by more than 90%, with some residual activity remaining.

title: Derivation conditions impact X-inactivation status in female human induced pluripotent stem cells.
text: Human female induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines exhibit variability in X-inactivation status. The majority of hiPSC lines retain one transcriptionally active X (Xa) and one inactive X (Xi) chromosome from donor cells, but a low frequency of lines produces two Xas. Sporadic epigenetic alterations of the Xi may occur during reprogramming. We show that X-inactivation status in female hiPSC lines is influenced by the derivation conditions. hiPSC lines generated through the Kyoto method (using leukemia inhibitory factor [LIF]-expressing SNL feeders) more commonly exhibit two Xas, while early passage lines generated on non-SNL feeders often retain their original Xa/Xi ratio. Supplementation with recombinant LIF can reactivate some X-linked genes in these cells. Our findings demonstrate that feeders play a significant role in determining X-inactivation status, and the efficient production of Xa/Xa hiPSC lines offers unparalleled opportunities to study human X-reactivation and -inactivation.

title: Loss of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine and ten-eleven translocation 2 protein expression in malignant melanoma.
text: Several recent studies have reported a decrease in 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) levels in various types of cancer, including breast, liver, lung, pancreatic, colon, prostate, brain, and myeloid cancers. In this study, we analyzed benign compound nevi (BCN), dysplastic compound nevi (DCN), superficial spreading melanomas (SSM) with tumor thickness <1 mm and >4 mm, and cutaneous metastatic disease (CMD). We used immunohistochemistry to detect 5hmC, 5-methylcytosine (5mC), and ten-eleven translocation 2 protein (TET2). Our findings showed that the median 5hmC levels were significantly higher in BCN and DCN compared to thin SSM, thick SSM, and CMD. In contrast, 5mC immunoreactivity did not differ significantly between nevi and melanoma. Interestingly, TET2 expression was predominantly weak and was found to be significantly more frequent in nevi than in thin SSM, thick SSM, and CMD.
