Our results suggest that 5hmC levels and TET2 expression are significantly reduced in advanced melanomas compared to nevi and thin melanomas, suggesting a potential role for these epigenetic marks in melanoma development and progression.

title: Estimation of the dietary requirement for vitamin D in healthy adults.
text:
Background: Knowledge gaps have led to disparities in international dietary recommendations for vitamin D. We aimed to determine the range of dietary vitamin D intakes required to maintain serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) concentrations above various proposed cutoffs (ie, 25, 37.5, 50, and 80 nmol/L) during winter after adjusting for the impact of summer sunlight exposure and diet.
Objective: To establish the dietary vitamin D requirements for adults aged 20-40 years to maintain optimal vitamin D status during winter.
Design: A randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind 22-week intervention study was conducted in men and women aged 20-40 years (n = 238) by varying supplemental doses of vitamin D(3) (0, 5, 10, and 15 microg/d) throughout winter. Serum 25(OH)D concentrations were measured using enzyme-linked immunoassay at baseline (October 2006) and endpoint (March 2007).
Results: There were dose-related increases (P < 0.0001) in serum 25(OH)D with increasing supplemental vitamin D(3) intake. The slope of the relationship between vitamin D intake and serum 25(OH)D concentration was found to be 1.96 nmol x L(-1) x microg(-1) intake. The vitamin D intake required to maintain serum 25(OH)D concentrations of >25 nmol/L in 97.5% of the sample was found to be 8.7 microg/d. This intake varied from 7.2 microg/d in those who enjoyed sunshine exposure, 8.8 microg/d in those who sometimes had sun exposure, and 12.3 microg/d in those who avoided sunshine. Vitamin D intakes required to maintain serum 25(OH)D concentrations of >37.5, >50, and >80 nmol/L in 97.5% of the sample were found to be 19.9, 28.0, and 41.1 microg/d, respectively.
Conclusion: Our findings indicate that the range of dietary vitamin D intakes required to ensure optimal vitamin D status in the vast majority (>97.5%) of 20-40-year-old adults, considering a variety of sun exposure preferences, is between 7.2 and 41.1 microg/d.

title: Rapid purification of homodimer and heterodimer HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by metal chelate affinity chromatography.
text: We have manipulated an Escherichia coli vector (p66) to express both 66-kDa HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (p66) and the polyprotein-coded protease simultaneously, resulting in high quantities of both enzymes. However, under these conditions, approximately 50% of the overexpressed p66 reverse transcriptase is processed, leading to the accumulation of large amounts of the p66/p51 enzyme. To facilitate the purification of these enzymes, we added a poly(histidine) affinity label to the amino terminus of the reverse-transcriptase-coding sequence (His-p66). This allows for the simple and rapid purification of milligram quantities of either p66 or p66/p51 enzyme from a crude lysate using metal chelate affinity chromatography. Purified His-p66 and His-p66/His-p51 reverse transcriptase exhibit both reverse transcriptase and RNase H activity. Additionally, we have used metal chelate chromatography to purify a p66/p51 enzyme where only the p66 component is labeled, further supporting the hypothesis that these enzymes exist as a heterodimer.

title: Polyphenols of Cocoa: Inhibition of Mammalian 15-Lipoxygenase
text: Some cocoa and chocolate products contain high levels of epicatechin and related oligomers, known as procyanidins. Fractions of these compounds, isolated from the seeds of Theobroma cacao, showed dose-dependent inhibition of rabbit 15-lipoxygenase-1, with larger oligomers being more active. The decamer fraction had an IC50 of 0.8 M. In contrast, monomeric flavanols, including epigallocatechin gallate (IC50 = 4 M) and epicatechin gallate (IC50 = 5 M), were more potent than ()epicatechin (IC50 = 60 M). ()Epicatechin and procyanidin nonamer also inhibited the formation of 15-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid from arachidonic acid in rabbit smooth muscle cells transfected with human 15-lipoxygenase-1. However, inhibition of the lipoxygenase pathway in J774A.1 cells transfected with porcine leukocytetype 12-lipoxygenase (a representative of the 12/15-lipoxygenase family) occurred only after sonication of the cells, suggesting a membrane barrier for flavanols in these cells. Notably, epicatechin (IC50 approx. 15 M) and the procyanidin decamer inhibited recombinant human platelet 12-lipoxygenase. These findings suggest that flavanols and procyanidins have general lipoxygenase inhibitory potency, which may contribute to their potential beneficial effects on the cardiovascular system in humans. Therefore, they may provide a plausible explanation for recent literature reports indicating that procyanidins decrease the leukotriene/prostacyclin ratio in humans and human aortic endothelial cells.

title: Quality of life in patients with advanced heart failure.
text: Although evaluating the treatment of congestive heart failure typically relies on clinical outcomes, patient self-assessment is increasingly recognized as a crucial component of evaluation. To assess the quality of life of 134 patients with advanced heart failure being evaluated for transplantation, a study used a combination of subjective and objective measures, including functional status, physical symptoms, emotional state, and psychosocial adaptation. Interestingly, there was no correlation between patients' cardiac ejection fraction and any quality-of-life measures. However, the results of a 6-minute walking test, New York Heart Association classification, and self-reported functional status were significantly linked to psychosocial adjustment. In fact, self-reported functional status, depression, and hostility accounted for 43% of the variance in total psychosocial adjustment to illness. These findings advocate for including quality of life as an outcome measure in any evaluation of treatment efficacy and underscore the importance of targeting interventions at reducing depression and hostility while boosting daily activity levels to improve the quality of life of patients with advanced heart failure.

title: Regional vascular resistance during exercise: role of cardiac afferents and exercise training.
text: The goal of this study was to investigate the effect of cardiac vagal afferents on changes in regional vascular resistance during exercise and to examine the impact of endurance exercise training on this effect. We measured regional vascular resistance in 12 rabbits at rest and during running at 12.6 m/min and 20% grade, before and after reversible denervation of cardiac afferents using intrapericardial procainamide HCl (2%). Additionally, these procedures were repeated in five of these rabbits following an 8-week endurance exercise training program. To determine the effects of blocking the efferent innervation on regional vascular resistance during exercise, we instrumented the rabbits with Doppler ultrasonic flow probes around the renal (R), mesenteric (M), ascending, and terminal aortic (TA) arteries. Catheters were positioned in the central ear artery and vein and pericardial sac. Our results showed that exercise significantly increased R (+37 +/- 4%), M (+88 +/- 9%), TA (-62 +/- 6%), and S (-34 +/- 3) resistances. However, blockade of cardiac efferents alone did not have a significant effect on regional vascular resistance during exercise. Combined efferent and afferent blockade resulted in significant increases in R (+62 +/- 6%) and M resistance (+134 +/- 13%) during exercise, while TA (-51 +/- 4%) and S (-27 +/- 2%) resistances remained unchanged. Notably, endurance exercise training significantly enhanced the inhibitory influence of cardiac afferents on R and M regional vascular resistance during exercise.

title: Serum Soluble Corin is Decreased in Stroke.
text:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Corin, a soluble form of corin protein, has been found to be decreased in coronary heart disease. Given the connections between cardiac dysfunction and stroke, circulating corin could potentially serve as a candidate marker for stroke risk. However, the association between circulating corin and stroke has yet to be explored in human populations. Therefore, we aimed to investigate this relationship in patients with ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke and community-based healthy controls.
METHODS: We analyzed serum soluble corin levels and certain conventional risk factors for stroke in 481 patients with ischemic stroke, 116 patients with hemorrhagic stroke, and 2498 healthy controls. Given previous reports of sex-specific differences in corin levels, we evaluated the association between serum soluble corin and stroke in men and women separately.
RESULTS: Our findings revealed that patients with ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke had significantly lower levels of serum soluble corin compared to healthy controls in both men and women (all P values <0.05). Furthermore, multivariate analysis showed that men in the lowest quartile of serum soluble corin were more likely to develop ischemic (odds ratio [OR], 4.90; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.99-8.03) and hemorrhagic (OR, 17.57; 95% CI, 4.85-63.71) stroke than those in the highest quartile. Similarly, women in the lowest quartile of serum soluble corin were also more likely to develop ischemic (OR, 3.10; 95% CI, 1.76-5.44) and hemorrhagic (OR, 8.54; 95% CI, 2.35-31.02) stroke than those in the highest quartile. Notably, the trend analysis revealed significantly increased odds ratios for ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke across the quartiles of serum soluble corin in both men and women (all P values for trend <0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Our study suggests that serum soluble corin levels are diminished in patients with stroke compared to healthy controls. These findings imply that serum soluble corin may have a pathogenic role in the development of stroke. Further research is warranted to validate these findings and explore the potential mechanisms underlying the observed associations.

title: Topical application of chlorhexidine to neonatal umbilical cords for prevention of omphalitis and neonatal mortality in a rural district of Pakistan: a community-based, cluster-randomised trial.
text:
In low-resource areas where home deliveries are common, umbilical cord infection (omphalitis) is a significant risk factor for neonatal sepsis and mortality. To assess the effectiveness of umbilical cord cleansing with 4% chlorhexidine (CHX) solution, with or without handwashing with antiseptic soap, on the incidence of omphalitis and neonatal mortality, we conducted a two-by-two factorial, cluster-randomised trial in Dadu, a rural area of Sindh province, Pakistan.
We randomly allocated 187 clusters to one of four study groups: CHX solution with soap and educational messages promoting handwashing, CHX solution only, handwashing only, and standard dry cord care in the control group. A total of 9741 newborn babies delivered by participating traditional birth attendants (TBAs) were enrolled in the study.
Our findings showed a significant reduction in the risk of omphalitis with CHX application (RR=0·58, 95% CI 0·41-0·82; p=0·002), but no evidence of an effect of handwashing promotion on omphalitis risk (RR=0·83, 0·61-1·13; p=0·24). Additionally, we found a significant reduction in neonatal mortality in neonates who received CHX cleansing (RR=0·62, 95 % CI 0·45-0·85; p=0·003), but no evidence of an effect of handwashing promotion on neonatal mortality (RR=1·08, 0·79-1·48; p=0·62). We recorded no serious adverse events during the study.
Our study suggests that application of 4% CHX to the umbilical cord is effective in reducing the risk of omphalitis and neonatal mortality in rural Pakistan. Providing CHX in birth kits may be a useful strategy for preventing neonatal mortality in high-mortality settings. The study was funded by the United States Agency for International Development.

title: The IKK complex, a central regulator of NF-kappaB activation.
text: The IKK kinase complex, the central component of the NF-κB signaling cascade, is composed of two kinases (IKKα and IKKβ) and a regulatory subunit, NEMO/IKKγ. Additional proteins may temporarily or permanently associate with the complex, but their identity and function are still unclear. Two distinct NF-κB signaling pathways have been discovered, depending on the activating signal and cell type: the canonical pathway dependent on IKKβ and NEMO and the noncanonical pathway that relies solely on IKKα. The primary question that remains unanswered is how an NF-κB activating signal leads to the activation of the kinase subunits, allowing them to phosphorylate their targets and ultimately induce nuclear translocation of the NF-κB dimers. Here, I will review the genetic, biochemical, and structural findings accumulated over the past decade regarding the function of the three IKK subunits.

title: Cognitive predictors of young children's readiness for powered mobility.
text:
Early childhood mobility independence has been linked to various cognitive and psychosocial skills. However, children with physical disabilities may struggle with independent mobility and experience delays in these areas. Providing young children with powered mobility can help overcome these challenges. Yet, there is a lack of information on when children have the cognitive skills to operate a powered wheelchair safely. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by identifying the necessary cognitive skills.
A battery of cognitive assessments and a wheelchair training and assessment program were developed. Twenty-six children with physical disabilities aged 20-36 months were evaluated on the cognitive assessment and participated in the wheelchair training. A stepwise regression analysis was used to determine which cognitive skills predict wheelchair mobility performance. The study found that spatial relations and problem-solving skills were significant predictors of wheelchair mobility, accounting for 57% of the variance in wheelchair skills. Developmental cut-off points for these skills in relation to wheelchair skills are presented, and clinical applications are discussed.

title: Knockdown of the co-chaperone Hop promotes extranuclear accumulation of Stat3 in mouse embryonic stem cells.
text: A pivotal event in the maintenance of mouse embryonic stem cell (mESC) pluripotency is the phosphorylation, dimerization, and nuclear translocation of the signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (Stat3). We employed RNA interference (RNAi) to reduce the levels of the co-chaperone protein Hop in an mESC line, which resulted in a 68% decrease in Stat3 mRNA levels, a decrease in soluble phosphorylated Stat3 (pYStat3) levels, and an accumulation of Stat3 in the extranuclear compartment. Hop's major binding partner, Hsp90, co-localized with a small non-nuclear fraction of Stat3 in mESCs, and both Stat3 and Hop co-precipitated with Hsp90. Interestingly, Hop knockdown did not affect the levels of the pluripotency markers Nanog and Oct4, but did result in a decrease in Nanog mRNA levels. Perhaps most noteworthy, we found that in the absence of Hop, mESCs lost their ability to form embryoid bodies with a basement membrane, suggesting a crucial role for Hop in maintaining mESC pluripotency. These data imply that Hop functions as a key component of the Hsp70/Hsp90 chaperone machinery, which is involved in pluripotency signaling.

title: B-cell self-tolerance in humans.
text: Two mechanisms contribute to the generation of the human antibody repertoire: V(D)J recombination during early B-cell development in the bone marrow and somatic mutation of immunoglobulin genes in mature B cells responding to antigen in the periphery. V(D)J recombination generates diversity through random joining of gene segments, while somatic mutation introduces random point mutations. Both mechanisms are essential to attain the level of antigen receptor diversification required for immune protection, as defects in either can lead to increased susceptibility to infection. However, the drawback of producing extensive random diversity in the antibody repertoire is the generation of autoantibodies. To prevent autoimmunity, B cells expressing autoantibodies are regulated through mechanisms that either alter the specificity of autoantibodies or the fate of cells producing them. Abnormalities in B-cell self-tolerance are associated with numerous autoimmune diseases, although the particular nature of the defects remains less clear. Here, we review recent data on the self-reactive B-cell repertoire in healthy individuals and patients with autoimmunity.

title: JMJD6 Promotes Colon Carcinogenesis through Negative Regulation of p53 by Hydroxylation
text: Jumonji domain-containing protein 6 (JMJD6) is a member of the Jumonji C domain-containing protein family. Although its cellular activity is not fully understood, JMJD6 has been found to physically associate with the tumor suppressor p53. Through experiments conducted in this study, it was discovered that JMJD6 acts as an α-ketoglutarate- and Fe(II)-dependent lysyl hydroxylase, catalyzing the hydroxylation of p53. The study found that p53 exists as a hydroxylated protein in vivo, with hydroxylation primarily occurring on lysine 382 of p53. Additionally, JMJD6 was found to antagonize p53 acetylation, promote the association of p53 with its negative regulator MDMX, and repress p53's transcriptional activity. Depletion of JMJD6 resulted in enhanced p53 transcriptional activity, cell arrest in the G1 phase, cell apoptosis, and increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agent-induced cell death. Furthermore, JMJD6 downregulation repressed p53-dependent colon cell proliferation and tumorigenesis in vivo, and high nuclear JMJD6 protein was found to be significantly associated with aggressive clinical behaviors of colon adenocarcinomas. These findings uncover a novel posttranslational modification for p53 and suggest JMJD6 as a potential biomarker for colon cancer aggressiveness and potential target for colon cancer intervention.

title: Spread of chloroquine resistance in Plasmodium falciparum.
text: Confirmation of malaria resistance to chloroquine has been reported in over 40 countries. Introduced in 1934, chloroquine was not widely used until the early 1950s. Early anecdotal reports of resistance emerged in Colombia and along the border area of Cambodia and Thailand as early as 1957. By 1960, resistance in these areas was confirmed, and it is believed to represent two separate events. The resistance spread rapidly, with a new focus of resistance confirmed in East Africa by 1977. Chloroquine resistance poses a significant challenge for both prophylaxis and treatment of malaria. In this article, David Payne examines the spread of resistance and discusses some of its implications.

title: Obesity occurring in apolipoprotein E-knockout mice has mild effects on fertility.
text: The Apolipoprotein (Apo) family is involved in lipid metabolism. There are five types of Apo: Apoa, Apob, Apoc, Apod, and Apoe. Apoe plays a central role in lipoprotein metabolism and is essential for efficient receptor-mediated plasma clearance of chylomicron remnants and VLDL remnant particles by the liver. Apoe-deficient (Apoe(-/-) mice) develop atherosclerotic plaques spontaneously and become obese. In this study, we investigated the impact of Apoe knockout on reproduction in female mice. Our results showed that Apoe(-/-) mice have significantly higher cholesterol levels, which lead to lipid accumulation in the ovaries, causing the ovaries to be heavier than those of WT mice. Moreover, the expression of certain genes involved in cholesterol metabolism (e.g., Cyp19a1, Hsd3b, Mtor, and Nfkb) decreased significantly at day 100, while the expression of genes involved in cell death (e.g., Bad and Tsc2) increased. Surprisingly, the knockout of Apoe did not significantly affect the fertility rates of the mice; however, it did result in an increase in the number of ovarian follicles and the ratio of ovarian follicle atresia and apoptosis. Overall, this work has provided valuable insights into the role of Apoe in reproduction.

title: Lipid metabolism and toxicity in the heart.
text:
The heart has the greatest energy requirements and is the most efficient at metabolizing fatty acids (FAs). However, under conditions like obesity and type 2 diabetes, the heart's ability to take up and metabolize FAs becomes impaired, leading to the accumulation of lipids in the heart tissue. This can potentially cause cardiac lipotoxicity, leading to heart dysfunction.
To begin with, we will discuss the routes by which the heart obtains FAs from the bloodstream and stores them inside the cells. Next, we will describe mouse models that demonstrate excess lipid accumulation leads to heart problems and detail the experiments performed to mitigate this toxicity. Finally, we will summarize the established relationships between heart lipid metabolism and disease in humans.

title: Malaria eradication back on the table.
text:
After a 40-year hiatus, the push for malaria eradication is gaining momentum. Inspired by the Gates Malaria Forum in 2007, key organizations are reassessing the feasibility of redefining eradication as an explicit goal of malaria control efforts. The past few decades have seen significant advances in our understanding of malaria's biology, the social and economic factors that contribute to its spread, and the demands placed on health systems in endemic countries. However, despite these advances, malaria remains a major public health burden, with 80% of cases occurring in sub-Saharan Africa.
In the past, regional malaria elimination campaigns have been successful in eliminating malaria from parts of Europe, North America, the Caribbean, and South-Central America. However, these efforts were not sustained in sub-Saharan Africa, where the burden of malaria is highest. The main reasons for the failure of the global eradication program in 1969 were technical challenges, especially in Africa.
In the post-eradication era, there was a focus on technical issues, such as drug and vaccine development, vector control, and insecticide-treated nets. These efforts led to significant advances in malaria research and development. However, there was little global support provided specifically for malaria control in newly independent states in Africa, which were struggling to establish broad-based health systems and primary health care.
The combination of a worsening malaria situation and promising technical developments in the 1990s led to a renewed global focus on malaria control. The Roll Back Malaria initiative, launched by WHO in 1998, led to the Abuja Declaration in 2000, which defined progressive intervention coverage targets for control designed to eliminate malaria as a public health problem. Increased resources through the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, the World Bank's Booster Program, and the US President's Malaria Initiative have meant that progress is finally being made in reducing malaria intervention coverage.
Against this background, there is a renewed call for elimination/eradication of malaria. The challenges are formidable, and it is clear that efforts must focus beyond simply developing better tools to include how existing and future tools can be strategically combined for maximum synergistic effectiveness when integrated into different health and social systems prevailing in endemic areas. Effective surveillance strategies must also be put in place to monitor progress, which will require a better understanding of malaria transmission heterogeneity in a globalized world with rapidly changing dynamics in environment, climate, migration, and transnational cooperation.
In conclusion, while we lack sufficient knowledge, systems, and tools to eradicate malaria today, we have a window of political will and financial resources to refocus on the goal of effective control through universal coverage of appropriate interventions. A successful strategy will require a synchronous global effort, locally adapted in all endemic areas, with a real rather than rhetorical emphasis on health systems.

title: CI-994 (N-acetyl-dinaline) in combination with conventional anti-cancer agents is effective against acute myeloid leukemia in vitro and in vivo.
text: N-acetyl-dinaline (CI-994) is an experimental anti-cancer drug that targets histone deacetylases. We investigated the potential of CI-994 to enhance the effects of conventional chemotherapeutics used in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) treatment in a rat model for AML and Brown Norway rat acute myelocytic leukemia (BNML). Our findings showed that CI-994 combined with cytarabine (ara-C), daunorubicin, and mitoxantrone exhibited moderate synergy in vitro. In vivo, higher doses of CI-994 resulted in complete remissions. The combinations of CI-994 with ara-C and daunorubicin were also effective against BNML. These results suggest that CI-994 has favorable in vitro and in vivo interactions with conventional anti-cancer agents used to treat AML.

title: CTCF and Cohesin in Genome Folding and Transcriptional Gene Regulation.
text: The functional efficiency of a genome depends on its dynamic structural organization during the cell cycle. The way chromosomes fold in interphase plays a crucial role in regulating transcription, facilitating proper replication, and maintaining genome integrity by limiting unwanted recombination. Recent high-resolution studies using chromosome conformation capture and functional analysis have provided valuable insights into the spatial and regulatory compartmentalization of mammalian genomes. These studies have shed light on the mechanisms employed by CTCF and cohesin in controlling the functional architecture of mammalian chromosomes.

title: Melatonin synthesized by T lymphocytes as a ligand of the retinoic acid-related orphan receptor.
text: Melatonin exerts a wide range of physiological effects on the immune system, influencing multiple biological functions through its various receptors. While the significance of specific melatonin receptors has been well established for various immune processes, retinoic acid-related orphan receptor alpha (RORα) has been proposed as a mediator of nuclear melatonin signaling based on pharmacological findings. However, it cannot be ruled out that melatonin may have an indirect impact on RORα. We aimed to investigate the direct interaction between melatonin and RORα. Our results indicate that RORα is predominantly located in the nucleus of human Jurkat T-cells and co-immunoprecipitates with melatonin. Immunocytochemistry studies also revealed co-localization of melatonin and RORα. Melatonin prompted a time-dependent decrease in nuclear RORα levels, suggesting its role in regulating RORα transcriptional activity. Interestingly, RORα plays a switch-like role in the generation of Th17 and Treg cells, which are involved in maintaining a balance between harmful and protective immune responses in conditions such as autoimmunity and organ transplant rejection. Our findings suggest that melatonin has tremendous therapeutic potential for treating various clinical disorders by modulating RORα activity.

title: Age- and infection intensity-dependent cytokine and antibody production in human trichuriasis: the importance of IgE.
text: The study investigated the cytokine and antibody response to Trichuris trichiura infection in 96 individuals living in an area where the parasite is highly prevalent and infection follows a curved age-intensity profile. Upon stimulation with T. trichiura antigen, a small proportion of the participants produced interleukin (IL)-4 (7%), IL-9 (5%), and IL-13 (17%). In contrast, a larger proportion produced IL-10 (97%), tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha (93%), and interferon (IFN)-gamma (32%). Notably, the levels of TNF-alpha (P = 0.016) and IFN-gamma (P = 0.012) increased with age, indicating a shift towards a more chronic infection phenotype. The dominant parasite-specific antibodies produced were IgG1, IgG4, IgA, and IgE. Unlike IgG subclasses and IgA, IgE correlated negatively with infection intensity, as measured by egg output (P = 0.008), and positively with host age (P = 0.010), suggesting a mixed cytokine response in trichuriasis and an IgE-associated level of protection.

title: The cryoprotective effect of trehalose supplementation on boar spermatozoa quality.
text: To enhance the quality of boar sperm during the frozen-thawed process, we investigated the effect of trehalose on the success of cryopreservation. We evaluated the freeze-thawing tolerance of boar spermatozoa in a basic cooling extender with varying concentrations of trehalose (0, 25, 50, 100, and 200 mmol/l). Our findings revealed that the optimum concentration of trehalose for improving the cryopreservation capacity of boar spermatozoa was 100 mmol/l. We observed significant improvements in sperm motility (49.89%), acrosome integrity (66.52%), and membrane integrity (44.61%) at this concentration. In contrast, the addition of 200 mmol/l trehalose resulted in a decrease in boar spermatozoa cryocapacitation during the freeze-thawing process. Moreover, before and after capacitation, the CTC score for semen diluted with an extender containing 100 mmol/l trehalose was 3.68% and 43.82%, respectively. Our results suggest that trehalose can provide a greater cryoprotective capacity to boar spermatozoa, and supplementation with 100 mmol/l trehalose in a basic extender can significantly improve sperm motility, membrane integrity, and acrosome integrity parameters during the cryopreservation process.

title: Roads to polyploidy: the megakaryocyte example.
text: Polyploidy, characterized by multiple copies of the haploid chromosome number, has been observed in various organisms, including plants, insects, and mammalian cells such as platelet precursors and megakaryocytes. These cell types attain high ploidy through distinct cell cycles, including an endomitotic process in megakaryocytes. In this review, we examine the mechanisms that lead to polyploidy in megakaryocytes and compare them to those seen in other systems where high ploidy is achieved. Overall, polyploidy is associated with a coordinated shift in the expression of several genes, some of which may be a direct result of high ploidy and therefore a determining factor in a new cell physiology. Others, however, are inducers of polyploidization and are worth further investigation in future studies.

title: Central memory and effector memory T cell subsets: function, generation, and maintenance.
text: The memory T cell pool serves as a dynamic storage of antigen-experienced T lymphocytes that accumulate throughout an individual's lifetime. Recent research has revealed that memory T cells comprise distinct populations of central memory (TCM) and effector memory (TEM) cells, each characterized by unique homing capabilities and effector functions. This review aims to elucidate the diversity of TCM and TEM, their developmental stages, and the current understanding of their generation and maintenance in both humans and mice.

title: The Werner and Bloom syndrome proteins help resolve replication blockage by converting (regressed) holliday junctions to functional replication forks.
text:
Cells have evolved strategies to deal with obstacles in the replication process, ensuring that DNA synthesis is completed and genome stability is maintained. Two helicases, WRN and BLM, play critical roles in maintaining genome stability and resolving replication blockages. Our study focuses on the actions of these helicases on a specific Holliday junction substrate that mimics a regressed replication fork.
We observed that both WRN and BLM, when ATP hydrolysis is required, convert the Holliday junction substrate into a four-stranded replication fork structure. This suggests that these helicases target the Holliday junction to initiate branch migration. Consistent with this finding, the Holliday junction-binding protein RuvA inhibits the WRN- and BLM-mediated conversion reactions. Moreover, the resulting conversion product can be used for replication with its leading daughter strand readily extended by DNA polymerases.
Our results also show that the optimal conditions for binding to and conversion of the Holliday junction occur at low MgCl2 concentrations, suggesting that WRN and BLM preferentially act on the square planar (open) conformation of Holliday junctions. Taken together, our findings suggest that, following fork regression events, WRN and/or BLM can restore functional replication forks to overcome blockage, a functionality that is consistent with the phenotypes associated with WRN- and BLM-deficient cells.

title: Do Montelukast Sodium and N-Acetylcysteine Have a Nephroprotective Effect on Unilateral Ureteral Obstruction? A Placebo Controlled Trial in a Rat Model.
text:
Background: Obstruction of the ureter can cause secondary renal damage, resulting in oxidative stress, inflammation, and tubular epithelial damage. Montelukast sodium and N-acetylcysteine are medications that have been shown to have nephroprotective effects. This study aimed to assess the effects of these medications on secondary renal damage due to unilateral ureteral obstruction in a rat model.
Methods: In this study, 30 male Wistar albino rats were randomly divided into three groups: placebo, N-acetylcysteine, and montelukast sodium. Three rats served as the control group. The left ureter of the rats was sutured with 4-zero polyglactin sutures. The medications were given for three days prior to obstruction and continued for 15 days. Dimercaptosuccinic acid renal scintigraphy was performed before obstruction and on day 15. The rats were sacrificed on day 15, and histopathological examinations were conducted. Oxidative stress markers, such as myeloperoxidase and malondialdehyde, sulfhydryl levels, and total nitrite levels for lipid peroxidation were biochemically assessed.
Results: Pathological examination revealed that inflammation and tubular epithelial damage in the N-acetylcysteine and montelukast sodium groups were significantly less than in the placebo group (p <0.05). There were no differences in normal kidneys. Biochemical analysis showed that myeloperoxidase, malondialdehyde, and total nitrite levels in the N-acetylcysteine group and myeloperoxidase and malondialdehyde levels in the montelukast sodium group were significantly lower than in the placebo group (p <0.05). No significant differences were seen in sulfhydryl levels (p >0.05) or among the N-acetylcysteine, montelukast sodium, and placebo groups on scintigraphy (p >0.05). No pathological, chemical, or scintigraphic differences were seen among the N-acetylcysteine, montelukast sodium, and sham-treated groups (p >0.05).
Conclusion: N-acetylcysteine and montelukast sodium have a protective effect against obstructive damage to the kidney. However, further investigations are needed.

title: Oxidative phosphorylation: synthesis of mitochondrially encoded proteins and assembly of individual structural subunits into functional holoenzyme complexes.
text: Most of the ATP required by cells in higher eukaryotes is typically produced through a process called oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), which involves five multimeric protein complexes (I-V) embedded within the inner mitochondrial membrane. Maintaining energy homeostasis under typical conditions depends on OXPHOS's ability to adapt to cellular changes in bioenergetic demand, and a chronic failure to do so often leads to human disease. Unlike Complex II, the structural subunits of OXPHOS complexes are encoded by both the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes. Due to the physical separation of these genomes, the expression of the 13 mitochondrially encoded polypeptides must be coordinated with that of relevant nuclear-encoded partners to assemble functional holoenzyme complexes. The assembly of these complexes is a highly ordered process, and several nuclear-encoded factors that play critical roles at different stages of complex biogenesis have been identified.

title: Familial gastroesophageal reflux and development of Barrett's esophagus.
text: The family of an elderly man with Barrett's esophagus underwent examination for gastroesophageal reflux and the development of Barrett's esophagus. All five living children have either gastroesophageal reflux or esophagitis, or both, and three have definitive Barrett's esophagus. Two third-generation descendants also have gastroesophageal reflux. This pattern suggests that the gastroesophageal reflux trait is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Additionally, the family has a high incidence of cancer, which may indicate the presence of the cancer family syndrome.

title: The effect of folate fortification on folic acid-based homocysteine-lowering intervention and stroke risk: a meta-analysis.
text:
Objective: Folate and vitamin B12 play a crucial role in the metabolic process of homocysteine, which is a risk factor for atherothrombotic events. Low folate intake or low plasma folate levels are associated with an increased risk of stroke. Previous randomized controlled trials have yielded discordant results on the effect of folic acid supplementation on stroke risk. This meta-analysis aimed to investigate how different folate fortification status affects the effects of folic acid supplementation on homocysteine reduction and stroke risk.
Design: Relevant randomized controlled trials were identified through a literature search, and homocysteine reduction was compared in subgroups stratified by folate fortification status. Relative risks with 95% confidence intervals were used to measure the association between folic acid supplementation and stroke risk.
Setting: The meta-analysis included 14 randomized controlled trials with a total of 39,420 participants.
Results: Homocysteine reductions were 26.99%, 18.38%, and 21.30% in the subgroups without folate fortification, with folate fortification, and with partial folate fortification, respectively. A significant difference was observed between the subgroups with and without folate fortification (P=0.05). The relative risk of stroke was 0.88 (95% CI 0.77, 1.00, P=0.05) in the subgroup without folate fortification, 0.94 (95% CI 0.58, 1.54, P=0.82) in the subgroup with folate fortification, and 0.91 (95% CI 0.82, 1.01, P=0.09) in the subgroup with partial folate fortification.
Conclusion: Folic acid supplementation may have a modest beneficial effect on stroke prevention in regions without folate fortification.

title: On the origin and impact of mesenchymal stem cell heterogeneity: new insights and emerging tools for single cell analysis.
text: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) exhibit substantial cell-to-cell variation, which is prevalent among donors, tissue sources, and within cell populations. This heterogeneity complicates the use of MSCs in regenerative applications and may limit their therapeutic efficacy. Conventional assays primarily measure MSC properties in bulk, thereby masking this cell-to-cell variation. Recent studies have revealed extensive variability within and amongst clonal MSC populations, encompassing functional differentiation capacity, molecular state (including epigenetic, transcriptomic, and proteomic status), and biophysical properties. The sources of these variations remain unknown, but potential mechanisms involve in vivo micro-anatomical heterogeneity, epigenetic bistability, and transcriptional fluctuations. Emerging single-cell analysis techniques may provide further insight into the mechanisms and implications of single-cell variation among MSCs, ultimately improving their clinical utility in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications. This review highlights the dimensions of MSC heterogeneity, elucidates known mechanisms governing it, and emphasizes emerging technologies poised to refine our understanding and enhance clinical application of this unique cell type.

title: Altered microRNA expression in bovine skeletal muscle with age.
text: Age-related decline in skeletal muscle function can lead to a range of inherited and acquired muscular disorders in older individuals. Small non-coding RNA molecules known as microRNAs (miRNAs) play a crucial role in muscle maintenance and repair, and their levels can be altered during the development and aging of skeletal muscle tissue. To investigate this further, we conducted a comprehensive next-generation sequencing analysis of miRNAs from five distinct stages of bovine skeletal muscle development. Our study identified a total of 511 miRNAs, including one putatively novel miRNA, which we submitted to the miRBase database. We found that 36 miRNAs were differentially expressed between prenatal and postnatal stages of muscle development, including several members of the myomiR (miR-1, miR-206, and let-7) families. In addition, we observed significant differences in miRNA expression between different muscle tissues, with 14 miRNAs up-regulated and 22 miRNAs down-regulated in the muscle of the postnatal stage. Furthermore, we used a dual luciferase reporter assay to demonstrate that a novel miRNA, predicted as bta-mir-10020, directly targeted the 3'-untranslated region (UTR) of the bovine ANGPT1 gene. Overexpression of bta-mir-10020 significantly decreased DsRed fluorescence in the wild-type expression cassette compared to the mutant type. Using three computational approaches - Miranda, PITA, and RNAhybrid - we predicted that the differentially expressed miRNAs could target 3609 bovine genes, and functional analysis revealed that these targets were enriched in muscle growth and developmental disorders. Our findings expand the repertoire of bovine miRNAs expressed in muscle tissue and could contribute to further studies on growth and developmental disorders in this tissue type.

title: Apoptosis occurs predominantly in bystander cells and not in productively infected cells of HIV- and SIV-infected lymph nodes
text: Although 13 years have passed since the discovery of human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) as the cause of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), we still do not fully understand how HIV kills its primary target, the T cell that carries the CD4 antigen. Although we and other researchers have observed an increase in the percentage of apoptotic cells among circulating CD4+ (and CD8+) T cells in HIV-infected individuals and an increase in frequency of apoptosis with disease progression, it is unclear whether this apoptosis occurs in infected or uninfected T cells. Our study, which used in situ labeling of lymph nodes from HIV-infected children and simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV)-infected macaques, reveals that apoptosis occurs predominantly in bystander cells and not in productively infected cells themselves. These findings have important implications for both the pathogenesis and therapy of HIV infection, suggesting that combination drug therapy may be necessary to target both viral replication in infected cells and apoptosis of uninfected cells.

title: Neuronal origin of a cerebral amyloid: neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer's disease contain the same protein as the amyloid of plaque cores and blood vessels.
text: The protein component of Alzheimer's disease amyloid, consisting of neurofibrillary tangles (NFT), amyloid plaque core, and congophilic angiopathy, is an aggregated polypeptide with a subunit mass of 4 kd (A4 monomer). According to the degree of N-terminal heterogeneity, the amyloid first deposits in the neuron and later in the extracellular space. Using antisera raised against synthetic peptides, we have shown that the N-terminal region of A4 (residues 1-11) contains an epitope for neurofibrillary tangles, while the internal region of the molecule (residues 11-23) contains an epitope for plaque cores and vascular amyloid. The non-protein component of the amyloid, aluminum silicate, may play a role in the deposition or amplification (possibly through self-replication) of the aggregated amyloid protein. The amyloid of Alzheimer's disease shares similarities in subunit size and composition but not sequence with the scrapie-associated fibril and its constituent polypeptides. In contrast, the sequence and composition of NFT are distinct from those of any known components of normal neurofilaments.

title: Pregnancy characteristics and maternal risk of breast cancer.
text:
During pregnancy, hormone levels are significantly higher than at other times in a woman's life. These hormones, including estrogen and progesterone, are primarily produced in the placenta, and any signs of placental impairment could potentially be used as indirect markers of hormone exposure during pregnancy. While inconsistent associations between these markers and breast cancer risk in mothers have been reported, the objective of this study was to examine the relationship between specific pregnancy characteristics, such as placental weight, and the risk of breast cancer in mothers.
The study was a population-based cohort study using data from the Swedish Birth Register, Cancer Register, Death Register, and Register of Population and Population Changes. The cohort included women who delivered singletons between 1982 and 1989 and were followed up until the occurrence of breast cancer, death, or the end of follow-up in 2001. The main outcome measure was the incidence of invasive breast cancer.
Of the 314,019 women in the cohort, 2216 (0.7%) developed breast cancer during the follow-up period. Of these, 2100 (95%) were diagnosed before the age of 50. The study found that women whose placentas weighed between 500 and 699 grams in their first pregnancy and at least 700 grams in their second pregnancy (or vice versa) had an increased risk of breast cancer, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.82 (95% CI, 1.07-3.08). The risk was doubled among women whose placentas weighed at least 700 grams in both pregnancies (adjusted hazard ratio, 2.05; 95% CI, 1.15-3.64). In contrast, a high birth weight (> or =4000 grams) in two successive births was associated with an increased risk of breast cancer before adjusting for placental weight and other covariates (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.76-1.59).
In conclusion, the study found that placental weight is positively associated with the risk of breast cancer in mothers, supporting the hypothesis that hormones produced during pregnancy play a critical role in modifying breast cancer risk.

title: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: a category or a continuum? Genetic analysis of a large-scale twin study.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the heritability of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and the distinction between categorical and continuum approaches using a large-scale twin sample.
Methodology:
A cohort of 1,938 families with twins and siblings aged 4 to 12 years was recruited from the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council Twin Registry. The families were assessed for ADHD using a DSM-III-R-based maternal rating scale. Probandwise concordance rates and correlations were calculated among monozygotic (MZ) and dizygotic (DZ) twins and siblings, and heritability was examined using the De Fries and Fulker regression technique.
Results:
There was a moderate to high heritability of ADHD (0.75 to 0.91) that was consistent across different familial relationships (twin, sibling, and twin-sibling) and across different definitions of ADHD as part of a continuum or as a disorder with various symptom cutoffs. No evidence was found for non-additive genetic variation or shared family environmental effects.

Conclusions:
These findings suggest that ADHD can be best understood as the extreme end of a behavior that varies genetically throughout the entire population rather than as a disorder with discrete determinants. These implications have significant consequences for the classification of ADHD, the identification of genes for this behavior, and diagnosis and treatment.

title: Antiapoptotic BCL-2 is required for maintenance of a model leukemia.
text: Resistance to programmed cell death, or apoptosis, is often observed in cancer cells, which can be attributed to the overexpression of proteins that inhibit apoptosis. However, it is unclear whether these defects are essential for the maintenance of cancer. To investigate this, we created mice that expressed a conditional BCL-2 gene and constitutive c-myc, leading to the development of lymphoblastic leukemia. When we eliminated BCL-2, we observed rapid loss of leukemic cells and significantly prolonged survival, confirming BCL-2 as a potential target for cancer therapy. Surprisingly, loss of this single molecule led to cell death, even in the presence of other oncogenic events. This suggests that cancer cells are subject to tonic death signals that would normally cause cell death if not countered by an essential apoptotic defect.

title: Cellular and histopathological changes in the infrapatellar fat pad in the monoiodoacetate model of osteoarthritis pain.
text:
Objective: The infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP) has been identified as a source of anterior knee pain, and its role in the progression of degenerative joint disease (DJD) has been explored using the monoiodoacetate (MIA) model of DJD in rats.
Methods: Rats were injected intra-articularly with MIA and the development of weight bearing asymmetry was monitored for 21 days. The IPFPs were removed from both ipsilateral and contralateral joints, and the inflammatory infiltrate and histopathological changes were analyzed.
Results: MIA injection caused significant weight bearing asymmetry, and ipsilateral IPFP wet weights were significantly increased on days 1 and 3 in MIA-treated animals. MIA treatment also resulted in increased total white blood cells, monocytes, and neutrophils in the IPFP, with these changes progressing to adipocyte necrosis, IPFP fibrosis, patellar cartilage and subchondral bone necrosis, and synovial hyperplasia at later time points.
Conclusions: The current study demonstrated that inflammatory changes in the IPFP occur during the early stage of the MIA model of OA, which may contribute to the pain observed at this stage. Further exploration of the IPFP's role in later stages of the model is warranted.

title: Angiogenesis therapy: amidst the hype, the neglected potential for serious side effects.
text: Until recently, angiogenesis therapy was largely unfamiliar as a therapeutic concept, but it has since gained significant attention in the cardiology community. However, along with the excitement surrounding its potential to treat patients with obstructed arteries supplying the myocardium or legs, there is a need to consider the potential side effects of this therapy. While clinical studies have failed to demonstrate primary end-point efficacy, careful consideration of the serious adverse effects that may occur has been largely overlooked in scientific communications. Recently, a tragic death due to injection of an adenoviral vector into the hepatic artery unrelated to angiogenesis therapy highlighted the potential dangers of this therapy. Despite this, there has been a lack of in-depth discussion among the scientific community of the potential complications of angiogenesis interventions. This discussion is important due to both the recent tragic event and the availability of mechanistic data that can identify specific potential side effects of angiogenesis therapy. Here, we will focus on potential complications based on our understanding of the biological activities of two of the most potent angiogenic cytokines: vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF). Angiogenic agents have the potential to induce neovascularization in many different tissues, and this can become a concern in clinical settings where their use is being investigated.

title: Body mass index and magnetic resonance markers of brain integrity in adults.
text:
Introduction:
Adulthood obesity and being overweight have been consistently linked to an increased risk of developing dementia in later life, particularly Alzheimer's disease. These conditions have also been associated with cognitive impairment and brain structural changes in otherwise healthy adults. Although proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) can differentiate between neuronal and glial components of the brain and reveal underlying neurobiological mechanisms for brain atrophy and cognitive decline, no MRS studies have yet examined the relationships between adiposity and brain metabolites.
Methods:
We analyzed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and proton MRS data from 50 healthy middle-aged participants (average age: 41.7 ± 8.5 years, 17 women) who served as control subjects in another study.

Results:
After adjusting for age and sex, greater body mass indices (BMIs) were associated with:
1. Lower concentrations of N-acetylaspartate (a spectroscopic marker of neuronal viability) in frontal (p = 0.001), parietal (p = 0.006), and temporal (p = 0.008) white matter.
2. Lower N-acetylaspartate levels in frontal gray matter (p = 0.01).
3. Lower concentrations of choline-containing metabolites (related to membrane metabolism) in frontal white matter (p = 0.05).

Interpretation:
These findings suggest that elevated BMI at midlife is associated with neuronal and/or myelin abnormalities, primarily in the frontal lobe. Since white matter in the frontal lobe is more susceptible to aging effects than in other lobes, our results may indicate accelerated aging in individuals with high BMIs, increasing their odds of developing age-related diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease.

title: Characteristics of medial temporal lobe epilepsy: II. Interictal and ictal scalp electroencephalography, neuropsychological testing, neuroimaging, surgical results, and pathology.
text:
In this study, the authors retrospectively analyzed the data of 67 patients with temporal lobe epilepsy without visible, potentially epileptogenic lesions, who underwent intracranial electrode embedding and subsequent temporal lobectomy. The study aimed to investigate the preoperative scalp electroencephalographic (EEG) findings, neuropsychological test results, neuroimaging findings, surgical outcomes, and pathology of resected tissue in these patients.
The study found that in 64 of the 67 patients (96%), interictal scalp EEG showed paroxysmal abnormalities during prolonged monitoring, with localization in the anterior temporal region in 60 patients (94%). Approximately 42% of the patients demonstrated bilateral independent paroxysmal activity, with the side of seizure origin experiencing preponderance in half of the cases. Ictal EEG changes were rarely observed during seizure onset, but lateralized buildup of rhythmic seizure activity occurred in 80% of patients. Interestingly, in 13% of the patients, the scalp EEG seizure buildup was contralateral to the side of seizure origin as confirmed by depth EEG and curative surgery. Furthermore, lateralized postictal slowing was observed in 80% of the patients, which was a reliable lateralizing finding.
Neuropsychological testing provided lateralizing findings concordant with the side of seizure origin in 73% of patients. However, in cases where neuropychological testing produced discordant results or non-lateralizing findings, the patients tended to have right temporal seizure origin. Intracarotid amobarbital (Amytal) testing demonstrated absent or marginal memory functions on the side of seizure onset in 63% of patients, while 26 patients (37%) had bilaterally intact memory. Interestingly, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was very sensitive in detecting subtle medial temporal abnormalities in 28 of the 28 MRI scans, with these abnormalities corresponding to mesial temporal sclerosis on pathological examination in all but 2 patients.
The study's findings suggest that preoperative evaluation of temporal lobe epilepsy patients using EEG, neuropsychological tests, neuroimaging, and intracarotid amobarbital testing can provide valuable information for surgical decision-making and lateralizing the seizure origin. These findings are consistent with the concept of lateralization of epileptogenicity and may help guide surgical resection to the appropriate hemisphere. This knowledge can be crucial for successful surgical outcome and improved quality of life for these patients.

title: OPA1-dependent cristae modulation is essential for cellular adaptation to metabolic demand.
text: Cristae, the structured invaginations of the mitochondrial inner membrane, adapt to the cell's energetic demands through dynamic changes in their structure. While the regulatory mechanisms behind these changes are largely unknown, one key player, Optic atrophy 1 (OPA1), has been revealed to play a significant role in maintaining cristae structure. OPA1 is a mitochondrial GTPase responsible for inner membrane fusion and has recently been found to regulate cristae structure independently of its role in fusion. In this study, we discovered that OPA1 is able to respond dynamically to changes in energy conditions, which enables it to regulate cristae structure without affecting its role in fusion. Moreover, we found that OPA1 is essential for cell survival under starvation conditions, respiration, growth in galactose media, and maintenance of ATP synthase assembly, regardless of its fusion activity. Further investigations revealed that mitochondrial solute carriers (SLC25A) interact with OPA1 and affect its function. Our findings suggest a novel mechanism by which OPA1 senses energy substrate availability and modulates its function in the regulation of mitochondrial architecture through SLC25A proteins.

title: Phenylpropanolamine and the risk of hemorrhagic stroke.
text:
Background: Phenylpropanolamine is frequently found in appetite suppressants and cough or cold remedies. Cases have been reported where individuals who use these products have suffered hemorrhagic strokes, often after the first use. To investigate this association, we conducted a case-control study.
Methods: We recruited men and women aged 18-49 from 43 US hospitals. Inclusion criteria were experiencing a subarachnoid or intracerebral hemorrhage within 30 days prior to enrollment, and no prior brain lesion diagnosis. Random digit dialing was used to find two matched control subjects per patient.
Results: A total of 702 patients and 1376 control subjects were included in the analysis. For women, the adjusted odds ratio was 16.58 (95% CI: 1.51-182.21; p=0.02) for the association between the use of appetite suppressants containing phenylpropanolamine and the risk of hemorrhagic stroke. The odds ratio for the association with the first use of a product containing phenylpropanolamine was 3.13 (95% CI: 0.86-11.46; p=0.08). All first uses of phenylpropanolamine were found in cough or cold remedies. For men and women combined, the adjusted odds ratio was 1.49 (95% CI: 0.84-2.64; p=0.17) for the association between the use of a product containing phenylpropanolamine and the risk of hemorrhagic stroke. No increased risk was found when analyzing cough or cold remedies that contained phenylpropanolamine, and appetite suppressants that contained phenylpropanolamine showed a statistically significant risk of 15.92 (95% CI: 1.38-184.13; p=0.03). No men in the study reported using appetite suppressants.
Conclusions: The results suggest that phenylpropanolamine in appetite suppressants, and possibly in cough and cold remedies, is a risk factor for hemorrhagic stroke in women.

title: The safety of intravenous fluorescein for confocal laser endomicroscopy in the gastrointestinal tract.
text:
BACKGROUND: Confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) is rapidly gaining recognition as a valuable tool for gastrointestinal endoscopic imaging. Fluorescent contrast agents are used to enhance imaging with CLE, with intravenous fluorescein being the most widely employed contrast agent. However, fluorescein is not FDA-cleared for use with CLE, despite its established safety profile in diagnostic angiography of the retina.
AIMS: To estimate the incidence of serious and total adverse events associated with intravenous fluorescein use during gastrointestinal CLE.
METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 16 prominent academic medical centers with active CLE research protocols that involved intravenous fluorescein. Centers using i.v. fluorescein for CLE and actively monitoring adverse events were included.
RESULTS: A total of 2272 gastrointestinal CLE procedures were performed at 16 centers. The most commonly administered dose of contrast agent was 2.5-5 mL of 10% sodium fluorescein. No serious adverse events were reported, but mild events occurred in 1.4% of participants, including nausea/vomiting, transient hypotension without shock, injection site erythema, diffuse rash, and mild epigastric pain. A limitation of the study was that only immediate post-procedure adverse events were actively monitored.
CONCLUSIONS: The use of intravenous fluorescein for gastrointestinal CLE appears to be relatively safe, with few acute complications.

title: Metabolic DNA as the origin of spontaneously released DNA?
text:
A fraction of DNA is released spontaneously from living, but not dead or dying, human, other mammalian, avian, amphibian, and plant cells. This released DNA fraction has been shown to be:
(a) Present in both dividing and nondividing cell populations.
(b) Labile and prone to degradation.
(c) Associated with DNA-dependent RNA or DNA polymerase.
(d) Associated with an RNA fraction.
And has the following characteristics:
(e) Lower molecular weight than the typical genetic DNA fraction.
(f) Increased proportions of Alu repeat sequences compared to unique genes in plasma/serum.
On the other hand, earlier studies using autoradiography and biochemical techniques identified a DNA fraction:
(1) Present in both dividing and nondividing, differentiated cell populations.
(2) Labile and prone to degradation.
(3) Having a lower molecular weight than the typical genetic DNA fraction.
This fraction was termed metabolic DNA (m-DNA) and was proposed as a potential precursor to the formation of the spontaneously released DNA fraction. Therefore, we suggest that the metabolic DNA fraction might represent the precursor to the spontaneously released DNA fraction.

title: The flavivirus precursor membrane-envelope protein complex: structure and maturation.
text: In the final stages of assembly, many viruses undergo a maturation process that is crucial for their infectivity. For flaviviruses, this maturation is catalyzed by proteolytic cleavage of the precursor membrane protein (prM), which transforms inert virus particles into infectious ones. Through the determination of the 2.2 angstrom resolution crystal structure of a recombinant protein consisting of the prM-envelope glycoprotein E (E) fusion, we have gained valuable insights into the maturation process of flaviviruses. The structure represents the prM-E heterodimer, which fits precisely into the cryo-electron microscopy density of immature virus at neutral pH. Of particular interest is the pr peptide beta-barrel structure, which covers the fusion loop in E, thereby preventing fusion with host cell membranes. Our structure provides a springboard for identifying the stages of the pH-directed conformational metamorphosis that flaviviruses undergo during maturation, culminating in the release of pr upon budding from the host.

title: Peptide and non-peptide G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) in skeletal muscle.
text: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) constitute a significant proportion of cell surface receptors that play a crucial role in various cellular processes. While GPCRs have been studied extensively in other muscle tissues such as cardiac and vascular smooth muscle cells, relatively little is known about their expression and function in skeletal muscle. To address this knowledge gap, we have compiled a comprehensive list of GPCRs expressed in skeletal muscle tissue, as well as their functional implications in both in vivo and in vitro skeletal muscle contexts.

title: Characterization of complete genome and small RNA profile of pagoda yellow mosaic associated virus, a novel badnavirus in China.
text: A newly discovered badnavirus was identified in pagoda trees exhibiting yellow mosaic symptoms on their leaves through high-throughput sequencing of small RNAs. The complete genome of this virus was determined to consist of 7424 nucleotides, showing 40.4%-45.1% identity to other badnaviruses. The genome encodes five open reading frames (ORFs) on the plus strand, including three conserved badnaviral ORFs. These findings suggest that this virus is a new member of the genus Badnavirus in the family Caulimoviridae. The virus has been tentatively named pagoda yellow mosaic associated virus (PYMAV). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that PYMAV forms a distinct group with gooseberry vein banding virus (GVBV) and grapevine vein-clearing virus (GVCV) within the family Caulimoviridae, while showing a distinct separation from other well-characterized badnaviral groups. Furthermore, analysis of the viral derived small RNA (vsRNA) profile of PYMAV showed that the most abundant vsRNAs are 21-nt in length, which differs from the predominance of 22- or 24-nt vsRNAs found in other viruses within the same family. Additionally, PYMAV vsRNAs showed a near-equal distribution of sense and antisense vsRNAs, while vsRNAs from other viruses in the family exhibit a preference for the sense strand of their genome. Moreover, PYMAV vsRNAs were found to be symmetrically distributed along the genome with no obvious vsRNA generating hotspots.

title: Experimental approaches for the treatment of malignant gliomas.
text: Malignant gliomas, including glioblastomas and anaplastic astrocytomas, are the most common primary brain tumors. In the last 30 years, the standard treatment for these tumors has evolved to include surgical resection, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy with temozolomide. While the median survival of patients with glioblastomas has increased from 6 months to 14.6 months, these tumors remain deadly for the majority of patients. However, significant progress has been made in understanding the molecular mechanisms of tumor growth and development, which is being translated into clinical trials.

title: Reversal of hyperglycemia in mice by using human expandable insulin-producing cells differentiated from fetal liver progenitor cells.
text: Beta-cell replacement therapy is widely considered the most promising approach for treating type 1 diabetes, yet a shortage of cells available for transplantation hinders its large-scale implementation. To overcome this challenge, we explored the potential of inducing stem/progenitor cells to differentiate into insulin-producing cells. We focused on fetal human progenitor liver cells (FH), which possess a high replication capacity and could be further expanded by introducing the gene for the catalytic subunit of human telomerase. By expressing the pancreatic duodenal homeobox 1 (Pdx1) gene, we found that FH cells could be directed to differentiate into insulin-producing cells that highly expressed beta-cell genes, stored significant amounts of insulin, and released insulin in a regulated manner in response to glucose challenge. When transplanted into hyperglycemic immunodeficient mice, the cells were able to restore and maintain euglycemia for extended periods, as evidenced by quantitative measurement of human C-peptide in the mouse serum. This approach holds promise as a novel source of cells for transplantation in patients with type 1 diabetes, offering a potential solution to the current cell shortage hindering the wide-scale implementation of beta-cell replacement therapy.

title: A review of the methods for human iPSC derivation.
text: The potential to reprogram somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) holds great promise for modeling human diseases and developing cellular therapies. Various methods exist for generating iPSC lines, but those most suitable for use in disease modeling and therapy development must be efficient enough to produce iPSCs from limited sample quantities, capable of reprogramming cells from both skin fibroblasts and blood, and free of unwanted cellular components. Several reprogramming techniques fulfill these requirements and can be used to derive iPSCs in research projects with both basic scientific and therapeutic objectives. Moreover, combining these reprogramming methods with small molecule modulators of signaling pathways can result in the successful generation of iPSCs from even the most resistant patient-derived somatic cells.

title: EB virus-encoded RNAs are recognized by RIG-I and activate signaling to induce type I IFN.
text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-encoded small RNAs (EBERs) are non-polyadenylated, untranslated RNAs that are most abundant in latently EBV-infected cells and are expected to form secondary structures with multiple short stem-loops. Retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) is a cytosolic protein that detects viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) inside the cell and initiates signaling pathways leading to the induction of protective cellular genes, including type I interferons (IFNs). We investigated whether EBERs are recognized by RIG-I as dsRNA. Transfection of RIG-I plasmid induced IFNs and IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) in EBV-positive Burkitt's lymphoma (BL) cells, but not in their EBV-negative counterparts or EBER-knockout EBV-infected BL cells. Transfection of EBER plasmid or in vitro-synthesized EBERs induced expression of type I IFNs and ISGs in RIG-I-expressing, EBV-negative BL cells, but not in RIG-I-deficient counterparts. EBERs activate RIG-I's substrates, NF-κB and IFN regulatory factor 3, which are essential for type I IFN activation. Moreover, our results show that EBERs co-precipitate with RIG-I, indicating that they are recognized by RIG-I. These findings suggest that EBERs are recognized by RIG-I as dsRNA and trigger signaling pathways that lead to the induction of type I IFN in EBV-infected cells.

title: Pregnancy in dialysis patients: a review of outcomes, complications, and management.
text: Although rare, pregnancy can occur in women on chronic dialysis. In 1980, the incidence of pregnancy in women on dialysis was approximately 0.9%. Studies conducted between 1992 and 2003 reveal that pregnancy occurred in 1-7% of women on chronic dialysis. Interestingly, intensive dialysis sessions of 16-24 hours per week have been associated with improved survival rates for infants born to mothers on chronic dialysis. In this article, we review the incidence, duration, fetal and maternal complications, and outcomes of pregnancy in women on chronic dialysis, as well as the management of anemia, hypertension, electrolytes, bone minerals, and acid-base parameters in pregnant dialysis patients. Additionally, we provide recommendations for the dialysis prescription for pregnant women on hemodialysis (HD) or peritoneal dialysis (PD). Given the complex and fragile nature of pregnancy in women on dialysis, close collaboration between the patient, nephrologist, dialysis staff, obstetrician, and neonatologist is crucial to increase the likelihood of a successful pregnancy.

title: Potent immunosuppressive activities of cytomegalovirus-encoded interleukin-10.
text: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) has developed sophisticated mechanisms to evade the host immune system. Recently, a novel gene consisting of non-contiguous open reading frames was discovered in the genomes of both human and primate CMV, with limited similarity to endogenous cellular interleukin-10 (IL-10). Here, we investigate the biological activities of the CMV IL-10-like gene product and reveal its immunosuppressive properties. We found that both recombinant bacteria-derived CMV IL-10 and CMV IL-10 expressed in supernatants of human cells inhibited the proliferation of mitogen-stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), with comparable potency to recombinant human IL-10. Moreover, CMV IL-10 suppressed cytokine synthesis in stimulated PBMCs and monocytes, leading to a significant decrease in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Additional findings showed that CMV IL-10 reduced the expression of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and class II molecules on the surface of cells, while increasing the expression of the non-classical MHC allele HLA-G. These results demonstrate for the first time that CMV possesses a biologically active IL-10 homolog that may contribute to immune evasion during viral infection.

title: Evidence for the presence of urease apoprotein complexes containing UreD, UreF, and UreG in cells that are competent for in vivo enzyme activation.
text:
In vitro activation of Klebsiella aerogenes urease, a nickel-containing enzyme, requires the presence of functional UreD, UreF, and UreG accessory proteins, as well as UreE. These accessory proteins are believed to play a role in metallocenter assembly (Lee et al., 1992). Three UreD-urease apoprotein complexes are present in cells that express high levels of ureD, and these complexes are thought to be essential for in vivo activation of the enzyme (Park et al., 1994).
We investigated the effect of deleting the genes for accessory proteins UreE, UreF, and UreG on urease complex formation. While these genes were not required for the formation of UreD-urease complexes, the complexes from the ureF deletion mutant exhibited delayed elution during size exclusion chromatography. This suggests that UreF may alter the conformation of UreD-urease complexes. Additionally, we identified a new series of urease apoprotein complexes present only in cells containing ureD, ureF, and ureG, along with the urease subunit genes. These complexes contain urease, UreD, UreF, and UreG. We propose that the UreD-UreF-UreG-urease apoprotein complexes represent the activation-competent form of urease apoprotein in the cell.

title: Human somatic cell nuclear transfer using adult cells.
text: Deriving patient-specific human pluripotent stem cells through somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) holds great promise for various therapeutic applications. However, achieving SCNT with human cells has proven to be challenging, and so far, only fetal or infant somatic cells have been successful. In this study, we sought to apply a novel method for generating human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) through SCNT using dermal fibroblasts from 35- and 75-year-old male donors. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of SCNT for adult human cells and warrant further exploration of this strategy in regenerative medicine.

title: "Natural" killer cells in the mouse. I. Cytotoxic cells with specificity for mouse Moloney leukemia cells. Specificity and distribution according to genotype.
text: In the spleens of young adult mice, there are naturally occurring killer lymphocytes with specificity for mouse Moloney leukemia cells. These cells exhibit lytic activity against both syngeneic and allogeneic Moloney leukemia cells, with the greatest activity observed when testing against in vitro grown leukemia cells. Interestingly, two leukemias of non-Moloney origin and the mastocytoma line P815 were resistant to lysis, while the killer cells showed specificity for Moloney leukemia cells as demonstrated by competition experiments using unlabeled Moloney or other tumor cells as inhibitors in the cytotoxic assays. Furthermore, the capacity to compete and sensitivity to lysis were found to be highly positively correlated. Analysis of the kinetics of the cytotoxic assay revealed a rapid induction of lysis within one to four hours, suggesting that the killer cells are not induced through an in vitro immune response. Additionally, there was no evidence found of soluble factors playing any role in the cytolytic assay.

title: Dose-response study on thyrotoxic patients undergoing positron emission tomography and radioiodine therapy
text: With acknowledged limitations in assessing thyroid function and associated radiation exposure, our previous policy involved administering 75 MBq of iodine-131 at 6-monthly intervals to patients with Graves' disease until they reached euthyroid status. However, with the integration of positron emission tomography (PET) at our hospital, the radiation dose to the thyroid has been calculated with an accuracy of approximately 20%, using an iodine-124 PET scan to determine the thyroid mass. To evaluate the optimal radiation dose for treating Graves' disease, a dose-response study was conducted on 65 patients who received cumulative radiation doses of less than 80 Gy. The results revealed that patients who received a low radiation dose (less than 20 Gy) at their initial treatment had a high likelihood of remaining toxic at 12 months. In contrast, patients who received higher radiation doses (more than 40 Gy) at their initial treatment had a higher probability of becoming euthyroid. Notably, the probability of becoming euthyroid increased more rapidly with increasing radiation dose than the probability of becoming hypothyroid. Based on these findings, a new treatment protocol has been implemented. Before receiving iodine-131 therapy, a 124I PET tracer study will be performed to ensure that a prescribed thyroid dose of 50 Gy is delivered to patients with Graves' disease. Additional 131I therapy will only be considered if patients remain toxic at 12 months.

title: Increased serum soluble corin in mid pregnancy is associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
text:
Here is a potential revision of the given text:
Background: The study of soluble corin in the circulation before hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) has been limited. In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between serum soluble corin levels in mid-pregnancy and the risk of HDP in a cohort of pregnant women.
Methods: We recruited 68 pairs of HDP patients and age- and gestational weeks-matched controls. Blood samples were collected between 16 and 20 gestational weeks, and serum soluble corin levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay methods. The relationship between serum soluble corin levels and the risk of HDP was examined using conditional logistic regression models.
Results: Our findings revealed that serum soluble corin levels were significantly higher in HDP patients compared to controls (median [interquartile range]: 1968 [1644-2332] pg/mL vs. 1700 [1446-2056] pg/mL, p=0.002). Participants were categorized into quartiles of serum soluble corin levels in the control group. We found that individuals in the highest quartile of serum soluble corin had a significantly higher risk of HDP compared to the lowest quartile (odds ratio [OR], 4.21; 95% confidence interval [95% CI], 1.31-13.53) after multivariate adjustment. However, we did not observe a significant increase in risk for individuals in the second (OR, 1.75; 95% CI, 0.44-7.02) and third (OR, 2.80; 95% CI, 0.70-11.18) quartiles. We then combined the second through fourth quartiles as a reference group and found that participants in the highest quartile had a significantly higher risk of HDP (OR, 2.28; 95% CI, 1.02-5.06).
Discussion: Our findings suggest that increased serum soluble corin levels in mid-pregnancy are associated with an increased risk of HDP.
