These findings suggest that screening for maltreatment, other traumatic experiences, and PTSD symptoms may improve prevention, treatment, and research strategies for childhood disruptive behavior disorders.

title: Exercise-induced asthma screening of elite athletes: field versus laboratory exercise challenge.
text: The study aimed to compare the effectiveness of a laboratory-based exercise challenge (LBC) and a field-based exercise challenge (FBC) in identifying exercise-induced asthma (EIA) in elite athletes. Twenty-three elite athletes who tested positive for EIA during the FBC and 23 gender- and sport-matched controls without asthma were included in the study. The athletes completed a medical history questionnaire before the FBC to assess EIA symptoms. During the FBC, baseline spirometry, actual or simulated competition, and spirometry tests at 5, 10, and 15 minutes after exercise were conducted. The results showed that 91% of the athletes who tested positive for EIA and 48% of the normal controls reported at least one symptom of EIA, with post-race cough being the most common. The baseline spirometry results were the same for both groups. The study concluded that self-reported symptoms of EIA by elite athletes are not reliable in identifying the condition, and the reference range for the decrease in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) in the elite athlete post-exercise is different from the current recommended guidelines. The study also found that a large number of false negatives may occur in this population if EIA screening is performed without adequate exercise and environmental stress.

title: Use of a targeted oncolytic poxvirus, JX-594, in patients with refractory primary or metastatic liver cancer: a phase I trial.
text:
Background: JX-594 is a targeted oncolytic poxvirus designed to selectively infect and destroy cancer cells with abnormal cell cycles and EGFR-ras signaling activation. In addition, it stimulates the production of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), which shuts down tumor blood vessels and boosts immune responses. To evaluate the safety and efficacy of JX-594 in patients with refractory primary or metastatic liver cancer, we conducted a phase I dose-escalation trial.
Methods: Between January 4, 2006, and July 4, 2007, we enrolled 14 patients with histopathologically confirmed refractory primary or metastatic liver tumors (up to 10.9 cm in diameter) that were amenable to image-guided intratumoral injections. The patients received JX-594 at one of four doses (10(8) plaque-forming units [pfu], 3x10(8) pfu, 10(9) pfu, or 3x10(9) pfu) every 3 weeks at Dong-A University Hospital in Busan, South Korea. Patients were monitored for at least 48 hours after treatment and for at least 4 weeks as outpatients, and adverse event monitoring was conducted according to the National Cancer Institute Common Toxicity Criteria (version 3) and standard laboratory toxicity grading for hematology, liver and renal function, coagulation studies, serum chemistry, and urinalysis. The primary objectives were to determine the maximum-tolerated dose (MTD) and safety of JX-594 treatment, and data were also collected on pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and efficacy.
Results: Of 22 patients with liver tumors evaluated for eligibility, eight did not meet inclusion criteria, and 14 patients were enrolled. The patients were heavily pretreated (5.6 previous treatments, SD 2.8, range 2.0-12.0) and had large tumors (7.0 cm in diameter, SD 2.7, range 1.8-10.9). Patients received a mean of 3.4 (SD 2.2, range 1.0-8.0) cycles of JX-594. All patients were evaluable for toxicity, and all patients experienced grade I-III flu-like symptoms, and four had transient grade I-III dose-related thrombocytopenia. Grade III hyperbilirubinaemia was dose-limiting in both patients at the highest dose; therefore, the MTD was established at 1x10(9) pfu. JX-594 replication-dependent dissemination in the blood was demonstrated, resulting in infection of non-injected tumor sites. GM-CSF expression led to grade I-III increases in neutrophil counts in four of six patients at the MTD. Tumor responses were shown in injected and non-injected tumors. Ten patients were radiographically evaluable for objective responses, and non-evaluable patients had contraindications to contrast medium (n=2) or no post-treatment scans (n=2). According to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), three patients had partial responses, six had stable disease, and one had progressive disease.
Interpretation: Intratumoral injection of JX-594 into primary or metastatic liver tumors was generally well-tolerated. Direct hyperbilirubinaemia was the dose-limiting toxicity. Safety was acceptable in the context of JX-594 replication, GM-CSF expression, systemic dissemination, and JX-594 had anti-tumoral effects against several refractory carcinomas. Phase II trials are now underway.

title: PTH Signaling in Osteoprogenitors Is Essential for B-Lymphocyte Differentiation and Mobilization.
text: Cells of the osteoblast lineage play a crucial role in supporting the development of B lymphocytes in the bone marrow (BM). Parathyroid hormone (PTH) signaling through its receptor (PPR) regulates hematopoietic stem cells, but its role in B lymphopoiesis is not well understood. Our study shows that deleting PPR in osteoprogenitors leads to a significant loss of trabecular and cortical bone. Interestingly, despite a reduction in B-cell progenitors in the BM, mature B cells were increased three and a half times in mice lacking PPR in osteoprogenitors. This retention of mature IgD(+) B cells in the BM was associated with increased expression of vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM1) by PPR-deficient osteoprogenitors, and treatment with VCAM1 neutralizing antibody increased mobilization of B lymphocytes from mutant BM. Our results demonstrate that PPR signaling in early osteoblasts is essential for B-cell differentiation via IL-7 secretion and for B-lymphocyte mobilization via VCAM1.

title: Snail coordinately regulates downstream pathways to control multiple aspects of mammalian neural precursor development.
text:
The Snail transcription factor is crucial for regulating various developmental processes, yet it is believed to play little role in mammalian neural precursor cells. In this study, we investigated radial glia precursor cells in the embryonic mouse cortex and found that Snail regulates their survival, self-renewal, and differentiation into intermediate progenitors and neurons through two distinct and separate target pathways.
Firstly, Snail promotes cell survival by inhibiting a p53-dependent death pathway, as demonstrated by the fact that p53 knockdown rescues survival deficits caused by Snail knockdown. Secondly, we reveal that Snail regulates the cell cycle phosphatase Cdc25b in radial precursors, and that coexpression of Cdc25b is sufficient to restore the reduced proliferation and differentiation of radial precursors observed upon Snail knockdown. Thus, Snail coordinates multiple aspects of mammalian embryonic neural precursor biology through p53 and Cdc25b.

title: Endothelial KLF2 links local arterial shear stress levels to the expression of vascular tone-regulating genes.
text: Lung Krüppel-like factor (LKLF/KLF2) is an essential transcription factor in murine vasculogenesis, specifically regulated by flow in vitro. We have now discovered a relation between local flow variations in the adult human vasculature and LKLF expression. Decreased LKLF expression was observed at the aortic bifurcations to the iliac and carotid arteries, concurrent with neointima formation. In vivo expression of LKLF was found to be directly inducible by shear stress in a murine carotid artery collar model, with a 4- to 30-fold increase in LKLF expression at high-shear sites. In vitro biomechanical analysis revealed that both steady flow and pulsatile flow induced basal LKLF expression at shear stresses greater than approximately 5 dyne/cm2, while cyclic stretch had no effect. Prolonged LKLF induction in the absence of flow led to changes in the expression of angiotensin-converting enzyme, endothelin-1, adrenomedullin, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase, similar to those observed under prolonged flow conditions. LKLF repression by siRNA also suppressed the flow response of these genes (P < 0.05). Our findings demonstrate that endothelial LKLF is regulated by flow in vivo and acts as a transcriptional regulator of several endothelial genes that control vascular tone in response to flow.

title: Synapsin I Cre transgene expression in male mice produces germline recombination in progeny.
text: The Cre/LoxP system can confer conditional loss of gene function in specific cell types, including neurons. A transgenic mouse line commonly used in research, which utilizes the Synapsin I promoter to drive Cre expression (SynCre), can achieve neuronal-specific Cre expression. Interestingly, we found that Cre expression is also observed in SynCre mice within the testes following breeding with a floxed transgenic mouse line. Cre transcript was expressed in testes, resulting in recombination of the floxed substrate in testes. Notably, in the majority of cases, offspring of male SynCre mice inherit a germline-recombined floxed allele, while this is never observed in offspring from female mice carrying the SynCre allele. This observation highlights a potential limitation in using these mice and enables male germ cell "deletor" strategies.

title: Hospital mortality, length of stay, and preventable complications among critically ill patients before and after tele-ICU reengineering of critical care processes.
text:
The association of a tele-intensive care unit (ICU) intervention with mortality, length of stay, and adherence to best practices in an academic medical center has not been previously reported. This study aimed to quantify the association of a tele-ICU intervention with these outcomes.
Methods:
In a prospective stepped-wedge clinical practice study, 6290 adult patients admitted to any of 7 ICUs (3 medical, 3 surgical, and 1 mixed cardiovascular) on two campuses of an 834-bed academic medical center were evaluated from April 26, 2005, through September 30, 2007. Electronic processes for best practice adherence, care plan creation, and clinician response times to alarms were evaluated. Mortality, length of stay, best practice adherence, and complication rates were the main outcome measures.
Results:
The hospital mortality rate during the pre-intervention period was 13.6% (95% CI, 11.9%-15.4%), which decreased to 11.8% (95% CI, 10.9%-12.8%) during the tele-ICU intervention period (adjusted odds ratio, 0.40 [95% CI, 0.31-0.52]). The tele-ICU intervention period was associated with higher rates of best practice adherence for deep vein thrombosis prevention (99% vs 85%, respectively; adjusted odds ratio, 15.4 [95% CI, 11.3-21.1]), cardiovascular protection (99% vs 80%, respectively; adjusted odds ratio, 30.7 [95% CI, 19.3-49.2]), and ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention (52% vs 33%, respectively; adjusted odds ratio, 2.20 [95% CI, 1.79-2.70]). The tele-ICU intervention also resulted in lower rates of preventable complications (ventilator-associated pneumonia, 1.6% vs 13%, respectively; adjusted odds ratio, 0.15 [95% CI, 0.09-0.23], and catheter-related bloodstream infection, 0.6% vs 1.0%, respectively; adjusted odds ratio, 0.50 [95% CI, 0.27-0.93]). Additionally, the tele-ICU intervention was associated with shorter hospital lengths of stay (9.8 vs 13.3 days, respectively; hazard ratio for discharge, 1.44 [95% CI, 1.33-1.56]). Similar results were observed in medical, surgical, and cardiovascular ICUs.


Conclusion:
Implementation of a tele-ICU intervention in a single academic medical center was associated with a reduction in adjusted odds of mortality and shorter hospital lengths of stay, as well as changes in best practice adherence and lower rates of preventable complications. These findings suggest that tele-ICU interventions may be effective in improving outcomes in critically ill patients.

title: CD11b+ monocytes abrogate Th17 CD4+ T cell-mediated experimental autoimmune myocarditis.
text: Experimental autoimmune myocarditis (EAM) serves as a mouse model for post-inflammatory heart disease, with Th17 T cells playing a central role. In wild-type BALB/c mice, EAM is a self-limiting condition that peaks 21 days after alpha-myosin heavy chain (MyHC) peptide/complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA) immunization and subsides thereafter. However, in IFN-gammaR(-/-) mice, the disease takes a chronic and progressive course. We found that this exacerbated disease course corresponds to persistently elevated levels of interleukin-17 (IL-17) from T cells infiltrating the heart of IFN-gammaR(-/-) mice 30 days after immunization. Specifically, IL-17 fosters the recruitment of CD11b(+) monocytes, the predominant heart-infiltrating cells in EAM. In turn, these CD11b(+) monocytes suppress MyHC-alpha-specific Th17 T cell responses in an IFN-gamma-dependent manner in vitro. In vivo, injecting IFN-gammaR(+/+)CD11b(+) monocytes, but not IFN-gammaR(-/-)CD11b(+), monocytes, aborted the progressive disease course in IFN-gammaR(-/-) mice. Lastly, co-injecting MyHC-alpha-specific, but not ovalbumin (OVA)-transgenic, IFN-gamma-releasing CD4(+) Th1 T cell lines with MyHC-alpha-specific Th17 T cells protected RAG2(-/-) mice from EAM. In conclusion, CD11b(+) monocytes play dual roles in EAM: as the primary cellular substrate for IL-17-induced inflammation and as mediators of an IFN-gamma-dependent negative feedback mechanism that limits disease progression.

title: The cytokine RANKL produced by positively selected thymocytes fosters medullary thymic epithelial cells that express autoimmune regulator.
text: The thymic medulla fosters the development of self-tolerance by creating a microenvironment where medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) express an array of autoimmune regulator genes and tissue-restricted genes. The process of positive selection is crucial for the formation of the thymic medulla, employing an obscure mechanism that has remained unexplored until now. Our findings indicate that the cytokine RANK ligand (RANKL), produced by positively selected thymocytes, plays a pivotal role in regulating the cellularity of mTECs through its interactions with RANK and osteoprotegerin. When RANKL is overexpressed, thymic medulla formation is restored in mice lacking positive selection, revealing the essential nature of this cytokine in establishing central tolerance. On the other hand, disrupting RANKL manifests a hindrance in medulla formation, underscoring the indispensable role of RANKL in the development of the thymic medulla.

title: Fibrosis and adipogenesis originate from a common mesenchymal progenitor in skeletal muscle.
text: The accumulation of adipocytes and collagen type-I-producing cells (fibrosis) is a hallmark of muscular dystrophies. While the origin of adipocytes has been previously identified as mesenchymal progenitors positive for platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (PDGFRα), the origin of muscle fibrosis remains unclear. In this study, clonal analyses revealed that PDGFRα(+) cells can differentiate into collagen type-I-producing cells, and PDGFRα(+) cells were found to accumulate in fibrotic areas of the diaphragm in a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Furthermore, expression of fibrosis markers was observed exclusively in the PDGFRα(+) cell fraction in the mdx mouse diaphragm, and TGF-β isoforms, known to induce fibrosis, induced expression of fibrosis markers in PDGFRα(+) cells but not in myogenic cells. Transplantation studies showed that fibrogenic PDGFRα(+) cells primarily originated from pre-existing PDGFRα(+) cells, with limited contribution from PDGFRα(-) cells and circulating cells. These findings indicate that mesenchymal progenitors are the primary source of both adipocyte accumulation and fibrosis in skeletal muscle.

title: The pecking order of free radicals and antioxidants: lipid peroxidation, alpha-tocopherol, and ascorbate.
Mitochondrial respiration in subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue from patients with morbid obesity.
text: Adipose tissue plays important endocrine and metabolic roles, but its bioenergetics are poorly understood, particularly in humans. Using high-resolution respirometry, we measured mitochondrial respiration in human abdominal subcutaneous and intra-abdominal visceral (omentum majus) adipose tissue obtained from 20 obese patients undergoing bariatric surgery. Mitochondrial density was determined through PCR analysis of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and genomic DNA (gDNA). Adipose tissue samples were permeabilized and respirometric measurements were performed in duplicate at 37°C, with sequential addition of glutamate, malate, octanoyl carnitine, and succinate to provide electrons to complex I + II. The addition of ADP (D) for state 3 respiration and the uncoupling agent FCCP were also performed. Our results showed that visceral fat contains more mitochondria per milligram of tissue than subcutaneous fat, but the cells are smaller. Stable and robust oxygen fluxes were observed in both tissues, with coupled state 3 (GMOS(D)) and uncoupled respiration being significantly higher in visceral adipose tissue (0.95 ± 0.05 and 1.15 ± 0.06 pmol O2 s1 mg1, respectively) compared to subcutaneous adipose tissue (0.76 ± 0.04 and 0.98 ± 0.05 pmol O2 s1 mg1, respectively). Furthermore, expressed per mtDNA, visceral adipose tissue had significantly lower mitochondrial respiration. Substrate control ratios were higher, and uncoupling control ratios were lower in visceral compared to subcutaneous adipose tissue. Our findings suggest that visceral fat is more bioenergetically active and responsive to mitochondrial substrate supply compared to subcutaneous fat, with higher relative activity of oxidative phosphorylation in visceral adipose tissue.

title: Endogenous gamma-H2AX-ATM-Chk2 checkpoint activation in Bloom's syndrome helicase deficient cells is related to DNA replication arrested forks.
text: The Bloom syndrome helicase (BLM) is crucial for maintaining genomic stability. A deficiency in BLM function leads to the development of Bloom syndrome (BS), a cancer-predisposing disorder. Our study reveals that BLM-deficient cell lines and primary fibroblasts exhibit an endogenously activated DNA double-strand break checkpoint response, characterized by high levels of phosphorylated histone H2AX (gamma-H2AX), Chk2 (p(T68)Chk2), and ATM (p(S1981)ATM) colocalizing in nuclear foci. Interestingly, the mitotic fraction of gamma-H2AX foci does not appear to be significantly higher in BLM-deficient cells, suggesting that these lesions occur transiently during interphase. Using iododeoxyuridine pulse labeling and immunofluorescence microscopy, we observed the colocalization of gamma-H2AX, ATM, and Chk2 with replication foci. These foci also co-stained with Rad51, indicating homologous recombination at these replication sites. To investigate replication in BS cells further, we employed a single-molecule approach on combed DNA fibers. In addition to a higher frequency of replication fork barriers, BS cells showed a reduced average fork velocity and a global decrease in interorigin distances, indicative of an increased frequency of origin firing. Considering BS is one of the most penetrant cancer-predisposing inherited diseases, it is likely that the absence of BLM entrains cells in a state similar to precancerous tissues with replication stress. Our findings are the first to report high ATM-Chk2 kinase activation and its connection to replication defects in a BS model.

title: Impact of TNF-alpha and IL-6 levels on development of cachexia in newly diagnosed NSCLC patients.
text: In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of cytokines tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) in cachexia development in newly diagnosed non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients. We evaluatend 44 NSCLC patients (41 male and 3 female) and 12 age-matched healthy smokers. We found that the Body Mass Index (BMI) of cachectic patients was significantly lower than that of non-cachectic patients and healthy controls. However, the serum levels of TNF-alpha did not differ between cachectic and non-cachectic patients, but were significantly higher in NSCLC patients compared to controls. IL-6 levels did not differ between the three groups, but there was a significant correlation between IL-6 and TNF-alpha levels, suggesting that these cytokines act as cofactors in weight loss. Additionally, there was a significant correlation between Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and TNF-alpha levels, suggesting that ESR could provide a valuable clue for considerable weight loss in the follow-up of NSCLC patients. Survival was not influenced by BMI or cytokine levels in the present study.

title: Treatment of antidepressant-associated sexual dysfunction with sildenafil: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Antidepressant use is a common cause of sexual dysfunction, leading to noncompliance with treatment. To investigate the efficacy of sildenafil citrate in improving sexual function in men taking selective and nonselective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SRI) antidepressants, we conducted a parallel-group, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at three US university medical centers from November 1, 2000, to January 1, 2001. Participants were 90 male outpatients (mean age 45 years) with major depression in remission who were experiencing sexual dysfunction due to SRI antidepressant treatment.
Patients were randomly assigned to receive either sildenafil (n=45) or placebo (n=45) at a flexible dose starting at 50 mg and adjustable to 100 mg before sexual activity for six weeks. The primary outcome measure was the Clinical Global Impression-Sexual Function (CGI-SF) score, and secondary measures included scores on the International Index of Erectile Function, Arizona Sexual Experience Scale, Massachusetts General Hospital-Sexual Functioning Questionnaire, and Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HAM-D).
Of the 90 patients randomized, 89 (93%) took at least one dose of study drug, and 85 (85%) completed the six-week assessment. At a CGI-SF score of 2 or lower, 54.5% (24/44) of sildenafil-treated patients were considered much or very much improved compared to 4.4% (2/45) of placebo patients (P<.001). Erectile function, arousal, ejaculation, orgasm, and overall satisfaction domain measures significantly improved in the sildenafil group compared to the placebo group. Mean depression scores remained consistent with remission (HAM-D score < or =10) in both groups throughout the study duration.
Our findings suggest that sildenafil citrate effectively improves erectile function and other aspects of sexual function in men experiencing sexual dysfunction due to SRI antidepressant use. These improvements may enable patients to maintain adherence to effective antidepressant treatment.

title: Noncoding transcription at enhancers: general principles and functional models.
text: Mammalian genomes display extensive transcriptional activity beyond the boundaries of protein-coding genes. Recent genome-wide studies have revealed that regulatory regions, including enhancers and locus-control regions, are major sites of noncoding transcription. These transcripts, while representing a small proportion of total cellular nonribosomal RNA, may have functional roles in some cases, rather than simply being transcriptional noise at accessible genomic regions. This article aims to provide an overview of the current knowledge on enhancer transcription and its potential implications.

title: Microarray analysis of pneumococcal gene expression during invasive disease.
text: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a significant cause of invasive bacterial infections. This study utilized whole-genome microarrays from The Institute for Genomic Research to investigate the expression of S. pneumoniae genes in vivo for the first time. Total RNA was obtained from pneumococci isolated from infected blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and bacteria attached to a pharyngeal epithelial cell line in vitro. microarray analysis of pneumococcal genes expressed in these models revealed body site-specific patterns of expression for virulence factors, transporters, transcription factors, translation-associated proteins, metabolism, and genes with unknown function. The study confirmed the contributions of several unknown genes to virulence by inserting duplication mutations and challenging mice with the mutants. Additionally, the results were cross-referenced with previous studies that used signature-tagged mutagenesis and differential fluorescence induction to identify genes that may be essential for invasive disease across a broad range of pneumococcal strains.

title: Integration of Smad and MAPK pathways: a link and a linker revisited.
text:
Cells develop by responding to complex mixtures of growth factors, as revealed by the highly dynamic processes of embryogenesis. In this issue, a report sheds light on an essential node for integrating diverse signaling pathways, particularly the Smad and Ras/MAPK pathways, during neural induction in Xenopus (Pera et al. 2003). The study uncovers a previously unknown function of FGF8 and IGF2 in promoting neural differentiation and mesoderm dorsalization by inhibiting BMP signaling.
BMP signaling, which induces differentiation of ectoderm into epidermal cell fates at the expense of neural fates, is ventralizes mesoderm development at the expense of dorsal fates. Conversely, neural differentiation and dorsal mesoderm formation are favored when BMP signaling is attenuated. FGF8 and IGF2, two growth factors that activate the Ras/MAPK pathway, favor neural differentiation and mesoderm dorsalization by inhibiting BMP signaling. This effect is surprising, given that neural induction can also be achieved through BMP signaling. The study raises the question of how FGF8 and IGF2's neuralizing effect is connected to BMP signaling.
The authors found that FGF8 and IGF2 activate the MAPK pathway, which inhibits the BMP signal-transduction factor Smad1. Smad1 is directly phosphorylated by the BMP receptor, resulting in Smad1 activation, and by MAPK in response to EGF, resulting in Smad1 inhibition. Smads 1, 5, and 8 act primarily downstream of BMP receptors, while Smads 2 and 3 downstream of TGF , Activin, and Nodal receptors. Smad proteins have two conserved globular domains—the MH1 and MH2 domains—with different functions. The MH1 domain is involved in DNA binding, while the MH2 domain is involved in binding to cytoplasmic retention factors, activated receptors, nucleoporins in the nuclear pore, and DNA-binding cofactors, coactivators, and corepressors in the nucleus. Receptor-mediated phosphorylation occurs at the carboxy-terminal sequence SXS, enabling the nuclear accumulation of Smads and their association with the shared partner Smad4 to form transcriptional complexes that are interpreted by the cell as a function of the context.
In conclusion, this study sheds light on the essential integration of distinct signaling pathways during neural induction in Xenopus, particularly through the crosstalk between the Smad and Ras/MAPK pathways. Further research into these crosstalk mechanisms may provide important insights into the regulation of developmental processes and diseases.

title: A brief analysis of clinical pharmacy interventions undertaken in an Australian teaching hospital.
text: During a 30-day data capture period, clinical pharmacists identified and analyzed a total of 67 interventions that they had implemented to address drug-related problems in patients. After initial review, 28 intervention reports were excluded from further analysis, leaving 39 interventions for review. Of the remaining interventions, 20 patients (51%) were under the care of a medical unit, and cardiovascular/antithrombotic agents accounted for 17 reports (43.5%). The majority of interventions (n=25, 64%) were implemented during inpatient medication order review by the clinical pharmacist. The most common category of drug-related problem addressed in the interventions was the prescription of inappropriately high doses of the correct drug for the patient (n=17, 43.6%). Technical knowledge deficiencies accounted for less than 25% of all cases.

title: Lethal complications of typhoid-cholera-vaccination. (Case report and review of the literature).
text: Simultaneous administration of typhoid and cholera vaccines resulted in death due to either anaphylactic shock or endotoxic shock in a 36-year-old male. Autopsy findings revealed characteristic signs of shock, as well as chronic interstitial myocarditis. Additionally, fresh histiocytic and lymphocytic nodules were found in the liver, heart, and meninges. A review of the literature on lethal complications following parenteral typhoid vaccinations revealed an increased risk in debilitated individuals, such as those with emaciation, stress, or cold exposure. Most fatalities occurred in individuals who had pre-existing cardiovascular problems, such as the case under investigation. Cardiac failure, Landry's paralysis, renal failure, and disturbances of skin, joints, and intestines may also follow typhoid vaccinations; however, these latter complications are generally not fatal. The patients in this case had many of the conditions that can exacerbate the situation and lead to a lethal outcome. The presentation of this case and the subsequent discussion highlight the importance of vaccination safety, particularly in healthy individuals. It is hoped that this information will help prevent similar fatalities in the future.

title: Functional genomics and proteomics approaches to study the ERBB network in cancer.
text: Advances in functional genomics and proteomics have significantly expanded the scope of biomedical research, offering novel insights into the complexity and regulation of biological processes. The completed human genome sequence has enabled deeper understanding of the intricate interactions between genes and their roles in health and disease. Emerging technologies like RNA interference (RNAi) and protein arrays have enabled researchers to gather comprehensive data on genes and their functions, far beyond single gene analysis. Adopting systems biology approaches, biological processes are increasingly being studied by integrating qualitative and quantitative data on the components involved to create models that can predict the effects of perturbations and refine these models through experimental validation. Here, we elucidate the potential of functional genomics and proteomics by using the ERBB family of growth-factor receptors as a case study to investigate signaling networks and their implications in cancer.

title: Evaluation of spatial filters to create smoothed maps of health data.
text: Spatial filters have been employed as a convenient and intuitive method for creating smoothed disease maps. Using birth weight data from New York State in 1994 and 1995, we compare the effectiveness of traditional filter types, such as fixed geographical sizes, with filters of constant or nearly constant population sizes. The latter are more suitable for mapping disease in areas with diverse population densities, such as New York State. We assess the implications of choosing different population sizes for the filter, the level of smoothing, the ability to detect genuine spatial patterns, and the capacity to remove random spatial noise.

title: Glucose tolerance and blood pressure: long term follow up in middle aged men.
text:
Objective: To investigate the role of glucose tolerance in the development of hypertension.
Design: A retrospective analysis was conducted on the results of a health check-up in a group of clinically healthy middle-aged men in the late 1960s (median year 1968). The subjects were then invited to participate in a primary prevention trial for cardiovascular disease in 1974, when they underwent clinical examination for risk factors. The trial ended in 1979, and the men were re-examined in 1986.
Setting: The study was conducted at the Institute of Occupational Health in Helsinki, Finland, and the second department of medicine at the University of Helsinki.
Subjects: In total, 3490 men born between 1919 and 1934 participated in the health check-up in the late 1960s. Of these, 1815 clinically healthy men were entered into the primary prevention trial for cardiovascular disease in 1974, and 1222 were considered at high risk of cardiovascular disease. Of these, 612 received an intervention and were excluded from the study, leaving 593 men without risk factors.
Methods: The study included all men who did not receive an intervention (n = 1203). In 1979, 1120 men were re-examined, and in 1986, 945 men attended follow-up. Two groups were created for analysis: one consisting of all subjects and the other consisting only of men who were normotensive in 1968 and for whom complete information was available. Interventions included antihypertensive drugs (by 1979) and drugs for hyperglycaemia (by 1986). Main outcome measures included blood glucose concentration one hour after a glucose load, blood pressure, and body weight measured in 1968, 1974, and 1979, and blood pressure and body weight measured in 1986.
Results: Men who were hypertensive in 1986 had significantly higher blood pressures (p < 0.0001) and (after adjustment for body mass index and alcohol intake) significantly higher blood glucose concentrations one hour after a glucose load at all examinations compared with those who were normotensive in 1986. Regression analysis showed that the higher the blood glucose concentration after a glucose load in 1968, the higher the blood pressure during the following years. Those men between the second and third tertiles of blood glucose concentration in 1968 had a significantly higher risk of developing hypertension (odds ratio 1.71, 95% confidence interval 1.05 to 2.77) compared with those below the first tertile.
Conclusion: The study found that men who developed hypertension tended to have shown an increased intolerance to glucose up to 18 years before the clinical manifestation of their disorder. Blood glucose concentration one hour after a glucose load was an independent predictor of future hypertension.

title: At the gates of death.
text: In the context of programmed cell death, or apoptosis, there is a specific pathway that involves the permeabilization of the outer membrane of mitochondria, known as the mitochondrial pathway. This pathway plays a crucial role in the release of certain proteins from the intermembrane space of the mitochondria, which is known as the mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP). The regulation and mediation of this essential step are governed by the Bcl-2 family of proteins. Specifically, the pro-apoptotic proteins Bax and Bak are necessary for MOMP, while the anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 proteins, including Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1, and others, work to prevent MOMP. Recently, an emerging view proposed by Certo et al. in this issue of Cancer Cell has shed light on the mechanisms by which these interactions lead to MOMP and ultimately apoptosis.

title: Structure of human RNase H1 complexed with an RNA/DNA hybrid: insight into HIV reverse transcription.
text: We report the crystal structures of human RNase H1 complexed with an RNA/DNA substrate. In contrast to B. halodurans RNase H1, human RNase H1 features a basic protrusion that forms a DNA-binding channel and, along with the conserved phosphate-binding pocket, confers specificity for the B form and 2'-deoxy DNA. The RNA strand is recognized by four consecutive 2'-OH groups, which are cleaved by a two-metal ion mechanism. Although RNase H1 is overall positively charged, the substrate interface is neutral to acidic, which likely influences the catalytic specificity. The positions of the scissile phosphate and two catalytic metal ions are interdependent and highly coupled. Additionally, modeling of HIV reverse transcriptase (RT) with RNA/DNA in its RNase H active site suggests that the substrate cannot occupy the polymerase active site simultaneously and undergoes a conformational change to toggle between the two catalytic centers. This region offers a potential target for developing HIV-specific inhibitors.

title: A diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging study of brain tissue from patients with migraine.
text:
Objective: To evaluate in vivo using diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging (DT-MRI) the extent of pathological damage in normal-appearing brain tissue (NABT) of migraine patients.
Methods: We acquired dual-echo and DT-MRI scans of the brain from 34 migraine patients and 17 sex and age-matched healthy volunteers. We obtained mean diffusivity (MD) and fractional anisotropy (FA) histograms of NABT from all subjects, measured the peak heights of the MD histogram, and analyzed the average MD and FA values of T2 visible lesions when present.
Results: Compared to healthy volunteers, migraine patients had lower peak heights in the MD histogram of NABT (p=0.02). No significant differences were found in FA histogram-derived metrics between migraine patients and healthy subjects. No significant differences were observed in MD and FA histogram-derived metrics between migraine patients with and without brain MRI lesions or between patients with and without aura.
Conclusions: This study suggests that while brain damage may extend beyond T2 weighted abnormalities in patients with migraine, the severity of these "occult" changes is relatively mild compared to other diseases associated with white matter abnormality.

title: Determination of chloramphenicol residues in milk by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay: improvement by biotin-streptavidin-amplified system.
text: An innovative biotin-streptavidin amplified enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (BA-ELISA) method was developed for the detection of chloramphenicol residues in milk. The incorporation of the biotin-streptavidin system significantly enhanced the sensitivity of the assay, leading to a detection limit of 0.042 +/- 0.006 ng/mL, which is 8-fold more sensitive than the traditional competitive ELISA using the same antibody and coating antigen. The present study explores the amplification mechanism of the biotin-streptavidin system and the key factors influencing sensitivity of detection. The method was successfully applied to determine chloramphenicol residues in milk samples using a simple and rapid extraction procedure, resulting in good recoveries (85.66-109.67%). These findings demonstrate the potential of the biotin-streptavidin system as a valuable tool for the specific detection of trace veterinary drug residues in food samples, and highlight its potential for routine monitoring applications.

title: Wedelolactone exhibits anti-fibrotic effects on human hepatic stellate cell line LX-2.
text:
Wedelolactone, a major coumarin derived from Eclipta prostrata, has been shown to prevent liver damage. However, its effect on hepatic fibrosis remains unexplored. This study aimed to investigate the anti-fibrotic properties of wedelolactone on activated human hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) and elucidate its underlying mechanisms.
Cell viability, collagen production, and apoptosis were analyzed using MTT assay, Hoechst staining, and western blot. Wedelolactone significantly decreased LX-2 cell viability in a time- and dose-dependent manner. Reductions in collagen I and α-smooth muscle actin expressions, two hallmarks of LX-2 activation, were also observed. Apoptosis induction in LX-2 cells was accompanied by decreased Bcl-2 expression and increased Bax expression. Moreover, wedelolactone up-regulated the phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), while suppressing phosphorylation of inhibitor of nuclear factor κB (IκB) and p65, even in the presence of tumor necrosis factor-α stimulation.
In conclusion, wedelolactone exhibited significant inhibition of LX-2 cell activation, which was mediated by inducing Bcl-2 family-mediated apoptosis, up-regulating ERK and JNK phosphorylation, and inhibiting NF-κB activity. These findings suggest that wedelolactone could be a valuable tool for preventing and treating hepatic fibrosis.

title: Adipose stem cells originate from perivascular cells.
text: Recent research has revealed that adipose tissues contain a rich source of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). However, the origin and location of these stem cells within adipose tissue remain unknown, hindering further purification and study. To investigate the origins of adipose stem cells, we used transgenic mice that express green fluorescent protein (GFP) in pericytes, which are a subtype of mesenchymal cells. We harvested adipose stromal cells (ASCs) from these mice and sorted them into GFP-positive and GFP-negative cells using flow cytometry. We then tested the pluripotency of these cells by applying multilineage differentiation tests. Immunofluorescent staining was used to identify GFP-positive cells and determine theirα-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) expression. These cells were then loaded onto a collagen-fibronectin gel with endothelial cells to evaluate their vascularization ability both in vitro and in vivo. Our results showed that all GFP-positive cells in adipose tissue are located near blood vessels. Only GFP-positive cells have multilineage differentiation ability, while GFP-negative cells can only differentiate into adipogenic cells. GFP-positive cells maintained expression of α-SMA during multilineage differentiation. These cells also exhibited the ability to promote endothelial cell vascularization in both in vitro and in vivo cultures. Based on these findings, we conclude that adipose stem cells originate from perivascular cells and congregate around blood vessels.

title: Interferon alpha and zidovudine therapy in adult T-cell leukaemia lymphoma: response and outcome in 15 patients.
text: Adult T-cell leukemia lymphoma (ATLL) is a severe disease caused by the human T-lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-I). Despite responses to interferon alpha (IFN-alpha) and zidovudine (AZT) in some cases, the disease has a poor prognosis. In this study, we treated 15 ATLL patients with IFN and AZT. Eleven patients had acute ATLL, two had lymphoma, and two had smouldering ATLL, with progression. Key features of the patients included organomegaly (14), skin lesions (10), high white blood cell (WBC) count (11), and hypercalcaemia (9). Eleven patients had previously received chemotherapy, and one had received an autograft. At the time of the study, seven patients had progressive disease, and eight were in partial or complete clinical remission. Responses (PR) lasting 2+ to 44+ months were seen in 67%, while 26% did not respond (NR) and one patient was not evaluable. Hypercalcaemia predicted a poor outcome, but the differences were not significant. Eight of the 15 patients have died within 3-41 months of diagnosis. The median survival for the 15 patients was 18 months. Survival for the non-responders (NR) ranged from 4 to 20 months, while six PR patients are alive from 8-82 months from diagnosis. The differences in survival between NR (median: 6 months) and PR (55% of patients alive at 4 years) were statistically significant (P = 0.002). In conclusion, IFN and AZT improves the outcome of ATLL patients and helps maintain responses.

title: Replisome stalling and stabilization at CGG repeats, which are responsible for chromosomal fragility
text: The expansion of CGG repeats in the human genome leads to chromosomal fragility and hereditary neurological disorders. In human and primate cells, replication forks tend to stall at CGG repeats in a length-dependent manner. Interestingly, the yeast proteins Tof1 and Mrc1 have been found to play a crucial role in facilitating replication fork progression through CGG repeats. Curiously, Mrc1's fork-stabilizing function does not rely on its checkpoint activity. As a result, forks that stall at expanded CGG repeats may escape the S-phase checkpoint, leading to chromosomal fragility.

title: Direct reprogramming of fibroblasts into neural stem cells by defined factors.
text: Recent research has revealed that specific sets of transcription factors can directly convert differentiated somatic cells into a different cell type without passing through a pluripotent state. However, the limited potential of the resulting cells restricts their applicability. Our study demonstrates that a combination of transcription factors (Brn4/Pou3f4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc, and E47/Tcf3) can convert mouse fibroblasts into induced neural stem cells (iNSCs) with properties similar to those of wild-type neural stem cells (NSCs). Direct reprogramming of fibroblasts into iNSCs is a gradual process during which the donor transcriptional program is silenced over time. iNSCs exhibit morphology, gene expression, epigenetic features, differentiation potential, and self-renewal capacity similar to those of wild-type NSCs, both in vitro and in vivo. Our findings suggest that differentiated cells can be directly converted into specific somatic stem cell types using defined sets of specific transcription factors, expanding the scope of their potential applications.

title: Epigenetics in lung fibrosis: from pathobiology to treatment perspective.
text: PURPOSE OF REVIEW Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a fatal disease with limited treatment options and extensive molecular changes in the lung parenchyma. Epigenetic factors are believed to contribute to the dysregulation of gene expression in IPF lung, and several lines of evidence support this notion. Importantly, well-established IPF risk factors, such as age, sex, and cigarette smoke exposure, also influence epigenetic marks. This review summarizes recent findings on the interplay between DNA methylation and histone modifications in IPF and their relationship to disease presence and fibroproliferation. RECENT FINDINGS In addition to focused studies on specific gene loci, comprehensive genome-wide analyses of DNA methylation in IPF lung tissue have revealed widespread changes in methylation patterns, which have a profound impact on gene expression. Genetic variants linked to IPF have also been found to harbor differentially methylated regions, suggesting that both genetic and epigenetic factors cooperate to disturb gene expression in IPF lung tissue. SUMMARY While our understanding of the role of epigenetics in IPF is still in its infancy, the potential for using epigenetic marks as diagnostic and therapeutic targets is significant, and recent discoveries in this field are likely to improve our ability to prognosticate and treat this fatal disease.

title: Novel roles for KLF1 in erythropoiesis revealed by mRNA-seq.
text: KLF1 (previously known as EKLF), regulates the development of red blood cells from bi-potent progenitor cells by activating the transcription of a diverse set of genes. Mice lacking KLF1 die in utero before E15 due to severe anemia caused by the insufficient expression of genes controlling hemoglobin production, cell membrane and cytoskeletal integrity, and cell cycle regulation. We recently identified the full spectrum of KLF1 binding sites in vivo through KLF1 ChIP-seq in primary fetal liver erythroid tissue (E14.5). This study provides novel insights into the function of KLF1 as a transcriptional activator and uncovered novel target genes not detectable by traditional microarray technology. We characterized a cis-regulatory module bound by KLF1, GATA1, TAL1, and EP300 that controls a core set of erythroid genes. Additionally, we identified a novel set of erythroid-specific promoters that drive high-level expression of otherwise ubiquitously expressed genes in erythroid cells. Our findings also revealed two novel long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) that are dynamically expressed during erythroid differentiation, and uncovered a role for KLF1 in directing the expression of genes involved in the terminal stages of erythroid maturation.

title: Self-assembling peptides optimize the post-traumatic milieu and synergistically enhance the effects of neural stem cell therapy after cervical spinal cord injury.
text:
Here is a possible revision of the text with some improvements in clarity and readability:
INTRODUCTION: After a spinal cord injury (SCI), the hostile environment can hinder the effectiveness of regenerative therapies. To address this challenge, we hypothesized that optimizing the post-traumatic environment with QL6 self-assembling peptides (SAPs) before transplanting neural precursor cells (NPCs) would enhance their survival, differentiation, and functional recovery.
METHODS: We conducted a rat model study involving 90 Wistar rats that received a clip-compression SCI at C7. The animals were randomly assigned to five groups: NPC, SAP, NPC+SAP, vehicle, and sham. SAPs were injected into the spinal cord 1 day after injury, while NPCs were injected 14 days later. The animals received growth factors over a period of 7 days and were immunosuppressed. Behavioral tests were conducted weekly for 8 weeks, and the corticospinal tract was assessed 9 weeks post-SCI using fiber-tracking.
RESULTS: Our findings revealed that SAP-treated animals had a significantly higher number of surviving NPCs that differentiated into neurons and oligodendrocytes compared to controls. Injecting SAPs alone or in combination with NPCs resulted in smaller intramedullary cysts and a larger volume of preserved tissue, with reduced astrogliosis and chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan deposition. Moreover, the combined treatment group exhibited increased synaptic connectivity. Additionally, corticospinal tract preservation and behavioral outcomes improved with combinatorial treatment.
CONCLUSION: Our study demonstrates that injecting SAPs after SCI can enhance the survival, integration, and differentiation of NPCs, leading to improved functional recovery. By creating a supportive environment for repair and regeneration, SAPs can significantly improve the efficacy of NPC treatment, offering promising results for individuals with SCIs.

title: A direct role for IFN-gamma in regulation of Th1 cell development.
text:
Investigating the relationship between IL-12 and IFN-gamma in promoting Th1 responses, we used naive CD4 cells from TCR transgenics and memory CD4 cells primed in vivo with KLH. Without exogenous IL-12 or IFN-gamma, these cells secreted varying levels of IL-2 and IFN-gamma. The amount of IFN-gamma secreted by the cells correlated with the level of endogenous IFN-gamma produced in primary cultures, and anti-IFN-gamma significantly inhibited the development of IFN-gamma-producing effectors.
Under optimal TCR stimulation conditions and costimulation, endogenous IFN-gamma, without IL-12, was sufficient to elicit Th1 cells via an autocrine mechanism. However, with suboptimal stimulation, exogenous rIL-12 or rIFN-gamma was required for Th1 development, with rIL-12 being more effective than rIFN-gamma. The enhanced autocrine production of IFN-gamma by rIL-12 played a crucial role in optimal Th1 development.
Our findings suggest that both IL-12 and IFN-gamma can regulate Th1 development, but the extent of differentiation depends on the strength of T cell stimulation and the availability of both APC-derived IL-12 and autocrine IFN-gamma. The relative contributions of these cytokines to Th1 development are determined by the conditions of T cell stimulation, and their synergistic actions are essential for optimal Th1 differentiation.

title: Neuregulin 1 promotes excitatory synapse development and function in GABAergic interneurons.
text: Neuregulin 1 (NRG1) and its receptor, ErbB4, have been identified as susceptibility genes for schizophrenia, but the underlying mechanisms of their dysfunction are not well understood. Although ErbB4 is enriched in GABAergic interneurons, the role of NRG1 in excitatory synapse formation in these neurons is poorly understood. Our study found that NRG1 significantly increased the number and size of PSD-95 puncta and the frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) in GABAergic interneurons, indicating that NRG1 stimulates the formation of new synapses and strengthens existing ones. In contrast, NRG1 had no effect on either the number or size of excitatory synapses in glutamatergic neurons, suggesting that its synaptogenic effect is specific to GABAergic interneurons. Treatment with ecto-ErbB4, which diminished both the number and size of excitatory synapses, suggested that endogenous NRG1 may be critical for basal synapse formation. NRG1 may stabilize PSD-95 in a manner that requires the tyrosine kinase activity of ErbB4. Furthermore, deletion of ErbB4 in parvalbumin-positive interneurons led to reduced frequency and amplitude of mEPSCs, providing in vivo evidence that ErbB4 is important in excitatory synaptogenesis in interneurons. Together, our findings suggest a novel synaptogenic role of NRG1 in excitatory synapse development, possibly via stabilizing PSD-95, and that this effect is specific to GABAergic interneurons. Given the association of NRG1 and ErbB4 with schizophrenia and dysfunction of the GABAergic system in this disorder, these resultsmay provide insight into its potential pathological mechanism.

title: Tolerance rather than immunity protects from Helicobacter pylori-induced gastric preneoplasia.
text:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Chronic infection with the bacterial pathogen Helicobacter pylori can lead to various gastric disorders, including chronic gastritis, gastric adenocarcinoma, and malignancies. However, only a subset of infected individuals will develop overt disease, while others remain asymptomatic despite lifelong colonization. This study aims to investigate the differential susceptibility to H pylori infection across and within populations.
METHODS: We have developed a C57BL/6 mouse model of H pylori infection with a strain that can deliver the virulence factor cytotoxin-associated gene A (CagA) into host cells through the activity of a Cag-pathogenicity island-encoded type IV secretion system.
RESULTS: Mice infected at 5-6 weeks of age with CagA(+)H pylori rapidly develop gastritis, gastric atrophy, epithelial hyperplasia, and metaplasia in a type IV secretion system-dependent manner. In contrast, mice infected during the neonatal period with the same strain are protected from preneoplastic lesions. This protection is mediated by H pylori-specific peripheral immunologic tolerance, which requires transforming growth factor-β signaling and is controlled by long-lived, inducible regulatory T cells. This tolerance develops in the neonatal period due to a biased ratio of T-regulatory to T-effector cells, and is favored by prolonged low-dose exposure to antigen.
CONCLUSIONS: Using our novel CagA(+)H pylori infection model, we report here that the development of tolerance to H pylori protects against gastric cancer precursor lesions. The age at initial infection may therefore explain the differential susceptibility of infected individuals to H pylori-associated disease manifestations.

title: Impaired mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation and insulin resistance in aging: novel protective role of glutathione.
text:
The following is a rewritten version of the text with some changes to improve readability and clarity:
Aging is linked to impaired fasted oxidation of nonesterified fatty acids (NEFA), which suggests a mitochondrial defect. Additionally, aging is associated with a deficiency of glutathione (GSH), an important antioxidant in mitochondria. This study aimed to determine whether GSH deficiency in aging contributes to impaired mitochondrial NEFA oxidation and insulin resistance, and whether GSH restoration reverses these defects.
Three studies were conducted:
* In 82-week-old C57BL/6 mice, the effect of naturally occurring GSH deficiency and its restoration on mitochondrial (13) C1 -palmitate oxidation and glucose metabolism was compared with 22-week-old C57BL/6 mice.
* In 20-week C57BL/6 mice, the effect of GSH depletion on mitochondrial oxidation of (13) C1 -palmitate and glucose metabolism was studied.
* The effect of GSH deficiency and its restoration on fasted NEFA oxidation and insulin resistance was studied in GSH-deficient elderly humans, and compared with GSH-replete young humans.
Chronic GSH deficiency in old mice and elderly humans was associated with decreased fasted mitochondrial NEFA oxidation and insulin resistance, and these defects were reversed with GSH restoration. Acute depletion of GSH in young mice resulted in lower mitochondrial NEFA oxidation, but did not alter glucose metabolism. These data suggest that GSH regulates mitochondrial NEFA oxidation and insulin resistance in aging. Chronic GSH deficiency promotes impaired NEFA oxidation and insulin resistance, and GSH restoration reverses these defects. Supplementing diets of elderly humans with cysteine and glycine to correct GSH deficiency could provide significant metabolic benefits.

title: Control of central and peripheral tolerance by Aire.
text: The elimination of self-reactive thymocytes relies on the expression of tissue-specific antigens by medullary thymic epithelial cells. The protein autoimmune regulator (Aire) plays a crucial role in activating these antigens, and the absence of even one Aire-induced tissue-specific antigen in the thymus can lead to autoimmunity in the target organ. Recently, Aire protein has been detected in peripheral lymphoid organs, suggesting that it also plays a complementary role in these areas. In these peripheral sites, Aire regulates the expression of a unique group of tissue-specific antigens that are distinct from those expressed in the thymus. Additionally, transgenic antigen expression in extrathymic Aire-expressing cells (eTACs) can induce deletional tolerance, but the immunological significance of Aire-dependent, endogenous tissue-specific antigens remains unclear.

title: Congenital Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism: A Trait Shared by Several Complex Neurodevelopmental Disorders.
text: Reproductive function is regulated by the gonadotropic axis, which is controlled by a complex neural network in the hypothalamus. This network matures postnatally through a neurodevelopmental program that starts in fetal life and ends at puberty. Disruptions to this program can lead to congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH), characterized by the absence of puberty. For many years, the genetic basis of CHH has been the focus of attention, with the majority of cases attributed to isolated genetic defects. However, recent advances in genomics have revealed a link between CHH and complex neurological dysfunctions, often associated with rare syndromes. This review aims to summarize the clinical and genetic features of syndromic CHH, highlighting the interplay between the ubiquitin pathway, synaptic proteins, and CHH. Additionally, unexpected mutations in genes encoding nucleolar proteins will be discussed.

title: Elevated expression of miR-24-3p is a potentially adverse prognostic factor in colorectal adenocarcinoma.
text:
Title: Prognostic Significance of miR-24-3p in Colorectal Adenocarcinoma: A Retrospective Cohort Study
Objective: miRNAs are altered in cancer, including colorectal adenocarcinoma. miR-24-3p has been implicated in cancer-related processes. We sought to determine the diagnostic and prognostic significance of miR-24-3p expression in colorectal adenocarcinoma.
Design and Methods: Total RNA was obtained from 182 colorectal adenocarcinoma tissues and 86 non-cancerous colorectal mucosae using an in-house reverse transcription real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) method based on SYBR Green chemistry, with SNORD43 (RNU43) as a reference gene. The study included 182 colorectal adenocarcinoma tissues and 86 non-cancerous colorectal mucosae.
Results: miR-24-3p expression levels were not significantly different between colorectal adenocarcinoma and non-cancerous colorectal mucosae, making it unsuitable for diagnostic purposes. However, high miR-24-3p expression predicted poor disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) of colorectal adenocarcinoma patients. Multivariate Cox regression analysis confirmed that miR-24-3p overexpression is an independent predictor of relapse in colorectal adenocarcinoma, retaining its unfavorable prognostic value in subgroups of patients with T3 and M0 disease, as well as those not treated with radiotherapy.
Conclusion: Strong expression of miR-24-3p predicts poor DFS and OS of colorectal adenocarcinoma patients, independently of clinicopathological parameters used for prognosis in this human malignancy.

title: Reforming the health sector in developing countries: the central role of policy analysis.
text:
Policy analysis has been an established field in industrialized nations, yet its application to developing countries has been limited, with the health sector being particularly overlooked. This is unexpected, as there is a recognized crisis in health systems and numerous recommendations for policy reforms. However, little attention has been paid to how countries can effectively implement these reforms, including the actors involved, the processes required for change, and the context within which policy is developed.
Conventional policy analysis often focuses primarily on the content of reform, neglecting the importance of understanding the processes involved in implementing policy changes. This can lead to a failure to address the underlying reasons why desired policy outcomes do not materialize.
This paper argues that a comprehensive approach to policy analysis is necessary, one that takes into account the actors involved at various levels (international, national, and sub-national), the contingent processes involved in implementing change, and the broader context in which policy is developed. By doing so, policy analysis can not only analyze the policy process but also inform the planning of effective policy interventions.
The paper is organized into four sections. The first section sets the stage by highlighting the shift from consensus to conflict in health policy and the resulting need for a greater emphasis on policy analysis. The second section provides a definition of policy analysis and its key components. The third section examines what other disciplines have contributed to the field of policy analysis, and the final section offers suggestions for how policy analysis can be used to both analyze and plan policy interventions.

title: The processing of Holliday junctions by BLM and WRN helicases is regulated by p53.
text: BLM, WRN, and p53 are integral to the homologous DNA recombination pathway. These DNA structure-specific helicases, BLM and WRN, unwind Holliday junctions (HJ), which could potentially inhibit inappropriate homologous recombination during DNA replication. In vitro, purified, recombinant p53 binds to these helicases and reduces their ability to unwind synthetic HJ. The p53 248W mutant reduces the binding of both to HJ, and the p53 273H mutant loses this ability. Of note, full-length p53 and a C-terminal polypeptide (residues 373-383) inhibit the BLM and WRN helicase activities, but phosphorylation at Ser(376) or Ser(378) completely abolishes this inhibition. Interestingly, following blockage of DNA replication, Ser(15) phospho-p53, BLM, and RAD51 colocalize in nuclear foci at sites likely to contain DNA replication intermediates in cells. These findings demonstrate a novel mechanism for p53-mediated regulation of DNA recombinational repair that involves p53 post-translational modifications and functional protein-protein interactions with BLM and WRN DNA helicases.

title: Trim and fill: A simple funnel-plot-based method of testing and adjusting for publication bias in meta-analysis.
text: We investigate recent nonparametric methods for estimating the number of undiscovered studies that could have influenced the outcome of a meta-analysis. These straightforward rank-based data augmentation techniques take advantage of funnel plots and offer potent tests for detecting publication bias. By accounting for missing studies, we find that the estimated overall effect size is approximately accurate, and the expanded confidence intervals for the effect size show a notable improvement in coverage, frequently recovering the nominal confidence levels in full. To illustrate the trim and fill approach, we apply it to existing meta-analyses in clinical trials and psychometrics.

title: Familial Barrett's esophagus associated with adenocarcinoma.
text: A family with six instances of Barrett's esophagus spanning three generations has been reported. Notably, the condition only affected males within the family, and there were three instances of associated adenocarcinoma. The mode of inheritance is consistent with an autosomal dominant pattern with near complete penetrance. This familial case of Barrett's esophagus and associated adenocarcinomas is compared with other reported cases in the literature.

title: Development of an insect model for the in vivo pathogenicity testing of yeasts.
text:
In order to investigate the feasibility of using the insect Galleria mellonella as a model system for in vivo pathogenicity testing of yeast isolates, we conducted a series of experiments. The goal of this work was to determine whether G. mellonella could serve as a suitable substitute for mammalian models, which are commonly employed in conventional in vivo assays to evaluate the relative pathogenicity of yeast isolates.
To achieve this, we inoculated the haemolymph of G. mellonella larvae with different doses of stationary phase yeasts from the genus Candida, including the pathogenic species Candida albicans and a range of other Candida species. The larvae were then incubated at 30 degrees C for 72 hours, during which time we monitored their survival. Our findings revealed that G. mellonella can indeed be killed by both pathogenic and non-pathogenic Candida species, although the kill kinetics varied depending on the species of yeast used. Specifically, we found that clinical and laboratory isolates of C. albicans were more pathogenic than the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
Our results suggest that G. mellonella may be employed as a reliable model system for in vivo pathogenicity testing, which could potentially reduce the need for mammalian models and alleviate suffering associated with their use. Additionally, the ease of culturing and manipulating G. mellonella larvae makes them an attractive alternative to mammals for certain types of experiments.

title: Use of TLS parameters to model anisotropic displacements in macromolecular refinement.
text: A crucial aspect of macromolecular refinement is selecting model parameters that accurately describe experimental data while maintaining a reasonable ratio of data to parameters. This is particularly important when it comes to choosing atomic displacement parameters, as the shift from individual isotropic to individual anisotropic refinement results in a sixfold increase in the number of required displacement parameters. To reduce the number of refinement parameters, collective variables can be employed instead of individual atomic variables, with one simplified example being the TLS parameterization for describing the translation, libration, and screw-rotation displacements of a pseudo-rigid body. This article describes the implementation of the TLS parameterization in the macromolecular refinement program REFMAC. The derivatives of the residual with respect to the TLS parameters are expanded in terms of the derivatives with respect to individual anisotropic U values, which can be calculated using a fast Fourier transform technique. As a result, TLS refinement is fast and can be performed routinely. Examples of TLS refinement are provided for glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) and a transcription activator GerE, both of which have data available only up to 2.0 Å resolution, making individual anisotropic refinement impractical. GAPDH was refined using between one and four TLS groups in the asymmetric unit, while GerE was refined with six TLS groups. In both cases, the inclusion of TLS parameters led to improved refinement statistics, including significant improvements in R and free R values. Additionally, both GAPDH and GerE have multiple molecules in the asymmetric unit, with significant differences in displacement parameters between molecules. The TLS parameterization effectively accounts for these differences, resulting in residual local displacements that are similar between molecules and can be fit with NCS restraints.

title: Sequence features surrounding the translation initiation sites assigned on the genome sequence of Synechocystis sp. strain PCC6803 by amino-terminal protein sequencing.
text:
To identify the sequence features surrounding the translation initiation sites on the genome of Synechocystis sp. strain 6803, total proteins were separated by two-dimensional electrophoresis and the amino-terminal sequences of the most abundant protein spots were determined. By comparing the determined amino-terminal sequences with the entire genome sequence, the translation initiation sites of 72 proteins were successfully located on the genome. The sequence features found near the translation initiation sites were as follows:
1. In addition to the commonly used initiation codons ATG, GTG, and TTG, evidence of the rare initiation codon ATT was also observed.
2. The core sequences (GAGG, GGAG, and AGGA) of the Shine-Dalgarno sequence were found in the appropriate position preceding the 35 initiation sites (48.6%).
3. A specific sequence surrounding the initiation codons, which was formulated as 5'-YY[...]R-3', where Y and R denote pyrimidine and purine nucleotides, respectively, and three dots represent the initiation codons, was identified.
The results of this study will provide valuable information for improving gene-finding software, and the approach used in this study can be applied for comprehensive analysis of cellular protein expression profiles.

title: Deregulated DNA polymerase beta induces chromosome instability and tumorigenesis.
text: To achieve the genetic alterations that define cancer, tumor cells must develop increased mutability due to a malfunction of a network of genetic stability systems, such as cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, and high fidelity of DNA synthesis during DNA replication. The most common genetic change observed in many types of solid tumors is numeric chromosomal imbalance, or aneuploidy. We find that ectopic expression of DNA polymerase beta, an error-prone enzyme frequently over-expressed in human tumors, leads to aneuploidy, abnormal centrosome localization of gamma-tubulin protein during mitosis, a weak mitotic checkpoint, and the promotion of tumorigenesis in nude immunodeficient mice. Therefore, altered polymerase beta expression appears to trigger significant genetic changes associated with a malignant phenotype.

title: Combinatorial signaling by Sonic hedgehog and Wnt family members induces myogenic bHLH gene expression in the somite.
text: In previous studies, we have shown that a combination of signals from the neural tube and the floor plate/notochord complex cooperatively activate the expression of myogenic bHLH genes and myogenic differentiation markers in unspecified somites. In this investigation, we demonstrate that Sonic hedgehog (Shh), which is expressed in the floor plate/notochord, and a subset of Wnt family members (Wnt-1, Wnt-3, and Wnt-4), which are expressed in dorsal regions of the neural tube, mimic the muscle-inducing function of these tissues. Combinatorially, Shh and either Wnt-1 or Wnt-3 are sufficient to induce myogenesis in somitic tissue in vitro, suggesting that myotome formation in vivo may be directed by the coordinated action of Shh secreted by ventral midline tissues (floor plate and notochord) and Wnt ligands produced by the dorsal neural tube.

title: Advances in osteoclast biology: old findings and new insights from mouse models
text: Maintaining adequate bone mass requires the controlled and timely removal of old, damaged bone tissue, which is performed by highly specialized cells called osteoclasts. Over the past 15 years, significant progress has been made in understanding the origin, differentiation, and activation of osteoclasts, primarily through the use of genetically modified mouse models. These models have revealed key factors involved in normal osteoclast function, including the RANK-RANKL-OPG system, ion transport and cellular attachment mechanisms, and the importance of matrix-degrading enzymes in resorptive activity. This review focuses on the principal observations in osteoclast biology derived from genetic mouse models and highlights emerging concepts that suggest how osteoclasts contribute to maintaining adequate bone mass and integrity throughout life.

title: DNA methylation in embryonic stem cells.
text: Embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are unique, self-renewing cells with the ability to differentiate into various cell types. These cells hold great promise for applications such as cell therapy, drug development, disease modeling, and the study of cellular differentiation. Unlocking the secrets of how ESCs function requires an understanding of the complex interplay between epigenetics, genetics, and gene expression. One of the most well-known epigenetic factors is DNA methylation, which plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression. This mechanism is particularly important in imprinted genes and X-chromosome inactivation, where DNA methylation of promoter regions leads to the repression of gene expression. Interestingly, studies have shown that the DNA methylation patterns of pluripotence-associated genes such as Nanog and Oct4/Pou5f1 differ between pluripotent and differentiated cells. It is clear that tight regulation of DNA methylation is essential for normal development. As more associations between aberrant DNA methylation and disease are reported, there is an increasing demand for high-throughput approaches for DNA methylation analysis. This article highlights some of these methods and discusses recent DNA methylation studies on ESCs.

title: Reserves, functional, immunoregulatory, and cytogenetic properties of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells in patients with myelodysplastic syndromes.
text: The function of bone marrow (BM) stroma supporting hematopoiesis has been implicated in the pathophysiology of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). This study aimed to investigate whether BM stroma progenitors, specifically mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), are primarily affected in MDS by evaluating their reserves, functional properties, and cytogenetic characteristics compared to BM hematopoietic cells in patients with de novo MDS (n=13). While the number and differentiation potential of MSCs towards adipocytes, chondrocytes, and osteoblasts did not significantly differ between patient and normal MSCs (n=20), patient MSCs failed to produce proinflammatory or growth-promoting cytokines and did not display cytogenetic abnormalities typical of hematopoietic cells. However, occasional patient and normal MSC cultures displayed irrelevant chromosomal alterations (trisomies 5 and 7) with uncertain pathophysiological significance. In contrast to controls, patient MSCs displayed impaired proliferative and clonogenic potential with passages, which may represent a nonspecific abnormality associated with the chronic inflammatory process present in patients' BM. These findings suggest that BM MSCs from MDS patients do not constitute the main cellular source contributing to the inflammatory marrow microenvironment.

title: Symmetric signalling within asymmetric dimers of the Staphylococcus aureus receptor histidine kinase AgrC.
text: The regulation of virulence in Staphylococcus aureus is primarily mediated by the accessory gene regulator (agr) quorum-sensing system. The AgrC receptor, a histidine kinase, senses its autoinducing peptide (AIP) ligand and generates an intracellular signal that leads to the secretion of virulence factors. Although the agr system is well-studied, the mechanism of AgrC activation remains poorly understood. Using co-immunoprecipitation analysis and intermolecular complementation of receptor mutants, we discovered that AgrC forms ligand-independent dimers that undergo trans-autophosphorylation upon interaction with AIP. Surprisingly, addition of specific AIPs to AgrC mutant dimers with only one functional sensor domain resulted in symmetric activation of both kinase domains, regardless of the asymmetry of the sensor domain. Furthermore, mutant dimers containing one constitutive protomer showed ligand-independent activity, regardless of which protomer was kinase deficient. These findings suggest that signaling through either individual AgrC protomer leads to symmetric activation of both kinase domains, likely through a mechanism involving dimer interface signaling. This mechanism may be an important way for dimeric quorum-sensing receptors to rapidly respond to signals upon detection.

title: Attachment of the ubiquitin-related protein Urm1p to the antioxidant protein Ahp1p.
text: Urm1p is a protein that plays a role in post-translational modifications by attaching to other proteins. This process, known as urmylation, has been associated with the budding process and nutrient sensing. In this study, we identified the first in vivo target of the urmylation pathway: the antioxidant protein Ahp1p. The attachment of Urm1p to Ahp1p requires the E1 enzyme Uba4p, which is part of the urmylation pathway. When the urmylation pathway is missing certain components, cells become sensitive to thiol-specific oxidants, suggesting that urmylation may play a role in the response to oxidative stress. Furthermore, treatment with thiol-specific oxidants affects the abundance of Ahp1p-Urm1p conjugates, leading us to propose that the conjugation of Urm1p to Ahp1p may regulate the function of Ahp1p in the antioxidant stress response in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

title: Sulfasalazine in the treatment of spondylarthropathy. A randomized, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
text:
Objective: To assess the effectiveness and safety of sulfasalazine (SSZ) in treating spondylarthropathy.
Methods: This was a 6-month, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicenter study involving patients with spondylarthropathy who had not responded to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Participants were randomly assigned to receive either SSZ (3g/day) or placebo. The primary efficiency outcomes were evaluated using physician and patient assessments, pain, and morning stiffness. The analysis was conducted on the intent-to-treat and completer patient populations, and the time course of effect was analyzed in the completer patient population.
Results: Of the 351 enrolled patients, 263 (75%) completed the 6-month treatment period. The withdrawal rates were 35 (20%) and 53 (30%) in the placebo and SSZ groups, respectively. In the intent-to-treat analysis of end point efficacy, the between-treatment difference did not reach statistical significance for any of the 4 primary outcome variables. However, laboratory markers of inflammation showed statistically significant changes in favor of SSZ.
