Subgroup analysis revealed the most impressive effects in patients with psoriatic arthritis, including improvements in the 4 primary efficacy variables and secondary efficacy variables such as the number of inflamed joints. Adverse events were more frequent in the SSZ group than the placebo group, but they were all transient or reversible after cessation of treatment.
Conclusion: The results of this study suggest that SSZ is more effective than placebo in treating active spondylarthropathy, particularly in patients with psoriatic arthritis. While adverse events were more common in the SSZ group, they were generally mild and reversible. These findings support the use of SSZ as a treatment option for patients with spondylarthropathy who have not responded to NSAIDs.

title: A randomized trial of aspirin to prevent colorectal adenomas in patients with previous colorectal cancer.
text:
BACKGROUND: Previous studies in animals and humans have suggested that regular aspirin use may reduce the risk of colorectal adenomas, which are the precursor cells to most colorectal cancers. To confirm these findings and determine the effectiveness of aspirin in preventing colorectal adenomas, we conducted a randomized, double-blind clinical trial.
METHODS: We randomly assigned 635 patients with a history of colorectal cancer to receive either 325 mg of aspirin per day or a placebo. We monitored the incidence of colorectal adenomas and the time to their detection during regular colonoscopic examinations. We adjusted our analyses for age, sex, cancer stage, the number of colonoscopic examinations, and the time to the first colonoscopy.
RESULTS: A total of 517 patients had at least one colonoscopic examination within a median of 12.8 months after randomization. Compared to the placebo group, patients taking aspirin had a lower incidence of colorectal adenomas (17% versus 27%, P=0.004). The average number of adenomas per patient was also lower in the aspirin group (0.30+/-0.87 versus 0.49+/-0.99, P=0.003 by the Wilcoxon test). The adjusted relative risk of any recurrent adenoma in the aspirin group was 0.65 (95% CI, 0.46 to 0.91). Additionally, the time to the detection of a first adenoma was longer in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (hazard ratio for the detection of a new polyp, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.43 to 0.94; P=0.022).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that daily aspirin use is associated with a significant reduction in the incidence of colorectal adenomas in patients with a history of colorectal cancer. These results provide evidence that aspirin may be a useful adjunct in colorectal cancer prevention.

title: The Wilms tumour suppressor protein WT1 (+KTS isoform) binds alpha-actinin 1 mRNA via its zinc-finger domain.
text:
Mutations in the WT1 gene are associated with developmental disorders that affect the urinary and reproductive systems, as well as various types of cancer, including Wilms tumor, acute myeloid leukemia, and breast and prostate cancers. The WT1 protein belongs to the early growth response family of zinc-finger transcription factors. Unlike other zinc-finger proteins, WT1 undergoes an evolutionarily conserved alternative splicing event that inserts a tripeptide, KTS, between zinc fingers 3 and 4. The KTS isoform of WT1 interacts with DNA and regulates transcription, while the -KTS isoform interacts with splice factors and RNA in vitro and in vivo. Although candidate DNA targets have been identified, the physiological mRNA targets of WT1 remain to be determined.
In this study, we investigated the distribution of WT1 in ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes in nuclear extracts from M15 cells, a mouse mesonephric fetal kidney cell line. We found that WT1 co-fractionated with the splice factor PSF in large RNP particles greater than or equal to 2 megadaltons. Additionally, we found that PSF co-immunoprecipitated with WT1, suggesting a functional interaction between these two multifunctional proteins.
Using a yeast three-hybrid library constructed from the co-immunoprecipitated RNA, we identified the first likely physiological mRNA target of WT1, alpha-actinin 1 (ACTN1) mRNA. We found that the WT1 zinc-finger domain (+KTS) binds to the start codon of ACTN1 mRNA in vitro, and a band shift assay confirmed this interaction. ACTN1 is a key component of the cytoskeleton and is involved in cell signaling and differentiation, and our findings suggest that WT1 may play a role in regulating its expression.

title: How safe are psychiatric medications after a voluntary overdose?
text:
Background: This study examined the use of psychiatric medications in suicide attempts and their potential lethality.
Methods: The study analyzed 563 suicide attempts in a general hospital in Madrid over a two-year period (1996-1998). Data on medication overdose and dosage were collected, and the ratio between the dose taken and the maximum recommended dose was used to assess medication toxicity.
Results: The study found that benzodiazepines were the most commonly used medications in suicide attempts (65%), followed by new antidepressants (11%), tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) (10%), and antipsychotics (8%). The study also revealed that patients prescribed antipsychotics were at a higher risk of overdose compared to those prescribed the other medications. Furthermore, 47% of TCA overdoses were potentially lethal. However, the study showed that all patients who overdosed on psychiatric medications fully recovered and were discharged without any lasting effects.
Discussion: The study suggests that psychiatric medications, particularly benzodiazepines, new antidepressants, and antipsychotics, are relatively safe when used for self-poisoning. However, if patients with mental illnesses are not properly treated, there is a higher risk of suicide.
Conclusion: Based on the findings of this study, it appears that prescribing psychiatric medications, particularly the new ones, may be preferable than withholding them due to an excessive fear of a lethal overdose.

title: Health benefits, costs, and cost-effectiveness of earlier eligibility for adult antiretroviral therapy and expanded treatment coverage: a combined analysis of 12 mathematical models.
text:
New World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines recommend initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV-positive individuals with CD4 cell counts ≤500 cells/µL, a higher threshold than previously advised. Country policymakers must deliberate whether to broaden ART eligibility in light of these revisions.
To evaluate the potential health impact, costs, and cost-effectiveness of different adult ART eligibility criteria, we employed multiple independent mathematical models in four settings: South Africa, Zambia, India, and Vietnam. Over a 20-year period, these models analyzed the consequences of expanding eligibility to include individuals with CD4 counts ≤500 cells/µL or all HIV-positive adults compared to the previous recommendation of ART initiation with CD4 counts ≤350 cells/µL. We assessed costs from a health system perspective and calculated the incremental cost per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted ($/DALY) to compare competing strategies. Strategies were considered 'very cost-effective' if the $/DALY was less than the country's per capita gross domestic product (GDP) and 'cost-effective' if $/DALY was less than three times per capita GDP.
Our findings indicate that expanding ART eligibility to CD4 counts ≤500 cells/µL in South Africa resulted in a cost per DALY averted ranging from $237 to $1691 compared to 2010 guidelines. Similarly, expanding eligibility in Zambia was found to be cost-effective, with costs per DALY averted ranging from $749 to $1691. Results were similar in scenarios with substantially expanded treatment access and for expanding eligibility to all HIV-positive adults. Expanding treatment coverage in the general population was found to be cost-effective in India, with costs per DALY averted ranging from $131 to $241. In Vietnam, eligibility for all HIV-positive persons cost $290 per DALY. In concentrated epidemics, expanded access among key populations was also found to be cost-effective.
In conclusion, the new WHO guidelines suggest that earlier ART eligibility is likely to be very cost-effective in low- and middle-income settings, although these questions should be revisited as further information becomes available. Scaling-up ART should be considered among other high-priority health interventions competing for health budgets. Funding for this study was provided by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation and the World Health Organization.

title: Chronic daily headache: long-term prognosis following inpatient treatment with repetitive IV DHE.
text:
In this study, we retrospectively examined the long-term (2-year) outcomes of 50 patients with chronic daily headache (CDH) who were admitted to an inpatient headache program due to overuse of analgesics, ergotamine, or both. The patients had been detoxified, given repetitive intravenous dihydroergotamine (IV DHE) and prophylactic medications as part of the program, and were headache-free on this regimen at the time of discharge. At the time of admission, 37 patients had transformed migraine (TM), 12 had new daily persistent headache (NDPH), and 1 had chronic tension-type headache; 29 of the patients with TM, 7 of those with NDPH, and the single patient with chronic tension-type headache had coexistent migraine. The patients were found to be abusing various substances, including caffeine, acetaminophen, aspirin, ibuprofen, narcotics, and ergotamine. Twenty patients were using preventive medication at the time of admission. Follow-up evaluations were conducted at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months after discharge, and 43 patients were analyzed at 3 months. Of these, 44% had an excellent or good result, and 28% had a fair result. At 24 months, 39 patients were analyzed, and 59% had a good or excellent result, while 28% had a fair result. Five patients were overusing analgesics, and four of them were doing poorly.
In summary, this study demonstrates the long-term effectiveness of an inpatient headache program in managing chronic daily headache due to overuse of analgesics, ergotamine, or both. The program resulted in significant improvements in headache frequency and duration, as well as reductions in the use of analgesics. However, some patients continued to experience headaches and were found to be overusing analgesics, highlighting the need for continued monitoring and management of headache symptoms.

title: Survival in a case of massive paraquat ingestion.
text: Severe exposure to the herbicide paraquat often leads to fatal outcomes, either due to gastrointestinal lesions resulting from caustic injury, shock, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), or due to the progressive development of pulmonary fibrosis associated with persistent hypoxemia. In a recent case of suicidal paraquat ingestion in a 59-year-old male patient, many of these indicators of poor prognosis were observed. The patient received early digestive decontamination and hemodialysis, followed by antioxidant therapy, including the administration of deferoxamine (100 mg/kg over 24 hours) and a continuous infusion of acetylcysteine (300 mg/kg/day for 3 weeks). While the patient developed nonoliguric acute renal failure, mild liver function abnormalities, and an impairment of carbon monoxide (CO) transfer factor, there were no respiratory complaints noted. Renal and hepatic disturbances resolved within 1 month, but CO transfer factor remained altered 14 months later. This observation suggests that early administration of antioxidant therapy, including deferoxamine and acetylcysteine, may be beneficially combined with measures aimed at preventing digestive absorption or enhancing elimination to limit systemic toxicity in potentially fatal paraquat poisoning.

title: Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase is a cytosolic DNA sensor that activates the type I interferon pathway.
text: The presence of DNA within the cytoplasm of mammalian cells serves as an alert signal, triggering the body's immune system to respond with the production of type I interferons. Specifically, the DNA induces the production of cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate (cyclic GMP-AMP, or cGAMP), which then binds to and activates the adaptor protein STING. Through the use of biochemical fractionation and quantitative mass spectrometry, we identified a cGAMS (cGAS) enzyme, which belongs to the nucleotidyltransferase family. Overexpression of cGAS resulted in the activation of the transcription factor IRF3, leading to the induction of interferon-β in a STING-dependent manner. Conversely, knockdown of cGAS inhibited IRF3 activation and interferon-β induction brought on by DNA transfection or DNA virus infection. cGAS was found to bind to DNA within the cytoplasm and catalyze cGAMP synthesis, thereby indicating that it is a cytosolic DNA sensor that triggers the production of interferons through the production of cGAMP.

title: Eating pathology, emotion regulation, and emotional overeating in obese adults with Binge Eating Disorder.
text:
The current study aimed to investigate the relationship between emotional regulation, emotional overeating, and general eating problems in a sample of adults seeking treatment for Binge Eating Disorder (BED).
METHODS: The sample consisted of 326 adults (248 women, 78 men) who were obese and met the DSM-IV-TR criteria for BED. Prior to treatment, participants completed the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), Emotional Overeating Questionnaire (EOQ), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), and Eating Disorder Examination-Questionnaire (EDE-Q) as part of a larger assessment battery.
RESULTS: Hierarchical regression analyses showed that difficulties with emotion regulation accounted for unique variance in both emotional overeating and general eating problems above and beyond sex and negative affect.
DISCUSSION: These findings suggest that emotion regulation may play a crucial role in the maintenance of emotional overeating and eating problems in obese adults with BED.

title: Monoallelic expression and methylation of imprinted genes in human and mouse embryonic germ cell lineages.
text: Epigenetic modification known as imprinting leads to the expression of some genes in only one of their copies, and altered imprinting is believed to be a hindrance to human stem cell transplantation, as studies have shown that epigenetic marks are unstable in mouse embryonic germ (EG) and stem (ES) cells. However, direct examination of stem cell imprinting in humans has not been conducted until now. Our findings reveal that three imprinted genes, TSSC5, H19, and SNRPN, display monoallelic expression in in vitro differentiated human EG-derived cells, while a fourth gene, IGF2, exhibits partially relaxed imprinting with a ratio ranging from 4:1 to 5:1, similar to that observed in normal somatic cells. Additionally, normal methylation of an imprinting control region (ICR) that regulates H19 and IGF2 imprinting suggests that imprinting may not be a significant epigenetic barrier to human EG cell transplantation. Furthermore, we were able to establish an in vitro mouse model of genomic imprinting by generating EG cells from 8.5-day embryos of an interspecific cross, resulting in undifferentiated cells exhibiting biallelic expression followed by preferential expression of one parental allele after differentiation. This model allows for manipulation of epigenetic modifications in cultured EG cells, a feat that may be difficult to achieve in human stem cell studies.

title: Functional in vivo interactions between JNK1 and JNK2 isoforms in obesity and insulin resistance.
text:
The c-Jun N-terminal kinases (JNKs) play a crucial role in regulating inflammation and insulin action, and obesity has been shown to increase total JNK activity. Interestingly, studies have revealed that JNK1, but not JNK2, deficiency results in reduced adiposity and improved insulin sensitivity. Surprisingly, high levels of JNK activation are observed in Jnk2(-/-) mice, particularly in the liver, suggesting an interplay between the two isoforms that may have obscured the metabolic effects of JNK2 in isolated mutant mice.
To investigate the unique role of the JNK2 isoform in metabolic homeostasis, we generated genetic combinations of Jnk1(-/-) and Jnk2(-/-) mice. We found that only Jnk1(-/-) and Jnk1(+/-)Jnk2(-/-) mice exhibited reduced body weight and increased insulin sensitivity compared to other genotypes. Additionally, these mice displayed decreased total JNK activity and cytokine expression in liver tissue. These findings suggest that the JNK2 isoform also plays a role in metabolic regulation, although its function is masked when JNK1 is fully expressed due to regulatory interactions between the two isoforms.

title: The immunological synapse of CTL contains a secretory domain and membrane bridges.
text: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) quickly eliminate their targets by rapid destruction. Here, we demonstrate that although the target cell dies within 5 minutes of CTL-target cell contact, a similar immunological synapse to that seen in CD4 cells forms rapidly in CTLs, characterized by a ring of adhesion proteins enclosing an inner domain rich in signaling molecules. Lytic granule secretion occurs in a distinct domain within the adhesion ring, effectively maintaining the organization of signaling proteins during exocytosis. Both live and fixed cell analysis reveal that target cell plasma membrane markers are transferred to the CTL as the cells separate. Additionally, electron microscopy shows the formation of continuities connecting the CTL and target cell membranes, suggesting a plausible mechanism for this transfer.

title: Compromised intestinal epithelial barrier induces adaptive immune compensation that protects from colitis.
text: Mice lacking the junctional adhesion molecule A (JAM-A, encoded by F11r) display enhanced intestinal epithelial permeability, bacterial translocation, and elevated colonic lymphocyte numbers, yet do not develop colitis. To investigate the contribution of adaptive immune compensation in response to increased intestinal epithelial permeability, we examined the susceptibility of F11r(-/-)Rag1(-/-) mice to acute colitis. While negligible contributions of adaptive immunity were observed in F11r(+/+)Rag1(-/-) mice, F11r(-/-)Rag1(-/-) mice displayed increased microflora-dependent colitis. We found that elimination of T cell subsets and cytokine analyses revealed a protective role for TGF-β-producing CD4+ T cells in F11r(-/-) mice. Additionally, loss of JAM-A led to elevated mucosal and serum IgA that was dependent upon CD4+ T cells and TGF-β. Interestingly, absence of IgA in F11r(+/+)Igha(-/-) mice did not affect disease, while F11r(-/-)Igha(-/-) mice displayed markedly increased susceptibility to acute injury-induced colitis. These findings establish a role for adaptive immune-mediated protection from acute colitis under conditions of intestinal epithelial barrier compromise.

title: Apoptosis and chemoresistance in transgenic cancer models
text:
Clinical oncology continues to grapple with the challenge of multidrug resistance, which has remained unresolved despite efforts over a decade ago to understand its underlying mechanisms. Initial studies showed that genes encoding cellular efflux pumps can confer resistance to a wide range of anticancer drugs, even before these compounds reach their intracellular targets. More recent research has revealed that many drugs trigger a common apoptotic program, which can also contribute to drug resistance. However, due to technical limitations, the significance of apoptotic defects in therapy-induced cell death has been difficult to evaluate.
To address these limitations, researchers have sought to develop more reliable models for studying drug resistance. For example, utilizing cancer cell lines may be biased by unphysiological conditions, and correlative analyses using patient specimens are limited by unknown background mutations in the biopsy material. To overcome these restrictions, a tractable transgenic cancer model was used to investigate the impact of apoptosis on treatment outcome.
While cell culture-based assays have their limitations, genetically engineered mice offer potential advantages as model systems. However, even these models have caveats to consider. For instance, the natural tumor microenvironment is often difficult to replicate in vitro, which can impact the accuracy of results.
In this study, the authors used a series of primary lymphomas with genetically defined lesions, treated at their natural site, to evaluate the impact of apoptosis on drug responses. By utilizing this tractable transgenic mouse model, the researchers were able to circumvent some of the challenges associated with studying drug resistance in vitro and in vivo.

title: NC-100717: a versatile RGD peptide scaffold for angiogenesis imaging.
text: The potential for detecting disease pathology using in vivo imaging technologies lies in targeting the molecular pathways involved in angiogenesis. The process of angiogenesis requires the activation and migration of endothelial cells, which are vital for the formation of new blood vessels. Endothelial cells interact with the extracellular matrix through specific cell adhesion receptors called integrins. Recognizing this interaction, peptides containing the tripeptide sequence RGD have been designed to bind with high affinity to the alphavbeta3 and alphavbeta5 integrins associated with angiogenesis. In this study, we report the synthesis and in vitro binding affinity of the RGD-containing peptide NC-100717 and a range of molecular probes derived from this intermediate.

title: Dose-dependent effect of statins on the incidence of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery.
text: Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) after cardiac surgery is linked to increased morbidity and mortality. Methods: We investigated whether statin treatment is associated with a lower incidence of postoperative AKI in 2,104 consecutive patients who underwent coronary artery bypass graft or valve surgery at the Minneapolis Veterans Administration Medical Center. AKI was defined as an absolute increase of greater than 0.3 mg/dL or a relative increase of greater than 50% in serum creatinine from baseline within 48 hours after surgery or requiring postoperative hemodialysis according to the AKI network criteria. Propensity scores were used to account for differences between the statin and no-statin treatment groups. All statins were converted to equivalent-dose simvastatin and divided at the median to construct high-dose (≥40 mg) and low-dose (<40 mg) statin groups. Results: Of the 2,104 patients, 1,435 (68%) were taking statins (638 high-dose), and 495 (24%) developed AKI (25% high-dose vs 40% low-dose vs 35% no-statin; p = 0.014). Independent predictors of AKI were estimated preoperative glomerular filtration rate (p = 0.003), diabetes mellitus (p = 0.02), valve surgery with or without coronary artery bypass graft (p = 0.024), cardiopulmonary bypass time (p = 0.001), and intraaortic balloon pump (p = 0.055). After propensity adjustment, statin treatment was not associated with postoperative AKI (odds ratio 0.79; 95% confidence interval 0.59-1.06; p = 0.11 for high-dose vs no-statin). After full adjustment for all independent predictors of AKI, the results did not change. Statins also had no effect on the incidence of postoperative hemodialysis (0.8% high-dose vs 1.9% low-dose vs 1% no-statin; p = 0.15). Conclusions: Statin treatment is not associated with a lower incidence of AKI after cardiac surgery.

title: Comparison of allogeneic vs autologous bone marrow–derived mesenchymal stem cells delivered by transendocardial injection in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy: the POSEIDON randomized trial.
text:
The POSEIDON study compared the safety and efficacy of allogeneic and autologous mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) in patients with left ventricular (LV) dysfunction due to ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM). The study was a phase 1/2 randomized controlled trial conducted at a tertiary-care referral hospital in the United States.
Thirty patients with LV dysfunction were enrolled in the study and randomly assigned to receive either allogeneic or autologous MSCs. The cells were delivered to the LV through transendocardial injection. The primary outcome measures included the incidence of treatment-emergent serious adverse events (SAEs) within 30 days of the procedure, as well as efficacy assessments such as the 6-minute walk test, exercise peak VO2, Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ), New York Heart Association class, LV volumes, ejection fraction (EF), early enhancement defect (EED; infarct size), and sphericity index.
The results showed that within 30 days of the procedure, one patient in each group (the allogeneic group) experienced a treatment-emergent SAE, which was less than the prespecified stopping event rate of 25%. The 1-year incidence of SAEs was 33.3% in the allogeneic group and 53.3% in the autologous group (P = .46). At 1 year, there were no ventricular arrhythmia SAEs observed among allogeneic recipients compared with 4 patients (26.7%) in the autologous group (P = .10).
In terms of efficacy, autologous MSC therapy was associated with improvements in the 6-minute walk test and MLHFQ score, but not exercise VO2 max. Allogeneic and autologous MSCs reduced mean EED by −33.21% (95% CI, −43.61% to −22.81%; P < .001) and sphericity index, but did not increase EF. Allogeneic MSCs reduced LV end-diastolic volumes. Low-dose concentration MSCs (20 million cells) produced the greatest reductions in LV volumes and increased EF. Allogeneic MSCs did not stimulate significant donor-specific alloimmune reactions.
In conclusion, the POSEIDON study found that both allogeneic and autologous MSCs were associated with low rates of treatment-emergent SAEs, including immunologic reactions. In aggregate, MSC injection favorably affected patient functional capacity, quality of life, and ventricular remodeling. However, the study could not determine whether the efficacy of allogeneic MSCs was inferior to that of autologous MSCs due to the lack of a placebo control group. Further research is needed to determine the optimal dosage and concentration of MSCs for treating ICM.

title: Periosteal bone formation--a neglected determinant of bone strength.
text: Life forms with low body mass are able to forage for food with ease on the undersides of branches or along sheer cliff faces, barely affected by the force of gravity. In comparison, larger creatures must engage in rapid movement to secure their next meal, relying on the lever function of their long bones to achieve this. These biomechanical marvels, made up of a unique combination of materials and structural design, possess the paradoxical qualities of both stiffness and flexibility, as well as strength and lightness. The stiffness of these bones is due to the triple-helical structure of collagen type I, which is encrusted with hydroxyapatite crystals, providing...

title: Triglyceride depletion of brown adipose tissue enables analysis of mitochondrial respiratory function in permeabilized biopsies.
text: Recent research has highlighted the crucial role of mitochondria in the onset and progression of obesity and related conditions. The classical methods for assessing mitochondrial function in brown adipose tissue (BAT) involve measuring enzymatic levels or respiration in isolated mitochondria, which requires significant tissue excision and disrupts the cellular structure. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a new, efficient protocol for analyzing mitochondrial respiratory states in BAT biopsies. Using this approach, we can now assess all mitochondrial respiratory states, including phosphorylation (OXPHOS), no-phosphorylation (LEAK), and uncoupled (ETS) states, as well as the use of specific substrates for complex I, complex II, and cytochrome c. This protocol enables the analysis of mitochondrial function in tiny BAT samples from humans and animal models, enabling researchers to better understand the mechanisms that regulate mitochondrial function in health and disease. By leveraging this protocol, scientists may be able to uncover novel insights into the role of mitochondria in obesity and related conditions, ultimately leading to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for these diseases.

title: HES-1 preserves purified hematopoietic stem cells ex vivo and accumulates side population cells in vivo.
text: Mouse long-term hematopoietic reconstituting cells reside in the c-Kit+Sca-1+Lin- (KSL) cell population, with CD34(low/-) cells representing the most highly purified population of hematopoietic stem cells in adult bone marrow. We demonstrate that retrovirus-mediated transduction of CD34(low/-)c-Kit+Sca-1+Lin- (34-KSL) cells with the HES-1 gene, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that regulates the growth phase of neural stem cells in the embryo, preserves the long-term reconstituting activity of these cells in vitro. We also find that cells derived from the HES-1-transduced 34-KSL population exhibit negative Hoechst dye staining, a characteristic of the side population, and retain a CD34(low/-) profile in the bone marrow KSL population in each recipient mouse at a ratio 3.5- to 7.8-fold higher than non-transduced 34-KSL-derived competitor cells. Our findings suggest that HES-1 maintains the long-term reconstituting hematopoietic activity of 34-KSL stem cells ex vivo. Additionally, up-regulation of HES-1 protein in the 34-KSL population without retrovirus transduction may represent a potent approach to expanding hematopoietic stem cells.

title: Measuring Absolute RNA Copy Numbers at High Temporal Resolution Reveals Transcriptome Kinetics in Development.
text: Transcript regulation is critical for cell function, and misregulation can lead to disease. Despite advances in surveying the transcriptome, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of transcript kinetics, which hinders quantitative biology. This is a significant challenge in embryonic development, where rapid changes in gene expression determine cell fate decisions. By ultra-high-frequency sampling of Xenopus embryos and absolute normalization of sequence reads, we have generated detailed gene expression trajectories in absolute transcript numbers. During a developmental period equivalent to the first 8 weeks of human gestation, transcript kinetics vary by eight orders of magnitude. Organizing genes based on expression dynamics, we found that "temporal synexpression" predicts shared gene function. Remarkably, a single parameter, the characteristic timescale, can globally classify transcript kinetics and distinguish genes involved in development from those involved in cellular metabolism. Our analysis provides unprecedented insight into the reorganization of maternal and embryonic transcripts and fundamentally alters our ability to perform quantitative biology.

title: Inflammasome activation by adenylate cyclase toxin directs Th17 responses and protection against Bordetella pertussis.
text:
The inflammasome plays a crucial role in both innate and adaptive immune responses, with key implications for autoinflammatory diseases and immunity to infection. While the inflammasome's role in driving adaptive immunity has been largely unexplored, our study provides evidence that it plays a critical role in promoting antigen-specific Th17 cells and immunity to Bordetella pertussis infection.
Using a murine respiratory challenge model, we found that B. pertussis infection significantly exacerbated in IL-1R type I-defective (IL-1RI(-/-)) mice, indicating that the inflammasome plays a crucial role in regulating immune responses to the bacteria. Our findings demonstrated that the bacterial toxin, adenylate cyclase toxin (CyaA), induces robust IL-1beta production by dendritic cells through activation of the NALP3-containing inflammasome complex.
We discovered that CyaA-mediated activation of caspase-1 is not dependent on adenylate cyclase enzyme activity but is rather dependent on the pore-forming capacity of CyaA. Moreover, CyaA promotes the induction of Ag-specific Th17 cells in wild-type mice but not in IL-1RI(-/-) mice, suggesting that the inflammasome plays a critical role in polarizing T cell responses toward the Th17 subtype.
Our findings also revealed that CyaA can promote IL-1beta-mediated Th17 cells, which promote clearance of the bacteria from the respiratory tract, suggesting that the toxin may manipulate the host immune response to protect itself from elimination. Overall, our study provides new insights into the mechanisms of immunity to B. pertussis and highlights the potential of the inflammasome as a target for modulating immune responses to infectious agents.

title: Infection and apoptosis as a combined inflammatory trigger.
text: While research has focused extensively on the phagocytosis of microbial pathogens and non-inflammatory phagocytosis of apoptotic cells, the consequences of innate immune recognition of host cells undergoing apoptosis as a direct result of infection are still unclear. In this scenario, the innate immune system encounters conflicting signals, with those from apoptotic cells and those from the infecting pathogen. Studies have implicated nuclear receptors in the response to apoptotic cell recognition, while Toll-like receptors are the prototypical inflammatory receptors activated during infection. When these signals intersect, a unique set of events unfolds, beginning with the repression of a subset of inflammatory genes and culminating in the induction of a T helper-17 adaptive immune response. This response is optimized for clearing the infecting pathogen and repairing the damage caused to host tissue during infection.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia with t(14;19)(q32;q13) is characterized by atypical morphologic and immunophenotypic features and distinctive genetic features.
text: The cytogenetic abnormality t(14;19)(q32;q13), which involves the IGH@ and BCL3 loci, is an uncommon alteration detected in B-cell malignancies, including chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL). In this study, we evaluated the clinicopathologic, cytogenetic, and molecular genetic characteristics of 14 cases of CLL/SLL with t(14;19)(q32;q13). All patients (10 men and 4 women) had lymphocytosis, and 10 had lymphadenopathy. The neoplastic cells in the blood and bone marrow were predominantly small but showed cytologic and immunophenotypic abnormalities. In all cases, the t(14;19) translocation occurred in the neoplastic stem cell clone, and it was the sole abnormality in 4 cases. Additional cytogenetic abnormalities, such as trisomy 12 and complex karyotypes, were present in 10 cases. Fluorescence in situ hybridization revealed the IGH@/BCL3 fusion gene in all cases, and the IGHV genes were unmutated in all cases, except for 7 cases that expressed the ZAP70 protein. Of note, 7 cases preferentially used IGHV4-39. Our findings suggest that t(14;19)(q32;q13) identifies a distinct subset of CLL/SLL with particular clinicopathologic and genetic features. Furthermore, t(14;19) may represent an early, potentially primary, genetic event.

title: Risk factors for the development of gallstone recurrence following medical dissolution. The British-Italian Gallstone Study Group.
text:
Objective: To investigate risk factors for gallstone recurrence after non-surgical treatment.
Design: Prospective follow-up of a multicentre cohort of post-dissolution gallstone patients.
Setting: Six gastroenterology units in the UK and Italy.
Participants: One hundred and sixty-three patients with confirmed gallstone dissolution following non-surgical therapy (bile acids or lithotripsy plus bile acids), followed up by ultrasound scan and clinical assessment at 6-monthly intervals for up to 6 years (median, 25 months; range, 6-70 months).
Outcome measures: Subject-related variables (sex, age, height, weight, body mass index), gallstone-related variables (number, diameter, presence of symptoms, months to complete stone clearance), treatment modalities (bile acid therapy, extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy), and follow-up-related variables (weight change, use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents, statins, pregnancies, and/or use of oestrogens) were examined using univariate and multivariate analysis as potential risk factors for gallstone recurrence.
Results: Forty-five gallstone recurrences were identified during the follow-up period. The only variables associated with an increased recurrence rate were multiple primary gallstones and the length of time to achieve gallstone dissolution. The appearance of biliary sludge during follow-up was also significantly related to the development of gallstone recurrence. Use of statins or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents did not provide protection against recurrence.
Conclusions: Patients with primary single stones are the best candidates for non-surgical treatment of gallstones, as they have a low risk of gallstone recurrence. The positive association of recurrence with biliary sludge formation and time to dissolution of primary stones suggests that impaired gallbladder motility plays a role in the pathogenesis of this condition.

title: Deletion of the developmentally essential gene ATR in adult mice leads to age-related phenotypes and stem cell loss.
text: Defects in the DNA damage response (DDR) have been associated with various abnormalities, including developmental disorders, cancer, and premature aging. Specifically, mutations in the ATR checkpoint regulator have been linked to developmental defects in mice (pregastrulation lethality) and humans (Seckel syndrome). Our findings show that deleting ATR in adult mice leads to a decline in tissue homeostasis and the sudden emergence of age-related phenotypes, such as gray hair, alopecia, kyphosis, osteoporosis, thymic involution, fibrosis, and other abnormalities. Through histological and genetic analyses, we discovered that ATR deletion causes rapid cellular loss in tissues where continuous proliferation is necessary for maintenance. Interestingly, thymic involution, alopecia, and hair graying in ATR knockout mice were found to be directly linked to significant reductions in tissue-specific stem and progenitor cells and a depletion of tissue renewal and homeostatic capacity. These results suggest that a lack of regenerative capacity in adults due to the deletion of a crucial DDR gene is sufficient to cause the premature appearance of age-related phenotypes.

title: Conventional and monocyte-derived CD11b(+) dendritic cells initiate and maintain T helper 2 cell-mediated immunity to house dust mite allergen.
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) are crucial for the development of allergic airway inflammation, but their specific role in this process is unclear. To investigate, we used CD64 and MAR-1 staining to separate CD11b(+) monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs) from conventional DCs (cDCs) and analyzed their antigen uptake, migration, and presentation abilities in response to inhaled house dust mite (HDM) in the lungs and lymph nodes (LN). Our findings revealed that mainly CD11b(+) cDCs, but not CD103(+) cDCs, induced T helper 2 (Th2) cell immunity in HDM-specific T cells in vitro and asthma in vivo. Interestingly, studies in Flt3l(-/-) mice, which lack all cDCs, showed that moDCs were also capable of inducing Th2 cell-mediated immunity, but only when high-dose HDM was administered. Our results demonstrate that migratory CD11b(+) cDCs are the primary subset responsible for inducing Th2 cell-mediated immunity in the LN, while moDCs play a key role in orchestrating allergic inflammation in the lung.

title: Interplay between the dividing cell and its neighbors regulates adherens junction formation during cytokinesis in epithelial tissue.
text: The formation of adherens junctions (AJs) during cell division is a poorly understood process. Here, we discovered that AJ formation is linked to cytokinesis and involves a complex interplay between the dividing cell and its neighboring cells. As the cytokinetic ring contracts, nearby cells accumulate Myosin II and generate the cortical tension necessary to establish the initial geometry of the daughter cell interface. However, the neighboring cell membranes hinder AJ formation. After midbody formation and the retreat of neighboring cells, Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerizationoriented by the midbody maintains AJ geometry and regulates AJ final length and the arrangement of epithelial cells during division. We propose that cytokinesis in epithelia is a multi-cellular process, where the cooperative actions of the dividing cell and its neighbors define a two-tiered mechanism that spatially and temporally controls AJ formation while maintaining tissue cohesion.

title: Cancer stem cells in solid tumours: accumulating evidence and unresolved questions
text: Solid tumors pose a significant cancer burden and therapeutic challenge. The cancer stem cell (CSC) hypothesis proposes a cellular mechanism to explain the resistance to treatment and dormancy exhibited by many of these tumors. Emerging evidence suggests that various solid tumors are organized in a hierarchical manner and sustained by a distinct population of CSCs. Recent studies in mouse models of epithelial tumorigenesis have provided direct evidence for the CSC hypothesis, although alternative models of tumor heterogeneity also exist. The clinical relevance of CSCs remains a crucial question, but early findings suggest that targeting these cells may be a viable strategy.

title: The structure of the follistatin:activin complex reveals antagonism of both type I and type II receptor binding.
text: TGF-beta ligands elicit a wide range of cellular responses by transmitting signals through type I and II receptors. Low-affinity ligand antagonists, such as follistatin, play an essential role in regulating these physiological responses. In this study, we have characterized the structure of activin A, a TGF-beta ligand, in complex with two follistatin molecules. This complex neutralizes the ligand by encapsulating one-third of its residues and receptor binding sites. Previous research suggested that type I receptor binding would not be affected by follistatin, but our crystal structure reveals that the N-terminal domain of follistatin adopts an unexpected fold resembling a universal type I receptor motif, thereby occupying this binding site. The stoichiometric and geometric arrangement of the activin:follistatin complex gives rise to the formation of follistatin:BMP:type I receptor complexes. The unique mode of ligand binding by follistatin has significant implications for its ability to neutralize homo- and heterodimeric Ligands of this growth factor family.

title: The activity of siRNA in mammalian cells is related to structural target accessibility: a comparison with antisense oligonucleotides.
text: The impact of siRNA on gene expression is influenced by the unique characteristics of the target RNA, including local RNA folding. To investigate the relationship between local target accessibility and the inhibition of the target gene by siRNA, we utilized a computational approach that had been previously shown to be consistent with experimental probing of target RNA. Specifically, we examined two accessible motifs and one inaccessible structure on the ICAM-1 mRNA in ECV304 cells. We compared the local target-dependent effectiveness of siRNA with antisense oligonucleotides (asON). Our findings indicate a >1000-fold difference in activity between active siRNAs (IC50 approximately 0.2-0.5 nM) and inactive siRNA (IC50 >= 1 microM). The extremely high activity of siRNA si2B (IC50 = 0.24 nM) suggests that not all siRNAs shown to be active at standard concentrations of >10-100 nM belong to this highly active species. These observations suggest a potential approach to assess target accessibility for siRNA, which could support the design of active siRNA constructs. This approach can be automated, work at high throughput, and is open to include additional parameters relevant to the biological activity of siRNA.

title: Rapid accumulation of mutations during seed-to-seed propagation of mismatch-repair-defective Arabidopsis.
text: During the repeated cell divisions that occur before the formation of plant gametes, their apical-meristem and floral precursors are exposed to both internal and external mutagenic threats. Although some deleterious recessive mutations may be removed during the development of haploid gametophytes and early haploid embryos (through a process known as "haplosufficiency quality-checking"), the diversity of plant genome-maintenance systems suggests that quality control is particularly important during earlier diploid growth. To investigate this hypothesis in Arabidopsis, we maintained parallel lines of 36 MMR-defective (Atmsh2-1) and 36 wild-type plants, and observed significant differences in their mutational profiles. Fifth-generation (G5) plants of the Atmsh2-1 lines displayed abnormalities in morphology, development, fertility, germination efficiency, seed/silique development, and seed set, whereas all 36 wild-type lines appeared normal at this stage. Analysis of insertion/deletion mutations at six repeat-sequence (microsatellite) loci revealed that each Atmsh2-1 line had developed its own unique "fingerprint," resulting from as many as 10 microsatellite mutations in a single line. These findings demonstrate that MMR during diploid growth plays a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the plant genome.

title: Archaeal chromatin and transcription.
text: Archaea have a diverse array of sequence-independent DNA binding proteins that have evolved to compact their genomes. Some of these proteins undergo post-translational modifications, such as lysine acetylation or methylation, which are similar to the histone modifications found in eukaryotes and play a role in regulating chromatin structure and transcription. In contrast to eukaryotes, Archaea do not have homologues of the multisubunit complexes that remodel chromatin and activate RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) initiation. Instead, they have sequence-specific regulators that repress and possibly activate transcription by mechanisms similar to the bacterial paradigm of regulating promoter binding by RNAP. These repressors compete with archaeal TATA-box binding protein (TBP) and TFB for the TATA-box and TFB-recognition elements (BRE) of the archaeal promoter, or with archaeal RNAP for the site of transcription initiation. Transcript-specific regulation by repressors binding to sites of transcript initiation is consistent with these sites having little sequence conservation. However, most Archaea have only one TBP and/or TFB, which must therefore bind to similar TATA-box and BRE sequences upstream of most genes. Repressors that function by competing with TBP and/or TFB binding must therefore make additional contacts with transcript-specific regulatory sites adjacent or remote from the TATA-box/BRE region. The fate of the archaeal TBP and TFB following transcription initiation is still unknown, but based on functional homology with their eukaryotic RNAPII-system counterparts, they should remain bound to the TATA-box/BRE region after transcription initiation. However, this seems unlikely due to the potential limitation of repressor competition at this site.

title: Temporal segregation of 4-1BB versus CD28-mediated costimulation: 4-1BB ligand influences T cell numbers late in the primary response and regulates the size of the T cell memory response following influenza infection.
text: In this report, we investigate the role of CD28 and 4-1BB/4-1BBL signaling in the expansion and function of CD8 T cells in response to influenza virus infection. We find that CD28(-/-) mice exhibit a defect in the initial expansion of D(b)/NP366-374-specific CD8 T cells, whereas 4-1BB ligand (4-1BBL)(-/-) mice show no such defect. In contrast, 4-1BBL(-/-) mice exhibit a decrease in D(b)/NP366-374-specific T cells during the late stages of the primary response, resulting in reduced CD8 T cell expansion and compromised cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) effector function during the in vivo secondary response. In contrast, anti- influenza virus Ab responses and secondary CD4 T cell responses are unaltered in 4-1BBL-deficient mice. Our findings suggest that CD28 plays a critical role in initial T cell expansion, while 4-1BB/4-1BBL signaling affects T cell numbers later in the response and is essential for the survival and function of the memory CD8 T cell pool.

title: Functional role of high-affinity anandamide transport, as revealed by selective inhibition.
text:
Anandamide, a chemical that occurs naturally in the brain, is released from neurons when they become depolarized. It is then rapidly broken down, but the exact mechanism isn't fully understood. Scientists believe that anandamide may be transported into cells or broken down by enzymes.
In a study, a compound called N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)arachidonylamide (AM404) was used to inhibit the accumulation of anandamide in rat neurons and astrocytes (a type of brain cell). This showed that the accumulation of anandamide in these cells was due to a specialized transport system. However, AM404 did not activate cannabinoid receptors or break down anandamide, but it did enhance the effects of anandamide on these receptors both in vitro and in vivo.
The study suggests that a specialized transport system may be important for ending the effects of anandamide. This transport system could be a potential target for drugs.

title: Silibinin inhibits the invasion of IL-6-stimulated colon cancer cells via selective JNK/AP-1/MMP-2 modulation in vitro.
text: Silibinin, a flavonoid with antihepatotoxic properties and pleiotrophic anticancer potential, was investigated for its ability to inhibit cell invasion in IL-6-stimulated LoVo colon cancer cells. This study showed that silibinin down-regulated matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2) expression by attenuating the activity of activator protein-1 (AP-1). Western blot analysis revealed that treatment with silibinin or a JNK inhibitor reduced MMP-2 protein expression by 1.6- or 1.7-fold compared to the control. similar results were observed in zymography and confocal microscopy. Pretreatment with silibinin also abolished the binding activity of AP-1 and MMP-2 promoter activity via AP-1 binding, as demonstrated by EMSA and luciferase assay. Furthermore, a [(3)H]-thymidine incorporation proliferation assay and cell migration assay indicated that silibinin inhibited IL-6-stimulated LoVo cell proliferation and invasion. These findings suggest that silibinin inhibits LoVo cell invasion by reducing MMP-2 expression through the attenuation of AP-1 binding activity, providing a novel antimetastatic application for silibinin in colon cancer chemoprevention.

title: Immigration cohorts and residential overcrowding in southern California
text: The extent to which immigrants reduce their high levels of residential overcrowding as they spend more time in the United States is explored through the use of a "double cohort" method that combines birth cohorts with immigration cohorts. This approach allows for the separation of aging effects from duration effects, enabling an examination of how cohort trends change over time. The analysis reveals that cohort trends diverge significantly from the cross-sectional pattern observed at a single point in time, with cohorts' growth in income contributing significantly to the decline in overcrowding over time. However, there are notable differences in cohort trends among Hispanic immigrants compared to other immigrant groups, with a less pronounced decrease in overcrowding and even increases in certain age ranges.

title: Expression of green fluorescent protein in the ureteric bud of transgenic mice: a new tool for the analysis of ureteric bud morphogenesis.
text: The development and growth of the ureteric bud is a complex process that plays a crucial role in organizing the collecting duct system and determining the number of nephrons in the metanephric kidney. Although some of the genes involved in this process have been identified, the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. To address this gap in knowledge, we generated transgenic mice that express a green fluorescent protein (GFP) in the ureteric bud under the control of the Hoxb7 promoter. In these mice, GFP is expressed in every branch of the ureteric bud throughout renal development and in its derivative epithelia in the adult kidney. The ability to visualize GFP in living tissue allows for the dynamics of ureteric bud growth and branching to be followed over several days when the kidneys are cultured in vitro. Using confocal microscopy, the three-dimensional branching of the ureteric bud can be analyzed. These mice represent a powerful tool to characterize the normal patterns of ureteric bud morphogenesis and to investigate the response of the bud to growth factors, matrix elements, and other agents that regulate its growth and branching.

title: Biological properties of herpes simplex virus 2 replication-defective mutant strains in a murine nasal infection model.
text: We employed a mouse nasal model of Herpes Simplex Virus 2 (HSV-2) infection to investigate the biological properties of HSV-2 wild-type (WT), TK-negative, and replication-deficient strains in vivo. Nasal septa tissue is the primary site of WT viral replication following intranasal (i.n.) inoculation. The HSV-2 strain 186 syn(+)-1 WT virus caused lethal encephalitis at doses above 104 PFU per nostril, and lower doses failed to demonstrate any positive neurons for latency-associated transcript in the trigeminal ganglia, indicating a lack of latent infection. In contrast, the 186ΔKpn TK-negative mutant virus replicated in nasal septa tissue but showed low-level replication in trigeminal ganglia at only one timepoint. In situ hybridization of trigeminal ganglia revealed that the number of LAT-positive neurons was directly proportional to the inoculum dose from 103 to 106 PFU per nare. Unlike the replication-defective mutant virus 5BlacZ, which showed no replication in nasal septa tissue and failed to maintain viral DNA at the inoculation site or trigeminal ganglia, the virus inoculated at distal sites reduced acute replication and latent infection of 186ΔKpn following i.n. challenge. This infection model provides a relevant system to analyze the characteristics of HSV-2 strains and demonstrates that replication-deficient mutant strains do not persist at injection sites or sensory ganglia but can induce immune protection that reduces the latent viral burden of a subsequent challenge virus.

title: The sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor agonist FTY720 modulates dendritic cell trafficking in vivo.
text: Clinical trials for the pro-drug FTY720 are underway for the prevention of allograft rejection. After phosphorylation, FTY720 targets the G protein-coupled sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (S1PR1) on lymphocytes, thereby inhibiting their egress from lymphoid organs and recirculation to inflammatory sites. The expression of all five S1PR subtypes (S1PR1-5) has been identified on murine dendritic cells (DCs). Administration of FTY720 to C57BL/10 mice markedly reduced circulating T and B lymphocytes within 24 hours, but not blood-borne DCs, which were enhanced significantly for up to 96 hours, while DCs in lymph nodes and spleen were reduced. In addition, the administration of the selective S1PR1 agonist SEW2871 significantly enhanced circulating DC numbers. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that the expression of CD11b, CD31/PECAM-1, CD54/ICAM-1, and CCR7 on blood-borne DCs was downregulated following FTY720 administration. Meanwhile, the transendothelial migration of FTY720-pre-treated immature DCs to the CCR7 ligand CCL19 was reduced. These findings suggest that FTY720 may modulate DC trafficking to contribute to its immunosuppressive effects.

title: Sustained survivin expression from OX40 costimulatory signals drives T cell clonal expansion.
text: The continuous interaction of T cell receptors (TCRs) and costimulatory molecules is believed to lead to the generation of high levels of effector T cells. In this study, we investigate the role of Survivin in peripheral T cells, which is controlled by OX40 cosignaling and sustained PI3k and PKB activity. Survivin is induced by OX40 regardless of cell division in late G1 phase, and its suppression leads to a decrease in S-phase transition and cell division, ultimately resulting in apoptosis. In addition, Survivin expression alone is sufficient to restore proliferation and prevent apoptosis in costimulation-deficient T cells, and can even rescue T cell expansion in vivo. Survivin promotes the proliferation of effector T cells, but Bcl-2 family proteins are essential for T cell survival after the active division phase. Therefore, sustained Survivin expression through costimulatory signaling allows for the maintenance of T cell division over time and regulates the extent of clonal expansion.

title: The Combination of Exercise and Respiratory Training Improves Respiratory Muscle Function in Pulmonary Hypertension
text:
Title: The Impact of Exercise and Respiratory Training on Respiratory Muscle Strength and 6-Min Walking Distance in Patients with Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: A Prospective Study
Background: Increased dyspnea and reduced exercise capacity are common symptoms in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Respiratory muscle dysfunction has been implicated as a primary contributor to these symptoms. Our study aimed to assess the impact of exercise and respiratory training on respiratory muscle strength and 6-min walking distance (6MWD) in PAH patients.
Methods: We conducted a prospective study in patients with invasively confirmed PAH who underwent 3 weeks of in-hospital exercise and respiratory training, followed by continued training at home for 12 weeks. Medication was held constant throughout the study period. Efficacy parameters were assessed by blinded observers at baseline, after 3 weeks, and after 15 weeks. Respiratory muscle function was evaluated using twitch mouth pressure (TwPmo) during non-volitional supramaximal magnetic phrenic nerve stimulation.
Results: Seven PAH patients (4 women) were enrolled in the study, with a median age of 53 years old, mean pulmonary artery pressure of 45 ± 11 mmHg, and median WHO functional class of 3.1 ± 0.4. The training program was found to be feasible and well-tolerated by all patients, with excellent compliance. TwPmo increased significantly from baseline to the final assessment by 0.41 ± 0.34 kPa (p = 0.012) and 6MWD increased by 81 ± 30 m (p = 0.001).
Conclusion: Our study suggests that exercise and respiratory training may be an effective adjunct to medical therapy in improving respiratory muscle strength and exercise capacity in patients with PAH. Future, randomized, controlled trials are warranted to confirm these findings.

title: Dual role of the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis in the development of autoimmune myocarditis: induction by IL-12 and protection by IFN-gamma.
text: The IL-12/IFN-gamma axis plays a double-edged role in the development of autoimmune myocarditis. On one hand, IL-12 and IFN-gamma positively regulate each other and boost type 1 inflammatory responses, which are believed to cause tissue damage in autoimmune diseases. However, our studies have shown that IL-12-deficient mice on a susceptible background are resistant to myocarditis, while IFN-gamma-deficient mice develop fatal autoimmune disease. Interestingly, blocking IL-4 receptor signaling did not confer susceptibility to myocarditis in IL-12-deficient mice, suggesting that IL-12 triggers autoimmunity through a mechanism independent of the effector cytokines IFN-gamma and IL-4. In conclusion, our findings suggest that the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis is a complex factor in the development of autoimmune myocarditis, with IL-12 mediating disease through the induction and expansion of Th1-type cells, while IFN-gamma production from these cells helps limit disease progression.

title: Somatic and Germline Diversification of a Putative Immunoreceptor within One Phylum: Dscam in Arthropods.
text: Arthropod Dscam, similar to the human Down Syndrome cell adhesion molecule, is a receptor utilized by both the nervous and immune systems. However, unlike in vertebrates, evolutionary pressures have resulted in an abundance of Dscam isoforms in arthropods, with the ability to specify neuronal identity during nervous system differentiation. This chapter examines the various methods of Dscam diversification in the context of arthropod evolution and immune system function, where its role is disputed. In contrast to insects and crustaceans, which possess a single Dscam gene with the capability of producing over 10,000 isoforms through mutually exclusive alternative splicing of three duplicated exon clusters, more basal arthropods, such as centipedes, exhibit a multitude of germline genes (over 80) with the potential for alternative splicing affecting a single exon cluster. Even more basic arthropods, such as chelicerates, lack splicing possibilities but possess dozens of germline Dscam genes. It is hypothesized that the somatic mutually exclusive alternative splicing within a single gene may provide a more simplified approach to expressing a large repertoire of Dscam. Expressed on the surface of hemocytes, Dscam serves as a phagocytic receptor and is also present in solution. Further research is needed to fully comprehend its binding properties to pathogens, its role in phagocytosis, its potential function in determining hemocyte identity, its expression kinetics, and the regulation of its RNA splicing to uncover how its diversity is linked to immunity.

title: Epidemiology, health-related quality of life and economic burden of binge eating disorder: a systematic literature review
text:
Objective: To conduct a systematic review of the epidemiology, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and economic burden of binge eating disorder (BED).
Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted using Medline, Embase, PsycINFO, PsycARTICLES, Academic Search Complete, CINAHL Plus, Business Source Premier, and the Cochrane Library. The search included articles published in English between 2009 and 2013. The studies included were assessed for quality, and data on epidemiology were extracted from 31 articles, HRQoL burden from 16 articles, and economic burden from 7 articles. The diagnosis of BED was determined using the 4th Edition of The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV) criteria in 46 studies. The lifetime prevalence of BED in the general population was found to be between 1.1% and 1.9%. BED was associated with significant impairment in both physical and mental aspects of HRQoL, as evidenced by mean scores on the Short Form 36 Physical and Mental Component Summaries that ranged from 31.1 to 47.3 and 32.0 to 49.8, respectively. Compared to individuals without eating disorders, BED was linked to increased healthcare utilization and costs, with annual direct healthcare costs per patient ranging between $2,372 and $3,731.
Results: BED is a serious eating disorder that has a significant impact on both physical and mental aspects of HRQoL and is associated with increased healthcare utilization and costs. The limited available literature warrants further research to better understand the long-term HRQoL and economic burden of BED.
Conclusion: The findings of this systematic review suggest that BED is a significant health concern that affects both physical and mental health outcomes, and is associated with increased healthcare utilization and costs. Further research is needed to fully understand the long-term HRQoL and economic burden of BED.

title: Subcellular steroid/nuclear receptor dynamics.
text: Steroid hormones, thyroid hormones, retinoic acids, and vitamin D bind to their respective receptors, which are now classified as steroid/nuclear receptors. These receptors, upon ligand binding, translocate either intracellularly or intranuclearly and form large protein complexes with cofactors to regulate gene expression. As such, steroid/nuclear receptors are ligand-dependent transcription factors. With the emergence of green fluorescent protein (GFP) and its color variants, the subcellular distribution of these receptors has been shown to be more dynamic than previously thought, with some receptors shuttling between the cytoplasm and nucleus. Steroid/nuclear receptors can be categorized into three groups based on their unliganded distribution: those primarily located in the nucleus, those in the cytoplasm, and those with mixed cytoplasmic and nuclear distributions. However, upon ligand binding, these receptors nearly completely translocate to the nucleus. Hormonal stimulation leads to a shift from a homogeneous nucleus distribution to a heterogeneous dot-like pattern of receptors. Ligand binding recruits additional proteins, including cofactors, which trigger the redistribution of receptor complexes in the nucleus. This nuclear reorganization could involve more intricate processes than simple DNA binding sites for transcription. By imaging and localizing the activities and interactions of steroid/nuclear receptors within a single cell, a more comprehensive understanding of their functions can be gained.

title: EMT, the cytoskeleton, and cancer cell invasion
text: The metastatic process, or the spreading of cancer cells throughout the body to form secondary tumors, involves cancer cells leaving the primary tumor and acquiring the ability to migrate and invade surrounding tissues. This process, known as epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), involves changes in the adhesive properties of cancer cells, as well as the acquisition of migratory and invasive capabilities through the reorganization of the cytoskeleton and the formation of membrane protrusions. Despite significant progress in understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying EMT and tumor metastasis, many aspects of these processes remain poorly understood. In particular, the functions of different types of migratory organelles, such as lamellipodia, filopodia, invadopodia, and podosomes, are not well characterized. Furthermore, there is currently a lack of direct experimental evidence linking the formation of migratory membrane protrusions and the process of EMT and tumor metastasis. In this review, we have summarized recent advances in our understanding of the molecular processes and players involved in EMT on one hand, and the formation of invasive membrane protrusions on the other hand.

title: Different response of human glioma tumor-initiating cells to epidermal growth factor receptor kinase inhibitors.
text: A subpopulation of cancer stem cells (TICs), believed to be responsible for the development, progression, and recurrence of many tumors, were evaluated for their sensitivity to epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) kinase inhibitors (erlotinib and gefitinib) in vitro. Human glioma TICs were isolated from seven tumors and grown under conditions that promote the expression of stem cell markers (CD133, nestin), and the ability to differentiate into multiple cell types. The TIC cultures were tested for their sensitivity to increasing concentrations of erlotinib and gefitinib, and the results showed that most TICs exhibited a time- and concentration-dependent cell death. However, one TIC (GBM 2) was completely insensitive to both drugs, while another (GBM 7) was only sensitive at the highest concentrations tested. To better understand the mechanisms underlying this variability, the study used a radioligand binding assay to determine if the TICs expressed EGFR. The results showed that all GBM TICs expressed EGFR, and the inhibition of EGFR and ERK1/2 phosphorylation/activation occurred in all GBMs, regardless of their antiproliferative response. However, some TICs, such as GBM 2, showed high levels of Akt phosphorylation that were insensitive to the drugs, while others, such as GBM 7, were only sensitive to gefitinib at high concentrations. The study suggests that the sensitivity of TICs to anti-EGFR drugs may depend on the expression of phosphatase and tensin homolog and Akt inhibition.

title: Structural features of the interaction of the 3'-untranslated region of mRNA containing exosomal RNA-specific motifs with YB-1, a potential mediator of mRNA sorting.
text: In a previous study, we demonstrated that YB-1 is the only protein in the cytoplasmic (S100) extract of HEK293 cells that specifically interacts with RNA hairpins containing specific motifs (ACCAGCUC, CAGUGAGC, and UAAUCCCA). Here, we investigated the interaction between YB-1 and a fragment of the 3'-untranslated region (UTR) of septin 14 mRNA (SEPT14 RNA), which contains all three motifs. We found that YB-1 can bind to SEPT14 RNA in a cooperative manner, with up to 5 moles of protein binding per mole of RNA. RNA hairpins containing motifs 1 and 2 competed with SEPT14 RNA for binding to YB-1, while those containing motif 3 were less competitive. Using YB-1-bound RNA, we identified protected nucleotides in all three motifs, with hairpins containing motif 2 containing many protected nucleotides outside the motif. Our analysis of the environments of motifs 1-3 in the HEK293 cell mRNA 3' UTRs derived from RNA-seq data revealed that the primary binding sites of YB-1 are hairpins containing some part of the motif, along with its specific surroundings. We derived a consensus sequence for these hairpins and concluded that our findings provide a new understanding of the structural basis of the interactions between YB-1 and mRNAs carrying these motifs.

title: Periodic screening for breast cancer: the HIP Randomized Controlled Trial. Health Insurance Plan.
text: This paper presents the findings of the first breast cancer screening trial, launched in December 1963 to evaluate the effectiveness of screening. Participants were female members of the Health Insurance Plan (HIP) of Greater New York aged 40-64 years, who were randomly assigned to either the study group or the control group. The study group underwent screening, including mammography (cephalocaudal and lateral views of each breast) and clinical breast examination, while the control group did not receive screening. Breast cancer and mortality from breast cancer were analyzed by treatment group (study vs. control) and by entry-age subgroup. By the end of 18 years from entry, the study group had a 25% lower breast cancer mortality rate among women aged 40-49 and 50-59 at time of entry compared to the control group. However, the majority of this reduction occurred among women in the 40-49-year-old subgroup who were diagnosed with breast cancer after passing their 50th birthday, raising questions about the utility of screening women in their forties.

title: Staphylococcus aureus infections.
text: Micrococcus, when restricted in scope and activity, can cause acute suppurative inflammation (phlegmon), but when more extensive and intense in its effects on the human body, it can lead to the most virulent forms of septicaemia and pyaemia.1 In a series of elegant clinical observations and laboratory studies published in 1880 and 1882, Ogston highlighted the role of staphylococcal infections in sepsis and abscess formation.1,2 More than a century has passed since then, and Staphylococcus aureus remains a versatile and dangerous pathogen in humans. Despite the steady increase in both community-acquired and hospital-acquired staphylococcal infections, the overall mortality rate has remained relatively unchanged. Treatment of these infections . . .

title: Structural overview of the nuclear receptor superfamily: insights into physiology and therapeutics.
text:
Nuclear hormone receptors are highly desirable drug targets due to their ability to bind to hydrophobic molecules and undergo ligand-induced conformational changes that recruit transcriptional coactivators to specific genes. However, the major challenge in developing drug targets that selectively activate or suppress a single gene has been identifying ligands that target specific genes without affecting the entire repertoire of genes under the receptor's control.
In this summary, we discuss the concepts and progress made in the development of steroidal and nonsteroidal receptor ligands, including the use of crystal structures, high-throughput screens, and rational design approaches to identify therapeutic molecules. Despite the challenges, a deeper understanding of receptor interdomain communication, posttranslational modifications, and receptor-protein interactions could potentially be exploited to develop selective receptor modulators that target specific genes.
In summary, nuclear hormone receptors are ideal drug targets, but the challenge lies in identifying ligands that selectively activate or suppress a single gene without affecting the entire repertoire of genes under the receptor's control. By leveraging advanced techniques such as crystal structures, high-throughput screens, and rational design approaches, it may be possible to develop selective receptor modulators that target specific genes and improve disease outcomes.

title: Differential assembly of inwardly rectifying K+ channel subunits, Kir4.1 and Kir5.1, in brain astrocytes.
text: The inwardly rectifying K+ channel subunit Kir5.1 is extensively expressed in the brain, but its precise distribution and function are not yet fully understood. To investigate the distribution and properties of Kir5.1 in the mouse brain, we compared the biochemical and immunological properties of Kir5.1 with its subunit Kir4.1. Immunoprecipitation experiments revealed that brain-expressed Kir channels consist of at least two subsets: heteromeric Kir4.1/5.1 and homomeric Kir4.1. Immunolabeling using specific antibodies showed that these channels are assembled in a region-specific manner, with heteromeric Kir4.1/5.1 identified in the neocortex and olfactory bulb glomeruli, and homomeric Kir4.1 in the hippocampus and thalamus. Notably, homomeric Kir5.1 was not detected. Both heteromeric Kir4.1/5.1 and homomeric Kir4.1 were found to be expressed only in astrocytes, specifically in membrane domains facing the pia mater and blood vessels or in processes surrounding synapses. Additionally, we found that these astrocyte Kir channels associate with PDZ domain-containing syntrophins, which may play a role in their subcellular targeting. Since heteromeric Kir4.1/5.1 and homomeric Kir4.1 have distinct ion channel properties (Tanemoto et al., 2000; Tucker et al., 2000), it is possible that these channels have differential physiological roles in K+ buffering actions of brain astrocytes in a region-specific manner.

title: Low-grade serous ovarian cancer: a unique disease.
text: Low-grade serous ovarian carcinomas account for about 10% of all ovarian carcinomas. Recent research has revealed significant differences between the clinical and molecular characteristics of these tumors and their high-grade counterparts. Patients with low-grade serous ovarian tumors are typically diagnosed at a younger age and have a longer overall survival than those with high-grade serous ovarian carcinomas, despite lower response rates to conventional chemotherapy. Additionally, low-grade serous ovarian carcinomas exhibit distinct pathologic and molecular features compared to high-grade serous carcinomas, yet similarities with serous tumors of low malignant potential. This suggests a shared underlying pathology and a continuum of disease progression from low-malignant potential tumors to low-grade serous carcinomas. Further investigation, focusing specifically on low-grade serous carcinomas, could help elucidate the roles of additional chemotherapeutic agents, hormonal therapy, or targeted biologic agents in their treatment.

title: Renal outcomes with different fixed-dose combination therapies in patients with hypertension at high risk for cardiovascular events (ACCOMPLISH): a prespecified secondary analysis of a randomised controlled trial.
text:
The ACCOMPLISH trial, conducted in five countries, compared the effects of initial antihypertensive therapy with benazepril plus amlodipine versus benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide on cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. The trial found that the combination of benazepril and amlodipine was superior to the combination of benazepril and hydrochlorothiazide in reducing cardiovascular events. However, the trial also found that the combination of benazepril and amlodipine slowed the progression of chronic kidney disease to a greater extent than the combination of benazepril and hydrochlorothiazide.
In analysis of the trial results, 113 events of chronic kidney disease progression occurred in the benazepril plus amlodipine group, compared with 215 events in the benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide group. The most common adverse event in patients with chronic kidney disease was peripheral oedema, which occurred more frequently in the benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide group. Angio-oedema was more frequent in the benazepril plus amlodipine group. In patients without chronic kidney disease, dizziness, hypokalaemia, and hypotension were more frequent in the benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide group than in the benazepril plus amlodipine group.
The results of the trial suggest that initial antihypertensive treatment with benazepril plus amlodipine should be considered in preference to benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide due to its potential to slow the progression of nephropathy. The trial was funded by Novartis.

title: Effects of exercise training on health status in patients with chronic heart failure: HF-ACTION randomized controlled trial.
text:
Background:
Previous studies have shown inconsistent results regarding the impact of exercise training on patient-reported health status in patients with heart failure. This study aimed to investigate the effects of exercise training on health status among patients with heart failure.
Methods:
This multicenter, randomized controlled trial enrolled 2331 medically stable outpatients with heart failure and left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less. Participants were randomly assigned to either usual care plus aerobic exercise training (n=1172) or usual care alone (n=1159). The exercise training program consisted of 36 supervised sessions followed by home-based training, while the usual care group received only standard medical care. Health status was assessed using the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) at baseline, every 3 months for 12 months, and annually thereafter for up to 4 years.
Results:
The median follow-up time was 2.5 years. At 3 months, the exercise group showed a significant improvement in the KCCQ overall summary score compared to the usual care group (mean difference=5.21, 95% CI=4.42-6.00). The additional improvement in the exercise group was statistically significant (P<.001). There were no significant changes in KCCQ score for either group after 3 months, resulting in a sustained, greater improvement overall for the exercise group (P<.001). Similar results were observed on the KCCQ subscales, and no subgroup interactions were detected.
Conclusion:
