Exercise training conferred modest but statistically significant improvements in self-reported health status compared to usual care without training. These improvements occurred early and persisted over time.
Trial Registration:
clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT00047437.

title: Acute respiratory failure in patients with severe community-acquired pneumonia: a prospective randomized evaluation of noninvasive ventilation.
text:
In uncontrolled studies, noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV) was found to be useful in avoiding endotracheal intubation in patients with acute respiratory failure (ARF) caused by severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). To evaluate the safety and efficacy of NPPV in patients with severe CAP and ARF, we conducted a prospective, randomized study comparing standard treatment plus NPPV delivered through a face mask to standard treatment alone.
We included patients meeting the American Thoracic Society criteria for severe CAP who had ARF (refractory hypoxemia and/or hypercapnia with acidosis). Exclusion criteria were severe hemodynamic instability, requirement for emergent cardiopulmonary resuscitation, home mechanical ventilation or oxygen long-term supplementation, concomitant severe disease with a low expectation of life, inability to expectorate or contraindications to the use of the mask. Fifty-six consecutive patients were enrolled, and the two groups were similar at study entry. The use of NPPV was well tolerated, safe, and associated with a significant reduction in respiratory rate, need for endotracheal intubation (21% vs. 50%; p = 0.03), and duration of intensive care unit (ICU) stay (1.8 ± 0.7 d vs. 6 ± 1.8 d; p = 0.04). The two groups had a similar intensity of nursing care workload, time interval from study entry to endotracheal intubation, duration of hospitalization, and hospital mortality. Among patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), those randomized to NPPV had a lower intensity of nursing care workload (p = 0.04) and improved 2-mo survival (88.9% vs. 37.5%; p = 0.05). We conclude that in selected patients with ARF caused by severe CAP, NPPV was associated with a significant reduction in the rate of endotracheal intubation and duration of ICU stay. A 2-mo survival advantage was seen in patients with COPD.

title: Smallest angiosperm genomes found in lentibulariaceae, with chromosomes of bacterial size.
text: Nuclear holoploid genome sizes (C-values) have been estimated to vary greatly in angiosperms, with the smallest known C-value of 157 Mbp recorded in Arabidopsis thaliana. However, recent findings in the carnivorous plant family Lentibulariaceae reveal that three taxa exhibit significantly lower C-values: Genlisea margaretae with 63 Mbp, G. aurea with 64 Mbp, and Utricularia gibba with 88 Mbp. These values are significantly smaller than the smallest mitotic anaphase chromatids in G. aurea, which are approximately bacterial in size (approximately 4 Mbp). Also, Utricularia species generally have lower C-values compared to A. thaliana or are similar in size. The highest C-value known from Lentibulariaceae was found in Genlisea hispidula with 1510 Mbp, resulting in approximately 24-fold variation among Genlisea and Lentibulariaceae. These findings suggest that genome miniaturization may have occurred in Genlisea and Utricularia, which are also terminal cablings in the eudicot phylogeny. Moreover, these genera exhibit one of the highest mutational rates in several genomic regions among angiosperms, which may be linked to their specialized patterns of genome evolution. Interestingly, ultrasmall genomes have not been found in the sister group of Genlisea-Utricularia, Pinguicula, which does not show accelerated mutational rates. C-values in Pinguicula varied only 1.7-fold from 487 to 829 Mbp.

title: Parasite multiplication potential and the severity of Falciparum malaria.
text: A comparison of the multiplication rates and invasiveness of Plasmodium falciparum parasites isolated from adult Thai patients hospitalized with uncomplicated malaria (n=34) and those from individuals with severe malaria (n=42) was conducted. To simulate severe malaria and account for host factors, in vitro cultures were adjusted to 1% parasitemia using the same red blood cell donor. Our findings revealed that P. falciparum isolates from patients with severe malaria exhibited significantly higher initial cycle multiplication rates in vitro (median [95% CI]: 8.3 [7.1-10.5] vs. 2.8 [1.7-3.9]; P<0.001). Additionally, parasites associated with severe malaria showed unrestricted red blood cell invasion, whereas those from uncomplicated malaria were restricted to approximately 40% (31%-53%) of red blood cells. Notably, P. falciparum parasites causing severe malaria were less selective and multiplied more rapidly at higher parasitemias compared to those causing uncomplicated malaria.

title: PHD3-dependent hydroxylation of HCLK2 promotes the DNA damage response.
text: The DNA damage response (DDR) is a dynamic regulatory network that plays a crucial role in maintaining genome integrity. Post-translational modifications are used to control the flow of signals in a spatiotemporal manner, but the response of the DDR to environmental cues, such as changes in oxygen levels, remains poorly understood. Our study found that an essential component of the ATR/CHK1 signaling pathway, the human homolog of the Caenorhabditis elegans biological clock protein CLK-2 (HCLK2), interacts with and is hydroxylated by prolyl hydroxylase domain protein 3 (PHD3). This hydroxylation is essential for HCLK2's interaction with ATR and the subsequent activation of the ATR/CHK1/p53 pathway. Inhibiting PHD3, either with a pan-hydroxylase inhibitor or through hypoxia, prevents the activation of the ATR/CHK1/p53 pathway and decreases apoptosis induced by DNA damage. Consistently, mice lacking PHD3 are resistant to the effects of ionizing radiation and have decreased thymic apoptosis, a marker of genomic integrity. Our discovery reveals the mechanism by which hypoxia inhibits the DDR, suggesting that hydroxylation of HCLK2 is a potential therapeutic target for regulating the ATR/CHK1/p53 pathway.

title: Economic implications of nighttime attending intensivist coverage in a medical intensive care unit.
text:
Objective: To investigate the cost implications of changing the intensive care unit (ICU) staffing model from on-demand presence to mandatory 24-hour in-house critical care specialist presence.
Design: A pre-post comparison was conducted among prospectively assessed cohorts of patients admitted to the ICU at a large academic center in the Midwest, 1 year before and 1 year after the staffing model change. Data were stratified by Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation III (APACHE III) quartile and admittance time (day or night). Costs were modeled using a generalized linear model with log-link and γ-distributed errors.
Setting: A large academic center in the Midwest.
Patients: All patients admitted to the adult ICU on or after January 1, 2005 and discharged on or before December 31, 2006, were included. Patients receiving care under both staffing models were excluded.
Intervention: The ICU staffing model was changed from on-demand presence to mandatory 24-hour in-house critical care specialist presence.
Measurements and Main Results: Total cost estimates of hospitalization were calculated for each patient from the day of ICU admission to the day of hospital discharge. Adjusted mean total cost estimates were 61% lower in the post period relative to the pre period for patients admitted during night hours (7 pm to 7 am) who were in the highest APACHE III quartile. No significant difference was seen at other severity levels. The unadjusted ICU length of stay fell in the post period relative to the pre period (3.5 versus 4.8 days) with no change in non-ICU length of stay.
Conclusions: The study findings suggest that 24-hour ICU intensivist staffing reduces lengths of stay and cost estimates for the sickest patients admitted at night. However, the cost of introducing such a staffing model must be weighed against the potential total savings generated for such patients in smaller ICUs, especially those that predominantly care for lower-acuity patients.

title: GENOTYPING OF THALASSEMIA IN MICROCYTIC HYPOCHROMIC ANEMIA PATIENTS FROM SOUTHWEST REGION OF IRAN
text:
Objective: To investigate the frequency of α-gene and s-gene mutations in individuals with microcytic hypochromic anemia in Southwest Iran.
Methodology: We analyzed 340 subjects with MCV <80fl; MCH <27pg from the Southwest region of Iran, including 171 with Beta-thalassemia trait, 88 with Alpha-thalassemia trait, 13 with thalassemia major, 11 with hemoglobin variants (HbS, HbC, and HbD Punjab), and 42 with iron-deficiency anemia. The remaining 15 patients had unknown etiology. Genotyping for -α 3.7, -α 4.2, – α PA, - α 5NT, and - - MED was conducted using gap-PCR. Additionally, direct mutation analysis by ARMS was performed for 23 known s-gene mutations.
Results: The overall frequency of - α 3.7 deletion was 20% in 325 individuals. Genotyping for the 23 most common s-gene mutations revealed a prevalence of CD 36/37 (9.7%), IVS II-I (11.7%), and IVS I-110 (3.5%). There were significant differences in MCV and MCH indices between Beta-thalassemia trait and Beta-thalassemia Major, and also between Beta-thalassemia trait and Hb Variants (P-value = 0.04).
Conclusion: α -gene and s-gene mutations are common in the Southwest region of Iran. Molecular genotyping can help diagnose unexplained microcytosis and prevent unnecessary iron supplementation.

title: Systemic biomarkers in exacerbations of COPD: the evolving clinical challenge.
text:
Background: Exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remain a significant cause of mortality and morbidity, despite advances in understanding their pathophysiology. Diagnosis and management of ECOPD rely heavily on clinical presentation, which can be unpredictable and variable. Researchers have investigated various biomarkers to improve the establishment and confirmation of ECOPD diagnosis, as well as prognosis and treatment guidance.
Methods: An online search of literature published until December 2010 included searching for terms related to ECOPD, biomarkers, and sampling methods. Biomarkers were assessed for their potential role in diagnosis, etiology, severity evaluation, prognosis prediction, and treatment guidance.
Results: Numerous systemic biomarkers have been measured in the context of ECOPD, with most showing increased levels at ECOPD onset and decreased levels during the course of exacerbations. Correlations among these biomarkers have been reported, but establishing direct associations with clinical variables has been challenging. Although there are still several limitations, some biomarkers, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) for ECOPD identification and procalcitonin (PCT) for antibiotic guidance, may provide clinically relevant information.
Conclusions: Currently, no single biomarker has gained widespread acceptance, but some biomarkers offer clinically useful information. Investigating these biomarkers in larger, decision-making studies is expected to be an area of intense research in the near future.

title: Preoperative Predictors of Weight Loss Following Bariatric Surgery: Systematic Review
text:
A startling 32% of adults in the United States struggle with obesity. While surgery can lead to remarkable weight loss, studies have shown that up to 30% of individuals do not achieve successful weight loss after bariatric surgery. Our investigation aimed to identify key psychosocial factors associated with weight loss following bariatric surgery.
We conducted a thorough search of PubMed® and the Cochrane Database of Reviews of Effectiveness, analyzing articles published between 1988 and April 2010. We evaluated a total of 115 studies, screening for factors such as preoperative weight loss, eating disorders, psychiatric disorders, and substance abuse.
Our findings revealed that mandatory preoperative weight loss may be positively associated with weight loss after surgery. On the other hand, factors such as preoperative BMI, super-obesity, and personality disorders may be negatively associated with weight loss. Additionally, we found that super-obese patients experienced a significant decrease in excess weight loss (EWL) of 10.1% (95% confidence interval (CI) [3.7–16.5%]), while patients with binge eating at 12 months after surgery displayed an increase in EWL of 5.9% (95% CI [1.9–9.8%]).
While these findings are encouraging, we recognize that further research is necessary to determine whether preoperative factors can accurately predict weight loss after bariatric surgery. If these factors are identified, patient selection and intervention strategies can be improved to ensure the best possible outcomes.

title: The tumor necrosis factor receptor stalk regions define responsiveness to soluble versus membrane-bound ligand.
text: The family of tumor necrosis factor receptors (TNFRs) and their ligands form a complex signaling network that regulates immune responses. Despite their similarities, different members of this receptor family respond differently to their respective ligands, and the underlying molecular mechanisms are not yet fully understood. Using a well-established system of chimeric TNFRs and novel ligand variants that mimic the bioactivity of membrane-bound TNF (mTNF), we uncovered that the membrane-proximal extracellular stalk regions of TNFR1 and TNFR2 play a crucial role in modulating responsiveness to soluble TNF (sTNF). We found that the stalk region of TNFR2, compared to the corresponding region of TNFR1, efficiently inhibits both the receptor's clustering on specific cell membranes and ligand-independent homotypic receptor assembly, thereby preventing sTNF-induced signaling but not mTNF-induced signaling. This discovery not only has implications for other TNFR family members but also identifies potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

title: A bird's-eye view of sex chromosome dosage compensation.
text: Extensive analysis of a select few genetically accessible species with XX/XY sex chromosomes has led to generalizations about the process of sex chromosome dosage compensation that do not accurately apply to ZZ/ZW sex chromosome systems, such as those found in birds. The inherent imbalance in the dose of sex chromosome genes has driven the evolution of sex-chromosome-wide mechanisms for balancing gene dosage between the sexes and relative to autosomal genes. Recent advances in our understanding of avian genomes have prompted a reevaluation of sex-specific dosage compensation (SSDC) in birds, which is less effective than in known XX/XY systems. Insights gleaned from studying SSDC in birds also highlight similarities and differences with respect to mechanisms in XX/XY species. The study of SSDC in birds offers new opportunities for investigating dosage compensation in a ZZ/ZW system, providing valuable insight into the evolution of SSDC more broadly.

title: The role of CHMP2BIntron5 in autophagy and frontotemporal dementia.
text: Charged multivesicular body protein 2B (CHMP2B) - an integral component of the endosomal complex required for transport-III (ESCRT-III) - plays a crucial role in the vital deformation of membranes during autophagy and endolysosomal trafficking. A specific mutation, CHMP2BIntron5, in the CHMP2B gene is associated with a subset of hereditary frontotemporal dementia (FTD-3). This mutation results in a C-terminal truncation, deleting an important Vps4 binding site and removing the normal autoinhibitory state of CHMP2B. CHMP2B is expressed in most cell types, but its importance is particularly pronounced in neurons. The CHMP2BIntron5 mutation leads to misregulation of transmembrane receptors, accumulation of multilamellar structures, abnormal lysosomal morphology, downregulation of a brain-specific microRNA (miRNA-124), abnormal dendritic spine morphology, decreased dendritic arborization, and cell death. To better understand the diverse phenotypes and develop therapeutic approaches, transgenic fly, mouse, and human cell lines are being employed as part of a Special Issue on Autophagy.

title: Restless legs syndrome and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a review of the literature.
text:
Objective: To review the existing literature on the relationship between Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), with a focus on the potential mechanisms underlying this association and the potential for shared pharmacological treatments.
Methodology: A PubMed search was conducted to identify studies examining the association between RLS and ADHD.
Results: Up to 44% of subjects with ADHD have been found to have RLS or RLS symptoms, while up to 26% of subjects with RLS have been found to have ADHD or ADHD symptoms. Several mechanisms may explain this association, including sleep disruption associated with RLS leading to inattentiveness, moodiness, and paradoxical overactivity, as well as diurnal manifestations of RLS mimicking ADHD symptoms. Additionally, there may be a common dopamine dysfunction underlying RLS and ADHD in some individuals. Limited evidence suggests that dopaminergic agents such as levodopa/carbidopa, pergolide, and ropinirole may be effective in treating RLS associated with ADHD symptoms in children.
Discussion: While evidence from clinical studies suggests an association between RLS and ADHD or ADHD symptoms, further research is needed to better understand the degree of association and the underlying mechanisms. Epidemiologic studies are required to assess the relationship between ADHD and RLS symptoms in non-clinical populations. Further investigations should explore the potential for shared pharmacological treatments for RLS and ADHD.
Conclusion: Although limited, the existing evidence suggests that there may be an association between RLS and ADHD, and that dopaminergic agents may be effective in treating RLS associated with ADHD symptoms. However, due to the lack of randomized and blinded controlled studies, evidence-based recommendations cannot be made at this time.

title: Impact of the KU80 pathway on NHEJ-induced genome rearrangements in mammalian cells.
text: Utilizing a substrate with an I-SceI-excised fragment, we investigated the impact of non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) on mammalian chromosome rearrangements. Through accurate and inaccurate rejoining, we determined that deletion is 2- to 8-fold more efficient than inversion, regardless of the DNA ends structure. KU80 regulates accurate rejoining, whereas in its absence, mutagenic rejoining, which relies on microhomology-mediated repair, occurs more efficiently. In cells carrying both NHEJ and homologous recombination (HR) substrates harboring a third I-SceI site, we found that NHEJ is at least 3.3-fold more efficient than HR. Moreover, translocation of the I-SceI fragment from the NHEJ substrate locus into the HR-I-SceI site can occur, but happens 50- to 100-fold less frequently than deletion. Both deletions and translocations exhibit both accurate and inaccurate rejoining, indicating that they are the result of a combination of KU-dependent and KU-independent processes. Therefore, these processes should represent prevalent pathways for DNA double-strand break (DSB)-induced genetic instability in mammalian cells.

title: The multi-zinc finger protein ZNF217 contacts DNA through a two-finger domain.
text: Classical C2H2 zinc finger proteins are prevalent transcription factors in eukaryotes, with extensive research devoted to elucidating their DNA recognition mechanisms. In general, a tandem array of three fingers separated by TGERP links is necessary for sequence-specific DNA binding. Nonetheless, a considerable number of zinc finger proteins deviate from this structure, raising questions about their DNA interaction capabilities. We investigate the multi-finger protein ZNF217, implicated in oncogenesis and E-cadherin repression, which contains eight classical zinc fingers. Using various methods, we uncover that two fingers, 6 and 7, can interact with DNA. Examining the potential binding site for ZNF217 in the E-cadherin promoter, we find that it is a suboptimal site. NMR analysis, mutagenesis, and fluorescence anisotropy titrations are used to characterize the DNA binding surface of ZNF217 and assess its specificity. Furthermore, sequence analysis reveals that some multi-finger proteins harbor two-finger units, suggesting the possibility of a distinct subclass of DNA recognition motifs.

title: Knowledge, attitudes, risk perception, and cancer screening behaviors among cancer survivors.
text: Background: Knowledge, attitudes, and perceived risk related to second primary cancer (SPC) screening among cancer survivors remain largely unexplored, with implications for their adherence to screening guidelines. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we recruited 326 cancer survivors (>1 year post-primary treatment) from six oncology clinics in the Republic of Korea. Participants' knowledge, attitudes, perceived risk, and screening practices were assessed, along with sociodemographic, behavioral, and clinical variables. Multivariate logistic regression identified behavioral factors associated with completion of appropriate SPC screening according to national guidelines. Results: Approximately 37.7% of survivors had undergone all recommended SPC screens. Survivors had a high perception of SPC risk and benefits, as well as positive attitudes toward cancer screening. However, they had limited knowledge of SPC screening tests and few had received a physician recommendation for screening. Although there was no association between perceived risk and positive attitudes, higher knowledge was found to be significantly associated with completion of all appropriate SPC screens (adjusted odds ratio, 1.81; 95% confidence interval, 1.03-3.33). Conclusions: Our study suggests that cancer survivors have limited knowledge of SPC screening tests, which may contribute to lower screening adherence in this population. Enhancing knowledge and physician recommendations may improve SPC screening uptake.

title: Ria1p (Ynl163c), a protein similar to elongation factors 2, is involved in the biogenesis of the 60S subunit of the ribosome in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
text: RIA1 (YNL163c) is a quasi-essential gene that encodes a protein with significant similarity to elongation factors 2. C-terminal deletions of the protein result in a severe growth defect, which can be alleviated by intragenic mutations in the RIA1 gene or dominant extragenic mutations in TIF6. The latter is thought to play a role in the production of the 60S subunit of the ribosome. In fact, dominant TIF6 alleles can also counteract the effects of a complete deletion of the RIA1 gene. Depletion of Ria1p leads to a drastic change in the polysome profile, characterized by a marked decrease in the abundance of 80S monosomes, an imbalance in the 40S/60S ratio, and the appearance of half-mers. Dissociation of monosomes and polysomes in Ria1p-depleted cells revealed a specific reduction in the amount of 60S subunits. Localization experiments using HA-tagged derivatives of Ria1p failed to detect any stable association of Ria1p with ribosome subunits, 80S monosomes, or polysomes. Furthermore, cell fractionation assays showed that Ria1p is present in both the cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions. Taken together, these findings suggest that Ria1p is involved in the biogenesis of the 60S subunit of the ribosome.

title: The Intestinal Immune System in Obesity and Insulin Resistance.
text: Obesity and insulin resistance are linked to chronic inflammation in metabolic tissues, such as adipose tissue and the liver. Recent research has highlighted the crucial role of the intestinal immune system in the development of metabolic disease. Obesity can lead to altered immune function in the gut, which in turn can result in changes to the gut microbiota, intestinal barrier function, and the number of immune cells in the gut. These alterations can lead to oral tolerance issues and may play a role in the development of insulin resistance. The gut immune system appears to be a promising new target for the treatment of systemic inflammation in insulin resistance. This review will examine the emerging field of intestinal immunity in relation to obesity-related insulin resistance and its impact on metabolic disorders.

title: Human placental lactogen and unconjugated estriol concentrations in twin pregnancy: monitoring of fetal development in intrauterine growth retardation and single intrauterine fetal death.
text: In this study, the concentrations of human placental lactogen and unconjugated estriol in the serum of 100 uneventful twin pregnancies were evaluated and compared to those in 16 twin pregnancies with intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) or single intrauterine fetal death (SIFD). In twin pregnancies with IUGR (n = 8), human placental lactogen levels were at the lower limit of normal range for singleton pregnancies, while estriol levels were normal in most cases. However, when one of the fetuses had died before week 33 of pregnancy (n = 5), both human placental lactogen and estriol levels were low and were almost at the levels seen in singleton pregnancies. In twin pregnancies where intrauterine fetal death occurred after week 36 of pregnancy (n = 3), both hormone levels remained normal until term. These findings suggest that human placental lactogen rather than estriol is a good indicator of IUGR in twin pregnancy, and both hormones are useful for monitoring the surviving fetus in the case of SIFD.

title: Low antioxidant enzyme gene expression in pancreatic islets compared with various other mouse tissues.
text: Using a delicate Northern blot hybridization technique, the expression of superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and glutathione peroxidase was investigated in pancreatic islets and compared to various other mouse tissues (liver, kidney, brain, lung, skeletal muscle, heart muscle, adrenal gland, and pituitary gland). gene expression of these antioxidant enzymes was typically in the range of ±50% of that in the liver. However, in pancreatic islets, gene expression was significantly lower, with levels of the cytoplasmic Cu/Zn SOD and mitochondrial Mn SOD at around 30-40% of those in the liver. Glutathione peroxidase gene expression was observed at 15%, and catalase gene expression was undetectable in pancreatic islets. These decreased levels of antioxidant enzyme gene expression may provide an explanation for the remarkable sensitivity of pancreatic beta cells to cytotoxic damage by diabetogenic compounds and during the progression of human and animal diabetes.

title: Cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase isozymes expressed in mouse skeletal muscle.
text: To investigate changes in cyclic nucleotide metabolism in muscle disorders, the expression of phosphodiesterase (PDE) isozymes was examined in normal mouse leg muscle. Fractions were generated by centrifugation at 10,000 x g and 100,000 x g, and PDE activity was found predominantly in the soluble fractions for cAMP, while cGMP activity was distributed equally among soluble and particulate fractions. Pharmacological inhibitors revealed that PDE4 is the major cAMP hydrolyzing enzyme, while PDE2 is the major cGMP hydrolyzing enzyme in mouse leg muscle. PDE1 was expressed at low levels, while PDE3 and PDE5 had intermediate expression. Findings showed that between 20 and 40% of total PDE activity remained in the presence of inhibitors for PDE1-PDE5, suggesting that other PDE families contribute to the total PDE pool. Reverse-transcription PCR using family-specific primers confirmed the presence of mRNA for PDE7-PDE9, supporting this conclusion. Total PDE activity was found to be elevated in tissue extracts from a mouse model of Duchenne's muscular dystrophy.

title: Exercise-induced asthma.
text: The study examined the impact of exercise on lung function in 7 patients with asthma. Three patients demonstrated a considerable decrease in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) after exercise. The degree of hyperventilation triggered by exercise correlated with the post-exercise decrease in FEV1. Voluntary hyperventilation at rest also decreased FEV1 in all patients with asthma. Inhaling 5.6% carbon dioxide during voluntary hyperventilation instead of room air resulted in a larger ventilation and greater decrease in FEV1. In contrast, neither exercise nor voluntary hyperventilation had a significant effect on FEV1 in normal subjects and patients with chronic bronchitis. Both exercise-induced and hyperventilation-induced decreases in FEV1 were inhibited by prior administration of isoproterenol but not by atropine. The study suggests that exercise-induced asthma may be a form of hyperventilation-induced asthma. Several underlying mechanisms, such as airway obstruction, may contribute to the development of asthma.

title: An antimicrobial protein of the gut symbiont Bacteroides fragilis with a MACPF domain of host immune proteins.
text: Bacteroidales, the most profuse Gram-negative bacteria of the human digestive tract microbiota, are said to constitute more than half of the bacterial flora in many individuals. Certain factors that contribute to their ability to thrive within this ecosystem are just beginning to be elucidated. Nevertheless, the role of ecological competition, particularly interference competition, where one organism detrimentally impacts another, remains largely unexplored. To gain further insight into the significance of this ecological phenomenon as it pertains to these ubiquitous gut bacteria and the factors that may facilitate such competition, we screened Bacteroides fragilis for the production of antimicrobial compounds. We discovered that the production of extracellularly secreted antimicrobial molecules is widespread in this species. The initial molecule identified, which is described in this manuscript, houses a membrane attack complex/perforin (MACPF) domain similar to that found in host immune molecules which kill bacteria and virally infected cells by pore formation, and mutations affecting key residues of this domain abolished its activity. This antimicrobial molecule, termed BSAP-1, is secreted through the cell's outer membrane vesicles and no additional proteins are required for its secretion, processing, or immunity of the producing cell. This investigation provides the initial insight into molecules that promote competitive interference among Bacteroidales strains within the human gut microbiota.

title: Directional perception of distributed sound sources.
text:
In an effort to investigate the perception of spatially distributed sound sources, two listening experiments were conducted in anechoic conditions using 13 loudspeakers evenly distributed in the frontal horizontal plane. The first experiment involved playing incoherent noise signals from widely distributed sound sources with gaps in their distribution, with the results showing that the accuracy of perceiving the exact loudspeaker distribution was limited and the perceived width of the distribution was narrower than the actual distribution.Up to three spatially distributed loudspeakers that were simultaneously emitting sound could be individually perceived, and the number of loudspeakers perceived as emitting sound was also smaller than the actual number.
In the second experiment, a reference with 13 loudspeakers and test cases with fewer loudspeakers were presented, and the perceived spatial differences were rated. The effect of noise bandwidth was particularly interesting, with noise with different bandwidths centered around 500 and 4000 Hz used. The results showed that as the number of loudspeakers increased from four to seven, the perceived auditory event was very similar to that perceived with 13 loudspeakers at all bandwidths. However, larger perceived differences were observed in wideband noise than in narrow-band noise.

title: Adoptive T cell transfer for cancer immunotherapy in the era of synthetic biology.
text: Adoptive T-cell transfer technology for cancer and chronic infections is an emerging field that holds great promise, as evidenced by recent trial results. By leveraging synthetic biology engineering techniques to enhance T lymphocytes with high-affinity antigen receptors, this approach can overcome the major limitation of immunotherapy, immune tolerance. Advances in cell engineering and culture methods have enabled the efficient gene transfer and ex vivo expansion of these cells, making this technology more accessible for broader application. However, a major challenge facing the field is improving the specificity of engineered T cells to target tumors, as targeting shared antigens can lead to off-target toxicities as observed in recent trials. As the technology matures, the major engineering challenge is the development of automated cell culture systems to make the approach widely available beyond specialized academic centers.

title: Bruce treadmill test in children: normal values in a clinic population.
text: The Bruce treadmill protocol is appropriate for children as young as 4 years of age. Maximal endurance time can serve as the sole indicator of exercise capacity, and normal values were established using 327 children with benign heart murmurs. Boys' mean endurance time increased from 10.4 minutes at age 4 to 13-15 years, while girls' mean endurance time increased from 9.5 minutes at age 4 to 10-12 years. The mean maximal heart rate ranged from 193 to 206 beats per minute, with small age differences in mean maximal and submaximal heart rates. There were negative correlations between endurance time and weight-to-height ratio, as well as between heart rates at treadmill stages 1-3 and endurance times. However, the correlation coefficient between endurance time and maximal oxygen uptake was 0.88, suggesting that endurance time alone can be a suitable indicator of exercise performance for clinical purposes.

title: Immunoproteasome and LMP2 polymorphism in aged and Alzheimer's disease brains.
text: In this research, we examined the presence and function of the immunoproteasome and its LMP2 subunit polymorphism at codon 60 in Alzheimer's disease (AD). The immunoproteasome was found to be present in brain regions such as the hippocampus and cerebellum, primarily in neurons, astrocytes, and endothelial cells. Our findings revealed that the expression of immunoproteasome was significantly higher in the brains of AD patients compared to non-demented elderly, with minimal or undetectable levels in young brain. Additionally, AD affected regions showed a partial decrease in proteasome trypsin-like activity. The study of LMP2 polymorphism (R/H) revealed that it did not influence LMP2 expression (neither the mRNA nor the mature protein) in brain tissue. However, brain areas of AD patients carrying the RR genotype showed an increased proteasome activity compared to RH carriers in control brain tissue. To investigate whether this effect of the genotype might be related to AD onset, we conducted a genetic study, which found no association between LMP2 codon 60 polymorphism and AD onset, despite its impact on proteasome activity in human brain.

title: The centrosome and its mode of inheritance: the reduction of the centrosome during gametogenesis and its restoration during fertilization.
text:
The inheritance of the centrosome during fertilization and gametogenesis, or the process of cell division, is not fully understood. Although it is known that both the sperm and egg contribute equally to the haploid genome during fertilization, the contribution of the centrosome is still a topic of debate. This article reviews evidence gathered from various experimental approaches to test Boveri's hypothesis that the sperm introduces the centrosome during fertilization, while the egg provides the missing protoplasmic substratum. However, the findings indicate that centrosome inheritance is not always universal, as parthenogenesis and de novo centrosome formation occur in some systems. The article proposes models of centrosome structure and mechanisms of centrosome restoration during fertilization, including the attraction of maternal centrosomal components to the paternal reproducing element and post-translational modifications. The study highlights the complexity of centrosome inheritance and the need for further research to fully understand this important aspect of development.
The restoration of the centrosome during fertilization and its reduction during gametogenesis are crucial events in development that have not been fully elucidated. Although it is well established that both the sperm and egg contribute equally to the haploid genome during fertilization, the contribution of the centrosome remains a mystery. This article aims to investigate centrosome inheritance patterns and evaluate nine essential activities of the centrosome.
Boveri once proposed that the ripe egg lacks an active division center, while the sperm possesses one but lacks the protoplasmic substratum to operate. Fertilization thus completes the missing element necessary for development. This idea is supported by the findings of 11 experimental approaches that indicate the sperm introduces the centrosome during fertilization. However, the study also suggests that centrosome inheritance is not universal, as parthenogenesis and de novo centrosome formation occur in some systems.
The article proposes models of centrosome structure and mechanisms of centrosome restoration during fertilization. The zygotic centrosome is believed to be recreated by attracting maternal centrosomal components, including gamma-tubulin and the 25S "gamma-some" particle, to the paternal reproducing element, followed by post-translational modifications, such as phosphorylation, disulfide reduction, and calcium ion binding. This process blends both maternal and paternal constituents to create a functional zygote centrosome.
In conclusion, the inheritance of the centrosome during fertilization and gametogenesis is a complex process that remains poorly understood. Further research is needed to elucidate the mechanisms of centrosome restoration and the role of maternal and paternal components in centrosome inheritance.

title: Aggregation of vascular risk factors and risk of incident Alzheimer disease.
text:
The following is a rewritten version of the given text:
BACKGROUND: The prevalence of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasing among the elderly population, and vascular risk factors may contribute to this trend. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the association between the aggregation of vascular risk factors and the risk of AD. METHODS: The study included 1,138 individuals without dementia at baseline (mean age 76.2) who were followed for a median of 5.5 years. The presence of vascular risk factors was evaluated, and the association with incident possible and probable AD was analyzed. RESULTS: Four vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, and current smoking) were significantly associated with an increased risk of AD (p < 0.10) when analyzed individually. The risk of AD increased with the number of risk factors, and the adjusted hazards ratio for probable AD was 3.4 (95% CI: 1.8, 6.3; p for trend < 0.0001) among individuals with three or more risk factors compared to those with no risk factors. Additionally, diabetes and current smoking were the strongest risk factors in isolation or when combined, while hypertension and heart disease were also associated with an increased risk of AD when clustered with diabetes, smoking, or each other. CONCLUSIONS: The risk of AD increases with the number of vascular risk factors. Diabetes and current smoking are the strongest risk factors, but clusters including hypertension and heart disease also contribute to the increased risk of AD. The associations are unlikely to be explained by misclassification of the outcome, given the strong associations when only probable AD is considered.

title: Hotspot mutations in H3F3A and IDH1 define distinct epigenetic and biological subgroups of glioblastoma.
text: Glioblastoma (GBM), a malignant brain tumor, exhibits significant heterogeneity and poor prognosis. Recent research has uncovered recurrent H3F3A mutations in approximately one-third of pediatric GBM, affecting specific amino acids on histone H3 (K27 and G34). Our findings indicate that each H3F3A mutation defines a distinct epigenetic subgroup of GBM, characterized by a unique global methylation pattern. Importantly, these mutations are mutually exclusive with IDH1 mutations, which define a separate subgroup. In addition, we identified three further epigenetic subgroups that are enriched for hallmark genetic events common in adult GBM and/or established transcriptomic signatures. Moreover, we observed that the two H3F3A mutations lead to the formation of GBMs in different anatomic compartments, with distinct regulation of transcription factors OLIG1, OLIG2, and FOXG1, suggesting different cellular origins.

title: Glucocorticoid with cyclophosphamide for paraquat-induced lung fibrosis.
text:
Background: Paraquat is a widely used herbicide, but it is also highly toxic and can lead to fatal poisoning in many developing countries. While standard treatments can help prevent further absorption and reduce the load of paraquat in the blood, their effectiveness is limited. The immune system plays a crucial role in exacerbating paraquat-induced lung fibrosis, and immunosuppressive treatment using glucocorticoid and cyclophosphamide has been developed and studied as a potential treatment.
Objectives: To assess the effectiveness of glucocorticoid with cyclophosphamide in reducing mortality in patients with paraquat-induced lung fibrosis.
Methods: The study searched several databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, to identify randomized controlled trials on the topic. The inclusion criteria were RCTs that included patients with moderate to severe paraquat poisoning and provided data on mortality at final follow-up. The data were analyzed using a meta-analysis with a fixed-effect model.
Results: The systematic review included three trials with a combined total of 164 participants. The results showed that patients who received glucocorticoid with cyclophosphamide in addition to standard care had a lower risk of death at final follow-up compared to those receiving standard care only.
Conclusion: Based on the findings of three small RCTs, glucocorticoid with cyclophosphamide may be a beneficial treatment for patients with paraquat-induced lung fibrosis. Further study is needed to establish the efficacy and safety of this treatment in larger samples. Hospitals may consider providing this treatment as part of a randomized controlled trial with allocation concealment to ensure the best possible results.

title: Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) versus other fluid therapies: effects on kidney function.
text: The study examined the effects of hydroxyethyl starches (HES) on kidney function compared to other fluid resuscitation therapies in different patient populations. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs were included if they compared HES to an alternate fluid therapy for the prevention or treatment of effective intravascular volume depletion. The primary outcomes were renal replacement therapy (RRT), author-defined kidney failure, and acute kidney injury (AKI) as defined by the RIFLE criteria. Secondary outcomes included serum creatinine and creatinine clearance. The review included 34 studies (2607 patients) and found that the risk of author-defined kidney failure was 1.50 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.87; n = 1199) and 1.38 for requiring RRT (95% CI 0.89 to 2.16; n = 1236) in HES-treated individuals compared to other fluid therapies. Subgroup analyses suggested an increased risk in septic patients compared to non-septic (surgical/trauma) patients. However, the limitations of the studies, including potential bias due to unblinding, made it difficult to draw firm conclusions. The authors concluded that the potential for increased risk of AKI should be considered when weighing the risks and benefits of HES for volume resuscitation, particularly in septic patients. Large studies with adequate follow-up are required to evaluate the renal safety of HES products in non-septic patient populations. The use of the RIFLE criteria in future studies and the re-analysis of existing studies could provide additional insights into the renal safety of HES products.

title: Dietary fat and obesity: evidence from epidemiology.
text:
The evidence from epidemiological studies on the relationship between a high-fat diet and the development of obesity is suggestive but not conclusive. The purpose of this review is to evaluate various epidemiological methods used to investigate this association and provide an updated summary of the existing evidence.
Ecological studies examining dietary fat intake and obesity at the population level have yielded mixed results due to potential confounding and data quality issues. Cross-sectional studies generally find a positive association between dietary fat intake and relative weight, while prospective studies of diet and weight change often provide inconsistent results, possibly due to behavioral factors such as dieting in response to weight gain. Intervention studies in free-living populations have provided more conclusive evidence of a short-term weight loss effect from low-fat diets, although the underlying biological mechanisms remain controversial.
Future epidemiological research directions include:
1. Longitudinal studies investigating the predictive role of dietary fat intake in childhood growth.
2. Observational studies examining the relationship between total dietary fat and specific types of fat and overall and regional adiposity.
3. Randomized intervention studies evaluating the effect of low-fat diets in various populations, including those with a genetic predisposition to obesity and other potential modifying factors.

title: Uncoupling of leading- and lagging-strand DNA replication during lesion bypass in vivo.
text: DNA molecules are subject to various attacks, leading to the formation of lesions that disrupt normal replication. In response, specialized DNA polymerases are activated to transiently replace the regular replicative polymerase and continue replication from the damaged sites, thus generating mutations that are a primary cancer-causing factor. In our study using Escherichia coli, we monitored the kinetics of replication of both strands of DNA molecules containing a single replication block in either the leading or lagging strand. Although a block occurred in the leading strand, lagging-strand synthesis progressed further, indicating a temporary separation of concurrent strand synthesis. Replication through the lesion requires specialized DNA polymerases and is similarly efficient and rapid in both strands.

title: Phosphoinositide 3-kinase signalling--which way to target?
text: Phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) play a central role in regulating cell growth, proliferation, and survival, and their dysregulation is a key factor in the development and progression of tumors. PI3Ks activate phosphoinositide-dependent kinase, protein kinase B, and the target of rapamycin, leading to downstream effects on cell motility and the regulation of cardiovascular parameters. Currently, there is evidence to suggest that PI3Ks may be viable drug targets for the treatment of various diseases, including cancer, chronic inflammation, allergy, and cardiovascular failure. However, PI3Ks also have critical functions in metabolic control and nutrient uptake, highlighting the potential risks and challenges associated with targeting these enzymes. This review summarizes recent mechanistic data and mouse phenotypic analyses and discusses the potential success of therapeutic inhibition of diverse PI3K isoforms.

title: Determination of the time course of capacitation in mouse spermatozoa using a chlortetracycline fluorescence assay.
text: Mouse sperm samples obtained 5 minutes after being removed from the epididymides showed a unique fluorescence pattern when exposed to the fluorophore chlortetracycline (CTC). Almost half of the sperm had a brighter line of fluorescence across their equatorial segments, which was labeled "F". After being incubated in culture medium (CM) containing 2% bovine serum albumin for 90 minutes, most of the sperm heads showed a dark non-fluorescent band across their equatorial and postequatorial segments, while the anterior portion of the head showed bright fluorescence. This pattern was labeled "B". The disappearance of pattern F and the appearance of pattern B occurred simultaneously over a period of 30 minutes, with complete transformation occurring in 90 minutes. Incubation of the sperm in CM for longer periods of time led to a decline in the percentage of sperm showing pattern B, and eventual loss of fluorescence across the entire head, indicating the sperm had undergone the acrosome reaction. Sperm showing pattern B were able to undergo the acrosome reaction both spontaneously and when exposed to acid-solubilized zonae pellucidae from mouse eggs. The use of 3-quinuclidinyl benzilate (QNB) as an inhibitor blocked this reaction. In contrast, sperm showing pattern F were unable to undergo the acrosome reaction when exposed to solubilized zonae. These findings suggest that the change from pattern F to pattern B occurs as a result of changes within the sperm that make them capable of undergoing the acrosome reaction. This change coincides with the previously determined time frame for capacitation of mouse sperm in vitro in CM. These results indicate that sperm showing CTC fluorescence pattern B are capacitated and can undergo the acrosome reaction rapidly when treated with acid-solubilized zonae pellucidae. The CTC fluorescence assay provides a means to monitor the time course of epididymal mouse sperm capacitation in vitro.

title: [Detection of CRISPR and its relationship to drug resistance in Shigella].
text:
Objective:
To investigate the presence of clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) in Shigella and evaluate its relationship with drug resistance.
Methods:
We used four primer pairs to detect CRISPR elements in 60 Shigella strains. The primers were designed based on CRISPR database sequences. CRISPR Finder was utilized to analyze CRISPR and susceptibilities of Shigella strains were tested using an agar diffusion method. Additionally, we examined the relationship between drug resistance and CRISPR-S4.
Results:
Our results showed a high positive rate (95%) for convincing CRISPR structures. The four CRISPR loci formed 12 spectra (A-L), with all except one containing convincing CRISPR structures. We discovered one new repeat and 12 new spacers. The multi-drug resistance rate was 53.33%. However, we found no significant difference between CRISPR-S4 and drug-resistant strains. However, the repeat sequence of CRISPR-S4 in multi- or TE-resistant strains was mainly R4.1 with AC deletions in the 3' end, and the spacer sequences of CRISPR-S4 in multi-drug resistance strains were mainly Sp5.1, Sp6.1, and Sp7.

Conclusion:
CRISPR is prevalent in Shigella. Variations in repeat sequences and diversity of spacer sequences may be linked to drug resistance in Shigella.

title: The helicase DDX41 senses intracellular DNA mediated by the adaptor STING in dendritic cells
text: The detection of viral DNA is crucial for the initiation of antiviral responses. In this study, we uncovered the role of DDX41, a member of the DEXDc family of helicases, as an intracellular DNA sensor in myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs). We found that suppressing DDX41 expression with short hairpin RNA hindered mDCs' ability to mount type I interferon and cytokine responses to both DNA and DNA viruses. Conversely, overexpressing DDX41 along with the membrane-bound adaptor STING resulted in a synergistic boost in Ifnb promoter activity. Notably, DDX41 interacted with both DNA and STING in the cytosol and its expression was necessary for the activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase TBK1 and transcription factors NF-κB and IRF3 in response to B-form DNA. Our findings suggest that DDX41 serves as an additional DNA sensor that relies on STING to detect pathogenic DNA.

title: Radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma.
text:
BACKGROUND Glioblastoma, the most common primary brain tumor in adults, is typically a rapidly fatal disease. The current standard of care for newly diagnosed glioblastoma involves surgical resection to the extent feasible, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy. In this clinical trial, we compared the effectiveness and safety of radiotherapy alone versus radiotherapy plus temozolomide in patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma.
METHODS We randomly assigned 573 patients from 85 centers to receive either radiotherapy alone (fractionated focal irradiation in daily fractions of 2 Gy given 5 days per week for 6 weeks, resulting in a total dose of 60 Gy) or radiotherapy plus continuous daily temozolomide (75 mg per square meter of body surface area per day for 7 days per week throughout the radiotherapy course, followed by 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide at a dose of 150-200 mg per square meter for 5 days per cycle). The primary endpoint was overall survival.
RESULTS At a median follow-up of 28 months, the median survival was 14.6 months in the radiotherapy plus temozolomide group and 12.1 months in the radiotherapy-alone group. The unadjusted hazard ratio for death was 0.63 (95% confidence interval, 0.52-0.75; P<0.001 by log-rank test). The two-year survival rate was 26.5% in the radiotherapy plus temozolomide group and 10.4% in the radiotherapy-alone group. Concurrent treatment with radiotherapy plus temozolomide resulted in grade 3 or 4 hematologic toxic effects in 7% of patients.
CONCLUSIONS Our results indicate that adding temozolomide to radiotherapy improves the survival of patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma, with minimal additional toxicity. These findings support the use of this combination as a new standard of care for this disease.

title: Drug interactions between oral contraceptives and antibiotics.
text: Objective: To evaluate the evidence on potential drug interactions between antibiotics and oral contraceptives (OCs) that may lead to OC failure. Data Sources: Medline and Lexis/Nexis Medical Library searches from 1966 to 1999 using the keywords "oral contraceptives," cross-indexed with terms "antibiotics," "adverse effects," and "pregnancy," and a MEDLINE search using the additional MeSH term "drug interactions." Study Selection: A total of 167 articles were retrieved for analysis, and 32 additional articles were identified by reviewing references cited in the selected publications. Articles were selected based on their ability to provide information on the relationship between antibiotic therapy and OC efficacy in otherwise compliant users. Data Extraction: The impact of antibiotics on the pharmacokinetics of OC components and the likelihood of OC failure due to concomitant use. Data Synthesis: At least 30 cases of pregnancies occurring in women taking OCs and antibiotics have been reported, particularly with rifampin. Approximately 20% of pregnant women reporting to family planning or abortion clinics reported concomitant OC and antibiotic use. Retrospective surveys from dermatology-based practices reported 24 pregnancies in OC users who received antibiotic therapy, most commonly with tetracyclines and penicillins. Apparent OC failure rates in clinical surveys were within the usual range expected for patterns of typical use. Pharmacokinetic studies of other antibiotics have not shown any systematic interaction between antibiotics and OC steroids. However, individual patients have been identified who experienced significant decreases in the plasma concentration of OC components and appeared to ovulate. Conclusion: Rifampin impairs the effectiveness of OCs, while pharmacokinetic studies of other antibiotics have not shown any significant interaction between antibiotics and OC steroids. However, individual patients may experience large decreases in the plasma concentration of OC components, particularly with tetracycline and penicillin derivatives. A cautious approach is advised as it is not possible to identify these patients in advance.

title: Male Japanese quails with female brains do not show male sexual behaviors.
text:
During fetal development, gonadal hormones (androgens and estrogens) are believed to organize the sexual differentiation of the brain in the heterogametic sexes of higher vertebrates (males in mammals, females in birds). The brains of the homogametic sexes (females in birds) develop without the need for hormonal influence, while the brains of males (heterogametic sex) are thought to be organized through the action of these hormones. In birds such as the Japanese quail, female brain development is thought to be influenced by estrogen, leading to a demasculinization of the default male brain phenotype.
To better understand the mechanisms of brain sexual differentiation, we performed isotopic, isochronic transplantation of the forebrain primordium in Japanese quail embryos before gonadal differentiation had occurred. The chimeras had a forebrain originating exclusively from donor cells, and their sexual behavior was influenced by the genetic sex of the host. In contrast to other chimeras, male-to-female (FM) chimeras showed reduced or absent reproductive behaviors, despite producing normal levels of steroid hormones. Morphological features of the medial preoptic nucleus, a sexually dimorphic brain area, were also not typical in FM males. These findings suggest a brain-intrinsic, genetically determined component that influences the production of gonadal hormones in adulthood and warrant a reevaluation of the mechanisms underlying brain sexual differentiation in other higher vertebrates.

title: DNA joint dependence of pol X family polymerase action in nonhomologous end joining.
text:
In this text, we investigate the role of the Pol X family polymerase Pol4 in nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) repair of DNA double strand breaks (DSBs). NHEJ is a critical pathway for repairing DSBs in eukaryotic cells, and it involves the use of enzymes and polymerases to accurately repair the breaks. Previous studies have shown that Pol4 is required for some but not all NHEJ events in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
To better understand the role of Pol4 in NHEJ, we analyzed the configurations of DSB ends and found that the presence of gaps on both strands and the polarity of the overhangs determines whether a joint requires Pol4 for repair. DSBs with 3'-overhangs and a gap on each strand rely heavily on Pol4 for repair, while DSBs with 5'-overhangs of the same sequence do not require Pol4. However, DSBs with 3'-overhangs that contain a gap on only one strand can be repaired without Pol4. Additionally, we found that Pol4 is equally required for all DSBs within the NHEJ-dependent range, but is dispensable outside of this range.
Loss of Pol4 does not affect the rejoining of DSBs that utilize recessed microhomology or DSBs bearing 5'-hydroxyls, but no gap. Additionally, mammalian Pol X polymerases can complement a pol4 mutation in yeast, demonstrating that these polymerases can participate in NHEJ with distinct properties.
In conclusion, our studies reveal that Pol4 plays a critical role in NHEJ repair of DSBs in yeast, and its requirements are determined by the configuration of the DSB ends. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms of NHEJ and highlight the complexity of this essential repair pathway.

title: ABC of burns. Introduction.
text:
Burns are a particularly challenging medical condition that affect individuals of all ages, from infants to the elderly, both in developed and developing countries. The pain and discomfort caused by even a minor burn can be intense, and the long-term psychological and physical scars can lead to chronic disability. Burn injuries present a complex and multifaceted challenge to medical and paramedical staff, requiring a skilled and comprehensive approach to management. This series of articles aims to provide a broad overview of the key aspects of burn injuries for hospital and non-hospital healthcare workers, with the goal of improving patient outcomes.
figure 1- A child with severe, 70% full-thickness burns, requiring resuscitation, intensive care, and extensive debridement and skin grafting. Left: The same child one year later at a burns camp, with a remarkable recovery. A favorable outcome is certainly possible...

title: DNA methylation is a critical cell-intrinsic determinant of astrocyte differentiation in the fetal brain.
text: Astrocyte differentiation, occurring late in brain development, is largely dependent on the activation of the transcription factor STAT3. We found that astrocytes, as identified by glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) expression, fail to emerge from neuroepithelial cells on embryonic day (E) 11.5 even when STAT3 is activated, unlike E14.5 neuroepithelial cells. A specific DNA sequence within the GFAP promoter, known as a STAT3 binding element, was found to be highly methylated in E11.5 neuroepithelial cells, making it inaccessible to STAT3. However, demethylation of this sequence in response to STAT3 activation allows for the expression of GFAP and the development of astrocytes. These findings suggest that methylation of a cell-specific gene promoter plays a crucial role in regulating lineage specification during brain development.

title: DNMT1 Inhibition Reprograms Pancreatic Cancer Stem Cells via Upregulation of the miR-17-92 Cluster.
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and other carcinomas exhibit a hierarchical organization, with cancer stem cells (CSC) residing at the top of the hierarchy and driving tumor progression, metastasis, and chemoresistance. Despite sharing a common genetic background, CSCs and non-CSCs exhibit distinct functional differences, which we hypothesize are due to epigenetic differences. Epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA methylation, play a crucial role in regulating stem cell differentiation and pluripotency, but the epigenetic landscape of pancreatic CSC is poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the genome-wide DNA methylation profile of PDAC CSCs and explored the role of DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) in CSC maintenance and tumorigenicity. Using high-throughput methylation analysis, we found that sorted CSCs have higher levels of DNA methylation than non-CSCs, regardless of the heterogeneity or polyclonality of the CSC populations present in the tumors analyzed. Moreover, we observed that CSCs express higher levels of DNMT1 than non-CSCs. Targeting DNMT1 in CSCs reduced their self-renewal and in vivo tumorigenic potential, providing a rationale to develop epigenetic modulators to target CSC plasticity and improve the poor prognosis of PDAC patients. Our findings also indicate that epigenetic reactivation of silenced microRNAs, including the miR-17-92 cluster, may contribute to the inhibitory effect observed. Overall, our study highlights the important role of epigenetics in CSC biology and the potential of epigenetic modulators as therapeutic strategies for treating PDAC.

title: Mutation spectrum in the nephrin gene (NPHS1) in congenital nephrotic syndrome.
text: Congenital nephrotic syndrome, Finnish type (CNF or NPHS1), is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by heavy proteinuria and the development of nephrotic syndrome shortly after birth. This disease is most prevalent in Finland, but it has also been identified in other populations. The condition is caused by mutations in the gene for nephrin, a crucial component of the glomerular ultrafilter and the podocyte slit diaphragm. To date, a total of 30 mutations have been discovered in the nephrin gene in individuals with congenital nephrotic syndrome worldwide. In the Finnish population, two predominant nonsense mutations account for over 94% of all mutations found. Non-Finnish patients, on the other hand, have a higher frequency of missense mutations, as well as nonsense, splice site, deletions, and insertions. This update on nephrin mutations includes information on all previously reported mutations and describes 20 novel mutations recently identified in our laboratory.

title: The HSA domain binds nuclear actin-related proteins to regulate chromatin-remodeling ATPases
text: Using biochemical and genetic assays, we have identified the helicase-SANT (HSA) domain as the primary binding platform for nuclear actin-related proteins (ARPs) and actin. Our findings indicate that individual HSA domains from chromatin remodelers (RSC, yeast SWI-SNF, human SWI-SNF, SWR1, and INO80) or modifiers (NuA4) can be reconstituted into their respective ARP-ARP or ARP-actin modules. In RSC, the HSA domain is located on the catalytic ATPase subunit Sth1, and this domain is essential in vivo. Our results show that the omission of the HSA domain in Sth1 leads to the specific loss of ARPs and a moderate reduction in ATPase activity. By using genetic selection methods, we were able to identify specific gain-of-function mutations in two new domains in Sth1, the post-HSA domain and protrusion 1, which are essential for RSC function in vivo but not ARP association. Overall, our findings establish the role of the HSA domain and provide evidence for a regulatory relationship involving the ARP-HSA module and two new functional domains conserved in remodeler ATPases that contain ARPs.

title: Increased dendritic complexity and axonal length in cultured mouse cortical neurons overexpressing methyl-CpG-binding protein MeCP2
text: Rett syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the MeCP2 gene, is characterized by diminished brain mass and neuronal complexity. In an effort to elucidate the role of MeCP2 in neuronal development, we investigated its influence on the morphological complexity of developing neurons. Our findings suggest that increasing the levels of MeCP2β (MECP2A) in cultured mouse neurons leads to more complex morphologies, featuring longer axons and dendrites, and a greater number of axon and dendrite terminals. To further explore the mechanisms underlying MeCP2's effects, we examined the impact of overexpressing a MeCP2β mutant lacking its carboxyl terminus. Interestingly, while neurons overexpressing this mutant failed to enhance axon and dendrite elongation, the complexity of their axon and dendrite branches retained significant elevation. Our results support the hypothesis that MeCP2 regulates neuronal maturation and/or synaptogenesis, and provide evidence that MeCP2 influences neuritic elongation and process branching through distinct mechanisms.

title: Folate affects apoptosis in human trophoblastic cells.
text: Research has investigated the impact of folate deficiency on the rate of programmed cell death (apoptosis) in human cytotrophoblastic cells. Apoptosis was measured in these cells after culture in three different mediums: control medium, folate-free medium, and folate-free medium supplemented with 10% fetal calf serum. Findings revealed that the rate of apoptosis was significantly higher in cells cultured in the folate-free mediums compared to those in the control medium (P < 0.02 and P < 0.03, respectively). In conclusion, the study demonstrates that cytotrophoblastic cells in vitro exhibit a pronounced increase in apoptosis when cultured in a folate-free medium, which may have implications for understanding the association between folate deficiency and pregnancy complications. Possible explanations for this association are discussed.

title: Role of KRAS and EGFR as biomarkers of response to erlotinib in National Cancer Institute of Canada Clinical Trials Group Study BR.21.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of KRAS and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) genotype on the response to erlotinib treatment in the BR.21, placebo-controlled trial. The study included 206 tumors for KRAS mutation analysis, 204 tumors for EGFR mutation analysis, and 159 tumors for EGFR gene copy analysis using fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH). The study found that:
15% of patients had KRAS mutations, 17% had EGFR exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R mutations, and 38% had high EGFR gene copy (FISH positive). Response rates were higher for patients with wild-type KRAS and EGFR compared to those with mutant KRAS and EGFR, respectively (5% vs 17%, P = .03, and 5% vs 27%, P = .003). Additionally, patients with EGFR FISH positivity had a significant survival benefit from erlotinib therapy compared to those with FISH negativity (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.43, P = .004 vs HR = 0.80, P = .35). In multivariate analysis, EGFR FISH-positive status was the only prognostic marker for poorer survival (P = .025) and predictive of differential survival benefit from erlotinib (P = .005).

In summary, the study found that EGFR mutations and high gene copy number are predictive of response to erlotinib, and EGFR FISH is the strongest prognostic marker for poorer survival and predictive of differential survival benefit from erlotinib.

title: Immune dysregulation in major depression: a critical review of existing evidence.
text: Emerging research has linked depression to immune system dysfunction. While it is unclear whether this dysfunction contributes directly to the development of major depression or simply makes depressed individuals more susceptible to immune-related disorders, studies have shown changes in white blood cell movement, lymphocyte function, and markers of immune activation in depressed individuals. This article provides a comprehensive review of existing evidence for immune dysregulation in major depression, including alterations in leukocyte trafficking, lymphocyte function, and potential mediators of immune dysfunction in depression. Additionally, the article critically reviews the relationship between major depression and various medical conditions, such as infections, allergies, autoimmune disorders, cardiovascular diseases, cancer, and AIDS.

title: Regulation of E2Fs and senescence by PML nuclear bodies.
text: The tumor suppressor PML (promyelocytic leukemia protein) controls cellular aging and terminal differentiation, both of which involve leaving the cell cycle permanently. We have shown that PML induces a permanent exit from the cell cycle by recruiting E2F transcription factors bound to their promoters and the retinoblastoma (Rb) proteins to PML nuclear bodies enriched in heterochromatin proteins and protein phosphatase 1α. If the Rb protein family or E2Fs are blocked or added back to PML-expressing cells, their defects in E2F-dependent gene expression and cell proliferation can be restored, reversing the senescent phenotype. In benign prostatic hyperplasia, a condition that exhibits features of cellular aging, PML is upregulated and forms nuclear bodies. In contrast, PML bodies are rarely observed in prostate cancers. The newly identified PML/Rb/E2F pathway may aid in distinguishing between benign tumors and cancers, and suggest E2F target genes as potential targets to induce senescence in human tumors.

title: The International Classification of Headache Disorders.
text: A collection of related medical conditions without a standardized classification system and diagnostic criteria is similar to a society without rules. This results in disorganization and confusion at best, or chaos at worst. Fortunately, the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD) has been a groundbreaking achievement in headache medicine over the past 50 years. The ICHD categorizes and groups over 100 distinct types of headaches in a logical and hierarchical system. Moreover, it provides clear diagnostic criteria for each of the headache disorders listed. The ICHD has been widely adopted and has received relatively minor criticism compared to other disease classification systems. Over the past 20 years, the publication of the ICHD has led to significant advancements in headache research, despite limited resources allocated to this effort. In summary, the ICHD has achieved widespread acceptance globally and has significantly facilitated both clinical research and patient care in the field of headache medicine.

title: Call to Develop a Standard Acquisition Charge Model for Kidney Paired Donation
text:
Sure, here is a possible revision of the text:
We propose a Medicare Demonstration Project to establish a uniform acquisition cost for kidney paired donation. As the current payment system may not adequately cover living donor expenses incurred to facilitate transplantation of a beneficiary belonging to a different insurance provider, a novel payment strategy is necessary. Prior to the 1970s, when organ procurement organizations were empowered to act as financial intermediaries, similar limitations existed in the recovery and placement of deceased donor organs. Similarly, kidney paired donation requires the evaluation of living donors before identifying their recipient, resulting in additional financial barriers, including tissue typing, crossmatching, and transportation costs. Furthermore, the administrative expenses incurred by organizations coordinating kidney paired donation transplantation need to be reimbursed, much like the reimbursement necessary for organ procurement organizations. To expand access to kidney paired donation for more patients, we propose a model to reimburse paired donation expenses using a strategy that has successfully been used for over 30 years to cover deceased donor solid organ transplantation in the United States.

title: Oxidant stress promotes disease by activating CaMKII.
text: Oxidation of methionine residues in the regulatory domain of CaMKII (CaMKII) leads to its activation. Activated CaMKII (ox-CaMKII) has been implicated in various diseases, including cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases, and cancer. This review aims to summarize the current understanding of the role of ox-CaMKII in disease, identify knowledge gaps, and suggest new areas of research.

title: Genetic diagnosis and prognosis of Alzheimer's disease: challenges and opportunities.
text: Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most common form of dementia in Western societies, is a complex and genetically influenced disorder. Recent advances in high-throughput genomic technologies have enabled researchers to rapidly analyze millions of polymorphisms in thousands of individuals, providing valuable insights into the genomic factors contributing to AD susceptibility. In the last five years, genome-wide association, whole-exome, and whole-genome sequencing studies have identified over 20 genetic loci associated with AD, shedding light on the underlying molecular mechanisms and revealing potential new therapeutic targets. This review article discusses the challenges and possibilities of utilizing genomic information for the diagnosis and prognosis of AD.

title: WNT5A regulates adipose tissue angiogenesis via antiangiogenic VEGF-A165b in obese humans.
text:
The study investigated the role of Wingless-related integration site 5A (WNT5A) in regulating angiogenesis in the adipose tissue of obese individuals. The results showed that WNT5A negatively regulates angiogenesis in adipose tissue by upregulating the expression of antiangiogenic factor Vascular endothelial growth factor A165b (VEGF-A165b). The study found that in both subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue, VEGF-A165b expression was strongly correlated with WNT5A protein expression. Additionally, exogenous WNT5A increased VEGF-A165b expression in both whole adipose tissue and isolated vascular endothelial cell fractions. However, the study also found that WNT5A increased the secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), a negative regulator of angiogenesis, in the sprout media. The study used a number of techniques, including Western blot analysis, to examine the expression of WNT5A and VEGF-A165b in adipose tissue biopsies from 38 obese individuals. The study found that elevated WNT5A expression in obesity may function as a negative regulator of angiogenesis, contributing to the development of metabolic dysfunction in this condition. The study's findings provide new insights into the regulatory nexus between WNT5A and antiangiogenic VEGF-A165b in the adipose tissue of obese subjects, and highlight the importance of this axis in the development of metabolic disorders.
In summary, the study demonstrates that WNT5A negatively regulates angiogenesis in adipose tissue by upregulating VEGF-A165b expression, contributing to metabolic dysfunction in obesity. The study suggests that targeting the WNT5A-VEGF-A165b signaling axis may provide a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of metabolic disorders associated with obesity.

title: At least 1400 base pairs of 5'-flanking DNA is required for the correct expression of the HO gene in yeast.
text: Homothallic yeast cells undergo a specific pattern of mating-type switching initiated by an endonuclease encoded by the HO gene. HO transcription is influenced by factors such as cell type (a, alpha, and a/alpha), cell age (mother or daughter), and the cell cycle. This study investigates the sequences involved in HO transcription by using mutated DNA copies in vitro. A region between -1000 and 1400 (called URS1) is required for transcription, in addition to a "TATA"-like region at -90. The 900 bp of DNA separating URS1 from the "TATA" box is not essential for transcription or a/alpha repression, but it is necessary for proper cell cycle regulation.

title: Inflammation and its role in neuroprotection, axonal regeneration and functional recovery after spinal cord injury.
text: Trauma to the central nervous system (CNS) leads to inflammation within the parenchymal tissue, which can exacerbate neuropathological changes and stimulate tissue repair mechanisms. Despite ongoing research, the underlying mechanisms that regulate these contradictory processes remain poorly understood. Immune-based therapies are thus gaining attention as a potential therapeutic approach. This review aims to address the complexities and controversies surrounding post-traumatic neuroinflammation, specifically in the spinal cord, and discuss current therapies targeting neuroinflammatory cascades.

title: Order of intron removal influences multiple splice outcomes, including a two-exon skip, in a COL5A1 acceptor-site mutation that results in abnormal pro-alpha1(V) N-propeptides and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type I.
text:
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) type I (classical variety), a dominantly inherited, genetically heterogeneous connective tissue disorder, is caused by mutations in the COL5A1 and COL5A2 genes, which encode type V collagen. These mutations occur in approximately 75% of individuals with EDS type I and affect either the triple-helical domain of the protein or the expression of one COL5A1 allele.
We recently identified a novel splice-acceptor mutation (IVS4-2A-->G) in the N-propeptide-encoding region of COL5A1 in one patient with EDS type I.
