They found that the serum miR-99a-5p levels were significantly increased in patients with ovarian cancer compared to the other two groups.
To investigate the role of exosomal miR-99a-5p in ovarian cancer progression, the researchers treated neighboring human peritoneal mesothelial cells (HPMCs) with exosomes derived from ovarian cancer cells and analyzed the expression of miR-99a-5p in HPMCs. They found that treatment with exosomes significantly increased miR-99a-5p expression in HPMCs. To further investigate the functional role of miR-99a-5p in ovarian cancer progression, the researchers transfected HPMCs with miR-99a-5p mimics and analyzed the effects of miR-99a-5p on cancer invasion using a 3D culture model. They found that miR-99a-5p promoted ovarian cancer invasion by affecting HPMCs through the upregulation of fibronectin and vitronectin.
The study's results suggest that serum miR-99a-5p is a promising biomarker for ovarian cancer diagnosis, and that exosomal miR-99a-5p plays a significant role in ovarian cancer progression. The researchers also found that miR-99a-5p regulates ovarian cancer invasion by targeting fibronectin and vitronectin in HPMCs.
In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the role of miRNAs in ovarian cancer progression and suggests that miR-99a-5p may be a potential target for inhibiting ovarian cancer invasion. The findings of this study have important implications for the diagnosis and treatment of ovarian cancer.

title: The Pfam protein families database.
text: Pfam is a widely utilized database of protein families, currently boasting over 13,000 manually curated protein families as of release 26.0. Pfam is accessible via servers located in the UK (http://pfam.sanger.ac.uk/), the USA (http://pfam.janelia.org/), and Sweden (http://pfam.sbc.su.se/). Here, we provide an update on the changes that have transpired since our 2010 NAR paper (release 24.0). Over the past two years, we have generated 1,840 new families and expanded coverage of the UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB) to nearly 80%. Furthermore, we have taken the initiative of sharing the annotation of our families with the Wikipedia community by linking Pfam families to relevant Wikipedia pages and inviting the Pfam and Wikipedia communities to collaborate on their improvement and expansion. We continue to enhance the Pfam website and add new visualizations, such as the 'sunburst' representation of the taxonomic distribution of families. In this work, we also address two topics of particular interest to the Pfam community. Initially, we expound upon the definition and application of family-specific, manually curated gathering thresholds. Next, we discuss some of the characteristics of domains of unknown function (also known as DUFs), which constitute a rapidly growing class of families within Pfam.

title: Exercise as a therapeutic approach to improve blood pressure in patients with peripheral arterial disease: current literature and future directions.
text:
INTRODUCTION: Patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD) often experience decreased functional capacity and increased mortality due to cardiovascular disease. Exercise has been a fundamental component of clinical treatment for improving walking capacity in these individuals; however, the impact of exercise on cardiovascular parameters has been inadequately explored. This review aims to examine the effects of exercise on blood pressure in patients with symptomatic PAD, as well as summarize the current evidence on the short-term (single bout of exercise) and long-term (chronic) effects of walking and resistance exercise on blood pressure and its underlying determinants.
AREAS COVERED: This review will focus on the following aspects:
1. The role of exercise in reducing blood pressure in patients with symptomatic PAD
2. The acute and chronic effects of walking and resistance exercise on blood pressure and its determinants.
EXPERT COMMENTARY: Our analysis reveals that exercise has a notable impact on blood pressure in patients with symptomatic PAD, particularly after walking and resistance exercise. Future studies should investigate the effects of alternative exercise modalities, including non-painful exercises, on cardiovascular function in patients with symptomatic PAD. By gaining a deeper understanding of the cardiovascular benefits of exercise in this population, we can optimize treatment strategies to improve patient outcomes.

title: Morin Exhibits Anti-Inflammatory Effects on IL-1β-Stimulated Human Osteoarthritis Chondrocytes by Activating the Nrf2 Signaling Pathway
text:
Background and Objectives: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a complex disease characterized by inflammation in joints. The present study aimed to investigate the anti-inflammatory effects of morin on human OA chondrocytes stimulated by Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β).
Methods: The study measured the levels of nitric oxide (NO) and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in the chondrocytes using the Griess method and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), respectively. The levels of matrix metalloproteinases (MMP1, MMP3, and MMP13) were also measured using ELISA.
Results: The results showed that IL-1β significantly increased the production of NO, PGE2, MMP1, MMP3, and MMP13. Treatment with morin significantly attenuated these increases. Additionally, IL-1β-induced activation of nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) was suppressed by morin. Furthermore, the expression of Nrf2 and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) was increased by morin, and knockdown of Nrf2 could block the anti-inflammatory effects of morin.
Conclusion: The study suggests that morin attenuates IL-1β-induced inflammation by activating the Nrf2 signaling pathway, thereby suggesting potential therapeutic applications for the treatment of osteoarthritis.

title: Impact of blood pressure variability on cardiovascular events in elderly patients with hypertension.
text: In older adults with hypertension, blood pressure variability is a common feature and its clinical significance remains unclear. To investigate the impact of blood pressure variability on cardiovascular events in these patients, we examined 106 hypertensive individuals aged 60 years or older (mean age: 73.9 ± 8.1 years; male: 54%). All participants underwent 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring and were followed up for a median of 34 months (range: 3-60 months). During the follow-up period, 39 cardiovascular events occurred, including 14 cases of cerebral infarction and 7 cases of acute myocardial infarction. We used the coefficient of variation (CV) of 24-hour systolic blood pressure (SBP) values as an index of blood pressure variability and divided the patients into two groups according to their CV values. The patients showed a mean CV value of 10.6%, and were categorized into a high CV group (n = 46) and a low CV group (n = 60). Although the baseline clinical characteristics were similar between the two groups, the Kaplan-Meier plots for event-free survival revealed that the rate of cardiovascular events was significantly higher in the high CV group than in the low CV group (p < 0.05). Cox's proportional hazards analysis also showed that increased blood pressure variability was an independent predictive variable for cardiovascular events. Furthermore, the CV value of daytime SBP and the SD value of both 24-hour SBP and daytime SBP were found to have positive correlations with the onset of cardiovascular events. These results suggest that increased blood pressure variability may be an independent risk factor for cardiovascular events in elderly hypertensive patients.

title: Reprogramming committed murine blood cells to induced hematopoietic stem cells with defined factors.
text: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are vital for maintaining the blood system throughout life, and they are the core cells used in bone marrow transplantation. We found that by briefly expressing six transcription factors (Run1t1, Hlf, Lmo2, Prdm5, Pbx1, and Zfp37) in lymphoid and myeloid progenitors and effector cells, we could impart multilineage potential onto these cells, making them more versatile and capable of differentiating into multiple blood cell types. Including the factors Mycn and Meis1 in the reprogramming process and using polycistronic viruses increased the efficiency of the reprogramming. The reprogrammed cells, known as induced-HSCs (iHSCs), have the ability to differentiate into multiple blood cell types in a clonal manner, reconstitute the stem/progenitor compartments, and can be serially transplanted. Analyzing these cells at the single-cell level revealed that those derived under optimal conditions had a gene expression profile nearly identical to that of native HSCs. These findings demonstrate that expressing a specific set of transcription factors is enough to activate the gene networks that control HSC function in committed blood cells. Our discoveries open up the possibility of using blood cell reprogramming as a means of generating transplantable stem cells for clinical applications.

title: Genetic variability in a frozen batch of MCF-7 cells invisible in routine authentication affecting cell function
text:
Here is a possible revision of the given text:
Common recommendations for cell line authentication, annotation, and quality control often fail to address the issue of genetic heterogeneity. In the Human Toxome Project, we have found that there can be significant cellular and phenotypic heterogeneity within a single batch of the human breast adenocarcinoma cell line MCF-7 obtained directly from a cell bank, which cannot be detected through standard cell authentication using short tandem repeat (STR) markers. STR profiling only serves as a basic authentication test, designed to detect cross-contamination and cell line misidentification. To fully understand cellular heterogeneity, alternative methods must be employed. Our results demonstrate the potential consequences of reproducibility issues caused by this unaccounted heterogeneity, as observed through morphology, estrogenic growth dose-response, whole genome gene expression, and untargeted mass spectrometry metabolomics experiments. By utilizing Comparative Genomic Hybridization (CGH), we found that genetic heterogeneity existed within the cells from the original frozen vials of the same ATCC lot even before differences were traced back to genetic heterogeneity, highlighting the need for more rigorous quality assurance measures in Good Cell Culture Practice and cell characterization, specifically involving alternative methods such as CGH to uncover potential genomic heterogeneity and genetic drift within cell lines.

title: The Mammalian-Specific Protein Armcx1 Regulates Mitochondrial Transport during Axon Regeneration
text: The importance of mitochondrial transport in neuronal and axonal function is well established, but its impact on neuronal injury responses, such as survival and axon regeneration, remains unclear. To investigate this, we utilized an established mouse model with robust axon regeneration to exam Armcx1, a mammalian-specific gene encoding a mitochondria-localized protein. Our findings show that Armcx1 is upregulated in adult retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) after axotomy in this high regeneration condition. Overexpression of Armcx1 enhances mitochondrial transport in these cells, and its mitochondrial localization is essential for these effects. Furthermore, Armcx1 promotes both neuronal survival and axon regeneration after injury, and these effects are dependent on its mitochondrial localization. In contrast, knockdown of Armcx1 undermines both neuronal survival and axon regeneration in this high regeneration model, further supporting a key role of Armcx1 in regulating neuronal injury responses in the adult central nervous system (CNS). Our findings suggest that Armcx1 controls mitochondrial transport during neuronal repair.

title: A diversity of beta diversities: straightening up a concept gone awry. Part 1. Defining beta diversity as a function of alpha and gamma diversity
text: The term "beta diversity" has been used eclectically to encompass a wide range of phenomena, despite not being related in any predictable way. In this two-part review, we aim to place these diverse concepts within a unified conceptual framework and clarify what each measures. In the first part, we focus on defining a beta component of diversity, which involves identifying the nature of diversity and how it is partitioned into alpha (a) and beta (b) components. Different definitions of "beta diversity" have been employed in the ecological literature, but true beta diversity represents the multiplicative partitioning of the total effective number of species in a dataset (true gamma diversity g) into the effective number of species per compositionally distinct group.

title: A cross-cultural study of wine consumers with respect to health benefits of wine
text: The current study aimed to investigate consumer preferences and consumption habits regarding the health benefits of wine among two culturally and geographically distinct consumer groups, specifically Koreans and Australians. Participants were required to be wine drinkers aged 18 or older. Data collection was conducted through an online questionnaire. The findings revealed that perceived health benefits of red wine were higher among the Australian sample compared to the Korean sample. Additionally, Australian consumers possessed more health-related wine knowledge than Korean consumers. Red wine was the preferred wine style among both groups, although the proportion of preference for red wine was significantly higher among Koreans. In terms of expenditure on wine products, $11-$19 was the preferred price range for both groups. The study also showed that health-oriented wine was more appealing to Korean consumers than Australian consumers. With respect to gender, Korean women preferred red wine equally as much as men, while Australian women consumed significantly more white wine than men. These findings provide insights for winemakers and wine marketers on the effectiveness of prioritizing health aspects in wine production and marketing to maximize consumer appeal.

title: DIASPORA BONDS: TAPPING THE DIASPORA DURING DIFFICULT TIMES
text: India and Israel have generated over US$35 billion in investments from their diaspora communities. These diaspora bonds provide a reliable and cost-effective source of external financing, often when other international capital markets are unavailable. For diaspora investors, these bonds offer the opportunity to support their country of origin while also providing a sound investment. The potential for diaspora bonds is substantial for many nations with sizeable diasporas overseas. However, for countries with weak governance and high sovereign risk, issuing diaspora bonds may require support for institutional capacity building and credit enhancement from multilateral or bilateral organizations. As an example, Haiti could potentially raise hundreds of millions of dollars through diaspora bond issuance if a guarantee structure is implemented to bolster trust in the country's public institutions.

title: Peroxisome Proliferator Activated Receptor gamma (PPARγ) Agonist Rosiglitazone Ameliorate Airway Inflammation by Inhibiting Toll-Like Receptor 2 (TLR2)/Nod-Like Receptor with Pyrin Domain Containing 3 (NLRP3) Inflammatory Corpuscle Activation in Asthmatic Mice
text:
Study Objective:
This study aimed to investigate the function and mechanism of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) agonists in the toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2)/nod-like receptor with pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammatory corpuscle pathway in asthmatic mice.
Methods:
Eighteen female mice (C57) were randomly divided into four groups: control, asthma model, rosiglitazone, and PPARγ agonist rosiglitazone treatment groups. The infiltration of peribronchial inflammatory cells and goblet cell hyperplasia were observed via hematoxylin and eosin and periodic acid-Schiff staining, and western blots were performed to assess the expression levels of TLR2, PPARγ, nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB), NLRP3, and ASC.
Results:
The results revealed that the number of inflammatory cells and eosinophils, as well as the levels of ovalbumin (OVA) IgE, interleukin-4 (IL-4), and IL-13, were significantly higher in the C57 asthma group compared to the C57 control group and treatment group (P < 0.05). Furthermore, peribronchiolar inflammatory cell infiltration, wall thickening, goblet cell hyperplasia, and mucus secretion were significantly decreased in the treatment group compared to the asthma group. PPARγ expression was significantly higher in the treatment group compared to the asthma group and control group (P < 0.05). Additionally, the protein expression levels of TLR2, NF-κB, NLRP3, and ASC were significantly lower in the treatment group compared to the asthma group but higher compared to the control group (P < 0.05).



Conclusion:

PPARγ rosiglitazone treatment inhibits NF-κB expression in asthmatic mice, thereby ameliorating airway inflammation via the TLR2/NLRP3 inflammatory corpuscle pathway.

title: Omi/HtrA2 Participates in Age-Related Autophagic Deficiency in Rat Liver
text: Liver is a crucial organ with various essential functions, and maintaining normal hepatic function is imperative for overall health. As a mechanism that helps maintain cellular homeostasis, autophagy plays a vital role in ensuring liver function. Research has revealed that degeneration of liver function is often associated with deficiencies in autophagy during aging. However, the underlying mechanisms are still not fully understood. The serine protease Omi/HtrA2 belongs to the HtrA family and promotes apoptosis through either the caspase-dependent or caspase-independent pathway. Mice lacking Omi/HtrA2 exhibited premature aging symptoms, which are similar to those of autophagic insufficiency. In this study, we found that both the protein level of Omi/HtrA2 in the liver and hepatic function decreased as rats aged, and there was a positive correlation between them. Furthermore, several autophagy-related proteins (LC3II/I, Beclin-1, and LAMP2) in the rat liver were significantly decreased with age. Finally, inhibition of Omi/HtrA2 resulted in reduced autophagy and hepatic dysfunction. These results suggest that Omi/HtrA2 plays a role in age-related autophagic deficiency in rat liver, offering a novel insight into the mechanisms involved in liver aging.

title: Macrosomia and Hyperinsulinaemic Hypoglycaemia in Patients with Heterozygous Mutations in the HNF4A Gene
text: Macrosomia, a condition where an infant is born significantly larger than average, is associated with high rates of neonatal and maternal complications. Despite being linked to several factors, the underlying predictors of macrosomia remain poorly understood. Interestingly, studies have shown that the offspring of pregnant women with diabetes and those with congenital hyperinsulinaemia are at a higher risk of macrosomia due to increased foetal insulin secretion. To explore the underlying mechanisms, we investigated the in utero and neonatal roles of two key pancreatic insulin regulators, HNF4A and HNF1A/TCF1, in patients with heterozygous mutations in these genes. We also examined the effect of pancreatic deletion of Hnf4a on foetal and neonatal insulin secretion in mice.

title: ART adherence clubs: A long-term retention strategy for clinically stable patients receiving antiretroviral therapy
text: The ART adherence club model outlined here offers patient-centric access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) for clinically stable patients, reducing the strain on healthcare facilities and allowing for more resources to be dedicated to new and at-risk patients. Under this model, 30 patients are grouped together in an ART club, which meets every 2 months for less than an hour at a designated facility or community location. A lay club facilitator oversees the meetings, conducting quick clinical assessments, referring patients as needed, and dispensing pre-packed ART. From January 2011 to December 2012, following adoption by the Western Cape Government for phased rollout, over 600 ART clubs were established in Cape Town, providing care to more than 16,000 patients. This widespread and rapid implementation illustrates the model's acceptance among patients and healthcare staff alike. Given South Africa's needs, it is suggested that a similar model be considered for national scale-up.

title: Exercise-linked FNDC5/irisin rescues synaptic plasticity and memory defects in Alzheimer’s models
text: Defective hormonal signaling in the brain has been linked to Alzheimer's disease (AD), a disorder marked by memory failure and synapse degeneration. Irisin, a myokine produced during exercise, is released upon cleavage of the membrane-bound precursor protein fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5 (FNDC5). This protein is also expressed in the hippocampus. Our findings reveal that levels of FNDC5/irisin are reduced in the hippocampi and cerebrospinal fluid of AD individuals, as well as in experimental AD models. Decreasing brain FNDC5/irisin impairs long-term potentiation and novel object recognition memory in mice, while increasing brain levels of FNDC5/irisin rescues synaptic plasticity and memory in AD mouse models. Furthermore, we found that overexpressing FNDC5/irisin in the periphery also rescues memory impairment, while blocking either brain or peripheral FNDC5/irisin attenuates the neuroprotective effects of exercise on synaptic plasticity and memory in AD mice. Our results demonstrate that FNDC5/irisin plays a vital role in the beneficial effects of exercise on synapse function and memory in AD models, suggesting that FNDC5/irisin may be a promising therapeutic agent for the treatment of AD.

title: Influence of antidepressant therapy on sick leave in primary care: ADAS, a comparative observational study
text:
Sweden has relatively modest annual sick leave expenditures compared to other European countries, but mental disorders such as depression, anxiety, and stress-related conditions are significant causes of sick leave. A Swedish register-based study found that antidepressant therapy for patients on long-term sick leave for these conditions resulted in longer sick leave and more frequent non-time-limited sickness compensation compared to psychotherapy, work-oriented rehabilitation, and other therapies.
The aim of this study was to determine if patients receiving antidepressant therapy while on long-term sick leave for mental disorders have longer sick leave than those treated with other therapies. This prospective, observational study included 192 patients at 28 primary health care centers in the Region Västra Götaland, Sweden, with a follow-up period of 12 months. The outcome measures included both gross and net sick leave days.
The study found that there were no significant differences in sick leave days due to mental disorders when comparing patients treated and not treated with antidepressants during the observation period. However, the groups differed at baseline in terms of frequency of exhaustion disorder, with a higher frequency of exhaustion disorder in the group without antidepressants.
The analysis also revealed associations between the patient's perception of returning to work and sick leave duration. Specifically, the patient's own perception of possibility of returning to work in the near and distant future was found to be an important factor associated with longer sick leave. This finding highlights the need to incorporate psychological rehabilitation and support in the rehabilitation process to help patients with mental disorders return to work more quickly.
In conclusion, while mental disorders are a major cause of sick leave in Sweden, this study suggests that antidepressant therapy may not necessarily lead to longer sick leave. However, the patient's own perception of returning to work and the support provided in the rehabilitation process may play a crucial role in determining sick leave duration.

title: CDX2 inhibits the proliferation and tumor formation of colon cancer cells by suppressing Wnt/β-catenin signaling via transactivation of GSK-3β and Axin2 expression
text:
The text can be rewritten as follows:
Caudal-related homeobox transcription factor 2 (CDX2), a nuclear transcription factor specific to the intestine, has been implicated in the tumorigenesis of various human cancers. However, its functional role in the development and progression of colorectal cancer (CRC) remains unclear. In this study, we investigate the impact of CDX2 on colon cancer cell proliferation and tumor formation.
Our findings demonstrate that CDX2 knockdown in colon cancer cells promotes cell proliferation in vitro and accelerates tumor formation in vivo, while CDX2 overexpression inhibits cell proliferation. Furthermore, we found that CDX2 regulates Wnt signaling activity, as determined by TOP/FOP-Flash reporter assay, western blot analysis, and dual-luciferase reporter assay. Specifically, CDX2 knockdown or overexpression altered the expression of downstream targets of Wnt signaling, including β-catenin, cyclin D1, and c-myc.
We also observed that CDX2 transcriptionally activates the expression of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) and axis inhibition protein 2 (Axin2) by directly binding to their promoters. These findings suggest that CDX2 inhibits the proliferation and tumor formation of colon cancer cells by suppressing Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
In conclusion, our results provide insights into the mechanisms underlying CDX2's role in CRC development and progression, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target for CRC treatment.

title: Prostaglandin E2 mediates sensory nerve regulation of bone homeostasis
text: The exact nature of whether sensory nerves can perceive bone density or metabolic activity to regulate bone homeostasis remains unexplored. However, our findings reveal that prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), produced by osteoblastic cells, activates PGE2 receptor 4 (EP4) in sensory nerves to modulate bone formation by suppressing sympathetic activity through the central nervous system. PGE2 production by osteoblasts increases when bone density decreases, as demonstrated in osteoporotic animal models. Ablation of sensory nerves leads to a deterioration of skeletal integrity. Specifically, the absence of EP4 in sensory nerves or cyclooxygenase-2 (COX2) in osteoblastic cells significantly reduces bone volume in adult mice. Elevated sympathetic tone is observed in sensory denervation models, and the use of propranolol, a β2-adrenergic antagonist, can rescue bone loss. In addition, injection of SW033291, a small molecule that increases PGE2 levels locally, significantly enhances bone formation, while this effect is obstructed in EP4 knockout mice, thus supporting the idea that PGE2 mediates the role of sensory nerves in controlling bone homeostasis and promoting regeneration.

title: The Bone and Joint Decade 2000-2010.
text: The World Health Organization has designated the period between 2000 and 2010 as the Bone and Joint Decade. This is a timely and appropriate move, as hundreds of millions of people worldwide are afflicted with a variety of disabilities caused by trauma, aging, and degenerative conditions that affect the musculoskeletal system. Advances in orthopedic surgery and rheumatology have significantly improved the treatment of bone and joint disorders, thanks to breakthroughs in pharmacology, updated imaging techniques, and innovative materials used for surgical repairs. However, man-made materials used for these repairs are prone to wear and tear and loosening within the host bone, highlighting the need for more research in this area. The Human Genome Project has provided valuable insights into disease genes and the potential for gene manipulation to prevent and treat specific diseases. Moreover, cartilage cell culture and transplantation are already a reality. Tissue engineering, which involves growing cells in three-dimensional collagen or synthetic biodegradable polymers, has shown promising results in replacing damaged bone and cartilage tissues. While significant progress has been made in this field, further research is necessary to fully realize its potential. It is not unreasonable to expect a major breakthrough in the treatment of bone and joint diseases by the end of this decade. Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore, 2002; 31:621-2.

title: Prevalence of late-life depression and gap in mental health service use across European regions.
text: Objective: To determine the prevalence and disparity in the use of mental health services among older adults with late-life depression in four European regions and identify factors associated with service utilization. Methods: Cross-sectional study based on data from the Survey on Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe. Participants were a population-based sample of 28,796 individuals aged 74 years or older residing in Europe. Mental health service use was estimated using information on depression diagnosis or treatment. Results: The prevalence of late-life depression was 29% in the entire sample, with the highest rates in Southern Europe (35%) and Central and Eastern Europe (32%), followed by Western Europe (26%) and the lowest in Scandinavia (17%). The strongest factors associated with depression were total number of chronic diseases, pain, limitations in instrumental activities of daily living, grip strength, and cognitive impairment. The gap in mental health service use was 79%. Conclusions: Interventions should focus on individuals with chronic somatic comorbidities and limited mental and physical functioning. Promoting help-seeking behaviors among older adults, de-stigmatizing mental illness, and educating general practitioners can help reduce the gap in mental health service utilization.

title: Impedance and Interface Properties of Al/Methyl-Red/p-InP Solar Cell
text: A solarto cell comprising an Al/methyl-red/p-InP layer was fabricated through solution processing and was characterized using current-voltage (I-V) and capacitance-voltage-frequency (C-V-f) measurements at room temperature. From the dark I-V characteristics, the ideality factor and barrier height of the device were calculated to be 1.11 eV and 2.02, respectively. It was observed that the device exhibited excellent photovoltaic performance with a maximum open circuit voltage of 0.38 V and short-circuit current of 2.8 nA under only 200 lx light intensity. The barrier height and acceptor carrier concentration values for the Al/methyl-red/p-InP devices were determined to be 1.27 eV and from the linear region of its characteristics, respectively. The difference between the I-V and C-V measurements for the Al/methyl-red/p-InP device was attributed to the distinct nature of the I-V and C-V measurements. Additionally, the energy distribution curves of the interface states and their time constants were obtained from the experimental conductance properties of the Al/methyl-red/p-InP structure at room temperature. The interface state densities and their relaxation times of the device were found to range from 6.1 x 10^10 to 2.4 x 10^11 cm^-2 and from 10^-11 to 10^-9 ps, respectively. It was observed that both the interface state density and the relaxation time of the interface states decreased with increasing bias voltage from the experimental results.

title: R: A Language for Data Analysis and Graphics
text: In this article, we share our experience in creating and deploying a novel statistical computing language. Drawing inspiration from existing computer languages, we deliberately integrated features we deemed valuable to foster a more efficient, portable, and manageable computational environment. Our innovation boasts improved portability, exceptional computational speed, efficient memory management, and enhanced scoping capabilities, placing it ahead of existing alternatives.

title: The Mouse Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates
text:
"The Mouse Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates" is the most widely used and cited brain atlas in print, providing researchers and students with both accurate stereotaxic coordinates for laboratory use and detailed delineations and indexing of structures for reference. The accompanying DVD contains drawings of brain structures that can be used as templates for making figures for publication. The third edition is a major revision and expansion of previous editions, featuring:
* Complementary delineations and photographs in the horizontal plane of section alongside the coronal and sagittal series
* All tissue sections depicted in high-resolution digital color photography
* High-resolution photographs of sections and intermediate sections provided on the accompanying DVD in JP 2000 format
* Revised delineations and consistent naming conventions based on Paxinos and Watson's "Rat Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates, 6th Edition"
The updated atlas is now available in a more practical 14"x11" format for convenient laboratory use and is in full color throughout. Additional material includes a CD containing all plates and diagrams, as well as Adobe Illustrator files of the diagrams and various other useful resources. Coronal and sagittal diagrams have been completely reworked and updated, and rhombomeric borders have been included in sagittal figures for the first time in mammals. Microscopic plates have been scanned using a new method resulting in significantly higher quality images.

title: ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis
text: Springer's "ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis" is the latest addition to their popular "UseR!" series, which has become a go-to resource for computational statistics. The books in this series are all centered around R, either showcasing new packages developed by the authors or providing guidance on how to apply statistical techniques using existing R packages. "ggplot2" is a unique implementation of The Grammar of Graphics (Wilkinson, 2005) in R, a systematic approach to creating statistical graphics that was first introduced in a book reviewed in the Journal of Statistical Software by Cox (2007). This implementation was developed by the talented Hadley Wickham, who is also the author of the book under review.

title: Multiple Imputation For Nonresponse In Surveys
text: Our book collection offers multiple imputation techniques for nonresponse in surveys, which can be accessed online with public access. This means you can download the text instantly and easily. Our book servers are located in multiple locations, allowing for faster download speeds and reduced latency. What's more, multiple imputation for nonresponse in surveys is compatible with any device, so you can read it on your computer, tablet, or eBook reader.

title: Inhibition of the dipeptidyl peptidase DPP4 (CD26) reveals IL-33-dependent eosinophil-mediated control of tumor growth
text: The dipeptidyl peptidase DPP4 (CD26) regulates post-translational modifications of chemokines in T lymphocyte trafficking, which negatively impacts lymphocyte migration and tumor defense. By investigating how DPP4 affects T cells and cancer cells in pre-clinical models of hepatocellular carcinoma and breast cancer, we discovered that blocking DPP4 improves anti-tumor responses. In these models, administration of the DPP4 inhibitor sitagliptin increased chemokine levels and eosinophil migration into solid tumors, resulting in enhanced tumor control. We found that the anti-tumor effect was dependent on the presence of eosinophils and could be abrogated by depleting them or treating them with degranulation inhibitors. Additionally, we found that tumor-cell expression of the alarmin IL-33 was necessary and sufficient for eosinophil-mediated anti-tumor responses, and this mechanism contributed to the efficacy of checkpoint-inhibitor therapy. These findings provide new insight into the role of eosinophils and IL-33 in tumor defense, revealing the importance of DPP4 immunoregulation in cancer treatment. Historically, eosinophils have been associated mainly with allergic responses, but they are increasingly recognized as contributors to other immune processes. Our study demonstrates the potential of using clinically approved DPP4 inhibitors to recruit eosinophils to tumors, leading to enhanced tumor destruction.

title: Cycling Quiescence in Temozolomide Resistant Glioblastoma Cells Is Partly Explained by microRNA-93 and -193-Mediated Decrease of Cyclin D
text: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a relentless and malignant brain tumor, commonly resistant to chemotherapy. The alkylating agent Temozolomide (TMZ) is the standard front-line treatment, but its effectiveness is often hindered by resistance. This phenomenon has been extensively studied, revealing mechanisms such as mismatch repair gene upregulation, ABC-mediated drug efflux, and cell cycle alterations. However, the precise mechanism by which TMZ induces cell cycle arrest in GBM cells remained unclear. Recent findings have linked TMZ-resistant GBM cells to microRNA (miRNA) and exosomes. Our investigation identified unique miRNAs present only in exosomes from TMZ-resistant GBM cell lines and primary spheres, and we narrowed these miRNAs down to miR-93 and -193. Through computational analyses, we discovered that these miRNAs target Cyclin D1, a key regulator of cell cycle progression. To validate this finding, we conducted cause-effect studies and observed that miR-93 and -193 blunt the expression of Cyclin D1. These two miRNAs also decrease cell cycling quiescence and induce resistance to TMZ. Our data provide a mechanism by which GBM cells develop TMZ resistance through miRNA-mediated inhibition of Cyclin D1. This study suggests several potential therapeutic approaches to reverse chemoresistance at the miRNA, exosomal, and cell cycle levels.

title: Longitudinal changes in maternal corin and mid-regional proatrial natriuretic peptide in women at risk of pre-eclampsia
text: Objectives: This study aimed to investigate the longitudinal changes in maternal plasma levels of corin and midregional proatrial natriuretic peptide (MR-PANP) in pregnancies that develop preeclampsia (PE) and gestational hypertension (GH). Methods: A nested case-control study was conducted among a larger prospective longitudinal study of singleton pregnancies at high risk for PE. Blood samples were collected every four weeks until delivery. The study compared maternal plasma corin and PANP levels in pregnancies that developed preterm-PE, term-PE, GH, and those that remained normotensive. The data were analyzed using a multilevel mixed-effects linear model (fixed effects and random effects) and compared to a one-level model using the likelihood ratio test. Results: A total of 471 samples were analyzed from 122 women, including 85 that remained normotensive, 12 with GH, 13 term-PE, and 12 preterm-PE. The study found that log10corin levels were associated with gestational age (p < 0.001) in the normotensive group. Corin levels did not differ significantly between the normotensive group and the GH and term-PE groups (p = 0.64 and p = 0.16, respectively). Compared to the normotensive group, MR-PANP levels were significantly higher in the preterm-PE and GH groups (p = 0.046 and p = 0.019, respectively), but not in the term-PE group (p = 0.47). Conclusions: The study suggests that maternal plasma corin and MR-PANP could potentially serve as useful biomarkers for the prediction of preterm-PE. Disclosures: A. Khalil has received research support and commercial interests from USCOM, Roche, Alere, NICOM, and Q-fFN. He has also spoken for Roche.

title: Children's Exercise Physiology
text:
The updated and revised "Children's Exercise Physiology, Second Edition," presents the most recent research, methodologies, and approaches related to children's physiological reactions to exercise. The book examines not only the current issues that distinguish children from adults but also the underlying reasons for these differences. Readers will learn what physiological differences exist between children and adults, such as size, biochemical differences, neuromuscular differences, and the lack of sexual and hormonal maturation. Those involved in working with young athletes, disease management, and health promotion will gain valuable insight into the physiological determinants of exercise performance. Children's exercise physiology is a rapidly developing field. In the eight years since the first edition of this book was published, a wealth of new information has emerged. This streamlined new edition contains 13 chapters instead of 15, an introduction, and updated features, including:
* Learning aids such as chapter objectives, discussion questions, and research directions.
* A reorganized table of contents for improved flow between chapters.
* An updated final chapter covering the role of the central nervous system.
* Enhanced discussion of the determinants of aerobic fitness and VO2 kinetics, as well as the significance of maximal aerobic power in children.
* Improved chapters on thermoregulation and metabolic and endocrinologic responses to exercise.
With this revised edition, you can be confident you're getting the most up-to-date information on "Children's Exercise Physiology."

title: Cost-effectiveness in health and medicine
text:
Chapter 1: Cost-Effectiveness Analysis as a Guide to Resource Allocation in Health: Roles and Limitations
Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) is a crucial tool for healthcare decision-makers to allocate resources efficiently. This chapter provides an overview of the roles and limitations of CEA in healthcare, including its theoretical foundations, methodological approaches, and potential biases.
Chapter 2: Theoretical Foundations of Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
This chapter delves into the theoretical basis of CEA, including the concept of effectiveness, the availability of health states, and the ethical principles that guide CEA. It also discusses the different types of costs and benefits considered in CEA, such as direct costs, indirect costs, and quality adjusted life years (QALYs).
Chapter 3: Framing and Designing the Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
This chapter provides practical guidance on how to frame and design a CEA study, including how to define the research question, identify the relevant populations and interventions, and select the appropriate study design.
Chapter 4: Identifying and Valuing Outcomes
This chapter discusses how to identify and value the outcomes of interest in CEA, including the use of utility values, quality of life scores, and other measure of health outcomes. It also provides examples of how to handle missing data and how to deal with non-linear relationships between costs and outcomes.
Chapter 5: Assessing the Effectiveness of Health Interventions
This chapter describes the different methods used to assess the effectiveness of health interventions, including randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and modeling exercises. It also discusses the challenges of assessing the effectiveness of complex interventions and how to handle uncertainty in the evidence.
Chapter 6: Estimating Costs in Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
This chapter provides guidance on how to estimate the costs associated with health interventions, including the use of cost data from different sources, the estimation of opportunity costs, and the consideration of indirect costs. It also discusses how to handle heterogeneity in cost estimates and how to account for the time value of money.
Chapter 7: Time Preference
This chapter explores the role of time preference in CEA, including how to discount future costs and benefits to their present value. It also discusses how to handle different time horizons and how to account for the uncertainty associated with time preference.
Chapter 8: Reflecting Uncertainty in Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
This chapter discusses the importance of uncertainty in CEA and how to handle it using different approaches, such as probabilistic sensitivity analysis and scenario analysis. It also provides guidance on how to report the results of CEA studies, including the use of uncertainty intervals and contingency tables.
Chapter 9: Reporting Cost-Effectiveness Studies and Results
This chapter provides practical guidance on how to report the results of CEA studies, including the use of standardized reporting templates and the inclusion of key information such as the reference case, the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve, and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio.

title: Weight gain during pregnancy: reexamining the guidelines.
text: As pregnant women of childbearing age have increasingly become heavier, the compromise between maternal and child health brought on by gestational weight gain variations becomes more challenging to reconcile. This book, "Weight Gain During Pregnancy," has been written in response to the need for a re-evaluation of the 1990 Institute of Medicine guidelines for weight gain during pregnancy. It expands on the theoretical framework that was used to support the 1990 weight gain recommendations and provides an in-depth examination of the existing literature, as well as independent evaluations of current databases. The book investigates the connections between weight gain during pregnancy and factors such as the mother's pre-pregnancy weight and height, and provides an in-depth analysis of the impact of weight gain on both mother and child health. This book includes specific, updated targets for weight gain during pregnancy, as well as guidelines for proper measurement. A new feature of this book is the recommendation of a specific range of weight gain for obese women. This book is designed to assist healthcare providers, policymakers, educators, researchers, and pregnant women themselves in understanding the importance of gestational weight gain and providing them with the necessary tools to promote optimal pregnancy outcomes.

title: To err is human. Building a safer health system
text:
Human beings are prone to making errors, and the healthcare industry is no exception. The Institute of Medicine's (IOM) report "To Err is Human" highlights the issue of medical errors and their impact on patient safety. The report notes that some healthcare systems are more prone to errors than others, and that these errors can be caused by various factors, including human errors and failures within the system.
The report emphasizes that human errors are the most significant contributor to medical errors, but these errors often stem from failures within the system. These failures can be hidden, such as in computer systems or within managerial layers, making them difficult to identify. To prevent errors, the report suggests designing systems that make it harder for people to make mistakes and easier for them to do the right thing. In healthcare, this means creating processes that prioritize patient safety and protect against accidental injuries.
As healthcare and delivery systems become more complex, the opportunities for errors increase. The IOM report proposes an approach to reducing medical errors and improving patient safety, which includes addressing the forces within the external environment that can drive quality improvement. While the risk of dying from a medical error is significantly higher than the risk of dying in an airline accident, public attention has been focused more on improving safety in the airline industry than in healthcare systems.
The report also clarifies the definitions of errors and adverse events. An error is described as the failure of a planned action to be completed as intended or the use of a wrong plan to achieve an aim. An adverse event, on the other hand, is an injury caused by medical management rather than the underlying condition of the patient. An adverse event attributable to an error is considered a "preventable adverse event."
In summary, the IOM report "To Err is Human" highlights the prevalence of medical errors in healthcare and the need to address the root causes of these errors, including failures within the system and a lack of standardized nomenclature. By designing systems that prioritize patient safety and adopting an evidence-based approach to quality improvement, healthcare providers can reduce the risk of medical errors and improve patient outcomes.

title: Excess risk of lymphomas, leukemia and myeloma in patients with rheumatoid arthritis
text: A study examining the incidence of malignant neoplasms among 11,483 male and 34,618 female individuals with rheumatoid arthritis was conducted using two national databases in Finland. The Social Insurance Institution's Population Data Register contained information on medication for certain chronic diseases, while the Finnish Cancer Registry provided data on all cancer patients diagnosed in the country. The follow-up period spanned a total of 213,911 person-years. The overall incidence of malignant neoplasms was higher in males compared to the expected incidence in females. The expected number of cases of leukemia, lymphomas, Hodgkin's disease, and myeloma in both sexes was 59·6, compared to the 130 actual cases observed. This difference was found to be statistically highly significant (p value).

title: Advanced Human Nutrition
text:
Advanced Human Nutrition, Second Edition offers a comprehensive overview of the human body and highlights the importance of nutrients from a biochemical, physiological, and molecular perspective. The text is accompanied by illustrative figures that enhance the reader's understanding of complex topics. For instance, complex pathways are presented in an accessible format, and diagrams illustrate metabolism and the molecular functions of nutrients. To reinforce key concepts, the text includes features such as "Here's Where You Have Been" and "Here's Where You Are Going," which provide real-world examples and drive home important points from each chapter.

The text covers a wide range of topics, including:

* Cellular aging, damage, and repair systems
* Human nutrition, digestion, and absorption, including the roles of organs, exocrine and endocrine functions, histology, and absorptive activities
* Microflora and satiety/hunger mechanisms
* Macronutrients during exercise and the role of liquids and sports drinks
* Prevalent diseases in Western cultures, such as coronary heart disease, cancer, and osteoporosis

In addition to the textbook, an Instructor's Manual, PowerPoint Presentations, and a TestBank are available as free downloads.

title: The Endothelium: Modulator of Cardiovascular Function
text:
Chapter 1: Introduction
Endothelium-dependent responses are a critical aspect of vascular physiology, involving the regulation of blood flow, blood pressure, and immune function. The endothelium, a layer of cells that lines the blood vessels, plays a central role in these responses through the release of various molecules that modulate vascular tone. This chapter will discuss the methods used to study endothelium-dependent responses, including the endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF), the physiological actions of endothelium-derived relaxing factors, other relaxing substances released by the endothelium, and the production of contracting agents.
Chapter 2: Methods to Study Endothelium-Dependent Responses
Understanding the mechanisms of endothelium-dependent responses requires the use of several experimental approaches. These include:
1. Isolation and culture of endothelial cells
2. Molecular biology techniques, such as PCR and Western blot, to detect and measure the expression of endothelial proteins
3. Immunophenotyping to identify and characterize endothelial cell populations
4. In vitro and in vivo experiments to study the effects of endothelium-derived molecules on vascular tone and blood flow

Chapter 3: Endothelium-Derived Relaxing Factor (EDRF)
EDRF is a potent vasodilator that is released from the endothelium and plays a key role in regulating vascular tone. EDRF is composed of various molecules, including nitric oxide (NO), prostacyclin (PGI2), and endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor (EDHF). These molecules act on smooth muscle cells to relax vascular tone and promote vasodilation.
Chapter 4: Physiological Actions of Endothelium-Derived Relaxing Factors
Endothelium-derived relaxing factors have a range of physiological actions, including:
1. Vasodilation: EDRFs promote vasodilation by relaxing smooth muscle cells and reducing vascular resistance.
2. Immune modulation: EDRFs can modulate the immune response by regulating the expression of adhesion molecules and cytokines on immune cells.
3. Neurohumoral regulation: EDRFs can interact with neural pathways to regulate vascular tone and blood pressure.
Chapter 5: Other Relaxing Substances Released By the Endothelium
In addition to EDRF, the endothelium releases other relaxing substances that modulate vascular tone. These include:
1. Prostacyclin (PGI2): PGI2 is a potent vasodilator that is released from the endothelium and acts on smooth muscle cells to promote vasodilation.
2. Endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor (EDHF): EDHF is a less well-characterized relaxing substance that is released from the endothelium and acts on smooth muscle cells to hyperpolarize them and promote vasodilation.
Chapter 6: Production of Contracting Agents
In addition to relaxing substances, the endothelium also produces contracting agents that regulate vascular tone. These include:
1. Endothelin: Endothelin is a vasoconstrictor that is produced by the endothelium and acts on smooth muscle cells to constrict vascular tone.
2. Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP): CGRP is a potent vasoconstrictor that is produced by the endothelium and acts on smooth muscle cells to constrict vascular tone.
Chapter 7: Local Regulation of Endothelium-Dependent Responses
The endothelium regulates vascular tone and flow through local mechanisms that involve the release of relaxing and contracting substances. These mechanisms are modulated by:
1. Vascular architecture: The spatial organization of the blood vessel wall, including the arrangement of endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and extracellular matrix, can influence the local distribution of relaxing and contracting substances.
2. Vascular shear stress: Vascular shear stress, which is generated by the movement of blood through the vessel, can modulate the release of relaxing and contracting substances from the endothelium.
Chapter 8: Neurohumoral Regulation of Endothelium-Dependent Responses
The endothelium also modulates vascular tone and blood pressure through neural pathways. This involves the release of neuropeptides and other signaling molecules from endothelial cells that interact with neural receptors and regulatory mechanisms in the brain.
Chapter 9: Heterogeneity and Chronic Modulation of Endothelium-Dependent Responses
The endothelium is a heterogeneous tissue, with different subpopulations of endothelial cells that have distinct functions and properties. Chronic modulation of endothelium-dependent responses can occur through changes in the expression of endothelial proteins and the activity of signaling pathways.
Chapter 10: Disease
Dysregulation of endothelium-dependent responses can contribute to a range of cardiovascular and inflammatory diseases, including:
1. Hypertension: Hypertension is associated with an imbalance in the release of relaxing and contracting substances from the endothelium, leading to vascular tone abnormalities.
2. Inflammation: Inflammation can disrupt the balance of endothelial homeostasis, leading to the release of pro-inflammatory mediators and the activation of immune cells.
3. Atherosclerosis: Atherosclerosis is associated with the accumulation of lipids and immune cells in the vessel wall, which can disrupt vascular tone and blood flow.
Chapter 11: Therapeutic Implications
Understanding the mechanisms of endothelium-dependent responses has important implications for the development of therapeutic strategies for cardiovascular and inflammatory diseases. These include:
1. Vasodilator therapy: Vasodilator therapy can be used to improve vascular tone and blood flow in hypertension and other cardiovascular diseases.
2. Anti-inflammatory therapy: Anti-inflammatory therapy can be used to reduce the release of pro-inflammatory mediators from the endothelium and to modulate the immune response.
3. Atherosclerosis therapy: Atherosclerosis therapy can be used to reduce the accumulation of lipids and immune cells in the vessel wall and to improve vascular tone and blood flow.
Chapter 12: References
This chapter provides a list of references cited in the text, including key articles, reviews, and books.
Chapter 13: Subject Index
This chapter provides an alphabetical listing of subject headings and their associated page numbers, making it easy to locate specific topics within the text.

title: Vegetarian vs. conventional diabetic diet – A 1-year follow-up
text:
Abstract
Objective: Our previous 6-month randomized study demonstrated the beneficial effects of a vegetarian diet (V) compared to a conventional diet (C) on cardiovascular risk factors for patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D), including improved insulin sensitivity, reduced body weight, decreased visceral and subcutaneous fat, lower LDL-cholesterol, and improved oxidative stress markers and adipokines. We conducted post-trial monitoring to assess whether these improvements persisted 1 year after the study ended.
Methods: We invited 62 participants who completed the study to attend a 1-year follow-up visit to measure weight, waist circumference, HbA1c, and blood lipids, without maintaining their assigned diets.
Results: Of the 62 participants, 44 (71%) attended the follow-up visit. The use of hypoglycemic agents increased by 14% in the vegetarian group and by 26% in the conventional group, respectively, while insulin therapy was introduced in 5% of the vegetarian group and 13% of the conventional group. Both weight and waist circumference changes were not significantly different between the groups. HbA1c levels increased (p ≤ 0.05) similarly in both groups (+0.49 ± 1.04% in the vegetarian group vs. +0.42 ± 0.8% in the conventional group). Blood lipids did not change significantly in either group.
Conclusion: One year after the end of the intervention, the beneficial effects of a vegetarian diet on cardiovascular risk factors compared to a conventional diet were only partially maintained.

title: Alcohol, wine, and health
text: For the past two decades, numerous epidemiological studies have explored the relationship between alcohol consumption and various disease states. These studies have consistently shown that moderate alcohol consumption is associated with a reduced risk of mortality, as well as a lower incidence of arteriosclerotic vascular diseases, hypertension, cancers, peptic ulcer disease, respiratory infections, gallstones, kidney stones, age-related macular degeneration, bone density, and cognitive impairment compared to abstinence. A thorough review of these studies reveals that each analysis has consistently revealed a U-shaped or J-shaped curve representing the reduced relative risk of disease for individuals who consume alcohol in moderation, with specific guidelines for men and women. Specifically, for men, moderate alcohol consumption should not exceed 2-4 drinks per day, while for women, it should not exceed 1-2 drinks per day. These findings suggest that alcohol has favorable effects on high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels, as well as the inhibition of platelet aggregation. Furthermore, the phenolic compounds present in wine, particularly red wine, have been shown to have a positive impact on various biochemical systems, including increased high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, antioxidant activity, decreased platelet aggregation, and endothelial adhesion, as well as the suppression of cancer cell growth and promotion of nitric oxide production.

title: Contraceptive practices of women requesting termination of pregnancy : A study from China
text: To develop a program for preventing unintended pregnancies, we conducted a survey of 1520 women seeking abortion at eight hospitals in Zheng Zhou City, Henan Province, China, from March to May 1996. The most common reason for unplanned pregnancies was contraceptive failure (71.9%), with 61.7% of these pregnancies being potentially predictable due to non-use or recognition of contraceptive failures. The leading causes of contraceptive failures were condom mishaps (29.7%), IUD failures (23.5%), and rhythm miscalculation (15.9%). Majority of abortion seekers (77.1%) had used some contraceptive methods previously, but only 19.7% used a method at their first sexual encounter. Among the abortion seekers, 57.6% had used condoms previously, and 50.9% of the condom users had experienced at least one instance of condom mishap. The rhythm method was used by 31.7% of abortion seekers, and 59.1% of the rhythm users had experienced at least one instance of rhythm failure. Of the 16.8% of abortion seekers who had used pills, 58.0% had experienced pill failures. User failure (46.4% of condom users and 56.0% of pill users) was the main category of failure among condom and pill users. Approximately 56.4% of the abortion seekers had experienced at least one previous abortion, and 5.3% had experienced two or more previous abortions. Only 10 subjects had utilized emergency contraception prior to their current pregnancy.

title: Oncologists' perceptions of the effects of cancer patients' companions on physician-patient interactions
text: To gain insight into oncologists' views on the impact of patients' companions on physician-patient communication, the study conducted semistructured interviews with 12 oncologists (6 medical, 4 surgical, and 2 radiation) out of a total of 21 oncologists. The physicians estimated that roughly three-quarters of their patients brought companions to consultations, which made these interactions more challenging for the physician. The behaviors of the companions varied widely, from dominating the conversation to passively taking notes. The most assertive companions were typically young professional men or older women who accompanied their spouses, and they tended to ask the most questions. The study observed all possible coalitions during medical visits, and the physicians noted that companions and patients often had different agendas. Additionally, the physicians observed differences in the companions' behaviors based on their gender and whether they lived in rural or urban areas.

title: Wolff's Headache and Other Head Pain.
text: Historically, no book on headaches has come close to the caliber of Dr. Harold Wolff's work. The second edition of his masterpiece was published a decade ago, and it remains an exhaustive and engrossingAccount of Wolff's long-standing study and understanding of headaches. The latest revision, conducted by Dalessio, updates certain aspects of the book, primarily in the area of drug therapy. However, the emphasis on holistic therapy rather than solely relying on drugs has been maintained. While Dalessio has modified the structure of the book, the new chapters on cluster headache and trigeminal neuralgia are essentially repurposed from other sections of the original work. The main section on migraine has been reorganized, with some anecdotal content removed, but very little new material has been added. It is worth noting that the section on methysergide (UML-491 in Wolff's work) has been slightly altered.

title: Ansichten von Hausärzten zur Versorgung von unheilbar kranken Patienten am Lebensende - Ergebnisse einer Befragung in Niedersachsen
text:
Background: Family physicians play a crucial role in the healthcare of terminal patients and those with serious illnesses. However, the current level of palliative care in Germany has been widely criticized, with limited empirical data available, particularly regarding family physicians' perspectives.
Methods: To investigate the attitudes of family physicians in four representative regions of Lower Saxony, semi-structured telephone interviews with a sample of 257 doctors were conducted as part of a larger health system researchers' expert report.
Results: Of the 257 doctors surveyed, 71 (28%) were interviewed. On average, these doctors cared for four palliative patients with cancer and eight patients with other diseases at the time of the survey. Many of the doctors reported being available to their patients around the clock, particularly in the final stages of their illness. While pain therapy was seen as an important aspect of palliative care, the main area for improvement identified by the doctors was psychosocial support. Additionally, there was a notable willingness among the doctors to establish new palliative care structures.
Conclusion: The study found that family physicians in Lower Saxony are highly motivated to provide palliative care and are open to improvements in this area. However, it is important to consider the diversity of opinions among professions and disciplines when addressing the current situation and developing palliative care further.

title: Novel Risk Factors for Systemic Atherosclerosis: A Comparison of C-Reactive Protein, Fibrinogen, Homocysteine, Lipoprotein(a), and Standard Cholesterol Screening as Predictors of Peripheral Arterial Disease
text:
In this study, the authors compared the predictive value of 11 biomarkers (lipid and nonlipid) as risk factors for the development of symptomatic peripheral arterial disease (PAD) in a nested case-control study of 140 PAD cases and 140 age- and smoking status-matched controls among 14,916 initially healthy US male physicians aged 40-84 years. The biomarkers included total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), total cholesterol-HDL-C ratio, triglycerides, homocysteine, C-reactive protein (CRP), lipoprotein(a), fibrinogen, and apolipoproteins (apo) A-I and B-100.
The results showed that plasma levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, triglycerides, apo B-100, fibrinogen, and CRP were significantly higher at baseline among men who subsequently developed PAD compared with those who did not. Specifically, the total cholesterol-HDL-C ratio was the strongest lipid predictor of risk, while CRP was the strongest nonlipid predictor. Additionally, the authors found that the addition of CRP to standard lipid screening significantly improved risk prediction models based on lipid screening alone. These findings suggest that a combination of lipid and nonlipid biomarkers may be useful for identifying individuals at high risk of developing PAD.

title: Assessment of older people: Self-maintaining and instrumental activities of daily living.
text: The trend towards utilizing standardized formal devices for assessing functional ability is gaining momentum within agencies catering to the elderly. In a recent contract study on functional assessment conducted by the Gerontological Society (Howell, 1968), a wide range of rating scales, checklists, and other evaluation techniques commonly used in practical settings were compiled. Currently, it appears that each investigator or practitioner feels an innate desire to create their own scale and to criticize existing ones for not suiting their specific setting. However, the authors contribute to this community by presenting two scales that have been standardized on their respective populations (Lawton, 1969). While one of the scales, the Physical Self-Maintenance Scale (PSMS), has been largely developed and utilized by other investigators (Lowenthal, 1964), the second scale, the Instrumental Activities of Daily Living Scale (IADL), taps a level of functioning that was previously underrepresented in attempts to assess everyday functional capacity. Both scales have been further tested in various institutions and facilities serving community-residing older people. Before delving into the specific behaviors measured by these two scales, the authors briefly outline the competence schema into which these behaviors fit (Lawton, 1969). This schema classifies human behavior based on the degree of complexity required for functioning in different tasks, with the lowest level being life maintenance, followed by increasingly complex levels of functioning.

title: Diabetes in pregnancy: management of diabetes and its complications from preconception to the postnatal period (NG3)
text:
In February 2015, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) released new guidance (NG3) on managing diabetes during pregnancy. Healthcare providers must familiarize themselves with this guidance and implement its recommendations. Specifically, the guidance includes the following elements:
* Preconception care: Target HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol for women with diabetes.
* Risk assessment: Women at risk of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) should undergo a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) for diagnosis. The diagnostic criteria have changed to a fasting glucose of 5.6 mmol/L or above or a 2-hour glucose of 7.8 mmol/L or above.
* Glycemic targets: Revised targets for glycemic control in all diabetic pregnancies include a fasting glucose below 5.3 mmol/L (4-5.2 mmol/L if on insulin) and a 1-hour postprandial glucose below 7.8 mmol/L if achieved safely.
* Continuous glucose monitoring and insulin pump therapy are not routinely recommended but can be used if glycemic control is a problem.
* Capillary ketone testing should be performed on women with type 1 diabetes when they are hyperglycemic, and all women with diabetes, including those with GDM, should undergo this test when acutely ill.
* Flexibility in delivery timings: Women with types 1 and 2 diabetes can deliver between 37+0 weeks and 38+6 weeks, while women with GDM can deliver prior to 40+6 weeks (or earlier if complications arise).
* Postnatal testing: After GDM, fasting glucose testing (not OGTT) should occur at 6-13 weeks postpartum. Later testing can use HbA1c.
* Resource implications: Introducing these changes will likely result in an increase in the number of women diagnosed with GDM.

title: Mental health difficulties across childhood and mental health service use: findings from a longitudinal population-based study.
text:
Over the past two decades, there has been a lack of change in the prevalence of mental health disorders among children in high-income countries despite increased investment in mental health services. Insufficient contact with mental health professionals may be a contributing factor, but there is limited knowledge on the proportion of children who receive adequate treatment. This study aimed to investigate the level of mental healthcare received by Australian children aged 4-14 years.
Using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, the study mapped trajectories of mental health symptoms in children. Health professional attendances and psychotropic medications dispensed were identified through linked national Medicare Benefits Schedule (MBS) and Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme records. The findings revealed four distinct trajectories of mental health symptoms: low, high-decreasing, moderate-increasing, and high-increasing.
The study found that most children with mental health symptoms had few MBS mental health attendances, and only a minority received care meeting the study's criteria for minimally adequate treatment. Children in the high-increasing and moderate-increasing trajectories were more likely to access care, yet there was no evidence of improvement in symptoms.
The study highlights the importance of providing mental health treatment that meets minimal clinical practice guidelines. Further research is needed to assess the quality of care currently provided to children with mental health difficulties and to identify how clinicians can be best funded and supported to provide adequate care.
Note: The study was conducted in Australia, so some of the terminology and data may not be applicable to other countries.

title: Rembrandt Scholz
text: This study examines the potential impact of changes in medical care on population health in Lithuania, Hungary, and Romania, with west Germany included for comparison. Using the concept of deaths from conditions that should not occur with timely and effective healthcare (amenable mortality), the study calculates the contribution of changes in mortality to changes in life expectancy between birth and age 75. The study finds that temporary life expectancy improved consistently in west Germany, with gains of 2.7 years for men and 1.6 years for women. In contrast, gains were relatively small in the other countries, except for Hungarian women, who gained 1.3 years. Romanian men experienced a loss of 1.3 years. In the 1980s, falling infant mortality contributed substantially to improvements in temporary life expectancy in all countries, with more than half of the gain attributable to amenable conditions. At older ages, falling amenable mortality contributed about 40% among those aged over 40 in Germany and Hungary, while causing a loss of life expectancy in Romania. In the 1990s, improvements in infant mortality continued to make substantial contributions to life expectancy in Lithuania and Hungary, but had little impact in either Germany or Romania. Among adults, improvements in amenable mortality continued to benefit Hungarians and west Germans. In Lithuania, up to two-thirds of the gain in temporary life expectancy were attributable to falling mortality from ischaemic heart disease, suggesting that medical care had a positive impact. In contrast, Romanian men and women experienced increases in amenable mortality that contributed up to half of the overall loss of life expectancy, suggesting a negative impact. The study finds that changes in medical care had considerable impact on mortality in the selected central and eastern European countries over the last 20 years, both positively and negatively.

title: The Women's Interagency HIV Study
text: The Women's Interagency HIV Study is the largest cohort in the United States to date, consisting of 2,058 HIV-seropositive women and a comparison cohort of 568 seronegative women. The study's methodology, training procedures, and quality assurance activities are detailed. The study population

title: Prevalence of the Metabolic Syndrome Among Us Adults: Findings From the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
text:
According to the text, metabolic syndrome is diagnosed when an individual exhibits three or more of the following criteria:
1. Abdominal obesity (waist circumference >102 cm in men and >88 cm in women)
2. Hypertriglyceridemia of 150 mg/dl or above
3. Low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol level (<40 mg/dl in men and <50 mg/dl in women)
4. Blood pressure of 130/85 mm Hg or higher
5. Fasting glucose of at least 110 mg/dl

Individuals with metabolic syndrome are at a higher risk of developing diabetes and cardiovascular disease, and have increased mortality rates from all causes, including cardiovascular disease.
An analysis of data from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey found that the age-adjusted prevalence of metabolic syndrome in the US population was 23.7%. The prevalence increased from 6.7% in those aged 20-29 to 42% in those aged 70 or older. There was little gender-related difference in prevalence rates between racial groups, but metabolic syndrome was most common in Mexican Americans and least common in whites, African Americans, and "others." In both African Americans and Mexican Americans, women had higher prevalence rates than men. Extrapolating from age-specific prevalence rates and US census data from 2000, the text estimates that 47 million US residents have metabolic syndrome. The text also emphasizes the importance of addressing the underlying causes of metabolic syndrome, including improper nutrition and insufficient physical activity, in order to reduce its prevalence in the US population.

title: Baseline cytology, human papillomavirus testing, and risk for cervical neoplasia: A 10-year cohort analysis
text:
The following is a rewritten version of the given text with improved readability and clarity:
As more research emerges on the development of cervical cancer, question marks have been raised over the value of annual Pap smear screening for all women. To investigate, we examined whether women at higher risk could be identified by testing for the presence of human papillomavirus (HPV) in cervical smears. At Kaiser Permanente in Portland, Oregon, we evaluated 23,702 women who underwent annual Pap smear screening between April 1989, and November 1990. Our results showed that over 20,000 women (83.6%) had at least one follow-up smear during the study period, but women with atypical squamous cells (ASC) or worse had more smears than women with normal results (mean, 4.4 vs. 3.3). We conducted follow-up screening more or less annually for a total of 122 months. HPV results were not used in deciding patient management. Of the 20,810 baseline Pap smears, 96% were diagnosed as negative (N = 20,156). Thirteen percent of these patients tested positive for HPV. The baseline smears of 654 women (3.1%) were classified as ASC or worse, and 417 (63.8%) were positive for HPV. One hundred seventy-eight women had a cytologic diagnosis of a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion or worse; of these, 143 (80.3%) tested positive for HPV. During the 10 years of follow-up, 171 patients developed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 3 or cervical cancer. Only half (49.2%) of the 58 patients diagnosed within the first 45 months of follow-up had an abnormal baseline smear. During this initial period, 7.85% of women whose initial Pap test was at least ASC were diagnosed with CIN 3 or cancer. The cumulative incidence at 10 years of follow-up was 10.2%. Sixty of the 171 women with CIN 3 or cancer had a negative baseline HPV test. Of the 118 women who were diagnosed during the first 45 months of follow-up, 89 (79.4%) were HPV positive initially. The cumulative incidence of CIN 3 or cancer among the group with a positive baseline HPV test was 6.92% over 10 years but only 1.73% at 45 months. The risk of developing CIN 3 or cancer remained elevated throughout the study in those women with a positive baseline HPV test. The predictive ability of the baseline Pap smear diminished as the follow-up interval increased. Fifteen percent of patients (N = 3216) had a positive Pap smear, a positive HPV test, or both at the initial examination. One hundred twenty-three (71.9%) were among the 171 women who developed CIN 3 or cancer. Eighty-six percent (102 of 123) of the patients who were diagnosed within the first 45 months were positive with at least one of the screening studies. The cumulative incidence over 45 months for women who had positive HPV testing and/or abnormal Pap smear results was 4.54%. Women with negative results in both screening tests had a cumulative risk of 0.16% for the same period. At 10 years, the cumulative risk incidence for these two groups was 6.83% and 0.79%, respectively, yielding a negative predictive value of 99.1% for combined testing.

title: Preconception Care and the Risk of Congenital Anomalies in the Offspring of Women With Diabetes Mellitus: A Meta-Analysis
